en: (Pas_1) KA_I,1.1-5 Ro_I,1-4 Now, the instruction of words (*śabdānuśāsana*). The word "now" (*atha*) is employed here in the sense of an introduction (*adhikāra*). It should be understood that the treatise on the instruction of words is now commenced. Of which words? Of both worldly (*laukika*) and Vedic (*vaidika*) words. Among these, first, the worldly ones:
"Cow, horse, man, elephant, bird, deer, Brahmin"—these are indeed [the examples]. And from the Vedic texts:
"May the goddesses be for our protection," "For food thee, for strength thee," "I praise Agni, the domestic priest," and "O Agni, come hither for the feast.
Now, in the word "cow" (*gauḥ*), what is the word? Is it that which possesses the dewlap, tail, hump, hooves, and horns?

"Is that word the form of the object? He said: "No; it is what is called a substance (*dravya*). "Then is that word the winking, the movement, or the blinking? He said: "No; that is what is called action (*kriyā*). "Then is that word 'white,' 'blue,' 'black,' 'tawny,' or 'dove-colored'? He said: "No; that is what is called a quality (*guṇa*). "Then [is it] that which [exists] in distinct things..."
"That word is not that which is undivided among divided [individuals], uncut, and common to all," he says. "What then is it? It is called the *ākṛti* (form).

"What then is the word (*śabda*)? "That by which, when uttered, there arises the cognition of those possessing a dewlap, tail, hump, hooves, and horns—that is the word. Or alternatively, in common usage, a sound (*dhvani*) whose referent is understood is called a "word" (*śabda*).

For example, one says, "Make a sound," "Do not make a sound," or "This boy is a maker of sound. Since it is spoken thus while he is actually producing a resonance (*dhvani*), therefore resonance (*dhvani*) is sound (*śabda*).
What, then, are the purposes of the instruction of words (*śabdānuśāsana*)? They are: preservation (*rakṣā*), addition (*hāga*), brevity (*laghu*), and absence of doubt (*asaṃdeha*).

The purpose [of grammar] is as follows: Grammar must be studied for the sake of protecting the Vedas; for one who knows [the rules regarding] elision, augmentation, and the modification of phonemes will properly preserve the Vedas. Furthermore, there is also the matter of adaptation (*ūha*): the mantras in the Veda are not recited with all possible gender markers nor with all case endings; therefore, they must necessarily be modified appropriately by one engaged in the sacrifice.
One who is not a grammarian is not able to transform those [words] correctly. Therefore, grammar must be studied.
Furthermore, there is traditional authority (*āgama*): "The Veda with its six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is the duty (*dharma*) of a Brahmin to be studied and known without [any other] motive.
And among the six ancillaries, grammar is the most important. Effort directed toward what is primary becomes fruitful.

Furthermore, grammar should be studied for the sake of brevity. It is held that words must necessarily be known by a Brahmin; yet, without grammar, words cannot be known through an easy means. Moreover, grammar should be studied to eliminate doubt. As the ritualists recite: "One should sacrifice a speckled cow, dedicated to Agni and Varuṇa, which is a draught-ox. [In this case, without grammar, one might be uncertain whether the word refers to a large speckled cow or a cow with large spots.]

Regarding this, there is doubt: "sthūlapṛṣatī" means both "she who is thick and spotted" and "she whose spots are thick. A person unversed in grammar cannot determine its meaning from the accent alone. If it has the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*), then it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; if, however, it is oxytone (*antodātta*), then it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
(4.1) Furthermore, these are the purposes of the instruction of words: "Those Asuras," "A corrupt word," and "That which has been studied."
But as for those who employ [the words], being ignorant,
they apply the case-endings.
He who indeed [knows] this [hymn],
the four [verses],
and "uta tvaḥ."
Like groats;
[the offering] to Sarasvatī;
on the tenth day, for the son.

"You are a good god, O Varuṇa," they said; those were the Asuras. Those Asuras, crying out "Helaya! Helaya! (in mockery), were utterly defeated. Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not speak barbarously nor speak incorrectly. That which is an incorrect word is indeed a barbarism (*mleccha*). One should study grammar so that one may not become a barbarian. Those were the Asuras.

(4.2) A corrupt word—a word that is incorrectly employed, whether in respect of its accent or its phoneme—does not convey its intended meaning. That word is a thunderbolt of speech which destroys the sacrificer, just as Indraśatru [the name of a demon] did through the error of accent. One should study grammar with the thought: "May we not employ corrupt words. A corrupt word...

(PS 4.3) That which has been studied, if it is studied without being understood and is merely recited like a chant, does not blaze at any time, like dry fuel in a fire that is not lit. Therefore, thinking "let us not study what is useless," one should study grammar. That which has been studied...

(PS 4.4) But he who employs words correctly according to their specific distinctions at the time of linguistic usage—that knower of the application of speech attains infinite victory in the hereafter; yet he is corrupted by corrupt words (*apaśabda*). Who is this? Precisely the knower of the application of speech. Why is this so? Because he who knows the correct words [also] knows the corrupt words.

Moreover, he knows this: just as there is merit (*dharma*) in the knowledge of correct words (*śabda*), so too is there demerit (*adharma*) in the knowledge of corrupt words (*apaśabda*). Or rather, a greater demerit would result; for corrupt words are more numerous than correct words. Indeed, for each single word there are many corrupt forms. For example, for the word *gauḥ*, there are *gāvī*, *goṇī*, *gotā*, *gopotalikā*, and so on.

Such are the corruptions. Now, as for one who does not know the yoga of speech, ignorance is his refuge. Yet, ignorance cannot serve as a refuge in an absolute sense. For if someone were to kill a Brahmin or drink liquor while being ignorant [of the rules], I consider him also to be fallen. In that case, however, the knower of the yoga of speech attains infinite victory in the hereafter.

And one is corrupted by corrupt words. Who? Only he who does not know the application of speech (*avāgyogavid*). But as for him who knows the application of speech, his knowledge is his refuge. Where, then, is this recited? In the verses known as the *Bhrāja-ślokas*. And, sir, are even verses an authority (*pramāṇa*)? What follows from that? If they are an authority, then this verse also ought to be an authority: "Even a man of low birth, if he is learned in grammar, is honored in the assemblies of the wise, just as a jewel of pure water is honored among the ornaments of the neck."* *Note: This verse is cited in the Mahābhāṣya (Paspaśāhnika) to support the importance of grammatical correctness.*

"If one drinks a great quantity of water from jars the color of *udumbara* fruit, would that not prevent one from going to heaven? Why then should one take such a thing as part of a sacrifice? This is merely the song of a careless person; however, that which is sung by those who are not careless is authoritative—namely, that which one actually employs.

(4.5) Those who are ignorant—those who do not know the protracted vowel (*pluti*) at the end of a name during a return-greeting (*pratyabhivāda*)—among them, one may, if one wishes, say "This is I" after returning from a journey, as one would among women. One should study grammar so that one does not become like women in the matter of greeting. [They are] the ignorant.
(4.6) They apply the case-endings (*vibhakti*). The ritualists recite:

"The *prayāja* offerings must be performed with their case-endings. And without grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), it is not possible to perform the *prayāja* offerings with their case-endings. (4.7) They apply the case-endings.

"Whoever indeed lays down this speech word by word, accent by accent, and syllable by syllable, he is fit for the office of a priest (*ārtvijīna*). [Thinking,] "May we be fit for the office of a priest," they apply the case-endings.
Grammar is to be studied. "He who indeed [knows] this... (Paspaśā 4.8). "Four...
"Four are his horns, three are his feet, two are his heads, seven are his hands; bound in three ways, the bull bellows loudly; the great god has entered into mortals. (Ṛgveda 4.58.3).

It has four horns—the four classes of words: nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles; it has three feet—the three tenses: past, future, and present; it has two heads—the two natures of sound: the eternal and the produced;
it has seven hands—the seven case-inflections; and it is bound in three ways—bound in three places.

"On the chest, on the throat, on the head. [He is called] *vṛṣabha* because of his raining down [of benefits]. "He roars loudly" means he makes a sound. Why is this so? Because the root *ru* has the sense of making a sound. "The great god has entered mortals"—the great god is the Sound (*śabda*). Mortals are humans whose nature is to die; he has entered them. [This is said so that] there may be for us equality with the great god.
Grammar is to be studied. Another says:
"Four are the measured steps of speech; those Brahmins who are wise know them. Three, hidden in the cave, do not stir;
the fourth of speech, humans speak. There are four measured steps of speech. Four.

The word-classes are nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles; those Brahmins who are wise know them. "Wise" (*manīṣiṇaḥ*) means masters of the mind (*manasa īṣiṇaḥ*). "Three are hidden in the cave and do not stir"—the three that are placed within the cave do not stir;
they do not move, which means they do not blink. Humans speak the fourth part of speech; [they speak] the fourth.

That which indeed exists among men is [but] a fourth part of speech; this is the meaning. There are four [parts]. (Pas_4.9) KA_I,4.5-8 Ro_I,18-19: "And some... And some, though seeing, have not seen Speech; and some, though hearing, do not hear her. But to some she has revealed her body, as a loving, well-clad wife to her husband. Indeed.

Indeed, one person, though seeing, does not see this speech; indeed, another, though hearing, does not hear it. It tells half [the truth] to the ignorant man. But to him [the wise], it reveals its body; it discloses its form, just as a loving, well-dressed wife reveals herself to her husband. Just as a wife, longing for her husband, reveals her own self while beautifully attired.

In this way, speech reveals its own self to the knower of speech. "May speech reveal itself to us"—thus should grammar be studied. And furthermore: "Like sifting flour with a sieve... (RV 10.71.2). Where the wise have fashioned speech with their mind, there friends recognize their friendships; auspicious is the mark deposited within them.

Regarding the word *adhi-vāci*: *saktu* is derived from the root *sac*, meaning it is difficult to shake off; or rather, from the opposite of the root *kas*, meaning it is scattered. *Titau* means a winnowing fan; it is so called because it is woven (*tatavat*) or because it pierces (*tunnavat*). The wise (*dhīrāḥ*), being contemplative (*dhyānavantaḥ*), have fashioned speech with their mind—that is, with their higher intelligence—they have produced speech. Here, friends recognize their friendships; they recognize their states of union (*sāyujyāni*). Where?

This path which is difficult to traverse, accessible by only one, and within the domain of speech—who, then, are they? They are the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇāḥ*). Why is this so? "Auspiciousness is deposited in their speech. Auspiciousness is deposited in their speech.
*Lakṣmī* [is derived] from the sense of being characterized (*lakṣaṇāt*), from shining (*bhāsanāt*), or from being preeminent (*parivṛḍhā*). "Like flour... [and so forth].

(4.11) Regarding the *sārasvatī*: the ritualists recite, "One who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), having employed a corrupt word (*apaśabda*), shall perform the expiatory (*prāyaścittīyā*) *sārasvatī* sacrifice. [Therefore,] one should study grammar so that we do not become subject to such expiations. [This refers to] the *sārasvatī*. (4.12) Regarding the tenth day for the son: the ritualists recite:

On the tenth day after the birth of a son, one should bestow a name upon him that begins with a voiced consonant, contains a semivowel (*antaḥstha*), does not contain a *vṛddhi* vowel, is inherited through three generations, and is not established as an enemy's name; for such a name becomes most firmly established. One should give a name consisting of two or four syllables, formed as a primary derivative (*kṛt*) and not as a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Furthermore, without grammar, there can be no primary derivatives nor secondary derivatives.
Or they can be understood [as follows]: on the tenth day, regarding the son—(Pas_4.13) KA_I,4.26-5.4 Ro_I,21-22:
"You are a good god, O Varuṇa; you are a good god, O Varuṇa, from whose palate the seven rivers flow like a hollow, well-burnished metal rod. You are a good god, O Varuṇa, a true god."

O Sword, you whose seven rivers—the seven case-inflections—flow along the *kākuda*. *Kākuda* means the palate; it is called *kākuda* because the tongue (*kāku*) is raised within it. It is like a hollow tube (*sūrmya*). Just as fire enters a beautiful, hollow tube and burns it from within, so too do your seven rivers—the seven case-inflections [pervade you].
They flow through the palate; therefore, you are a true deity (*satyadeva*). "May we be true deities"—for this reason, grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) should be studied. You are a good deity (*sudeva*).

"But what is it that is being proclaimed as the purpose for those desiring to study *just* this grammar, and not something else as well? Having said, "Yes," [he spoke] according to the tradition: "Peace."

They recite such words as these. In a former age, it was thus: after the performance of the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*), the Brāhmaṇas used to study grammar. From them—who were knowledgeable regarding the places of articulation (*sthāna*), the points of production (*karaṇa*), and the secondary efforts (*anupradāna*)—the Vedic words were taught. But nowadays it is not so; having studied the Veda, people become hasty speakers.

"Vedic words are established for us from the Veda, and worldly words from common usage; therefore, grammar is useless. To those students who hold such a contrary view, the Teacher expounds this treatise, saying:
"Grammar must be studied for these purposes."

(PS_6) KA_I,5.11-22 Ro_I,23-24: Word has been discussed; its essential nature has also been stated; its purposes have also been stated. Now, the instruction of words (*śabdānuśāsana*) must be undertaken. How should it be undertaken?

Should there be an instruction of correct words (*śabda*), or an instruction of corrupt words (*apaśabda*), or an instruction of both? [The answer is: by the instruction of either one, the task is accomplished.

It may be so. For example, by a restriction regarding what is to be eaten, the prohibition of what is not to be eaten is understood. When it is said, "Five five-nailed animals are to be eaten," it is understood that others than these are not to be eaten. Or, by the prohibition of what is not to be eaten, the restriction regarding what is to be eaten is understood. For example, when it is said, "The domestic cock is not to be eaten; the domestic pig is not to be eaten," [it is understood that other things are to be eaten].
This is as follows: "The forest-dweller is to be eaten. Likewise here too:
if the instruction of the word is given, namely "cow," when this has been taught, it is understood that:

"Words such as *gāvī* and the like are corrupt forms (*apaśabda*). Now, if instruction regarding corrupt forms is given—meaning that when words such as *gāvī* have been taught, it is understood that "this word is *go*"—then which of these two is superior? Instruction regarding the correct words is superior because of its brevity. Instruction regarding the correct words is more concise, whereas instruction regarding corrupt forms is more cumbersome; for there are many corruptions for every single correct word. Therefore...

For example, "gāvī," "goṇī," "gotā," "gopotalikā," and so forth, are corruptions (*apabhraṃśa*) of the word "gauḥ. Furthermore, there is indeed the desired grammatical derivation [of these forms]. Now, given this instruction regarding words, should one perform a word-by-word recitation (*pratipadapāṭha*) for the comprehension of words—reciting such words as "cow," "horse," "man," "elephant," "bird," "deer," "Brahmin," and so on? No, he says; this word-by-word recitation is not a means for the comprehension of words.
For it is heard thus:
Bṛhaspati taught Indra the *śabdapārāyaṇa*—the complete mastery of words—consisting of words explicitly mentioned, for a divine thousand years;
yet he did not reach the end. Bṛhaspati was the teacher and Indra was the student, and the duration of the study was a divine thousand years.

And he did not reach its end; how much less so today? He who lives long at all lives for a hundred years. Furthermore, knowledge is put to use in four ways: by the time of its acquisition, the time of its study, the time of its exposition, and the time of its practical application. And in that regard, one's lifespan is exhausted by the time of its acquisition alone.

Therefore, the recitation of every single word (*pratipadapāṭha*) is not a means for the comprehension of words. How, then, are these words to be understood? A definition (*lakṣaṇa*) possessing both general and specific features must be formulated, by which one may comprehend vast masses of words with little effort. What, then, is that [definition]? It is the general rule (*utsarga*) and the exception (*apavāda*).

Some general rule (*utsarga*) must be formulated, and some exception (*apavāda*) must be formulated. Of what kind, then, should the general rule be, and of what kind the exception? The general rule should be formulated in a general manner; for example, the suffix *aṇ* after a verbal root (*karmaṇi aṇ*).
Its exception should be formulated in a specific manner; for example, *ka* after a root ending in long *ā* when there is no prefix (*ātaḥ anupasarge kaḥ*).

(Pas_8) KA_I,6.8-11 Ro_I,25-26: Is it then the *ākṛti* (form/structure) that is the word-meaning, or rather the *dravya* (substance)? He says: "Both. How is this known? For the Teacher has taught the *sūtras* in both ways. Having taken the *ākṛti* as the word-meaning, he states [Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.58]: "In the case of a name for a genus (*jāti*), the plural may optionally be used for a single [entity]. Having taken the *dravya* as the word-meaning...
Having understood this, the *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one from among similar forms) is commenced by the rule *sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣa ekavibhaktau*.

(Pas_9) KA_I,6.12-14 Ro_I,26-27: Is word (*śabda*) eternal (*nitya*), or is it something produced (*kārya*)? This has been primarily examined in the *Saṃgraha*, as to whether it might be eternal or produced. In that regard, both the faults (*doṣa*) and the purposes (*prayojana*) have been stated.

They have indeed been stated. In that regard, however, this is the conclusion: whether [the word] is eternal or whether it is produced, in both cases the grammatical definition (*lakṣaṇa*) must be applied.
But how is this [to be understood] regarding the venerable teacher Pāṇini?

The definition has been set forth: "When the relationship between word and meaning is established" (*siddhe śabdārthasambandhe*). That is to say, when the word, the meaning, and the relationship are established (*siddha*).

Now, what is the referent of the word *siddha*? The word *siddha* is a synonym for "eternal" (*nitya*). How is this known? Because it is used in reference to entities that are immovable and unchanging. For example: "The sky is established" (*siddhā dyauḥ*).

"The earth is established (*siddhā*); space is established (*siddham*). But surely, sir, the word *siddha* is also used in the sense of "prepared" with respect to products (*kārya*), as in: "the rice is prepared," "the soup is prepared," "the gruel is prepared. Since it is used even in the sense of products, why is it that here the term is understood as a synonym for "eternal" (*nitya*) and not as the word *siddha* used in the sense of a product? [The answer is: In the *Saṃgraha*, first of all, because of its state of being the opposite of a product (*kārya*).

We consider that the term "grahaṇa" (taking) expresses a synonym for "nitya" (eternal/permanent). Here too, it is exactly that. Alternatively, there are even single-word expressions that function as restrictive particles (*avadhāraṇa*).

For example: *abbhakṣaḥ* (water-drinker) or *vāyubhakṣaḥ* (air-drinker); from these, it is understood that he eats *only* water or he eats *only* air. In the same way, here too, [the word] is already established and not something to be proven. Or else, there is an elision of the first member of the compound (*pūrvapadalopa*).

In this regard, it should be understood that "siddha" means "extremely established. For example, Devadatta is called Datta, and Satyabhāmā is called Bhāmā. Alternatively, the specific meaning is understood through explanation, for there is no rule [of grammar] based on ambiguity.

We shall explain that this is the inclusion of words expressing the sense of "eternal" (*nitya*). But what is the purpose of this elaborate description? Why not simply employ the word "eternal" itself, by using which there would be no doubt? It is for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).
The Teacher, being one who observes auspicious rites, employs the word *siddha* at the beginning for the sake of auspiciousness for the great flood of this treatise.

For treatises that begin with auspicious words become renowned, and they come to possess heroic men and long-lived men. This is so that the students may achieve their purpose. Furthermore, this word *nitya* does not necessarily refer only to things that are immutable and unchanging; rather, it also refers to frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*). For example: [the word *nityaprahasita* means "one who laughs constantly"].

"Always laughing" and "always talking"—since these words also denote frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*), their meaning there too would have to be something else [than the intended one]. For a specific understanding is derived from the commentary; indeed, a rule is not invalid simply because of doubt. But the Teacher sees that the word *siddha* has been employed at the beginning for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), and he thinks: "I shall be able [to complete this work]."

And [the author] intends to describe this [word] as a synonym for "eternal" (*nitya*); therefore, the word *siddha* alone is employed, not the word *nitya*. Now, with reference to what object is this analysis (*vigraha*) performed:
"when the word, the meaning, and the relationship are established"? He says: "with reference to the form (*ākṛti*). Why is this so? Because the form is eternal.

Substance is impermanent. Now, if substance (*dravya*) is the category (*padārtha*), how should the analysis (*vigraha*) be formulated? [It should be: "When the word and its relation to the meaning are established" (*siddhe śabde arthasambandhe ca*). For the relation of words possessing meaning with their meanings is eternal. Alternatively, this analysis—“when the word, the meaning, and the relation are established”—is appropriate precisely when substance is the category. For substance...

The form is eternal, while the individual manifestation is impermanent. How is this known? It is observed thus in the world: clay, when possessed of a certain form, becomes a lump; having destroyed the form of the lump, small jars are made; having destroyed the form of the small jars, water-pots are made. Likewise, gold, when possessed of a certain form, becomes a lump; [having destroyed] the form of the lump...

Having destroyed the form of the *rucaka* (necklace), bracelets (*kaṭaka*) are made; having destroyed the form of the bracelet, swastikas (*svastika*) are made. Again, when the gold mass returns and is endowed with another form, it becomes two earrings (*kuṇḍala*) having the color of khadira-wood charcoal. The form becomes one thing and then another, but the substance remains that very same thing. This is due to the destruction of the form.

Only the substance (dravya) remains. Even when the generic form (ākṛti) is the word-meaning, this analysis is logical: "when the word, its meaning, and their relationship are established. But was it not said that the generic form is non-eternal? This is not so; the generic form is eternal. How so? Because it does not cease anywhere, it is therefore considered to have ceased everywhere [in the sense of being absent from specific instances]; it resides in other substances.

But it is perceived. Alternatively, this alone is not the definition of the eternal—that which is firm, immutable, immovable, free from loss, gain, or transformation, and characterized by non-origination, non-increase, and non-decay; that is eternal. Even that is eternal in which reality (*tattva*) is not destroyed. But what is reality? Reality is its essential nature (*tadbhāva*). Even in the case of a generic form (*ākṛti*), reality is not destroyed.

Alternatively, what is the use of this [distinction] between "this is eternal" and "this is non-eternal"? Having considered that eternal category of things (*padārtha*), this analysis is performed [in the rule]: "when the word, the meaning, and the relationship are established. But how is it known that the word, the meaning, and the relationship are established? From common worldly usage (*loka*). For in the world, having taken up a meaning, people employ words...

They employ [words], yet they do not exert effort toward their production (*nirvṛtti*). On the other hand, effort is indeed exerted for the production of those things that are effects (*kārya*). For example, one who intends to perform a task with a jar goes to the potter’s workshop and says, "Make a jar; I shall perform a task with it. It is not so when one is about to employ words.

Having gone to the house of a grammarian, he says: "Make words; I shall employ them. It is precisely by taking up the meaning that people employ words. (Pas_11) KA_I,8.1-22 Ro_I,32-35 If, then, the world is the authority regarding these, what is accomplished by the treatise?

When the employment of words is prompted by meaning from the world, the treatise effects a restriction for the sake of merit (*dharmaniyama*). [This applies] when the employment of words is prompted by meaning from the world.

In the application of words, a restriction regarding merit (*dharma*) is established by the treatise. What is this "restriction regarding merit"? A restriction for the sake of merit is a "restriction regarding merit" (*dharmaniyama*); or a restriction whose purpose is merit is a "restriction regarding merit"; or a restriction whose objective is merit is a "restriction regarding merit. It is as in the case of worldly and Vedic [usages]. The Southerners are fond of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*). As in common usage: [the word *vaidika* is used].

When "vede ca" ought to have been used, they employ "yathā laukikavaidikeṣu. Alternatively, the sense of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is indeed appropriate, as in "yathā laukikeṣu vaidikeṣu ca kṛtānteṣu. In common worldly usage, it is said: "The village cock is not to be eaten; the village pig is not to be eaten. And that which is called "edible" is taken up for the purpose of warding off hunger.

Furthermore, it is possible to satisfy hunger even with dog meat and the like; yet, a restriction is established therein: "This is edible; this is inedible. Similarly, engagement with women occurs out of weariness; and the removal of that weariness is the same whether with a woman who is approachable or one who is unapproachable. In that regard, a restriction is established:

"This woman is to be approached; this woman is not to be approached. Indeed, even in the Veda it is said: "The Brāhmaṇa has milk as his vow, the Kṣatriya has rice-gruel as his vow, and the Vaiśya has curdled milk as his vow. Now, what is called a "vow" (vrata) is undertaken for the purpose of consumption.
It is possible for one to consume even rice, meat, and so forth as a vow; however, a restriction is made therein. Likewise [with regard to sacrificial wood]: "made of Bilva or Khadira."

Or it is said that there may be a sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Now, a sacrificial post is indeed employed for the purpose of tethering the animal. And it is possible to tether an animal by raising some piece of wood or even without raising one at all. In that regard, a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is established.
Likewise, having placed the potsherds (*kapāla*) upon the fire, he consecrates them with the mantra: "Of the Bhṛgus, of the Aṅgirases, of the Gharma..."
"Perform penance through austerity. Even without a mantra, fire—whose function is burning—warms the potsherds;

in that case, a restriction is established: "When performed in this manner, it becomes a cause of prosperity. Likewise here, although the comprehension of the meaning is the same whether by means of a word or a corrupt form (*apaśabda*), a restriction regarding *dharma* is established: [the goal is achieved] only by means of the correct word.

The meaning—that which is to be expressed—is not [conveyed] by an ungrammatical word (*apaśabda*). When it is done in this way, it becomes a cause of prosperity (*abhyudaya*). There are words that are not used. Indeed, there are words that are not employed;
for example: *ūṣa*, *tera*, *cakra*, *peca*. What follows from the fact that they are not used? For [the correctness of a word] depends upon usage.
You determine the correctness (*sādhutva*) of words; yet those which are currently not in use would not be correct.

This is contradictory that it is said, "there indeed are words that are not in use. If they exist, they are not un-used; if they are un-used, they do not exist. To say "they exist and are un-used" is a contradiction.

Indeed, while you yourself are currently employing them, you say that there are words which have not been employed. And what other person like yourself could be proficient in the employment of words? This is not a contradiction. We say first of all that they exist, because those who know the treatises conform to them by means of the treatise; we say, however, that they have not been employed.

Regarding the statement that "they are not used in the world," and as for what is further said—"Who else now, being of your kind, would be proficient in the usage of words?"—we do not say that they are not used by us; rather, we say that they are not used in the world. But surely you too are an insider in the world? I am indeed an insider in the world.

If it is argued that "the world is not [composed of] words that have never been used," we say no, because words are employed for the sake of meaning. If it is argued that "there exist [words] that have never been used," that is not so. Why? Because words are employed for the sake of meaning. Words are employed for meanings, and these words possess meanings for which they are employed. The claim of non-usage is based on a different kind of usage; thus, there is no total non-usage.

Indeed, this [usage] of these words is logical. Why? Because of the difference in usage (*prayogānyatvāt*). That they employ other words for the meaning of these words is as follows: for the meaning of the word *ūṣa*, they say "Where have you stayed?";
for the meaning of *tera*, "Have you crossed over?"; and for the meaning of *cakra*, "What have you done?"
Regarding the meaning of *peca*, do you mean "you have cooked"? [This occurs] in the case of words not currently in use (*aprayukta*), like the *dīrghasattra* sacrifice.

Even though they are not currently in use, they must necessarily be followed by means of a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*), just like the *dīrghasattra*. For example, there are *dīrghasattra* sacrifices lasting a hundred years and even a thousand years; yet nowadays, no one at all employs them in practice. They exist only...
Considering that dharma consists in the tradition of the seers (*ṛṣi*), the ritualists conform to it by means of the scripture. All [words] exist in other regions;

indeed, all these words are employed in other regions, yet they are not perceived here. Let an effort be made to perceive them, for the scope of a word's usage is vast: the earth has seven islands, and there are three worlds.

The four Vedas, along with their auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) and secret doctrines (*rahasya*), are divided in many ways: there are one hundred and one branches of the *Adhvaryu* (Yajurveda), the Sāmaveda has a thousand paths, the *Bāhvṛca* (Ṛgveda) is twenty-one-fold, and the Atharvaveda is nine-fold; furthermore, there are the dialogues (*vākovākya*), history (*itihāsa*), ancient lore (*purāṇa*), and medicine (*vaidyaka*).
Such is the scope of the application of words. This much is the scope of the application of words.

The statement that there are those who do not apply [words] without having reflected upon them is mere recklessness. Within this vast domain of linguistic usage, various words are seen to have restricted domains in their respective contexts. For example, the root *śavati*, which denotes the act of moving, is used only among the Kambojas; however, in its derivative form, the Āryas use it as *śava* (corpse).
Thus: *hammati* is used in the Surāṣṭra region, *raṃhati* in the eastern and central regions, but the Āryas employ only *gam*.

*Dāti* is used in the sense of "cutting" among the Easterners, while *dātra* is used by those in the North. Furthermore, even those words which are not currently in common usage but are accepted [by tradition], their employment is observed. Where? In the Veda: "O wealthy ones (*revatī*), that wealth (*revatya*) of yours... and so forth. *Uṣa*... [text fragment].

"The prayer (*brahman*) which men have fashioned for me as something to be heard—that through which they have brought old age upon our bodies. (Pas_13) KA_I,10.4–11.14 Ro_I,39–42 Furthermore, does merit (*dharma*) reside in the knowledge of the word, or in its employment?
And what is the distinction here? If it is argued that merit resides in knowledge, then demerit (*adharma*) would likewise [reside there]. If merit resides in knowledge...

If that were so, demerit (*adharma*) would follow. For he who knows correct words (*śabda*) also knows incorrect words (*apaśabda*). Just as there is merit in the knowledge of correct words, so too there would be demerit in the knowledge of incorrect words. Or rather, even greater demerit would follow;
for incorrect words are more numerous than correct words—there are many corruptions (*apabhraṃśa*) for every single correct word.

For example: *gauḥ*—its corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśas*) include *gāvī*, *goṇī*, *gotā*, *gopotalikā*, and so forth. Regarding usage, there is a restriction. Furthermore, the Seer (the Veda) makes known a restriction regarding usage: "Those Asuras were defeated because they uttered 'helayaḥ, helayaḥ'. Well then, let it be regarding actual usage. [But] regarding usage, it applies to all people. If [it concerns] usage...

The entire world would be endowed with prosperity through Dharma. And what envy could you possibly have now if the entire world were endowed with prosperity? Indeed, there would be no envy at all. However, effort would become purposeless.
Yet effort must indeed be fruitful, and effort cannot be separated from its fruit. Is this not so?

Furthermore, those who have made an effort will employ words more correctly; they alone shall be joined with greater prosperity. Indeed, a distinction is also observed: for we see both those who have made an effort but are unskilled, and those who have not made an effort yet are skilled. In that case, there may also be a difference in the result. If this is so, then [the result] does not reside in knowledge either.

Dharma does not reside in the word alone, nor even in its mere employment. What then? Prosperity results from employing words preceded by knowledge of the *śāstra*; this is equivalent to the Vedic word (*vedaśabda*). He who employs words preceded by knowledge of the *śāstra* is joined with prosperity; this is equivalent to the Vedic word. The Vedic words themselves declare thus: "He who sacrifices with the Agniṣṭoma, and he who [teaches] it..."

Thus it is known: "He who piles the *Nāciketa* fire-altar, and he who knows it thus. Another says: "That is equivalent to the word *veda* (the Veda). Just as the words of the Veda become fruitful when studied according to the prescribed rules, so too he who employs words according to the rules of the science [of grammar] is joined with prosperity (*abhyudaya*). Or, again:

"Let it be that merit (*dharma*) resides in knowledge alone. But has it not been said: "If merit resides in knowledge, then demerit (*adharma*) likewise resides in [the knowledge of] what is contrary"?

This is not a fault. We take scripture as our authority; whatever the scripture declares is our authority. And the scripture declares merit in the knowledge of correct words, not demerit in the knowledge of corrupt words (*apaśabda*). Furthermore, as for that which is neither enjoined nor prohibited by the learned...

That [knowledge] leads neither to demerit nor to spiritual merit. For example: sneezing, laughing, and scratching lead neither to demerit nor to spiritual merit. Alternatively, the knowledge of corrupt words (*apaśabda*) is itself a means (*abhyupāya*) for the knowledge of correct words (*śabda*);
for he who knows the corrupt words also knows the correct words. Thus, for one who asserts that merit resides in such knowledge—

The implication is that merit (*dharma*) resides in the knowledge of words preceded by the knowledge of incorrect words (*apaśabda*). Alternatively, this is like the case of a well-digger: just as a well-digger, while digging, may indeed be covered with mud and dust, yet once water has arisen, he gains from that very source the benefit by which that very defect is removed.

Furthermore, there is a connection with great prosperity; likewise here too, even if there is demerit in the knowledge of corrupt words (*apaśabda*), nevertheless, that fault will be eradicated by the merit (*dharma*) that exists in the knowledge of correct words (*śabda*), and there will be a connection with great prosperity. As for what was said regarding the restriction on conduct in sacrificial rites:

That is the restrictive rule (*niyama*). For it is heard in scripture thus: "There were sages named Yarvāṇas and Tarvāṇas, who had directly perceived Dharma, who knew what was prior and what was subsequent, who had known all that is to be known, and who had realized the true nature of reality. When those venerable ones ought to have used the forms 'yat vā naḥ' or 'tat vā naḥ,' they instead employed 'yar vā ṇaḥ' and 'tar vā ṇaḥ' during the sacrificial rite."
They did not speak incorrectly. However, by those Asuras, incorrect speech was uttered during the sacrificial rite; consequently, they were defeated.
(Pas_14) KA_I,11.14-12.27 Ro_I,42-47 Now, what is the meaning of the word "grammar" (*vyākaraṇa*)? It is the *sūtra*. [Objection:
In the case of the *sūtra* being grammar, the sense of the genitive case is untenable. [Response: Regarding the *sūtra* as grammar, the sense of the genitive case...

"It is not tenable that the *sūtra* is the grammar (*vyākaraṇa*). For what else is grammar apart from the *sūtra*, such that this [collection] would be its *sūtra*? It would result in a failure to understand words. And indeed, it follows that there would be no understanding of words [if grammar were merely the *sūtra*], based on the claim:
"We understand words from grammar. For one does not understand words from the *sūtra* alone. What then?

And [it is established] by way of explanation (*vyākhyāna*). But is it not the case that the very sūtra itself, when analyzed (*vigṛhīta*), constitutes the explanation? No; mere words of inquiry (*carcāpada*) do not constitute an explanation—for instance, [the rule] *vṛddhir ādaic*. What then? An example (*udāharaṇa*), a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), and the supplying of ellipsis (*vākyādhyāhāra*): this collection taken together constitutes an explanation. If that is so, then [let us consider] the word *śabda*. In the word...

The meaning of the suffix *lyuṭ*. If "word" (*śabda*) were [the referent of] *vyākaraṇa* in the sense of *lyuṭ*, it would not be tenable; for [the definition] "that by which something is analyzed (*vyākriyate*) is grammar (*vyākaraṇa*)" does not apply, since nothing whatsoever is analyzed by a word. By what, then, is it analyzed? By the sūtra. Furthermore, the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) in the sense of "occurring in" (*bhave*) would not be tenable, as in: "that which occurs in grammar (*vyākaraṇe bhavaḥ*) is the connection (*yoga*); thus, one who possesses that is a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇaḥ*). For [analysis] does not occur in a word.

"Bhava" means "yoga" (connection). Where, then? In the Sūtra. Furthermore, the secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) such as *prokta* and others would not be applicable; for [according to your view], [words like] *pāṇinīyam* ("taught by Pāṇini") and *āpiśalam* ("taught by Āpiśali") would not be possible.

"Kāśakṛtsna. For words were not taught by Pāṇini; rather, it was the *sūtra*. Why are both stated here—"in the sense of 'taught' (*prokta*) and so forth, and [the suffixes] are *taddhita*s"—instead of simply "in the sense of 'taught' and so forth, and [the suffixes] are *taddhita*s"? Even in the sense of "become" (*bhava*), the *taddhita* suffix would have been enjoined. Previously, this was seen by the Teacher: that in the sense of "become," there is a *taddhita* suffix.

Thus that was recited. Subsequently, this was seen and [the rule] "proktādyaś ca taddhitāḥ" was also recited. Furthermore, teachers do not compose and then set aside their own sūtras. This is not a fault regarding what is said, namely that the suffix *lyuṭ* has the sense of the verbal root (*dhātu*). For *lyuṭ* is not necessarily prescribed only for the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

What then? [The rule] "kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam" applies even to other *kārakas* (grammatical factors). For example: *praskandanam* ("leaping forward"), *prapatanam* ("falling down"). Alternatively, words are explained by means of words themselves. For example, when the word "cow" (*gauḥ*) is uttered, all doubts are removed: it is not a horse, nor is it a donkey. But then this fault would arise: that the *taddhita* suffixes such as *-bhava* and others [would also function as explanations].

Thus [it is said]. If that is so, then grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) consists of both the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); this combination of the characterized and the characteristic constitutes grammar. But what, then, is the characterized and what is the characteristic? The word (*śabda*) is the characterized; the rule (*sūtra*) is the characteristic. Even so, there is this fault: the term "grammar" applies to the whole (*samudāya*), yet it is not applicable to its individual parts (*avayava*).

And one who studies the Sūtras is indeed desired to be called a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*). This is not a fault, for words that have been applied to wholes also function with respect to their parts. For example: "the eastern Pañcālas" and "the northern Pañcālas."
Oil has been consumed; ghee has been consumed;
[he is] white.

"Blue," "black"—in this way, this word *vyākaraṇa*, which is applied to the whole, also functions with respect to its parts. Or rather, let it be the *sūtra* [itself]. But was it not said that the sense of the genitive case is untenable in the phrase "in the *vyākaraṇa*-sūtra"?

This is not a fault. It will be accounted for by the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). As for what was said—that there would be no comprehension of the words—that has already been refuted by the fact that one does not comprehend words from the sūtra alone; rather, it is through the commentary (*vyākhyāna*) as well.
For that very sūtra, when analyzed, becomes the commentary itself. But was it not said that [words] are not [used] alone?

The "words for discussion" (*carcāpadāni*) constitute the explanation; [the rule] *vṛddhir ādaic*—what then? Is it the example (*udāharaṇa*), the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), or the supplying of the sentence (*vākyādhyāhāra*)? This collection [of elements] constitutes the explanation. This is so for one who does not understand. For they grasp words from the sūtra itself. And therefore, if someone were to speak contrary to the sūtra, that would not be accepted, since [the meaning] is derived from the sūtra alone.

(Pas_15) KA_I,13.1–14.22 Ro_I,47–53 Now, for what purpose is the instruction of the phonemes? The instruction is for the sake of their occurrence and combination. The instruction of the phonemes must be performed for the sake of their occurrence and combination. What is this "for the sake of occurrence and combination"?
Occurrence and combination (*samavāya*) for the purpose of usage (*vṛtti*) is "occurrence-and-combination."

The term *vṛttisamavāya* means either the inherence (*samavāya*) that serves as the basis for occurrence (*vṛtti*), or the inherence whose purpose is occurrence. What, then, is occurrence? It is the operation of the treatise. Now, what is inherence? It is the arrangement of phonemes in a specific sequence. Furthermore, what is instruction (*upadeśa*)? It is pronunciation. Why?

This [is the purpose]: the direction [of the teacher] is the act of pronunciation. For, having pronounced the phonemes, he says: "These phonemes have been taught. And it is for the sake of applying the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters). The teaching of the phonemes must be performed for the sake of applying the *anubandhas*, thinking, "I shall attach the *anubandhas*. For indeed, without having taught the phonemes, the *anubandhas* [cannot be applied].

They can be attached [to others]. This instruction of the phonemes (varṇas) serves both for the purpose of forming grammatical operations (vṛtti-samavāya) and for the purpose of creating indicatory markers (anubandha). The formation of grammatical operations and the creation of indicatory markers serve the purpose of abbreviation (pratyāhāra). Abbreviation serves the purpose of grammatical operations. And it serves the purpose of achieving desired cognition. The instruction of the phonemes is for the purpose of achieving desired cognition; [the teacher thinks: "I shall understand the desired phonemes."

If it is argued that [the instruction of phonemes] is for the purpose of producing the intended cognition, then the instruction of acute (udātta), grave (anudātta), circumflex (svarita), nasalized (anunāsika), long (dīrgha), and protracted (pluta) vowels must also be provided, on the grounds that they too are intended [to be cognized]. For phonemes are indeed desired to possess such qualities. [Reply: This is established through the instruction of the *ākṛti* (general form). It is established by virtue of the instruction of the general form.

This is established: the form of the vowel *a* (avarṇa) as it is taught will include the entire class of *a*-sounds; likewise for the form of the class of *i*-sounds (ivarṇa), and likewise for the form of the class of *u*-sounds (uvarṇa). If it is argued that this is established by the teaching of the general form (*ākṛti*), then an exception must be stated regarding the closed [lips] and so forth.
If it is argued that this is established by the teaching of the general form, then an exception must be stated regarding the closed [lips] and so forth. But what are the "closed [lips]" and so forth?
It is *saṃvṛta*, *kala*, *dhmāta*, *eṇīkṛta*, *ambūkṛta*, *ardhaka*, *grasta*, *nirasta*, *pragīta*, *upagīta*, *kṣviṇṇa*, and *romaśa*. Another says:
*grasta*, *nirasta*, *avilambita*, *nirhata*, *ambūkṛta*, *dhmāta*, and also *vikampita*, *sandaṣṭa*.

"Half-eṇīkṛta, druta, and vikīrṇa—these are the conceptualizations of defects in vowels. Therefore, the others are defects of consonants. [Objection: This is not a defect. [Response: By the inclusion of the *garga* and *bidādi* groups in the list, the exclusion of *saṃvṛta* and the rest will occur. [Question: Is there another purpose for the inclusion of the *garga* and *bidādi* groups? [Answer: What is it? It is so that the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the collective groups may be established. Thus.

In that case, I shall explain the restoration of the unvoiced vowel (*avarṇa*) which has been divided into eighteen types and from which the *kalā* and other markers have been removed. If so, then that [restoration] must be stated. But the restoration is for the sake of gender (*liṅga*). Then it will be for the sake of gender. If so, then that must be stated. Even if this is said, or rather, even now, a hundred secondary markers (*anubandha*) need not be uttered, because they would be designated as *it*.

And it need not be stated that there is elision [of the *it*], nor need it be stated that there is no elision. Whatever is accomplished by means of *anubandhas* will be accomplished by means of *kalā* and so forth. This being so, [the rule] is established; however, it would then become non-Pāṇinian. Let it remain exactly as it was originally formulated. If it is argued that it is established because the teaching is given in terms of the general form (*ākṛti*), then the prohibition regarding the closed vowels (*saṃvṛta*) and so forth has already been addressed. This has been resolved by the fact that [the *it* markers] are read within the *gargādi* and *bidādi* groups.
The cessation of *saṃvṛta* and the others will occur. But has not another purpose for the recitation of the *garga-* and *bidā-* groups been stated?
What is it? That there should be grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) for the composite wholes. If that is so, then both are accomplished by this [recitation]:
the recitation itself is specified, and *kalā* and the others are excluded. But how can both be accomplished by a single effort?
"It is possible; it is possible," he said. How so? Because causes can also be twofold. For example:

"The mango trees have been watered and the ancestors have been gratified. Likewise, sentences also can be situated in two places, as in: "The white one runs" and "He has gone to the Alambusas. Or rather, first this person must be asked: "Where are these [categories] such as the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and so forth?"

"They would be heard. [In] the *āgamas*, the *āgamas* are recited in their pure form. "Then [in] the *vikāras*, the *vikāras* are recited in their pure form. "Then [in] the *pratyayas*, the *pratyayas* are recited in their pure form. "Then [in] the *dhātus*, the *dhātus* are also recited in their pure form. "Then [in] the *prātipadikas*, the *prātipadikas* are also recited in their pure form."

As for those nominal stems (*prātipadika*) that are not [phonetically] grasped [as such], their instruction must also be provided for the purpose of knowing the sequence of their vowels and consonants, so that there may not be the confusion of *śaśaḥ* for *ṣaṣaḥ*, nor *palāśaḥ* for *palāṣaḥ*, nor *mañcakaḥ* for *mañjakaḥ*. Furthermore, augments (*āgama*), substitutes (*vikāra*), and suffixes (*pratyaya*) are uttered together with verbal roots (*dhātu*); therefore, among them—
These [sounds], *ka* and so forth, have not been attained [as substitutes]. (Śs 1.1) The teaching of the vowel *a* as "open" (*vivṛta*) is for the purpose of including the vowel *ā*.
The vowel *a* must be taught as open. What is the purpose? It is for the purpose of including *ā*. [For] by the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrahaṇa*), the vowel *a* [includes *ā*].

How could it not also grasp the *ākāra*? And for what reason would it not grasp it? Because of the difference in mouth-opening (*vivāra*). Why is it said "because of the difference in mouth-opening" and not also because of the difference in time (*kāla*)? For just as there is a difference in mouth-opening, so too is there a difference in time. This is true; however, [the author] will state the purpose of including the term "mouth" (*āsya*) in the rule: "That which has the same place and effort of articulation is a homogeneous sound" (*tulyāsyaprayatnaṃ savarṇam*). In that context, the inclusion of the word "mouth" serves a specific purpose.

Those whose place of articulation (*sthāna*) and effort (*prayatna*) within the mouth are identical are designated as *savarna* (homogeneous). Furthermore, time (*kāla*) is external to the mouth; therefore, there should indeed be the inclusion of that which differs in time, but not of that which differs in openness (*vivāra*). Now, is this grammatical explanation (*anvākhyāna*) provided for the sake of the open [vowel] being taught, or rather for the sake of the closed [vowel]?

It is argued that when something is being taught, the teaching of it as "open" (*vivṛta*) is enjoined; the purpose of teaching that which is open is thus explained. How is this known? Because [the rule] teaches the restoration of the closed (*saṃvṛta*) state for the vowel *a*, which is [otherwise] open, by stating "a a. This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*). For there is indeed another purpose for its enunciation. What is it? [The word] *atikhaṭvaḥ*.

In the case of *atimālaḥ*, by virtue of proximity, a *vivṛta* [vowel] would result from a *vivṛta* [vowel]. It is for the purpose that it should be *saṃvṛta* that this restoration (*pratyāpatti*) is stated. This is not so. Neither in common usage nor in the Veda is the vowel *a* *vivṛta*. What then? It is *saṃvṛta*. That which exists will remain as it is. Thus, this statement regarding restoration will serve merely as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

"The purpose of teaching the *vivṛta* [open] vowel is being explained. But what is the distinction here—whether the purpose of teaching the *vivṛta* vowel is to be explained, or whether the teaching of the *saṃvṛta* [closed] vowel is to be questioned?
Indeed, there is no distinction whatsoever. You have merely spoken out of self-importance regarding the *saṃvṛta* vowel.

It is argued that for that which is being taught, the teaching as an open articulation (*vivṛta*) is enjoined. We, however, say that the purpose of the open articulation of that which is being taught is explained [by the rule]. Because of the teaching of that [vowel] as an open articulation, there must also be an open articulation elsewhere for the sake of including its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). Due to the teaching of this very vowel belonging to the *akṣarasamāmnāya* as an open articulation, an open articulation must also be applied elsewhere.

Where else [could it apply]? To that which stands within a root (*dhātu*), a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), an affix (*pratyaya*), or an indeclinable (*nipāta*). What is the purpose? It is for the sake of including the homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*). So that its inclusion may occur by means of a sound belonging to the traditional phonetic list (*akṣarasamāmnāyika*). And what is the reason why it would not otherwise occur? Precisely because of the difference in the opening of the articulation (*vivāra*). The activity of the Teacher (*ācārya*) indicates that there is inclusion by means of a phonetic-list sound even for that which stands at the beginning of a root and so forth.

When [Pāṇini] says "akaḥ" in the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*, he employs the term *akaḥ* as a pratyāhāra (abbreviated designation). How does this serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? For it is not possible for two phonemes belonging to the *akṣarasamāmnāya* (the traditional alphabet) to exist simultaneously. This is not an indicator. Indeed, there is another purpose for its mention. What is that? [It concerns] that which [is combined] with a phoneme of the *akṣarasamāmnāya*.

There is indeed the inclusion [of the vowel *a*]; for that purpose, this [rule] would apply, as in the cases of *khaṭvāḍhakam* and *mālāḍhakam*. Since there is a specific purpose, it cannot be considered a mere *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark). Therefore, the teaching of the vowels must be given as "open" (*vivṛta*). What kind of effort is being urged here, namely, the "open teaching"? Should they be taught as open or as "closed" (*saṃvṛta*)? What, then, is the distinction here? All of this is for that very purpose.

This effort—that these nominal stems (*prātipadika*) which are not [explicitly] mentioned are taught by this means—is cumbersome. Therefore, it should be stated: "and that which is open (*vivṛta*) when situated at the beginning of a verbal root (*dhātu*)," etc. Furthermore, the teaching of the open [articulation] serves to exclude the closed (*saṃvṛta*) articulation when long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels are being spoken. Thus, the instruction of the open [articulation] is for the purpose of excluding the closed [articulation] in the case of the mention of long and protracted vowels.

It must be stated [that the vowels] are open (*vivṛta*), lest the long and protracted vowels be closed (*saṃvṛta*). For example, in *vṛkṣābhyām* and *devadattā*, neither in common usage nor in the Veda do the long and protracted vowels exist as closed. What then? They are open. Those two which exist will be [open]. Just as the *anusvāra* would cause the substitution of the *yaṇ* [vowels], so too the closed original vowel (*sthānin*) would cause the substitution of the closed long and protracted vowels.

One should substitute the *anusvāra* for the *yaṇ*, just as [one substitutes it] for the semivowels. For example: *sayṃyantā*, *savṃvatsaraḥ*, *yalṃ lokam*, *talṃ lokam*. The *anusvāra* replaces the *sthānin* (*yaṇ*) with a nasalized *yaṇ*. This is an unequal comparison. It is appropriate that there is a substitution of what already exists; for there are indeed *yaṇ*s that are both nasalized and non-nasalized.

Furthermore, the long and protracted [vowels] exist neither in common usage nor in the Vedic tradition. Which ones, then? Those that are *vivṛta* (uncovered). Those two which exist will be the future [long and protracted forms]. Even so, how is it known that they will be those with identical places of articulation (*sthāna*) but different efforts (*prayatna*), and not rather those with identical efforts but different places of articulation, such as the vowel *ī* or the vowel *ū*? He will state [the answer] under the rule *sthāne*.

Regarding the term *antaratamaḥ* ("most similar"), since the word *sthāne* ("in place of") is already understood from the context, the purpose of mentioning *sthāna* again here is so that where there is more than one kind of similarity (*āntarya*), the similarity based on *sthāna* (place of articulation) alone may be considered stronger. (Śs 1.2) In that regard, when a grammatical element is indicated by a continued reference (*anuvṛtti-nirdeśa*), its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*) are not included, because it is not an *aṇ* vowel.

In that case, when there is a reference by recurrence (*anuvṛtti*), the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) would not be obtained [by the term *a*]. [As in the rules] *asya cvau* and *yasyeti ca*. What is the reason? Because they are not *aṇ*. For those which occur in the recurrence are not *aṇ*. Which ones, then? Those which are taught in the traditional list of phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*). [Objection: This is established because the sound *a* is one; this *a* is one and the same, whether it is in the traditional list of phonemes...

Both that which occurs in the *anuvṛtti* (the subsequent application) and that which resides at the beginning of a verbal root [would be affected]. However, there would be a confusion of *anubandhas*. Indeed, a confusion of *anubandhas* would result:

even for the suffix *ka* prescribed by the rules "the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇy aṇ*) and "the suffix *ka* after a vowel when no prefix is present" (*āto ’nupasarge kaḥ*), the operations dependent on the marker *ṇ* would apply. Furthermore, there would be an impossibility regarding the rules concerning the terms *ekāc* and *anekāc*.

Furthermore, there will be an impossibility regarding the application of [grammatical rules] to both single-vowel and multi-vowel [bases]. What is the fault in that? In the case of *kiriṇā* and *giriṇā*, the rule for a single vowel (*ekāj-lakṣaṇa*) would result in the final syllable being udātta. And here, in the case of *ghaṭena tarati ghaṭikaḥ*, the suffix *ṭhan*—which is conditioned by two vowels (*dvyaj-lakṣaṇa*)—would not apply. Moreover, metaphorical designations (*upacāra*) would follow the pattern of substantial entities (*dravyavat*). Indeed, metaphorical designations would occur as if they were substantial entities.

For example: among substances, one single jar does not perform multiple functions simultaneously. In the same way, many people should not pronounce this sound *a* simultaneously. However, it is established by the fact that [the grammarians] employ the sound *a* with various genders (*nānāliṅga*) for each respective object (*viṣaya*). That they employ the sound *a* with various genders—such as in the rule "the suffix *aṇ* after a verbal root" (*karmaṇy aṇ*), and "the suffix *ka* after a root ending in *ā*, provided no prefix is present" (*ātaḥ anupasarge kaḥ*)—makes this known.

There is no confusion of the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters). For if there were, the employment of various *liṅgas* (indicatory markers) would be purposeless; one would simply pronounce a single [root] possessing all the qualities. This is not a [valid] indicator. This [employment of various markers] must be for the sake of establishing the designation (*sañjñā*) of *it*.
For it is not possible to pierce this [root] with *anubandhas* like a stake; indeed, there would be a fault if they were designated as *its*.

For if [the *it* designation] were applied to both, to which two would it apply? To the first and the last. If that is the case, then it is established by the fact that the indicator (*liṅga*) is applied again with respect to the specific domain (*viṣaya*). Since he applies the indicator *a* again for each respective domain—such as "after *prāgdīvyat*, there is *aṇ*" and "after *śiva* and others, there is *aṇ*"—it is known that there is no confusion of *anubandhas*. For if there were such confusion, [he would not have done so].

The prescription of gender would be purposeless. Or rather, let it be that it is established by the very fact that there is a cause for various genders in the object [of the action]. But was it not said that this [prescription] must exist for the sake of establishing the technical designation *it*? This is not a fault; for this is established from common usage (*loka*). For example:
In the world, someone says to Devadatta:
"Be shaven-headed here; be matted-haired here."

In this case, as in the expression *śikhī bhava*, whatever gender is used for a word in a particular context, it appears there with that same gender. Likewise, the vowel *a* will appear with whatever gender is used for it in a particular context. As for the objection raised—that there would be an inconsistency regarding the mention of both single-vowel (*ekāc*) and multi-vowel (*anekāc*) elements—it is because in the mentions of both single-vowel and multi-vowel elements, the number refers to the repetition [of the vowel]. Thus, in the mentions of single-vowel and multi-vowel elements...

And because of repetition and enumeration, there will be the status of having multiple vowels (*anekāctva*). For example, in the case of "there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses," where one recites the first verse three times and the last verse three times, the number seventeen is achieved through repetition. In the same way here as well, there will be the status of having multiple vowels through repetition. Thus, the objection regarding the grammatical operation [based on a single vowel] would be avoided. Here...

But indeed, in the case of *kiriṇā giriṇā*, the property of being udātta on the final syllable (*antodāttatvam*) resulting from the rule for a single vowel (*ekāj-lakṣaṇam*) certainly applies; this too is established. How? From common usage (*lokataḥ*). Just as in the world, when a thousand sages each give a single tawny cow (*kapilā*) a thousand times, they all become recipients of a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*sahasradakṣiṇa*), so too here there will be the status of having multiple vowels (*anekāctvam*).

Furthermore, as for what was said—that figurative designations would result [for the letter *a*] just as they do for substances—it may be that one person cannot simultaneously perform an action that is impossible to perform by many; however, that which is indeed a possible action can be performed simultaneously even by many. For example, the seeing or the touching of a jar. And this action regarding the vowel *a* is indeed possible.

As for the utterance [of the phoneme], even many people might perform it simultaneously. However, there is a difference in its state because of the intervention of time and sound. Indeed, there is a difference in the state of the letter *a*. Why? Because of the intervention of time and sound. That is, due to the intervention of time and the intervention of sound. Due to the intervention of time: *daṇḍa*,...

The first [reason] is because of the intervention of sound: for example, "daṇḍaḥ. Now, there can be no intervention for a single self (ātman). If such intervention were to occur, it would imply that the letter *a* undergoes change into something else. Furthermore, because we perceive them as occupying different locations simultaneously; indeed, from the perception of their simultaneous existence in distinct locations, we conclude this.

"The letter *a* possesses a different state (*anyabhāvya*), because it is perceived simultaneously in distinct locations—as in *aśvaḥ*, *arkaḥ*, and *arthaḥ*. For a single Devadatta cannot exist simultaneously in both Srughna and Mathurā. If [this is argued]:

Furthermore, these phonemes might be like birds. Just as birds, because of their rapid movement, are seen behind after having flown ahead, so too this sound *a*, which was perceived in the word *da*, is perceived in the word *ṇḍa*. This cannot be so; for in that case, there would be impermanence (*anityatva*), yet words are eternal (*nitya*). And since words are eternal, they must be immutable (*kūṭastha*).

The phonemes must be unchanging, neither subject to disappearance, appearance, nor modification. For if this [phoneme] *da* which is perceived here were perceived as *ṇḍa* there, it would not be immutable (*kūṭastha*). Furthermore, if these phonemes were like the sun, just as the single sun, situated in multiple locations, is perceived simultaneously in various distinct places.
The comparison is unequal. One single observer does not perceive the sun as residing simultaneously in multiple locations across various distinct places;

yet one perceives the letter *a*, and at other times, one does not perceive the letter *a*. What is the reason? [The letter *a*] is perceived by the auditory organ and is grasped by the intellect through its production.

The region of space (*ākāśadeśa*) is ablaze, yet space is one; however, the regions of space are many. Since they are many, there must be a difference in the nature of the vowel *a*. [Objection: This is established by the apprehension of the form (*ākṛti*). The form of the *a*-vowels (*avarṇākṛti*) has been taught, and it will include the entire family of *a*-vowels. Likewise for the form of the *i*-vowels (*ivarṇākṛti*), and likewise for the form of the *u*-vowels (*uvarṇākṛti*). And the same applies to the use of the *ta*-marker (*taparakaraṇa*).

And it is for this reason that *tapara* markers are employed [in the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ*], on the grounds that there would be over-extension (*atiprasakta*) due to the inclusion of the general form (*ākṛtigrahaṇa*). But surely, they should be employed because there would be over-extension due to the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrahaṇa*)? That [objection] is rejected: "The mention of *aṇ* with respect to a homogeneous sound is not a universal rule (*aparibhāṣya*), because the general form is included and because [the specific instance] is non-different [from the class]. And this applies to the mentions of *hal* as well. What [is the result]? It is established precisely by the inclusion of the general form. As in the rule *jhalo jhali*: [the *jhal* markers are used because otherwise there would be over-extension].
*avāttām*, *avāttam*, *avātta*—where this [rule] does not apply:

"a vowel includes its homogeneous counterparts" (*aṇ savarṇān gṛhṇāti*). Or rather, it is established by the similarity of form (*rūpasāmānyāt*). It is established by the similarity of form. For example:
"We are wearing those very same garments that we wore in Mathurā."
We eat those very same *śāli* rice grains that are found in Magadha;

and this very same *kārṣāpaṇa* coin which was taken in Mathurā is the one before you. In one case and in another, because of the similarity of form, the thought "this is that very same thing" arises. Thus, here too, it is established by the similarity of form.

(Śs_2) KA_I,19.10–21.28 Ro_I,70–79: What is the purpose of the instruction of the phoneme *ḷ*? Why is the instruction of the phoneme *ḷ* specifically questioned, rather than the instruction of other phonemes as well? If there is some purpose for the instruction of other phonemes, that same purpose should also apply to the instruction of the phoneme *ḷ*. Or who [could object otherwise]?

There is this distinction. Indeed, there is this distinction: the scope of usage for this *ḷ*-sound is extremely limited, and even that scope of usage belongs only to the root *kḷp*. Furthermore, the substitution of *ḷ* for *ṛ* in the case of *kḷp* is not established (*asiddha*). Because it is not established, the vowel-based grammatical operations (*ackārya*) will apply to the *ṛ*-sound alone. Thus, there is no purpose in the instruction (*upadeśa*) of the *ḷ*-sound. To this, he recites the following reply:

The instruction of the phoneme *ḷ* is for the sake of arbitrary words (*yadṛcchā*), imitation of what arises from inability (*aśaktijānukaraṇa*), prolation (*pluti*), and so forth. The instruction of the phoneme *ḷ* is formulated for the purpose of [denoting] arbitrary words, for the purpose of imitating what arises from inability, and for the purpose of prolation and the like. First, regarding the purpose of arbitrary words: suppose there is someone arbitrarily named *ḷtaka*; [the instruction is so that] vowel-operations may apply to him, as in: "O *ḷtaka*, give me curd" (*dadhi ḷtaka dehi*); "O *ḷtaka*, give me honey" (*madhu ḷtaka dehi*).
‘Ṛtaka’ went north; ‘ṛtaka’ went west. There are four ways in which words function:

genus-words (jātiśabda), quality-words (guṇaśabda), action-words (kriyāśabda), and fourthly, arbitrary words (yadṛcchāśabda). This [example] is for the purpose of imitating that which arises from incapacity. Due to some incapacity, when a certain Brāhmaṇa woman ought to have used the word *ṛtaka*, she used the word *ḷtaka*. This is an imitation of that.

The Brahmin woman says "ḷtakaḥ"; the young girl says "ḷtakaḥ. Furthermore, the instruction of the phoneme *ḷ* must be formulated for the sake of *pluta* (protracted vowels) and other such phenomena. What, then, are these *pluta* and others? They are protraction (*pluti*), reduplication (*dvirvacana*), and circumflex (*svarita*): as in *kḷptaśikha*, *kḷptaḥ*, *prakḷptaḥ*.

In operations such as protraction and the like, the substitution of *l* for *ḷ* in the root *kḷp* is established. Because that [substitution] is established, the grammatical operations pertaining to vowels (*ackāryāṇi*) apply.

[The forms] are not established. Therefore, the instruction of the phoneme *ḷ* must be made. [Vārttikakāra: These are not valid purposes. Because of the existence of what is logical, there is an assumption regarding names (*saṃjñā*) and so forth. Because of the existence of the logically correct word *ṛtaka*, they consider it appropriate to assume that in names and so forth, "this is indeed *ṛtaka*, not *ḷtaka*. Another says:

The word *ṛtaka* exists as a legitimate term consistent with the grammatical treatises (*śāstra*). It should be considered correct when used as a proper name (*saṃjñā*) and so forth; it is indeed *ṛtaka*, not *ḷtaka*. In that case, this arbitrary word (*yadṛcchāśabda*) is unavoidable: *ḷphiḍa*, *ḷphiḍḍa*. This too is [derived from] *ṛphiḍa* and *ṛphiḍḍa*. How so? Because in common usage, the application of the root *ṛ* is observed, along with the roots *phiḍ* and *phiḍḍ*.

The two suffixes [in question] belong to the *auṇādika* group. Furthermore, there are three ways in which words function: they are words denoting genus (*jāti*), words denoting quality (*guṇa*), and words denoting action (*kriyā*).

There are no arbitrary words (*yadṛcchāśabda*). Having formulated the purpose [of the inquiry] on one basis, the refutation is offered on another. Having assumed that arbitrary words exist, the purpose was stated; having assumed that they do not exist, the refutation is given. This being the case...

Furthermore, a word that conforms to the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) serves to exclude a word that does not conform to the treatise with respect to its meaning. For example, the word *devadatta* excludes the word *devadiṇṇa*, but it does not exclude words such as *gāvī* and the like. This is not a fault, for there are also solutions through alternative positions. There is imitation (*anukaraṇa*) among the learned, the unlearned, and those who are neither prohibited nor prescribed, as in the case of worldly and Vedic expressions. Thus, there is imitation.

For that which is practiced by the cultured (*śiṣṭa*) is good; or rather, that which is neither prescribed nor prohibited by the cultured does not lead to either fault or spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*), just as in the case of worldly and Vedic matters. As in worldly and Vedic established doctrines (*kṛtānta*): first, regarding the world, if one gives, sacrifices, or studies in such a manner as others do, and one imitates them by giving, sacrificing, and studying, one is joined with spiritual prosperity.
Also in the Veda:

"Those who thus sit for the sacrificial sessions (*sattra*) of the world-creators (*viśvasṛj*),"—emulating them, one should likewise sit for those sessions, and he too is joined with prosperity. This is not prohibited by the cultured (*aśiṣṭa*). He who hiccups in this manner, he who... [thus].

If one mimics another who laughs, saying, "He laughs," or who scratches, saying, "He scratches," and then laughs and scratches oneself, that shall result neither in fault nor in merit. But if one, mimicking another, were to kill a Brahmin, saying, "He kills a Brahmin," or drink liquor, saying, "He drinks liquor," he too [would incur the same].
I think it must have fallen; this is an unequal comparison. He who kills in such a manner and he who kills in imitation—both are killers. He who drinks and he who drinks after him—both are drinkers.

But as for one who, having bathed and anointed himself, with a garland around his neck, imitates [the act] thinking, "In this way that man kills a Brāhmaṇa" or "In this way that man drinks liquor"—[he is not the same].

One might cut down a plantain trunk or drink milk, yet I do not consider him fallen. Likewise here, if someone uses an incorrect word (apaśabda) and another person, imitating him, were to use that same incorrect word, he too would be a partaker of an incorrect word. But this is a different word whose referent is the incorrect word itself, for the sake of which instruction must be given; it is not [the same as the original].
And a word that has an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) as its meaning is itself an incorrect word. This must necessarily be understood in this way;

for if one were to think that "a word that has an incorrect word as its meaning is an incorrect word," then for him, the very term *apaśabda* would itself be an incorrect word, yet this is not an incorrect word. Indeed, this is further a word of imitation (*anukaraṇa*).

The purpose for which the instruction must be given is not avoidable: "He studies *sādhu-ḷkāra*" and "He studies *madhu-ḷkāra*. But of what is this an imitation? It is the imitation of that which stands in the *kḷpi*-position. If it belongs to the *kḷpi*-position, then since the substitution of *l* for *ḷ* in *kḷp-* is unestablished (*asiddha*), because of that unestablished status, the operations dependent on vowels (*ackāryāṇi*) will apply to the vowel *ṛ* itself. This would be the case for that purpose.

It would not serve any purpose. But this is another word whose referent is established by convention (*klṛpta*), for the sake of which an instruction must be given. It need not be given. This must necessarily be stated: "An imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is like its original form (*prakṛti*). What is the purpose? [For example: *dviḥ pacantu*.

He says: "tiṅ atiṅaḥ" [Pāṇini 8.1.28] so that the *nighāta* (accentual suppression) may apply. He says "agnī": "īdūded dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam" [Pāṇini 1.1.11] so that the designation *pragṛhya* may apply. If it is said that an imitation is like the original form (*prakṛtivat*), then this becomes a mere corrupt word (*apaśabda*):
he says "kumārīḷtakaḥ"; he says "brahmaṇīḷtakaḥ". For this is indeed a corrupt word.

The base form (*prakṛti*) [is the subject]. And an ungrammatical word (*apaśabda*) is not the base form; for ungrammatical words are not taught. Furthermore, there can be no base form that has not been taught. [Objection: Because that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original], [rules such as] prolation (*pluti*) and so on will apply. Since that which is modified in one part is treated as non-different [from the original], prolation and so on will indeed take effect. [Reply: If it is said that "that which is modified in one part is treated as non-different,"...

In the case of *rājñaḥ* and *rājakīyam*, the elision (*allopa*) of the *an* [portion] would result in its disappearance. To this we reply: "That which is modified in one part is not different from the original"; thus I shall state that the rule applies to what is specified by the genitive case. If it is said that the rule applies to what is specified by the genitive, then in the case of *kḷptaśikhaḥ*, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) would not apply, for here the *ṛ*-vowel is not specified by the genitive. What then? The *repha*. [The genitive refers to] the *ṛ*-vowel.

But here [in the rule], it is indicated by the genitive case. How so? The instruction is without case endings (*avibhaktika*); it is stated as *kṛpa uḥ raḥ laḥ*, meaning "for *kṛp*, *u* becomes *r* and *l*.
