Or rather, let it be without distinction. But was it not said: "In the case of *rājñaḥ ka ca* (P.

4.2.140) forming *rājakīyam*, the elision of the *an* stem (*allopaḥ anaḥ*) would result in the elision [of the final vowel]? This will be explained: "When there is vocalization (*prasāraṇa*), the mention of words ending in *n* applies to *śvan* and others."

"It is for the purpose of prohibiting [the elision] of that which does not end in *n*. That [rule] under discussion will carry over into what follows: 'There is elision of the *an* [suffix], provided it does not end in *n*.

In this case, then, in *kḷptaśikha*, the prohibition 'if it is not *ṛt*' would apply. And because of the prohibition regarding those ending in *rav*. This is established by the prohibition regarding those ending in *rav*. I shall state: 'of a heavy syllable that does not end in *rav*. If [it applies] to that which does not end in *rav*..."

Thus it is said: [the rule] "of the *ṛ*-vowel of the *hotṛ*" would not apply here in the case of *hotṛṛkāra*. I shall state: "of a heavy short vowel ending in *r*. This *ḷ*-vowel, which exists for the sake of *pluti* and other purposes, is thus rejected by splitting the rule (*sūtrabheda*). This is the great...

Similarly, in the case of *hotṛṛkāraḥ*, the substitution of *au* would apply only to the *au* that has the *tapara* marker, and consequently, the substitution of *ru* for the *ṛ* would not occur. Therefore, they should be taught without the *tapara* marker. But if they are taught without the *tapara* marker, then in the case of *khele*, the substitution of *e* would apply to both types of *e*, and consequently, the elision of the final vowel would not occur. In the case of *āstīrṇam barhiḥ*, the substitution of *o* would apply to both types of *o*, and consequently, the substitution of *v* for the *m* would not occur. Or rather, [the vowels] with *t* as their limit (*tapara*) are as they are in the original arrangement. What is the distinction here? If there is the teaching of *tapara* for the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*), then there must be the pronunciation of *tapara*. If there is the teaching of *tapara* for the diphthongs, then the pronunciation of *tapara* must be performed.

Regarding the rules for *pluti* (protracted vowels) and others: in cases such as *pluti*, a grammatical operation (*vidhi*) dependent on a vowel (*aj-āśraya*) is not established. For instance, in the example *gotrāt* / *nautrāt*, the doubling (*dvirvacana*)—which occurs according to the rule *anaci ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.47) whereby a consonant (*yar*) following a vowel becomes doubled—is not obtained. Furthermore, in the examples *pratyaṅ aitakāyana* and *udaṅ aupagava*, the insertion of *ṅam* (*ṅamuṭ*)—which occurs according to the rule *aci* (Pāṇini 8.3.2)—is not obtained. [This concerns] the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *pluta*.

Furthermore, the designation *pluta* (protracted) would not be established. [For example,] in *aitikāyana* and *aupagava*, the designation *pluta*—as prescribed by the rule "The vowel *ū* is *pluta* when followed by *k* or *l*" (*ūkalaḥ*)—would not apply to the vowels *e* and *o*. In that case, let them [the vowels *ai* and *au*] be without a following *t* (*atapara*). [The rule] "When a short vowel is substituted for *ec*, [the substitute] is *i* or *u* if it is without a following *t*" (*atapare ecaḥ ik hrasvādeśe*) would then apply. If they are without a following *t*, then it must be stated: "When a short vowel is substituted for *ec*, [the substitute] is *i* or *u*. What is the purpose? [It is for the sake of] the rules prescribing short vowel substitutes for *ec*.

[The objection is: "Let it not be that one half is *e* and the other half is *o*. But surely this must also be stated by one for whom the [phonemes] are followed by *t* (*tapara*). These two diphthongs (*ai* and *au*) are composite sounds: one mora belongs to the *a*-sound, and one mora each to the *i*-sound and the *u*-sound. Consequently, when there are rules prescribing short substitutes for these two, sometimes the *a*-sound would occur, and sometimes the *i*-sound or the *u*-sound. Let this never happen.

"It is incorrect," he says. This is rejected on the grounds that "the *ai* and *au* [substitutes] are greater in their subsequent components. If the position of rejection is maintained, then this too is rejected:
"It is established because of the common place of articulation (*saṃsthāna*) with *eṅ*. But surely, the half-*ekāra* and half-*okāra* are more closely similar in place of articulation to *eṅ*?

And those two do not exist. For if they did exist, he would have taught them as such. But surely, O venerable one, the Sātyamugris and Rāṇāyanīyas among the Chandogas recite [the words] "ardha-e-ka-ra" and "ardha-o-ka-ra" in the passage:
*sujāte eśvasūnṛte*.
"O Adhvaryu, [bring] the pressed [juice] with the wooden vats;
this of yours is bright, this of yours is worthy of sacrifice"—this is the manner of the disciples of those venerable ones.
For indeed, neither in common worldly usage nor in any other Veda does there exist a half-e sound or a half-o sound. The mention of "long" (dīrgha) refers to the single-substitute (ekādeśa).

In the case of a single substitute (ekādeśa), the term "long" (dīrgha) must be explicitly stated [in the rules]. [Namely: "The *guṇa* [substitute] for *ā* is long," and "The *vṛddhi* [substitute] for *eC* is long. What is the purpose? It is so that, by virtue of similarity (*āntarya*), substitutes consisting of three or four morae (*mātra*) do not occur in place of original elements (*sthānin*) consisting of three or four morae. For example: *khaṭvā*.
Indra is a bed; Indra is a bed;
water is bed-water.
A bedstead, a pole for a bedstead, a bedstead, a bedstead.
A woman who has been carried away is *ūḍhā*;
a bed is *khaṭvā*; a small bed is *elakā*; a small bed that is a bed is *khaṭvailakā*.
A bedstead; rice; "bedstead-rice" (a compound of *khaṭvā* and *odanaḥ*);
a bedstead.
Aitikāyanaḥ, khaṭvaitikāyanaḥ;
khaṭvā, aupagavaḥ, khaṭvaupagavaḥ. In that case, then, the mention of "long" (dīrgha) must be made. It need not be made. [It will be understood] from what follows.

A division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: first, "a vowel (*akaḥ*) becomes one (*ekaḥ*) with its homogeneous (*savarṇa*) counterpart"; then, "it becomes long (*dīrghaḥ*). And that which is designated as "that which is one [result] of the preceding and following sounds" is what is called "long. If this were so, then it would also apply here in the cases *paśum* and *viddham*.
[They say: "They cook [it]. This is not a fault. In this case, it is already established by the rule *paśum am-eka-* alone.

Since this is already established, the purpose of employing the mention of *pūrva* (the preceding) is so that the same kind of operation that applies to the preceding [element] shall apply to both. In the case of *viddham*, the word *pūrva* continues to be understood from the previous rule.

Alternatively, the activity of the Teacher indicates that a long vowel does not occur for a *samprasāraṇa* by this rule, since he teaches the lengthening of a *samprasāraṇa* that follows a consonant (*halaḥ*). In forms such as *pacanti*, the result is already established by the rule "when followed by [a suffix] beginning with a vowel, the substitution of *guṇa* occurs" (*ato guṇe paraḥ*). Since this is already established, the fact that he employs the term "form" (*rūpa*) here has the following purpose:
The purpose of this [rule] is so that whatever the nature of the form of the other [element] may be, the nature of both [elements] shall be the same.

In that case, however, in forms such as *khaṭvarśyaḥ* and *mālarśyaḥ*, because of the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*), the substitution of the short *a* does not occur due to immediate proximity (*ānantarya*), nor do the substitutions of *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*.
What would be the fault there? It would follow that the separated [vowels] would be heard. We do not say [this applies] wherever the rule is being applied.
In that case, there would be a fault; what then? It should be done where no fault arises when it is performed.
And where is there no fault when it is performed? In the formulation of technical names (*saṃjñāvidhi*): "vṛddhi" is *āt* and *aic*, "long" (*dīrgha*); "guṇa" is *at* and *eṅ*, "long" (*dīrgha*).
Then, should the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) be made? No, it need not be made. Why? Because of proximity (*āntarya*) alone.

Substitutes consisting of three or four morae do not occur in place of original elements (sthānins) that consist of three or four morae. [The rule] "guṇa and vṛddhi [substitutions] are followed by *t*"—but surely, sir, that which has *t* after it is called *tapara*? No, he says; for *tapara* is also that which follows *t*. If *tapara* were also that which follows *t*, then [the rule] *ṛdoḥ ap* would apply only here [in this specific instance].

In the case of *yavaḥ*, *stavaḥ*, *lavaḥ*, and *pavaḥ*, [the rule] would not apply here. This is not the letter *t*; what then? It is the letter *d*. What is the purpose of the letter *d*? And what is the purpose of the letter *t*? If the letter *t* is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity, the letter *d* is also [for that same purpose]. If the letter *t* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation, the letter *d* is also [for that same purpose].

(Śs 3-4.2) KA_I,23.24–26.27 Ro_I,84–93 This is now investigated: Are those parts of phonemes (*varṇaikadeśa*) which have forms identical to other phonemes perceived through the perception of their constituent parts, or not? Why, then, this investigation? Because here both wholes (*samudāya*) and parts (*avayava*) are taught, and [the part] is internal.
A part [is included] within a whole. For example:

when a tree moves, it moves together with its parts. In that case, a deliberation arises as to whether or not a part situated within the whole is included by the mention of the whole. And what is the distinction here? [It concerns] the parts of phonemes (*varṇaikadeśa*).

If it is argued that by the mention of "phoneme" (*varṇa*), the rule concerning homogeneous vowels (*samānākṣara*) is prohibited in the case of diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*): if it is argued that parts of phonemes are included under the term "phoneme," then a rule based on homogeneous vowels would apply to diphthongs; that must be prohibited—as in *agne indram* and *vāyo*.

In *udaka*, the rule "a long vowel is substituted for [a short vowel] followed by a homogeneous vowel" (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*) would result in a long vowel. Regarding the substitution of a long vowel, there is a prohibition of rules concerning short vowels. When a long vowel is substituted, a rule depending on a short syllable would apply; that must be prohibited—as in *grāmaṇīḥ* and *ālūya*.

[Regarding the rule] *pralūya*: since [the rule] "a *tuk* is inserted after a short vowel before a *kṛt*-suffix ending in a *pit*" applies, the *tuk* would result [here]. This is not a fault. The activity of the Teacher indicates that a rule dependent on a short vowel does not apply when there is a long vowel, because he teaches the *tuk* after a long vowel in the case of the suffix *cha*. This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*). For there is another purpose for this statement. What is it? [It concerns the case] from the end of a word (*padāntāt*).

"I shall state that 'vā' (or) indicates an option. If that is so, then why does he perform this division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*)? For otherwise, he would simply have said "after a long vowel at the end of a word, optionally" (*dīrghāt padāntād vā*). In that case, consider these examples: *khaṭvābhiḥ*, *mālābhiḥ*.

Therefore, by the rule *bhiḥ sau ais*, the substitution of *ais* would apply. It will not occur, however, due to the force of the inclusion of the marker *t* (in *bhis*). But then, in this case—*yātā*, *vātā*—the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *ato lopaḥ ārdhadhātuke* would apply. [Objection: But surely here too, it is due to the force of the inclusion of the marker *t*...

Thus it will not occur. For there is another purpose for the addition of the *t* (the *tapara* marker): what is it? That the elision (*lopa*) of the entire [substitute] should not take place. Now, even when the *tapara* marker is employed, once the elision of the subsequent [element] has been effected, why does [the elision] not also occur for the preceding one? Because of the status of the subsequent elision as *sthānivat* and because it is considered *asiddha*. If this is so, then the activity of the Teacher indicates [this rule].

The fact that [Pāṇini] adds the *k* as an *anubandha* in the rule "after a verbal root ending in long *ā*, when no preposition precedes, the suffix *ka* is added" (*ātaḥ anupasarge kaḥ*) indicates that the elision of the vowel *a* does not occur for an *a* situated within the long *ā*. How does this serve as an indicator? The purpose of adding the *k* is so that the elision of the long *ā* may take place by the rule "before a suffix marked with *k*" (*kiti*). If the elision of the vowel *a* were to occur even for an *a* situated within the long *ā*, then the addition of the *k* would be purposeless.

If the elision (*lopa*) of the subsequent *a* were performed, then by applying the single-substitute rule (*pararūpa*) to the two *a*s, the forms would be correctly established as *godah* and *kambaladah*. However, the Teacher perceives that the elision of the *a* situated within the [suffix] *-an* does not occur;
therefore, he makes the letter *k* an indicatory mark (*anubandha*). This is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*), for it may be for the sake of the subsequent rule concerning *tuṇḍa* and *śoka*.

Regarding the rule *parimṛjāpanudoḥ*: if that is so, then in the rule *gāpoṣṭhak*, he attaches the marker *k* as an *anubandha* for no other purpose [than to indicate the formation of a single syllable]. And it is like a single syllable (*ekavarṇavat*). It should be stated that "it becomes long like a single syllable. What is the purpose?
[So that] in the case of *vācā tarati*, the suffix *ṭhan*—which is conditioned by a base of two syllables (*dvyajlakṣaṇa*)—does not apply. And here, [the word] *vācaḥ* is the cause.

The reason for this is that [the rule] "saṃyogotpattau" (P. 6.1.26) applies to what is characterized by two consonants (*dvyajlakṣaṇa*); thus, it is intended that such a case should not occur. In this regard as well, the mention of *go-naus* (in P. 6.1.89) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that a grammatical operation (*vidhi*) characterized by two consonants does not apply after a long vowel. However, this is the resolution for all cases: a grammatical operation prescribed for a whole does not apply to its part, just as in the case of substances. A grammatical operation based on a part of a non-separate whole does not occur with respect to that part, just as in the case of substances. For example, as in the case of substances...

Regarding the statement, "There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses," it does not follow that a piece of wood exactly seventeen *aratnis* long is to be placed into the fire. This is an unequal comparison. For that ritual action is enjoined for each individual verse, and such a length is impossible both for the fire and for the altar. Just so, when it is said, "One should place seventeen fuel-sticks (*samidh*) made of *aśvattha* wood, each a span (*prādeśa*) long," it does not mean a single stick exactly seventeen spans long.

Wood is placed upon the fire. In this case as well, this ritual act is enjoined for each specific occasion, and the impossibility [of performing it otherwise] is equal regarding both the fire and the altar. Just as, for instance, oil must not be sold and meat must not be sold, so too that which is separated [from its source] is not sold.
Cows and mustard seeds are sold while they are not separated [from their source]. Likewise, one should perform purification after touching hair and nails;

however, it must be performed as a rule after touching them when they are separated, whereas when they are not separated, there is freedom of action. Where, then, is there separation? And where is there separation? It is in the case of the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*), because of the openness (*vivṛtatva*) in the diphthongs. That which...

In this context, the vowel *a* is more open than other vowels; likewise, the vowels *i* and *u* are also more open than other vowels *i* and *u*. Alternatively, however, they are not included [in the definition]. If they are not included, then the vowel *ṛ* must be explicitly mentioned in the rules for the augment *nuṭ*, for the substitution of *l*, and for the process of vocalization (*vināma*). If they are not included, the vowel *ṛ* must be mentioned in the rules for the augment *nuṭ*, for the substitution of *l*, and for the process of vocalization.

Therefore, it must be stated that the augment *nuṭ* occurs after a root with two consonants (*dvihala*) and before the vowel *ṛ*, so that forms such as *ānṛdhatuḥ* and *ānṛdhuḥ* may also be correctly derived here. For one who holds that [the rule] applies only to roots with two consonants, however, this is already established.

Even for one who does not accept [the application of] this [rule], there is no fault. The mention of "having two *hal*s" (*dvihal*) will not be made; rather, it will simply be that "therefore *nuṭ* occurs. If it were not done, then [the augment] would also apply in cases such as *āṭatuḥ* and *āṭuḥ*. The mention of the root *aś* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): [the *nuṭ* occurs] only after *aś*, which has a vowel (*avarṇa*) as its penultimate (*upadhā*), and not after any other [root] having a vowel as its penultimate. Furthermore, the mention of the letter *ṛ* must be made in the rule for the substitutes of *lā* (i.e., *liṭ*): *kṛpaḥ raḥ laḥ*.

It should be stated that "and of the vowel *ṛ*" [is included] so that it may apply here as well, as in the cases *kḷptaḥ* and *kḷptavān*. For one who accepts [the rule] simply as "of *r*" (*raḥ*), it is established. Even for one who does not accept it, there is no fault; for the vowel *ṛ* is also indicated here. How? The indication is without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*). [The words are] *kṛpa*, *uḥ*.

"raḥ", "laḥ", and "kṛpo ro laḥ". Alternatively, only the *sphoṭa* (the pure phonemic essence) is indicated on both sides [of the rule], meaning that upon the hearing of the sound *ra*, there occurs the hearing of the sound *la*. The vowel *ṛ* must be included in the rule for elision (*vināma*). [This is required] in the rule "raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ samānapade" (Pāṇini 8.4.1).

It should be stated here as well that [the rule applies] "after the vowel *ṛ*" (*ṛkārāt ca*), so that forms such as *mātṝṇām* and *pitṝṇām* may be obtained. For one who holds that [the *ṇatva* rule] is governed solely by the words "after *ra* and *ṣa*" (*raṣābhyām*), it is already established. But it is not established.

Because that which follows the *repha* (the *r*) is separated from the suffix by the *bhakti* (the inherent part of the consonant), the rule does not apply. Let it not be so; [it will apply] when there is no intervention by a vowel (*aḍvyavāye*).

Thus it is established. [But] it is not established. Which parts of letters (*varṇaikadeśāḥ*) are included by the mention of "letters" (*varṇagrahaṇena*)? Those which, though being parts of letters, exist as distinct [from them]. Furthermore, that which follows the *repha* (the letter *r*) in the case of a *bhakti* (a partial sound) is never seen to be distinct [from the *repha*]. If this is so, then a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: "After *ra* and *ṣa*, *na* becomes *ṇa* within the same word (*samānapade*). Then [the second part]:...

"In the case of separation (vyavāya), when there is separation by *ra* or *ṣa*, *na* becomes *ṇa*. Then [there is the rule]: "When there is separation by *aṭ*, *ku*, *pu*, *āṅ*, or *num* [the same applies].

Now, what is the purpose of this [present rule]? It is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). [The meaning is: "Only when there is separation by these very letters belonging to the alphabet (*akṣarasamāmnāyika*) does [the substitution] occur, and not by others.
Even for one who does not accept [the previous rule], this is not a fault. The activity of the Teacher (*ācāryapravṛtti*) indicates that it is so.

As for the claim that there is a rule for the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* after the vowel *ṛ* because [Pāṇini] lists the word *nṛnamana* among the *kṣubhādi* group, this is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*).
This listing would instead be for the purpose of applying *vṛddhi*:
[as in] *nārnamaniḥ*. What then is the point of his listing the word *tṛpnoti*, and also the word *nṛnamana*?
But was it not said that this [substitution] would be for the sake of *vṛddhi*? The *vṛddhi* is external (*bahiraṅga*), while the substitution of *ṇa* is internal (*antaraṅga*).

That which is external is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal. Or rather, a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made later: first, "after *ṛ*, *na* becomes *ṇa*"; then, "in the Veda (*chandasi*), [this occurs] after a word-break (*avagraha*)," [referring back to] "after *ṛ*" alone; and finally, "in the case of protracted vowels (*pluti*), [the substitution applies] to *ai* and *au*."

And this must be stated: for one who does accept [the rule] *guroḥ ṭeḥ*, it is established by means of prolation (*pluti*) itself. For one who does not accept it either, there is no fault here; this is addressed in the *Nyāsa* itself: "In a conjunction of identical forms, the rule for double consonants [does not apply]. In a conjunction of identical forms, a rule dependent on a double consonant is not established: as in *kukkuṭaḥ*.

"Pippalaḥ" and "pittam. For one who [pronounces] them with the nasalization (anunāsika), there are two *k* sounds, two *p* sounds, and two *t* sounds. For one who does not pronounce them with the nasalization, there are likewise two *k* sounds, two *p* sounds, and two *t* sounds. How so?

In this context, the duration of a *mātrā* is understood; however, there is no consonant (*vyañjana*) consisting of a single *mātrā*. Since it has not been taught, how can it be known? Even if one could argue that this [rule] applies where the principle "a vowel includes its homogeneous counterparts" (*aṇ savarṇān gṛhṇāti*) does not exist, how would it apply here in cases such as *sayṃyantā*, *savṃvatsaraḥ*, *yalṃ lokam*, and *talṃ lokam*?

This [rule] states: "A vowel (*aṇ*) includes its homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*). Even here, only that which possesses a duration of one *mātrā* is grasped, and there is no consonant (*vyañjana*) that possesses a *mātrā*.
Since it has not been taught, how could it be understood?
(Śs_5.1) All the phonemes (*varṇa*) have been taught once; this letter *ha*, however, is taught twice.

Both the preceding and the following [forms] are taught. If, however, only the preceding were taught, or only the following, what would be the distinction here? When the letter *h* is taught as following [the vowel], the mention of *h* must be made in the rules concerning *aṭ*. When the letter *h* is taught as following, the mention of *h* must be made in the rules concerning *aṭ*, such as in the rule "ātaḥ aṭi nityam" (Pāṇini 7.3.101).

"Śaḥ chaḥ aṭi" [Pāṇini 8.4.63], "dīrghāt aṭi samānapade" [Pāṇini 8.4.52]. It should be stated that [the rule] "hakāre ca" [Pāṇini 8.4.62] applies here as well, so that [the change occurs] in this case too:

*mahāṃ hi saḥ*. And regarding the substitution of *u* [for *m*]: the mention of the letter *h* must also be made when there is the substitution of *u*, [as in] "ataḥ roḥ aplutāt aplute" [Pāṇini 6.1.113].
And [the rule] "haśi ca" (Pāṇini 6.1.110) should be stated as "hakāre ca" (and when *ha* follows), so that it may apply here as well:

*puruṣo hasati*, *brāhmaṇo hasati*. Let it be, then, that the instruction is given first. If the instruction is given first, the rules concerning *kit* status, the prohibition of *iṭ*, and the inclusion of *jhal* [must be formulated].

Furthermore: if the previous instruction were followed, *kittva* (the status of being marked with *k*) would have to be prescribed. In the case of *snihitvā*, *snehitvā*, *sisnihiṣati*, and *sisnehiṣati*, the rule "after a root ending in *ra* or *la*, having *y* or *v* as its penultimate letter, and beginning with a consonant" would not apply to provide *kittva*. The prescription of *ksa*: *ksa* must also be prescribed.

In the cases of *adhukṣat* and *alikṣat*, the rule "after a root ending in *śal*, having *i*, *u*, or *ṛ* as its penultimate letter, and being *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*), *ksa* [is applied]" would not apply to provide *ksa*. The prescription of *iṭ*: [the augment *iṭ* must also be prescribed].

And *iṭ* should be prescribed [as part of the root]. [In forms like] *rudihi*, *svapihi*, the *iṭ* characterized by the suffix beginning with a consonant (*valādi*) would not be obtained. And the mentions of *jhal*—what [would happen]? They would be devoid of the letter *ha*. What fault would there be in that? [The rule] *jhalaḥ jhali* would not apply here: [the forms] *adāgdhām*, *adāgdham* [would be incorrect]. Therefore, it should be taught both before and after [the *ha*]. And if there is some purpose for teaching it elsewhere as well, it should be taught there too.

(Śs 5.2) KA_I,27.21–28.15 Ro_I,95–97 This is now considered: should this *repha* (the letter *r*) be taught only before the letters *ya* and *va*, as in *hara ya vaṭ*; or should it be taught only after them, as in the established arrangement (*yathānyāsam*)? And what is the distinction here? [The answer is: If the *repha* were taught after [the other letters], there would be a prohibition against nasalization (*anunāsika*), doubling (*dvirvacana*), and the *parasavarṇa* rule.

When the letter *r* is taught as following [another sound], a prohibition must be stated regarding the nasalization (*anunāsika*), the doubling (*dvirvacana*), and the substitution of a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*). Regarding nasalization:

in the examples "svaḥ nayati" and "prātaḥ nayati," the rule "when a *y*, *r*, *l*, or *v* follows, a preceding nasal may optionally become nasalized" would result in the application of nasalization. Regarding doubling: [the same applies].
In *bhadrahradaḥ* and *madrahradaḥ*, the doubling [of the consonant] prescribed by the rule *yaraḥ* would apply; however, this is superseded by the rule for *parasavarṇa*:
as in *kuṇḍam rathena*.

In the word *vanam rathena*, the rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ* would require the substitution of the following semivowel (*yay*) for the *anusvāra*. Let it be, then, that there is instruction regarding the preceding [element]. If there is instruction regarding the preceding element, there is the prohibition of *kittva* and the mention of the elision of *v*. If there is instruction regarding the preceding element, then *kittva* must be prohibited; for example, in *devitvā* and *dideviṣati*, the rule *ralo vyupadhāt* would cause *kittva* to apply. This is not a fault. It is not so.

Thus it is understood that [the suffix -aṇ applies] after a root ending in *r* or *l* when there is an intervening vowel (*vyupadhāt*). What then? It is [after a root ending in *r* or *l*] when there is no intervening vowel (*avyupadhāt*). What is this "when there is no intervening vowel"? It means: from a root ending in *v* or *y* which has an intervening vowel, [it is called] "without an intervening vowel. And there must be a statement regarding the elision of *v* and *y*: there is also elision of *v* and *y*, as in *gaudheraḥ*.

In *paceran* and *yajeran*, and in *jīradānuḥ* (from *jīveḥ radānuk*), the elision [of the semivowel] by the rule *vali* would not apply. This is not a fault, for here the letter *r* is also indicated; thus, the rule *lopo vyoḥ vali* means "elision of *v* and *y* when *val* [follows] and when *r* [follows]. Or rather, let it be taught as subsequent (*paropadeśa*). But surely—

And it has been stated: "In the case of the letter *r* being taught as subsequent [to another], there is a prohibition of nasalization (*anunāsika*), doubling (*dvirvacana*), and homogeneity (*parasavarṇa*). Now, a prohibition regarding nasalization and homogeneity need not be stated; for the letter *r* and the sibilants (*ūṣman*) have no homogeneous counterparts. Furthermore, regarding doubling, these two—*r* and *h*—are not the subjects (*kāryin*) of the doubling. What then? These two—*r* and *h*—are the causes (*nimitta*) of the doubling.

For example: "Let the Brahmins be fed; let Māṭhara and Kauṇḍinya serve the food. Now, those two do not eat [at that moment]. This is what is being considered: these *ayogavāha* sounds are not taught anywhere, yet they are heard. An instruction for them must be made for the sake of their grammatical function. But which are the *ayogavāha* sounds?

The *visarjanīya*, *jihvāmūlīya*, *upadhmānīya*, *anusvāra*, *anunāsikya*, and the *yamas*. But how are these *ayogavāhas* [defined]? They are so called because they carry [their sounds] when not joined [to a vowel], and they are heard even though they have not been explicitly taught. Where, then, should their instruction be placed? The *ayogavāhas* should be taught among the *aṭ* [consonants]. What is the purpose of this?

Regarding the substitution of *ṇ*: in the forms *uraḥkeṇa* and *uraḥpeṇa*, the substitution of *ṇ* is established by the rule *aḍvyavāye*. Regarding the status of *jaś* and *ṣatva* in the case of *śar* sounds: the teaching [of the root] should be stated with respect to *śar* sounds.
What is the purpose? It is for the sake of the status of *jaś* and *ṣatva*. This root *ubj* is recited with the *upadhmānīya* as its penultimate letter.

When *jaś*-ness (*jaśtva*) has been applied to it, so that the forms *ubjitā* and *ubjitum* may result—if the root *ubj* were taught with the *upadhmānīya* as its penultimate letter, then in the case of *ubjijiṣati*, reduplication would apply only to the form beginning with the *upadhmānīya*. However, when it is taught with a *da* as its penultimate letter, the prohibition established by the rule *na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ* becomes effective. If it is taught with a *da* as its penultimate letter, what is the derivation of the form?

Regarding the form *ubjitā* [from the root] *udj*: since the substitution of *bh* for *udj* is not established, there is this rule: "When *st* is followed by *śc*, *śc* is substituted [in place of both]. Therefore, one might say: "The substitution of *bh* for *udj* occurs when it comes into contact with *śc*. That must then be stated. It need not be stated;

it is established simply through a formal exception (*nipātana*). What is the exception? It is: "*bhuj* and *nyubj* are used in the sense of 'eating' and 'bending down,' respectively. This applies here as well.

In that case, it would follow that *abhyudgaḥ* and *samudgaḥ* [should not occur]. That [formation] is an irregularity (*nipātana*) in a context where *kutva* does not apply. Alternatively, this is not a form derived from the root *ubj*. Rather, the suffix *ḍa* is prescribed after the root *gam* when preceded by two prefixes: *abhyudgataḥ* becomes *abhyudgaḥ*, and *samudgataḥ* becomes *samudgaḥ*. Furthermore, the change to the sibilant *ṣ* is also a purpose [of this rule].

In the cases of *sarpiḥṣu* and *dhanuḥṣu*, the substitution of *ṣ* is established by the rule *śarvyavāye*. Consequently, the mention of *visarjanīya* in the rule *numvisarjanīyaśarvyavāye api* need not be made. In that case, the mention of *num* could also be omitted. How then [would one derive] *sarpīṃṣi* and *dhanūṃṣi*? Once the *anusvāra* has been applied, it is already established by the rule *śarvyavāye* alone. This is necessarily so.
The mention of *num* must be made as a qualifier for the *anusvāra*. The mention of *num* is so that [the rule] may apply to the *anusvāra* that follows *num*, but not here:

*puṃsu*. Alternatively, the instruction should be given without distinction. What is the purpose? Without distinction, there are the following: the technical designation of a *saṃyoga*, the designation of a penultimate (*upadhā*), the designation of the final letter (*al-antyam*), the prohibition of doubling (*dvirvacana*), and the prohibition of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).

The purpose of the technical designation *saṃyoga* (conjunction) is without distinction [of vowels or consonants]. For example: *ūbjaka*. By the rule "consonants that are not separated by vowels are a *saṃyoga*," the designation *saṃyoga* is applied; and by the rule "a syllable containing a *saṃyoga* is heavy (*guru*)," the designation *guru* is applied; and by the rule "after a heavy syllable," a protracted vowel (*pluta*) occurs. Furthermore, the designation *upadhā* (penultimate) is also a purpose. As in: *duṣkṛtam*, *niṣkṛtam*.

In the cases of *niṣpītam* and *duṣpītam*, the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] is established by the rule *idudupadhasya cāpratyayasya*. This purpose is not necessary; for the letter *visarjanīya* is not qualified by the mention of *idudupadha*. What then? It is the letter *s* that is qualified.

It is qualified [as follows]: "the *visarjanīya* that belongs to a *sakāra* which has *i* or *u* as its *upadhā*. Alternatively, the mention of *upadhā* will not be made; rather, we shall qualify the *visarjanīya* by means of *i* and *u*: "of the *visarjanīya* following *i* and *u*. The purpose [of the rule] is the application of the operation to the final letter of the *ala* (the substitute). For example: *vṛkṣas tarati*, *plakṣas tarati*; [here the substitution applies] to the final letter of the *ala*.
If it is argued that "rules [apply] to all," then the substitution of *s* for the final letter would be established; however, this too is not a purposeful requirement.
Since "substitutions apply to that which is being specifically indicated," the rule will apply to the *visarjanīya* alone. Furthermore, reduplication is a purpose: as in *uraḥkaḥ*.

Regarding the rule *uraḥpaḥ* and *anaci ca*: since the doubling (*dvirvacana*) is established by the principle that "the consonants *ya*, *ra*, and *la* following a vowel become doubled," this is already accomplished. However, the prohibition of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva-pratiṣedha*) is also a purpose [of this rule]. For instance, just as in the examples *uraḥkeṇa* and *uraḥpeṇa* the substitution of *ṇ* occurs even when there is an intervening *a* (by the rule *aḍvyavāye ’pi*), so too here in the cases *vyūḍhoraskena* and *mahoraskena*, the substitution would apply due to the status of being a substitute. In that regard, the prohibition is stated as *analvidhau* ("not in the case of an operation concerning a phoneme").
It is established.
(Śs 5.4) KA_I,30.1–32.11 Ro_I,101–106 But are these phonemes (*varṇa*) meaningful or meaningless?
The phonemes are meaningful, because meaning is observed in roots, nominal stems, suffixes, and particles that consist of a single phoneme.
Roots consisting of a single phoneme are seen to be meaningful, as in *eti*,
*adhyeti*,
and *adhīte*. Nominal stems (*prātipadika*) consisting of a single phoneme are also meaningful, as in *ābhyām*.
In these [words], *ebhiḥ* and *eṣu*, suffixes consisting of a single phoneme are meaningful: *aupagavaḥ*, *kāpaṭavaḥ*. Particles (*nipāta*) consisting of a single phoneme are meaningful: [e.g., *a*].

"Go away! Look at Indra! Arise! Since we observe meaning in monosyllabic roots (*dhātu*), nominal stems (*prātipadika*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), and particles (*nipāta*), we consider that phonemes (*varṇa*) possess meaning. Furthermore, because a change in meaning occurs when there is a transposition of phonemes, we consider that phonemes possess meaning. For example: *kūpaḥ* (well), [and *upakūpaḥ* (near the well)].

Regarding the words *sūpaḥ*, *yūpaḥ*, and *kūpaḥ*: by means of the letter *ka* in *kūpaḥ*, a certain meaning is understood. When the letter *ka* is removed and the letter *sa* is added in *sūpaḥ*, a different meaning is understood. When both the letters *ka* and *sa* are removed and the letter *ya* is added in *yūpaḥ*, yet another meaning is understood. Therefore, we consider:

That which is the meaning of "well" (*kūpa*) belongs to the letter *k*; that which is the meaning of "soup" (*sūpa*) belongs to the letter *s*; and that which is the meaning of "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*) belongs to the letter *y*. Furthermore, because no meaning is perceived when the letters are not perceived, we maintain that the letters possess meaning. For example: *vṛkṣaḥ* (tree).

*ṛkṣaḥ*, *kāṇḍīraḥ*, *āṇḍīraḥ*. Through the presence of the letter *ka* in the word *vṛkṣaḥ*, a certain meaning is understood; when that *va* is removed, as in *ṛkṣaḥ*, that [meaning] is no longer conveyed.

The meaning is not understood. In the word *kāṇḍīraḥ*, a certain meaning is understood when the letter *k* is present; in the word *āṇḍīraḥ*, when the letter *k* is removed, that meaning is no longer understood. Why, then, is it said "because of the non-understanding of the meaning"? For in this case, the understanding of the meaning is certainly not as clear. If that is so, then this should have been stated as: "when the phoneme is not perceived."

And because of the non-comprehension of that meaning. What is this "because of the non-comprehension of that meaning"? That which has that as its object is "tadartha" (that-meaning). The comprehension of that meaning is "tadarthagati. The absence of the comprehension of that meaning is "atadarthagati. [The phrase is] "because of the non-comprehension of that meaning" (*atadarthagateḥ*). Alternatively, that which is the object is "tadartha. The comprehension of that meaning is "tadarthagati. The absence of the comprehension of that meaning is "atadarthagati."

“Because it does not convey that meaning. [Objection: In that case, the expression should be stated in such a way. [Response: It need not be so stated; here, the elision of the final member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*) is to be understood. For example:
“one whose face is like the face of a camel” is called *uṣṭramukhaḥ*.

"Kharamukha" means one whose face is like a donkey's face; thus, it is because of the failure to convey that meaning, and because of the failure to convey any meaning at all, and because of the meaningfulness of the aggregate. And because of the meaningfulness of the aggregate, we consider the phonemes (*varṇas*) to be meaningful. For those whose aggregates are meaningful, their parts are also meaningful; but for those whose parts are meaningless, their wholes are also [meaningless].
Those whose parts are meaningless. For example:

a single person with sight is capable of seeing, and a collection of them—even a hundred—is also capable; a single sesame seed is capable of yielding oil, and even a *khārī* measure of them is capable. However, for those [words] whose parts are meaningless—
Their aggregates, too, are devoid of meaning. For example:

a single blind person is incapable of seeing, and even an aggregate of a hundred such persons is incapable; and a single grain of sand is incapable of yielding oil, and even an aggregate of a hundred *khārī* measures of them is incapable. If, then, these phonemes...

Meaningful [elements] acquire the properties produced by meaningful [elements]. Which ones? By the rule *arthavad adhātur apratyayaḥ prātipadikam*, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) is applied;

by the rule *prātipadikāt*, the derivation of case-endings (*svādi*) occurs; and by the rule *sup-antam padam*, the technical designation "word" (*pada*) is applied. What is the fault in that? By the rule *padasya*, the elision of the *n* (and other such operations) would apply. For example, in the word *dhanam*.

Regarding the word *vanam*: because the aggregate (*saṅghāta*) has a single meaning, there is an absence of case-endings (*sub*) after the phoneme (*varṇa*). The meaning of the aggregate is oneness; therefore, the production of case-endings will not occur after the individual phonemes. However, the phonemes are devoid of meaning (*anarthaka*), because no meaning is perceived for each individual phoneme.
Indeed, the phonemes are meaningless. Why? Because no meaning is perceived for each individual phoneme; for it is not the case that [meaning is perceived] for each individual phoneme.

Meanings are perceived. What does this "with respect to each phoneme" (*prativarṇam*) mean? It means "for every single phoneme. Because meanings are observed even when there is the transposition, elision, addition, or modification of phonemes, we consider that phonemes are themselves devoid of meaning. Regarding the transposition of phonemes: [example omitted].
From *kṛti* comes *tarku*; from *kasi* comes *sikatā*;

from *hiṃs* comes *siṃha*. This is a transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*), not a change in meaning (*arthavyatyaya*). Elision (*apāya*) is disappearance (*lopa*). [Examples of elision: *ghnanti*,...

*Ghantu*, *aghnat*: there is a loss of phonemes (*varṇāpāya*), but no loss of meaning (*nārthāpāya*). *Upajana* is an augment (*āgama*). *Lavitā*, *lavitum*: there is an addition of phonemes (*varṇopajana*), but no addition of meaning (*na arthopajana*). *Vikāra* is a substitute (*ādeśa*). *Ghātayati*.

The destroyer [of the word] is a modification of the phoneme (*varṇa*), not a modification of the meaning (*artha*). Just as there are modifications consisting of the transposition, elision, addition, and alteration of phonemes, so too there ought to be modifications consisting of the transposition, elision, addition, and alteration of meanings. But here it is not so.
Therefore, we consider that phonemes are devoid of meaning. Both of these [possibilities] have been stated regarding phonemes: that they possess meaning and that they are devoid of meaning.
And so it is. What is logical here? He says: both. Why? By their very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*). For example:

among those who exert equal effort and study equally, some are endowed with meaning and others are not. Now, it is not possible for everyone to become meaningful simply because someone is meaningful, nor for everyone to become meaningless simply because someone is meaningless. In that case, what can be done by us?

That verbal roots (*dhātu*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), nominal stems (*prātipadika*), and particles (*nipāta*) consisting of a single phoneme (*ekavarṇa*) are meaningful, whereas others are meaningless—this is inherent (*svābhāvika*). How so? This reason which was taught by you for the meaningfulness of phonemes—"phonemes are meaningful because we observe meaning in those consisting of a single phoneme belonging to verbal roots, nominal stems, suffixes, and particles"—is undermined when there is a transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*).

And because there is a transition to a different meaning, because no [individual] phoneme is perceived when the meaning is not understood, and because the composite possesses meaning— these very types of composites function with respect to different meanings: *kūpaḥ* (well),
*sūpaḥ* (soup).

[Regarding the word] *yūpaḥ*: for if there were a shift to a different meaning caused by the transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*), then the meaning of "well" (*kūpa*) would mostly be found in "soup" (*sūpa*), the meaning of "soup" in "well," the meaning of "well" in "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*), the meaning of "sacrificial post" in "well," the meaning of "soup" in "sacrificial post," and the meaning of "sacrificial post" in "soup. Since, however, none of these occurs—neither the meaning of "well" in "soup," nor that of "soup" in "well," nor that of "well" [in the others]...

Or [the word] *yūpa* in the sense of a sacrificial post, or *kūpa* in the sense of a well, or *sūpa* in the sense of a sacrificial post, or *yūpa* in the sense of a well, or *sūpa* in the sense of a sacrificial post—therefore we consider that these and other such compounds function with distinct meanings. Indeed, by you who assert that phonemes possess meaning, their lack of meaning has been more effectively demonstrated. For one who thinks that whatever [meaning] exists in the word *kūpa* is the meaning of the well...

That [suffix] which serves the purpose of the root *sūpa* in the case of *kakāra*, and that which serves the purpose of the root *yūpa* in the case of *sakāra*, would be meaningless in the case of the word *iti-ūpa*. Regarding this, the point that "it is because the composite whole possesses meaning" has not been refuted; he will address this very matter when discussing the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
a, i, uṇ, ṛ, ḷk, e, o, ai, auṃ, aḥ.

Oṃ ai, auc. [Question: Why is it that in the *pratyāhāra* [system], these *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) are not included when there is the mention of vowels (*aj*)? [Explanation: These *anubandhas* are attached to the phonemes (*akṣa*) for the purpose of forming *pratyāhāras*;
why then do they not become included when there is a mention of vowels (*aj*)? What would be the consequence [if they were included]?

In the cases of *dadhi ṇakārīyati* and *madhu ṇakārīyati*, the substitution of *yaṇ* [for the semivowel] by the rule *ikaḥ yaṇ aci* would apply. [This objection arises] from usage (*ācārāt*). What is meant by "from usage"? It means from the conventional practice of the teachers (*ācāryāṇām upacārāt*). The teachers have not applied vowel-related operations (*ackāryāṇi*) to these [diphthongs].
Because they are not primary (*apradhānatvāt*). And because they are not primary, there is indeed no instruction (*upadeśa*) regarding them as being primarily vowels (*akṣu*).

[It] is performed. Where, then? Among the *hal*s (consonants). Why is this so? For this style of the Teacher (*ācārya*) is observed: that he teaches similar [elements] among similar [elements]. Just as *ac* [vowels] are taught among *akṣ* [vowels], and *hal* [consonants] among *hal*s. Furthermore, elision (*lopa*) is more powerful. Indeed, elision does indeed take place. Or rather, the rule *ūkālo ’j* should apply to the inclusion of vowels (*ac*) of that duration.

Therefore, this undesirable consequence will not arise for these [sounds]. Alternatively, a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: "A vowel (*ac*) having the duration of *ū*. This means that a vowel having such a duration—as in *u*, *ū*, *u3*—becomes [the subject]. Then follows: "Short, long, and protracted (*hrasva-dīrgha-pluta*). And thus, a vowel having the duration of *ū* receives the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of short, long, and protracted. Even so, [the designation would] undesirably apply here as well: in the word *kukkuṭaḥ*. Therefore, the previously stated [solution remains necessary].
This is the solution; this is the very meaning. Another says:

Let the rule (*yoga*) apply only as far as "short" (*hrasva*) and so forth, prior to [the mention of] *tāvat*, so that vowel-operations (*ackāryāṇi*) may take place when the vowels (*akṣu*) are in that state.
(Śs 5.6) Now, for what purpose is the teaching (*upadeśa*) of the semivowels (*antaḥstha*) among the vowels (*aṇ*) performed?

In this case, in *saṃyamyantā saṃvatsaraḥ* and *yal lokaṃ tal lokam*, because the substitution of a homogeneous following sound (*parasavarṇa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), there is doubling only of the *anusvāra*. In that situation, once the *parasavarṇa* has been applied to the following sound, since that [new sound] is included by the term *yay* (the *yama* sounds), one might think that the *parasavarṇa* should also apply to the preceding sound. However, this purpose is not necessary; for he will state this later.

It must be stated that the substitution of the *parasavarṇa* [homogeneous sound] after a reduplication is established. To the extent that its establishment is asserted, the *parasavarṇa* itself occurs first. Now, once the *parasavarṇa* has been applied, since that [resulting sound] is included by the mention of *y* and *v*, let there be reduplication.
Let there not be reduplication. But surely there is a difference: when there is reduplication, it would consist of three *i*-sounds.

If there were no doubling (dvirvacana), it would consist of two *y* sounds (*dviyakāra*). There would be no difference [between the cases]. Even when there is doubling, it would still consist of two *y* sounds. How so? By the rule "there is elision of *yam* after a consonant (*hal*) before a *yam*" (*halaḥ yamām yami lopaḥ*), one of them must be elided. Even so, there is a difference:
when there is doubling, sometimes it consists of two *y* sounds and sometimes it consists of three *y* sounds. How is this difference accounted for?

It would not [be so] if that elision were permanent. And that elision is optional. Let it be as there is no difference. The term "optionally" (vibhāṣā) continues [to apply]. This [rule] prevents reduplication when a *śar* sound precedes a vowel. In that the Teacher teaches this prohibition of reduplication by stating "when a *śar* sound precedes a vowel," he makes known that the term "optionally" continues to apply. How?

Having made this an indicator (*jñāpaka*): for if its elision were compulsory (*nitya*), there would be no purpose whatsoever for the prohibition. If the elision were compulsory, the statement of the prohibition would be meaningless. Let there be doubling (*dvirvacana*) here; the elision will occur by the rule "of a *jhara* before a homogeneous *jhara*" (*jharaḥ jhari savarṇe*). But the Teacher perceives that the elision is optional (*vibhāṣā*); therefore, he [formulates] the prohibition of doubling.
This is not a proof [for the permanence of the elision]. Even if that elision were permanent, that prohibition must necessarily be stated.

This doubling [prescribed] by the rule *acaḥ rahābhyām* is understood as an exception (*apavāda*) to that elision. How so? Because it is said "of *ya* and *ra*" (*yaraḥ*). And there are only these many *yar*s: namely, either *jhar*s or *yam*s. And if in this case [the elision] were permanent...

There would be elision; reduplication would be purposeless. What, then, is the illustrative example for those two rules? It is that case where there is a conjunction of three consonants when reduplication has not yet occurred: *prattam*, *avattam*.

In the case of *ādityaḥ*, because of the force of the doubling [of the *y*], the elision does not occur here and now, such that it is called "the agent" (*karttā*) or "the remover" (*harttā*). Likewise, in this instance as well, the elision would not occur:

*karṣati*, *varṣati*. Therefore, even though the elision is obligatory, that prohibition must necessarily be stated. This point remains utterly doubtful: do the teachers intend the option (*vibhāṣā*) to apply here?
"Or not.

(Śs 6) This *ṇ* is attached twice, both before and after [the vowel]. In that regard, a doubt arises concerning the mention of *aṇ* and the mention of *iṇ*: they might belong to the preceding [rule] or to the following one.

Thus [it is asked]: "In which instance, then, is there doubt regarding the mention of *aṇ*? [In the rule] 'When *ḍha* or *ra* is elided, the preceding vowel becomes long, provided it is an *aṇ*'? There is no doubt; [the reference is] to the former [rule], not to the latter. Why is this so? Because of the absence of [other] subsequent [vowels]. For when *ḍha* or *ra* is elided, there are no subsequent *aṇ* vowels. But is this not the case: [there is such a subsequent vowel]?

[The question is raised: "Is it *ātṛḍham* or *āvṛḍham*? [The answer: In that case, by virtue of the context, [the rule applies] with the preceding [term], not with the following. For if it were with the following, the mention of *aṇ* would be purposeless. One could simply have said, "When there is elision of *ḍh* or *r*, there is lengthening of the preceding vowel (*acaḥ*). Or rather, one might not even say this; for these—short, long, and protracted—are indeed properties of a vowel (*acaḥ*). Well then, in this case...

There is a doubt regarding the mention of *aṇ*: [does it mean] "of which *aṇ*"? It is not doubtful; it refers to the preceding [rule], not the subsequent one. Why is this so? Because of the absence of anything subsequent. For there are no *aṇ* sounds following *ke*. But is this not the case here: *gokā*, *naukā*? If that is so, then by virtue of the logical necessity (*sāmarthya*), it refers to the preceding one, not the subsequent one. For if it were due to the subsequent one, the mention of *aṇ* would be purposeless. [The rule is thus: *ke acaḥ* ("after *ke*, [the substitution of] *aci*").

One should say this; or rather, one should not even say this, for [the classification] short, long, and protracted applies only to vowels (*ac*). If that is so, then there would be doubt regarding the mention of *aṇ* in the rule "an *aṇ* which is not a *pragṛhya* becomes nasalized. It is without doubt [that it refers] to the former [rule] and not to the latter. Why? Because of the absence of subsequent [vowels]. For there are no final *aṇ* sounds in words that follow. But surely—

And this [agent] exists as both doer and taker. If that is so, then by implication it is [governed] by the former rule and not the latter. For if it were governed by the latter, the mention of *aṇ* would be purposeless; one could simply have said, "the nasalization of a non-pragṛhya vowel.
Or rather, one need not even say that; for only vowels can be pragṛhyas. If, then, there is this mention of *aṇ*...

There is doubt regarding the rule *uḥ aṇ raparaḥ*. It is not doubtful that [the substitution] is by the preceding [rule] and not by the subsequent one. Why is this so? Because of the absence of subsequent [vowels]. For there are no *aṇ* vowels in the place of *u* that follow it. But is this not the case in *kartrartham* and *hartrartham*? What would happen then? If *raparatva* (the substitution of *ra*) were to apply here, the hearing of two *r*s would result. [This is because of the rule] *halaḥ*.

By the rule *yam-ām yami lopaḥ*, there is the elision of one [of the two] here. That elision is optional (*vibhāṣā*). Consequently, its audible pronunciation would follow as an alternative. Well then, let this be a compulsory elision by the rule *raḥ ri*. But that [elision] applies only to what stands at the end of a word (*padāntasya*). It is not possible to understand it as applying to the end of a word, for in that case, the elision would not occur here: in *ajarghāḥ* from the root *jargṛdh-* in the *laṅ* tense, or in *pāspardh-* [from *pāspṛdh-*].

[Objection: "In that case, [the rule] *apāspāḥ* would entail the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* in the forms *mātṝṇām* and *pitṝṇām*. [Response: The activity of the Teacher indicates that the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* does not occur here, since he employs the term *dhātu-* in the rule *ṝta id dhātoḥ*. How does this serve as an indicator? The purpose of employing the term *dhātu-* is so that [the substitution] does not occur here: *mātṝṇām*, [and likewise *pitṝṇām*]."

Regarding the word *pitṝṇām*: if *rapara* (the substitution of *r*) were to apply here, the mention of the term "dhātu" (root) would be purposeless. Once *rapara* is applied, because [the *r*] would not be final, the substitution of *it* (the short *i*) would not occur. However, the Teacher perceives that *rapara* does not apply here, and therefore he includes the mention of "dhātu. If that is so, then in these cases as well—*cikīrṣati* and *jihīrṣati*—the substitution of *it* would not be applicable.

[Objection: Let it not be so; [the rule] "and after a penultimate vowel" (*upadhāyāś ca*) will apply here as well. [Reply: In that case, it would also apply here in *mātṛṇām* and *pitṛṇām*. Therefore, the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) must be made there [in the rule]. [Objection: If that is so, then by the force of the mention of *aṇ*, [the substitution applies] by the former [rule] and not by the latter. For if it were by the latter, the mention of *aṇ* would be purposeless. [The latter rule is: "The *u* [of the root] is replaced by *ṛ*, followed by *r*. (*uḥ ac raparaḥ*).

One should speak thus. But then, regarding this mention of *aṇ*, there arises a doubt: [does it mean] "an *aṇ* and that which is designated by *u* are substitutes for their homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*), provided they are not suffixes"? It is beyond doubt that [the rule applies] with the subsequent [term], not the preceding one. Why is this so? Because in the case of a homogeneous sound, *aṇ* has a following *t*; for instance, in the rule *uḥ ṛt*, the fact that he makes the letter *ṛ* have a following *t* indicates this.

The Teacher [intends] the subsequent [iṇ], not the preceding one. If that is so, there is doubt regarding the mentions of *iṇ*. It is without doubt that [the reference is] to the subsequent, not the preceding. Why is this? Because elsewhere, *iṇ* occurs after *y* and *v*. Where he intends a combined mention (*sammṛdya-grahaṇa*) with the preceding [vowel], he uses the term *yvoḥ*. And that becomes cumbersome. How does it function as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? In that case, when there is a mention by means of a case-ending...
In the case of grasping [the sound] by rubbing together, there are three and a half *mātrās*; however, in the case of grasping it through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), there are three *mātrās*.

Since this is already established by such a lighter method, the fact that the Teacher undertakes a more laborious effort indicates that [the rule applies] by the subsequent [letter] and not by the preceding one. Furthermore, why is the letter *ṇ* doubled in the production of the phonemes, as if it were being uttered twice?

By this, the Teacher makes it known that this is a *paribhāṣā* (metarule): "The understanding of a specific meaning arises from the explanation, for there is no rule based on doubt. We shall explain that, setting aside the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ*, the mention of *aṇ* [in Pāṇini 1.1.69] refers to the preceding [vowels], while the mention of *iṇ* [in Pāṇini 1.1.70] refers to the following [consonants].
(Śs 7–8.1) KA_I,35.20–36.4 Ro_I,115–116 For what purpose are these two classes of phonemes articulated by both the mouth and the nose?

Both [the *m* and the *ñ*] should be attached as markers (*anubandha*), not the *ñ* alone. Why? Because there are certain rules involving the letter *m*, such as "the *hal* [consonants] before *yam* [semivowels and nasals], when followed by a *yam*, undergo elision" (*halaḥ yamām yami lopaḥ*). [If only *ñ* were used, one might argue: "Let it be that the *hal* before *yañ* [nasals and semivowels], when followed by a *yañ*, undergo elision" (*halaḥ yañām yañi lopaḥ*). This cannot be done. For then the elision of the *jh* and *bh* sounds would also undesirably follow when they are followed by *jh* and *bh* sounds; yet the *jh* and *bh* sounds are not to be elided.

[The rule] "jhakārabhakārayoḥ staḥ" [is problematic]. How so? Because of the rule "pumaḥ khayyi ampare. Let this also be stated as "pumaḥ khayyi añpare" with the letter *ñ*. It cannot be done thus; for if it were so, the substitution of *ru* would undesirably apply when *khay* is followed by *jh* or *bh*. There is no *khay* followed by *jh* or *bh*. How about the rule "ṅamaḥ hrasvāt aci ṅamuṭ nityam"? This...

"Let it be that by means of the letter *ṇ*, [the forms] *ṅ* and *ña* are obtained through the rule *hrasvāt aci ṅañuṭ nityam*. This cannot be so. For then, even after word-final *jha* and *bha*, the augments *jha* and *bha* would have to occur. But there are no word-final *jha* or *bha*. Even if this were the case, there would be five augments and only three bases; because of this discrepancy in number, the principle of correspondence (*saṅkhyātānudeśa*) would not apply."

Let it be for those who have traditional scriptures (*āgama*) and followers of those scriptures (*āgamika*). However, since the phonemes *jha* and *bha* do not exist as word-final sounds (*padānta*), their augmentations (*āgama*) will likewise not occur.
(Śs 7–8.2) KA_I,36.5–11 Ro_I,117 Now, what is this that is called a "syllable" (*akṣara*)? One should know that a syllable is that which does not perish (*na kṣaram*).

It is called *akṣara* because it does not perish (*na kṣīyate*) or does not flow away (*na kṣarati*). Alternatively, *akṣara* is derived from the root *aś* with the suffix *saran*. Or again, this suffix *saran* is an *auṇādika* (irregular) formation added to the root *aś*. Or they say that *varṇa* (phoneme) was intended in the previous rule; or rather, in the previous rule, the term *akṣara* is established as a technical designation (*sañjñā*) for *varṇa*.

(Śs_7-8.3) For what purpose is this taught? Why, indeed, is this taught? Knowledge of the phonemes is the domain of speech, wherein Brahman resides; it is taught for that purpose, for the sake of understanding the desired [meaning], and for the sake of brevity. This very traditional collection of syllables, the traditional collection of speech, is in full bloom and bears fruit.
The mass of Brahman should be understood as being adorned like the moon and the stars. Furthermore, the attainment of the fruit of the merit of all the Vedas occurs through his knowledge,
and his mother and father are glorified in the heavenly world.
Why does the substitution of *k* for *c* (as prescribed by the rule *coḥ kuḥ padasya*) not occur here? Because it is designated as a *bha*. How is it designated as a *bha*?

By the rule *ayasmayādīni chandasi*. It is said that this applies "in the Veda" (*chandasi*). But this is not the Veda. [Objection: The Sūtras are like the Veda (*chandovat sūtrāṇi*). [Reply: If it were designated as a *bha*, then by the rules *vṛddhir ādaic* and *adeṅ guṇaḥ*, the substitution of *jaś* would also not apply.
123–124. Furthermore, what is the meaning of this term *tadbhāvita* (produced by that)?
Does it refer to the inclusion of those vowels *ā*, *e*, and *o* which are produced as "vṛddhi" [by specific rules], or does it refer to the entire class of *ādaij* [vowels] in general?

And what follows from this? If it were the inclusion of those produced as such, then in the words *śālīyaḥ* and *mālīyaḥ*, the suffix *cha*—which is prescribed for bases ending in a *vṛddhi* vowel—would not apply.

[The suffix] *mayaṭ* would not apply to form *āmramayaḥ* or *śālamayaḥ* when [the base] is characterized by the marker *vṛddhi*. [The suffix] *phiñ* would not apply to form *āmraguptāyaniḥ* or *śālaguptāyaniḥ* when [the base] is characterized by the marker *vṛddhi*. Now, if there were the inclusion of every [instance of] *aij*, then in the case of *sarvabhāsaḥ* (from *sarva-bhāsaḥ*), when there is *vṛddhi* of the second member (*uttarapada*), this rule—namely, "and *sarva*"—would apply.

And in this case, in a compound such as *tāvatī-bhāryaḥ* (having so many wives), where the first member ends in *ī*, the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would apply because the first member is the cause of the vowel increase (*vṛddhi*) in the second member. Let it be, then, that the rule applies to every instance of *ai*. But has it not been said that in a compound like *sarva-bhāsaḥ* (all-illuminating), when there is vowel increase in the second member, this rule [of *aij*] would also apply by the principle "and *sarva*"? This is not a fault; for it is not understood thus: [the rule applies] to the second member...

[The objection: "In the rule *vṛddhir uttarapadavṛddhiḥ uttarapadavṛddhau*, how is it then [to be understood]? [The answer: Having introduced the topic with the words "of the second member" (*uttarapadasya*), this is to be understood as meaning "when the second member possesses that *vṛddhi*. And this must necessarily be understood in this way; for even if the term *tadbhāvita* ("produced by that") were included, the [undesired] application would still occur here: [e.g., in *pārikhīya*, where the *vṛddhi* is not produced by the suffix].

"Every agent is a 'sarvakāraka' (an agent of all). As for what is said—that in the case of *tāvadbhāryaḥ* (having so many wives), where *yāvadbhāryaḥ* [is used] because it is caused by a vowel-strengthening (*vṛddhi*), the prohibition of the masculine-like form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would apply—this is not a fault. It is not understood thus: "the cause of strengthening is *vṛddhinimitta*; [the rule applies] to that which has *vṛddhinimitta*. How then? [It is understood as: "that which is the cause of strengthening is *vṛddhinimitta*; [the rule applies] to that which has *vṛddhinimitta*. How? [It is understood as: "strengthening is the cause; that which has strengthening as its cause is *vṛddhinimitta*; [the rule applies] to that which has *vṛddhinimitta*. Thus, there is no fault.

In that case, "vṛddhinimitta" means that which is the cause (nimitta) of *vṛddhi*; [the expression] "of that which has *vṛddhi* as its cause" (*vṛddhinimittasya*). And what is the cause of *vṛddhi*? It is that [substitute] which is the letter *k*, *ṇ*, or *ñ*. Alternatively, it is that which is the cause of the entire *vṛddhi*. And what is the cause of the entire *vṛddhi*? It is that which [is the cause] of the three vowels: *ā*, *e*, and *o*.

The section on technical terms (*saṃjñā-adhikāra*) is for the purpose of making known the technical designations. Now, having introduced the topic with "Now, the technical terms," the words *vṛddhi* and so forth are to be recited. What is the purpose? For the purpose of making known the technical designations of the words *vṛddhi* and the rest.

The purpose is so that there may be this understanding: "This is a technical name (*saṃjñā*). For otherwise, there would be no such understanding, as is the case in common worldly usage. If the heading on technical names were not established, there would be no understanding that *vṛddhi* and the others are technical names. Consequently, these many subsequent sūtras would now be rendered meaningless. He asks: "In what way would they be meaningless? [He replies: "As in common worldly usage. In the world...

For indeed, sentences are seen to be both meaningful and meaningless. First, those that are meaningful: "Devadatta, drive the white cow here with a staff"; and "Devadatta, drive the black cow here. And those that are meaningless:
"Ten pomegranates, six cakes, a bowl, a goat-skin, a lump of meat, a short tunic—this is the girl's [property]."

"‘The father of Sphaiyakṛta is Pratiśīna’—thus there would be confusion regarding the name and the named. Even if the heading *sañjñādhikāra* (the domain of technical names) were established, it must be stated that there should be no ambiguity between the name and the named. For how could it be known that the word *vṛddhi* is the name and *ādaic* [the vowels ā, ai, au] are the named, rather than *ādaic* being the name and the word *vṛddhi* being the named? As for what was said regarding the heading *sañjñādhikāra*..."

"It should be formulated for the sake of establishing a conventional designation"—it need not be formulated. The establishment of a designation follows from the practice of the teachers. The establishment of a designation will indeed follow from the practice of the teachers. What is this "practice of the teachers"? It is the customary usage of the teachers, just as it occurs among worldly and Vedic traditions.
For example, as it occurs in worldly and Vedic systems of established doctrine (*kṛtānta*). First, regarding the world:
When a son is born, his parents give him a name—such as Devadatta or Yajñadatta—in a private place. Through their usage, others also come to know, "This is his designation.
In the Veda, the ritualists establish designations such as *sphya*, *yūpa*, and *caṣāla*. Through the usage of those venerable ones, others [come to understand them].
Do they not know that "this is its name"? Others, however, having stated "there is vṛddhi in the case of *sic*," cite the vowels *ā*, *e*, and *o*.

We consider that by which [the objects] are made known is the name (*saṃjñā*), and those which are made known are the named entities (*saṃjñin*). Furthermore, as for what is said regarding [the rule] being formulated...

Furthermore, even within the section on technical designations (*saṃjñā*), it must be stated that there should be no ambiguity between the designation and the designated object. [Thus: "No ambiguity between the designation and the designated object. The absence of ambiguity between the designation and the designated object is established. Why? Precisely from the practice of the Teacher (*ācāryācāra*). The practice of the Teacher has been explained: [the designation] is without form (*anākṛti*). Alternatively, the designation is without form, while the designated objects possess form. For even in the world, [one uses] those possessing form...

The designation "Devadatta" is applied to a lump of flesh; or [it is applied] by means of a characteristic mark (*liṅga*). Alternatively, having attached some characteristic mark, I shall say that the designation possesses such a mark. And in the word *vṛddhi*, that mark will be established, not in the word *ādaic*. First of all, this which is stated—that [the usage is derived] from the practice of the Teacher—is improper. What is improper here? Having censured that very point:

To say that "your sūtra is without basis" and yet to subsequently treat that very same [sūtra] as authoritative is illogical. Indeed, dissatisfied with this resolution, you have stated, "It is by means of the *ākṛti* (form) or the *liṅga* (mark). That too must be explained.
Even if it were said: "Alternatively, in this case, the designation *it* need not be stated, nor need the elision (*lopa*) be stated."

The technical name (*saṃjñā*) will serve as the indicator (*liṅga*) for the *anubandhas*. Nor is the cessation of the technical name explicitly stated; rather, technical names cease by their own nature once they have conveyed the named object (*saṃjñin*). Therefore, the cessation of the *anubandhas* will also follow.

This is indeed established. However, it would not be in accordance with Pāṇini’s system. Let it remain exactly as it was originally formulated. But has it not been said that this is a governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning technical names?
It is for the purpose of providing clear recognition; otherwise, there would be a lack of clear recognition, as is the case in the world. It is not as it is in the world that it is so in grammar.

The Teacher, who has become an authoritative means of knowledge, sat down on a pure spot with *darbha* grass in his hand, facing the east, and composed the Sūtras with great effort. In that context, it is impossible for even a single phoneme to be meaningless.

But what follows from this much of a sūtra? What follows from that which is impossible? From this, it follows that there is only a relationship between the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*). Why indeed is it said that there is only a relationship between the name and the named, and not rather that in this science—which is an instruction on correctness (*sādhvanuśāsana*)—correctness (*sādhutva*) is being produced by it? The correctness of these two has already been established. How so? Because *vṛddhi* has been taught to him without distinction.

In the list of primary elements (*prakṛti-pāṭha*), the suffix *ktin* follows from that [root]. Furthermore, the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* (*ādaic*) are also taught in the traditional recitation of phonemes (*akṣara-samāmnāya*). If so, this [rule] must be for the purpose of regulating usage, meaning that the vowels *ādaic* should be employed after the word *vṛddhi*. No, a regulation of usage is not being initiated here. What then? Words are set forth after they have been individually refined; of these, [the order] is according to one's preference.
There is a mutual connection [between the two]. For example:

"bring the bowl" (*āhara pātram*) and "bring the bowl" (*pātram āhara*). In that case, these would be substitutes (*ādeśa*): the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* (*ādaic*) would be the substitutes for the term *vṛddhi*. [This applies to] that which is designated by the genitive case.

Substitutes (ādeśas) are being taught here, yet we do not see a genitive case ending [indicating the element to be replaced]. In that case, these must be augments (āgamas). That is, the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* are augments of the word "vṛddhi. But augments are also taught only for that which is indicated by a genitive case ending and by a specific formal characteristic (liṅga). Here, however, we neither see a genitive case ending nor indeed any formal characteristic of an augment. Furthermore, this is even more so:

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the possession of a single case-ending belong to two things. Which two? Either the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*), or the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*). In this regard, one might think it refers to the qualifier and the qualified; but that is not so.

For in common worldly usage, the relationship of qualifier and qualified exists between two things whose referents are already known (*pratītapadārthaka*). And the word *ādi* does not have a known referent.

Therefore, there are only the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*). However, in that regard, this much doubt arises: which is the named and which is the name? And where does that doubt occur? It occurs where both [terms] have the same number of syllables. But where one is light, that which is light is the name. Why is this so? For the purpose of brevity is the making of a technical name. Even in that case, this is not necessarily [the case].
One ought to observe only the relative weight [of the rules]. What then? One must also observe the lack of formal shape (*anākṛtitā*). "Lack of formal shape" refers to a name (*saṃjñā*);

those possessing a formal shape are the named objects (*saṃjñin*). For in the world, a name such as "Devadatta" is applied to a mass of flesh that possesses a formal shape. Alternatively, names are recurring; the word *vṛddhi* recurs, but the word *ādaiC* does not.

For example: elsewhere too, it is the word "Devadatta" that recurs, not the lump of flesh. Or rather, that which was previously uttered is the named object (*saṃjñin*), and that which is uttered later is the name (*saṃjñā*). Why is this so? Because an existing thing that is to undergo an operation must exist prior to the operation. For example: elsewhere too, the name "Devadatta" is assigned to an existing lump of flesh. How so?

"Vṛddhiḥ āt aic"—let this one [sūtra] be tolerated by the Teacher for the sake of auspiciousness. The Teacher, being auspicious-minded, employs the word *vṛddhi* at the beginning for the sake of the auspiciousness of this great flood of treatises. For treatises that begin with auspiciousness flourish, and they come to have heroic men as their authors and long-lived men as their students. And the students...

[The purpose is] so that [the terms] may be established as having their meanings realized. For in every grammatical treatise (*vyākaraṇa*), the name-bearer (*sañjñin*) is uttered first, and the name (*sañjñā*) is uttered later, just as in the rule *at eṅ guṇaḥ*.

However, the section on names (*sañjñādhikāra*) is indeed defective; for even in the eighth book, a name is formed in the rule *tasya param āmreḍitam*, and there too this [section on names] would have to be supplied by way of anuvṛtti. Now...

Or rather, this effort is being made in the wrong place; for this does not differ from common worldly usage. If this were different from worldly usage, then it would merit such effort. For example, someone might point to a cow and, grasping it by the leg or the ear, instruct [a person] who does not know cows, saying, "This is a cow. And he does not tell him, "This is its technical name. Yet, the understanding arises in that person.
In this regard, it might be argued: "The connection has been established by previous [teachers]. Here too, the connection has been established by previous [teachers].
By whom? By the teachers (*ācāryas*). In that case, it might be argued: "For the one to whom he is currently teaching, it has not been established.

Even in the world, for the one to whom he is currently teaching, it has not been established. Therefore, if it has been established there, it should be understood as having been established here as well.

(P_1,1.1.4) Since the technical designation (*sañjñā*) does not exist for *vṛddhi* and the like while they are already existent, there is a lack of establishment due to mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) based upon them. Because the designation does not exist for the designatum (*sañjñin*) while it is already existent, there is non-establishment (*aprasiddhi*) because of mutual dependence regarding the designatum upon which the designation *vṛddhi* and so forth depend.

What constitutes this mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*)? There must be the designation (*sañjñā*) for the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* (*ādaic*), and by means of that designation, *ā*, *ai*, and *au* are brought into being.
That results in mutual dependence;
and operations (*kārya*) characterized by mutual dependence do not function. For example: a boat tied to another boat does not serve as a support for either.

It happens. But, sir, are not effects also seen to be mutually dependent? For example: a boat carries a cart, and a cart carries a boat. Furthermore, there is something else present there—either water or land.
On land, the cart carries the boat; on water, the boat carries the cart. It is just like a tripod stand [which supports itself].
In that case as well, there would ultimately be a circular argument (*sūtraka*). But this is indeed a case of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

It is established, however, because words are eternal. This is established. How? Because words are eternal. Words are eternal. Since words are eternal, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is applied to the existing vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au*. The vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* are not brought into existence by the designation. If, then...

If words are eternal, for what purpose is the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*)? If it is asked, "For what purpose is the treatise?", [the answer is: it is established because it serves as a means of exclusion (*nivartaka*). The treatise is an agent of exclusion. How so? The root *mṛj* has been taught to him without distinction; consequently, the notion of *mṛj* would apply to it everywhere. In that regard, an exclusion is effected by this [treatise] in the case of suffixes other than those marked with *k* or *ṅ*, where *mṛj* would otherwise be applicable.
"It is correct that *mārjiḥ* [is formed]," so it is said.

(P. 1.1.1.5) It should be stated that the technical designations (*sañjñā*) of *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* apply to each [element] individually. What is the purpose? [So that they do not apply] to the aggregate.

"Let it not be so. Because of the mention of "together" (*saha*) elsewhere, there would be the undesirable consequence of the technical designation (*sañjñā*) applying to the aggregate. Because of the mention of "together" elsewhere, the designations of *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* would not apply to the aggregate. Wherever one intends for an operation to be performed upon things that exist together, there the word "together" is employed.
