For example: *saha supā* ("with a *sup* [ending], together") and *ubhe abhyastam saha* ("both together are called *abhyasta*"). [This applies] to each individual member.

And because the completion of a sentence is observed in each individual member. For instance, in the case of "Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra, let them eat," although it is not explicitly stated that [the action] applies to each one individually, the act of eating is completed with respect to each person. Now, is there not also this example where the completion of a sentence occurs with respect to a collective whole? For example: "The Gargas..."
"Let a hundred be punished. Kings act for the sake of wealth, yet they do not punish each individual.

Given this example, if the word "together" (*saha*) were used there, it would have to be stated here as well that [the action applies] to each individually. Alternatively, if in that case the effect pertains to those who are together even without the use of the word "together," then here too the word is unnecessary.
By the statement "each one" (*pratyekam*).
Now, for what purpose is the vowel *ā* made *tapara*? The making of *ā* *tapara* is for the sake of including its homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*).

The addition of *t* after the vowel *ā* (*taparakaraṇam*) is made for what purpose? For the sake of including its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇārtham*). According to the rule "that which has *t* as a marker [denotes] that which has the same duration," there should be the inclusion of those sounds that have the same duration. Of which sounds? Of the acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and circumflex (*svarita*). And why would it not be so? Because accent is a differentiator (*bhedakatvāt svarasya*). The acute and other accents are differentiators. But how is it known that they are differentiators?

"Regarding the statement 'the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth': for this is observed in the world. When Khaṇḍika the teacher applies the grave accent (*anudātta*) when the acute accent ought to be applied, he gives him a slap, saying, 'You are doing something else! This [distinction] serves a purpose. What then?

It must be stated that it is because a quality (*guṇa*) is a differentiator. What is the purpose? There is a quality called nasality (*ānunāsikya*); [it serves to distinguish] that which is different from it."
It might be so. And what is the reason it would not be so? Because a quality (*guṇa*) is a differentiator. Qualities are differentiators.
But how is it known that qualities are differentiators? For it is observed thus in the world: this single entity called "water" becomes distinct due to the difference in its qualities.

"This is cold, this is hot"—[thus they appear distinct]. But surely, sir, qualities are also seen to be non-differentiating. For example: Devadatta does not abandon his own name even when he is shaven-headed, or has matted hair, or wears a top-knot.

Likewise, [the same individual is called] a child, a youth, an old man; a calf, a steer, or a bull. Both of these cases have been stated regarding qualities: those that differentiate and those that do not.
"Are they non-differentiators? What, then, is the correct view here? It is correct that qualities (*guṇas*) are non-differentiators. Why is this so?

Because [the author] makes the mention of "acute" (*udātta*) in the rule *asthidadhisakthyakṣṇām anaṅ udāttaḥ*. If qualities were differentiators, he would have pronounced only the acute vowel. If, then, qualities are non-differentiators, [how do we account for the rule regarding] words beginning with an unaccented vowel (*anudāttādi*)?

Furthermore, that which is prescribed after a word with an acute accent on the final syllable would also apply to words having a circumflex accent on the first syllable and a circumflex accent on the final syllable. This is not a fault.
A quality that is being relied upon serves as a differentiator. For example: "One should sacrifice a white [animal]," "One should sacrifice a black [animal].
In that case, if one were to sacrifice a black animal when a white one is to be sacrificed, he has certainly not done what was prescribed.

In that case, the letter *t* is for the purpose of removing doubt. If it were stated simply as *aic*, a doubt might arise: "Are these only the vowels *ai* and *au*, or is the vowel *ā* also indicated here? This is merely a doubt; and in all cases of doubt, this principle applies: "The specific meaning is understood through interpretation, for there is no rule [that remains] due to doubt."

We shall explain that there is the mention of "three. For elsewhere too, in regard to doubts of this kind, he makes no effort whatsoever; for example, in the rule *auto 'mśasoḥ*. However, this is the purpose: so that, by virtue of proximity (*āntarya*), substitutes consisting of three or four morae (*mātra*) do not replace original elements (*sthānin*) consisting of three or four morae.
A bedstead that is Indra is *khaṭvendra*;

a bedstead that is water is *khaṭvodaka*; a bedstead that is a pole is *khaṭveṣā*; a bedstead that is carried is *khaṭvoḍhā*; a bedstead that is a goat-hair rug is *khaṭvailakā*; a bedstead that is rice is *khaṭvaudana*.
Khaṭvaudana, Khaṭvaaitikāyana, Khaṭvaitikāyana.

[The examples are] *khaṭvā aupagavaḥ* and *khaṭvaupagavaḥ*. Now, even if the letter *t* were applied [as a marker], why would substitutes of three or four morae (*mātrā*) not occur in place of original elements (*sthānin*) consisting of three or four morae? Because of the restrictive rule: "A vowel followed by *t* [indicates] its own duration. But is it not the case that [the substitute] is *ta*...?

"Since it is subsequent to that [ta], this is *tapara*. He says: "No; for it is also subsequent to *tāt* (the sound *t*). If it were *tapara* because it is subsequent even to *tāt*, then [the rule] *ṛdoḥ ap* would apply only here: *yavaḥ*, *stavaḥ*; but it would not apply in cases such as *lavaḥ* and *pavaḥ*. This is not the letter *t*; what then? It is the letter *d*. What is the purpose of the letter *d*? Or rather, what is it?

What is the purpose of the letter *t*? If it is for the sake of removing ambiguity, then the letter *d* would serve that purpose as well. If it is for the sake of ease of pronunciation, then the letter *d* would serve that purpose as well. (P 1.1.3.1) What is the purpose of the mention of *ig*? The mention of *ig* is for the sake of excluding *āt*, diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*), and consonants (*vyañjana*).

The mention of *ig* is made for the purpose of excluding the long vowel *ā*, for the purpose of excluding diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*), and for the purpose of excluding consonants. First, regarding the exclusion of the long vowel *ā*: in the case of *yātā* and *vātā*, the substitution of *guṇa* would apply to the long vowel *ā*; however, because of the mention of *ig*, it does not occur. Regarding the exclusion of diphthongs: in the case of *glāyati* and *mlāyati*, the substitution of *guṇa* would apply to the diphthong.
[The mention of] *ig* [in the rule] prevents [the application of the rule]. It is for the purpose of excluding consonants.

In the cases of *umbhitā*, *umbhitum*, and *umbhitavyam*, the *guṇa* substitution would apply to the consonant; however, because of the mention of *ig*, it does not occur. First of all, there is no need for the mention [of *ig*] for the purpose of excluding the vowel *ā*. The activity of the Teacher indicates that the *guṇa* substitution does not apply to the vowel *ā*, since he [proceeds as follows]:
Therefore, by adding the *k* as an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) in the rule *ātaḥ anupasarge kaḥ*, he provides an indication. How does this serve as an indication?

The purpose of making it *kit* is so that the elision of the long *ā* (*ākāralopaḥ*) may occur by the rule *kiti*. If there were *guṇa* substitution for the long *ā*, the addition of the *kit* would be redundant; for once *guṇa* is applied, the desired form would be established by the single-substitute rule (*pararūpa*) between the two short *a*s, as in *godah*.

Regarding the term *kambaladaḥ*: the Teacher perceives that [the substitution of] *guṇa* does not apply to the vowel *ā*. Therefore, he adds the letter *k* as an *anubandha*. Nor is there a need for it to serve the purpose of including the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*). By virtue of the power of the original instruction (*upadeśa*), the *guṇa* substitution will not apply to a diphthong. Nor is there a need for it to serve the purpose of excluding consonants. The Teacher’s action makes this known.
The fact that [Pāṇini] teaches the suffix *ḍa* after the root *jan* indicates that there is no guna substitution for a consonant. How does this serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)?

The purpose of making the suffix *ḍit* is so that, by the rule "when a *ḍit* suffix follows," the elision of the *ṭi* portion may occur. If there were guna substitution for a consonant, the teaching of the *ḍit* suffix would be redundant; for once the guna had been applied, the desired form would already be established through the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) of the three *a*-sounds.

[The examples would be] *upasarajaḥ* and *mandurajaḥ*. However, the Teacher perceives that [the substitution] is not a quality (*guṇa*) of the suffix (*vyañjana*). Therefore, he teaches the suffix *ḍam* after the root *jan*. These are not the purposes [for teaching it]. As for what was said—that the inclusion of the marker *k* (*kit*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding the long vowel *ā*.
"It is not a *guṇa* substitution. This [statement] must be for the sake of what follows: namely, "in the case of *tuṇḍa* and *śoka* with *parimṛja* and *apanuda*.

If that is so, then why does he attach the *k* as an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) in the rule *gāpoṣṭhak*, which serves no other purpose? Furthermore, as for what was said—that by the force of the original instruction (*upadeśa*), there is no *guṇa* substitution for a diphthong (*saṃdhyakṣara*)—if whatever applies to a diphthong were indeed [to be blocked], [then the *k* would be necessary].

If that [substitution] is set aside by the force of the instruction, then the *āya* and other suffixes would also not apply. This is not a fault. That rule for which the instruction is purposeless is set aside; however, that rule whose very cause [the substitution] exists is not set aside. For the instruction regarding the *guṇa* is purposeless, whereas for the *āya* and others, it is the cause.

As for what is said—that the statement of the suffix *ḍa* after the root *jan* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that a *guṇa* substitution does not occur for a consonant—this is so because a rule being initiated when [the result] is already established serves as an indicator. However, it is not established by a *guṇa* substitution in the case of *jan*. For why should it be that when a *guṇa* is prescribed for *jan*, it becomes the vowel *a*, and not perhaps the vowel *e* or the vowel *o*?

By way of proximity (*āntaryataḥ*), the vowel *a* consisting of one *mātrā* would become [the substitute] for a consonant consisting of half a *mātrā*. Even so, it would follow that it becomes nasalized (*anunāsika*).
It will become pure (*śuddha*) by means of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). If that is the case, then this suffix *ḍa* must also be prescribed after the root *gam*.
And since *guṇa* is being prescribed for *gam*, by way of proximity, the vowel *o* would result as the substitute. Therefore, the mention of *ig* (vowels) must be made.
If the term *ig* were included [in the definition], then [the forms] *dyauḥ*,
*panthāḥ*,
and *saḥ* [would not be accounted for].

Do these [rules] also apply to *ika*? There is a restriction regarding rules formulated by means of technical names (*saṃjñā*). The restriction applies to those which are prescribed by means of technical names.
Is this something that needs to be stated? No, it need not. How is it understood even without being stated? By the force of the mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.
But how could *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* belong to *ika* without the mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*? The mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is the subject under discussion.

It follows [from the previous rule]. Where was it introduced? In the rules "vṛddhir ād aic" and "at eṅ guṇaḥ. If that [term *vṛddhi*] were to follow, then by the rule "at eṅ guṇaḥ vṛddhiś ca," the designation *vṛddhi* would undesirably apply even to the vowels *a*, *e*, and *o*. [Objection: It will follow as connected [to the specific context]:
"vṛddhir ād aic" and "at eṅ guṇaḥ vṛddhir ād aic"; then, from there, "ikaḥ guṇavṛddhī" [will apply]. [Thus,] the mention of both *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [is necessary].

The mention of *āt* and *aic* continues [from the previous rule], while [the mention of] *eṅ* has ceased. Alternatively, governing rules (*adhikāra*) proceed like the movements of frogs (*maṇḍūkagati*); just as frogs go by leaping again and again, so too do governing rules. Or else, a single compound rule (*ekayoga*) will be formulated: "Vṛddhi is *āt* and *aic*; *guṇa* is *at* and *eṅ*"; and then [the next rule]: "Guṇa and Vṛddhi substitutions occur in place of *ik*. Furthermore, there is no continuation (*anuvṛtti*) within a single compound rule.

Alternatively, because another designation is stated and because the particle *ca* (and) is not employed, it is understood that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to what has been previously introduced. Just as an exception sublates that which is applicable by way of a general rule (*utsarga*), so too, because another technical term (*saṃjñā*) is stated and the particle *ca*— which would serve to carry over [the previous term]— is not used, the designation *vṛddhi* will sublate the designation *guṇa*, just as an exception sublates a general rule.

An exception (*apavāda*) serves as a sublater (*bādhaka*) of that which has been previously applied. Alternatively, he will state this: although rules (*vidhi*) do indeed continue to apply, they do not come into effect merely by such continuation; rather, they come into effect through a specific effort (*yatna*). Or else, both [the general rule and its exception] have ceased to apply; we shall take that into account.

Is this [rule] a supplement (*śeṣa*) to the rule concerning the final letter (*alontya*), or rather an exception (*apavāda*) to it? How could it be a supplement to that, or how could it be an exception to it? If there were a single sentence consisting of both "of the *al*" (*alaḥ*) and this [present rule]:

The rules [prescribing] *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* apply to the final [element] by the rule "the operations [apply] to the final [element of the base]" (*alaḥ antyasya*). Therefore, this [present rule] is a supplement (*taccheṣa*) to that. Alternatively, it is a separate sentence: "Operations apply to the final [element]," and "the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions apply to both the final and the non-final [elements]. Therefore, this [present rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to that. And what is the case here?

[Objection: If it is argued that "vṛddhi and guṇa [substitutions] apply to the final letter of the stem" (Pāṇini 1.1.54), then [the sūtra] must include the mention of *ik* in the case of *mid*, *pu-ganta-laghu-upadha*, *ṛcchi*, *dṛśi*, *kṣipra*, and *kṣudra*. If it is argued that "vṛddhi and guṇa apply to the final letter of the stem," then one must state the inclusion of *ik* in the rules for *mid*, *pu-ganta-laghu-upadha*, *ṛcchi*, *dṛśi*, *kṣipra*, and *kṣudra*. For in the case of *mid*, the guṇa substitution would not otherwise apply because [the *m*] is not final.
[Response: It should be stated that for *mid*, the guṇa applies to the *ik*. Since it is not final, [the rule] would not otherwise apply.

It should be stated that "there is *guṇa* substitution for an *ik* vowel which has a light penultimate syllable. For, because it is not final, [the rule] would otherwise not apply. It should be stated that "there is *guṇa* substitution for an *ik* vowel in the root *ṛcch* when the *liṭ* suffix follows. For, because it is not final, [the rule] would otherwise not apply. It should be stated that "there is *guṇa* substitution for an *ik* vowel in the roots *ṛ*, *dṛ*, and *sṛ* when the *aṅ* suffix follows. For, because it is not final, [the rule] would otherwise not apply. It should be stated that "there is *guṇa* substitution for an *ik* vowel in the words *kṣipra* and *kṣudra*. For, because they are not final, [the rule] would otherwise not apply.

Because [the substitute] is infinite in scope, it would not apply; furthermore, there is the undesirable consequence of it being a replacement for the entire word (*sarvādeśa*) in the case of a stem that does not end in *i*. For both the substitution of the whole and the *guṇa* substitution would apply to a stem not ending in *i*: as in *yātā* and *vātā*. Why? Because the genitive case in the rule *alaḥ antyasya* has indeed shifted to refer to the final *ik* vowel.

And the term *aṅgasya* is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). Consequently, for that member (*aṅga*) which now does not end in *i*, a *guṇa* substitution would result as a replacement for the whole. This is not a fault. For just as the genitive in *alaḥ antyasya* has shifted to refer to the final *ik*, so too the genitive in *aṅgasya* is a genitive of location. Thus, when the member now does not end in *i*, [the rule still applies].

In that case, the sixth [case ending] does not exist at all; how then could there be a *guṇa* substitution, and how could there be a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*)? If this is so, then this is not a collection of faults. What then? This fault is relative to what precedes it; furthermore, this particle *ca* is read here in the sense of *hi* (for). Regarding the rule "in *mideḥ*, *puganta-laghūpadha*, *ṛcchi*, *dṛśi*, *kṣipra*, and *kṣudra*, there is the mention of *ik*, which results in the undesirable consequence of a whole-stem replacement (*sarvādeśa-prasaṅga*) because [the rule] applies to that which does not end in *ik*: in the case of *mideḥ*, the *guṇa* is [prescribed] by the statement "of *ik*" (*ikaḥ*), and therefore it does not apply to the final [phoneme].

Because of the statement "of the last [element]," the *ik* [vowel] does not [undergo the substitution]. However, it is stated that the *guṇa* [substitution] occurs; that would result in being a substitute for the whole word (*sarvādeśa*). This applies everywhere. Let it then be an exception to that. If it is argued that it applies to the mere *ik*, then there is a prohibition against [the rule applying to] non-final [elements] in the case of *guṇa* substitutions for *jus*, *sārvadhātuka*, *ārdhadhātuka*, and short vowels. If it is argued that it applies to the mere *ik*, then [there is a prohibition] in the case of *jus*, *sārvadhātuka*, *ārdhadhātuka*, short vowels, and so forth, regarding the *guṇas*.

A prohibition of the infinity [of the rule] regarding the *guṇa* substitutions must be stated. [The rule] "there is *guṇa* before *jusi*" applies here as follows: just as in *ajuhavuḥ* and *abibhayuḥ*, so too in *anenijuḥ*.
They served [the food] around;
here too, the rule would apply: "There is *guṇa* substitution for [the final vowel of a verbal root] before a *sārvadhātuka* or *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. Just as it occurs here:
*kartā*, *hartā*, *nayati*, *tarati*, *bhavati*.
In this way, [the rule] would also apply here to *īhitā* and *īhitum*. [The rule states: "There is guna for a short vowel. Just as it occurs here:
*he agne*, *he vāyo*.

In this way, [the rule] would also apply here to "he agnicit" and "he somasut. There is a *guṇa* substitution in the *jas* case-ending. Just as it occurs here in "agnayaḥ" and "vāyavaḥ," so too [it would occur] in "agnicitaḥ."

In this case as well, the rule for *somasutaḥ* would apply. According to the rule "there is guna substitution for an *ṛt* [stem] before the endings *ṅi*, *sarvanāmasthāna*, and *su*," just as it occurs here in *kartari*, *kartārau*, and *kartāraḥ*, so too would it apply here in *sukṛti*, *sukṛtau*, and *sukṛtaḥ*. Furthermore, according to the rule "there is guna substitution for a stem ending in *ghi* before an ending marked with *ṅ*," just as it occurs here in *agnaye* and *vāyave*, so too would it apply in *agnicite* and *somasute*.

In this case as well, the rule "oḥ guṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.84) would apply. Just as it occurs here in *bābhravyaḥ* and *māṇḍavyaḥ*, so too would it apply here in *suśrut* and *sauśrutaḥ*. This is not a fault, because the mention of "the penultimate light vowel" (*pugantalaghūpadha*) is for the purpose of restricting [the application] to non-final vowels.

The mention of "having a light penultimate vowel" (*laghūpadha*) in the rule for *puganta* [roots] will serve to restrict it to non-final vowels; that is, it will apply only to a non-final vowel that follows a root ending in *pu* or *g*, and not to any other non-final vowel. This restriction would apply to what is under discussion. And what is under discussion? It is the rule "before *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes. Consequently, by virtue of this restriction, [the substitution] would not occur here in the case of *īhitā*.

Regarding the forms *īhitum* and *īhitavyam*: the substitution of the *guṇa* vowel for short vowels and the like is not restricted. Consequently, it would apply even to a non-final vowel. Now, suppose there were such a restriction: that the *guṇa* substitution occurs only for the penultimate light vowel (*laghūpadha*) when followed by a *sārvadhātuka* or *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.

Even so, the *guṇa* substitution for the roots ending in *puk* and those having a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*) before *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes would remain unrestricted; it would thus apply even to non-final vowels, as in *īhitā*, *īhitum*, and *īhitavyam*. Alternatively, if there were a restriction from both sides—namely, that *guṇa* applies only to roots ending in *puk* or having a light penultimate vowel before *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes—[the rule would still require further qualification].

[The rule] "pugantalaghūpadhasya" applies only to [roots ending in] *puK* or having a light penultimate vowel when followed by a *sārvadhātuka* or *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. Even so, this *guṇa* substitution before *jus* would be unrestricted; it would apply even to a non-final vowel, as in *anenijuḥ* and *paryaviviṣuḥ*. If that is the case, then this is neither a supplement (*taccheṣa*) to that [rule], nor is it an exception (*tadapavāda*) to it; rather, this is something entirely different.
Another paribhāṣā is unrelated to this paribhāṣā. Regarding it as another paribhāṣā, the followers of Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana (Kroṣṭrīyas) recite:

"By way of restriction, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* apply to the *ik* vowels through *vipratiṣedha*. If this [present rule] were a supplement (*taccheṣa*) to that, then a *vipratiṣedha* between them would be improper. Moreover, even if it were an exception (*apavāda*) to that, there can be no *vipratiṣedha* between a general rule (*utsarga*) and its exception.
This is an improper contradiction. In that case, the scope for the restrictive rule (*niyama*) is:
*rājñaḥ ka ca*, [as in] *rājakīyam*. The scope for the rule "guna and vṛddhi substitute for *ik*" is: *cayanam*.
*cāyakaḥ*,
*lavanam*, and *lāvakaḥ*. In these cases, both [suffixes] would apply:

[The opponent argues: "In the case of *medyati* and *mārṣṭi*, the rule 'ikaḥ guṇavṛddhī' (P. 1.1.3) prevails by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). [The author replies: "This conflict is not appropriate. For it is said that in a conflict, 'the latter' prevails; however, this preceding rule is a general prescription (*yoga*), while the subsequent one is a restrictive rule (*niyama*). The word 'latter' (*para*) denotes what is desired. In a conflict, that which is desired is the latter.
[The opponent replies: "Even so, the conflict is still inappropriate. For a conflict occurs when two operations apply simultaneously."

And here, it is not the case that a single [element] is joined with two operations. Furthermore, conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) does not necessarily consist only in the conjunction of two operations; rather, it is also [defined by] impossibility (*asambhava*). And such impossibility exists here. What is this impossibility? First, in this case: *vṛkṣebhyaḥ*.

In the case of *plakṣebhyaḥ*, there is one substituendum (*sthānin*) and two substitutes (*ādeśau*). However, it is impossible for there to be two substitutes for a single substituendum. Here, in the forms *medyati*, *medyataḥ*, and *medyanti*, there are two substituenda and one substitute. Furthermore, it is impossible for there to be a single substitute for two substituenda; thus, this [proposed situation] is impossible.

It is true that in this case of impossibility, a contradiction is logical. Even so, the contradiction remains illogical; for a contradiction occurs only when two rules are established with their respective scopes (*sāvakāśa*). Yet, this present rule (*yoga*) is without scope (*anavakāśa*). But was not its scope just now established: namely, the piling of the altar (*cayana*)?
*cāyakaḥ*, *lavanam*, *lāvakaḥ*. Here too, a restriction would apply; however, this rule (*yoga*) is commenced precisely because the restriction does not [otherwise] apply.
Therefore, this *yoga* (rule) serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to that. And between a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*), a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is improper.
Even if, by some means, there were scope for the rule "guṇa and vṛddhi replace *ik*" [P.
1.1.3], even so, just as here [in the case of *cayanīyam*] the guṇa of *ik* occurs due to conflict:
[The roots] *medyati*, *medyataḥ*, [and] *medyanti* [are formed];
likewise, here too, it would be so: *anenijuḥ*, *paryaveviṣuḥ*. If that is the case, then wherever one says "vṛddhi occurs" or "guṇa occurs," [it refers to] the *ik* [vowels].
Thus, this [interpretation] should be seen as applicable there. What is accomplished? The genitive case is manifested as a second [alternative]. In that regard, there is freedom of choice:
either to qualify the *ik* by means of what is being grasped, or to have the *ik* qualify what is being grasped. Since there is such freedom of choice here, [the following applies]:
In the rules concerning *mid*, *puganta*, *laghūpadha*, *cchi*, *dṛśi*, *kṣipra*, and *kṣudra*, we shall qualify the *ik* by that which is being grasped [as the cause of the operation]:
namely, "that *ik* which belongs to these.

Now, here in the rules concerning *jus*, *sārvadhātuka*, *ārdhadhātuka*, short vowels (*hrasva*), and so forth, regarding the *guṇa* substitutions, we shall qualify the *ik* by that which is being grasped [as the cause of the operation].

The quality *guṇa* applies to these [roots] that end in an *ik* vowel, according to the rule "of those ending in an *ik*. Alternatively, the substituend (*sthānin*) is indicated everywhere. Here, first of all, in the case of *mideḥ*, it is an indication without a case-ending: *mid-eḥ*, [which is equivalent to] *mideḥ*.

Regarding the term *mideḥ*: alternatively, it will be a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), namely *midiḥ* [from] *midaḥ iḥ*, meaning "the *i*-substitution for *mid*. Thus, the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya* is not to be understood in that way.

[The rule] "of a stem ending in *puk* and having a light penultimate vowel" [is incorrect]. How then [should it be understood]? "That which has *puk* at its end is *puganta*; that which has a light penultimate vowel is *laghūpadhā*;

[the compound] *pugantalaghūpadham* means 'that which both ends in *puk* and has a light penultimate vowel'. And this must necessarily be understood in this way; for if [the term *pugantalaghūpadham*] were a qualifier of the stem (*aṅga*), then [the rule] would apply here [undesirably].

"Bhinatti" and "chinatti": this is also a combined (praśliṣṭa) mention of the root *ṛcch*. [The forms are] *ṛcchati*, *ṛ*, *ṛ*, and *ṝtām ṛcchaty-ṝtām*. A separate rule (*yogavibhāga*) will also be made for *dṛś*: "There is guṇa substitution for *u* before the suffix *aṅ*. Thus, there is guṇa for *u* before *aṅ*. Then, [the second part is] "and for *dṛś*"; there is also guṇa for *dṛś* before *aṅ*. [The condition] "for *u*" remains in force. [This applies] in the sense of "quick" and "small."

Even by the rule "guṇa is substituted for [an *ik*] followed by a vowel or a consonant beginning with *yaṇ*" (*yari*), this much is established. Now, since this is already established, the purpose of the mention of the word "pūrva" (preceding) is so that it may apply to an *ik*, and not to what is not an *ik*. (Pāṇini 1.1.50–51)

155–161. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *vṛddhi*? Why is the mention of *vṛddhi* specifically questioned, and not also the mention of *guṇa*? If there were some purpose for the mention of *guṇa*, that same purpose ought to apply to the mention of *vṛddhi* as well. Or what is the distinction? This is the distinction: in the prescription of *guṇa*, [the term *vṛddhi*] never occurs.

The original element (*sthānin*) is being specified. In that regard, the mention of "guṇa" must necessarily be made for the purpose of specifying the original element. However, in the rule prescribing *vṛddhi*, the original element is specified everywhere: in *acaḥ ñṇiti*, *ata upadhāyāḥ*, and *taddhiteṣv acām ādeḥ*. To this, he replies: the mention of "vṛddhi" is for the sake of what follows; thus, the mention of "vṛddhi" is made.

For the sake of what follows: he will state the prohibition [of vṛddhi] by the rule *kṅiti*. That [prohibition] should apply to vṛddhi as well. Vṛddhi is prescribed for *mṛj* without distinction; let that not occur before a *kṅit* suffix: [as in] *mṛṣṭaḥ*.

Vṛddhi occurs before both suffixes ending in ñ and those ending in ṇ. [The rule applies] only to vowels (acaḥ). If it is stated that vṛddhi applies to a vowel, then in the case of *nyamārṭ*, vṛddhi would also apply to the augment *aṭ*. But it has been stated regarding the augment *aṭ*: what was stated? That when a modification does not affect the final letter, the operation applies to that which is in the vicinity of the final letter (*antyasadeśasya*). However, the prohibition of vṛddhi is untenable because this falls within the section on the suffix *ik*; for the prohibition of vṛddhi [is intended only there].
It is not applicable. What is the reason? Because of the context of *ik* vowels. The prohibition applies to *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* characterized by *ik* vowels;

however, this being the case, there is no *vṛddhi* characterized by *ik* for the root *mṛj*. Therefore, a *vṛddhi* characterized by *ik* must be desired for *mṛj*. If that is so, then here other grammarians introduce an optional *vṛddhi* for *mṛj* when followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) in the process of transition (*saṅkrama*).

[The forms] *parimṛjanti*, *parimārjanti*, *parimṛjantu*, *parimārjantu*, *parimamṛjatuḥ*, *parimamārjatuḥ*, and so forth [are derived]. That [rule] must also be established here. Once that is established, a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: "In place of the vowel of the root *mṛj*, there is *vṛddhi*. Then: "Before an affix beginning with *ac* that has *k* or *ṅ* as an indicatory letter (*kṅit*). Thus, before an affix beginning with a vowel that has *k* or *ṅ* as an indicatory letter, there is *vṛddhi* for the root *mṛj*.

They rub; let them rub. For what purpose is this? It is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*): [the substitution] occurs only before *kṅit* suffixes beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*), and not elsewhere. Where else should it not occur? In forms such as *mṛṣṭaḥ* and *mṛṣṭavān*. Then, optionally (*vā*): optionally, there is *vṛddhi* for the root *mṛj-* before a *kṅit* suffix beginning with a vowel. [Examples: *parimṛjanti*,...

[Examples are] *parimārjanti*, *parimamṛjatuḥ*, and *parimamārjatuḥ*. For this very purpose—that is, for the sake of the *sic* suffix—the mention of "vṛddhi" (vowel strengthening) must be made. Vṛddhi is prescribed for *sic* without distinction; it [should apply] so that it occurs in place of an *ik* vowel.

[The rule] "let there not be a single vowel" (anika) [is stated]. For what, then, would a single vowel be obtained? For the vowel *a*: as in *acikīrṣīt* and *ajihīrṣīt*. This is not the case; here, elision (*lopa*) will be the sublater. Then it would apply to the long vowel *ā*: as in *ayāsīt* and *avāsīt*. There is no difference here whether the *vṛddhi* [substitution] occurs or does not occur. Then it would apply to a diphthong (*sandhyakṣara*).

A diphthong is certainly not the final [element]. But is it not the case that this occurs when the elision of *ḍh* has taken place, as in *udavoḍhām*, *udavoḍham*, and *udavoḍha*? This is not so; the elision of *ḍh* is *asiddha*. Because it is *asiddha*, this does not become the final [element]. In that case, would it not then apply to a consonant, as in *abhaitsīt*?

[The form] *acchaitsīt* [is derived as follows]: the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule for stems ending in a consonant (*halanta-lakṣaṇā*) will be the sublater [of the *guṇa*]. But where is that [vṛddhi] prohibited? In cases such as *akoṣīt* and *amoṣīt*. This prohibition applies to the *vṛddhi* even in the case of the suffix *sic*. How so? For a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) wavers, it stumbles; it does not remain steady even for a moment. [The suffix] *prāpnoti* [is obtained]. For that [suffix], the *vṛddhi* substitution conditioned by a final consonant (*halanta*) is an exception (*bādhikā*). For that [vṛddhi] as well, there is a prohibition by the rule *na iṭi*.

[Otherwise,] cessation [of the application of the rule] would occur; it would also apply to this [case]: *kartṛ-hartṛ*. The vowel *r* is elided in *abhāji rāgaḥ* and *upabarhaṇam*. From the root *sriv*, [we have] *āsremāṇam*. Upon the elision of the *anubandha*:
from *lūñ*, [we have] *lavitā* and *lavitum*. If a formal enumeration (*parigaṇana*) is made, [the following are included]: *syadaḥ*,...

[The rule] would also apply here in the cases of *praśrathaḥ* and *himaśrathaḥ*. In the case of *māgadha-kaḥ* and *dṛṣada-kaḥ*, [the substitution] would not apply here because of the status of the original locus (*sthānivadbhāva*) regarding the elision of the vowel. Therefore, there is elision (*lopa*). Then, regarding the rule *yasya*: "there is elision of that which belongs to [a stem] ending in *a*"—this is understood from the previous rule *ataḥ* itself. For what purpose is this stated? It is for the purpose of superseding the *luk*-elision that will be taught later. Then, regarding the rule *halaḥ*: "and there is elision of that which follows a consonant. Here too, because of the subsequent position and due to the division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*), [the elision applies].
Or rather, the elision (*lopa*) would subvert the zero-substitution (*luk*):

[in the case of] *kṛṣṇaḥ nonāva vṛṣabhaḥ yad idam*, from the root *nonūyati* we derive *nonāva*. A zero-substitution (*luk*) that has the same locus as an elision (*lopa*) is subverted by that elision. And what is "having the same locus"? That which has the suffix as its locus. And here, the zero-substitution (*luk*) occurs prior even to the production of the suffix.
It occurs. How so?
*syadaḥ*, *praśrathaḥ*, *himaśrathaḥ*.

"Jīradānuḥ" and "nikucitaḥ. It was stated regarding the remainder [of the rules]: what was stated? That by virtue of being an irregular formation (*nipātana*), it is established in cases such as *syadādi*; because it does not depend on a suffix (*pratyaya-śruti*), it is established elsewhere. Regarding *jya* with the suffix *rak*, there is vocalization (*prasāraṇa*). It was also stated regarding *nikucita*: a grammatical operation characterized by a specific configuration (*sannipāta-lakṣaṇa*) [is not nullified by that which destroys the configuration].
"‘That [term] is without a cause for its own destruction’—

this refers to the mention of ‘that which is the cause of it’ in the prohibition concerning *kṅit* suffixes. In the prohibition concerning *kṅit* suffixes, there must be a mention of that which is the cause of it."

It must be stated: "Those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions which would otherwise apply when *kṅit* suffixes follow do not take place. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of [the forms] *upadhā* and *roravīti*. That is, for the sake of *upadhā* and for the sake of *roravīti*. First, regarding the sake of *upadhā*: [the forms] *bhinnaḥ* and *bhinnavān*. Why, then, are these not established? Because it is stated that [the rule applies] "when *kṅit* follows. Therefore, it would only apply where there is a *guṇa*-subject immediately preceding a *kṅit* suffix.

The *guṇa* substitution has been stated [to apply] when there is a *kit* or *ṅit* affix following. But here it would not apply in cases such as *bhinnaḥ* and *bhinnavān*. Now, one might argue: "We shall qualify that for which *guṇa* is prescribed by the condition of being followed by a *kit* or *ṅit*. However, *guṇa* is prescribed for that which ends in *puk*, as well as for that which has a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*), and in these instances, that [element] is indeed followed by a *kit* or *ṅit*. Yet, the rule "for that which ends in *puk* or has a light penultimate vowel" is not to be understood in that way.

[This refers to the rule] "of a root ending in *puk* and of that which has a light penultimate vowel. How, then, [is the compound formed]? That which ends in *puk* is *puganta*; that which has a light penultimate vowel is *laghūpadha*.
[The two are conjoined as] *puganta* and *laghūpadha*, resulting in *pugantalaghūpadham*.

[The rule] *pugantalaghūpadhasya* [applies]. And this must necessarily be understood in this way. For if it were taken as a qualification of the *aṅga* (the verbal base), then it would undesirably apply here: *bhinatti*, *chinatti*. And it is for the sake of *roravīti*: "The bull, bound in three ways, bellows loudly" (*tridhā baddho vṛṣabho roravīti*). If, however, the mention of that cause (*tannimitta*) is made, there is a fault with forms ending in *śyan*: *riyati*, *piyati*, *dhiyati*, and *prādudruvat*.

[In the case of] *prāsusruvat*, [the rule] would apply here because that which ends in *śapa* (the present tense marker) is an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation. Since it is an internal operation, once *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* have been applied, there will be no *guṇa* substitution because the vowel is no longer penultimate (*anupadhātva*). This is done, and this inclusion of "that as its cause" (*tannimittagrahaṇa*) does not give rise to any fault. Furthermore, these are the purposes for including "that as its cause": [e.g.,] *hataḥ*.
hathaḥ,
upoyate, auyata.
*lauyamāniḥ*, *pauyamāniḥ*,
and *nenikte*— these do not serve as purposes [for the formation of the denominative]. Here, first of all, [we have] *hataḥ*.

[The objection is] "by force" (*hatha*). It is possible to effect the cessation of that which has been introduced [into the rule] but not yet realized, by means of its prohibition; and here, the vowel *a* exists precisely at the stage of the verbal root's instruction (*dhātūpadeśa*). And here [we have examples such as]:
*upoyate*, *auyata*, *lauyamāniḥ*.

Regarding the example *pauyamāniḥ*: the prohibition is internal (*antaraṅga*), whereas the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions are external (*bahiraṅga*). An external operation is considered unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to an internal one. Therefore, in the case of *nenikte*, [the substitution] will not occur because it is intervened by the subsequent form [of the suffix]. First of all, there is no need for the purpose of "penultimate" (*upadhā*). The term "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*) is understood from the context. We shall qualify the root by its being followed by *k* or *ṅit* suffixes. If the root is thus qualified, [the rule] would not apply to the *vikaraṇa* suffixes.
cinutaḥ, sunutaḥ, lunītaḥ.

[Objection: "It would be purified" (punītaḥ). [Response: This is not a fault. The mention of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is a qualifier of what has been prescribed (*vihita*). That is, "that which has been prescribed after a verbal root. [Objection: In that case, it would not apply even to [the form] derived from a verbal root. [Response: It is not understood in this way, as "after a verbal root, when *k* or *ṅit* follows.

How then? As "when *k* or *ṅit* follows that which has been prescribed after a verbal root. Or rather, for technical definitions and rules of interpretation (*saṃjñā-paribhāṣā*), the time of their application is determined by the specific grammatical operation (*kāryakāla*).

Where there is an operation, there it should be observed. Since "there is guna for a root ending in a *puk* or *ant* [consonant] when the penultimate vowel is light" is present, this [rule] "not before *kṅit*" becomes applicable. Alternatively, the mention of *kṅit* in this rule is without scope;
because it is without scope, guna and vṛddhi will not occur. Or rather, the activity of the Teacher indicates [this].

There is a prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution for that which is characterized by the condition of having an *upadhā*. This is indicated by the fact that [Pāṇini] makes the suffixes *knū* and *san* *kit* in the rule "trasigṛdhidhṛṣikṣipeḥ knuḥ" and "ikaḥ jhal halantāt ca. How does this serve as an indicator? The purpose of making them *kit* is so that the *guṇa* substitution might not occur. For if there were no prohibition of *guṇa* in these cases, the *kit*-designation would be meaningless.

[Otherwise, the rule] would be purposeless. However, the Teacher perceives that there must be a prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution conditioned by the *upadhā*. Therefore, he makes *knus* and *na* both *kit*. [He might argue: "There is no point even in the sense of *roravīti*, for it is stated that [the rule applies] 'before a *kṅit* suffix. And we do not see a *kṅit* suffix here. [To this, the reply is: It would apply by virtue of the suffix being a condition (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). [But] it is stated: "Not when [a suffix] has been elided by *lumat*."

This is the negation of the characteristic of being a condition (*pratyayalakṣaṇapratiṣedha*). Now, even if it is stated that "by [an affix] marked with *lu*, there is no [application of a rule] to the stem" (*na lumatāṅgasya*), even so there is no fault. How so? When something is elided by an affix marked with *lu*, the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for the "stem" (*aṅga*) is not being referred back. What then? It means that when something is elided by an affix marked with *lu*, whatever operation was to apply to the stem (*aṅga*) in relation to that [elided affix] does not take place. Furthermore, even if the governing heading for the "stem" (*āṅgādhikāra*) [is still in force]...

Even if it is pointed out in this way, there is no fault. How so? For technical definitions (*saṃjñā*) and rules of interpretation (*paribhāṣā*) apply at the time of their operation; they are to be understood wherever the operation occurs. When it is stated, "There is *guṇa* substitution for [the vowels of] *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes," this [rule], "Not before *kṅit* suffixes," becomes present [as a counter-exception]. Alternatively, this is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). And in the Veda, one follows what is actually observed.

Alternatively, the *guṇa* substitution is external (*bahiraṅga*) and the prohibition is internal (*antaraṅga*). That which is external is not established (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal.
Alternatively, in the preceding rule, the mention of the term *ārdhadhātuka* is without scope (*anavakāśa*). Because it lacks scope, the *guṇa* substitution will take place.
177–180. Why does [the rule] not apply here:

*laigavāyanaḥ*, *kāmayate*? Because of the context of the suffixes (*taddhita*) and the desiderative (*kāmya*) which involve *ik*-vowels. The prohibition applies to *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* that are characterized by an *ik*-vowel; it does not [apply to others].

And these [are] characterized by *i*. Because the letter *l* has the property of being *ṅit*, there arises the contingency of the substitute being treated like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) in the case of the substitutes. Because the letter *l* has the property of being *ṅit*, the status of being like the original applies to the substitutes:
[as in] *acinavam*, *asunavam*, *akaravam*. Thus, because the letter *l* has the property of being *ṅit*, there is the contingency of the substitute being treated like the original.

If [it is argued that the rule] is established by the statement that *yāsuṭ* is treated as having the marker *ṅ*, then this very teaching of the marker *ṅ* for *yāsuṭ* indicates that the teacher [Pāṇini] intends: "Substitutes that have the marker *ṅ* do not themselves possess the marker *ṅ*. If this is indicated, how is it that [the rule] says "always [augment *iṭ*] after that which has the marker *ṅ* and after an *it*" (A 7.2.45)? The effect that belongs to what has the marker *ṅ* does indeed occur, but the effect that belongs to a substitute *marked* with *ṅ* does not occur. Why?

This must be stated: for how would it be understood if it were not explicitly stated? [It is understood] from the fact that *yāsuṭ* itself is designated as having the marker *ṅ*. Indeed, *yāsuṭ* alone is insufficient for the status of being *ṅit* with respect to the entire complex; rather, it renders that [complex] *ṅit*.
The purpose of this is so that whatever operation applies to what is *ṅit* may take place, but whatever operation applies to what is *ṅit* [as a suffix] may not occur.
(P_1,1.6) For what purpose is this stated? [It is] so that *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions do not occur:
as in *ādīdhyanaṃ*, *ādīdhyakaḥ*.

Regarding the rule "āvevyanam" and "āvevyakaḥ": this *yoga* (rule) can be omitted. How so? Because the roots *dīdhī* and *vevī* pertain to the Vedic domain (*chandoviṣayatvāt*), and because the Veda follows what is observed (*dṛṣṭānuvidhitvāt*), as we see the presence of *guṇa* (vowel strengthening) in forms such as *adīdhet* and *adīdhayuḥ*, there is no prohibition [of *guṇa*]. [The reason is: "because *dīdhī* and *vevī* pertain to the Vedic domain. *Dīdhī* and *vevī* are Vedic; and because of following what is observed...

In the Vedic language (*chandas*), there is conformity with what is observed. Because the *guṇa* [strengthening] is seen in forms such as *adīdhet* and *adīdhayuḥ*, there is no prohibition [of it]. A prohibition that is purposeless is a "non-prohibition" (*apratiṣedha*).
