In the case of the *daśarājña* (the battle of the ten kings), this would be a suitable example:
*adīdhet*. However, this is unsuitable:
*adīdhayuḥ*. This guna substitution in the *jus* suffix is introduced within the scope of the prohibition.

Just as that [rule] "na kṅiti" sublates the prohibition [of guṇa], so too does it sublate this one as well. This is not a fault. The rule "guṇaḥ jasi" (guṇa before *jus*), being introduced within the scope of the prohibition, sublates only a prohibition of the same class. And what is a prohibition of the same class? One that depends on the affix (*pratyayāśraya*). But this [prohibition regarding *jus*] depends on the base (*prakṛtyāśraya*).

Alternatively, that which has not yet come into operation cannot be sublated. And the prohibition "not before *kṅ*" has not yet come into operation when the rule "there is *guṇa* before *jus*" is introduced; however, this [present] rule applies both when it has come into operation and when it has not. If, then, this rule were not introduced, how would one account for *dīdhyat*? *Dīdhyat* is derived through the transposition (*vyatyaya*) of the *śyan* suffix. Thus, *dīdhyat*.

This *śyan* will occur by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). Furthermore, the mention of *iṭ* could also have been omitted. How so? [In the case of] *akaṇiṣam*, *araṇiṣam*, *kaṇitā śvaḥ*, and *raṇitā śvaḥ*: since the word *iṭ* is already present in the rule *ārdhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ*, the repetition of the mention of *iṭ* [in the present rule] serves to indicate that this *iṭ* is not subject to augmentation.

The purpose is that only what is desired should occur, and whatever else might result should not. But what else results? A *guṇa* [substitution]. If a restriction (*niyama*) is made, then from the desiderative stem *pipaṭhiṣati*, the form *pipaṭhīḥ* (without the suffix) would not obtain the lengthening of the vowel. This is not a fault, because it is the operation pertaining to a *prakṛti* (*āṅga*) that is restricted, and this [lengthening] does not pertain to a *prakṛti*. Alternatively, the lengthening is not yet established (*asiddha*). Because it is not established, [the rule does not apply].
There will be no restriction (*niyama*).
Regarding the term *anantarāḥ* ("immediately preceding"), how is this to be understood?
Does this mean that there is no interval between these [sounds], or that those which are in between them do not exist? And what follows from this?

If it is understood as "there is no interval between these," then the designation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) would not apply to the word *apsu*, as in *ap-su*; for indeed, an interval exists here. On the other hand, if it is understood as "those which are in between them do not exist" [then the designation applies].

Thus, there is no fault. Let it be as there is no fault. Or rather, let it be that there is no interval (*antaram*) between these [sounds]. But has it not been stated that in the case of *avagraha*, the designation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) does not apply—as in *ap-su* and *apsu*—since an interval indeed exists here? No, there is neither a fault nor a purpose [for this objection].

(P_1,1.7.2) Regarding the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), the mention of "together" (*saha*) must be made, as is done elsewhere. In the definition of conjunction, it should be stated: "Consonants that are contiguous are a conjunction when they occur together. What is the purpose? [It is] for those that have occurred together.

The designation *saṃyoga* (conjunction) should apply to [groups of] two or more, so that it does not apply to each individual consonant, as is the case elsewhere. Just as elsewhere, wherever one intends for a grammatical operation to apply to things that occur together, there the word "together" (*saha*) is employed. For example:

*saha supā* ("with a nominal suffix") and *ubhe abhyastam saha* ("both [halanta and vowel] are called *abhyasta* when they occur together"). What would happen if the designation *saṃyoga* were applied to each individual consonant? In this case, [the form] *niryāyāt* [would be incorrect].

Otherwise, the substitution of *e* would undesirably apply in the case of *nirvāyāt* due to its being preceded by a conjunct consonant; and here in *saṃhṛṣīṣṭa*, the augment *iṭ* would undesirably apply according to the rule *ṛtaśca saṃyogādeḥ*; and here in *saṃhriyate*, the *guṇa* substitution would undesirably apply according to the rule *artisṛyūṭyūtām*.

In this case, in *dṛṣat* and *karoti*, and *samit* and *karoti*, the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would undesirably apply. And here, in *śaktā* and *vastā*, the elision of the *sk* and *k* sounds at the beginning of a conjunct (*skoḥ saṃyogādyor lopaḥ*) would undesirably apply. And here, in *niryātaḥ* and *nirvātaḥ*, the substitution of *ṇ* for the final *t* of a root ending in *yaṇ* that begins with a conjunct (*saṃyogāder ātaḥ dhātoḥ yaṇvato niṣṭhāyām ṇatvam*) would undesirably apply. This is not a fault. As for what was said first regarding *niryāyāt*:

[Otherwise], if [the rule were interpreted as] "or for another [consonant] beginning with a conjunct," the substitution of *et* (e) would undesirably apply to *nirvāyāt*. It is not understood in this way—that "saṃyogādi" means "that which has a conjunct as its initial element.
How then? "Saṃyogādi" means "that which has two conjuncts as its initial elements," [as in the case of] "saṃyogādeḥ.
In this manner, first of all, the entire objection regarding the suffix *āṅ* is avoided. Furthermore, as for what is said regarding "dṛṣat" here...

[If it were argued that] in *karoti* and *samit*, the rule "there is elision of what ends in a conjunct" (*saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*) would apply—this is not so. It is not understood thus: "that which has a conjunct at its end is 'ending in a conjunct' (*saṃyogāntam*)," [and then] "of that which ends in a conjunct. How, then? "That which has two conjuncts at its ends is 'ending in a conjunct' (*saṃyogāntam*)."

Regarding the rule *saṃyogāntasya*: as for what was said—that here in the words *śaktāḥ* and *vastāḥ*, the elision (*lopa*) [of the final consonant] would apply by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca*—it is not understood in that way. It is not [understood] as "the two *saṃyogas* are at the beginning [of the word], thus *saṃyogādī*; [the rule applies to] those two *saṃyogādī*s. How, then? It is understood as "the beginnings of the two *saṃyogas* are *saṃyogādī*; [the rule applies to] those two *saṃyogādī*s. As for what was also said regarding the word *niryātaḥ* here...

[Objection: It would follow that the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* for the *t* of the suffix *niṣṭhā*—namely, "the *t* of a root ending in a semivowel (*yaṇ*) preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) or the letter *ā*"—would apply [undesirably] to [the root] *nirvāta*. [Reply: It is not understood in this way: that "this is a *saṃyogādi* (beginning with a conjunct) which has a *saṃyoga* as its initial element. How then? It is understood that "this is a *saṃyogādi* which has two conjuncts (*saṃyogau*) as its initial elements," [and thus the rule applies to] "that which begins with a *saṃyoga*. [Question: How can the designation *saṃyoga* apply to each individual [consonant]? [Answer: Because the completion of the sentence [defining the term] occurs for each one individually.
It has been observed that, for example, the technical designations *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* apply to each [element] individually. But is there not also this illustrative example:

"the completion of a sentence occurs with respect to a collective"? For instance, in the case of the command, "Let the Gargas be fined one hundred," kings who desire gold do not fine them individually. This being the case, here is the illustrative example.
If it is said that [the designation applies] individually (*pratyekam*) in that [previous rule], then here too the mention of "together" (*saha*) should be made. Alternatively,
if in that case the designations of *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* occur individually even without the expression "individually," then here too there is no purpose in mentioning "together."

186–190. Now, where there is a series of many [consonants] forming an *ānantarya* (immediate succession), does the designation of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) apply to every pair of two, or rather without distinction? And what is the distinction here? [Objection: There is the elision of the initial consonant of a conjunction (*saṃyogādilopa*) in the case of the root *masj-* when it occurs as a whole; this elision of the initial of a conjunction is not established for *masj-* in its entirety. Thus, [the forms] *maṅktā* and *maṅktum* would not be correct. Furthermore, in the case of *nirgle-yāt*, [the same fault would apply].
In *nirglāyāt*, *nirmleyāt*,
and *nirmlāyāt*, the substitution of *e* (by the rule *vā anyasya saṃyogādeḥ*) does not apply. And here [in the following example], *saṃsvariṣīṣṭa*.

In the case of *ṛtaḥ ca saṃyogādeḥ*, the augment *iṭ* would not apply. And here, in *saṃsvaryate*, the rule *arti-saṃyogādyoḥ* would prevent the *guṇa* substitution from applying. And here, in *gomān karoti* and *yavamān karoti*, the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* would prevent the elision of the final consonant from applying. And here, in *nirglānaḥ*...

In the case of *nirmlānaḥ*, the rule *saṃyogāder ātaḥ dhātoḥ yaṇvataḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.43) prescribing the substitution of *ṇ* for the *t* of the suffix *niṣṭhā* would not apply. Well then, let it be that a "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) consists of two [consonants] at a time. If it is argued that a conjunction consists of two consonants, then reduplication (*dvirvacana*) would not be established. For example: one desires Indra → *indrīyati*; from *indrīyati*, the desiderative suffix *san*: [indriyi-sa].

In *indidrīyiṣati*, because of the rule "the first elements of a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) beginning with *n* or *d* are not reduplicated," the doubling of the letter *d* does not occur. [Objection: This fault does not arise. [Question: For what reason? [Answer: Because it is a prescription regarding vowels (*ajvidhi*). The rule "the first elements of a consonant cluster beginning with *n* or *d* are not reduplicated" is stated [in reference to consonants], but the term "beginning with a vowel" (*ajādeḥ*) continues to apply [from the previous sūtra]. Now, whether the designation of "consonant cluster" (*saṃjñā*) applies to many [consonants] or even to two, [the result remains the same].
Is this [definition] understood by means of this much of the sūtra, or must further sūtra be composed for one of the two positions?
He says: "It is understood. How so? First, when the technical term *saṃyoga* applies to many [consonants], then the analysis (*vigraha*) will be made thus:
"those for whom there is no interval" (*avidyamānam antaram eṣām*). When it applies to each pair of two, then the analysis will be made thus: [“those between whom there is no interval”].

"Because there is nothing existing between them. Does something exist or not exist between two [sounds]? Even so, it would follow that the designation applies only to many [sounds]. For those which you point out with the genitive case, there should be no occurrence [of the rule] when they are separated by another. Let it be, then, that the designation applies to the aggregate. But was it not said that, if it applied to the aggregate, there would be the elision of the *saṃyoga* and other [initial sounds]?

Regarding the objection "there would be *masji*": this is not a fault. This will be explained: "The letter *m* preceding the final letter of the root *masj* is designated as *mit* for the purpose of the elision of the *anuṣaṅga* (the nasal) and the initial of the *saṃyoga*. Alternatively, the technical term *saṃyoga* shall be understood without distinction, applying to both two letters and many. In that case, the elision will occur based on that designation of *saṃyoga* which applies to two letters. As for what was said regarding *nirgleyāt* here:
In *nirglāyāt*, *nirmleyāt*,

and *nirmlāyāt*, the substitution of *e* (by the rule *vā anyasya saṃyogādeḥ*) does not apply; therefore, we shall qualify the "consonant cluster" (*saṃyoga*) by means of the *aṅga* (the verbal base).

Regarding the rule *aṅgasya saṃyogādeḥ* ("of a stem beginning with a conjunct"): thus, first of all, everything concerning the stem (*aṅga*) has been resolved. As for what is said here—that in the cases *gomān karoti* and *yavamān karoti*, the elision (*lopa*) of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*) does not apply—it is because we shall qualify "conjunct" by means of the word "word" (*pada*). That is, [the rule applies to] a word-final conjunct (*padasya saṃyogāntasya*). Furthermore, as for what is said here regarding *nirglānaḥ*:

Regarding the form *nirmlānaḥ*, the rule stating that the *niṣṭhā* suffix receives the nasal substitute (*ṇatva*) after a root beginning with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādi*) and ending in a vowel followed by a semi-vowel (*yaṇvat*) would not apply. Therefore, we shall qualify the term "beginning with a conjunct" (*saṃyogādi*) by means of the word "root" (*dhātu*). That is to say: "after a root beginning with a conjunct. (Pāṇini 8.2.43). [The sūtra] states "not separated by vowels" (*svarānantarhita*). Consonants that are not separated by vowels receive the technical designation "conjunct" (*saṃyoga*).

Thus it should be stated. What is the purpose? So that [the rule] does not apply to those that are separated. As in: *pacati panasam* ("he cooks the breadfruit"). But has it not been said that they must be "immediate" (*anantara*)? By that, it will not apply to those that are separated. However, immediacy is observed even in the case of what is separated; the word "immediate" is seen to apply even to what is separated. For example: [text follows].
These two villages are called "immediate" (*anantara*). Between them there are both rivers and mountains.

If, then, the word *anantara* applies even when there is an intervention, what would be the purpose of the expression "immediacy" (*ānantarya*) now? If it is asked, "What is the purpose of the expression 'immediacy'?", it is for the sake of excluding the case of a single [consonant]. For a single consonant (*hal*) [would otherwise receive] the technical designation of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*).

"Let it not be so. Furthermore, what would happen if the designation *saṃyoga* were applied to a single consonant? [In forms such as] *iyeṣa* and *uvoṣa*, the suffix *ām* would undesirably apply by the rule "after a root beginning with *ij* and having a heavy vowel (*gurumat*), except for *ṛcch*" (*ijādeśca gurumato 'nṛcchaḥ*). [Response: "Or rather, there is no such fault, because of the intervention of a dissimilar element.
Indeed, this fault does not arise. Why? Because of the intervention of a dissimilar element. For in common usage, [a *saṃyoga*] consists of [consonants] of a similar class.

It becomes an intervening factor. But how is it known that in the world that which is of a different kind acts as an intervening factor? For instance, someone asks another: "Are these two [houses] in immediate proximity? He replies: "They are not in immediate proximity; there is a *vṛṣala* family between them. What, then, is the reason that in some cases that which is of a different kind [acts as an intervention]?

In some cases it does not act as an interposer; for indeed, only that which is of a different class acts as an interposer. How so? [In the expression] "these two villages are contiguous" (*anantarau*). This word *grāma* has many meanings.
It refers to a collection of houses, as in "the village is burned. It refers to the enclosure of a fence, as in "he goes to the village."

It has entered; it exists among humans. For example: "the village has gone," or "the village has come. It exists in the wilderness, together with its boundaries and its open spaces. For example: "the village has been acquired. Having observed that which exists in the wilderness, together with its boundaries and its open spaces, this [expression] is employed:
"These two villages are adjacent. For in every case, that which is of a different kind acts as an intervening element.
(P_1,1.8.1) What is this "spoken through the mouth and nose"? The mouth and the nose together constitute "mouth-and-nose" (*mukhanāsika*). Mouth-and-nose...

This [term] *mukhanāsikāvacanaḥ* refers to that which has speech through both the mouth and the nose. If this is so, one would expect it to be *mukhanāsikavacanaḥ*. [To this we reply: the lengthening of the vowel will occur by virtue of a formal exception (*nipātana*). Alternatively, it means that its speech (*āvacana*) is through the mouth and the nose; thus it is *mukhanāsikāvacanaḥ*. What is this "speech" (*āvacana*)? It is slight speech (*īṣadvacana*). That is to say, some portion is speech through the mouth, and some portion is speech through the nose.

Alternatively, his organ of speech (*vacana*) is the nose together with the mouth; thus he is "one whose organ of speech is the mouth and nose" (*mukhanāsikāvacana*). Or else, his organ of speech is the nose associated with the mouth; thus he is "one whose organ of speech is the mouth and nose" (*mukhanāsikāvacana*).

193–194. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "mouth" (*mukha*)? If it were stated merely as "an *anunāsika* is that which is uttered through the nose," it would follow that the term applies only to the *yamas* and the *anusvāras*. However, when the mention of "mouth" is made, no such fault occurs. Next, for what purpose is the mention of "nose" (*nāsikā*)? If it were stated merely as "an *anunāsika* is that which is uttered through the mouth," [the term] would apply to the [consonants] *ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa*, etc.

[Otherwise] this undesirable consequence would follow. However, when the mention of "nose" (*nāsikā*) is made, no fault arises. The mention of "mouth" (*mukha*) could then be omitted. By what means, then, would there be [the application of the rule] for those words that denote both? By the principle of the "dweller in the palace" (*prāsādavāsin*). For example:
some are dwellers in the palace, some are dwellers on the ground, and some are dwellers in both. Those who are dwellers in the palace...
Those who dwell in palaces are included by the term "palace-dwellers"; those who dwell on the ground are included by the principle of "ground-dwellers";

and those who dwell in both are included by both the term "palace-dwellers" and the principle of "ground-dwellers. Likewise, here too, some are mouth-sounders, some are nose-sounders, and some are both-sounders. Among them, those who are mouth-sounders...

Those which are designated by the term "mouth" are included by the mention of "mouth"; those which are designated by the term "nose" are included by the mention of "nose"; and those which are designated by both are indeed included by both the mention of "mouth" and the mention of "nose. This would be established for those designated by both;
however, it would also apply to the *yama*s and the *anusvāra*s. This is not a fault, nor is there any need [to state it].

But this results in mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). What is this mutual dependence? There must be a designation (*saṃjñā*) for that which already exists as an *anunāsika* (nasalized sound), and by means of that designation, the sound is made to become an *anunāsika*. Thus, it becomes a case of mutual dependence.

Furthermore, operations that involve mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) are not logically tenable. This was stated regarding the technical name *anunāsika* (nasalized) when there is mutual dependence:

"But [the definition] is established because words are eternal. Words are eternal. Since words are eternal, the designation (*saṃjñā*) is applied to an existing nasalized sound; the nasalized sound is not brought into being by the designation. If, then, words are eternal, for what purpose [is this rule]?

The treatise (*śāstra*). If it is asked, "For what purpose is the treatise?", it is established because it is a means of exclusion (*nivartaka*). The treatise is a means of exclusion. How so? The *āṅ* [prefix] has been taught without distinction as being non-nasal (*ananunāsika*). Consequently, the notion that it is non-nasal would apply everywhere. In that regard, its exclusion is effected by this [treatise]. [Namely,] in the Vedic language (*chandas*), when a vowel (*ac*) follows, the non-nasal *āṅ* [is excluded].
In the context of grammatical derivation (*prasaṅge*), a nasalized sound (*anunāsika*) is correct.

(Pāṇini 1.1.9.1) *Tulya* means "equal to" (*tulayā sammitam*). "Oral effort" (*āsyaprayatna*) refers to both the mouth (*āsya*) and the effort (*prayatna*). [The compound] *tulyāsyam* [means "having an equal oral [location and effort]"].

And that which possesses an equal effort receives the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous). But what is "the mouth" (*āsya*)? The mouth in common usage is that which extends from the lips up to the throat-joint (*kākalaka*). How, then, is it called "the mouth"? It is called "the mouth" because one emits sounds (*varṇa*) by means of it; or alternatively, it is called "the mouth" because food flows (*āsyandate*) into it. Now, what is "effort" (*prayatna*)? Effort is the act of striving (*prayatana*), derived from the prefix *pra-* [with the root *yat*].
The suffix *naṅ* is used here to denote the state (*bhāva*) of the root *yat*. If "mouth" (*āsya*) refers to the ordinary mouth, what is the purpose of mentioning the mouth?
For that [ordinary mouth] is common to all. This will be explained later:
the mention of the "mouth" serves as a qualification of the effort (*prayatna*).

(P_1,1.9.2) Regarding the technical designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous), there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to sounds produced in different locations because their effort (*prayatna*) is common. In the case of the designation *savarṇa*, there is over-extension to sounds produced in different locations, such as *ja, ba, ga, ḍa, da, śa*. What is the reason? Because their effort is common.

For their effort (*prayatna*) is indeed the same. [The rule] "But it is established that those [sounds] produced in the mouth with the same place and effort are *savarṇa*"—this is established. How so? It should be stated: "Those whose place and effort in the mouth are the same receive the designation *savarṇa*.
Even so, what is the purpose of including the term "in the mouth" (*āsya*)? For that [effort] is the same for all. [Answer: It is a qualifier of the effort.

This is the inclusion [of these qualities]. For there are external efforts (*bāhya-prayatna*) belonging to the mouth; they are abandoned here. Whether those [external efforts] exist or do not exist, the designation of *savarṇa* (homogeneous) is established. What, then, are they? They are: openness (*vivāra*), closure (*saṃvāra*), aspiration (*śvāsa*), sonority (*nāda*), voicedness (*ghoṣavat*), voicelessness (*aghoṣatā*), weak breath (*alpaprāṇatā*), and strong breath (*mahāprāṇatā*). Among them, the first and second letters of the classes (*varga*) have an open throat (*vivṛtakaṇṭha*) and are characterized by aspiration (*śvāsānupradāna*).

The unvoiced [consonants] are such that some are of weak aspiration (alpaprāṇa) and others are of strong aspiration (mahāprāṇa). The third and fourth [classes of consonants] have a closed glottis, are produced with resonance (nādānupradāna), and are voiced (ghoṣavat). Among them, some are of weak aspiration and others are of strong aspiration. Just as it is with the thirds, so it is with the fifths, with the exception of nasality (ānunāsikya). Nasality is an additional quality for them. Even so, the designation "homogeneous" (savarṇasañjñā) does not apply to the sound *a* (avarṇa).

What is the reason? For the place of articulation for the sound *a* is outside the mouth. Some maintain that the sound *a* has its place of articulation throughout the entire mouth. Even so, the designation "those whose place of articulation within the mouth is the same" would not be possible. [Reply: The designation will be established by treating it as if it possessed a specific designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). Thus, it is established.

In that case, the Sūtra would be contradicted. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. But was it not stated that in the definition of *savarṇa* (homogeneous), there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding sounds produced in different locations because their articulatory effort (*prayatna*) is common? This is not a fault. For "mouth" (*āsya*) is not used here in its ordinary sense. What then? It is a derivative term (*taddhitānta*): "that which belongs to the mouth."

That which exists in the mouth is "oral" (*āsya*). [The suffix] *yat* is applied after a word denoting a part of the body. But what, then, is that which exists in the mouth? It is both the place of articulation (*sthāna*) and the instrument of articulation (*karaṇa*).

Even so, effort (*prayatna*) remains unspecified. And yet, effort is indeed specified. How so? For effort is not the act of striving; rather, effort is the initiation of striving. If it is the initiation...

If it is argued that the effort [of pronunciation] is the same, even so, the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) would apply between the vowel *a* and the diphthongs *e* and *o*. For these two consist of closely joined phonemes (*praśliṣṭavarṇa*).
In that case, the designation *savarṇa* would apply between the vowel *a* and the diphthongs *ai* and *au*. For these two have the vowel *a* pronounced more opened (*vivṛtatara*).

Then, the designation *savarṇa* would apply only between these two [diphthongs] themselves. But these two do not have the same place of articulation (*tulyasthāna*), [as they differ] regarding the acute accent (*udātta*) and the other [vowel qualities].

In that case, the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) would not apply, because accents such as the acute (*udātta*) and so forth are non-differentiators. Alternatively, what is the point of this effort, namely the exertion (*yatna*)? Exertion is simply the act of striving (*prayatana*). And that very [act] is the "effort" (*prayatna*) ending in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*). We shall rely upon that which is common [to all]. [Question: When there is a difference? [Answer: He says, "when there is. For it is precisely when there is a difference [that we must rely on the commonality].

The designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) must apply. Why is this so? Because the designation *savarṇa* is based on difference. For if it were to apply where everything is identical, the rule for the *savarṇa* designation would be purposeless. If, then, the *savarṇa* designation applies because there is something in common despite the existence of difference—as in the case of the letters ś and ch, or ṣ and ṭh—[then it follows].
The designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) would apply to the letters *sa* and *tha*, for among these, everything else is identical except for the articulatory organ (*karaṇa*).

If that is so, then "effort" (*prayatna*) is simply the term ending in a secondary suffix (*taddhita*), and "oral" (*āsya*) is its qualifier; thus, it is not a *dvandva* compound meaning "the oral and the effort" (*āsyam ca prayatnaś ca āsyaprayatnam*). What then? It is a three-word *bahuvrīhi* compound.
"The effort in the mouth (*āsye prayatnaḥ*) of these is equal. Alternatively, it is a *tatpuruṣa* first, followed by a *bahuvrīhi*:
"equal in the mouth" is *tulyāsyaḥ*; [the compound means] "those whose effort in the mouth is equal" (*tulyāsyaḥ prayatna eṣām*). Or else, it is a *tatpuruṣa* last, followed by a *bahuvrīhi*.

"Effort in the mouth" means effort within the oral cavity; "those whose effort in the mouth is equal" refers to those [sounds] for whom the articulatory effort in the mouth is identical. (Pāṇini 1.1.9.3) KA_I,62.15-26 Ro_I,174.10-180.10; T_1,34.14-35.12; J_1,108.1-109.10; C_1,108.1-109.10; B_1,108.1-109.10; W_1,108.1-109.10; M_1,108.1-109.10; S_1,108.1-109.10; P_1,108.1-109.10; K_1,108.1-109.10; H_1,108.1-109.10; N_1,108.1-109.10; A_1,108.1-109.10;

202–203. Regarding the phrase *tasya tasya* (of that, of that), it should indeed be stated. What is the purpose? It is so that whatever has the same place of articulation (*sthāna*) and effort (*prayatna*) as something else shall have the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) with respect to that very thing; it should not be the case that what has the same place of articulation and effort as one thing should have the designation *savarṇa* with respect to another thing. [Objection: The word *tasya* need not be stated, because the authority of the explicit statement [in the sūtra] is sufficient. [Response: The word *tasya* must be stated. [Otherwise,] what has the same place of articulation and effort as one thing...
Why does the designation *savarṇa* not apply to one [sound] with respect to another? Because of the authority of the statement;

that is, by virtue of the force of the statement establishing the *savarṇa* designation. For if a sound that possesses the same place and effort of articulation were to be the *savarṇa* designation for another, the statement establishing the *savarṇa* designation would be purposeless. Or rather, it is similar to the case of correlative terms (*sambandhiśabda*). It is like correlative terms.
Or again, this is equivalent:

for example, [the expressions] "one should behave properly toward one's mother" and "one should serve one's father. It is not said "toward one's own mother" or "toward one's own father," because [the relationship] is understood through the connection [of the terms].

And this is understood: that "she who is someone's mother" and "he who is someone's father. Likewise here as well, in the rule *tulyāsyaprayatnaṃ savarṇam* ("that which has the same place and effort of articulation is homogeneous"), these two words are relative terms. Therefore, by virtue of their relationship, it must be understood:
with respect to whatever [sound] something has the same place and effort of articulation, that [latter] receives the technical designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) with respect to that [former].

The rule for homogeneous (*savarṇa*) status regarding the phonemes *ṛ* and *ḷ*. The designation of homogeneity (*savarṇasañjñā*) must be prescribed for the phonemes *ṛ* and *ḷ*. [Examples: *hotṛ*, *ḷkāraḥ*.

The *ḷkāra* is the *hotṛ*. What is the purpose? So that the lengthening prescribed by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* may occur. This is not a necessary purpose, for he will state this: "In the case of lengthening with a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇadīrghatva*), there is the statement 'optionally *ṛ* when *ṛ* follows' and 'optionally *ḷ* when *ḷ* follows'. Thus it shall apply where there is a homogeneous vowel; but let it not apply here: *dadhi*.

The sound *ḷ*, honey, the sound *ḷ*. Regarding this [rule] concerning the long vowel of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇadīrgha*) which states "before *ṛ*" (*ṛti*), I shall state it as "before *ṛ*" (*ṛtaḥ*). Then, [it applies] before *ḷ* (*ḷti*).
And [if one were to say] "or *ḷ* becomes *lḷ*," it would be exactly the same as saying "from *ṛ*. Therefore, that need not be stated. Yet, it must necessarily be stated:

"A vowel (*ac*) having the duration of *ū* is designated as short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), or protracted (*pluta*). Now, neither the sound *ṛ* nor the sound *ḷ* is a vowel (*ac*). Regarding the sound *ṛ*...

And I shall state that the letter *ḷ* possesses the status of a vowel (*actva*). That must necessarily be stated so that the protracted (*pluta*) form may occur: *hotṛ*, *ṛkāraḥ*, *hotṝkāraḥ*, *hotṛ*.

The sound *ḷ*, the sound *hotṛ*, and the sound *hotṛ* (with protracted length). What, then, is superior here? The statement regarding the technical designation of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇasañjñā*) alone is superior; [for it results in] longness.
For this indeed becomes established. Moreover, when the phoneme *ṛ* is mentioned, the inclusion of the phoneme *ḷ* is also present. As it occurs here:
"before *ṛ*, [the substitution of] *akaḥ" [applies], as in *khaṭva-ṛśyaḥ*.
The *māla-ṛśya* also includes this: *khaṭva*, the letter *ḷ*,
and *māla*.
Regarding the letter *ḷ*: according to Āpiśali, [the substitution of *ṛ* for *ḷ*] occurs before a word ending in *su*; thus, one says *uparkārīyati* or *upārkārīyati*.
This also becomes established:
*upalkārīyati*, *upālkārīyati*. If, then, the inclusion of the sound *ḷ* is present when the sound *ṛ* is mentioned—as in the rule *uḥ aṇ raparaḥ*—then [the following applies].

The substitution of *ra* for *ḷ* would also apply to the sound *ḷ*. I shall state that the substitution of *la* for *ḷ* will take place; and that must necessarily be stated for the sake of a specific injunction in the absence of the technical term *savarṇa* (homogeneous). That same rule, when the term *savarṇa* exists, will serve to block the substitution of *ra*. In this case, then, the inclusion of the letter *ṛ* is required by the rule "after *ra* and *ṣ*, *ṇa* replaces *na* within the same word," as in the example *mātṝṇām*.

[The rule] "of the ancestors" (pitṝṇām) is for this very purpose. Consequently, it would also apply here in the case of *kḷpyamānaṃ paśya*. Now, even if the designation of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*) does not exist, why does [the substitution] not occur here in *prakḷpyamānaṃ paśya*? I shall state that [the substitution] does not occur when there is an intervention by *c*, *ṭ*, *t*, *t*, *l*, *ś*, *ṣ*, or *s*. Another says:

"I shall state that [the substitution of *ṇ*] does not occur when there is an intervention by any of the three middle classes [of consonants] or by *l* and *s*. Furthermore, since parts of phonemes (*varṇaikadeśa*) are included under the term 'phoneme' (*varṇagrahaṇa*), the prohibition will apply based on the *l* sound that is part of the phoneme *ḷ*.
If this is so, there is no need for the mention of the phoneme *ṛ* in the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* after *r* and *ṣ*, because parts of phonemes are already included under the term 'phoneme'."
Regarding the statement "they are grasped": since that *ṛ* sound possesses a *repha*, the substitution of *ṇ* will take place based upon it.

(Pāṇini 1.1.10) In the prohibition concerning vowels (*ac*) and consonants (*hal*), there is a prohibition of the letter *śa*, because it belongs to the category of both vowels and consonants (*ajjhaltvāt*). [In the rule] regarding the prohibition of vowels and consonants, [the letter *śa*...]

Regarding the letter *ś*, there arises the contingency of prohibiting its designation as a *savarṇa*. What is the reason? Because it possesses the nature of both a vowel (*ac*) and a consonant (*hal*). For this *ś* is indeed both a vowel and a consonant. How, then, does it have the nature of a vowel? It has the nature of a vowel because the vowel *i* includes the *ś* by virtue of the rule for the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrahaṇa*). It has the nature of a consonant because it is taught among the consonants. What is the fault in that? In that case, there would be the fault of the elision of a homogeneous sound (*savarṇalopa*).

There is a fault. In that case, there is a fault regarding the elision of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇalopa*). In the expression *paraśśatāni kāryāṇi*, the elision prescribed by the rule *jharaḥ jhari savarṇe* would not apply. [Objection: This is established because it is not a vowel (*anactva*). [Reply: This is established. How? Because it is not a vowel. How is it not a vowel? The articulation (*karaṇa*) of the stops (*sparśa*) is complete contact (*spṛṣṭa*); that of the semivowels (*antaḥstha*) is slight contact (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*); and that of the sibilants (*ūṣman*) is open (*vivṛta*).

The word "slightly" (*īṣat*) is understood [from the previous rule]. [The rule states: "The vowels are *vivṛta* (open). The word "slightly" is no longer applicable. Or rather, it is established by the incompleteness of the sentence (*vākyāparisamāpteḥ*). Or rather, this is established because the sentence is not yet complete. What is meant by "because the sentence is not yet complete"? First, there is the instruction (*upadeśa*) of the phonemes (*varṇa*). Subsequent to the instruction is the designation (*saṃjñā*) as *it*. Subsequent to the *it*-designation is the rule: "The first [phoneme], together with the last..."

*Itā* is a pratyāhāra (abbreviation). The designation of *savarṇa* (homogeneous) occurs subsequent to the pratyāhāra. Subsequent to the *savarṇa* designation, in the rule *aṇ udit savarṇasya ca apratyayaḥ*, there is the mention of *savarṇa*. By this entire collection of statements, there is the inclusion of homogeneous sounds elsewhere. And here, the vowel *i* does not include the letter *ś*. Just as...
In that case, if the letter *i* does not include the letter *ś*, it likewise would not include the letter *ī*. What fault is there in that? [Consider the example:

*kumārī īhate* → *kumārīhate*. The rule for the long vowel of homogeneous sounds (*akaḥ savarṇadīrghatvam*) would not apply. This is not a fault. Because of this inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* in the rule "a long vowel replaces a homogeneous sound following a short *a*" (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*), the letter *i* includes the letter *ī*, but it does not include the letter *ś*.
It does not include it. Another says:

"In the prohibition concerning vowels (*ac*) and *hal* consonants, there is a prohibition of the letter *ś*. Because of its being an *ajhal* [neither vowel nor *hal*]. When there is a prohibition concerning vowels and *hal* consonants, the designation of homogeneous (*savarṇa*) for the letter *ś* with respect to the letter *ś* would result in being prohibited. What is the reason? Because of its being an *ajhal*. For the letter *ś* is indeed a vowel (*ac*)."

And furthermore: how, first of all, is it a vowel (*ac*)? Because the letter *i* includes the letter *ś* by virtue of the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrahaṇa*), it is a vowel. It is a consonant (*hal*) because it is taught as such among the consonants. What is the fault in that? In that case, there is a fault regarding the elision of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇalopa*). There is a fault regarding the elision of homogeneous sounds in this instance: in the expression *paraśśatāni kāryāṇi*, the elision prescribed by the rule *jharaḥ jhari savarṇe* would not apply.

[The objection: "It is established because it lacks a vowel (*anactvāt*). [The response: This is established. How? Because it lacks a vowel. How is there a lack of a vowel? Either because the sentence is not yet complete (*vākyāparisamāpteḥ*), or because the non-completion of the sentence has already been stated. In this view, the word "or" (*vā*) remains unestablished; however, this [objection] is indeed established. How? Let there be the designation of *śakāra* as homogeneous with *śakāra*, or let there not be. But was it not said:
“There are more than a hundred grammatical operations [to be performed]. [If this were so,] by the rule *jharaḥ jhari savarṇe* (P. 8.4.65), elision would not apply. “Let there be no elision.
“But surely there is a difference: when there is elision, it has two *śa*s; when there is no elision, it has three *śa*s. “There is no difference.
Even when there is no elision, it has exactly two *śa*s. “How so? “Because the doubling is optional (*vibhāṣā dvirvacanam*). “Even so, there is still a difference.”

If the elision were non-existent, it would sometimes have two *śakāra*s and sometimes three *śakāra*s; if the elision were present, it would always have exactly two *śakāra*s. How then could this difference not occur? It would so occur if the elision were obligatory (*nitya*). But that elision is optional (*vibhāṣā*); let it be such that there is no difference.

For what purpose is the designation *pragṛhya* prescribed for vowels such as *ī* that are followed by *t* (*tapara*)? It is so that, according to the rule *taparas tatkālasya*, there may be the inclusion of homogeneous (*savarṇa*) vowels of that same duration. Of which [vowels]? Of those that are acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and circumflex (*svarita*). There is [a need for this].

This is the purpose [of the rule]. But what then? The designation *pragṛhya* does not apply to the protracted (*pluta*) vowels. What is the reason? Because they do not share the same duration (*atatkālatvāt*). For the protracted vowels do not have that same duration. The protracted vowel is not established (*asiddha*). Because it is not established, they would indeed [otherwise] have that same duration. The protracted vowel is established in the context of vowel coalescence (*svarasandhi*). How is it known that the protracted vowel is established in the context of vowel coalescence?

Thus [it is said]. Since this [sūtra] teaches the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of a *pluta* vowel by means of the rule "pluta-pragṛhyā aci," how does it serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? For an operation must apply to that which already exists as the subject of the operation. What is the purpose of this indication?

It is that the phrase "from what is not a *pluta*, before what is not a *pluta*" need not be stated. What follows from this, given that the *pluta* is established in the context of vowel coalescence (*svarasandhi*)?

In the formulation of technical names (*saṃjñā*), [the rule] is not established. Because it is not established, only those [sounds] belonging to its own time [period] occur. And in the formulation of technical names, it is established. How so? The rules for technical names and interpretive rules (*paribhāṣā*) are operative at the time the operation [is to be applied]. Wherever there is an operation, there these rules should be seen as present. Thus, when the rule "a *pragṛhya* remains in its original form" is present, this [rule] "a dual ending consisting of *ī*, *ū*, or *e* is *pragṛhya*" is also present.

Thus [it is said]. But what, then, is the purpose of prescribing the *pragṛhya* designation for a protracted (*pluta*) vowel? [The answer is: so that the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) dependent on being a *pragṛhya* may occur. Let it not be so; it will be possible by the rule "a protracted vowel is [treated] as its original form" (*plutaḥ prakṛtyā*). It cannot be so; for a fault would arise when [the word] is present (*upasthite*). For the Teacher will indeed recite here: "it is as if it were not protracted when [the word] is present" (*aplutavad upasthite*).
That statement is for the purpose of prohibiting the *pluta* operation;

for if there were a prohibition of *pluta*, it would follow that the *pragṛhya-pluta* [operation] is also prohibited, since it is prescribed by another rule. Therefore, the designation *pragṛhya* must be desired for the *pluta* vowel so that the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) dependent upon the *pragṛhya* designation may occur. If, however—

If the designation *pragṛhya* were stated for long vowels that do not have a following *at* (i.e., are not followed by a vowel), even so, only the phoneme *e* would include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), while the phonemes *ī* and *ū* would not include theirs. Why? Because they are not *aṇ*. But if, on the other hand, the designation *pragṛhya* were stated for short vowels that do not have a following *at*, it could not be done in this way; for in that case, it would also undesirably apply here: *akurvahi*.

In this case [the rule] "akurvahi atra" applies. Therefore, it must be stated that the designation *pragṛhya* applies only to long vowels followed by *t* (tapara). And since it is being stated for long vowels, it does not apply to protracted (*pluta*) vowels. If that is so, what is the point of this effort [to establish a rule], given that it has already been established that "the *pluta* vowel is not subject to vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*)"? The *pluta* vowel is considered *asiddha* (unestablished). Because it is *asiddha*, only those [vowels] of its same duration [are affected].

[They] exist. How so? That which was stated as the indicator (*jñāpaka*)—namely, "pluta vowels and *pragṛhya* vowels [retain their original form] before a vowel"—is understood thus: "that which is about to become a *pluta* remains in its original form. How so? That which was stated as the purpose (*prayojana*)—namely, that it is formulated in the rule itself as "before a non-*pluta* vowel" (*aplutāt aplute*)—even so, that operation of the *pragṛhya* which is established [by the rule] does not apply to a *pluta* vowel.

[The rule] "an *a* that is not a *pragṛhya* becomes nasalized" [applies]. If that is so, what is the use of this principle that "technical definitions (*saṃjñā*) and interpretive rules (*paribhāṣā*) apply at the time of their operation"? Let it be that technical definitions and interpretive rules apply exactly as they are enunciated (*yathoddeśam*). In that case, this [rule regarding the nasalization] is not established [at the time of its operation].
Because it is not established, only those [operations] belonging to its own time occur.

(P_1,1.11.2) KA_I,67.3-68.7 Ro_I, 217-220 How, then, is this to be understood: that *īd* and so forth are the dual endings, or rather, that the dual ending which has *īd* and so forth at its beginning [is intended]? And what is the distinction here?

If it is argued that [the rule] "the dual endings *ī*, *ū*, and *e* are *pragṛhya*" applies to the final [sound], then the designation *pragṛhya* must be prescribed for the final [sound]. For example, in *pacete* and *pacethe*. [Objection: It will occur by virtue of the explicit statement [of the rule]. [Reply: There is a purpose for the explicit statement. What is it? As in *khaṭve*.

[Objection: Let it be that "the dual ending in *ī*, *ū*, or *ā*" [is what is meant]. [Response: If it is "ending in *ī*, *ū*, or *ā*," then the rule would apply to a single [word]. If it is "ending in *ī*, *ū*, or *ā*," then the designation *pragṛhya* must be prescribed for a single [word], as in *khaṭve* and *māle*. [Response: Or rather, this is not a fault. Why? Because of the principle of "treating a single entity as having both an initial and a final. According to the rule "a single entity is treated as having both an initial and a final," the designation will apply even to a single [word]. Or else, it is thus:

"Regarding the rule 'that which ends in *ī* etc., being dual-ended' (*īdādyantaṃ yad dvivacanāntam*): if it is argued that 'it refers to that which ends in *ī* etc., being dual-ended,' then a prohibition must be stated regarding elision (*luk*). [Otherwise, one would get] *kumāryor agāram*, [which should instead be] *kumāry-agāram*;
[and] *vadhvor agāram*."
*vadhvāgāram*. For this [word] is heard with the vowels *ī* and *ū* at its beginning and end, and it also becomes dual-ended by virtue of the technical designation of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*).

The mention of "meaning" (*arthagrahaṇa*) in the rule for the locative case is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the prohibition of the designation of the suffix. By the fact that the Teacher employs the mention of "meaning" in the rule *īdūtau ca saptamyarthe*, he indicates that [the suffixal status] does not apply in the matter of the designation of *pragṛhya*.

"It becomes a condition (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*). Well then, for the sake of providing an explanatory indication (*jñāpaka*), the mention of "meaning" (*artha*) should be made. It need not be made. We shall qualify the dual ending (*dvivacana*) by means of *ī*, *ā*, and so on; and through that dual ending qualified by *ī*, *ā*, etc., there will be an application of the rule regarding what ends in that (*tadanta-vidhi*).
That is to say: "that which is a dual ending ending in *ī*, *ā*, etc., [and] which itself ends in *ī*, *ā*, etc. Even so, in the case of *aśukle*...

In the case of *vastraśukle sampadyetām* and *śuklī āstām vastrai*, [the substitution of] *śī* would result here, because the dual ending beginning with *ī* (i.e., *au*) follows that which ends in *ī*, by virtue of the rule regarding the presence of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Even in this instance, the elision (*luk*) will occur before the substitution of *śī* has taken place. This is what must be considered here.

"Let there be elision (*luk*); let there be the substitution of *śī*. What should be done here? The substitution of *śī* [is applied] because it is subsequent (*paratvāt*). Elision (*luk*) is permanent (*nitya*), for it applies whether the substitution of *śī* has been made or not yet made. [But] elision is not permanent (*anitya*), for it applies when one thing has been made and another when it has not been made. A rule that applies to a different word-form (*śabdāntara*) is considered non-permanent; such is the case with the substitution of *śī*."

[The substitution of] *śī* is also non-eternal (*anitya*). For it does not apply once the elision (*luk*) has taken place. Between two non-eternal operations, the substitution of *śī* occurs by virtue of its being subsequent;
once *śī* has been applied, then the elision (*luk*) occurs. Even if, for some reason, the elision were eternal (*nitya*), there would still be a fault. This will be stated [later]:

"In the definition of a word (*pada-sañjñā*), the mention of 'end' is for the purpose of prohibiting the rule of 'inclusion of what ends with that' (*tadantavidhi*) when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned in other rules prescribing technical designations."
220–226. Regarding the designation *pragṛhya*: because that [substitution] is not established (*asiddha*), there is a prohibition of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) forms *ay* and *av*.

Since that substitution of *ī* and *ū* is not established when the *pragṛhya* designation applies, the single-substitute forms *ay* and *av* would occur. A prohibition of these must be stated. For example: *amī atra*.

"Amī āsate," "amū atra," "amū āsāte. But surely, by the force of the rule prescribing the *pragṛhya* designation, the substitutions *ay* and so forth will not occur? [Reply: This is for the sake of the specific statement [of the rule].
For this is already established. This cannot be obtained from the rule itself; indeed, there is another purpose for stating it. What is that?

It would be for the sake of that grammatical operation which applies to a *pragṛhya* when it is already established—namely, the rule "an *aṇ* that is not a *pragṛhya* becomes nasalized" (*aṇo 'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ*). A single purpose does not justify the commencement of a rule; if this were the only purpose, then [the rule] would have been stated right there.
One might say this: "Let there be a nasal substitute for a non-pragṛhya *a* [following] *adas*, except when it is *na*. Or rather, [one might argue] by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*):

"Either let the *pragṛhya* designation be applied, or let the *ay*-substitutes be applied; the *pragṛhya* designation will prevail through conflict. This conflict is not appropriate. For it is said that in a conflict, the subsequent rule prevails, yet the *pragṛhya* designation is the prior one.

The words beginning with *para* (the others) are *ayādi*. The designation *pragṛhya* will be applied to those [others]. Thus, a reversal of the order of the sūtras has been made. If that is so, then the designation *pragṛhya* applies only to the others. How? For the technical rules (*saṃjñā-paribhāṣā*) are operative at the time the operation (*kārya*) occurs; wherever the operation is, there the rule should be seen as present. When it is stated, "A *pragṛhya* remains in its original form" (*pragṛhyaḥ prakṛtyā*), this rule is understood to apply to the word *adas*.

[Objection: "Māt"—even so, this contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*) is improper. How so? For a contradiction consists in the application of two grammatical operations (*kārya*) [simultaneously]. And here, no single element is joined with two operations. [The rules are: "ec" [vowels] undergo the substitution of "ay" and so forth; "ī" and "ū" ending in a word-final syllable receive the designation *pragṛhya*. [Response: A contradiction does not necessarily consist only in the application of two operations. What then? It is also impossibility (*asambhava*). And that impossibility exists here.

What is this impossibility? The designation *pragṛhya*, while being established, subverts the *ayādi* substitutions; the *ayādi* substitutions, while being established, obstruct the cause of the *pragṛhya* designation. This is the impossibility.
When there is such an impossibility, a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is appropriate. Even so, the conflict is improper; for a conflict occurs only when both [rules] are present.

It occurs; however, in this case, neither the substitution of *ī* nor *ū* exists, nor is there the letter *m*. Both are unestablished (*asiddha*). But there is establishment by virtue of its basis (*āśrayāt siddhatva*), as in the case of the substitution of *ū* for *ru*. There will be establishment by virtue of its basis. For example, *ru* is established by virtue of its basis when the substitution of *ū* [is to occur]. What, then, is the reason that *ru* is established by virtue of its basis when the substitution of *ū* [is to occur], but not where...?

In that very context, the substitution of *ru* is established, and the substitution of *utva* is also stated there. But it cannot be so. For if *utva* were unestablished, the *ādguṇa* [rule] would not be established. Indeed, if *utva* were unestablished, the *ādguṇa* [rule] would fail to apply in cases such as *vṛkṣaḥ atra* and *plakṣaḥ atra*. Therefore, in that case, its established status must be accepted on account of its basis (*āśrayāt*). In that regard, it is established by virtue of its basis.

It will be so here as well. Alternatively, by virtue of the explicit mention of the term *pragṛhya*, the substitutes *ay* and so forth will not occur. Or else, a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: first, "of *adas*"; vowels beginning with *ī* belonging to *adas* receive the designation *pragṛhya*. Then, "after *m*" [is added]; vowels beginning with *ī* that follow *m* also receive the designation *pragṛhya*.
It is indeed *adas*. For what purpose is this separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*)? One [purpose] is for that which is already established, namely for the function of being a *pragṛhya*;

the other is for that which is not yet established. If so, would it not follow here as well in the cases *amuyā* and *amuyoḥ*? And what would happen if the designation *pragṛhya* were applied? The preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) would depend upon that *pragṛhya* designation.

It would follow [as an over-extension]. This fault does not apply; for *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) occurs within the context of word-final elements (*padānta*), and this [word] is not word-final. Even so, it would still apply in cases such as *amuke atra*. The term "dual number" (*dvivacana*) is understood [to carry over from the previous rule]. If "dual number" is understood to carry over, then it would not apply in the case of *amī atra*. In that case, then, the term "ending in /e/" (*edanta*) has been withdrawn. Or else:

He says: "This is the mother of *adas*. But neither the substitution of *ī* (īttva) nor the substitution of *u* (uttva) occurs there, nor does the letter *m*. We shall understand it thus: [the rule applies] to those words whose meaning is that of *adas*, such as those beginning with *ī*. Or rather, it has already been stated. What has been stated? It has been stated: "The substitutions of *ī* and *u* in *adas* are established when they occur before a vowel, when they are characterized by being outside the word (*bahiṣpada*), and when they are subject to the designation *pragṛhya*. In that case, there is a fault regarding the suffix *sak*. There is a fault regarding the letter *s* in that context.

[The objection: "It would follow [that the rule applies] here, in the case of *amuke*. [The response: Or rather, there is no such fault, because it is a qualifier of the term *grahaṇa*. What is the reason? Because it is a qualifier of the term *grahaṇa*. It is not the case that what ends in *ī*, *īd*, etc., is qualified by the mention of *māt*; rather, it is *ī*, *īd*, etc., that are qualified. [The meaning is: "those *ī*, *īd*, etc., which follow after *māt*."

(P_1,1.13) KA_I,70.5-10 Ro_I, 226-227 Why does [the rule] not apply here in the cases *kāśe*, *kuśe*, and *vaṃśe*? Because of the mention of *śe* as having meaning (*arthavat*). There is a mention of the word *śe* when it possesses meaning; and [in these examples, it does not].

This [rule] applies to that which possesses meaning (*arthavat*). Even so, it would still apply here in the case of *hariśe* and *babhruśe*. If that is the case, then according to the principle that "between that which is taught by a general rule and that which is taught by a specific rule, the specific one prevails," it will not occur. Alternatively, let it be that the mention of "possessing meaning" excludes that which is meaningless. But how is it in the case of *hariśe* and *babhruśe*? In this instance, one [element] is meaningful by virtue of the meaning of the case-ending.
Another [view holds that] the entire complex is meaningless because its purpose is already served by the secondary derivative (*taddhita*). (P.
1.1.14) [Question: For what purpose is the term "particle" (*nipāta*) used here? [Answer: The particle *ca* is used here.

[The rule] "jahāra atra" [is given]. Why is it stated that "it consists of a single vowel" (*ekāc*)? [Consider the examples: *pra idam brahma*, *pra idam kṣatram*. Even though "consisting of a single vowel" is stated, [the rule] would apply here as well; for this too consists of a single vowel. This term "consisting of a single vowel" (*ekāc*) is not a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that in which there is one vowel"—but rather, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound in apposition: [meaning "a single vowel itself"].

"Single" (*eka*) means "having a single vowel" (*ekāc*). If it were a *tatpuruṣa* compound with a coreferential member (*samānādhikaraṇa*), there would be no purpose in mentioning the word "single. Why does [the rule] not apply here in the case of *pra idam brahma* and *pra idam kṣatram*? [Because] it will be understood that the term refers to a particle (*nipāta*) that consists of exactly one vowel. Is this something that needs to be stated? [No.]
Indeed not. How would it be understood if it were not explicitly stated? By the force of the mention of *aj*.
For if it were the case that [the rule applied] both to what is *aj* and to something else, the mention of *aj* would be purposeless. But there is another purpose for the mention of *aj*:
so that it may apply to that which ends in *aj*, and not to that which ends in a consonant (*hal*). This is not a fault, nor is it a purpose. Thus [it is].

But from what [source] does it follow that when these two rules of interpretation (*paribhāṣā*)— namely, "in a single [element], as if it had a beginning and an end" (*ādyantavad ekasmin*) and "that by which an operation is prescribed applies to that which ends with it" (*yena vidhis tadantasya*)— are both simultaneously applicable and present, this rule of interpretation "that by which an operation is prescribed applies to that which ends with it" will apply here, and not this rule "in a single [element], as if it had a beginning and an end"? The activity of the Teacher (*ācāryapravṛtti*) makes it known that this [latter rule]...

In this context, there is a metarule (*paribhāṣā*) stating "that which has a single [element] is treated like the beginning and the end. This [rule] does not apply here because of the rule "that by which an operation is prescribed applies to that which ends with it," since the author teaches the prohibition "not *anāṅ*. If that is so, then since the desired result is already established, the fact that the Teacher makes a mention of "single" (*eka*) even when the mention of "vowel" (*aj*) is being made indicates that elsewhere, when a letter (*varṇa*) is mentioned, there is an inclusion of the entire class (*jāti*).

Thus [it is stated]. What is the purpose of making this known? That which was stated—that the inclusion of *hal* in the rule for the root *dambh-* is established because it denotes a genus (*jāti*)—becomes justified. For what purpose is the restriction *anāṅ* [stated]? [Examples: *ā*, *udakāntāt*, *audakāntāt*. Why does it not apply here: [example follows]...?
"Do you think so? Is that indeed the case? [The reply is: "There is a mention of the vowel *ā* with its *anubandha*, and here the vowel *ā* is without an *anubandha*.

But where is this [vowel] with an *anubandha*, and where is it without an *anubandha*? [It occurs] in the sense of 'slightness' (*īṣadartha*), in connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*), and in the senses of 'limit exclusive' (*maryādā*) and 'limit inclusive' (*abhividhi*)."

And he who would know this *ātaṅ* as having the marker *ṅ*—[it is used] in the senses of speech (*vākya*) and recollection (*smaraṇa*), when it lacks the marker *ṅ*. What is the example? It is "āho. 231–233. *Otaścvipratiṣedhaḥ*. Regarding the rule *odanto nipātaḥ*, a prohibition must be stated for that which ends in *cvi*. For example: *anadaḥ*, *adaḥ*, *abhavat*: [the form] *adobhavat* [is incorrect].

"It disappears. It should not be said [that it disappears]. Because of the rule "between that which is taught by a definition and that which is taught by its own specific form, the latter prevails," this will not occur. Even so, in the case of *agauḥ gauḥ sampadyate* (the non-cow becomes a cow), expressed as *gobhavat*, the [application of the suffix] would still result here.

If that is the case, then according to the principle "between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*), the operation applies to the primary," just as when it is said "a cow is to be sacrificed" or "a goat dedicated to Agni and Soma," a *bāhīka* (a low-caste person) is not sacrificed. How then do the rules for *vṛddhi* and *ātva* apply to the *bāhīka*? [The answer follows:]...

"The cow stands," "Bring the cow. This occurs when there is reliance on meaning (*arthāśraya*). For that which relies on the word (*śabdāśraya*) applies only to the mere word (*śabdamātra*). And [the rules regarding] *vṛddhi* and *āttva* rely on the word. Why does it not occur here: "āho"? [Because it relies on meaning.]

[Question: "Or rather, it is said that [the rule applies] to *uñ*. But we do not see *uñ* here. [Answer: This single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of *uñ* with another sound is included by the mention of *uñ*. [Objection: The activity of the Teacher indicates that the single-substitute of *uñ* is not included by the mention of *uñ*, since he teaches the *pragṛhya* designation for the particle ending in *o* by stating "ot" (Pāṇini 1.1.15). [Reply: This is not a valid indicator.

This has been stated: this undertaking is for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of] that which has already been forbidden. Indeed, there would be a fault if the *uṅ* substitute were not included by the mention of *uṅ*: in the case of *jānu*, *u*, and *asya rujati*, one would have *jānū asya rujati* or *jānvasya rujati*. [In these cases,] the substitution of *v* for *uṅ* according to the rule *maya uño vo vā* would apply.

It would not [be so]. If that is the case, then these are single phonemes (*ekanipāta*). Alternatively, there are two *u*-phonemes here: one is without an indicatory letter (*ananubandhaka*), and the other is with an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*). Of these, this single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) applies to the one that is without an indicatory letter.

234–235. There is a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) regarding *uñ*. A split of the rule regarding *uñ* must be made: according to the opinion of the teacher Śākalya, the designation *pragṛhya* applies to *uñ*, [resulting in] *u* and *v*. Then, from *uṃ*: according to the opinion of the teacher Śākalya, this substitution *ūṃ* occurs; it is long, nasalized, and bears the designation *pragṛhya*.

"Um. For what purpose is this separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*)? [It is] "um optionally according to Śākalya. According to the opinion of the teacher Śākalya, there should be an option regarding *um*: namely, *ūm* or *uṃ*.
According to the opinion of other teachers, it is *v*.
