Regarding the rule "like a dried leather bag lying in a lake" (*dṛtim na śuṣkam sarasī śayānam*), it does not apply here when there is a specific purpose, as in the case of "Soma has settled upon the *gaurī*" (*somo gaurī adhi śritaḥ*). Even in that instance, [the rule applies] if there is a "lake" (*sarasī*). That too is established. How so? If the word *sarasī* is in active usage. And the word *sarasī* is indeed in active usage in the world. How so? For in the Deccan (*dakṣiṇāpatha*)...

Large lakes are called *sarasyaḥ*. This would serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the fact that [the term] ends in that [suffix]. If that is so, then the Teacher indicates that in the application of the technical designation *pragṛhya*, the characteristic of being a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not apply. What is the purpose of this indication?
[For example: *kumāryor agāram* becomes *kumāryagāram*.

In the case of *vadhvoḥ agāram*, which becomes *vadhvagāram*, the designation *pragṛhya* does not apply because it is conditioned by a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*). Alternatively, let there be [the designation *pragṛhya*] for the preceding member; or rather, the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*arthagrahaṇam*) is for the purpose that it should not apply to the preceding member—as in *vāpyām aśvaḥ* becoming *vāpyaśvaḥ*.

In *nadyām ātiḥ*, [we get] *nadyātiḥ*. Now, even if the term "meaning" (*artha*) is included [in the rule], why does this not occur here? Because it is a *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) compound. But if it is a *ajahatsvārthā* (not abandoning its own meaning) compound, then there is indeed a fault. And there is no fault in the case of a *ajahatsvārthā* compound, because the collective meaning of the whole is expressed. [The fault would arise] only if "ī and ū" were taken as the seventh case endings when they have been elided; however, because of the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*), [the rule applies].

If [the vowel] were homogeneous with the preceding one, then this substitution of *āṬ* for *ām* would result by virtue of the rule; even where there is lengthening, if *sarasī* were the indicator (*jñāpaka*) [of the application of the rule], then let it not apply to the finality of the preceding member.

239–241. Regarding the designation *ghu*, the mention of the "original form" (*prakṛti*) is for the sake of [the suffix] *śit*. In the definition of the *ghu* designation, the mention of the original form must be made;

it should be stated that "those whose original forms are *dā* and *dhā* receive the *ghu* designation. What is the purpose? This designation is made for those [roots] that have undergone the change to *āt* (i.e., *adāp*). It would apply only to those that have become *āt*, and not to those that have not become *āt*. But surely...

The majority of operations conditioned by the designation *ghu* occur in the *ārdhadhātuka* domain, and therein these [roots] are seen having undergone the substitution of *ā*. For the sake of the *śit* suffixes:

the mention of the "original form" (*prakṛti*) must be made for the sake of the *śit* suffixes; it is for the purpose of prohibiting the substitution of *ā* when a *śit* suffix follows, as in *praṇidayate* and *praṇidhayati*. The followers of Bhāradvāja recite that the mention of the "original form" applies to the designation *ghu*.

The term *ghu* is prescribed for the sake of both the original form (*prakṛti*) and its modified forms (*vikṛta*). Regarding the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *ghu*, the mention of the "original form" is made. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of the original form and for the sake of the modified forms. An example for the original form has already been cited. Now, an example for the sake of the modified forms: *praṇidātā*, *praṇidhātā*. But why is it not established? Because, between that which is [defined] by a general rule (*lakṣaṇa*) and that which is [stated] by a specific word (*pratipadokta*), the specific word takes precedence.

If [the word] "eva" is used, it would apply only to those that have become *āt* by virtue of each specific rule (*pratipada*), but it would not apply to those that have become *āt* by virtue of a general grammatical definition (*lakṣaṇa*). Now, even if the mention of "roots" (*prakṛti*) is made, how is this to be understood: are the roots *dā* and *dhā* intended, or are the forms *dā* and *dhā* intended as roots? What follows from this? If it is understood that the roots *dā* and *dhā* are intended...

That very same fault remains: [the rule] would apply only to those that have undergone *āt* substitution, and not to those that have not. Now, if it is understood that "the roots *dā* and *dhā*" are the bases (*prakṛti*), then it would apply only to those that have not undergone *āt* substitution, and not to those that have. In that case, it should not be understood as "the roots *dā* and *dhā*" are the bases, nor as "the bases are *dā* and *dhā*. How then? It is simply "*dā-dhāḥ*."

"The bases (prakṛti) become [roots] designated as *ghu*, and these are their [original] forms. If that is so, then the mention of "base" (*prakṛti*) must be made. It need not be made. This mention of "meaning" (*artha*), which is the subject under discussion, continues to apply here. Where was it introduced? In the rule *īdūtau ca saptamyarthe*. Following that, I shall state: *dādhā ghu adāp* [in the sense of meaning]. But it cannot be done in this way.

They say that *rāti*, *āsati*, *dāśati*, *maṃhati*, *prīṇāti*, *prabhṛti*, and so on, have the same meaning as *dadāti*. These [roots] would also obtain the designation *ghu*; therefore, it cannot be [the case that the rule applies] in this way. If it were not so, the mention of the root-form (*prakṛtigrahaṇa*) would have to be made.
For the sake of the suffix *śit*, there is no purpose in mentioning the root-form; however, the mention of the root-form must necessarily be made there for the sake of the suffix *mā*.

The purpose is to show that [the rule] applies to *praṇamayate* and *praṇyamayata*. That will be explained later: "In the case of the roots *mā* and *mī* when they are in their original form (*prakṛti*). If the mention of "original form" (*prakṛtigrahaṇa*) were made, it would also apply here in *praniminoti* and *pranimīnāti*. Now, even if the mention of "original form" is not made, why does it not apply here?

Regarding the statement "one who wishes to measure" (*pramimātā pramātum*): it will be understood that the term *ṅit* refers to that which ends in the vowel *ā*. In that case, just as when the mention of the "original form" (*prakṛti*) is not made, it is understood that *ṅit* refers to that which ends in *ā*, so too when the mention of the "original form" is made, it will be understood that *ṅit* refers to that which ends in *ā*. Furthermore, there is no purpose served by [the mention of] the modified form (*vikṛta*).

This very rule constitutes a flaw in this technical definition (*paribhāṣā*): namely, that regarding the conflict between what is taught by a general definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and what is taught by a specific word-for-word statement (*pratipadokta*), the latter alone prevails; thus, there would be no distinction in the case of rules involving the mention of *gām*, *ādā*, and *gra* (as in Pāṇini 6.1.43).
Furthermore, a prohibition must be stated regarding words that are identical in form (*samānaśabda*). A prohibition of identical words must be formulated.

In *praṇidārayati* and *praṇidhārayati*, the designation *ghu* would apply because of the rule "the roots *dā* and *dhā* receive the designation *ghu*. [Objection: There is no prohibition for identical forms, because of the inclusion of meaningful items (*arthavad-grahaṇāt*). [Response: There is no prohibition for identical forms; thus, the prohibition is non-existent, which means there is no prohibition. Why does the designation *ghu* not occur? Because of the inclusion of meaningful items. [The designation applies] to two meaningful items.

The mention of *dā* and *dhā* [in the rule] is for the sake of including the causative forms; however, these two [causatives] do not possess their own independent meaning. Or rather, the rule applies when the prefixes (*pra*, etc.

are connected with an action, for it is in relation to that [action] that they receive the designations "motion" (*gati*) and "preverb" (*upasarga*). But there is no connection with an action in relation to these two roots *dā* and *dhā*.
If this is so, then the designation would not apply here either: *praṇidāpayati*, *praṇidhāpayati*; for in this case as well, there is no [connection with an action].

These two *dādhau* possess meaning, yet there is no connection with a verbal action (*kriyā*) regarding these two *dādhau*. Or rather, an augment (*āgama*) that is subordinate to a meaningful element is included by the mention of that [meaningful element], as is the case elsewhere. Or rather, this is not a fault. Why? Because an augment subordinate to a meaningful element is included by the mention of that meaningful element, just as is the case elsewhere.

For example: elsewhere too, an *āgama* (augment) that possesses meaning is included by the mention of "that which possesses meaning. Where else? In the cases of *lavitā* and *cikīrṣitā*. But it is indeed logical that there should be a teaching regarding augments in the case of eternal words; for eternal words must consist of phonemes (*varṇa*) that are fixed, unchanging, and devoid of loss, addition, or modification.
Furthermore, what is called *āgama* (an augment) is the addition of a previously non-existent sound. Now, it would be logical that there should be substitutes (*ādeśa*) for eternal words.

Certainly, that is logical. In this case, there must be different words [involved]. Therein, the comprehension of one word from another word is logical. In that case, these will be augments for those [words] that originally lacked them, making them possessed of augments. How so?
All [grammatical] substitutes are replacements for entire words, according to Pāṇini, the son of Dākṣī; for if only a single part were modified, permanence (*nityatva*) would not be tenable. (P.

1.1.20.3) Regarding the substitution of *i* for the roots *sthā* and *ghu*, a prohibition must be stated for the root *dīṅ*. That is, a prohibition of the substitution of *i* for *sthā* and *ghu* must be stated in the case of the root *dīṅ*.

[The opponent says: "He took the accent of this teacher. [In the case of] *mīnāti* and *minoti*, once the substitution of *ā* (by *āttve*) has been applied, the substitution of *i* (by *sthāghvoḥ it ca*) would also apply. But from what does this fault arise? Is it from the mention of the root (*prakṛti*), or from the mention of the form (*rūpa*)? He says: it is from the mention of the form. Indeed, in this case, the fault arises from the mention of the root.

One might object: [the form] *upadidīṣate* [should not occur], because of the rule "after *mī*, *mā*, *ghu*, *rabh*, and *labh* [the suffix *san* takes *iṭ*]. This is not a fault. It is stated that [the root] has *dā* as its base (*prakṛti*), but this [root *do*] does not have *dā* as its base. For roots ending in long *ā* have bases ending in *e*, and bases ending in *e* have bases ending in long *ī*. Furthermore, a base of a base is not included by the mention of the "base" itself. Therefore, that prohibition must indeed be stated.

It should not be stated [that it is]. Why does the designation *ghu* not occur? [Because] "a rule conditioned by a specific combination [of sounds] is not the cause for the destruction of that very combination"—thus it will not occur.

246–247. Regarding the prohibition of *dāp*, the prohibition does not apply to *daip* because it does not end in a vowel (*anejantatvāt*). In the case of the prohibition of *dāp*, the prohibition would not apply to *daip*: for example, *avadātaṃ mukham*. But surely [the form] will be established once the substitution of *ā* (āttva) has taken place? That substitution of *ā* does not indeed apply here. What is the reason? Because it does not end in a vowel. [Objection: It is established because the indicatory letter (*anubandha*) is non-exclusive (*anekānta*). This is established. How so?

Because the suffixes (anubandhas) are not invariably determinative; the suffixes are indeed non-invariable. Or else, because of the prohibition regarding the *pit* marker. Alternatively, I shall state that *dā* and *dhā* are *ghu* when they do not have the *pit* marker. And that must necessarily be stated. For if it were simply stated as "except for *dāp*," then [the rule] would undesirably apply here as well: *praṇidāpayati*. However, by one who says "except for *dāp*," it is possible to understand that the prohibition applies to that which ends in *ba*.

In that case, the Sūtra is contradicted. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. But was it not said: "When there is a prohibition of *da*, [the rule] *na daip* does not apply"? This has been answered: "It is established because an *anubandha* is not invariably [indicative of its grammatical function]. Now, if there is indeed a fault in the case of those [roots] where the *anubandha* is invariably [indicative], there is no fault in the case of those where it is not. Once *āttva* (the substitution of *ā*) has been applied, it will be so. But was it not said that this *āttva*...?

It does not obtain. What is the reason? Because it is immovable (*anejantatvāt*). [Objection: It will apply once the letter *p* has been elided. [Reply: For in that case, this is no longer a substitute ending in *āp*. [Objection: It will apply by way of its previous state (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*). And this is what is logical here: that in all instances involving the mention of an element with an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*), the understanding is based on its previous state. For the elision of an indicatory letter is not conditioned by any external cause.

It remains exactly as it was. Alternatively, the activity of the Teacher (Ācārya) indicates that the status of not ending in a vowel (*anejantatva*) is not determined by an *anubandha*, since he makes a mention of the root *meṅ*—which has undergone the change to *ā*—in the rule "udīcāṃ māṅo vyatīhāre" (*Pāṇini 1.3.59*). Or rather, this is simply the root *dāp*; there is no such root as *daip*. As for how one says "avadāyayati," the suffix *śyan* will be applied [to form the causative].

For what purpose is this stated? "Because there is the status of being like the beginning and the end when another exists; [therefore] the statement regarding being like the beginning and the end applies to that which is single.
When another exists, that which has nothing before it and has something after it is called the "beginning" (*ādi*). When another exists...

Because that which has nothing beyond it and has something before it is called "the end" (*anta*). Since there is another [element] when there is a state of having a beginning and an end, for this reason, grammatical operations prescribed for the beginning and the end do not apply to a single [element]. Yet, it is desired that they should apply; therefore, the statement regarding the beginning and the end with respect to a single element is made so that these [operations] may be accomplished without further effort. This is the purpose of this [rule].

It is said: there is indeed a purpose for this. What then? In that regard, there must be a statement regarding "that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivad-vacana*). In that context, the state of being like that which possesses a designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) must be stated; it must be stated that "an operation occurs as if it were in that which possesses a designation, even when [the element] is singular. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of the rule "of a monosyllable, two [are uttered] for the first" (*ekāco dve prathamasya*). He will state: "of a monosyllable, two [are uttered] for the first."

It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound designation. If this were applied, it would occur only in cases such as *papāca* and *papāṭha*, but it would not occur here in *iyāya* and *āra*. However, by the principle that "an operation applies to a single entity as if it possessed distinct designations," this is also established in these cases.

And [the genitive case ending] in the word *ṣatve* is for the purpose of indicating that it is a substitute (*ādeśa*). He will state [in Pāṇini 8.3.59], "In the place of a substitute and a suffix," that this is indeed a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). If this were done, [the rule] would apply only here:
*kariṣyati*, *hariṣyati*; but it would not apply here: [e.g., *iṣyati*].
"May Indra lead me;
may he sacrifice to the gods. Since an operation applies to a single entity as if it were that which possesses a designation (*vyapadeśivat*), this [rule] is also established here.
Well then, that state of being "as if possessing a designation" must be explicitly stated. It need not be stated; it is established through common worldly understanding, as no such statement is made.
This is established even without an explicit statement, due to common worldly understanding. For example:
in the world, a collection of houses is called a "village" (*grāma*). And yet, this occurs even in the case of a single house, as in "a village consisting of a single house" (*ekaśālo grāmaḥ*).
This is an unequal comparison. This word *grāma* has many meanings; it indeed exists as referring to a collection of houses.
For example, "the village is burned" refers to that which exists within the enclosure of the boundary wall; for example, "he has entered the village.

It refers to that which exists among the people; for example, "the village has gone," or "the village has come. It refers to that which exists together with its pasture lands, its boundaries, and its common grounds; for example, "the village."
It has been established [that a word denotes a class]. Therefore, having observed that which exists within a forested area, together with its boundaries and its open spaces, this term is applied:

"a village consisting of a single hall" (*ekaśālo grāmaḥ*). Just as it is said that a collection of phonemes is a word (*pada*), a collection of words is a verse (*ṛc*), and a collection of verses is a hymn (*sūkta*), so too does this occur even in a single instance: a word consisting of a single phoneme, a verse consisting of a single word, and a hymn consisting of a single verse.
"It is a *sūkta*. Here too, the designation is based on its meaning: "word" (*pada*) has a specific meaning, and "hymn" (*sūkta*) has a specific meaning.
In that case, it is just as appropriate when there are many sons:
"This one is my eldest, this one is my middle child, and this one is my youngest. It occurs thus.
And even in the case of a single thing, one says: "This is my eldest," "This is my middle one," and "This is my youngest.

Likewise, regarding a woman who has not yet given birth or will not give birth, it is said: "She has been destroyed by her first pregnancy. Similarly, one who has not yet arrived but intends to come says: "This is my first arrival. Furthermore, it is possible to speak of a state of having both a beginning and an end.

How so? Because of the characteristics of being unprecedented (*apūrva*) and unsurpassed (*anuttara*), [the operations] established for the beginning and the end apply even to a single [syllable]. The beginning has the characteristic of being unprecedented; the end has the characteristic of being unsurpassed. And this occurs even in the case of a single [syllable]. For this reason—that it possesses the characteristics of being unprecedented and unsurpassed—the grammatical operations prescribed for the beginning and the end will take place even with respect to a single [syllable]. There is no purpose in [formally] treating it as having the status of "beginning-like" (*ādivat*) or "end-like" (*antavat*).
But Gonardīya says: "This is true, provided that there is another [suffix].

What, then, are the purposes of this rule? Its purpose is with regard to the status of being "like the beginning" (*ādivat*), specifically for the acute accent on the first syllable of a suffix (*pratyaya*). For it is stated: "The beginning of a suffix is acute," and this applies right here.

It might be argued: [the rule] should apply to *kartavyam*, *taittirīyaḥ*, *aupagavaḥ*, and *kāpaṭavaḥ*; however, it would not apply here. [If one were to say] "before suffixes marked with ñ or ṇ, the initial [augment] is obligatory," then it would apply only in this case: [kartavyam].

In the case of *ahicumbakāyaniḥ*, *agniveśyaḥ*, *gargyaḥ*, and *kṛtiḥ*, [the suffix] would not [be added]. The augment *iṭ* applies to an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant (*val*). The purpose of the *iṭ* for an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant is as follows: here, the *iṭ* of the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix occurs only when it begins with a consonant (*val*).

In cases such as *kariṣyati*, *hariṣyati*, *joṣiṣat*, and *maṃsiṣat*, [the rule] would not apply. [The principle is: "When a grammatical operation (*vidhi*) is prescribed with reference to a certain element, it applies when that element is at the beginning. There is a purpose in stating:

"When a grammatical operation is prescribed with reference to a certain element, [it applies] when that element is at the beginning, provided that the mention of the letter *a* (*al-grahaṇa*) is made. When that [principle] is applied, [the rule] *aci śnudhātubhruvām...* [is established].

The substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* should apply only here: *śriyaḥ*, *bhruvaḥ*. [Otherwise], they would not apply in cases such as *śriyau* and *bhruvau*. Regarding the *āṭ* augment for roots beginning with vowels: the purpose of the *āṭ* augment for roots beginning with vowels is that it should apply only here: *aihiṣṭa*, *aikṣiṣṭa*. [Otherwise], it would apply in *ait*.

In the case of *adhyaiṣṭa*, [the rule] would not apply here. Now, what are the purposes served by the property of having an end (*antavattva*)? It serves the purpose of [applying] the status of being a *pragṛhya* for dual endings that have an end. The purpose of [the property of] having an end for dual endings that are *pragṛhya* is this: it would apply only in cases such as *pacete* and *pacethe*; however, it would not apply in cases such as *khaṭve* and *māle*. The marker *mit* follows after the final vowel. The purpose of [the marker] *mit* following after the final vowel is this: it would apply only in this very case.

Regarding the rules *kuṇḍāni vanāni* and *tāni yāni*, [the substitution of the final vowel] would not occur here. The purpose of the rule *acaḥ antyādi ṭi* is as follows: by the rule *ṭita ātmanepadānām ṭeḥ e*, the substitution of *e* for the *ṭi* of the *ātmanepada* endings would apply only in cases such as *kurvāte* and *kurvāthe*; it would not apply in cases such as *kurute* and *kurve*. The purpose of the rule *alaḥ antyasya* (substitution applies to the final phoneme of the *al*) is as follows: by the rule *ataḥ dīrgho yañi supi ca*, the lengthening of the vowel after *at* would apply only in cases such as *ghaṭābhyām*.

255–256. Regarding the designation *gha*, there is a prohibition concerning the crossing of a river (*nadītara*). It should be stated that regarding the designation *gha*, there is a prohibition concerning the crossing of a river, as in the example *nadyās taraḥ* = *nadītaraḥ*. [Objection: Regarding the designation *gha*, there is no prohibition concerning the crossing of a river. A prohibition that is purposeless is called "no-prohibition" (*apratiṣedhaḥ*). Why does the designation *gha* not apply here? [Response: Because the inclusion of the suffix *-tara-* refers to what is directly taught (*aupadeśika*). For that which is directly taught...

[The suffix] *tarap* is what is being referred to. And yet, this word *tarap* does not exist in actual usage (*upadeśa*). Should it be stated [that it exists]? No, it need not. How is it understood even though it is not explicitly stated? For in this grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), in all cases involving the mention of items with indicatory letters (*sānubandhaka*), the formal shape (*rūpa*) is relied upon, according to the principle:
"wherever this form occurs. And the apprehension of that form cannot occur without recourse to worldly usage (*laukika-prayoga*). And in that case...
Since there is no usage of words with *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) in common worldly usage, a second usage is adopted;
what is that? It is called "instruction" (*upadeśa*). And this word *tarap* does not exist in the state of instruction. Alternatively, let it have the designation *gha*;

what would be the fault? Since it is stated that "in the case of [stems ending in] *gha* etc., the feminine suffix *nadī* becomes short," the shortening of the vowel would undesirably apply here in the case of co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) compounds.

[The rule applies] "in the case of words beginning with *gha*," and thus it is so. But then, when that very same river is [referred to by] that very same word *taraḥ*, [the suffix] would apply. [To avoid this, it must mean] "only in the case of feminine words beginning with *gha*. And this must necessarily be understood in this way; for if it were stated as "in the case of words beginning with *gha* that are in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*)," then it would undesirably apply here in cases such as *mahiṣī-rūpam* and *brāhmaṇī-rūpam*.
Regarding the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "number" (*saṅkhyā*), the term "number" must be explicitly mentioned. In the rule for the designation of number, it should be stated:

"The terms *bahu*, *gaṇa*, and those ending in the suffixes *vat* and *uṭ* receive the designation 'number' (*saṅkhyā-saṃjñā*)," and furthermore, "the word 'number' itself receives the designation 'number'."
It must be stated. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of ensuring the recognition of number.

This is so that there may be the recognition of "number" for numbers such as one and so forth in the rules concerning number. But surely, in common usage, numbers such as one and so forth are already understood as "number";
therefore, their recognition as "number" will occur in the rules concerning number even without this. Even so, it must still be stated.

Otherwise, there would be a lack of comprehension because [the term "number"] is not artificial, as is the case in common worldly usage. For if the mention of "number" were not made [in the rule], there would be no comprehension that numbers such as "one" and so forth are indeed "numbers. What is the reason? Because they are not artificial.

Terms such as *bahu* (many) and so forth are artificial designations (*saṃjñā*). And when there is a choice between an artificial and a non-artificial [term], the application of the grammatical operation occurs with respect to the artificial one.

As it is in the world: for example, in common usage, when one says, "Bring the cowherd" (*gopālaka*) or "Bring the mat-born" (*kaṭaja*), it is the person who has that designation who is brought, not merely one who herds cows or one who was born on a mat. If, then, between an artificial (*kṛtrima*) and a non-artificial (*akṛtrima*) term, the understanding applies to the artificial one, then the rule *nadīpaurṇamāsyāgrahāyaṇībhyaḥ* would also apply there [to the artificial forms].

It will not apply because of the inclusion of *paurṇamāsī* and *āgrahāyaṇī*. In that case, it would apply to its specific instances, such as *gaṅgā* and *yamunā*. If this is so, then the activity of the Teacher indicates that it does not apply to its specific instances, since he recites the word *vipāṭ* among the items beginning with *śarad*. In that case, it would apply here: [the example follows].

Regarding the phrase "and by means of rivers" (*nadībhiś ca*): because of the indication in the plural number, [the application of the rule] will not occur. If it is argued that a rule concerning the actual form (*svarūpavidhi*) would then apply, [we reply] that precisely because of the indication in the plural number, it will not occur. Thus, this principle—that between the artificial (*kṛtrima*) and the non-artificial (*akṛtrima*), there is comprehension of the artificial—is not left unfulfilled, and there is no fault whatsoever. Furthermore, it is for the sake of what follows; the mention of "number" (*saṅkhyā*) is for the purpose of subsequent rules.

It must be stated [as a rule]: "Those ending in *ṣ* and *n* are called *ṣaṭ*. This is so that the technical designation *ṣaṭ* may apply to numbers ending in the letters *ṣ* and *n*. It should not apply here: *pāmānaḥ* (scabs) or *vipruṣaḥ* (drops). Now, for the time being, there is no need for the mention of "number" (*saṅkhyā*) in this rule. But was it not said: "Otherwise, there would be a lack of comprehension because [the word] is not artificial, as in common usage"? This is not a fault. For, by virtue of the meaning or the context...

Or, in the world, between an artificial and a natural thing, trust is placed in the artificial; or its meaning is understood through such a designation; or the context is present there, such that "this must be done by one with such a designation. Therefore, it is from the meaning or from the context. Indeed, you might as well speak to a rustic, a barefooted man ignorant of the context, who has arrived here.

"Bring the cowherd," "Bring Kaṭajaka"—in such cases, there is a dual possibility for him: he will either go to the one who holds a staff, or [to the other], whichever is more appropriate. Just as in common usage, based on the meaning or the context, there is a comprehension of the *kṛtrima* (technical/assigned) sense over the *akṛtrima* (natural/common) sense among both types, so too here it would follow. For he knows that this technical name has been assigned to the words beginning with *bahu*.

It is not as it is in the world that it is so in grammar; rather, here there is a dual application (ubhayagati). Furthermore, this is not necessarily restricted to this [treatise] alone, but occurs elsewhere as well. For example:
"The object most desired by the agent is the *karman*"—this is an artificial designation (*kṛtrimā saṃjñā*). And in the sections dealing with the *karman*, there is a dual application.

In the rule *karmaṇi dvitīyā* ("the second case ending is used for the object"), the technical (*kṛtrima*) [term "object"] is understood; whereas in the rule *kartari karmavyatihāre* ("the third case ending is used for the agent when there is a reciprocal action"), the non-technical (*akṛtrima*) [term "agent"] is understood.

Likewise, in the rule *sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam* ("the most effective means is the instrument"), the technical designation "instrument" (*karaṇasaṃjñā*) is applied. And in the various contexts where "instrument" occurs, both [the technical and non-technical] applications are intended.

Thus, in the rule *kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā* ("the third case ending is used for the agent and the instrument"), the technical [term "agent"] is understood; however, in the rule *śabdavairakalahābhrakaṇvameghebhyaḥ*... [the non-technical term is understood].

In the case of the term *karaṇa*, it refers to the non-technical (*akṛtrima*) sense; likewise, the designation *adhikaraṇa* as "the locus" (*ādhāra*) is technical (*kṛtrima*). In the rules (*pradeśa*) concerning the locative, both interpretations apply: the mention of the technical sense occurs in the rule *saptamī adhikaraṇe ca*, while the non-technical sense occurs in the rule *vipratiṣiddham ca anadhikaraṇavāci*. Alternatively, this is not a formal assignment of technical designations (*saṃjñākaraṇa*).

In the same way, this is an extended application (*atideśa*): "The words *bahu*, *gaṇa*, *vatu*, and *ḍati* are treated like numerals (*saṃkhyā*). Well then, that instruction should be formulated using the suffix *-vat*; for without the suffix *-vat*, an extended application is not understood. [Objection: Even without the suffix *-vat*, an extended application is understood. For example:

This is Brahmadatta. Although he is not Brahmadatta, he says "Brahmadatta. We understand from this that he is like Brahmadatta. Similarly here as well, when he says "number" (*saṅkhyā*) for what is not number (*asaṅkhyā*), it is understood that it is "like a number" (*saṅkhyāvat*). Alternatively, the activity of the Teacher indicates that numbers beginning with one are included in the rules concerning numbers (*saṅkhyāpradeśa*).

Regarding the statement "there is comprehension of number": this refers to the rule *saṅkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan*, which teaches a prohibition for those [numerals] ending in *ti* or *śat*. How does this serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? For there exists no artificial (*kṛtrima*) number that ends in *ti* or *śat*. But is it not the case that such a thing exists in the form of the suffix *ḍati*? [The answer is: That is why the rule teaches a prohibition for those ending in *śat*; and also for those ending in *ti*.

It teaches a prohibition. But was it not said that this would be for the sake of [the suffix] *ḍati*? In the rule regarding the mention of meaningful items (*arthavat*), an item that is meaningless is not included; therefore, the word *ti* is understood as being meaningful. However, the word *ti* is not meaningful when it belongs to *ḍati*. Alternatively, this is a very long technical term (*saṃjñā*) being created. And a technical term is certainly not something to be made unnecessarily cumbersome. Why is that? For the sake of brevity (*laghu*).

For this is the making of a technical name (*saṃjñākaraṇa*). In that regard, the purpose of employing this long technical name is so that it may be understood as a "significant name" (*anvarthasaṃjñā*): "that by which something is counted is a 'number' (*saṃkhyā*). And indeed, things are counted by means of [the series] beginning with one.

Furthermore, there is no need for the mention of "number" (*saṃkhyā*) here, because the word from the subsequent rule will also apply here by way of *anuvṛtti*. This—[namely, the word "number"]—is what is under discussion. This—[namely, the word "number"]—...

It is indeed for the sake of providing a designation, and furthermore, for the sake of qualifying the designated object hereafter. A term introduced for one purpose does not become something else merely by being used for another purpose. Nor indeed does one thing become something else simply because it follows after another that was previously introduced. For a lizard, though it crawls, does not become a snake merely by the act of crawling. As for what was said—that a term introduced for one purpose does not become something else [for another]—that is so.
Thus, even that which was introduced for one purpose may serve another purpose. For example:

canals are dug for the sake of rice, yet from them water is drunk, it is used for ritual sipping, and the rice is cultivated. Furthermore, it is said that indeed one thing does not become something else merely by following after what was previously introduced.
For a lizard does not become a snake merely by crawling. This might be so in the case of substances;

however, a word indeed becomes a qualifier of whatever specific property it is connected with. Alternatively, this designation is made dependently (*sāpekṣa*), and there is nothing else to be depended upon; we shall depend on number alone.

The mention of *adhyardha* is for the purpose of [regulating] compounds and primary derivatives (*kan*). The mention of *adhyardha* must be made. What is the purpose? For the purpose of [regulating] compounds and primary derivatives; that is, for the purpose of the rules concerning compounds and for the purpose of the rules concerning primary derivatives (*kan*).
First, for the purpose of prescribing compounds:
*adhyardhaśūrpa*. For the purpose of prescribing the suffix *kan*:
*adhyardhakam*. And regarding elision (*luk*): there is no mention of "elision. When there is elision, the mention of *adhyardha* need not be made.

Regarding the rule *adhyardhapūrvadvigor luk asaṃjñāyām*: it is already established by the rule *dvigoḥ* alone. However, it must be stated that a compound whose prior member is *ardha* and which ends in a ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*) is designated as a number (*saṅkhyā*). What is the purpose? It is for the sake of the rules governing compounds and the rules governing *kan* suffixes. That is, for the sake of the rules for compounds and for the rules for *kan* suffixes.
And [the mention of] *ardha* is for the purpose of the rule on compounds:
*ardhapañcamaśūrpa*. It is for the purpose of the suffix *kan*:

*ardhapañcamakam*. Furthermore, the inclusion of the term *adhika* is for the purpose of causing the vṛddhi-strengthening of the final syllable of the compound when there is no elision (*aluk*). This is the inclusion of *adhika*.

And the elision (*aluk*) must be applied. What is the purpose? For the sake of the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the final member of a compound—that is, for the sake of the *vṛddhi* of the compound as a whole and for the sake of the *vṛddhi* of the subsequent member. First, for the sake of the *vṛddhi* of the compound: *adhikaṣāṣṭhikaḥ*.

*adhikasāptatikaḥ*. For the sake of the vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the final member, [examples are] *adhikaṣāṣṭhikaḥ*, *adhikasāptatikaḥ*. Why is it stated "when there is no elision" (*aluki*)? [To show that it does not apply when there is elision: *adhikaṣāṣṭhikaḥ*, *adhikasāptatikaḥ*. Furthermore, there is no need to mention the word *adhika* in the context of the *bahuvrīhi* compound; for in a *bahuvrīhi*, the mention of the word *adhika* need not be made.

[The rule] "In the sense of a numeral, indeclinables, *avyasanna*, *adūra*, and *adhika* [are compounded] with numerals when they denote a thing to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*)"—this is established by the word "numeral" (*saṃkhyā*) alone. There is no need to mention *bahu* and so forth. It would be possible to omit the mention of *bahu* and so forth. [Objection: By what means, then, will there be the understanding of "numeral" (*saṃkhya*) in the various rules concerning numerals? [Response: It is established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*). What is the indicator? That this [rule] mentions *vat*...

265–269. Regarding the technical designation *ṣaṭ* (six): the term "upadeśa" (original enunciation) must be included in the definition of *ṣaṭ*. It should be stated that "in the original enunciation, a numeral ending in the letter *ṣ* or *n* receives the designation *ṣaṭ*. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of applying the augment *num* to *śata* and others, and the augment *nuṭ* to *aṣṭan*. [Examples: *śatāni*, *sahasrāṇi*. Once the augment *num* has been applied, the designation *ṣaṭ* would apply by the rule "those ending in *ṣ* or *n* are called *ṣaṭ*"; [this is prevented] by the inclusion of the term "upadeśa."

It does not occur. In the case of *aṣṭānām*, once the substitution of *ā* (for *aṣṭan*) has been applied, the designation *ṣaṣ* would not apply. It does, however, apply because of the inclusion of the term "original instruction" (*upadeśagrahaṇa*). Or rather, it has already been stated. What has been stated? First, regarding the forms *śatāni* and *sahasrāṇi*: "A grammatical operation conditioned by a specific configuration (*sannipātalakṣaṇa*) is not the cause for the destruction of that very configuration. This has also been stated regarding *aṣṭan*. What has been stated? "The mention of the long vowel [in the rule] for *aṣṭan*."

"The term *ṣaṭ* (six) is taught as a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for the purpose of applying the augment *nuṭ* to words ending in long *ā*. Alternatively, the long vowel *ā* itself is also indicated here; thus, a numeral ending in *ṣ*, *n*, or *ā* receives the designation *ṣaṭ*. "In that case, would this [designation] not also apply here: *sadhamadhaḥ*, *dyumnaḥ*, *ekāḥ*, *taḥ*, *ekāḥ*? "This is not a fault. This word *eka* has multiple meanings. There is indeed a usage where it is a numeral term, as in: *ekaḥ*..."
"Two" and "many": there is also a word expressing "without a companion," such as *ekāgnayaḥ* (those who maintain a single fire) and *ekahalāni* (single-ploughed fields).
"By those alone, by the lowly, victory was won"—this means "by those without companions. There is, however, another meaning in which it occurs. For example:

"One protects the offspring, one [protects] the strength"—here the meaning is "another. "The glorious ones are the sole sharers of the intoxication"—here the meaning is "others. This is the usage of that [word *ekā*] when it functions in this other sense.
But in this case, would it not then apply?
"By two and by twenty for the sake of the desired [form]. If that is so, then a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) will be made in the seventh [chapter]: "From *aṣṭan*, *auś*"; then "from six":

whatever was stated regarding "from eight" also applies from "six. Then "elision" (*luk*): elision also occurs from "six. Alternatively, a *yogavibhāga* will be made later: "for *aṣṭan*, *āt* before a case-ending"; then "for *rāya*."

In the case of the word *rāyaḥ*, there is the substitution of the vowel *ā* when followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*). The rule *hali* applies as a remainder for both [the preceding and following rules]. If this were so, forms such as *priyāṣṭau* and *priyāṣṭāḥ* would not be established, and forms such as *priyāṣṭānau* and *priyāṣṭānaḥ* would result. [The answer is: "According to the grammatical rules, [these forms apply] to words that are not actually used in common speech" (*yathālakṣaṇam aprayukte*).

This mention of *ḍati* is repeated twice: for the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "number" and for the technical designation of "six. One [of these] could be omitted. How so? If it is first performed for the designation of "number," it will not be performed for the designation of "six. Why? Because in the rule *ṣṇāntāḥ ṣaṭ*, the term *ḍati* will be understood by way of anuvṛtti (carrying over). On the other hand, if it is performed for the designation of "six"—

The designation *saṅkhyā* (number) will not be applied [here]. In the rule *ḍati ca*, the designation *saṅkhyā* will be carried over [as an anuvṛtti]. (P. 1.1.26) Regarding the designation *niṣṭhā*, there is a prohibition of words that are identical in form (*samānaśabda*). In the designation *niṣṭhā*, there is a prohibition of those words which are identical in sound.
It should be stated: "The *loṭ* [imperative] and the *garta* [grave]. Regarding the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *niṣṭhā*, there is no prohibition against identical sounds.

[Objection: Regarding the designation of *niṣṭhā*, there is a prohibition against identical sounds. [Reply: A prohibition that is purposeless is not a prohibition. Why does the designation of *niṣṭhā* not apply? Because the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) effects difference. An *anubandha* is applied; it will effect difference.

If it is argued that "an *anubandha* causes a change [in identity]," we say no, because of its elision (*lopa*). If it is argued that an *anubandha* causes a change [in identity], that is not so. What is the reason? Because of its elision. Here, the *anubandha* is elided; once the *anubandha* has been elided here, there will be no change [in identity]. For example:

"Which is Devadatta’s house? That one where that crow is. When the crow has flown away, that house is lost [from view]. In the same way here too, when the *anubandha* is elided, the suffix is considered lost. Even though it is elided, one still knows: "This technical designation (*saṃjñā*) was made for the form together with its *anubandha*. Just as it is in other cases as well:

"Which is Devadatta’s house? That one where that crow is. Even if the crow flies away and that house is no longer visible, he nevertheless knows that location in the end. Furthermore, there is the subversion of what is established;
that is, even if he knows it, doubt arises in him.

This is that word "ta": "the well has collapsed" (*lotaḥ gartaḥ*); this is that word "ta": "it has been cut off" (*lūnaḥ*) or "swallowed" (*gīrṇaḥ*). Just as in other cases: "Which is Devadatta’s house? That one where that crow is. Even if the crow flies away and that house is lost to sight, he nevertheless knows that location; yet a doubt arises for him:

"This is that house, this is that house. If that is so, then [the desired form] is established through the specific distinctions of the *kāraka* (participant) and tense (*kāla*). The specific distinctions of *kāraka* and tense must be taken into account. The suffix *ta*, which occurs in the past tense, applies to the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), and the impersonal state (*bhāva*). This is just as it is elsewhere:
a person who acts with foresight, by means of an unstable cause, [perceives] a stable cause.
One takes up an altar or a lotus. Even so, [the rule] would apply here in the case of *prākīrṣṭa*, because the *sij* affix and others are seen in the *luṅ* tense.

It will not apply because the *sij* affix and others are seen in the *luṅ* tense. But where the *sij* affix and others are not seen, as in *prābhitta*? The *sij* affix and others are seen there as well. Is this something that needs to be stated? No, it need not be stated. How so, if it is not being stated?
It will be understood as follows: just as this [grammarian] understands these specific agents and tenses even though they are not explicitly taught, so too he ought to understand this:
that where the *sij* and other affixes do not occur.

Regarding the rule *sarvādīni*: what kind of compound is this? He says it is a *bahuvrīhi*. What is its analysis (*vigraha*)? It is: "those for which the word *sarva* is the first. If this is so, the designation of pronoun (*sarvanāma-saṃjñā*) would not apply to the word *sarva*. Why? Because a *bahuvrīhi* has another word as its referent (*anyapadārtha*). This *bahuvrīhi* [refers] to a meaning other than the words [it is composed of].

It occurs. Therefore, whatever else remains apart from the word "all" (*sarva*) would obtain the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). For example, when it is said, "Let Citragu be brought," he who possesses those cows is brought, not the cows themselves. This is not a fault;
for in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is also "cognition of its qualities" (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*). As for example:

"Bring the one with variegated clothing. "The priests, wearing red turbans, proceed [with the sacrifice]. That which possesses those qualities is brought; and those who possess those qualities proceed.
(P_1,1.27.2) Regarding the rule *iha sarvanāmāni*, the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] would apply by the rule *pūrvapadāt sañjñāyām agaḥ*. Of that...

An objection must be raised: [if the rule were applied as stated,] there would be an absence of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) due to the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*). [The response is: Due to the technical designation of "pronominal," there will be no *ṇatva* because of a specific rule of exception (*nipātana*). What is this thing called an "exception"? And what is this thing called an "objection"? Having stated something in a general sense, it is subsequently stated that it is "not" so in a specific case. In that context, the intention of the Teacher is clearly understood.

"This does not occur"—an irregular formation (*nipātana*) of this kind is precisely for that purpose. Having stated the substitution of *ṇ* without distinction, an irregular formation is then made with specific restriction. In that case, the teacher’s intention is clearly understood as:
"this does not occur. But surely, by virtue of the irregular formation, there would be the absence of *ṇ*, while the substitution of *ṇ* would remain as it was originally obtained?

Are there other instances of this kind? Here, by the rule *ikaḥ yaṇ aci*, both the *yaṇ* substitution would occur and the original *ik* vowel would also be heard as it was. This is not a fault; there is a distinction here. In this case, a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is employed for the reference. Furthermore, the genitive case displaces the original element (*sthānin*). What then of this instance: [text missing] ?

Because of the rule "the suffix *śyan* is applied after [roots] beginning with *div* when the agent is expressed," the suffix *śyan* would apply, and the suffix *śap* would also be heard as it occurs by default.
This is not a fault, for *śyan* and the others will be treated as substitutes (*ādeśa*) for *śap*. If that is so, then the mention of *śap* must be made.

It need not be made; the previously stated [rule] continues to apply. Where was it stated? In the rule "the suffix *śap* is applied when the agent is expressed. But that [term *śap*] was mentioned in the nominative case.

And here, the meaning is determined by what is indicated in the genitive case. This fifth [ablative] case in *divādibhyaḥ* will effect a transformation of the first [nominative] case *śap* into a genitive:

"from that" (*tasmāt*) [is used] for what follows. This is a rule for the prescription of an affix (*pratyayavidhi*). And in a rule for the prescription of an affix, fifth cases do not function as transformers [of other case endings]. This is not a rule for the prescription of an affix; rather, the affix has already been prescribed.

And the original [rule] continues to apply here as well. In this case, then, regarding the rule *avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ*: because of the explicit statement (*vacana*), *akac* would be applied, and the *ka* [of the original suffix] would also be heard as it was originally obtained.
This is not a fault. For *akac* is introduced when *ka* has not yet been established; therefore, it will be the sublater (*bādhaka*). It is an irregularity (*nipātana*).
Even in such cases, the irregularity (*nipātana*) is not undertaken when the substitution of *ṇatva* has not yet been reached; therefore, it will serve as an exception (*bādhaka*).

If, however, irregularities are of this same kind, then there is a fault in the case of *samaḥ tate*. Here, other grammarians undertake the optional elision (*vibhāṣā lopa*) of *samaḥ* when followed by *tate*.
For it is equal in both cases: *satatam*,
*santatam*, and *sahitam*.

Regarding the word *saṃhitam*: here, however, you desire the elision of the *m* by means of a nipātana (irregular formation), as in the case of *aparaspārāḥ* when there is continuity of action; yet you also accept the non-elision as it stands in the form *santatam*. This is not established. An effort must be made in this matter, for nipātanās serve only as exceptions that override [the general rules].

Prohibition regarding technical terms (*saṃjñā*) and subordinate members (*upasarjana*). A prohibition must be stated for those words beginning with *sarva* when they function as technical terms or as subordinate members. For example: "A certain person is named *Sarva*; give to that *Sarva*" (*sarvo nāma kaścit; tasmai sarvāya dehi*). Or: "Give to one who has surpassed all" (*atisarvāya dehi*). How is this so?

An exclusion (*paryudāsa*) must be made based on the recitation. The designation (*sañjñā*) applies only to those [words] that have been recited. Therefore, the exclusion must be made based on the recitation itself; the designation must be applied only to those pure items that have been recited. "The words beginning with *sarva* receive the designation of pronoun (*sarvanāman*). Those that have become subordinate members (*upasarjanībhūta*) are not included among the words beginning with *sarva*. Is this so without distinction? He says: "No. It is so even with distinction. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of the grammatical operations (*kārya*) that apply immediately after the words beginning with *sarva*.

[The rule] stating that for the words beginning with *sarva*, whatever grammatical operation (*kārya*) is prescribed [to apply] immediately [after them], should not also apply when they have become subordinate members (*upasarjana*) of a technical name (*saṃjñā*). What is the purpose? The purpose is for the substitution of *at* in place of *ḍatara* and the others. The purpose is for the substitution of *at* in place of *ḍatara* and the others:
"This Brahmin family has surpassed [others]; which one is it? (*atikrāntam idaṃ brāhmaṇakulaṃ kataram*).

"An excessively eminent Brāhmaṇa family. And regarding the rule for *tyad* and so forth (*tyadādividhi*). There is a purpose for the rule for *tyad* and so forth: "This Brāhmaṇa has passed beyond [others]; he is an *atitat* Brāhmaṇa. First of all, the prohibition regarding technical names (*saṃjñā*) need not be stated. A division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) will be made later: "The terms *pūrva*, *para*, *avara*, *dakṣiṇa*, *uttara*, *apara*, and *adhara* [are used] when there is a restriction (*vyavasthā*). From that [follows]:

Regarding the term *asañjñāyām*: those [words] enumerated as beginning with *sarva* which occur in the context of "not being a name" (*asañjñāyām*) are to be understood in this way. Furthermore, the prohibition concerning secondary members (*upasarjana*) need not be formulated. This rule (*yoga*) beginning with *anupasarjanāt* is rejected.
We shall connect it [with the present rule] in this manner:

"Anupasarjana a at. What is this "a at"? The two *a*-sounds (*akāra*) that remain [in the rule] should be understood as referring to what is not an *upasarjana*. If this is so, then forms such as *atiyuṣmat* and *atyasmat* would not be established.
This is a *praśliṣṭanirdeśa* (a compound-like reading):
"anupasarjana a a at. The two *a*-sounds that remain [in the rule] should be understood as referring to what is not an *upasarjana*, following a word ending in *a* and a word beginning with *a*.

Alternatively, that which is stated under the heading of "members" (*aṅga*) applies to the case-ending that is being perceived. If this were so, then in the cases *paramapañca* and *paramasapta*, the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *ṣaḍbhyaḥ luk* would not apply. This is not a fault, for in this compound, the number six (*ṣaṣ*) is the primary element. In that case, however, in the example *priyasakthnā brāhmaṇena*, the substitution of *anaṅ* would not apply. [This is because the rule] specifies that which is indicated by the locative case...

It is said: that [substitution] occurs when the case-ending (vibhakti) of the present context is applied. If this is so, then in the forms *atitat*, *atitadau*, and *atitadaḥ*, the substitution of *a* would result;
and that too must be stated. It need not be stated. For in this case, first, *adḍ* [is substituted].

In the rule *ḍatarādibhyaḥ pañcabhyaḥ*, the word *pañcabhyaḥ* is in the ablative case, while *aṅgasya* is in the genitive case. Since they possess different case endings, it is impossible for the ablative *ḍatarādibhyaḥ* to qualify the genitive *aṅga*. Under these circumstances, what else could possibly be qualified other than the suffix that is prescribed? [The answer is: "that which is prescribed after *ḍatara* and the others. Now, in this context of *asthi*, *dadhi*, *sakthi*, and *akṣi*:

Regarding the rule *anaṅ udāttaḥ* ("the substitute *anaṅ* is acute"): since there are genitive forms such as *tyadādīnām aḥ bhavati*, *asthyādīnām*, and *aṅgasya*, as well as genitive forms such as *tyadādīnām* and *aṅgasya*, there is freedom of choice (*kāmacāra*). That is, one may either qualify the case-ending by means of that which is being grasped (*gṛhyamāṇa*), or qualify it by means of the stem (*aṅga*). Since there is such freedom, we shall here qualify the case-ending by means of the stem in the rule *asthidadhisakhthyakṣṇām anaṅ udāttaḥ*.

By means of [the rule] "anaṅ for *asthi* etc.," it is understood that *anaṅ* occurs in place of the final vowel of the stem (*aṅga*) when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows, specifically for stems beginning with *asthi*. Now, in this context, regarding the rule "for *tyad* etc., *aḥ* occurs," we shall qualify the case-ending by means of the stem (*aṅga*), so that *aḥ* replaces the final vowel of the stem when a case-ending follows: "for *tyad* etc., *aḥ* occurs in place of the final vowel of the stem when a case-ending follows. If this is the case, then [in the word] *atisaḥ*:

[Objection: You do not obtain the substitution of *atva* (the replacement of *sma* by *at*). [Response: This is not a fault. This compound has *tyad* and so forth as its predominant element. Alternatively, this is not a formal technical name (*saṃjñā*); rather, it is a qualifier for the recitation: "those which are the names of all [things] are the *sarvādi* [words]. And both the technical name and the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) remain restricted to their specific scope. If this is so, then that grammatical operation which depends upon the technical name does not succeed;
namely, [the rule] "for a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), *smai* [is substituted for the nominative-accusative dual ending]."
Regarding the rule *āmi sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ*, it should be understood there as a definition-based (*anvartha*) designation:

that which is the name for all things is a "sarvanāman" (pronominal). For a sarvanāman, the case ending *ṅe* becomes *smai*. For a sarvanāman, the suffix *ām* receives the augment *suṭ*. If this is so, then [the words] *sakalam* and *kṛtsnam*—
In this case, [the designation *sarvanāman*] would also apply to the word *jagat*. Furthermore, each of these words has its own respective referent (*viṣaya*).

For whichever word occurs in whichever particular referent, that word, while occurring in that referent, would undergo the grammatical operations prescribed for *sarvanāman*. If that is so, then both [functions] are performed by this [sūtra]: the recitation [of the word *jagat*] is indeed specified.

And the designation (*sañjñā*). But how can both be obtained by a single effort? He says: they are obtained. How? Because of the indication by means of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one from among identical items). This is an indication by *ekaśeṣa*: "sarvādīni" and "sarvādīni" [together] become "sarvādīni"; "sarvanāmāni" and "sarvanāmāni" [together] become "sarvanāmāni. Thus, the group beginning with *sarva* receives the designation "sarvanāman" (pronoun). And those which are the names of all...

Those [words] beginning with *sarva* remain restricted to specific [meanings], as do [words] that are technical names (*saṃjñā*) or secondary members (*upasarjana*). Alternatively, this technical name is made extensive; for a technical name is not something to be made concise. Why is that? Because the purpose of making a technical name is for the sake of brevity. In that case, [the purpose of] the extensive [name]...

The purpose of this rule regarding the formation of the technical name (*sañjñā*) is so that it may be understood as a term based on its meaning (*anvarthasañjñā*). [The words] beginning with *sarva* receive the designation "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*) because they are the names (*nāma*) of all things; therefore, they are called "pronominals. Furthermore, both the technical name and the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) remain restricted to their specific meanings.

286–289. Now, what is the purpose of *ubha* being a pronoun (*sarvanāman*)? [The purpose] of *ubha* being a pronoun is for the sake of the suffix *akaC*. When the reading "for the sake of *akaC*" is made regarding *ubha* being a pronoun, it results in the form *ubhakau*. Why is it said that it is "for the sake of *akaC*" and not that other operations of pronouns also apply? There is an absence of others because it is the domain of the dual number and the feminine suffix *ṭāP*. There is an absence of other operations of pronouns. What is the reason? Because it is the domain of the dual number and the feminine suffix *ṭāP*.

This word *ubha* is restricted to the dual number and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Other pronominal operations (*sarvanāmakārya*) are prescribed for it in the singular and plural numbers. But when this word *ubha* is restricted to the dual and *ṭāp*, what then occurs elsewhere? Elsewhere, it becomes *ubhaya*. The form *ubhaya* occurs for it elsewhere; for example, *ubhaye devamanuṣyāḥ* ("both gods and humans").

"Both [forms] would be *ubhaya-maṇi*. Furthermore, what would happen if *akac* were not applied here? What would be the consequence? And what now is the difference between *ka* and *kakac*? It has been stated that this word *ubha* is restricted to the domain of the dual number and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. In that case, when *akac* is present, because it falls within the middle of that [base], it can be said: [that both forms would result].
"This [suffix] occurs when followed by a dual ending. But in what case would it not be followed by a dual ending? In that case, its being followed by a dual ending must be stated.

Well then, just as it would not be followed by a dual ending in the presence of *ke*, so too it would not be followed by a dual ending in the presence of *āpi*; therefore, its being followed by a dual ending must be stated even there. [Reply: Even without such a statement, it is understood that it is followed by that [dual ending].
Even without an explicit statement, this [suffix] will be followed by a dual ending (*dvivacana*). What need is there to state this? Indeed, there is none.

How is it understood when it is not explicitly stated? Once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, this [suffix] is followed by a dual ending by virtue of the rule regarding "the end and the beginning" (*antādivadbhāva*).

If it is argued that the understanding of it being followed by that [dual] occurs even without a statement because of the absence of such a statement, then the same applies to *ke* as well. Because of the absence of a statement, the understanding of it being followed by that [dual] occurs.

If it is argued that even without an explicit statement, [the suffix] will be one that follows a dual form—how so? Because derivative suffixes (*svārthika-pratyaya*) are not distinct from their base forms (*prakṛti*), the mention of the base form includes the derivative suffixes as well. Now, what are the purposes served by *bhavat* being a pronoun (*sarvanāman*)? [The purposes are]: *akac*, *śeṣa*, and *ātva* for *bhavat*. [Examples: *bhavataḥ*.
The purposes for the suffixes *akac* and *ātva* are as follows.
*Akac*: *bhavakān*. *Śeṣaḥ*:
*saḥ ca bhavān ca bhavantau*. *Ātva*: [resulting in *bhavantau*].

"Like you. Now, is this an exhaustive enumeration or merely an illustration? He says it is merely an illustration; for [the use of] the third case and others is also desired. [As in: "by the reason that is 'you'"; here, from a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), the third case is employed.
"Because of your reason," [it is said].
(P_1,1.28) KA_I,90.5-26 Ro_I, 289-291 For what purpose is the mention of *dig*? One will state the prohibition "not in a *bahuvrīhi*"; in that case, it is not [necessary].

It is understood where there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) and where there is a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). However, when the mention of "direction" (*dig*) is made, no fault arises; for when direction is indicated, there is an option, and elsewhere there is a prohibition. Now, what is the purpose of mentioning "compound" (*samāsa*)? It is so that [the rule] may apply only to that which is a *bahuvrīhi* compound by its very nature, and not to that which is a *bahuvrīhi* by virtue of the treatment as a *bahuvrīhi* (i.e., through the application of the *tadvat* principle).

"Give it to the one who is most skillful on the right. Now, what is the purpose of including the term *bahuvrīhi*? It is so that [the rule] does not apply in a *dvandva* compound, as in "of the south, north, and east. This is not a valid purpose, for there will be a prohibition by the rule "and in a *dvandva*.

But this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is commenced when the prohibition has not yet taken effect; it applies specifically to the case of *bahuvrīhi*. Just as in the case of *bahuvrīhi*, [so too should it be here].
In this way, it would indeed subvert the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 2.4.13], namely that "also in a *dvandva* [compound]. It does not subvert it. What is the reason?

Subversion occurs only when [a rule] has not already taken effect (*aprāpte*). This *paribhāṣā* is not commenced when that prohibition—"not in a *bahuvrīhi*"—has not yet taken effect; however, in the case of "also in a *dvandva*," it is both already taken effect and not yet taken effect.

Or rather, since exceptions (apavāda) set aside the rules immediately preceding them, this option (*vibhāṣā*) will set aside the prohibition "not in a *bahuvrīhi*," but it will not set aside the prohibition "also not in a *dvandva*. Or again, first he must be asked this: why does [the suffix] not occur here?
That which is the east is the north for this person who is disoriented; thus he is "disoriented with respect to the east and north" (*pūrvottara-unmugdha*).

Give it to him, the one disoriented with respect to the east and north. [This is because of the rule: "Between that which is indicated by a general rule and that which is expressed by its specific form, the latter alone [is taken].

If this is so, there is no purpose in mentioning the *bahuvrīhi* compound. Why does it not apply in the case of a *dvandva*? Because of the rule: "Between that which is indicated by a general rule and that which is expressed by its specific form..."
[The objection: "Only for that which is explicitly stated [as a *bahuvrīhi*]. [Response: Then the mention of *bahuvrīhi* must be made for the sake of the subsequent rule. [Reply: It need not be made;
it is already included in the very word *bahuvrīhi*. [Objection:

A second mention must be made so that the rule applies only to that which is a *bahuvrīhi* by its own nature, and not to that which becomes a *bahuvrīhi* through the application of the *bahuvrīhi*-like treatment (*bahuvrīhivadbhāva*).
"Give it to each one individually. This too is not a purpose [for the rule]. The term "in a compound" (*samāse*) is understood [from the previous rule]; therefore, we shall qualify the *bahuvrīhi*:

"that which is a compound and is a *bahuvrīhi*. Well then, this is the purpose: so that there may be a prohibition even for a *bahuvrīhi* that constitutes a member [of a larger compound]. Let it not be the case here: "those for whom clothing is internal," i.e., *vastrāntarāḥ* (clothed). "Clothing" (*vasanam*).

The interval (*antara*) between these [two] is what is meant by *vasanāntara*; thus, *vasanāntara* refers both to an interval between garments (*vastra*) and an interval between coverings (*vasana*), hence the compound *vastrāntaravasanāntara*.

What is an example? *priyaviśvāya*. This is not a valid example, for there must be a prohibition of a *bahuvrīhi* compound whose final member begins with *sarva* and so forth; and this will be stated later.
Regarding the statement, "In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is an addition [to the rule] for pronouns and numerals," in that case, it should be *viśvapriyāya*. But then consider this:
*dvyanyāya*, *tryanyāya*. Is it not the case that here too, by the rule of prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*), the pronoun itself ought to come first? This is not a fault. He will state this:
in a *bahuvrīhi* compound consisting of a numeral and a pronoun, because of the principle of posteriority (*paratva*), the numeral takes the prior placement.

Thus [it is said]. And this example, *priyaviśva*, is also for the sake of those who hold that it should be *viśvapriya*. For he will say: "Or, [the suffix] after *priya*. Indeed, the prohibition does not necessarily apply only to a *bahuvrīhi* compound whose final member begins with *sarva* and so forth.

It must be so. But what then? It must also apply to words that do not begin or end with *sarva*. What is the purpose? So that *akac* does not occur. And what would happen if *akac* were to occur? [The form] *kaḥ* would not occur. But what now is the difference between *ka* and *kakac*? There is a difference in the case of words ending in consonants. For example: *ahakam* (I am) is his father—[the compound] is *makatpitṛkaḥ*.
[Otherwise], one would arrive at the form *tvakat-pitṛkaḥ* ("whose father is you"),

whereas *matkapitṛkaḥ* ("whose father is mine") and *tvatkapitṛkaḥ* ("whose father is yours") are what is desired. But how, even if you so desire, can an internal rule (*antaraṅga*) be set aside by an external prohibition (*bahiraṅga*), since "an external [rule] sets aside even internal rules"?
The rule *vidhiḥ bādhate gomatpriyaḥ* ("the rule sets aside [the prohibition] in the case of *gomatpriyaḥ*") shows that an effort is made there [to prevent the application of the prohibition];

namely, the rule *pratyayottarapadayoś ca*. But is not an effort also made here [in this very context], namely by the rule *na bahuvrīhau*? There is another purpose for stating this [separate rule]. What is it? It is for the sake of *priyaviśvāya*, by means of the prohibition concerning the *upasarjana*.

This is indeed established. This *bahuvrīhi* compound is indeed of two kinds: there is the primary type (*prāthamakalpika*) in which there is identity of word-form (*aikapadya*), identity of accent (*aikasvarya*), and identity of case-ending (*aikavibhaktikatva*). There is also the type where the name of the whole is applied to its parts because they serve that purpose (*tādarthyāt tācchabdyam*):

namely, words whose meaning is that of a *bahuvrīhi* are themselves called "the *bahuvrīhi*. This [usage] belongs to the latter, which is based on the application of the name of the whole to its constituent parts due to their serving that purpose.

293–294. An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made regarding that which was previously so in the case of a prohibition. An addition must be made regarding that which was previously so in the case of a prohibition: [e.g.,] "one who was formerly wealthy" (*āḍhyabhūtapūrva*) becomes *āḍhyapūrva*;

thus, one says, "Give to the one who was formerly wealthy" (*āḍhyapūrvāya dehi*). [Objection: The addition regarding that which was previously so in the case of a prohibition is unnecessary, because of the rule stating "of *pūrva* and the others, when used in a restrictive sense" (*pūrvādīnām vyavasthāyām*). [Response: The addition regarding that which was previously so in the case of a prohibition is not unnecessary. Why? Because...

The reason is that it is stated [in Pāṇini’s rule] "pūrvādīnām vyavasthāyām" (for *pūrva* and the others, when there is a restriction). The designation of pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is prescribed for *pūrva* and the others when there is a restriction; however, no such restriction is perceived here.

While the term "in a compound" (*samāse*) is already in force, what is the purpose of mentioning "compound" (*samāsa*) again? This third-case compound (*tṛtīyāsamāsa*) certainly exists as a primary (literal) sense, wherein there is oneness of word (*aikapadya*), oneness of accent (*aikasvarya*), and oneness of case-ending (*aikavibhaktikatva*). There is also a figurative usage based on the purpose (*tādarthyāt tācchabdyam*): words that serve the purpose of a third-case compound are called "the third-case compound. This mention refers to that figurative usage based on the purpose. Alternatively, while "in a compound" is in force, the purpose of mentioning "compound" again is...
This is the purpose:

so that the status of being a "limb of yoga" (*yogāṅga*) may arise. Once the status of being a limb of yoga exists, the analysis of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) will be performed. [The result is that] in a compound with the third case (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*), words beginning with *sarva* do not receive the designation of "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*). For example: *māsapūrvāya dehi* ("Give to one preceded by a month"), *saṃvatsarapūrvāya dehi* ("Give to one preceded by a year").

Therefore, in a non-compound (*asamāsa*), the words beginning with *sarva* do not receive the designation of pronominal (*sarvanāman*) when they follow a word in the third case. For example: *māsena pūrvāya*.
