298–299. The mention of *upasaṃvyāna* (the inner garment) is purposeless, because it is already accounted for by the rule regarding external connection (*bahiryoga*). [Objection: The mention of *upasaṃvyāna* is purposeless. What is the reason? Because it is already accounted for by the rule regarding external connection. It is already established by the very rule "in the case of external connection" (*bahiryoge*). [Response: Or rather, it is not purposeless, as it is for the sake of a pair of garments and so forth. Indeed, it is not purposeless. What is the reason? It is for the sake of a pair of garments and so forth; it is for the sake of a pair of garments and so forth.
In that case, this must be stated: where it is not known what is the inner garment and what is the upper garment.
Even in this regard, for that person who acts with foresight, it becomes clearly known: "This is the inner garment; this is the upper garment."

It should be stated that [the word] *puri* [is used]. Let it not apply here: *antarāyāṃ puri vasati* ("he lives in the inner city"). In the section concerning the optional rule (*vā-prakaraṇa*), there must be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the suffix *tīya* before case-endings beginning with *ṅ*. In the section concerning the optional rule, an addition must be made for the suffix *tīya* before case-endings beginning with *ṅ*.

[The forms] *dvitīyāyai*, *dvitīyasyai*, *tṛtīyāyai*, and *tṛtīyasyai* [are established]. The rule "optionally after *dvitīyā* and *tṛtīyā*" (*vibhāṣā dvitīyātṛtīyābhyām*) need not be stated. What, then, is better here? An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) is indeed better here. By this, the following is also established:
For the second, for that which is second; for the third, for that which is third. (P.
1.1.37) Why is a separate mention made of the *svarādi* group? Why could they not have been read among the *cādi* group instead? [Answer: Because of the *cādi* group...

The designation *nipāta* applies to those words denoting non-entities (*asattvavacana*), whereas for the words beginning with *svara*, the designation applies both to those denoting entities (*sattvavacana*) and those denoting non-entities.
Now, for what purpose are both designations applied? Why not let there be only the designation *nipāta*? It cannot be done in this way;

for it has been stated that "a monosyllabic *nipāta* other than *āṅ* is called *pragṛhya*. That [designation of *pragṛhya*] would then undesirably apply even to the monosyllabic words beginning with *svara*.
If that were the case, then let there be only the designation *avyaya* (indeclinable). But that is impossible. For he will say this:

"In the case of an *avyaya*, [the rule applies] to *nañ*, *ku*, and particles (*nipāta*). Consequently, one would have to provide an exhaustive enumeration (*parigaṇana*) by means of a more cumbersome formulation (*garīyasā nyāsena*). Therefore, they must be mentioned separately, and both designations must be established.

300–301: An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for those [words] that do not occur with all case-endings (*asarvavibhakti*) when they are not caused by a case-ending (*avibhaktinimitta*). An addition must be made for those that do not occur with all case-endings when they are not caused by a case-ending: namely *nānā* and *vinā*. But what is the reason it is not established? Because it applies to all case-endings without distinction. For this [suffix] occurs with all case-endings. Why? Because there is no distinction; because it is prescribed without distinction. And an addition must also be made for the suffixes beginning with *tral*.
And an addition must be made for *tral* and the others. In that regard, *tatra*, *yataḥ*, and *tataḥ* [are formed]. But surely these are prescribed specifically:
*tasil* after the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) and *tral* after the seventh case-ending (*saptamī*). To this he will say: "They are seen after other case-endings as well."

302-303 If, on the other hand, it were stated that "an indeclinable word is one that lacks case-endings (*avibhaktiḥ*)," then because of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*), the designation would not be established. Because of mutual dependence regarding the state of lacking case-endings, the designation [of "indeclinable"] would fail to be established.

What constitutes this mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*)? When there is the state of being devoid of case-endings (*avibhaktitva*), there must be a technical designation (*sañjñā*); and by means of that designation, the state of being devoid of case-endings is brought about. Thus, it becomes a case of mutual dependence, and grammatical operations (*kāryāṇi*) involving mutual dependence do not take effect. Alternatively, [the word *avyaya*] is without gender (*aliṅga*) and without number (*asaṅkhya*). Or rather, it is without gender.

It should be stated that [the terms] "innumerable" (*asaṅkhya*) and "imperishable" (*avyaya*) [apply]. Even so, this results in a circular dependency (*itaretarāśraya*). What is this circular dependency? When there is the state of being without gender and number, there must be a technical name (*saṃjñā*); and by means of that technical name, the state of being without gender and number is brought about. Thus, it becomes a circular dependency.

Furthermore, effects that depend upon one another cannot be logically established. This lack of gender (*aliṅgatā*) and number (*asaṅkhyatā*) is not something based on scriptural injunction (*vācanika*); rather, it is inherent (*svābhāvika*). For example: among those who exert equal effort and study equally, some are successful in their goals while others are not. In such a case, what can we do? This is inherent. Therefore, it must be stated that [the word *brahman*] is without gender and without number. [Objection: No.

It must be stated. But it is established by the recitation [of the sūtras]. This is established by the recitation. How should the recitation be performed? "The suffixes beginning with *tasil* and ending before *pāśap*, and those beginning with *śas* and ending before the *samāsānta* suffixes."
The suffix *mān*,
the sense of "times" (*kṛtvas-artha*),
and the suffixes *tasi* and *vat*.
Regarding the rule *nānāñau* (P. 1.1.38):
Alternatively, let it be that a word which lacks case endings (*avibhaktika*) receives the designation *avyaya*. But is this not so?

And it has been said that [the definition] is unestablished because of mutual dependence when the case-endings are not present. This is not a fault. First, this person must be asked: although grammarians, when beginning their work on the elision of case-endings, employ words devoid of endings, how do those other people who are not grammarians employ words devoid of endings?
They employ [these terms] as follows: furthermore, worldly supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) refer to objects such as oneness and so forth. And for this reason, there are supernormal knowledges:
for by one price they buy one cow, and by another, two.
Others [employ] three [cases], and they do not employ the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Let this be observed in this way:
the nature of the meaning here is such that no case-ending (*vibhakti*) occurs. Furthermore, let this be understood accordingly:
some indeclinables (*avyaya*) have the meaning of a case-ending as their primary sense, while others have action as their primary sense. For example, *uccaiḥ*.

The word *nīcaiḥ* is primarily expressive of the meaning of a case ending (*vibhaktyartha*), whereas *hiruk* and *pṛthak* are primarily expressive of an action (*kriyā*). Among secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) as well, some are primarily expressive of the meaning of a case ending and some are primarily expressive of an action. In this regard, *yatra* is primarily expressive of the meaning of a case ending, while *nānā* and *vina* are primarily expressive of an action. Furthermore, these two types of meanings do not possess connection with gender (*liṅga*) or number (*saṅkhyā*).

(P_1,1.38.4) KA_I,95.23-96.5 Ro_I, 304-307 Now, even if it is said that [the word *sarvanāman*] does not take all case-endings (*asarvavibhakti*), even so there is no fault. How? Even now, this much is done in abundance:
"The singular number is used for one thing, the dual for two, and the plural for many."

"The dual number is used for two things, and the plural number for many. How then [is it explained]? The singular number shall be established as the general rule (*utsarga*). For that [singular], the dual and plural numbers will serve as exceptions (*bādhaka*) when applied to the meanings of duality and plurality.
Nor, moreover, will the analysis (*vigraha*) be formulated in this way:
"Not all" means "not every";

[the compound] *asarvā vibhaktayaḥ* means "case-endings that are not all. How then? It is "not all" because "a case-ending (*vibhakti*) that is not all" occurs after this [word]. Furthermore, the technical term *vibhakti* applies to a triplet (of suffixes). This being the case, the same principle applies to *kṛt* suffixes as well.

This inclusion [of the suffix] *mān* is for the sake of its specific grammatical operation; it is not intended there [in that context]. Furthermore, the three desired operations involving *kṛt*-suffixes should follow after that. However, regarding the inclusion of *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes, it must be stated that "there is a prohibition" for those which are based upon a specific number. Let this not apply here: *ekaḥ*.
"Two," "many"— therefore, the inclusion of the vowels and so forth must be made, as well as the recitation of the primary derivatives (*kṛt*) and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*).

By means of the recitation [of the sūtra], this designation as an indeclinable (*avyayasañjñā*) is established. That [designation] does not apply here in the cases of *paramoccaiḥ* and *paramanīcaiḥ*. It will apply by means of the rule of extension to what ends with that (*tadantavidhi*). But then it would also apply here: [e.g., *atyuccais*].

[The forms] *atyuccaiḥ*, *atyuccaisau*, and *atyuccaisaḥ* [are derived from *aty-uccais*]. There will be a prohibition [of the designation *sarvanāman*] by the rule "not for a subordinate member" (*upasarjanasya na*).

Well then, that prohibition must be stated. It need not be stated; the prohibition established in the context of the technical designation *sarvanāman* will carry over here. Indeed, that [prohibition] is rejected in that [original] context. Just as it is rejected there...

Here too, it can be rejected in the same way. How is it rejected there? A very long technical name (saṃjñā) is being made. But this [other] technical name is also being made as something very long. And a technical name should not be anything other than concise. Why is that? For the purpose of brevity is the making of technical names. In that case, regarding the making of a long technical name, this...
The purpose [of this definition] is so that the technical name may be understood according to its literal meaning:

that which "does not pass away" (*na vyeti*) is called "indeclinable" (*avyaya*). But where does it not pass away? It does not pass away from the genders—feminine, masculine, and neuter—nor from the qualities of being, nor from singularity, duality, and plurality.
Some things pass away from these states, while others do not; that which does not pass away is the indeclinable. It remains constant.
That which does not change across the three genders, all case endings (*vibhakti*), and all numbers (*vacana*) is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
(Pāṇini 1.1.39) How is this [sūtra] to be understood?

Does this mean "a *kṛt* suffix that ends in *m*" or "a *kṛdanta* [word] that ends in *m*"? What follows from this? On the other hand, if it is understood as "a *kṛdanta* [word] that ends in *m*," then it would also apply in cases such as *pratāmau* and *pratāmaḥ*. It is as you wish.

Let it be. For now, let it be that [the suffix] *kṛt* has the marker *m*. But how [does one derive] *kārayām cakāra* and *hārayām cakāra*? Furthermore, what is sought here by means of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) "indeclinable" (*avyaya*)? [It is so that] the elision (*luk*) may occur according to the rule *avyayāt*. Let it not be thus. It will be accomplished by the rule *āmaḥ*. It is not established. Because the mention of *li* (the marker *l*) follows there. The mention of *li*...
It will be withdrawn. If it were withdrawn, elision (*luk*) would apply to the suffix alone; and this is indeed desired for the suffix alone.
Moreover, it is so intended, for thus he says:
"And *kṛ* is employed after [the root] in the *liṭ* [perfect]. If, however, elision of the suffix alone occurs, then this [statement] is justified.
Or rather, let it be that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix and contains the letter *m*. How then [do we account for] *pratāmau*, *pratāmaḥ*?

The activity of the Teacher indicates that the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) does not occur by virtue of the characteristic of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), since he recites the word *praśān* among the *svarādi* group.

(P_1,1.39.2) Kṛt suffixes ending in a consonant (*mejanta*) and those whose base is not *i*, *u*, or *ū* [are termed *sarvanāmasthāna*]. It should be stated: "Kṛt suffixes ending in a consonant and those whose base is not *i*, *u*, or *ū*. This is so that [the designation does] not apply here:
*ādhaye*, *ādheḥ*.

[The forms] *cikīrṣave* and *cikīrṣoḥ* [are explained]. Or rather, [the rule] "that which does not have another as its base" [is intended]. Alternatively, it should be stated that "that which does not have another as its base becomes designated as a *kṛt*-suffix and an indeclinable (*avyaya*). What, then, is better here? The statement regarding "not having another as its base" is indeed better. By this, the following is also established:

[The examples] "kumbhakārebhyaḥ" and "nagarakārebhyaḥ" [are cited]. In that case, it must be stated [as a rule]. Or rather, it need not be stated. Why? Because a grammatical operation (*vidhi*) characterized by a coalescence (*sannipāta*) does not serve as the cause for the destruction of that very coalescence.
It need not be stated. What is the reason? A grammatical operation characterized by a coalescence is not the cause for the destruction of that [coalescence].

The technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "of its prevention" (*tadvighātasya*) must be formulated. But what is the distinction here: should this *paribhāṣā* be made, or should it be stated that "it has no other base-form" (*ananyaprakṛti*)? This *paribhāṣā* must certainly be formulated, for there are many purposes served by it. What, then, are they? The purpose is [to prevent] the application of the *tuṅ* augment after a short vowel, as in *grāmaṇikulam*. [In the case of] *grāmaṇikulam*,...

In the case of *senānikula*, once the shortening (*hrasvatva*) has been applied, the rule "a *tuK* augment occurs before a *kṛt* suffix beginning with a *pit* vowel after a short vowel" would apply, resulting in the insertion of *tuK*. However, there is no fault here because of the principle: "A grammatical operation conditioned by a specific configuration (*sannipātalakṣaṇa*) does not cause the destruction of that very configuration. This is not a valid purpose [for the rule], for the shortening is external (*bahiraṅga*), whereas the *tuK* augment is internal (*antaraṅga*). And that which is external is considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*) in relation to that which is internal.

In the case of *vṛtrahabhiḥ* and *bhrūṇahabhiḥ*, when the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) has been applied, the rule "the augment *tuk* occurs before a *pit* *kṛt* suffix after a short vowel" would result in the application of *tuk*. However, there is no fault here because of the principle: "A grammatical operation conditioned by a specific configuration [of sounds] does not become the cause for the destruction of that very configuration. This also applies here.

There is no purpose [in this objection]. The elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). Because it is unestablished, [the rule] will not apply. The state of having *u* as a penultimate letter (*udupadhatva*) is not a cause for the absence of *kṛt* suffixes marked with *k* (*akittva*) in the case of *nikucita*. Where? In *nikucita*. Here, once the elision of *n* has been applied in the word *nikucitaḥ*, the absence of *k* would apply by the rule "after a root with *u* as its penultimate letter, when expressing a state or a passive/reflexive action, [the *kṛt* suffix is optional]."

The rule characterized by the conjunction [of causes] is without cause for its own sublation; thus, there is no fault. This too serves no purpose. Let there be the status of *akittva* (non-*kit*) here. The prohibition "not when there is elision of a verbal root (*dhātulopa*) before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix" will apply.

The substitution of *nā* for *na* is not the cause for the lengthening of the vowel in the case of the *yañ* suffix. The substitution of *nā* for *na* is not the cause for the lengthening of the vowel in the case of the *yañ* suffix.

Where? When *nā* has been substituted by this [rule], then the lengthening prescribed by the rule "yañi supi ca" would apply. However, there is no fault, because of the principle that "a grammatical operation conditioned by a specific configuration does not cause the destruction of that very configuration. This also is not a valid purpose, for he will say this:

Regarding the statement "na mu ṭādeśe" (the substitution of *mu* does not occur when there is an *ā* substitute): the substitution of *ā* is not the cause for the *kittva* (the status of having a *k*-marker). Where? In the example "upādāsta asya svaraḥ śikṣakasya. Once the substitution of *ā* has been made, the rule "sthāghvoḥ it ca" would require the substitution of *it*. [The answer is: There is no fault, because a grammatical operation conditioned by a specific configuration (*sannipātalakṣaṇa*) is not the cause for the destruction of that very configuration. This also applies here.
There is no purpose [for this objection]. This has already been stated:

"The prohibition of *dīṅ* applies to the substitution of *it* for *sthā* and *ghu*. The forms *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* are not causes for the application of the suffix *ṅīp*. For example: *tisras tiṣṭhanti*, *catasras tiṣṭhanti*. Once the substitution of *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* has been effected...

The suffix *ṅīp* would apply by the rule "after *ṛn*, *ṅīp*. [Objection: There is no fault, because "a grammatical operation conditioned by a specific configuration (*sannipātalakṣaṇa*) does not cause the destruction of that very configuration. [Reply: Even this is not a valid purpose. The activity of the Teacher indicates that the suffix *ṅīp* does not occur once the forms *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* have been produced, since he prohibits the lengthening of the vowel in strong cases (*nāmi*) for these words with the rule "not for *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*."

[The author] teaches: "In that case, these are the purposes [of the rule]: hundreds, thousands. When the *num* suffix is applied, the designation *ṣaṭ* (six) would apply by the rule "those ending in *ṣ* or *n* are called *ṣaṭ*. There is no fault, because a grammatical operation conditioned by a specific configuration (*sannipātalakṣaṇa*) does not become the cause for the destruction of that very configuration. [Examples: *śakaṭau*, *paddhatau*. When the substitution of *at* has been made...

Therefore, the suffix *ṭāp* would apply [to the vowel *i*]. However, there is no fault, because "a rule conditioned by a specific combination [of sounds] (*sannipātalakṣaṇa*) is not the cause for the destruction of that very combination. Thus, in *iyeṣa* and *uvoṣa*, once *guṇa* has been applied, the suffix *ām* would apply by the rule "after a root beginning with *ij* and having a heavy syllable, except for *ṛcch*" (*ijādeśca gurumato 'nṛcchaḥ*). This is because it is conditioned by a specific combination.

The rule is not a cause for its own obstruction; thus there is no fault. The fault of that [rule] is that a suffix depending on a phoneme (*varṇāśraya*) is not a cause for the displacement of a phoneme (*varṇavicāla*). This fault of the present definition would mean that a suffix depending on a phoneme is not a cause for the displacement of a phoneme. Where? For example, in *dākṣiḥ* derived from *ata iñ*.

Plākṣi says: [The suffix] is not a condition characterized by immediate contiguity (*sannipātalakṣaṇa*). In that case, the designation of the stem (*aṅgasañjñā*) would not be the cause [for the application of a rule]. The substitution of *ā* [for the final vowel of the root] in the context of the prescription of *puk* [augment], as in *krāpayati*, would then not be the cause for the prescription of *puk*. Where? In *krāpayati*. The *puk* augment in the context of the shortening [of the penultimate vowel], as in *adīdapat*, would then not be the cause for the shortening. Where? In *adīdapat*. [Furthermore,] the *a* of the pronouns beginning with *tyad*...

Regarding the rule for *ṭāp*: the vowel *a* of words such as *tyad* would not be a cause for the application of *ṭāp*. Where? In the case of *yā sā*. Regarding the rule for *iṭ*: it would not be a cause for the elision of the long *ā*. Where? In the cases of *papivān* and *tasthivān*. Regarding the acute accent on the suffix *matup* and the case endings: they would not be causes for the suppression of the preceding word’s accent (*pūrvanighāta*). Where? [In the examples where this suppression applies.]

[The sūtra] *agnimān vāyumān paramavācā paramavāce* [is cited]. Regarding the shortening of a *nadī* stem, this would not be the cause for the elision of the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi-lopa*). Where? In the cases of *nadi*, *kumāri*, *kiśori*, *brāhmaṇi*, and *brahmabandhu*. Once the shortening has been applied, the elision [of the vocative suffix] prescribed by the rule *eṅhrasvāt sambuddheḥ* would not apply. Let it not be so; [the elision applies] from that which ends in a *ṅī* suffix.
Thus it would be; [the rule] does not succeed. It is stated that [the elision occurs] "after a long vowel," yet it does not apply after one ending in a short vowel.
This must be considered here:

should the shortening be performed first, or the elision of the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi*)? What should be done in this case? The shortening takes precedence because it is [prescribed by a rule] of higher priority.

The elision of the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi-lopa*) is permanent (*nitya*). It applies whether the shortening (*hrasvatva*) has occurred or not. [Objection: The elision of the vocative suffix is not permanent; for it does not apply once the shortening has occurred. What is the reason? Because "a rule conditioned by a specific combination [of sounds] (*sannipāta-lakṣaṇo vidhiḥ*) is not a cause for the destruction of that very combination. These faults are equal or even greater [in both views]. Therefore, there is no purpose in this *paribhāṣā*.

Indeed, one should not make a rule stating that "faults do not exist," nor should a definition be formulated to that effect. For it is not the case that because there are no beggars, cooking pots are not placed on the fire; nor is it the case that because there are no deer, barley is not sown. Furthermore, the faults have indeed been enumerated in their entirety; this [list] is merely an illustration of the purposes. Why is this so? Because... [the text continues].

There are defects [in this rule]. Therefore, for the sake of those purposes which this technical rule (paribhāṣā) serves, this paribhāṣā must be formulated, and a remedy must be applied against the defects.
