The purpose of the indeclinability (*avyayatva*) of an *avyayībhāva* compound is [to ensure] the elision (*luk*), the accent on the first member (*mukhasvara*), and its treatment as an indeclinable (*upacāra*). What is the purpose of the indeclinability of the *avyayībhāva*? [It is] the elision, the accent on the first member, and its treatment as an indeclinable. Regarding elision (*luk*): in *upāgni* and *pratyagni*, the elision [of the case-ending] is established by the rule "after an indeclinable" (*avyayād*). Regarding the accent on the first member (*mukhasvara*): in *upāgnimukhaḥ* and *pratyagnimukhaḥ*, the prohibition [of the accent on the first member] established by the rule "not after an indeclinable, a word denoting direction, *go*, *mahat*, *sthūla*, *pṛthu*, or *vatsa*" becomes applicable. Regarding its treatment as an indeclinable (*upacāra*): [this applies when it functions as an indeclinable].

"upapayaḥkāraḥ" and "upapayaḥkāmaḥ. Therefore, the prohibition established by the rule "anavyayasya" [Pāṇini 8.3.46]—which states that the substitution of *ṣatva* does not occur after an indeclinable when followed by *kṛ*, *ka*, *mi*, *kaṃsa*, *kumbha*, *pātra*, *kuśā*, or *karṇī*—is thus validated.
But is this a complete enumeration (*parigaṇana*), or is it merely illustrative (*udāharaṇamātra*)? It is a complete enumeration.

Thus he said. Furthermore, they indeed say: "Whatever else is applicable to an *avyayībhāva* compound as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) formation, its prohibition must be stated. What, then, is that? It is the status of being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*). Regarding the status of being like a subordinate member, the prohibition of indeclinables has been enjoined for such purposes as "reading loudly" (*uccair adhīyāna*) and "reading softly" (*nīcair adhīyāna*). That [prohibition] would also apply here.

The mention of "indeclinables" (*avyaya*) in the rule for *akac* is made for the sake of forms such as *uccakaiḥ* and *nīcakaiḥ*. Consequently, that [application of *akac*] would also apply here in the cases of *upāgnikam* and *pratyagnikam*. Furthermore, a prohibition regarding *avyayas* is stated in the rule for *mum*: *doṣāmanyam ahaḥ*.
The purpose [of the rule] is so that one may think "it is day" when it is night. This [suffix] would also apply here:

*aupakumbhamanyaḥ* ("one who considers himself near the water-jar"), *upamaṇikammanyaḥ* ("one who considers himself near the water-pot"). Regarding this, a prohibition for the suffix *cvī* after an indeclinable is stated: *doṣābhūtam ahaḥ* ("the day became night").
[The rule] "the night has become day" is for that purpose. That [designation] would apply here as well:

*upakumbhībhūtam*, *upamaṇikībhūtam*. If an enumeration is made, there is no need for the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) for the *avyayībhāva* compound. Why? Because those purposes which [are cited] for the indeclinability of the *avyayībhāva* do not exist [in these cases].
As for what is said regarding *luk*:

the activity of the Teacher indicates that there is elision (*luk*) after an *avyayībhāva* compound, since he teaches the prohibition "not [after] an *avyayībhāva* ending in *ataḥ*. Regarding the term *upacāra*:

the phrase "not standing in a final member" (*anuttarapadasthasya*) continues to apply. In that context, the accent on the first syllable (*mukhasvara*) is the sole motivating factor; and it is not a single [factor].

If it is argued that "the *śi* [ending] is a *sarvanāmasthāna* and takes the augment *suṭ* except for the neuter," then there would be a prohibition of *śi* in the case of *jas*. If it is argued that "the *śi* [ending] is a *sarvanāmasthāna* and takes the augment *suṭ* except for the neuter," then a prohibition of *śi* would apply in the case of *jas*: *kuṇḍāni tiṣṭhanti*, *vanāni tiṣṭhanti*. Furthermore, this should be understood as an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound) regarding the term "except for the neuter" (*anapuṃsakasya*). For the negative particle *nañ* has no semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) with the neuter; with what, then, does it have a connection?

Regarding the word *bhavati*: [it is stated] "there is no [application of the rule] for the neuter. As for what was said—"If *śi* is a *sarvanāmasthāna*, then by the rule 'the augment *suṭ* is not for the neuter,' there would be a prohibition of *śi* before the ending *jas*"—this is not so, because there is no prohibition. This is not a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation).
"Not for the neuter. What then? This is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*):
"that which is other than the neuter. There is no operation [of the rule] with respect to the neuter. If it is applicable by something else, it shall take place by that.
And it is applicable by the preceding [rule]. Or rather, because it is not otherwise applicable. Or else, the application that follows immediately is what is prohibited.

Why is this so? Because a rule (vidhi) or a prohibition (pratiṣedha) applies to what is immediately preceding. Thus, the prior attainment (prāpti) remains unprohibited; by that [attainment], the result will come about. But does not this [subsequent] attainment sublate the prior attainment? No, for being itself prohibited, it is not capable of sublating. Furthermore, as for what is said—that this should be regarded as an "incapable compound" (asamartha-samāsa)—even if...

It should be said: "Now there are many purposes [for this]. Which ones? Faces that are not to be seen by the sun, verses that are not to be sung again, and a Brahmin who eats the food of one lacking faith."

(P_1,1.44.1) KA_I,101.18–102.10 Ro_I, 322–323: Regarding the option (*vibhāṣā*) expressed as "or not" (*na vā*), there must be the designation of its meaning. That is to say, for the option "or not," a technical name (*sañjñā*) for its meaning must be established; it should be stated that the name applies to whatever is the meaning of the word "or not. What is the purpose?

For when there is a technical name for a word (*śabda-sañjñā*), there is no comprehension of the meaning, as in other cases. Indeed, when a technical name for a word exists, there would be no comprehension of the meaning, just as in other instances. Even in other cases where there is a technical name for a word, there is comprehension of the word itself, but not of its meaning. Where else? In the rules concerning the technical name *ghu*, such as "the roots *dā* and *dhā* [except *adāp*] are *ghu*" and "the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* are *gha*. In these instances involving the mention of *ghu*, there is no comprehension of the meaning.
In the case of verbal roots (*ghañ*-affixes), there is a cognition of the word itself, not of its meaning. If that is so, then it must be stated [that the meaning is understood].

It need not be stated. The particle *iti* serves the purpose of indicating the meaning. The particle *iti* is employed; it will serve the purpose of indicating the meaning. Is this [understanding of the meaning] already established by the particle *iti*, or does the addition of the meaning follow from the addition of the word? He says: it is already established.

Why? From common usage (*loka*). For example, in common usage, when one says "this is a cow" (*gauḥ ayam iti*), the particle *iti* employed after the word "cow" causes that word "cow" to fall away from its own referent. Having fallen away from its own referent, that word becomes a signifier of the word itself rather than a signifier of the external object-referent. It is the same here.

Furthermore, when the particle *iti* is employed after the word *navā*, it causes the word *navā* to deviate from its own primary meaning. Having thus deviated from its own meaning, that [particle] brings to light the conventional meaning of the fact that words possess their own referents. This is what is understood by "or not" (*na vā*), and this is what is cognized by "or not."
(Exclusion of identical words. An exclusion of identical words must be stated:

[the prohibition applies] to cases such as *navā kuṇḍikā* and *navā ghaṭikā*. Furthermore, what would happen if these too were subject to the designation *vibhāṣā*? [The rule] "optionally [so] in a *bahuvrīhi* compound involving a directional term" (*vibhāṣā diksamāse bahuvrīhau*) [would apply].

In the southeast hall, there would be a perception [of it] as recently built. Or rather, there is no such perception because the negation is preceded by an injunction, just as in common worldly usage. Or rather, this is not a fault. What is the reason? Because it is preceded by an injunction. Having first enjoined something, one says "not" or "no"; therefore, the suffix *sam* occurs with a word expressing a negation. For example, in common worldly usage:

"Is the village to be gone to by you, or not?"—"It is not so"—thus it is understood. There exists a reason why, in common usage, there is a comprehension of a word expressing negation as being identical [in form]. What is the reason? For you, sir, provide an illustration in common usage that possesses a different gender. Indeed, let an illustration be provided with the same gender, and there will be a comprehension of what expresses "presently. For example: [the following occurs]...

It is understood that "the village is to be gone to" means "new" or "fresh. And we do not even know whether, in some grammatical system, a designation is made using words of the same gender. Furthermore, the speaker has freedom in the connection of words. For example:

"The gruel is to be eaten by you, fresh. When the word *yavāgūḥ* (gruel) is connected with the verb *bhuj* (to eat), and the verb *bhuj* is connected with the word *navā* (fresh), then there arises the understanding of a prohibition [of eating it when it is not fresh].

When it is said, "The gruel (yavāgūḥ) is to be eaten by you fresh (navā)," it is understood that it is not [to be eaten otherwise]. When the word *yavāgūḥ* is connected with the word *navā* and not with the verb *bhuj*, then there is the comprehension of that which expresses "freshness": "The gruel is to be eaten by you fresh"; it is understood as "fresh. And here, we do not connect the words beginning with *sarva* with the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*).

"In a *bahuvrīhi* compound that is a directional compound (*diksamāsa*), the words beginning with *sarva-* are optionally [treated as *sarvanāman*]. What then? The verb *bhavati* ("they become") is connected [to the rule]:
"In a *bahuvrīhi* compound that is a directional compound, the words beginning with *sarva-* optionally become [treated as *sarvanāman*]. (P.
325–328. The non-eternality of the rule is untenable because of the application of the designation "prohibition. The non-eternality of the rule is not established: *śuśāva*, *śuśuvatuḥ*, *śuśuvuḥ*.
*śiśvāya*, *śiśviyatuḥ*, *śiśviyuḥ*. What is the reason? Because of the creation of a technical designation for the prohibition. This designation is made for the prohibition.
Therefore, in the sections of the *Vibhāṣā*, there would be an understanding of only a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). But it is established through a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).
This is established. How? Through a simple negation. Having applied something, it is said "not" or "no.
By that, both [the affirmation and the negation] will occur. But there is a contradiction. Indeed, there is a contradiction. In this case, it is not known:

With what intention does one engage [in an action], and with what intention does one desist? Or rather, it is not by the force of engagement that one acts elsewhere than in the object of prohibition. Nor is this a fault. Why? Because of the force of engagement. By the force of engagement, there will be an injunction (vidhi) elsewhere than in the object of prohibition; and by the force of prohibition, there will be a prohibition.

It will apply except in the domain of a specific rule (*vidhi*). Where, then, is this established? It is established in the case of an option (*vibhāṣā*) that applies where [a rule] has not yet been reached.

For in the case of an option that applies where [a rule] has already been reached, since its capacity has already been exercised, one would understand it as a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) on the grounds that the previous rule has already taken effect. This too is established. How so? The designation "option" (*vibhāṣā*) is made as a great technical term (*mahatī-sañjñā*). And a technical term...
Because it is not simpler. Why is that? For the purpose of brevity is the making of technical designations (*saṃjñā*).
In this case, the purpose of employing such a long designation is so that both [designations] may be understood:

namely, "not" (*na*) and "or" (*vā*). Among these, in the case of an option (*vibhāṣā*) where [the rule] was not previously established, since there is nothing to be prohibited, the alternative will be effected by the word "or" (*vā*). However, as for the option where [the rule] was already established...
In that case, both "not" (na) and "or" (vā) are presented together. Therein, when [a rule] is negated by "not," there will be an option (*vikalpa*) by means of "or.
Even so, the simultaneous expression of two contradictory [rules] is untenable; the simultaneous expression of two contradictions is not possible.

*śuśāva*, *śuśuvatuḥ*, *śuśuvuḥ*; *śiśvāya*, *śiśviyatuḥ*, *śiśviyuḥ*. What is the reason? If [the rule] "it occurs" (*bhavati*) is accepted, then there is no prohibition. If "it occurs" is accepted, then the prohibition does not apply. If "it does not occur" (*na*) is accepted, then there is no injunction. If "it does not occur" is accepted, then the injunction is not established. However, it is established because the former is sublated by the latter. It is established.

This [is the case]. How so? A subsequent rule (*uttaravidhi*) sublates a preceding rule (*pūrvavidhi*). It has been stated that the particle *iti* serves the purpose of indicating the meaning (*arthanirdeśārtha*).

In this grammatical system which teaches what is correct (*sādhvanuśāsana*), that for which an option (*vibhāṣā*) is prescribed possesses correctness (*sādhutva*). In this system which teaches what is correct...

In the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), that for which an option (*vibhāṣā*) is prescribed shall be correct (*sādhu*) optionally. And indeed, the compound (*samāsa*) is the very thing for which an option is prescribed. Therefore, the correctness of the compound alone would be optional. Let it be so. That which is correct will be employed; that which is incorrect will not be employed. Furthermore, in this particular state, there is never any incorrectness regarding the form *rājapuruṣaḥ*.

It is accepted. Furthermore, there is a twofold understanding; that is, a twofold non-understanding of words. Moreover, we desire that in the rules concerning *vibhāṣā* (optionality), there should be a twofold understanding of words, yet that is not established. For one who holds that words are produced (*kāryāḥ śabdāḥ*), he brings about the formation of a compound by means of optionality (*vibhāṣā*). But for one who holds that words are eternal (*nityāḥ*), [it is not so].
This fault does not apply even to that [interpretation]. How so? It is not with the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionality) that grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is connected.
What then? It is the designation of "compound" (*samāsa-sañjñā*) that is connected: the designation "compound" is optional (*vibhāṣā*). For example:

It is stated that "the sacrificial animal (medhyaḥ paśuḥ) is optional," and "the ox (anaḍvān) is optional. This is not being deliberated upon as to whether it is an ox or not an ox; rather, it is being deliberated upon as to whether it should be sacrificed or not sacrificed. Regarding the ritual acts, there is simultaneity through collective mention (anvācaya). In the case of words denoting ritual acts, when something is expressed simultaneously and by way of collective mention, the status of being expressed simultaneously applies to it.

[The suffixes] *tavyat*, *tavya*, *anīyar*, and *ra* [are taught], and *ḍhak* [is taught] after [the word] *maṇḍūka*. But for one for whom words are eternal, this [Pāṇini’s grammar] explains the correctness (*sādhutva*) of those that have been employed. Now, is it not the case that even for one for whom [words] are produced (*kārya*), this is not a fault? How so? Because a suffix occurs subsequent [to a base].

Thus it is said. Furthermore, it is not possible for multiple suffixes to follow a single base simultaneously. Nor do we say that a "chain of suffixes" (pratyayamālā) results. What then? When [an action] is to be expressed as "it must be done" (*kartavyam*), the simultaneous application of a second and a third suffix would result. This is not a fault, because [the suffixes serve] the purpose of conveying the meaning.

The employment of a word: a word is employed with the intention, "I shall cause the meaning to be understood. In that case, since that meaning has already been expressed by one [word], there should be no employment of a second [word] for it, according to the principle that "what has already been expressed need not be employed again. Furthermore, regarding the study of the practices of those who follow the Teacher's tradition, the scope of that [rule] extends to what is stated through such study; thus, the rule applies to the *ika* vowels.

According to Gālava, the suffix *phin* is applied diversely after a non-*vṛddha* [stem] ending in a short vowel among the Easterners; thus, only the Gālavas would employ [names with] short vowels, for it is precisely among the Easterners that the suffix *phin* occurs. For example:
"Jamadagni indeed offered this fifth portion; therefore, no one who is not a descendant of Jamadagni offers a five-portioned oblation."

He performs the oblation. For one, however, for whom words are eternal (*nitya*), the mention of Gālava is for the sake of honor, and the mention of the region is for the sake of renown. But surely, even for one for whom [words] are produced (*kārya*), the mention of Gālava would be for the sake of honor, and the mention of the region for the sake of renown; and in that case, there would be a twofold understanding upon such renown. And in that renown, there is a duality regarding words.
There would be no comprehension [of the forms]. Yet we desire that in the case of the inclusion of teachers and the inclusion of regions, there should be a twofold comprehension of words;
however, that is not established.
Or it is not subject to further instruction because it is already known. Furthermore, this *yoga* (rule) is not subject to instruction. What is the reason? Because it is already known;

for that purpose which is sought by means of this *yoga* is already known. Indeed, even those who do not undertake this technical designation (*sañjñā*) understand the non-mandatory nature (*anityatva*) when the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) is uttered. This is also the case with the ritualists (*yājñika*s).

When "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) is stated, those who do not rely on a technical name (*saṃjñā*) understand it as meaning "non-eternality" (*anityatva*). For example: "A sacrificial animal is optionally [to be sacrificed]"; "An ox is optionally [to be sacrificed]"; from this it is understood that it is both to be sacrificed and not to be sacrificed. Indeed, even when the Teacher (Pāṇini) introduces a technical name, he most frequently expresses this very same thing by other words as well.

"It conveys the meaning abundantly, optionally, or in both ways, according to some. (P. 1.1.44). Regarding those [rules] where [the operation] has not [otherwise] been established, there is a threefold doubt. From here onwards, those *vibhāṣā*s (optional rules) that we shall enumerate should be understood as applying where [the operation] has not [otherwise] been established. However, they give rise to a threefold doubt: 1. Is the rule intended to enjoin something that was not previously established? 2. Or is it intended to restrict what was already established by another rule? 3. Or is it intended to provide an option (*vibhāṣā*) for what was already established? These are the three doubts. Furthermore, regarding the term "where [the operation] has not [otherwise] been established" (*aprāpte*): it refers to cases where, in the absence of this *vibhāṣā* rule, the desired grammatical form would not be obtained through any other rule. It does not refer to cases where the form is already established by a mandatory (*nitya*) rule; for in such cases, an optional rule is unnecessary. Nor does it refer to cases where the form is already established by a preceding optional rule; for in such cases, the subsequent optional rule would be redundant. Therefore, the phrase "where [the operation] has not [otherwise] been established" is used to exclude these two situations. As for the "threefold doubt": when an optional rule is encountered, one must consider all three possibilities mentioned above. For example, in the case of the rule "one may optionally apply the suffix *kha* after the word *pūga*," one must investigate whether it is meant to enjoin something new, to restrict what is already established, or to provide an option for what is already established. This threefold investigation is necessary because, without it, one cannot correctly determine the scope and application of the optional rule. Thus, the "threefold doubt" serves as a methodological guide for interpreting the intent of the *vibhāṣā*s.

Regarding the phrase "whether it is *prāpta*, *aprāpta*, or both": there is a doubt concerning the rule "optionally in the *jas* [case-ending] after a *dvandva* compound" as to whether it is *prāpta*, *aprāpta*, or both. How is it *prāpta*, how is it *aprāpta*, and how is it both?
The word *ubhaya* is listed among the *sarvādi* group, and the suffix *tayap* undergoes the substitution of *ayac*. Therefore—

[The question is: Is it when [the suffix] is already established as obligatory, or when it is not established elsewhere, or when it is not established in both cases? [Answer: It is when it is not established. [In that case,] *ayac* would be a different suffix. If it were a different suffix, then the long vowel *ī* in the word *ubhayī* would not be obtained. Let it not be so; it will be so by virtue of the rule for *mātrac*. How so? The term *mātrac* here is not a reference to a specific suffix; what then? It is a reference to a *pratyāhāra* (a grammatical abbreviation).

Wherein are the *pratyāhāras* (abbreviations) located? From the word *mātra* up to the letter *ā* in *āyac*, including the letter *ca*. If there is a mention of *pratyāhāra*, then [the rule] would also apply here in the case of *kati tiṣṭhanti*. [Answer: The term *ataḥ* (from *at*) is understood [as a governing rule]. Even so, it would still apply here in *tailamātrā* and *ghṛtamātrā*. [Objection: It will not apply to a similar sound that is not included [in the *pratyāhāra*], because it is not grasped by the *pratyāhāra*.
[Vārttika: There is an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the root *ūrṇu*.

There is a doubt as to whether [the rule] applies when [the condition] is already present, when it is not yet present, or in both cases. How so when it is already present? How so when it is not yet present? And how so in both cases? [The opponent argues: Because there is no connection [between the two conditions], the *liṭ* suffix is always *kit* by the rule *liṭ kit*; thus, it is either always applicable, or otherwise inapplicable, or in both cases. [The proponent replies: It is inapplicable. For *kittva* (the property of being *kit*) is one thing, and *ṅittva* (the property of being *ṅit*) is another. If they were one and the same, then *ṅit* and *kit* would be identical. If they were one...

There is doubt regarding whether [the augment] *ṅit* or *kit* follows from that. For if they are distinct, there is no doubt; yet even if they are not distinct, there is still doubt. How so? In the case of *praurṇuvi*. Is it when the *sārvadhātuka* suffix is marked with *apit*, such that [the rule] is obligatory, or when it does not apply elsewhere, or when it applies to both? It is when it does not apply. [This is indicated by the rule: "The option (*vibhāṣā*) applies in the sense of 'marrying' (*upayamana*)."

There is a doubt as to whether [the rule applies] when [the condition] is already present (*prāpte*), when it is not yet present (*aprāpte*), or in both cases (*ubhayatra*). How is it when present? How is it when not present? And how is it in both cases? Regarding the term *gandhane*: does it apply when [the condition] is eternally present, or when it is absent elsewhere, or in both cases?
It applies when not yet present. The term *gandhane* is excluded. Or, [it applies] when there is no prefix (*anupasargāt*).

There is a doubt as to whether [the rule applies] when [the condition] is present, when it is absent, or in both cases. How so when present, how so when absent, or how so in both? Is it that *kram* is optionally applied when the rule *vṛtti-sarga-tāyaneṣu kramaḥ* is eternally applicable, or when it is not applicable elsewhere, or in both cases?
It is when it is not applicable. The phrase "in *vṛtti* and so forth" is no longer operative. [The rule is: "Optionally, for *vṛkṣa*, *mṛga*, and so forth."

There is a doubt as to whether [the rule] applies when [the suffix] is already present (*prāpte*), when it is not yet present (*aprāpte*), or in both cases. How so when it is already present? How so when it is not yet present? Or how so in both cases? Is it because the rule "for non-living beings" (*jātir aprāṇinām*) applies when the suffix is already present, or when it is otherwise not yet present, or in both cases? It applies when it is not yet present. The phrase "for non-living beings" has ceased to apply. [The rule] "after the roots *uṣ*, *vid*, and *jāgṛ*, optionally" (*uṣavidajāgṛbhyo 'nyatarasyām*) [applies].

There is a doubt as to whether [the rule applies] when [the suffix] is already present, when it is not yet present, or in both cases. How so when it is already present? How so when it is not yet present? Or how so in both cases? Is it when the suffix is already present because it is obligatory after a word ending in a suffix, or when it is not yet present elsewhere, or in both cases? It is when it is not yet present. Words ending in suffixes are distinct verbal roots (*dhātu*). Regarding the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) for *dīp* and others: [the suffix is applied] when it is not yet present.

There is a doubt as to whether [the rule applies] when [the suffix] is already applicable, when it is not yet applicable, or in both cases. How is it applicable? How is it not applicable? And how is it applicable in both cases? Is it applicable because of the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (P. 3.1.67) as a constant requirement, or is it applicable elsewhere, or in both cases? It is not yet applicable. The word *kartari* (P. 3.4.67) is understood [as governing the context]. Even so, there remains a doubt:

Or rather, it is logical that this applies either to an agent (*kartṛ*) or to a reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*); there is no doubt about this. The agent of a transitive verb (*sakarmaka*) behaves like the object (*karmavat*), and there are also intransitive verbs such as *dīp* (to shine) and others. Indeed, even intransitive verbs become transitive when accompanied by prepositions (*upasarga*). Rules prescribed with reference to the object apply to those whose state (*bhāva*) resides in the object and to those whose action (*kriyā*) resides in the object; however, [rules] concerning the agent do not apply to those whose state resides in the agent.
And [the examples] such as *dīpa* (lamp) and so forth. Regarding the rule *vibhāṣā agreprathamapūrveṣu*:

there is a doubt as to whether it applies when [the action] has been performed (*prāpte*), when it has not been performed (*aprāpte*), or in both cases (*ubhayatra*). How is it applied when performed? How when not performed? And how in both cases? Or, regarding the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇye*), is it applied when [the action] is constant (*nitye*), or otherwise when not constant, or in both cases?

Regarding "aprāpte" (when [the rule] has not applied): the phrase "in the sense of frequency" (*ābhīkṣṇye*) is no longer operative. There is a doubt concerning the suffixes *tṛn* and so forth: does it apply when [the rule] has already applied, when it has not yet applied, or optionally in both cases? And how is it when it has already applied, or when it has not yet applied, or in both cases? Is it because the rule "in the sense of abuse" (*ākrośe*) applies invariably, or because it does not apply elsewhere, or because it applies optionally in both cases? [The answer is: it is when it has not yet applied.

The term *ākrośe* (in the sense of "abuse") is excluded. Regarding the rule [Pāṇini 6.3.60] stating that when a single consonant (*ekahal*) or more follows, the substitution may optionally (*anyatarasyām*) take place: there is a doubt as to whether it applies when the substitution is already applicable (*prāpte*), when it is not applicable (*aprāpte*), or in both cases (*ubhayatra*). How is it applicable? How is it not applicable? And how is it in both cases? For example, regarding the form *uda* in the sense of *udaka* (water) by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.63] *udakasyodaḥ sañjñāyām*, there is a doubt as to whether it applies when the substitution is obligatory (*nitye prāpte*), when it is not applicable elsewhere (*anyatra vā aprāpte*), or in both cases (*ubhayatra vā*). [In this case, it is] *aprāpte*.

The word *sañjñāyām* has ceased [to apply]. Regarding the rule *śvāder iñi padāntasyānyatarasyām*: there is a doubt as to whether it applies when [the rule] is already established, when it is not yet established, or in both cases. How is it "when established," how is it "when not established," and how is it "in both"? Is it when the suffix *iñ* is invariably established, or when it is not established elsewhere, or in both? It is "when not established. The word *iñi* has ceased [to apply].

Regarding the rule *sapūrvāyāḥ prathamāyā vibhāṣā*: there is a doubt as to whether it applies when [the case ending] is already present (*prāpte*), when it is not present (*aprāpte*), or in both cases (*ubhayatra*). How does it apply when present? How when not present? Or how in both cases? If one considers the rule *cādibhir yoge* (Pāṇini 8.1.59), which prescribes the substitution of *sa* for *samāna* when joined with particles beginning with *ca*, then the question arises: does this [new rule] apply where that [previous rule] is eternally present, or where it is not present, or in both cases? It applies where it is not present. In that case, the phrase *cādibhir yoge* is no longer operative. As for *graḥ*...

Regarding the rule *yaṅi aci vibhāṣā*: there is a doubt as to whether it applies when [the condition] is present, when it is absent, or in both cases. How is it "when present," how is it "when absent," and how is it "in both"? Is it when the [rule] *yaṅi* is eternally present, or when it is absent elsewhere, or in both? It is "when absent. It is "when absent. The term *yaṅi* has ceased to apply.

And when [an operation] has already been established, those optional rules (*vibhāṣā*) which we shall enumerate hereafter are to be understood as applying to that which is already established. However, they give rise to three types of doubt:
whether [the rule applies] when [the condition] is established, when it is not established, or in both cases. [For example: "Optional (*vibhāṣā*) in the case of confused speech."

There is a doubt as to whether [the rule applies] when [the condition] is present, when it is absent, or in both cases. And how is it when present? How when absent? Or how in both? Regarding the phrase "of articulate speech" (*vyaktavācām*), does it apply when [the condition] is eternally present, or when it is absent elsewhere, or in both cases? It applies when present; for the phrase "of articulate speech" indeed continues [from the previous rule]. [The rule] is optional (*vibhāṣā*) when the sense is understood through a co-occurring word (*upapada*).

There is a doubt as to whether [the rule] applies when [the condition] is already present (*prāpte*), when it is not yet present (*aprāpte*), or in both cases (*ubhayatra*). How so? In what sense does it apply when already present, in what sense when not yet present, and in what sense in both? Is it because the rule *svaritañitaḥ* (P. 1.3.72) applies invariably (*nitye*) when the condition is already present, or otherwise when it is not yet present, or in both cases? It applies when already present; for the word *svaritañitaḥ* is understood [from the previous sūtra]. [The rule] *tiraḥ antardhau vibhāṣā kṛñi* (P. 1.4.71) [illustrates this].

There is a doubt as to whether [the rule] applies when [the condition] is present, when it is absent, or in both cases. How is it applied when present? How when absent? And how in both? Or, regarding the term *antardhau* (in the sense of "disappearance"), is it applied when the [condition] is necessarily present, or when it is absent elsewhere, or in both cases?

It is applied when present; for the word *antardhau* is understood [as a governing condition]. Regarding the rule *adhir īśvare vibhāṣā kṛñi* ("*adhi* is optionally [a karmapravacanīya] in the sense of 'lordship' when used with the root *kṛ*"):
There is a doubt as to whether [the rule applies] when [the condition] is present, when it is absent, or in both cases. And how is it when present? Or how when absent? Or how in both?

Is it when "īśvara" is present, or when it is eternally present, or when it is absent elsewhere, or in both? When it is present: for the word "īśvara" indeed occurs [in the context]. Regarding the suffix *div*, there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) when a prefix (*upasarga*) expresses that same meaning.

There is a doubt as to whether [the rule applies] when [the condition] is already present, when it is not yet present, or in both cases. And how is it when present? Or how when not present? Or how in both? Is it "for the sake of that" (*tadarthasya*) when [the condition] is permanently present, or when it is elsewhere not yet present, or in both cases?
It is when [the condition] is present; the phrase "for the sake of that" (*tadarthasya*) continues to apply.
Furthermore, from here onwards, those optional rules (*vibhāṣā*) that we shall enumerate should be understood as applying in both cases. However, they give rise to three types of doubt:

whether [the rule] applies when [the condition] is present, when it is absent, or in both cases. For example: *hṛkror anyatarasyām* ("after the roots *hṛ* and *kru*, [the suffix *niṣṭhā* takes the augment *iṭ* optionally]").

There is a doubt as to whether [the rule applies] when [the object] is reached (*prāpta*), not reached (*aprāpta*), or both. How so when reached, how so when not reached, or how so in both cases? Is it when [the rule] is eternally applicable according to the sūtra *gati-buddhi-pratyavasānārtha-śabda-karma-akarmakāṇām*, or when it is otherwise not applicable, or in both cases? It applies in both cases. First, regarding when it is applicable:
He causes the Saindhavas to eat;
he causes [them] to eat with the Saindhavas;
he causes the Saindhavas to undergo a change [of state].
He transforms [the horse] with Sindhava salt. When [the agent] has not yet reached [the object]:
Devadatta carries the load; he causes Devadatta to carry the load, or he causes the load to be carried by Devadatta. Devadatta makes a mat; he causes Devadatta to make a mat.

He has Devadatta make a mat (*kārayati kaṭaṃ devadattena*). If there were no option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding whether [the rule] applies when [the suffix] is required, when it is not required, or in both cases, there would be doubt: how is it in the case of what is required, how in the case of what is not required, and how in both cases? That is, does it apply when [the suffix] is required by the rule *yádi*, or when it is not required elsewhere, or in both cases? It applies in both cases. First, regarding what is required:
Do you remember, Devadatta, that we were thinking, "We shall dwell in Kaśmīra," that we dwelt in Kaśmīra,
and that there we would eat boiled rice?
That we ate rice there before it was [properly] obtained:
"Devadatta, do you recall that we were going to Kaśmīra?
We went to Kaśmīra."
In that case, we shall eat rice (*odanaṃ bhokṣyāmahe*);
there, we ate rice (*odanān abhuñjmahi*). Regarding the rule *vibhāṣā śveḥ*:

there is doubt as to whether it applies when [the suffix] is already present (*prāpte*), when it is not yet present (*aprāpte*), or both. How is it when already present? Or how is it when not yet present? How?

Regarding the rule "vā ubhayatra" (or both cases): when [the substitution] is obligatory in one case, or not applicable in another, or applicable in both—this refers to "both cases. First, regarding that which is applicable: *śuśuvatuḥ*, *śuśuvuḥ*.
*śiśviyatuḥ*, *śiśviyuḥ*. [This applies] when [the rule for *guṇa*] has not been reached:
*śuśāva*, *śuśavitha*, *śiśvāya*, *śiśvayitha*. [The rule] "optionally [applies] to *saṃ-ghuṣ* and *asvan*" [is as follows]:

There arises a doubt regarding the prefix *sam* [in the rule for the verb] *ghuṣ*: is it in a case where [the suffix] is already applicable, or where it is not applicable, or in both cases? And how is it applicable, or how is it not applicable, or how is it in both cases? Is it because *ghuṣ* is restricted to "not making a sound" (*aviśabdane*), thus being always applicable, or is it otherwise—either not applicable or applicable in both ways? It is in both cases. First, as for where it is applicable:
A rope that has been twisted;
a rope that has been made to resound. Regarding what has not yet occurred: a sentence that has been uttered.

Regarding the word *saṅghuṣitam*: there is a doubt as to whether [the rule] applies when the suffix is already present (*prāpte*), when it is not yet present (*aprāpte*), or in both cases (*ubhayatra*). How is it "already present," how is it "not yet present," and how is it "in both"? Is it when the suffix is eternally present after the root *svan* with the prefix *āṅ* in the sense of "in the mind" (*manasi*), or when it is not yet present elsewhere, or in both? It applies in both cases. First, regarding the case where it is already present:
The word *āsvāntam* means "the mind is comforted" (*āsvanitaṃ manaḥ*). Regarding the case where [the vowel] has not been reached:
*āsvānto devadattaḥ*.
"Devadatta has been called out.
(Pāṇini 1.1.45) Is this the designation *samprasāraṇa* being applied to a sentence?
Does this sentence, "ik yaṇaḥ," receive the technical designation *samprasāraṇa*, or does it refer to the phoneme:
"that *ik* which occurs in place of a *yaṇ* receives the designation *samprasāraṇa*"? And what is the difference here regarding the designation *samprasāraṇa*?

If the designation *vākya* (sentence) applies, then it is a rule concerning phonemes (*varṇavidhi*). If the designation *vākya* applies when there is the designation *samprasāraṇa*, then the rule concerning phonemes—namely, "that which precedes the *samprasāraṇa* becomes [the single substitute], and a long vowel is substituted for the *samprasāraṇa*"—is not established; for the designation *samprasāraṇa* does not apply to a sentence.

This explanation is untenable, nor is the occurrence of these two effects possible. Let it be then for the phoneme (*varṇa*). If it is the designation of a phoneme, then [the term] "origination" (*nirvṛtti*) [is required]. If it is the designation of a phoneme, then "origination" is not established;
for in the rule *ṣyaṅaḥ saṃprasāraṇam*, that very *ik* whose designation is being made is itself difficult to find. Now, if...
Furthermore, how could it possibly be obtained by anyone, since it would not exist in its proper place? For it is by this very [rule] that it is established;

thus, this results in a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), and operations involving mutual dependence are not logically tenable. However, the specific mention of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the dual designation (*ubhaya-sañjñātva*).

In that he provides an instruction using specific case endings—stating "that which follows a *samprasāraṇa* becomes the preceding [vowel]" and "there is lengthening of the *samprasāraṇa*"—it is understood by this that both [the preceding vowel and the *samprasāraṇa*] receive the designation [*samprasāraṇa*].
As for what he said: "that which follows a *samprasāraṇa* becomes the preceding [vowel]" and "there is lengthening of the *samprasāraṇa*."

By this it is known that the designation applies to a phoneme (*varṇa*). Furthermore, by what he says—"there is *samprasāraṇa* of *ṣyaṅ*"—it is known that the designation also applies to a sentence (*vākya*). Or rather, let it be only for the sentence. But was it not said: "If the designation *samprasāraṇa* applies to a sentence, then it would be a rule concerning phonemes (*varṇavidhi*)"? This is not a fault.

Just as one born from a crow is a crow, and one born from a hawk is a hawk, so too that which is produced from *samprasāraṇa* is called *samprasāraṇa*. That which is produced from *samprasāraṇa*—being *samprasāraṇa*—is followed by [another vowel], and the preceding [vowel] becomes long in its place. Now...
For indeed, one is seen employing parts of sentences within sentences and parts of words within words. First, regarding parts of sentences within sentences:
"Enter, [eat] the cake," [is used for "Enter, eat the cake"].
Enter the principle of *tarpaṇa* (satisfaction). Just as one uses parts of words for the whole words—
as in *devadattaḥ* for *dattaḥ*,
or *satyabhāmā* for *bhāmā*— so too here, [the rule applies] from that which is produced by semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) to that which is produced by semivowel substitution.

Regarding the meaning of this statement, the phrase "of the *samprasāraṇa*" is employed as a part of the rule "after a *samprasāraṇa*. By this, we shall understand it as a prescription for that which has been produced [from] a *samprasāraṇa*: namely, "of that which has been produced from a *samprasāraṇa*. Alternatively, he says: "this [subsequent vowel] becomes the preceding [vowel] after a *samprasāraṇa*, and there is lengthening of the *samprasāraṇa*."

[The objection continues: "It would be so; however, if the term *samprasāraṇa* were applied to the entire sentence, this specific designation would not be tenable, nor would these two grammatical operations be possible. [Response: In that case, they will occur by virtue of an explicit statement (*vacana*). Or rather, let it be [the application] to the individual phoneme (*varṇa*). [Objection: But was it not said that if it is a designation for a phoneme, there would be a lack of completion? [Response: This is not a fault; it is merely a case of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*)."

This has been raised: all cases of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) have been resolved by treating them as identical, as in the established rule, "But [the term *vṛddhi*] is established because of the eternality of words. This is not equal to other instances of mutual dependence. For in those cases, it is not stated that "those forms—*ā*, *e*, and *o*—which are substituted in place of this [element], receive the technical designation *vṛddhi*. Here, however, it is stated: "The *ik*..."

"That which occurs in place of a semi-vowel (yaṇ) receives the technical designation *saṃprasāraṇa*. If this is so, then this designation should be understood as referring to what is yet to come (*bhāvinī*). For example, someone says to a weaver:
"I am weaving a cloth for this thread. He observes:
"If it is a cloth, it is not to be woven; if it is to be woven, it is not yet a cloth. To say 'the cloth is to be woven' is a contradiction.
Indeed, he intends a future designation. I believe that which, when woven, will be called a cloth, is what is to be woven.

"This is what happens": in this case as well, that which arises in place of *yaṇ* will receive the technical designation "samprasāraṇa" once it has been produced. Alternatively, it is indeed observed in common usage that the application of suffixes such as *ij* and *yaj* occurs; however, due to the instruction regarding *yaj* and other roots, the application of *ij* and others would otherwise be precluded. Yet people in the world do employ them, as in the words *iṣṭam* and *uptam*.

Thus we consider it: they employ this *ik* in place of that *yaṇ*. In that regard, the correctness (*sādhutva*) of that which was previously regarded as incorrect is established by the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), [stating] "it is correct when followed by a *kit* suffix," "it is correct when followed by a *ṅit* suffix."

This is a compound designation (*samāsanirdeśa*). In that case, it is not known which is the beginning and which is the end. For example, when it is said, "Devadatta and Yajñadatta [possess] goats and sheep," it is not known whose the goats are and whose the sheep are.

346–349: Furthermore, [it might be argued that] the *ṭakita* suffixes occur at the beginning and the end [of the word]. To this he replies: "They are augments (*āgama*s). But it is more reasonable that there should be a teaching regarding augments only for words that are eternal; for eternal words must consist of letters that are fixed, immovable, and devoid of loss, addition, or modification. And an "augment" is indeed the production of a previously non-existent sound-element. Now...

It is logical that there should be substitutes for eternal words. Certainly, it is logical. In this case, there must be other words [involved]. Therefore, it is logical that one word is understood from another word. In that case, these will be substitutes for those [words] which lack an augment (anāgamaka), namely those which possess an augment (sāgamaka). How so? This is a section concerning technical designations (saṃjñā-adhikāra); furthermore, here both "the initial" (ādi) and "the final" (anta) are being mentioned.
The *ṭ* and *k* sounds occurring at the beginning and end [of the augment] are cited as examples. In that context, the *ṭ* and *k* sounds at the beginning and end will serve as markers (*sañjñā*).

Here, the rule "the augment *iṭ* is added to an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant" (*ārdhadhātukasya iṭ valādeḥ*) is applicable, and the word "beginning" (*ādiḥ*) is present. By this, the substitute will begin with the letter *i*. Thus far, the sūtra here is simply "the augment *iṭ*. But how [is this so]?
By this much of the sūtra, a substitute beginning with the vowel *i* is obtained. He says: "it is obtained. How? From the indication by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
This is an indication by a *bahuvrīhi*:
"that which has *i* as its initial [element]. Even if that can be stated in this case, how is it here?

In the rule *luṅlaṅlṛṅkṣv aṭ udāttaḥ*, where it is impossible to qualify the vowel *a* by means of the mention of "udātta," what would be the fault? The fault would be that the *aṅga* (the stem) itself would become udātta. This is not a fault; for this is a three-word *bahuvrīhi* compound.
In that case, within the very sentence, the vowel *a* is qualified by the mention of "udātta."

The vowel *a* is acute (*udātta*) because it is its initial [element]. But in cases where this occurs through the application of a rule (*anuvṛtti*), such as "the augment *āṭ* is added to those beginning with a vowel" (*āṭ ajādīnām*), he will state: "it is established for those beginning with a vowel by means of the augment *aṭ*. Or rather, that much which he is able to teach in a general sense—

First he teaches the root *prakṛti*, then the *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes beginning with *val*, and after that the vowel *i*. By this means, he understands the specific composite whole as a distinct word. It is just as in the case of the *khadira* and the *burbura*: [one first says] "the *khadira* and the *burbura* have white trunks and fine leaves," and only afterwards does one say, "the *khadira* is thorny."
By that means, he understands that specific [element] as a distinct substance within the aggregate. Alternatively, by this sequence he teaches it as a different word:
first the base (*prakṛti*), then the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *val*, and subsequently the letter *i*; regarding that [letter], there arises the cognition that it is an augment (*āgama*).

(P_1,1.46.3) Regarding the prescription of initial and final elements for *ṭ* and *kit*, there must be a prohibition of the suffix. When prescribing initial and final elements for *ṭ* and *kit*, a prohibition of the suffix must be stated: [lest] a suffix be considered the beginning or the end [of the word], as in the rules "ṭa" (*Pāṇini 3.2.18*), "ātaḥ" (*Pāṇini 3.2.3*), and "anupasarge kaḥ" (*Pāṇini 3.2.3*). This is established by the rule of posteriority; by virtue of the rule of posteriority, the suffix is [treated as] the beginning.

Or else it will not exist internally. If it is argued that [the desired form] is established by a subsequent rule, we say no, because this is an exception (*apavāda*). If it is argued that it is established by a subsequent rule, we say no. What is the reason? Because it is an exception. This rule is an exception; for example, the rule "after a short vowel, an augment follows the final letter" is an exception to the rules concerning the *sthāni* relation and the condition of being followed by an affix (*pratyaya-paratva*).

This is an unequal comparison. It is appropriate in that case for the introduction of the marker *ṭ* (ṭit-karaṇa) to override the rules of positional connection (*sthāneyoga*) and the requirement that an affix follow [the base] (*pratyayaparatva*), as it has no other scope. But here, both have scope. What is their scope? The scope of the introduction of the marker *ṭ* is so that the long vowel *ī* may occur by the rule "of that which ends in *ṭ*" (*ṭitaḥ*). The scope of the introduction of the marker *k* (kit-karaṇa) is...

The elision of the vowel *ā* in the word *kiti* is intended so that it may occur. That which must necessarily occur is called a "purpose" (*prayojana*). If this [suffix] were necessarily subsequent, then this would be its purpose. But how indeed is it known that, because of the marker *ṭ*, this will be subsequent and not initial? And because of the marker *k*, it will be subsequent.

But it is not the case that [the suffix] *ki* is an "end" (*anta*). Indeed, this is a valid rebuttal in cases where it is impossible for something to be both subsequent (*para*) and initial (*ādi*). However, regarding *kit*, there is no such rebuttal; for it is indeed possible for something to be both subsequent and an "end. What fault is there in that? Consider the rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*: *ādhyoḥ*.

In the case of *pradhyauḥ*, the prohibition [of the substitution of *au* for *as*] by the rule *na uṅdhātvoḥ* would apply. Furthermore, there would be no escape from the difficulty regarding the suffix marked with *ṭ*. For, because of the addition of the marker *ṭ*, this [augment *i*] would indeed be initial, and not final. Where, then, would this [rule] now apply? To the rule stating that "the vowel *ī* occurs after a suffix marked with *ṭ*. It applies where [the suffix] possesses both [the markers *ṭ* and *k*].

Regarding the rule *gāpoṣṭak*: it is established by the statement within the governing context (*adhikāra*) of the genitive case. This is established. How? This rule should be formulated within the governing context of the genitive case as follows:

"The markers *ṭ* and *k* are placed at the beginning and the end of that which is designated by the genitive. Alternatively, because the beginning and the end serve the purpose of the genitive, in the absence of the genitive, there is no cognition [of those positions]. Or rather, since the beginning and the end have the sense of the genitive, in the absence of the genitive, there is no cognition [of them]. [Thus, the marker] *ādiḥ* [is understood].
Or else, it will not exist at all. It is more logical, however, that the meaning should be caused by the word, rather than the word having to be caused by the meaning.
Indeed, the word is caused by the meaning. How so? [The rule] "the first and the last" refers to the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*).
Yet we do not see a genitive here. Therefore, we consider:
In this case, neither the beginning nor the end exists; since those two are absent, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) also does not occur. (P.

1.1.47.1) Why is this stated? It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the [general] rule regarding position and what follows (*sthānapara*), namely: "A *mit* augment comes after the final vowel (*acaḥ antyāt*)."

By the rule *acaḥ antyāt paraḥ* ("after the final vowel"), an exception is stated to both the principle of *sthāneyoga* (substitution in the place of the original) and the requirement that an element follow immediately after a suffix.
First, regarding *sthāneyoga*:
*kuṇḍāni*, *vanāni*, *payāṃsi*, *yaśāṃsi*. Regarding the requirement of following a suffix:

"It splits," "it cuts. This example would be appropriate—such as *kuṇḍāni* or *vanāni*—where there is no possibility [of the rule applying], because here [the vowel] follows something other than a vowel (*anyat*) and occurs in place [of another]. But this [example], *payāṃsi* and *yaśāṃsi*, is inappropriate.
For there is indeed the possibility that [the suffix -ām] follows something other than a vowel and occurs in place [of another]. This too is appropriate. How so?
Neither does the Lord command this, nor do the authors of the *Dharmasūtras* state that "general rules (*utsarga*) are to be set aside by exceptions (*apavāda*).
What then? This is a worldly illustration. For in the world, even when it is possible [to follow both], setting aside occurs; for example:
"Let curd be given to the Brahmins, but buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya"—even though it is possible to give curd [to Kauṇḍinya as well].

The gift of buttermilk (*takradāna*) is a preventive measure. Likewise, here too, even though it is possible [for both to apply], the status of being subsequent to the final vowel (*antyāt paratva*) will set aside the status of being a connection with the place of substitution (*ṣaṣṭhīsthāneyoga*).

352–353. *Masj* [is to be defined as] having the letter *m* preceding its final consonant, for the purpose of the elision of the *anuṣaṅga* and the first member of a *saṃyoga*. It should be stated that *masj* has the marker *mit* placed before its final consonant. What is the purpose? For the purpose of the elision of the *anuṣaṅga* and the elision of the first member of a *saṃyoga*. First, for the purpose of the elision of the *anuṣaṅga*: *magnaḥ*.

[The root] *majj* has [the augment *niṣṭhā-takāra* changed to *na*]. This is for the purpose of the elision of the initial consonant of the *saṃyoga*: *maṅktā*, *maṅktum*, *maṅktavyam*. And in the case of *bharj* and *mṛc*, it should be stated that the augment *miṭ* occurs before the final letter. Thus: *bharūjāḥ*, *marīcayaḥ*. If so, it must be stated. No, it need not be stated; it is established by means of a *nipātana* (irregularity). What is the *nipātana*?
The word *bharūja* is listed among the *aṅguli* group, while the word *marīci* is listed among the *bāhu* group.

(Pāṇini 1.1.47.3) Now, is this [augment] one whose initial part belongs to the preceding element (*pūrvānta*), or one whose initial part belongs to the following element (*parādi*), or is it independent (*abhakta*)? And how is this so?

How could it be a prior-final (*pūrvānta*) element, or how could it be a subsequent-initial (*parādi*) element, or how could it be an independent (*abhakta*) element? If the term "final" (*anta*) is understood [to carry over], then it is a prior-final element. If the term "initial" (*ādi*) is understood, then it is a subsequent-initial element. If both have ceased to apply, then it is an independent element. What is the distinction here? In the case of an independent element, there is the lengthening of vowels, the elision of *n*, vowel-accentuation (*svara*), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*, the nasalization (*anusvāra*), and the substitution of *śī*. If it is an independent element...
Lengthening does not occur:

in *kuṇḍāni* and *vanāni*, lengthening—prescribed by the rule "there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel before a nominal ending (*sarvanāmasthāna*) other than the vocative"—does not take effect. [In the case of] *dīrgha*, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is also not established.
In the case of *agne trī te vajrinā trī sadhasthā*,
the elision of the *n* in *trīṇi* (as prescribed by the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*) does not occur.
Furthermore, the accent (*svara*) also does not become established.

In the case of *sarvāṇi jyotīṣi*, the rule *sarvasya supi* (Pāṇini 6.1.192) does not result in the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*). Regarding the accent and the substitution of *ṇ*: in *māṣavāpāṇi* and *vrīhivāpāṇi*, the substitution of *ṇ* is not established. [However, it is] established by the rule *prātipadikāntanakārasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.12), provided that [the word] ends in the prior member.

In the case of the *n* of a case-ending (*vibhakti*) that begins with a vowel, the inclusion of *num* when it is not followed by a vowel (*abhakta*) must be made. It need not be made; it is already accomplished in the very formulation (*nyāsa*) [of Pāṇini’s rule]:
"in the final syllable of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), in *num*, and in case-endings" (*prātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu*). [This applies to] the substitution of *ṇ* (*ṇatva*) and the *anusvāra*.

And the *anusvāra* is not established in cases such as *dviṣantapaḥ* and *parantapaḥ*. Since the rule "the *anusvāra* replaces *m* before a consonant" (*maḥ anusvāro hali*) applies, the *anusvāra* would not occur here. Let it not be so; rather, it will occur by the rule "and [the *anusvāra* replaces *n*] when it is not at the end of a word and followed by a *jhal* sound" (*naś cāpadāntasya jhali*). But what about that [instance] where it is not followed by a *jhal* sound?
The word *gaur abhraṃlihaḥ* (the cloud-licking cow) and *vāyur abhraṃlihaḥ* (the cloud-licking wind). Regarding the anusvāra and the substitution of *śī*: the substitution of *śī* is not established.

In the case of *trapuṇī*, *jatunī*, and *tumburuṇī*, since the substitution of *śī* for *auṅ* occurs after a neuter [stem], the substitution of *śī* does not apply. [Objection: But the substitution of *śī* [is indeed required]. [Response: In that case, it will be treated as having its initial letter added (*parādi*). When it is treated as having its initial letter added, there is a prohibition of the application of *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, *auttva*, lengthening (*dīrgha*), *nalopa*, *anusvāra*, *śībhāva*, and the vowel *e*.
If it is treated as having its initial letter added, then *guṇa* must be prohibited.

In *trapuṇe*, *jatune*, and *tumburuṇe*, the rule "guṇa is substituted for [the final vowel] before a suffix marked with Ṅ" (*gher ṅiti*) would result in *guṇa*. [But this is not desired. As for *vṛddhi*: *vṛddhi* must be prohibited;

for example, in *atisakhīni brāhmaṇakulāni*. Since the suffix is marked with Ṇ by the rule "after *sakhi*, when not in the vocative" (*sakhyur asambuddhau*), the rule "vṛddhi is substituted for the vowel [of the base] before a suffix marked with Ñ or Ṇ" (*acaḥ ñṇiti*) would result in *vṛddhi*. [But this is not desired. As for *auttvam* (the substitution of *au*): [this is also prohibited].

And the substitution of *aut* must also be prohibited [in the case of] *trapuṇi*, *jatuni*, and *tumburuṇi*. By the rule "after *i* and *u*, *aut* and *at* [are substituted] for *ghi*," the substitution of *aut* would apply. Regarding the substitution of *aut*: the lengthening [of the vowel] is also not established.

In the case of *kuṇḍāni* and *vanāni*, the lengthening [of the penultimate vowel] prescribed by the rule *nopadhāyāḥ sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau* does not apply. Let it not be so; rather, the lengthening will occur by the rule *ato dīrgho yañi supi ca*. But then, consider these cases:
*asthīni*, *dadhīni*, *priyasakhīni*, and *brāhmaṇakulāni*. [The rule for] lengthening [does not apply here]. [Therefore, there must be] elision of *n* (*nalopa*).
Furthermore, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is not established:

in the case of *agne trī te vajinā trī sadhasthā*, [the form] *ta tā piṇḍānām* results. By the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*, the elision of *n* would not apply. [Thus, there is the elision of *n*. Regarding the *anusvāra*:

And the *anusvāra* is not established in cases such as *dviṣantapaḥ* and *parantapaḥ*. Since the rule "the *anusvāra* replaces *m* before a consonant" (*maḥ anusvāro hali*) applies, the *anusvāra* should occur. Let it not be so; rather, it will be governed by the rule "and [the *anusvāra* replaces *n*] when it is not at the end of a word, before a *jhal* sound" (*naś cāpadāntasya jhali*). What then of those cases where [the *n*] is not followed by a *jhal* sound?
"Sky-licking" refers to a cow;
"cloud-licking" refers to the wind. Regarding the *anusvāra*: a prohibition of the *śī* substitution must be stated for the letter *n*.
That is, in the case of the *śī* substitution, a prohibition of the letter *n* must be formulated.

In the case of *trapuṇī*, *jatunī*, and *tumburuṇī*, the substitution of *ś* for *num* would apply. This is not a fault. Since grammatical substitutions apply only to that which is explicitly mentioned (*nirdiśyamāna*), it will not occur here. But then, it would not apply to that which is actually being mentioned [as the base]. Why? Because it is separated by *num*. In that case, let it be treated as a prior element (*pūrvānta*). If it is a prior element, then the shortening of the neuter gender (*napuṃsaka*) and the secondary member (*upasarjana*) applies.

And regarding the accent of *dvigu* compounds: if [the feminine suffix] were applied as a final element (*pūrvanta*), then both the shortening of the vowel in neuter secondary members (*napuṃsakopasarjana-hrasvatva*) and the accent of *dvigu* compounds would not be established. As for the shortening of the vowel in neuter secondary members: *ārāśastriṇī*, *dhānāśaṣkulinī*, *niṣkauśāmbinī*, *nirvārāṇasinī*. As for the accent of *dvigu*: [this would likewise fail].

[In the case of] *pañcāratninī* and *daśāratninī*, once the augment *num* has been applied, these rules [of Vṛddhi substitution] would not apply because the word is no longer final. Or rather, it is not so, because they are characterized as external (*bahiraṅga*). Or rather, this is not a fault. What is the reason? Because they are characterized as external. The augment *num* is external, while these rules are internal (*antaraṅga*). [And that which is external is] as if unestablished (*asiddha*) [with respect to what is internal].

An external [rule] is superseded by an internal one. There is a more extensive avoidance of conflict regarding the accent of a *dvigu* compound: considering that this [accent] is dependent on the aggregate (*saṃghātabhakta*) and is not capable of subverting the status of the final vowel of a member (*avayava*) as having an *ik* vowel, the accent of the *dvigu* will take effect.

357–359. For what purpose is this stated? It is for the purpose of excluding the homogeneous *ā* vowel from the *ec* vowels. When it is said that "the *ic* [vowels] replace the *ec* vowels," it is stated for the purpose of excluding their homogeneous counterparts and for the purpose of excluding the vowel *ā*. First, regarding the exclusion of the homogeneous counterpart: it is so that in the rules prescribing short vowels for *eṅ*, half of the *ekāra* or half of the *okāra* does not occur. Regarding the exclusion of the vowel *ā*: [it is so that *ā* is not substituted].

And these two, *ai* and *au*, are composite phonemes (*samāhāravarṇa*). There is one mora for the vowel *a*, and one mora each for the vowels *i* and *u*. In the rules concerning short vowels, there might sometimes be the vowel *a*, and sometimes the vowels *i* and *u*. It is for the purpose that it should never be the vowel *a* that this [rule] is stated. This is indeed a valid purpose. But what then? There would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the vowels *ai* and *au*] being long. However, they are long...

[The vowels] attain [the status of *ik*]. What is the reason? Because "in place [of a vowel], the most similar one (*antaratama*) occurs. But does it not say "when there is a substitution of a short vowel"? Therefore, long vowels will not occur. This [rule] would be for the sake of a specific application (*viṣya*), namely: "when there is the contingency of a short vowel for *ec*, *ik* occurs. However, the non-occurrence of long vowels is due to their being excluded; for the *ik*s [which are short], there is no contingency of long vowels.

What is the reason? Because it is a rule of exclusion (*nivartaka*). By this [rule], the *ik* vowels are not excluded; rather, the *anik* vowels are excluded. For both the short vowels and the *ik* vowels as well as the *anik* vowels are already established. In that case, by this [rule], the *anik* vowels are excluded. First of all, there is no purpose for it to serve as an exclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*). This is already established because of the common place of articulation (*saṃsthāna*) of the *eṅ* vowels. How so? Because of the common place of articulation of the *eṅ* vowels.

The *ekāra* and *okāra* will come into being; however, there will be no half-*ekāra* or half-*okāra*. But surely, for the *eṅ* sounds, there exist half-*ekāra* and half-*okāra* which have a more similar place of articulation (*saṃsthānatara*). They do not exist. For if they did exist, he would have taught those very ones. But surely, O venerable one, among the Chāndogas, the Sātyamugris and Rāṇāyanīyas [teach] a half-*ekāra* and a half...?
And they recite the syllable *oka*:
"O well-born one, rich in horses and gifts!
O Adhvaryu, [press] the pressed [juice] with the wooden vats!"
"‘śukram te enyat’, ‘yajatam te enyat’—this is merely a manner of speaking on the part of those venerable ones.

Neither in common usage nor in any other Veda does there exist an *ekāra* or an *okāra* that consists of two equal halves. Nor is there any purpose served by [assuming] the exclusion of the vowel *a*. This is because in the diphthongs *ai* and *au*, the subsequent element predominates; and because the subsequent element predominates in *ai* and *au*, they will not be instances of the *avarṇa* (the sound *a*)."

The quantity of *ivarṇa* and *uvarṇa* is greater, while that of *avarṇa* is smaller. Therefore, the references will be to the more numerous [sounds]. It is just as when it is said, "Let a village of Brāhmaṇas be brought," and there, at the very least, there are five craftsmen present.

360. What is this [expression] *sthāneyogā*? It means that for which there is a connection (*yoga*) with a position (*sthāna*). This is *sthāneyogā*. The elision of the locative case-ending (*saptamī*) occurs by virtue of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Alternatively, there is the substitution of *e* for the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*): that for which there is a connection by way of position is *sthāneyogā*. P_1,1.49) [Question] Why is it stated [in the rule] that "the substitute (*ādeśa*) takes the place of that which is designated by the term *sthāna*," rather than simply stating "the substitute takes the place of that which is designated by the term *sthānin*"? [Answer] It is because the designation of the original element (*sthānin*) is not established unless the substitute (*ādeśa*) is first established. For instance, in the case of the expression *aster bhūḥ*, the designation of the original element *asti* is established only after the substitute *bhū* has been established. Furthermore, if the substitute were not established, it would be impossible to know what the original element is. Moreover, since the original element is something already existing, it cannot be said to "take the place of" anything. On the other hand, since the substitute is something not yet existing, it can be said to "take the place of" the original element. Therefore, it is stated that "the substitute takes the place of that which is designated by the term *sthāna*. [Question] But even so, how is it known that the substitute takes the place of the original element, and not that the original element takes the place of the substitute? [Answer] Because the original element is something already existing, it cannot be said to "take the place of" anything. On the other hand, since the substitute is something not yet existing, it can be said to "take the place of" the original element. Furthermore, the word *sthāna* is used in the sense of "that which is situated" (*sthitam atra*), and it refers to the original element. Therefore, it is understood that the substitute takes the place of the original element. [Question] If that is so, then in the case of the expression *aster bhūḥ*, the designation of the original element *asti* would be established only after the substitute *bhū* has been established. However, since the substitute *bhū* is not yet established at that time, the designation of the original element *asti* could not be established. Consequently, the substitute *bhū* would not take the place of the original element *asti*. [Answer] That fault does not arise. For the designation of the original element *asti* is established by means of the substitute *bhū*. That is to say, the designation of the original element *asti* is established by means of the substitute *bhū*. Therefore, the designation of the original element is established by means of the substitute.
