360–364. Why, then, is this stated? The statement that the genitive [case-ending] is used in the sense of "substitution" (*sthāne-yoga*) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). This undertaking is for the sake of restriction. There are one hundred and one meanings of the genitive, or however many there may be; all of them would apply when the genitive is uttered.
However, it is desired in grammar that whichever genitive occurs, it should be used only in the sense of substitution. And that cannot be achieved without an effort.

The statement that [the genitive] "of the sixth case" (*ṣaṣṭhyāḥ*) is an expression of *sthāneyoga* (the relation of substitution) is for the purpose of restriction; this is stated for this very purpose. There is indeed a need for this. What, then, is it? It is to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as the genitive of a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), as in the rules *śāsaḥ* and *gohaḥ*. For the genitive of a part and so forth would not be established. In that case, what is the fault? [The fault would be that the rule] *śāsa it aṅhaloḥ* would apply [inappropriately].

And for the root *śās*, [the substitution] would apply both to the final letter and to the penultimate (*upadhā*) alone; and by the rule *ūdupadhāyā gohaḥ*, for the root *guh*, [the substitution] would apply both to the final letter and to the penultimate alone. Furthermore, there would be no application of the genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth, because the rule (*yoga*) is unambiguous.
Moreover, there would be no application of the restriction regarding the genitive of part and so forth. Why? Because the rule is unambiguous.

There is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding doubt, and there is no doubt concerning [the use of] the genitive case for parts (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth. Should this be stated? No, it need not be stated. How will it be understood without being stated? This is a worldly example. For instance, in common usage, someone asks another:

"I shall go to another village; please instruct me on the path. He explains it to him: "In that place, the right hand must be grasped; in that place, the left hand. However, as for the diagonal path that exists there, since there is no doubt regarding it, it is not instructed. In this case as well, there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding doubt.

And there is no doubt regarding the genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth. Alternatively, [the term] *sthāneyogā* [is analyzed as] *sthāne ayogā*. What is this *ayogā*? It means having an unmanifest connection (*avyakta-yogā*). Or rather, it is *yogavatī yogā*. Which one is *yogavatī*? That which has many connections (*yogāḥ*). Why is this so? Because the suffix *matup* occurs in the sense of abundance (*bhūmani*). Or else, it is a specific genitive, namely the "genitive of substitution" (*sthāneyogā*). Now...

Or, having attached some indicative mark (*liṅga*), I shall say: "The genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by such a mark is used in the sense of 'substitution' (*sthāne-yoga*). That mark will not be applied to the genitive of parts (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth. If this is the case, then in the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ*, the mention of *śās-* in *śā hau* must be made for the sake of indicating that it is used in the sense of substitution.

One should not think, "I shall supply [the word]. That which was previously introduced as having the sense of a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) will, by continuing (*anuvṛtta*) into what follows, serve the purpose of denoting the relation of substitution (*sthāneyoga*). How so? An *adhikāra* (heading) is of three kinds: some, situated in one place, illuminates the entire treatise, just as a well-kindled lamp [illuminates everything].

It causes the entire house to blaze up. Another application [of the rule] is that, just as a piece of wood bound with a rope or iron is dragged along, so too is it dragged along; this is indicated by the word "ca" (and). Another application is that it stands over each individual rule (*pratiyogam*) for the purpose of not having to specify it every time; thus, it applies to each and every rule. This refers to the position where the application (*adhikāra*) stands over each individual rule for the purpose of its non-specification.

For in that case, whatever was previously introduced as having the sense of a partitive genitive (avayava-ṣaṣṭhī) will, by being carried forward (anuvṛtta) in what follows, serve the purpose of denoting substitution (sthāne-yoga). This [genitive] is merely for the sake of conveying understanding; for it is not possible to attach a grammatical indicator (liṅga) without pronouncing the word itself. If that is so, then that indicator will be applied to the substitute (ādeśa), and it will belong to its original base (prakṛti).

It will apply. If a restriction is made [to the effect that the rule applies only where there is one genitive case and multiple qualifiers], then it would not be established in cases such as *aṅgasya*,
*halaḥ*, and *aṇaḥ*.

Regarding the rule *samprasāraṇasya*: both *hal* (a consonant) and *aṇ* (a vowel) are to be qualified, as is *samprasāraṇa*. However, in the absence of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), one may qualify several things with a single genitive case. For example: "Devadatta’s son, his hand, [and] his blanket. Therefore, there is no purpose for a restriction. But was it not said that there are one hundred and one meanings of the genitive?
"Or rather, all those [words] that are obtained when the genitive case-ending is uttered—this fault does not apply.

Even though in common usage there are many types of relations—those based on wealth, those based on marriage, those based on speech, and those based on ritual action—what other relation could possibly exist between one word and another word, except for the relation of *sthāna* (position)? [This refers to] the relation of one word with another word.

The terms *anantara* (immediate), and so forth, are relations. Regarding the rule "for *as*, there is *bhū*" (*aster bhūḥ*), a doubt arises as to whether it means "in place," "immediately after," or "nearby. This remains merely a doubt. And in all cases of doubt, this principle applies: "Specific understanding comes from the explanation; for there is no rule based on mere doubt. We shall explain [the term] as "in place" (*sthāne*).

In that case, this rule (*yoga*) need not be stated now. Yet it must be stated. What is the purpose? So that a word ending in the genitive case may be joined with a "position" (*sthāna*), since the genitive has been uttered. What is thereby accomplished? This interpretive maxim (*paribhāṣā*)—"substitutes (*ādeśa*) apply to that which is being specifically indicated (*nirdiśyamāna*)"—need not be formulated.
(P_1,1.50.1) What is the example? *ikaḥ yaṇ aci*:
"dadhi atra" (yogurt here), "madhu atra" (honey here).

[The rule] "that which has the palate as its place of articulation [should have] the palate as its place of articulation; that which has the lips as its place of articulation [should have] the lips as its place of articulation" is not necessary, for this is already established by the principle of correspondence according to number (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*). In that case, consider this: "For *ta*, *tha*, *tha*, and *mi*, there are *ta*, *ta*, *ta*, and *ma*"—so that that which has a single meaning may have a single meaning, that which has two meanings may have two meanings, and that which has many meanings may have many meanings. But surely this too is established by the principle of correspondence according to number alone. In that case, consider this:
Regarding the rule "akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ" (a short *a* vowel followed by a homogeneous vowel becomes long): examples are *daṇḍāgram*,
*kṣupāgram*,
and *dadhi indraḥ*.
Regarding "madhu-uṣṭraḥ":

[the rule] is so that for two [sounds] having the throat as their place of articulation (*sthāna*), there is [substitution] by one having the throat as its place; for two having the palate as their place, by one having the palate; and for two having the lips as their place, by one having the lips. Now, since the word *sthāne* (in the place) is already being carried over [from a previous rule], what is the purpose of mentioning *sthāna* again? In cases where...

Among the various types of proximity (*āntarya*), proximity by place of articulation (*sthāna*) is the most powerful. What, then, is that? In the case of *cetā* and *stotā*, by the rule of quantity (*pramāṇataḥ*), the vowel *a* would obtain the quality [of length], whereas by place of articulation (*sthānataḥ*), it would become *e* or *o*. Because of the repeated mention of "place" (*sthāna*), they become *e* and *o*. Now, what is the purpose of including the superlative suffix *-tama*? It is for the sake of excluding the [substitution] prescribed by the rule *jhayaḥ haḥ anyatarasyām*, which applies to a voiceless aspirated consonant (*soṣman*).

The second [class of consonants] are those possessed of *ūṣman* (aspirates); the third are those possessed of *nāda* (voiced). By the inclusion of the suffix *-tamap*, those that are both possessed of *ūṣman* and possessed of *nāda* become the fourth: "Speech devours; the *triṣṭubh* meter devours."

(P_1,1.50.2) KA_I,120.14–121.29 Ro_I, 366–370: For what purpose, then, is this stated? Because the substituend (*sthānin*) is indicated as a single unit and because multiple substitutes (*anekādeśa*) are indicated, there is the undesirable consequence that [the substitute] would apply everywhere; therefore, the statement "the most similar [substitute] in place" (*sthānentaratama*) is made. The substituend is indicated by its oneness: namely, *akaḥ*.

Furthermore, multiple substitutes are specified, such as "long" (*dīrgha*). Because the original element (*sthānin*) is indicated in the singular and because multiple substitutes are indicated, there arises the undesirable consequence that all [substitutes] would apply everywhere.
All [substitutes] would thus apply in all instances. However, it is desired that only the most similar (*antaratama*) should occur. And that cannot be achieved without an effort.

It is not established. Therefore, the statement "in its place, the most similar" (*sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ*) is for the purpose of restriction. This is stated for this very purpose. There is indeed a need for this. What then? Is this production of the most similar [substitute] derived from the original form (*prakṛti*)?

Is the genitive case [used] in reference to the *sthānin* as that which is most similar (*antaratama*), or rather in reference to the substitute (*ādeśa*)—that is, "among those things obtained at the place [of substitution], the most similar one becomes the substitute"? Why, then, this deliberation? Because the phonetic combination (*saṃhitā*) is the same in either case.
[The rules] "sthānentaratama" and "uraṇ raparaḥ. What follows from this? If [the substitution] were based on the original form (*prakṛti*): "ikaḥ yaṇ aci" [would apply].
Wherever there is an *ik* sound that is most similar [to the substitute], there the genitive case applies;
and wherever the genitive applies, there the substitutes occur. Thus, it would apply only here:

*dadhi atra*, *madhu atra*. But in the case of *kumārī atra brahmabandhvartham*, it would not apply. However, when the most similar form is established through substitution, the genitive applies everywhere.

Where there is a genitive case, there the substitutes occur; thus it is established everywhere. Likewise, in the rule *ikaḥ guṇavṛddhī* ("for *ik*, there are *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*"), the genitive refers to those *ik*-sounds which are most similar to the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*;
since the substitutes occur where there is a genitive, this would apply only in such cases as follows:

In cases such as *netā*, *lavitā*, *nāyakaḥ*, *lāvakaḥ*, *cetā*, *stotā*, *cāyakaḥ*, and *stāvakaḥ*, [the substitution] would not occur [if the genitive were not used]. However, when the most similar (antaratama) replacement is established through the use of the genitive case—since substitutions apply wherever there is a genitive—the result is established in all instances. Likewise, when a *ṛ*-vowel is subject to the application of *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*, the genitive is applied to that *ṛ*-vowel which is the most similar to the *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*.
Since the substitutes occur where there is a genitive case, they would apply only in this instance:
*kartā*, *hartā*,
*āstārakaḥ*.

In cases such as *nipārakaḥ*, *āstaritā*, *niparitā*, *kārakaḥ*, and *hārakaḥ*, [the rule] would not apply. However, when the substitution occurs through the most similar (*antaratama*) replacement, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) applies everywhere; since substitutions take place wherever there is a genitive, the rule becomes established in all instances. Now, if this substitution occurs through the most similar replacement, there is this fault:

Regarding the rule for *vānt* (the substitution of *au* and *ai*) before a semivowel (*y*), the original element (*sthānin*) must be specified; it should be stated that this applies to the vowels *o* and *au*, so that it does not apply to *e* and *ai*. However, since the most similar (*antaratama*) substitute is established by virtue of the original form (*prakṛti*), the genitive case is used for that original which is the most similar to the substitute *vānt*.
Since it is established that "where there is a genitive case, there the substitutes occur," this is accomplished even without an explicit mention of the original element (*sthānin*).
Furthermore, there is no fault even if the most similar (*antaratama*) substitute is produced through the application of the rule for substitutes. How so? The term *vānta* will not be employed;
rather, it will simply be stated: "when a *yi*-affix follows, the *ec*-vowels become *ay*, etc. If [the term *vānta*] is not used, then [the following applies]: *ceyam*.

In this case as well, [the suffix] *yat* would apply [to other roots]. The rule "kṣayya and jayya are used in the sense of possibility" (*kṣayyajayyau śakyārthe*) will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the substitution of *ec* occurs only for the roots *kṣi* and *ji*. However, in that case, it would still apply to those two roots even outside the sense of possibility, as in "sin is to be destroyed" (*kṣeyam pāpam*) and "the low-born man is to be conquered" (*jeyaḥ vṛṣalaḥ*). Therefore, the restriction will be understood as being twofold: [it applies only to these two roots and only in the sense of possibility].

[The rule] "only after *kṣi* and *ji*, and only for these two [roots], when the sense is that of possibility" applies here as well; thus, by virtue of this restriction, [the substitution] would not occur in cases such as *lavyam*, *pavyam*, *avaśyalāvyam*, and *avaśyapāvyam*. The restriction applies to those of the same class (*tulyajātīya*). And what is of the same class? That which is of the same nature as the *ec* vowels of *kṣi* and *ji*. Of what nature is the *ec* of *kṣi* and *ji*? It is the vowel *e*. Even so, [it would apply] to *rāyam*.
In the case of *icchati* and *rāyati*, [the substitution] would also apply here. *Rāyiḥ* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). In the Veda, there is conformity with what is observed.
Regarding the rule "ū is substituted for the penultimate vowel of *gūh*" (*ūdupadhāyā gohaḥ*):

when the substitution is based on the *ādeśa* (the substitute), the mention of "penultimate" (*upadhā*) must be made. However, when the substitution is based on the *prakṛti* (the original element), since the most similar (*antaratama*) original of the *ūkāra* of *gūh* is [the vowel *ū* itself], [the mention of "penultimate" is unnecessary].
In that case, since the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used where it occurs, the substitutes (*ādeśāḥ*) are established even without the explicit mention of the term *upadhā*.

Furthermore, there is no fault even when the most similar (*antaratama*) replacement is effected through the application of the substitute itself. This very point is addressed in the *Nyāsa* under the rule *radābhyām*.
Regarding the rule "niṣṭhātaḥ naḥ pūrvasya ca daḥ":

if the substitution were determined by the *ādeśa* (the substitute sound), then since the most similar (*antaratama*) [substitute] would be established, the mention of the letter *t* would have to be made [in the rule]. However, if the establishment of the most similar [substitute] is determined by the *prakṛti* (the original sound), then when the *niṣṭhā* suffix follows, the genitive case refers to that *prakṛti* which is the most similar to the *n*.

Since the substitutes occur where there is a genitive case, this is established even without the mention of the letter *t*; thus, there is no fault even when the most similar [substitute] is produced through substitution.
This is done precisely in the *Nyāsa*.
370–372. Furthermore, what is this [term] that brings about [the formation]?
Is it that which is brought about by this [process] as being most similar, or rather is it that which expresses [it]?
The application of this [rule] concerns those things produced by another. And what is the distinction here?

When there is a substitute (*sthānin*) that is most similar (*antaratama*), there is the replacement of the original element (*sthānin*). If it were the case that when there is a substitute that is most similar, there is the replacement of all original elements, then this would also apply:
*dadhi madhu*. Let it be so; however, no other substitute is specifically indicated there. Therefore, by virtue of similarity (*āntaryataḥ*), it is the word *dadhi* [that is replaced].

The word *dadhi* itself will be the substitute for the word *madhu*, and the word *madhu* itself will be the substitute for [the word *dadhi*]. And if there were any dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) in such a case, that would constitute a fault:
as in *bisam bisam*.
In the case of *musalam musalam*, the rule for the substitution of *ṣ* (as in *iṇkoḥ*) would apply. Furthermore, the desired systematic arrangement would not be established.
Just as sesame seeds thrown into a heated frying pan do not remain there even for a moment, so too these phonemes would not persist for even a moment. Let it be, then, that [the word] is expressive.
The realization [of the suffix] occurs by means of that which has been produced by another [element]. When there is realization of what has been produced, there is production. [Objection:

In the case of the realization of what has been produced, production is not established; [if it were so], all [suffixes] would apply everywhere. What, then, is meant by saying "production is not established"?
[Response: It is not that production is better established; we do not say that production is not established.
[Objection: What then? [Reply: The desired restriction would not be established. It is not accepted that all [suffixes] apply everywhere.

For what purpose would this [present rule] be now? And it would be useless. This would be useless; for if one were to say to someone who has already eaten, "Do not eat," what would he have accomplished by it? Or has it already been stated? What has been stated? [It has been stated: "But it is established under the heading of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyadhikāre*)."

Regarding the statement "because of the mention": this rule (*yoga*) should be formulated under the heading of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhy-adhikāra*): "In place of that which is designated by the genitive, the most similar [element] occurs. (Pāṇini 1.1.50).

372–373. And there is the mention of "each for itself" (*pratyātmam*). It should be stated that it is "each for itself. What is the purpose? So that whichever [sound] is the most similar (*antaratama*) to a given [original] shall take its place, and not so that the most similar [sound] to one thing might take the place of another. The mention of "each for itself" is unnecessary to be taught (*aśiṣya*), because it is established by its own nature (*svabhāvasiddha*). The mention of "each for itself" is unnecessary to be taught.
What is the reason? Because it is established by its own nature (*svabhāva*). This is established by its very nature. For example:

when it is said in assemblies, gatherings, and congregations, "Sit down," it is not explicitly stated "sit individually," yet they sit individually. Furthermore, there is the rule regarding the closest relative (*antaratama*); however, the rule regarding the closest relative need not be taught, for it is a natural connection (*yoga*).
And furthermore, this [distinction] is not something to be taught. Why? Precisely because it is established by its own nature (*svabhāva*). For example:
when it is said in assemblies, gatherings, or meetings, "Let there be sitting," those who are emaciated do not sit together with the emaciated, nor do the pale sit with the pale.
Only those among whom there exists some internal connection based on a common purpose sit together. It is just so.
Cows that have wandered during the day lie down together with whichever calf is their offspring. Likewise, those groups of cattle-yoked carts that are clattering see one another and make a sound.
Such is the case among sentient beings; even among insentient things, a clod of earth, when thrown, travels with the speed of an arm and does not veer off to the side.

It does not go upward nor does it ascend; being a modification of earth, it goes to the earth by way of its inherent nature (*āntaryataḥ*). Likewise, those subtle waters belonging to the intermediate space—their modification is smoke; that, in a windless region of the sky, neither moves horizontally nor descends downward; being a modification of water, it goes to the waters themselves by way of its inherent nature. The same applies to light.
A modification, such as a flame, when well-kindled in a windless space within the ether, does not move sideways nor does it descend;
being a modification of light, it moves toward the light itself by virtue of its internal nature.

373–377. Furthermore, in the case of the transposition of consonants and vowels, there would be the consequence of [the substitution] occurring at that same time. In the event of the transposition of a consonant and the transposition of a vowel, it follows that the substitution would take place at that very moment. Regarding the transposition of a consonant: in the examples *iṣṭam* and *uptam*, by virtue of proximity (*āntaryataḥ*), a short *iK* consisting of half a mora (*ardhamātrika*) would result for the consonant which consists of half a mora.
However, neither in common usage (*loke*) nor in the Veda is there such a short *iK* consisting of half a mora. What then? It is one consisting of a full mora (*mātrika*). That which exists is this.
It will occur. In the case of a vowel substitution (*svaravyatikrama*):

*dadhi atra*, *madhu atra*, *kumārī atra*, *brahmabandhvartham*. Due to proximity (*āntaryataḥ*), for an *ik* vowel of one mora (*mātrika*) or two moras (*dvimātrika*), a *yaṇ* of one mora or two moras would result; however, this does not occur either in common usage (*loke*) or in the Veda (*vede*).

Is the *yaṇ* one measure (*mātrika*) or two measures (*dvimātrika*)? What then? It is half a measure (*ardhamātrika*). That which exists will be so. And in the case of vowels (*akṣu*) where there is the substitution of multiple phonemes (*anekavarṇādeśa*), the same duration would result. For instance, in the rule *idama iś*, by virtue of internal similarity (*āntaryataḥ*), a palatal vowel (*ivarṇa*) of two and a half measures (*ardhatṛtīyamātra*) would result in place of the *idam* which has two and a half measures. This is not [the case].

This is the fault: that there would be no inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) by what is being taught. This will not be the case [if we accept the following]. And in the cases of *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, *ej*-substitution, and the absence of a sound (*abhāva*), the same duration would result:
*khaṭvā indraḥ* → *khaṭvendraḥ*; *khaṭvā udakam* → *khaṭvodakam*; *khaṭvā īṣā* → *khaṭveṣā*; *khaṭvā ūḍhā* → *khaṭvoḍhā*; *khaṭvā elakā* → *khaṭvailakā*; *khaṭvā odanaḥ* → *khaṭvaudanaḥ*.

In the examples *khaṭvā aitikāyanaḥ* > *khaṭvaitikāyanaḥ* and *khaṭvā aupagavaḥ* > *khaṭvaupagavaḥ*, by virtue of proximity (*āntaryataḥ*), substitutes consisting of three or four morae (*trimātra-caturmātra*) would result for original elements (*sthānin*) that consist of three or four morae. This is not a fault, because of the rule: "The *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [substitutes] are followed by *t*. But is it not the case that *taḥ paraḥ* means "that from which *t* follows"?
"This [tapara] is that very one. He says: "No; it is *tapara* because it follows a *tā* as well. If it were *tapara* because it follows a *tā*, then [the rule] *ṛdorap* would apply only here:
*yavaḥ*, *stavaḥ*; *lavaḥ*."

In this case, [the form] *pavaḥ* would not occur. This is not the letter *t*; what then? It is the letter *d*. What is the purpose of the letter *d*? And what is the purpose of the letter *t*? If the letter *t* is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity, the letter *d* is also [for that same purpose]. If the letter *t* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation, the letter *d* is also [for that same purpose]. [This applies] in the absence of *ej*.

In *kurvāte* and *kurvāthe*, by virtue of proximity, an *e*-sound consisting of two and a half morae (*ardhatṛtīyamātra*) would result for that which is designated as *ṭi* and consists of two and a half morae. However, such a two-and-a-half-mora *e*-sound exists neither in common usage nor in the Veda. When there is the possibility of *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* for an *ṛ*-vowel, there is over-extension (*sarvaprasaṅga*), because there is no distinction [specified]. When there is the possibility of *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* for an *ṛ*-vowel, there is over-extension; all [sounds] would then be subject to the designations *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.

[The substitutes] would apply in place of the *ṛ*-vowel. What is the reason? Because there is no distinction. For no such distinction is specified as to which [substitute] bearing the technical names *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* occurs in place of the *ṛ*-vowel. Since no distinction is specified, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all [substitutes] would apply. Or rather, it is not so; for there is no lack of internal similarity (*āntarya*) for the *a*-vowel, because in place of the *ṛ*-vowel, a substitute followed by *r* (*rapara*) is required. Or rather, it is not so.

This is a fault. Why? Because of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [the substitute] would have *r* as its final element (*rapara*) in place of the vowel *ṛ*. It is stated that when an *aṇ* is prescribed in place of *u*, it necessarily has *r* as its final element. In that case, by virtue of similarity (*āntaryataḥ*), among those containing *r*, the vowel *a* alone—which also contains *r*—is the most similar (*antaratama*). However, there is the undesirable consequence of it being a substitute for the whole word (*sarvādeśaprasaṅga*) because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāltvāt*). Indeed, there is the undesirable consequence of it being a substitute for the whole word.

The designation *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would apply to the vowel *ṛ*. Why? Because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*). [According to the rule] "that which has more than one phoneme and is marked with *ś* applies to the whole. Or rather, this is not a fault. Why? Because the status of having more than one phoneme depends upon that very [substitution]. There is no obstruction to the substitution for the vowel *ṛ*. Why? Because the status of having more than one phoneme depends upon that. When this [substitute *ar*, etc. takes the place of *uḥ*, then it consists of more than one phoneme. [Thus, the rule regarding *anekāl* applies.]

Because the substitution of the vowel *ṛ* has that [substitution of *u*] as its basis, there will be no obstruction. Alternatively, the very lack of proximity (*anāntarya*) between these two constitutes their proximity (*āntarya*). For one [the substitute], there is no most similar original form (*prakṛti*); for the other [the original], there is no most similar substitute (*ādeśa*). This alone is the proximity between these two. Or rather, their association is like that of a man who has lost his horse and another whose chariot is burnt. Now...

Or rather, there is a conjunction [of the two], like that of a man whose horse has been lost and another whose chariot has been burnt: "Your horse is lost and my chariot is burnt; let us both join together. So it is here as well:
"You have no most similar *prakṛti*, and I have no most similar substitute (*ādeśa*); let us be joined."
Regarding the term "conjunction" (*samprayoga*): this is an unequal comparison. In the world, conjunction occurs among sentient beings—either by implication or from the context.
Furthermore, phonemes (*varṇa*) are insentient. In that case, what would constitute their conjunction?
Even though phonemes are insentient, he who employs them is sentient. In the substitution of *e* and *o* for the original form (*sthānin*), [the substitute] is the vowel *a*.
Because the original element (*sthānin*) is primarily characterized by the vowel *a*. When there is a substitution for the vowels *e* and *o*, the vowel *a* would result:

as in *khaṭvā-elakā* and *mālā-aupagavaḥ*. What is the reason? Because the original element here is primarily characterized by the vowel *a*. For in these cases, the original element is indeed primarily characterized by the vowel *a*.
But it is established that [the substitute] occurs because of being the most similar to both. This is established. How? That which is the most similar to both must be the substitute;
and no *a*-vowel is the most similar to both.
378–381: Does this statement regarding *aṇ* followed by *r* (uraṇ rapara) serve to exclude other [substitutes], meaning that in the place of *u*, only *aṇ* occurs and it is followed by *r*;
or rather, is the quality of being followed by *r* (raparatva) itself prescribed by this rule?

In place of *uḥ*, both *aṇ* and *anaṇ* [are substituted], but *aṇ* alone is followed by *r*. What is the distinction here? If the statement of *uraṇ raparaḥ* is for the purpose of excluding others, there is a fault regarding the acute (*udātta*) and other accents. If the statement of *uraṇ raparaḥ* is for the purpose of excluding others, a fault arises with respect to the acute and other accents. Which, then, are the acute and others? They are the acute (*udātta*), the grave (*anudātta*), the circumflex (*svarita*), and the nasalized (*anunāsika*). For example: *kṛtiḥ*.
Taking away,
done, taken.
[This concerns] the subject at hand:

"Protect men who have struck [the enemy]. Let it be then that in place of *u*, there is both an *aṇ* and a non-*aṇ* vowel, and that the *aṇ* is followed by *r*. If it is argued that "whatever is in place of *u* is followed by *r*," then there would be no realization of the *avarṇa* (vowels *a*, *ā*) in the case of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions. [For if the rule were simply] "whatever is in place of *u* is followed by *r*," [then the *a* in *dadhyatra* would not be understood as *avarṇa*].

If this is argued, then there would be no realization of *a*-vowels for the purposes of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions; [for example,] *kartā* or *hartā* according to Vārṣagaṇya. For what is more appropriate than that, when an *ṛ*-vowel meets a non-homogeneous vowel, it should become an *a*-vowel rather than *eṅ* or *aic*? This fault applies even to the former position.
For what is more appropriate there as well—that when an *ṛ*-vowel meets a non-homogeneous vowel, it should become an *a*-vowel rather than an *i*-vowel or an *u*-vowel?

Now, if it is thought that—since there is an occasion for both an *aṇ* and a non-*aṇ* vowel in place of *ū*, only an *aṇ* occurs, followed by *r*—then the realization of the *avarṇa* is established under the first view. As for what was said—that a fault arises regarding the acute (*udātta*) accents and so forth—here that fault arises. It does not arise. That fault does arise. How? [In the case of] the acute.
By this [rule], both *aṇ* vowels and non-*aṇ* vowels are indicated. Even though they are indicated, they do not [all] apply.

What is the reason? Because that which is most similar (*antaratama*) occurs in place of the original. But how is it that when two paribhāṣās with scope stand together—namely, "that which is most similar occurs in place" and "the *u* [substitute] is followed by *r*"—[the latter applies]? [The answer is: "that which is most similar occurs in place."
Thus, by this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), the determination will be established, and not by the rule *uḥ aṇ raparaḥ*. What follows from this?
From this, the following fault arises:

there is a fault regarding the acute-accented vowels (*udātta*) and so forth. Furthermore, regarding those substitutes (*ādeśa*) that are prescribed word-for-word (*pratipadam*) in place of the vowel *ṛ*, the property of being followed by *r* (*raparatva*) would not apply to them.

[The rule] *ṛta id dhātor ut oṣṭhyapūrvasya* [is stated]. But it is established by virtue of being followed by *r* (*raparatva*) when there is an occasion [for substitution]. This is established. How? By virtue of being followed by *r* when there is an occasion. An *aṇ* that is to be substituted in place of *u* becomes followed by *r* as soon as it is occasioned. Is this something that needs to be explicitly stated? No, indeed. How will it be understood without being stated? The word "in place of" (*sthāne*) is understood from the context; the word "place" (*sthāna*) is what is carried over.
And [the word *sthāne*] has the sense of "occurrence" (*prasaṅga*). If it were so, the substitute (*ādeśa*) would be unspecified; yet the substitute is specified. How so?

The second mention of the term *sthāna* is understood as a reference back to the topic at hand. There, the connection will be made thus: "in the place of *u*, in the place of *aṇ*. Thus, when *u* occurs, the *aṇ* that is being applied is precisely that which is followed by *r*.

How would it be a preceding part, how a following part, or how independent? If the term "end" (*anta*) is understood to carry over, then it is a preceding part; if the term "beginning" (*ādi*) is understood to carry over, then it is a following part; if both are withdrawn, then it is independent.

And what is the distinction here? [If it were] not a part of the suffix (*abhakta*), there would be a prohibition of lengthening, the substitution of *la*, the elision of *ya* and *ga*, the remaining of the vowel and the initial consonant, and the visarga;

[The rule] "of a word ending in *r* or *v*, [the substitution of *ī* for] the *ik* of a root" [is proposed]. "Alternatively, [the rule applies] in the case of the teaching of *kṛt* suffixes for the sake of those beginning with *ta* and for the sake of the augment *iṭ*. Thus, there is the accent on the suffix beginning with *ta*. As for the lengthening:
391–392. Is this *al*-grahaṇa a qualifier of the final [phoneme], or rather a qualifier of the substitute (*ādeśa*)? And what follows from this?

If it is a qualifier of the final [phoneme], then the substitute remains unqualified. What is the fault in that? Even a substitute consisting of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*) would apply to the final [phoneme]. But if, on the other hand, it were stated that "the *al* [substitute] replaces the final [phoneme]," then in that case, even a substitute consisting of more than one phoneme [would be restricted to the final].

It need not be stated that [the substitute] replaces "everything" (*sarvasya*). This will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): namely, that the substitution occurs only for the final [element], and not for anything else. Even so, the final element remains unspecified. What is the fault in that? It would follow that the substitution applies to the final element of both a sentence (*vākya*) and a word (*pada*). If, however, this is the intended meaning...

It would not be performed; even when the final-suffix condition (*antyaviśeṣaṇa*) is present, it will not be applied. How so? The rule *ṅicca* (Pāṇini 1.1.53), which states that [an operation] affecting more than one letter (*anekāl*) applies to the final [letter], will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): namely, that only an element marked with the *ṅit* designation applies to the final [letter], and no other.
(P_1,1.52.2) KA_I,130.12-20 Ro_I, 392-394 For what purpose, then, is this stated? [It is] a restatement of that which was understood as applying "in place" by the rule *alaḥ antyasya*.
A restatement is made of that which was understood as applying "in place" (*sthāne*) by the rule *alaḥ antyasya*. Otherwise...

For indeed, there would be the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*). Otherwise, the undesirable consequence would follow: even the markers *ṭ*, *k*, and *m* would apply to the final [sound]. If, however, this were understood as a supplement to the preceding rule (*yogaśeṣa*), then in that case what undesirable consequence would follow? Even the markers *ṭ*, *k*, and *m* would apply to the final [sound]. Therefore, it is well said:
The rule *alaḥ antyasya* is a restatement (*anusaṃhāra*) of that which has already been understood as "of the final [element]"; otherwise, an undesirable consequence would follow.
(P. 1.1.53) Why does *tātaṅ* not apply to the final [element]? Because the rule *ṅicca* and *alaḥ antyasya* would then apply to *tātaṅ*. In the case of *tātaṅ*:

Because the inclusion of the marker *ṅ* has its own scope, [the substitution of] *tāt* for *hi* is a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*) due to the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). What is the scope for the inclusion of *ṅ* in *tāt*? The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Since the inclusion of *ṅ* in *tāt* has its own scope, it will be a total replacement by virtue of the rule of conflict. That which must necessarily be stated is indeed called a "purpose" (*prayojana*).

It would be so if this [substitution] were necessarily a replacement for the whole (sarvādeśa). In that case, this purpose [of the marker] would be valid. But why indeed should it be understood from the addition of the marker *ṅ* that this will be a replacement for the whole and not merely for the final letter? If that is the case, then this very fact—that it is marked with *ṅ*—indicates that *tātaṅ* does not occur in place of the final letter.

He says this because otherwise he would have stated [the rule] only in the section concerning *er* for the imperative (*loṭ*), as in: "For the two [suffixes] *ti* and *hi*, *tāt* is optionally used in the sense of benediction" (Pāṇini 7.1.35).

Due to the conflict between exceptions (*apavāda*) and prohibitions (*vipratiṣedha*), according to the principles "of the final letter of *ala*" (Pāṇini 1.1.52) and "a substitute consisting of more than one letter or marked with *ś* replaces the whole" (Pāṇini 1.1.55), it becomes a replacement for the entire form.

The rule *alo 'ntyasya* ("of the final [alphonetic element]") is the general rule (*utsarga*). The rules *tasyādeḥ parasya* ("of that which follows, [the substitute takes the place] of its initial [element]") and *anekāl śit sarvasya* ("a substitute consisting of more than one phoneme or marked with Ś replaces the whole") are exceptions (*apavāda*) to it. However, due to the conflict between a general rule and an exception (*apavādavipratiṣedha*), there will be a replacement of the whole. The scope of application for *tasyādeḥ parasya* is, for example, *dvyantarupasargebhyo 'pa īt*: "after the words *dvi*, *antaḥ*, and prepositions, the word *apaḥ* is replaced by *ī*."

Regarding the rule *anekāl-śit sarvasya* ("that which has more than one letter or is marked with Ś replaces the whole"), this is its scope: *asteḥ bhūḥ* ("*bhū*" replaces *as*") and *bhavitā*, *bhavitum*. Here, both [rules] would apply:

*ataḥ bhisa ais* ("*ais* replaces *bhis* after a stem ending in *at*") and *anekāl-śit sarvasya*. By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the latter prevails. Regarding the rule *śit sarvasya* ("that which is marked with Ś replaces the whole"), this is its scope: *idama iś* ("*iś* replaces *idam*") and *itaḥ*.

In this case, the scope of the rule *ādeḥ parasya* ("of the substitute for what follows, [the replacement] is of the first element") is exactly that same [situation]. Here, both [rules] would apply: *aṣṭābhya auś* and *śit sarvasya*. By means of the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the latter prevails. (P. 1.1.55) KA_I,131.19–132.7 Ro_I,148.10–149.10; T_2,6.18–24; J_1,131.19–132.7; C_1,56b1–57a2; W_1,108.1–109.10;

396–397. What is an example for [the rule] "śit replaces the whole"? [The example is: from *idam*, *iś* [is substituted], as in *itaḥ* and *iha*. This is not a necessary purpose; because of the very presence of the marker *ś*, there will be substitution of the whole in this case. Then what [is the example]? [The example is: *aṣṭābhyaḥ auś*. But surely, even here, because of the very presence of the marker *ś*, there will be substitution of the whole. Then what [is the example]?

*Jasaḥ śi jaśśasoḥ śiḥ*. Now, one might object: even here, the substitution will be for the whole word simply because of the presence of the *śit* marker. There is another purpose for the *śit* marker. What is it? It is for the sake of specification (*viśeṣaṇa*). Where is there a need for specification? In the rules: *śi sarvanāmasthānam* and *vibhāṣā ṅiśyoḥ*. [If that were so,] one could have omitted the rule *śit sarvasya*. How so?

If this [element] were to occur in place of the final [sound], it would not be a suffix (*pratyaya*). If the designation "suffix" does not exist, the designation *it* would not exist. If the designation *it* does not exist, there would be no elision (*lopa*). If there is no elision, it is "multi-sound" (*anekāl*). When it is multi-sound, then it is a total substitute (*sarvādeśa*). When it is a total substitute, then it is a suffix. When it is a suffix, then the designation *it* exists. When...

"In that case, there is elision of its designation. If this is so, then since the result is already established, the fact that the Teacher states "that which has a *ś* [as an indicatory letter] replaces the whole" indicates that there exists this metarule (*paribhāṣā*): "The property of having more than one phoneme (*anekāltva*) does not arise on account of an indicatory letter (*anubandha*). What is the purpose of indicating this? In that regard—

Regarding the statement that "in the prohibitions of *asarūpa* [substitutes] and *sarvādeśa* [total replacements], there must be a separate mention because [the original form] does not end in the vowel *ā*," it is said that this need not be stated.

398–401. What is the purpose of employing the term *vat*? If it were stated merely that "the substitute (*ādeśa*) is [treated as] the original (*sthānin*) except in rules concerning vowels (*analvidhi*)," this would fall under the jurisdiction of technical designations (*saṃjñā-adhikāra*), and in that case, the designation of "original" would apply to the substitute itself. What would be the fault in that? [The rule] "the *ātmanepada* occurs after the roots *yama* and *hana* following the prefix *āṅ*" would apply only to the root *vadhi*, but not to the root *han*. However, when the term *vat* is employed, there is no such fault.

It occurs. An operation pertaining to the original element (*sthānin*) is extended to the substitute (*ādeśa*), just as in the case of "the son of a teacher is like the teacher. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "substitute" (*ādeśa*)? If it were stated merely as "like the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) except in the case of an operation concerning a phoneme (*analvidhi*)," then what would now be considered "like the original element"?
That which exists in place [of another]. And what exists in place? The substitute. Then this is the purpose: that it should apply to every substitute whatsoever.

[The term *sthānivadbhāva*] should apply as if it were the original element (*sthānin*). [An objection: One will raise the point that an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for that which has undergone partial modification (*ekadeśavikṛta*). [Reply: That need not be stated. Now, what is the purpose of including the word "rule" (*vidhi*)? It is so that the compound may be understood as ending in all case endings:
"a rule concerning what follows an *al*" (*alaḥ parasya vidhiḥ*) is an *al-vidhi*.
"Al-vidhi" means an operation concerning *al*; "ali-vidhi" means an operation concerning *ali*; "alā-vidhi" means an operation concerning *alā*.
This purpose is not necessary; this is a reference to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). These are references to the nominal stem.

And they are dependent on the meaning; they do not rely on any particular case-ending as being primary. In that case, when the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) has been indicated, whichever case-ending the intention arises to employ—that one should be employed. This, then, is the purpose:
so that the elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapadalopa*) may be understood [as follows].

That which depends on *al* is "dependent on *al*" (*alāśraya*); a rule dependent on *al* is an "*al*-rule" (*alvidhi*). The prohibition would apply only in cases where *al* is depended upon as the primary element;
it would not apply in cases where *al* is depended upon merely as a qualifier. What is the purpose [of this distinction]?
In the examples *pradīvya* and *prasīvya*, the augment *iṭ*—which would otherwise be triggered by the rule regarding roots beginning with *val*—must not occur.

But for what purpose is this stated? Because the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*) are distinct, the designation "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies to the substitute.

Just as in the case of "the guru's son is like the guru," where one is the original element (*sthānin*) and another is the substitute (*ādeśa*), because of this distinction between the original element and its substitute, the operation applicable to the original element does not apply to the substitute. What is the fault in that? [According to the rule] "the *ātmanepada* occurs after *āṅ-yama-han*," it would apply only to *han*, but not to *vadh*. Yet it is desired that it should also apply to *vadh*. Therefore...

And [the desired result] is not accomplished without effort. Therefore, the rule "it should be treated like the original" (*sthānivad-anudeśaḥ*) is stated for this purpose, just as in the case of "the son of the teacher is like the teacher. For example, just as one should behave toward the teacher's son as one would toward the teacher, whatever operation applies to the teacher is extended (*atidiśyate*) to the teacher's son.

In this case as well, the operation pertaining to the original element (*sthānin*) is extended by analogy to the substitute (*ādeśa*). This is not necessary, for it is established by common worldly usage. Just as in the world, whoever appears in someone else's place receives that person's functions;
for example, a teacher’s pupil, having gone to the households of those for whom he performs sacrifices, receives the seat of honor and other such privileges. Even so...

In the world, this is a commonly observed principle: even an illustration serves to preclude the application of a person's [usual] effort. And here, there is indeed a certain effort on the part of a person. He says: "There is. What is it? It is a rule regarding the essential form (*svarūpavidhi*). When the *ātmanepada* affix is prescribed for the root *han*, it would apply only to *han* and not to *vadh*. If that is so, then the activity of the Teacher indicates that [the substitute] is as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*).

The fact that there is an injunction [of a prohibition]—namely, that this [sūtra] teaches a prohibition of substitution by stating "yuṣmadasmadoḥ anādeśe" (for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, except when there is a substitute)—is the indicator. How does it function as an indicator? Since an operation is prescribed for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* in relation to a case-ending (*vibhakti*), what occasion would there be for it to apply to a substitute? However, the Teacher perceives that a substitute is indeed like the original (*sthānivadbhavati*). Therefore, he teaches the prohibition regarding the substitute.
In that case, the purpose is this:
[the rule] will state the prohibition "not in a rule prescribing an *al*," so that it does not apply here: *dyauḥ*.

"The path," "that"—even this [objection] serves no purpose. The activity of the Teacher indicates that the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) does not apply in a rule concerning an *al* (vowel); for, although the form would have been established by the rule *adaḥ jagdhiḥ lyap ti kiti* simply by the mention of *ti-kit*, the explicit mention of *lyap* [in the rule *lyapi laghupūrvāt*] is intended to convey this very point.
Therefore, there is no purpose served by this rule (*yoga*).

Even if this rule were to be undertaken, there would be no application of it in the case of a prohibition regarding the prescription of an *al* (vowel) substitute, because no specific distinction has been made.

Because it is not seen. Even when a prohibition regarding an *al*-rule is applied without relying on a qualifier, in the absence of that qualifier, there is no application of the rule—as in *pradīvya* and *prasīvya*. What is the reason? Because it is not seen. It is stated [in the rule] "after a consonant beginning with *v*" (*valādeḥ*), and we do not see a consonant beginning with *v* here. But surely this effort is made for this very purpose: so that an operation being prescribed for one thing may apply to another. True, it is for this purpose, but it does not actually obtain.
What is the reason? When there is an extension of a general rule, there is no extension of the specific details. For when the general is being extended, the specific is not extended. For example:
"One should behave toward this Kṣatriya as one does toward a Brāhmaṇa. In this case, that which is the duty of a Brāhmaṇa is the general [rule] applied to the Kṣatriya.

That which is specified [as a condition] for Māṭhara or Kauṇḍinya is not extended [by analogy]. Likewise here as well, that general operation of the suffix which is common is extended, but that which is specified as belonging to [roots] beginning with *val* is not extended. If this were so, in the case of *agrahīt*, the elision of the *sic* suffix by the rule "when *īṭ* follows *iṭ*" would not apply. However, when it is stated again "in a rule not concerning a letter" (*analvidhau*), [the desired result is achieved].

In this case as well, there will be a prohibition [of the augment *iṭ*] in the forms *pradīvya* and *prasīvya*, for here it relies upon a specific capacity (*bala*) called *alam*. And in this case, there will be no prohibition in *agrahīt*, for here it relies upon a specific incapacity (*an-alam*) called *iṭ*. If, then, both the general rule and the specific rule are extended, and a rule is desired to apply when its basis exists—then, since [the basis] exists...
Since [the root] belongs to the *valādi* group, the augment *iṭ* ought to occur:

*aruditām*, *aruditam*, *arudita*. What follows from this? That it ought to occur when it exists. However, a prohibition would apply because it is not a rule concerning vowels (*alvidhi*). A prohibition would indeed apply. Why? Because it is not a rule concerning vowels; this is a rule concerning vowels (*alvidhi*).

In that case, the prohibition [stated in the rule] "analvidhau" would apply. Or rather, there is no such fault; for while there is a prohibition of the *ādeśika* (substituted) form, the existence of the other [the original] remains. Why? Because of the prohibition of the *ādeśika*. Let there be here a prohibition of the *valāditva* (the status of having *val* as its initial element) of the *ādeśika*; however, the *valāditva* will exist here by virtue of its own basis (*svāśraya*).

We do not dispute whether [the substitute] begins with *v* or does not begin with *v*. What then? Because of the status of being a *sthānin*, the property of being a *sārvadhātuka* must be admitted. In that case, the prohibition "not in the case of a rule concerning a vowel" (*analvidhau*) would apply.

406–408. Furthermore, when the substitute (*ādeśin*) *ali* (a vowel) is relied upon, does the prohibition apply, or does it apply without distinction to both the substitute and the original (*ādeśya*)? And what is the difference here? If the prohibition applies to the original (*ādeśya*), then a prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* must be stated for the roots *kṛ*, *vadh*, and *pā*. That is to say, in the case of the original [roots] *kṛ*, *vadh*, and *pā*, a prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* must be formulated. For example, in the form *kuru*.

In this case, by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the designation of the stem (*aṅga-sañjñā*) and the condition of having a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhatva*) dependent upon it [the *ā*] are present. Consequently, the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel would apply. In the word *vadhakam*, by virtue of the status of being a substitute, the designation of the stem and the condition of having a short vowel as the penultimate (*adupadhatva*) dependent upon it [the *k*] are present. Consequently, the *vṛddhi* substitution would apply. In the word *piba*, by virtue of the status of being a substitute, the designation of the stem and the condition dependent upon it...

There is the state of having a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhatva*). In that case, *guṇa* substitution would apply. Let it be, then, without distinction, whether with respect to the substitute (*ādeśa*) or the original element (*ādeśin*). If it is argued that [the rule applies] when there is both an original element and a substitute, then an addition must be made for those cases where *sup*, *tiṅ*, and *kṛt* suffixes are extended by analogy (*atideśa*). If it is argued that [the rule applies] when there is both an original element and a substitute, then an addition must be made for those cases where *sup*, *tiṅ*, and *kṛt* suffixes are extended by analogy. *Sup*:

In the case of *vṛkṣāya* and *plakṣāya*, because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the designation *sup* applies and its own inherent property of beginning with *yañ* etc. also applies. In that situation, the prohibition [of the elision of the final vowel] would apply. Regarding *sup* and *tiṅ*: in *aruditām*, *aruditam*, and *arudita*, because of the status of being a substitute, the designation *sārvadhātuka* applies and its own inherent property of beginning with a *val* sound also applies. In that situation, the prohibition [of the substitution of *guṇa* for *ṛ*] would apply. Regarding *tiṅ*: in the case of forms taught as *kṛt*-derivatives, such as *suvaṇam*, [the same applies].

In the case of *dhuvana*, because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), it would possess both the technical designation of an affix (*pratyayasañjñā*) and its own inherent property of beginning with a vowel (*ajāditva*). Consequently, the prohibition [of the augment *it*] would apply there. What, then, is better in this regard? It is better that the prohibition applies when the original element (*ādeśin*) is understood as not being an affix.

Why is this so? Because in this way, one transfers a specific operation pertaining to the original element to the substitute, just as one treats the son of a teacher as a teacher himself (*guruvat guruputre*).
Thus, as it is said:
"One should behave toward the teacher's son just as one behaves toward the teacher, except for eating his leftovers and performing the clasping of his feet.
And if the teacher's son is also a teacher, then that [behavior] must also be performed. Let it be so, then, when *ali* is resorted to as the substitute (*ādeśin*).

[This is] a prohibition. But was it not said that when there is a prohibition of a rule concerning that which is to be substituted (*ādeśya*), there is a prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* for the roots *kṛ*, *han*, and *pā*?

This is not a fault. It is established because of the mention of the vowel *t* (in *karoti*) as having a following *ṛ* (*tapara*). The root *pā* ends in *a*. As for *vadhaka*, this is not the suffix *ṇvul*; rather, this is another word *aka* which is a *kit* suffix belonging to the *uṇādi* class, just like *rucaka*.

(P_1,1.56.5) KA_I,136.5-137.2 Ro_I, 408-411 An addition must be made regarding that which is modified in one part. An addition must be made regarding that which is modified in one part. What is the purpose? [So that] *pacatu* and *pacantu* may be included by the mention of *tiṅ*. [This applies to] that which is modified in one part.

It is established because of non-difference. Since that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original], it will be included by the mention of *tiṅ*. For example: when a dog's ear or tail is cut off, it remains a dog; it does not become a horse or a donkey. However, there is the understanding of non-eternality; therefore, an additional rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) is required. For there is the understanding of non-eternality [in the world, yet] words are eternal. Among eternal things...

A name must consist of phonemes (*varṇa*) that are fixed, unchanging, and devoid of loss, addition, or modification. In that regard, the fact that "this very same [name] is modified" is not possible among eternal things. Therefore, an additional rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be formulated. The followers of Bhāradvāja recite:

An addition must be made regarding those forms in which a single part has been modified. An addition must be made regarding those forms in which a single part has been modified. What is the purpose? [So that] in cases such as *pacatu* and *pacantu*, there may be inclusion by the mention of *tiṅ*. And for what reason would it not be so? Because they are not substitutes (*ādeśa*). It is stated that "a substitute is like its original" (*sthānivadbhavati*), but these are not substitutes. Furthermore, because the form is different; indeed, the form of *pacati* is one thing, while the form of *pacatu* is another.

Thus [it is said]. These also are substitutes (*ādeśa*). How so? That which is pointed out (*ādiśyate*) is a substitute; and these too are pointed out. If it is argued that "a substitute is like the original" (*sthānivat*), we say no, because it has not been established. If it is argued that "a substitute is like the original," that is not so. What is the reason? Because it has not been established. That which is the substitute here is not what is relied upon, and that which is relied upon is not the substitute.

This is the instruction. It should not be thought that when the whole (samudāya) is resorted to, the part (avayava) is not resorted to; for the part is indeed internal to the whole. Just as, for example, a tree moving moves along with its parts. If it is argued that [the whole] is the locus (āśraya), then there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of an operation concerning a vowel (al-vidhi). [If it is said that] the locus...

If this is argued, then since this is a rule concerning vowels (*al-vidhi*), the prohibition "in the case of what is not a rule concerning vowels" (*analvidhau*) would apply. This is not a fault; for if that were the case, there would be no rule concerning vowels at all, yet this term "analvidhau" is indeed stated. Therefore, it should be understood as referring to the superlative degree (*prakarṣagati*).
"Better is that which is an *al*-vidhi. And what is better? That where *al* is relied upon primarily. Where *al* is relied upon as an inseparable adjunct (*nāntarīyaka*), that is not an *al*-vidhi.
Or rather, the purpose of mentioning "substitute" (*ādeśa*) has already been stated: so that every substitute whatsoever should be treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*).

(P_1,1.56.6) The relationship between a substituend (*sthānin*) and a substitute (*ādeśa*) is untenable because words are eternal (*nitya*). This notion that "there is a substituend and a substitute" is not applicable to eternal words. Why? Because of their eternity. For that which is called a "substituend" is something that, having existed, no longer exists; whereas a "substitute" is something that did not exist before but now exists.

Indeed, that which comes into being after not having existed is not possible in the case of eternal words, namely, that there should be the destruction of what exists or the manifestation of what does not exist. But this is established by the use of the term "place" (*sthāna*) even for things that have never previously existed, as seen in both worldly and Vedic treatises. This is established. How so? Just as in worldly and Vedic systems of thought (*kṛtānta*).

The word *sthāna* (place/position) is used even for that which has not previously existed. In common worldly usage, for instance, it is said, "the pupil is in the place of the teacher," yet the teacher was not previously present there. Likewise in the Veda:
"One should press the *pūtīka* grass in the place of *soma*," yet the *soma* was not previously present there.

It occurs. Or it is established through the transformation of the effect (*kāryavipariṇāmāt*). Alternatively, this is established through the transformation of the effect. What is this "transformation of the effect"? The effect is cognition (*buddhi*); that is what undergoes transformation. But should it not rather be "through the non-transformation of the effect" (*kāryāvipariṇāmāt*)? For there are indeed instances of shortening at the end of a compound. Furthermore, cognition is comprehension (*sampratyaya*).

Thus, there is no difference in meaning. "The effect" refers to cognition (*buddhi*); "the effect" refers to comprehension (*sampratyaya*); "the transformation of the effect" refers to the transformation of comprehension;
[the term] "due to the transformation of the effect" is stated having considered this to be a different resolution.

And how would this be a different resolution? If the word *sthāna* (place/position) is used in the sense of what has occurred previously (*bhūtapūrva*). [That is, it means] "in what has occurred previously."

Furthermore, the word "place" (sthāna) is used [in this context]. How so? By means of cognition (buddhi). For example, someone instructs another, saying, "The mango trees are to the east of the village. In that person, a cognition of mango trees has arisen everywhere. Thereafter, he says, "Those which have milky sap, aerial roots, and broad leaves are banyan trees. Thus, he replaces the cognition of mango trees there with the cognition of banyan trees.
He proceeds; then, by means of his intellect (*buddhi*), he perceives mango trees being removed and banyan trees being planted.
Yet the mango trees remain eternally in their own place, and the banyan trees likewise remain eternal. It is only his intellect that undergoes transformation.
In the same way here, the verb "to be" (*asti*) is taught to him without distinction; consequently, the notion of existence (*astibuddhi*) becomes attached to him everywhere.

Thinking "the root *as* becomes *bhū*," he transitions from the cognition of *asti* to the cognition of *bhavati*. Thereupon, through his intellect, he perceives *asti* being withdrawn and *bhavati* being introduced. While *asti* remains eternally established in its own object and *bhavati* likewise remains eternal, it is only his cognition that undergoes transformation.

But there arises the contingency of the application of an exception (*apavāda*) because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). Furthermore, that which is effected by a general rule (*utsarga*) would also apply to an exception. For instance, in the case of the suffix *ka* [as in *kāraka*], even though it is an exception to the rule "the suffix *aṇ* occurs after a verbal root when an object is expressed" (*karmaṇy aṇ*) and "the suffix *ka* occurs after a root ending in long *ā* when no prefix is present" (*ātaḥ anupasarge kaḥ*), that which is effected by the suffix *aṇ* would still apply. What is the reason? Because of the status of being a substitute.
Or has it been stated? What has been stated? It was stated that "it is established by the fact that different genders are employed for the object. Or else:
"It is established, however, because of the statement that what is designated by the genitive is like the original (sthānin). This is established. How so?

It must be stated that "the substitute (ādeśa) of that which is designated by the genitive is like the original. In that case, the mention of "that which is designated by the genitive" must be made. No.

It must be performed. The subject under discussion continues. Where was it discussed? In the rule *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā* ("the genitive [case ending] is used in connection with that which takes its place"). Alternatively, the activity of the Teacher indicates that what is prescribed by a general rule (*utsarga*) does not apply when an exception (*apavāda*) is present, since he forms certain *śit* suffixes for *śyan* and others: namely, *śyan*.
*śnam*,
*śnā*, *śaḥ*, and *śnuḥ*.

There is a fault in this [rule]; regarding the substitution of *tay* and so forth, there must be a prohibition of both. This is the fault of this very rule: when there is the substitution of *tay* and so forth, a prohibition of both must be stated.

Both gods and humans [are included]. Since the term *tayap* is included by the inclusion [of the suffix], the optional application of the *jasi* case-ending would follow. This is not a fault. The suffix *ayac* is a different suffix. If it were a different suffix, the form *ubhayī* (with the long vowel *ī*) would not be obtained.
Let it not be so; it will be formed by the rule for the suffix *mātrac*. How so? Because this "mātrac" is not a mention of a specific suffix.
What then? It is the inclusion of a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated reference). Of which [elements] is there this *pratyāhāra*? From the word *mātra* up to the letter *ca* in *āyac*.
If it is the inclusion of a *pratyāhāra*, then [the suffix] would also apply here in the case of *kati tiṣṭhanti*. [Answer: The word *ataḥ* (from *at*) is understood [as a governing rule].
Even so, it would still apply here in *tailamātrā* and *ghṛtamātrā*. [Objection: It would also apply to similar forms.

For that which is not established [as a substitute], there will be no grasping by means of *pratyāhāra*. In the case of a transfer of number (*vacanātideśa*) when expressing a genus (*jātyākhyā*), there must be a prohibition of the status of being a *sthānin*. In the expression "come from the rice-grains" (*vrīhibhya āgataḥ*), the rule *gher ṅiti* would result in the application of *guṇa*. This is not a fault; for this has already been stated:

"It is established by the extension of the meaning. Regarding the mention of *ṅī* and *āp*: "In the mention of *ṅī* and *āp*, a short substitute is not *sthānivadbhūta* (does not behave like its original). This must be stated. What is the purpose? [To ensure that] in *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* and *atikhaṭvaḥ*, the elision of *su* (*sulopa*) does not occur because they are included by the mention of *ṅī* and *āp*. But surely it is said, "after a long vowel" (*dīrghāt*). Therefore, that need not be stated. What, then, is better here? The prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* itself is indeed better.
This also is established:

*atikhaṭvāya*, *atimālāya*. By the rule *yāṭ āpaḥ*, the suffix *yāṭ* does not occur. Now, even though there is no status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), once the lengthening has been performed, why does *yāṭ* not occur by the rule *yāṭ āpaḥ*, on the grounds that this [suffix] was previously a *pit*?

"Between that which is taught by its technical definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and that which is taught by its specific wording (*pratipadokta*), the latter alone [is to be taken]. But now, even though there is the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), can this paribhāṣā not apply here? No, he says; for in that case, the status of being a substitute would not occur anywhere at all. Then it must be stated? It need not be stated. It is established through a *praśliṣṭanirdeśa* (a combined or contiguous formulation). This is indeed a *praśliṣṭanirdeśa*:

[The rule] "from those ending in *ī*, *ī*, and *īkāra*, and from those ending in *ā* and *āp*" [is intended]. There must be a prohibition of *īṭ* for the roots *ah* and *bhū*. A prohibition of *īṭ* for *ah* and *bhū* must be stated: [otherwise, one would derive] *āttha* and *abhūt*. Since these are included by the mention of *asti* and *brū*, *īṭ* would apply. First, it need not be stated for *ah*; the activity of the Teacher indicates that *īṭ* does not occur after *ah*, since he prescribes the substitution of *th* for *ah* in the section concerning [suffixes] beginning with *jhal* by stating "the *th* of *ah*."

[The opponent] teaches: "This purpose does not exist. For there is indeed another purpose for stating this [the substitution of *tha*]. What is it? So that the understanding of what was previously so (*bhūtapūrvagati*) may be known: 'that which was previously beginning with a *jhal* [consonant]'. If this were the case, the mention of *tha* would be useless. He should have simply pronounced *ātha*: "In place of the five [roots], beginning with *bru*, *ātha* is substituted for *bru*. And [the substitution] for the root *bhū* need not be stated either. [The rule] *astisico 'pṛkte* contains a dual *s* (i.e., *asti-s-icaḥ*), as an indication [of this].

Regarding the statement "from the root *as* ending in *s*": there must be a prohibition of *vṛddhi* and *tattva* (the substitution of *t*) when the substitute *vadha* is applied. When the substitute *vadha* is applied, a prohibition of *vṛddhi* and *tattva* must be stated; otherwise, [in the case of] *vadhakam puṣkaram*, *vṛddhi* and *tattva* would occur due to the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*. This is not a fault. It has already been said: this is not the suffix *ṇvul*; this is another word *aka*, a *kit* suffix belonging to the *uṇādi* class, just as in the case of *rucaka*. And there is the rule for *iṭ*: the augment *iṭ* is to be prescribed.

[In the case of] *āvadhiṣīṣṭa*, the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 7.2.10], "of a monosyllabic root which is unaccented in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*)," would apply. This is not a fault; for we shall effect an accentuation by means of a nipātana (irregular assignment) as being acutely accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*). That nipātana-accent will be the sublater of the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Even so, the status of being "as if in its original enunciation" (*upadeśivadbhāva*) must be stated; for just as the nipātana-accent [sublates] the natural accent, [so too must the rule regarding the prohibition apply].

In this way, it would indeed override even the accent of the suffix, as in *āvadhiṣīṣṭa*. This is not a fault. The rules pertaining to *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes apply generally while the suffixes have not yet been fixed. Therefore, once the substitution of *vadhi* has occurred by virtue of the general category of *ārdhadhātuka*, the accent of the suffix prevails because it is the remaining (or subsequent) rule.

It will be so. There must be a prohibition of *nuk* and *śuk* after a stem ending in long *ā*: [the forms] *vilāpayati* and *bhāpayate*. Since these stems are included by the mention of the roots *lī* and *bhī*, the suffixes *nuk* and *śuk* would apply. This is established by the mention of *lī* and *bhī* as a conjunctive compound (*praśliṣṭanirdeśa*). This is a conjunctive compound of *lī*—meaning a root ending in long *ī*—and *bhī*—meaning a root ending in long *ī*. In the case of substitutes for the imperative (*loḍādeśa*), there must be a prohibition of the following: the substitution of *śā* for *sa*, the substitution of *jha* for *jhi*, the substitution of *dhi* for *hi*, the elision (*hilopa*) of *hi*, and the substitution of *it* for *hi*. A prohibition of these must be stated for the substitutes of the imperative.

From *śiṣtāt*, *hatāt*, *bhintāt*, *kurutāt*, and *stāt*: when the substitutes for the imperative (*loṭ*) have been applied, the following rules would apply—the substitution of *ś* for *s*, the substitution of *j* for *h*, the substitution of *dh* for *t*, the elision of *hi*, and the substitution of *e* for *a*. This is not a fault; for here, this must be deliberated upon.

"Let the substitutes for the imperative (loḍādeśa) be applied; these rules [of substitution] are to be followed. What should be done here? The imperative substitute applies because it is subsequent [in the order of rules].

Now, once the imperative substitute has been applied, why do these other rules not apply again by virtue of the principle of "re-occurrence" (punaḥprasaṅga)? Because of the principle: "In the case of a conflict where a rule has been applied once, that which was superseded remains superseded. [Objection: There is a prohibition regarding forms ending in *-s* when the *trayādeśa* (the substitution of *traya*) occurs.
An exception must be stated regarding the substitution of *traya-* for a stem ending in *tisṛ*:

[the rule would otherwise apply to] *tisṛṇām*. Once the substitution of *tisṛ* has been effected, the substitution of *traya-* for *tri-* (P. 7.2.99) would then apply. This is not a fault. Here, this must be considered:
should the substitution of *tisṛ* be applied, or the substitution of *traya-*? What should be done here? The substitution of *tisṛ* applies because it is subsequent. Now...

Now, since the substitution of *tisṛ* has been applied, why does the substitution of *traya* not occur again due to the principle of "reapplication" (*punar-prasaṅga-vijñāna*)? [The answer is: "In the case of a single application when there is a conflict, that which is superseded remains superseded. And regarding the rule for *ām*: in the prescription of *ām*, a prohibition must be stated for a stem ending in *sr*.

The four [forms] remain. When the substitution of *catasṛ* has been made, the rule "the *ām* of *catur* and *anaḍuh* is acute" would cause *ām* to apply. This is not a fault. Here it must be considered: let either the substitution of *catasṛ* be applied, or the *ām* of *catur* and *anaḍuh* (by which *ām* is prescribed)—which of these two should be done here? Because of its higher status in the order of rules (*paratva*), the substitution of *catasṛ* takes effect. Now, once the substitution of *catasṛ* has been performed, why does *ām* not occur again by virtue of the principle of "reapplication" (*punaḥprasaṅga*)?
"When there is a conflict between two rules that apply simultaneously, that which is sublated remains sublated. Regarding the substitution of *vas* [for *as*] before a vowel:

a prohibition must be stated regarding the substitution of *vas* before a vowel; [otherwise], in the case of *viduṣaḥ paśya*, this accent would apply by the rule "the suffix *śatṛ* ending in a vowel other than *u*, not preceded by a nasal, is udātta when it follows a stem ending in an udātta vowel": namely, the rule "the suffix *śatṛ* is udātta after a stem ending in an udātta vowel, provided it is not a feminine stem in *nadi* or beginning with a vowel. This is not so.
There is a fault. [Objection: There will be a prohibition by the word "anumaḥ. [Response: It is said "anumaḥ," yet we do not see a *num* augment here. [Clarification:

This "anumaḥ" is not a mention of an augument (*āgama*). What then? It is a mention of a *pratyāhāra* (a grammatical abbreviation). Of which elements is this *pratyāhāra* composed? From the letter *u* up to the *m* of *num*. If it is a mention of a *pratyāhāra*, then [the rule applies to] *lunataḥ*, *punataḥ*.

In this case as well, [the objection] would apply: by the mention of *anum*, the present participle ending in *-śatṛ* is not qualified; rather, it is the suffix *-śatṛ* itself that is qualified, meaning "that which is a *-śatṛ* suffix having the augment *anum*. And this must necessarily be understood in this way. For if there were a mention of the augment (*āgama*), then [the rule] would undesirably apply here in cases such as *muñcatām* and *muñcataḥ*. Regarding the word *go*: a prohibition must be stated concerning the initial *ṇit*-strengthening, the substitution of *āt*, and accentuation when following the word *go*. That is to say, a prohibition must be stated for the word *go* with respect to the initial *ṇit*-strengthening, the substitution of *āt*, and accentuation.

In *citragvagram* and *śabalagvagram*, the rule *sarvatra vibhāṣā goḥ* would result in the optional substitution of the penultimate vowel (*pūrvatva*). This is not a fault. The term *eṅaḥ* is understood [from the previous rule]; therefore, the prohibition by the rule *analvidhau* will apply there. Even so, [in the vocative] *he citrago*.

In this case, the status of being a *ṇit* would apply first: *citraguḥ*, *citragū*, *citragavaḥ*. By the rule *goto ṇit*, the status of being a *ṇit* would apply. Then the substitution of *ā* would apply: *citragum paśya*, *śabalagum paśya*. By the rule *ā ot*, the substitution of *ā* would apply. This is not a fault; it is established by the inclusion of the marker *t* (in *gotaḥ*). By the force of including the marker *t*, the status of being a *ṇit* and the substitution of *ā* will not occur.

Regarding the *svara* (accent): in the case of *bahugumān*, the prohibition [of the acute accent] by the rule *na gośvansāvavarṇa* would apply. There is a prohibition regarding the roots *kṛ* and *pā*. A prohibition must be stated for the roots *kṛ* and *pā*: [otherwise, one would have to say] *kuru* and *piba*. Due to the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) would apply. Or, it has already been stated. What has been stated? It has been stated that [the form] is established by the mention of the vowel *a* with a following *t* (*tapara*) in the rule for the root *kṛ*.
"pibatiḥ adantaḥ" (the root *pā* ending in *i* when followed by *ad*).
(P. 1.1.57.1) KA_I,141.24–144.17 Ro_I, 421–431. Why [is it said] "of vowels" (*acaḥ*)? This is the question.

In the forms *dyūtvā* and *ākrāṣṭām āgatya*, as well as in *praśnaḥ* and *viśnaḥ*, the substitution of the letter *ś* for the letter *ch* is conditioned by a subsequent cause (*paranimittaka*). Due to the status of that [substitute] as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original), the rule *che ca* applies.
Thus, the insertion of *tuk* would occur. It does not occur because of the mention of *acaḥ*. This is not a valid purpose [for the mention].

Even if the mention of *ac* were made, an effort must certainly be exerted here to prevent the occurrence of *tuk*; for *tuk* would apply by virtue of being an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation. In that case, consider this:

In the case of *dyūtvā*, the substitution of *ūṭ* for the letter *v* is conditioned by a subsequent element (*paranimittaka*).
