Due to the status of that [substitute] as "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), the rule for *yaṇ*-substitution—namely, *aci*—would not apply. However, because of the explicit mention of *acaḥ* [in the rule], it does take place. This too is not a valid purpose [for the rule]. Here, the status of being a vowel (*actva*) will exist by virtue of its own nature (*svāśraya*). Alternatively, that which is the substitute here is not relied upon, and that which is relied upon is not the substitute.
[This is] an instruction (*ādeśa*). Then this is the purpose:

[in the case of] *ākrāṣṭām*, the elision (*lopa*) of *sic* is caused by a subsequent element (*paranimittaka*). Due to its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original), the substitution of *k* for *ṣ* and *ḍh* according to the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* would apply. It occurs, however, because of the mention of *acaḥ* [in that rule]. This too is not a purpose; for he will say this:

[The rule] "in the case of what is not established in the preceding [context], there is no *sthānivadbhāva*" [applies]. What then is the purpose [of this sūtra]? [Consider the forms] *āgatya* and *abhigatya*. The elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) is caused by what follows (*paranimittaka*). Because of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, the *tuk* augment [prescribed] by the rule "after a short vowel" (*hrasvasya*) would not apply. It does, however, apply because of the explicit mention of "vowels" (*acaḥ*). Now, for what purpose is the phrase "when [the substitute is] subsequent" (*parasmin*)? [Consider] *yuvajāniḥ*.
Dvipadikā,
Vaiyāghrapadya,
Ādīdhye, Yuvajāni.
Regarding the form *vadhūjāniḥ*:

the substitution *niṅ* for *jāyā* is not caused by what follows it (*paranimittaka*). Due to its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, the elision of *y* (*yalopa*)—which occurs "before a *val*" (*vali*)—would not apply.

However, because of the rule stating "when there is something following" (*parasmin*), it does take effect. This, however, is not a necessary purpose; for here, the *val*-elision occurs by virtue of its own inherent nature (*svāśrayam*).
It will be so. Or rather, that which is an *ādeśa* (substitute) here is not resorted to, and that which is resorted to is not an *ādeśa*.
In that case, this is the purpose:

in the forms *dvipadikā* and *tripadikā*, the elision (*lopa*) of the word *pāda* is not caused by a subsequent element (*paranimittaka*). Because of its status as a *sthānivat* (as if it were the original), the substitution of *pad-* [for *pāda-*, as in *padbhyām*, etc. would otherwise apply.

[The objection: It does not obtain [the designation of *bha*] because of the statement "in the subsequent [element]. [The response: This too is not a purposeful restriction; by the force of the repeated mention of elision (*lopa*), the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) will not occur. [The objector asks: Then what is the purpose? [The response: Consider the case of *vaiyāghrapadyaḥ*. [The objector says: But even here, it will not occur simply by the force of the repeated mention. [The response: There is indeed another purpose for the repeated mention of elision. What is it? [It applies] where there is the technical designation *bha*.
Not so:
*vyāghrapāt*, *śyenapāt*. And this too is an example: *ādīdhye*.

In *āvevye*, the substitution of *e* for the vowel *i* is not caused by a subsequent element (*paranimittaka*). Because that [substitution] would be treated as if it were the original (by the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*), the elision prescribed by the rule *yīvarṇayor dīdhīvevyoḥ* would apply. However, by virtue of the statement "when there is a subsequent [element]," it does not occur. Now, what is the purpose of the phrase "in the case of an operation concerning a preceding element" (*pūrvavidhau*)? [Consider the examples: *he gauḥ* and *bābhravīyāḥ*.

In the case of *naidheyaḥ*—wherein the vowel *au* in *gauḥ* is caused by a subsequent element—the elision of the vocative ending prescribed by the rule *eṅhrasvāt sambuddheḥ* would apply because of the status of that [substitute] as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). However, this does not occur due to the statement "in the case of a rule concerning what precedes" (*pūrvavidhau*). This, however, is not a valid purpose [for the rule]. The activity of the Teacher indicates that there is no status as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) in the elision of the vocative ending.
As for the fact that he employs the term *eṅ* in the rule *eṅhrasvāt saṃbuddheḥ*, this is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*). This would merely be for the sake of brevity (*laghvartham*).
If so, then why does he employ the mention of the *pratyāhāra*? For otherwise, he would simply have said *ohrasvāt*.
In that case, the purpose is this:

In the case of *bābhravīyāḥ* and *mādhavīyāḥ*, the substitution of *v* for *au* is conditioned by what follows (*paranimittaka*). Because of its status as a *sthānivat* (as if it were the original element), the elision of *y* prescribed by the rule *halaḥ taddhitasya* would not apply. [However], due to the statement "in a rule concerning what precedes" (*pūrvavidhau*), this does not occur. Yet, even this is not a valid purpose [for the rule].

In this case, the status of being a consonant (*hal*) will belong to its own substratum. Alternatively, that which is the substitute here is not what is relied upon, and that which is relied upon is not the substitute. In that case, the purpose [of the rule] is this:

*naidheyaḥ*. Here, the elision of the vowel *ā* is conditioned by a subsequent element; because of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original), the suffix *ḍhak* would be characterized by having two syllables (*dvyac*).
It does not apply. Because of the statement "in a preceding rule" (*pūrvavidhau*), it does not occur. Now, for what purpose is the mention of the word "rule" (*vidhi*)?
So that the compound may be understood as ending in every case-ending:
"a rule concerning what precedes" (*pūrvasya vidhiḥ*) is "a preceding rule" (*pūrvavidhiḥ*).

The rule concerning what precedes is "pūrvavidhi" (a rule based on what precedes). Now, what are the purposes for the treatment as a *sthānin* (original element) in a rule concerning what precedes? They are: *bebhiditā*, *māthitikaḥ*, and *apīpacan*. [In the case of] *bebhiditā*: 1. *bebhiditā*: [This is derived from the root √bhid with the desiderative suffix san, followed by the periphrastic future suffix tṛc. Here, the substitution of *iṭ* after the reduplicated stem (*abhyāsa*) is not considered to have occurred in place of the original element; thus, the prohibition of *iṭ* by P. 7.2.11 does not apply, and the augment *iṭ* is inserted. 2. *māthitikaḥ*: [This is derived from *mathita* with the secondary suffix *ṭhak*. Here, the substitution of *t* for *th* in *mathita* is not considered to have occurred in place of the original element; thus, the application of the suffix *ṭhak* is not blocked by P. 7.3.3, which prohibits it after words ending in *t*. 3. *apīpacan*: [This is derived from the root √pac with the causative suffix nic, followed by the imperfect suffix laṅ. Here, the substitution of *guṇa* (*o*) for the vowel of the reduplicated stem is not considered to have occurred in place of the original element; thus, the shortening of the reduplicated vowel by P. 7.4.59 does not apply. These are the purposes for the treatment as a *sthānin* in a rule concerning what precedes. *Bebhiditā*.

In the case of *cecchiditāḥ*, once the elision of the vowel *a* has occurred, the prohibition of the augment *iṭ*—which applies to a monosyllabic base—would result; however, it does not occur because of the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). In the case of *māthitikaḥ*, once the elision of the vowel *a* has occurred, the substitution of *ka* (by the rule *tāntāt kaḥ*) would result; however, it does not occur because of the status of the substitute. In the case of *apīpacan*, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has occurred, the change to *jus* (by the rule *abhyastāt jher jus bhavati*) would result.

[The objection: "It does not occur because of the status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). [The reply: These are not valid purposes [for the rule]. Why? Because this is a mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). And mentions of nominal stems are dependent on the meaning; they do not depend primarily on any particular case-ending (*vibhakti*). Therefore, when the meaning of the nominal stem has been specified, whatever case-ending the mind may conceive of employing—[in that case, the rule applies].
Each [substitute] must be resorted to [as a basis for the rule]. Then this is the purpose:

so that the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) may apply even when the original form (*prakṛti*) is not being resorted to, in the case of a mere rule (*vidhimātra*). For example, in *vāyvoḥ* and *adhvaryvoḥ*, let there not be the elision of *y* and *v* (*yalopa*) by the rule *lopo vyor vali*. This is indeed a purpose. What [else]?

If so, it should rather be stated as "in the prescription of another. What is the purpose? So that the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the place of the original) may apply even in the prescription of its own [element].
But what, then, are the purposes for the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* in the prescription of its own [element]? [The forms] *āyan*, *āsan*, etc.
They satisfy and prepare the curd here;
they made it sweet here, they did so. Here, for instance: *āyan*.

In the case of *āsan*—where the *yaṇ* and elision (*lopa*) have been applied to the roots *iṇ* and *as*—the augment *āṭ* does not apply because the root does not begin with a vowel (an-aj-ādi), according to the rule *āṭ ajādīnām*. However, it does occur by virtue of the status of the substitute being as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). In the cases of *dhinvanti* and *kṛṇvanti*, once the *yaṇ* substitution has been made, the augment *iṭ* would apply by the rule governing suffixes beginning with a consonant (*valādi*). It does not occur, however, due to the status of the substitute being as if it were the original. In the examples *dadhi atra* and *madhu atra*, once the *yaṇ* substitution has been made, there occurs the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*).

[The substitution] would apply; however, due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), it does not occur. In the forms *cakratuḥ* and *cakruḥ*, once the *yaṇ*-substitution has been applied, reduplication would not apply because [the resulting form] is no longer a vowel (*anact*). Due to the status of being a substitute, it does occur. If, then, the status of being a substitute applies even in the case of a rule concerning itself (*svavidhi*), then [in the case of] "it should be given by two" (*dvābhyāṃ deyam*), [the same problem would arise].

In this case, *lavanam* would also result [as an undesired form]. In the word *dvābhyām*, because of the status of the substitute as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the vowel *at*, lengthening (*dīrghatva*) would not apply. In the word *deyam*, because of the status of the substitute as being like the original for the substitution of *ī*, the *guṇa* replacement would not apply. In the word *lavanam*, because of the status of the substitute as being like the original for the *guṇa*, the substitution of *av* would not apply. This is not a fault; for in these cases, the operations depend on their own inherent bases (*svāśraya*).

[Objection: Then rules (*vidhayaḥ*) will have to be stated [separately] for each subsequent rule (*aparavidhau*). [Reply: It need not be stated. It is established by the very phrase "in the preceding rule" (*pūrvavidhau*). How so? By the mention of "preceding," the substitute (*ādeśa*) is not connected [as the subject]; rather, the sense is:

"A substitute for a vowel (*ajādeśaḥ*) conditioned by what follows (*paranimittakaḥ*) is like the original (*sthānivat*) with respect to a rule concerning what precedes. From what does it belong to what precedes? From the substitute. What then? The cause (*nimitta*) is connected [to the preceding].

A substitute for *ajādi* (a vowel) which is caused by a subsequent element (*paranimittaka*) is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhavati*) with respect to an operation concerning what precedes it. From where [does the rule apply] to what precedes? From the cause (*nimittāt*). Now, when the cause is connected [to the rule], even that most celebrated example of this rule is included. What, then, is that? "paṭvyā" and "mṛdvyā. Certainly.
[It is] included. But surely, because it is separated by the *yaṇ* substitute for the vowel *ī*, this [substitute] does not precede the cause [of the substitution].
Even when separated, the word "preceding" (*pūrva*) is used;

for example: "Pāṭaliputra is before Mathurā. Alternatively, the term "substitute" (*ādeśa*) itself is connected [to the rule]. How so? Regarding those purposes for which the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) is required in its own rule (*svavidhi*), these do not exist here.

In this context, first of all, there are the forms *āyan*, *āsan*, *dhinvanti*, and *kṛṇvanti*. This word "vidhi" (injunction) indeed exists as having an object (*karman*) as its means of derivation (*sādhana*).
The word *vidhi* is prescribed [as a technical term]. There is a derivation based on the abstract action (*bhāvasādhana*):

"the act of prescribing" (*vidhāna*) is *vidhi*. Since the adoption of the word *vidhi* as a derivative based on the object (*karmasādhana*) would not encompass everything that is intended, it should be understood that the word *vidhi* is adopted here as a derivative based on the abstract action.

Thus, [the rule] "that which precedes a *vidhi*—with respect to the preceding [element], with respect to the preceding [action]—should be as if it were the original" means that it becomes like the original (*sthānivat*).
"In this way, *āṭ* will occur, and *iṭ* will not occur. [The author] will state the resolution regarding the forms *dadhi atra*, *madhu atra*, *cakratuḥ*, and *cakruḥ*.
What, then, are the purposes of this rule (*yoga*)? "I shall praise Pādikaudavāhin. Thus he speaks.

On the following day, [the teacher said: "O Śātanī and Pātanī, come as leaders; after that, bring Dhāraṇī and Rāvaṇī, for then it will fall away and be destroyed. Here, in the case of *pādikam audavāhim*—namely *śātanīm*, *pātanīm*, *dhāraṇīm*, and *rāvaṇīm*—when the short *a* is elided, the rules for the substitution of *pad-* (for *pada-*) by *ūṭh*, the elision of *al*, and the elision of *ṭi* would apply. This is because of the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).
[The suffixes] do not occur. [In the case of] *sraṃsyate* and *dhvaṃsyate*:

once the *ṇi*-affix has been elided, the elision of the *n*—prescribed by the rule *aniditām hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti*—would apply. It does not occur because of the status of being "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*). These are not valid purposes [for the rule]. By the rule *asiddhavat atra ā bhāt*, these [cases] are also [covered].

[The forms] are established. However, this is the purpose [of the rule]: consider the case of *yāpyate*. When the *ṇi*-affix is elided, the rule "vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs for roots beginning with *yaj* before a *kit* suffix" would apply. [But] due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), it does not occur.
This too is not a valid purpose. We shall qualify the *kit* suffix here by means of the roots beginning with *yaj*, [specifying that it applies only] to those beginning with *yaj*.

Regarding the rule *yaḥ kit*: what is *kit*? It is that *ya* which is prescribed after the roots beginning with *yaj*. Then this is the purpose: [to account for forms like] *paṭvyā* and *mṛdvyā*. When the substitution of *yaṇ* has been applied to the following vowel, the substitution does not apply to the preceding one because it is separated by the *yaṇ* substitute for the long *ī*. It occurs, however, by virtue of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*. But what is the reason that it occurs first for the following vowel and not for the preceding one?

Because it is obligatory (*nityatvāt*). The substitution of *para-yaṇ* (the subsequent semivowel) is obligatory; it applies whether the substitution of *pūrva-yaṇ* (the preceding semivowel) has already taken place or not yet taken place. Since it is obligatory, once the substitution of *para-yaṇ* has occurred, the [substitution of] the preceding [element] does not apply. [But] it does occur by virtue of the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāvāt*). Even this is not a purpose [for the rule], because that which is characterized by being external (*bahiraṅga*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is characterized by being internal (*antaraṅga*), and thus it is non-existent.
The external rule (*bahiraṅga*) for the substitution of *yaṇ* [for *v*] shall be superseded by the internal rule (*antaraṅga*) for the prior substitution of *yaṇ*.

Furthermore, this *paribhāṣā* must necessarily be resorted to for the sake of accentuation, so that the accent prescribed by the rule "udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt" may apply in forms such as *kartryā* and *hartryā*. This accent is also established by the present rule. How? Because it is an obligatory (*nitya*) rule that is being introduced.

When this rule (*yoga*) is being formulated, the substitution of *yaṇ* for the preceding vowel (*pūrvayaṇādeśa*) is obligatory; it applies whether the substitution of *yaṇ* for the subsequent vowel (*parayaṇādeśa*) has already occurred or has not yet occurred. The substitution of *yaṇ* for the subsequent vowel is also obligatory; it applies whether the substitution of *yaṇ* for the preceding vowel has already occurred or has not yet occurred. Furthermore, this [substitution] is subsequent (*para*), and it is subsequent by virtue of its fixed status (*vyavasthā*). Simultaneous occurrence is impossible.

And there is no possibility of their simultaneous occurrence. How, then, is it established? It is established by means of what is external (*bahiraṅga*). This is established by the rule: "That which is characterized as external is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is characterized as internal (*antaraṅga*). If this is so, then the accent will depend on that *udātta-yaṇ* (vowel with an acute accent) which occurs here. [Objection: Because it is separated by the *yaṇ*-substitute for the long vowel *ī*, the [desired] accent does not apply. [This is said] regarding the rules for accents (*svaravidhi*).

A consonant (vyañjana) becomes as if non-existent; thus, there is no intervention. In that case, this technical rule (paribhāṣā) must indeed be formulated. But should not this other one also be formulated:

"That which is characterized by being external (bahiraṅga) is unestablished (asiddha) with respect to that which is characterized by being internal (antaraṅga)"? This technical rule has many purposes; it is certainly necessary.
This [usage] must be established. And this too is established from common worldly usage. How so? Worldly practice is observed to follow each individual limb [of speech]. For example:

this person, having risen in the morning, first performs those duties of his that pertain to his own body, then those for his friends, and then those for his relatives. Furthermore, even a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is taught to function in a general sense.

For that which exists in a general form (*sāmānya*), the particular (*vyakti*) arises. Once it has become manifest and is endowed with gender and number, it enters into connection with an external object. Just as there is a sequential emergence of objects, so too must there be a sequential emergence of words; likewise, their effects must also follow that same sequence. These, then, are the purposes [of the suffix]: *paṭayati*, etc.

In *avadhīt* (he killed), as in *bahukhaṭvakaḥ*, and in *paṭayati* or *laghayati*, once the *ṭi*-elision has been performed, the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* would require the substitution of a *vṛddhi* vowel for the penultimate *a*. This does not occur because of the status of the substitute as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). In *avadhīt*, once the elision of the *akāra* has been made, [the rule] *ato halāder laghoḥ* [would otherwise apply].

The *vṛddhi* substitution would apply [to the final vowel]. It does not occur because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). In the case of *bahukhaṭvakaḥ*, when the shortening of the feminine suffix *āp* has optionally been applied according to the rule "optionally after a short vowel," this accent—namely, that which applies to the syllable preceding the final one—would result. It does not occur because of the status of being a substitute.

435–436. Here, in the case of *vaiyākaraṇaḥ* and *sauvaśvaḥ*, the substitution of *āy* and *āv* would result from the status of the [substitutes] as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). A prohibition of these two must be stated.

[This is not necessary,] because the *ai* and *au* are established through the understanding that [the rule applies] to what precedes a vowel (*acaḥ pūrva-vijñānāt*). Regarding a prescription for that which precedes a vowel which has not been previously specified (*anādiṣṭāt acaḥ pūrvaḥ*), [the substitute is treated as non-existent].

The status of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva). And this [substitute] precedes the vowel that is prescribed. Should this be stated? No, it need not. How is it understood even without being stated? The word *acaḥ* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*); thus, it means "of what precedes the vowel. If this is so, then the substitute remains unspecified. Yet the substitute must be specified. How?
We do not say that the mention of *aj* (vowel) which is indicated by the genitive case must be changed to one indicated by the ablative case. What then?

Something else must be done; yet nothing else need be done. That very mention of *aj* indicated by the genitive case becomes [the basis for] the ablative case when it is in construction with words denoting direction (*dik-śabda*).

A substitute for *ac* (a vowel), which has a subsequent element as its cause, is treated like the original (*sthānivadbhavati*) with respect to an operation concerning what precedes it. From what does "what precedes" derive? From the rule "of *ac*" [P. 1.1.57]. For example, a substitute is designated in the nominative case; when used in conjunction with words denoting direction, the ablative case is employed: "A substitute for *ac*, having a subsequent element as its cause, is treated like the original with respect to an operation concerning what precedes it. From what does "what precedes" derive? From the substitute [itself].

In that case, there is a prohibition regarding the characteristics of a substitute (*ādeśa*). An operation characterized by a substitute would apply there; its prohibition must be stated: in *vāyvoḥ* and *adhvaryvoḥ*, the elision of *y* (*yalopa*)—by the rule "there is elision of *vy* before a consonant" (*lopo vyor vali*)—would apply. [This is] established because of the statement that [the former] is not established (*asiddha*). [The substitute is] one beginning with a vowel (*ajādeśaḥ*).
It should be stated that "that which has a subsequent cause is not established (*asiddha*) with respect to the rule for the preceding one.

If it is argued that "it is established because of the statement of its being *asiddha*," then there must be a restatement (*anudeśa*) of the rules concerning general operations (*utsarga*). If it is argued that "it is established because of the statement of its being *asiddha*," then a restatement of the rules concerning general operations must be made.

"By means of the sharp [or] the soft. But is this not already established by the statement "it is unestablished"? If you say it is established because of the statement that it is unestablished, we say no; for the existence of one thing does not follow from the statement that another is unestablished. If you say it is established because of the statement that it is unestablished, that is not so. What is the reason? Because the existence of one thing does not follow from the statement that another is unestablished. Indeed, it is not from the statement that another is unestablished [that the other exists].

The reappearance of another [element] occurs; for when the killer of Devadatta has been killed, there is no reappearance of Devadatta. Therefore, both the rule regarding "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) and the status of being "unestablished" (*asiddhatva*) must be stated. Thus, the state of behaving like the original must be declared, as well as the status of being unestablished. In the case of *paṭvyā* and *mṛdvyā*, there is the state of behaving like the original. In *vāyvoḥ*,...

[The objection that] the status of being unestablished (*asiddhatva*) applies to the two *adhvaryu* [forms] has already been addressed. What was said? That "the statement regarding the *sthānivadbhāva* (treating a substitute as the original) is purposeless because of the unestablished status of the rule. This comparison is unequal. It is appropriate in that case that the rule for the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) should be unestablished with respect to the rule for the *tuk* augment—since one [rule] pertains to one thing and the other to another. But here, it is not appropriate. For how could that very same thing be unestablished with respect to itself? And yet, even that very thing is indeed unestablished with respect to itself. For the Teacher will say: [P. 6.1.86].

Regarding the statement: "When there is *luk* of *ciṇ*, the mention of *ta* is useless, because the entire complex [of suffixes] is not a suffix (*apratyaya*), and because the elision of *ta* (*talopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*)," [the reply is: When there is *luk* of *ciṇ*, the *luk* of *ciṇ* itself remains non-existent. Or rather, let it be extended [by analogy] whether it exists or does not exist;
here there is no burden. For the remainder of the sentence must be inferred, for a sentence depends upon the speaker. Now...
This is an instruction using the suffix *vati*. And in an instruction with *vati*, there is freedom of usage (*kāmacāra*) to justify the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*).
For example: "In the Madra country, there are barley-grains like in Uśīnara; they exist, or they do not exist. "Her arts are like her mother's; they exist, or they do not exist.
In the same way here too, we shall justify the remainder of the sentence: "it is as if the original element (*sthānin*) were present" or "it is not as if the original element were present."

In this case, first of all, just as the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs for the substituendum (*sthānin*) in the words *paṭvyā* and *mṛdvyā*, so too does it occur for the substitute (*ādeśa*). Now, in this instance,
just as the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) does not occur for the substituendum in the words *vāyvoḥ* and *adhvaryvoḥ*, so too it does not occur for the substitute.

438–441. Furthermore, does the status of being *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the position of the original) apply with respect to what is immediately preceding, or rather to everything that precedes?

And what is the distinction here? If it applies to what is immediately preceding, then an addition must be made regarding the cases of *ekānanudātta*, *dvigusvara*, and *gatinighāta*. If it applies to what is immediately preceding, an addition must be made regarding the cases of *ekānanudātta*, *dvigusvara*, and *gatinighāta*. [Example: *ekānanudātta*: * **ekānanudātta**: [The rule states: "In a compound consisting of two members, the first member is unaccented (*anudātta*) except when it is a monosyllable. If the *sthānivadbhāva* applied only to what is immediately preceding, this would not hold in cases where the first member is more than one syllable long and separated from the suffix by other elements. Therefore, an addition is required to ensure the rule applies even when there is an intervention. * Example: *vīrapuruṣakaḥ* ("having heroic men"). Here, the suffix *-ka* causes the first member to lose its accent. If the *sthānivadbhāva* were restricted to the immediate predecessor, it would fail to apply to *vīra-* because the suffix is not directly attached to it. Thus, the rule must be extended. * **dvigusvara**: [The rule states: "In a *dvigu* compound, the first member takes the acute accent (*udātta*). If the *sthānivadbhāva* were restricted to the immediate predecessor, this would not apply to compounds like *pañcakapālī* ("an oblation prepared in five pots") where the suffix intervenes. An addition is therefore necessary. * **gatinighāta**: [The rule states: "A word preceding a verb loses its accent (*nighāta*). If the *sthānivadbhāva* were restricted to the immediate predecessor, this would not apply to cases where the verb is separated from its prefix by other words. An addition is therefore necessary. Thus, if the *sthānivadbhāva* is limited to the immediately preceding element, an explicit extension (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be formulated for these three specific grammatical operations.
"Cut here! Purify here!"—the rule "anudāttaṃ padam ekavarjam" (an unaccented word has one [vowel] excepted) does not apply here. Regarding the accent of *dvigu* compounds:

in *pañcāratnyaḥ* and *daśāratnyaḥ*, the rule "igantakāla" (a word ending in an *ik* vowel or denoting time is acute on the final syllable) does not apply. Regarding the suppression of the accent of a *gati* particle:
In the case of *yat pralunīhi atra* and *yat prapunīhi atra*, the accent prescribed by the rule *tiṅi codāttavati* does not apply. Let it be, then, for the preceding *mātrā*.

If it is for the preceding *mātrā*, then the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatva*) must be stated. If it is for the preceding *mātrā*, then the shortening of the penultimate vowel must be stated.

He caused [the lute] to be played; he had the lute played by a lutanist (*parivādaka*). But what is the reason it is not established? Because that *ṇi* which is elided in the presence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) would, by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, prevent the application of the rule for shortening (*hrasvatva*). Furthermore, the designation "heavy" (*gurusañjñā*) is also not established. Indeed, the designation "heavy" is not established.

In *śleṣmāghna*, *pittāghna*, *dādhyaśva*, and *mādhvaśva*, the consonants that follow one another constitute a *saṃyoga* (conjunction), according to the rule "consonants occurring without an intervening vowel are termed *saṃyoga*. By the rule "a syllable containing a *saṃyoga* is heavy," it receives the designation of being "heavy" (*guru*). Consequently, the protracted (*pluta*) vowel substitution prescribed by the rule "after a heavy syllable" does not apply. But surely, even for that which undergoes the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) with respect to a rule concerning what immediately follows it, there exists a rule characterized by immediate succession, namely the designation of *saṃyoga*.

[The rule] is to be applied. Or rather, it is not [required], because the *saṃyoga* (conjunction) is a previously unestablished injunction (*apūrvavidhi*). Or rather, this fault does not arise. Why? Because the *saṃyoga* is a previously unestablished injunction. The *saṃyoga* is not a rule for what has already been established (*pūrvavidhi*). What then? The *saṃyoga* is a rule for both the preceding and the following (*pūrvaparavidhi*).
An addition must be made regarding the *ekādeśa* (single-substitute). An addition must be made for the *ekādeśa*.
In *śrāyasau*, *gaumatau*, *cāturau*, *ānaḍuhau* (in the sense of "foot"),
and *udavāhe*, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, the rules for *num*, *ām*, *padbhāva*, and *ūṭh* would [otherwise] apply. Why, then...

The reason is not established. Because it has both as its cause: it is stated that "a substitute for *ac* has the subsequent element as its cause," yet this [substitute] has both as its cause; and because it is a substitute for two [sounds]. Furthermore, it is stated that "a substitute for *ac* occurs before *ic*," yet this is a substitute for two vowels (*ac*). This is not a fault. As for what was said regarding "because it has both as its cause":
In this case, when someone has many tasks in a village or a city, they are able to designate one of them, saying:

"We dwell here for the sake of our teacher," or "We dwell here for the sake of study. As for what was said—that it is because of being designated by both—here, when there is an occasion involving two things specified in the genitive case, that [result] obtains from either one of them.

441–443. Now, is a substitute for a *hal* (consonant) or an *ac* (vowel) treated as the original (*sthānivadbhavati*), or is it not? And what is the distinction here? If it is held that a substitute for a *hal* or an *ac* is treated as the original, then regarding the elision of the *ti* of *viṃśati*, a single substitution (*ekādeśa*) must be stated. If a substitute for a *hal* or an *ac* is treated as the original, then in the case of the elision of the *ti* of *viṃśati*, a single substitution must be prescribed: [as in] *viṃśakaḥ*.

*Viṃśam śatam*, *viṃśaḥ*. Regarding the substitution of *ava* for the final vowel of words beginning with *sthūla* when *yaṇ* and other subsequent sounds are elided: when the elision of *yaṇ* and following sounds has been performed in the case of words beginning with *sthūla*, the substitution of *ava* must be stated; as in *sthavīyān* and *davīyān*. Regarding the substitution of *etva* (the change to *e*) for the *iy* of *kekaya* and *mitrayu*: the substitution of *etva* for the *iy* of *kekaya* and *mitrayu* is not established; [as in] *kaikeyaḥ*.

Regarding Maitreya: the substitution of *e* (*etva*) for *aci* is not established. Furthermore, there is a fault when the final member of a compound is elided (*uttarapadalopa*). When the final member is elided, as in *dadhyupasiktāḥ saktavaḥ* (barley meal mixed with curd), which becomes *dadhisaktavaḥ*, the substitution of *yaṇ* for *aci* would apply. Regarding the elision of *yaṅ*: the substitutions of *yaṇ*, *iyaṅ*, and *uvaṅ* are not established when *yaṅ* is elided; thus, forms such as *cecyah* and *nenyah* would not be correct.

In the case of *cekriyaḥ*, *loluvaḥ*, and *popuvaḥ*, the rules for *yaṇ*, *iyaṅ*, and *uvaṅ* substitutions before a vowel (*aci*) would not be established. Let it then be that [the substitute] is not like the original (*na sthānivat*). If it is not like the original...

Prohibition of Guṇa and Vṛddhi in the Elision of Yaṅ: When there is non-substitution [of the original form] due to the elision of *yaṅ*, a prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* must be stated: *loluvaḥ*, *popuvaḥ*, *sarīsṛpaḥ*.

[The objection: "In *marīmṛjaḥ*, this fault [of the rule] would apply. [Response: This is not a fault. The prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 1.1.5]—"when there is elision of a verbal root (*dhātu*) before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix"—will apply here. [Question: But when is the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original element) operative? Is it when a specific base (*prakṛti*) is relied upon, or is it without distinction? Which [is it]?

And here there is a distinction. If it is argued that [the substitute] is *sthānivadbhūta* (behaves like the original) without qualification, then the rule regarding the designation of "heavy" (*guru*) would not be established in the case of elision (*lopa*) and the substitution of *yaṇ*. For example: *śleṣmā3ghna*, *pittā3ghna*, *dā3dhyaśva*, *mā3dhvaśva*. [In these cases,] the technical term "consonant cluster" (*saṃyoga*) applies according to the rule: "Consonants that are not separated by vowels are called a cluster."

If [the vowel] in a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is designated as "heavy" (*guru*), then the designation "heavy" (*gurusañjñā*) applies, and consequently, the protracted (*pluta*) vowel [rule] beginning with *guroḥ* would not apply. Furthermore, regarding the prohibition [of doubling], cases such as doubling (*dvirvacana*) and so forth must be stated.
Regarding the prohibition, doubling and the like must be mentioned:

namely, "doubling, the suffix *vara*, and elision of *ya*" (*dvirvacanavareyalopa*). Regarding the elision of *ks*, the rule for elision (*luk*) must be stated: "elision (*luk*) occurs when *ks* is elided," as in *adugdha*.

*adugdhāḥ*: [The form] is derived by the rule *luk vā duhadihalihaguhām ātmanepade dantye* (P. 6.4.91). For the root *han*, there is the substitution of *gh*. It must be stated that for *han* there is the substitution of *gh*: *ghnanti*, *ghnantu*, *aghanan*. Let it be then that [the rule applies] when the original base (*prakṛti*) is being resorted to. If it is argued that "in the case of operations involving the mention [of a specific form], the substitute is like the original" (*sthānivad ādeśo 'nalvidhau*), then there would be a prohibition of the substitute in the case of *jagdhi* and so forth. If it is argued that "in the case of operations involving the mention [of a specific form], the substitute is like the original," then [there would be a problem] with *jagdhi* and the others.
A prohibition must be stated for this substitution:

in *nirādya* and *samādya*, the substitution of *jagdhi* [for *ad*] would apply by the rule *adaḥ jagdhiḥ lyap ti kiti*. There is a prohibition of the substitution of *yaṇ*, the elision of *y*, *it*-ness, and *anunāsika-ittva* when there is the substitution of *yaṇ*. That is, there is a prohibition of the substitution of *yaṇ*, the elision of *y*, *it*-ness, and *anunāsika-ittva* when the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs.

It must be stated [as an exception]: regarding the elision of *y* (*yalopa*): in *vāyvoḥ*, *adhvaryvoḥ*. Since the rule "there is elision of *vy* before a consonant" (*lopo vyor vali*) would apply, there would be elision of *y*. Regarding the elision of *u* (*ulopa*): in *akurvi āśām*, *akurvy āśām*. Since the rule "the *u* of the root *kṛ* is always elided before the suffix *ya*" would apply, there would be elision of *u*. Regarding the substitution of *ī* (*ītva*):...

In *ālunī āśām*, *aluny āśām*, the substitution of *ī* (by the rule *ī hali aghoḥ*) would apply. In *ajajñī āśām*, *ajajñy āśām*, the substitution of the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) [by the rule *ye vibhāṣā*] would apply. Furthermore, there must be a prohibition of the substitution of *āt* for *rāi*: in *rāyī āśām*, *rāyy āśām*, the substitution of *āt* for *rāi* (by the rule *rāyaḥ hali*) would apply. When a long vowel follows, there must be a prohibition of the elision of *y* (*yalopa*): [in *rāyyā*].

In the case of *saurye*, which is the name of a peak of the Himavat mountains, [the form] *tadvān* becomes *sauryī* [by adding *ī*]; when the lengthening of the vowel *i* (*sau*) has been applied, the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) would result. Therefore, there is a rule for the elision of *y* after a long vowel. Thus, the elision of *y* must be stated after a long vowel: as in *gārgābhyām*.

In the case of *vātsābhyām*, once the lengthening has been applied, the prohibition "the substitution [of the long vowel] for the descendant-suffix (*āpatya*) does not take place before a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) other than *āN*" would apply. This is not a fault. For in that rule, the term "before a secondary suffix" (*taddhite*) is understood as referring to the original base (*prakṛti*). The resolution for all these cases is as follows:

it has already been stated that the purpose of employing the term "prescription" (*vidhi*) is so that the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) should apply to every prescription, even when [the condition of] not being based on the original base is not explicitly invoked.

"Or even in the original form (*prakṛti*). Or rather, let it be that "as in the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies without distinction. But was it not said: "If 'as in the original' applies without distinction, then there would be a prohibition regarding the rule for a heavy syllable (*guru-vidhi*) in the case of elision (*lopa*) and the substitution of *yaṇ*, as well as regarding reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and so forth; and regarding the elision of *ksa*, there would be the need for an explicit statement of elision (*lug-vacana*)"?

Regarding the statement "there is the substitution of *gh* for *han*": this fault does not apply. As for what was said—that if the rule were without qualification, then by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, the rule regarding the heavy syllable (*guru*) would apply to the elision (*lopa*) and the substitution of *yaṇ*—this has already been addressed:

"Or rather, it is not so, because the rule concerning a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) is not a rule that applies to something previously unestablished. Furthermore, as for what was said—that rules such as reduplication (*dvirvacana*) must be stated as exceptions to the prohibition—[that too is resolved].

It is stated that "with respect to a rule concerning the end of a word (*padāntavidhi*), [a substitute] is not treated as the original (*na sthānivat*). In that case, in the word *vetasvān*, the substitution of *ru* would apply. This is not a fault; for here the designation *bha* will be the sublater, by the rule *tasau matvarthe*. With respect to the designation *bha*, this [word *vetasvant-*] ends in the vowel *a*; with respect to the designation *pada*, it ends in the consonant *s*. But surely it will be understood thus: "that which is currently at the end of a word"? This would be the case if the word *vidhi* were employed in its passive sense (*karmasādhana*). And this word *vidhi* is indeed used in the passive sense: [meaning "a rule concerning that which is to be effected"].
The term *vidhi* is prescribed. There is a derivation based on the abstract action (*bhāva-sādhana*), namely:
"the act of prescribing" (*vidhāna*) is *vidhi*. In that case, if the derivation based on the abstract action were adopted, this fault would arise. And here [in the following examples]:
*brahmabandhvā*, *brahmabandhvai*.

The substitution of a *jaś* sound (a voiced unaspirated stop) would apply to the letter *dh*. However, when the word *vidhi* is employed in its sense of "action" (*bhāva-sādhana*), is something desired included, or is there merely the end of a fault? He says: "There is. In this case, what are those [forms] that exist?
*kau staḥ*, *yau staḥ*—that *y* or *v* which is heard at the end of a word is not heard [in these cases]. For example: *ṣaḍikaḥ*.

Furthermore, [the term] *siddha* (established) is [possible], but the vocal [form] (*vācika*) is not established. Let it then be a derivative based on the object (*karmasādhana*). If it is a derivative based on the object, then *ṣaḍika* is not established. Let it then be a derivative based on the action/state (*bhāvasādhana*). In that case, the vocal [form] is not established; the vocal and the *ṣaḍika* do not agree. An effort must be made here. How [is it formed] for *brahmabandhvā* and *brahmabandhvai*?
"Regarding both bases, it is not like [the rule for] the end of a word and so forth. How then is *vetasvān* [formed]? It is not understood thus:

"The end of a word (*padānta*) is that which is within a word (*pade antaḥ*), with respect to an operation concerning the end of a word (*padāntavidhim prati*). How then? It is understood as: "That which is within a word (*pade antaḥ*) is the end of a word (*padānta*), with respect to an operation concerning the end of a word (*padāntavidhim prati*). Or else, just as other word-operations (*padakāryāṇi*) also apply, so too does the substitution of *r* (*rutvam*).

And likewise, this *padakārya* (operation pertaining to a word) would also be sublated: namely, the designation *bha*. It is stated that [the substitute] is not *sthānivadbhūta* with respect to the rule for the elision of *y* when followed by a vowel (*vare*). In that case, in the example *te apsu yāyāvaraḥ pravapeta piṇḍān*, it would be *sthānivadbhūta* with respect to the rule for the elision of the vowel (*avarṇa*). This is not a fault; for it is not understood in that way.

"In the case of a *vārṇa* [substitution], there is no *sthānivadbhāva* with respect to the rule for the elision of *ya*. How then? "In the case of a *vārṇa*, with respect to the rule for the elision of *aya*. What does this mean, "with respect to the rule for the elision of *aya*"? It means "with respect to the rule for the elision of *avarṇa* and with respect to the rule for the elision of *ya*. Alternatively, a split of the *yoga* (rule) will be made:

What is elided by *vare* (in the context of *vārṇād āṅgaṃ balīyaḥ*) is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. Therefore, with respect to the rule for the elision of *y*, it is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*.

What is an example for the elision of *y*? [The answer is: from the root *kaṇḍūyati*, the suffix *ap* is elided, resulting in *kaṇḍūḥ*. This is not correct, because what is elided by *kvip* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. Then, what is the example here?

"Saurī balākā" (the crane belonging to Sūrya). This is not a valid example; with respect to a rule concerning the substitution of an element, [the substitute] is not treated as the original (sthānivadbhāva). Then this is the purpose: "ādityaḥ" (belonging to Āditya). This is not a valid example; when a preceding operation is not yet established (asiddha), [the substitute] is not treated as the original. Then this: "kaṇḍūtiḥ", "valgūtiḥ". This is not a valid purpose; it should be "kaṇḍūyā", "valgūyā". Then this:
From the root *kaṇḍūyati* with the suffix *ktic*:
*brāhmaṇakaṇḍūtiḥ* (the itching of a Brahmin), *kṣatriyakaṇḍūtiḥ* (the itching of a Kṣatriya).

Regarding the prohibition [of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule], it should be stated that "in the case of a substitution consisting of an elision (*lopa*), when there is a prohibition concerning accent (*svara*), lengthening (*dīrgha*), or the elision of *y* (*yalopa*), such a substitute is not like the original (*na sthānivat*). Accent (*svara*):
*ākarṣikaḥ*.
*cikīrṣakaḥ* (one who wishes to do), *jihīrṣakaḥ* (one who wishes to take). For any other substitute that occurs is indeed like the original (*sthānivadbhavati*): *pañcāratnyaḥ* (five cubits long).
Ten cubits. Vowel. Long.
*pratidīvna* for *pratidīvne*. For any other substitute is indeed treated like the original (sthānivat): *kiryoh*, *giryoh*. Long vowel. Elision of *y*.

The itching of a Brāhmaṇa, the itching of a Kṣatriya. For any other substitute that occurs is indeed like the original (sthānivadbhavati), as in the cases of *vāyvoḥ* and *adhvaryvoḥ*. If so, then it must be stated [as a rule]. It need not be stated; for here, even elision (*lopa*) is a substitute under discussion.
The term *vidhi* (rule) also follows from the present context. Long vowels (*dīrgha*) and so forth are also being indicated here. Only the necessary connection must be made:

in rules concerning vowel quality (*svara*), lengthening (*dīrgha*), and the elision of *y* (*yalopa*), a substitute for an elided element (*lopājādeśaḥ*) is not treated as if it were the original (*na sthānivat*). This applies to those [elements] arranged in their proper sequence.
A desired connection can be established [between words]. Moreover, these [words] are not arranged in a fixed sequence;
even for those arranged out of sequence, a desired connection occurs. For example:
"O sister, did you see the ox carrying water, you who carry a jar upon your head, as it was running sideways? In that case, a desired connection is established.
"O sister water-carrier, as you carry the jar upon your head, did you see the ox running sideways? (Pāṇini 1.1.58.3).

An addition [to the rule] should be made regarding the cases of *kvip*, elision (*luk*), the state of being a penultimate vowel (*upadhātva*), the suffix *acaṅ*, the reduction of syllables (*paranirhrāsa*), and the substitution of *ku* (*kutva*). [This applies] in the cases of *kvip*, elision, the state of being a penultimate vowel, the suffix *acaṅ*, the reduction of syllables, and the substitution of *ku*.

An addition must be made [to the rule]. What is the example for *kvau*? From the root *kaṇḍūyati*, with the suffix *apratyaya*, we have *kaṇḍūḥ*. This is not correct; with respect to the rule for the elision of *y*, it is not as if it were in its original state (*na sthānivat*). Then what is the example? From the desiderative *pipaṭhiṣati*, with the suffix *apratyaya*, we have *pipaṭhīḥ*. This is not correct; with respect to the lengthening of the vowel, it is not as if it were in its original state. Then what is the example?

From *lāvayateḥ*, *lauḥ*; from *pāvayateḥ*, *pauḥ*. This is not correct; for the elision of the *ṇi* suffix occurs without [the application of] the *vṛddhi* and *āv* substitutions. The *vṛddhi* will occur by virtue of the characteristic of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Then consider this: one causes *lava-* to be expressed, which is *lavayati*. From *lavayateḥ*, the suffixless form is *lauḥ*.

[Objection: Due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the original position), the substitution of *ūṭh* for *ṇi* does not occur. [Response: It follows that what is elided before a *kvip* suffix is not subject to *sthānivadbhāva*.

[Objection: Even so, it is still not established. How? In the case of *kvip*, there is the elision of *ṇi*; in the case of *ṇi*, there is the elision of the vowel *a*. Because of the *sthānivadbhāva* of that [elided *a*], the substitution of *ūṭh* does not occur. [Response: This is not a fault. It is not understood in this way:

"Regarding *kvip*, that which is elided is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were present). How then [is it explained]? Regarding a rule concerning *kvip*, that which is elided is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. What is the example for elision (*luk*)? *bimbam*, *badaram*. This is not correct; this is already established by the rule of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment). Then what is the example? *āmalakam*. This too is not correct; he will state this later:"
"The statement regarding the elision [of the feminine suffix] in the case of a derivative (*phala*) is purposeless, because it is a different base form (*prakṛti*). If so, then consider this:

"bought for five clever women" (*pañcapaṭuḥ*), "bought for ten clever women" (*daśapaṭuḥ*). But surely even this is established by the rule of masculine-like behavior (*puṃvadbhāva*). How is there masculine-like behavior?

Regarding the rule that "in the case of a *bha* [stem], when a *taddhita* suffix follows, it becomes like the masculine," the word "*bhasya*" (of the *bha*) is stated. Now, a stem is called *bha* when it begins with an element of the *yajādi* class, and we do not see such an element here. [Objection: It is a *yajādi* element by virtue of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). [Response: There is no application of the suffix-characteristic (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) when the operation depends on a phoneme (*varṇāśraya*).
[Objection: In that case, it will be so by the rule "*ṭhakchasośca*. [Response: The rule "*ṭhakchasośca*" is stated, but it does not apply here.

Here we observe the suffixes *ṭhak* and *cha*. [One might argue that] by the rule of "characterization by a suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), [the suffix would still apply]; however, there is a prohibition of characterization by a suffix by the rule "not when [a suffix] is elided by *lumat*" (*na lumatā tasmin*). Furthermore, it is not only the suffix *ṭhak* that has the sense of "purchased" (*krīta*), nor are only those secondary nominal suffixes (*taddhita*) that have meanings such as "purchased" [excluded].
What then? There are other secondary nominal suffixes as well which cause elision (*luk*).
One who has five Indrāṇīs as his deities is called "pañcendra," one who has ten Indras is "daśendra," and one who has five Agnis is "pañcāgni."

*Daśāgniḥ*. What is an example regarding its status as a *upadhā* (penultimate vowel)? [Consider] the suffixless form *pipaṭhīḥ* derived from *pipaṭhiṣati*. This is not correct; with respect to the rule for lengthening (*dīrghavidhi*), it is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. Then consider this: *saurī balākā*. This is not correct; with respect to the rule for the elision of *y* (*yalopavidhi*), it is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. Then consider this: *pārikhīyaḥ*. An addition must be made regarding the shortening of the vowel following *caṅ*: one who caused someone who had played [a musical instrument] to play.

He played the lute with a lute-player. But what is the reason that [the desired form] is not established? Because of the status of that *ṇi* which is elided before the causative suffix *ṇic* as being "as if it were in its original position" (*sthānivadbhāva*), the shortening of the vowel does not apply. Is it not already established by the rule that "this [substitute] is not treated as the original in respect to a rule prescribing the status of a penultimate vowel (*upadhā*)"? This must be stated as a specific restriction. Where? In the context of the prescription of a suffix (*pratyayavidhi*). Let it not apply here: [in cases such as *avīvadata*].

459–461. *Pūrvatrāsiddhe ca* (And when [an operation] is not established in what precedes). It should be stated that "even when [an operation] is not established in what precedes, [the substitute] is not like the original (*sthānivat*). What is the purpose? The purpose is the elision of *ksa* (*ksalopa*) when there is the elision of *s* (*salopa*). Regarding the elision of *s*, the elision of *ksa* is the purpose: *adugdha*, *adugdhāḥ*. Because of the rule "there is optionally elision (*luk*) of the *ksa* of the roots *duh*, *dihi*, *lih*, and *guh* when the *ātmanepada* ending begins with a dental," the mention of *luk* need not be made. [Furthermore, regarding] the elision of the vowel *ā* of the root *dadh* when there is the fourth sound (*caturtha*) at the beginning: when there is the elision of the vowel *ā* of *dadh* and the fourth sound at the beginning...
The purpose [of this rule] is as follows:

in forms such as *dhatse*, *dhaddhve*, and *dhaddhvam*, the letter *ca* in the rule *dadhaḥ tathoś ca* need not be stated. Regarding the rule *halaḥ yamām yami lopaḥ*: its purpose is seen in the word *ādityaḥ*; thus, the elision (*lopa*) of the semivowels (*yam*) after a consonant (*hal*) before another semivowel (*yami*) is established. Regarding the elision of *a* (*allopa*) and the elision of *ṇi* (*ṇilopa*): their purpose is seen in rules such as *saṃyogāntalopa*. Thus, the elision of *a* and the elision of *ṇi* are established in the context of the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), and so forth.
From *pāpacyate* comes *pāpakti*;
from *yāyajyate* comes *yāyaṣṭi*;
from *pācayate* comes *pākti*.

The suffix *yaṣṭi* [is established] for the root *yājayati*. And the rules concerning reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and so forth—these need not be recited; they are already established by the principle that what is *asiddha* (not yet proven) with respect to what precedes it is nonetheless effective. Is this without distinction? No, he says; "with the exception of *vareya*, elision (*lopa*), accent (*svara*), and [the rule regarding] *vara*. That is, excluding *vareya*, elision, and accent. Its fault [applies] in the cases of the elision of the first member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādilopa*), the substitution of *la* (*latva*), and the substitution of *ṇa* (*ṇatva*). Of that...

There is a fault in this definition regarding the elision of the first member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*), the substitution of *l* (*latva*), and the substitution of *ṇ* (*ṇatva*). Regarding the elision of the first member of a conjunct:

in the cases of *kākyartham* and *vāsyartham*, the elision [of the *k*] would apply by the rule "there is elision of the *s* and *k* which are the first members of a conjunct at the end of a word. Regarding the substitution of *l*: [the same fault applies].

461–462. Because of the extension [of properties] to the substitute (ādeśa) as being like the original (sthānin), reduplication (dvirvacana) applies to that which possesses such a substitute. Because of the extension [of properties] to the substitute as being like the original, reduplication applies to that which possesses the substitute. Like what? Like that which possesses the substitute. Consequently, what is the fault? In that case, the form of the reduplicated syllable (abhyāsa-rūpa) [is not established]. In that case, the form of the reduplicated syllable is not established: *cakratuḥ*.

They say "they made [the rule]. However, the mention of *aj* (vowel) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies to the form (*rūpa*). By the fact that the Teacher includes the mention of *aj*, he indicates that it is the form that becomes like the original. How does this serve as an indicator? The purpose of mentioning *aj* is so that [the rule] does not apply here: [Example omitted for brevity] ...so that it might not occur in this case.

[The forms] *jeghrīyate* and *dedhmīyate* [are cited]. If the form (*rūpa*) is treated as if it were the original (*sthānivat*), then the mention of the vowel (*aj-grahaṇa*) becomes meaningful. However, if the operation (*kārya*) [is what is meant], there is no purpose for the mention of the vowel. In this case, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) indeed occurs.

462–466. Regarding the prohibition of *gāṅ*: In that context, a prohibition of *gāṅ* must be stated [in the case of] *adhijage*, because the status of having an *i*-vowel as its reduplicated syllable would apply. It need not be stated. The expression *gāṅ liṭi* is a dual-lakāra (two-letter) reference, meaning "when *liṭ* begins with the *lakāra*. The form of the reduplicated syllable in the case of roots ending in *kṛt* suffixes, roots ending in *yaṅ*, roots beginning with *div*, and nominal roots is not established. [In the case of] *kṛt*: [the form is not obtained].
*acikīrtat* (from *kṝ*, with *iṭ*); *ejanta*:
*jagle*, *mamle* (both from roots ending in *e*); *divādi*:
*dudyūṣati*, *susyūṣati* (both from the *div* class); *nāmadhātu*: [examples of denominative verbs].

One desires to cause to become; from the root *bhū* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), followed by the desiderative suffix (*san*), we have *bibhavanīyiṣati*. If that is so, I shall state [the rule] as "when there is a suffix. If it is stated "when there is a suffix," then the form of the reduplication (*abhyāsa-rūpa*) in the case of roots ending in *kṛt* suffixes or those beginning with a vowel would not be established. If it is stated "when there is a suffix," then the form of the reduplication in the case of roots ending in *kṛt* suffixes or those beginning with a vowel is not established.

Some [grammarians] have already rejected the examples beginning with *div*. If that is so, then I shall state: "When there is a cause for reduplication (*dvirvacana*), a substitute (*ādeśa*) for a vowel (*ac*) is treated as the original (*sthānivat*).

In that case, the word "cause" (*nimitta*) must be explicitly included [in the rule], for the meaning of "cause" is not understood without the word "cause. [Objection: The meaning of "cause" is understood even without the word "cause. For example:
"Curd and cucumber" (*dadhitrapusa*) is directly perceived as fever; it is understood to be the cause of fever. "Reed-water" (*naḍvalodaka*) is foot disease;

it is understood to be the cause of foot disease. "Clarified butter" (*ghṛta*) is longevity; it is understood to be the cause of longevity. Alternatively, the negative particle *a-* has the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).
That which has "doubling" (*dvirvacana*) in this context is called *dvirvacana*;

thus, [the locative form] is *dvirvacane*. Even so, it is not known for how long a duration it remains as a substitute (*sthānivadbhavati*). However, for one who says, "when doubling is to be performed," once that doubling has been completed, it will no longer be treated as a substitute.

If that is so, then the prohibition under discussion is what will follow here. Where was it introduced? In the rule *na padāntadvirvacana*, which states that when a vowel is the cause of doubling (*dvirvacana*), a substitute for a vowel (*ajādeśa*) does not take place. Even so, it is not known for how long a duration that [prohibition] remains in effect. However, for one who says "when doubling is to be performed," [the prohibition applies] once that doubling has been completed.
The substitute *ajādeśaḥ* will occur. If that is so, then both are effected by this [rule]:

the suffix (*pratyaya*) is qualified, as is the reduplication (*dvirvacana*). But how can both be obtained through a single effort? He says: they are obtained. How? By means of an indication using the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) compound. This is an indication by *ekaśeṣa*.

Reduplication, reduplication, reduplication. When reduplication is to be performed, [the rule] "when there is an *ac* suffix" means that [the substitute] is treated as the original (*sthānivat*) when the *ac* suffix is the cause of the reduplication. If it is argued that "when there is an *ac* suffix which is the cause of reduplication, it is treated as the original," then it must be stated that the status of being treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies even in the case of the causative suffix (*ṇau*). If it is argued that "when there is an *ac* suffix which is the cause of reduplication, it is treated as the original," then the status of being treated as the original must be explicitly stated for the causative suffix (*ṇau*).

One might object that [the forms] *avanunāvayiṣati* and *avacukṣāvayiṣati* should not be stated [as examples]. However, the statement regarding "oḥ puyaṇjiṣu" is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) in the case of a causative suffix (*ṇi*). When the Teacher says "when *pu*, *yaṇ*, or *ji* follow," he indicates that in the case of a causative suffix, the original form is treated as a substitute.
If this is intended as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), then the form *acīkīrtat* would also fall under its scope. [Objection: It is an indicator for that which belongs to the same class (*tulyajātīya*).

[Question: And what is of the same class? [Answer: Those of the same nature as *pu*, *yaṇ*, and *ja*. [Question: And of what nature are these [cases]? [Answer: They are followed by vowels other than *a* (*avarṇa*). [Question: How then do we account for *jagle* and *mamle*? [Answer: The substitution of *ā* is unconditional (*anaimittika*), whereas the prohibition applies when a *śit* affix follows.
What, then, are the purposes of this grammatical rule (*yoga*)? [For example: *papatuḥ*, *papuḥ*.
They two stood;
they [all] stood;
they two went.
They went;
he wandered about; he sharpened.

In the forms *cakratuḥ* and *cakruḥ*, once the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*), the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*), the elision of the *ṇi*-affix (*ṇilopa*), and the *yaṇ*-substitution have been applied, reduplication would not apply because the root would then be devoid of vowels (*anackatvāt*). [However, it] occurs by virtue of the status of being "as if occupying the original position" (*sthānivadbhāvāt*). These are not valid purposes [for the rule], for [the result] is achieved even by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).
These [rules] are established. How so? For the Teacher will say:

"The doubling [of a consonant] takes precedence over *yaṇ*-substitution, the substitution of *ya*, *v*, *āy*, and *āv*, elision (*lopa*), elision of the penultimate (*upadhā-lopa*), and the substitution of *u* for *kikin*. Thus, that rule regarding priority (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) need not be recited. But what is superior here? The status of being as if the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) alone is superior; whereas in the case of priority, [the rule would have to be stated].
If this were the case, then this should have been stated:

"For a substitute beginning with *o* or *au*, an *u* occurs in place of a reduplicated syllable beginning with *c*, *ṭ*, *t*, *u*, *ś*, or *r*. But surely you too must state the substitution of *i*. It will serve my purpose: "In the presence of the suffix *san*, an *i* occurs in place of *at*. In that case, for me as well, the substitution of *u* will serve another purpose: [it will apply to the rule] "In the presence of the suffix *san*, an *u* occurs in place of *at*."
469–471. A technical name (*sañjñā*) should be assigned to the object (*artha*), so that it does not apply to the word (*śabda*). Furthermore, this results in mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
What constitutes this mutual dependence? There must be a name for an existing non-perception, and by means of the name, the non-perception is brought about.
This, then, is mutual dependence. And tasks characterized by mutual dependence cannot be accomplished.

Regarding the technical designation of elision (*lopasañjñā*), it has been stated that [the rule applies] to both that which exists as a meaning (*arthasat*) and that which exists as a word-form (*satsat*). What was stated? First, regarding that which exists as a meaning: it was stated that "the particle *iti* is for the purpose of indicating a meaning. Regarding that which exists as a word-form, it was also stated: "But [the form] is established because words are eternal" (*nityaśabdatvāt*). Words are eternal. And in the case of eternal words, there is the non-perception of that which exists.

A technical designation (*sañjñā*) is being applied. It is not the case that non-perception (*adarśana*) is produced by the designation. However, there would be the over-extension (*sarvaprasaṅga*) [of the designation] because everything is not perceived elsewhere. Indeed, there would be the over-extension: the designation of elision (*lopa*) would apply to every non-perception.
What is the reason? Because everything is not perceived elsewhere. For every word is [potentially] within the domain of usage for something else.

That [suffix] is not seen elsewhere; in *trapu* and *jatu*, there is the non-appearance of the *aṇ*. In that case, the designation "elision" (*lopa*) applies by the rule "non-appearance therein is elision. What is the fault in that? There is the prohibition of operations conditioned by an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). In that situation, an operation conditioned by an affix would apply, and its prohibition must be stated. [This is required for rules such as] *acaḥ ñṇiti*.

Thus, the rule for *vṛddhi* would apply. This is not a fault. It is stated that *vṛddhi* occurs for the vowel (*ac*) of the stem (*aṅga*) when followed by an affix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*. That which serves as the basis for the prescription of an affix is the "stem" (*aṅga*) with respect to that affix. Now, in this case, the basis for the prescription of the affix is not that [element] after which the affix follows; and that which follows the affix is not the basis for the prescription of the affix. [If so,] then what about the *kvip* affix?

[The term] "non-appearance" (adarśana). In that case, the technical designation "elision" (lopa) applies by the rule *adarśanaṃ lopaḥ*. What is the fault in that? Therein, there would be a prohibition of operations conditioned by an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). An operation conditioned by an affix would apply there; its prohibition must be stated. [For example,] by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk*, the augment *tuk* would apply. But it is established [that this is unnecessary] because [the rule applies to] the non-appearance of what was present.
Because it is designated as *lopa* (elision), this is established. How so? It should be stated that "the non-appearance of what was applicable is designated as *lopa*.

If it is stated that "the non-appearance of what was applicable is designated as *lopa*," then in the cases of *grāmaṇīḥ* and *senānīḥ*, the *vṛddhi* substitution would apply here. [The rule applies only to] that which is specified by the genitive case, such that the non-appearance of what was applicable is designated as *lopa*.

If it is stated that [the designation *lopa*] applies only to what is indicated by the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdiṣṭasya*), and restricted to cases where there is the elision of *ca* and so forth (*cāhalope eva*), then the designation *lopa* would not apply here in the rule "optionally when *ca* and so forth are elided" (*cādilope vibhāṣā*). Now, if it is argued that the designation *lopa* applies to the non-perception of that which was expected to appear (*prasaktādarśanaṃ lopasañjñaṃ bhavati*), how is this established? What is the "expectation" (*prasaṅga*) of a word? It is that situation where the meaning is understood, yet the word itself is not.

471–476. What is the purpose of mentioning "affix" (*pratyaya*)? The mention of "affix" when *lumat* occurs is for the purpose of prohibiting the designation of non-affixes. When *lumat* occurs, the mention of "affix" is made so that these designations do not apply to what is not an affix. What is the purpose? The purpose is [to prevent the application of rules] regarding the elision (*luk*) of *taddhita* suffixes, such as in the case of *kaṃsīya* and *paraśavya*, and also for the purpose of the cessation of the original base (*prakṛti*) in the case of the elision of *go*. Regarding the elision of *taddhita* suffixes...

In order to prevent the elision of *go*, and in order to prevent the elision of the base in the case of *kaṃsīya* and *paraśavya* when there is elision [of the suffix], the rule "when there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix" (*luk taddhitaluki*) would result in the elision of *go* as well. It does not occur because of the mention of the "suffix" (*pratyaya*). In the case of *kaṃsīya* and *paraśavya*, where the suffixes *yañ* and *añ* are elided, the elision of the base would also apply. It does not occur because of the mention of the "suffix. This is for the purpose of preventing the elision of *go*.

In that case, it would not serve the purpose [of the rule]. It is established by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule). A *yogavibhāga* will be made: "Of *go* when it is an *upasarjana*. A short vowel occurs for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *go* when it is an *upasarjana*.
Then: "Of the feminine. A short vowel occurs for a nominal stem ending in a feminine suffix when it is an *upasarjana*. Then...

Regarding the rule *luk taddhitaluki*: the term *striyāḥ* (of the feminine) continues to apply, while *goḥ* (of the word *go*) has ceased to apply. [The desired forms] are established by the specific mention of *kaṃsīya* and *paraśavya*. A specific mention must also be made for *kaṃsīya* and *paraśavya*, as follows: "In place of *kaṃsīya* and *paraśavya*, the suffixes *yañ* and *añ* occur, and there is elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *cha* and *yat*. And that specific mention must necessarily be made; for even if the term *pratyaya* (suffix) were included [in the rule], [the result would not follow].
[Objection: This would apply to the words *ukāra* and *saśabda*.

[For example,] from the root *kam*, we have *kaṃsaḥ*; and "that which shatters others" (*parāñ śṛṇāti*) is *paraśuḥ*. [Reply: This fault does not arise, because *uṇādi* formations are underived nominal stems (*prātipadika*). Therefore, this specific mention must be made for its own sake, or else the term "affix" (*pratyaya*) must be explicitly mentioned.

It must be stated, or it has already been stated. What has been stated? That "the mention of *ṅī*, *āp*, and nominal stems (*prātipadika*) is for the sake of the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of *aṅga*, *bha*, and *pada*, and for the sake of the elision (*luk*) of *yat* and *śas*.
But it is for the sake of the mention of the genitive case. If so, then the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*) must be made for the sake of the mention of the genitive case;
for if it were not mentioned, the meaning of the genitive case would not be established. For if the mention of the suffix were not made, the meaning of the genitive case [would remain unestablished].

There would be a lack of established application (*aprasiddhi*). Of what? Of the status of being connected with a substitute (*sthāneyoga*). But what is the purpose here of the mention of "pratyaya" (affix) for the sake of indicating a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), since a genitive is indeed uttered everywhere—in [the rules] *aṇiñoḥ*, *tadrājasya*, *yañañoḥ*, and *śapaḥ*? In this [present rule], however, there is no genitive at all.

Regarding the rule *janapade lup*: here too, the previously mentioned term *pratyayagrahaṇam* (the mention of "affix") is understood to carry over. Where was it mentioned? In the rule *pratyayaḥ paraś ca*. However, that [mention] was indicated in the nominative case (*prathamānirdiṣṭam*), whereas here [in the current rule], the sense requires it to be indicated in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdiṣṭena*). Consequently, this fifth-case form (*pañcamī*)—namely, *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*—will cause the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) to be substituted for the first case (*prathamā*) of the word *pratyayaḥ*.

Therefore, this is a rule for the introduction of an affix (*pratyayavidhi*) regarding what follows. Furthermore, in a rule for the introduction of an affix, ablative case endings do not serve as the basis for the derivation [of the substitute].

This is not a rule for the introduction of an affix; rather, an affix that has already been prescribed and the previously mentioned [element] continue to apply. Or, it is for the sake of making it a total substitute (*sarvādeśa*), by virtue of the authority of the statement. If so, then the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) must be made for the sake of making it a total substitute, [as in the case of] *luk*, *ślu*, and *lup*.

[The purpose is] so that all [elements] may be replaced. Now, even if the term *pratyaya* (suffix) is included [in the rule], how indeed can *luk*, *ślu*, and *lup* be obtained as replacements for the whole? [Answer: By virtue of the authority of the statement;
by the force of the inclusion of the term *pratyaya*. This too is not a purpose. The activity of the Teacher indicates [the following].

Since the substitutes *luk*, *ślu*, and *lup* are replacements for the whole [stem], why does [Pāṇini] prescribe *luk* in the rule "or *luk* occurs for the roots *duh*, *diha*, *liha*, and *guh* when followed by an ending of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) that begins with a dental"? It is for the sake of what follows. But then, the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) must be made for the sake of what follows. No, it need not be made; it is indeed done right there [in the previous rule].

"Where there is the elision of an affix, the operation conditioned by that affix [should take place]" (*pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam*). A second rule must be formulated: "The operation conditioned by an affix should take place when there is the elision of the entire affix, so that it does not occur when there is the elision of only a portion [of it]. For example: *āghnīta sam rāyaspoṣeṇa gmīya*.

476–478. What is the purpose of including the term *pratyaya* (suffix)? If it were stated merely as "there is the operation based on a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) when [a suffix] is elided (*lope*)," then in the case of *saurathī vahatī*, the suffix *ṣyaṅ*—which is conditioned by the rule regarding a heavy penultimate syllable (*gurūpottama*)—would undesirably apply. This is not a fault. It is not understood in this way: "When a suffix is elided, there is the manifestation (*prādurbhāva*) of the suffix. How, then? It means: "That grammatical operation for which the suffix is the condition (*lakṣaṇa*) occurs even when the suffix has been elided. Well then, consider this:

The purpose [of this rule] is as follows: that which applies when a suffix is present should occur by virtue of the suffix being the formal cause (*pratyayalaksana*); however, that which applies after the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix should not occur by virtue of the suffix being the formal cause. What is the purpose? [Consider the example:
*grāmaṇikulam*.

In the case of *senānikulam*, once the shortening (*hrasvatva*) has been applied according to the rule for the *auttarapadika* suffix, the augment *tuk* would apply by the rule "the augment *tuk* occurs before a *kṛt* suffix beginning with a vowel (*pit*) after a short vowel. To prevent this from occurring: if, then, that which applies when a suffix is present is to occur by virtue of the characteristic of that suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), [then the following applies].

That which would apply after the elision (*lopa*) does not occur in the case of *jagat*, because the augment *tuk* does not apply here in the word *janagat*. For in this instance, the augment *tuk* occurs after the elision. Therefore, there is no purpose served by the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*) for such a reason. Why then does it not occur in *grāmaṇikulam* and *senānikulam*? Because the shortening (*hrasvatva*) is external (*bahiraṅga*), whereas the *tuk* is internal (*antaraṅga*). That which is external is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal. In that case, this is the purpose:

The purpose [of the second mention of *pratyaya*] is so that the rule regarding the characteristics of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) should apply when the entire suffix is elided, but not when only a portion of it is elided; as in: *āghnīta sam rāyaspoṣeṇa gmīya*. This same purpose for the mention of *pratyaya* was already stated in the preceding rule (*yoga*). One or the other [mention] could have been omitted. Now, what is the purpose of the second mention of *pratyaya*? It is so that the rule regarding the characteristics of a suffix applies.
So that there might be the characteristic of the phonetic form (*varṇalakṣaṇa*), let it not be [otherwise]: *gave hitam* becomes *go-hitam*,
and *rāyaḥ kulam* becomes *rai-kulam*.

(P_1,1.62.2) Why, then, is this stated? [The rule] "when a suffix is elided, that which is conditioned by the suffix [still applies]" is stated because the science [of grammar] provides a formal description of what exists. It is said, "when a suffix is elided, that which is conditioned by the suffix [applies]," because the science provides a formal description of what exists (*sat*).

The treatise (śāstra) provides an exposition of what already exists, or the treatise serves as an expositor of what is existent. Because the treatise expounds upon what is existent, [the rule] "ugidacām sarvanāmasthāne 'dhātoḥ" would apply only here:
*gomantau* and *yavamantau*; it would not apply in cases such as *gomān* and *yavamān*. Yet, it is desired that it should apply there as well.

And that [result] is not accomplished without effort; therefore, there is the statement regarding the "characteristic of an affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) even when an affix is elided (*pratyayalopa*). This is stated for this very purpose. There is indeed a need for this. What then? An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for cases of elision by *luk*. An addition must be made for cases of elision by *luk*:
