Five, seven. But what is the reason that [the rule] is not established? Because the prescription applies when there is elision (*lopa*). For it is prescribed that the characteristic of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) applies when there is elision; therefore, it does not apply when there is *luk*. Or rather, it need not be stated. Why? Because non-appearance is designated by the term "elision" (*lopa*). It is said that non-appearance receives the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "elision. [The same applies to] the designations *lumat*.

And [the operations] of non-appearance (adarśana) are performed. Therefore, it will also apply when there is elision (luk). If this is so, then the non-appearance of an affix would also receive the technical designation *lumat*. What is the fault in that? In that case, there would be the undesired application of the rule for *ślu* even when there is *luk*; that must be prohibited.

In the case of *atti* (from √ad) and *hanti* (from √han), reduplication would apply by the rule *ślau*. This is not so, however, because of the assignment of separate technical names (*saṃjñā*). Indeed, this fault does not arise. Why? Because of the assignment of separate technical names. By virtue of the assignment of these separate technical names, the rule for *ślu* will not apply when there is *luk*. Therefore, on account of their commonality as non-observation (*adarśana*), the *lumat* designations subsume the designation *lopa*. Just as...

In that case, just as the designation *lopasañjñā* (the designation "elision") would encompass the *lumatsañjñās* (the designations *lu*, *lup*, and *luṅ*) because they share the common property of non-observation (*adarśana*), so too the *lumatsañjñās* would also encompass the *lopasañjñā*. What would be the fault in that? [Consider the example: *agomatī gomatī saṃpannā gomatībhūtā*.
By the rule *luk taddhitaluki*, the elision (*luk*) of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would undesirably follow. But surely, even here, because the designations are made separately...

Thus it is established. If that is so, then just as the *lummat* designations do not subsume the *lopa* designation by virtue of the power of their being established as separate designations, so too the *lopa* designation should not subsume the *lummat* designations. In that case, the same fault remains:
"there must be an additional rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for *luk*. There is, however, another purpose for establishing the *lopa* designation as a separate designation.

What [is the purpose]? It is so that what is prescribed in rules concerning the technical designation *lumat* should not apply to mere elision (*lopa*). Or rather, it is because of the prohibition regarding *lumat*.

Alternatively, by teaching this prohibition—namely, "not when there is *lumat*, [the operation] of the stem (*aṅga*) [does not take place]"—the Teacher makes it known that even when there is elision (*luka*), the formal characteristics of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) still apply.

Because of the absence of a cause, there is an absence of the designation *pada*. The suffix *san* is the non-cause for those grammatical operations [that would otherwise apply]; [for example,] in the case of *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*, even though that [suffix] has been elided, it would still be a non-cause.

Regarding the example *rājapuruṣaḥ*: let it be that for that [word], the designation *pada* defined as "that which ends in a vowel or a consonant" (*svādau padam*) is not the cause; however, the designation *pada* defined as "that which ends in a *sup*-affix" (*subantaṃ padam*) will indeed apply. When this suffix is present, one can say:
"By this [designation] it will be so, by that it will not be so. Now, when the suffix has been elided, from whatever limit [the designation applies]...

The designation *pada* applies to as much as "a word ending in a *sup* suffix" (*subantaṃ padam*)—that is, from the rule *svādau padam*. And since there is the status of being followed by *yaj* and so on by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of the suffix), the designation *bha* would consequently apply. Furthermore, the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between the *tug* augment and lengthening (*dīrghatva*) in the case of *parivīḥ* is untenable, because they are characterized by a single rule (*ekayogalakṣaṇatvāt*). Thus, the conflict between the *tug* augment and lengthening does not hold.

Where [is] *parivīḥ*? What is the reason? Because they are characterized by a single rule (*ekayogalakṣaṇatvāt*). In the case of the *tuk*-augment and lengthening (*tugdīrghatve*) which are characterized by a single rule, when the suffix is elided here, all operations dependent upon that suffix have already been completed. These very operations are now being reinstated: "by this very [rule] the *tuk*-augment, and by this very [rule] the lengthening. Thus, this constitutes a single rule.

[The objection is: "It occurs [as a fault], and the characteristics of a single application (*ekayoga*) are not possible. [The reply: "But it is established by the designation of the substituendum (*sthānin*). This is established. How? It must be stated that the designation of the substituendum applies to that which has become something else. What is accomplished by this? Only its existence is established; the *tug*-augment and the lengthening will occur according to what is already applicable. That is so.

It must be said: even if it is stated that "now, furthermore, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is not commenced," and one were to say, "I shall state that the designation of a substitute applies to that which has become something else, except in the case of a rule concerning an *al* (phoneme)," [the following problem arises]: if this were so, then in the rule "the *ātmanepada* occurs after *āṅ* with *yama* and *hana*," it would apply only to *hana*, but not to *vadh*. For there is no designation for *hana* that belongs to *vadh*.

It would be extended [to other cases] as well. There is also a technical name (*saṃjñā*) for the root *han*. What is it? It is *han* itself. How so? Because of the rule stating "the own form of a word is its technical name, provided it is not itself a technical name," the own form of a word becomes its technical name; thus, *han* will also have *han* as its technical name. Furthermore, this is established in the case of the technical name *bh*, in the feminine suffix *aṅīp*, in the suffix *ṣpha*, and in the substitution of *ā* for *go*. [This applies] in the case of the technical name *bh*, in the feminine suffix *aṅīp*, in the suffix *ṣpha*, and in the substitution of *ā* for *go*.
And [the following] is established: the technical designation *bha*.

In the case of *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king's man), [the compound] *rājapuruṣaḥ* results. By the rule for the characteristic of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the designation *bha* would apply according to the rule *yaci bham*; however, it does not occur because of the statement "the designation of the original base (*sthānisañjñā*) applies to that which has become something else, except in the case of a rule concerning an *al*. [Similarly in] *ṅīp*:

In the case of *citrāyām jātā citrā*, the suffix *ī* would apply after a stem ending in *aṇ* by virtue of the definition of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). It does not occur because of the rule stating that the designation of the original base (*sthānisañjñā*) applies to what has become something else, except in the case of an operation concerning a phoneme (*analvidhi*). Regarding *ṣpha*: [in the case of] *vataṅḍī*. The suffix *ṣpha* would apply after a stem ending in *yañ* by virtue of the definition of a suffix. It does not occur because of the rule stating that the designation of the original base applies to what has become something else, except in the case of an operation concerning a phoneme (*analvidhi*). Regarding the substitution of *ā* for *go*: [in the case of] *gām icchati gavyati*. By virtue of the definition of a suffix...

The substitution of *ā* [for *i*] in the case of *ami* and *aḥ* (the nominative and accusative plural endings) would apply by the rule "ami pūrvaḥ" and "aṃśasoḥ". However, it does not occur because of the statement: "The designation of the original element (*sthānin*) applies to that which has become something else, except in the case of a rule concerning an *al*. The fault of this [rule] is regarding the elision of the *ṅ* and *u*, and the elision of the *nakāra*. This fault of the aforementioned definition concerns the elision of the *ṅ* and *u* in *ārdre carman* and *lohite carman*. [Otherwise], by the characteristic of the suffix according to the rule "yañi bham," [the word would be designated as a *bha* stem].

The designation *bha* is established. However, the designation *sthāni* would not apply because of the rule stating that "the designation *sthāni* does not apply to what has become something else when a rule concerning *al* is not being prescribed. Regarding the substitution of *it*: in the case of *āśīḥ*, the substitution of *it* by the rule *hali* (Pāṇini 6.4.119) is established by means of the characteristic of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). However, the designation *sthāni* would not apply because of the rule stating that "the designation *sthāni* does not apply to what has become something else when a rule concerning *al* is not being prescribed. Regarding the substitution of *im*: in the case of *atṛṇet*, the substitution of *it* by the rule *hali* is established by means of the characteristic of the suffix. [However, the designation *sthāni* would not apply because of the rule stating that "the designation *sthāni* does not apply to what has become something else..."]
Because of the statement "in the case of *anal*," [the designation *pada*] does not apply; furthermore, the rule (*sūtra*) would have to be split. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated.

But has it not been said that, since the cause no longer exists, the designation *pada* is absent, and thus the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between the *tuṅ* and the long vowel is untenable because they are characterized by a single application (*ekayogalakṣaṇa*), as in the case of *parivīḥ*? This is not a fault; he will provide the resolution for this here as well. In this case too—
In the case of *parivīḥ*, because it is subsequent [to the rule for *guṇa*], lengthening will occur by virtue of the prohibition of the subsequent [rule] in the treatise.
What, then, are the purposes of this rule? Its purpose is that when the single-consonant suffix (*apṛkta*) *śi* is elided, the augment *num* applies to words ending in *am* and *au*.

The purposes [of the rule] are the application of *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, lengthening (*dīrghatva*), *im*, *āṭ*, and the prescription of *śnam*. When the elision of the *apṛkta* suffix and the elision of *śi* have been performed, these are the results: *num*, *am*, *ām*, *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, lengthening, *im*, *āṭ*, and the prescription of *śnam*. Regarding *num*:
"O Agni, three are thy powers (*vajinā*), three thy abodes (*sadhasthā*)."
The forms *tā*, *tau*, *tāni*, *num*, and *am* and *ām*: *he anaḍvan*, *anaḍvān*. Guṇa:
*adhok*, *aleṭ*. Vṛddhi:
*ni amārṣṭi*. The lengthening [of the vowel]:
*agne trī te vajrinā trī sadhasthā*, these are for the lumps (*piṇḍa*). *im*:
atṛṇeṭ; the affixes aṅ and āṭ: adhok, aleṭ, aiyaḥ.
The rule for the suffix *śnam*:

*abhinaḥ atra*, *acchinaḥ atra*. Once the elision (*lopa*) of the *apṛkta* suffix has been performed, these rules would not apply. [This objection is met] by means of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the technical designation of an element as a suffix).

These purposes do not exist. These are established even by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being like the original). They are not established. It is said that "a substitute (*ādeśa*) is like the original" (*sthānivat*). But elision (*lopa*) is not a substitute. Elision is indeed a substitute. How so? That which is prescribed is a substitute; elision is also prescribed. Indeed, there would be a fault if...

Elision (*lopa*) should not be considered a substitute (*ādeśa*). In this context, there would be no examples of elision under the rule *acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau* (P. 1.1.57), and those [examples] would not exist. Therefore, this rule must be stated for the sake of cases where the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply. And where does the status of being a substitute not apply? Where there is a rule concerning an *al* (a phoneme) (*alvidhi*). What is the purpose? This is the purpose.

These rules apply when the suffix *ṅa* has been elided. There is a fault regarding the designation *bha*, as well as regarding the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, the suffix *ṣph*, and the substitution of *ā*. There is a fault regarding the designation *bha*, the suffix *ṅīp*, the suffix *ṣph*, and the substitution of *ā*. First, there is no fault regarding the designation *bha*. The activity of the Teacher indicates that the designation *bha* does not occur by virtue of the characteristic of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), since he teaches the prohibition with respect to the locative case ending *ṅi* in the rule "not in the case of *ṅi* or the vocative" (*na ṅisambuddhyoḥ*). The same applies to the suffix *ṅīp*:
It is not understood thus: "from that which ends in *aṇ* and ends in *akāra*. How then? It is understood as: "that *akāra* which [follows] *aṇ*. This also applies to *ṣpha*:
it is not understood thus.

[The objection: "From that which ends in *yañ* [and] from that which ends in *a*. [Response: How then? [It means] "the *a* that follows *yañ*, [which itself ends in] *ya*. Even regarding the substitution of *ā* for *go*: it is not understood as "before *ami* when followed by *aci*. How then? It is understood as "before *aci* when *ami* [follows]. [Objection: In that case, those purposes [of the rule] do not exist either. As for what was said—that the elision of the *ṅ* and the *n* is performed—it is already accomplished in the *Nyāsa* itself.
"Not after the two [roots] *sam* and *budh*"—this also applies to the substitution of *it*. He will state this:

"In the case of the substitution of *it* for *śās*, [the rule] 'after *āśās* before *kvip*' applies. There is also the prescription of *im*: the condition "before a consonant" (*hali*) has been removed. If "before a consonant" is removed, then [the substitution] would also apply here in the case of *tṛṇahāni*. If that is so, then...

The word *aci* will also carry over [from the previous rule]. If that is so, then this present rule (*yoga*) need not be stated. Yet it must be stated. What is the purpose? It is so that what is prescribed by taking a suffix (*pratyaya*) as the basis should apply by virtue of the "suffix-condition" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), whereas what is prescribed by taking a word-form (*śabda*) as the basis should not apply by virtue of the "suffix-condition. What is the purpose? [For example, in the case of] *śobhanāḥ*...

[The rule] "dṛṣadaḥ asya sudṛṣat brāhmaṇaḥ" [is cited]. [The objection is: "In 'soḥ' and 'manasī', let there not be this accentuation [of the first member]. (P. 1.1.63.1) When there is a prohibition regarding the elision (*lumat*), an addition must be made for the accentuation of a single word (*ekapadasvara*). When there is a prohibition regarding the elision, an addition must be made for the accentuation of a single word.

An addition must be made: it should be stated that when a suffix is elided by *lumat*, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the grammatical operation conditioned by a suffix) does not apply even with respect to the accent of a single word (*ekapadasvara*). Is this to be stated without qualification? No, he says; [it should be stated] excluding the accent of the entire word (*sarva*), the accent of the vocative (*āmantrita*), and the accent of the elision of *sij*. That is, excluding the accent of the entire word, the accent of the vocative, and the accent of the elision of *sij*. [Regarding] "the accent of the entire word":
*sarvastomaḥ* and *sarvapṛṣṭhaḥ*:
[the rule] *sarvasya supi* is applied so that the initial syllable may be udātta. [This is an example of] the accent of the vocative (*āmantrita-svara*).
"Let *sarpiḥ* come;
let the seven come"—this is so that the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) may apply by the rule *āmantritasya ca*. Regarding the accent of the *sij*-elision: "let them not give."

Let it be that the accent [of the root] is applied by the rule *ādiḥ sico 'nyatarasyām* so that this accentuation may occur. What is the purpose? The purpose is the accents of *ñni*, *kit*, and *luk*. The accents of *ñni*, *kit*, and *luk* serve as the purpose [for this rule]. For example: *gargaḥ*, *vatsaḥ*.
Bida, Urva, and Uṣṭragrīva.
The term *vāmarajjuḥ* [is cited] so that, by the rule *ñniti*, the initial accentuation (*ādyudāttatva*) might not occur. And here:
*atrayaḥ*.

[The rule] *kitaḥ* [is stated] so that the word-final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) does not occur. Regarding *pathimathoḥ sarvanāmasthāne*: the purpose of [the rule] *pathimathoḥ sarvanāmasthāne* regarding elision (*luk*) is [as follows]: in *pathipriyaḥ* and *mathipriyaḥ*, this accent [prescribed by] *pathimathoḥ sarvanāmasthāne* should not occur. Regarding *ahnaḥ ravidhau*: it must be stated that when a suffix is elided by *lumat*, the technical designation of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not apply to the rule for the substitution of *ra-* in place of *ahan*.
In the examples *ahaḥ dadāti* and *ahaḥ bhuṅkte*,

the prohibition [of the substitution of *ru* for *visarga*] by the rule *raḥ asupi* should not apply; therefore, the term *pratyayalakṣaṇena* (by virtue of the technical designation of being a suffix) is used [to ensure that the suffix status of *sup* is not considered].

(Regarding the rule for the final member of a compound: When it is the final member of a compound, and when a rule concerning what is not the beginning of a word applies, it must be stated that when a suffix is elided by *lumat*, the grammatical operation conditioned by that suffix does not take place. For example: *paramavācā* and *paramavāce*; *paramagoduhā* and *paramagoduhe*.

In *paramaśvalihā* and *paramaśvalihe*, [the rules] such as *kutva* (the substitution of *k*) should not apply by virtue of the definition of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) under the rule *padasya*. Why is it stated "in the case of a rule applying to what is not the beginning of a word" (*apadādividhau*)? It is so that the prohibition in the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* may apply to forms such as *dadhisecau* and *dadhisecaḥ*. If it were stated "in the case of a rule applying to what is not the beginning of a word," then the governing heading concerning the subsequent member of a compound (*uttarapadādhikāra*) would be excluded.
It would not be applicable. What fault is there in that? Rules such as *karṇo varṇalakṣaṇāt* would not be established.

Furthermore, if it were stated that in rules concerning the elision of *n* (nalopa) and so forth—up to the rule for prolation (*pluti*)—the designation of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not apply when [an affix] is elided by *lumat*, this cannot be maintained. For in this case:

[If it were so], the rule for *śākala* would apply [erroneously] to forms such as *rājakumāryau* and *rājakumāryaḥ*. This is not a fault. Regarding this point—that *śākala* does not apply when there is a *sit* (the marker *s*)—I shall state that *śākala* does not apply when there is an affix (*pratyaya*). If it is stated that *śākala* does not apply when there is an affix, then [it applies to] *dadhy-adya* and *madhv-adya*.

In this case as well, it would not follow [that the rule applies]. [The rule] "Śākala does not occur before a suffix" (A 8.3.19) [would apply]; before what? Before whatever suffix is prescribed. But then, in cases such as *paramadivā* and *paramadive*, the substitution of *ut* for *diva-* (A 6.1.131) would result. Let it be, then, without distinction. But was it not said that the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "the second member of a compound" (*uttarapada*) could not be established? It will be established by virtue of the explicit statement. Therefore, that must indeed be stated.

It need not be stated. The recurrence [of the rule] will be applied. This exists: "That from which a suffix-rule [is derived], beginning with that, is a stem (*aṅga*) when a suffix follows; that which ends in a *sup* or *tiṅ* is a word (*pada*). Also: "That from which a *sup* or *tiṅ* rule is derived, beginning with that, is a word ending in a *sup*. [And: "In the case of *kye*, [the final letter] of a word ending in *n* [is replaced by *r*]. [And: "In the case of *kye*, [the final letter] of a word ending in *n* [is replaced by *r*]."

It receives the designation *pada* because of the rule for *kyap* suffixes and because it ends in a *sup* (nominal) suffix. And with respect to a *sit* suffix, that which precedes it receives the designation *pada*, as well as that which begins with it and ends in a *sup* suffix, because of the rule for *sit* suffixes. Among the suffixes beginning with *sva* (i.e., case endings), except when they are *asarvanāmasthāna* (non-neuter nominative/accusative singular), that which precedes them receives the designation *pada*, as well as that which begins with it and ends in a *sup* suffix, because of the rule for those *sva*-beginning suffixes.

*Yaci bham*: when a suffix beginning with *yaj* follows, that which precedes it receives the designation *pada*, as well as everything from the beginning of that element up to the end of the inflected word (*subanta*) upon which the rule for *yaj* and the others applies. In this case, however:
*paramavāk*.

The prohibition [of the term *pada*] by the rule "not in a *sarvanāmasthāna*" would apply. Let that prohibition apply to the case where the technical designation *pada* is defined as "that which ends in a *svādi* suffix"; however, the designation *pada* defined as "that which ends in a *sup* suffix" will still apply. When this suffix is present, one might think, "it was so by this [designation], but it will not be so by that [designation]. Now, when the suffix has been elided, to whatever extent...

By the rule *avadheḥ svādau padam*, the technical designation *pada* applies to that very extent of the suffix beginning with a *su*-affix; and since there is the status of being followed by a *sarvanāmasthāna* by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of the suffix), a prohibition would apply—given that prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) are stronger [than general rules]. [Reply: No, because it is not a prohibition. This is not a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (an absolute negation).

"In the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna*, [the substitution] is not *na*. What then? This is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*): 'that which is other than a *sarvanāmasthāna*. Thus, there is no operation regarding the *sarvanāmasthāna*. If it is applicable by some [rule], it will take place by that; and it is applicable by the preceding rule. Or rather, because it was not previously obtained; or else, it is the application that follows immediately."

That [subsequent application] is prohibited. Why is this so? Because a rule or a prohibition applies to what immediately precedes it. The prior attainment remains unprohibited; therefore, it will take effect by virtue of that. But does not this [subsequent] attainment subvert the prior attainment? No, for once it has been prohibited, it is unable to subvert. If this is so, then in the case of *paramavācau* and *paramavācaḥ*, [the subsequent rule would apply].
Thus, by the rule "that which ends in a sup or a tiṅ affix is a *pada*," the designation *pada* would apply [to the entire word]. If that is so, then a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) will be made:

first, among the *svādi* suffixes, what precedes is designated as a *pada*. Then, before a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix other than *ayac*, what precedes is designated as a *pada*. Then, "bha": that which begins with *yaj* and so forth, when not a *sarvanāmasthāna*, receives the designation *bha*. If, then...
Even a single word (*pada*) is subject [to this rule];

however, he will raise an objection regarding the mention of "end of a word" (*padānta*) in the section on protracted vowels (*pluta*), so that it does not apply here in cases such as *bhadraṃ karoṣi gauḥ*.
Even when that [rule] is being applied, it will still occur; for that [rule] applies to the final sound of a sentence or a word. But in this case, then:
*dadhisecau*, *dadhisecaḥ*—the prohibition characterized by "being at the beginning of a word" (*sātpadādyoḥ*) would not apply. Let it not be so.
"Padādi" means the beginning of a word (*padasya ādiḥ padādiḥ*);
[the prohibition] "not after *padādi*" would apply. How then?
It is "that which begins after a word" (*padāt ādiḥ padādiḥ*).
[Objection: It will be so by the rule "na" [Pāṇini 1.4.17], which applies to words beginning with *pad*. [Reply: That cannot be; for then it would also undesirably apply here:

in the case of *ṛkṣu*, *vākṣu*, *tvakṣu*, *kumārīṣu*, and *kiśorīṣu*. [Objection: The prohibition of the suffix *sāt* [in Pāṇini 1.4.16] is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the prohibition does not apply to those things which receive the designation *pada* by virtue of being among the items beginning with *sva* [i.e., by Pāṇini 1.4.14]. [Reply: Then what about this case: *bahusecau*?

*bahusecaḥ*: this suffix *bahuc* [is the example]. Here, "beginning of a word" (*padādi*) refers to that which stands at the beginning of a word (*padāt ādiḥ*). Even though it is stated that [the rule] does not apply to what is at the beginning of a word (*padādeḥ na*), the desired result is still not achieved. If that is so, then I shall state: "And when there is the status of being a subsequent member (*uttarapadatve*), in a rule concerning the beginning of a word, the presence of the suffix is to be recognized even when it has been elided by *lumat*" (P.
1.1.62 vt.). That [statement] will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtham*): [it will restrict the application of the rule to cases where the suffix is elided by *lumat*].

[The rule] applies only when a rule concerns the beginning of a word (*padādi*), not when it concerns the end of a word (*padānta*). How so? [In the case of] *bahusecau* and *bahusecaḥ*: since the suffix *bahuc* precedes, [the rule] applies to the beginning of a word, not to the end of a word. Regarding *dvandva* (copulative compounds): it must be stated that when the final member is elided by *lup*, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the effect of a suffix) does not apply. [Example: *vāk-srak-tvacam*.

(P_1,1.63.3) Here, in the case of *abhūvan*, the substitution of *jus* would apply by virtue of the characteristic of being a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). There is no possibility for the *us* [substitution] of *sic*, because of the context of the vowel *ā*. There is no possibility for the *us* of *sic*. What is the reason? Because of the context of the vowel *ā*. [This is indicated by the rule] *ātaḥ*.
This will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*):
[the suffix *śnā* applies] only after a root ending in long *ā* from which the *sic* has been elided, and not after any other root from which the *sic* has been elided. For example:
*iti yuṣmatputro dadāti*.

In the case of *iti asmatputraḥ dadāti* ("Thus our son gives"), the substitutions *vām*, *nau*, *āva*, and *āma* would apply to *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when they stand in the sixth, fourth, or second case, because of the inclusion of the term *sthā* (standing) in the rule *yuṣmadasmadoḥ ṣaṣṭhīcaturthīdvitīyāsthayor vāmnāvau*. That inclusion of *sthā* is made there [in the sūtra] for a specific purpose. It should be understood as a qualifier of the actually occurring (*śrūyamāṇa*) case-ending. There is another purpose for the inclusion of *sthā*.

Is it so that [the rule] "vām-nau-ādayaḥ" (vām, nau, etc. should apply to the form including the case-ending? This purpose does not exist. The term "pada" (word) is understood [from the previous rule], and a word is that which ends in a case-ending. Therefore, even without the mention of *sthā* (in the sense of "standing in place of"), the reference will be to the form including the case-ending alone. This would be established in cases where the word ends in a case-ending; however, where indeed...
In that case, the status of being a *pada* (a complete word) when followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*) is not established:
*grāmo vām dīyate*,
*grāmo nau dīyate*, *janapado vām dīyate*.

"The country is given to us. The term *sarva* (all), though previously introduced, also continues to apply here. Therefore, it will apply only to that which possesses a case-ending (*savibhaktika*). In this instance:

"He caused one desiring sight to sacrifice" (*cakṣuṣkāmaṃ yājayāṃ cakāra*), by the rule *tiṅ-atiṅaḥ*, the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) of the former [verb] follows from the latter, and the absence of *nighāta* for the latter follows from the former. Due to the elision of the *ām* suffix, there is the absence of *nighāta* for the former and the presence of *nighāta* for the latter. Due to the elision of the *ām* suffix, there is... for the former.

And because there is no [designation of] *aṅga*, the designation of *nighāta* (accentual suppression) will consequently be established. Regarding the rules for the prescription and prohibition of *iṭ* under the heading of *aṅga*:
the prescription and prohibition of *iṭ* under the heading of *aṅga* are not established;
[for example], in *jigamiṣa* and *saṃvivṛtsa*, the prescription and prohibition of *iṭ* do not apply to the *aṅga*. [Furthermore,] the lengthening of *kram-* [would not occur].

500–502. Here, in certain matters concerning the status of a suffix (*aṅga*), [an operation] occurs by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of a suffix) even when it has been elided by *lumat* (a marker indicating elision);

however, in other cases, it does not occur. Now, if instead it were stated as *na lumatā tasmin*, then what would be established if *na lumatā tasmin* were so stated? [The following: the prescription and prohibition of *iṭ* (augment), the [prohibition of *iṭ*] for the root *kram*, and the lengthening [of the vowel].

Certainly, it is established. It is not said that "the prohibition of *iṭ* and the rule for *ītv* apply to the *parasmaipada*s. How then? It is said [they apply] "before an affix beginning with *s*. Thus, the mention of *parasmaipada* is a qualifier of that [affix]. Nor indeed is it said that "the lengthening of the vowel of *kram-* applies to the *parasmaipada*s. How then? It is said [it applies] "before a *śit* [affix]. Thus, the mention of *parasmaipada* is a qualifier of that [affix].
If it is argued that [the rule] *na lumatā tasmin* applies, then the substitutes for *han*, *iṇ*, and *ṅī* would not be established when *t* is elided; for instance,
in the case of *avadhi bhavatā dasyuḥ*.

"You sang the village" (*agāyi bhavatā grāmaḥ*) and "you studied the section" (*adhyagāyi bhavatā anuvākaḥ*). When the *l* suffix is elided by the rule *luṅi*, the substitutes for *han*, *iṇ*, and *ṅī* would not apply.
This is not a fault. The substitutes for *han*, *iṇ*, and *ṅī* are not prescribed by the condition "in the *luṅ* tense. What then? They are prescribed by the condition "in an *ārdhadhātuka* affix."

The mention of *luṅ* is for the purpose of qualifying that [term]. And in this case, in the examples *sarvastomaḥ* and *sarvapṛṣṭhaḥ*, the rule *sarvasya supi* (Pāṇini 6.1.193) would not result in the initial udātta accent; therefore, that too must be stated.

It should not be stated [that the rule *na lumatāṅgasya* is necessary], for it is already established by the very rule *na lumatāṅgasya*. How so? When an element is elided by *lumat*, the governing heading (*adhikāra*) regarding the stem (*aṅga*) is not referred back [to that elided element]. What then? When something is elided by *lumat*, whatever grammatical operation was applicable to the stem (*aṅga*) that precedes it does not take place. Even so, the accentuation of *sarvasvara* is not established; therefore, an effort must be made in this regard.
Is this mention of *al* a qualifier of the final [sound]? It ought to be so.

If, in the definition of the technical term *upadhā*, the mention of *al* is an indication of the final [sound], then there must be a prohibition regarding the whole cluster (*saṅghāta*). In the definition of the technical term *upadhā*, the mention of *al* is an indication of the final [sound].
If that were so, the prohibition regarding a composite (*saṅghāta*) would have to be stated. [Otherwise] the designation *upadhā* would apply to the composite.
What fault would there be in that? [The rule] "after *śās*, [the substitute] *īt* occurs before *aṅ* and *hal*" would apply:
*śiṣṭvā*, *śiṣṭaḥ*.

The shortening (*ittva*) would apply to the entire cluster (*saṅghāta*). If, however, it were stated that "the [shortening] occurs before the final [letter]," even so, the final letter would remain unspecified.
What would be the fault in that? The designation of *upadhā* (penultimate) would undesirably apply to what precedes the entire cluster as well.
What would be the fault in that? [It would affect the rule] *śāsaḥ it aṅhaloḥ*: [the root] *śās-* [takes *it*] before *aṅ* and *hal*, resulting in *śiṣṭaḥ*.
[The opponent] said: "The substitution of *ī* for *ś* would result [in an over-extension], and the sūtra would be contradicted. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. [The proponent asks:

"But was it not stated that regarding the technical designation *upadhā*, if there were no mention of *al* and the reference were to the final [letter], there would be a prohibition against a cluster?

[The proponent replies: "This is not a fault. It is established by understanding [the term *upadhā*] as referring to the final [element]. This is established. How? By the rule *alaḥ antyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52)."
"If it is argued that the rules [of substitution] apply to the final [element], then it will apply to the last one.

If it is argued that this is established by the recognition of the final element, we say no; for the rule "an operation applies to the final letter" does not hold when the element is meaningless (*anarthaka*) or in the case of modifications of a reduplicated syllable (*anabhyāsavikāra*).
If it is argued that [the desired result] is established by the rule regarding the final letter (*antyavidhi*), that is not so. What is the reason?

Because the rule concerning the final letter does not apply to meaningless elements (*anarthaka*) when there is no modification of a reduplicated syllable (*anabhyāsavikāra*). This *paribhāṣā* must be formulated: "The rule concerning the final letter does not apply to meaningless elements. Is this without qualification? No, he says; it applies except in the case of a modification of a reduplicated syllable—that is, excluding modifications of reduplicated syllables. [As in the example: *bhṛñām it*.

Regarding the rule *arti-pipartyośca*: what are the purposes of this paribhāṣā? The purpose is in the case of *avyaktānukaraṇasyāta itau*: [if this were not a paribhāṣā], the substitution would apply to the final letter. [But] since the rule *anarthake 'lontyavidhiḥ* does not apply, there is no fault. This is not a valid purpose; for the activity of the Teacher indicates that the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) does not apply to the final letter.

Regarding this, since he says "but [the substitution] is optionally [of] the final [phoneme] of the reduplicated [root]" (*āmreḍitasya antyasya tu vā*), [one might object that] in the rule *ghvasor et hau abhyāsalopaś ca*, the substitution of *et* for *gh* and *s* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable would apply to the final [phoneme]. However, there is no fault, because the rule *anarthake 'lontyavidhir na bhavati* (when [a grammatical operation] is purposeless, it does not apply to the final phoneme) prevents this. Furthermore, even this [objection] is not necessary, because of the force of the explicit mention of "elision" (*lopa*) once again.

It will apply to the whole [stem]. Or rather, the *śit* designation will be applied; since that *śit* [element] applies to the whole, it will become a substitute for the entire [stem]. In that case, the letter *ś* must be included. It need not be included; it is indeed included in the formulation itself. The statement is made with two *ś*s:

"In place of *ghu* and *as*, *et* and *hau* are substituted, and there is elision of the reduplication. The rule "there is elision of *āp* after an *ak* vowel when followed by a non-consonant" remains as a sūtra. It is explained otherwise:

[Objection: By the rule *āpi hali lopaḥ*, the elision would apply to the final [letter]. [Response: There is no fault, because the rule *anarthake 'lontyavidhiḥ* (the operation of a single substitute for several letters applies only to the final letter when the substitute is meaningless) does not apply here. [Objection: Even this is not a purposeful argument; I shall state the elision of *ana-* itself. [Response: Then the mention of *ana-* must be made. [Objection: It need not be made. [Response: The previously stated [term] is understood by way of reference (*anuvartate*). [Question: Where was it previously stated? [Answer: In the rule *an āpi akaḥ*.

Thus it is said. That [term] is indeed indicated in the nominative case (*prathamā-nirdiṣṭa*). And here, the meaning is conveyed by that which is indicated in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdiṣṭa*). This locative case (*saptamī*), namely *hali*, will effect a change of the nominative *an* into the genitive; for when something is indicated [by a locative], the rule "that which precedes" (*tasmin nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya*) applies. Here, there is elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsa-lopa*). Here, there is elision of the reduplication.

Thus, it would follow that [the operation] applies to the final [element]. However, there is no fault because the rule "when [an element] is meaningless, the operation does not apply to the final" does not hold here. Even this is not a purpose [for the mention of *atra*]; by the force of the mention of *atra*, it will apply to the whole. There is another purpose for the mention of *atra*. What is it? The governing context (*adhikāra*) of *san* is required.

Let it not be so here: *dadhau*, *dadau*. Even without the mention of *atra* (here), we shall expect the governing rule for *san* (*san-adhikāra*). [Objection: Then one must expect *san* beginning with *s* (*sakārādi*), as in the rule "before *san* beginning with *s*" (*sani sakārādau*), so that it does not apply here: *jijñāpayiṣati*. [Response: Even without the mention of *atra*, we shall expect *san* beginning with *s*. [Objection: Then the original bases (*prakṛti*) are expected; [the purpose being] that the elision (*lopa*) of these original bases may occur.

Let it not be that [the rule applies] here: *pipakṣati*, *yiyakṣati*. Even without the mention of "here" (*atra*), we shall refer to these bases (*prakṛti*). But then the context (*viṣaya*) must be referred to; otherwise, in the case of the rule "there is optionally a *guṇa* for *muc* when it is intransitive," let it not apply here:
*mumukṣati gām* ("he desires to release the cow"). Even without the mention of "here," we shall refer to the context. How so? By the phrase "when it is intransitive."
Thus it is said. Therefore, this [term] *muc* will apply only where it is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Consequently, there is no purpose for this *paribhāṣā*.

506. "The *al* preceding the final [phoneme] is the *upadhā*"—or rather, it should be stated explicitly: "The *al* preceding the final [phoneme] receives the designation *upadhā*. If that is so, then it must be stated. It need not be stated; for it is established through worldly convention even without being stated. This is established through worldly convention even without a formal statement. How so?
When it is said in the world, "Let one who precedes these Brāhmaṇas by one position be brought forward," a person of the same caste as the last one is brought forward as the one preceding the last.
507–511. What is an example? Here, for instance:
"When that [element] is specified, [the operation applies] to what precedes it" (Pāṇini 1.1.66);
and "The *yaṇ* replaces *ik* before a vowel" (Pāṇini 6.1.77).
"Dadhi" is here, "madhu" is here;
from this [it follows] "iti" and "uttarasya";
[the substitution of] "ī" for "ap" occurs after two vowels or a prefix.

"Dvīpa," "antarīpa," and "samīpa" are instances where a designation is made by means of a word of one kind, yet an example of a different kind is cited. What, then, is the example? Here, first of all:
when it is said "tasmin" (in that), [the rule] "pūrvasya" (of the preceding) applies;

as in "tasmin aṇi ca yuṣmākāsmākau" (when that suffix *aṇ* follows, the forms *yuṣmāka-* and *asmāka-* are substituted). When it is said "tasmāt" (from that), [the rule] "uttarasya" (of the following) applies.

Therefore, [the rule] "śasaḥ naḥ puṃsi" (Pāṇini 7.1.19) is an example of this. And this too is an example: "ikaḥ yaṇ aci" (6.1.77), "dvyantarupasargebhyaḥ apaḥ īt" (6.3.97). How so? This reference is made by means of a pronominal (sarvanāman), and a pronominal denotes a general category. When a general category is thus indicated, specific instances are also included as examples.
They exist. But what, then, is the universal (*sāmānya*) and what is the particular (*viśeṣa*)? "Cow" is the universal; "black" is the particular.
In that case, the black [cow] would no longer be the universal, and the cow would become the particular. Yet it is both.
If the universal were also the particular, and the particular were also the universal, then the categories of universal and particular could not be established. And yet they are established. How so?
It depends on the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). When "cow" is intended as the general category and "black" as the specific quality, then "cow" is the general and "black" is the particular.
When "black" is intended as the general category and "cow" as the specific quality, then "black" is the general and "cow" is the particular. Another says:
And they are both designated. How? Like father and son.

For example, the very same person is a father with respect to someone and a son with respect to someone else; likewise here too, that very same thing is a generality with respect to something and a particularity with respect to something else. Indeed, these are even more frequently used than those [terms] formed with secondary suffixes (*nairdeśika*), namely those expressed by pronouns (*sarvanāman*).
Explanations are being given. For by these [rules], a much greater portion [of the domain] is covered. Now, for what purpose is the explanation made with a prefix (*upasarga*)?

When a word is specified in the locative case, the grammatical operation should apply to what precedes it, and not to its meaning—for example, in the cases *janapade* and *atiśāyane*. Is this understood through the prefix, or does the addition of a word imply the addition of a meaning? He says: "It is understood. How so? This prefix *niḥ* functions in the sense of exclusion (*bahirbhāve*).
For example:

"departed from the country" (*niṣkrānto deśāt*) means "outside the country" (*bahirdeśaḥ*). In this case, the word is external to the word, while the referent (*artha*) is not external. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "specified" (*nirdiṣṭa*)? The mention of "specified" is for the sake of indicating immediate proximity (*ānantarya*).
The mention of "nirdiṣṭa" (specified) is made for the purpose of immediate sequence (*ānantarya*). This is so that the operation may apply only when there is immediate sequence, as in *ikaḥ yaṇ aci*:
*dadhy atra*, *madhv atra*. It should not apply here:
*samidhau*, *samidhaḥ*.

*dṛṣadau*, *dṛṣadaḥ*. For what purpose, then, is this stated? Because there is no distinction between the preceding and following rules regarding the terms "in that" (*tasmin*) and "from that" (*tasmāt*).

The statement is for the purpose of restriction: "He cooks rice with curd and water. Since there would be no distinction between the preceding and following rules regarding the phrases "in that" (*tasmin*) and "from that" (*tasmāt*), this [present rule] is commenced for the sake of restriction. In the case of *grāme devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta is in the village"), there is doubt as to whether he is the one in front or the one behind. In the case of *grāmād devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta is from the village"), there is doubt as to whether he is the one in front or the one behind. Likewise here as well:

*ikaḥ yaṇ aci*: "In place of an *ik*, there is *yaṇ* before a vowel (*ac*). For example: *dadhy udakam* ("water with curd"), *pacaty odanam* ("he cooks rice"). Here, there is ambiguity: both are *iks* and both are vowels (*acs*), so it is uncertain whether the substitution applies to the preceding vowel or the following one. Similarly, regarding *tiṅ atiṅaḥ*: "A finite verb (*tiṅ*) is followed by a non-finite verb (*atiṅ*)," there is ambiguity as to whether the preceding element is the non-finite verb or the following element is the non-finite verb.
And in this case, it is desired that the substitution apply to the preceding vowel.
"Of that which follows after *atiṅ*. Since this [result] is not established without an effort, the statement is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

This purpose exists. But what then? Now, where both [the preceding and the following] are indicated, does the operation apply to the preceding or rather to the following? In the case of an indication of both, because of the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the indication by the ablative (*pañcamī*) [prevails].

Because there would be a conflict in the case of a dual designation, the designation by the ablative case (*pañcamī*) will take effect. What is the purpose? The purpose is for the sake of the low-pitched accent (*anudātta*) of the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes. It will be stated [in the rule] that "the designation by the locative case (*saptamī*) after roots beginning with *tās-* is for the sake of the *abhyasta* and *sij*" [Pāṇini 6.1.186]. If that were applied, [there would be a problem regarding] the *lasārvadhātuka* following those beginning with *tās-*, when a *lasārvadhātuka* follows.

There is a doubt regarding the phrase "after *tāsi* and so forth": does it mean "of the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes that follow *tāsi* and so forth"? Regarding the phrase "the elision of the initial [vowel] of *iṣṭha* and so forth after *bahu*": there is a doubt as to whether it means "of *iṣṭha*, *imani*, and *īyasun* which follow *bahu*" or "after *bahu* [comes the elision of the initial of] *iṣṭha*, *imani*, and *īyasun*. Regarding the rule "after *gota* [comes] a *ṇit* [suffix]": it refers to the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix that follows *gota*.

There is an ambiguity regarding the rule *gotaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.90]: does it mean "after *got* when a *sarvanāmasthāna* follows," or "of a *sarvanāmasthāna* that follows *got*"? There is an ambiguity regarding the rule *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke* [Pāṇini 7.2.76]: does it mean "of a *sārvadhātuka* affix following *rud* etc. when a *sārvadhātuka* follows," or "of *rud* etc. when a *sārvadhātuka* follows"? There is an ambiguity regarding the rule *āne muk īt āsaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.82]: does it mean "the augment *muk* with the vowel *ī* is added to *ān* which follows *ās*," or...?

Regarding the rule *ānaḥ parataḥ āsaḥ*, there is doubt as to whether it refers to the *ān* that follows *āsaḥ*. Regarding the rule *āmi sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ*, there is doubt as to whether it refers to the *ām* that follows a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) when *ām* follows [the pronoun]. Regarding the rule *sarvanāmnaḥ uttarasya*, there is doubt as to whether it refers to what follows a pronoun. Regarding the rule *gheḥ ṅiti āṭ nadyāḥ*, there is doubt as to whether it refers to the *ṅit* suffixes that follow a feminine stem ending in *nadī* when those *ṅit* suffixes follow [the stem]. [The answer is: [It refers to] the *nadī* [stem].

Regarding the *ṅit* suffixes that follow: [the rule] *yāṭ āpaḥ* [applies]. There is a doubt concerning the phrase *āpaḥ uttarasya ṅitaḥ ṅiti parataḥ āpaḥ*: does it mean "of the *ṅit* suffix following *āp*, when a *ṅit* suffix follows"? Regarding the phrase *ṅamaḥ hrasvāt aci ṅamuṭ nityam*: there is a doubt concerning the phrase *ṅamaḥ uttarasya acaḥ aci parataḥ ṅamaḥ*: does it mean "of the vowel (*ac*) following a *ṅam* suffix, when a vowel follows"? Because there is no scope for the specific mention of case-endings (*vibhakti*).
There is no contradiction. This contradiction is improper because the specific mention of a case-ending (vibhakti-viśeṣa-nirdeśa) leaves no room [for conflict].

In all such instances here, the locative case (saptamī) has already exercised its function, whereas the ablative case (pañcamī) has not yet exercised its function; therefore, the mention of the ablative will take effect.
515–518. Or, the genitive case-assignment is according to the actual meaning. Alternatively, the genitive case-assignment must be made according to the actual meaning.

Where an operation is intended for the preceding element, the genitive must be assigned to the preceding element; where an operation is intended for the subsequent element, the genitive must be assigned to the subsequent element. In that case, such an assignment should indeed be made. It need not be made.
The formulation will be achieved by this very means:

when [an element] is designated by the word "in that" (*tasmin*), the genitive case of what precedes it is understood; when [an element] is designated by the word "from that" (*tasmāt*), the genitive case of what follows it is understood. If that is so, then the mention of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) must be made. It need not be made; the previously mentioned term continues to apply. Where was it previously mentioned? In the rule for the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*).

Regarding the phrase "sthāneyogāḥ" (connected with the place [of substitution]): if it is argued that they are "prakalpaka" (determinative), then there would be an absence of restriction (*niyamābhāva*). If it is argued that they are "prakalpaka," then there is an absence of restriction. And this has already been stated:
"This undertaking is for the purpose of restriction. Furthermore, in the prescription of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) would indeed be determinative.

In that case, what is the fault? [The rule] *guptijkibhyaḥ san* contains a fifth-case ending (*pañcamī*), which would establish a sixth-case relationship (*ṣaṣṭhī*) with the first-case term *san*, according to the principle "from that [the preceding], [there is substitution] for the following. Let it be so. No substitute is being specifically indicated there. Therefore, by virtue of proximity (*āntaryataḥ*), the suffix *san* itself will simply follow the suffix *san*. This cannot be maintained; for in that case, the designation *it* would not be established.

In the *upadeśa*, the designation *it* is stated; furthermore, there would be no established distinction between the original form (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*). And if there were no established distinction between the original form and its modification, [the rule] "ikaḥ yaṇ aci" would be problematic:
the locative case "aci" would have to be interpreted as a genitive case for "yaṇ," according to the principle that "when a specific element is mentioned, it refers to what precedes it."

Thus, because both the seventh (locative) and fifth (ablative) case endings are present, the sixth (genitive) case ending is prescribed in both instances; consequently, there arises the contingency of both operations applying simultaneously. Since both the seventh and fifth case endings are present, the sixth case ending would apply to both: the fifth case ending in *tāsyādibhyaḥ* would prescribe the sixth case ending for the seventh case ending in *lasārvadhātuke*, and [the sixth case ending] would likewise apply to that which follows, starting from "therefrom" (*tasmāt*).

Thus, in the rule *lasārvadhātuke*, this locative (*saptamī*) would effect a change of the ablative (*pañcamī*) in *tāsyādibhyaḥ* into a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), according to the principle that "when [an element] is specified by the locative, it refers to what precedes. What fault is there in that? The fault is that both operations would apply there simultaneously.
This is not a fault, as for what was stated:

If it is argued that [the rule] "prakalpakam" (that which effects a designation) applies, then there would be a lack of restriction (*niyamābhāva*). Let there be no restriction. When a seventh-case (*saptamī*) element is specified, a sixth-case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is supplied for what precedes; when a fifth-case (*pañcamī*) element is specified, [a sixth-case] is supplied for what follows. To the extent that a sixth-case is supplied for what precedes when a seventh-case is specified, so too is it supplied for what follows when a fifth-case is specified. It is not possible [for the operation] of what follows to apply when a seventh-case is specified.

Nor can it be [the cause] when that which is designated by the fifth case (pañcamī) is intended to become [the result]. As for what is said—"In the prescription of an affix (*pratyaya-vidhi*), the fifth case endings indeed serve as the basis for the formation [of the sixth]"—let them be so formed as bases. But has it not been stated: "In the rule *guptijkibhyaḥ san*, this fifth case ending should effect a change of the first case ending *san* into a sixth case ending"?

Therefore, regarding the phrase "of the subsequent [element]," this has already been answered: no substitute (*ādeśa*) is being specifically indicated there. Rather, by virtue of proximity (*āntarya*), it will be the *san* itself that replaces the *san*. But was it not said: "It cannot be so; otherwise, the designation *it* would not be applicable"? For the designation *it* is prescribed [only] for what is taught in the original instruction (*upadeśa*). This would indeed be the case.

This fault would arise if the *itsaṃjñā* were to wait for the substitute (*ādeśa*). For once the *itsaṃjñā* has been applied and the elision (*lopa*) has been performed, the substitute will take place; indeed, the *itsaṃjñā* is prescribed with respect to the original form (*upadeśa*). Alternatively, the formation (*prakḷpti*) must not occur as long as the suffix *san* has not yet arisen. And when the *san* has arisen, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) has already fulfilled its purpose.
Once [the substitution] has been made, there will be no further application of the rule.

As for what is also said—that there would be a lack of distinction between the original form (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*)—even in that case, the genitive case is applied to the original form in the rule "ikaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.77), while the nominative case is applied to the modification in the rule "yaṇ" (Pāṇini 6.1.77). And where indeed there is no genitive case in a sūtra, there the application of the rule must occur. Now...

Or, let it be for now that *ikaḥ* [is the ablative] and *yaṇ aci* [is the locative], where indeed there is a Vedic (sautrī) genitive. And if, now, this locative *aci* were to effect a transformation of the nominative *yaṇ* into a genitive—let it be according to the rule *tasminn iti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya* ("when that [word] is specified [in the locative], [the operation applies] to what precedes it")—then no other substitute is specifically indicated; in that case, by virtue of proximity (*āntarya*), a *yaṇ* [would replace] a *yaṇ*.
It will be so. As for what was said—

that because both the seventh and fifth cases occur due to the existence [of the action], the sixth case is prescribed in both instances, and thus there is the contingency of both operations applying simultaneously—
the activity of the Teacher indicates that both do not apply at once, since he [uses] this one [term].
Regarding the phrase "of the preceding and the following," he provides the mention of "preceding.

There will be a designation for the word (*śabda*). For a word has no "self" (*sva*) other than its form (*rūpa*). If that is so, since [the definition] is already established, the fact that the Teacher employs the term "form" (*rūpa*) indicates that there is a "self" of the word other than its form. What, then, is that? It is the meaning (*artha*). What is the purpose of indicating this? [It is for the sake of the rule regarding] the inclusion of meaningful items (*arthavattva*).

The metarule (*paribhāṣā*) "not [of] that which is meaningless" (*anarthakasya*) need not be formulated. Why, then, is this stated? Because meaning is understood through the word; since a meaning is impossible [without a word], [the rule applies] to that which expresses it.

When a word is uttered, its meaning is understood; for instance, in "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*) or "Eat the curd" (*dadhi aśāna*), the object is brought and the food is eaten.
