34. This formulation is incorrect. By the word *ū*, both time (*kāla*) and this phoneme (*varṇa*) are indicated. In that case, it is improper for a phoneme to be placed in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with time. How, then, should the formulation be made? It should be: *ūkālakālasya* ("of that which has the duration of the long *ū*"). What is meant by "of that which has the duration of the long *ū*" (*ūkālakālasya*)? The duration of this [phoneme] *ū* is "the *ū*-duration" (*ūkāla*). [That which has] the *ū*-duration...

[The objection: "It is the time of this [vowel], thus it is 'ū-kāla-kāla'. [The reply: Then that designation must be made in that way. [Objection: It need not be so made. [Reply: Here, the elision of the final member of the compound (uttarapadalopa) is to be understood. Just as one whose face is like a camel's face is called "uṣṭramukha" or "kharamukha," so too "ū-kāla-kāla" is simply called "ū-kāla. Alternatively, by virtue of association (sāhacarya), the term will apply figuratively: the phoneme (varṇa) associated with time is also called "time" itself.

The establishment of an equal number [of terms] regarding the short vowels and so forth is not achieved because of the disparity in their formulation. Regarding the short vowels and so forth, there is no establishment of an equal number. What is the reason? Because of the disparity in their formulation. There are three technical names (*saṃjñā*) and only one object to be named (*saṃjñin*). This is due to the disparity.

The designation according to number (*saṅkhyātānudeśa*) would not apply. But it is established by virtue of having an equal number. This is established. How? By virtue of having an equal number. How is there an equality of number? For there is a mention of modification (*vikāra*) for three [sounds];
this is a conjunctive mention (*praśliṣṭanirdeśa*) of three. But how is it known that this is a conjunctive mention of three?

Because of the functional capacity of the three designations (*sañjñā*). Even if it is understood from the functional capacity of the three designations that this is a conjunctive mention (*praśliṣṭanirdeśa*) of three [terms], how is it known that the designations will apply to those arranged in this specific sequence: first the one-measure (*mātrika*), then the two-measure?

Then [the rule] "trimātraḥ" [is stated]. It cannot be that a *mātrika* [vowel] occurs either in the middle or at the end; nor can a *dvimātra* [vowel] occur either at the beginning or at the end; nor can a *trimātra* [vowel] occur either at the beginning or in the middle. This *trimātra* [vowel], for its part, is impossible to place either at the beginning or in the middle. Why? Because it would follow that the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form) would depend upon a *pluta* [vowel], whereas [it applies to] *mātrika* and *dvimātrika* [vowels].

Furthermore, according to the rule that "the shorter [term] is placed first," the *mātrika* (one-mora) will be placed first. As for what was said—that this three-mora [vowel] cannot be produced at the beginning or in the middle, because it would result in the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) based on a *pluta* (protracted) vowel—[we reply]: the preservation of the original form is based on a *pluta*, and the designation (*saṃjñā*) of *pluta* is established by this very [rule]. And if it were indeed three morae...

Whether it occurs at the beginning or in the middle, it would simply not have the designation *pluta*; how then could there be the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) for it? As for what is said—that since "that which ends in a *ghi* [stem] precedes" applies even to monosyllabic (*mātrika*) and disyllabic (*dvimātrika*) words, the monosyllabic one will take the prior position—it is because the designation *ghi* depends upon short vowels (*hrasva*), and the designation *hrasva* is established by this very rule. And if it were a monosyllabic word...

Whether it occurs in the middle or at the end, this [vowel] would simply not have the designation *hrasva* (short); how then could it have the designation *ghī*, and how could there be its *pūrvanipāta* (preceding placement)?

Thus, this systematic arrangement is not possible. If that is so, then the activity of the Teacher indicates that a *mātrika* (one-mora) vowel does not occur at the end, since he prescribes the *pluta* (three-mora) substitute for a *mātrika* vowel in the rule: "Optionally, the particle *hi* is replaced by a *pluta* when used in response to a question."

How does this serve as an indicator? That which is at the end is designated as *pluta*. If a single-mora (*mātrika*) sound were at the end, it would receive the designation *pluta*. In that case, the mention of the duration of a mora for a sound of one-mora duration would be purposeless. [One might then argue: "In that case, it must occur in the middle. To this, the activity of the Teacher indicates that a single-mora sound does not occur in the middle.

That this [rule] teaches the lengthening of the vowel *i* before the suffixes *yañ* and *sup*—namely, that "this [vowel] becomes long"—serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). How does it function as an indicator?

That which is in the middle is designated as "long. If a single-mora (*mātrika*) vowel were in the middle, it would receive the designation "long. In that case, the mention of a duration of one mora for what already has a duration of one mora would be purposeless. Therefore, the two-mora vowel must be at the end.

In this matter also, the activity of the Teacher indicates that a [vowel] consisting of two morae (dvimātra) does not occur at the end [of a word], since he prescribes a protracted vowel (pluta) for that which consists of two morae in the rule *om abhyādāne*. How is it a *jñāpaka*? That which occurs at the end is designated as "protracted" (*pluta*).

If a [vowel] consisting of two morae were to occur at the end, it would receive the designation "protracted. In that case, there would be the prescription of a duration of two morae for what already has a duration of two morae.

It would be purposeless. Furthermore, since its prior placement (pūrvanipāta) has been superseded by the *mātrika* rule, where else could it possibly occur except in the middle? Thus, this arrangement is established. [Objection: Such an arrangement may indeed be established; however, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the prior designation would apply to long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels as well. For the prior designation would also obtain for long and protracted vowels.

What is the short designation? What is the reason? [It is because] "an [vowel] includes its homogeneous counterparts" (P. 1.1.69). But this is established by the mention of *tapara* [vowels]. How so? The mention of *tapara* must be made: "that which has the duration of *u*, ū, or *ū3*" (P. 1.2.27). If that is the case, when the *tapara* is applied to the quick (*druta*) tempo, there must be an addition for the medium (*madhyama*) and slow (*vilambita*) tempos.

Because of the difference in duration. And it has been stated regarding [the vowels] *druta* (quick), etc. What was stated? "But it is established that the phonemes (*varṇa*) remain constant; it is their modes of articulation (*vṛtti*) that are distinguished by the speaker’s utterance being slow or quick. In that case, then, the mention of *tapara* (the *t* following the vowel) must be made. It need not be made. Here, the term "duration" (*kāla*) is employed; and as long as the *tapara* marker is used, so long is the term "duration" understood.
And the word *kāla* (time/measure) is completed with each [term] individually:

*ukālaḥ*, *ūkālaḥ*, *ū3kālaḥ*. Alternatively, this rule (*yoga*) should be formulated under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) "one designation" (*ekasañjñā*). In that case, there is only one designation—namely, whichever is subsequent and which has no other scope—and thus the previous designation does not apply to the long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels.
It will be so. Alternatively, this rule—"the own form of a word [is used] when it is not a technical grammatical term" (*svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasyāśabdasaṃjñā*)—is rejected.

In that case, the phrase "when it is not a technical grammatical term" (*aśabdasaṃjñā*) will be understood as being qualified by whatever case-ending through which its indication becomes meaningful; thus, it will follow accordingly.

"A vowel (aṇ) and [the vowels] u, i, ṛ, and ḷ (it), when not themselves suffixes, denote their homogeneous sounds (savarṇa), except for technical terms. Alternatively, by virtue of the explicit statement of the technical term "short" (hrasva), the previous designation [of "vowel"] will not apply to long (dīrgha) and protracted (pluta) vowels. But would this not serve as a purpose:
namely, that I shall state a restriction regarding the application of the technical term, such that whatever is expressed by the term "short" occurs in place of a vowel?
"So that it might be so. This would be the purpose [of the rule] if the teachings regarding short vowels were effective;

however, since the mention of "short" (hrasva) applies only as long as the mention of "a" (aj) applies, the teachings regarding short vowels are therefore ineffective. In that case, this is the purpose:

"I shall state that *ekah ik hrasvādeśe* (in the case of a short substitute, *ekah* [the single substitute] becomes *ik*). For if this were not stated, it would have to be said at every instance where a short vowel is prescribed: "In the case of a neuter nominal stem (*prātipadika*), *ekah* becomes *ik*"; "In the case of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) when *ṇic* followed by *caṅ* is applied, *ekah* becomes *ik*"; "The remaining initial consonant (*halādi-śeṣa*) is short, and *ekah* becomes *ik*."

"Let *ik* be [the name for *ec*]," [one might say]. But a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not lighter than this. Why? Because the purpose of creating a technical name is for the sake of brevity (*laghu*). And in the six instances where "short vowels" (*hrasva*) are mentioned, it would be more concise to say "let *ekāra*, *aikāra*, *okāra*, and *aukāra* become *ik*" rather than creating a technical name. There are six mentions of "short vowels" where one could simply say "let *ec* become *ik*. However, if a technical name were created, there would be eight [mentions]. [The first is] the definition of the term "short vowel" (*hrasvasaṃjñā*).
It must be stated that in the rules concerning short vowels (*hrasva*), the term "short" (*hrasva*) should be mentioned three times— as *hrasvaḥ*, *hrasvaḥ*, *hrasvaḥ*—

in the rule *eca ig hrasvādeśe*. Since this [result] is already established by a simpler formulation, the reason he undertakes this more cumbersome effort is so that the previous designation (*pūrvasañjñā*) shall not apply to long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels.

Is this a supplement (*śeṣa*) to the rule *al-antyasya*, or rather an exception (*apavāda*) to it? How could it be a supplement to that, or how could it be an exception to it? If there were a single sentence consisting of both [the rule *al-antyasya*] and this [rule], such that the operations concerning *al* apply to the final [element], and the short, long, and protracted vowels [apply] to the final vowel (*acaḥ*), then this would be a supplement to that. But if they are separate sentences:

The rules regarding the final [element] state that "the short, long, and protracted vowels apply to both the final and the non-final [vowel]. Therefore, this present rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to that. What, then, is the distinction here? If it is argued that the rules for short vowels and so forth apply to the final [consonant], then there would be an anomaly in the case of the lengthening of the vowels in *vac*, *pracch*, *śam* and others, as well as in *han*, *gam*, and *dīrgha*.

Regarding the mention of *aj* (a vowel): if it is argued that the rule for short vowels and so forth applies to the final letter of the stem (*alaḥ antyasya*), then the mention of *aj* must be made in the case of the lengthening of *vac*, *pracch*, *śam* and others, as well as *han* and *gam*. It must be stated that the lengthening of *vac* and *pracch* occurs by the rule "lengthening of a vowel" (*acaḥ*). [Otherwise], because they are not final letters, the rule would not apply. It must be stated that the lengthening of *śam* and others occurs by the rule "lengthening of a vowel" (*acaḥ*). [Otherwise], because they are not final letters, the rule would not apply. [The same applies to] *han* and *gam*.

It should be stated that [the substitution] applies to a long vowel (*dīrgha*) following a vowel (*acaḥ*). Since it does not occur at the end of a word (*anantyatvāt*), the rule would not apply. Let it then be an exception (*apavāda*) to that. If [the substitution] follows a vowel (*acaḥ*), then there must be a prohibition of the non-final [vowel] in the case of neuter short vowels, *kṛt* suffixes, *sārvadhātuka* suffixes, and the lengthening of *nām* suffixes. That is to say, if [the substitution] follows a vowel, then a prohibition of the non-final [vowel] must be stated for neuter short vowels, *kṛt* suffixes, *sārvadhātuka* suffixes, and the lengthening of *nām* suffixes. [This concerns the rule: "A neuter nominal stem (*prātipadika*) has a short vowel."
As it occurs here:
*rai*,
*atiri*, *nau*.
In the case of *atinau* [in the rule] "thus, *suvāk*, in a Brāhmaṇa family," the long vowel would also apply here. Regarding the rule "the long vowel for *akṛt* and *sārvadhātuka* suffixes":
just as it occurs here in *cīyate* and *stūyate*, so too would it apply here in *bhidyate*. Regarding the rule "the long vowel for *nām*"...

Just as it occurs here in the case of *agnīnām* and *vāyūnām*, so too would it apply here in the case of *ṣaṇṇām*. This is not a fault. The rule *nopadhāyāḥ* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). This restriction will apply to that which is under discussion. And what is under discussion? It is *nāmi*. Therefore, [the rule] shall apply.

In this case, by virtue of the restriction (*niyama*), it would not apply to *ṣaṇṇām*. [The rule] would also apply here in *anyate* and *tanyate*. Furthermore, even if the restriction were formulated thus:
"only for *nām* [suffixes] following a penultimate vowel (*upadhā*)", still, by virtue of that restriction, it would not apply in this instance.

[The vowels] *anyate* and *tanyate* [would be affected]; here, the rule would apply to the six [vowels]. Furthermore, if there were a restriction from both sides—namely, "only for a penultimate vowel" and "only when *ām* follows, and only when *ām* follows, not otherwise"—even so, the rule would be split; thus, in *suvāk brāhmaṇakulam*, the rule would undesirably apply here as well. Therefore, in that case, wherever one says "short," "long," or "protracted," one should specify "of a vowel (*ac*)."

This [ambiguity] must be seen as present there. What is accomplished [by this]? A genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is manifested alongside the accusative (*dvitīyā*). In that situation, there is freedom of choice: either to qualify the vowel (*ac*) by means of what is being grasped [as the head], or for what is being grasped to be qualified by the vowel. Since there is such freedom of choice, in cases such as *vac*, *pracchi*, *śamādi*, *prabhṛti*, *han*, *gam*, and *dīrgha*, we shall qualify the vowel by means of what is being grasped [as the head], so that "the long vowel replaces the vowel of these. Now, in cases such as *napuṃsakahrasva*, *akṛt*, *sārvadhātuka-nāmi-dīrgha*, we shall qualify what is being grasped by means of the vowel.

41–43. Why does it not occur here: *dyauḥ*, *panthāḥ*, *saḥ*? There is a restriction (*niyama*) regarding what is prescribed by means of a technical name (*saṃjñā*). The restriction applies to those things that are prescribed by means of a technical name. Is this something that needs to be stated?

This [is not so]. For how would it be understood if it were not explicitly stated? The term *ac* (vowel) is understood to carry over. In that case, the connection will be made as follows: "In place of a vowel (*ac*), there occurs a short, long, or protracted vowel (*ac*)"—thus it is being formulated. Now, when the term *ac* was included in the preceding rule (*yoga*), what was the purpose? The inclusion of *ac* is for the purpose of excluding a collection (*samudāya*) consisting of a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) and a vowel. [Therefore,] the inclusion of *ac* [is necessary].

This is done for the purpose of excluding [the application of] *saṃyoga* and for the purpose of excluding [the application of] a collection of vowels (*acsamudāya*). First, for the purpose of excluding *saṃyoga*: in the cases of *pratakṣya* and *prarakṣya*, let there not be the insertion of *tuk* by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk*. Second, for the purpose of excluding a collection of vowels: in the case of *titaucchatram*.
[In the case of] *titaucchāyā*, let there not be the optional application (*vibhāṣā*) [of the rule] "after a long vowel at the end of a word" (*dīrghāt padāntāt vā*).
Does the mention of the vowel (*aj-grahaṇa*) specified in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdiṣṭa*) carry over [from the previous sūtra], or does it not? And what follows from this? If it carries over...

If a consonant has obtained a vowel [as its preceding element], the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating that "a consonant is as if non-existent" does not apply. How indeed could a consonant obtain a vowel? In that case, this [rule] is set aside. There are many purposes for this technical rule. Now, does the mention of *aj* (vowel) specified in the first [sūtra] carry over, or does it not? And what is the purpose of its carrying over?

"Certainly, it would be meaningful if these qualities were perceived as belonging to the consonant (*vyañjana*) as well. But are they not directly perceived [as such], for example, in 'iṣe tvā' and 'ūrje tvā'? These are not qualities of the consonant; they are qualities of the vowel (*ac*). However, due to its proximity to that [vowel], the consonant is also perceived as possessing those qualities. It is just as when a white cloth is placed between two red cloths."

When an empty bronze vessel is placed inside a basket of jujube fruits, it is perceived as having the quality of those [fruits]. From where indeed do these qualities come to the vowel? Rather, because of its proximity to them, the consonant is also perceived as having that quality.
But these qualities would not belong to the consonant; rather, because of its proximity to it, the vowel is also perceived as having that quality.
Thus, even without a consonant, these qualities are observed in vowels alone; however, there is no utterance of a consonant without a vowel. Indeed, the etymological definition is significant:
"The vowels shine by themselves (*svayaṃ rājante svarāḥ*)," while "the consonant follows after" (*anvak bhavati vyañjanam*).
Because "high" and "low" are not fixed, the establishment of their technical designation is impossible. This "high and low" refers to unstable meanings;
for that very same thing is high in relation to one person and low in relation to another. Thus, someone says to another who is studying:

"Why do you recite loudly? Now, let it proceed softly. To him who was reciting in that manner, another said: "Why do you recite with your teeth clenched? Let it proceed loudly. Thus, [the instruction] is characterized by high and low tones and unstable meanings. Because of this instability, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) cannot be established. If that is the case, then a formal definition (*lakṣaṇa*) shall be formulated:
Length, harshness, and narrowness of the oral cavity are the factors that raise the pitch of sound. Length refers to the contraction of the limbs;

harshness refers to the roughness and dryness of the voice; and narrowness of the oral cavity refers to the constriction of the throat. These are the factors that raise the pitch of sound. Now, the factors that lower the pitch of sound: relaxation, softness, and width of the oral cavity are the factors that lower the pitch.

Relaxation of the vocal organs is the loosening of the limbs; softness of the voice is its mildness and smoothness; and breadth of the oral cavity is the largeness of the throat—these are the factors that lower the pitch of the sound. This, however, is inconclusive, because what is highest for a voice of weak effort (alpa-prāṇa) may be lowest for one of strong effort (mahā-prāṇa). But it is established by the statement regarding the uniformity of the mode of articulation.
This is established. How so? It should be stated: "when the process is the same. But what is this "process" (*prakrama*)? It is the chest, the throat, and the head.
(Pāṇini 1.2.31) It is said that a combination (*samāhāra*) is called *svarita*. Of which [sounds] does the combination receive the designation *svarita*? Of two vowels (*ac*).

Thus he said: "If it is a combination (*samāhāra*) of two vowels (*ac*), [then there is no *eka-śeṣa*], because of their non-existence. If it is a combination of two vowels, that is not so. What is the reason? Because of their non-existence. For there is no such thing as a combination of two vowels. But is this not the case in *gāṅge-nūpe*? This is not a combination of two vowels; rather, this single [substitute] is prescribed in place of an acute and a grave accent. If that is so, then [it applies] to the two qualities (*guṇa*).

If it is argued that [the term *guṇa*] refers to the two qualities [of *vṛddhi* and *guṇa*], no; because this is not the section on vowels (*ac*). If it is argued that there is a collective reference (*samāhāra*) to the two qualities, that is not so. What is the reason? Because this is not the section on vowels. The term *ac* (vowel) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. But it is established that, since there is no such thing as a "collection of vowels" (*acsamudāya*), there is a cognition of the quality belonging to that [vowel].
This is established. How? By considering that there is no collection of vowels, [the term *guṇa*] refers to the vowel possessing that quality, namely, the quality of the collective [operation].
There will be comprehension. But how can "samāhāra" (collection) be referred to by this [term] ending in *ac*?

Here, the elision of the *matup* suffix (*matub-lopa*) is to be understood. For example: those who have flowers are "puṣpakāḥ"; those who have blackness are "kālakāḥ. In this way, that which possesses a collection is "samāhāra. Alternatively, the vowel *a* has the sense of the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*). For example: "tundaḥ" (one who has a protruding belly).

[The word] *ghāṭaḥ*. If this were so, the threefold accent (*traisvarya*) would not be established. What fault is there in that? [The objection is: "We study with the threefold accent"—this would not be tenable. This does not depend on the qualities [of the vowels]. What then? It depends on the vowels themselves. "We study with the threefold accent" means we study by means of three kinds of vowels: some with the quality of acute (*udātta*), some with the quality of grave (*anudātta*), and some with both qualities. For example: [text follows].

That which possesses the quality of white is "white," and that which possesses the quality of black is "black. Now, that which possesses both qualities receives a third designation, either "variegated" (*kalmāṣa*) or "spotted" (*sāraṅga*). In the same way here as well, that which possesses the quality of high pitch is "high-pitched" (*udātta*), and that which possesses the quality of low pitch is "low-pitched" (*anudātta*). Now, that which possesses both receives a third designation: "circumflex" (*svarita*).

It is stated that [the vowel] is half-a-short [mātrā]. In that case, [the designation] does not apply to long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels, as in *kanyā śaktike3 śaktike*. This is not a fault; here, the suffix *mātrac* is to be understood as elided. "Half-a-short" means simply half of a short [vowel].
Thus [it is asked]: for what purpose is this stated? It is because this [world] becomes as if mixed together. For example:

when milk and water are joined, because they have become mixed, it is not known how much is milk and how much is water, nor in which place is the milk and in which place is the water. Likewise here too, because they have become mixed, it is not known.

"How much is acute (udātta)? How much is grave (anudātta)? In what position is it acute? In what position is it grave?"—the Teacher, acting as a friend, explains this: "This much is acute; this much is grave; in this position it is acute; in this position it is grave. If he is such a friend, why does he not also teach other matters of this same kind? What, then, are those? They are the places of articulation (sthāna), the organs of articulation (karaṇa), and the modes of emission (anupradāna).

Grammar is this higher science (*uttarā vidyā*). One who has been thoroughly trained in the treatises on metrics (*chandaḥśāstra*) is capable of understanding it through comprehension. If this is so, there is no purpose served by this [grammar]; this too will be understood through comprehension.
In that case, this is merely a matter of applying a technical designation (*sañjñākaraṇa*).
"Of that *svarita* [vowel], the first half-mora is designated as *udātta*. What is accomplished by this? In the three rules concerning the *udātta*, the mention of *svarita* need not be made:

namely, in the rules *udāttasvaritaparasya sannataraḥ*, *udāttasvaritayoḥ yaṇaḥ svarito 'nudāttasya*, and *nodāttasvaritodayam*. This is the purpose of establishing the technical designation (*saṃjñākaraṇam*)."

Indeed, it is certainly not lighter. Why is that? For the purpose of a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is to achieve brevity. And in the three instances where the *udātta* is prescribed, the mention of the *svarita* is lighter than establishing a technical name. In the three instances where the *udātta* is prescribed, there are nine syllables; but in establishing a technical name, there are eleven. If that is so, then both [options] are covered by this.

Both the grammatical description and the technical designation are being established. But how can both be obtained by a single effort? He says: they can be obtained. How so? It will be understood as a designation based on the literal meaning (*anvarthagrahaṇa*):
"Of that *svarita* vowel, the first half-mora is designated as *udātta* (acute). [The term *udātta*] means "raised up" (*ūrdhvam ātta*).

And therefore, [the rule] concerning the acute accent (*udātta*) applies. If that is so, then whatever is stated regarding that which begins with an acute accent would also apply to that which begins with a circumflex accent (*svarita*). In that case, this is merely an explanatory restatement (*anvākhyāna*) for the sake of one of dull intellect. (P_1.2.32.2) KA_I,209.5-25 Ro_II,

50–52: [The rule] "from the half-mora of the acute preceding a svarita" (svaritasyārdhahrasvodāttāt) up to [the rule] "of the grave following an acute-svarita" (udāttasvaritaparasya sannataraḥ)—this section of sūtras follows from the sūtra "after an acute, the grave becomes svarita" (ūrdhvam udāttād anudāttasya svaritaḥ), for the purpose of establishing the svarita [quality]. This section of sūtras follows from that very sūtra: "from the half-mora of the acute preceding a svarita" (svaritasyārdhahrasvodāttāt) up to "of the grave following an acute-svarita" (udāttasvaritaparasya sannataraḥ). Thus [is established] the svarita of the grave following an acute.

What is the purpose? It is for the sake of establishing [the rule] "after a svarita" (svaritāt). It is so that the establishment [of the rule] "anudāttas following a svarita in saṃhitā" (svaritāt saṃhitāyām anudāttānām) may occur, as in: *imam me gaṅge yamune sarasvati śutudri*. Where, then, would it apply? To that svarita which is already established.

The compound *kāryam* [is used] for the sake of *devadattayajñadattau*. And it is for the sake of the circumflex (*svarita*) and the acute (*udātta*). That [substitution] must be applied only there; it does not apply in the *Subrahmaṇyā* formula, where the circumflex becomes acute: "indra āgaccha. Where, then, would it apply? Wherever the circumflex is already established: "subrahmaṇyom indra āgaccha. And from the acute following a circumflex, it is for the sake of the non-circumflex. And from the acute following a circumflex, it is for the sake of the non-circumflex.

It should be performed in that very place. [The mantra] "indra āgaccha hariva āgaccha" [is an example]. And for the sake of the lower pitch (*sannatara*) following a circumflex (*svarita*). And for the sake of the lower pitch following a circumflex, it should be performed in that very place. That which follows a circumflex which is itself acute (*udātta*) has a lower pitch:
"maṇavaka jaṭilakādhyāpaka nyaṅ. Where, then, would it apply? To that circumflex which is established [by rule].
"O young brahmin, O matted-hair ascetic, O handsome one! Where then should that be stated? It need not be stated.

The prescription of the *anudātta* accent for *deva* and *brahman* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that [the rule] "from a *svarita*" is already established. The prescription of the *anudātta* accent for *deva* and *brahman* is the indicator that here the *svarita* is established. If this is what is being indicated, then [it applies to] the *anudātta* following a *svarita* and an *udātta*."

The *svarita* accent would follow. We do not say that the statement regarding the *anudātta* (unaccented) nature of *deva* and *brahman* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the *svarita* is established here. What then? This subsequent section [of the grammar] is the indicator.

53. Is this the inclusion of the technical term *sambuddhi* (vocative singular), meaning "the singular number is *sambuddhi*," or is it an inclusion based on the etymological meaning, meaning "*sambuddhi* is addressing"? What follows from this? If it were the technical term, it would not apply in cases such as *devāḥ* or *brahmāṇaḥ*. If, however, it is an inclusion based on the etymological meaning, there is no fault. As for example:
There is no fault; let it be so.
(P_1.2.33.2) What then: is this *ekaśruti* acute (*udātta*) or grave (*anudātta*)? It is not acute. How is this known?

As for this statement, "The *vaṣaṭ*-call is even higher (*uccaistarām*)," how does it serve as an indicator? The mention of "higher" is not a restrictive rule; rather, it means that to whatever degree it is "high" (*uccaiḥ*), it is "even higher" (*uccaistarām*). If, then, there are neither acute (*udātta*) nor grave (*anudātta*) accents, and if there is no grave accent at all, how is this known? It is known from the statement, "That which follows an acute or a circumflex (*svarita*) is lower (*sannatara*). How so?

This is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). The mention of "crossing over" (*tara*) is not restrictive; for as long as there is "low" (*sanna*), so long there is "lower" (*sannatara*). Thus, by these two indicators, the single tone (*ekaśruti*)—which is the intermediate interval between the acute (*udātta*) and the grave (*anudātta*)—is brought into effect. Another says: "But is this *ekaśruti* acute or grave? It is acute. How is this known? Because this...
"The *vaṣaṭ*-call is indeed higher," so it is said. How is this an indicator? Because the reference to "crossing over" (*tara*) is used as a technical term (*tantra*).

Having perceived [the preceding vowel] as high (*uccaiḥ*), the term "higher" (*uccaistarām*) comes into being. If, then, it is acute (*udātta*) and not grave (*anudātta*), yet it is also grave—how is this known? Because he says, "that which follows an acute or a circumflex (*svarita*) is lower" (*sannataraḥ*). How is this so?
This is the indicator: the rule concerning the comparative degree (*taranirdeśa*). Having perceived the "lowered" (*sanna*), there occurs that which is "more lowered" (*sannatara*).
Thus, in this rule concerning the comparative degree, there are these seven accents:
the acute (*udātta*) and the more acute (*udāttatara*).
The unaccented (anudātta),
the more unaccented (anudāttatara), and the circumflex (svarita).
That which is the acute (*udātta*) within a circumflex (*svarita*) is distinguished by another; this is the seventh [type of accent], known as monotone (*ekaśruti*).
(Pāṇini 1.2.37)

55–56. In the *subrahmaṇyā* formula, the syllable *o* is acute (*udātta*). In the *subrahmaṇyā*, the syllable *o* becomes acute: *subrahmaṇyom*. In a verb, the syllable *ā* and the following initial syllable are also acute. In a verb, the syllable *ā* and the following initial syllable become acute: *indra āgaccha*; *harivo āgaccha*. And at the beginning of a sentence, two syllables each are acute. At the beginning of a sentence, two syllables each become acute: [e.g., *indra āgaccha*].
*indra āgaccha*, *hariva āgaccha*, *maghavann varjam āgaccha*, *maghavan sutyāparāṇām antaḥ*. In the case of *sutyāparāṇām antaḥ*, the final syllable is acute (*udātta*):
*dvyahe sutyam*, *tryahe sutyam*. In the case of *asau iti antaḥ*, the final syllable is acute:
*asau gārgyo yajate*, *asau vātsyō yajate*. In the case of *amuṣya iti antaḥ*, the final syllable [is acute]: *amuṣya...*

In the case of *dākṣeḥ pitā yajate*, the penultimate syllable of a word ending in *-syā* is acute, as is the final syllable. In the case of *gārgyasya pitā yajate* and *vātsyasya pitā yajate*, the penultimate syllable of a name ending in *-syā* is optionally acute. Alternatively, for a name ending in *-syā*, the penultimate syllable becomes acute.
The father of Devadatta sacrifices. The father of Devadatta sacrifices.
(P_1.2.38) Some [teachers] maintain that the words *deva* and *brahman* are unaccented (*anudātta*). Some desire that the words *deva* and *brahman* be unaccented.
"Devas, Brahmanas; Devas, Brahmanas.

(Pāṇini 1.2.39) If it is argued that [the rule] "in *saṃhitā*, for the *anudātta* vowels following a *svarita*" applies, then the single tone (*ekaśruti*) must be prescribed for two or one [such vowels]. If it is argued that [the rule] "in *saṃhitā*, for the *anudātta* vowels following a *svarita*" applies, then the single tone (*ekaśruti*) must be stated for two or one [vowels].

"Agniveśya cooks. But what is the reason it does not succeed? The instruction is made using the plural number; therefore, there would be a single accent for many, but not for two or one. This is not a fault. Here, the specific mention [of the number] is not the governing factor (*tantra*). But how can that very same mention be made while it is not the governing factor? And one who acts according to that—
And you are a hater of that [repetition]. Because it is inseparable [from the act of expression], a designation is made here by means of the plural number;
for a designation must necessarily be made by some case-ending and some number. For example:
someone desiring rice brings a bundle of *śāli* grain together with its stalks and husks because it is inseparable from them. As long as...

First, having taken what is to be taken, one discards the husks and the straw. Similarly, someone seeking meat takes fish along with their bones and scales because they are inseparable; having taken as much as is needed, he discards the scales and bones.
Likewise here too, because they are inseparable, the designation is made by means of the plural number. Thus, there is a uniformity of accent without distinction.

If it is argued that there is a single accentuation (*ekaśrutya*) without distinction, then there would be no application of it to words separated [by others]. If it is argued that there is a single accentuation without distinction, then a single accentuation would not apply to separated words, as in:
*imam me gaṅge yamune sarasvati śutudri*. However, this is established by the rule stating "even more than one" (*anekam api*). [Thus, it applies to] more than one.
It should be stated that even a single [vowel] following a svarita becomes *ekaśruti* in *saṃhitā*. [Objection: This is established. [Response:
In that case, the sūtra is altered. [Proposer: Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. [Objection: But was it not said:

"If it is argued that 'in *saṃhitā*, [the rule] applies to the anudātta vowels following a svarita,' then one must state the *ekaśruti* for two or one [vowels]; otherwise, there would be *ekaśruti* without distinction."
[Objection: "There would be no application [of the rule] for those [words] separated [by others]. [Response: This is not a fault. How so? This is an *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) enumeration:

*anudāttasya ca*, meaning "of two *anudātta*s" and "of many *anudātta*s. Even so, it would apply only to six or more [words]. [Response: The *ekaśeṣa* is completed within the group of six or more; however, since the completion of a sentence is observed to occur for each individual member, it will apply even to the case of two or one.

Regarding the designation *apṛkta*: the mention of *hal* [in the rule] is for the purpose of excluding *hal* [as a suffix] when there is elision of the *svādi* group. The mention of *hal* must be made in the definition of *apṛkta*. It should be stated that a suffix consisting of a single consonant (*ekahal*) receives the designation *apṛkta*. Why?
The purpose [of the mention of *al*] is to prevent the application of the rule *svādilope halaḥ*. When there is elision of suffixes beginning with *su*, the mention of *hal* need not be made;

for by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisi apṛktam hal*, the elision of the single-consonant (*apṛkta*) suffix is already established simply by the mention of *apṛktasya*. The mention of *al* is for the sake of the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ*. The mention of *al* must be made for the sake of the elision of *aṇ* and *iñ*. What is the purpose? For the elision of *aṇ* and *iñ*.
No separate mention need be made [of the elision of *ṇya*]:

by the rule "there is elision (*luk*) of *aṇ* and *iñ* after a *ṇya*, a *kṣatriya*, or an *ārṣa* [patronymic] in the sense of a younger descendant," the desired result is established simply by the condition that the suffix is *apṛkta*. If it is argued that the mention is for the sake of causing the elision of *aṇ* and *iñ*, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the case of *ṇya*. If it is argued that the mention is for the sake of causing the elision of *aṇ* and *iñ*, then an over-extension occurs regarding *ṇya*;
for [the elision] would apply here as well: [example omitted].
The son of Phāṇṭāhṛti is the youth Phāṇṭāhṛta. [Objection: It will not occur because of the force of the explicit mention of *ṇa*. [Reply:

If it is argued that this is due to the authority of the explicit statement, then the statement is for the purpose of excluding *phaṅ*. If it is argued that it is due to the authority of the explicit statement, this would be for the purpose of excluding *phaṅ*, so that *phaṅ* does not occur after this [name]. [Reply: It is established by the inclusion [of the name] among the *pailādi* group. If this were the only purpose, [it would have been stated] among the *pailādi* group.

One should read the rule in this way: *eva-pāṭhaṃ kuryāt*. By reading it thus, the suffix *phak* is excluded even for others besides those mentioned. Since this is already established, the fact that the Teacher prescribes the suffix *ṇam* indicates that there is no elision (*luk*) of this [suffix]. These are the three instances of the mention of "hal" (*hal-grahaṇa*). In the definition of the term *apṛkta*, the mention of "hal" must be made; [and] in the rule for the elision of the *svādi* group, the mention of "hal" is required.

The mention [of *apṛkta*] need not be made. When there is elision (*luk*) of *aṇ* and *iñ*, the mention [of *apṛkta*] must be made. Even when the mention of *al* is made, those same three mentions would still occur. In the definition of the technical term *apṛkta*, the mention of *al* must be made. In the case of the elision of suffixes beginning with *su* and others, the mention of *hal* must be made. Thus, the mention [of *apṛkta*] is not required for the elision of *aṇ* and *iñ*. [Therefore,] the mention of *apṛkta* [is superfluous].

It must be formulated. In that case, there is no distinction made on the basis of brevity (*lāghava*). This is the distinction: when the term *al* is employed, the term *ekāc* will not be used. Why does it not apply to *darviḥ* and *jāgṛviḥ*? Because [the rule applies] only to a suffix that consists of a single phoneme (*al*). Is this something that needs to be explicitly stated? No, it need not be. How so, even if it is not stated?

It will be understood [that the suffix consists of] a vowel (al) by virtue of the force of the mention of *al*. If it were the case that there could be both a vowel (*al*) and something else, the mention of *al* would be purposeless.

Even if the mention of *hal* were made, the mention of *eka* (single) need not be made. Why does it not occur in the case of *darviḥ* and *jāgṛviḥ*? Because the suffix consists of a consonant (*hal*) alone. Is this something that needs to be stated? No, indeed. How is it understood without being stated?

It will be understood [that the rule applies] by virtue of the mention of *hal*. If it were the case that something other than *hal* were also intended there, the mention of *hal* would be purposeless. There is another purpose for the mention of *hal*: so that it may apply to what ends in *hal*, and not to what ends in a vowel (*al*). If that is so, then since the desired result is already established, why is the mention of *eka* made when the mention of *al* is being formulated?

By doing so, the Teacher indicates that, except in the case of the mention of a specific phoneme (*varṇa*), there is a mention of the class (*jāti*). What is the purpose of this indication? It has been stated that [the rule] for *dambh-* is established because the mention of the consonant (*hal*) denotes the class;
that [statement] now becomes justified.
If it is argued that "a *tatpuruṣa* compound whose members have the same referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is a *karmadhāraya*," [we reply] that this is untenable because a compound has a single meaning;
for the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) [of *karmadhāraya*] applies to the compound as a whole which possesses a single meaning.

[The objection: There is no established proof. This single entity called a *tatpuruṣa* compound relies upon multiple meanings, yet grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) depends on a single substratum.

[The reply: But it is established by virtue of the coreferentiality of the words. This is indeed established. How? It should be stated that a *tatpuruṣa* compound whose members are coreferential is designated as a *karmadhāraya*. [Objection: It is thus established. [Reply: In that case, the rule (*sūtra*) is altered. [Objection: Let it remain as it was originally formulated.

"Let it be so. But has it not been said that "a *tatpuruṣa* compound whose members have a common referent is a *karmadhāraya*"? If this is argued, [the response is] that there would be a lack of established usage because a compound possesses a single meaning. This is not a fault. There is a primary type of *tatpuruṣa* in which there is a single word-form (*aikapadya*), a single accent (*ekasvarya*), and a single case-ending (*ekavibhaktikatva*). There is also [the designation of *karmadhāraya*] applied to it by virtue of its being for that purpose (*tādarthyāt*).

"The words whose purpose is that [other word] constitute a *tatpuruṣa*. Here, the term "that" (*tat*) refers to the designation [of the compound] by virtue of being for the sake of that [other word]. (P_1.2.43.1) If it is argued that "in a compound, that which is designated by the first case-ending is the subordinate member (*upasarjana*)," [we reply: because there is no such designation by the first case-ending, the application of this technical name (*saṃjñā*) in a compound is not established.

If it is argued that "in a compound, that which is designated by the first case [ending] is the subordinate member (*upasarjana*)," then because there is no such designation by the first case, the technical term *upasarjana* would not be established for a compound. For we do not observe the first case ending in words such as *kaṣṭa* when they are part of a compound. However, this is established through an explicit statement in the rule prescribing compounds. How so? In the rule prescribing a compound, that which is designated by the first case receives the technical name *upasarjana*.

It must be stated that [the term *samāsa*] applies [to the treatise]. If so, then it must be stated. Or rather, it need not be stated. Why? Because a designation is applied to something based on its being for the sake of that thing (*tādarthyāt*). The treatise is for the sake of the compound; therefore, it is designated by the word "compound" (*samāsa*).

64–67. If there is an occurrence of the nominative case in the formulation of a rule, then the designation *upasarjana* would undesirably apply even elsewhere. When the nominative case is employed in the formulation of a rule for something, the designation *upasarjana* would consequently apply to that same item even in other contexts.

For example: *rājñaḥ kumārīm śritaḥ* ("he has resorted to the king's daughter," i.e., *rājakumārīṃ śritaḥ*). In a compound beginning with *śrita*, the word ending in the second case (*dvitīyānta*) is indicated by the nominative case [in the rule].

Even in the case of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the designation *upasarjana* would apply [to the first member]. However, it is established by the rule stating "with respect to that for whose prescription [it is used]. This is established. How? It should be stated: "In the prescription of anything, that which is indicated in the nominative case becomes designated as *upasarjana* with respect to that. Then that must be stated. No, it need not be stated.

The term *upasarjana* is made into a technical designation (*saṃjñā*). And a designation is certainly not something to be made unnecessarily light. Why is that? For the purpose of brevity is the reason for making a designation. In this case, the purpose of making it a long designation is so that it may be understood as a descriptive designation (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), namely: "that which is non-principal is the *upasarjana*. Thus, the principal is the *upasarjana*.
And these two are relative terms (*sambandhi-śabda*). In this regard, it must be understood from their relationship as follows:

that which is subordinate with respect to something else receives the designation "subordinate" (*upasarjana*) with respect to that thing. Now, why is it that in a case where there are two words ending in the genitive case, the primary word does not receive the designation "subordinate"?

In the case of *rājñaḥ puruṣasya* [becoming] *rājapuruṣasya*, it has been stated that when two words ending in the genitive case function as subordinate members (*upasarjana*), a certain rule applies. What was stated? It was stated that in a compound of two words ending in the genitive, because there is no difference in meaning, the principal member (*pradhāna*) does not undergo initial placement. Thus, this [rule] "the subordinate member comes first" would not be rendered redundant; for, while the meaning remains unchanged, the principal member is placed first.
It will not be so. Even if this treatment as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) has been avoided, another [rule] still applies:

in the case of *rājñaḥ kumāryāḥ* (the king’s daughter), the form *rājakumāryāḥ* results, and by the rule *go-striyor upasarjanasya*, shortening would apply. But it has already been stated. What has been stated? That "gender follows that of the [subordinate] word" (*paravat liṅgam*), and that both the word and its meaning [are governed by this]. In that regard, for that which is directly taught...
The shortness [of the vowel] will be heard as a result of an extended application (*atideśika*). (P.

1.2.44.1) By this rule, the designation *upasarjana* would also apply to [words] beginning with the second [member of a compound]. What fault is there in that? In that case, the prohibition "when it is not the first member" (*apūrvanipāte*) would be triggered. No, for there is no such prohibition.
This is not a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) in the sense of "the word *na*" being placed first [in the compound]. What then? This is a *paryudāsa* (relative negation):
"that which is other than the first placement. Thus, there is no operation regarding the first placement; if something is applicable by some rule, it applies by that.

It will occur. And it would also occur by virtue of the preceding [rule]. Therefore, it will occur. Or rather, because [the former] has not been attained. Alternatively, that attainment which is immediate is what is prohibited. Why is this so? Because a rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediate. 68. Regarding the rule *ekavibhaktau*: it should be stated that this applies to words ending in case-suffixes other than the genitive (*aṣaṣṭhyanta*). This is so that [the rule] does not apply here: *ardham pippalyāḥ* (half of a long pepper), which becomes *ardhapippalī*. Or rather, it has already been explained. What has been explained? That "gender is like that of the word with which it is compounded" (*paravat liṅgam*) and that "the meaning is the meaning of the word" (*śabdārtha*). In that case, the shortening (*hrasvatva*) applies to the directly taught form (*aupadeśika*), while the original form will be heard (*śravaṇa*) in the case of the transferred form (*ātideśika*).

What, then, are the purposes of this yoga? The purpose is stated in the rule: "Dvigu, *prāpta*, *āpanna*, and compounds preceded by *alam* or a prefix [are bahuvrīhis] when they have the sense of a *kta*-suffix. Regarding *dvigu*: that which is bought for five cows is *pañcagu*. Regarding *prāpta* and *āpanna*: [e.g., *prāptam udakam yam sa prāptodakaḥ*].

One who has obtained a livelihood is *prāptajīvikaḥ*; one who has entered upon a livelihood is *āpannajīvikaḥ*. With *alam* preceding [a noun]: *alaṃkumāriḥ* (sufficient for a maiden). Prepositions (*upasarga*) [are compounded] with a word ending in a *kta* suffix: *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* (departed from Kauśāmbī), *nirvārāṇasiḥ* (departed from Vārāṇasī).

The term *arthavat* ("possessing meaning") is used for the sake of designation so that it does not apply to individual phonemes (*varṇa*). What would [the consequence] be? [In the case of the word] *vanaṃ*,...

In the word *dhanam*, the elision of the *n* [by the rule] "the *n* at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is elided" would otherwise apply. Why is it stated "not a verbal root (*adhātuḥ*)"? [Consider the example: *ahan vṛtram* ("he slew Vṛtra"). It could be said that "not a verbal root" need not be stated. Why does [the elision] not occur in *ahan vṛtram*? The teacher’s practice indicates that a verbal root does not receive the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), since he [teaches] the suffix *sup*.

In the rule *dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*, he makes the mention of *dhātu*. This is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*). It would rather be for the purpose of prohibition, as in the case of *api kākaḥ śyenāyate* ("even a crow behaves like a hawk"). [Question: What is the purpose of the term *apratyayaḥ* ("not a suffix")? [Example: *kāṇḍe kuḍye* ("in the stalk, in the wall"). [Objection: The term *apratyayaḥ* can be omitted. [Question: Why does it not occur in *kāṇḍe kuḍye*? [Answer: The mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
The designation *prātipadika* applies only to that which ends in a suffix—namely, that which ends in a *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffix—and not to anything else.

If the designation *prātipadika* were applied to whatever possesses meaning (*arthavat*), there would be the undesirable consequence of multiple words [being called *prātipadika*]. If the designation *prātipadika* were applied to whatever possesses meaning, the designation *prātipadika* would result even for multiple words.

"Ten pomegranates, six cakes, a pot, a goat-skin, a ball of minced meat, and a lower garment—this is what the father of the girl from Sphaiyakṛta has sent. [Objection: "The whole (samudāya) is meaningless. [Response: If it is argued that "the whole is meaningless," [we reply] that because the parts possess meaning, the whole possesses meaning, just as in common worldly usage. If it is argued that "the whole is meaningless," [it is not so], because the parts are meaningful.

Aggregates also possess meaning, just as in common worldly usage. For example, in the world it is said, "This city is wealthy," or "This city possesses cattle," even though not everyone therein is wealthy or everyone possesses cattle.
When it is said, "as in the world," it is meant that in the world only the constituent parts possess meaning, not the aggregate; and for this reason, [the meaning resides in] the constituents.

Thus, the individual [words] possess meaning, not the aggregate; for he who owns that substance performs the action with it, and he who has cows consumes their milk and clarified butter. This cannot even be perceived by others. What, then, is this mode of expression?

"This city is wealthy; this [city] possesses cattle"—this is the manner of expression. In this regard, first, in the phrase "this city is wealthy," the suffix *a* (akāra) is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).

"Riches exist in this" means "this is rich. In the expression "this has cows," the possessive suffix *mat* is elided from the word ending in *mat*. Even so, there must be a prohibition of the [application of the] sentence, because it possesses meaning. A prohibition of the technical designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) for a sentence must be stated;
for example: "Devadatta, drive the white cow hither," and "Devadatta, drive the black cow hither. What is the reason? Because they possess meaning.

For this sentence is indeed meaningful. Indeed, no meaning other than the meanings of the word-components (padārtha) is perceived within a sentence. If it is argued that nothing other than the word-meanings is perceived, [we reply] that what is perceived is the connection between the word-meanings.
If it is further argued that nothing other than the word-meanings is perceived, it is stated as follows:

The apprehension of the mutual relation between word-meanings occurs within a sentence. Here, when "Devadatta" is uttered, the agent is specified, while the object, the action, and the quality remain unspecified. When "cow" is uttered, the object is specified, while the agent, the action, and the quality remain unspecified. When "drive toward" (*abhyāja*) is uttered, the action is specified, while the agent, the object, and the quality remain unspecified. [When "white"] is uttered... *śuklām* (the white one).

When it was stated thus, the quality (*guṇa*) was specified, but the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), and the action (*kriyā*) were not specified. Now, when it is said here, "Devadatta, drive the cow toward [me], the white one," everything becomes specified:
Devadatta alone is the agent, and no other; the cow alone is the object, and nothing else; the act of driving alone is the action, and no other.

"Only white, not black"—the fact that these words, which function in a general sense, come to rest in a specific instance is the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*). Therefore, there is a prohibition. Therefore, a prohibition must be stated. It need not be stated.

The mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) with respect to meaningful aggregates (*arthavat-samudāya*) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). [The mention of "compound" with respect to meaningful aggregates...]
It will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*):

"Only a compound (*samāsa*) consisting of meaningful constituents (*arthavat*) receives the designation *prātipadika*, and no other. If this restriction is applied, the designation *prātipadika* would not apply to the aggregate of a base (*prakṛti*) and its suffix (*pratyaya*).

"Bahupaṭavaḥ" and "uccakaiḥ"—what, then, is sought here by means of the technical designation *prātipadika*? It is so that the suffixes beginning with *su* (i.e., case endings) may arise [according to the rule] "after a *prātipadika*" (*prātipadikāt*). This is not a fault; for just as in these cases, because they are not *prātipadikas*, the arising of the *svādi* suffixes does not occur.
In that case, even the *luk* elision would not occur; the very case-ending (*vibhakti*) that remains internal would simply be heard.

This is not possible, for there would be a fault regarding the accent (*svara*). Specifically, the accent of "bahupaṭavaḥ" [as derived from "bahupaṭu-aḥ"] would result, whereas "bahupaṭavaḥ" [with a different accent] is what is desired. For the Teacher will indeed state:

"It is for the sake of many meanings that [the suffix] *cita* is added along with its own base (*saprakṛti*). Furthermore, when that [suffix] has been elided, whatever other case-ending (*vibhakti*) arises, it will not have the udātta accent on the final syllable because it is only a portion of the base. If this is so, then the activity of the Teacher indicates that the designation "nominal stem" (*prātipadika-sañjñā*) applies to the aggregate of base and suffix, since he uses the term "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*).

Thus he teaches a prohibition; and that is a prohibition of [suffixes] ending in those [kṛt and taddhita]. Well then, that prohibition of suffixes must be stated for the sake of providing an indicator (jñāpaka). But surely it must also be stated for the sake of obtaining [the application of the rule]? No, there is no need for its being for the sake of obtaining [the application]; the mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita* will serve as a restrictive rule (niyama).

The designation *prātipadika* will apply only to that which ends in an affix—namely, a word ending in a *kṛt* or *taddhita* affix—and not to any other word ending in an affix. Therefore, this prohibition of affixes must be stated for the sake of nothing else [but to restrict the scope], or else the designation *prātipadika* must be stated for the aggregate of base and affix. Neither of these need be stated; the restriction applies to those of the same class. Which [is the class]?

And [the compound] consists of members of the same class (*tulyajātīya*). Of what kind of items is there a compound? Of items ending in *sup* suffixes (*subanta*). In that case, the designation *prātipadika* would apply to a collection of both *sup* and *tiṅ* suffixes. Therefore, the designation *prātipadika* is prescribed for a collection of *sup* and *tiṅ* suffixes by the rule: "The root *jahāti* frequently denotes the agent along with the object" (*jahi karmaṇā bahulam ābhīkṣṇye kartāram ca abhidadhāti*). That [prescription] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).
It will be so:

the designation *prātipadika* applies to this very collection of *suptiṅ* [suffixes], and not to anything else. In that case, the designation *prātipadika* would then apply to a collection of *tiṅ* [suffixes] as well. Therefore, the designation *prātipadika* is also prescribed for a collection of *tiṅ* suffixes.

Regarding the rule "a verb [is compounded] with a verb to express continuity of action" (*ākhyātam ākhyātena kriyāsātatye*), that will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): the designation of *prātipadika* applies only to this specific collection of verbal forms (*tiṅ-samudāya*) and not to any other.

77–79. Meaningfulness is not possible because [the word] does not denote by itself. Meaningfulness is not possible for the word *vṛkṣa*. Why? Because it does not denote by itself. The meaning is not understood by the word *vṛkṣa* alone. By what, then? By that which is accompanied by an affix (*sapratyayaka*). Or rather, there is no usage of the word alone because of its eternal connection with the affix. It is not [the case that it lacks meaning].

Or rather, this fault does not arise. What is the reason? Because of the constant connection with the suffix (*pratyaya*). These two entities—the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix—are constantly connected. Because of the constant connection with the suffix, there will be no usage of the base alone. You are asked one thing, yet you explain something else; it is like being asked about mango trees and explaining about *kovidāra* trees. [The objection that] meaningfulness (*arthavattā*) [does not apply to the base alone]... [is not valid].
"You have been questioned by us as to how [the meaning] arises from the mere [word] because of its non-utterance; you state the reason for not employing the mere [word].

And indeed, having made such an assumption, the objection is raised: 'Because the whole is employed for the sake of the meaning, the parts are not established. But it is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka)."
This is established. How? Through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). What is this positive concomitance or negative concomitance?
Here, when "tree" (*vṛkṣaḥ*) is uttered, a certain word is heard: the word "tree," ending in the vowel *a*, and a suffix ending in the letter *s*. A certain meaning is also understood:

[The tree] possesses roots, trunk, fruit, and foliage, and yet there is oneness. When "two trees" (*vṛkṣau*) is said, one word is lost, another arises, and another persists: the *sakāra* is lost, the *aukāra* arises, and the word *vṛkṣa*, ending in the vowel *akāra*, persists. The meaning also is such that something is lost, something arises, and something persists.
Unity is lost and duality arises; that which possesses roots, trunk, fruit, and foliage is the persisting entity. We consider it thus:
the meaning belongs to that word which is lost, and the meaning belongs to that word which arises;
the meaning belongs to that word which persists, and the meaning belongs to that [persisting] meaning.
[Objection: It follows [that the word "cow" applies to all four-footed animals]. [Reply: This is an unequal comparison. For many words have a single meaning; for example:
*indra*, *śakra*, *puruhūta*, *purandara*; or *kandu*, *koṣṭha*, *kuśūla*. And one word may have many meanings; for example:

[The examples are] *akṣāḥ*, *pādāḥ*, and *māṣāḥ*. What follows from this? Is it not the case that the meaningfulness [of words] is more effectively established? We do not say that meaningfulness is not established; rather, meaningfulness has already been described through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) alone. In that regard, how is it determined that "this is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)" and "this is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*)," rather than the base itself expressing both meanings?

Or rather, it is simply a matter of convention. These words would be general terms in this way; and general terms do not settle upon specific meanings without [the aid of] a specific context. However, since a cognition necessarily arises regarding some particular object by its very nature when the word "tree" is uttered, we consider that these are not general terms. No.

If these are general terms, then the base (*prakṛti*) occurs in the sense of the base, and the suffix (*pratyaya*) occurs in the sense of the suffix. (P_1.2.45.4) KA_I,220.9-24 Ro_II, 79-80 But are these phonemes (*varṇa*) meaningful, or are they meaningless? Regarding the meaningfulness or meaninglessness of a phoneme...

It has been stated. What has been stated? "Phonemes possess meaning, because we observe meaning in monosyllabic roots, nominal stems, suffixes, and particles; because when there is a transposition of phonemes, there is a shift to another meaning; because when a phoneme is not perceived, there is an absence of meaning; and because of the meaningfulness of a composite. Furthermore, because the composite has a single unified meaning, the case-ending (*sub*) does not occur after a single phoneme. [Therefore,] they are meaningless.

"But [the word is not the letters], because no meaning is perceived from each individual letter; for the meaning is seen when there is a transposition, elision, addition, or modification of the letters. To this, it was not yet answered: "And because the aggregate possesses meaning. The answer to that is: if it is argued that "because the aggregate possesses meaning," it is observed [that the aggregate has meaning].

If it is argued that the substratum (guṇin) possesses its functional purpose through a quality (guṇa) that does not itself possess that purpose—on the grounds that the composite whole must have a purpose—[we reply: indeed, it is observed that a substratum can possess its functional purpose even through a quality that does not possess that purpose. For example: a single thread is incapable of providing protection against cold, yet a blanket, which is a collection of them, is capable. A single grain of rice is incapable of warding off hunger.

And their collection is capable of forming a *vardhatika* (a type of mat). A single blade of *balvaja* grass is incapable of binding, yet its collection becomes a rope that is capable. This is an unequal comparison. For in that case, there exists both the specific nature and the extent of the purposeful capacity. Indeed, with respect to certain things, a single thread is capable of protecting the skin, and a single grain of rice [is capable of satisfying hunger].

A single blade of *balvaja* grass is capable of warding off hunger, and a single bond is capable of holding fast; yet these phonemes (*varṇas*) are utterly useless by themselves. Just as, for example, when the parts of a chariot are disassembled, each individually is incapable of the act of moving, whereas their collection—the chariot—is capable, so too the collections of these phonemes possess meaning.

"The members [of a compound] are meaningless" (Pāṇini 1.2.45). A particle that is meaningless is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); that is, a particle that is meaningless receives the designation of a nominal stem.

It should be stated: "it limps," "it limps down," "it hangs," "it hangs down. But what is sought here by means of the technical designation *prātipadika*? [The purpose is] that from a *prātipadika* there is the derivation of case-endings (*svādi*), and that "that which ends in a case-ending is a *pada*"—this is the designation *pada*.

[The opponent says: "So that there might be the *nighāta* accent [of the first syllable] in the word *padāt* according to the rule *padasya padāt*. [The author replies: This is not a valid purpose. Even if the designation *prātipadika* were present, the derivation of case-endings (*svādi*) would not occur. Why? Because the derivation of case-endings is not restricted solely by the designation *prātipadika*. What then? Case-endings are prescribed when the meanings such as singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth are present; and these [words *pada*, etc. do not possess singularity and the other numbers.

[Objection: This fault does not arise. [The suffixes] arise without distinction; the restriction (*niyama*) is applied to those that have arisen. Alternatively, the restriction is made with reference to the subject matter under discussion (*prakṛta*). And what are the subjects under discussion? Singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth. The singular number is used for one object only, not for two, nor for many. The dual number is used for two only, not for one, nor for many. [The plural number is used] for many...

Thus, the plural number is used for multiple meanings, not for one or two. Alternatively, the activity of the Teacher indicates that these [terms] apply even when they are meaningless, because he teaches that "what is done by those possessing meaning" applies here; for he prescribes the technical term *karmapravacanīya*—which supersedes the technical terms *gati* and *upasarga*—for the two [words] *adhi* and *pari* when they are meaningless, by stating: "*adhi-parī* are meaningless."
But what is this? Is it an exclusion (*paryudāsa*)—that which is other than the suffix—or is it a prohibitive negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*)?

"It is not a suffix. And what is the distinction here? If it is argued that "it is not a suffix," then there would be a prohibition regarding the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) for *ti* and *ip*, because it would possess the quality of having an end (*antavat*). If it is argued that "it is not a suffix," then there would be a prohibition regarding the single-substitute for *ti* and *ip* in forms such as *kāṇḍe* and *kuḍye*. What is the reason? Because of its having an end. The single substitute for *ti* and *ip* would have the status of having an end like *ip*. Thinking that "there is something other than *tip*," the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-sañjñā*) would consequently apply.
Let it be, then, a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*).

[Objection: It is not a suffix (*pratyaya*). [Reply: If it is argued that it is not a suffix, then a prohibition would apply to the single-substitute *ūṅ* because it is treated like the initial [element]. If it is argued that it is not a suffix, then a prohibition would follow regarding the single substitute *ūṅ*: as in *brahmabandhūḥ*. What is the reason? Because it is treated like the initial. According to the rule "between a suffix and a non-suffix, the suffix is treated like the initial," the suffix [in this case] would be treated like the initial; thus, the prohibition "it is not a suffix" would apply there. This is not a fault, for such is the practice of the Teacher.

It indicates that the case endings beginning with *su* arise after a stem ending in *ūṅ*, since [the author] teaches the prohibition of the accent of the case ending in the rule "not after *ūṅ* or a verbal root" (*na ūṅ-dhātvoḥ*). Alternatively, there are indeed two designations as nominal stems (*prātipadika-sañjñā*) here:

one for the constituent part and one for the whole. In that regard, by virtue of the designation as a nominal stem belonging to the constituent part, the status of being "as if at the end" (*antavadbhāva*) applies.

The production of the *su*-affix will occur. And in the case of the elision of *su*, because of the application of the rule regarding the presence of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), a prohibition would result even after the elision of *su*: as in "rājā" (king) and "takṣā" (carpenter). Because of the rule regarding the presence of an affix, the prohibition "there is no [application of an operation] when there is an affix" would apply. This is not a fault.

The activity of the Teacher indicates that the prohibition does not apply by virtue of the technical definition of a suffix (*pratyaya*), since he teaches the prohibition "not after [stems ending in] *ṅi* or the vocative. Alternatively, let it be a relative exclusion (*paryudāsa*). But was it not said: "If it is an 'non-suffix' (*apratyaya'), then there would be a prohibition in the case of the single-substitute for *tiP*, because it possesses the character of being final"? This same fault applies even in the case of a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*). For in this case, there are indeed two designations as nominal stems (*prātipadika*).

[The rule applies] both to the individual constituent (*avayava*) and to the aggregate (*samudāya*). Furthermore, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from the combination of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and a non-nominal stem is also included under the term "nominal stem. Therefore, it would have to be stated by both [the proponent and the opponent]: "That which is short in the neuter gender... Moreover, [the question arises: "In what is it neuter? It is neuter that of which the neuter is a quality (*guṇa*). And of what is the neuter a quality? Of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). 85. What is the purpose of mentioning "compound" (*samāsa*)? It has been stated regarding the mention of "compound. What was stated? That the mention of "compound" for meaningful aggregates (*arthavat-samudāya*) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

What is the purpose of mentioning "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*)? The mention of "nominal stem" in the rule concerning the shortening of the neuter is for the purpose of excluding the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*).

The mention of the *prātipadika* (nominal stem) is made in the rule for the shortening of neuter stems in order to exclude forms ending in *tiP*. Let there not be shortening for that which ends in *tiP*: as in *kāṇḍe*, *kuḍye*, and *ramate brāhmaṇakulam*. A prohibition must be stated regarding indeclinables (*avyaya*). A prohibition regarding indeclinables must be stated: as in *doṣā brāhmaṇakulam* and *divā brāhmaṇakulam*. Should that [prohibition] then be stated? It need not be stated.
In this case, the indeclinable does not function as a neuter [noun]. What then? Here, the indeclinable functions as the locus (adhikaraṇa) of the neuter.
In that case, it would apply here: *kāṇḍībhūtaṃ vṛṣalakulam* ("the low-born family has become a mere stalk").
"The family of the *vṛṣala* has become like a wall. Or rather, it need not be stated at all. Why?

Because of the absence of a gender marker (*liṅga*). An indeclinable (*avyaya*) lacks a gender marker. But is this an exception only for indeclinables, or also for forms ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*)? He says: it applies even to forms ending in a verbal suffix. How so? For some indeclinables have the meaning of a case-ending as their primary sense.

Some [words] have action as their primary meaning; for example, *uccais* (loudly) and *nīcais* (softly) have the meaning of a case ending as their primary meaning, while *hiruk* and *pṛthak* (separately) have action as their primary meaning. Furthermore, even among words ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*), some have the meaning of a case ending as their primary meaning and some have action as their primary meaning; for instance, *kāṇḍe* and *kuḍye* (in the stalk and in the wall) have the meaning of a case ending as their primary meaning.

The phrase *brāhmaṇakulaṃ ramate* ("the Brahmin family delights") has the action as its primary meaning. Furthermore, these two meanings do not possess a connection with gender and number. And this must necessarily be understood in this way; for even if the term "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) were included [in the definition], it would still result in the following application here: *kāṇḍe kuḍye* ("in the stalk, in the wall"). For in these cases, there are two designations of "nominal stem"—one for the constituent part and one for the whole—and both would be grasped.

Furthermore, the single substitute for both a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and a non-nominal stem would be included under the term "nominal stem. Therefore, it would have to be stated by both [the sūtra and the vārttika]:

"The short vowel that occurs in the neuter [state] belongs to that [stem]. Moreover, in what sense is it "in the neuter"? It means "that whose quality (*guṇa*) is the neuter. And of what is the neuter the quality? Of the nominal stem.

88. An exception must be stated regarding the single-substitute long vowel (*ekādeśa-dīrgha*) and the substitution of *ai* (*aittva*). [Exception: An exception must be stated regarding the single-substitute long vowel and the substitution of *ai*: for example, *yugavaratrāya*, *yugavaratrārtham*, and *yugavaratrebhyaḥ*. [Response: This is established because these are characterized as "external" (*bahiraṅga*). These rules are external; the shortening (*hrasvatva*) is internal (*antaraṅga*). That which is external is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) [with respect to that which is internal].
Regarding internal elements:

(P_1.2.48.1) KA_I,223.18–21 Ro_II, 88–89. And regarding the shortening of a subordinate element (*upasarjana*). And regarding the shortening of a subordinate element: what [is the problem]? A prohibition must be stated concerning the long vowel resulting from a single-substitute replacement (*yañekādeśa*) and the substitution of *it*.

89–94. The mention of *goṭāṅ* is for the purpose of excluding *kṛt*-derived forms. The mention of *goṭāṅ* must be made. What is this "*ṭāṅ*"? It is a pratyāhāra (a grammatical abbreviation). Of which [elements] is it a pratyāhāra? It is the pratyāhāra of those beginning from *ṭāp* up to the *ṅ* of *ṣyaṅ*. What is the purpose? For the purpose of excluding *kṛt*-derived forms. [The rule] "the shortening [of the vowel] shall not apply to feminine *kṛt* derivatives and feminine verbal roots (*dhātu-strī*)" is intended.

"atitantrīḥ," "atiśrīḥ," and "atilakṣmīḥ. If that is so, then it must be stated [as a rule]. It need not be stated; for the mention of the word "strī" (feminine) is intended to indicate the accent (*svarita*). In that case—

The understanding of the governing scope (*adhikāra*) occurs through the use of the circumflex accent (*svarita*). It will be understood that the term refers to those [suffixes] prescribed under the heading "in the feminine" (*striyām*). Since the understanding of the governing scope occurs through the circumflex accent, there is no fault. If this is so, then this is a reference to a suffix (*pratyaya*). In that case, according to the rule "when a suffix is mentioned, it includes that which begins with it," [the rule] would not apply here.

"atirājakumāriḥ" (one who surpasses the princess) and "atisenānīkumāriḥ" (one who surpasses the commander-in-chief's daughter)—this is so because of the rule regarding non-feminine suffixes (*astrīpratyaya*). Regarding the suffix *īyas*, it is stated that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the treatment as masculine (*puṃvadbhāva*). It must be stated that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the feminine suffix *īyas* undergoes the transformation into the masculine form. For example: "bahuśreyasī" (one who has many excellent things) or "vidyamānaśreyasī" (one in whom excellence exists).

And there is a prohibition of the first member [of the compound], for the purpose of excluding the *go-samāsa*. A prohibition of the first member must be stated. What is the purpose? For the purpose of excluding the *go-samāsa*—that is, for the purpose of excluding *go* and for the purpose of excluding *samāsa*. First, for the purpose of excluding *go*: *gokulam*, [which would otherwise be *go-kulam*].
"cow's milk," "cowherd. For the purpose of excluding compound formations:
"the son of the king's daughter."

Regarding the example *senānīkumārīputraḥ*: why is it said that [the prohibition] is for the sake of excluding compounds (*samāsa*)? Is it not the case that there might also be a non-compound (*asamāsa*) where this prohibition would apply? It is stated that "there is shortening of a feminine-final nominal stem (*prātipadika*) when it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*"); however, without a compound, a feminine-final nominal stem cannot be a subordinate member.
It exists. But surely this [usage] exists:

*khaṭvāpādaḥ* ("the leg of a bed"), *mālāpādaḥ* ("the stalk of a garland").
