Once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, it would follow [that the rule applies] because of the status of being "like the end" (*antavadbhāva*) or "like the beginning" (*ādivadbhāva*). However, when there is dependence on both sides, it is not "like the end" or "like the beginning."

First of all, there is no purpose [for the rule] regarding the suffix *-go*. It is stated that "the short vowel occurs for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *-go* when it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*"), and this [word *strī*] does not end in *-go*. But is it not the case that this too ends in *-go* by virtue of the treatment as a named entity (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*)?

[The answer is: the treatment as a named entity applies only when not preceded by a nominal stem. Furthermore, there is no purpose [for the rule] regarding the exclusion of compounds (*samāsa*). [This is because the rule already applies to] that which ends in the feminine suffix (*stryanta*).

It is stated that "the short vowel occurs for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). These two terms, "principal" (*pradhāna*) and "subordinate" (*upasarjana*), are relative terms. In this context, it must be understood through their relationship as follows: "whenever something is subordinate in relation to another, and if that [other] constitutes its final element (*anta*)," [then the shortening applies]. Furthermore, this must necessarily be understood in this way; for even if a prohibition were explicitly stated, the rule would still apply here [in the following case]: [example omitted].

"Priyapañcakumāri" means "one who has five beloved daughters," and likewise "daśakumārīpriyaḥ. [Regarding the rule] "kapi ca": a prohibition must be stated with respect to the suffix *kap*; for example, "bahukumārīkaḥ."

"Bahuvṛṣalīkaḥ. [Regarding] "And in a Dvandva compound": a prohibition must be stated for Dvandva compounds as well; for example, *kukkuṭamayūryau* ("the cock and the peahen"). Or rather, it has already been stated. What has been stated? First, regarding the suffix *kap*, it was stated that there is a prohibition by the rule "not before *kap*. But this is not what was stated. For the shortening [of the final vowel] that would otherwise apply by the rule "ke aṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.13), [that is what was addressed].
It is a prohibition. Why is this so? Because a rule or a prohibition applies specifically to what immediately precedes it.

Furthermore, this must necessarily be understood in this way; for if one were to think that there is a prohibition of every instance of the application of *hrasva* (shortening)—whether it be of such-and-such a type or to such-and-such an extent—then a prohibition would undesirably follow even in this case.
"O village chief, the Brahmin family is dear to him; thus he is a *priyagrāmaṇika*. Now, this has been said:

"Since the suffix *kap* is applied last, there will be no shortening [of the vowel] because it is not final. This must be considered here: should *kap* be applied first, or should the shortening take place? What should be done in this case? Because it is subsequent, *kap* should be applied; the shortening is internal (*antaraṅga*).

The suffix *kap* is more internal (antaraṅgatara). But surely this *kap* is prescribed as a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) after [stems ending in] *ic*; [if so, how can it apply here]? It will receive that designation by virtue of being for that purpose (*tādarthyāt*). For those words whose compound is formed, nothing else occurs until they await the application of *kap*. This has also been stated regarding the *dvandva*: what was stated? That "the gender is like the latter" (*paravat liṅgam*), and that "the word and its meaning" (*śabdaśabdārthau*). In that regard—
The short vowel will belong to that which is taught directly (*aupadeśika*), while the long vowel will be heard in that which is extended by rule (*ātideśika*).

(Pāṇini 1.2.49) Regarding the elision of *taddhita* suffixes (*taddhitaluki*), there is a prohibition for *Avanti* and others. It must be stated that there is a prohibition for *Avanti* and others when a *taddhita* suffix is elided.

*Avantī*, *Kuntī*, *Kurūḥ*. Regarding the non-prohibition of *avantī* and others when there is elision (*luk*) of a secondary suffix (*taddhita*), it is because [the rule] applies to cases where elision does not occur. When there is elision of a secondary suffix, there is no prohibition for *avantī* and others. "Non-prohibition" (*apratiṣedhaḥ*) means a prohibition that is purposeless. Why does elision (*luk*) not occur? Because elision does not apply here. It is stated that [elision occurs] "when there is elision" (*luki*). Yet we do not observe elision in this case. Therefore, "when there is elision" (*luki*) is not a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*).

It is possible to understand [the rule]. For there is no sequence of prior and posterior (*paurvāparya*) by means of elision (*luk*). What then? It is a locative absolute (*satsaptamī*): "when *luk* occurs. If it is a locative absolute, then this would apply. In that case, this [term] which ought to be mentioned here—the Teacher does not mention it. What is it? The word "of the subordinate member" (*upasarjanasya*) is understood [from the previous rule]. And a genus (*jāti*) is not a subordinate member.

(P_1.2.50) It should be stated that [the suffix] does not apply after *goṇī*. Indeed, it should be stated as "not after *goṇī*. There is no purpose for [marking the word with] the indicatory letter *it*. What is the formal derivation?
*pañcagoṇiḥ* ("five she-goats").

In the case of *daśagoṇiḥ*, shortness is indeed prescribed; for here, shortness is prescribed by the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya*. Whether it is stated as *iti* or as *na*, what difference is there here? It may have been done for the sake of brevity (*mātrārtha*). Or rather, this must be stated for the sake of brevity: [the rule] *gostriyor upasarjanasya* applies to both [masculine and feminine].

"This is merely the word *goṇī* [as in] *goṇīmātram*. Another says: "The substitution of *it* (short *i*) for *goṇī* occurs by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*). The substitution of *it* for *goṇī* need not be taught. What is the reason? Because of the context. Shortness (*hrasvatva*) is the subject under discussion; the term "short" (*hrasvaḥ*) is understood to carry over. But [does this apply to] *sūcī*? It applies for the sake of *sūcī* and others. Indeed, this should be understood as being for the sake of *sūcī* and so forth.

Regarding *pañcasūciḥ* and *daśasūciḥ*, it should be stated that [the rule] "not after *goṇī*" applies; for shortness (*hrasvatā*) is indeed prescribed. Or rather, if such a statement were made, it would be intended for the sake of the measure (*mātrārtha*).
The substitution of *it* for the final vowel of *goṇī* occurs by virtue of the context; or else, it is for the sake of [the formation of] *sūcī* and so forth.
(Pāṇini 1.2.51.1) What is the purpose of the expression "denoting an individual" (*vyaktivacana*)? [Consider: a village not far from *śirīṣa* trees is called *śirīṣāḥ*. Of that...

The village forest is a *śirīṣa* forest. Furthermore, what would happen? By the rule "optionally after names of herbs and trees" (*vibhāṣā oṣadhivanaspatibhyaḥ*), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* would undesirably apply. Another says:
a village not far from a *kaṭubadarī* is called *kaṭubadarī*; this is so that, through the application of the feminine form (*yuktavadbhāva*), the genitive case ending does not occur.

Now, even when it is stated that "the word *vacana* [means] 'individual' (*vyakti*)," why does [the rule] not apply here? For the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is also a *vacana*. This is not a reference to the technical term *vacana*; what then? It is a reference to the etymological meaning:

that which is spoken (*ucyate*) is called *vacana*. Even so, the genitive case still applies, for the genitive is also spoken of. This is because [the sense] has already been expressed by the elision (*lup*).

"There should be no employment of that second meaning, because 'that which has already expressed its meaning is not employed' (*uktārthānām aprayogaḥ*). In that case, it would follow by extension (*ātideśikī*). If this is so, then it is appropriate both before the formation of the compound and after the formation of the compound. To this extent, it is appropriate; furthermore, the speaker has freedom of choice regarding gender and number before the formation of the compound. Even before the formation of the compound, it is appropriate [to say], 'by the *vanaspati*s'."

The word *nagara* is both a compound (*vṛtta*) and something joined with trees (*vanaspati*). The status of being "joined" (*yuktavadbhāva*) is prescribed for it when it is a compound. Furthermore, there is freedom for the speaker as to whether he intends to extend the gender and number that existed prior to the formation of the compound, or those that belong to the compound itself. Since there is such freedom, it is the gender and number belonging to the compound itself that are extended, and not those that existed prior to the formation of the compound.

(P_1,2.51.2) For what purpose, then, is this stated? "In other cases, because the gender and number [of the derivative] do not follow those of the expressed meaning, there is the designation 'like that which is joined' (*yuktavad-anudeśa*) when *lup* occurs. In other cases, the gender and number are like those of the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*). Where else? In the case of *luk*.
"Lavaṇaḥ sūpaḥ" (salted soup),
"lavaṇā yavāgūḥ" (salted gruel),
"lavaṇam śākam" (salted vegetable)— in these cases, when there is elision (*luk*), the gender and number are like those of the expressed object (*abhidheya*). This also applies elsewhere.
The gender and number [of the elided word] would follow those of the thing denoted (*abhidheya*), whereas it is desired that they be like those of the designation (*abhidhāna*).
Since this cannot be established without an effort, there is the rule "the mention of what is joined with the elision" (*lupi yuktavad-anudeśaḥ*). This is stated for this purpose.
There is indeed a need for this; but what is it? Because elision (*lup*) is designated as non-appearance (*adarśana*), the comprehension of the meaning is not possible.

The term *lup* is applied as a designation for non-appearance (*adarśana*). However, it is not possible to extend (*atideṣṭum*) gender and number to non-appearance. Because *lup* is designated as non-appearance, the comprehension of meaning is not logically established. Alternatively, there is no such fault; for although non-appearance is impossible [to designate directly], the comprehension of meaning occurs through association (*sāhacaryāt*). Why? Because non-appearance is impossible [to designate].

Since the gender and number of "non-perception" (*adarśana*) cannot be extended [to other things], there will be an understanding of that object which is accompanied by non-perception, on account of their association (*sāhacarya*), and because no other [object] is connected [with it]. And since there is no connection with non-perception itself, there will be an understanding of that object which is accompanied by non-perception, on account of their association.

In a compound, there is the elision (*lup*) of the plural ending of the final member. In a compound, it must be stated that the final member undergoes the behavior of the corresponding singular form (*yuktavadbhāva*):
*madhurā-pañcālāḥ*. What is the purpose? For the sake of restriction: [the elision applies] only to the final member of a compound. Where should it not apply? As in *pañcāla-madhurāḥ*.
(P_1,2.52.1) KA_I,228.5-10 Ro_II, 102-103 How is this to be understood:
that the genus (*jāti*) is the qualifier, or rather that those which are qualifiers of the genus [are the qualifiers]? And what follows from this? If it is understood...

If it is established that a genus (*jāti*) is the qualifier, then while "The Pañcālas are a country" is established, "It is well-supplied with food, abundant in water, and rich in garlands and fruits" is not established. On the other hand, if it is understood that [the rule applies] to those qualifiers of a genus,
then while "It is well-supplied with food, abundant in water, and rich in garlands and fruits" is established, "The Pañcālas are a country" is not established.

103–104. Why, then, is this stated? The statement of qualifiers is for the purpose of excluding the genus (*jāti*). This undertaking is for the purpose of excluding the genus. Why is it said that it is "for the purpose of excluding the genus," and not rather so that the application of the suffix *yuk* (the feminine suffix *ī*) might also apply to the qualifiers? [It is already] established because they are in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Because the qualifiers are in coreferentiality, the application of the suffix *yuk* is established.

It will be so. If this is the case, there is no purpose served by this [rule]. Even elsewhere than in the case of *lup*, the treatment as having the same gender and number (*yuktavadbhāva*) does not apply to a genus (*jāti*).

Where else? As in: "The *badarī* tree has fine thorns and is sweet. But what is the reason that even elsewhere the treatment as having the same gender and number does not apply to a genus? Because a genus possesses fixed genders (*āviṣṭaliṅgā*), and it is by adopting whichever gender [it happens to have]...

It persists from its production until its destruction and does not abandon its gender (*liṅga*). If that is so, then this rule need not be stated now. Yet it must be stated. What is the purpose? It is stated here and there that for words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*), the gender and number are determined by the substrate (*āśraya*); that is what is being established by this [rule].

In the case of *harītakī* and similar words, there is the expression of the individual entity (*vyakti*). In the case of *harītakī* and similar words, the expression of the individual entity occurs through the application of the rule for "behaving like that which it is joined with" (*yuktavadbhāva*): [the fruit of] *harītakī* is called *harītakyaḥ phalāni*. In the case of *khalatika* and similar words, there is the expression [of the location]. In the case of *khalatika* and similar words, the expression occurs through the application of the rule for "behaving like that which it is joined with": [the forest near] *khalatika* is called *khalatikam*.

The forests situated near the Khalatika mountain are called "Khalatika-vanāni. There is a prohibition regarding the elision of the word "manuṣya" (man); a prohibition must be stated concerning the elision of "manuṣya":
for example, "Cañcā abhirūpaḥ" (handsome as a puppet) and "Vadhrikā darśanīyaḥ" (beautiful as a female weaver).
Is it because of the authority of these artificial technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as *ṭi*, *ghu*, and *bh* that [the rule] need not be taught? No, he says. A designation is a naming.

106–109. This is incorrect. What here is incorrect? There are many objects [denoted] there; in that case, the plural number is appropriate. Therefore, it is incorrect that when the singular number ought to be taught, the plural is taught instead. One should rather say, "the singular is used for the plural. To this, he recites the following reply:

When a genus is denoted, there is a single referent because a commonality is expressed. When a genus is denoted, there will be a single referent because a commonality is expressed. That which is the "rice-ness" in rice, the "barley-ness" in barley, and the "Gārgya-ness" in a descendant of Garga—that is one, and it is what is intended to be expressed. Because of its oneness, only the singular number would result. Yet, the plural number is desired [to occur].

Thus, since that [result] cannot be accomplished without effort, the plural number is used for a single entity when expressing a genus (*jāti*). This is stated for this very purpose. There is indeed a purpose for this. What, then, is it? In that regard, it was stated concerning the substitution of the singular number.
What was stated? That in the case of *vrīhibhya āgataḥ* ("come from the rice-grains"), the rule *gher ṅiti* would result in a *guṇa* [substitution]. This is not so.

There is a fault. [The rule] is established by the extension of meaning (*arthātideśa*). This is an extension of meaning; it is not a reference to the technical term (*paribhāṣika*) "vacana. What then? It is a reference according to the literal sense (*anvarthagrahaṇa*): that which is spoken is "speech" (*vacana*). Thus, "bahuvacana" means the speech of many things. This applies as long as one might say "one thing" (*ekaḥ arthaḥ*).

"It becomes plural" means that the plural number is used for a single entity. There is a prohibition when a numeral is employed. A prohibition must be stated regarding the employment of numerals: "A single grain of rice, when harvested, brings about an abundance of food. There is also a prohibition for the word *asmad* (I/we) when used with a name or with a suffix denoting youth (*yuva*). A prohibition must be stated for *asmad* when used with a name and when used with a suffix denoting youth. Regarding the use with a name:
"I, Devadatta, speak. "I, Yajñadatta, speak. When using a *yuvan* (patronymic) suffix:

"I, Gārgyāyaṇa, speak. "I, Vātsyāyana, speak. There is no need for the mention of the *yuvan* suffix; it is sufficient simply to say that [the substitution] does not occur when the name-suffix (*nāmapratyaya*) is used in conjunction with the pronoun *asmad*. By this, the following is also established: "I, Gārgya, speak. "I, Vātsya, speak. Another says:
When the pronoun *asmad* (we/I) is used with a qualifier, the singular alone [is employed]. This is also established:

"I, being clever, speak"; "I, being wise, speak. Alternatively, the plural form is not to be taught, because it expresses plurality. Or rather, the plural usage is not something to be prescribed as a rule. Why? Because it expresses plurality. For substances are indeed distinct.

They are denoted by many objects; therefore, the use of the plural is appropriate. Why is it said that "it is because of the denotation of distinctness," when it was just stated that "in the case of a name for a genus, there is a single referent due to the denotation of a commonality"? For it is by means of a genus-word (*jātiśabda*) that the substance is denoted. By means of a genus-word...

For indeed, both a substance (*dravya*) and a genus (*jāti*) are denoted [by a word]. But how is it known that a substance is also denoted by a genus-word? It is as follows: someone asks a cowherd sitting in a large herd of cows, "Do you see any cow here? and he sees [one].

He sees the cows and asks someone there, "Do you see a cow? [The other replies,] "Surely he intends to speak of a substance. Therefore, when there is a denotation of a substance, there will be the plural number; when there is a denotation of a universal, there will be the singular number.
(P_1,2.59) This rule, too, can be stated as unnecessary. How so? [In the case of the singular,] I say;
[in the case of the dual,] we two say.
We say this: these sense-faculties (*indriya*) are sometimes intended to be independent, as for example:
"This eye of mine sees well; this ear of mine hears well. Sometimes they are intended to be dependent:
"By means of this eye I see well; by means of this ear I hear well. That is when they are independent.

In that case, the plural number will occur when there is a desire to express [the stars] as independent entities; whereas the singular and dual numbers will occur when they are expressed as dependent. (Pāṇini 1.2.60) This rule, too, can be dispensed with. How so? [In the expression] "The two Phalgunīs have risen," [the dual is used because the stars are conceived as a single unit].

"The *pūrvā-phalgunyaḥ* have risen," "the *pūrve proṣṭhapade* have risen," or "the *pūrvāḥ proṣṭhapadāḥ* have risen. The word *phalgunī* is applied when the moon has reached the vicinity of the *phalgunī* constellation.

There are many meanings [denoted] by those two; therefore, the plural number is appropriate there. When, however, only those two are denoted, then the dual number will occur. (Pāṇini 1.2.61–62) These two rules could also be omitted. How? By the rule *supām sulukpūrvasavarṇa* [Pāṇini 7.1.39], the forms *punarvasū* and *viśākhau* are established. [The rule *supām sulukpūrvasavarṇa* applies to the case-endings (*sup*) of *punarvasu* and *viśākha*.]
Thus it is established. (Pāṇini 1.2.63) [Question:
For what purpose is the rule *tiṣyapunarvasvoḥ* [stated]? [Example: *kṛttikārohiṇyaḥ* ("Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī"). [Question:

For what purpose is the term *nakṣatra* [in the rule]? [Counter-example: *tiṣyaś ca māṇavakaḥ punarvasū māṇavakau tiṣyapunarvasavaḥ* ("Tiṣya the boy and the two Punarvasus the boys: Tiṣya-and-Punarvasu").

Now, while the term "constellation" (*nakṣatra*) is already understood from the context, for what purpose is "constellation" mentioned again? This word *tiṣyapunarvasu* exists as referring to the celestial bodies themselves, and it also exists as a designation of time. For example:
"Many *tiṣyapunarvasus* have passed; by which *tiṣya* did he go? That [usage] which refers to the celestial bodies...
This term "grahaṇa" (mention) applies to it. Alternatively, while the word "nakṣatre" (in the case of a lunar mansion) is already in effect, the purpose of mentioning "nakṣatra" again is this:

so that even when Tiṣya and Punarvasu are located in another region, their specific grammatical operation should apply only to them as lunar mansions. Thus, regarding the rule "the elision of *y* should be stated for the lunar mansions Tiṣya and Puṣya," the mention of "nakṣatra" need not be made [separately]. Or rather, while the word "nakṣatre" is in effect, the mention of "nakṣatra" again...

The purpose of this inclusion is so that it may also apply to those terms that are synonyms for Tiṣya and Punarvasu, such as *puṣya-punarvasū* and *siddhya-punarvasū*. Now, what is the purpose of the rule "in a dvandva compound"? [It is to ensure that] "that which is Tiṣya, those two are Punarvasu."

[The rule applies] to those for whom these [stars] Tiṣya and Punarvasu are [the names]. Why is the plural marker used? [Because the form] *tiṣyapunarvasū* is stated in the singular. How is there a singular here? Because a *dvandva* compound denoting a genus (*jāti*) becomes singular. [Objection: In that case, the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 2.4.6] "for non-living beings" (*aprāṇinām*) would apply. [Response:
Since the desired result is already established, the fact that the teacher includes the mention of the plural marker indicates the following:

"Every *dvandva* compound may optionally be treated as a singular. What is the purpose of this indication? [The forms] *bābhravaśālaṅkāyanam* and *bābhravaśālaṅkāyanāḥ* are thereby established. Alternatively, those venerable ones here are not living beings;
rather, it is their vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) that are venerable here.

114-116 What is the purpose of including the term *rūpa* ("form")? If it were stated merely as "there is a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of similar things when there is a single case-ending," it would apply only where everything is identical— both the word-form and the meaning— as in the case of *vṛkṣāḥ*.

Regarding the term *plakṣāḥ*: here [the rule] would not apply to *akṣāḥ*, *pādāḥ*, and *māṣāḥ*. However, when the mention of "form" (*rūpa*) is made, no fault arises; for the form itself is taken as the basis (*nimitta*).

And there is the mention of "form" (*rūpa*) in the *Śruti*. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "one" (*eka*)? If it were stated merely as "of those having the same form, there is elision (*śeṣa*) when there is a single case-ending," then elision would undesirably apply even to two or many [words]. However, when the mention of "one" is made, this fault does not occur. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "elision" (*śeṣa*)? If it were stated merely as "of those having the same form, one [remains] when there is a single case-ending"—

If this were stated [as a rule], this substitution would be understood [in that way]. What is the fault in that? In the case of *aśvaś ca aśvaś ca* = *aśvau*, because of proximity (*āntaryataḥ*), a substitute possessing two udātta accents would result for a base (*sthānin*) that possesses two udātta accents. Furthermore, the status of being "subject to elision" (*lopya*) or "having undergone elision" (*lopita*) would not be established. What is the fault in that? [In the formation of] *gargāḥ*, *vatsāḥ*, etc. [the desired forms would not be obtained].

*bidāḥ*, *urvāḥ*. If it is stated that "the suffix *añ* when it occurs in the plural" and "the suffix *yañ* when it occurs in the plural," then elision (*luk*) would not apply. Let it not be so. It will be understood as: "that which ends in *añ* when it occurs in the plural" and "that which ends in *yañ* when it occurs in the plural. This cannot be done; for in this case, there would be a fault. Thus: [text follows]

“Those who are images of Kāśyapa are called ‘Kāśyapas’. Why is it stated that “the case endings must be identical” (*ekavibhaktau*)? [Consider these examples: *payaḥ payaḥ jarayati* (“he digests milk after milk”), *vāsaḥ vāsaḥ chādayati* (“he covers garment after garment”), and *brāhmaṇābhyāṃ ca kṛtaṃ brāhmaṇābhyāṃ ca dehi* (“it was done by two Brahmins; give to those same two Brahmins”).

117–119. Why, then, is this stated? Because a word is applied to each respective object (*pratyartha*), there is no denotation of many by one. Words are applied (*abhiniviśante*) to each respective object. What does "to each respective object" mean? It means "with respect to each object" (*artham artham prati*). For this reason—that words are applied to each respective object—there is no denotation of many by a single word.

It follows that there would be the denotation of multiple meanings. What is the fault in that? In that case, when multiple meanings are denoted, there would be the status of having multiple words. When multiple meanings are denoted, it follows that there must be multiple words; yet, it is desired that there should be the denotation of multiple [meanings] even by a single [word]. And that is not accomplished without effort. Therefore, there must be *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one).
This is stated for this purpose; there is indeed a specific motive. What is it?

It is that, by relying on the example that "words adhere to each individual object," the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of words with identical forms is undertaken; whereas, by not relying on the example that "words do not adhere to each individual object," the *anekaśeṣa* (non-retention of one) of dissimilar forms is undertaken.
It is begun [here]. In this regard, it might be thought:

"The cessation of those of similar form is lighter, whereas the comprehension of those of dissimilar form is more burdensome. But that is not so; the comprehension of those of dissimilar form is lighter. What is the reason? For where one remains out of many of similar form, there—at the very least—[the comprehension is simpler].

In the case of two similar forms, the cessation [of one] would have to be stated. Even so, while this is the case, the Teacher considers something to be easier; indeed, he considers the formulation of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) to be the easier option.

119–133. Furthermore, does this *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) occur when there is a single case-ending? It ought to be so. If it is argued that it occurs "when there is a single case-ending," that is not correct. Why? Because of the absence of a case-ending. If it is argued that it occurs "when there is a single case-ending," that is not so. What is the reason? Because of the absence of a case-ending. For there is no case-ending following the entire aggregate [of stems]. Why? Because it is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadikatvāt*).

But surely, by the rule "that which possesses meaning is a nominal stem" (*arthavat prātipadikam*), the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika-sañjñā*) will apply. [Response: It does not apply because of a restrictive rule (*niyama*). For the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) in the rule regarding meaningful clusters is for the purpose of restriction. However, if it were instead stated that a single-remainder elision (*ekaśeṣa*) applies to all [stems] individually when followed by case-endings—[then one might ask: if it is said that they are all separate, would there not be the perception of separate case-endings in the case of *ekaśeṣa*?
Because it is based on that [the base]. If it is argued that "all [bases] are separate," then in the case of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), the occurrence of separate case-endings would follow.

Why is it said that "in *ekaśeṣa* there is the occurrence of separate case-endings," when the established rule (*samaya*) has been made that "neither the base alone nor the suffix alone should be used"? It follows [that separate endings occur] because it is based on that [base].
For where the cessation of the suffix is caused by the base, there the base is employed without a suffix,
as in *agnicit* and *somasut*. And where the cessation of the base is caused by the suffix, there the suffix is employed without a base, as in *adhunā*.

"It is this much," as for example. Let it be established by the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). But why indeed should there be the removal of the two subsequent instances of the word *vṛkṣa*, and not rather of the two preceding ones? In that regard, one might argue:

"Even if the preceding ones were removed, it would be established by the elision of the initial consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*). It is not so established. For in that case, at the very least...

The hearing of two *sakāra*s would result; furthermore, it would not be established in cases where there is no elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*). And where is there no elision of a final consonant cluster? In the dual and plural numbers. If, however, a single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*) were stated for the compound, what would be accomplished? A certain loss of number would be avoided. That [is the case].
In that case, the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) must be made. It need not be made; the previously stated [rule] continues to apply. Where was it previously stated? In the rule:

"In a dual compound of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra-dvandva*), the dual replaces the plural invariably. If it is argued that [the term "compound"] must be mentioned, there is a fault regarding accent (*svara*) and compound suffixes (*samāsānta*). If it is argued that "compound" must be mentioned, there is a fault regarding accent and compound suffixes. [Example of] accent: *tiṣya-punarvasū*.

*aśvaś ca aśvaś ca* becomes *aśvau*. Once the accentuation of the final member of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*) has been applied, the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) would apply. Here, this must be deliberated: "Should the accentuation of the final member of the compound be performed first, or the *ekaśeṣa*? What should be done here? Because it is subsequent in the order of rules, the accentuation of the final member of the compound takes effect. And when the accentuation of the final member of the compound has occurred, a fault arises regarding the accent (*svara*). [End of section on] the final member of a compound.

"Ṛk" and "ṛk" form "ṛcau. Once the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) has been applied, *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one of two identical words) does not apply because of the lack of similarity in form (*asārūpya*). This must be considered here: should the compound-final suffix be applied first, or should *ekaśeṣa* be applied? What should be done in this case? The compound-final suffix applies because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. And when the compound-final suffix is applied, a fault arises. Furthermore, the statement regarding *ekaśeṣa* depends upon the base (*aṅga*). Thus, *ekaśeṣa* must be stated as an operation that depends upon the base.

*Svasā* (sister), *svasārau*, and *svasāraḥ*. When the operation dependent on the stem (*aṅgāśraya*) has been applied, because of the lack of uniformity (*asārūpya*), the rule for "single-remainder" (*ekaśeṣa*) does not apply. This must be deliberated here: should the operation dependent on the stem be performed first, or the single-remainder? What should be done here? Because it is subsequent, the operation dependent on the stem [should be performed]. [This applies] in the case of a compound of finite verbs (*tiṅsamāsa*).

Regarding the statement "tiṅsamāsavacanam": in the context of *tiṅsamāsa*, the term *tiṅsamāsa* must be explicitly stated. [Objection: One mention of the word *tiṅ* is redundant; for it would be established by the rule itself, namely, "in a compound (*samāsa*), there is *tiṅsamāsa*. [Response: It is not redundant. Since the general topic is *tiṅsamāsa*, the specific *tiṅsamāsa* must be mentioned. Furthermore, there is both a prescription and a prohibition regarding *tiṅ*: some *tiṅ* forms are to be prescribed, while others are to be prohibited.
"He cooks and he cooks" becomes *pacataḥ*;

here the word ending in *-taḥ* is that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), while the word ending in *-ti* is that which is to be negated (*pratiṣedhya*). Furthermore, if it were stated that the single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*) occurs even in non-compounds (*asamāsa*), then [the rule] would require the statement:

"In the case of a non-compound, there is the elision of the suffix. If, in the case of a non-compound, the elision of the suffix must indeed be stated, then surely [this elision] occurs precisely at the moment of arising (*utpattau*).
We have been questioned. He will state the rule for the dual and plural numbers and the prohibition of the *dvandva* compound;
for that purpose, it is questioned again. Regarding the rule for the dual and plural: the dual and plural endings are to be prescribed:
"the tree and the tree" (*vṛkṣaś ca vṛkṣaś ca*) becomes "two trees" (*vṛkṣau*).
"Vṛkṣaś ca vṛkṣaś ca vṛkṣaś ca vṛkṣāḥ. There must also be a prohibition of the *dvandva* compound. A prohibition of the *dvandva* must be stated:
"vṛkṣaś ca vṛkṣaś ca vṛkṣau" and "vṛkṣaś ca vṛkṣaś ca vṛkṣaś ca vṛkṣāḥ," because the *dvandva* would otherwise apply by the rule "the *dvandva* [compound occurs] in the sense of 'ca' (and)."

This is not a fault. The *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) will have no scope and will be superseded by the *dvandva* (copulative compound). The *ekaśeṣa* does have its scope. What is that scope? Verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) are its scope. But if *ekaśeṣa* were stated to apply to all words ending in case-suffixes (*vibhaktyanta*) individually, what would be achieved? Some loss of expression (*vacanalopa*) would be avoided. [However, this applies only] to those ending in case-suffixes.

In the case of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), when there is *ekaśeṣa* of items ending in case-suffixes, it is indeed the items ending in case-suffixes that are eliminated. However, the phrase "of those ending in the same case-suffix" (*ekavibhaktyantānām*) is for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of *ekaśeṣa*] to those with different case-suffixes. It should be stated: "of those ending in the same case-suffix. What is the purpose? For the purpose of prohibiting [the application of *ekaśeṣa*] to those with different case-suffixes; let it not apply to those ending in different case-suffixes.

"Give to two Brahmins" and "Give by means of two Brahmins"—is there not a simultaneous expression [of both meanings] here? No, this is not a fault. Why? Because of a contradiction in meaning (*arthavipratiṣedha*). These two meanings—"agent" (*kartṛ*) and "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*)"—are contradictory; it is impossible to designate them simultaneously. Of these two...
Because they are mutually contradictory, there will be no simultaneous expression. Furthermore, *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) has multiple meanings as its basis.
*Ekaśeṣa* is commenced with the intention, "I shall cause multiple meanings to be understood. Therefore, there is not a single word [for each meaning];
consequently, there will be no single-word status. In that case, this is the fault:

There is a certain omission of number [in the rules], namely the rule for the dual and plural, and the prohibition of *dvandva* compounds. If, however, *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) were stated to apply to nominal stems (*prātipadika*), what would be accomplished? The omission of number would be avoided.
In the case of *ekaśeṣa* of nominal stems, there is a prohibition regarding *mātṛ* and *mātr̥* because they are of the same form. This is in the case of *ekaśeṣa* of nominal stems.
A prohibition regarding *mātṛ* and *mātṛ* must be stated:

[the forms] *mātā* (mother) and *janayitrī* (progenitress), as well as *mātārau* (two mothers) and *dhānyasya mātāraḥ* (those who measure grain). What is the reason? Because they are similar in form (*sarūpa*). For these nominal stems (*prātipadika*) are indeed similar in form. Why, then, is it said that there is a prohibition of *mātṛ* and *mātṛ* when there is a single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*) of nominal stems?

It must be stated [as a restriction]; for even by one who maintains that there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of words ending in case-suffixes (*vibhaktyanta*), a prohibition regarding "mother" and "measuring" (*mātṛ-mātroḥ*) would still have to be stated. For even according to him, these forms are sometimes identical in form when ending in case-suffixes, as in *mātṛbhyām ca mātṛbhyām ca*. Now, if it is thought that identity of form (*sārūpya*) must apply only to those [words] ending in case-suffixes...

Thus, by means of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), a fault arises specifically regarding the retention of one among nominal stems (*prātipadika*). And having established this, the following objection is raised:

"An addition must be made for the feminine forms of *harita*, *hariṇa*, *śyeta*, *śyena*, *rohita*, and *rohiṇa*. An addition must be made for the feminine forms of *harita*, *hariṇa*, *śyeta*, *śyena*, *rohita*, and *rohiṇa*. The feminine of *harita* is *hariṇī*; the feminine of *hariṇa* is also *hariṇī*."

*Hariṇa* and *hariṇī* form *hariṇyau*. The female of *śyeta* is *śyenī*, and the female of *śyena* is also *śyenī*; *śyenī* and *śyenī* form *śyenyau*. The female of *rohita* is *rohiṇī*, and the female of *rohiṇa* is also *rohiṇī*;
*rohiṇī* and *rohiṇī* form *rohiṇyau*. Or rather, this is not a fault, because [the feminine suffix] is applied to the meaning of the word-base (*pada*). Indeed, there is no such defect.

What is the reason? Because a word is employed in the sense [of its meaning]. A word is employed in the sense, and a word is that which ends in an inflection (*vibhakti*). Furthermore, it is the form (*rūpa*) that is relied upon here. And the apprehension of the form of a word does not occur without worldly usage (*laukika-prayoga*). And in that worldly usage, these [words] are of identical form. Another says:

Or rather, [this is not so] because a word is employed in the sense of its meaning. Nor indeed is this position tenable—that there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of nominal stems (*prātipadika*). What is the reason? Because a word is employed in the sense of its meaning, and a word is that which ends in an inflection (*vibhakti*). Furthermore, it is the form (*rūpa*) that is resorted to here, and the apprehension of the form of a word does not occur without worldly usage (*laukika-prayoga*).

And in that worldly usage, there is no employment of nominal stems (prātipadika). Now, if the purpose were served by this alternative—that there is a single-remainder (ekaśeṣa) of nominal stems—then certainly the purpose is served. But is this something that needs to be explicitly stated? No, it need not be. How is it understood even without being stated? It is already expressed by this very rule: "There is a single-remainder of similar forms when they occur in the same case-ending."

Thus [it is asked]: how? The case-ending (*vibhakti*) is relied upon by way of similarity of form (*sārūpya*). The *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is not conditioned [by the presence of a specific suffix]. The *ekaśeṣa* occurs for those items that have the same form when they appear with a single case-ending. Where? Anywhere at all. Now, if the purpose were served by this position—that the *ekaśeṣa* applies to words ending in case-endings—then certainly the purpose is served. But should this be explicitly stated? No, it need not be. Why?

Even that which is not explicitly stated will be understood. This too has been expressed by this very sūtra: *sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣa ekavibhaktau* ("of those having the same form, there is a single remainder when [they occur] in one case-ending").
How so? This is not a reference to the technical (paribhāṣika) case-ending (*vibhakti*). What then? It is a reference to the term according to its etymological meaning (*anvartha*):

"division" (*vibhāga*) is "case-ending" (*vibhakti*). Thus, it means: "when there is a single division, there is a single remainder for those things that have the same form. But was it not already said?

[Objection: There is a certain loss of number, namely the application of the dual and plural numbers and the prohibition of *dvandva* compounds. [Response: This is not a fault. As for what was said—that there is a certain loss of number and the application of the dual and plural—it is because *ekaśeṣa* occurs when there is a desire to express [the items] together (*sahavivakṣā*).
When there is a simultaneous desire to express them, there must be *ekaśeṣa*. [Question: In that case, this [following] does not occur now: [text missing].
"Tree and tree are two trees;
tree and tree and tree are [many] trees"—this does not occur when there is an intention to express them together. Furthermore, if one intends to demonstrate it, it should be demonstrated thus:
"two trees and two trees are [four] trees."

"Vṛkṣaḥ ca vṛkṣaḥ ca vṛkṣaḥ ca vṛkṣaḥ" [i.e., "tree and tree and tree and tree"]. As for what was said—that a prohibition of *dvandva* must be stated—this is not a fault. The *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) rule, having no other scope, will subvert the *dvandva*. But was it not said that the *ekaśeṣa* does have a scope? What is its scope? Verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) are its scope. No, verbal suffixes do not necessitate the formulation of *ekaśeṣa*.

What is the reason? *Ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) occurs for items of such a kind as have the capacity for the employment of a second word; however, finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) do not have the capacity for the employment of a second word. What is the reason? Because there is only one action (*kriyā*). Since that meaning has already been expressed by one [verb], there should be no employment of a second.

"There is no application of [suffixes] for meanings already expressed. If, then, a single action does not account for the dual and plural endings—as in *pacataḥ* ("they two cook") and *pacanti* ("they cook")—these do not depend upon the action. What, then? They depend upon the means (*sādhana*). Or alternatively:

"Let it be that [the rule] 'in the case of a single inflection' applies. But was it not said: "If it is argued that it applies when there is a single inflection, no, because of the absence of an inflection"? This is not a fault. This has already been resolved:
by the rule "that which possesses meaning is a nominal stem," the designation of *prātipadika* will apply. But was it not further said, on account of the restrictive rule (*niyama*)?

It does not follow that the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) for groups of words that possess meaning is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). This is not a fault, because the restriction applies to those of the same class (*tulyajātīya*). And what is of the same class? That which is of the same nature as compounds. Of what nature are compounds? They are of the nature of those ending in case-terminations (*subanta*).
An addition must be made in all cases regarding offspring and the like. An addition must be made for all alternative views concerning offspring and the like, as in:

"a collection of alms" (*bhikṣāṇām samūhaḥ* = *bhaikṣam*). It is said, "in all cases"; this is established even in the case of the single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of nominal stems. It is said, "regarding offspring and the like"; and there are many such categories as offspring and so forth.

The descendants of Garga are many: *gargāḥ*. There is one base (*prakṛti*) and many secondary suffixes (*yañ*). Because they are not identical in form (*asārūpyāt*), the rule of single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) does not apply. But surely, just as there are many suffixes, there could likewise be many bases? This cannot be maintained; for in that case, a fault would arise here: *gargāḥ*.

[Vatsas, Bidas, Urvās. Since it is stated that "the suffix *añ* when there are many [is elided], and the suffix *yañ* when there are many [is elided]," the elision (*luk*) would not apply here. Let it not be so. It will be understood as: "that which ends in *añ* when there are many, and that which ends in *yañ* when there are many."
But was it not said:

"It cannot be so; for in this case there would be a fault, namely that those who are images of Kāśyapa would [also] be Kāśyapas"? This is not a fault, because in that context the worldly lineage (gotra) is what is being referred to.

And this lineage is not worldly. Or rather, let there be one *prakṛti* and many *yañ* suffixes. But was it not said: "Because of dissimilarity (*asārūpyāt*), the retention of one (*ekaśeṣa*) does not apply"? [The answer is: It is established, however, because of the rule stating that for words having the same meaning, there is *ekaśeṣa*. This is established. How? It must be stated: "For words having the same meaning, there is *ekaśeṣa*. If they have the same meaning...

The rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is stated: how is it that [forms such as] *akṣāḥ*, *pādāḥ*, and *māṣāḥ* [are formed]? It must be stated that *ekaśeṣa* applies even to words of different meanings (*nānārtha*) that are identical in form (*sarūpa*). It must also be stated that *ekaśeṣa* applies even to words of the same meaning (*ekārtha*) that are dissimilar in form (*virūpa*).
It should be stated:

*vakradaṇḍa* and *kuṭiladaṇḍa*, or [the compound] *vakradaṇḍau kuṭiladaṇḍau*. For those words differentiated by accent (*svarabhinna*), that one whose rule for the subsequent accent applies should be stated as the single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*). That is to say, among words differentiated by accent, there should be a single remainder for that one whose rule regarding the subsequent accent applies.
*Akṣaś ca akṣaś ca akṣau* (the die and the die are two dice);
*mīmāṃsakaś ca mīmāṃsakaś ca mīmāṃsakau* (the Mīmāṃsaka and the Mīmāṃsaka are two Mīmāṃsakas).
Why does this not occur here:

*ekaś ca ekaś ca*, *dvau ca dvau ca*? Because the meaning of the number is not clearly understood and because it functions as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), there is no *anekaśeṣa* (retention of one from many).

Because the meaning of the number is not understood [in that way], the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) will not occur. For the meaning is not conveyed by the word "ekau" (two ones). Furthermore, because the number is the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*), the *ekaśeṣa* will not occur. The meaning of "ekaśca ekaśca" is "dvau" (two); the meaning of "dvau ca dvau ca" is "catvāraḥ" (four). These two [cases] do not apply here.

There are two rebuttals. First, as for what was said—that because the meaning of the number is not understood—[the objection is invalid], for even when the meaning is not understood, *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) occurs.
For example: *gārgyaś ca gārgyāyaṇaś ca gārgyau*. Although it is not explicitly stated that they are "an elder and a youth," *ekaśeṣa* nevertheless takes place. Furthermore, as for what was said:
"And because it refers to another word-meaning (anyapadārthatvāt). The *ekaśeṣa* [elision] also occurs when there is another word-meaning. For example:

*viṃśatiś ca viṃśatiś ca* [twenty and twenty] results in *viṃśatī* [two twenties]; the meaning is "forty" (*catvāriṃśat*) for those two. If this is so, then these are not two separate solutions. This is a single solution:
"because of the non-comprehension of the meaning of the number and because it refers to another word-meaning. For in a case where there is a non-comprehension of the meaning—
Or rather, there is either the status of being the meaning of another word (*anyapadārthatā*) or *ekaśeṣa* occurs there, as in "two Gārgyas" (*gārgyau viṃśatī*).

Alternatively, these are not words denoting *ekaśeṣa*. If, then, these are not words denoting *ekaśeṣa*, they are instead collective words (*samudāyaśabda*). What is the fault in that? The singular number would result, for collectives have a single referent. For example, "a herd" (*yūtham*).

"Śataṃ" and "vanam"—let them then be words subject to *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one). What produces their similarity? Their mutual production of similarity. But are there other words as well for which their state [of similarity] is produced by one another? He says: "There are."

"It is like [the words] 'mother,' 'father,' or 'brother'. This is an unequal comparison. Those words are applied once and continue to apply even when [one of the referents] has departed. Here, however, even with the departure of just one, the word "four" does not apply. Now, as for what you say—that these words are applied once and continue to apply even when [one of the referents] has departed—[that is true]; but as for what you [say] to us...
An objection is raised: "Are there not other words as well whose existence is mutually dependent?

To this, we have presented these [examples]. Regarding that, you have said: "These words, having been applied once, continue to function even when [the object] has passed away. But this is incorrect. For how could it be so in a case where not even a single person is able to lift the burden?
Would each one be the agent, or would all of them be so? How is this logically tenable?
If exertion is the cause, yet one does not exert oneself, then [the result] is the same as in its absence;
therefore, those agents are each distinct, but they are dependent upon one another.
There is a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of the first, middle, and last [persons] because they are of the same form. A single remainder of the first, middle, and last persons must be stated:
*pacati ca pacasi ca* results in *pacathaḥ*.
"Thou cookest and I cook" (*pacasi ca pacāmi ca*) becomes *pacāvaḥ*;

"he cooks, thou cookest, and I cook" (*pacati ca pacasi ca pacāmi ca*) becomes *pacāmaḥ*. But what is the reason that [the desired forms] are not established? Because they are not of the same form (*asarūpatvāt*).

140–144. Furthermore, there would be no establishment of the dual and plural numbers because there is only a single referent. There would be no establishment of the dual and plural numbers. What is the reason? Because there is only a single referent. Only this one remains; therefore, it must function for that purpose. For what purpose? For the purpose for which the one exists. And for what purpose does the one exist? The one has a single referent. It is not [the case that there are multiple referents].

"Identity of meaning. This is not a single meaning; rather, it is a dual meaning and a plural meaning. If you say, "It is not identity of meaning," then the formulation [of the rule] would be purposeless. If it is not identity of meaning, then the commencement of the *ekaśeṣa* (the rule for retaining one of identical forms) would be useless. For in this case, the multiplicity of meanings of a word must be either inherent (*svābhāvikī*) or stipulated by convention (*vācanikī*). Now, if it were inherent...

The *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is not subject to further rule (*aśiṣya*), because it has already been expressed by one [word]. The *ekaśeṣa* is not subject to rule. What is the reason? Because it has been expressed by one;

since that meaning has already been conveyed, there should be no employment of a second [word], according to the principle that "those whose meaning has already been expressed are not employed. Or rather, that must be stated as a formal injunction (*vācanikī*).

"This single [word] is undifferentiated, and it possesses both a dual meaning and a plural meaning"—this need not be stated. It is already established by the very rule "ekaśeṣa" (retention of one). But how, by the phrase "this single [word] is undifferentiated," can a dual or plural meaning be obtained? And that is accomplished by *ekaśeṣa*. For indeed, without a word expressive of that [meaning], [it could not be so].

The comprehension of that meaning occurs through the employment [of a word]. Furthermore, we observe that the comprehension of that meaning occurs even without the employment of a word expressive of it, as in the case of "Agnicit" (fire-piler) and "Somasut" (Soma-presser).
We consider this to be due to elision (lopa), by which the comprehension of that meaning occurs here even without the employment of a word expressive of it.
The meaning "it becomes the case" [is understood]. Thus, here too, this is accomplished by *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one), by which this single [word] remains;

through this, there occurs either a dual sense or a plural sense. If it were argued [otherwise], then the meaning would not be understood. For if one were to say "cow-horse" (*gām aśvaḥ*) or "horse-cow" (*aśvam gauḥ*), no comprehension would ever arise. Therefore, in the expression of multiple meanings, [the *ekaśeṣa* is necessary].
One who exerts effort must necessarily follow the world [in its usage], [inquiring]:

"In what matters do worldly people employ which words? And in the world, they employ the word *vṛkṣaḥ* (a tree) when there is one, *vṛkṣau* (two trees) when there are two, and *vṛkṣāḥ* (trees) when there are many. If, then, the world is necessarily the authority regarding words, for what purpose [is grammar]?

The rule for *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is being introduced. Now, for what purpose is elision (*lopa*) being introduced? The Teacher introduces elision while seeking the application of the term "characterized by an affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). However, once *ekaśeṣa* has been introduced, this [elision] serves no further purpose. But has it not been stated: "Because a word is applied to each individual meaning, there is no denotation of many by one"? And if, by means of a single word...

There would be the denotation of many objects, and the application of the word would not have been made for each individual object. If it is argued that because the word is applied to each object, and because many are denoted by one, it is therefore "not for each object" (*apratyartham*), even that is indeed "for each object. If it is argued that because the word is applied to each object, and because many are denoted by one, it is therefore "not for each object," this is what is being said:

Even when there is the expression of many by means of one, that too is indeed "per object" (*pratyartha*). For whether it is [an expression] directed toward each individual object (*artham artham prati*), or whether it is directed toward objects collectively (*arthān arthān prati*), that too is indeed "per object. The application of as many [words] as there are expressions is logical; for as many objects as there are, so many [expressions] come to be.

The position that there should be the employment of as many words as there are [meanings] is the logical one. If it is argued that the employment of as many words as there is denotation is logical, then even by a single word there is the denotation of many. If it is argued that the employment of as many words as there is denotation is logical, this is said in reply:

This too is indeed logical, since even by means of one [word], there can be the denotation of many. If, then, the denotation of many occurs by means of one—as in "plakṣanyagrodhau" (the *plakṣa* and the *nyagrodha*)—then because it has been expressed by one, the employment of the other is untenable. Since that meaning has been expressed by one, there should be no employment of another for that same meaning. Why? Because "that which has already expressed its meaning is not to be employed again. This is because it has already been expressed by one.

If it is argued that the employment of another word is untenable because [the meaning] has already been stated, we reply: no, because it has not been stated. Since the *plakṣa* tree does not denote the *nyagrodha*, the employment of the word *nyagrodha* is necessary.

If it is argued that the employment of another word is untenable because the meaning has already been expressed by one, we reply: since the meaning of the *nyagrodha* has not been expressed by the word *plakṣa*, the word *nyagrodha* is employed. How has it not been stated, when it was just now said that it has been stated by one?

There is also the expression of many by means of one. Even by a single [word], there is the expression of many that are similar in form (*sarūpa*), but not of those that are dissimilar in form (*virūpa*). What, then, is the reason that there is expression of many by a single [word] when they are similar in form, but not when they are dissimilar in form? Expression, moreover, is natural (*svābhāvika*). Expression is natural, because both cases are observed.
Indeed, both cases are observed:
there is the designation of many by means of one, even when they are dissimilar. For example:
*dyavā ha kṣamā*; *dyavā cit asmai pṛthivī namete*. If the designation of many by means of one can indeed occur even for dissimilar things, how much more so for those that are similar?

Or, because it denotes the form (*ākṛti*), Vājapyāyana considers it logical that there is only one [word] in the case of an inflection (*vibhakti*). The teacher Vājapyāyana considers it logical that there is only one word denoting the form in the case of an inflection;
namely, that the form is one and it is that which is denoted. But how is it known that the form is one and that it is that which is denoted?

Thus, because of the lack of distinction in cognition. For when "cow" is said, no specific distinction is cognized, such as whether it is white, blue, tawny, or pigeon-colored. Even if, for the sake of argument, it is known from the lack of distinction in cognition that there is a single form (ākṛti), on what basis is it understood that this [form] is what is denoted?
And because of the non-separation [of the form from the individual]. Because of the non-separation, we consider that the form is what is denoted.

Thus it is said. For when "cow" is uttered, a specific distinction is not understood—whether it be white, black, tawny, or pigeon-colored. Yet that which is taught once is indeed known; indeed, that which is taught once is certainly known. Suppose a cow has been taught to someone at some time;
having seen it in another place, at another time, and in another stage of life, he recognizes it: "This is that."

"An ox. But what is its specific distinction? It is from the "distinction in cognition" (prakhyāviśeṣa). This [statement] serves as a corroboration of that very point: it is known from the distinction in cognition that [the word] is taught as a single unit. And the Dharmaśāstra is likewise. Having established this, the Dharmaśāstra proceeds:
"A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," "Liquor must not be drunk. It is not merely any Brāhmaṇa who is not killed, nor merely any liquor that is not drunk.

And [the rule] "nor does one drink" [would be meaningless]. If the word-meaning were a substance (*dravya*), then by not killing a single Brāhmaṇa and not drinking a single draught of *surā* liquor, there would be freedom of action (*kāmacāra*) elsewhere. What, then, is the distinction here? It is because [the result] does not proceed until completion (*avyapavargagati*).
Therefore, this [statement regarding the non-completion of the act] serves as a corroboration (*upodbalaka*) of that very point.
And because there is no cessation [of the perception], so it is with the treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*). Furthermore, there is one thing that exists simultaneously in multiple locations.
Indeed, there is one thing perceived simultaneously in multiple locations. What is it? The sun.
For example, the single sun is perceived simultaneously as being situated in multiple locations. [Objection: This is an unequal comparison.

A single observer does not simultaneously perceive the sun as residing in multiple locations. If that is so, then the object [of perception] is like Indra. Just as a single Indra, when summoned at a hundred sacrifices, is present everywhere simultaneously, so too will the generic form (*ākṛti*) be present everywhere simultaneously. And this must necessarily be understood in this way: [the universal] is one.

"It is perceived simultaneously as residing in multiple substrata. If it is argued that "one [entity] cannot reside in multiple substrata simultaneously," then the same fault would apply to the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one). For whoever thinks that "one [word] is not perceived simultaneously as residing in multiple substrata" would incur this defect regarding *ekaśeṣa*. Even in the case of *ekaśeṣa*, the single word "tree" does not denote multiple objects simultaneously.

It must necessarily be understood in this way: that it is the *ākṛti* (form) which is denoted. For if the substance (*dravya*) were denoted, there would be no cognition of the form. If the substance were denoted, there would be no cognition of the form. What is the fault in that? In that case, there would be no comprehension of all substances. In that case, the non-comprehension of all substances would follow. Regarding this non-comprehension of all substances...

What is the fault? [The injunctions] "A cow is to be sacrificed" and "A goat is for Agni-Soma"—one person would perform what is prescribed by the scripture, while another would perform what is not prescribed by the scripture. And when that which is not prescribed by the scripture is performed, the ritual action becomes deficient in its qualities (*viguṇa*). When the ritual action is deficient, there is no attainment of the fruit. But surely, even for one for whom the *ākṛti* (form) is the meaning of the word...

Furthermore, if it is objected that [the action] is performed without its constituent parts and yet is not subsequently connected [to the result], the ritual act becomes deficient (*viguṇa*). When a ritual act is deficient, the fruit is not obtained. Moreover, the thesis that "there is a single form" (*ekākṛti*) would be abandoned. Furthermore, the purpose for adopting this position—that "one need not state the *ekaśeṣa* [rule]"—must now be stated. Thus...

In that case, it is enjoined without parts and is completed in each individual instance, just as with the sun. But surely, for one for whom the word-meaning is a substance (*dravya*), it too is enjoined without parts and is completed in each individual instance.
However, you must explain the phenomenon of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one). In that case, you too must establish the dual and plural endings when there is an injunction.

And because there is an application of a single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) [to multiple individuals], and because there is an injunction regarding a single application of a limiting adjunct, we consider that the *ākṛti* (form/genus) is what is denoted. For instance, in the injunction "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni" (*āgneyam aṣṭākapālam nirvapet*), after one has been offered, a second and a third are also offered. And if the individual substance (*dravya*) were the meaning of the word, then [only] one...

Having performed the offering for the first, the offering for the second and the third would not be possible. What, then, is the distinction between these two injunctions of genus (*jāti*)? One is by means of that which has been accomplished (*nirvṛtta*), while the other is by means of that which is to be accomplished (*nirvartya*).

150–152. Vyāḍi maintains that the word denotes the substance (*dravyābhidhāna*). The teacher Vyāḍi considers it logical that the word denotes the substance; thus, "the substance is denoted. And in this way, the establishment of gender and number is achieved. By adopting this view, gender and number become established: *brāhmaṇī*, *brāhmaṇaḥ*.

"Two Brahmins," "Brahmins"—because it is initiated in the injunctions. Because it is initiated in the injunctions, we consider that the substance is denoted [by the word]. For instance, in the cases "The cow is to be bound," "The goat is for Agni-Soma":
when the generic form (*ākṛti*) is enjoined, actions such as touching, seizing, sprinkling, and immolation are performed upon the substance. And yet, it is not one [of these two].
[If it were so,] it would exist simultaneously in many locations. Indeed, a single thing is never perceived as existing simultaneously in many locations;

for a single Devadatta cannot be in Srughna and Mathurā at the same time. In that case, everything would be subject to both destruction and manifestation simultaneously. What [would happen]? It would both perish and come into being. [For example,] when one says "the dog is dead," it is still called a "dog."
It would not function in common usage; for if [the rule] were "gauḥ jātaḥ," everything that has become a cow would be [denoted by] *gobhūta*, leaving no room for distinction.
Furthermore, there is indeed a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*);

for there is indeed a lack of uniformity in such cases as "gauś ca gauś ca khaṇḍo muṇḍaḥ" (both a cow and a cow, the spotted one and the hornless one). And thus the analysis (*vigraha*) is possible. By doing it this way, the analysis becomes logically established.

153–159. The establishment of gender and number [is possible] because quality is non-eternal. Gender and numbers are established. Why? Because quality is non-eternal. Qualities are non-eternal; they come and go. Are these [qualities] the white and so forth? No, he says. Feminine, masculine, and neuter are qualities of *sattva*, as are singularity, duality, and plurality. At times...

The generic form (*ākṛti*) is sometimes associated with singularity, sometimes with duality, sometimes with plurality; sometimes with femininity, sometimes with masculinity, and sometimes with neuter gender. While the abandonment of gender might be tenable, the abandonment of number is not tenable. For if the generic form were sometimes associated with singularity and sometimes with duality...

If there were a plurality [of universals], the thesis that "the form (ākṛti) is one" would be abandoned. Furthermore, the purpose stated for adopting this position—that "the *ekaśeṣa* need not be mentioned"—would now have to be mentioned. If that is so, then the establishment of gender and number follows from the non-constancy of the intention to express qualities (*guṇavivakṣā*). Thus, genders and numbers become established. Why? Because the intention to express qualities is non-constant.
The intention regarding gender is non-eternal. Sometimes the form (*ākṛti*) is intended to be expressed as singular, sometimes as dual, sometimes as plural;

sometimes as feminine, sometimes as masculine, and sometimes as neuter. While the avoidance of gender might be tenable, the avoidance of number (*vacana*) is not tenable. If [you argue] that sometimes...

The generic form (*ākṛti*) is intended to be expressed sometimes in the singular, sometimes in the dual, and sometimes in the plural; thus, the thesis that "the generic form is one" would be abandoned. Furthermore, the purpose stated for adopting this position—that the rule of *ekaśeṣa* need not be taught—would now have to be taught after all. Moreover, the avoidance of gender distinctions is also untenable. What is the reason?

The gender-inherent-in-the-universal (*āviṣṭaliṅgā jātiḥ*) is that which, having adopted a particular gender, does not abandon that gender from its origin until its destruction. Therefore, it is not possible for grammarians to rely upon worldly gender. Some established doctrine (*svakṛtānta*) must necessarily be adopted. What is this established doctrine? Contraction (*saṃstyāna*) and procreation (*prasava*) are the genders. Contraction and procreation...

The gender [of words] must be accepted. What is this that is called "contraction" (*saṃstyāna*) and "procreation" (*prasava*)? From the root *styai* with the suffix *ḍraṭ*, we derive *strī* in the sense of contraction; from the root *sū* with the prefix *sap*, we derive *pumān* in the sense of procreation. But is it not the case in common usage (*loka*) as well that a woman is derived from *styai* and a man from *sū*? In common usage, the word for "woman" (*strī*) functions as a locus (*adhikaraṇasādhana*): "the embryo is conceived in her" (*styāyaty asyām garbhaḥ*). And the word for "man" (*pumān*) functions as an agent (*kartṛsādhana*): [he is one who procreates].
"A male procreates. Here, however, both [terms] function as abstract nouns (*bhāvasādhana*):
*styāna* (concretion) and *pravṛtti* (activity). Of what, then, is there concretion? A woman; or of what is there activity? A man. [They belong to] the qualities (*guṇa*).
Which qualities? Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Furthermore, all material forms (*mūrti*) are of this nature, characterized by the qualities of concretion and production.
They possess sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Wherever there are fewer qualities, there are at least three:
sound, touch, and form. Taste and smell are not present everywhere. Furthermore, activity is indeed constant;
for here no one remains still within their own self even for a moment, as long as they continue to grow by means of it.

[The term *vardhamāna*] ought to be connected with either increase (*vṛddhi*) or decrease (*apacaya*). And both of these [states] exist everywhere. If both exist everywhere, how is there a fixed determination? It is due to the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). When there is an intention to express contraction, it is feminine; when there is an intention to express production, it is masculine; and when there is no intention to express either, it is neuter. In that case, the establishment of gender and number results from the non-constancy of the intention to express qualities (*guṇa*); thus is the objection regarding gender refuted.
[The objection] is established; however, the verbal resolution is not established. And yet, the verbal resolution is indeed established.
First, he should be asked this:
"Now, for one for whom a substance (*dravya*) is the word-meaning (*padārtha*), how do the singular, dual, and plural number endings come to be? To this, he will reply:

"Singular for one, dual for two, and plural for many"—if even these were merely conventional and not inherent, I too would say: "Singular for one, dual for two, and plural for many. For it is not the case that for one who holds the *ākṛti* (form) to be the referent of a word, the *dravya* (substance) is not the referent; nor is it the case that for one who holds the *dravya* to be the referent, the *ākṛti* is not the referent. Both [referents] belong to both [theories].

Regarding the meaning of a word (*padārtha*), for some, one thing is primary and another is secondary. For one who holds that the form (*ākṛti*) is the word-meaning, the form is primary and the substance (*dravya*) is secondary. For one who holds that the substance is the word-meaning, the substance is primary and the form is secondary. Or, it will be like words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*); that is, the gender and number will be like those of words expressing qualities.
For example, the gender and number of words expressing qualities depend upon their substratum:
*śuklaṃ vastram* (a white cloth),
*śuklā śāṭī* (a white garment), *śuklaḥ kambalaḥ* (a white woolen blanket).

"Two white blankets," "white blankets"—whatever gender and number belong to that substance upon which a quality rests, those same belong to the quality as well. Likewise here too, whatever gender and number belong to that substance upon which the generic form (ākṛti) rests, those shall belong to the generic form as well. This is a case of reaching the substratum through association.

Since the commencement and other [processes] cannot possibly exist in the generic form (*ākṛti*), it follows that the commencement and so forth must occur in the substance (*dravya*) that accompanies the generic form. Furthermore, it is not the case that a single entity can simultaneously occupy multiple locations; thus, the object is like the sun. Indeed, a single entity is never perceived as occupying multiple locations at once, as is the case with the sun.

It will be the object [of cognition]. For example, a single sun is perceived simultaneously as being situated in many locations. This is an unequal comparison. A single observer does not perceive a single sun as being situated in multiple locations simultaneously. In that case, the object is like Indra; for example, a single Indra is invoked in a hundred sacrifices at once.
Just as this form exists simultaneously everywhere, so too it will exist simultaneously everywhere. It is indestructible because it is non-dependent.
Even upon the destruction of the substance, there is no destruction of the form. Why? Because it is non-dependent. The form does not depend on the substance.
As for what was said just now—that its existence in a locus is due to concomitance—why is it said that it is "non-dependent"? [Because it is not dependent on the substance.]

If that is the case, then there is no destruction [of the configuration], because they are not identical. When the substance is destroyed, the configuration is not destroyed. Why? Because they are not identical. The nature of the configuration and the substance is manifold. For example, a creeper situated on a tree is not destroyed even when the tree is cut down. Deformity and disintegration also result from the difference in substances. Deformity and disintegration likewise arise from the difference in substances.

[The forms] will come into being. And [the derivation] is established through commonality even for words with different meanings; everything is established through commonality even among things that have distinct referents.

From the root *aś* (to pervade) comes *akṣa*; from *pad* (to go) comes *pāda*; from *mā* (to measure) comes *māṣa*. In those cases, it is established through the commonality of action. But another says: in a former age this was so—that sixteen *māṣas* made one *kārṣāpaṇa*, and the *māṣa-śambaṭyas* had sixteen fruits.
In that case, it is established by virtue of the commonality of number. (Pāṇini 1.2.65) Why does [the rule] not apply here? [Example: *iha* (here).

"A goat and a kid," "a horse and a foal," "a camel and a young camel"— if it is argued that the distinction here consists solely in those characteristics, yet in this case the distinction does not consist solely in those characteristics; for a distinction consists solely in those characteristics when [the objects] are otherwise identical...
There is a difference in words regarding form. (P.
1.2.66.1) This is considered in all instances where the term "feminine" (*strī*) is employed: [Is it based on gender or on form?]

In the mention of the word *strī* (female), there might be the mention of the feminine suffix (*strī-pratyaya*), or the mention of the feminine meaning (*stry-artha*), or the mention of the word *strī* itself. And what follows from this? If it were the mention of the suffix or the mention of the word, then in the case of *gārgī* and *gārgyāyaṇau* [forming] *gargāḥ*, by what rule would the suffix *ya* not be heard? For it is stated that the elision (*luk*) occurs "when not denoting a female" (*astriyām*). And here, in the case of *gārgī* and *gārgyāyaṇau* [forming] *gargān paśya* ("see the Gargas"), [the same difficulty arises].

Therefore, the substitution of *n* for *śas* in the masculine does not apply [to the word *go*]. Now, if the term "meaning" (*artha*) is included, there is no fault. Let it be so that there is no fault.
Why, then, does it not occur here?

"A ewe and a ram," "a mare and a foal," "a female camel and a colt"— if it is argued that the distinction [between these] is based solely on their defining characteristics (*tallakṣaṇa*), it is not the case here that the distinction is based solely on their defining characteristics. That the distinction is based solely on their defining characteristics is when [the individuals] are of the same...
There is a difference of words regarding the form (*ākṛti*). (Pāṇini 1.2.64) Why does this [rule] not apply here? [KA_I,248.8-10; Ro_II, 162]

"The swan and the female swan, the tortoise and the female tortoise, the male deer and the female deer"—if it is argued that the distinction here consists precisely in those characteristics, we reply: no, for in this case the distinction does not consist merely in those characteristics. That the distinction consists merely in those characteristics is when there is a difference of words despite the identity of the general form (*ākṛti*).

(P_1,2.68.1) Why is this stated? Is it not already established by the rule *pumān striyā*? It is not so established. This is said because the distinction must be based on that specific characteristic (*tallakṣaṇa*). However, in this case, the distinction is not based solely on that characteristic; rather, it is indeed based on that characteristic alone.

The distinction is that there is a difference in words despite the identity of the form (*ākṛti*). If this is so, then since [the formation of the dual] is already established, the fact that the Teacher teaches this specific rule (*yoga*) indicates the following: "Where a distinction characterized by the base itself occurs after the base, there *ekaśeṣa* takes place. What is the purpose of this indication? For example, *haṃsaś ca varaṭā ca*.

In the case of *kacchapaśca ḍulī ca*, *ṛśyaśca rohitaśca*, there is no application of the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) rule. In the two preceding rules (*yogau*), there is a more extensive exception (*parihāra*). As far as one might say "the lineage (*gotra*) with the youth," so far [does the rule apply] "the elder (*vṛddha*) with the youth. In the previous sūtra, it was the lineage that was [qualified] by the elder.
Thus the designation is made.
(Pāṇini 1.2.68.2) Because, among dissimilar [forms]— such as young and old, female and male— the distinction is not intended to be expressed, and only the general [form] is intended.

It is established because of the intended meaning (*vivakṣitatvāt*). For "unlike" (*asarūpa*) young and old, female and male, the distinction is not intended to be expressed, while the commonality (*sāmānya*) is intended to be expressed.
