Since the distinction is not intended and the commonality is intended, the rule "of like forms there is a single remainder when a single case-ending follows" (*sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣa ekavibhaktau*) is indeed established. Why does the rule "the masculine [remains] in place of the feminine" (*pumān striyā*) not apply here?

In the case of *brāhmaṇavatsā* and *brāhmaṇīvatsaḥ*, because the gender (*liṅga*) following the case-ending (*vibhakti*) expresses a specific distinction, there will be no *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one). Since the gender following the case-ending in *brāhmaṇavatsā* and *brāhmaṇīvatsaḥ* expresses a specific distinction, *ekaśeṣa* will not occur. This is where the gender alone, following the case-ending, expresses a specific distinction.

In that case, there is the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*). Here, gender is not the only indicator of distinction when it follows a case-ending. If, then, *ekaśeṣa* occurs only where gender is the sole indicator of distinction following a case-ending, then it would not apply here:
*kārakaś ca kārikā ca kārakau*. For in this instance, gender is not the only indicator of distinction following a case-ending. How, then, is this to be understood?

Is the distinction [intended] that the word itself must be characterized as feminine, or rather that the meaning itself must be characterized as feminine? What follows from this? If it is understood that the distinction is that the word itself must be characterized as feminine, then *kārakaḥ* (masculine) and *kārikā* (feminine) would both be established as *kārakau* (dual neuter). However, this [following case] would not be established: [the dual form *kārakau*].

*gomān* and *gomatī* become *gomantau*. Now, if it is understood that the meaning is such that this distinction applies only when the feminine is characterized by that [masculine] quality, then *gomān* and *gomatī* are established as *gomantau*. However, this is not established: *kārakaḥ* and *kārikā* do not become *kārakau*; likewise, even in both cases, *paṭuḥ* and *paṭvī* do not become *paṭū*.
It is established. If that is so, then it is not understood that the word [itself] is the distinction characterized by whatever woman [is meant];

nor is it understood that the meaning [itself] is the distinction characterized by whatever woman [is meant]. How then? Both the word and the meaning are taken as the basis for the distinction characterized by the existence of whatever woman [is meant]. And having done so, the application [of the rule] occurs here as well.

[The examples would be] *brāhmaṇavatsā* and *brāhmaṇīvatsaḥ*. If that is so, then although this [distinction] ought to be specified here, the Teacher does not specify it. What [is left unsaid]? The word *tat* (that) is understood to follow. By this word *tat*, both the feminine and masculine forms in the base state (*prakṛti*) are referred to. And what are the two bases? The primary ones: the primary one which is a feminine word-form, and the primary one which is a feminine meaning.

(P_1,2.69) This application (*yoga*) cannot be stated [as a fault]. How so? "The blanket is white and the cloth is white; this here is white; these two are white. [In such cases, the rule would apply.]
"A white blanket, a white upper garment, and a white cloth—this is 'white' (śuklam);

these are 'whites' (śuklāni). Because the grammatical operation applies to the principal element, the remainder [is understood]. Since the grammatical operation applies to the principal element, the remainder will be established. And what is the principal element? It is the neuter. But how is it known that it is neuter?
Regarding the term "pradhāna": for it is observed thus in the world;
when an object is not yet identified and there is doubt as to its qualities, the neuter gender is employed. One asks, "What has been born?
and indeed, only two things are born: either a female or a male. Likewise, having seen something indistinct and formless at a distance...

People say, "It is like the form of a buffalo," or "It is like the form of a Brahmin woman. Because the understanding of the effect resides in the primary [referent], the neuter gender will remain as the residue. Now, this is the purpose:
I shall state that "it may optionally be treated as a singular. Even this is not a purpose, because [the word] denotes a generic form (*ākṛti*).

The singular number [is used]. Because it denotes the form (ākṛti), the singular number will occur. When there is the denotation of the substance (dravya), then the dual and plural numbers will occur.

Why is this stated? Is it not already established by the rule *na pumān striyā* ("the masculine is not [used] with the feminine")? [It is stated] for the sake of the brother, son, father, and father-in-law (*bhrātṛ-putra-pitṛ-śvaśura*).

The application of the term [to denote] a substance occurs because of a causal factor. The application of the term to a substance occurs because of the causal factors of brother, son, father, and father-in-law. If it is argued that the application of the term to a substance is due to these causal factors, it is established by virtue of having the same causal basis. For if one sustains, he is a "brother" (bhrātṛ), and this [term] applies to a sister as well. Likewise, if he purifies...

One is called a "son" (*putra*) because he "pleases" (*prīṇāti*); this [etymology] applies to a daughter as well. Likewise, if one protects (*pāti*) or guards (*pālayati*), one is called a "father" (*pitā*);

this applies to a mother as well. Similarly, if one is to be quickly reached (*āśu āptavyaḥ*), one is called a "father-in-law" (*śvaśura*); this applies to a mother-in-law as well. Indeed, the basis is direct observation (*darśana*). For the word "brother" (*bhrātṛ*) is not observed to apply to a sister; thus, direct observation is the basis.

If this is argued, it is the same. If it is argued that "observation is the cause," this is equally applicable: let the word *bhrātṛ* (brother) be observed to apply to a sister as well, for the reason is the same. But indeed, such a conventional understanding does not exist in the world; for when it is said in common usage, "Let the brother be brought," a sister is not brought. And it must be understood that this [usage] has that specific scope.

“Sisterhood” [is used] for a brother. With reference to what? With reference to the domain of *ekaśeṣa* (the grammatical retention of one of two identical words). But it is logical that words should have restricted domains. Certainly, it is logical, because such domains are observed elsewhere as well. Indeed, words with such domains are seen elsewhere too. For example:

When the color red is the same, one says "the cow is red" (*lohita*) and "the horse is crimson" (*śoṇa*). When the color black is the same, one says "the cow is black" (*kṛṣṇa*) and "the horse is bay" (*hema*). And when the color white is the same, one says "the cow is white" (*śveta*) and "the horse is dappled white" (*karka*).

169–170. *Tyadāditaḥ śeṣe puṃnapuṃsakataḥ liṅgavacanāni*. After [words] beginning with *tyad* (demonstrative pronouns), when there is a remainder [in a compound], the gender and number are those of the masculine or neuter. For example: *sā ca devadattaś ca tau* ("she and Devadatta—those two"), and *sā ca kuṇḍe ca tāni* ("she and the two bowls—those"). It should be stated: "Except for dvandva compounds, tatpuruṣa compounds, and qualifiers. This is so that it does not apply here: *sa ca kukkuṭaḥ sā ca...* ("he who is a cock and she who is...").

*mayūrī* and *kukkuṭamayūryau*—these two; *ardhaṃ pippalyāḥ* and *tad ardhapippalī ca sā*—this is *ardhapippalī*; *ardhapippalyau*—these two. (P_1.2.72.2) This rule (*yoga*) as well can be omitted. How so? Because the pronouns beginning with *tyad* have a general sense. [This applies to] the pronouns beginning with *tyad*.

The referent (*artha*) is the commonality (*sāmānya*), and therefore it is the commonality. For this [commonality] exists in Devadatta as well as in Yajñadatta. Since pronouns such as *tyad* and so on possess the sense of commonality, the remainder (*śeṣa*) will apply. However, this is for the purpose of stating that the remainder applies to the subsequent [word]. And because the subsequent [pronoun] denotes both; the subsequent [pronoun] denotes both. Furthermore, because the remainder of the preceding [word] is observed. Indeed, the remainder of the preceding [word] is also observed:
"Bring both him and whoever [it may be]," or "Bring those two who [were mentioned]. In that case, this is the purpose:
so that a *dvandva* compound does not occur. But even this is not a valid purpose, because there is no *dvandva* compound between words expressing a general term and its specific instance.

Success! It should be stated that a *dvandva* compound does not occur between words expressing a general term and its specific instance (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*). If it is said that a *dvandva* does not occur between words expressing a general term and its specific instance, [examples such as] *śūdrābhīram* and *gobalīvardam* [would be problematic].

The form *tṛṇolapam* is not established [as a valid compound]. This is not a fault. First, regarding *śūdrābhīram*: the Ābhīras are a distinct caste. Regarding *gobalīvardam*: "cows" refers to those from which the males have been removed for the purpose of being yoked or sold; thus, only females remain. As for *tṛṇolapam*: [it would likewise not be established].

"Apām ulapam" is a name. If so, then it ought to be stated. It need not be stated; because it has been stated in a general sense, there will be no application of the specific term. Since that meaning has already been expressed generally, there should be no application of the specific term. What is the reason? Because "that which has already expressed its meaning is not to be applied again. If that is so, then this [following] case does not occur: [text missing].

"Bring that Brāhmaṇa, Gārgya. Since it is by rule that only he is brought, [it follows that] if this is so, then for the very same reason that this sentence "Bring that Brāhmaṇa, Gārgya" occurs, the compound (vṛtti) would also result. Therefore, there is no dvandva compound of two words expressing a general term and a specific term.
"It exists" should be stated. (Pāṇini 1.2.73) This rule (*yoga*) as well can be omitted. How so? [In the case of] "these cows are grazing," [the action is understood].
These goats are wandering about—cows from which the males have been removed—for the purpose of being yoked or sold; only females remain. This, then, is the purpose:
I shall say "among domestic animals," so that it does not apply here:
"these are *nyaṅkavaḥ*."

"These are pigs. But who would dare to drive away men from the countryside who cannot even be captured? How much less so for the purpose of yoking them as draft animals or selling them? "In that case," he thought, "I shall state this purpose regarding livestock. Let it not be applied here: "These are Brahmins."
"These are low-caste men (vṛṣala). Furthermore, who would be entitled to drive away those males that are not cattle—those which are incapable of being used as draft animals or for sale?

This, then, is the purpose: [to ensure] that I shall say 'in groups' (saṅgheṣu). Let it not be the case here: 'These two cows are grazing. Furthermore, who would be entitled to employ a word otherwise when the meaning is already well-known? This, then, is the purpose:"
I shall say "among those that are not young. Let it not apply here:

*uraṇakā ime*, *barkarā ime*. But who would dare to drive away young males that are incapable of being used for transport or sale? It should be stated "among animals with uncloven hoofs," so that it does not apply here.
"Horses move; donkeys move.

(Pāṇini 1.3.1) From where does this letter *va* come? If the instruction is given in *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination), it should be "bhv-ādayaḥ"; if, however, it is not in *saṃhitā*, it should be "bhū-ādayaḥ."
To this, he recites the following reply:

"This letter *va* is employed at the beginning of the *bhūvādi* class for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). The teacher, being auspicious-minded, employs the augment *va* for the sake of auspiciousness for this great flood of treatises. [For it is said: 'Those works which have auspicious beginnings, auspicious middles, and auspicious ends..."

For indeed, treatises become renowned and possess heroic persons as well as long-lived persons, so that the students may achieve their purpose. Now, what is the purpose of including the word "beginning" (*ādi*)? If they are already recited [in the text], there is no need for the inclusion of "beginning. For even elsewhere, this reciter does not employ the inclusion of "beginning. Where else?

Regarding the rule *mṛḍamṛdagudhakuṣakliśavadavasaḥ ktvā*: if these [roots] are not recited, then their meaning cannot be included by the mention of "etc. (*ādi*), for those that are not recited cannot be specified by the mention of "etc. If this is so, then since the matter is already established, the fact that the teacher includes the mention of "etc. indicates that there is indeed a recitation [of these roots] external to the Sūtra. What is the purpose of this indication?

The purpose [of this rule] is as follows: it becomes established that "designation as a verbal root (*dhātusañjñā*) is by virtue of being recited [in the Dhātupāṭha]. Regarding the designation as a verbal root by virtue of being recited, there must be a prohibition of identical-sounding words (*samānaśabda*). When the designation as a verbal root is based on recitation, a prohibition of identical-sounding words must be stated. For example, *yā* [as a root] and *yā* [as a feminine suffix ending in long -ā]; *vā* [as a root] and *vā* [as a particle (*nipāta*]); *nu* [as a root] and *nu*.

Thus, *pratyaya* is both a suffix and a particle; *div* is both a verbal root (*dhātu*) and a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). What would happen if these were also designated as verbal roots? It would follow that suffixes such as *-tavya* and others would be produced [after them] by the rule "after a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*). This is not a fault. Suffixes such as *-tavya* are prescribed for the sake of the "means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*), and the means of accomplishment belongs to an action (*kriyā*). In the absence of an action, there is an absence of the means of accomplishment.

Because there is no means of proof, even if the designation *dhātu* (verbal root) were present, suffixes such as *tavya* would not occur. But in this case—*yāḥ paśya* ("look at those which")—the elision [of the long vowel] by the rule *āto dhātoḥ* would undesirably apply. This is not a fault; for that [elision] applies only to what is not *āp*. But then, in this case...

Because *vā* is a particle (*nipāta*) and not a verbal root (*adhātu*), there would follow the prohibition of its designation as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Due to this lack of nominal stem status, the derivation of case endings such as *sva-* would not occur. This is not a fault. For it has been stated that a particle is designated as a nominal stem when it is devoid of meaning;
in that context, the mention of "devoid of meaning" will not be employed.

[The rule] "a particle is a nominal stem" (nipātaḥ prātipadikam) applies here as well. In this case, however, for the word *trasnū*, the substitution of *uvaṅ* [for the final *u*] would undesirably apply by the rule "in place of *y* and *v* of *śnu*, verbal roots, and *bhrū*, there is *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* before a vowel. This is not a fault, because it is the established practice of the Teacher [to indicate that the rule does not apply].
It indicates that the substitution of *uvaṅ* does not apply to the suffix; for he employs the mention of *śnu* in that rule.
However, in this case, the word *div* would be subject to the prohibition of the designation "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) because it is not a verbal root (*adhātu*).
Due to its lack of being a nominal stem, the derivation of case endings such as *svādi* would not occur. This is not a fault, for the activity of the Teacher indicates [otherwise].

As for the claim that "the *svādi* suffixes arise after the word *div*," because [Pāṇini] teaches the substitution of *au* for the *s* of *div*, this is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*). For there is indeed another purpose for stating this rule. What is it? It would apply to the case where *div* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
[Objection: "In the case of *akṣadyūḥ*, [the rule] does not apply here. For what is undesired follows, and what is desired is not established.

[Response: In that case, because of the principle that "when a term without an *anubandha* is mentioned, it does not include one with an *anubandha*," this will not occur. [Objection: Even so, since there is no word *div* without an *anubandha*, it must be understood as referring to the one with an *anubandha*.

179–185. If, however, this definition were made—that a verbal root (*dhātu*) is that which expresses action (*kriyā*)—then what is action? Endeavor (*īhā*). And what is endeavor? Effort (*ceṣṭā*). And what is effort? Activity (*vyāpāra*). In every way, you are merely describing words by means of words;
you do not point out any class of meaning whatsoever.

"Action of such a kind": this so-called action is entirely imperceptible. It is impossible to point out action as a solidified mass, like an embryo extracted [from the womb]. That action is to be understood through inference. What is that inference?
Here, when all the means [of cooking] are present, sometimes "he cooks" occurs, and sometimes it does not.

That action in which, when a particular means is present, the expression "he cooks" occurs—that is surely *kriyā*. Alternatively, that by which Devadatta, having been here, comes to be in Pāṭaliputra—that is surely *kriyā*. But how is it known that roots such as *pac* (to cook) denote *kriyā*? It is because they stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb *karoti* (he does).

"What does he do? "He cooks. "What will he do? "He will cook. "What did he do? "He cooked. In that context, there is a prohibition regarding prefixes (*upasarga*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) when the word expresses an action (*kriyāvacana*). A prohibition must be stated regarding prefixes and suffixes when the verbal root (*dhātu*) expresses an action; for example, *pacati* ("he cooks") and *prapacati* ("he cooks thoroughly"). But what is the reason that [the suffix] would otherwise apply? Because it applies to the entire complex (*saṅghāta*).
Because meaning is understood through a combination; for meaning is understood through a word that consists of a root together with its suffix and its prefix.

[Objection: The status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*) belongs to the roots *as*, *bhū*, and *vid*. It must be stated that *as*, *bhū*, and *vid* receive the technical designation of "verbal root" (*dhātusañjñā*).
For just as you have demonstrated the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of roots such as *pac* with the verb *karoti*, it is not so with roots such as *asti*.

It is demonstrated [as follows]: for it does not occur that "what does he do? is synonymous with "he exists. Because the meaning of the suffix remains invariant across different verbal roots (*prakṛti*), we consider that the root itself expresses the action (*kriyā*). In cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks") and *paṭhati* ("he reads"), the meaning of the root is different in each case, yet the meaning of the suffix is the same. And because the meaning of the root remains undifferentiated even when other suffixes follow, [the root alone expresses the action].

And because there is no difference in the meaning of the verbal root across various suffixes, we consider that the root alone expresses the action. For instance, in *paktā* (the cooker), *pacanam* (the act of cooking), and *pākaḥ* (cooking), while the meaning of the suffix varies from one to another, the meaning of the base remains the same. But how is it known that "this is the meaning of the base" and "this is the meaning of the suffix"? This is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). [It is known] from positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
And because of exclusion (*vyatireka*). What is this positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or exclusion (*vyatireka*)? Here, when "he cooks" (*pacati*) is said, a certain word is heard:
the word *pac*, ending in the letter *c*, and the suffix *ati*. A certain meaning is also understood:
softening (*viklitti*), agency (*kartṛtva*), and singularity (*ekatva*). When "he reads" (*paṭhati*) is said, one word is lost, another arises, and one remains constant (*anvayī*).
The word *pac* disappears, the word *paṭh* arises, and the word *ati* persists. Likewise, some meaning disappears, some arises, and some persists:

the state of being softened (*viklitti*) disappears, the act of reciting (*paṭhikriyā*) arises, and both agency (*kartṛtva*) and singularity (*ekatva*) persist. We consider that the meaning which disappears belongs to the word that disappears; the meaning which arises belongs to the word that arises.

That meaning which arises is the meaning of that word which is recurrent; that word which is recurrent is the word of that meaning which is recurrent. This formulation is flawed, for many words have a single meaning. For example:
Indra, Śakra, Puruhūta, and Purandara.

"Kandu," "koṣṭha," and "kuśūla"—these are examples where a single word has multiple meanings. For instance: *akṣāḥ*, *pādāḥ*, and *māṣāḥ*. Therefore, why would it not be even more established that [words] possess meaning? Nor do we say that the possession of meaning is not established; rather, the possession of meaning has already been described through the very methods of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). In that regard, from what [source] does this [objection arise]?

"This is the meaning of the base (prakṛti), this is the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya)"—the base itself should not express both meanings, nor should the suffix alone. These would thus be general terms (sāmānyaśabda). And general terms do not settle upon specific meanings without context or a specific indicator. For indeed, when "he cooks" (pacati) is said by necessity, [the specific action] arises from its own nature.
The word *pacati* (he cooks) applies to a specific instance; therefore, we consider that these are not general terms (*sāmānya-śabda*).
If they are not general terms, then the base (*prakṛti*) occurs in the sense of the base, and the suffix (*pratyaya*) occurs in the sense of the suffix. A prefix (*upasarga*) qualifies the action.
In the word *pacati*, an action is understood; the prefix *pra-* qualifies that [action]. Even though this is so here—

It can be said: where a verbal root (*dhātu*) deviates from a prefix (*upasarga*), and where it certainly does not deviate from it, how is it [to be explained] in cases such as *adhyeti* and *adhīte*? Even though here the verbal root does not deviate from the prefix, the prefix, however, deviates from the verbal root. This is what we consider.

Whatever meaning this prefix *adhi* has elsewhere, that same meaning it has here as well. But what is the meaning of *adhi* elsewhere? The prefix *adhi* occurs in the sense of "being above. In this case, however, a distinct meaning is clearly perceived:
[in the words] *tiṣṭhati* and *pratiṣṭhate*. *Tiṣṭhati* signifies the cessation of the action of going (*vrajikriyā*), whereas *pratiṣṭhate* signifies the action of going.
It is understood. We consider this to be caused by the prefix (*upasarga*), by which the action of going (*vrajikriyā*) is understood here.

This prefix *pra-* is observed to have a deviation [from its primary meaning] in that it functions to indicate the commencement of an action (*ādikarma*). And it is not the case that there is no such thing as verbal roots having multiple meanings. For example:
the root *vapi-* is seen in the sense of scattering, yet it also functions in the sense of cutting.
"He shaves his hair and beard. The root *īḍ* is seen in the senses of praise, instigation, and entreaty, but it also functions in the sense of impelling:

"Agni indeed impels rain from here; the Maruts cause it to fall from yonder. The root *kṛ* is seen in the sense of bringing into existence what did not previously exist, but it also functions in the sense of cleansing: "Make the back clean, O cook."
"Kuru" (do/make) is understood as "unmṛdāna" (crush/prepare). It also functions in the sense of placing:

"kuru kaṭe" (place on a mat), "kuru ghaṭe" (place in a jar), "itaḥ kuru aśmānam" (move the stone from here)—it is understood as "sthāpaya" (set down). In this way, here too, the root *tiṣṭhati* itself expresses the act of going (*vrajikriyā*), and *tiṣṭhati* itself expresses the cessation of the act of going. If that is so, then this is the fault:

Regarding the statement that *asti*, *bhavati*, and *vidyati* possess the nature of verbal roots (*dhātutva*): (Pāṇini 1.3.1.3) If, however, the definition were formulated as "a root is that which expresses an action" (*bhāvavacana*), how then would it be known that *pacati* and other such forms express an action? It is because they stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb *bhavati*.

[The forms] *bhavati*, *pacati*, *bhavati pakṣyati*, and *bhavati apākṣīt* [are used]. But what is *bhāva* (being)? The meaning of the root *bhū* itself is *bhavana* (the act of becoming); that is *bhāva*. If the meaning of the root *bhū* itself—namely, *bhavana*—is *bhāva*, then [it would apply to] contradictory things...
The notion of "element" (dhātu-sañjñā) does not apply [to the following]:
"breaking" (bheda), "cutting" (cheda). For existence (bhāva) is one thing and non-existence (abhāva) is another; moreover, existence is distinct from non-existence.
For he who desires the existence of something does not desire its non-existence, and he who desires the non-existence of something does not desire its existence.

Furthermore, the designation "root" (dhātu-sañjñā) would not apply to *pac* and other such verbs. For while you have demonstrated the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of *pac* and others with *karoti* when the root expresses action (*kriyāvacana*), it is not so demonstrated when the root expresses the state of being (*bhāvavacana*). *Karoti* follows *pac* and others across all tenses, all persons, and all numbers; *bhavati*, however, does not.
[The suffix expresses] both the present time and singularity. What, then, is the meaning of this linguistic expression:
"he is cooking" (*bhavati pacati*), "he will cook" (*bhavati pakṣyati*)?
"It has become cooked" (*bhavati apākṣīt*). This is the linguistic formulation:

actions such as "cooking" (*pacādi*) are the agents of the action of "becoming" (*bhavatikriyā*). Even if it can be said in this case where one action is distinct from another, how is it so in a case where that very same action [is involved]?
"Bhavet" means "bhavet," and "syāt" means "syāt. Here too, there is a difference. Why? Because of the difference in time and the difference in the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
In this case, for one [form], the root *bhū* is the means of accomplishment and the suffix has all three times; for the other, it is external.

The means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and the present tense are the indicators (*pratyaya*). Since there is indeed a difference here as well—in that *pac* and other roots are actions and they become the agents (*kartṛ*) of the action of "being" (*bhū*)—let this be a derivation based on the agent (*kartṛ-sādhana*), such that "being" (*bhavati*) is the state (*bhāva*). What is accomplished by this? The designation of verbal root (*dhātu-sañjñā*) for those [roots] whose meanings are mutually contradictory is established. It would be desirable if the designation of verbal root were established even for those whose meanings are contradictory.

[The suffix] would also apply to nominal stems (*prātipadika*), as in *vṛkṣaḥ* and *plakṣaḥ*. What is the reason? For these too are [entities]. [This is done] by the *sūtra*: P. 1.3.2: *upadeśe 'j anunāsika it* ("In the *upadeśana*, a non-consonant nasal vowel is designated as *it*").

In that case, it is split off. Let it remain exactly as it was originally arranged. But was it not said that in the case of the designation *it*, there would be over-extension (*sarvaprasaṅga*) because there is no distinction? This is not a fault. In the word *upadeśa*, this suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). [Objection: It is not established; because it is subsequent, the suffix *lyuṭ* would apply. [Response: We do not say [that it applies] by the rule "also when denoting an agent other than the subject and when it is a technical name" (*akartari ca kārake sañjñāyām*). What then?

Regarding the rule *halośca*: there too, the phrase "in the case of a technical name" (*sañjñāyām*) is understood to carry over. However, this [term *prāya*] is not a technical name. Because it is stated as a general tendency (*prāya*), it will apply even when it is not a technical name. Due to being stated as a general tendency, it may or may not apply specifically to a technical name. For a limiting factor cannot be a limiting factor for another limiting factor, nor can a qualifier be a qualifier for another qualifier. If it were not a limiting factor for a limiting factor, or a qualifier for a qualifier...

Or, if it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of words such as *kalyāṇī*, the suffix *inaṅ* would not optionally apply to the word *kulaṭā*. In this case, *inaṅ* alone is the primary element; the suffix that has been prescribed and introduced is what is being carried forward (*anuvartate*). In that case, here:

regarding the rule "for *vākina* and others, *kuk* [is added] after *putra*, optionally," the optional application of *kuk* would not occur. In this instance too, it is *kuk* [that is the primary element].

Thus, the primary element [is established]; the prescribed suffix and the contextual element both persist. In this way, this does not become unformed, nor does it constitute a qualification of a qualification, or a qualifier of a qualifier; thus, no fault whatsoever arises. And by doing so, the *ghañ* suffix would not apply. If that is the case, then [the formation occurs] by the rule "kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam" (Pāṇini 3.3.113).

In this case, the suffix *ghañ* will occur. (Pāṇini 1.3.3.1) KA_I,261.5-15 Ro_II, 202-203: Regarding the rule "a consonant is the final [element] of a word" (*halantyam*), there is the undesirable consequence that it would apply to all [consonants], because every [consonant] is final in some context. Regarding the rule "a consonant is the final [element] of a word," there is the undesirable consequence that it would apply to all [consonants]. This is because every [consonant] is final in some context.

The designation *it* would apply to every consonant (*hal*). Why? Because it is the final element of everything. For every consonant is indeed final with respect to its respective limit. But this is established by virtue of being the final element of what is determined (*vyavasita*). This is established. How? By virtue of being the final element of what is determined. It should be stated: "A consonant that is the final element of what is determined receives the designation *it*. What, then, are the determined elements? They are roots (*dhātu*), nominal stems (*prātipadika*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), particles (*nipāta*), augments (*āgama*), and substitutes (*ādeśa*).

[The rule] is established. But then the Sūtra is contradicted. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. [Objection: Was it not said that if [the term *hal*] were placed at the end [of the rule], there would be over-extension (*sarvaprasaṅga*) because every consonant is final with respect to something? [Response: This is not a fault. He says: "A consonant (*hal*) becomes marked with the technical designation *it* when it is final.
And every consonant is final with respect to its respective limit. In that case, the sense of superlative degree (*prakṛṣṭagati*) will be understood [to apply].

"Better is that which is final. And what is better? That which is final in its determination (*vyavasitāntya*). Alternatively, this reference is made with a requirement (*sāpekṣa*); and there is nothing else to be required.
We shall simply require that which has been determined.

203–205. Because the *lakāra* is not indicated by an *anubandha*, the inclusion of *hal* is not established. Since the *lakāra* is not indicated as an *anubandha*, the inclusion of *hal* is not established. It is stated that "the final [sound] is designated as *it*"; however, the designation of *it* does not even apply to the *lakāra* itself. But it is established by the mention of the *lakāra*. This is established. How?
A specification of the letter *l* must be made; it should be stated that "the final consonant (*hal*) bears the designation *it*, and so does the letter *l*.

Alternatively, this is due to a mention by means of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from a class): or rather, this is a mention by *ekaśeṣa*: "consonant (*hal*) and consonant (*hal*) are [collectively] *hal*; the final *hal* bears the designation *it*. Or else, this is the mention of the letter *ḷ* itself as a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*). In that case, regarding the instruction (*upadeśa*):
The designation *it* will apply by the rule "an *ac* [vowel] is called *it*. Alternatively, the activity of the Teacher indicates that the designation *it* applies to the letter *l*,
since he treats the *ṇal* [suffix] as having the designation *lit*.

205–207. Prohibition regarding nominal stems (*prātipadika*): [The rule applies] to that which does not end in a *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffix. A prohibition must be stated for a nominal stem that ends in a *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffix, as in the examples *udaśvit* and *śakṛt*. Why is it specified "that which does not end in a *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffix"? [Consider the following: *kumbhakāraḥ*, *nagarakāraḥ*, *aupagavaḥ*, *kāpaṭavaḥ*. This is established because of the absence of the purpose [of the marker]. Due to the absence of any grammatical operation (*it-kārya*) [triggered by such markers], the designation *it* will not apply here.

[Objection: This [is necessary] so that the *svarita* accent may apply according to the rule "this [suffix] has the *it*-kārya [of *it*], it is *svarita*. [Response: This is not necessary. He will raise the objection there regarding the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*). Then what [is the purpose]? [Consider] *rājā*, *takṣā*. So that the rule "the first syllable is *udātta* when followed by a suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*" may apply. Although it is stated "when followed by a suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*," because there is no distinct separation (*vyapavarga*) there, [the rule would not otherwise apply].

"It will not occur. Well then, this is for the sake of the *svara* (accent): so that this *svara* [the *svarita*] might apply by the rule "the penultimate (*upottama*) vowel in a *riti* [vowel sequence]. It will not occur due to the power of the application of the *svarita* itself, as it is stated: "The *nyaṅ* and *svar* [vowels] are *svarita*. "Well then, let it be here in the word *antaḥ*. The word 'penultimate' (*uttama*) applies to words consisting of three or more syllables, and there are not three or more syllables here. "Well then, let it be here in the word *sanutaḥ*. [This is governed by] the rule: 'The penultimate (*upottama*) vowel in a *riti*...'"

Let this be the accent. An *antodātta* (final acute) will be prescribed by way of exception (*nipātana*). And that exceptional accent will be an obstructor of the accent [prescribed] for the *rit* suffix. Furthermore, it is logical here that because there is no operation of an *it*, the designation *it* should not apply. Where an operation of an *it* occurs, there the designation *it* applies. For example: in the case of *āgastya* and *kauṇḍinya*, [the forms] *agasti* and *kuṇḍina*.

(P_1.3.4) KA_I,262.19–263.9 Ro_II,207–209: A prohibition of the *tavarga* [dental stops] must be stated regarding case endings (*vibhakti*) when they are not *taddhita* suffixes. It should be stated: "A prohibition of the *tavarga* [applies] in case endings, provided they are not *taddhita*. This is so that it does not apply here: *kimaḥ at* [Pāṇini 5.3.12], as in *kve prepsan dīpyase* ("Where, seeking, do you shine? and *kva ardhamāsāḥ* ("Where are the half-months?"). That [is the rule].

In that case, a prohibition must be stated. It need not be stated. The activity of the Teacher indicates that there is no prohibition regarding a *taddhita* suffix when it follows a case-ending (*vibhakti*), because he attaches the marker *u* as an *anubandha* to the *m* of *thamu* in the rule *idamas-thamuḥ* for the purpose of protecting it from being designated as an *it*. If this is what is indicated, then [the designation of *it*] would apply here as well in the word *idānīm*. [But it does not,] because there is no function for an *it* in that case.

In this case, the designation *it* will not apply. This is the function of *it*: [the rule] "a *mit* [augment] follows after the final vowel" so that it may follow after the final vowel among the vowels. Once the substitution of *i* has been made, there is no difference whether one says "a *mit* follows after the final vowel" or "an affix follows. However, that very substitution of *i* does not even obtain. What is the reason? Because [the condition for it] occurs previously.

It is said that the substitution of *iś* occurs in the case of suffixes [denoting] directions. But who is entitled to state that the substitution of *iś* occurs in suffixes [denoting] directions before the word "diś"?

What then? The substitution of *iś* occurs for meanings prior to "diś"; the production of the suffix occurs after words beginning with *kim*, all pronouns (*sarvanāman*), and *bahu*, excluding *dvi* and so on.
If this is so, then this must also be stated for *tad*: and for *tad*, it is not established by being placed after the final vowel because of the rule *mit acaḥ antyāt paratvena*.

But surely, even here, once *attva* (the substitution of *at*) has been applied, there is no difference whether the suffix is considered "after the final vowel" (*mit-acaḥ antyāt paraḥ*) or "a suffix that follows" (*pratyayaḥ paraḥ*). For in that case, *attva* would not apply. What is the reason? It is because it is stated [in the rule] "before a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*). If that is so, then we shall now treat it as ending in the letter *y*. Why is the *y* not heard? The *y* is indicated as elided.

(P_1,3.7.1) Regarding *cuñcup* and *caṇap*: there must be a prohibition of the letter *c*. A prohibition of the letter *c* in *cuñcup* and *caṇap* must be stated [as an exception]. For example: *keśacuñcuḥ*, *keśacaṇaḥ*. This is established because of the absence of the operation of the *it*-marker. Due to the absence of the operation of the *it*-marker, the designation (*sañjñā*) of *it* will not apply here.

This suffix *it* has the effect that [the word] becomes oxytone (*anta-udātta*), so that it may have an acute accent on the final syllable. Now, for what purpose is the marker *p* used? If it is asked, "For what purpose is the marker *p*?", it is for the sake of providing an alternative (*paryāya*). If it is asked, "For what purpose is the marker *p*?", this would be for the sake of an alternative. In that case, [the suffixes] *cuñcup* and *caṇap* begin with the letter *y*. What is the purpose of the letter *y*?
It is not heard [in the rule]. The letter *y* has been elided and indicated as such. (P. 1.3.7.2) An addition must be made for *iraḥ*: an addition of *iraḥ* must be formulated.
Regarding the root *rudh*:

[the forms] *arudhat* and *arautsīt* are established by virtue of the mention of the constituent parts. Here, the letter *r* will receive the technical designation *it* by the rule *halantyam*, and the vowel *i* will receive it by the rule *upadeśe 'janunāsika it*. If it is argued that this is established by the mention of the constituent parts, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the rule prescribing *it* for the roots *id* and *id*.

If it is argued that [the rule applies] because of the mention of the "parts" (avayava), then the undesired application of the *it* designation would follow. For example, in the case of *bhettā* and *chettā*, by the rule "a *num* augment follows a verbal root marked with *it*," the *num* augment would have to occur. However, if this rule for the *it* designation were understood according to the maxim of "one whose grain is in a jar" (*kumbhīdhānyanyāya*), then it would be as follows: one is called a "Vedic scholar whose grain is in a jar" (*kumbhīdhānyaḥ śrotriyaḥ*) when his grain is kept only in a jar.

"One who has grain in a jar" (*kumbhīdhānyaḥ*). But for one who has [grain] both in a jar and elsewhere, he is not "one who has grain in a jar. This rule cannot be understood according to the logic of "one who has grain in a jar," for in that case a fault would arise here: [the word] *nandathuḥ* from the root *ṭunadi*. If that is so, then it is not to be understood thus: "that which has the vowel *i* as its *it* is *idit*; of that which is *idit* [the nasal is inserted]."

How, then, [is this to be understood]? It is simply that the letter *i* is the *it*, according to the rule "that which has an *it* as its final element. Alternatively, this is a mention of the vowel *ṛ* itself when it has become *irt*.

In that case, the designation *it* will apply by the rule "in the original instruction (*upadeśa*), a nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) is an *it*. Or else, the activity of the Teacher indicates that the rule for *it*-designation does not apply to such types [of sounds], since he uses the term *iritaḥ* for certain [roots] that are followed by the augment *num*.

He recites: *ubundi* means "to perceive"; *skandi* means "motion" and "drying up. Alternatively, the activity of the Teacher indicates that the designation *it* applies to the sound *i*, since he says "or [the root] is marked with *i*" (*iritah vā*). Or rather, the word "at the end" (*ante*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].

211–212. What is the purpose of mentioning *tasya*? It is intended to refer back to that which has the designation *it*. This is not necessary as a purpose, because the word *iti* from the previous context continues to apply. Where was it previously mentioned? In the rule: "In the original instruction (*upadeśa*), a vowel (*ac*) is nasalized (*anunāsika*). But that [vowel] was designated in the nominative case, whereas here the meaning requires it to be designated in the genitive case. Therefore, there will be a change of case endings by implication (*arthāt*).
For example: "High are Devadatta’s houses. From this it is understood: "Address Devadatta.
[In the phrase] "Devadatta’s cows, horses, and gold," [the meaning] "The wealthy son of Vaidhava" is understood to be Devadatta.
That which was previously indicated by the genitive case becomes, by implication, indicated by the accusative and the nominative cases.
In this case as well, although "sat" is mentioned first [in the rule], it will effectively become that which is designated by the genitive case [referring to the substitute].

This, then, is the purpose: so that for those [elements] having multiple phonemes (*anekāla*) that are designated by the technical term *it*, their elision (*lopa*) may be a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*).
Now, even if the mention of "tasya" (of that) is made, how indeed can the elision be obtained as a total replacement? It is obtainable.
Thus he says. Why? Because of the authority of the statement; because of the force of the mention of that [suffix].

An addition must be made regarding the elision of *it* after roots ending in *i* before the suffixes *ṇa*, *ktvā*, and the *niṣṭhā*; for there is a prohibition of *it* in these cases. [This applies] to the elision of *it* after roots ending in *i* before *ṇa*, *ktvā*, and the *niṣṭhā*.

An addition must be made [to the rule]: [the suffixes] *ṇal*, *ktvā*, and *niṣṭhā*. Examples: *ṇal*—*aham papaca*; *ktvā*—*devitvā*, *sevitvā*; *niṣṭhā*—*śayitaḥ*, *śayitavān*. But for what reason is this not established? Because of the prohibition of the *it*-designation. Here, the *it*-designation is prohibited:

*ṇal* is optionally treated as having the *ṇit* designation when it is in the first person; *ktvā* with the augment *iṭ* is not treated as having the *kit* designation; and *niṣṭhā* with the augment *iṭ* is not treated as having the *kit* designation.

[Objection: This is established, however, because of the prohibition of the mention of *ṇal* and the others. [Response: This is indeed established. How? The mentions of *ṇal* and the others are prohibited. [Namely: "The *uttama* person ending in *ṇal* is optionally included by the mention of *ṇit*; *ktvā* with an indicatory *ṣ* (*seṭ*) is not included by the mention of *kit*; the *niṣṭhā* suffix with an indicatory *ṣ* (*seṭ*) is not included by the mention of *kit*. Or else, it is due to the elision of what is explicitly stated (*nirdiṣṭalopa*). It is due to the elision of what is explicitly stated.

Or rather, it is already established. Or else, this elision (*lopa*) is applied to that which has been specifically prescribed. Therefore, this is established. In that regard, there is a prohibition concerning *t*, *u*, and *m*. In that case, a prohibition of *t*, *u*, and *m* must be stated. [Examples would be: *tasmāt*, *tasmin*, *yasmāt*, *yasmin*, *vṛkṣāḥ*, *plakṣāḥ*, *acinavam*, *asunavam*, *akaravam*. [Objection: No, because of the power of its pronunciation. It is not so.

Or rather, it should be stated [that the elision does not occur]. What is the reason? Because of the power of its pronunciation (*uccāraṇasāmarthyāt*), there will be no elision here. There is non-establishment [of the rule] because of the conflict between the presence and absence [of the elision] when an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) is elided. Since there is a contradiction between the presence and absence [of the elision] when an indicatory letter is elided, there is non-establishment;
it is not known with what intention [the rule] applies and with what it effects the cessation [of the operation]. However, it is established by the principle of the exception (*apavādanyāya*).
This is established. How? By the rule of the exception (*apavāda*). But how is it here that there is a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*)?

For the presence (*bhāva*) of an element is for the sake of an operation (*kārya*), whereas elision (*lopa*) is not for the sake of another purpose. An indicatory letter (*anubandha*) is attached with the thought, "I shall perform an operation," so that nothing other than the operation [intended] may occur; thus, elision is employed.
(P_1,3.9.3) KA_I,265.18–267.6 Ro_II, 214–217 Now, regarding that to which a suffix is attached, is it invariably related to that [base], or is it non-invariably related?
It is invariably related there, because it is perceived there. He says: "It is invariably related. Why? Because it is perceived there; it resides therein.

For that [suffix] is perceived [as such]. Just as a branch situated on a tree is perceived as being exclusively part of the tree. In this regard, regarding the prohibition of *asarūpa* (non-identical) suffixes and of substitutes for the whole (*sarvādeśa*) after *dāp*, there is a separate mention because [the suffix *ka*] does not end in the vowel *ā*. Therein, a fault arises in the rule concerning non-identical suffixes: namely, "the suffix *aṇ* is applied after a verbal root ending in *ā* when an object is expressed, and the suffix *ka* is applied after a root ending in *ā* when no prefix is present. Thus, even in the domain of *kaṇ*, the suffix *aṇ* would also apply. Furthermore, a fault arises regarding the substitution of the whole.

In that case, the substitution of *au* for the entire word (*sarvādeśa*) would result. To prevent this, a separate mention must be made in the prohibition regarding *dāp*. It should be stated as "adāp-dai-pau. But what is the reason it is not established? Because it does not end in the vowel *ā*. [Objection: But once the substitution of *ā* (*āttva*) has been applied, it will be established. [Response: That substitution of *ā* does not apply. What is the reason? Because it does not end in a vowel (*anejantatvāt*). In that case, let it be so.

It is non-exclusive (*anekānta*). If [the suffix] is non-exclusive, then the specific occurrence (*vṛttiviśeṣa*) is not established. If the specific occurrence is not established, then the grammatical operations prescribed for suffixes marked with *k* or *ṇ* (i.e., *kit* and *ṇit*) are not established. For how could that [suffix] be "its" (*tasya*) [i.e., belong to the preceding element], such that an operation conditioned by *it* would apply? If that is so, then [let it be] immediate (*anantara*). If it is argued that it is immediate, then there arises the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the operation conditioned by *it* would apply to both the preceding and the following elements. [The opponent replies: It is immediate.

If this were the case, the substitution of *it* would apply to both the preceding and the following [elements], such as in the case of the suffixes *vuñ* and *chaṇ*. However, it is established by the reading of the *vyavasita* (the settled or determined) text.
This is established. How? The *vyavasita-pāṭha* must be performed. That is, *vuñ* and *chaṇ*. And that *vyavasita-pāṭha* must necessarily be performed;
otherwise, even in a clear case (*ekānta*), there would be doubt. For if the *vyavasita-pāṭha* were not performed, even in a clear case—

There would be doubt; in that case, it would not be known whether this belongs to the preceding [rule] or rather to the subsequent one. This is merely a doubt, and in all cases of doubt, this principle applies: "The specific understanding arises from the explanation, for there is no non-characteristic due to doubt. We shall explain it as belonging to the preceding [rule]. Or, it is from what has occurred (*vṛtta*). Or, it is from what has occurred.

Furthermore, this is established: having observed that [a form] has the *vṛddhi* substitute and is acute-accented on the first syllable, one should determine that the suffix is *ñit*; having observed it to be acute-accented on the final syllable, one should determine it is *kit*. It is indeed proper, however, that the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) should be caused by the grammatical operation (*vṛtti*), and not that the grammatical operation should be caused by the *anubandha*. The *anubandha* is indeed caused by the grammatical operation; for the Teacher is one who knows the grammatical operations.

He attaches the *anubandhas*. Both of these—namely, that they are "exclusive" (*ekānta*) or "non-exclusive" (*anekānta*)—have been stated regarding the *anubandhas*. What is the correct view here? It is correct that they are exclusive. Why is this so? Because here a reason (*hetu*) has been specified; and whatever possesses a reason is indeed correct. But was it not said there: "In order to prohibit [the substitution of] *asarūpa* [suffixes], *sarvādeśa* [suffixes], and *dāp*, there is a separate mention"?

"Because it does not end in a suffixal marker (*anākārāntatvāt*). First, there is no fault regarding the rule for non-identical forms (*asarūpavidhi*). The activity of the Teacher indicates that dissimilarity caused by a suffixal marker (*anubandha*) does not exist, since he teaches the optional form *śam* in the rule "there is an option for *dadāti* and *dadhati*. Furthermore, as for what was said regarding "it being a replacement for the whole" (*sarvādeśe*), here too the activity of the Teacher indicates that [dissimilarity] caused by a suffixal marker does not exist.

The fact that [the substitute] becomes multiallic (anekāl) is indicated by the statement "this *śit* replaces the whole. Furthermore, as for what was said—that a separate mention must be made regarding the prohibition of *dāt*—it need not be made. The activity of the Teacher indicates that the status of being non-final (*anejantatva*) is not caused by an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), since he [uses] *meṅ*, which possesses an indicatory letter, in the rule "of *māṅ* in the sense of exchange among the Northerners."
It effects the inclusion of that which has become *āt*.
1.1.56) What is the example here? "A *yaṇ* replaces an *ik* before a vowel": as in *dadhy atra*, *madhv atra*. This is not [an example], because it concerns a substitute (*sthāne*).

This is also established by the closest [substitute]. Why? Because of proximity: that which has the palate as its place of articulation will have the palate as its place of articulation; that which has the lips as its place of articulation will have the lips as its place of articulation. But then consider this: *tasthasthamipām tāmtamtāmaḥ*. Is it not the case that this too is established by the closest [substitute] according to place of articulation? Why? Because of proximity: that which has a single meaning will have a single meaning.

That which has two meanings will have two meanings, and that which has many meanings will have many meanings. But then, what about this: "From *tūdī*, *śalātura*, *avarmatī*, and *kūcavāra*, [the suffixes] *ḍhak*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *ḍhañ*, and *yak* [are applied]"?
218–220. Why, then, is this stated? Because designations (*saṃjñā*) and compounds (*samāsa*) are employed in the rules, there would be an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) of subsequent rules (*anudeśa*).

The statement "according to order" (*yathāsaṅkhyam*) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Designations and compounds are used in the rules. First, by way of designation: *parasmaipadānām ṇalatususthalathusaṇalvamāḥ*. By way of compounds: *tūdīśalāturavarmatīkūcavārāt*.

Regarding the rule *ḍhak-chaṇ-ṭhañ-ya-kak*, because the technical terms (*sañjñā*) and compounds (*samāsa*) are indicated [in the sūtra], there is the possibility of over-extension (*sarvaprasaṅga*). The statement of "correspondence" (*anudeśa*) according to order (*yathāsaṅkhya*) is for the purpose of restriction. For every [term in the] original enunciation (*uddeśa*), every [term in the] subsequent application (*anudeśa*) would otherwise apply. However, it is desired that they be equal in number. Since this cannot be established without effort, the statement of correspondence is made therein.

For the sake of restriction. This is stated for this purpose. But what is the reason that the indications are made by means of technical names (*saṃjñā*) and compounds (*samāsa*)? The indication by means of technical names and compounds is for the purpose of avoiding the separate utterance of the case endings and the named items (*saṃjñin*). Indications are made by means of technical names and compounds so that one might not have to utter the case endings and the named items separately. In this context...

And it is for the purpose of ensuring universal comprehension; that is, so that there may be a comprehensive understanding of all [the elements] within the context, such as [in the rule] *vidaḥ* or *laṭo vā*.
But does the correspondence of number (*saṅkhyātānudeśa*) occur on the basis of phonetic form (*śabda*), or rather on the basis of meaning (*artha*)? Which [is it]?

And here there is a distinction: if numerical equality were based on the word-form, then there would be no designation [of specific elements] such as "ṇalādayaḥ" for the *parasmaipada*s, "ḍāraurasaḥ" for the first person, or "ayavāyāvaḥ" for the *ec* vowels; a designation that fails to convey the intended meaning is called a non-designation (*anirdeśaḥ*). For instance, in the rule "parasmaipadānām ṇalatususthalathusaṇalvamāḥ," the term "ṇalādayaḥ" refers to many individual elements, while "parasmaipadānām" is a single word.

Due to the inequality [in number], the designation according to numerical correspondence (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) does not obtain. In the rule *ḍāraurasaḥ prathamasya*, the word *ḍāraurasaḥ* consists of many [sounds] while *prathamasya* is a single word; due to this inequality, the designation according to numerical correspondence does not obtain. In the rule *ecaḥ ayavāyāvaḥ*, the word *ayavāyāvaḥ* consists of many [sounds] while *ecaḥ* is a single word; due to this inequality, the designation according to numerical correspondence does not obtain.

Let it be, then, by way of meaning (*arthataḥ*). If it is by way of meaning, there is a fault regarding the *lṛ* and *luṭ* [affixes] in the case of *nandi*, *arīhaṇa*, *sindhu*, *takṣaśilā*, and so forth. There is a fault regarding the *lṛ* and *luṭ* [affixes] in the case of *nandi*, *arīhaṇa*, *sindhu*, *takṣaśilā*, and so forth. Regarding the rule *syatāsī lṛluṭoḥ*: "the two, *syat* and *tāsī*, [are applied] after *lṛ* and *luṭ*"—this has three meanings. Because of this inequality, the application of the number (*saṅkhyātānudeśa*) does not obtain. [This applies to the rules for] *nandi*, *grahi*, *pac* and so forth.

Regarding *lyu*, *ṇini*, and *ac*: there are many [bases] beginning with *nandi*, while *lyu*, *ṇini*, and *ac* are three. Due to this inequality, a correspondence based on numerical sequence (*saṅkhyātānudeśa*) is not obtained. Regarding *arīhaṇa* and so forth: there are many [bases], while *vuñ* and the others are seventeen. Due to this inequality, a correspondence based on numerical sequence is not obtained. Regarding *sindhu*, *takṣaśilā*, and so forth: there are many [bases], while *aṇ* and *añ* are two.

Because there are two [pairs], a numerical correspondence (*saṅkhyātānudeśa*) based on inequality does not apply in the case of the rules for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), the suffixes *niṣṭhā*, and the designation of *sārvadhātuka*. Furthermore, there is a fault in the mention of the rules for the middle voice, the suffixes *niṣṭhā*, and *sārvadhātuka*; specifically, the rule for the middle voice would not be established. This is because the rule "the middle voice is used after roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or the letter *ṅ*" would imply that both [types of roots] marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel or the letter *ṅ* take the middle voice.

There are two meanings [for a term]. In that case, a numerical correspondence (saṅkhyātānudeśa) would apply. For example, regarding the rule *niṣṭhā* and *radābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ pūrvasya ca daḥ*: the terms "repha" (the letter r) and "dakāra" (the letter d) are two, and "niṣṭhā" has two meanings; thus, a numerical correspondence would apply there. Furthermore, an error occurs in the case of the mentions of *sārvadhātuka* and *dvirvacana*. In the rules *śnasoḥ allopaḥ* and *śnamastī*, there are two [meanings for each].

The term *sārvadhātuka* has two meanings; in that case, a correspondence based on numerical order (*saṅkhyātānudeśa*) would apply. Regarding the substitution of a single substitute for the preceding [vowel] in place of *eṅ*, a prohibition must be stated: "A prohibition regarding the substitution of a single substitute for the preceding [vowel] in place of *eṅ* must be stated. [This applies to the rule: "In place of *eṅ* at the end of a word, and in place of *ati* before the endings *ṅasi* and *ṅas*.
Since *ṅasi* and *ṅas* are two, and *eṅ* is also two, a correspondence based on numerical order would apply there. Let it be so.

If it is by way of the word-form (*śabda*), then [one might object]: "But was it not said that if there were numerical equality by way of the word-form, there would be no specific designation for *ṇal* and so forth among the *parasmaipada* endings, nor for *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* among the first person endings, nor for *ay*, *āv*, and *āva* in place of *ec*? This is not a fault. The determination will be made by the rule "in place of [an original], the most similar [substitute occurs] (*sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ*). From what does this similarity arise? From that which has one referent (*ekārtha*) [replacing] that which has one referent.

That which has two meanings [is the substitute] for that which has two meanings; that which has many meanings [is the substitute] for that which has many meanings. That which has a closed vowel is [the substitute] for that which has a closed vowel; that which has an open vowel is [the substitute] for that which has an open vowel. There is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* before *kṅit* suffixes. An over-extension occurs regarding the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* before *kṅit* suffixes. There are two *guṇas* and two *vṛddhis*, and there are two *kṅits*. In that case, a correspondence based on numerical order (*saṅkhyātānudeśa*) would result. This is not a fault.

The letter *ga* is also indicated here. Should that mention of *ga* also be made? It need not be made; it is already provided in the *Nyāsa* itself. In the rule for the letter *ka*, the letter *ga* is indicated as having become a *cartva* (the cerebral substitute). [As in] *gi*, *kiti*, *ṅiti*. [And in] *udi kūle rujivahoḥ*. Here, *udikūle* consists of two [words], and *rujivahau* consists of two [roots]. In that case, the principle of "designation according to number" (*saṅkhyātānudeśa*) would apply.

This is not a fault. *ud* is not the *upapada*; rather, it is a qualifier of the roots *ruj* and *vah*. [The rule means: "When *kūla* is the *upapada*, [the suffix *kha* is added] after the two roots *ruj* and *vah* preceded by *ud*. Regarding the inclusion of the term *dhātu* (root) in the rules for those characterized by such habits (*tacchīla*) and so forth: there is a fault in the rules for those characterized by such habits where the term *dhātu* is included three times. In the rule *vidi-bhidi-chidibhyaḥ kurac*, there are three instances of *tacchīla* and so forth: [1] *vidi-bhidi-chidibhyaḥ*, [2] *kurac*, and [3] *tacchīla-ādiṣu*.

There are three [cases]. In that regard, the application of numerical correspondence (*saṅkhyātānudeśa*) would result in the following instances involving the mention of "two" (*dvi*) among the *ghañ*-affixes and others: in the rules for *ghañ* and others where "two" is mentioned, a fault arises. For example, in the rule *nirabhyoḥ pūlvoḥ*, there are two prefixes (*nir* and *abhi*) and two roots (*pū* and *lū*). There, the application of numerical correspondence would result. This is not a fault; indeed, the application of numerical correspondence is intended here: [as in] *niṣpāvaḥ*.

[The word] *abhilāvaḥ* [is an example]. If that is so, then in the rule "after roots meaning 'to cut' (*pūlva*), when there is neither an agent nor another kāraka, but rather the action itself (*bhāve*)", there are two [roots] and two [suffixes]; thus, a correspondence based on number (*saṅkhyātānudeśaḥ*) would result. In the rule "after the roots *ava-tṛ* and *ava-stṛ*, when there is an instrument (*karaṇa*) or a locus (*adhikaraṇa*)," there are two roots (*tṛ* and *stṛ*) and two [meanings], instrument and locus; thus, a correspondence based on number would result. And in the rule "after the roots *bhū* and *kṛñ*, when there is an agent (*kartṛ*) or an object (*karman*)," there are the agent and the object...

There are two [roots] *bhū* and *kṛ*, and two [suffixes]. In that case, a numerical correspondence (*saṅkhyātānudeśa*) would apply. [The pair] "impossibility" (*anavaklṛpti*) and "impatience" (*amarṣa*), even when not preceded by *kim*; there are two [meanings] "impossibility" and "impatience," and two [particles] "those preceded by *kim*" and "those not preceded by *kim*. In that case, a numerical correspondence would apply. Regarding *kṛ* and *bhū*, there are *ktvā* and *ṇamul*; there are two [roots] *kṛ* and *bhū*, and two [suffixes] *ktvā* and *ṇamul*. In that case, a numerical correspondence would apply.

Regarding the terms *chandobrāhmaṇāni* and *vedam*: there are two instances of *chandobrāhmaṇāni*, and two instances of *vedam*. In that case, a correspondence based on numerical order would apply.

[The rule] applies there. In that case, according to your explanation, from the [roots] *kratu* and *yajña*, there would be two [derivatives] ending in the suffix *aṇ*. This is not a fault, because the mention of *ghoṣa* [is intended].

In this case, the following should be done: for *veśoyaśas* and so on, from the *bhaga* [element], there are two *yal* and two *kh* [substitutions]. Or rather, it is not so, because of the statement regarding their being joined together in a common operation (*samānayogavacanāt*). Indeed, this fault does not arise.

What is the reason? Because of the statement regarding equal application (*samānayogavacana*). The fault of this [rule] is that for *vid* or for the present tense (*laṭ*), this correspondence according to number does not apply due to the fault of this definition. [The suffix] *ini*, *tra*, *kaṭya*, and *ac* [after the word *khalagoratha*] does not obtain its application. Therefore, one should adopt that alternative in which there are fewer faults.

thereafter is the governing rule (adhikāra); and there is a governing rule by means of a circumflex accent (svarita). 228–229. For what purpose is this stated? It is for the purpose of not specifying [the application] with every individual rule (*pratiyoga*). An *adhikāra* (governing heading) is established with every individual rule for the purpose of not having to specify it [again] with each one. What is meant by "with every individual rule" (*pratiyogam*)? It means "rule by rule" (*yogam yogam prati*). [The intention is: "May I not have to grasp it in every single rule. Is this point already understood by this much?

"It is established by the Sūtra," he says. Why? From common usage (*loka*). For example, in the world it is said, "He is appointed over this village," or "He is appointed over this city," of one who engages in activity therein. And what other activity can be understood from the word "appointed" (*adhikṛta*) than being present at each respective task (*yoge yoge upasthāna*)? Or rather, it is not so, because that which is being pointed out is itself the one appointed.

As in common usage. Or rather, this [objection] is not a valid purpose. What is the reason? Because that which is being specified is understood as the subject under discussion, as in common usage. That which is being specified is understood as the subject; for example: "Let a cow be given to Devadatta, to Yajñadatta, and to Viṣṇumitra. Here, "cow" is understood [as the subject]. So it is here as well: in the rule *pada-ruja-viśa-spraśo ghañ sṛ sthire*, [the root *sṛ* is understood as the subject].

It is understood that [the suffix] *ghañ* occurs when there is an abstract state (*bhāva*). However, the mention of "another" (*anyanirdeśa*) serves as a displacer; therefore, it is a *paribhāṣā*. For in common usage, the mention of another thing acts as a displacer. For example: "Let a cow be given to Devadatta, a blanket to Yajñadatta, and [one] to Viṣṇumitra. Here, the blanket displaces the cow. In the same way, here too, in the sense of an inclusive limit (*abhividhi*) regarding an abstract state...
The suffix *inuṇ* would then exclude *ghañ*. Therefore, a restrictive rule (*paribhāṣā*) must be formulated.

(P_1.3.11.2) Regarding the lack of knowledge concerning the extent of a governing heading (*adhikāra*): indeed, there is a lack of knowledge concerning the extent of the governing heading; it is not known [how far it extends].

To what extent does the governing authority (adhikāra) continue? [It is asked] for the purpose of knowing the limit of that authority. But then, this rule (yoga) must indeed be stated for the very purpose of knowing the limit of the authority—thinking, "I shall know the extent of the authority. How, moreover, can the limit of the authority be understood by means of this statement, "The authority [is indicated] by a circumflex accent" (svarita)? I shall state it thus: "By a circumflex accent (*svarita*)," [and so forth].
[The question is: "Is it an *adhikāra*? [The answer is: "Upon seeing a circumflex (*svarita*) accent, it is not an *adhikāra*. [The question is: "By what, then, will there be an *adhikāra*?

[The answer is: "It is a worldly (*laukika*) *adhikāra*. [The question is: "If you say it is not an *adhikāra*, has this not already been stated? [The question is: "What has been stated? [The answer is: "'But a different designation is a canceller; therefore, it is a *paribhāṣā*. [The conclusion is: "In that case, this rule (*yoga*) must indeed be stated for the purpose of an *adhikāra*."

But was it not said that there is ignorance regarding the extent of the governing rule (*adhikāra*)? This is established by the statement: "As many rules as there are *al*-suffixes [as *anubandhas*]. It must be stated: "The governing rule continues for as many rules as the number of *al*-suffixes that are attached. Now, however, there are cases where there are fewer *al*-suffixes, yet the governing rule continues over more rules.

How should it be done there? The statement "in the case of a plurality" should be made; the statement "in the case of a plurality" must be made. It should be stated as "prior to this. If so, then it must be stated. No, it need not be stated. This results in mere doubt.
And in all cases of doubt, this principle applies: "The specific meaning is understood through the commentary, for [a rule] does not [stand] on account of doubt."

Regarding the term *alakṣaṇam*: we shall explain [the meaning of] *prāk amutaḥ* later on. If this is so, there is no purpose served by this [term]. By what, then, will the governing authority (*adhikāra*) be established? It is the worldly governing authority. If it is argued that "it has already been stated that there is no governing authority," then it has indeed been stated. What was stated? That "but a reference to something else is a canceller; therefore, it is a *paribhāṣā*. This is merely a doubt.

230–232. In that case, this rule (*yoga*) need not be stated now. Yet it must be stated. What is the purpose? So that the scope of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) may be understood through the *svarita* accent:
[the sense of] "more" (*adhika*), "further action" (*kārya*), and "additional cause" (*kāra*). Regarding the understanding of the governing heading:
Regarding the rule *gostriyor upasarjanam*, it was proposed that the mention of *go* (cow) and *tāṅ* (the feminine suffix *tāp*) should be included. That need not be done.

The mention of *strī* (feminine) will be marked with a svarita accent. Since the scope of a governing rule (*adhikāra*) is determined by a svarita accent, it will be understood that the reference is to those suffixes prescribed under the heading *striyām*. In this way, the scope of the governing rule is established by the svarita accent.
There is no fault in saying "it exists. The additional purpose [of the rule] is this:

what does the Teacher consider to be the proper definition of the *apādāna*? It is that from which there is a cessation upon reaching it. Therefore, it would apply only in cases such as these: "He comes from the village," "He comes from the city," and "The people of Pāṭaliputra are more handsome than those of Sāṅkāśya."

Thus, in this case, [the designation *adhikaraṇa*] would not apply. Since the operation of *adhikaraṇa* occurs by virtue of the circumflex accent (*svarita*), it is established here as well. Furthermore, what does the Teacher consider to be the correct definition of *adhikaraṇa*? It is where the entire substratum is pervaded.
Therefore, it would apply only in this instance: [kūpe ghaṭaḥ].
"Oil in sesame seeds," "clarified butter in curds," "cows in the Ganges," and "the family of Garga in the well"—in these cases [the designation *adhikaraṇa*] would not apply.

However, since it is stated that "the operation of *adhikaraṇa* occurs by means of the *svarita* accent," this is also established here. [The term] *adhikam kāryam* means "an additional operation"; [the term] *adhikaḥ kāraḥ* means "an additional action.
Thus, the *pūrvavipratiṣedha*s (prior exceptions) need not be recited. [The rule for] *num* [takes precedence] over *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, *auttva*, and *tṛjvadbhāva*.

The rule *nuṭ* is a prior exception (*pūrvavipratiṣiddha*) to *num*, *aci-rat*, and *ṛjvadbhāva*. The *num* and *nuṭ* will be marked with the circumflex accent (*svarita*). Since an operation accompanied by the circumflex accent is more powerful, *num* and *nuṭ* will take effect. But how can prior exceptions be stated by this [method of accentuation], given that it says "an operation accompanied by the circumflex accent"? [Answer: From common usage (*loka*). For example, in common usage, something is called "additional" (*adhika*)...

It is said that "this one performs an action" (*kāram karoti*) when one who is weak carries a burden together with those who are strong. Likewise, here too, it is said that "this one performs an excessive action" (*adhikam kāram karoti*) when one who was previously [present] obstructs another. The understanding of "excessive authority" (*adhikāra*) has the sense of a feminine noun; for the sake of distinction, there is an "excessive task. Now, as for that other "excessive action":
That [rule] is for the purpose of a prior prohibition (pūrvavipratiṣedha).
A prohibition must be stated regarding the *vikaraṇas*: *cinutaḥ*, *sunutaḥ*, *lunītaḥ*, *punītaḥ*. [This applies to those] ending in *ṅit*.

Thus, the *ātmanepada* ending would follow. This is not a fault. It is not understood in this way: "the letter *ṅ* is its [marker], therefore it is *ṅit*; [the suffix] belonging to that which is *ṅit*. How then? The letter *ṅ* itself is the *ṅit*, [and the suffix] belongs to that which is *ṅit*. Or rather, the word "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*) is understood to carry over. Or else, it has been stated: "But it is established by the extension of the operation of the preceding [element]. And in every case, [this applies] because of the *caṅ* and *aṅ* affixes.

[It] obtains [the designation "root"]. If that is so, then the term *dhātoḥ* ("from the root") is understood [as a governing rule]. Where was it introduced? In the rule *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ* ("*bhū*, etc., are roots"). That [term] was indeed indicated in the nominative case (*prathamā*), whereas here [in the present context] there is a need for it in the ablative case (*pañcamī*). Therefore, by the force of the sense, there will be a change of case-ending (*vibhaktivipariṇāma*). For example: "Devadatta’s houses are high; call him. [In this case, although *devadattasya* is in the genitive, it is understood as the vocative.]

Thus it is understood: "Devadatta’s cows, horses, and gold. [One understands: "The wealthy son of Vidhavā is Devadatta. That which was previously indicated by the genitive case becomes, by implication, indicated by the accusative and the nominative. Likewise here too, that which was previously indicated by the nominative will, by implication, be indicated by the ablative.

(P_1,3.12.2) Why, then, is this stated? The mention of the *ātmanepada* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). This undertaking is for the sake of restriction. It is asked: why is it said that this is for the sake of restriction, and not also for the sake of an injunction (*vidhyartha*)? [The answer is: because the rule for the suffix *la* has already been prescribed.

It has been prescribed. For by the rule for the suffix *la*, both the *ātmanepada* and *parasmaipada* endings have been prescribed. This purpose is indeed established. But what then? Because they are intervened by the *vikaraṇa* suffixes, the restriction does not apply. Here, this must be deliberated: let the *vikaraṇas* be applied first, or the restriction? What should be done here? The *vikaraṇas* [should apply] because they are subsequent; moreover, they are obligatory (*nitya*).

Indeed, the *vikaraṇas* occur both when the restriction (*niyama*) has been applied and when it has not been applied. Because they are obligatory (*nitya*) and because they follow [the root], once the *vikaraṇas* have been applied, the restriction does not apply because [the suffix] is separated by those *vikaraṇas*. This is not a fault; for the restriction is without scope (*anavakāśa*). It does have scope (*sāvakāśa*). What is its scope? Those which are *luk-vikaraṇas* and *ślu-vikaraṇas*.
And [the rule] regarding the *liṅ* and *liṭ* [affixes]. If, however, this were understood as a *paribhāṣā*, what would be accomplished?

[The principle that] "a technical definition (*saṃjñā*) and a *paribhāṣā* are to be applied wherever the operation (*kārya*) occurs" would apply; thus, when it is stated "for *la*, there are *tiP* and so on," the following would be present: "from a root marked with an indicatory *anudātta* or *ṅ*, the *ātmanepada* affixes occur; from the remainder, when denoting the agent, the *parasmaipada* affixes occur. Even so...

It results in mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). What is this mutual dependence? Once the suffixes beginning with *tiP* have been produced in place of *la*, they must receive the designations of *ātmanepada* or *parasmaipada*; and by means of those designations, the suffixes beginning with *tiP* are to be produced. Thus, it becomes a case of mutual dependence. And grammatical operations that involve mutual dependence are not established. [This applies] to the *parasmaipada* suffixes.
In that case, there would be no mutual dependence. The enumeration of the *parasmaipada* endings will not be performed.

It must necessarily be performed for the sake of [the rule] "after *anu* and *parā*, [the suffixes are used] after the root *kṛ*. But surely this too will be done within the very enumeration of the *ātmanepada* endings? [It is said: "When the fruit of the action accrues to the agent, the *ātmanepada* occurs after a root marked with a svarita accent or a ñit marker."
