The designation will be understood as something yet to come to be (*bhāvinī saṃjñā*), like the example of the cloth and the threads. For instance, someone says to a weaver: "Weave this cloth. [The weaver understands that the word "cloth" refers to what is yet to be produced. Similarly, here too, the designation is understood prospectively. Thus, when one says, "He cooks for himself," the agent is already designated as the object by virtue of the future application of the reflexive sense. Therefore, there is no fault of mutual dependence. Furthermore, because the suffix *śānac* (the present middle participle) is taught immediately after the rule for the *ātmanepada*, it is understood that the *ātmanepada* endings themselves are intended here. Consequently, since the *ātmanepada* endings are not applied in the examples *anukriyate* and *parakriyate*, the designation of object does not apply there either. Thus, the rule is established without flaw. Alternatively, the word *na* may be supplied from the previous rule; thus, the meaning becomes: "In the case of the *ātmanepada*, the designation of object is not applied to the roots *kṛ* preceded by *anu* and *para*. In this way, the rule is explained without any logical inconsistency. As for the statement "the designation is understood as something yet to come to be," it means that the designation is determined based on the future state of the action. This is just as when someone says to a weaver: "Weave this cloth. [The weaver knows that the term "cloth" applies to the material that is currently being woven. "I am weaving a cloth for this thread. He observes: "If it is a cloth, it should not be woven; if it is to be woven, it is not yet a cloth. To say 'the cloth is to be woven' is a contradiction. Indeed, he intends a future designation. He thinks: "That which, when woven, becomes what is called a 'cloth,' is what must be woven. In the same way, here too, that [suffix] of *la*.

The designation *ātmanepada* shall apply to that which is produced after the suffix *lyap* has been applied; this will be its technical name. Alternatively, let it be a restrictive rule (*niyama*). But was it not stated that because of the intervention by the *vikaraṇas*, the restriction would not apply?
This is not a fault. The teacher’s practice indicates that the restriction is stronger than the *vikaraṇas*, since—

This rule regarding the prescription of suffixes (*vikaraṇa-vidhi*) relies upon the *ātmanepada* and *parasmaipada* terminations, as seen in the rules: "after roots beginning with *puṣ*, those beginning with *dyut*, and those marked with *ṛt* or *ḷt*, the *parasmaipada* [is used]," and "the *ātmanepada* [is used] optionally. This, however, is not an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*). For the *ātmanepada* and *parasmaipada* terminations are already established as substitutes for *la*. If that is so, then what about the fact that he teaches the optionality in the rule "optionally when there is no prefix"?

(P_1,3.12.3) KA_I,275.16–277.18 Ro_II, 237–244: But what, then, is this restriction regarding the suffixes (*pratyayaniyama*)? Is it that the *ātmanepada* occurs only after roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or the letter *ṅ*?

Is it that the *ātmanepada* occurs only in the sense of the action for oneself (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), or rather is it a restriction on the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha-niyama*)—namely, that the *ātmanepada* occurs only after roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or the suffix *ṅ*, and that the *ātmanepada* occurs only in the sense of the action for oneself and the object? And what is the distinction here? In that case, if it were a restriction on the suffix (*pratyaya-niyama*), there would be the need for a supplementary statement (*śeṣavacana*).

Because the *parasmaipada* has not been excluded. In that case, if there were a restriction on the suffixes, the term "śeṣa" (remainder) must be included for the purpose of restricting the *parasmaipada*: "After a root other than those [already specified], the *parasmaipada* occurs when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. What is the reason? Because the *parasmaipada* has not been excluded. The suffixes are restricted, but the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) are unrestricted. In such a situation, the *parasmaipada* would apply. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "śeṣa" is necessary.

This must be stated for the purpose of restricting the *parasmaipada* endings: that the *parasmaipada* occurs only after the "remainder" (*śeṣāt*) and not from anything else. The statement regarding the *ātmanepada* for *kyaṣ* is necessary because of the restriction [of *parasmaipada*] elsewhere. It should be stated that *kyaṣ* takes the *ātmanepada*:
*lohitāyati*, *lohitāyate*. But what is the reason that it is not established? Because of the restriction of that [the *parasmaipada*] elsewhere. That...

For [the suffix] is restricted elsewhere, yet it is stated that it does not apply there; therefore, it will occur by virtue of that specific statement. Well then, let there be a restriction regarding the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha-niyama*). If there is a restriction regarding the meaning of the verbal root, there would be an absence of others. If there is a restriction regarding the meaning of the verbal root, other suffixes would not occur; thus, the *anudātta-ṅit* suffixes such as *tṛc* and so forth would not apply. This is not a fault, because they have no scope [otherwise].

The suffixes beginning with *tṛc* are also prescribed; they will occur by virtue of an explicit statement (*vacana*). The suffixes beginning with *tṛc* have their own scope (*sāvakāśa*). What is their scope? Their scope consists of [roots] that take the *parasmaipada* endings. Even there, they do not apply because of a restrictive rule (*niyama*). In that case, the suffixes beginning with *tavya* would not apply to the sense of the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*) due to the restrictive rule. But the suffixes beginning with *tavya* also lack scope. They too will occur by virtue of an explicit statement.

In that case, because of the restriction regarding the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), the suffix *ciṇ* would not apply. [Response: Even so, *ciṇ* will occur by virtue of an explicit statement (*vacana*). In that case, because of the restriction regarding the abstract action and the object, the suffix *ghañ* would not apply. [Response: In that instance as well, the previously mentioned mention of "object" (*karma-grahaṇa*) applies. Where was it mentioned? In the rule *aṇ karmaṇi ca*. But in that context, it is a qualifier of the *upapada* (governing word), whereas here it is a qualifier of what is to be expressed (*abhidheya*).

And this is the meaning here: that which is commenced for one purpose does not become something else for another purpose. Indeed, even if one thing is commenced, it does not become something else merely by following after [another]; for a lizard, though it crawls, does not become a snake simply because of its crawling.

As for what was said—that "that which is commenced for one purpose does not become something else for another purpose"—even that which is commenced for one purpose [can] become something else for another purpose.

It is as follows: canals are constructed for the sake of rice; from them water is drunk and used for ritual sipping, and the rice is cultivated. As for what was said—that indeed nothing other than the original subject arises through a subsequent application—it may be so in the case of substances, for a lizard does not become a snake simply by crawling.

This would indeed be so. However, a word, when connected with this or that specific attribute, becomes a qualifier of each of those attributes. Furthermore, there is the mention of the "remainder" (śeṣa). And the term "remainder" must be employed [in the rule], as in: "From the remainder, when the agent is expressed, the *parasmaipada* endings are used. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of restricting the remainder. The meanings of the verbal roots (*prakṛti*) are restricted; the suffixes (*pratyaya*) are unrestricted.

Those [suffixes] would also apply to the *śeṣa* (the remainder). Therefore, the mention of *śeṣa* must be made [in the rule], so that it may be understood: "From the *śeṣa*, when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed, only the *parasmaipada* suffixes occur, and no others. Furthermore, a second mention of *śeṣa* must be made for the purpose of prohibiting the *parasmaipada* suffixes in cases where the *ātmanepada* would otherwise apply to the agent. Thus, a second mention of *śeṣa* is required to prohibit the *parasmaipada* in those instances where the *ātmanepada* is the proper domain regarding the agent.

It should be stated: "After the remainder [the suffixes apply] to the remainder. This [rule] should not apply here: *bhidyate kuśūlaḥ svayam eva* ("The granary bursts open by itself"). In which view does this fault occur? In the view where the meaning of the base is restricted. First, there is no fault in the restriction of the meaning of the base. For in that case, the meanings of the bases are fixed, while the suffixes are unfixed. Therefore, there is no purpose in including the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*), and it is precisely because of the mention of the agent that the fault arises.
In that case, this is the fault when the restriction applies to the suffixes (*pratyaya*): the suffixes are restricted, while the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) are unrestricted.

In that situation, the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) must be made for the purpose of excluding the passive (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). And because of the mention of the agent, this fault arises. However, when the restriction applies to the meanings of the base, the mention of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) can be omitted. How so? Because the meanings of the base [are already restricted].
The suffixes are unrestricted, while the *niyama* (restriction) is fixed; therefore, I shall state that "the *parasmaipada* occurs. That will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning:

"where both *parasmaipada* and another [suffix] would otherwise apply, there the *parasmaipada* alone occurs. In that case, if the restriction applies to the suffixes, a second mention of the term *śeṣa* must be made. It need not be made; rather, there is a division of the *yoga* (sūtra).

It will be performed [as follows]: *anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam* (the Ātmanepada occurs after roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel or Ṅ); then *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (the Ātmanepada occurs in the sense of the abstract action and the object); then *kartari* (the Ātmanepada occurs in the sense of the agent).

And in the sense of the agent, the Ātmanepada occurs in the sense of both the abstract action and the object. Then [comes] *karmavyatihāre* (the Ātmanepada occurs when there is a reciprocal action); here too, "in the sense of the agent" (*kartari*) applies alone, while "in the sense of the abstract action and the object" (*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*) is discontinued. If that is so, then just as it occurs in the sense of the object and the agent, it would likewise occur in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*).

[The rule] would apply to the agent: "Joy comes to one who lives; nothing harms him. A second *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) will be made: first, *anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam* ("the *ātmanepada* [suffixes] follow roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel or the letter ṅ"); then, *bhāve* ("in the sense of the abstract state"); then, *karmaṇi* ("in the sense of the object"). And in the sense of the object, the *ātmanepada* occurs.
Then, *kartari* ("in the sense of the agent"). And in the sense of the agent, the *ātmanepada* occurs. [This applies] when there is the sense of the object.

[The word] *anuvartate* [is understood]. [The word] *bhāve* has ceased [to apply]. Then, after [the rule for] *karmavyatihāra*, [the word] *kartari* alone [applies]. [The word] *karmaṇi* has ceased [to apply]. Even so, the mention of *śeṣa* must be made for the sake of [the rule] *anuparābhyāṃ kṛñaḥ*. Let it not occur here: *anukriyate svayam eva* ("he acts for himself"), *parākriyate svayam eva* ("he acts against himself"). But surely this [result] also follows from the analysis of the rules (*yogavibhāga*)?
Thus it is established. It is not established. That acquisition (*prāpti*) which follows immediately can be set aside by means of a rule-separation (*yogavibhāga*).

Why is this so? Because a rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediate. The subsequent acquisition is not prohibited; therefore, it will take effect. But does this acquisition not set aside the preceding acquisition? No, for once it has been prohibited, it lacks the power [to do so].
[This is] so that [the suffix] may not be barred. If that is the case, then the mention of *kartṛ* (agent) in the rule *kartari karmavyatihāre* is rejected.

That [term], being the subject under discussion, will carry over (*anuvartate*) into the subsequent rule: *śeṣāt kartari*. Why is it stated *kartari kartari*? It is so that [the suffix] may apply only where the agent is indeed the agent; whereas in the case of one who is both an agent and something else...

"Let there not be an agent in that case. Therefore, [the rule] "after *anu* and *pari*, [the suffix *lyap* is used] after the root *kṛ*" applies when the agent is the referent; this is understood from the very statement "when the agent is the referent. (P. 1.3.14.1) It should be stated: "when there is a mutual exchange of action. For if it were stated as "when there is a mutual exchange of object," it would undesirably apply in this instance: [karma-vyatihāra].

In the case of "they cut the grain of Devadatta mutually" (*devadattasya dhānyam vyatilunanti*), the forms *vyatilunate* and *vyatipunate* would not occur here. Therefore, that [rule] must be stated. It need not be stated. For in common usage, people metaphorically designate an action as the "object" (*karman*). One asks, "What action will you perform? or "What object will you perform? Even so, it must be formulated thus: [the rule applies] between the artificial (*kṛtrima*) and the non-artificial (*akṛtrima*).

Trust arises toward that which is artificial. Action (*kriyā*) is also an artificial object (*karma*). [The definition] is not established, for it is said that "the object is that which is most desired by the agent.
How indeed could action itself be that which is most desired by action? Action is also that which is most desired by action. By what action?
By the action of perceiving (*sampaśyati*), by the action of desiring (*prārthayati*), and by the action of determining (*adhyavasyati*).

Or rather: here, a person who acts with foresight first perceives some object through his intellect. Once it is perceived, there arises a desire; once desired, a determination; once determined, an undertaking; once undertaken, an accomplishment; and once accomplished, the attainment of the fruit. Thus, action (*kriyā*) is also an artificial object (*karma*). In this way, both [action and its object]—

[If this were not stated,] it would follow that both artificial (*kṛtrima*) and non-artificial (*akṛtrima*) [objects] would be included. Therefore, it should be stated: "when there is a reciprocal action" (*kriyāvyatihāre*).

It need not be stated. Here, it is established by merely saying "when there is a reciprocal action in the sense of the agent" (*kartari vyatihāre*). Now, since this is already established, the purpose of employing the mention of "object" (*karman*) is so that [the rule] may apply when there is a reciprocal action, but not when there is a reciprocal object (*karmavyatihāra*).

(P_1,3.14.2) Now, what is the purpose of mentioning the *kartṛ* (agent)? The mention of the agent in rules such as those concerning the exchange of actions (*karmavyatihāra*) is for the purpose of excluding the *bhāva* (impersonal action) and *karman* (passive).
The mention of the agent is made in the case of the exchange of actions so that the *ātmanepada* ending may not occur here by virtue of [the rule governing] the *bhāva* and *karman*.

Thus [it is said]. For otherwise, if there were a prohibition [of the *ātmanepada*] in that context, there would be a prohibition regarding both the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). If the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*) were not made, the *ātmanepada* would undesirably apply even to the state and the object. What is the fault in that? If there were a prohibition in that case, there would be a prohibition regarding the state and the object as well. What is the fault in that? If there were a prohibition in that case, by this [rule], the *ātmanepada* would [also] apply to the state and the object.

A prohibition would apply [to all]. For example, in the cases *vyatigamyante grāmāḥ* ("the villages go against one another") and *vyatihanyante dasyavaḥ* ("the bandits strike at one another"). Or rather, this fault does not arise. Why? Because of the prohibition of what is immediately preceding.

That is to say, there is a prohibition of that which is the immediately preceding rule for prescribing the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). How is this so? Because the rule applies to what is immediately preceding.

Or rather, there is a prohibition [of the previous rule]. The prior application remains unprohibited; by that [prior application], the desired result will occur. But does this [subsequent] application not sublate the prior application? No, for once it has been prohibited, it is unable to sublate. Then the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) must be made for the sake of the subsequent rule. It need not be made. It is indeed performed right there [in the previous rule] under the heading of "the remainder" (*śeṣāt*).

247. An addition must be made regarding the prohibition of *has* and others. An addition must be made to the prohibition concerning *has* and so forth: *vyatihasanti*, *vyatijalpanti*, *vyatipaṭhanti*. There is no prohibition for *hari* and *vahi*. It should be stated that there is no prohibition for *hari* and *vahi*: *sampraharante rājānaḥ*, *saṃvivahante gargaḥ*.

Thus, *vahiḥ* does not have the sense of "going outside. *Vahiḥ* refers to the action of reaching another location. (Pāṇini 1.3.16) It should also be stated: "and when *pra* or *paraspara* are used as upapadas. For example: *parasparasya vyatilunanti* ("they cut each other's [hair]"), *parasparasya vyatipunanti* ("they pierce each other").
The mention of *upasarga* (preverb) must be made [in the rule], as in the example: *parā jayati senā* (“the army conquers”). Well then, it must be stated.
No, it need not be stated. For even though this word *parā* is seen to deviate [from its status as a preverb], it is both a preverb and a non-preverb.

Furthermore, this particle *vi* is indeed a prefix whose application is never seen to fail; what else besides a prefix could possibly serve as its companion? For example, if one says, "There is need for a second for this cow," it is the cow itself that is brought forward, not a horse or a donkey.

(P_1.3.20) Regarding *āṅo daḥ avyasanakriyasya*: it should be stated that [the rule] "after *āṅ*, [the root] *dā* [is replaced by *āda*], provided the action is not one of separating" applies here as well, so that forms such as *vipādikām vyādadāti* ("he opens his foot-sore") and *kūlam vyādadāti* ("he opens the bank") may occur. Therefore, that [restriction] must indeed be stated.

It need not be stated. Here, the rule is already established by the [Pāṇinian sūtra] *āṅo do 'nāsye*. Since this is already established, the reason he includes the mention of "moving" (*viharaṇa*) is so that [the substitution of *da* for *dā*] may also apply when the action is identical to moving the mouth (*āsyaviharaṇa*). And of the same nature as the action of moving the mouth is the action here as well. [This also applies] from [the rule concerning roots whose object is] one's own limb (*svāṅgakarma*).
It should be stated that [the rule applies] "also when the action concerns one's own limbs. This should not apply here: *vyādadate pipīlikāḥ pataṅgamukham* ("the ants open the mouth of the moth").
(Pāṇini 1.3.21) The mention of *upasarga* (preverbs) must be made. This should not apply here: *anu krīḍati māṇavakam* ("he plays along with the boy"). [This applies only after] *sam*.

Regarding *akūjane* (not making a sound): it should be stated that [the rule] applies when there is no making of a sound. Let it not apply here: *saṅkrīḍanti śakaṭāni* ("the carts play"). Regarding *āgameḥ kṣamāyām*: an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for *āgam* in the sense of "endurance" (*kṣamā*). Example: *āgamayasva tāvat māṇavaka* ("wait a moment, young man"). Regarding *śikṣeḥ jijñāsāyām*: an addition must be made for *śikṣ* in the sense of "desire to know" (*jijñāsā*). Example: *vidyāsu śikṣate* ("he trains in the sciences"), *dhanuṣi* ("in archery").

One learns [the following]. Regarding the root *kṛ* (kirati) in the senses of "joy," "livelihood," and "making a dwelling": an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the root *kṛ* in the senses of joy, livelihood, and making a dwelling. "The bull leaps about (*apaskirate*) out of joy. "The cock leaps about seeking food. "The dog leaps about seeking shelter. Regarding the root *hṛ* (harati) in the sense of habitual movement: an addition must be made for the root *hṛ* in the sense of habitual movement.

Horses imitate their father; cows imitate their mother. Regarding the rule "with *āṅ* [the suffix *ātmanepada* is used] with *nu* and *pracchi*": an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for *nu* and *pracchi* when preceded by *āṅ*. Example: "The jackal howls at" (*ānute śṛgālaḥ*); "He asks leave of his teacher" (*āpṛcchate gurum*). Regarding the rule "with *nāth* in the sense of benediction" (*āśiṣi nāthaḥ*): an addition must be made for *nāth* in the sense of benediction. Example: "He hopes for clarified butter" (*sarpiṣo nāthate*); "He hopes for honey" (*madhuno nāthate*). Regarding the rule "with *śap* in the sense of cursing" (*śapa upalambhane*).

An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the perception of an oath (*śapaḥ upalambhane*): *devadattāya śapate*, *yajñadattāya śapate*. (Pāṇini 1.3.22) Regarding *āṅaḥ sthaḥ pratijñāne*: it should be stated that *stha* following *āṅ* [governs the dative] in the sense of promising (*pratijñāne*). *astim sakāram ātiṣṭhate* ("He promises the letter *s* for the root *as*"). *Āgamau guṇavṛddhī ātiṣṭhate* ("He promises the augmentations *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*"). *Vikārau guṇavṛddhī* ("The modifications *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*... [are promised].

[The rule] *ātiṣṭhate* (Pāṇini 1.3.24). Regarding *uda īhāyām*: it should be stated that [the substitution of *sthā* for *āṅ* occurs] after *ud* when there is "striving" (*īhā*). This should not apply here: *uttiṣṭhati senā* ("the army stands up").

(P_1,3.25) *upāt pūjāsaṅgatakaraṇayoḥ*. It should be stated: "after *upa*, [the *ātmanepada* endings are used] in the senses of honoring (*pūjā*) and joining together (*saṅgatakaraṇa*). In the sense of honoring: *ādityam upatiṣṭhate* ("he honors the sun"); *candramasam upatiṣṭhate* ("he honors the moon"). In the sense of joining together: *rathikān upatiṣṭhate* ("he joins with the charioteers"); *aśvārohān* ("[he joins with] the horsemen").

He attends upon [the sun]. Even among many who are without minds, there is one who possesses a mind. Behold, in this army of monkeys, he who attends upon the sun—do not think that he alone possesses a mind just as we do. This too is his monkey-nature that he attends upon the sun. Another said:

It should be stated that [the prefix *upa*] is used in the senses of "worshiping a deity," "forming an association," and "making a friend. An example for "forming an association" has already been cited. For "making a friend": *rathikān upatiṣṭhate* ("he courts the charioteers"), *aśvārohān upatiṣṭhate* ("he courts the horsemen"). For "on a path":

*ayaṃ panthāḥ srughnam upatiṣṭhate* ("this path leads to Srughna"), *ayaṃ panthāḥ sāketam upatiṣṭhate* ("this path leads to Saketa"). Or, it is used optionally when there is a desire to obtain (*lipsā*). Or, it is used optionally when there is a desire to obtain.

Thus it should be stated: "A beggar approaches a Brahmin family," or "A beggar waits upon a Brahmin family" (Pāṇini 1.4.27). [The rule] applies only after an intransitive verb (*akarmaka*). For example: "The goldsmith heats the gold. And [the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied] after a verb whose object is one's own body part (*svāṅgakarmaka*).

It should be stated that [the rule applies] "also after [roots] whose object is one's own limb (*svāṅga-karmaka*). Examples: *uttapate pāṇī* (he warms his hands); *vitapate pāṇī*; *uttapate pṛṣṭham* (he warms his back); *vitapate pṛṣṭham*. Now, regarding the rule *udvibhyām*, what is given as a counter-example? It is *niṣṭapyate*.
But for what reason is only the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) cited as an example, rather than the active voice (*parasmaipada*) which should have been cited as a counter-example?
But this [verb] *tap* is intransitive (*akarmaka*). And even intransitive verbs become transitive (*sakarmaka*) when accompanied by a prefix (*sopasarga*).

It is not the case that transitive verbs become intransitive without a reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*). As for what was said—"it is not the case that transitive verbs become intransitive without a reflexive agent"—even without a reflexive agent, transitive [verbs] [become intransitive].
They become intransitive. For example: "the river flows" (*nadī vahati*) is intransitive; "he carries a load" (*bhāraṃ vahati*) is transitive.
Therefore, "he heats [it] out" (*niṣṭapati*) should be cited as a counter-example.

256–257. An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the roots *vid*, *pracchi*, and *svar* after the prefix *sam* when used with verbs such as *gami*. An addition must be made for the roots *vid*, *pracchi*, and *svar* after *sam*: *saṃvitté*, *saṃpṛccháte*, *saṃsvaraté*. And [an addition must be made] after *ṛ*, *śru*, and *dṛśi*.
It should be stated: "And after *ṛ*, *śru*, and *dṛśi*": *mā samārta*, *mā samarṣātām*, *mā samarṣata*. [The root] *ṛ*; *śru*.

He hears (*saṃśṛṇute*). He sees (*sampaśyate*). Regarding the rule "after a prefix (*upasarga*), [the *ātmanepada* endings are used] for the roots *as* and *ūh*, there is an option (*vāvacana*)": it should be stated that after a prefix, [the *ātmanepada* endings are used] optionally for *as* and *ūh*. Thus: *nirasyati* / *nirasyate*; *samūhati* / *samūhate*. (P_1.3.40) KA_I,282.20–21 Ro_II, [page number].

257. [The rule applies] when there is the rising of luminaries (*jyotiṣām udgamane*). It should be stated: "when there is the rising of luminaries. This is so that it does not apply here: *ākrāmati dhūmo harmyatalam* ("the smoke ascends to the roof-terrace"). (P. 1.3.48) [Question: For what purpose is the phrase "of those with distinct speech" (*vyaktavācām*) used? [Example: *varatanu saṃpravadanti kukkuṭāḥ* ("O slender-limbed one, the cocks are crowing"). [This is an example of] "those with distinct speech."

Even when this is said, the rule would still apply here, for these [birds] also have distinct speech. Furthermore, when a cock crows with distinct speech, it is said, "the cock speaks. If that is so, then the term "vyaktavācām" (of those with distinct speech) is stated; for indeed, all [birds] have distinct speech. In that case, the understanding will be one of degree: "those who have more clearly distinct speech. Which ones?

And it is even better. For those [beings] in whose speech the phonemes beginning with *a* are manifested, and for whom the phonemes beginning with *a* are not manifested in speech—[it is argued that] for these too, the phonemes beginning with *a* are indeed manifested in speech. And thus they are manifested; for so it is said:
"The chickens [cry] 'kukkuṭ, kukkuṭ'. But they do not speak in that way. This is merely an imitation of their [sound]. Now...

Or rather, it is not understood thus: "those whose speech is distinct are these 'distinct-speakers' (vyaktavācaḥ). How then? It is: "those in whose speech the phonemes (varṇāḥ) are distinct are these 'distinct-speakers'.
Regarding the rule *avād graḥ*: here, it should be stated that [the root] is *gṛ* (from *girati*). It should not apply to *gṛṇāti*.
Well then, must it be stated? No, it need not be stated, because such usage does not exist. When it is said *avād graḥ*, there is no usage of *gṛṇāti* preceded by the prefix *ā*.

What is the purpose of [the rule] "after that which is joined with the third case"? [Consider: *ubhau lokau cañcarasi imam ca amum ca devala* ("O Devala, you wander through both worlds, this one and that one").
Even when the rule "after that which is joined with the third case" is stated, it would still apply here, for there too there is a connection with the third case. Thus...

If it is said that this third case ending (tṛtīyā) occurs in the sense of the fourth (caturthī), how indeed could a third case ending occur in the sense of a fourth? In that case, by this rule, both the third case ending and the middle voice (ātmanepada) are prescribed in the usage of the unrefined (*aśiṣṭa*): *dāsyā saṃprayacchate* ("he gives with a female slave"), *vṛṣalyā saṃprayacchate* ("he gives with a low-caste woman"). For as for the usage of the refined (*śiṣṭa*), one says: *brāhmaṇībhyaḥ saṃprayacchati* ("he gives to the Brahmin women").

Thus it must be understood in that case. If this is so, there is no purpose served by this grammatical rule (*yoga*). By what, then, will the third case (*tṛtīyā*) and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) be established? [Response: The third case shall apply when joined with *saha* (along with), and the rule for the middle voice shall apply in the sense of reciprocal action (*vyatihāra*). [Objection:

The third case will indeed occur by the rule "the third case is used for the subordinate element when joined with *saha*," and the middle voice will occur by the rule "the middle voice is used for the agent when there is reciprocal action."

(P_1,3.56) Why does [the suffix] not occur here: *svaṃ śāṭakāntam upayacchati* ("he takes his own end of the cloth")? It should occur when one makes what is not one's own (*asva*) one's own (*sva*). If that is so, then [the suffix] would apply in the sense of "appropriating" (*svīkaraṇa*). The formations of secondary derivatives (*taddhita-vṛtti*) are diverse.

A secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix is not produced from this [root]. (Pāṇini 1.3.58). Regarding the prohibition of the root *jñā* after the prefix *anu*, the mention of "transitive" (*sakarmaka*) is for the sake of the prohibition of *jñā* after *anu*. The mention of "transitive" in the prohibition of *jñā* after *anu* [is necessary].

It should be stated that [the prohibition] does not apply here: *auṣadhasya anujijñāsate*. Or rather, it need not be stated. Why? Because the subsequent rule prescribes [the ātmanepada] for an intransitive verb. It need not be stated. What is the reason? Because the subsequent rule prescribes [the ātmanepada] for an intransitive verb. For the root *jñā*, when it is intransitive, the ātmanepada is prescribed by the subsequent connection [Pāṇini 1.3.57], namely "as before, after *san*" (*pūrvavat sanaḥ*). Thus, the prohibition applies to the preceding rule.

And this is a prohibition of the preceding rule. Furthermore, that [preceding rule] was formulated for the sake of transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*). How, then, is it known that this is a prohibition of the preceding rule? Because a grammatical operation—whether a prescription (*vidhi*) or a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*)—applies only to what is immediately contiguous. How, then, is it known that the formulation is for the sake of transitive verbs? From the fact that the suffix *san* occurs after the intransitive verb *jñā*.
Since there is no purpose for the mention of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), it is understood as being for the sake of [the verb] having an object (*sakarmaka*).

Because the root *śad* with the suffix *śit* depends upon the active voice (*parasmaipada*), there is an absence of the middle voice. This is because the root *śad* with the suffix *śit* depends upon the active voice.

There is an absence of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). [The forms are] *śīyate*, *śīyete*, *śīyante*. Furthermore, sir, it is said that for the root *śad*, [the substitution of *śnā* occurs] before *śit* affixes in the active voice (*parasmaipada*). Indeed, it is not explicitly stated "in the active voice," yet it is understood to apply in the active voice. How so?

After stating these two rules—"the middle voice after roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or *ṅ*" and "the middle voice in the sense of state (*bhāva*) or object (*karman*)"—[the rule] "from the remainder... (*śeṣāt*) [is stated].

The *parasmaipada* is stated [to apply] in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Thus, it is not stated specifically for the *parasmaipada* endings, yet it is understood to apply to the *parasmaipada* endings. But who would be so bold as to state these two rules and then say "from the remainder, the *parasmaipada* applies in the sense of the agent"?
What then? Having followed the entire section on *ātmanepada* without distinction, one should simply state: "from the remainder, the *parasmaipada* applies in the sense of the agent."
Thus it is said. Even so, there remains the basis for the *parasmaipada*. How? First, this must be asked:

if this were not stated, what would occur here? He says: "the *parasmaipada*. If [it is] "the *parasmaipada*," then there remains the basis for the *parasmaipada*. But it is established by the statement that the *ātmanepada* applies to the *laṭ* and other suffixes. It is established.

This [is the point]. How so? It must be stated that for the root *śad*, the *ātmanepada* endings occur after the *laṭ* and other [tenses]. [If this is said,] it is established. But then the rule (*sūtra*) is split. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. But was it not said that because the suffix *śit* (the marker of the present tense) depends on the *parasmaipada*, there is an absence of the *ātmanepada*? This is not a fault. The term *śitaḥ* is not a fifth case (ablative). What then? It is a sixth case (genitive) expressing a relationship.

[The question is: What is the *śit* [augment] of the root *śad*? [The answer is: It is the *prakṛti* (the base form). [This is understood from the rule] "of *śad* which has *śit* as its *prakṛti*. Alternatively, one might say: "this [rule] refers to the *śit* of *śad*," yet there is no *śad* that possesses *śit*. Therefore, we shall understand it thus: "of *śad*, when it is in the domain of *śit*. Or else, even if this [principle] applies elsewhere—that the restriction (*niyama*) is stronger than the verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*)—[the interpretation remains the same].
In this case, this [rule] does not apply, for here the suffix *śit* is relied upon [in the rule].

(P_1.3.60.2) Regarding the restriction that [the augment *ṭuk*] occurs only when preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*), there must be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for cases where it is separated by an *aṭ*-augment. In the restriction concerning what is preceded by a prefix, when there is an intervention by an *aṭ*-augment...

An addition must be made [to the rule]: *nyaviśata*, *vyakrīṇīta*. For what reason, then, is it not established? Because it is separated by the augment *aṭ*. But surely this *aṭ* is a part of the verbal root (*dhātubhakta*) and will be included by the mention of "the root"? It is not established.

For the *aṭ* is said to belong to the base (*aṅga*), and the base ends with the suffix (*vikaraṇa*). Thus, that [augment] belongs to the entire complex (*saṅghātabhakta*) and cannot [be treated as part of the root].
[This would be] to include it by the mention of "dhātu" (root). If that is so, then this must be considered here:

let there be the augment *aṭ*, or let there be the suffix (*vikaraṇa*). What should be done in this case? Because it is subsequent, the augment *aṭ* [should apply]. The suffixes are obligatory; they apply whether the augment *aṭ* has been applied or not. The augment *aṭ* is also obligatory; it applies even when the suffixes have been applied.

It applies even when [the suffixes] have not been applied. The augment *aṭ* is non-eternal (*anitya*). It applies when the *vikaraṇas* (conjugational affixes) of one [element] have been applied, but not when those of another have been applied.

And a rule that applies to a different word-form becomes non-eternal. If this is so, then this must be considered here: "Let *aṭ* be applied, or let the substitution for *l* (the *l*-suffixes) be applied"? What should be done in this case? Because it is subsequent, the augment *aṭ* is applied.

The substitution of *l* (the *l*-affixes) is obligatory. It applies whether the augment *aṭ* has been applied or not. Because the substitution of *l* is obligatory, the augment *aṭ* will occur only in the case of the *ātmanepada*. If it is argued that because the substitution of *l* is obligatory, the augment *aṭ* occurs in the *ātmanepada*, [we reply: due to the fact that *aṭ* is the cause for the non-occurrence of the *ātmanepada*, there is no *ātmanepada*. Because the substitution of *l* is obligatory, the augment *aṭ* occurs only in the *ātmanepada*.

If this is said, it is replied as follows: *aṭ* is also of permanent cause (*nityanimitta*). It applies whether the substitution for the *l*-suffixes (*lādeśa*) has been made or not yet made. Because *aṭ* is of permanent cause, there is an absence of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). Therefore, an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made; therefore, an addition must be formulated. [Objection: It need not be formulated. In that case, the substitution for the *l*-suffixes is internal (*antaraṅga*). [Reply: We do not dispute that it is internal.

"It is not internal. Let it be that this [rule] is both eternal (*nitya*) and internal (*antaraṅga*). For here, when the substitute *l* (the verbal suffix) has been applied, three operations simultaneously present themselves:
the *vikaraṇa* affixes, the augment *aṭ*, and the restriction (*niyama*). Now, if the restriction were obtained from all sides, the task would be accomplished.

But that [suffix] cannot be obtained. Even if *aṭ* were obtained because of the rule "after a verbal root (*vikaraṇāt*) comes *aṭ*," it would still be applied after the suffix has been added. However, even so, that [desired form] cannot be obtained. Why? Because the *vikaraṇas* must be desired to precede the *āṅga* (the base with its suffixes) for the sake of forms such as *tarataḥ* and *taranti*. Furthermore, something else besides *aṭ* and *āṭ* must be desired to precede the *āṅga*, as in the case of *upārcchati*.

For this reason: for if *āṭ* were applied there first, the substitution of *ṛcchi* would apply to that which is preceded by *āṭ*. [Objection: But once the substitution of *ṛcchi* has been made, since it is a different word (*śabdāntara*) from that to which *āṭ* was previously applied, *āṭ* will be applied again. [Response: Then the substitution of *ṛcchi* again and *āṭ* again—this results in a cycle (*cakraka*) and a lack of finality (*avyavasthā*). [Reply: This is not a fault. As for what was said—that [the operation] must precede the *aṅga*...

The *vikaraṇas* are to be sought for the purpose that "those who were crossing over cross over. This would be established in cases where the *vikaraṇas* are obligatory (*nitya*) and the suffix (*āṅga*) is non-obligatory (*anitya*); there, the *vikaraṇas* would indeed precede the suffix. However, in cases where both are obligatory, the suffix takes precedence due to its higher status. As for what was said—that even in the presence of *aṭ* and *āṭ*, another suffix (*āṅga*) should come first—[that is not so].

"It should be sought because it approaches"—this is the meaning. Let there be *āṭ* here. Once *āṭ* has been applied, and the substitution of *ṛcchi* has been made for that which is accompanied by *āṭ*, since *āṭ* has not yet been applied to the other word-form, *āṭ* will be applied once again. But was it not said that the repeated application of *ṛcchi* and the repeated application of *āṭ* would result in a cycle (*cakraka*) and thus lead to an infinite regress? This is not a fault; for in cases involving cycles...

The determination is based on what is desired. Alternatively, *neḥ* is not a genitive case; what then? It is a genitive of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*). [The meaning is: "that which is qualified by *ni-*.

And what is qualified by *ni-*? The qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Furthermore, even that which is separated [by other words] can be qualified. Alternatively, both *niḥ* is a word and *viśiḥ* is a word. And a rule concerning words (*pada-vidhi*) applies to those [words] that are semantically connected (*samarthānām*), even when they are separated.
The capacity [for the application of the rule] exists.

(P_1.3.62.1) KA_I,287.7-15 Ro_II, 268-269 What is this mention of "prior" (*pūrva*)? It refers to those roots for which the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) was prescribed prior to the suffix *san*. From those, [the suffix *sa* is applied].

Does it apply even to those [roots] ending in *san*? Or does it depend on the [preceding] rule (*yoga*)? That is to say, for those roots to which the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) was previously stated, the middle voice occurs after they end in *san*. What follows from this? If the condition depends on *san*, then the cause would be unspecified; as before, it would not be known whether the middle voice should occur after what ends in *san*. Or else...

In what follows, a rule dependent on the suffix *san* is not applicable, as in the cases of *bubhukṣate* and *upayuyukṣate*. Let it be as you wish. For now, let it be that [the suffix] *san* is indeed depended upon. But was it not said that the cause (*nimitta*) would be unspecified? And yet, the cause is specified. How so? We shall depend upon *san* itself here as the cause, just as before.

The suffix *san* takes the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). Why? Because of the word "of *san*" (*sanaḥ*). Alternatively, let it rather depend on the [preceding] rule (*yoga*). But was it not said that a prescription cannot be established for what follows? Yet the prescription is indeed established. How so? Even in the subsequent rule, the phrase "of *san*" (*sanaḥ*) will continue to apply just as before.
(P_1,3.62.2) KA_I,287.16–288.17 Ro_II, 269–271 Why, then, is this stated? [The rule] "pūrvavat sanaḥ" is for the sake of *śad* and *mriyati*.
This undertaking is for the sake of *śad* and *mriyati*: lest there be the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) after the roots *śad* and *mriyati* when they are followed by the suffix *san*. Otherwise...

For by those two [rules], the prohibition of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) applies to the forms ending in *san*. Otherwise, if this were not stated, a prohibition of the middle voice would have to be explicitly formulated for those two forms ending in *san*: namely, *śiśitsati* and *mumūrṣati*. But how, then, does the rule "as before, after *san*" effect the prohibition of the middle voice for the forms ending in *san* derived from the roots *śad* and *mṛ*?

It is possible to understand [the rule]. This is an instruction using the suffix *vati*, and in an instruction using *vati*, one may supply an ellipsis according to one's preference. For example: "In Madra there are barley-grains, like in Uśīnara"—[one may supply] "they exist" or "they do not exist. "Her artistic skills are like her mother's"—[one may supply] "they exist" or "they do not exist.
In the same way here as well, one may supply the ellipsis "it occurs" or "it does not occur. We shall support the ellipsis with the words "it does not occur."

Just as in the previous rules (*pūrvayoga*) the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) does not occur after roots ending in *san*, so too here it does not occur after the roots *śad* and *mri* when they end in *san*. If, then, this rule is intended for the sake of the roots *śad* and *mri*, the prescription would not apply to cases such as *āsisiṣate* and *śiśayiṣate*. Alternatively, if it is for the sake of the general prescription, [it applies] to *śad* and *mri* when they end in *san*.

The *ātmanepada* ending would apply. Let it be as you wish. Let it be, for the time being, for the purpose of prohibition. But was it not said that a positive injunction (*vidhi*) cannot be established? Yet a positive injunction is indeed established. How so? This very fact indicates that the *ātmanepada* occurs after a root with the suffix *san*, since [the rule] prescribes the *ātmanepada* for the roots *śad* and *mriyati* when they are followed by *san*.

It teaches a prohibition. Or, alternatively, let it have the sense of a positive injunction (*vidhi*). But was it not stated that the *ātmanepada* would result from the two roots *śad* and *mṛ*, when they are followed by *san*? This is not a fault. The previously mentioned "not" (*na*) after *san* will be carried over (*anuvartate*). Where was it previously mentioned? In the rule "Not [the *ātmanepada*] after *san* following *jñā*, *śru*, *smṛ*, and *dṛś*; nor after *jñā* preceded by *anu*; nor after *san* following a transitive root; nor after [roots] preceded by *prati* and *āṅ*."

[The rule] "after *san*" applies to *śadeḥ* (from *śad*), as in *śiṣatsati*; it applies to *mriyateḥ* (from *mṛ*), as in *mumūrṣati*; and it applies to the *luṅ* and *liṅ* [optative] after *san*, as in *sisaniṣati*.

Now, in this context, the phrase "as before" (*pūrvavat*) and "after *san*" (*sanaḥ*) continue to apply, while "not" (*na*) has ceased to apply. By doing so, that which was stated—that the cause [of the substitution] would be unspecified—is also rendered faultless. Or rather, there is no concern here regarding the roots *śad* and *mṛ*.

The *ātmanepada* affix would result after [roots ending in] *san* and *na*. What is the reason? It is stated that "after the root *śad*, when followed by a *śit* [affix], [the *ātmanepada* occurs]," yet the root *śad* alone is not the cause for the *ātmanepada*. What then? The *śit* affix is also a cause. Or, even if it is the root *śad* itself that is the cause, it must be followed by a *śit* affix. And this [root *śad*] followed by *san* does not become followed by a *śit* affix. In that case where the *śit* is not relied upon—what then?

Regarding the rule *mriyateḥ luṅliṅoḥ ca*: here too, it is not the root *mri* alone that is the cause for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). What then? Both the *luṅ* and *liṅ* suffixes are also causes. Or, even if it were the root *mri* itself, it would be the cause only when followed by *luṅ* or *liṅ*;
and this [desiderative] *san* suffix is not followed by *luṅ* or *liṅ*.

(P_1,3.62.3) KA_I,288.18-289.8 Ro_II, 271-272 But is it the case that the observation of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) belonging to the original [root] is extended (*atidiśyate*) to the [root] with the suffix *san* as well? It ought to be so; for since the original [root] was observed to take the middle voice, there is the occurrence of the middle voice for the [root] with *san*.

If it is argued that [the rule] is not established for *gup* and the others because we observe the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) for the preceding [roots], then the application of the middle voice would not occur after the desiderative suffix (*san*) in the case of *gup* and the others—such as in *jugupsate* and *mīmāṃsate*.
For we do not see either the middle voice or the active voice (*parasmaipada*) for these roots prior to the addition of *san*. However, [the desired result] is established.

This is established by the extension of the characteristic (liṅga) of the preceding [root]. How so? That which is the characteristic of the middle voice (ātmanepada) belonging to the preceding [root] is extended to that which ends in *san* as well. However, there must be a prohibition of the characteristic in the case of *kṛñ* and others.

Indeed, a prohibition of the characteristic must be stated for *kṛñ* and others, as in *anucikīrṣati* and *parācikīrṣati*. Let it be, then, that the middle voice occurs for those [roots] prior to *san*.

"It is observed that [the suffix] *san* is added even after those [roots] which already possess [the *ātmanepada* endings]. Now, if it is argued: "But was it not stated that because the *ātmanepada* is seen after the preceding [root], the *ātmanepada* status applies to the [derivative root] ending in *san*? [The reply is: "If so, there would be no established application for *gup* and the others. This is not a fault; it will occur by virtue of the power of the assignment of the *anubandha*. Alternatively, a characteristic (*liṅga*) applied to a part becomes a qualifier of the whole. For example:

A grammatical marker (*liṅga*) applied to the thigh or the ear of a cow becomes a qualifier of the whole (*samudāya*). If a marker applied to a part becomes a qualifier of the whole, then it would follow [undesirably] even in cases such as *jugupsayati* and *mīmāṃsāyati*.
This is not a fault. Of which whole does a marker applied to a part become a qualifier? That [whole] to which it belongs.

That which is a part (*avayava*) does not deviate from the whole (*samudāya*), nor does it deviate from the suffix *san*, but it does deviate from the causative suffix *ṇic*. For example, a mark made on the thigh or the ear of a cow serves as a distinguishing characteristic (*viśeṣaka*) of that very cow, and not of the entire herd of cows.

The mention of "pratyaya" (affix) is for the sake of the causative suffix *ṇic*. The mention of the affix must be made; it should be stated that [the rule applies] "as before, after an affix. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of the causative suffix *ṇic*, so that [the operation] may also apply after a stem ending in *ṇic*. For example: *ākusmayate*, *vikusmayate*, *hṛṇīyate*, *mahīyate*. What is the fault in that? In that case, there would be a prohibition regarding the causative *ṇic* used in the sense of "motive" (*hetu*).

In that case, a prohibition must be stated for the causative suffix *ṇic* when it follows a root with a causal meaning, as in *āsayati* and *śāyayati*. Furthermore, the rule would have to be modified. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. How then are forms such as *ākusmayate*, *vikusmayate*, *hṛṇīyate*, and *mahīyate* explained? They will be accounted for by the power of the inclusion of the indicatory letter (*anubandha*). Alternatively, a characteristic mark applied to a constituent part serves to distinguish the whole; just as, for example:

A marker (liṅga) applied to the thigh or the ear of a cow serves as a distinguishing characteristic of the whole animal. If a marker applied to a part serves as a distinguishing characteristic of the whole, then [the rule] would also apply here in the cases of *hṛṇīyayati* and *mahīyayati*.
To which whole does a marker applied to a part serve as a distinguishing characteristic? It serves as a distinguishing characteristic of that whole of which the part is not a constituent.

It deviates [from its primary referent], yet it does not deviate from one thing; however, it does deviate from the *ṇic* suffix. For example, a mark made on the thigh or the ear of a cow serves as a distinguishing characteristic only for that specific cow, and not for the entire herd of cows.

274. What is the purpose of including *kṛñ*? It is so that it does not apply here: *īhāmāsa*, *īhāmāsatuḥ*, *īhāmāsuḥ*. And how is it that there is the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of the verb *as* in these cases? It is understood that in those instances, a pratyāhāra (a grammatical abbreviation) is intended. But how is it known that a pratyāhāra is intended there? From the inclusion of *kṛñ* here. Why, then, is a pratyāhāra intended here [in this specific rule]?

It does not apply here, precisely because of the inclusion of the root *kṛ* [in the rule]. Now, why does it not apply here: *udumbhām cakāra*, *udubjām cakāra*? Is it not said that "it is like [a verb] having the affix *ām*"? And yet, we do not see an *ātmanepada* ending here following from the affix *ām*.
We do not say "by this [rule]. What then? The *ātmanepada* occurs for roots marked with a circumflex (*svarita*) or the marker *ṇi* when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent.
"It happens"—this is not a fault. Here, it will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), namely: "only like the *āmpratyaya*.

If it were a restrictive rule, the injunction would not apply to cases such as *īhām cakre* and *ūhām cakre*. But the injunction does indeed apply. How so? Because the phrase "as before" (*pūrvavat*) continues [from the previous rule]. Thus, it means "like the *āmpratyaya* and as before."
(P_1,3.64) It should be stated: "after [a root] preceded by a prefix beginning with a vowel. As in: *udyuṅkte*, *anuyuṅkte*. Another says: it should be stated:
"after [a root] preceded by a prefix beginning or ending with a vowel. As in: *prayuṅkte*, *niyuṅkte*, *niniyuṅkte*.

(P_1,3.65) Why is the mention of [the root] situated in a different location made? Why could it not simply be stated as "samaḥ gamādiṣu" (after *sam*, in the case of *gam* and so on)? [The answer is: "After *sam*, [the suffix *liṭ* is used] for *kṣṇuva* when it has an object (*sakarmaka*). This undertaking is for the sake of cases where there is an object; for in that context, the term "akarmakāt" (when it is intransitive) continues to apply.

It should be stated: "not in the sense of bending or crookedness. This is so that it may also apply here, as in: *prabhujati vāsasī* (he unfolds the two garments) and *nibhujati jānuśirasī* (he bends the knees and the head). Then, must it be stated? It need not be stated. For that root *bhuji* which means "not bending" (*anavanam*)—[it is by that meaning that the rule applies].
And its meaning is "seizing" (*grahaṇa*). Nor is "not bending down" (*anavana*) the meaning of this root *bhuji*.

When the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is prescribed after the suffix *ṇi*, the object of the non-causative (*aṇyanta*) verb is found there [as the agent]. When the middle voice is prescribed after the suffix *ṇi*...

It should be stated that when that which is the object of the non-causative (*aṇyanta*) verb becomes the very same object in the causative (*ṇyanta*), then the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*sarvaprasaṅga*). Otherwise, indeed, there would be an over-extension everywhere. It would even apply here:

"The elephant-keepers mount the elephant" (*ārohanti hastinam hastipakāḥ*); [and then] "the mounting elephant causes the men to mount the platform" (*ārohamāṇo hastī sthalam ārohayati manuṣyān*). If so, then it must be stated. No, it need not be stated. Why does it not occur?

"Elephant-drivers mount the elephant. "The mounting elephant causes the men to mount the elephant-back. I shall state it thus: the *ātmanepada* suffix occurs after the causative (*ṇi*). Then: "if that which was the object in the non-causative (*aṇau*) is also the object in the causative (*ṇau*). If that which was the object in the non-causative state becomes the very same object in the causative state, then it [the object] becomes the agent (*kartā*). "If it becomes that agent in the causative," so it is said.

If it is thus [argued] that this is the result of the object (*karman*), then it is established by virtue of being both object and agent (*karmakartṛtva*). If it is argued that it is established by virtue of being both object and agent, [we reply: this statement must be made for the purpose of excluding *yak* and *ciṇ*. If it is argued that it is established by virtue of being both object and agent, this must be stated so that *yak* and *ciṇ*, which are prescribed based on the object, do not occur. Or rather, there is no need to exclude *yak* and *ciṇ*.
Because of the prohibition. Or rather, this fault does not arise. Why? Because of the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ*.

Here, *yak* and *ciṇ* are prohibited. [The rule] "In the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ*, there is an addition for causative *ṇic* roots, as well as for *śri* and *brū*" applies. If that is so, then for the sake of those [roots] which are not causative *ṇic*, this must be stated: "Let *yak* and *ciṇ*, which are prescribed with respect to the object, not occur for that [non-causative root]."

"He raises his tail by himself" (*utpucchayate puccham svayam eva*). "He raised his tail by himself" (*udapuppucchata puccham svayam eva*). In this case as well, it must be according to what the followers of Bhāradvāja recite:

"When there is a prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ*, there is an extension [of the rule] to include the roots *ṇi*, *śri*, *granthi*, *brū*, those that are reflexive (*ātmanepada*), and those that are intransitive (*akarmaka*).
And that prohibition must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, where there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*), there would be a prohibition elsewhere.
For if this were not stated, then wherever the restriction applies, one would have to state a prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ* elsewhere than that;

for example, in *gaṇayati gaṇaṃ gopālakaḥ* ("the cowherd counts the herd") and *gaṇayati gaṇaḥ svayam eva* ("the herd counts itself"). Furthermore, a prohibition of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would also have to be stated.

The group (*gaṇa*) itself counts by itself. However, this [rule] must be stated for the purpose of prohibiting the middle voice (*ātmanepada*): "The group itself counts. Yet, the middle voice is indeed desired here. Is it merely desired, or does it also actually occur? It is both desired and it occurs. How so? This [restriction] applies to the *ṇi*-affix that follows what [otherwise] begins with *aṇ*.

The inclusion [of this rule] is for the purpose that, prior to this *ṇi*-affix, there may exist either an object (*karman*) or an agent (*kartṛ*); however, in this case, prior to this *ṇi*-affix, neither an object nor an agent exists.

If so, then this is the purpose: I shall state "provided it is not in the sense of remembering" (*anādhyāne*). Let it not apply here: *smarati vanagulmasya kokilaḥ* ("the cuckoo remembers the thicket"). [In such a case, one would instead say] *smarayati*.

"The forest thicket [will] itself [eat] him"—even this purpose does not exist. Prescriptive rules taught with reference to an action apply to those whose state (*bhāva*) resides in the object and those whose action (*kriyā*) resides in the object; however, this [root *ad*] has its state residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*). If that is so, since the matter is already established, the fact that the Teacher teaches the prohibition "not when there is mental attention" (*anādhyāne*) indicates that such a class of [roots] exists.

Regarding the term *ātmanepada*: what is the purpose of making this known? [Examples: *paśyanti bhṛtyā rājānam* ("The servants see the king"); *darśayate bhṛtyān rājā* ("The king causes the servants to see himself");
*darśayate bhṛtyai rājā* ("The king causes the servants to see himself"). In these cases, the *ātmanepada* ending is established.

285. Prohibition regarding the self as the object. A prohibition must be stated regarding the self being the object [in the case of causative verbs]: "He kills himself" (*hanty ātmānam*) and "He causes himself to be killed" (*ghātayaty ātmā*). Then it must indeed be stated. Or rather, it need not be stated. Why? Because in the causative (*ṇyanta*), there is a different agent. What is meant here by "a different [agent]"? That which is the object in the non-causative (*aṇyanta*).

The agent of the causative verb is different [from the agent of the simple verb]. How so? There are two selves: the inner self (antarātman) and the bodily self (śarīrātman). The inner self performs that action by which the bodily self experiences pleasure and pain; the bodily self performs that action by which the inner self experiences pleasure and pain. Thus it is said.

(P_1,3.72) For what purpose is the rule *svaritañitaḥ* [stated]? [Examples: *yāti*, *vāti*, *drāti*, *psāti*. The term *svaritañitaḥ* could be omitted. Why does [the ātmanepada] not occur in *yāti*, *vāti*, *drāti*, *psāti*? Because [in these cases] the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (*kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*).

Thus it is said: for all [roots], the fruit of the action belongs to the agent (*kartṛ*). We shall understand it in this way: the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs for those [roots] whose fruit of the action belongs both to the agent and to one who is not the agent. And for these [roots], the fruit of the action does not belong both to the agent and to one who is not the agent; such is their nature.

Indeed, the Ācārya has taught that those roots marked with the svarita accent or the ñ letter have a fruit of action (*kriyāphala*) that belongs either to the agent (*kartṛ*) or not to the agent. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *abhiprāya* (intention/aim)? If it were stated merely as "the fruit of the action of roots marked with svarita or ñ belongs to the agent," it would apply only where the fruit of the action accrues to the agent at that very moment. [This would exclude cases like: *lūñ*—*lunīte*; *pūñ*—*punīte*.
In this case, it would not apply [to the following]: *yajate* (he sacrifices) and *vapate* (he shaves). However, when the inclusion of the sense of "towards" (*abhi*) is made, there is no fault.

Here, *abhi* functions in the sense of "facing toward," while *pra* functions in the sense of "commencement of an action. Therefore, with respect to that which one is currently facing toward, that which one will face toward, and that which one has already faced toward—in all these cases, the rule is established simply by the presence of "facing toward."

What is the purpose of the rule *kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale* ("when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent")? [Examples: *pacanti bhaktakārāḥ* (the cooks cook), *kurvanti karmakārāḥ* (the laborers work), *yajanti yājakāḥ* (the priests sacrifice). Even if the rule *kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale* were stated, it would still apply here; for even in these cases, the fruit of the action accrues to the agent. The priests sacrifice with the thought, "We shall obtain cows," and the laborers [work with the thought, "We shall receive wages"].

"They perform the *pādika* rite [thinking], 'We shall obtain [the reward]'. If that is so, then it is stated that [the *ātmanepada* suffix is used] "when the fruit of the action is intended for the agent" (*kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*).
And in all cases, the agent intends the fruit of the action for himself. In that regard, the application of the term will be understood as referring to excellence:

namely, where the agent more effectively intends the fruit of the action for himself. Furthermore, there is no attainment of the fruit of the sacrifice (*yajiphala*) without the act of sacrificing (*yajati*), nor the fruit of sowing (*vapiphala*) without the act of sowing (*vapati*).
The sacrificers obtain the fruit of the sacrifice; however, the priests obtain cattle even without performing the sacrifice, and laborers obtain their wages.

(Pāṇini 1.3.78) Regarding the mention of "remainder" (*śeṣa*), there is a prohibition when it occurs in the sense of the fifth case (*pañcamī*). [This applies] if the mention of "remainder" occurs in the sense of the fifth case.
An exception must be stated: "The granary bursts of its own accord; the rope breaks of its own accord.

If that is so, I shall state the rule as "in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe*). If it is [the case] of a base ending in the seventh case (*saptamī*), an exception must be stated: "He sits, he lies down, they fall, they float. But this is established by the mention of both. This is indeed established.
How so? Both [terms] must be specified. It should be stated: "from the remainder, to the remainder.

For what purpose, then, would the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*) be necessary now? The mention of the agent is for the sake of excluding *anu*, *pari*, and others. This would be for the sake of excluding *anu*, *pari*, and others. Let it not apply here: *anukriyate svayam eva* ("it is performed by itself"), *parākriyate svayam eva* ("it is performed away by itself"). [In this way,] it is established. Thus, the sūtra is [correct].

In that case, it is split [into two rules]. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. But was it not said that the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) serves as a prohibition when there is the sense of the fifth case? This is not a fault. In the rule *kartari karmavyatihāre*, the mention of the word "agent" (*kartṛ*) is rejected.
That which is established there will be carried over (*anuvartate*) here: "from the remainder, when the agent is the agent. What does this "when the agent is the agent" mean?

Thus: [the rule] is so that it may apply where there is an agent who is indeed the agent; and it is so that it may not apply where there is an agent who is both an agent and something else. (Pāṇini 1.3.79) Why is this stated? Because of the prohibition of the *parasmaipada* endings, there is a prescription for the roots beginning with *kṛ*. Because of the prohibition of the *parasmaipada* endings...

The *parasmaipada* endings are prescribed for the roots beginning with *kṛñ*. Therein, the *parasmaipada* is prohibited by the rule: "The *ātmanepada* occurs for roots marked with a circumflex (*svarita*) or the marker *ñ*, when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent. This serves a purpose. What, then, is it? In that case, there would be a prohibition of the *ātmanepada* because [the *parasmaipada*] has not been prohibited. In that context, there is a prohibition of the *ātmanepada*.

It should be stated. What is the reason? Because it is not prohibited. For the *ātmanepada* is not prohibited; rather, by this [rule], the *parasmaipada* is prescribed. Or rather, there is no such fault, because of the optionality (*vāvacana*) regarding roots beginning with *dyut*. What is the reason? Because of the optionality regarding roots beginning with *dyut*; for this [author] makes the optionality apply to roots beginning with *dyut*.

The Teacher indicates by this that the *ātmanepada* does not occur in a domain where the *parasmaipada* is required. Alternatively, it is a prohibition regarding the restriction of the *ātmanepada*. Or rather, a prohibition must be stated concerning the restriction of the *ātmanepada*: "When the fruit of the action accrues to the agent, the *ātmanepada* occurs for roots marked with a svarita vowel or a ñ letter; however, it is not so after the prefixes *anu* and *parā* when used with the root *kṛ*. This is established. [This is] the Sūtra.

In that case, it is split [into two rules]. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated [in the original sūtra]. But was it not said there that the prohibition of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) does not apply because it is not prohibited? This has been answered: "Or rather, because of the optional rule (*vāvacana*) regarding the *dyut* group. Or else, first this person must be asked: "Does the middle voice occur when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent for roots marked with a circumflex accent (*svarita*) or the marker *ñ*?"

294. For what purpose is the inclusion of those [roots] such as *budh* that are intransitive? It is for the sake of [including] those that are transitive, or for the sake of those whose agent is not conscious (*acittavat*).

(P_1.3.88) Regarding the rule *aṇau akarmakāt*, the prescription of the *parasmaipada* ending after a root of the *curādi* class followed by *ṇic* must be stated. That is, the *parasmaipada* should be prescribed after a root of the *curādi* class followed by *ṇic*, provided it is intransitive in its *aṇ* form. This applies here as well.

For example, it might be intended that "one who is willing causes another to will" (cetayamānaṃ prayojayati cetayati). If, then, this [causative] is also accepted here, for what purpose would the mention of *aṇ* be now?
It is so that the mention of "intransitive" (*akarmaka*) may be understood as a qualifier of that which does not end in *aṇ*. Otherwise, if it were not done...

Of what would the mention of *ani* be a qualifier? It would be a qualifier for the mention of *akarmaka*. [The word] *ṇeḥ* is understood [from the previous rule]. Thus, it is a qualifier for that which ends in *ṇi*.
What is the fault in that? In this case, it would apply only here:
*cetayamānaṃ prayojayati cetayati* ("he causes one who is conscious to act"); but it would not apply here: [where the agent is not conscious].

"It causes to sit" (*āsayati*) or "causes to lie down" (*śāyayati*). But this is established by the statement: "In the case of that which is not [the causative suffix] *ṇi*. This is established. How? It should be stated: "In the case of that which is intransitive when it does not have the suffix *ṇi*. Thus it is established. But then the rule (*sūtra*) is altered. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. But was it not said that, because of the rule "from an intransitive root after the suffix *aṇ*," there is a prescription for the *parasmaipada* ending from a causative (*ṇic*) of the *cur*-class?

295–296: An addition regarding *dheṭ* after roots beginning with *pā*. An addition must be made for *dheṭ* after roots beginning with *pā*: "She causes her child to drink milk alone, being well-disposed" (*dhāpayate śiśum ekaṃ samīcī*).

(Pāṇini 1.3.93). Why is the letter *ca* used? It is for the purpose of carrying forward the term *syasanoh* [from the preceding rule]. If that were not the case, without the letter *ca*, [the rule would not apply].

In the rule *dyudbhyo luṅi*, there too the letter *ca* should have been included for the purpose of drawing forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the term *vibhāṣā*. Now, even without the letter *ca*, the continuation [of that rule] occurs here as well; thus, the letter *ca* serves no purpose here. In this manner, all instances of the letter *ca* are rejected.

(P_1,4.1.1) KA_I,296.2–10 Ro_II, 297–298: For what purpose is this stated? This statement is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), because elsewhere there is a coalescence of technical names (*saṃjñāsamāveśa*). Where else does this coalescence of names occur? In common usage (*loka*) and in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*). First, in common usage: Indra, Śakra...

"Puruhūta," "Purandara," "Kandu," "Koṣṭha," and "Kuśūla"—thus there are many designations for a single object. In grammar as well, in the case of *kartavyam* and *hartavyam*, there is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the technical designations (*sañjñā*) of suffix (*pratyaya*), agentive affix (*kṛt*), and gerundive (*kṛtya*). In the case of *pāñcālaḥ*, *vaidehaḥ*, and *vaidarbhaḥ*, there is a co-occurrence of the designations of suffix (*pratyaya*), secondary derivative (*taddhita*), and patronymic (*tadrāja*).

There would be a co-occurrence [of technical names]. Because of this reason—that there is no co-occurrence of technical names elsewhere—it follows that even up to the word *kaḍāra*, there would be a co-occurrence of technical names. However, it is desired that there should be only one technical name at a time. And since that cannot be established without an effort, the statement is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*). This is said for this purpose. There is indeed a point in this; what then?

(P_1,4.1.2) How, then, is this sūtra to be read? Is it "up to *kaḍāra*, there is one technical designation (*saṃjñā*) [for each item]," or rather, "prior to *kaḍāra*, that which follows [is the operation (*kārya*)"]? But whence does this doubt arise? For in both ways, the Teacher has instructed his pupils.

The Sūtras have established two positions: some hold that "up to *kaḍāra*, there is only one designation" (*eka-sañjñā*), while others hold that "prior to *kaḍāra*, the subsequent operation prevails" (*paraṃ kāryam*). What, then, is the distinction here? In that regard, under the heading of "one designation" (*ekasañjñā-adhikāra*):
That statement [is made]. In that context, within the governing rule concerning "a single designation" (*ekasañjñādhikāra*), that must be stated. What? That "there is a single designation.

But surely, even for one for whom [the designation] is a subsequent operation (*parakāryatva*), the mention of "subsequent" (*para*) must be made; it will serve my purpose through the rule "in case of conflict" (*vipratiṣedhe*). In that case, my mention of "single" (*eka*) will also serve the purpose of others.

"Of those that have the same form, there is a single remainder when they occur with the same case-ending. This is a governing rule (*sañjñā-adhikāra*). In this context, what else could be understood [from it] other than a technical designation (*sañjñā*)? Regarding this, only this much needs to be stated: "Up to the word *kaḍāra*, [the rule] is one. What does this mean? It means that there is only one technical designation. Consequently, there is no co-occurrence (*asamāveśa*) of the designations *aṅga* and *bha* or *pada*; rather, by virtue of the designation *aṅga*...
The simultaneous application (*samāveśa*) of the designations *bha* and *pada* would not be possible [in the following cases]: *sārpiṣkaḥ*, *bārhiṣkaḥ*, *yājuṣkaḥ*, *dhānuṣkaḥ*;

and *bābhravyaḥ*, *māṇḍavyaḥ*. Since the designations *bha* and *pada* have no other scope [for application], they would subvert the designation *aṅga*. For if they were stated as subsequent [rules], a restrictive rule (*niyama*) would be impossible, and thus there would be an absence of both designations. However, for one [view] where it is a subsequent operation, a restrictive rule is impossible.

The status of both those designations is established. How so? First, it has the designations *bha* and *pada*; subsequently, it has the designation *aṅga*. How so? He will state this: "That from which a suffix is prescribed, beginning with that, is a word (*pada*) ending in a *sup* or *tiṅ* [suffix]; in the case of *kye*, it is not [a *pada*] when followed by *naḥ*; and in the case of *sit* [suffixes], likewise. [Then: "In the presence of suffixes beginning with *sva-* and excluding *sarvanāmasthāna*, a stem ending in *yaC* or *jaC* is called *bha*. Thus, when that [stem] ends in a suffix...

Regarding the term *aṅga*: in that context, the designation *bha* and the designation *pada* will occur by virtue of the capacity of the initial operation (*ārambhasāmarthya*), and the designation *aṅga* will occur because it is an operation pertaining to what follows (*paraṅkāryatva*). But surely, even for one who maintains the rule "only one designation applies" (*ekasañjñādhikāra*), the designations *bha* and *pada* are preceded by the designation *aṅga*. How so? Because the [designation *aṅga*] is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) [from the previous rule]. [If you say this,] then an option (*paryāya*) would result. This is not the case, because of the explicit statement "only one designation."

Simultaneous occurrence [is required]. Regarding the status of a *karmadhāraya*, the mention of *tatpuruṣa* must be made; that is, "a *tatpuruṣa* with a common substratum is a *karmadhāraya*. It has been argued that this falls under the governing rule for a single designation (*ekasañjñādhikāra*). For if it were not so stated, the *karmadhāraya* designation, having no other scope, would subvert the *tatpuruṣa* designation. This is because of the subsequent statement.

Indeed, for one [who holds that the subsequent rule] is not subject to a restrictive rule (*niyama*), there is an absence of both designations (*saṃjñā*). However, for one for whom the subsequent [rule] is subject to a restrictive rule, the existence of both designations is established. How so? The former designation for it is *karmadhāraya*, and the latter is *tatpuruṣa*. How so? He will state this: "The words *pūrvakāla*, *eka*, *sarva*, *jarat*, *purāṇa*, *nava*, and *kevala* [are placed first in a *karmadhāraya*]."

"A *karmadhāraya* [compound] occurs with a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Having thus followed the entire section on *karmadhāraya* compounds, at its conclusion it states: "The class beginning with *śrita* forms a *tatpuruṣa* compound. In that case, by the force of the initial rule and because the *tatpuruṣa* designation is a subsequent operation (*paraṅkārya*), the *karmadhāraya* designation will indeed apply. But surely, for one who maintains the governing rule of "only one designation" (*ekasañjñādhikāra*)...

For that [compound] as well, the designation *karmadhāraya* is preceded by the designation *tatpuruṣa*. How so? Because the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) [of the rule for *tatpuruṣa*] is applied. A synonymy (*paryāya*) would result. Since it is stated that "there is one designation," simultaneous occurrence is not possible. Regarding the status of being a *tatpuruṣa*, there must be the mention of *dvigu* as well. That is to say, regarding the status of being a *tatpuruṣa*, the mention of *dvigu* must be made: "a *tatpuruṣa* and a *dvigu*."
The particle *ca* must be supplied. For if the *ca* were not employed, the designation *dvigu*, having no other scope, would sublate the designation *tatpuruṣa*.

Indeed, when a subsequent rule is stated, a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is untenable; consequently, there would be an absence of both designations. However, for one for whom the subsequent operation is [the result], because a restrictive rule is untenable, the existence of both designations is established. How so? Its prior designation is that of *dvigu*.

The designation *tatpuruṣa* is subsequent. How so? He will state thus: "In the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), in the case of a final member, and in a collective (*samāhāra*), a compound preceded by a numeral is a *dvigu*. Having thus followed the entire section on *dvigu*, he will place "the *tatpuruṣa* beginning with *śrita*" at the end of that.
In this regard, the designation *dvigu* applies by virtue of its initial formulation, while the designation *tatpuruṣa* applies because it is a subsequent operation.

It will be so. But surely, even for one who maintains the governing rule of "one designation" (*ekasañjñādhikāra*), the designation of *dvigu* is preceded by the designation of *tatpuruṣa*. How so? Because the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) is applied. [If that were the case,] a mutual option (*paryāya*) would result. Since it is stated that "there is one designation," simultaneous occurrence is impossible. The mention of *ca* [in the rule] applies to cases involving prefixes (*gati*), the roots *div*, *karma*, and *hetumat*. [The rule applies] to cases involving prefixes, the root *div*, *karma*, and *hetumat*.

The mention of the word "ca" (and) must be made [in the rule]. In the rule *upasargāḥ kriyāyoge gatiśca*, the word "ca" must be included. For if the word "ca" were not employed, the designation *upasarga* (prefix), having no other scope, would subvert the designation *gati*. Indeed, since a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is impossible when a subsequent statement is made, there would be an absence of both designations. However, for one for whom the subsequent status is established, because a restrictive rule is impossible, there is the presence of both designations.
