The state [of being both] is established. How? Its prior designation is *upasarga* (prefix), and its subsequent designation is *gati* (particle). Here, by virtue of the force of the initial formulation (*ārambhasāmarthyāt*), it will have the designation *upasarga*, and by virtue of the fact that the subsequent operation takes precedence (*paraṅkāryatvāt*), it will have the designation *gati*. But surely, even for one who maintains the rule of "one designation at a time" (*ekasañjñādhikāra*), the designation *gati* would be preceded by the designation *upasarga*. How so? Because the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) is maintained. [In that case,] an alternation (*paryāya*) would result.

Because of the statement "there is one designation," simultaneous occurrence is not possible. Even the designation *gati* (motion) would be without scope; however, it will apply by virtue of that specific rule. The designation *gati* does have scope. What is its scope? The group beginning with *ūry-ādi* is its scope. The designation *gati* for prefixes (*prādayaḥ*) is without scope [in this context]. [The rules are: *gati*, *divaḥ karma* (the object of *div*), and *sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam divaḥ* (that which is most effective in accomplishing the action is the instrument of *div*).

And the particle *ca* must be supplied after the word *karma*. For if the particle *ca* were not employed, the designation *karman* (object), having no scope [elsewhere], would subvert the designation *karaṇa* (instrument). Indeed, when a subsequent rule is stated, a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is impossible, and thus both designations would be absent. However, for one for whom the subsequent element is to be applied, because a restrictive rule is impossible, the existence of both designations is established. How so? His prior designation is that of *karman*.

The designation *karaṇa* (instrument) takes precedence. How so? He will say this: "That which is most effective (*sādhakatama*) in relation to *div* is the *karman* (object); after that, it is the *karaṇa*. And thus, it receives the designation of *karaṇa* while being *sādhakatama*. [In this case,] the rule for *div* has ceased to apply. In that situation, by virtue of the force of the original formulation (*ārambha-sāmarthya*) and because the designation of *karaṇa* is a subsequent operation (*para-kāryatva*), the designation of *karaṇa* will indeed prevail. But surely, even for one who maintains the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "only one designation applies," [the same would hold]?
Furthermore, the designation of "object" (*karma-sañjñā*) is preceded by the designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa-sañjñā*).

How so? Because [if both were applied simultaneously], a recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) would be required; otherwise, a confusion of categories (*paryāya*) would result. Since it is stated that "there is only one designation," their simultaneous occurrence is impossible. [The rule states: "That which is the object of *div* [is the agent]. [It is] "possessing a cause" (*hetumat*). "The independent one is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*); "the instigator of that [agent] is the cause" (*tatprayojako hetuḥ*).

And the particle *ca* must be supplied. For if the *ca* were not employed, the designation *hetu* (cause), having no other scope, would sublate the designation *kartṛ* (agent). Since a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is impossible when a subsequent [rule] is stated, there would be an absence of both designations. However, for one for whom the subsequent operation is [intended], because a restrictive rule is impossible, the existence of both designations is established. How so? His prior designation is that of *hetu*.
The designation "agent" (kartṛ) takes precedence. How so? He will state as follows: "The independent instigator is the cause (hetu).

From that [rule], it follows that there is an agent; and that which is independent receives the designation "agent. The term "instigator" (prayojaka) is withdrawn. In that case, by the force of the original formulation and because the designation "cause" is subsequent, the designation "agent" will prevail. But is it not the case that...

Even for one who holds that there is a governing rule of "only one technical designation" (*ekasañjñādhikāra*), the designation of "cause" (*hetu*) is preceded by the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*). How so? Because the [designation of agent] is carried over [by *anuvṛtti*].

[If both were applied simultaneously,] a conflict of options (*paryāya*) would result. Since it is stated that "there is only one designation," simultaneous occurrence is not possible. [For example,] the designations "heavy" (*guru*) and "light" (*laghu*), as well as the designations "nadī" and "ghi," would mutually sublate one another [if applied at once]. As in the case of *gārgībhandhuḥ*.
Vātsībandhu [says] that after having analyzed the *vaitra* [sūtra]: "For if it were a subsequent [designation], a restriction would not be possible, and thus both designations would be absent.
But for one [who holds] that it is a subsequent operation, because a restriction would not be possible, the existence of both designations is established.
How so? Its designations as *nadī* and *ghi* apply to what precedes; its designations as *guru* and *laghu* apply to what follows. This is because of the force of the initial formulation."
Furthermore, the designations *nadī* and *ghi* will exist because they must be applied to others, and the designations *guru* and *laghu* will likewise exist.

But surely, even for one who maintains the governing rule of "only one designation" (*ekasañjñādhikāra*), the designations *guru* and *laghu* would be preceded by the designations *nadī*, *ghi*, and *saṃghi*. How so? Because the [previous] application continues. [Objection: A simultaneous occurrence (*paryāya*) would result. [Response: No, because of the statement "only one designation," there is no simultaneity.

[The suffix] *sambhava* [would incur] the designation *parasmaipada* and the designation *puruṣa*. The designation *parasmaipada* would sublate the designation *puruṣa*. For if the latter were stated, a restriction would be impossible; thus, there would be an absence of both designations. However, for one for whom the subsequent operation [is primary], because a restriction is impossible, the existence of both designations is established. How so? His prior designation is that of *puruṣa*.

The designation *parasmaipada* [is established] as subsequent. How so? He will state thus: "Of the *tiṅ*s, three each are the first, middle, and last persons. Having thus set forth the entire restriction regarding the persons (*puruṣa*), at the end of that [section] he will say: "The *la*s are *parasmaipada*. In that case, the designation of the person (*puruṣasañjñā*) will occur by virtue of its initial formulation, and the designation *parasmaipada* will occur because it is a subsequent operation (*paraṅkāryatva*).

But surely, for one who holds that there is a single designation (*eka-saṃjñā*), even for him the designation of person (*puruṣa-saṃjñā*) is preceded by the designation of *parasmaipada*. How so? Because the [previous rule] is carried over (*anuvṛtti*). [Objection: A conflict of options (*paryāya*) would result. [Response:

Due to the statement "there is a single designation," simultaneous occurrence is impossible. [Objection: The designation *parasmaipada* is also without scope; it will nonetheless come into effect by virtue of the explicit statement.
The designation *parasmaipada* has scope [for application]. What is its scope? The affixes *śatṛ* and *kvasu* are its scope.

1.4.1.3) When there is an instruction regarding what follows (*para*), a word ending in *sit* is called *pada*. When there is an instruction regarding what follows, a word ending in *sit* would also incur the designation *bha*.

"This is your seasonal womb; may we obtain offspring through this seasonal rite. Due to the force of the initial formulation (*ārambha-sāmarthya*) and because it is a subsequent operation (*para-kāryatva*), the designation *pada* would apply, and due to the same reasons, the designation *bha* would also apply. For roots such as *gati*, *buddhi*, etc., when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), their object receives the designation *kartṛ*. Thus, for roots such as *gati*, *buddhi*, etc., when followed by the causative suffix, it follows that their object would also receive the designation *kartṛ*, due to the force of the initial formulation.

The designation *karman* (object) and the designation *pada* (inflected word) apply, and because it is an operation dependent on another (*parakāryatva*), the designation *kartṛ* (agent) would also result. This is not a fault. The activity of the Teacher indicates that the designation *kartṛ* does not apply when the designation *karman* is present, since he employs the mention of the option (*anyatarasyām*) in the rule *hṛkror anyatarasyām*. Furthermore, the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) is for the purpose of excluding the designation *ghisamjñā*. Thus, the mention of "the remainder" is made.

And [the rule] *śeṣo dhy asakhi* must be formulated. What is the purpose? To prevent the application of the technical term *ghi*. [The intention is: "When the term *nadī* applies, let the term *ghi* not apply. For example: *śakaṭyai*, *paddhatyai*, *buddhyai*, *dhenvai*. Otherwise, because the subsequent operation (*paraṅkārya*) takes precedence and because of the force of the formulation [of the *ghi* rule], the term *nadī* would apply by the rule *ṅiti hrasvaś ca*. [Objection: No, for there is no possibility [of conflict].
Or rather, it need not be done because of impossibility. Why does the designation *ghī* not apply when the designation *nadī* is to be applied?

Because of impossibility. What is this impossibility? For the designation *nadī* is characterized by short vowels (*hrasva*), whereas in the case of the designation *ghī*, there must be a *guṇa* [vowel].

Since the designation *nadī* is characterized by short vowels, and a *guṇa* would have to occur in the case of the designation *ghī*, [the latter does not apply] there due to the authority of the specific rule.

When the designation *nadī* (feminine) applies, the designation *ghi* does not exist. In that case, by virtue of the authority of the rule itself, the designation *ghi* will not apply when the designation *nadī* is present. What is the reason? Because of the absence of a basis (*āśraya*). If it is argued that the cessation of the designation *ghi* occurs when the designation *nadī* is present due to the absence of a basis, then there would be an absence of the substitution [of *yaṇ* for *i*]. If it is argued that the cessation of the designation *ghi* occurs when the designation *nadī* is present due to the absence of a basis, then it is so.

It is said that even the substitution of *yaṇ* does not apply. This is not a fault. Because the substitution of *yaṇ* depends upon the [designation] *nadī*, there is no application of the technical term *nadī* to a short vowel. The substitution of *yaṇ* has the *nadī* as its basis. When the designation *ghis* has been superseded by the designation *nadī*, then subsequently the substitution of *yaṇ* must take place. Since the substitution of *yaṇ* depends upon the *nadī*, the short vowel does not receive the designation *nadī*.
It will be so. However, for the sake of the *bahuvrīhi* [compound], the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) must be made in order to exclude the *bahuvrīhi*.
That is, "the *bahuvrīhi* is the remainder. What is the purpose? The purpose applies to *avyayībhāva*, comparison (*upamāna*), *dvigu*, and the elision of the suffix *kṛt*.

Regarding *avyayībhāva*: *unmattagaṅgam* (the Gaṅgā is out of its course), *lohitagaṅgam* (the Gaṅgā is red). Regarding comparison: *śastrīśyāmā* (dark as a knife), *kumudaśyenī* (white as a water-lily).

In the case of *dvigu* compounds: *pañcagavaṃ* (five cows), *daśagavaṃ* (ten cows). In the case of elision (*lopa*) [of the second member]: *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* (one who has departed from Kauśāmbī), *nirvārāṇasiḥ* (one who has departed from Vārāṇasī). Therein, because of the statement regarding the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), there is a fault: namely, a prohibition of the *bahuvrīhi* in compounds consisting of numerals in grammatical apposition (*saṃkhyā-samānādhikaraṇa*). Because of that statement regarding the "remainder," a fault arises; for in compounds consisting of numerals in apposition, a prohibition of the *bahuvrīhi* would otherwise apply. [This concerns] numerals.
A region possessing two *rāvatī*s; a region possessing three *rāvatī*s. [These are examples of] appositional compounds (*samānādhikaraṇa*). A village possessing heroic men (*vīrapuruṣaka*);

a region not possessing Brāhmaṇas (*abrāhmaṇaka*) due to a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*); a region not possessing Śūdras (*avṛṣalaka*). Furthermore, when there is elision of the *kṛt*-suffix, because of the rule concerning the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), a Bahuvrīhi compound is not formed with prefixes such as *pra*. When there is elision of the *kṛt*-suffix, because of the rule concerning the "remainder," it would not be possible [to form a Bahuvrīhi] with prefixes such as *pra*. [For example: one from whom leaves have fallen is *praparṇaka*.

[The word] *prapalāśakaḥ* [is derived from] *prapatitapalāśaḥ*. Now, how is this established under the heading "one technical name" (*ekasañjñādhikāra*)? Under the heading "one technical name," the *bahuvrīhi* [compound] prevails due to the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). Under the heading "one technical name," the *bahuvrīhi* will prevail because of the rule of conflict. If it is argued that under the heading "one technical name" the *bahuvrīhi* prevails due to the rule of conflict, then there is a prohibition regarding the sense of the *kta* suffix. Under the heading "one technical name"...

If it is argued that the *bahuvrīhi* compound is used because of a conflict [with other rules], then a prohibition must be stated regarding the sense of the *kta* suffix: as in *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* ("one who has departed from Kauśāmbī") and *nirvārāṇasiḥ* ("one who has departed from Vārāṇasī"). In these cases, the *tatpuruṣa* compound will serve as the sublater. If it is argued that the *tatpuruṣa* applies, then a prohibition must be stated for cases other than the sense of the *kta* suffix: as in *prapatitaparṇaḥ* ("one from whom leaves have fallen"), which becomes *praparṇakaḥ*.

[The objection: [In that case,] *prapalāśakaḥ* would mean "one whose leaves have fallen" (*pratita-palāśaḥ*). [The reply: This is established, however, because it is stated that for prefixes (*prādi*) in the sense of a *kta*-suffix, a *tatpuruṣa* compound occurs.
313–317. What, then, are the purposes of this yoga? The purpose is [to establish] the designation "short" (hrasva) for the long (dīrgha) and protracted (pluta) vowels.
The designations "long" and "protracted" sublate the designation "short. *tiṅ* and *sārvadhātuka* [are designated as such]; *liṅ* and *liṭ* are *ārdhadhātuka*.
The *ārdhadhātuka* designation of *liṅ* and *liṭ* sublates the *sārvadhātuka* designation of *tiṅ*. An offspring who is old [is designated as such], while a youth [is not].
The designation *vṛddha* subverts the designation *yavuṣ*. The designation *nadī* subverts the designation *ghi*.
The designation *guru* subverts the designation *laghu*. The designation *bha* subverts the designation *pada*. [Examples:

*apādānam uttarāṇi* (the word following an ablative case is called *bha*), *dhanuṣā vidhyati* (he pierces with a bow), *kaṃsapātryām bhuṅkte* (he eats from a bronze vessel), *gām dogdhi* (he milks a cow), *dhanuḥ* (a bow).

Regarding the statement "he pierces" (*vidhyati*): subsequent *kāraka* designations supersede the designation of the ablative (*apādāna*). Where? In cases such as: "He pierces with a bow" (*dhanuṣā vidhyati*), "He eats from a bronze plate" (*kaṃsapātryām bhuṅkte*), and "He milks the cow" (*gām dogdhi*). In the case of "The bow pierces" (*dhanur vidhyati*) or "He pierces with a bow" (*dhanuṣā vidhyati*), the designation of the ablative would apply because it is connected with departure (*apāya*), according to the rule: "That which is fixed (*dhruva*) in relation to a departure is the ablative" (*dhruvam apāye 'pādānam*). However, the designation of the instrument (*karaṇa*) also applies, according to the rule: "That which is most effective in accomplishing an action is the instrument" (*sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam*).

That [designation] becomes the subsequent one. In the case of "he eats from a bronze vessel" (*kaṃsapātryām bhuṅkte*), because it is connected with departure (*apāya*), the designation *apādāna* (ablative) would apply by the rule "that which is fixed in relation to departure is the *apādāna*. However, the designation *adhikaraṇa* (locative), by the rule "the substratum is the *adhikaraṇa*," applies as well.

That [designation] becomes the subsequent one, namely the *adhikaraṇa*. In the case of "he milks the cow" (*gām dogdhi*), because it is connected with departure, the designation *apādāna* would apply.
And there is the technical designation (saṃjñā) of "object" (karman) according to the rule: "That which is most desired by the agent is the object. That [designation] is subsequent.

In the example "he pierces with a bow" (*dhanur vidhyati*), because it involves separation (*apāya*), the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) applies; and because of the rule "the independent one is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*), the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) applies. That [designation] is subsequent. [Furthermore, by the rule] "when *krudh* and *druh* are preceded by a prefix, the object is the recipient" (*krudhadruhor upasṛṣṭayoḥ karma saṃpradānam*).

The designation *karma* (object) subverts the designation *saṃpradāna* (recipient) when the roots √krudh (to be angry) and √druh (to bear malice) are used with a prefix. Later rules [in the Aṣṭādhyāyī] override the designation *karaṇa* (instrument). For example: *asiḥ chinatti* ("the sword cuts"). Later rules override the designation *karaṇa*. Where? In cases such as *dhanur vidhyati* ("he pierces with a bow") and *asiḥ chinatti* ("he cuts with a sword"). The designation *karman* (object) overrides the designation *adhikaraṇa* (locus). For example: *gehaṃ praviśati* ("he enters the house"). The designation *karman* overrides the designation *adhikaraṇa*.

It subverts [the designation]. Where? In the case of "he enters the house," [the agent] is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). The designation of the agent (*kartṛ*) subverts the designation of the locus. Where? In the case of "the pot cooks. An object (*karman*) preceded by the prefix *adhi*—an object preceded by *adhi* subverts the designation of the locus. The designations of motion (*gati*) and prefix (*upasarga*) are subverted by the designation of a particle governing an object (*karmapravacanīya*). The designations of motion and prefix...

The designation *karmapravacanīya* sublates [the designations of case endings]. The *parasmaipada* [designation] sublates the *ātmanepada* [designation]; that is, the *ātmanepada* designation sublates the *parasmaipada* designation. And the *samāsa* designations: whichever *samāsa* designations are subsequent and without scope (*anavakāśa*), they sublate those which are prior and have scope (*sāvakāśa*).

(P_1.4.1.5) A meaningful item is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). An item that possesses meaning receives the designation "nominal stem. Furthermore, that which expresses a quality (*guṇavacana*) also receives the designation "quality-expressing" provided it possesses meaning. A compound (*samāsa*), a primary derivative (*kṛt*), a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), an indeclinable (*avyaya*), a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), and that which does not possess all genders (*asarvaliṅga*) are [also] genus (*jāti*). 41.

The term *samāsa* [compound] must be stated, and the designation *samāsa* must be stated. The term *kṛt* [primary derivative] must be stated, and the designation *kṛt* must be stated. The term *taddhita* [secondary derivative] must be stated, and the designation *taddhita* must be stated. The term *avyaya* [indeclinable] must be stated, and the designation *avyaya* must be stated. The term *sarvanāman* [pronoun] must be stated, and the designation *sarvanāman* must be stated.

It must be stated that "jāti" (genus) does not possess all genders; this also must be stated. "Number": the technical designation of "number" must also be stated. "Ḍu": the technical designation of "ḍu" must also be stated. But what is the technical designation of "ḍu"? It is the technical designation of "ṣaṭ" (six). "A designation that resides in a single substance":
it must also be stated that [a designation] resides in a single substance. For what purpose is this being said?
The designations (saṃjñās) are for the most part made according to the original arrangement; however, there are indeed some new designations here as well.

Furthermore, it is so that there may be an exclusion (bādhanam) of those [terms] arranged in this sequence, and so that there may be an exclusion of the designation "quality-word" (guṇavacana-saṃjñā) by these [new ones].

Regarding the term *vipratiṣedha*: what kind of word is this? It is derived from the root *sidh* preceded by the prefixes *vi-* and *prati-*, with the suffix *ghañ* used in the sense of reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*). Thus, *vipratiṣedha* means mutual exclusion, or reciprocal exclusion. It is the negation of one another.
What, then, is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*)? When two applications have different purposes and both apply simultaneously to a single instance, that is a conflict.
When two applications have different purposes and both obtain simultaneously in one place, that is a conflict.
Where, then, do they have different purposes, and where do they both apply simultaneously? [In the case of] *vṛkṣābhyām*.

In the case of *vṛkṣeṣu*, [the suffixes] for the other meanings apply; in the case of *vṛkṣebhyaḥ*, both would apply simultaneously. What would follow? Because simultaneous occurrence in a single instance is impossible, there would be the contingency of both [suffixes] due to the application of both the preceding and the succeeding rules. Because simultaneous occurrence in a single instance is impossible, and because of the application of both the preceding and the succeeding rules, there is the contingency of both. This which is stated—that "because simultaneous occurrence in a single instance is impossible, [there is the contingency of both] due to the application of both the preceding and the succeeding rules"—is a contradiction.

Regarding the statement "there would be the application of both": how indeed could there be a simultaneous impossibility in a single case? Since both the prior and the subsequent rules would apply, there would be the application of both. This is not contradictory. As for what was said—that there is a simultaneous impossibility in a single case—it refers to the simultaneous impossibility of the two *effects*, whereas the application of both refers to the two grammatical rules (*śāstra*).

It is equivalent to the suffixes beginning with *tṛc*. It follows that there is an alternation (*paryāya*) [between the suffixes], just as the suffixes beginning with *tṛc* occur alternatively. But what is the reason that the suffixes beginning with *tṛc* occur alternatively? Because it would otherwise entail non-comprehensiveness (*anavayaprasaṅga*) and because they are prescribed for each specific word (*pratipada*). They would entail non-comprehensiveness and are prescribed for each specific word. Alternatively, there would be no comprehension of either.
Because they possess equal force. Or else, there would be non-comprehension of both treatises. What is the reason? Because they possess equal force;

for both treatises are of equal strength. It is just as when there is a single servant belonging to two people of equal power: he performs their work in turn. But when both send him simultaneously in different directions...

And if both [suffixes] occur in the same function, then, if that speaker desires non-contradiction, he does not employ both. But what is the reason he does not employ both? Because of the impossibility of simultaneity; there is no possibility of their occurrence simultaneously.
To clarify this point, a statement must be made: "In that case, for the sake of clarification, this should be stated regarding the suffixes *tavyat* and so forth."

But [in that case] there would be non-establishment. However, regarding the suffixes such as *tavyat* and so on, there is a non-establishment of their function; for no rule (*śāstra*) is initiated with respect to *tavyat* and the others that would cause them to occur. And the reason you have pointed out—namely, "non-comprehension because both [alternatives] possess equal force"—is equally applicable to *tavyat* and the others. This is not a fault.

The suffixes *tavyat* and so forth are said to have no scope [for application]. They will nevertheless occur because of an explicit statement (*vacana*). Furthermore, as for the reason you have pointed out—that an alternation (*paryāya*) would result, just as with the suffixes *-tṛc* and others—that same reasoning applies equally to the suffixes *tavyat* and the rest. In this matter, the rule is simply: "In the case of conflict, the subsequent [rule prevails]. For the Teacher will indeed state: "When two rules apply simultaneously in a conflict..."
"What has been refuted is indeed refuted. And he will state again: "It is established through the understanding of recurrence.

But how, by this much of a sūtra, can both [alternatives] be obtained? He says: they are obtained. How so? Here you have pointed out two reasons: that an alternation (paryāya) would result as being similar to the *tṛj*-affixes and the like, or else there would be a lack of comprehension (*apratipatti*).

And [it is argued] "because both have equal force. Now, when this reason—that the suffix *tṛc* and others apply as alternatives (*paryāya*) with equal force—is present, then what is accomplished by the rule *vipratiṣedhe param*? It is a restriction (*niyama*). That is to say: in a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), only the subsequent [rule] applies. In that case, it becomes logically consistent that in a conflict where there is a single application (*sakṛdgati*), that which has been sublated [is not applied again].

That [rule] is indeed set aside. But when this reason—that there is non-comprehension because both [rules] possess equal strength—applies, then what is accomplished by the rule *vipratiṣedhe param*? It serves as a gateway. First, in a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the subsequent [rule] takes effect;
once that has been performed, if the preceding [rule] also applies, then that too takes effect. In that case, this [application of the subsequent rule] is justified.

Furthermore, it is established through the understanding of the recurring application (*punaḥprasaṅga*). Having stated "in case of conflict, the latter [rule prevails]," one must state "the former" within the section on *aṅga* (bases). What is accomplished by this? The rules for "prior conflict" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) need not be explicitly recited.

[The rule] "num [takes precedence] in prior conflict with *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, *aut*, and *tṛjvadbhāva*" [is thus established]; [and the rule] "from *num*, *aci-ra*, and *tṛjvadbhāva*... [is likewise established].

[The objection is: "But what about the term *nuṭ*? How can those [rules] that are *paravipratiṣedhas* (subsequent counter-rules) be justified? [For instance,] it is said that by way of a *vipratiṣedha*, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* take precedence over *ittva* and *uttva*. In this case, the *sūtra* would have to be altered. [The reply is: "Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. How then are those *pūrvavipratiṣedhas* (prior counter-rules) to be explained? They are established simply by the rule *vipratiṣedhe param* ('in the case of a conflict, the subsequent [rule prevails]'). How so? This word *para* has many meanings; there is indeed..."

It occurs in the sense of "distinction" (*vyavasthā*), as for example: "prior" or "subsequent. It occurs in the sense of "another" (*anyārtha*), as for example: "another's son" or "another's wife"; here it is understood as "son of another" or "wife of another. It occurs in the sense of "predominance" (*prādhānya*), as for example: "this Brāhmaṇī woman is supreme (*param*) in this family"; here it is understood as "foremost" (*pradhāna*). It occurs...

The word *para* signifies that which is desired (*iṣṭa*). For example, in the expression "he has gone to the highest abode" (*param dhāma gataḥ*), it is understood that the abode is one that is desired. Therefore, this is the inclusion of the word *para* as signifying that which is desired. In the case of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), that which is desired is considered the "later" (*para*) rule.
(Pāṇini 1.4.2)

325–335. And that which is internal (*antaraṅga*) is stronger; this must be stated. What is the purpose? The purpose is [to show] that the substitution of *yaṇ*, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*), the substitution of *it*, and the substitution of *uttva* take precedence over guna, vṛddhi, reduplication (*dvirvacana*), elision (*alopa*), and accent (*svara*). Regarding the substitution of *yaṇ* in preference to guna: in the case of *syonaḥ* and *syonā*, both guna and the substitution of *yaṇ* would apply. Since the latter is subsequent (*para*), guna would occur. However, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs because it is internal (*antaraṅga*).

Regarding the substitution of *yaṇ* for *vṛddhi*: in *dyaukāmiḥ* and *syaukāmiḥ*, both *vṛddhi* and the *yaṇ* substitution would apply. Because of its priority (*paratva*), *vṛddhi* would occur; however, the *yaṇ* substitution takes place because it is *antaraṅga*. Regarding the *yaṇ* substitution prior to reduplication: in *dudyūṣati* and *susyūṣati*, both reduplication and the *yaṇ* substitution would apply. Because of its permanence (*nityatva*), reduplication would occur; [nevertheless,] the *yaṇ* substitution [takes place].

It occurs by virtue of being *antaraṅga*. Furthermore, there is no comparative weighing (*sampradhāraṇā*) between elision (*allopasya*) and the substitution of *yaṇ* (*yaṇādeśasya*). The *yaṇ* substitution takes precedence over the vowel (*svarāt*). For example, in *dyaukāmiḥ* and *syaukāmiḥ*, both the vowel (*svaraḥ*) and the *yaṇ* substitution would apply; however, because it is subsequent (*paratvāt*), the vowel [accentuation] would occur. But the *yaṇ* substitution occurs by virtue of being *antaraṅga*. Regarding the substitution of a single substitute (*ekādeśaḥ*) for *guṇa*: [in the case of] *kādraveyaḥ*, he saw the mantra.

Both *guṇa* and *ekādeśa* apply. Because it is subsequent (*paratva*), *guṇa* would occur; however, *ekādeśa* occurs because it is *antaraṅga*. In the case of *vṛddhi*, *ekādeśa* [occurs]. As in *vaikṣmāṇiḥ* and *sausthitiḥ*. Both *vṛddhi* and *ekādeśa* apply. Because it is subsequent, *vṛddhi* would occur; however, *ekādeśa* occurs because it is *antaraṅga*. In the case of reduplication (*dvirvacana*), *ekādeśa* [occurs]. As in *jñāyā odanaḥ*.

*jñaudanaḥ*. One desires *jñaudana* [as food]: *jñaudanīyati*. From *jñaudanīyati*, the desiderative suffix (*san*) is applied: *jujñaudanīyiṣati*. Here, both reduplication (*dvirvacanam*) and the single-substitute replacement (*ekādeśaḥ*) would apply. Because it is permanent (*nityatvāt*), reduplication should occur; however, the single-substitute replacement occurs because it is more internal (*antaraṅgataḥ*). In the case of *allopāt* (the elision of *a*) in *śunā* and *śune*, both the elision of *a* and the single-substitute replacement would apply. Because it is subsequent (*paratvāt*), the single-substitute replacement occurs.

There should be elision of *al*. An *ekādeśa* (single-substitute) occurs by virtue of being *antaraṅga* (more internal). This is not a valid purpose [for the rule]. There is no difference here whether the cessation occurs through the elision of *al* or through its being treated as the preceding element (*pūrva*). However, there is this distinction: if the cessation occurred through the elision of *al*, the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (accent resulting from the removal of an acute accent) would result. But the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* does not apply here.

What is the reason? Because of the prohibition: "The *go* and *aśva* [stems] do not have the vowel *sa* as a non-color-vowel" (*na gośvansāvavarṇaḥ*). This is not a prohibition of the accent resulting from the removal of the acute (*udāttanivṛttisvara*). Of what, then, is it a prohibition? It is a prohibition of the third and subsequent accents (*tṛtīyādisvara*). But then, in cases where the third and subsequent accent does not exist, such as in *śunaḥ paśya*, what happens? In that case, we do not teach a prohibition for that which is merely derivative (*lākṣaṇika*). What, then? [We teach it] by means of that...

This is a prohibition of the accent of a case-ending that has been obtained by some specific characteristic. But what about where there is no case-ending, as in *bahv-śunī*? Furthermore, if this were understood as a prohibition even of the accent resulting from the removal of an acute (*udāttanivṛtti-svara*), it would not be possible; for then it would also apply here: [the following example].

[Regarding the word] *kumārī*: if this is so, then the activity of the Teacher indicates that the accent of the "substitution for the acute" (*anudāttanivṛttisvara*) does not descend upon *śunī*, since he recites the word *śvan* in the *gaurādi* group. He makes an effort [to include it there] for the sake of the final acute accent; for [the desired result] would already be established by the suffix *ṅīp* alone. [The rule] "the single-substitute [vowel] resulting from an accent [and another vowel]" applies: as in *sautthitiḥ* and *vaikṣmāṇiḥ*. And the accent would [otherwise] apply [only to the first syllable].

And as for the single-substitute (ekādeśa) rule: the accent would apply because it is subsequent; however, the single substitute occurs because it is more internal (antaraṅga). There is no conflict between the *guṇa* rule and the rules for *it*-substitution and *ut*-substitution. [In the case of] *vṛddhi*, there is *it*-substitution and *ut*-substitution, as in *staurniḥ* and *paurtiḥ*. Here, both *vṛddhi* and *it*-substitution/*ut*-substitution would apply; the *vṛddhi* would apply because it is subsequent, but *it*-substitution and *ut*-substitution occur because they are more internal than the doubling (*dvirvacana*).

Regarding the rules for *ittva* (the substitution of *i*) and *uttva* (the substitution of *u*): in the case of *āste*, *tīryate*, and *āpyāyate*, both reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and *ittva*/*uttva* would apply. Because reduplication is obligatory (*nitya*), it would occur first. However, *ittva* and *uttva* take precedence due to their being *antaraṅga* (internal). Furthermore, there is no conflict between the elision of *a* (*allopasya*) and *ittva*/*uttva*. There is no difference in accent (*svara*). In the case of the roots *iṇ*, *niṣ*, and *śī*, the substitution of *guṇa* for *ā* occurs because of the rule for homogeneous long vowels (*savarṇadīrghatvāt*).

In the case of *iṇ* and *niś*, there is the substitution of *guṇa* for the vowel *ā* [of the suffix], which serves as the purpose for applying the rule of homogeneous long-vowel (*savarṇadīrghatva*) [substitution]. For example: *ayaje indram*, *avape indram*, *vṛkṣe indram*, *plakṣe indram*, *ye indram*, *te indram*. Here, both the substitution of *guṇa* for *ā* and the substitution of a homogeneous long vowel would apply. Since the latter is subsequent, the substitution of the homogeneous long vowel would occur; however, the substitution of *guṇa* for *ā* occurs because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*). Or rather, [the substitution of *guṇa* does not occur] because of the substitution of the homogeneous long vowel.

Because it has no scope (*anavakāśatvāt*). Nor is this established even by means of an *antaraṅga* [rule]. What is the reason? Because the substitution of a long vowel for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*) has no scope. The substitution of a long vowel for homogeneous vowels, having no scope, would subvert the *āt-guṇa* [rule]. It is not the case that in an *antaraṅga* rule there is a subsequent [rule] which has no scope. Here too, in the case of *syonaḥ*,...

It may be said that [the term] "syonā" [is formed] or not, because the quality [of the substitute] is subsequent. The single-substitute (ekādeśa) for *ūṅ* and *āp* occurs by virtue of *ītva* and elision (*lopa*), due to its being *antaraṅga*. There is a purpose [for this]. From *ītva*, the single-substitute occurs:
as in *khaṭvīyati* and *mālīyati*. Both *ītva* and the single-substitute apply; however, because it is subsequent, *ītva* would occur. [But in fact,] the single-substitute occurs.

The single-substitute (ekādeśa) occurs because it is internal (antaraṅga). For example: *kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ*, *bhādrabāheyaḥ*. Here, both elision (*lopa*) and the single substitute would apply; however, by virtue of its priority (paratva), the elision would occur. But the single substitute prevails because it is internal. Now, for what purpose is it stated "by means of *īt* and elision" (*ītvālopābhyām*), rather than simply stating "by means of elision and *īt*" (*lopaitvābhyām*)? It is so that there may be no application of numerical correspondence (*saṅkhyātānudeśa*).
Thus, the substitution of *āp* also serves as a cause for elision. For example:

*cauḍiḥ*, *bālākiḥ*. The rules for the substitution of *āt*, the shortening of neuter stems, and the shortening of secondary members (*upasarjana*) take precedence over the rules for the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of *aya*, *ava*, and *āy*, and over the rules for the insertion of the augment *tuK*. This is because they are more internal (*antaraṅga*).

[The roots] *veñ*, *śo* [for *śyai*], *glai*, *mlai*, and *glācchattram* / *clācchattram* undergo the substitution of *ā* (āttva), and these grammatical operations [such as lengthening] also apply. Because they are subsequent rules, these operations would take effect; however, the substitution of *ā* occurs because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*).
Furthermore, the shortening of neuter secondary members (*napuṃsakopasarjana*) is also a purpose [of this rule]. Examples: *atiri atra*, *atinu atra*, *atiricchattram*.

In *atinucchatram*, *ārāśastri*, *idam dhānāśaṣkuli*, *idam niṣkauśāmbi*, and *idam nirvārāṇasi*, the shortening of the feminine secondary member (*napuṃsakopasarjanahrasvatvam*) applies, as do these other rules [of sandhi]. Since these rules are subsequent, they would take precedence; however, the shortening of the feminine secondary member does indeed occur.

By virtue of being *antaraṅga* (internal), the *tuk* augment occurs prior to the rules for *yaṇ*-substitution, single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) formation, *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, *auttva*, lengthening (*dīrghatva*), *itva*, *um*, *ettva*, and the rule for *rī*. The *tuk* augment occurs by virtue of being *antaraṅga* before the following operations:
1. From *yaṇ*-substitution: as in *agnicit atra* and *somasut atra*. 2. From single-substitute formation: as in *agnicid idam* and *somasud udakam*.

From the presence of a *guṇa* vowel: in *agnicite* and *somasute*. From the presence of *vṛddhi*: in *praṛcchakaḥ* and *prārcchakaḥ*. From the presence of *aut* (the diphthong *au*): in *agniciti* and *somasuti*. From the presence of a long vowel (*dīrgha*): in *jagadbhyām* and *janagadbhyām*. From the presence of *īt* (the diphthong *ī*): in *jagatyati* and *janagatyati*. From the presence of the augment *muṭ*: in *agnicinmanyaḥ* and *somasunmanyaḥ*. From the presence of *et* (the diphthong *e*): in *jagadbhyaḥ* and *janagadbhyaḥ*. From the prescription of *rī* (the diphthong *rī*).

Regarding *sukṛtyati* and *pāpakṛtyati*: it should be stated that [the suffix] applies after both *anaṅ* and *aṅ*. Thus we have *sukṛt* and *sukṛt-duṣkṛtau*. Both the insertion of the augment *tuk* and these grammatical operations would apply; however, because they are subsequent rules, these operations should take effect first. The *tuk* occurs by virtue of being an *antaraṅga* (internal) operation. The substitution of *iyaṅ* takes precedence over *guṇa* because it is an *antaraṅga* operation. An example of this is *dhiyati* and *riyati*.

Both the substitution of *iyaṅ* and *guṇa* would apply; however, because it is subsequent, *guṇa* would occur. The substitution of *iyaṅ* occurs because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*). It should also be stated that there is the substitution of *uvaṅ*: as in *prādudruvat* and *prāsusruvat*. Regarding the root *śvi*, the priority of the *samprasāraṇa* substitution over the *yaṇ* substitution is due to its being more internal; this serves as the purpose [for stating the rule].

*śuśuvatuḥ*, *śuśuvuḥ*. Both the substitution of the preceding vowel (*pūrvatva*) and the substitution of *yaṇ* apply. Because the latter [rule for *yaṇ*] is subsequent, it would be the *yaṇ* substitution that occurs. However, the substitution of the preceding vowel takes place because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*). This is due to the elision of the vowel *ā* in the root *hve*. The substitution of the preceding vowel occurs because it is more internal; this is the purpose [of the rule]. Examples: *juhuvatuḥ*, *juhuvuḥ*. Both the substitution of the preceding vowel and the elision of the vowel *ā* apply.

Because it is subsequent, there would be the elision of the vowel *ā*. Priority [of the accent] arises due to its being internal (*antaraṅga*). Accent arises from elision; accent arises from elision due to its being internal. This is the purpose: *aupagavī*, *saudāmanī*. Both accent and elision apply; because it is subsequent, elision would occur. Accent arises due to its being internal. The rule for the suffix applies prior to the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*).

The rule for the formation of suffixes takes precedence over a single-substitute (ekādeśa) operation on account of its being *antaraṅga* (more internal). For example: *agniḥ*, *indraḥ*, *vāyuḥ*, *udakam*. Here, both the rule for the suffix and the single-substitute operation would apply; however, because it is subsequent (*para*), the single-substitute operation would [otherwise] occur.
But the rule for the suffix prevails due to its being *antaraṅga*. It should also be stated that this applies even over the *yaṇ*-substitution: *agnir atra*, *vāyur atra*.

In this case, the substitution of *la* (the imperative suffix) takes precedence over the phonetic rule (*varṇavidhi*) because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*). For example, in *pacatu atra* and *paṭhatu atra*, both the substitution of *la* and the substitution of *yaṇ* would apply; however, by virtue of being subsequent (*paratva*), the *yaṇ* substitution would occur. But the substitution of *la* occurs because it is more internal. Furthermore, the final acute accent (*antodātta*) of the *tatpuruṣa* compound prevails over the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*).

The final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) of a *tatpuruṣa* compound arises from the original accent of the prior member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*). For example, in *pūrvaśālāpriyaḥ* and *aparaśālāpriyaḥ*, both the final acute accent of the *tatpuruṣa* and the original accent of the prior member would apply; however, by virtue of its priority, the original accent of the prior member would prevail. But [in fact], the final acute accent of the *tatpuruṣa* occurs because it is more internal.

These are the purposes of this *paribhāṣā*, for the sake of which this *paribhāṣā* must be formulated. Why?
