"An external grammatical operation (*bahiraṅga-lakṣaṇa*) is not established when an internal grammatical operation (*antaraṅga-lakṣaṇa*) is to take effect. What is the purpose [of this rule]? [In the examples] *pacāvedam* and *pacāmedam*, because the external operation of *guṇa* is not established, let there not be the internal operation of *aitva*.
[Objection: "Then both must be applied. [The author] says: "No; it is already established by this very [rule]. For even here in *syonaḥ* and *syonā*, because [the *guṇa*] is not established...

The substitution of *yaṇ* (semivowels), which is an internal (*antaraṅga*) rule, will take effect in place of the quality (*guṇa*), which is an external (*bahiraṅga*) rule. If it is stated that "an external rule is as if unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to an internal rule," then in the cases of *akṣadyūḥ* and *hiraṇyadyūḥ*, because the external rule for *ūṭh* is unestablished, the internal rule for the *yaṇ* substitution would not apply. This is not a fault.

Having stated that "an external rule (*bahir-aṅga-lakṣaṇa*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to an internal rule (*antaraṅga-lakṣaṇa*)," he will subsequently state: "In the case of non-proximity (*ajānantarya*), there is no designation of externality. Therefore, this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) must be formulated. It need not be formulated; for the Teacher’s practice indicates that this rule exists, since he says: "The [substitution] of *ṣatva* and *tuk* is unestablished. Well then, what about this?

A paribhāṣā must be formulated stating that "that which is characterized by being external (bahiraṅga) is not established when [it comes into conflict with] that which is characterized by being internal (antaraṅga). However, this paribhāṣā need not be formulated.

The activity of the Teacher (Ācārya) indicates that this paribhāṣā exists, insofar as he teaches the substitution of *ūṭh* in the rule *vāha ūṭh*. The fault in that regard is that the *vṛddhi* and accentuation of the preceding and following members would [otherwise] take precedence over the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*). This is the purpose of that rule.

The *vṛddhi* and accentuation rules for the first and second members of a compound would not apply due to the fact that the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has already taken effect as an internal operation (*antaraṅga*).

For example, in *pūrva-eṣukāmaśamaḥ*, *apara-eṣukāmaśamaḥ*, *guḍa-udakam*, and *tila-udakam*, the rule "in the case of *udaka* when it does not mean 'entirely'" would not apply because there is no distinct separation (*vyapavarga*) between the first and second members. This is not a fault; for the activity of the Teacher indicates that [the rule applies] to the first and second members [of the compound].

The operation must take place first, and not the single-substitute (ekādeśa) replacement; this is because the rule prohibits [the substitution] in the case of "para-indra" by stating "not after *indra*. How does this serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? In the word *indra*, there are two vowels (*ac*). Of these, one is removed by the elision (*lopa*) according to the rule "of that which has *ī*" (*yasyeti ca*), and the other is replaced by a single substitute (*ekādeśa*). Consequently, *indra* becomes devoid of vowels (*anacka*). Under such circumstances, what possibility is there for the application of *vṛddhi*?

The Teacher, however, perceives that the operation of the preceding and following members must first take place before the single-substitute (ekādeśa) occurs; therefore, he teaches the prohibition "not when *indra* follows. Regarding the substitution of *iy* and *uv* for *yaṇ*: the substitutions of *iy* and *uv* do not apply because they have already been established by the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) of the *yaṇ*-substitution—as in the cases *vaiyākaraṇaḥ* and *sauvaśvaḥ*. For indeed, there is a rule concerning *y* and *v*.
"In the event of *vṛddhi*, *iy* and *uv* should occur"—this is not a fault. *Iy* and *uv* are without scope [elsewhere], for it is stated that they occur "before a vowel" (*aci*).

But what is the reason for saying "before a vowel"? It is so that they do not occur here: *aitikāyanaḥ*, *aupagavaḥ*. Let *iy* and *uv* occur here; there will be elision by the rule "elision of *y* and *v* before a consonant" (*lopo vyoḥ vali*). But where, then, is there no elision?

There is [the example] *praiyamedhaḥ*, *praiyaṅgavaḥ*. Because of the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) in the case of the suffix *usi*, the substitution of *iy* would not apply because it is superseded by that which is established as more internal (*antaraṅga*).
[Examples would be: *paceyuḥ*, *yajeyuḥ*. This is not a fault. It is not understood thus:
"for this [stem] *yā*, *iy* occurs. How then? It is understood: "for this [stem] *yās*, *iy* occurs. [In the case of *paceyuḥ*, etc.,] there is elision (*luk*).

It should be stated that elision (*luk*) is stronger than elision (*lopa*), *yaṇ*-substitution, *ay*-substitution, *vāy*-substitution, and *ekādeśa* (single-substitute) operations. [Example] From elision (*lopa*): *gomān priyo 'sya* becomes *gomatpriyaḥ*; *yavamatpriyaḥ*. [Also]: *gomān ivācarati* becomes *gomatyate*;
*yavamatyate*. [Example] From *yaṇ*-substitution: *grāmaṇyaḥ kulam* becomes *grāmaṇikulam*; *senānyaḥ kulam* becomes *senānikulam*.

Regarding the rule *ayavāyāvekādeśebhyaḥ*: *gave hitam* becomes *go-hitam*; *rāyaḥ kulam* becomes *rai-kulam*; *nāvaḥ kulam* becomes *nau-kulam*; *vṛkādbhayam* becomes *vṛka-bhayam*. Both the elision (*luk*) and these specific grammatical operations apply. Since these operations are subsequent [to the rule for elision], they would take effect first. It must be stated that elision is stronger; thus, elision (*luk*) should take place.

(P_1,4.3.1) What is the purpose of [specifying] *yū*? [Consider the examples: *khaṭvā*, *mālā*. What would happen? In the case of *khaṭvābandhuḥ* and *mālābandhuḥ*, the accent prescribed by the rule *nadī bandhuni* would apply. And here, in the case of *bahukhaṭvakaḥ*, the rule *nadyṛtaś ca* [would also apply].

Thus, the suffix *kap* would apply permanently [to all feminine bases]. This is not a fault. The activity of the Teacher indicates that the term *āp* does not receive the designation *nadī*, since he makes a separate mention of *āp* in the rule "ṅer ām nadyāmnībhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.116). However, in this case—such as *mātre* and *mātuḥ*—the augment *āṭ* prescribed by the rule "āṭ nadyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.112) would apply. But is this mention of the long vowels (*dīrgha*) intended for those two [specific cases], or rather...?
[The rule applies] to the two short vowels. What follows from this? If [the term] *yū* refers to the long vowels, then the grammatical instruction (*nirdeśa*) is not tenable;

for after a long vowel, the substitution of a homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*) is prohibited. Furthermore, in the subsequent rule, the qualification "the two short vowels" (*yū hrasvau*) could not be established.
If they are *yū*, they are not short; if they are short, they are not *yū*. To say "the two *yū* are short" is a contradiction.

Now, [if the rule applied] to both short vowels, it would also undesirably apply here: *he śakaṭe*. This fault does not arise; for in this case, the designation *nadī* must necessarily be understood as optional (*vibhāṣā*). For both forms are desired:
*he śakaṭi* and *he śakaṭe*. But then, in the case of *śakaṭibandhuḥ*, there would be this accent [of the first member] by the rule *nadī bandhuni*.

[Otherwise] it would follow [that the suffix *kap* would apply]. And in the case of *bahuśakaṭiḥ*, the suffix *kap* would necessarily apply by the rule "after a feminine stem ending in long *ṛ*, [the suffix *kap* is applied]" (*nady-ṛtaś-ca*). This is not a fault. The rule "a short vowel followed by a *ṅit* [suffix] is also [called *nadī*]" (*ṅiti hrasvaś-ca*) will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). It means that only when followed by a *ṅit* suffix are the *yū* (feminine stems in long *ī* and *ū*) and short vowels designated as *nadī*, and not otherwise. Why does a restriction occur? Because there is no other thing to be prescribed (*vidheya*). Thus it is considered.

And here there is something to be prescribed. What is it? The designation *nadī* (river) is established as permanent; that [designation] must be prescribed as optional (*vibhāṣā*). In that case, let it be a new injunction (*apūrvo vidhiḥ*) or let it be a restrictive rule (*niyamaḥ*); it will be a new injunction alone, not a restrictive rule. If this were a permanent rule (*nityo yogaḥ*), then a restriction could be assumed. Certainly, a restriction could be assumed. But in that case, it would be permanent.

How is that so? A division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) will be made as follows: First, this rule exists: "The two vowels *yū* (i.e., *ī* and *ū*), when feminine in gender, are designated as *nadī*, provided they do not stand in the place of *iyaṅ* or *uvaṅ*;

or, [according to another view], they are *nadī* except before the suffix *ām*. Then comes the rule: "Before a suffix marked with *ṅ*. This means that the two vowels *yū*, standing in the place of *iyaṅ* or *uvaṅ*, are not designated as *nadī* before a suffix marked with *ṅ*, unless they are feminine.

Then comes the rule: "The two short vowels. This means that the two short vowels *yū* (i.e., *i* and *u*), when feminine in gender, are designated as *nadī* before a suffix marked with *ṅ*. [This applies] to those standing in the place of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*.

And the word "or not" (*vā na*) has been removed [from the rule]. If this were so, then in the case of *śakaṭaye*, the substitution of the *guṇa* vowel would not be obtained. A second *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) will be made: the mention of *śeṣa* (remainder) will not be employed. How? This exists: "The feminine stems *yū* called *nadī* that do not stand in the place of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are optionally called *nadī* before the endings *āma* and *su*, provided they are not *strī*. Then, from the rule "before a suffix marked with *ṅ*" (*ṅiti*): "And before a suffix marked with *ṅ*, the feminine stems *yū* that stand in the place of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are optionally designated as *nadī*, provided they are not *strī*."
Not [the case] for you. Therefore, they are short. And the two short vowels *yū* (i and u) denoting feminine are designated as *nadī* when followed by a suffix beginning with *ṅ*.

Then, "short" [is repeated]. And the two short vowels *yū* denoting feminine are designated as *nadī* when followed by a suffix beginning with *ṅ*. The rule "or those which are the substitutes for *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*" and "not *na*" are also removed. Then, *ghi*. And the two short vowels *yū* denoting feminine are designated as *ghi*.

[The rule] "before a suffix marked with Ṅ" [is established]. Then, [the rule] "not *sakhi*": both *yū* (i.e., *ī* and *ū*) that are short and exclude *sakhi* receive the technical designation *ghis*. Furthermore, the phrase "feminine in name before a suffix marked with Ṅ" is no longer in force. If, then, the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) were not made, there would be no need for even one division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). Without distinction, the designation *nadī* would be the general rule (*utsarga*); the designation *ghi* would be its exception (*bādhaka*) for the two short vowels; and while that [designation *ghi*] is permanent, [the designation *nadī* would apply otherwise].

The option (*vibhāṣā*) is commenced when a *ṅit* suffix follows. Or rather, let it be that [the rule applies] after two long vowels (*dīrgha*). But was it not said that the grammatical instruction (*nirdeśa*) is untenable? For a *pūrvasavarṇa* [diphthong] is prohibited after a long vowel. [Reply: It will be so by virtue of the rule "optionally in the Veda" (*vā chandasi*). [Objection: It is stated "in the Veda," yet this is not the Veda. [Reply: The Sūtras are like the Veda (*chandovat*). Furthermore, even if...

It is said: "In what follows, the specific distinction would not be applicable, namely that 'yū' are short vowels. If they are *yū* but not short, or if they are short but not *yū*, then the statement "yū are short" is contradictory. This is not contradictory.
He says this: "yū are short. If they are *yū* but not short, or if they are short but not *yū*, we shall understand it in this way.

"Regarding *yvoḥ* [in the rule] 'the two short ones (*hrasvau*)': which are the two short *y* and *v*? They are those that are homogeneous (*savarṇa*). Now, as for the term *stryākhyau*: what kind of word is this? Those that denote a female (*strī*) are called *stryākhyau*. If that is so, one would expect the form *stryākhyāyau*. For the suffix *ka* is prescribed only when there is no preceding prefix (*anupasarga*). In that case, the following [Vedic example] would not be valid: *yasmin daśa sahasrāṇi putre jāte*."

"He gave cows to the Brahmins who were called *priya*. "This man lives by gleaning (*uñcha*). "The poets compose according to the Vedic meters (*chandovat*). "For this is not an *iṣṭi* sacrifice. If that is so, then it will be a word derived from an object (a *karmasādhana*): "those two which are designated as feminine are called *stryākhyau*. If it is a *karmasādhana*, then it would not apply to feminine words formed with *kṛt* suffixes or feminine verbal roots (*dhātustri*).
[If it is argued: "Let there be a *bahuvrīhi* compound:

those two whose designation (*ākhyā*) is 'female' (*strī*) are 'feminine-designated' (*stryākhyau*). [Response: Even so, it would not apply to feminine nouns derived from verbal roots (*dhātu-strī*) or feminine nouns formed with primary suffixes (*kṛt-strī*), such as *tantryai*, *lakṣmyai*, *śriyai*, and *bhruvai*. [Objection: "In that case, let there be the *vic* suffix. Or rather, let it simply be "the feminine" (*strīm*).

They state that [the suffix *ka*] is applied to words denoting females (*stryākhyau*). But has it not already been said that the form *stryākhyāyau* would result? For the suffix *ka* is prescribed only after a word that does not have a prefix (*anupasarge*). [Reply: The suffix *ka* will occur by virtue of its inclusion in the group beginning with *mūlavibhuja*. And by doing so, that which was stated also becomes free from fault:
"When ten thousand cows were given to the Brāhmaṇas who announced the pleasant news upon the birth of a son."
This very person lives by gleaning grains.

Now, what is the purpose of including the term *ākhyā* [in the rule]? The inclusion of the term *ākhyā* in the definition of the technical term *nadī* is for the sake of referring to feminine objects.

In the definition of the term *nadī*, the inclusion of the word "designation" (*ākhyā*) is for the purpose of restricting it to feminine objects. This is so that the designation *nadī* applies only to those two [words] which are always feminine in meaning. It should not apply here: *grāmaṇye*, *senānye* (when used as feminine). And there must be the inclusion of the "original gender" (*prathamaliṅga*). That is to say, it must be stated: "those two which have the designation 'feminine' in their original gender [are called *nadī*]."

What is the purpose? The purpose is for the sake of the *kvip*, *lup*, and compound formations. [Examples: *kumāryai brāhmaṇāya* (for a Brahmin who is a young girl); *lup*: *kharakuṭyai brāhmaṇāya* (for a Brahmin who is a donkey-stable), *atitantryai brāhmaṇāya* (for a Brahmin who has transcended the loom), *atilakṣmyai brāhmaṇāya* (for a Brahmin who has surpassed Lakṣmī). Then it must be stated. It need not be stated. It is established because the feminine reference applies to the constituent part (*avayava*). In this case, the constituent part is feminine; the [grammatical operation] is based upon that.

[Objection: "The designation *nadī* will apply [to the whole], because it is established on the basis of its having a feminine part. [Reply: If that were so, then in the prohibition of the *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutes, there would follow the undesirable consequence of prohibiting the *yaṇ* substitute as well, because the parts [of the whole] occupy the place of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*. [Objection: "If it is argued that it is established because the designation applies to the feminine parts," [Reply:
Then in the prohibition of the *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutes, there would follow the undesirable consequence of prohibiting both *y* and *v* even when they occupy the place of *yaṇ*.

[The forms] *ādhyai*, *pradhyai*, and *brāhmaṇyai* [are established]. What is the reason? Because the constituent part (*avayava*) occupies the place of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*. Here, the constituent part occupies the place of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*. [This is] established, however, by virtue of the mention of the form of the stem (*aṅga*). For there is a prohibition against that stem for which *iy* and *uv* occur. This is established. How? By mentioning the form of the stem: "of that stem for which *iy* and *uv* occur."

This is the inclusion [of the term *hrasva*]. And for this member (*aṅga*), the substitutions *iy* and *uv* do not occur. It must be stated: "When the short vowels *i* and *u* (standing in the place of *iy* and *uv*) are about to occur, and when they are in the feminine gender, they receive the technical designation *nadī* both while they are short and standing in the place of *iy* and *uv*, as well as prior to their occurrence. [Examples: *śakaṭyai*, *atiśakaṭyai*, *brāhmaṇāṇyai*. Where [is it] not?
[It was] for Bhūta, for Atiśakaṭa, for the Brāhmaṇa; for Dhenu, for Atidhenu, for the Brāhmaṇī. Where should it not be?

For Dhenu, for Atidhenu, for the Brāhmaṇa; for Śrī, for Atiśrī, for the Brāhmaṇī. Where should it not be? For Śrī, for Atiśrī, for the Brāhmaṇa; for Bhru, for Atibhru, for the Brāhmaṇī. Where should it not be? For Bhru, for Atibhru.

To a Brāhmaṇa woman. Another says: it should be stated that short vowels in the place of *i* and *u*, even when they have undergone modification (*pravṛtta*), are designated as *nadī* (feminine) only when they express the feminine gender; for example, *śakaṭyai*, *atiśakaṭyai*, *brāhmaṇāṇyai*. Where should this not apply? As in *śakaṭaye*, *atiśakaṭaye*, *brāhmaṇāya*. [And] *dhenvai*.

[The rule applies] for *atidhenvai* and *brāhmaṇyai*. [Question: Where would it not apply? [Answer: For *dhenave* and *atidhenave*, for *brāhmaṇāya*. For *śriyai* and *atiśriyai*, for *brāhmaṇyai*. Where would it not apply? For *śriye* and *atiśriye*, for *brāhmaṇāya*. For *bhruvai* and *atibhruvai*, for *brāhmaṇyai*. Where would it not apply? For *bhruve* and *atibhruve*, for *brāhmaṇāya*. Why, then, is this stated? [It is stated] so that the gender of the first member [of the compound] is taken.

This has been objected: one should understand that all this is subject to conceptual construction (*vikalpate*). Therefore, the Teacher, acting as a friend, explains: both the short vowels and those in the place of *i* and *u*, whether they have undergone *pravṛtti* or have not yet undergone *pravṛtti*, are indeed feminine in gender.

349–350. A division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) must be made: "In the Veda, that which is joined with a genitive [is called *ghi*]. When joined with a genitive, the word *pati* is designated as *ghi* in the Veda. From this follows: "Or optionally. In the Veda, all rules are optional: there is the transposition of case endings (*sup*), the transposition of verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), the transposition of phonemes (*varṇa*), the transposition of gender (*liṅga*), the transposition of tense (*kāla*), and the transposition of person (*puruṣa*).

The substitution of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*); the substitution of the active voice (*parasmaipada*); the substitution of case endings (*sup*). "The mother was yoked to the pole of the sacrificial fee" (*dhuri dakṣiṇāyāḥ*), where one would have expected *dakṣiṇāyām*. This is the substitution of verbal endings (*tiṅ*). "Those who carve the wooden post for the horse" (*ye aśvayūpaya takṣati*), where one would have expected *takṣanti*. This is the substitution of phonemes (*varṇa*). "The *triṣṭubh* [verse], powerful, brightened, and of fierce heroism."

When *suhitam* was expected, there is a change of gender: *madhoḥ gṛhṇāti*, *madhoḥ tṛptā iva āsate*. When *madhunaḥ* was expected, there is a change of time: *śvaḥ agnīn ādhāsyamānena*, *śvaḥ somena yakṣyamāṇena*, *śvaḥ ādhātā*, *śvaḥ yaṣṭā*. When [the present tense] was expected, there is a change of person: *atha sa vīraiḥ daśabhir viyūyāḥ*.

Regarding the form *viyūyāt*: where *viyuñjīta* was expected, there is a substitution of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). Regarding *brahmacāriṇam icchate*: where *icchati* was expected, there is a substitution of the active voice (*parasmaipada*). "One wave fights against another wave;
another wave fights along with [another]"—where *yudhyate* was expected, there is a substitution of the active voice.

The word *yasmāt* is used for the sake of designation. Now, what is the purpose of mentioning the term *pratyaya*? If it were stated merely that "that which begins with the element from which a rule is prescribed (*vidhi*) is the *aṅga* when a suffix (*pratyaya*) follows," then [the rule] would undesirably apply even in cases such as *strī iyatī* and *strīyati*.

However, when the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) is made, there is no fault. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "rule" (*vidhi*)? Because if it were stated merely that "that which begins with an affix is a stem (*aṅga*) when an affix follows," then [the designation of stem] would undesirably apply here as well: *dadhi-adhunā* and *madhu-adhunā*. But when the mention of "rule" is made, there is no fault. This is achieved by the mention of "affix."

And by the mention of "vidhi" (prescription) in combination [with "tadādi"], a restriction (*sanniyoga*) is established: namely, that whatever suffix is prescribed, that which begins with it receives the technical designation *aṅga*. Now, what is the purpose of the mention of "tadādi" (that which begins with it)? In the matter of the *aṅga* designation, the mention of "tadādi" is for the sake of the case-endings (*syādi*) and for the sake of *num*. Thus, the mention of "tadādi" is made in the *aṅga* designation for the sake of the case-endings and for the sake of *num*.

And [the following examples serve] as illustrations: *kariṣyāvaḥ* (we two shall do), *kariṣyāmaḥ* (we all shall do). For the sake of the augment *num*: *kuṇḍāni*, *vanāni*. There must be an addition regarding *mit* and *suṭ*. An addition must be made for that which has *mit* and for that which has *suṭ*. Regarding that which has *mit*: *bhinatti*, *chinatti*, *abhinat*, *acchinat*. Regarding that which has *suṭ*: *sañcaskāra*, *sañcaskaruḥ*. But what is the reason?

It is not established [by the rule], because *suṭ* is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). *Suṭ* is extrinsic; *guṇa* is intrinsic (*antaraṅga*). That which is extrinsic is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is intrinsic. He will state this: in the prescription of *guṇa* for roots beginning with a conjunct consonant, the mention of "having a conjunct as a penultimate" (*saṃyogopadha*) is for the sake of *kṛñ*. If the mention of "having a conjunct as a penultimate" is made, there is no purpose in the mention of "beginning with a conjunct" (*saṃyogādi*). Here...

[The forms] *sasvaratuḥ* and *sasvaruḥ* are already established by the rule *saṃyogopadhasya*. This would be so, and there would be no need for this [separate] purpose; however, this [other case] is not established: *sañcakaratuḥ* and *sañcaskaruḥ*. What, then, is the reason it is not established? In this context, the reference is either to that [specific root] itself or to something beginning with it; yet this is neither that nor does it begin with it. But it is established as follows:

This is established by the expression "tadādyādi. How so? It should be stated that "that which begins with what begins with it" receives the technical designation *aṅga*. What is this "tadādyādi"? "Tadādi" means its beginning (*tasya ādiḥ*);

"tadādyādi" means that of which the beginning begins with that (*tadādir ādir yasya*). Well then, that should be the formulation. No, it need not be; here an elision of the final member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*) is to be understood. For example:
"One whose face is like that of a camel is *uṣṭramukhaḥ*;
[one whose face is like that of a donkey is] *kharamukhaḥ*.

In this way, [the compound] *tadādi* is formed from *tad-ādi*. Alternatively, it is established through the principle of "understanding by means of a part" (*tadekadeśavijñānāt*); that is, through understanding by means of a part."
This is established. A part that constitutes a portion of a whole is included by the mention of that whole. For example: "The Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and Devadattā.

When many rivers have entered the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, they are included by the mention of the "Gaṅgā-Yamunā. Likewise, the fetus residing within Devadattā is included by the mention of "Devadattā. [Objection: This is an unequal comparison. Here, some...
Words are denoters of objects whose measure has been specified— namely, those words which are numerals and those which are measures of capacity,
such as "five" and "seven," which do not apply when even one is removed; and such as "droṇa," "khārī," and "āḍhaka."

They are neither more nor less; they say exactly as much as there is. These words for genus (*jāti-śabda*) and words for quality (*guṇa-śabda*)—such as "oil" and "clarified butter"—apply whether it be in a *khārī* measure or even in a *droṇa*. [Words for] qualities such as "white," "blue," and "black" apply to a substance as large as the Himalayas, and even to a substance the size of a small ball of cow dung. Furthermore, the technical designation of "base" (*aṅga-sañjñā*) applies to those whose quantity has not been specified.

It is being done. By what means would it apply to something additional? If that is so, then the activity of the Teacher indicates that a part belonging to a whole is included by the mention of that whole, since he teaches a prohibition for those forms containing the letter *ka* in the rule "not for *idam* and *adas* when they lack *ka*" (*na idamadasoḥ akoḥ*). How does this serve as an indicator? Since the grammatical operation is stated for *idam* and *adas*, what occasion could there be for it to apply to those forms containing the letter *ka*?

The Teacher, however, perceives that because [the whole] is a part of that [whole], it is grasped by the mention of that [part]; therefore, he teaches the prohibition for the two [sounds] beginning with *ka*.

Now, what is the purpose of the second mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*)? The mention of "affix" is for the sake of preventing [the designation of *aṅga*] from applying to the beginning of a word (*padādau*). The mention of "affix" is made so that the technical name *aṅga* does not apply to the beginning of a word.
[The word] *bhūta* [is used]. And what would be the result? For the sake of feminine forms, for the sake of *śrī*, and for the sake of *bhū*:
by the rule "of a stem" (*aṅgasya*), *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* would apply. And it is for the sake of measurement; and the second [word *bhūta*] is for the sake of measurement.

The mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) is made. If it were stated merely that "that which begins with what an affix is prescribed after is a stem" (*aṅga*), then even the *dāśataya* [Vedic hymns] would incur the designation of "stem. Should that [designation] then be applied? It need not be applied. But by what means will the operations pertaining to the stem (*aṅgakārya*) now take place? Having introduced the rule with "when an affix follows" (*pratyaye*), I shall teach the operations pertaining to the stem. [This applies] when an affix follows.
Having stated this, [the question arises: "In *adhīṣe*, *prākarot*, and *upaihiṣṭa*, do the augments *aṭ* and *āṭ* apply before the prefix?

[The answer is: This is established by the rule regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇe*), through the understanding that [the term refers to] what begins with that [suffix] and ends with it (*tadāditadanta-vijñānāt*). How so? When there is a mention of a suffix, the mention includes that which begins with the element after which that suffix is prescribed and that which ends with it.

Thus, this *paribhāṣā* must be formulated. But what is the distinction here between formulating this *paribhāṣā* and [merely] using the term "affix" (*pratyaya*)? This *paribhāṣā* must necessarily be formulated, for there are many purposes for this *paribhāṣā*. The purposes are: rules concerning verbal roots (*dhātu*), nominal stems (*prātipadika*), affixes (*pratyaya*), compounds (*samāsa*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and accents (*svara*). Regarding verbal roots: *devadattaś cikīrṣati* ("Devadatta desires to do").
The designation *dhātu* (verbal root) would apply to the entire aggregate [of sounds]. [Example: *devadattaḥ*, *gārgyaḥ*.
The designation *prātipadika* (nominal stem) would apply to the entire aggregate. [Example: *mahāntam putram icchati*. The production of a suffix (*pratyaya*) would result from the entire aggregate.
[Example: *ṛddhasya rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*. The designation *samāsa* (compound) would apply to the entire aggregate.

Regarding the rule for the formation of *taddhita* derivatives: [in the case of] *devadatta-gārgyāyaṇaḥ*, the production of a *taddhita* suffix would result from the entire compound (*saṃghāta*). Regarding accent: [in the case of] *devadatta-gārgyaḥ*, the initial syllable of the compound would necessarily acquire the acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) by the rule "that which begins with *ñ* or *ṇ* is always [acute]. However, there is no fault here, because when a suffix is mentioned, it refers to that suffix along with whatever precedes it and whatever ends with it. That being so, this [rule]...
An explanatory rule (*paribhāṣā*) must be formulated. It need not be formulated. I shall state it thus:

"That which begins with the element from which a suffix is prescribed is included when that suffix is being apprehended; therefore, it is called a stem (*aṅga*). And it becomes designated as a stem—that which begins with the element from which a suffix is prescribed—when that suffix is being apprehended.

359–360. If it is stated that when a suffix is mentioned, there is the inclusion of that [suffix] and what precedes it, then in the case of *avatape nakulasthitam* and *te etad udake viśīrṇam*, a compound with *sanakula*—which includes the prefix (*sagatika*)—would not be obtained. If this is so, then having stated that when a suffix is mentioned, there is the inclusion of that [suffix] and what precedes it, I shall thereafter say:

When there is a mention of a *kṛt* suffix, there is also the inclusion of that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*. This *paribhāṣā* (metarule) must be formulated: "When there is a mention of a *kṛt* suffix, there is also the inclusion of [a compound] preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*. What are the purposes (*prayojana*) of this *paribhāṣā*? The purposes are the rules for compounds (*samāsa*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and accentuation (*svara*). Regarding compounds: *avatapena kulasthitam te etat*, *udake viśīrṇam te etat*; [here we have] with the *gati* and the *nakula*: *sagatikena sanakulena*.

And the compound is established. Regarding compounds: in the rule for secondary derivation (*taddhita-vidhi*), [the forms] *sāṅkūṭinam* and *vyāvakrośī* are established as the production of a secondary derivative from a composite whole. Regarding the rule for secondary derivation: in the case of accent (*svara*), in the example "come from afar" (*dūrād āgataḥ* → *dūrādāgataḥ*), this accent is established by the rule "the acute accent falls on the final syllable of words ending in *thā*, *tha*, *ghan*, *ktā*, *ac*, *ap*, *tra*, or *ka*. This applies when there is the mention of *kṛt*-suffixes.

There is no fault, because there is also the inclusion of that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*. If so, then this *paribhāṣā* must be formulated. It need not be formulated; for the Teacher’s practice indicates that this *paribhāṣā* exists, insofar as he employs the term "immediate" (*anantara*) in the rule *gatiḥ anantaraḥ*.

(P_1.4.14) Why is the mention of "end" (*anta*) stated? Why not simply say, "a word (*pada*) consists of [stems ending in] case-endings (*suptiṅ*)"? By what means, then, would the designation apply to those [stems] that end in them? It would be by the rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*). Therefore, he recites the following answer: "In the case of the technical term 'word' (*padasañjñā*), the mention of 'end' [is necessary], because it is otherwise."

In a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, the prohibition of the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadanta-vidhi-pratiṣedha*) applies. In the case of the technical name *pada*, however, the mention of the word "end" (*anta*) is made for the purpose of providing a *jñāpaka* (an indicator). What is indicated? The Teacher indicates this: that in other rules prescribing technical names, when a suffix is mentioned, the rule of extension to what ends with that does not apply. What is the purpose of this indication? [It serves to establish the forms] *tarap* and *tamap*.

The suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* do not receive the designation *gha*. What would be the consequence? In the case of *kumārī gauritarā*, the rule "in the presence of *gha*-suffixes and others, the feminine suffix *nadi* becomes short" would undesirably apply, resulting in shortening. If this [the fact that *tarap* and *tamap* are not *gha*] is to be indicated, then in the rule "sanādyantāḥ dhātavaḥ" (P. 3.1.32), the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) must be made; and in the rule "kṛttaddhitasamāsāś ca" (P. 1.2.46), the inclusion of the word "end" must also be made.

This is the third indicator for this purpose. First, two [terms] are indeed provided in the very *nyāsa* [commentary]. As for what is said—that in the rule *kṛttaddhitasamāsāś ca*, the mention of the final element (*antagrahaṇa*) must be made—it need not be made. The term *arthavat* (meaning-bearing) is understood to carry over; and it is only that which ends in a *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffix which is meaning-bearing, not the *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffixes alone.

(P_1,4.15) Why is this stated? It is already established that "a word (*pada*) is that which ends in a *sup* suffix. This undertaking is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Only that which ends in *n* is designated as a *pada* when followed by *kye*, and nothing else. Where should it not apply? As in *vācyati* and *srucyati*.

It is stated: "in a case that is not a *sarvanāmasthāna*. In that context, for [the forms] *te*, *rājā*, and *takṣā*, there would follow the prohibition of the technical designation *pada* because it is "not a *sarvanāmasthāna*. This is not so, because it is not a prohibition. This is not a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) regarding the *sarvanāmasthāna*.

"No"—what then? This is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), namely: "that which is other than a *sarvanāmasthāna*. There is no operation regarding the *sarvanāmasthāna*. If it is obtained by something else, it will occur by that; and it is obtained by the preceding rule. Or rather, because [the subsequent rule] has not yet been reached.
Or else, the application that follows immediately is what is prohibited. Why is this so? Because there is a rule for that which is intermediate.

There is either an option or a prohibition. The prior application remains unprohibited; by that, it will take effect. But does this [subsequent] application not sublate the prior application? No, for once it has been prohibited, it is unable to sublate.

Alternatively, a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: among the suffixes beginning with *sva*, the preceding element receives the designation "word" (*pada*); thereafter, [it receives it] before a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix.

First, it receives the designation *pada*; then it receives the designation *bha* by the rule "it is called *bha* when followed by an affix beginning with *yaj* that is not a *sarvanāmasthāna*. If, then, even in the case of the nominative singular (*su*), it is a *pada*, then the mention of "end of a word" (*padānta*) in the rule regarding the modification of *ec* vowels into protracted forms (*pluta*) would apply here—namely, in the example "bhadraṃ karoṣi gauḥ"—even though that [designation of *pada*] is indeed applied; for [the rule] applies to the final sound of both a sentence and a word.
Thus it is so. The designation *pada* should be stated for these two [words] when they are followed by forms ending in *-vat* or *-vatī*, namely, those ending in *-bhū-vat* and *-dhārayat-vat*.

(Pāṇini 1.4.18) Regarding the designation *bha*, there is a prohibition of the [substitution of *ṣaṣ* for *ṣaṣṭhī*] when there is elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapadalopa*). Regarding the designation *bha*, when there is elision of the subsequent member...

The prohibition of the suffix *ṭhak* must be stated [in the rule for *anukampita*]. [Examples: *anukampitaḥ ṣaḍaṅguliḥ* → *ṣaḍikaḥ*. This is established by virtue of the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) of the vowel (*ac*).

This is established. How? Because of the status of the substitute of the vowel, the designation *bha* will not occur. But then it would follow here as well: *vāgāśīrdattaḥ* → *vācikaḥ*. To this he will say:

It is established [that the elision occurs] because it is stated that for compounds whose prior member consists of a single syllable, there is the elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapadalopa*). If so, would this not also apply here in the cases *ṣaḍaṅguliḥ* and *ṣaḍikaḥ*? This will be explained:

"It is established by the rule stating *ṭha*, *ja*, and so forth after the word *ṣaṣ*. An addition must be made regarding the suffix *vati* for the words *nabhas*, *aṅgiras*, and *manus*: an addition must be made for *nabhas*, *aṅgiras*, and *manus* with respect to the suffix *vati*.
[The forms are] *nabhasvat*, *aṅgirasvat*, and *manusvat*. [An addition must also be made] for *vṛṣan* before the words *vasu* and *aśva*.
The designation *bhas* should be stated for the word *vṛṣan* when it occurs before the two words *vasu* and *aśva*. [Examples: *vṛṣaṇvasuḥ*, *vṛṣaṇaśvasya yat śiraḥ*, *vṛṣaṇaśvasya mene*.
(Pāṇini 1.4.19) For what purpose is the mention of "meaning" (*artha*)? Why not simply say *tasau matau*? If only *tasau matau* were stated...

If [the rule] were stated thus, one would possess milk and fame only here [in this world], and would not possess milk and fame here [in this world]. However, when the term "meaning" (artha) is included, it becomes established for both the suffix *matup* and for any other suffix that has the same meaning as it.
If the inclusion of the word "meaning" is made, then [the forms] *payasvān* and *yaśasvān* would not be obtained here. What is the reason? It is because...

For the suffix *matup* occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), and the suffix *matup* also occurs in the sense of possession. For example, when it is said, "Let the Brāhmaṇas be brought to Devadatta’s house," if Devadatta himself is also a Brāhmaṇa, he too is brought. 367. It should be stated that [the term *bahuvacana*] applies even when there is a notion of both [singular and plural]. "He with his well-praising, hymn-like host.
(P_1,4.21.1) KA_I,321.2-27 Ro_II, 368-372. It is said: "The plural is used for many. For which many? For many objects (*arthas*). If this is so, [then in the case of] *vṛkṣaḥ*...

In this case, the term *plakṣa* would also incur [the designation of being plural], for it has many referents: the root, the trunk, the fruit, and the leaves. If that is so, then "singular," "dual," and "plural" are merely technical names (*saṃjñā*) for words; they apply when many meanings are intended for which the suffixes beginning with *su-* (the case endings) are prescribed. And for which meanings are the suffixes beginning with *su-* prescribed? For [meanings such as] the object (*karman*) and so forth.

Indeed, *karman* and the others are not the meanings of the case endings (*vibhakti*). What then? They are *ekatva* (singularity) and so forth. Even when *ekatva* and the others are the meanings of the case endings, *karman* and the others must necessarily be adopted as the causes [of their application], as in "in the singularity of the object" (*karmaṇa ekatve*), "in the duality of the object" (*karmaṇo dvitve*), or "in the plurality of the object" (*karmaṇo bahutve*). Therefore, that [expression] should be stated in such a way; for it is not possible without [specifying them].

In the case of abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*), the grammatical instruction is one in which the quality (*guṇa*) is primary. And here, some maintain that because of the rule "tat eke manyante" (so some think), the singular number would apply due to its subsequent position. However, the rule "bahuvacanaṃ bahuṣu" (the plural is used for the plural) will be placed later [as a subsequent rule]. Thus, a reversal of the order of the *sūtras* has been made. Here...

And as for [the example] "much rice" (*bahuḥ odanaḥ*) and "much soup" (*bahuḥ sūpaḥ*), the plural number would apply because it is subsequent [in the rules]. This is not a fault. As for what was said:

It is not the case that a designation involving a quality and a primary substance cannot occur without an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*); rather, a designation involving a quality and a primary substance does occur even without an abstract suffix. How so? Here, sometimes a quality serves as a qualifier of the qualified substance, as in "the cloth is white. And sometimes a quality is designated by means of the qualified substance, as in "the whiteness of the cloth."

Regarding the term "white" (*śukla*): when a quality (*guṇa*) serves as a qualifier for a substance (*guṇin*), as in "the cloth is white," there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the quality and the possessor of the quality. In that case, the designation does not have the quality as its primary referent without the addition of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). However, when the quality is designated by means of the possessor of the quality, as in "the white of the cloth," the quality then becomes the primary referent in its own right.

In that case, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply to the substance (*dravya*). Consequently, the designation would be one in which the quality (*guṇa*) is primary rather than the state-suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). Furthermore, we shall not qualify the object (*karman*) and so forth by means of singularity (*ekatva*) and the rest; rather, we shall qualify singularity and the rest by means of the object and the rest. How so? "The singular number (*ekavacana*) occurs when there is oneness. Oneness of what? Of the object (*karman*).

The dual number is used for two; for which two? For two objects (*karman*). The plural number is used for many; for which many? For many objects. How is it that the plural number is used for "many"? This very point makes known that the Teacher intends the word "many" (*bahu*) here as signifying "different substrata" (*nānādhikaraṇa*), and not as signifying "vastness" (*vaipulya*). What is the purpose of this making known?

As for what was said—that because of the rule for plurality (*bahuvacana*), the forms *bahuḥ odanaḥ* and *bahuḥ sūpaḥ* would result in the plural number—that fault does not occur. Furthermore, as for what is said—that because of the rule for singularity (*ekavacana*), the form *iti eke manyante* would result in the singular number because of the subsequent rule—that is not a fault. This word *eka* has multiple meanings; it indeed exists as a term denoting number. That...

As in the cases of "one," "two," or "many. There is [the sense] expressing "without a companion," as for example: "those who maintain a single fire" (*ekāgnayaḥ*), "single-ploughed fields" (*ekahalāni*), or "conquered by solitary wretches" (*ekākibhiḥ kṣudrakaiḥ jitam*). There is [also the sense] in which it functions in the meaning of "other" (*anyārthe*), as for example: "those *ekāḥ* [days] are for shared revelry" (*sadhamādaḥ dyumnaḥ ekāḥ*); the meaning is "others" (*anyāḥ*). This is the usage of that [word *eka*] which functions in the sense of "other."

(P_1,4.21.2) KA_I,322.1-25 Ro_II, 372-375 Why, then, is this stated? Because *sup* and *tiṅ* suffixes are prescribed without distinction, and because they are seen to be used in ways that deviate [from their expected application], this statement is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*). *Sup* suffixes are prescribed without distinction after any nominal stem (*prātipadika*) whatsoever; likewise, *tiṅ* suffixes are prescribed without distinction.
They are prescribed merely by way of their elements (*dhātu*). In this regard, it might be argued: "Even if they are prescribed without distinction, no dissociation is observed.
However, because dissociation is indeed observed, and because dissociation is actually seen—as for example:
"My eyes are beautiful to behold."

"My feet are delicate"—since there is no distinction made between nominal suffixes (*sup*) and verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), and because their usage is observed to be interchanged, a confusion of the two would result. However, it is desired that there be no such confusion; and since this cannot be accomplished without an effort, the statement is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*). This is said for that very purpose. Now, when this purpose of restriction is established, what further...?
This is the rule for grammatical conditions: the singular number is used only for one thing,
and the dual number only for two.
Is it that the plural number is used only for many [things], or is there a restriction of meaning:
that the singular is used only for one,
and the dual only for two?

"In the case of many [objects], there is only the plural number. And what is the distinction here? In that case, if the rule were restricted to the suffixes, indeclinables (*avyaya*) would lack the designation "word" (*pada*), because they do not end in a *su*-affix. If the rule were restricted to the suffixes, the designation "word" would not apply to indeclinables such as *uccais* ("high") and *nīcais* ("low"). What is the reason? Because they do not end in a *su*-affix. [The rule is] established if the restriction is on the meaning; in the case of a restriction on the meaning, it is established.

It is established. Let there be a restriction on the meaning (*arthaniyama*). Or rather, let there be a restriction on the suffix (*pratyayaniyama*). But was it not said: "In that case, under a restriction on the suffix, indeclinables would lack the designation *pada* because they do not end in a *sup* [case-ending]"? This is not a fault.
For the meanings of the *sup* suffixes include both the object (*karman*) and so forth, as well as number; likewise for the *tiṅ* suffixes. And the meaning of the *sup* suffixes is indeed number.

And [the same applies] to the objects of action (*karman*) and so forth, as well as to the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*). In that case, the restriction (*niyama*) is well-known; the restriction there is well-established. Or rather, the restriction applies to those topics under discussion (*prakṛta*). Alternatively, the restriction is with reference to the meanings currently under discussion. And what are those topics under discussion? They are singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth. The singular number (*ekavacana*) is used for one alone, not for two, nor for many. The dual number (*dvivacana*) is used for two alone.

The plural number is used neither for one nor for many; rather, the plural is used only for many, not for two or for one. Alternatively, the activity of the Teacher indicates that case-endings (*svādayaḥ*) arise even from indeclinables (*avyaya*), since he teaches the elision (*luk*) of case-endings after an indeclinable by stating "after an indeclinable, the elision of *āp* and *sup*" (*avyayād āpsupaḥ*).

376–379. "What is this [term] *kārake*? It is a designation (*saṃjñā-nirdeśa*). Should this be stated? No, it need not. How is it understood even when not explicitly stated? For in this grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), designations are made using those words whose referents are well-known in the world, such as "animal," "offspring," or "deity"; or by means of these artificial designations (*kṛtrima-saṃjñā*) such as *ṭi*, *ghu*, *ap*, and *bha*.

[The opponent replies: "By those [words]. And this word *dhruva* and so forth is not one whose referent is not well-known in the world; nor indeed is it an artificial technical term (*saṃjñā*), because it has not been prescribed elsewhere. Furthermore, this is a section concerning technical terms (*saṃjñā-adhikāra*). In that case, what else could be understood there other than a technical term? If the mention of "in a kāraka" is an indication of a technical term, then it is also an indication of the bearer of the technical term (*saṃjñin*). [The question remains: "In a kāraka..."?

If this is the definition of a "designation" (*sañjñā*), then the "designated" (*sañjñin*) must also be defined. It should be stated that "that which accomplishes [an action] and brings it about is the designation 'kāraka' (participant in an action). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence [of over-extension]; for instance, in the case of *grāmasya samīpād āgacchati* ("he comes from near the village"), the [word *samīpa*] would be subject to the designation of a non-kāraka. Otherwise, an undesirable result would follow: even that which is not a kāraka would incur the designation of *apādāna* (ablative).
[Question: "From where does he come? He comes from near the village. [Answer: This is not a fault. In this case, the village is not connected with departure (*apāya*).

What then? It is the vicinity (*samīpa*). And when the village is connected with departure, then it receives the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "ablative" (*apādāna*), as in: "He comes from the village. [Objection: There would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the designation "object" (*karman*) for the son of a Brahmin who has not been specifically mentioned.

[One might object: "In the case of *panthānaṃ pṛcchati* (he asks the way), the designation of *karman* (object) would apply because it is 'unspoken' (*akathita*) [by another rule]. Where? In the case of *brāhmaṇasya putraṃ panthānaṃ pṛcchati* (he asks the Brahmin's son for the way). This is not a fault. This word *akathita* indeed refers to that which has been mentioned; for example, someone, having pointed out a certain person, says, "That one here is unmentioned" (*akathita*), meaning he is not mentioned [in the sentence].

Thus it is understood. [The word] *aprādhānye* means "in the sense of non-primacy. For example, one says "he is unmentioned (*akathita*) in the village" or "he is unmentioned in the city" regarding someone who is not the primary subject in a given context. When the word *akathita* functions in the sense of non-primacy, then this fault arises: the undesirable application of the technical designation *karman* (object) to the son of an unmentioned Brahmin on the road.

[The opponent] asks: "In the case of *vṛkṣasya parṇaṃ patati* ('the leaf of the tree falls'), the designation of *apādāna* (ablative) would also apply. Where? In cases such as *vṛkṣasya parṇaṃ patati* and *kuḍyasya piṇḍaḥ patati* ('the lump from the wall falls'). [Reply: Or rather, this is not a fault, because the departure (*apāya*) is not intended to be expressed. Why? Because the departure is not intended to be expressed here; the departure is not what is meant to be conveyed in this instance."
What then? It is the relationship (*sambandha*). And when the separation (*apāya*) is intended to be expressed, then the designation "ablative" (*apādāna*) applies.
For example: "A leaf falls from the tree. However, at that time, the specific relationship is not intended to be expressed;
it is not known whether [the leaf belongs] to a *kaṅka* or a *kurara*.

(P_1,4.23.2) KA_I,324.6-326.17 Ro_II, 380-386 Then this fault arises: the designation *karman* would undesirably apply to the unmentioned Brāhmaṇa in the sentence "He asks the Brāhmaṇa for his son's path.
This is not a fault. The term *kāraka* is made a great designation (*saṃjñā*). And a designation, by its very nature...
Because it is not more concise. Why is this? For the purpose of a technical term (*saṃjñā*) is brevity.

In that case, the purpose of employing a long technical term is so that it may be understood as a descriptive term (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), such that "it performs" (*karoti*) means "a performer" (*kāraka*).

If it is argued that it is a descriptive term, then the word "performer" (*kartṛ*) would be inapplicable to one who is not a performer. If it is a descriptive term, the word "performer" cannot apply to a non-performer.

It is established that the instrument (*karaṇa*) is a factor of action (*kāraka*), as is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). However, it is proven that for verbs such as *pac* ("to cook"), the status of agent (*kartṛbhāva*) belongs to both the instrument and the locus, because the action differs according to each factor of action. It is proven that the status of agent belongs to the instrument and the locus.

Why? Because for verbs such as *pac*, the action differs according to each factor of action. For indeed, in the case of verbs like *pac*, the action varies with respect to each individual factor of action.
"What is this 'counter-agent' (*pratikāraka*)? A counter-agent is that which acts against each agent (*kāraka*). What is this counter-agent?

It is a differentiation of action belonging to the roots such as *pac* (to cook). The cooking of the primary agent consists of the actions of placing [the pot] on the fire, pouring water, pouring in the rice, and adding fuel. Even while performing these actions—placing on the fire, pouring water, pouring in the rice, adding fuel, and so forth—[the agent is said to be "cooking"].
It is said, "Devadatta cooks. In that case, at that time, the root *pac* (to cook) is operative. This is the cooking of the primary agent;

this is the agency of the primary agent. In expressions such as "he cooks a *droṇa*" or "he cooks an *āḍhaka*," the cooking of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) consists of the action of containing and the action of supporting. In "he cooks a *droṇa*" or "he cooks an *āḍhaka*," [the cooking] refers to the action of containing.

When it is said that "the pot cooks" while performing the action of holding [the contents], the root *pac* (to cook) is operative therein; this is the cooking of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). This is the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the locus. When it is said, "The fuel-sticks (*edhas*) will cook until they are softened; they will burn," the action of burning is the cooking of the instrument (*karaṇa*). When it is said, "The fuel-sticks will cook until they are softened; they will burn," they are performing [that action].

It is said that "the pieces of wood cook. In that case, the root *pac* (to cook) is operative there. This is the cooking belonging to the instrument; this is the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the instrument. Raising and lowering [the axe] is the agent's act of cutting. While performing the raising and lowering, Devadatta is said to "cut. In that case, the root *chid* (to cut) is operative there. This belongs to the primary agent (*pradhānakartṛ*).
This is the agency of the primary agent: that which is not the cutting of the grass by the axe;
rather, that which is cut by the axe—and not by the grass—despite the effort and the downward stroke being equal, that is the cutting of the axe.
And this must necessarily be understood in this way; for otherwise, there would be no distinction between the cutting of the sword and the cutting of the grass.

For if one were to think that "cutting" occurs merely from the raising and lowering [of the instrument], then there would be no distinction in the act of cutting between a sword and grass; what is cut by a sword would likewise be cut by grass. Furthermore, there would be no established status for the *apādāna* (ablative) and other factors; that is, the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the *apādāna* and others would not be established. This is just as you have [already] stated regarding the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

Agency has been demonstrated [in the case of the agent], but agency is not demonstrated in the same way for the *apādāna* and other kārakas. Nor is there an issue, because those two—the independent and the dependent—are expressed alternately, and the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is based on that expression. Or rather, this is not a fault. Why?
Because of the nature of independence and dependence; in every instance here, both independence and dependence are intended to be expressed.
The expression of those two alternately: there will be an alternating expression of those two, namely independence (*svātantrya*) and dependence (*pāratantrya*).

And the designation will be based on that expression. For example: "It lightens from the cloud," "It lightens in the cloud," or "The cloud lightens. Why, then, is it said that "the status of the ablative (*apādāna*) and the other [kārakas] is not established"? It is thus.

In that case, we do not say that the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the ablation (*apādāna*) and the other [kārakas] is unestablished. The agency of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) has been sufficiently demonstrated as an illustration for the demonstration of the agency of the ablation and the others. For a single grain of rice (*pulāka*) is sufficient to demonstrate the nature of a cooking pot. What then? It is the technical designation (*sañjñā*) that is unestablished; for in all these cases, there is indeed independence (*svātantrya*).

And since dependence exists therein because of the otherness [of the agent], the designation "agent" (kartṛ) alone would necessarily apply. To this also, the answer is: "Or rather, it is not so, because of their independence and dependence; they are expressed alternately, and the designation depends upon that expression. Just as this independence of the pot has been demonstrated with respect to the action of containing and the action of supporting.

If the pot is independent while performing [its own functions], where would it be dependent now? That washing or turning over [is not its primary purpose]. Indeed, the pot is not employed for the sake of performing washing or turning over. How then? It is for the sake of performing the action of containing and the action of supporting. And in that regard, it is independent.
Where, then, is the dependent [agency] (paratantra)? If that is so, then when effort residing in the pot is being expressed, the pot is independent (svatantra);

but when effort residing in the agent is being expressed, it is dependent. But surely, sir, even when effort residing in the agent is being expressed, the pot performs the action of coming into being and the action of supporting; in that case, it is independent. Where, then, [is the dependent agency]?

[The pot] is dependent. If that is so, then in its conjunction with the primary [agent], the pot is dependent; in its separation from it, it is independent. For example, in the case of ministers and others, there is dependence when they are in conjunction with the king, and independence when they are separated from him. But what, then, is the primary? The agent. How, then, is it known that the agent is the primary? Because among all the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), [the agent is the most predominant].

When things are present, the agent becomes the instigator. But surely, sir, even in the case of a conjunction with the primary factor, there is a need for the pot; [for] the locus is a *kāraka*. Indeed, by the term "kāraka," the state of being a locus is not expressed, nor is the state of being a *kāraka* expressed by the term "locus. Both [terms]—
And these two become qualifiers of one another. How? Because they reside in the same substance (*ekadravyasamavāyitvāt*). For example, "Gārgya Devadatta.

Indeed, by the term "Gārgya," the state of being Devadatta is not expressed, nor by the term "Devadatta" is the state of being Gārgya expressed. Yet both serve as qualifiers for one another because they reside in the same substance. If that is so, then...

Action exists as a common property; that which brings about [the accomplishment] of that action is the *kāraka*. Alternatively, just as one might say "in respect to action" (*kriyāyām*), so too should one say "in respect to the *kāraka*" (*kārake*). By adopting this view, the grammatical instruction "in respect to the *kāraka*" (*kārake*) becomes logically justified. Otherwise, one would have to say "in respect to the *kārakas*" (*kārakeṣu*).

(P_1,4.24.1) For what purpose is the word *dhruvam* [stated]? [Example: *grāmāt āgacchati śakaṭena* ("He comes from the village by means of a cart"). This is not necessary; for here, the technical designation *karaṇa* (instrument) will serve as the sublater [of the designation *apādāna*]. Then consider this: *grāmāt āgacchan kaṃsapātryām pāṇinā odanam bhuṅkte* ("Coming from the village, he eats rice with his hand in a bronze bowl").

Thus, even here, the designation *adhikaraṇa* (locus) will be the sublater [of the *apādāna*]. But then consider these cases: *vṛkṣasya parṇaṃ patati* ("the leaf of the tree falls") and *kuḍyasya piṇḍaḥ patati* ("the lump from the wall falls"). An addition must be made for verbs meaning "disgust," "cessation," and "negligence. An addition must be made for verbs meaning disgust, cessation, and negligence. Disgust: *adharmāt jugupsate* ("he feels disgust at unrighteousness"), *adharmāt bībhatsate* ("he loathes unrighteousness"). Cessation: [...]

He desists from dharma; he turns away from dharma. He is negligent regarding dharma; he is deluded regarding dharma. Furthermore, this addition must be made here: "The inhabitants of Pāṭaliputra are more handsome than the inhabitants of Sāṃkāśya.
Well then, should this be stated? It need not be stated. For in this case, [the forms] "he feels aversion toward adharma" and "from adharma... [are already accounted for].

Regarding the term *bībhatsate*: that person who acts with foresight perceives that unrighteousness (*adharma*) is suffering and that there is no purpose in it; having understood this through his intellect, he desists. In that case, the status of the ablative as the point of departure (*apādāna*) when there is a certain removal is already established by the rule *dhruvam apāye ’pādānam*. And here, in expressions such as "he abstains from dharma" (*dharmād viramati*), "he turns away from dharma" (*dharmān nivartate*), or "he neglects dharma" (*dharmāt pramādyati*).

"From *dharma* he becomes deluded. This person, whose intellect is confused, perceives: "This thing called *dharma* does not exist; I shall not perform it. Having reached [the conclusion] through his intellect, he desists. In that case, the status of the *apādāna* (ablative) is established by the rule: "That from which there is a certain departure is the *apādāna*. And here: "The people of Pāṭaliputra are more handsome than the people of Sāṃkāśya."

Thus, one who has attained equality with them employs this [formula]. In the case of those joined with a motion (*gati*), the designation of *apādāna* (ablative) is not tenable because of instability (*adhruvatva*). In the case of those joined with a motion, the designation of *apādāna* is not tenable: "He fell from a frightened horse," "He fell from a driven chariot," "He was left behind by a departing caravan. What is the reason? Because of instability.

Or rather, this is not a fault because non-permanence (*adhrauvya*) is not intended to be expressed. What is the reason? Because non-permanence is not intended to be expressed here. What, then, is intended? Permanence (*dhrauvya*). In the example "He fell from a horse that was running away," that which belongs to the horse—the state of being a horse (*aśvatva*) and its quality of swift movement—is permanent, and that is what is intended to be expressed.

Regarding the statement "he has fallen from the chariot," that which constitutes the "chariot-ness" (*rathatva*) in the chariot—namely, that it is called a *ratha* because people delight (*ramante*) in it—is constant (*dhruva*), and that is what is intended to be expressed. Regarding the statement "he has fallen from the caravan," that which constitutes the "caravan-ness" (*sārthatva*) in the caravan—namely, the state of being a companion (*sahārthībhāva*)—is constant, and that is what is intended to be expressed. Even though this may be possible in these cases...

But as for those who say that these [terms] are endowed with an absolute state—namely, "he fell while running" or "he fell while hurrying"—here too, it is established by the very principle that non-permanence (*adhrauvya*) is not intended to be expressed. But how can there be a non-intention to express something that exists? Even that which exists may not be intended to be expressed; for example, "a hairless ewe" or "a girl with no belly."

Regarding the term *kanyā* ("maiden"): there is also the desire to speak of what is non-existent, as in "the ocean is a small water-pot" (*samudraḥ kuṇḍikā*) or "the Vindhya mountains are a cooking-pot" (*vindhyaḥ vardhitakam*). This grammatical rule (*yoga*) could be omitted. How so? [In cases such as] "he fears wolves," "he fears bandits," or "he fears thieves."
"It protects from robbers, it protects"—this is how it is said here: "He fears wolves, he fears robbers.

A person who acts with foresight perceives: "If the wolves see me, my death is certain. Having reached this conclusion through his intellect, he turns back. In that case, that from which there is a certain departure is the *apādāna* (ablative).

Thus it is established: here, in the cases "he protects from thieves" (*caurebhyaḥ trāyate*) and "he protects from bandits" (*dasyubhyaḥ trāyate*), that person who acts with foresight perceives: "If they see this [person], there will certainly be for him execution, imprisonment, or affliction. Having reached this conclusion through his intellect, he desists. In that case, it is already established by the rule "that which is fixed (*dhruva*) in relation to a departure (*apāya*) is the *apādāna*."

(P_1,4.26) KA_I,328.5-8 Ro_II, 393 This construction, too, can be explained otherwise. How so? [The question is: "How does one fail because of study? A person who acts with foresight perceives that study is painful, difficult to master, and that teachers are difficult to serve.

Thus, having reached [the beans] through the intellect, he turns back. In that case, it is established by the rule itself: "That from which there is a departure is the *apādāna* (ablative). (Pāṇini 1.4.24). What is the example? "He keeps the cows away from the beans. This would apply to one who has beans but no cows.
Beans may be desired. But for one who indeed has cows and not beans, how could beans be desired by him?

Even for him, it is the beans themselves that are desired. And because they are desired, he wards off the cows from the barley. Here, in the case of "he wards off the blind man from the well," the designation of *apādāna* (ablative) would not apply; for the well is not desired by him.

Who then? A blind man. For him, too, the well is indeed desired [to be avoided]. This blind man sees that "the well must not be reached. Or rather, just as there is a desire for this [blind man] elsewhere when he does not see, so it is with respect to the well. Here, in the expression "he wards off the boy from the fire," the designation of *apādāna* (ablative) would apply to the boy. The designation of *karman* (object) will be the sublater in this case.

In that case, it would also be sublated even by the word *agni* (fire). Therefore, it must be stated as "that which is desired by the action" (*karmaṇo yad īpsitam*) or "that which is desired by the desired" (*īpsitepsitam*). Regarding the words expressing prevention, the mention of *karman* is redundant, because of the rule stating "the object most desired by the agent is the *karman*.
In the case of words expressing prevention, the mention of *karman* is purposeless. Why? Because [the definition] is "the object most desired by the agent is the *karman*."

Because of this statement, it is already established that "the object most desired by the agent is the *karman*. This rule (*yoga*) as well can be omitted. How so? In the case of "he keeps the cows away from the beans" (*māṣebhyaḥ gāḥ vārayati*). This person perceives: "If these cows go there, the destruction of the crops is certain; and with the destruction of the crops, there will be both unrighteousness (*adharma*) and fear of the king. Having thus reached [this conclusion] through his intellect...

It ceases. In that case, it is already established by the rule *dhruvam apāye 'pādānam* (Pāṇini 1.4.24). This rule (*yoga*) as well can be dispensed with. How [would one explain] "he hides from the teacher"? He sees this:

"If the teacher sees me, there will certainly be a mission or a reprimand. Having reached this conclusion through his intellect, he turns back. In that case, the rule "the fixed point in departure is the *apādāna*" is already established. (Pāṇini 1.4.29) KA_I,329.6-22 Ro_II,250.17-251.10: *yadi mām upādhyāyaḥ paśyati dhruvam preṣaṇam upālambho vā*—having understood this, he turns back.
