396–398. [Question: For what purpose is the term *upayoge* (in the sense of "attention" or "application") stated? [Counter-example: *naṭasya śṛṇoti* ("He listens to the actor"), *granthikasya śṛṇoti* ("He listens to the storyteller"). Even if *upayoge* were stated, this [rule] would still apply here; for this too is indeed an instance of *upayoga*. Furthermore, there is *upayoga* in that those who initiate [the performance] go to the stage with the thought, "We shall listen to the actor."

"We shall listen to the reciter (granthika). If that is so, then it is said "in the case of application" (*upayoge*), and every [instance] is an application. In that case, a distinction of excellence will be understood: "that which is the more excellent application. And what is the more excellent? That which pertains to both the text and its meaning. Or rather, what can truly be called "application"? That which is preceded by formal discipline (*niyamapūrvaka*). For example, it is said, "the students have applied themselves" (*upayuktā māṇavakāḥ*).

Those who have studied [the Veda] preceded by the observance of restrictive rules (niyama). Furthermore, regarding the verb (ākhyāta) in the sense of "non-utilization" (anupayoga), is it a *kāraka* or is it not a *kāraka*? And what is the distinction here? If it is argued that the verb is a *kāraka* in the sense of non-utilization, then because it has not been specifically assigned [by another rule], the designation of "object" (*karman*) would undesirably follow. If it is argued that the verb is a *kāraka* in the sense of non-utilization, then because it has not been specifically assigned, the technical term "object" would apply.

Let it then be that [the agent] is not a *kāraka*. If it is argued that it is not a *kāraka*, then the statement regarding its "employment" (*upayoga*) is purposeless; for if it is not a *kāraka*, the statement of its employment would be meaningless. Let it then be that it is a *kāraka*. But was it not said that [the agent] is a *kāraka* only when there is no employment? If it is argued that, because it is not explicitly mentioned (*akathita*), the designation of "object" (*karman*) would undesirably follow, this is not a fault, because there is an exhaustive enumeration (*parigaṇana*).

In that regard, it is stated: "The rule applies to *duh*, *yāc*, *rudh*, *pracch*, *bhikṣ*, and *ciñ*. This rule (*yoga*) can also be omitted. How so? [In the case of] "he learns from the teacher" (*upādhyāyād adhīte*), that learning departs from him. If it departs, why does it not depart forever? Because it is continuous. Alternatively, cognitions are like lights.

(P_1,4.30) This formulation (*yoga*) can also be stated as follows: How is it that a scorpion is born from cow dung? How is it that *dūrvā* grass is born from cow-hair and sheep’s wool? [Answer: Those [qualities] depart from them. [Objection:
If they depart, why do they not depart completely?
Because of continuity. Or rather, others and yet others appear. This rule (*yoga*) as well could have been omitted. How so? [In the case of] "the Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat. They depart.
Therefore, those are the waters. If it departs, why does it not depart forever? Because of their continuity;
or rather, others and yet others continue to appear.

400–401. What is the purpose of including the mention of *karman* (the object)? If it were stated merely as "that which one intends [to reach] through the action is the *sampradāna*," then the designation *sampradāna* would undesirably apply to the *karman* itself. However, when the mention of *karman* is made, no such fault arises;

for the *karman* is relied upon here as the cause (*nimitta*). Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *yam* (whom)? It is so that [it may be understood]: "one intends [to reach] by means of the *karman*."

If it were stated merely as "the recipient" (*sampradāna*), the designation of "recipient" would undesirably apply only to that which one intends to reach. However, when the mention of *yaṃ* (whom) is made, no such fault arises. Because of the mention of *yaṃ*, the designation of "recipient" is restricted to that which one intends to reach. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *abhi-pra*? If it were stated merely as "that which one reaches by means of the object is the recipient," [the fault would remain].
It would apply only to that which is currently being reached, as in: *upādhyāyāya gām dadāti* ("He gives a cow to the teacher"). Here it would not apply:

*upādhyāyāya gām adāt* ("He gave a cow to the teacher") or *upādhyāyāya gām dāsyati* ("He will give a cow to the teacher"). However, when the inclusion of the prefix *abhi-* is made, there is no fault.

The prefix *abhi-* functions in the sense of "facing toward" (*ābhimukhya*), while the word *pra-* functions in the sense of "commencement of action" (*ādikarman*). Therefore, it applies to both that which one is facing toward and that which one is beginning to act upon.
And that which one intends to go toward and that which one has already gone toward—this is established everywhere by the mere fact of being directed toward it.

(Pāṇini 1.4.32) It should also be stated that "action" (*kriyā*) must be mentioned [in the rule], so that it may apply here as well: *śrāddhāya nigṛhṇate* ("he reproaches for the sake of the funeral rite").

"One prepares for battle"; "she lies down for her husband. If that is so, then it must be stated [as a rule]. It need not be stated. How so? For in common usage, people employ the term *karman* (object) as a metaphorical designation for action (*kriyā*). One asks: "What action will you perform? or "What work (*karman*) will you do? Even so, the rule must still be formulated: "Between the artificial (*kṛtrima*) and the non-artificial (*akṛtrima*), the understanding applies to the artificial one. [And in this case, *kriyā* is the artificial object.]

Furthermore, even an artificial action does not [function as] an object (*karman*). It is stated that "the object is that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma*); how, then, could one action be most desired by another action? Yet, an action can indeed be most desired by another action. By what action?
Either by the action of perceiving (*sandarśana*), or by the action of desiring (*prārthayati*), or by the action of determining (*adhyavasyati*). In this case...

A person who acts with foresight first perceives some object through the intellect (*buddhi*). Once it is perceived, there arises a desire; from desire, a determination (*adhyavasāya*); from determination, an undertaking (*ārambha*); from the undertaking, an accomplishment (*nirvṛtti*);

and from accomplishment, the attainment of the fruit. Thus, even action (*kriyā*) is an artificial object (*karma*). In this way, too, there is the designation of "object" (*karman*) for the instrument (*karaṇa*).

403–404. Are these [terms] synonymous or do they have different meanings? And what follows from this? If they are synonymous, for what purpose are they mentioned separately? On the other hand, if they have different meanings, how can they be qualified by the word *kupita* (enraged)? In that case, they have different meanings; however, there is a commonality among them in relation to *kupa*. For one who is not enraged (*akupita*) does not become angry, nor does one who is not enraged bear malice (*druhyati*).

"One who is not provoked does not envy, nor does one who is not provoked find fault. (Pāṇini 1.4.42) [Question: What is the purpose of including the word *tam*? Why not simply state "the instrument is that which accomplishes"? [Answer: Because the term "instrument" (*karaṇa*) refers to that which is effective in bringing about an action.

If this much were stated, the designation *karaṇa* (instrument) would undesirably apply to all *kārakas*, for all *kārakas* are indeed accomplishers (*sādhaka*). However, when the mention of "that" (*tam*) is made, no such fault arises. But this is not a necessary purpose;

for the preceding designations will set aside [the subsequent ones] because they are exceptions (*apavāda*), while the subsequent ones will prevail due to their posteriority (*paratva*) and lack of occasion (*anavakāśatva*).

And here, then, in the case of "he pierces with a bow" (*dhanuṣā vidhyati*), because it is connected with departure (*apāya*) the designation *apādāna* would apply, and because it is the instrument (*sādhaka*) the designation *karaṇa* would apply. However, when the mention of "that" (*tam*) is made, there is no fault. If that is so, this is established by common usage (*loka*). For example, in the world one says, "Water should be brought for the handsome man," or "A maiden should be given to the handsome man"; and yet...

Activity occurs toward that which is not the most effective (*anabhirūpa*). In that context, it is understood to mean "toward the most effective" (*abhirūpatamāya*). Likewise here, although it is stated that "the instrument is the achiever" (*sādhakaṃ karaṇam*), all *kārakas* are achievers, and there is no activity toward that which is not an achiever.

Therefore, it will be understood there as "the most effective achiever" (*sādhakatamam*). If this is so, since [the meaning] is already established, why does [the author] employ the mention of the superlative suffix (*tamap*)?

The Teacher indicates thereby that in the technical designation of *kāraka*, the application of degrees of comparison (*taratama-yoga*) does not occur. What is the purpose of this indication? The Teacher considers what [definition of] *apādāna* (ablative) to be correct? [He considers it to be: "that from which there is a cessation upon reaching.

By this, it would apply only in cases such as "he comes from the village" (*grāmād āgacchati*) or "he comes from the city" (*nagarād āgacchati*), but not in cases such as "the inhabitants of Pāṭaliputra [are superior] to those of Sāṅkāśya" (*sāṅkāśyakebhyaḥ pāṭaliputrakāḥ*).

In the case of "abhirūpataraḥ" (more handsome), [the designation of *kāraka*] would not apply here. It is thus established that the application of the comparative suffixes *-tara* and *-tama* does not occur within the technical term *kāraka*. Likewise, what does the Teacher consider to be the proper locus (*ādhāra*)? [He considers it to be] where the entire nature of the locus is pervaded. Therefore, it would apply only in cases such as "oil in sesame seeds" (*tileṣu tailam*) or "clarified butter in curds" (*dadhi sarpiḥ*), but not in "cows on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyām gāvaḥ*).

406–407. A prohibition must be stated for the root *vas* when it has the sense of "eating. [Objection: A prohibition must be stated for the root *vas* when it has the sense of "eating," as in the example: "He fasts near the village" (*grāmam upavasati*). [Reply: Then it must indeed be stated. [Objection: It need not be stated. In this case, the village is not the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the root *vas* preceded by the prefix *upa*. [Question: Of what, then, is it the locus? [Answer: It is the locus of the root *vas* without a prefix. [That is to say,] while staying in the village, he fasts for three nights.

(P_1.4.49.1) KA_I,332.10–13 Ro_II,407: What is the purpose of including the word *tama* [in the sūtra]? If it were stated merely as "the object desired by the agent (*kartuḥ īpsitaṃ karma*)," then in the example "he wards off the boy from the fire" (*agner māṇavakaṃ vārayati*), the technical designation *apādāna* would undesirably apply to the boy (*māṇavaka*). This fault does not arise.

In that case, the technical designation *karman* (object) will serve as the sublater [of the designation *apādāna*]. But then it would also serve as the sublater in the case of fire (*agni*). However, here again, when the mention of *tama* (the suffix *-tama*) is made, that which was stated—that the mention of *karman* is redundant in the context of prohibitions because of the rule "the object is that which is most desired by the agent"—becomes justified.
Regarding this, it is said: "He cooks rice (*odanaṃ pacati*). If the rice were being cooked [in the sense of being produced], then another substance would have to be brought into existence.
This is not a fault. Because they are for that purpose, the designation will apply to them; the grains of rice are for the sake of the rice, and thus they are called "rice."

Thus it is said. Now, in this case, how should one understand the expression "he cooks rice-grains into porridge" (*taṇḍulān odanaṃ pacati*)? Should it be *taṇḍulān odanaṃ pacati* or *taṇḍulānām odanaṃ pacati*? It should be understood in both ways. How so? For here, in the expression "he cooks rice-grains into porridge," the verb *pacati* has two meanings: "while cooking the rice-grains, he brings about the porridge. Now, in the expression "of the rice-grains... [the genitive is used].

The verb *pac* (to cook) has two meanings; and when it is used in the sense of transformation (*vikāra*), the genitive case is employed, as in "he prepares rice (*odana*) which is a transformation of rice-grains (*taṇḍula*). Here, someone addresses another, saying, "The meal is ready; let it be eaten. The one being addressed says, "We have already eaten enough. The one addressing him says, "There will surely be curd and milk."

[The opponent says: "Indeed, it will be so. When being addressed, one says: 'I would indeed eat with curds,' or 'I would indeed eat with milk. In this case, the designation of *karman* (object) would apply [to the curds and milk], for that is what is most desired by him. [The author replies: Even for him, the rice (*odana*) alone is what is most desired; he has no regard for the subordinate qualities (*guṇa*). It is just as when one says, "I would eat rice."
"If it were soft and clear"— in this case as well, one would think, "I shall eat rice with the quality of curd," or "I shall eat rice with the quality of milk.

Since that which is desired is designated as the *karman*, there arises the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even an accomplished factor (*nirvṛtta-kāraka*) would receive the designation of *karman*, because it is desired by the action.

If the designation *karman* (object) applies only to that which is desired (*īpsita*), then the designation *karman* would not apply to that which has already been accomplished (*nirvṛtta*) while functioning as a *kāraka*, as in the example "he eats molasses" (*guḍaṃ bhakṣayati*). What is the reason? Because it is the action that is desired; the action is what he desires. Or rather, there is no such fault, because both are desired. Why? Because both are desired by him. Therefore...

For he whose mind is intent upon eating molasses does not become satisfied by eating a clod of earth. Even though it might be possible to say this here, suppose some person among those royal officials says to another, "Make a mat," and that person replies, "I will not make a mat; I shall make a jar."

411–412. What is the example? "He eats poison. This is not [an example]. This is already established by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 1.4.49]. It is not established. For it is stated that "the object most desired by the agent is the *karman*"; and who indeed would desire the eating of poison?
Even the eating of poison is desired by someone. How so? Here, this person who...
Afflicted by suffering, having reflected upon other miseries, he considers the consumption of poison itself to be better;

consequently, he consumes that which was his desired object. Furthermore, when one intends to do one thing but does another, that is the illustration. What, then, is that? For example, while going to another village, he encounters thieves and leaps over a snake.

"One crushes thorns. Here, the designation *karman* (object) is prescribed for both that which is desired (*īpsita*) and that which is not desired (*anīpsita*). Now, what should be the case regarding that which is neither most desired nor undesired? For example: "While going to another village, he passes by the roots of trees; he passes by the bases of walls. This too is established [as an object]. How so?

Regarding the term *anīpsita* ("undesired"), this is not a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) meaning "not desired. What then? This is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), meaning that what is other than the desired is the undesired. And that which is other than the desired is neither [simply] desired nor undesired.

(P_1.4.51.1) KA_I,333.25–334.15 Ro_II, 413–418: By what is it "unspoken" (*akathita*)? By specific designations such as *apādāna* and so forth. What is the example? [The rule states: "In the case of the roots *duh*, *yāc*, *rudh*, *prach*, *bhikṣ*, and *ci*, that which is the cause of the application (*upayoga-nimitta*), and in the case of *brū* and *śās* when there is no prior rule [establishing another designation], that which is connected with them by virtue of their quality—that is called 'unspoken' (*akīrtita*) by the Poet. Regarding *duh*: [Example: *gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ*. (He milks the cow for milk. [Commentary: Here, the cow (*go*) is not designated as an *apādāna* because there is no separation (*viśleṣa*). Nor is it designated as a *karman* because the milk (*payas*) is the primary object of the action. Therefore, by this rule, it is designated as *kartṛ* (agent). Since it is not designated by any other term, it is called *akathita*. Thus, the cow is the agent of the action of milking. However, since the cow is the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) of the action of milking, it would have been designated as *adhikaraṇa* by the rule *adhi-śīṅ-sthā-ās-ām karma* (P_1.4.46). But because of the word *ca* ("and") in the rule *akathitaṃ ca* (P_1.4.51), the designation of *adhikaraṇa* is superseded, and it is instead designated as *kartṛ*. Why is it said "when there is no prior rule"? Because if there were a prior rule, the designation established by that rule would prevail. For example, in *māṇavakaṃ dharmaṃ bhāṣate* (He speaks the dharma to the boy), the boy is designated as *saṃpradāna* by the rule *kriyāgrahaṇam api kartavyam* (Vārttika on P_1.4.32), and thus he is not called *akathita*. Similarly, in *māṇavakaṃ dharmam anuśāsti* (He instructs the boy in the dharma), the boy is designated as *saṃpradāna* by the rule *ādhāro ’dhikaraṇam* (P_1.4.45) [interpreted here as *ādhāraḥ saṃpradānam*]. Why is it said "by virtue of their quality (*guṇena*)"? Because if it were not so stated, then in the case of *pauravaṃ gāṃ yācate* (He begs a cow from the descendant of Puru), the descendant of Puru (*paurava*) would also be called *akathita*. This is because the root *yāc* is included among the group of roots beginning with *duh*; therefore, the descendant of Puru would be designated as *apādāna* by the rule *dhruvam apāye ’pādānam* (P_1.4.24), and thus would not be called *akathita*. Hence, the phrase "by virtue of their quality" is used to exclude such cases. Why is it said "that which is connected (*yat sacate*)"? Because if it were not so stated, then in the case of *pauravo gāṃ yācyate* (The descendant of Puru is begged for a cow), the descendant of Puru would be called *akathita*. This is because the descendant of Puru is connected with the root *yāc* through its quality of being the object of the action; therefore, the phrase "that which is connected" is used to exclude such cases. Why is it said "in the case of *brū* and *śās* when there is no prior rule (*apūrva-vidhau*)"? Because if it were not so stated, then in the case of *māṇavako mātaram anuśāsti* (The boy instructs his mother), the mother would be called *akathita*. This is because the root *śās* is included among the group of roots beginning with *duh*; therefore, the mother would be designated as *apādāna* by the rule *dhruvam apāye ’pādānam* (P_1.4.24), and thus would not be called *akathita*. Hence, the phrase "when there is no prior rule" is used to exclude such cases. Why is it said "the cause of the application (*upayoga-nimittam*)"? Because if it were not so stated, then in the case of *pauravo gāṃ yācate* (The descendant of Puru begs a cow), the cow would also be called *akathita*. This is because the cow is connected with the root *yāc* through its quality of being the object of the action; therefore, the phrase "the cause of the application" is used to exclude such cases. Why is it said "that which is the cause of the application (*upayoga-nimittam*)"? Because if it were not so stated, then in the case of *pauravo gāṃ yācate* (The descendant of Puru begs a cow), the descendant of Puru would also be called *akathita*. This is because the descendant of Puru is connected with the root *yāc* through its quality of being the object of the action; therefore, the phrase "that which is the cause of the application" is used to exclude such cases. This is because the descendant of Puru is connected with the root *yāc* through its quality of being the object of the action; therefore, the phrase "that which is the cause of the application" is used to exclude such cases. This is because the cow is connected with the root *yāc* through its quality of being the object of the action; therefore, the phrase "that which is the cause of the application" is used to exclude such cases. This is because the descendant of Puru is connected with the root *yāc* through its quality of being the object of the action; therefore, the phrase "that which is the cause of the application" is used to exclude such cases. "He milks the cow for milk" (*gām dogdhi payaḥ*). This is not [an example of *apādāna*]. The designation *apādāna* was already stated for this case under the rule *duhi-yāci*. Then consider: "He begs the Paurava for a cow" (*pauravam gām yācate*). This is not [an example of *apādāna*] either. The designation *apādāna* was already stated for this case under the rule *duhi-yāci*. It is not from the mere act of begging that the separation (*apāya*) occurs. If, having been begged, he gives it, then he is connected with the separation. [This applies to] *yāci*. [Now for] *rudhi*: "He obstructs the village" (*grāmam rundhe*). This is not [an example of *apādāna*]. The designation *apādāna* was already stated for this case under the rule *ā-kartr̥-sthānāc cet vīpsāyām*. It is not from the mere act of obstructing that the separation occurs. If, having been obstructed, he departs, then he is connected with the separation. [This applies to] *rudhi*.
"He shuts the cow in the pen" (*anvavaruṇaddhi gām vrajam*). This is not correct. The designation of "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*) has already been stated for this case. [In the rule] *rudhi* (to obstruct):

"He asks the boy the way" (*māṇavakam panthānam pṛcchati*). This is not correct. The designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) has already been stated for this case. Separation does not occur merely from the act of asking. When he is asked and then explains it, only then is he connected with separation. [In the rule] *pracchi* (to ask). [In the rule] *bhikṣi* (to beg):

"One begs a cow from the Paurava. This is not so. The designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) has already been stated for this case. The departure does not occur solely from the act of begging; rather, if that person, having been begged, gives [the cow], then he is connected with the departure. [The roots] *bhikṣ* (to beg) and *ci* (to gather): "He gathers fruits from the tree. This is not so. The designation of "ablative" has already been stated for this case by virtue of the quality of the roots *brū* (to speak) and *śās* (to instruct).

And that which is associated with [the action] is called *akīrtita* (unmentioned) by the wise. Furthermore, that which is associated with—that is, connected to—a verb having the sense of *brū* (to speak) or *śās* (to instruct) is also an example. What, then, is that? "He speaks the Dharma to his son" (*putraṃ brūte dharmam*), and "He instructs his son in the Dharma" (*putram anuśāsti dharmam*).
This is not so; for in these cases, the designation *sampradāna* (recipient) has already been stated previously. Therefore, there are only three examples.
"He asks the Paurava for a cow," "he asks the young boy the way," and "he begs a cow from the Paurava.

Now, regarding those verbal roots that take two objects (*dvikarmaka*), do the *lādi* suffixes (the passive and reflexive voices) occur when [one object] is expressed (*kathita*) or when it is not expressed (*akathita*)?

When [the object] is expressed by the *l*-class [suffixes], etc. When [the object] is expressed (*abhihita*) by the *l*-class suffixes, what should be done regarding the secondary object (*guṇakarma*)? If the *l*-class suffixes should occur when [the primary object] is expressed, then one should employ the genitive case for the secondary object. If the *l*-class suffixes should occur when [the primary object] is expressed, then the genitive case must be employed for the secondary object. For example: *duhyate goḥ payaḥ* ("milk is milked from the cow") and *yācyate pauravasya kambalaḥ* ("a blanket is asked for from the descendant of Puru"). How so? Because it is not a [primary] factor of action (*akāraka*).

Because it has not been designated [as a specific *kāraka*]. For this is indeed not a *kāraka*. What is the reason? Because it has not been designated. But if it were a *kāraka*, it would not be undesignated. Now, if it is a *kāraka* but not designated, then when a *kāraka* exists, what [designation] should be applied?

If one should recognize it as a *kāraka*, whichever [designation] one considers appropriate for it, that should be used. If one recognizes it as a *kāraka*, whichever [designation] applies, that is what should be employed.

That [action] is to be expressed [by the verb]: *goḥ payo duhyate* ("milk is being milked from the cow"), *pauravāt kambalo yācyate* ("a blanket is being requested from the descendant of Puru"). Regarding the rule "when [the object] is stated (*kathita*) or expressed (*abhihita*), however, there is no prescription" (*tvavidhiḥ*): this refers to the prescription of *la*-suffixes (*lādividhiḥ*) when there is a secondary action (*guṇakarmaṇi*). When [the object] is stated by the *la*-suffixes or expressed, this is the rule of "no prescription" (*tvavidhiḥ*). What is this "rule of no prescription" (*tvavidhiḥ*)? It is a prescription for you (*tava vidhiḥ*). "When there is a secondary action" (*tvamatiḥ*). What is this?
Regarding the term *tvamati*: *tvamatiḥ* means "your mind" (*tava matiḥ*). Others do not think so. How then do others think?

They hold that the rule for the introduction of *l*-affixes and so forth applies when there is a subordinate object (*guṇakarma*), provided it is accompanied by another [object]. That is to say, the rules for *l*-affixes and so forth apply to roots whose meanings involve motion, cognition, eating, or which have sound as their object, or which are intransitive, when the agent of the root in its non-causative form (*aṇikartā*) becomes the object in the causative (*ṇau*), provided the action involves something stable (*dhruva*) or movement (*ceṣṭita*). This occurs in connection with a subsequent [object].

Furthermore, remember that statement of the one of no small intelligence regarding the absence of the [secondary] object (*aguṇa*). In cases where the primary object is intended, and in cases where the effort is intended, the *l*-affixes and others occur even when the action lacks a [secondary] object; let that statement of the teacher of no small intelligence be remembered. Another says:

"Regarding verbs with two objects (*dvikarman*), they say that the *l*-affixes and others are used when the primary object is to be expressed. When the primary object among those with two objects is to be denoted, [the *l*-affixes are employed].

It should be stated that the *l*-affixes and others occur in the sense of the object (*karman*) of verbal roots (*dhātu*). For example: *ajāṃ nayati grāmam* (he leads the goat to the village), *ajā nīyate grāmam* (the goat is being led to the village), and *ajā nītā grāmam* (the goat has been led to the village). Regarding the roots beginning with *duh* (to milk): it should be stated that for the roots *duh* and others, the *l*-affixes and others occur in the sense of the object when that object is not the primary factor (*apradhāna*). For example: *duhyate gauḥ payaḥ* (the cow is milked of its milk). And [the *l*-affixes occur] in the sense of both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) in the case of causative forms (*ṇyanta*).

It should be stated that *la*-affixes and others occur [in such cases]. "Devadatta is being made to go to the village by Yajñadatta. Which roots, however, have two objects? It is the settled conclusion that among those with two objects, the inclusion of *nī* (to lead), *vah* (to carry), *hṛ* (to take), and likewise those with the meaning of motion (*gatyartha*), is to be understood.
[Examples: "He leads the goat to the village"; "He carries the load to the village"; "He carries the load..."

"He takes the village" (*harati grāmam*). Regarding roots meaning "to go": "He causes Devadatta to go to the village" (*gamayati devadattam grāmam*); "He causes Devadatta to travel to the village" (*yāpayati devadattam grāmam*).
Or rather, it is established by the rule *apo anyakarmaṇaḥ*. Or again, this is established. Why? Because of the phrase *anyakarmaṇaḥ*.

Here, the goat (*ajā*) is the object (*karman*) of one [agent], while the village is the object of another. Having taken hold of the goat, he leads her to the village. This is "another action" (*anyakarman*).

If it should be argued that there would be no application of the *l*-affixes (*la* etc. [in such cases], or if it should be argued that this would be the case when it is another action [that is expressed], then consider the example: *ajā nīyate grāmam* ("The she-goat is led to the village"). In the case of a passive construction (*parasmaipada*), the expression of the she-goat by the *l*-affix being produced would not be obtained.

425–428. Time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), and the distance to be traversed (*adhvagantavya*) are designated as the object (*karman*) for roots that are otherwise intransitive (*akarmaka*). It should be stated that time, state, and the distance to be traversed receive the designation of "object" when used with intransitive verbal roots. *Time*: He sits for a month; he sleeps for a month. *State*: He sits during the milking of the cows; he sleeps during the milking of the cows. *Distance to be traversed*: He sits for the duration of a *krośa*.

"One sleeps for a *krośa*" (*krośaṃ svapiti*). It should be stated that a location (*deśa*) becomes designated as an "object" (*karman*) when it is not itself an action. For example: "He sleeps in the Kurus" (*kurūn svapiti*), "He sleeps in the Pañcālas" (*pañcālān svapiti*). However, the wise know that which is the opposite of an object to be "kalma. What is this "kalma"? An incomplete action is "kalma. Or rather, it is so called because in it all the grammatical operations pertaining to an object (*karmakāryāṇi*) are not performed. Why? [Because the action is not fully realized there.]

In that case, the second case ending alone [is used]. However, regarding that object (*karman*) in which another [action] arises through connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and where the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs—that object is called *kalma*. And it is not stated that the function of the verbal root exists by virtue of its being *ralatva* (the state of having *ra* or *la* as its final phoneme). By this which has been explained, the entire technical designation of "object" (*karmasañjñā*) is established. In that regard, what would be the purpose of [specifying] that which is desired (*īpsita*)?

[This rule applies] to that which is designated as the object of the action (*karmasañjñā*). However, that which was previously stated [in Pāṇini 1.4.51] regarding "that which is connected with what is intended" (*īpsitatama*) is for the sake of establishing its status.
But for that which is *only* intended (*īpsita*), it will be established by the previous statement [Pāṇini 1.4.49]. Now, how should it be in this case:
*netā aśvasya srughnam* ("the leader of the horse to Srughna") or *netā aśvasya srughnasya* ("the leader of the horse of Srughna")? Gonikāputra says it can be both ways.

Regarding the expression *śabdakarma* ("having sound as its object"): how is this to be understood? Is it "those for whom sound is the action" (*kriyā*), or rather "those for whom sound is the object" (*karman*)? And what is the distinction here? If [the compound] were taken as "those whose action is sound" (*śabdakriyāṇām*) in the context of the designation *śabdakarma*, then [it would apply] to verbs such as *hvayati* ("he calls").

[This is] a prohibition. If it is argued that [the rule applies to] "verbal actions" when there is a mention of "words as actions," then a prohibition must be stated for verbs such as *hvayati* ("he calls") and others.
Which, then, are these verbs beginning with *hvayati*? They are: *hvayati*, *krandati*, and *śabdāyate*. For example: *devadatto hvayati* ("Devadatta calls");

*hvāyayati devadattena* ("He causes Devadatta to call"). *Devadattaḥ krandati* ("Devadatta cries out"); *krandayati devadattena* ("He causes Devadatta to cry out"). *Devadattaḥ śabdāyate* ("Devadatta makes a sound").

"One causes Devadatta to sound" (*śabdāyayati devadattena*). There must also be an addition [to the rule] for verbs such as *śru* ("to hear"), because their action does not consist of producing sound (*aśabdakriyatvāt*). An addition must be made for verbs such as *śru*. Which, then, are the verbs beginning with *śru*? They are: *śṛṇoti*, *vijānāti*, *upalabhate*. "Devadatta hears" (*śṛṇoti devadattaḥ*), "he causes Devadatta to hear" (*śrāvayati devadattam*). "Devadatta understands" (*vijānāti devadattaḥ*), "he causes Devadatta to understand" (*vijñāpayati*).

[One causes] Devadatta [to speak]. Devadatta perceives. [One causes] Devadatta to perceive. But what is the reason that [the rule] is not established? Because it does not have sound as its action (*aśabdakriyatvāt*). Well then, let it be that for those [verbs] where sound is the object (*karma*). If it is argued that [the rule applies to] "that which has sound as its object," then there must be an addition (*upasamkhyāna*) for [verbs] such as *jalpati* ("murmurs"). If it is argued that [the rule applies to] "that which has sound as its object," then there must be an addition for [verbs] such as *jalpati*.
[The suffix ṇic] should be applied. What, then, are the roots beginning with *jalpati*? They are *jalpati*, *vilapati*, and *ābhāṣate*. [Examples: *devadatto jalpati* ("Devadatta talks");

*devadattaṃ jalpayati* ("He causes Devadatta to talk"). *devadatto vilapati* ("Devadatta laments"); *devadattaṃ vilāpayati* ("He causes Devadatta to lament"). *devadatta ābhāṣate* ("Devadatta addresses");
*devadattam ābhāṣayati* ("He causes Devadatta to address"). For the root *dṛś*, it should be added everywhere: an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the root *dṛś* in all cases.
One perceives a *kārṣāpaṇa* coin by examining its appearance; one shows a *kārṣāpaṇa* coin by examining its appearance.

(P_1,4.52.2) KA_I,337.14-27 Ro_II, 431-432 A prohibition must be stated for the roots *ad* (to eat), *khād* (to chew), and *nī* (to lead). A prohibition must be stated for *ad*, *khād*, and *nī*: Devadatta eats; [the food] is eaten by Devadatta. Another says:
It must be stated that every result of eating (*pratyavasāna*) does not belong to the root *ad-*;
this applies even to the *parasmaipada* [terminations]. Only this one [result] is accepted:
the *kta* suffix [is used] in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), following roots whose meanings involve duration (*dhrauvya*), motion (*gati*), or eating (*pratyavasāna*).

This is their eaten [food]. *khādi* (the act of eating). Devadatta eats (*khādati*). He causes Devadatta to eat (*khādayati*) by means of Devadatta. *nī* (to lead): Devadatta leads (*nayati*). He causes Devadatta to lead (*nāyayati*) by means of Devadatta. Regarding *vah* (to carry), it should be stated that it applies when the agent is not a driver: "of *vah* whose agent is not a driver. Devadatta carries the load (*vahati bhāram*). He causes Devadatta to carry the load (*vāhayati bhāram*) by means of Devadatta. [This applies] when the agent is not a driver.

For what purpose [is this rule stated]? [In the examples: "The oxen carry the barley" (*vahanti yavān balīvardāḥ*) and "They cause the oxen to carry the barley" (*vāhayanti balīvardān yavān*). [Regarding the root] *bhakṣ* (to eat): it should be stated that [the rule applies] to the root *bhakṣ* when it does not mean "injury. [Examples: "Devadatta eats the cake" (*bhakṣayati piṇḍīm devadattaḥ*) and "He causes Devadatta to eat the cake" (*bhakṣayati piṇḍīm devadattena*). For what purpose is the phrase "when it does not mean injury" used? [Counter-example: "The oxen eat the barley" (*bhakṣayanti yavān balīvardāḥ*). Here, since the eating involves injury to the grain, the passive construction with the instrumental case is not applied.

The oxen eat the barley. Regarding the mention of "intransitive" (*akarmaka*), there is a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) concerning those [verbs] that have time as their object: when "intransitive" is mentioned, it includes those whose objects are time.
An addition must be made [to the rule]: "Devadatta sits for a month"; "He causes Devadatta to sit for a month"; "Devadatta lies down for a month";

"He causes Devadatta to lie down for a month. But this is already established by the statement that roots having time as their object (kālakarmaka) are treated like intransitive roots (akarmakavat). How so? It should be stated: "Roots having time as their object are treated like intransitive roots. Therefore, that...

It must be stated; it need not be stated. It is said [in the rule] "of intransitive verbs" (*akarmakāṇām*), yet there are no verbs that are ever intransitive with respect to time, action, or distance. Therefore, we shall understand it thus: "those which are intransitive in some instances. Alternatively, it refers to those intransitive verbs by virtue of that same object (*karman*) by which they become both transitive and intransitive; and no verb becomes intransitive by this particular object.

Furthermore, it is also intransitive. Alternatively, regarding those [verbs] that have an object which sometimes exists and sometimes does not, they are called "having objects" (*sakarmaka*); however, this [object] never fails to exist in any case whatsoever.
(Pāṇini 1.4.53)

435. Regarding the optional application of *hr̥* and *kr̥*, there is an addition [to the rule] for the *ātmanepada* when used with *abhivādi* and *dṛś*. An addition must be made to the rule concerning the optional application of *hr̥* and *kr̥* regarding the *ātmanepada* when used with *abhivādi* and *dṛś*. Devadatta greets the teacher: *abhivadati guruṃ devadattaḥ*. He causes himself to be greeted by the teacher: *abhivādayate guruṃ devadattam*. He causes himself to be greeted by Devadatta: *abhivādayate guruṃ devadattena*. The servants see the king: *paśyanti bhṛtyā rājānam*. He causes himself to be seen: *darśayate*.

435–436. Is he who has his own *tantra* independent (*svatantra*)? And what follows from this? [If so,] it would apply to a weaver (*tantuvāya*). This fault does not arise; for this word *tantra* exists as referring to a canopy (*vitāna*). For example: "the canopy is spread out," "the canopy is prepared"—it is understood to mean a canopy. It also exists as referring to predominance (*prādhānya*).
For example, when it is said, "this Brāhmaṇa is independent" (*svatantra*), it is understood that he is "one who has himself as his primary authority" (*svapradhāna*). Therefore,
this is the inclusion of the word *tantra* when it occurs in the sense of primacy (*prādhānya*).

436–438. Regarding the designation of the independent agent (*svatantra*), there must be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the case of that which possesses a cause (*hetumat*), because [the agent] is not independent. When the independent is designated as the agent, an addition must be made for the case of that which possesses a cause, as in: "Devadatta causes Yajñadatta to cook rice. But what is the reason that it is not established? Because [the agent] is not independent. Or rather, it is not so, because of independence; otherwise...

For it would follow that one causes another to act even while not acting oneself; or rather, [the action] should not be performed at all. What is the reason? Because of independence (*svātantrya*). He becomes independent. Otherwise, it would follow that one causes another to act even while not acting oneself. For if one thinks that he is not independent, then for him the statement "he causes [another] to act even while not acting" would be impossible. If you say, "It is not the case that he does not act," [we reply:]...

He is independent (*svatantra*). If one does not act while another causes him to act, it follows that he is independent. At least this much can be said by one who provides this supplementary rule (*upasamkhyāna*): "One who acts is independent; one who does not act is not.
This is a more convincing indicator (*jñāpaka*). For, it is said, when someone has been dispatched, he determines [his status] by observing both the action and the non-action.
"Acting independently, not acting [otherwise]. And if, having been commanded, he does not act, he becomes independent.

1.4.55) Because in the case of a command (*praiṣa*), there is the status of being a motivator (*hetu*) due to being a prompter who is not himself dependent. Because in the case of a command, there is the status of being a prompter who is not himself dependent.
The designation "cause" (*hetu*) is not established [in this context]. It is stated that "that which independently prompts [an action] is designated as a cause.

However, this [agent] does not prompt [the action] independently. This is established because of its independence. This is established. How? Because of its independence. If it is argued that "it prompts independently," then there is the state of being both independent and dependent.

It is contradictory. If he is independent, he cannot be directed; if he is to be directed, he is not independent. To say that he is both directed and independent is a contradiction. Or rather, it has already been stated. What has been stated? First, it was said: "Or rather, it is not so, because of independence; for otherwise, one would be making someone act even when they are not acting. Another point has also been stated: "Or rather, not so..."

If it is argued that [the suffix] is not *aprayojaka* because it is produced by a general rule (*sāmānyakṛtatvāt*) and is thus indistinguishable from a causal factor (*hetutaḥ*), since it functions independently (*svatantraprayojakatvāt*), then it has been stated that this is equally true for the case without doubt (*muktam asaṃśayena tulyam*).
(P_1.4.56) KA_I,340.2-25 Ro_II,440-442 For what purpose is the word *īśvara* taken with the addition of the letter *r*? [It is so that] it does not apply after *rīśvara* or *vīśvara*.

It is said [in the rule] "from *īśvara*"; let it not be [taken] from the root *īś* (meaning "to be able"), as in the rules "after the root *śak*, the suffixes *ṇamul* and *kamul*" and "in the sense of 'being able,' the suffixes *tosun* and *kasun*. This purpose is not necessary. The activity of the Teacher indicates that the word *īśvara* which is immediately preceding is what is intended to be included, since he applies the designation of indeclinable (*avyaya*) to a form ending in *kṛt* that ends in *m* or *e*.

[The rule] teaches [that the word *īśvara* is included]. A *kṛt*-suffix ending in *m* and a suffix ending in *e* exist even beyond this [word *īśvara*]. For that purpose, this [teaching] would be necessary. However, insofar as [the rule] teaches the designation of "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) for the *avyayībhāva* compound, the Teacher indicates that the word *īśvara* which follows immediately [after *anu*] is what is intended to be included. Among compounds, the *avyayībhāva* is [the first]. Of the compound...
This would be an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that only the *avyayībhāva* compound receives the designation "indeclinable" (*avyaya*), and no other.

If that is so, then this is established by common usage (*lokataḥ*). For example, in common usage, when it is said, "One should follow a dear traveler as far as the edge of the forest (*ā vanāntāt*) or as far as the edge of the water (*ā udakāntāt*)," one follows him from whichever is the first edge of the forest or the edge of the water. This is a matter of common usage.
And it exceeds [the limit]. One follows a second and a third forest edge or the edge of water.

Therefore, the word *īśvara* beginning with the letter *r* (repha) is to be understood. Now, what is the purpose of the mention of "prior" (*prāk*)? The mention of "prior" is for the purpose of excluding the technical designation (*saṃjñā*).
The mention of "prior" is made so that there may be no exclusion of the designation "particle" (*nipāta*). For if the mention of "prior" were not made, [the designation would cease].

The technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of *gati*, *upasarga*, and *karmapravacanīya* would subvert the designation of *nipāta*. To prevent them from subverting it, the rule stating "prior [to the designation of *karmapravacanīya*]" is formulated. Now, even though this rule "prior" is formulated, why do these [other] designations not nonetheless subvert it, given that they are of no occasion (*anavakāśa*)? For when the rule "prior" is formulated, once the designation of *nipāta* has been established, these [other] designations become merely partial designations (*avayavasaṃjñā*).
They are commenced. In that regard, there is a coalescence [of meanings] due to the explicit statement.
(Pāṇini 1.4.57) This word *sattva* indeed exists as having "substance" (*dravya*) as its referent. For example: "This Brāhmaṇa is a *sattva*."

"In this [example], *brāhmaṇī* is a word denoting a substance (*sattva*). There exists a word whose referent is an action (*kriyā*); "existence" (*sadbhāva*) is "substance" (*sattva*). Of what kind is this [word] being taken?

It is of that which has a substance as its referent. Why is this so? Because by taking it thus, both the positive injunction (*vidhi*) and the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) are established. But is this [the term *asattvavacana*] a preclusion (*paryudāsa*)—"that which is other than words denoting substance"? Yes.

Or rather, is this a prohibitive negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), [meaning] "no" when there is a word denoting an existent (*sattva*)? And what follows from this? If it were an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*), then the designation would also apply here in the case of *vipra*. This compound denotes an action or a substance, and as a substance, it is distinct from that which is governed by the rule. Furthermore, since it shares a commonality with words beginning with *pra* and so forth, the technical name "particle" (*nipāta*) would apply to it by means of the rule governing suffixes at the end of a compound (*tadantavidhi*).
Now, if it is a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), there is no fault. Let it be as there is no fault.
(P_1,4.58-59.1) The rule *prādayaḥ* is a split rule (*yogavibhāga*). The rule *prādayaḥ* must be split: "The words beginning with *pra* [are indeclinables] when they denote a substance (*sattva*)."

They receive the designation of *nipāta*. Then [the rule] "prepositions (*upasarga*) [are so called] when in connection with a verb" (*upasargāḥ kriyāyoge*) follows. What is the purpose of this separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*)?
It is for the sake of the designation *nipāta*. So that the designation *nipāta* may apply. For if there were a single rule (*ekayoga*), there would be an absence of the designation *nipāta*.

Indeed, if there were a single rule, there would be no application of the designation *nipāta*, because the designations of *gati*, *upasarga*, and *karmapravacanīya* would apply to that very same specific category.
The designation *nipāta* should apply to that very same specific instance.
An addition must be made for the word *marut*. An addition must be made for the word *marut*. [Example: *maruddatta*.

Regarding the word *kārikā*: an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the word *kārikā*. [The example is] *kārikākṛtya*. Furthermore, regarding *punar* and *canaḥ*: it should be stated that *punar* and *canaḥ* receive the designation of *gati* in the Vedic language (*chandas*). [Examples are:
*punarutsyūtaṃ vāso deyam* (a garment to be given after being sewn again), *punarniṣkṛto rathaḥ* (a chariot repaired again), and *uśig dūtaś canohitaḥ* (the eager messenger, well-disposed).

Regarding the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of "motion" (*gati*) and "preverb" (*upasarga*) in connection with an action: the statement "with respect to that action with which they are connected" means that it must be stated: "The designations 'motion' and 'preverb' apply with respect to that action with which they are connected. Why?

The purpose [of this rule]. The purpose is [to illustrate] the application of *ghañ*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*, and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. [Example of *ghañ*: An increased state is "increase" (*prabhāvaḥ*). [This is taught by Pāṇini 3.3.18: *ghañ* is used after a root when there is no prefix (*anupasarge*). Let there not be a prohibition [of *ghañ*] in this case. [Example of *ṣatva*: A village from which the sprinklers have departed is a "sprinklerless" (*visecakaḥ*) village.

[This is taught by Pāṇini 8.3.65: The substitution of *ṣ* occurs after a prefix (*upasargāt*). Let there not be the substitution of *ṣ* here. [Example of *ṇatva*: A village from which the leaders have departed is a "leaderless" (*pranāyakaḥ*) village. [This is taught by Pāṇini 8.4.14.]

In the word *grāmaḥ*, let there not be the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] by virtue of the rule "after a prefix" (*upasargād*...). Furthermore, the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) in the rule prescribing *vṛddhi* is redundant. In the rule for *vṛddhi*, namely "after a prefix, before a root ending in *ṛ*" (*upasargād ṛti dhātau*), the purpose of mentioning the "root" is so that it should not apply here in the case of *prarṣabhaṃ vanam*. Even if the mention of the "root" were made, [the form] would still be *prarcchaka*.

Thus, [the rule] would apply here. However, because of the statement "that toward which the action is directed," it does not occur. There is a fault regarding the rules for *vat* (substitution), *vidhna*, *bhāva*, *abīt-tva*, *svāṅga-ādi-svara*, and *raṇatva*. Regarding the rule for *vat*: *udvataḥ nivataḥ yāsi bapsat* ("you go up and down, devouring"). This is the rule for *vat*. Regarding *nas-bhāva*: *praṇasam mukham*, *unnasam mukham* ("a face with a prominent nose," "a face with an upturned nose"). This is *nas-bhāva*. Regarding *abīt-tva*: *prepam*, *parepam*. This is *abīt-tva*. Regarding *svāṅga-ādi-svara*...

*Prasphik*, *prodaraḥ*, [the rule for] vowels in *svāṅga* and so forth, and [the rule for] *ṇatva*: *pra ṇaḥ śūdraḥ*, *pra ṇaḥ ācāryaḥ*, *pra ṇaḥ rājā*, *pra ṇaḥ vṛtrahā*. These rules [prescribed] by the [sūtra] "after a preposition" (*upasargāt*) do not apply. [Objection: This is established by the authority of the explicit statement (*vacana-prāmāṇyāt*) regarding those rules for *vat*, *vidhi*, absence of *nas*, *bīttva*, vowels in *svāṅga* and so forth, and *ṇatva*. [Reply: These rules have no scope [elsewhere]. They will apply by virtue of the authority of the explicit statement.

There is a prohibition regarding *su* and *dur* in the rules for the application of the augment *num*, the substitution of *t* for *d*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*, and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. It must be stated that there is a prohibition of *su* and *dur* in the rules for the application of *num*, the substitution of *t*, the substitution of *ṣ*, and the substitution of *ṇ*. Regarding the application of *num*:

in the case of *sulabham* and *durlabham*, let there not be the *num* [augment] prescribed by the rule "after a preverb" (*upasargāt*). [The answer is: it does not apply when *su* and *dur* are used alone.

Thus, this need not be stated; there is no purpose for it. This is accomplished by the very *nyāsa* (exclusion). [The purpose is: "Let there not be *tattva* (substitution of *ta*) by the rule *acaḥ upasargāt taḥ*," as in *sudattam*. [And: "Let there not be *ṣatva* (substitution of *ṣa*) by the rule *upasargāt*," as in *susiktam ghaṭaśatena* ("well-sprinkled with a hundred jars") and *sustutam ślokaśatena* ("well-praised with a hundred verses"). [In these cases,] *suḥ* is used in the sense of praise (*pūjā*).

This need not be stated; there is no purpose for it. This [application of] *ṇatva* is already accomplished by the rule itself (*nyāsa*). [For example, in the cases of] *durnayam* and *durnītam*, let there not be *ṇatva* on account of the rule "after a preverb" (*upasargāt*).

It should be stated that [the rule] applies "in connection with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*," so that it may apply only in these cases: *ūrīkṛtya* and *ūrībhūya*. It should not apply here: *ūrī paktvā*. Well then, it must be stated. No, it need not be stated; for the term "in connection with an action" (*kriyāyoge*) is understood [from the previous rule], and there is no connection between the words beginning with *ūry-* (such as *ūrī*) and the suffixes *ciṭ* and *ḍāc* with any other action.

(P_1,4.62.1) KA_I,343.14-22 Ro_II, 449-450 How is this to be understood? Is *itipara* "that which follows *iti*" [and] *anitipara* "not followed by *iti*," or rather, is *itipara* "that from which *iti* is subsequent"? What follows from this? If...

If [the compound] *itipara* is understood as "that which follows after *iti*," then in the case of "having made the sound *khāṭ*, he spat" (*iti khāṭ iti kṛtvā niraṣṭhīvat*), the rule would apply here. Alternatively, if [the compound] *itipara* means "that from which *iti* is subsequent," then in the case of "having made the sounds *śrauṣaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ*, he spat" (*iti śrauṣaṭ vauṣaṭ iti kṛtvā niraṣṭhīvat*), the rule would apply here. Let it be, for now, that [the compound] *itipara* means "that from which *iti* is subsequent."
"This [word] *iti* is not the limit, nor is it beyond the limit; thus it is 'not beyond the limit' (*an-itiparam*). But was it not stated that, having uttered "śrauṣaṭ" or "vauṣaṭ," one spits?
In that case, the rule would apply here as well. This is not a fault. First, he should be asked this:

"Now, in this context, since the rule says 'before the verbal root' (*prāk dhātoḥ*), how is it that there is the prior application of the mere *gati*? He provides the answer: "It extracts [the *gati*]."

Thus, the form of the action (*gatyākṛti*) is being specified. In this case as well, then, the form of the imitation (*anukaraṇākṛti*) is being specified. Why is this stated? To prohibit the occurrence of the particle *iti* after an imitation, for the purpose of avoiding unintended words.

A prohibition regarding the suffix *iti* following an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is stated. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of avoiding undesirable forms. That is to say, so that undesirable forms do not occur. This will be examined [later]: "The statement 'before the verbal root' (*te prāk dhātoḥ*) is intended either as a restriction on usage (*prayoga-niyama*) or as a restriction on technical designation (*saṃjñā-niyama*). When it is intended as a restriction on usage, then it serves to avoid undesirable forms.
This must be said: for when it is for the purpose of restricting the application of technical terms (*saṃjñā*), then there is no fault.

1.4.63) This is being made far too much of—[the distinction between] "when there is respect" and "when there is disrespect," or "when [something] exists" and "when it does not exist. It is established simply by saying "when there is respect."

"How is it that [the term] *asatkṛtya* is formed? It will be by means of the rule for the end of a compound (*tadanta-vidhi*). "By what, then, would there be the sense of disrespect? We shall understand the negation of respect through the negative particle (*nañ*): [the compound] *anādara* meaning "disrespect. "It cannot be so," [says the opponent]. For [if it were so], it would apply only when respect is the context; it would not apply when disrespect is the context. However, when the term *anādara* ("disrespect") is explicitly included, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

This is understood [from the rule]: "when there is no regard" (*avidyamānādare*) means "in the absence of regard" (*anādare*). Therefore, the mention of "non-regard" (*anādara*) should be made [explicitly]. However, for that which does not exist (*asataḥ*), it is established by the rule of "specification of what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*).

452. An addition must be made [to Pāṇini’s rule] regarding the word *antaḥ* in the cases of the prefix *āṅ*, the application of the *ki* suffix, compounds, and the substitution of *ṇ*. An addition must be made for the word *antaḥ* in the cases of *āṅ*, the application of *ki*, compounds, and the substitution of *ṇ*. 1. *Āṅ*: *antardhā*. 2. Application of *ki*: *antardhiḥ*. 3. Compound: *antarhatya*. 4. Substitution of *ṇ*: *antarhaṇyāt gobhyo gāḥ*.

(P_1,4.74) Regarding the words beginning with *sākṣāt*, there must be an inclusion of the sense of the suffix *cvī*. An inclusion of the sense of *cvī* must be made for the words beginning with *sākṣāt*. [Examples:
*asākṣāt* having become *sākṣāt* → *sākṣātkṛtya*. For when something is indeed already *sākṣāt*, then [the suffix] should not apply.

Thus [it is stated]. Furthermore, the status of having "m" as a final phoneme (*makārāntatva*) is prescribed in conjunction with the technical designation *gati*. It must be stated that the status of having "m" as a final phoneme is contingent upon its connection with the designation *gati*, as in *lavaṇaṃ kṛtvā* ("having made salty"). In that case, there is a prohibition regarding the suffix *cv-*; it must be stated that there is a prohibition for that which ends in *cv-*, as in *lavaṇīkṛtya* ("having made salty"). Or rather, it need not be stated. Why? Because it has already been accomplished by the preceding rule.

"Let it be that by this [rule] there is an option (*vibhāṣā*). By the preceding [rule], it will be obligatory (*nitya*). "But then this is the purpose: it has been stated that the status of having *m* as its final sound (*makārāntatva*) is conditioned by the designation 'gati' (*gatisañjñā*). Therefore, let this not apply to a word ending in the suffix *cv-*. "This too is not a purpose. This optional substitution of the word *lavaṇam* for the word *lavaṇa* is made. And if [the form] *lavaṇī-*..."

453–456. Is this statement "before the verbal root" intended as a restriction on usage— meaning that these [suffixes] must be employed only before the verbal root— or is it intended as a restriction on technical designation (saṃjñā)—
meaning that these may be employed both before and after the verbal root?

"The designation *gati* applies to those [words] used before [the verb]. What is the specific purpose here? If it is argued that the statement "before the verbal root" (*prāgdhātu*) is for the sake of restricting usage, then there would be the undesirable consequence of a prohibition against the particle *iti* following an imitation-word (*anukaraṇa*). If it is argued that the statement "before the verbal root" is for the sake of restricting usage, then there would be the prohibition against the particle *iti* following an imitation-word.

It must be stated. For what purpose? To exclude undesirable forms. That is, so that undesirable words do not occur. And in the Vedic language (*chandas*), there is the rule for [elements] separated by others. It should be stated: "In the Vedic language, [an element] may be separated by others and even by intervening elements. This is established by the restriction of technical names (*saṃjñāniyama*). This is accomplished through the restriction of technical names. Let it then be a restriction of technical names.

The statement of both [alternatives] is useless because no undesirable consequence is observed. For both positions, the verbal expression is purposeless. Why? Because no undesirable consequence is observed. Indeed, no one uses the form *pacatipra* when they ought to use *prapacati*. And if an undesirable consequence were observed, then it would merit such effort. This is the case regarding the occurrence of a subordinate element (*upasarjana*).

But it is for the sake of establishing the order of precedence between the prior and the subsequent. However, this must be stated for the sake of establishing the order of precedence when there is a conjunction with a subordinate element (*upasarjana*):

*ṛṣabhaṃ kūlamudrujam*, *ṛṣabhaṃ kūlamudvaham*. [The purpose is] so that the verb may be used before the root (*dhātu*) [in the compound]. If this is stated for the sake of establishing the order of precedence when there is a conjunction with a subordinate element, then [it applies to forms such as] *sukaṭaṃkarāṇi*.

In the case of *vīraṇāni*, the application [of the suffix] would have occurred before the verbal root due to the rule for *gati*. However, the activity of the Teacher indicates that here the application does not occur before the *gati*, since he adds the indicatory letter *kh* (in *khal*) in the rule *īṣadduḥsuṣu kṛcchrākṛcchrārtheṣu khal*. How is this an indicator? By the addition of the *kh*, this is the purpose: [to ensure that the accent falls on the root].
The purpose is so that *mum* may occur after the suffix *khit*. If, however, the verbal root were used here before the suffix *gati*, the application of *khit* would be purposeless.

Let it be that *mum* occurs here; the prohibition "not for an indeclinable" (*anavyayasya*) will apply. But the Teacher perceives that in this case the verbal root is not used before the suffix *gati*; therefore, he adds the indicatory letter *kh*.

This is not a valid indicator. Even if there were a prior application of the prefix (*pra*) here, the augment *mum* would still occur; for how so? Because when a *kṛt*-suffix is mentioned, that which is preceded by a prefix (*gati*) or a kāraka is also included. Therefore, there is no purpose in the rule stating "prior to the verbal root" (*prāgdhātu*) for this specific reason. How then [do we explain] examples such as *ṛṣabham kūlamudrujam* ("the bull pushing up the bank") and *ṛṣabham kūlamudvaham* ("the bull carrying away the bank")?

456–457. For what purpose is this extensive designation (*sañjñā*) made? So that the designation may be understood according to its meaning (*anvartha*), namely: "those who have expressed an object (*karman*) are *karmapravacanīya*s. But who are those who have expressed an object? Those which do not currently express an action (*kriyā*). And which are those that do not currently express an action? Those which express the action of an unexpressed [verb] are the *karmapravacanīya*s.

(P_1.4.84) KA_I,346.20–347.21 Ro_II,458–460 For what purpose is this stated? So that the technical designation *karmapravacanīya* may apply, and the designations *gati* and *upasarga* may not apply. And what would [follow] from that? [In the example: *śākalyasya saṃhitām anu prāvarṣat*.

The rule "gatiḥ gatau" would result in the *nighāta* (elision of accent) [of *vi*]. If that were so, the designation *karmapravacanīya* should also be stated for *vi*. However, the *nighāta* of *vi* is not desired in such cases, as in: *prādeśam prādeśam viparilikhati* ("he traces around every span"). There is a distinction here: in this case, *vi* does not have a connection with the action (*likhi*) in its expressed form. What then? It is used in its unexpressed form, as in: *prādeśam prādeśam vimāya parilikhati* ("having measured out every span, he traces around"). If that is the case...
Even for *anu*, there is no purpose in assigning it the technical designation of *karmapravacanīya*. For even in the case of *anu*, there is no connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*) toward *vṛṣi*;

rather, [the connection is] with that which is not being employed [in the sentence]. [Example: "Having followed the well-composed *saṃhitā* of Śākalya, the god rained. In that case, this is the purpose:
so that the accusative case may occur, according to the rule "the accusative is used when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*. Therefore...

He recites the reply: "The statement that *anu* is used in the sense of a mark (*lakṣaṇa*) is redundant, because it has already been established by the general rule. The statement that *anu* is used in the sense of a mark is redundant. What is the reason? Because it has already been established by the general rule. By the general rule itself, the designation *karmapravacanīya* will apply here, according to [Pāṇini 1.4.90]: "The terms *prati*, *pari*, and *anu* [receive this designation] when used in the senses of a mark, description of a state (*itthambhūtākhyāna*), a share (*bhāga*), and distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). However, the statement is made for the sake of indicating the causal sense (*hetu*).

This must be stated for the sake of the cause (*hetu*). The *saṃhitā* of Śākalya is the cause of the rain, not its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Is this something that needs to be stated? No, indeed. How will it be understood without being stated? For that which is called a "characteristic" is that by which something is characterized again and again, not that which is fit to serve merely as a cause even once. And this [connection] was well-established by Śākalya only once.
"The god rained after having studied the *Saṃhitā*. In that case, it should have been taught as "the particle *anu* [is used] in the sense of cause (*hetu*).
But now, since the sense of cause is already included within the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), there is no need for this [separate rule]. The sense of cause is indeed included within the definition;
for not everything that serves as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is necessarily one by which something is characterized again and again. Why?

In that case, even that which serves as a cause (*nimitta*) only once becomes a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). For example, as when one says, "You saw the student with the water-pot in his hand" (*kamaṇḍalupāṇim chātram adrākṣīḥ*). Even though that student was seen with the water-pot in his hand only once, that very thing remains his defining characteristic. Therefore, that is precisely the purpose [of the rule]: so that the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) may occur when there is a connection with a *karmapravacanīya*.

It should be stated that *āṅ* is used in the sense of both limit (*maryādā*) and inclusion (*abhividhi*). This is so that [the rule] may apply here as well in the example: *ākumāraṃ yaśaḥ pāṇineḥ* ("The fame of Pāṇini extends even to children"). Then it must indeed be stated. No, it need not be stated; for it is already established by the rule *maryādāvacane*. This is the limit of his fame. (Pāṇini 1.4.89) KA_I,348.2-6 Ro_II,257.1-5.10.2023. Of what things are the meanings beginning with "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) being taught? Of trees and so forth. But for what purpose is this stated?
So that they may receive the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *karmapravacanīya*; [it is] so that they do not receive the designations of "motion" (*gati*) or "prefix" (*upasarga*).

This is not a necessary purpose, because the designations of motion and prefix apply only toward that action (*kriyā*) with which [the words] are connected, and [in these cases, they are not connected to any such action].

The connection with action (*kriyāyoga*) applies to [words such as] *vṛkṣa* and so forth. In that case, however, this is the purpose: so that the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) may occur according to the rule "the second case ending is used when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*. For example: *vṛkṣaṃ prati vidyotate* ("It flashes toward the tree") and *vṛkṣam anu vidyotate* ("It flashes along the tree"). 462–464. For what purpose is the designation *karmapravacanīya* prescribed for *adhi* and *pari* when they are devoid of meaning? [The answer is: so that the designation *karmapravacanīya* may apply; [it is] lest the designations *gati* and *upasarga* should apply. This is not a valid purpose. For the designations *gati* and *upasarga* apply toward that [action] with which they are connected, and these two [words] are here devoid of meaning. In that case, this is the purpose:

How is it that the fifth case (pañcamī) occurs here, as in the rule *apādāne pañcamī*? From what is it approached? Here, the fifth case is established by the very rule *apādāne*. Therefore, this is indeed the fifth case in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*). Even in cases where the fifth case is not specifically prescribed in connection with the word *adhi*, it is nevertheless heard: "From where is it approached? (*kutaḥ adhyāgamyate*). If that is so, then [the point] is established.

In that the Teacher teaches the designation *karmapravacanīya*—which sets aside the designations of *gati* and *upasarga* for those [particles] that are meaningless—it indicates that for these [particles], even when they are meaningless, the property of having meaning (*arthavat*) applies. What is the purpose of this indication? It is so that the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) may be enjoined for a meaningless particle; thus, it need not be stated.

Alternatively, these two [prefixes] are not indeed meaningless. What then is meant by "meaningless"? They are called "meaningless" because they do not denote a different meaning [from the verbal root]. They express the action already expressed by the verbal root; that [action] remains undistinguished, just as milk [is indistinguishable] in a conch shell.

If this is so, since that meaning has already been expressed by the verbal root, the employment of a prefix for that meaning would not be appropriate, according to the principle that "that which has already been expressed [need not be expressed again]."

Regarding the term *aprayoga* ("non-application"): the application of words whose meaning has already been expressed is also observed. For example: *apūpau dvāv ānaya* ("bring two cakes"), *brāhmaṇau dvāv ānaya* ("bring two Brahmins").
Why does it not occur here: *sarpiṣo 'pi syāt*, *gomūtrasyāpi syāt*? And what else?

[Objection: A second case ending would also follow [unnecessarily], because of the rule stating that the second case is used when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*. [Response: This is not a fault. These are not being indicated as meanings [of the particle *api*] itself. What then? These are being indicated as meanings belonging to another word. The sense is that the particle *api* receives the designation *karmapravacanīya* with respect to whatever word occurs in these meanings. Now...

In the rule *adhir īśvare* (Pāṇini 1.4.97), it is asked: "What has been stated? [The answer is: "If the mention of the agent in the phrase *yasya ca īśvaravacanam* is intended as a designation of the agent (*kartṛnirdeśa*), then [the desired result] is established by the absence of such a statement. However, the occurrence of the nominative case is not justified. Therefore, it is established by its own statement: it must be stated that *adhi* receives the technical designation *karmapravacanīya* when it relates to 'one's own' (*sva*)."

Regarding the mention of *parasmaipada* in the rule for the substitutes of *l*: [this] must be stated. What is the reason? Because it would be sublated by the [rules for] person (*puruṣa*). For in this case, there would be a sublation of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*). Here...

For if [the term] *puruṣa* were being formulated [as a technical name], it would, having no scope of its own, sublate the technical name *parasmaipada*. But the technical name *parasmaipada* also has no scope [if *puruṣa* were used]. It will exist by virtue of an explicit statement (*vacana*). The technical name *parasmaipada* does have scope. What is its scope? The affixes *śatṛ* and *kvasu* are its scope. Furthermore, the mention of *parasmaipada* in the rule for the *vṛddhi* substitution after the suffix *sic* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that [the name *puruṣa*] does not sublate [the name *parasmaipada*].

Regarding the technical designations *prathama*, *madhyama*, and *uttama*, the mention of the *ātmanepada* [voices] is for the sake of establishing a one-to-one correspondence. The mention of the *ātmanepada* must be made in the rule defining the *prathama*, *madhyama*, and *uttama* designations. It should be stated that the *prathama*, *madhyama*, and *uttama* designations apply to the *ātmanepada* endings as well. What is the purpose? For the sake of establishing a one-to-one correspondence, so that there may be a sequential application (*anudeśa*) according to the number of items.

For if the mention of *ātmanepada* were not made, there would be three technical terms (*saṃjñās*) and six things to be named (*saṃjñins*); due to this inequality, the assignment of names according to numerical correspondence (*saṅkhyātānudeśa*) would not obtain. Furthermore, even when the mention of *ātmanepada* is made, the statement of sequential order (*ānupūrvya*) must also be provided. For if it were not made, the first technical term might apply to one triad [of suffixes] and a different one to another.

In this way, for some [roots] there is the designation "middle" (madhyama), and for others the designation "highest" (uttama). It is not because of a reference by means of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one from a group of identical items). As for what was said—that the mention of the term *ātmanepada* must be made for the sake of equality in number—that need not be done. For only six designations (*saṃjñā*) are actually specified. How so? Because of a reference by means of *ekaśeṣa*. This is a reference by means of *ekaśeṣa*. Now...

In this case of the teaching of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), is this a *dvandva* compound of those for which *ekaśeṣa* has already been applied— namely: "the first and the first are the two firsts," "the middle and the middle are the two middles," "the last and the last are the two last," and then "the two firsts, the two middles, and the two last" [forming] "first-middles-last"— or rather, is it *ekaśeṣa* of those for which a *dvandva* has already been formed?

"First," "middle," and "last" constitute "first-middle-last. [The compound] "first-middle-last" and [the compound] "first-middle-last" and [the compound] "first-middle-last"—thus [it is]. And what follows from this? If a *dvandva* compound were formed among those [terms] ending in the singular case-ending, then the designation "first" (*prathama*) would apply to the first and middle [persons], and the designation "middle" (*madhyama*) would apply to the last and first [persons].

[The designation] *madhyama* would obtain; [the designation] *uttama* would obtain for both *madhyama* and *uttama*. Now, if there is a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of those that have formed a *dvandva* compound, there is no fault. Let it be so, in such a way that there is no fault. But what is the correct principle here? He says: "Both. For both are observed. For example: *bahu śaktikiṭakam* (many spears and clubs), *bahūni śaktikiṭakāni* (many spears and clubs).

"Pot and pan" (sthālīpiṭharam) means many pots and pans. As for what was said—that even if the mention of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is made, the statement regarding "successive order" (*ānupūrvya*) must be formulated—it need not be formulated. This is established from common usage (*loka*). For example, in the world it is said, "The fire of the *vihavya* hymn is to be approached with two [verses] at a time," yet no statement regarding successive order is made.
Thus it is approached in regular succession.
(Pāṇini 1.4.104) Does "three, three" carry over [from the previous rule], or does it not? And what follows from this? If it carries over, then [the rule applies] to *aṣṭan*.

In the case of *ā vibhaktau*, the substitution of *ā* would not apply. Furthermore, if [the rule] *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ* has been withdrawn, it follows that only the two suffixes (*au*) would be understood here. Let it be as you wish; let us assume for now that [the previous rule] continues to apply. But was it not said that, because of the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*, the substitution of *ā* would not apply? It will occur by virtue of an explicit statement.

Alternatively, let it be that [the rule] has ceased. But was it not said that in the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*, there would result the application of the term "suffixes" (*pratyayayoḥ*) alone? This is not a fault. The word *aci* (before a vowel) is understood from the previous context. And the two suffixes beginning with a vowel (*ajādī*) do not exist as the first two [suffixes]. But is it not understood thus: "those two which begin with a vowel among the vowels"? Or "among those beginning with a vowel"?

Regarding the words "yau prathamau": when the rule *tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi* subsequently refers back to the previously mentioned long vowel of homogeneous quality (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*), that indicates the Teacher’s intention that the two case endings (*vibhakti*) are being referred to. Alternatively, he could have simply used the mention of the number (*vacana*), stating: "In the case of *au* and *jas*, there is the long vowel of homogeneous quality."

Why is this stated? The statement regarding the remainder of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). This undertaking is for the sake of restriction. Now, when this is understood as having the purpose of restriction, is this a restriction concerning the *upapada* (governing word) in the case of *yuṣmad*, or...

Is it that the second person (*madhyama*) occurs only with *asmat* (the first person pronoun) and the third person (*uttama*) only with *yuṣmat* (the second person pronoun)—that is, a restriction based on the person—or is it that the second person occurs only with *yuṣmad* and the third person only with *asmat*? And what follows from this? If it were a restriction based on the person, then the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) would have to be made [in the rule], as in: "The first person (*prathama*) occurs in the remainder. What is the reason? Because the second and third persons are restricted to *yuṣmad* and *asmat* respectively, while the persons [of the pronouns] themselves would be unrestricted; in that case, the first person would apply.

[The suffix] would indeed apply [there as well]. In that case, the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) must be made for the sake of the first restriction: that the first person occurs only in the remainder and not elsewhere. Or, even if it were a restriction regarding the *upapada* (governing word), the mention of "the remainder" must still be made, stating that the first person occurs in the remainder;
for while the second and first persons are restricted to *yuṣmad* and *asmad* respectively, the two [second and first persons] are unrestricted and would thus also apply in the case of the remainder.
