In that case, the term *śeṣa* (the remainder) must be included for the purpose of restricting the remainder; [it serves to show] that in the case of the remainder, only the first person occurs and no other. If the restriction were based solely on the *upapada* (the accompanying word), the inclusion of *śeṣa* could be omitted. How so? The words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are restricted [to the second and first persons respectively], while the middle and first persons are not restricted; thus, those two would apply even in the case of the remainder. Therefore, one would have to state, "the first person occurs," and that [statement] would serve as a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

It will be so: where both the first [suffix] and another would apply, there the first shall take effect. In that case, regarding *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when followed by other [words], there must be a prohibition of the first [suffix] because they are "remainder" (*śeṣa*). Thus, a prohibition of the first [suffix] must be stated for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when followed by others: *tvam ca devadattaś ca pacathaḥ* ("you and Devadatta cook"); *aham ca devadattaś ca pacāvaḥ* ("I and Devadatta cook").

What is the reason? Because of being the remainder (*śeṣa*). Since it is stated that "the first [person] occurs in the remainder," the first person would result. However, this is established by means of the prohibition regarding *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. How is it established? By the prohibition regarding *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. It should be stated: "The first person occurs in the remainder, but not for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. By means of this prohibition, the second person (*madhyama*) is used for *yuṣmad*, and the third person (*uttama*) is used for *asmad*. Thus, for *yuṣmad*, the second person is used.

The rule "the first person is used for *asmad*" (Pāṇini 1.4.107) takes precedence by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of the rule "the second person is used for *yuṣmad*" (Pāṇini 1.4.105) is, for example, *tvam pacasi* ("you cook"). The scope of the rule "the first person is used for *asmad*" is, for example, *aham pacāmi* ("I cook"). In the case where both would apply, such as *tvam ca aham ca pacāvaḥ* ("you and I cook"), the rule "the first person is used for *asmad*" prevails by way of conflict. Therefore, that [rule]...

The objection regarding contradiction must be stated. It need not be stated. According to the rule "among the words beginning with *tyad*, whichever comes last remains," the remainder will be *asmad* (the word for "I/we"). In that case, it is already established by the rule "when *asmad* is present, the first person [suffix] is used. However, it must be stated that this contradiction exists for the sake of allowing multiple remainders (*anekaśeṣa*). When is it that there is no single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*)? When...

And there is no *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one). *Ekaśeṣa* occurs when there is the intention to express [the items] together (*sahavivakṣā*). When there is no intention to express them together, then *ekaśeṣa* does not exist.
Or rather, there is no contradiction because of the non-existence of *ekaśeṣa* for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, since those which have them as their substrata (*tadadhikaraṇa*) also lack *ekaśeṣa*.

Or rather, there is no purpose served by the rule of "contradiction" (*vipratiṣedha*). What is the reason? Because of the non-existence of *ekaśeṣa* for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, [and consequently] for those which have them as their substrata.

Furthermore, even in the case of bases (*adhikaraṇa*) such as *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, there should not be a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*), as in: "you and I cook" (*tvam ca aham ca pacasi pacāmi ca*). And when there is a plurality of actions, the observation of a plurality of substances serves as the inferential mark for the non-existence of a single-remainder compound in subsequent cases.
Indeed, when there is a plurality of actions, a plurality of substances is observed, as in: "you cook and I cook."

"And I" (*aham ca*). That inference is that there is no *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) even for the two subsequent actions. And by doing so, that which was stated there—"the prohibition of [the forms] *yuṣmad* and *asmad* in the presence of others is not [applicable] because of their being the remainder"—is also free from fault. For in that case as well, it should be thus: "You and Devadatta cook" (*tvam ca devadattaś ca pacasi pacati*).

And: "I and Devadatta cook" (*aham ca devadattaś ca pacāmi pacati ca*). As for what was said—that there is no contradiction because the *yuṣmad* and *asmad* [pronouns] do not undergo the single-remainder elision (*ekaśeṣa*), whereas those standing in the same grammatical relation as them do undergo it—it is observed that both the *yuṣmad* and *asmad* [pronouns] undergo the single-remainder elision, and those standing in the same relation as them also undergo it. For example: "you and I" (*tvam ca aham*).

"And let us both, O slayer of Vṛtra, join together. Furthermore, as for what is said—that the observation of the distinctness of substances when there is a distinctness of actions serves as an inference for the existence of multiple *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) formations later on—it is indeed observed that even when there is a distinctness of actions, there occurs a single-remainder formation of the substance.
For example: "The dice should be broken, eaten, and played with. Thus it is.

And having done so, that fault which was stated there—namely, "the prohibition of the first person [suffixes] applies to *yuṣmad*, *asmad*, and others because they remain as the remainder"—does not apply. This fault has already been resolved by the statement: "But it is established by the prohibition of [the suffixes] for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*.
Well then, that prohibition must be stated. It need not be stated. For the first person [suffixes] are prescribed for the remainder.

For that which is "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) and that which is "other" (*anya*) are not both grasped by the mention of "the remainder. [If they were so grasped,] the first person would occur, but it would not [be intended here]; furthermore, the middle and highest persons would also not be obtained. What is the reason? The middle and highest persons are prescribed when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are the attendant words (*upapada*).
And neither *yuṣmad* nor *asmad*, nor that which is other than them, is grasped by the mention of *yuṣmad-asmad*. Whatever is here [the word] *yuṣmat*...

[Objection: In that case, the second and first persons would depend on *yuṣmad* and *asmad* respectively. Just as it is here that the second and first persons occur depending on *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, so too it follows that the first person should occur depending on whatever remains (*śeṣa*) here.
[Response: In that case, the first person is prescribed when the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is the governing word (*upapada*). A word that is uttered near [another] is a "governing word" (*upapada*).

And that which is uttered here as a subordinate element (*upoccāri*) is not a *śeṣa*; and that which is a *śeṣa* is not uttered as a subordinate element. [If this were so,] the first person would not exist, and the middle and highest persons would also not be obtained. What is the reason? The middle and highest persons are prescribed when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are the subordinate elements (*upapada*). A word that is uttered as a subordinate element is an *upapada*. And those two, *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, are not what is uttered here as a subordinate element.

And since *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are not uttered as secondary elements (*upoccārita*), then [if your view were correct], the first person would be prescribed when there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). However, in this case, there is no coreferentiality with the "remainder" alone; thus, the first person would not occur. Furthermore, the second and first persons (*madhyama* and *uttama*) would also not be obtained. What is the reason? Because [the rule for those persons] applies when there is coreferentiality with *yuṣmad* and *asmad*.

The middle and the highest [persons] are prescribed, yet here there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. If that is so, then by the rule "the pronouns beginning with *tyad* are always [retained] when followed by all [other words]," the remainder (*śeṣa*) of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* will occur here; thus, it is established that the middle person is used for *yuṣmad* and the highest person for *asmad*. It is not so established.

[If it were so], the first person would also apply to the *sthānin* (the original element). Indeed, according to the rule "among *tyad*-type pronouns, whichever is subsequent remains," when there is the retention (*śeṣa*) of *bhavat*, then the first person would apply.
It is stated [in the rules] that "the second person is used for *yuṣmad* and the third person for *asmad*"; however, those two do not apply here.

[One might argue: "The status of *parama* [as a substitute] applies in cases such as *paramastvaṃ pacasi* and *paramāhaṃ pacāmi*; this will be achieved by the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) [which allows the operation to apply to words ending in *tvam* and *aham*]. [Response: In that case, the same extension would also apply here: *atitvaṃ pacati* and *atyahaṃ pacati*. Furthermore, in the case of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) functioning in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the second and first persons would not be obtained: *tvattaraḥ pacasi* and *mattaraḥ pacāmi*; *tvadrūpaḥ pacasi* and *madrūpaḥ pacāmi*; *tvatkalpaḥ*... [and so forth].
"You cook; I, who am like you, cook. If that is the case, then [the suffixes] will occur as *yuṣmad-vat* and *asmad-vat*.
But then they would also apply here:

*atitvaṃ pacati* ("he cooks, surpassing you") and *atyahaṃ pacati* ("he cooks, surpassing me"). If so, then [the meaning should be] "when *yuṣmad* is the agent" (*sādhana*) and "when *asmad* is the agent."

It will be so. And by doing it this way, that which was stated there—namely, "the prohibition of the first person [suffixes] in the case of *yuṣmad*, *asmad*, and others, because they are the remainder"—is also rendered faultless. Alternatively, the first person shall be established as the general rule (*utsarga*). When *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are used as attendant words (*upapada*), the second and first persons will serve as exceptions (*apavāda*). In that context, there is both the presence of the sense of *yuṣmad* and the presence of the sense of *asmad*.
And because [the suffix] *asti* exists, the middle and highest persons will occur. Now, how should it be here?
Is it *atvam tvam sampadyate*, *tvadbhavati*, *madbhavati*; or rather, *tvadbhavasi*, *madbhavāmi*?
It should be *tvadbhavati*, *madbhavati*. Why do the middle and highest persons not occur?

When there is a choice between the secondary (gauṇa) and the primary (mukhya) meaning, comprehension occurs with respect to the primary. For example, in the injunctions "The cow is to be sacrificed" (*gaur anubandhyaḥ*) and "The goat dedicated to Agni and Soma" (*aja agnīṣomīyaḥ*), it is not the Bāhīka man who is bound for sacrifice. How then do the rules regarding *vṛddhi* and the substitution of *āt* apply to the word *bāhīka* in such cases as "The cow stands" (*gauḥ tiṣṭhati*) or "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*)? This occurs when the application depends on the meaning; however, that which depends on the word applies to the mere word-form itself.
[The term *vṛddhi* occurs] with reference to sound (*śabda*), and [the terms] *āt* and *utva* [occur] with reference to the locus [of sound].
1.4.109) The closest proximity [of sounds] is *saṃhitā*; however, in the case of [speech] that is not rapid, there is no *saṃhitā*. The closest proximity [of sounds] is *saṃhitā*.

If that were so, the designation *saṃhitā* would not apply in the non-rapid (*adrutā*) mode of speech. For the closest proximity (*paraḥ sannikarṣaḥ*) of phonemes occurs only in the rapid mode, not in the non-rapid mode. [Reply: The proximity is equal. The proximity of phonemes is equal in the rapid, medium, and slow modes of speech. [Question: What then is the distinction? [Answer: It is the greater duration of time for the phonemes; that is, there is a greater duration of time for the phonemes in those [modes].

For example: the proximity between an elephant and a mosquito is equal, yet there is a difference in the magnitude of their bodies. If this is so, then when the *tapara* (the letter *t*) is used in the rapid (*druta*) tempo, an addition must be made for the medium (*madhyama*) and slow (*vilambita*) tempos because of the difference in duration. When the *tapara* is used in the rapid tempo, an addition must be made for the medium and slow tempos. What is the reason? Because of the difference in duration. Those [sounds] which occur in the rapid tempo...

In the *vṛtti* style, the phonemes (*varṇa*) are increased by one-third; those which are increased by one-third in the *madhyamā* style are [further increased] in the *vilambita* style. Or it has been said: what was said? "It is established, however, that while the phonemes remain fixed, the styles (*vṛtti*) are distinguished by the speaker’s speech being slow or rapid. Alternatively, this definition shall be formulated: "The absence of interruption between sounds is *saṃhitā*."

When there is no cessation of sound, there is a pause at every syllable. When there is no cessation of sound, the designation "pause" (avasāna) would apply to every syllable. What does this "at every syllable" mean? It means "with respect to each syllable" (prati-varṇam). By the very same effort with which one syllable is uttered, when that syllable is finished, one withdraws that effort and, taking up another, employs the second syllable.

Likewise for the third [letter], and likewise for the fourth. If this is so, then the designation *saṃhitā* (continuous junction), having no scope [elsewhere], will subvert the designation *avasāna* (pause). Alternatively, regarding the designation *avasāna*, it should be understood as referring to a superior degree (*prakarṣagati*): that which is a more complete cessation (*sādhīyo virāmaḥ*). And what is more complete? That which is the cessation of both sound and meaning. Or else, it is the cessation of resonance (*hrādāvirāmaḥ*).

The definition *saṃhita* will be formulated as follows: "In the absence of a pause (*hrādāvirāma*) and in the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) of unaspirated (*aghoṣa*) consonants (*sparśa*), [the term] *asaṃhita* [applies] due to the non-proximity (*asannidhāna*).

In cases such as *kukkuṭaḥ*, *pippakā*, and *pittam*, because there is no proximity in the conjunction of unaspirated consonants following a pause, the designation *saṃhitā* does not apply. Why is it said "in conjunction" (*saṃyoge*)? For instance, in a case like *ekaḥ pacati*.

One [sound] is masked by the resonance (*hrāda*) of those preceding and following it. For example: between two red garments, a white garment is perceived as having that same quality; or an empty bronze vessel within a heap of jujube fruits is perceived as having that same quality.
The proximity is equal in both cases. Just as one phoneme is masked by the resonance, so too are many.

Alternatively, the definition of *saṃhitā* will be formulated as: "The sequence of preceding and following [sounds] without an interval of time is *saṃhitā*. If the sequence of preceding and following [sounds] without an interval of time is *saṃhitā*, then because of the absence of prior and posterior [in a single sound], the designation of *saṃhitā* would not apply to what is not joined (*asaṃhita*). For there is no sequence of preceding and following among individual phonemes (*varṇa*).

It exists. For what reason? Because speech resides in each individual phoneme (*varṇa*) and because phonemes perish as soon as they are uttered. Speech resides in each individual phoneme; it does not utter two [phonemes] simultaneously. In the word "gauḥ," for instance, while the speech resides in the sound *g*, it does not reside in the sound *au* nor in the visarga (*ḥ*). While it resides in the sound *au*, it does not reside in the sound *g* nor in the visarga. While...

[The rule does not apply] when there is a *visarjanīya*, nor when there is the letter *ga*, nor when there is the vowel *au*. This is because [phonemes] perish as soon as they are uttered. Indeed, phonemes perish as soon as they are uttered; once uttered, they are destroyed. Then another [phoneme] is employed. One phoneme is not the companion of another phoneme. If that is so, then the wise agent, whose conduct is based on reality, performs all actions by means of the word after having formed them in the intellect (*buddhi*).
Having perceived the meanings to be expressed in the intellect, one should establish their sequence. The sequence of words belongs exclusively to the domain of the intellect.
Here, a person who acts with foresight perceives: "With regard to this meaning, this word is to be employed; in this word, first this phoneme, then this, then this."

This is now considered: should *avasāna* (the pause at the end of a word) be characterized as non-existence (*abhāva*) or as cessation (*virāma*)? And what is the distinction here? If non-existence were the characteristic of *avasāna*, there would be a mention of non-existence above [in the rule]. If non-existence were the characteristic of *avasāna*, there would be the inclusion of the term "non-existence" above.

It must be stated: "that which is non-existence (abhāva) above [the word]. For otherwise, the non-existence of the word even before it might not be included there. What would be the consequence? In the case of *rasaḥ* and *rathaḥ*, the rule *kharavasānayor visarjanīyaḥ* would result in the occurrence of the *visarjanīya*.

Let it be, then, that it is *virāma* (pause). In the case of *virāma*, the mention of *virāma* is required; for it is the *virāma* of that [word] which necessitates the inclusion of the term *virāma*.

Therefore, it must be formulated. But surely, even for one for whom there is non-existence (abhāva), that non-existence must also be apprehended. It will serve my purpose: "non-existence" (abhāva) means elision (lopa); from that, [the rule] "and the pause" (avasāna) [will apply]. In that case, for me as well, the mention of "cessation" (virāma) will serve another's purpose: "cessation" (virāma) means elision (lopa) and pause (avasāna). [However,] it should be stated that "the cessation which occurs above [is what is meant]."

[The objection is: "Let there not be a pause (*virāma*) even before the word [in that case]. And what would happen? In the case of *rasaḥ* and *rathaḥ*, the rule ‘the visarga occurs in place of [a final] *khara* (voiceless consonant) and *avasāna* (pause)’ would apply, resulting in a visarga. [The response is: My "pause" is preceded by an actual commencement [of speech]. Or rather, this is not being considered as a definition of *avasāna* (pause). What then? It is the named entity (*sañjñin*). Non-existence (*abhāva*) is the name (*sañjñā*) for *avasāna*.

It might be that there is a pause (*virāma*). What is the distinction here? Regarding the absence [of a following sound] when the term "pause" (*avasāna*) applies: one must state that the absence of what follows is intended. When the term "pause" applies, it should be specified as "the absence of what follows. For it should not apply to the absence of a word even when it occurs before [another]. And what would be the consequence? [In the case of] *rasaḥ*, *rathaḥ*.

[If it were not so defined,] by the rule *khar-avasānayor visarjanīyaḥ*, the *visarjanīya* would [inappropriately] apply. Let it then be *virāma* (the pause). [But] in the case of *virāma*, there must be an explicit mention of *virāma*. For that which has a *virāma*, the mention of *virāma* must be made. But surely, for that which is non-existent (*abhāva*), the mention of non-existence must also be made? It will serve my purpose for the sake of another. [That other is] non-existence (*abhāva*).

[The rule] *lopaḥ* [is stated]; then [the rule] *avasānaṃ ca*. In that case, for me as well, the mention of *virāma* will be for the sake of another purpose: [the definition] "non-occurrence (*virāma*) is elision (*lopa*) and also the pause (*avasāna*). It must be stated that "the pause which occurs above [in the sequence]. But surely, even by one for whom there is non-existence [of the sound], the mention of non-existence must be made. For me, it will be for the sake of another purpose: [the term] "non-existence" [is used].

[The rule is: "elision" (*lopaḥ*); then, "and pause" (*avasānam ca*). In that case, for me too, the mention of *virāma* will be for the sake of another [rule]: "pause, elision, and pause. It must be stated: "the pause which occurs above [the letter]. But was it not said that [the term] is preceded by its formal commencement? No; this root *ram* does not necessarily denote only "commencement" (*pravṛtti*). What then? It denotes "non-commencement" (*apravṛtti*).

Furthermore, for example: "The vows have ceased in this family; the study of the Veda has ceased. Yet, in that case, there was no prior occurrence of Vedic study, nor are there vows [currently being performed]. Because the word arises from the non-cessation of its existence, it does not have cessation as its characteristic. Since the word arises from the non-cessation of its existence, it is not tenable that cessation is its defining characteristic.

"What is this [meaning of] 'because it arises from the non-cessation of existence' (*bhāvāvirāmabhāvitvāt*)? The non-cessation of existence is *bhāvāvirāma*; that which comes into being through the non-cessation of existence is *bhāvāvirāmabhāvī*; the state of being such is *bhāvāvirāmabhāvitvam*. Another says:
because sound arises from existence and arises from non-cessation, its characteristic of having an end is not tenable."

Or rather, "that which is followed by a pause" (*tatpara*) is the term for the end of a syllable (*avasāna*). It should be stated that a syllable followed by a pause is designated as "end. Or else, the final syllable is the end. Or again, it should be read explicitly: "the final syllable is designated as 'end'. If so, then it must be stated. No, it need not be stated, because [the rule] concerns both *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) and *avasāna* (pause).

It is established because it is well known in the world. "Samhitā" and "avasāna" are these two meanings well known in the world. For instance, someone says to another who is studying: "Recite this *śanno devī* [verse] according to the *samhitā*. He then recites it with the closest possible proximity [of sounds]. Another says:

491–496. Regarding the word *vidhi*: what is this term? It is derived from the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *vi*, with the suffix *ika* used in the sense of the object (*karmasādhana*). Thus, that which is prescribed (*vidhīyate*) is called a *vidhi*. What, then, is prescribed? A compound, the prescription of case endings (*vibhakti*), and the treatment as if it were a subsequent member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*). Furthermore, is this an *adhikāra* (heading) or a *paribhāṣā* (metarule)? And what is the distinction between an *adhikāra* and a *paribhāṣā*?

The heading (*adhikāra*) is for the purpose of non-specification regarding each individual rule (*yoga*); thus it applies to every rule. A technical definition (*paribhāṣā*), however, while situated in one place, illuminates the entire treatise like a lamp. Just as a well-kindled lamp, though situated in one spot, illuminates the entire house—what, then, is the distinction between these two in terms of effort?

When there is a governing heading (*adhikāra*), [the rule] must be vocalized; however, when a general metarule (*paribhāṣā*) is present, everything must be taken into account. Thus, another duality arises: is *sāmarthya* (semantic competency) to be understood as *ekārthībhāva* (unification of meaning), or as *vyapekṣā* (mutual expectancy)? In that regard, if *sāmarthya* is understood as *ekārthībhāva* and there is a governing heading, then the single *samāsa* (compound) is subsumed, as is the prescription of case-endings (*vibhakti*).

And the treatment as if it were a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) is not included [in the definition of *samartha*]. However, when *sāmarthya* (semantic connection) and *adhikāra* (governing context) exist in the sense of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), the prescription of case endings (*vibhaktividhāna*) and the treatment as if it were a subordinate member are included; yet the compound (*samāsa*) alone remains unaccounted for. Furthermore, in other instances, the terms *samartha* and *yukta* must indeed be explicitly mentioned. Where else? In the rules concerning *is* and *us* in the sense of *sāmarthya*, and in the rule "not when joined with *ca*, *vā*, *ha*, *āha*, or *eva*" (*na cavāhāhaivayukte*).

Thus, when there is mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), as well as semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) and the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), whatever trace of "words" exists in grammar is entirely subsumed; however, the compound (*samāsa*) alone remains unaccounted for. In that case, by taking semantic integration (*ekārthībhāva*) as both the semantic capacity and the technical rule, the sūtra becomes more concise. Even so, in some instances...

In some cases, that which ought not to be stated is stated, and that which ought to be stated is not stated. First, that which ought not to be stated is stated in the rule: "after a word capable [of forming a compound], or after the first [member]. And that which ought to be stated is not stated in the rule: "the suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word capable [of expressing the agent] when it denotes the object. But is it not understood there that the capacity exists, as in the examples *kumbhakāraḥ* ("pot-maker") and *nagarakāraḥ* ("city-builder")? True, it is understood.
But when the condition has arisen, that very [suffix] is to be produced from that which is capable. (P.
2.1.1) Now, for what purpose is the mention of *samartha* ("capable")? It will be stated that a word ending in the second case is compounded with words such as *śrita*.

"Dependent on hardship" (*kaṣṭaśritaḥ*) means "dependent on hell" (*narakaśritaḥ*). What is the purpose of including the term *samartha* ("having the same referent")? Consider: "Devadatta, look at the hardship! [Here, *kaṣṭam* is not a compound. And: "Viṣṇumitra has resorted to the teacher's family" (*gurukulam*). [The rule] "With a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*), [a compound is formed] with that which has its meaning produced by the third case" (*tṛtīyā tatkṛtārthena guṇavacanena*) applies here: "broken by a wedge" (*śaṅkulākhaṇḍaḥ*), "cut by a knife" (*kirikāṇaḥ*).
What is the purpose of including the term *samartha*? Consider: "Stay there with a wedge! [Here, *śaṅkulayā* is not a compound. "The broken one runs."

[The suffix *tasi*] is used with *musalena*. [The suffix *caturthī* (the fourth case ending) is used] with words meaning "for that purpose," "wealth," "beneficial," "pleasurable," and "protected": *go-hitam* ("beneficial for cows"), *aśva-hitam* ("beneficial for horses"). Why is the requirement of semantic connection (*samartha*) mentioned? [Consider: *sukham gobhyaḥ* ("happiness for the cows") and *hitam devadattāya* ("beneficial for Devadatta"). [The suffix *pañcamī* (the fifth case ending) is used] with *bhaya* ("fear"): *vṛka-bhayam* ("fear of a wolf"), *dasyu-bhayam* ("fear of a bandit"), *cora-bhayam* ("fear of a thief"). Why is the requirement of semantic connection mentioned? [Consider: *gaccha tvam mā vṛkebhyaḥ* ("Go, do not [fear] from wolves") and *bhayam devadattasya* ("Devadatta's fear").
The genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is compounded with a word ending in a *sub*-suffix:

*rājapuruṣaḥ* (the king’s man), *brāhmaṇakambalaḥ* (the Brahmin’s blanket). For what purpose is the mention of "semantic competency" (*samartha*)? [To exclude cases such as: *bhāryā rājñaḥ* (the king’s wife) and *puruṣaḥ devadattasya* (Devadatta’s man). [Also, the locative case ending is compounded] with words meaning "skilled" (*śauṇḍa*), etc.: [e.g., *akṣaśauṇḍaḥ* (skilled at dice)].

"Addicted to dice," "addicted to women. For what purpose is the mention of *samartha* (semantic compatibility) made? [To exclude cases such as: "Devadatta is skillful at dice," or "The drunkard drinks in the tavern. Now, even when the mention of *samartha* is made, why does it not apply here in the case of *mahat kaṣṭam* ("great hardship")?

Regarding the term *śrita*: the form *mahākaṣṭaśrita* does not occur [in that specific sense]. It occurs when the sentence is as follows: "great suffering" is *mahākaṣṭam*; "one who has resorted to great suffering" is *mahākaṣṭaśritaḥ*. But when the sentence is as follows: [it does not occur].

When it is said that "he has resorted to great hardship," then [the suffix] should not occur; yet at that time, it does occur. Why does it not occur then? For what reason does it not occur for whom? Is it for two [words], or rather for many? Why does it not occur for many?
The rule *sup supā* ("noun with noun") is understood [to apply here]. But surely, sir, grammatical rules operate upon forms (*ākṛti*). For example, [the rule] "from a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*).
While this is the case, the production [of a suffix] occurs from one nominal stem after another. This is true;

however, the *ākṛti* (form/essence) is completed in each individual instance. To whatever extent this is completed, to that extent there must be production from the nominal stem. And this is completed in each individual instance, not in the aggregate. Thus.

In this case as well, a compound must occur only for as many words as the rule *sup supā* ("a nominal ending with a nominal ending") covers; however, this rule applies to pairs of words, not to many. Why, then, does it not apply to two [words] taken individually? Because of a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*). How is there a lack of semantic connection? Because that which is dependent (*sāpekṣa*) is semantically disconnected. If that which is dependent is semantically disconnected—

It is said: "The king’s man is handsome," "the king’s man is beautiful. In these cases, the formation of a compound (*vṛtti*) does not occur. This is not a fault. Here, the principal member (*pradhāna*) is dependent (*sāpekṣa*). And a compound is indeed permitted for a principal member even when it is dependent. But where then the non-principal member (*apradhāna*) is dependent, there your rule for compound formation does not apply.

In cases such as *devadattasya gurukulam* ("Devadatta’s teacher’s family"), *devadattasya guruputraḥ* ("Devadatta’s teacher’s son"), and *devadattasya dāsabhāryā* ("Devadatta’s servant’s wife"), this fault does not apply. Here, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is dependent upon the whole aggregate; it refers to the entire "teacher’s family. However, where the genitive is not dependent upon an aggregate—there [the fault remains].
The application [of the rule] does not obtain:
"Rice of śālī-grains," "A measure of groats from the market," "From where do you come? From Pāṭaliputra," and also here:
"Devadatta’s teacher’s family."
In the cases of "the teacher’s son of Devadatta" (*devadattasya guruputraḥ*) and "the wife of the servant of Devadatta" (*devadattasya dāsabhāryā*),
if this genitive case were one depending on the whole compound, it would not necessarily follow that [the son or wife] belongs to Devadatta’s teacher.

Regarding the phrase "tasya yaḥ putraḥ" (the son of him): what then? The meaning would be understood as "the son of someone else, [namely] Devadatta’s teacher, [is] Devadatta’s something. However, since the meaning understood is necessarily "the son of him who is Devadatta’s teacher," we consider that the genitive case here does not depend upon a collective whole. Indeed, in other cases...

Even when the requirement of semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) is observed, an operation may still take place even for that which is dependent (*sāpekṣa*). Where else? In the rule *isusoḥ sāmarthye* (Pāṇini 5.4.150). For example:
*brāhmaṇasya sarpiḥ karoti* ("He prepares ghee for the Brahmin"). Therefore, it cannot be said that "that which is dependent is semantically incompetent. [Objection:

Why then does no compound formation (*vṛtti*) occur in the case of *mahat kaṣṭam śritaḥ* ("he has resorted to great hardship")? [Answer: Because [the rule] applies only to those [words] accompanied by qualifiers (*saviśeṣaṇānām*).

It must be stated that either a compound (*vṛtti*) does not occur with a qualifier, or a qualifier is not employed after a compound has been formed. If it is asserted that "a compound does not occur with a qualifier, or a qualifier is not employed after a compound has been formed," then in cases such as *devadattasya gurukulam* ("Devadatta’s teacher’s family"),

*devadattasya guruputraḥ* ("Devadatta’s teacher’s son"), and *devadattasya dāsabhāryā* ("Devadatta’s servant’s wife"), the formation of a compound would not be possible for *agurukula-*, *aputra-*, and so forth.

Thus it should be stated. In that case, it must be stated: "The formation of a compound occurs for those [words] accompanied by qualifiers, but a qualifier is not employed for that which has already been compounded," as in the cases of *aguru*, *kulaputra*, and so forth. It need not be stated. Why, then, does the compound formation not occur?

Because it would fail to convey the intended meaning (*agamakatvāt*). In this instance, there ought to be both a sentence and a compound expressing the same meaning; yet, such is the meaning here [in the case of *agurukulaputra*].

The meaning "he has resorted to great hardship" is understood through a full sentence (*vākya*), but it is never understood through a compound (*samāsa*) as "mahatkaṣṭaśritaḥ. For this reason, we say [the compound is not used] because it would not convey the meaning (*agamakatvāt*). We do not say that it would be an incorrect word (*apaśabda*); for wherever there is a means of conveying the meaning, there the formation of a compound occurs. For example:

In the cases of "Devadatta’s teacher’s house," "Devadatta’s teacher’s son," and "Devadatta’s servant’s wife," if the lack of semantic connection (*agamakatva*) were the reason [for the absence of the genitive], then the inclusion of the term "samartha" (semantically connected) would be purposeless.

In this case as well, the meaning conveyed by the sentence "the wife of the king" (*rājño bhāryā*) or "the man of Devadatta" (*devadattasya puruṣaḥ*) is never conveyed by the compound *bhāryārājapuruṣo devadattasya*. Therefore, the purpose [of the rule] is not served by the inclusion of the term "samartha" (capable/connected). This...

In that case, there is a purpose. There is the *nañ*-compound known as the "incompetent compound" (*asamarthasamāsa*), which serves as an indicator [of a specific meaning]. Its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) must not apply [universally]—as in the cases of "one doing nothing" (*akiñcit kurvāṇam*), "not taking beans" (*amāṣam haramāṇam*), or "cast from a depth" (*agādhād utsṛṣṭam*). This too is not a valid purpose. For one must necessarily state the grammatical correctness of at least some *nañ*-compounds that serve as indicators, such as "those who do not see the sun" (*asūryampaśyāni*).

Examples include *mukhāni*, *apunar-geyāḥ ślokāḥ*, *aśrāddha-bhojī*, and *alavaṇa-bhojī* Brāhmaṇa. [The rule] *suṭ anapuṃsakasya* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) for this very *nañ*-compound which is an *asamartha-samāsa* (an unconnected compound) that conveys meaning: it ensures that grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) belongs only to this specific type of *nañ*-compound that conveys meaning, and not to any other. Therefore, there is no purpose in including the mention of *samartha* (connected).
(P_2,1.1.3) Now, even if the term *samartha* ("capable") is included [in the sūtra], it is stated: "What indeed is meant by 'capable'?

The statement regarding capability is the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) of words that have separate meanings. It is the unification of meaning of words that possess distinct individual senses.

It is said [of a word] that it is "capable" (*samartha*). In a sentence, such as *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), the meanings are distinct; but in a compound, such as *rājapuruṣaḥ*, they constitute a single meaning. Why is it said that the meanings are distinct, when—upon being told, "Let the king’s man be brought"—it is that very same person who is meant by "the king’s man"? Nor do we say that there is the bringing of someone else. Who [is it]?

In that case, the distinction is produced by the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). [The distinctions are: the elision of the nominal suffix (*sup*), intervention, connection with either [member] as desired, and accent. In a sentence, there is no elision of the nominal suffix, as in *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"). In a compound, however, it does not occur, as in *rājapuruṣaḥ*. Furthermore, in a sentence there is intervention, as in *rājñaḥ ṛddhasya puruṣaḥ* ("the man of the wealthy king").

In a compound, [the desired relationship] does not occur. For example, in the case of *rājapuruṣaḥ*, in a sentence there is a connection with either [term] as one wishes: *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king’s man) or *puruṣo rājñaḥ* (the man of the king). But in a compound, it does not occur; it is simply *rājapuruṣaḥ*. In a sentence, there are two accents: *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*. But in a compound, however, there is only one: *rājapuruṣaḥ*.

Thus, these distinctions are not produced by the state of having a single meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). What then? These are based on explicit scriptural injunctions (*vācanika*). For the Blessed One has said:

"In a compound, the *sup*-suffixes [of the members] are placed first before the verbal root and the nominal stem (*prātipadika*); the final syllable of the compound is acute-accented. If so, then these are indeed the distinctions produced by the state of having a single meaning: the specific number (*saṅkhyāviśeṣa*), the denotation of the individual (*vyaktābhidhāna*), and the qualification of the subordinate member (*upasarjana-viśeṣaṇa*).

"Is it not the case that conjunction (*caya*) is a specific number (*saṅkhyāviśeṣa*) occurring in a sentence, as in *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*, *rājñoḥ puruṣaḥ*, and *rājñām puruṣaḥ*? It does not occur in a compound, as in *rājapuruṣaḥ*. There is a reason why this is so.
What is the reason? Because that word which expresses the specific [number] is absent. Come now, please pronounce that [word]."

That distinction will be understood. But surely it should not be so; for meaning should not be determined by the word, but rather the word should be determined by the meaning. Let this be viewed in this way:
the very nature of the meaning is such that no distinction is perceived here. And this must necessarily be so.

This should be understood as follows: for one who thinks that because a word expressive of a particular [quality] is not present here, the particular is not understood, [it would follow that] its particular would be understood in this case—
such as *apsucaraḥ*, *goṣucaraḥ*, and *varṣāsujaḥ*— where there is an explicit denotation of the individual in the sentence, as in "of the Brāhmaṇa."

"In *kambalaḥ tiṣṭhati* (the blanket stands), it is indistinct; but in the compound *brāhmaṇakambalaḥ tiṣṭhati*, there arises a doubt as to whether it is a vocative or a genitive compound. This too is not a distinction. For there is something indistinct in a sentence that becomes distinct in a compound. First, it is indistinct in the sentence: *ardham paśoḥ devadattasya* (half of Devadatta’s animal)."

Thus, a doubt arises: does it refer to half of the quality belonging to Devadatta, or to that which has become the named object—the animal—of which there is a half? And this becomes clear in a compound: *ardhapuruṣo devadattasya* ("half of Devadatta's person"). In a sentence, however, it functions as a qualifier of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*), as in *ṛddhasya rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the man of the wealthy king"); but in a compound, it does not.

[The example] "rājapuruṣaḥ" (the king's man) occurs. This too is not a fault; even in a compound, there is qualification of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*). For example: "devadattasya gurukulam" (Devadatta’s teacher’s family), "devadattasya guruputraḥ" (Devadatta’s teacher’s son), and "devadattasya dāsabhāryā" (Devadatta’s servant’s wife). In a sentence, there is a connection with a possessor (*sva*); namely, connection with a possessor and connection with an owner (*svāmin*). Connection with a possessor is, for example, "rājño gauḥ" (the king’s cow).

And [the rule] does not apply to "horse" (*aśva*) and "man" (*puruṣa*) when they are in a compound, as in *rājño gavāśvapuruṣāḥ* ("the king's cows, horses, and men"). Nor does it apply to the connection with a possessor (*svāmiyoga*), as in *devadattasya ca yajñadattasya ca viṣṇumitrasya ca gauḥ* ("the cow belonging to Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra"); it does not apply in the compound *devadattayajñadattaviṣṇumitrāṇāṃ gauḥ*. Now, regarding this specific state produced by the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāvakṛte viśeṣe*), what [is the case]?

Is the denotation of meaning by words innate (*svābhāvika*) or is it based on explicit instruction (*vācanika*)? He says: it is innate. Why is this so? Because meanings are not explicitly taught. For meanings are certainly not taught [in the grammatical rules]. But how could one who is not teaching meanings say, "meanings are not taught"? This is because you yourself have stated: "The *dvandva* compound occurs when there are multiple [words] whose referent is another word-meaning (*anyapadārtha*), or in the sense of 'and' (*cārthe*), or in the sense of 'progeny' (*apatye*)."

Regarding the phrase "when red has come about": these are not instructions on the meanings [of the words]. Rather, the grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) of these words, which are by their very nature fixed upon these meanings, is performed for the sake of providing a formal sign (*nimitta*). For example: "The path to the well is to the right of the hand," or "Look at the moon in the cloud. By their very nature, [these indicate] the path situated there [at the well] and the moon.
And thus, an explanation is provided by way of indicative signs (*nimitta*). Likewise here as well: that which has the sense of "and" (*ca*) is a *dvandva* compound;

that which has another word as its referent (*anyapadārtha*) is a *bahuvrīhi*. But what is the reason they are not explicitly taught? It is for the sake of brevity (*laghu*). Indeed, meanings are not explicitly taught for the sake of brevity; for one who must necessarily teach these meanings must do so by means of some word or other.

An explanation must be provided. By whom, then, was that [explanation] made, such that it could now be made? If it were made by someone, then by whom was that [person's explanation] made? Thus, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, an explanation of that [grammar] is simply impossible. For who indeed is capable of prescribing the meanings of verbal roots (*dhātu*), nominal stems (*prātipadika*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), and particles (*nipāta*)? And yet...

This must be understood: when the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is specified, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) remains unspecified. For indeed, when a quality (*guṇa*) is denoted, there is a comprehension of the possessor of that quality (*guṇin*). For example, [one understands] "white" or "black.
This is an unequal comparison. These would be general terms (*sāmānyaśabda*); and general terms do not [function] without...

They abide in specific particulars, whether as a distinction or as a context. However, since the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) necessarily refers by its very nature to one particular instance when it is uttered, we consider that these are not general terms (*sāmānya-śabda*). If they are not general terms, then the base (*prakṛti*) functions in the sense of the base itself, and the suffix (*pratyaya*) [functions accordingly].
It functions for the sake of providing a conventional meaning. Indeed, there is even non-application of the instruction of meaning;

for there are many words whose meanings are not understood, such as *jarbharī* and *turpharītū*. Furthermore, even without the employment of words, many meanings are understood through the contraction of eyes and the movements of hands. Moreover, it is not the case that [a word is used] for a meaning already fully known.
And the mention of the word *vā* (or) is useless because [the alternative] is established by its own nature (*svabhāva*). The mention of *vā* is useless. For what reason?

Because it is established by its own nature. Here there are two positions: the position of derivation (*vṛtti*) and the position of non-derivation (*avṛtti*). And by its very nature, this results in both a sentence (*vākya*) and a compound (*samāsa*). In that case, since a compound is permanently established by its own nature within the domain of derivation, [the use of *vā* is redundant].

What else could possibly be connected by the use of the word *vā* other than a name (*saṃjñā*)? Furthermore, the existence or non-existence of a name is not what is intended here. Therefore, there is no purpose in using the word *vā*.
517–525. Now, as for those who maintain that [the word] has a function (*vṛtti*), what do they say? They say that the function is the expression of another’s meaning (*parārthābhidhāna*).

Now, for those who speak thus, is the function one that abandons its own meaning (*jahatsvārthā*) or one that does not abandon its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*)? And what follows from this? If the function were one that abandons its own meaning, then when it is said, "Bring the king's man," there would be the bringing of a mere man.

When it is said, "Bring the descendant of Upagu," [the suffix] applies to the offspring alone. Now, if the operation (*vṛtti*) were one that does not abandon its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*), then since both meanings would be present, the dual number would apply according to the rule "the dual is used for two things whose own meanings are present. Which operation, then, is logical?

The one that abandons its own meaning (*jahatsvārthā*). But is it indeed appropriate that there should be such a thing as an operation called "abandoning its own meaning"? Certainly, it is appropriate.
For it is observed thus in the world: a man engaged in the work of another abandons his own work;

just as a carpenter, while engaged in the king’s work, abandons his own. In the same way, it is logical that the king, while engaged in the purpose of a man, should abandon his own purpose, and Upagu, while engaged in the purpose of others, should abandon his own purpose.

But has it not been said that when "Bring the king's man" is uttered, the bringing of any man whatsoever would follow; and when "Bring the son of Upagu" is uttered, the bringing of any offspring whatsoever would follow? This is not a fault. Although this [word] abandons its own primary meaning, it does not abandon it entirely. It abandons only that primary meaning which is incompatible with the purpose of another. For example, a carpenter engaged in the service of the king [abandons his own work].

One does not abandon one's own act of carving, nor indeed [one's] hiccuping, laughing, or scratching. Furthermore, this thing called a "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*) is not something that contradicts the purpose of another; therefore, it will not be abandoned. Alternatively, it will be a qualifier by way of concomitance (*anvaya*). For example, in the case of "a jar of ghee" (*ghṛtaghaṭaḥ*) or "a jar of oil" (*tailaghaṭaḥ*), once the ghee or oil has been poured out, it remains a qualifier by virtue of its prior concomitance.

"This is a jar of ghee; this is a jar of oil. This is an unequal comparison. For in that case, there exists both the substance and its full extent. Come now, my friend, heat the jar of ghee over a fire and wash it with a bunch of grass;
that distinction will not remain. But as for [the cases of] "a jasmine-bag" or "a campaka-bag," when the flowers have been removed...
Furthermore, even in the case of flowers (*sumanas*), a qualification occurs through association, as in "this is a cluster of *mallikā* flowers" or "this is a cluster of *campaka* flowers.

Alternatively, this rule regarding semantic competency (*samartha*) is applied within a compound (*vṛtti*). Semantic competency consists of either distinction (*bheda*) or conjunction (*saṃsarga*). Another says: "Semantic competency is either distinction or conjunction. But what, then, is distinction or conjunction? Here, in the word "of the king" (*rājñaḥ*)...

When it is said "all one's own," the person is implicated; when it is said "the person," everyone who is an owner is implicated. Now, however, when "the king's man" is said, the king excludes the man from other owners, and the man also excludes the king from his other subjects. Thus, when both sides have been delimited, if [the word] should abandon [its meaning], let it abandon it at will; it certainly does not.
There will be the bringing of a mere person. Or rather, let there be a function (*vṛtti*) that does not abandon its own primary meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*).

It is indeed appropriate that there should be such a function as "not abandoning its own meaning. Certainly it is appropriate; for it is observed thus in the world: this beggar, having obtained a second alms-offering, does not abandon the first, but proceeds to accumulate them.

But has it not been stated that since both [words] possess their own meanings, the dual number applies because "the dual occurs for two"? For which [word], then, does the dual apply? For the nominative. But the king is not capable of being construed with the nominative. Then for the genitive? But the man is not capable of being construed with the genitive. In that case, it would follow that the dual applies to the nominative alone.

But has it not been stated that "the king" (*rājā*) is not the meaning of the first case? That meaning has been brought forward; it has become included within the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). In that case, since the first case applies to the meaning of the nominal stem, only the dual number of the first case would result. Because the aggregate possesses a single meaning, the suffix does not arise based on the number of its individual parts. This is because the aggregate [is what is intended].

The meaning is oneness (*ekatva*). Therefore, the case-ending (*sub*) will not be produced based on the number of the individual components. "Oneness" refers to mutual expectancy (*parasparavyapekṣā*); some maintain that oneness consists in mutual expectancy. But what is this mutual expectancy between two words? We do not say it is between two words; rather, it is between two meanings. Here, when "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) is said, the king...
The king considers the man, thinking, "This one belongs to me," and the man also considers the king, thinking, "I belong to him.

The genitive case-ending expresses the relationship between these two. Likewise, in the expression "he has resorted to hardship" (*kaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ*), the accusative case-ending expresses the relationship between the action and its factor (*kāraka*).

whether *sāmarthya* (semantic competency) consists in the state of having a single meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) or in mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), is this [distinction] already understood from this very sūtra,
or must a further sūtra be composed for one of these two positions? It is understood.

He asks: How so? This is a compound with the word *artha*. And *sam* is a prefix (*upasarga*). Furthermore, prefixes are of such a nature that where some word expressive of an action is employed, they express a particularization of that action. But here no word expressive of an action is employed, by which *sam* might possess semantic force (*sāmarthya*).

In this regard, it must be understood from usage that there is certainly some word suitable for usage which is not being employed here, such that [the meaning] is "equal in capacity. For example: upon seeing smoke, it is understood that "fire is here," and upon seeing a *triviṣṭabdhaka* (a specific posture), it is understood that "this is a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*). But what is that word suitable for usage? It is said: the word whose meaning is connected [to the context].

"Capable" (*samartha*) means having a combined meaning (*saṃsṛṣṭārtha*), capable means having a mutually perceived meaning (*samprekṣitārtha*), and capable means having a connected meaning (*sambaddhārtha*). When "capability" (*sāmarthya*) refers to the state of having a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), then the analysis (*vigraha*) will be performed as follows: "capable" means having a combined meaning or having a unified meaning. For example, it is said that "the ghee is mixed" or "the oil is mixed."

It is understood that [the meanings] have become one. When *sāmarthya* (semantic competency) consists in mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), then the analysis (*vigraha*) will be made thus: "that which has its meaning fully considered is competent," or "that which has its meaning connected is competent. But what here is the meaning of the root *bandh*? It is said to be "connected" (*sambaddha*).
That which is interlaced with a rope or iron at a stake is called "bound"; however, the root *bandh* does not necessarily denote mere physical interlacing.

It functions in this way. What then? It also functions in the sense of "not abandoning. For example, two young bulls are said to be "connected" when they do not abandon one another. Alternatively, the verb *badhnāti* (to bind) occurs in such contexts as well. For example: "We have a connection with the Gargas"; "We have a connection with the Vatsas. This refers to a conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

This is the meaning. Now, regarding this [notion of] semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) consisting in mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), that specific distinction produced by "becoming a single unified meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) must be stated. In that regard, there is a prohibition of the accentual depression (*nighāta*) and the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when derived from different grammatical roles (*nānākāraka*). In this context, while semantic capacity consists in mutual expectancy, the accentual depression and the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* would otherwise apply to those [words] derived from different grammatical roles; therefore, their prohibition is established.

It must be stated [as a rule]: "The *nighāta* (elision of accent) occurs. This is a staff. "Take it with this. Since there is a mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) between the word *daṇḍa* and the verb *harati*, the *nighāta* would consequently apply. Regarding the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*: "Cook the rice; it will be yours. "Cook the rice; it will be mine. Since there is a mutual expectancy between the word *odana* and the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the substitutes *vām*, *naus*, etc., would consequently apply.

[They] attain [the status of instrument]. A prohibition regarding them must be stated. Why is it said "not from a different factor" (*nānākārakāt*) when it is carried away by being attached to that very [factor]? Nor do we say that it is carried away by being attached to something else. What then? We take the word as our authority (*śabdapramāṇaka*).
Whatever the word says is our authority. And here, the word expresses existence (*sattā*): "this is a staff."

It is understood that "it exists. That stick, having been the agent (*kartṛ*), becomes the instrument (*karaṇa*) when it is connected with another word. For example: someone asks another, "Where is Devadatta? He replies to him, "He is in the tree. "In which one? "The one that stands there. That tree is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

Having become [a subordinate element], it becomes the agent when connected with another word. A prohibition of compounding must be stated for the case of accumulation (*pracaya*). [For example: "The king's cow, horse, and man" (*rājño gauś cāśvaś ca puruṣaś ca*) would result in *rājagavāśvapuruṣāḥ*. Alternatively, the compounding will take place between those words that are more closely related (*samarthatarāṇām*). But which are they?
[The compounds] consisting of two members are more capable. Why is this so? Because for these, a more rapid application (vṛtti) is obtained.
It is just as when it is said, "This boy is more capable for study"; it is understood that he has studied the texts more rapidly. Another says:

Or rather, there will be a compound of those words that are more semantically capable (*samarthatarāṇām*). But which ones are more semantically capable? Those that are intended to form a *dvandva* (copulative) compound. Why is this so? Because these [words] possess the same case endings (*samānavibhaktīni*), whereas the word "king" (*rājā*) has a different case ending. There is a distinction between one's own brother and the son of a paternal uncle. Or rather, it is established by the semantic power of the aggregate (*samudāyasāmarthyāt*); it is established by the semantic power of the aggregate.
Or rather, this is established: the capacity of a king resides in the aggregate, not in a single part. Another says:

or because of the capacity of the aggregate, there is a compound of words that are more capable. Why is this so? Precisely because of the capacity of the aggregate. On this view, the word "or" (*vā*) is not justified.

This is established. How so? It is not the case that here, when the king is related to both the horse and the man, there is a compound with the cow. What then? When the cow is related to the king, there is a compound with the horse and the man. In this context, the cow is the primary element (*pradhāna*), and it is indeed possible for the primary element [to be compounded].
A compound is formed even for that which is dependent [on another word].

(Pāṇini 2.1.1) A sentence consists of a verb accompanied by indeclinables, kārakas, and qualifiers. That is, a sentence is a verb together with indeclinables, together with kārakas, and together with the qualifiers of the kārakas.

It should be stated that [a word] is designated as a sentence (*vākya*) when it is accompanied by an indeclinable (*avyaya*), by a kāraka, or by a qualifier of a kāraka, and also when it is accompanied by a qualifier of the action (*kriyā*). Examples: "He recites loudly" (*uccaiḥ paṭhati*); "He recites softly" (*nīcaiḥ paṭhati*); "He cooks rice" (*odanam pacati*); "He cooks rice that is soft and clear" (*odanam mṛdu viśadam pacati*). And it should be stated that it includes qualifiers of the action: "He cooks well" (*suṣṭhu pacati*); "He cooks poorly" (*duṣṭhu pacati*). Another says:
A verb (ākhyāta) is [considered] together with its qualifiers (saviśeṣaṇa). For all these are indeed qualifiers of the action. "That which has a single finite verb" (ekatiṅ):

it should be stated that what possesses a single finite verb receives the designation of a "sentence" (vākya). "Speak! Speak! [In this case, the rules for] the elision (nighāta), and the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, apply within a single sentence.
Having begun with the rule "within a single sentence," the elision, and the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, must be stated. What is the purpose?

"Lest there be elision (*nighāta*) and other such operations in the case of separate sentences. This is the rule: *daṇḍo 'yam*, *hara anena*, *odanaṃ paca*, *tava bhaviṣyati*, *odanaṃ paca*, *mama bhaviṣyati*. There is a prohibition when joined with particles beginning with *ca* (*cādi*). It must be stated that there is a prohibition when joined with particles beginning with *ca*: *grāmas tava ca svam mama ca svam*. For what purpose is this stated?

The prohibition regarding the use of particles such as *ca* is stated according to the original formulation. This [new rule] establishes that "this" (*idam*) is something unprecedented: the designation of a sentence (*vākya-sañjñā*) and the governing rule concerning a single sentence (*samāna-vākya-adhikāra*). One should understand this objection thus: "All of this is rendered optional. Therefore, the Teacher, acting as a friend, explains it in accordance with the original formulation: when in conjunction with particles such as *ca*, the rule remains as it was originally stated.

It is thus: for, in the case of the *samartha-nighāta* (the suppression of accentuation when a word is semantically connected), an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for compounds with words in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), and for those joined with words that are themselves joined (*yuktayukta*), because they lack semantic connection (*asamarthatva*).

Indeed, in the case of the *samartha-nighāta*, an addition would have to be made for compounds with words in apposition and for those joined with words that are themselves joined. Examples: 1. Apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*):

*paṭave te dāsyāmi* ("I will give to you for the sake of a cloth"), *mṛdave te dāsyāmi* ("I will give to you for the sake of softness"). 2. Joined with what is itself joined (*yuktayukta*): *nadyāḥ tiṣṭhati* ("He stands by the river").

The branch hangs on the tree’s bank. I give you rice-porridge of *śāli* grains; he gives me rice-porridge of *śāli* grains. What, then, is the reason it is not established? Because of incapacity. There would be the consequence of a double genitive in the case of "the milk of a royal cow" (*rājagavīkṣīre*), because of the occurrence of two genitives. There would be the consequence of a double genitive in the case of "the milk of a royal cow. For what reason? Because of the occurrence of two genitives.

For there are two genitive relations here, as in "the milk of the cow belonging to the king. Why is it said that there is the contingency of a double compound (*dvisamāsa*), given that the rule *sup* [ending] with *sup* [ending] is still in force? The expression "the contingency of a double compound" is not to be understood as "the contingency of a compound of two words ending in *sup*-suffixes. How then? It refers to a compound of two types.
There would be the contingency of compounding; there would be the contingency of a double compound. Thus, *rājagokṣīram* would also result, yet it ought not to be so.

And it ought to occur when this is the analytical sentence: "the cow's milk is *gokṣīram*; the king's *gokṣīram* is *rājagokṣīram*. But when the analytical sentence is "the king's cow's milk" (*rājño goḥ kṣīram*), then...

In that case, it would follow that [the compound] should not exist. Why does it not exist then? But it is established by virtue of the capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the milk belonging to a cow distinguished by a king. This is established. How so? A compound occurs with the milk of a cow distinguished by a king, not with a cow alone. Is this something that needs to be stated? No, indeed. How is it understood even when it is not explicitly stated?

Just as one exerts effort toward this cow and does not find satisfaction with the milk alone, so too one exerts effort toward the king [thinking], "the milk of that cow which belongs to the king. Alternatively, in this case, there is no possibility of a compound between the milk and the cow that depends upon the king. What is the reason? Because of a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*). How is there a lack of semantic capacity?

"That which is dependent becomes incapable [of forming a compound]. How then does a cow that is dependent on its milk form a compound with "king" (*rājan*)? In this case, the cow is the primary element (*pradhāna*). And a compound is indeed possible for a primary element, even when it is dependent.

537–540. Now, for what purpose is the governing rule of "samartha" (semantic competency) established in the context of rules concerning words (*padavidhi*)? The statement regarding "samartha" in rules concerning words is made because, in grammatical rules based on individual phonemes (*varṇāśraya*), there is a tendency to understand [the operation] as occurring merely upon immediate sequence (*ānantarya*). Therefore, the governing rule of "samartha" is established in rules concerning words so that the operation might be understood as applying only when there is semantic competency. For example: *tiṣṭhatu dadhi, aśāna tvam śākena* ("Let the curd stand; you eat with the vegetable"). [In this case, although the words are in immediate sequence, they lack semantic competency.]

"Let the maiden stand; Devadatta, take the umbrella. Because this governing rule of semantic competency (*samarthādhikāra*) stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the element to be prescribed (*vidheya*), its explicit mention would be redundant. This governing rule of semantic competency is coreferential with that which is to be prescribed. And what is it that is to be prescribed? It is the compound (*samāsa*). To the extent that one might say "semantic competency belongs to the compound," it follows that "semantic competency governs the rules for word formation (*padavidhi*). And yet...

In this state, such as in the case of *rājapuruṣaḥ*, nothing at all can be introduced or excluded by virtue of the governing rule of semantic competency (*samarthādhikāra*). Because the governing rule of semantic competency requires grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the element to be prescribed, its mention [in this context] would be purposeless.
However, this is established by the statement "of semantically competent words" (*samarthānām*). How so? By the statement "of semantically competent words" (*samarthānām padānām*).

It should be stated that this is the prescribed rule (*vidhi*). Even so, it would not apply to two or one [entities]. Alternatively, it is because of the mention by means of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one). Or rather, this is a mention by means of *ekaśeṣa*: "of the capable," "of the two capable," "of the many capable," and "of the many capable. Even so, it would apply only to six or more. For it is among six or more that the *ekaśeṣa* is fully established.
This fault does not arise. Since the completion of a sentence is observed to occur for each individual word, it will likewise occur for two or one.

Even so, the rule would not apply to words with different case-endings, because [the rule] states: "from a capable word, [to another] capable word. In that case, by means of the word *vidhi* ("prescription"), the compound consists of two capable words ending in all case-endings.
A rule for that which is capable is a *samarthavidhi*;
a rule for two things that are capable is a *samarthavidhi*;
a rule [arising] from that which is capable is a *samarthavidhi*.
An operation prescribed for that which is capable [of performing it] is an "operation for the capable" (*samarthavidhi*). An operation prescribed for a word is a "word-operation" (*padavidhi*);
an operation prescribed for two words is a "word-operation";
an operation prescribed for many words is a "word-operation."

A rule concerning a word (*pada*) is a *padavidhi*; a rule [applying] within a word is a *padavidhi*. A rule concerning semantic connection (*samartha*) is a *samarthavidhi*; a rule concerning semantic connection is a *samarthavidhi*; a rule concerning semantic connection is a *samarthavidhi*;

a rule concerning semantic connection is a *samarthavidhi*; a rule concerning semantic connection is a *samarthavidhi*; a rule concerning semantic connection is a *samarthavidhi*. A rule concerning a word is a *padavidhi*; a rule concerning a word is a *padavidhi*; a rule concerning a word is a *padavidhi*; a rule concerning a word is a *padavidhi*.

And there is the rule concerning words (*padavidhi*), and there is the rule concerning words. A rule concerning words that applies when there is semantic connection (*samarthavidhi*) is "a rule concerning words with semantic connection" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*).

540–546. An addition must be made for words in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), because [the rule] does not apply due to a lack of semantic capacity (*asamarthatva*). An addition must be made for words in apposition: *vīraḥ puruṣaḥ* (a brave man) becomes *vīrapuruṣaḥ*. But what is the reason it is not established? Because of a lack of semantic capacity. Why is there a lack of semantic capacity? If it is argued that the referent of a word is a substance (*dravya*), then if the referent of a word is not a substance, [the rule does not apply].

In that case, there is capacity (*sāmarthya*). For when a quality (*guṇa*) is the referent of a word, then there is capacity. For heroism (*vīratva*) as a quality is one thing, while manhood (*puruṣatva*) is another; yet because there is no difference [between the two in this context], there is capacity by virtue of that much. For Devadatta is distinct from cows and horses, yet he does not possess capacity merely by virtue of that. Or who indeed...?

The distinction is this: there would be semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) with respect to the category of quality (*guṇa*), but not with respect to the category of substance (*dravya*). This is the distinction. For those two, the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) is one and the same, yet "heroism" (*vīratva*) as a quality is one thing, and "manhood" (*puruṣatva*) is another. Even for one who holds that the category of substance is the meaning of a word, there will be semantic capacity due to the difference in qualities. However, it is impossible for one who holds that the category of substance is the meaning of a word [to maintain that] the substance...

The benefit produced by a quality (*guṇa*) is what is to be asserted. But is it not already included [within the substance]? Even if it is included, it is nevertheless not understood. For when "molasses" is said, its sweetness is not understood; nor, when "ginger" is said, is its pungency understood. In that case, even for one who holds that qualities are real entities (*guṇapadārthika*), it would be impossible to assert a benefit to the quality produced by the substance. Now, if...

The proponent of the category of quality (*guṇa-padārthika*) maintains [this view]; why does the proponent of the category of substance (*dravya-padārthika*) not maintain it as well? Thus, there may or may not be such functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) for these two. And where indeed would this [usage] occur by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*)? It would occur where everything is synonymous, such as: "Indra, Śakra, Puruhūta, Purandara," or "Kandu, Koṣṭha, Kuśūla. But it is not so for words of that kind.
It should exist as a compound or it should arise as a derivative suffix. What is the reason? The employment of words is for the purpose of conveying meaning.

A word is employed with the thought, "I shall cause the meaning to be understood. Since that meaning has already been expressed by one [word], there should be no employment of a second [word] for that same meaning. What is the reason? Because "that which has already expressed its meaning is not to be employed again. Is this not so?
If that is so, then this [compound] *bhṛtyabharaṇīya* would mean "one who is to be supported as a servant. These two [suffixes] do not have the same meaning.
In this case, one [suffix], the *kṛtya*, occurs in the sense of possibility (*śakya*), while the other occurs in the sense of entitlement (*arhati*).
A servant (*bhṛtya*) is one who is possible to support; one who is entitled to support is "to be supported" (*bharaṇīya*). Thus, a servant who is to be supported is *bhṛtyabharaṇīya*.

Thus [it is said]. If, then, [the rule] must apply wherever there is some similarity and some distinction, then it would follow here as well: *darśanīyāyā māta* (the mother of a beautiful woman) becomes *darśanīyamātā*. In this case too, there is some similarity and some distinction. But what are those? They are existence (*sadbhāva*) and difference-in-existence (*anyabhāva*). Nowhere do existence and difference-in-existence not exist.

And it is said, "by means of a coreferential [term]. In that context, the sense of excellence will be understood: where the coreferentiality is more complete. And where is the coreferentiality more complete? Where everything is identical—namely, existence and non-existence, as well as the substance. Alternatively, by the phrase "by means of a coreferential [term]," that which is common [to both] is relied upon.
That which is common both exists and does not exist; yet this "common" [quality] is not non-existent anywhere at all.

Alternatively, as far as one might say "by means of a common substance," so far it is "by means of a common substratum. For in common usage, a substance (*dravya*) is said to be the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*). For example: "uttered with respect to a single substance," or "with respect to a single substratum."

It has been stated thus. Likewise, in grammar, the rule *vipratiṣiddhaṃ cānadhikaraṇavāci* is understood to mean "that which does not denote a substance. Even so, this must necessarily be formulated: "A co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) compound is treated as if it were incapable [of syntactic connection with other words]. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of forms such as *sarpiḥkālakam* ("clarified butter that is black") and *yajurpītakam* ("a Yajus formula that is yellow"). If [the term] *samānādhikaraṇa*...

It is said that [the compound] becomes as if it were incapable [of expressing its meaning]. In cases such as *sarpiḥ pīyate* ("ghee is drunk") and *yajuḥ kriyate* ("a Yajus formula is performed"), the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) would not apply. This is because [the rule] states "not when expressed by a verbal root" (*adhātvabhihita*). And having established this, an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for words in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), as in *vīraḥ puruṣaḥ* → *vīrapuruṣaḥ*. What is the reason? Because of the lack of capacity (*asamarthatva*). Or rather, it is not so, because of the authority of the explicit statement (*vacanaprāmāṇyāt*).

Or rather, it need not be formulated. What is the reason? Because of the authority of the explicit statement (*vacanaprāmāṇyāt*). By virtue of the authority of the statement, the compound will be formed here.

What is the authority of the statement? It is the rule: *samānamadhyamadhyamavīrāś ca*. And in the case of [compounds] where the verb is elided (*luptākhyāteṣu*). An addition must be made for cases where the verb is elided: *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*, *nirvārāṇasiḥ*. [Question: In the case of those where the verb is elided, what [is the purpose]?

On account of the authority of the statement. What is the authority of the statement? It is the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18). There is another purpose for this statement. What is it? [The formation of] *surājā* and *atirājā*. We do not say "on account of the authority of the statement in the *vṛtti*-sūtra. What then? On account of the authority of the statement in the *vārttika*. But it is established by the mention of *kvāṅksva* and *atidurgati*.

"Words beginning with *pra* [are used] in the sense of the past participle (*kta*)," or "because its meaning is understood. Or rather, this is established because its meaning is understood. What does "because its meaning is understood" mean? Its meaning is "that-meaning" (*tad-artha*); the understanding of that meaning is "understanding of that-meaning" (*tad-arthagati*); [it is so called] because of that understanding of that meaning. That meaning which has a functional connection (*sāmarthya*) with Kauśāmbī is expressed by the word *niṣ*. Alternatively, that meaning is "that-meaning" (*tad-artha*).

The compound *tadarthagati* means "the understanding of that meaning," as in the expression *tadarthagateḥ*. That which is capable [of being reached] from Kauśāmbī is called *niṣā*. (Pāṇini 2.1.10) Now, where there is the possibility of a compound involving many [words], does the compounding occur between each pair of two?

Or rather, [should it apply] without distinction? And what is the distinction here? If a compound consists of two by two, then the term "multiple" (*aneka*) must be mentioned in the rule for *dvandva*.

If a compound consists of two by two, then the mention of "multiple" must be made in the rule for *dvandva*, because the rule states "a *dvandva* is for the sense of 'and' (*ca-artha*). It must be stated that it is "multiple," so that it may also apply here: *plakṣanyagrodhakhadirapalāśāḥ*. This is not a fault.

In this case as well, there will be a compound of two by two. If it is argued that there is a compound of two by two, we say no, because duality does not exist among many. If it is argued that there is a compound of two by two, that is not so. What is the reason? Because duality is absent among many. Duality does not exist among many. It is not necessarily the case that the analysis (*vigraha*) must be performed in this way:

[If it were as you say,] one would have "plakṣaś ca nyagrodhaś ca khadiraś ca palāśaś ca. What then? The analysis will be done in this way: "plakṣaś ca nyagrodhaś ca" becomes "plakṣanyagrodhau"; "khadiraś ca palāśaś ca" becomes "khadirapalāśau";
[and finally] "plakṣanyagrodhau ca khadirapalāśau" becomes "plakṣanyagrodhakhadirapalāśāḥ. [In that case,] then [the compound for] "hotṛ-potṛ-neṣṭodgātāraḥ" [would be formed accordingly].
[If it were otherwise], the term *hotāpotāneṣṭodgātāraḥ* would not be established; rather, [the undesired form] *hotāpotāneṣṭodgātāraḥ* would result. And it should not be so.
It must be so when the analysis (*vigraha*) is performed as follows: "The *hotṛ* and the *potr* are the *hotāpotārau*; the *neṣṭṛ* and the *udgātṛ* are the *neṣṭodgātārau*;
and the *hotāpotārau* and the *neṣṭodgātārau* are the *hotāpotāneṣṭodgātāraḥ*. [Thus, the correct form is] *hotṛpotraneṣṭodgātāraḥ*.

But [the compounds] are not established, and there is a prohibition regarding the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). A prohibition of the compound-final suffix must also be stated for cases such as *vāktvaksrugdṛṣadam*; otherwise, one would obtain the form *vāktvacasrugdṛṣadam*. This is not a fault; for here too, the composition will occur with each subsequent member: *sruc* and *dṛṣad* form *srugdṛṣadam*, and then *tvac* and...

[The compound] *srugdṛṣadam* and *tvaksrugdṛṣadam* [would be formed]; [furthermore], *vāk* and *tvaksrugdṛṣadam* would result in *vāktvaksrugdṛṣadam*. In this way, then, the cases of the *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, and *udgātṛ* priests are established. However, in this case—*susūkṣmajaṭakeśena*, *sunatājīvasanā*, *samantaśitirandhreṇa*—the formation of a dual compound is not established. Let it be, then, without distinction; let it be without distinction.

In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the contingency of multiple words. If, without distinction, there is the contingency of multiple words in a *bahuvrīhi*, what is the fault in that? In that regard, the fault lies in the accent (*svara*), the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*), and the masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*).
