There is a fault concerning the accent, the compound-final suffix, and the masculine substitution. Regarding the accent: *pūrvaśālāpriyaḥ* (one who loves the eastern hall), *aparaśālāpriyaḥ* (one who loves the western hall). Regarding the accent. Regarding the compound-final suffix: *pañcagavapriyaḥ* (one who loves five cows).

[Regarding] the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) and the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*): *khādiretaraśamyam*, *rauravetaraśamyam*. Or rather, there is no fault, because it is a partitive *tatpuruṣa* compound. Why? Because it is a partitive *tatpuruṣa* compound. In this case, the constituent member is designated as a *tatpuruṣa*; therefore, the compound-ending suffix and the substitution of the masculine form will occur based upon that [constituent]. How is the accent? It has the udātta accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*).

"Because of conflict: let the final acute accent (antodāttatva) be applied, or let the original accent of the first member (pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara) be applied; thus, by conflict, the final acute accent prevails. This conflict is not logical. It is said that "in a conflict, the later [rule] prevails"; however, the final acute accent is earlier, while the original accent of the first member is later. We do not speak of a conflict between what is later and what is earlier.

What then? It is an internal conflict (antaraṅga-vipratiṣedha). Or rather, it is because the accent of the *nimittin* is stronger. Alternatively, it should be stated that the accent of the *nimittin* is stronger than the accent of the *nimitta*. What, then, is the *nimitta* and what is the *nimittin*? The *bahuvrīhi* is the *nimitta*; the *tatpuruṣa* is the *nimittin*. Therefore, it must be stated that the accent of the *nimittin* is stronger than the accent of the *nimitta*.

This should not be said. However, the mention of the accent of *ekaśitipād* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the accent of the *nimittin* (the base) is stronger than the accent of the *nimitta* (the cause).

In that the Teacher recites the word *ekaśitipad* among the *yuktārohī* and other such groups, he thereby indicates that the accent of the *nimittin* is more powerful than the accent of the *nimitta*. But who is qualified to recite the word *ekaśitipad* among the *yuktārohī* and others?

It is indeed recited thus: "one white [mark], one white [mark], one white foot"—meaning that of which one foot is white. But that is not so; the analysis (vigraha) will be made in this way: "one white [mark] among these, those are the 'ekaśitayas';
he whose feet are ekaśitayas. Or, furthermore, the analysis may be made thus: "one white [mark], one white [mark], one white foot"—meaning that of which one foot is white.
Even so, there is no purpose in this recitation. The accent prescribed by the rule *igante dvigau* will serve as the sublater of this [accent].

But then, the designation *tatpuruṣa* would apply to this member of a *bahuvrīhi*, as in *susūkṣmajaṭakeśena*, *sunatājivāsanā*, and *samantaśitirandhreṇa*. What is the fault in that? Its final acute accent [would result] due to the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).

There would be final acute accent by way of conflict (vipratiṣedha). This is not a fault. This rule is not being formulated as a definition for a *tatpuruṣa* that is a member of a *bahuvrīhi*. What then? For that *tatpuruṣa* which is a member of a *bahuvrīhi* and possesses that [specific] definition, there will be final acute accent by way of conflict. But does this [present case] not also possess it? What is the distinguishing factor?

Regarding the rule *viśeṣyeṇa bahulam* ("frequently with the qualified object"): because of the mention of "frequently" (*bahula*), [the designation will not apply]. However, in this case, the designation *tatpuruṣa* would then apply to that member of the *bahuvrīhi*, as in *adhikaṣaṣṭivarṣaḥ*. What is the fault in that? Because of the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), it would result in the final syllable being accented (*antodāttatva*).

[Objection: Because of the contradiction [with other rules], this fault does not arise. [Response: This accent will apply by the rule *igante dvigau* ("in a *dvigu* compound ending in an *ik*-vowel"). [Objection: But what about a case that does not end in an *ik*-vowel, such as *adhikaśatavarṣaḥ*? And here too, in the case of *adhikaṣaṣṭivarṣaḥ*, the suffix for a compound-final member (*samāsānta*) would apply. [Response: In the section on the suffix *ḍac*, there is an extension of the rule for *tatpuruṣa* compounds beginning with *niḥtriṃśa*. [Objection: This is not so.

There is a fault. That [rule] is formulated as "avyayādeḥ" (beginning with an indeclinable). What, then, is the reason for formulating it as "avyayādeḥ"? It is so that [the designation of a compound] does not apply here in cases such as *gotriṃśat* (thirty cows) or *gocatvāriṃśat* (forty cows). In that case, the technical name *bahuvrīhi* would apply [by the rule]: "A numeral combined with an indeclinable, 'āsanna' (near), 'adūra' (not far), or 'adhika' (more), when denoting a number to be counted, forms a *bahuvrīhi*. We shall not, however, allow the numeral to function while denoting the thing to be counted. How so? The analysis (*vigraha*) will be constructed in this way: [and so forth].

"It has more than sixty years"—if that rule (*yoga*) is thus rejected, then [the desired form] is obtained by the preceding one. And how is that rule rejected? [It is rejected on the grounds that] "a compound whose final member is a number is not subject to the rule, because it denotes a number-like entity. When that rule is rejected, we shall apply the word *saṃkhyā* (number) to the thing numbered (*saṃkhyeya*).

In this case, the analysis of the compound will be made thus: "sixty years plus something more belong to him. In every respect, we are not released from being over sixty years old. How so? Because that [compound] *yoga* is rejected, and this analysis remains: "there are sixty years plus something more belonging to him. As for what was said—that "over-sixty-years-old" (*adhikaṣaṣṭivarṣaḥ*) is not established—[that is incorrect].

555–561. What is the purpose of [the condition] *sup*? [Example: *karoṣi aṭan*. This is not [a valid case]. Because of a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*), it will not apply here. Why is there a lack of semantic connection? Because "that which has a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is treated as if it were semantically disconnected. Then what [is an example]? *pīḍye pīḍyamāna*. And this too is an example: *karoṣi aṭan*. But was it not already stated that because of a lack of semantic connection, it does not apply here?

It will be so. How is there a lack of capacity? [The objection is: "That which is in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is treated as if it were incapable. This is not a fault. That [rule] refers to what is not expressed by a verbal root (*adhātvabhihita*). Regarding the treatment of a vocative as a subsequent member (*parāṅgvadbhāva*), there is the statement concerning the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and the vocative case-factor (*āmantritakāraka*). When a vocative is treated as a subsequent member, that which ends in the sixth case and the vocative case-factor become like the constituent element (*aṅga*) of the following word.

This is what should be stated: first, [the examples] ending in the genitive case, such as *madrāṇāṃ rājan* ("O King of the Madras") and *magadhānāṃ rājan* ("O King of the Magadhas"). This refers to the case-role (*kāraka*) that is the object of address. [Examples include: *kuṇḍena aṭan* ("wandering with a bowl"). In this regard, there is no difference whether the status of being like a subsequent member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) applies or not. But consider this: *paraśunā vṛścan* ("cutting with an axe"). Alternatively, the mention of "that cause" (*tannimittagrahaṇa*) should be made; that is, the mention of the cause of the address (*āmantritanimitta*).

It must be stated that [the compound] becomes like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavat*) of the following word; and that [condition] must necessarily be stated as one of the two alternatives. For if it were not stated, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of this rule applying to every form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). Indeed, if this were not mentioned, the status of being like a subordinate member of the following word would apply to every form ending in a case-suffix. This [undesirable application] would also occur in cases such as: *kṣatreṇa agne svāyuḥ saṃrabhasva*, *mitreṇa agne mitradheye*.

Exert yourself. What, then, is superior here? Taking that as the cause (the basis for the application of the rule) is indeed superior. By this, the following is also established: *goṣu svāmin*, *aśveṣu svāmin*. For this [word *svāmin*] is neither in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) nor is it a vocative (*āmantrita*) functioning as a kāraka.

Since there is a prescription (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) to behave like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavat*) when it is in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), [this rule applies] because of its non-immediate proximity (*ananantaratvāt*). [This applies] to a word ending in a case-suffix.

An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made [to the rule] regarding the status of being like a member of a subsequent word (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) when there is coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*): for example, *tīkṣṇayā sūcyā sīvyan* ("sewing with a sharp needle") and *tīkṣṇena paraśunā vṛścan* ("cutting with a sharp axe"). But what is the reason that it is not established? Because they are not immediate (*ananantaratvāt*). [Objection:

Once the status of being like a member of a subsequent word has been applied to the subsequent element, will it not also apply to the preceding one? [Response: No, because of the restriction regarding accent (*svara*).
It is not established because the restriction applies to accent (*svara*). The restriction is made with respect to accent, not with respect to immediate sequence (*ānantarya*). It should be stated:

"In the Veda (*chandas*), even that which follows [an *upasarga*] is treated like a verbal root (*aṅga*) with respect to what precedes it. Examples: *ā te pitaḥ marutām sumnam etu*, *prati tvā duhitaḥ divaḥ*, and *vṛṇīṣva duhitaḥ divaḥ*. [This rule also serves as] a prohibition regarding indeclinables (*avyaya*).

And a prohibition must be stated for indeclinables (*avyaya*): *uccair adhīyāna*, *nīcair adhīyāna*. It must be stated that [the rule applies] to what is not an *avyayībhāva* compound: it should not apply here—*upāgnir adhīyāna*, *pratyagnir adhīyāna*. Now, for what purpose is the restriction made regarding accent (*svara*)? The restriction regarding accent is for the sake of the elision of the case-ending (*sub-lopa*). Regarding accent...

A restriction is made so that [the rule] does not apply when a *sub* suffix has been elided. For example, in *paraśunā vṛścan*. Or rather, it need not be stated. Why? Because it applies exclusively to forms ending in a *sub* suffix. The treatment as if it were a member of another word (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) occurs exclusively for forms ending in a *sub* suffix; however, when the *sub* suffix is elided, it applies exclusively to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Indeed, when the *sub* suffix has been elided, it becomes exclusive to the nominal stem.

By the definition of a suffix (*pratyaya*), there would be an absolute restriction to forms ending in *sup*. Therefore, the restriction regarding accent (*svara*) need not be made for the sake of the elision of *sup*; for it is the *sup* situated within the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that is said to undergo elision (*luk*). Consequently, there is no purpose in mentioning the accent. If this is so, then the purpose is this: let the rules for the substitution of *ṣ* and *ṇ* not apply [in cases such as] "kūpe siñcan" (sprinkling in a well) and "carman naman" (bending the hide). [Otherwise, these rules would wrongly apply.]
This purpose, too, does not exist. Here, first of all, in the case of *kūpe siñcan* ("pouring into the well"), the status of being a word-initial (*padāditva*) will apply to its own base.

In the case of *carman naman* ("bending the hide"), it will not apply due to this restriction: "after a preceding member [of a compound], when a name is formed, [the suffix *ṇatv* applies] except after *ag*" (Pāṇini 8.4.3). But surely, in a compound, there is such a distinction as "preceding member" and "subsequent member"? No, he says; this occurs without such a distinction.

The former word is the *pūrvapada* (first member), and the latter word is the *uttarapada* (second member). (Pāṇini 2.1.3) Why is the expression "before" (*prāk*) used? The expression "before" is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] technical names (*saṃjñā*). The expression "before" is employed.

This is so that the designation "compound" (*samāsa-sañjñā*) may not be precluded. For if the word "prior to" (*prāk*) were not employed, the designations such as *avyayībhāva* and the rest—which have no other scope—would subvert the designation "compound. To prevent them from subverting it, the word "prior to" is employed.
Now, even if the word "prior to" is employed, why is it that the designations such as *avyayībhāva*, having no other scope, do not [subvert it] nonetheless?

[They] obstruct [the application of other rules]. For when the previous rule [regarding technical names] is being applied, these member-designations (*avayava-sañjñā*) are initiated while the designation of a compound (*samāsa-sañjñā*) already exists. In that case, there will be a co-occurrence (*vacana-samāveśa*) of the designations. The designation of a compound would also be without scope; it will nevertheless occur by virtue of the explicit statement. But the designation of a compound has its scope. What is its scope? Words such as *vispaṣṭa* constitute its scope: e.g., *vispaṣṭa-paṭuḥ*.

Regarding the term *vispaṣṭapaṭuḥ*: there is no room for this [objection]. For the style of the Teacher is observed to be such that by whatever [rule] the operation of a constituent part occurs, by that very same [rule] the operation of the whole also occurs. Just as the accent, which is the operation of a constituent part, applies, so too will the compound (*samāsa*), which is the operation of the whole, apply. This is because [the rule] "vispaṣṭādīni guṇavacaneṣu" [applies].
In that case, this would be like the "crow-and-palm" (kākatālīya) or the "goat-and-sword" (ajākṛpāṇīya) coincidences.

Even here, by the very same [constituent] which performs the operation on the parts—namely, the production of the suffix—the same will perform the operation on the whole, namely, the designation of a compound (*samāsa*). And from the compound, because it has that as its domain.
In that case, consider *punārājaḥ* and *punargavaḥ*. Here too, the designation of a *tatpuruṣa* must necessarily be stated, for it depends upon the *tatpuruṣa*.

[The rule] for the suffix of a compound (*samāsānta*) should apply. Consider this case: *punarādheyam*. Here too, the designation "gati" must necessarily be stated so that the accent prescribed by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* may occur. Consider this case:
*punarutsyūtaṃ vāso deyam*. Here too, the designation "gati" must necessarily be stated so that the elision of accent (*nighāta*) prescribed by the rule *gatir gatau* may occur.

If that [term] does not exist, then again, by the rule *chandasi* (Pāṇini 3.4.117), it would apply. When that [term] exists, the desired result is established by that very [rule]. Even so, because of the statement "only one designation [applies]," simultaneous occurrence is impossible; rather, an alternation (*paryāya*) would result.
Therefore, the mention of the word *prāk* (before) must be made.
(P_2.1.4) For what purpose is the word *saha* used? The mention of *saha* is for the sake of excluding compounds that are not [formed] separately.

The inclusion of *saha* is made so that the technical designation of *samāsa* (compound) may apply to two things that exist together (*sahabhūta*), and not to each one individually. What would happen if it applied to each one individually?

In this case, the designation "compound" (*samāsa*) would apply; thus, in the example *ṛkpādaḥ*, the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) would result. And here, in *rājāśvaḥ*, there would be two vowels [resulting in the loss of the elision]. Furthermore, how is it that the designation applies to each individual? It is observed that the completion of a sentence occurs for each [word] individually. For example, the designations "vṛddhi" and "guṇa" apply to each [element] individually. But is there not also this illustrative example?

"The completion of the sentence occurs with respect to the aggregate," as in the example: "Let the Gargas be fined one hundred. Kings are desirous of gold, yet they do not fine them individually. Since this example exists, if it is stated there that [the action applies] "individually," then here too the mention of "together" (*saha*) must be made. Or else, even without that [mention],...

The expression "each" (*pratyekam*) indicates that the technical designations *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* apply to each [element] individually; thus, even here, there is no purpose for including the word "together" (*saha*). If that is so, since the desired result is already established, the reason he includes the word "together" is so that it may be understood as a subordinate member of the rule (*yogāṅga*). And when it functions as a subordinate member of the rule, the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made as follows: "It is compounded with a *sup*-ending word together [with another]. With what is it "together"? [With a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix.]

[The word] *samarthena* [is used]. *Anuvyācalat* means "he entered after. Then, with a *sup*-ending word, a *sup*-ending word is compounded. This is both a governing rule (*adhikāra*) and a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). For that compound for which there is no other defining rule, this shall be the defining rule.
As in: "A garment that has been sewn again is to be given; a chariot that has been repaired again. With the particle *iva*, there is no elision of case-endings.

569. Why is this great designation (mahatī sañjñā) employed? So that it may be understood as a designation based on its meaning (*anvarthasañjñā*). [The rule] "that which is not indeclinable becomes indeclinable" refers to the *avyayībhāva*. Thus, it need not be stated that "the *avyayībhāva* compound also receives the designation 'indeclinable'."

(P_2,1.6) Why does [the suffix *ka*] not occur here in the cases of *sumadrāḥ*, *sumagadhāḥ*, *saputraḥ*, and *sacchātraḥ*? For [the rule] "in the sense of prosperity" (*samṛddhau*) and "in the sense of completeness" (*sākalye*) would apply. This is not a fault. For in this context, some compounds have the meaning of the prior member as their predominant factor (*pūrvapadārthapradhāna*).
Some [compounds] have the meaning of the final member as predominant, some have the meaning of another word (the first member) as predominant,
and some have the meanings of both members as predominant. The *avyayībhāva* has the meaning of the first member as predominant.
A *tatpuruṣa* compound has the meaning of the final member as its predominant element;

a *bahuvrīhi* has the meaning of another word [external to the compound] as its predominant element; and a *dvandva* has the meanings of both members as its predominant elements. Furthermore, in this case, predominance of the meaning of the first member is not perceived. Alternatively, it is not these meanings of the compounds that are being indicated here; rather, it is the meanings of the indeclinables (*avyaya*) that are being indicated.
"In these meanings, that indeclinable which occurs is compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix" (Pāṇini 2.1.7).

[Question: For what purpose is the condition "provided there is no similarity" (*asādṛśye*) stated? [Example: "As Devadatta is, so is Yajñadatta. Since it is stated "provided there is no similarity," this [following example] would not be established: [example omitted].

"According to one's capacity, according to one's strength. What is the reason? [The word] *yathā* is a suffix *thāl* used in the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*), and that [suffix] occurs in the sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*). This fault does not apply. This word *yathā* exists as an unanalyzed nominal stem (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*) expressing distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). It also exists as a suffix *thāl* used in the sense of manner. Therefore, that which is the unanalyzed nominal stem expressing distributive repetition—[it is this that is intended here].
This is its inclusion [in the rule]. Now, why is there not an inclusion of that *thāl* suffix which expresses a manner (*prakāra*)?
It would follow from the preceding rule because of the expression "similarity" (*sādṛśya*) and "attainment" (*sampatti*). It will not occur because of the force of the statement of the prohibition.

While *sup* is already understood [from the previous rule], what is the purpose of mentioning *sub* again? It is so that the designation *avyaya* may apply even when there is merely a *sup* suffix, as in *māṣaprati*, *sūpaprati*, and *odanaprati*.

2.1.10) Just as *akṣa* and others ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) do not become [the first member] of the aforementioned [compound], so too *akṣa* and others ending in the third case [do not become the first member] in the case of *pari*.

It should be stated that [the suffix *pari*] is compounded together with [the word it follows]. It is not as in the case previously mentioned; rather, it is used when something of a different nature is to be indicated. For example: *akṣapari* and *śalākāpari*, meaning "it did not turn out as it did before by means of the die" (*akṣeṇa*). This applies when the die (*akṣa*) and the counter (*śalākā*) are singular. It should also be stated that [the words] *akṣa* and *śalākā* must end in the singular number. Let this not apply here: *akṣābhyām vṛttam*.

The suffix *kta* is applied after the word *akṣa* [in the sense of "played"] when it refers to the practice of gamblers. It should be stated: "when it refers to the practice of gamblers. Let it not be so here:
*akṣeṇedam na vṛttaṃ śakaṭena yathā pūrvam* ("This was not played with a die, as was done before with a cart").

574–575. A *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) must be made. "Optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) is this governing heading (*adhikāra*). Then follows: "After *apa*, *pari*, *bahis*, and [roots] ending in *añc*, when used with the fifth case. The mention of the "fifth case" (*pañcamī*) can be omitted. How so? The term "ending in a nominal suffix" (*subanta*) is understood [from the preceding rule], and since the fifth case is prescribed here in connection with these *karmapravacanīya*s, there the fifth case occurs even without the explicit mention of the "fifth case."

The compound will indeed occur with that which ends in the fifth case (pañcamyanta). However, this is the purpose [of the rule]: the fifth case is not prescribed when used in conjunction with the word *bahiḥ*; therefore, it is so that [the rule] may apply there as well, as in *bahir grāmāt* ("outside the village"). Now, even if the mention of the fifth case (*pañcamī-grahaṇa*) were made, since the fifth case is not prescribed in conjunction with the word *bahiḥ*, how is this established?
By the force of the inclusion of the fifth case (*pañcamī*).

2.1.13) It would have been possible not to include the mention of both "limit" (*maryādā*) and "inclusiveness" (*abhividhi*). How so? Because the phrase "by that which ends in the fifth case" (*pañcamyantena*) continues [from the previous rule], and [the particle] *āṅ* [is understood].

575–576. What is the example? *anugaṅgaṃ hāstinapuram* (Hastināpura is along the Ganges), *anugaṅgaṃ vārāṇasī* (Vārāṇasī is along the Ganges), *anuśoṇaṃ pāṭaliputram* (Pāṭaliputra is along the Śoṇa). Regarding the rule "and that which has its length [is compounded with it]," both the Ganges and Vārāṇasī are long. In that case, why does the compound occur with the Ganges and not with Vārāṇasī? If this is so, then [the answer is] by means of the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇena*).

Thus it follows that the Ganges alone is the defining characteristic, not Vārāṇasī. Alternatively, regarding what is called "the length" (*āyāma*), both the Ganges and Vārāṇasī are long; however, the sense of excellence will be understood there [by the suffix], namely: "that whose length is greater. And the length of the Ganges is greater than that of Vārāṇasī.

(P_2,1.17) What is the purpose of the particle *ca*? It serves the purpose of the restrictive particle *eva*. [The rule applies to] only those beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu*. Where should it not apply? In cases such as *paramaṃ tiṣṭhadgu*. [The term] *tiṣṭhadgu* refers to a specific time. It should be stated that *tiṣṭhadgu* refers to a specific time.
The words *tiṣṭhadgu*, *vahadgu*, and *khaleyavādi*—being nominative singular—are compounded when they denote another word-meaning (*anyapadārtha*).

Words such as *khaleyava* and others, being nominative singular, are compounded when they denote another word-meaning. Examples include: *khaleyava*, *khalebusa*, *lūnayava*, *lūyamānayava*, *pūtayava*, and *pūyamānayava*.

(P_2,1.18) What is the purpose of the mention of *vā*? It is so that there may be an optional compound (*vibhāṣā samāsaḥ*). That is, when the compound is not used, there may also be a sentence (*vākya*), such as *pāraṃ gaṅgāyāḥ*. This purpose is not necessary, because the *mahāvibhāṣā* is the subject under discussion.

By that [rule], the compound will also be a verbal expression (*vākya*). In that case, this is the purpose: so that when the *avyayībhāva* is excluded, the *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* may occur, as in *gaṅgāpāram*. This too is not a purpose; for this *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* is also optional (*vibhāṣā*). Both of them will occur by virtue of the explicit statement [of the rule]. Therefore, he recites the subsequent sūtra: "With *pāra* and *madhya*, with the genitive."

Regarding the word *vā* (the optional particle): it should be stated that [the compound] with *pāre* and *madhye* is optional after a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyā vā*). For if it were not stated, there would be an absence of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), as in the case where the part-whole relation is predominant (*ekadeśipradhāna*). Indeed, if the optional particle *vā* were not employed, there would be an absence of the genitive compound, just as in the case where the part-whole relation is predominant. That is to say, when one is excluded by the part-whole compound (*ekadeśisamāsa*), the genitive compound does not occur. Why?

Furthermore, when the *ekadeśisamāsa* (compound denoting a part) is excluded, the *ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa* (genitive compound) does not occur. The formation of compounds and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) is optional (*vibhāṣā*). Within the domain of such formations, an exception (*apavāda*) is obligatory. However, if the optionality (*vāvacana*) were applied here, one [rule] would be an optional formation, while the other would be an optional exception within the domain of formations. And there is the irregular substitution (*nipātana*) of the final vowel /e/. This refers to the irregular substitution of the final vowel /e/.

And it should not be formulated as *pāregaṅgam*. It need not be formulated, for it is established by means of the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case. [Objection: It would be established when the locative case is used;

579–582. A prohibition must be stated regarding the formation of a *saṃkhyā-samāsa* (numeral compound) with feminine nouns denoting rivers (*nadī*) when the meaning of the compound is something other than the members themselves. [Objection: A prohibition must be stated for a *saṃkhyā-samāsa* with rivers in the sense of another word [as the referent]. For example: *dvīrāvatīkaḥ deśaḥ* ("a region having two Āravatīs"), *trīrāvatīkaḥ deśaḥ* ("a region having three Āravatīs"). [In these cases,] the rule *nadībhiḥ saṃkhyā* would apply. [Reply: It need not be stated. In this context, some compounds have the meaning of the prior member as their predominant sense (*pūrvapadārthapradhāna*).

Some [compounds] have the meaning of the final member as predominant, some have the meaning of another word (the external referent) as predominant, and some have the meanings of both members as predominant. The *avyayībhāva* has the meaning of the prior member as predominant.
A *tatpuruṣa* compound has the meaning of the final member as its predominant sense;
a *bahuvrīhi* has the meaning of another word [external to the compound] as its predominant sense;
and a *dvandva* has the meanings of both members as its predominant sense. And here, the predominance of the meaning of the prior member is not perceived. Now, one might object: [is it not so?]

And that which is expressed by a word is its meaning. Here, moreover, we perceive this very meaning being expressed by these two words. We know precisely this: that whatever is expressed by something is the meaning of that thing.

Furthermore, the status of being the meaning of another word (*anyapadārthatā*) would not be possible [in such cases as] "one who has brindled cows" (*citraguḥ*) or "one who has variegated cows" (*śabalaguḥ*). What is the reason?

For even here, we perceive this meaning being expressed by these two words. Even though this meaning is expressed by these two words, it is nevertheless understood as the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*). In that case, the *bahuvrīhi* compound will have its basis in the meaning of another word. But in this instance as well, the meaning of another word is understood, as is the meaning of its own constituent words (*svapadārtha*).

Nevertheless, it is understood that in this case, the *avyayībhāva* compound would apply by virtue of its own constituent meaning. If that is so, then this must be considered here: "Let the *avyayībhāva* be formed, or let the *bahuvrīhi* be formed? The *bahuvrīhi* will prevail by way of a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*). This would be established if there were a governing rule for a single designation; however, it is not established when the subsequent operation is to take effect. [This is] because of the force of the original formulation.
The *avyayībhāva* compound would apply [first] because it is a subsequent operation (*paraṅkārya*), whereas the *bahuvrīhi* applies later. And there is no fault in its being a subsequent operation.

It should be stated that when a numeral is combined with river names in a collective sense (*samāhāra*), an *avyayībhāva* is formed. And that must certainly be stated, as in the examples: *sarvanadī*, *ekanadī*, and *tarenadī*.

(P_2,1.23) What are the purposes for treating a *dvigu* as a *tatpuruṣa*? When a *dvigu* is treated as a *tatpuruṣa*, the addition of compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) is the purpose: *pañcagavam*, *daśagavam*, *pañcarājam*, *daśarājam*.

582–587: An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for *gami*, *gāmi*, and others among the words beginning with *śrita*. An addition must be made for *gami*, *gāmi*, and others among the words beginning with *śrita*. For example: *grāmaṃ gamī* (one who will go to the village), *grāmagaṃmī*, *grāmaṃ gāmī*, and *grāmagāmī*. Regarding the rule for compounds with words beginning with *śrita*: since it expresses non-separation (*ahīna*), the prescription of a compound with a word in the accusative case is redundant, because it is already accomplished by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound. That is to say, the statement regarding the formation of a compound with an accusative case-ending when used with words beginning with *śrita*—provided it does not signify separation—is purposeless, as the desired form is already produced by a *bahuvrīhi*.

What is the reason? Because it is formed as a *bahuvrīhi* compound. For in this case, when someone has resorted to hardship (*kaṣṭa*), it is understood that "hardship has been resorted to by him. In that instance, the formation is already established by the *bahuvrīhi*. Furthermore, the rule regarding the accentuation of the second member in an *ahīna* compound would be redundant; namely, the statement that "in an *ahīna*, the second member is the first member [of the compound], which retains its original accent" (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) would be purposeless. What is the reason?

Precisely because it is formed as a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there would be the undesirable consequence of the accent of a genus (*jāti*). That is, the accent of a genus would apply [to the final syllable], as in *grāmagataḥ* (gone from the village) and *araṇyagataḥ* (gone to the forest). This is because of the rule: "The past passive participle suffix *kta* [has an acute accent on the first syllable] after words denoting genus, time, pleasure, and so forth, provided they do not mean clothing, except when used with *akṛta*, *mita*, or *pratipanna*. In that regard, the desired result is established by the optional statement regarding "born" (*jāta*) and the others. I shall state this: "Or, [the accent is optionally on the first syllable] when *jāta* follows," which I will express as "or, [the accent is optionally on the first syllable] when *jāta* and the others follow."

These [words] beginning with *jāta* will occur [as examples]. But surely there is a difference? For if it were a *bahuvrīhi*, it would have to be oxytone due to the suffix applied at the end of the compound (*samāsāntodātta*), whereas if it were a *tatpuruṣa*, it would be [oxytone] precisely by the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*). There is no difference; for even one who begins with a *tatpuruṣa* does not have the *bahuvrīhi* barred by a staff (i.e., it is not prohibited).

In that case, when it is a *tatpuruṣa*, there are two compounds and two accents; when it is a *bahuvrīhi*, there is one compound and the state of having two accents. If this is so, then since [the desired form] is already established, the fact that the Teacher teaches the *tatpuruṣa* rule indicates that when the meaning is the same, even though there is only a difference in the analytical expression (*vigraha*), where both a *tatpuruṣa* and a *bahuvrīhi* would otherwise apply, the *tatpuruṣa* alone occurs.

Thus [it is stated]. What is the purpose of making this known? [The example is: *rājñaḥ sakhā* (the king’s friend) becomes *rājasakhaḥ*. [Otherwise,] the compound *rājā sakhā asya* would result in a *bahuvrīhi*, which does not occur. This is not something that must be established by a *jñāpaka* (an indicator), because general rules (*utsarga*) are sublated by exceptions (*apavāda*). There must be a sublating factor here, since a rule prescribed in a general way is sublated by one prescribed for a specific case. Now, if it were not prescribed in a general way...

As for what was said—that [the suffix] is due to it being formed as a *bahuvrīhi*—that is incorrect. Indeed, there is a distinction between the *bahuvrīhi* and the *tatpuruṣa*. Is this distinction based on the word-form (*śabda*) or based on the meaning (*artha*)? It is both based on the word-form and based on the meaning. First, regarding the word-form: when it is a *bahuvrīhi*, the suffix *kap* must occur; when it is a *tatpuruṣa*, it must not occur.

[The suffix] *kta* is applied based on the meaning [of the action]. When it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the *kta* suffix following roots such as *ruh* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) when there is no completion (*anapavarga*) of the root-meaning;

for example: "Devadatta has climbed the tree" (*ārūḍho vṛkṣaṃ devadattaḥ*). In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, it occurs when the object (*karman*) is completed; for example: "The tree has been climbed by Devadatta" (*ārūḍho vṛkṣo devadattena*). Indeed, the comprehension of the meaning through direct perception is of a different nature altogether.

It is of a different nature due to the relationship. In the case of *rājasakha* ("the king's friend"), because of the relationship, it must be understood that "surely the king is also his friend. Indeed, both cases are intended:
*svasti somasakha punar ehi* ("Hail, O friend of Soma, come back again") and *gavāṃsakhaḥ* ("friend of cows").

(P_2,1.26) What is the example? "The rogue has mounted the couch" (*khaṭvārūḍho jālmah*). It is stated that this occurs in the sense of censure (*kṣepe*). What indeed is this so-called censure? One who has studied, performed the ceremonial bath (*snāta*), and been permitted by his teachers should mount the couch; he who now acts otherwise than that is [the one censured].
"This rogue has mounted the bed; he is not one who observes his vows strictly.

(Pāṇini 2.1.29) Since the formation of a compound with a word ending in the *kta* suffix in the sense of "continuous connection" (*atyantasaṃyoga*) is stated without qualification, the specific rule for compounding with the *kta* suffix would be redundant. [This applies] in the case of continuous connection.

Since the formation of compounds is stated without distinction—namely, that "times" (kālāḥ) form compounds with both words ending in *kta* and those not ending in *kta*—the specific rule for compounding [time with] a word ending in *kta* is redundant; it is already established by the rule *atyantasaṃyoge*. However, this must be stated for the sake of cases where there is no absolute connection (*anatyantasaṃyoga*). For example: "six muhūrtas are moving and non-moving"; they sometimes pass during the day, and sometimes [they do not].

Regarding the phrase *tatkṛtārthena* (by that which has its purpose accomplished by it), for what purpose [is it stated]? [Examples: *dadhnā paṭuḥ* (clever because of curd), *ghṛtena paṭuḥ* (clever because of ghee). This case does not exist. Because of a lack of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*), [the suffix] will not occur here. Why is there a lack of capacity? Because that which is dependent is incapable. For there is no syntactic capacity between the curd and the cleverness; rather, [the capacity exists] with the act of eating. [The meaning is: "He eats cleverly because of the curd."

[Objection: In that case, it would not apply here either, as in *śaṅkulākhaṇḍaḥ kirikāṇaḥ* ("a woodcutter with a wooden mallet"). For here too, there is no semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) between the wooden mallet and the fragment; rather, [the connection is] with the verb *karoti* ("to make"), as in "a fragment made by means of a wooden mallet. [Response:

It will occur here as well because of the explicit statement (*vacana*), just as in the cases *dadhnā paṭuḥ* ("clever because of yogurt") and *ghṛtena paṭuḥ* ("clever because of ghee"). Therefore, the mention of "that which has its purpose accomplished by it" (*tatkṛtārtha*) is necessary.

It must be stated [as a rule]. Why is it said "by means of a word expressing a quality" (*guṇavacanena*)? [Consider these examples: "possessing fat because of cows" (*gobhir vapāvān*), "possessing wealth because of grain" (*dhānyena dhanavān*). But what, then, is the illustrative example here? It is "Devadatta is broken by a wedge" (*śaṅkulākhaṇḍo devadattaḥ*). But how can a compound, when being taught as occurring with a word expressing a quality, apply to a word expressing a substance (*dravyavacana*)? In this case, it is established by the rule: "The third case ending [is compounded] with a quality produced by that [instrument], or with the object [of the action]. (*tṛtīyā tatkṛtārthena guṇena*)—this much is sufficient.

Now, since this [rule] is thus established, the purpose of employing the term *vacana* (word) is so that it may be understood: "by a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*) which has expressed a quality. But how does this word, being an expression of a quality, come to be an expression of a substance (*dravyavacana*)? In that regard, the elision of the possessive suffix *matup* is commenced; for there is the elision (*luk*) of *matup* after words expressing qualities.

Thus: just as that which has the quality of white is "white," and that which has the quality of black is "black," so too that which has the quality of being broken is "broken. If this is the case, there is no purpose in including the term *kṛtārtha* (that which has its purpose accomplished). For indeed, there is a functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) between a wedge and a piece [of wood]; however, because there is no such capacity here in cases like *dadhnā paṭuḥ* ("clever with curd") or *ghṛtena paṭuḥ* ("clever with ghee"), it will not apply. Therefore, there is no need for the inclusion of the term *tatkṛtārtha*.

In the case of a third-case compound (*tṛtīyāsamāsa*), the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) is redundant, for the meaning is understood even without its explicit mention. In a third-case compound, the mention of "meaning" is unnecessary. Why? Because the meaning is understood even without its being stated; the meaning will be grasped even in the absence of an explicit statement. If it is argued that [the meaning] must be explicitly indicated, then there would also have to be an explicit indication of the sense of the third case. Even so, such an indication would still have to be made.

If this is so, then a specification of the meaning of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) would also have to be made; one would have to say: "The third case [is used] with that which is produced by it (*tad-artha-kṛta*) and with a word expressing a quality (*guṇa-vacana*). Well then, it must be stated. No, it need not be stated. This is not a specification of meaning; rather, this is a specification of a component of the rule (*yogāṅga*). And when there is a component of the rule, a division of the rule (*yoga-vibhāga*) will be made: "The third case [is used] with that which is produced by it" (P. 2.1.30), and then "with a word expressing a quality" (P. 2.1.31).
It is compounded. Then, with the word *artha* (meaning), the third case ending is compounded. Examples are *dhānyārthaḥ* (for the sake of grain) and *vasanārthaḥ* (for the sake of clothing).
Thus, the inclusion of the term *artha* in the rule "with *pūrva*, *sadṛśa*, *sama*, and *unārtha*" need not have been made.

592–593: An addition [to the rule] regarding "avaras" (younger/lower) after words such as "pūrva" (prior). An addition [to the rule] regarding "avaras" after words such as "pūrva": *māsāvaraḥ* (this is younger by a month), *saṃvatsarāvaraḥ* (this is younger by a year). It was stated [in the commentary] concerning the mention of "sadṛśa" (similar). What was stated? "The mention of 'sadṛśa' is useless because of the statement regarding the *tṛtīyā*-compound. [Objection: "If it is for the sake of the genitive case, then the statement regarding the *tṛtīyā*-compound is useless."

"The agent and the instrument [are compounded] with a *kṛt* [derivative] ending in a *kta* suffix. It should be stated: "The agent and the instrument [are compounded] with a *kṛt* [derivative] ending in a *kta* suffix. Examples: *ahir hataḥ* ("killed by a snake"), *nakhanirbhinnaḥ* ("split by claws"), *dātralūnaḥ* ("cut by a sickle"), *paraśucchinnaḥ* ("felled by an axe"). Why specify "with a *kṛt* [derivative] ending in a *kta* suffix"? So that it does not apply here: *dātreṇa lūnavān* ("one who has cut with a sickle").
"He cut with an axe. If that is so, then it must be stated [as a rule]. It need not be stated; it is established by the use of the term *bahula* ("in various cases").

[This is seen] elsewhere as well, in the expression of an additional meaning by means of gerundives (*kṛtya*). [This is seen] elsewhere as well in the expression of an additional meaning by means of gerundives.

It should be stated that [the compound] is seen even when [the object] is visible: *busopendhyam* (to be burned with chaff), *tṛṇopendhyam* (to be burned with grass), *ghanaghātyam* (to be struck with a mallet). Or rather, it should be stated that the word *sādhana* (instrument) is compounded with words ending in a *kṛt* suffix for the sake of terms such as *pādahāraka*. Alternatively, it should be stated that *sādhana* is compounded with words ending in a *kṛt* suffix. What is the purpose? For the sake of terms such as *pādahāraka*. That which is carried by the feet is *pādahāraka*; that which is suspended from the neck is *galecopaka*.

"Vyañjana with food" (*annena vyañjanam*) and "mixing with solid food" (*bhakṣyeṇa miśrīkaraṇam*): this should be understood as an *asamartha-samāsa*. What is the reason? [Because] of the [separate] case-relations (*kāraka*).
[The capacity of factors] exists through action. The capacity of the *kārakas* arises through action, not through their mutual [relation].

For example, a ladder has its capacity through two pieces of wood, but not through those [pieces of wood] being mutually related. If that is so, then one says, "There is a mixing of sauce with the food, and of condiment with the meal," yet there is no [inherent] capacity [between them]. In that case—

If it is argued that the compound will occur by virtue of a specific rule—that is, on the authority of a formal statement—then a prohibition must be stated regarding [compounds of] different case-roles (*nānākāraka*), even on the authority of such a statement. For example: *tiṣṭhatu dadhnā odano bhujyate devadattena* ("Let the curd remain; the rice is eaten by Devadatta"). However, this is already established: under the heading of "coreferentiality" (*samānādhikaraṇa*), a past passive participle (*kta*) preceded by a word in the third case undergoes the elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapadalopa*).

And this is established. How so? It should be stated under the section on *samānādhikaraṇa* (co-referential compounds): "A word ending in the suffix *kta* preceded by a third-case word is compounded with a *sup*-ending word, and there is elision of the final syllable of the second member. Thus: *dadhnā upasiktaḥ* becomes *dadhyupasiktaḥ*; *dadhyupasikta odanaḥ* becomes *dadhyodanaḥ*. Similarly, *guḍena saṃsṛṣṭāḥ* becomes *guḍasaṃsṛṣṭāḥ*.

"Popped rice mixed with molasses" (*guḍasaṃsṛṣṭā dhānāḥ*) is "molasses-popped-rice" (*guḍadhānāḥ*). This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), and it is a rule that a genitive compound ending in *yukta* or *pūrṇa* is formed, with the elision of the final member being stated [as an option]. For example: "yoked to horses" (*aśvānāṃ yuktaḥ*) is "horse-yoked" (*aśvayuktaḥ*);

a "horse-yoked chariot" (*aśvayukto rathaḥ*) is "horse-chariot" (*aśvarathaḥ*). "Filled with curds" (*dadhnāḥ pūrṇaḥ*) is "curd-filled" (*dadhipūrṇaḥ*); a "curd-filled jar" (*dadhipūrṇo ghaṭaḥ*) is "curd-jar" (*dadhighaṭaḥ*).

In that case, much would have to be said. Or rather, it need not be stated, because [the forms] are not seen in non-compounds. Why? Because they are not seen in non-compounds. For when something is seen in a non-compound but not seen in a compound, that necessitates the formulation of a rule for elision (*lopa*). And the words *upasikta*, *saṃsṛṣṭa*, or *pūrṇa* are not seen in non-compounds.

How, then, is semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) understood? Semantic capacity arises from the comprehension of a connected meaning. Through the word "curd" (*dadhi*), a state of having a connected meaning is comprehended. But how is it known that a state of having a connected meaning is comprehended through "curd"? It is because of such comprehension that the determination of that meaning occurs; it is from comprehension that the meaning of that [word] is determined.

And this must necessarily be understood in this way. For if there were the elision (*lopa*) of meanings currently being perceived, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). For one who thinks that there is elision of words whose meanings are currently being perceived, for him there would be an infinite regress of such elisions. When the word "curd" (*dadhi*) is uttered, many meanings are understood—such as "thick," "watery," or "congealed"—and [if one were to posit elision] of the words expressing those [specific meanings], the same fault would follow.

Omission must be stated [as a rule]. For instance, when "molasses" (*guḍa*) is said, the word "sweet" (*madhura*) is understood; and when "ginger" (*śṛṅgavera*) is said, the word "pungent" (*kaṭu*) is understood.

Indeed, even without the employment of words, many meanings are comprehended through the contraction of eyes and the movements of hands. Therefore, the omission of the words expressing those meanings must be stated.

(P_2,1.36) KA_I,388.6–390.19 Ro_II, 598–603: Is there a compound of a word ending in the fourth case with that which has the sense of "for its sake" (*tadartha*) alone? It ought to be so. But if a word ending in the fourth case were compounded with anything having the sense of "for its sake," there would be over-extension (*sarvaprasaṅga*), because there is no distinction made. [Regarding] a word ending in the fourth case with that which has the sense of "for its sake" alone...

If this were so, there would be an over-extension (*sarvaprasaṅga*); a compound with anything ending in the fourth case (*caturthyanta*) would result with just that which has its meaning (*tadartha*).
This [rule] would also apply [inappropriately] to such cases as *randhanāya sthālī* ("a pot for cooking") and *avahananāya ulūkhalam* ("a mortar for threshing"). What is the reason?
Because there is no distinction (*aviśeṣāt*). For no specific distinction is stated regarding a word ending in the fourth case of such a kind [as being compounded] with that which has its meaning.

[The rule] "there is a compound" would apply [universally]. If no specific distinction were stated, there would be the undesirable consequence [of over-extension] to all cases. Furthermore, the mention of *balirakṣita* (the offering and the protector) would be purposeless. The statement regarding the compounding of *balirakṣita* is indeed useless; for that which is an offering (*bali*) for a Great King (*mahārāja*) is already considered to be for the sake of the Great King (*mahārājārtha*). In that case, it is already established by the rule "that which is for its sake" (*tadartha*). However, if it is a modification (*vikṛti*)...

The rule should be formulated as follows: "That which ends in the fourth case is compounded with its source (*prakṛti*). If it is argued that the rule is "the modification (*vikṛti*) is compounded with its source," then an addition must be made for cases such as *aśvaghāsa* ("horse fodder") and the like. If it is argued that the rule is "the modification is compounded with its source," then an addition must be made for cases such as *aśvaghāsa*, *śvaśrūsuram*, and *hastividhā*. Furthermore, it should be stated that there is an obligatory compound with a word expressing purpose (*artha*).

It must be stated that there is an obligatory compound with the word *artha*. [Examples: *brāhmaṇārtham*, *kṣatriyārtham*. [Question: Is it because a word ending in the dative case is compounded with its base (*prakṛti*) that it must be stated there is an obligatory compound with *artha*? [Answer: No, he says; rather, an obligatory compound with *artha* must be stated in every respect so that no analytical statement (*vigraha*) occurs. And there is the taking of all genders (*sarvaliṅgatā*). [That is,] the taking of all genders.

And it must be stated that [the compound] "milk for the sake of the Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇārthaṃ payaḥ*), "soup for the sake of the Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇārthaḥ sūpaḥ*), and "gruel for the sake of the Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇārthā yavāgūḥ*) takes all genders. Is it being said that there is an obligatory compound with the word *artha*? Therefore, it must be stated that [the compound] takes all genders. No, he says;

rather, it must be stated that it takes all genders in every respect. What is the reason? This word *artha* is masculine and has the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) as its predominant sense.

And since it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound, only a masculine compound would be expressed, while feminine and neuter compounds would not. Therefore, much must be stated: it should be stated that "the modification [is expressed] by the original form" (*vikṛtiḥ prakṛtyā*). An addition must be made for cases such as *aśvaghāsa* ("horse fodder") and so on. It should be stated that there is an obligatory compound with the word *artha* ("meaning"). And it should be stated that [such compounds] possess all genders.
It need not be stated. As for what is said—that it should be stated that "a derivative (*vikṛti*) [is compounded] with its base (*prakṛti*)"—it need not be stated.
The activity of the Teacher indicates that a derivative ending in the fourth case is compounded with its base;

this is shown by the fact that he makes the mention of *balirakṣita*. How does this serve as an indicator? It indicates which types of words are included in the compound by the mention of *balirakṣita*.

The meaning is that there is a compounding of words belonging to that same class. If a word ending in the dative case, when it denotes a modification (*vikṛti*), is compounded with its source material (*prakṛti*) rather than with the mere sense of that [dative] alone, then the mention of *bali* and *akṛṣita* becomes purposeful. As for what was said—that an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for *aśvaghāsa* and so forth—it need not be made; *aśvaghāsa* and the like will be genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
For when something exists for the sake of another, there is also this relationship expressed as "this belongs to that.

For example, "this is of the teacher" (*guror idam*) means "for the sake of the teacher" (*gurvartham*). But surely there is a difference in accent? Indeed, if it were a dative compound (*caturthīsamāsa*), it would have to be accented on the first member by virtue of its original accent; however, in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), it would instead be oxytone (accented on the final syllable).

There is a distinction. Even when it is a compound with the fourth case (caturthī-samāsa), it must necessarily be oxytone (antodātta). How so? The activity of the Teacher (ācārya) indicates that a modification ending in the fourth case retains the accent of its original base (prakṛti-svara), and not merely the fourth case itself; for this reason, in the rule *caturthī tadarthe 'rthe kte ca*, he employs both the mention of "artha" and the mention of "kta. How is this so?

This is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For those items of a similar kind for which there is a purpose through the mention of "meaning" (*artha*) and the mention of "the suffix -kta" (*kta*), there is likewise the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*) for those of that same kind. And if it is the case that a derivative form (*vikṛti*) ending in the dative case becomes [accented] by its original base (*prakṛti*), and not merely the dative case-ending itself, then the mention of "meaning" and the mention of "-kta" become meaningful. Furthermore, as for what is said—that there is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*) with "meaning" (*artha*)—[it is also indicated].

"It should be stated. "It need not be stated. The suffix *sartha* will be employed. What is accomplished by this? First, there is never a case where it would be analyzed [as a separate compound]. Furthermore, the fact that it possesses all genders (*sarvaliṅgatā*) is established. If the suffix *sartha* is employed, however, the designation *it* does not apply. Even if, somehow, the designation *it* were to apply, it would still be for the sake of [the accentuation of] *śrī*."

If it were for the sake of *bhū*, then *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* would apply to the stem (*aṅgasya*). If that is so, then it will be a *bahuvrīhi* compound. What is achieved by this? Indeed, there are certain *bahuvrīhi*s whose analysis (*vigraha*) does not consist of its own constituent words (*asvapadavigraha*). For example: "she has a beautiful face" is expressed as *sumukhī*. This cannot be maintained; for in the case of *mahadartham*, the rules for *āttva* and *kap* would undesirably apply.

In that case, the word *artha* shall be substituted for the final member (*uttarapada*) which has that same meaning. What is thereby accomplished? First, there is never an analysis (*vigraha*) using the substitute form itself. Furthermore, the attainment of all genders (*sarvaliṅgatā*) is established. If so, then it must be stated. It need not be stated; rather, a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: [first] "the fourth case ending [is compounded] with a word ending in a case-suffix."

It is compounded together. Consequently, *tadarthārtha*: for the word *artha* which is the final member (*uttarapada*) signifying "for that purpose" (*tadartha*), the substitute *artha* occurs. If so, would this compounding not also apply here: *chātrāya rucitam* (pleasing to the student) and *chātrāya svaditam* (tasting good to the student)?
The activity of the Teacher indicates that only a dative case ending used in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*) is compounded, and not every dative case ending whatsoever.

That this [sūtra] includes the mention of *hita* and *sukha* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). How does it function as an indicator? It indicates that the compound is formed with those types of words for which there is a purpose by means of the inclusion of *hita* and *sukha*. If the dative case ending is compounded when it denotes "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*)—and not merely any dative case ending—then the inclusion of *hita* and *sukha* becomes meaningful.

In that case, even here, the word *artha* would result as a substitute for the final member whose meaning it expresses, as in *yūpāya dāru* → *yūpadāru* and *rathadāru*. [Objection: An option (*vāvacana*) will be prescribed. [Reply: In that case, an option would still apply here: *brāhmaṇārtham*, *kṣatriyārtham*. [Conclusion: Therefore, the activity of the Teacher indicates that this is a compound consisting of a base and its modification (*prakṛti-vikṛtyoḥ*).

In that case, the word *artha* is substituted for the final member (*uttarapada*) signifying that same meaning, except when it is obligatory; this is why [the author] makes the mention of *bali* and *hita*. If that were so, in the case of *udakārtho vīvadhaḥ*, the substitution of *uda-* would result by virtue of the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*). Therefore, it cannot be thus. If it is not thus, then an obligatory compound with the word *artha* must be stated, as well as its taking all genders (*sarvaliṅgatā*).

And this is not a fault. First, he should be asked this: now, in the expression "to the Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇebhyaḥ*), what is this dative case? He says it is used in the sense of *tādarthya* (purpose). If the dative is used in the sense of *tādarthya*, then the word "artha" should not be employed, because of the rule that words whose meaning has already been expressed are not used. In that case, even a compound would not be possible. [But] the compound occurs by virtue of an explicit statement (*vacana*).

It will be so. As for what was said—that "the fact of having all genders must also be stated"—it need not be stated. Gender is not subject to formal prescription, because gender depends upon common usage (*lokāśrayatvāt*).
(Pāṇini 2.1.37)

"This is stated too briefly when it says 'by fear' (*bhayena*). It should rather be stated as 'by fear, one who is afraid, fearfulness, and dread' (*bhaya-bhīta-bhīti-bhībhiḥ*). For example: 'fear from a wolf' is *vṛkabhaya*; 'one afraid of a wolf' is *vṛkabhīta*; 'fearfulness toward a wolf' is *vṛkabhīti*; and 'dread of a wolf' is *vṛkabhī*. Another says:
"It should be stated as 'by fear, departure, and aversion' (*bhaya-nirgata-jugupsubhiḥ*)."

"One who has gone out from the village [is called] *vṛkabhaya* (fear of wolves), and one who loathes unrighteousness [is called] *adharmajugupsu*. (Pāṇini 2.1.40). It should be stated that [the rule applies] "with *śauṇḍa*-type words" so that it may also apply here: *akṣadhūrtaḥ*, *strīdhūrtaḥ*, *akṣakitavaḥ*.

"Regarding the term *strīkitava*: if that is so, then it ought to be stated [as a separate rule]. It need not be stated; for by the mention of the plural number in the rule *śauṇḍādibhiḥ*, it will be understood [that the list includes such terms].
As for *dhvāṅkṣeṇa*, this is a reference to the meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*). A reference to the meaning must be made regarding *dhvāṅkṣeṇa*; for even here [the same applies]."
It should be as follows: "a crow at a sacred bathing place" (*tīrthakāka*). This is said in the sense of censure (*kṣepa*). What, then, is meant here by "censure"?
Just as crows do not remain for long at a sacred bathing place, so too one who goes to the teachers' households (*gurukula*) but does not stay for long is called a "crow at a sacred bathing place."

(P_2,1.43) Regarding the mention of *kṛtya* suffixes in the rule for "injunction" (*niyoga*): it should be stated that [the rule] applies "by means of *kṛtya* suffixes in the sense of an injunction. This is so that it may also apply here: "The *sāman* is to be sung before midday; the *anuvāka* is to be studied in the morning. Well then, must that be stated? No, it need not be stated.
605. What is the example? "This [effort] of yours is like a mongoose in a heated [pan]. It is stated that this occurs in the sense of censure (*kṣepa*). What is meant here by "censure"?

Just as mongooses do not remain for long in a heated [pan], so too one who does not persist for long after having begun tasks is said to be "like a mongoose in a heated [pan]" regarding this effort of yours. In the sense of censure, the locative case-ending is used.
It is stated that [a word] is compounded with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix. In that case, a compound would not be obtained for one preceded by a *gati* or for *sanakula*.

Regarding censure (*kṣepa*), it has been stated that [the rule applies] when a word preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* is involved. What was stated? That when there is the mention of a *kṛt* suffix, [the rule applies] even to that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*.

606. What is the purpose of the particle *ca*? It has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*. [The rule applies to] only those compounds beginning with *pātresamitāḥ*. Where should it not apply? As in *paramaṃ pātresamitāḥ*. (Pāṇini 2.1.49) Why does the *avyayībhāva* compound not occur here in the case of *ekā nadī = ekanadī*, where the rule *nadībhiḥ saṅkhyā* would otherwise apply? In this regard, some compounds have the meaning of the prior member as their predominant factor (*pūrvapadārthapradhāna*).

Some [compounds] have the meaning of the final member as predominant; some have the meaning of another word as predominant; some have the meanings of both members as predominant. The *avyayībhāva* has the meaning of the prior member as predominant.
A *tatpuruṣa* compound is one in which the meaning of the final member is predominant;
a *bahuvrīhi* is one in which the meaning of another word (external to the compound) is predominant;
and a *dvandva* is one in which the meanings of both members are predominant. Furthermore, predominance of the meaning of the prior member is not perceived here. Alternatively:

"Let the *avyayībhāva* be formed; let the *bahuvrīhi* be formed. The *bahuvrīhi* will prevail by way of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). This would be established if there were a governing rule for a single designation (*ekasañjñādhikāra*), but it is not established when the subsequent operation (*paraṅkāryatva*) applies. By virtue of the very fact of its formulation, the *avyayībhāva* would apply, and by virtue of the subsequent operation, the *bahuvrīhi*. And there is no fault in the case of the subsequent operation. [This applies to the compound] "number with river-names" (*nadībhiḥ saṅkhyāyāḥ*).

It should be stated that the *avyayībhāva* compound occurs in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*). And that must necessarily be stated [in the rule], as in: "The word *sarva-* [forms an *avyayībhāva*] with *ekanadītare*" (Pāṇini 2.1.51).

What is this word *samāhāra*? It is derived from the root *hṛ* preceded by the prefix *samāṅ*, with the suffix *ghañ* used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). It is that which is brought together (*samāhriyate*).

Regarding the term *samāhāraḥ*: if it is derived as an object (*karmasādhana*), as in "five girls have been gathered together" (*pañca kumāryaḥ samahṛtāḥ*), then the shortening [of the final vowel] prescribed by the rule *pañcakumāri*, *daśakumāri*—based on the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya*—would not apply; furthermore, the rule *dvigur ekavacanam* would have to be stated [separately]. Therefore, in that case, it will be derived as an action (*bhāvasādhana*). *Samāhāraḥ* means the act of gathering (*samāharaṇam*). Now, if it is derived as an action...

When [the term] *sati* is present, what is being denoted? It is that which constitutes the state of being one above and another below (*auttarādharya*). But what is the "collection" (*samāhāra*) of cows? It is their acquisition, purchase, driving, or bringing back. If this is so, it would not be established when the cows are scattered about or grazing in separate herds. In that case, then, "collection" is the act of bringing them together into proximity (*samabhyāśīkaraṇa*). Even so, [the forms] *pañcagrāmī* ("a group of five villages") and *ṣaṇṇagarī* ("a group of six cities") would still not be accounted for.

The form *tripurī* is not established. What is the reason? The prefix *sam* expresses oneness (*ekatva*), while the prefix *āṅ* denotes facing toward (*ābhimukhya*). The root *harati* means "to bring to another place" (*deśāntaraprāpaṇa*). However, the root *harati* does not necessarily denote only bringing to another place; what then? It also denotes similarity (*sādṛśya*), as for example in "he resembles his mother" (*mātuḥ anuharati*) or "he resembles his father" (*pituḥ anuharati*). Alternatively, [the term refers to] a group of five villages (*pañcagrāmī*).

The term *ṣaṇṇagarī* (the six cities) or *tripurī* (the three cities) does not terminate with just this much; it necessarily requires something further from that—either an action (*kriyā*) or a quality (*guṇa*). That which it requires is a single unit, and that constitutes a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*). But then, this fault arises when the formation is based on an abstract action (*bhāva-sādhana*): when the command "Let the five-bundle be brought" (*pañcapūlī ānīyatām*) is given, there would be the bringing of a substance (*dravya*) instead of the bringing of the action.

[The opponent says: "It does not obtain. [The proponent replies: This is not a fault. First, he should be asked this: Now, in the case of the injunctions, "A cow is to be bound for sacrifice" (*gauḥ anubandhyaḥ*) and "A goat dedicated to Agni and Soma" (*aja agnīṣomīyaḥ*), since the generic form (*ākṛti*) is what is enjoined, how is it that the acts of touching, seizing, sprinkling, and immolation are performed upon the individual substance (*dravya*)?

Because they are impossible [in the generic form]. Since the acts of touching and so forth cannot possibly exist in the generic form, they are therefore performed upon the individual substance that accompanies the generic form.

The acts of "commencing" (*ārambhaṇa*) and so forth are performed upon a substance (*dravya*). This [case] is of the same nature. Since it is impossible to bring the abstract state (*bhāva*), there will be the bringing of the substance. Or rather, because there is no distinction between the substance and its form (*ākṛti*).
609–612. But how can the designation *dvigu* apply to [a compound] ending in a suffix or a final member? It ought to be so.

If the designation *dvigu* applies to [a compound] ending in a suffix or a final member, there is non-establishment due to mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatvāt*). If the designation *dvigu* applies to [a compound] ending in a suffix or a final member, there is non-establishment due to mutual dependence. What is this mutual dependence? [It concerns] the cause for the *dvigu* designation.

When the subsequent member is a suffix (*pratyaya-uttara-pada*), the designation *dvigu* is conditioned by that subsequent member being a suffix. This results in mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). And things characterized by mutual dependence are not logically tenable. If this is so, then I shall state [the rule] as "when there is a meaning" (*arthe*). If it is "when there is a meaning," then the non-occurrence of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) follows, as in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*. If it is "when there is a meaning," the production of the secondary derivative does not obtain, as in the case of *pāñcanāpitiḥ*.

*dvimāturaḥ*, *traimāturaḥ*. What is the reason? Because it has already been expressed by a *dvigu* compound, [the rule] applies as if it were a *bahuvrīhi*. Just as in the case of *citraguḥ*, because the possessive sense (*matvartha*) has already been expressed by the *bahuvrīhi*, a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) does not occur. If that is so, then in the formulation of rules for compounds and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*),...

I shall explain this. If it is argued that [the rule] "in the prescription of compounds and secondary derivatives" (samāsa-taddhita-vidhau) applies, then the designation of "compound" (samāsa-sañjñā) would not occur elsewhere. If it is argued that [the rule] "in the prescription of compounds and secondary derivatives" applies, then the designation of "compound" does not obtain elsewhere. Where else? In the matter of accent (svara). In *pañcāratniḥ* and *daśāratniḥ*, the accent prescribed by the rule "in a dvigu compound ending in an *ik*-stem" (igante dvigau) would not obtain. However, [the desired result] is established by the rule "in the case of a suffix and a subsequent member" (pratyayottarapadayoḥ).

Because of the statement "and" (ca), this is established. How? Because of the statement "and [the designation *dvigu* applies] to the suffix (*pratyaya*) and the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). It should be stated that the designation *dvigu* applies to both the suffix and the subsequent member. But was it not said that if the designation *dvigu* were to apply to the suffix and the subsequent member, there would be a lack of establishment due to mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*)? This is not a fault; this is merely a case of mutual dependence.

All [the arguments] raised regarding mutual dependence have been resolved by [accepting them as] a unity, as established by the fact that "the word is eternal. This is not equal to other cases of mutual dependence; for a name (*saṃjñā*) is not eternal. If that is so, then the name will be understood as prospective (*bhāvinī*). For example:

Someone said to a certain weaver: "Weave a cloth from this thread. He reflects: "If it is a cloth, it need not be woven; if it is to be woven, it is not yet a cloth. That 'it is a cloth and it is to be woven' is a contradiction. Indeed, he intends a future designation for it.

I think that it is that which is to be expressed [by the compound], because in its case the designation "cloth" (śāṭaka) occurs. Likewise here as well, the designation "dvigu" applies to that whose completion results in the subsequent member being a suffix (pratyaya); thus these two designations will apply.
Or rather, let it be in the sense of "artha. But was it not said: "If it is in the sense of 'artha,' there would be no production of a taddhita suffix, just as in the case of a bahuvrīhi"?

Thus [it is argued]. This is not a fault. The word *artha* does not necessarily refer only to that which is denoted (*abhidheya*). What then? It also refers to the purpose (*syād-artha*). For example: "We strive for the sake of a wife" (*dārārtham ghaṭāmahe*), "We beg for the sake of wealth" (*dhanārtham bhikṣāmahe*), "May we have wives," or "May we have wealth. In the same way, here too, a *dvigu* compound occurs in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).

It should be that a *taddhita* suffix occurs. Alternatively, the statement regarding the elision (*luk*) of the suffix after a *dvigu* compound is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that a *taddhita* suffix arises [there]. Or rather, when the Teacher teaches the elision of the *taddhita* suffix following a *dvigu*—in the rule "there is elision of the *taddhita* following a *dvigu*, except for those denoting offspring" (*dvigor lug anapatye*)—that indicates that a *taddhita* suffix is produced after a *dvigu*.

Since there is no distinction between *samāhāra* (aggregation) and *samūha* (collection), the mention of *samāhāra* [in the rule] is redundant, because it has already been accounted for by the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
These two meanings—*samāhāra* and *samūha*—are indistinguishable. Because there is no difference between *samāhāra* and *samūha*, the mention of *samāhāra* [is unnecessary].

It is purposeless. What is the reason? Because it has already been formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Since it is stated that "a *dvigu* compound occurs in the sense of a secondary derivative," the *dvigu* will apply here in this manner. If the *dvigu* applies here because it occurs in the sense of a secondary derivative, then the production of the secondary suffix would follow. Let it be produced; there will be its elision (*luk*). But then the grammatical operations conditioned by elision would apply. Which ones? [The feminine suffix] *-ī* in *pañcapūlī*.
Regarding *daśapūlī*: the prohibition [of the feminine suffix] "na taddhitaluki" (Pāṇini 4.1.88) would apply to words such as *aparimāṇa*, *bista*, *ācita*, and *kambala*.

In *pañcagava* and *daśagava*, the suffix *ṭac* (Pāṇini 5.2.29), which applies to the word *go* when no *taddhita* suffix follows, would not apply. This is not a fault. Having stated that the suffix *ṅīp* applies to a *dvigu* compound without qualification, I shall subsequently state that it applies specifically to a collective (*samāhāra*) compound. That [subsequent rule] will serve the purpose of a restriction (*niyama*).

"Only in a collective compound (*samāhāra*), and not elsewhere. [Objection: Since it has been stated that the suffix *ṭac* is applied to the word *go-* without distinction in a *dvigu* compound, one might say: "I shall state 'in a *dvigu* compound' [specifically] for a collective. That [specification] would then serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning "only in a collective, and not elsewhere. [Response: However, it must be stated for the sake of expression (*abhidhānārtha*). Indeed, the mention of "collective" (*samāhāra*) must be made for the purpose of expressing [the specific meaning].

The purpose is so that there may be expression by means of a collective compound (*samāhāra*), and not by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) sense. What would be the consequence? The production of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) would result. Let it be produced. [But] elision (*luk*) will occur. [If so,] the grammatical operations conditioned by elision would apply. [Reply: All such cases have been avoided. [Objection: They are not all avoided. For example, *pañcakumāri* and *daśakumāri*. By the rule *liṅg-taddhita-luki*, there would be elision of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.

[Otherwise] it would follow [that the rule does not apply]. It must be stated that for *dvandva* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds, there is obligatory composition (*nityasamāsa*) when a subsequent member follows. [Examples are: *vāgdṛṣadapriyaḥ*, *chatropānahapriyaḥ*, *pañcagavapriyaḥ*, *daśagavapriyaḥ*. What is the purpose? So that when the whole functions [as a compound], the parts do not occasionally fail to function [as such].

Thus it is said. Then that must be stated. It need not be stated. Here there are two positions: the position of occurrence (*vṛttipakṣa*) and the position of non-occurrence (*avṛttipakṣa*). When it is the position of occurrence, then there is occurrence for all [the members]. But when it is non-occurrence, then there is non-occurrence for all. The statement regarding the compound (*samāsa*) of a *dvigu* with a word denoting a measure (*parimāṇin*) by means of a subsequent member: the *dvigu* is a compound with a subsequent member denoting a measure.

It should be stated: "two months old," "three months old. But what is the reason that it is not established? [Because] the rule *sup supā* (noun with noun) continues to apply. If that is so, then this would be the case:
*dvau māsau* becomes *dvimāsam*.

Regarding the expression *dvimāsa-jātasya*: it cannot be so. For there would be a fault in the accent; *dvimāsajātaḥ* would result, whereas *dvimāsajātaḥ* (with a different accent) is desired. Furthermore, *dvyāhnajātaḥ* would not be established; *dvyahajātaḥ* would result, and it ought not to be so. It should indeed be so when [the compound] is a *dvigu* in the sense of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*). However, in the case of *dvyahnajātaḥ*, it is not.

It is established. Why is it said [only] "by that which possesses a measure" (*parimāṇin*), and not elsewhere as well? For example, *pañcagavapriyaḥ* ("one who loves five cows") and *daśagavapriyaḥ* ("one who loves ten cows").

Elsewhere, because it is a collective *bahuvrīhi*, the status of being the final member (*uttarapada*) is established. Elsewhere, there is the designation of a collective *bahuvrīhi*. Because it is a collective *bahuvrīhi* elsewhere, the status of being the final member is established. When the status of being the final member is established, [the rule applies] in the case of the final member.

Thus, it will be a *dvigu* compound. There is a prohibition regarding the possessive sense (*matvartha*) in all cases. In all these alternative views, a prohibition of the *dvigu* designation must be stated when the possessive sense is intended. What is the purpose? [In examples such as] *pañcakhaṭvā* ("five beds") and *daśakhaṭvā* ("ten beds"), let there not be the feminine suffix *īkāra* [prescribed] by the rule "after a *dvigu*. [And in examples such as] *pañcaguḥ* ("worth five cows") and *daśaguḥ* ("worth ten cows"), let there not be the suffix *ṭac* [prescribed] by the rule "after *go*, except when a *taddhita* suffix follows that causes *luk*."

(P_2.1.52) KA_I,396.13–23 Ro_II,617–618: Is that which is preceded by a numeral designated as *dvigu* only when it occurs in the immediately following rule, or even when it occurs merely before [the rule]? And what follows from this? If it were only in the immediately following rule, then in the case of *ekaśāṭī*, the feminine suffix *īkāra* would not apply according to the rule "of a *dvigu*. If, however, it applies merely before [the rule]...

In this case as well, the form *ekabhikṣā* would result. Let it be so for the immediately preceding case. As for *ekaśāṭī*, let there be a compound with a word ending in the vowel *ī*; thus, "one garment" is *ekaśāṭī*. But then, in the case of *ekāpūpī*, the suffix *ī* prescribed by the rule *dvigoḥ* would not apply. Well then, let it be so for the [word] ending in the first vowel (*ā*) alone.
