How then is *ekabhikṣā* formed? It will be a compound with a word ending in the suffix *ṭā*; thus, "one alms-begging" is *ekā bhikṣā*.

[Objection: In this case, for *ekabhikṣā*, the accent [of the final member] would apply by the rule "in a *dvigu* compound ending in a vowel. [Response: Let it be so then in the case of the immediately preceding [rule]. [Question: How then is *ekāpūpī* formed? [Response: It is established by the very rule "in a collective (*samāhāra*) [compound]. [Question: But what is the "collection" (*samāhāra*) here? [Response: It is that gift or that haste. [Objection: In this case then, for *pañcahotāraḥ* and *daśahotāraḥ*, [the accent would apply] by the rule "in a *dvigu* compound ending in a vowel."
This accent does not apply. Let it then be [the case] where there is only a preceding [vowel]. How is *saptarṣayaḥ* [accounted for]?

This is established by the rule *tricakrādīnāṃ chandasi* within the section concerning words with an udātta on the final syllable (*antodātta*). Or rather, let it be [the case] where there is no interval (*anantara*). How are *pañcahotāraḥ* and *daśahotāraḥ* [accounted for]? This is likewise established by the rule *divodāsādīnāṃ chandasi* within the section concerning words with an udātta on the initial syllable (*ādyudātta*).

(P_2,1.53) What is the example? *vaiyākaraṇakhasūciḥ*. Is it that grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is contemptible, or rather the grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*)? It is the grammarian who is contemptible. When that [person] is contemptible, even that which resides in him (*tatstha*) becomes contemptible.

It is stated: "The standards of comparison (*upamāna*). But what, then, are the standards of comparison? Is that which is the standard of comparison the very same as the object of comparison (*upameya*), or is the standard of comparison one thing and the object of comparison another? And what follows from this? If that which is the standard of comparison...

If it were that very same thing which is the object of comparison (*upameya*), what would be the purpose of the comparison here, as in "a cow is like a cow"? Or, if the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) were one thing and the object of comparison another, what would be the purpose of the comparison here, as in "a cow is like a horse"? In that case, the standard of comparison and the object of comparison exist only where there is some commonality and some distinction. Is this something that needs to be stated? No, indeed. Why?

It will be understood even when not explicitly stated. For a means of knowledge (*māna*) is indeed employed for the purpose of knowing what is not yet known, with the thought, "I shall know an object not yet known. That which measures something nearby, but not definitively, is a means of comparison (*upamāna*), as in "the *gavaya* is like a cow.
Here, the cow is already known, while the *gavaya* is unknown. Therefore, by this very same reason, [comparison applies] to one for whom the *gavaya*—

The cow would be already known; therefore, the gavaya would have to be made known as "the cow is like that," just as it is not yet known. Certainly, it must be so made known. But what is the example here? "Dark as a sword-blade" (*śastrīśyāmā*). But where does this word *śyāmā* (dark) apply? He says: "To the sword-blade. By what, then, is Devadatta denoted now? By the compound. If this is so, then [the compound] is "Devadatta is dark as a sword-blade" (*śastrīśyāmo devadattaḥ*).

Thus, it is not established. [Objection: The shortening will occur because [the word] is an *upasarjana*. [Reply: If, then, even such items as these are considered *upasarjana*s, then in the case of *tittirikalmāṣī* and *kumbhakapālalohinī*, the long vowel *ī*—which is conditioned by the rule for non-*upasarjana*s—would not be obtained. [Reply: In that case, the word *śastrī* applies only to the knife, while the word *śyāmā* applies to Devadattā.
Even so, the quality remains unspecified. There are many qualities of a sword, such as being sharp, fine, or broad;

yet, even when a quality is not explicitly specified, it is understood in common usage. For example, in the expression "Devadatta has a moon-like face," although there are many qualities in the moon, that specific quality of being pleasant to behold is what is conveyed. In this same way...

The phrase "even with a word in grammatical apposition" (samānādhikaraṇena) continues to apply here. Because [the words] are in different grammatical relations (vyadhikaraṇatvāt), the compound does not obtain. Why indeed would it not occur by virtue of an explicit rule? Even if a compound were to occur by virtue of such a rule, in this case—namely, *mṛgacapalā* (as fickle as a deer)—the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) characterized by grammatical apposition would not obtain. If that is so, then in that very same [case]...

Both [qualities] reside [in Devadattā]. And this is logical here: that both reside in her alone. For otherwise, much would have to be taken into account. If first the analysis (vigraha) is made thus: "Devadattā is dark like a sword-blade," then "darkness in the sword-blade" would have to be taken into account. But if the analysis is made thus: "as dark as a sword-blade," [then it is not so].

In the same way, if one says "this is Devadattā," then regarding Devadattā, it would still be necessary to specify that she is "dark-complexioned. Even so, the quality remains unspecified. There are many qualities in a sword, such as being sharp, fine, and broad. Yet, even when a quality is not explicitly specified, there is a conventional understanding of it in the world; for example, when one says, "Devadattā has a moon-like face. There are many [qualities].

The qualities [of the moon], such as that which is its "lovely appearance," are understood [in the expression *candra iva priyadarśanā*]. In a compound where the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is the first member, because the word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*) partakes of a specific [quality], there would be no application of a word expressing a general quality (*sāmānyavacana*). In a compound where the standard of comparison is the first member, because the word expressing a quality partakes of a specific [quality], there would be no application of a word expressing a general quality. For example, in *śastrīśyāmā*: this word *śyāmā*, when connected with the word *śastrī*, [functions as a specific quality].

It becomes a term expressing a specific quality (*viśeṣavacana*). In that case, a compound [formed] with "terms expressing general qualities" (*sāmānyavacanaiḥ*) would not be applicable. Alternatively, there is no such fault. Why? Because the quality of blackness (*śyāmatva*) exists in both places, and because the word expresses that [quality], it is established as a term expressing a general quality (*sāmānyavacanaprasiddhi*). Indeed, the quality of blackness exists in both places; it is precisely in both places that blackness resides.

It exists in both the knife (*śastrī*) and Devadatta, because the word denotes that [quality]. The conventional usage of it as a term for a universal (*sāmānya-vacana*) is established, and here the word "dark" (*śyāma*) is employed as a denoter of that. What does it denote? It denotes both. Since the quality of darkness (*śyāmatva*) exists in both and the word denotes that, its status as a term for a universal is well-established. In the case of a term for a universal—

The compound will be formed as *prasiddhe sāmānyavacanaiḥ*. Furthermore, it is not necessarily only that which expresses the commonality of many things that is called "expressive of a general property" (*sāmānyavacana*). That which expresses the commonality of even two things is also indeed expressive of a general property. Alternatively, it is said "by those expressive of a general property"; and every word, when connected with another word, [is so].
It becomes a term expressing a specific quality (*viśeṣavacana*). We shall understand it thus: prior to its connection [with another word], it is a general term (*sāmānyavacana*). (P.
2.1.56) For what purpose is the phrase "when there is no employment of a general term" (*sāmānyāprayoge*)? It is so that it does not apply here: "This man is brave like a tiger."

This person is strong like a tiger. The phrase "when not used with a common term" (*sāmānyāprayoge*) could have been omitted. Why does it not occur in such cases as "this person is brave like a tiger" or "this person is strong like a tiger"? Because of a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*). How is there a lack of competency? Because that which is dependent [on another] is semantically incompetent. If that is so, then...

Since the rule *siddhe sati yat sāmānyāprayoge* (P. 2.1.57) teaches a prohibition, the Teacher thereby indicates that a compound is indeed formed even when the principal member is dependent (*sāpekṣa*). What is the purpose of this indication? [In examples such as] *rājapuruṣo 'bhirūpaḥ* ("the king's man is handsome") and *rājapuruṣo darśanīyaḥ* ("the king's man is beautiful"), the formation of the compound is thereby established.

Because both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) are qualifiers of each other, and because both are also the qualified, there is no established status of being a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). Since both the qualifier and the qualified are qualifiers of each other, and both are also the qualified, there is no established status of being a subordinate member.

In the expression "black sesame seeds" (*kṛṣṇatilāḥ*), this word "black" (*kṛṣṇa*) becomes a qualifier when connected with the word "sesame" (*tila*); likewise, the word "sesame" becomes a qualifier when connected with the word "black. Thus, both are qualifiers and both are the qualified. This is because both the qualifier and the qualified function as qualifiers for one another.

Because both [members] are qualificands (*viśeṣya*), there would be no established status of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*). Or rather, this is not a fault. Why? Because one of the two is the principal (*pradhāna*). Since the other qualifies it, the status of the subordinate member is established for that [other]. Or rather, this is not a fault. What is the reason?
Because one of the two is the principal. In this case, one is the principal, and because the other qualifies it, [the status of the subordinate member is established].

And there is another [reason] for its being a qualifier: because one member possesses the status of the principal (*pradhāna*) and the other possesses the status of a qualifier (*viśeṣaka*), the other will receive the designation of the subordinate (*upasarjana*). When the sesame seeds are intended to be expressed as the principal and "black" as the qualifier, then the sesame seeds are the principal and "black" is the qualifier. Well then, let it be by this very reason.

If blackness is intended to be the primary factor and sesame seeds are intended as a qualifier, then one should form the compound *tilakṛṣṇāḥ*. It should not be formed [otherwise], for this is not a *dvandva* compound meaning "sesame seeds and black things. Nor indeed is it a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound meaning "the black ones of the sesame seeds. What then? These two words, both being primary, are simultaneously restricted to a single referent.

Furthermore, there is no purpose whatsoever in two principal words being simultaneously restricted to a single referent. From their usage, this must be understood: "Surely, in this case, one is the principal [term] and the other is its qualifier. However, in that regard, there is this much doubt: which is the principal and which is the qualifier?

And where does that doubt arise? Where both words denote qualities, as for example: *kuñjakhañjakaḥ* (the hunchbacked-lame) or *khañjakubjakaḥ* (the lame-hunchbacked). For where one [term] denotes a substance and the other a quality, there the substance is primary. As for example: "One should sacrifice a white [animal]," "One should sacrifice a black [animal]"—one does not perform the sacrifice by offering a ball of flour.

One who has completed his task necessarily requires a substance possessing those qualities. How then can these two primary terms, "tree" and "śiṃśipā," be simultaneously restricted to a single referent? There is no necessity for their co-occurrence;
for there is no such thing as a *śiṃśipā* that is not a tree.

(P_2,1.58) Now, for what purpose is such a sequential enumeration made hereafter, since it would already be established by the rule *viśeṣaṇam viśeṣyeṇa bahulam*? Because the expression "frequently" (*bahula*) is not all-inclusive, there is the necessity for a sequential enumeration hereafter.

The statement "it is incomplete" is a frequent expression; therefore, it is repeated later on. If it is incomplete, then whatever has been done by this [author] remains undone. If that is so, then we do not say it is "incomplete"; rather, it is complete, effective, successful, and accomplishing. And whatever has been done by him has been well-done. For what purpose, then, is there such a sequence of statements?

It is done because of the abundance of examples. Indeed, those rules (*vidhi*) are well-grasped which include both the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and the elaboration (*prapañca*). A mere definition or a mere elaboration is not so effective as an instrument of instruction. We must certainly state this: [the rule applies] frequently, optionally, in both ways, or according to some authorities.

Thus [it is said]. For this treatise is the seat of all the Vedas; therein, it is not possible to adhere to a single path. (Pāṇini 2.1.59) The *śreṇyādi* group is recited. The *kṛtādi* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. Regarding the *śreṇyādi* group, there is the mention of the sense of the suffix *cvy-* (*cvi-artha*). In the *śreṇyādi* group—

The inclusion of the term *cvyartha* (the sense of the suffix *cvi*) must be stated [as a restriction]. [For example: *aśreṇayaḥ śreṇayaḥ kṛtāḥ* = *śreṇikṛtāḥ*. This is so that when the very things that are already guilds (*śreṇi*) are made into something else, [the rule] should not apply. Elsewhere, in these instances where *cvyartha* is mentioned, it teaches a prohibition of that which ends in *cvi*; however, it is not so here. What is the reason? Because elsewhere, first the operation pertaining to the form ending in *cvi* takes effect, and subsequently the operation pertaining to the sense of *cvi*.
In this case, however, the operation concerning the *pūrva* (the prior element) takes precedence over the operation concerning the *para* (the subsequent element).

2.1.60) Regarding that which is qualified by the negative particle (*nañ*), there must be a statement concerning the common base form. That is to say, one must provide a rule regarding the common base form when [a compound] is qualified by the negative particle.

In this case, let it not be [the case that] "accomplished" (*siddha*) and "not yet enjoyed" (*abhukta*) [form a compound]. Furthermore, a prohibition must be stated regarding the term *anañ* (negations other than *na*). In this case, let it not be [the case that] "to be done" (*kartavya*) and "not done" (*akṛta*) [form a compound]. And [a rule] concerning the addition of the augment *nuṭ* and the suffix *iṭ*: a compound must be stated for cases involving the addition of *nuṭ* and *iṭ*. So that it may also apply here: "he lives by what has been eaten and what has not been eaten" (*aśitānaśitena jīvati*), "he lives by what has been afflicted and what has not been afflicted" (*kliṣṭākliśitena jīvati*). Why is this said?

The inclusion of the term "of the same nature" (*samānaprakṛti*) must be made when it is stated that [the rule applies] "by means of what is qualified by *nañ*. And here, the distinction is not caused by *nañ* alone; rather, it is also caused by the root [meaning]. This word "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*) indeed exists and functions in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). For example: "Devadatta and Yajñadatta are wealthy, handsome, beautiful, and winged."

But Devadatta is distinguished from Yajñadatta by his Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). It is understood that it is by Vedic study alone [that he is distinguished]; other qualities are equal. It functions in the sense of superiority. For example: "Devadatta and Yajñadatta are wealthy, handsome, beautiful, and strong; however, Devadatta is distinguished from Yajñadatta by his Vedic study."

By means of *svādhyāya* (repetition for study), other qualities become unintended (*avivakṣita*). Thus, when the word *viśiṣṭa* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), then there is no purpose served by the inclusion of "having the same base" (*samānaprakṛti*); it will not apply here in the case of *siddham ca abhuktam ca*. Nor is there a need for the prohibition regarding *anañ*; it will not apply here in the case of *kartavyam akṛtam*.

But even with the addition of *nuṭ* and *iṭ*, a compound would not be obtained at that time. When the word *viśiṣṭa* (qualified) is used to denote an excess, then the mention of "having the same base" (*samānaprakṛti*) must be made; otherwise, it would apply here to cases such as *ṣiddham ca abhuktam ca*. Furthermore, a prohibition of the negative particle (*anañ*) must be stated; otherwise, it would apply here to cases such as *kartavyam akṛtam*. However, even with the addition of *nuṭ* and *iṭ*, the formation of the compound is established.

In that regard, considering that the mention of "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*) implies an excess [of elements], the inclusion of "having the same base" (*samānaprakṛti*) is enjoined. If the restriction were made by means of the negative particle (*nañ*), it would not be applicable to those qualified by the augment *nuṭ* or *iṭ*. Alternatively, if there is an intention to express an excess, the operation applies to that which has the same base. Furthermore, there must be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for cases such as *kṛtāpakṛta*; indeed, there must be an addition for cases such as *kṛtāpakṛta*. [The example is: *kṛtāpakṛtam*.
"‘Eaten and uneaten,’ ‘drunk and undrunk. This is established by the rule *siddhaṃ tu ktena viṣamāptāv anañ* (P. 2.1.60). How so?

It should be stated that a word ending in a *kta*-suffix is compounded with another word ending in a *kta*-suffix when there is an incompleteness of action (*kriyāviṣamāpti*), provided it is not preceded by the negative particle *nañ*. And there must be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for cases such as *gatapratyāgata* ('gone and returned'). An addition must be made for *gatapratyāgata* and similar forms. [Example: *gatapratyāgatam*."
*yātānuyātam*, *puṭāpuṭikā*, *krayākrayikā*, *phalāphalikā*, *mānonmānikā*.

(Pāṇini 2.1.67) This formulation is incorrect. The term *samānādhikaraṇena* (with words in apposition) continues to apply [from the previous rule]. What possibility is there for [the formation of] words with different referents (*vyadhikaraṇa*)?

There would be a compound. If that is so, then the Teacher indicates that a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) of a certain grammatical type is compounded with a preceding member (*pūrvapada*) of that same type. What is the purpose of this indication? It is that the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*)—"when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, the mention includes that which is qualified by gender" (*liṅgaviśiṣṭasya*)—need not be formulated.
This is now considered: is this a compound with the third case ending [expressing] "by means of a letter"? Or is it otherwise?

Is *kṛṣṇasāraṅgaḥ* a compound formed with a coordinate term (*sāmānādhikaraṇa*), as in "a black-spotted [animal]"—that is, "the black one is spotted"—or is it something else? And what is the distinction here? A third-case compound (*tṛtīyāsamāsa*) is formed with a color-word; however, in the prohibition of that [third-case compound], the mention of "color" (*varṇagrahaṇa*) must be made. A third-case compound is formed with a color-word; but in the prohibition of that, the mention of "color" must be performed. Third case...

The preceding word has its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). It should be stated that [the rule applies] when there is no *avarṇa*. Now, what is the purpose of the second mention of the term "vowel" (*varṇa*) as a qualifier for *eta*? Certainly, there is a purpose, provided that the word *eta* exists without an *avarṇa*. But does such a word exist? Yes, for example: *āitaḥ*, *etaḥ*, *kṛṣṇetaḥ*.

Regarding the word *lohitetaḥ*: there is no purpose served by the inclusion of the term "color" (*varṇa*) for this specific meaning. If, first of all, this *kta* suffix is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), then by the rule "the third [acute accent] is on the word ending in the *kta* suffix when it denotes the object" (*tṛtīyā karmaṇi*), this accent ought to occur. Alternatively, if it is used in the sense of the agent, then because it is a subsequent rule, the accent of the *kṛt* suffix (*kṛtsvara*) ought to occur. Now, if it is in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), then in the case of apposition, the term "color" (*varṇa*) is mentioned twice; that is, in the section concerning apposition.

The mention of "color" (varṇa) must be stated twice. It should be said: "A color [is compounded] with colors. One mention of "color" must be made so that this does not apply here: *paramaśuklaḥ* (extremely white), *paramakṛṣṇaḥ* (extremely black). A second mention of "color" must be made so that this does not apply here: *kṛṣṇatilāḥ* (black sesame seeds). One mention of "color" is redundant; why is it not [applied] to one or the other?

It does not occur; for between that which is expressed by a technical term (*lakṣaṇa*) and that which is expressed by its specific wording (*pratipadokta*), the preference goes to the one expressed by its specific wording. This being the case, there are these three occurrences of the mention of "vowel" (*varṇagrahaṇa*): two in the rule prescribing compounds (*samāsavidhi*) and one in the rule prescribing accent (*svaravidhi*).
Even for one who holds that the compound is formed with the third case, there are likewise those same three occurrences of the mention of "vowel": two in the rule prescribing compounds.

And regarding the rule for accentuation (*svaravidhi*), [the word] *ekam* [is used]. In general, my position will be that there is a third-case compound (*tṛtīyāsamāsa*) according to the rule: "A word in the third case is compounded with a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) when it denotes that which is produced by it. However, a specific compound (*pratipada-samāsa*) with *varṇena* must necessarily be stated for those cases where it is not established by that [general rule]. And where is it not established by that? In cases such as *śukababhruḥ* ("light-brown") and *haritababhruḥ* ("greenish-brown"). This being so...

There are exactly three mentions of *varṇa*: two in the rule for compound formation (*samāsa-vidhi*) and one in the rule for vowel application (*svara-vidhi*). Now, if the term *samānādhikaraṇa* were established by general rule, [the answer is]: "Certainly it is established. "How? "By the rule: *viśeṣaṇam viśeṣyeṇa bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.57). Even so, two mentions of *varṇa* must be made; [the mention] in the rule for vowel application refers specifically to that which is explicitly stated (*pratipadokta*).
Because of its non-existence [as a separate entity], this position— that it is a term in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*)— is superior.
Regarding the section on terms in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇādhikāra*), among primary and secondary members, the subsequent [rule] prevails by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).
In the section concerning words in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), among principal and subordinate members, the subsequent [term] prevails by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*):

among principals, the principal; among subordinates, the subordinate. First, regarding the principal: the scope for the rule "one being honored with *vṛndāraka*, *nāga*, or *kuñjara*" is, for example, *govṛndārakaḥ* (an excellent bull) and *aśvavṛndārakaḥ* (an excellent horse). Next, the scope for the rule concerning *poṭā* and *yuvati* [is as follows].

*ibhyayuvatiḥ* (the wife of a wealthy man), *āḍhyayuvatiḥ* (the wife of a rich man). Here, both [rules] would apply. In *nāgayuvatiḥ* (the wife of a Nāga) and *vṛndārakayuvatiḥ* (an excellent woman), that which follows the principal members occurs by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). For subordinate members (*upasarjana*), that which follows the subordinate member occurs. The scope of the rule *sanmahatparamotkṛṣṭāḥ* is, for example, *sadgavaḥ* (an excellent ox) and *sadaśvaḥ* (an excellent horse). The scope of the rule *kṛtyatulyākhyā ajātyā* is, for example, *tulyaśvetaḥ* (as white as snow).
*tulyakṛṣṇaḥ*. Here, both [rules] would apply:

*tulyasat* and *tulyamahān*. By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the subsequent member becomes the subordinate element (*upasarjana*) among subordinate elements. The *bahuvrīhi* takes precedence over the *samānādhikaraṇa* compound; by way of conflict, the *bahuvrīhi* occurs in place of the *samānādhikaraṇa* compound. [This applies] to the *samānādhikaraṇa* compound.

*Avakāśaḥ* (opportunity), *vīraḥ puruṣaḥ* (a brave man), and *vīrapuruṣaḥ* (having brave men) [are examples]. *Kaṇṭhekālaḥ* (one whose throat is black) is an opportunity for the *bahuvrīhi* compound. Here, both [compounds] would apply: *vīrapuruṣakaḥ grāmaḥ* (a village having brave men). By means of *vipratiṣedha* (conflict/exception), the *bahuvrīhi* occurs. Sometimes the *karmadhāraya* occurs for the sake of words such as *sarvadhanādi*. Sometimes the *karmadhāraya* occurs instead of the *bahuvrīhi*. What is the purpose?

The purpose [of this rule] concerns all types of wealth and so forth: *sarvadhanī* (possessing all wealth), *sarvabījī* (possessing all seeds), *sarvakeśī naṭaḥ* (an actor possessing all hair), *gaurakharavat vanam* (a forest possessing white donkeys), *gauramṛgavat vanam* (a forest possessing white deer), *kṛṣṇasarpavān valmīkaḥ* (an anthill possessing black snakes), and *lohitaśālimān grāmaḥ* (a village possessing red rice). What is the purpose? So that there may be expression by means of possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*) applied to the bases of *karmadhāraya* compounds. And what is the reason it would not otherwise occur? Because the meaning has already been expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound.

Regarding the possessive suffix (*matvartha*): if "already being expressed" (*uktatva*) is the reason, then it would not apply even in the case of a *karmadhāraya*, because [the meaning] is already expressed by that as well. Furthermore, the possessive suffix does not depend on the technical name (*saṃjñā*); rather, it depends on the meaning (*artha*). Just as it does not occur because the meaning is already expressed by a *bahuvrīhi*, so too it will not occur because the meaning is already expressed by a *karmadhāraya*. If that is the case, then this [rule] should be formulated as follows:
"Those who acquire all wealth are 'possessors of all wealth' (*sarvadhanī*). This is not possible.

If it were always thus, it would necessarily be a *karmadhāraya* compound. Therefore, what was said—that sometimes it is a *karmadhāraya*—is incorrect. If that is so, then indeed some teachers recite [the word] having formed an understanding of it as having a specific purpose.
Words should be formed [accordingly]. Similarly, this has been stated: "From a *samānādhikaraṇa* compound, a *bahuvrīhi* should be made;

sometimes a *karmadhāraya* is made for the sake of [expressing] 'all wealth' (*sarvadhanādi*) and so forth. As for the claim that "a *bahuvrīhi* occurs from a *samānādhikaraṇa* compound by way of *vipratiṣedha* (conflict of rules)," this *vipratiṣedha* is not tenable, because the *karmadhāraya* is *antaraṅga* (internal/within the domain).

What is the internal nature [of the rule]? A *karmadhāraya* compound occurs when the meaning of its own constituent members is intended; a *bahuvrīhi* compound occurs when the meaning of another word is intended. Let it be so. There is an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the *karmadhāraya*:

when it is not a *karmadhāraya*, then it will be a *bahuvrīhi*. Even so, if at some point a *karmadhāraya* does occur here, there would be expression by means of possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*) based on the original forms of the *karmadhāraya*.

[The suffix] is obtained. And all this effort for such a purpose is so that there may not be expression by means of possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*) based on *karmadhāraya* compounds. If that is the case, then this is not an example of that rule [Pāṇini 2.4.2], "In the case of conflict, the subsequent [rule prevails]. What then? This is stated as a desired result (*iṣṭi*). A *bahuvrīhi* compound is desired over a *samānādhikaraṇa* compound.

Sometimes the *karmadhāraya* compound is used for the sake of expressing "all wealth" and so forth. If the *iṣṭi* has been recited, there is no purpose served by this [compound]. For here, all human beings desire great objects with little effort: a hundred thousand for a single *māṣa*, or a thousand *khārīs* for a single spade. In that case, the expression is formed by adding possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*) to the bases of the *karmadhāraya* compounds.

"Let it be by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound"—it will be so by means of a *bahuvrīhi* because of its brevity. [Objection: How then do we account for forms such as *sarvadhanī*, *sarvabījī*, and *sarvakeśī naṭaḥ*? [Response: In the section on the suffix *-in*, I shall state that *-in* is added after words beginning with *sarva*. And this must necessarily be stated in order to supersede the suffix *-ṭhan*. [Objection: How then do we account for *gaurakharavat vanam*, *gauramṛgavat vanam*, and *kṛṣṇasarpavān*?
"Valmīkaḥ" refers to a village possessing red rice; there is a distinction here: the connection is made by way of genus (*jāti*).

"Kṛṣṇasarpaḥ" means a species of snake; that [species] exists in this anthill (*valmīka*). For when the connection between those possessing [the quality] is made without [explicitly mentioning] the genus—as in "a black snake anthill"—then it will be so [expressed]. [This applies] when there is an excellence in the first member of the compound.

A *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed after a superlative suffix (*ātiśāyika*) for the purpose of expressing meanings such as "one whose garment is finer" (*sūkṣmavastratara*). When there is a superlative in the first member of the compound, a *bahuvrīhi* occurs by way of a counter-exception (*vipratiṣedha*). What is the purpose? It is for the sake of forms such as *sūkṣmavastratara*. The scope of the superlative suffix is, for example, *paṭutaraḥ* ("more clever") or *paṭutamaḥ* ("most clever"). The scope of the *bahuvrīhi* is, for example, *citraguḥ* ("one who has variegated cows") or *śabalaguḥ* ("one who has brindled cows"). In this case, both [rules] apply.

[One might argue that] *sūkṣmavastrataraḥ* and *tīkṣṇaśṛṅgataraḥ* would result [from the application of the comparative suffix], because the *bahuvrīhi* compound takes precedence by way of prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*). This prohibition is not correct. It is stated that "in a prohibition, that which is subsequent prevails. However, the *bahuvrīhi* is prior, while the superlative suffix (*ātiśāyika*) is subsequent. The word "subsequent" (*para*) denotes what is desired. In a prohibition, that which is desired is what prevails.

Even so, it is incorrect. [The suffix] expressing excellence (*ātiśāyika*) is internal (*antaraṅga*). What is its internality? The suffix expressing excellence is applied after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṅī* or *āp*; whereas the *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed from words ending in case-terminations (*subanta*). Thus, the suffix expressing excellence is not internal either. How so? A secondary derivative (*taddhita*) arises from a word that has semantic capacity (*samartha*), and this semantic capacity resides in what ends in a case-termination. Even so, it is internal. How? Because the suffix expressing excellence applies to the meaning of its own constituent members (*svapadārtha*).

The *bahuvrīhi* compound occurs when there is a referent other than the constituent words. Even so, it is not *antaraṅga*. Why? Because the suffix expressing excellence (*ātiśāyika*) occurs in relation to competition (*spardhā*), and competition does not occur without a counterpart (*pratiyogin*). Or rather, the suffix expressing excellence would not even apply here at all. What is the reason? Because of a lack of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*). How is there a lack of capacity? That which is dependent [on another] lacks capacity.

Thus [it is said]. To the extent that garments depend upon one who possesses them, and depending upon one who possesses them, there arises a simultaneous rivalry between the garments and the garments themselves. But surely this superlative suffix (*ātiśāyika*) is prescribed when such a mutual dependence exists? True, it is of such a nature; yet it occurs when that dependence exists without which its application would not take place.

It must be so. And without dependence on what [else], would there not be the application of the comparative suffix (*ātiśāyika*)? For that dependence which is toward a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), and that which is toward one who possesses it (*tadvant*), in those cases it should not occur. In that case, even the *bahuvrīhi* compound would not be obtained. What is the reason? Precisely because of a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*). How is there a lack of semantic capacity? Because that which is dependent is semantically incapable.

It occurs thus: to the extent that garments require other garments, there is a connection with that [requirement]. If this is so, then this is not an illustration of that rule "in case of conflict, the latter [prevails]. What then?
This is a desired reading. When there is excellence of the prior member, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is desired after a superlative suffix (*ātiśāyika*).

"Regarding the phrase 'for the sake of finer garments and so forth': if this *iṣṭi* (desire) were merely recited, there would be no purpose served by it. How then is this reasoning stated—namely, that garments require other garments, and thus there is a connection with those [possessing them]—since when a garment is connected with other garments without opposition, it is indeed without a rival?"
In that case, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. From a *bahuvrīhi*, the superlative suffix (*ātiśāyika*) is applied. If so, then this form would not occur now:

*sūkṣmataravastraḥ* ("one whose garment is more subtle"). It does occur. When, without reference to a possessor of the quality (*tadvant*), there is a simultaneous rivalry among garments themselves, then the superlative suffix is applied. But how can the excellence of one thing [be expressed] by means of another?

There would be excellence [of one thing] by means of the excellence of another; however, it is not the case that through the excellence of one thing there must necessarily be excellence of another. Just as one exerts effort regarding substances, thinking, "May I have garments," so too does one exert effort regarding qualities, thinking, "May they be finer. In this case, the suffix denoting comparative excellence (*ātiśāyika*) does not apply. What is the reason? It is said: "Because [the word] expresses a quality (*guṇavacanāt*)."

And a compound is not denotative of a quality (*guṇavacana*). [Objection: But a compound is indeed denotative of a quality. [Question: How so? [Answer: Because the operation [of a compound] is one that does not abandon its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthā vṛttiḥ*). [Objection: But if it were one that abandons its own meaning (*jahatsvārthā*), there would certainly be a fault. [Reply: Even in the case of abandoning its own meaning, there is no fault; for even in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there occurs "cognition of that as possessing the quality" (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*). For example: "Bring the one with white clothes," or "The priests wearing red turbans perform the ritual."

Thus it is said: its quality is brought forth, and its qualities prevail. Regarding the excellence of the meaning of the final member [of a compound], the *ātiśāyika* suffix occurs after a *bahuvrīhi* for the sake of expressing meanings such as "more very-wealthy" (*bahvāḍhyatara*). The *ātiśāyika* suffix occurs after a *bahuvrīhi* when there is excellence of the meaning of the final member, by way of an exception (*vipratiṣedha*) [to other rules]. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of expressing meanings such as "more very-wealthy" (*bahvāḍhyatara*), "more very-delicate" (*bahu-sukumāratara*). What [is the need for this]? *Note:* This passage discusses the formation of comparative forms from *bahuvrīhi* compounds. According to Pāṇinian grammar (P. 5.3.55), the *ātiśāyika* suffixes (*tama*, *iṣṭhan*, etc. are generally applied to simple words to form superlatives and comparatives. However, this rule allows them to be applied to *bahuvrīhi* compounds when the excellence pertains to the referent of the final member of the compound, thereby forming terms like *bahvāḍhyatara* ("more very-wealthy") rather than the expected *bahvāḍhyatama*. The term *vipratiṣedha* here indicates that this specific rule overrides other general restrictions. The examples provided illustrate the application of these comparative suffixes to *bahuvrīhi*s. The question at the end (*kaḥ*) likely introduces a further inquiry or objection regarding the necessity or scope of this rule.

Furthermore, there is a distinction here: either the comparative suffix (*ātiśāyika*) may be added after a *bahuvrīhi* compound, or the *bahuvrīhi* may be formed with a word ending in a comparative suffix. There is a difference regarding accent (*svara*) and the suffix *ka*. If the *bahuvrīhi* were formed after the comparative suffix, then in the case of *bahvāḍhyatara*, the accent would result as *bahvāḍhyataraḥ*, whereas *bahvāḍhyataraḥ* is what is intended. Furthermore, [if the comparative were applied first], one would obtain *bahvāḍhyakataraḥ* instead of the desired *bahvāḍhyatarakaḥ*.

And this is accepted: under the rule concerning *samānādhikaraṇa* (co-referential) compounds, there should be an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the class beginning with *śākapārthiva*, and the elision (*lopa*) of the middle word must be stated. Under the rule concerning *samānādhikaraṇa* compounds, an addition must be made for the class beginning with *śākapārthiva*, and the elision of the middle word must be prescribed. For example: a king (*pārthiva*) who eats vegetables (*śāka-bhojin*) is a *śākapārthiva*; a descendant of Suśruta (*sauśruta*) who wears a woolen blanket (*kutapa-vāsas*) is a *kutapasauśruta*.
*ajāpaṇyaḥ* (one who does not sell goats), *taulvaliḥ*, *ajātaulvaliḥ*; *yaṣṭipradhānaḥ maudgalyaḥ* (a Maudgalya for whom a staff is the primary characteristic), *yaṣṭimaudgalyaḥ*.

Why does this not occur here:

*grāmārdhaḥ* (half of a village), *nagarārdhaḥ* (half of a city)? This inclusion of the word *ardha* refers to its neuter gender, yet this word *ardha* is also masculine. Where, then, is it neuter, and where is it masculine?
In the sense of an equal division, it is neuter;

when denoting a part, it is masculine. Why does [the rule] not apply here in the case of *ardhaṃ pippalīnām*? It is not necessarily so; for *ardhapippalyaḥ* is indeed used when there is a collection of parts.

"Half-pippalī, half-pippalī, half-pippalī, [half-pippalīs]"—thus it should be. But when this sentence occurs, "half of the pippalīs," then it should not be so. Why does it not occur then? Because the phrase "in the case of making one thing out of many" (ekādikaraṇe) is understood to apply here. If that is the case, then why does this [form] not occur now: [half-pippalī, half-pippalī, half-pippalī]?
"Half of a heap" (*ardharāśiḥ*). This occurs; this is a single grammatical topic (*adhikaraṇa*), namely that which is called a "heap.
(Pāṇini 2.2.3) Why is the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") included? So that the compound may optionally occur; [otherwise] it would always occur by means of compounding.

[Objection: "The purpose is so that there may also be a sentence (vākya) when the [compound] is excluded, namely 'the second [portion] of alms' (bhikṣāyā dvitīyam). [Reply: This is not a valid purpose, because the Great Option (mahāvibhāṣā) is under discussion; by that, the sentence will also be possible. [Objection: Then this is the purpose: so that when the partitive compound (ekadeśisamāsa) is excluded, the genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa) may also occur, as in 'bhikṣādvitīyam'. [Reply: This too is not a valid purpose.

This *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* (genitive compound) is also [subject to] the *vibhāṣā* (optionality). Both of these will occur by virtue of the explicit statement. Therefore, he recites the following reply: The statement of optionality (*vibhāṣā-vacana*) within the section on optionality (*vibhāṣā-prakaraṇa*) regarding the second case (*dvitīyā*) and the others is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is no general rule (*sāmānya-vidhāna*) for the prescription of a part [of a compound].
The statement of optionality regarding the second case and the others is made within the section on optionality for the purpose of providing an indication. What is indicated?

The Teacher indicates this: that in a rule prescribing a specific component (*avayava-vidhi*), a general rule (*sāmānya-vidhi*) does not apply. What is the purpose of this indication? [Consider] *bhinatti* and *chinatti*. Once the suffix *śnam* has been applied, the suffix *śap* would not occur. This is not a valid purpose, because the substitutes for *śap*, namely *śyan* and so forth, will be prescribed. In that case, the mention of *śap* must indeed be made.

It should not be applied. The original subject (*prakṛta*) is being followed. Where is the original subject? It is "the *śap* [augment] when the agent is expressed" (*kartari śap*). Now, that [rule] was indicated in the nominative case, whereas here the requirement is for something indicated in the genitive case. This word "from *rudh*-etc. (*rudhādibhyaḥ*), being in the fifth case, will cause the first-case word *śap* to be understood as having a genitive sense, according to the principle "from that [which is indicated in the ablative], the following [is affected]. This is a rule for the prescription of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*), and in the prescription of suffixes, [the genitive is not used].

The fifth case endings are used in the sense of "forming" (prakalpika). This is not a rule for the introduction of a suffix (*pratyayavidhi*); rather, a suffix already prescribed and the context under discussion (*prakṛta*) continue to apply. If that is so, then the Teacher indicates this: where there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) between a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*), once the exception has applied, the general rule does not subsequently apply. What is the purpose of this indication? [It is to explain the formation of] *dikpūrvapadāt ṅīp*.

*prāṅmukhī* [is formed with] *ṅīp*, and *prāṅmukhā* [is formed with] *ṅīṣ*; likewise, *pratyaṅmukhī* [is formed with] *ṅīp*, and *pratyaṅmukhā* [is formed with] *ṅīṣ*. When *ṅīp* is applied, *ṅīṣ* does not occur. This is not a valid purpose [for the rule]. He will state this: "The *anudātta* accentuation of *ṅīṣ* after a compound whose first member is a direction-word [is taught]; for if *ṅīp* were prescribed, then even elsewhere—where *ṅīṣ* would otherwise apply—there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *ṅīp*. If that is so, then this is the purpose: *ardhapippalī*.

In the case of *ardhakośātakī*, when the *ekadeśisamāsa* (partitive compound) is excluded, a *ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa* (genitive compound) does not occur. In the cases of *unmattagaṅgam* and *lohitagaṅgam*, when the *avyayībhāva* is excluded, a *bahuvrīhi* does not occur. In the cases of *dākṣiḥ* and *plākṣiḥ*, when the suffix *iñ* is excluded, the suffix *aṇ* does not occur. If this is made known, then in the case of "the offspring of Upagu" (*upagoḥ apatyam*), [the form] *aupagavaḥ* occurs; when the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix is excluded, one would have "Upagu’s offspring" (*upagvapatyam*).

It is not established. There is a distinction here: for there are two options (*vibhāṣā*) in this case. Namely, "after *daivayajñi*, *śaucivṛkṣi*, *sātyamugri*, and *kāṇṭheviddhi*, optionally" (*anyatarasyām*), and "from among those [words] that are semantically connected, optionally from the first" (*samarthānām prathamāt vā*). In that regard, by means of one [rule], the compound (*vṛtti*) will be formed;

by means of the other, it serves as an optional exception (*vibhāṣāpavāda*) to the scope of the compound. Even when the mention of "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is made, the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) would still occur.

It does not apply. What is the reason? Because of the prohibition by the word *pūraṇa*. This [word] does not end in a *pūraṇa* suffix; it ends in *an*. Even this [suffix] ends in a *pūraṇa* suffix. How so? The meaning called "filling" (*pūraṇa*) is expressed by the word *tīya*. Therefore, it is a *pūraṇa*. That which is added after a *pūraṇa*-ending word in the sense of a part (*bhāga*) with the suffix *an*—that too is indeed a *pūraṇa*. Thus.
In that case, by virtue of the inclusion of the word "anyatarasyām" (optionally), a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) will also be possible.
(Pāṇini 2.2.4) Why is the particle *ca* used? It is for the purpose of attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*). The word "anyatarasyām" is attracted [to this rule]. What [is its purpose]?

The purpose [of this rule] is so that there may optionally be a compound; and when there is no compound, so that there may also be a sentence, as in *jīvikāṃ prāptaḥ*. This is not a valid purpose, because the *mahāvibhāṣā* (the great option) is under discussion, and by it the sentence will occur. Then this is the purpose: so that there may also be a second-case compound, as in *jīvikāprāptaḥ*.

This too is not a purpose [for the *ca*]. This [compound] is also called a second-case compound (*dvitīyā-samāsa*). Both of those will occur by virtue of the explicit statement. If that is so, then this *ca* is not for the purpose of attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*). What then? By this, the substitution of *at* is prescribed: *prāpta* and *āpanna* are compounded with a word ending in the second case, and the substitution of *at* occurs for *prāpta* and *āpanna*.

Thus: *prāptajīvikā* means one who has obtained a livelihood; *āpannajīvikā* means one who has fallen into a livelihood. (Pāṇini 2.2.5.1) KA_I,409.6-12 Ro_II, 661-662 What is the predominant element in this compound? The meaning of the final member (*uttarapadārtha*). If it is predominant in the meaning of the final member, [then...]

By this [example], it must be understood that others are also compounds whose meaning is dominated by the final member (*uttarapadārthapradhāna*). And in other cases where the meaning is dominated by the final member, whatever case-ending (*vibhakti*) exists internally within the compound is indeed heard even when the compound is formed:

for example, *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king's man) becomes *rājapuruṣaḥ*. But here, however, there is the genitive case in the sentence, whereas in the compound there is the nominative. By what [reasoning] is this so?

Thus it occurs: that connection between the two words *māsa* and *jāta*, which exists [in the analytical state], is removed when there is a compound (*samāsa*). That meaning, having been expressed, becomes internalized and results in the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). In that case, since the rule "the first case ending occurs in the sense of a nominal stem" applies, the first case ending (*prathamā*) is used. If this is so, then this [following example] would not occur:

Regarding the expression *māsajātasya*: the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs in relation to an external object. Since that with which time is compounded is itself not a measure, it is not specified; for that with which time is compounded [is not a measure].

It is immeasurable. Because it is immeasurable, there is no designation for it. A designation that does not convey understanding is a non-designation. For a month is not the measure of one who is born. Of what, then, is it the measure? Of thirty nights. It is just as in the case of: "Devadatta’s *droṇa* of jujube fruits. The *droṇa* is not the measure of Devadatta; of what, then, is it the measure? Of the jujube fruits. This is established.

But [the term] *kāla* refers to that which has a measure of time (*kālaparimāṇa*); [the compound is formed] with that. This is established. How? It should be stated that "that which has a measure of time is a *kāla*, and it is compounded with that. Thus it is established. But in that case, the rule (*sūtra*) is altered. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. [Objection: Was it not already stated that there is no designation [of the word] because that with which time is compounded lacks a measure?

Furthermore, considering what time do you say that there is no designation of time because it is immeasurable? They call that "time" by which the increase and decrease of material forms are perceived. When that very [time] is joined with a certain activity, it becomes "day" and "night. By what activity? By the movement of the sun.

By that very [unit of time] repeated many times, there comes to be what is called a "month" (*māsa*) and a "year" (*saṃvatsara*). If it is thus the case that a month is the measure of one who is born, then an addition must be made regarding the singular number and *dvigu* compounds. It should be stated: "[The suffix *ṭhañ* applies] after words ending in the singular number. This should not apply here: *māsau jātasya*, *māsāḥ jātasya*. And it should be stated: "[The suffix *ṭhañ* applies] after a *dvigu* compound," so that it may also occur here: [e.g., *dvimāsikaḥ*].

"Born two months ago," "born three months ago. Or rather, it has already been stated. What has been stated? First, regarding the singular number, it was stated: "because of non-expression [of the meaning]. Regarding the *dvigu* compound, what has been stated? It was stated: "the designation of a *samāsa* for a *dvigu* when the measure-possessor (*parimāṇin*) follows as the final member."

(P_2,2.6) What is the predominant element of this compound? Is it the meaning of the final member (*uttarapadārtha*)? If it were the meaning of the final member, then when one says, "Bring a non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇam ānaya*), the bringing of any Brahmin whatsoever would result. [Therefore,] it must have the meaning of another word as its predominant element (*anyapadārthapradhāna*).

In that case, it will be so. If [the compound] has the meaning of another word as its predominant element, then in the case of *avarṣā hemantaḥ* ("a non-rainy winter"), whatever gender and number belong to *hemantaḥ* would also apply to the compound. If, then, it has the meaning of the prior member as its predominant element, then the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) would apply.
"For its first member is indeclinable"—this objection does not hold. The designation *avyaya* (indeclinable) is established by way of formal recitation (*pāṭha*).
And the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) is not recited therein. Even if the negative compound is not recited, the particle *nañ* itself is recited.
When the designation *avyaya* is established even by way of such recitation, [the compound] nevertheless possesses gender and number, just like that which is to be expressed. And that which...

In this case, it is the meaning that is denoted, and that [meaning] has no connection with gender or number. This lack of gender and number is not something established by rule (*vācanika*); rather, it is inherent (*svābhāvika*). For example:
among those who strive equally and study equally, some are endowed with the results while others are not; and yet, there is no [rule] governing this at present.

Thinking that because one [word] has meaning, all [words] must have meaning, or because one is meaningless, all must be meaningless—what can be done by us in this regard? That which occurs before the compound—that there is no connection with gender and number—is not the case once the compound is formed; this is simply its inherent nature. Now...
Or rather, the gender and number will be determined by the substratum (*āśraya*). For words that express qualities (*guṇavacana*), the gender and number are those of the substratum.
For example:
"a white cloth" (*śuklaṃ vastram*).

"A white cloth," "a white blanket," "two white blankets," "many white blankets"— in these cases, whatever gender and number the substance (dravya) possesses which the quality (guṇa) depends upon, those same gender and number belong to the quality as well. Thus, here too, that which this [quality] depends upon...

The gender and number belonging to that [constituent] will also belong to the compound. Alternatively, let it be that the compound has the meaning of the final member as its predominant sense. But was it not said that when "Bring the non-Brāhmaṇa" is uttered, the bringing of any Brāhmaṇa whatsoever would follow? This is not a fault. First, this person should be asked:
Now, when it is said here, "Bring a king's man," why does the bringing of just any man not occur?

There is a distinction here: the word "king" is employed as a qualifier. Therefore, the bringing of one qualified by him occurs. In this case as well, then, the negative particle *nañ* is employed as a qualifier; therefore, there will be the bringing of that which is qualified by *nañ*. Which [is that]?

Furthermore, this [negation] has its referent withdrawn (*nivṛttapadārthaka*). When, moreover, its referent is withdrawn, is that withdrawal inherent (*svābhāvikī*) or is it based on explicit statement (*vācanikī*)? And what follows from this? If it is inherent, what does the negative particle (*nañ*) accomplish when it is employed?
Or if it is based on explicit statement, then that must be explained.
"When the negative particle (*nañ*) is employed, it excludes the meaning of the word. If that is so, then the exclusion is inherent. But was it not said:
"What does the negative particle do when it is employed? When the negative particle is employed, it excludes the meaning of the word.
How? Like a wedge and its counter-wedge. Just as a wedge, being driven in, drives out a counter-wedge. If...

This would be the greatness of the negative particle (*nañ*): kings would never carry elephants and horses; they would simply say "no" to them. If that is so, then the cessation [of action] is inherent. But was it not asked: what does the negative particle do when it is employed?
It is rather the perception [of absence] caused by the negative particle. For example, as in the case of objects situated in deep darkness.

The perception of the lamp is for the purpose of illumination, yet the lamp itself is not the producer of that perception. If, however, this [word] has its referent already ceased, for what purpose is the word "brāhmaṇa" employed? It is so that it may be understood that "the referent of this [word] ceases. For if only "not" were said, there would be doubt as to which referent ceases.

Thus, the word *brāhmaṇa* is employed there for the sake of removing doubt. Or rather, it is like this: all these words—*brāhmaṇa*, *kṣatriya*, *vaiśya*, and *śūdra*—refer to collections of qualities (*guṇasamudāya*). "Austerity, sacred learning, and birth"—this is what constitutes a *brāhmaṇa*. One who is devoid of austerity and sacred learning is merely a *brāhmaṇa* by birth.

Thus it is. Likewise, they also regard these internal qualities as constituting Brahminhood: being fair-complexioned, pure in conduct, tawny-eyed, and having reddish-brown hair. Furthermore, words that function with reference to a whole may also function with reference to its parts. For example:
"the eastern Pañcālas," "the northern Pañcālas," "oil has been eaten," "clarified butter has been eaten," or "white," "blue," and "tawny."

Regarding the word "Kṛṣṇa": in this way, this word *brāhmaṇa*, which is applied to the whole [collection of qualities], also applies to its parts, even when [the person] is devoid of [the] caste (*jāti*) and devoid of [the] qualities (*guṇa*). First, regarding one devoid of qualities: "This is a non-Brāhmaṇa who urinates while standing;
this is a non-Brāhmaṇa who eats while walking. Regarding one devoid of caste, the word *brāhmaṇa* is applied due to doubt and due to false instruction. First, regarding doubt:

Having seen someone who is fair-complexioned, of pure conduct, tawny-eyed, and with reddish-brown hair, one determines, "This is a Brāhmaṇa. Subsequently, however, one perceives, "This is not a Brāhmaṇa; this is a non-Brāhmaṇa. In that case, because of doubt, the word "Brāhmaṇa" continues to be applied, yet there is a cessation of the object's status as determined by birth (*jāti*). This is due to erroneous instruction (*durupadeśa*).
He receives incorrect instruction, such as, "O Brahmin, bring him from that place.
Having gone there, he perceives whoever he sees and concludes, "This is a Brahmin. Only afterwards does he realize, "This is not a Brahmin; this is a non-Brahmin."

In that case, the word "brāhmaṇa" is applied due to incorrect instruction (*durupadeśa*), and there is an exclusion of the meaning based on caste (*jāti*). Furthermore, it is because of doubt or because of incorrect instruction. For one does not, upon seeing a person with the color of a heap of black beans sitting in a marketplace, determine, "This is a brāhmaṇa. His [status] is already known [to him]. Moreover, this is even more so:

When the meaning of the final member of the compound is predominant, it is included [in the scope of the rule]. What is included? "Aneka" (more than one). What is included here? The singular number (*ekavacana*). But how can there be a cognition of "many" through the negation of "one"? This [negation] applies as a simple prohibition (*prasajya*) to the action and the quality, and only afterwards does it effect the exclusion. For example:

"Make him sit, make him lie down, feed him—many [people]. Even if it can be said here that this applies where the action and its quality are predicated, how is it so when they are not predicated, as in "many stand"? And yet, even for such cases, there is a comprehension of many through the negation of one. For example: "Not one thing is dear to us; not one thing is our happiness. Here, [the term] *abrāhmaṇatva* (non-Brahminhood) [functions similarly].

Because it is a *para* (subsequent) element, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* would apply to form *abrāhmaṇatā*. What fault is there in that? There would indeed be a fault regarding the accent (*svara*). It should be stated that the words beginning with *pra-* are compounded when they have the sense of a *kta*-suffix. Thus: *pragata ācāryaḥ* = *prācāryaḥ*; *prāntevāsī*; *prapitāmahaḥ*. And this very rule has been recited by the followers of Śākalya (*saunāgaiḥ*) in even greater detail.

The term *su* is used in the sense of praise; it should be stated that it occurs in the sense of praise. Examples: *surājā* (a good king), *atirājā* (an excellent king). The term *duḥ* is used in the sense of censure; it should be stated that it occurs in the sense of censure. Examples: *duṣkulam* (a bad family), *durgavaḥ* (a bad ox). The particle *āṅ* is used in the sense of slightness; it should be stated that it occurs in the sense of slightness. Examples: *ākaḍāraḥ* (slightly tawny), *āpiṅgalaḥ* (slightly reddish-brown). The particle *ku-* is used in the sense of evil; it should be stated that it occurs in the sense of evil. Examples: *kubrāhmaṇaḥ* (a bad Brahmin), *kuvṛṣalaḥ* (a bad Śūdra).

*Prādayaḥ* (particles beginning with *pra*) are compounded with a word in the first case when they convey meanings such as "gone" (*gata*) and so forth. It should be stated that *prādayaḥ* are compounded with a word in the first case when they convey meanings such as "gone. Examples: *pragata ācāryaḥ* → *prācāryaḥ*; *prāntevāsī*; *prapitāmahaḥ*. *Atyādayaḥ* (particles beginning with *ati*) are compounded with a word in the second case when they convey meanings such as "transcended" (*krānta*) and so forth. It should be stated that *atyādayaḥ* are compounded with a word in the second case when they convey meanings such as "transcended. Example: *atikrāntaḥ...*

*Ati-khaṭvaḥ* (one who has surpassed a bed) and *ati-mālaḥ* (one who has surpassed a garland). It should be stated that words beginning with *ava*, when used in the sense of "called" (*kruṣṭa*) and so forth, are compounded with a word in the third case. For example: *avakruṣṭaḥ kokilayā* (called by the cuckoo) becomes *avakokilaḥ* (the spring). Words beginning with *pari*, when used in the sense of "afflicted" (*glāna*) and so forth, are compounded with a word in the fourth case. It should be stated that words beginning with *pari*, when used in the sense of "afflicted" and so forth, are compounded with a word in the fourth case.

"Pariglāna" means exhausted by study; "paryadhayana. It should be stated that words beginning with *nis* (nirādayaḥ) are compounded with a word in the fifth case when they have the sense of "having gone beyond" (*krāntādyarthe*). For example: one who has gone out from Kauśāmbī is *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*; one who has gone out from Vārāṇasī is *nirvārāṇasiḥ*. It should be stated that an indeclinable (*avyayam*) is compounded with words such as *pravṛddha*. Thus, an indeclinable is compounded with words beginning with *pravṛddha*.

Furthermore, *punarvṛddham*, *punarnavam*, and *punaḥsukham* are examples where the case-ending (*vibhaktyanta*) is elided after the particle *iva*, and the preceding member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Examples include *vāsasī iva* and *kanye iva*. It should be stated that an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is compounded with a finite verb (*tiṅ*) that possesses an udātta accent and expresses motion. Examples are *anuvyacalat*, *anuprāviśat*, and *yat pariyanti*.

(P_2.2.19) Why is it stated that "not [a word] ending in a verbal suffix" (*atiṅ*)? [Examples: *kārakaḥ vrajati* ("the doer goes"), *hārakaḥ vrajati* ("the taker goes"). It could have been formulated without the restriction "not [a word] ending in a verbal suffix. Why does [the rule] not apply in the cases *kārakaḥ vrajati* and *hārakaḥ vrajati*? Because of the rule *sup supā* ("a noun with a noun").

[The objection] persists. Therefore, he recites the following answer: "The prohibition [of the designation *upapada*] applies to that which has the same meaning as *atiṅ*. This prohibition of that which has the same meaning as *atiṅ* must be stated. Of what? Of that which has the meaning of a *tiṅ*-suffix. But what is the meaning of a *tiṅ*-suffix? It is action (*kriyā*). Or rather, it is a prohibition of action. Alternatively, this should have been read quite explicitly as: "An *upapada* [is not designated as such if it has the same meaning as *atiṅ*]."

"By non-action. Now, what is the counter-example for "by non-action"? "The doer has gone," "the remover has gone. This does not denote an action; what then? It denotes a substance (*dravya*). Then consider this: "the going of the doer," "the movement of the doer. This too denotes a substance. How so? Because "an action expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix functions like a substance."

If that is the case, then since [the formation] is already established, the fact that the Teacher teaches the prohibition "not after a verbal suffix" (atiṅ) indicates that the rule "noun with noun" (sup supā) has ceased to apply in these two rules. What is the purpose of this indication? This technical rule—that there is compounding of prefixes (gati), objects (kāraka), and secondary words (upapada) with primary derivatives (kṛt)—need not be formulated. If this is indicated...

By what [word] will there now be a compound? By that which is "capable" (*samartha*). If this is so, then a compound would also result between a verbal root and a prefix (*upasarga*), because it is said that "first the root is joined with the prefix, and afterwards with the means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*). This is not the case;
rather, first the root is joined with the means of accomplishment, and afterwards with the prefix. For it is the means of accomplishment that brings about the action.

The prefix (*upasarga*) qualifies that [noun]. And it is possible to state a distinction for an already established meaning by means of a prefix. The compound with a prefix (*upasargasamāsa*) takes precedence over the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) by way of a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of the genitive compound is, for example, *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king's man), which becomes *rājapuruṣaḥ*. [In contrast,] this is the scope of the compound with an accompanying word (*upapadasamāsa*).

In the case of *avakāśaḥ*, *stamberamaḥ*, and *karṇejapaḥ*, both [rules] would apply here: *kumbhakāraḥ* and *nagarakāraḥ*. [One might argue that] the *upapada* compound occurs by way of a prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*) [of the genitive compound]. Or rather, there is no need for a prohibition; the *upapada* compound occurs because of the absence of the genitive compound. What is the reason? There is no need for a prohibition; the *upapada* compound occurs because of the absence of the genitive compound.

It will be so. How? Because of the rule stating that "there is an option for the compounding of words denoting direction, agent, or object with words ending in kṛt-suffixes, prior to the addition of case-endings. Alternatively, there is an optional sixth-case compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). When it is not a sixth-case compound, then it will be an *upapada* compound. This is so that it may occur by this very rule and not by that one. And what is the difference here between the two?

It may be that this is an *upapada* compound or a compulsory (*nitya*) compound; however, a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound is optional (*vibhāṣā*). But surely, a compound that is compulsory is a "compulsory compound" (*nityasamāsa*), meaning one for which there is no analytical expansion (*vigraha*)? No, he says. A compound that occurs under the governing rule of "compulsorily" (*nitya*) is a compulsory compound. This cannot be so, for in that case, the *avyayībhāva* would be an inconstant (*anitya*) compound.

[Otherwise] it would follow [that the rule applies excessively]. Therefore, a compound that is obligatory is an "obligatory compound" (*nityasamāsa*), one for which there is no analytical expansion (*vigraha*).

(Pāṇini 2.2.20) [Question: What is the purpose of the particle *eva*? [Answer: It is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). [Objection: This purpose is not necessary. For a rule is commenced even when [the desired result] is already established.
Even without the particle *eva*, it will serve the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). If that is so, it will then serve the purpose of limitation according to what is desired (*iṣṭataḥ*);
namely, so that it may be understood as "only with an indeclinable (*avyaya*) [following] *amā*," and not so that it might be understood otherwise.

"Only with an indeclinable (*avyaya*)," it is said. But there is also a non-indeclinable word *am* for which this rule would apply. He says: "There is," namely in the case of *khaśayam brāhmaṇakulam*. This is not a valid purpose; because it is *antaraṅga* (internal), the compound will occur here by its own nature. Then this is the purpose: that the *upapada* which is prescribed under the same conditions as *am* alone [should be compounded].

It should be so only in that specific case. This is so that the rule does not apply where the *upapada* is prescribed by both the particle *am* and another [particle]. For example, in *agre bhojam* (having eaten first), since the rule is not otherwise applicable to words beginning with *agra*, one might object to the prohibition of compounding; however, such an objection need not be stated.

It is stated: "the remainder" (*śeṣa*). What is this so-called "remainder"? That compound for which no [specific] rule has been stated is the remainder. If it is argued that the mention of the "remainder" is based on the words, that is not so. Why? Because [of their] non-existence. If the mention of the "remainder" were based on the words, that would not be correct. What is the reason?

Because they do not exist. For those words for which composition has not been stated do not exist [as such]. In that case, then, the mention of "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is based on meaning. That composition which has not been stated regarding certain meanings is the "remainder. If it is based on meaning, then it is indistinct. If it is based on meaning, this becomes indistinct. Why? Because of the words. For those meanings for which [composition has not been stated] do not exist.

The compound has not been mentioned [in the rules]. In that case, the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) refers to the triad; that triad for which the compound has not been mentioned is the "remainder. And for which [case] has it not been mentioned? For the nominative (*prathamā*).

699–704. What is the purpose of including the word *pada* (word)? If it were stated merely as "anekam anyārthe" (when more than one [word] occurs in the sense of another), the *bahuvrīhi* compound would apply even to the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*). For example: "Just as my mother, so too my father; O, you are well-bathed! However, when the word *pada* is included, this fault does not arise. Now, what is the purpose of including the word *anya* (other)? If it were stated merely as "anekam padārthe" (when more than one [word] occurs in the sense of a word-meaning) ...

If it were stated [that a compound occurs] when its own constituent meaning is expressed, then even a *bahuvrīhi* would apply in cases such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* (king’s man) and *takṣapuruṣaḥ* (carpenter’s man). This is not a valid objection; for a *tatpuruṣa* will serve as an exception (*bādhaka*) in the case of its own constituent meaning. [The rule] would be established under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "only one technical name" (*ekasañjñā*).

However, it is not established when the status of being a subsequent operation (*parakāryatva*) applies. And by the very force of its formulation, the *tatpuruṣa* prevails because it is a subsequent operation.

And thus, a *bahuvrīhi* would result. However, there is no fault if it is a subsequent operation (*paraṅkāryatva*). The term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is understood [from the previous rule]. Because it is a remainder, it will not occur. This was stated regarding the mention of "remainder. What was stated? Therein, because of the mention of "remainder," there is a fault: namely, the prohibition of *bahuvrīhi* in the case of compounds with numerals, coreferential terms, and the negative particle (*nañ*). Now, within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for "one technical designation" (*ekasaṃjñā*), there is no purpose for the mention of "another" (*anya*). Within the governing heading for one technical designation—

And [the word *anya*] must be employed. For if *anya* were not employed, just as a *tatpuruṣa* compound subverts a *bahuvrīhi* in its own constituent meaning (*svapadārtha*), it would likewise subvert it in the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*). Now, for what purpose is the mention of *aneka* (more than one)? If only "in the meaning of another word" (*anyapadārthe*) were stated, the *bahuvrīhi* would apply even to a single word; for example, there would be [the undesirable formation] *sarpiṣo* and *madhuno*.

It might be so; it might also apply to *gomūtra*. But this is not a purpose [for the rule]. The rule *sup supā* (a case-ending word with a case-ending word) continues to apply. Then what is the purpose? So that there may be a compound even of many words, as in: *susūkṣmajaṭakeśena sunatājinavāsasā* ("by one whose hair is very fine and matted, and who is clothed in a beautiful deerskin").

Furthermore, the mention of "many" (*aneka*) must be made for the sake of the subsequent rule: "A *dvandva* compound occurs in the sense of 'and' (*cārthe*), consisting of many [words]. So that here too, as follows: [it applies].

It might be argued that [the compound] *plakṣanyagrodhakhadirapalāśāḥ* [is required]. This too serves no purpose. The activity of the Teacher indicates that a compound of many [elements] also occurs, since he teaches the *dvigu* when there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*). In that case, would it not follow that a *tatpuruṣa* could also consist of many elements? A *tatpuruṣa* is expressed by the specific mention [of the term]; therefore, it will not apply to many [elements].

Therefore, he recites the following answer: "The mention of 'many' is for the sake of the *upasarjana*. The term 'many' is employed for the sake of the *upasarjana*, so that the technical designation *upasarjana* may apply to many *sup*-suffixes [ending words] which are designated as such by being stated in the nominative case in a compound (*samāsa*), according to the rule: 'That which is designated in the nominative case in a compound is the *upasarjana*'—as in *citraguḥ* and *śabalaguḥ*. "No, this is not a purpose, because they share the same case-ending. Or rather, even this is not a purpose.

It exists. What is the reason? Because they share the same case-ending (*ekavibhaktitvāt*). And by the rule "when there is no prior occurrence [of another word], that which has the same case-ending receives the designation of *upasarjana*," the term will be designated as *upasarjana*. For example: *citraguḥ*, *śabalaguḥ*. In the case of *citraguḥ tiṣṭhati* ("the one whose cows are brindled stands"), *citrāḥ yasya gāvaḥ* ("whose cows are brindled") is the analysis. In *citragum paśya* ("see the one whose cows are brindled"), *citrāḥ yasya gāvaḥ* is the analysis. In *citraguṇā kṛtam* ("done by the one whose cows are brindled"), *citrāḥ yasya gāvaḥ* is the analysis. In *citrāḥ yasya gāvaḥ* (as a standalone analysis), it is the same.

"Give to Citragu" (citragave dehi)—one whose cows are variegated. "Bring Citragu" (citragor ānaya)—one whose cows are variegated. "The property of Citragu" (citragoḥ svam)—one whose cows are variegated. "Place Citragu" (citragau nidhehi)—one whose cows are variegated. "O Citragu! (he citrago iti)—one whose cows are variegated.
If, then, a connection with a single case-ending is established by supplying some word or other from anywhere at all;

This [term] also becomes joined with a single case ending; here too it would apply: *rājakumārī*, *takṣakumārī*. "The princess who belongs to the king" is *rājakumārī* standing [there]. "Look at the princess who belongs to the king" is *rājakumārīm*. "Done by the princess who belongs to the king" is *rājakumāryā*. "Give to the princess who belongs to the king" is *rājakumāryai*. "Of the princess who belongs to the king" is *rājakumāryāḥ*.
"Bring [the girl] belonging to the king. "The girl who belongs to the princess is [her] own. "Place the girl who belongs to the king within the princess.

"O girl who belongs to the king, O princess! Should this be stated? No, indeed. How would it be understood without being stated? By the force of the mention of the singular number (*eka*). For if that which is joined with a single case-ending and that which is joined with multiple case-endings—

Furthermore, in that case, the inclusion of the word *eka* would be purposeless; one should simply have stated, "when joined with a case-ending, provided it does not occur as the first member. Regarding the expression of the meaning of a word (*padārtha*), the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) is untenable because the meaning has already been expressed. This is because the meaning of the word has already been denoted.

The subsequent employment [of the verb] would be untenable in the case of "citragur devadattaḥ" (Devadatta is the possessor of brindled cows). What is the reason? Because it has already been expressed.
Since that meaning has been expressed by the word *citragu*, the subsequent employment [of the verb] does not apply. Or rather, it is not so, because it is not expressed.
Or rather, this fault does not arise. What is the reason? Because it is not expressed. That [meaning] is not expressed by the word *citragu*.

The suffix will be applied on the grounds that it expresses the meaning (*artha*). But how can it be said that the meaning is not already expressed, when it was just stated that the application of a subsequent suffix is untenable because the meaning of the word has already been expressed? For while the general sense is expressed, the specific detail remains unexpressed. Indeed, when the general is expressed, the particular is unexpressed; therefore, one who desires the specific must necessarily [seek it].

A specific term (*viśeṣa*) must be employed [to specify the referent]. For example: "Citraguḥ" (the one possessing brindled cows). Who is he? Devadatta. This would be established when the word functions in a general sense. But when it functions in a specific sense, it is not established; namely, when one says: "Devadatta’s brindled cows are *citraguḥ* (the brindled-cow-possessor), Devadatta. That too is established. How so? Because these two [general and specific] do not occur simultaneously.

There is both the sentence (*vākya*) and the compound (*samāsa*). When it is a sentence, it is not a compound; when it is a compound, it is not a sentence. When it is a compound, its function is with respect to the general (*sāmānya*). In that case, one who desires the specific (*viśeṣa*) must necessarily employ the specific [verb]. For example: "The one possessing brindled cows" (*citraguḥ*). Who is he? "Devadatta. But then, the employment of the general alone would not be possible.
"Belonging to the brindled cow," "something belonging to the brindled cow," or "everything belonging to the brindled cow"—just as a universal can function as a particular, so it is here.

When "belonging to the brindled cow" is stated, a doubt may arise: whether it refers to everything or to the whole universe. In that case, for the sake of removing the doubt, one who seeks a specific meaning must necessarily employ a further qualifier. Alternatively, the meaning of the case-ending is expressed; and this is...

In this regard, it is logical that the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is what is expressed. For in that context, the word "of this" (*asya*) occurs at the very end of all [the other elements]. If the meaning of the case-ending were being expressed, then for that which is not a substance (*adravya*), the figurative application (*upacāra*) of gender and number would be untenable. If the meaning of the case-ending were expressed, the figurative application of gender and number to that which is not a substance is logically impossible. [Examples would be: *bahuyavam*, *bahuyavā*, *bahuyavaḥ*.
"Bahuyava" and "bahuhavāḥ. Another says:

"In the denotation of the meaning of a case-ending, it is untenable for that which is not a substance (adravya) to have the metaphorical application (upacāra) of gender and number.
