When the meaning of a case-ending is denoted, the metaphorical application of the gender and number belonging to the substance to the meaning of the case-ending is untenable. [As in] *bahuyavam*."

*bahuyavāḥ*, *bahuyavaḥ*, *bahuyavau*, *bahuyavāḥ*. For how could there be a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the gender and number of one thing to another? But it is established as being like the case of adjectives expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*). This is established. How? Just as in the case of adjectives expressing qualities. Regarding adjectives expressing qualities, it has been stated:

The gender and number of words expressing qualities (guṇavacana) are determined by their substratum (āśraya). For example: *śuklaṃ vastram* (a white cloth), *śuklā śāṭī* (a white garment), *śuklaḥ kambalaḥ* (a white blanket), *śuklau kambalau* (two white blankets), *śuklāḥ kambalāḥ* (many white blankets). Whatever gender and number belong to that substance (*dravya*) upon which the quality rests, those same belong to the quality as well. Thus it is here.

Furthermore, whatever gender and number belong to that substance which is resorted to by the meaning of the case-ending, those same will also belong to the compound. If, then, the meaning of the case-ending is expressed [by the compound], how is the entire word-meaning—possessing substance, gender, and number—expressed? It is by the force of the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*). Here, in the rule "anekam anyapade... [Pāṇini 2.2.24]...

Thus much is established by this. But how, indeed, can there be an operation (*vṛtti*) upon a word (*pada*), since this is a linguistic item (*śabda*)? Because [the operation] is impossible with respect to the word itself, it will be understood to apply to the meaning (*artha*). Now, since this is already established, the purpose for which he provides the mention of "meaning" (*arthagrahaṇa*) is so that the entire meaning of the word may be expressed—possessing substance (*sadravya*), possessing gender (*saliṅga*), and possessing number (*sasaṅkhya*).

And [as for] "ca": if, then, the entire meaning of the nominal stem (*padārtha*) were expressed, the rules concerning gender (*liṅga*) and number (*sāṅkhya*) would not be established. But it has already been stated. What was stated? First, regarding gender: "But it is established that the feminine suffixes *ṭāp* and so on occur in their own meaning (*svārthe*), because the feminine is a qualifier of the nominal stem. Regarding number as well, it has been stated, taking it as a fact that "unity and so on [are expressed], while [the roles of] object and so on are not yet expressed."

They will be *sāṅkhyā* [numerals]. In that case, however, the first case ending (*prathamā*) would not be obtained. It will be obtained by convention (*samaya*). If it is based on convention, why do the others not occur by rule? Because of the absence of [the conditions for] the object (*karman*) and so forth. In that case, the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would be obtained.

The sixth case is characterized as being used for the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). It will not occur because there is no remainder. Even so, there would be confusion (*vyatikara*), since it would apply even to a single thing.

The dual and plural endings would apply [where they are not intended], as there would be a dual and singular where there are two, and a singular and dual where there are many. An arrangement will be made based on the meaning (*arthataḥ*). Alternatively, this thing called "number" is subordinate to another; the thing to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*) is the qualifier. And if the nominative case were not used here, the thing to be numbered would remain unqualified. Or else:

This will be explained later. In that context, the purpose of including the term "vacana" (number) is so that the nominative case (*prathamā*) may apply even when [the meanings of] singularity and so forth have already been expressed. Even so, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would still result. What is the reason? For this compound indeed deviates from gender and number; however, it does not deviate from the sense of the genitive. That meaning has already been expressed.

The meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is included [within the case-meaning] and thus becomes established. In that case, the nominative will occur by the rule "the nominative is used for the meaning of the nominal stem. If this is so, then how does this form come to be:
*citragor devadattasya* ("of Devadatta, who has brindled cows")? It does occur; the genitive is used here with reference to an external object.

A complete enumeration must be made: "The *bahuvrīhi* compound consists of [words] in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). It should be stated that the *bahuvrīhi* compound consists of words in apposition. What is the purpose? So that it does not apply to words in different cases (*vyadhikaraṇa*). For example: *pañcabhir bhuktam* ("eaten by five").

Regarding the word *asya*: "And [the formation] of indeclinables. A *bahuvrīhi* compound of indeclinables must be stated; for example, *uccairmukhaḥ* ("high-faced") and *nīcairmukhaḥ* ("low-faced"). "Of that which has a locative case as its prior member or a word denoting a standard of comparison as its prior member, there is elision of the final member.

A *bahuvrīhi* compound of that which has a locative case as its prior member or a word denoting a standard of comparison as its prior member must be stated, and the elision of the final member must also be stated; for example, *kaṇṭhesthaḥ kālo 'sya* ("he who has black [soot] on his neck").
*Kaṇṭhekālaḥ* ("Black-throated") [is an example]. *Uṣṭramukhaḥ* ("Camel-faced") and *kharamukhaḥ* ("Donkey-faced") [are examples where the first member denotes] a part of a whole (*samudāya-ṣaṣṭhī*).

Furthermore, a *bahuvrīhi* compound should be stated for both the genitive of a whole (*samudāya-ṣaṣṭhī*) and the genitive of a modification (*vikāra-ṣaṣṭhī*), and the elision (*lopa*) of the final member should also be stated. [Examples: A collection of hair (*keśānāṃ samāhāraḥ*) is his crest (*cūḍā*); thus, *keśacūḍaḥ*. An ornament made of gold (*suvarṇasya vikāraḥ alaṅkāraḥ*) is his; thus, *suvarṇālaṅkāraḥ*.

[The compound] *suvarṇālaṅkāraḥ* [is formed]. Regarding the rule *prādibhyaḥ dhātujasya vā*: a *bahuvrīhi* compound [of words beginning with] *pra* and others with a word derived from a verbal root (*dhātujam*) should be stated; and furthermore, the optional elision (*lopaḥ*) of the final member (*uttarapadasya*) should be stated. Examples: *prapatitaparṇaḥ* (one whose leaves have fallen) becomes *praparṇaḥ*; *prapatitapalāśaḥ* becomes *prapalāśaḥ*. Regarding the rule *nañaḥ astyarthānām*: a *bahuvrīhi* compound [of the negative particle] *nañ* with words having the sense of "existent" (*astyarthānām*) should be stated, [along with the optional elision] of the final member.

Or rather, the elision (*lopa*) [of the suffix] should be stated. For example: *avidyamānaputraḥ* becomes *aputraḥ*; *avidyamānabhāryaḥ* becomes *abhāryaḥ*. In that case, much would have to be stated. Or rather, it need not be stated, because of non-expression (*anabhidhānāt*). There is no application of the technical name (*sañjñābhāva*) when the members are not in grammatical coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇa*). Or rather, it need not be stated at all. Why does the *bahuvrīhi* compound not occur for words that are not in coreferentiality?

"Because it has been eaten by five"—this is due to non-expression (*anabhidhāna*). And this non-expression must necessarily be accepted. Even if a formal enumeration (*parigaṇana*) were made, the *bahuvrīhi* compound does not occur where there is no expression;

for example, "five have eaten [food] belonging to him. Now, if such non-expression exists, even if there were an enumeration of the types of formations (*vṛtti*), [the compound would still not apply].

A listing of the *varti*s must also be made. How should that be done? When the meaning is restricted, the inclusion of the sense of possession (*matvartha*) is necessary. When the meaning is restricted, the inclusion of the sense of possession must be stated: "That which occurs in the sense of possession is a *bahuvrīhi*. This is so that it does not apply here: *kaṣṭaṃ śritam anena* ("suffering has been resorted to by him"). And thus the purpose of the subsequent statement is fulfilled. By doing this, the purpose of the statement of the subsequent rule becomes justified. Some, however, say:

Regarding what is stated in the *vṛtti-sūtra*: "Numerals, indeclinables, words meaning 'near,' 'not far,' and 'more than,' when denoting a number, [form a compound] with a word denoting the thing numbered. Another says: regarding what is stated in the *vārttika*: "With a word expressing an object (*karman*), [there is a compound] other than the first case. A *bahuvrīhi* compound should be stated with a word expressing an object, excluding the first case. For example:

"A chariot has been carried by him" → *ūḍharatha* (one who has carried a chariot), [referring to] an ox; "An animal has been offered to Rudra" → *upahṛtapaśu* (one to whom an animal has been offered).

"Rudra" is the rice that has been removed; "sthālyā uddhṛtaudana" is the pot from which the rice has been removed. If it is said [the compound is formed] with a word expressing the object (*karman*), how is it when the word expresses the agent (*kartṛ*)? For example: *prāptam udakam grāmam* (water reached the village) becomes *prāptodako grāmaḥ* (a village reached by water); *āgatā atithayo grāmam* (guests came to the village) becomes *āgatātithir grāmaḥ* (a village whose guests have arrived). It must also be stated that [the compound is formed] even with a word expressing the agent. It must be stated that it is [formed] even with a word expressing the agent.

What is the purpose of the condition "not being in the nominative case" (*aprathamāyāḥ*)? [Consider the example: *vṛṣṭe deve gataḥ* ("When it had rained, he went"). If the condition "not being in the nominative case" were stated, why would [the rule] not apply here: *vṛṣṭe deve gatam paśya* ("See that when it had rained, [he] went")? In this case, the non-nominative case is extrinsically conditioned (*bahiraṅga*). [The answer is: Under the heading governing *sub*-suffixes (*sub-adhikāre*), there must be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for words such as *astikṣīrā* ("having milk"). Under the heading governing *sub*-suffixes, an addition must be made for *astikṣīrā* and similar forms. [Example: *astikṣīrā*.
[Objection: Then it must be stated [that the feminine suffix *ṅīp* applies after *brāhmaṇa*]. [Reply: Or rather, it need not be stated. Why?
Because of its indeclinability (*avyayatva*). This word *asti* is an indeclinable; it is not the present tense (*laṭ*) of the root *as*. How is it an indeclinable?

By the rule "Particles (*nipāta*) are those that resemble prepositions (*upasarga*), case-endings (*vibhakti*), or accents (*svara*)," it receives the designation of a particle. And a particle [is indeclinable].
"Indeclinable" (*avyaya*) refers to the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "indeclinable.
Now, regarding the compound *kiṃsabrahmacārī*: what kind of compound is this? It is said to be a *bahuvrīhi*. What is its [meaning]?
[The opponent proposes: "The analysis [of the compound] is: 'Of whom is he a fellow-student (sabrahmacārī)? If this is so, the reply 'Kaṭha' is not tenable;

for one who is asked about one thing does not state another. If that is the case, then the analysis shall be made thus: 'A fellow-student of whom?—a Kiṃsabrahmacārī. But even then, the reply is not tenable, and there is also a fault regarding the accent."

A fault arises. [If the compound were analyzed as] *kiṃ sabrahmacārī*, then such an accent (*svara*) would result; however, *kiṃsabrahmacārī* is what is intended. If that is the case, then the analysis will be performed thus: *kaḥ sabrahmacārī* = *kiṃsabrahmacārī*. In this way, the response would be appropriate, but there remains a fault regarding the accent. Therefore, the analysis shall be as follows: [the analysis of *kiṃsabrahmacārī*].

It will be explained as follows: "Who is your fellow religious student? What kind of fellow religious student are you? Alternatively, let the analysis be this: "Whose are his fellow religious students? But was it not said that the response "Kaṭha" would be untenable? This is not a fault; it will be understood according to the maxim of "I shall place [the oblation] in the fire" (*agnau karavāṇi*). For example, someone says to another:

"I shall perform [the rite] in the fire. When the agent is authorized with "Do so," the action is also authorized. Another says: "[The rite] will be performed in the fire. When the object is authorized with "Let it be done," the agent is also authorized. Just as, for instance, when it is asked, "Who are his fellow-students? and the answer is given, "The Kaṭhas," this is understood through the relationship [of the students to him].
"Surely he too is a Kaṭha. When it is said "thus [is] a Kaṭha," this must be understood through connection:

"surely they too are Kaṭhas. Indeed, they cannot be designated by means of a compound; for they become subordinate members (*upasarjana*). Now, regarding the term *arthatṛtīyāḥ*, what kind of compound is this? He says: it is a *bahuvrīhi*. Which one?
The analysis (*vigraha*) of this is: "the third part of these. What is the meaning of the compound? The meaning of the compound is not tenable.
For that which is called the "meaning of another word" (*anyapadārtha*) is the meaning of a word other than those words whose compound it is;
thus, it would be the meaning of a word external to the compound. If that is so, then the analysis will be formulated thus: "the third part of these two."
Thus [it is asked]: even so, what is the meaning of the genitive? The meaning of the genitive is not tenable. For what indeed becomes the "half" of those two?

Let it be that the analysis is thus: "the third part of these is a half. But was it not said that the meaning of the compound is not tenable? This is not a fault; the analysis is by means of a part, while the meaning of the compound is the whole. If...

The analysis (*vigraha*) by means of a constituent part is that the collective whole is the meaning of the compound: "he followed the Pāṇḍava with a sword as his second" (*asidvitīyaḥ*). [One might object: "May the strength of Kṛṣṇa increase, who has Saṃkarṣaṇa as his second"—in this case, the dual number would apply to the two [entities]. Let it be that this very analysis is correct: "the half is the third of these two. But was it not said that the sense of the genitive case is not applicable? No, this is not so.
This is a fault. First, he should be asked this: now, in the expression "Devadatta’s brother," what is the meaning of the genitive case?

To that, one might say: "Arising from the same source. But that is untenable. For example, when members of a caravan have stayed together in a single lodging and set out in the morning, there is no mutual relationship between them whatsoever.

Such is the nature of this so-called "brotherhood. If the sense of the genitive case is seen to be appropriate here, let it be seen as appropriate here as well. But in that case, when it is said, "Let two and a half [people] be brought," the bringing of the "half" would not be obtained. Let this analysis then be: "the half is the third of these. But has it not already been stated?

He followed the Pāṇḍava [with the thought]: "May the strength of Kṛṣṇa, who has Saṅkarṣaṇa as his second, increase. [Objection: "In the case of two things, the dual number ought to be used. [Response: This is not a fault. This word ending in *-tīya* exists both as a ordinal (*pūraṇa*) and as a term denoting a companion (*sahāyavācin*). Here, it is the one denoting a companion that is being taken; thus, "having a sword as his second" (*asidvitīyaḥ*) is understood to mean "having a sword as his companion" (*asisahāyaḥ*). It is the same here.

Regarding the expression *api ardhatṛtīyāḥ*, since there is the rule that "the singular number is used for a single thing," the singular would be required; for aggregates consist of a single referent, as in the cases of "a hundred," "a herd," or "a forest. Alternatively, let this be the analysis: "half is the third of these two" (*ardham tṛtīyam anayoḥ*). But was it not said that when it is commanded, "Let two-and-a-half [measures] be brought," only half is brought?

"It does not obtain"—this is not a fault. In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is also the "cognition of its qualities" (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*). For example: "Bring the one who wears white clothes" (*śuklavāsasam ānaya*); "The priests wearing red turbans proceed" (*lohitoṣṇīṣāḥ ṛtvijaḥ pracaranti*). The one possessing that quality is brought, and those possessing that quality proceed. Or rather, let this analysis be: "Half is the third part of these."

Thus [it is said]. Now, it was objected that the singular number would result; however, this is not a fault. This thing called "number" is subordinate to something else; by it, the object to be numbered (saṅkhyeya) is to be qualified. And if the singular were used here, the object to be numbered would remain unqualified. In this case, however, as in "three and a half *droṇas*," this word *droṇa* applies to the aggregate, yet [it is also used] for a part.
This is not tenable. This is not a fault. Words that are applied to wholes also function with respect to their parts.

For example: "the eastern Pañcālas," "the northern Pañcālas," "oil has been eaten," "ghee has been eaten," and "white," "blue," "tawny," "black. In this same way, the word *droṇa*, though applied to a whole measure, also functions with respect to its constituent parts.

In that case, by this very same reasoning, when two *droṇas* and half of a half-*āḍhaka* are to be expressed, one should say "two and a half *droṇas*" (*ardhatṛtīyā droṇāḥ*). It need not be so. For words that have been applied to wholes also function with respect to their parts. With respect to which parts? To those parts which do not deviate from that whole.
And what aggregate does it not deviate from? "Half a *droṇa* is a *droṇa*" [it does not deviate]. However, "half an *āḍhaka*" does deviate.
What kind of compound is this in "two or three" (*dvitrāḥ*) and "three or four" (*tricaturāḥ*)? He says: it is a *bahuvrīhi*. What is its analysis (*vigraha*)?

"Two or three," they say. When there is the bringing of many, then the plural number is appropriate; but when indeed only two are brought, it is not established. Even then, it is established. How? Some first say: "The plural number should be employed when the object is not specifically determined. For example: [as follows].

“How many sons do you have? How many wives do you have? Another says: when “two” is said, “three” is understood; when “three” is said, “two” is understood. This speech has five bases. In this case, the plural number is appropriate. Now, [consider] “the twelve” and “the thirty-three.”

"What kind of compound is this? "It is a *bahuvrīhi*," he says. "What is its analysis (*vigraha*)? "'Twice ten' means 'two tens'. "In a numerical compound, because it ends in the suffix *suc*, there is no establishment of the number [ten]. In a numerical compound, because it ends in the suffix *suc*, the term "number" is not established; for there is no such thing as a "number" that ends in *suc*. If that is the case, then the analysis shall be formulated in this way: [dvi-daśau = two tens].

"Two tens are *dvidaśāḥ*. Even so, because it ends in the suffix *-at*, it would not be recognized as a "number" (*saṅkhyā*), for there is no number that ends in the suffix *-at*. Well then, let this analysis be: "ten twice" is *dviśaśāḥ*. But was it not said that in a numeral compound (*saṅkhyā-samāsa*), because it ends in the suffix *suc*, it would not be recognized as a "number"? No, for it does not end in *suc*.

Or rather, this is not a fault. What is the reason? Because it is not a form ending in *su*. It is said that [the suffixes] end in *su*; however, we do not perceive anything here ending in *su*. But what is the reason that *su* is seen in a sentence (*vākya*) but is not seen in a compound (*samāsa*)? The state of having *su* does not exist in a compound because its meaning has already been expressed. There is an absence of *su* in a compound. What is the reason? Because its meaning has already been expressed (*abhihitārthatvāt*). It has been expressed.

If it is argued that the *su* suffix will not occur in a compound because the sense of *su* (*suj-artha*) has already been expressed by the compound, we reply: Why, sir, is it said that the compound is formed "in the sense of *su*"?

Indeed, it is not explicitly stated that it is "in the sense of *su*," yet the sense of *su* is understood. How so? Because that which is to be numbered (*saṅkhyeya*)—that which is counted by a number—is for the purpose of repeating an action (*kriyābhyāvṛtti*), and that [repetition] has already been expressed by the compound.

Once the compound has been formed, the suffix *suc* will not apply. A *bahuvrīhi* with a numeral as its final member is unnecessary to be taught, because it expresses a countable object (*saṃkhyeya*). It is unnecessary to teach a *bahuvrīhi* with a numeral as its final member. Why? Because it expresses a countable object. For both the numeral and the meaning "object" (*artha*) are expressed [by the compound]. In that case, it is already established by the rule itself for the sense of "another word's meaning" (*anyapadārtha*). It would indeed be established.

Regarding the forms *adhikaviṃśāḥ* and *adhikatriṃśāḥ*, it is deliberated here whether words such as *viṃśati* and so on denote the sense of "ten" (*daśadartha*) or the possessor of that measure (*parimāṇin*). However, the form *adhikadaśāḥ* is not established [by this rule], because in that case the word necessarily refers only to the thing numbered (*saṅkhyeya*). Now, what kind of compound is *upadaśāḥ*? He says: it is a *bahuvrīhi*. What is its [analysis]?

The compound is *upadaśāḥ*, meaning "near ten. But to what does "nearness" (*sāmīpya*) refer? It refers to the word *upa*. If this is so, then it is not the meaning of another member of the compound (*anyapadārtha*). In that case, it would be possible to omit the mention of "number" (*saṅkhyāgrahaṇa*) when [the rule] is stated with the nominative case.

Or rather, because the preceding rule was formulated for the sense of possession (*matvarthe*), this present rule is for the non-possessive sense (*amatvartha*). Alternatively, the preceding rule applies to the possessive sense, whereas this one applies to the non-possessive sense.
[This is] the introduction. Or rather, it is for the sake of preventing the *kap* suffix; that is, so that *kap* might not occur.

[The rule applies] in the case of a compound of directions (*dik-samāsa*) and in the case of association (*sahayoga*), because these denote the intermediate space as the primary meaning. [This refers to] compounds of directions and associations.

And the *aśiṣya* [example] is a *bahuvrīhi*. What is the reason? Because it denotes the intermediate space as the primary meaning. In a compound of directions (*dik-samāsa*) and in the sense of accompaniment (*saha-yoga*), the intermediate space is denoted as the primary element. In that case, it is already established by the rule "in the sense of another word" (*anyapadārthe*). If this is so, then in the case of *dakṣiṇapūrvā dik* ("the south-eastern direction"), the masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) characterized by coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) would not apply. But now, moreover—

If one considers that "this is that very same *dakṣiṇā*" and "that is the very same *pūrvā*," then the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*)—characterized by grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*)—would be established.

But it is not so established. The substitution of the masculine form applies only to words that have been used in the masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*). And these two [words] have not been used in the masculine. [Objection:
But surely, sir, the word *dakṣiṇa* and the word *pūrva* are used in the masculine. [Reply: Only when they belong to the same generic form (*ākṛti*).

[The words] *dakṣiṇā* and *pūrvā* are [examples of] those that have been mentioned as having a masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*). These two also have masculine forms in other morphological configurations (*ākṛtyantara*): *dakṣiṇaḥ* and *pūrvaḥ*.

The words *dakṣiṇā* and *pūrvā* are terms denoting direction (*dikśabda*), whereas *dakṣiṇaḥ* and *pūrvaḥ* are terms denoting relative position (*vyavasthāśabda*). Now, if even the terms denoting direction were also terms denoting relative position, how would those grammatical operations prescribed for "directions" apply? When the directions express a relative position—if...

If [the term] "dikśabda" (direction-word) refers to whatever exists in a direction, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to words such as *ramaṇīyā* (pleasant), as in "the pleasant direction" (*ramaṇīyā dik*) or "the beautiful direction" (*śobhanā dik*). Now, if it is held that "dikśabda" means a word seen in the direction—a word seen in the direction (*digdṛṣṭa*) or directed toward the direction (*digdiṣṭa*)—that is, a word which does not deviate from denoting a direction, then there is no over-extension to words such as *ramaṇīyā*. [In this case], the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) applies.

[The objection continues: But [the desired form] is not obtained. If that is so, then it must be stated that for a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), there is *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution) in all instances of its occurrence (*vṛtti*), for the sake of forms such as *dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām*.

And having done this, [it follows] that in the case of a compound of directions (*dik-samāsa*) and in the case of association (*sahayoga*), there is indeed [only one form] because of the denotation of the intermediate space as the primary meaning. But was it not already said that in the case of "the direction south-east" (*dakṣiṇapūrvā dik*), the *puṃvadbhāva* characterized by grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) does not apply?

"It follows [that the rule applies]. This is not a fault. It has been resolved by the application of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) for all pronouns (*sarvanāman*) in every kind of compound formation (*vṛtti*). Or rather, because the preceding rule was prescribed for the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Alternatively, the preceding rule pertains to the sense of possession; this present rule is commenced for what is not the sense of possession (*amatvartha*). Or else, it is for the sake of avoiding the suffix *kap*; that is, so that *kap* does not occur.

Furthermore, because the action is expressed when [words] ending in the third or seventh case are used, the *bahuvrīhi* compound is not subject to further rule (*aśiṣya*). What is the reason? Because the action is expressed. The action is expressed there in the sense of another word (*anyapadārtha*).

Thus it is established. Or rather, it is not for the purpose of prohibiting *ekaśeṣa*. Nor is it something that need not be taught. What is the reason? This must be stated for the purpose of prohibiting *ekaśeṣa*, and also for the sake of the lengthening of the preceding vowel (*pūrvadīrgha*). And this must be stated for the sake of the lengthening of the preceding vowel in forms such as *keśākeśi*. This would be a valid purpose if its lengthening were necessarily produced by this [rule] alone. But now—

The rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate* [Pāṇini 6.3.137] shows that lengthening is not required [for the vowel of *mālā*]. Alternatively, because the preceding rule [Pāṇini 5.2.115] was formulated for the purpose of expressing possession (*matvartha*), this [present] formulation [of Pāṇini 5.2.120] concerns a case where there is no possessive sense. Or rather, it is for the sake of preventing the suffix *kap*; that is, so that *kap* does not occur.
Regarding the statement "in the sense of *ca* (*cārthe*)," since *ca* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), it follows that the compound would receive the designation of an indeclinable.
This is not a fault. The designation of an indeclinable is established by formal recitation (*pāṭha*). And the compound is not recited there [among the indeclinables]. By virtue of the recitation...

Even when the designation "indeclinable" (avyaya-sañjñā) applies, gender and number occur just as they do for that which is denoted. And the meaning that is expressed here has no connection with gender or number. This lack of gender and number is not something established by formal rule (vācanika); rather, it is inherent (svābhāvika). For example:

Among those who strive equally and study alike, some are joined with results while others are not. Yet, one cannot assume that because someone is successful now, everyone must be successful; nor can one assume that because someone is unsuccessful now, everyone must be unsuccessful. In this matter, what can we do regarding that which occurred prior to the composition of the *Pāṇinīya-samāsa*?

Furthermore, there is no connection of the meaning with gender and number in a compound, yet it occurs; this is its inherent nature. Alternatively, the gender and number will be determined by the substratum (āśraya). For words that express qualities (guṇavacana) take their gender and number from the substratum.
For example: "a white cloth" (*śuklaṃ vastram*).

"A white cloth," "a white blanket," "two white blankets," "many white blankets"— in these cases, whatever gender and number the substance (dravya) which the quality (guṇa) depends upon possesses, those same gender and number belong to the quality as well. Thus, here too, that which this [quality] depends upon...
The gender and number belonging to that [prior member] will also belong to the compound.

Now, why does it not occur here: "he is both a ritualist (yājñika) and a grammarian (vaiyākaraṇa)," "he is both a Kaṭha and a Bahvṛca," or "he is both an Aukthika and a Mīmāṃsaka"? The word "remainder" (śeṣa) is understood [from the previous rule]; because these are not remainders, it will not occur.

If the term "remainder" (śeṣa) continues to apply, then [the rule would not hold] for a place that has been sprinkled with water, drenched with thick liquid, or for a silent stream, a great lake, or a *droṇa*—if one is unable to go there, [thinking] "let them not afflict you," [and thus] this [rule] would not be established. This is not a fault; for one thing is done (*kṛta*) and another thing is left undone (*akṛta*).

If the term *dvandva* were prescribed for the sense of *ca*, there would be the undesirable consequence [of the rule applying] even in the case of a non-compound (*asamāsa*), because the sense of *ca* is understood even in a non-compound. If the term *dvandva* were prescribed for the sense of *ca*, since the sense of *ca* is understood even in a non-compound, an undesired result follows: [one would have to apply the rule to] *ahaḥ ahaḥ nayamānaḥ*.

Vaivasvata is not satisfied with cattle, horses, men, or livestock, just as one intoxicated by liquor is never satiated. [The deities are] Indra, Tvaṣṭṛ, Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Āditya. But this is established by the rule stating that a *dvandva* compound denotes things that occupy the same substratum simultaneously. How so? This is established because it must be stated: "A *dvandva* compound occurs when words denote things that occupy the same substratum simultaneously. In that case, there is a prohibition against the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*).

In this regard, regarding this characteristic, a prohibition of the masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) must be stated. In the case of *paṭvīmṛdvyau*, the masculine-like treatment conditioned by grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) would apply. Furthermore, there is an impossibility in the case of contradictory things. There is an impossibility of simultaneous predication of a single substratum (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*) in the case of contradictory things, such as cold and heat, pleasure and pain, or birth and death. What is the reason? Because of the mutual exclusion of pleasure [by its opposite].

For indeed, suffering is [defined] by its opposition to pleasure. As for what was said regarding the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) in that context, this person must first be questioned:
why then does it not occur here in the case of *darśanīyāmātā* (the mother of a beautiful woman)? If it is thought thus: [that the rule applies only when the feminine suffix is elided].

Since the rule for the masculine-like transformation (*puṃvadbhāva*) applies wherever there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) prior to compounding, there is no fault here either. As for what was said—that there is an impossibility in the case of contradictory terms—all words are indeed contradictory. Even here, in the expression *plakṣanyagrodhau*, when the word *plakṣa* is employed, it denotes the sense of a *plakṣa* tree.

It causes the understanding of the *nyagrodha* and excludes the *plakṣa*. When the word *nyagrodha* is employed, it causes the understanding of the object *nyagrodha* and excludes the object *plakṣa*. If simultaneous denotation of the substrata (*adhikaraṇavacanatā*) is seen to be appropriate here, let it be seen as appropriate here as well. Even so, because of the sequential employment of the words, there is the expression of a sequence of meanings.

From the employment of the sequence of words, it follows that there must be an expression of the sequence of meanings. What follows from this? It results in the impossibility of simultaneous denotation of the substrata, as in the cases of *plakṣanyagrodhau* and *plakṣanyagrodhāḥ*. For just as there is a sequence among words, so too must there be a sequence among their meanings. Because of the employment of the sequence of words, there is an expression of the sequence of meanings.

If this is the case, then the dual and plural number endings would be untenable. If it is argued that the sequence of meanings is expressed based on the sequence of word-usage, then the dual and plural number endings would still be untenable; for example, in the cases *plakṣanyagrodhau* (the *plakṣa* and *nyagrodha* trees) and *plakṣanyagrodhāḥ* (the *plakṣa* and *nyagrodha* trees). [In such a view,] the meaningful word *plakṣa* would have ceased [to function], and the word *nyagrodha* [would be the sole representative].

When [the two words] are presented as having a single meaning, because they have a single meaning, only the singular number would apply. However, the simultaneous expression [of both meanings] in the analytical statement (*vigraha*) is an indicator of that simultaneous expression. Indeed, simultaneous expression is observed even in the analytical statement:
"Heaven and Earth," and "Even Heaven and Earth bow down before him. What is this? It is the state of expressing a common substratum simultaneously (*yugapad-adhikaraṇa-vacanatā*).

[This is] a supporting argument. It is said that in a *vigraha* (analytic statement), there might be simultaneous denotation of multiple substrates (*yugapad-adhikaraṇavacanatā*), so how much more so in a compound (*samāsa*)?

[Objection: This is established from the whole (*samudāya*). [Response: This is indeed established from the whole. What is meant by "established from the whole"? It has been urged that this would result in the occurrence of dual and plural numbers. This is the rebuttal to that: if it is argued that it is established from the whole, we say no, because the whole possesses a single meaning (*ekārthatva*).

If it is argued that [the meaning] is established from the aggregate (*samudāya*), that is not so. What is the reason? Because the aggregate has a single referent. For aggregates possess a single referent, as for example: "a hundred," "a herd," or "a forest. But this does not have a single referent; it is not a single referent. What then? It has two referents and many referents. The *plakṣa* tree also has two referents, as does the *nyagrodha*.

Furthermore, [the word] *plakṣa* has two referents; if *nyagrodha* also has two referents, then because those two have multiple referents, there would be the undesirable consequence of using the plural number. Because those two have multiple referents, the rule "the plural is used for many" (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*) would apply, resulting in the use of the plural. If it is argued that there is the undesirable consequence of the plural because those two have multiple referents, we say no, because plurality is absent. Even though those two have multiple referents...

If it is argued that there would be the contingency of using the plural number, that is not so. What is the reason? Because of the absence of plurality. Plurality does not exist here. Why is it said that there is an absence of plurality, when it was just stated that the *plakṣa* tree has two meanings and the *nyagrodha* tree also has two meanings? For by those very same [meanings] by which one is "having two meanings," by those very same ones the other is as well.

Furthermore: if it is argued that it is impossible for one thing to be expressed by a word denoting another—that is, it is not possible for one thing to be expressed by a word denoting something else—if you say, "it is impossible for one thing to be expressed by a word denoting another," then because a *plakṣa* tree is a *nyagrodha* and a *nyagrodha* tree is a *plakṣa*, it would follow that they are denoted by their own respective words; thus, it is impossible for one thing to be expressed by a word denoting another.

If this is argued, it is said: that is not so. What is the reason? Because a *plakṣa* tree is a *nyagrodha* and a *nyagrodha* is a *plakṣa*, they are denoted by their own respective words; thus, a *plakṣa* is also a *nyagrodha*, and a *nyagrodha* is also a *plakṣa*. But how can a *plakṣa* be a *nyagrodha* and a *nyagrodha* be a *plakṣa*, given that the application of a word to a substance [is based on a specific cause]?

If it is argued that the application of the word [to the substance] is due to its cause, [we reply: it is established because the cause is the same. If it is argued that the application of the word to the substance is due to its cause, this is stated as follows:
that is not so, because the cause is the same; for the cause is indeed identical. If, first of all, it is called a *plakṣa* because it exudes sap (*prakṣarati*), [then the same applies].

This [etymology] might apply to the *nyagrodha* tree as well: if it grows downwards (*nyak rohati*), it is a *nyagrodha*. This same [etymology] would also apply to the *plakṣa* tree. If you say that observation is the basis [for usage], it is the same in this case; for the word *plakṣa* is not observed to be applied to a *nyagrodha*. If you say that observation is the basis, then it is the same: let the word *nyagrodha* also be observed to be applied to a *plakṣa*. It is the same.

For this is the reason: indeed, such a conventional understanding does not exist in the world. For when it is said, "Let a *plakṣa* tree be brought," a *nyagrodha* tree is not brought. And this [usage] has that as its scope; one must see that the status of being a *nyagrodha* belongs to the *plakṣa*.
What is its scope? Its scope is the *dvandva* compound. Furthermore, it is appropriate that words should have restricted domains.
"Certainly, it is logical; for that is observed elsewhere as well. Indeed, words are seen to have restricted referents even in other cases. For example:
although the color red is the same, one says 'the cow is red' (*lohita*) and 'the horse is crimson' (*śoṇa*). And although the color at the same time is the same..."

A cow is "black" and a horse is "golden. Even when the color is the same, white, a cow is called "white" and a horse is called "karka. If that is so, then since a *plakṣa* tree is also a *nyagrodha* and a *nyagrodha* is also a *plakṣa*, the use of one term after the other is untenable because it has already been expressed by the first; since that meaning has already been expressed by one, the use of the other is redundant.

It is not tenable that the term *nyagrodha* is employed in connection with a *plakṣa*. If it is argued that the employment of the second term is untenable because the first has already expressed it, [we reply] that the employment of *nyagrodha* in connection with the *plakṣa* is indeed possible because it has not been expressed. If it is argued that the employment of the second is untenable because the first has already expressed it, that is not so. Why? Because it has not been expressed.

The application of the word *nyagrodha* [occurs] by means of the word *plakṣa*. The meaning of *nyagrodha* is not explicitly stated by the word *plakṣa*; therefore, the word *nyagrodha* is employed. How is it not stated, given that it was just said that "the *plakṣa* is also the *nyagrodha*, and the *nyagrodha* is also the *plakṣa*"? These two express each other's meaning when they are co-occurrent, but not when they are separate.
But what is the reason that these two, being co-existent, express their meaning for one another when not separate?

Furthermore, the designation is intrinsic; the designation is intrinsic. Alternatively, in this case, there may be certain *plakṣa* and *nyagrodha* trees belonging to the first aeon, or something may be called a *plakṣa* because of its action or quality, such as "this is a *plakṣa* because it is like a *plakṣa*."
"This is a *nyagrodha*, like a *nyagrodha*. In that case, when it is said "two *plakṣas*," doubt might arise:

"Are these two *plakṣas*, or are they a *plakṣa* and a *nyagrodha*? To eliminate such doubt, the word *nyagrodha* is employed. This so-called "simultaneous expression of multiple substrates" (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*) is both difficult and hard to justify. And furthermore—

Furthermore, its basis has been stated as *dyāvā ha kṣāmā*; that too is Vedic (*chāndasa*). In that case, it is established by the rule *supām supo bhavanti* (substitutes of case endings take the place of case endings). Moreover, the Sūtra would have to be modified. Let it remain exactly as it is. But was it not said that, since the meaning of "conjunction" (*cārtha*) is understood even in a non-compound when expressing conjunction (*dvandva*), there would be the undesirable consequence [of such compounds being formed]? This is not so.

There is a fault here. This [rule] is already established by the rule *ce dvandve*. How, then, could there be an application (*vṛtti*) for *ca*? For this is a word; since [the operation] is impossible with respect to the word itself, it will be understood to apply to the meaning. Now, since this is already established, the purpose of his making the mention of "meaning" (*artha*) is so that it may be understood that the meaning is not effected by *ca*.

"And what is the meaning of *ca*? What, then, is the meaning conveyed by *ca*? It is: conjunction (*samuccaya*), sequential mention (*anvācaya*), mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*), and collective totality (*samāhāra*). Conjunction: when it is said, 'And the *plakṣa* tree,' it is understood that 'and the *nyagrodha* tree' [is also implied]. Sequential mention:
when it is said, 'And the *plakṣa* tree,' it is understood that 'this is employed with reference to something else. Mutual connection..."

When it is said, "the *plakṣa* and the *nyagrodha*," it is understood that the *plakṣa* has the *nyagrodha* as its companion and the *nyagrodha* has the *plakṣa* as its companion. Even when a collective (*samāhāra*) is intended, the form *plakṣanyagrodham* is employed. In that case, this rule regarding the singular form of a *dvandva* need not be explicitly stated; for it is established by the very fact that the collective is a single entity.

Regarding the expressions *ekādaśa* and *dvādaśa*, what kind of compound is this? It is a *dvandva* compound of *eka* and the others with *daśa* and the others. If it is a *dvandva* compound of *eka* and the others with *daśa* and the others, then there would be the undesirable consequence of applying the plural number to *viṃśati* and so forth.

If it is argued that there is a *dvandva* compound of "one" and so forth with "ten" and so forth, then the rule would apply to numbers such as twenty and beyond, resulting in forms like *ekaviṃśatiḥ* (twenty-one) and *dvāviṃśatiḥ* (twenty-two). However, this is established: in the section concerning grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), a number ending in "additional" (*adhika*) is compounded with another number, and the word "additional" is elided. This is thus established. How? It should be stated in the section on coreferentiality that a number ending in "additional" is [compounded] with another number.
It is compounded together with the word *saha*, and there is the elision (*lopa*) of the word *adhika*. Thus: "twenty exceeded by one" is *ekaviṃśati*;

"twenty exceeded by two" is *dvāviṃśati*. If it were a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the accent would not be established. For that rule which states that "the first member, being a numeral, retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*)" applies specifically to *dvandva* compounds. What, then, is the reason?

It is thus in the case of a *dvandva* compound. Let it not be so here in the case of "a hundred thousand" (*śatasahasram*). Well then, let it be a *dvandva*. But was it not said that if there were a *dvandva* of "one" and so on with "ten" and so on, there would be the undesirable consequence of plural number in the words for twenty and so forth? This is not a fault, because every *dvandva* optionally functions as a singular. When, then, it is in the singular, [it is as follows].

It would result in the neuter gender. Gender is not subject to formal prescription, because gender is based on common usage in the world. (Pāṇini 2.2.30) Why is this stated? It is for the purpose of ensuring that the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is placed first, thereby precluding its occurrence at the end of the compound.

The rule stating that the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) must be placed first is formulated so that its usage at the end [of the compound] might not occur. Or rather, this is not necessary, because no undesirable consequence is observed. Why? Because no undesirable result is seen. Indeed, no one uses the form *puruṣarājaḥ* when they ought to use *rājapuruṣaḥ*. If...

And since undesirable [results] are seen [otherwise], therefore it must be for the sake of effort. Now, when there are two words ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), why does the primary element not occur first in a compound such as *rājñaḥ puruṣasya* (the king’s man) becoming *rājapuruṣasya*? In a compound of two words ending in the genitive, because there is no difference in meaning, the primary element does not occur first. This is the case in a compound of two words ending in the genitive.

744–746. Is this rule mandatory (*tantra*) or optional (*atantra*)? And what follows from this? If it is mandatory, there is a restriction regarding two items, but no restriction regarding many. What fault is there in that? The compound *śaṅkhadundubhivīṇānām* would not be established; furthermore, the word *dundubhi* would also have to appear first [in the compound]. If, on the other hand, it is optional, then [the forms] *mṛdaṅgaśaṅkhatūṇavāḥ* and so forth are possible.

“They cry out separately in the assembly” [is formed]. [The rule] “in the palace of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), Rāma, and Keśava” is not established. Let it be as you wish. Let the *tantra* (the governing rule) apply for now. But was it not said that there is a restriction when there are two [words], and no restriction when there are many? In that case, [the compound] “of the conch, the drum, and the lute” would not be established; for even the word *dundubhi* (drum) would have to appear first [according to the rule of alphabetical order].

[The objection: "It follows [that the rule applies incorrectly]. [The response: This is not a fault. That which is stated as *alpāctaram* (the one with fewer syllables), I shall state as *alpāc* (the one with fewer vowels). Or rather, let it be that the mention of *atantra* (non-essential) is not intended. But was it not said that the following would not be established: *mṛdaṅgaśaṅkhatūṇavāḥ pṛthak nadanti saṃsadi* ("The drum, conch, and flute resound separately in the assembly") and *prāsāde dhanapatirāmakeśavānām* ("In the palace of Dhanapati, Rāma, and Keśava")? [The response: When the mention of *atantra* is not intended, [the rule applies] to the conch and the flute.

The compound with *mṛdaṅga* is as follows: when the mention of the suffix *tarap* is not mandatory (*atantra*), the compound of *śaṅkha* and *tūṇava* will be formed with *mṛdaṅga*. Thus: *śaṅkhaśca tūṇavaśca* = *śaṅkhatūṇavau*; *mṛdaṅgaśca śaṅkhatūṇavau ca* = *mṛdaṅgaśaṅkhatūṇavāḥ*. Similarly: *rāmaśca keśavaśca* = *rāmakeśavau*; *dhanapatiśca rāmakeśavau ca* = *dhanapatirāmakeśavāḥ*.

Regarding the example "teṣām dhanapatirāmakeśavānām" (of them, Dhanapati, Rāma, and Keśava): now, where there is the possibility of multiple [words] being placed first, does the restriction apply to only one of them, or without distinction? When several [options] are possible, there is a restriction for one, and no restriction for the rest. When several [options] are possible, there is a restriction for one, and no restriction for the rest. For example: *paṭumṛduśuklāḥ* or *paṭuśuklamṛdavaḥ*.

(P_2,2.34.2) Regarding seasons and lunar mansions that have the same number of syllables, when listed in their natural order, the one mentioned first [the shorter one] should be stated as the prior member of the compound. For example: *śiśiravasantau* (winter and spring), *udagayanasthau* (those situated in the northern course of the sun), and *kṛttikārohiṇyaḥ* (the lunar mansions Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī). This applies to what is more venerable (*abhyarhitam*).

It should be stated that "that which is more venerable comes first. For example: *mātāpitarau* (mother and father), *śraddhāmedhe* (faith and wisdom). It should be stated that "that which has fewer syllables comes first. For example: *kuśakāśam* (grass and reeds), *śaraśīryam* (reed and *śīrya* grass). Another says: "In all cases, it should be stated that 'that which is more venerable comes first,' even over that which has fewer syllables. For example: *śraddhātapasī* (faith and austerity).

Regarding *dīkṣā* and *tapas*: it should be stated that among the social classes (*varṇa*), the one that precedes in the traditional order takes the first position [in a compound]. Example: *brāhmaṇakṣatriyaviṭśūdrāḥ*. Regarding "the elder brother": it should be stated that the elder brother takes the first position [in a compound]. Example: *yudhiṣṭhirārjunau*. Regarding "the smaller number": [it should be stated that] the smaller number...
It should be stated that the shorter [member] takes the first position: *ekādaśa* (eleven), *dvādaśa* (twelve). Regarding the group beginning with *dharma*, both [alternatives] apply:
it should be stated that regarding the group beginning with *dharma*, both [members] may optionally take the first position. Thus: *dharmārthau* or *arthadharmau*; *kāmārthau* or *arthakāmau*;
*guṇavṛddhī* or *vṛddhiguṇau*; *ādyantau* or *antādī*.

(P_2.2.35) An addition must be made regarding the application of the rules for *sarvanāman* (pronominal) and *saṃkhyā* (numeral) in a *bahuvrīhi* compound. An addition must be made regarding the application of the rules for *sarvanāman* and *saṃkhyā* in a *bahuvrīhi*:
*viśvadevaḥ*, *viśvayasāḥ*, *dviputraḥ*, *dvibhāryaḥ*. Now, in cases where...
A *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed only from a numeral and a pronominal; in that case, which of the two should undergo prior placement? The numeral, because it is subsequent [in the rule]:

*dvyanya* (one other than two), *tryanya* (one other than three). Alternatively, regarding the word *priya*: it should be stated that *priya* may optionally take prior placement. Thus: *priyaguḍa* (one for whom molasses is dear) or *guḍapriya*. Regarding the prior placement of the locative (*saptamī*): there is a statement concerning words such as *gaḍu* to ensure their subsequent placement. This applies when the locative is to be placed first.

It should be stated that the locative case [ending] follows words such as *gaḍu* and others: *gaḍukaṇṭhaḥ* ("one with a goitre on the neck"), *gaḍuśirāḥ* ("one with a goitre on the head"). Regarding the rule concerning the prior placement of the past participle (*niṣṭhā*), there is a statement [to the effect] that it occurs after words denoting genus (*jāti*), time (*kāla*), pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth. This refers to the prior placement of the past participle.

It should be stated that the suffix *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) follows words denoting genus (*jāti*), time (*kāla*), pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth. Examples are: *śārṅgajagdhi* ("eaten by a horned animal"), *palāṇḍubhakṣitī* ("eaten by an onion"), *māsajātā* ("born after a month"), *saṃvatsarajātā* ("born after a year"), *sukhajātā* ("born in happiness"), and *duḥkhajātā* ("born in suffering"). Alternatively, it need not be stated. Why? Because the rule prescribing that the final syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) be acute (*antodātta*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of its posteriority [to the preceding word]. It need not be stated. What is the reason? Because of the rule prescribing that the final syllable of the subsequent member be acute.

This is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the posteriority of the suffix: the fact that the Teacher teaches the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) of the second member following a *niṣṭhā* (past participle) after words such as *jāti*, *kāla*, and *sukha* indicates that, in this context, the *niṣṭhā* occurs later. However, if there were a prohibition [of the posteriority], there would be the undesirable consequence of the prior placement [of the *niṣṭhā*]; therefore, it is read in the *rājadantādi* group. For if there were a prohibition, the prior placement [of the *niṣṭhā*] would follow.

[The suffix *kta*] is obtained [in the sense of the past]. [In the case of compounds like] *akṛtamitapratipannāḥ*, it should therefore be included in the list of *rājadantādi* compounds. It need not be included; for here too, the statement of the prohibition is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the *niṣṭhā* suffix occurs after [the first member]. And [this applies] after words meaning "weapons.
It should be stated that the *niṣṭhā* and the locative (*saptamī*) suffixes occur after words meaning "weapons": *asyudyataḥ*.

"Musalyudyataḥ," "asipāṇiḥ," and "daṇḍapāṇiḥ. Regarding the rule *dvandve ghi*, the rule *ajādyantam* takes precedence by way of prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*). From the rule *dvandve ghi*, the rule *ajādyantam* prevails through prohibition. The scope (*avakāśa*) of *dvandve ghi* is exemplified by *paṭuguptau*; the scope of *ajādyantam* is exemplified by *uṣṭrakharau*. In the case of *indrāgnī*, both rules would apply.

The rule *ajādyadantam* (A 2.2.33) applies by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The rule *ubhābhyām alpāctaram* (A 2.2.34) also applies. The scope of *dvandve ghi* (A 2.2.32) is, for example, *paṭuguptau*; the scope of *alpāctaram* is, for example, *vāgdṛṣadau*. In the case of *vāgagnī*, both rules would apply; therefore, *alpāctaram* prevails.

It occurs by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). "That which begins with a vowel other than *a* and ends in a short *a*" (*ajādyadantam*) has its scope in the case of *uṣṭra-kharau*. "That which has fewer syllables" (*alpāctaram*) has the same scope. Here, both rules would apply to *vāg-indrau*. By way of conflict, the rule "that which has fewer syllables" prevails.

It should be stated that "kaḍārādayaḥ" [beginning with *kaḍāra*] applies here as well, so that forms such as *gaḍulaśāṇḍilyaḥ* / *śāṇḍilyagaḍulaḥ*, *khaṇḍavātsyaḥ* / *vatsyakaṇḍaḥ* may occur. Then, should it be stated? No, it need not be stated; for it is established by the use of the plural number.
It will be understood that "kaḍārādayaḥ" [refers to those beginning with *kaḍāra*]. (P_2.3.1.1) It is stated:
"when not already expressed" (*anabhihite*). What is this that is called "not already expressed"? That which has been spoken of, pointed out, or expressed is called "expressed" (*abhihita*).
This is not a different meaning. As far as one might say "when unspoken" or "when unspecified," so far does it mean "when not expressed.

The mention of "not expressed" (anabhihita) is redundant because, elsewhere, that which is prescribed [by a suffix] is absent when it is already expressed. The mention of "not expressed" is purposeless. Why? Because elsewhere, too, that which is prescribed is absent when it is expressed; for even elsewhere, it is prescribed only when [the number] is not expressed.

It does not occur. Where else? In *citraguḥ* and *śabalaguḥ*. Because the possessive sense (*matvartha*) has already been expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound, a secondary suffix denoting possession (*matvarthīya*) does not occur. In *gargāḥ*, *vatsāḥ*, *vidāḥ*, and *urvāḥ*, because the meaning of "offspring" has already been expressed by the suffixes *yañ* and *añ*, the regular derivation [of further patronymic suffixes] does not occur. In *saptaparṇaḥ* and *aṣṭāpadam*, because the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) has already been expressed by the compound, [the distributive particle *dvis* or *tris* is not used].

The reduplication does not occur. As for what was said—that because the possessive sense (*matvartha*) has already been expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound, a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is not applied—this is incorrect, because the suffix *matup* is prescribed only when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb "to be" (*asti*).

And in this case, there is no coreferentiality with "to be. Furthermore, as for what was said regarding "the Gargas," "the Vatsas," "the Vidas," and "the Urvās": [these are explained by the fact that the suffix is applied to denote a group].

Because the meaning of "offspring" (*apatya*) has already been expressed by the suffixes *yañ* and *añ*, its further production [by another suffix] is not logically possible. The rule *samarthānām prathamād vā* ("from the first of the capable [words]") continues to apply here. However, this [word *saptaparṇaḥ*] is not the first among the capable words; rather, it has shifted to a second meaning. Furthermore, as for what was said—that in the case of *saptaparṇaḥ* and *aṣṭāpadam*, because repetition (*vīpsā*) has already been expressed by the compound, there should be no doubling [of the word]—[that is incorrect].

"It does not occur" means that what is joined with repetition (*vīpsā*) here is not employed [as a separate word]. What, then, is that? "In every joint (*parvaṇi parvaṇi*) there are seven leaves of this [tree]"; "in every row (*paṅktau paṅktau*) there are eight steps. Now, regarding the suffixes *śnam*, *bahuc*, and *kak*: *śnam*: *bhinatti*, *chinatti*. Because the agency (*kartṛtva*) is already expressed by *śnam*, the *śap* [suffix] does not occur in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). *Bahuc*: *bahukṛtam*.

Regarding the term *bahubhinnam*: because it has already been expressed by the suffix *bahu*, the suffixes such as *kalpa* do not occur when there is only slight completion (*īṣadasamāpti*). Regarding *akac*: in forms such as *uccakaiḥ* and *nīcakaiḥ*, because it has already been expressed by *akac*, the suffixes such as *kā* (denoting contempt, etc. do not occur. [Objection: But surely *śna*, *bahu*, and *akac* are exceptions (*apavāda*); being exceptions, they will necessarily supersede [the general rules]. [Reply: In the case of *śna*, *bahu*, and *akac*, because their positions (*nānādeśatva*) differ from those of the general rules (*utsarga*), there is no prohibition of the general rules.

An exception (apavāda) subverts a general rule (utsarga) when they occupy the same location; because they occupy different locations, [the subversion] does not apply here. But what is it that is being done here? Is the governing heading "when not expressed" (anabhihitādhikāra), which ought to be applied elsewhere, being applied here, or is it being omitted where it ought to be applied? It is being applied here, though it ought not to be. For this indeed is the logical position: that which is prescribed when [the number] is already expressed.

It would not [be necessary]. However, the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is not already expressed; therefore, there is the mention of "not being expressed" (*anabhihitavacana*). Indeed, the meaning of the case-ending is not already expressed.

But what, then, is the meaning of the case-ending? Singularity and so forth are the meanings of the case-endings. It is so that when these are not already expressed, factors such as the object (*karman*)—which serve as the cause for the production of case-endings even when they are already expressed—should not [act as causes] here. Therefore, there is the mention of "not being expressed."

Therefore, the governing rule *anabhihite* ("when not already expressed") is established. Furthermore, this must necessarily be understood thus: that "oneness" (*ekatva*) and so forth are the meanings of the case-endings (*vibhakti*). [Otherwise,] there would be no occurrence of the nominative (*prathamā*) when [the number] is already expressed. For one who thinks that "object" (*karman*) and so forth are the meanings of the case-endings, and that when these are expressed, the case-endings will not arise by virtue of the semantic requirement (*sāmarthya*), for such a person the nominative would not be applicable.

[Question: Where [is the first case used]? [Example: *vṛkṣaḥ plakṣaḥ* ("The tree is a *plakṣa*"). [Question: What is the reason? [Answer: Because the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) has already been expressed by the nominal stem itself. [Objection: Nowhere is the meaning of the nominal stem unexpressed by the nominal stem, yet the first case is still employed. [Response: That will occur by virtue of the explicit rule (*vacana*). [Reply:
But this fault belongs only to you, for whom the meanings of the case endings are singularity and so forth; thus, when those are already expressed, there would be an absence of the first case.

In this case, the nominative case does not apply [to *devadatta*]. Where? In the sentence: *pacati odanaṃ devadattaḥ*. What is the reason? Because singularity and the other numbers are already expressed by the *tiṅ* suffix. Furthermore, you both establish the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "when not already expressed" (*anabhihite*) and provide an enumeration [of the cases where it applies].

Nowhere is it said that singularity and the other numbers are not expressed by a *tiṅ* suffix, yet the nominative is prescribed [in such instances]. That [nominative] will occur by virtue of the specific statement [of the rule].

But surely, in this case there is no expression [of the verb], as in "a tree is a *plakṣa*. Even here, however, there is expression. How so? This will be stated: "The verb *as* (to be), followed by the present participle suffix *-ant*, in the third person, is understood even when not explicitly employed. Thus, in "a tree is a *plakṣa*," it is understood that "it exists. But this fault belongs only to you, for whom the object (*karman*) and other factors are the meanings of the case-endings.

"When [the object] is already expressed, the first case-suffix (*prathamā*) does not occur. In that case, the first case-suffix would apply [to *bhīṣma*, etc.]. Where? In the example: *kaṭaṃ karoti bhīṣmam udāraṃ śobhanaṃ darśanīyam* ("He makes a mat that is formidable, magnificent, beautiful, and handsome"). Since the object is already expressed by the second case-suffix (*dvitīyā*) arising from the word *kaṭa*, the second case-suffix would not apply to *bhīṣma* and the others. What, then, would apply? The first case-suffix. For example: [as in the following:]...

In the example "The mat (kaṭaḥ) has been made (kṛtaḥ) formidable (bhīṣmaḥ), noble (udāraḥ), beautiful (śobhanaḥ), and handsome (darśanīyaḥ)," since the object (*karman*) is already expressed by the *kta* suffix arising from the root *kṛ*, the second case (*dvitīyā*) does not occur after words such as *bhīṣma*. What then? The nominative (*prathamā*) occurs.
This is not a fault; for I have neither the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "when not expressed" (*anabhihita*) nor an explicit enumeration (*parigaṇana*). [This follows] by implication (*sāmarthyāt*).
The production of case endings for me will occur, and there is indeed the necessary capacity. What is that? A specific object (*karmaviśeṣa*) must be expressed.

Or rather, both the mat (*kaṭa*) and the formidable ones (*bhīṣma*) and so forth are objects; thus, it is established by the rule "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*) alone. Or else, the mat itself is the object, and because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the second case ending will occur after *bhīṣma* and the others as well. It exists.

Furthermore, there is indeed a distinction: in the cases of *kaṭaṃ karoti bhīṣmam udāram śobhanaṃ darśanīyam* (he makes a mat that is formidable, magnificent, beautiful, and handsome) and *kṛtaḥ kaṭo bhīṣmaḥ udāraḥ śobhanaḥ darśanīyaḥ* (the mat has been made formidable, magnificent, beautiful, and handsome), the suffix *kta* arising from the root *kṛ* denotes the entire object (*karman*) without exception. However, by the accusative case ending arising from the word *kaṭa*, that which resides in the mat [is expressed].

That action cannot be expressed, for it is not a specific type of action. However, this fault belongs to you alone, for whom oneness and so forth are the meanings of case-endings, and for whom there is an absence of the nominative when [these meanings] have already been expressed. Thus, the nominative does not apply to you in cases such as *ekaḥ*, *dvau*, or *bahavaḥ*. What is the reason? Because oneness and so forth have already been expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

Even in the case of the meanings of case-terminations such as the object (*karman*), singularity and so forth must necessarily be adopted as the basis [for grammatical operations], as in "in the singularity of the object," "in the duality of the object," or "in the plurality of the object. However, singularity and so forth do not possess further instances of singularity and so forth. If they do exist for you, they exist for me as well; when these are not already expressed, the nominative case (*prathamā*) will apply. Alternatively, [the terms] denote both.

For these [words] denote both substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*). Since the number one and so forth—which reside in that which possesses the quality—are not explicitly stated [as qualities], the nominative case will apply. Alternatively, this thing called "number" is subordinate to another; by it, the thing to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*) is qualified. And if the nominative were not used here, the thing to be numbered would remain unqualified. Now...

Or he will state there the purpose of including the mention of "word" (*vacana*): so that the nominative case (*prathamā*) may occur even when [numbers such as] singularity and so forth have already been expressed. Alternatively, it will arise by convention (*samaya*). If it is conventional and not mandatory, why do the other cases not occur? Because of the absence of [grammatical relations such as] object (*karman*) and so forth. In that case, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would result; however, the genitive characterized by the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) does not apply because there is no remainder.
It will not be so. Even in this case, a confusion of usage would result: the dual and plural endings would apply even to a single thing;

the singular and plural endings would apply even to two things; and the singular and dual endings would apply even to many things. [Objection: The restriction will be determined by the meaning (*arthataḥ*).

A complete enumeration must be made. [The enumeration is: by means of finite verbs (*tiṅ*), primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*). A complete enumeration must be made by means of finite verbs, primary derivatives, secondary derivatives, and compounds. [Examples: finite verb (*tiṅ*): *kaṭaḥ kriyate* ("the mat is being made"). Primary derivative (*kṛt*): *kaṭaḥ kṛtaḥ* ("the mat was made"). Secondary derivative (*taddhita*): *aupagavaḥ* ("a descendant of Upagu").

[Kātyāyana] Kāpaṭava [says]: [This is] a compound. *citraguḥ* (one who has brindled cows), *śabalaguḥ* (one who has dappled cows). For in the general rule, when there is coreferentiality with a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the case ending must be stated. Indeed, in the general rule, when there is coreferentiality with a nominal stem, the case ending must be prescribed. Where? In cases such as *kaṭaṃ karoti bhīṣmam udāraṃ śobhanaṃ darśanīyam* ("He makes a mat that is formidable, magnificent, beautiful, and lovely"). [The case ending] arises from the word *kaṭa*.

If it is held that "the accusative case is prescribed for what is expressed by the second [case-ending]," then the accusative would not apply to *bhīṣma* and so forth. What, then, would be the case? It would be the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). [Objection: The genitive is characterized as being used for the "remainder" (*śeṣa*); since there is no remainder here, it will not occur. [Reply: Other cases would likewise not apply. What is the reason? Because the categories of object (*karman*) and so forth are absent. Furthermore, a convention has been established that a base (*prakṛti*) should not be uttered alone.

It is not the case that the condition (*pratyaya*) alone [is the object]. Furthermore, since other words being produced are not capable of expressing this specific relationship, the accusative case will apply. Alternatively, both the mat (*kaṭa*) and the formidable ones (*bhīṣma*) and so forth are objects (*karman*). In that case, it is established by the rule "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*) alone. Or else, the mat alone is the object; because of its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the accusative case applies to the words *bhīṣma* and the rest.
It will be so. Therefore, there is no purpose in enumerating them.

(Pāṇini 2.3.1.3) When a *kāraka* involved in two actions is expressed by one [of those actions], there arises the undesirable consequence of the absence of case-endings (*vibhakti*). When a *kāraka* involved in two actions is expressed by one [of those actions], a case-ending does not apply.

In what [case] does it occur? For example, in "He sits in the palace" (*prāsāde āste*) or "He sits on the bed" (*śayane āste*). What is the reason? Since the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is already expressed by the suffix *sat* (the present participle suffix), the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) would not be applicable.
[Response: This is not a fault, because it is not expressed by either one of them. Why? Because it is not expressed by either one.

Because of non-expression. Here, there is non-expression by one [of the two]. There is expression by the suffix *sat* (present participle), but non-expression by the suffix *as* (past passive participle). Since there is non-expression, the locative case (*saptamī*) will be based upon that. Why? Indeed, whether there is expression or non-expression, the locative case will be based on what is not expressed (*anabhihita*), and not on what is expressed (*abhihita*).

[The rule] is a prohibition. For the prescription [of the locative case] applies when [the action] is not already expressed. Indeed, the seventh case (locative) is prescribed when [the action] is not expressed; it is not a prohibition when it is expressed. Even if this can be said in cases where there are two different actions—such as "he sits on a seat" (*āsane āste*) or "he lies on a bed" (*śayane śete*)—how is it in cases where it is indeed the same action? [In such cases,] even here...

There is a difference [between them]. Why? Because of the difference in time and the difference in the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Here, for one [verb] *ās* (to sit), the means of accomplishment is *ās* itself and the suffix denotes all three times; for the other, the means of accomplishment is external and the suffix denotes the present time. But is the substance the means of accomplishment, or is it a quality (*guṇa*)? And what follows from this? If the substance is the means of accomplishment, then...

This is different from what has been stated. For if a quality (*guṇa*) is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), this is different from what has been stated; for the quality of "being" (*sadiguṇa*) is one thing, and the quality of "sitting" (*āsiguṇa*) is another. What, then, is the logical means of accomplishment? He says: it is the quality (*guṇa*).
How is this known? For instance, someone asks another: "Where is Devadatta? and he [responds] to him...

He says, "That [is] on the tree. "On which one? "The one that stands. That tree, having been the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) when connected with another word. Furthermore, when a substance is the means (*sādhana*), that which is the object remains the object, that which is the instrument remains the instrument, and that which is the locus remains the locus.

(P_2,3.1.4) The statement regarding "what has not been expressed" (*anabhihitavacana*) is purposeless, because the prescription of the nominative case (*prathamā*) would have no scope. The statement regarding "what has not been expressed" is purposeless. For what reason? Because the prescription of the nominative case would have no scope. The nominative case would have no scope.

It will be so by virtue of the statement. The first [case] has scope. What is its scope? That which is not a kāraka; for example, "vṛkṣaḥ" (tree) or "plakṣaḥ" (fig tree). If it is argued that its scope is that which is not a kāraka, we say no; for the verb *as* ("to be"), in the present tense (*bhavantī*) and in the third person (*prathamapuruṣa*), exists even when it is not explicitly employed. If it is argued that its scope is that which is not a kāraka, that is not correct. Why? Because the verb *as*, in the present tense and in the third person, [exists].

Even when not being employed [as a specific case ending], it is understood that [the thing] exists, as in: "The tree is a *plakṣa*"; it is understood that it exists. Alternatively, due to conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), there is an absence of the first case (*prathamā*). Or rather, let the second case and so forth be applied, or the first; by virtue of conflict, the first case shall prevail. The scope for the second case and others is, for example: "He makes a mat" (*kaṭam karoti*), or "splendid, noble, beautiful, and lovely."

Thus [it is said]. The scope for the first case (nominative) is where there is no grammatical relation (*akāraka*), as in "the tree is a *plakṣa*. Here, however, both [the first and sixth cases] would apply, as in "the mat was made formidable, noble, beautiful, and handsome. The first case will occur by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). But this is not established; because it is subsequent, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply. [Reply: The sixth case characterized as "remainder" (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇā*) will not occur because there is no remainder (*aśeṣatvāt*).

But when there is the employment of a *kṛt* suffix, the subsequent rule for the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) applies; therefore, for the purpose of prohibiting that, the governing heading (*adhikāra*) "when not already expressed" (*anabhihita*) must be applied. For instance, in the case of *kartavyaḥ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat is to be made"). How is that [heading] to be applied? If singularity and so forth are the meanings of the case-endings (*vibhaktyartha*), then it is so. But if, on the other hand, the object (*karman*) and so forth are the meanings [of the suffixes], then it is likewise.

The meanings of case endings are not the [referent] (*artha*) by virtue of the governing rule concerning what has not been expressed (*anabhihitādhikāra*). (Pāṇini 2.3.2) An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the usage of *samayā*, *nikaṣā*, and *hā*. An addition must be made for the usage of *samayā*, *nikaṣā*, and *hā*. For example: *samayā grāmam* ("near the village"), *nikaṣā grāmam* ("near the village"). Regarding the usage of *hā*: *hā devadattam* ("Alas, Devadatta!").
"Alas for Yajñadatta! Another says:

"In the rule prescribing the second case (dvitīyā), an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made regarding the usage of *abhitaḥ*, *paritaḥ*, *samayā*, *nikaṣā*, *adhi*, *adhi* [in the sense of superiority], and *dhik*. An addition must be made to the rule prescribing the second case concerning the usage of *abhitaḥ*, *paritaḥ*, *samayā*, *nikaṣā*, *adhi*, *adhi*, and *dhik*. For example: *abhitaḥ grāmam*."

[The word *dvitīyā* (the second case) is used] with *paritaḥ*, *samayā*, *nikaṣā*, and *adhi* [when used in the sense of "around" or "near"] as in: *parito grāmam*, *samayā grāmam*, *nikaṣā grāmam*, *adhi adhi grāmam*. [It is also used] with *dhik* [in the sense of reproach], as in: *dhik jālmam*, *dhik vṛṣalam*. Another teacher says: "The second case should be employed after *ubha* and *sarvatas*; it is seen after the three beginning with *dhik* and *upari* when they are reduplicated; furthermore, it is seen elsewhere as well. The second case must be stated after *ubhaya* and *sarva* when they end in the suffix *tas*.

[The accusative case is used] with *ubhayataḥ* (on both sides), *sarvataḥ* (on all sides), and in connection with *dhik* (fie/shame). For example: *dhig jālmam* (Fie on the wretch!), *dhik vṛṣalam* (Shame on the low-born!). With the three words beginning with *upari* (above) when they are repeated [as *āmreḍita*], the accusative should be prescribed: *upari upari grāmam* (Above the village, above the village); *adhi adhi grāmam*; *adhaḥ adhaḥ grāmam*. Furthermore, it is seen elsewhere than that: *na devadattam pratibhāti kiṃcit* (Nothing occurs to Devadatta's mind); *bubhukṣitam* (the hungry one).
Nothing occurs to me.
(P_2.3.3) Why is this stated? So that the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) may apply. But is not the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) already established? It is indeed established.

[The rule] "in the case of an object" (*karmaṇi*) is sufficient; thus, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is also established. How? By the very principle that "the substitutes for *sup* [case endings] take the place of *sup*. If this principle—that "substitutes for *sup* take the place of *sup*"—did not exist, then this present rule would have been formulated for the sake of the third case. For example: "He offers the *agnihotra* with barley-gruel" (*yavāgvāgnihotraṃ juhoti*).

If that is so, then the third case is indeed established. How? Simply by the rule "for the agent and the instrument" (*kartṛkaraṇayoḥ*). This word *agnihotra* [is used here in the sense of the instrument].
