Alternatively, the restriction is made with reference to the meanings under discussion. And what are the meanings under discussion? Singularity and so forth. In the case of one...

The singular number is used for one, not for two nor for many; the dual number is used for two only, not for one nor for many; the plural number is used for many only, not for one nor for two. Alternatively, the activity of the Teacher indicates that case-endings (*svādayaḥ*) arise from indeclinables (*avyaya*), since he teaches the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*) by the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ*.

(P_2,4.83.1) KA_I,498.14-23 Ro_II, 903: The rule "na avyayībhāvāt ataḥ" is a separation of the *yoga*. That is, the rule "na avyayībhāvāt ataḥ" is to be understood as a distinct application. [The meaning is: after an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) ending in the vowel *a*, there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*). Then follows: "am tu apañcamyāḥ" [Pāṇini 5.4.11]. For what purpose [is this]?

There is a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). It is for the purpose of prohibiting *am* after the fifth case-ending. The prohibition of *am* after the fifth case-ending must take effect. For if there were a single rule (*ekayoga*), there would be a prohibition of both; indeed, if there were a single rule, there would be a prohibition of both *am* and *aluk*. [Objection: Then that division of the rule must be made. [Response: It need not be made. The particle *tu* is the restrictor. The particle *tu*...
It is being formulated. That will serve as the regulator: "only for [the case ending] other than the fifth.

(Regarding *ami apaṃcamyāḥ*): when there is a prohibition of the fifth case ending by *ami*, the mention of the ablative (*apādāna*) is required. When there is a prohibition of the fifth case ending by *ami*, the mention of the ablative is required.

It should be stated: "The ablative case ending [is used] after a word in the sense of *apādāna*. What is the purpose? To prevent the prohibition from applying when a word is joined with a *karmapravacanīya*. Let it not be so when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*, as in: "It rained as far as Pāṭaliputra" (*āpāṭaliputram vṛṣṭo devaḥ*). Or rather, it need not be stated; because the subsequent member of the compound is joined with a *karmapravacanīya*, there is no occurrence of the ablative case after the compound. Thus, it need not be stated.

What is the reason? Here, the final member (*uttarapada*) is joined with a *karmapravacanīya*. Because the final member is joined with a *karmapravacanīya*, the ablative case will not occur after the compound. And when the compound itself is joined with a *karmapravacanīya*, then the prohibition applies. For example: *ā upakumbhāt* (as far as near the jar) and *ā upamaṇikāt* (as far as near the water-pot).

(P_2,4.84) After [words denoting] prosperity (*ṛddhi*), a river compound (*nadīsamāsa*), or a numeral part (*saṅkhyāvayava*), the seventh case suffix is always [elided]. It should be stated that after [words denoting] prosperity, a river compound, or a numeral part, the seventh case suffix is always [elided]. Examples of prosperity: *sumaram*, *sumagadham*. Examples of a river compound: *unmattagaṅgam*, *lohitagaṅgam*.
[The rule concerning] the components of a number: "twenty-one Bhāradvājas" and "fifty-three Gautamas.

(Pāṇini 2.4.85.1) Regarding the rule that substitutes the final phoneme (*ṭi*) of *ṭit* [pratyayas] with *ṭā*, *ṅasi~* and *ṅas* [are applied] by prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣiddha*) to the rule for *luṭ* [ending] *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras*. This refers to the rule that substitutes the final phoneme (*ṭi*) of *ṭit* [pratyayas].

The substitutes *ḍā*, *aur*, and *as* take the place of the *luṭ* suffix by means of an anterior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). The scope for the substitution of *et* (for the final *ṭi*) is, for example: *pacate*, *pacete*, *pacante*. The scope for *ḍā*, *aur*, and *as* is, for example: *śvaḥ kartā*, *śvaḥ kartārau*, *śvaḥ kartāraḥ*. In this case—namely, *śvaḥ adhetā*, *śvaḥ adhyetārau*, *śvaḥ adhyetāraḥ*—both rules would apply; however, *ḍā*, *aur*, and *as* prevail by means of an anterior counter-exception.

In that case, a *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior exclusion) must be stated. It need not be stated; it is established by the rule "and for the *ātmanepada*s. One must state: "And for the *ātmanepada*s, there are *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras*. And that is for the sake of equal number (*samasaṅkhyārtham*).
And that mention of *ātmanepada*s must necessarily be made for the sake of equal number. [Otherwise] there would be an assignment according to the number of items enumerated (*saṅkhyātanudeśaḥ*).

So that it may be so. For if the mention of the *ātmanepada* were not made, there would be three substitutes for the single locus *śa*; because of this inequality, the rule of "correspondence according to number" (*saṅkhyātānudeśa*) would not apply. First of all, the mention of the *ātmanepada* serves no purpose for the sake of [establishing] a priority by prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).
This must be considered here: let the replacements *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* be applied, or let the substitution of *e* for the final *ṭi* be applied. What should be done in this case?

The substitution of *et* (the vowel *e*) [for the final *i*] is [considered] non-eternal (*anitya*). The suffixes *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* are eternal (*nitya*). They apply whether the substitution of *et* has already taken place or has not yet taken place.

The substitution of *et* for the final syllable (*ṭi*) is also eternal; it applies whether the suffixes *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* have been applied or have not been applied. However, the substitution of *et* is non-eternal, because it applies to one thing when the suffixes *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* have been applied, and to another thing when they have not been applied. And since it applies to a different word-form (*śabdāntara*), [it is considered non-eternal].

The rule is non-eternal (*anitya*). The suffixes *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* are also non-eternal; they apply when one thing has undergone the change to *etva*, but not when another has. Since they apply to a different word-form, they are non-eternal. Between these two non-eternal rules, *etva* takes precedence because it is subsequent. Once *etva* has been applied, the suffixes *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* will still occur, because of the principle that a rule applies again once its conditions have been met (*punaḥprasaṅgavijñāna*). This is also for the sake of maintaining an equal number [of items].

There is no purpose in mentioning the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). The distinction will be established by proximity (*āntarya*). Why is there proximity? By way of meaning (*arthataḥ*): that which has a single meaning is replaced by that which has a single meaning; that which has two meanings, by that which has two meanings; and that which has many meanings, by that which has many meanings. Alternatively, only six substitutes are indicated. How so? By means of an indication using the *ekaśeṣa* (the "one-remainder" compound). It is an indication by *ekaśeṣa*.

Now, regarding this instruction by means of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), is this a *dvandva* compound of those for which *ekaśeṣa* has already been applied— namely, *ḍā* and *ḍā*, *rau* and *rau*, *raḥ* and *raḥ*— resulting in *ḍā-rau-raḥ*? Or rather, is it *ekaśeṣa* of those for which the *dvandva* has already been applied— namely, *ḍā*, *rau*, and *raḥ*— resulting in *ḍā-rau-raḥ*, and then [the addition of] *ḍā-rau-raḥ*?

[The forms] *ḍā-aurasaḥ* and *ḍā-aurasaḥ*. What follows from this? If the *dvandva* compound is formed after the *ekaśeṣa* [has already been applied], an undesirable result occurs where the number [of the suffixes] would be incorrect: the suffix *ḍā* would apply to both the singular and the dual; the suffix *rau* would apply to both the plural and the singular;
and the suffix *ra* would apply to both the dual and the plural. On the other hand, if the *ekaśeṣa* is applied after the *dvandva* has been formed...

There is no fault. Let it be as there is no fault. But what is superior here? He says: "Both. For both are observed: *bahu-śakti-kiṭakam* (many small spears), *bahūni śakti-kiṭakāni* (many small spears); *bahu-sthālī-piṭharam* (many pots and pans), *bahūni sthālī-piṭharāṇi* (many pots and pans). When *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* are substituted for *ṭi*, let there be *ey* as before; when there is a vowel-prolongation (*prasāraṇa*), let it be by equal number.

There is no purpose [in the rule]. It is established that, in their respective places, they are internal (*antara*) by virtue of meaning. The arrangement is based on proximity (*āntarya*). Let these three alone be [the substitutes] for all [cases]. And since the substitution of *et* for *ṭi* is subsequent, let these [substitutions] remain even when that [substitution of *et*] has been performed.

907–911. The addition of the marker *ś* to the substitute *ḍā* is for the purpose of making it a universal replacement (*sarvādeśa*). The substitute *ḍā* should be marked with *ś*. What is the purpose? It is for the purpose of making it a universal replacement. By the rule "that which is marked with *ś* replaces the whole," it should be a universal replacement. For if the letter *ś* were not employed, the rule "operations apply to the final [element] of the *ala*" would result in its application only to the final [portion]. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the *nighāta* accent; that is, the *nighāta* accent would apply.

But [in the case of] *prapnoti* and *śvaḥ kartā*, this accent would apply by the rule "the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix following *tās-* is unaccented. As for what was said—that the addition of the marker *ś* to the substitute *ḍā* is for the purpose of making it a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*)—this is already established by the principle that "a substitute replaces only the final phoneme of the original" (*alaḥ antyavikārāt*). This is established. How? By the principle that "a substitute replaces only the final phoneme of the original. Let this [substitution] apply to the final phoneme of the original. What then is the resulting form?

[The suffix] *kartṛ*. [Objection: Because of the rule "there is elision of the final vowel and what follows it (*ṭi*) when a *ḍit* suffix follows," there would be elision by the elision of the *ṭi*. [Response: It does not apply because it is not an *abha* element. [Objection: It will apply by virtue of the fact that the marker *ḍ* is attached. Or else, it is established by the fact that it is not an *it*. [Question: What is meant by "by the fact that it is not an *it"? [Answer: If this were to occur in place of the final letter, it would not be designated as a suffix. If the designation "suffix" is absent, [the rules governing suffixes do not apply].

If the designation *it* does not exist, there is no elision (*lopa*). If elision does not exist, [the substitute] has more than one phoneme (*anekāl*). When it has more than one phoneme, then it is a total substitute (*sarvādeśa*). When it is a total substitute, then it is an affix (*pratyaya*). When it is an affix, then there is the designation *it*. When there is the designation *it*, then there is elision. Or else, because of the contiguous mention (*praśliṣṭanirdeśa*): or rather, this is a contiguous mention; [namely,] *ḍā*.

By the rule *āḍ ajādīnām*, [the augment] *āṭ* will be a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*) because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*) and is marked with the indicatory letter *ś*. However, when this [augment] occurs in place of the final [phoneme], it would not be included by the mention of *tiṅ*. [Reply: Because that which is modified in one part is not different from the original, the mention of *tiṅ* will include it. That which is modified in one part is treated as non-different; thus, there will be inclusion by the mention of *tiṅ*.

How is the accent [established]? It is established by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) regarding the accent. Let the suffixes *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* be applied, and let there be the state of being unaccented (*anudāttatva*).

What should be done here? The state of being unaccented [should apply] because it is subsequent. The suffixes *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* are permanent (*nitya*). They apply whether the state of being unaccented has been performed or not yet performed. The state of being unaccented is also permanent; for even when the suffixes *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* have already been applied, [the unaccented state still applies].

It applies even when [the conditions] have not been fulfilled. The state of being unaccented (*anudātta*) is non-eternal (*anitya*). When the suffixes *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* have been applied to one thing, it applies; when they have not been applied to another, it applies. A rule that applies to a different word-form is non-eternal. The suffixes *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* are also non-eternal; for they apply when the accent has been altered by the application of the unaccented state, and they do not apply when the accent has not been so altered.

And for those [suffixes] that undergo *svarabhakti* (vowel-insertion), they become non-eternal (*anitya*). Between two non-eternal operations, the one that follows takes precedence; thus, the *anudātta* accent is applied first. Once the *anudātta* accent has been applied, the suffixes *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* apply again by virtue of the principle of "reapplication" (*punaḥprasaṅga*). [Objection: It is established by the accent of the disappearance of the high-pitched vowel (*udāttanivṛttisvara*) when the *ṭi*-portion is elided. [Reply: It is not established. Why? Because the substitution of *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* is more internal (*antaraṅga*). In that case, because it is more internal—

When the suffixes *ḍā* and *auras* have been applied, should the state of being unaccented (*anudāttatva*) be performed first, or the elision of the *ṭi*? What must be done here? The elision of the *ṭi* must take place because it is subsequent. If that is so, then [the desired result] is established through the conflict of accents (*svaravipratiṣedha*). This conflict of accents is indeed logical. This must be deliberated upon here: should the state of being unaccented be performed, or the accent of the cessation of the acute (*udāttanivṛttisvara*)?

Thus [it is asked]: what should be done here? Because it is subsequent, the *anudātta* (unaccented) quality [should apply]. Once the *anudātta* has been applied, by the principle of "reapplication" (*punaḥprasaṅga*), the accent called *udāttanivṛttisvara* will occur. Where, then, is this established? It is established where there is a rule for a suffix with the marker *pit*. Where there is a rule for a suffix with the marker *apit*, it is not established there. But even in that case, it is established. How so? This [rule] regarding the *anudātta* nature of *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes applies today [as well].

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accent of an affix (*pratyayasvara*). Furthermore, a general rule (*utsarga*) does not apply where an exception is operative; for exceptions take effect first, and only afterwards do the general rules apply. Or rather, having set aside the domain of the exception, the general rule then applies. Therefore, the accent of the affix never occurs [in such cases], because the exception—the lack of udātta for *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes—takes precedence.

It awaits [the operation of another rule], thinking: "Let the state of being *anudātta* (unaccented) be applied, and let there be elision (*lopa*). Even though elision occurs because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], that very elision takes place while the *udātta* accent is still non-existent; thus, an *udātta* vowel is elided when it is *anudātta*. This is an exception to the accent of suffixes (*pratyayasvara*). By this, the accent of the suffix does not apply there at all. However, the accent of the suffix *tās-* is taught as being conditioned by its occurrence in a specific grammatical context (*vṛtti-sanniyoga-śiṣṭa*).
And by that [rule], this acute accent would also be elided; thus there is no fault.

This designation of "affix" (*pratyaya*) is established by way of a governing rule (*adhikāra*). Consequently, it would also apply to the base (*prakṛti*), the subordinate word (*upapada*), and the qualifying attributes (*upādhi*).

Its prohibition must be stated. [The following are the cases: (1) *prakṛti*: *san* after roots ending in *gup*, *tij*, and *kita*; (2) *upapada*: *san* after *stambh* with *karṇa*, and after *ram* and *japa*; (3) *upādhi*: *san* after *hṛ* when *dṛti* and *nātha* follow, provided the agent is an animal. The prohibition of these must be stated. Furthermore, what would happen if these also were designated as *pratyaya*? [There would be] the status of being subsequent (*paratva*), the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*), and the designation of the *aṅga*.

Thus, these rules would apply [undesirably]. Therefore, he recites the reply: "In the governing context of suffixes (*pratyayādhikāra*), there is no prohibition of the base (*prakṛti*), the attendant word (*upapada*), or the condition (*upādhi*). Even when the technical designation of a suffix (*pratyayasañjñā*) exists by virtue of the governing context, there is no prohibition of the base, the attendant word, or the condition. "No prohibition" (*apratiṣedha*) means that the prohibition is purposeless. Why does the technical designation of a suffix not apply to them? Because they are merely the causes (*nimitta*).

Because the cause exists for the sake of the effect that it causes, this applies elsewhere as well. For causes indeed exist for the sake of the effects they cause. What, then, is the cause, and what is the caused? The bases (*prakṛti*), prepositions (*upapada*), and affixes (*upādhi*) are the cause; the suffix (*pratyaya*) is the caused.
This principle is observed elsewhere too. Where else? In common worldly usage. For example, when many people are sitting together...
Someone asks another: "Which one is Devadatta? Which one is Yajñadatta? He explains it to him:
when it is said, "the one who is on the horse, the one who is on the seat," because the indicative mark (nimitta) exists for the sake of the effect based on that mark (nimittika), he determines:
"This is Devadatta; this is Yajñadatta. It does not mean that Devadatta is [identical with] the horse or the seat at that moment.

A perception arises. What, then, is the indicator (*nimitta*) and what is the indicated (*nimittin*)? A known meaning is the indicator; an unknown meaning is the indicated. And here, the suffix (*pratyaya*) is unknown, while the base (*prakṛti*), the subordinate element (*upapada*), and the condition (*upādhi*) are known. Where? In the instruction of verbal roots (*dhātu*) and in the instruction of nominal stems (*prātipadika*).
These known elements are taken as indicators, because the grammatical operation is understood to apply to the principal element.

Or rather, it is established. Alternatively, the application of the operation will occur with respect to the principal element. And what is the principal element? It is the suffix (*pratyaya*). For example, when many people are traveling, someone asks another, "Who is going? He replies, "The king. Since the operation is understood to apply to the principal element when "the king" is mentioned, it applies to both: the one who asks and the one who answers.

There arises a conviction [regarding the meaning]. But what constitutes this predominance? It is constituted by the purpose (*artha*). Just as in the world predominance is constituted by the purpose, so now, what constitutes the predominance of the word (*śabda*)? The predominance of the word consists in its instruction of something not previously known (*apūrvopadeśa*).
That which has an instruction of something not previously known is predominant. And the verbal roots (*prakṛti*), prefixes (*upapada*), and limiting conditions (*upādhi*) have already been taught.

Where? In the teaching of roots (*dhātūpadeśa*) and in the teaching of nominal stems (*prātipadikopadeśa*). If it is argued that this is because a cause exists for the sake of the effect produced by that cause, or even if it is argued that the effect is understood as belonging to the primary element (*pradhāna*), then [the augment] would not apply to the base (*prakṛti*), the prefix (*upapada*), or the limiting condition (*upādhi*), but it would apply to the modification (*vikāra*) and the augment (*āgama*). For instance, [in the rules] *hanaḥ ta ca* and *trapujatunoḥ ṣuk*, these [modifications and augments] possess primacy because they are taught as something previously non-existent (*apūrvopadeśa*).

And these [substitutions] are characterized by their cause (*nimittin*). Furthermore, because they occur subsequent to the cognition of another element, the designation "suffix" (*pratyaya*) will not apply to the occurrences of modifications (*vikāra*) and augments (*āgama*). It is stated that a suffix is "that which follows" (*paraḥ*); however, modifications and augments do not occur as subsequent elements. What, then, is the reason that, although the instruction of what was previously unknown (*apūrvopadeśa*) is common to both, the suffix is "that which follows" while modifications and augments are not?

Not for others, because that which is indicated by the genitive is connected with it. That which is indicated by the genitive is connected with a modification (*vikāra*) or an augment (*āgama*), whereas the suffix (*pratyaya*) is prescribed after that which is indicated by the ablative. However, the prescription of the suffix is untenable; indeed, the rule for the suffix does not hold. Where? In cases where modifications and augments are prescribed, such as in *hanaḥ ta ca* ("the substitute *ta* [is applied] after the root *han*") and *tarpujatunoḥ ṣuk* ("the augment *ṣuk* is added after *tarpu* and *jatun*"). But what then?

The reason is not established, because it is not joined with the occurrence of a modification (*vikāra*) and because it is not specified by the fifth case (*pañcamī*). Therefore, it is established there by the specification of the fifth case. Consequently, the specification of the fifth case should be made there. [Objection: It need not be made. First, consider the rule *hanaḥ te*: the term *dhātoḥ* ("from a verbal root") is understood to carry over here. Next, consider the rule *trapujatunoḥ ṣuk*: [the term] *prātipadikāt* ("from a nominal stem") [is understood to carry over].
Thus it continues. If this is so, then since the suffix *kyap* occurs after the root *han* with the replacement *ta*, the suffix *kyap* would apply to every root whatsoever.

This is not a fault. The activity of the Teacher indicates that *kyap* does not occur after every root, since he provides a restricted enumeration by stating: "The suffix *kyap* occurs after the roots *i*, *tu*, *śas*, *vṛ*, *dṛ*, and *juṣ*. Alternatively, in this context, only the root *han* is intended by the mention of "root."
We shall fully understand. *ta* is substituted for the root *han*. The suffix *kyap* occurs after a verbal root. From what [root]? From *han*.

Or rather, because it depends on the meaning. Alternatively, the rule for suffixes (*pratyaya-vidhi*) is based on meaning. That which conveys that meaning is a suffix. Should this be stated? No, it need not. How is it understood even when not explicitly stated? [It is understood from] "suffix" (*pratyaya*).

Thus, a long designation (*sañjñā*) is being made. And a designation, by its very nature, ought not to be overly cumbersome. Why is this so? For the purpose of a designation is brevity. In that regard, the purpose of employing such a long designation is so that it may be understood as a *anvarthasañjñā*—a designation based on its own meaning.
[For example: "it causes to understand" (*pratyāyayati*) is a *pratyaya*. If "that which causes to understand" is a *pratyaya*, then [the rule applies] to *avika* and the others.

The designation *pratyaya* (suffix) would not apply [to *san* and so on], for they do not convey any meaning (*pratyāyayanti*). If that is the case, then let it be defined as: "that by which something is conveyed is a *pratyaya*. Even so, the designation still does not apply to *san* and the others. If that is the case, then this term has a dual derivation: it is derived both from the agent (*kartṛ-sādhana*) and from the object (*karman-sādhana*). Even so, why is it that when the instruction of what was previously unknown (*apūrvopadeśa*) is the same, [the suffix is applied] in cases such as *trāpuṣam* and *jātuṣam*, but not elsewhere?

The letter *a* conveys that meaning, but the letter *ṣ* does not. Furthermore, because that same meaning is expressed by the letter *a* elsewhere as well, we consider it to be the letter *a* that conveys that meaning, and not the letter *ṣ*. Where else? In the case of the suffix *aṇ* after words such as *bilva*: *bailvaḥ*.

(P_3,1.2) KA_II,3.15–6.2 Ro_III, 12–19: For what purpose is this stated? [So that] the subsequent [suffix] may occur, and not the preceding one. This is not a valid purpose. Whatever [suffix] he desires as preceding, he states that:

namely, *vibhāṣā supo bahuc purastāt tu* ("optionally, *bahuc* is added after a nominal ending, and it precedes"). Then, [it is said: "Let it not occur in the middle. Even in the middle, whatever [suffix] he desires, he states that.

Regarding the rule *avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ*: since any other suffix that remains [after the application of this rule] will necessarily follow [the base] even without an explicit statement, there is no purpose in the rule prescribing "subsequent" (*para*) status. Even so, only those suffixes whose position is restricted by this rule would have a fixed position; however, any suffix whose position is currently unrestricted might occasionally appear before [the base].

Sometimes it may be further away, and sometimes it may be in between. For example, a calf is sometimes in front of its mother, sometimes behind her, and sometimes at her side. The mention of "further away" (*para*) is for the purpose of ensuring that it is indeed further away. The mention of "further away" is redundant because the word "further away" is already indicated by the use of the fifth case (*pañcamī*). Therefore, the inclusion of the term *para* is unnecessary.

What is the reason? Because an operation is stated to apply to that which is designated by the fifth case (pañcamī). For example: "after *dvi*, *antar*, and prefixes, *apa* becomes *īt*" (*dvyantarupasargebhyaḥ apaḥ īt*). This is an unequal comparison. In that [other] case, an operation is stated to apply to something that already exists as the subsequent element. But here now, of what existing thing could an operation apply as the subsequent element? Here too, it must apply to something that already exists. How so? Because its status as being subsequent is inherent (*svābhāvika*).

Alternatively, if the status of being "subsequent" were based on explicit statement (*vācanika*), then there would be a purpose for employing the term "subsequent. However, in this case, it is not based on explicit statement, nor is there any purpose [for the term]. For that which is subsequent has its function precisely in being subsequent; or rather, its function is in having a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) when it is subsequent. In that case, this rule (*yoga*) must be stated for the sake of those instances where the ablative (*pañcamī*) does not exist. And where [is that]?

The fifth case [ending] does not exist where modifications (*vikāra*) and augments (*āgama*) are taught. And where are modifications and augments taught? [For example: "In place of *han*, *ta* is substituted" (*hanaḥ ta ca*), and "the augment *ṣuk* is added after *trapu* and *jatun*" (*trapujatunoḥ ṣuk*). Regarding these modifications and augments, it has been stated: "But the application of suffixes is untenable.

Therefore, in those cases, the rule is established by the use of the fifth case. Or rather, [the fifth case is used] for the purpose of indicating that [the modification or augment] occurs subsequent to elements never previously observed.

In that case, the mention of "another" (*para*) must be made for the sake of the elision of those elements that follow [the base], since these *kvip* suffixes and others are absolutely unobserved [elsewhere]. This is so that the elision of those which have become "other" may occur, and not of those that have not become "other. But what is the purpose of stating the elision of those that are absolutely unobserved as being "other"? It is for the sake of operations conditioned by *kit* and *ṇit*.

"May they be [visible]"—this purpose also does not exist. The activity of the Teacher indicates that those suffixes which are entirely unseen elsewhere are elided, since he attaches *kādi* indicatory letters (*anubandha*) to them. How is this an indicator?
The purpose in attaching the indicatory letters is so that operations prescribed for *kit* and *ṇit* suffixes may take place. And if...
In this context, since those elements that follow immediately after [the preceding element] are not observed elsewhere, they would be elided; therefore, the attachment of suffixes becomes meaningful.

Or rather, it is for the purpose of restricting usage. If it is for the sake of restricting usage, then the mention of "following" (*para*) must be made so that the application occurs only for those elements that follow, and not for those that do not follow. Is there, however, anything undesirable [if this were not done] for which this purpose is intended?

There must be a restrictive rule (*niyama*). He says: "It exists," because when the base (*prakṛti*) expresses the meaning, the suffix (*pratyaya*) is not observed. When the base expresses the meaning, forms lacking a suffix are seen, such as: "Where is that Devadatta? Where is that Yajñadatta? Babhru, Maṇḍu, Lamaka. These should have been used as *Bābhravyaḥ*, *Māṇḍavyaḥ*, and *Lāmakāyanaḥ*, yet they appear as *babhruḥ*, *maṇḍuḥ*.

The term *lamaka* is employed because suffixes such as *dvayasaC* and others are observed only in their isolated forms. Indeed, the usage of *dvayasaC* and the like is seen in isolation, as in: "What is its *dvayasa*? ("What is its measure?"), and "What is today's lunar day (*tithi*)? Suffixes such as *dvayasaC* are indeed similar to those produced in compounds (*vṛttija*), yet they are not produced in compounds; they are just like *bahu*. Furthermore, the mention of the option (*vāvacana*) is for the purpose of preventing their production [in compounds]. This is because of the mention of the option.

And the mention of "another" (*para*) must be made for the sake of non-origination, so that non-origination may occur by means of the expression "or" (*vā*). Now, even when the mention of "another" is made, how indeed is non-origination obtained through the expression "or"? When the mention of "another" is made, the expression "or" is connected with this very word "another. But when the mention of "another" is not made, [the connection is different].

What else could possibly be connected by the use of the word *vā* (or) other than a technical name (*saṃjñā*)? Furthermore, neither the existence nor the non-existence of a technical name is desired [in this context]. And it has already been stated regarding the use of *vā*. What was stated? "The use of *vā* is purposeless there, because the suffix *san* is compulsory. [Objection: In that case, the mention of the subsequent element (*para*) must indeed be made for the sake of restricting usage. Now...

Given this rule regarding the application [of linguistic elements], is it a restriction on the suffix (*pratyayaniyama*), meaning that a suffix must be employed only when followed by a base (*prakṛti*) and not otherwise? Or is it a restriction on the base (*prakṛtiniyama*), meaning that a base must be employed only when followed by a suffix and not otherwise? And what is the distinction here? In that case, if it were a restriction on the suffix, there would be no restriction on the base.

In that case, if there is a restriction on the suffix (*pratyaya*), a restriction on the base (*prakṛti*) would not obtain; the employment of a base without a suffix would result. [For example: "Where is Devadatta? Where is Yajñadatta? Babhru, Maṇḍu, Lamaka? Let it be, then, a restriction on the base. If there is a restriction on the base, there is no restriction on the suffix. When there is a restriction on the base, regarding the suffix—

A restriction (*niyama*) would not apply. What is its dual? What is its measure? What is the lunar day (*tithi*) today? The employment of a suffix without a corresponding base (*prakṛti*) would result. But it is established by means of a double restriction. How so? By means of a double restriction. This is a double restriction: a suffix must be employed only when followed by a base, and a base [must be employed] only when followed by a suffix.
And thus it is the *prakṛti*. Should this be stated? No, indeed. How would it be understood without being stated?
By the force of the mention of "para" (*paragrahaṇa*). Even without the mention of "para," this [suffix] would be "para. The mention of "para" is for the purpose that it be *para* alone.

(P_3,1.3.1) KA_II,6.4-14 Ro_III, 20-21 For what purpose is this stated? [It is] so that it may have the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*), and not the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*). This purpose is not necessary; for regarding that which he intends to have the acute accent on the final syllable, he employs the letter *c* as an indicatory mark (*anubandha*).

[If it were so,] the *cita* suffix would have its acute accent (*udātta*) at the end. [Therefore,] lest it be mid-acute (*madhyodātta*), he attaches the marker *r* (repha) where he desires the penultimate syllable to be acute; as it is said: "The penultimate [is acute] before *rit*. Then, lest it be grave (*anudātta*), he attaches the marker *p* (pakāra) where he desires even that [penultimate] to be grave; as it is said: "The two [substitutes] are grave (*anudāttau*)."

[Regarding the rule] *suppitau*: "In that case, let there not be a circumflex (*svarita*). [The author replies: Even for that which he desires to be circumflex, he introduces the marker *t* there and states, "A *t* is circumflex. Now, as for any other suffix remaining besides this, it will be necessarily acute on the first syllable even without an explicit statement; therefore, the statement regarding the acute on the first syllable serves no purpose.

Even so, only those words whose accent is specifically regulated would possess a fixed accent. That which is currently of unfixed accent might at one time be acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*), at another time acute on the final syllable (*antodātta*), at another time acute on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*), at another time unaccented (*anudātta*), and at another time circumflex (*svarita*). It is for the purpose that it should always be acute on the first syllable that this [rule] is stated.

(P_3,1.3.2) Now, for what purpose is the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) prescribed in conjunction with the technical designation of an affix (*pratyayasañjñā*), rather than the grave accent (*anudāttatva*); [why] is this not prescribed only where another accent occurs? [The answer is: "In an affix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*, the first syllable is always acute."
And because it is taught as having an *a* in the upadeśa, the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes and those ending in *su* and *pit* are *anudātta*. In that case, this further point follows:
the mention of "initially acute" (*ādyudātta*) need not be repeated twice, nor need the mention of "grave" (*anudātta*) be repeated twice. The previously established [rule] continues to apply.
Therefore, he recites what follows:

The purpose of prescribing initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) in connection with the technical designation of a suffix (*pratyayasañjñā*) is for the sake of making that which receives the designation acutely accented on its first syllable. In establishing this connection between initial acute accent and the designation of a suffix, the purpose is so that whatever receives the designation shall have its initial syllable acutely accented. For, were it not connected [to the designation], the rule "whatever [suffix] follows, the initial syllable of that and what precedes it is acutely accented" would apply to the end of that [word].

And [the rule for] the anudātta accent. For if [the anudātta rule] were not established, then while the initial udātta accent is prescribed in conjunction with the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "suffix" (*pratyaya*), according to the principle that when a suffix is mentioned, it includes the element from which that suffix begins, it would follow that the initial syllable of that entire complex (beginning with the root) would be udātta, and the final syllable would be anudātta. However, even when the initial udātta accent is prescribed in conjunction with the designation of "suffix," [the anudātta rule must still be stated].

And why is it that, in such cases, the initial syllable of that [stem] does not become udātta, nor the final syllable of that [suffix] become anudātta? A suffix that has already arisen is the cause for the grammatical operations dependent upon that suffix, not one that is in the process of arising. For example, a jar that has been made is the cause for the functions dependent upon the jar, not one being made. Or rather, [the rule applies] to the base (prakṛti).

The statement regarding the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the rule does not apply to what begins with that [suffix]. Or rather, this is not a fault. Why? Because when the teacher teaches that the initial syllable of the base (*prakṛti*) is invariably acute by the rule "that which ends in *ñ* or *ṇ* is always [acute] on its first syllable" (*ñniti ādir nityam*), he thereby indicates that the acute accent on the first syllable does not belong to what begins with that [suffix]. In that case, would it not follow that the final syllable of that [base] becomes grave (*anudātta*)? [No,] because of the accent of the base.

And because of the force of the rule itself, there is an absence of the accent of the suffix. Since the Teacher teaches that the final syllable of the root and the final syllable of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) are udātta—by stating "the end of the root" and "the end of the nominal stem"—he indicates that the final syllable of a compound ending in such a word does not become anudātta. How is this an indicator? For in cases where the suffix is anudātta, the accent of the base (*prakṛti-svara*) prevails.

It serves as a purpose [for the rule]. Or rather, it is for the sake of making the augments (*āgama*) unaccented. If that is so, then the property of being acutely accented on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) is stated in conjunction with the technical designation of "suffix" (*pratyaya-sañjñā*), so that when the acute accent on the first syllable has been applied in conjunction with the designation of "suffix," the augments may be unaccented. No; this is not even a purpose, because the augment is already declared to be unaccented.

What is the reason? Because it is stated that augments (*āgama*) are unaccented (*anudātta*). I shall state that "augments are unaccented. But which augments necessitate this unaccented quality? [The augment] *iṭ*. As in *lavitā*. First of all, *iṭ* does not necessitate it. This must be considered here: "Let there be *iṭ*, or let there be the initial accent (*ādyudāttatva*). What should be done in this case? [The latter,] because it is subsequent (*paratvāt*).

There is the introduction of the augment *iṭ*. The quality of being always acute-accented (*ādyudāttatva*) applies both when *iṭ* has been applied and when it has not been applied; thus, *iṭ* is also constant. The quality of being always acute-accented applies both when *iṭ* has been applied and when it has not been applied; thus, *iṭ* is not constant. For otherwise, the accent would result in one way when the acute-accent is applied and in another way when it is not applied; and a rule that applies to something whose accent has changed is considered non-constant.

It is non-eternal (*anitya*). The fact that it has the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) is also non-eternal. For when the augment *iṭ* is applied for one purpose, it does not apply for another; and a rule that applies to a different word-form is non-eternal. Between these two non-eternal rules, the addition of the augment *iṭ* prevails because it is subsequent. If so, then having the acute accent on the first syllable is an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation. What constitutes its internality? Its internality consists in the fact that the acute accent on the first syllable occurs simultaneously with the production of the word-form.

It is said: when the suffix has arisen, the augment *iṭ* is applied to the base (*aṅga*) by depending upon both the base and the suffix. Furthermore, the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) is not *antaraṅga*, because while the suffix is being resorted to, the base is also necessarily resorted to. [Therefore,] the acute accent on the first syllable is indeed *antaraṅga*. How so? For it was just stated that in a rule prescribing the accent of a suffix, there is no application of the "rule of the beginning of that" (*tadādividhi*).

[It is argued: "The augment *sīyuṭ* then becomes the cause [for the accentuation]. For if it were not stated [that augments are unaccented], the initial syllable of that which begins with *sīyuṭ* would be udātta. For if the rule "augments are unaccented" (*āgamā anudāttāḥ*) were not formulated—even if the rule for the initial udātta [of a suffix] were applied in conjunction with the technical designation of a suffix (*pratyaya-sañjñā-sanniyoga*)—it would follow as a consequence that the initial syllable of the optative (*liṅ*) beginning with *sīyuṭ* would be udātta, as in *laviṣīya*, *paviṣīya*. Therefore, it must be stated that "augments are unaccented."

"It is not necessary to state that [the suffixes] become unaccented (*anudātta*). The activity of the Teacher indicates that the *āgamas* are unaccented, since he says: 'The augment *yāsuṭ* is acute (*udātta*) and marked with *ṅ* in the case of parasmaipada endings. This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*), for he will say: 'The mention of *ṅ* for *yāsuṭ* is for the sake of the *piṭ* designation, and the mention of the acute accent is likewise. It is possible for him to say this:"

"The *yāsuṭ* occurs in the *parasmaipada* endings and it is also *apit* when it is the *liṅ*. Since this is established by such a concise formulation, the fact that the Teacher undertakes a more cumbersome effort indicates that augment (*āgama*)s are unaccented (*anudātta*). This can be understood either from the explicit statement or from the indicator (*jñāpaka*): that augment-sounds are unaccented.

[The suffixes] occur. However, because they are separated by augments (*āgama*), the quality of having an acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) does not apply. I shall state that augments are as if non-existent. If it is stated that augments are as if non-existent, then in the case of *lavitā*, the substitution of *ava* would not apply. I shall state [the solution]: "in a rule concerning accent" (*svaravidhau*). Even so, in the case of *lavitā*, there would be a circumflex accent (*svarita*) for the unaccented vowel following an accented one.

In this case, the svarita accent would not be obtained. I shall state [the rule] as "in the case of the sixth [type of] accent. Even so, in the case of *śikṣitaḥ*, this accent [prescribed by] "and the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) when the stem consists of two syllables and does not begin with a vowel" would still apply. I shall state [the rule] as "in the prescription of the accent of a suffix.
Then that must be stated: "they (the augments) are as if non-existent. It need not be stated. The activity of the Teacher indicates that the augments [are as if non-existent].

As for the statement that "they become as if non-existent," namely that he says, "the *yāsuṭ* [augment] in the *parasmaipada* endings is acute (*udātta*) and has the *ṅit* designation," this is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*). He will state this later:
"The mention of the *ṅit* designation for *yāsuṭ* is for the sake of the *pit* designation, and the mention of the acute accent is likewise. This can be stated by him.

"The *yāsuṭ* occurs in the *parasmaipada* endings and it is also *apit*, and [the *liṅ* occurs] in the *liṅ*. Since this is established by such a concise formulation, the fact that the Teacher undertakes a more cumbersome effort indicates that he intends to teach: "augments (*āgama*) are as if non-existent. Or rather, it is for the sake of the elision of what is *ādyudātta*; for then, the designation of a suffix (*pratyaya-sañjñā*) is applied simultaneously with the purpose of eliding what is *ādyudātta*.

The property of having the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) is stated. When the acute accent on the first syllable is applied by virtue of its association with the technical designation of a suffix (*pratyayasañjñā*), the accent known as *udāttanivṛttisvara* becomes established—as in *sraughnī* and *māthurī*. For in these cases, because it is subsequent in order, the elision (*lopa*) would otherwise override the accent of the suffix. Or rather, this is not a valid objection, because [the elision] is characterized as being external (*bahiraṅga*). It does not serve as a motive for that [objection]. Why? Because it is characterized as external. It is external in its character.

The elision (*lopa*) characterized by an internal rule (*antaraṅga*) [occurs], while the vowel [substitution] characterized by an external rule (*bahiraṅga*) is not yet established (*asiddha*) with respect to the internal one. Furthermore, this *paribhāṣā* must necessarily be resorted to; for if it were not stated, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the suffixes marked with *ñ*, *ṇ*, and *k*. If this *paribhāṣā* were not relied upon, even if the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) were applied in conjunction with the technical designation of a suffix (*pratyayasañjñā*), there would still be an over-extension regarding the suffixes marked with *ñ*, *ṇ*, and *k*.

[Regarding the forms] *autsī*, *kāṃsikī*, and *ātreyī*: here, because it is subsequent, the elision (*lopa*) would indeed subvert the accentuation rules for suffixes ending in *ñi*, *ni*, or *kit*. This is not a fault. The accentuation rules for *ñi*, *ni*, and *kit* are exceptions (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of suffixes (*pratyayasvara*). And a general rule (*utsarga*) does not apply where an exception is operative. For exceptions take effect first, and subsequently the general rule applies. Or rather, having first set aside the domain of the exception, [the general rule applies].
Then the general rule (*utsarga*) applies. In this case, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the suffixes and so forth does not occur at all;

rather, it awaits the exceptions (*apavāda*), namely the accents of *ñi*, *ni*, and *kit*. In the case of *kaṃsikī*, there is a greater displacement: here, the acute accent belongs to one [element] while another is elided; the initial syllable receives the acute accent while the final syllable is elided. In that case, consider the word *ātreyī*.

For in this case, because it is subsequent, the elision (*lopa*) would subvert the accent of the *kit* suffix. Therefore, this *paribhāṣā* must be resorted to. And when this is established, it is possible to state that the initial vowel is acute (*ādyudātta*) by way of its connection with the suffix.

27–30. Because of the rule that the beginning of an affix is acute (pratyayādyudāttatva), the final syllable of the root [is acute] by way of conflict (vipratiṣedha). This results from the conflict between the two rules: "the beginning of an affix is acute" and "the final syllable of the root is acute. The scope of the rule for the acute beginning of an affix is where the base (prakṛti) is unaccented (anudātta); examples include *samatvam* and *simatvam*. The scope of the rule "the final syllable of the root is acute" is where the affix is unaccented.

In the case of *pacati* and *paṭhati*, both [rules] would apply here. In *gopāyati* and *dhapāyati*, by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the rule "the final of a root" (*dhātor antaḥ*) prevails. Regarding the accent of a *pit* suffix versus the accent of a *tit* suffix when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied: by way of conflict, the accent of the *tit* suffix prevails over the accent of the *pit* suffix when *ṭāp* is applied. The scope for the accent of the *pit* suffix is, for example, *pacati* and *paṭhati*. The scope for the accent of the *tit* suffix is, for example, *kāryam*.

[The suffix] -ya is subject to removal. Here, both [rules] would apply: *kāryā* and *hāryā*. By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the accent of the *ti*-suffix prevails. Furthermore, the accent of the *cit* suffix prevails over the accent of the *pit* suffix; by way of conflict, the accent of the *cit* suffix prevails over the accent of the *pit* suffix. The scope for the accent of the *cit* suffix is, for example, *calanaḥ* and *copanaḥ*. The scope for the accent of the *pit* suffix is the same [as previously stated]. Here, both [rules] would apply: *āmbaṣṭhyā*.

The acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) occurs by way of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). Or rather, there is no need for a conflict; because the designation of "affix" (*pratyaya-sañjñā*) is applied simultaneously with the acute accent on the first syllable. Why? Because the designation of "affix" is applied simultaneously with the acute accent on the first syllable. Once the acute accent on the first syllable has been established through the simultaneous application of the affix designation, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātu-svara*) will prevail due to its being the "remaining" (*satiśiṣṭa*) accent.

Moreover, this contradiction between the accent of the *pit* (the feminine suffix) and the accent of the *ti* (the nominal stem) is improper. What is the reason? Because there is a single substitution (*ekādeśa*) with the circumflex (*svarita*) when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added; that is, a single substitution occurs with the circumflex when *ṭāp* is applied. Here, it must be considered: "Should the circumflex be applied first, or the single substitution? What should be done here? The circumflex should take effect because it is subsequent (*para*). The single substitution is obligatory (*nitya*).
It applies whether the *svarita* accent has been applied or not; it applies whether the *svarita* accent has been applied or not. Furthermore, the *svarita* accent itself is constant:

it applies whether the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied or not. However, the *svarita* accent is non-constant, because it applies to one thing when the single-substitute has been applied, and to another thing when it has not been applied. A grammatical rule that applies to a different word-form is considered non-constant; and this applies to the single-substitute as well.

[The rule] is non-permanent (*anitya*). [For] when the *svarita* accent is applied to a word that has a different accent, it applies; and when the word that has a different accent has not yet been applied, the rule applies to that which is distinct in accent. Thus, the rule, while applying to that which is distinct in accent, becomes non-permanent. In that case, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*). What is its internality? The single-substitute depends upon two phonemes (*varṇa*), whereas the *svarita* accent of the word [depends upon the whole word]. [Objection: The *svarita* accent is also internal. How so?

This will be explained later: "The mention of the word *pada* is for the sake of defining its measure. Because it is subsequent (*para*) to both internal rules (*antaraṅga*), the *svarita* accent is applied. Once the *svarita* has been applied, by virtue of proximity (*āntarya*), a *svarita* will arise from a *svarita* and an *anudātta*. Furthermore, this conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between the accent of a *pit* suffix and the accent of a *cit* suffix is also improper. What is the reason? Because... [the rule] *cāpi*...
Because it is marked with *cit*, and also by virtue of the capacity of the *cit* marker, the final syllable will be udātta.
3.1.5) Why is the *anubandha* added to the roots beginning with *gup*? The addition of the *anubandha* to the roots beginning with *gup* is for the sake of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).

The indicatory letters (*anubandhas*) are attached to roots such as *gup* so that the *ātmanepada* endings may occur. Even though these indicatory letters are attached, the *ātmanepada* still does not apply. What is the reason? Because [the root] is separated by the suffix *san*. [Objection: It will be so by the rule "as before, after *san*" (*pūrvavat sanaḥ*).
[Reply: The rule "as before, after *san*" is stated; however, the *ātmanepada* does not occur for these roots prior to the addition of *san*.
Nor do we see [any rule for] the *parasmaipada* [ending]. If that is so, it will come about through the power of the indicatory letter (*anubandha*).

Or rather, a characteristic mark applied to a part will serve as a differentiator for the whole. Just as a mark made on the thigh or the ear of a cow serves as a differentiator for the cow; if a mark made on a part [serves as a differentiator] for the whole...

[Objection: In this case, [the suffix] would also apply to [the roots] *viśeṣayati*, *jugupsayati*, and *mīmāṃsayati*. [Question: A grammatical marker (*liṅga*) applied to a member (an *avayava*) serves as a specifier for which aggregate (*samudāya*)? [Answer: It specifies that aggregate which the member does not deviate from. Now, [the marker] does not deviate from *san* (the desiderative suffix), but it does deviate from *ṇic* (the causative suffix). For example, as in the case of "the leg of a cow" (*goḥ sakthani*).

A mark placed on the ear belongs to the specific cow, not to the entire herd of cows. (Pāṇini 3.1.6) In the case of the lengthening of the reduplication, there would be the undesirable consequence of lengthening for the vowel *a*; that is, the vowel *a* would undergo lengthening in the reduplicated syllable.

It obtains [the substitution]. It undergoes investigation. But surely, once the *ittva* (substitution of *i*) has been applied, the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) will occur. How, then, can the lengthening—which is prescribed as being conditioned by the very occurrence [of the root]—wait for the *ittva*? Or rather, how does it wait for the reduplication (*abhyāsa*)? It waits for the reduplication because of an explicit statement; however, it does not wait for the *ittva*. For there is no [rule] that would block an exception (*apavāda*) in the case of modifications of the reduplicated syllable.
Because an exception does not subvert a general rule. Or rather, this fault does not arise. Why?

Because among the modifications of reduplication (*abhyāsa-vikāra*), an exception (*apavāda*) does not subvert the general rule (*utsarga*). Thus, when lengthening (*dīrghatva*) is prescribed, it will not subvert the substitution of *it*. Alternatively, [the rule] "after the roots *mā*, *badh*, *dā*, and *śā*, there is also *ī* for the reduplication" applies.

I shall explain it thus: even so, the long vowel *ī* would still result as an exception to the rule for the retention of the initial consonant (*halādiśeṣa*). To this I reply: I shall state that "the *ī* [is substituted] for the vowel (*acaḥ*) [of the reduplicated syllable]. Alternatively, I shall state: "after the roots *mān*, *badh*, *dān*, and *śān*, there is a long vowel, and the *i* of the reduplicated syllable [is replaced by *ī*]. This is established. But then the Sūtra is altered. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. An objection is raised: "But was it not said that when the reduplicated syllable is long, the *a*-vowel [is affected]?"

"The consequence would be over-extension" (*dīrghaprasaṅgaḥ*). This has been refuted by the statement: "Or rather, not so, because an exception does not subvert a general rule (*utsarga*) in cases of modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsavikāra*).

Alternatively, it is not understood thus: "and the long vowel [applies] to the reduplicated syllable" (*dīrghaś cābhyāsasya*). How then? It is understood as: "and the long vowel [applies] to that which belongs to the reduplicated syllable" (*dīrghaś cābhyāsasya*). What is this "belonging to the reduplicated syllable"? That which is a modification of the reduplicated syllable is "the reduplicated syllable" (*ābhyāsa*); [it means] "to that."

(P_3,1.7.1) KA_II,12-14.7 Ro_III, 33-39: What is the purpose of [specifying] "from a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*)? [Consider: *prācikīrṣat* ("he desired to act upon"). [This should not apply] after a preposition (*sopasargāt*). Because of the mention of "object" (*karma*), the mention of "verbal root" (*dhātugrahaṇa*) is redundant in the rule prescribing the suffix *san*. [Response: Because of the mention of "object," the mention of "verbal root" is necessary in the rule prescribing *san*.

[The suffix] would be useless. Since [the suffix] *san* occurs when there is a desire for an action that has the same agent as another action, the derivation will occur from the verbal root itself. But the object (*karman*) is accompanied by a prefix (*sopasarga*). Therefore, the derivation would have to occur from that [root plus prefix]. If it is argued that the object is accompanied by a prefix, [we reply: because the prefix serves to qualify the object, the object is [in fact] without a prefix (*anupasarga*). If it is argued that the object is accompanied by a prefix, [we reply: the prefix is a qualifier of the object.

[The prefix] is an *upasarga*. For the object (*karman*) is indeed without an *upasarga*. And this must necessarily be understood thus: that the object is without an *upasarga*. For if that which possesses an *upasarga* were considered the object, then even under the heading of verbal roots (*dhātu*), there would be no prescription for the suffix *san*, because [the complex with the prefix] is not an object. For one who thinks that the object possesses an *upasarga*, even if the mention of the verbal root were made, there would still be no application of *san* for him.

What is the reason? Because it would not be an object of action (*akarmatvāt*). Then this is the purpose: let there be no derivation from that which ends in a *sub*-suffix. Furthermore, there is no possibility [of deriving] *kyac* and so forth from a *sub*-ending form, because they are exceptions (*apavāda*). Nor is there any possibility of deriving *san* from a *sub*-ending form. What is the reason? Because *kyac* and so forth are exceptions. *Kyac* and the others are prescribed after a *sub*-ending form; since they are exceptions, [they supersede the general rule].

They will be obstacles. Or rather, because of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*). Alternatively, due to non-expression, the suffixal derivation will not occur from that which ends in a *sup*-suffix. For if it were derived from a form ending in a *sup*-suffix, the desire (*icchā*) would not be expressed by the desiderative suffix (*san*);
because it is not expressed, the derivation from that [form] will not take place. This "non-expression" is indeed a recourse for those who have no other way out.

As for what is said—that there is no possibility [of the application] of *kyac* and the others after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) because they are exceptions (*apavāda*)—this might indeed be the case in some instances regarding one's own desire (*ātmecchā*). However, in the case of another's desire (*parecchā*), it would apply:
as in "he desires the king's son" (*rājñaḥ putram icchati*). If that is so, then this [application] should have been explicitly stated here, yet the Teacher does not state it.

What is it? It is stated that [the suffix *san*] occurs after a verb having the same agent (*samānakartṛka*). However, a noun ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) does not have a common agent. Even so, this might apply to something where there is no agent at all. But here it would apply:

*āsitum icchati* ("he wishes to sit"), *śayitum icchati* ("he wishes to lie down"). Since the suffix *san* is prescribed in the sense of wishing (*icchā*), and the suffix *tumun* is also prescribed after verbs meaning "to wish," the suffix *san* will not occur because that meaning has already been expressed by *tumun*.

Even so, it would follow here [that the suffix applies] in cases such as *āsanam icchati* ("he desires a seat") and *śayanam icchati* ("he desires a bed"). In this regard, whatever specific distinction or limiting condition (*upādhi*) is introduced when that which is to be expressed is indicated, the suffix must occur by means of that. And what meaning is understood here is "he desires to sit" (*āsitum icchati*) and "he desires to lie down" (*śayitum icchati*).

It is not understood here that "he desires to perform that action himself," as in the cases of *āsanam icchati* ("he desires a seat") or *śayanam icchati* ("he desires a bed"). Furthermore, the meaning "he desires a seat for another" is also understood. And this must necessarily be understood in this way; for even when [the suffix] is applied, he who thinks that it must exist when that [meaning] is not expressed [is mistaken].
If the term *dhātu* (verbal root) were not included here, it would apply in cases such as:

*saṅgatam icchati devadatto yajñadattena* ("Devadatta desires union with Yajñadatta"). Furthermore, the mention of "the same agent" (*samānakartṛka*) and "object" (*karman*) would be redundant, because the suffix is prescribed when expressing desire. Why? Because the mention of "the same agent" and "object" would be purposeless. What [is the point]?
The reason is that the suffix is prescribed when "desire" (icchā) is to be expressed. When desire is the meaning to be denoted, the suffix *saN* is prescribed.

For [the suffix *saN*] is not prescribed after a root that is either intransitive (*akarmaka*) or has a different agent (*asamānakartṛka*). Indeed, when desire is the meaning to be denoted, *saN* is prescribed;
and it would not be possible for desire to be expressed by a *saN* produced after a root that is intransitive or has a different agent.

Because it is not so designated, its production [as a verbal root] will not occur. However, it is for the purpose of determining the extent of the verbal base (*aṅga*). If it is for the purpose of determining the extent of the verbal base, then one of the two—either the mention of "action" (*karman*) or the mention of "verbal root" (*dhātu*)—must be made, with the thought: "I shall know the extent of the verbal base. But which of these is better here? The mention of "verbal root" alone is better; thus, the extent of the verbal base is indeed understood.

Furthermore, since a suffix prescribed after a verbal root (dhātu) is designated as *ārdhadhātuka*, the designation *ārdhadhātuka* for the suffix *san* is established. As for what was said—that because of the mention of "object" (*karman*), the mention of "verbal root" (*dhātu*) is redundant in the rule prescribing *san*—if it is argued that the object [of the action] includes the prefix (*upasarga*), we reply: no, because the prefix serves to qualify the object; thus, [the root] is without a prefix.

For his own position is described here by this [argument]: "Even though the domain of verbal roots (*dhātu*) is under discussion, the suffix *san* is not prescribed for that which has a prefix as its object, because it is not an object [of the root]. Here, one must consider what is logical: what constitutes the proper object?

And in this case, it is logical that the object should be that which includes the prefix. Now, it was indeed stated: "For if that which has a prefix is the object, while the domain of verbal roots..."

"But [the suffix] *san* would not apply because there is no object (*akarmatvāt*). This is not a fault. The ablative case in "from an object" (*karmaṇaḥ*) is not a genitive in grammatical apposition with the verbal root (*dhātu*). It is not [meant as] "from a root that is an object. What then? This is a genitive expressing a part-whole relationship (*avayavayoga*). [It means] "that which is a root which is a part of the object. If this is a genitive expressing a part-whole relationship, then derivation from a simple [root] would not be obtained. [For example, in the case of] *cikīrṣati*.

"He wishes to take" (*jihīrṣati*). Here too, by the principle of "acting like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the verbal root (*dhātu*) becomes a part of the object (*karman*). In that case, one might argue that *kyac* should also be applied for this very reason: "he desires a great son" (*mahāntam putram icchati*), on the grounds that "that which ends in a case-ending (*subanta*) belonging to the object becomes a part [of the verbal base]. It need not be applied. It will not occur because of a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*). How is there a lack of semantic connection?

"That which is dependent becomes semantically deficient (*asamartha*). Furthermore, the mention of the option (*vāvacana*) is purposeless because the suffix *san* is obligatory (*nitya*) in that case. The mention of the option is indeed useless. Why? Because the suffix *san* is obligatory there. For here there are two positions: the position of composition (*vṛttipakṣa*) and the position of non-composition (*avṛttipakṣa*). And by its very nature, this results in both the compound and the sentence.

And there is the condition (*pratyaya*). In that case, since a suffix (*pratyaya*) is already established as being inherent in its scope of application and eternal, what else could possibly be connected by the statement "optionally" (*vāvacana*), other than a technical name (*saṃjñā*)? Furthermore, the presence or absence of a technical name is not intended [as a matter of fact]. Therefore, the statement "optionally" serves no purpose.

(P_3,1.7.2) KA_II,14.8-15.4 Ro_III, 39-42: An option regarding the suffix *tumun*; and the statement that there is elision (*luk*) of it. It should be stated that the desiderative suffix *san* may optionally follow a word ending in *tumun*, and there should be elision (*luk*) of that *tumun*.

For example: *kartum icchati* → *cikīrṣati*. Or, [the suffix *san*] may optionally follow the first person singular of the optative (*liṅ*). It should be stated that the desiderative suffix *san* may optionally follow the first person singular of the optative.

And the elision (*luk*) of that potential suffix (*liṅ*) must be stated. [For example: "he wishes to do" (*cikīrṣati*) [is derived from] "he would do" (*kuryām*). An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for non-sentient things when there is a sense of apprehension (*āśaṅkā*). An addition must be made for non-sentient things when there is apprehension: "the stone wishes to roll down" (*aśmā luluṭhiṣate*), "the bank wishes to fall" (*kūlam pipatiṣati*). But what is the reason it is not established? He thinks thus: [it applies only] to that which possesses consciousness.

This constitutes "desire" (*icchā*). And the riverbank is insentient. There is no purpose in including the term "insentient. It is simply [to be understood] as "in the case of doubt. This also becomes established: "The dog is about to die. Or rather, it need not be stated, because desire is perceived through its activity, since the cause is the same. Why? Because the cause is the same. It is the same.

For [the agent] is the cause, whether in the case of the conscious Devadatta or in the case of the unconscious bank. Why? Because activity is perceived through desire. Indeed, activity is observed to arise from desire. Even one who intends to make a mat does not announce, "I shall make a mat. What then? [He is seen] with his hands equipped with cords, stakes, and bundles of grass.

Having seen this, then the desire [to fall] is understood. Even for one wishing to fall from the bank, clods of earth crumble, fissures arise, and he moves from one place to another. Furthermore, dogs that are about to die become solitary in their habits and have swollen eyes.
Or rather, it is established through analogy; indeed, this is established through analogy. How so? [One says: "He wishes to roll" (*luluṭhiṣate*).

[The forms] *luluṭhiṣate* and *pipatiṣati* are as if [they were] *pipatiṣati*. There is no comparison with a verbal form ending in a *tiṅ* suffix. If that is so, then it is like "desire as it were desire. Or rather, because everything possesses consciousness. Or else, everything is conscious; for thus it is said:
"The pots move," "The śirīṣa tree sleeps on its side," and "The suvarcalā plant revolves following the sun."
When it is said, "āskanda kapilaka," [the dog] leaps upon the grass; iron moves toward a magnet; a seer recites, "Listen, O pressing-stones.
(Pāṇini 3.1.7.3) Many such forms are taught here. In this regard, it is not known for whose sake the suffix *saN* is prescribed.

Thus [it is said] regarding the root *iṣ*, which does not undergo the substitution of *ś* for *s*. If this is so, then since one "seeks to act" (*kartum anvicchati*), the suffix *-an* would also apply here to form *anveṣaṇā*.

If that is the case, then this form is a *nipātana* (irregular formation) for the expression "one whose desire is for a woman" (*yasya striyām icchā*). And for which [root] is this *nipātana* applied? For the root meaning "to love" (*kānti-karman*). Now, in the phrase "he desires to go to the village" (*grāmam gantum icchati*), what is the object (*karman*) of what?

Both [types of] objects belong to the root *iṣ* (to desire). If this is so, then in the cases "he wishes to go to the village" (*grāmaṃ gantum icchati*) and "he wishes to go for the sake of the village" (*grāmāya gantum icchati*), the second and fourth case endings would not apply to the object of a verb meaning "to go. If that is the case, then the village is the object of the root *gam* (to go), and it is the object of *gam* which is itself the object of *iṣ*.

Even so, in the expression "the village is desired to be gone to" (*iṣyate grāmo gantum*), the village is denoted by the passive suffix *la*, which arises in connection with the operation of another agent.

[The suffix *san*] would not be obtained. If that is so, then in the case of *gami*, the village (*grāma*) is the object; in the case of *iṣ*, both are objects. Now, [if it were argued that] *san* must occur after a stem ending in *san*, as in "he desires to wish to do" (*cikīrṣitum icchati*) or "he desires to wish to take" (*jihīrṣitum icchati*), it need not occur. What is the reason? The employment of words is for the purpose of conveying meaning. A word is employed with the thought, "I shall cause the meaning to be understood. In that case, since [the meaning] has already been expressed by one [element], [the second is unnecessary].

There should be no application of another [verbal root] for that same meaning. What is the reason? Because there is no application of roots whose meaning has already been expressed. If that is so, then how is it that the forms *eṣitum icchati* and *eṣiṣiṣati* do not occur now? There is a distinction here: in this case, one instance of the root *iṣ* (to desire) is the means (*sādhana*) for the other instance of *iṣ*.
And the suffix (*pratyaya*) [of the first verb] has the present tense. For the other [verb], the external means (*sādhana*) is [the object] and the suffix has all tenses.
In this case as well, for one [instance of the root] *iṣ* (to desire), the means is the *iṣ* qualified by the act of "doing" (*karoti*), and the suffix has the present tense;
for the other, the external means is [the object] and the suffix has all tenses. Indeed, it is by that very same reason that this [is so].

The statement "he wishes to desire to do" (*cikīrṣitum icchati*) and "he wishes to desire to take away" (*jihīrṣitum icchati*) implies that for that very reason, the application [of the suffix] would also occur after a form ending in *san*. Therefore, a prohibition of *san* after [another] *san*-ending form must be stated. And while stating that, one must say "after the root *iṣ* and after *san*" (*iṣisanaḥ*). For indeed, forms such as *jugupsiṣate* ("he wishes to feel aversion") and *mīmāṃsiṣate* ("he wishes to investigate") occur. Furthermore, from a secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*) expressing the sense of the possessive suffix (*matup*), another secondary derivative may arise.
A suffix of similar form (*sarūpa*) having the sense of the *matup* suffix is not desired [to apply]. A *san* suffix is not desired after a stem already ending in *san*.

(Pāṇini 3.1.8.1) What is the purpose of the letter *c* [in the rule]? It is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*). By the rule "the final syllable of that which has the marker *cit* is acute," it serves to establish the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*).

Let it be so. This purpose is not necessary. This [root] has a single vowel (*ekāc*); therefore, there is no need for the marker *c* (the *anubandha*) for the sake of the accent. It is already established by the accent of the suffix itself. If you say it is for the sake of specification (*viśeṣaṇa*), then where is the need for specification?
[In the rule] "asya cvau kyaci ca" (Pāṇini 7.4.32). For even if it were stated as "kye ca," [the form] "kākaḥ śyenāyate" would also [be included].

One might object: "This is not so; when there is a mention of something with a specific suffixal marker (*tadanubandhaka*), there is no mention of that which lacks such a marker. To this we reply: it will not apply in this way [to the present case]. [Objection: Then it is for the purpose of not obstructing the general inclusion. [Reply: And where is there a need for the purpose of not obstructing the general inclusion? [In the rule] *naḥ kye*. Now, what is the purpose of mentioning *ātman*? So that it may apply when one desires for oneself (*ātma-icchā*), and not when one desires for another (*para-icchā*).

Lest this [undesired consequence] should occur—namely, that one would say *rājñaḥ putram icchati* ("he desires the king's son") even when the word *ātman* (self) is included [in the rule]. Why? Because in the expression *ātmanaḥ*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes the agent; whereas in *icchā*, the suffix *-ā* denotes the action (*bhāve*). Thus, whether it is "the desire of oneself" or "the desire of another," it remains simply "the desire of the self. Therefore, the inclusion of the word *ātman* does not exclude the desire for another.
What is connected [to the word]? Rather, it is that which ends in a *sup* suffix (*subanta*) that is connected. [The meaning is: "that which is one's own *subanta*.

If the mention of "one's own" (*ātman*) were made, it would not apply in the Vedic language (*chandasi*) when referring to another's desire, as in: *mā tvā vṛkā aghāyavo vidan*. Therefore, there is no purpose in the mention of "one's own. Why does it not occur here?

[The objection: "One desires a son for the king" (*rājñaḥ putram icchati*)—this is impossible due to a lack of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*). How is there a lack of capacity? [Because] that which is dependent [on another] lacks capacity. [The reply: In that case, it would not even be possible in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), as in: *mā tvā vṛkā aghāyavo vidan* ("May the harmful wolves not find you"). [Objection: There is a distinction here. Even without the employment of a third word, the desire for another is understood. How so?

Furthermore, even without the employment of a third word here, the desire of another is understood; for those very wolves are of such a nature as to be harmful. And who would wish to seek their own misfortune? Therefore, even without the employment of a third word here, the desire of another is understood. Just so, then, in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), from the word *agha*—

If the suffix *kyac* occurs when *parasmaipada* is intended, then it would also apply in the *bhāṣā* (common speech) in the sense "he desires evil" (*agham icchati*). Therefore, the mention of *ātmanepada* must be made. How about in the *chandas* (Vedic)? The activity of the Teacher indicates that in the *chandas*, *kyac* occurs after the word *agha* when *parasmaipada* is intended; for this reason, he [Pāṇini] provides the rule *aśvāghasyāt* when *kyac* has been introduced, in order to prevent the substitution of *ī*.

[The rule] teaches the form [of the suffix]. Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *sup* (the nominal suffix)? It is so that the production [of the suffix] may occur after a word ending in a *sup* suffix, and not after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). This is not a valid purpose. There is no distinction here between the production occurring after a word ending in a *sup* suffix and after a nominal stem. However, there is this distinction: when the production occurs after a word ending in a *sup* suffix, the designation *pada* is established.

If [suffixes] were to arise from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the designation "word" (*pada*) would not apply. But is it not the case that if they arise from the nominal stem, the designation "word" is already established? How so? Because the rule *naḥ kye* is formulated. And that must necessarily be stated for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*) when [suffixes] arise from a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). That very same [rule], however, serves as an injunction (*vidhyartha*) when [suffixes] arise from the nominal stem.
It will be so. Then this is the purpose: that the suffixation should occur after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), and not after a verbal root (*dhātu*).
This too is not a valid purpose. For the suffix *san* is prescribed after a verbal root; it will therefore act as an exception (*bādhaka*).
Indeed, rules that have no other scope (*anavakāśa*) are exceptions, whereas *san* has its own scope. What is its scope? The desire of another.

The suffix *san* should not occur after [a verb] expressing the desire of another. What is the reason? It is stated that [the suffix occurs] after [a verb] having the same agent (*samānakartṛka*). And as long as there is the mention of "self" (*ātman*) here, so long is there the mention of "having the same agent" there. Then what is the purpose [of this rule]? So that the derivation may occur from a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), and not from a sentence (*vākya*). For example: *mahāntaṃ putram icchati* ("he desires a great son"). Or rather, it does not occur.
Regarding the form *mahāputrīyati*: this occurs when the analysis of the word is as follows—*mahān putraḥ* (a great son), *mahāputraḥ*;
