then, "he desires a great son" results in *mahāputrīyati*. However, when the analysis is *mahāntam putram icchati* ("he desires a great son"), it should not occur; yet it would [otherwise] result there. Therefore, it is said: "let it not be so."

(P_3,1.8.2) KA_II,17.12–18.15 Ro_III, 48–50: Now, even if the mention of *sub* is made, why does [the rule] not apply here? For this sentence consists of words ending in *sup*. It is not *subanta*. Why? Because when there is a mention of a suffix (*pratyaya*), the mention includes that which begins with it.

Thus [it is said]. Now, why does derivation not occur from that which ends in a nominal suffix (*subanta*) in this case? Because there is no application (*avṛtti*) of co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) terms everywhere, due to their lack of connection with a single [word]. There is no application of co-referential terms in all cases whatsoever. In what cases "everywhere"? In the rules for compound formation (*samāsa-vidhi*) and in the rules for suffixation (*pratyaya-vidhi*). First, regarding the rules for compound formation: [as in] *ṛddhasya rājñaḥ* ("of the prosperous king").

"The man has resorted to great hardship. [This occurs] in the formation of a derivative (*pratyaya*): "the offspring of the wealthy Upagu," or "he desires a great son. But what is the reason that a compound formation (*vṛtti*) does not occur everywhere among words in apposition? Because there is no connection with one [word]. For there is no connection with a single word. In this case, for instance: "the king's man, who is wealthy."

Thus, a compound is prescribed when there is semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) between a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) and a word ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*). Now, that which ends in the sixth case here has no semantic connection with the word ending in a nominal suffix; and that which possesses semantic connection does not end in the sixth case. That is a sentence, as in: "the offspring of Upagu the wealthy" (*ṛddhasya upagoḥ apatyam*). Furthermore, a secondary suffix (*pratyaya*) is prescribed when there is a connection with "offspring" (*apatya*) following a word that is semantically connected with the sixth case.

Furthermore, that which is governed by a genitive case ending here does not have a connection with the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*), and that which has a connection with the sense of "offspring" is not in the genitive case. That is a sentence (*vākya*). It is stated [in the rule] "of those in apposition" (*samānādhikaraṇānām*). Now, how is it for those in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*)? For example: *rājñaḥ putram icchati* ("he desires the king's son"). If this is so, then this should be recited: "of those accompanied by qualifiers" (*saviśeṣaṇānām*).

There is no application [of the suffix] in all cases because it is not possible with one [object]. However, a second [object] is not possible; indeed, a second [object] does not occur in such expressions as *mahāntaṃ putram icchati* ("he desires a great son"). What is the reason? A son is not the object of the act of desiring (*iṣikarma*). If a son is not the object of the act of desiring, then it is not necessarily only the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) that occurs. What then? All case endings beginning with the accusative—such as the instrumental (*mahatā*)—may occur.

"Done by the son" (*putreṇa kṛtam*). "Give to the great son" (*mahate putrāya dehi*). "Bring from the great son" (*mahaḥ putrāt ānaya*). "The property of the great son" (*mahataḥ putrasya svam*). "Place [the gift] in the great son" (*mahati putre nidhehi*). Therefore, it cannot be said that "the son is not the object of the act of shooting. The son himself is indeed the object of the act of shooting. Because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [verb], the second case endings and so forth will occur. [Objection: Then why is there a formal rule (*vṛtti*)?

It does not occur. It must be stated that "there is no compound formation (*vṛtti*) of words accompanied by qualifiers, nor is a qualifier applied to a word that has already undergone compound formation.

If it is said that "there is no compound formation of words accompanied by qualifiers, nor is a qualifier applied to a word that has already undergone compound formation," then in the case of *muṇḍayati māṇavakam* ("he causes the boy to be shorn"), compound formation would not be obtained. It must be stated that [the rule applies] to words such as *amuṇḍa* and the like. Therefore, that must indeed be stated.

[The objection: "The formation of a compound (*vṛtti*) does not occur for words that have qualifiers, nor is a qualifier applied to a word that has already been compounded; this is the case with *amuṇḍa* and so forth. [Response: This need not be stated. Why does the compound not occur in the expression *mahāntam putram icchati* ("he desires a great son")? Because it is not expressive (*agamakatvāt*).
In this case, there ought to be a sentence with the same meaning as the form ending in a suffix (*pratyayānta*). And whatever meaning is here expressed by the sentence...

In the expression "he desires a great son" (*mahāntaṃ putraṃ icchati*), it is understood that he wishes for a great son; however, this is never understood from the derivative form *putrīyati* ("he treats like a son"). For this reason, we say [the objection is invalid] because of its lack of expressiveness (*agamakatvāt*). We do not say that it would be an ungrammatical word (*apaśabda*).
Where there is expressiveness, there is the application of a verbal derivative (*vṛtti*). For example, as in "he shaves the boy" (*muṇḍayati māṇavakam*).

(P_3,1.8.3) Now, what are the factors (*sādhana*) for this [verb] ending in *kyac*? They are the action (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kartṛ*). What then of the object (*karman*)? There is no object. But is it not the case that this root *iṣ* is transitive, and it is precisely for its meaning that *kyac* is prescribed?

That expressed action is included within [the root], and thus becomes the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Now, there is no other action remaining by which it could be transitive (*sakarmaka*). How then does this [root] become transitive, as in "he treats the boy like a son" (*putrīyati māṇavakam*)? There is a distinction here: for in this case, there are two objects—the object of comparison (*upamānakarman*) and [the object of the action itself].

And the object of the thing compared (*upameya*) is included within the object of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). By means of the object that is the thing compared, [the verb] becomes transitive (*sakarmaka*).
For example: "Even a crow acts like a hawk" (*api kākaḥ śyenāyate*). Here, there are two agents: the agent who is the standard of comparison and the agent who is the thing compared.
The agent who is the standard of comparison is included; by means of the agent who is the thing compared, [the verb] comes to have an agent (*sakartṛka*). How then is this [to be explained]?

It becomes transitive, as in "he causes the boy to be shaved" (*muṇḍayati māṇavakam*). Here too, there are two objects: the general object and the specific object. The general object is included [within the verbal base], and it becomes transitive by virtue of the specific object. But surely, in this case, there should not even be a verbal derivation (*vṛtti*)? What is the reason? Because of a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*). How is there a lack of competency?

[Objection: "That which is dependent becomes semantically deficient (*asamartha*). [Response: This is not a fault. In this case, neither *muṇḍaḥ* nor *māṇavakaḥ* is connected with the verb *karoti*. For the boy (*māṇavaka*) is not being made; rather, it is only when both are connected with *karoti* that the compound formation (*vṛtti*) does not occur. For example: "He makes a bull strong, and he makes him shaven. Well then, [let us grant that].

For this very reason, one should also apply the suffix *kyac* in the case of *māṇavakam muṇḍam icchati*. [Objection: It should not be applied, because both [the boy and the state of being shaven] are connected with the verb *iṣ* ("to desire"). [Response: It should indeed be applied. For here, both the state of being shaven (*muṇḍa*) and the boy (*māṇavaka*) are connected with *iṣ*. How so? Because he does not find satisfaction in the mere state of being shaven; rather, he desires the state of being shaven as it resides in the boy. If that is so, then in this case as well—

One does not obtain [the application of the suffix] in the case of *muṇḍayati māṇavakam* ("he shaves the boy"). For here too, both are connected with the action of making (*karoti*): namely, the shaving and the boy. Indeed, he does not bring satisfaction by means of the shaving alone; rather, he brings about that shaving which resides in the boy. If that is so, then words such as *muṇḍa* are qualifiers (*guṇavacana*). And qualifiers are dependent (*sāpekṣa*). [The rule applies] because of the statement regarding those that are dependent.

Or rather, there will be a derivative formation (*vṛtti*). Or else, *muṇḍa* and so forth are indeed verbal roots (*dhātu*). For it is not the case that meanings are being prescribed [as primary], yet their status as denoters of action (*kriyāvacanatā*) is understood. Or else, these two do not occur simultaneously: neither the sentence (*vākya*) nor the suffix (*pratyaya*). When it is a sentence, then there is no suffix; when there is a suffix in its general sense, then there is a derivative formation. In that regard:

One who desires a specific distinction must necessarily employ that distinction; for example, "he shaves" (*muṇḍayati*)—whom? "The boy" (*māṇavakam*). Or rather, he does not wish to attain that [shaving] by means of the root *kṛ* (to do) as qualified by "shaving. Alternatively, this has already been stated: "In this case, no further operation (*vyāpāra*) is to be understood. Because it possesses the sense of "going" (*gamakatvāt*), the derivative form will occur here: "he shaves the boy" (*muṇḍayati māṇavakam*). Now, in this case, by means of the suffix *kyac*...

It must be [expressed as] *bhavitavyam* (it is to be), *iṣṭaḥ putraḥ* (a desired son), or *iṣyate putraḥ* (a son is desired). First, some say that it need not be expressed. What is the reason? Because it has already been stated by its own word (*svaśabda*). Others say: it must be expressed. What is the reason? This suffix *kyac* is prescribed in the sense of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and that sense of the root [is what is intended].
It must be designated by some word or other; however, the venerable ones say that it should not be so.

What is the reason? In this case, there ought to be a sentence with the same meaning as that which ends in a suffix; yet the meaning understood here from the sentence—such as "the son is desired" (*iṣṭaḥ putraḥ*) or "a son is being desired" (*iṣyate putraḥ*)—is never conveyed by a form ending in a suffix.

A prohibition regarding words ending in *m* and indeclinables (*avyaya*) must be stated for the suffix *kyac*. [Otherwise], it would apply here: *idamicchati* ("he desires this"), *kimicchati* ("what does he desire?"), *uccairicchati* ("he desires loudly"), *nīcairicchati* ("he desires softly"). [The rule applies] after a word ending in a letter identical to that of *go* (i.e., *o*).
Thus say some. [The suffix *kyac* is applied] after the word *go*: *gavyati*. After a word ending in a homogeneous vowel: *dadhīyati*, *madhyati*, *kartrīyati*, *hartrīyati*.
After a word ending in *n*: *rājīyati*, *takṣīyati*.

56–57. What is the purpose of the letter *ca*? It is for the sake of accent (*svarārtha*). [The rule] "the final syllable of that which is marked with *cit* is acute" ensures that it has an acute accent on the final syllable. This is not a necessary purpose, for this is already established by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*). [Objection: Then the letter *ca* should be placed at the beginning for the sake of protecting the letter *ka* from receiving the designation *it*. To this, he recites the following: *kāmyacaḥ*.

The designation *cit* is purposeless because there is no object for it. The designation *cit* for [the suffix] *kāmyac* is useless. Why, then, does the letter *k* not receive the technical name *it*? Because there is no object for it; since there is no operation (*kārya*) to be performed by an *it*, the designation *it* will not apply here. But surely, elision (*lopa*) itself is the operation of an *it*. Elision is not an operation. For in this system, a linguistic element exists for the sake of an operation.

Or rather, the instruction (upadeśa) is for the purpose of hearing [the rule]. And here there is no grammatical operation (kārya). If, in the absence of an operation, even the hearing were not to take place, the instruction would be useless. Well then, this is the purpose of the *it*: in *agnicit-kāmyati*, so that the prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule *kiti* may apply. This is not a valid purpose; for [the prohibition of *guṇa*] applies to *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes.

It is stated that a suffix is a "quality" (*guṇa*) of the stem (*aṅga*). Furthermore, a suffix prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*) receives the technical designation *ārdhadhātuka*, provided it is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*).

However, this [suffix in question] is not prescribed after a verbal root. [Objection: Then consider this example: *upayaṭkāmyati*. [In this case,] the vowel substitution known as *samprasāraṇa* should occur by the rule "before a *kit* suffix. [Response: This too is not a valid purpose. We shall qualify the *kit* suffix here by means of the roots beginning with *yaj* (i.e., *yaj*, *yāc*, *vep*, *vyadh*, *vye*, and *vraśca*). Thus, the *samprasāraṇa* will occur only where appropriate.

Regarding the rule *yajādīnām yaḥ kit*: what is it that makes the suffix *ya* after the roots beginning with *yaj* marked as *kit*? It means the *ya* prescribed after the roots beginning with *yaj*. Even if, for some reason, there were an operation dependent on the *it*-marker (*itkārya*), there would still be no fault. One could simply provide a dual-consonant notation (*dvicakāraka*) in the formulation itself: *supa ātmanaḥ kyac ca kāmyac ca*. Alternatively, this is a Vedic usage; it follows the observed forms (*dṛṣṭānuvidhi*).

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), [the suffix *kyac*] occurs; however, no vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) is observed here. (P_3.1.10) And because of the locus (*adhikaraṇāt*). It should be stated: "and because of the locus. Just as in the case of *prāsādayati* ("he causes to dwell in a palace") and *kuṭīyati* ("he acts like a hut"), so too in the case of *prāsāde* ("in the palace").
The suffix *kyaṅ* is prescribed by way of conjunction with the elision of the *s*. Therefore, it should occur only where there is the elision of *s*.

[Examples would be: *payāyate*. Here it should not occur: *api kākaḥ śyenāyate*. This is not a fault. The suffix *kyaṅ* is taught as the primary element; the elision of *s* is taught as a secondary (concomitant) element. And it is only where you perceive the letter *s* that [the rule applies]. For example, it is like someone being told:

"Go for alms in the village and bring Devadatta. He goes for alms in the village; if he sees Devadatta, he brings him as well. "Or there is elision of *s*. It should be stated: "Or there is elision of *s*. [In these cases: *payāyate*, *payasyate*. "In the case of *ojas* and *apsaras*, it is obligatory. It should be stated that in the case of *ojas* and *apsaras*, the elision of *s* is obligatory: [the serpent] who was acting with vigor (*ojāyamānam*)... the serpent.
"He slew" (*jaghāna*). "He acts like an *apsaras*" (*apsarāyate*). [Regarding] *apraḥ* [the rule] says there is elision of the *s*, as in *apsarasaḥ* itself. It must be that it becomes *payasyate*.

How [is it explained] in the case of *ojāyamānam yaḥ ahim jaghana* ("he who slew the serpent while displaying vigor")? This is a Vedic usage. And in the Veda, the rule is prescribed according to what is observed.

58–59. *Ācāre galbhaklībahoḍebhyaḥ kvip vā*. It should be stated that the suffix *kvip* optionally applies after the words *galbha*, *klība*, and *hoḍa* when they denote conduct (*ācāra*). [Examples: *avagalbhate* / *avagalbhāyate*; *viklībate* / *viklībāyate*; *vihoḍate* / *vihoḍāyate*. What is the purpose? So that they may express an action (*kriyāvacanatā*). This is not a necessary purpose.

The roots *galbh* and so forth are indeed verbal roots (*dhātu*). For it is not their meanings that are being indicated, yet they are understood to denote actions. In that case, this is the purpose: [to ensure that] in the forms *avagalbhā*, *viklībā*, and *vihoḍā*, the suffix *a* occurs by the rule "after a root ending in a non-suffix" (*apratyayāt*). Let it not be so; for it will occur by the rule "after a heavy vowel and a consonant" (*gurośca halaḥ*). In that case, this is the purpose: [the form] *avagalbhām*.
He made him tremble; he made him limp; he made him stagger. [The suffix] *ām* is applied so that, by the rule *kāspratyayād ām amantre*, the form *ām* may occur. Another says:

"The suffix *kvip* must be stated after all nominal stems (*prātipadika*) in the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*), for the sake of forms such as *aśvati* and *gardabhati*. In that case, the enumeration of roots beginning with *galbha* need not be performed now. Yet it must indeed be performed. What is the purpose? For the sake of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).

"I shall consider the consequences. [The suffix] *ky-aṅ* is prescribed after [roots ending in] a consonant (*hal*) in conjunction with its elision (*lopa*). Therefore, it applies only where there is elision of that consonant. *Galbha*, *klība*, *hoḍa*. (Pāṇini 3.1.12.1) KA_II,21.20-22 Ro_III, 60. This *ky-aṅ* is prescribed in connection with the elision of a consonant; thus, it occurs only where there is elision of a consonant.

[The objection: It would follow [that the rule applies even where there is no *hal*]. [The response: This fault does not arise. The suffix *kyaṅ* is taught as the primary element (*pradhāna*), whereas the elision of the *hal* (*halaḥ lopaḥ*) is taught as a secondary or incidental element (*anvācaya*). And it is only where you perceive a *hal* that [the elision occurs]. (P. 3.1.12.2) KA_II,21.23–22.17 Ro_III,105.16–106.18: *nanu caivam api kṛte 'ntaraṅgatvād dīrgheṇa bhavitavyam / naiṣa doṣaḥ / āśrīyamāṇe 'pi dīrghe tasya sthānivadbhāvāt kyaṅo halantād iti lopasiddhiḥ / athavā punar astv antaraṅgatvād dīrghatvam / nanu coktam evam api kṛte 'ntaraṅgatvād dīrgheṇa bhavitavyam iti / naiṣa doṣaḥ / vakṣyaty etad dīrghavidhim prati na sthānivad iti / athavā punar astu pūrvam dīrghatvam / nanu coktaṃ kṛte dīrghe 'ntaraṅgatvāt kyaci kṛte 'lvidhitvāt sthānivadbhāvābhāvād dīrghāprasaṅga iti / naiṣa doṣaḥ / vakṣyaty etad dīrghavidhim prati na sthānivad iti / athavā punar astu pūrvam dīrghatvam / nanu coktaṃ kṛte dīrghe 'ntaraṅgatvāt kyaci kṛte 'lvidhitvāt sthānivadbhāvābhāvād dīrghāprasaṅga iti / naiṣa doṣaḥ / vakṣyaty etad dīrghavidhim prati na sthānivad iti / athavā punar astu pūrvam dīrghatvam / nanu coktaṃ kṛte dīrghe 'ntaraṅgatvāt kyaci kṛte 'lvidhitvāt sthānivadbhāvābhāvād dīrghāprasaṅga iti / naiṣa doṣaḥ / vakṣyaty etad dīrghavidhim prati na
