60–61. Regarding the *bhṛśādi* group, there must be an inclusion of the sense of "becoming that which it was not" (*abhūtatadbhāva*). An inclusion of the sense of "becoming that which it was not" must be made in the case of the *bhṛśādi* group.

This is so that [the suffix] does not apply here: *kva divā bhṛśā bhavanti* ("Where do they become intense by day?"). Furthermore, the prohibition of the *cvī* suffix is rendered purposeless because of the rule prescribing *kyaṅ* in the sense of "becoming. Moreover, the prohibition of *cvī* is useless. Why? Because of the prescription of *kyaṅ* in the sense of "becoming."

For the suffix *kyaṅ* is prescribed in the sense of "becoming" (*bhavati*). The prescription of *cvi* occurs in connection with the verb *bhavati*. Since that meaning has already been expressed by *cvi* in that context, *kyaṅ* will not apply. But then it would not apply even after a form ending in *ḍāc*, as in *paṭapaṭāyate*; for *ḍāc* is also prescribed in connection with *bhavati* in the sense of "becoming."

[Kyaṣ occurs] after [words ending in] ḍāc, because of the authority of the explicit statement. It will occur because of the authority of the explicit statement. What is the authority of the statement? It is the rule: "After *lohita* and those ending in *ḍāc*, there is *kyaṣ*. Here, some things are raised as objections when they are not being performed, while other things are rejected even though they are being performed. Thus, a division of the sūtra is made. Let it remain exactly as it was originally formulated. But has it not been said?

Why does this not occur here: *kva divā bhṛśā bhavanti* ("Where are they very intense during the day")? [The answer is: "That which is joined with *nañ* or *iva* [is understood] as referring to something else similar; for such is the comprehension of the meaning. Whatever is seen here joined with *nañ* or joined with *iva*, there the grammatical operation is understood to apply to something else that is similar to it; for such is the meaning comprehended. For example, when it is said, *abrāhmaṇam ānaya* ("Bring a non-Brahmin").

A person resembling a Brahmin is being brought; he does not become satisfied by bringing a clod of earth. In the same way here as well, because of the prohibition against *cvī* in the rule "not after *acvī*," the operation will be understood to apply to something other than *cvī*-ending, yet similar to *cvī*. And what else is there that is non-*cvī*-ending yet similar to *cvī*? It is the state of becoming that which it was not before (*abhūtatadbhāva*).
(P_3,1.12.3) Here, certain nominal bases (*prakṛti*) are recited with prefixes (*upasarga*): *abhimanas*, *sumanas*, etc.
*unmanas*, *durmanas*. In this regard, it is considered:
in the case of [words] such as *bhṛśa* and others, would the prefix (*upasarga*) be a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix?

[The forms] *abhibhavat*, *subhavat*, *udbhavat*, and *durbhavat*—or rather, [the forms] *abhimanas*, *sumanas*, *unmanas*, and *durmanas*—are qualifiers of the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*). However, it is appropriate to consider this further:
surely the qualifiers of the meaning of the verbal root ought to be listed before the root itself, since they are currently recited after it?

For if [the term *bhṛśa*] were a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), it would have been recited before the root *bhū*. These [words] cannot be recited before the root *bhū*; for if the meaning of the suffix were thus qualified, the production [of the suffix] would result from the mere category of *bhṛśādi* (intensive) words.
Therefore, it cannot be done in this way. If this is not the case, then such an inquiry arises: what then is the distinction here?

If it is argued that in the case of *bhṛśa* and other such words, the prefix (*upasarga*) qualifies the meaning of the suffix, there is a fault regarding the accent (*svara*). If it is argued that in the case of *bhṛśa* and others, the prefix qualifies the meaning of the suffix, there arises a fault in the accent: in the form *abhimanāyate*, the rule *tiṅ atiṅaḥ* would entail the occurrence of the *nighāta* (elision of accent). Let it be, then, that [the prefix] qualifies the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). If it is argued that [the suffix applies] "after that which has a prefix" (*sopasargāt*), there is a fault in the case of the augment *aṭ*.

If it is argued that [the rule] applies "after a word with a prefix," then there is a fault in the case of *aṭ*. For example: *svamanayata*. This which is said—"there is a fault in the case of *aṭ*"—is stated too little. It should be stated: "In the cases of *aṭ*, *lyap*, and reduplication (*dvirvacana*). *Aṭ*: as has been illustrated. *Lyap*: [example follows].

Regarding *sumanāyya*: in the case of reduplication, as in *abhimimanāyiṣate*, this fault does not arise. It must necessarily be stated that the derivation of *saṃgrāmayate* occurs only when it is accompanied by a prefix, for the sake of such examples as "the hero does not engage in battle" (*asaṃgrāmayate śūraḥ*). That [rule] will therefore serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), [stating] that [the derivation] applies only to *saṃgrāmayate*.
"Only from that which has a prefix, not from any other [word] having a prefix. If this restriction is made, the accent is not established.

In that case, I shall state that for words beginning with *bhṛśa*, the prefix behaves as if it were part of the subsequent member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*). If the behavior of being part of the subsequent member is stated, then the augment *aṭ*, the substitution of *yaṇ*, and reduplication would not be established. I shall state "in the rule for accent" (*svaravidhau*). And having done so, [the desired results follow].

Let it be a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārthaviśeṣaṇa*). But was it not said that if a prefix (*upasarga*) is a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix in the case of *bhṛśādi* words, there is a fault regarding the accent (*svara*)? That has been resolved by the rule of "behaving like a subordinate element" (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) with respect to the accent. Then this is the fault when it is a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix: since that meaning has already been expressed by the *kyaṅ* suffix, the employment of the prefix would not be justified. Why?

The reason is that "there is no application [of an element] when its meaning has already been expressed. For example, in the expression *api kākaḥ śyenāyate* ("even a crow acts like a hawk"), because the sense of conduct (*ācāra*) is already expressed by the suffix *kyaṅ*, the prefix *āṅ* is not employed. There is a distinction here: in that case, the suffix arises with respect to a single qualified meaning of the suffix, whereas here it arises with respect to many. In that regard, when *manāyate* is said, there might be doubt regarding the root *abhibhū* ("to overcome").

Regarding the forms *subhavati* and *durbhavati*: in those cases, a prefix (*upasarga*) is employed for the sake of removing ambiguity. But where [a form] occurs with only one [prefix], such as *utpucchayate*? Even there, it occurs with more than one: namely, *pucchād udsane*, *pucchād vyasane*, and *pucchāt paryasane*.

64–66. What is the purpose of the letter *k* [in the suffix *kit*]? It is so that there may be the prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule *kṅiti*. This is not a valid purpose. For it is taught that *guṇa* applies to the *aṅga* (stem) before *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes. Furthermore, a suffix is designated as *ārdhadhātuka* only when it is prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*), and this suffix is not prescribed after a root. [The suffixes in question] follow nominal stems (*prātipadika*) such as *lohita* and others.

[Objection: Then it must be for the purpose of grasping the general category (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*). [Question: Where is there a need for grasping the general category? [Answer: In the rule *naḥ kye*. This [suffix] is not prescribed after a word ending in *n*. [Objection: Then here [is the case]: *yasya halaḥ kyasya vibhāṣā*. This [suffix] is not prescribed after a word ending in a consonant (*hal*).
[Objection: Then here [is the case]: *āpatyayasya ca taddhite anāti kyacvyoḥ ca*. This [suffix] is not [prescribed] after a patronymic (*āpatya*).

It is prescribed. In this case, then, regarding the rule *kyāt chandasi*, one should simply say *yāt chandasi* for the sake of forms such as *caraṇyūḥ*, *turaṇyuḥ*, and *bhuraṇyuḥ*. However, there is this purpose: in the rule concerning the substitution of the long vowel (*dīrghatva*) in the section on *akṛtya*-suffixes, the mention of *kṅit* is carried over; therefore, it should apply here as well, as in *lohitāyate*.

But what is the reason that the mention of *kṅit* continues there [in the rule for *rīṅ*]? [It is so] lest it apply here in cases such as *uruyā* and *dhṛṣṇuyā*. If the mention of *kṅit* continues, then in the case of *itryam*, the substitution of *rīṅ* for *pitṛ-* would not be obtained.

[Reply: The mention of *kṅit* will be discontinued in the rule for the substitution of *rīṅ*. [Objection: If it is discontinued, how do we account for *asūyā* and *vasūyā*? [They come] from the root *asūyati*.

*Asūyā* is derived from the root *vasūyati*; thus it is *vasūyā*. Alternatively, this is a Vedic (chāndasa) form; for in the Veda, one follows whatever forms are observed. If being a Vedic form is the reason [for the lengthening], then there is no need for the continued application of the rule regarding *kṅit* suffixes. Why does it not occur in the case of *uruyā* and *dhṛṣṇuyā*? Because they are Vedic forms. Or rather, let there be lengthening here; it is Vedic.
There will be shortening [of the vowel]. For example: "May my wives, pregnant and young, sing in accompaniment to me.

Now, for what purpose is the letter *ṣ*? It is for the sake of specification (*viśeṣaṇa*). Where is there a need for the purpose of specification? In the rule "optionally after a root ending in *kyaṣ*" (*vā kyaṣaḥ*). For if it were stated simply as "*vā kyāt*," then [the suffix] would also apply after [roots ending in] *ataḥ*. This is not a purpose of yours; [the result would be] the Parasmaipada [suffixes].

Thus it is said. We do not see here either a *parasmaipada* ending nor an *ātmanepada* ending. In that case, its purpose will be to prevent the obstruction of the general inclusion (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*). Where is there a need for the purpose of preventing the obstruction of the general inclusion? [In the rule] "kyāt in the Veda" (*chandasi*). It should rather have been stated as "yāt in the Veda" (*chandasi*) for the sake of forms such as *caraṇyūḥ*, *turaṇyuḥ*, and *bhuraṇyuḥ*.

(P_3,1.13.2) Regarding *lohita* and *ḍāj* suffixes, the rule for *kyaṣ* must be stated: *kyaṣ* should be prescribed after *lohita* and *ḍāj* suffixes. Examples: *lohitāyati*, *lohitāyate*; *paṭapaṭāyati*, *paṭapaṭāyate*. Now, as for other words such as *lohita* and so on: the others [belong] among the *bhṛśādi* group; they are in the *bhṛśādi* group.
The others should be recited. What is the purpose? So that the *ātmanepada* ending may occur by virtue of the rule *ṅitaḥ*.

Why is *kaṣṭāya* treated as an irregular formation (*nipātyate*)? From the word *kaṣṭa*, when it is in the dative case (*caturthīsamartha*), the suffix *ky*ṅ is irregularly formed in the sense of "striving" (*kramaṇa*) toward something that is not upright (*anārjava*). [Thus: he strives toward a difficult task; *kaṣṭāyate*. This is too little.

This is stated as "for *kaṣṭa*. [The rule] "after *sattra*, *kakṣa*, *kaṣṭa*, and *gahana*, when there is a desire to do harm" must be formulated. After *sattra*, *kakṣa*, *kaṣṭa*, and *gahana*, when there is a desire to do harm, it should be stated. Thus: *sattrāyate* (he intends to perform a sacrificial session); *sattra*. *kakaṣa*; *kakṣāyate* (he intends to enter the thicket); *kaṣṭa*.

*kaṣṭāyate*, *kaṣṭa*, *gahana*, *gahanāyate*. Another says: the suffix *kyaṅ* should be prescribed after words beginning with *sattra* when they end in the dative case, provided there is "stepping" (*kramaṇa*) in the sense of crookedness (*anārjava*). These very forms are the examples. [Question: For what purpose is the rule "after *sattra* and so forth"? [Example: *kuṭilāya anuvākāya krāmati* ("he proceeds crookedly through the lesson"). [The rule specifies] "after those ending in the dative case."

68. It is said: "romantha. What is this so-called *romantha*? *Romantha* is the chewing (*mantha*) of that which has been regurgitated or swallowed. If this is the case, it should be stated as "in the movement of the jaw" (*hanucalane*). Let it not apply here: "The insect performs *romantha*. Then it must be stated. No, it need not be stated. Why does it not occur? [Because] the insect [performs] *romantha*.
69. It should be stated that [the suffix *kyac* is applied] after *phena* as well: *phenāyate*.
(Pāṇini 3.1.17) The inclusion of *aṭā*, *aṭṭā*, *āśīkā*, *akoṭā*, *apoṭā*, *asoṭā*, *pruṣṭā*, and *pluṣṭā* must be made. *aṭā*: *aṭāyate*. *aṭṭā*: [aṭṭāyate].

*āṭṭāyate*, *śīkā*, *śīkāyate*; *koṭā*, *koṭāyate*; *poṭā*, *poṭāyate*; *soṭā*, *soṭāyate*; *pruṣṭā*, *pruṣṭāyate*; *pluṣṭā*, *pluṣṭāyate*. It should be stated: "and from *sudinā* and *durdinā*"; thus, *sudināyate*, *durdināyate*. It should be stated: "and from *nīhāra*"; thus, *nīhārāyate*.

(P_3,1.18) Regarding the phrase "in the case of the agent's feeling" (*kartṛvedanāyām*), for what purpose is it stated? It is so that [the rule] does not apply here: *prasādhakaḥ devadattasya sukhaṃ vedayate* ("The attendant causes Devadatta to feel pleasure"). Even when "in the case of the agent's feeling" is stated, [the suffix] would still apply here. What is the reason? Because this [term] *kartuḥ* ("of the agent") occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).

The genitive [case] in the phrase "in feeling" (*vedanāyām*) expresses the abstract state (*bhāve*). Whether one feels for oneself or for another, that [feeling] remains the feeling of the agent (*kartṛvedanā*). It is not the term "agent" (*kartṛ*) itself that is connected with "feeling"; rather, it is pleasure and so forth that are connected. [That is to say, it refers to] those pleasures and so forth belonging to the agent.

(P_3,1.19.1) Regarding the suffix *kyac* after the word *namas*, the occurrence of the second case is untenable. When *kyac* follows *namas*, the second case does not apply; as in *namasyati devān*. What is the reason? Because the fourth case is prescribed in connection with the word *namaḥ*. That [fourth case] would thus result. [But it does not,] because [the form *namasyati*] is a different base (*prakṛtyantara*).

Siddham. The dative case is prescribed when used in conjunction with the word *namaḥ*. And this is the word *namasyati*. But surely, the word *namaḥ* exists within the word *namasyati*; therefore, [the dative] would apply by virtue of that connection. This is not a fault, because the word *namaḥ* is understood here as having a specific meaning. Furthermore, the word *namaḥ* does not possess that specific meaning within the word *namasyati*. Alternatively, [this is explained] by means of the case of the subordinate word (*upapada-vibhakti*).

Since the case-ending denoting the agent (*kāraka-vibhakti*) is more powerful, the accusative case will apply. Regarding the suffixes *kyac* and others, there must be a specification of the meaning of the suffix; that is, a specification of the meaning of the suffixes *kyac* and others must be made.

The suffix *namas* is used in the sense of worship; *varivas* in the sense of service; *citraṅ* in the sense of wonder; *bhāṇḍa* in the sense of gathering together; *cīvara* in the sense of acquisition or wearing; and *puccha* in the sense of lifting up or casting away. What is the purpose? So that they may function as verbal expressions. This is not a necessary purpose, for the activity of the Teacher indicates [the rule].
The statement that "kyaj and the others denote action" is because [Pāṇini] teaches the technical designation of verbal root (*dhātu*) in the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*.

The purpose of this teaching of the designation "verbal root" is so that suffixes such as *tavyat* may arise according to the rule *dhātoḥ*. This would not be possible if, in these cases, there were no denotation of action.

The statement regarding the designation of verbal roots (*dhātusañjñā*) would be purposeless. Even if the designation of verbal roots were present, the suffixes *tavyat* and so forth would not occur. Why? Because the suffixes *tavyat* and others are prescribed for the sake of the "means" (*sādhana*), and the means belongs to an action (*kriyā*). Due to the absence of action, there is an absence of the means. Due to the absence of the means, even if the designation of verbal roots were present, the suffixes *tavyat* and others would not occur. [Objection: One observes [them occurring].

But the Teacher [Pāṇini], by stating that "the suffixes *kyac* and others denote action" (*kriyāvacanāḥ*), thereby teaches the technical designation "root" (*dhātu*) for those ending in *san* and so forth, according to the rule "those ending in *san* and others are roots. Now, one might argue that this purpose would be: "I shall state their production in relation to another factor of action (*sādhana*). But it should not be their production in relation to another factor of action. Why? Because the term "factor of action" (*sādhana*) is a relative term; and relative terms—

Furthermore, things of this nature imply a related entity; for example: "one should behave properly toward one's mother," and "one should serve one's father. It is not explicitly stated that [this applies] only to "one's own mother" or "one's own father," yet this is understood from the relationship itself—that she is the mother of a particular person and he is the father of a particular person. So too here, it is understood through relationship.
This is to be understood as: "that which is the means (sādhana) of whichever verbal root (dhātu) [is to be expressed]. Alternatively, the suffixes such as *kyac* are themselves verbal roots;

for their meanings are not being taught [as primary], and yet they are understood to denote action (*kriyā*). Indeed, who would even exert effort to establish that roots such as *pac* denote action? For by the very same reason that roots such as *pac* denote action, [so too do these suffixes].

The same applies to *kyac* and the others as well. For this reason, the Teacher illustrates [the matter] in such a way: in some places he indicates the meaning, and in others he does not. Even so, the indication of the meaning must be provided, so that these ignorant ones might understand. Alternatively, it is possible not to provide the indication. How so? Because the word "instrument" (*karaṇe*) is understood [from the previous rule]. And the instrument is the act of doing, which is the root *kṛ*.
And it occurs in the sense of action in general.
(Pāṇini 3.1.21) These two, *hali* and *kali*, end in the vowel *i*. There also exist the words *hala* and *kala* which end in the vowel *a*. Of which [two]?

This is the inclusion [of the roots *hal* and *kal*]. The substitution of *a* for those two which end in *i* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). What is the purpose? The prescription of the substitution of *a* for *hal* and *kal* is for the sake of prohibiting the treatment as *san*-like (*sanvadbhāva*). The substitution of *a* for *hal* and *kal* is performed so that the *sanvadbhāva* shall not occur. [Examples would be: *ajahalat*, *acakalat*. This is not a valid purpose; for once the elision of the *i* has been effected, [the rule] "for those that lose a penultimate *a*" (*aglopinām*) applies.

"No"—this will be the prohibition. Once the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) has been applied, there is elision (*lopa*). Consequently, that stem (*aṅga*) does not have an elided *a* (*aglopi*). This must be considered here: "Should the *vṛddhi* be performed, or the elision of the *a*? What should be done in this case? The *vṛddhi* [should take effect] because it is subsequent. The elision is permanent (*nitya*); for it applies whether the *vṛddhi* has been performed or not yet performed. [But if so, it would be] non-permanent (*anitya*).

[The rule for] elision applies to one [element], while the [rule for] *vṛddhi* applies to another, whether it has been performed or not. A grammatical operation that applies to a different word-form (*śabdāntara*) is considered non-permanent (*anitya*). The *vṛddhi* is also non-permanent; it applies to one [element] when the elision has been performed, and to another when it has not been performed. Since both rules are non-permanent, [the *vṛddhi* prevails] by virtue of its posteriority (*paratva*).

There is *vṛddhi*. Once *vṛddhi* has been applied, there is elision (*lopa*). Consequently, that base (*aṅga*) does not have an *aglopi* vowel (one where an *ak* vowel is elided). However, when the substitution of *at* occurs, one might think: "Let *vṛddhi* be applied first, and then let there be elision. Even if *vṛddhi* is applied because it is subsequent, once *vṛddhi* has been performed, only the *ak* vowel is elided. Therefore, it is rightly said that the specific substitution of *at* for *halika* and *kalika* is for the purpose of prohibiting the treatment as *sanvadbhāva*.

Regarding the term *samabhihāra*: what kind of word is this? It is derived from the root *hṛ* preceded by the prefixes *sam* and *abhi*, with the suffix *ghañ* used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva-sādhana*). Thus, *samabhiharaṇaṃ* is *samabhihāraḥ*. For example, as in *puṣpābhihāraḥ* (a collection of flowers) or *phalābhihāraḥ* (a collection of fruits). [Objection: This is an inappropriate comparison. For those flowers are many; therefore, a "collection" (*samabhihāra*) is appropriate in that case.

In this case, however, there is a single action. Although the general action is one, the constituent actions are many—namely, the actions of placing [the pot] on the fire, pouring water, adding rice, stirring the fuel, and so forth.

One person performs these completely, while another performs them incompletely. He who performs them completely is said to "cook thoroughly" (*pāpacyate*). Alternatively, he who cooks again and again is said to "cook repeatedly" (*pāpacyate*).

(P_3,1.22.2) KA_II,28.19–29.12 Ro_III, 75–76 Now, for what purpose is the mention of *dhātu* (verbal root)? [So that it] does not apply here in the case of *prāṭati bhṛśam*. To this, he recites the answer: "It has been stated regarding the mention of *dhātu* in the rule prescribing *yaṅ*. What was stated? First, it was stated there [in the discussion on Pāṇini 3.1.7] because of the mention of *karman* (object).

In the rule for *san*, the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) is redundant. If it is argued that [the root] with a prefix (*sopasarga*) is the object (*karman*), then because the prefix merely qualifies the object, the root without a prefix would be the object. For if that which has a prefix were the object, then even under the governing heading of "root," *san* would not be prescribed [for such a root], because it would lack the status of being an object. Similarly here as well, because of the mention of "intensive repetition of action" (*kriyāsamabhihāra*) in the rule for *yaṅ*, the mention of "root" is redundant; [the root] with a prefix [would be intended].

If it is argued that [the term] *kriyāsamabhihāra* (intensive repetition) [is intended], then because the prefix (*upasarga*) qualifies the intensive repetition of the action, the intensive repetition itself would not be a prefix. For if the intensive repetition belonged to the verb together with its prefix, then even within the governing rule for verbal roots (*dhātu*), the suffix *yaṅ* would not be prescribed, because it would not belong to the intensive repetition of the action alone.

Now, what is the purpose of specifying "a single vowel" (*ekāj*) and "beginning with a consonant" (*jhalādi*)? It is so that [the suffix] does not apply here: [Example omitted in source] ...so that it does not occur in this case.

"He wakes intensely," "He looks intensely. And regarding the inclusion of roots beginning with a single vowel followed by a *jhal* consonant: it has been stated concerning the inclusion of roots beginning with a single vowel followed by a *jhal* consonant. What was stated? First, it was stated therein that the mention of "having the same agent as the action" (*karmasamānakartṛka*) is redundant, because the suffix is prescribed when there is an expression of desire (*icchā*). For there is no expression [of the desiderative] from a root that lacks an object or from one that does not have the same agent. Here too, the inclusion of roots beginning with a single vowel followed by a *jhal* consonant is redundant.

Because of the rule prescribing *yaṅ* for the intensification of action (*kriyāsamabhihāre*), it follows that there is no designation [of the suffix] for roots with multiple vowels (*anekāc*) or those beginning with a non-consonant (*ahalādi*). And this non-designation must necessarily be accepted; for even if the mention of "single-vowel" (*ekāc*) and "beginning with a consonant" (*halādi*) were made, in cases where the meaning is not expressed by the *yaṅ* being produced after a single-vowel root beginning with a consonant, the production of the suffix does not occur.

For example: it shines intensely; it gleams intensely. Furthermore, where the meaning is expressed by a *yaṅ* suffix arising after a root with more than one vowel (*anekāc*) that does not begin with *ha*, there the suffix arises. For example: *aṭāṭyate*, *arāryate*, *aśāśyate*, *sosūcyate*, *sosūtryate*, *momūtryate*.
(Regarding *ūrṇoti*): An addition must be made for the root *ūrṇu*. An addition must be made for the root *ūrṇu*, as in *prorṇonūyate*. This which is stated—"for *ūrṇu*"—is too limited.

[The rule] "the mention of *sūci*, *sūtri*, *mūtri*, *aṭi*, *arti*, *aśi*, *ūrṇu* [is required] in the prescription of *yaṅ* for the sake of roots with multiple vowels and those beginning with a consonant."

The inclusion of the roots *sūci*, *sūtri*, *mūtri*, *aṭi*, *arti*, *aśi*, and *ūrṇoti* must be made. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of [applying the rules] regarding the *yaṅ* suffix when the root has more than one vowel (*anekāc*) or begins with a consonant (*ahal-ādi*). Examples: *sosūcyate*, *sosūtryate*, *momūtryate*, *aṭāṭyate*, *arāryate*, *aśāśyate*, *prorṇonūyate*. It should be stated that *ūrṇu* undergoes the substitution of *ṇuvat*; the purpose is the successful formation of the *yaṅ* forms. Furthermore, it is for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of the rule] to the form ending in *ām*.

And [the suffix] *yaṅ* follows a monosyllabic root that takes the augment *iṭ*. (Pāṇini 3.1.22) Regarding the intensive (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), the prescription of the imperative (*loṭ*) takes precedence by way of an exception over *yaṅ*. In the sense of the intensive, the imperative occurs.

Furthermore, by way of prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*): the scope of the rule "the *yaṅ* affix occurs in the sense of frequent repetition of an action" (*kriyāsamabhihāre yaṅ bhavati*) is when a root consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*), begins with a consonant (*halādi*), denotes frequent repetition of an action, and is not connected to another verb; for example, *lolūyate*. The scope of the *loṭ* affix is when a root consists of more than one vowel (*anekāc*), does not begin with a consonant (*ahalādi*), denotes frequent repetition of an action, and is connected to another verb.

Thinking "May you wake up, wake up," he indeed wakes up; thinking "May you exert yourself, exert yourself," he indeed exerts himself. When there is a root that consists of a single vowel, begins with a consonant, and denotes the repetition of an action (kriyāsamabhihāra), and when there is a connection between roots (dhātusambandha), both [the suffixes *yaṅ* and *loṭ*] would apply.

He [the agent] says, "Sir, cut! Cut! and thus he cuts; here the *loṭ* (imperative) suffix occurs by way of prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*). But then this would not occur now: "Sir, cut repeatedly (*lolūyasva*)! Cut repeatedly! and yet it does occur. Or rather, it is not so, because of the difference in meaning.

For the rule for *yaṅ* is prescribed after verbal roots when there is an agent or an object, and it expresses its own meaning with reference to a specific action. Or rather, there is no need for a prohibition.

What is the reason? Because there are multiple meanings. What is this multiplicity of meaning? For the suffix *la* is prescribed for both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*). Indeed, the imperative (*loṭ*) is prescribed for both the agent and the object. Furthermore, the intensive suffix *yaṅ* occurs in its own sense when there is a specification of action. In that case, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), the *yaṅ* ought to occur first. If that is so, then this [example] would not now be possible: "May you cut, may you cut!"—in which case he cuts thus. But it does occur.
And: *vibhāṣā yaṅ*. When there is no *yaṅ*, then there is *loṭ*.

Regarding the two subsequent [rules], since no specific distinction is understood through the analysis (*vigraha*), the mention of "always" (*nitya*) is redundant. This refers to the two subsequent rules (*yoga*).

Because no specific meaning is understood from the verbal base alone, the inclusion of the word "eternal" (nitya) would be purposeless; for it is not understood that one who "walks crookedly" (*kuṭilaṃ krāmati*) is "wandering about" (*caṅkramyate*). Now, the suffix *yaṅ* ought to occur after these [roots] to express the intensification of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*).

However, *yaṅ* does not occur after these [roots] even in the case of the intensification of an action; *yaṅ* ought not to occur after these [roots] even in the case of the intensification of an action. [Example: He mutters intensely (*bhṛśaṃ japati*).
The Brahmin burns the fuel intensely; such is the meaning.

(Pāṇini 3.1.25) What is the irregularly formed word *satyāp*? It is derived from *satya* with the root *kṛ*, and the suffix *āpuk* is applied. Thus, *āpuk* is irregularly applied after *satya* when combined with the root *kṛ*.

And [the suffix] *ṇic* [is added]. One makes true: *satyāpayati*. This which is stated is too little. It should be stated: "After the words *artha*, *veda*, and *satya*, when followed by *ṇic* or *vid*, there is the augment *apuk*. Thus: *arthāpayati*, *vedāpayati*, *satyāpayati*. If *āpuk* were applied, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) would result. In that case, then, *puk* will be applied. Thus...

But then, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) would result. In that case, we shall employ *āk*. Even so, the elision of the *ṭi* still results. In that case, we shall employ *ak*. Even so, because it does not end in *ā*, the augment *puK* would not apply. In that case, we shall employ *apuṭ*. Or rather, let there simply be *āpuk*. But was it not said: "The elision of the *ṭi* results"? [No,] because of the force of the explicit mention of *āpuk*.

It will not occur. Or rather, let there be *puk* alone. But has it not been stated that even so, the elision of the *ṭi* suffix would still apply? It will not occur by virtue of the expressive power (*sāmarthya*) of the mention of *puk*. Or rather, let there be *āk* alone. But has it not been stated that even so, the elision of the *ṭi* suffix would still apply? It will not occur by virtue of the expressive power of the mention of *āk*.

(P_3,1.26.1) KA_II,31.7–32.26 Ro_III, 80–86 How is this to be understood? Is it that the causative suffix *ṇic* occurs when the causal agent (*hetumat*) is to be expressed, or rather that it occurs when the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself functions in a causal sense? It is indeed appropriate to investigate this; for surely, by means of this [rule], there would be no doubt.

The term must be a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), since it is stated as "in the sense of that which possesses a cause" (*hetumati*). For if it were a qualifier of the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), one would have said "of that which possesses a cause" (*hetumataḥ*). This is not the case; for here there are also locative cases of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*).
For example: "the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which occurs in the sense of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇe*)," or "the nominal stem which occurs in the feminine."

Thus, here too, when the meaning is "caused by an instigator" (*hetumat*), the question arises: "Does the *ṇic* suffix apply to whatever verbal root occurs in the sense of being caused? To this, he recites the following reply: The mention of "the instigator" (*hetumat*) as a factor (*kāraka*) is for the purpose of including the meaning of the suffix;

just as in the case of the root *takṣ*, which [is used] in the sense of thinning. The term "instigator" is taken as a factor. What is the purpose? It is for the purpose of including the meaning of the suffix.

This being the case, the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is well-grasped. Just as in the expression "a carpenter (*takṣan*) in the act of thinning," the act of thinning is taken as the basis; if, in that same way, it serves as a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), then indeed it is understood there as a qualifier of the meaning of the base. That is to say, "a carpenter" [is defined] in relation to the action of thinning. Let it be a qualifier of the meaning of the base.

What is the fault? For here, since it is said "he causes [someone] to act" or "being sent, he acts," the causative suffix (*ṇic*) would apply. However, when the meaning of the suffix is qualified [by the object], this fault does not arise; because the meaning has already been expressed by its own word (*svaśabda*), the suffix will not occur. Even when the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is qualified, this fault does not arise; for where the comprehension of the meaning cannot occur without a word, there the word [is employed].
[A word] is employed [only where necessary]. For indeed, where the meaning is understood even without a word, a word is not employed there.

But then, in this case—"Devadatta causes Yajñadatta to cook the rice"—it would follow that the *ṇic* suffix denotes both agents. However, when the agent is used as a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), there is no fault; [the suffix denotes] the principal agent.

Since the *l*-class suffixes occur [in this context], the primary agent (*pradhānakartṛ*) is expressed by the *l* suffix. As for that which is non-primary (*apradhāna*), since it is established as the agent (*kartṛ*) there, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) applies by the rule "the agent" (*kartari*). Now, in the example "Devadatta was made to go to the village by Yajñadatta," because the sense of motion (*gatyartha*) is not distinct [from the causative], the suffix *kta* would result in the sense of the agent according to the rule "for roots meaning motion" (*gatyarthānāṃ kartari*). And here [in the following example], they mutually pierce one another (*vyatibhedayante*).

Since the meaning of "vyaticchedayante" (they cut across) is not distinct from the meaning of "hiṃsā" (injury), the prohibition "na gatihiṃsārthebhyaḥ" (there is no [application of the *ṇic* suffix] after roots meaning motion or injury) would apply. Let it then be a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārthaviśeṣaṇam*). If it is a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix, then in the case of "pācayati odanaṃ devadatto yajñadattena" (Devadatta causes Yajñadatta to cook rice), the designation of "object" (*karmasañjñā*) would apply to the instigator (*prayojya*) who is the agent (*kartṛ*).

For in that case, there is indeed a desire for that [object]. And here, in the examples *grāmam gamayati* ("he causes to go to the village") and *grāmāya gamayati*, since the meaning of "going" (*gatyartha*) is considered distinct [from the causative], the second and fourth cases would not apply to the object of a verb meaning "to go. Furthermore, in the example *edhodakasya upaskārayati* ("he prepares fuel and water"), since the meaning of "doing" (*karotyartha*) is considered distinct, the sixth case would not apply by the rule *kṛñaḥ pratiyatne* ("the sixth case after the root *kṛ* when there is a preparatory effort").

In this case, [the rule] does not apply. Furthermore, in the expression *bhedikā devadattasya yajñadattasya kāṣṭhānām* ("the splitter of the wood belonging to Devadatta and Yajñadatta"), the genitive case would not apply to the agent (*kartṛ*) of the prompted action (*prayojya*). Moreover, in the expressions *abhiṣāvayati* and *pariṣāvayati*, since the meaning of the root *su* (to press) is considered distinct [from the meaning of the prefix], the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] by the rule *upasargāt sunotyādīnām* would not apply. This is not a fault. As for that which...

It is said: in the case of "Devadatta causes Yajñadatta to cook the rice," the designation *karman* (object) would apply to the agent (*kartṛ*) who is the one being prompted (*prayojya*). [To this we reply: the rule "of those roots meaning motion, cognition, eating, having sound as their object, or being intransitive, when followed by a suffix other than *ṇic*" will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). It will mean that only for these roots, when they are not followed by *ṇic*, the one who is the agent becomes designated as the *karman* when *ṇic* is added, and not for others. As for...

Furthermore, it is said here that in the cases "he causes him to go to the village" (*grāmaṃ gamayati*) and "he causes him to go for the sake of the village" (*grāmāya gamayati*), since the action of going is considered distinct [from the causative], the second and fourth case endings do not apply to the object of the action of going. This is because he is not commanded in this way:
"Go to the village. How then? He is commanded to perform the action qualified by its means (*sādhana*). [The object is] the village.

"Go," "go to the village"—even regarding what is said here, namely that in the expression *edhodakasyopaskurute* ("he prepares fuel and water"), since the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do/make) is distinct [from the sense of "preparing"], the genitive case prescribed by the rule *kṛñaḥ pratiyatne* does not apply. But it is not the case that he is commanded in this way: "Prepare the fuel and water. How then? [He is commanded] with respect to the object qualified by the instrument (*sādhanaviśiṣṭām*).

This [agent] is prompted toward an action, as in: "Prepare fuel and water. Furthermore, regarding what was said—that in the example "the splitting of Devadatta's and Yajñadatta's wood," the genitive case would not apply to the agent who is the object of the prompting—it has been stated that the purpose of including the term *kṛt* [in the rule] is so that the genitive may occur even when the agent is merely one who was previously an agent (*kartṛbhūtapūrvamātra*).

Thus it is said: "And since one says here 'he presses out' (*abhiṣāvayati*) and 'he presses around' (*pariṣāvayati*), the meaning of the root *su* is distinct [from the prefixes]; therefore, by the rule 'after a prefix, in the case of *su* and so on,' the substitution of *ṣ* does not apply. This is not so; for he is not commanded thus: "Press out, [you who are] facing toward" (*sunv abhi*). How then? He is commanded to perform the action as qualified by the prefix.

It is sent forth; [he] presses. However, it is appropriate to investigate this further. Is it not the case that there ought to be an unambiguous qualification of the meaning of the suffix, since a distinct meaning is clearly understood from both *pacati* ("he cooks") and *pācayati* ("he causes to cook")? Certainly, it is appropriate. Here, what is the primary meaning of the root *pac*? It is that which is the softening (*viklitti*) of the rice grains.

Now, if at present the sending or the requesting were preceded by that intention (*abhisandhi*), it would be logical for everything to be the meaning of the root *paci*. Furthermore, the mention of a cause (*hetu*) is merely an occasion (*nimitta-mātra*), as seen in the case of *bhikṣā* and so forth; indeed, the mention of a cause is merely an occasion.
It should be observed that as far as one might say "sign" (*nimitta*) or "cause" (*kāraṇa*), so far [does] "reason" (*hetu*) [extend]. What is the purpose [of this definition]?

Because it is seen in the case of *bhikṣā* and so forth. For the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is observed in cases such as *bhikṣāḥ vāsayanti* ("the alms cause [him] to dwell") and *kāriṣo 'gniḥ adhyāpayati* ("the fire causes [the child] to study"). But what is the reason that it is not established in the case of a technical (*pāribhāṣika*) "reason"? He thinks thus:
This [act of] sending or requesting belongs to one who possesses volition (*cetanā*). And alms-food (*bhikṣā*) is insentient.
This is not a fault. It is not necessarily the case that only he who says "stay" causes the residence;
even one who remains silent but performs actions conducive to it causes the residence. Furthermore, the alms-food is abundant and accompanied by various condiments.
When they are obtained, they serve as the occasion for residing. Likewise, a fire of dried cow-dung, when well-kindled in a secluded place free from wind,
serves as the occasion for Vedic study.
88–89. Here, someone says to another: "May your honor question me; may your honor interrogate me.

Why is the causative suffix (*ṇic*) not applied here? Because there is no agency (*akartṛtva*). For he is not questioning at this very moment; he remains silent. Furthermore, O sir, must there necessarily be an agent only for an action in the present tense, and not for one in the past or future?
Even for [actions belonging to] past and future times, there must be something that "is to be" (*bhavitavyam*). In those cases, a connection is made such as:
"He performed this action," or "He will perform this action. But here, however, no such connection is made, nor does he ask at present; he remains silent. If, then, there is no agent, how is it so?
The imperative (*loṭ*) denotes the agent (*kartṛ*). Now, how is it that when this [agent] asks, this verb *pracchi* (to ask) occurs?

In that case, a connection is made there: "Perform this action. But then, a connection is also made by means of the agent: "And you, be the agent of this action. Thus, the agent is not [denoted] by the verbal suffix (*kartṛpratyaya*).

And it is expressed by the imperative (*loṭ*). Even if, somehow, there were an agent [of the action denoted by the root], even so there would be no fault; because the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) has already been expressed by the imperative, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) will not occur. For the imperative and other such suffixes are prescribed for these meanings, such as instigation (*praiṣa*) and so forth.
And where there is a second object to be impelled (*prayojya*), there the causative suffix occurs, as in "make him sit" (*āsaya*) or "make him lie down" (*śāyaya*).

And there would be the non-arising [of the result] in the case of ploughing and so forth. It must be stated that there is no production of results in the case of ploughing and such activities. For instance, one who is sitting silently in a secluded place is said to be "ploughing with five ploughs. In that case, [the action] ought to exist; [yet it is said] "with five ploughs."

"It draws forth" (*karṣayati*). Furthermore, there is no [separate] production of various actions in the case of "plowing" (*kṛṣi*) and so on, because those various actions have plowing as their purpose. Thus, it is established that there is no separate production of various actions in the case of plowing and so on. Why? Because the various actions have plowing as their purpose; the various actions are the purposes of plowing. Plowing does not necessarily consist only of the act of scratching the soil (*vilekhana*); rather, it also consists of the act of preparing the ground (*pratividhāna*).
That which he performs by means of servants, seeds, and oxen is for the purpose of agriculture; thus, it exists within the context of preparation (*pratividhāna*).

On the very day that he does not prepare, on that day that ritual action does not proceed. Furthermore, there is no reversal in the case of sacrifices and the like. It must be stated that there is no reversal in sacrifices and the like: "Puṣyamitra sacrifices," [and] "the officiating priests."

"They cause [him] to sacrifice" (*yājayanti*). In that case, it must be so: "Puṣyamitra causes [the priests] to sacrifice" (*puṣyamitraḥ yājayate*), while "the sacrificers sacrifice" (*yājakāḥ yajanti*).

Furthermore, there is no reversal of roles regarding the act of sacrificing and so forth, because various actions have the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) as their purpose. Thus, the absence of reversal regarding the act of sacrificing and so forth is established.
Why? Because various actions have the root *yaj* as their purpose; various actions are the meanings of *yaj*. It is not necessarily [the case that] *yaj* itself [is the action].

It refers only to the act of throwing the oblation [into the fire]. What then? It also refers to the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*). Indeed, one who performs a perfect relinquishment is said to "sacrifice" (*yajate*).
And Puṣyamitra performs that [relinquishment]; the officiating priests (*yājaka*) cause it to be performed.

91–92. The addition *tat karoti* ("he makes that") should be stated for the sake of [derivatives] such as *sūtrayati*. The addition *tat karoti* must be formulated. What is the purpose? For the sake of [derivatives] such as *sūtrayati*. [Examples: *sūtram karoti* (he makes a sūtra) becomes *sūtrayati* (he composes a sūtra).
Here, in the case of *vyākaraṇasya sūtram karoti*, it becomes *vyākaraṇam sūtrayati* (he composes a sūtra of grammar). When the suffix has been produced, the genitive case occurs in the sentence.

The second [case ending]. By what means does this occur? That connection (*abhisambandha*) between the *sūtra* and the *vyākaraṇa* which exists ceases once the suffix has been produced. However, since the root *kṛ* possesses a functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) with respect to the *vyākaraṇa*, the second case ending will indeed occur.

92–97. *Ākhyānāt kṛtaḥ*: "From a *kṛt*-derived word denoting a narrative, in the sense of 'he tells that,' there is elision of the *kṛt* suffix, restoration of the original form (*prakṛti-pratyāpatti*), and the grammatical relation (*kāraka*) remains as it was in the original. It should be stated: when the sense is "he tells that" from a *kṛt*-derived word denoting a narrative, there is elision of the *kṛt* suffix, restoration of the original form, and the grammatical relation remains as it was in the original. Example: *kaṃsavadham ācaṣṭe* ("He tells the slaying of Kaṃsa") becomes *kaṃsaṃ ghātayati* ("He causes Kaṃsa to be slain"). *Balibandham* ("The binding of Bali").

"One relates" (*ācaṣṭe*) means "he causes [someone] to compose" (*bandhayati*). And there is a prohibition based on the word *ākhyāna*. A prohibition must also be stated based on the word *ākhyāna*: "he relates a narrative" (*ākhyānam ācaṣṭe*). Now, should the suffix arise from those narratives which have become technical names (*saṃjñā*), or rather from the mere narration of an action? What follows from this? If [the suffix arises] from those that have become technical names...

In this case, it does not apply: one says "he announces the king's arrival" (*rājāgamanaṃ ācaṣṭe*) or "he causes the king to arrive" (*rājānam āgamayati*). Now, if there is no fault simply because of the mere verbal expression of the action, let it be so that there is no fault. And regarding the occurrence of roots meaning "to see": when roots meaning "to see" occur, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) should be stated after a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix in the sense of "he tells that [someone]"; in this sense, there is the elision of the *kṛt* suffix and the restoration of the original form (*prakṛti-pratyāpatti*).

And a *kāraka* (participant in an action) remains as it was by its original nature (*prakṛti*). For example: "He describes the deer's sporting" becomes "he causes the deer to sport" (*mṛgān ramayati*). Why is the rule "of roots meaning 'to see'" (*dṛśyarthānām*) stated? Because when one says, "He describes the deer's sporting in the village," the form remains simply "he describes the deer's sporting" (*mṛgaramaṇam ācaṣṭe*). Furthermore, there is the elision of the prefix *āṅ* when expressing a limit (*maryādā*) involving an absolute connection with time (*kālātyantasaṃyoga*). [This applies] when there is an absolute connection with time and a limit.

The suffix *ṇic* should be stated after a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix in the sense of "he describes that"; furthermore, there is the elision of the prefix *āṅ*, the elision of the *kṛt* suffix, the restoration of the original form of the base, and the grammatical relation (*kāraka*) remains as it was in the original base. Thus, from *ārātrivivāsa* (one who causes the night to pass), in the sense of "he describes him as causing the night to pass," one says *rātriṃ vivāsayati*. This should also be stated when the meaning is "to cause wonder" (*citrīkaraṇa*). When the meaning is "to cause wonder," the suffix *ṇic* should be stated after a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, with the elision of the *kṛt* suffix and the restoration of the original form of the base.

And the *kāraka* remains as it was in the base form (*prakṛti*). One who has set out from Ujjayinī and expects the rising of the sun at Māhiṣmatī is said to "cause the sun to rise" (*sūryam udgamayati*). Regarding the connection with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatrayoga*): when the sense of "knowing" (*jñā*) follows a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix denoting the connection with a lunar mansion, a causative suffix (*ṇic*) should be stated; there is the elision of the *kṛt* suffix (*kṛt-luk*), the restoration of the base form (*prakṛti-pratyāpatti*), and the *kāraka* remains as it was in the base form. [Example: *puṣyayogam*.

[One] knows [it]; [one] joins it with Puṣya; [one] joins it with Maghās. In that case, much would have to be said. Or rather, it need not be stated, because it is established by the general rule. For it is not distinct from the cause. Or rather, it need not be stated. What is the reason? Because it is established by the general rule. Here the causative suffix (*ṇic*) will apply by the general rule itself, namely, "when there is a motive" (*hetumati*). What is the reason? For it is not distinct from the cause. From the cause.

For [the status] would be undifferentiated; for the causality is indeed equal in the case of Devadatta and the sun. It is not established [that the sun is the cause]. It is stated that "one who is an independent instigator receives the designation 'cause' (hetu)," yet he (Devadatta) does not instigate the sun. If it is argued that [the sun] is not an instigator because it is an independent instigator, then this is equivalent to the case of one whose agency is beyond doubt. That which you consider to be an independent instigator whose agency is beyond doubt—

It is considered logical that one says, "Devadatta causes Yajñadatta to cook the rice"; this is similar to that [case]. How so? For in both instances, activity occurs independently. Indeed, activity occurs entirely without dependence on anything else, whether in the case of Devadatta or the sun. Here, no one acts with the thought, "I must favor another."

All these proceed for the sake of their own welfare. Those who are intent on serving their teacher also proceed solely for the sake of their own welfare, thinking: "There will be benefit for us in the next world, and here our teacher, being pleased, will teach us.
Likewise, those known as slaves and laborers also proceed solely for the sake of their own welfare, [thinking]: "We shall receive food..."

"We shall obtain clothing and there will be no reproaches against us. Likewise, those who are craftsmen also act solely for their own benefit, thinking, "We shall receive wages and we shall gain friends.
Thus, while all these are acting for their own benefit, if it is argued that the instigator is the one who acts [on behalf of another], [the response follows].

It is the same. If someone is called an "instigator" (*prayojaka*) of one who acts, it is the same as this. If, then, all these beings proceed for the sake of their own well-being, what is the purpose of the "one to be instigated"? It is that in which they become attached to the intentions [of others], such as:
"Make the two oxen like this," or "Make them skillful. And the sun also becomes attached to his intention.
This is his intention: having set out from Ujjayinī, he might expect the rising of the sun at Māhiṣmatī.
And the Sun fulfills this intention of his. In this case, the use of the present tense would be appropriate:
"Having set out from Ujjayinī, he expects the rising of the sun at Māhiṣmatī; he causes the sun to rise."

Thus [it is said]. For him who is situated there, the sun rises; but here, how can there be a present tense in such cases as "he causes Kaṃsa to be killed" (*kaṃsaṃ ghātayati*) or "he causes Bali to be bound" (*baliṃ bandhayati*), when Kaṃsa was killed long ago and Bali was bound long ago? This too is logical. How so? First, those who are called "spectators" (*śobhikāḥ*) actually kill Kaṃsa before their very eyes and [bind Bali] before their very eyes.
"And they perform the *bali* offering. How so in the case of paintings? For even in paintings, blows are seen—both those raised and those fallen—as well as the dragging of Kaṃsa.
How so in the case of knotted texts (*granthika*) where only a mere mass of words is perceived?
For they too, explaining their supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) from their origin until their destruction, [describe] things that are objects of the intellect.
They reveal this. Furthermore, existing things are indeed seen to be mixed:

some are devotees of Kaṃsa, while others are devotees of Vāsudeva. Indeed, they even exhibit a difference in color: some have red faces, while others have black faces. Moreover, the three times are observed in the world: "Go, Kaṃsa is being killed."

"Go! Kaṃsa will be slain. [Question: "What is the point of going? Kaṃsa has already been slain. (Pāṇini 3.1.27) [Question: What is the purpose of the letter *k*? [Answer: So that there may be the prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule *kṅiti*. [Objection: This is not a necessary purpose.

It is stated that *guṇa* substitution occurs for the *aṅga* [stem] before both *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes. Furthermore, a suffix prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*) receives the technical designation *ārdhadhātuka*. However, this [suffix in question] is not prescribed after a verbal root. For *kaṇḍū* and the others are nominal stems (*prātipadika*). [Objection: There should be an option regarding the suffixes after *kaṇḍū* and the others. That is to say, it should be stated: "after *kaṇḍū* and the others, [the suffix is] optional. For if it were not so stated, the suffix would be obligatory.

For if the word *vā* (optionally) were not employed, the rule for affixes would necessarily apply [universally]. What fault would there be in that? In that case, there would be a prohibition regarding the designation of "root" (*dhātu*) and the augment *tuk*. There, a prohibition of both the designation of "root" and the augment *tuk* would have to be stated.

[Otherwise, in the forms] *kaṇḍvau* and *kaṇḍvaḥ*, the substitution of *uvaṅ*—by the rule "in place of *y* and *v* of *aci*, *śnu*, roots, and *bhrū*, there are *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*"—would undesirably apply.
And here, in the case of *kaṇḍū* and *kaṇḍve*, the prohibition [of *ūṅ*] by the rule *ūṅ dhātvoḥ* would apply; furthermore, the *tuk* augment would also have to be prohibited.

In the case of *valguḥ* and *mantuḥ*, the *tuk* augment would apply before a *kṛt* suffix beginning with a *pit* vowel. Moreover, the shortening of the vowel (*hrasva*) and the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) must be stated;
indeed, both the shortening of the vowel and the elision of *y* would have to be stated in the case of *valguḥ* and *mantuḥ*. Why is this so? Is it not already a short vowel (*hrasva*)?

Thus, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), this [suffix] would undergo lengthening by the rule *akṛd-yakāre* (Pāṇini 6.4.149). [Objection: There must also be the elision of *y* (*yalopa*). [Examples: *kaṇḍūḥ*, *valguḥ*, *mantuḥ*. [Question: For what purpose is this? Is it not already established by the rule *na vali* (Pāṇini 6.1.66)? [Reply: It is stated as *vali*. And we do not see a *val* [augment] here. [Objection: But isn't the *kvip* suffix *valādi*? [Reply: Once the elision of *kvip* has occurred, there is an absence of *valādi*.

[The rule for *yaṇ*] does not apply. This must be considered here: should the elision of *kvip* be performed, or the elision of the *val* sounds? What should be done in this case? The elision of *kvip* [should take place], because it is subsequent. Furthermore, the elision of *kvip* is indeed obligatory; it applies whether the elision of *ya* has already occurred or has not yet occurred. Because it is both obligatory and subsequent, once the elision of *kvip* has taken place, [the rule for *yaṇ*] does not apply due to the absence of a *val*-initial suffix.
If that is so, then it will be by means of the characteristic of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). [But] there is no characteristic of the suffix with respect to the phonemes (*varṇa*).
Now, even if the option (*vāvacana*) were applied, why would these faults not occur when *kvip* follows a stem ending in *yaṅ*?
They would not occur because *kvip* is not seen after those [stems]. What is the reason? It is stated that [the suffix *kvip*] is seen after other stems as well.

And yet, at that time, the *kvip* suffix is not observed after these [roots]. If it is argued that just as when the option (*vāvacana*) is applied, the suffix is seen after other roots as well, so here too *kvip* does not occur; even so, when the option is not applied, it will likewise not occur. Therefore, the *kvip* suffix must necessarily be desired after these [roots] at that time. What is the purpose? So that these forms may be produced. That...
In that case, should the word *vā* (or) be stated? It need not be stated. Both [categories]—the *kaṇḍvādi* group and the verbal roots—are both verbal roots and nominal stems (*prātipadika*).
And for this reason, there are both: the form *kaṇḍūyati* is employed when one is performing an action, while [the form] *asti me kaṇḍūḥ* is used in the presence of mere sensation. Another says:

Because it belongs to the section on verbal roots (*dhātu-prakaraṇāt*), the term *dhātu* [is understood here] even by way of association with something else. And he says: "This long vowel [in *dīrgha*]—I consider this verbal root to be optionally specified (*vibhāṣita*).

(Pāṇini 3.1.30) For what purpose is this letter *ṇ*? It is for the sake of *vṛddhi*. So that *vṛddhi* may occur according to the rule "before an affix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*" (*ñṇiti*). [The *ṇ*] is employed...

Indeed, the *vṛddhi* substitution does not apply even when the suffix *ṇak* is present. What is the reason? Because of the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 1.1.5]: "And [there is no *vṛddhi*] before *ki*t and *ṅi*t. [Objection: It will occur by virtue of the functional force (*sāmarthya*) of the inclusion of the marker *ṇ*. To this, he recites the following reply: "Since the inclusion of the marker *ṇ* in *ṇiṅ* has its own scope, there arises the contingency of the prohibition of *vṛddhi*. The inclusion of the marker *ṇ* in *ṇiṅ* has its own scope. What is that scope? The letter *ṇ* is for the purpose of including the general term. Where is it used for the purpose of including the general term?"

The meaning [of the rule] is: "after a suffix marked with *ṇ*, [the penultimate vowel takes *guṇa*] except before an affix marked with *ṅ*. Since the addition of the marker *ṇ* has its own scope of application, a prohibition of *vṛddhi* would follow. But then the addition of the marker *ṅ* also has its own scope. What is that scope? The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of not obstructing the general reference [to the suffix]. Where is there a need for it to serve as a non-obstruction to the general reference? Precisely here. It is possible for it to serve as a non-obstruction to the general reference in this very case.

There is another *anubandha* [the letter Ṅ] attached [to the root]. In that case, due to the requirement of the letter Ṅ, a prohibition of *vṛddhi* would apply. Therefore, the letter Ṅ must necessarily be attached as an *anubandha* for the sake of the *ātmanepada* endings, so that the *ātmanepada* may occur by the rule "after a root marked with Ṅ" (*ṅitaḥ*). Thus, since both [the rules for *vṛddhi* and the prohibition] have their own scope of application, the prohibition prevails by virtue of its greater strength. If this is so, then...

The activity of the Teacher indicates that there is no prohibition of *vṛddhi* for the root *kam*, since he teaches the prohibition of the designation *mit* by stating "not for *kam*, *yam*, and *cam*. And because the prohibition of *mit* is purposeful, the prohibition [of *vṛddhi*] would otherwise apply. The prohibition of *mit* is indeed purposeful. What is its purpose? It is for the sake of the root ending in *ṇiṅ*.

[The objection: "Let there not be shortening of that *vṛddhi* which occurs in the causative (*ṇic*). [The response: But surely this too must be subject to the prohibition by the rule *kṅiti ca*. [The objection: It need not be so. For it has been stated that in the prohibition concerning *kṅit* suffixes, the term "caused by that" (*tannimitta*) must be understood. [The response: In that case, the shortening would not apply to the *vṛddhi* that occurs in the causative of a root ending in *ṇiṅ*. What is the reason?

Because of the intervention of the *ṇiṅ* [suffix]. When the [suffix] is elided, there is no intervention. But because of the status of being "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is indeed intervention.

[Objection: Then let it not apply when there is *ṇiṅ*. [Response: It does not apply even when there is *ṇiṅ*. What is the reason? Because that which is characterized by being external (*bahiraṅga*) is unestablished with respect to that which is characterized by being internal (*antaraṅga*). Or rather, the *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution] does not at all apply to the *ṇic* [derivative] of that which ends in *ṇiṅ*. What is the reason?

Because of the intervention by *ṇiṅ*, [the rule] does not apply. When the elision (*lopa*) has been performed, there is no intervention; yet due to the status of being "as if in the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is indeed an intervention.

In that case, this is the purpose: so that the lengthening (*dīrgha*) prescribed by the rule "there is optionally lengthening for *ciṇ* and *ṇamul*" should not occur for the root *kam* when *ṇiṅ* follows. But what is the reason that "optionally lengthening" is stated in that rule?

One could simply say "na hrasvo 'nyatarasyām" (or "it is not short, optionally"). And since the shortening of the root *kram* is already established by rule, there is this further purpose: the mention of "short" (*hrasva*) need not be made. The previously mentioned [rule] continues to apply. Where was it previously mentioned? In the rule "mitāṃ hrasvaḥ" (the short vowel for roots ending in a marker *m*). What is the resulting form?

*aśami*, *aśāmi*, *śamam*, *śamam*, *śāmam*, *śāmam*. [The form] is established by means of *vṛddhi* [substitution]. It is not established; it is not established. Because of the rule "there is no *vṛddhi* for a root taught with an udātta vowel that ends in *m*, except for *ācam*" (*na udāttopadeśasya māntasyānācameḥ*), the prohibition of *vṛddhi* would apply. That prohibition applies to the *ciṇ* and *kṛt* suffixes, but not to the *ṇic* suffix. In that case, consider this: *ajani*, *ajāni*, *janam*, *janam*, *jānam*, *jānam*. [This concerns the roots] *jan* and *vadh*.

And thus, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* would apply. That [prohibition] also applies only to the cases of *ciṇ* and *kṛt* suffixes. In that case, an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for those instances where the causative suffix (*ṇic*) intervenes and for the elision of *yaṅ*: *aśami*, *aśāmi*, *śamam*, *śamam*, *śāmam*, *śāmam*;
and from *śaṃśamayati*: *aśaṃśami*, *aśaṃśāmi*, *śaṃśamam*, *śaṃśamam*, *śaṃśāmam*, *śaṃśāmam*.

What, then, is the reason it is not established? It is stated that "when a causative suffix (ṇi) follows a *ciṇ* or a *ṇamul* suffix, there is shortening of the vowels of bases (*aṅga*) ending in *mit*. However, the causative suffix (*ṇi*) here which follows a *ciṇ* or *ṇamul* suffix does not have a base (*aṅga*) ending in *mit*; and the base (*aṅga*) which ends in *mit* does not have that causative suffix (*ṇi*) followed by a *ṇamul*. Once the elision (*lopa*) of the *ṇi* has been performed, although it [the base] would follow a *ciṇ* or *ṇamul* suffix by virtue of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), it is not [actually] followed by a *ciṇ* or *ṇamul* suffix.

Now, if it were stated simply as *dīrgho 'nyatarasyām* ("the long vowel optionally"), since the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) would apply, how would this be established? This is precisely the purpose of the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*). By stating that a substitute for a short vowel (*aj-ādeśa*) is not like its original with respect to a rule concerning a long vowel, the prohibition of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāvapratiṣedha*) becomes established. Furthermore, when the affixes *āya*, etc., [are applied] in the domain of the *ārdhadhātuka*...

104–107. How is this to be understood? Does it mean that when an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix follows [a root] such as *āya*, there is the optional cessation (*nivṛtti*) of those *āya*-suffixes; or rather, that when an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix follows the base (*prakṛti*) to which *āya* etc.
were originally applied, there is the optional production (*utpatti*) of those *āya*-suffixes? Is this established by this much of a rule, or is it [established] in one way or another?

In this alternative view, the sūtra must be formulated again. He says: "It is understood. How so? First, when the *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes beginning with *yat* are present, the cessation (*nivṛtti*) of the *āy*-class suffixes occurs; at that time, having proceeded through the entire section on the *āy*-class suffixes without distinction, it is stated: "The *āy*-class suffixes are optional before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. Furthermore, when [the rule applies] to the base (*prakṛti*) of the *āy*-class suffixes...
When that *ārdhadhātuka* suffix is present, the occurrence of *āya* and the others takes place; thus, there are two statements: this one and the following:

"After the roots *gup*, *dhūp*, *vicch*, *paṇ*, and *pani*, *āya* is optionally applied before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix"; "After the root *ṛt*, *īyaṅ* is optionally applied before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix";

and "After the root *kam*, *ṇiṅ* is optionally applied before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. What, then, is the distinction here? [The distinction is] that the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix follows after *āya* and the others.

There is the undesirable consequence [of the rule] "yat after āya and so forth" applying in two ways: namely, both as "the *ārdhadhātuka* affix *yat* after āya and so forth" and "the *ārdhadhātuka* affix *yat* after the base that begins with āya. In both cases, an undesired result follows.
If it is understood that when the *ārdhadhātuka* affix *yat* follows āya and so forth, there is either the persistence of those [affixes] or the disappearance of āya and so forth.

If [the rule] were "it becomes" (*bhavati*), then the desired forms *jugopa* ("he protected") and *gopā* ("protector") would not be established, and this undesirable consequence would follow: *gopām cakāra* ("he made a protector") and *gopāḥ*. However, the following desired forms are established: *gopāyām cakāra* ("he caused to protect") and *gopāya* ("for the sake of protecting"). Now, it is understood that when an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix follows a base such as *āya*, the derivation of *āya* and the other affixes occurs optionally while that [suffix] remains present.

Thus, it is established that *guptiḥ* means "he protected" (*jugopa*), which is desired; however, this undesired form *gopāyām cakāra gopāya* does not follow. But this desired form *gopayām cakāra gopāya* is not achieved. On the other hand, this desired form *gopayām cakāra* is indeed established. How? Let there be the suffix *āy* here for the base [ending in] *ā*.

Since the *liṭ* suffix is an *ārdhadhātuka*, when it is present, the *āya*-class suffixes (*āyādayaḥ*) may optionally apply; they will fall in between [the root and the suffix], just like the *vikaraṇas*. But then this desired form *gopāyā* would not be established. However, it is established because of the rule stating that [the *āya*-suffixes] are obligatory before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, without depending on the optional application (*vā-vidhāna*). This is established. How? By the optional application of the *āya*-class suffixes being stated without distinction [between *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka*].

I shall state that [the substitution] is obligatory (*nitya*) in the domain of *sārvadhātuka* suffixes. However, the greater force of the *syat*-class [suffixes] arises by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), because they share identical conditions. Indeed, it follows that the *āya*-class [suffixes] would be superseded by the *syat*-class suffixes through conflict. What is the reason? Because they share identical conditions. The conditions for the *syat*-class and the *āya*-class are the same. The scope of the *syat*-class suffixes is, for example: *kariṣyati*, *hariṣyati*.

There is scope for the suffixes *āya* and so forth [in the forms] *gopāyati* and *dhūpāyati*. Here, both [suffixes] would apply: [one might derive] *gopāyiṣyati* and *dhūpāyiṣyati*. However, because they are subsequent [rules], the *sya*-suffixes (the future tense markers) would prevail. Or rather, this is not a fault. Why? Because the prescription of *āya* and so forth has no scope [elsewhere]. Indeed, the suffixes *āya* and so forth are said to be without scope [for application elsewhere].
And they will come to be by virtue of that statement. But was not the scope [of the rule] already established just now with the examples "gopāyati" and "dhūpāyati"?

In these cases too, the suffix *śap* and so forth occur. Even though it occurs here as well, there is no distinction whether *śap* is present or absent. Now, this other point is being stated: "there is no distinction. As for that which...

It was stated that there is no scope [for the substitution of *āya* etc. not covered by *syati* and the others; therefore, such scope does not exist. Indeed, in this case, the affix *śap* must necessarily be desired [after roots ending in long vowels]. What is the reason? [In forms such as] *gopāyantī* and *dhūpāyantī*, so that the augment *num* may always apply according to the rule "after [roots ending in long vowels], *num* is added before *śap* and *śyan*" (*śap-śyanoḥ nityam*). If, then, the substitutes *āya* and the others have no scope because of *syati* and the others...

An annulment of the rules for *sy-* and so forth would result. However, this objection is resolved by splitting the rule (*sūtra-bheda*): if it were stated that [the augment] is "always" (*nityam*) applied when the suffix *śap* follows, then [the desired forms] are established. But in that case, the rule is split. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. But has it not already been stated that, regarding the *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes following *āya* and so forth, there are two ways of interpreting the statement: "the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix following *āya* and so forth" and "the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix following the base that begins with *āya* and so forth"?
"An undesirable consequence [would follow]. This is not a fault. The term *ārdhadhātuke* is not a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*). What then?

It is a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*), meaning "in the domain of the *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes. In that case, within the domain of the *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes, once the *āya*-class suffixes and others have been applied to the base, whichever suffix is applicable from whichever [base] shall occur from that.

What is the purpose of including the mention of the "end" (*anta*)? Why not simply say, "the *san*-class and others are verbal roots"? By what means, then, would the designation apply to those [roots] ending in them? It would be by the rule of extension to that which ends in such elements (*tadantavidhi*). Therefore, he recites the following answer regarding the inclusion of the "end" in the *san*-class and others:

It has been stated. What was stated? That in the rule for the designation *pada*, the mention of "final" (*anta*) is for the purpose of prohibiting the extension of a rule (*tadantavidhi*) when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned in any other rule prescribing a technical designation (*saṃjñāvidhi*). And this [rule defining *dhātu*] is also a prescription of a technical designation, and this too is a mention of a suffix.
Why then is this stated again? Is it not already established by the rule "the roots beginning with *bhū* are *dhātus*"? It is not so established.

The designation *dhātu* (verbal root) is established by means of recitation (*pāṭha*), yet these [roots] are not recited therein. How then does the designation *dhātu* apply to others that are not recited? [For example:
*bhū* is substituted for *as*; *vac* for *brū*; and *khyāñ* for *cakṣiṅ*. Even though these are not recited there...

But their original forms (*prakṛti*) are recited there. In that case, it is established by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). [Objection: Even so, what about those which are not recited there, yet for which meanings are assigned? Those [original forms] for which meanings are assigned are indeed recited there. In that case, it is established by virtue of the status of being a substitute. [Reply: It is not established. For it is stated that "the substitute (*ādeśa*) is like the original" (*sthānivat*); it is not stated that "the original is like the substitute."
And these are substitutes (*ādeśāḥ*). These also are substitutes. How so? That which is pointed out (*ādiśyate*) is a substitute. And these also are pointed out.

Even so, it is stated that "substitutes of that which is indicated by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdiṣṭasya*) are like the original (*sthānivat*). If it is withdrawn, then [the rule] would apply even to an exception (*apavāda*) as if it were the general rule (*utsarga*).

Regarding the rule *karmaṇy aṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1) and *ātaḥ anupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3), one might argue that even when the suffix *ka* is applied, the effect of the suffix *aṇ* would still occur. This is not a fault. The activity of the Teacher indicates that what is effected by a general rule (*utsarga*) does not apply when an exception (*apavāda*) is present; for this reason, he treats certain suffixes such as *śyan* and others as having the marker *śit*, as seen in the rules *śnam*, *śnā*, and *śnuḥ*.

In that case, *yak* is prescribed for the passive and middle voices (*bhāva-karman*), while *śap* is prescribed for the active voice (*kartṛ*). Regarding the term *śap*: here, that which is indicated in the nominative (*prathamā*) has its purpose [fulfilled] by that which is indicated in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). The word "divādibhyaḥ" is in the ablative;

This is not a rule for introducing an affix (*pratyayavidhi*). An affix has already been prescribed, and the current topic (*prakṛta*) continues to apply. Or rather, the continuity (*anuvṛtti*) will be maintained:

So that there may be subsequent application (*anuprayoga*). This is not a valid purpose.

[The objection: "Because it ends in *ā* and its meaning is indistinct, the sense [of the action] remains incomplete; therefore, there will be a subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) [of another verb].
