And usage occurs neither exclusively for those denoting the general nor exclusively for those denoting the specific. In that regard:

The roots expressing specific actions arise; those expressing general action will be employed as subsequent applications (*anuprayoga*). Or rather, it is for the sake of [restricting] that which follows *liṭ*.

In that case, the rule regarding the subsequent application of *kṛñ* is made for the sake of that which follows *liṭ*. It is so that the subsequent application occurs only after *liṭ*, and not after anything else. After what else, then, would it occur? After that which follows *laṭ*. It does not occur after that which follows *laṭ* by virtue of the subsequent application.

Then the past time would be qualified [by the auxiliary]. Well then, let it be for that which follows a *niṣṭhā* (past participle). No; for that which follows a *niṣṭhā*, the person and voice (*puruṣa-upagraha*) would be qualified by the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*). Well then, let it be for that which follows *luṅ* (the aorist). No; for that which follows *luṅ*, the non-recent past time (*anadyatana-bhūtakāla*) would be qualified by the subsequent application. Well then, let it be for that which follows *laṅ* (the imperfect). No; for that which follows *laṅ*, the non-recent past time that is remote (*anadyatana-parokṣa*) [would be qualified].

The time [of the action] would be specified. In that case, the *laṅ* is prescribed for what is past, non-evident, and not of today, as in the rule: "After *ha* and *śaśvat*, the *laṅ* also. This is so that it does not occur after something else. But even that is not a purpose, because once an application has been made for one generic form (*ākṛti*), it does not occur for a second or a third. It is just as when someone is the master of cows, he is not the master of horses.

And as for the word *ca*: there is no such usage as "the owner of cows and horses" (*goṣu ca aśvānām ca svāmī*). Alternatively, because the meaning is already complete, there would be no subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) [of a verb]. That is to say, because the meaning is complete, there would be no subsequent application. Since the meaning is completed by the suffix *-ām*, one might think that there should be no subsequent application. But even this is not a valid objection; for it was just stated that the suffix *-ām* [is used]...
[The word *kṛ*] has its meaning unmanifested. Therefore, because the meaning is not fully completed [by it alone], there will be the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) [of another verb].

Or, it is for the purpose of preventing inversion. If it is for the purpose of preventing inversion, then the rule regarding the subsequent application of *kṛ* is stated so that one does not say "he made effort" (*īhām cakre*) when it should be "he made" (*cakre īhām*). And it is for the purpose of preventing separation; that is, for the purpose of preventing [the application of the rule] when there is an intervention [between the two verbs].
125–130. Where is this *cli* heard? It is not heard anywhere. [If so,] substitutes such as *sij* and others are prescribed;

since it is not heard anywhere, for what purpose then is the general rule (*utsarga*) for *clu* formulated? Should not the general rule for *sic* alone be made? Its exceptions (*apavāda*) will be *ksa* and the others. To this, he recites the following reply: "The general rule for *cli* is for the sake of including the general category."

The substitution of *cli* is prescribed for the purpose of including [the affixes] in general. Where is there a need for this inclusion in general? In the rule *mantra-ghasahvaraṇaśavṛdahādvṛckṛgamijanibhyaḥ leḥ*, where at least three [affixes] would have to be mentioned: *caṅ*, *aṅ*, and *sic*. Furthermore, in the prescription of *kṣa* and in the mention of roots as being "without *iṭ*" (*aniṭ*), the purpose is to ensure the correct understanding of *cli*.

Furthermore, in the rule for *ksa*, the suffix *cli* is introduced as a general substitute (*utsarga*) for the purpose of conveying the sense of the *liṭ* (perfect) tense; thus, the substitution of *ksa* for the *aniṭ* *cli* becomes established. And in the case of the substitution of *ghas* [for *ad*], when *cli* itself has been applied, the suffix *aṅ* becomes established by the rule "after roots marked with *ḷ*" (*lṛditaḥ*). Now, what is the purpose of adding the marker *c* to *cli*? The addition of the marker *c* to *cli* is for the sake of specification. [The marker *c* serves to specify that the following rule applies] to *cli*.
The addition of the marker *it* is made for the purpose of specification. Where is there a need for the purpose of specification? In the rule *cleḥ sic*.
If it were stated as *leḥ sic*, it would undesirably apply to the *liṅ* and *liṭ* suffixes as well. This is not a valid objection, for it is stated [in the context] of the *luṅ* tense;
and the *liṅ* and *liṭ* do not occur in the *luṅ*. Now, what is the purpose of adding the marker *it*? The addition of the marker *it* is for the purpose of including the general form.

And the addition of the marker *it* is made for the purpose of general reference (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*). Where is there a need for general reference? In the rules "In a mantra, after the roots *ghas*, *hvaraṇa*, *śavṛ*, *dṛ*, *hā*, *dṛc*, *kṛ*, *gam*, *ji*, and *ni*, [the suffix] *liṭ* [is replaced by *kvasu*]" and "after [the root *mā*], *ām* [is substituted for *liṭ*]. Now, since the marker *it* is being added for the purpose of general reference, the letter *ca* must necessarily be included to ensure that the general reference is not obstructed.

What is the purpose of the particle *ca* for the sake of ensuring the inclusion of the general term? It is precisely here. As for what is stated—that the elision of *cl* is for the sake of including the general term—even when the elision of *cl* is applied, those same three mentions remain:
"cl" in the rule for *luṅ*, "cleḥ" in the rule for *sic*, and "leḥ" in the rule for *liṭ*. This mention of "leḥ" will serve another purpose. How so?

Regarding this rule, *gāti-sthā-ghu-pā-bhū-bhyaḥ sicaḥ parasmaipadeṣu*, the mention of *sicaḥ* here—I shall state that it refers to *leḥ*. If it is stated as *leḥ*, then for the root *dheṭ*, a fourfold verbal expression (*cātuḥśabdyam*) would result: *adadhat*, *adhāt*, *adhāsīt*, and [the fourth form] *adadhāt* would also result. Furthermore, when there is elision (*luk*) of the *caṅ* suffix, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) should not take place. Why?

The rule is stated as *caṅi*. However, we do not see the suffix *caṅ* here. [One might argue that it exists] by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations conditioned by a suffix). [To this we reply: there is a prohibition against *pratyayalakṣaṇa* by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya*. In that case, regarding the plural, four forms would result:
*adadhan*, *adhuḥ*, *adhāsiṣuḥ*, and *adhān* would also result. This is not a fault, because the substitution of *jus* occurs by the rule *ātaḥ*.
It will occur; it is not established. The mention of *sij* follows there [from the previous rule]. The mention of *sij* will be discontinued.

If it is discontinued, then in the case of *abhūvan*, the substitution of *jus* would apply by virtue of the characteristic of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). If that is so, then the elision (*luk*) will be understood as an exception (*apavāda*) to *sij*. If the elision is understood as an exception to *sij*, then [the forms] *mā hi dātām* and *mā hi dhātām* [would be incorrect].

In this case, the accent prescribed by the rule *ādiḥ sico 'nyatarasyām* would not apply. Therefore, it cannot be said that the *luk*-elision is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *sic*-affix. If this were not stated, then in forms such as *abhūvan*, the substitution of *jus* for *śn* would apply by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of the affix). Consequently, in the rule *ātaḥ*, the mention of *sic* must be carried over (*anuvartyam*). And while that [mention of *sic*] is being carried over, [it applies] to the root *dheṭ*.

It would result in a fourfold application of the term. Therefore, in the rule *gāti-sthā-ghu-pā-bhūbhyaḥ sicaḥ parasmaipadeṣu*, the mention of *sic* must be made. And when that is done, there are exactly three mentions:

*cli luṅi*, *cleḥ sic*, and *leḥ*. As for what is also said—that in the prescription of *kṣa*, the mention of *cli* is for the purpose of indicating the absence of the augment *iṭ*—[that too is unnecessary].

Thus, we shall qualify the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself here by its state of being *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*), as in "of a verbal root that is *aniṭ*. But how can a verbal root be called *aniṭ*? A verbal root is indeed *aniṭ*. How so? Either it is *aniṭ* because it lacks the cause for *iṭ*, or because there is no *iṭ* after it; thus it is called *aniṭ*. Now, if the verbal root is being qualified, where will you apply the qualification "that which is *aniṭ*"?

Furthermore, what follows from this? If it is understood as "of that which is *aniṭ* in the *niṣṭhā* [suffixes]," then the rule would apply to the vast majority [of roots]. For the vast majority of roots ending in *śal* with a *laghu* vowel (*igupadha*) are *aniṭ* in the *niṣṭhā*. On the other hand, if it is understood as "that which is *aniṭ* in the *liṭ*," then it would not apply to anything at all; for all roots ending in *śal* with a *laghu* vowel are [in fact] *seṭ* in the *liṭ*.

"Regarding the rule *liṭi seṭaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.45]: what, then, is the reason that when the verbal root (*dhātu*) is being qualified, these two specific conditions are qualified? Why is it not the case here that the prescription and prohibition of *iṭ* apply generally? Where do they apply generally? To *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes beginning with *val*.
As for what is said regarding the substitution of *ghas*, the *ārdhadhātuka* rules apply generally to those suffixes that have not yet been fixed."
Regarding the suffixes: in that case, when the substitution of *ghas* has been applied in general for all *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes, the designation *aṅ* will apply by virtue of the rule *lṛdito ’ṅ*.

(P_3.1.44.1) KA_II,51.2–52.8 Ro_III,130–132 What is the purpose of the letter *c*? It is for the sake of specification. Where is there a need for it to serve as a specifier? [In the rule] *sici vṛddhiḥ* (P_7.2.1).
Regarding the rule *parasmaipadeṣu*: if it were stated simply that "there is vṛddhi before *su*," then it would undesirably apply even in cases such as *agniḥ* and *vāyuḥ*.

This objection has no force, for the term *parasmaipadeṣu* is indeed stated [in the rule], and we do not perceive a *parasmaipada* ending here. Well then, it is for the sake of the accent; for by the rule *citaḥ anta udātto bhavati*, there would otherwise be an acute accent on the final syllable.

This too is not a valid purpose. This [suffix] is without an *ac* vowel; therefore, there is no need for the marker *c*, which serves the purpose of indicating accent (*svarārtha*). Once the augment *iṭ* has been applied, it will possess an *ac* vowel. In that case, the *iṭ* will become acute by virtue of the rule that the first syllable of an affix is acute (*pratyayādyudātta*). [Objection: That is not established. Since augments (*āgama*) are unaccented (*anudātta*), the *iṭ* would consequently be unaccented.

To this, he recites the following reply: "The marking of *sic* with the *cit* designation is purposeless because it would behave like its original (*sthānivat*). The marking of *sic* with *cit* is useless. Why? Because of its status as a substitute (*sthānivat*); due to the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, it will possess the *cit* designation [automatically]. "But the marking with *cit* is indeed purposeful, for by the power of that *cit* designation, the augment *iṭ* becomes acute-accented (*udātta*). The marking with *cit* is meaningful. What is the meaning?"

Indeed, by virtue of the *cit* designation, the vowel of the suffix *iṭ* will be acute. This rule for the unaccented nature of an augment (*āgama*) is commenced when the accent of the suffix has not yet applied. Just as it sets aside the accent of the suffix, so too would it set aside that which is obtained through the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). Therefore, the *cit* designation is necessary; therefore, the letter *c* must be added. Now, as for the purpose of the *it* designation:

For what purpose? The designation *idit* is made for the sake of preventing the elision of the letter *n*. The designation *idit* is applied so that the elision of *n* does not occur—as in *amaṃsta* and *amaṃsthāḥ*, [which would otherwise be subject to] the rule *aniditām hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti*. Or rather, the designation *kit* for the suffix *sic* after the root *han* serves as the reason for the absence of the elision of *n*; indeed, this is not the purpose. What is the reason?

The fact that the Teacher teaches the *kittva* of the suffix *sic* in the rule "yat ayam hanaḥ sic" (Pāṇini 6.4.63) indicates that there is no elision of the letter *n* in a stem ending in *sic*. This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*). For there is another purpose for this statement. What is it? It is so that the elision of *n* occurs only when *sic* follows, and not when some other cause (*nimitta*) follows. But what [is the problem] here?

There is this distinction regarding the *sic* affix, whether there is elision of *n* or when another cause follows. This is the distinction: when there is elision of *n* after *sic*, because that elision of *n* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the elision of the vowel *a* does not take place. However, when another cause follows and the elision of *n* occurs, the elision of the vowel *a* would result. This [elision of *a*] depends on different bases (*vyāśraya*), whereas [the elision of *n*] is non-existent [for the purpose of the former] only when it shares the same basis (*samānāśraya*). But surely, in the case of another [cause] following...

Even when the *nimitta* (condition) for the elision of *n* has ceased to exist, the elision of the vowel *a* will not occur. How so? Because of the rule that "an external operation (*bahiraṅga*) characterized by a formal feature is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to an internal operation (*antaraṅga*) characterized by a formal feature. Thus, the fact that the suffix *sic* is marked with the *kit* designation after the root *han* is itself an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the elision of *n* does not take place for a stem ending in *sic*. Alternatively, [the elision of *n* is prevented] either because of the *idit* marker [of *sic*] or because of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitute). Or else, there might be some other purpose served by this *idit* marker.

This substitution will be treated as if it were *idit* due to its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*. (P_3,1.44.2) It should be stated: "The suffix *sic* is optionally [treated as having an indicatory *k*] after the roots *spṛś*, *mṛś*, *kṛṣ*, *tṛp*, and *dṛp*. (KA_II,52.9-53.5; Ro_III, 133-135) *spṛś-mṛś-kṛṣ-tṛp-dṛpaḥ sic vā*. It should be stated that the suffix *sic* is optionally [treated as having an indicatory *k*] after *spṛś*, *mṛś*, *kṛṣ*, *tṛp*, and *dṛp*.

*Spṛśa*: *aspṛkṣat*, *asprākṣīt*. *Mṛśa*: *amṛkṣat*, *amrākṣīt*. *Kṛṣa*: *akṛkṣat*, *akrākṣīt*. *Tṛpa*: *atṛpat*, *atrāpsīt*. *Dṛpa*: *adṛpat*, *adrapsīt*. What is the purpose? So that the suffix *sic* may apply. But is not *ksa* already established? It is established by the rule: "The suffix *ksa* is applied after roots ending in *śal*, having *ik* as their penultimate letter, and being non-*iṭ*. [Therefore,] *sic* [is required for other cases].

It is also established. How? The insertion of *c* after the *cli* affix is rejected. In that case, when the augment *am* has been applied to the *cli* itself—which is characterized as a *jhal*—the *ksa* suffix will not occur because its cause has been removed. If this were so, the *sij* and other suffixes would apply to the final letter. But it is established by the fact that *sic* begins with *ya*. This is indeed established. How? *Sic* will be made to begin with *ya*.

By the rule *anekāl-śit sarvasya*, it will be a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*). Why is the letter *y* not heard? The letter *y* has been indicated as elided. How about in the case of *caṅ* and *aṅ*? It is established by the fact that *caṅ* and *aṅ* are taught as a conjunctive compound (*praśliṣṭanirdeśa*). This is a conjunctive compound of *caṅ* and *aṅ*: *ca-aṅ* = *caṅ*; *a-aṅ* = *aṅ*. By the rule *anekāl-śit sarvasya*, it will be a total replacement. How about in the case of *ciṇ*?

It is established because *ciṇ* is not marked with *it*. It is established because *ciṇ* is not marked with *it*. What does "because it is not marked with *it*" mean? Since this [augment] would occur in place of the final letter, it would not be designated as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. If the designation *pratyaya* (suffix) is absent, the designation *it* does not apply. If the designation *it* is absent, there is no elision (*lopa*). If there is no elision, [the augment] consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*). When it consists of more than one phoneme, it is a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). When it is a substitute for the whole, [the rule is established].
First there is the condition (*pratyaya*); when there is the condition, then there is the designation *it*; when there is the designation *it*, then there is elision (*lopa*).

And thus, in that regard, the determination of the author of the *Vārttika* is that the marking with the acute accent (*cit*) serves a purpose. Furthermore, the threefold verbal form would not be established: *aspṛkṣat*, *asprākṣīt*, and *aspārkṣīt* would not be possible. But when the suffix *sic* is present, there is an option (*vibhāṣā*).

Thus it is. Even in this case, the augment *am*, which is conditioned by a *jhal* sound, is optional (*vibhāṣā*). Indeed, for that [root] whose cause for the augment *am* is not obstructed, that augment would certainly occur. Therefore, it is rightly said: "After the roots *spṛś*, *mṛś*, *kṛṣ*, *tṛp*, and *dṛp*, the suffix *sic* is optionally [used].
(Pāṇini 3.1.45).

135–136. Regarding the rule for *ksa*: there is an absence of the *ig-upadha* [condition] because the *cli* is the cause of the *guṇa*. In the rule prescribing *ksa*, there is an absence of the *ig-upadha* condition.

What is the reason? Because the *cli* is the cause of the *guṇa*. The *cli* is the cause of the *guṇa*. Therefore, once the *guṇa* has been applied specifically to the *cli*, the *ksa* suffix does not apply by virtue of the rule "after a root with an *ik* vowel as its penultimate (*ig-upadha*)". Or rather, it is not so; for since *ksa* is without scope (*anavakāśa*), it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *guṇa*. It is not [the case that *ksa* is without scope].
Or rather, this fault does not arise. What is the reason? Because *ksa* has no scope. *Ksa*, having no scope, will supersede the *guṇa*.

The mention of "not taking *iṭ*" (*aniṭ*) is not a qualification [of the root], because *cli* is invariably prescribed [to follow it]. The mention of "not taking *iṭ*" is not a qualification. What is the reason? Because *cli* is invariably prescribed. *Cli* is never heard [in its own form] anywhere; in that context, the rule applies as "of *cli* which does not take *iṭ*."

[The suffix] *ksa* is not obtained. Or rather, it is not a fault, because *ksa* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *sic*, and that [suffix *sic*] depends on the absence of *iṭ* (*aniṭ*); thus, once the absence of *iṭ* is established, the addition of *ksa* occurs. Or rather, this is not a fault. Why? Because *ksa* is an exception to *sic*. *Ksa* is an exception to *sic*, and it depends on the absence of *iṭ*. Furthermore, a prefix (*upasarga*) does not apply to the domain of an exception. For previously...

Exceptions (*apavāda*) apply first, and subsequently the general rules (*utsarga*). Or, having first determined the scope of the exception, the general rule applies. Therefore, in this case, the suffix *sic* never occurs at that stage. It awaits the [application of] *ksa*, because *ksa* is an exception to *sic*, and since *ksa* depends on the root being *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment), its status as *aniṭ* is well-established. Once it is established that the root is *aniṭ*, the substitution of *ksa* for *vid* occurs; thus, it is only when the root is *aniṭ* that [the rule applies].

[Objection: Since [the substitution of] *kṣa* will be established [by P. 7.3.72], where then will *sic* apply? [Response: The rule for *sic* applies to the remainder (*śeṣe*). The rule for *sic* will apply to the remainder, as in *akoṣīt* and *amoṣīt*. (P. 3.1.46) KA_II,54.2-24 Ro_III,108.19–110.10; ŚVTib 125b7–126b1; ŚVtrTib 249a4–250a2; ŚVK 342.14–343.14; ŚVV 243.17–244.12; ŚVT 222.15–223.12;

136–138. Why is this stated? For the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*). [The rule] is intended so that the suffix *kṣa* occurs only after the root *śliṣ* in the sense of "embracing" (*āliṅgana*). It should not occur here: *upāśliṣaj jatu ca kāṣṭhaṃ ca* ("the lac and the wood stuck together") or *samāśliṣad brāhmaṇakulam* ("the group of Brahmins gathered"). To this, he recites the following reply: "The restriction regarding the root *śliṣ* in the sense of embracing is untenable because it is already established by another rule. There is no possibility of a restriction for the root *śliṣ* in the sense of embracing.

What is the reason? Because there is something to be enjoined (*vidheya*). A restriction (*niyama*) occurs because of the purposelessness [of a rule] when there is nothing to be enjoined; however, here there is something to be enjoined. What is it? Since the suffix *aṅ* would apply by virtue of the word *puṣ* being listed in the *puṣādi* group, the suffix *ksa* must be enjoined in order to set that aside. In this case, whether it be an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*) or a restriction (*niyama*), it must be an original injunction alone.

There is no such restriction. Furthermore, what would happen if this restriction did not exist? The suffix *ksa* would undesirably apply in the *ātmanepada* and in the sense of embracing (*āliṅgana*). Just as *ksa* sets aside the *aṅ* substitution, it would likewise set aside the *ciṇ* substitution, as in: *upāśleṣi kanyā devadattena* ("the girl was embraced by Devadatta"). But [this result] is established by the rule: "The root *śliṣ* takes *ksa* in the sense of embracing when it does not concern the domain of *ciṇ*. This is established. How so?

It should be stated that for the root *śliṣ* in the sense of "embracing," *ksa* occurs when *aci* follows, provided it is not within the scope of *ciṇ*. Furthermore, it should be stated that for the root *śliṣ*, when *aṅ* is prescribed, it applies in the sense of "not embracing. [Objection: This is established. [Response: In that case, the rule (*sūtra*) is split.

Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. [Objection: But was it not said that, regarding *śliṣ* in the sense of "embracing," a restriction (*niyama*) is untenable because there is nothing to be prescribed (*vidheya*)?

[Objection: This is not a fault. It is established by means of a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*). A split in the rule will be made: "After the root *śliṣ*. [The suffix] *ksa* occurs after *śliṣ*. For what purpose is this? Because of its inclusion in the *puṣādi* group, the suffix *aṅ* would otherwise apply; it is for the purpose of excluding that. Then: "And in the sense of embracing. After *śliṣ*, *ksa* occurs when the sense is embracing. Now, what is the purpose of this [second rule]? It is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

The root *śliṣ* occurs only in the sense of "embracing. Where should it not [apply]? [In cases such as: *upāśliṣaj jatu ca kāṣṭhaṃ ca* ("the lac and the wood adhered together") and *samāśliṣad brāhmaṇakulam* ("the group of Brahmins gathered together"). Furthermore, as for what is said—that just as *ksa* subverts the *aṅga*, so too should it subvert *ciṇ*:
since "exceptions subvert the immediately following rules, not those that follow later," in this way *ksa* will subvert the *aṅga*.

The *ciṇ* affix will not cause an obstruction. Alternatively, he will state there [in the commentary]: "The purpose of mentioning *ciṇ* is so that it may apply only when *ciṇ* itself is applicable; let that which else would apply not take place. (Pāṇini 3.1.48) KA_II,55.2-16 Ro_III,109.1-110.10. [Objection: But how can this be? For even when *ciṇ* is mentioned, the rule for *ciṇ* does not prevent the application of other rules. For example, in the case of *apāci*, although *ciṇ* applies by virtue of Pāṇini 3.1.66 (*ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*), the rule for *luṅ* (the aorist suffix) also applies by virtue of Pāṇini 3.2.110 (*luṅ*). Furthermore, in the case of *abhāji*, although *ciṇ* applies by virtue of Pāṇini 3.1.66, the rule for *caṅ* (the reduplication of the aorist) also applies by virtue of Pāṇini 3.1.48 (*sanvallaghuni caṅpare 'naglope*). Moreover, in the case of *akāri*, although *ciṇ* applies by virtue of Pāṇini 3.1.66, the rule for *sic* (the aorist suffix *sic*) also applies by virtue of Pāṇini 3.1.44 (*cleḥ sic*). Therefore, the mention of *ciṇ* does not serve as an obstruction to other rules. [Response: This is not a fault. While *ciṇ* is already in force, what is the purpose of mentioning *ciṇ* again? It was not so that it might be negated (*na*). This is for the sake of prescribing (*vidhi*). (P_3,1.67.1) KA_II,56.15-57.17 Ro_III, 141-146 Here we observe that dual and plural endings are cited for the object (*karman*): *pacyete odanau* ("two rice-messes are being cooked"), *pacyante odanāḥ* ("rice-messes are being cooked"). However, in the case of the abstract state (*bhāva*), there is only the singular ending:

"It is sat by you," "It is sat by you two," "It is sat by you all. By what means does this occur? Because the object (*karman*) is manifold; due to its manifoldness, there are dual and plural endings.

[The action] exists [as one]. But the state (*bhāva*) is indeed only one. How then do the dual and plural numbers occur here, as in *pākau* (two cookings) and *pākāḥ* (many cookings)? Because of the difference in their substrates (*āśrayabheda*). Since the state rests upon a substance (*dravya*), the dual and plural numbers occur due to the difference in that [substance]. In this case as well, then, all those who perform that action [should be expressed by the plural].

They serve as its substrata; due to their differentiation, dual and plural forms are obtained. If this is so, then first this must be asked: with what in view is this employed—namely, *pākau* (two cookings) and *pākāḥ* (many cookings)?
If it is with specific types of cooking in view—such as that of rice, that of molasses, and that of sesame seeds—then [the forms follow].

There are many words that are identical in form; in such cases, it is appropriate to employ both the plural number and the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one). Even when the state [of the action] is expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the plural is heard [in usage]. For example:
"The camel-sittings are being sat" (*uṣṭrāsikā āsyante*) and "The dead-lying-downs are lying" (*hataśāyikāḥ śayyante*). Now, as for that which [is formed] having regard for specific times...
Furthermore, there are many words that are identical in form (*sarūpa*) for the cooking of today, yesterday, and tomorrow;

in those cases, the use of the plural number and the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) are appropriate. However, even when the action is expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), because the abstract state (*bhāva*) lacks identity of form, *ekaśeṣa* does not occur—as in the case of *āsi* and *āsyate*.

It will exist. Indeed, there is a distinction between a state (*bhāva*) expressed by a *kṛt* suffix and one expressed by a *tiṅ* suffix. A state expressed by a *kṛt* suffix behaves like a substance (*dravyavat*). What does "behaving like a substance" mean? A substance enters into a relation of inherence (*samavāya*) with an action. What kind of relation? A substance attains the status of an instrument (*sādhana*) in the accomplishment of an action. And this state [expressed by a *kṛt*] is like that.

That which is expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix [denotes] a state (*bhāva*). For example, in the expression "pākaḥ vartate" ("the cooking is occurring"), it does not possess action (*kriyāvat*). What is this "possessing action"?

It means that one action does not enter into a relation of inherence (*samavāya*) with another action, as in "he cooks" (*pacati*) or "he reads" (*paṭhati*). And that [quality of possessing action] does not belong to this [state] expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix, as in "pākaḥ vartate. Indeed, there is a distinction between a state expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix and one expressed by a *tiṅ*-suffix.

Furthermore, time, person, and voice (upagraha) are manifested by the action expressed through a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), but they are not manifested by the action expressed through a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*). Indeed, there is a distinction between the action expressed by a *kṛt* suffix and that expressed by a *tiṅ* suffix:
the action expressed by a *tiṅ* suffix is connected with an agent, whereas the action expressed by a *kṛt* suffix is not so connected. To this extent...
There is some commonality and some distinction; it is logical that this [distinction] should also exist as being caused by gender and caused by number.

(P_3.1.67.2) KA_II,57.18–58.23 Ro_III, 146–149 This is now considered: do the meanings of the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes consist of the state (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), and the agent (*kartṛ*), or do they consist of the meanings of the *vikaraṇa* suffixes?

Or rather: how would they have the sense of *sārvadhātuka* suffixes, or how would they have the sense of *vikaraṇa* suffixes? [The former view holds: "When a *sārvadhātuka* suffix expresses the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), the suffix *yak* occurs;

when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix expresses the agent (*kartṛ*), the suffix *śap* occurs"—thus they have the sense of *sārvadhātuka* suffixes. [The latter view holds: "The suffix *yak* occurs when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix expresses the action or the object; the suffix *śap* occurs when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix expresses the agent"—thus they have the sense of *vikaraṇa* suffixes.

And what is the distinction here? If the meanings of the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes were [only] the state (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), and the agent (*kartṛ*), then a restriction regarding the singular, dual, and plural would be untenable, because those [suffixes] would not have that as their meaning. If the meanings of the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes were the state, the object, and the agent, a restriction regarding the singular, dual, and plural would be untenable. What is the reason? Because they do not have that as their meaning. For in that case, singularity and so forth would not be the sole meanings of the case-endings (*vibhakti*). Why?

In that case, let the agent (*kartṛ*) as well as the object (*karman*) and the state (*bhāva*) [be expressed by the suffixes]. If it is argued that they serve the purpose of introducing verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*), then if it is said that they serve the purpose of introducing verbal suffixes, there would be an absence of the verbal suffix when the meaning is already expressed by a *kṛt* suffix. If it is argued that they serve the purpose of introducing verbal suffixes, then a verbal suffix would not apply when the meaning is already expressed by a *kṛt* suffix—as in *dhārayaḥ* and *pārayaḥ*. Why is it said "when expressed by a *kṛt* suffix"? For expression also occurs by means of the *laṭ* (present) suffix.
It is impossible for the suffix *la* to be the means of expression [for the agent]. This alternative position has been adopted:

that the meanings of the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes are either the object, the action, or the agent, or else they are the meanings of the *vikaraṇa* suffixes. And if the expression were indeed by means of *la*, this would not be an alternative position. How is it impossible? When you yourself have stated: "The *l*-suffixes [denote] the object and also the action."

And [the rule] "and from intransitives" (*akarmakebhyaḥ*). I shall state it thus: "The suffixes *la* [denote] the object, the state (*bhāva*), and from intransitives. But in that case, where the affixes (*vikaraṇa*) are not heard, what will express the state, the object, and the agent? And where are they not heard? In those cases where these affixes undergo elision (*luk*) or elision by *ślu*. Even here, when the status of the agent has been expressed, the elision (*luk*) will take place.

In that case, when no *vikaraṇas* (verbal suffixes) arise at all, what will express the action (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), or the agent (*kartṛ*)? And where do they not arise? In the *liṅ* and *liṭ* [moods]. Therefore, it cannot be said that there is no expression by means of the *laṭ* [suffix]. If there is expression, then there is simply an absence of *vikaraṇas*. If that is so, then this would be the case: when...

When *la* [the verbal suffix] denotes the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), then the *vikaraṇas* denote the agent (*kartṛ*). When *la* denotes the agent, then the *vikaraṇas* denote the action or the object. This is both natural and based on formal rule:
"The base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) together express the meaning of the suffix. And it is not possible for one [of them] alone...

There would be a simultaneous co-occurrence (*anusahāyībhāva*) of two distinct meanings of the *prakṛti*. And by doing so, this [interpretation] becomes one-sided: namely, that the meanings of the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes are exclusively [the agent]. But was it not said: "If the meanings of the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes are the state of being (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), and the agent (*kartṛ*), then a restriction regarding the singular, dual, and plural numbers is untenable because they do not have those as their meanings"? This is not a fault, for the meanings such as the object (*karman*) belong to the nominal suffixes (*sup*).
Furthermore, the meaning of *sup*-suffixes is number as well as [the categories] beginning with *karman* (object);

likewise for *tiṅ*-suffixes. In that regard, the restriction is well-known; the restriction there is well-established. Or rather, the restriction applies to those [meanings] under discussion. And what are the things under discussion? Singularity and so forth. In the case of one [thing],...
Thus, the singular number is used for one, not for two, nor for many; the dual number is used for two only, not for one, nor for many;
and the plural number is used for many only, not for two, nor for one.

149–153. Regarding the prescription of *yaṅ* for the passive (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), an addition must be made for the case of the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*). An addition must be made to the rule prescribing *yaṅ* for the passive and the object: "It is cooked by itself" (*pacyate svayam eva*); "It is studied by itself" (*paṭhyate svayam eva*).
But what is the reason that it is not established? Because of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the personal ending *śap* is stronger. It is because of conflict.
Indeed, the *śap* [suffix] obtains greater force. The scope of *śap* is: *pacati*, *paṭhati*. The scope of *yak* is:

*pacyate odanaḥ devadattena*, *paṭhyate vidyā devadattena*. Here, both would apply: *pacyate svayam eva*, *paṭhyate svayam eva*. Because it is subsequent (*paratva*), *śap* would apply; [this is avoided] by means of a formal split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*).

Success! A division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: *ciṇ* [is applied] in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*); *yak* [is applied] in the sense of the abstract state and the object when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix follows. Then, for the agent (*kartṛ*):

*yak* also occurs in the sense of the agent, [but only] in the sense of the abstract state and the object. If that is so, then just as *yak* occurs in the sense of the object and the agent, it would likewise follow that it occurs in the sense of the abstract state and the agent. [As in: "Bliss comes to one who lives. It does not [apply] to this.

"Something pains him due to disease. A second rule-separation (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: "The affix *ciṇ* occurs in the sense of the impersonal state (*bhāva*). Then: "In the sense of the object (*karman*)," meaning that *ciṇ* also occurs in the sense of the object. Then: "In the presence of a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, *yak* occurs," both in the sense of the impersonal state and in the sense of the object. Then: "In the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*)," meaning that *yak* also occurs in the sense of the agent. The term "in the sense of the object" (*karmani*) is carried over (*anuvartate*), while the term "in the sense of the impersonal state" (*bhāve*) ceases to apply (*nivṛttam*).

Then [the rule] "śap" and "śap" also occurs; [the condition] "in the sense of the agent" (kartari) remains, while "in the sense of the object" (karmaṇi) has also ceased to apply. Even so, an addition must be made, for due to the conflict (vipratiṣedha), the suffix *śyan* would otherwise prevail. The scope (*avakāśa*) of *śyan* is:
*dīvyati*, *sīvyati*. The scope of *yak* is: *odanaḥ pacyate devadattena*, *vidyā paṭhyate*.

In the case of *devadattena*, both [suffixes] would apply here: *dīvyate* (he plays) by himself, and *sīvyate* (he sews) by himself. Because it is subsequent, the suffix *śyan* would apply. But is this not already established by means of the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*)? It is not established. Only that application which is immediate can be set aside by the division of the rule. Why is this so? Because a grammatical operation applies either to what is immediately preceding or...

Or rather, it is a prohibition. The subsequent application (prāpti) remains unprohibited; by that, [the suffix] is applied. But would this application not sublate the subsequent application? No, for being prohibited, it is unable to sublate. If that is the case, then the substitutes for *śa*, namely *śyan* and so on, will be employed. And *śap* is sublated by *syati* and the others. In that regard, for roots of the *div*-class, *śap* applies in the domain of *yaṅ*.
In that case, [the suffixes] *śyan* and so forth would not exist; from what [source] would they arise? Well then, the mention of *śap* must be made. It need not be made.

The previously stated [rule] continues to apply. Where was it stated? In the rule *kartari śap* ("*śap* occurs when the agent is expressed"). But that [term *śap*] was indicated in the nominative (*prathamā*), whereas here the requirement is for something indicated in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). [This is because] *divādibhyaḥ* is a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*), while *śap* is a word ending in the first case (*prathamā*).

"He will prescribe the sixth [case-ending] from that," namely, "of the subsequent. This is a rule for the prescription of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*). And in a rule for the prescription of suffixes, ablative case-endings do not serve as prescribers. This is not a rule for the prescription of suffixes; rather, the suffix has already been prescribed, and the previously mentioned [suffix] continues to apply. Alternatively, since the desired result is already established by the continued application of the rule "in the sense of the action or the object" (*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*), there is no cessation of the application of *yak*.
Regarding the rule *bhāvāya iha sārvadhātuke yak*, this is established even without the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*.

Since it is thus established, the purpose for which he continues the phrase *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* is so that [the suffix *yak*] may also apply in the case of the reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*). Furthermore, the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) as *kartari* is intended to prevent the need for stating a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) regarding the suffix *śyan*.

A *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) must be made for the rule *kartari*, so that one might not have to state a *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior contradiction) regarding *śyan*. Alternatively, by the force of the statement regarding *karmavadbhāva* (the treatment as an object), *yak* will occur. Is there another purpose for the statement of *karmavadbhāva*? What is it? So that the *ātmanepada* endings may occur. The *ātmanepada* will occur because of the explicit statement. [This applies to] *ciṇ*.

In that case, it should be so. [The augment] *ciṇ* will also occur because of the explicit statement. But then, how can there be the state of being like *ciṇ* (*ciṇvad-bhāva*)? A single purpose does not necessitate the commencement of a grammatical rule (*yoga*). In this matter, the suffix *yak* will occur by virtue of the force of the statement regarding the status of being like the object (*karmavad-bhāva*). Alternatively, the activity of the Teacher indicates that *yak* occurs in the case of the reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*), since he [formulates the rule].
The rule *na duhasnunamām yakciṇau* teaches the prohibition of the suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* after the roots *duh*, *snū*, and *nam*. (Pāṇini 3.1.89) [Question:
For what purpose is the condition "not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasargāt*) stated? [Examples: *āyasyati*, *prayasyati*. [Answer: The condition "not preceded by a prefix" could have been omitted.

153–154. What is the purpose of the marker *ś*? It is for the sake of [designating] *sārvadhātuka*. By the rule "that which has *ś* as its marker is *sārvadhātuka*," the technical designation *sārvadhātuka* is applied. By the rule "a *sārvadhātuka* suffix that is not marked with *p* is treated as having the marker *ṅ*," the status of having the marker *ṅ* is established. This is so that the prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule "before a suffix marked with *ṅ*" may take effect, as in the forms *bhinatti* and *chinatti*. But this is not a valid purpose. For by the rule "there is *guṇa* of the stem before a *sārvadhātuka* or *ārdhadhātuka* suffix," [the desired result is already achieved].

It is said: because the rule for an affix applies, that which is the cause (yasmāt) of that rule receives the technical designation "base" (aṅga) with respect to that affix. Now, that which is the cause of the rule for an affix here does not stand before that affix; and that which stands before the affix is not the cause of the rule for that affix. If so, then this is the purpose: lest the designation "ārdhadhātuka" (pertaining to half-roots) should apply. And what would happen [if it did]? [The suffix] characterized by having *val* as its initial [would apply].

[If that were so,] *iṭ* would result [as an augment]. This too is not a valid purpose. *Iṭ* is prescribed for an *aṅga* (stem) that begins with a consonant (*valādi*) followed by an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. Furthermore, that which is the basis for the rule prescribing a suffix (*pratyayavidhi*) is designated as an *aṅga* only when that suffix follows it. However, in this case, the basis for the rule prescribing the suffix is not that which precedes the suffix; and that which follows the suffix is not the basis for the rule prescribing the suffix.

Therefore, he recites the following reply: "The addition of the marker *ś* in *śnam* is for the sake of [triggering] the shortening of roots beginning with *pū*, etc., when followed by a *śit* affix, so that forms such as *pṛṇasi* and *mṛṇasi* may occur. [Objection: "Or rather, it need not be done. Why? Because they are different verbal roots (*dhātu-anyatvāt*). *Pṛṇi* and *mṛṇi* are distinct roots from those [beginning with *pū* and *mṛ*]. [Reply: "Where [the rule applies], [they are indeed the same]."

You choose (*vṛṇase*). This is not *śnam*; this shortening belongs to *śna*. If this were the shortening of *śna*, the accent would not be established in *vṛṇase*. Because of the rule "that which follows a root-final *a* (adupadeśāt) is unaccented (*anudātta*) when it is a *lasārvadhātuka* suffix," this accent would not apply. Therefore, this is *śnam*. If it were *śnam*, then by the rule "there is elision (*allopa*) of [the *n*] before *snas*," elision would result. [This is prevented] by the rule "of the penultimate (*upadhā*)."

It occurs. Because it is not a penultimate vowel (*anupadhātva*), [the substitution] will not take place. It is not possible to understand that [the rule] applies "to the penultimate vowel" (*upadhāyāḥ*). For in this case, there would be a fault: *aṅktaḥ*, *añjanti*. Therefore, the shortening belongs only to the suffix *śna*. How about the accent? "In the Veda, the *sārvadhātuka* is frequently treated as *pit*. It should be stated that in the Veda, the *sārvadhātuka* is frequently treated as *pit*.
The sonship of one who is not a son is observed, and the non-sonship of one who is a son. First, regarding the sonship of one who is not a son: "I honor my mother, my progenitor.
Regarding the non-sonship of one who is a son: "Listen, O pressing-stones! In that case, the shortening [of vowels] must be stated;
indeed, the shortening must necessarily be stated in the Vedic language for such purposes as: "May the pregnant young wives sing my praises."

[Objection: Then it is for the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇārtha*). Where is there a need for the purpose of specification? [In the rule] *śnān nalopaḥ* ("there is no elision of *n* after [a stem ending in] *śnā"). If it were stated simply as *nāt nalopaḥ*, then it would also apply in cases such as *yajñānām* and *yatnānām*. [Reply: Once the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) has been applied, it will not occur. [Objection: This must be considered here: should the lengthening be performed first, or the elision of *n*? What should be done in this case?

155–156. Now, for what purpose is *karoti* mentioned separately? Why not simply say "from *tan* and the others"?
