Let it not be that [the rule] "after roots beginning with *tan* and so on, as well as after *as*, [the suffix *sic* takes the augment *iṭ*]" applies here. But surely, the rule "after a short-stemmed *aṅga*" does indeed apply here;
by that rule alone let it be as it should, and by this [present rule] let it not be. And what is the difference here between that [previous rule] being present or this one?

When that [previous rule] is present, because the elision of *sic* (*sijlopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the treatment as if it were *ciṇ* (*ciṇvadbhāva*) is established. But when this [present rule] is present...

The *ciṇvadbhāva* (the treatment of the root as if it were followed by the suffix *ciṇ*) would not occur. By this [rule], however, the *ciṇvadbhāva* is established even when [the suffix] is present. How? Through the option (*vibhāṣā*) of elision (*luk*). When there is no elision, then by that [rule] there is deletion (*lopa*). Since the deletion of the *sij*-suffix is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) in that context, the *ciṇvadbhāva* becomes established. Because the root *kṛ* belongs to the *tanādi* class, [the form] is established; and even with the deletion of the *sij*-suffix, there is no fault. However, there is a fault here regarding the *ciṇvadbhāva*.
It may be so; that too has been stated as optional.
(Pāṇini 3.1.80) Where is this letter *a* heard? It is not heard anywhere. Its elision occurs by the rule "elision of *at*" (*ato lopaḥ*).

Regarding the term *ārdhadhātuke*: if [the substitution] were not heard anywhere, for what purpose is the substitution of *at* prescribed rather than simply *lopa*? It cannot be so; for if *lopa* were applied, *guṇa* would result. But even if *lopa* were applied, would there not be a prohibition by the rule *na dhātulope ārdhadhātuke*? That prohibition applies only when the *lopa* is caused by an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.
Furthermore, this elision is not caused by an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. Moreover, that rule (*yoga*) is rejected;

when it is rejected, the *guṇa* substitution would indeed occur. Therefore, the substitution of *at* must be stated. Now, for what purpose is the mention of the forms with the *num* augment included, rather than simply saying "of *dhi* and *vikṛvī*"? If it were stated as "of *dhi* and *vikṛvī*," then once the *at* substitution had been applied—
The augment *num* would undesirably apply [in cases such as *bhavān*]. This must be considered here: should *atva* (the substitution of *a*) be applied first, or *num*?

What should be done here? Because it is subsequent, *num* should be added. But *atva* is internal (*antaraṅga*). In what sense is it internal? *Atva* is prescribed in conjunction with the arising of the suffix; whereas *num* is added to the stem (*aṅga*) after the suffix has arisen, depending upon both the base and the suffix. *Num* also...

[The suffix] is internal (*antaraṅga*). How so? He will state this [in the rule for *num*]: "The statement 'as if taught' (*upadeśivad-vacana*) regarding the prescription of *num* is for the sake of the prescription of suffixes.
Between the two internal [operations], because of its posteriority, the augment *num* occurs. Therefore, it should be stated: "after *dhi* and *vikṛtyoḥ*" (Pāṇini 3.1.83).

157–160. For what purpose is the *śit* [marker] applied? It is so that the designation *sārvadhātuka* may apply by the rule *śit sārvadhātukam*, that the property of being *ṅit* may apply by the rule *sārvadhātukam apit*, and that the prohibition [of Guṇa] by the rule *ṅiti* may take effect—as in the forms *kuṣāṇa* and *puṣāṇa*. To this, he replies: The application of the *śit* marker to the substitute for *śnā* is redundant because it is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). [The purpose of] applying the *śit* marker to the substitute for *śnā*...

[The objection: It is purposeless. Why? Because it would be *sthānivat* (like its original). This substitute [for *śnā*] will be *śit* by virtue of the status of being *sthānivat*. [The response: But the meaningfulness of the *śit*-marker is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that in the case of a substitute for a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, the *anubandha* does not behave as *sthānivat*. Indeed, the application of the *śit*-marker to the modification of *śnā* is meaningful. What is its purpose? It is for the sake of providing an indicator. What is indicated? The Teacher indicates this: that in the case of a substitute for a *sārvadhātuka* suffix...

"Anubandhas do not function as *sthānivats*. What is the purpose of making this known? The purpose is that the *hit* and *ataṅ* suffixes are not considered *pit*. The *pit*-ness of *hi* need not be prohibited. This substitute would be considered *pit* by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva*; however, since "anubandhas do not function as *sthānivats* in the case of a substitute for a *sārvadhātuka* suffix," this [substitute] will not be *pit*.

And in the case of the suffix *tāt*, the letter *ṅ* is not to be pronounced. This substitute *pit* (having *p* as its marker) would become *pit* by virtue of being "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*). However, since markers (*anubandha*) do not function as "as if they were the original" when they belong to a substitute for a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, this will not be considered *pit*. Furthermore, the property of being *ṅit* applies to the *tab* group of suffixes; indeed, the purpose [of the marker] is that the *tab* group of suffixes possess the quality of *ṅit*. For example: *śṛṇota grāvāṇaḥ* ("Listen, O pressing-stones!"). [This is because the suffix is] *ṅit*.

These substitutes would be marked with the *ṅ*-sign (*ṅit*) by virtue of being *sthānivadbhāva* (behaving like the original). However, since the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) do not persist in a substitute for a *sārvadhātuka* affix, these [substitutes] do not become *ṅit*. The fault of this rule is that the *pit* designation is absent in the substitute for *mip*. This is the defect of this grammatical principle: the absence of the *pit* designation in the substitute for *mip*, as in *acinavam*, *asunavam*, and *akaravam*; for this [substitute] is *pit*.

The substitute would be marked with the *pit* designation due to its being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). However, since markers (*anubandha*) do not function as *sthānivat* when they belong to a substitute for a *sārvadhātuka* affix, this [substitute] would not be marked with *pit*. This statement is too narrow; it should be stated that "the substitutes for *tip*, *sip*, and *mip* [are not *sthānivat*].

[Examples are: *veda* and *vettha*. Regarding the rule "the *śit* designation for the *vasu* following *vid*"—the *śit* designation must be stated for the *vasu* following the root *vid*. [This is because] of the *śit* [designation].

This substitute would be treated as having the marker *p* (pit) due to the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*. Since markers (*anubandha*) do not function as *sthānivat* when they belong to a substitute for a *sārvadhātuka* affix, this [substitute] would not be treated as having the marker *ś* (śit). Alternatively, it is established by the employment of the marker *k* (kit). Or rather, the marker *k* must necessarily be attached here in order to prevent the obstruction of the general reference (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*). Where is there need for the marker *k* to prevent the obstruction of the general reference? [In the rule: "There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the final vowel of the element ending in *vas*."
By that very effort, no merit will be gained. This indicator (jñāpaka) has faults; it has purposes.
The faults are equal or greater [than the purposes]. Therefore, there is no purpose served by this indicator. How so?

Those purposes which are achieved are accomplished simply through the formal rule (nyāsa). Even so, it might be argued that [the desired result] would occur by virtue of the power of the designation *pit*, or by virtue of the power of the designation *ṅit*.
That which is designated as *ṅit* when it follows a *pit* [suffix]—and that which is designated as *pit* when it follows a *ṅit* [suffix]—by what means would that not occur?

Therefore, it must be stated: "A *pit* suffix does not behave like a *ṅit*, nor does a *ṅit* suffix behave like a *pit*. It need not be so stated. I shall express it thus: "The *sārvadhātuka* suffix is *ṅit*, but not *pit*. In this way, first, the *ṅit*-status of a *pit* suffix is prohibited.
Therefore, because it is not a *saṃyoga*, the *liṭ* suffix is *kit*; thus, it is neither *ṅit* nor *pit*. In this way, the *pit*-status of a *ṅit* suffix is prohibited.
(Pāṇini 3.1.84) It should be stated: "The suffix *śāyac* occurs everywhere in the Vedic language. Wherever? Everywhere.

And *ahau* and *aha*. What is the purpose? [The forms] *mahī askabhāyat*, *yaḥ askabhāyat*, *udgṛbhāyata*, and *unmathāyata*—these are for the sake of that meaning. (Pāṇini 3.1.85) A separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made: "There is a transposition (*vyatyaya*) of the *si*-class suffixes. [Thus we have] *āṇḍā śuṣṇasya bhṝdati*.
When *bhinatti* (he pierces) was expected, [the text has *bhinte*]; when *mriyate* (he dies) was expected, [the text has *na mriyate*]. Thence, "variously" (*bahulam*).
In the domain of the Vedic language (*chandas*), all grammatical rules apply variously. There is the transposition of case endings (*supām vyatyayaḥ*);

the transposition of verbal suffixes (*tiṅām vyatyayaḥ*); the transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyayaḥ*); the transposition of gender (*liṅgavyatyayaḥ*); the transposition of tense (*kālavyatyayaḥ*); the transposition of person (*puruṣavyatyayaḥ*); and the transposition of voice (*ātmanepadavyatyayaḥ*).

There is the transposition of *parasmaipada* endings; there is the transposition of case-endings (*sup*). "The mother was yoked to the pole of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)"—where "in the sacrificial fee" (*dakṣiṇāyām*) would have been expected. There is the transposition of verbal endings (*tiṅ*): "those who fashion the top-ring for the horse-sacrifice pillar" (*aśvayūpāya takṣati*)—where "they fashion" (*takṣanti*) would have been expected. There is the transposition of phonemes (*varṇa*): "the *triṣṭubh* [verse], powerful, adorned with fierce heroes"—where "well-endowed" (*suhitam*) would have been expected. There is the transposition of gender (*liṅga*).
"He takes from honey" (*madhoḥ gṛhṇāti*); "they sit as if satiated with honey" (*madhoḥ tṛptā iva āsate*). Where *madhunaḥ* was expected, there is a change of time (*kālavyatyaya*).

"By one who intends to establish the sacred fires tomorrow" (*śvaḥ agnīn ādhāsyamānena*), "by one who intends to sacrifice with Soma tomorrow" (*śvaḥ somena yakṣyamāṇena*). Where "the establisher" (*ādhātā*) and "the sacrificer" (*yaṣṭā*) were expected, there is a change of person (*puruṣavyatyaya*). "Then he might be separated from his ten heroes" (*adhā sa vīraiḥ daśabhir viyūyāḥ*). Where *viyūyāt* was expected, there is a change of voice (*ātmanepadavyatyaya*).

He desires [the form] *brahmacāriṇam icchate*. Although *icchati* was expected, there is an exchange of the *parasmaipada* (active voice). Another wave [of grammatical variation] fights against [the norm]. Although *yudhyate* was expected, the author of the treatise intends an exchange of these: of the suffixes (*suptiṅ*), the auxiliary verbs (*upagraha*), gender (*liṅga*), number (*nara*), tense (*kāla*), the suffix *hal*, accent (*svara*), the agent (*kartṛ*), and the *yaṅ* affix. And that too is established by means of the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*).

(P_3,1.86) This suffix *aṅ* is prescribed in the sense of benediction (*āśis*). What is its purpose? The purpose of *aṅ* in the sense of benediction is [to apply] to the roots *sthā*, *gā*, *gam*, *vac*, and *vid*. *sthā*: "May I attend upon the bull" (*upa stheṣam vṛṣabham*). *gā*: "May I truly approach with sincerity" (*añjasā satyam upa geṣam*). *gami*: [example follows].
Through sacrifice may I attain a firm foundation. *gami* (I shall go). *vaci* (to speak): "May we utter the mantra to Agni. *vaci*. *vidi* (to know):
"May I find her who has entered my mind. It should be stated that *śaki* and *ruhaḥ* [take the suffix *aṅ*]. "May we be able to kindle you.
"May we ascend the flowing river for our well-being. *dṛśoḥ* (in the two eyes): "May I behold the father and the mother. *dṛśoḥ* ak.

It should be stated [as a rule] for the purpose that one might see both father and mother, thinking, "Let us attend upon them here. The suffix *āṭ* must also be stated; it is not established by the *aṅ* augment alone. It need not be stated: because of its status as a *sārvadhātuka*, there is the elision of *s*; because of its status as an *ārdhadhātuka*, there is the change to *e*.
In this case, it is established because it possesses the characteristics of both.

(P_3,1.87.1) KA_II,66.2–8 Ro_III, 162–164: What is the purpose of employing the term *vat*? So that [the operation] may also apply to its own locus (*svāśraya*), as in "it is split by a granary" (*bhidyate kuśūlena*). This is so that the suffix *la* may occur according to the rule "for intransitive verbs, *la* occurs in the sense of the action" (*akarmakāṇām bhāve laḥ*). Why is it said "by the object" (*karmaṇā*)? [To exclude cases involving] the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

Let it not be that an agent whose action is equal [to that of the object] is treated like the object—as in: "The sword cuts well" (*sādhu asis chinatti*) or "The pot cooks well" (*sādhu sthālī pacati*). Why is the phrase "whose action is equal" (*tulyakriyaḥ*) stated? [Consider: "Devadatta cooks rice" (*pacati odanaṃ devadattaḥ*). Even if "whose action is equal" were stated, [the rule] would still apply here; for even in this case, the agent has an action equal to that of the object. [But this is not desired,] because of the inclusion of the term "equal action."

164–167. *Karmavat akarmakasya kartā* (The agent of an intransitive verb is treated like the object). It should be stated that "the agent of an intransitive verb becomes like the object. What is the purpose? So that the agent of a transitive verb does not become like the object. For example: *bhidyamānaḥ kuśūlaḥ pātrāṇi bhinatti* ("The granary, being split, splits the vessels"). Likewise, [the rule applies] if it is seen as an object within the same verbal root (*samānadhātu*). That is, if it is seen as an object within the same verbal root.

Thus it should be stated. Let it not be so here: *pacati odanaṃ devadattaḥ* (Devadatta cooks the rice); *rādhyati odanaḥ svayam eva* (the rice ripens by itself). Likewise, for roots whose state (*bhāva*) resides in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka*) and those whose action (*kriyā*) resides in the object (*karmasthakriyā*), it should be stated: "The agent (*kartṛ*) of roots whose state or action resides in the object becomes like the object (*karmavat*). [This does not apply] to those whose state or action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka* or *kartṛsthakriyā*).

[The objection: "Let it not be that the agent [of an intransitive verb] behaves like the object. As for what was said—that it must be stated that "the agent of an intransitive verb behaves like the object"—it need not be stated. This will be explained [later]: "There is a prohibition for transitive verbs, as in the case of 'they embrace each other' (*anyonyam āśliṣyataḥ*). Furthermore, as for what was said—that it must be stated "if the object is seen within the same verbal root" (*samānadhātau*)—[that too is unnecessary].

It should not be stated [that "of the root" is understood]. The word "dhātoḥ" (of the root) is understood [from the previous rule]. This treatment as the object (*karmavadbhāva*) is extended to the case where a root has an agent who is simultaneously its object. There, by virtue of the connection, this must be understood: "if the agent of a root is that which was its object. It is just as in the case of the rule "the suffix *aṇ* occurs after a root when there is an object"; there, by virtue of the connection, it is understood that it applies to the root whose object [is the agent].

Regarding the phrase "that which is the object" (*yat karma*): let it not apply here in cases such as *āhara kumbham* ("bring the jar") or *karoti kaṭam* ("he makes a mat"). Furthermore, as for what is said—that "the agent of verbs whose state or action resides in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka* or *karmasthakriyā*) is treated like the object"—it should be stated that this is so that the agent of verbs whose state or action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka* or *kartṛsthakriyā*) shall not be treated like the object. It need not be stated; for by means of an action residing in the object, this [agent]... [is understood].

[The agent] compares [it]. Furthermore, for verbal roots whose state (*bhāva*) resides in the agent or whose action (*kriyā*) resides in the agent, there is no occurrence of the action with respect to the object (*karman*).

(P_3.1.87.3) KA_II,67.3-9 Ro_III, 167 But then, in the case of a reflexive object (*karmakartṛ*), does [the action] reside solely in the object, or does it also reside in the agent? What [is the case]?

And therefore: if the rules for *caṅ*, *śap*, and *kṛt* suffixes apply only when the action is based on the object (*karmāśraya*), these would not be established. Regarding *caṅ*: *acīkarata kaṭaḥ svayam eva* ("the mat made itself"). Regarding *śap*: *namate daṇḍaḥ svayam eva* ("the staff bends itself"). Regarding the rule for *kṛt* suffixes: *bhiduram kāṣṭham svayam eva* ("the wood splits itself"). If, however, [these rules] are established even when the action is based on the agent (*kartṛāśraya*), then what is the problem? It is this: the prohibition of the rules for *ātmanepada* endings, *śap*, and so forth.
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) should be prescribed, and the prohibition [of *śap*] for roots beginning with *śo* must be stated. Both are accomplished precisely in the *Nyāsa*.
Why, then, is this stated? Because even in the case of a reflexive object (*karmakartṛ*), agency is intended on account of independence (*svātantrya*).

Agency exists in the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*). Why? Because independence (*svātantrya*) is intended to be expressed. Here, the agent is intended to be expressed precisely by way of its independence. But is this an expression of an existing independence, or is it merely an intention to express it? He says: "of an existing one. How is this known? From the example: "The grain is split by itself" (*bhidyate kuśūlena*). And no other agent is perceived.

Furthermore, action is perceived. Moreover, sir, must an agent of action necessarily possess a physical body, such that even wind, heat, and time could not be agents? This would be established if one of these—wind, heat, or time—were the agent.
But as for that granary which, being recently made, splits in a place free from wind and rain, what is its [agent]?

There is no agent other than this granary. Even if it could be argued that there is no other agent in that case, how could it not be so here when it is said, "The field is being reaped by itself," while Devadatta is seen running about on all sides with a sickle in his hand? In this case too, there is that very ease [of the action].
Its name is not anything other than that; there is no agent other than the field. There is a purpose for this. What is it?

In that case, there is the extension of the "object-like" status (*karmavad-anudeśa*) to that which ends in *l*. In that case, the extension of the "object-like" status must be stated for that which ends in *l*;
it must be said that "the agent of that which ends in *l* becomes like the object. Otherwise, in the case of *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal-artha* suffixes...
This is a prohibition. For if the mention of the term *l* (the personal endings) were not made, a prohibition would have to be stated regarding the *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal-artha* suffixes.

Regarding the *kṛtya*: in the case of "the granary is to be split" (*bhettavyaḥ kuśūlaḥ*), where the object is expressed, when that [object] is intended to be expressed as independent, it would undergo the status of being like an agent (*karmavadbhāva*). A prohibition of that must be stated. When that [status] is prohibited, [the rule applies] to intransitive verbs (*akarmaka*).

Since *kṛtya* suffixes occur in the sense of the action (*bhāve*), [the rule] should apply to the action, as in "it is to be broken by the granary" (*bhettavyaṃ kuśūlena*). However, when the *kta* suffix is used, as in "the granary is broken" (*bhinnaḥ kuśūlaḥ*), it denotes the object (*karman*). When that [granary] is intended to be expressed with independence (*svātantryeṇa*), then it should undergo the treatment of an object (*karmavadbhāva*).
A prohibition of that must be stated. When that is prohibited, the *kta* suffix occurs in the sense of the action for intransitive verbs (*akarmakāṇām*).

Thus, so that the suffix *kta* may occur in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), [the rule] is stated. For example: *bhinnaṃ kuśūlena* ("split by means of a granary"). The sense of the suffix *khal* is as follows: "the granary is easily split" (*īṣadbhedyaḥ kuśūlaḥ*). This is the object (*karman*). When that [granary] is intended to be expressed as the agent (*svātantryeṇa*) due to its independence, then it would undergo the treatment of an object (*karmavadbhāvaḥ*). A prohibition of that must be stated. When that [treatment] is prohibited, since the suffix *khal* occurs in the sense of an abstract state for intransitive verbs (*akarmakāṇām*), it should occur in the sense of an abstract state.

"It can be distinguished slightly by means of the *kuśūla*. [Objection: "In that case, then, the mention of *la* (the marker for the optative) must be made. [Reply: "It need not be made; it is already accomplished in the *Nyāsa* itself.
In the rule *liṅi āśiṣy aṅ*, the mention contains two *l*s. But it is established because it is an original object (*prākṛta-karman*).
This is established. How? Because it is an original object. This very thing is an original object, just like 'a mat' (*kaṭam*)."

"He makes a cart," "he makes. But how is it known that this action is indeed *prākṛta* (inherent)? Because an action is observed in the case of an agent who is not [otherwise] an object when there is contact with the self (*ātmasaṃyoga*). An action is observed in the case of an agent who is not [otherwise] an object when there is contact with the self. Where? In "he kills himself" (*hanty ātmānam*) and "he is killed by himself" (*hanyata ātmanā*). This is an unequal comparison. In "he kills himself," an object is observed.

An agent is not perceived. [In the phrase] "it is killed by itself," an agent is perceived; yet no object of action is perceived. Furthermore, there is an elision of words (*padalopa*). One must recognize this elision of words: [the full sense is] "it kills itself by itself" or "it is killed by itself. But who is it that kills itself, or who is it that is killed by itself? There are two selves: the inner self (*antarātman*) and the bodily self (*śarīrātman*).

The inner self (*antarātman*) performs that action by which the bodily self (*śarīrātman*) experiences pleasure and pain; the bodily self performs that action by which the inner self experiences pleasure and pain.
172–176. Prohibition for transitive verbs: "They embrace each other.

A prohibition must be stated regarding transitive verbs. What is the purpose? [To exclude cases such as] "they embrace each other," "they touch each other," or "they seize each other. Alternatively, the mention of the transitive verb *tap* (to heat) is for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyama*). Or rather, it concerns the transitive verb *tap*.

The statement will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): [it applies] only to the root *tap* when it has an object, and not to any other transitive root. But then it would apply even to that [root *ut-tap*] which has a different object, as in: "The goldsmith heats the gold" (*uttapati suvarṇaṃ suvarṇakāraḥ*). [And one might say: "The gold being heated heats the goldsmith" (*uttapyamānaṃ suvarṇaṃ suvarṇakāram uttapati*). And for that [root *ut-tap*], it would apply only when *tapas* is the object. And for that [root *ut-tap*] when *tapas* is the object...

In this way, the agent becomes like the object, and not [like] that which has another object. What is this "tapaḥ"? This *askāra* suffix is derived from the root *tap-* by means of an *uṇādi* suffix, and it functions as a noun denoting an abstract state (*bhāva*). What is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)? What is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*)? It is simply "the act of heating" (*santapaḥ*).
But how can the very same thing be both the meaning of the base and the meaning of the suffix? [This is so] because of the general sense of the root *tap-*.

The heating of a part (*avayavatāpa*) becomes the object (*karman*). For example: "He nourished these [parts]—the nourishment of cattle, the nourishment of horses, the nourishment of wealth. The heating of a whole (*avayavitāpa*) is the object of the general act of heating (*sāmānyatapa*); likewise here too, the heating of a part is the object of the general act of heating.
[The rule] *duhipacyor bahulaṃ sakarmakayoḥ* applies to the roots *duh* and *pac* when they are transitive (*sakarmaka*). That is, for *duh* and *pac* when they take an object...

It should be stated that "the agent [of the causative] frequently behaves like the object [of the primary verb]. For example: *gaur dugdhe payaḥ* ("The cow yields milk") and *tasmād udumbaraḥ sa lohitam phalam pacyate* ("Therefore, that *udumbara* tree ripens red fruit"). What is the purpose of the word "frequently" (*bahula*)? It is for the sake of the *parasmaipada* (active voice). If this is so, there is no need for the word "frequently," for the *parasmaipada* is not intended here. Rather, it is the *śyan* suffix that applies to the roots *sṛj* and *yuj*. [This applies] to *sṛj* and *yuj*.

It should be stated that for two transitive roots, the agent (*kartṛ*) frequently behaves like the object (*karmavat*). However, the suffix *śyan* occurs [in this case]. For the root *sṛj*, when the agent is endowed with faith (*śraddhopapanne*), the behavior like the object should be prescribed for the sake of the *ciṇ* affix and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*): *sṛjyate mālām* (he creates a garland) and *asarji mālām* (he created a garland). But for the root *yaj*, in the case of a legitimate reflexive object-agent (*nyāyye karmakartari*), it is for the sake of the absence of the *yak* affix: *yujyate brahmacārī yogam* (the student applies himself to yoga).

An agent whose action is similar to that of an instrument [is often treated] like an object. It should be stated: "An agent whose action is similar to that of an instrument is frequently treated like an object. For example: *parivārayanti vṛkṣaṃ kaṇṭakaiḥ* ("They surround the tree with thorns") and *parivārayante vṛkṣaṃ kaṇṭakāḥ* ("The thorns surround the tree"). There is a prohibition for verbs such as *sravati* ("to flow"). It should be stated that there is a prohibition for verbs such as *sravati*. For example: *sravati kuṇḍikā* ("The water-pot flows").
"Water flows from the water-pot; the roof-tiles flow [water]; water flows from the roof-tiles.

In that case, a prohibition must be stated. It need not be stated. For it is said, "that which has the same action [as the agent]," yet here a different action is understood. In the first instance, "the water-pot flows water," it means "it releases [water]."

"It is understood as 'it goes' when one says, 'the water flows from the pitcher' (*kuṇḍikāyā udakaṃ sravati*); it is understood as 'it comes out' [when one says, 'the water flows from the pitcher']. It is understood as 'they let loose' when one says, 'the roof-tiles shed water' (*valīkāni udakaṃ sravanti*); it is understood as 'it falls' when one says, 'the water flows from the roof-tiles' (*valīkebhya udakaṃ sravati*). [The suffix *śatṛ* is used] after verbs meaning 'to adorn,' 'to scatter,' and 'to strive,' except when the *ātmanepada* is employed. [And also after verbs meaning 'to adorn,' 'to scatter,' and 'to strive.']

The prohibition must be stated except in the case of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). The maiden adorns herself. The maiden desired to adorn herself. The maiden decks herself. The maiden decked herself.
[The root] *kṛ* (to scatter): The elephant scatters [dust] upon himself. The elephant scattered [dust] upon himself. [With the desiderative suffix] *saN*: The mat desires to be made.
The mat wished to be made by itself; [the mat] wished to be made by itself.

(P_3.1.89) Regarding the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ*, there is an addition [to the rule] for the causative suffix *ṇic* and the roots *śri*, *brū*, and *ñi*. Regarding the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ*...

An addition must be made [to the rule] regarding roots ending in the causative suffix *ṇi*, as well as for *śri* and *brū*: *ṇi*: "The mat makes itself" (*kārayate kaṭaḥ svayam eva*); "The mat caused itself to be made" (*acīkarata kaṭaḥ svayam eva*).

*ṇi śri*: "The staff raises itself" (*ucchrayate daṇḍaḥ svayam eva*); "The staff raised itself" (*udaśiśriyata daṇḍaḥ svayam eva*). *śri brūñ*: "The story tells itself" (*brūte kathā svayam eva*); "The story told itself" (*avocata kathā svayam eva*). [Thus say] the followers of Bhāradvāja.

They recite [the following]: "In the prohibition regarding *yak* and *ciṇ*, there is an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the roots *ṇi*, *śri*, *granthi*, *brū*, and those that are *ātmanepada* and intransitive.

(Pāṇini 3.1.90) Regarding the rule for the application of *śyan* after the roots *kuṣ* and *rañj*, there is the mention of "sārvadhātuka" [in the sūtra]. In the rule for the application of *śyan* after *kuṣ* and *rañj*, the term "sārvadhātuka" is included.
It must be stated [that the term *sārvadhātuka* applies here]. For if it were not stated, there would be a prohibition regarding the *liṅ* and *liṭ* [affixes].

Indeed, if the mention of *sārvadhātuka* were not made, a prohibition would have to be formulated for the *liṅ* and *liṭ* [affixes]: "The foot healed itself" (*cukuṣe pādaḥ svayam eva*); "the garment colored itself" (*rarañje vastram svayam eva*);
"may the foot heal itself" (*koṣiṣīṣṭa pādaḥ svayam eva*); "may the garment color itself" (*raṅkṣīṣṭa vastram svayam eva*). Even when the mention of *sārvadhātuka* is made...
In this case, it follows [that a rule applies]. How many black feet are there here? It follows that *śyan* would subvert the application of *sy*-class suffixes:

*koṣiṣyate pādaḥ svayam eva* ("the foot will expand by itself"), *rañkṣyate vastram svayam eva* ("the garment will color itself"), *akoṣi pādaḥ svayam eva* ("the foot expanded by itself"), *arañji vastram svayam eva* ("the garment colored itself"). As for what was said—that the mention of *sārvadhātuka* must be made—it has already been established.

It follows [from the previous rule]. Where was it introduced? In the rule *sārvadhātuke yak* ("the affix *yak* occurs before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix"). If that is what follows, is there a conjunction (*samuccaya*) in the preceding rule, meaning "before *le* and before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix"? Or is the mention of *le* a qualifier of *sārvadhātuka*? What follows from this? If it is a conjunction, then [the affix *yak*] would also apply here in the case of *kati iha bhindānāḥ kuśūlāḥ*.

Now, if the mention of *l* is a qualifier of the *sārvadhātuka* [affix], it would not apply to the *liṅ* and *liṭ* [moods]. For example, in the cases "the granary split by itself" (*bibhide kuśūlaḥ svayam eva*) and "may the granary split by itself" (*bhitsīṣṭa kuśūlaḥ svayam eva*). Let it be that the mention of *l* is a qualifier of the *sārvadhātuka*.
But was it not said that it would not apply to the *liṅ* and *liṭ*? The mention of *liṅ* and *liṭ* also follows as a contextual remainder from what precedes.

Where is the subject under discussion? It is: "After which suffixes does *ām* occur—after *liṭ*, *liṅ* in the sense of benediction (*āśis*), and after *āṅ* when not used in a mantra. By doing so, that objection which was raised—"the form *kati iha kuṣṇāṇāḥ pādāḥ* would result"—is also rendered faultless. For here too, the mention of *sārvadhātuka* qualified by *la* continues to apply. As for what was further stated—that there would be an exclusion (*bādhanam*) of *syādi* suffixes by *śyan*—that also does not hold.

I shall explain *śyan* by way of its connection with the prohibition of *yak*. [Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.89: "The affixes *yak* and *ciṇ* are not used after the roots *duh*, *snū*, and *nam*. Then [3.1.90]: "After the roots *kuṣ* and *rañj*, according to the Eastern grammarians, *yak* and *ciṇ* do not occur. Then [3.1.69]: "*śyan* and the Parasmaipada endings [occur after the roots of the fourth class]. In that case, just as *śyan* occurs in the domain of *yak*, it would likewise apply in the domain of *ciṇ*. [Thus one would get] *akoṣi pādaḥ svayam eva* ("the foot was scratched by itself") and *arañji* ("it was colored").

"Regarding the word *vastraṃ svayam eva*. If that is so, then a second *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) will be made: "The *ciṇ* affix does not occur after the roots *duh*, *snū*, and *nam*. Then: "The *yak* affix also does not occur after *duh*, *snū*, and *nam*. Then: "The *yak* affix does not occur after the roots *kuṣ* and *rañj* according to the Eastern grammarians. Then: "The *śyan* affix and the *parasmaipada* endings [occur]. Alternatively, an *anuvṛtti* (carrying over of a previous rule) will be performed: "*syatāsī*"...

Regarding *lṛ* and *luṭ*: [Pāṇini 3.1.43] *cli luṅi* [states that] *sic* is substituted for *cli* in the *luṅ* [tense]. Regarding the agent (*kartṛ*): [Pāṇini 3.1.68] *śap syatāsī lṛluṭoḥ* [states that] *śap* is added; [Pāṇini 3.1.43] *cli luṅi* [states that] *sic* is substituted for *cli* in the *luṅ*. Regarding *kuṣ* and *rañj*: [Pāṇini 3.1.90] *kuṣirajoḥ prācām śyan parasmaipadam ca* [states that] *śyan* is added and the *parasmaipada* is used; [Pāṇini 3.1.43] *cli luṅi* [states that] *sic* is substituted for *cli* in the *luṅ*.
Alternatively, the *syat* suffixes and others are *antaraṅga*. What is their *antaraṅga* status? It is their presence at the stage of the *lakāra* (the verbal suffix).
Thus [the suffixes] sya and so forth [are introduced]. Before a sārvadhātuka [affix], the suffix śyan is applied.

(Pāṇini 3.1.69) From what point does this governing heading (adhikāra) of "dhātu" (verbal root) extend? Does it extend prior to the substitution of l-substitutes (lādeśa), or rather until the conclusion of the third chapter?

The governing authority of the verbal root (*dhātva-dhikāra*) extends prior to the substitution of *l* (the *l*-affixes). The governing authority of the verbal root extends prior to the substitution of *l*. For if it were [extended] to the substitution of *l*, there would be non-application due to intervention. Indeed, if the substitution of *l* were still in force while the governing authority of the verbal root continued, there would be non-application because of the intervention. And what would happen? In the first rule, the *tiṅ* affixes would not occur when there is intervention. This is because in the first rule, they would be separated by the *vikaraṇa* affixes.

The *tiṅ* suffixes would not occur [in their proper place]. In "pacati" and "paṭhati," this must be deliberated: should the *vikaraṇas* be applied first, or the substitutes (*ādeśas*)? What should be done here? The substitutes, because they are subsequent. The *vikaraṇas* are permanent (*nitya*). They apply whether the substitutes have been made or not yet made. Because they are permanent, once the *vikaraṇas* have been applied, the substitutes [cannot apply] because they are separated by the *vikaraṇas*.
[The substitutes] do not obtain. [Objection: Then the substitutes would have no scope. [Response: The substitutes do have scope. What is that scope?

It is those [suffixes] which have *luk* as their *vikaraṇa*, those which have *ślu* as their *vikaraṇa*, and the *liṅ* and *liṭ* [tenses]. The substitution of *et* for the final vowel (*ṭi*) would not occur when [the suffix] prescribes something for those [suffixes] marked with *ṭ*. Furthermore, the substitution of *et* prescribed for those marked with the technical term *ṭit* would also not occur because it is intervened by the *vikaraṇas*. [This applies to] *eś*.

The status of being *śit* [must be applied]. The letter *e* should be designated as *śit*. What is the purpose? So that, by the rule "that which is *śit* replaces the whole," it may serve as a replacement for the entire [stem]. For if the letter *ś* were not employed, then after the substitution of *e* for the *t* of the following element according to the rule "from that, [the substitute takes the place] of the initial," there would result the undesirable consequence of hearing two *e*s. However, once the designation of *l* has been withdrawn and the governing heading of "root" (*dhātu*) is in force, the rule "of the final [element]" (*alaḥ antyasya*) applies.

Since the suffixes are prescribed [for the whole], there is no purpose for the singular ending of the word *eka*; therefore, even without the letter *ś*, it will become a substitute for the whole. Furthermore, that which is prescribed for the *loṭ* [imperative] would not apply because it is separated by the *vikaraṇas*. What, then, is that? It is: "The *loṭ* is like the *laṅ*; *e* becomes *u* after *si*; *hi* and the *apit* [augment] are optionally so in the Veda. That which...

Moreover, that which was stated regarding the *laṅ* and *liṅ* [tenses] would not apply. What, then, is that? It is: "After a root ending in *ṅ*, and after *ita*, [the substitutes] for *tas*, *thas*, *tha*, and *mip* are always *tām*, *tām*, *tām*; for the *liṅ* [optative], *sīyuṭ* is added; and in the *parasmaipada* [voices], *yāsuṭ* is added, which is acute-accented and marked with *ṅ*. Therefore, the governing rule for roots (*dhātvadhikāra*) applies prior to the substitution of the *l*-suffixes. If the governing rule for roots applies prior to the substitution of the *l*-suffixes, then the vowel *a* must be designated as having the *śit* marker. What is the purpose of this?

The rule *śit sarvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.55) ensures that [the substitute] replaces the whole [stem]. However, while the governing context of the affix *l* (*lādeśa*) and the governing context of the verbal root (*dhātvadhikāra*) are still in effect, the rule *tasmād ity uttarasya ādeḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.54–57) would apply; thus, when the substitution of *a* for the letter *th* is made, the resulting form would be established by the single-substitute rule (*pararūpa*) between the two *a*s, as in *peca yūyam* and *cakratha yūyam*. But surely, even if the governing context of the affix *l* and the governing context of the verbal root have ceased?

Since rules apply to the final [element], there would be no purpose for the mention of the letter *a* (in the rule *alo’ntyasya*) as being replaced by *a*; thus, even without the letter *ś*, it would become a replacement for the whole word (*sarvādeśa*). However, there is another purpose for the mention of *a* in place of *a*. What is it? He will state this: "The mention of *a* in place of *a* is for the sake of ensuring an equal number [of elements]."

Regarding the technical designation *ārdhadhātuka*, the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) must be made so that the designation *ārdhadhātuka* applies only to what follows a root. It should not apply here in cases such as *vṛkṣatvam* and *vṛkṣatā*. Therefore, the governing rule for roots (*dhātvadhikāra*) must be carried over into the section concerning substitutes for *l*-suffixes. But was it not already stated in the first [section]?

"If [the suffixes] *tiṅ* are not to occur in the case of *yoga* (conjunction) or *vyavāya* (separation)," [it is argued]. This is not a fault. This is established through sequential order (*ānupūrvyāt*). Here, the *vikaraṇa* suffixes do not apply before the substitutes (*ādeśa*) have been made. What is the reason? The *vikaraṇa* suffixes are prescribed for the *sārvadhātuka* [suffixes].
And the status of being *sārvadhātuka* does not exist when the substitutes have not yet been made. As for those [suffixes] which are not prescribed under this specific condition—

But what are those *syādi* suffixes? In that case as well, the mention of "dhātu" (root) is a qualifier of what is prescribed (*vihita-viśeṣaṇa*). [The meaning is: "of the *la* suffix prescribed after a root. If this is so, then in the case of *vindati*, the *ṇal* and other suffixes would result. We shall, however, qualify what is prescribed by the root with the specific root *vid*, and [qualify] the immediate succession (*ānantarya*) by means of *vid*. [The meaning is: "of the *la* suffix prescribed after a root, which is immediately followed by *vid*. In that case, here [in the example] *ajakṣiṣyan*...

In the case of *ajāgar-iṣan*, the substitution of *jus* for *jhi* after a reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*) would apply; however, we shall qualify that which is prescribed by the root (*dhātu*) as being immediate (*ānantarya*) with respect to the reduplicated stem—that is, [the substitute applies] to that which is prescribed after a root and is immediately following a reduplicated stem. But how will you qualify [the rule] in the case of *ātaḥ*? If, first of all, the mention of "root" (*dhātugrahaṇa*) is a qualifier of "prescribed" (*vihita*).

If the mention of *ākāra* is a qualifier of immediate succession (*ānantarya*), then it would also apply here in the case of *alunāt*. Now, if the mention of *ākāra* is a qualifier of what is prescribed (*vihita*) and the mention of *dhātu* is a qualifier of immediate succession, then it would also apply here in the case of *apibat*. Let it be, then, that the mention of *dhātu* is a qualifier of what is prescribed and the mention of *ākāra* is a qualifier of immediate succession. But was it not already stated?
[Objection: In this case as well, [the substitution of] *alunaḥ* would result. [Reply: This is not a fault. Once the elision (*lopa*) has been performed, it will not occur.

[Objection: Elision does not apply here. [Question: For what reason? [Reply: It is superseded by the substitution of *ī*. [Objection: The substitution of *ī* does not apply here. [Question: For what reason? [Reply: It is superseded by the substitution of *ant*.

In this case, the substitution of *anti* would not apply. What is the reason? It is sublated by the substitution of *jus*. In this case, the substitution of *jus* would not apply. What is the reason? It is sublated by elision (*lopa*). Elision is sublated by the substitution of *ī*; the substitution of *ī* is sublated by the substitution of *anti*; the substitution of *anti* is sublated by the substitution of *jus*; and the substitution of *jus* is sublated by elision. Thus, a circularity (*cakraka*) and a lack of finality (*avyavasthā*) would result. There is no such contingency of circularity.

For a grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) cannot be one that fails to establish a fixed rule; indeed, a treatise must be one that establishes a fixed rule. And here, it is not possible for [the substitute] *hal* and so forth to remain even for a moment; at that very point, there must be the state of *antibhāva*. Once *antibhāva* has occurred, there is elision (*lopa*). Through elision, the establishment of the rule will be achieved. As for what was said regarding the *śit*-nature of *eś*:
Thus it is done in the very *nyāsa*.
What, then, are the purposes (*prayojana*) of this rule? The purpose is the prohibition [of the application of the suffix] to nominal stems (*prātipadika*).

The purpose [of the prohibition] is to prevent [the application of suffixes] to nominal stems (*prātipadika*). [The rule] "the suffixes *tavya* and so on [should apply] after a verbal root (*dhātu*)" is intended so that they do not apply after a nominal stem. This is not a valid purpose. The suffixes *tavya* and so on are prescribed with respect to the instrument (*sādhana*), and the instrument belongs to the action (*kriyā*). Since there is no action, there is no instrument. Because there is no instrument, even in the absence of the governing heading for verbal roots (*dhātu-adhikāra*), [the suffixes would not apply] after a nominal stem.

The suffixes beginning with *tavya* will not occur [in cases such as *svaptavyam*]. [Objection: Then there is a purpose in the case of roots beginning with *svap*, such as *svapiti*; let it not be [erroneously] *supati*. [Response: And the designation *aṅga* is also a purpose. The designation *aṅga* is a purpose because, by the rule "that which precedes a suffix is called *aṅga* when a suffix follows," the designation *aṅga* for the root is established. And the designation *kṛt* is also [a purpose]. The designation *kṛt* is also [a purpose].

The purpose [of this rule] is as follows: the designation *kṛt* for a suffix prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*) becomes established; and the designation *upapada* is also a purpose. Furthermore, the designation *upapada* is established by the rule: "In this context governed by *dhātu*, that which is indicated by the locative case receives the designation *upapada*. As for the designations *kṛt* and *upapada*, they do not yet serve a purpose [at this stage].

These [rules] are established by virtue of the governing context (*adhikāra*). In that case, however, the designation "member of a complex" (*aṅga*) for roots such as *svap* is also a purpose [for the mention of *dhātu*]. The mention of *dhātu* is useless in the rule prescribing *yaṅ*, because the governing context of *dhātu* applies to the prescription of *yaṅ*. The mention of *dhātu* is useless. Why? Because the governing context of *dhātu* applies to the prescription of *yaṅ*. In the prescription of *yaṅ*, the mention of *dhātu* is carried over from the previous context; and it must necessarily be carried over.

For if there were no governing context (*anadhikāra*), there would be an absence of the designation "stem" (*aṅga*). However, the mention of the causal agent (*hetumat*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that [the suffix *ṇic*] does not occur elsewhere. That which...
By stating "and this [suffix] occurs when there is a cause," the Teacher indicates that the causative suffix *ṇic* does not occur from a mere verbal root (*dhātu*).

This is because, among the *kaṇḍū* and other such roots, the designation [of the group] applies as if it were a single individual entity (*vyapadeśivad-vacana*). Therefore, by stating "the suffix *yak* occurs after the roots *kaṇḍū* and others," he indicates [the following].

185–186. What is the purpose of including the word *stha*? If it were stated merely as "in that case, the *upapada* [is governed] by the locative," then [the rule] would apply only where the locative case is actually heard, such as in *stamberamaḥ* ("elephant") and *karṇejapaḥ* ("whisperer in the ear"), or where the designation is made by this very term [in a rule], such as in *saptamyām janeḥ ḍaḥ* ("after the root *jan*, when preceded by a word in the locative, the suffix *ḍa* is applied"). But in cases like *kumbhakāraḥ* ("potter") and *nagarakāraḥ* ("city-builder"), it would not apply. However, when the word *stha* is included, then wherever...

The locative case is heard both where it is explicitly stated and where it is not; it occurs wherever this word [“tatra”] provides the designation, as well as wherever it is indicated by another term. Since the rule is established simply by the presence of the locative case, what is the purpose of including the mention of “tatra”? The inclusion of “tatra” is for the sake of defining the scope. The scope is thus specified: within this governing context of verbal roots (dhātu-adhikāra), whatever is designated by the locative case—
Thus, it becomes designated as an *upapada*; in this way, the designation *upapada* is established.

Regarding the designation *upapada*, there must be a statement concerning its semantic competency (*samartha*). When the designation *upapada* is applied, the term "semantically competent" (*samartha*) must be included [in the rule].

It should be stated that a *upapada* must be semantically connected (*samartha*) with the suffix. This [restriction] should not apply here: *āhara kumbham* ("bring the jar") and *karoti kaṭam* ("he makes a mat"). Even if the term "semantically connected" (*samarthagrahaṇa*) were included, it would still apply in the case of *mahāntaṃ kumbhaṃ karoti* ("he makes a large jar"). [Objection: It should not apply in the case of *mahākumbhakāraḥ* ("a maker of large jars"). [Response: It should indeed apply when this is a single sentence (*vākya*).

It occurs as follows: *mahān kumbhaḥ* (a large jar), *mahākumbhaḥ* (a large jar); one who makes a *mahākumbha* is a *mahākumbhakāraḥ* (a maker of large jars). However, when the sentence is *mahāntaṃ kumbhaṃ karoti* (he makes a large jar), then [the compound] should not occur; yet it does occur then. To prevent it from occurring then, it is said: "The mention of *samartha* (semantic compatibility) must be made. But that is not necessary.

It must be stated [that the suffix *aṇ* is applied]. The term "from a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) is understood [from the previous rule]. The suffix *aṇ* occurs after a verbal root when there is an object (*karmani*). This is to be understood here through connection as follows: "of whichever verbal root there is an object. Furthermore, regarding the objection that even if the term "capable" (*samartha*) were included, the suffix would still apply in the case of "he makes a large jar" (*mahāntaṃ kumbhaṃ karoti*), [the answer is]: the designation "immediate constituent" (*upapada*) is a very extensive one.
It is being done. Furthermore, a name (*saṃjñā*) is not something to be made unnecessarily light. Why is this so? For the purpose of brevity is the reason for creating a name.

In that regard, the purpose of employing such a long name is so that it may be understood as a descriptive designation (*anvarthasaṃjñā*): "a word uttered near [another] is an *upapada*. And here, that which is uttered near is not necessarily a word, and that which is a word is not necessarily uttered near.

To the extent that there is currently the presence of a word (*pada*), this rule for words (*padavidhi*) applies. And a rule for words applies to those [words] that possess semantic capacity (*samartha*).
In this case, because there is no such capacity, it will not apply. Now, when a derivative ending in *cv-* is the attendant word (*upapada*), should the suffix *aṇ* occur? As in:
"He makes what was not a jar into a jar" (*akumbhaṃ kumbhaṃ karoti*), resulting in *kumbhīkaroti mṛdam*. It should not occur. What is the reason?

The suffix *cvi* is prescribed when there is the intention to express a change from the original state (*prakṛti*). That [suffix] is dependent [on another word]. And that which is dependent is semantically incapable (*asamartha*) [of forming a compound].
If that is so, then this would not occur now:
"I desire a maker of mats of *kāśa* grass" (*icchāmi ahaṃ kāśakaṭīkāram*). This is indeed desired by Gonardīya. Furthermore, there is the mention of the cause (*nimitta*).

And the mention of the "cause" (nimitta) must be made. It should be stated that the cause is the "governor word" (upapada) of the suffix. For if it were not mentioned, there would be the undesirable consequence of the suffix applying even when there is no governor word. Indeed, if the mention of the cause were not made, it would follow [that the suffix applies] even in the absence of a governor word. What, then, would be the purpose of the specific instruction now? The instruction is for the purpose of establishing a technical name (saṃjñā). When the suffix occurs upon a governor word...
"In that case, I shall explain the technical designation *upapada*. [Objection: "Then the mention of the cause (*nimitta*) must be made. [Response: "It need not be made.
The mention of 'therein' (*tatra*) is for the purpose of connecting it with the *upapada*. The mention of 'therein' is made;

it will serve to connect it with the *upapada*, such that the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed when there is an object (*karman*), provided that the suffix occurs therein. [Objection: "But surely it is something else?"

The purpose of the mention of *tatra* has been stated: what is it? That the mention of *tatra* is for the sake of specifying the domain (*viṣaya*). This is also established by virtue of the governing context (*adhikāra*). (P.
3.1.93) KA_II,77.2-17 Ro_III, 190-192 For what purpose is *atiṅ* [stated]? [In examples such as] *pacati karoti*. It could be said that *atiṅ* need not be mentioned. Why not?

[In examples such as] *bhavati*, *pacati*, and *karoti*, the designation *kṛt* applies to what follows a verbal root (*dhātu*). Furthermore, the governing rule for verbal roots (*dhātvadhikāra*) extends up to the point before the substitutes for *l* (the *lādeśa*). Even so, by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the designation *kṛt* would still apply [to the *l*]. For instance, when it is stated "not a *tiṅ*" (*atiṅ*), since there is the status of being a substitute, how is this [exclusion] established? It is established by the force of the explicit statement of the prohibition. Alternatively, [it refers to] the *lakāra* which is to become a *tiṅ*.
There is a prohibition of the designation *kṛt*. Furthermore, what would happen if the designation *kṛt* were applied here?

By the rule "a *kṛt*-affix forms a nominal stem" (*kṛt-prātipadika*), the designation *prātipadika* (nominal stem) would apply. Consequently, by the rule "after a nominal stem," the occurrence of case-endings (*svādi*) would follow. This is not a fault. Case-endings are prescribed for meanings such as singularity and so forth; and since those [meanings], namely singularity and so forth, are already expressed here by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), [the application of case-endings does not occur].

Since their meaning has already been expressed, the suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth will not occur. [Objection: In that case, let them not occur after a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*).
