[Response: That is not so. Because the suffix *ap* is taught [immediately] after the suffix *ṅīp*, the suffix *ap* would supersede the suffix *ṅīp*. [Objection: Even if the suffix *ap* were applied, there would be no fault, because the suffix *ṅīṣ* would apply by the rule "the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after the root *kṛ*. [Response: That is not so. Because the suffix *ap* is taught [immediately] after the suffix *ṅī

256–257. There is no establishment [of the technical terms] because of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) when they have already been established. What is this mutual dependence? The suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* must exist for the technical name (*sañjñā*) to apply, and by means of the technical name, the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* are brought into being. Thus, this results in mutual dependence; and things characterized by mutual dependence are not logically tenable.

The mention of *kta* and *ktavatu* should be stated twice. [Namely: "The suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* occur when an action is completed (*bhūte*)," and "The suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* are termed *niṣṭhā*. Alternatively, if the designation *niṣṭhā* were also stated right here—[namely: "The suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* occur when an action is completed; then they are *niṣṭhā*; and the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* receive the designation *niṣṭhā*"—what would be achieved?
It is so. Or rather, the mention of *kta* and *ktavat* need not be repeated twice. Even so, it would still have to be stated that "those two [are called *niṣṭhā*]";

for he will say this: "The statement 'those two when [the action is] completed' (*tau sat*) is for the purpose of excluding [other meanings]. This is so that the designation *niṣṭhā* may apply to those two roots when they are connected with past time (*bhūtena kālena*), as in *ñimidā* → *minnaḥ* and *ñikṣvidā* → *kṣvinnaḥ*. But what if [the action] has neither been seen nor heard?

If, having taken only the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu*, the technical designation *niṣṭhā* were stated, this would not be possible. It would not apply to forms that are seen or heard, such as *minnaḥ* from the root *ñimidā*. Therefore, it cannot be done in this way. If it were not done thus, one would either have to mention *kta* and *ktavatu* twice, or there would be mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). This is not a fault; it is merely a case of mutual dependence.

And all those [cases] involving mutual dependence have been resolved by [the principle of] unity, as established by the rule "But [it is] established because of the eternality of words. This is not equal to other cases of mutual dependence; for a name (*saṃjñā*) is not eternal. If that is so, then the name will be understood as prospective (*bhāvinī*). For example:

Someone said to a certain weaver, "Weave a cloth from this thread. He reflects: "If it is a cloth, it need not be woven; if it is to be woven, it is not yet a cloth. To say 'a cloth is to be woven' is a contradiction. Indeed, he intends for it to have its future designation.

I think that it is to be explained thus: "In which [action], when completed, this term *śāṭakaḥ* (a garment) comes into being. Likewise here as well, those two [actions] exist in the past time, for which, once they have been accomplished, this designation *niṣṭhā* will apply.

258–259. *Niṣṭhā* [the past participial suffixes] should be prescribed for the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*). [Example: *prakṛtaḥ kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta has begun the mat"). Why, then, is it not established? Because it is used in the sense of "becoming" (*bhavanti-artha*), as in: *prakṛtaḥ kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ* meaning *prakaroti kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta is making the mat"). But it is logical [to apply the suffix] because of the completion at the very beginning.

But this past tense is logical. Why? Because of the completion of the beginning (*ādyapavarga*). Here, the beginning has been completed. And it is indeed logical that a past tense should apply where something is seen to have been completed. Or rather, it is expressed in the aorist (*adyatany*): "Devadatta made a mat" or "Devadatta has made a mat."

Is it because these words can be employed that this past tense is logical? Not necessarily from mere usage alone. This thing called "action" (kriyā) is entirely imperceptible and accessible only through inference; it is impossible to point to it as a concrete entity, like an embryo extracted [from the womb]. In whatever word it is connected, to that extent— [The action] is manifested. It is not possible to show it as a solidified mass, like an embryo drawn out. That very action, in whatever word it is associated with, to that same extent [is manifested].

It is brought to completion. For example, someone wishing to go to Pāṭaliputra, having traveled one day, says, "This much has been gone today. Yet, by that much alone, his act of going is not finished. Rather, it is with reference to what has already been traversed that he employs this expression, "This much has been gone today. In the same way here too, that which has been performed—
Having perceived this, one employs the expression "Devadatta is making a mat. For when the mat is perceived within the reeds,
then indeed the expression "he is making a mat" occurs.

260. Why is the option (*vāvacana*) regarding the suffixes *kānac* and *kvasu* prescribed? The option regarding *kānac* and *kvasu* is for the sake of observing finite verb forms (*tiṅ*) in the Vedic language (*chandas*). An option regarding *kānac* and *kvasu* is prescribed because finite verb forms are observed in the Veda:
"I have seen the sun on both sides" (*aham sūram ubhayataḥ dadarśa*), and "I have stretched out heaven and earth" (*aham dyāvāpṛthivī ātatāna*). Or rather, it is not by this [rule].

Because there is a statement of substitution for that which is prescribed [by this rule]. Or rather, this is not the purpose [of the rule]. What is the reason? Because there is a statement of substitution for that which is prescribed by this [rule]. Let it be that there is a substitution for that which is prescribed by this. But now, by what means will there be the hearing (actual occurrence) of the *liṭ* [perfect tense] prescribed in the Veda (*chandas*)? [It will be by] the rule "In the Veda, [the endings of] *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* [are used]. Therefore, let this alternative formulation (*vā-vacana*) remain as a mere incidental addition (*sānnyāsika*).
(P_3.2.106–107.2) KA_II,115.3–8 Ro_III, 260–261 Now, for what purpose is the marker *k* added? Is it not already established by the rule "the *liṭ* [affixes] following a non-conjunct are *kit*"?

The addition of the marker *k* is for the sake of [avoiding] a conjunct. The marker *k* is added for the sake of a conjunct; those ending in a conjunct cause [the application of the rule]. As in the case of *vṛtra*sya...
Regarding the [Vedic] forms *badbadhānasya* (from *bādh*) and *arṇavān badbadhānān aramṇāḥ*, [the commentary states]: "He who has won the prize (*ājivān*) has anointed himself.

Here, the suffixes *kānac* and *kvasu* are Vedic (*chāndasau*). Furthermore, in the Veda, the *liṭ* [perfect] tense also functions as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. In that context, because the rule "an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix that is not marked with *p* is treated as having the *ṅ*-marker" applies, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*guṇa*) due to its being *ṅit*. This is for the purpose of preventing *guṇa* substitution in the case of roots ending in *ṛ*.

Or rather, the *kit* designation must be applied for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* in roots ending in *ṛ*. This rule concerning *guṇa* is introduced for roots ending in *ṛ* in the domain of the prohibition [of *guṇa*] in the *liṭ* tense. Just as *guṇa* occurs here by overriding the prohibition—as in *teratuḥ*, *teruḥ*—so too would it occur here as well, as in *titīrvān* and *tirirāṇaḥ*. However, by the further application of the *kit* designation, it is prohibited.

(P_3.2.108) *bhāṣāyām sadādibhyaḥ vā liṭ*. In common usage (*bhāṣā*), the *liṭ* [perfect] suffix may optionally be prescribed after roots such as *sad* and others. What is the purpose? To prevent the exclusion of the *luṅ* [aorist] in that domain. There must be no exclusion of the *luṅ* in the domain of that *liṭ*.

It should be as follows: *upasedivān kautsaḥ pāṇinim* (Kautsa approached Pāṇini). [The form] *upāsadat* [is used]. And in the cases of the non-recent past (*anadyatana*) and the remote past (*parokṣa*), the *liṭ* [affix] should be stated as optional. Thus, one may say *upasedivān kautsaḥ pāṇinim*, *upāsīdat*, or *upasasāda*. Indeed, their occurrence is due to the prohibition of exceptions (*apavāda-vipratiṣedha*). For by the prohibition of exceptions, those two [the *laṅ* and *liṭ*] would occur. In what cases? In the cases of the *laṅ* and *liṭ*. For that [root], there is the suffix *kvasu*.

"Regarding the rule *aparokṣe nityam*: it should be stated that for that *liṭ*, in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), *kvasu* occurs invariably when not in the immediate past (*aparokṣe nityam*). There is no purpose in including the mention of *aparokṣe*; it should simply be stated as *tasya kvasur nityam*. [Objection: By what means, then, will the hearing of *liṭ* occur in the case of the remote past (*parokṣe*)?
[Answer: By the rule *parokṣe liṭ*. [Objection: Then that must be stated. [Answer: It need not be stated; the subsequent application (*anuvṛtti*) will be carried out."

In the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), the *liṭ* suffix optionally occurs after roots such as *sad* and others, and for the *liṭ*, the *kvasu* suffix occurs. From that, the *luṅ* [suffix occurs]. The *luṅ* occurs in the past tense. In the spoken language, the *liṭ* suffix optionally occurs after roots such as *sad* and others, and for the *liṭ*, the *kvasu* suffix occurs. From that, the *laṅ* [occurs] in the non-todays-past (*anadyatana*). The *laṅ* occurs in the non-todays-past tense. In the spoken language, the *liṭ* [optionally occurs] after roots such as *sad* and others.

The *liṭ* [affix] occurs, and the *kvasu* [affix] also occurs. The *liṭ* occurs in the sense of the remote past (*parokṣa*). In common speech (*bhāṣā*), the *liṭ* optionally occurs after roots such as *sad*, and the *kvasu* also occurs after that *liṭ*. In this regard, the following point is also established: it need not be stated that "the *kvasu* [occurs] after that [root] necessarily even when not in the remote past."

Why is the irregular form *upeyivān* prescribed? The irregularity regarding *upeyuṣ* is for the sake of the augment *iṭ*. The irregularity regarding *upeyuṣ* is prescribed so that the augment *iṭ* may occur. This purpose is not necessary; it is already established here.

Regarding the rule *iṭ vasvekākād ghasām*: once reduplication has been performed, because the root now consists of more than one vowel (*anekāctvāt*), the augment *iṭ* does not apply. This must be considered here: "Should reduplication be performed first, or the augment *iṭ*? What should be done in this case? The introduction of the augment *iṭ* [should take place] because it is subsequent (in the order of rules). Reduplication is obligatory; it applies whether *iṭ* has been added or not. The augment *iṭ* is also obligatory; it applies even when reduplication has already occurred.
And [the substitution] would apply both when the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been effected and when it has not yet been effected. But in this case, the single-substitute does not apply. Why?

Because it is superseded by the lengthening [rule] *dīrgha iṇaḥ kiti*. Therefore, this irregularity (*nipātana*) is made for the sake of the augment *iṭ* in the word *upeyuṣi*. If it is argued that the irregularity is for the sake of *iṭ* in *upeyuṣi*, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to forms beginning with vowels such as *ajādau*. [The answer is: the irregularity applies only to *upeyuṣi*.

If it is argued that [the rule applies] for the sake of *iḍ*, there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases beginning with vowels such as *aj*. For example: *upeyuṣā*, *upeyuṣe*, *upeyuṣaḥ*, *upeyuṣi*. However, the substitution of *īy* is for the sake of the form of that which has undergone the single-substitute (*ekādiṣṭa*). Indeed, the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) is performed for the sake of the form of that which has undergone the single-substitute becoming *īy*. That is to say, this form *īy* is derived as an irregularity for that which has undergone the single-substitute. But was it not already stated that here the single-substitute does not apply? What is the reason?

[The objection: "By the rule *dīrgha iṇaḥ kiti*, [the substitution of] a long vowel sublates [the substitution of *yaṇ*]. [Response: That is not well stated. For the substitution of a long vowel does not sublate the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule. What, then, sublates it? The substitution of *yaṇ*. And where does that sublate? Where its cause exists. For where the cause does not exist, the single-substitute rule prevails there without opposition.

Or rather, it is for the sake of the substitution of *yaṇ* when a consonant follows. Or else, the substitution of *yaṇ* is specifically prescribed (*nipātyate*) only when a consonant follows. Once the substitution of *yaṇ* has been made, the augment *iṭ* is established by the rule "for monosyllabic roots" (*ekācaḥ*). Another says: *upeyivān* is not to be treated as a specific irregularity (*nipāta*). Because the augment *iṭ* applies later in order, it will occur after reduplication. Let the reduplication be performed first.

The augment *iṭ* will occur by way of a conflict between rules (*vipratiṣedha*). In that case, would *iṭ* not also apply here [before reduplication] in forms such as *bibhidvān* and *cicchidvān*? Others say that for other monosyllabic roots, reduplication is obligatory. For others, reduplication is indeed obligatory;
it applies whether *iṭ* has been added or has not been added. But for this [root *bhī*], both *iṭ* and reduplication are obligatory.
Furthermore, for this [root], the augment *iṭ* is indeed obligatory, as is reduplication (*dvirvacana*). And when reduplication has been performed, it becomes a monosyllable (*ekāc*).
How so? When the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied. Therefore, *iṭ* subverts reduplication; therefore, *iṭ* subverts reduplication.

[The word] *anūcānaḥ* [is formed] in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). It should be stated: "*anūcānaḥ* in the sense of the agent. One who has studied [the Veda] repeatedly is *anūcānaḥ*. [That which is] studied repeatedly is *anūktam*.

Thus it is elsewhere; *upeyivān* is not to be treated as an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) word. The augment *iṭ* will occur because of its priority over reduplication. Others say that for other monosyllabic roots, reduplication is obligatory. But for this [root], both the augment *iṭ* and reduplication are obligatory. For its [application] is not obstructed by reduplication, since it is a monosyllable even after reduplication. Therefore, *iṭ* supersedes reduplication.

There arises the contingency that the *luṅ* and *lṛṭ* [suffixes] would supersede [the rules for the past and future], because there is no specification regarding the past and the future. It follows that *luṅ* and *lṛṭ* would act as exceptions [to the general rules]. For example:

"We went to the cowherd settlements" (*agāma ghoṣān*), "We drank milk" (*apāma payaḥ*), "We lay down on *pūtīka* grass" (*aśayiṣmahi pūtīkatṛṇeṣu*); and likewise, "We shall go to the cowherd settlements" (*gamiṣyāmaḥ ghoṣān*).

"We shall drink milk; we shall lie down on *pūtīka* grass. For what reason? Because there is no distinction made between the past and the future. The *luṅ* (aorist) and *lṛṭ* (future) suffixes are prescribed without distinction for both the past and the future. Since the *laṅ* (imperfect) and *lṛṭ* (periphrastic future) are prescribed specifically for those [two times], they would apply as exceptions (*apavāda*). Not so, because the exception lacks its necessary condition. For the prescription of those two [suffixes] applies only to non-today time (*anadyatana*). Or rather, this is not the case.

There is a fault. What is the reason? Because there is no occasion for an exception (*apavāda*). There is no occasion for an exception here. What is the reason? For those two are prescribed for non-today time (*anadyatana*). Indeed, *laṅ* and *luṭ* are prescribed for non-today time;
however, in this case, non-today time is not intended to be expressed. What then? It is the general past time and the general future time.

Furthermore, even if one could say in this case, "We shall go to the cowherd stations," "we shall drink milk," or "we shall lie down on *pūtīka* grass," where it is not known *what* or *when*, here [in the past tense] how could one say, "We went to the cowherd stations," "we drank milk," or "we lay down on *pūtīka* grass," when it is already ascertained that "on such-and-such a day we went"?

Thus [it is said]. Here too, it is simply because there is no occasion for an exception (*apavāda*), for those two [suffixes] are prescribed for the non-current day (*anadyatana*). But how can there be a lack of intention to express (*avivakṣā*) that which exists? Even that which exists may not be intended to be expressed. For example: "a hairless ewe" (*alomikā eḍakā*), "a girl with no belly" (*anudarā kanyā*). And there is also the intention to express that which does not exist. For example: "the ocean" (*samudraḥ*).
*kuṇḍikā*, *vindhyaḥ*, *vardhitakam*.

Regarding the root *vas-* [in the sense of "to dwell"], the *luṅ* suffix is prescribed when the night has passed. It should be stated that the *luṅ* suffix is used for *vas-* when the night has passed. When it was the proper time to rise, he rose.

Someone asks another: "Where did you stay? He replies: "I stayed there. [The objection is: One would expect him to say, "I dwelt there" (*avasam*), because it is a continuous state of waking; it should be stated that it is a continuous state of waking. For even one who sleeps for only a moment, in that case he must simply say, "I dwelt there" (*avasam*).

(P_3,2.111) KA_II,118.22–119.7 Ro_III, 268–269: *anadyatane* is a Bahuvrīhi compound. [For example: *adya hyo 'bhukṣmahi* ("we ate yesterday"). The term *anadyatane* must be explained as a Bahuvrīhi compound: "that for which the current day (*adyatana*) does not exist" is *anadyatana*. What is the purpose [of this]?
[The rule] "We ate today and yesterday" (*adya hyo 'bhukṣmahi*)—where both "today" (*adya*) and "yesterday" (*hyaḥ*) are involved—the *luṅ* (aorist) alone should apply.

If this is so, then the *laṅ* (imperfect) would also apply to the "recent past" (*adyatana*). [Objection: For in the recent past, there is no such thing as a "non-recent past. [Response: Even in the recent past, there exists a "non-recent past. How? By virtue of being treated as if it were designated (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). And in the case of what is "beyond the senses" (*parokṣa*) yet known in the world, for the speaker...

Regarding the scope of the speaker's perception (*darśanaviṣaya*) and that which is beyond perception (*parokṣa*), it should be stated that the *laṅ* (imperfect) suffix is used for what is known by the world (*lokavijñāta*) and within the scope of the speaker's perception. For example: *aruṇad yavanaḥ sāketam* ("The Yavana besieged Sāketa"); *aruṇad yavano mādhurikām* ("The Yavana besieged Mādhurikā"). Why is "beyond perception" (*parokṣe*) specified? [To exclude cases like: *udagād ādityaḥ* ("The sun rose").

Why is "known by the world" (*lokavijñāte*) specified? [To exclude cases like: *cakāra kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta made a mat"). [And why is] "within the scope of the speaker's perception" (*prayoktur darśanaviṣaye*) specified? [To exclude cases where the action is not witnessed by the speaker.]
For what purpose did Vāsudeva kill Kaṃsa?
What is the example? "In that place we shall drink barley-meal. "Do you remember, Devadatta, the barley-meal in that place?"

"Let us drink. [The word] *pūrvam* (first) would be expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) because it expects a subsequent [word], [thinking] "it should be [drinking]. But how is the subsequent [word] expectant? The subsequent [word] is also expectant. How is it expectant? Because there is an expectation toward this [subsequent word], it is therefore expectant. Regarding the rule "optionally when expectant, in all cases": it should be stated that "optionally when expectant, in all cases. In what sense "in all cases"? When *yadi* is present and *ayadi* is also present.

And furthermore: "Devadatta, do you remember that we were going to Kaśmīra, that we went to Kaśmīra, that we would eat rice there, and that we ate rice there? Do you remember, Devadatta, that we were going to Kaśmīra, that we went to Kaśmīra, that we would eat rice there, and that we ate rice there?"

It is stated [in the rule] "when out of sight" (*parokṣe*). What, then, is meant by "out of sight"? That which is beyond the eye (*akṣi*) is "out of sight. But what is the eye? This word *akṣi* is derived from the root *aś* with the suffix *si*, which is formed according to the *uṇādi* rules and functions as an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*). It is called *akṣi* because one perceives (*anuśyati*) by means of it.

If this is so, it would follow that [the form] should be *parākṣam*. This is not a fault. Let the substitution of *para-* for *parasya* be seen as applying when the word *akṣa-* follows, i.e., in the case of *parokṣe* (in the sense of "out of sight"). It should be stated that the substitution of *para-* occurs for the word *para-* when the word *akṣa-* is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Or rather, let it be stated that the substitution of *u* occurs for the word *akṣi-* when it follows the word *para-*. Thus, the desired form is established.
Or [it is] from this irregular derivation (*nipātana*).

(P_3.2.115.2) KA_II,120.5–23 Ro_III, 271–273 But in reference to what "past" (*parokṣa*) time? There is indeed no governing rule (*adhikāra*) regarding time. If that is so, then [the suffix applies] after a verbal root (*dhātu*).

Thus it continues: "when the verbal root (*dhātu*) is beyond the range of perception" (*parokṣe*). Now, "verbal root" (*dhātu*) is indeed a word (*śabda*). And it is not possible for a word to be either perceptible or imperceptible. Since this [distinction] is impossible in the case of a word, the operation (*kārya*) will be understood as applying to the meaning (*artha*). That is to say: "when the verbal root is imperceptible" means "when the meaning of the verbal root is imperceptible. But what, then, is the meaning of a verbal root? It is action (*kriyā*). [The rule thus applies] when the action is imperceptible. If this is so—

In the case of *hyo 'pacat* ("he cooked yesterday"), the *liṭ* suffix would also apply here. What is the reason? This thing called "action" (*kriyā*) is entirely imperceptible, cognizable only through inference, and impossible to point out as a concrete entity, just like an embryo that has not been extracted. If this is so, then [the suffix applies] when the means (*sādhana*) are beyond perception. And what is your understanding regarding the means? If it is a collection of qualities (*guṇasamudāya*).

The means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is also to be understood through inference. Now, if the means of accomplishment were something other than the qualities (*guṇa*), there would be the possibility of it being either perceptible or imperceptible. Furthermore, when he sees rice-water on the street, how should one understand that? If the means of accomplishment were imperceptible, one should say "he cooked" (*papāca*); for his means of accomplishment do indeed exist.

Regarding the *parokṣa* [tenses]: now, as for those specific actions consisting of sounds such as *cītkāra* and *phūtkāra*, even when they are *parokṣa*, the form should likewise be *papāca*. But of what nature, then, is that which is called *parokṣa*? Some first say:
"That which occurred a hundred years ago is *parokṣa*. Others say: "That which is separated by a wall (*kaṭa*) is *parokṣa*. Still others say:

Regarding the cases of "occurring for two days" (*dvyahavṛtta*) and "occurring for three days" (*tryahvṛtta*): in no way is the [intended] excellence established. It should rather be stated as "of one who is asleep or intoxicated" (*suptamattayoḥ*).

For example: "I indeed prattled while asleep," "I indeed prattled while intoxicated," "Did I perhaps prattle while asleep? or "Did I perhaps prattle while intoxicated? Or else, it may be that someone is actually awake.

Furthermore, one does not perceive the present time. For example, Śākaṭāyana, among grammarians, while sitting on the path of a chariot, did not perceive a caravan of carts passing by. What, then, is the reason that even when awake, one does not perceive the present time? The sense organs, when conjoined with the mind, are the instruments for perception; [in this case], it is due to the non-proximity of the mind.

*liṭ* is used for the remote past (*parokṣe*) and also for absolute denial (*atyantāpahnave*). Regarding the rule *liṭ* is used for the remote past, it should be stated that it is also used for absolute denial:
"He did not go to the Khaṇḍikas; he did not go to the Kaliṅgas. "I did not drink Soma; I did not [drink] the juice of the Dārvaja tree."

275–278. It should be stated: *sma* is used for the simple past (*bhūtamātra*) and not for the recent past (*adyatana*). Regarding the rule for *sma* and so forth ending in *purā*: does it apply to the simple past without distinction? In that case, it must be stated that the characteristics of *sma* and the characteristics of *purā* do not apply to the recent past. Or rather—

The suffixes *sma* and *purā* occur without distinction before any verbal root (*bhūtamātra*) [to express the sense of the present]. In that case, it should have been stated: "The suffixes beginning with *sma* [occur] before *purā*, but not when [the time is] contemporary (*adyatana*). What follows from this? If the rule for the suffixes beginning with *sma* were applied without distinction up to the word *purā*, what would be accomplished by Kātyāyana’s statement here: "But not when [the time is] contemporary (*adyatana*)"? [By stating this, he indicates that] the rule for the suffixes beginning with *sma* applies only in specific cases.

If [the term] *purā* were [applicable] without distinction, why would the author of the Vārttika provide this prohibition, stating "not in the sense of 'formerly' (*purā*) when used with *adyatana* (today)"? The rule *anadyatanasya lāt sme* (3.2.115) already excludes the non-recent past (*anadyatana*); therefore, there is no need for the function of the negative particle (*nañ*) here. In the rule *laṭ sme* (3.2.117), the term *anadyatane* will continue to apply [from the previous rule]. Furthermore, in the rules *aparokṣānadyatanaḥ* (3.2.111) and *nanau ca nanvoḥ* (3.2.121), [the same applies].

And regarding the cessation [of the rule], one might say that it does not apply when "purā" (formerly) is used with the sense of the present day; in that case, only this much should have been stated: "not when 'purā' is used with the sense of the present day. And in that context, there is the mention of *laṅ*. There, the mention of *laṅ* serves as an indicator (*jñapaka*) that the rule characterized by "purā" does not apply when the sense is the present day. Now, if the thought arises: "Because there is no distinction, [the suffixes] *sma* and *purā* are the causes [for the application of *laṅ*]," then...

Previously, it was understood that *buddhi* [is used] without distinction as a cause (*hetu*). Listen further to this matter: the rule *ca-aparokṣe* (and when not perceptible) applies everywhere prior to the mention of the word *puruṣa*, and it pertains to all non-present [tenses]. This being the case, what function does the negative particle (*nañ*) serve here? Know also that it is possible to say: "In the case of the *smād-* group and when not perceptible, [the rule] should not apply. For it is indeed possible.

Regarding the rule *nivartayitum parokṣe* and the rule *lṛṭ sme*, you might think: "This [usage] of yours would be established even by the rule for *sma* (*sma-lakṣaṇa*) in exactly the same way. [To this we reply: The rule *lṛṭ sme* would then become redundant. Therefore, it must serve another purpose. In that case, the Teacher indicates that the rules for *sma* (*sma-lakṣaṇa*) and for the remote past (*purā-lakṣaṇa*) apply to non-contemporary time (*anadyatana*).

Regarding the rule *nanau pṛṣṭaprativacane* ("when *nanu* occurs in a response to a question"), the use of the present tense (*laṭ*) is not to be prescribed, because the completion of the action is intended to be expressed. As for the rule *nanau pṛṣṭaprativacane*, the present tense is not to be prescribed. What is the reason? Because the completion of the action is intended to be expressed. In this case, there is no non-completion of the action.
This indeed is the proper present time, wherein there is the non-termination of an action;

in that case, it is already established by the rule "In the present tense, *laṭ* [is used]. If *laṭ* occurs only when the present tense is intended, then the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* would also result.
However, *śatṛ* and *śānac* are desired [in these cases].

"Behold me making," "nanu māṃ kurvantam"; "behold me doing," "nanu māṃ kurvāṇam. (Pāṇini 3.2.122). Regarding *ha* and *śaśvat*: that which is characterized by *purā* occurs in place of that characterized by *ha* and *śaśvat* by way of a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*).

[The particle] *ha* provides scope for the characteristic [of the temporal adverb] *śaśvat*. Thus: *ha akarot* ("he did so indeed"), *iha ha cakāra* ("here he did so indeed"). [The particle] *śaśvat* provides scope for the characteristic of *purā* ("formerly"). Thus: *śaśvat akarot* ("he did so repeatedly"), *śaśvat cakāra* ("he did so repeatedly"). [The particle] *purā* provides scope for the characteristic of *ratha* ("chariot"). Thus: *rathena ayam purā yāti* ("this man goes by chariot formerly"), *rathena ayam purā ayāsīt* ("this man went by chariot formerly"). In this case, both [characteristics] apply simultaneously: *rathena ha śaśvat purā yāti* ("he indeed goes by chariot repeatedly formerly"), *rathena ha śaśvat purā ayāsīt* ("he indeed went by chariot repeatedly formerly").

The suffix *purā* (indicating "formerly") prevails by way of exception over all [other suffixes]. The suffix *sma* prevails by way of exception over all [others]. The suffix *sma* prevails by way of exception over all [others], including those characterized by *purā*. [The suffix *sma*] also prevails over those characterized by *ha-śaśvat* and those characterized by *purā*. The scope for the suffix characterized by *ha-śaśvat* is as follows: *iti ha akarot* ("Thus he did"), *iha ha cakāra* ("Here he did"). *Śaśvat* [is used]: *śaśvat akarot*, *śaśvat cakāra*. As for the suffix characterized by *purā*: [it is used as follows].

There is scope [for the application of the rule]. "This man used to go by chariot" (*rathena ayam purā yāti*); "This man used to go by chariot" (*rathena ayam purā ayāsīt*). This is the scope for the characteristic *sma*.

"The Kurus used to fight according to dharma" (*dharmeṇa sma kuravaḥ yudhyante*). Here, everything is obtained. "In former times, one never used to burn what was not cut with an axe" (*na ha sma vai purā śaśvat aparaśuvṛkṇam dahati*). The *laṭ* (present tense) occurs in place of the *sma*-characteristic by way of prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*).

(P_3,2.123) When there is no cessation of an action that has already commenced, the suffixes of the present tense (*śatṛ* and *śānac*) apply, because [the action] is not currently occurring [in its entirety]. When there is no cessation of an action that has already commenced, the suffixes of the present tense apply:
"We study here," "We dwell here," "We perform the sacrifice for Puṣyamitra here. But what is the reason [for this]?

It is not established because it is not currently occurring; and because there is no division of time in that which is eternally active. Furthermore, when [the action] is eternally active, there would be things to be taught such as "the mountains stand" and "the rivers flow. What, then, is the reason it is not established? Because there is no division of time. Here, the present time is the opposite of the past and the future; and in this case, neither the past nor the future exists.
The two times [past and future] exist. However, the present time is logical because of the non-cessation of the commencement. Indeed, this status as the present time is logical. Why?

Because of the non-cessation of the commencement (*ārambhānapavargāt*). Here, the commencement has not ceased. This indeed is the logical present time where the commencement has not ceased. And there is a cessation in the case of one whose doubt has been resolved. Regarding that which you—
One considers the present time to be logically established when one says, "Devadatta is eating," as there is no doubt about it; this [example] is similar to that case.

For even while necessarily eating, he may laugh, talk, or drink water. If the application of the present tense is seen to be appropriate here, let it be seen as equally appropriate in this case as well. Furthermore, divisions of time do exist; they are indeed present.

Indeed, there are divisions of time: "the mountains stand," "the mountains will stand," and "the mountains stood. Are these words capable of being employed? Therefore, divisions of time exist. It is not necessarily only from their actual employment [that we know this]. Here, the actions of past, future, and present kings constitute the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the verb "to stand" (*tiṣṭhati*).

"In this case, first: 'the mountains stand'—this refers to the actions of those kings who exist at present, while those actions are currently occurring. 'The mountains will stand'—this refers to the actions of those kings who will exist hereafter, while those actions are yet to occur. 'The mountains stood'—this refers to the actions of those kings who existed in the past. [And so on for the actions] of those kings who have already been.
When those [arguments] had been stated, another said:
"There is no present time. Furthermore, they cite these verses on this point:
"The wheel does not turn; the arrow is not shot; the rivers do not flow toward the ocean; this world is immutable."
The world is not devoid of activity; for he who sees thus is indeed not blind. A young man of great intelligence, considering himself a Mīmāṃsaka, once asked a crow here:
"What is the characteristic of your flight? You do not fly before [the object] has arrived, nor after it has passed, O crow; if you fly only when it is present."

This entire world falls; even the Himavat mountain moves. Regarding the three—what has not yet come, what has passed, and the present—there is no movement whatsoever. Why, then, is it said that "it moves"? Having observed that specific effort which is the cause for the initiation of an action, one should employ the expression "it moves" without further deliberation.
Apra said: "Present time exists; it is simply not perceived, like the movement of the sun. Furthermore, they cite a verse on this point:

'Just as the fibers of a lotus stalk being burned, their transformation is not noticed during the process, yet those who possess the three states of being testify that it exists—for a subtle state is to be known through inference.'"

(P_3,2.124.1) KA_II,125.2-20 Ro_III, 286-288 Because *la* cannot be coreferential with anything other than the first case (*prathamā*), its substitution is untenable, as is the case elsewhere. Because *la* cannot be coreferential with anything other than the first case, the two substitutions are untenable, as is the case elsewhere. That is just as it is elsewhere.

Furthermore, there is no connection of *laṭ* with that which is not in grammatical coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇa*) with the first case. Where else? In *laṅ*: "Devadatta cooked the rice" (*apacat odanaṃ devadattaḥ*). If it is argued that there is a connection [of *laṭ*], then there would be a connection elsewhere as well. Now, if this thought occurs—that there is a connection—then there would be a connection elsewhere too. Where else? In *laṅ*: "Devadatta cooked the rice" (*apacat odanaṃ devadattaḥ*).

Thus, one should not conclude that because there is no application [of a word] in some instances, it must therefore apply everywhere; nor should one conclude that because there is non-application in some instances, it must therefore be non-applicable everywhere. For example: among those who exert equal effort and study equally, some are successful in their aims while others are not. Yet, one does not conclude from this that no one at present is successful in their aims; rather, [one concludes] that all [words] are meaningful.

It is possible that something might be meaningless by virtue of all [the elements] being meaningless. In that case, what can be done by us? That there is a connection with the non-first-case (aprathamā) coreferentiality of the *loṭ* suffix, but not of the *laṅ*—this is not inherent. Alternatively, having observed the coreferentiality in the substitute (*ādeśa*), one must infer through reasoning that the coreferentiality belongs to the original base (*prakṛti*) as well.

"It exists. For example, having seen smoke, it is understood that "there is fire here," and having seen a triple-staff (triviṣṭabdhaka), it is understood that "this is a wandering mendicant (parivrājaka). This is an unequal comparison. In those cases, a perceptible connection has been established between fire and smoke, and between the triple-staff and the wandering mendicant; therefore, even upon seeing them in a different location, one recognizes [the presence of the other].
"Fire is here; a wandering mendicant is here. Indeed, inference is stronger even than direct perception.
For example, a circle of firebrands (*alātacakram*) is seen directly, yet through inference it is understood that "this does not exist.
Furthermore, for someone, a connection established once becomes established for all time. For example:
Regarding a tree and its leaf, one says, "this is the tree" and "this is the leaf. Even when seeing [the leaf] located in a different place from that [tree], he knows,
"this is the leaf of this tree."

Furthermore, is this a *paryudāsa* (an exclusionary negation), namely "that which is other than what is in grammatical agreement with the nominative," or is it a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (a simple prohibitive negation)?

[The rule] "not when there is no coreferentiality with the first case-ending" (*aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe na*). What is the distinction here? If [the rule] "the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* replace *laṭ* when there is no coreferentiality with the first case-ending" is stated, then an addition must be made for the cases of suffixes and subsequent members of compounds (*pratyayottarapadayoḥ*). If "the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* replace *laṭ* when there is no coreferentiality with the first case-ending" is stated, then an addition must be made for the cases of suffixes and subsequent members of compounds: *kaurvataḥ*, *pācataḥ*, *kurvadbhaktiḥ*.

[The examples would be] *pacadbhaktiḥ*, *kurvāṇabhaktiḥ*, and *pacamānabhaktiḥ*. Well then, let it be a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (a simple negation). [In that case, the rule would be: "not when there is coreferentiality with a word ending in the first case. If it is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha*, the substitution [of *-at* for *-ant*] in the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is untenable. In a *prasajya-pratiṣedha*, the two substitutions in the subsequent member are untenable. [For example,] she who is cooking is the devotion; thus, *pacadbhaktiḥ*, *kurvāṇabhaktiḥ*, and *kurvadbhaktiḥ*.

Regarding the term *pacamānabhaktiḥ*: even in those cases where secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) function as coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* would not otherwise apply [in their present participial sense]. For example: *kurvattaraḥ*, *pacattaraḥ*, *kurvāṇataraḥ*, *pacamānataraḥ*;
*kurvadrūpaḥ*, *pacadrūpaḥ*, *kurvāṇarūpaḥ*, *pacamānarūpaḥ*; *kurvatkalpaḥ*, *pacatkalpaḥ*, *kurvāṇakalpaḥ*, *pacamānakalpaḥ*.

[Objection: This is established by the rule *pratyayottarapadayoś ca*. [Response: It is indeed established. How? It should be stated that the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* occur both after a suffix (*pratyaya*) and after a subsequent member of a compound (*uttarapada*). In that case, because the suffix is the cause for the substitution [of the stem], there would be no application [of the rule]. In that case, because the suffix is the cause for the substitution, there would be no application. [The suffix] is the cause for the substitution, and [the substitution] is the cause for the suffix.

And there is the substitution [of *śatṛ* for *laṭ*]. This results in a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). And things that involve mutual dependence are not logically tenable. Furthermore, because the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is conditioned by a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), the application of the affixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* would not be established. Because the subsequent member is conditioned by a word ending in a case-suffix, the application of *śatṛ* and *śānac* is not established. The case-suffix conditioned by the subsequent member is itself conditioned by a word ending in a case-suffix.

And [the suffix] *uttarapada* [is required]. Thus, this results in mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). And things characterized by mutual dependence are not logically tenable. Or rather, there is no such fault; for since the letter *l* (representing the verbal suffix) is a *kṛt* suffix, it possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and the rule for the application of the suffix is based upon that. Or rather, this is not a fault. Why? Because the letter *l* has the status of a nominal stem due to being a *kṛt* suffix; the letter *l* is a *kṛt*, and a *kṛt* is a nominal stem.

Thus, the designation *prātipadika* is established. Based upon that, the prescription of suffixes (*pratyaya*) occurs. The production of case-endings such as *su* and others will take place based on the *prātipadika*. [Objection: Since the substitution of *tiṅ* [for verbal roots] occurs first, the production of *sub* endings should follow. [Response: Let the substitution of *tiṅ* be made; however, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], the production of *sub* endings will occur. Therefore, the status of being an "uttarapada" (final member of a compound) is established. Consequently, the *uttarapada* is established.

When the subsequent word is established, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* will apply to that subsequent word. In that case, would there not also be the production of a case ending (*sub*) after a verbal substitute (*tiṅ*), as in *pacati* and *paṭhati*? There is a distinction here: the substitution of *tiṅ* is obligatory. It applies whether the case ending has already been produced or has not yet been produced. Because it is obligatory, once the substitution of *tiṅ* has taken place, the production of the case ending occurs.

It will not occur. In that case, even here, because of its permanence (*nityatva*), there would be a substitution by a *tiṅ* affix, as in *kurvadbhaktiḥ*, *pacadbhaktiḥ*, and *pacamānabhaktiḥ*. There is a distinction here: the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes are exceptions (*apavāda*) to *tiṅ*, and they are conditioned by specific causes. Furthermore, the general rule (*utsarga*) does not apply where an exception is operative; for the exceptions apply first, and subsequently [the general rule applies].
The general rule (*utsarga*) applies after having set aside the domain of the exception (*apavāda*). Thus, the general rule does not apply here at all;
it awaits the two exceptions, *śatṛ* and *śānac*. Where is this established?

It is established where there is an origin from a general category. For where there is [an origin] from a specific category—as in the case of "from this, *iñ*"—there is indeed mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

[The word] *vaikṣamāṇiḥ* [is derived from] *apatyam vaikṣamāṇasya* ("the offspring of one who gazes"). And here, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* would be applicable: *pacatitarām*, *jalpatitarām*, *pacatirūpam*, *jalpatirūpam*, *pacatikalpam*, *jalpatikalpam*, and *pacati paṭhati*.
How, then, is this established? If *śatṛ* and *śānac* are optionally [substituted] for *laṭ*. If *śatṛ* and *śānac* [are applied].

If [the suffix] *laṭ* optionally becomes [the present participial suffixes] *śatṛ* and *śānac*, and this is a rule of restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), then here we shall have: *bhaviṣyataḥ kaurvataḥ*, *pācataḥ*;

*kurvadbhaktiḥ*, *pacadbhaktiḥ*, *pacamānabhaktiḥ*; *kurvattaraḥ*, *pacattaraḥ*, *pacamānataraḥ*; *kurvadrūpaḥ*, *pacadrūpaḥ*, *pacamānarūpaḥ*; *kurvatkalpaḥ*, *pacatkalpaḥ*, *pacamānakalpaḥ*; and *pacan*.

Regarding the phrase *paṭhan*, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* [are applied] to the present tense marker (*laṭ*). And here they will not occur [in the following cases]: *pacatitarām jalpatitarām*, *pacatirūpam jalpatirūpam*, *pacatikalpam jalpatikalpam*, and *pacati paṭhati*. [Objection: In that case, the rule for optionality (*vāvacana*) must be stated. [Response: It need not be stated; the previously established context continues. Where was it established?
Regarding the rule *nanvoḥ vibhāṣā*: if that [rule] continues to apply, then by the rule *vartamāne laṭ*, the suffix *laṭ* would also optionally (*vibhāṣā*) apply.
[Reply: It will continue to apply in its specific connection: *nanvoḥ vibhāṣā*; *puri luṅ ca asme vibhāṣā*;
*vartamāne laṭ puri luṅ ca asme vibhāṣā*; and *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacau vibhāṣā*. [In this way,] the phrase *puri luṅ ca asme* ceases to apply.

In that case, it should not now be stated that [the suffixes] apply when they do not have the same referent as a word ending in the first case (*aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe*). And yet, it must be stated. What is the purpose? For the sake of obligatoriness (*nityārtham*): so that the two [suffixes] may be obligatory when they do not have the same referent as a word ending in the first case. Where, then, would there be an option (*vibhāṣā*) now?
When they have the same referent as a word ending in the first case: *pacan pacati*, *pacamānaḥ pacate*.

An addition must be made [to the rule] regarding the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) and the cause (*hetu*) of an action when it refers to a quality (*guṇa*). An addition must be made regarding the indicator and the cause of an action when it refers to a quality:
*tiṣṭhan mūtrayati* ("he urinates while standing"), *gacchan bhakṣayati* ("he eats while walking"). And for the agent (*kartṛ*), when there are two indicators, they may optionally alternate.

Regarding the rule *ac-yoge*: an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the case where two characteristics of the agent (*kartṛ-lakṣaṇa*) occur alternately (*paryāyeṇa*) in connection with a non-vowel (*ac*). For example: "He who, while studying, sits, is Devadatta"; "He who, while sitting, studies, is Devadatta. Why does it say "in connection with a non-vowel" (*ac-yoge*)? [Consider: "He who both sits and studies is Caitra. Furthermore, an addition must also be made in the case of a descriptive statement of reality (*tattvānvākhyāne*).
[The suffix *kṛtya*] should be applied. "The *dūrvā* grass grows while lying down; the lotus root grows while sitting. And [the suffixes] *sat* and so forth are used diversely.

It should be stated that "*sat* and so forth are used diversely": *san* brāhmaṇaḥ ("an existing Brāhmaṇa"), *asti* brāhmaṇaḥ ("there is a Brāhmaṇa"), *vidyate* brāhmaṇaḥ ("a Brāhmaṇa is found"), *vidyamānaḥ* brāhmaṇaḥ ("a Brāhmaṇa who exists"). Regarding the roots *iṅ* and *hu*, there is an option. It should be stated that "for *iṅ* and *hu*, there is an option": *adhīte* ("he studies").

"One who is studying. "One who is offering oblations. Regarding the rule *māṅi ākrośe* (Pāṇini 3.3.174), it should be stated that this applies when there is an expression of censure. Examples: *mā pacan*, *mā pacamānaḥ*. Then, should that [restriction] be stated? It need not be stated. It is already established by the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.126). Take first the example: *tiṣṭhan mūtrayati* ("he urinates while standing"). Here, the action of standing (*tiṣṭhati-kriyā*) is the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) of the action of urinating (*mūtrayati-kriyā*).

"He eats while walking": the action of walking is the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) of the action of eating. "He who sits while studying is Devadatta": the action of studying is the indicator of the action of sitting. "He who sits and studies is Devadatta": the action of sitting is the indicator of the action of studying. In that case, this is the purpose [of the rule].

"I shall state [the rule] 'in connection with accumulation' (acayoge)"; let it not apply here in the case of "He who both sits and studies is Caitra. This too is not a purposeful restriction. Why? Because this is not a definition of the action (*kriyā*); rather, it is a definition of the agent (*kartṛ*). As in "The *dūrvā* grass grows while lying down": the act of lying down is the defining characteristic of the act of growing. [Likewise,] he grows while sitting.

*bisam* [is used] as such. The action of sitting (*āsikriyā*) is the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) of the action of growing (*vṛddhikriyā*). And it must indeed be stated that *sad-* and the others [are used] diversely (*bahulam*) with *iṅ* and *hu-*; or [it is used] with *māṅ* in the sense of abuse (*ākrośe*).

294–296. What is the purpose of mentioning *tau*? Are *śatṛ* and *śānac* being referred back? This serves no purpose, for *śatṛ* and *śānac* will follow from their original context (*prakṛti*). In what original context? From the rule: "After *laṭ*, *śatṛ* and *śānac* [are used] when not in grammatical apposition with the first case. Therefore, he recites the following answer: The mention of *tau sat* is for the sake of non-association; thus, the mention of *tau* is made.

For the sake of non-association: so that the technical designation (*sañjñā*) of *śatṛ* and *śānac* may apply only when they are not associated with these specific [temporal] qualifiers. But surely these specific qualifiers would be excluded? Even if these specific qualifiers were excluded, this present time must certainly be carried over for the sake of subsequent rules. When that is carried over, [the rule applies] to those two [suffixes] prescribed for the present time.

In this way, the designation *sat* would apply to the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*, but it would not apply to those prescribed for past and future time. But what is the purpose of stating the designation *sat* for those prescribed for past and future time? [It is so that the prohibition] "in the case of *pūraṇa*, *guṇa*, *suhita*, and *sat*" applies: e.g., *brāhmaṇasya pakṣyan* ("a Brāhmaṇa who is about to sacrifice") and *brāhmaṇasya pakṣyamāṇaḥ* ("a Brāhmaṇa who is being about to sacrifice"). Now, even if the mention of *san* is made, how is it that [the two suffixes] are not connected with these specific [prohibitions]?

The designation (*sañjñā*) is obtainable. He says it is obtainable. How? By means of the word "those two" (*tau*). When the connection with "being" (*sat*) is made, the mention of "those two" becomes an integral part of the rule (*yogāṅga*). And when that part of the rule exists, the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be performed. "Those two": these two, the *śatṛ* and *śānac*, occur after a suffix following a verbal root (*dhātu*) alone. Then, "being" (*sat*): those two are designated as "being."
The suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* apply to verbal roots (*bhūvādīnām*). In that case, they would also apply here: *kārakaḥ*, *hārakaḥ*. [Response:

The rule for the future tense (*lṛṭ*) is a restrictive one. The rule "after a root ending in *lṛt*, there is optionally *sat*" will serve as a restriction: namely, that [the suffixes] apply only after a root followed by *lṛṭ*, and not after anything else. A restriction occurs because of the question "for what purpose? (*kaimarthyakāt*), since there is no other element to be enjoined.

And here there is something to be prescribed. What is it? The suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are obtained as being obligatory (*nitya*); these two must be prescribed as optional (*vibhāṣā*). In that case, one might ask whether this should be a new injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*) or a restrictive rule (*niyama*). It will be a new injunction alone, not a restrictive rule. And since it is already established through the analysis of the sūtra (*yogavibhāga*), [the question arises]: "If that is so, then let the analysis of the sūtra be performed thus: *lṛṭaḥ sat* (after the suffix *lṛṭ*, the suffix *sat* is used)."

The two [suffixes] *śatṛ* and *śānac* are designated as *sat* when following the suffix *lṛṭ*. For what purpose is this? It is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*): that these occur only after a verbal root (*dhātumātra*) following *lṛṭ*, and not after anything else. Furthermore, there is the option (*vā*): *śatṛ* and *śānac* are optionally designated as *sat* when following *lṛṭ*. In that regard, this is also the meaning: he will state that the rule for *sat* applies invariably (*nityam*) when not coreferential with a word in the nominative case (*aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe*).
Therefore, that need not be stated.
Now, regarding these two following *śatāna*s: are they substitutes for *l* (*lādeśau*), or are they not substitutes for *l* (*alādeśau*)? And which [is it]?

In this regard, there is a specific point: regarding the substitution of *la* in the latter two [tenses], the rule should be stated as "optionally. That is, it should be stated that "in the latter two, when *la* is substituted, it is optional. Thus, forms such as *pavamānaḥ* and *yajamānaḥ* would be established, and forms such as *pavate* and *yajate* would also occur. Furthermore, the designation of the instrument (*sādhana*) would also apply; for by the rule "the suffixes *la* are used in the sense of the object and the agent, and after intransitive verbs, in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) and the object," they would also apply in the sense of the action and the object.

Regarding accent (*svara*): accent is also something that must be established. [In the example] *kati iha pavamānāḥ*, the rule "the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix following a root taught with a short *a* is unaccented" would result in this accent being applied. Furthermore, there is the prohibition of voice (*upagraha*).
A prohibition of voice must also be stated; [in the example] *kati iha nighnānāḥ*, the designation "ātmanepada" [by the rule] "the *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes are ātmanepada" would apply.
In that case, let there be substitutes for *al*. [Objection: There must be a prohibition of the genitive case when there is a substitute for *al*. [Examples:

*somam pavamānaḥ* ("purifying the Soma"), *naḍam āghnānaḥ* ("striking the reed"), *adhīyan pārāyaṇam* ("studying the Pārāyaṇa"). [The rule] "there is no [genitive] in the usage of *lap*" would not apply. [Response: Let it not be so; it will simply be by the suffix *tṛn*. [Question: How? [Answer: This mention of *tṛn* is not a reference to the suffix itself.

What then? It is the inclusion of a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated reference). Wherein are those [sounds] situated for which there is this *pratyāhāra*? Starting from *laṭaḥ śatṛ* and extending up to the *nakāra* of *tṛn*. If it is an inclusion of a *pratyāhāra*, then [the suffix] would also apply here in the case of *caurasya dviṣan* and *vṛṣalasya dviṣan*. [Response: It should be stated that after the root *dviṣ*, the *śatṛ* suffix is optional. One must say: "after the root *dviṣ*, the *śatṛ* suffix is optionally [applied]."

298–300. Regarding the rule for the suffix *tṛn* and regarding officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), it should be stated: "The suffix *tṛn* applies after a verb that is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*) when referring to officiating priests. Examples: *hotā*, *potā*. Why is it specified "not preceded by a prefix"? [To exclude cases such as] *praśāstā*, *pratihartā*. Regarding the root *nī*: it should be stated that the augment *ṣuk* is added to *nī*, and that the suffix *tṛn* is also applied. Example: *neṣṭā*. Alternatively, this is not necessary, because [in the case of *praśāstā* and *pratihartā*] there is a difference in the verbal roots [due to the presence of prefixes].

Or rather, it need not be stated. What is the reason? Because of the difference in verbal roots (*dhātu*). *neṣati* is not a different root. How is this known? From the observation that "he may lead" (*neṣatu*) and "may he lead" (*neṣṭāt*). The usage "neṣatu neṣṭāt" is observed: "May Indra lead us by that," and "May he lead your cows. Furthermore, in the case of the root *tviṣ*, there is the substitution of *a* for the penultimate vowel and the absence of the augment *iṭ*. This applies to the root *tviṣ*.

Regarding the deity (*devatā*), it should be stated that the suffix *tṛn* is applied, that there is substitution of *a* for the penultimate vowel, and that the root is *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*). Thus, *tvaṣṭṛ*. Now, does this *aniṭ* status apply only to the root *tviṣ*? No, he says; this *aniṭ* status applies as a supplement to everything that has been enumerated and everything that will be enumerated. And [the suffix *tṛn* is applied] after the root *kṣad* when joined with [the prefix *pra*]. After the root *kṣad*, when joined with [the prefix *pra*], the suffix *tṛn* should be stated. Thus, *kṣattṛ*.
In the Vedic language, the suffix *tṛc* [should also be mentioned]. In the Vedic language, both *tṛc* and *tṛn* should be stated. [Examples: *kṣattṛbhyaḥ saṅgrahītṛbhyaḥ*;
*kṣattṛbhyaḥ saṅgrahītṛbhyaḥ*. (Pāṇini 3.2.139; Kāśikā II,131.15–132.20; Rūpāvatāra III).

Regarding the *kit* status of the suffix *snu*: an exception must be stated for the long vowel *ī* in the case of the root *sthā*. [Otherwise,] in the word *sthāsnuḥ*, the substitution of *ī* would apply by the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām hali*. If that is so, then let it not be treated as *kit*. [Objection: If it is not *kit*, then an exception to *guṇa* must be stated. [For example,] in *jiṣṇuḥ*.
Thus [it is said]. And there must be a prohibition of *iṭ* for the root *bhū*. What else?

And a prohibition of *guṇa* [must be stated] for the form *bhūṣṇuḥ*. Let it then be that [the suffix] is *kit*. But was it not said that if *snu* is *kit*, a prohibition of the vowel *ī* for the root *sthā* must be stated? This is not a fault. *Snu* occurs after the roots *sthā* and *daṃś* in the Veda. After *sthā* and *daṃś*...

The suffix *snu* should be stated as occurring in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), as in the examples "sthāsnu" (stationary) and "jaṅgama" (moving), and "daṅkṣṇavaḥ paśavaḥ" (animals with fangs). This [suffix] will now be prescribed after the root *sthā* without distinction. In that case, the rule would have to be split. Let it remain as it is in the original formulation. But was it not said that if *snu* were marked with the *k*-sign (*kit*), a prohibition of the long *ī* in *sthā* must be stated? In that case, it will be marked with the *g*-sign (*git*). [Thus, the forms] *sthoḥ*...
Because [the suffix] *stha* has the marker *g*, the long vowel *ī* does not occur. Because *stha* has the marker *g*, the long vowel *ī* will not occur. What is the reason?

Because the substitution of *ī* is prescribed only for [suffixes with] the markers *k* and *ṅ*. The substitution of *ī* is taught specifically for *k* and *ṅ*. In that case, however, in the form *jiṣṇuḥ*, the substitution of *guṇa* would apply.
The absence of *guṇa* must be remembered in three cases: when there is a *g*-marker, a *k*-marker, or a *ṅ*-marker. That is so.

The inclusion of the letter *ga* must be made. It need not be made; it is already provided in the *Nyāsa* itself. In the rule regarding the letter *ka*, the letter *ga* is indicated as having undergone the change to a *cari* sound [by *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*], as in the rule *kkṅiti ca*. In that case, here in the word *bhūṣṇuḥ*, the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *śryukaḥ kiti* would not apply. [Objection: The status of being *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*) applies to roots ending in *śrī*, *yuk*, and *ruk*. [Response: It must be stated that the status of being *aniṭ* applies to roots ending in *ga* and *ka*.

In that case, the letter *ga* should be mentioned [in the rule]. It need not be mentioned; it is already provided by the very placement [of the letters]. In the word *kakāra*, the letter *ga* is indicated as having undergone the substitution of a *cari* sound [to *ka*], according to the rule *śryukaḥ kiti*. If this were so, since the *cari* substitution would be considered asiddha (non-existent), the substitution of *u* by the rule *haśi ca* would apply. This is a Vedic-style (sautra) mention. Alternatively, the mention will be made without *saṃhitā* (without coalescence).

Regarding the rule *śryukaḥ kiti*: because of the *gittva* (indicatory *g*) of the root *sthā*, the long *ī* does not occur for *sthā* before *kṅit* suffixes, due to the teaching of *īttva* (the substitution of *ī* for *sthā*). The absence of *guṇa* in these three cases is to be remembered. Furthermore, the roots *śri*, *yu*, and *ru* are *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*) before suffixes beginning with *ga* or *ka*. (Pāṇini 3.2.141; Kāśikā II,132.22–133.4; Rūpāvatāra III).

This should be stated as *ghinaṇ*. For if *ghinuṇ* were applied, then in the case of *śaminau*, *śaminaḥ*, *taminau*, and *taminaḥ*, the augment *num* would undesirably apply by the rule *ugidacāṃ sarvanāmasthāne 'dhātoḥ*. This is not a fault; he will raise that objection regarding the mention of *jhal* there. But then consider this: *śaminitarā*, *śaminītarā*, *taminitarā*, *taminītarā*.

[Objection: Since it is stated that "for a word ending in *ugit*, before suffixes such as *gha* etc., the *nadī* [vowel] optionally becomes short," the shortening would apply optionally here as well. [Response: Shortening is indeed desired. [Objection: It should be stated that [the suffix] *ghinuṇ* occurs after roots that are intransitive (*akarmaka*). [Response: It must be stated that *ghinuṇ* occurs after intransitive roots. [Objection: This should not apply here: *saṃpṛṇakti śākam* ("he mixes vegetables"). [Response: Or rather, it has already been stated. [Question: What has been stated? [Answer: That it does not occur because of non-usage (*anabhidhānāt*).

(P_3,2.146) KA_II,133.7-19 Ro_III, 301-302 For what purpose is the suffix *vuñ* prescribed after words such as *nindā*? Is it not already established by *ṇvul* alone? Indeed, there is no difference whether *ṇvul* or *vuñ* is used after words like *nindā*; the form remains the same and the accent is the same. [But] *vuñ* is for polysyllabic bases (*anekāc*).

The suffix *vuñ* is employed after roots with more than one vowel: *asūyakaḥ*. Now, for what purpose is the mention of those roots that are recited here as having only one vowel? Is it not already established by *ṇvul* alone? It is not so established. This suffix *tṛn* is prescribed for the sense of "one who habitually does that" (*tacchīla*) and so forth;
being prescribed for a specific case, it would supersede *ṇvul*, which is prescribed for general cases. [Objection: By the rule of alternative forms (*vāsarūpa*), *ṇvul* will also occur.

Therefore, he recites the following reply: "The prescription of *vuñ* after [the group beginning with] *nindā* is for the purpose of prohibiting *ṇvul* after other [roots]. The prescription of *vuñ* after *nindā* and so forth is made for the sake of providing a technical indicator (*jñāpaka*). What is indicated? The Teacher indicates this: that by the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa*), *ṇvul* does not occur after other [roots] when [suffixes] such as *tacchīla* (denoting habit) are intended. It is also for the purpose of prohibiting *tṛc* and other [suffixes].

Or rather, the Teacher indicates this: that among suffixes such as those denoting habit (*tacchīla*), all suffixes beginning with *tṛc* do not apply by the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa*). The mention of the root *pad* is redundant, because [the desired forms] are already established by the rule "from roots ending in an *anudātta* vowel and beginning with a consonant. [This is the purpose of] the mention of *pad*.

It is purposeless. Why? Because the suffix *yuc* is already established here by the rule "after a root that begins with a consonant and ends in an unaccented vowel. It is not established. This suffix *ukañ* is prescribed for the root *pad* by the rule "the suffix *ukañ* comes after the roots *laṣ*, *pad*, *pad*, *sthā*, *bhū*, *vṛṣ*, *han*, *kam*, *gam*, and *śṝ*.

Since that [suffix *ukañ*] is prescribed as a specific exception, it would supersede the general suffix *yuc*. [Objection: By the principle of alternative forms (*vāsarūpa-nyāya*), the suffix *yuc* will also occur.
"But for the purpose of excluding those of dissimilar form. [Objection: "In that case, the mention of the root *dīp* is made for the purpose of excluding those of dissimilar form.

By this, the Teacher indicates that among suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*), suffixes expressing habitual action do not occur by way of non-similarity of form (*vāsarūpa*). [Reply: "If this is indicated, then the mention of *dīp* in the rule *dū-dīpa-dīkṣaś ca* is useless. This suffix *ra* is prescribed after the root *dīp*."

"Namika-pi-smy-aja-sahiṃsa-dīpa-raḥ" [Pāṇini 3.2.167]. This suffix *ra*, being specifically prescribed, will supersede the general suffix *yuc*. If that is so, since the desired form is already established, the fact that the teacher includes the mention of "dīpa" (in the rule) indicates that there is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of *yuc* and *ra*. What is the purpose of this indication? [The forms] "kamrā kanyā" and "kamanā kanyā" [are both derived accordingly].
This is established.
(Pāṇini 3.2.158) Why is *āluc* prescribed? Why not simply *luś*? What would the resulting form be?

[The forms] *spṛhayāluḥ* and *gṛhayāluḥ*: once the suffix *śap* has been applied, the lengthening [of the vowel] will occur by the rule "lengthening occurs before a suffix beginning with *yañ*" (*ato dīrgho yañi*). If this is so, then since the form is already established, the fact that the teacher prescribes the suffix *āluc* indicates that this suffix also occurs after other roots. What is the purpose of this indication? It is that he will raise the objection regarding the mention of the root *śīṅ* in the rule for *āluc*; that [mention] need not be made.
It occurs. Regarding the suffix *āluc*, there must be a mention of the root *śīṅ*; that is, the mention of *śīṅ* must be made in the rule for *āluc*. [Thus we have] *śayāluḥ*.

(Pāṇini 3.2.171) Why is the *kittva* (the property of being marked with *k*) prescribed for the suffixes *kikin*? Is it not already established by the rule "the *liṭ* [suffixes] following a non-conjunct consonant are *kit*"? [The answer is: regarding *kikin*...

The *kittva* [designation] of the suffixes *ki* and *kin* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *ṛ*. The *kittva* of *ki* and *kin* is prescribed in order to prohibit *guṇa* for the vowel *ṛ*.
This rule, which begins with "ṛcchatyṝtrām," prohibits *guṇa* in the case of roots ending in *ṛ* when the *liṭ* [perfect tense] affix follows within the scope of that prohibition.
Just as it applies here in cases such as *ātastaratuḥ* and *ātastaruḥ*, so too would it apply here in the case of *mitrāvaruṇau*.

*taturiḥ* and *jaguriḥ*, for the path is far and difficult to traverse. That [suffix] is again superseded when *kittva* (the property of having a *k*-marker) applies. There is a general rule (*utsarga*) that in the Veda (*chandas*), [the suffixes] *sad* and others are seen; thus, it should be stated that in the Veda, the suffixes *ki* and *kin* are used as a general rule. What is the purpose? Because they are seen after *sad* and others. For *ki* and *kin* are indeed seen after *sad* and others: *sed-iḥ*, *men-iḥ*, *rem-iḥ*.

*nemiḥ* (wheel-rim) is formed like *cakram*. *viviciḥ* is the best among those that hold jewels (*ratnadhātama*). Regarding the suffixes *kikin* and *ki*, they should be stated as applicable after the roots *dhā*, *kṛ*, *sṛ*, *jan*, and *nam* in the spoken language (*bhāṣāyām*). *dhāñ*: *dadhiḥ*. *dhāñ*: *kṛ*: *cakriḥ*. *kṛ*: *sṛ*: *sasriḥ*. *sṛ*: *jani*: *jajñiḥ*. *jani*: *nam*: *nemiḥ*. [The suffixes apply] to *sāsahi*, *vāvahi*, *cācali*, and *pāpati*.

This is a matter of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Irregular derivations must be formulated for the forms *sāsahi*, *vāvahi*, *cācali*, and *pāpati*. Thus: *vṛṣā sahamānam* [is] *sāsahiḥ*; likewise *vāvahiḥ*, *cācaliḥ*, and *pāpatiḥ*. Another says: after the roots *sah*, *vah*, *cal*, and *pat* when followed by the suffix *yaṅ*, the suffixes *kikin* should be stated; these very forms are the examples.

(P_3,2.174) KA_II,135.14 Ro_III, 305: It should also be stated that *krukan* follows *bhī-* [to form] *bhīrukaḥ*. (P_3,2.178.1) KA_II,135.16–136.4 Ro_III, 306: [The suffix *vuñ* is applied after words denoting a cause, such as *hetu*, *nimitta*, etc., to express the result. *hāyanāntayuvādibhyo 'ṇ* (P_3,2.178). [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after words ending in *hāyana* and after *yuvan* etc., to express the result. *hāyana* means "year. *dvaihāyanaḥ* ("two years old"), *traihāyanaḥ* ("three years old"). *yuvan* etc.: *yauvanaḥ*, *sthāviraḥ*, *vārdhaḥ*, *pākaḥ*, *śaucaḥ*, *mārdavaḥ*. *yuvan* etc. is an *ādi*-group (*yuvādi-gaṇa*). *prāṇabhṛjjāti-vayo-vacanād vuñ* (P_3,2.179). [The suffix *vuñ* is applied after words denoting a genus of living beings or an age, to express the result. *mānuṣakaḥ*, *bālakaḥ*, *sthavirakaḥ*. *vatsokṣāśvarṣabhebhyaś ca tanutve* (P_3,2.180). [The suffix *īya* is applied after *kiśora* to express thinness. *kiśorīyaḥ*. *vṛddhokṣāt pramāṇe* (P_3,2.182). [The elision of the *taddhita* suffix does not occur after a *dvigu* ending in *āḍhaka* when it is a proper name. *āḍhakajambukaḥ*. *anāsikāyāḥ saṃjñāyāṃ ṇas cāsthūlāt* (P_3,2.191). [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after *anāsikā* to form a proper name, and *nas* is substituted for *anāsikā*, provided the word is not *sthūla*. *vigranthinasaḥ*, *sugranthinasaḥ*. *naḍād ibhaḥ* (P_3,2.192). [The suffix *phak* is optionally applied after *droṇa*, *parvata*, and *jīvanta* to denote a descendant. *drauṇāyanaḥ*, *drauṇiḥ*; *pārvatāyanaḥ*, *pārvatiḥ*; *jaivantāyanaḥ*,

305–306. Why is this stated? [Is it not already] established by the rule "the suffix *kvip* is seen after other roots as well"? The prescription of *kvip* is for the sake of cases where there is no accompanying word (*anupapada*). This new formulation is undertaken for the sake of cases where there is no accompanying word: from *pac*, *pak*; from *bhid*, *bhit*; from *chid*, *chit*. Now, what is the purpose of including those [roots] here that have prefixes? Is it not already established by that very rule? No.

It is established. Here, some read the rule as *ā kveḥ*, while others read it as *prāk kveḥ*. Among them, those who read *ā kveḥ* imply the suffix *kvip* as well; [they do so] so that *kvip* may occur in the senses of "having such a habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. This purpose is not necessary, because that very suffix which is prescribed without distinction applies in the senses of "having such a habit" and so forth.

It will occur elsewhere as well; [otherwise] it would not be established. This suffix *tṛn* is prescribed for the sense of "having that habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. Since it is prescribed as a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*), it would supersede the general suffix *ṇvul*. [Objection: By the principle of *vāsarūpa*, *ṇvul* will also occur. [Reply: It is not established.
For it was just stated that in the senses of "having that habit" and so forth, suffixes such as *tṛc* do not occur by virtue of the *vāsarūpa* rule.

And also *kvip*, as well as *tṛc* and so forth. (Pāṇini 3.2.178.2) Regarding the roots *vac*, *pracch*, *āyata*, *stu*, *kaṭapru*, *ju*, and *śrī*, there is lengthening [of the vowel]. [The rule applies] to *vac*, *pracch*, *āyata*, *stu*, *kaṭapru*, *ju*, and *śrī*.

The lengthening of the vowel and the suffix *kvip* must also be stated. From the root *vac*, we have *vāk*. From *pracch*, we have *śabdaprāṭ*. From *prach*, we have *āyatastūḥ*. From *kaṭapru*, we have *kaṭaprūḥ*. From *ju*, we have *jūḥ*. From *śri*, we have *śrīḥ*. Another teacher says:

312–313: An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the future tense (*bhaviṣyati*) when it does not refer to the current day (*anadyatana*). An addition must be made for the future tense when it does not refer to the current day: *śvo grāmaṃ gamī* ("he will go to the village tomorrow"). But what is the reason that [the rule] is not established? This instruction is formulated using the suffix *lṛṭ*. And since *lṛṭ* is superseded by *luṭ* in the case of the future not referring to the current day, these suffixes would apply only in the domain of *lṛṭ*.

They would not apply in the domain of the periphrastic future (*luṭ*). Furthermore, there is mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). And indeed, there is mutual dependence. What constitutes this mutual dependence?

The designation is made by means of a word denoting the future tense; yet the state of being the future tense occurs only after the designation has been made. Thus, this results in mutual dependence. And things characterized by mutual dependence are not logically tenable. Or rather, it has already been stated.

What has been said? First, it was said: "No, because there is no occasion for an exception; for the prescription of those two [suffixes] applies to what is not of today. Furthermore, it was also said: "It is established by the mention of the indeclinable (*avyaya*). The mention shall be made by means of a word possessing the nature of an indeclinable, namely:
"not being present" (*avartamāne*) and "not having come into being" (*abhūte*). Therefore, that mention must indeed be made by means of a word possessing the nature of an indeclinable.
It should not be so [interpreted]. This word *bhaviṣyat* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*); it is not the *lṛṭ* (future) suffix of the root *bhū*. How is its status as an indeclinable established?

It receives the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "particle" (*nipāta*) by the rule: "And those that resemble case-endings (*vibhakti*) or accents (*svara*) are particles. It then receives the designation of "indeclinable" by the rule: "A particle is an indeclinable. Even if it were indeed the *lṛṭ* suffix of the root *bhū*, even then it would still be an indeclinable. Why? Because it does not "pass away" (*na vyeti*).

Thus, it is an *avyaya* (indeclinable). But where does it not change (*na vyeti*)? These two specific times, the past and the present. By its very nature, it exists only in the future. If it is an *avyaya* because it does not change therein, or rather, because there is no other rule for its formation elsewhere;
or rather, there is no purpose for the heading concerning the future. What is the reason? Because there is no other rule for its formation elsewhere.

Because of their non-existence. Even those suffixes (*pratyaya*) that remain hereafter do not exclude these two specific times, namely the past and the present. By their very nature, they exist only as "will be" (*bhaviṣyat*). Therefore, he recites what follows: the purpose of the section on the future (*bhaviṣyad-adhikāra*) is for the sake of avoiding incorrect forms (*anapaśabda*) in such cases as *yāvat pacati* ("while cooking") and *purā pacati* ("before cooking").

Regarding the rule for the present tense (*laṭ*) after words such as *yāvat* and *purā*, it is a prior exception (*pūrvavipratiṣiddha*) to the future tense (*luṭ*). The rule for the present tense (*laṭ*) applies after words such as *yāvat* and *purā* by means of a prior exception to the future tense (*luṭ*). The scope of the rule "the present tense (*laṭ*) occurs after the particles *yāvat* and *purā*" is as follows: *yāvat*... [text continues].

[The rule for] *laṭ* [applies]: "He eats," "He used to eat. [The rule for] *luṭ* has its scope: "He will do tomorrow" (*śvaḥ kartā*), "He will study tomorrow" (*śvo 'dhyetā*). Here both [rules] would apply: "As far as tomorrow he eats" (*yāvac chvo bhuṅkte*), "Before tomorrow he eats" (*purā śvo bhuṅkte*). By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), *laṭ* takes effect.

Then that [rule for *luṭ*] must be stated as a prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). It need not be stated; because in the rule "In the non-recent past, *luṭ*" (*anadyatane luṭ*), the terms "as far as" (*yāvat*) and "before" (*purā*) [are understood].
The term *laṭ* will be carried over [from the previous rule].

That [suffix], being specifically prescribed, would supersede the general suffix *ṇvul*. This too is not a valid purpose.
