(P_3,3.11) For what purpose is this stated? It is not the case that those suffixes prescribed for the sense of abstract action (*bhāva*) will apply without distinction—both when there is a verbal root denoting an action as a subordinate element (*upapada*) intended for another action, and otherwise. This is for the sake of a specific rule (*pratipadavidhi*) regarding those suffixes prescribed for the sense of abstract action exactly as they have been ordained.

This undertaking is for the purpose of a specific rule (*pratipadavidhi*) regarding verbal derivatives expressing abstract action (*bhāvavacana*) as prescribed [in previous rules]. For it was just stated that when a word denoting an action is used as an attendant circumstance (*upapada*) for another action, suffixes such as *tṛc* and others do not occur by virtue of the optionality of different forms (*vāsarūpa*). Yet, suffixes such as *tṛc* and others also express abstract action. This indeed serves a purpose. What then? It must be stated that they occur "as prescribed" (*yathāvihita*).

What is the purpose? Here, so that from whatever bases (*prakṛti*) and by whatever specific rule affixes (*pratyaya*) are prescribed for the abstract state (*bhāva*), they may likewise apply from those same bases and by that same specific rule when there is an object of action (*upapada*) denoting an action intended for the sake of another action;
[this is] so that there be no confusion (*vyatikara*). If that is so, then it must be stated. It need not be stated. For here, the affixes are prescribed for the abstract state (*bhāva*).

Thus, this [rule] is established. Since this is already established, the purpose of employing the term *vacana* (word) is so that [the suffixes] may function as denoters (*vācaka*). And if, from whichever bases (*prakṛti*) and by whichever specific distinction the suffixes are prescribed for the abstract state (*bhāva*), then from those same bases and by that very same distinction they [should apply] to the action (*kriyā*).
317–318. Why is this stated? [Objection: The suffix *aṇ* has been prescribed for the object (*karman*) without distinction;

it will therefore apply when there is a verbal root as an attendant word (*upapada*) whose purpose is an action, as well as in other cases. [Response: The restatement of *aṇ* is for the sake of preventing its exclusion in the domain of exceptions.
The restatement of *aṇ* is made so that there may be no exclusion even in the domain of exceptions. For example: *godāyo vrajati* ("He goes to fetch cows").

[The example] "kambaladāyo vrajati" (he goes, giving blankets) is stated so that there might be no non-application [of the general rule] in the domain of an exception (*apavāda*), but not so that it would apply again in the domain of a general rule (*utsarga*) for the sake of a specific injunction (*pratipadavidhi*). For it was just now stated that when a verb is an attendant word (*upapada*) to another action, suffixes such as *tṛc* and others do not occur by the rule of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpa*). And the suffix *aṇ* is also included among those beginning with *tṛc*. If that is so, then...

By this, two things are accomplished: the non-occurrence [of the suffix] in the domain of the exception (*apavāda*), and the application of the specific rule (*pratipadavidhāna*) in the domain of the general rule (*utsarga*).
But how can both be obtained by a single effort? He says: they are obtained. How? By the force of the mention of the word "object" (*karman*).
But how is it that the suffix *aṇ* is obtainable in the sense of an object even without the mention of the word "object"? The term "mention" (*vacana*) is understood from the context.
It follows. There is this purpose [for the rule]. But what is it? It must be stated that [the suffix] occurs "not alternately" (*aparyāyeṇa*).

For sometimes it would apply to the object (*karman*), and sometimes when a verbal root expressing an action is the attendant word (*upapada*) for the sake of another action. Then it must indeed be stated. No, it need not be stated. By means of the word *ca* ("and"), a simultaneous application (*sanniyoga*) will be effected: "the suffix *aṇ* [is used] in the sense of the object and also [when a verbal root expressing an action is the attendant word]. 318–319. What is the purpose of the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*)? The mention of "the remainder" regarding the future tense suffix *lṛṭ* is for the sake of a specific rule (*pratipadavidhi*) concerning action. The mention of "the remainder" regarding *lṛṭ* is made for the sake of a specific rule concerning action, so that there may be a specific rule. If it were prescribed without distinction, there would be an absence of *lṛṭ* because it has been prohibited. If it were prescribed without distinction, there would be an absence of *lṛṭ*.
[One] goes thinking, "I shall do," or [one] goes thinking, "I shall take. What is the reason? Because it has been prohibited.

For it was just stated that when a verbal root meaning an action is used as an *upapada* for another action, the suffixes beginning with *tṛc* (the agentive suffixes) do not occur by virtue of the rule *vāsarūpa*. And the suffix *lṛṭ* (the future tense marker) is also among those beginning with *tṛc*. This [objection] does indeed serve a purpose. But what then? [The answer is: It is certainly better [to state the following].

By the inclusion of the word *śeṣa* (the remainder), the future suffix *lṛṭ* is excluded from that which has a word expressing an action as its *upapada*. What is the reason? Because [in those cases] there is no *upapada* expressing an action. It is stated: "in the *śeṣa*. And what is the *śeṣa*? That which is other than an action directed toward another action. If this is so, then the mention of the *śeṣa* regarding *lṛṭ* is for the purpose of a specific rule (*pratipadavidhi*) concerning action. The mention of the *śeṣa* regarding *lṛṭ* is made as a specific rule concerning action.

So that it may be: *lṛṭ* [is used] in the remaining cases as well, as in *kariṣyati*, *hariṣyati*. And where? When a verb expressing an action is the *upapada* (governing word) for the sake of another action. Then, should the particle *ca* ("and") be inserted? It need not be inserted. This is established by the mere statement "here *lṛṭ* occurs. Since this is already established, the purpose of his employing the term *śeṣe* ("in the remainder") is to indicate that it is an integral part of the rule (*yogāṅga*).

Where, then, does the option (*vibhāṣā*) apply? It applies when there is grammatical agreement with a word ending in the first case: "He will cook" (*pākṣyan pakṣyati*), "He is about to cook" (*pakṣyamāṇaḥ pakṣyate*).

(P_3,3.15.1) A split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made: in the sense of "not today" (*anadyatana*), the suffixes *lṛṭ* and those termed *sat* occur. For example: *śvo ’gnīn ādhyāsyamānena* ("by one who will maintain the sacred fires tomorrow") and *śvaḥ somena yakṣyamāṇena* ("by one who will sacrifice with Soma tomorrow"). Then follows *luṭ*: *luṭ* occurs in the sense of "not today. For example: *śvaḥ kartā* ("he will do tomorrow"). Tomorrow...

[The opponent asks: "By whom is it prescribed that the two [suffixes] *sat* and *sañjñau* are designated as such for the future tense (*lṛṭ*) not referring to the current day (*anadyatana*)? [The proponent replies: This very fact makes it known that the future tense (*lṛṭ*) occurs even when not referring to the current day, since this [sūtra] prescribes that the two [suffixes] *sat* and *sañjñau* apply to the future tense (*lṛṭ*) not referring to the current day.
And by doing so, that which was stated—"there must be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) regarding the future tense not referring to the current day"—is also rendered faultless.

Regarding lamentation, [the suffixes] expressing the sense of the future tense (*bhaviṣyantī*) and the tomorrow-tense (*śvastanī*) should be stated [to occur]. Regarding the sense of lamentation expressed by the future tense and the tomorrow-tense, it should be stated: "When indeed will she go, who places her feet thus? When indeed will he study?"
"One who is thus unengaged" [is the meaning]. However, there is a comparison based on the lapse of time; however, there is a comparison based on the lapse of time.

"This one is a goer, as it were"—this one will not go. "This one is a reciter, as it were"—this one will not recite. Indeed, there is no comparison with a finite verb form (*tiṅanta*). If that is so, then [the rule applies] as in the case of "as if in the non-recent past" (*anadyatane iva anadyatane*).

It should be stated: "in the case of *vādhimatsyabala*. *Atīsāra* means disease; *visāra* means fish; in the sense of *bala*, [it refers to] *śālasāra* and *khadirasāra*.

(Pāṇini 3.3.18) Regarding the state (*bhāva*), there is an indication of all genders. An indication of all genders must be made for the state. [This applies to] the occurrence (*bhūti*) and the coming into being (*bhavana*).

Regarding the word *bhāve*: what is the purpose? It is so that these suffixes may occur when the abstract state (*bhāva*) is expressed in all genders. But what is the reason that this is not established? This instruction is made using the masculine gender and the singular number; therefore, these suffixes would occur only in the masculine gender and only in the singular number, and not in the feminine or neuter genders, nor in the dual or plural numbers.

And they would not exist. In this case, the specific mention [of gender] is not the governing factor. But how can it be that the mention is made by that very [word], and yet that [mention] is not the governing factor? You are both a practitioner of that and a hater of that. Because it is inseparable, the mention here is made with the masculine gender and the singular number. It must necessarily be by some case-ending and some gender.

An explanation must be given. For example, suppose someone seeking rice brings a bundle of rice together with its husks and its straw because they are inseparable; having taken as much as is needed, he discards the husks and the straw. Similarly, suppose someone seeking meat brings fish together with their scales and their bones because they are inseparable; [having taken] as much as is needed...

In that case, having taken [the pieces], one discards the fragments and thorns. Similarly here as well, because of the invariable concomitance (*nāntarīyakatva*), the designation is made using the masculine gender and the singular number. For in this context, the specific form of the designation is not the essential factor; the designation could have been made with any particular case-ending and any particular gender. Alternatively, the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* denote action in general, while they also denote specific actions.

The roots beginning with *pac* [are used]. Now, that which is the root *bhū* (to become) for *pac* (to cook) is not the root *pac* for *bhū*; and that which is the root *pac* for *bhū* is not the root *bhū* for *pac*. Furthermore, what is the *bhū* of *pac*? It is the universal (*sāmānya*). And what is the *pac* of *bhū*? It is the particular (*viśeṣa*). For example:

The pupil of the preceptor went to the nephew of his maternal uncle and said, "Please pay your respects to the preceptor. He went and paid his respects to the maternal uncle. Likewise, the nephew of the maternal uncle went to the pupil of the preceptor and said, "Please pay your respects to the maternal uncle. He went and paid his respects to the preceptor.
In this case as well, that which is indicated by the root *pac* when it functions as *bhū* is [the object].

(Pāṇini 3.3.19) Why is the term "kāraka" (participant in action) mentioned? The mention of "kāraka" is for the purpose of understanding that [the substitution] applies to its own meaning (*svārtha*) when there is no other designation. The mention of "kāraka" [is necessary].

"In the absence of a specific instruction, [a suffix] is understood to have its own meaning (*svārtha*); that is, suffixes whose meanings are not specifically prescribed apply in their own sense. For example:

*guptijkidbhyaḥ san* ("the suffix *san* after roots *gup*, *tij*, and *kit*") and *yāvādibhyaḥ kan* ("the suffix *kan* after *yāva* and others"). These suffixes here too would thus apply in their own sense.
It is for this purpose—that they should not apply in their own sense but rather in the sense of a *kāraka* (grammatical participant)—that this is stated. But this is not a valid purpose.

The suffix *ghañ* has been prescribed in its own sense to denote the abstract state (*bhāva*). Therefore, since there is no possibility [of the rule applying otherwise] in this case, this [sūtra] should be understood as having a restrictive purpose (*niyamārtha*), namely: "only when denoting a name (*saṃjñā*) and not when denoting the agent. And indeed, there exists at present some abstract state that has become a name for which this rule would apply. He says: "there is," namely *āvāha*.

Regarding the term *vivāha*: a restrictive rule (*niyama*) would apply because of the principle of "uselessness" (*kaimarthakya*), on the grounds that there is nothing else to be enjoined. However, in this case, there is something to be enjoined: namely, that the suffix *ghañ* is to be enjoined for the sake of forming a name (*saṃjñā*) when the action does not involve the agent as the primary factor (*akartari kārake*). In that situation, since one must choose between an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*) and a restrictive rule (*niyama*), it will be an original injunction and not a restrictive rule. Therefore, that very [original injunction] is the purpose.
"Lest they [the suffixes] apply in their own primary sense (*svārtha*). But has it not been stated that "the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed in its own primary sense, in the sense of 'being' (*bhāva*)"?

That "being" is different; it is external to the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*). By this rule, it would now apply to the internal "being. What, then, is the distinction between these two types of "being"? The distinction between types of "being" has already been explained in the Bhāṣya. Even this purpose is not necessary.

That which is joined with *nañ* (the negative particle) or *iva* (the particle of comparison) is understood to apply to something other than that [negated object] or to what is similar to it; for such is the comprehension of the meaning. That which is joined with *nañ* and that which is joined with *iva* are to be understood as referring to another thing or to something resembling it; for such is the meaning perceived. For example, when it is said, "Bring a non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇam ānaya*), one brings a person who resembles a Brahmin. One does not become satisfied by bringing a clod of earth.

In this case as well, because of the prohibition of agency by the term "non-agent" (*akartari*), the operation is understood to apply to something other than the agent, namely that which resembles an agent. Furthermore, what else is a non-agent that resembles an agent? A *kāraka* (participant in action). If so, the mention of *kāraka* must be made for the sake of the subsequent rule, so that [the operation] may apply to all *kārakas* when expressing measure (*parimāṇa*). Let it not be the case here: "one *tila*-height" (*ekā tilocchritiḥ*).

Regarding the rule *deve sṛtī* (Pāṇini 3.3.49): the enumeration of the suffix *ghañ* in this context is for the sake of excluding its application where the agent (*kartṛ*) is not intended; for it will be stated later that even when feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*) are not explicitly mentioned, they are understood as being excluded. Therefore, that [separate mention] need not be stated. Furthermore, there is no purpose for this [separate mention] either, because here too the condition *akartari* ("when not denoting the agent") will simply carry over [from the previous rule]. Moreover, the mention of the term *saṃjñā* ("technical name") is redundant, since the suffix *ghañ* is observed everywhere [in such cases].

And the mention of *sañjñā* (name) is purposeless. Why? Because the suffix *ghañ* is seen everywhere. For *ghañ* is indeed seen even when it is not a name (*asañjñāyām*): "What gift (*dāya*) was given by you? and "What gain (*lābha*) was obtained by you?
If the mention of *sañjñā* were not made, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). In the case of "the mat (*kaṭa*) was made," [the suffix] *kāra* [would apply].

[If it is argued that] the suffix *kaṭac* would apply [to words like *paṭu*], resulting in an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), [we reply: this is established because the application of a suffix is characterized by its actual usage (*abhidhānalakṣaṇatva*). If it is argued that there is an over-extension, that is not so. What is the reason? It is established because the application of a suffix is characterized by its actual usage. Formations consisting of *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and *samāsa* suffixes are characterized by their actual usage; therefore, they will not occur where there is no such usage (*anabhidhānāt*).

What is the purpose of including the word *sarva* ("all")? It is so that the suffix *ghañ* may occur after all verbal roots (*dhātu*), even in cases where [the suffixes] *ap* and *ac* would otherwise apply. For example: *ekaḥ taṇḍulaniścāyaḥ* ("one winnowing of rice") and *dvau śūrpaniṣpāvau* ("two winnowings with a winnowing-basket"). The inclusion of the word *sarva* is redundant when the meaning is a measure (*parimāṇa*).

Because [the suffix] is already established by this rule, the inclusion of the word *sarva* (all) is purposeless. What is the reason? Because it is already established by the rule "when expressing a measure" (*parimāṇākhyāyam*). Thus, the suffix *ghañ* is established even in the domain of the suffixes *ac* and *ap*. There is no need for the inclusion of *sarva*. However, there is another purpose for stating this [rule]. What is it? [To account for forms such as] *ekaḥ pākaḥ*, *dvau pākau*, *trayaḥ pākāḥ*.

[Objection: This is already established by the preceding rule. [Reply: It is not so established. The previous rule applies when there is a technical name (*saṃjñā*). But this is not a technical name. [Objection: The mention of "technical name" (*saṃjñā*) is rejected. [Reply: Even if it were retained, there would still be no fault.
In the case of *aj* as well, it occurs only when it is a technical name. For whatever kind the general rule (*utsarga*) is, the exception (*apavāda*) must be of that same kind.

Then it is for the sake of the subsequent rule: so that [the suffix] may apply after *iṅ* as well as after all [other roots]. But surely this *iṅ* is unique, like a seedless pomegranate; how can it apply to all derivational bases? [The forms are: "having approached, one studies" (*upetya adhīyate*), therefore it is an *adhyāya*;
"it is studied in that," therefore it is an *adhyāya*. This is a formal irregularity (*nipātana*) based on the rule: "and [the words] *adhyāya*, *nyāya*, *āyodha*, *āvasa*, *saṃhāra*, and *āvāya*."
It need not be formulated; even this purpose does not exist, for it is already accomplished by the rule for *nyāsa* itself. [Objection:

Then it must be stated for the sake of what follows, so that the suffix *ṇac* may apply after all roots in the sense of reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*) when a feminine noun is intended. [Response: Even this purpose does not exist, for he will say this: "In the case of reciprocal action, the mention of 'feminine' is for the sake of the meaning of *vyatipāka*."

The separate mention is for the purpose of subverting an objection and for the purpose of excluding [the application of] *vyāvacorī* and *vyāvacarcī*. In that regard, there would be a fault in the case of *vyatīkṣā* and so on. But it is established that when "strī" is mentioned in the context of the base form (*prakṛti*), there is the mention of both *ṇac* and *ṇic*. If it is argued that it is for the sake of what follows—so that *inuṇ* may apply to all roots in the sense of "pervasion" (*abhividhi*) in the abstract state (*bhāva*), as in *sāṃrāviṇam*—this too is not the case.

The purpose [of this rule] will be stated: the inclusion of the term *bhāva* (state/being) in the sense of "pervasion" (*abhividhi*) is for the sake of excluding the suffix *kta* and others in the neuter;

the separate mention [of *bhāva*] is for the sake of subverting what is obstructive [to it], but not [for the sake of subverting] the suffix *lyuṭ*. If so, then this is the purpose: there should be the subversion of that exception which depends on the verbal root (*prakṛti*), as well as the subversion of that exception which depends on the meaning (*artha*).
Let it not be that there is one *tila*-measure and two paths. The enumeration of the suffix *ghañ* is for the sake of excluding the domain of *ajap* [suffixes].
For if it were not stated, one would raise the objection that there would be an understanding of exceptions even for feminine suffixes; therefore, this need not be said.

329–330. *Ghañ-anukramaṇam aj-ab-viṣaye*. It should be stated: "The sequence of *ghañ* [suffixes] applies in the domain of *aj* and *ap*. For if this were not stated, it would be understood that this [sequence] is an exception (*apavāda*) even for feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*). If this were not mentioned, it would be understood that this is an exception even for feminine suffixes, as in: *ekā tilocchritiḥ* (one height of a sesame seed) and *dve sṛtī* (two paths). [Furthermore, in the case of] *dāra* and *jāra*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *ṇi* suffix when they denote the agent (*kartṛ*).

330. Regarding the rule *iṅaśca*, there is an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the feminine when it denotes the ablative (*apādāna*); and after a word ending in that [root], the suffix *ṅīṣ* is optionally prescribed. In the rule *iṅaśca*, an addition must be made for the feminine when it denotes the ablative; and it should be stated that after a word ending in that [root], *ṅīṣ* is optionally applied. She from whom one studies by approaching her is called *upādhyāyī* or *upādhyāyā*. Regarding the root *śṝ*: after this root, [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] in the sense of wind, color, and cessation.

The suffix *ghañ* should be stated [as applicable here]. *Śāraḥ* means wind; *śāraḥ* means color. "Like a cow that has not been fully grazed (*akṛtanīśāraḥ*), one is generally emaciated in the winter.

(Pāṇini 3.3.36). The statement "in the sense of a fist" (*sami muṣṭau*) is redundant, because it is already established by the rule "when expressing a measure" (*parimāṇākhyāyām*). [Thus, the addition] "in the sense of a fist" (*sami muṣṭau*) is unnecessary.

Thus, this statement is purposeless. Why? Because it is already established by the rule *parimāṇākhyāyām*. It is indeed established by the very words *parimāṇākhyāyām*. However, this undertaking is for the sake of things that are not measures (*aparimāṇa*); for example, *mallasya saṅgrāhaḥ* (the grip of the wrestler) and *muṣṭikasya saṅgāhaḥ* (the grasp of the boxer). Furthermore, *udgrābha* and *nigrābha* [are used] in the Veda (*chandasi*) in the sense of lifting up and lowering down the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*).
The two words *udgrābha* and *nigrābha* are to be stated as Vedic forms [used] in the sense of lifting up and lowering down the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*).
"The gods have increased the *brahman* for both the *udgrābha* and the *nigrābha*. (Pāṇini 3.3.43).
*Kaṭha Upaniṣad* II,148.11–149.3; *Rgveda* III. [End of citation].

331–332. What is the purpose of including the word *strī* (feminine)? The inclusion of the word *strī* in the rule for the reciprocal exchange of actions (*karmavyatihāra*) is for the sake of the meaning "exchange" (*vyatipāka*). The inclusion of the word *strī* in the rule for the reciprocal exchange of actions is made for the sake of the meaning "exchange. [Otherwise] it would not apply here in the case of *vyatipāko vartate*. Now, what is the purpose of the separate mention? The separate mention is for the purpose of subverting a sublater (*bādhakabādhanārtha*). This is the separate mention.

It is formulated for the purpose of refuting those who would refute it—that is, for the purpose of refuting those who are its refuters. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of avoiding the faults of *vyāvacorī* and *vyāvacarcī*. The fault of *vyāvacorī* occurs; the fault of *vyāvacarcī* occurs. In that regard, there is a fault concerning *vyatīkṣā* and the others. In that regard, there is a fault concerning *vyatīkṣā* and the others. [Examples: *vyatīkṣā vartate*, *vyatīhā vartate*. [The desired form is] established.
But regarding the current mention of *strī* (the feminine suffix), there is the mention of *ṇac* and the mention of *ṇic*. This is established. How?

332–333. What is the purpose of including the term *bhāva* (state/abstract action)? The inclusion of *bhāva* in the sense of "inclusively" (*abhividhi*) is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] the suffixes *kta* and others in the neuter gender.

The inclusion of *bhāva* in the sense of inclusively is made for the purpose of excluding *kta* and other suffixes in the neuter gender, so that they do not occur in the neuter. Now, what is the purpose of the separate mention? The separate mention is for the purpose of subverting the sublater [of the rule].

The separate mention [of *saṃkūṭana*] is made for the purpose of subverting those [rules] that would otherwise subvert it; that is, for the purpose of subverting those which would subvert it. But this does not apply to the suffix *lyuṭ*. For the subversion of *lyuṭ* is not intended; rather, the form remains simply as *saṃkūṭanam*.

333–334. An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) regarding *bhaya* must be made in the rule for suffixes beginning with *ac*. An addition regarding *bhaya* must be made in the rule for suffixes beginning with *ac*. [The example is: *bhayam* (fear). It is said that this is too limited when it says "of *bhaya*"; it should rather be stated as "of *bhaya* and so forth" (*bhayādīnām*), so that it may apply here as well:
*bhayam*, *varṣam* (rain). What is the purpose? To exclude suffixes such as *kta* in the neuter gender. For suffixes such as *kta* occur in the neuter gender.
"Let them not be"—this is the prohibition regarding *kalpa* and so forth. A prohibition must be stated regarding *kalpa* and so forth;
[in these cases], *kalpa* means "purpose" and *mantra* [is implied]. Regarding *jāvasau* in the Veda: the forms *jāva* and *sāva* must be stated as occurring in the Veda. For example:
"May there be speed (*java*) for my thighs," and "This five-gruel offering (*pañcaudana-sāva*) is mine."

For what purpose is *ap* prescribed after the root *ci* preceded by *nis*, when it would already be established by *ac* alone? For there is no difference whether *ap* or *ac* follows *ci* preceded by *nis*; the form would be the same and the accent would be the same. [Reply: It is not so established.

In the case of *hastādāna* ("taking by the hand"), the suffix *ghañ* would otherwise apply; [the following rule] is intended to preclude that. Therefore, he recites the subsequent [explanation]: "The mention of *niś* in the rule prescribing the suffix *ap* is purposeless, because there is a prohibition against *ghañ* in the case of *steya*. The mention of *niś* in the rule prescribing the suffix *ap* is purposeless. Why? Because there is a prohibition against *ghañ* in the case of *steya*. [This refers to] the *ghañ* prescribed for *steya*.

The suffixes that have been prescribed for the immediate vicinity of the present time (*vartamāna-sāmīpya*) should apply after every verbal root (*dhātu*). However, if the particle *vat* is employed [in the rule], no fault arises. Furthermore, if from whichever bases (*prakṛti*) and by whichever specific condition suffixes were prescribed for the present time, they likewise occur from those same bases and by that very same condition for the immediate vicinity of the present, then it is "like the present" (*vartamānavat*).

[The suffixes] would have been formed [by this rule]. For if they were derived from the base alone, or if they were merely the suffix alone, they would not be formed like those used for the present. Here, after stating "or like the present in proximity to the present," only the imperative (*loṭ*) is cited as an example.

If, on the other hand, it were simply stated that "the present tense (*laṭ*) optionally occurs," then [this objection would arise]. Therefore, he recites the subsequent [sūtra]: "In proximity to the present..."

The statement "it is like the present" is for the sake of [the forms] *śatṛ* and so on. The rule that it is "like the present" when there is proximity to the present time is formulated for the sake of *śatṛ* and so on; this undertaking is for the purpose of *śatṛ* and the rest, as in: "Here I am cooking" (*eṣo 'smi pacan*) and "Here I am cooking" (*eṣo 'smi pacamānaḥ*).
This is not a necessary purpose, because *śatṛ* and *śānac* are substitutes for *laṭ*; therefore, *laṭ* occurs there by virtue of the general rule.

Thus it is established. But what about those two substitutes for *laṅ*? [For example: "I am this purifying one" (*eṣo 'smi pavamānaḥ*) and "I am this sacrificer" (*eṣo 'smi yajamānaḥ*). And those two which are substitutes for *laṭ* also serve as a purpose [for this rule]: the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are prescribed for *laṭ* when it is ordained to denote the present tense. Furthermore, this rule is prescribed without distinction; indeed, it is stated that it is for the sake of *śatṛ* and the others. There are many...
And [the suffixes] *śatṛ* and so forth: "I am one who adorns" (*alaṅkariṣṇuḥ*), "I am one who procreates" (*prajaniṣṇuḥ*).

(Pāṇini 3.3.132.1) Expectation (*āśaṃsā*) refers to the future time. When there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the past tense (*bhūtavat*) in the sense of expectation, there is a prohibition of the *laṅ* and *liṭ* suffixes.

When there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the past tense (*bhūtavat*) to express a wish (*āśaṃsā*), it should be stated that the *laṅ* and *liṭ* suffixes are prohibited. Or rather, it need not be stated. Why? Because the occasion for the exception (*apavāda*) does not exist; for those two [suffixes] are prescribed only for what is not of the current day (*anadyatana*). Or rather, it need not be stated. What is the reason? Because the occasion for the exception does not exist. There is no occasion for the exception here. How so? Because those two are prescribed for what is not of the current day. [And this applies] when it is not of the current day.

For those two, the *laṅ* and *liṭ*, are prescribed [by rules other than this one]. And here, the non-contemporary (*anadyatana*) time is not intended to be expressed. What then? It is the general past time (*bhūtakālasāmānya*). (P_3.3.132.2) Because there is no distinction between *āśaṃsā* (expectation) and *sambhāvanā* (possibility), the prescription for them would not otherwise apply. *Āśaṃsā* is possibility.

Thus, these two meanings are indistinguishable. Because there is no distinction between *āśaṃsā* (hope) and *sambhāvanā* (possibility), there is no application of the specific rules [prescribed for them].

Those suffixes that are prescribed for *āśaṃsā* would also apply to *sambhāvanā*, and those prescribed for *sambhāvanā* would also apply to *āśaṃsā*. Why, then, is it said that there is "no application"? It is not that they do not apply at all; rather, they do not apply in a more appropriate manner.

[The following] occurs: the desired systematic arrangement would not be possible; it is not the case that [all things] are intended to exist everywhere. Or rather, [this is not a fault], because hope (*āśaṃsā*) is a constituent part of possibility (*sambhāvanā*). Or again, this is not a fault. Why? Because hope is a constituent part of possibility. Hope consists essentially of the constituent parts of possibility. What is called "hope" is a determined object that is both realized and unrealized. Possibility...

The meaning intended by the name has indeed been demonstrated. Or rather, there is no doubt regarding the meaning because the suffix *sambhāvana* (possibility) is sufficient for that purpose. Alternatively, there is indeed no doubt regarding its meaning. What is the reason? Because the suffix *sambhāvana* is sufficient for that purpose. In the case of *sambhāvana*, sufficiency (*ālamarthya*) is understood; however, in the absence of doubt, there is insufficiency (*anālamarthya*). This is the activity of the Teacher.

It indicates that even when expressing possibility (*sambhāvana*), a sense of incapacity (*anālamarthya*) is understood, since he [the author] says "possible" (*alam*) in the context of possibility. Therefore, it is rightly said: "Or rather, because hope (*āśaṃsā*) is a constituent part of possibility. (Pāṇini 3.3.133.1) KA_II,159.16–201.2 Ro_III,159.16–201.2.

350. *Lṛṭ* occurs in expressions of speed; *liṅ* occurs in expressions of hope, by way of prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*). In expressions of speed, *lṛṭ* occurs; in expressions of hope, *liṅ* occurs, by way of prohibition. "In expressions of speed, *lṛṭ* occurs" is the scope for this [rule]. For example: "If the teacher has come, we shall study quickly. "In expressions of hope, *liṅ* occurs" is the scope for that [rule]. For example: "The teacher..."

If the teacher has arrived, I hope that I shall be able to study; here both [the optative and the conditional] apply. If the teacher has arrived, I hope that I may study quickly. The optative occurs by way of prohibition [of the conditional].

350–351. The term "accomplished" (*niṣpanna*) is applied to what is not yet accomplished; the student is so called because he is not yet accomplished. The student, though not yet accomplished, is designated by the word "accomplished" and is to be instructed. For what reason? Because he is not yet accomplished. Just as when it has rained, one says, "The rice is accomplished," meaning that the rice will come to be there and will be perfected. But this is established [as a valid usage] because it serves to preclude the future.

This is established. How so? Because of the prohibition regarding the future. That which the world does not tolerate is the use of a word expressing the future. Someone says: "If it rains, the rice will be successful. He is told: "Do not speak thus; say instead, 'the rice has been successful,' because [the result] is perceived as having occurred at the time when the cause was present."

Or rather, this is established because it is observed at the time when it has become a cause; for rain is the cause, and the rainy season is the action. If that is so, and the object is already accomplished, why are the tasks that have been accomplished not performed? Which ones? Eating and so forth.
This objection—"why are the tasks that have been accomplished not performed?"—is now addressed as something different. As for that which is accomplished...

"The purpose has not been accomplished"—that is the purpose which has been accomplished. Indeed, even when rice is already in the granary, threshing and other such processes must necessarily still be awaited. In the same way here as well, the purpose has been accomplished; yet, birth and other such processes must necessarily still be awaited.

All case endings are used after words having the sense of *asti* (is/exists) in the sense of the root *bhū*. All case endings are used after words having the sense of *asti* in the sense of the root *bhū*. For example: *kūpaḥ asti* (there is a well), *kūpaḥ bhaviṣyati* (there will be a well), *kūpaḥ bhavitā* (there is to be a well), *kūpaḥ abhūt* (there was a well), *kūpaḥ āsīt* (there was a well), and *kūpaḥ babhūva* (there came to be a well). But how is it known that this is the meaning of the root *bhū*?
Because the agent exists; the agent exists here. But how is it known that the agent exists here?

[It is known because] this well was seen by him at some time, and he does not perceive any loss whatsoever on its part. He, however, determines through his intellect its eternal existence there, thinking, "The well exists. But it is established according to its own nature.

This is established by the simultaneous utterance of the [temporal] times. How so? Because these case-endings (*vibhakti*) are employed according to their respective times. But how is it known that these case-endings are employed according to their respective times? Because they are not heard; for they are not actually uttered. Furthermore, there would be a reversal of what is unestablished (*asiddha*). It is unestablished.
And there is no such reversal [of meaning]. For one does not employ the expression "the well came into being" when it should have been said "there is a well.

What, then, is the reason? [It is that] they are not so spoken of, and the reversal is unestablished. Here, some actions belong to the senses (*indriya*) and some belong to the intellect (*buddhi*). The action of the sense is contact (*samāsādana*); the action of the intellect is determination (*vyavasāya*). For in this way, who...

Someone wishing to go to Pāṭaliputra says: "On this road that is to be traveled as far as Pāṭaliputra, there will be a well. [Another says: "Having reached it, having passed it, and having stayed there, there was a well. [Or: "Having reached it, having passed it, and having stayed there, having forgotten it, there came to be a well. When these are the functions of the sense organs, then these case-endings [are used].
For when there is the action of cognition (*buddhi*), then [the suffix] will be present (*vartamāna*).
(Pāṇini 3.3.135) Why are these two prohibitions stated? Why is it not simply said, "as in the case of the present day" (*adyatanavat*)? It is not [sufficient].

Regarding the prohibition [of the *laṅ* and *luṭ* suffixes] as if they were not pertaining to the current day (*anadyatana*), there is no prohibition of *laṅ* and *luṭ*. One should not view it as a prohibition of *laṅ* and *luṭ* when there is a prohibition as if they were not pertaining to the current day. For, when there is the statement "as if pertaining to the current day," this is understood as a positive injunction (*vidhi*). What is the fault in that? In that case, there would be the contingency of the injunction for *laṭ*. In that situation, the injunction for *laṭ* would apply.

It would follow that the *luṅ* and *lṛṭ* [tenses] would be used out of their proper time. That is, the application of *luṅ* and *lṛṭ* would occur at the wrong times: *lṛṭ* would occur where *luṅ* is required, and *luṅ* would occur where *lṛṭ* is required. But now, having stated these two prohibitions, he remains silent; thus, it will be according to what is naturally obtained, namely, in the sense of "today" (*adyatana*).

For what purpose is this stated? Is it not already established by [the rule] *na anadyatanavat*? It is for the sake of ensuring that there is no continuity of action (*akriyāprabandha*) when a future limit (*maryādā*) is expressed as being "subsequent" (*avarasmin*). This formulation is undertaken for the sake of ensuring no continuity of action. Why is this said?

It is a prohibition of continuity (*akriyā-prabandha*), and not for the sake of continuity of action (*kriyā-prabandha*). If it were for the sake of continuity of action, the statement would be purposeless. If it were for the sake of continuity of action, the statement would be redundant; for the continuity of action is already established by the preceding rule alone. In that case, this is the purpose: I shall say "not of those [periods] lasting less than a day and night" (*an-ahorātrāṇām*), so that it does not apply here.

Regarding this upcoming period of thirty nights, [the rule applies] to its latter fifteen nights. If it is argued that this is for the purpose of excluding the day-and-night (*ahorātra*), we say no, because such an exclusion is not desired. If it is argued that it is for the purpose of excluding the day-and-night, that is not so, because it is not desired. What is the reason? Because it is not desired. For here too, it is precisely intended that the rule does not apply as if it were referring to the immediate past (*anadyatana*). Then what is the purpose?

"I shall say 'it will be' so that it does not apply here: 'that which is this path already traversed as far as Pāṭaliputra, the portion of it prior to Sāketa. No, because it is not desired. For here too, it is intended that the rule 'not like the immediate past' (anadyatanavat) applies.
Then this is the purpose: I shall say 'in the expression of a limit' so that it does not apply here: that which is this path..."

"The destination is immeasurable; that which is 'lower' than Sāketa [is the limit]. Even here, it is desired that the rule "not as if referring to the immediate past" (*anadyatanavat*) applies. Therefore, it is rightly said: "In the case of a statement of a limit (*maryādāvacana*), when it is the lower one, [the *luṅ* tense is used] for the sake of not implying continuity of action (*akriyāprabandha*).
If it is argued that it is for the sake of implying continuity of action (*kriyāprabandha*), then the statement is redundant.

(P_3,3.137) KA_II,162.15-21 Ro_III, 356: Regarding the phrase *anahorātrāṇām*, a prohibition must be stated concerning their division. [This refers to: "Of this thirty-night period that is to come, that which is the subsequent half-month"—in the case of a division by those [units].
And they should state that this applies to the division [of time]:

"That which is the coming month, the latter fifteen nights of it. One should understand this as a prohibition against dividing days and nights by means of other days and nights. Therefore, the Teacher, acting as a friend, explains it thus:

The phrase "of non-daily periods" (*anahorātrāṇām*) is a prohibition regarding their division; and [the phrase] "by means of them" (*taiḥ ca*) refers to division. In what subsequent context? In the context of the division of time (*kālavibhāge*). Why is this so? Because of the force of making a formal split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*).

It should also be stated that [the rule applies] when there is a failure of the means (*sādhanātipatti*), so that it may apply here as well: "You would have eaten meat if you had sat near me. If that is so, then it must be stated. It need not be stated; for without a means, [the action cannot occur].

357. *lṛṅ* is used for the past tense when *uta*, *api*, and so forth follow. *lṛṅ* should be understood as used for the past tense in the presence of *uta*, *api*, and others: *uta adhyaiṣyata* ("perhaps he studied"), *api adhyaiṣyata* ("even he studied").

(P. 3.3.141) It should be stated: "Optionally (*vibhāṣā*) [the use of *lṛṅ* applies] from *garhā* onwards, prior to *uta* and *api*. For if it were simply stated "optionally (*vā*) before *uta* and *api*," there would be uncertainty.

358. The prescription of the *laṭ* (present tense) for the purpose of censure (*garhā*) is purposeless, because the completion of the action is intended to be expressed. The rule prescribing the *laṭ* for censure is useless. Why? Because the completion of the action is intended to be expressed. Here, the non-completion of the action is understood. And this is indeed the proper time for the present tense (*vartamāna-kāla*), wherein the action remains uncompleted. In that case—

[The desired form] is already established by the rule *vartamāne laṭ* ("the suffix *laṭ* occurs when the action is present"). If *laṭ* occurs here according to *vartamāne laṭ*, then the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* would result. And yet, *śatṛ* and *śānac* are desired:
"Look at me while I am sacrificing" (*api mām yājayantam paśya*), and "Look at me while I am sacrificing" (*api mām yājayamānam paśya*).

Since there is no governing rule (*anadhikāra*) for that which is formed with an interrogative pronoun (*kiṃvṛtta*), the mention of "not being formed with an interrogative pronoun" (*akiṃvṛttagrahaṇa*) in the subsequent rule is redundant.

Because there is no governing rule for the interrogative pronoun, the mention of "not being formed with an interrogative pronoun" in what follows is purposeless; [the previous rule] "in the case of an interrogative pronoun" (*kiṃvṛtte*) has ceased to apply. In that [subsequent rule]:

When *nivṛtta* occurs without distinction—whether it is formed with *kiṃvṛtta* or *akiṃvṛtta*—it will still apply. Then this is the purpose: I shall state the technical term *upapada*. What is the purpose of stating the term *upapada*? It is so that there may be a compound by the rule "an *upapada* [is compounded] with what is not a finite verb (*atiṅ*)". Otherwise, the prohibition "not when it is a finite verb" (*atiṅ*) would apply. When, however, the future suffix *lṛṭ* has the technical designation *sat*, then the designation *upapada* applies.

It will be so. The two [suffixes] *sat* and *san*, which are prescribed under the heading of the future (*bhaviṣyat*), are stated to have the technical designation *satsañjñā*; and this [present rule] is also prescribed without distinction.

3.3.147) Regarding the prescription of the optative (*liṅ*) after the words *jātu* and *yad*, there is an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the words *yadā* and *yadi*. Regarding the prescription of the optative after *jātu* and *yad*, [there is an addition] for *yadā* and *yadi*.

An addition must be made: "when one such as you should officiate for a Kṣatriya," or "if one such as you should officiate for a Kṣatriya" (Pāṇini 3.3.151). Regarding the prohibition of *yad* in the sense of "wondering" (*citrīkaraṇa*), the prohibition is redundant because the meaning is different; that is, the prohibition of *yad* applies when there is the sense of wondering.
It is meaningless. What is the reason? Because the meaning is different. For when *yadi* is used as an upapada, it does not convey wonder (*citrīkaraṇa*).
What then? It conveys possibility (*sambhāvanā*).

360. *Liṅ* may optionally be used for both cause (*hetu*) and effect (*hetumat*). It should be stated that *liṅ* is optionally used for both cause and effect: "If he were to go by this [path], the cart would not overturn"; "If he will go by this [path], the cart will not overturn. Regarding the section on the future (*bhaviṣyat*): it should be stated that this applies within the scope of the future. Let it not apply here: "He runs because it rains" (*varṣati iti dhāvati*); "He strikes because... (*hanti iti*).

[The suffix] *palayate* [is used]. Now, why do the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* not occur here? [The rule] "In connection with *devatrātaḥ*, *galaḥ*, and *grāhaḥ*, the prescription for *sat* [applies]"—these are not optionally applied to one another. [Examples are: *gavākṣaḥ* and *saṃśitavrataḥ*.
(Pāṇini 3.2.157; Kāśikā II,165.7–8; Rūpāvatāra III).

361. If it is intended to express a desire (*kāmapravedana*), it should be stated that [the suffix *liṅ*] is used when a desire is understood. This should not apply here: "Desiring a mat, he makes it" (*icchan kaṭaṃ karoti*).
What is the difference between an injunction (*vidhi*) and a request (*adhīṣṭi*)? An injunction (*vidhi*) is a command (*preṣaṇa*). A request (*adhīṣṭi*) is preceded by respect (*satkāra*).

[The term *vyāpāraṇā* means] causing to act. Now, what is the distinction between *nimantraṇā* (invitation) and *āmantraṇā* (request)? [Some say: *Nimantraṇā* occurs with one who is present, while *āmantraṇā* occurs with one who is absent. This is not a valid distinction; for *nimantraṇā* can occur even with one who is absent, and *āmantraṇā* can occur with one who is present. If that is so, then that which must necessarily be performed is *nimantraṇā*.

What, then, is that? Whether it be an offering to the gods (*havya*) or an offering to the ancestors (*kavya*). When it is said, "Let the *siddha* food be eaten by the Brāhmaṇa," unrighteousness (*adharma*) accrues to the one who refuses. In the case of an invitation (*āmantraṇa*), there is freedom of action (*kāmacāra*).

362–365. Furthermore, how is this to be understood: [does it mean] "in the sense of invitation (*nimantraṇa*) and so forth," or rather, "when invitation and so forth are being conveyed"? And what is the distinction here? If it were "in the sense of invitation and so forth," then in the case of *āmantraye bhavantam* ("I invite you") or *nimantraye bhavantam*, the suffix would be untenable, because the meaning is already expressed by the verbal base (*prakṛti*). [This applies to] invitation and so forth...

If it is argued that [the suffix occurs] when there is a meaning (*arthe*), then in expressions such as *āmantraye* or *nimantraye bhavantam*, the application of the suffix would be untenable. What is the reason? Because the meaning is already expressed by the base form (*prakṛti*). Since that meaning is already expressed by the base form, the suffix does not apply. Furthermore, there would be no occurrence of the dual and plural numbers because there is only a single meaning; thus, the dual and plural numbers would be unestablished.

What is the reason? Because the meaning is one. This single meaning is called "invitation" (*nimantraṇa*). Since that [meaning] is one, only the singular number would be applicable. Let it be then when invitation and so forth are implied. But then it would apply here as well: "Devadatta invites you" (*devadatta āmantrayate bhavantam*) and "Devadatta invites you" (*devadatto nimantrayate bhavantam*). However, [the rule] is established for that which requires a second [object].

This is established because the suffix is prescribed for the meaning of the suffix when that meaning is the base (prakṛti). How so? It should be stated that "the suffix occurs after a verbal root that requires a second [object], when that meaning is the base. And what are the base meanings?
They are the action (bhāva), the object (karman), and the agent (kartṛ). Thus it would be established: "May you come," "May you receive the invitation," "May you experience [it]."
"Addressing" (*āmantraṇa*) is that in which a second [person] is expected. However, this [usage] is not established: *āmantrayai*, *nimantrayai*.
Here too, a second [person] is expected. Who? The very person being invited (*nimantri*). *Āmantrayai* means addressing; *nimantrayai* means inviting.
But how could the person being invited expect an invitation? And it is observed.
The connection of a state (*bhāva*) is with a state; for example, a desire (*iṣi*) is connected with a desire, and femininity with femininity.

To the extent that a second [factor] is required here, it follows that [the suffix occurs] in the sense of invitation (*nimantraṇa*) and so forth. But has it not been said that [this applies] "in the sense of invitation and so forth"?

If so, then in the case of "I invite you" (*āmantraye*) or "I invite you" (*nimantraye*), the application of the suffix would be untenable, because [the object] has already been expressed by the verbal base (*prakṛti*).

[Objection: This is not a fault. That which is required as the second [factor] shall be the meaning of my suffix (*pratyaya*). [Reply: Then this is the fault: the non-establishment of dual and plural numbers because there is only a single referent (*ekārthatva*). [Objection: This is not a fault. For the meanings of nominal suffixes (*sup*) include both the object (*karman*) and so forth, as well as number (*saṅkhyā*); likewise for verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*). For nominal suffixes, number alone is the meaning.

And [the same applies] to the object (*karman*) and so forth, as well as to the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*). In that case, the restriction (*niyama*) is well-known. The restriction is well-known there. Or, the restriction applies to those topics under discussion. Alternatively, the restriction is with reference to the meanings currently under discussion. And what are those topics under discussion? They are singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth. The singular number (*ekavacana*) occurs only for one, not for two, nor for many. The dual number (*dvivacana*) occurs only for two.

"Not in one, nor in many. The plural number occurs only in the case of many, not in one or in two. (Pāṇini 3.3.163) Why are the *kṛtya* suffixes prescribed for meanings such as "command" (*praiṣa*) and so forth, rather than being prescribed without distinction?

These shall apply to the *praiṣa* (commands) and so forth, as well as elsewhere. Regarding the *praiṣa* and so forth, the prescription of the *kṛtya* suffixes is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

This undertaking is for the sake of restriction: namely, that the *kṛtya* suffixes should occur only in the *praiṣa* and so forth. If it is argued that the mention of the *kṛtya* suffixes in the *praiṣa* and so forth is for the purpose of restriction, that is undesirable. [The objection continues: "The mention of the *kṛtya* suffixes in the *praiṣa* and so forth is for the purpose of restriction."

If this is argued, then an undesirable consequence follows. For it is not intended that *kṛtya* suffixes occur only in the sense of commands (*praiṣa*) and so forth. What then? They are intended without distinction, as in: *busopendhyam*, *tṛṇopendhyam*, *ghanghātyam*. However, for the sake of expressing an injunction (*vidhi*), there is the statement "before the feminine [suffixes]. Indeed, the mention of *kṛtya* suffixes in the context of commands and so forth is for the purpose of expressing an injunction. This [is the rule for] the *loṭ* suffix in the sense of commands and so forth.

It is prescribed. That [suffix], being specifically prescribed, would supersede the *kṛtya* suffixes prescribed in a general manner. [Objection: The *kṛtya* suffixes will also occur by virtue of the rule *vāsarūpa*. [Reply: They would not. What is the reason? Because of the statement "prior to [the formation of] the feminine. Or rather, [the rule applies] prior to the feminine, as in the case of *asarūpa*.

It should be stated that [the rule applies] "to those ending in the nominative case. What is the purpose? So that it does not apply here: *kāle bhuṅkte* ("he eats at the time"). Then it must be stated. It need not be stated. The term "in the case of commands and so forth" (*praiṣādiṣu*) continues [from the previous rule]. And that mention of "commands and so forth" must necessarily be carried over.
For if it were stated as "to those ending in the nominative case," it would undesirably apply even here: *kālaḥ pacati bhūtāni* ("Time cooks all beings").
Time destroys all creatures.

(Pāṇini 3.4.2) The mention of *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* in the rule for *hi* and *sva* is for the purpose of prohibiting [the substitution of] *lādeśas*. The mention of *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* in the rule for *hi* and *sva*...

The rule *hiḥ* must be stated so that *hi* applies to the *parasmaipada* endings and *sva* applies to the *ātmanepada* endings. What is the purpose? To prohibit the substitution of *l* [for the verbal root]. That is, so that *hi* and *sva* do not become substitutes for *l*. And what would happen if *hi* and *sva* were substitutes for *l*?
The designation *pada*—by the rule "that which ends in a *tiṅ* is a *pada*"—would not apply. Let it not be so; [let it be] that which ends in a *sup*.

The term *pada* will function as the technical designation *padasañjñā*. How, then, does the derivation of case-endings (*svādi*) occur? Because the letter *l* (the verbal root marker) possesses the status of a *kṛt* suffix, it has the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*); based on that, the rule for the introduction of suffixes applies. The letter *l* is a *kṛt* suffix; because it is a *kṛt*, by the rule "a *kṛt*-formed item is a nominal stem," it receives the designation *prātipadika*. Based on its being a nominal stem, the derivation of case-endings such as *su* and so forth will also occur. If there is the derivation of case-endings, there would be the audible pronunciation of those case-endings (*supām śravaṇam*).

[The suffix] is obtained. By the rule *avyayāt*, there will be the elision (*lup*) of the case-ending (*sup*). How is it an indeclinable (*avyaya*)? It receives the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "particle" (*nipāta*) because of the rule *vibhaktisvarapratirūpakāś ca nipātā bhavanti*. It receives the technical designation of "indeclinable" by the rule *nipātam avyayam*. In that case, here [in the example] *sa bhavān lunīhi lunīhi evāyaṃ lunāti*, the suppression of accent (*nighāta*) prescribed by the rule *tiṅ atiṅaḥ* would not obtain.

And for the sake of equal number: the mention of *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* in the rules for *hi* and *sva* must be made for the sake of equal number, so that *hi* may apply to the *parasmaipadas* and *sva* to the *ātmanepadas*, lest there be a confusion. Or rather, it is not necessary; the statement regarding the substitutes for *ta* and *dhvam* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the substitution applies to the *pada*. Thus, the mention of *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* in the rules for *hi* and *sva* is unnecessary.

It must be stated. What is the reason? The mention of substitutes for *ta* and *dhvam* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that these are substitutes for words (*pada*). When the Teacher says, "and optionally for *ta* and *dhvam*," he indicates that *hi* and *su* are substitutes for words. In that case, when they are substitutes for words, there must be a prohibition of the *pit* designation and of *āṭ*. Thus, when they are substitutes for words, a prohibition of the *pit* designation and of *āṭ* must be stated.

Regarding *pit* [the suffix]: that venerable one cuts [the grass] thinking, "Cut! Cut! Indeed, it is also because of *āṭ*. I, for my part, cut thinking, "Cut! Cut! First of all, *pit* need not be mentioned. A split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made regarding the prohibition of *pit*: first, "here [the augment] *hi* occurs after *si*"; then, "and it occurs after what is not *pit* (*apit*)," meaning as far as [the suffixes] are concerned.

Indeed, the designation *hi* need not be mentioned, nor even *āṭ*. Once *āṭ* has been applied, the substitute will belong to that which is accompanied by *āṭ*. This must be considered here: "Let *āṭ* be applied, or let the substitute be applied"? What should be done in this case? The augment *āṭ* [should be applied] because it is subsequent. The substitute is obligatory (*nitya*); for it applies whether *āṭ* has been applied or not. *Āṭ* is also obligatory; for it applies whether the substitute has been applied or not. [Objection: *Āṭ* is also obligatory. It applies even when the substitute has been applied.

[A grammatical operation] is non-eternal (*anitya*) even when it applies to that which has not been performed. The augment *āṭ* is non-eternal: it applies when one [element] has been substituted, and it also applies when another has not been substituted.

A rule (*vidhi*) that applies to a different word-form becomes non-eternal; the substitution (*ādeśa*) is also non-eternal, as it applies when one [element] has been augmented by *āṭ*, and it does not apply when another has not. A rule that applies to a different word-form is non-eternal.

[The augment] *āṬ* occurs. Because both [the root and the suffix] are impermanent (*anitya*), the augment *āṬ* applies by virtue of being subsequent [in the rules]. Once *āṬ* has been applied, the substitute will apply to that which is accompanied by *āṬ*. In that case, however, in forms such as *saḥ aham*, *bhuṅkṣva bhuṅkṣva*, and *bhuñjāvai*, the elision of the vowel *a*—prescribed by the rule *śnasoḥ allopaḥ*—would not take place. Furthermore, the requirement for an equal number [of elements to correspond] remains unresolved. But [the desired result] is established for the singular middle person of the imperative (*loṭ*).

This is established by the reduplication [of the verb] in the sense of frequent repetition (*kriyāsamabhihāra*). How so? It should be stated that "the second person singular imperative (*loṭ*) undergoes reduplication in the sense of frequent repetition. To what [form] is this reduplication of the second person singular imperative prescribed in the sense of frequent repetition? By this very statement, the Teacher indicates that the suffix *loṭ* occurs in the sense of frequent repetition.

Since this [grammarian] teaches the doubling of the second person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*) in the sense of the frequent repetition of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), how indeed is it known that the imperative occurs here by virtue of that very indicator (*jñāpaka*)? It is not the case that when that very [imperative] which is prescribed without distinction occurs in the sense of the frequent repetition of an action, then its doubling takes place. [This applies specifically] to the second person singular of the imperative.

In this way, indeed, it would be established. Furthermore, these two suffixes *hi* and *sva* are intended for all persons (*puruṣa*) and all numbers (*vacana*). And the sūtra would have to be split. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. But was it not said that the mention of *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* with respect to *hi* and *sva* is for the purpose of prohibiting their substitution for *l*-suffixes, and for the sake of ensuring an equal number? This is not a fault, because it is established through the division of the yoga (yogavibhāga).
A grammatical split (yogavibhāga) will be made: first, "In the sense of frequent repetition of an action (kriyāsamabhihāra), the imperative (loṭ) occurs";

then, "From that [rule], for the imperative, *hi* and *sva* occur. The word "imperative" (loṭ) continues to apply [to the second rule]. Thus, it is understood as: "For those *hi* and *sva* which belong to the imperative. And how about [the rule] "or also for *ta* and *dhvam*"? It is understood thus: "Or also for that imperative which is subject to becoming *ta* and *dhvam*."

(P_3,4.4) Why is this stated? So that there may be an *anuprayoga* (subsequent application of a verb). This purpose is not necessary. For [the form] ending in *hi* or *sva* has its meaning unmanifested; therefore, since the sense is incomplete, the *anuprayoga* will occur by virtue of that.

"In that case, this is the purpose: I shall say 'according to the rule' (*yathāvidhi*). Even this is not a purpose, for he will state that "in the case of a combination (*samuccaya*), there is the use of the general term. In that regard, even without an explicit statement, the application will occur according to the rule. (P_3,4.5) KA_II,170.21-24 Ro_III,4.5)
