374. Regarding the injunctions for *upasaṃvāda* (mutual agreement) and *āśaṅkā* (apprehension), the explicit statement is redundant because [the sense] is already conveyed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*). The statement concerning *upasaṃvāda* and *āśaṅkā* is purposeless. What is the reason? Because it is the meaning of the optative suffix. It is already established by the rule that the subjunctive suffix (*leṭ*) occurs in the sense of the optative (*liṅ*). But what, then, is the meaning of the optative? Some say: "The optative occurs in the sense of cause and effect" (*hetu-hetumatoḥ liṅ*). Others say:
In this specific case, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) must indeed be employed; for it is used in common worldly usage as in: "If you would do this for me, I too would give this to you.

It is stated [in the rule] that it is used "in the sense of *tumun*. What is the sense of *tumun*? It is the agent (*kartṛ*). If this is so, there is no purpose in the mention of the sense of *tumun*.

Indeed, by the very same reason for which the suffix *tumun* occurs when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed, the suffixes *sayā* and others will also occur. If that is so, since [the meaning] is already established, the fact that the Teacher includes the mention of "for the sake of the meaning of *tumun*" (*tum-artha-grahaṇa*) indicates that there is another meaning of *tumun* besides the agent. But what is this? It is "being" (*bhāva*). How, indeed, is it known that *tumun* occurs in the sense of "being"?
It will apply [to the agent], but not to the *kārakas* such as the object (*karman*) and so forth. Because of this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), this [suffix] is drawn away from the agent;

nor is it prescribed for any other meaning. Since suffixes whose meanings are not specifically prescribed occur in their own inherent sense (*svārtha*), it will apply in its own sense—just as in the rules "after roots ending in *gup*, *tij*, and *kit*, the suffix *san* occurs" and "after *yāva* and others, the suffix *kan* occurs. Thus, that [suffix] occurring in its own sense...

[The suffix] will occur in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). What is the purpose of making this known? It means that it need not be stated that "kṛt suffixes introduced by an *avyaya* [particle] occur in the sense of the abstract action. Why is the root *meṅ*, which possesses an *anubandha* and has undergone the substitution of *āt*, [mentioned]?

The inclusion [of the root *mā*] is not made; rather, it should simply be stated as "of *meṅ* according to the Northern Grammarians. In that case, this further purpose is achieved: the mention of "reciprocity" (*vyatihāra*) need not be made in the rule "of *meṅ* according to the Northern Grammarians. Why? Because that [rule] pertains specifically to that [root]; the root *mayati* has reciprocity as its sole domain. If that is so, then since the result is already established, why is there the mention of *meṅ*, which includes an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*)?

By making the inclusion of that which has undergone *āt*-vṛddhi, the Teacher indicates that the status of being "non-consonantal-final" (*anejantatva*) is not determined by the presence of an *anubandha*. What is the purpose of this indication? In that context, regarding the prohibition of the substitution of *dāp* for all [stems] when they are not of dissimilar form (*asarūpa*), it was stated that "the separate mention is because [the stem] does not end in the vowel *ā*. That need not be said; for what reason?
376–377. Why does [the suffix -ktvā] not occur here:

*pūrvaṃ bhuṅkte paścād vrajati* ("first he eats, later he goes")? It does not occur because it has already been expressed by its own word (*svaśabda*). If that is so, then why does this not occur now: *pūrvaṃ bhuktvā tato vrajati* ("having first eaten, he then goes")? This is not a case of the priority of the action (*kriyāpaurvakālya*); rather, it is a case of the priority of the agent (*kartṛpaurvakālya*).

For previously he eats, and after that he goes from among other eaters; and here, why does [the form] *āsyate bhoktum* ("he sits in order to eat") not occur? Why does it not occur? Is it because of the root *ās* (to sit), or rather because of the root *bhuj* (to eat)? It is because of the root *bhuj*. Why?

It does not occur because it is not preceded by [the condition of] "apūrva" (not having occurred before). If so, why does it not occur after the root *ās*? Because in this case, the suffix *laṭ* occurs.
This is what must be asked here: how does *laṭ* occur in this instance? And *laṭ* will occur here by virtue of the rule of "non-similarity of form" (*vāsarūpa*).

Regarding the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.21), there is non-application in the case of many [actions]. Because of the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ*, the suffix *ktvā* does not apply when there are many [actions], such as in the example: *snātvā bhuktvā pītvā vrajati* ("having bathed, eaten, and drunk, he goes"). What, then, is the reason it is not established? Because of the mention of the dual number. This mention is made by means of the dual; therefore, it would apply only when there are two [actions] in a temporal sequence, but not for many.
It would not be so. But it is established because the action is the primary element. This is established. How? Because the action is the primary element.

This instruction has the action as its primary focus; here, the specific wording of the instruction is not the governing factor. But how can an instruction be made by that very same [word] while that [word] itself is not the governing factor? You are both a practitioner of that and a hater of that. [This is so] because of its invariable concomitance.

In this case, the indication is made by means of the dual number. An indication must necessarily be made by some case-ending and some number. For example, suppose someone seeking rice brings a bundle of *śāli* grain together with its husks and its straw because they are inseparable; having taken as much as was to be taken, he discards the husks and the straw. In the same way, who...

One who desires meat brings fish along with their scales and bones because they are inseparable [from the meat]. Having taken as much as is required, he discards the scales and bones. Likewise here too, the dual number is employed because of this inseparability. For in this case, the specific mention [of the dual] is not the governing factor. Even so, it is not established due to common worldly understanding, as for example:

In the world, when it is said, "Let the Brāhmaṇas be brought first," the very first one is brought. In this case as well, [the suffix -ktvā] would apply to the action that is absolutely first. However, it is established by the mention of "non-final" (anantya). It should be stated: "Of two actions having the same agent, [the suffix -ktvā applies] to the non-final one.
Thus it is established. But then the sūtra is altered. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. But was it not already stated that [the suffix applies] to two actions having the same agent?

Thus, [the objection] that there is no application in the case of many [actions] has been answered by the established principle: "But it is established because the action is the primary element. Now, it was argued that even so, this is not established because of common worldly understanding. This is not a fault, for in all these cases, there is a priority of time with respect to the action of going: "Having bathed, he goes; having eaten, he goes; having drunk, he goes. And having done so—
The application [of the rule] is indefinite: one goes after having bathed, eaten, and drunk; or one goes after having drunk, bathed, and eaten.

(P_3.4.21.3) Regarding "he sleeps with his mouth open" (*vyādāya svapiti*), there must be an addition to the rule because the action [of opening the mouth] does not precede [the action of sleeping]. There must be an addition for the case of "he sleeps with his mouth open."

It must be performed. But what is the reason it is not established? Because it occurs at a later time. For he sleeps first and afterwards opens his mouth. Or rather, it need not be performed. What is the reason?
Because sleep occurs at a non-time (*avakālatvāt*). Sleep is a non-time; he necessarily sleeps for even a moment after having opened his mouth.

(P_3,4.24) Is this an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding what is already established, or rather regarding what is not yet established? And how is it "already established," or how is it "not yet established"? Is it "already established" by the rule *ābhīkṣṇye* [P. 3.4.22] when there is constant repetition (*nitya*), or is it "not yet established" in other cases? What follows from this? If it is "already established" in the case of constant repetition...

An undesired option (*vibhāṣā*) would result, and elsewhere the desired [result] would not be established. Now, [if you argue that the rule applies] when [the condition] has not yet been reached: regarding *agra* and so forth, a prohibition of compounding must be stated for a rule that has not otherwise been reached. That, then, must be stated. It need not be stated. For this has already been explained in the context of the rule "only with *am*" (*am-eva-avyayena*), by means of the employment of the particle *eva*.

381. For what purpose is the *makārānta* (ending in *m*) form prescribed for the word *svādumi*, when the suffix *khamuñ* is already under discussion and would naturally apply? The prescription of the *makārānta* form for *svādumi* is for the sake of preventing the *īkāra* (the vowel *ī*). The *makārānta* form is prescribed for *svādumi* so that the *īkāra* does not occur. [Examples: *svādvīṃ kṛtvā yavāgūṃ bhuṅkte* (having made the gruel sweet, he eats it); *svāduṅkāraṃ yavāgūṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats the gruel, making it sweet).

382–385. *Ā ca tumunaḥ samānādhikaraṇe*. The suffixes up to and including *tumun* should be stated to have the same referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*) [as the verb they qualify]. By what means? By the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of the verb. What is the purpose? So that the third case ending may occur in "devadattena svāduṅkāraṃ yavāgūḥ bhujyate" (The gruel is eaten by Devadatta making it tasty). And for what reason would it not otherwise occur? Because the agent has already been expressed by the suffix *ṇamul*.

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might argue: since the agent is not expressed by the suffix *bhuj* (in *yavāgūṃ bhuñjānaḥ*), the rule based on the "unexpressed" (*anabhihita*) will apply, and thus the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) will occur. If, whether there is expression or non-expression, the rule based on the "unexpressed" applies simply because it is "unexpressed" for some reason, then the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) would result for *yavāgvām*. Why?
The reason is that the object (*karman*) is not already expressed by the suffix *ṇamul*. If, however, this [suffix] were understood as expressing the object, it would not be possible in this way.

For in the case of "Devadatta eats the gruel pleasantly" (*svāduṅkāraṃ yavāgūṃ bhuṅkte devadattaḥ*), there would be no accusative case ending for the word *yavāgū* (gruel). What is the reason? Because the object is already expressed by the suffix *ṇamul*. But is it not the case that [the object] is not expressed by the suffix of the verb *bhuj*?

Considering that [the agent] is expressed by the term *karma*, the rule [for the accusative] will apply as one based on what is not already expressed (*anabhihitāśraya*). Even if it is expressed, if for some reason it is considered "not expressed," then the rule based on what is not expressed will apply; thus, when the accusative case applies, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) would also result for *devadatta*. What is the reason? Because the agent is not expressed by the suffix *ṇamul*.
Now, by this [rule], the meaning is as follows:

"Having cooked the rice, it is eaten by Devadatta. Certainly, that is the meaning. [The purpose is] so that the third case ending may occur for Devadatta. But what is the reason it would not occur? Because the agent has been expressed by the suffix *ktvā*. [Objection: But is it not the case that [the agent] is not expressed by the suffix of the verb *bhuj* (to eat)?

If it is argued that the rule for the third case will apply based on the agent being unexpressed (*anabhihita*), then even when [the agent] is expressed, if for some reason it is considered unexpressed, the rule for the third case would apply; yet, in the case of *odane*, the second case (*dvitīyā*) is obtained. What is the reason? Because the object (*karman*) is not expressed by the suffix *-ktvā*. If...

Furthermore, this [suffix] might be understood as applying to the object (*karman*); however, it cannot be so. For in the case of the sentence, "Having cooked the rice, Devadatta eats" (*paktvā odanaṃ bhuṅkte devadattaḥ*), the accusative case would not occur for *odana*. What is the reason? Because the object has already been expressed by the suffix *-ktvā*. But surely, since the object is not expressed by the suffix of the verb *bhuj*, the rule regarding the accusative will apply on the basis of that which is unexpressed (*anabhihita*). If that were the case...

Whether there is expression or non-expression [of the agent], since there is non-expression for some reason, the rule will apply based on that which is not expressed; thus, when the second case (*dvitīyā*) is used for Devadatta, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) would result. What is the reason? Because the agent is not expressed by the suffix *ktvā*. Now, if this is the meaning of the suffix *tumun*: "Rice is cooked by Devadatta in order to eat" (*bhoktum odanaḥ pacyate devadattena*). Certainly, this is the meaning.

[The opponent asks: "How can the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) be applied in the case of *devadatta*? Furthermore, for what reason would it not be applied? [The proponent replies: "Because the agent has already been expressed by the suffix *tumun*. [The opponent objects: "But surely, since the agent is not expressed by the verbal suffix (*pac*) itself, the rule will apply based on that which is unexpressed, and thus the third case ending will occur. [The proponent replies: "If this were so, whether there is expression or non-expression, one could arbitrarily assume non-expression; therefore, how could the rule be based on what is truly unexpressed?"

The rule would apply to the third case (instrumental), whereas the second case would be required for the *odana*. What is the reason? Because the object (*karman*) has not been expressed by the suffix *tumun*. If, however, this [suffix] were understood as expressing the object, it would not be possible in this way. For in the example "Devadatta cooks rice in order to eat" (*bhoktum odanam pacati devadattaḥ*), the second case would not occur for *odana*. What is the reason? Because the object has already been expressed by *tumun*.

[Objection: But surely, since the object (*karman*) is not expressed by the suffix of the root *pac* (in *pacyate*), the rule for the second case will apply on the basis of that unexpressed [object]. [Response: If, whether there is expression or non-expression, the rule for the second case were to apply on the basis of some kind of non-expression, then in the case of "Devadatta," the third case would also result.

What is the reason? [It is] because the agent (*kartṛ*) has not been expressed by the suffix *tumun*. Now, here in this case, the meaning "having cooked the rice, Devadatta goes to the village" is indeed expressed by this [suffix]. Certainly, the meaning is there; [the rule is intended] so that the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) may occur for Devadatta. And what is the reason it would not occur? Because the agent has been expressed by the suffix *ktvā*. But is it not the case that [the agent] has not been expressed by the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*) of the root *gam*?

Considering that the agent is expressed, the rule based on what is not expressed will apply, and the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) will occur. Even if it is expressed, if for some reason it is considered as if unexpressed, the rule based on what is not expressed will apply and the third case ending will occur. Thus, the fault mentioned—that the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) would apply to "rice" (*odana*)—does not arise.

In that case, it should be stated: "up to and including the suffix *tumun*, [these suffixes] occur when they have the same referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*). It need not be stated. Since suffixes formed with indeclinables (*avyayakṛt*) denote the abstract action (*bhāva*), they will apply in the sense of the abstract action. Is this something that needs to be stated? No, it is not. How is it understood even though it is not stated? The phrase "in the sense of *tumun*" (*tum-arthe*) is understood from the preceding context. And what is the sense of *tumun*? It is the abstract action (*bhāva*).
And there is the elision of *ū* in this case;

furthermore, the mention of the word *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") can be omitted. How so? In the example "The god has rained upon the footprint of a cow" (*goṣpadam vṛṣṭo devaḥ*), the root *prā* has the sense of filling (*pūraṇa*). From that [root], this suffix *ka* is applied. If it were *ka*, the hearing of the case-endings (*vibhakti*) would result.

The case endings are indeed heard here; for example, in the expression *ekena goṣpadapreṇa*. [Vārttika: The rule regarding the instrument (*karaṇe*) for the root *han* is redundant, because the suffix *ṇamul* is already prescribed after roots meaning "to injure" (*hiṃsārtha*) when used with an instrument. Thus, the mention of the instrument for *han* is purposeless.

The statement [is necessary]. What is the reason? Because the suffix *ṇamul* is prescribed after roots meaning "to injure. Indeed, *ṇamul* is prescribed after roots meaning "to injure"; thus, the rule is already established by that. However, the explicit mention of *ṇamul* for the root *han* is purposeful, because it is prescribed for the sense of non-injury. What is the purpose? It is so that *ṇamul* may occur after roots whose meaning is non-injurious. But does it [otherwise] occur?

In some instances, this root *han* has the meaning of non-injury (*ahiṃsā*), for which there would be an injunction. He says: "It exists," as in "he strikes the altar so as to avoid injuring it with his hand. And for the sake of obligatory compounds (*nityasamāsa*): indeed, even from the root *han* meaning injury, an injunction by means of this [suffix] must be sought. But how, even if one desires it, can an injunction by means of this [suffix] be obtained from the root *han* meaning injury?

By this [rule], let it be by that [other rule]—thus there would be a conflict (vipratiṣedha). The priority of the former rule regarding the root *han* is indicated by the Vārttika itself. In that the Teacher says "and for the sake of obligatory compounds," he indicates that this rule applies even to the root *han* when it means "to injure."

Why does [the suffix] not occur here in the case of *grāme baddhaḥ* ("bound in the village")? I shall state it thus: "The root *bandh-* [takes the suffix *kta*] when expressing the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), provided it forms a name (*sañjñā*). Then, "after [roots ending in] *naś-* and *vah-*, [the suffix *kta* is used] with the agent (*kartṛ*) when the object is *jīva* or *puruṣa*. How then is one said to be "bound in a prison" (*aṭṭālikābandham baddhaḥ*)?
"Caṇḍālikābanadham baddhaḥ" [is formed] by the rule "upamāne karmaṇi ca" (Pāṇini 3.4.45). This [explanation] is incorrect; it should be "tiraści. This is a Vedic (sautra) usage.

What is the purpose of including the word *artha*? If it were stated simply as *nādhāpratyaye*, [the rule] would apply only here: *dvidhākṛtya*; it would not apply here: *dvaidhaṅkṛtya*. However, when the word *artha* is included, there is no fault; [the rule applies] even when an *ādhā-pratyaya* follows.

It is established that this applies to whatever else has the same meaning as that [word *kṛt*]. Now, for what purpose is the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*)? It is so that it should not apply here: *hiruk kṛtvā*, *pṛthak kṛtvā*.
This formulation is incorrect; it should be *anūcī*. This is a Vedic (sautra) formulation.

For what purpose is this stated? Because the rule regarding *kṛt* suffixes [denoting] the agent (*kartari*) is understood to retain its own original meaning when there is no substitution. [The suffix denotes] the agent.

It is said that they "become [active]" because, in the absence of an explicit instruction, suffixes are understood to express their own inherent meaning (*svārtha*). Suffixes whose meaning is not specifically prescribed function in their own inherent sense. For example: *guptijkidbhyaḥ san* ("the suffix *san* follows *gup*, *tij*, and *kid*") and *yāvādibhyaḥ kan* ("the suffix *kan* follows *yāva* and others"). In this way, these suffixes would also apply in their own inherent sense. It is for this purpose—that they should not remain in their own inherent sense but rather apply in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*)—that this rule is stated.

This purpose does not exist. Whatever [a speaker] intends for his own meaning, he expresses that; thus, the suffix *ghañ* occurs in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). [Objection: Then let it not occur in the sense of an object (*karman*). [Response: Even in the sense of an object, whatever he intends, he expresses that; thus, the suffix *ṣṭran* occurs after the root *dhā* in the sense of an object (*dhaḥ karmaṇi ṣṭran*).
[Objection: Then let it not occur in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) or a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). [Response: Even in the sense of an instrument or a locus, whatever he intends—

He says: "The suffix *lyuṭ* occurs in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). [Objection: "In that case, let it not occur in the sense of the recipient (*sampradāna*) and the point of departure (*apādāna*). [Response: Even in the sense of the recipient and the point of departure, he states that which he intends: "The suffixes *dāś* and *goghna* occur in the sense of the recipient (*sampradāna*); *bhīma* and others occur in the sense of the point of departure (*apādāna*). As for any other remaining suffix at present, it will occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) even without an explicit statement.

Then that very purpose [is the reason for the rule]: let them not occur when the sense is that of the agent itself (*svārtha*). But has it not already been stated: "Whatever one desires in the sense of the agent, he expresses that; the suffix *ghañ* occurs in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*)"? That *bhāva* is something else—it is external to the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*). By this [rule], they would now apply in the sense of the internal *bhāva*. Therefore, the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) is made so that they do not occur there. But what, then, is the difference between these two?

There is a distinction between the two states (*bhāva*). The difference between the states has been stated in the Bhāṣya. This purpose is indeed established. What then? In that regard, there is a prohibition of *khyun* and the others because they constitute separate rules (*nānāvākya*). In that case, a prohibition of *khyun* and the others must be stated so that *khyun* and the others do not occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). But surely *khyun* and the others are prescribed in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*); how could they [then] apply to the agent?

[The suffixes] would not occur; by that [rule], they would apply in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), and by this [present rule], in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). But surely, because they are exceptions (*apavāda*), the suffixes beginning with *khyun* should supersede [the general rules]? They would not. Why? Because they belong to different sentences (*nānāvākya*). That [previous rule] and this [present rule] are different sentences. Exceptions supersede general rules only within the same sentence (*samānavākya*); because they belong to different sentences, supersession does not take place.

And likewise, the particle *eva* is employed with gerundives (*kṛtya*). Having established this, the particle *eva* is used with gerundives [in the rule] "only for those two [roots] are there gerundives, past participles, and words having the sense of *khal*; and [gerundives are formed] from intransitive roots in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). What is the purpose? It is for the sake of *bhavya* and so on.

Thus, the inclusion of *bhavya* and others is established. For example: "The boy is to sing the *Sāman* chants" (*geyo māṇavakaḥ sāmnām*), and "The *Sāman* chants are to be sung by the boy" (*geyāni māṇavakena*).

Regarding the term *sāmāni*: the statement concerning the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the agent and the deity with the *kṛt* suffixes is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is no such co-occurrence. Since the rule *kartari ca ṛṣidevatayoḥ* would already establish co-occurrence [if it were desired], the fact that the Teacher teaches the use of the particle *ca* for the purpose of co-occurrence indicates that, in reality, there is no co-occurrence. Why, then, is the restrictive particle *eva* used in the case of *kṛtya* suffixes?
It is so stated. And the inclusion of the particle *eva* (only) is for the sake of conjunction (*ca*). The inclusion of the particle *eva* should be understood as serving the purpose of conjunction:

"The *kṛtya* affixes occur after those two—bhāva and karman—and also after [roots] such as *bhavya* when the agent is expressed. What is the purpose? That is for the sake of [roots] such as *bhavya*. Thus, their inclusion among [roots] such as *bhavya* is established: *geyaḥ māṇavakaḥ sāmnām* ("The boy is one to whom the Sāmans are to be sung").

The *geyāni* are the *sāman*s sung by a young brahmin. As for what was said—that the statement regarding the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the deity with the composers (*kṛt*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of non-co-occurrence—that is not something to be established by an indicator; rather, general rules (*utsarga*) are set aside by exceptions (*apavāda*).
This is precisely the logical principle: that general rules are set aside by exceptions. But was it not said that this is because they are distinct sentences?

It does not incur [the fault of] being a separate sentence on the grounds that it refers to something situated in a different location; even though it refers to something situated in a different location, it remains a single sentence. For example, in the second chapter, *luk* (elision) is taught, and for that, in the fourth and sixth chapters, *aluk* (non-elision) is taught as an exception (*apavāda*). Furthermore, regarding what was said—that the use of the particle *eva* is for the sake of the sense of *ca* (and)—how indeed...

One thing indeed exists for the sake of another. How then does the particle *eva* function in the sense of "and"? This very *eva* functions in its own inherent sense (*svārtha*). What is the purpose? It is for the sake of providing an indicator (*jñāpaka*). By this, the Teacher indicates that from here onwards there is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) [of suffixes]. What is the purpose of this indication? It is for the sake of [suffixes] such as *bhavya*, and so on; [it applies] to the *bhavya*-class and others.

The co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) is established: "the boy is to sing the *sāmans*" (*geyo māṇavakaḥ sāmnām*), and "the *sāmans* are to be sung by the boy" (*geyāni māṇavakena sāmāni*). If this is being made known, then here too the co-occurrence would apply [to the following rules]: "the *dāśa* and *goghna* suffixes occur when there is a recipient" (*dāśagoghnau sampradāne*), and "the *bhīma*-class [suffixes] occur when there is an ablative" (*bhīmādayaḥ apādāne*). In this case as well, it is established; for this very reason [Pāṇini teaches] that the *kta* suffix occurs after a root denoting the beginning of an action, and [it also occurs] in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
When the immersion (*samāveśa*) has been accomplished, the teacher instructs that immersion; he makes it known that "prior to this [state], the immersion occurs.
What, then, is this restriction regarding the suffixes?

Is it a restriction of the technical designation (*saṃjñā-niyama*)—that an *akāra* or the word *aka* following a verbal root (*dhātu*), necessarily expressing the agent, receives both the designations *kṛt* and *pratyaya*? Or rather, is it a restriction of the nature of the elements (*svabhāva-niyama*)—that an *akāra* or the word *aka* following a verbal root, by its very nature expressing the agent, receives both the designations *kṛt* and *pratyaya*? And what is the distinction here? In that case, if it were a restriction of the designation, there would be the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*).

In that case, if there were a restriction on the suffixes, an undesirable consequence would follow: *kāṣṭhabhid* (wood-cutter) and *balabhid* (Indra) would not be considered non-Brahmins [as they would be excluded from the category of "non-Brahmin" by the rule]. Furthermore, this [term *abrāhmaṇa*] would, by necessity, denote the agent and would possess both the designation of *kṛt* and the designation of *pratyaya*. It is established when there is a restriction on the designations. When there is a restriction on the designations, it becomes established. This is so if there is a restriction on the designations.

There is a fault regarding examples such as *vibhakta* and others; [the forms] *vibhaktā bhrātaraḥ* ("the brothers have divided") and *pītā gāvaḥ* ("the cows have drunk") would not be established. However, when there is a restriction on the suffix, the suffix *kta* following the enumerated bases necessarily denotes the agent (*kartṛ*). And these bases are not enumerated therein. Furthermore, there is non-attainment [of the desired form] in cases like *vibhakta* because of the rule stating that the suffix follows the base.

Furthermore, there would be no application of the restriction regarding suffixes in the case of [words like] *vibhakta* and so on. What is the reason? Because it is stated that the suffix follows the base (*prakṛti*).

By its very nature, the suffix *kta* following enumerated bases denotes the agent; however, these [bases] are not enumerated therein. If that is so, then this word is not correct at present. It is indeed correct, but not in the sense of the agent.
How, then, is agency understood here? The suffix *a* has the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*):

those for whom partitioned property exists are "the partitioned" (*vibhaktāḥ*); those for whom drinking exists are "the drinkers" (*pītāḥ*). Alternatively, one should see here an elision of the latter member of the compound: those whose wealth is partitioned are "the partitioned" (*vibhaktāḥ*); those who have drunk water are "the drinkers" (*pītāḥ*).

(P_3,4.69) Why is this stated? [It is said] so that *la*-suffixes may occur with these means of accomplishment (*sādhana*): namely, in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), in the sense of the object (*karman*), and in the sense of the state (*bhāva*) for intransitive verbs. This purpose is not necessary, because the *ātmanepada* occurs in the sense of the state and the object.

It is prescribed that, by virtue of what remains, the *parasmaipada* endings occur when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. And this *la* [suffix] consists only of the *parasmaipada* and the *ātmanepada*. This very [category] has been thus prescribed. Therefore, he recites the following: "The mention of *la* is for the purpose of excluding transitive verbs.
The mention of *la* is made for the purpose of excluding transitive verbs, so that the *la* suffix may not occur in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) for transitive verbs.

If, however, the mention of "intransitive" (*akarmaka*) were made only there [in the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca...*], then the mention of "intransitive" would have to be repeated here as well. But is it not already stated here too in the rule *bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ*? This will serve another purpose: namely, that the *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khalartha* suffixes apply to those two [roots] alone, and the *bhāva* (passive) suffixes apply to intransitive roots. As long as the mention of *la* is present here, so long...

In this regard, there is the mention of "intransitive" (*akarmaka*), or else the mention of "the suffix *la*" (*la-grahaṇa*) should be made here, or the mention of "intransitive" should be made there. What, then, is the distinction here? This is the distinction: when the mention of "*la*" is made here, the suffix *āna* is established for the agent (*kartṛ*).
But when the mention of "intransitive" is made there [in the previous rule], *āna* would not apply to the agent. Therefore...

Even when the mention of "intransitive" (*akarmaka*) is made, the suffix *āna* is established in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). How so? Because [the rule] "in the sense of the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*)" [is followed by] all other subsequent listings of middle endings (*ātmanepada*), which are entirely for the purpose of the agent. Or else, by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), *āna* occurs in the sense of the agent. Indeed, by way of conflict, *āna* will occur in the sense of the agent; therein, [the rule] "in the sense of the state and the object" [applies].

Let it be that "kṛt affixes [denote] the agent" (kartari kṛt). This rule "kṛt affixes [denote] the agent" will apply by way of a conflict (vipratiṣedha). But there is the undesirable consequence (sarvaprasaṅga) that the affix āna would apply to all roots in the sense of the agent, even to those that are parasmaipada. This is not a fault; for the rule "anudāttaṅitaḥ" will serve as a restrictive rule (niyamārtha). If this rule...

If the rule is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), then it does not apply to cases such as *āste* (he sits) and *śete* (he lies down). If, on the other hand, it is for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartha*), then a restriction regarding the prefix *ā-* would not be obtained in cases such as *āsīnaḥ* (seated) and *śayānaḥ* (lying down). Likewise, the sequential enumeration beginning with *neḥ viśaḥ* (after *ni-*, [the root] *viś*) would not be applicable if the rule were for the purpose of restriction; if it is for the purpose of an injunction, then a restriction regarding *ā-* would not be obtained. Let it then be for the purpose of restriction.

But was it not said that the prescription [of the *ātmanepada*] is not possible? Yet the prescription has indeed been established. How so? In the rule "bhāvakarmaṇoḥ," the phrase "anudāttaṅitaḥ" will be carried over (anuvartate). If it is carried over, even so, the *ātmanepada* would only apply after roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or the letter *ṅ*, in the sense of the action itself (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). In that case, a separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: first, "anudāttaṅitaḥ."

The *ātmanepada* [voice] occurs. Then, [the rule] "in the sense of the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). Then, "in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). And in the sense of the agent, the *ātmanepada* occurs by the very rule "after a root marked with an indicatory vowel *ṅ* that is grave (*anudātta*). The phrase "in the sense of the state and the object" has ceased to apply. Then, [the rule] "in the case of mutual action (*karmavyatihāra*). The word "in the sense of the agent" continues to apply. The phrase "after a root marked with an indicatory vowel *ṅ* that is grave" has also ceased to apply. As for what is said regarding the prefix *ni-*...

If the sequential enumeration beginning with "viśaḥ" and so forth is for the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha), then a rule (vidhi) cannot be established. If, on the other hand, it is for the purpose of a rule, then the restriction of the suffix *āna* would not be obtained. Let it be for the purpose of a rule. But was it not said that the restriction of *āna* is not obtained? This is not a fault; for just as the *taṅ* suffixes occur here even though they were not previously obtained, so too does *āna*.

[If that were so,] it would indeed occur; however, there would be no over-extension (*aprasaṅga*) in all cases. For in all [other] *sādhana*s (grammatical operations), the suffix *āna* would not apply.

Alternatively, due to conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), by the rule "the suffix *āna* [is used] when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed," it would not occur in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*); it would occur only when the agent is expressed. But here, since the mention of *la* is being made, let this [rule] "a *kṛt* suffix [is used] when the agent is expressed" apply, while the rule "the *la*-suffixes are used in the sense of the object and in the sense of the action for intransitive verbs" applies.

Thus, by the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ*, this will occur through subsequent sublation (*vipratiṣedha*). However, there would be the undesirable consequence (*sarvaprasaṅga*) that the substitutes for *l* would apply to all means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Furthermore, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *kvasu* would also apply even in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). This is not a fault; for by the rule *śeṣāt parasmaipadaṃ kartari*, those two [suffixes] are restricted to the agent (*kartṛ*).

(P_3,4.77.1) KA_II,181.8–25 Ro_III, 400–402: Regarding the substitution of *ḷ*, there is the undesirable consequence of it applying to all [lakāras], because no distinction is made. If there is a substitution of *ḷ* for a *lakāra*, it would follow that this substitution applies to every *lakāra*. It would thus apply even here: *lunāti*, *labhate*. Why? Because no distinction is specified; indeed, no specific qualification is introduced.

[The rule] states that this substitution occurs for a *lakāra* of such a kind. If no specific distinction were made, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it applying to all [instances].

[Objection: It is established by the principle of "mentioning what is meaningful" (*arthavad-grahaṇa*). Only a meaningful *lakāra* is mentioned here, and this [substitution] does not apply to a meaningful one. [Reply:

If it is argued that it is established by "mentioning what is meaningful," [we say] no, because this concerns the mention of individual phonemes (*varṇa*). It is not established by "mentioning what is meaningful."
If that is so, it is not [the case]. What is the reason? This is a mention of phonemes (*varṇa*). And this [rule] does not apply to the mention of phonemes;

rather, it applies to the mention of meaningful units (*arthavat*), not to what is meaningless. Therefore, there must be a specific mention. Consequently, a specific mention of the letter *l* must be made. It need not be made. The term "of a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) is understood [from the previous rule]. Even so, [in the word] *śālā*—

In the case of *mālāmalla*, [the designation *it*] would apply here. [But] the *uṇādi* suffixes are underived nominal stems (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*). Even so, [the designation *it*] would still apply here in the case of *nandana*. [Objection: In this case, the designation *it* will serve as an exception (*bādhaka*). [Reply: Then it would also exclude [the designation *it*] in cases such as *pacati* and *paṭhati*. [Objection:

Since there is no operation for an *it* element (*itkāryābhāva*) here, the designation *it* will not occur. [Reply: This is indeed an operation for an *it* element: [the rule] "in the presence of *li*" (*liti*).

The rule "that which precedes a suffix marked with *l* (lit) is acute" is stated so that this accentuation may occur. However, we do not see any suffix marked with *l* (*lit*) here. Even if, somehow, by virtue of a specific statement or through the influence of a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*), there were a substitution of those [suffixes] designated as *it*, even then there would be no fault; for the activity of the Teacher indicates that the operation of *lit*-markers does not apply when there is a substitute for a *l*-suffix (*lādeśa*).

Thus, since this [rule] makes the letter *ṇ* a *liṅga* (indicatory marker), even though the *uṇādi* suffixes are indeed derived [by other rules], there is still no fault. For a specific mention of *la* is made [in the rule]:
"of *la*" (*lasya*).

The substitution of *la* (the imperative suffix) takes precedence over a rule concerning individual phonemes (*varṇavidhi*), by virtue of the "prior contradiction" (*pūrvavipratiṣiddham*). The substitution of *la* occurs by means of the prior contradiction with regard to a rule concerning phonemes. The scope of the substitution of *la* is, for example, *pacatu* ("let him cook") and *paṭhatu* ("let him recite"). The scope of a rule concerning phonemes is, for example, *dadhyatra* ("curd here") and *madhvatra* ("honey here"). In the case of *pacatu atra* and *paṭhatu atra*, both [rules] would apply; however, the substitution of *la* occurs by virtue of the prior contradiction.
In that case, then, a prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) must be stated. It need not be stated; for it has already been said. What has been said?
That "the substitution of *l* [for *ś*] takes precedence over a rule concerning phonemes (*varṇavidhi*).

403–404. Regarding the substitution of *e* for the *ṭit* [affixes] in the *ātmanepada*: the prohibition of *āna* must be stated. When there is the substitution of *e* for the *ṭit* [affixes] in the *ātmanepada*, the prohibition of *āna* must be stated. For example: *pacamānaḥ*, *yajamānaḥ*. By the rule "for the *ṭit*," the substitution of *e* would apply. Or has this been stated? What has been stated? It has been stated that there is a *jñāpaka* (indicative mark) that when a substitute is prescribed for a [suffix] with an *anubandha*, there is an absence of *it*-operations. This has not been stated.

It would indeed have been stated thus if it were understood in this way: "That which has *ṭ* as its *it* is *ātmanepada*; [the rule] 'of those *ātmanepadas* that have *ṭ* as their *it*'. But that is not the case. It is understood rather as: "Of those *ātmanepada* suffixes belonging to the *l*-class (*lakāra*) that have *ṭ* as their *it*. And this must necessarily be understood in this way: "That which has *ṭ* as its *it* is *ātmanepada*; [the rule] 'of those *ātmanepadas* that have *ṭ* as their *it*'."
If it were understood in this way, then [the substitution] would undesirably apply here as well. This is not *ṭit*; what then? It is *ṭhit*.

And that must necessarily be stated as *ṭhit* so that it does not become the initial element. How is it that [the rule] "of *iṭ*, *at*" is interpreted? I shall state it as "of *iṭha*, *at*. And that must necessarily be stated so that it does not apply to *paryavapādya*. [For example: *laviṣīṣṭa*. In this case, then, regarding *iṣam*...

In the word *ūrjam aham*, since [the suffix] begins with *i*, the rule "there is elision of the *ā* of *itaḥ* before an *iṭ*" would not apply; therefore, this [suffix] must be *ṭit*. If that is so, why does it not become initial (*ādi*)? Seventeen substitutes bring about the status of being a substitute for a specific locus (*sthāneyoga*).
Considering that no single one of them is capable of setting aside all those [rules], it will not be initial. Why, then, is it not [treated as] *paryavapādya* (that which is set aside)?

[The form] *laviṣīṣṭa* [is derived]. [But this is incorrect because] "that which is characterized by being external (*bahiraṅga*) is not established when [confronted with] that which is characterized by being internal (*antaraṅga*). In that case, it was stated previously: "the substitution of *e* occurs for the primary middle-voice endings (*ātmanepada*). And what are the primary ones? They are those beginning with *ta*. But [if you argue that] the suffix *muk* [added to the root *jñā*] is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the substitution of *e* in the case of the *ṭi*-marked endings and the *taṅ* group; [and that] the substitutes *i*, *sīr*, and *ic* occur before *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras*; [and that] the *ṭi*-marked ending is not [included] in the *aṭitaḥ* list; [and that] in the present context, that [substitution] applies—then how [do you explain] the *guṇa* [vowel]?

The addition of the marker *ś* to *ṇal* is for the purpose of making it a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*). *Ṇal* should be made *śit*. What is the purpose? For the sake of being a universal substitute.

By the rule "that which has *ś* as its marker replaces the whole," it may serve as a universal substitute. For if the *ś* were not present, the rules would apply only to the final phoneme of the *alaḥ* (the stem).
[If it were so,] the [suffix] *antya* would follow as a consequence. Or has it already been stated? What has been stated? That "it is established because of the absence of *it*.
The letter *ṇ* is employed; because of its lack of *it*, it is established. Which of these two solutions is logical? You have been urged toward the letter *ś*;
you say, "I shall employ *ṇ*, I shall not employ *ś*. In this case, *ṇ* would be employed, and *ś*...

Or rather, what indeed is the distinction here? In this case, the letter *ṇ* must necessarily be made for the sake of *vṛddhi*, so that the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule "before a *ṇit*" may occur. There is no need for the letter *ṇ* for the purpose of *vṛddhi*. A split of the *yoga* (separation of the rule) will be made regarding the status of being *ṇit*: first, "after *go*, [the suffix] is *ṇit*"; then, "the *al* [suffix]"; and then, "and the *al* is *ṇit*"; and finally, "or the last [vowel]". If that is so, then...

The letter *l* is employed [in the suffix]. Because it is not marked with *ṅ* (i.e., it is not *an*), the rule is established. What kind of solution is this that is considered logical? You have been urged toward the letter *ś*; you say, "I shall employ *l*, I shall not employ *ś*. Whether *l* is used here or *ś*, what indeed is the distinction? In this case, the letter *l* must certainly be employed for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*), because of the rule regarding the suffix ending in *lit*.

[The opponent says: "It must be that the preceding [syllable] is acute (udātta), so that this accent may occur. [The proponent replies: This purpose is not necessary. Once the accent of the root (dhātusvara) has been applied, reduplication (dvirvacana) takes place. Therein, by virtue of internal correspondence (āntarya), an acute-final substitute will arise for an acute-final [original]. [The opponent asks: But how can this be acute-final when it consists of a single vowel (ekāc)? [The proponent replies: By means of the treatment as if possessing a designation (vyapadeśivadbhāva). [The opponent says: In that case, by the very same principle of vyapadeśivadbhāva—

Just as [the rule] for an oxytone (antodātta) applies, so too does it for an ādyudātta. In that case, by virtue of proximity (āntarya), an ādyudātta substitute would result for an ādyudātta [original]. This is true; however, there is no such rule as "the beginning of a root is udātta.
Rather, this rule exists: "the end of a root is udātta. Thus, by that rule, it is an oxytone (antodātta).

In that case, by virtue of proximity (*āntaryataḥ*), an acute-accented substitute (*antodātta*) will arise for an acute-accented [original]. This also does not apply to the substitute itself, because there is no rule stating that the end of the substitute must be acute. Rather, the accent is obtained from the original form (*prakṛti*). And just as its original form is acute on the final syllable, it may likewise be acute on the initial syllable. Furthermore, in the case of reduplication (*dvirvacana*) involving double application, both [the original and the substitute] would be affected.

Otherwise, the property of having an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*) would result. Since it is a rule that "a word has one [syllable] which is not grave" (*anudāttaṃ padam ekavarjam*), simultaneous occurrence is impossible. Consequently, an alternation (*paryāya*) would result. Therefore, the letter *l* must be inserted for the sake of the accent. The letter *l* is inserted; because it is not an *it*, the desired form is established.
407–408. The addition of the marker *ś* to the letter *a* is for the purpose of making it a substitute for the whole. The letter *a* must be provided with the marker *ś*. What is the purpose?

It is for the purpose of making it a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). By the rule "that which has *ś* as its marker replaces the whole," it should be a substitute for the entire [stem]. For if the marker *ś* were not applied, then by the rule "operations apply to the final [element] of an *al*," it would result in being a substitute for only the final [letter]. But surely, when the letter *a* is spoken of as the letter *a*...

[Objection: Since there is no purpose [for it], it will be a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*) even without the letter *ś*. [Response: There is another purpose for stating the letter *a* as *a*. What is it? The statement of *a* is for the sake of equality in number (*samasaṅkhyārtha*), so that there may be a correspondence according to the number of elements (*saṅkhyātānudeśa*).
Therefore, the letter *ś* must be employed; therefore, the letter *ś* should be made. [Objection: It need not be made. [Response: It is indeed made.

In the very *nyāsa*, this is a *praśliṣṭanirdeśa* (a conjoined indication): *a-a-a*. By the rule "that which has more than one letter or is marked with *ś* is a substitute for the whole," it will be a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*).

3.4.85) Regarding the extension (*atideśa*) of being like the *laṅ* [tense], there is a prohibition of the substitution of *jus*. In the extension of being like the *laṅ*, there is a prohibition of the substitution of *jus*.

It must be stated: "Let them go" (*yāntu*), "let them vomit" (*vāntu*). Since the rule "for Śākaṭāyana alone [the substitution of] *jus* applies to the *laṅ* [optative]" would result in the substitution of *jus*, [the following is said]: "The statement regarding the change to *u* (utva) establishes the correct form. Here, the change to *u* will be the sublater (*bādhaka*). For rules that have no other scope (*anavakāśa*) are sublaters. But the change to *u* does have scope. What is its scope? "Let him cook" (*pacatu*), "let him read" (*paṭhatu*). Even here, the elision of the vowel *i* (*ikāralopa*) would apply.

Just as *utva* subverts the elision of the vowel *i*, so too does it subvert the substitution of *juṣ*. It does not subvert it. What is the reason? Because subversion occurs only when [the rule] has not already taken effect. Now, *utva* does not begin its operation when the elision of *i* has not yet taken effect; however, regarding the substitution of *juṣ*, it applies both when that substitution has taken effect and when it has not. Alternatively, these are exceptions (*apavāda*) that precede [the general rules].
"Subsequent rules set aside preceding ones"—thus, the substitution of *u* sets aside the elision of the vowel *i*, but it does not set aside the change to *ju*.

If that is so, he will state the purpose of the mention of *laṅ* there: "So that it may apply only to that which is actually *laṅ*; let it not apply to that which is *laṅ* by virtue of the treatment as *laṅ* (*laṅvad-bhāva*)."

185.3–9. Prohibition of *utva* for *hin*. A prohibition of the substitution of *u* for the vowel of *hin* must be stated. [In examples such as] *lunīhi*, *lunāni*, the substitution of *u* (by rule *eḥ uḥ*) would apply. Or rather, it need not be stated, because of the force of the pronunciation itself. Why? Because of the force of the pronunciation itself. It need not be stated. What is the reason?

409–410. *Etaḥ aitve ādguṇapratiṣedhaḥ*. A prohibition of the *ādguṇa* [substitution] must be stated when *etaḥ* undergoes the change to *ait*. For example: *pacāva idam* (*pacāvedam*) and *pacāma idam* (*pacāmedam*). Once the *ādguṇa* has been applied, the rule for changing *eta* to *ait* would apply. [Objection: It need not be stated, because [the *ādguṇa* substitution] is characterized as being external (*bahiraṅga*). [Response: No, it need not be stated.

What is the reason? Because it is a rule conditioned by external factors (*bahiraṅga*). The substitution of *guṇa* for *āt* [in *ā + i*] is conditioned by external factors, whereas the substitution of *ait* [for *ai*] is conditioned by internal factors (*antaraṅga*). That which is conditioned by external factors is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is conditioned by internal factors. But [the rule] *apakarṣavijñāna* (understanding by attraction) applies; thus, the *suṭ* augment would be understood as being attracted from the rule for the *ti* and *th* endings: *kṛṣīṣṭa*, *kṛṣīṣṭhāḥ*. Furthermore, the statement regarding *suṭ* must apply even to that which does not begin with [an *t* or *th*]. Thus, *suṭ* should be prescribed for *kṛṣīyāstām* and *kṛṣīyāsthām*; otherwise, because the rule specifies "of the *liṅ* [optative] beginning with *t* or *th*," *suṭ* would not apply. [Response: Not so; because the *ti* and *th* endings are the primary elements, the mention of *liṅ* serves as their qualifier.

Or rather, it should not be stated. What is the reason? Because the *ti* and *th* are the primary elements. In this context, the *ti* and *th* alone are the primary elements; the mention of "liṅ" (*liṅgrahaṇa*) is merely a qualifier for them. It is not understood thus: "the *suṭ* augment occurs after the *liṅ* [affix] when it consists of *t* or *th*. How then? It is understood as: "the *suṭ* augment occurs after *t* and *th*, provided that these two belong to the *liṅ* [affix]."

(P_3.4.103) For what purpose is the *ṅit* designation stated for *yāsuṭ*? The statement that *yāsuṭ* is *ṅit* is for the sake of [the rules concerning] *pit*. The rules concerning *pit* serve as their purpose. Now, for what purpose is the statement that it is *udātta* made? And the statement that it is *udātta*—for what? It is for the sake of [the rules concerning] *pit*.
Or rather, it is for the sake of making the augment (āgama) unaccented (*anudātta*). Alternatively, the Teacher indicates this: that augments are unaccented.

When there is no other purpose, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). And this has been stated: "The mention of *ṅit* for *yāsuṭ* is for the sake of the *pit* designation, and the mention of the acute accent (*udātta*) is likewise. By this, it can be said that *yāsuṭ* occurs in the *parasmaipada* endings.

Moreover, there is the suffix *liṅ*. Since this [result] is already established by such a simpler formulation (*nyāsa*), the fact that the Teacher undertakes a more laborious effort indicates that *āgamas* are *anudātta* (unaccented).
