412–414. Is this inclusion of the long *ā* in the rule for the *jus* suffix intended as a restrictive (*niyamārtha*) one, or rather as an inclusive (*prāpaka*) one? How would it be restrictive, and how would it be inclusive? If the mention of *sic* (from P. 3.4.109) is understood to carry over [into this rule], then it is restrictive; if it has ceased to apply, then it is inclusive. What, then, is the distinction here? If the inclusion of the long *ā* in the rule for *jus* is for the sake of restriction, then there must be a mention of the elision of *sic*.

If it is argued that the mention of the *ākāra* (the vowel *ā*) is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), then the mention of the elision of *sij* (*sijluggrahaṇa*) must be made. It should be stated: "after a root ending in *ā* from which *sij* has been elided. This is so that [the rule] does not apply here: *akārṣuḥ*, *ahārṣuḥ*. Let it then be an inclusive statement (*prāpaka*). If it is an inclusive statement, then there must be a prohibition regarding the application of suffix-characteristics (*pratyayalakṣaṇapratiṣedha*). If it is an inclusive statement, then a prohibition regarding the application of suffix-characteristics must be stated.

Because [the forms] "abhūvan" and so on possess the characteristic of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the substitution of *jus* would apply; therefore, the use of the particle *eva* is necessary. Indeed, the use of *eva* must be made, as in the rule: "The *laṅ* [suffixes] are replaced by *jus* according to Śākaṭāyana alone. However, when the restriction is already established, the particle *eva* serves no purpose.
But surely, even when the rule is already applicable, a prescription (*vidhi*) being commenced—even without the particle *eva*—serves the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

It will be so. If it is for the sake of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) according to what is desired, then the particle *eva* must be employed. So that it may be understood thus: "The *laṅ* [suffix] is [used] only for Śākaṭāyana"; let it not be understood as "Only for Śākaṭāyana is there the *laṅ*. And what would be the consequence? For Śākaṭāyana, the *luṅ* [suffix] would not be [used]; [for example, the forms] *aduḥ*, *apuḥ*, *adhuḥ*, *asthuḥ*. Furthermore, the mention of *laṅ*—the mention of *laṅ* [is necessary].

And it must be stated [as a rule]: "The substitution [of *jus*] for the *laṅ* occurs according to Śākaṭāyana alone. However, since this is already a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), there is no purpose in mentioning *laṅ*. The phrase "after an *ā*, before a *ṅit*" continues to apply. And there is no other *ṅit* suffix immediately following an *ā*-vowel other than the *laṅ*; therefore, let it be a restrictive rule. But was it not said that the mention of the vowel *ā* in the rule for *jusi* is for the sake of restriction? [In response: It is the mention of the elision of *sic* (*sij-luk*) [that serves as the basis].

[Objection: This is not a fault. The restriction applies to that which is of the same class (*tulyajātīya*). And what is of the same class? That which follows immediately after both [the root and the suffix *sica*] and which begins with *ā*. [Reply: In that case, the employment of the particle *eva* need not be made at all. [Objection: It must indeed be made. [Question: For what purpose? [Reply: For the sake of the subsequent rule. So that, in the case of the *liṭ* and the *liṅ* used in the sense of benediction (*āśis*), it may be understood as being exclusively an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.

Otherwise, by virtue of the explicit statement, it would receive the designation *ārdhadhātuka*, and because it is included by the mention of *tiṅ*, it would receive the designation *sārvadhātuka*. Now, that mention of *laṅ* need not be made at all. [Objection: It must indeed be made. [Question: For what purpose? [Answer: So that the rule may apply only to that which is actually *laṅ*; let it not apply to that which is *laṅ* only by virtue of being treated as *laṅ* (*laṅvadbhāva*).

Regarding the technical designation *ārdhadhātuka*: the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) must be made in the rule for the *ārdhadhātuka* designation. This is so that the designation *ārdhadhātuka* applies to what follows a root. It should not apply here, however, in the case of *vṛkṣatva*.

Regarding the term *vṛkṣatā*: even if the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) were made, there would still be a prohibition regarding *svādi* [suffixes]. A prohibition of *svādi* suffixes must be stated so that it does not apply here in cases such as *lūbhyām* and *lūbhiḥ*. The mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) depends on what has been previously enumerated. Even so, [the rule] would undesirably apply to forms like *agnikāmyati* and *vāyukāmyati*. Therefore, the mention of "root" must be made. [Objection: It need not be made.

The governing rule for verbal roots (*dhātu-adhikāra*) continues in force until the end of the third chapter. Where was it introduced? It was introduced in the rule *dhātor ekāco halādeḥ*. Even so, [undesired forms] such as *śrīkāmyati* and *bhūkāmyati* would result. This is established by treating the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) as a qualifier of what is prescribed (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*). That is, [the meaning is]: "that which is prescribed after a root. This [suffix] is prescribed after a root.
"Having mentioned 'from a root' (*dhātoḥ*), that which is prescribed in this manner [is intended].

4.1.1) Why is there the mention of "feminine suffixes, *āp*-suffixes, and nominal stems" (*ṅyāpprātipadika*)? It is so that [the suffixes] may occur after a feminine suffix, an *āp*-suffix, or a nominal stem, rather than after a root.

[Objection: "Let them not occur. [Response: This is not a valid purpose. The suffixes beginning with *tavya* are prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*); they will act as exceptions (*apavāda*) and thus supersede [the case endings]. [Objection: Then let them not occur after a word ending in a personal ending (*tiṅanta*). [Response: The case-endings beginning with *su* (*svādayaḥ*) are prescribed for meanings such as singularity and so forth.

Since those [meanings]—singularity and the rest—are already expressed here by the personal endings (*tiṅ*), the case-endings will not occur because their meaning has already been expressed (*uktārthatvāt*).

In that case, let it be that the *ṭāp* suffixes and others do not occur after verbal forms (*tiṅanta*). The *ṭāp* suffixes and others are prescribed for feminine gender; however, there is no connection of a verbal form with femininity. Then let it be that the *aṇ* suffixes and others do not occur after verbal forms. The *aṇ* suffixes and others are prescribed in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth; however, there is no connection of a verbal form with offspring and the like. Even so, how [is this explained]?

Even if this were a *cit*-yoga (an operation marked by the indicator *cit*), there would still be no fault. The activity of the Teacher makes it known that suffixes such as *aṇ* and others do not follow verbal roots (*tiṅanta*);

for he employs the term *tiṅ* in certain rules prescribing secondary nominal suffixes (*taddhita*), such as: "The suffixes *tamap* and *iṣṭhan* occur after a word expressing excellence, and also after a *tiṅ*. Therefore, he recites the following answer: "The mention of *ṅī*, *āp*, and nominal stems (*prātipadika*) is for the sake of [defining] the technical designations of *aṅga*, *bha*, and *pada*."

The mention of *ṅī*, *āp*, and *prātipadika* is made for the sake of the technical designations (*saṃjñās*) of "stem" (*aṅga*), "base" (*bha*), and "word" (*pada*). [The purpose is] so that these designations of stem, base, and word may apply to the *ṅī*, *āp*, and *prātipadika*. But where, in this context, is there a need for the mention of *ṅī*, *āp*, and *prātipadika* for the sake of the designations of stem, base, and word? [It is needed] in the case of the suffixes *ṭāp* and so on. This is not a valid purpose; for the suffixes *ṭāp* and so on are prescribed after those [bases] that possess the designation of being "marked by a mention" (*grahaṇavat*). [They are also prescribed] after those ending in *ugit*.
"The suffix *ṅīp* occurs; from this [base], the suffix *ṭāp* occurs"—thus, the production of those [suffixes] is from that very form of the word which is apprehended.

These [suffixes] will be its designations (*saṃjñā*). Or, even if someone does not accept [the base as the cause], there is still no fault. The suffixes *ṭāp* and so on are prescribed when [the word] denotes a female (*strī*). The production of those [suffixes] is from that very form of the word which exists in the feminine.

These designations will apply to it. But then, regarding the suffixes *aṇ* and so forth: even *aṇ* and the others are prescribed after bases that are themselves subject to the designation "grahaṇavat" (possessing the status of being mentioned), such as in the rules "yañ after *garga* and so forth," and "phak after *naḍa* and so forth. Since that specific verbal form (*śabdasvarūpa*) is what is being grasped, the suffix arises from that; these designations will apply to it. Furthermore, suppose there were someone who did not grasp [the form].

Even so, there is no fault. The suffixes *aṇ* and others are prescribed with respect to meanings such as "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth. That which is the very form of the word (*śabdasvarūpa*) occurring in the sense of offspring and the like—its derivation [of the suffix] occurs from that; these technical designations (*saṃjñā*) will apply to it. But what about in the case of suffixes added in their own meaning (*svārthika*)? Suffixes added in their own meaning are also prescribed after bases that possess the capacity for being mentioned (*grahaṇavat*). For example, *kan* is prescribed after words beginning with *yāvat*, and [suffixes] after words beginning with *prajña*.

Regarding the term *aṇ*: that which is grasped as the very form of the word (*śabdasvarūpa*) arises from that; these [suffixes] will be its designations (*saṃjñā*). As for the case where there is no such grasping, as in "whiter" (*śuklatara*) or "blacker" (*kṛṣṇatara*): even here, it is not the case that whatever is white is "whiter. Rather, "whiter" refers to a white thing that is preeminent (*prakṛṣṭa*). That which is the very form of the word functions with respect to what is preeminent.

Therefore, their production [occurs] from that. These will be its designations. But then, in the case of the *svādi* suffixes: the *svādi* suffixes are prescribed for meanings such as singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth. Since that very form of the word (*śabdasvarūpa*) occurs with respect to meanings such as singularity, its production [occurs] from that. These will be its designations. But how is it that the *svādi* suffixes are mentioned here?

The meanings such as "oneness" (*ekatva*) and so forth can be understood [from this rule], because it constitutes a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*). That [previous rule] is one sentence and this [present rule] is another; yet, if they form a single sentence, why are they placed in different locations? The Teacher demonstrates mere skill (*kauśalamātra*) in that he places what is a single sentence in different locations, thinking: "I shall also include other [rules] in this manner."

And [the mention of] *ṅy-āp-prātipadika* is for the sake of elision (*luk*) after *yac* and *yaccha*. If it is asked: "Then why is *ṅy-āp-prātipadika* mentioned for the sake of elision after *yac* and *yaccha*?
[The answer is: It is so that the elision may apply to what follows a *ṅy-āp-prātipadika*, according to the rule *kaṃsīyaparaśavyayoḥ yañañau luk ca*.
For if the mention of *ṅy-āp-prātipadika* were not made, the elision would undesirably apply even to the base (*prakṛti*). This too is not [correct].

There is a purpose [for this rule]. Just as it has been stated that "the *luk*, *ślu*, and *lup* [suffix-removals] apply to a suffix," [one might argue that the elision would apply] to the suffix. Even so, [the elision] would undesirably apply (*prasajyeta*) to the phonemes *u* and *s*. For instance, from the root *kameḥ* [we derive] *kaṃsaḥ* ("a vessel"), and from *parāñ śṛṇāti* ["he cuts others"] we derive *paraśuḥ* ("an axe"). [Therefore, the answer is: the *uṇādi* formations are underived nominal bases (*avyutpannāni prātipadikāni*). This is because [the formation of these words] is characterized by the presence of long vowels (*vṛddhi*), short vowels (*avṛddha*), vowel-sounds (*avarṇa*), accents (*svara*), and double-consonant clusters (*dvyañ*).

And [the mention of] *prātipadika* in the rule for the prescription of suffixes is for the purpose of ensuring that understanding of it. If that is so, then in the rule for the prescription of suffixes characterized by *vṛddhi*, non-*vṛddhi*, vowel-initial, or two-syllable [bases], the mention of *ṅyāpprātipadika* is made for the purpose of ensuring that understanding of it—so that these may serve as qualifiers of the *prātipadika*: "from a *vṛddha* [base]," "from a non-*vṛddha* [base]," "from one ending in a vowel," "from one beginning with an *anudātta*," and "from a two-syllable [base]. Now...

If the mention of *ṅy-āp-prātipadika* were not made, of what would these [terms] be qualifiers? They would be qualifiers of "samartha" (semantically connected). What would be the fault in that? The rule *udīcām vṛddhād agotrāt* would apply here as well: *jñānām brāhmaṇānām apatyam* ("the offspring of Jña Brāhmaṇas").
For this [compound] is semantically connected (*samartha*) and contains a *vṛddha* stem. And in the case of *jñayoḥ brāhmaṇayoḥ apatyam* ("the offspring of two Jña Brāhmaṇas"), it would not apply.

For this [term *jña*] is capable [of being a Bahuvrīhi compound] and is not a *vṛddha* [stem]. [If the rule were applied without qualification: "The offspring of two *jña* Brāhmaṇas" (*jñayor brāhmaṇayor apatyam*), here too the suffix *-phin* would frequently apply according to the rule "for the Easterners, *-phin* is frequent after a non-*vṛddha* [stem]" (*prācām avṛddhāt phin bahulam*). For this [compound] is capable and is not a *vṛddha*.

And in the case of "the offspring of many *jña* Brāhmaṇas" (*jñānām brāhmaṇānām apatyam*), it would not apply here. For this [compound] is capable but is a *vṛddha*. [Furthermore, the term *avṛddha* refers to a stem] that does not begin with the vowel *a*.
Therefore, the suffix *iñ* applies; it should apply here:
*dakṣasya apatyam* (the offspring of Dakṣa) = *dākṣiḥ*. For this [compound] is "samartha" (capable of forming a derivative) and ends in the vowel *a*. But it should not apply here:
*dakṣayoḥ apatyam* (the offspring of two Dakṣas) or *dakṣāṇām apatyam* (the offspring of many Dakṣas). For these are "samartha" but do not end in the vowel *a*—that is, they do not end in *avarṇa*.

Regarding accent (*svara*): if [the suffix] *añ* were applied to stems beginning with an *anudātta* (unaccented) vowel, it would undesirably apply here in the cases of *vāco vikāraḥ* ("a modification of speech") and *tvaco vikāraḥ* ("a modification of the skin"). This [word *vāk*] is indeed capable [of being called] "beginning with an *anudātta" vowel. However, it would not apply here in the case of *sarveṣām vikāraḥ* ("a modification of all [sounds]"). This [word *sarva*] is indeed capable [of being called] "beginning with an *udātta* (accented) vowel. Regarding accent: if [the suffix] *ṭhan* were applied to stems characterized by having two vowels (*dvyañ-lakṣaṇa*), it would undesirably apply here in the case of *vācā*.

"One crosses by means of the skin, one crosses"—this [compound] is indeed capable and consists of two syllables (*dvyañ*). But here [the rule] would not apply to "one crosses by means of a jar" (*ghaṭena tarati*), for although this too is capable, it does not consist of two syllables. Now, when there is a qualification of "capability," is something desired [by the author] included, or is it merely the end of a fault? He says: "It is so. What is it? "One crosses by means of the *sāman*."
"By means of *vemā* one crosses. For this is indeed capable [of being a base], and it is also a *ṅyāpprātipadika*.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of *ṅī* and *āp*? Is it not already established by the rule "from a *prātipadika*"? It is not so established.

If [the term] *apratyayaḥ* (non-suffix) is intended as a prohibition of the designation *prātipadika*, then if this is the reason for including the mention of *ṅī* and *āp*, the mention of *ti* and *ū* must also be made; for those two are also suffixes. Regarding the mention of *ti*, however, it is unnecessary; for by the rule "a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)," the designation *prātipadika* will apply. And regarding the mention of *ū*, it is also unnecessary.

The suffix *ūṅ* is prescribed after a stem ending in the vowel *ū*. In that case, there is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [for the final of the stem and the initial of the suffix]. Once the single-substitute has been made, the designation "nominal stem" (*prātipadika-sañjñā*) will apply by virtue of the treatment of the substitute as being like the final (of the original stem) or the initial (of the following element). If this is the reason for not including *ūṅ* [in the rule], then the inclusion of *āp* should also not be made; for *āp* is also prescribed after a stem ending in the vowel *a*. In that case too, there is a single-substitute. Once the single-substitute has been made, the designation "nominal stem" will apply by virtue of the treatment of the substitute as being like the final (of the original stem) or the initial (of the following element).

It will be so. What then of those words ending in *anakāra* (other than *a*), such as *kruñcā*, *uṣṇihā*, and *devaviśā*? Even here, the application [of the rule] is observed from words ending in *akāra*: "one should sacrifice *kruñcās*," "*uṣṇihakakubhau*," and "*devaviśam ca manuṣyaviśam ca*. Regarding the example *uṣṇihakakubhau* first: this shortening of the vowel is indeed due to the suffix *āp* when it follows a subsequent member of a compound. Here...

Indeed, there is no difference between the word *devaviśam* and *manuṣyaviśam* when the suffix arises after a stem ending in a vowel or after one ending in a consonant. As for what was said regarding *uṣṇihakakubhau* here: this shortening of the final vowel of the second member (*auttarapadika-hrasvatva*) applies only to the word *āpaḥ*. This is so because of the rule *sañjñā-cchandasoḥ*; however, this [the word *uṣṇihakakubhau*] is not a technical name (*sañjñā*).

Nor is this a *chandas* [Vedic] usage. As for what is said here—"the host of gods (*devaviśam*) and the host of men (*manuṣyaviśam*)"—there is no difference whether the suffix arises after a word ending in a vowel or after one ending in a consonant. There is a difference in accent.
If the suffix were to arise here after a word ending in a consonant, the accent would result as in *devaviśam*. [But it is not so. *Devaviśam*.

And this is accepted. Therefore, what is the scope for such [a rule]? Well then, consider this: *pādo ’nyatarasyāṃ ṭāp ṛci* ("The suffix *ṭāp* optionally occurs after *pāda* when it refers to a Vedic verse"). It is stated "in a Vedic verse" (*ṛci*). In that case, it will apply because of its Vedic character (*chāndasatvāt*). But "in a Vedic verse" (*ṛci*) does not here intend to refer to the Vedic corpus itself—whether it be the *Kāṭhaka*, the *Kāpālaka*, the *Amudaka*, or the *Paippalādaka*. What then? It is a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārthaviśeṣaṇam*).

As for this [objection] that "the word *ṛk* would be the meaning of the suffix": even this is not a valid purpose. The word *pada*, ending in the vowel *a*, is seen in the Veda (*chandas*) as having the same meaning as the word *pāda*. The sense is: "one *pada* of it consists of seven syllables" means "one *pāda*. Therefore, the derivation will take place. In that case, however, the suffix *ḍāp* is optionally applied after both [of these].

Thus: *bahurājā*, *bahurāje*, *bahurājāḥ*. The mention of the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* is purposeless, because when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included. The mention of *ṅī* and *āp* is purposeless. Why? Because when a nominal stem is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included; this is a metarule (*paribhāṣā*).
It must be formulated. But what is the distinction between formulating this as a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) or simply including the mention of *āP*?
This *paribhāṣā* must necessarily be formulated. There are many purposes for this *paribhāṣā*. What are they?

The purpose is for the sake of the rules concerning pronouns (*sarvanāman*), accents, compounds (*samāsa*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and for the application and removal of suffixes (*vidhi-luk-aluk*). The rule concerning pronouns is a purpose: [the rule] "of a pronoun" (*sarvanāmnaḥ*).

The augment *suṭ* would apply only in cases such as *teṣām*, *tāsām*, and *yāsām*, but it would not apply here [in the case of *bhavatyāḥ*]. This is not a valid objection. The suffix *ṭāp* is prescribed after a stem ending in the vowel *a*. In that situation, there is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [of *a* and *ā*]. Once the single-substitute has been formed, *suṭ* will apply by virtue of the rule regarding the treatment of a substitute as the final element of the preceding member (*antavad-bhāva*) or the initial element of the following member (*ādivad-bhāva*).
In that case, this is the purpose: the third-case suffixes of the pronominal class (*sarvanāman*) should apply only here, as in *bhavatā hetunā* and *bhavataḥ*.

Regarding the term *hetoḥ*: [if it were not a pronominal], in the case of *bhavatyā hetunā* or *bhavatyā hetoḥ*, the substitution would not occur here. [The rule applies to] pronominals (*sarvanāman*). Regarding accent (*svara*):

in the case of *kuśūla-kūpa-kumbha-śālam* followed by *bile*, it would occur only here as *kuśūla-bilam*; in the case of *kuśūlī-bilam*, it would not occur here. [The rule applies to] accent (*svara*). Regarding compound (*samāsa*): the accusative case is compounded with words such as *śrita*; it would occur only here, as in *kaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ*.

In the case of *kaṣṭaśritaḥ*—where [one might argue] *kaṣṭam śritā* is *kaṣṭaśritā*—it would not apply here. But even this is not a valid objection. The word *śrita* ends in the vowel *a*; there, a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) occurs. Once the single-substitute has been made, it will function by virtue of the rule regarding "that which precedes" (*antavadbhāva*) and "that which follows" (*ādivadbhāva*). Well then, consider this: in the case of *pūrvasadṛśa*, it would apply only here, as in *pitṛsadṛśaḥ* ("similar to the father") and *pitṛsadṛśī* ("similar to the father").

In the case of *pitṛsadṛśī*, there would not be a compound here; rather, it would be a rule for secondary derivation (*taddhita-vidhi*). According to the rule *acittahasti-dhenoṣ ṭhak*, the suffix *ṭhak* would apply only here: *hastinām samūhaḥ* = *hāstikam*. However, in the case of *hastinīnām samūhaḥ*, the form *hāstikam* would not be obtained. This objection, too, is not valid as a purpose [for the rule], because this is already established by the rule of masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*). Then what [is the purpose]?

Regarding the rule for the suffix *dvayasaC*: just as here one says *hastidvayasam* ("measuring two elephants") or *hastimātram* ("the size of an elephant"), so too there should be the forms *hastinīdvayasam* and *hastinīmātram*. [This is] the rule for *taddhita* suffixes. [The elision (*luk*) applies] by the rule *na indasiddhabadhnātiṣu ca*;

it would apply only in this case, such as *sthaṇḍilaśāyī* (masculine) and *sthaṇḍilaśāyinī* (feminine), whereas in other cases it would not. [The elision (*luk*) does not apply] by the rule *aluk śayavāsavāsiṣu*.

Due to the incorrect timing [of the application], the form *grāmevāsī* would occur here, but *grāmevāsinī* would not occur here. Furthermore, regarding the suffix *mānin*, there is a purpose for both a rule (*vidhi*) and a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). First, for the sake of the rule: the suffixes *kyaṅ* and *mānin* would apply here, as in *darśanīyamānī*; however, they would not apply here in the case of *darśanīyamāninī*. Also, for the sake of the prohibition:

[The suffix] *īta* follows [the word] *vākya* and *svāṅga*, except when expressing a feminine who is not conceited (*amānin*). When that [suffix] is applied here, it would result in *dīrghamukhamānī*; however, in the case of *dīrghamukhamāninī*, it would not occur. And regarding the inclusion of the mention of the suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇopacāreṣu*): there is a purpose for including the mention of the suffix. In the rule "by means of *tṛc* and *aka* when denoting the agent" (*tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari*), it would apply only here, as in *apām sraṣṭā* ("the creator of waters"); but in *apām sraṣṭrī*, it would not occur. "Inclusion" (*upacāra*) refers to: [the inclusion of the mention of the suffix].

Therefore, in cases such as *kṛka*, *mika*, *kaṃsa*, and *kumbha*, there should only be [the suffix] *itha* (i.e., *ī*), as in *ayaskumbhī*. However, in the case of *ayaskumbhaḥ*, it should not occur.

These are the purposes of this *paribhāṣā* for which this *paribhāṣā* must be formulated. And when this [rule] exists, there is no need for the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* [in the sūtra]. There is over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in rules conditioned by an *upapada*. In rules conditioned by an *upapada*, there is over-extension.

It occurs. Regarding the root *tāp* with the words *dviṣat* and *para*, just as here we have *dviṣantapaḥ*, so too would *dviṣatītapaḥ* occur here as well. Regarding the suffix *phak* after *yañ* and *iñ*: there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the suffix *phak* after *yañ* and *iñ*. Just as here we have *gārgyāyaṇaḥ* and *dākṣāyaṇaḥ*, so too would *gārgeyaḥ* and *dākṣeyaḥ* occur here as well. This is not so.
There is a fault. Here, the suffix *ḍhak* will serve as an exception. Furthermore, regarding the compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*), there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Just as *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣ ṭac* applies here to form *madrarājaḥ* and *kaśmīrarājaḥ*, it would also apply here to form *madrarājñī* and *kaśmīrarājñī*. But it does not; rather, [the form] *madrarājñī* occurs when [the feminine suffix] follows from the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*).

The vowel *ī* [is the cause]. However, if there were an inclusion of the word qualified by its gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭagrahaṇa*), then a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) would result after a stem ending in *ī*. What is the fault in that? There would be the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) and the elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*). In that case, the form would be *madrījī*, whereas *madrarājñī* is what is intended. Regarding the substitution of *mahat* for *mahat* when preceded by words such as *priya*: there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of the substitution of *mahat* for *mahat* when preceded by words beginning with *priya*. [This is because of the rule] "after *āt* [comes the substitute] for *mahat*."

Regarding the rule *samānādhikaraṇajātīyayoḥ*: just as here [in the masculine] it occurs that "his great beloved" is *mahāpriyaḥ*, so too here [in the feminine] it would also occur that "his great beloved" is *mahatīpriyaḥ*. Why, then, is it said "in the case of *priyā* and so on"? It is because the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is prohibited there; however, where it is not prohibited, the substitution of *ā* (*āttva*) must certainly take place.

Regarding the rule for the acute accent on a *ñnit* suffix: there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of this rule. According to the rule "the first syllable is acute when a *ñnit* suffix follows," just as it occurs here in *dākṣiḥ* and *āhicumbukāyaniḥ*, it would also apply here in *dākṣī* and *āhicumbukāyanī*. Regarding the rule for the accent of the word *rājan*: there is an over-extension of the rule concerning *rājan* in relation to the words *brāhmaṇa* and *kumāra*. [The example is] *rājā*.

And [the rule] regarding "brahmin boy" (*brāhmaṇakumāra*)—just as here we have *rājakumāraḥ* (king’s son) and *rājabrāhmaṇaḥ* (king-brahmin), so too would there be *rājakumārī* (king’s daughter) and *rājabrāhmaṇī* (king-brahmin woman) in this case as well. Furthermore, in the case of references to compounds (*samāsa*) and groups (*saṅghāta*), there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For example, in the rule "after *bahu*, like *nañ*, when the final member denotes abundance," just as we have *bahugomān* (possessing many cows) here...

In cases such as *bahuyavamān*, *bahugomatī*, and *bahuyavamatī*, this [rule] would also apply. Why then is it said that "in the case of rules involving the mention of a composite whole (*saṃghāta*)"?

For the very purpose of that maxim (*paribhāṣā*) is the mention of its constituent parts (*avayava*), just as in the examples *kumbhaśālam* (a hole with a jar) and *kuśūlībilam* (a hole with a granary). And it has been stated regarding case-endings (*vibhakti*). What was stated? "Or rather, there is no [need for a separate rule], because when a case-ending follows, the feminine form qualified by gender is not separately mentioned."

"Or rather, it is the sublation of the gender-indicator (*liṅga-bādhanam*).
(P. 4.1.3.1) It is stated: "in the feminine" (*striyām*). What indeed is this thing called "feminine"? These words are well-known in the world as denoting female and male.

"Neuter. That which, when observed in the world, leads to the determination: "this is female," "this is male," or "this is neuter"—that is the female, that is the male, and that is the neuter. But what is it in the world, upon seeing which, this is determined:
"this is female," "this is male," or "this is neuter"? It is the *liṅga* (gender-mark). But what is that? A woman is one who possesses breasts and hair.

It may be that a man is traditionally known as *lomaśa* (hairy). That which is the interval between the two [feminine and masculine] is the neuter in their absence. If the knowledge of feminine and masculine were based on gender (*liṅga*), then the suffix *ṭāp* would apply to the word *bhrūkuṃsa*. If the knowledge of feminine and masculine were based on gender, then *ṭāp* would result for *bhrūkuṃsa*. For that by which it is determined in the world upon seeing someone, "this is a woman," exists in the case of *bhrūkuṃsa* as well.
[Objection: One sees that the feminine suffix *ṭāp* does not apply to words like *vadhrikā*. [The rule states: "One sees *cañcā*, one sees *vadhrikā*, one sees *kharakuṭī*";

thus, by the rule *śasaḥ naḥ puṃsi*, the substitution of *na* for the final vowel of the stem should occur. For that which, upon being seen, leads one to determine "this is a male" exists in the case of *vadhrikā* and so on. However, the forms *khaṭvā* and *vṛkṣaḥ* are not established. It is not established. For that which is perceived in the world and by which it is determined "this is a woman" or "this is a man" does not exist in the case of a bed (*khaṭvā*) or a tree (*vṛkṣa*). What, then, would be the appropriate gender for those two? It should not be neuter; rather, the neuter gender would be the appropriate gender for the bed and the tree. What is this [term] *nāpuṃsaka*? That which exists in the neuter is *nāpuṃsaka*. In the absence of that—

The neuter. In the absence of that—that is, in the absence of the feminine and masculine genders—the neuter gender is logical. But [in this case] it is non-existent, like a mirage. However, the gender of the words *khaṭvā* (bed) and *vṛkṣa* (tree) should be regarded as non-existent. But how can a non-existent gender be perceived? Like a mirage. For example, thirsty deer perceive streams of water; yet they do not exist.

They exist. Just like a city of Gandharvas: just as cities of Gandharvas are seen from afar but are not perceived upon approaching them, so too should the *liṅga* of the bed and the tree be regarded. It is not non-existent like the movement of the sun; rather, it is like the movement of the sun, which, though existent, is not perceived—so too the existent *liṅga* of the bed and the tree.

It is not perceived. And it is like being hidden by a cloth; just as objects hidden by a cloth are not perceived, so too the existing mark of the bed and the tree is not perceived. This is an unequal comparison. Objects hidden by a cloth are perceived once the cloth is removed; however, even those carpenters who possess axes and hatchets [do not perceive them].

From the root to the tip, they fashion the trees, yet they do not perceive the mark (*liṅga*) of those two [the bedstead and the tree]. By what means is it determined that the existing mark of the bedstead and the tree is not perceived? There are six ways in which existent entities (*bhāva*) fail to be perceived: due to proximity, due to extreme distance, due to being obstructed by another form, and so forth.

"Because it is shrouded by darkness, because of the weakness of the senses, and because of extreme negligence. Therefore, some cause must be observed here by which the existent mark (*sat-liṅga*) of the bed and the tree is not perceived. By what is it determined that the existent mark of the bed and the tree is not perceived? By seeing the effect produced by them; that is, by seeing the sound produced by the woman.

A woman is determined as such upon seeing what is produced by a man, and a man is determined as such [upon seeing what is produced by a woman]. Just as by means of space one understands that "the light is here"; for space has light as its cause. But this is a case of mutual dependence; indeed, this becomes a case of mutual dependence: the word is produced by the feminine gender, and the feminine gender is produced by the word.

This results in a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). And things that involve mutual dependence cannot be established. It contradicts perception (*pratyakṣa*). Indeed, he who says that no mark of existence is perceived for a bed or a tree contradicts perception. In that case, one has acted in contradiction to one's own senses; and surely, one should not act in contradiction to one's own senses.

It must be so. Even when all the gender-markers (*liṅga*) are seen on the riverbank, who can determine them? Indeed, even after seeing all the gender-markers on the bank, who is able to determine that "this is a bank," "that is a bank," or "the other is a bank," or that "this is female," "this is male," or "this is neuter"? Therefore, it is not possible for grammarians to rely upon worldly gender (*laukika-liṅga*). It is necessary [to rely on something else].

And some [philosopher] must maintain a certain *svakṛtānta* (established conclusion). What is this *svakṛtānta*? "Dissolution (*saṃstyāna*) and production (*prasava*) are to be maintained as the mark (*liṅga*) according to one's own established conclusion. Dissolution and production are to be maintained as the mark. What is this "dissolution and production"? [The suffix] *ḍraṭ* is applied to the root *styai* in the sense of dissolution.

"A woman (*strī*) is so called because of the root *styai* (to congeal), and a man (*pumān*) because of the root *sū* (to bring forth). But is it not the case that even in common worldly usage, a woman is derived from *styai* and a man from *sū*? In the world, "woman" is derived from the locus (*adhikaraṇa*):

she is the one "in whom the embryo congeals" (*styāyati asyām garbhaḥ*). And "man" is derived from the agent (*kartṛ*): he is the one "who brings forth" (*sūte pumān*). Here, however, both are derived from the action itself (*bhāva-sādhana*).

Styāna (concretion) is female activity, and prasava (procreation) is male. Of what, then, is styāna female activity or prasava male? Of the *guṇas*. Which ones? Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Furthermore, all material forms (*mūrti*) are of this nature: they possess the qualities of styāna and prasava, and they possess sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Wherever there are fewer qualities, there are at least three, beginning with sound.

Touch and form [exist] everywhere, but taste and smell do not exist everywhere. Furthermore, activity is indeed constant; for here no one remains even for a moment within their own self. Rather, one either increases as far as it is possible to increase, or is joined with decline. And both of these occur everywhere. If both occur everywhere, how can there be any fixed distinction?

[Gender is determined] by the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). When there is the intention to express contraction (*saṃstyāna*), it is feminine; when there is the intention to express procreation (*prasava*), it is masculine; and when there is no intention to express either, it is neuter. Regarding its expression—that is, in its verbal designation—it receives its name from common usage (*loka*); that is to say, in its verbal expression, it becomes known as "feminine," "masculine," or "neuter" based on worldly convention. Alternatively, in the case of the elision of a suffix (*lup*), the word behaves like that which it was joined with (*yuktavat*). This provides a more extensive resolution regarding words such as *vadhrikā* and others.

In the case of elision (*lup*), the gender and number are treated as if they were present; thus, the *guṇa* substitution occurs here. Nor should it be thought that this is stated merely according to one's own whim.
For the Teacher will state: "Gender is not to be taught, because gender depends upon worldly usage. Furthermore, he will state:

"A difference in gender is observed when there is a single referent despite a difference in words, and also due to a difference in constituent parts. [This applies] in the sense of contraction (*saṃstyāna*).

From the root *styā* comes the suffix *ḍraṭ*, forming *strī*; from the root *sū* with the suffix *saP* comes *pums* in the sense of procreation. A vowel (*varṇa*) may be *ugit*, a suffix (*pratyaya*) may be *ugit*, and a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) may also be *ugit*.

What is the purpose of including the term *anyatarasyām*? It is so that the suffix *ḍāp* may optionally apply; and when *ḍāp* is not applied, the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) may also optionally apply. This is not a valid purpose, because here both *ḍāp* and the prohibition are being taught; both will occur by virtue of the explicit statement. Then what is the purpose? It is so that, when [the suffix] is released from both *ḍāp* and the prohibition...

[The questioner asks: "So that the suffix *ṅīp* may also occur here [in the case of *anaḥ*]. But the *ṅīp* is already established by the rule *ana upadhālopino ’nyatarasyām*. Now, can that mention of *anyatarasyām* be omitted? [The respondent says: Certainly it can. How so? Here, the suffix *ḍāp* is also prescribed, as is the prohibition, and the *ṅīp* as well; all of that will come about through the explicit statement [of the rule]. [The opponent replies: It is not possible to understand it in this way."
For if that option (*anyatarasyām*) were not stated there, the *ṅīp* and the prohibition of *ḍāp* would lack scope and would subvert [the application of] the *ḍāp* and its prohibition.

But the *ḍāp* and its prohibition also lack scope. They will nevertheless occur by virtue of the explicit statement. The *ḍāp* and its prohibition do have scope. What is their scope? "suparvā" and "cāruparvā. Therefore, that option (*anyatarasyām*) must be stated.

Indeed, this mention of "one or the other" (*anyatarasyām*) could have been omitted; however, it must certainly be included. What is the purpose? It is so that when [the suffixes] *ḍāp* and *pratiṣedha* (the prohibition of *ṭāp*) are excluded, both *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* may occur. Furthermore, the addition of the rule for *rap* after a *bahuvrīhi* compound was proposed; that need not be stated.

(P_4,1.13.2) KA_II,204.23–205.5 Ro_III, 469–470 Now, how should it be in these cases: *bahavaḥ śvānaḥ asyām rathyāyām* ("many dogs are in this street") and *bahavaḥ śvānaḥ asyām śālāyām* ("many dogs are in this hall")? It should be *bahuśūkā* and *bahuyūkā*. What is the derivation of the form? [The suffix] *ḍāp* [is applied], and there is elision (*lopa*) of the *ṭi* [portion].

Regarding the rule *prasāraṇam prasāraṇaparapūrvatvam nadṛtaśca* [Pāṇini 6.1.108], which prescribes the substitution of *kaP*: first of all, *kaP* should not occur here. What is the reason? That rule is understood to apply specifically to a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in a feminine noun (*nadī*) [as in *nadanta-bahuvrīhi*]. However, this is not a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in a *nadī*. Furthermore, the substitution of *prasāraṇa* (vocalization) should also not occur. This will be explained later in the section concerning the vocalization of words beginning with *śvan*, etc. (*śvādīnām prasāraṇe*).

The mention of a word ending in *nakāra* (the letter *n*) is for the purpose of excluding those not ending in *nakāra*. Therefore, even by virtue of the rule regarding "preceding by the other" (*parapūrvatva*), [the substitution] should not occur.

This will be stated later: "In the case of a vowel-substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) being preceded by another, the mention of 'having the same stem' (*samānāṅga*) is for the purpose of excluding cases where the stems are different. Consequently, the forms should be *bahuśvā* and *bahuyuvā*.

(P_4,1.14) Why is it stated "not when [the compound] is a subordinate member" (*anupasarjanāt*)? [Consider the examples: *bahukurucarā mathurā* ("Mathurā where many Kurus dwell") and *priyakurucarā mathurā* ("Mathurā dear to those who dwell among the Kurus").
This is not a valid purpose [for the rule]. The suffix is prescribed after the word *kurucara*; therefore, what occasion is there for [the application of the rule] in these cases?

[If it were argued: "It would apply from the word *bahukurucara*; [but] it does not even apply there, so what is the purpose of the prohibition?"—it applies by means of the rule for inclusion of that which ends in such a word (*tadantavidhi*). Therefore, he recites the following answer: "The mention of *anupasarjana* (non-derivative) is purposeless, because the prohibition of *tadantavidhi* applies to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
The mention of *anupasarjana* is purposeless. Why? Because the prohibition of *tadantavidhi* applies to a nominal stem.

The rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) to that which ends in a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is prohibited when [the suffix] is preceded by a word expressing possession. However, there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the non-prohibition of such extension in the preceding rules. If this is so, then the Teacher indicates that in the preceding rules, the prohibition of extension to that which ends in [a specific element] does not apply. What is the purpose of this indication? It is so that in forms such as *bhavatī*, *atibhavatī*, *mahatī*, and *atimahatī*, the rule of extension to that which ends in [the base] is established.

It occurs. This purpose is not valid, for it has already been stated that the *varṇa* (phoneme) is an *ugit-pratyaya*, the suffix is an *ugit*, and the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is also an *ugit*. Well then, consider the forms *bahudhīvarī* and *bahupīvarī*. Even this is not a valid purpose, for it has already been stated that an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) is required for the rule regarding *ra* in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because [the application of the suffix] is otherwise prohibited.

Thus [it is said]. In that case, however, [the forms] *atidhīvarī* and *atipīvarī* [would not be formed]. Or rather, this is a reference to the previous rule, as in the example "he studies the Āpiśala [grammar]. Furthermore, this should be regarded as a reference to the previous rule. In the previous rule, the technical term *upasarjana* (secondary member) is applied to that which is non-principal (*apradhāna*). As long as one says that [the suffix] must be produced from the principal and not from the non-principal, [the condition] is expressed by the word *anupasarjana* (not being a secondary member).

What is the purpose [of this]? [It is so that we may understand] "one studies the Āpiśala. [In the case of] "an Āpiśala Brāhmaṇī who studies the Āpiśala," the suffix *ī* should not occur after a word ending in *aṇ*. Now, if it is stated that [the rule applies] "only when [the word] is not a secondary member (*anupasarjana*)," why does it not apply here?
For this [word "Āpiśala"] ends in *aṇ* and is not a secondary member. [Answer: The word ending in *aṇ* is not qualified by the mention of "not being a secondary member."

[The rule] "from a word ending in *aṇ*, provided it is not a secondary member (*anupasarjana*)"—what then? It is *aṇ* itself that is qualified: "that *aṇ* which is not a secondary member. However, there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) with respect to genus-words (*jātiśabda*). Indeed, there is over-extension with respect to genus-words: [the forms] *kuntī* and *gāndhārī*. But this is established because a genus-word is not a secondary member. This is established. How so? Because [the rule applies to] what is not a secondary member.

Thus it is said. Nor is *jāti* a subordinate element (*upasarjana*). This too serves no purpose. The term "in the feminine" (*striyām*) is understood [from the previous rule]. Therefore, we shall qualify the suffix *aṇ*: "that *aṇ* which is prescribed in the feminine. Even so, in the case of "the *Mīmāṃsā* taught by Kāśakṛtsni is the *Kāśakṛtsnī*; she studies the *Kāśakṛtsnī*; [she is] a *Kāśakṛtsnā* Brāhmaṇī woman," the [desired] application occurs here.

This is not a fault. When the feminine suffix *ī* is to be applied, it must be added to the *aṇ* [suffix]. Now, that *aṇ* which was prescribed here when the feminine is to be expressed has been elided; and since the *ī* is added to that which is heard as having been produced [by the suffix], it will not be added again. However, this is for the purpose of ensuring that the rule of "specification by the final letter" (*tadantavidhi*) applies, as in the case of *kumbhakārī*.

Regarding *nagarakārī*: for here, when there is a mention of a suffix (*pratyaya*), the rule "that which begins with the element from which it is prescribed" applies, and thus the suffix would result in derivation from a single constituent part. However, by the principle that "when a *kṛt* suffix is mentioned, it includes that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*," the suffix will instead result in derivation from the entire complex. It is said, "when a *kṛt* suffix is mentioned," yet this is not a mention of a *kṛt* suffix.

This [term] refers to both that which is formed by a *kṛt* suffix and that which is not. This *aṇ* is indeed a *kṛt* suffix, yet it is also a *taddhita* suffix. If that were the case, then the compound would occur with a word ending in the vowel *ī*.

If that were possible, it would be accomplished; however, that is not possible. Why? Because in this context, the rule "there is compounding of prefixes (*gati*), objects (*kāraka*), and subordinate words (*upapada*) with *kṛt*-formed words" applies, and thus compounding occurs first of all.

When a compound is formed, the suffix [ṅīṣ] would result from the constituent member. If the suffix were produced from the constituent member, what fault would there be? The form *kaumbhakāreyaḥ* would not be established; the *vṛddhi* and accentuation would apply to the non-indeclinable part. Therefore, there must be the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "provided it is not a secondary member" (*anupasarjana*). When the governing rule "provided it is not a secondary member" is in effect for the prescription of the suffix *ṅīṣ* after a genus-name (*jāti*), there must be an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) regarding *suparṇī*. Regarding the prescription of the suffix *ṅīṣ* after a genus-name when the governing rule "provided it is not a secondary member" is in effect, [the case of] *suparṇī* [must be mentioned].

An addition must be made [to the rule]: *suparṇī*. Or rather, there is no fault, because the suffix *ṅīṣ* is prescribed generally for a word that is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*) and which denotes a genus (*jāti*), since the compound here is not a subordinate member and it denotes a genus. Why? Because the compound is not a subordinate member;
in this case, the compound is not a subordinate member, and it denotes a genus. Therefore, due to the compound being not a subordinate member, [the suffix applies].

And because the word [ending in *śvan*] denotes a genus (*jāti*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* will apply by the general rule: "The suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after a genus-denoting word that does not refer exclusively to females and whose penultimate vowel is not *y*. How is the objection raised? How is the resolution given? The objection is raised on the basis that it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; the resolution is given on the basis that it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

(P_4,1.15.1) Regarding the mention of *ḍha*, there must be an addition for that which possesses an *anubandha*. An addition must be made regarding the mention of *ḍha* for that which possesses an *anubandha*:
*kārikeyī*, *hārikeyī*. But what is the reason that it is not established? Because when there is a mention [of a term] without an *anubandha*...

"When there is the mention of that which has an *anubandha*, [the rule] 'ne' does not apply to that which lacks such an *anubandha*. What are the purposes of this *paribhāṣā*? Should these two *paribhāṣās* be formulated? They need not be formulated. The activity of the Teacher (*ācārya*) makes it known."

These two technical designations (*paribhāṣā*) of yours—namely, that in the rule *vāmadevād ḍyaḍḍyau*, he makes *ḍya* and *ḍya* *ḍit*—require an additional statement (*upasaṅkhyāna*). Since there is no word ending in the suffix *ḍha* in the feminine that lacks an indicatory letter (*ananubandhaka*), it will be understood that the suffix with its indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*) is what is intended to be included. But is there not this [suffix] *ḍha* in the rule *śilāyā ḍhaḥ*?

The mention of *añ* is redundant, because the suffix *ṅīn* is prescribed after that which ends in it. The mention of *añ* is purposeless. Why? Because *ṅīn* is prescribed after that which ends in it; for *ṅīn* is prescribed after a stem ending in *añ*, according to the rule: "After *añ* [stems] such as *śārṅgarava* and others, *ṅīn*. And there is no difference whether *ṅīn* or *ṅīp* follows a stem ending in *añ*; the form is the same and the accent is the same.

Or rather, it is not so, because of the governing context of "jāti" (genus). Nor is it purposeless. Why? Because of the governing context of "jāti. The word "jāteḥ" (of genus) carries over from that [preceding rule]. This present undertaking is for the sake of excluding "jāti. [The examples are] *autsī* and *audapānī*. Furthermore, the mention of "jāti" must necessarily be carried over. For if there were no governing context, there would be the undesirable consequence of the suffix *ṅīn* being applied by the rule "in the sense of a name derived from connection with a male" (*puṃyogād ākhyāyām*). Indeed, if the mention of "jāti" were not carried over...

If it were designated by connection with a male, the suffix *ṅīn* would apply: for example, "the wife of a Baida" (*baidī*). If, then, there is a basis for this [rule], this very rule must be formulated. That need not be formulated. Even so, it must certainly be formulated; for if it were not formulated, [the word] "the sister of a Baida" (*baidī*) would also [incorrectly] follow.

Because it is subsequent, the suffix *ṅīṣ* characterized by the class-marker *jāti* would supersede *ṅīp*. However, when *ṅīn* is present, because it is subsequent, *ṅīn* would supersede *ṅīṣ*. (P_4.1.15.3) KA_II,209.6-11 Ro_III, 480-481 An addition must be made for *khyun*: an addition for *khyun* must be formulated. [Examples: *āḍhyaṅkaraṇī*, *subhagaṅkaraṇī*. This that is stated is too little:

Regarding "khyun": there is an extension (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for *nañ*, *snañ*, *īkak*, *khyun*, *taruṇa*, and *taluna*. An extension must be made for *nañ*, *snañ*, *īkak*, *khyun*, *taruṇa*, and *taluna*. *Nañ* and *snañ*: *straiṇī*, *pauṃsnī*. *Īkak*:
*śāktīkī*, *yāṣṭīkī*. *Khyun*: [example follows].

The mention of *apatya* (descendant) must be made in order to prohibit [the suffix] *yañ* after the word *dvīpa*. This is so that [the form] *dvaipyā* does not occur here. Then, should that be stated? It need not be stated. For it is not understood thus: "after *kañ*, *kvarap*, and *yañ*.
How then? It is understood as: "after *kañ*, *kvarap*, and [stems] other than those ending in *yañ*."

(P_4,1.17) For what purpose is the mention of "taddhita" [in the rule]? The mention of "taddhita" is for the sake of the long vowel *ī* after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) marked with the marker *ṣ*. The mention of "taddhita" is made so that the long vowel *ī* may occur after a nominal stem marked with *ṣ*. This purpose does not exist; for it follows by the force of the application of the marker *ṣ* itself.

In this case, the suffix *īkāra* will indeed occur. However, just as the suffix *īkāra* occurs even after what is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*) by virtue of the power of the inclusion of the marker *ṣit*, so too, by virtue of the power of the continued application (*anuvartana*) of the term "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*), the suffix *īkāra* would also occur after a nominal stem that does not have the marker *ṣit*. There is another purpose for the continued application of the term "nominal stem. What is it? It is for the sake of the subsequent rule: "From *ataḥ* [comes] *iñ*: *dākṣiḥ*."

(P_4,1.18.1) KA_II,210.2-4 Ro_III, 482-483: What is the purpose of including the term *sarvatra* ("everywhere")? [Otherwise] it would apply only for the easterners (*prācām*). This is not a valid purpose, because for the easterners, the rule is already established by the preceding sūtra. Then what is the purpose? So that it may apply for all [grammarians]. [Example: *āvaṭyāyanī*.
The substitution of *ṣpha* should take place even when *cāp* is prohibited.
An addition [to the rule] should be made for Śākalya regarding the words beginning with *lohita*. An addition [to the rule] should be made for Śākalya regarding the words beginning with *lohita*.

It must be done. [The form] *śākalyāyanī* [is derived as follows]. However, if this word *śakala* were recited among the [words beginning with] *lohita*, it would not be possible in this way. For in this case, the pupils of Śākalya are called *śākalāḥ*; [if *śakala* were in the *lohita* group], the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule "from *kaṇva* etc., in the sense of a lineage" (*gotre*) would not apply. If that is so, then: "But *śakala* comes before *kaṇva*. The word *śakala* should be recited before the word *kaṇva*.
*Kata* is desired as the subsequent [term]. The word *śakala* should be recited after the word *kata*.

The preceding and succeeding groups (*gaṇas*) should be understood as ending with and beginning with those [terms] respectively. Those who begin with *kaṇva* are those who begin with *śakala*; those who end with *kata* are those who end with *śakala*. What is the purpose? The purpose there is for the suffixes *ṣpha* and *aṇ*. This being so, in that case—

The suffixes *ṣpha* and *aṇ* are established [as applicable]. However, *śakala* is desired before *kaṇva*, and [the suffix] after *kata*. The former and the latter [refer to] that which ends in and begins with them; in those cases, *ṣpha* and *aṇ* are the purpose [for their application].

484. An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) should be made for *kauravya* and *māṇḍūka* after [the patronymic suffix] *āsureḥ*. An addition should be made for *kauravya* and *māṇḍūka* after *āsureḥ*: *āsurāyaṇī*. And the suffix *cha* should also be stated: "and *cha*" should be said. *āsurīyaḥ kalpaḥ*.

484–486. It should be stated that the rule applies "in a non-final age" so that it would also apply here in cases such as *vadhūṭī* and *ciraṇṭī*. Why does it not apply here in cases such as *uttānaśayā*, *lohitapādikā*, *dvivarṣā*, and *trivarṣā*? These words do not denote age.

493–495. Regarding the statement that "in all cases, when suffixes (*liṅga*) are elided, there is the application of what was caused by them" in the context of the prescription of augments (*āgama*) and substitutes (*ādeśa*): if augments and substitutes were prescribed in all cases by way of association with the suffix, then that which was caused by them would apply even when the suffix is elided. For example: *pañcendrāṇyo devatā asya* ("the five Indrāṇīs are its deities") results in *pañcendraḥ*, *pañcāgniḥ*, and *daśāgniḥ*. Why is it said "in all cases"? Because [the rule] applies elsewhere as well.

It is not necessarily only here [in this specific case]. Where else? As in "purchased for five female fishermen" (*pañcabhir dhīvarībhiḥ krītaḥ*), resulting in *pañcadhīvā* or *daśadhīvā*. There is no purpose in mentioning the gender (*liṅga*). In every case, when rules concerning augments (*āgama*) and substitutes (*ādeśa*) are stated, the application of those [rules] occurs even when there is elision (*luk*). By this, the following is also established: "he buys with five" (*pañcamena gṛhṇāti*) results in *pañcakaḥ*. This is not so.

[to form] *ṣaṭkaḥ* in the sense of "he grasps with six. There is no purpose in including the mention of the "feminine section" (*strīprakaraṇa*). It is already established by the rule that "substitutions for [numerals] and so forth apply on the basis of the stem" (*āgamādeśānām aṅgataḥ vacanāt*).

By this, the following is also established: *ṣaṣṭhena gṛhṇāti* (he buys with six), *ṣaṭkaḥ*. Alternatively, there is the statement regarding the restoration of the original form (*prakṛtipratyāpatti*) when there is elision of gender (*liṅgaluki*). Or rather, the restoration of the original form should be stated only in the case of the elision of gender; there is no purpose in the mention of "gender" (*liṅga*).

Or rather, it is precisely the statement regarding the restoration of the base form (*prakṛtipratyāpatti*) even when there is elision (*luk*) [that is intended]. By this, the following is also established: *ṣaṭkena gṛhṇāti* → *ṣaṭkaḥ*. But what is superior here? It is precisely the statement regarding the restoration of the base form even when there is elision that is superior.
By this, the following is also established: *pañcabhiḥ paṭvībhiḥ krītaḥ* → *pañcapaṭuḥ*, *daśapaṭuḥ*. That...

If so, it must be stated; yet it need not be stated. For when those prescribed as being joined together (*sanniyogaśiṣṭa*) are present, upon the absence of either one, there is the absence of both. Just as, for example: "This task is to be performed by Devadatta and Yajñadatta. Upon the absence of Devadatta, Yajñadatta also does not perform it.

496. There is a prohibition regarding *asita* and *palita*. A prohibition regarding *asita* and *palita* must be stated: *asitā*, *palitā*. According to some, there is the suffix *kna* in the Veda: according to some, they desire the suffix *kna* in the Veda:

*asiknī asi oṣadhe* ("O herb, you are black"); *paliknīḥ* indeed are the young women. Regarding the rule for the application of the suffix *ṅīp* after a word denoting color, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the word *piśaṅga*: *piśaṅgī*.

(P_4,1.42) Regarding the rule *nīlāt oṣadhau*: it should be stated that [the suffix] applies after *nīla* when referring to a plant; for example, *nīlī oṣadhiḥ* ("a blue herb"). Regarding the rule *prāṇini ca*:

it should be stated that [the suffix] applies also when referring to a living being; for example, *nīlī gauḥ* ("a blue cow") and *nīlī vaḍavā* ("a blue mare"). Regarding the rule *vā sañjñāyām*: [it should be stated] "optionally when it is a name."
It should be stated: *nīlī* means "blue. (P.

4.1.44) It is said, "from words denoting qualities" (*guṇavacanāt*). What, then, is called a "quality" (*guṇa*)? That which enters into a substance (*sattva*), departs from it, is seen in various classes [of substances], is capable of being imposed, is not produced by action, and is non-substantial by nature—that is a quality.

Another says: it approaches one thing and abandons another; this is observed even in the case of different substances. A quality (*guṇa*) is traditionally held to be distinct from substance (*dravya*), as it is the designator of all genders. [The suffix] *ṅīp* should be prescribed after words denoting qualities, for the sake of making the first syllable acute (*ādyudātta*). [Therefore: *ṅīp* should be stated after words denoting qualities.

What is the purpose? It is for the sake of making [the word] have an acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*). Words with an acute accent on the first syllable serve as the motivation [for this rule]. For example, *vasvī*. Furthermore, there is the prohibition regarding words ending in *kharu* or having a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) as their penultimate element (P.
4.1.48). A prohibition must be stated for words such as *gopālikā* and others.

A cowherd woman is a *gopālikā* or a *paśupālikā*. What, then, is the example here? It is *praṣṭhī* and *pracarī*. But how does this word *praṣṭha*, which ends in the vowel *a*, denote a female? It is through the connection expressed by the rule "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*).
For just as she receives the bathing, anointing, and sprinkling performed by him, so too does she receive the application of the word *praṣṭha*.

[He] obtains [the desired form]. If it is thus, then regarding the designation based on connection with a male (*puṃyogāt ākhyāyām*), there must be a statement concerning the elision (*luk*) of the *taddhita* suffix. [Otherwise], the suffix [denoting] "belonging to him" (*tasyedam*) would apply. In that case, the forms *prāsthyaḥ imāḥ* ("these are the women of Prastha") and *prācaryaḥ imāḥ* ("these are the women of the Ācāryas") would not occur; yet they do occur. Therefore, the elision (*luk*) must be stated as optional (*vibhāṣā*). When there is elision...

In that case, when there is elision (*luk*), it is *praṣṭhī*; when there is no elision, it is *prāṣṭhī*. If this is so, there is no purpose for the elision. The formation of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is optional. When the secondary derivative is formed, it is *prāṣṭhī*; when the secondary derivative is not formed, it is *praṣṭhī*. Even so, elision must still be stated; for a word does not function for the sake of another meaning without the elision of the secondary derivative. If...
Furthermore, the word *praṣṭha* would have to apply to that very [cow]. But how could the word *praṣṭha* apply to her when she does not stand still?

For just as she receives the slaughter, imprisonment, and afflictions caused by someone even though she has committed no evil at all, so too does she receive the designation *praṣṭha*. Moreover, because it is stated to be a compound ending in a *subanta* (inflected nominal), its ending in the vowel *a* is untenable.

Furthermore, because it is stated that a compound consists of words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*), the state of ending in the vowel *a* is not tenable. A compound is formed of words ending in case-suffixes; in that case, by virtue of being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the feminine suffix *ṭāp* would arise first. Once *ṭāp* has arisen, the compound is formed, and the word *sthā* would be compounded. In that situation, the rule "after a word ending in *a*, when denoting a female through connection with a male" (*puṃyogād ākhyāyām*) would not apply to produce the long *ī*. However, this is established [as correct] because a female is expressed by means of a masculine word. Thus, this is established.

How so? Because a woman is designated by a masculine word. A woman is expressed by a masculine term. But was it not stated that "there is a rule for the elision of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) when a name is derived from connection with a man"? This is not a fault. The Teacher’s practice indicates that no such secondary suffix arises here, since he teaches the long vowel *ī* in the case of a name derived from connection with a man.

This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*). For there is another purpose for stating this rule: it would apply to those feminine suffixes that do not end in *ī*. But then why does [the author] employ the term "name" (*ākhyā*)? For a word ending in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is not a "name. Alternatively, let it be understood through the connection "this belongs to him. But was it not already stated that [the feminine form arises] from connection with a male (*puṃyogāt*)?

Regarding the statement "there is a rule for the elision of the *taddhita* suffix when it denotes a name," this is not a fault. It is not necessarily the case that the relationship [expressed by the suffix] is only "this belongs to that" (*tasyedaṃ*);
there is also this relationship: "this is that" (*so 'yam*). But how can the expression "this is that" apply to something that is not that? It occurs in four ways: through location (*tātsthya*),...

"By virtue of having that property (*tāddharmyāt*), by virtue of proximity to it (*tatsāmīpyāt*), and by virtue of association with it (*tatsāhacaryāt*). First, regarding "by virtue of being located there" (*tātsthyāt*): "The platforms laugh" (*mañcāḥ hasanti*); "The mountain burns" (*giriḥ dahyate*). Regarding "by virtue of having that property" (*tāddharmyāt*): One says, "Brahmadatta is going, wearing matted hair" (*jaṭinam yāntam brahmadattaḥ iti āha*). Since whatever functions are performed by Brahmadatta are also performed by the one with matted hair, for this reason the one with matted hair is called "Brahmadatta. Regarding "by virtue of proximity to it" (*tatsāmīpyāt*): [As in] "In the Ganges... (*gaṅgāyām*)...

The word *ghoṣaḥ* [is used] as in "the Garga family at the well," due to association with that [well]. [Examples of ellipsis include] "bring in the spears" (*kuntān praveśaya*) and "bring in the staffs" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*). Alternatively, let the word *praṣṭha-* itself [denote the horse]. But was it not said that because of the rule regarding compounds ending in a *subanta*, the form ending in short *a* (*praṣṭha-*) is untenable? This is not a fault, because there is a rule stating that prefixes (*gati*), verbal roots with objects (*kāraka*), and secondary words (*upapada*) form compounds with *kṛt*-derived suffixes.

The following *paribhāṣā* must be formulated: "There is a compound (*samāsa*) of words denoting direction (*gati*), agent (*kāraka*), or subordinate word (*upapada*) with [words ending in] primary suffixes (*kṛt*). What are the purposes of this *paribhāṣā*? The purpose is [illustrated by] the rule regarding the formation of feminine nouns from *kṛt*-suffixes when the action is of small extent (*alpākhyā*): *abhraviliptī*, *sūpaviliptī*. Here, the compound is formed between words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*). In that case, because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the feminine suffix *ṭāp* would apply first; however, once *ṭāp* has been produced, the compound is formed. Thus, the word *viliptā* [is established].

It would be compounded there. In that case, because it ends in *a* and denotes a small quantity (*alpākhyā*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* would not apply by the rule "after a word ending in *a*, [if it denotes] a small quantity. [But this is incorrect, for] the application of *ṅīṣ* is prescribed after words denoting a genus (*jāti*). The purpose of prescribing *ṅīṣ* after a genus is as in *vyāghrī* ("tigress") and *kacchapī* ("tortoise"). [Objection: The compound is formed from words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*). In that case, *ṭāp* applies first because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*).

Once *ṭāp* has been produced, the compound is formed; thus the word *ghrā* would be compounded. In that situation, [the rule] "after a genus-word that is not feminine (*astrīviṣaya*) and does not have *ya* as its penultimate letter (*ayopadha*)" [would apply].

The suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply after a word ending in the vowel *a*. Regarding the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* for the final letter of a compound (*samāsānta*): there is a purpose for this rule of *ṇ*-substitution for the final letter of a compound.

It will be stated that the mention of "the final letter of a compound" in the rule for the *ṇ*-substitution of the final letter of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is for the sake of prohibiting it in cases where the word is not the final member of a compound.

When that [mention] is made, in the case of *māṣavāpiṇī* ("one who sows beans") and *vrīhivāpiṇī* ("one who sows rice"), the compound is formed from words ending in case-suffixes (*sup*). In that situation, because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), [the *ṇ*-substitution would apply].

Because it ends in the letter *na*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Once *ṅīp* has been produced, the compound is formed; the word *vāpinī* would then be compounded. In that case, by the rule "of the final member of a compound" (*samāsāntasya*), the substitution of *ṇa* would not apply. Furthermore, regarding the rule "after a *kṛt*-derived stem, the suffixes [introduce] *vṛddhi* and accentuation in secondary derivation" (*taddhite vṛddhisvarau ca*): after a *kṛt*-derived stem, the introduction of *vṛddhi* and accentuation in secondary derivation serves as the purpose—as in *sāṅkuṭinam* and *vyāvakrośī*. Here, the production [of the suffix] from a constituent part would otherwise result. [This is governed by the rule: "A preverb (*gati*), a kāraka, or an upapada [is compounded] with *kṛt*-derived stems."

There is no fault in saying that the compound occurs simultaneously. Even if this paribhāṣā were present, the suffix would still result from the member [of the compound]. Why? Because of the rule: "When there is a mention of a suffix, there is the inclusion of that which begins with it. Furthermore, by the rule: "When there is a mention of a *kṛt* suffix, there is the inclusion of even that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*," the suffix will arise from the entire aggregate.

If, then, this technical rule (paribhāṣā) exists, there is no purpose for this [other] technical rule; it is established by this very one. It is not established. Why? Because it is not a nominal stem (aprātipadikatvāt). [Objection:
The designation "nominal stem" (prātipadika-sañjñā) will apply because it ends in a kṛt suffix. [Reply: But even now, when the designation "nominal stem" applies...

It might be possible to provide this as a general definition (*paribhāṣā*). [The author] says: "No. For in this case, even in a sentence such as *mūlakena upadaṃśam bhuṅkte* ("he eats with a radish as a side-dish"), the elision (*luk*) would undesirably apply. Furthermore, there would be a fault regarding the accent (*svara*). In the case of *prakārakaḥ* and *prakaraṇam*, according to the rule that "a *kṛt*-derived word following a prefix (*gati*), a kāraka, or a subordinate word (*upapada*) retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*)," this accent would not occur. [Objection: This is not a fault.
In these cases, there are two designations as *prātipadika*:

that of the constituent part and that of the whole. In that regard, the accent will be based on the *prātipadika* designation of the constituent part. If so, then here too—in the case of *sāṅkuṭinam* and *vyāvakrośī*—there are likewise two *prātipadika* designations.

[This applies] both to the member and to the aggregate. In that case, since the designation *prātipadika* belongs to the member, the production [of a suffix] would follow from the member as its basis. If production were to occur from the member, what fault would there be? The form *kaumbhakāreyaḥ* would not be established;
furthermore, the *vṛddhi* and accentuation would belong to the member. Therefore, this *paribhāṣā* indeed serves a purpose [only when applied] to both.
Now, it is indeed established. However, there is the contingency of the suffix *ṅīp* in the case of *avadātā*.

In the case of *avadātā*, the suffix *ṅīp* would apply [by the rule] "after a word denoting color (*varṇa*) that is anudātta and has *t* as its penultimate letter, *taḥ* becomes *naḥ*"—as in *avadātā brāhmaṇī*. But this [word *avadāta*] does not denote color; rather, it denotes purity (*viśuddha*). And it denotes purity because of the following statement: "He whose three are pure—learning, birth, and conduct..."

510–511. Regarding the greatness of snow and forest: it should be stated that [the suffix *ān* is applied] to express the greatness of snow and forest. A great mass of snow is *himānī*; a great forest is *araṇyānī*. Regarding barley when it is defective: it should be stated that [the suffix *ān* is applied] to *yava* when it denotes something defective. Barley that is defective is *yavānī*. Regarding script from the Yavanas: it should be stated that [the suffix *ān* is applied] to *yavana* when it denotes a script. The script of the Yavanas is *yavanānī*. [The suffix *ān* is applied] after *upādhyāya* and *mātula*...

Or rather, it should be stated: "or from *upādhyāya* and *mātula*. Thus: *upādhyāyī*, *upādhyāyānī*; *mātulī*, *mātulānī*. It should be stated: "after *mudgala*, in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), there is also the suffix *lit*. Thus: *rathīr abhūt mudgalānī*. And it should be stated: "after *ācārya*, there is also the substitution of *aṇ*. Thus: *ācāryānī*. [The same applies] after *ārya* and *kṣatriya*.
Or rather, it should be stated as "from *ārya* and *kṣatriya*" (*āryakṣatriyābhyām vā*). [Thus,] *āryā* and *āryāṇī*; *kṣatriyā* and *kṣatriyāṇī*.

(Pāṇini 4.1.50) Why is it said "preceded by an instrument" (*karaṇapūrvāt*)? [Examples: *gavāt krītā* ("purchased with a cow"), *aśvena krītā* ("purchased with a horse"). If it were stated [only] "preceded by an instrument,"...
Does this [rule] not apply here as well? For this word *krīta* also has an instrument (*karaṇa*) preceding it. It will not apply because it is separated by a case-ending (*vibhakti*).

If, then, the case-ending also acts as an intervention, the form *manasākrītī* would not be established. In that case, it should not be understood thus: "that which has an instrument preceding this word *krīta*. Rather, it is this: [the compound is formed with the word *krīta*].

[The objection: "It is *karaṇapūrva*; therefore, from that word *krīta* which has *karaṇa* as its prior member, [the suffix applies] provided it is not a subordinate element (*anupasarjana*).
