512–513. Prohibition regarding that which has an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*). It should be stated that there is a prohibition for that which is *jāta* (born/arisen) when it has an acute accent on the final syllable. For example: *dantajātā*, *stanajātā*. Regarding *pāṇigṛhītī* and others, there is a specific rule. It should be stated: "In the case of *pāṇigṛhītī* and others, there is a specific [application]. *Pāṇigṛhītī* refers to a wife. She is called *pāṇigṛhītā* by whomsoever her hand is taken in any manner whatsoever. This occurs diversely (*bahulam*).

Regarding the suffix *taṇ*: it should be stated that *taṇ* occurs diversely (*bahulam*). What is this "*taṇ*" [referring to]? It is the inclusion of both technical names (*sañjñā*) and Vedic forms (*chandas*). What is the purpose? For the sake of forms such as *prabaddhavilūnā*. [Examples: *prabaddhavilūnī*, *prabaddhavilūnā*. It should be stated: "after a word that is oxytone (*antodātta*), provided it is not preceded by *bahu*, *nañ*, *su*, or a word denoting time or happiness (*kāla-sukha-ādi*)."

*bahu* [is used] as *bahukṛtā*; *nañ* [is used] as *akṛtā*; *su* [is used] as *sukṛtā*. *Kāla*: *māsajātā*, *saṃvatsarajātā*. *Sukhādi*: *sukhajātā*, *duḥkhajātā*. Regarding the rule *jātipūrvād vā*: alternatively, it should be stated that [the suffix applies] after a word preceded by *jāti*. (P_4,1.54.1) KA_II,222.8-18 Ro_III,

513–513. It is stated: "And [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] after a word denoting one's own limb (*svāṅga*) that is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). What is called "one's own limb" (*svāṅga*)? A limb belonging to a living being (*prāṇistha*), which is not liquid (*adrava*), possesses form (*mūrtimat*), and is not produced by modification (*avikāraja*)—even if it is not currently located on that [particular] body, provided it was seen there before; and if it is joined with that [body] in such a way. [Furthermore,] even for non-living beings, there are their own limbs. Why is it specified "not liquid" (*adrava*)? [Consider the example: *bahulohitā* ("having much blood"). This is not a valid case, because of the rule: "Not after a word with many vowels (*bahvac*)."

There will be a prohibition [of this rule]. In that case, what about *bahukaphā*? Why is it specified as "possessing form" (*mūrtimat*)? [Examples would be] *bahubuddhiḥ*, *bahumanāḥ*. This is not necessary, because the word "from that" (*ataḥ*) continues to apply from the previous rule. In that case, what about *bahujñānā*? Why is it specified as "residing in a living being" (*prāṇistham*)? [An example would be] *ślakṣṇamukhā śālā* (a hall with a smooth entrance). Why is it specified as "not produced by modification" (*avikārajam*)? [Examples would be] *bahugaḍuḥ*, *bahupaṭikā*.

This is not so. Here, first of all, in the case of *bahugaḍuḥ*, the word *ataḥ* (from that) continues to apply. In the case of *bahupaṭikā*, there will be a prohibition by the rule *na bahvacaḥ*. Then what about *bahuśophā*? [The definition] "that which is not situated in it, but is seen in it" applies. That which is not situated in a living being, yet is seen in a living being, receives the technical designation *svāṅga* (body-part). For example, *dīrghakeśī rathyā* ("a street with long hair"). Regarding that...

If it is so endowed [with the suffix], then even for inanimate objects, there occurs the designation "one's own limb" (*svāṅga*). For example: *dīrghanāsikī arcā* ("an image with a long nose"), *tuṅganāsikī arcā* ("an image with a prominent nose").

Now, what is the purpose of the mention of the term *upasarjana* ("secondary member")? It is so that [the designation does not apply] here: *śikhā* ("crest"). The mention of *upasarjana* [is necessary].

The mention of *upasarjana* is redundant because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning *bahuvrīhi*. What is the reason? Because of the governing rule concerning *bahuvrīhi*; the word "of the *bahuvrīhi*" (*bahuvrīheḥ*) is understood [from the previous sūtra]. Where was it introduced? In [Pāṇini 6.2.172]: "And [the final syllable] of a *bahuvrīhi* that is oxytone. In that case, the mention of *upasarjana* must be made for the sake of words with many syllables (*bahvac*). For he will state a prohibition: "not [if it has] many syllables" (*na bahvacaḥ*). That [prohibition] refers to the mention of "many syllables" (*bahvac*).

This is so that the qualifier may be understood as qualifying the *upasarjana* (the subordinate member), [namely]: "not after an *upasarjana* that has many vowels. Now, if the mention of *upasarjana* were not made, of what would the mention of "many vowels" (*bahvac*) be the qualifier? It follows from the previous context that "of a *bahuvrīhi*";
thus, it would be understood as a qualifier of the *bahuvrīhi*. And there now exists a certain *bahuvrīhi* that does not have many vowels, for the sake of which [this rule is intended].

It should be a rule. He says: "it exists," namely *svaḍā* and *svaḍī*. If it is argued that this is for the sake of including words with many syllables (*bahvac*), [we reply] that it is already established by the mention of *svāṅga* (body parts). The term *svāṅga* is employed; we shall qualify that by the mention of *bahvac*: "not [after a word] consisting of many syllables that is a *svāṅga*. If that is so, then [the rule applies] after a word that is oxytone (*antodāttāt*).

Thus it proceeds. This commencement is for the purpose of ensuring the final acute accent (*antodātta*). If it is argued that this is already established because [the word] is formed with *saha* and so forth, [we reply:

since the Teacher teaches the prohibition in the rule "after words preceded by *sa*, *nañ*, or *vidyamāna*," he thereby indicates that [the suffix] also occurs after words that have the final acute accent. However, it is for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of the suffix] to a collection of body parts (*svāṅga-samudāya*). It is indeed for the purpose of prohibiting [the suffix] from a collection of body parts.

In that case, the mention of the term *upasarjana* (secondary member) must be made so that [the rule] applies when [the word] is a part of the body (*svāṅga*), but not when it is a collection of parts of the body. For example, in the case of *kalyāṇapāṇipādā*. Now, even if the mention of *upasarjana* is made, why does [the rule] not apply here?

For this is indeed a part of the body that is a secondary member; however, a collection of parts of the body is not grasped by the mention of "part of the body" (*svāṅga*) in the same way as [a single part is].

A collection of districts (*janapadasamudāya*) is not included by the term "district" (*janapada*). Therefore, in the case of *kāśikosalīyāḥ*, the suffix *vuñ*—prescribed by the rule *janapadatadavadhyoḥ*—does not apply. This objection also has no force. The phrase "not preceded by a word denoting a body part" (*asvāṅgapūrvapadāt*) continues to apply. By that, we shall qualify "body part": [the rule applies] to a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in a body part that follows a non-body-part as its prior member.

Thus [it is said]. And here, that which follows after a non-body-part (*asvāṅga*) prior member is not the end of a *bahuvrīhi* compound; and that which is the end of a *bahuvrīhi* compound does not follow after a non-body-part prior member, even though it is a body part (*svāṅga*). But surely, in the preceding rule (*yoga*), that was a qualifier of the *bahuvrīhi*. No, he says: it is a qualifier of the prior member. "Non-body-part" (*asvāṅga*) means a prior member that is not a body part; thus, "prior member" (*pūrvapada*) refers to a prior member that is a non-body part.

The term *pūrvapada* [in the rule] refers to a *pūrvapada* that is not a body part (*asvāṅga-pūrvapada*). [The rule states: "from a [bahuvrīhi] having a *pūrvapada* that is not a body part. If this is so, then in the preceding rule, the *bahuvrīhi* remains unspecified, while the *bahuvrīhi* is here specified. How? The word *ktāt* (after a suffix ending in *kta*) is understood to carry over. By means of it, we shall specify the *bahuvrīhi*: "from a *bahuvrīhi* ending in a suffix *kta* that follows a *pūrvapada* which is not a body part."

This, then, is the purpose: the term "of the *bahuvrīhi*" is understood [from the previous rule], so that [the suffix] may apply even after a mere subordinate member (*upasarjana*). For example: *niṣkeśī yūkā* ("a louse without hair") and *atikeśī mālā* ("a garland with excessive hair").

517. Regarding the optional application (*vibhāṣā*) for words such as *nāsikā* (nose), it should be stated that it applies after the word *puccha* (tail) as well: "The optional application [of the feminine suffix] for words such as *nāsikā* should be stated to apply after *puccha* as well.

Examples: *kalyāṇapucchī* or *kalyāṇapucchā*. Regarding the rule for *kabara*, *maṇi*, *viṣa*, and *śara*, it should be stated that it is obligatory (*nityam*): "The [obligatory application of the feminine suffix] after *kabara*, *maṇi*, *viṣa*, and *śara* should be stated to be obligatory. Examples: *kabarapucchī*, *maṇipucchī*, *viṣapucchī*, *śarapucchī*. [The rule applies] after the word *pakṣa* (wing) when preceded by a standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

And it should be stated that [the suffix] is applied from the side (*pakṣa*), from the wing (*pakṣa*), and from the tail (*puccha*). For example: *ulūkapakṣī śālā* ("an owl-winged hall") and *ulūkapakṣī senā* ("an owl-winged army").

Regarding the optional application (*vibhāṣā*) [of the suffix] after words beginning with *nāsikā*, there is a prohibition when preceded by *sa-* or *nañ*, by way of a counter-exception (*vipratiṣedha*).

There is a prohibition by way of conflict (vipratiṣedha) against the optional application [of the feminine suffix] after words beginning with *nāsikā* when preceded by *sa-* (*saha-*) or *nañ*, or by the word *vidyamāna*. The scope for the optional rule after words beginning with *nāsikā* is, for example, *kalyāṇanāsikī* or *kalyāṇanāsikā*. The scope for the prohibition characterized by being preceded by *sa-*, *nañ*, or *vidyamāna* is, for example, *samukhā*, *amukhā*, or *vidyamānamukhā*. In the present case, both rules would apply.

Regarding the examples *sanāsikaḥ*, *anāsikaḥ*, and *vidyamānanāsikaḥ*: the prohibition [of the suffix *ka*] after words preceded by the negative particle (*nañ*), the word *saha*, or the word *vidyamāna* occurs by way of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). This conflict is not logical. This is a rule (*vidhi*) and that is a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*);
and a conflict between a rule and a prohibition is illogical. Furthermore, this is also a rule; it is not like a prohibition applied to soft cotton.

It is now commenced. Just as that [rule] subverts the prohibition characterized by having many vowels (*bahvac*) and characterized by having a prefix ending in a consonant (*saṃyogopadha*), so too would it subvert the prohibition characterized by being preceded by *saha*, *nañ*, or *vidyamāna*. What, then, is the solution? In this case, for instance, in the word *nāsikodara*, both the prohibition characterized by having many vowels and the prohibition characterized by being preceded by *saha*, *nañ*, or *vidyamāna* would apply. [The former applies] first...

Since exceptions (apavāda) set aside the rules immediately preceding them, this option (*vibhāṣā*) will set aside the prohibition characterized by the presence of a multiple consonant cluster (*bahvac*). However, it will not set aside the rule characterized by the presence of the prefix *sa-* or the words *nañ* and *vidyamāna*. In the case of *oṣṭha*, *jaṅghā*, *danta*, *karṇa*, and *śṛṅga*, both the prohibition characterized by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) and the rule characterized by the presence of *sa-*, *nañ*, or *vidyamāna* would apply simultaneously in the middle.

Since exceptions (*apavāda*) set aside preceding rules (*vidhi*), this optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) will set aside the prohibition characterized by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*); however, it will not set aside the prohibition characterized by being preceded by *saha*, *nañ*, or *vidyamāna*. 518–519. Regarding the *anudātta* (low-pitched) nature of the *ṅīṣ* suffix after a compound whose first member is a direction (*dik*). It should be stated that the *ṅīṣ* suffix following a compound whose first member is a direction is *anudātta*. For example: *prāṅmukhī*, *pratyaṅmukhī*. For if the rule for *ṅīp* were applied [instead], there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *ṅīp* occurring even in cases where *ṅīṣ* is otherwise required. Indeed, if the rule for *ṅīp* were established, *ṅīp* would wrongly apply even in other instances where *ṅīṣ* is intended, such as in *prāggulphā* and *pratyaglalāṭā*. But surely [one might object]?

These specific rules would continue to apply: "not after a word with many syllables that has a non-conjunct as its penultimate. Even if these specific rules were to continue—namely, "not after a word with many syllables that has a non-conjunct as its penultimate"—nevertheless, when the suffix *ṅīp* is excluded by the rule for words preceded by a cardinal direction (*dik-pūrvapada*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* would still result.

This is not a fault; for it has been stated: "Where there is an option between a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*), once the exception has applied, the general rule does not apply."
"It does not occur. Or rather, the *ṅīp* will be made as a substitute for the *ṅīṣ*. In that case, then, the mention of *ṅīṣ* must be made.
It need not be made; the previously mentioned [term] is understood here. Where was it previously mentioned? In the rule "the suffix *ṅīṣ* after other [words].

But that was specified in the nominative case (*prathamā-nirdiṣṭa*), whereas here the sense requires something specified in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdiṣṭa*). The word "from a compound whose first member is a direction" (*dik-pūrvapadāt*) is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*), which [corresponds to] the nominative *ṅīṣ*.

519–521. It is said: "On account of the genus (*jāti*). What, then, is this so-called genus? Genus is that which is grasped through form; it does not possess all genders, nor is it grasped by being denoted [by a single word] only once. It includes both lineage (*gotra*) and Vedic schools (*caraṇa*). Another says:
That genus is characterized by the simultaneous appearance and disappearance of an entity along with its qualities, and it possesses multiple meanings while not having all genders.

The poets know [the distinction between] *gotra* and *caraṇa*. But what is the difference between these two characteristics of *jāti*? According to the former definition of *jāti*, it should be "one whose wife is a maiden" (*kumārībhārya*); according to the latter, it should be "one who has married a maiden" (*kumārabhārya*).

(P_4,1.63.2) KA_II,225.22–26 Ro_III, 522 Now, regarding the phrase "provided it does not refer to a feminine," how is this to be understood? Does it mean "that which, within the same general form (*ākṛti*), does not refer to a feminine"?
Or rather, "that which, in some instances, does not refer to a feminine"? And what follows from this? If it is understood [as] "within the same..."

If [the rule] "that which does not have the feminine as its scope" is understood as referring to *ākṛti* (form/class), then forms such as *droṇī*, *kuṭī*, and *pātrī* would not be established. Alternatively, if it is understood as "in some cases that which does not have the feminine as its scope," then [the suffix] would also apply here to *mālā* and *balākā*. Let it be that "in some cases that which does not have the feminine as its scope. But how [is it then that they are feminine]? They will be included in the list beginning with *ajā* (*ajādi*).

(P_4,1.63.3) Why is it stated "provided it does not have *ya* as an upadhā"? [Counter-example: *ibhyā*, *kṣatriyā*. This statement "provided it does not have *ya* as an upadhā" is too limited. It should also be stated "provided it does not have *ka* as an upadhā," so that [the rule] may apply here as well: *caṭakā*, *mūṣikā*. If it is stated "provided it does not have *ka* as an upadhā," then *kākī*, *kokī*, *śukī* would not be established. Well then, let it be exactly "provided it does not have *ya* as an upadhā. But how [is the rule applied] in the case of *caṭakā* and *mūṣikā*?

The word *puṣpa* should be included in the list beginning with *aja*. (P. 4.1.64) There is a prohibition [of the suffix *cha*] after the words *sada*, *kāṇḍa*, *prānta*, *śata*, and *eka*, when followed by *puṣpa*. [Namely, the suffix *cha* is not applied after *sada*, *kāṇḍa*, *prānta*, *śata*, and *eka* when *puṣpa* follows. After *sada*, *kāṇḍa*, *prānta*, *śata*, and *eka*...

A prohibition must be stated regarding the word *puṣpa* (flower): *satpuṣpā*, *prākpuṣpā*, *kāṇḍapuṣpā*, *prāntapuṣpā*, *śatapuṣpā*, *akapuṣpā*. A prohibition must be stated regarding the word *phala* (fruit) after the words *sam*, *bhastrā*, *ajina*, *śaṇa*, and *piṇḍa*: [after] *sam*, *bhastrā*, *ajina*, *śaṇa*, and *piṇḍa*, a prohibition regarding *phala* must be stated. *sam*: *samphalā*. *bhastrā*: *bhastrāphalā*. *bhastrā*.

*Ajina*, *ajinaphalā*; *piṇḍa*, *piṇḍaphalā*; *piṇḍa*; *śaṇa*, *śaṇaphalā*; *śaṇa*. It should be stated that [the suffix] also applies after *śveta*: *śvetaphalā*. Also after *tri*: a prohibition must be stated for *tri*: *triphalā*. After *mūla* when preceded by the negative particle *nañ*: [the suffix applies].

While the term *jāteḥ* ("from a genus") is understood [from the previous rule], for what purpose is *jāti-* mentioned again? [The answer is: The term *ayopadhāt* ("from that which has *ya* as its penultimate letter") is also understood; [the repetition is so that the suffix applies] even after a word with *ya* as its penultimate letter, such as *audameyī*. There is an addition [to the rule] regarding *iñ* after a human genus beginning with *it-*: "after a human genus beginning with *it-*."
The addition of *iñaḥ* must be stated [as an exception]. Examples: *sautaṅgamī*, *maunicitī*.
Why is the letter *ṅ* used? For the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇārtha*). Where is there a need for the purpose of specification? Not in the case of *ūṅ* or verbal roots (*dhātu*).

Thus [it is said]. If it were stated as "na ūdhātvoḥ," then it would also undesirably apply here in the case of *yavāgvā* and *yavāgvai*. Now, for what purpose is the long vowel pronounced? Why not simply state "na ūṅ utaḥ"? What is the formal derivation (*rūpasiddhi*)?
[It is] *brahmabandhūḥ*.

Regarding the form *brahmabandhūḥ*: it is established by the rule for lengthening a vowel with a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇadīrghatva*). It is not [correctly] established. For, by the rule "of a feminine stem ending in *go* or a word denoting a female (*strī*), when it is a secondary member (*upasarjana*)" (*gostriyor upasarjanasya*), shortening would undesirably apply. Furthermore, in the case of *brahmabandhūchatram* (from *brahmabandhū-chatram*) and *brahmabandhūcchatram* (from *brahmabandhū-cchatram*), because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) according to the rule "the substitution of *ṣ* and *t* are non-existent" (*ṣatvatukoḥ asiddhaḥ*), the obligatory *tuk* augment would undesirably apply. And here, in the case of *brahmabandhūḥ*,...

In the case of *brahmabandhūḥ* and *dhīvabandhūḥ*, since they end in the suffix *kap*, the suffix *kap* would [otherwise] be attached. This is not a fault. As for what was said—that in *brahmabandhūḥ* and *dhīvabandhūḥ*, the shortening [of the final vowel] would apply by the rule *go-striyor upasarjanasya*—[the answer is: when there is a dependence on both sides, the [operations of] "end" and "beginning" do not apply. Furthermore, as for what was said regarding *brahmabandhūchatram* and *brahmabandhūcchatram* [in relation to] the rules concerning the substitution of *ṣ* and *tuk*: [this is also not a fault].

[Objection: Because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the obligatory *tuk* augment would result [inappropriately]. It depends on something. Of three, two are indeed "risen" (*udgata*). It occurs that one which is "risen" is so only in relation to one that is "not risen.

Of three, two are indeed "risen"; of three, two indeed become "risen. [The suffix] *ṣyaṅ* must be applied starting from four; it is not established for *vārāhī*. *Ṣyaṅ* must be stated for those beginning with four; it is not established for *vārāhī*.

It does not apply in the case of *vārāhyā*. What is the reason? Because there is an absence of four or more [syllables]. Its accent is different; therefore, by that superlative word (*ātiśāyika*), the rule for the suffix *ām* is not observed. Indeed, its accent is different from that superlative word; thus, the rule for *ām* is not observed. And the rule for *ām* is not observed anywhere at all.
This is a different word [from *tama*], seen to function internally within the three [suffixes]. If that is so,
then this *tama* has a meaning identical to the superlative suffix (*ātiśāyika*) and occurs after words beginning with *tri*.

530–538. Furthermore, is this [the suffix] *ṣyaṅ* a substitute for *aṇ* and *iñ*, or is it something that follows after *aṇ* and *iñ*? And what is the distinction here? If *ṣyaṅ* were not a substitute, there would be a need to state the elision of *y*. If *ṣyaṅ* were not a substitute, the elision of *y* must be stated [as a special rule]. For example: "The students of Audameghī" (*audameghyāyāś chātrāḥ*) become "Audameghas" (*audameghāḥ*). Furthermore, there would be a double application of the *aṇ* rule. That is, the *aṇ* suffix would have to be applied twice. For example: "The students of Audameghī" (*audameghyāyāś chātrāḥ*) become "Audameghas" (*audameghāḥ*).

In the case of *audameghyānāṃ saṅghaḥ* ("the assembly of the Audameghas"), the suffix *aṇ*—which would apply by the rule *iñaḥ*—is not obtained. Let it then be a substitute (*ādeśa*). [Objection: If it is a substitute, the elision of the *n* must be stated, as in *auḍulomyā* and *śāralomyā*. [Furthermore,] by the rule *ye ca abhāvakarmaṇoḥ*, the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) would undesirably apply. [Response: Not so, because the *ṣyaṅ* is the cause for the elision.

Or rather, this fault does not arise. What is the reason? Because *ṣyaṅ* is the cause for the elision [of the penultimate vowel]. *Ṣyaṅ* is the cause for the elision; *ṣyaṅ* does not apply when the elision has not yet occurred. What is the reason? It is stated that [the rule applies] "when the two syllables preceding the penultimate are heavy" (*gurūpottamayoḥ*), and when the elision has not occurred, the penultimate syllable is not heavy. Alternatively, let it be the subsequent [form]. But was it not said that there must be a statement regarding the elision of *y* when *ṣyaṅ* is substituted for [the suffix] *an*?

Regarding the statement that "the rule for *aṇ* would apply twice": this is not a fault. As for what was said concerning the mention of the elision of *y*, there is no fault here. Why? Because of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) when a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *yaj* follows. When a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *yaj* follows, *puṃvadbhāva* will occur, according to the rule: "In place of *bha*, when a *taddhita* suffix other than one beginning with *aṭ* follows, the masculine form is used. If so, then this is the fault: "the rule for *aṇ* applies twice. No.

This is the fault. And [the rule] regarding the prescription of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*) is established; that [rule] is established in the prescription of suffixes. Both of these have been stated: "it is a substitute" (*ādeśa*) and "it is subsequent" (*para*). What is logical here? That it is a substitute (*ādeśa*) is logical. Why is this so? For it is precisely by adopting this view that the Teacher has recited the *sūtra* and made the reference using the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).

Therefore, this position is faultless. Now, it may be argued that even if the other [position] were accepted, those faults would have been avoided: the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) was avoided by means of the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*), and that masculine treatment occurs when the suffix is not *aṅ*. In that case, however, *Audameghyaḥ* would not be established.
You must, therefore, apply two indicatory marks (*anubandha*). Those who provide the substitute must apply them: one is for the purpose of general inclusion.

Another [purpose] is for the sake of not obstructing the inclusion of the general term (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*). Where is there a need for the inclusion of the general term? [In the rule] *yaṅaś ca cāp*. Now, where is there a need for the inclusion of the general term for the sake of not obstructing it? Precisely here. What is the purpose? For the sake of *cāp*, so that *cāp* may occur. How is *cāp* [obtained] in your view? It is by the prescription of *ṭāp* in my view. In my view, it is established by *ṭāp*. But is it not true that...?

[Objection: For me as well, the suffix *ṭāp* is established [by P. 4.1.4]. [Reply: It is not established. Because of the rules "after *aṇ*" (P. 4.1.78) and "after *iñ*" (P. 4.1.95), the long vowel *ī* would be obtained. [Objection: This fault does not arise. It is not understood thus: "after that which ends in *aṇ*, after that which ends in *a*; after that which ends in *iñ*, after that which ends in *i*. How then? It is understood: "the *a* which belongs to *aṇ*, and the *i* which belongs to *iñ*. [Objection: In that case, for the sake of the accent (*svara*), you must state the suffix *cāp*. [This is because of the rule] "before a suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*..."

[The objection is: "In this way, let there not be an acute accent on the first syllable (by the rule *ādyudāttaḥ*); rather, let there be an acute accent on the final syllable (by the rule *citaḥ anta udāttaḥ*). [The reply is: "Even for you, then, since femininity has already been expressed by the suffix *ṣyaṅ*, the suffix *ṭāp* would not apply. [The opponent replies: "For these [suffixes] do occur even when [the meaning] has already been expressed; for even when femininity has been expressed, these suffixes such as *ṭāp* and so on do occur. [The proponent says: "It has been stated that the suffixes *ṭāp* and so on are *svārthika* (added in their own sense)."

[Objection: "In that case, for me as well, the substitute (ādeśa) along with its suffixal connection (sānubandhaka) does not undergo the operation of *it*. Therefore, the marker *ñ* will not occur. [Reply: There is a fault if it is treated as non-substituted (*asthānivattva*). For you, the *vṛddhi* [vowel lengthening] is not established here. There is a fault if it is treated as non-substituted; the *vṛddhi* does not apply in the cases of *auḍulomī* and *śāralomī*. And one cannot now adopt the "half-old-woman" approach (*ardhajaratīya*) regarding the *vṛddhi*.
[Otherwise] it would follow that my [vowel] would not have its own accent. For example, it is as if one desires half of an old woman and not the other half.
In this case, you too would have to provide a qualifier for the sake of distinction; you too would have to provide an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) here for the sake of distinction.
Where is the need for the purpose of a qualifier? [In the rule] "there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of *ṣyaṅ*. [If there were no *anubandha*,] there would be no application [of the rule].

In this case, the distinction (*viśeṣa*) is accompanied by its consequence (*sānubandha*), whereas for me, the distinction itself is accompanied by its consequence. Why would it not apply to *pāśyā* in the case of *pāśyāputraḥ*? For me, one [element] would be the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). One [element] serves my purpose as a qualifier. By you, however, two must be made. Now, even in the case of a single [element]...

If it exists, what will be done? And what follows from this? There would be a split in the sūtra. If something other than these two is made, a split in the sūtra occurs. If it is marked with *ṣit*, the characteristic of being *ṣit* would entail the application of the vowel *ī*. If it is marked with *ṅit*, there is a fault in the case of the *cekrīyita* (intensive) formation. If it is marked with *ṅit*, there is a fault in the *cekrīyita* formation.

Regarding the forms *lolūyāputraḥ* and *lolūyāpatiḥ*: because of the intervention, there is no fault. Since it is separated by the vowel *a*, no defect arises. That which is immediate is not a verbal root (*dhātu*). The term "of a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) continues to apply; and that which is immediate here is not a verbal root. That which is a verbal root is not immediate. And that which is a verbal root is indeed immediate. No.
If there were equality on both sides, it would follow that [the rule] applies in both cases.

If there is no equality on both sides, it does not apply in both cases. Furthermore, if the verbal root (*dhātu*) were to be qualified by the *yaṅ* suffix—whether the verbal root here is qualified by the *yaṅ*, or whether the *yaṅ* is qualified by the verbal root—it would be the same in either case. That is, if the verbal root is indeed qualified by the *yaṅ*.

If it is further specified by means of a verbal root (*dhātu*), this results in the same situation as *yaṅ*. If both are primary, there is no fault here; if both are primary, there is no fault in this case. However, in that case, the Lord of Speech (*vākpati*) would undergo vocalization (*prasāraṇa*). Such being the case, in the word *vākputra*, vocalization would apply [to the *u*]. This is because of the context of the verbal root.

The certainty here is that "there is no occurrence. This certainty is established on the grounds that there is no occurrence of the section concerning verbal roots (*dhātu*) here. The mention of "verbal root" (*dhātu*) must necessarily be made for the sake of the substitution of *āt*. Let it not apply here: *gobhyām*, *gobhiḥ*, *naubhyām*, *naubhiḥ*. If it is to be made for the sake of the substitution of *āt*, it will be done right there, in the context of the original instruction (*upadeśe*).

If it is intended that the substitution of *āt* applies to that which is "moving" (*ejat*), this refers to the primary enumeration (*uddeśa*) of conventional words (*rūḍhiśabda*). Therefore, it will not apply to the word *go*.
If that is so, then [the rule] says "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*); however, for nominal stems (*prātipadika*), there is an enumeration (*uddeśa*) but no original instruction (*upadeśa*).

538–540. For what purpose is this stated? It is for the sake of [denoting] those who do not belong to the lineage (*agotra*) from that which is a part of the lineage (*gotrāvayava*). It is said: "from that which is a part of the lineage. This undertaking is for the sake of those who do not belong to the lineage. If it is argued that "it is for the sake of those who do not belong to the lineage from that which is a part of the lineage," then that is undesirable. If it is argued that "it is for the sake of those who do not belong to the lineage from that which is a part of the lineage," then that undesirable consequence follows; for in this case as well, it would apply to [the words] *āhicchatrī* and *kānyakubjī*.

If that is so, then [the suffix] is applied from the *gotra* itself, which is a part of the *gotra*. If it is argued that it is "from the *gotra*," then the statement is redundant; if it is argued that it is "from the *gotra*," then the statement is purposeless, for it is already established by the preceding rule (*pūrveṇa*) with respect to the *gotra*. In that case, this is the purpose: it is stated that [the suffix applies] when the penultimate syllable is heavy (*gurūpottama*). This undertaking is for the sake of cases where the penultimate syllable is not heavy (*agurūpottama*). If it is argued that it is for the sake of cases where the penultimate syllable is not heavy, then [the rule would apply] to all [names].

Because they are constituent parts (*avayava*), there would be the undesirable consequence that [the suffix] applies to all. If it is argued that this is for the sake of excluding those whose penultimate syllable is not heavy (*agurūpottama*), [we reply that] since all are constituent parts, it would apply everywhere—for example, "there were eighty-eight thousand sages who were perpetual celibates (*ūrdhvaretas*). Among them, procreation was undertaken by the sages with Agastya as the eighth. The offspring of those venerable ones constitute the *gotras*; others are merely subordinate parts (*avayava*) of the *gotras*.
In that case, the [suffix] *ut* would apply; and that is undesirable. Therefore, there is no purpose for this rule. How so?
Because it is desired for those words whose penultimate syllable is not heavy (*agurūpottama*). But it is established by means of an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for *rauḍhi* and others.
This is established. How? By an addition for *rauḍhi* and others. An addition must be made for *rauḍhi* and others.

Who, then, are the Rauḍhyas and others? They are the same as the Krauḍyas and others. The followers of Bhāradvāja recite: "But it is established that [the suffix] is applied after names of families (kulākhyā) which are recognized as lineages (gotra) in common usage. This is established. How so? Because in common usage, those called "family names" (kulākhyā) are said to be subdivisions of lineages (gotrāvayava). Alternatively, what can be considered a subdivision of a lineage? One who is separated from the lineage. And who is that?
"Separated from the *gotra*," "that which is immediate," and "Daivadatti" and "Yājñadatti" [are examples].
4.1.82) Why is the word *samartha* ("having capacity") stated? So that the suffix may arise from what has capacity (*samartha*).

[The compound] *upagoḥ apatyam* ("the offspring of Upagu")—lest [this rule apply] when there is a lack of semantic connection (*asamartha*), as in: "The blanket is Upagu’s offspring, [belonging] to Devadatta. The statement regarding semantic connection (*samartha*) is redundant. For there is no expression of meaning by means of what is semantically unconnected. The statement regarding semantic connection is redundant. Why? Because there is no expression of meaning by means of what is semantically unconnected.

For indeed, there can be no expression of meaning by an affix produced from that which lacks [the status of] being the first member. Because it does not express [the meaning], its production from that [base] will not occur. Now, what is the purpose of the mention of "the first" (*prathama*)? The mention of "the first" is for the sake of qualifying the base (*prakṛti*).
It is so that the production of the affix may occur after that which is the first, and not after that which is not the first—as in the case of *upagoḥ apatyam* ("the offspring of Upagu").

From the word *apatya*, the nominative case is redundant. For there is no denotation of meaning by that which is not the nominative. The nominative case is redundant. Why? Because there is no denotation of meaning by that which is not the nominative. Indeed, there would be no denotation of meaning by an affix produced from something other than the nominative. Since there is no such denotation, its production [as a nominative] will not occur. Now, if...

What is the purpose of the word *vā* (‘or’)? So that there may also be a sentence such as: "the offspring of Upagu. Regarding the mention of *vā*, what was said? First, it was said there: "The mention of *vā* is useless because the suffix *san* is compulsory.
Here too, the mention of *vā* is useless. For what reason? Because in that case the suffix is compulsory; here [it would be] likewise.

There are two positions: the position of application (*vṛttipakṣa*) and the position of non-application (*avṛttipakṣa*). By its very nature, this consists of both the sentence (*vākya*) and the compound (*vṛtti*). In that regard, when an obligatory suffix would apply to a natural case of application, what else could possibly be connected by means of the word "optionally" (*vā*), other than a technical name (*saṃjñā*)? And yet, the existence or non-existence of a technical name is not intended here.

Therefore, there is no purpose for the mention of the word "artha" (meaning). Now, this mention of "samartha" (semantically connected) need not be made at all. Yet it must be made. What is the purpose? So that the suffix may arise from what is semantically connected, and not from what is not semantically connected. But what, then, is "samartha"? That which is capable of expressing a meaning. And what is that? A word (*pada*) consisting of a specific sequence of phonemes (*varṇa*).

[The examples] *sautthitiḥ* and *vaikṣamāṇiḥ*. Now, that statement (*vāvacana*) should not be made at all; yet it must be made. What is the purpose? Words are eternal (*nitya*). By means of this [statement], the correctness (*sādhutva*) of a sentence is explained with respect to eternal words. yuktaḥ prayujyante kecin neti | yadi tarhi nityāḥ śabdāḥ kathaṃ kecid vacanaviśeṣayuktāḥ kecin neti | ucyate— yathā nityo ’py ātmā kecid vacanaviśeṣair yukto bhavati kecin neti | evam ihāpi nityāḥ bhavati kecin neti | evam ihāpi nityāḥ śabdāḥ santo ’pi kecit puruṣaviśeṣair yuktaḥ prayujyante kecin neti | yadi tarhi nityāḥ śabdāḥ kathaṃ kecid arthaviśeṣayuktāḥ kecin neti | ucyate— yathā nityo ’py ātmā kecid arthaviśeṣair yukto bhavati kecin neti |
544–545. This formulation is incorrect. For no word *dīvya* is recited there; rather, it is the word *dīvyati*. How, then, should the formulation be made? It should be "prior to *dīvyati*.
Then that formulation "prior to *dīvyati*" must be made. It need not be made. [For] within the word *dīvyati*, the word *dīvya* is present.

It exists. Therefore, this is the ablative case (*pañcamī*). But what is the reason for making this statement with a modified form? The Teacher intends to indicate this: there is this metarule (*paribhāṣā*):
"that which has undergone a partial modification is not different [from the original]. What is the purpose of indicating this? [It applies] to those things that have undergone a partial modification.
The supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) has been proposed; however, it need not be formulated. Alternatively, this word *prāk* is a directional term (*dikśabda*).

And when used in conjunction with directional terms, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) occurs. In that case, the rule "provided it is not in grammatical apposition with a word ending in the nominative" (*aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe*) will apply, and thus [the form] *śatāt* will result.

545. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "prior" (*prāk*)? The mention of "prior" is for the sake of enjoining [the suffix] once. The mention of "prior" is made so that the suffix may be enjoined only once, thinking: "Let me not have to refer to it in every individual rule (*yoga-yoge*). This purpose is not necessary; for this is established even by virtue of the governing heading (*adhikāra*). [The word *prāk* is used because] it is a governing heading (*adhikāra*).

The purpose of the phrase "for each [instance] of that" (*pratiyogam tasya*) is to ensure that it applies to every individual instance (*yoge yoge*). If it is argued that this is established by virtue of the governing context (*adhikāra*), then the suffix *aṇ* would undesirably apply even in the domain of exceptions (*apavāda*). If it is argued that this is established by virtue of the governing context, then *aṇ* would occur in the scope of an exception.
Consequently, since the rule states "both *iñ* and *aṇ*," *aṇ* would also apply. Therefore, the explicit mention of "prior" (*prāk*) must be made; for that reason, the word "prior" must be stated.

(P_4,1.83.3) KA_II,235.235.18–236.8 Ro_III, 545–547 Now, even if the expression "prior to" (*prāk*) is employed, how is this to be understood: are those *prakṛtis* (bases) which occur prior to the [suffix] *divya*, or are those meanings (*arthas*) which occur prior to the [suffix] *divya*? And what follows from this? If it is understood as "prior to the [suffix] *divya*..."

If [the rule] is understood as "those which are *prakṛtis*," then that same fault remains: the contingency of *aṇ* even in the domain of exceptions (*apavāda*). However, if it is understood as "those meanings which occur prior to gambling" (*prāk dīvyataḥ*), then there is no fault. Since both [suffixes] arise for the same meaning, the suffix *iñ*, being produced from a specific *prakṛti*, supersedes *aṇ*. Let it be so, in such a way that there is no fault; thus, it is understood that [the rule applies to] "those meanings which occur prior to gambling."

Why is this so? Because this [sūtra] indicates the meaning primarily; otherwise, many *prakṛti*s would be recited, and one might take whichever among them as the cause (*nimitta*). Or rather, let it be that "the *prakṛti*s which occur prior to the suffix *divya*. But has it not been said that there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the suffix *aṇ* in the domain of exceptions (*apavāda*)?

Or rather, there is no fault because of the mention of the option (*vā*) in certain instances. Why? Because of the mention of the option in certain instances. When the Teacher employs the option in the rule "optionally after *pīlu* and *udaśvit*" (*pīlūnāṃ vā udaśvito 'nyatarasyām*), he indicates that the suffix *aṇ* does not occur in the domain of exceptions (*apavāda*). If this is indicated, there is no need for the introductory statement (*prāgvacana*). This follows from the governing context (*adhikāra*).

Success! Now, if it is argued that [the desired form] is established by virtue of the governing rule (*adhikāra*), then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the suffix *aṇ* even in a domain where an exception (*apavāda*) applies.

This is not a fault. For this has already been resolved by the statement: "Or rather, it is not so, because of the mention of 'or' (*vā*) in certain instances. But what is the reason for taking this specific limit? Why not simply say "prior to *ṭhak*"? This indicates that [the suffix *aṇ*] occurs in the sense of "in these [specific] meanings."

Thus [it is stated]. What is the purpose of making this known? The suffix *iñ*, which arises from a specific base, supersedes *aṇ*. (P_4.1.85.1) An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) should be made for *vān*, *mati*, and *pitṛmat* in the Vedic language (*chandas*). An addition should be made for *vān*, *mati*, and *pitṛmat* in the Vedic language.

The suffix *ka* should be applied: *vāk*, *vācyaḥ*. The suffix *matup*: *matiḥ*, *mātyaḥ*. The suffix *paitṛmatya* [is derived from] *pitṛmat*. The suffixes *ñ* and *añ* are to be stated after *pṛthivī*:
the suffixes *ñ* and *añ* should be stated after *pṛthivī*; [thus] *pārthivaḥ*, *pārthivī*. The suffixes *yañ* and *añ* are to be stated after *deva*:

the suffixes *yañ* and *añ* should be stated after *deva*; [thus] *daivyam*, *daivam*. After *bahiṣ*, there is elision of the *ṭi* [portion] and the suffix *yañ*: after *bahiṣ*, there is elision of the *ṭi* and the suffix *yañ*.

And it should be stated: [the suffix] *bāhya* means "external. And *īkak* should also be stated; thus, *bāhīka*. And *īkan* should be stated in the Vedic language (*chandasi*); thus, "May there be prosperity for you, O *bāhīkas*. An *akāra* should be stated [as a substitute] for *sthāman*; thus, *aśvatthāman*. [The suffix] *īkan* is applied after *loman* when referring to many descendants. Thus, *lomaṇī*.

The suffix *aṇ* should be stated [as the substitute for *taddhita*] when the word refers to many: *uḍulomāḥ*, *śaralomāḥ*. Why "when referring to many"? [To show the difference: *auḍalomiḥ*, *śāralomiḥ*.

In all cases, when there is the possibility of suffixes beginning with vowels (*aj-ādi*) following the word *go*, the suffix *yat* should be stated. When there is the possibility of suffixes beginning with vowels following *go*, *yat* should be stated:

*gavi bhavam* (existing in a cow) = *gavyam*; *goḥ idam* (this belongs to a cow) = *gavyam*; *goḥ svam* (the property of a cow) = *gavyam*; *gauḥ devatā asya sthālīpākasya* (a cow is the deity of this sacrificial oblation).
The *sthālīpāka* prepared from cow’s milk (*gavya*).

The suffixes beginning with *ṇya* (i.e., *ṇya*, *ṭya*, etc. [are applied] by prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) to the *aṇ* suffix prescribed by specific rules for particular meanings. The suffixes beginning with *ṇya* [supersede] those [prescribed] by specific rules for particular meanings.

By the rule of prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the suffix *aṇ* supersedes [the application of] *ṇya* and others. The scope of *ṇya* and others is, for example: "Diti is his deity" → *daityaḥ*. Now, the scope of the specific rule for *aṇ* (which is an exception to other rules) is, for example: "The offspring of Duli" → *dauleyaḥ*; "The offspring of Bali" → *bāleyaḥ*. In this case, both would apply: "The offspring of Diti" → *daityaḥ*. This refers to another specific rule for *aṇ* which is an exception [to the general rule].

The scope [of the suffix *ṭhak*] is for words such as *acitta*, *hastin*, and *dhenu*: e.g., *āpūpikaṃ* and *śāṣkulikaṃ*. The scope [of the suffixes] beginning with *ṇya* is for words such as *bārhaspatyam* and *prājāpatyam*.

Here, both [rules] would apply: e.g., a collection of trees (*vanaspati*) is *vānaspatyam*. The suffixes beginning with *ṇya* occur by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Well then, that prior counter-exception must be stated. It need not be stated.

The word *iṣṭa* signifies "desired. In the case of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), that which is desired takes effect. [The suffix *añ* is applied] after the words *diti* and *vanaspati* to denote offspring and a collection, respectively.

(Pāṇini 4.1.86). In the section concerning the suffix *añ*, it should be stated: "After the word *grīṣma*, [the suffix *añ* is applied] except in Vedic usage" (Pāṇini 4.3.158). In the section concerning the suffix *añ*, it should be stated: "After *grīṣma*, [the suffix *añ* is applied] except in Vedic usage."

Regarding the term *graiṣma*: [the rule] says "not in Vedic meters" (*acchandasi*). Why? [Because otherwise it would apply to] *triṣṭubh graiṣmī*. If it is said "not in Vedic meters," then this [suffix] would not apply here to these two months, *graiṣmau*. It is said "not in Vedic meters. This is not a Vedic meter that has been examined—such as the *kāṭhaka*, *kāpālaka*, *maudaka*, or *pāppalādaka*. What then? This is a qualifier for the meaning of the suffix.
"If *chandaḥ* is not for the sake of the condition (*pratyayārtha*).
(P_4.1.87.1) KA_II,238.2-13 Ro_III, 550-551 For what purpose are both *nañ* and *snañ* stated? Why not state *nañ* alone? What is the resulting form (*rūpasiddhi*)?

Regarding *pauṃsnam*: if the word *pum* ends in *s* and *na* is the suffix, it is not established; for by the rule "there is elision of what ends in a conjunct," elision would result. If that is so, then the meaning is neither expressed by *nañ* nor by *snañ*. Since *añ* is the subject under discussion, it will be carried over [as a governing rule], and the letter *n* must be stated as an augment. Now, when the augment *n* is added, is it to be considered as part of the preceding element (*pūrvānta*)?

Is it to be treated as a *pūrvānta* (an integral part of the preceding element) or as a *parādi* (an initial part of the following suffix)? What follows from this? If it were a *pūrvānta*, then in the case of the word *straiṇāḥ* (feminine), the elision [of the feminine suffix] would apply when forming a plural.

For example, in the formation of *straiṇānām saṅghaḥ* ("a group of feminine things"), the rule *saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇeṣv añyañiñām aṇ* would require the substitution of *aṇ*. If, on the other hand, it were a *parādi*, then in the case of *pauṃsam* (masculine), the same fault would arise: the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would apply. Let it then be a *pūrvānta*. But how is the form *straiṇāḥ* derived?

Regarding the phrase "a group of women" (*straiṇānāṃ saṅghaḥ*): in both cases, the worldly *gotra* (clan/lineage) is intended. However, this is not a worldly *gotra*. [If so,] would the long vowel *ī* not then apply? This is indeed desired as being included; it must be *straiṇī* and *pauṃsī*. For thus do the followers of Śākalya recite: "There is an addition for *nañ*, *snañ*, *īkak*, *khun*, and for *taruṇa* and *taluna*."

552. Now, do these two suffixes, *nañ* and *snañ*, apply before the word *bhavana*, or rather before the suffix *vati*? And what is the distinction here? If it is held that *nañ* and *snañ* apply before *bhavana*, then a prohibition must be stated regarding the sense of the suffix *vati*. [For example,] "like a woman" (*strīvat*) and "like a man" (*puṃvat*). But what is the reason that it is not established? These...

The suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* are said to occur before the word *bhavana*. Since these two are prescribed as specific rules (*viśeṣavidhi*), they would supersede the suffix *vati*, which is prescribed as a general rule (*sāmānyavidhi*). Therefore, that [supersession] must be stated. It need not be stated. I shall say "before *vati*. If it is "before *vati*," then an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the sense of "state" (*bhāva*). If it is "before *vati*," then an addition must be made for the sense of "state": *strībhāvaḥ* ("the state of being female").
[If it were argued that] the feminine form becomes masculine, or the masculine form becomes feminine, then the sūtra would have to be split. Let it remain exactly as it is. If it is objected:

"But was it not stated that since *nañ* and *snañ* occur after the root *bhū*, there is a prohibition regarding the sense of the suffix *vati*? This is not a fault. The Teacher’s practice indicates that *nañ* and *snañ* do not occur in the sense of *vati*, because he provides the instruction: "The feminine [stem] is like the masculine" (*striyāḥ puṃvat*).
[The suffix] *ka* is applied. Even so, [the form] *strīvat* is not established. The *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) depends upon the specific grammatical connection (*yoga*).

Why does it not occur here in the cases of *traividyaḥ*, *pāñcanadaḥ*, and *ṣāṭkulaḥ*? First, regarding *traividyaḥ*, it is not understood in this way: "one who studies three sciences is *traividyaḥ*."

Thus [it is asked]. How then? *trividyā* means knowledge consisting of three parts; one who studies the *trividyā* is called *traividya*. Here too, in the case of *pāñcanada*, it is not understood in this way—that *pāñcanada* means "that which exists in five rivers. How then? The collection of five rivers is *pañcanada*; that which exists in the *pañcanada* is *pāñcanada*.

Regarding the term *ṣāṭkula*: it is not understood as "that which exists in six families (*ṣaṭsu kuleṣu bhavaḥ*). How then? It is "the collection of six" (*ṣaṇṇām kulam*) which is *ṣaṭkulam*; that which exists in the *ṣaṭkula* is *ṣāṭkula*. Furthermore, the inclusion of the group beginning with *ajādi* must be made [in the rule]. This is so that it does not apply here: *pañcagarbharūpyam*, *pañcagarbhamayam*.

(P_4,1.88.2) Regarding the elision (*luk*) of a *taddhita* suffix after a *dvigu* compound, there must be a mention of that which causes it. When there is elision after a *dvigu*, one must state that there is elision of that *taddhita* suffix which is caused by the *dvigu*. This should be stated so that [elision] does not occur here: *pañcakapālasya*.

"This section is called *pāñcakapāla*. It should be stated: "Even when the specific meaning is not understood, [the suffix applies] even from that which is not its cause. What is the purpose? [So that] one prepared on five potsherds is *pañcakapāla*;
and even by analyzing it as "prepared in a *pañcakapālī*," it should result in exactly *pañcakapāla*. Now...

Even when the apprehension of that cause (*nimitta*) is being performed, how is this understood? Is it "that is its cause" (*tasya nimittam*), thus "its cause" (*tannimittam*), and "from its cause" (*tannimittāt*); or rather, "that is the cause of this," thus "this is caused by that" (*tannimittaḥ*), and "from that which is caused by that" (*tannimittāt*)? And what follows from this? If it is understood as "that is its cause" (*tasya nimittam*), thus "its cause" (*tannimittam*), and "from its cause" (*tannimittāt*), then [the following applies] even when [the rule] is being performed.
Furthermore, if it were taken as "the grasping of that cause," then the rule would apply here [to the word *pañcakapāla*] in the sense of "this is a fragment of a five-pan vessel.

However, if it is understood as "that is its cause; this is caused by that; from that which is caused by that," then there is no fault. Let it be so, in such a way that there is no fault: it is understood as "that is its cause; this is caused by that; from that which is caused by that."

Why is this so? Because he says: "When a specific meaning is not understood, [the suffix is applied] even from that which is not its cause. In that case, then, the mention of "its cause" (*tannimitta*) should be made. It need not be made. The word "of the *dvigu*" (*dvigoḥ*) is not in the ablative case. What then? It is a genitive of relation (*sambandha-ṣaṣṭhī*). There is elision (*luk*) of the *taddhita* suffix after a *dvigu*. And what is the *taddhita* suffix of the *dvigu*? Its cause (*nimitta*).

In what case does this rule "dvigu" apply? And in what case does it apply? It applies when there is an affix (*pratyaya*). Then this must be stated: "Even from that which is not the cause [of the formation], provided there is no comprehension of a specific meaning. But this need not be stated. Here, we must establish three forms: *pañcakapālaḥ* (prepared in five dishes), *pañcakapālī* (prepared in a vessel for five), and *pañcasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ* (prepared in five dishes).

Regarding the terms *pañcakapālaḥ* and *daśakapālaḥ*: there, since two words have the same meaning, the analysis (*vigraha*) will be performed by one, while the suffixal derivation (*utpatti*) will occur from the other, according to the maxim of the sheep and the ram (*aviravikanyāya*). For example, having analyzed it as "the meat of a sheep" (*aveḥ māṃsam*), the derivation occurs from the word *avika*. Likewise, having analyzed it as "prepared in five potsherds" (*pañcasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ*), [the compound] *pañcakapālaḥ* is formed.

556–557. If it is argued that there is no *aluk* (non-elision) in the case of a *gotra* [patronymic] before a vowel-initial suffix (*aci*), we reply: there would be non-establishment due to mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). If it is argued that there is no *aluk* in the case of a *gotra* before a vowel-initial suffix, we say: because of mutual dependence, there is non-establishment. What is this mutual dependence? The vowel-initial suffix is the cause for the *aluk*, and the *aluk* is the cause for the vowel-initial suffix. This constitutes mutual dependence. And things characterized by mutual dependence cannot be established, due to contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*).

[Objection: There is the provision for *luk* elision. [Response: But by virtue of the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), *cha* will take effect in place of *luk*. The scope of *luk* is, for example, *gargāḥ*, *vatsāḥ*, *bidāḥ*, *urvāḥ*. The scope of *cha* is, for example, *śālīyaḥ*, *mālīyaḥ*, *gārgīyaḥ*, *vātsīyaḥ*. In the present case, both would apply: "the pupils of the Gargas" (*gargāṇāṃ chātrāḥ*) results in *gārgīyāḥ* and *vātsīyāḥ*. [Response: By the rule of conflict, *cha* occurs. No.

This is an improper contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*). Elision (*luk*) is applicable when there is abundance (*bhūman*), yet the *ajādi* suffix is prescribed for an external meaning (*bāhya-artha*). Since that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is weaker than that which is internal (*antaraṅga*), it would be improper on account of this contradiction. By prescribing non-elision (*aluk*) for the *taddhita* suffix beginning with *aj* where elision had been obtained due to abundance, he declares—while performing [this]—that non-elision (*aluk*) and elision (*luk*) are simultaneous. That this...

The Teacher teaches the non-elision (*aluk*) of the suffix that would otherwise have been elided (*luk*) when a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a vowel follows a word in the sense of "abundance" (*bhūman*), thereby making it known that these two—elision and non-elision—are simultaneous. Alternatively, the suffix *cha* is well-known to occur in place of elision; or rather, non-elision occurs in place of elision, and thus the suffix *cha* is well-established for it. [This was] previously stated.

For exceptions (*apavāda*) apply first, and general rules (*utsarga*) afterwards. Or rather, the non-elision (*aluk*) awaits the occasion for elision (*luk*); thus, when there is non-elision after *cha*, it is likewise. Furthermore, if the non-elision (*aluk*) again awaits the occasion for elision (*luk*), then its non-elision after *cha* is established.
Or, having first conceived the domain of the exception, the general rule subsequently applies.

(Regarding the rule P_4.1.89.2) When a *gotra* [patronymic] stem that undergoes elision (*lopin*) in the plural is used to denote two or one [descendants], the non-elision (*aluk*) of the suffix must be stated. When a *gotra* stem that undergoes elision in the plural is used to denote two or one [descendants], the non-elision of the suffix must be stated. [Example: *bidānām apatyam* ("the offspring of the Bidas").

*Māṇavakaḥ baidaḥ*, *baidau*. For what purpose is this [rule] stated? Is it not already established by the rule *na aci* (Pāṇini 6.4.135), whereby the elision (*aluk*) is accomplished? It is stated that [the elision occurs] when a vowel (*ac*) follows. But here we do not see a vowel at the beginning of a suffix (*ajādi*). [This would be so] by means of the "characteristic of a suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). However, there is no application of the "characteristic of a suffix" when the operation depends on a phoneme (*varṇāśraya*). In the case of the application of the singular and dual endings, there is elision of the suffix *yuvan* when there is a plurality. This applies to that which ends in the singular or dual.

In the case of multiple descendants, the elision (*lopa*) must be stated for the *yuvan* (younger generation) suffix. For example: the offspring of Baida are many young men, [called] *bidāḥ*. From two Baidas, they are *bidāḥ*. If it were stated that "the suffix *añ* is elided when there are many" or "the suffix *yañ* is elided when there are many," then elision would not apply here. Let it not be so; rather, it should be understood as: "that which ends in *añ* when there are many" or "that which ends in *yañ* when there are many."

Thus it would be. But it cannot be so; for in this case there would be a fault: [the name] *kāśyapa* would apply to images of Kāśyapa as well. This is not a fault. As for what was said—that since the stem *gotra* undergoes elision when plural, it must be stated that there is no elision (*aluk*) when it occurs in the dual or singular—it need not be stated. The non-elision is established by the rule itself regarding vowels (*aci*). It is indeed by the rule "before a vowel" (*aci*) that the non-elision is secured.

It is said: "And here we do not see [the application of] *ajādi* (beginning with a vowel) by means of the characteristic of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). But has it not been stated that "there is no *pratyayalakṣaṇa* when depending on a phoneme (*varṇa*)"? Or rather, if some things that depend on phonemes also occur by means of the characteristic of an affix, then this [case] will also be so. Alternatively, having stated the non-elision (*aluk*) without distinction, [it is then specified] "not before a consonant" (*hali na*).

I shall explain. If, after stating the non-elision (*aluk*) without qualification, one were to say "except before a consonant" (*hali na*), then in the case of *bidāḥ*—meaning many young students (*māṇavaka*) who are the descendants of the *Bidas*—the non-elision would also apply here. Let it be so; however, since this [term] now denotes a plurality of youth (*yuvan*), elision (*luk*) will occur again. Why does the non-elision not occur once more? Because the rule applies to the first among the semantically related [elements] that ends in a *gotra* suffix.

The *aluk* [compound] is being discussed. And this [word] is not the first among the capable [compounds] ending in a *gotra* suffix; rather, it has transitioned to a second meaning. Furthermore, this must necessarily be understood in this way for the sake of forms such as *atribharadvājikā*, *vasiṣṭhakaśyapikā*, *bhṛgvaṅgirasikā*, and *kutsakuśikikā*. Alternatively, the mention of *gargabhārgavikā* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

Alternatively, the mention of *gargabhārgavika* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): the elision does not occur for any other [patronymic] that has entered into this very second meaning, but only for this one. Furthermore, regarding what was said—that when [the suffixes] ending in the singular or dual are applied, their elision must be stated in the sense of the younger generation (*yuvan*)—[this is unnecessary], because it is stated that "the *añ* which occurs in the plural" and "the *yañ* which occurs in the plural."

[The suffix] *luk* would not apply. Let it not be so; [let it be] "that which ends in *añ* when there are many" and "that which ends in *yañ* when there are many. It will be understood as "that which ends in *añ* when there are many" and "that which ends in *yañ* when there are many. But was it not said that this is not possible? For in this case, a fault would arise:
[the form] *kāśyapāḥ* meaning "images of Kāśyapa. This is not a fault, because in that context, the word refers to a worldly lineage (*gotra*).

And this inclusion does not refer to the worldly *gotra*. If it were stated that "that which ends in *añ* when there are many [descendants]" or "that which ends in *yañ* when there are many," then in the case of "the descendant of the Bidas is a young student (*māṇavaka*), a Baida; [and] two Baidas," the suffix would also apply here. [Objection: In this case, the *aluk* will block the *luk*. [Response: But once the *aluk* has been applied, since the cause for *luk* no longer exists, [the *luk*] would not apply again.

It will not be elided. Or rather, it has already been stated. What has been stated? That "a descendant (*apatya*) is indeed a lineage (*gotra*)," and that "a descendant of the ultimate progenitor (*paramaprakṛti*) is [also] a lineage.

From a descendant who belongs to a living generation, a second [suffix] is applied in the sense of the base itself, and it receives the designation *yuvan*. And that [designation] does not apply in the feminine. Furthermore, the mention of "single lineage" (*ekagotra*) is redundant.

It is established even in the case of those [formations] where the plural suffix is elided. In that regard, having analyzed "the young boy who is the descendant of the Bidas" (*bidānām apatyam māṇavakaḥ*), [the following applies].

From the word *bida*, the suffix will arise in the sense of "two" or "one": *baidaḥ* (a descendant of Bida), *baidau* (two descendants of Bida). Having analyzed [the compound] as "many young students who are the offspring of Bida," the suffix will arise from the word *bida* in the sense of "many," according to the maxim of the sheep and the ram (*aviravikanyāya*), resulting in *bidāḥ*.

562–563. If it is argued that "there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix after a *yuvan* [derivative] when followed by a vowel (*aci*)," then an undesirable result would follow for the suffix. If it is argued that "there is elision of the suffix after a *yuvan* [derivative] when followed by a vowel," then an undesired suffix would occur; while the undesired suffix remains present, its elision (*luk*) would not take place, and consequently, the hearing (*śravaṇa*) of that undesired suffix would result. [Response: But it is established (*siddham*) by the rule stating that elision occurs without distinction, and there is a prohibition (*pratiṣedhaḥ*) when a consonant (*hal*) follows. It is thus established.

This [is the solution]. How so? Having stated the elision (*luk*) without distinction, I shall say "not before a consonant" (*hali na*). [Objection: This is established; however, the rule (*sūtra*) is then altered. [Response: Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. [Objection: But was it not said that if [the elision occurs] when a vowel follows (*aci*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the affix appearing inappropriately? [Response: This is not a fault. The term "in a vowel" (*aci*) is not a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*). What then? It is a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*).

"Regarding the domain beginning with vowels (*ajādau viṣaye*): when *luk* elision has occurred there in the domain of a vowel, whichever suffix is applicable shall apply from that very [base]. What, then, are the purposes of this rule? Its purpose is [to provide for] the suffixes *ṇa*, *ṭhak*, and *cha* after the *sauvīra* gotras.

The descendant of Phāṇṭāhṛti is the youth Phāṇṭāhṛta. The students of the youth Phāṇṭāhṛta are the Phāṇṭāhṛtas. [The suffix] *ṇa*. The descendant of Bhāgavitti is the youth Bhāgavittika. The students of the youth Bhāgavittika are the Bhāgavittas. [The suffix] *ṭhak*. The descendant of Tailāyani is the youth Tailāyanīya. [The suffix] *cha* (forming *Tailāyanīya*).

The students who are young [descendants] of Tailāyani are called *tailāyanīyāḥ*. The suffixes *iñ* and *ṇya* apply everywhere; that is, *iñ* and *ṇya* are used everywhere for the purpose [of deriving names]. The students who are young [descendants] of Aupagavi are called *aupagavīyāḥ*. If there were an extension (*atideśa*) treating it like a *vṛddha* [stem], then by the rule "after *iñ* expressing a lineage," the suffix *aṇ* would be required. This is not a fault, for that extension is rejected. How then are those purposes [of the extension] achieved? They are achieved through an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
[The suffixes] are established. Now, what is the purpose of *iñ* after [stems ending in] *yat* and *kha*? *Yat*: The offspring of a father-in-law (*śvaśura*) is *śvaśuryaḥ*.

The offspring of *śvaśurya* is *śvāśuriḥ*. The students of the young *śvāśuri* are *śvāśurāḥ*. *Kha*: The offspring of a family (*kula*) is *kulīnaḥ*. The offspring of *kulīna* is *kaulīniḥ*. The students of the young *kaulīni* are *kaulīnāḥ*.

Kha. Cha. The offspring of a sister is *svasrīyaḥ*; the offspring of a *svasrīya* is *svāsrīyiḥ*; the young students of a *svāsrīya* are *svāsrīyāḥ*. Indeed, even these [examples] do not serve as purposes [for the application of the rule]. In this case as well, when referring to a youth (*yuvan*), it should simply be *śvaśuryaḥ*, *kulīnaḥ*, or *svasrīyaḥ*. This has already been stated: "When there is elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ*, [the patronymic suffix is applied] from any [stem] except for those that are non-Brāhmaṇa *gotras*."

Regarding the statement "there is an addition [to the rule] concerning the suffix *yuva*": it is said that [the suffix applies] after a non-Brāhmaṇa gotra-name only. However, this [term in question] is not merely a non-Brāhmaṇa gotra-name. The expression "after a non-Brāhmaṇa gotra-name only" is not a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion) meaning "that which is other than a Brāhmaṇa gotra-name only. Rather, it is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (a simple negation) meaning "not after a Brāhmaṇa gotra-name only. And this must necessarily be so.

This should be understood as follows: for the sake of [forming] *māyūriḥ*, *kāpotiḥ*, and *kāpiñjaliḥ*. If that is so, then the suffixes *aṇ* and *ṇya* are useful everywhere. *Aṇ*: the descendant of Glucukāyani is a young student (*māṇavaka*), [named] Glaucukāyana. The students of the young Glaucukāyana are the Glaucukāyanas. *Ṇya*: and [the suffix] *ṇya* is for the sake of [words like] *kāpiñjali*. The descendant of Kāpiñjali is a young student [named] Kāpiñjali.
*Kāpiñjalādi*: the pupils of that youth are *kāpiñjalādāḥ*.

Under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "prior to *dīvya*," there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the status of an elder (*vṛddha*) to a youth (*yuvan*). Under the governing rule "prior to *dīvya*," there is an extension of the status of an elder to a youth.
It must be stated that "a youth becomes like an elder. A collection of Gārgyāyaṇas is *gārgyāṇakam*.

Something belonging to the Gārgyāyaṇas is *gārgyāṇakam*. One whose devotion is to the Gārgyāyaṇas is *gārgyāyaṇakaḥ*. This is so that the suffix *vuñ* may apply based on the *gotra* (clan) designation. If the extension of the status of an elder (*vṛddhavad-atideśa*) were applied [without qualification], then the students of a youth named Aupagavi would be called *aupagavīyāḥ*.

Thus, by the rule *iñaḥ gotre*, the suffix *aṇ* would apply. If, however, non-occurrence were to be extended by the rule *yuvā vṛddhavat*, [one might ask]: how can non-occurrence be extended by the rule *yuvā vṛddhavat*? This is because the mention of the suffix *-vat* is optional, and when the suffix *-vat* is mentioned, it is used to justify a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*). For example:

Just as among the Madras there is the expression, "Do barley-corns exist or not exist in Uśīnara?", and regarding its parts, "Do they exist or not exist like those of a mother?", so too here we shall justify the remainder of the sentence by saying, "In this case, a youth becomes like an old man, or he does not become like an old man. Just as the suffix *yuvan* is not applied within a *gotra*, so it is under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of "prāgdīvyataḥ" (before the suffix *dīvya*).

"It does not occur even in the case of a youth"—this must be stated. Even if it were said, "Or rather, let there be elision (*luk*) in the case of a youth," this [rule] would not be formulated. How then [would one account for] the rule *phakphiñoḥ anyatarasyām*? I shall state that when a youth is denoted by the suffixes *phak* or *phiñ*, he may optionally be treated like an elder (*vṛddha*). But when he is not treated like an elder, then [we have forms such as] *gārgyāyaṇānām*.

The collective term *gārgyāṇakam* refers to a certain group of *gārgyāyaṇas*. Since the suffix *vuñ* is prescribed for one who has devotion (*bhakti*) toward a lineage (*gotra*), such as in the form *gārgyāyaṇakaḥ*, it would not apply here. However, if the meaning were extended by the rule "the youth is treated like the elder" (*yuvā vṛddhavat*), then under the governing heading of "before the suffix *dīvyat*," the meaning of the youth would be treated as that of the elder. That must be stated; even if [that is so]...

This is what is said: alternatively, the rule *atha vā etarhi yūni luk* will not be formulated. How, then, [will one explain] the rule *phakphiñoḥ anyatarasyām*? I shall state that the meaning of the youth (*yuvan*) residing in the suffixes *phak* and *phiñ* optionally behaves like the meaning of the elder (*vṛddha*). When it does not behave like the elder, then [the forms] *gārgyāṇakam*—meaning a collection of *gārgyāyaṇas*—and *gārgyāṇakam*—meaning something belonging to the *gārgyāyaṇas*—are derived.

[Gārgyāyaṇa says: "In the case of *bhakti* (devotion) belonging to one who is a Gārgyāyaṇa, the suffix *vuñ*—which depends on a *gotra* name—would not apply. [The author replies: "If that is so, then the mention of *rājanya* and *manuṣya* in the rule for *vuñ* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the worldly [usage]. By the fact that the Teacher makes the mention of *rājanya* and *manuṣya* in the prescription of *vuñ*, he indicates that the mention of *gotra* refers to the worldly [usage]. And in common usage, a youth (*yuvan*) is also considered a *gotra*."

Thus it is treated as a conventional designation (*upacaryate*). "What is your lineage (*gotra*), young man? "I am a Gārgyāyaṇa. "What is your lineage, young man? "I am a Vātsyāyana. If this is intended to be made known [by the rule], then in the case of "the students of the young Aupagavi" (*aupagavīyāḥ*), the suffix *iñ* being based on a lineage, the suffix *aṇ* would apply by the rule "after *iñ*, when referring to a lineage" (*gotre*). [Therefore,] this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding collective formations (*sāmūhika*). If it is an indicator regarding collective formations, then in the case of the Gārgyāyaṇas—

In the case of *gārgyāṇaka*—where *gārgyāyaṇa* has devotion (*bhakti*) toward [the lineage of] Gārgya—the suffix *vuñ* would not apply to form *gārgyāyaṇaka*, as it relies on a specific lineage (*gotra*). This is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding the application of *vuñ*. Regarding the application of *vuñ*: in the case of "the students of Śālaṅki, who is young," the term is *śālaṅkāḥ*;

here, the suffix *aṇ* (prescribed by the rule *iñaḥ gotre*) would not apply. Let it be then without distinction. How then [would one explain] "the students of Aupagavi, who is young" as *aupagavīyāḥ*?
We shall qualify this *iñ* by means of the *gotra*: "the *iñ* prescribed after a *gotra*.
Regarding the rule "this belongs to him" (*tasyedam*), the suffix *aṇ* is established even for the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*). These are specific instances of that [rule].

For these [suffixes] are taught for the sake of offspring (*apatya*), collection (*samūha*), modification (*vikāra*), and residence (*nivāsa*). Why, then, is this [present rule] stated? It is intended for the purpose of supersession (*bādhanārtha*). That is, it serves to supersede those [suffixes] that would otherwise apply to it. But how can a suffix not belonging to the *śeṣa* category supersede one belonging to the *śeṣa* category? This [present rule] is indeed an *utsarga* (general rule), and an *utsarga* is precisely what is called *śeṣa*. For whatever is an *utsarga* is also indeed a *śeṣa*.
Now, when this sublation of the sublater occurs, what is the purpose? Its purpose is the *vṛddhi* [vowel lengthening].

They cause the *vṛddhi* to be applied: *bhānoḥ apatyam* becomes *bhānavaḥ*; *śyāmagoḥ apatyam* becomes *śyāmagavaḥ*. But how, even if one desires it, can an exception (*apavāda*) which is applicable be prevented from taking effect? By the force of the mention of *tasya* [in the rule]. What is this?
Your Honor has stated the purpose of that very rule (*adhyāroha*), but not of the entire yoga.

An explanation of the meaning must necessarily be provided for the sake of what follows. In that case, the case-ending expressing capability (*samartha-vibhakti*) must also necessarily be specified for the sake of what follows. If this is so, then it is by virtue of the power of making a division of the yoga (*yoga-vibhāga*); otherwise—

For one should simply say: "The suffix *iñ* occurs after that which is its offspring. This rule is stated in the masculine gender and in the singular number; therefore, the suffix arises only after a word in the masculine gender.

It might be that this [rule] would not apply after a word ending in the singular number, nor after a word in the feminine or neuter gender ending in the dual or plural numbers. Regarding the specification of the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), gender and number are not authoritative, because they are not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitatvāt*). Regarding the specification of the meaning of a secondary derivative, gender and number are not authoritative. What is the reason? Because they are not intended to be expressed. Here, the specific mention [of gender and number] is not the governing factor (*tantra*).

But how can there be a designation by that very [word], while that [designation] is not the primary factor? You are both its practitioner and its detractor. Because it is inseparable [from the meaning], the designation here is made using the masculine gender and the singular number.
Since a designation must necessarily be made with some case-ending and some number, it is as follows:

Someone seeking rice might bring a bundle of rice together with its stalks and husks, not because he intends to keep them, but because they were included; having taken as much as he requires, he discards the husks and stalks. Similarly, someone seeking meat might bring fish together with their bones and scales, not because he intends to keep them, but because they were included; having taken as much as he requires, he discards the scales and bones.

Thus, here too, because of the necessary connection (*nāntarīyakatva*), the reference is made using the masculine gender and in the singular number. For in this case, the specific grammatical form of the reference is not the governing factor (*tantra*). When there is a reference by means of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), no specific [gender or number] is understood, because it is a general reference. When there is a reference by a pronoun, no specific [gender or number] is understood. What is the reason? Because it is a general reference. By means of a pronoun...

This explanation is being given: the term *sara* is a general expression. Therefore, only that which expresses a general category would undergo production (*utpatti*), and not that which expresses a specific instance. However, injunctions regarding the general apply to the specific instances; indeed, injunctions regarding the general are established within the specific instances. For example:

"The cow is to be tied up; the goat is for Agni-Soma"—when the generic form (*ākṛti*) is thus enjoined, actions such as touching, seizing, sprinkling, and immolation are performed upon the individual substance (*dravya*). This is an unequal comparison. There is a reason why this is so. What is the reason? Because of impossibility. Since touching and the other acts are impossible in the generic form, they are performed upon that which accompanies the generic form.

In the case of a substance (*dravya*), operations such as *ārambhaṇa* (cutting) and so forth are performed; this [case] is of the same nature. Because it is impossible [for a general term to denote the specific], when there is the production [of a derivative], the production will be of that which denotes the particular. Regarding the denotation of offspring (*apatya*), the feminine and masculine genders are not established because of its neuter gender. When there is the denotation of offspring, the feminine and masculine genders are not established. What is the reason? Because of its neuter gender.

The word *apatyam* (offspring) is neuter in gender; therefore, it would denote only that which is neuter, and not the feminine or masculine genders. But has this not already been raised as an objection and resolved previously? In that case, the objection concerned the *origination* [of the offspring]; here, however, the objection concerns the *denotation* by means of what has already originated. This is established, however, because the intention is to express procreation.

This is established. How so? Because "procreation" (prajana) is intended to be expressed. Here, "procreation" is what is intended to be expressed, and it possesses all genders. But what is the reason that, while the activity is the same, "offspring" (apatya) is neuter gender whereas "procreation" (prajana) has all genders?
