Because different words are used for the same meaning, a difference in gender is observed. Due to the difference in words for the same meaning, a difference in gender is seen.

It is observed [that gender varies]. For example: *puṣya* (masculine), *tārakā* (feminine), *nakṣatra* (neuter); or *geha* (neuter), *kuṭī* (feminine), *maṭha* (masculine). And because of the difference in constituent parts (*avayava*), a difference in gender is observed. For example: *kuṭī*, *kuṭīra*; *śamī*, *śamīra*; *śuṇḍā*, *śuṇḍāra*. Indeed, if a difference in gender were to arise merely from a difference in constituent parts, how much more so where there is also a difference in the word-form (*śabda*) itself?

(P_4,1.93) For what purpose is this stated? Because the offspring is connected to the progenitor, and because that [progenitor] is intended to be expressed, the singular number is used for the *gotra*. The progenitor is connected with the offspring as "progenitor after progenitor"; and because that [progenitor] is intended to be expressed.

Furthermore, that relationship [of "offspring"] is intended to be expressed in relation to the progenitor. Since the offspring is connected to the progenitor, and since that relationship is intended to be expressed, if one were to denote the offspring of each and every progenitor, it would follow that there would be multiple suffixes; yet it is desired that there be only one. And that cannot be accomplished without an effort.

Thus, the singular number is used in reference to the lineage (*gotra*). This is stated for this very purpose. But how is it known that the progenitor is connected with the offspring through the term "progenitor"? For it is observed thus in the world: when a child is sitting on his grandfather’s lap, someone asks, "To whom does he belong? and he replies, "To Devadatta" or "To Yajñadatta. [The word refers to] the progenitor.

He does not designate himself. There is a purpose for this. What, then, is it? In that regard, there is a prohibition [of the suffix] after a secondary derivative (*pratyayānta*) when referring to a lineage (*gotra*), because [the application of the suffix] is restricted to the lineage. In that case, a prohibition must be stated regarding a secondary derivative when it refers to a lineage—for example, "the descendant of Aupagava. What is the reason? Because it is restricted to the lineage. For this restriction applies specifically to the lineage.
It is being done. Therefore, that *gotra*-suffix which would otherwise apply—both as to its identity and its specific type—would be only one.
Which one would apply? That which follows a [secondary] suffix; and there would be the production from the ultimate base (*paramaprakṛti*).
And the production from the ultimate base must be stated, for it does not apply due to non-connection. He will recite the resolution of these two very points.

For the Teacher [states] that when the grandson (*yuvan*) has disappeared, there is no application [of the suffix]; and just as in that case it ends with a suffix denoting a derivative or a part, and just as that very same [suffix] transfers to the second and third derivatives, so too here, that very same [suffix] ending in the patronymic suffix will transfer to the second and third descendants. This may be so.
Success! The descendant of Aupagava is Aupagava; where that very person is intended as the immediate one, he alone is [intended] in the sense of a *gotra*.

However, this indeed is not established: "the descendant of Garga is Gārgya. For here, one person is intended as the immediate one and another as the *gotra*. And regarding the feminine, there is no fixed rule; thus, regarding a young woman (*yuvatī*), a restriction does not apply.

*Aupagavī* [is] *māṇavakī*. For, by the restrictive rule (*niyamāt*), the feminine gender is excluded by the sūtra: "In the case of a lineage name (*gotra*), there is only one [suffix]; in the case of a youth (*yuvan*), it is applied after the lineage name, except for the feminine. In which view does this fault lie? In the view that [the suffix] applies to the progenitor when he is connected with offspring. First, there is no fault when the progenitor is connected with offspring; for when the progenitor is connected with offspring, it need not necessarily follow from the very fact of procreation.

In that case, a restriction is not possible. If there were no restriction, this fault would not arise. However, this fault applies to all cases involving offspring. For in all cases involving offspring, there ought to be production from every [direction]. In that situation, a restriction becomes appropriate. When there is a restriction, this fault exists: namely, that when the progenitor possesses offspring, it would belong to a young woman.

The designation [of *yuvan*] is not obtained. What is the reason? The technical name *gotra* subverts the technical name *yuvan*. A suffix is prescribed after a *gotra* stem for a *yuvan* descendant, provided it is not feminine. When the *yuvan* descendant is further removed (i.e., when there is an intervening generation), there is no application [of the rule]. When the *yuvan* descendant is further removed, the restriction does not apply, as in the case of "the offspring of Gārgyāyaṇa. In which of the two positions is this fault found? In all of them.

Regarding those connected with offspring: first, there is no fault in all cases where they are connected with offspring, for when all are connected with offspring, it must occur through production from every [source]. In that case, a restriction is appropriate; since the restriction exists, this fault does not arise.
However, this fault applies when the progenitor is connected with offspring, for when the progenitor is connected with offspring, it pertains to the ultimate primary source.

It does not apply because of the immediate [succession] and because of the lack of connection to the lineage (*gotra*). Nor does it apply to one who is merely young. What is the reason? Because of the restriction "from the lineage. Well then, how is it known that all [descendants] are connected by the term *apatya* (offspring)? For the ritualists (*yājñika*) recite thus: "He whose house has had no Śūdras for ten generations may drink the Soma. If...
And since all [beings] are possessed of offspring, this [following] is established: how so?
It is as when someone asks of a child sitting on his grandfather’s lap, "Whose is this? and he replies, "Devadatta’s" or "Yajñadatta’s.
He designates the progenitor, not himself; thus, it is the act of procreation that is intended to be expressed by him, and this applies to all.

"This is not the offspring; rather, Devadatta is its progenitor. Now, since all [the terms] are connected with the sense of offspring, what is accomplished by the rule "ekaḥ gotre" (only one [suffix occurs] in the sense of lineage)? Because all are connected with the sense of offspring, the rule "ekaḥ gotre" is for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of] a suffix after a form that already ends in a suffix in the sense of lineage. Because all are connected with the sense of offspring, "ekaḥ gotre" is for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of] a suffix after a form that already ends in a suffix in the sense of lineage.

It is said: there is indeed a purpose for this. What, then, is it? It is not known which one [the suffix] is—that which comes from the remote base (*paramaprakṛti*) or that which comes from the immediate base (*anantarāt*). Furthermore, there would be an impossibility of restriction; and a restriction is not tenable. For what reason? Because the application of multiple suffixes does not occur for a single offspring (*apatya*); indeed, in the case of a single offspring...
It would follow that there is a plurality of suffixes. What then?
In the case of another descendant, from a different base word, a different suffix is obtained. In the case of another descendant, from yet another base word, a further suffix is obtained.

From a word ending in *phak*, *iñ* is applied; from a word ending in *iñ*, *phak* is applied. Thus, a chain of suffixes extending through ten stages (*dāśatayī pratyayamālā*) beginning with *phak* and *iñ* would result. In which [case] does this occur?
In this view, there is this fault: [the fault applies] to all cases involving offspring. Regarding all cases involving offspring, first of all, there is no fault;
for in all cases involving offspring, it must occur through production from every [source]. In that case, a restriction is appropriate. When there is a restriction, this fault does not exist.

In that case, this fault applies when the progenitor is associated with offspring. For if the progenitor were associated with offspring, he would not necessarily exist through universal production; thus, a restrictive rule (*niyama*) would not be possible there. In the absence of such a rule, this fault arises. However, there is no fault when the progenitor is associated with offspring. How so? If "offspring" (*apatya*) is understood as a collective whole (*samudāya*), then a restrictive rule is observed in this context.

In that case, many suffixes would apply; there will be a restriction for this: "offspring" (apatyam)—all offspring having Upagu and others as ancestors is considered here. In that case, many suffixes would apply; there will be a restriction for this: "only one [suffix] in the lineage" (gotre). As for what was said, "and there is no restriction regarding the feminine," I shall state it thus: "after a lineage-name (gotra), [a suffix is applied] in the sense of a younger generation" (yūni).
[The suffix] becomes a *pratyaya*. [If it is argued: "Not in the feminine," even so, the designation of a young woman (*yuvati*) as feminine would not be obtained.

If that is the case, then I shall state it thus: "After a *gotra* [suffix], a *pratyaya* occurs for the younger generation (*yuvan*); in the feminine, there is elision (*luk*). Even so, in the case of *aupagavī māṇavikā*, the long vowel *ī* [prescribed by Pāṇini 4.1.15] would not be obtained because of the rule "after what is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*). Let it not be so; let it be the case that the *aṇ* which is not a subordinate member [is intended].

[Objection: It will be so because of the rule "after a word ending in *aṇ*, provided it is not a secondary derivative (*anupasarjana*). [Reply: It cannot be so; for in this case there would be a fault. Consider:

*kāśakṛtsnī mīmāṃsā* (the Mīmāṃsā taught by Kāśakṛtsna); she who studies that is a *kāśakṛtsnā brāhmaṇī*. Because of the rule "after a word ending in *aṇ*," the suffix *īkāra* would be improperly applied. [Reply: This is not a fault; when the female student is the meaning to be expressed, the suffix *īkāra* must indeed follow the *aṇ*.

Furthermore, regarding this [suffix], since the *aṇ* [which was applied] to the base (*adhyetryām*) has been elided, and since the *īkāra* is heard as having been produced [by the rule for feminine suffixes], it will not occur again. If that is so, then in the case of *aupagavībhāryaḥ* (where *aupagavī* is a young woman who is his wife), the prohibition of the masculine-like form (*puṃvadbhāva*) characterized by the genus (*jāti*) would not apply. Let it not be so; [the prohibition applies] when there is a cause for *vṛddhi*.

Thus it will be so. But what then of that which is not caused by *vṛddhi*? For example, "the young girl Glucukāyanī is his wife" results in *glucukāyanībhāryaḥ*. Therefore, only the designation *yuvatī* ("young woman") for a female must be excluded [from the application of the suffix *yañ*]. And when that [designation] has been excluded, this [term] ending in the *gotra* suffix refers to the *yuvan* (descendant), here in the sense of one who produces offspring.

A prohibition must be stated regarding [the suffix] after a form ending in a secondary suffix (pratyayānta), and the production [of the suffix] from the ultimate base (paramaprakṛti) must also be stated.

In all cases involving descendants (apatya), a prohibition must be stated regarding [the suffix] after a form ending in a secondary suffix. Therefore, a prohibition must be stated. Therefore, a prohibition must be stated. Alternatively, the production of the suffix occurs after those that function as technical names (sañjñākārin). Or rather, the production of the suffix occurs after those that function as technical names.

It must be stated. If it is said that suffixes arise from those that form names (*saṃjñākārin*), how [does one derive] *gārgyāyaṇaḥ* or *vātsyāyanaḥ*? [The rule] "from the *gotra*, for the *yuvan*"—this must be stated. And that is for the purpose of excluding [the application of the suffix to] genus (*jāti*) and so forth.

Furthermore, that mention of "those that form names" (*saṃjñākārin*) must necessarily be made. What is the purpose? It is for the purpose of excluding [the application of the suffix to] genus and so forth.

Lest there be production from genus (*jāti*) and so forth, genus does not occur; number (*saṃkhyā*) does not occur; the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) does not occur. Genus does not occur [in such cases as]: "the offspring of a crow" (*kākasya apatyam*), "the offspring of a curlew" (*kurarasya apatyam*). Number does not occur [in such cases as]:
"the offspring of nine" (*navānām apatyam*), "the offspring of ten" (*daśānām apatyam*). The pronoun does not occur [in such cases as]: "the offspring of all" (*sarveṣām apatyam*).

Regarding the statement, "the offspring of all": as for what was said—that the genus (*jāti*) does not apply in cases such as "the offspring of a crow" or "the offspring of an osprey"—by the very same cause that one is a crow, so too will a second and a third be crows. Furthermore, regarding what was said—that number (*saṃkhyā*) does not apply in cases such as "the offspring of nine" or "the offspring of ten"—[the same principle holds].

Thus, number operates in dependence upon that which is to be numbered. Since that [number] is dependent, and what is dependent is incapable [of forming a compound], it will not occur due to this incapacity. As for what is also said—that the pronominal does not apply in cases such as *sarveṣām apatyam* ("the offspring of all") or *viśveṣām apatyam* ("the offspring of the Viśvas")—the pronominal operates in dependence upon that which is to be designated; thus, it is dependent.

And since that which is dependent is incapable [of independent function], it will not occur due to this incapacity. As for what was said—that by the very same cause there is one crow, so by that same cause there will be a second and a third crow—we do not dispute whether it is a crow or not a crow. What then? We dispute rather that by which this sentence comes to be.

By that very same reasoning, the application [of the suffix] would also follow in the case of "the offspring of a crow" (*kākasya apatyam*) and "the offspring of a osprey" (*kurarasya apatyam*). As for what was said—that number proceeds in dependence upon that which is to be numbered, and that which is dependent is incapable [of forming a compound]—it is indeed possible that for someone the object of dependence is determined through either the sense or the context. When...

When [the referent] is fully known, then the compound formation (*vṛtti*) occurs. As for what was said—that a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) functions in dependence upon that which is to be specified, and that being dependent, it is "incapable" (*asamartha*) [of forming a compound]—it is indeed the case that for someone, the object of dependence may be fully known from the context or from the sense. When it is fully known, then the compound formation occurs. If this is so, then...

Because it is not denoted, there will be no production [of the suffix] from *jāti* and the like. And that non-denotation must necessarily be accepted. For even when the mention of the name-former (*sañjñākārin*) is made, production occurs only where there is the denotation of the meaning by the suffix being produced from *jāti* and the like; for example: "From where does the peahen (*māyūrī*) come?"
Why is Kāpiñjali thin? Because he was bitten by a snake. [The names] Pāñci, Sutamasa, Tādāyani, Yādāyani, and Kaimāyani are considered [to be derived from patronymic suffixes].
Therefore, this mention of "one who forms a name" (*sañjñākārin*) must be made so that it does not apply to other purposes, specifically when a suffix follows another suffix.

A prohibition must be stated. Both [the mention of *gotra* and the prohibition] need not be done. The mention of *gotra* will not be made; it will simply be stated that "only one suffix occurs in the sense of offspring. For if a suffix were now to occur even after a form already ending in a suffix, then there would not be "only one suffix" in the sense of offspring. If the mention of *gotra* is not made, how [is the form] *gārgyāyaṇa* derived?

Regarding the term *vātsyāyana*: this must indeed be stated as "from a *gotra* [name], in the sense of a young descendant (*yuvan*), provided it is not feminine. Even if the mention of *gotra* is made, there is still no fault. It is not by the mention of "one" (*eka*) that the suffix is connected—meaning "only one suffix occurs in the *gotra* sense"—but rather, the base (*prakṛti*) is what is connected.

A single base produces a suffix in the sense of a lineage (*gotra*). If, moreover, a suffix were to be produced even after [a word] that already ends in a suffix, then a single base would not produce a suffix in the sense of a lineage. Alternatively, this effort is made at the wrong place; for this does not differ from common usage. In the world, people employ the term "one" when referring to a number as it occurs.
Or rather, it is the first [rule]. As long as one says "the first produces a suffix for the offspring," so long does "one [applies] to the lineage" hold.

4.1.95) Regarding *iñ* and the others: *phiñ* and *phin* take precedence over *vṛddha* and *avṛddha* by way of prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*). [This applies] to *iñ* and the others over *vṛddha* and *avṛddha*.

The suffixes *phiñ* and *phañ* occur by way of mutual exclusion (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of *iñ* is, for example, *Dākṣiḥ* and *Plākṣiḥ*. The scope of *phiñ* is, for example, *Tādāyaniḥ* and *Yādāyaniḥ*. In the case of *Tāpasāyaniḥ* and *Sāmmitikāyaniḥ*, both would apply; therefore, *phiñ* prevails. The scope of *phañ* is, for example, *Tvacāyaniḥ* and *Srucāyaniḥ*. The scope of *iñ* is the same as before. In the case of *Glucukāyaniḥ* and *Mulucukāyaniḥ*, both would apply; therefore, *phañ* prevails.

The suffixes *phiñ* and *phin* prevail by way of exception (*vipratiṣedha*). Why does it not occur here in the case of *dākṣiḥ* and *plākṣiḥ*? Because of the rule of diversity (*bahulavacana*). And [the suffix] *tadrāja* also [prevails]. The suffix *tadrāja* also prevails over *iñ* by way of exception. The scope of *tadrāja* is, for example, *aikṣvakaḥ*; the scope of *iñ* is the same. Here, both would apply in the cases of *pāñcālaḥ*, *vaidehaḥ*, and *vaidarbhaḥ*. The suffix *tadrāja* prevails by way of exception.

Regarding those [names] whose occurrence in the *bāhvādi* group and others is observed in the worldly state of lineage (*gotrabhāva*), there is a prohibition of them when that state is other than worldly.
Regarding those [names] whose occurrence in the *bāhvādi* group and others is observed in the worldly state of lineage, there is a prohibition of them when that state is other than worldly.

It must be stated: *bāhoḥ apatyam* [is] *bāhiḥ*. For that which is called *bāhu*, its offspring is *bāhiḥ*. *Naḍasya apatyam* [is] *nāḍāyanaḥ*. For that which is called *naḍa*, its offspring is *nāḍiḥ*. A prohibition must be stated regarding suffixes that denote relations from words that resemble them; for suffixes denoting relations, a prohibition must be stated from words resembling them.

The offspring of a father-in-law (*śvaśura*) is *śvaśurya*. For that which is called a "father-in-law" indeed belongs to the "son-in-law" (*śvaśuri*). There is no need for the explicit mention of the suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*); for words that denote a relationship (*sambandhi-śabda*) exclude [the application of a suffix] to something similar to them. By this, the following is also established: from the words *mātṛ* and *pitṛ*, the word *svasṛ* [forms] *mātṛṣvasā* ("mother's sister") and *anyā mātṛsvasā* ("another mother's sister").
(P_4,1.97) Regarding *sudhātṛ* and *vyāsa*: it should be stated that [the suffix *iñ* applies] after *sudhātṛ* and *vyāsa*; for example, *saudhātakiḥ*.
Śuka is the son of Vyāsa. This that has been said is too little; it should be stated as "of Sudhātṛ, Vyāsa, Varuḍa, Niṣāda, Caṇḍāla, and Bimba":
namely, Saudhātaki, Vaiyāsika Śuka, and so forth.
A descendant of Vāruḍa, a descendant of Naiṣāda, and a descendant of Caṇḍāla.
[Baimbakiḥ]. In that case, it should be stated [as a separate rule]. It need not be stated; these are distinct base forms (*prakṛti*).

For what purpose is the letter *c* [in the suffix *cha*]? It is for the sake of accent (*svarārtha*). By the rule "that which has the marker *cit* has an acute accent on its final syllable" (*citaḥ anta udāttaḥ bhavati*), it results in the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*).
So that it may be so. Now, what is the purpose of the letter *ñ*? The letter *ñ* is for the sake of *vṛddhi*. It is so that *vṛddhi* may occur by the rule "before *ñ*, *ṇ*, and *it*" (*ñṇiti*).

[Objection: Both purposes are accomplished by the single letter *k*. [Response: Nevertheless, another *anubandha* must necessarily be made here for the sake of specification (*viśeṣaṇa*). Where is there a need for the purpose of specification? In the rule "after *vrāta* and *cphañ*, provided it is not feminine" (*vrātacphañoḥ astriyām*). For [otherwise], it would be read as "after *phak*."

If it were stated [simply as] "phañ," then the suffix would also apply in the case of *nāḍāyana*. Furthermore, if it were stated as "phañ," then the suffix would also apply in the case of *āśvāyana*. Therefore, the letter *c* must indeed be added so that the word-final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) may also occur.
And now, since the letter *c* is being employed for the purpose of specification, another marker (*anubandha*) must necessarily be added for the purpose of [triggering] *vṛddhi*.

And that [suffix] must indeed be *ñ*, so that there may not be a division of the sūtra. Now, even if *c* were employed, the quality of being udātta on the final syllable would not be obtained. What is the reason? Because of its posteriority, the quality of being udātta on the initial syllable (by the rule *ñ-n-iti*) would apply.
[Objection: By virtue of the power of the marker *c*, there will be udātta on the final syllable; by virtue of the power of the marker *ñ*, there will be udātta on the initial syllable.

[The suffix] is obtained. There is another purpose for the addition of the marker *ñ*: the letter *ñ* is for the sake of *vṛddhi*. But there is also another purpose for the addition of the marker *c*: the letter *c* is for the sake of specification (*viśeṣaṇa*). In this case, it would have been possible to attach another marker for the sake of specification; however, because of the presence of the letter *c*, the final syllable becomes udātta. [Thus, the letter *ñ* serves the purpose of *vṛddhi*.]

Nevertheless, another [type of] suffix (*anubandha*) could have been attached. In that case, by virtue of the presence of the *ñ* as an indicatory letter (*it*), the rule for the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) would apply. If this is so, then a split in the grammatical connection (*yogavibhāga*) will be made regarding the accent: "This [rule] exists: *citaḥ*. That which has the *cit* suffix has its final syllable (*anta*) accented acute. Then: "*taddhitasya*. And that which has the *cit* suffix belonging to a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) has its final syllable accented acute. For what purpose?

This [suffix] would, by virtue of being marked with *ñ*, undergo the rule *ñniti* (Pāṇini 6.1.197), which prescribes that the first syllable is acute (*ādyudātta*). To prevent that, [the rule] *tataḥ kitaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.165) applies:

"The final syllable of a *taddhita* suffix marked with *k* is acute. But why is there this marker *c* added for the sake of accent, since the suffix *ñya* is prescribed after a stem ending in *cphañ*? In that case, it ought to be the first syllable that is acute by the rule *ñniti*. It is not so.

This is the case: so that when many [suffixes] have been elided, the word-final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) may apply, as in *kauñcāyanāḥ*. Here, some prescribe the suffix *phyañ* for the dual and singular, and *phak* for the plural; others [prescribe it] from a stem ending in *cphañ*.

[Objection: What is logical here? [Response: Only the mention of *ñya* is logical. For if *phyañ* were applied to the dual and singular, and *phañ* to the plural, then in the case of "a young student who is the descendant of the Krauñcāyanas" (*krauñcāyanānām apatyam māṇavakaḥ*), one would have *kauñjāyanyaḥ* (singular), *kauñjāyanyau* (dual). By what [rule] would the sound *ya* be heard [in the plural]? Since it is stated that [the suffix applies] to the dual and singular, it would not apply [to the plural]. Here, however, there are many descendants of Kauñjāyana.
"O Kauñjāyanas, young men, why is this word not heard? Since it is stated that [the suffix *cha*] applies to two or one, it would follow [that it does not apply here].

How, then, is the mention of *ñya* superior? If that were not the case, then the offspring (*apatya*) is the lineage (*gotra*). And the offspring is derived from the ultimate source (*paramaprakṛti*). From an offspring that is a living descendant, a second [suffix] is applied in the sense of the base itself, and it receives the designation 'yuvan' (junior)."

And that [suffix] is not feminine. Furthermore, the mention of the singular number in the rule for *gotra* is redundant, as it is already established in the case of suffixes that elide the plural marker (*bahuvacana-lopi*).

For if that [mention of the singular] were present, there would be no fault even when the suffix *phyañ* applies to two or one, or when *phañ* applies to many. In that regard, having analyzed the compound "the young boy who is the descendant of the Kauñjāyanas," the suffix will arise from the word *kuñja* to denote two or one.

595–596. Regarding the statement "not being a seer (*anṛṣi*) and [committing] an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*)," this is established therein: namely, Kauśika and Viśvāmitra. What is the reason? Viśvāmitra performed ascetic penance (*tapas*) thinking, "May I not be one who is not a seer. Thus, the venerable one became a seer. He again performed ascetic penance thinking, "May I not have a son who is not a seer. Thus, the venerable Gādhi also became a seer.

Furthermore, he performed austerities with the thought, "May I not be the grandson of a non-seer (anṛṣi). Thereupon, the venerable Kuśika also became a seer (ṛṣi). Thus, this constitutes a case of "uninterrupted succession of seers" (ṛṣyānantarya). In that case, the prohibition [stated in the rule] "when there is no uninterrupted succession of seers" (anṛṣyānantarye) would apply. This is not a fault. It is not understood in this way: "it does not occur when there is an uninterrupted succession of seers. How, then?

Then [the question arises]: "Is it not so in the case of an immediate descendant of a seer (*ṛṣi*)? If this is the case, then the mention of "not being an immediate descendant of a seer" (*anṛṣyānantarya*) is purposeless, because the governing topic is names (*saṃjñā*) and lineages (*gotra*).

The mention of "not being an immediate descendant of a seer" is purposeless. Why? Because the governing topic is names and lineages; the phrase "in the case of names and lineages" (*saṃjñāgotre*) continues to apply. What possibility is there for [the suffix] to occur in the case of an immediate descendant? It does not even apply there, so there is no need for a prohibition.

If this is so, then since [the formation of the word *nānāndra*] is already established, the fact that the Teacher teaches the prohibition "not after a non-seer" (*anṛṣyānantarye*) indicates that for those [patronymics] listed in the *bidādi* group which are not seers, the suffix *vṛddhi* occurs even when they follow immediately [after a feminine base]. What is the purpose of this indication? It is that [the forms] *nānāndraḥ*, *pautraḥ*, and *dauhitraḥ* are thereby established.

(P_4,1.108) Why is this stated? [Is it not the case that] it is already established by the rule *gargādibhyo yañ* alone? [One might say: "I shall state *luk striyām* [there]. But if it were stated right there [in that rule], it would not be possible;
for the mention of *Āṅgirasa* would be cut off.

(P_4,1.112) Why is the suffix *aṇ* prescribed after the group beginning with *śiva*, rather than simply saying "as prescribed"? If it were stated merely as "after *śiva* and so on, as prescribed," then the suffix *iñ* would be applicable; for *iñ* is prescribed [after these] by default. Therefore, there is a restatement.

What would be the purpose of this repetition now? What would be the purpose of repeating it now? It is for the sake of setting aside those [rules] that would otherwise sublate it. Indeed, there is no such thing that could sublate it. In that case, by the force of its very commencement, that which has been prescribed but does not otherwise apply will come into effect. And what is that? It is *aṇ* alone. If so, it is for the sake of subsequent rules:

[The rule applies] "to names of rivers and female humans that are not aged (avṛddha), provided they have those [specific] names. Here, if only "as prescribed" (*yathāvihita*) were stated, the suffix *ḍhak* would apply excessively. Since *ḍhak* is already prescribed after such [names], what would be the purpose of this repetition?

It is for the sake of subverting those [suffixes] which are its superseded exceptions. But there is indeed no such suffix that could supersede it; therefore, by the force of its very formulation [in this specific context].
Who is it that, though prescribed, does not obtain [the suffix], and will therefore come to be [by this rule]? It is *aṇ* alone. But then [this rule] is for the sake of what follows:

namely, the rule *ṛṣyandhakavṛṣṇikurubhyaś ca*. If only "as prescribed" (*yathāvihita*) were stated here, *iñ* would be over-extended. Since *iñ* is already prescribed after [names ending in] *at*, what would be the purpose of the repetition? It is for the purpose of setting aside those [suffixes] which are its sublaters.

Indeed, there is no such thing that could obstruct it. In this regard, by virtue of the capacity of the rule's formulation (*ārambha-sāmarthya*), that which is prescribed but does not otherwise obtain will come to pass. And what is that? It is precisely the suffix *aṇ*. [Objection: Then it is for the sake of the subsequent rule alone:
"After *mātṛ*, when preceded by a numeral, *saṃ*, or *bhadrā*..."

Regarding the rule *kanyāyāḥ kanīnaś ca*: if only "as prescribed" (*yathāvihitam*) were stated here, the suffix *ḍhak* would apply [to both]. Since *ḍhak* is already prescribed after [the word] *mātṛ*, what would be the purpose of this repetition? [The answer is: "I shall state the substitution of *ukāra* for *mātṛ* and the change of *kanyā* to *kanīna*. If this were the only purpose, he would have said that very thing right there.
"The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after feminine stems; the vowel *u* is substituted for the final of *mātṛ*; and the form *kanyā* undergoes the change to *kanīna*. If so, then this is the purpose:

This word *ṛṣṭiṣeṇa* is listed among the *śivādi* group. In that context, if it were stated simply as "in this much" (*iyati*), the suffix *iñ* would apply; however, because of its subsequent position, the suffix *ṇya* [prescribed] after words ending in *senā* would supersede it. In that case, by virtue of the force of the initial rule's formulation, *iñ* would still apply. But because of the re-introduction of the suffix *aṇ*, only *aṇ* occurs.

The suffixes *ḍhak* and *ḍhrak* [are applied] after the *aṇ* suffix [denoting] a seer (*ṛṣi*), by way of an exception (*vipratiṣedha*). The suffixes *ḍhak* and *ḍhrak* occur after the *aṇ* suffix [denoting] a seer by way of an exception. The scope (*avakāśa*) of the *aṇ* suffix is: *vāsiṣṭhaḥ*, *vaiśvāmitraḥ*. The scope of the *ḍhak* suffix is: ...
*duli* becomes *dauleyaḥ*;
*bali* becomes *bāleyaḥ*. Here, both [rules] would apply: *atri*, *ātreyaḥ*. This is the scope for the suffix *ṣyaṅ*:
*Makandikā* becomes *mākandika*. *Ḍhraka* is the occasion [for the suffix]: *kāṇikera*. Here both [suffixes] would apply:
*pauṇikera*.

Regarding *maudgalikera*: by means of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the suffixes *ḍhak* and *ḍhrañ* take precedence over *ḍhak*. While the rule "for a word of two syllables, the suffix *ḍhak*" applies, the suffixes *ḍhrañ* and *ḍhañ* occur instead by virtue of this conflict. The scope (*avakāśa*) of the rule "for a word of two syllables, the suffix *ḍhak*" is, for example, *dātteyaḥ*.
The suffix *gaupteya* is the same as *ḍhraka*. Here, both [suffixes] would apply:
*naṭī* → *nāṭeraḥ*, *dāsī* → *dāseraḥ*. [However,] *ḍhañ* has its own scope:

*Kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ*, *bhādrabāheyaḥ*. *Ḍhaka* is the same [as *ḍhak*]. Here, both [suffixes] would apply: *jambū-jāmbeyaḥ*. By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), *ḍhraṅ* and *ḍhañ* occur. Or rather, it is not so; for there is a restatement of the suffix *aṇ* [which applies] after the names of sages (*ṛṣi*).

For the purpose of excluding others. Or rather, this contradiction between the suffix *aṇ* [from the rule for seers] and the suffix *ḍhak* is not logical. What is the reason? The restatement of *aṇ* [in the rule for seers] is for the purpose of excluding others. In this case, *aṇ* is already established by the general rule (*utsarga*) alone. The purpose of its restatement is to set aside those other exceptions (*apavāda*) that would otherwise apply.

Just as that *apavāda* (*iñ*) sublates the former [rule], so too would it sublate the *ḍhak*. Therefore, when the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed after the word "ṛṣi," there must be a prohibition of [the application of] *atri* and others. Thus, when the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed after the word "ṛṣi," a prohibition of *atri* and others must be stated. It need not be stated. For it is a principle that intermediate *apavādas* sublate preceding rules; thus, this *ṛṣya-aṇ* sublates the *iñ*.

It will supersede *ḍhak*, yet it will not supersede [it]. Furthermore, this contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*)—namely, that between *ḍhak* and *ḍrag-ḍhañ*—is improper. What is the reason? The restatement of *ḍhak* is for the purpose of excluding others. In this case, *ḍhak* is already established by the rule "from feminine stems, *ḍhak*" (*strībhyaḥ ḍhak*). Its restatement serves this purpose: to exclude those other suffixes which are exceptions (*apavāda*) to it.

They apply for the purpose of subverting that [general rule]. Just as that [rule] subverts the suffix *aṇ* which bears the same name as its exception, so too would it subvert the suffixes *ḍhak* and *ḍhrañ*. Therefore, the suffix *aṇ* is not applied after a non-dvysvara (non-two-syllabled) word. Thus it should be stated: "Therefore, the suffix *aṇ* is not applied after a non-dvysvara word. It need not be stated. For it is a principle that intermediate exceptions subvert preceding rules; thus, this [case] is explained in that manner.

The suffix *ḍhak*—which includes the *aṇ* prescribed by the rule *tannāmikāṇ*—will set aside that exception (*tadapavāda*), but it will not set aside the suffixes *ḍhrak* and *ḍhañ*. By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the suffix *ṇya* applies after [names of] sages (*ṛṣi*), Andhakas, Vṛṣṇis, and Kurus, as well as after words ending in *senā*. The scope (*avakāśa*) of the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* is, for example: *vāsiṣṭhaḥ*.
The scope of the suffix *ṇya* is:
*pāriṣeṇyaḥ*, *vāriṣeṇyaḥ*. There is a seer named Jātasena; from him both [suffixes] would apply. By the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), *ṇya* occurs. The scope of *andhakāṇa* is:

Śvāphalkaḥ, śvaitrakaḥ. For [the patronymic] in -ṇya, it is the same. Ugrasena by name is an Andhaka; from him both [suffixes] would apply. By the rule of conflict (vipratiṣedha), the suffix -ṇya occurs: *augrasenyaḥ*. The scope of the vṛṣṇi-ṇa [suffix] is: Vāsudeva.
*Bāladeva*: [The patronymic] *bāla* belongs to him; he is the Vṛṣṇi named Vaiṣvaksena. From that, both suffixes would apply. By the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the suffix *ṇya* applies:

*vaiṣvaksenya*. The scope of *kurvaṇa* is: *nākula*, *sāhadeva*. [The patronymic] *bhīma* belongs to him; he is the Kuru named Bhīmasena. From that, both suffixes would apply. By the rule of conflict, the suffix *ṇya* applies: [the form *bhaimaseniya*].
The suffix *ṇya* occurs after [stems ending in] *senā* by way of an exception (*vipratiṣedha*). It should be stated that [the suffix applies] after *jāta*, *ugra*, *viṣvak*, and *bhīma*.

(Pāṇini 4.1.115) For what purpose is the reference made in the feminine gender? Why not simply say "not after [a word] preceded by a numeral or *saṃbhadra*"? [The answer is: so that it may apply to the word *mātṛ* when it is in the feminine gender. In this case, [it would not apply] to *mā*...
The word *bhūt* [is explained as follows]: one who measures is a *sammātṛ*; the offspring of a *sammātṛ* is a *sāmmātra*.
This is a contradiction. What is the contradiction? The term "offspring" (*apatya*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. If she is a maiden (*kanyā*), she is not offspring;
if she is offspring, she is not a maiden. To say "she is both a maiden and offspring" is a contradiction. This is not so.

This is contradictory. How so? This word *kanyā* (virgin) ceases to apply when there has been sexual intercourse preceded by union with a man. Yet, for that girl who at present has not yet had sexual intercourse with a man prior to such union, the word *kanyā* still applies. Thus, the offspring of a *kanyā*—one who is called a *kanyā*, one who is regarded as a *kanyā*, one who is beautiful to behold—is called *kānīna*.

This is deliberated upon in all instances where the term *strī* ("woman") is mentioned: does it refer to the technical suffixes (*strī-pratyaya*), or to the word-form *strī* itself, or to the meaning "female"? What follows from this? If it were a reference to the word-form or the meaning, then [the rule would apply to] *iḍaviḍ*.

Aiḍadiṭ, pṛth, pārtha, uśij, auśija, śarat, and śārada—here too [the suffix] would apply. Now, if there is a mention of the *pratyaya* (suffix), then forms such as *laikhābhreyaḥ* and *vaimātreyaḥ* would not be established. Let there be a mention of the *pratyaya*. How then are *laikhābhreyaḥ* and *vaimātreyaḥ* formed? They will be included in the list of *śubhra* and others (*śubhrādi*). [This applies] when the offspring of a *vaḍavā* is to be expressed as a male. [The rule applies] to the *vaḍavā*.

When the meaning is "bull" (*vṛṣa*), the suffix *ḍhak* should be stated [after the word *vaḍavā*]. A bull belonging to a mare is *vāḍaveya*. (P_4.1.128) Regarding *caṭakā*, there must be a specification in the masculine gender; that is, a specification in the masculine gender must be made for *caṭakā* here.

It might also be as follows: the offspring of a *caṭaka* (sparrow) is a *cāṭakaira*. If the masculine gender is specified—as in "the offspring of a *caṭakā* (female sparrow) is a *cāṭakaira*"—this would not be established. However, when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included;
thus it will be so. [But] there must be elision (*luk*) in the case of a female offspring. Elision must be stated for the feminine when it is an offspring.

The feminine offspring of a *caṭaka* is a *caṭakā*. (P_4.1.130) The mention of *āraṅ* is purposeless, because it is already established by the suffix *rak*. The mention of *āraṅ* is purposeless. What is the reason?

[The suffix] *rak* is established [by rule]. [In the case of *godhā*,] it ends in the vowel *ā*, and *rak* is the suffix. If this is so, then since [the form] is already established, the fact that the Teacher teaches [the suffix] *ārak* indicates that this [suffix *rak*] also occurs after other [bases]. What is the purpose of this indication? It is so that forms such as *mauṇḍāraḥ*, *jāṇḍāraḥ*, and *pāṇḍāraḥ* may be established.
It is said, "from low-born women" (*kṣudrābhyaḥ*). Who is called a "low-born woman"? One who has had sexual relations with many men or one who is physically deformed.

605. Regarding the offspring of a *rājan*, there must be a mention of the caste (*jāti*). One must specify the offspring of a *rājan* as a caste; [the term] *rājanya* refers to a caste. In what case should it not apply? As in *rājanaḥ*. (P_4.1.145) KA_II,260.2-6 Ro_III, 606. The statement regarding the suffix *vyan* is purposeless because there is no referent for the suffix. The statement regarding *vyan* is purposeless. For what reason?

Because of the absence of the meaning of the suffix. What is this "because of the absence of the meaning of the suffix"? Because of the absence of the meaning of offspring (*apatya*). The term "offspring" is understood [from the context], yet the word *bhrātṛvya* is also used for one who is not an offspring, namely for an enemy (*sapatna*), as in "by the evil enemy, the *bhrātṛvya*. Let it be granted, then, that in that case *bhrātṛvya* means both offspring and enemy. But how [is it used] in the phrase "by the evil enemy, the *bhrātṛvya*"?
Thus, it is established by way of analogy: *bhrātṛvya* is like an adversary (*bhrātṛvya*). (P.
4.1.147) What is the purpose of the letter *ṇ*? It is for the sake of *vṛddhi*. So that there may be *vṛddhi* according to the rule *ñṇiti*; as in *gārgyaḥ*.

[Objection: A fool! The addition of the marker *ṇ* to the affix after a feminine word denoting a lineage (*gotra*) is purposeless, because the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is already "vṛddha" (possessing a long vowel in its first syllable). [Response: The addition of the marker *ṇ* to the affix after a feminine word denoting a lineage is indeed purposeless. What is the reason? Because the nominal stem is already "vṛddha. This nominal stem is already "vṛddha" by nature. [Objection: Then the marker *ṇ* must be made for the sake of elision (*luk*). [That is, it applies] to that which ends in elision.

The non-elision (*avṛddha*) is for the sake of ensuring that elision (*vṛddhi*) occurs where it ought to. [Example: *vātaṇḍaḥ* [is] a rogue. If it is argued that this is for the sake of elision (*luk*), we say no, because of the prohibition of elision. If it is argued that it is for the sake of elision, that is not so. What is the reason? Because of the prohibition of elision. For here, elision is prohibited by the rule:

"There is no elision (*aluk*) in the case of a *gotra* [patronymic] when followed by a vowel (*aci*). If it is argued that there is no prohibition because of the intervention [of a sound], we say no; because of the intervention of the long *ī* (*īkāra*), the prohibition applies.

[The suffix] is not obtained [after *mālā*]. If it is argued that there is no prohibition because of the intervention [of the *taddhita* suffix], we say no, because of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution). If it is argued that there is no prohibition because of the intervention, that is not so. What is the reason? Because of the *puṃvadbhāva*. Here, *puṃvadbhāva* occurs;

for when a *taddhita* suffix follows, *puṃvadbhāva* occurs for a *bha*-stem provided the suffix does not begin with the augment *aṭ*. However, the letter *ṇ* is for the sake of the *phin* suffix. But the letter *ṇ* is indeed for the sake of the *phin* suffix.

It must be prescribed so that the augment *vṛddhi* occurs where there is a suffix ending in a *phin* that does not have *vṛddhi*. For example: *glaucukāyanaḥ* [is] a rogue (*jālmaḥ*). Furthermore, the letter *ṇ* must be prescribed for the purpose of prohibiting the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). For the purpose of prohibiting the masculine form, the letter *ṇ* must be made; otherwise, in the case of *gārgī bhāryā asya* ("he whose wife is a Gārgī"), the prohibition of the masculine form would apply by the rule "of that which has *vṛddhi* as its cause" (*vṛddhinimittasya*), just as [in the following].

It might be argued that this is unnecessary because of the rule "from the *gotra* [stem], for the *yuvan* [derivative], provided it is not feminine" (*gotrād yūni astriyām*). Because of the statement "from the *gotra* [stem], for the *yuvan* [derivative], provided it is not feminine," this [suffix] would be without purpose. [Objection: There is no such thing as a "Gārgā" [in the sense of a *yuvan* descendant]. Or rather, the purpose is for the sake of the feminine, because she does not belong to the lineage (*avaṃśyatvāt*).

Or rather, the purpose is for the sake of the feminine because she does not belong to the lineage; a woman does not belong to the lineage. [Reply: There is indeed a woman who is a Gārgā. Another says:
There are only two lineages: the maternal lineage (*mātṛvaṃśa*) and the paternal lineage (*pitṛvaṃśa*). To the extent that there is a maternal lineage, O Gārgī, it does not exist [independently]. (P.

4.1.148) From a feminine name belonging to a *gotra* that ends in a *vṛddhi* vowel, the suffixes *ṭhak*, *pheḥ*, *cha*, and *phāṇṭāhṛti* apply; these are four rules. Among them, three concern contempt (*kutsana*), and the third concerns the *Sauvīra* *gotra*. The first rule applies only in the sense of contempt.
The suffix *paraḥ* belongs to the Sauvīra clan alone.
(Pāṇini 4.1.150) What is the purpose of the letter *ṇ*? It is for the sake of *vṛddhi*. So that the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed by the rule *ñṇiti* may occur, as in *phāṇṭāhṛtaḥ*.

The addition of the marker *ṇit* to the suffix after the stem *phāṇṭāhṛti* is purposeless because the nominal stem is already *vṛddha*. The addition of the marker *ṇit* to the suffix after *phāṇṭāhṛti* is redundant. Why? Because the nominal stem is already *vṛddha*; this nominal stem is indeed *vṛddha*. However, it is for the sake of prohibiting the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*); that is, it serves to prohibit the application of the masculine form.

The letter *ṇ* must be applied [as a marker]. In the case of *phāṇṭāhṛtabhāryaḥ*, meaning "one whose wife is from Phāṇṭāhṛta," the prohibition of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) by the rule *vṛddhinimittasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.40) is intended so that it may occur. Or rather, it has already been stated. What has been stated? It was stated that because of the rule *gotrāt yūni astriyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.95), there is no purpose [for the prohibition]; or, because the woman does not belong to the lineage (*avaṃśyatvāt*), there is a purpose for the prohibition.

(P_4.1.151) *Vāmaratha* is like *Kaṇva* and others, with the exception of the accent. It should be stated that *vāmaratha* undergoes the same treatment as *kaṇva* and others. Is this without qualification? No, he says; it is with the exception of the accent. What is the purpose? [To apply it to] *vāmarathyasya*.

The students are the Vāmarathas. [This is stated] so that the suffix *aṇ* may apply according to the rule *kaṇvādibhyo gotre*. If it were said "as in the case of *kaṇva* and others," then the basis for the suffix (*pratyayāśraya*) would not be extended. What is the fault in that? [In the case of] the Vāmarathas: the elision (*lopa*) in the plural would not apply. [And in the case of] a group (*saṅgha*) of Vāmarathas: the suffix *aṇ*—prescribed by the rule *saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇeṣv añyañiñām aṇ*—would not apply.

If, on the other hand, it were stated as *yañvat*, even so, that which depends on the base (*prakṛti*) would not be extended [to the derivative]. What fault would there be in that? [The fault is that] for *vāmarathāḥ*—meaning "the pupils of Vāmarathya"—the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule *kaṇvādibhyo gotre* would not apply.
Let it be, then, simply *kaṇvādivat*. But how [would one explain] *vāmarathānām saṅghaḥ* ("an assembly of Vāmarathas")? That which...
"This [rule] excludes the accent," says the Teacher; this indicates that even that which is extended by analogy (*atideśa*) is dependent upon the suffix (*pratyaya*).

4.1.153) Regarding the rule for the suffix *añ* according to the Northern Grammarians (*udīcām*), the suffix *aṇ* must be stated after the word *takṣan*. In the rule for the suffix *añ* according to the Northern Grammarians, the suffix *aṇ* should be prescribed after *takṣan*.

*Tākṣṇaḥ*. If, however, this word *takṣan* were recited among the *śiva*-group [in the list of *gotra* names], then, if it belonged to the *śiva*-group, the suffix *ṇya* would be prescribed. If it belonged to the *śiva*-group, then *ṇya* would have to be applied; thus, the form would be *tākṣṇyaḥ*. But this is established by the statement that for the Northerners (*udīcām*), the suffix *ṇya* is optional.
This is established. How? By the statement that for the Northerners, *ṇya* occurs optionally. One must state: "For the Northerners, *ṇya* is optional. Thus, the form *tākṣṇyaḥ* is also established.
"Whatever one obtains from whatever [source] when liberated by means of that [source], he shall become that [source].

(Pāṇini 4.1.155). Why is there this mention of *kausalyaka* and *kārmārya*, which are derivatives (*vikṛti*)? It is so that [the rule] may apply to these two derivatives. This is stated too little; for [the following applies]:

"And from *dagu*, *kausala*, *karmāra*, *chāga*, and *vṛṣan*. It should be stated that in the section on the suffix *phiñ*, "for *dagu*, *kausala*, *karmāra*, *chāga*, and *vṛṣan*, there is also [the substitution of] *yuṭ*. [Thus we have: from *dagu*: *dāgavyāyaniḥ*; from *kausala*: *kausalayāyaniḥ*;
from *karmāra*: *karmāryāyaṇiḥ*; from *chāga*: *chāgyāyaniḥ*; from *vṛṣan*: *vārṣyāyaṇiḥ*. If...

The *yuṭ* augment is applied; once *yuṭ* has been applied, because it is not initial, the substitution does not apply. This must be considered here: "Should *yuṭ* be applied, or the substitution? What should be done in this case? The substitution [should take place] because it is subsequent. *Yuṭ* is obligatory (*nitya*); it applies whether the substitution has occurred or not. *Yuṭ* is also non-obligatory (*anitya*), for it applies when another [element] has undergone substitution.

Furthermore, a grammatical rule (*vidhi*) that applies when another word-form has not yet been produced becomes non-eternal (*anitya*). In that case, *yuṭ* would be more internal (*antaraṅga*). What constitutes its internality? *Yuṭ* is prescribed as being co-occurrent with the production [of the suffix]. Once the suffix has been produced, the substitution for the stem (*aṅga*) is prescribed by depending upon both the stem and the suffix. But the substitute (*ādeśa*) is also internal. How so? This will be explained in the section concerning *āyan* and other such forms.

"The statement 'it is like an *upadeśa* for the sake of establishing its own form' [is incorrect]. In that case, the suffix *yuṭ* would have no scope. If that is so, then it shall be treated as a *pūrvānta* (belonging to the preceding element).

If it is treated as a *pūrvānta*, then in the case of *dāgavyāyaniḥ*, the rule 'guṇa for *o*' (*oḥ guṇaḥ*) would not apply. Let it then be a *parādi* (belonging to the following element). But was it not said that once *yuṭ* is applied, because it does not begin with the original root, the substitution would not apply? No, this is not so."

There is a fault. But it is established by the statement that *yuṭ* is prescribed for that which has been substituted. This is established. How? By the statement that *yuṭ* is prescribed for that which has been substituted. It should be stated: "*yuṭ* [is applied] to that which has been substituted. Then it must indeed be stated. No, it need not be stated. For by the word "and" (*ca*), a simultaneous application (*sanniyoga*) will be made: "*yuṭ* and whatever else follows. And what else follows? "Substitution" (*ādeśa*).

Furthermore, if this *kuṭ* were made to follow after [the root], then the substitution for the beginning of the suffix would be untenable because it would not be initial. When *kuṭ* is present, the substitution for the beginning of the suffix is not possible. What is the reason? Because it would not be initial. When *kuṭ* is present...

Because it is beginningless (*anāditva*), the substitution (*ādeśa*) does not apply. If that is so, then let it be treated as a prior element (*pūrvānta*). [Objection: If it is treated as a prior element, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) must be stated. For example, in *cārmikāyaṇiḥ* and *vārmikāyaṇiḥ*, the elision of *n*—by the rule "the *n* at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is elided"—does not apply. However, if it occurs at the beginning of the subsequent element (*parādau*), then the elision of *n* by the rule "the *n* at the end of a nominal stem" applies.

Thus, the elision of *n* is established. Let it then be that [the suffix] begins with *par*. But was it not said that if there is *kuṭ*, because it is not initial, the substitution does not apply? It is established, however, by the statement that *kuṭ* applies to that which has been substituted. This is established. How so? It should be stated: "and *kuṭ* applies to that which has been substituted. Then that must be stated. No, it need not be stated; for by the particle *ca*, there is a conjunction [of conditions].

It will be formed. And [the suffix] *kuṭ* [is added]. What else? Whatever else is applicable. What else is applicable? A substitute (*ādeśa*). It is thus established. In that case, the rule (*sūtra*) is altered. Let it remain exactly as it was originally formulated. But was it not said that there must be a statement regarding the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) at the end of the preceding word? This is provided for in the very original formulation itself: "In the case of *carmin* and *varmin*, there is also the elision of *n*. [This applies to] those who act.

The suffix *phiñ* [is applied] after [patronymics] other than those of the *gotra* class by way of an exception (*vipratiṣedha*). [The rule] "the suffix *iñ* occurs after [words ending in] *kārin*" is set aside by the rule "the suffix *phiñ* occurs after [patronymics] other than those of the *gotra* class. The scope (*avakāśa*) of the rule "the suffix *iñ* occurs after [words ending in] *kārin*" is, for example, *āyaskāriḥ* and *lauhakāriḥ*. The scope of the suffix *phiñ* is, for example, *tāpasāyaniḥ* and *sāmmitikāyaniḥ*. In the case of *nāpitāyaniḥ*, both [rules] would apply; [therefore, *phiñ* prevails].
The suffix *phiñ* occurs by way of prohibition [of other suffixes].

If *ṣuk* were made a prior element (*pūrvānta*), then in the case of *mānuṣa-* [with the suffix *aṇ*], when forming a plural, the elision (*lopa*) would apply. [For example,] "an assembly of humans" (*mānuṣāṇāṃ saṅghaḥ*).

In the case of the technical term *saṅgha* (assemblage), the suffix *aṇ* would apply by the rule for words ending in *añ* or *iñ*. Let it then be a *parādi* (having the augment as its initial element). If it were a *parādi*, the long vowel *ī* would not apply in the case of *mānuṣī* derived from a word ending in *añ*. Let it then be a *pūrvānta* (having the augment as its final element). [Objection: How then do we get *mānuṣāḥ* and *mānuṣāṇāṃ saṅghaḥ*? [Response: In both cases, the term *gotra* refers to a worldly (secular) lineage, and this [the word *mānuṣa*] is not such a worldly lineage.

In that case, for the word *mānuṣyaka*, the elision [of the final vowel] prescribed by the rule *halas taddhitasya* would apply. This same fault occurs even if [the suffix] is at the beginning. For the mention of *hal* in the rule *halas taddhitasya* cannot be understood as a qualifier of the stem (*aṅga*).
In that case, there would be a fault here: from *vṛka* with the suffix *ṭeṇyaṇ*, the form *vārkeṇī* [would be incorrect]. Therefore, it must be stated by both [rules].
By nature, [the suffix] *aka* is applied after words meaning "king," "man," and "youth" (Pāṇini 4.1.162).
When the technical designation *gotra* applies to descendants starting from the grandson, the designation "starting from the grandson" is applied to that which is the offspring.

Regarding the technical designation *gotra* for those beginning with the grandson: it should be stated that the designation *gotra* applies to the grandson and subsequent descendants of whichever person one intends to be the progenitor (*apatya*). For even Garga may be a grandson to someone, and Kuśika as well. Therefore, [the rule] should not apply in such cases. [Objection: Then that must be stated. [Reply: It need not be stated. The phrase "from the first among those capable [of forming a compound]" (*samarthānām prathamāt vā*) continues to apply.

It is understood that among capable [ancestors], the offspring of the first [ancestor] beginning with the grandson is designated as such. And one whose lineage is living, if he is contemptible, should be stated to bear the name of his *gotra*. "You are a Gārgya, you wretch! You are a Vātsya, you wretch! But what is the contempt here? [Contempt for] one who possesses a designation in the world derived from his father.

One must be dependent. He who is now independent because he has a father is addressed [as follows]: "O Gārgya, you are a fool! You do not deserve to be designated by [the patronymic] derived from your father. (Pāṇini 4.1.163) KA_II,265.10–266.15 Ro_III, [179]–[180]1.1.62. *svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasyāśabdasamjñā* || P_4,1.163 || Kāśikāvṛtti: "In this section, one's own form (*svarūpa*) is understood to be the meaning of the word, except when it is a technical grammatical term (*saṃjñā*). [Question] Why is it stated that "except when it is a technical grammatical term"? [Answer] It is for the purpose of excluding cases such as "the *kṛt* suffixes" (*kṛt-pratyayāḥ*). [Question] What is the purpose of this rule? [Answer] It is so that one's own form may be understood as the meaning of the word. [Question] Of what kind of word? [Answer] Of a word that is not a technical grammatical term. [Question] Is it not already established that "one's own form" is understood as the meaning of the word even without this rule?
