Regarding the rule *jīvati tu vaṃśye yuvā* ("But while the ancestor lives, [the grandson] is called 'yuvan'"), it should be stated that this refers to those starting from the grandson (*pautraprabhṛti*). That is to say, it must be stated: "But while the ancestor lives, [the grandson] is called 'yuvan'; and this refers to those starting from the grandson. Well then, should it be stated? It need not be stated.
The term "starting from the grandson" (*pautraprabhṛti*) is understood [from the previous rule]. If that is so, then he is merely restating that "starting from the grandson" is understood.
What is the purpose of providing this grammatical explanation? It is for the sake of *devadattīya*. [The derivation is as follows:
"the offspring of Devadatta" is *devadattiḥ*; [this is stated] so that the designation *yuvan* (younger descendant) does not apply to the offspring immediately following [the father].
But then, the designation *yuvan* would apply to the grandson of Devadatta. This too occurs starting from the grandson; it does not start from the grandson.
By this [rule], "offspring" (apatya) is connected:
namely, that offspring which begins with the grandson (pautra). What then? It is connected to the lineage (vaṃśya):
namely, that offspring while a member of the lineage beginning with the grandson is living. Even so, in the case of Devadatta’s two sons...

[Objection: "In the case of the younger [brother], the designation 'yuvan' (younger) would apply even to an elder brother. [Response: In that case, it is *apatyam* (offspring) itself that is connected [as the referent], not an offspring that stands in grammatical apposition with [the term] *pautra-prabhṛti* (starting from grandson). It is not understood thus: "that which is an offspring starting from the grandson. How then? [It is understood as] "the offspring of one starting from the grandson. And [this applies] for the sake of honoring an elder.

And in the case of honoring an elder, the designation "youth" (yuvasañjñā) should be stated [as applicable]. For example: "The venerable Gārgyāyaṇas; the venerable Vātsyāyanas. But what here constitutes "honor"? In the world, being desired as a youth is metaphorically designated as "honor. Thus, those venerable ones become pleased when they are treated as youths. Alternatively, a descendant is the lineage (gotra); or rather, the descendant is designated by the term "lineage."

It should be stated: "There is [a suffix]. And [there is] a descendant of the ultimate progenitor (*paramaprakṛti*). It should be stated: "And there is a descendant of the ultimate progenitor. From a descendant who belongs to a living lineage, a second suffix is to be stated for the sake of the base meaning itself (*svārthe*), and it is to be stated that it receives the technical designation *yuvan* (young descendant). And that...

"It should be stated that [the suffix] *sa-* occurs when not feminine (*astriyām*). Furthermore, the mention of the singular and the lineage (*eka-gotra-grahaṇa*) is unnecessary. By doing so, the mention of the singular and the lineage becomes purposeless. Moreover, it is established for those cases where the plural number is elided. For instance, having analyzed 'the descendant of the Bidas is a young boy' (*bidāṇām apatyam māṇavakaḥ*), from the word *bida*, [the suffix is applied] in the sense of two or one."

The suffix will arise [in the singular]: *baidaḥ*, *baidau*. Having analyzed [the compound] as "many young students (*māṇavakāḥ*) who are the offspring (*apatyam*) of Baida," the suffix will arise from the word *bid-* in the sense of plurality:
*bidāḥ*.

620–621. What is the purpose of mentioning "another" (*anyagrahaṇam*)? [The word] "brother" (*bhrātari*) is understood from the preceding context; [the mention of "another"] is so that [the rule may apply] to any *sapiṇḍa* relative.

Now, what is the purpose of mentioning "one who is older" (*sthavirataragrahaṇam*)? It is so that [the rule applies] to one distinguished on both counts: by position (*sthānataḥ*) and by age (*vayastaḥ*).

Now, while the word "living" (*jīvati*) is already understood from the context, what is the purpose of mentioning "living" (*jīvati*) again? It is so that [the rule applies] when [the elder] is living and [the younger] is also living.
It might be argued: "Let it not be so when [the person] is dead. For when one is dead, it must simply be 'the dead man is to be sought' (*mṛto mārgyaḥ*).
Now, does the coexistence of the *gotra* and the *yuvan* suffixes occur, or rather not? And what follows from this? It certainly follows.

For this is not a governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning a single notion. What follows from this? What fault would there be in the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of two *gotra* suffixes? That which is caused by it would occur. What fault is there in the co-occurrence of two *gotra* suffixes? That which is caused by it results: rules based on *gotra* would apply even to the *yuvan* (descendant) degree. For example, in the case of *Yāskāyanayaḥ* and *Lāhyāyanayaḥ*, the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule "from *yaska*- etc., in the sense of *gotra*" would result.

There is no fault regarding the *yaska*-class [of names], because of the continued application of the rule "not in the case of a youth" (*na yūni*). There is no fault regarding the *yaska*-class. What is the reason? Because of the continued application of the rule "not in the case of a youth. The phrase "not in the case of a youth" is carried over there from that [preceding rule]. Where was it introduced? From the rule "not after *taulvali* and others" (*na taulvalibhyaḥ*).

There is a fault regarding the *atri*, *bida*, and *pañcāla* [classes], because of the continued application of the rule "not in the case of a youth. If the rule "not in the case of a youth" is indeed carried over...
In this regard, forms such as *ātrayaḥ*, *baidaḥ*, *pāñcālaḥ*, and *māṇavakaḥ* would not be established. This is not a fault; the connection [of the rule] will continue.

[The rule] "not after *taulvali*" applies: the elision (*luk*) of the *tadrāja* suffix occurs when many [descendants] are denoted, provided it is not feminine, but it does not occur in the case of a *yuvan* (grandchild) after *taulvali*. The elision of the *gotra* suffix occurs after *yaska* and others, but not in the case of a *yuvan*. The phrase "after *taulvali*" is no longer operative. [This concerns the rule regarding] *yañ* and *añ*.
And there is elision (*luk*) after *Atri*, *Bhṛgu*, *Kutsa*, *Vasiṣṭha*, *Gotama*, and *Aṅgiras*. The phrase "not when [denoting] a younger descendant" (*yūni na*) has ceased to apply here.

In this case, for example: "the students of Kāṇvyāyana" (*kāṇvyāyanīyāḥ*). By the rule "after *Kaṇva* and others, [the suffix] *aṇ* [is applied] in the sense of a lineage" (*gotre*), the suffix *aṇ* would be required.

There is no fault regarding *Kaṇva* and the others; it does not apply to a younger descendant, and beyond that, there is no fault. Why? Because there is no fault in the case of *Kaṇva* and the others. What [fault could there be]?
The reason is that there is nothing further [to be added] after the youth (yuvan). It is stated [in the rule] "after a nominal stem ending in that which is prescribed after Kaṇva and others.
Now, that which is prescribed after Kaṇva and others here is not a nominal stem ending in it;

and that nominal stem which ends in it does not [itself] come after Kaṇva and others. In this case, however, [one might argue]: "the offspring of Aupagava is Aupagavi"—thus [there would be] one [derivative].

Because of this restriction, namely that "in the sense of *gotra*," the suffix would not be applicable. [For] there is only one [rule]: "In the sense of *gotra*, [the suffix is applied] word-for-word (*pratipadam*).

Here, the suffixes are prescribed word-for-word by the rule: "After a *gotra* [stem], in the sense of a younger descendant (*yuvan*), provided it is not feminine. If that were the case, then multiple suffixes would apply after a stem ending in a *gotra* suffix. One should remember that [the rule applies] "after a *gotra* [stem], in the sense of a *yuvan*"; one should remember that [the rule applies] "after a *gotra* [stem], in the sense of a *yuvan*, provided it is not feminine. Why?

[Objection: It is stated that the elision (*aluk*) occurs in the *gotra* [suffix] when there is only one [descendant]. That [elision] would then apply even in the case of a *yuvan* [descendant]. [Reply: Let it be so. There will be elision (*luk*) again in the case of the *yuvan*. [Objection: This cannot be done. There would be a fault regarding the suffixes *phak* and *phiñ*. For example, the students of a *yuvan* descendant of Śālaṅki would be called *śālaṅkāḥ*, and the students of Paila would be called *pailāḥ*. Because of the rule "the suffixes *phak* and *phiñ* may optionally [be elided]," the optional hearing of those suffixes would result [even where they should not appear].

Therefore, it must be stated that the designation "lineage" (*gotra*) is prohibited when the designation "youth" (*yuvan*) applies. It need not be stated. The particle *tu* is restrictive; since *tu* is employed, it will serve as the restrictor:

namely, that while the ancestor (*vaṃśya*) is living, the descendant receives only the designation "youth. If, then, the designation "lineage" [is applied] when the designation "youth" [is to be applied],...

Those rules which are desired to apply when [the suffix] *ya* is present do not succeed when it depends on a *gotra* (patronymic). For example: *gārgyāyaṇānāṃ samūhaḥ* ("a collection of Gārgyāyaṇas") results in *gārgyāyaṇakam*; *gārgyāyaṇānāṃ kiṃcit* ("something belonging to the Gārgyāyaṇas") results in *gārgyāyaṇakam*; and *gārgyāyaṇo bhaktir asya* ("he whose devotion is to a Gārgyāyaṇa") results in *gārgyāyaṇakaḥ*. In these cases, the suffix *vuñ*, which depends on a *gotra*, would not be obtained. If that is so, then the rule "from *rājanya* and from *manuṣya* [the suffix] *vuñ*" serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the worldly usage.

Furthermore, the fact that the Teacher makes mention of "rājanya" and "manuṣya" in the rule prescribing the suffix *vuñ* indicates that the mention of "gotra" refers to the worldly sense. In common usage, a youth is called a "gotra": "What is your gotra, young man? "I am a Gārgyāyaṇa. "What is your gotra, young man? "I am a Vātsyāyana. If this is what is being indicated...

In the case of *aupagaveḥ yūnaḥ chātrāḥ aupagavīyāḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* would apply by virtue of the rule regarding *gotra* (lineage). [This indicates that] it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for collective formations (*sāmūhika*). If it is an indicator for collective formations, then in the case of *gārgyāyaṇānām kim cit gārgyāyaṇakam*—meaning "something belonging to the Gārgyāyaṇas"—or *gārgyāyaṇo bhaktir asya gārgyāyaṇakaḥ* ("Gārgyāyaṇa is his devotion"), the suffix *vuñ* based on *gotra* would not apply. Therefore, this [example] is an indicator with respect to the prescription of *vuñ*. It is an indicator in the rule prescribing *vuñ*.

It is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). If it is an indicator regarding the rule for *vuñ*, then in the case of "the students of Śālaṅki, who is young, are Śālaṅkāḥ," the suffix *aṇ*—which applies by the rule "after a patronymic ending in *iñ*"—would not be obtained. Let it then apply without distinction. [Objection: How then would "the students of Aupagavi, who is young, are Aupagavīyāḥ" be formed?

[In this case] the suffix *aṇ* would be obtained by the rule "after a patronymic ending in *iñ*. [Response: This is not a fault. We shall qualify the suffix *iñ* by means of the term "patronymic" (*gotra*). [That is, we will specify that the rule applies only when the *iñ* denotes a *gotra*. In the case of a *gotra*...
Regarding the rule "yaḥ iñ vihitaḥ":
[it is stated] "from a *kṣatriya* who is a single king" (*kṣatriyāt ekarājāt*) for the purpose of excluding a *saṅgha*. It should be stated: "from a *kṣatriya* who is a single king."

What is the purpose? It is for the sake of excluding the *saṅgha*. Let it not be [the case that] "the descendant of the Pañcālas" or "the descendant of the Videhas" refers to the *saṅgha* itself. If so, then it must be stated. It need not be stated. For without the elision (*luk*) in the plural, the form *pañcālāḥ* does not occur; rather, the secondary suffix (*yuvan-pratyaya*) which arises from that [base] would be the one applied. And if it is a secondary suffix...
In that case, there will be elision (*luk*) of the suffix and non-elision (*aluk*) of the other. But then consider this: "the offspring of the Kṣaudrakas" and "the offspring of the Mālavas.

Here too, one would expect [the forms] *kṣaudrakyāḥ* and *mālakyaḥ*. However, these terms do not refer to their slaves or laborers; rather, they refer to someone among those very people themselves. Since the secondary suffix denoting youth (*yuvan-pratyaya*) arises from someone among those very people themselves, [the rule applies].
That [suffix] shall be the *yuvan* suffix; if it is a *yuvan* suffix, there will be its elision (*luk*), and in that case, there will be non-elision (*aluk*) [of the feminine suffix].

(P_4.1.168.2) KA_II,269.4-8 Ro_III, 626 Now, for what purpose is the mention of "Kṣatriya"? It is so that it may not apply here: Videha is a Brāhmaṇa by name; his offspring is Vaidehi. And regarding the pointlessness of mentioning "Kṣatriya," it has been said: what...?
It has been stated. First, one point was stated:

that those [suffixes] which are seen after words such as *bāhu* and so forth in the sense of "lineage" (*gotra*) when it is worldly (*laukika*), their application is prohibited elsewhere. Another point was stated:
"because they are not expressed."

(P_4,1.168.3) From a country name that has the same form as a *kṣatriya* [name], when expressing its king, suffixes are applied as they are for a descendant (*apatya*). It should be stated: "From a country name that has the same form as a *kṣatriya*, when expressing its king, suffixes are applied as they are for a descendant. For example: the king of the Pañcālas (*pāñcāla*).

The suffix *añ* should be stated [after the word] *pāñcāla*: *pāñcālaḥ*. The suffix *aṇ* should be stated [after the word] *pūru*: *pauravaḥ*. The suffix *ḍyaṇ* should be stated [after the word] *pāṇḍu*: *pāṇḍyaḥ*.
(Pāṇini 4.1.170) By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the suffixes *ṇyaṅ*, *ṇya*, and *iñ* take precedence over *aṇ*. That is to say, *ṇyaṅ*, *ṇya*, and *iñ* occur by virtue of conflict with *aṇ*.

The scope of *aṇ* is, for example, *āṅga* and *vāṅga*. The scope of *ñyaṅ* is, for example, *āmbaṣṭhya* and *sauvīrya*. Here, both [suffixes] would apply: *dārvya*. The scope of *ṇya* is, for example, *nicaka* and *naicakya*. The scope of *aṇ* is the same [as above]. Here, both would apply: *nīpa* and *naipya*. The scope of *iñ* is, for example, *ājamīḍhi* and *ājakrandi*. The scope of *aṇ* is the same [as above]. Here...

One obtains both: *budha* and *baudhi*. The suffixes *ṇyaṅ*, *ṇya*, and *ñya* apply by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). From the rule "from *kuru*, *nādi*, etc., there is *ṇya*" [regarding *ṇyaṅ*], and from the rule "from *kuru*, *nādi*, etc., there is *ṇya*" [regarding *ṇya*], the suffix *ṇya* applies by way of conflict. The scope for *ṇyaṅ* is, for example, *āvantyaḥ* and *kauntyaḥ*; the scope for *ṇya* is the same. There is a country named *naiśaḥ*. From that, one obtains both; [specifically] *ṇya*.
It occurs by way of contradiction. *naiśyaḥ*. (P.

4.1.175) Regarding the statement that there is elision (*luk*) after [the names] beginning with *kamboja*, it is for the sake of [the tribes] beginning with *coḍa*. Elision must be stated after *kamboja* and the others. What is the purpose? For the sake of [the tribes] beginning with *coḍa*: *coḍaḥ*, *kaḍeraḥ*, *keralaḥ*.

Why does [the rule] not apply here: *āmbaṣṭhyā*, *sauvīryā*? It is stated that [the rule applies] "from this" (*ataḥ*). Yet this is not the vowel *a*; it would [otherwise] apply by means of the rule for inclusion of what ends with that (*tadantavidhi*). Therefore, he recites the subsequent answer: "In the word 'ataḥ', there is no inclusion of what ends with that."

Because of the rule regarding the elision (*luk*) for *Avanti* and others, the term "from this" (*ataḥ*) does not include that which ends in it. What is the reason? Because of the rule regarding the elision for *Avanti* and others. In that the Teacher prescribes the elision (*luk*) for *Avanti* and others, he indicates that here there is no application of the rule concerning the inclusion of what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*).

628. It should be stated that there is elision (*luk*) after [the word] *pārśva* and others. For example: *parśūḥ*, *rakṣāḥ*, *asurī*. The prohibition regarding the *yaudheya*-class [in Pāṇini 4.1.178] is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the elision after *pārśva* and others. Since the Teacher teaches the prohibition "not from the Easterners, nor from the *bhargādi* group, nor from the *yaudheyādi* group," this indicates that there is elision after *pārśva* and others.

(P_4,2.1) What is the purpose of [the word] *rāgāt*? [Example: *devadattena raktam vastram* ("a cloth dyed by Devadatta"). Since the suffix is prescribed when expressing the meaning of "dyed" (*rakta*) and so forth, the mention of the qualifier (*upādhi*) is redundant; because the suffix is prescribed for the expression of the meanings of "dyed" and so forth, the inclusion of the term *upādhi* is useless.
For an object cannot be denoted by a causal condition that arises from non-attachment (*arāga*). Since there is no denotation, there will be no arising from it.

629–630. In the section on the suffix *ṭhak*, an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the words *śakala* and *kardama*. [The forms] *śākalika* and *kārdamika* [are thus derived]. Regarding the word *nīlī*, the suffix *an* should be stated. That which is dyed with *nīlī* is *nīla*. Regarding the word *pīta*, the suffix *kan* should be stated. That which is dyed with yellow is *pītaka*. This is the word *pītaka*.

Or [it may be] another base form. Therefore, elision (*luk*) must be stated. From *haridrā* and *mahārajana*, the suffix *añ* must be stated: *hāridram*, *māhārajanam*. It is said [in the rule] "from a color" (*rāgāt*). In that case, this is not established:

"the two feet of a cock are yellow" (*hāridrau kukkuṭasya pādau*), or "the two ears of a donkey are saffron-colored" (*kāṣāyau gardabhasya karṇau*). [This is] established by way of comparison (*upamāna*): [they are] like turmeric (*haridrau*).
Like two yellow-green things (*haridrāu*); like two saffron-colored things (*kāṣāyau*).
This formulation is incorrect; for what is called a "connection" (*yoga*) exists only between two things that possess proximity (*sannikarṣa*) and distance (*viprakarṣa*).
[They] exist. And there is no proximity or remoteness between time and the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), for both time and the lunar mansion are eternal.

How, then, should the rule be formulated? It should be stated: "The suffix is prescribed for the time connected with that [lunar mansion] because of the conjunction of the moon with the lunar mansion. That is to say, "The suffix occurs for the time connected with that [lunar mansion] because of the conjunction of the moon with the lunar mansion. [Example: *puṣyeṇa*...
"Yukta" means joined with Puṣya;
when the moon is joined with Puṣya at this time,
it is the day of Pauṣa.

[The word] *pauṣī* refers to the night [of the full moon]. In that case, there is the elision of the final member [of the compound]. In that case, the elision of the final member must be stated. For the suffix is prescribed after the word *puṣyayukta*. Furthermore, there is the impossibility of [the proper application of] gender and number. There is an impossibility regarding both gender and number; whatever the gender and number of the moon are, those would apply to [the word *pauṣī*] by virtue of its behaving like the [word it is joined with]. [This is] established through connection with time.

"Let it be that time is designated as being 'conjoined with a lunar mansion' (*nakṣatra*). But has it not been said that this designation is improper? For "conjunction" (*yoga*) occurs only between two things that possess proximity (*sannikarṣa*) and distance (*viprakarṣa*), yet there is no proximity or distance between time and a lunar mansion, since both time and lunar mansions are eternal. This is not a fault; for when the moon has approached the vicinity of Puṣya, the word "Puṣya" is applied [to the time].

It occurs. By that [term] so designated, time is qualified, and thus there is correct understanding (*sampratyaya*). And it is by doing so that common usage in the world comes to be understood: when the moon has approached Puṣya, speakers say, "Today is [the day of] Puṣya," or "Today is [the day of] Maghā."

Why does [the suffix] not occur here: *pauṣī rātriḥ* (the night of Pauṣa), *pauṣam ahaḥ* (the day of Pauṣa)? It is stated that [the rule applies] when there is no distinction (*aviśeṣe*). But here a distinction is understood: when "night" is mentioned, it is understood that it is not "day"; when "day" is mentioned, it is understood that it is not "night."
[Objection: In that case, it would not apply here either, as in the expression "Today is Puṣya. [Response: For even here, a distinction is understood;
when "today" is said, it is understood that it is neither yesterday nor tomorrow. [Objection: Even if a distinction is understood here, a lack of distinction is also understood.
When "today" is said, it is not known whether it is at night or by day. Since there is this lack of distinction, it is based on that.
[The suffix] will be elided (*lup*). In this case as well, although a specific [time] is understood, a non-specific [time] is also understood.

When "night" is mentioned, it is not known when; since there is this non-specificity, the elision (*lup*) would apply based on that. If that is so, then the rule "time conjoined with a lunar mansion" (*nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ*) continues to apply. In the case of a non-specific time conjoined with a lunar mansion—

What, then, is the time that is conjoined with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*)? A day and night (*ahorātra*). Why does the treatment as if it were the same as its component (*yuktavadbhāva*) not apply here in the case of *śravaṇā rātriḥ* ("the night of Śravaṇā")? This is established by an irregular derivation (*nipātana*). What is the irregular derivation? [It is] from the rule: "After *phālgunī*, *śravaṇā*, *kārttikī*, and *caitrī*..."
Thus [it is said].

(Pāṇini 4.2.7) Regarding the rule *dṛṣṭaṃ sāma kaleḍḍhak* ("The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after *kali* when meaning 'a Sāman seen by'"): here, in the expression *dṛṣṭaṃ sāma*, it should be stated that the suffix *ḍhak* follows *kali*. A Sāman seen by Kali is called the *Kāleya* Sāman; thus the *Kāleya* Sāman is sung. Another says:

In all cases, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied after the words *agni* and *kali*. It should be stated that the suffix *ḍhak* is applied in all instances after *agni* and *kali*: *āgneyam* (belonging to Agni): a *sāman* seen by Agni; existing in Agni; come from Agni; belonging to Agni; having Agni as its deity. *kāleyam* (belonging to Kali): a *sāman* seen by Kali; come from Kali; [existing] in Kali.

*Kāleyam* means belonging to *Kali*. *Kāleyam* [is derived from] *kali* with the suffix *cha* (*iya*). *Kāleyaḥ caruḥ* (the sacrificial porridge for Kali) is that for which *Kali* is the deity; [this is formed by adding] *cha* (*eya*) to the word *kali*. Regarding the rules for the suffix *aṇ* and the suffix *ḍit*, it is stated that when a *sāman* is seen or when one is born [under a certain asterism], the suffix *aṇ* and the suffix *ḍit* are optionally applied twice. It should be stated that when a *sāman* is seen or when one is born, the suffix *aṇ* and the suffix *ḍit* are optionally applied twice. *Ausanasam* (the *sāman* seen by Uśanas) is [formed from] *uśanas* with the suffix *aṇ*. *Ausanam* [is the same]. *Śātabhiṣajaḥ* (born under Śatabhiṣaj) is [formed from] *śatabhiṣaj* with the suffix *aṇ*. *Śātabhiṣaḥ* [is the same, formed with the suffix *ḍit*].

The suffix *īkak* should be prescribed after ordinal numbers ending in *tīya*. For example: *dvaitīyikaḥ*, *tārtīyikaḥ*. It should be stated that it does not apply after the word *vidyā*; thus, one says simply "the second science" (*dvitīyā vidyā*) or "the third science" (*tṛtīyā vidyā*). After a *gotra* name, it is desired that the suffixes behave like those of the *aṅka* (numeral) class; for example: *aupagavakam*. Furthermore, when a *sāman* has been seen or a [descendant] has been born, the suffix *aṇ* with the marker *ḍit* is optionally prescribed twice; however, *īkak* is not applied after an ordinal number.
The [patronymic suffix] is desired after the word *vidyā* as if it were a *gotra* [name], like *aṅka*.

(Pāṇini 4.2.9) Why is the letter *ḍ* used? So that there may be elision by the rule *ḍiti* (Pāṇini 1.1.54). This purpose is not necessary, because [the required result] is achieved by the elision of *ya* (*yasyeti-lopa*).

This is already established. If that is so, then since this is already established, the fact that the Teacher prescribes the markers *ḍ* and *t* for *yayati* indicates these two paribhāṣās: "When there is a mention of a [root] without an indicatory letter (*ananubandhaka*), there is no inclusion of one with an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*); when there is a mention of one with a specific indicatory letter (*tadanubandhaka*), there is no inclusion of one with a different indicatory letter (*atadanubandhaka*). What is the purpose of this indication? [The example is: *avāmadevyam*.

Thus, this is established: once [the rule] *yasyeti ca* has been established by means of elision (*lopa*), for what purpose are *yayatau* prescribed as having the marker *ḍit*? [The answer is: so that their mention may not apply to cases where that [elision] does not occur, such as in the case of *vāmadevasya* due to the accentuation of the negative particle (*nañ*).

Regarding the rule *parivṛto rathaḥ* ("a chariot surrounded by..."), that restriction to the specific object (*tadekāntagrahaṇam*) must be applied here. It should be stated that when something surrounds a chariot, it becomes "exclusive to the chariot" (*rathaikānta*) only if it is indeed part of the chariot's equipment. This [restriction] should not apply in cases such as *putraiḥ parivṛto rathaḥ* ("a chariot surrounded by sons") or *chātraiḥ parivṛto rathaḥ* ("a chariot surrounded by students"). If so, then that [restriction] must be explicitly stated. No, it need not be stated. Why does it not apply [in those other cases]?

"A chariot surrounded by sons" and "a chariot surrounded by students"—[these are not formed] because [the suffix] is not prescribed [in such cases]. Regarding the rule *kaumārāpūrvavacane* (Pāṇini 4.1.35): it must be stated that in this case, "in the expression *kaumārāpūrvavacana*, when there is the unprecedentedness (*apūrvatva*) of the woman on both sides. A husband who has approached a maiden who has never had a husband before is called *kaumāra*. A maiden who has never had a husband and has approached a husband is called *kaumārī*. Thus, in the expression *kaumārāpūrvavacana*, [the term refers to] the maiden.

The suffix *aṇ* is prescribed [with the sense] of "being unprecedented" (*apūrvatva*) when it occurs in relation to a maiden (*kumārī*). Alternatively, *kaumāra* means "belonging to a maiden" (*kumāryām bhavaḥ*). If this were the case, the form *kaumārī bhāryā* ("the wife who belongs to a youth") would not be established. [Response: It will be a designation for a woman based on her connection with a male (*puṃyogāt stryabhidhānam*). Based on her connection with a male, there will be a designation for a woman: "the wife of one who is youthful" (*kaumārasya bhāryā kaumārī*).

"In this [month], that [night] is the full moon"—this is the mention of a technical term (*saṃjñā*). The mention of a technical term must be made in the form "in this [month], that [night] is the full moon. For if it were not a technical term, there would be a more cumbersome connection (*garīyān upasaṃyogaḥ*). Indeed, if the mention of a technical term were not made, there would be a more cumbersome connection.

It would have to be prescribed. It should be stated [as] "in the month and the half-month. Let it not apply here: "The full moon day of Pauṣa in this fifteen-night period" or "in this ten-night period. And it should also be stated [as] "at the seasonal junctures of the year," so that it does not apply to a hired month (*bhṛtakamāsa*). Well then, it must be stated. No, it need not be stated; the particle *iti* is employed. Therefore, [the rule applies] only when there is such an intention to express.

Why does the elision (*lopa*) not occur for *yasya*? Because of the power of the pronunciation of the vowel *i*. Now, if it is *yat*, and the word is *kāyam* as in *haviḥ*, how should the injunction (*sampraiṣa*) be formulated? If, first of all, there is the substitution of *kā* for *kimaḥ*, then [the injunction would be]: *kasmai anubrūhi*.

Thus it should be: *atha na kimaḥ kāya anubrūhi*. Even if it is *kimaḥ*, or even if it is *na kimaḥ*, in both cases it should be *kasmai anubrūhi*. For the designation "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*) is applied to all [words]. And *sarvaḥ* is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is *kaḥ*. Another says:

Whether it be *kimaḥ* or even *na kimaḥ*, in both cases it must be *kāyānubrūhi*. For the designation of "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*) is prohibited for technical names (*sañjñā*) and secondary members (*upasarjana*). And this [term *kāya*] is a technical name belonging to the Venerable One. It is because the ending in the vowel *ṛ* is prescribed in conjunction with the suffix; therefore, when that suffix is absent, it should not occur.

(Pāṇini 4.2.34) How is this to be understood?

[Does this mean: "The suffixes that are prescribed after words denoting time (kāla) when [the sense] 'origin' (bhava) is intended, those same suffixes occur after words denoting time in the sense of 'this is its deity' (sā asya devatā)"? Or rather: "The suffixes that are prescribed after words denoting time when [the sense] 'origin' is intended, those same suffixes occur after words denoting time in the sense of 'this is its deity'"? And what is the difference here? [In the former case,] there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of suffixes being applied to words denoting time merely for the sense of 'origin'.

If it is understood that "those suffixes which are prescribed after words denoting time (kāla) when [the sense] is 'existence' (bhave) become [applicable] after those [words] when [the sense] is 'his deity' (sā asya devatā)," then in this meaning, one would obtain merely a suffix (*pratyayamātra*). There would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [the suffix] would apply from the nominal stem alone (*prātipadikamātrāt*) in the prescription of that which occurs after words denoting time when [the sense] is 'existence'. Alternatively, if it is understood that "those suffixes which are prescribed after words denoting time when [the sense] is 'existence' become [applicable] after words denoting time [in the sense of] 'his deity'," [then the rule is correctly formulated].

In the sense "this is its deity," [the suffixes] would apply from the nominal stem alone. But it is established by the mention of both. This is established. How? By the mention of both. The mention of both must be made: "from words for time, like *bhava*, from words for time. Then that mention of both must be made. It need not be made; [it is understood] by the rule "like *bhava*."

This is the explanation provided by the Vārttikakāra: If those suffixes are prescribed with a specific qualification after certain bases in the sense of *bhava* (origin), and they also occur after those same bases with that same qualification in the sense of *sā asya devatā* (that is its deity), then these [suffixes] would be formed like those of *bhava*. However, if they were to occur either from the base alone or as a mere suffix [without such qualification], [the rule would not apply].

These [names] would not be formed with the suffix *bhava* (as in *bhavavat*). In the section on the suffix *ṭhañ*, there is an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) stating that for words such as *navayajña*, the sense "that occurs in this" applies; this is within the section on *ṭhañ*.

The rule "it occurs in this" (*asmin vartate*) requires the addition of *navayajña* and others to the list. For example: "the *navayajña* occurs at this time" → *nāvayajñika*. *Pākayajñika*. From *pūrṇamāsa*, the suffix *aṇ* should be stated. [Example:

Here, the masculine substitution will apply according to the rule: "In the case of a *bha*-stem, before a *taddhita* suffix that begins with a vowel and has an indicatory letter *ḍ*, the feminine stem becomes like the masculine. It is stated that the suffix *vuñ* occurs after a word denoting a *gotra* (clan name); however, the word *kṣudramālavaka* is not a *gotra*, nor is a collection of *gotras* included under the term "gotra. For example, a collection of countries (*janapada*) is not included under the term "country" (*janapada*);

thus, the suffix *vuñ* does not apply in the case of "the inhabitants of Kāśi and Kosala" (*kāśikosalīyāḥ*). [One might argue that] it would apply by the rule of "that which ends in such" (*tadantavidhi*), but that is not the case for everything.

The rule of "application to that which ends in [X]" (*tadantavidhi*) applies only to those cases enumerated [in the rule]. This case is not enumerated there. It would serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the existence of *tadantavidhi*. If that is so, then the Teacher indicates that here *tadantavidhi* does indeed apply. And thus is the rule of Āpiśali. By doing so, the rule of the teacher Āpiśali becomes justified: *dhenuḥ*.

It produces the suffix *anañ*. *Dhainukam* is a collection (*samūha*) of milch-cows (*dhenu*). Why [is it specified] "after *anañ*"? [Consider: *ādhenavam*, a collection of non-milch cows. Or rather, this is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*) regarding the army (*senā*). That is to say, this undertaking is for the sake of restriction: [the suffix *aṇ* occurs] after the words *kṣudraka* and *mālava* only when referring to an army. Where should it not occur? [In the case of] *kṣaudrakamālavakam*, meaning something other than an army. Thus, it may be so that the suffix *vuñ* would be superseded by *aṇ*.

Alternatively, the Teacher indicates that even the suffix *vuñ* (Pāṇini 4.2.119) subverts the suffix *añ* (Pāṇini 4.2.112) which follows it. But was it not said: "The suffix *vuñ* [is applied] after a *gotra* name, and that is not a *gotra*"? It would follow [the application of *vuñ*] by means of the rule regarding elements ending in such a word (*tadantavidhi*).

But was it not also said: "It does not apply from everything [ending in that]"? That would be an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the state of being an element ending in such a word. If that is so, then the Teacher indicates that [the suffix *añ*] occurs [after a *gotra* name].

"In this case, there is the rule of *tadanta* (application to that which ends with the specified element). But how can both of these be made known—that there is the *tadanta*-rule, and furthermore, that the suffix *vuñ* precedes and subverts the suffix *añ*? Both are made known. It is said, "beginning with *uktha*. What are the *ukthas*? They are the *sāmans*. If this were the case, the term *aukthika* would apply to anyone who merely knows the *sāmans*. This is not a fault; for the name will be applied by virtue of being for that purpose (*tādarthyāt*). That which is for the sake of the *uktha* is called an *uktha*.

In this context, one who studies the *ukthas* is called an *aukthika*, and one who studies the sacrifice (*yajña*) is called a *yājñika*. Now, for one who currently studies both the *aukthika* and the *yājñika*, how should it be expressed? It should be expressed as *aukthikaḥ* and *yājñikaḥ*. How so?

Because there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix denoting "belonging to that" (*tasyedaṃ-pratyaya*). There is elision of the suffix denoting "belonging to that. And [there is elision] of that suffix denoting "belonging to that. Therefore, that [is the case].

It should be stated; it should not be stated. Here, we must establish a threefold terminology: *ukthāny adhīte*, *aukthikyam adhīte*, and *aukthikaḥ*. In that case, since two [terms] have the same meaning, the analysis (*vigraha*) will be made with one, and the suffixal derivation (*utpatti*) will occur from the other, according to the maxim of the sheep and the ewe (*aviravikanyāya*). For example, having analyzed *aveḥ māṃsam* ("the meat of a sheep"), the derivation occurs from the word *avika*.

It becomes *āvikam*. Having analyzed *evam ukthāni adhīte* as "one who studies the Ukthas," it will become *aukthikaḥ*. Having analyzed *aukthikyam adhīte*, it is simply a sentence [of analysis]. (P_4,2.66.1) For what purpose is this stated? Because elsewhere the subject matter is non-eternal, there is a statement regarding the *chandas* and *brāhmaṇas* concerning that domain. Elsewhere the subject matter is non-eternal; it may be called "Pāṇinīya," for example.
Or [one might say] "the followers of Pāṇini. In that case, because the subject matter elsewhere is non-eternal, it would follow that even the *chandas* (Vedic texts) and *brāhmaṇas* are non-eternal.

Yet it is desired that they alone should be the subject matter; and since that cannot be established without effort, the statement "of the *chandas* and *brāhmaṇas*" is made to specify that as the subject matter. This is stated for this purpose. There is indeed a point.

What then? In that regard, there is an application to those objects according to their respective scopes. There, the status of being the object applies according to the scope; the phrase "one who has studied the Veda" (adhīte veda) is understood to carry over. Consequently, the status of being the object would apply only to the one who studies and the one who knows it. Other metaphorical applications (*upacāra*) would not occur therein. For example, as it occurs here: *pāṇinīyaṃ mahat suvihitam* ("the great and well-composed work of Pāṇini").

Thus, it might be argued here as well: "How can [the term] *mahat* be properly established? This, however, is already established, because within the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning "proclaimed" (*prokta*), its specific scope has been stated. How so? Within that very governing rule concerning "proclaimed," its application must be specified:

"That which is proclaimed [is so called] only with respect to the student and the knower of the *Chandas* and *Brāhmaṇas*. Therefore, the mention of the "student and the knower" (*adhyetṛ-veditṛ*) must indeed be made.

But is it not the case that here too [the suffix] is applied, as in: "he studies this for the sake of another" or "he knows this"? If that is so, then wherever there is the mention of *chandas* and *brāhmaṇas*, there the mention of the "student" (*adhyetṛ*) and "knower" (*veditṛ*) is intended. But is it not the case that [the suffix] is also applied there? That will be for the sake of others, [as in the rule]: "after Śaunaka and others, in the case of *brāhmaṇas* and *kalpas* proclaimed by ancient sages."

657–659: Prohibition regarding Yājñavalkya and others. A prohibition must be stated regarding Yājñavalkya and others: [the suffix does not apply] after Yājñavalkya and others, as in *yājñavalkyāni brāhmaṇāni* ("the Brāhmaṇas spoken by Yājñavalkya") and *saulabhāni*. Is it the case that, within the governing rule for words "spoken by" (*prokta*), the scope is restricted to those [specific types of texts]?
Therefore, a prohibition regarding Yājñavalkya and others must be stated. He says: "No. In every respect, [the suffix applies] after Yājñavalkya and others.

A prohibition must be stated; or rather, the suffix *ini* applies when [the work] has been proclaimed (*prokta*) and refers to that subject. Alternatively, it should be stated that the suffix *ini* occurs when [the work] has been proclaimed and refers to that subject. If it is said that *ini* occurs when [the work] has been proclaimed and refers to that subject, then the form *paiṅgī kalpaḥ* would also result here. Furthermore, the mention of *kāśyapa* and *kauśika* in the rule for *kalpa* is for the purpose of restriction. This is the mention of *kāśyapa* and *kauśika*.

And this [rule] should be understood as being for the purpose of restriction: namely, that the suffix *ini* occurs after *kāśyapa* and *kauśika* when a *kalpa* is the object, and not after others. Even so, the status of having that [kalpa] as the object would not apply to suffixes such as *chaṇ*, as in *taittirīyāḥ* and *vāratantavīyāḥ*. If, however, it were said that suffixes such as *chaṇ* have that [kalpa] as their object when they denote "proclaimed" (*prokta*), even then, the *paiṅgī kalpaḥ* [would remain problematic].

In this case as well, [the undesired consequence] would follow. Furthermore, the mention of *Kāśyapa* and *Kauśika* in the rule (*kalpa*) is precisely for the sake of restriction. Even so, the general rules (*autsargika*) would not obtain their scope regarding those [specific cases]. For instance, the *Krauḍas*, *Kāṅkatas*, *Maudas*, and *Paippalādas*—and also the suffixes beginning with *chaṇ*—would supersede the general rules only in the case of the student (*adhyetṛ*) and the knower (*veditr*), but they would not supersede them in other metaphorical applications (*upacāra*).

"These verses were spoken by Tittiri. In that case, it would apply without distinction. But was it not stated that there is a prohibition regarding Yājñavalkya and others? This will be explained: "There is a prohibition regarding Yājñavalkya and others because they belong to the same period. That must be stated right there [in that context]: "And it does not have them as its scope. How then [could it apply] to the followers of Kāśyapa or the followers of Kauśika?

Thus, when it is stated that "the suffix *ini* occurs when [a word] is mentioned as having that as its object," the mention of *kāśyapa* and *kauśika* in the rule must necessarily be understood as a restriction (*niyamārtha*). That very same [mention] will now serve as an injunction (*vidhyartha*). How so? For example: "The mendicants are *pārāśariṇaḥ*; the actors are *śailālinaḥ*. Here too, the phrase "and having that as its object" (*tadviṣayatā*) will be understood as carrying over (*anuvartisyate*).

(P_4,2.67–70) KA_II,286.24–287.10 Ro_III, 660–661: Is this one single *yoga*, or rather several distinct *yogas*? And what follows from this? If it is one single *yoga*, then in the subsequent rules for designating meanings, the phrase "in that country, when [the name] is that [of the country]" (*deśe tannāmni*) must be carried over (*anuvṛtti*).

For there is no recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) when there is a single rule (*ekayoga*). How is this known? Because [Pāṇini] makes the mention of "that" twice in the statement, "He studies that; he knows that. Now, if these were separate rules (*nānāyoga*), such as "oḥ," "añ," and so forth, then [the recurrence] would apply only to the domain of the very last item in the sequence, which serves as the actual designation of meaning. Let it be as you wish. For now, let it be a single rule.

But has it not been stated that in the subsequent rules concerning the designation of regions (*deśa*), the phrase "in that region, having that name" must be understood as recurring? For recurrence does not occur within a single rule (*ekayoga*). [Reply: Recurrence does occur even within a single rule.
How is this known? Because in the rule *tat asya asti asmin iti matup*, he does not repeat the mention of *tat* twice.

"How does one study that? How does one know that? [The answer is: What was done by the teacher through negligence can be undone. Or rather, let there be various applications (*yoga*). But has it not been said that the sequential enumeration beginning with "oḥ" and "añ" would apply only to that which is the final element in its entirety, namely the substitution of meaning (*arthādeśana*)? This is not a fault. The governing rules (*adhikāra*) function like a herd of cows; therefore...
Just as a herd of cows, when struck by a single staff, all move together with a uniform sound, so it is with these grammatical operations.

4.2.71) Regarding the rule for *oḥ* (*aṅ*), the suffix *matup* takes precedence over the application of *nadi* by way of conflict; that is, *matup* occurs after a stem ending in *oḥ* (*aṅ*) before a *nadī* vowel, due to the principle of conflict.
The scope for *añ* is: *kannavat* and *kānnavat*. The scope for *matup* is: *udumbarāvatī* and *maśakāvatī*.
In the case of *ikṣumatī* and *drumatī*, both [suffixes] would apply; therefore, by the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), *matup* occurs.

661–662. What is the purpose of including the term *aṅga*? It is so that the inclusion of the term *bahvac* may be understood as a qualifier of *aṅga*, [meaning] "from a stem (*aṅga*) consisting of many vowels. Now, if the term *aṅga* were not included, of what would the inclusion of the term *bahvac* be a qualifier? It would be a qualifier of *matvant* (a word ending in the suffix *-mant*). What fault would there be in that? It would undesirably apply here as well: *mālāvatām ayam nivāsaḥ* → *mālāvatam*. [In this case, the suffix would apply] because [the word *mālāvat*] exists.

662. For what purpose is the suffix *matup* prescribed for feminine nouns (*nadī*)? It is already established by the rule "the suffix *matup* occurs when [the sense] is 'this belongs to him' or 'this exists in this'. The prescription of *matup* for feminine nouns is made because the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). This suffix *aṇ* is prescribed in the sense of possession; it is prescribed as a specific rule (*viśeṣavihita*), whereas *matup* is prescribed as a general rule (*sāmānyavihita*).

It would [otherwise] subvert [the application]. And for the sake of meanings such as "completed" (*nirvṛtta*): the suffix *matup* is prescribed after the word *nadī* for the sake of meanings such as "completed," so that *matup* may occur in the sense of "completed" and so forth. 662. It should be stated that [the suffix] is also applied after *mahiṣa*: *mahiṣmān*.

(P_4.2.91) If, however, this *kuṭ* were made to begin with the subsequent element (*parādi*), then the substitution of the initial part of the suffix would be untenable, because it would not be the beginning of the word.

If [the substitution] *kuṭ* were applied first, the substitution [of *ku* for *kṛ*] would be untenable; once *kuṭ* has been applied, because it is not at the beginning [of the word], the substitution would not apply. If that is the case, then let it be treated as a *pūrvānta* (an element forming part of the preceding stem). If it is a *pūrvānta*, then shortening (*hrasvatva*) must be stated. For example, in *kuñcakīyāḥ*. However, if it were at the beginning of the following [element], then shortening would be established by the rule *ke 'ṇaḥ*.
It occurs. Let it then be *parādi* (beginning with the subsequent element). But was it not said that once *kuṭ* has been applied, the substitute does not apply because it is not initial?

This is established, however, by the statement that the substitute applies to that which has been subjected to *kuṭ*. This is established. How? It should be stated: "to that which has been subjected to *kuṭ*.
Then that must be stated. No, it need not be stated; it is established through simultaneous prescription (*sanniyoga*). Simultaneous prescription will be made.

What is this effort being enjoined called "conjunction" (*sanniyoga*)? The letter *ca* must be added [to the rule], as in: "and *kuṭ*. And what else is obtained? An *ādeśa* (substitute). It is thus established. But then the *sūtra* is altered. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. But was it not said: "there would be shortening in the case of *pūrvānta*"? This is established by means of a technical designation (*nipātana*). What [is the point]?

[The rule] "nipātanam. kruñcaḥ hrasvatvaṃ ca" [is proposed]. In that case, the irregularity (nipātana) must be applied when it occurs at the beginning of the preceding word. But this same fault applies even if it were placed at the beginning of the subsequent word. For that shortening [prescribed] by the rule "ke 'ṇaḥ" cannot be understood as applying to every suffix beginning with *ka*; otherwise, it would undesirably apply here as well: *nadīkalpaḥ*, *parīvāhaḥ*, and *kumārīkāmyati*. Therefore, it must be [placed] after both.
This must be stated: "The [suffix] *kruñc* and the shortening of the vowel. (Pāṇini 4.2.92).

It is said, "in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe*). What, then, is this so-called "remainder"? It refers to those [meanings] other than those beginning with "offspring" (*apatya*) and ending with the fourfold meanings (*cāturarthya*).

Other meanings constitute that which is the *śeṣa* (remainder). But for what purpose is the term *śeṣa* mentioned? It is so that the suffixes *gha* and others may apply to the *śeṣa*, and not to the primary meaning (*svārtha*). This is not a valid purpose. First, he must be asked this: why do the suffixes *aṇ* and others not apply in their own primary meaning? [The answer is: the suffixes *aṇ* and others are prescribed for meanings such as "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth; therefore, they do not apply in their own primary meaning.
[They] will not [apply]. But then, these [suffixes] are also prescribed for meanings such as "born" (*jāta*) and so forth. Therefore, they will not apply in their own primary sense (*svārtha*).

However, how can the *gha*-class suffixes and others, being mentioned here, be understood to apply to meanings such as "born"? The *gha*-class suffixes will carry over (*anuvartiṣyante*) there. If the *gha*-class suffixes carry over, then for whichever subsequent base [is mentioned], the preceding [suffixes] will apply to each respective one.

The suffixes would thus obtain [their application]. If that is so, then we shall depend upon the suffixes *gha* and others for the meanings such as "born" (*jāta*) and so forth. Such a dependence on many [suffixes] is improper. One who is depending [on them] would have to depend on the immediately following rule. There is indeed dependence on many; for example, in the case of the *kaṣ*-class and others, there is the subsequent application according to the rule—this applies to everything, both the general and the specific.

It is expected. Or rather, let there be recurrence (*anuvṛtti*). But has it not been said that for whichever subsequent base (*prakṛti*) there is, the preceding affixes (*pratyaya*) would apply to each of them? This is not a fault; the connection will recur.

[The rule] "from *rāṣṭra* and *avārapāra*, the suffixes *gha* and *kha*" [recurs]. "From *grāma*, the suffixes *ya* and *khañ*; from *rāṣṭra* and *avārapāra*, the suffixes *gha* and *kha*. [And so on] from *kattry-ādi*.

"From *rāṣṭra* and *avārapāra*, the suffix *ḍhakañ*; from *grāma*, *gha* and *kha*; [and] *yakhañ*. To this, he recites the following: "The mention of the 'remainder' (*śeṣa*) is for the purpose of preventing the application of *gha* and the other suffixes in the sense of 'descendant' (*apatya*) and so forth. The mention of the 'remainder' is made so that *gha* and the others may apply in the remainder, and not in the sense of 'descendant' and so forth. But how could they possibly apply? They would apply by virtue of the rule stating 'this belongs to that' (*tasyedam*)."

Its specific instances are these: offspring, collection, residence, and modification. [Objection: It is established by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). Let the suffixes beginning with *aṇ* (P. 4.1.83ff. and those beginning with *gha* (P. 5.1.78ff. both apply; by virtue of conflict, the suffixes beginning with *aṇ* occur. [Response: Or rather, it is not so, because the suffixes beginning with *gha* are subsequent. This conflict is not tenable. Why? Because the suffixes beginning with *gha* are subsequent. In a case of conflict...

It is said [in the rule] "param" (subsequent). The *aṇ* suffixes and others are prior, while the *gha* suffixes and others are subsequent. The *aṇ* suffixes and others will be made subsequent; thus, a reversal of the order of the rules is effected. Furthermore, because they are exceptions (*apavāda*) to *aṇ*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *gha* suffixes and others applying in the domain of *aṇ*. Because the *gha* suffixes and others are exceptions to *aṇ*, the *gha* suffixes and others would indeed apply in the domain of *aṇ*. This is not a fault, for the activity of the Teacher (*ācāryapravṛtti*) indicates [the intended meaning].

The claim that "the suffixes *gha* and others do not occur when [the base] is not denoting a country (*a-deśe*)"—on account of which this rule *pheś cha ca* prescribes the suffix *cha* after a base ending in *phiṭ*—is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*). This rule could instead be for the sake of the suffix *phin*. The term "among the Sauvīras" (*sauvīreṣu*) is understood [from the previous rule], and there is no *gotra* name among the Sauvīras that ends in *phin*. The mention of *gotra* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding the *sāmūhika* (collective) suffixes, while the mention of *daivayāta* is an indicator regarding the *vaiṣayika* (territorial) suffixes.
The mention of *bhāstrāyaṇa* does not apply to those who are permanent residents (*naivāsika*).

(P_4.2.93) Regarding the rule for *avārapāra*: it should be stated that [the suffix applies] even when the compound is split. Thus, from the split form *avārapārāt*, we have *avārīṇaḥ*, *pārīṇaḥ*, and *avārapārīṇaḥ*. It should also be stated that [the suffix applies] even when the order is reversed. Thus, from the reversed form, we likewise obtain these forms.

Regarding *pārāvārīṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.95), it should be stated that [the suffix] applies after the word *grāma* as well; thus, *grāmeyakaḥ*. If that is so, then it must be stated. It need not be stated. For in the rule *kattryādibhyaḥ ḍhakañ* (Pāṇini 4.2.95), the term *grāmāt* will be understood by way of anuvṛtti (carrying over).

This grammatical rule (*yoga*) can be dispensed with. How so? [In the case of] *kauleyaka*: it is the offspring (*apatyam*) of the family (*kulasya*). [One might argue that] the suffix *kan* applies after *kukṣigrīva*, whereas *ḍhañ* applies after *kula*.
Thus, [the form] *kauleyaka* will be derived as "the offspring of the family. Furthermore, the suffix *kan* will also apply after *kukṣigrīva* when it ends in *ḍhañ*.

(P_4,2.99) It should be stated that [the suffix] is also applied after *bāhli*, *ūrdi*, and *parḍi*: *bāhlāyanī*, *aurdāyanī*, *pārdāyanī*. (P_4,2.100) KA_II,292.4–14 Ro_III, [671b]... Regarding the phrase "amanuṣye" (in the sense of 'non-human'), for what purpose is it stated? [Example: *rāṅkavakaḥ* is a human being. The mention of "amanuṣya" (non-human) in the rule for *raṅku* is redundant, because the suffix *vuñ* is prescribed after *raṅku* when the meaning is either a human or something belonging to a human (*manuṣyatatstha*). Thus, the mention of "amanuṣya" in the rule for *raṅku* is useless. Why? Because the suffix *vuñ* is prescribed after *raṅku* when the meaning is either a human or something belonging to a human. This suffix *vuñ* is indeed prescribed for the case of a human and for that which belongs to a human.
That would be an obstacle [to the rule]. If that is the case, then the Teacher indicates that *ṣpha* and *gaṇa* occur when [the suffix] refers to a non-human being residing in a human.
If it is argued that this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for *ṣpha* and *gaṇa* when [the suffix] refers to a non-human being residing in a human, we say no, because it is not desired.

If it is argued that this is an indicator for *ṣpha* and *gaṇa* when [the suffix] refers to a non-human being residing in a human, that is not so. For what reason? Because it is not desired; for indeed...
The suffixes *ṣpha* and *gaṇa* are not intended [to apply] when the word *amanuṣya* (non-human) refers to a human being. What then? Only the suffix *vuñ* is intended.

Furthermore, the mention of the suffix *aṇ* [in the rule] is for the sake of [excluding it from] words such as *kaccha*, because of the specific prescription of *aṇ* for those words. Moreover, the mention of the suffix *aṇ* is redundant. Why? Because of the specific prescription of *aṇ* for words beginning with *kaccha*. Since these words are listed in the *kacchādi* group, the suffix *aṇ* will apply here by that very rule.

A comprehensive enumeration must be made: the suffix *tyap* is prescribed after the words *am*, *ihak*, *kvat*, and *sitre*; that which is traditionally taught as occurring after an indeclinable is also included. Examples: from *amā* comes *amātyaḥ* (minister), and *amā* itself; from *iha* comes *ihatyah* (belonging here), and *iha* itself; from *kva* comes *kvatyaḥ* (wherefrom?), and *kva* itself; from *tasi* comes *tatastyaḥ* (henceforth), and *yatastyaḥ* (whenceforth).

*Tra*, *tatratya*, and *yatratya*. Otherwise, a prohibition would have to be stated for *auttarāha*, *aupariṣṭa*, and *pārata*: namely, *auttarāhaḥ*, *aupariṣṭaḥ*, and *pārataḥ*. [The suffix] *tyap* [is applied] after *ni* when meaning "fixed" (*dhruva*). It should be stated that *tyap* follows *ni* in the sense of "fixed": *nityaḥ*. [The suffix] *tyap* should be stated [after *nis*] in the sense of "gone" (*gata*): *niṣṭyaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṇa* [is applied] after *araṇya*. [The suffix] *ṇa* [is applied] after *araṇya*.

It should be stated: [the word] *āraṇyāḥ* [is formed from] *sumanasaḥ*. It should be stated that [the suffix] *dūretya* occurs after *dūrāt*. [The form] *auttarāhaḥ* [is derived from] *uttarāt* with the suffix *āhañ*; it should be stated that [the suffix] *āhañ* occurs after *uttarāt*. Regarding the rule "after an indeclinable (*avyaya*), [the suffix] *tyap*," there must be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the case where *āviṣṭa* occurs in the Vedic language (*chandas*). That is to say, in the rule "after an indeclinable, *tyap*," an addition must be made for *āviṣṭa* in the Vedic language. [Thus, the form] *āviṣṭyaḥ* [is obtained].
And the beautiful one increases in these [villages].

By way of a counter-exception (*vipratiṣedha*), the suffix *cha* takes precedence over the rule prescribing [the suffix *aṇ*] for villages in the northern regions that have a long vowel (*vṛddha*) as their penultimate letter, provided they do not end in *ayaya*, *tīra*, or *rūpya*.

By way of an exception (*vipratiṣedha*), the suffix *cha* occurs after a word ending in *vṛddhi* that has *ayana*, *tīra*, *rūpya*, or a Northern village name as its final member. [The rule] "after an indeclinable, *tyap* occurs" has its scope in *amātyaḥ*. The scope of *cha* is in *śālīyaḥ* and *mālīyaḥ*.
In the case of *ārāt*, both would apply; thus we have *ārātīyaḥ*. [The rule] "after a word ending in *tīra*, *añ* occurs" has its scope in...

*Kakhatīra* and *kākhatīrī*. For the suffix *cha*, it is the same [as before]. From *vāyastīra*, both [suffixes] apply: *vāyastīrīyaḥ*. The suffix *ñya* applies after a word ending in *rūpya*; this is its scope: *caṇārarūpya* and *cāṇārarūpyā*. For *cha*, it is the same [as before]. From *māṇirūpya*, both [suffixes] apply; however, because of its subsequent position, the suffix characterized by having *y* as the penultimate letter (*cha*) takes precedence.

The suffix *vuñ* (forming *bādhate*) is excluded. Regarding the rule "the suffix *añ* occurs after a polysyllabic name of a village in the North that has an udātta accent on the final syllable," its scope is, for example, *śivapur- > śaivapuraḥ*. The scope of the suffix *cha* is the same. In the case of *vāḍavakarṣa*, both [suffixes] would apply: *vāḍavakarṣīyaḥ*. Regarding the rule "the suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word having *k* as its penultimate letter (*kopadha*)," its scope is, for example, *nilīnaka- > nailīnakaḥ*. The scope of the suffix *cha* is the same. [This applies to] *aulūka* as well.

One obtains both [results]. The follower of Ulūka (aulūkīya). From those [words] beginning with *tyap*, the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha* occur by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of the rule "from an indeclinable, *tyap* occurs" is, for example, *amātyaḥ*. The scope of *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha* is, for example, *kārantavikī* and *kārantavikā*.

*Āratantavikī* and *ārātantavikā*: *Ārāt* is the name of a Vāhīka village. From that [name], both suffixes apply: *ārātkī* and *ārātkā*. The scope of the rule "the suffix *añ* occurs when *tīra* is the final member" is, for example, *kakhatīra* and *kākhatīrī*.
The same applies to the two suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha*: *kāstīraḥ*.

*Kāstīra* is the name of a Vāhīka village. From that [name], both suffixes would apply: *kāstīrikī* and *kāstirikā*. The scope for the rule "the suffix *ñ* occurs after a word ending in *rūpya*" is, for example, *cāṇārarūpya* and *cāṇārarūpyā*. For *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha*, it is the same. *Dāsarūpa* is the name of a Vāhīka village. From that, both suffixes would apply; however, those two, *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha*, are superseded by the suffix characterized by having *y* as the penultimate vowel (*yopadhā-*) due to its higher status in the order of rules.

The suffix *vuñ* is obstructed [by other rules]. Regarding *dāsarūpyakaḥ*: the scope of the rule "the suffix *añ* occurs after a village name of the Northern region that has many vowels and is oxytone" is, for example, *śivapura* → *śaivapuraḥ*. For the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha*, the same applies. Now, there is a Vāhīka village named Śākala; from it, both [suffixes] would apply: *śākalikī* (with *ñiṭha*) and *śākalikā* (with *ṭhañ*). The scope of the rule "the suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word ending in the letter *k*" is as follows: *śākalikaḥ* (with *aṇ*) [In this case, the suffix *aṇ* prevails over the others.]

*Nilīnakaḥ* and *nailīnakaḥ*: [the suffix] *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha* apply in exactly the same way. *Sausukam* is the name of a Vāhīka village. From that, both [suffixes] would be applicable. However, those two, *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha*, are superseded by the suffix *cha*, which is characterized by having *ka* as its penultimate letter (*kopadha*), because of its higher status in the order of rules. Thus, [the form is] *sausukīyaḥ*. Alternatively, this is not so, because *ṭhañ* and the others are exceptions (*apavāda*) to *cha*, and since they do not exist within the domain of that [exception], the others [do not apply]. Or rather, it is not so.

The meaning [of the rule] is established by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). What is the reason? Because the suffixes beginning with *ṭhañ* are exceptions (*apavāda*) to *cha*; that is, the suffixes beginning with *ṭhañ* are exceptions to *cha*. Furthermore, because the others do not exist in that domain; that is, in the domain of *cha*, there is an absence of suffixes such as *tyap*. Moreover, the restatement of the suffix *aṇ* after a word ending in *ka* is for the purpose of excluding others. And this conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) which has been cited here is also improper.

[The rule applies] after a stem having *k* as its penultimate letter (*kopadha*), [to the suffix] *aṇ* and to *cha*. What is the reason? The repetition of *aṇ* after a stem having *k* as its penultimate letter is for the purpose of excluding others.

Here, *aṇ* is already established by the general rule (*utsarga*). The purpose of repeating it is to set aside those other exceptions (*apavāda*) that would otherwise apply. Just as it sets aside the suffix *añ*, which is an exception to it, so too does it set aside *cha*.

It would subvert [the rule]. Therefore, there must be a prohibition of *añ* after a word ending in *k* with an acute accent on the final syllable. Consequently, a prohibition of *añ* after a word ending in *k* with an acute accent on the final syllable must be stated. It need not be stated. Since intermediate exceptions (*apavāda*) subvert preceding rules, this will subvert only *añ* after a word ending in *k*, but it will not subvert *cha*. From *cha*, when denoting a place, *ṭhañ* is applied after a word ending in *u*. From *cha*, when denoting a place...

The suffix *ṭhañ* [prescribed] after a word denoting time (*kālāt*) takes precedence over the rule "after a word ending in *o*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is used when referring to a place" (*or deśe ṭhañ*), by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope (*avakāśa*) of the former [the rule for *ch*] is: *śālīyaḥ*, *mālīyaḥ*. The scope of the latter [the rule for *ṭhañ* after *o*] is: *niṣāhakarṣū* (a place named Niṣāhakarṣū) → *naiṣāhakarṣukaḥ*. In the present case, both would apply: *dākṣikarṣukaḥ*.

The scope for the rule "the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after a word denoting time" is, for example, *ārdhamāsikam* ("half-monthly") and *sāṃvatsarikam* ("yearly"). The scope for the suffix *cha* is the same. [In the case of] *māsa*, both would apply: *māsikam*. After a word denoting a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the suffix *aṇ* applies by way of supersession (*vipratiṣedha*) over *cha*. The scope for *aṇ* is, for example, *taiṣaḥ* ("belonging to the month of Tiṣya") and *pauṣaḥ* ("belonging to the month of Puṣya"). The scope for *cha* is the same. In the case of *svāti*, both would apply: *sauvātaḥ*.

After an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* are applied by way of supersession (*vipratiṣedha*) [of the suffix *cha*]. The scope (*avakāśa*) of *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* is, for example, *doṣāntanam* and *divātanam*. The scope of *cha* is the same. From the word *prātar*, both would apply; thus, *prātastanam*. After a word denoting a limb of the body (*śarīrāvayava*), the suffix *yat* is applied by way of supersession [of the suffix *cha*]. The scope of *yat* is...

The suffix *cha* occurs after a word ending in a dental or labial. For the word *pāda*, both [suffixes] would apply: *padya*. Furthermore, after a word ending in a class-consonant (*vargānta*), when not followed by the word *aśva*, the suffixes *yat* and *kha* occur. After a word ending in a class-consonant and not followed by *aśva*, *yat* and *kha* occur in place of *cha* by way of an exception (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope for *yat* and *kha* is, for example, *akrūravagyaḥ* and *akrūravargīṇaḥ*. The scope for *cha* remains the same as before. In the case of the word *vāsudevavarga*, both [suffixes] would apply.

*vāsudevāvargyaḥ* (one who belongs to the class of Vāsudeva), *vāsudevavargīṇaḥ* (one who belongs to the class of Vāsudeva). [The suffix] *vuñ* applies after a polysyllabic word that has udātta on the final syllable. [However,] *ṭhañ* occurs instead of *cha* by way of prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*) after a polysyllabic word with udātta on the final syllable. The scope of *ṭhañ* is, for example, *natanana* → *nātānatikaḥ*. The scope of *cha* is the same. In the case of *sāmasta*, both would apply; thus, *sāmastikaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṭhak* applies after words denoting places of business (*āyasthāna*). After words denoting places of business...

The suffix *ṭhak* takes precedence over *cha* by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of *ṭhak* is, for example, *śaulkika* and *gaulkika*; the scope of *cha* is the same. In the case of *āpaṇa*, both would apply; [the result is] *āpaṇika*. From words denoting a relationship through learning or birth, the suffix *vuñ* applies. From words denoting a relationship through learning or birth, *vuñ* takes precedence over *cha* by way of conflict. The scope of *vuñ* is, for example, *aupādhyāyakam* and *paitāmahakam*; the scope of *cha* is the same.

That same [suffix] applies here to both: *ācāryaka* and *mātulaka*. From the suffix *ṛt*, the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs by way of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of *ṭhañ* is, for example, *hautṛka* and *svāsṛka*; the scope of *cha* is that same [suffix]. Here, both would apply: *śāstṛka* and *bhrātṛka*. The suffixes *rūpya* and *mayaṭ* occur after *cha*.

By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*): the scope of the suffixes *-mayaṭ* and *rūpya* is, for example, *devadattarūpyam* and *devadattamayam*. The scope of *cha* is the same. From *vāyudatta*, both would apply: *vāyudattarūpam* and *vāyudattamayam*. [In this case,] after a word denoting something inanimate (*acitta*), the suffix *ṭhak* applies by way of conflict with *cha*. The scope of *ṭhak* is, for example, *āpūpikaḥ* and *śāṣkulikaḥ*.

The suffix *cha* [is applied] after the word *maudakika*; it is the same [as before]. After the word *pāyasa*, both [suffixes] apply: *pāyasikaḥ*. After words denoting a *gotra* (lineage) or a *kṣatriya* name, the suffix *vuñ* is applied diversely (*bahulam*). After words denoting a *gotra* or a *kṣatriya* name, the suffix *vuñ* occurs in place of *cha* by way of an exception (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of *vuñ* is, for example, *glaucukāyanaḥ* and *traigartakaḥ*. The scope of *cha* is the same as before. Here, both [suffixes] would apply: *gārgikaḥ*.

The suffix *ṇini* [is applied] after the names of Vātsakas and Mālavakas; [the suffix] *cha* is applied after the names of pupils (*antevāsī*) and Brāhmaṇas, by way of an exception (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of *ṇini* is, for example, *Hāridraviṇaḥ*, *Taumburaviṇaḥ*, and *Bhāllavinaḥ*. The scope of *cha* is the same. In this case, both would apply: *Āruṇinaḥ* and *Śāṭyāyaninaḥ*. [The suffix] *añ* is applied after a name preceded by *pattra*.

After a word ending in *pattra*, the suffix *añ* occurs in preference to *cha* by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of *añ* is, for example, *uṣṭra-auṣṭra-* and *auṣṭra-ratha-*. The scope of *cha* is the same. In this case, both would apply: *vāmī-vāma-* and *vāmī-ratha-*. After a *dvandva* compound, the suffix *vun* occurs in the sense of enmity or sexual union in preference to *cha*. The scope of *vun* is, for example, *ahinakulikā*.
That same [suffix] applies for *cha*. Here, both [suffixes] would apply: *kākolūkikā* and *śvāvarāhikā*.

From the rule "vuñ after a *gotra* or *caraṇa*," *vuñ* occurs in supersession of *cha*. The scope of *vuñ* is, for example, *glaucukāyanakam*, *mlaucukāyanakam*, *kāṭhakam*, and *kālāpakam*. For *cha*, it is that same [scope]. Here, both would apply: *gārgakam*, *vātsakam*, and *maudakam*.

Regarding *paippalādakam*: [the suffix] *vuñ* occurs by way of supersession (*vipratiṣedha*) over the rule prescribing *aṇ* after [names in] the *kaṇva* group and over the rule prescribing *aṇ* after [names ending in] *īñ*. The scope (*avakāśa*) of the rule "after [names in] the *kaṇva* group, *aṇ* occurs" and "after [names ending in] *īñ*, *aṇ* occurs" is, for example, *kāṇvāḥ daṇḍamāṇavāḥ* and *dākṣāḥ daṇḍamāṇavāḥ*. The scope of *vuñ* is the same. In this case, both [rules] apply.

[The suffix] *kāṇvaka* and *dākṣaka* are obtained. Regarding the rule "after [stems ending in] *o*, when denoting a place, there is *ṭhañ*": this occurs by way of supersession (*vipratiṣedha*) over the rule "after [stems ending in] *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh*, when denoting a place, there is *ṭhañ*. The scope (*avakāśa*) of *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh* is [the formation of] *kāraṃtavikī* and *kāraṃtavikā*. The scope of the rule "after [stems ending in] *o*, when denoting a place, there is *ṭhañ*" is [the formation of] *niṣāhakarṣū* and *naiṣāhakarṣukaḥ*.

The place named Niṣādakarṣū is called Naiṣādakarṣuka. In this case, two [suffixes] would apply: [the suffix] -cha (as in *nāpitavāstuka*) and the suffix -ṭhañ. By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), -ṭhañ prevails. Or rather, there is no need for a conflict, because -ṭhañ has no scope [elsewhere]. Why? Because -ṭhañ has no scope. Since -ṭhañ has no scope, it will simply supersede [the other suffixes], namely -ṭhañ and -ñiṭh. But is it not so that...?
And now, the scope [of the rule] has been established: that which is a Vṛddha name ending in a vowel other than *u* and designating a Vāhīka village is the scope for the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭ*.

That which is not Vṛddha and ends in *u* is the scope for the suffix *ṭhañ*. When it is a Vṛddha name ending in *u* and designates a Vāhīka village, both [suffixes] would apply. If this is so, then this is not a valid objection to this conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). To whom [does it apply]?

In that case, [the rule] "from a word denoting a place or time, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after a word ending in *ū*" [would apply]. But surely, even there, an opportunity [for application] has been established: that which is a *vṛddha* word ending in *ū* is the scope for *cha*; that which is not a *vṛddha* word ending in *ū* is the scope for *ṭhañ*. When it is a *vṛddha* word ending in *ū* and also denotes a place, both [suffixes] would apply. Therefore, [the rule] "after a *vṛddha* [word]"...

What is accomplished by this mention of *vṛddha* in the rule *prācām*? It would have been sufficient to say that in the preceding rule [the suffix applies] after both *vṛddha* and *avṛddha* bases. This mention of *vṛddha* in the present rule is therefore without scope (*anavakāśa*). Because it lacks scope, the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is improper. [The suffix] *vuñ* applies after bases ending in *y* and after *prastha* etc.; *vuñ* [applies] after bases ending in *y* and after *prastha* etc., [while] *ṭhañ*, *ñiṭha*, and [others apply] by virtue of the subsequent rules.
There is a conflict [between rules]. The scope for the rule "vuñ occurs after a word with *y* as an upadhā" is, for example, *sāṅkāśya* → *sāṅkāśyaka*.

The same applies to the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha*: *dāsarūpya*, which is the name of a village of the Vāhīkas. From that, both [suffixes] would apply: *dāsarūpyaka*. The scope for the rule "vuñ occurs after a word ending in *prasthānta*" is, for example, *mālāprastha* → *mālāprasthaka*.

The suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ṭhañ* [are applied] in the same way. *Pātānaprastha* is the name of a Vāhīka village; from it, both [suffixes] would apply: *pātānaprasthakaḥ*. The scope for the rule "from a word ending in *pur*, the suffix *vuñ* occurs" is, for example, *kāñcīpura*: *kāñcīpurakaḥ*. [In this case,] *ṭhañ* and *ṭhañ* apply in the same way. *Nāndīpura* is the name of a Vāhīka village; from it, both [suffixes] would apply.

*Nāndīpurakaḥ*. Since the suffix *vuñ* occurs after words ending in *vah*, this is its scope: *vātavaha* → *vātavahakaḥ*. For the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha*, it is the same. *Kaukkuḍīvaha* is the name of a Vāhīka village. From that, both [suffixes] would apply: [by *ṭhañ*] *kaukkuḍīvahakaḥ*. [Now consider] *oś ca ṭhañaḥ*. After a word ending in *o*, *vuñ* occurs by way of supersession (*vipratiṣedha*) over *ṭhañ*. The scope of *ṭhañ* after *o* is: *naiṣāhakarṣukaḥ*. [The scope of *vuñ* is: *kaukkuḍīvahakaḥ*. Here, *vuñ* applies by supersession. Thus, *kaukkuḍīvahakaḥ*. [And finally: *oś ca ṭhañaḥ*. After a word ending in *o*, *vuñ* occurs by way of supersession over *ṭhañ*. The scope of *ṭhañ* after *o* is: *naiṣāhakarṣukaḥ*. [The scope of *vuñ* is: *kaukkuḍīvahakaḥ*. Here, *vuñ* applies by supersession. Thus, *kaukkuḍīvahakaḥ*. [And finally: *oś ca ṭhañaḥ*. After a word ending in *o*, *vuñ* occurs by way of supersession over *ṭhañ*. The scope of *ṭhañ* after *o* is: *naiṣāhakarṣukaḥ*. [The scope of *vuñ* is: *kaukkuḍīvahakaḥ*. Here, *vuñ* applies by supersession. Thus, *kaukkuḍīvahakaḥ*. [And finally: *oś ca ṭhañaḥ*.
