*Naiṣādakarṣukaḥ*: this is the same as the suffix *vuñ*. Regarding [the word] *āprītamāyu*, both [suffixes] apply: *āprītamāyavaḥ* and *āprītamāyavakaḥ*. Regarding the rule "for country names, the suffixes *aka* and *aṇ*" (*janapadānām akāṇau*): for country names, the suffixes *aka* and *aṇ* occur by way of supersession (*vipratiṣedha*) of the suffix *oḥ ṭhañ*. The scope of *aka* is, for example, *aṅgāḥ* and *āṅgakaḥ*. The scope of *oḥ ṭhañ* is the same [as that of *aka*]. There is a country named *jihlava*; from that, both [suffixes apply].

[The suffix] *aṇ* applies [to form] *Jaihnavaka*. The scope of *aṇ* is, for example, *ārṣika* from *Ṛṣika*. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* [also applies] after *oḥ* (the word *ikṣvāku*), as in *Aikṣvāka*, which is the name of a country (*janapada*). Thus, both [suffixes] would apply [simultaneously], resulting in *Aikṣvāka*. [Objection: Or rather, there is no need for the rule of mutual exclusion (*vipratiṣedha*), because *aṇ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *vuñ*.
[Reply: No, there is no purpose served by the mutual exclusion. What is the reason? Because *aṇ* is an exception to *vuñ*; that is, *aṇ* is an exception to *vuñ*.

And *vuñ* will supersede *oḥ ṭhañ*. [The rule] "after a word with *k* as its penultimate letter, *cha* is applied after a word ending in *a* that does not have *ka* as its penultimate letter" [supersedes the rule] "after a word with *k* as its penultimate letter, *aṇ* is applied. By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), *cha* is applied after a word with *k* as its penultimate letter that does not have *ka* as its penultimate letter. The scope (*avakāśa*) of the rule "after a word with *k* as its penultimate letter, *aṇ* is applied" is, for example, *nilīnaka*, *nailīnaka*. The scope of the rule "after a word ending in *a* that does not have *ka* as its penultimate letter, *cha* is applied" is, for example, *ārīhaṇaka*, *ārīhaṇakīya*. [An example of the former is] *brāhmaṇaka* by name.

The *janapada* (name of a country) [ending in *dhanvan*] therefore obtains both [suffixes]. It belongs to the Brāhmaṇas. Regarding the rule "and after *dhanvan* there is *vuñ*": the suffix *cha* occurs by way of prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of the rule "after *dhanvan*, *vuñ* occurs" is, for example, *pāredhanva* and *pāredhanvaka*. The scope of *cha* is the same. There is a desert named Āṣṭaka; from that, both [suffixes] would apply.

Regarding the suffix *āṣṭakīya*: Or rather, the repetition of *cha* is for the purpose of precluding its exceptions (*chāpavāda*). Or rather, there is no need [for this], because it is established by the rule of mutual exclusion (*vipratiṣedha*). What is the reason? The repetition of *cha* is for the purpose of precluding its exceptions. Here, the suffix *cha* is already established by the rule "after a word ending in *vṛddhi*, the suffix *cha* [is applied]. The purpose of its repetition is to set aside those other exceptions that would otherwise apply.
Just as it subverts other exceptions to that [rule], so too will it subvert this one as well.

(P_4.2.124) Regarding the prescription of the suffix *vuñ* after the names of countries (*janapada*) and their inhabitants (*tadavaha*), there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it would apply even to a mere constituent part [of such a name]. In the prescription of *vuñ* after the names of countries and their inhabitants...

[The suffix] would apply from a mere constituent part. For example, there is a village among the Vāhīkas named Mauñja; that which exists in it is *mauñjīya*. If that is so, [the rule should be] "from a country (*janapada*)," meaning "having a country as its limit. If it is argued that it should be "from a country," then the mention [of the word] is redundant. If it is "from a country," then the inclusion of the term "limit" (*avadhi*) is purposeless, because the result is already established by the rule "from a country" alone. In that case, this is the purpose [of the mention]:
[The rule] "vuñ should apply after a *janapada* [name]" is stated so that *vuñ* occurs where it is prescribed; [the purpose is] lest something else should apply. And what else might apply?

The suffix *cha*. Regarding the prescription of *cha* for names where the second member is *gartá*, he will state that *vuñ* applies after a *janapada* by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).
That prior counter-exception need not be explicitly taught.
This which is stated—"in the case of *manuṣya*"—is too little. It should be stated as: "in the case of *pathin*, *adhyāya*, *nyāya*, *vihāra*, *manuṣya*, and *hastin*."

685. Regarding the rule *kuruyugandharebhyo vāvacanāt manuṣyatatsthayor vuñ* (A 4.2.130): because of the optionality (*vāvacana*) [of the suffix *cha*] after *kuru* and *yugandhara*, the application of *vuñ* for [denoting] a human being or one residing therein occurs by way of supersession (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of the optionality of the suffixes after *kuru* and *yugandhara* is: *kauravaḥ*, *kauravakaḥ*; *yaugandharaḥ*, *yaugandharakaḥ*. [The scope of *vuñ*] is for [denoting] a human being or one residing therein.

The scope for the suffix *vuñ* is when there are other [suffixes], such as *kaccha*. For example: *kācchakaḥ manuṣyaḥ* (a person from Kaccha), *kācchakam asya īkṣitam jalpitam hasitam smitam* (his looking, speaking, laughing, or smiling). Here, both [suffixes] would apply: *kauravkaḥ manuṣyaḥ* (a person from Kurava), *kauravakam asya īkṣitam jalpitam hasitam smitam*. The suffix *vuñ* occurs by way of a prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*). This is not correct.

There is a contradiction. For there is no scope for other [words] such as *kaccha* etc. for the word *kuru*. The reading of the word *kuru* among the *kaccha*-group is without scope. Furthermore, the word *kuru* does not necessitate an option (*vibhāṣā*). By this [rule], the suffix *vuñ* will apply due to its inclusion in the *kaccha*-group, while the suffix *aṇ* will apply by virtue of the option; thus, this option is for the sake of [the formation of the name] *Yaugandhara*.

(P_4.2.133) Why is the inclusion of *sālva* among the *kaccha*-class words made? The inclusion of *sālva* among the *kaccha*-class words is for the purpose of prescribing the suffix *aṇ*. The inclusion of *sālva* among the *kaccha*-class words is made so that *aṇ* may apply; let there not be *vuñ*.

Or rather, the mention of *apadāti* and *yogavāh* is not for the sake of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Nor is there any need for this purpose. What is the reason? The mention of *apadāti* and *yogavāh* will serve as a restriction: [the suffix *cha*] shall apply after *sālva* only when it means "not on foot" (*apadāti*), and only when it means "cattle and draught-oxen" (*goyavāgvoh*) after *sālva*. 686. From a *janapada* (name of a country) that has *gartta* as its final member, the suffix *vuñ* is applied by way of prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣiddha*) against the rule for the suffix *cha*. The suffix *vuñ* occurs from a *janapada* having *gartta* as its final member by means of prior prohibition. The scope (*avakāśa*) of the rule "the suffix *cha* occurs after [a *janapada*] having *gartta* as its final member" is, for example: *śvāvidgarta*, *śvāvidgartīyaḥ*. The scope of *vuñ* is, for example: *aṅgāḥ*, *āṅgakaḥ*. In this case [where both would apply], [the latter prevails].

One obtains both [suffixes]. For example, *traigartakaḥ*. The suffix *vuñ* occurs by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Well then, that prior counter-exception must be stated. It need not be stated. The purpose of including the mention of "limit" (*avadhi*) has already been explained: so that *vuñ* may apply after a country name (*janapada*) as well as after a word denoting the limit of a country (*janapadāvadi*), and so that whatever else might otherwise apply shall not occur.

In the *gahādi* group, the middle portion of the word *pṛthivīmadhya* should be stated as having the status of the middle [portion]. That which exists in the middle of the earth is *madhyamīya*. By virtue of its connection with the feet (*caraṇa*), it is characterized by residence; hence the suffix *aṇ*.

The suffix *aṇ* should be stated [after a word denoting a place] in the sense of residence (*nivāsa*) when there is a connection with a person who has traveled there. Three [suffixes] belong to the East (*prācya*), and three belong to the Middle Country (*mādhyama*).
All [of these] denote residence.

687–688. It should be stated that [the suffix] applies even after *īkānta*, so that it may occur here as in *aiṇīkīyaḥ*. Well then, it must be stated. No, it need not be stated. When there is the mention of *akekānta*, the mention of *kopadha* is for the sake of forms such as *sausukīya*. When there is the mention of *akekānta*, the mention of *kopadha* must be made. What is the purpose? For the sake of forms such as *sausukīya*. As in *sausukīyaḥ*.

(P_4.3.1) Regarding the prescription of suffixes after *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, there should be a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). In the prescription of suffixes after *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, a division of the rule must be made: after *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the suffix *cha* optionally occurs. [Examples: *yuṣmadīyaḥ*, *asmadīyaḥ*.

Then follows *khañ*. The suffix *khañ* optionally occurs after the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. [Examples: *yauṣmakīṇaḥ*, *āsmākīnaḥ*. For what purpose is this split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*)? It is for the purpose of preventing an equal number of correspondences (*saṃkhyāpratiṣedhārtha*). [That is,] so that there may not be a one-to-one correspondence (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) [between the two sets of suffixes].
And regarding the statement of the *ādeśa* (substitute): what [is the purpose]? A split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made. First: "In that *aṇ* suffix, *yuṣmāka-* and *asmāka-* occur.

Thus: *yauṣmākaḥ*, *āsmākaḥ*. Then: "In the *khañ* suffix. And in the *khañ* suffix, *yuṣmāka-* and *asmāka-* occur. Thus: *yauṣmākīṇaḥ*, *āsmākīnaḥ*. For what purpose is this split of the rule? It is precisely for the sake of prohibiting [the application of] equal numbers [of substitutes]. In that regard, again—

Regarding the mention of *khañ*: in that context, the mention of *khañ* must be made again. For indeed, without the mention of *khañ*, the application of the suffix does not arise. If so, then it ought to be stated. It need not be stated. I shall express it thus: "In that *khañ*, *yuṣmāka-* and *asmāka-* occur"; then [the rule] "and in *aṇ*" follows; thus, "in *aṇ* as well, *yuṣmāka-* and *asmāka-* occur."

And there must be the inclusion of the term "having a single referent" (*ekārtha*). One must state: "of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when they have a single referent. Why is it not already established by the rule "in the singular" (*ekavacane*) alone? It is not established. What is the reason?

Because of the absence of the singular number. It is stated [in the rule] "in the singular" (*ekavacane*), yet we do not see a singular here. If, on the other hand, *aṇ* and *khañ* were to be qualified by their being followed by the singular, this would not be possible. For in that case, they would apply even here: *yuṣmākaṃ chātraḥ* → *yauṣmākīṇaḥ*, *āsmākīnaḥ*; and they would not apply here: *tava chātrāḥ* → *tāvakīnāḥ*.

[The suffixes] belonging to me [are meant]. Therefore, it cannot be so. If it is not so, then the term "singular" (*ekavacana*) must be taken in its literal sense (*anvartha*). It need not be so. This is not a reference to the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) term "singular. What then? It is a reference to the literal meaning. That which is spoken is "utterance" (*vacana*). An utterance of a single object is a "singular utterance" (*ekavacana*).

(P_4,3.4) When the suffix *ya* is prescribed after the word *ardha*, the suffix *ṭhañ* should be stated [as an alternative] when it is preceded by another word. Examples: *bāleyārdhikaḥ*, *gautamārdhikaḥ*. Furthermore, when the word *ardha* is preceded by a word denoting a direction (*dik*), both the suffix *yat* and *ṭhañ* are applied.
And it should be stated: *pūrvārdhyaḥ*, *paurvārdhikaḥ*; *dakṣiṇārdhyaḥ*, *dākṣiṇārdhikaḥ*;

*uttarārdhyaḥ*, *auttarārdhikaḥ*. For what purpose is this said, when both [suffixes] were already stated in the initial rule (*ādyanyāsa*) following a directional word as the first member of the compound ending in *ardha*?
This is being done now for the first time: [to provide specific forms].

Regarding the rule "after *ardha* and after that which has a preceding member, *ṭhañ* [is applied]," one should recognize that it is undesirable because it implies that everything is optional. Therefore, the Teacher, acting as a friend, explains:
"After a compound whose first member is a direction-word (*dik*), it occurs exactly according to the original rule."

(P_4,3.15) Regarding *śvas*, the substitution of *tuṭ* is untenable because it is not original (*anāditva*). Once *tuṭ* has been applied to *śvas*, the subsequent substitution is untenable. What is the reason? Because it is not original. Once *tuṭ* has been applied, because it is not original, the [further] substitution does not take effect. If that is so, then [the augment] belongs to the prior boundary (*pūrvānta*).

It will be so performed. There is a prohibition of *kā* in the case of the prior limit (*pūrvānta*). If it is the prior limit, then a prohibition of the substitution of *kā* must be stated; otherwise, in the word *śauvastikam*, the substitution of *kā* would apply by the rule "after that which ends in *t*. Let it then be the subsequent element (*parādi*). But was it not said that the addition of the augment *tuṭ* is untenable because [the word] lacks an initial point? It is established, however, because *tuṭ* is prescribed for that which has been substituted. Thus it is established.

This [is the case]. How so? It should be stated: "of that which has been substituted by *tuṭ* etc. Or rather, the conjunction *ca* will be used to establish a simultaneous application (*sanniyoga*): "*tuṭ*" and "whatever else follows. What else follows? Substitution (*ādeśa*).

693–694. The prescription of the elision of the *tal* suffix after *hemanta* when the *aṇ* suffix follows is purposeless, because *heman* is a different base form (*prakṛti*). The statement regarding the elision of the *tal* suffix after *hemanta* when the *aṇ* suffix follows is redundant. What is the reason? Because *heman* is a different base form.
The word *heman* is indeed a distinct base form; for it is said: "O winter, O winter, you come near to my ears."

Therefore, these two do not lose the suffix *hemanta*. Furthermore, because the elision of *a* is observed. Indeed, the elision of *a* is also seen, as in the example: *paṅktir haimantī*. Another says: "The prescription of the suffix *aṇ* for *hemanta*, and the prescription of its elision when *aṇ* follows, are redundant. What is the reason? Because *heman* is a separate base (*prakṛtyantara*) and because the elision of *a* is observed. In that case, [the rule] "from the seasons... applies.
Thus it is established.
(P_4,3.23.1) It should be stated that the suffix *tna* is added after *cirapara*, *parut*, and *parāri*: *ciratnam*, *paruttnam*, *parāritnam*. [The suffix *tanaC* is added] after *praga*.

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), it should be stated that there is both the elision (*lopa*) of *ga* and the suffix *tna*. [Examples: *pratnam ātmānam* ("the ancient self"). After *agra-* and so forth, the suffix *ḍimuc* is prescribed:
*agrimam*, *ādimam*, *paścimam*. It should also be stated that [the suffix applies] after *anta-*: *antimam*.

695–696. Now, what is prescribed for the words *sāyam* and *ciram*? The fact that *sāyam* and *ciram* end in the letter *m* is prescribed as being in conjunction with a suffix. That is to say, the status of ending in *m* for *sāyam* and *ciram* is prescribed by virtue of their connection with a suffix; [as in] *sāyantana-* and *cirantana-*. This is not necessary, however, because the word *sāyam* already ends in *m*. [Question: How then is *sāyāhnaḥ* formed? [Answer: It is from *sāyamaḥ* + *ahne*.

There is the elision of *m*. It should be stated that there is elision of *m* in *sāyam* when followed by *ahan*. How do we account for *sāyatara*? It should be stated that [the suffix] *tara* also [follows]. How do we account for *sāyam* and *sāye*? It should be stated that [the elision occurs] optionally in the locative case (*saptamī*). Now, what is the irregularity (*nipātana*) regarding *prāhṇa* and *pragaya*?
The fact that *prāhṇa* and *pragaya* end in the vowel *e* is an irregularity; the ending in *e* for *prāhṇa* and *pragaya* is prescribed as an irregularity. [Example: *prāhṇetana*.

[Objection: This is not a purpose [for the rule]. It is established even by the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case. [Reply: It would be established when the locative case is present; however, when another case ending is used, it is not established. Regarding *tuṭ*, it has been stated. What was stated?
That the substitution of *tuṭ* is untenable because there is no beginning (*anāditva*). Once *tuṭ* has been applied, because there is no beginning, the substitution does not apply. Thus.

In that case, let it be a prior element (*pūrvānta*). [If it is] a prior element, then the *visarjanīya* [is applied]. If the *visarjanīya* is to be stated as a prior element, [consider the examples] *prātastanam* and *punastanam*. However, if it is at the beginning of the subsequent element (*parādi*), then by the rule "the *visarjanīya* occurs before a *khar* consonant or at the end of a word" (*kharavasānayoḥ visarjanīyaḥ*), the *visarjanīya* is established. Let it then be a subsequent element (*parādi*). But was it not said that once the augment *tuṭ* is applied, because it is not at the beginning, the substitution [of *visarjanīya*] would not occur?

[The objection is: "It follows [that the augment *tuṭ* would not apply]. [The reply is: It is established, however, because of the statement that *tuṭ* applies to that which is designated (*ādiṣṭa*). This is established. How? It should be stated: "*tuṭ* applies to that which is designated. Alternatively, a conjunction will be made so that there is a simultaneous application (*sanniyoga*): "*tuṭ*, and also whatever else follows. And what else follows? A substitute (*ādeśa*).

(P_4.3.24) Regarding *pūrvāhṇa* and *aparāhṇa*, the statement that they are *subanta* (ending in case-suffixes) is for the purpose of hearing the locative (*saptamī*). It must be stated that *pūrvāhṇa* and *aparāhṇa* are *subanta*. What is the purpose? For the purpose of hearing the locative; that is, the hearing of the locative case-ending.

It should be so: *pūrvāhṇetana* and *aparāhṇetana*. If that is the case, then it must be stated. It need not be stated. The activity of the Teacher indicates that the locative case (*saptamī*) occurs here, since he teaches the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative in the rule "ghakālataneṣu kālanāmnaḥ. If it is argued that the mention of non-elision (*alugvacana*) is the indicator [of this], then there would be the undesirable consequence of the locative occurring after an indeclinable (*avyaya*). [This is because] the mention of non-elision...

If it is argued that this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*), then the seventh case ending would be required after an indeclinable (*avyaya*): *doṣātanam*, *divātanam*. Let it be so; [if you say] "after an indeclinable," then the elision (*luk*) will occur. But here too, elision would apply: *pūrvāhṇetanam*, *aparāhṇetanam*. [We reply: In this case, the non-elision (*aluk*) will block the elision. But in this case too it would block it: *doṣātanam*, *divātanam*. Elision is blocked by non-elision only when they share the same basis (*samānāśraya*).
And what is "having a common locus" (*samānāśraya*)? It is that which has the suffix (*pratyaya*) as its locus. And in this case, the elision (*luk*) occurs even before the production of the suffix.

[Objection: This is not established. For here, when the suffix exists, there must be elision; when elision exists, there must be non-elision (*aluk*). But in that situation, the suffix itself does not exist. How then will there be elision? Thus, by means of this indicator (*jñāpaka*), it is shown that [the rule] does not apply when [the suffix] is absent.

The case ending (*vibhakti*) is attracted [to the compound]. Just as it serves as a sublater (*bādhikā*) here in the cases of *pūrvāhṇetana* and *aparāhṇetana*, so too would it be here in the cases of *doṣātanam* and *divātanam*. If that is so, we do not say that the statement regarding the absence of elision (*aluk-vacana*) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the locative (*saptamī*) is present here. What then? It is that the production [of the suffix] occurs after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). But what exactly is being indicated?

This applies as far as the rule "from the first among those that are capable" (*samarthānām prathamāt vā*) continues; and "capability" (*sāmarthyam*) [in this context] refers to [the capacity to be connected with] a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). Thus he says: "It is to be made known. How so? Because the rule "from a *ṅī*, *āp*, or nominal stem" (*ṅyāpprātipadikāt*) also continues [in the present context]. In that case, why should the derivation (*utpatti*) occur from a word ending in a case-suffix and not rather from a *ṅī*, *āp*, or nominal stem? Regarding what was stated: "In the case of [suffixes] characterized by *vṛddhi*, non-*vṛddhi*, vowels, accents, or two consonants..."

And [it is said] "for the sake of making that understood in the rule for suffixes. This is understood to mean: "that which is *vṛddha* among the *samartha* [elements], namely a *ṅī*, *āp*, or *prātipadika*. If this is what is being indicated, how is it that we have forms such as *dvipadaḥ āgatam* (come from a two-footed one) → *dvipādrūpyam*;

*praṣṭhauhaḥ āgatam* (come from a draft-ox) → *praṣṭhvāḍrūpyam*; *kīlālapaḥ āgatam* (come from a drinker of gruel) → *kīlālapārūpyam*; and *papuṣaḥ āgatam* (come from one who has drunk) → *papivaḍrūpyam*?

The rules for *padbhāva*, the elision of the form *ūha*, and *prasāraṇa* would apply [here]. Once *luk* has been applied, they will not occur. But in this case, regarding *sāmanyaḥ* and *vemanyaḥ*—meaning "one who is skilled in the *sāmans*" or "one who is skilled in weaving"—the elision of *n* according to the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* would apply.
Once *luk* has been applied, it will not occur because the word then possesses the designation *bha*. This must be considered here: should *luk* be applied?

"Regarding the rule *nalopaḥ*: what should be done here? The elision of *n* (*nalopaḥ*) [should take place], because it is subsequent. If that is so, then this must be considered here: should the elision of *n* be performed first, or the derivation of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*)? What should be done here? The elision of *n*, because it is subsequent. The elision of *n* is not established (*asiddha*). Because it is not established, the derivation of the secondary suffix will take place. [This applies] to those operations that have been specifically enumerated."

"The elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is not established (*asiddha*), and this [elision] is not included in that enumeration. This too is included there. How so? The term *subvidhi* (rule concerning *sup*) is a compound ending in all case endings:
*supo vidhiḥ* is *subvidhiḥ*."
"Subvidhi" means a rule concerning that which ends in a case-ending (*subanta*).
4.3.25) Why are the meanings such as "born" (*jāta*) and so forth specified? [It is so that] suffixes such as *gha* and others may apply when these meanings, beginning with "born," are present.

[The objection is: "They should [apply] in their own sense; let them not apply in the sense of the base itself. [Response: This is not a valid purpose. The term *śeṣe* ("in the remaining cases") is understood [from the previous rule].

Therefore, they will not apply in their own sense. Consequently, he recites the following reply: "In the case of *tatrajāta* and so on, the statement is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*). This undertaking is for the sake of restriction: that the suffixes *gha* and others should apply only in the case of *jāta* and so on, and not here [in other senses].

In that case, [the rule] "he sits there" or "he sleeps there" would apply. If a restriction is made such that [the suffix applies only when the grain is] "ground on a stone" (*dārṣada*) or "boiled in a mortar" (*aulūkhala*), then the form *yāvaka* ("barley-gruel") would not be established. It will be established by the term "prepared" (*saṃskṛta*). Thus, *dārṣadāḥ saktavaḥ* ("flour ground on a stone") would be established;
however, this [other form] is not established: [namely, *yāvaka*].
"The mortar" and "the barley-gruel"—for that indeed is called "prepared" which is extracted from that very source and then consumed.

But barley-gruel is not extracted and consumed directly from the mortar; it necessarily requires cooking and other such processes. Therefore, there is no purpose served by this restrictive rule. Why does it not apply?

In that case, one says "he sits there" or "he lies there. This is because [the suffix] is not prescribed [for such meanings]. And this non-prescription must necessarily be accepted. For even when the meanings are specified, in cases such as *jāti* (genus) and so forth, where the meaning is not expressed by the suffix being produced, the suffix does not arise there. For example:

"He digs with his finger; he has come from the foot of the tree. In that case, the meanings such as "born" (*jāta*) and so forth should not be specified [as separate senses]. Yet they must be specified. For what purpose? To provide an exception (*apavāda*). [The rule] *prāvṛṣaṣ ṭhaP* [states]: "born in the rainy season" (*prāvṛṣi jātaḥ*) is *prāvṛṣakaḥ*. Where should it not apply? [In the case of] "occurring in the rainy season" (*prāvṛṣi bhavaḥ*), as in *prāveṣeṇyāḥ balāhakāḥ* ("clouds belonging to the rainy season"). As for these [other forms], however...

Those [rules] which are beyond reproach and are merely explanatory statements can be left unformulated. [For example, one might say: "Devadatta is from Sraugha" (*sraughno devadattaḥ*), being skilled in what is made, obtained, or purchased.

In the section concerning elision (*luk-prakaraṇa*), there should be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the words *citrā*, *revatī*, and *rohiṇī* when denoting a female. In the section concerning elision, [the suffix is elided] after *citrā*, *revatī*, and *rohiṇī*.

An addition must be made for the feminine gender: one born under Citrā is a woman called Citrā; Revatī is a woman called Revatī; Rohiṇī is a woman called Rohiṇī. After *phalgunī* and *aṣāḍhā*, the suffixes *ṭāp* and *ṅīp* should be stated: *phalgunī*; [the bricks] he lays down as the *aṣāḍhās*. After *śraviṣṭhā* and *aṣāḍhā*, the suffix *chaṇ* [should be stated]. After *śraviṣṭhā* and *aṣāḍhā*...

It should be stated that [the suffix] *chaṇ* applies [after the names of asterisms]. For example: *śrāviṣṭhīyaḥ*, *āṣāḍhīyaḥ*. Or rather, it need not be stated. Why? Because of the rule stating the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *balu* after asterisms. It need not be stated. What is the reason? Because of the rule stating the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *balu* after asterisms. By the rule "there is elision (*luk*) of *balu* after asterisms," the elision will occur here in this manner.

The inclusion of the term *prāyabhava* (“mostly existing there”) is purposeless, because that [designation] is already established by the term *tatra-bhava* (“existing there”). The inclusion of *prāyabhava* is purposeless. Why? Because it is already accomplished by *tatra-bhava*. For indeed, one who exists mostly in a kingdom—

In that case, the form *tatra bhavaḥ* results in *asau bhavati*. [Objection: It is already established by the rule *tatra tatra bhavaḥ*. [Reply: It is not so established; for there would be the forms *anityabhavaḥ* and *prāyabhavaḥ*. If you argue that *anityabhavaḥ* and *prāyabhavaḥ* are like *muktasaṃśayaḥ*, then just as you consider it correct to cite *muktasaṃśayaḥ* as an example for that [rule governing] *bhava*, namely *sraughnaḥ devadattaḥ*, by that same logic—

This is equivalent. For he too necessarily departs from the region of water and so forth. Now, if you consider this to be a valid example for "arising in that place" (*prāyabhava*), then what is the example for "being in that place" (*tatra bhava*)? It is that which is permanent there, such as "the palaces of Sraughna" or "the ramparts of Sraughna. If that is the case, then [the rule] should be formulated as *tatra bhavati*.

The suffix *cha* is prescribed after [the words] *jihvāmūla* and *aṅguli*. Just as it occurs in the sense of "found there" (*tatra-bhava*) in the form *aṅgulīya*, so too will it occur in the sense of "mostly found there" (*prāya-bhava*). However, this is the purpose: having introduced the topic as "mostly found there" (*prāya-bhava*), he will prescribe the suffix *ṭhak* after [the words] *upajānu*, *upakarṇa*, and *upanīvi*. That [suffix] should apply only in the sense of "mostly found there," and not in the sense of "found there" (*tatra-bhava*). [Otherwise], it would result in the form *aupajānubhava*.

Regarding the word *gaḍu*: now, since the rule "the suffix *yat* is prescribed after words denoting parts of the body" (*śarīrāvayavāt yat*) is formulated with the governing term *tatra bhavaḥ* ("originating therein"), why does that suffix not apply here? Because of non-usage (*anabhidhānāt*). Just as *yat* does not apply due to non-usage, so too *ṭhak* will not apply.

Regarding a derivative (*vikāra*), the suffix *ḍhañ* should be prescribed after the word *kośa*. A derivative of *kośa* is *kauśeya* (silk). For if it were stated [simply] "in the sense of *saṃbhūta*" (produced from), there would be a lack of logical consistency regarding the meaning. Indeed, if "in the sense of *saṃbhūta*" were stated, there would be an impossibility of the intended meaning.

For that [word *kośaja*] cannot apply to what is produced within a sheath (*kośa*). What then? It refers to a modification (*vikāra*) of the sheath. If it is said to be a "modification," then it would also apply to ashes; for ashes too are a modification of the sheath. If, on the other hand, it is said to be "produced within" (*sambhūta*), why does it not apply to a worm? For a worm is also produced within a sheath. [The answer is: because of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*). Just as...

In that case, because it is not so designated, [the suffix] does not apply to *krimi*; likewise, it will not apply to *bhasman* either. And thus the meaning becomes logically consistent. (P_4.3.48) This instruction is improper. The word *kālāt* (from time) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Yet there is no such thing as a "time" (*kala*) named *kalāpin*. This is not a fault; the designation will occur through association (*sāhacarya*). [The term *kalāpin*] refers to that which is associated with *kalāpi*.
"Kālaḥ kalāpī kālaḥ" (P.

While the word "tatra" is already understood [from the previous rule], for what purpose is "tatra" mentioned again? It is for the sake of [specifying] that particular context within the section on "tatra."

The repetition of the word "there" (*tatra*) is for the purpose of terminating the [preceding] section on time (*kāla*). In that context, the repetition of "there" is made to terminate the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning time. For governing rules do not cease merely because a crow caws.
Or rather, what connection is there such that the mention of "there" would terminate the governing rule of time? This is [the answer]:...

Connection: the mention of *tatra* (in that place), which is connected with time, continues [from the previous rule]. And this mention of *tatra* serves as a displacer of the previous mention of *tatra*. When that has been displaced, the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning time is also displaced.

706. In the section concerning the suffix *ñya*, an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for words beginning with *parimukha*. An addition must be made in the section concerning *ñya* for words such as *parimukha*: *pārimukhyam*, *pārihanavyam*. Regarding the rule for the formation of *avyayībhāva* compounds, a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) must be stated for words beginning with *upakūla*: *aupakūlaḥ*, *aupamūlaḥ*, *aupaśālaḥ*.
This which has been stated is too little. It is intended that [the substitution] of *samāna* and of that which begins with it occurs in the case of *adhyātma* and so forth. Regarding *samāna*:
*sāmānikaḥ*. Regarding that which begins with it: [e.g., *sāmānyatvaḥ*].

The suffix *ṭhañ* is prescribed after the words *samānagrāma* and *samānadeśa*, as well as after *adhyātman* and others—namely, *ādhyātmika*, *ādhidaivika*, and *ādhibhautika*. The suffix *ṭhañ* should also be stated [after the compound] *ūrdhvandama* and *ūrdhvadeha*; thus: *aurdhvandamika* and *aurdhvadehika*.

The suffix *ṭhañ* should also be stated after the word *lokottara*; thus: *aihalaūkika* and *pāralaukika*. [The suffix *ṭhañ* is also prescribed] after the words *mukha* and *pārśva* when followed by the suffix *tasi*.

The suffix *īya* should be prescribed after the words *mukha* and *pārśva* when they end in the suffix *tas*. Thus: *mukhatīyaḥ*, *pārśvatīyaḥ*. The suffix *īya* should be prescribed after *jana* when it is preceded by *ku* or *para*. Thus: *janakīyam*, *parakīyam*. The suffix *īya* should be applied; furthermore, it should be applied to *madhya*. Thus: *madhyīyaḥ*. Moreover, the two suffixes *maṇ* and *īya* should also be prescribed. Thus: *maṇ* and *īya* are also suffixes to be stated.

*Mādhyamaḥ* means "belonging to the middle. From *madhya*, the suffix *dinaṇ* is added. The word *madhya* undergoes the change to *madhyama*, and from it the suffix *dinaṇ* occurs. Thus: *mādhyandina udgāyati* ("the midday priest chants"). Likewise, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix after *sthāman* and *ajina*. After *sthāman*...

The elision (*luk*) should be stated [after these]. *Aśvatthāmā*. The elision (*luk*) should also be stated after words ending in *ajina*: *ulājinaḥ*, *siṃhājinaḥ*, *vyāghrājinaḥ*. For *bāhya*, *daivya*, and *pāñcajanya*, the suffix *ñya* is desired to express depth (*gāmbhīrya*).

709–710. For what purpose is the simultaneous governing (*adhikāra*) of *bhava* and *vyākhyāna* established? The simultaneous governing of *bhava* and *vyākhyāna* is for the purpose of prescribing exceptions (*apavāda*). The simultaneous governing of *bhava* and *vyākhyāna* is established for the purpose of prescribing exceptions, [with the intention]: "I shall state the exceptions simultaneously. Why is it said that it is "for the purpose of prescribing exceptions"?

Thus, it would not be for the purpose of further instruction, for those two have already been instructed; indeed, these two meanings have already been explained: one is "that which exists there" (*tatra-bhava*), and the other is "belonging to that" (*tasyedam*). Now, for what purpose is the mention of the name of the term to be explained? The mention of the name of the term to be explained therein is for the sake of the meaning of "existence there. [The mention of] the name of the term to be explained therein...
The inclusion is made for the sake of existence (*bhavārtha*). Why is it said "for the sake of existence" and not also "for the sake of explanation"?
For in the case of an explanation, it is established even without being stated; when there is an explanation, it is established even in the absence of a statement.
That toward which there is an explanation—this is what will constitute its origin. Toward what does this [explanation] occur?

Regarding the name of that which is to be explained (*vyākhyātavyanāman*): it is not the case that [the rule] applies only for the sake of the object being explained (*bhavārtha*). The name of that which is to be explained is also employed for the sake of the explanation itself. This is so that [the designation] "Sukosalā is the explanation of Pāṭaliputra" does not occur here. Now, even if the name of that which is to be explained is included, why does it not occur in this instance? For [in this case], the explanation is partial (*avayavaśas*).

[The word] *vyākhyāna* [is used]. One also explains *Pāṭaliputra* by its constituent parts, saying, "Its ramparts are like this. This is indeed true. However, in some cases, a certain mode of explanation becomes more prevalent. And in the treatises on words (*śabda-grantha*), this mode of explanation is more prevalent: "The *Nirukta* is being explained," or "The *Vyākaraṇa* is being explained."
It is said: No one says, "Pāṭaliputra is being explained. (Regarding the rule P. 4.3.66:
In the case of mantras used in the sense of "occurring in," elision must be stated. [For example: A mantra occurring in the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is called *agniṣṭoma*.
The *agniṣṭoma*, the *rājasūya*, and the *vājapeya*. Regarding the *kalpa* and the *vyākhyāna*: in the case of the *kalpa* and the *vyākhyāna*, the elision (*luk*) should be stated.

The *kalpa* that is the exposition (*vyākhyāna*) of the *agniṣṭoma* is [called] *agniṣṭoma*; [the *kalpas* of] the *rājasūya* and the *vājapeya* [are likewise called by those names]. Then it must be stated [that this elision occurs]. Or rather, it need not be stated; for there is designation by the name of the object because of its being for that purpose (*tādarthyāt tācchabdyam*). It need not be stated. What is the reason? Because there is designation by the name of the object because of its being for that purpose.
The designation [of the cup] will be based on its being for the sake of that [sacrifice]. That which is for the sake of the Agniṣṭoma is called "Agniṣṭoma"; likewise, the Rājasūya and the Vājapeya.

4.3.68) For what purpose is the mention of *kratu*? If it were stated simply as "from sacrifices" (*yajñebhyaḥ*), the derivation would occur only from those sacrifices that have already become established technical names (*saṃjñībhūta*).

[The suffix -ika is applied] after words such as *agniṣṭoma*, *rājasūya*, and *vājapeya*; or wherever the word *yajña* occurs, as in *nāvayajñika* and *pākayajñika*. However, it would not apply here: *pāñcaudanikaḥ*, *sāptaudanikaḥ*, and *śātaudanikaḥ*. But if the term *kratu* is used instead [of *yajña*], there is no fault. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *yajña*? If only "after *kratu*s" were stated, then those [compounds] which—

The mention of *nāman* and *ākhyāta* is for the purpose of including both their compounded and uncompounded forms. The mention of *nāman* and *ākhyāta* should be understood as intended to include both the compound and the analysis [of the compound]: *nāmikaḥ*, *ākhyātikaḥ*, and *nāmākhyātikaḥ*.
(P_4.3.84) This formulation is incorrect; for it does not originate from Vidūra. What then? It originates from Bālavāya.

"It occurs in the sense of 'originating from' and it is derived [from *vidūra*]. If that is so, then [the derivation] of *vālavāya* from *vidūra* would require that the word *vidūra* undergoes a change into *vālavāya*, and furthermore, the suffix *ñya* must be stated [as the cause of this change]. Or rather, it is simply a different base form (*prakṛtyantara*).
Alternatively, the word *vidūra* is a different base form for *vālavāya*. Indeed, people do not apply the designation "it is *vidūra*" to what is *vālavāya* there. Indeed not.

If one should say, "In that case," then one should apply the term as in the case of *jitvarī*. Just as merchants address Vārāṇasī as *jitvarī*, so do grammarians address Vālavāya as *vidūra*. [The forms] *vālavāya* and *vidūra* are either two distinct bases (*prakṛti*) or [the latter is derived from the former]. If one should say, "Indeed, it is not so in that case," then one should apply the term as in the case of *jitvarī*.
This formulation is incorrect. Departing or exiting belongs to that which possesses consciousness, whereas a door is insentient. How, then, should it be formulated? "The door for departing."
In that case, should such an instruction be given? It need not be given. For even in the case of insentient things, metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) as if they were sentient is observed.
For example: "This corner of his has gone out"; "this one has entered.
(Pāṇini 4.3.87) KA_II,313.20–22 Ro_III, [text missing]

713. Regarding the rule *adhikṛtya kṛte granthe* (P. 4.3.87), it should be stated that after *ākhyāyikā* ("narrative"), the suffix is frequently elided (*bahulaṃ lup*). Thus, for a work composed concerning [a person], the suffix is optionally elided after the name of a narrative: *vāsavadattā*, *sumanottarā*. But it does not occur in the case of *bhaimarathī*.

713. A prohibition [of the suffix *cha*] must be stated for compounds beginning with *devāsura* and others when they are *dvandva*s. [The forms are: *daivāsuraṃ*, *rākṣosuraṃ*, *daivāsurī*, *rakṣosurī*. What is the difference between *nivāsa* (residence) and *abhijana* (ancestral home)? *Nivāsa* is that place where one currently dwells; *abhijana* is that place where one's ancestors have dwelt.

(P_4,3.98) Why is the suffix *vun* prescribed after the word *vāsudeva*, when it would already be established by the rule "after [words denoting] *gotra* or *kṣatriya* names, *vuñ* is applied diversely"? For there is no difference between the *vun* derived from the word *vāsudeva* and the *vuñ*; the form is identical in either case.
That is indeed the [correct] accent. In that case, however, this is the purpose: [the rule] will state that the word *vāsudeva* is to be placed first.
Alternatively, this is not a designation for a Kṣatriya; it is a name (*sañjñā*) of that venerable one.

715. What is the purpose of the mention of *sarva*? The mention of *sarva* is for the sake of the reduction of the base form (*prakṛtinirhrāsa*). The mention of *sarva* is made so that there may be a reduction of the base form. And that [mention] is for the sake of *madravṛji*. That should be understood as being for the sake of *madravṛji*: one whose devotion is to the Madras, or whose devotion is among the Madras, is a *Madraka*.

It should be exactly thus: *vārjya-bhaktir asya* or *vārjyau bhaktir asya*, [resulting in] *vṛjikaḥ*. (P. 4.3.101) The mention of *prokta* (proclaimed) is useless, because it is not observed there. The mention of *prokta* is useless. Why?

The reason is that it is not observed there. In every village, the *Kāṭhaka* and the *Kālāpaka* are recited; however, it is not observed there [in those texts]. Furthermore, it is observed in the *grantha* (text). And wherever the *grantha* is observed, it is established by the very fact that the *grantha* has been composed there. If so, this must be stated for the sake of the Vedic meters (*chandas*). No, it need not.

For the Vedic meters (*chandas*) are being composed [now]. The Vedic meters are eternal. If it is argued that they are for the sake of the meter, that is an equal position. If it is argued that they are for the sake of the meter, this becomes an equal case: in every village the *Kāṭhaka* and the *Kālāpaka* are recited.
Because they are not seen there, and because no suffix (*pratyaya*) is observed there; yet because they are seen in the text where they do appear.

That is a literary work (*grantha*). In that case, it is already established by the rule *tatra kṛte granthe*. But was it not said: "The Vedas (*chandas*) are not created; the Vedas are eternal"? Even if the meaning is eternal, that sequence of phonemes (*varṇānupūrvī*) is non-eternal. And it is due to the difference in that [sequence] that these names arise: *Kāṭhaka*, *Kālāpaka*, *Maudaka*, *Paippalādaka*.

[Objection: "In that case, this should not be stated now. [Response: It must indeed be stated. [Question: What is the purpose? [Answer: That which was proclaimed by him but not composed by him—the *Mādhurī* recension. [Objection: If there is a basis for this, then this alone should be stated.
[Response: That need not be stated. [Objection: Even that must necessarily be stated—that which was composed by him but not proclaimed by him.
The *vāraruca* poetry and the *jālūkā* verses [are examples].
The inclusion of the term "one who performs it before one's eyes" (*pratyakṣakārin*) must be made; [it applies] to the words *antevāsin* and *antevāsin*.

"Let it not be so. Then that [distinction] must be stated. It need not be stated. The mention of Kalāpin and Khāḍāya is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the inclusion of those who act as direct pupils (*pratyakṣakārin*) among the disciples of Vaiśampāyana. In that the Teacher makes this mention of Kalāpin and Khāḍāya, he indicates that [the suffix *cha*] does not occur after the grand-disciples of a disciple (*antevāsyantevāsibhyaḥ*). How is this an indicator?

Kaṭha was a pupil of Vaiśampāyana; Khāḍāyana was a pupil of Kaṭha; and Kalāpin was a pupil of Vaiśampāyana. If [the rule] were to apply even to the pupils of pupils, then the mention of Kalāpin and Khāḍāyana would be redundant. However, the Teacher perceives that it does not apply to the pupils of pupils; therefore, there is the mention of Kalāpin and Khāḍāyana.
[The word] "desire" (chanda) is included [in the rule]; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). The inclusion of "desire" must be made;
otherwise, there would indeed be an over-extension. Otherwise, there would be an over-extension even here:
[the undesired application] that "these are verses (śloka) proclaimed by Tittiri."
Regarding the rule "in the case of Brāhmaṇas and Kalpas proclaimed in ancient times," a prohibition must be stated for Yājñavalkya and others, because they belong to the same period.
In this rule, "in the case of Brāhmaṇas and Kalpas proclaimed in ancient times," a prohibition regarding Yājñavalkya and others must be formulated.
The *Yājñavalkīya-brāhmaṇas* and the *Saulabhāni*—for what reason? Because they are of equal time. These also are of equal time. (P_4,3.116) KA_II,316.18–317.4 Ro_III, [116]

319–320. Regarding the rule *kṛte granthe* (P. 4.3.116), the suffix *aṇ* should be stated after the group beginning with *makṣikā*. In this context of "when a book is made," the suffix *aṇ* must be prescribed after words such as *makṣikā*. [Example: *mākṣikam* ("honey"), meaning "made by bees. And it should also be stated after its specific sub-varieties. The suffix *aṇ* should also be prescribed after its specific sub-varieties. [Examples: *sāragham* ("bee-honey"), meaning "made by *saraghā* bees"; *gārmutam* ("honey from *garmut* bees"); *pauttikam* ("honey from *pauttika* bees"). Therefore, that [rule] must indeed be stated.

It need not be stated. It is established through the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). The division will be made as follows: [First: *kṛte granthe* (after a word meaning "composed," when it refers to a book); [Second: *tataḥ sañjñāyām* (after that, when it is a name). And in the sense of "made by that" (*tena kṛte*), a suffix occurs according to the prescribed rules when it is a name (*sañjñāyām*). For example: *sāragham* (made by bees), *gārmutam*, *pauttikam*. Then, after words such as *kulāla* ("potter"), the suffix *vuñ* is applied. This is only in the sense of being a name (*sañjñāyām*).

(P_4,3.120) KA_II,318.2–319.13 Ro_III, 720–722: There is no application [of the suffix] in the sense of "this belongs to that" when the referent is not present, because the word *idam* denotes what is perceptible. There is no application in the sense of "this belongs to that" when the referent is not present. What is the reason? Because the word *idam* denotes what is perceptible. This [word] *idam*— The word *idam* denotes that which is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*). Since it denotes only that which is currently present before one's eyes, it cannot express a relationship with something that is absent or remote. Therefore, a suffix such as *cha* (forming adjectives like *tasyedam*) cannot be applied to form a derivative meaning "this belongs to that" when the object referred to by *idam* is not in proximity. Why? Because the denotation of *idam* is restricted to the perceptible. The term *idam* refers specifically to this immediate, manifest reality. Thus, in the absence of the object, the grammatical operation fails to apply.

The genitive case occurs when there is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, it would apply only in this instance: "this belongs to him" (*tasyedaṃ*); but it would not apply in cases such as "that belongs to him" (*tasyādaḥ*) or "that belongs to him" (*tasya tat*). [Objection: But this is already established, since the genitive occurs wherever there is a connection (*yadyoga*). [Reply: This is indeed established. How so? It should be stated that the genitive occurs where there is a connection with *yat*. Furthermore, there is a prohibition regarding [words] beginning with *anantara*. There is a prohibition regarding [words] beginning with *anantara*.

It must be stated: "that which is immediate to it" means "that which is near to it. Is it because the genitive case occurs through connection [with a word] that a prohibition regarding "immediate" (*anantara*) and so forth must be stated? He says: No. A prohibition regarding "immediate" and so forth must be stated in every respect. But this is established by enumeration. How so? An enumeration must be made.

[The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after one's own village, district, and person. It should be stated: "after one's own village, district, and person. Examples: *sraughnaḥ* (one from Sroghna), *māthuraḥ* (one from Mathurā)—these refer to villages; *āṅgakaḥ*, *vāṅgakaḥ*—these refer to districts. Regarding persons: *daivadattaḥ*, *yājñadattaḥ*. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after a leaf when it is outside [the body]. It should be stated: "after a leaf when it is outside. Examples: *āśvam* (made from horse-leather), *auṣṭram* (made from camel-leather), *gārdabham* (made from donkey-leather). After a chariot [the suffix *aṇ* is applied].

Regarding *rathāṅga*: it should be stated that [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after *ratha* when *rathāṅga* follows. Thus: *āśvaratha*, *auṣṭraratha*, *gārdabharatha*. Regarding *vahi*: after a word ending in the suffix *tṛ*, the suffix *aṇ* should be stated, and the augment *iṭ* should also be stated. Thus: the property of one who carries is *sāṃvahitra*. Regarding *agnīdh*: the suffix *rañ* should be stated after *agnīdh* when *śaraṇa* follows, and it should be designated as *bha*. Thus: *āgnīdhra*.

And it should be stated [as follows]: *āgnīdhra* is the name for the fire-priest’s shed (*śaraṇa*). Regarding the suffix *ṣeṇyaṇ* in the sense of "the placing of fuel" (*samidhām ādhāne*), the suffix *ṣeṇyaṇ* should be stated [after the word *samidh*]. Thus, the mantra used for the placing of fuel is called *sāmidhenī*; the *ṛc* verse is a *sāmidhenī*. Regarding the rule "from *caraṇa*, in the sense of *dharma* and *āmnāya*," it should be stated that [this applies] after the word *caraṇa*. For example: the *dharma* of the Kaṭhas is the *kāṭhaka*.

Or rather, the traditional recensions (*āmnāya*) are [named] after them, such as the *Kāṭhaka*, *Kālāpaka*, *Maudaka*, and *Paippalādaka*. In that case, much would have to be said, and the Sūtra would be split. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. But was it not already stated that if something is not present, there is no application of the rule "this belongs to that"? Are you now merely criticizing the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), and not the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)?

Furthermore, just as the term *idam* (this) applies to what is perceptible (*pratyakṣa*), so too the term *tat* (that) applies to what is imperceptible (*parokṣa*). Consequently, [the rule] would apply here: *tasyedam* ("this belongs to that"). But it would not apply in the case of *asyāmuṣya* ("this belongs to that one over there"). There is a distinction here: an elliptical expression (*ekaśeṣanirdeśa*) will be used here; thus, from *tasya* and *asya* and *amuṣya*, the form *tasya* arises.
In this case as well, there will be a reference by means of a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member): "that," "this," and "this" [will be expressed as] simply "this.

As for what was said—that a prohibition must be stated regarding "immediate succession" (*anantara*) and so forth—it need not be stated; because of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*), the application of the suffix will not occur in the case of "immediate succession" and the like.

An exception must be stated regarding the word *vaira* after [compounds] such as *devāsura*: an exception regarding *vaira* after [compounds] such as *devāsura* must be stated. [Examples: *daivāsura*, *rākṣosura*.
723. The mention of *ghoṣa* in the rule for *saṅgha* and others. The mention of *ghoṣa* must be made in the rule for *saṅgha* and others: [examples are] *gārgyo ghoṣaḥ*, *vātsyo ghoṣaḥ*.

(P_4.3.127.2) KA_II,319.20–320.4 Ro_III, 723. What is the purpose of the letter *ṇ*? It is for the sake of *vṛddhi*. So that the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule *ñṇiti* may occur in the case of *saṅgha* and others.

The addition of the marker *ṇit* to the suffix is purposeless because the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is already "vṛddha" (possessing a long vowel in its first syllable). Regarding the addition of the marker *ṇit* to the suffix in the case of *saṅgha* and other such stems, it is purposeless. Why? Because the nominal stem is already "vṛddha. This nominal stem is indeed already "vṛddha. However, it is for the sake of prohibiting [the application of] gender and masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*). That is to say, it is for the purpose of prohibiting gender and masculine substitution.
However, the letter *ṇ* must be applied for the sake of the gender (*liṅga*). [In the case of] *vaidī*, it is for the sake of prohibiting the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*).
[For example: *baidī-sthūṇaḥ* ("one whose pillar is female"). This is so that the prohibition of the masculine form by the rule *vṛddhinimittasya...* (Pāṇini 1.1.73) may apply.
(Pāṇini 4.3.131; Kāśikā II,320.6–21; Rūpāvatāra III)

724–725. The suffix *aṇ* is prescribed after *kaupiñjala* and *hāstipada*. The suffix *aṇ* should be stated [after these]: *kaupiñjalāḥ*, *hāstipadāḥ*. For *ātharvaṇika*, there is the elision of the *ik* suffix and the suffix *aṇ* should also be stated.

[The forms] *ātharvaṇo dharmaḥ* (the dharma of the Atharvavedins) and *ātharvaṇa āmnāyaḥ* (the tradition of the Atharvavedins) [are derived thus]. This [section] is for the sake of *ātharvaṇa* and for the sake of *ātharvaṇika*.

The word "four" (catur) is mentioned [in the rule]. In the section beginning with "vasanta," the words *atharvan* and *ātharvaṇa* are recited. Their mention in the sixth chapter is for the sake of preserving the original stem-form (*prakṛtibhāva*). This fourth mention, however, is for the purpose of the elision of the suffix *ik*. It might be argued that the double mention could be avoided. How so? By taking the rule *tena proktam* as the starting point, one should state that there is an elision (*luk*) after the names of sages (*ṛṣi*), as in the case of Vasiṣṭha.

The term *anuvāka* [is used] for the sake of [denoting] Viśvāmitra as an *anuvāka*; therefore, it should be stated that [the word] is derived from *Atharvan*. By this, both *Atharvā* and *Ātharvaṇaḥ* are established. Alternatively, the word *Ātharvaṇa* should be recited among the *vasantādi* group [of words].

In that case, there is no purpose served by the rule regarding the preservation of the original stem form (*prakṛtibhāva*), nor by the elision of the suffix *ik*. If [it were included] in the *vasantādi* group...

The word *ātharvaṇa* is recited [in the rule], but the form *ātharvaṇikaḥ*—meaning "one who studies the Atharvan"—is not established. This is not a fault. Here, we must establish three forms. In that case, between two words of identical meaning, the analysis (*vigraha*) will be made with one, and the derivation (*utpatti*) will occur from the other, according to the maxim of the sheep and the ewe (*aviravikanyāya*). For example: *aveḥ māṃsam* ("the meat of a sheep").
Thus, by analyzing [the compound] as *avika-śabdāt*, its derivation occurs. Similarly, by analyzing *ātharvaṇam adhīte*, it will become *ātharvaṇikaḥ*;

or, by analyzing *atharvāṇam adhīte*, it remains a mere sentence. In that case, one must simply establish the connection as "of the Ātharvaṇikas. And at present, nothing else can rightfully belong to the Ātharvaṇikas.
"Other than this dharma or the sacred tradition" (Pāṇini 4.3.134).

While the word *tasya* ("of that") is already in effect [from the previous rule], for what purpose is *tasya* mentioned again? This repetition of *tasya* within its own section (*prakaraṇa*) serves to restrict the application of the rule.

It is for the purpose of excluding the *śaiṣika* suffixes. Within this section, the phrase "of that" (*tasya*) is stated again for the purpose of excluding the *śaiṣika* suffixes; thus, the *śaiṣika* suffixes are set aside. But how do they apply? Their application follows from the rule "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*). For these [categories]—offspring, collection, modification, and dwelling—are indeed specific instances of "that which belongs to it. Why is this stated? For the purpose of superseding [the general rule].

It would be accomplished [by the general rule]. Those [suffixes] which are obstructors of it [would apply] for the purpose of obstructing that [general rule]. But how can a non-śaiṣika suffix obstruct a śaiṣika suffix? This [non-śaiṣika] is indeed a general rule (*utsarga*) regarding the remainder (*śeṣa*). For whatever is a general rule is also indeed a remainder. Which [suffixes], then, among the śaiṣikas would apply to products (*vikāra*) and parts (*avayava*), since everything here is pervaded by exceptions (*apavāda*)? In this case—

Nothing is said [here]. [The rule] "after *hala* and *sīra*, the suffix *ṭhak*" applies. But how, even if one wishes it so, can an exception (*apavāda*) that is applicable be set aside? By the force of the mention of the word *tasya*. Do you state this purpose for the mention of *tasya* alone by way of an assumption (*adhyāroha*), and not rather for the entire rule (*yoga*)? [Reply: The statement of the purpose must necessarily be for the sake of what follows.

It must be stated. Furthermore, the case-ending expressing capability (*samartha-vibhakti*) must necessarily be specified for the sake of what follows. [Objection: The case-ending under discussion, namely "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*), continues to apply. [Reply: There is no such understanding. Or rather, there is no need for such an understanding, because the secondary suffixes (*śaiṣika*) are excluded by this very rule. For grammatical governing rules (*adhikāra*) do not cease merely because a crow caws.
If, indeed, secondary derivatives (*śaiṣika*) are not desired for both modifications and parts, then an exclusion must be stated by means of a lengthy rule:

"And [the suffix] does not apply to parts of non-living beings, herbs, and trees. Since the non-exclusion for parts of non-living beings, herbs, and trees is intended, yet an exclusion would result there; for example, *pāṭaliputrakāḥ prāsādāḥ* ("the palaces of Pāṭaliputra") and *pāṭaliputrakāḥ*.

Regarding the words "prākārāḥ": the contradiction between the suffixes *aṇ* and *mayaṭ* is untenable because *mayaṭ* is the general rule (*utsarga*). A contradiction between *aṇ* and *mayaṭ* is not possible. For he will state the contradiction:
"After a word ending in a *vṛddhi* vowel, *mayaṭ* takes the place of *aṇ*. That contradiction is untenable. What is the reason? Because *mayaṭ* is the general rule.

For when the secondary suffixes (*śaiṣika*) are excluded, the general rule (*utsarga*) is that *mayaṭ* follows a base ending in a *vṛddhi* vowel; this [suffix] is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rule for] *aṇ*. And a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between a general rule and an exception is improper. For if they were included, then by the conflict between the general rule and the exception, *mayaṭ* would apply; for when the secondary suffixes are included, *cha* is the general rule following a base ending in a *vṛddhi* vowel, while *aṇ* and *mayaṭ* are its exceptions. [The former view is rejected] because of the conflict with the exceptions.

The suffix *mayaṭ* will apply. As for what was said—that there is no comprehension [of the intended meaning] because the secondary (*śaiṣika*) suffixes are excluded by this much of a rule—there is indeed comprehension. For the suffix *aṇ* is not difficult to obtain here; it is established here simply by the rule "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*).

This very same *aṇ*, however, by virtue of the mention of "that" (*tasya*), would otherwise have the occasion to apply as that *aṇ* which possesses exceptions; [the present rule] makes this [suffix] free from exceptions.

It establishes the *aṇ* suffix. Among those [suffixes], it will sublate the second ones because they are exceptions (*apavāda*), and the third ones because they are subsequent (*para*). Regarding the fourth ones, some are exceptions that precede and thus sublate the immediately following rules, so they will not sublate this one; others are exceptions in the middle and thus sublate the preceding rules.

And these [parts] would be only so many, namely the second, the third, or the fourth; there are no fifth parts, nor sixth. As for what is said—that "there is no exclusion [of the suffix] in the case of parts belonging to non-living beings, herbs, and trees"—it is stated that there is an exclusion [of the suffix] in the case of living beings, herbs, and trees. In that case, what occasion is there for there to be an exclusion in the case of non-living beings, herbs, and trees?

As for what is said—that the contradiction regarding *aṇ* and *mayaṭ* is untenable because *mayaṭ* is a general rule (*utsarga*)—let there be no contradiction. According to the principle that "exceptions (*apavāda*) set aside the immediately preceding rules," *aṇ* and *añ* will be set aside, but *mayaṭ* will not be set aside.
730–731. For what purpose is there a simultaneous governing rule (*adhikāra*) for both *vikāra* (modification) and *avayava* (part)? It has been stated regarding *vikāra* and *avayava*.

What was stated? In that context, it was stated: "There is a simultaneous governing rule for *bhāva* (state/condition) and *vyākhyāna* (explanation/commentary) for the purpose of prescribing exceptions (*apavāda*), because those two have already been specified. Here too, there is a simultaneous governing rule for *vikāra* and *avayava* for the purpose of prescribing exceptions.
For those two [the suffixes *cha* and *ña*] have already been prescribed by the rule "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*).
Why is the word *gavīdhukā* listed among the *bilva*-group, when it would already be established by the rule "the suffix *aṇ* after a stem ending in *ka*"?

The inclusion of *gavīdhukā* among the *bilva*-type words is for the purpose of prohibiting the suffix *mayaṭ*. The inclusion of *gavīdhukā* among the *bilva*-type words is made in order to prohibit *mayaṭ*; thus, let there not be *mayaṭ* after this [word]. (Pāṇini 4.3.140) KA_II,323.4–24 Ro_III, [140]

731–733. Regarding the prescription of *añ* after a word beginning with an *anudātta* vowel, there must be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the case of a word that is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable). When the suffix *añ* is prescribed after a word beginning with an *anudātta*, an addition must be made for the case of a word that is *ādyudātta*. [Examples: *kuvalī* (the *kuvala* fruit), *kauvalam* (a product of the *kuvala*); *badarī* (the *badara* fruit), *bādaram* (a product of the *badara*). Then, should this be stated? It need not be stated. For once the *nighāta* (suppression of accent) has been applied, the rule "after a word beginning with an *anudātta*" is already established.

It is not established. What is the reason? Because a word (*pada*) begins with an unaccented vowel. For the suppression of accent (*nighāta*) applies to a word, and a word is that which ends in a case-suffix (*sup*).

Furthermore, suffixes are prescribed after nominal stems (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or *prātipadika*. Or rather, it need not be stated. What is the reason? Because of the unaccented initial of the meaningful unit (*samartha*). It is by virtue of having an unaccented initial that the meaningful unit [is characterized].

We shall specify [the meaning]. It cannot be done in this way; for in that case, it would follow that [the term applies to] "a modification of speech" and "a modification of skin. Indeed, this [term *vikāra*] is capable [of being understood] as beginning with the low-pitched accent (*anudātta*) and so forth. And in this case, it would not apply to "a modification of all [parts]. Therefore, it cannot be done in this way. If it is not so, then an additional rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made. It need not be made; for such is the practice of the Teacher.
It indicates that the *nighāta* (enclitic accent) of the preceding word occurs at the very moment the second vowel appears;
for this reason, he includes the word *garbhiṇī* among the *bhikṣādi* group [of words ending in *aṇ*]. How does this serve as an indicator?
By including *garbhiṇī* in the *bhikṣādi* list, the purpose is to prevent the suffix *aṇ* from being applied by the rule concerning words beginning with an *anudātta* vowel.

And if there were the *nighāta* (non-accentuation) of the word, this word *garbha* would be acute on the first syllable; therefore, whatever suffix would apply after that which ends in *in*, that alone would occur. That being established, the *nighāta* would follow. In that case, what possibility would there be for the suffix *añ* characterized by having an initial low tone (*anudātta*)?
However, the Teacher perceives that as soon as the second accent appears, [the process is complete].

4.3.156.2) Regarding the rule *aṇo vṛddhāt mayaṭ* ("after a word ending in *aṇ* that is *vṛddha*, the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied"), this occurs by way of *vipratiṣedha* (conflict between rules).

The scope of *oḥ añaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.136) is *tittiḍīka*, [yielding] *taittiḍīkam*. The scope of *mayaṭ* (Pāṇini 4.3.82) is *kāṣṭhamayam*. In the case of *śākamayam*, both would apply. By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), *mayaṭ* applies after a word ending in *oḥ añaḥ* and after a word beginning with an anudātta vowel that ends in *añ*. The scope of *oḥ añaḥ* is *āraḍavam*; the scope of *mayaṭ* is the same. In the case of *dārumayam*, both would apply.

The suffix *añ* occurs after a word beginning with an *anudātta* vowel; this is its scope: *kauvalam*, *jāradvṛkṣam*. The suffix *mayaṭ* has the same scope. Here, both would apply: *āmramayam*. By way of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), *añ* takes the place of *mayaṭ* when referring to living beings (*prāṇin*). By way of conflict, *añ* occurs in place of *mayaṭ* for living beings. The scope of *añ* for living beings is, for example, *gārdhram* (from *gṛdhra*). The scope of *mayaṭ* is the same.
Thus, in this case, both [suffixes] would apply: to *cāṣa* and *bhāsa*. [The suffix] *añ* would prevail by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). Or rather, it is not so;

because it has no scope (*anavakāśatvāt*), *mayaṭ* is an exception (*apavāda*). Indeed, this conflict between *añ* and *mayaṭ* is not appropriate. Why? Because *mayaṭ* is an exception due to having no scope; *mayaṭ* has no scope, whereas *añ* has scope.

It will be superseded. How can it be without scope? If the secondary suffixes (*śaiṣika*) are still in force, [then there is no conflict]. But if the secondary suffixes have ceased to apply, then *mayaṭ* has its scope in the case of words with a *vṛddhi* vowel in the first syllable, as does *añ* after words denoting living beings (*prāṇi*). Furthermore, this conflict between *mayaṭ* and *añ* is improper. Why? Because, due to its lack of scope, *mayaṭ* is simply an exception (*apavāda*).

The suffix *mayaṭ* has no scope [to apply]. Just as it sets aside both the suffix *añ* after words beginning with a non-anudātta vowel and the suffix *añ* after words denoting living beings (*prāṇin*), so too would it set aside the suffix *añ* after words denoting living beings. Therefore, when *mayaṭ* is prescribed, there must be a prohibition regarding living beings. Thus, when *mayaṭ* is prescribed, a prohibition regarding living beings must be stated.
But then, it must indeed be stated. No, it need not be stated; for intermediate exceptions (*apavāda*) [set aside] the preceding [rules].

Since intermediate exceptions (*madhye apavādāḥ*) set aside preceding rules (*purastāt apavādāḥ*), this suffix *mayaṭ* will thus set aside the suffix *añ* prescribed after [stems] beginning with an unaccented vowel, as well as the suffix *añ*. It will not, however, set aside the suffix *añ* prescribed after words denoting living beings (*prāṇyañ*). If it were the case that "intermediate exceptions set aside preceding rules," then the secondary suffixes (*śaiṣikāḥ*) would not apply here; for intermediate exceptions set aside only those rules immediately following them, and thus this suffix *aṇ* will set aside the suffix *añ*.

The suffix *mayaṭ* will not supersede [the suffix *añ*]. By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the suffix *añ* derived from a word with an initial low-pitched vowel (*anudāttādi*) supersedes the suffix *añ* used for living beings (*prāṇyañ*). The scope of the rule "the suffix *añ* occurs after a word with an initial low-pitched vowel" is, for example, *jaradvṛkṣa* → *jāradvṛkṣam*. The scope of the suffix *añ* used for living beings is the same [as previously stated]. In this case, both [suffixes] would apply: *kapota* → *kāpotam*. [In such instances, the *prāṇyañ* applies.]

It occurs by way of contradiction. But what is the distinction here between that [rule] being present or this one? That rule is subject to exceptions; this one, however, is without exception. If it were by that [rule], it would not apply here: *śauvāvidham*, meaning "a modification of a porcupine" (*śvāvidh*).

747. Is he who has a *mṛdaṅga* as his craft a *mārdaṅgika*? And what follows from this? It would follow that the term applies to a potter (*kumbhakāra*). If that is so, then a deletion of the final member of the compound must be understood: "craft" (*śilpa*) is like "craft. One whose craft is the playing of the *mṛdaṅga* is a *mārdaṅgika*. [Similarly,] a *paiṭharika*.

(P_4,4.59) Why is this stated? Is it not the case that *kak* alone is stated, and the formation of the forms is established as *śāktīkaḥ* and *yāṣṭīkaḥ*? [In these cases], the vowel *ī* is at the end of *śakti* and *yaṣṭi*, and the suffix *ka* follows. [Yet] it is not established.

Furthermore, because there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the suffixes *śakti* and *yaṣṭi*, the long vowel *ī* would also apply; moreover, by the rule *ke 'ṇaḥ*, the shortening of the vowel would result. If that is the case, then [the suffix] is stated as *ikak*. What is the formal derivation (*rūpasiddhi*)? It would be *śāktīkaḥ* and *yāṣṭīkaḥ*. This is established by the lengthening of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*). It is not established; for the elision of the final vowel (*yasyeti ca lopaḥ*) would also apply. [Objection: It will not occur due to the power of the explicit pronunciation of the vowel *i*.

If, then, a rule that would otherwise apply is set aside by the power of pronunciation (*uccāraṇasāmarthya*), then the long vowel substitution for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*) would not apply either. That rule is set aside for which the instruction is rendered purposeless; however, a rule whose very cause [for application] remains is not set aside. In this case, the pronunciation of the vowel *i* is purposeless with respect to the elision (*lopa*).
But [the substitution] of a long vowel of the same class (*savarṇadīrghatva*) is indeed the cause [of the application of the rule].

The student is to be shielded by the teacher as by an umbrella, and the teacher is to be protected by the student as by an umbrella.

otherwise, there would be no such instruction. Otherwise, the instruction would not exist. Furthermore, when used in conjunction with the word *hita*, the dative case is employed.

It is prescribed. That [suffix] would then apply. In that case, the use of the dative case must be stated. It need not be stated. 750–751. [Objection: The prescription of suffixes after the words *ratha*, *śakaṭa*, *hala*, and *sīra* when expressing the sense "carrying" (*vahati*) is redundant because it has already been prescribed.

When expressing the sense "carrying," the prescription of suffixes after *ratha*, *śakaṭa*, *hala*, and *sīra* is purposeless. Why? Because it has already been prescribed; for the suffix [denoted by] *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120) has already been prescribed here. [Response: It is not prescribed because of the difference in the word-form.
Because of the difference in words, that would not be a prescription. For one word means "he carries the chariot," while another means "the carrier of the chariot.

If it is argued that there is no prescription because of the difference in words, [we reply: it is established because the prescription of suffixes depends on the meaning, and because the meanings are identical. If it is argued that there is no prescription because of the difference in words, [we say] the prescription of suffixes is based on the meaning; that very meaning is the same.

"He who draws the chariot is the drawer of the chariot"—this is established there by virtue of the commonality of meaning. However, this is the specific purpose: one who draws two chariots is *dvirathya*, whereas one who is the drawer of two chariots is *dviratha*. Therefore, when [the suffix] is present, the elision (*luk*) occurs. Why does it not occur when [the suffix] is present according to this [rule]? It is stated that [the rule applies] "prior to the suffix *divyat*."

(P_4,4.82) KA_II,334.2-6 Ro_III, 751-752 What is being prescribed as an irregular form (*nipāta*)? The state of being a mother (*janī-bhāva*) for the word *jananī* is prescribed, as well as the suffix.

[Objection: The irregular prescription (*nipātana*) of the form *janyāḥ* is redundant because of the mention of the ablative case (*pañcamī*). The irregular prescription of the form *janyāḥ* is purposeless. For what reason?

Because of the mention of the fifth case. This is the fifth case from the word *jananī*. Then this is the purpose: so that the rule for the suffix may be understood as applying to all times—as in *janyā janīm vahanti* ("the bridegrooms carry the bride"), *janyā janīm voḍhāraḥ* ("the bridegrooms are those who will carry the bride"), and *janyā janīm avākṣuḥ* ("the bridegrooms have carried the bride").
(P_4,4.83) It pierces by means of non-instrumentality (*akaraṇena*). It should be stated: "it pierces by means of non-instrumentality. Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If it were stated as "by means of what is not a bow" (*adhanuṣā*), an over-extension would occur; it would [incorrectly] apply here as well: *śarkarābhiḥ* ("with pebbles").

"He pierces. "He pierces with thorns. If that is so, then it ought to be stated [by rule]. It need not be stated. Why? Because [the usage] "he pierces with pebbles" or "he pierces with thorns" does not occur. This is because such expressions are not part of the linguistic convention (*anabhidhānāt*). It is said [in the rule] "connected with the householder" (*gṛhapatisaṃyukte*). In that case, it would follow that [the offering] applies even to the *dakṣiṇāgni* (southern fire), for the *dakṣiṇāgni* is also connected with the householder. If that is so, then since everything is connected with the householder, the term "connected with the householder" must be understood as referring to the highest degree [of connection]. Thus, there will be a sense of excellence (*prakarṣagati*) in its application.

It is better [to apply the designation] to that which is connected with the *gṛhapati*. And what is better? That in which the *patnīsaṃyājyā* verses are performed. Or else, *gṛhapati* is the name of a mantra; it is that in which [the word] is uttered.

753. Regarding the suffixes for the months and bodies, it should be stated that they occur in the sense of "immediately following" (*anantara*). It should be stated: "Regarding the months and bodies, [the suffix occurs] in the sense of 'immediately following'.

Thus, *madhu* is in this [month], or *madhu* is immediately following; hence *madhavyaḥ* or *mādhavaḥ*. Furthermore, the suffixes *luk*, *akāra*, *ikāra*, and *repha* should be stated. *Luk*: *madhuḥ*, *tapaḥ*, *nabhaḥ*. *Akāra*: *iṣaḥ*, *ūrjaḥ*. *Ikāra*: *śuciḥ*.
And *repha* is *śukra*. (P_4.4.140) An addition [to the rule] regarding a collection of syllables of the Veda (*chandas*): an addition regarding a collection of syllables of the Veda.

The word *kartavyam* consists of three syllables; *o śrāvaya* consists of four syllables; *astu śrauṣaṭ* consists of four syllables; *ye yajāmahe* consists of five syllables; *yaja* consists of two syllables; and the *vaṣaṭ*-call consists of two syllables. This Prajāpati, consisting of seventeen syllables and belonging to the meters, is indeed fashioned according to the sacrifice. In the meter, there is an addition of many riches.

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), there is an extension of the rule for the case of "many *vasavya*s. [Examples: "Fill your two hands with many *vasavya*s"; "Agni is the lord of *vasavya*. An extension of the rule must be made regarding "Agni is the lord of *vasavya*. Well then, that extension must be made. It need not be made; it is established through the understanding of its own meaning. This is established through the understanding of its own meaning: "*vasavaḥ*" [is used].
"May the *vasavyas* protect you thus.
(Pāṇini 5.1.1) What is the purpose of the expression "prāk" (before)? It has been stated regarding the word "prāk. What was stated?

First, it was stated there that the mention of "prāk" is for the sake of a single application (*sakṛdvidhāna*). If it is argued that [the desired result] is established by virtue of the governing heading (*adhikāra*), [the answer follows].

"In the scope of exceptions (*apavāda*), there is the possibility of the application of *aṇ*. Here too, the introductory statement (*prāgvacana*) is made for the purpose of a single enunciation; that the affix should be enjoined only once. [The concern is: "May I not have to mention it in every individual rule (*yoga-yoge*). This purpose is not necessary. This is established even by virtue of the governing heading (*adhikāra*). The governing heading serves the purpose of indicating that [the rule] applies to each individual connection.

Thus [the suffix] occurs in every instance [of application]. If it is argued that this is established by virtue of the governing context (*adhikāra*), then the suffix *cha* would undesirably apply even in the domain of exceptions.
