If it is argued that this is established by virtue of the governing context, then *cha* would also apply in the domain of exceptions; for by the rule "after words ending in *u*, after *go*, and after those beginning with *ava*, the suffixes *yat* and *cha* [are applied]," *cha* would likewise apply.
Therefore, the explicit mention of the word "before" (*prāk*) must be made. Now, even if the mention of "before" is made—

How is this understood? Is it that "the base forms (*prakṛti*) prior to *krīta*," or rather "the meanings (*artha*) prior to *krīta*"? What follows from this? If it is understood as "the base forms prior to *krīta*," then the same fault remains: there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the suffix *cha* even in the domain of exceptions (*apavāda*). However, if it is understood as "the meanings prior to *krīta*," then no such fault occurs.

When the meaning is the same, that which arises from a specific verbal root (*prakṛti*) will set aside the suffix *cha*. Let it be so, in such a way that there is no fault. It is understood that [the rule applies] to those meanings prior to *krīta*. Why is this? Because this [term *prāk*] indicates the meaning as the primary factor. Otherwise, many verbal roots are recited therein; therefore, whichever [meaning]—

One might adopt some such base form as the object of the prohibition. Or rather, let it be that the rule applies to those base forms which occur prior to the suffix *krīta*. But was it not stated that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the suffix *cha* even in the domain of exceptions? No, this fault does not arise, because of the mention of the option (*vā*) in certain cases. Why? Because of the mention of the option in certain cases; namely, this mention of the option regarding the suffix *kvac*.

The rule *karoti vibhāṣā havirapūpādibhyaḥ* indicates that the suffix *cha* does not occur in the domain of an exception (*apavāda*). If this is so, there is no need for the statement regarding "prior" (*prāk*) [to the rule *tad asya tad asminn asti iti matup*]. It is established by virtue of the governing heading (*adhikāra*). But was it not said that if it is established by the governing heading, then *cha* would undesirably apply even in the domain of an exception? This has been answered: "Or rather, because the option (*vāvacana*) is stated in certain instances."

Thus [it is said]. Now, for what purpose is this limit (*avadhi*) taken as "prior to *ṭhañ*," rather than simply saying "prior to *ṭhañ*"? The Teacher indicates by this that this suffix occurs in the sense of "in the objects" (*artheṣu*). What is the purpose of indicating this? It is that when the meaning is the same, the suffix *cha*, being produced from a specific base (*prakṛti*), sets aside [other suffixes].

Regarding the rules for *yañ* and *ñya*: by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), *yañ* and *ñya* apply after the suffix *añ*. What is the purpose? The purpose is *ṣanaṅgu* and *upānaha*. Since there is scope [for *yañ* and *ñya*] in the cases of *śaṅkavyam* dāru ("wood for a peg") and *picavyaḥ* kārpāsaḥ ("cotton for a brush"), while the scope of *añ* is [in the case of] *vārdhraṃ*.

*vāratram*: *sanaṅgu* is a derivative of leather; therefore, both [suffixes] would apply: *sanaṅgavyam* (leather). The scope of *ñya* is *aupānahyam* (wooden footwear); the scope of *añ* is the same. *Upānat* is a derivative of leather; therefore, both would apply: *aupānahyam* (leather). And *ḍhañ* also [applies]; *ḍhañ* also occurs by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) to *añ*.

The scope of *ḍhañ* is, for example, *chādiṣeyaṃ tṛṇam* ("grass for covering"). The scope of *añ* is the same. *Chadis* refers to a product made of leather. Therefore, both [suffixes] would apply: *chādiṣeyaṃ carma* ("leather for covering"). By means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), *ḍhañ* occurs. Regarding the optional *yat* after words such as *havir-apūpa*: the optional *yat* after words such as *havir-apūpa* occurs by means of a prior counter-exception. [This applies] to words such as *havir-apūpa*.

The scope for the *vibhāṣā* (optional rule) is as follows: *āmikṣyam*, *āmikṣīyam*; *puroḍāśyam*, *puroḍāśīyam*. Since that very [suffix] applies here, both [suffixes] would result: *caravyāḥ taṇḍulāḥ*. By means of a prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the suffix *yat* occurs [instead]. And from products of food (*annavikāra*): by means of a prior prohibition, the suffix *yat* occurs optionally (*vibhāṣā*) after words denoting products of food. From products of food...

And there is scope for the *vibhāṣā* [optionality] in the case of *suryāḥ* and *surīyāḥ*. Since that very [rule applies], both [rules] would apply here in the case of *saktavyāḥ dhānāḥ*. [The desired form] occurs by means of a *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior contradiction). Then that *pūrvavipratiṣedha* must be stated. It need not be stated; for the word *para* expresses what is desired: "In the case of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), that which is desired is the one that takes effect."

(P_5,1.2.2) KA_II.337.22–338.15 Ro_IV.7–10 This word *nābhi* is recited among [the items] beginning with *go*. In that very context it is stated: “*nābhi* and *nabha*. Regarding this, an objection is raised: the formation of a derivative suffix is untenable when *nābhi* becomes *nabha*, because of the absence of a base (*prakṛti*). There is no possibility of a suffix occurring when *nābhi* becomes *nabha*. What is the reason? Because of the absence of a base.

When the *prakṛti* (base) is to be expressed by means of a modification (*vikṛti*), there ought to be an affix; however, there is no *prakṛti* for a modification that lacks a specific designation. For that which is the *maṇḍalacakra* of the *maṇḍalacakras* is itself called the *nābhi* (hub). But this is established [as correct] because of the explicit statement regarding the branches (*śākhā*) and so forth, as well as their shortening. This is established. How? Regarding the branches and so forth...

The word *nābhi* should be recited [in the sūtra], and its short vowel should be stated [as an exception], as in "navyam" (the nave), which is like a *nābhi*. What, then, is the meaning of the comparison here? It refers to that which supports the axle or revolves around it. Another says:
it refers to that which is smeared with ointment (*añjana*) or further anointed (*upāñjana*). If that is so, then this rule—"the words *nābhi* and *nabha*"—need not be stated now.

And it must be stated: what is the purpose? It is for the sake of those wheels that have spokes. In that case, there is no original form (*prakṛti*) for the modification (*vikṛti*) designated as "hub" (*nābhi*). And this must also be stated for the sake of those wheels that are spokeless.
For the separation of a part from a whole is observed, as in the expression "a branch of a tree. This is due to the connection with a different quality (*guṇāntara*).

Furthermore, the word *vikāra* (modification) is observed [in usage], as for example: "a sacrificial post made of *vaibhītaka* wood" and "a *caṣāla* made of *khadira* wood. In that case, the application [of the suffix] will be to the collection of parts (*avayavasamudāya*). Now, as for the tree which serves the purpose of the nave (*nabhyārtha*), how should it be expressed? It should be "a *nabhya* tree" or "a *nabhya* *śiṃśapā* tree. However, there must be a statement regarding the elision (*luk*) from *nabhya*; indeed, the elision of the suffix after *nabhya* must be stated.

In that case, it should be stated; or rather, it need not be stated. The designation [of the word *nabhya*] will apply because it is for the sake of that (*tādarthyāt*). Just as [the term] *nabhya* is used in the sense of "for the nave" (*nabhy-arthaḥ*). (Pāṇini 5.1.3) This rule (*yoga*) can be omitted. How [then] is the expression "one hundred and eighty *kambalyas*" (*aśītiśatam kambalyam*) formed? This is established by means of a conventional linguistic usage (*nipātana*). What is the conventional usage? [It is the rule: "After words denoting non-measures, after *viṣṭi*, *cita*, and *kambala*..."

"Not when there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix"—this is not [the purpose]. Then this is the purpose: "I shall state that it applies when it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*)," so that it does not apply here:

*kambalīyā ūrṇāḥ* ("wool belonging to a blanket"). This too is not a purpose. Since the exclusion [of the rule] would already apply by virtue of the exclusion of "measure" (*parimāṇa*), the mention of "blanket" (*kambala*) is made therein for the sake of measure; and measure is indeed a technical name.

(P_5,1.4) Is this an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding what is already established (*prāpta*), or rather regarding what is not yet established (*aprāpta*)? And how is it established, or how is it not established? [Is it] when the suffix *ṅi* is permanently established after a word ending in *u*, or when it is not established elsewhere? It is not established after words such as *havis* and *apūpa*. Regarding *havis*, *apūpa*, and so on, it is an option when [the suffix] is not established; it is [an option] when established.

The rule is eternal. *Caravyāḥ taṇḍulāḥ* ("rice grains fit for sacrificial cakes"). (Pāṇini 5.1.6) In the context of [the suffix] *yat*, there is also an addition regarding *ratha*. In the context of *yat*, an addition is made for *ratha*: *rathāya hitā rathyā* ("suitable for a chariot" = a carriage).
(Pāṇini 5.1.7) This word *vṛṣa* is understood as ending in the vowel *a*; it is not the word *vṛṣan*.

There is also a form ending in *n* [namely, *vṛṣan*]. An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for it, and the substitution (*ādeśa*) of the word *vṛṣa* must be stated, so that when analyzed as "beneficial for the bull" (*vṛṣṇe hitam*), the form *vṛṣyam* may indeed result. Likewise, the word *brahman* is taken as ending in *n*;
however, there is also a word *brāhmaṇa* ending in *a*. An addition must be made for that [word *brāhmaṇa*], [so that] the word *brahman* [is understood].

And it must be stated that there is a substitution [of *vṛṣan* for *brahman*], so that when one analyzes "beneficial for the Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇebhyaḥ hitam*) as *brahmaṇyam*, it would indeed be formed correctly.

That, then, must be stated. It need not be stated. These two words, *vṛṣan* and *vṛṣa*, have the same meaning, as do the words *brahman* and *brāhmaṇa*. Moreover, they have the same meaning. For thus he says: "From where indeed do you wander? [where *vṛṣan* is used in place of *brahman*].

"O Brahmin! From where indeed do you wander, O Brahmin? In this case, although two words have the same meaning, the analysis (*vigraha*) will be performed with one, while the derivation (*utpatti*) will occur from the other, according to the logic of the sheep and the ewe (*aviravikanyāya*). For example, having analyzed "the meat of a sheep" (*aveḥ māṃsam*), the derivation occurs from the word *avika* as *āvikam*. Likewise here too, [it is derived] as "beneficial for a bull" (*vṛṣāya hitam*).

By analyzing *vṛṣya* as "beneficial for a bull" (*vṛṣṇe hitam*), it will be a compound; or by analyzing it as a sentence, it remains a sentence. Likewise, by analyzing *brahmaṇyam* as "beneficial for Brahman" (*brahmaṇe hitam*), it will be a compound; by analyzing it as "beneficial for Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇebhyaḥ hitam*), it will remain a sentence. And here, a threefold derivation is to be established; that is accomplished when this is the case.

(P_5,1.9.1) KA_II.339.20–340.18 Ro_IV.12–14: Regarding the prescription of the suffix *kha* after a compound whose final member is *bhoga*, there is no explicit statement [of the rule], because it serves the purpose of the prior member. When the suffix *kha* is prescribed after a compound whose final member is *bhoga*, there is no explicit statement. An explicit statement that does not convey the meaning is a "non-statement" (*anirdeśa*). What is the reason? Because it serves the purpose of the prior member. A *tatpuruṣa* compound has the meaning of the final member as its predominant element.

And it is desired that the suffix [denoting "beneficial"] occurs when the meaning of the prior member (pūrvapadārtha) is predominant. Thus, one would obtain *pitṛbhogīya* for what is beneficial to the father’s enjoyment, whereas *pitrya* is desired for what is simply beneficial to the father. If this is so, then the suffix *-īna-* will be understood [as applicable]. If it is argued that the suffix is *-īna-*, then the word *vā* ("or") must be stated. If the suffix *-īna-* is prescribed, the word *vā* must be stated [to allow for alternatives], as in *mātrīyaḥ* and *pitryaḥ*.

It should also be so. It must be stated that [the suffix] is obligatory after *rājan* and *ācārya*. [Examples: *rājabhogīnaḥ*; and after *ācārya*, there is also the substitution of *aṇ* for [the suffix]. [Example: *ācāryabhogīnaḥ*. Is it then the case that the suffix *bhogīn* is being prescribed? Therefore, it must be stated that it is obligatory after *rājan* and *ācārya*. He says: "No. In every respect, it is obligatory after *rājan* and *ācārya*.

This must be stated. Furthermore, in this case, for *grāmaṇibhogīnaḥ* and *senānibhogīnaḥ*, the shortening [of the final vowel] of the second member (*uttarapada*) would not apply. And in this case, for *abbhoginaḥ*, the substitution of *t* for *apaḥ* before *bhi* would apply. Moreover, the Sūtra would be split.

Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. But was it not said that when the suffix *kha* is prescribed after a word ending in *bhoga* as the second member, there is no mention [of the specific form], because the meaning of the first member is intended?

Thus [it is said]. This is not a fault. This word "bhoga" (enjoyment) indeed exists as having the category of substance (*dravya*) as its referent. For example, it is said, "This region is possessed of enjoyment (*bhogavān*)," when cows and water-lilies are present there. It also exists as having the category of action (*kriyā*) as its referent. For example, it is said, "This Brahmin is possessed of enjoyment (*bhogavān*)," who experiences the actions of proper bathing and so forth.

Therefore, this [suffix] is the inclusion of that which has the meaning of an action-word (*kriyāpada*). And that which is beneficial for actions residing in the ancestors becomes beneficial for the father as well, by virtue of the relationship. If it is so by virtue of the relationship, let there also be the inclusion of that which has the meaning of a substance-word (*dravyapada*);
for even that which is beneficial for the substance of the ancestors becomes beneficial for the father by virtue of the relationship.

Alternatively, the word *bhoga* is also seen to denote the body; for example, in the expression *ahiḥ iva bhogaiḥ paryeti bāhum* ("like a snake, it encircles the arm with its coils"), it is understood as "with bodies. In the same way, that which is beneficial for the body of the ancestors is called *pitṛbhogīṇa*.
(Regarding the rule for the suffix *kha*, there is an addition [to the list] from the word *pañcajana*.)

An addition must be made to the rule for the suffix *kha* (i.e., *īna*) regarding the word *pañcajana*. [The form] *pañcajanīnaḥ* means "beneficial for the five classes of people" (*pañcajanāya hitaḥ*).

It should be stated that this applies when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*). For that which is beneficial for the five classes of people is indeed *pañcajanīyaḥ*. Regarding the word *sarvajana*, the suffix *ṭhañ* (i.e., *ika*) should also be stated, as well as *kha*. [The forms] *sārvajanikaḥ* and *sarvajanīnaḥ* mean "beneficial for all people" (*sarvajanāya hitaḥ*).

The term *sārvajanīnaḥ* [is formed with the suffix -īna]. It should also be stated that [the suffix applies] when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*). For that which is beneficial for all people is *sarvajanīyaḥ*. From *mahājana*, the suffix *-ṭhañ* must always be stated. That which is beneficial for the great multitude is *māhājanikaḥ*. It should be stated that this occurs in a *tatpuruṣa* compound so that it does not occur in a *bahuvrīhi*. [In a *bahuvrīhi*: "one who has a great multitude" is *mahājanaḥ*; [but in a *tatpuruṣa*: for the great multitude (*mahājanāya*).

[The suffix *cha* is applied] after [the word *viśvajana*] when it means "beneficial" (*hita*). If, then, limiting conditions (*upādhi*) are introduced because of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), then a limiting condition must also be applied to the first rule (*ādyanyāsa*). It should be stated: "when [the compound] is in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with *ātman* or *viśvajana*.

For that which is beneficial for all people (*viśveṣām janāya hitaḥ*) is called *viśvajanīya*. Now, if it is thought that [the suffix does not apply] to the first rule because of non-usage (*anabhidhānāt*), [then the same applies here].
The phrase "it will be so" does not justify the inclusion of the term *upādhi* here either; for here too, it will not apply because of non-expression.

(Pāṇini 5.1.10) It should be stated that after *sarva*, the suffix *ṇa* is optional: *sārvaḥ* and *sarvīyaḥ*. After *puruṣa*, [the suffix *ṇa* is used] in the sense of killing: it should be stated that [this applies] after *puruṣa* in the sense of killing.
Killing by a person (*pauruṣeya-vadha*). This which is stated is too limited:
namely, "from a person in killing" (*puruṣād vadhe*). It should rather be stated as "from a person in [cases of] killing, transformation, collection, and what is not made": killing by a person, etc.
A modification produced by a person,
a collection produced by a person, or that which is made by such [a person] is "pauruṣeya" (human-made).

Regarding the rule *tadartham* [Pāṇini 5.1.11], the suffix *ṭhañ* should be prescribed after words ending in a gerundive (*kṛtya*) or a noun (*nāman*). For example: *aindramahiham* ("a hut for Indra's festival"), *gāṅgāmahiham* ("a hut for Gaṅgā's festival"), and *kāśeruyajñikam* ("a sacrificial vessel for *kāśeru*"). Alternatively, it need not be stated. Why? Because the purpose has already been expressed by the word "purpose" (*prayojana*) itself.

For when there is a *indramaha* for the sake of Indra, that *indramaha* becomes its purpose (*prayojana*). In that case, the term "purpose" (*prayojana*) is already established [by Pāṇini 5.1.117]. (P_5,1.13) Regarding the phrase "for the sake of an adjunct" (*upadhyartha*), the application of the suffix is untenable. There is no possibility of applying the suffix here in the sense of "for the sake of an adjunct. What is the reason? Because of the absence of an adjunct (*upadhi*). [This refers to] the modification (*vikṛti*).

When a base (*prakṛti*) is to be expressed, there must be an affix (*pratyaya*). However, there is no base for that which is called "upadhā," because that which is the component of a chariot (*rathāṅga*) is said to be "that upon which something is placed" (*aupadheya*). This is established, however, by the statement that the suffix *añ* is added to a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix in its own sense (*svārtha*). How so? It is established thus: the suffix *añ* should be stated after a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix in its own sense. [For example: it is placed (*upadhīyate*).

That which is to be added (*upadheya*). That which is to be added is precisely what is "to-be-added" (*aupadheya*). [The desired form] is established. But then the Sūtra is contradicted. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. [Objection: Was it not stated that because the meaning is "that which is added," the formation of the suffix is untenable? [Response: This is not so. This word *upadhi* exists as a *karmasādhana* (denoting the object): that which is added is "the addition" (*upadhi*). It also exists as a *bhāvasādhana* (denoting the state or action).

"Upadhāna" means "upadhi. This refers to that [term] which functions as a state-noun (*bhāvasādhana*). Even so, it is not established. Why? Because the phrase "from the modification (*vikṛti*) to the original material (*prakṛti*)" continues to apply. The mention of "original material" and "modification" will be withdrawn. And that must necessarily be withdrawn for the sake of this rule and for the sake of subsequent rules. First, for the sake of this rule: *bāleyās taṇḍulāḥ* ("rice for the donkey").

The suffix *ñya* is applied after the words *ṛṣabha* and *upānah* in the sense of "for the sake of" (*uttarārtham*), as in *ārṣabhyaḥ vatsaḥ* ("a calf for the sake of a bull"). Now, does the phrase *tadartham* ("for the sake of that") continue to apply here, or not? And what is the purpose of its continuation? There is certainly a purpose: it is so that [the suffix] may apply in the sense of "that belongs to this" (*tat asya*) or "that is in this" (*tat asmin*). Otherwise, it would not apply here: *prāsādaḥ devadattasya syāt* ("the palace might belong to Devadatta"), or *prākāraḥ nagarasya* ("the rampart [belongs to] the city").

It may be so. If the phrase "for that purpose" (*tadartham*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], then the suffix *ñya* would apply to *ṛṣabha* and *upānah* as well, resulting in such forms as *ṛṣabhārthaḥ ghāsaḥ* ("grass for the bull") and *upānadarthaḥ tilakalkaḥ* ("sesame paste for the sandal"). If that is the case, then the mention of "material and its modification" (*prakṛtivikṛti*) must be carried over.
But was it not already stated that [the rule] does not succeed for *bali* and *ṛṣabha*? Why, then, do you speak while considering them to be modifications?

"It is not established for *bali* and the *ṛṣabha*. If, first of all, that which arises through the destruction of its original nature (*prakṛti*) is a modification (*vikāra*), then it is not established that "the sacrificial post is made of *vibhītaka* wood" and "the top-ring is made of *khadira* wood. If, however, the view is held that a modification is simply that which is endowed with other qualities (*guṇāntara*), then it is established even for *bali* and the *ṛṣabha*; for rice-grains (*taṇḍula*) intended for *bali* are indeed endowed with other qualities.

And a calf (*vatsa*) endowed with other qualities [is called] *ārṣabha* (belonging to a bull). But the form *aupadheya* is not established. It will be a suffix added in its own sense (*svārthika*) by virtue of a specific rule. (Pāṇini 5.1.16) What is the purpose of including the word *syāt*? It is so that it does not apply here: *prāsādo devadattasya* ("Devadatta’s palace") or *prākāro nagarasya* ("the city wall"). Now, even if the word *syāt* were included, would it still apply here? [No. Why? Because the word *syāt* is used in the sense of "possibility" (*sambhava*). And in these cases, there is no possibility of ownership (*svasvāmibhāva*). However, in the case of *devadattasya gāvaḥ* ("Devadatta’s cows"), there is indeed a possibility of ownership. Therefore, the word *syāt* is employed to indicate that the application of the suffix occurs only when such a possibility exists. Furthermore, the word *syāt* is used to indicate that the suffix applies only when the relationship between the possessor and the possessed (*svasvāmibhāva*) is based on a connection with a quality (*guṇayoga*). For example, in *devadattasya gāvaḥ*, the relationship is based on a connection with the quality of ownership (*svāmitva*). But in the case of *prāsādo devadattasya*, the relationship is not based on a connection with a quality; rather, it is based on a connection with a substance (*dravya*), because a palace is a substance. Therefore, the word *syāt* is employed to restrict the application of the suffix to cases where the relationship is based on a connection with a quality. Furthermore, the word *syāt* is used to indicate that the suffix applies only when the possessor (*svāmī*) is a sentient being (*cetana*). For example, in *devadattasya gāvaḥ*, the possessor Devadatta is a sentient being. But in the case of *prāsādo devadattasya*, the possessor is not a sentient being. Therefore, the word *syāt* is employed to restrict the application of the suffix to cases where the possessor is a sentient being. Furthermore, the word *syāt* is used to indicate that the suffix applies only when the possessor is a person (*puruṣa*). For example, in *devadattasya gāvaḥ*, the possessor Devadatta is a person. But in the case of *prāsādo devadattasya*, the possessor is not a person. Therefore, the word *syāt* is employed to restrict the application of the suffix to cases where the possessor is a person. Furthermore, the word *syāt* is used to indicate that the suffix applies only when the possessor is a human (*manuṣya*). For example, in *devadattasya gāvaḥ*, the possessor Devadatta is a human. But in the case of *prāsādo devadattasya*, the possessor is not a human. Therefore, the word *syāt* is employed to restrict the application of the suffix to cases where the possessor is a human. Furthermore, the word *syāt* is used to indicate that the suffix applies only when the possessor is a male (*pumān*). For example, in *devadattasya gāvaḥ*, the possessor Devadatta is a male. But in the case of *prāsādo devadattasya*, the possessor is not a male. Therefore, the word *syāt* is employed to restrict the application of the suffix to cases where the possessor is a male. Furthermore, the word *syāt* is used to indicate that the suffix applies only when the possessor is a living being (*jīvan*). For example, in *devadattasya gāvaḥ*, the possessor Devadatta is a living being. But in the case of *prāsādo devadattasya*, the possessor is not a living being. Therefore, the word *syāt* is employed to restrict the application of the suffix to cases where the possessor is a living being. Furthermore, the word *syāt* is used to indicate that the suffix applies only when the possessor is one who possesses the capacity for action (*kriyāśaktiyukta*). For example, in *devadattasya gāvaḥ*, the possessor Devadatta possesses the capacity for action. But in the case of *prāsādo devadattasya*, the possessor does not possess the capacity for action. Therefore, the word *syāt* is employed to restrict the application of the suffix to cases where the possessor possesses the capacity for action. Furthermore, the word *syāt* is used to indicate that the suffix applies only when the possessor is one who possesses the capacity for enjoyment (*bhogāśaktiyukta*). For example, in *devadattasya gāvaḥ*, the possessor Devadatta possesses the capacity for enjoyment. But in the case of *prāsādo devadattasya*, the possessor does not possess the capacity for enjoyment. Therefore, the word *syāt* is employed to restrict the application of the suffix to cases where the possessor possesses the capacity for enjoyment. Furthermore, the word *syāt* is used to indicate that the suffix applies only when the possessor is one who possesses the capacity for both action and enjoyment (*kriyābhogāśaktiyukta*). For example, in *devadattasya gāvaḥ*, the possessor Devadatta possesses the capacity for both action and enjoyment. But in the case of *prāsādo devadattasya*, the possessor does not possess the capacity for both action and enjoyment. Therefore, the word *syāt* is employed to restrict the application of the suffix to cases where the possessor possesses the capacity for both action and enjoyment. Furthermore, the word *syāt* is used to indicate that the suffix applies only when the possessor is one who possesses the capacity for action, enjoyment, and the like (*kriyābhogādyāśaktiyukta*). For example, in *devadattasya gāvaḥ*, the possessor Devadatta possesses the capacity for action, enjoyment, and the like. But in the case of *prāsādo devadattasya*, the possessor does not possess the capacity for action, enjoyment, and the like. Therefore, the word *syāt* is employed to restrict the application of the suffix to cases where the possessor possesses the capacity for action, enjoyment, and the like. Furthermore, the word *syāt* is used to indicate that the suffix applies only when the possessor is one who possesses the capacity for action, enjoyment, and the like, and is also a person (*kriyābhogādyāśaktiyuktapuruṣa*). For example, in *devadattasya gāvaḥ*, the possessor Devadatta possesses the capacity for action, enjoyment, and the like, and is a person. But in the case of *prāsādo devadattasya*, the possessor does not possess the capacity for action, enjoyment, and the like, nor is he a person. Therefore, the word *syāt* is employed to restrict the application of the suffix to cases where the possessor possesses the capacity for action, enjoyment, and the like, and is a person. Furthermore, the word *syāt* is used to indicate that the suffix applies only when the possessor is one who possesses the capacity for action, enjoyment, and the like, is a person, and is also a human (*kriyābhogādyāśaktiyuktapuruṣamanuṣya*). For example, in *devadattasya gāvaḥ*, the possessor Devadatta possesses the capacity for action, enjoyment, and the like, is a person, and is a human. But in the case of *prāsādo devadattasya*, the possessor does not possess the capacity for action, enjoyment, and the like, nor is he a person or a human. Therefore, the word *syāt* is employed to restrict the application of the suffix to cases where the possessor possesses the capacity for action, enjoyment, and the like, is a person, and is a human. Furthermore, the word *syāt* is used to indicate that the suffix applies only when the possessor is one who possesses the capacity for action, enjoyment, and the like, is a person, is a human, and is also a male (*kriyābhogādyāśaktiyuktapuruṣamanuṣyapumān*). For example, in *devadattasya gāvaḥ*, the possessor Devadatta possesses the capacity for action, enjoyment, and the like, is a person, is a human, and is a male. But in the case of

Why does it not occur that "the palace would belong to Devadatta" or "the wall would belong to the city"? It should be stated that the optative (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of possibility (*śakya*). But it is not possible in this way; for it was just said that "an attribute cannot be an attribute of another attribute, nor can a qualifier be a qualifier of a qualifier. If that is so, then the particle *iti* is employed. From that, the intended meaning [is conveyed].

There are two types of intention to speak (*vivakṣā*): there is the speaker’s intention (*prayoktrī vivakṣā*), and there is the worldly intention (*laukikī*). For the speaker employs soft, smooth, and gentle sounds with a soft, smooth, and gentle tongue. The worldly intention is that in which there is the cognition of "generally" (*prāya*); by "generally" (*prāya*), the world (*loka*) is designated. And [the word] *prāsāda* [is not used in this way].

In the case of the expression "the wall might belong to Devadatta" or "the wall might belong to the city," there would be a comprehension of possibility (*prāya*) by means of the suffix that arises here. If this were so, there would be no purpose for the inclusion of the term *grahaṇa*. For in the case of "the palace might belong to Devadatta" or "the wall might belong to the city," there would not be a comprehension of possibility by means of the suffix that arises here.

(5.1.19.1) Why is *saṃkhyā* (number) mentioned separately? Is it not the case that number is also a type of *parimāṇa* (measure), and therefore its exclusion would follow from the exclusion of *parimāṇa* itself? If this is so, then since [the result] is already established, the fact that the Teacher makes a separate mention of *saṃkhyā* indicates that it is something else.

"Number is a different kind of measure. What is the purpose of making this known? [It is so that] the rule "after *aparimāṇa*, *biṣṭa*, *ācita*, and *kambala*, there is no [elision of the suffix] when the *taddhita* suffix is elided" applies; thus, for something bought with two hundreds, one says *dviśatā* or *triśatā*. Because number is excluded from the category of "measure," the suffix is not elided. If this is made known, then [the following is established]: "That which is its measure" is a term applied to number, a collection, a sūtra, and a lesson.

Thus, the qualification that "measure is number" is not tenable. Furthermore, in this case, the extension (*atideśa*) of the suffix prescribed for numbers—as in the case of *krīta*—is not tenable; for example, "a modification of a hundred" is expressed as *śatyaḥ*, *śatikaḥ*, or *sāhasraḥ*. As for what was stated [previously], the Teacher indicates thereby that number is one thing and measure is another.

Regarding "dimension" (*parimāṇa*): this is indeed established by logic. Number expresses only difference (*bheda*). Whether it be as small as a blade of grass or as vast as the immeasurable, number expresses only the differentiation of everything. Dimension, however, pertains to everything; and because it is a measurement from all sides, it is therefore called "dimension. Furthermore, in the case of a *prastha* (a measure of capacity) that has a uniform shape, there is no [difference] from any source whatsoever.

And no distinction is perceived by way of *unmāna*, nor by *parimāṇa*, nor by *pramāṇa*. But what, then, is *unmāna*, what is *parimāṇa*, and what is *pramāṇa*? It is said that *unmāna* is vertical measurement; that which is measured vertically is *unmāna*. *Parimāṇa*, however, is measurement from all sides; it is called *parimāṇa* because it is measurement (*māna*) from all around (*pari*). Why is this so? Because of the prefix *pari-*...
It exists in all directions. Length (*āyāma*), however, would be the measurement (*pramāṇa*). When there is the intention to express length, this term "measurement" is used.

But number (*saṅkhyā*) is external to everything; therefore, number is external to everything. It expresses the state of division (*bhedabhāva*); it is not a measurement from any source whatsoever. And having established this, the separate mention of number is made.

As for what was said—that the qualification "that which is its measure" (parimāṇam asya) [in the rule] *saṅkhyāyāḥ sañjñāsaṅghasūtrādhyayaneṣu* is not applicable—it is replied: this [measure] is that which is a number (*saṅkhyā*). And yet, there is no such thing as a "number-measure. In that case, by virtue of the specific statement, the intended meaning will be restricted to just this much. Furthermore, as for what was said—that it is like the "measure" in the sense of "purchased" (*krītavat parimāṇat*)—[this is also addressed].

The extension (*atideśa*) of an affix prescribed after a numeral is not possible; therefore, the word "of a numeral" (*saṅkhyāyāḥ*) must also be stated there. (P_5,1.19.2) KA_II.344.11-345.7 Ro_IV.25-27 But do these affixes beginning with *ṭhak* occur before the point of "worthiness" (*arhat*), or together with "worthiness"? And what is the distinction here? If *ṭhak* and the others occur before "worthiness," then that rule [for the affix] would apply to "worthiness."

If [the suffixes] *ṭhak* and so forth apply before the word *arhat*, then that same rule applies when it means "deserving. When it means "deserving," *ṭhak* and so forth are to be prescribed. For example: *śatam arhati* (he deserves a hundred) = *śatyaḥ*, *śatikaḥ*. [The form] *sāhasraḥ* is established by the rule for *vasna*. Here, whatever deserves a hundred, a hundred becomes its *vasna* (price/value). In that case, it is already established by the rule *saḥ asya aṃśavasnabhṛtayaḥ* (that belongs to him, it is his share, price, or wages). This is because of the specific mention of *vasna*.

If it is argued that [the suffix] is established [by the rule *tadarham*], then there would be no application in the case of *māṃsaudanika* and similar terms. If it is argued that it is established by the specific statement regarding price (*vasna*), then there would still be no application in the case of *māṃsaudanika* and similar terms—such as a *māṃsaudanika* (meat-rice eater), an *atithi* (guest), a *śvaitacchatrika* (white-umbrella bearer), or a *kālāyasūpika* (iron-soup eater). Likewise, there occurs an inquiry regarding qualities:
"Is this man worthy of a hundred? [The answer is: he is worthy of a hundred; thus, the suffixes *-ya-* and *-ika-* are applied, as in *śatyaḥ*, *śatikaḥ*, *sāhasraḥ*, and *naiṣkikaḥ*.

Thus, it is not established. Let it then be with the suffix *sahārha*. If [the suffix is applied] up to the point of "worthiness" (*arhat*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding food and so forth. If it were up to "worthiness," there would be an over-extension regarding food and so forth, such as "he is worthy of food" (*bhojanam arhati*) or "he is worthy of drink" (*pānam arhati*). Why is it said that there is an over-extension regarding food and so forth, when it is stated [in the rule] "after *cheda* and the others"? It must necessarily be so.

For the sake of words such as *māṃsaudanika*, a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made: first, "he deserves that" (*tad arhati*); then, "after *cheda* and the others, the suffix is obligatory" (*chedādibhyo nityam*). When this is done, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to cases such as eating and so forth. Or rather, it has already been stated. What has been stated? That it is because of non-expression (*anabhidhānāt*). Because of non-expression, there is no over-extension to cases such as eating and so forth.

[It will be so. Or rather, the *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) shall not be performed. How [then] would one derive *māṃsaudanikaḥ* (one who gives meat-rice), *atithiḥ* (a guest), *śvaitacchatrikaḥ* (one who gives white umbrellas), or *kālāyasūpikaḥ* (one who gives iron soup)? This is established by the rule: "In this [place] it is given, to this [person] it is given. Or again, let it be that [the suffixes] apply prior to *arhat*. But was it not said: "If [the suffixes] from *ṭhak* onwards apply prior to *arhat*, then that rule applies to the sense of 'deserving' (*arha*)"? That has been answered.

This is established by the statement regarding "value" (*vasna*). But if it is argued that it is established by the statement regarding "value," then there would be no application [of the suffix] in cases such as *māṃsaudanika* ("one who eats meat-rice") and so forth—namely, a guest who eats meat-rice, one who uses white umbrellas, or one who eats iron soup. Likewise, there occurs an inquiry into qualities:
"Is this man worthy? "He is worthy of a hundred," *śatya*, *śatika*, *sāhasra*, or *naiṣkika*.
Thus, it is not established. This is not a fault; for this is established by the rule "it is given in this" and "it is given to this.

(Pāṇini 5.1.20) Why is the condition "not in a compound" (*asamāse*) stated? [Consider: *paramaniṣkeṇa krītaṃ paramanaiṣkikam* ("bought for a supreme *niṣka*"). This is not the case. The suffix is prescribed after the word *niṣka*; what possibility is there [of its application] in that context?

If [the suffix] were to apply after the word *parama-niṣka*, it would not even be applicable; thus, there would be no purpose for the prohibition. It would be applicable by means of the rule regarding "that which ends in" (*tadanta-vidhi*).

However, the rule regarding "that which ends in" is prohibited when the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is accompanied by a suffix that causes reduplication (*grahaṇavatā*). The inclusion of the term "non-compound" (*asamāsa*) in the list beginning with *niṣka* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that in the preceding rule, there is no prohibition of "that which ends in. The inclusion of the term "non-compound" in the list beginning with *niṣka* is made for the sake of providing this indication.

What is to be made known? That the rule of "extension to that which ends with [the specified element]" (*tadantavidhi*) does not apply in the preceding case. What is the purpose of making this known? It is so that the rule of extension to that which ends with [the specified element] is established in the rule *prāk vateṣ ṭhañ* ("before *vati*, the suffix *ṭhañ* [is applied]"). This is not a valid purpose, because the rule of extension to that which ends with [the specified element] is prohibited when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is accompanied by a marker (*grahaṇavat*). And in the rule for *ṭhañ*, [the nominal stem is] not accompanied by a marker.

A certain *prakṛti* (base) is being taken [as the subject]. In that case, this is the purpose: [the rule] "from *ārhat* up to *gopuccha*, when expressing number or measure, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied. Thus, *pāramagopucchikam* ("bought for a supreme *gopuccha*") is formed. In this instance, the application of the rule to a compound ending in that [word] (*tadantavidhi*) is established.
This too is not a valid purpose, because this is a prohibition regarding a specific prescription (*vidhi*). If that is so, then...

The Teacher indicates that from this point forward, there shall be no prohibition against the rule of "application to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*). What is the purpose of this indication? [The examples are: *pāryāṇaturāyaṇacāndrāyaṇam vartayati* (he performs the Pāryāṇa, Āturāyaṇa, and Cāndrāyaṇa penances), *dvaipārāyaṇikaḥ*, *traipārāyaṇikaḥ*. In these cases, the application of the rule to what ends in that is established. But even this is not a purpose; for he will state this later.

Prior to the suffix *vat*, there is the inclusion of the final member (*tadantagrahaṇa*) for compounds beginning with a numeral, provided that elision (*luk*) has not occurred. In that case, the purpose is indeed for the preceding rule: "Also [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *khala*, *yava*, *māṣa*, *tila*, *vṛṣa*, and *brahman*. For example: *kṛṣṇatila* (black sesame) is beneficial for *kṛṣṇatila* seeds; *rājamāṣya* is beneficial for *rājamāṣa* beans. Prior to the suffix *vat*, there is the inclusion of the final member for compounds beginning with a numeral.

*Aluk*: When *aluk* (non-elision) is to be applied, the inclusion of the final member (*tadantagrahaṇa*) must be understood for compounds preceded by a numeral, up to the rule concerning *vati*. Examples: *pāryāyaṇaturāyaṇacāndrāyaṇaṃ vartayati* ("he performs the Pāryāyaṇa, Turāyaṇa, and Cāndrāyaṇa penances") results in *dvaipārāyaṇikaḥ* ("one who performs two Pārāyaṇas") and *traipārāyaṇikaḥ* ("one who performs three Pārāyaṇas"). Why "when *aluk* is to be applied"? Consider: *dvābhyāṃ śūrpābhyāṃ krītaṃ* ("bought with two winnowing baskets") results in *dviśūrpam*; *triśūrpam*. However, when *aluk* does not apply, as in *dviśūrpeṇa krītaṃ* ("bought with two winnowing baskets"), the result is *dvaiśaurpikam*; *traiśaurpikam*.

(P_5,1.21) When there is a negation of "one hundred" (*śata*), there is no negation [of the suffix] when it refers to another "hundred. It should be stated: "When there is a negation of 'one hundred,' there is no negation [of the suffix] when it refers to another 'hundred'. This is so that [the suffix] does not occur here: *śatyam śāṭakaśatam* ("a set of one hundred garments bought for one hundred"). Why say "when it refers to another 'hundred'"? [Observe: *śatakam nidānam* ("a bundle of one hundred").

It should be stated that [the suffix] *ḍati* also applies here, so that forms such as *katika-* ("bought for how many? may be obtained. But what is the reason it is not established? Because the prohibition "not after a stem ending in *ti*" would apply. If it is argued that the mention of *ḍati* is for the sake of prohibiting *ti*, [we reply: it is established by the principle of mentioning only that which is meaningful (*arthavad-grahaṇāt*). [Only] that which is meaningful [is affected].

The word *ti* is not included [in the rule], nor is the word *ti* meaningful when it follows the suffix *ḍati*. This *paribhāṣā* cannot be understood to apply here, for a meaning is not conveyed by a suffix alone; rather, it is conveyed by the suffix together with its stem (*saprakṛtika*). Where, then, does this *paribhāṣā* apply? It applies to those instances where there is the mention of a collection of sounds (*śabdasamghātagrahaṇa*). If that is so, then it must be stated.

It need not be stated. It is established by the inclusion of that which possesses meaning (*arthavat*). But was it not said that this *paribhāṣā* cannot be understood here? For a meaning is not understood from a suffix alone. A meaning is indeed understood even from a suffix alone. How so? It has been stated: by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

(P_5,1.23) For whom is this *iṭ* prescribed? He says: "For the suffix *kan*. Therefore, the mention of *kan* must be made. For if the mention of *kan* were not made, this [augment] would be understood as a suffix because of the governing context of suffixes (*pratyayādhikāra*). [Objection: By the force of the marker *ṭ*, it will be at the beginning. [Reply: There is another purpose for the application of the marker *ṭ*.

[The suffix] *ī* should be [understood as] *ṭit*. However, in the section concerning bases ending in *a*, the suffix *ī* does not apply, and this [base] does not end in *a*. Even so, why [is it *ṭit*]? By virtue of the power of its being marked with *ṭ*, it will be initial; otherwise, even though we are in the section concerning bases ending in *a*, the suffix *ī* might occur after a base that does not end in *a*. Therefore, the mention of *kaṇ* must be made. It need not be made, for it is already under discussion (*prakṛta*).

[The word] *anuvartate* [is supplied]. Where was it introduced? In the rule: *saṅkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan*. That [word] was indeed indicated in the nominative case (*prathamānirdiṣṭam*), and here the sense is with that which is indicated in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdiṣṭena*). This [word] *vatoḥ*, being in the fifth case (*pañcamī*), will effect a sixth-case interpretation for the first-case [word] *kan*, according to the principle: "from that [which is in the ablative], [the suffix is applied] to what follows. This is a rule for the introduction of a suffix (*pratyayavidhi*). And in a rule for the introduction of a suffix...

The suffixes [beginning with *kan*] apply after the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*). This is not a rule for the introduction of a suffix; rather, the suffix already prescribed and the base (*prakṛta*) under discussion continue to apply. (Pāṇini 5.1.24) For what purpose is the condition "provided it is not a technical name" (*asañjñāyām*) stated? [Consider the examples: *triṃśatkaḥ*, *viṃśatkaḥ*. How does the suffix *kan* apply here? It applies by the rule "the suffix *kan* comes after a numeral" (Pāṇini 5.1.22). [But then] there is a prohibition by the rule "after a numeral ending in *atiśat*" (Pāṇini 5.1.24). [Therefore, the condition *asañjñāyām* is necessary.]

[The suffix *kan*] is obtained. If that is so, then the activity of the Teacher indicates that *kan* occurs here, because he provides this irregular derivation (*nipātana*) ending in a suffix by stating "after *viṃśatika*, [the suffix] *kha*. This might be an indication regarding *viṃśati*. [Patañjali] says: No; the indication depends on the specific rule (*yoga*). Or rather, a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: after *viṃśati* and *triṃśat*, *kan* occurs.

Thus [ends the discussion]. Then, regarding the rule *ḍvun asaṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.1.25): "And *ṭithan* after *ardha*. It should be stated that *ṭithan* follows *ardha*. [Examples: *ardhikaḥ*, *ardhikī*. "And *prati* after *kārṣāpaṇa*. It should be stated that *ṭiṭhan* follows *kārṣāpaṇa*, and there is also the alternative [suffix *ḍvun*].
The substitute *prati* should be stated [as an option]. [Examples: *kārṣāpaṇikaḥ*, *kārṣāpaṇikī*; *pratikaḥ*, *pratikī*. (P.

5.1.28) It has been stated regarding the elision (*luk*) of a *dvigu* compound. What was stated? First, it was stated there: "When there is elision of a *dvigu*, the mention of that which causes it [is required]. And: "When the specific meaning is not understood, [the suffix is applied] even from that which does not cause it."

In this case as well, when there is elision (*luk*) of a *dvigu* compound, the rule regarding "that which is caused by it" (*tannimittagrahaṇa*) must be applied. It should be stated that the elision occurs of that *taddhita* suffix which is the cause of the *dvigu*. This is so that [the elision] does not occur here: *dviśūrpa* (purchased with two winnowing baskets) and *triśūrpa* (purchased with three winnowing baskets). [Otherwise, one would have to derive] *dvaiśaurpika* (purchased with two *dviśūrpa*s) and *traiśaurpika* (purchased with three *triśūrpa*s). [This is necessary] because the specific meaning would not be understood.

"Also from that which is not its cause. When there is no comprehension of a specific meaning [derived] from that which is not its cause, it should be stated [that the suffix is applied] even from that which is not its cause. What is the purpose?

[The compound] *dviśūrpī* (two winnowing baskets) is a collective (*samāhāra*) of two *śūrpa*s. Having analyzed [the compound] as "purchased for two *śūrpa*s," it should be such that the form *dviśūrpa* itself is obtained. Now, even if the mention of "that which is its cause" (*tannimitta*) is made, how is this understood? Of that...

Does "tannimittāt" mean "the cause of that is *tannimitta*, [and] from that which has that as its cause"? Or does it mean "that is the cause of this, therefore this is *tannimitta*, [and] from that which has that as its cause"? And what follows from this? If it is understood as "the cause of that is *tannimitta*, [and] from that which has that as its cause," then even if the term *tannimitta* were included [in the rule], it would still apply here: for example, in the case of *dviśūrpa*, meaning "purchased with two winnowing baskets."

"Triśūrpa. "Dvaiśaurpika," meaning "bought with two śūrpa-measures," and "traiśaurpika. Now, if it is understood that "he is the cause of this" (sa nimittam asya), then "this is caused by that" (sa ayam tannimittaḥ) and "from that which is caused by that" (tannimittāt); thus there is no fault. Let it be so, in such a way that there is no fault. It is understood that "he is the cause of this" (sa nimittam asya), and therefore "this is caused by that" (sa ayam tannimittaḥ) and "from that which is caused by that" (tannimittāt). Why?

This refers to what he said: "When a specific meaning is not understood, [the suffix is applied] even from that which is not its cause. If that is so, then the mention of "its cause" (*tannimitta*) must be made.
It need not be made. The word *dvigoḥ* is not in the ablative case. What then? It is a genitive of relation (*sambandha-ṣaṣṭhī*).

Elision (*luk*) occurs of the *taddhita* suffix belonging to a *dvigu* compound. And what is the *taddhita* suffix belonging to the *dvigu*? Its cause—that is, that on account of which the *dvigu* is formed.

This is the case. And in what does this occur? In a derivative suffix (*pratyaya*). Then it must be stated: "Even from that which is not the cause [of the specific meaning], provided there is no cognition of a specific meaning. But this need not be stated. Here, we must establish three forms: *dviśūrpa* (bought with two winnowing baskets), *triśūrpa* (bought with three winnowing baskets), and *dvaiśaurpika* (bought with two winnowing baskets).

Regarding the term *traisaurpikam*: in that case, between two words having the same meaning, the analysis (*vigraha*) will be made with one, while the suffixal derivation (*utpatti*) will occur from the other, according to the maxim of the sheep and the ram (*aviravikanyāya*). For example, having analyzed it as "the meat of a sheep" (*aveḥ māṃsam*), the derivation occurs from the word *avika*. Likewise here, having analyzed it as "bought with two winnowing baskets" (*dvābhyām śūrpābhyām krītam*), [the compound] *dviśūrpa* is formed.

Thus it will be: having analyzed the compound as *dviśūrpyā krītam* (bought for two winnowing-baskets), it will remain a mere sentence. Now, what is the purpose of the restriction "provided it is not a technical name" (*asañjñāyām*)? [Consider] *pāñcalohitikam* and *pāñcakalāpikam*. Furthermore, the prohibition regarding technical names is useless because the elision is caused by that very [technical name].
The prohibition of the technical name is indeed useless. Why? Because the elision is caused by that [technical name].

Without a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix and without the elision (*luk*) of that secondary derivative, there is no designation as a *dvigu* compound. Therefore, a suffix that would arise from such a compound could not have that [the *dvigu*] as its cause. If that is so, then this [form] might occur: *pañcalohitī* (a collection of five red things) or *pañcalohityā krītam* (bought for five red things). Even here, it should necessarily be *pañcalohitam*. Why? Because it has been stated:

For it has been stated that when a specific meaning is not understood, [the designation applies] even from what is not its cause. The purpose for [the term] being a number (*saṅkhyātva*) has already been explained;

therefore, the mention of *adhyardha* here is redundant. It has been stated that there is a purpose for the mention of *adhyardha* as a number. What was stated? That "the mention of *adhyardha* is for the sake of the rules regarding compounds and primary suffixes (*kan*), and there is no mention [of it] when elision (*luk*) occurs. Therefore...

In this case, the mention of *adhyardha* is redundant. Therefore, the mention of *adhyardha* here is purposeless; for the elision (*luk*) is already established by the rule "of a *dvigu*" (Pāṇini 5.1.28).
[Addition: An inclusionary statement (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made regarding *kārṣāpaṇa-sahasra* and *suvarṇa-śatamāna*.

[The suffix *ka*] should be applied [after a word ending in *suvarṇa*, *śatamāna*, or *śāta* when preceded by *adhyardha*, *dvi*, or *tri*]. *Adhyardhasuvarṇam*, *adhyardhasauvarṇikam*; *adhyardhaśatamānam*, *adhyardhaśātamānam*;
*dviśatamānam*, *dviśātamānam*. After *dvi* and *tri*, [the suffix *ya* is applied]: *dvitribhyām*. "After *dvi* and *tri*" [is the rule].
As for what is said—"this should be understood as having a dual application"—what is this "dual application"? It means occurring in two *yoga*s;

the state of being in two *yoga*s is "dual application" (*dvaiyogya*). One should understand it as something to be desired: from here onwards, [the rule] applies without distinction to both two and three. Therefore, the Teacher, acting as a friend, explains it further:

"From *dvi* and *tri*, [the suffix] *dvaiyogya* [is applied]. And in that case, the mention of *bahu* is required; in that case, the mention of *bahu* must be made: *bahuniṣkam*, *bahunaiṣkikam*; *bahuvistam*, *bahubaistikam*. "After *khārī*, [the suffix] *īkan* is applied, and also after the solitary [word *khārī*]. It should be stated: "After *khārī*, *īkan* is applied, and also after the solitary [word *khārī*]": *khārīkam*. There is also an addition regarding *kākiṇī*: there is an addition regarding *kākiṇī*.
The suffix -ka should be applied. [Examples: *adhyardhakākiṇīkam*, *dvikākiṇīkam*. It should be stated that it is also applied after the word *kevalā*: [examples: *kākiṇīkam*.
(Pāṇini 5.1.35) It should be stated that the suffixes -ka and -ya are optionally applied after the words *śata* and *śāṇa*:
[examples: *adhyardhaśatam* and *adhyardhaśatyam*, *pañcaśatam* and *pañcaśatyam*; *adhyardhaśāṇam* and *adhyardhaśāṇyam*.

*pañcaśāṇam*, *pañcaśāṇyam*. [The rule] "after *dvi* and *tri* preceded by [a word], there is also *aṇ*" should be stated. After *dvi* and *tri* preceded by [a word], there is also *aṇ*: *dviśāṇam*, *triśāṇam*, *dvaiśāṇam*, *traiśāṇam*, *dviśāṇyam*, *triśāṇyam*. (P_5.1.37) From the rule "purchased with that" (*tena krītam*), because it is the instrument (*karaṇa*). From the rule "purchased with that."

In this case, it should be stated: "because of being the instrument" (*karaṇāt*). Let it not apply here: *devadattena krītam* ("bought by Devadatta"), *yajñadattena krītam* ("bought by Yajñadatta"). It should be stated: "because of being exclusively non-agents" (*akartrekāntāt*). Let it not apply here: *devadattena pāṇinā krītam* ("bought by Devadatta with his hand"). There should be an addition [to the rule] for numerals and for *dvigu* compounds. It should be stated: "of a numeral" (*saṃkhyāyāḥ*).

In this case as well, it should be so: "purchased for five" (*pañcaka*). But what is the reason that it is not established? He will state [later] that [the suffix *kan* is added] after a word ending in the singular number. This present rule is an exception (*apakarṣa*) to that, placed before it. It should be stated: "after a singular [word]," meaning "after a word ending in the singular. Let it not apply here: "purchased with two winnowing baskets" (*śūrpābhyām krītam*) or "purchased with many winnowing baskets" (*śūrpaiḥ krītam*). And [it applies] after a *dvigu* compound.

It should be stated that [the suffix applies] even after a *dvigu* compound. This is so that forms such as *dviśūrpa* ("purchased for two winnowing baskets") and *triśūrpa* ("purchased for three winnowing baskets") may also be obtained here. If it were said [that the suffix applies] only after a word ending in the singular number, then forms such as *maudgika* ("purchased with mung beans") and *māṣika* ("purchased with black gram") would not be established. It should rather be stated that [the suffix applies] after that which ends in the singular number of a measure or a numeral.

In that case, it should be stated that [the suffix] occurs after a word ending in the singular number. And if that were done, much would have to be explained. It need not be stated. Why does [the suffix] not occur in *śūrpābhyāṃ krītam* ("bought with two winnowing baskets") or *śūrpaiḥ krītam* ("bought with many winnowing baskets")? It has already been stated. What was stated? That it is because such forms are not used (*anabhidhānāt*). If this is so, then it should also not be stated that [the suffix occurs] "after an instrument (*karaṇa*) that is not restricted to being a non-agent (*akartrekāntāt*)."
Why does it not occur solely from the agent (*kartṛ*)? Because it is not so expressed (*anabhidhānāt*).
What is the difference between conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and occurrence (*nipāta*)? Conjunction is that which is expressed as:
"Having done this, this is obtained. Occurrence is that which is an accidental event (*yādṛcchika-bheda*).

Or [the suffix -ika is used] after the words *cheda*, *padma*, or *parṇa*. In the section concerning its cause (*tasyanimittaprakaraṇe*), an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the words *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman* when followed by the terms *śamana* (pacification) or *kopana* (provocation). An addition must be made in the section concerning its cause for the words *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman* when followed by *śamana* or *kopana*.
For example: that which is the pacification or provocation of wind (*vāta*) is *vātika*; likewise, *paittika* and *ślaiṣmika*. Also from *sannipāta*.

And it should be stated: "and from *sannipāta*"; thus, *sānnipātika*. In the section concerning *yat*, there should be an addition for *brahmavarcasa*: "and from *brahmavarcasa*" in the section on *yat*. That which is the cause of *brahmavarcasa* is *brahmavarcasya*; or it is a portent (*utpāta*).

(P_5,1.47) KA_II.351.20–352.2 Ro_IV.41: "And [the rule] *tad asmin dīyate asmai* (‘that is given to this’). It should be stated: “*tad asmin dīyate asmai*. When five—whether interest (*vṛddhi*), profit (*āya*), gain (*lābha*), toll (*śulka*), or gift (*upadā*)—is given to this, it is called *pañcakaḥ*. [Similarly,] *saptakaḥ*, *aṣṭakaḥ*, *navakaḥ*, *daśakaḥ*. That being so...
An addition [to the rule] should be made. It need not be made; for when something is given to someone, it is also given in that [which belongs to him].

Thus, the expression "it is given in this" is already established. (P_5,1.48) In the section concerning the suffix *ṭhan*, an addition should be made for words ending in *ananta*. In the section concerning *ṭhan*...

An addition must be made for the word *ananta*. [Examples: *dvitīyakaḥ*, *tṛtīyakaḥ*. But what is the reason that it is not established? It is said: "Because it is a word denoting a ordinal number (*pūraṇa*). And this [word *ananta*] does not end in a term denoting a ordinal number. This is the conclusion: "Ordinal number" is a meaning; the word *tīya* expresses that meaning. That [suffix] occurs after a word ending in a term denoting a ordinal number, in its own sense (*svārthe*).
In the case of a fraction (*bhāga*), *an* [is applied]; that also indeed becomes a filler (*pūraṇa*).

(Pāṇini 5.1.52) Regarding the rule "from *droṇa*, when it means 'he cooks that', the suffix *aṇ* is also applied": it should be stated as "from *droṇa*, when it means 'he cooks that', the suffix *aṇ* is also applied. Examples: *droṇam pacati* ("he cooks a *droṇa* measure"), *drauṇī*, *drauṇikī*.
Since the formation is already established by the rule "also from *kulija*," the mention of the elision (*luk*) is redundant.

Because of the presence of the "trika" (the set of three suffixes) in the preceding rule, it is already established by the phrase "and from *kulija*. There is no purpose in the explicit mention of the elision (*luk*).
Why? Because of the presence of the "trika" in the preceding rule. In the preceding rule, this entire "trika" is indicated:
*dvyāḍhakī*, *dvyāḍhikī*, and *dvyāḍhakīnā*.

(P_5.1.57–58.1) KA_II.352.18–354.6 Ro_IV.43–46: Regarding names (*sañjñā*), a suffix is to be applied in its own sense (*svārthe*). For example: *pañcakāḥ śakunayaḥ* ("five birds"), *trikāḥ śālaṅkāyanāḥ* ("the Śālaṅkāyana [clan] has three [members]"), *saptakā brahmavṛkṣāḥ* ("the Brahmavṛkṣa [trees] have seven [leaves]"). After that, it should be stated: "The suffix following that [base] is applied when the possessor of the measure (*parimāṇin*) is to be expressed."

A *pañcaka* (a group of five) is a *saṅgha*. A *daśaka* (a group of ten) is a *saṅgha*. There should be an addition regarding the measure of life (*jīvitaparimāṇa*). An addition must be made regarding the measure of life. One whose measure of life is sixty is called *ṣāṣṭika*; one whose measure of life is seventy is called *sāptatika*.
The mention of "and regarding the measure of life" is redundant, because [the formation] is already established by the rule "from time" (*kālāt*). And [it applies to] the measure of life.

Thus, this statement is purposeless. Why? Because it is already established by the rule *kālāt*. It is indeed established by *kālāt* alone. In this case, for one whose lifespan is sixty years, having been engaged for sixty [days], he is called *bhūta*. There, it is already established that he is *adhīṣṭa*, *bhṛta*, *bhūta*, or *bhāvī*. Furthermore, this must necessarily be understood in this way; otherwise, in the present statement...
For there would be the undesirable consequence of *luk* (elision). For if [the suffix] were applied here, *luk* would indeed apply:

*dviṣāṣṭikaḥ*, *triṣāṣṭikaḥ*. Since *luk* occurs by this [rule], why does it not occur by that [other rule]? It is stated: "up to and including *arhat*. But it is not established. What is the reason? Because these are not words denoting time (*kālaśabda*). What then?

These are words for number; these too are words for time. How so? Number functions with respect to that which is numbered. If, then, whatever functions with respect to time is a word for time, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to [words] such as *ramaṇīya* (pleasant), as in: "he became at a pleasant time" (*ramaṇīyaṃ kālaṃ bhūtaḥ*), or "he became at a beautiful time" (*śobhanaṃ kālaṃ bhūtaḥ*). Now, if this is your view: [it is not so, because] it must be seen in relation to time.

The word *kāla* (time) is that which does not deviate from time; thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to [words like] *ramaṇīya* and so forth. However, an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the measure of life. And here too, an addition must be made: *vārṣaśatikaḥ* ("lasting a hundred years") and *vārṣasahasrikaḥ* ("lasting a thousand years"). But what is the reason that it is not established? For the word *varṣaśata* ("hundred years") is not a numeral (*saṅkhyā*).

What then? The word "hundred" (*śata*) is used here in the sense of a countable number. If that is so, then [the suffix] is seen after other words as well, for the sake of expressing "a hundred *khāra*s" and so forth. It should be stated: "[the suffix] is seen after other words as well. What is the purpose? For the sake of expressing "a hundred *khāra*s" and so forth: *khāraśatikaḥ rāśiḥ* (a heap consisting of a hundred *khāra*s); *khārasahastrikaḥ rāśiḥ* (a heap consisting of a thousand *khāra*s). But then this fault arises: for in this case...

[There would be] the undesirable consequence (*luk-prasaṅga*) [of elision]. We do not say that a rule must be applied wherever a fault arises when it is applied. What then? It must be applied where no fault arises when it is applied. And where does no fault arise when it is applied? In the case of *param* and *arhāt*. In that case, then, this addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made. No, it need not be made; for it is already established by the rule itself [beginning with] *kālāt*. But surely—

And it has been said: "These are not words for time; what then? They are words for number. But has it not been said that these too are words for time? How so? Because "number" (saṅkhyā) applies to that which is numbered (saṅkhyeya). But has it not been said: "If, then, whatever applies to time is a word for time, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) to [words] such as 'delightful' (ramaṇīya)"? It has indeed been stated.

What has been said? "Because it is not so stated. Because it is not so stated, there will be no production [of the suffix] in the case of *ramaṇīya* and the like. Regarding the rule for the suffix *ḍa* in the sense of a *stoma*: the suffix *ḍa* is to be prescribed in the sense of a *stoma*. What is the purpose? For the sake of expressing "fifteen" and so forth. [Examples: *pañcadaśaḥ stomaḥ* ("a fifteenfold hymn"), *saptadaśaḥ stomaḥ* ("a seventeenfold hymn").

(P_5.1.59) KA_II.355.2–357.8 Ro_IV.46–56 These words beginning with *viṃśati* are established as irregular forms (*nipātana*) together with their bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*). In that regard, it is not known which is the base, which is the suffix, and what is the meaning of the suffix. Therefore, it must be stated: "this is the base, this is the suffix, and this is the meaning of the suffix. We shall state them starting from the word *dvi*.
This suffix *śati* is prescribed in the sense of its own referent (*svārthe*) for the word *daśan*, with the substitution of *vin* [for *daśan*]. Thus, two tens (*daśatau*) are twenty (*viṃśatiḥ*).

If [it is argued that] words such as *viṃśati* are derived from *daśan*, then the formation of a compound would be impossible. If words such as *viṃśati* were derived from *daśan*, a compound such as *viṃśatigavaḥ* ("twenty cows") would not be possible. Why? Because the substance (*dravya*) would not be expressed. Of that...

Because [the word *go*] is not expressed [by the case-ending], the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply; and in a compound, that which ends in the genitive is placed first. In that case, *goviṃśatiḥ* would result, but it ought not to be so. Furthermore, *viṃśatigavam* would not be established.
And here, in the cases of *triṃśatpūlī* and *catvāriṃśatpūlī*, a compound characterized by grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) would not apply.

And the word must be prescribed as such: "twenty. Because there are two groups of ten, the dual number would apply according to the rule that "the dual occurs for two things," and thus the dual form would result. If this is the case, then words like *viṃśati* will denote the possessor of the measure (*parimāṇin*). But if they denote the possessor of the measure, then a suffix must again be prescribed in its own sense (*svārthe*). If they denote the possessor of the measure, then a suffix must indeed be prescribed in its own sense: [the form] *viṃśakaḥ*.

The Saṅgha [is the subject]. There is a rule for the sixth case (genitive) ending; the sixth case must also be prescribed. "A group of twenty cows" (*gavāṃ viṃśatiḥ*). Since the substance (*dravya*) is already expressed [by the word *viṃśati*], the sixth case does not apply because it has already been expressed. Furthermore, the singular number must be prescribed. In "twenty cows" (*viṃśatir gāvaḥ*), since there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "cows" (*gobhiḥ*), the plural number would apply according to the rule "the plural is used when there is a plurality. [Therefore, this rule] is not undertaken [as a separate one].

Or rather, [the formation of *viṃśati* and so on] is established through their recognition as primary nominal stems (*prātipadika*), just as in the case of *sahasra* and other such words. Alternatively, it is more logical that *viṃśati* and the following are not derived [by rule]. How is this established? Through their recognition as primary nominal stems. How is there recognition as primary nominal stems? *Viṃśati* and the others are underived primary nominal stems, just as in the case of *sahasra* and so on. For example: *sahasram*, *ayutam*, *arbudam*.
Thus, there is no formal grammatical derivation (*anugama*) performed here, yet the designation (*abhidhāna*) does occur, as is said in the case of "thousand" (*sahasra*) and so forth.

Now, how should it be in the case of "thousand" and so forth? [The forms are: *sahasraṃ gavām* (a thousand cows), *sahasraṃ gāvaḥ* (a thousand cows), *sahasragavam* (a thousand cows), and *gosahasram* (a thousand cows). Since there is doubt even in this case, one should not be critical where a formal derivation is not performed.

But has it not been stated that if *viṃśati* and the others [denote] "ten," then the formation of a compound is untenable; if they denote the possessor of the measure (*parimāṇin*), then there would be the prescription of a suffix in its own sense (*svārthe*) and the application of the genitive case? This is not a fault. The words *viṃśati* and so on will apply to the aggregate (*saṅgha*). Should this be explicitly stated? No, it need not be. How then is it understood without being stated? As an aggregate (*saṅgha*).

Thus it continues. *Saṅgha*, *samūha*, and *samudāya* are synonymous. These terms beginning with *viṃśati* (twenty), while existing as designations for a collection (*samudāya*), become expressions of state (*bhāvavacana*). Being expressions of state, they become expressions of quality (*guṇavacana*).
Being expressions of quality, they become indistinguishable from other expressions of quality. And in the case of other expressions of quality, sometimes the quality [is perceived].

It becomes a qualifier of the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), as in "a white cloth. Sometimes the quality is designated by means of the possessor of the quality: "the whiteness of the cloth. Now, regarding the statement that "if [numbers] such as twenty and so on are [treated as] tens, the formation of a compound would be impossible," if there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) at that time, then it is between the quality and the possessor of the quality. Let the resolution of the objection regarding the number of words stand for now; [it applies] to the possessor of measure (*parimāṇin*).

If, however, the suffix is prescribed in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), then that which occurs in the sense of "conjunction" (*saṃhanana*) will occur in the sense of "conjunction"; that which occurs in the sense of "numerical conjunction" (*saṅkhyā-saṃhanana*) will occur in the sense of "substantial conjunction" (*dravya-saṃhanana*). Now, if it is the genitive case [that is used], then the quality (*guṇa*) is qualified by the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*). The resolution regarding the number applies to both cases as well. If, then, these words beginning with *viṃśati* were qualifiers (*guṇavacana*), they would share the same properties as other qualifiers.
It must be so. Furthermore, other words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*) follow the gender and number of the substance (*dravya*). For example:

*śuklaṃ vastram* (a white cloth), *śuklā śāṭī* (a white garment), *śuklaḥ kambalaḥ* (a white blanket), *śuklau kambalau* (two white blankets), *śuklāḥ kambalāḥ* (many white blankets). Whatever gender and whatever number belong to that quality which resides in the substance, those same belong to the quality as well.

Furthermore, the numbers twenty and so forth do not follow [the gender and number of the noun they qualify]. Indeed, other quality-words (*guṇavacana*) also do not necessarily follow the gender and number of the substance (*dravya*). For example: *gāvo dhanam* ("cows are wealth"), *putrā apatyam* ("sons are offspring"), *indrāgnī devatā* ("Indra and Agni are the deity"), *viśvedevā devatā* ("the Viśvedevas are the deity"), and "as many as follow the barren cow, all those are the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the sake of prosperity."
Now, a reason for this non-application [of the rule] can indeed be stated. Certainly, it can be stated. Well then, let it be stated:
here, sometimes a quality (*guṇa*) is intended to be expressed as the primary factor (*prādhānyena*). For example:
"five hundred rafts have crossed," "five hundred planks have crossed," "a battle with horses," or "a battle with swords. And yet, it is not the swords that fight.

Men fight by means of their qualities (*guṇa*), yet it is indeed the quality that is intended to be expressed as primary. Here, first of all, in the expression "cows are wealth" (*gāvo dhanam*), "wealth" (*dhanam*) is a single quality derived from the root *dhinoti* (to satisfy); that is intended to be expressed as primary. In the expression "sons are offspring" (*putrā apatyam*), "offspring" (*apatyam*) is a single quality derived from the sense of "not falling away" (*apatanāt*); that is intended to be expressed as primary. [Likewise,] Indra and Agni are the deity (*indrāgnī devatā*).

"The Viśvedevas are the deity": from the root *div*, meaning "to rule" (*aiśvarya-karman*), comes *deva*. From that, the suffix *tal* is added in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*). This is one quality (*guṇa*), and it is intended to be expressed as the primary element. "As many as they follow the command (*vāśitām anuyanti*), all those [are] the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the sake of prosperity (*samṛddhi*). From the root *dakṣ*, meaning "to increase" (*vṛddhi-karman*), comes *dakṣiṇā*. This is one quality, and it is intended to be expressed as the primary element. Of that...

Because it is a single entity, the singular number will be used. Furthermore, in words such as *viṃśati* ("twenty") and so on, there is also a single quality (*guṇa*); since that is intended to be expressed as the primary meaning, the singular number will be used because of its singularity. But then, this is a fault regarding the abstract nouns (*bhāvavacana*) among words like *viṃśati*: when the command "Let twenty cows be brought" is given, if the bringing of the action (*bhāva*) is enjoined, the bringing of the substance (*dravya*) would not follow. This is not so.
This is a fault. First, this must be asked:

if it is here stated that "the cow is to be bound" and "the goat is for Agni-Soma," how is it that when the generic form (*ākṛti*) is enjoined, actions such as touching, sprinkling, and slaughtering are performed upon the individual substance (*dravya*)? Because it is impossible; since touching and the other acts cannot possibly occur in the generic form, they are [performed] upon that which is associated with the generic form.

The acts of "commencing" (*ārambhaṇa*) and so forth are performed upon a substance (*dravya*). This [case] is of the same nature. Since it is impossible to bring the abstract state (*bhāva*), there will be the bringing of the substance. Or rather, because there is no distinction (*avyatireka*).
Since the analysis (*vigraha*) is seen after words such as *cheda* and *pathin*, the mention of the word "eternal" (*nitya*) is redundant.

The inclusion of the term *nitya* (always) in the rule for suffixes such as *-cha* after words like *cheda* and *pathin* is redundant. Why? Because the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is observed. The analysis is seen as follows: "he deserves cutting" (*chedam arhati*) and "he goes along the path" (*panthānam gacchati*). If it is argued that this inclusion of *nitya* is made for the sake of expressing a modification (*vikāra*), so that the analysis does not occur through a modification [of the base], then consider the forms *virāga* and *viraṅga*. [In these cases,] the suffix *ṇa* is applied to *pathin* always.

If it is argued that [the suffix] is for the sake of denoting a modification (*vikāra*), then this is equivalent to the case of *akaṅ* and the others. Just as there is no analysis (*vigraha*) with modifications such as *akaṅ* and so forth, so too there will be none with these two.
Furthermore, what is the point here? Should the mention of "permanence" (*nitya*) be made here, or should it be made elsewhere and not here?

In this case, that which ought not to be done is being done. This is precisely the principle: namely, that when two things are enjoined as being mutually dependent (*sanniyogaśiṣṭa*), upon the absence of one, there is the absence of both. For example: "This must be done by Devadatta and Yajñadatta together. Upon the absence of Devadatta, Yajñadatta also does not do it.

(P_5,1.71) KA_II.357.22–24 Ro_IV.58: An addition [to the rule] should be made stating "from *yajña* and *ṛtvij*, [the suffix *cha* is applied] in the sense of 'deserving that action'. An addition must be made stating "from *yajña* and *ṛtvij*, [the suffix *cha* is applied] in the sense of 'deserving that action'. For example: *yajñiyaḥ deśaḥ* ("a place deserving the performance of a sacrifice") and *ārtvijīnaṃ brāhmaṇakulam* ("a Brahmin family deserving the duties of a priest").
Regarding the statement "he performs that," this is not a definitive designation because it is not observed there.

The phrase "he performs that" is not a definitive designation; a designation that does not convey understanding is called "non-designation. Who performs the *pārāyaṇa*? He who acts for another. Who performs the *turāyaṇa*? He who offers the sacrificial pap (*caru*) and the cake (*puroḍāśa*). In that case—

Because it is not observed; for no suffix (*pratyaya*) is observed there. And because it is observed in the case of *iṅ* and *yaj*; for a suffix is indeed observed in the case of *iṅ* and *yaj*. One who studies the *pārāyaṇa* is called a *pārāyaṇika*; one who sacrifices with the *turāyaṇa* is called a *taurāyaṇika*. Both he who studies and he who performs [the sacrifice] for another cause [the suffix] to occur.
He who sacrifices and he who prepares the *caru* and *puroḍāśa* offerings—both of them perform the action. Why does [the suffix] not occur in both cases? Because it is not so prescribed.
(Pāṇini 5.1.74) An addition should be made for the cases of *yojanam gacchati* (he goes a *yojana*) and for *krośaśata-yojanaśata* (a hundred *krośas* or a hundred *yojanas*).
