Regarding the rule "he goes a *yojana*," an addition must be made for the cases of "a hundred *krośas*" and "a hundred *yojanas*. Thus, one who goes a hundred *krośas* is called *krauśaśatikaḥ*, and one who goes a hundred *yojanas* is called *yaujanaśatikaḥ*. Furthermore, there is the rule "he deserves to go from there"; and regarding this "he deserves to go from there," the same applies to the cases of "a hundred *krośas*" and "a hundred *yojanas*."

An addition must be made [to the rule]: one who deserves to be approached from a distance of a hundred *krośas* is called *krauśaśatika*; a teacher (*guru*) who deserves to be approached from a distance of a hundred *yojanas* is called *yaujanaśatika*.
(Pāṇini 5.1.77) In the section concerning things brought (*āhṛta-prakaraṇa*), [the suffix *ṭhan* is applied] after words preceded by *vāri*, *jaṅgala*, *sthalaka*, and *kāntāra*.

An addition [to the rule] must be made: in the section concerning "brought" (*āhṛta*), an addition should be made for compounds preceded by *vāri*, *jaṅgala*, *sthala*, and *kāntāra*. One who goes by way of water is a *vāripathika*; that which is brought by way of water is *vāripathika*. Water (*vāri*). Jungle (*jaṅgala*): one who goes by way of the jungle path is a *jāṅgalapathika*; that which is brought by way of the jungle path is *jāṅgalapathika*.

*Jaṅgala*. One who goes by land (*sthala*) is a *sthālapathika*; that which is brought by land is *sthālapathika*. *Sthala*. One who goes by a wilderness path (*kāntārapatha*) is a *kāntārapathika*; that which is brought by a wilderness path is *kāntārapathika*. And [the suffix applies] after *ajapatha* and *śaṅkupatha*. And after *ajapatha* and *śaṅkupatha*.

Thus it should be stated: one who travels by way of the *ajapatha* is *ājapathika*; that which is brought by way of the *ajapatha* is *ājapathika*. One who travels by way of the *śaṅkupatha* is *śāṅkupathika*; that which is brought by way of the *śaṅkupatha* is *śāṅkupathika*. Regarding *madhuka* and *marica*, the suffix *aṇ* should be stated [after the word] *sthālapatha*. *Madhuka* from the *sthālapatha* is *sthālapatham madhukam*; *marica* from the *sthālapatha* is *sthālapatham maricam*.

(P_5,1.80) KA_II.12-18 Ro_IV.60-61: The prescription of the accusative case for the meanings of *adhīṣṭa* and *bhṛti* is purposeless, because it is not observed there. The prescription of the accusative case for the meanings of *adhīṣṭa* and *bhṛti* is purposeless. What is the reason? Because it is not observed there.
For one does not say, "He will study for a month" (*māsam adhīṣyate*). Rather, having been requested for a moment (*muhūrta*), he performs that work for a month.
But it is established by the mention of the dative case. This is established. How? By the mention of the dative case.
The mention of the dative case must be made: "that for which one is commissioned" (*tasmai adhīṣṭaḥ*). Then that mention of the dative case must indeed be made. It need not be made;
for there will be a designation [of the whole] by the name of its purpose. A *muhūrta* whose purpose is a month is called a "month."

In the rule *avayasi ṭhañ ca*, there is an attraction (*anukarṣa*) of the immediately preceding [element]. One should understand that *avayasi ṭhañ ca* is an attraction of what is immediately prior; [furthermore,] one should recognize that *yap* also continues [from the previous rule]. Thus, the Teacher, acting as a friend, explains this.

In the rule *avayasi ṭhañ ca*, there is an attraction (*anukarṣa*) of the immediately preceding [element]. (P_5.1.90) Regarding the word *ṣaṣṭika*, there must be a mention of it as a technical term (*saṃjñā*). A mention of it as a technical term must be made so that [the suffix] does not apply to *mudga* beans, which also ripen in sixty nights. Or rather, it has already been stated.
What has been stated? "Because it is not expressed" (anabhidhānāt).

Regarding the rule *tat asya brahmacaryam* (Pāṇini 5.1.94), an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the words *mahānāmnī* and others: the addition *tat asya brahmacaryam* must be formulated for *mahānāmnī* and so forth.

The *brahmacarya* of the *mahānāmnī* verses is called *māhānāmnikam*. There is also [the term] *ādityavratikam*. Regarding the rule "he performs that" (*tat carati*), an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for words such as *mahānāmnī* and others. Thus: one who performs the *mahānāmnī* verses is a *māhānāmnika*; an *ādityavratika*. This formulation "he performs that" (*tat carati*) is not appropriate, because the *mahānāmnīs* are [merely] names of *ṛc* verses.

"And yet those [rites] are not performed; rather, the vow belonging to them is performed. This is not a fault. The designation will apply by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*); that is, the vow associated with the *Mahānāmnī* verses is called "the *Mahānāmnī* vow. The suffix *ḍin* should be stated after words such as *avāntaradīkṣā*. [Thus we have] *avāntaradīkṣī* ("one who has undergone the intermediate consecration") and *tilavratī* ("one who observes the sesame-vow"). [The suffix applies] after the word *aṣṭācatvāriṃśat*.
And *ḍvun* [is added] after *aṣṭācatvāriṃśat*; both *ḍvun* and *ḍini* should be stated [as suffixes]. [Examples: *aṣṭācatvāriṃśakaḥ*, *aṣṭācatvāriṃśī*.
And for *cāturmāsya*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of *y*. Both *ḍvun* and *ḍini* should be stated [as suffixes] along with the elision of *y* for *cāturmāsya*.
[Examples: *cāturmāsikaḥ*, *cāturmāsī*. Now, what is this "of the *cāturmāsyas*"? [The suffix] *ṇya* is applied after *caturmāsa* when referring to a sacrifice.

In that context, regarding the sense "occurring therein," the suffix *ṇya* should be prescribed after the word *caturmāsa* when it means "occurring therein. Thus, sacrifices occurring in four months are called *cāturmāsyāni*. Regarding technical names (*saṃjñā*), the suffix *aṇ* should be prescribed. Thus, the full moon day occurring in four months is called *cāturmāsī*.

(P_5,1.95) What is the purpose of including the term *ākhyā* ("name")? If it were stated merely as "its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) [comes] from sacrifices (*yajña*)," then the suffix would arise only from those sacrifices that have become technical names (*saṃjñībhūta*), such as *agniṣṭomikī*, *rājasūyikī*, and *vājapeyikī*. It would not apply where the word *yajña* is actually present, as in *nāvayajñikī* or *pākayajñikī*.

In this case, [the forms] *pāñcaudanikyaḥ* and *dāśaudanikyaḥ* would not be possible. However, when the mention of "name" (*ākhyā*) is made, there is no fault. Whether they have become technical names (*sañjñībhūta*) or not, and whether the word *yajña* is present or absent, the desired suffix occurs based on the mere name itself. (Pāṇini 5.1.96) The mention of "occurrence" (*kārya*) is redundant, because it has already been accomplished by the rule for "being therein" (*tatra-bhava*).

The mention of *kārya* (effect) is redundant. What is the reason? Because it has already been established by the term *tatra-bhava*. For whatever is an effect (*kārya*) in a month, being produced in that month, is simply "that which exists there" (*tatra-bhava*). In this case, the rule is already established by the expression *tatra-bhava*. Why, then, does your honor reject only the mention of *kārya* and not the mention of *dīyate* as well? For just as that which is an effect in a month [is called] "in a month,"...

That which occurs in a month is "bhavam" (occurring in that); thus, even that which is given in a month is "bhavam" in the sense of occurring in that month. In this regard, it is already established by the rule *tatra bhavaḥ*. It is not so established. That [gift] is not given in the month; rather, it is given when the month has passed.

If that is the case, then the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) should be understood as one of immediate proximity (*aupaśleṣika*). If that is so, then [the rule] should follow after the division of the *yoga* (sūtra).

This [sūtra] should be recited: "The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) belongs to those called sacrifices (*yajña*)," and it is given therein. From that, [the suffix] *bhavavat* applies according to time [rule P. 4.3.53]. (P.
5.1.97) In the section on the suffix *aṇ*, there is an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for words beginning with *agnipada*. In the section on *aṇ*:

An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for *agnipada* and so forth. There are three mentions of the suffix *aṇ* here: (1) *aṇ* after *vyuṣṭa* and so forth, in the sense of "that time has arrived for him" (*samayas tat asya prāptam*); (2) *aṇ* after words denoting a season (*ṛtu*), in the sense of "purpose" (*prayojana*); and (3) *aṇ* after *viśākhā* and *āṣāḍhā*, in the sense of "churning-stick" (*mantha*) and "staff" (*daṇḍa*). In this regard, it is not known in which *aṇ*-rule the addition for *agnipada* and so forth should be applied, because there is no distinction [specified].
Having stated that the suffix *aṇ* occurs after *vyuṣṭa* and others in all cases, it should be further stated: "and after *agnipada* and others.

That which is given or the task to be performed at *agnipada* is called *āgnipada*. [Similarly] *pailumūla*. When the time has arrived for him, the suffix *aṇ* is applied after words denoting a season (*ṛtu*). It should be stated: "and after *agnipada* and others. That for whom the fast (*upavasta*) has arrived is called *aupavastra*. [Similarly] *prāśita*.

The *prāśitra* has been obtained; this is its purpose (*prayojana*). [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after *viśākhā* and *āṣāḍhā* when referring to the *mantha* and the *daṇḍa*. It should be stated that [the suffix *aṇ* is also applied] after *agnipada* and others. That for which the *cūḍā* is the purpose is *cauḍa*; that for which the *śraddhā* is the purpose is *śrāddha*. (Pāṇini 5.1.111) In the section concerning *cha*, [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the verbal roots *viś*, *pūr*, *pad*, and *ruh*, provided they do not end in *ā*.

An addition [to the rule] regarding compounds with a preceding member (*sapūrvapada*): in the section on *cha*, an addition must be made for the roots *viś*, *pūr*, *pad*, and *ruh* when preceded by a non-vocalic (*anāt*) preceding member. *Viś*: *gehānupraveśanīyam* (that which is to be entered into the house). *Pūr*: *prapāpūraṇīyam* (that which is to be filled by a water-trough).

*Pad*: *goprapadanīyam* (suitable for the treading of cows); *aśvaprapadanīyam* (suitable for the treading of horses). *Ruh*: *prāsādārohaṇīyam* (suitable for ascending the palace). [Furthermore, the suffix] *yat* is applied after words such as *svarga*.
The suffix *yat* occurs after words such as *svarga*. [Examples: *svargya*, *dhanya*, *yaśasya*, *āyuṣya*. [Rule:

Elision (*luk*) should be stated for words beginning with *puṇyāhavācana*. [Examples: *puṇyāhavācana*, *śāntivācana*, *svastivācana*. [Commentary: The mention of *ekāgāra* is unnecessary because it falls within the scope of the section on the suffix *ṭhañ*.

The inclusion of "from *ekāgāra*" (a single house) is purposeless. Why? Because it occurs within the section on the suffix *ṭhañ*. The suffix *ṭhañ* is the subject under discussion; it will continue to apply here. If that is so, then this is the purpose: I shall state "in the case of a thief" (*caure*). Let it not apply here: "this monk has a single house as his purpose. If this were the only purpose, one would simply have said "from *ekāgāra* in the case of a thief."
The rule for *nipātana* (irregular formation) from *ākāla* is purposeless because of the context of the suffix *ṭhañ*.

The *nipātana* from *ākāla* is purposeless. Why? Because of the context of *ṭhañ*. The suffix *ṭhañ* is the subject under discussion; it will continue to apply here as well. If this is so, then this is the purpose: I shall perform the *nipātana* for this specific case when there is a desire to express the beginning and end of that which is simultaneous (*samānakāla*).

Thus [it is stated]. "And *ṭhan* after *ākāla*": it should be stated that *ṭhan* also [is applied] after *ākāla*. [The forms are] *ākālikī* and *ākālikā*. (Pāṇini 5.1.115) This is incorrect. What is incorrect here? That which is stated as "when that which is in construction with the third case is an action (*kriyā*). And how can there be construction with the third case?

[Objection: There would be an action [denoted by the term]. [Response: This is not a fault. All these words refer to collections of qualities (*guṇasamudāya*): "Brāhmaṇa," "Kṣatriya," "Vaiśya," and "Śūdra. For it is said regarding this very collection of qualities: "Austerity (*tapas*), sacred learning (*śruta*), and birth (*yoni*)—these are the makers of a Brāhmaṇa. One who is devoid of austerity and sacred learning is merely a Brāhmaṇa by birth (*jātibrāhmaṇa*)."

"He is thus fair-complexioned, of pure conduct, tawny-eyed, and with reddish-brown hair"—they apply these qualities to a Brāhmaṇa as well. And words that function for a whole are also applied to its parts. For example:
"the eastern Pañcālas."
The Northern Pañcālas; oil has been eaten;
ghee has been eaten.
"White," "blue," and "black. In this way, this word *brāhmaṇa*, which functions with reference to a collection, also functions with reference to its individual parts, if—
In that case, the word qualified by the third case-ending (*tṛtīyāsamartha*) is specified, while the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) remains unspecified. What is the fault in this?

[The fault is that] from a word qualified by the third case-ending that denotes an action (*kriyāvācin*), the suffix would also occur when there is equality of quality (*guṇatulya*). For example: *putreṇa tulyaḥ sthūlaḥ* ("He is as stout as his son") and *putreṇa tulyaḥ piṅgalaḥ* ("He is as tawny as his son"). Let it be, then, that the meaning of the suffix is what is specified. That which is equal is the action (*kriyā*).

If it is said that "it becomes that," even so, the third-case construction remains unspecified. What is the fault in that? From a word in the third case that does not denote an action, a suffix would undesirably apply even when [the object of comparison] is not an action. This is not a fault, because it is stated that "if that which is equal is an action. And that which is measured by a scale (*tulā*) is "equal" (*tulya*). If...

And even if [the word] is in construction with the third case (*tṛtīyāsamartha*), it is still an action (*kriyā*); since the meaning of the suffix is also an action, it becomes equivalent [to the standard example]. Alternatively, let it be simply this: that which is in construction with the third case, provided that it is an action. But was it not said that "the meaning of the suffix is unspecified"? What is the fault in that? [The fault is that] from a word in construction with the third case denoting an action, [the suffix would apply] to something equal in quality (*guṇatulya*).

[Objection: There would also be the possibility [of the suffix] in cases such as *putreṇa tulyaḥ sthūlaḥ* ("as fat as the son") and *putreṇa tulyaḥ piṅgalaḥ* ("as tawny as the son"). [Response: This is not a fault, because it is stated that "that which is in grammatical agreement with the third case [word] must be an action (*kriyā*). Furthermore, *tulya* means "measured by means of a balance" (*tulayā sammitam*).
And if both that which is in agreement with the third case and the meaning of the suffix are actions, then [the rule] applies.
It occurs. But which of these two is superior? Qualifying the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) alone is superior. Why is this so?

Because it is precisely by adopting this view that the Teacher has recited the Sūtra. He has established grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *vat*. Furthermore, the inclusion of *vati* among the indeclinables (*avyaya*) would not need to be made. Since this [suffix] occurs as an action (*kriyā*), it will not be connected with gender or number.

(P_5,1.116) KA_II.365.12–17 Ro_IV.75–77 For what purpose is this stated? Is it not already established by the rule *tena tulyaṃ kriyā ced vatiḥ*? It is not so established. That suffix is produced from a word in the third case when one person performs an action that ought to be performed by another; however, no such [action] is expressed by the word *iva*.

The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is prescribed in connection with the word *yoga*. But surely, the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) is not prescribed either? If that is so, then since [the formation] is already established, the fact that the teacher teaches the suffix *vati* after a word governed by the seventh case when joined with the word *iva* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*): namely, that the seventh case occurs in connection with the word *iva*. What is the purpose of this indication? For example: *deveṣv iva nāma* ("as it were among the gods"), *brāhmaṇeṣv iva* ("as it were among the Brahmins").
This application [of the suffix] is thus established.

(P_5.1.117) KA_II.364.19-22 Ro_IV.77-79 For what purpose is this stated? Is it not already established by the rule "When [something] is equal to that in action, the suffix *vati* is used"? It is not so established. The suffix would [otherwise] be applied there from a word in the third case (*tṛtīyāsamartha*), whereas [the intended meaning is] when [the equality is] with another.

In another case, when one person performs an action that ought to be performed by another, a suffix is produced [denoting comparison]. But here, however, from a word in the second case-relationship (*dvitīyāsamartha*), a suffix is produced to denote an action worthy of oneself—that is, an agent capable of performing it—where the capacity to perform it is firmly established: "You behave like a Brāhmaṇa. This means that the conduct [of yours] is worthy of a Brāhmaṇa.

(P_5,1.118.1) KA_II.365.2-6 Ro_IV.79 What is the purpose of including the term *artha*? One might simply say: "In the Vedic language, [the augment *naṭ* is applied] after a prefix before a verbal root (*dhātu*). Now, a verbal root is indeed a word (*śabda*). Since an operation cannot apply to a word itself, it will be understood to apply to its meaning (*artha*). But what is the meaning of a verbal root? It is action (*kriyā*). In that case, this is the purpose: the elision of the final member of a compound (*uttarapadalopa*).

It is so that it may be understood that "the meaning produced by the root" (dhātukṛto 'rthaḥ) is what is meant by "the meaning of the root" (dhātvarthaḥ). But what is the meaning produced by the root?

It is the *sādhana* (the means of accomplishment). What is the purpose? When this [suffix] occurs in the sense of a *sādhana*, it will be connected with gender and number, as in: *udgatāni udvataḥ* ("those which have gone up are high places") and *nigatāni nivataḥ* ("those which have gone down are low places").

(P_5,1.118.2) KA_II.365.7-12 Ro_IV.80 An addition should be made regarding the suffix *vati* after the words *strī* and *pums*. An addition must be made for *strī* and *pums* with the suffix *vati*: namely, *strīvat* and *puṃvat*. But what is the reason that [these forms] are not established? These two suffixes, *nañ* and *snañ*, are said to apply "before the word *bhavana*. Since those two are prescribed as specific exceptions (*viśeṣavihita*), they [block] the suffix *vati*, which is prescribed as a general rule (*sāmānyavihita*).

[If it were argued that] they would cause harm [to the rule], this is not a fault. The activity of the Teacher indicates that the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* do not occur in the sense of the suffix *vati*, since he provides the instruction "striyāḥ puṃvat" (as in the masculine, when referring to a feminine). Even so, the form "strīvat" is not established. [The answer is:
the indicator depends upon the presence of the letter *y*.
(P_5,1.119.1) KA_II.365.14–366.6 Ro_IV.81–82: An addition must be made regarding the suffixes *tva* and *tal* after the words *strī* and *pums*.

An addition must be made regarding the suffixes *tva* and *tal* after the words *strī* and *pums*: [the forms] *strībhāvaḥ*, *strītvam*, and *strītā*. But what is the reason that [these forms] are not established? These two suffixes, *nañ* and *snañ*, are said to apply before the word *bhavana*; they are prescribed as specific exceptions.

The suffix *vati*, which is prescribed as a general rule, would be superseded [by the two suffixes *nañ* and *snañ*]. Furthermore, the word "or" (*vā*) must be stated. What is the purpose? So that the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* may also apply: for instance, *strībhāvaḥ* (the state of being female) becomes *straiṇam*, and *pum̐bhāvaḥ* (the state of being male) becomes *pauṃsnam*. Alternatively, this is established through the co-occurrence with exceptions (*apavāda*). Indeed, this is established through the co-occurrence with exceptions; just as, for example, by the exceptions beginning with the suffix *imanij*.

Inclusion occurs in this manner; it will be the same for these two as well. Neither the Lord (Īśvara) commands, nor do the authors of the Dharmasūtras state that inclusion occurs through exceptions such as *imanij* and so forth. Rather, inclusion occurs through exceptions such as *imanij* and so forth by virtue of this specific effort [of the rule] beginning with "up to and including *tvatal*" (*ā ca tvāt*).

And these two are not included here. These two also are included here. How so? Because exceptions (*apavāda*) occur in the same domain as the general rules (*utsarga*). And we do not even know this: that exceptions occur in the same domain as the general rules.
Furthermore, from what [source] do we know that these two also are included here, and not rather the preceding ones or the subsequent ones?
In that case, [the author] will state the purpose of employing the letter *ca* in the rule *ā ca tvāt*: "There is also a combination with *nañ* and *snañ*.
(Pāṇini 5.1.119). Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the term *tasya bhāvaḥ* to unintended meanings such as intention (*abhiprāya*) and the like.
If it were defined as "the state of that," there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to cases such as intention (*abhiprāya*). This [undesirable consequence] would apply here as well:

"Devadatta’s intention regarding sweetmeats and food"; "those things which are our states (*bhāva*) are our sons"; and "they act by means of their sons. However, the rule is established as follows: when a word is applied to a substance (*dravya*) on account of the presence of a certain quality (*guṇa*), the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used to denote that very quality.

This is established. How so? When a word is applied to a substance because of the presence of a certain quality, then when that quality is to be expressed, there must be a suffix. However, the word *devadatta* does not apply to the substance because of the presence of intentions (*abhiprāya*) and so forth. What, then, is substance? And what are qualities? Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the qualities. Therefore—

Is the substance different [from its qualities], or is it not different from sound and the other qualities? By applying the term "substance" to that which possesses the state of being a quality, he makes known that the substance is different from sound and the others. Yet the substance is not different from sound and the others; for nothing else is perceived. Indeed, even when an animal has been dissected, [its parts] are found within the hundred-fold mass of leaves...
When something is placed [on a scale], nothing other than sound and so forth is perceived. Yet there is a substance distinct from sound and the rest, which is accessible through inference.
For example, the growth and decay of medicinal herbs and trees, and the motion of the luminaries. What is this inference?
In this world, when the height and circumference are equal, the weight of iron on one end of the scale is different from that of cotton.

That which produces a distinction is substance (*dravya*). For instance, one person cuts while merely touching, whereas another does not cut even though hanging [over the object]. That which produces this distinction is substance. One person brings about completion with a single blow, while another does not do so even with two. That which produces this distinction is substance. Or rather, that of which...
Even when other qualities (*guṇa*) appear, that reality (*tattva*) is not destroyed; that is substance (*dravya*). What, then, is reality?

Reality is its state of being (*tadbhāva*). For example, although qualities such as redness or yellowness manifest in fruits such as the *āmalaka*, they remain simply "the *āmalaka*" or "the *badara*. Indeed, the etymological definition is consistent with the actual meaning.

[Objection: "A substance (*dravya*) is a collection of qualities (*guṇasandrāva*). [Response: If, then, suffixes are produced after a word ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīsamartha*) in the sense of a quality (*guṇa*), what is the purpose of this rule? It would suffice to say simply: "after a word ending in the genitive case, in the sense of a quality. If only "after a word ending in the genitive case, in the sense of a quality" were stated, then [the form] *dviguṇā rajjuḥ* ("a two-fold rope") [would not be accounted for].

In this case as well, it would follow that the word *guṇa* means "cord" (*rajjū*). This is not a fault. This word *guṇa* has many meanings. It indeed occurs in the sense of equal constituent parts (*avayava*), as for example: "a two-fold cord," "a three-fold cord.
It also has the meaning of a substance (*dravyapadārthaka*), as for example when it is said, "this region is rich in *guṇas*," meaning in which there are cattle and crops.

And it occurs [in various senses]. It occurs in the sense of being non-primary (*aprādhānya*). For example, when someone is not the primary agent in a matter, he says, "We are subordinate here. It occurs in the sense of conduct (*ācāra*). For example, one who performs correct conduct is called "this Brāhmaṇa is virtuous" (*guṇavān*). It occurs in the sense of refinement (*saṃskāra*). For example, "refined" (*saṃskṛta*).
It is said that "food possesses qualities" (*guṇavat*). Alternatively, this word *guṇa* is used everywhere to refer to equal constituent parts.

For example, it is said, "the study is twofold" (*dviguṇam adhyayanam*) or "the study is threefold" (*triguṇam adhyayanam*). This occurs in relation to the qualities of *carcā* (repetition) and the qualities of *krama* (step-by-step recitation), and not in relation to the qualities of *saṃhitā* (continuous junction) and the qualities of *carcā*. If food is thus possessed of qualities...

Thus, the term "accessory" (*guṇa*) is not appropriate. For the soup and other such items are not necessarily equal to the rice as accessories; equality does not consist solely of identity of color or quantity. Rather, it must also be by way of propriety (*yukti*). Therefore, it is also by way of propriety: for if one were to throw a *prastha* of salt into a *prastha* of mung beans, that would not be proper.

If, first of all, *anna* is derived from the root *ad* ("to eat"), then that which is eaten would not be *anna*. If, on the other hand, it is derived from the root *an* ("to breathe"), then one would not breathe after having eaten. In that case, however, since there is no substrate (*vartin*) for words such as *śukla*, the application (*vṛtti*) [of the suffixes] would not be possible in forms such as *śuklatva* and *śuklatā*. Furthermore, what is the reason that only words like *śukla* are cited as examples and not words like *vṛkṣa* as well? [The answer is: *vṛkṣatva* and *vṛkṣatā*.

Thus it is said. There is a distinction here: for these words denote both; they express both substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*). Since they are expressive of substance, the compound formation (*vṛtti*) will take place. But then these [words] also denote both. How so? The elision of the possessive suffix *matup* is commenced by the rule "there is elision (*luk*) of *matup* after words expressive of qualities. Since they are expressive of substance, the compound formation will take place.

In that case, since there is no substratum (vartin) in words such as *ḍittha*, the occurrence [of the suffixes] would not be possible; for instance, in *ḍitthatva*, *ḍitthatā*, and *ḍāmbhiṭṭatva*. To this it is replied:

even here, there is some primary person named *ḍittha* or *ḍāmbhiṭṭa*. Whoever performs an action or a quality performed by him is called "your *ḍitthatva*" or "your *ḍāmbhiṭṭatva*. Thus, the occurrence is established.

Thus do those named *Ḍittha* act; thus do those named *Ḍāmbhiṭṭa* act. In that case, for a person who was a *Ḍittha* or a *Ḍāmbhiṭṭa* at the very beginning of time (*prāthamakalpika*), since there is no prior mode of subsistence (*vṛtti*), the formation of a compound would not be possible. This is not a fault. Just as his usage [of the name] occurs somehow or other, so too will the compound formation occur. Or rather, all entities exist by their own inherent nature (*svena bhāvena*).
They exist; that is their state (*bhāva*), and [the suffixes] occur when there is the expression of that. What is accomplished by these three mentions of *bhāva*?
By one [mention], the word (*śabda*) is indicated; by two, the meaning (*artha*). Or rather, all words "exist" (*bhavanti*) by means of their own meaning;
that is their meaning, and thus the suffixes *tva* and *tal* occur when there is the expression of that.

It should be stated as "bhavataḥ. It does not occur otherwise. For in the case of the expression *na hi tena raktam rāgāt*, suffixes do not arise with respect to the word *rakta*; because it is impossible for them to apply to the word, they will apply to the object (*artha*) colored by passion. In that case, one of the two [options] must be adopted, and the Sūtra would be split. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. But is this not so?

And it has been stated that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of the suffix] to "intention" (*abhiprāya*) and so forth, because [the suffix] denotes "the state of that" (*tasya bhāvaḥ*). Or rather, it has been said: what was said?
That "because of non-expression" (*anabhidhānāt*). Because of non-expression, the production [of the suffix] will not occur in the case of intention and so forth.
(Pāṇini 5.1.119.3) KA_II.368.5–369.2 Ro_IV.93–95: A *nañ*-compound with the suffixes *tva* and *tal* is prescribed as a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣiddham*).

[The rule] "tvataloḥ" is for the sake of establishing the correct accentuation of the suffixes *tva* and *tal*. A negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) occurs with the suffixes *tva* and *tal* by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). What is the purpose? For the sake of establishing the correct accentuation of *tva* and *tal*, so that the accentuation of *tva* and *tal* may be properly established. The scope (*avakāśa*) of *tva* and *tal* is the expression of a state (*bhāva*) and the non-expression of a negation; [examples are] *brāhmaṇatvam* and *brāhmaṇatā*.

The scope for a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) is the expression of a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) without the expression of a positive state (*bhāva*). For example: *abrāhmaṇaḥ* (non-Brahmin), *avṛṣalaḥ* (non-Śūdra). When both [the prohibition and the state] are expressed, both would apply: *abrāhmaṇatvam* (the state of being a non-Brahmin) and *abrāhmaṇatā* (the state of being a non-Śūdra). The negative compound occurs by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). [Objection: Then that prior counter-exception must be stated. [Response: It need not be stated; it is not necessary here.

The suffixes *tva* and *tal* would apply. What is the reason? Because of a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*). How is there a lack of competency? [Because] "that which is dependent is incompetent. To what extent does the word *brāhmaṇa* depend on a negation? In that case, even the *nañ*-compound would not be possible.
What is the reason? Precisely because of a lack of semantic competency. How is there a lack of competency? [Because] "that which is dependent is incompetent."

It occurs because the word *brāhmaṇa* requires a state (*bhāva*). In that case, the word *brāhmaṇa* is the primary element; and a compound is indeed formed even when the primary element is dependent. However, this is the purpose: he will state that "other words expressing a state, other than those with the negative particle *nañ*, serve the purpose of [preserving] the accent and the vowel-lengthening of the subsequent member. In that context, it is for the sake of establishing a fixed rule.
This must be stated: "Or in the Vedic language" (*vā chandasi*). In the Vedic language, a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) must be stated [as permissible]. [For example:

"The sacrificer prays for lack of virility, for the state of having no sacrificial animals, for the state of not being born from a womb, for the state of not being loose, for the state of having no cattle, and for the state of having no offspring.

This would be a suitable example: "for the state of not being born from a womb" and "for the state of not being loose. But this [example], "for the state of having no sacrificial animals," is inappropriate.

Thus [it is said]. For he does not desire the state of being a compound (*samāsa-bhāva*). What then? He desires the absence of the final member (*uttara-pada-abhāva*), meaning "not the state of the animal" (*na paśor bhāvaḥ*).

A word expressing a state (*bhāva-vacana*) other than a *nañ*-compound exists; by way of a counter-exception (*vipratiṣedha*), there is a word expressing a state other than a *nañ*-compound. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of the accent (*svara*) and for the sake of the vowel-lengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the final member. That is, for the sake of the accent and for the sake of the vowel-lengthening of the final member.

And [the particle *ca*]. First, for the sake of accent: *aprathimā*, *amradimā*. For the sake of the vṛddhi of the second member: *aśauklyam*, *akārṣṇyam*. (Pāṇini 5.1.120) KA_II.369.4–16 Ro_IV.95–97. What is the purpose of the particle *ca*? It is for the purpose of attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*). The suffixes *tva* and *tal* are attracted [from the previous rule]. This is not a valid purpose, because *tva* and *tal* will follow from the original context (*prakṛti*). Therefore, the following [is stated]:

[The author] recites: "And up to *tv-*. The inclusion of the letter *ca* in the expression *ā ca tvāt* is for the purpose of allowing co-occurrence with exceptions (*apavāda*). The inclusion of the letter *ca* in *ā ca tvāt* is made so that there may be co-occurrence with exceptions such as *imanij* and others.
This is not necessary; by the expression *ā tvāt* alone, co-occurrence with exceptions such as *imanij* and others [is already established]."

It will be so. Well then, this is the purpose: so that *tv* and *tal* may occur from those bases (*prakṛti*) up to [the end of] *ā*, as well as from that [specific base] from which they are prescribed. This too is not a purpose. For by the rule "up to *ā*" (*ā tvāt*), *tv* and *tal* will occur from whatever bases [are included], and they will occur from that [specific base] from which they are prescribed. Well then, this is the purpose: those [bases] up to *ā*...

The purpose [of the rule] is that the suffixes *tva* and *tal* should apply to those meanings where they are prescribed. But even this is not a valid purpose; for by the rule *ā tvāt* itself, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* will apply to those meanings up to the limit of *ātvāt*, and they will be prescribed wherever they are required. In that case, this is the purpose: so that the suffixes *tva* and *tal* may apply from those bases (*prakṛti*) which fall within the scope of *ā tvāt*. From whichever base—be it a feminine ending in *ī* or *ū*, or one ending in *an*, *as*, or *tṛc*—the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are desired, they should apply from that very base. Otherwise, if the suffixes were applied only to the meaning of "femininity" (*strītva*), then from a base such as *kārīṣagandhyā*, the form *kārīṣagandhyātva* would result, whereas the intended form is *kārīṣagandhyātvam*. Similarly, from *sraughnī*, the form *sraughnyātva* would result, whereas the intended form is *sraughnyātvam*. Likewise, from *aupagavī*, the form *aupagavyātva* would result, whereas the intended form is *aupagavyātvam*. Therefore, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* must apply from the bases themselves. Furthermore, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* should apply to the meanings of "being a son" (*putratva*) and "being a grandson" (*pautratva*). If the suffixes were applied only to the meaning of "son," then from the word *putra*, the form *putratva* would result, whereas the intended form is *putratvam*. Similarly, from *pautra*, the form *pautratva* would result, whereas the intended form is *pautratvam*. Thus, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* must apply to those meanings. This is the purpose. And because of this [extension], another suffix arises for a specific quality that does not belong to the base form (*prakṛti*). What is thereby accomplished? It is stated that there should be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) of the suffixes *tva* and *tal* after the words "woman" (*strī*) and "man" (*pums*). That need not be stated. (P. 5.1.121) [Question: Of what is this a prohibition? [Answer: He says it is a prohibition of *tva* and *tal*. [Objection: This is not a purpose [for the rule]. For [the suffixes] are desired after a *tatpuruṣa* compound preceded by the negative particle *nañ*.
Regarding the suffixes *tva* and *tal*: [the forms] *abrāhmaṇatvam* and *abrāhmaṇatā*. To this, he recites the subsequent [sūtra]: "Not after that which is preceded by the negative particle *nañ*.

This is a prohibition of the subsequent [suffix]. That is to say, a prohibition is made regarding the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) following that which is preceded by the negative particle *nañ*. Not.

This is the purpose: the suffix denoting abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) is prescribed after enumerated base-stems (*prakṛti*), and no base-stem preceded by the negative particle *nañ* is included therein. [However,] it would apply there by means of the rule of extension to what ends with that (*tadantavidhi*). The extension to what ends with [a specific element] is prohibited when the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is accompanied by a marker of inclusion. Where, then, does the extension to what ends with [a specific element] exist? It exists in cases such as *patyantapurohitādibhyaḥ*.

Regarding the suffix *yak*: if this were the only purpose [of the rule], he would have stated it right there, saying: "The suffix *yak* occurs after a *tatpuruṣa* compound preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, provided it ends in a primary derivative (*apatya*). If that is the case, then the Teacher indicates that a subsequent abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) occurs after a *bahuvrīhi* compound preceded by *nañ*. But this is not desired; rather, only the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are desired.
"Non-existent are the broad ones of this [man]; he is not broad (apṛthuḥ).

The state of being not broad is 'apṛthutvam' or 'apṛthutā'. If that were the case, it would imply that the teacher teaches: "A subsequent abstract suffix occurs after a *tatpuruṣa* compound whose prior member is different [from the one currently under discussion]. This is not desired;
rather, only the suffixes *-tva* and *-tal* are desired.

*Paramaḥ pṛthuḥ* means "extremely broad"; *paramapṛthoḥ bhāvaḥ* is "the state of being extremely broad," namely *paramapṛthutvam* or *paramapṛthutā*. If this is so, then it indicates that the subsequent abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) occurs after a compound that is dependent [on another word]. What is the purpose of this indication? [It serves to explain the formation of] a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*).

It was stated that another [sūtra] containing the word *bhāva* is for the purpose of causing vṛddhi in the initial vowel of the subsequent member; that is now rendered consistent. However, even this does not serve as a purpose. The activity of the Teacher indicates that all these taddhita suffixes occur after a word that is dependent on something else, since he states: "When there is a negation of a quality (*guṇa-pratiṣedha*), the taddhita suffixes having the senses of 'accomplished' (*sampādya*), 'worthy' (*arha*), 'beneficial' (*hita*), and 'capable' (*alam*) occur after the negative particle *nañ*."

(P_5,1.122) KA_II.370.14–19 Ro_IV.100–101: What is the purpose of the mention of the word *vā* ("or")? So that a sentence (*vākya*) may also occur. This is not a valid purpose, because the Great Option (*mahāvibhāṣā*) is in force; by means of it, a sentence will also occur. Then this is the purpose: so that the suffixes *tva* and *tal* may also occur. This too is not a valid purpose.

Since [the suffixes] *tva* and *tal* would also occur by virtue of this very effort [of the rule], he recites the following: "The option regarding the *pṛthu*-class is for the purpose of allowing the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) with the suffix *aṇ*. The option regarding the *pṛthu*-class is prescribed so that there may be co-occurrence with the suffix *aṇ*: *pārthavaṃ* (derived from *pṛthu*) and *prathimā* (derived from *pṛthu*)."

(P_5,1.124) An addition should be made regarding the words *cāturvarṇya* and so forth in the list beginning with *brāhmaṇa*. An addition must be made for *cāturvarṇya* and the others in the *brāhmaṇa*-group [of Pāṇini 5.1.124]: *cāturvarṇyam*, *cāturvaidyam*, *cāturāśramyam*. Regarding the word *arhat*, the suffix *num* and also the suffix *ṣyañ* should be stated: the state (*bhāva*) of an *arhat* is *ārhantyam* or *ārhatī*.

(P_5.1.125) KA_II.371.4–6 Ro_IV.101–102: Is this [reference] to the letter *n* in the rule for its elision (*nalopa*) a reference to a single phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*), or rather a reference to the entire cluster (*saṅghātagrahaṇa*)? And what follows from this? If it is a reference to the phoneme, then in the case of *steya*, once the elision of *n* has occurred, the substitution of *ay* would apply. If, on the other hand, it is a reference to the cluster, why does the elision not occur for the final [element of that cluster]? [The answer is: The elision of the final [element] is already established by the rule *yasya*.

Thus it is. In that case, by the force of the initial statement, it will apply to all. (Pāṇini 5.1.130) In the section on *aṇ* suffixes, [the addition of] "śrotriya" must be supplied; and there is the elision of the *gha* suffix. The state of being a *śrotriya* is *śrautra*.

(P_5.2.4) KA_II.372.2-21 Ro_IV.103-105: *tilādibhyaḥ khañ ca*. It should be stated: "The suffix *khañ* [is applied] after *tila* and others. Examples: *tilyam*, *tailīnam*. Why is this stated? Is it not already established by the rule: "The suffix *khañ* is applied after names of grains when the sense is 'a field where they grow' (*dhānyānām bhavane kṣetre*)"? It is not so established. What is the reason? Because *umā* and *bhaṅgā* are not considered grains (*adhānyatvāt*).

The suffix *khañ* is prescribed for a field that is the place of production (*bhavana*) of grains. However, [the word] *umābhaṅga* does not denote a grain. Only that which is recited among the grains is considered a grain, and these two [words] are not recited there. In that case, then, the mention of *khañ* must be made. It need not be made; the previously stated rule continues to apply. Where was it previously stated? "The suffix *khañ* is prescribed for a field that is the place of production of grains."

Thus [it is said]. If that [condition] were to follow, then for *vrīhi* and *śāli*, since there is the rule "the suffix *ḍhak* after *vrīhi* and *śāli*" and also the rule "the suffix *khañ* after *yava*, *yavaka*, and *ṣaṣṭika*," the suffix *khañ* would also apply. [Objection: The connection will be carried over: "the suffix *khañ* is used for a field where grains grow;
the suffix *ḍhak* applies to *vrīhi* and *śāli*; the suffix *khañ* is used for a field where grains grow; the suffix *yat* applies to *yava*, *yavaka*, and *ṣaṣṭika*; [this applies to] grains."

In the case of *bhavana* (a threshing floor) and *kṣetra* (a field), the suffix *khañ* occurs. [The rule] "optionally after *tila*, *māṣa*, *umā*, *bhaṅgā*, and *ṇu*" follows. The mention of *bhavana* and *kṣetra* continues; however, the mention of "of grains" (*dhānyānām*) has ceased. Alternatively, governing rules (*adhikāra*) proceed by "frog-leaps," just as frogs go by leaping from one place to another; such is the nature of these governing rules. Or else, because of the statement of something else and because the particle *ca* is not employed.

An exception (*apavāda*) to what has been introduced is understood, just as an exception applies to that which is applicable by way of a general rule (*utsarga*). Because another suffix is explicitly stated and because the particle *ca* is not used for the purpose of attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*), the two suffixes *ḍhak* and *yañ* will be exceptions that supersede the *khañ* under discussion; just as an exception becomes a superseder of that which is applicable by way of a general rule. Or rather, this is [the case].

It indicates that although grammatical rules (vidhis) do indeed follow [from a general principle], they do not come into effect merely by such following. Rather, they come into effect through deliberate effort (yatna). Alternatively, when a field is prepared for the cultivation of grains, the suffix *khañ* is already established [by the rule *dhānyānām bhavane kṣetre khañ*]. But was it not said: "It is not established"? For what reason? Because *umā* and *bhaṅgā* are not grains (*adhānya*). This is not so.

The word *doṣa* [is derived from the root] *duṣ*. *Dhānya* is from the root *dhinoti*. And these two also nourish (*dhinutaḥ*). Alternatively, there are seventeen types of grain (*dhānyāni*), including hemp (*śaṇa*).

(Pāṇini 5.2.6) What is the irregular formation (*nipātyate*) of the word *sammukha*? In the word *sammukha*, there is the elision of the final vowel of the prefix *sam*. In the word *sammukha*, the elision of the final vowel of the prefix *sam* is an irregular formation (*nipātyate*).
One who faces toward the same direction as the face is *sammukhīnaḥ*. (i.e., one who is facing.)
It is said that one should lead [the pieces] in *ayānaya*. In this regard, it is not known what *aya* is and what *anaya* is. *Aya* is clockwise; *anaya* is counter-clockwise.

That position in which the moves of the pieces (*śāra*) moving clockwise and counter-clockwise do not overlap with those of the opponents is *ayānaya*. One should lead [the pieces] in *ayānaya*; such a move is called *ayānayīna*.

(P_5.2.10) What is the irregular formation (*nipātana*) of *parovara*? *Parovara* is a statement regarding the substitution of *o* for *para*. In *parovara*, the substitution of *o* for *para* is prescribed as an irregularity. If that were so, one would expect the expression "the substitution of *au* for *para*" (*parasyautvavacanam*). This is stated according to the analogy of *śakandhu*. Alternatively, it should not be understood as "the substitution of *o* for *para*."
"It is an irregular formation (*nipātyate*). How so? "The substitution of *u* for the initial of the subsequent word-form is an irregular formation.
[In the case of] *parovarīṇaḥ*, it means one who experiences both those beyond (*parān*) and those below (*avarān*). Now, what is irregularly formed in the case of *parampara*?

It is the state of being a succession (*paramparabhāvaḥ*) of those further and further beyond (*paraparatarāṇām*). The state of being a succession of those further and further beyond is irregularly formed. [It refers to] those beyond (*parān*) and those even further beyond (*paratarān*).
And it is experienced through tradition.

(Pāṇini 5.2.12) Here, in the case of *samāṃsamīnā gauḥ*, the elision of the *sup* suffix [after the first member] would apply by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*. However, because of the statement regarding the elision of *ya* in *samāṃ samāṃ vijāyate*, it is understood that there is no elision (*aluk*). *Samām*...
Regarding the statement "she gives birth every year" (*samām samām vijāyate*), the understanding that there is no elision (*aluk*) will result from the rule concerning the elision of *ya*.

Since the Teacher prescribes the elision of *ya* here, he indicates that elision (*luk*) does not occur in this case. If it is argued that the understanding of non-elision follows from the rule for the elision of *ya* in the expression "she gives birth every year," [we reply: there is a specific prescription for the elision of the final member (*uttarapada*). This is because of the rule for the elision of *ya* in the expression "she gives birth every year."

If it is argued that there should be elision (*luk*) of [the *y*] of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), it must be stated that there is elision of the subsequent member. However, this is already established by the rule concerning the elision of the *y* of the prior member (*pūrvapada*).

How so? It must be stated that there is elision of the *y* of the prior member. Furthermore, regarding its non-occurrence, it must be stated as an optional rule (*vāvacana*) for the subsequent member. That is to say, when it does not occur, the elision of the *y* of both the prior member and the subsequent member must be stated as an option. [Thus, the form] *samām* is established.

"Samām vijāyate" means "she gives birth every year. (Pāṇini 5.2.14). What is the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) of *āgavīna*? It is derived from the word *go* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, with the suffix *kha* applied in the sense of one who performs an action until the return of that cow. That is to say, from *go* preceded by *āṅ*, with the suffix *kha* applied in the sense of one who performs an action until the return of that cow.
It is treated as a *nipātana* (irregular formation). Because of the repayment of that cow, one who performs labor is called *āgavīna*, a laborer.

(Pāṇini 5.2.20) [Question: Is it that one who is not bold (*adhṛṣṭa*) in a house (*śālā*) is *śālīna*, or that which is an improper act (*akārya*) in a well (*kūpa*) is *kaupīna*? [Answer: No, he says. Here, the elision of the latter member (*uttarapadalopa*) is to be understood. [The full forms are] *śālā-praveśanam* (entering the house) and *kūpa-apavāraṇam* (covering the well).

One who is unassailable is called *śālīna*. That which deserves descending into a well is an unworthy act; that is *kaupīna*. (Pāṇini 5.2.21) It is said: "He lives by means of a *vrāta*. What is this thing called a *vrāta*? A *vrāta* consists of groups of people of various castes, of unsettled livelihoods, who live by manual labor. Their work is called *vrāta*.
One who lives by the rites of a *vrāta* is called a *vrātīna*.

(Pāṇini 5.2.23) What is the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) of *haiyaṅgavīna*? In the sense of a name, there is the substitution of *hiyaṅgu* for *hyogodoha*; [and] in the sense of its modification, the substitution of *hiyaṅgu* for *hyogodoha* is irregularly derived as a name.

The term *viṣaye* [is used] in the sense of "in the modification thereof. For example: *hyogodohasya vikāraḥ* = *haiyaṅgavīnam* (butter made from yesterday's milk). Why is it said "*sañjñāyām*" (when it is a name)? It is so that [the suffix] does not apply here: *hyogodohasya vikāraḥ* = *udaśvit* (whey). (P. 5.2.25) It should be stated: "*mūle*" (at the root). For example: *pakṣasya mūlam* = *pakṣatiḥ* (the root of a wing).

In that case, it should be stated. It need not be stated. The word "mūle" (at the root) is understood [from the previous rule]. Where was it introduced? In the rule: "After words beginning with *pīlu* and *karṇa*, the suffixes *kuṇap* and *jāhac* are added [respectively] to denote 'its fruit' (*tasya pāka*) and 'its root' (*mūla*). If that [word *mūla*] were to follow [into this present rule], then [the suffixes] would also apply when the meaning is "fruit" (*pāka*). [Answer: The word "mūle" is understood; the word "pāke" has ceased to apply. But how can one part of two things specified in a single grammatical rule (*ekayoganirdiṣṭa*) be understood [to carry over]?

Or rather, only a portion [of the rule] would apply. Even for those elements taught within a single *yoga*, there is the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of only a portion. For example: [the suffix] *ṅīp* [is applied] after words beginning with a numeral and after words ending in *vayas*; and [it is applied] after words ending in *dāman* and *hāyana*. [In this case], "after a word beginning with a numeral" (*saṃkhyādeḥ*) is carried over (*anuvartate*), while "after a word beginning with an indeclinable" (*avyayādeḥ*) has ceased to apply (*nivṛttam*). (Pāṇini 5.2.27) In this context, the sense of "together" (*sahārtha*) would be understood from the word *nānā*. For two negations [yield an affirmative].

[The opponent asks: "Does it not convey the intended meaning that [the prefix *vi-*, etc. occurs only together with [the negative particle *nañ*]? [The author replies: This is not a fault. This is not the meaning of the suffix; rather, this is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*). By means of these two—*vi-* and *nañ*—which denote non-concomitance (*asahavācin*), the suffixes *nānāñ* are applied. In what sense? In their own sense (*svārthe*).

In what sense do *śālaja* and the others occur? The word "not" (*na*) from the preceding rule is understood here. It would be established that [the forms] *viśāle śṛṅge* and *viśaṅkaṭe śṛṅge* are correct. However, in this case, in the word *saṅkaṭam*, the sense of "conjoined" (*saṅgata*) is understood; in *prakaṭam*, the sense of "spread out" (*pragata*) is understood; and in *utkaṭam*, the sense of "risen up" (*udgata*) is understood.

"It is understood. If that is so, then [the suffixes] *śālā-j* and so forth would apply to the instrument (*sādhana*). Is this something that needs to be stated? No, indeed. How will it be understood without being stated? These suffixes are prescribed after prefixes (*upasarga*). Furthermore, prefixes are of such a nature that wherever a word expressing an action is employed, they express a particularization of that action. For where there is no...

An action is employed along with its means; therein they say that the action [is expressed]. These suffixes, being prescribed after prepositions, will apply to an action accompanied by its means. Even so, the forms *viśāle* and *śṛṅge* would be established. But this is not established: *viśālaḥ* and *viśaṅkaṭaḥ*. This too is established. How? The vowel *a* is a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*). [Thus, *viśāla-* means] "possessing width."
He has two large [shoulders]; he has two broad [shoulders], thus "viśaṅkaṭaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.2.29).

In the section concerning the suffix *kaṭac*, there should be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the words *alābū*, *tila*, and *ūma* when "dust" (*rajas*) is to be expressed. In the section concerning *kaṭac*, an addition must be made for *alābū*, *tila*, and *ūma* when "dust" is the meaning to be conveyed.

*alābūkaṭaḥ*, *tilakaṭaḥ*, *umākaṭaḥ*. It should also be stated: "and from *bhaṅgā*"; thus, *bhaṅgākaṭaḥ*. The suffixes beginning with *goṣṭha* are to be prescribed after words denoting cattle and the like, in the sense of place and so forth; that is, the suffixes beginning with *goṣṭha* are to be stated [after words] denoting cattle and the like, in the senses of place and so forth. Examples: *gogoṣṭham* (a cow-pen), *avigoṣṭham* (a sheep-pen). It should also be stated that the suffix *kaṭac* occurs [in these senses].

The suffix *kaṭa* should be stated [after *uṣṭra*] when not preceded by *avi*: *avikaṭaḥ*, *uṣṭrakaṭaḥ*. The suffix *paṭa* should also be stated: *avipaṭaḥ*, *uṣṭrapaṭaḥ*. The suffix *goyuga* should also be stated as a secondary derivative: *uṣṭragoyugam*, *kharagoyugam*. The suffix *taila* should also be stated as a secondary derivative:
*iṅgudatailam*, *sarṣapatailam*. The suffix *śākaṭa* should also be stated as a secondary derivative: *ikṣuśākaṭam*.

Regarding *mūlaśākaṭam*: it should be stated that the suffix *śākin* [is added] after *mūla*. Thus, we have *ikṣuśākinam* and *mūlaśākinam*. Alternatively, this is established through comparison (*upamāna*). This is indeed established through comparison: just as a place for cows is called a *goṣṭha*, so too is a place for camels.
It should be stated that the suffix *kaṭac* [is added]. Just as a collection of various materials is a *kaṭa*, so too is a collection of sheep.

They are joined together and not separated; and it should be stated that the suffix *paṭ* is applied. Just as a cloth (*paṭa*) is spread out, so too are the feathers (*avayaḥ*) spread out—thus it is "not a cloth" (*avipaṭaḥ*). And it should be stated that the word *goyuga* is a secondary derivative (*pratyaya*). A pair of cows is a *goyuga*. Just as it is for a cow, so it is for a camel: a pair of camels is an *uṣṭragoyugam*. And it should be stated that the word *taila* is a secondary derivative; it is a different base form (*prakṛti*).

The word *taila* occurs in the sense of a derivative (*vikāra*). By doing so, the form *tilataila* ("sesame oil") is also established. Furthermore, the suffix *śākaṭa* must be stated; and the suffix *śākina* must also be stated.
(Pāṇini 5.2.33) The suffixes *ina*, *cipiṭa*, and *ca* must be stated as well, [as in] *cikaci*.

And these substitutions for the base (*prakṛti-ādeśāḥ*) should be stated: *cikinaḥ*, *cipiṭaḥ*, *cikkaḥ*. Regarding the rule "for *klinna* [there are] *cil* and *pil*, and *la* is its suffix when meaning 'his eyes'": the two substitutions *cil* and *pil* for *klinna* should be stated, along with the suffix *la*, in the sense of "his eyes. When his eyes are moist, he is called *cillaḥ* or *pillaḥ*. Furthermore, *cul* should also be stated [as a substitute].

[Cullaḥ]. If it were stated as *asya* ("of this"), then forms such as *cille cakṣuṣī* ("two eyes that blink") and *pille cakṣuṣī* ("two eyes that squint") would not be established. Therefore, there is no purpose in including *asya*. How then are *cillaḥ* and *pillaḥ* derived? The suffix *-a* has the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). [The derivation is: "he who has blinking eyes is *cillaḥ*"; "he who has squinting eyes is *pillaḥ*."

Regarding the rule *pramāṇe*: is this the meaning of the suffix? No, "the measure" (*pramāṇa*) is not the meaning of the suffix. "In the sense of a measure" (*pramāṇe*)—this is not the meaning of the suffix. Then where do the suffixes occur? In the sense of that which possesses it (*tadvati*). Why is this so? Because of the recurrence of the word *asya* ("of this"). The word *asya* recurs. Where was it introduced? [It was introduced] in the previous rule.

Therefore, the suffix *itac* is applied to this [word] by the rule *tārakādibhya itac*. In my opinion, both the first and the second [measurements] are considered when measuring upwards: *ūrudvayasam* (reaching to the thighs), *ūrudaghnam* (reaching to the thighs). Regarding measurement, the suffix *la* should be stated: *śamaḥ*, *diṣṭiḥ*.

*vitastiḥ* (the word *vitasti* [is included]). Regarding *dvigoḥ nityam*: it should be stated that after a *dvigu* compound, the suffix *la* is obligatory. Examples: *dviśatam*, *triśatam*; *dvidiṣṭiḥ*, *tridiṣṭiḥ*; *dvivitastiḥ*, *trivitastiḥ*. For what purpose is this stated? [The answer is: He will state later that for a word ending in the suffix *śrāvin*, there is an elision (*apakarṣaḥ*) of the preceding [suffix]. Regarding the suffix *ḍaṭ* in the sense of a *stoma*: it should be stated that the suffix *ḍaṭ* occurs in the sense of a *stoma*. Example: *pañcadaśaḥ*.

The suffix *ḍini* is applied after the words *stoma*, *śat*, and *śan*. It should be stated that *ḍini* is applied after *śat* and *śan*: *triṃśinaḥ māsāḥ* ("months consisting of thirty days"), *pañcadaśinaḥ ardhamāsāḥ* ("fortnights consisting of fifteen days"). It should also be stated that it is applied after *viṃśati*: *viṃśinaḥ aṅgirasaḥ* ("the Aṅgirasas numbering twenty"). The suffix *mātrac* is applied after words denoting measure (*pramāṇa*), quantity (*parimāṇa*), and number (*saṅkhyā*) when there is uncertainty (*saṃśaya*): *śamamātram* ("perhaps a cubit"), *diṣṭimātram* ("perhaps a span"), *vitastimātram* ("perhaps a span").

*kuḍavamātram* (just a *kuḍava*), *pañcamātrāḥ* (about five), *daśamātrāḥ* (about ten). The suffixes *dvayasaC* and *mātraC* are applied diversely (*bahulam*) after a word ending in *vat* in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). It should be stated that *dvayasaC* and *mātraC* are applied diversely after a word ending in *vat* in the sense of the base itself: *tāvat* alone is *tāvaddvayasam*; *tāvanmātram*. *yāvat* alone is *yāvaddvayasam*; *yāvanmātram*. [The meaning of the suffix is the measure (*pramāṇa*).]

Because of the application of the rule "tadvati asya" [Pāṇini 5.2.94], both the first and the second [suffixes] are considered by me in the context of vertical measurement (*ūrdhvamāna*). [The suffix] *la* occurs after a word denoting a measure (*pramāṇa*). [The suffix *ḍa*] always occurs after a *dvigu* compound. [The suffix] *ḍat* occurs after a word denoting a collection (*stoma*). [The suffix] *ḍini* occurs after the suffixes *śas* and *śan*. [The suffix *kan* occurs] after a numeral following words denoting measure (*pramāṇa*), capacity (*parimāṇa*), or when there is doubt (*saṃśaya*) [Pāṇini 5.2.37–46].

(P_5,2.39.1) Why is it stated "in the case of *parimāṇa*"? Does [the term] "measure" (*pramāṇa*) not continue [from the previous rule]? If that is so, since [the desired result] is already established, the fact that the teacher makes the mention of "*parimāṇa*" indicates that "measure" (*pramāṇa*) is one thing and "dimension" (*parimāṇa*) is another. The two suffixes, *ḍāp* and *vatu*, are mentioned separately because of the distinction in their meanings.

This is not something to be established by an explanatory indicator (*jñāpaka*), namely that "one [suffix] is a different means of proof (*pramāṇa*) and another is a different measure (*parimāṇa*). The distinction in this regard has already been stated:
"so that there may be no obstruction of *mātra* and the others. By doing so, there is no obstruction of *mātra* and the other suffixes.

Furthermore, the formation of abstract nouns (*bhāva*) from those ending in *ḍāp* and *ḍāv* is established; thus, the formation of abstract nouns such as *mātraj* and the like from bases ending in *ḍāp* and *ḍāv* becomes established.

In the section on the suffix *vatup*, there should be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when expressing similarity in the Vedic language (*chandas*). An addition must be made in the section on *vatup* for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* in the Vedic language when expressing similarity: "No other [being] like you has been born, nor will be born, whether divine or earthly"—that is, *tvavat*.
"O Purūvasu! [Accept] the sacrifice of the inspired singer (vipra), of one like me, of one like you.

[The dual ending -au is mentioned separately because of the distinction in meaning; it is for the sake of not obstructing the measure (mātrā) and so forth. The state of being [the dual ending] is established by the two forms -au. (Pāṇini 5.2.40). By what is the substitution of *gh* for *v* in the suffix *vatup* ordained after the words *kim* and *idam*?

It is said: the Teacher indicates this very point by means of the rule *kim-idam-bhyāṃ vatup*, since he teaches that the *va* of the suffix *vatup* following *kim* and *idam* becomes *gh*. Alternatively, a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: first, *kim-idam-bhyāṃ vatup* [the suffix *vatup* occurs after *kim* and *idam*];
then, *vaḥ ghaḥ* [and the *va* of this [suffix] becomes *gh*]. Thus, the *va* of this [suffix] becomes *gh*.

It should be stated that [the rule applies] when there are many. Let it not apply here: *kiyān* (how much?), *kiyanto* (how many?). Then it must be stated? It need not be stated. Why? Because this [word *kiyat*] functions in the sense of inquiry (*paripraśna*), and inquiry occurs regarding what is not yet known; and what is not yet known pertains to many things. However, in the case of two or one, it is already known. Because it is already known.

A cross-questioning (*paripraśna*) does not occur between two [entities] or one. Due to the absence of such a cross-questioning, how could there even be [the notion of] "one," let alone a derivative suffix (*pratyaya*)?

(Pāṇini 5.2.42) Why does it not occur here: *bahavaḥ avayavā asyāḥ saṅkhyāyāḥ* ("there are many parts of this number")? It is said that [the suffix applies] to the number which belongs to the part; however, no such number exists at all.

That [word] of which "many" (*bahu*) is a constituent part. But is this not already the word "number" (*saṃkhyā*) itself? This is not a number; it is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*). When there is a prescription regarding a constituent part, the suffix is applied to the whole (*avayavin*). It should be stated: "When there is a prescription regarding a constituent part, the suffix occurs with reference to the whole. Let it not be so in cases such as "five parts" or "ten parts. Now, regarding the whole...

When it is stated thus, why does [the suffix] not occur in the case of the owner of the parts, as in "five limbs of Devadatta"? This word *avayava* (limb/part) is a quality-word (*guṇa-śabda*) and functions with the sense of "belonging to this. Therefore, the suffix must occur in relation to that whole (*avayavin*) for whom the part is a subordinate quality (*guṇa*). And in relation to what is the part a subordinate quality? In relation to the aggregate (*samudāya*).
If this is so, then one should not even say "in the whole" (*avayavini*). Why does it not occur in the parts (*avayaveṣu*)? [The word] *asya* ("of this") is understood from the previous rule.

(Pāṇini 5.2.44) For what purpose is it stated that [the suffix] is *udātta*? So that it may be *udātta*. This is not a necessary purpose, for this accent is already established by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). It is not established.

If it were stated that "the *cita* suffix is acute (*udātta*) at the end," then the property of being acute at the end would result [for all *cita* suffixes]. Now, if it is simply stated that "it is acute," how is it determined that this acuteness belongs to the beginning and not rather to the end? It will belong to that for which the accent has not otherwise been prescribed, by virtue of the force of the explicit mention of "acute. And for what is it not prescribed? For the beginning; but for the end, it is already prescribed.
It is established by the very mention of *citsvara*.

Why does it not apply here: "In this hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*, eleven *māṣas* are additional"? [The rule applies] when the additional element belongs to the same class (*samānajāti*); it is desired that the additional element belong to the same class.

Now, why does it not occur here: "There are eleven *kārṣāpaṇas* in addition to this thirty *kārṣāpaṇas*"? [The rule] is intended for the case of "hundred" (*śata*) and "thousand" (*sahasra*). It is desired that [the suffix] occurs when there is an addition to a hundred or a thousand. But in the case of "eleven hundred-thousands," to what addition should it apply? In my opinion, the suffix *ḍa* should be applied to the addition of that which possesses the number.

If, first of all, hundreds are being counted, there ought to be an excess of hundreds; if thousands are being counted, there ought to be an excess of thousands. In the rule for the suffix *ḍa*, because there is no locus for the excess of words denoting measure (*parimāṇa*), there is no specification [of such an excess]. In the rule for the suffix *ḍa*, because there is no locus for the excess of words denoting measure, there is no specification; it is non-informative.

It is a designation (*nirdeśa*), not a non-designation (*anirdeśa*). For it is not the case that one hundred is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of eleven. But this is established by the designation of the ablative (*pañcamī*). This is established. How? By the designation of the ablative. The designation of the ablative must be made: "that is more than this. Well then, that designation of the ablative must be made. It need not be made. Even so—

Since [the sense of] "possible" (*sambhava*) does not exist in either a pervasive (*vyāpaka*) or a subjective (*vaiṣayika*) locus, it shall be understood as a locative of contact (*aupaśleṣika*). For example:
"In this hundred, eleven *kārṣāpaṇas* are attached; thus it is 'one hundred and eleven' (*ekādaśam śatam*).
(Pāṇini 5.2.46) Why, when the word *śat* ("hundred") is mentioned, is the mention of the final element (*anta*) included? When the word *śat* is mentioned...

The mention of "the end" (*anta*) in the rule concerning the mention of an "affix" (*pratyaya*) is for the purpose of including that which begins with the element from which [the affix] is prescribed. When there is a mention of *śat*, the mention of "the end" is made; however, in the case of a mention of an "affix," the inclusion of that which begins with the element from which it is prescribed and ends with that affix does not apply here.

"One hundred and thirty-one" is also desired here; and since that cannot be established without effort, the mention of "end" (*anta*) is made. This is stated for this purpose. There is indeed a need for this. What then?
It is the mention of "number" (*saṅkhyā*). The mention of "number" must also be made, so that it does not occur here: *gotriṃśad adhikarmā*.

Regarding the rule *asmin śate* ("in this hundred"): the mention of the limit (*anta*) must also be made for *viṃśati*. This is so that it may also apply here: *ekaviṃśaṃ śatam* ("a hundred plus one"). Furthermore, because of the word *ca* ("and"), the mention of "number" (*saṅkhyā*) must also be made. This is so that it does not apply here: *goviṃśatiḥ adhikam asmin śate* ("twenty cows are in excess in this hundred").

(P_5,2.47) KA_II.381.18–382.16 Ro_IV.126–129: "In the case of comparison, when there is a possessor of qualities. It should be stated: "in the case of comparison, when there is a possessor of qualities.

What is the purpose? So that it does not apply to the qualities themselves. "Of the greater" (*bhūyasaḥ*). And it should be stated: "of the greater. What is the purpose? So that the [suffix] may arise from a number expressing a greater quantity, and not from a number expressing a smaller quantity.

[The rule] "let there be no arising" [applies]. One is "the other. It must be stated that "if one is the other. Let it not apply here: *dvau yavānām traya udaśvitaḥ* ("two of barley, three of buttermilk"). [It must be stated: "of similar things. And it must be stated: "and of similar things. Let it not apply here:
*ekaḥ yavānām adhyardha udaśvitaḥ* ("one of barley, one and a half of buttermilk"). Therefore, that [rule] is manifold.

It should be stated; it should not be stated. First, regarding what was said—that "it should be stated [the word] *guṇini*": it need not be stated. Why does it not apply to qualities (*guṇa*)? Because the term *asya* ("of this") continues to apply from the previous rule. Regarding what was said—that "it should be stated [the word] *bhūyasaḥ* (of the greater)": it need not be stated. Why does the production of a number denoting fewer [qualities] not occur?
Because it is not so expressed. As for what was said—that if there is one [of two kinds], it must be stated that it is "either one"—it need not be stated.

Why? Because it does not occur in such cases as "two of barley" (*yavānām*) and "three of buttermilk" (*udaśvitaḥ*). The case-ending indication is governed by the *tantra* (the principle of common application).
Furthermore, as for what is said—that it must be stated "and of similar things" (*samānānām ca*)—it need not be stated. Why? Because it does not occur [in those cases].

"One [measure] of barley for one and a half [measures] of whey. This is because it is not so designated. Furthermore, the suffix is seen even in the sense of that which is measured (*nimeya*). The suffix is indeed observed in the sense of that which is measured, as in "barley measured by two" (*dvimayā yavāḥ*) or "measured by three" (*trimayāḥ*). But what, then, is the measure (*nimāna*) here, and what is the thing measured (*nimeya*), since both are being abandoned? True, this is so; however, in some cases, one or the other is more prominent.

Such is the usage. For example, when there is an equal relinquishment [of value], one says "he sells grain" or "he sells barley," but no one says "he sells a kārṣāpaṇa. Alternatively, that by which something is acquired is the *nimāna* (the means of exchange), and that which is acquired is the *nimeya* (the object of exchange).

Regarding the rule *tasya pūraṇe*, there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). There is an over-extension in the application of *tasya pūraṇe*; it would apply here as well: "a jar that fills five water-pots" (*pañcānām uṣṭrikāṇām pūraṇo ghaṭaḥ*). However, this is established by the explicit statement "in the sense of filling a number" (*saṅkhyāpūraṇe*). How is this established? By the statement "in the sense of filling a number."

Thus it should be stated. Even so, [the suffix] would apply to the word *ghaṭa* (pot), for one fills that [pot] with water, which is a thing to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*). We say "in the completion of a number" (*saṃkhyāpūraṇe*), not "in the completion of a thing to be numbered" (*saṃkhyeyapūraṇe*). Or rather, it should be stated: "in that case where, by virtue of its existence, there is the state of being another number. Or else, it should be stated: "in that case where, by virtue of its existence, another number comes into operation. Even so, [this applies] in the second chapter.

[If it were so,] the eighth [offering] would follow; for a number applies to all of them because they exist. It should be stated that [the number applies] when the last has arisen and the preceding one has not yet passed away. Even so, the two offerings to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt—the eleventh and twelfth—would be designated as "this is the second" and "this is the third," and the expression "ten decads" would not be established. Furthermore, the sūtra would be contradicted. Therefore, let it remain as it was originally formulated.

"Let it be so. But was it not said that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because of the rule *tasya pūraṇe*? This has been answered by the statement that [the suffix] is established by the rule *saṅkhyāpūraṇe*. "In that case, then, the mention of *saṅkhyā* (number) must be made. No, it need not be made; the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) is carried over [from the previous rule]. Where was it introduced? In the rule *saṅkhyāyā guṇasya nimāne mayaṭ*. Thus [it is understood].

In that case, this application [of the suffix] is not being criticized. What then? It is the locus of the application that is criticized; for in this instance, the application itself does not even occur. Why? Because of the absence of the meaning of the suffix. This is not a fault, because by virtue of the explicit statement, it will be a *svārthika* (a suffix added without changing the original meaning). Alternatively, it must be stated that the arising of the subsequent number occurs in dependence upon the preceding number.

Furthermore, the subsequent enumeration must be stated as an instruction (*ādeśa*). Alternatively, this word "all" (*kṛtsna*) should be understood as being used for a lesser number, just as the word "five" is used for four. Or rather, all numbers beginning with two depend upon one another. If that were so, then in the second chapter it would follow that it is called the "eighth. This indeed occurs; for every grammatical operation (*vṛtti*) takes place outside of the meaning of the base form (*prakṛti*).

It is generally observed that [the rule] would apply in the sense of completion (*pūraṇa*). How then can there be its application? Let it be understood from the explicit statement. Let the *taddhita* suffix be applied to that number which precedes it; and the subsequent number shall likewise be properly treated as a substitute (*ādeśa*). Or rather, this word "entire" (*kṛtsna*) may apply to the preceding [number] if there is a semantic connection with the succeeding one.

And thus, by that [number], its application will be logical. Or, if all numbers beginning with "two" (dvi) function by depending upon one another, then such an operation is logical in the case of completion (*pūraṇa*). A number designating many is intended, and the "completer" (*pūraṇa*) is held to be one. Because of the distinctness of both, the branch of a tree (*vārkṣī śākhā*) is the appropriate illustration.
(P_5,2.49) Regarding the rule for *maḍādi* and others: "the mention of that which is the beginning.

In the case of *maḍādi* and others, the mention must be made of that which is placed at the beginning; it should be stated that "this is the beginning. For if it were not so stated, because of the governing context of suffixes (*pratyaya-adhikāra*), this would be understood as a suffix. What would be the fault in that? [The fault would be that] it would apply to other suffixes.

For there would be a fault regarding the accent (*svara*). Indeed, if another suffix were present, there would be a fault regarding the accent. [In the case of] *viṃśatitamaḥ*, this accent would result. However, *viṃśatitamaḥ* is what is intended. Then that [term] must be stated in such a way. It need not be so stated. The mention of *ḍaṭ* from the previous context continues. Where was it previously mentioned? In the rule: "The suffix *ḍaṭ* occurs in the sense of 'completing' that."

That which is indeed indicated in the nominative case [in the rule *nāntāt*] has its purpose fulfilled by that which is indicated in the genitive case. The word "from" (*nāntāt*), being in the ablative case, will cause the genitive case to be understood for the word "ḍaṭ," which is in the nominative case—according to the principle that "that [which is mentioned] from which [something arises] belongs to what follows.

This, however, is a rule for the introduction of an affix (*pratyayavidhi*), and in a rule for the introduction of an affix, ablative cases do not function as indicators (*prakalpikā*). This is not a rule for the introduction of an affix; rather, it is an affix that has already been prescribed.
The term *pratyaya* (suffix) and *prakṛta* (base) are carried over [from the previous rule].

(Pāṇini 5.2.51) Regarding the word *catur*, the suffixes *cha* and *yaṭ* are applied, and there is the elision of the initial syllable. It should be stated that for the word *catur*, the suffixes *cha* and *yaṭ* are applied, and the elision of the initial syllable must also be stated. Thus: *turīyam* and *turyam*.

(P_5,2.51.2) Now, for what purpose are *thaṭ* and *thuk* treated separately? Why not let everything be *thaṭ* alone, or *thuk* alone? The separate treatment of *thaṭ* and *thuk* is for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of] rules concerning word-final elements (*padāntavidhi*).
