The separate treatment of *thaṭ* and *thuk* is performed for the purpose of prohibiting rules concerning word-final elements; that is, for the sake of the rules regarding word-final elements.

And for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of rules] at the end of a word (*padānta*). First, for the purpose of the rule concerning the end of a word: "The sacrificial vessels (*pātrāṇi*) are made of *parṇa* wood; the chariot is the seventh (*saptathaḥ*). So that there may be the elision of *n* (*nalopaḥ*) by the rule "of the end of a word" (*padantasya*), [the term *apadādau* is used]. For the purpose of prohibiting [the application of rules] at the end of a word: "the sixth (*ṣaṣṭhaḥ*). So that there may not be the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*) by the rule "of the end of a word. And here, in the case of "the fourth (*caturthaḥ*)," so that there may not be the substitution of the visarga (*visarjanīya*) by the rule "of the end of a word."

(P_5,2.52) The suffixes expressing "one of many" or "one of a few" arise from a base qualified by gender. It should be stated that the suffixes expressing "one of many" or "one of a few" arise from a base qualified by gender, so that they may also occur here:
*bahvīnām pūraṇī* = *bahutithī* ("the one completing many"), *katipayānām pūraṇī* = *katipayathī* ("the one completing a few"), and *tāvatīnām pūraṇī* = *tāvatithī* ("the one completing so many").

The derivation of suffixes from a nominal stem qualified by gender for words consisting of many or several syllables is established. How so? Because when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included. Furthermore, there must be a statement regarding the masculine-like form (*puṃvadbhāva*). For example, *bahutithī*, the feminine ordinal of *bahvī*. Why is this not already established by the rule: "In the case of a *taddhita* suffix other than one beginning with *aṭ*, the feminine base becomes masculine-like"? [This is not established because the rule applies only to bases ending in *ī* or *ū*].
It is said: "of *bha*. And *bha* occurs when [a suffix] beginning with *yaj* follows. But here we do not see anything beginning with *yaj*. What is the reason?

Because it is not preceded by [a suffix beginning with *yaj*], the *tithuk* augment does not apply. This must be considered here: should the *tithuk* augment be applied, or the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*)?
What should be done here? The masculine form, because it is subsequent. The *tithuk* is obligatory; even when the masculine form has been applied, [the *tithuk* still applies].

It applies even when [the condition] has not been performed; it applies even when the suffix *tithuk* is optional. It applies when *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment) has been applied to one thing, yet has not been applied to another. And a rule that applies to a different word is considered non-eternal (*anitya*). In that case, *tithuk* is *antaraṅga* (inherently internal). What is its *antaraṅga* nature? *Tithuk* is prescribed in conjunction with the very arising [of the suffix], whereas the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) exist once the suffix has already arisen.

The substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is based on this [rule]. The substitution of the masculine form is also *antaraṅga*. How so? This has been stated: "And [the rule] is established when the suffix is prescribed. Between these two *antaraṅga* operations, the substitution of the masculine form occurs because it is subsequent. Once the substitution of the masculine form has been performed, the suffix *tithuk* is established by the principle of "reapplication" (*punaḥprasaṅga-vijñāna*): thus we have *bahutithī*.

(P_5,2.58) Why is it stated "not beginning with a numeral" (*asaṅkhyādeḥ*)? So that it does not apply here: *ekaṣaṣṭaḥ* ("the sixty-first"), *dviṣaṣṭaḥ* ("the sixty-second"). It could have been said without the phrase "not beginning with a numeral. Why would [the suffix] not occur in *ekaṣaṣṭaḥ* and *dviṣaṣṭaḥ*? Because the suffix is prescribed after the word *ṣaṣṭi* ("sixty"). What possibility is there for it to occur after the word *ekaṣaṣṭi* ("sixty-one")?

It would not apply at all; there would be no purpose for the prohibition. [The rule] applies by means of the *tadantavidhi* (the rule that a grammatical operation applies to that which ends with the specified element).

However, the *tadantavidhi* is prohibited when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is accompanied by a suffix that itself possesses a specific marker (*grahaṇavat*). If this is so, then the Teacher indicates that in this case the *tadantavidhi* does indeed apply. What is the purpose of this indication? [The form] *ekaviṃśatitamaḥ* (the twenty-first) is thereby established.

(P_5,2.59) KA_II.385.22–386.14 Ro_IV.137–140: In the section concerning *cha*, it should be stated that [the suffix] occurs even after a multi-word compound: "In the section concerning *cha*, it should be stated that it occurs even after a multi-word compound," so that it may apply here as well in forms such as *asyavāmīyam* and *kayāśubhīyam*. But what is the reason that it is not established? Because they are not nominal stems (*aprātipadikatvāt*). It is, however, established through their being understood as nominal stems (*prātipadikavijñānāt*).

This is established. How? From the recognition of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). How is there recognition of the nominal stem? Because of the rule: "The form itself of a word [is the referent], except when it is a technical grammatical term. Thus, the meaning of this [word] is that very word *asyavāma* which is recited in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). But what, then...

These words of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) are different from others. He says, "Om. Why is this so? Because the nature of the words of the sacred tradition is distinct, being restricted by their accents, phonemes, sequence, place, and time. In the sacred tradition, the accent of the word *asyavāma* is fixed; indeed, the sequence of its phonemes is also fixed in the sacred tradition; and the place [of recitation] is also fixed in the sacred tradition—at the cremation ground.

"One should not study [at certain places]: 'One should not study at a crossroads. Indeed, time is also restricted by tradition: "Not on the new moon day, nor on the fourteenth day. And because we observe the elision of case-endings (*sup*) from parts of words. Indeed, parts of words with elided case-endings are observed in the tradition, such as *asyavāmīyam*. But surely this would be a case of the elision of a case-ending? Yes, because we observe the elision of case-endings; it is an elision of a case-ending.

Indeed, it is also seen [in usage], as in "asyavāmīyam. If, then, these words denoting possession (*matvartha*) are different from other Vedic (*āmnāya*) words, it would not be logical [to say] that the word *asyavāma* exists in this [text]. A name (*saṃjñā*) does not deviate from the thing named (*saṃjñin*). (Pāṇini 5.2.60) Alternatively, there should be an elision (*luk*) after the words *adhyāya* and *anuvāka*. An elision should be stated [after these]: *stambhaḥ*, *stambhīyaḥ*; *gardabhāṇḍaḥ*.
*gardabhāṇḍīyaḥ*, *anukaḥ*, *anukīyaḥ*. (Pāṇini 5.2.65) Regarding the rule for *dhana* and *hiraṇya*:

it should be stated that [the suffixes apply] when desire (*kāma*) is expressed. For if they were applied in the sense of the genitive case, an undesirable result would follow. Indeed, if they were to occur in the sense of the genitive...

[An objection: One incurs an undesirable consequence: [the word *dhana-kāma* would mean] "one who has desire for wealth. [Response: Then that must be stated. [Objection: It need not be stated. Why does [the meaning] "one who has desire for wealth" not occur? [Response: Because it is not so expressed (*anabhidhānāt*).
(Pāṇini 5.2.72) Is one who produces cold called *śītaka*, or one who produces heat?

He who acts slowly is called *uṣṇaka*. What follows from this? It would follow that the term applies even when the sun is cold (*tuṣāra*). If that is so, then a deletion of the latter member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*) must be understood here: "cold-like" is *śītam*, and "hot-like" is *uṣṇam*. One who performs tasks that ought to be done quickly only after a long time is called *śītaka*; whereas one who performs tasks that ought to be done quickly, indeed quickly, is [called *uṣṇaka*].

It is called *uṣṇaka*. (Pāṇini 5.2.73) What is derived as *adhika*? It is formed by the elision of the final member of the compound *adhyārūḍha* and the addition of the suffix *kan*. Thus, *adhyārūḍham* becomes *adhikam*. This would indeed be established for *adhyārūḍhaḥ*.

"A *droṇa* is more than a *khārī*; a *droṇa* [is] in a *khārī*"—this is established. But this is not established: "a *khārī* exceeded by a *droṇa*; a *khārī* more than a *droṇa*. For the suffix *kta* after roots meaning "to go" is prescribed in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Indeed, the suffix *kta* after roots meaning "to go" is also prescribed in the sense of the object (*karman*).

(P_5,2.75) KA_II.387.15–17 Ro_IV.142) Is it that one who seeks by the side (*pārśvena*) is a *pārśvaka*? And what follows from this? It would [incorrectly] apply to the term *rājapuruṣa* (the king’s man). If that is so, then a deletion of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*) should be understood here:
"like the side" is *pārśvam*. One who seeks those objects that ought to be sought by a straightforward means through a crooked means.

He is called *pārśvaka*. (Pāṇini 5.2.76) KA_II.387.19–388.2 Ro_IV.142: Is it that one who seeks [something] with an iron hook (*ayaḥśūla*) is *āyaḥśūlika*? What follows from this? [The term] would apply to Śivabhāgavata. If that is so, then in this case, the elision of the final member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*) is to be understood.
Like an iron spike, like an iron spike. He who seeks those matters that ought to be sought by a gentle means, but seeks them by a violent means, is called *āyaḥśūlika*.
(Pāṇini 5.2.77) [In the rule *tāvatithaṃ grahaṇaṃ*], the mention of the option (*vā*) for elision (*luk*) is redundant.

Because of the context of the *vibhāṣā* (optional rule). The statement that there is an optional elision (*luk*) for the suffix *tāvatitha* when it means "he takes [a portion]" is redundant. Why? Because of the context of the *vibhāṣā*. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* is the subject under discussion; by it, this is already established: [the form] *tāvatithena gṛhṇāti* is formed with the suffix *tāvatitha*, and there is also elision (*luk*). An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made: "there is elision (*luk*) [of the suffix] when it means 'he takes [a portion] by that many'. For example: *ṣaṣṭhena gṛhṇāti* = *ṣaṭkaḥ* ("one who takes a sixth part").
"The statement 'A chain is its bond for a young elephant' is an improper designation (*anirdeśa*). An improper designation is one that does not convey the meaning.
For a young elephant has no bond consisting of a chain; rather, it is bound by a rope provided with a chain. But [the point] is established by designating it as being like that."

"And *luk* [is also used]. This is established. How so? The designation should be made as "like that," and *luk* should be stated; for example, "binding like a chain" (*śṛṅkhalavat bandhanam*). Then, that designation "like that" must be made. It need not be made. For in this context, when something does not occur without another, that [latter] is capable of being the cause (*nimitta*) for the former. And without a chain, [the binding] does not occur.

The bond comes into operation. Alternatively, by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), the term itself will denote that which is associated with it: "the bond associated with a chain" is called "the chain-bond.

(Pāṇini 5.2.82) Regarding the sense of "mostly" (*prāye*) and when it is a name (*sañjñā*), the suffix *ini* is added after the word *vaṭaka*. The suffix *ini* should be stated [after *vaṭaka*] in the sense of "mostly" and when it is a name: *vaṭakinī paurṇamāsī* ("the full moon day on which there is mostly *vaṭaka* cakes").

(P_5,2.84) What is derived [as a nipātana]? The word *śrotriya* is used in place of the meaning of the sentence "he studies the *chandas*. That is to say, in the sense of the sentence "he studies the *chandas*," this word *śrotriya* is derived as a nipātana. Alternatively, there is the substitution of *śrotṛ* for *chandas*, and the suffix *ghan* is applied in the sense of "one who studies that. [The derivation is] from *chandas*.
Or rather, the form *śrotra* is substituted [for *chandas*], and the suffix *ghan* is applied in the sense of "one who studies that. Thus, one who studies the *Chandas* is a *śrotriya*.

(Pāṇini 5.2.85) The simultaneous application of both the suffixes *ini* and *thañ* must be specified. A simultaneous application of *ini* and *thañ* must be made so that [the suffix *thañ*] does not apply in a case such as: "One who ate today is a *śrāddhika* tomorrow. Or it has already been stated. What has been stated? That it does not occur because of non-expression (*anabhidhānāt*).

(P_5,2.91) For what purpose is the mention of *sañjñāyām* ("in the sense of a technical name")? [It is used because] something is directly witnessed by three parties: he who gives, he to whom it is given, and the witness. In all such cases, the suffix would otherwise apply. By the force of the mention of *sañjñā*, [the suffix] does not apply in the case of the creditor (*dhanika*) and the pupil (*antevāsin*).
(P_5.2.92) What is the irregularly formed word (*nipātyate*)? *Kṣetriyaḥ* is like *śrotriyaḥ*.

The word *kṣetriyaḥ* is irregularly formed just as *śrotriyaḥ* is. In the sense of the sentence "curable in another's field," this word *kṣetriyaḥ* is irregularly formed. Alternatively, [it is derived] from the sense "curable there because of another's field," whereby the syllable *para-* is elided.

And *ghac*: in the sense of "to be treated there" (*tatra cikitsyaḥ*) from the word *parakṣetra*, the elision of the final vowel (*paralopa*) is prescribed as a nipātana, and *ghac* is also applied. One who is to be treated in another's field (*parakṣetre cikitsyaḥ*) is called *kṣetriya*.
Why are both these meanings specified?

The relation "this belongs to that" is not such that whatever belongs to someone must also reside in him, nor is it the case that whatever resides in something must also belong to it. There is no necessary coexistence between these two. For Devadatta possesses cows, yet they do not reside within him; and trees exist on a mountain, yet they do not belong to it.

[They] exist. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *asti*? So that the suffix may occur when the meaning is "existence" (*sattā*). This is not a valid purpose; for a word-meaning (*padārtha*) never deviates from existence. Then this is the purpose:
so that it may occur when there is "present existence" (*sampratisattā*).
Let it not be that [the suffix] applies to the existence of past or future entities, as in:

"He had cows" (*gāvo 'syāsan*) or "He will have cows" (*gāvo 'sya bhavitāraḥ*). In that case, this would not occur now: "He was possessed of cows" (*gomān āsīt*) or "He will be possessed of cows" (*gomān bhavitā*). It does occur, but not in this specific sentence. If it were to apply in this sentence, then just as the use of the verb *as* (to be) does not occur here in expressions such as "possessed of cows" (*gomān*) or "possessed of barley" (*yavamān*), [it would likewise not occur in those past and future cases].
In this case as well, it would not be so:

[one would not say] *gomān āsīt* ("the owner of cows was") or *gomān bhavitā* ("the owner of cows will be"). Even though the verb *as-* is employed, just as here the plural form is heard—namely, *gāvaḥ asya āsan* ("his cows were") or *gāvaḥ asya bhavitāraḥ* ("his cows will be")—so too here it should be: *gomān āsīt*, *gomān bhavitā*.

[Objection: What then is the meaning of this linguistic usage: "He was possessed of cows" (*gomān āsīt*) and "He will be possessed of cows" (*gomān bhavitā*)? [Response: This is that very linguistic usage. It is not the existence (*sattā*) of the cows themselves that is being expressed here. What then? It is the existence of the possessor of cows (*gomat-sattā*) that is being expressed. In this case, there is the verb *asti* ("is") referring to the present time. [Question: How then is the existence in the past or future understood? [Response: By the rule "suffixes [denoting tense] are related to the verbal root" (*dhātu-sambandhe pratyayāḥ*).

Then this is the purpose: so that [the suffix] may occur after a word joined with *asti*, but not after a word joined with *anantara* and so forth—as in "his cows are immediate" (*gāvo 'syānantarāḥ*) or "his cows are near" (*gāvo 'sya samīpe*). Now, even when the mention of *asti* is made, why does it not occur here:
"his cows exist immediately" (*gāvo 'sya santi anantarāḥ*) or "his cows exist nearby" (*gāvo 'sya santi samīpe*)? Because of a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*).

How is there a lack of capacity? It is because that which is dependent lacks capacity. If that is so, then just as [the rules] do not apply to *anantara* and the others when the mention of *astrī* is made due to a lack of capacity, they likewise will not apply even when the mention of *astrī* is not made. There is a distinction here: when the mention of *astrī* is made, [the rule does not apply] without the employment of a third word.

The meanings [expressed by] *antarā* and so forth are understood. However, if the mention of *as* were not made, the meanings of *antarā* and so forth would be understood even without the employment of a third word. (P_5.2.94.2) KA_II.391.24–392.19 Ro_IV.153–156 Now, why does this not occur here in the case of *citraguḥ*?

"Śabalaguḥ"—this is because the possessive sense (*matvartha*) has already been expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound. Now, why does it not occur here: "citragavo 'sya santi" (he has brindled cows)? Why does it not occur? Is it because of a member [of the compound] or because of the whole?
Why does it not occur because of a member? Because of a lack of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*). How is there a lack of capacity? That which is dependent is incapable [of forming a compound].
"It occurs. [Objection: Why then does it not occur from the whole aggregate? [Response: Because it is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadikatvāt*). [Objection:

But surely, sir, grammatical rules operate with reference to the general form (*ākṛti*). For example, while the rule *sup supā* ("a case-ending with a case-ending") is in force, a compound occurs between one word and another. [Response: This is indeed true; however, the general form is fully realized in each individual instance (*pratyekam parisamāpyate*). To whatever extent...

This [rule] concludes with the words *ṅy-āpprātipadikāt*; therefore, the suffix must arise from that much. And this rule concludes with respect to the individual member, not the whole aggregate. Now, why does it not occur here: *pañca gāvo 'sya santi* (he has five cows) → *pañcaguḥ*, *daśaguḥ*? Because there is no semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*) in each individual word, and because the aggregate is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadikatva*). [Rather, it occurs] from the compound (*samāsa*).

Because it has been stated in brief, this is not the essence [of the matter]. For even when the meaning of the suffix has been expressed, a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) arises from a *dvigu* compound;
for example, *dvaimāturaḥ* ("born of two mothers") and *pāñcanāpitiḥ* ("descendant of five Nāpitis"). This is not a *dvigu*. What then is it? It is a *bahuvrīhi*.
Since it is an exception (*apavāda*), the *dvigu* would apply. But the *bahuvrīhi* will prevail because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*). What is its internality?

The *bahuvrīhi* compound occurs when there is a meaning other than that of the constituent members (*anyapadārtha*), specifically when that distinct meaning is qualified; the *dvigu* compound occurs when that [meaning] is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) meaning. And in that context of the secondary derivative, the term "existence" (*asti*) is included. If, then, there are over-extensions (*atiprasaṅga*), the inclusion of "existence" must also be made for the *bahuvrīhi*, so that it may apply when [the word] is joined with "existent" (*asti-yukta*), but not when it is joined with words such as "immediate" (*anantara*) and so forth. Now...

Even in the rule for the derivation of secondary nominal suffixes (*taddhita*), there is no purpose in including the mention of "exists" (*asti*). This is indeed true. Nevertheless, the mention of "exists" is now made in the rule for secondary suffixes; however, even when it is included, it is for the sake of prescribing the suffix itself, not for the sake of a qualifying condition (*upādhi*). [The purpose is] so that the suffix *matup* may apply in the sense of "possessing existence" (*astimān*). And what is the reason why it would not otherwise apply? Because [the word "asti"] is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadikatvāt*).

This is not a fault. This word *asti* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). It is not the present tense (*laṭ*) of the root *as*. How is it an indeclinable? Because particles (*nipāta*) are those that resemble case-endings or accents; thus it receives the designation "particle. By the rule "a particle is an indeclinable," it receives the designation "indeclinable. Even so, it is still not established. What is the reason? Because when there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *asti*, the possessive suffix *matup* [would apply].

It is prescribed [by P. 2.4.82]. And there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the verb *as* "to be" and the noun *asti*. Therefore, even though this [rule] is being formulated for the purpose of prescribing a suffix, it is not for the purpose of a qualifier (*upādhi*). Consequently, a prohibition must be stated regarding the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) after a *dvigu* compound, if that [prohibition] does not exist; for if it did exist, the desired result would be established by that very [prohibition] in all cases where a possessive sense (*matvartha*) is intended.

Now, it might be argued that from a suffix denoting possession (*matvarthīya*), there ought to be another suffix denoting possession. But this need not be so. Why? Because the employment of words is for the purpose of conveying meaning. A word is employed with the thought, "I shall cause the meaning to be understood. Since that meaning has already been expressed by one [suffix], there is no purpose for the employment of a second.
It should not be so. What is the reason? Because "that which has already expressed its meaning is not employed [again]. If that is so, then this would not occur now:
*daṇḍimatī śālā* ("a hall possessing staffs") or *hastimatī upapadyakā* ("a courtyard possessing elephants"). Yet it does occur. This is because there is a shift from one meaning to another meaning;
or rather, what was used in the sense of the genitive case occurs in the sense of the locative case, or what was used in the sense of the locative case occurs in the sense of the genitive case.
It occurs. Now, one might argue that a suffix *matup* should follow a word ending in *mat*, as in "he has *gomant*s" or "he has *yavamat*s. It should not so occur. Why?
Because for one who possesses *gomant*s, he necessarily possesses cows (*gāvaḥ*). In that case, the suffix has already been stated [by rule P. 5.2.119] in connection with the cows themselves.

If this is so, then the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix will not occur. [Objection: In that case, the following would not occur: *daṇḍimatī śālā* ("a hall possessing staffs") and *hastimatī upapādukā* ("a cave possessing elephants"). [Response: It does occur. This is because a word used in one sense is employed in another sense. Alternatively, what was used in the sense of a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of a locative (*saptamī*), or what was used in the sense of a locative is used in the sense of a genitive.

It occurs here as well: that which is used in the sense of the locative case may occur in the sense of the genitive case, or that which is used in the sense of the genitive case may occur in the sense of the locative case. Indeed, the suffix [denoting possession] when connected with "cows" (*gobhiḥ*) is of one kind, while [the suffix] when connected with "possessing them" (*tadvatā*) is of another kind. For by whatever cause this sentence "He has cows" (*gomanto 'sya santi*) arises, [by that same cause the other form arises].

Because the phrase "those who possess barley" exists, by that very reason, the formation of a derivative meaning (vṛtti) would also result. Therefore, a prohibition must be stated regarding the suffix *matup* and others used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). And while stating that, it must also be said that in a compound with a similar form (*sarūpa*), the same applies.

For indeed, one finds such forms as *daṇḍimatī śālā* ("a hall possessing staffs") and *hastimatī upapadyakā* ("a courtyard possessing elephants"). [Furthermore,] from a secondary suffix (*śaiṣika*) used in the sense of possession (*matubarthīya*), another secondary suffix may arise.

A suffix of the same form as one expressing the sense of *matup* is not desired [to apply after another such suffix]. A *san* suffix is not desired after a [verbal base] already ending in *san*. (Pāṇini 5.2.94.4) [Question:
But do these suffixes beginning with *matup* occur only after the mere existence [of a quality]?

[Answer: It ought to be so. [Objection: If suffixes beginning with *matup* occurred after the mere existence [of a quality], there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [Explanation: Suffixes beginning with *matup*...

If [the suffix were applied] to mere existence (*sanmātra*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); it would then apply here as well: *vrīhir asya* ("rice belongs to him") and *yavo 'sya* ("barley belongs to him"). Therefore, the mention of "abundance" (*bhūma*) and the other conditions must be made. What, then, are these conditions beginning with "abundance"? The suffixes such as *matup* occur in the senses of abundance (*bhūman*), censure (*nindā*), praise (*praśaṃsā*), constant connection (*nityayoga*), excellence (*atiśāyana*), association (*saṃsarga*), and when the sense of existence (*asti*) is intended to be expressed. Regarding abundance:
One who possesses cows (*gomān*), one who possesses barley (*yavamān*). In the sense of censure:
one with a hump on the back (*kakudāvartī*), one who eats from a conch-shell (*saṅkhādakī*). In the sense of praise:
one who is handsome (*rūpavān*), one who has a fair complexion (*varṇavān*). In the sense of constant connection:
Examples of trees that bear milk and trees that bear thorns. Regarding excellence: "a girl with a protruding belly. Regarding conjunction:

"One with a staff," "one with an umbrella. In that case, then, should the mention of "abundance" (*bhūman*) and so forth be made? It need not be made. Why does [the suffix] not occur in cases such as *vrīhir asya* ("rice belongs to him") or *yavo 'sya* ("barley belongs to him")? It has already been stated. What was stated? That it is due to "non-expression" (*anabhidhāna*). Furthermore, the particle *iti* is indeed employed; therefore, if there is a desire to express [the sense], it is only when there is a desire to express that which is joined with abundance and so forth, as in *gomān* ("possessing cows") or *yavamān* ("possessing barley").
Existence is predicated only of that which is possessed of abundance and the like; for there is no one for whom barley does not exist.

[The statement] "she is a *saṅkhādakī* (one who eats everything) and has a hump on her back" expresses existence only of that which is characterized by censure; for there is no one who is not a *saṅkhādakī*. [The statements] "he is handsome" (*rūpavān*) or "he is well-colored" (*varṇavān*) express existence only of that which is associated with praise; for there is no one who lacks beauty.
"Milky trees," "thorny trees"—the existence of these is spoken of only as being constantly possessed [of those qualities].
For there is no one who lacks milk [entirely]. "A girl with a protruding belly"—the existence of this is spoken of only as being characterized by an excess [of that quality].
For there is no one who lacks a belly entirely. "One with a staff," "one with an umbrella"—the existence of these is spoken of only as being joined with [those objects].

For there is no one for whom the suffix *daṇḍa* does not exist. Indeed, existence (*sattā*) is predicated of as many cows as suffice for the purposes of carrying, milking, or breeding; for some, these purposes are served by three, while for others, even a hundred do not suffice.

Furthermore, because it is seen by the seers (*ṛṣi*), [the suffix] applies to mere existence (*sanmātra*). Moreover, the seer indicates the possessive suffix *matup* in the sense of "mere existence," as in the case of *yavamatībhiḥ*.
"One sprinkles the sacrificial post with water" (*adbhir yūpaṃ prokṣati*). Regarding the elision of the suffix *matup* after words expressing qualities:

it should be stated that there is elision of *matup* after words expressing qualities, as in "white" (*śuklaḥ*) and "black" (*kṛṣṇaḥ*). This is established because there is no distinction [between the quality and the possessor of the quality]; for a quality does not [exist] apart from the possessor of the quality.

[Objection: It deviates [from the rule]. [Reply: If it is argued that [the deviation] is established because there is no non-exclusion (*avyatireka*), [we reply: exclusion (*vyatireka*) is indeed observed. Exclusion is seen, as for example in the case of "the whiteness of a cloth. And thus, the establishment of gender and number is achieved. By doing so, genders and numbers are established: *śuklaṃ vastram* (a white cloth), *śuklā śāṭī* (a white garment), *śuklaḥ kambalaḥ* (a white blanket), *śuklau kambalau* (two white blankets).
"White blankets. When a quality (*guṇa*) is dependent upon a substance (*dravya*), whatever gender (*liṅga*) and number (*vacana*) that substance possesses, those same belong to the quality as well.
(Pāṇini 5.2.95) Why is this stated? [Is it not already established by] *tat asya asti* (5.2.94) and *asmin* (5.2.94)?

Thus, the suffix *matup* is already established [by Pāṇini 5.2.94]. However, the repetition of the rule for *rasa* and so forth is for the purpose of excluding others. The repetition of the rule for *rasa* and so forth is made to prohibit other possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*), so that only *matup* may apply. [The intention is: "Let those other possessive suffixes which would otherwise apply not occur. This is not a valid purpose, for [other suffixes] are seen [to occur].

For other [suffixes] than those expressing "possessing" (*matvarthīya*) are used after words such as *rasa* and others: e.g., *rasikaḥ naṭaḥ* ("the actor possesses taste"), *urvaśī vai rūpiṇī apsarasām* ("Urvaśī is indeed the most beautiful among the Apsarases"), and *sparśikaḥ vāyuḥ* ("the wind possesses touch"). Why does [the suffix] not occur here? [In the following examples: (P_5.2.96) KA_II.395.2-4 Ro_IV.163 iha kasmāt na bhavati: [Why does it not occur in these cases?]

"He has the desire to act" (*cikīrṣā asya asti*), "he has the desire to take" (*jihīrṣā asya asti*). It should be stated that [the suffix applies] after a word denoting a limb of a living being (*prāṇyaṅgāt*). Then it must indeed be stated. No, it need not be stated. Why does it not apply in the case of: "He has the desire to act" (*cikīrṣā asya asti*)?

"He has the desire to take" (*jihīrṣā asya asti*). Because [the suffix *lac*] is not prescribed [in this case]. (Pāṇini 5.2.97). Regarding those words in the *sidhma*-group that end in short *a*, when the suffix *lac* is excluded, the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* would apply; however, *ini* and *ṭhan* are not desired here. The phrase "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) indicates a conjunction with *lac*.

The rule *lac anyatarasyām* is a conjunction (*samuccaya*), not an option (*vibhāṣā*). That is to say, both *lac* and *matup* [are applied]. How, then, is it known that *lac anyatarasyām* is a conjunction and not an option? The fact that *tunda* and the others are joined with *piccha* and the others in separate rules is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of their non-coexistence. For this reason, he [the author] joins *tunda* and the others to *piccha* and the others.

The Teacher indicates by this separate formulation (*nānāyoga*) that this is a mandatory rule (*samuccaya*), not an optional one (*vibhāṣā*). If it were optional, the separate formulation would be purposeless; for in that case, he could have simply listed *tunda* and the others within the *piccha* group itself. This, however, is not the indicator [you suggest]. For there is indeed another purpose for the separate formulation. What is it? It is for those items in the *tunda* group that do not end in the vowel *a*.

So that the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* may apply after those [words]. But what is the purpose of the recitation of those words which already end in *a*? It is for the sake of providing an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Another says: the separate formulation of the *tunda* group from the *piccha* group is an indicator of their non-co-occurrence. In that the Teacher makes a separate formulation of the *tunda* group from the *piccha* group, he indicates that this is a mandatory combination (*samuccaya*) and not an option (*vibhāṣā*).

If it were an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*), the formation of separate rules would be purposeless; one could simply have read words such as *piccha* and others under the same group as *tuṇḍa* and so forth. This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*). For there is indeed another purpose for the formation of separate rules. What is it? It is so that the suffixes *-ini* and *-thañ* may apply after those words beginning with *piccha* that do not end in the vowel *a*. But what about those that do end in *a*?

What is the purpose of their recitation? It is solely for the sake of providing an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Furthermore, the repetition of *va* is for the sake of making it optional in all cases (*sarvavibhāṣā*).
Indeed, the repetition of *va* is made for the sake of making it optional in all cases, as in the rule: "After *keśa*, *vaḥ* is optionally [used].

By this very fact, the Teacher indicates that this is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) and not an option (*vibhāṣā*). [The repetition] after *dyu* and *dru* is for the sake of making it obligatory (*nitya*).
Some desire the inclusion of the word *anyatara* [in this rule]. How so? This rule (*yoga*) is placed in the middle of the *vibhāṣā* section;

thus, those rules which are established within the *vibhāṣā* section become obligatory (*nitya*). (Pāṇini 5.2.100) In the section on the suffix *naṅ*, there is the shortening of the vowel in *dadru*. In the section on the suffix *naṅ*...
The addition of *dadru* must be stated, as must its shortening when not in the context of [the suffix] *na*. [That is,] it should be stated that for *dadru*, there is shortening [of the vowel]:
*dadruṇaḥ*. This which is stated is too little; it should be stated: "For *śākin*, *palālin*, and *dadru*, there is shortening": *śākinam*, *palālinam*.

Regarding *dadruṇam*: [the suffix *naṅ* is applied after *viṣvañc*] with the elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*) and without the application of sandhi (*akṛtasaṃdheḥ*). An addition (*upasaṅkhyānam*) must be made for *viṣvañc*, and it should be stated that there is elision of the final member and no sandhi. [Example: *viṣvag gatāny asya* = *viṣuṇaḥ*. (Pāṇini 5.2.101) And [the suffix *naṅ* is applied] after *vṛtti*. It should be stated: "and after *vṛtti*. [Example: *vārttam*.

(Regarding Pāṇini 5.2.102–103.1) Why is the suffix *vin* prescribed after the word *tapas*, since it would already be established by the rule "after a word ending in *as*"? [The answer is: the prescription of *vin* for *tapas* is made because [otherwise] the suffix *aṇ* would be applied. The suffix *vin* is prescribed for *tapas*; however, the suffix *an* is prescribed after the word *tapas*.
That [suffix *an*], being prescribed as a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*), would supersede the *vin* prescribed as a general rule (*sāmānyavidhi*). Therefore, the suffix *vin* is prescribed.
In the section on the suffix *aṇ*, there is an addition [to the rule] regarding words such as *jyotsnā*.
An addition must be made to the section on *aṇ* for words beginning with *jyotsnā*: *jyautsnaḥ*, *tāmisraḥ*, *kauṇḍalaḥ*, *kautapaḥ*, *vaipādikaḥ*.

(P_5,2.107.1) KA_II.397.5–7 Ro_IV.167 This word *madhu* exists as denoting a substance (*dravyapadārthaka*), and it exists as denoting taste (*rasavācī*). And therefore, [it is] also [used] when denoting taste; for indeed, the expression "this honey is sweet" (*madhuram*) applies only to honey. Therefore, this is the inclusion of that which denotes taste. For if there were an inclusion of that which denotes a substance, [the rule would not apply].
In this case too, it would follow [that the suffix applies]: *madhu asmin ghaṭe asti* ("there is honey in this jar").

In the section concerning the suffix *ra*, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) should be made for the words *kha*, *mukha*, and *kuñja*: *kharaḥ*, *mukharaḥ*, *kuñjaraḥ*. It should also be stated that [the suffix applies] after *naga*:
*nagaram*.

(P_5.2.109) KA_II.397.12–20 Ro_IV.168–169: An addition [to the rule] regarding *vapa*: an addition should be stated concerning *maṇi* and *hiraṇya* within the section on *vapa*. [Examples: *maṇivaḥ*, *hiraṇyavaḥ*.
In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the suffixes *ī* and *vanip* should also be stated; that is, both *vaḥ* and *matup* [should be stated]. [Example: *mudgalanī rathīr abhūt*.
In *gaviṣṭau*. "This bride is auspicious. [The word] *ṛtavānam*. We pray to *maghavānam*. *Udvā* and *udvatī*.
*Medhārathābhyām iraniracau*: after *medhā* and *ratha*, the suffixes *iran* and *irac* should be stated. [Examples: *medhiraḥ*, *rathiraḥ*. Another says:
In the section on *vā*, it should be stated that [the suffix] is seen after other words as well: *bimbāva*, *kurarāva*, *iṣṭakāva*.
In the section on *valac*, it is seen after other words as well; it should be stated that in the section on *valac* it is seen after other words as well: *bhrātṛvalaḥ*, *putravalaḥ*, *utsaṅgavalaḥ*.

(P_5.2.115) KA_II.398.2–11 Ro_IV.169–170: A prohibition [of the suffixes] *ini* and *thañ* must be stated after a monosyllabic word. [The rule says: "A prohibition of *ini* and *thañ* after a monosyllable must be stated: *svavān*, *khavān*. This statement is too limited. [It should rather be: "After a monosyllable, after a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, after a genus (*jāti*) word, and in the locative case, those two [suffixes] are not prescribed. After a monosyllable: *svavān*, *khavān*. After a *kṛt* suffix: *kārakavān*.
Possessing a necklace; [possessing] a genus: possessing a tree, possessing a *plakṣa* tree, possessing a tiger.

[The suffix] *vān* occurs [after a word ending in the seventh case]. And in the seventh case, those two [suffixes, *ini* and *ka*,] do not occur. For instance: "In this hall there are staff-bearers" (*daṇḍā asyāṃ śālāyāṃ santi*).

If it is said that [the suffix] does not occur after a word denoting an action (*kṛta*), then forms such as *kāryī* and *kāryikaḥ* would not be established. Likewise, if it is said that [the suffix] does not occur after a word denoting a genus (*jāti*), then forms such as *tuṇḍilī* and *tuṇḍilikaḥ* would not be established. If this is so, then this is not a collective conjunction (of the conditions) "after a word denoting an action and after a word denoting a genus."
What then? The mention of *kṛt* is for the purpose of qualifying the genus (*jāti*):

[it means] "the genus that is *kṛt*. [If so, how do we derive] *kārakavān*, *hārakavān*? This will not occur because of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*). If this is the case, there is no need for this [rule]. How then [do we derive] *svavān*?
In cases such as *vṛkṣavān*,
*siṃhavān*, and *vyāghravān*— meaning "there are trees, lions, or tigers in this hall"— the suffix will not occur because there is no conventional usage (*anabhidhānāt*) for it.

The suffix *ini* should be prescribed after [the group] beginning with *śikhā*, and the suffix *ikan* after [the group] beginning with *yavakhada*. What is the purpose? For the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*). That is, *ini* alone [is used] after *śikhā* and so on, and *ikan* alone [is used] after *yavakhada* and so on.
Because the non-statement of a restriction for *śikhā*, *yavakhada*, and so on serves as a negator (*nivartaka*), there is no restriction for *śikhā*, *yavakhada*, and so on.
[The rule is] "non-expression. For what reason? Because it is a negator (*nivartaka*). What is the negator? Non-expression (*anabhidhāna*). (Pāṇini 5.2.118) [Question:

What is the purpose of including the term *nitya* ("always")? [Answer: So that there may not be an option (*vibhāṣā*). [Objection: This is not a valid purpose, because the mention of *vibhāṣā* was already ceased in the preceding rule itself. Thus...

In that case, since [the desired result] is already established, the fact that the teacher employs the term "nitya" (obligatory) indicates that the rule "vibhāṣā" (optionally) continues to apply prior to this yoga. Now, does the phrase "atha ataḥ" (from here onwards) continue to apply, or not? And what follows from this? If it does continue to apply, then "ekagavikaḥ" would not be established. [Objection: It will be established once the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is applied. [Reply: Even so, "gauśakaṭikaḥ" would not be established.

Now, [the suffix] *nivṛtta* would also apply here: "He has twenty cows" (*goviṃśatir asyāsti*). Why does it not occur in the case of "He has twenty cows" (*goviṃśatir asyāsti*)? It will not occur because of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*).
In the section on *yaP*, it is observed after other [roots] as well. It should be stated that in the section on *yaP*, it is observed after others as well: "The snowy mountains" (*himyāḥ parvatāḥ*).

The Brāhmaṇas are possessed of qualities. (Pāṇini 5.2.122). In the section concerning Vedic meters (*chandovinprakaraṇa*), there is the rule: "In the section concerning Vedic meters, there is lengthening of the vowels in the words *aṣṭṛ*, *mekhalā*, *dvaya*, *ubhaya*, *ruj*, and *hṛdaya*. Thus it is stated.

It should be stated: *aṣṭrāvī*, *mekhalāvī*, *dvayāvī*, *ubhayāvī*, *rujāvī*, *hṛdayāvī*. It should also be stated: "and after *marman*. Thus: *marmāvī*. In all cases, [the suffix] is applied to *āmaya*. An addition must be made for *āmaya* in all cases: *āmayāvī*. After *śṛṅga* and *vṛnda*, the suffix *ārakan* is applied. It should be stated that *ārakan* follows *śṛṅga* and *vṛnda*: *śṛṅgārakaḥ*.

The suffix *inan* is applied after the words *phala* and *barhas*. It should be stated that *inan* is added after *phala* and *barhas*: *phalinaḥ* (fruitful) and *barhiṇaḥ* (peacock). The suffix *cālu* is optionally applied after the word *hṛdaya*. It should be stated that *cālu* is optionally added after *hṛdaya*:

*hṛdayāluḥ*, *hṛdayī*, *hṛdayikaḥ*, and *hṛdayavān* (all meaning "sensitive" or "having a heart"). The suffix [meaning "one who does not endure"] is applied after the words *śīta*, *uṣṇa*, and *tṛpra*. [It is applied] after *śīta*, *uṣṇa*, and *tṛpra*.

The suffix *ālu* should be stated [after a word] in the sense of "not enduring that": *śītāluḥ* ("sensitive to cold"), *uṣṇāluḥ* ("sensitive to heat"), *tṛprāluḥ* ("sensitive to pain"). The suffix *celu* should be stated after the word *himāt* in the sense of "not enduring that": *himāc celuḥ*. The suffix *ūla* should be stated after the word *balāt* in the sense of "not enduring that": *balūlaḥ* ("powerful"). [The suffix *ūla* is also applied] after the word *vātāt* in the sense of a collection (*samūha*).

And: the suffix *ūla* should be stated [after the word *vāta*] in the sense of "not being able to endure that collection. *Vātūla*. Regarding the words *parvan* and *marut*, the suffix *tap* should be stated: *parvataḥ* (mountain), *maruttaḥ* (Marutta). Or alternatively, this will be understood as a derivative from the root *dā* ("to give"): Marutta is one who was given by the Maruts (*marudbhir dattaḥ*).

It should be stated that [the suffix] applies when there is contempt (*kutsita*). For one who speaks much correctly is indeed called *vāgmī* ("eloquent"). If that is so, then it must be stated. It need not be stated. By the power of forming separate rules (*nānāyoga*), it will not apply [in the case of *vāc*]. Why does it not apply here: *svam asyāsti* ("this belongs to him")?

This is not a fault. This is not the meaning of the suffix; rather, this is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*). [The word *svāmin*] is an irregular form (*nipātana*) in the sense of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). (Pāṇini 5.2.129) It should be stated that [the suffix *ṅīṣ*] also occurs after *piśāca*. *Piśācakī* refers to Vaiśravaṇa.

In the section on the suffix *ini*, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for words preceded by *bala*, *bāhu*, and *ūru*. In the section on *ini*, an addition must be made for words preceded by *bala*, *bāhu*, and *ūru*: *bāhubalī* ("strong-armed"), *ūrubalī* ("thigh-strong"). Furthermore, the suffix *ini* should be stated [to apply] after words beginning with *sarva*: *sarvadhanī* ("possessing all wealth"), *sarvabījī* ("possessing all seeds"), *sarvakeśī* ("having all one's hair").

And [the suffix] *ini* should be stated [after the word *artha*] when it means "not present" (*asannihita*). [Thus: *arthī*. Why is it said "when not present"? [To exclude: *arthavān* (possessing wealth). And it should be stated that [the suffix applies] after that which ends in this [word]. [Examples: *dhānyārthī*, *hiraṇyārthī*. Why is it stated "after that which ends in this"? Is it not already established by the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*)? [No,] because [the suffix] is applied by a term that includes its own mention (*grahaṇavatā*).

The rule regarding the inclusion of that which ends in a nominal stem (*tadantavidhi*) is prohibited by the nominal stem itself. If that is the case, then the compound will be formed with that which ends in the suffix *in*.

For example: *dhānyenārthī* ("one who desires grain"). However, that compound does not apply here. But if this were the *ṇini* suffix derived from the root *arthayati*, even so it would apply only to one who is performing an action. Even one sitting silently who [performs actions] conducive to that [desire] would [be included].

He practices; it is understood that by means of this, one attains what is to be sought (*arthyam*). If this is so, then this word *artha* certainly exists as having "substance" (*dravya*) as its referent (*padārtha*). For example, it is said, "This region is rich in resources" (*arthavān*), meaning that in it cattle and crops exist.
It also exists as having "action" (*kriyā*) as its referent, functioning as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*). [In this sense] *artha* is the act of seeking (*arthanam*). Therefore, that which...
This [term *idam*] is the inclusion of that which has the meaning of a verbal action (*kriyā*). By doing so, the terms *arthika* and *pratyarthika* are also established.

(Pāṇini 5.3.1) What is the purpose of its being a case-ending (*vibhakti*)? The purpose of its being a case-ending is the prohibition of the *it*-augment. In the word *idānīm*, the prohibition of the *it*-augment by the rule "not in a case-ending after *t* or *s*" (*na vibhaktau tusmāḥ*) becomes established.

If this is so, [the rule] "kimaḥ at" [would apply]; where would you seek to shine? Where are the half-months (*ardhamāsāḥ*)? Here too, [the substitution] would result. But those two have already been discussed. What has been said? That there is a prohibition of the *tavarga* [substitution] when a case ending (*vibhakti*) follows that is not a *taddhita* suffix. And the accent of the case ending of *idam* is also a purpose [for the rule]. The accent of the case ending of *idam* is also a motive: *itaḥ*, *iha*. [In these cases], the third case ending and those following are [governed by] *idamaḥ tṛtīyādiḥ vibhaktiḥ*.

"It becomes acute" (*udātta*); this is the accent. And there are the rules concerning *tyad* and so forth (*tyadādividhayaḥ*). And the rules concerning *tyad* and so forth are the purpose. Because [it is said] "in the case of a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*), the rules concerning *tyad* and so forth are established. (Pāṇini 5.3.2) In the mention of *bahu*, there is the inclusion of numerals (*saṅkhyā*). In the mention of *bahu*, there is the inclusion of numerals.
It must be stated that [the rule] should not apply here: *bahau*, *bahoḥ*. Now, for what purpose is the supplementary inclusion (*upasaṅkhyāna*) of *kim* made?
Is it not already established by the rule "of a pronoun" (*sarvanāmnaḥ*) alone? The inclusion of *kim* is made because of the prohibition regarding two or more.

The inclusion of *kim* is made because of the prohibition regarding two or more; for otherwise, when the prohibition "not after two or more" (*advyādibhyaḥ*) would have applied, [this inclusion is necessary].
The addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of *kim* is made [to the rule].
Where is this *n*-sound heard? It is not heard anywhere.
Its elision occurs by the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*. If it is not heard anywhere, for what purpose is it [mentioned]?

It is stated [in the rule]: "That which has more than one letter (anekāl) and ends in ś replaces the whole. This is so that it may be a universal substitute (sarvādeśa). Even when the letter *n* is inserted, the status of being a universal substitute would not be obtained. Why? Because once the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) has taken place, it consists of only one letter (*ekāl*). Here, this must be considered: "Should the elision of *n* be performed first, or the universal substitution? What should be done here? The elision of *n* [should take place] because it is subsequent. However, the elision of *n* is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*).

Because that [substitution] is not yet established, it becomes a replacement for the whole (sarvādeśa). The elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is considered unestablished (*asiddha*) only with respect to those operations specifically enumerated, and this [substitution] is not included among them. If that is so, then this is established through sequential order: the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-sañjñā*) does not apply until the whole-replacement has occurred, and the elision of *n* does not apply until the designation of a nominal stem has been effected.

That [argument] is established by sequence. This purpose does not exist: since rules apply to the final [element] (*alaḥ antyasya*), and there is no purpose for pronouncing an *a* in place of an *a*, it will be a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*) even without the letter *n*. There is another purpose for pronouncing an *a* in place of an *a*. What is it? Those other substitutes that begin with *a*.

[They] undergo [substitution] for the purpose of excluding that [anusvāra]. For example, in the rule *maḥ rāji samaḥ kvau*, by the force of the explicit mention of the letter *m* as *m*, [substitutions such as] *anusvāra* and the like do not occur. Therefore, the letter *n* should be employed. It need not be employed; it is indeed included in the formal statement (*nyāsa*). This is a *praśliṣṭa-nirdeśa* (a conjoined indication) consisting of *a a a*. By the rule *anekāl-śit sarvasya*, it will become a replacement for the whole.

(P_5,3.5.2) KA_II.403.16–24 Ro_IV.180: The rule *etado 'ti* is a split rule (*yogavibhāga*). The rule *etado 'ti* must be split. From *etado*, the two substitutes *eta* and *iti* occur; then [the rule] *an*. And *an* also occurs from *etado*.
By which prescribed [suffix] is the substitution of *etado* stated when the suffix *thak* occurs? There must be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for *etado* before the suffix *tham*.

And this *thamu* suffix must be added as an optional supplement (*upasaṅkhyāna*). [The example is: "of this kind," "in this manner. Then, that supplementary rule must indeed be formulated. No, it need not be formulated. This very fact—that he teaches a substitute for a word beginning with the letter *tha*—indicates that *thamu* occurs here. But how can it be known from this indicator (*jñāpaka*) that *thamu* will occur here, and not [some other suffix] which...?
Thus, that [suffix] beginning with *tha*, which is prescribed without distinction, shall be the substitute for it. We shall qualify this [suffix] beginning with *tha* by means of *idam*:
"that which begins with *tha* belonging to *idam*.
(P. 5.3.7, 10) This is now considered: KA_II.404.3-23 Ro_IV.180-182.

These suffixes beginning with *tasil* are either substitutes for case-endings (*vibhaktyādeśa*) or they follow after them (*pare*). How could they be substitutes, and how could they be subsequent? If [the rule] were in the genitive case—as in "of the fifth" or "of the seventh"—then they would be substitutes. But if it is in the ablative case, then they are subsequent. Why is there this doubt? Because the grammatical indication (*nirdeśa*) is the same. And what is the distinction here? That the suffixes beginning with *tasil* are substitutes for case-endings.

If *tasil* and the others are substitutes for case endings (*vibhakti-ādeśa*), then a prohibition must be stated regarding the elision of the case ending (*sub-luk*), accent (*svara*), *guṇa*, *vṛddhi* (long vowel), *aitva*, *autva*, and the application of the suffix *smāyādi*. Regarding the elision of the case ending (*sub-luk*): from *tatas* comes *tatastyaḥ*; from *yatas* comes *yatastyaḥ*;

from *tatra* comes *tatratyaḥ*; from *yatra* comes *yatratyaḥ*. [In these cases,] by the rule "the case ending is elided after a verbal root or a nominal stem" (*supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*), the elision of the case ending would apply.

[Substitution of] *subluk* (elision of case endings). [Regarding] accent (*svara*): when that occurs, the accent prescribed by the rule "the *sup* and *pit* suffixes are unaccented" (*anudāttau suppitau*) would apply.

[Regarding] accent: [regarding] quality (*guṇa*). Why? From what? The quality (*guṇa*) prescribed by the rule "for *ghi*-stems before a suffix beginning with *ṅ*" (*gheḥ ṅiti*) would apply. [Regarding] quality: [regarding] lengthening (*dīrgha*). In that case, lengthening (*dīrghatva*) prescribed by the rule "lengthening of *at* before a suffix beginning with *yañ* or a *sup* suffix" (*ataḥ dīrgho yañi supi ca*) would apply. [Regarding] lengthening: [regarding] the substitution of *et* (*ettva*). In those cases...

In that regard, when a *jhali* suffix follows a plural ending, the substitution of *et* (by Pāṇini 7.3.103) would apply [to the final vowel]. Regarding the substitution of *aut*: in *kasmin* and *kutra*, the substitution of *aut* (by Pāṇini 7.3.118, *idudbhyām aut at ca gheḥ*) would apply. Regarding the rules for *smāyādi* (the forms *smāt*, *smin*, etc.):
from *tasmāt*, *tataḥ*, *tasmin*, and *tatra*, the *smāyādi* substitutions (*smāt* and *smin*) would apply by virtue of the mention of the fifth case (*pañcamī*).

Success! May others be well. If it is argued that a prohibition must be stated for those words that are identical [to the original], then [in the case of] *tasmāt tasyati* and *yasmāt tasyati*, the suffix *tasil* would apply because of the rule "the suffix *tasil* occurs after a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) with the sense of *tasi*. [Response: There is no prohibition of identical words because the meaning of the base itself is understood when there is no substitution. There is no prohibition of identical words because the meaning of the base itself is understood when there is no substitution.

The negation is meaningless; it is not a negation [of the suffix]. Why does *tasil* not occur? Because its own meaning (*svārtha*) is already understood. According to the rule, *tasil* should occur after a word ending in the fifth case when it functions in its own sense (*svārtha*). However, in this instance, *tasi* does not occur after a word ending in the fifth case in its own sense.

(P_5,3.8) Why is *tasil* prescribed for *tasi*? The prescription of *tasil* for *tasi* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*). The prescription of *tasil* for *tasi* is made for the sake of the accent, so that this accent may occur: "when a suffix marked with *L* follows, the syllable preceding the suffix is acute. But will not this *tasil* supersede *tasi*? It is not established.

Because it is subsequent, *tasi* would apply. The scope for *tasil* is: *tataḥ hīyate* ("he departs from there"), *tataḥ avarohati* ("he descends from there"). The scope for *tasi* is: *grāmataḥ āgacchati* ("he comes from the village"), *nagarataḥ āgacchati* ("he comes from the city"). Here, both [suffixes] would apply:

*tataḥ āgacchati* ("he comes from there") and *yataḥ āgacchati* ("he comes from whence"). Because it is subsequent, *tasi* would apply. Therefore, it is well said [that the rule for] *tasi* [takes precedence].

The mention of *tasil* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*). (Pāṇini 5.3.9) Regarding what is stated as "also with *pary-* and *abhi-*," that should be understood as having the sense of "all around" (*sarva*) and "on both sides" (*ubhaya*). To the extent that there is "from all sides" (*sarvataḥ*), so is there "around" (*paritaḥ*); to the extent that there is "on both sides" (*ubhayataḥ*), so is there "on both sides" (*abhitaḥ*).

Why does [the substitution] not occur here: *saḥ*, *tau*, *te*? It should be stated: "[The substitution occurs] when in conjunction with *bhavat* and so forth. But what are *bhavat* and so forth? They are: *bhavān*, *dīrghāyuḥ*, *devānāmpriyaḥ*, and *āyuṣmān*. Thus: *sa bhavān*, *tatra bhavān*, *tataḥ bhavān*, *taṃ bhavantam*, *tatra bhavantam*.
From him, Your Honor; by him, Your Honor; there, Your Honor;
from there, Your Honor; to him, Your Honor; there, Your Honor; from there, Your Honor; from him, Your Honor; there, Your Honor;
from there, Your Honor; in him, Your Honor; there, Your Honor; from there, Your Honor. He is long-lived; there, he is long-lived.

Then Dīrghāyus; that Dīrghāyus; there Dīrghāyus; from there Dīrghāyus. He is Devānāmpriya; there Devānāmpriya; from there Devānāmpriya. That Devānāmpriya; there Devānāmpriya; from there Devānāmpriya. He is Āyuṣmān; there Āyuṣmān; from there Āyuṣmān.

To that venerable one... there the venerable one... from that the venerable one. (P_5.3.17) KA_II.406.2-3 Ro_IV.184: What is [the word] *adhunā* derived as? It is the substitution of *aś* for *idam*, with the suffix *dhunā*; or else, there is the elision (*lopa*) of *idam*, with the suffix *adhunā*. At this time: *adhunā*.

Now, since the rule states that the third case and subsequent case endings of the pronoun *idam* are acute, this accent would apply [to the syllable *da*]. However, the accent is established by means of the irregular form (*nipātana*) *dānīm*. The accent will be established through the irregular form *dānīm*; an irregular form beginning with an acute accent (*ādyudātta-nipātana*) will be prescribed. That irregular accent [of *dānīm*] supersedes the accent of the case ending.
It will be an obstacle. Or has it been stated? What has been stated? That "it is established from the beginning. (Pāṇini 5.3.19).
The mention of *dā* after *tad* is purposeless because it has already been prescribed.

The mention of *dā* after *tad* is purposeless. For what reason? Because it has already been prescribed. Here, the suffix *dā* has already been prescribed [by the rule] *sarva-ekānya-kim-yat-tadaḥ kāle dā*.

Regarding the phrase "of those two" (*tayoḥ*), it is a reference to nominal stems (*prātipadika-nirdeśa*). One should understand that "of those two" is a reference to nominal stems. [The question arises: "Of which two?
Of the two rules (*yoga*) or of the two suffixes (*pratyaya*)? Therefore, the Teacher, acting as a friend, explains: "It is a reference to nominal stems."

(P_5,3.22) What is the irregularly formed (*nipātita*) word *sadyas*? It is the substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* and the suffix *dyas*, [occurring] when "day" (*ahani*) is to be expressed. The substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* is irregularly formed, and the suffix *dyas* is added when "day" is to be expressed. Thus, *sadyas* means "on the same day. What is the irregularly formed word *parut* and *parāri*? It is the substitution of *para-* for *pūrva-* and *pūrvatara-* [respectively].

And *udārī* [is used] in reference to a year. The forms *parut* and *parāri* are derived by the application of the suffixes *udārī* and *udārī*, respectively, when the word "year" (*saṃvatsara*) is to be expressed. In the preceding year, it is *parut*; in the more remote preceding year, it is *parāri*. What is the derivation of *aiṣamaḥ*? It is the substitution of the suffix *samasaṇ* for *idam*. When the word "year" is to be expressed, the suffix *samasaṇ* is applied to *idam*.

In this year, [the form] *aiṣamaḥ*. What is the irregular derivation (*nipātyate*) of *paredyavi*? It is the suffix *-edyavi* after the word *para*, when "day" (*ahani*) is to be expressed. When "day" is to be expressed, the suffix *-edyavi* is irregularly derived after *para*; thus, *paredyavi* means "on the following day. What is the irregular derivation of *adya*? It is the substitution of *aś* for *idam* and the addition of *dya*. The substitution of *aś* for *idam* is irregularly derived, followed by the suffix *dya*.

And the suffix *edyusuc* is a *pratyaya* [occurring] when "day" (*ahar*) is to be expressed. In this sense, [we have] *adya* ("on this day"). What is the rule for the formation of *pūrvedyuḥ*, *anyedyuḥ*, *anyataredyuḥ*, *itaredyuḥ*, *aparedyuḥ*, *adharedyuḥ*, *ubhayedyuḥ*, and *uttaredyuḥ*? The suffix *edyusuc* is prescribed after the words *pūrva*, *anya*, *anyatara*, *itarā*, *apara*, *adhara*, *ubhaya*, and *uttara*, [when the word *ahar* follows]. Thus, the suffix *edyusuc* is prescribed after *pūrva*, *anya*, *anyatara*, *itarā*, *apara*, *adhara*, *ubhaya*, and *uttara* when the word *ahar* follows.

In the sense of "on the day": *pūrvedyus* (on the previous day), *anyedyus* (on another day), *anyataredyus* (on one or the other day), *itaredyus* (on the other day), *aparedyus* (on the following day), *adharedyus* (on a lower day), *ubhayedyus* (on both days), *uttaredyus* (on a subsequent day). [The suffix] *-dyus* [is added].
And [the suffix] *dyu* should also be stated after the word *ubhaya*. Therefore, from *manuṣyebhyaḥ*, we have *ubhayadyuḥ*.
(Pāṇini 5.3.27) Why does it not occur here: "He dwells in the eastern region" (*pūrvasmin deśe vasati*)? This is not a [simple] region; this is a qualifier of a region.
(Pāṇini 5.3.28) For what purpose is *atasuc* prescribed, rather than simply *tasuc*?

In this regard, there is also this point: the *ca* (the letter *c*) need not be used for the sake of accentuation, as it is already established by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). What is the formation of the forms?
[They are] *dakṣiṇato grāmasya* and *uttarato grāmasya*. The words *dakṣiṇa* and *uttara* end in the vowel *a*; [the suffix] is the word *tasu*.

[The rule] would be established when [the words] end in *akāra*; however, when they indeed end in *ākāra*, it is not established. Even then, it is established. How? By means of the masculine-like form (*puṃvadbhāva*). How is there the masculine-like form? [By the rule] "In the case of *tasil* and so on, up to *kṛtvasuc*. It is not established. The masculine-like form applies to that which has been previously mentioned as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), and these two are not such that they have been previously mentioned as masculine.

But surely, sir, the words *dakṣiṇa* and *uttara* are used in the masculine; and it is stated that "that which has been mentioned as having the masculine gender" (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) applies when there is a common form. Yet these two have different forms when they are *bhāṣitapuṃska*: *dakṣiṇā* and *uttarā* are directional terms (*dikśabda*), whereas *dakṣiṇaḥ* and *uttaraḥ* are terms of relative position (*vyavasthāśabda*). If, however, directional terms are also terms of relative position...

[The question arises: How can there be [words] designated as "directions" (*dig-apadiṣṭa*) for actions? [Answer: When the directions (*diś*) shall express a fixed determination (*vyavasthā*). If, however, every word that exists in a direction were a "direction-word" (*dik-śabda*), then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to such things as "the beautiful direction" (*ramaṇīyā dik*) or "the auspicious direction" (*śobhanā dik*). Now, if it is thought that a "direction-word" is a word seen in a direction—that is, a word perceived in a direction—[then the definition holds].

[The rule] "that which does not deviate from its direction" prevents over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to words such as *ramaṇīya* (pleasant) and so on. However, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would still apply. If that is the case, then the masculine substitution for a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) must be stated to apply in all compound formations (*vṛtti*), for the sake of forms such as *dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām*. If you say it is for the sake of providing a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), then where is there a need for a qualifier? [Answer: It is necessary in connection with a genitive case ending followed by an affix expressing the sense of "from that" (*atasarthapratyaya*).

Thus, if it were stated "with a word ending in the sixth case [denoting the starting point] and a suffix having the sense of *tasi*," then it would also apply here: *tataḥ grāmāt* ("from that village") and *yataḥ grāmāt* ("from which village"). What is the irregular formation (*nipātana*) of *upari* and *upariṣṭāt*? The substitution of *upa* for *ūrdhva*, along with the suffixes *ri* and *liṣṭātil*. The substitution of *upa* for *ūrdhva*, as well as the suffixes *ri* and *liṣṭātil*, are irregularly prescribed. Thus: *upari* and *upariṣṭāt*.

(P_5,3.32) What is the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) of *paścāt*? It is the substitution of *pañca* for *apara*, along with the suffix *āti*. That is to say, the substitution of *pañca* for *apara* is irregularly prescribed, as is the suffix *āti*. Thus: *paścāt*.

Furthermore, it must be stated that for a compound whose prior member is a direction-word (*dik-pūrvapada*), the substitution of *pañca* for *apara* occurs, along with the suffix *āti*. Thus: *paścima*.

[The suffix] *paśca* [is substituted for *apara*] in the sense of "western" when it follows *dakṣiṇa*, *uttara*, or a compound whose final member is *ardha*. It should be stated that in a compound whose final member is *ardha*, *paśca* is substituted for *apara*. [Examples: *dakṣiṇapaścārdhaḥ* (the southwestern half), *uttarapaścārdhaḥ* (the northwestern half). Furthermore, it should be stated that when *ardha* follows, *paśca* is substituted for *apara*. [Example: *paścārdhaḥ* (the western half).

(P_5.3.35) KA_II.409.18–20 Ro_IV.191: Regarding the rule *apañcamyāḥ* ("except for the fifth case"), it should be understood as applying prior to *asaḥ* ("before the suffix *as*"). As for what is stated as *apañcamyāḥ*, that must be seen as applying prior to *asaḥ*. One might think that the subsequent rule applies without distinction as *apañcamyāḥ*. Therefore, the Teacher, acting as a friend, explains:
"*apañcamyāḥ* [applies] prior to *asaḥ*."

(P_5,3.36) What is the purpose of the letter *ca*? It is for the sake of accent (*svarārtha*). [The rule] "the end of that which has the marker *cit* is acute" would ensure that it has an acute accent on the final syllable. But this is not a necessary purpose, because this [suffix] consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*); therefore, there is no need for the marker *ca* as an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) for the sake of accent, since it is already established by the accent of the suffix itself. [Then what is its purpose? It is for the sake of specification (*viśeṣaṇārtha*).

In that case, where is the purpose for the meaning of the qualifier? [It is stated in the rule: "When joined with *anya*, *ārāt*, *itara*, *ṛte*, words denoting direction (*dikśabda*), a word ending in *añc*, a word standing as the second member (*uttarapada*), or *āja* and *ahi*, [the fifth case ending is used]. It is said, "[The fifth case ending is used] in the sense of separation (*vidhā*)". What indeed is the meaning of "separation" (*vidhārtha*)? The meaning of separation is "separation-sense" (*vidhārtha*). If this is so, then in cases such as *ekā govidhā* ("one cow-separation") and *ekā hastividhā* ("one elephant-separation"), here too—

[He] attains [it]. If that is so, then the rule for verbal roots (dhātu) applies when there is a separation from the meaning of the verbal root. It should be stated: "The rule for verbal roots applies when there is a separation from the meaning of the verbal root. But what is this "separation from the meaning of the verbal root"? Is it that Devadatta eats rice with his hand from a bronze bowl? No, he says; this is a separation of the *kārakas* (factors of action). What then is that which occurs at the proper time?

"He eats in the evening; he eats. [Objection: No, he says, "this is a distinction of time. [Objection: Then what about "he eats cold food; he eats hot food"? [Reply: No, he says, "this is a distinction of qualities (*guṇa*). [Question: What then is the distinctness of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)? [Reply:

Action (*kriyā*) is a specific mode of activity of the factors of action (*kāraka*). If this is so, then this [distinction] occurs within the varieties of action. [This applies to] those cases involving injunctions (*vidhi*).
And there are [words] in the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*): *evaṃvidham*, *evaṃyuktam*, *evaṅgatam*, *evamprakāram*.
(Pāṇini 5.3.44) The suffix *dhyamuñ* is prescribed in the sense of "being together" (*sahabhāva*). It should be stated that *dhyamuñ* occurs in the sense of being together.

[Example: *ekadhyam rāśim kuru* ("make the heap into one"). [Question: Then, must it be stated? [Answer: No, it need not be stated. [For this meaning is already covered by the rule] *adhikaraṇavicāle* ("when there is a change of location").

It is said: that alone is not *adhikaraṇavicāla* where one thing is made many; rather, when many things are made one, that too is *adhikaraṇavicāla*. (Pāṇini 5.3.45) The suffix *ḍa* is observed after a word ending in *dhamuñ* in its own sense (*svārthe*). The suffix *ḍa* is seen after a word ending in *dhamuñ* in its own sense, and it is to be prescribed [as such]. Examples: *pathidvaidhāni*.
In the case of doubt, there are two alternatives.
(Pāṇini 5.3.47) Regarding the suffix *pāśa*, the mention of "contemptible" (*kutsita*) must be made. [The suffix *pāśa* is applied] when contempt is intended:

*vaiyākaraṇapāśaḥ* ("a contemptible grammarian"), *yājñikapāśaḥ* ("a contemptible performer of sacrifices"). For it is that which is to be kept at a distance, that is called *yāpya*; in that case, [the suffix *pāśa* applies].

[The opponent says: "It must be so. [Vājapyāyana replies: "Now, a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*) should be one who is emaciated in body and excellent in grammar; thus he should be called a 'wretched grammarian' (*vaiyākaraṇapāśa*). [Vājapyāyana says: "He should not be so called. Why? Because when a word is applied to a substance based on the existence of a certain quality, a suffix must be used to express that quality when it is to be denoted. However, the word *vaiyākaraṇa* is not applied to the substance because of the existence of emaciation (*kārśya*)."

The mention of *pūraṇa* (“ordinal”) could have been omitted. For there exists no word ending in *-tīya* that is not an ordinal where a fault might arise. But is this not the case with forms such as *mukhatīyaḥ* and *pārśvatīyaḥ*?
[To this we reply: Since the rule applies to what is meaningful (*arthavat*), it will not apply to what is meaningless. If so, the mention of *pūraṇa* is for the sake of the subsequent rule.

It must be stated [as a rule]: "before the suffixes up to the eleventh, in non-Vedic usage," so that it may apply to the ordinal numbers. (Pāṇini 5.3.52) The suffix *ākinic* is prescribed after the word *eka* when expressing a dual or plural sense.
The suffix *ākinic* is to be prescribed after *eka* in the sense of two or many: *ekākinau*, *ekākinaḥ*. But why [is this necessary]?

The reason is not established. This word *eka* is a numeral (*saṅkhyāpada*), and the meaning of a numeral is that which is to be numbered (*saṅkhyeya*). [Objection: But it is established by the statement regarding the substitution for numerals. [Response: This is indeed established. How? The word *eka* must be stated as the substitute for a numeral having the sense of two or many; or alternatively, the word *eka* must be stated as the substitute for that which is without a companion (*asahāya*).

"Without a companion" means *ekākī* (solitary); "without companions" means *ekākinau* (two solitary ones); "without companions" means *ekākinaḥ* (many solitary ones). [The form] *sidhyati* (is established). In that case, the sūtra is contradicted. Let it remain exactly as it was originally formulated. But has it not been stated that the suffix *ākinic* is prescribed after the word *eka* when a dual or plural sense is intended? This is not a fault. This word *eka* is indeed a numeral (*saṅkhyāpada*). For example: *ekaḥ*, *dvau*.

Regarding the word *bahavaḥ*: it exists in the sense of "others. For example, in the phrase *sadhamādo dyumna ekāstāḥ*, the meaning is "others. It also signifies "without companion. For example: *ekāgnayaḥ* (those who maintain a single fire), *ekahalāni* (single-ploughed fields), and *ekākibhiḥ kṣudrakaiḥ jitam* ("it was won by solitary, insignificant men").
This present usage refers to that which signifies "without companion."

(P_5,3.55.1) It is stated: "in the sense of excellence" (*atiśāyane*). What is this "in the sense of excellence"? Descriptive formulations of the sūtras are being composed. As much as one might say "in the sense of pre-eminence" (*prakarṣe*) or "in the sense of superiority" (*atiśaye*), so much is meant by "in the sense of excellence. Of what, then, does the suffix arise in the sense of pre-eminence? The term "from a *ṅī*-ending or a *āp*-ending nominal stem" (*ṅyāpprātipadikāt*) is understood to carry over. [It arises] from a *ṅī*-ending or *āp*-ending nominal stem.

Regarding the term *prakarṣe* (in the sense of excellence): the word *ṅyāpprātipadika* refers to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a feminine suffix (*ṅī*) or a long vowel (*āp*). Now, excellence and deficiency do not exist in a word itself, because such qualities are impossible in a word. Therefore, it should be understood that the operation applies to the meaning. But what is the meaning of a nominal stem ending in a feminine suffix or a long vowel? It is substance (*dravya*). However, excellence is not desired in the case of a substance. If that is so, then it must be a quality (*guṇa*). Even so, the explicit mention of "quality" (*guṇa*) must still be made.

Substance (*dravya*) is also the meaning of a nominal stem ending in *ṅī* or *āp*, and quality (*guṇa*) is also [the meaning]. In that case, why should this [suffix] occur when there is excellence of a quality and not rather when there is excellence of a substance? Furthermore, even if the mention of "quality" (*guṇa*) were made, one would have to specify "a similar quality" (*samānaguṇa*), so that it does not apply in a case such as "from white to black. If that is so, then this [following example] would not occur now: [the formation of *paṭīyas* from *paṭu*].

"The Adhvaryu is indeed superior; the Pratiprasthātṛ is inferior. Among the blind, he is the most one-eyed. This rivalry occurs between those of equal merit. The Adhvaryu is indeed superior to other praiseworthy ones; the Pratiprasthātṛ is inferior to other blameworthy ones. Regarding "among the blind, he is the most one-eyed," this word *kaṇi* refers to subtlety (*saukṣmya*). All [are thus compared].
"These people see something; this one among them is the most blind. It should be stated that [the comparison applies] when there is no great distance [between the objects].

Let it not apply here: "The mustard seed is large," "The Himalayas are large. It should be stated that [the comparison does not apply] to a genus (*jāti*). Let it not apply here: "This is a tree," "This is a *plakṣa* tree. In that case, this [usage] would not occur now: [e.g., "This is the largest among trees"].

*gotaraḥ*, *gotarā*, *aśvataraḥ*. This is not a superiority of the genus (*jāti*). Of what, then? Of a quality (*guṇa*). This is a cow that draws a cart; this is a *gotara* which draws both a cart and a plow. This is a cow that gives birth every year; this is a *gotarā* that gives birth every year and has a female calf. [Likewise,] a horse...

This is the mule which travels four *yojanas*; this is the one which travels eight *yojanas*. Likewise, in the rule "and [the suffix] *tiṅ*," the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) must be supplied so that it does not apply when there is excellence of the "means" (*sādhana*). This fault does not arise. As for what was said—that the mention of "quality" (*guṇa*) must be made—it need not be made. For excellence belongs only to that [which is a quality].
Its excellence will exist in that [quality]. Furthermore, excellence belongs to the quality alone, not to the substance. How is this known?

For it is observed thus in the world: here, when the length and breadth are equal, the price of a cloth from Kāśī is one thing, while that of one from Mathurā is another. Indeed, when artisans produce a different quality, they wash away the previous substance with a different liquid.

With one [cloth] they make a *dhautaka* (washed) cloth, with another a *śaiphālika*, and with another a *mādhyamika*. As for what is said—that even when excellence is being grasped, the grasping of equal excellence must be performed so that [the designation does not apply] from "white" to "black"—it need not be done. For rivalry occurs only between equals; indeed, the wealthy and the handsome do not compete with one another.

Furthermore, the expressive word (*vācaka*) must indeed arise [from its cause]; for if a cognition were to arise from something black with respect to something white, it could not be the expressive word.

As for what was said—that it should be stated that [the relationship] exists when there is no great distance—that need not be stated. Rivalry occurs only when there is no great distance; for one who possesses a single *niṣka* does not rival one who possesses a hundred *niṣkas*. As for what was further said...

It should be stated that [the suffix] does not apply to a genus (*jāti*). It need not be stated. That which is attained through birth is a genus, and there is no excellence (*prakarsa*) or deficiency (*apakarṣa*) in this category of meaning.
