Furthermore, as for what was said—that in the rule *tiṅaś ca* (Pāṇini 5.3.56), the word "action" (*kriyā*) must be included so that [the suffix] does not apply to the excellence of a means (*sādhana*)—it need not be included. For a means is indeed a substance (*dravya*), and there is no excellence of a substance.

There exist excellence (*prakarṣa*) and deficiency (*apakarṣa*). But is whiteness one, or is it manifold? And what follows from this? If it were one, excellence would not be possible; for a thing cannot possess excellence through itself alone. If, on the other hand, it is manifold, then the apprehension of common qualities must be stated [as a rule], so that [the suffix] does not occur after "white" when there is "black. There is indeed one whiteness, but it...
It possesses distinctions. By what are these distinctions made? They are made by smallness and greatness. Alternatively, let it be one and without distinction.
But was it not said that excellence (prakarpa) is not possible? For excellence cannot belong to a thing by means of itself.
Excellence will arise from the concealment [of one quality] by another quality. Or again, let it be manifold. But was it not...

And it has been said that one must specify "the apprehension of a common quality" so that [the suffix] does not apply from "white" to "black. This need not be specified; for rivalry occurs only between things possessing a common quality. Indeed, a wealthy man and a handsome man do not compete with one another. Furthermore, the suffix must arise as a designator (*vācaka*); and a suffix arising after "white" in relation to "black" would not be a designator.
(P_5,3.55.2) From what ending in the accusative case (*kimanta*) should there be the production [of the suffix]?

From that which is being surpassed (*atiśayyamāna*), ending in the second case. For example: *śuklam atiśete* (he surpasses the white) results in *śuklataraḥ*; *kṛṣṇam atiśete* (he surpasses the black) results in *kṛṣṇataraḥ*. If it were from an ending in the second case that which is being surpassed, then in the case of *kālaḥ atiśete kālīm* (time surpasses a dark woman), one would obtain *kālitaraḥ*, whereas [the desired form] is *kālataraḥ*.

And this is also accepted: likewise, in the case of *kāla*, one would obtain *kālātaraḥ* when it surpasses *kāla*, yet *kālitarā* is what is accepted. Likewise, in the case of *gārgya*, one would obtain *gargātaraḥ* when he surpasses the *Gargas*, yet *gārgyātaraḥ* is what is accepted. Likewise, in the case of the *Gargas*, one would obtain *gargatarāḥ* when they surpass *Gārgya*, yet *gārgyatarāḥ* is what is accepted.

If that is the case, then [the suffix] will be a *svārthika* (denoting its own meaning) following a word ending in the nominative case. For example: *kālaḥ atिशेते* (he surpasses in time) becomes *kālataraḥ*;

*kālī atिशेते* becomes *kālitarā*; *gārgyaḥ atिशेते* becomes *gārgyataraḥ*; *gargāḥ atिशेरते* becomes *gargatarāḥ*. If it is a *svārthika* following a nominative-ending word, then in the case of *kumāritarā* and *kiśoritarā*, since the age is not distinct [from the state of being a girl or a young woman], it is used in reference to age (*vayasi*).

[Objection: In the first case, the suffix *ṅīp* would apply. [Response: Because it has already been expressed by the comparative suffix *tarap*, the feminine suffix will not occur. [Objection: In that case, the suffix *ṭāp* would also not apply. [Response: Even when [the quality] has been expressed, these suffixes such as *ṭāp* do occur. [Response: It has already been stated that *ṭāp* and the others are *svārthika* (suffixes expressing the same meaning as the base). [Objection: In that case, the suffix *ṅīp* would still apply. [Response: In that case, a quality (*guṇa*) is being denoted. [Objection: Even so, gender and number [would remain problematic].
They are not established as *śuklataram*, *śuklatarā*, *śuklataraḥ*, *śuklatarau*, or *śuklatarāḥ*.

The gender and number will follow from the substrate (*āśraya*). For words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*), the gender and number are determined by the substrate: for example, "the white cloth" (*śuklaṃ vastram*).

"A white cloth," "a white blanket," "two white blankets," "white blankets"—whatever gender and number the substance (dravya) possesses which the quality (guṇa) depends upon, those same will belong to that quality as well. Alternatively, the action (kriyā) is expressed; thus it is.

Furthermore, gender and number would not be established. Gender and number will be determined by the substratum (*āśraya*). Even so, the dual number would result; for both that which excels and that which is excelled are its two substrata. This is not a fault. How so? The root *śī* is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Even roots that are intransitive become transitive (*sakarmaka*) when accompanied by a prefix (*upasarga*).

The rules prescribed for *karman* (the object) apply to those verbal roots whose action resides in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka*) or whose action resides in the object (*karmasthakriyā*). However, the root *śī* (to lie down) has its action residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*). Now, whether the suffix arises from a word ending in the accusative case or from a word ending in the nominative as a self-descriptive (*svārthika*), and whether it denotes a quality (*guṇa*) or an action (*kriyā*), does this follow from the extent of this very sūtra, or rather from one of the two [alternative interpretations]?

In this case, the rule (*sūtra*) should be formulated again. He says: it has already been explained. How so? First, when there is derivation from a word ending in the accusative or a primary suffix (*svārthika*) added to a word ending in the nominative, then the suffix *lyuṭ* will apply here by the rule "the *kṛtya*, *lyuṭ*, and others are used diversely" (*kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*).
When a quality (*guṇa*) is denoted, it is established by logic alone. Even when the action (*kriyā*) is denoted, it is likewise established by logic.

Thus it is. Alternatively, *atiśāyana* means "that which causes to excel. What is the meaning of the object being acted upon (*prayojya*)? Qualities cause the possessor of qualities to act, or the possessor of qualities causes the qualities to act. Furthermore, what here is the meaning of "lying down" (*śeti*)? Here, that which exists in a certain place lies down there. And qualities lie down in the possessor of qualities. This designation is considered to express either the sense of lying down or the sense of causal agency (*kāritārtha*).

In the sense of "belonging to" (*śeṣa*), there is nothing to be said; I speak to you in the sense of "causative function" (*kāritārtha*). Whether it be a possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) manifested through connection with a quality (*guṇa*), or a quality manifested through connection with its possessor, by virtue of that connection, there will be the sense of causative function. In this case, for example: "His garments are fine," or "His [garments are fine]."

In the case of *api sūkṣmāṇi vastrāṇi*, the superlative suffix (*ātiśāyika*) would apply because of the remoteness [of the comparison]. Regarding the superlative in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, it has been stated:

what was stated? That when there is excellence in the first member (*pūrvapada*), the *bahuvrīhi* follows the superlative suffix for the sake of meanings such as "one whose clothes are more subtle" (*sūkṣmavastratara*); and when there is excellence in the final member (*uttarapada*), the superlative suffix follows the *bahuvrīhi* for the sake of meanings such as "one who is much wealthier" (*bahvāḍhyatara*). Here, there are three white clothes characterized by degrees of excellence and deficiency.

In this regard, with respect to the preceding [word], the two subsequent ones end in the suffix *tarap*. Of these two words ending in *tarap*, the production [of the suffix] would result from one that possesses excellence, namely from the word *śuklatara*; however, it is desired that it arise from the word *śukla* itself. Since the state of being white (*śuklabhāva*) belongs to the "whiter" (*śuklatara*), the suffix is understood to belong to the base (*prakṛti*). The word *śukla* exists within the word *śuklatara*; therefore, the production [of the suffix] will occur [from *śukla*].

We do not dispute whether the word *śukla* exists within the word *śuklatara*. What then? The word *śuklatara* also exists. From that, the [suffix] *ut* would result. Furthermore, there is an observation of the suffix expressing the same meaning (*svārthe*) after that which ends in such a suffix, in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), as in *śreṣṭhama* and *āyīyas*.

After that which ends in such a suffix—that is, after that which ends in a comparative suffix (*ātiśāyika*)—a comparative suffix is observed in the Vedic language for the sake of the same meaning, as in *devaḥ vaḥ savitā*.

"Let it be assigned for the sake of the best action. If that is so, then the production [of the suffix] must be stated from the middle *śukla* word, which depends on both what precedes and what follows. And the middle *śukla* word, depending on what precedes, is superior; depending on what follows, it is inferior. Now, something inferior does not function [as the base]. Or rather, let it be produced; there will be elision (*luk*). For indeed, by means of the expressive word...

Furthermore, [the suffix] *utpattavya* should not be derived from the word *śuklatara*, for that which is being produced would not be a denotative term. Indeed, the comparative suffix *tarap* cannot be applied to many things; rather, it is by means of the superlative suffix *tamap*. Competing with the preceding [term], this [word] *sita* attains [the status of a denotative]; whereas the subsequent [term] undergoes diminution, and what is diminished does not function [as a denotative]. The middle [term] functions by depending on the preceding one.

The white [moon] attains increase; in another case it reaches diminution, just as a minister does when the king is present. Or rather, let there be *tara* after that; it will not be an incorrect word (*apaśabda*). If it is expressive, it should be employed; if it is expressive, let it be employed.
(Pāṇini 5.3.57) It is stated [in the rule] "in the dual" (*dvivacane*). In that regard, this [is not so].

It is established: "The teeth of Dantoṣṭha are smoother; the feet of Pāṇipāda are more delicate; and between us and Devadatta, Devadatta is more handsome. However, if it were stated that "the upapada consists of two meanings," then this meaning [of the rule] would also apply: the mention of *upapada* need not be separated [into two parts]. This also applies here in the case of "from among the Śāṅkāśyakas."

[If it were argued that] the rule is already established by the phrase "when there is a two-fold referent (*dvyarthopapada*)," as in the case of "The inhabitants of Pāṭaliputra are more handsome [than those of Śaṅkāśya],"—such a two-fold referent cannot be understood in this way. For in that case, the rule would also apply here: "Among the inhabitants of Śaṅkāśya and the inhabitants of Pāṭaliputra, the inhabitants of Pāṭaliputra are the most handsome. Therefore, one must certainly perform the inclusion of the *upapada* by means of analysis (*vibhajya*).

For that which is a division among many is for the sake of that [distinction], as in: "The people of Mathurā are more handsome than those of Śākya and those of Pāṭaliputra. If that is so, then it should be stated that [the rule applies] when there is a dual-worded upapada. It need not be stated. This is not a reference to the technical (paribhāṣika) dual number; rather, it is a reference to the etymological (anvartha) sense. It is said: "the statement [is made]."

The term *dvivacana* means "the expression of two meanings. Even so, there must be an addition [to the rule] regarding the suffixes *tarap* and *īyasun* when they denote the excellence or inferiority of a single substance; that is, it must be stated that there is an addition for *tarap* and *īyasun* when they express the excellence or inferiority of a single substance. For example: "Last year you were clever (*paṭu*), but this year you are more clever (*paṭutara*). However, this is established because the quality is subordinate [to the substance].
This is established. How so? Because of the distinction between the subordinate and the principal. This designation is made with the subordinate as the principal.

Furthermore, through connection with other qualities, there arises a state of being "other. For example, speakers say of that very same person when he is joined with other qualities, "You have become someone else."

(P_5,3.58) KA_II.417.9-12 Ro_IV.215 What is the purpose of the particle *eva*? It is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). This is not necessary; since a rule is being commenced when [the formation] is already established, it will serve as a restriction even without the particle *eva*. Then, is it for the sake of emphasizing what is desired? So that it may be understood thus: "only from a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) [is there a feminine suffix] beginning with *aj*."

Let it not be understood thus: "only after a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) [the suffixes] beginning with *aj* [are applied]. What would be the consequence? [The suffixes] beginning with a consonant would not be applied after a quality-word.
This is incorrect. What is incorrect here?
Having stated that [the suffixes] beginning with *aj* apply only after a quality-word, the substitutes for *aj* and *ādi* are prescribed even for words that are not quality-words. It is not so.

This is the fault. This very point makes it known to you that even from these non-qualifier words (*aguṇavacana*), the suffix *ṅīp* applies after those beginning with *aja*, since he prescribes the substitutes when *aja* and so forth follow. Even so, it would have to be stated as "after those two" (*tayoḥ*). That is, [it should say] "when those two follow. But if this were understood as a rule (*vidhi*), it could not be so; for [the suffixes] do not begin with a consonant (*vyañjana*).

Furthermore, there would be a confusion of the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) because of the re-enactment of the rules for *aja* and so forth. [Objection: But surely these specific features (*viśeṣa*) would continue to apply.

[Response: Even if these were to continue, then [the suffixes] *vyañjanādī* would not occur. In that case, the activity of the Teacher (*ācārya*) indicates that the suffixes *ajādī* occur even after these [words] when they do not denote a quality (*aguṇavacana*), since he [prescribes them] after *aja* and so forth.

He teaches the substitutes. But was it not said that one must say "of those two"? It need not be said. The mention of "beginning with *aj*" (*ajādī*) from the original context continues here. Where was it mentioned? In the rule: "Only after a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*) [is there substitution] when beginning with *aj*. That [mention] was indeed indicated in the nominative case, whereas here the meaning requires it to be indicated in the locative case. By implication, there will be a change of case-ending (*vibhaktivipariṇāma*). For example:
"Devadatta’s houses are high. It is understood that "him," namely Devadatta, is being addressed.

[In the phrase] "Devadatta’s cows, horses, and gold," it is understood that "the wealthy son of Vaidhas, Devadatta," is meant. That which was previously indicated by the genitive case becomes, by implication, indicated by the accusative and the nominative cases. Thus, here too, previously...

That which is designated by the first case ending [in the rule] will, by implication, be that which is designated by the seventh case ending. The designation is made in the feminine gender and in the singular number;
therefore, the suffix should arise only from a feminine base and only from a singular form, and not from masculine or neuter bases, nor from dual or plural forms.
And it would not [apply]. This is not a fault. This is not the meaning of the suffix; what then? It is a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*).

The suffix *rūpap* occurs after that nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which functions in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*). In what sense? In its own sense (*svārthe*). And since these are suffixes used in their own sense (*svārthika*), they follow the gender and number of the base. This is because the base lacks gender and number [of its own].

The substitution of *am* for the verbal root must be stated. Since the verbal root lacks gender and number, it must be stated that the formative suffix *rūpa* undergoes the substitution of *am* after a verbal root: *pacatirūpam*, *pacatorūpam*, *pacantirūpam*. But this is already established because the verb has action as its primary meaning. This is established. How? Because it has action as its primary meaning. A finite verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning, and action is singular.

A noun has substance as its primary meaning. But how is it known that a verb has action as its primary meaning and a noun has substance as its primary meaning? When one is asked about an action, one expresses it by means of a *tiṅ*-suffix (a finite verb): "What is Devadatta doing?"—"He cooks. When one is asked about a substance, one expresses it by means of a *kṛt*-suffix (a nominal suffix): "Which is Devadatta?"—"The one who is the agent [of the action], the one who brings [the object]. If, then, there is only one...

Dual and plural endings for the action (*kriyā*) are not established [in such forms as] *pacataḥ* ("they two cook") and *pacanti* ("they cook"). These do not depend on the action; rather, they depend on the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). If that is so, then [plural endings] would also apply here in the case of *pacatirūpam*, *pacatorūpam*, and *pacantirūpam*. This will not happen because that connection has already been expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*); therefore, the singular ending applies.

But then, it would not be obtained. It will be obtained by convention (*samaya*). In that case, the dual and plural numbers would also be obtained by convention. Well then, let the singular number be established as the general rule (*utsarga*); for it, the dual and plural numbers will serve as exceptions (*apavāda*) when there are two or many [objects]. Even so, the neuter gender must be stated. It need not be stated; gender is not something to be prescribed (*aśiṣya*).
Because the gender [of the derivative] depends on the world [usage].

(Pāṇini 5.3.66.2) An addition should be made for words such as *vṛṣala*. An addition must be made for words such as *vṛṣala*: *vṛṣalarūpaḥ* ("one who has the form of a low-born man"), *dasyurūpaḥ* ("one who has the form of a robber"), *corarūpaḥ* ("one who has the form of a thief"). But this is established by stating that there is a specific qualification of the meaning of the base word (*prakṛti*).

This is established. How so? It must be stated that [the suffix occurs] when there is a qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). For example: "This man has the appearance of a low-born person (*vṛṣala*)," yet he might even drink wine with onions; "This man has the appearance of a thief (*cora*)," yet he might even take away collyrium from the eyes;
"This man has the appearance of a bandit (*dasyu*)," yet he might even drink the blood of those who are running.

(P_5,3.67) KA_II.419.8–420.17 Ro_IV.222–226: Because [the suffixes] expressing slight incompleteness (*īṣadasamāpti*) have action as their primary meaning, there is no application of gender and number. Since those expressing slight incompleteness have action as their primary meaning, there is no application of gender and number. For example: *paṭukalpaḥ*, *paṭukalpau*, *paṭukalpāḥ*. This single meaning called "slight incompleteness" is one; because it is singular, the singular number is used.

[The objection: It follows [that the rule is unnecessary]. [The response: It is established because it qualifies the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). This is established. How so? This is not the meaning of the suffix; rather, this is a qualifier of the meaning of the base. The suffixes *kalpa* and so forth occur after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that functions in the sense of "slight incompleteness" (*īṣadasamāpti*). In what sense? In its own sense (*svārthe*). And since these are suffixes used in their own sense (*svārthika*), they inherit the gender and number from the base.

[The suffixes] follow [the gender and number of the base]. If they were to apply to the meaning of the base itself, there would be an impossibility of gender and number. If they applied to the meaning of the base itself, there would be an impossibility of gender and number, as in: "grapes are like molasses," "clear liquor is like oil," and "barley gruel is like milk. This is established, however, because the suffix is prescribed when the meaning of the subsequent member is connected with that [meaning of the base]. This is established. How? Through connection with that.

It should be stated that the suffix occurs when the meaning of the subsequent word is connected with "slight incompleteness. [Objection: Then the rule (*sūtra*) is altered. [Response: Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. [Objection: But was it not already said that because the slight incompleteness has the action as its primary element, there is no possibility of gender and number? [Response: This has been answered: it is established because it serves as a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*).

But has it not been said that if [the suffix] is used in the sense of the base (prakṛtyartha), there would be an impossibility of gender and number? This is not a fault. The activity of the Teacher indicates that even for self-descriptive (svārthika) suffixes, gender and number may be disregarded, since he employs the mention of the feminine in the rule "añ after ṇac in the feminine. If this were indicated, then *bahuguḍā drākṣā* ("grape with much molasses") and *bahutailā prasannā* ("clear liquor with much oil") would be formed.
In the case of "rice-gruel with many ingredients" (*bahupayā yavāgūḥ*), this [suffix] would also apply there; yet they do not overstep [the rule]. What, then, is the example here?

"Almost clever" (*paṭukalpaḥ*) and "almost soft" (*mṛdukalpaḥ*). This is not correct. For there is either the completion or the non-completion of a meaning already determined, whereas a quality (*guṇa*) is not [previously] determined. In that case, consider this: "grapes almost like molasses" (*guḍakalpā drākṣā*) and "clear liquor almost like oil" (*tailakalpā prasannā*).
"Yavāgū is like milk"—here too, the substance is not specifically determined. Well then, consider these: *kṛtakalpa* ("almost done"), *bhuktakalpa* ("almost eaten"), and *pītakalpa* ("almost drunk").

There is an impossibility of forming a suffix from a word ending in the *kta* suffix, because the *kta* suffix characterizes the past tense, whereas words such as *kalpa* express incompleteness. Thus, there is an impossibility of forming a suffix from a word ending in *kta*. What is the reason?

Because the suffix *kta* has the characteristic of denoting the past tense; the suffix *kta* is characterized by the past tense. And because [the words] "kalpa" and so forth denote non-completion; "kalpa" and the others denote non-completion. Furthermore, it is impossible that something could be both in the past tense and yet be incomplete. But this is established because there is a statement regarding the past as if it were present when there is an expression of hope (*āśaṃsā*). This is established. How? In the case of hope...

And because it has actually become so, the suffix *kta* will be used here [in the sense of "become"]. Furthermore, this is also an example: *paṭukalpaḥ* (nearly clever) and *mṛdukalpaḥ* (nearly soft).

Now, it was argued that for a quality already known, there is either completion or non-completion, whereas a quality is not yet known. [The answer is: The quality is known through observing worldly usage. For example, [one says] "he is clever."

He who accomplishes his goals by a simple means is called a "brāhmaṇa. He who does not accomplish them in such a way is called "one who is nearly proficient" (*paṭukalpa*). And this too is an example: "grapes are like molasses," "clear liquor is like oil," and "barley-gruel is like milk. But was it not said that even a substance is unascertained? [It is ascertained] from common worldly usage.
The substance (*dravya*) has also been fully understood.

(P_5.3.68.1) KA_II.420.19–422.4 Ro_IV.226–229: What is the purpose of including the term *vibhāṣā*? It is so that the suffix *bahuc* may optionally (*vibhāṣā*) occur; and when *bahuc* is not used, so that the sentence itself may remain. This is not a necessary purpose.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā* is the subject under discussion. By means of it, the rule for the sentence will be established. "In that case, this is the purpose:
so that [the suffix] *kalpa* and others may also occur. This too is not a valid purpose. For *bahuc* is also said to include *kalpa* and others;
thus both will occur by virtue of the explicit statement. "It is not possible in this way," [he says], "for if the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionally) were not made, [the rule] would have no scope."

It would contradict many rules concerning the beginning of a compound (*kalpa*) and so forth. Furthermore, the rules concerning the beginning of a compound and so forth would also be left without scope. [Objection: They will apply by virtue of an explicit statement (*vacana*). [Response: The rules concerning the beginning of a compound and so forth do indeed have scope. [Question: What is their scope? [Answer: Verbal endings (*tiṅanta*) are their scope. [Question: Now, what is the purpose of including the term *sub* (the nominal suffix)? [Answer: So that the derivation may occur from a word ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*), and not from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). [Objection: This is not a valid purpose. It is not necessary.

In this case, the distinction is whether the suffix arises from a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) or from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). If that is so, then here too there is no need for the mention of *sub* [in the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*]. Even here, there is no distinction between the suffix arising from a word ending in a case-suffix or from a nominal stem. However, this distinction does exist: if the suffix arises from a word ending in a case-suffix, it receives the technical designation *pada*.

[The suffix] becomes established. If [the suffix] were to arise from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the designation "word" (*pada*) would not apply. But is it not the case that even when arising from the nominal stem, the designation "word" is established? How so? Because the rule *naḥ kye* is commenced. And that must necessarily be formulated for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*) if [the suffix] arises from an inflected word (*subanta*). That very same [rule], however, serves as an injunction (*vidhyartha*) if [the suffix] arises from the nominal stem.
It will be so. Then this is the purpose: that the suffixation should occur after a word ending in a *sup* (nominal) affix, and not after a word ending in a *tiṅ* (verbal) affix.

This too is not a valid purpose, because the term "from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or *pratyaya*" is understood [as a governing rule] from the previous context. Therefore, he recites the following answer:

"Because of the mention of *sup* in the case of *bahuc*, there is the prescription of [suffixation] after a *tiṅ* in the preceding rule. The mention of *sup* is made in the case of *bahuc* for the sake of the preceding rule.

[The purpose is] so that the rule for *tiṅ* [suffixes] may be understood. This is not a necessary purpose, because the mention of *tiṅ* from the previous context continues here. Where was it mentioned? In the rules "the suffixes *tamaP* and *iṣṭhan* are used in the sense of excellence" and "and after *tiṅ*. If that is the case, then the mention of *sub* is made in the rule for *bahuC*, because in the preceding rule there was a prescription for *tiṅ*. The mention of *sub* is made in the rule for *bahuC*. For what reason? Because in the preceding rule there was *tiṅ*.

Because of the rule of prescription (*vidhāna*). In the previous [sūtra], the phrase "and after a verbal suffix" (*tiṅaś ca*) is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*). That [rule] would therefore apply here as well. But surely the mention of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ-grahaṇa*) should be excluded? It must necessarily be carried over for the sake of the subsequent [sūtra]: *avyaya-sarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ* ("the suffix *akac* is added before the final phoneme of indeclinables and pronouns"), for the purpose of forms such as *pacataki* and *jalpataki*. If the mention of the nominal suffix (*sub-grahaṇa*) were made, the accent would not be established, as in *bahupaṭavaḥ*.

In this way, the accent would apply [to the whole], and the form *bahupaṭavaḥ* is also desired. For the Teacher will state: "The compound ending in *cita-* retains its original accent for the sake of the suffixes *bahu-* and *akac*. How is the accent [established]? The accent follows from the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Once the case-ending elision (*subluk*) has been performed, the accent will occur because of the status of being a nominal stem. Now, what is the purpose of mentioning *tu*? The mention of *tu* is for the sake of making it obligatory (*nitya*) that the preceding element retains its accent. This is the mention of *tu*.
It is done so that the former [term] may always be [the first], lest there be an option (*vibhāṣā*). This purpose does not exist.

The term "option" (*vibhāṣā*) is not connected with the former; what then? It is connected with *bahuc*: "there is optionally *bahuc*. And when it occurs, then the former [term] occurs. In that case, this is the purpose:

[Objection: That gender and number which belong to the base before its production should also apply when the suffix has been produced, as in *bahuguḍā drākṣā* ("grapes with much molasses"), *bahutailā prasannā* ("clear liquor with much oil"), and *bahupayā yavāgūḥ* ("gruel with much milk"). [Response: This too is not a purposeful requirement.
This suffix is *svārthika* (denoting its own meaning), and *svārthika* suffixes follow the gender and number of their base (*prakṛti*). [Objection: If that is so, then...

Since [the formation of the word] is already established, the fact that the Teacher employs the mention of *tu* (in Pāṇini 5.3.70) indicates that derivative suffixes added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthika*) may also deviate from the gender and number [of the original]. What is the purpose of this indication? [For example: *guḍakalpā drākṣā* ("grapes that are almost like molasses") and *tailakalpā prasannā* ("clear liquor that is almost like oil").
The phrase "gruel resembling milk" (*payaskalpā yavāgūḥ*) is thus established.
(P_5,3.68.2) *Kāśikā* II.422.5–10; *Rūpāvatāra* IV.229–230: "After words beginning with *tam*, the suffixes *kalpa* and so forth [are applied] by way of an exception (*vipratiṣedha*).
After words beginning with *tam*, the suffixes *kalpa* and so forth occur by way of an exception. The scope of the suffixes beginning with *tam* is the expression of excellence."

The suffixes *kalpa* and so forth are not prescribed for the sense of "slight incompleteness" (*īṣadasamāpti*), because [in that case] excellence (*prakarṣa*) is not expressed. For example: *paṭutaraḥ* ("more clever") and *paṭutamaḥ* ("most clever"). However, when *kalpa* and so forth are used in the sense of slight incompleteness, excellence is not expressed. For example: *paṭukalpaḥ* ("somewhat clever") and *mṛdukalpaḥ* ("somewhat soft"). When both meanings are expressed, both suffixes would apply. For example: *paṭukalpataraḥ* ("somewhat more clever") and *mṛdukalpataraḥ* ("somewhat softer"). By way of a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*), the suffixes *kalpa* and so forth take precedence. If this is the case...

The suffixes *tamap* and so forth apply to express excellence when there is slight incompleteness; however, it is desired that they apply to the base (*prakṛti*) itself. The suffixes *tamap* and so forth occur after that which is slightly predominant. They also occur after that which is slightly predominant. Of what is there excellence? Of the base itself. When there is excellence of that [base], the suffix will occur. And of what is there excellence? Of the base itself.

(P_5,3.71–72.1) KA_II.422.16–21 Ro_IV.230: Does this [suffix] apply to a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) before *ṭi*, or rather to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or *ṅap*? Whence the doubt? Both have been introduced as the subject matter; it is possible to specify either one. And what follows from this? If it applies to a word ending in a case-suffix, then [the forms] *yuṣmakābhiḥ*, *asmakābhiḥ*, *yuṣmakāsu*, *asmakāsu*, and *yuvakayoḥ* [would not be established].
If [the suffix] were applied to the base (*prātipadika*), then forms such as *tvayakā*, *mayakā*, *tvayaki*, and *mayaki* would result; however, this is not desired.
Suppose it is applied to the inflected word (*subanta*). Then how do we account for *yuṣmakābhiḥ*, *asmakābhiḥ*, *yuṣmakāsu*, *asmakāsu*, *yuvakayoḥ*, and *āvakayoḥ*?
It must be stated that [the suffix applies] when the following element begins with *an*, *o*, *ka*, *ra*, *sa*, *bha*, or *ā*.

(P_5,3.71–72.2) KA_II.422.22–423.2 Ro_IV.230–231: In the section on *akac*, [the suffix] *kāmu* should be stated after *tūṣṇīm*. In the section on *akac*, it should be stated that *kāmu* follows *tūṣṇīm*: "It was indeed thought by one observing this while remaining silent (*tūṣṇīkām*). Regarding the sense of habit (*śīla*), [the suffix] *ka* is applied and there is elision of *m*. Regarding the sense of habit, it should be stated that *ka* is applied and there is elision of *m*: *tūṣṇīśīlaḥ* ("one whose habit is silence"), *tūṣṇīkaḥ* ("silent").

(P_5,3.71-72.3) KA_II.423.3-8 Ro_IV.231: Here, when *śnam* is applied in *bhinatti* and *chinatti*, *śap* would follow. When *bahuc* is applied in *bahukṛtam*, *bahubhuktam*, and *bahupītam*, *kalpa*-suffixes and the like would follow. When *akac* is applied in *uccakaiḥ* and *nīcakaiḥ*, *kādi*-suffixes would follow. But surely, *śnam*, *bahuc*, and *akac* are exceptions (*apavāda*)?

These will be subverters [of the general rules]. Regarding the suffixes *śna*, *bahuc*, and *kak*, because they occur in different locations, a prohibition of the general rule must be stated. Subverters (*apavāda*) that occupy the same location as the general rules (*utsarga*) do indeed subvert those general rules;
however, because these occur in different locations, the subversion does not apply.

(P_5,3.71–72.4) KA_II.423.9–24 Ro_IV.231–232: The suffixes *tama* and so forth [supersede] the rule for *ka*; by way of prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the suffixes *tama* and so forth occur in place of the rule for *ka*. The scope (*avakāśa*) of the rule for *ka* is the expression of contempt (*kutsā*) and so forth without expressing excellence (*prakarṣa*), as in *paṭukaḥ* ("slightly clever") and *mṛdukaḥ* ("slightly soft"). The scope of the suffixes *tama* and so forth is [the expression of] excellence.

The non-occurrence of the suffixes *kutsā* and so forth [is the result]. [Examples: *paṭutaraḥ*, *paṭutamaḥ*. When both [suffixes] are applicable, both would apply: *paṭutarakaḥ*, *paṭutamakaḥ*. By means of a prior counter-rule (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the suffixes *tamap* and so forth [apply]. Sometimes [the suffixes] *chinnakatara* and so forth [apply];
sometimes *chinnakatara* and so forth occur by means of a counter-rule (*vipratiṣedha*). [Examples: *chinnakataram*, *chinnakatamam*.

And there is a compound whose predominant element is the first member (*ekadeśipradhāna*). And a compound whose predominant element is the first member occurs by way of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) to the rule for the suffix *ka*. Examples: *ardhapippalikā* (half a pippalī), *ardhakośātakikā* (half a kośātakī). And there is a compound whose predominant element is the second member (*uttarapadārthapradhāna*) when it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*), for the purpose of the rule for the suffix *kan*.
And a compound whose predominant element is the second member occurs by way of a prior counter-exception to the rule for the suffix *ka*. What is the purpose?

The suffix *kan* is prescribed for the purpose of forming names (*sañjñā*). So that *kan* may occur in the sense of a name: *navagrāmakam*, *navarāṣṭrakam*, *navanagarakam*. Sometimes there is a *dvandva* compound; sometimes a *dvandva* occurs by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) to the rule for *kan*: *plakṣakanyagrodakau*, *plakṣanyagrodhakau*.

(P_5,3.74. Here, in the cases of *kutsitakaḥ* (“one who is despised”) and *anukampitakaḥ* (“one who is pitied”), because that meaning has already been expressed by the word itself (*svaśabdena*), the suffix would not apply. This is not a fault. [The suffix] will apply when there is pity for one who is despised, or contempt for one who is pitied. Alternatively, a word, having denoted its own primary meaning, is independent.

He states that the substance (*dravya*) is that which is inherent (*samaveta*). And in the expression of what is inherent, there is the gender, the number, and the case-ending (*vibhakti*). Having denoted those specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), and while still requiring them, that word ending in a case-suffix proceeds again toward its entire self in relation to likes, dislikes, and so forth. But how is this to be understood?

Is it "in the sense of contemptible things (*kutsita*) and so forth," or rather "from that which is in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with contemptible things and so forth"? And what is the distinction here? If [it were] "in the sense of contemptible things and so forth," there would be an impossibility of gender and number. If it were "in the sense of contemptible things and so forth," there would be an impossibility of gender and number [as follows]: *paṭukam*, *paṭukā*, *paṭukaḥ*, *paṭukau*, *paṭukāḥ*. This is a single meaning.

The term *kutsita* (contemptible) is singular; therefore, by rule, only the singular number would apply. [Objection: But there is the rule stating "after a word that is in grammatical apposition with *kutsita* and so forth. [Response: If it were "after a word in apposition with *kutsita* and so forth," there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), as occurs in the case of the feminine suffixes *ṭāp* and others. If it were "after a word in apposition with *kutsita* and so forth," there would be an over-extension, just as in the case of *ṭāp* and others. And how is it in the case of *ṭāp* and others? It has been stated therein: "after a word in apposition with a feminine."

If it is argued that this leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *bhūta* and so forth, then here too, if it is argued that [the suffix applies] because of coreferentiality with words such as *kutsita*, there would likewise be an over-extension. [For instance,] from the word *idam* itself, one would obtain the forms *idaṃ ghṛtakam* ("this is ghee") and *idaṃ tailakam* ("this is oil"). However, the desired result is established by the rule that prescribes the suffix in its own sense (*svārthe*) after a word joined with that which expresses contempt (*kutsita*) and so forth. This is thus established.

How so? It should be stated that when meanings such as "contemptible" (kutsita) and so forth are understood, the suffix occurs in its own sense (svārthe) after a word joined with that [suffix]. [If this is done,] it is established. But then the Sūtra is altered. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. [Objection: Was it not said that if [the suffix] were used in the sense of contempt and so forth, there would be an impossibility regarding gender and number? [Response: This is not a fault. For this...

This is not for the sake of a suffix-meaning (*pratyayārtha*); rather, it is a qualifier of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*). The suffixes *ka* and so forth occur after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that denotes something contemptible and the like. In what sense? In its own meaning (*svārthe*). And as derivative suffixes (*svārthika*), they follow the gender and number of the base.

(P_5,3.83.1) From a word ending in the dative case, elision should be stated [of the suffix -ka]. For example: *bṛhaspatidattakaḥ* becomes *bṛhaspatikaḥ*; *prajāpatidattakaḥ* becomes *prajāpatikaḥ*. And when the following word begins with a consonant other than *a*, elision should also be stated. For example: *devadattakaḥ* becomes *devakaḥ*; *yajñadattakaḥ* becomes *yajñakaḥ*. There is also elision of the preceding member [of the compound].

And the elision of the first member [of the compound] should also be stated. *Devadattakaḥ* becomes *Dattakaḥ*; *Yajñadattakaḥ* becomes *Dattakaḥ*. This is desired in the same way when there is no suffix (*apratyaye*). *Devadattaḥ* becomes *Dattaḥ*; *Yajñadattaḥ* becomes *Dattaḥ*. After a vowel ending in *u* (*uvarṇāt*) and after the syllable *il*, elision should also be stated. *Bhānudattakaḥ* becomes *Bhānulaḥ*.

Vasudattakaḥ, Vasulaḥ. (P_5,3.83.2) Now, for what purpose is the mention of *ṭhak*? Is it not already established by the rule "after [a word ending in] *ika*, when an affix beginning with a vowel follows"? The mention of *ṭhak* is for the purpose of prescribing the suffix *ka* when there is a second occurrence of the suffix *uka*. This is the mention of *ṭhak*.

The suffix *uka* is prescribed so that the rule for *ka* may apply when it is the second [suffix]. For example: *vāyudattakaḥ* and *vāyukaḥ*; *pitṛdattakaḥ* and *pitṛkaḥ*. For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the suffixes characterized by beginning with a vowel (*ajādi*), just as in the case of *māthitika*. Indeed, in the case of those characterized by beginning with a vowel, the same undesirable consequence would arise as in *māthitika*: just as from *mathitam paṇyam asya* ("this has churned [milk] as its merchandise") one derives *māthitikaḥ*, once the elision of the short *a* has been made, [the suffix *ṭhan* applies] because it ends in *ta*.

Thus, the substitution of *kā* does not occur; likewise, it should not occur here either. Regarding the elision of a vowel after the second vowel, when there is the status of being the second element of a diphthong (*sandhyakṣara*), the elision of that which begins with it must be stated. When the elision of a vowel after the second vowel is to be performed, if it is the second element of a diphthong, the elision of that which begins with it must be prescribed. Examples: *lahoḍaḥ*, *lahikaḥ*; *kahoḍaḥ*, *kahikaḥ*.

(P_5,3.84) And for *varuṇa* and the others, the [suffix] *sa* is [substituted] for the third [vowel], and that is [to be applied] when no sandhi has been performed. For *varuṇa* and the others, the elision (*lopa*) is prescribed; and that must be stated as occurring when no sandhi has been performed: *suparyāśīrdattaḥ*, *suparikaḥ*, *supariyaḥ*.

Regarding *suparīlaḥ*: here, in the case of *ṣaḍaṅguliḥ* and *ṣaḍikaḥ*, once the elision of the *aj*-class suffixes has occurred, the designation *pada* would not apply. What is the fault in that? The substitution of *jaś* (the voiced unaspirated stops) would not take place. Regarding the substitution of *jaś* in *ṣaḍikaḥ*, it has already been stated. What was stated? That it is established by the rule "it is as if the original [vowel] remained" (*acaḥ sthānivadbhāvāt*). If this is so, then there must be a prohibition of the application of *pada*-rules in the case of *vācika* and similar forms. There is indeed a prohibition of the application of *pada*-rules in the case of *vācika* and similar forms.

It should be stated: [the formation] is established by the rule concerning the elision of the second member (*uttarapada-lopa*) for compounds whose first member consists of a single syllable (*ekākṣara-pūrvapada*). This is established. How so? It should be stated that there is elision of the second member of compounds whose first member consists of a single syllable. In that case, would this not also apply here to *ṣaḍaṅguliḥ* and *ṣaḍikaḥ*? It is established by the rule stating that the suffixes *ṭhañ* and those beginning with *añ* follow the word *ṣaṣ*. This is established by the rule stating that the suffixes *ṭhañ* and those beginning with *añ* follow the word *ṣaṣ*.

(P_5,3.85-86) Why are these two meanings taught? Is it not the case that whatever is small (*alpa*) is also short (*hrasva*), and whatever is short is also small? There is no necessary co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) between these two. One says, "small ghee," "small oil"; no one says, "short [ghee]."

"Ghee" (*ghṛtam*) is short; "oil" (*tailam*) is short. Likewise, one says "a short cloth" (*hrasvaḥ paṭaḥ*) or "a short garment" (*hrasvaḥ śāṭakaḥ*). No one says "a small cloth" (*alpaḥ paṭaḥ*) or "a small garment" (*alpaḥ śāṭakaḥ*).
(Pāṇini 5.3.88) In the case of *kuṭī*, *śamī*, and *śuṇḍā*, there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāvaḥ*) by virtue of the application of the suffix.
The masculine transformation (*puṃvadbhāva*) should be stated as occurring in connection with the suffixes added to *kuṭī*, *śamī*, and *śuṇḍā*. [Examples: *kuṭī* (feminine) / *kuṭīraḥ* (masculine);

*śamī* (feminine) / *śamīraḥ* (masculine); *śuṇḍā* (feminine) / *śuṇḍāraḥ* (masculine). But what is the reason that it is not already established? This suffix is one that expresses the same meaning as the base (*svārthika*), and suffixes expressing the same meaning as the base follow the gender and number of the base. Or has this been stated? What has been stated?
"Words denoting one's own [possession] (*svārthika*) may deviate even from gender and number.

(Pāṇini 5.3.91). Regarding the rule for *vatsa* and others, there is a prohibition when referring to thinness or emaciation. A prohibition must be stated regarding *vatsa* and others when referring to thinness or emaciation, so that forms such as *kṛśo vatsaḥ* ("a thin calf") or *vatsataraḥ* ("a very young calf") do not occur.

In that case, a prohibition must be stated. It need not be stated. For when a quality exists such that a word is applied to a substance on account of that quality, then a suffix ought to occur to express that quality. However, the word *vatsa* is not applied to the substance because of the presence of leanness (*kārśya*).

(P_5,3.92-93) KA_II.427.16–428.4 Ro_IV.242: Since suffixes are prescribed for *kim* and the others when there is a dual or plural sense, the mention of the qualifier (*upādhi*) is redundant. Why? Because "selection" (*nirdhāraṇa*) consists in setting something apart from a group. To what extent? Selection occurs only when one out of two [or more] is set apart.
It occurs. Another says:

regarding the rule *bahūnāṃ jātiparipraśne ḍatamac*, the mention of *bahu* ("many") is redundant. What is the reason? This word *kim* functions in the sense of inquiry (*paripraśna*), and inquiry occurs when something is not yet known; and that which is not yet known pertains to "many," not to two or one.

Furthermore, it is already known. Because it is already known, there is no inquiry regarding two or one. Since there is no inquiry, why would [the suffix] not exist at all? From what [source] would the suffix arise? (Pāṇini 5.3.94) For what purpose is the mention of *prāk* ("before")? So that the option (*vibhāṣā*) may apply.

And the mention of "prior" is redundant because of the context of the *vibhāṣā* rule. The mention of "prior" is purposeless. What is the reason? The *mahāvibhāṣā* is the subject under discussion; it is already established by that very rule. (Pāṇini 5.3.95) The suffix *kan* is prescribed in the sense of "throwing down," while the suffix *ka* is prescribed in the sense of "contempt. Which of these two [is intended here]?

There is a distinction between the two meanings. *Avakṣepaṇa* (contempt) is the instrument; it is a contemptible action. Indeed, *avakṣepaṇa* is a contemptible instrument. By means of that, whatever is made contemptible also becomes contemptible. In that case, the status of being "contemptible" is already established. If this is so, then that which is employed for the purpose of censuring another is the example here: *vyākaraṇakena*.

"This one is named Garvita. "This one is named Yājñikya. That which is employed for the purpose of denoting contempt for oneself is the illustrative example in this context: *devadattakaḥ*, *yajñadattakaḥ*. (Pāṇini 5.3.98) Why is it stated that there is *lup* in the case of a human being, rather than simply stating *luk*?

For the sake of establishing gender, there is elision (*lup*) in the case of "human" (*manuṣya*). Elision is prescribed in the case of "human" for the sake of establishing gender. For example: *cañcā* (a straw doll) as if it were a woman;

*vadhrikā* (a leather bag) as if it were a woman; *kharakuṭī* (a donkey-stall) as if it were a woman. Why is elision prescribed in the case of "human," rather than simply non-elision (*luk*) being prescribed? [This refers to Pāṇini 1.2.52.]
It is stated [in the rule] that "it does not apply to merchandise" (*apaṇye*). In that case, this is not established:

*śivaḥ*, *skandaḥ*, *viśākhaḥ*. What is the reason? These images were commissioned by the Mauryas, who were seekers of gold. [The rule] would not apply to those; however, it will apply to those which are intended for worship as objects of veneration.

(P_5,3.106) KA_II.429.6-9 Ro_IV.244-245 By this word "tat" (*that*), what is being referred to? [It refers to] the suffix *cha*. But how can a compound (*samāsa*) be the domain of the suffix *cha*? In that case, it has the sense of "like" (*iva*). If, then, the compound also occurs in the sense of "like," since the meaning is already expressed by the compound, the suffix would not apply. In that case, there are two [possibilities].
The two [suffixes] have the sense of *iva* ("like"). How so? *Kākāgamanam iva tālapatanam iva* is *kākatālam*. *Kākatālam iva* is *kākatālīyam*. (Pāṇini 5.3.118) Regarding the suffix *aṇ*:

from a *gotra* [stem], there must be a mention of *gotra*. From the suffix *aṇ*, when it follows a *gotra* stem, the mention of *gotra* must be made. It should be stated: "from a *gotra* [stem]. This is so that it does not apply here: *ābhijitaḥ muhūrtaḥ* ("the hour belonging to Abhijit").

Regarding the rule "from *ābhijit*, [the suffix] *sthālīpāka*": it must also be stated that [the word refers to] a *gotra*. What is the purpose? So that forms such as *ābhijitakaḥ* may be produced; [this is so that] the suffix *vuñ* may apply based on a *gotra*. It could have been possible to omit the mention of "*gotra*. How then would *ābhijitakaḥ* be formed?
This [suffix *ka*] is applied to a *gotra* in its own sense (*svārthika*), and thus it remains a *gotra* itself.
The mention of "a hundred pādas" is purposeless, because [the suffix] is seen elsewhere as well.
The mention of "a hundred pādas" is purposeless. Why? Because it is seen elsewhere as well. For indeed, the suffix *vun* is seen elsewhere too: e.g., *dvimodikām dadāti*.

In the section on the suffix *kan*, an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the words *cañcat* and *bṛhat*. An addition must be made in the section on *kan* for *cañcat* and *bṛhat*: *cañcatkaḥ* and *bṛhatkaḥ*.

Regarding the rule that suffixes such as *tamap* follow a word ending in the past passive participle (*ktānta*) when the action has not reached its ultimate completion, this is a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣiddha*).

The suffixes *tama* and so forth occur after a word ending in the *kta* suffix when there is no absolute completion [of the action], by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). The scope (*avakāśa*) of the rule "the suffix *kan* occurs after a word ending in *kta* when there is no absolute completion" is a statement of non-absolute completion without a statement of excellence (*prakarṣa*):
*bhinnakam*, *chinnakam*. The scope of the suffixes *tama* and so forth is a statement of excellence without a statement of non-absolute completion.

*paṭutaraḥ*, *paṭutamaḥ*. When both [suffixes] are applicable, both are obtained. *bhinnatarakam*, *chinnatarakam*. The suffixes beginning with *tama-* occur by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Furthermore, the suffix *kan* is prescribed after that which ends in those [suffixes] in the sense of the same meaning (*svārthe*): after that which ends in those [suffixes], *kan* should be stated in the sense of the same meaning. *bhinnatarakam*.

(P_5,4.5) KA_II.431.2–4 Ro_IV.248: The prohibition [of the suffix *kan*] when a word expressing "a portion" (*sāmivacana*) is present is redundant, because the meaning is already expressed by the base form (*prakṛti*). The prohibition regarding words expressing "a portion" is unnecessary. Why? Because the meaning is already expressed by the base form.
Since that meaning is already expressed by the base form, the suffix *kan* will not occur.

(P_5,4.7) KA_II.431.6–23 Ro_IV.248–251: The prescription of a suffix after a compound whose final member is *adhi* is untenable because there is no analytical dissolution (*vigraha*). The prescription of a suffix after a compound whose final member is *adhi* is untenable. Why? Because there is no analytical dissolution. The production of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is preceded by an analytical dissolution; however, no analytical dissolution is observed with *adhi* as the final member. Therefore...

In that case, [the word] *sadhīnaḥ* means "dependent on this. Therefore, the suffix *pratyaya* [should be stated as] *tatra-idam-sadhīnaḥ*. For example: *rājani idam* = *rājādhīnam* ("dependent on the king"). If it were formed as *sadhīnaḥ*, the designation *itsaṃjñā* (elision marker) would not apply to the letter *s*. Furthermore, in cases such as *śryadhīnaḥ* and *bhrvadhīnaḥ*, the rules for *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* would apply to the base (*aṅga*). Moreover, the sūtra would have to be altered. [Therefore, it should remain] as it is in the original formulation (*yathānyāsam*).

"Let it be so. But was it not stated that the formation of a suffix after a compound whose final member is *adhi* is untenable because there is no analytical statement (*vigraha*)? This is not a fault. There is a reason why no analytical statement occurs here. What is the reason? This is an obligatory suffix (*nityapratyaya*). Which, then, are the obligatory suffixes? Those beginning with *tama* up to before *kan*, and those beginning with *ñya* up to before *ka*.

[The suffixes] beginning with *vun* and ending with *mayaṭ*, as well as those ending in *bṛhatī* and generic terms (*jāti*), are compound-terminating suffixes (*samāsānta*). If this is so, then this is not a rule for the derivation of a suffix (*pratyayavidhi*) that is being criticized; rather, it is the base form (*prakṛti*) that is being criticized. There is no base form consisting of a word preceded by *adhi*. What is the reason? Because of the absence of an analytical statement (*vigraha*). The application of a compound is preceded by an analytical statement, and there is no such statement with *adhi*.
A separate analysis (*vigraha*) is observed. If that is so, then it will be a *bahuvrīhi* compound. What is achieved by this?

Indeed, there are certain *bahuvrīhi* compounds even without an analysis using their own constituent words (*asvapadavigraha*). For example, "she has a beautiful face" is expressed as *sumukhī*. This cannot be the case; for in the instance of *mahadadhīnam*, the suffixes *ātva* and *kap* would undesirably apply. If that is so, then...

It will be an *avyayībhāva* compound. Even so, the rule for the prior placement of *adhi* would still apply. [Response: It will be included in the list of *rājadantādi* compounds. Alternatively, this is a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*); for *adhi* is recited among the *śauṇḍādi* group. (Pāṇini 5.4.8) Question: What is the purpose of mentioning "direction" (*dig*)? [Objection: If it were stated merely as "provided it is not feminine" (*astriyām*),...

In the case of "the Brāhmaṇī is facing east" (*prācīnā*) and "the tuft of hair is facing west" (*avācīnā*), the same [undesired] application would also occur. However, when the term *diś* (direction) is explicitly mentioned, no such fault arises. Now, for what purpose is the mention of the word *strī* (feminine), since a direction-word (*dik-śabda*) refers exclusively to the feminine? Indeed, there are certain direction-words that do not refer to the feminine; for example, *prāk* and *prācīnam*, as well as *pratyak*.
*pratīcīnam*, *ucak*, *udīcīnam*.

(P_5.4.14) Why is there the mention of "feminine" (*strī*)? Is this not a suffix used in its own sense (*svārthika*), and since suffixes used in their own sense follow the gender and number of the base (*prakṛti*), the feminine form would be established by default? Even so, since it is already established, why is there the mention of "feminine"?

By doing this, the Teacher indicates that even when suffixes are used with a self-referential (svārthika) sense, they may deviate from the original gender and number. What is the purpose of indicating this? [The examples] "grapes are like molasses" (*guḍakalpā drākṣā*), "clear wine is like oil" (*tailakalpā prasannā*), and "barley gruel is like milk" (*payaskalpā yavāgūḥ*) are thereby established.
In the rule regarding *sakṛdādeśa* (a single substitution), the mention of *abhyāvṛtti* (repetition) should be removed.
What is the purpose? *Abhyāvṛtti* means repetition again and again. And there can be no repetition again and again of that which is singular.
Now, does the term *kriyā* (action) continue to apply [from the previous rule], or not? And what is the point of its continuation? Certainly.

The meaning [of the rule] is as follows: let it not apply here: *ekaḥ bhuṅkte* ("one eats"). Now, even though the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) continues [from the previous rules], why does it not apply here in *ekaḥ pākaḥ* ("one cooking")? And why does it not apply in the two preceding rules [regarding numbers]? For example: *dvau pākau*, *trayaḥ pākāḥ*, *catvāraḥ*.

"Five *pākāḥ* (cooks)," "ten *pākāḥ*. This is not a counting of actions; what then? This is a counting of substances (*dravya*). How so? Because "a state (*bhāva*) expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix functions like a substance. In that case, it would also not apply here because it is a counting of substances: *sakṛd bhuktvā* ("having eaten once") and *sakṛd bhoktum* ("in order to eat once"). And in the two preceding rules, [it applies] as in *dvis bhuktvā* ("having eaten twice").

If "repetition" (*abhyāvṛtti*) means repeating an action twice, three times, five times, or ten times—such as eating twice after having eaten once, eating three times after having eaten once, eating five times after having eaten once, or eating ten times after having eaten once—then it would not apply to the counting of substances. Furthermore, if repetition indeed means a repeated occurrence, then when there is a double occurrence it would be "once," and when there is a triple occurrence it would be "twice. If that is the case, then:

The term *abhyāvṛtti* (repetition) is understood here, but it does not mean repetition in the sense of occurring again and again (*punaḥ punar*). Rather, *abhyāvṛtti* means an action directed toward something (*abhimukhī pravṛtti*). Both the preceding [action] is directed toward the subsequent one, and the subsequent ones are directed toward the preceding one.

Furthermore, as for what was said: "Even though the mention of 'action' (*kriyā*) is carried over [from the previous rule], why does [the suffix] not occur here in the case of *ekaḥ pākaḥ* (one cooking)? [This is because the action is not repeated.]

[Objection: Why does this [suffix] not occur after the two previous *yogās*, as in "two *pākās*," "three *pākās*," "four *pākās*," "five *pākās*," or "ten *pākās*"? [Response: This has already been answered. This is not a counting of actions (*kriyā*). What then? This is a counting of substances (*dravya*). How so? Because "a state (*bhāva*) expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix functions like a substance (*dravyavat*)."

But has it not been stated that even here, because of the counting of substances (*dravyagaṇanāt*), [the suffix] would not apply in cases such as *sakṛd bhuktvā* (having eaten once) and *sakṛd bhoktum* (to eat once)? And in the two preceding rules, [it would not apply] in cases such as *dvis bhuktvā*, *dvis bhoktum*, *tris bhuktvā*, *tris bhoktum*, *pañcakṛtvo bhuktvā*,
*pañcakṛtvo bhoktum*, *daśakṛtvo bhuktvā*, and *daśakṛtvo bhoktum*, due to the counting of substances.

[The desired result] is not obtained. This is not a fault; it will be accomplished by counting the actions (*kriyā*). How so? A state (*bhāva*) expressed by a *kṛt* suffix functions both like a substance (*dravyavat*) and like an action (*kriyāvat*).
(Pāṇini 5.4.24) It is stated [in the rule] "after a word ending in the name of a deity" (*devatāntāt*). Consequently, this [form] is not established.

Regarding the term *pitṛdevatyam*: what is the reason? Is it not the case that the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) are not deities (*devatā*)? This is not a fault. The word *deva* is derived from the root *div*, which means "to exercise sovereignty. Therefore, the suffix *tal* is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*). By doing so, the form *devadevatyam* is also established. (Pāṇini 5.4.27) Regarding the suffix *tal*: the feminine gender must be stated for *tal*. The feminine gender [of words ending in *tal*] must be explicitly mentioned.
[The word] *devatā* [is feminine]. But what is the reason that it does not succeed? This word *deva* is masculine, and this [suffix -tā] is a svārthika suffix.
And svārthika suffixes follow the gender and number of their base (*prakṛti*). Or rather, it has already been stated. What has been stated?
That "svārthika suffixes may even deviate from the gender and number [of their base]."

(P_5.4.30) KA_II.433.22–435.3 Ro_IV.257–259: "Or, there is the subversion of gender after *lohita*. It should be stated: "Or, there is the subversion of gender after *lohita*. [Examples: *lohitaka*, *lohinikā*. "An addition must be made for Vedic meters regarding groups of syllables. An addition must be made for Vedic meters regarding groups of syllables. [For example: *o śrāvaya* consists of four syllables; *astu śrauṣaṭ* [consists of four syllables].

The four-syllabled [formula] is *ye yajāmahe*; the five-syllabled is *yaja*; the two-syllabled is *vaṣaṭ*. This seventeen-syllabled Prajāpati, consisting of meters, is indeed fashioned according to the sacrifice. In the Vedic meter (*chandas*), there is an addition of many riches; in the Vedic meter, there is an addition of many riches: "Fill your hands with many riches; Agni is the lord of riches."

The addition of *agnirīśeva* to the category of *savya* must be stated. Or rather, it has already been stated. What has been stated? That it is established through the understanding of its own meaning (*svārtha*).
[Examples: *apasyaḥ vasānāḥ* [should be] *apaḥ vasānāḥ*; *sve okye* [should be] *sve oke*; *kavyaḥ asi havyasūdana* [should be] *kaviḥ asi*;
*raudreṇa anīkena kavyatāyai* [should be] *kavitayai*; *āmuṣyāyaṇasya* [should be] *amuṣyaputrasya*.

He rules over security; he rules over well-being. He settles in security; he settles in well-being. Long life is conducive to splendor; splendor itself is that which is conducive to splendor. It is exclusive; it is absolute. It is praiseworthy; it is a hymn of praise. It is born of the people; through them, it is accompanied by the people. Through them, it is the people; through them, it is accompanied by the people. With these hymns of praise, I generate something new.

Ninefold. Lead us with new [hymns], with new ones. The ancient prayer (*brahma*). The ancient path (*pāthaḥ*). The ancient [protection] within our bodies. Ancient. Of ancient days. Of ancient mornings. Ancient clans. Ancient clans. Most ancient. Most ancient.
He is the most ancient; he is the first. Agni indeed is the most ancient. The first. Delight in him, O youngest one!
O youngest one! O carrier of the oblation, O most youthful one! O youngest one! Since you, O most youthful one, [are so];

O youngest one! He dwells equally, he grasps equally; he dwells in equality, he grasps in equality. His hands are equal in the sacrifice to the gods. Equal. He performs deeds that bring equal vigor; equal. He performs deeds of equal vigor; equal.
[The suffix *u* is applied] after *īvat*, as well as after *lokam*. After *īvat*, after *brahmaṇe*, and after *iyate*. Regarding *nava*:
the substitute *nū* should be stated for *nava*, and the suffixes *tnap*, *tanap*, and *kha* should also be stated. [Thus we have] *nūtnam*, *nūtanam*, and *navīnam*.

Furthermore, regarding the word *purāṇa*, the substitute *prāt* should be stated for *nava*, and the suffixes *tnap*, *tanap*, and *kha* should also be stated. [Thus we have] *prāt*, *prātanaḥ*, and *prātkhaḥ*.
The following [words] should be stated: *praṇam*, *pratnam*, *pratanam*, *prīṇam*.

(P_5,4.36) KA_II.435.5-436.4 Ro_IV.259-260 By this word *tat* (that), what is being referred to? It is speech (*vāk*) itself. Whatever is expressed by speech is performed by action. In the section on the suffix *aṇ*, [the rule applies] from the words *kulāla*, *varuḍa*, *niṣāda*, *caṇḍāla*, and *amitra*.

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), an addition must be made to the section on the suffix *aṇ*: [the suffix *aṇ* applies] after *kulāla*, *varuḍa*, *niṣāda*, *caṇḍāla*, and *amitra*. Examples: *kaulālaḥ*, *vāruḍaḥ*, *naiṣādaḥ*, *cāṇḍālaḥ*, *āmitraḥ*. The suffix *dheya* should be stated [as applying] after words meaning "portion" (*bhāga*), "form" (*rūpa*), and "name" (*nāman*). Examples: *bhāgadheyam*, *rūpadheyam*, *nāmadheyam*.

In the Vedic language (*chandas*), [the suffix] *dheya* should be stated after *mitra*: *mitradheya*. One should strive for the acquisition of a friend (*mitradheye yatasva*). The suffix *aṇ* should also be stated after *amitra*: it should be stated that *aṇ* follows *amitra*. Thus: *maitraḥ* (belonging to a friend) and *āmitraḥ* (hostile). The following words are established as irregular formations (*nipātyante*): *sānnāyya*, *ānujāvara*, *ānuṣūka*, *cātuṣprāśya*, *rākṣoghna*, *vaiyāta*, *vaikṛta*, *vārivaskṛta*, *āgrāyaṇa*, *āgrahāyaṇa*, and *sāntapana*. Examples: *sānnāyyam* (the milk offering), *ānujāvaraḥ* (one who is inferior by birth), *ānuṣūkaḥ* (a small amount of grain), *cātuṣprāśyaḥ* (that which is to be eaten by four), *rākṣoghnaḥ* (destructive of demons), *vaiyātaḥ* (a type of garment).

*vaikṛtaḥ*, *vārivaskṛtaḥ*, *āgrāyaṇaḥ*, *āgrahāyaṇaḥ*, *sāntapanaḥ*. The suffix *añ* should be stated [after the word] *agnīdhrasādhāraṇa*. *āgnīdhram*, *sādhāraṇam*. The suffix *añ* should be stated after *ayavasa* and *marut* in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). *āyavase vardhante*, *mārutam*.
The host [of Maruts], for those who are most youthful among mortals; that which is to be spoken for those who are most youthful among mortals:
the new one, the sun, the mortal, the most youthful. He who, from security, from security is to be spoken of: secure, standing, a furtherer, a hero of good lineage.

(P_5,4.42) KA_II.436.6–9 Ro_IV.260–261: Regarding words expressing abundance or scarcity, a term indicating auspiciousness [or rather, a term indicating auspiciousness or inauspiciousness] should be employed after words expressing abundance or scarcity. One should say, "Give abundantly" (*bahuśo dehi*). This is so that it does not apply to inauspicious things such as funeral offerings (*śrāddha*), but so that it may apply to auspicious things such as the *prāśitra* portion.
"Give in small measure"—let it not be so in the case of desired things such as the *prāśitra* portion, but let it be so in the case of undesired things such as the *śrāddha* offerings.

(Pāṇini 5.4.44) An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for words beginning with *ādi* in the section concerning the suffix *tasi*: an addition must be made for words beginning with *ādi* in the section concerning *tasi*. [Examples: *āditaḥ*, *madhyataḥ*, *antataḥ*.

Regarding the rule for *cvī*: the inclusion of the phrase "the state of becoming what it was not" (*abhūtatadbhāva*) must be made in the rule for *cvī*. This is so that [the suffix] does not apply here: *yavāḥ sampadyante* ("barley is being prepared") and *śālayaḥ sampadyante* ("rice is being prepared"). Now, even if the inclusion of the phrase "the state of becoming what it was not" is made, why does it not apply here?

"In this field, rice-grains are produced. And there must be the inclusion of the phrase "intention to express the material cause" (*prakṛtivivakṣāgrahaṇa*). Furthermore, an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for words such as *samīpa* ("near"). An addition must be made for *samīpa* and so forth:
[the forms] *samīpī bhavati*, *abhyāśī bhavati*, and *antikī bhavati* [are required]. But what is the reason that [these forms] are not established?
For that which is not proximate does not become proximate. What then? That which stands in proximity becomes proximate.
If so, then it must be stated. It need not be stated; by virtue of being located therein (*tātsthyāt*), there will be designation by that term (*tācchabdyam*).
(Pāṇini 5.4.57) For what purpose is the *ca* [in the rule]? For the sake of accent (*svarārtha*). [The suffix] *cit* has an acute accent on its final syllable (*citaḥ antaḥ*).

"It becomes acute" means that the acute accent (*udāttatva*) should apply. This purpose is not necessary; for this [suffix] consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*). In that case, there is no need for the marker *c* (*cakāra*) as an *anubandha* for the sake of the accent, since it is already established by the accent of the suffix itself (*pratyayasvara*). Therefore, he recites the following: "The addition of the marker *c* in *ḍāc* is for the purpose of specification. The marker *c* is added in *ḍāc*.

It is for the sake of specification (*viśeṣaṇa*). Where is there a need for the purpose of specification? In the rule *lohitādi-ḍājbhyaḥ kyaṣ* (Pāṇini 3.1.13). For if it were stated simply as *ḍāḥ*, then [the suffix *kyaṣ*] would also apply after *iḍā*. [Objection: This will not apply because of the principle that when a meaningful element (*arthavat*) is mentioned, an element lacking meaning (*anarthaka*) is not included. [Response: Even so, it would still apply here: *nābhā pṛthivyāḥ nihito davidyutat*. Therefore, the letter *c* must be added.

(P_5,4.67) It should be stated: "And after *bhadrā*. [The result is: *bhadrā karoti*. (P_5,4.68) For what purpose is the mention of "end" (*anta*)? So that it may occur at the end. This is not a necessary purpose; for this is already established by the fact that [the suffix] follows the affix (*pratyaya*). Then [the purpose is this]:
The purpose [of the rule] is so that there may be inclusion by means of the mention of "that" (*tad*). What, then, are the purposes of mentioning "that"?

The purposes are the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of *avyayībhāva*, *dvigu*, *dvandva*, *tatpuruṣa*, and *bahuvrīhi*. The *avyayībhāva* is one such purpose. For example: *pratirājam*, *uparājam*. Since an *avyayībhāva* compound is neuter in gender, it acquires the status of being neuter.

It might be so. But this purpose is not necessary, because gender is not to be prescribed, as gender depends upon common usage. Then this is the purpose: so that this rule—"after an *avyayībhāva* compound ending in *a*, the suffix *am* is used, except in the case of the fifth case"—may apply. [The examples are] *avyayībhāva* and *dvigu*. Furthermore, the designation *dvigu* is also a purpose: *pañcagavam* (five cows), *daśagavam* (ten cows). [These are] *dvigu* compounds.

And [the rule] "and a compound is neuter" is intended so that the neuter gender may apply. This purpose is not necessary, because gender is not subject to formal prescription, as gender depends upon common usage. Well then, this is the purpose: [to form] *dvipurī* and *tripurī*, so that the suffix *īkāra* may apply according to the rule "after a *dvigu* compound ending in *akāra*. Even this purpose is not necessary.

This word *pura* ends in the vowel *a*; therefore, it will form a compound. And because it ends in *a*, he says [the following]. [In the verse: "They subdue their anger in cities that are secure, well-supplied with food, and where stores have been prepared. It is stated: "from the remainder" (*śeṣāt*). What is this so-called "remainder"?

In that case, then, the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) does not depend on [the word] *kapa*, nor does it depend on the compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*). What then? That which is the immediately preceding governing rule (*adhikāra*) for *bahuvrīhi* is what is expected. This is because, in the immediately preceding *bahuvrīhi* governing rule, no compound-final suffix has been prescribed for the *bahuvrīhi*. How then [do we derive] *anṛcaḥ* and *bahvṛcaḥ*? "Of a monosyllabic [root] (*ekācaḥ*). And what follows from this? Therefore, he recites the subsequent answer: "The mention of *ekācaḥ dve prathamasya* is a *bahuvrīhi* designation."

The statement "ekācaḥ dve prathamasya" is a Bahuvrīhi compound. How does it apply to monosyllabic words? It applies to monosyllabic words by virtue of the principle that "the designation [of a property] applies to what possesses that property even when it is singular" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). It should be stated that an operation occurs for a single entity as if it were designated [by a plural]. In this way, reduplication will occur for monosyllabic words. When it is said, "there are two of that which has a single vowel," it is not known which [vowel] it refers to.

"Two [syllables] occur for that which has a single vowel (*ekāc*). He will state later: "In the *liṭ* [perfect], for a root (*dhātu*) that is not reduplicated. By this, it is understood that [the rule applies] to a root that has a single vowel. If it were understood as "for a root that has a single vowel," then forms such as *papāca*, *papāṭha*, *jajāgāra*, and *puputrīyiṣati* would be established; however, they are not established. This genitive case in the word *dhātoḥ* is not a genitive of apposition with *ekāc*; rather, it means "of a root that has a single vowel."

What then? This genitive case is one denoting a relation with a part (*avayavayoga*); that is, "that which is a one-syllable (*ekāc*) part of the verbal root (*dhātu*). If it is argued that this genitive denotes a relation with a part, then while forms such as *jajāgāra* and *puputrīyiṣati* are established, forms such as *papāca* and *papāṭha* are not established [as they would have two syllables]. Even in these cases, by virtue of being treated as if possessing a designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), it becomes a one-syllable part of the verbal root. [The rule applies: "Of the first [monosyllabic root], there is reduplication."

Thus it is said. Therefore, reduplication should occur only where there is both a "first" (prathama) and a "non-first" (aprathama), as in *jajāgāra* and *puputrīyiṣati*. It would not occur here in *papāca* and *papāṭha*, because [the root] is a first [instance]. And regarding the state of being a first [instance]: what is the purpose of this? It is established simply by the rule of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). Well then, that behavior like that which possesses a designation must be explicitly stated.

It need not be stated; or rather, it has already been stated. What has been stated? Therein, the rule "like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivad-vacana*) was mentioned; [the rule] "two [syllables] of a monosyllabic word" (*ekāco dve*) was for the sake of the first [case]; and [the rule] regarding the substitution of *ṣ* (*ṣatva*) was for the sake of ensuring the recognition of the substitute. It is established simply by the absence of such a statement and by common worldly understanding. Or else, there is a division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*). Alternatively, a division of the rules will be made: "Two [syllables] of a monosyllabic word occur. For what purpose is this division of the rules?
The purpose of [the mention of] "ekāc" (a single-vowel root) is for the sake of reduplication. Reduplication should apply to that which consists of a single vowel, as in *iyāya* and *papāca*.
Then, regarding "of the first": two forms of the first [vowel] occur. Now, what is the purpose of this? It is for the sake of restriction (*niyama*).
Where there is both a first and a non-first [vowel], reduplication of the first single-vowel [root] should occur therein.

It might be so. Let it not apply to that which is not a single syllable (*ekāc*), such as *jajāgāra* and *puputrīyiṣati*. Because the parts [of a multi-syllabic root] are themselves single-syllabled, there arises the contingency of doubling those parts. Since the parts are single-syllabled, doubling of the parts would follow for a single-syllable [root].
In the case of *nenijati*, here the word *nij* is a single syllable, the word *ij* is a single syllable, the letter *i* is a single syllable, and the word *ni* is also a single syllable.

In that case, if there is doubling of the word *ni*, the form is established and no faults arise. If there is doubling of the word *ij*, the form is not established, yet no faults arise. If there is doubling of the phoneme *i*, the form is not established, yet no faults arise. If there is doubling of the word *ni*, the form is established, but faults do exist. What, then, is the fault in that case?

In that regard, there is the statement concerning the substitution of *jus*. In that case, the substitution of *jus* must be stated [as an exception]. In forms such as *anenijuḥ* and *paryaveviṣuḥ*, the substitution of *jus* for the suffix *jhi* after a reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*) does not apply because of the intervention of the letter *j*. Furthermore, the accentuation is also not established; in forms such as *nenijati* and *yat pariveviṣati*, the rule that "the first syllable of reduplicated stems is acute" would fail to apply.

In the case of *nenijati* and *pariveviṣati*, the accent prescribed by the rule "there is [anudātta] before a sārvadhātuka beginning with a letter other than 'a' or 'j'" does not apply; nor is the substitution of *at* established. Furthermore, the prohibition of *num* is not established. [Objection: The substitution of *at* [for the final vowel of the root] would not apply because of the rule "after a reduplicated stem" (*abhyastāt*). Also, the prohibition of *num* would not be established. [Response: No. It is not so. The substitution of *at* is indeed established here by the rule "the substitution of *at* occurs after a reduplicated stem ending in a consonant" (*abhyastasya cātaḥ*), which is an exception to the aforementioned rule.
