Moreover, the prohibition of *num* is established by the rule "the prohibition of *num* applies after a reduplicated stem ending in a consonant" (*abhyastānām ādiḥ*), which is an exception to the rule "the augment *num* is added after a reduplicated stem ending in a vowel" (*aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti*). Thus, there is no fault.

The prohibition of *num* after a root ending in a *śatṛ* suffix following a reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*) would not apply because of the intervention of the letter *j*. Furthermore, there would be a loss of the grammatical rule (*śāstrahāni*). Indeed, a loss of the rule occurs; the rule concerning that which consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*) as a whole is abandoned. But this is established by virtue of the fact that the whole (*samudāya*) consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*), thus there is no loss of the rule. This is established. How? By virtue of the fact that the whole consists of a single vowel. What does "by virtue of the fact that the whole consists of a single vowel" mean?

Thus: "its collection" means the collection of that. "The state of being a single vowel" (*ekāctva*) means the condition of having one vowel. "The state of being a single vowel belonging to that collection" means the collection’s possession of a single vowel.

[The reduplication] will occur because of that collection’s state of having a single vowel. Why? Because of the non-abandonment of the grammatical rule (*śāstra*). For in this way, the rule remains unviolated. But surely, if there is reduplication of a collection that has a single vowel...

Even when [the operation] is being performed, the rule concerning the single-syllable (*ekāc*) member is abandoned. It is not abandoned. What is the reason? Because the whole (*samudāya*) consists of its parts (*avayava*). The whole consists of its parts;
for the part is internal to the whole. Just as, for example, a tree moving moves together with its parts.
It moves forward. In that case, when there is a reference by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, reduplication would apply to a vowelless element because it constitutes the meaning of another word.

When there is a reference by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, reduplication would result for what is without a vowel. For example: *āṭatuḥ*, *āṭuḥ*. What is the reason? Because of the *bahuvrīhi* being the meaning of another word.
A *bahuvrīhi* occurs when it denotes the meaning of another word; therefore, reduplication applies to that which is other than the vowel.

It might be so. For example, when it is said, "Let Citragu be brought," he who possesses those cows is brought, not the cows themselves. But this is established through the inclusion of the quality (tadguṇasaṃvijñāna) according to Pāṇini, as is seen in common usage. This is established. How? Through the inclusion of the quality, according to the venerable teacher Pāṇini, as in the world. In the world, [one says] "the one with white clothes" (*śuklavāsasam*).
"Bring [the one] with a red turban; those with red turbans are proceeding. Here, the quality is brought, and those possessing that quality proceed. It is the same here as well.

(P_6.1.1.2) KA_III.3.24-5.19 Ro_IV.287-293 Now, regarding that for which duplication (*dvirvacana*) is prescribed: does it occur in place of [the original], or is it a double utterance? And what is the distinction here? In the case of duplication in place of [the original]...

The statement regarding the elision of *ṇi* is necessary because it is a substitute for the entire complex. When there is reduplication in place of the original, the elision of *ṇi* must be stated. As in *āṭiṭat* and *āśiśat*. What is the reason? Because it is a substitute for the entire complex. The substitute is for the whole complex; therein, because the complex consisting of the stem and the suffix has become completely merged, the *ṇi* is lost, and thus the rule "the elision of *ṇi* before a non-iṭ [suffix]" does not apply.

This must be considered here: let there be reduplication, or let there be the elision of the *ṇi* affix—what should be done in this case? The elision of the *ṇi* takes effect because it is subsequent. Reduplication is obligatory; it applies both when the elision of the *ṇi* has occurred and when it has not. Reduplication is also obligatory; it applies to one form when the elision of the *ṇi* has occurred, and to another when it has not. And since it would apply to a different word-form...

The rule is non-eternal; however, reduplication is indeed eternal. How so? Because of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) of the form. Whatever objection is raised regarding the reduplication of a root ending in *san* or *yaṅ*, that same objection applies here as well. What, then, is that objection? [It concerns the rules]: "If [the root] ends in *san* or *yaṅ*, [the penultimate vowel is lengthened]," "if it is not *aś* before *san*," "if it is a root lacking *iṭ*," "lengthening," "the substitution of *ku* for *kū*", "vowel-vocalization (*prasāraṇa*)," and "the substitution of *ṣ*."

[Objection: Because the reduplication applies to the *adhika* (the additional part), there would be a conflict with the rule for *abhyasta* (repeated) forms regarding the roots *āp* and *br̥h*. Furthermore, since the entire complex (*samudāya*) is the substitute for the entire complex when based on *saṅ*, and since it is indistinguishable [from the original] when based on *jhal*, there would be no designation [of the reduplicated form as such]. [Response: Let it be then that *dvirvacana* (reduplication) is the double utterance (*dviḥprayoga*). [Objection: If *dvirvacana* means double utterance, then the substitution of *ṇakāra* and *ṣakāra*, etc., and the substitution of *et* must be stated in the case of the *liṭ* suffix. [Response: It is double utterance.

If this is argued, then it must be stated that the substitution of *e* occurs in the *liṭ* [perfect] after roots beginning with the substitutes *ṇa* and *ṣa*: *nematuḥ*, *nemuḥ*, *sehe*, *sehāte*, *sahire*.

However, the prohibition [of *guṇa*] would apply because of the rule "not after a root beginning with a substitute" (*anādeśādeḥ*). But when there is reduplication in place [of the whole], the substitute is for the whole; therein, because the root and suffix are completely merged (*sampramugdhatvāt*), that "beginning with a substitute" has been lost.

It occurs. Even when there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*) through double application (*dviḥprayoga*), there is no fault. He will state there the purpose of the mention of *liṭ*: "In *liṭ*, that which begins with a substitute (*ādeśa*)—of that which begins with it, [the rule] does not apply. And the mention of *iṭ* is for the case of *yaṅ*-lopa. The augment *iṭ* must also be stated in the case of *yaṅ*-lopa: *bebhiditā*, *bebhiditum*. Otherwise, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "after a monosyllabic root (*ekāc*) which is unaccented (*anudātta*) in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*)" would apply.

Furthermore, when reduplication occurs in its proper place, the entire complex (samudāya) is the substitute for the entire complex. In that case, because the root and the suffix are completely obscured, that [root] which was monosyllabic and unaccented in its original instruction (upadeśa) becomes lost. Even when reduplication involves double usage, there is no fault. We shall qualify the stem (aṅga) by means of the mention of "monosyllabic" (ekāj): [the rule applies] from a monosyllabic stem.

But surely, each individual element here is a single *aṅga*. The designation *aṅga* will apply to that which constitutes the completion of the sentence within the aggregate. Why is this so? Because it avoids the abandonment of the technical rule (*śāstra*). For in this way, the rule remains unviolated. Furthermore, there would be a need to prohibit the augment *iṭ* and the lengthening of vowels. [Examples: *jarīgṛhitā*, *jarīgṛhitum*, *grahaḥ*.

The rule "aliṭi dīrghaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.7) would result in lengthening [of the vowel]. However, when there is reduplication in place [of the whole], the substitute is for the entire unit. In that case, because the root and the suffix are completely merged, the root *grah-* is lost. Even if reduplication involves double application, there is no fault. We shall qualify the stem by means of *grah-*, [interpreting the rule as] "from the stem *grah-*. But is it not the case that each [element] is individual?

In this case, it is a member (*aṅga*). The designation "member" will apply to that which constitutes the completion of the sentence within the aggregate. Why is this so? Because of the non-abandonment of the technical rule (*śāstra*). For in this way, the technical rule remains unviolated. Furthermore, there is the prohibition of rules concerning word-initial elements (*padādi*). A prohibition must be stated regarding the rule defining word-initial elements; for example, in *siṣeca* and *suṣvāpa*, there would otherwise be a prohibition of the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*.

[The objection] applies. However, when there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*) in place [of the whole], the substitute is the whole for the whole. In that case, because the stem and the suffix are completely obscured, that which was the beginning of the word is lost. Furthermore, there is no fault even if reduplication consists in the double employment [of the whole]. We shall qualify the term *pada* by means of the suffixes *sup* and *tiṅ*: that from which the rule for *sup* and *tiṅ* begins is a *subanta* (ending in a *sup*) or a *tiṅanta* (ending in a *tiṅ*).

But surely, the rule for *sup* and *tiṅ* applies even from each individual [element] here? The designation of "word" (*pada*) will occur by virtue of that completion of the sentence which takes place in the aggregate. Why is this so?
Because of the non-abandonment of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*). For in this way, the treatise remains unviolated; those very *sup* and *tiṅ* suffixes are subsequent to that [aggregate].

And that very [suffix] is the original (*prakṛti*). The mention of "original" (*ādi*) is what is under discussion. By this, the status of being a word for a composite whole (*samudāyapadatva*) is established. (P_6.1.2.1) Regarding the statement "of the second," there is no need for its explicit mention. The term *ajādeḥ* is a genitive case derived from a *karmadhāraya* compound. It is possible to omit the word "of the second. How so? Because the genitive in *ajādeḥ* does not belong to a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

That which has *ac* as its initial element is "beginning with *ac*" (*ajādi*). [The question is: Is this [the word *ajādeḥ*] in the ablative case derived from a *karmadhāraya* compound? [Answer: No; rather, it is a fifth-case [ablative] form derived from a *karmadhāraya*. [That is to say,] *ac* is the beginning [of it], thus it is *ajādi*; [the rule means] "of that which follows what begins with *ac*. In that case, even without the explicit mention of "the second" (*dvitīya*), it will apply to the second [syllable] alone. (P_6.1.2.2) KA_III.6.1-8.7 Ro_IV.294-301 In the case of the reduplication of the second [syllable], the exclusion of the first [syllable] follows naturally.

In the case of the second reduplication, the cessation of the first must be stated, as in *aṭiṭiṣati* and *aśiśiṣati*. What is the reason? Because it would otherwise apply. For [the rule] "of a monosyllabic root, the first is reduplicated" would apply. But surely the reduplication of the second will supersede the reduplication of the first. How could that which is prescribed for one thing be a superseder of another? [This would be so] if it did not exist.

Furthermore, an obstruction occurs when there is a possibility [of both], and there is indeed such a possibility that both might exist. Or rather, it should not be stated [that there is an obstruction]. What is the reason? For when the first cognition exists, there is no attainment of a second, because there is no second. Nor should it be said [that there is an obstruction]. What is the reason? For when the first cognition exists, there would be no attainment of a second. What is the reason? Because there is no second. Indeed, this is not the case now regarding the doubling of the first.

When duplication has been performed, the second [element] becomes the second. What then? It becomes the third. Just as when two people are sitting and a third person is born, the second does not remain the second; what then? He becomes the third. For nothing is said to the effect that "before duplication has been performed, that which was the second must remain so. Rather, it is said that this occurs when duplication has been performed.
That which is the second [syllable] will belong to it. In this way, it would be equivalent to not undertaking [the rule at all]. There would be reduplication of the first syllable of *aṭ*.

[Then] *halādiśeṣaḥ* [would apply]. There would be reduplication of the second [syllable]. [Then] *halādiśeṣaḥ* [would apply again]. When there is the substitution of a single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) for the three *a*-vowels, the resulting form would be *aṭiṣati*. It is not equivalent to not undertaking [the rule]. There is reduplication of the first syllable of *aṭ*.

The *halādi-śeṣa* [remains]; the short *i* vowel (*ittva*); doubling of the second [consonant]; *halādi-śeṣa*; the short *i* vowel; for the two *i*-vowels, there is long-vowel substitution for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa-dīrghatva*); and for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) before a non-homogeneous vowel, there is the substitution of *iyaṅ*. Thus, the form *iyiṭiṣati* is obtained. And from the root *oṇ*, *uvaṇiṣati* is formed. The application of the grammatical rules cannot possibly be intended to produce undesirable results.

Or, just as in the case of a rule concerning the initial [element] (*ādivikāra*), there is no application of a rule concerning the final [element] (*antyavikāra*); or just as in the case of a rule concerning the initial (*ādividhi*), a rule concerning the final (*antyavidhi*) does not occur—so too, in the case of a second doubling (*dvitīyadvirvacana*), a first doubling (*prathamadvirvacana*) will not occur. [Reply: This is an unequal comparison.

For the rule concerning the initial (*ādividhi*) is not commenced when the rule concerning the final (*antyavidhi*) has not already become applicable; therefore, it shall be an exception (*bādhaka*) to that.

This too is of the same nature: the second doubling is not commenced while the first doubling has not yet been reached; therefore, it will be the sublater. As for what was said—that sublation occurs only when coexistence is impossible, and that here there is indeed the possibility for both to exist—this is not so; for sublation occurs even when coexistence is possible.

It occurs as follows: "Let curd be given to the Brahmins; let buttermilk be given to Kauṇḍinya. Even though the giving of curd is possible, the giving of buttermilk serves to exclude it. In the same way here as well, even though the first doubling is possible, the second doubling will set it aside. In that case, when the preceding vowel is removed—

The non-cessation of the consonant must be stated [as a rule], as in the case of *aṭiṭiṣati*. Just as there is the cessation of the vowel (*ac*), so too would the cessation of the consonant (*vyañjana*) result. In that regard, when the preceding vowel ceases, the non-cessation of the consonant follows because there is no instruction for its cessation.
Thus, when the preceding vowel ceases, the non-cessation of the consonant is established. Why? Because there is no instruction [to the contrary].

Regarding the preceding [rule]: we do not here teach a prohibition of the preceding [element]. What then? We are about to introduce the doubling of the second [element]. As for consonants, however, they are like the wives of actors. For example, when the wives of actors have gone to the stage, whomever asks, "Whose are you? Whose are you? they say to each of them, "Yours! Yours!"

In this way, consonants take on the operations prescribed for whichever vowel they follow. Furthermore, because of the prohibition regarding *n*, *d*, and so forth—specifically, the rule "the first elements of a conjunct (*saṃyoga*) are not doubled" (*na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ*)—the Teacher indicates that when the preceding [vowel] is removed, the consonant is not removed. In that case, since doubling of the first [consonant] is prohibited in the absence of a second, [the second is the one that is doubled].

In that case, if the second monosyllable (*ekāc*) is absent, the doubling of the first would not apply—as in *āṭatuḥ* and *āṭuḥ*. Why? Because it is prohibited; specifically, because of the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 6.1.2] that "the second [monosyllable] beginning with a vowel (*ajādih*) is doubled. This is not a fault. The prohibition applies when that [second monosyllable] exists; the prohibition of the first applies only when there is the doubling of the second. When that [second monosyllable] exists...

If it is argued that there is a prohibition [of the rule] when that [suffix] follows, then there is a fault regarding the *halādiśeṣa* (the retention of the first consonant). If it is argued that there is a prohibition when that [suffix] follows, then a fault arises in the case of *halādiśeṣa*. When *halādiśeṣa* applies, there would be the elision of everything except the initial consonant (*anādyasya lopaḥ*) whenever a consonant follows. This would occur only in cases such as *papāca* and *papāṭha*; it would not occur in cases such as *āṭatuḥ* and *āṭuḥ*. Regarding the *halādiśeṣa*, it is like what is observed in common usage (*lokavat*). It is like what is observed in common usage regarding the *halādiśeṣa*.

Success! It is as follows: in the world, a lord issues a command: "Let men be brought from every village; let Brahmins be brought from the villages east of Aṅga. If there are no Brahmins in those villages, then there can be no bringing of anyone else from them. This is because the existence of a Brahmin is present somewhere [or, according to R: everywhere] therein.

Just as [the suffix] *nivartikā* excludes what is not a Brahmin, so too here, in some cases, that which begins with a consonant (*hal-ādya*) becomes the displacer of every preceding vowel (*an-ādya*) consonant. If it is argued that in other cases there is elision (*lopa*), then reduplication (*dvirvacana*) would likewise result in elision in other cases. Furthermore, in some instances, being the second element, it would displace the entire first element.

It would be a negator. Therefore, let it be simply that there is a prohibition when that [suffix] exists. But was it not said: "If it is argued that there is a prohibition when that exists, then there is a fault in the rule for the substitution of *halādiśeṣa*"? This will be remedied under the rule for *halādiśeṣa*. (P_6.1.3) KA_III.8.9-22 Ro_IV.301-302 For what purpose is this stated? Because there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of reduplication (*dvirvacana*) for [roots] beginning with *n* and *d*.

In that context, there is a prohibition regarding the letters *n*, *d*, and *r*. For a monosyllabic root beginning with *n*, *d*, or *r*, reduplication would otherwise apply; therefore, a prohibition is stated for those [roots] beginning with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) that contain *n*, *d*, or *r*.
Regarding the root *īrṣya*: it should be stated that "the third syllable of *īrṣya* becomes doubled.
First, some say: "it is a monosyllabic root" [and thus the rule applies]; hence *īrṣyiṣiṣati*. Another says:

Regarding the rule *vyañjanasya*: [the augment] *īṭ* is applied in *īrṣyiyiṣati*. And regarding the *kaṇḍvādi* group: it should be stated that for the *kaṇḍvādi* verbs, the third [suffix] undergoes doubling.
Thus: *kaṇḍūyiyiṣati*, *asūyiyiṣati*. Regarding nominal stems (*nāmadhātu*): optionally, for nominal stems, the third [suffix] undergoes doubling. Thus: *vā nāmadhātūnām*.

Thus it should be stated: *aśvīyiyiṣati*, *aśiśvīyiṣati*. Another says: "Or as one pleases," because "the name-formations (*nāmadhātu*) may be treated as one pleases. Thus: *puputrīyiṣati*, *putitrīyiṣati*, *putrīyiyiṣati*. (P_6.1.4) It is said that "the preceding [part] is the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsa*). Of what is the preceding part designated as the reduplicated syllable?

It occurs. The word "two" (dve) is understood [from the previous rule]. It should be stated as "of two" (dvayoḥ). Then that instruction must be made accordingly. It need not be made; for by implication, there will be a change of case-ending. For example: "The houses of Devadatta are high. [When one says] "Address him," it is understood that [the address is] "Devadatta. Or: "The cows, horses, and gold of Devadatta."
Thus, it is understood that "Āḍhya" is the son of a widow, [and] "Devadatta" is the subject.

That which was previously indicated by the genitive case becomes, by implication, indicated by the accusative and the nominative. In the same way here as well, that which was previously indicated by the nominative will, by implication, become indicated by the genitive.

Regarding the designation *abhyasta* (repeated), the mention of "together" (*saha*) must be made. What is the purpose? It is so that the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) does not apply separately. The acute accent on the first syllable should belong to the two [syllables] when they are together; it should not belong to each one individually. There is no fault in this very same operation regarding the *abhyasta*.

That very rule has been recited: "The word that is to be pronounced with an *anudātta* accent is [so treated] except for one [other vowel]. Simultaneity is not possible. In that case, an alternation (*paryāya*) would follow. And indeed, there would be alternation. First, for the preceding [vowel], it will not occur because it is separated by the form of the subsequent [vowel]. But then it might occur for the subsequent [vowel]. Regarding that, the activity of the Teacher indicates that it does not occur for the subsequent one.

Thus, he says that for *bibheti* and so forth, the syllable preceding the *pit* affix becomes acute (*udātta*). In this way, it is stated that [the rule] does not apply to the preceding [syllable] due to intervention, nor to the following [syllable] due to the *jñāpaka*. Furthermore, it is taught that "for reduplicated (*abhyasta*) roots, the first syllable becomes acute.
In that case, the same fault would result in an undesirable alternative (*paryāya*). Therefore, the mention of *saha* must be made. It need not be made.

The mention of "both" (*ubhe*) is made so that it may be understood as having the sense of "together" (*saha*). Is there another purpose for the mention of "both"? What is it? The mention of "both" is for the purpose of indicating the technical term (*saṃjñī*). Even without the mention of "both," the indication of the technical term is already established. How so? Because the word "two" (*dve*) is understood from the previous context. Then what is the purpose [of the mention of "both"]? It is where both forms of the word are actually heard.
In that case, so that the designation "abhyasta" (repeated) applies there, it should not apply here: *īrtsanti*,
*īpsanti*, *īrtsan*.

*īpsan*, *airtsan*, *aipsan*. Furthermore, what would happen? The rules for the substitution of *at*, the prohibition of *num*, and the substitution of *jus*—these operations would undesirably apply. Regarding the substitution of *at*, there is no fault; for a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made in the seventh [chapter].
This is the case:

[the rule] "from that which ends in *at*" (P. 7.1.5), and then "in the *ātmanepada* endings" (P. 7.1.5). And in the *ātmanepada* endings, there is the substitution of *at*. The term "not ending in *a*" (*anataḥ*) is a remainder (*śeṣa*) for both. As for what is said—that there is a prohibition of the augment *num*—once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, it will not occur because of the absence of distinct separation (*vyapavarga*).

This must be considered here: let there be the prohibition of *num*, or let there be the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [operation]. What should be done here? The prohibition of *num* [should take effect] because it is subsequent. The single-substitute operation is permanent (*nitya*), for it applies whether the prohibition of *num* has been performed or not. The single-substitute operation is also permanent, for it applies when one thing has been performed and another when it has not been performed; [it concerns] a different word-form.

And if [the substitution] were to apply first, the rule would become non-eternal (*anitya*). In that case, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is *antaraṅga*. What is its *antaraṅga* nature? The single-substitute depends upon two phonemes (*varṇa*). Regarding the scope of the rule, there is a prohibition of the augment *num*;

however, the single-substitute occurs before the arising of the *sarvanāmasthāna* [case ending]. In that situation, because it is both eternal (*nitya*) and *antaraṅga*, the single-substitute [takes effect first].

Once the single-substitute (ekādeśa) has been applied, [the rule] will not apply because there is no distinct separation (*vyapavarga*). As for what was said—that the substitution of *jus* would occur—once the single-substitute has been applied, it will not occur because there is no distinct separation. It is said, "after a single-substitute," but by what is there a single-substitute here? By the suffix *-anti*. But the state of being *-anti* does not apply here. What is the reason? Because it is superseded by the substitution of *jus*. Not so here.
The substitution of *ju* would result [in *juhavatu*]. What is the reason? Because it is separated by the suffix *śap*. Once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been made, there is no separation.

But since "a single substitute is treated as the original in place of what precedes" (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is indeed still a separation. Furthermore, for what reason does the element *anti*, which possesses the cause [for the substitution], wait for the single-substitute, rather than [acting] immediately when the cause itself exists?
It should be understood as the absence of *anti*. In that case, since the cause [for the substitution] exists even here to that same extent, there would be the form *anti*. [Examples would be:

*anenijuḥ*, *paryaveviṣuḥ*. Let it be so. Once the absence of *anti* has been effected, because of the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), it will be included by the mention of *jhi*, and thus the substitution of *jus* will occur. Or alternatively, even though this *anti* possesses the cause [for its own application], the substitution of *jus* applies to it.
This is an exception (*apavāda*). General rules (*utsarga*) do not apply to the domain of an exception. For exceptions apply first, and only afterwards do general rules apply.
Or rather, having set aside the domain of the exception, the general rule then proceeds. In this case, the substitution of *ant* never occurs at all;
it awaits the substitution of *jus* as an exception. Indeed, it is not even the case that...

In some cases, there is immediate succession (*ānantarya*) between the affix *jhi* and the roots that have been repeated; however, in all cases, there is intervention by the *vikaraṇas*. Therefore, by this [rule], the disappearance of the *vikaraṇa* must necessarily be awaited—sometimes by means of *luk*, sometimes by *ślul*, and sometimes by means of a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*).
Just as it awaits *ślul* and *luk*, so too it awaits the single-substitute. If this is so, then this [point] must be explained here.

The teacher does not teach that there is the status of being like the original (sthānivadbhāva). [Objection: Because of the status of being like the original, there would be an intervention; because of the intervention, [the desired result] will not occur. [Response: The status of being like the original applies in a rule concerning what precedes, and this is not a rule concerning what precedes.

[Objection: A rule concerning what precedes is one that follows from what precedes. Therefore, since there is no other purpose, the mention of "both" (ubhe) is for the sake of expressing conjunction (sahārtha).

It will be understood. How so? Because the designation (*saṃjñā*) of "repeated" (*abhyasta*) applies to each individual [syllable]. It is observed that the completion of a sentence occurs for each [member] individually; for example, the designations *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* apply to each [element] separately. But is there not also this observed example where the completion of a sentence occurs with respect to a collective whole? For instance: "Let the Gargas be fined one hundred. [This refers to] those who are liable.

And kings possess gold, yet they do not punish each individual [offender] separately. Given this analogy, if it is said that "separately" applies there, then here too the inclusion of the word "together" (*saha*) should be made. Alternatively, if in that case the designations of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* apply separately even without the mention of "separately," then here too there is no purpose for the inclusion of the word "together."

(P_6,1.6) Regarding the rule *jakṣityādiṣu saptagrahaṇam vevītyartham*: the mention of "seven" (*sapta*) in the context of *jakṣityādi* must be made. It should be stated that seven roots beginning with *jakṣ* receive the designation *abhyasta*. What is the purpose? For the sake of *vevī*. So that the designation *abhyasta* may apply to *vevī*.

It is recited [in the list]. Or rather, it is not included because the list ends with *agaṇ*. Or rather, there is no purpose in including it in the list. Let the designation *abhyasta* apply up to the end of the *agaṇ* group. In that case, it would follow here as well for *āṅ-śāsu*. Let it be so. Why then do the operations pertaining to *abhyasta* not take place? Because the majority [of such operations] occur in the *parasmaipada*, and this [root] is *ātmanepada*. In that case, the accent (*svara*) would follow.

Even in those cases where there is an accentual operation for the *abhyasta* (repeated) forms among the *ātmanepada* endings, there too—by the rule that "an *lasārvadhātuka* suffix following an *anudātta* [root] becomes *anudātta*"—once the *anudātta* quality has been applied, there is no distinction whether the root-accent (*dhātusvara*) results in an *udātta* or the *abhyasta*-accent does. The roots *ṣas* and *vaś* are Vedic; in the Veda, one follows the observed usage. This is the *carkarīta* [reduplication].

[Objection: Then [the substitution] would apply even to *hnu* because it is a reduplicated (*abhyasta*) root. [Response: Let it be so. Why do the operations pertaining to reduplicated roots not take place? [Objection: Because the majority [of such operations] occur in the *parasmaipada*, and this [root *hnu*] is *ātmanepada*. [Response: Then the accent (*svara*) would apply. [Response: The accent will not occur due to the force of the rule enjoining the prohibition "in the case of *ah* and *iṅ*" (*ahnviṅoḥ*). Alternatively, these are only seven verbal roots.

They are recited [in the sūtras]: "The root *jakṣ* receives the designation *abhyasta*," and so forth; there are six such roots beginning with *jakṣ*. Regarding the rule "(P_6,1.7) KA_III.11.21-12.9 Ro_IV.309-310": "In the case of *tuj* and the others, the mention of the Vedic suffix must be made. That is to say, in the case of *tuj* and the others, the mention of the Vedic suffix must be performed; one must state that "in the Veda (*chandasi*), the lengthening of vowels occurs for *tuj* and the others."

And it should be stated that [the rule applies] "in this and that specific condition. It should not apply here: *tutoja śabalān harān*. Alternatively, there is no need to begin [this rule], because it is not included in the enumeration. Or rather, it is more logical not to initiate the lengthening in Vedic usage. Why? Because it is not included in the enumeration. For it is impossible to provide a complete enumeration of the instances of lengthening in the Veda. What is the reason?

And because it is observed in others: even for those [grammarians] for whom lengthening is not prescribed, lengthening is nevertheless seen in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), as in *pūruṣaḥ* and *nārakaḥ*. Furthermore, because of its non-universality: even for those for whom it is prescribed, there is non-universality; for in the very same grammatical condition (*pratyaya*) where lengthening is observed, it is not [observed] in that very same condition.
It is observed that [the forms] *mamahānaḥ* and *ukthapātram* occur as *mamahānaḥ*.
(P_6.1.8) Why is the word "dhātoḥ" (of a root) stated? [Consider the example: *īhām cakre*. This is not valid.

It is stated [in the rule] "when *liṭ* follows," yet we do not see *liṭ* here. [If you argue it exists] by virtue of the characteristic of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*), [we reply: no, because of the prohibition "not when [a suffix] marked with *lu* follows" (*na lumatā*).
In that case, there is a prohibition of the application of the rules concerning suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). What then? [The example is: *sasṛvāṃsaḥ viśṛṇvire*.

Regarding the reduplication in the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, there is an option for the root *jāgarti*. It should be stated: "In the *liṭ* tense, when reduplication occurs, there is an option for the root *jāgarti*. [Examples:

*yaḥ jāgara tam ṛcaḥ kāmayante* (He who is awake—the Ṛgvedic verses desire him) and *yaḥ jajāgāra tam ṛcaḥ kāmayante* (He who has awakened—the Ṛgvedic verses desire him). Why is it said "of that which is not a reduplicated base" (*anabhyāsasya*)? [Consider: *kṛṣṇaḥ*.

"Nonāva vṛṣabhaḥ yadi idam. [The form] *nonāva* is derived from the root *nonūyate*. Furthermore, the prohibition of reduplication (*abhyāsa-pratiṣedha*) is purposeless because of the rule stating "optionally in the Veda" (*chandasi vā-vacanāt*). The prohibition of reduplication is indeed useless. Why? Because of the rule "optionally in the Veda. It must necessarily be stated that "in the Veda, there is optionally a doubling [of the root]. What is the purpose? The purpose is for the sake of [the forms] *ādityān*, etc.
When *yāciṣāmahe* and *yiyāciṣāmahe* are expected [as forms], [the Vedic forms] are *devatā no dāti priyāṇi* (the deity grants us dear things) and *dadāti priyāṇi* (he gives dear things);

*maghavā dātu* (may Maghavan give) and *maghavā dadātu* (may Maghavan grant); *sa naḥ stuto vīravat dhātu* (he, being praised, may bestow upon us heroic sons) and *vīravat dadhātu* (may he bestow heroic sons).
Since it is stated that in the Veda (*chandasi*) there are two forms optionally, there is no purpose even in mentioning the word "root" (*dhātu*).

Why does [the form] *sasṛvāṃsaḥ* not occur as *viśṛṇvire*? Because of the statement "optionally in the Veda" (*chandasi vā*). Let this mention of the verbal root (*dhātugrahaṇa*), which belongs to the section on technical rules (*sānnyāsika*), stand for now. (P_6.1.9) Is this a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) or a locative (*saptamī*)? Why?

There is doubt. The instruction is identical. What follows from this? If it is the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), then the reduplication must apply to that which ends in *san* or *yaṅ*. If, however, it is the locative case (*saptamī*), then the reduplication applies to the preceding element when *san* or *yaṅ* follow. What is the distinction here? If it is "when *san* or *yaṅ* follow," then there would be reduplication of the augment *iṭ*, because it is treated as if it were at the beginning of the following element. If it is "when *san* or *yaṅ* follow" [and the rule applies to the preceding], then...

The augment *iṭ* should undergo reduplication: *aṭiṭiṣati*, *aśiśiṣati*. But for what reason is it not established? Because it is initial (*parādi*). The *iṭ* is initial. And [the reduplication] of *iṭ* after the root *han*: the reduplication of *iṭ* after the root *han* must also be performed: *jeghnīyate*. [Objection: But would not the same contingency of *sthānivadbhāva* (treatment as the original element) apply even to that which undergoes reduplication when followed by *san* or *yaṅ*?

In this case, because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), reduplication (*dvirvacana*) would not apply to the augment *īṭ*. This is not a fault. It is stated that [the substitute] is treated as the original when there is a vowel (*ac*) that is the cause of reduplication; however, this [augment *īṭ*] is not the cause of reduplication. Whatever causes reduplication, and whatever undergoes reduplication—all of that is the cause of reduplication. Therefore, reduplication applies to *īṭ*. Therefore...

The augment *iṭ* must undergo reduplication by both [rules]. Furthermore, a fault that applies to both [sides] cannot be charged against one alone. If the mention of "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśe*) in the rule *ekāca upadeśe 'nudāttāt* is intended as a qualifier of "acute" (*udātta*), then there would be a prohibition of *iṭ* for the suffix *san*.

If the mention of "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśe*) in the rule *ekāca upadeśe 'nudāttāt* is intended as a qualifier of "acute" (*udātta*), then there would be a prohibition of *iṭ* for the suffix *san*.

It must be stated: *bibhitsati*, *cicchitsati*. Once reduplication has occurred, the prohibition of *iṭ*—based on the rule "after a monosyllabic root that is unaccented in its original form (*upadeśa*) and is actually heard"—does not apply. Let it be, then, for a stem ending in *san* or *yaṅ*. If it is argued that it applies to what ends in *san* or *yaṅ*, then in the case of the root *aś* followed by *san*, which is otherwise *aniṭ*, reduplication must be stated [as an exception]. If it is argued that it applies to what ends in *san* or *yaṅ*, then for the root *aś* followed by *san*, which is *aniṭ*, reduplication must be stated.

Those who desire to sacrifice, being in agreement with the Bhṛgus—by whomsoever the reduplication is prescribed even when [the root] *sanyaṅ* follows, by that person also an effort must certainly be made here to prevent the insertion of *iṭ*. What is the reason? For *iṭ* is prescribed for the root *aś* specifically by the rule "smipūṅrañjaśām sani" (Pāṇini 7.2.74). By that very [rule], the second reduplication will also not occur. Or else:

This is not the form of the root *aś* (to eat). This is a Vedic elision of phonemes belonging to the root *yaj* (to sacrifice). For example: *tubhyam idam agne* [is used] where *tubhyam idam agne* was expected; *nāmbānām carum* where *āmbānām carum* was expected;
*āvyādhinīr ugaṇāḥ* where *sugaṇāḥ* was expected; and *iṣkartāram adhvarasya* where *niṣkartāram* was expected. [Also: *śivā*.

Regarding the forms *udrasya bheṣajī* and *śivā rudrasya bheṣajī*, when [the root] *rudh* is reached, it is understood in the sense of *aś* (to pervade). But what is the meaning of *aś*? The root *aś* has the sense of pervasion (*vyāpti*). The root *yaj* also functions in the sense of *aś*. How, then, can one [root] function in the sense of another? Roots have many meanings; for example: [The text continues with examples of roots having multiple meanings.]

The root *vap* is observed in the sense of scattering, but it also occurs in the sense of cutting, as in "he cuts the hair" (*keśān vapati*). The root *īḍ* is observed in the senses of praising, inciting, and begging, but it also occurs in the sense of impelling, as in "Agni indeed impels rain from here; the Maruts cause it to fall from yonder. This root *kṛ* is observed in the sense of the manifestation of what was previously non-existent, but it also occurs in the sense of cleansing, as in "make the back clean" (*pṛṣṭham kuru*).

"Make the feet"—it is understood as "rub them. It is also seen in the sense of "placing," as in "make [them] on a mat," "make [them] on a pot," or "make the stone here"—it is understood as "place it. If that is so, then [the rules for] lengthening, *kutva*, *prasāraṇa*, and the substitution of *ṣ* would apply to what is additional to the reduplication. However, lengthening is not established for what is additional to the reduplication, as in *cicīṣati* and *tuṣṭūṣati*.

The substitute is the entire complex (samudāya) for the entire complex. In that case, because the stem and the suffix are completely obscured, the [stem] having been lost, [the rule] "lengthening occurs for those ending in a vowel before the suffix *san*" does not apply. Here, this must be deliberated:
should the lengthening be performed, or the reduplication? What should be done here? Lengthening, because it is subsequent; and it is obligatory.
Regarding the reduplication: it applies whether the lengthening has already occurred or whether it has not yet occurred. Lengthening, too, is permanent;

it applies whether the reduplication has already occurred or whether it has not yet occurred. However, reduplication is not permanent, for it does not apply once the reduplication has already taken place. What is the reason? Because the substitute is a whole for the whole; in that case, [the original] is completely obscured.

Since the base and suffix do not end in a vowel (*ajantatā*), the rule for lengthening does not apply. Furthermore, reduplication is also non-obligatory (*anitya*): when the lengthening has been applied to one element, it applies to another; and a grammatical operation that applies to a different word-form is considered non-obligatory. Between these two non-obligatory operations, lengthening takes precedence because it is subsequent. As for that which [applies] when it has not yet been performed—

In the case of reduplication, the lengthening [of the vowel] is not established, as in *juhūṣati*. The substitution of *k* (kutva) for the root *han* is not established when it occurs beyond the stage of reduplication, as in *jighāṃsati* and *jaṅghanyate*. What is the reason? Because the entire complex is replaced by another entire complex. In that state, because the root and the suffix are completely merged, the root *han* becomes lost.

In that case, due to the repetition [of the root], the substitution of *k* for *h* in the reduplicated syllable (*kutva*) is not established. Furthermore, the *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) is not established for that which exceeds the reduplication, as in *juhūṣati* and *johūyate*. Here, the entire complex is replaced by another entire complex; consequently, because the root and suffix are obscured, the form *havayati* is lost. In that situation, the *samprasāraṇa* of the root *hve-* applies to the reduplicated stem.

Thus, the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) would not be obtained. This is not a fault; for he will state this: "of *hva* when it has an *abhyasta* [repeated] cause. And to the extent that it is now stated, "of *hva* when it has an *abhyasta* cause," even that is free from fault. As for what was said—"in that case, since lengthening does not occur when reduplication (*dvirvacana*) has not yet taken place, that is not established"—and as for the rule for *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*): [these are also resolved].

The rule does not apply to that which exceeds the reduplication, as in *pipakṣati* and *yiyakṣati*. Here, the entire complex is substituted for the entire complex; consequently, because the root and the suffix are completely obscured, the [suffixal] *s* is lost. Thus, the rule "the *s* following *iṇ* and *ku*" for the suffixal *s* would not obtain. This matter of reduplication must be considered here.

"Let there be *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*); what must be done here? "By virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), let there be *ṣatva*. "Regarding what is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to what precedes it, there can be no comparison between what is established and what is unestablished. And regarding *ā* and *br̥dh*, there is a prohibition of rules based on the reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*). For *ā* and *br̥dh*, a rule dependent on the reduplicated stem would apply; that must be prohibited. [Examples: *īpsati*, *īrtsati*.

*īpsan*, *īrtsan*, *aipsan*, *airtsan*. Furthermore, what would happen? The rules for the elision of *at*, the prohibition of *num*, and the substitution of *jus* would all apply [erroneously]. This is not a fault, for the solutions have already been stated here: in the case of depending on *saṅ*, because the whole is the substitute for the whole; and in the case of depending on *jhal*, there is no designation because of the intermingling. And in the case of depending on *saṅ*...

Because the whole [substitute] takes the place of the whole [original], and because there is no designation when a *jhal* [consonant] is the basis [of an operation]. What is the reason? Because of being mixed (*āmiśratva*).

This becomes intermingled. For example, as when milk and water are mixed together. Because of being mixed, it is not known how much is milk and how much is water; nor is it known in which part is the milk and in which part is the water.

In this case as well, because they are mixed together, it is not known which is the base (*prakṛti*) and which is the suffix (*pratyaya*), nor in what position the base occurs and in what position the suffix occurs. What is the fault in that? The rules for *kutva* and so forth—such as "when *saṅ* follows a *jhal*"—would not be established. Here, one must deliberate between performing reduplication (*dvirvacana*) or applying *kutva* and so forth; what should be done in this instance?

Because they are subsequent, the *kutva* changes and so forth [apply]. When what precedes is not established (*pūrvatrāsiddha*), there is no comparative evaluation (*sampradhāraṇā*) between what is established and what is unestablished regarding the *kutva* changes and so forth.

If that is the case, then it must be stated: "That which is unestablished with respect to what precedes does not apply when there is reduplication. And this must certainly be stated, because [certain rules] cause optional application (*vibhāṣita*): *drogdhā* / *drogdhā*, *droḍhā* / *droḍhā*. To whatever extent "that which is unestablished with respect to what precedes" [applies], [so much applies] now.

Regarding the statement "in the case of reduplication," that too is not a fault. As for what was said—that the substitution of *ṣ* is not established—it is because here, in the case of reduplication by way of substitution (*sthāne-dvirvacana*), the elision of the *ṇi*-affix (*ṇilopa*) has not been addressed. When reduplication occurs after the suffixes *san* and *yaṅ*, it must be stated that there is reduplication of the augment *iṭ*. Furthermore, when reduplication occurs after a root ending in *san* or *yaṅ*, the change of *han* to *k* (*kutva*) has not been addressed; in that regard, [the rule applies] to that which ends in *san* or *yaṅ*.

The position that there is both reduplication and double application is faultless. Regarding that, this objection—that there would be a prohibition of the *iṭ* augment after the suffix *san*—has not yet been answered. He will provide the answer for this as well, stating that it is established because both [the root and the suffix] serve as qualifiers.
How is it that *jeghnīyate* is formed? He will explain this in the section on *yaṅ* (intensive) that after the root *han*, when meaning "injury," the substitute *ghnī* occurs.

(P_6,1.12.1) KA_III.16.9-23 Ro_IV.317-318: What is the irregular formation (*nipātana*) of *dāśvān*? In the case of the suffix *vas*, there is the prohibition of reduplication and the augment *iṭ* for the root *dāś*. In the case of the suffix *vas*, the prohibition of reduplication and the augment *iṭ* are irregularly prescribed for *dāś*: *dāśvaṃsaḥ*, *dāśuṣaḥ sutaṃ*, *dāśvān*. What is the irregular formation of *sāhvān*? There is the lengthening of the vowel for the root *sah*, and furthermore, the prohibition of reduplication and the augment *iṭ*.

And: *sāhvān*, *balāhakaḥ*, *sāhvān*, *mīḍhvān*—what is here irregularly formed (*nipātyate*)? [The answer is: from the root *miha* (to sprinkle), there is the substitution of *ḍha*. And what else? That which belongs to the two preceding [roots]. And what belongs to the two preceding? The prohibition of reduplication and of the augment *iṭ*, as well as lengthening. "O bountiful one (*mīḍhvaḥ*), be gracious to our offspring and progeny. "As this [earth], O Indra, O bountiful one (*mīḍhvaḥ*). Indeed, the sense of "greatness" is understood. Which [root]? [It is *mah*, "to honor," etc.]

Furthermore, [the root] *mahi* has the sense of "greatness" (*mahyartha*). The root *mahi* has the action of giving as its meaning. What follows from this? Its short vowel form (*itva*) must also be prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation). If it is argued that [the form is] established because the root *mihi* has that same meaning—namely, if it is argued that the root *mihi* also occurs in the sense of "greatness"—how indeed can one root function in the sense of another? Roots have many meanings.

Thus [it is said]. But does the root *mihi* also occur elsewhere in the sense of "to rain"? He says: it does. From *mihi*, [we derive] *megha*. And why is it called *megha*? Because it gives water (*apaḥ dadāti*).
In the section on reduplication (*dvirvacana-prakaraṇa*), [there is the rule]: "The suffix *ke* is applied after *kṛñ* and others in the section on reduplication."

An addition must be made to the rule regarding the roots *kṛñ* and others, stating that the suffix *ke* applies: as in *cakram*, *ciklidam*, and *caknam*. It should be stated that this applies to the roots beginning with *kā* as well, so that it may occur here too: as in *babhruḥ* and *yayuḥ*. Regarding the roots *car*, *cal*, *pat*, and *vad*, it should be stated that when the suffix *ac* follows, they undergo reduplication and the augment *āk* is added to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Thus, for the roots *car*, *cal*, *pat*, and *vad*, there is reduplication before the suffix *ac*, and the augment *āk* is applied to the reduplicated syllable.

*carācaraḥ*, *calācalaḥ*, *patāpataḥ*, *vadāvadaḥ*. The suffix *gha* should also be prescribed after the root *han*. When the suffix *ac* follows, the root is reduplicated and the augment *āk* is added to the reduplicative syllable (*abhyāsa*). Thus: *ghanāghanaḥ*. The elision of the *ṇi* suffix and the lengthening of the reduplicative syllable should also be prescribed for the root *pāṭ*. Furthermore, the substitution of *ūk* for the reduplicative syllable should be prescribed for the root *pāṭ*. It should be stated that when the suffix *ac* follows, the root is reduplicated. Thus: *pāṭūpāṭaḥ*.
The long vowel and the augment *ūk* are added [to the reduplicated syllable]. *pāṭupaṭaḥ*. (P.

6.1.12.3) Reduplication takes precedence by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) over the substitution of *yaṇ*, *ay*, *av*, and *āv*; elision (*lopa*); elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*); elision of the suffix *ṇi*; the substitution of *ki* and *kī*; and the substitution of *ut*. Reduplication occurs in preference to the substitutions of *yaṇ*, *ay*, *av*, and *āv*; elisions; elision of the penultimate vowel; elision of the suffix *ṇi*; the substitutions of *ki* and *kī*; and the substitution of *ut*.

The scope for reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is, for example, *bibhidatuḥ* and *bibhiduḥ*. The scope for the *yaṇ*-substitution is, for example, *dadhi atra* and *madhu atra*. In this case [of *cakratuḥ* and *cakruḥ*], both rules would apply. The scope for the substitutions of *ay*, *av*, and *āv* is, for example, *cayanam*, *cāyakaḥ*, *lavanam*, and *lāvakaḥ*. The scope for reduplication is the same as before. In this case [of *cāyakaḥ* and *lāvakaḥ*], both rules would apply.

*cicāya*, *cicayitha*; *lulāva*, *lulavitha*. The scope for the elision of *ā* (ā-lopasya) is: *godaḥ*, *kambaladaḥ*. The scope for reduplication (dvirvacanasya) is the same. Here, both [rules] would apply: *yayatuḥ*, *yayuḥ*; *tasthatuḥ*, *tasthuḥ*. The scope for the elision of the penultimate vowel (upadhālopasya) is: *śleṣmaghnam madhu*, *pittaghnam ghṛtam*. The scope for reduplication is...

That very same [rule] applies here to both cases: *āṭitat*, *āśiśat*. The scope for the substitution of *ut* is seen in forms such as *nipūrtāḥ piṇḍāḥ*; the scope for reduplication is that same [form]. Here, both would apply simultaneously: *mitrātvaruṇau taturiḥ* and *dūre hyadhvā jaguriḥ*.
Reduplication occurs by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Well then, what is that prior counter-exception?

It should be stated; it need not be stated. The word *para* signifies "desired. In a conflict [of rules], that which is desired is the one that prevails. Rules for reduplication, rules for *prasāraṇa*, rules for *atva*, rules for changes at the beginning of a root, rules for *rītv*, *ittva*, and *uttva*, and rules for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* take precedence over reduplication. That is to say, rules for reduplication, rules for *prasāraṇa*, rules for *atva*, rules for changes at the beginning of a root, rules for *rītv*, *ittva*, and *uttva*, and rules for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* prevail over reduplication.

[This is] by way of conflict. The scope for reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is, for example, *bibhidatuḥ* and *bibhiduḥ*. The scope for vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) is, for example, *iṣṭam* and *suptam*. Here, both would apply: *ījatuḥ* and *ījuḥ*. This is not a valid objection. Let there be reduplication here; once reduplication has been performed, the form of the subsequent [root] will apply to the preceding [portion] by virtue of the rule "before a *kit* suffix."

Regarding the rule *liṭi abhyāsasya ubhayeṣām*: this then is *soṣupyate*. And this also is an example: *ījatuḥ*, *ījuḥ*. But has it not been said: "Let there be reduplication here; once reduplication is performed, the [guṇa] substitution for the subsequent form will occur by the rule *kiti*, and for the preceding [reduplicated] syllable, it will occur by the rule *liṭi abhyāsasya ubhayeṣām*"? It is not established; for when there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), [the rule does not apply].

The prohibition [of *samprasāraṇa*] by the rule "samprasāraṇam" would apply; however, it will not apply because [the vowel] is separated by the letter *a*. Once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been made, there is no separation. But since a single-substitute is treated as the original (sthānivat) for the sake of a preceding rule, there is indeed still a separation due to that *sthānivadbhāva*. If that is the case, he will raise the objection there regarding the mention of "belonging to the same constituent" (*samānāṅga*). This is the scope for the substitution of *ā*.

*glātā*, *mlātā*. In the case of reduplication (*dvirvacana*), that same [rule applies]. Here, both [rules] would apply: *jagle*, *mamle*. The scope for changes at the beginning of the root (*dhātu*) is, for example, *namati*, *siñcati*. In the case of reduplication, that same [rule applies]. Here, both [rules] would apply: *nanāma*, *siseca*, *sasnau*. The scope for the substitution of *r* (*rītvam*) is, for example, *mātrīyati*, *pitrīyati*.

That same [rule] applies to reduplication. Here, both [rules] would apply: *cekrīyate*, *jehrīyate*. [The rule for] *ītva* has its scope in cases such as *pīyate*, *gīyate*; [the rule for] reduplication has that same scope. Here, both would apply: *pepīyate*, *jegīyate*. [The rules for] *ittva* and *uttva* have their scope in cases such as *āstīrṇam*, *nipūrtāḥ*; [the rule for] reduplication has that same scope. Here, both [would apply].

[The suffix] *prāpnoti* [is applied]; it is spread (*ātistīryate*); it is filled (*nipoṣyate*). There is scope for both *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [substitutions]: as in *cetā* and *gauḥ*. For *dvirvacana* (reduplication), the same [scope applies]. Here, both would apply: *cicāya*, *cicayitha*; *lulāva*, *lulavitha*. This is not a valid purpose [for the rule]. Let there be reduplication here; once reduplication has been performed, let the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions apply to the subsequent form.

[The forms] *iyāya* and *iyayitha* will result. But then this is the purpose [of the rule]: [to prevent the substitution of] *iyāya* and *iyayitha*. However, it has been stated that there is no need for this. Let there be reduplication here. Once reduplication is performed, the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions will apply to the subsequent form. This is not established; because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the substitution of a long vowel with a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇadīrghatva*) would take effect first. [But] an operation concerning the constituent parts of a word (*āṅga*) is stronger than one concerning phonemes (*vārṇa*).

The *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions will occur. Should this be stated? No, it need not. How is it understood without being explicitly stated? The activity of the Teacher indicates that an internal (*āṅga*) operation is stronger than one based on a phoneme (*vārṇa*), since he employs the term "non-homogeneous" (*asavarṇa*) in the rule *abhyāsasya asavarṇe*.

It functions [as an indicator]. How does it function as an indicator? Because, without *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) would not have a dissimilar vowel (*asavarṇa*) following it. This is not a valid indicator, for this [rule] might be intended for the sake of *arti*: *iyartaḥ*, *iyṛthaḥ*, [and *uvoṇa*, *uvoṇithaḥ*].
If that is so, then what about the fact that it teaches the lengthening in the rule "lengthening of *iṇ* before a *kit* suffix"? Even for this, there is a purpose in its statement.

What [is the purpose]? This [rule] would be for the sake of subverting the long vowel of homogeneous quality (*savarṇadīrgha*). If that is so, then just as it subverts the long vowel of homogeneous quality, it would likewise subvert the *yaṇ* substitution as well. If this is the case, then a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made regarding the *yaṇ* substitution:
first, "for *iṇ*, *yaṇ* occurs"; then, "for *e* that has more than one vowel. Thus, *yaṇ* occurs for *e* that has more than one vowel and is also *iṇ*.

Then, regarding the rule *asaṃyogapūrvasya*, it is simply *eḥ anekācaḥ*. In that case, the mention of *asavarṇa* (non-homogeneous) is indeed the indicator (*jñāpaka*). But was it not said that this [mention of *asavarṇa*] would be for the sake of [the forms] *artya* and so on? No; a single example does not necessitate the inclusion of the term *asavarṇa*.

Even so, due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), *iyaṅ* would not apply. Now, even if there were a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), to the extent that the status of being a substitute exists—
How is this established? That which precedes an *ac* that has not been explicitly prescribed (*anādiṣṭa*) undergoes the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) with respect to an operation;
and this [element] precedes an *ac* that has been explicitly prescribed (*ādiṣṭa*).
(Regarding the rule *ṣyaṅaḥ saṃprasāraṇe putrapatyoḥ tadādau*)...

There is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). When there is *saṃprasāraṇa* of the suffix *ṣyaṅ*, there is an over-extension in the case of words beginning with "son" (*putra*) and "husband" (*pati*), for *saṃprasāraṇa* would apply to words such as "son" and "husband. For example: *kārīṣagandhyāputrakulam* and *kārīṣagandhyāpatikulam*. This is established by the mention of the phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇāt*). This [rule] applies when there is a mention of a specific phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇe*) in which...

The rule applies at the beginning of that [compound] and so forth; however, this is not a mention of a *varṇa* (phoneme). If it is argued that it is a mention of a *varṇa*, then a prohibition must be stated regarding that which ends in such a [phoneme].

If it is a mention of a *varṇa*, then a prohibition must be formulated for that which ends in it. Otherwise, *samprasāraṇa* would apply to words ending in *putra* and *pati*, as in *kārīṣagandhyāparamaputraḥ*.
The husband of Kārīṣagandhyā’s younger sister; the son of Kaumudagandhyā’s younger sister;

the husband of Kaumudagandhyā’s younger sister. What is the reason? For where there is no rule concerning that which begins with [a specific element], there must be a rule concerning that which ends with it.
But this is established by the mention of the "subsequent member" (uttarapada). How is it established? By the mention of the "subsequent member."
It should be stated that [the rule applies] when *putra* and *pati* are the subsequent members (*uttarapada*). If so, then it must be stated. No, it need not be stated.

These two terms, "prior member" (*pūrvapada*) and "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), are relative terms: there is a "subsequent member" only when there is a "prior member," and there is a "prior member" only when there is a "subsequent member. And in this case, *putra* and *pati* are not the subsequent members. If that is so, then here too—

One does not obtain [the forms] *kārīṣagandhīputraḥ* or *kārīṣagandhīpatiḥ*. What is the reason? It is stated that [the term] "prior member" (*pūrvapada*) [is intended]. For in this case, the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is not the prior member;
rather, the prior member ends in *ṣyaṅ*. How so? When there is a mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*), the inclusion of everything beginning with that [suffix] is understood.

It occurs as follows: if it is stated that when there is a mention of a suffix (*pratyaya*), the inclusion of that [word] and what begins with it is understood, then forms such as *paramakārīṣagandhīputraḥ* and *paramakārīṣagandhīpatiḥ* would not be established. [The rule applies] when there is a mention of a suffix, the inclusion of that [word] and what begins with it is understood, provided it is not a feminine suffix (*astrīpratyaya*). If it is stated "provided it is not a feminine suffix," then in the case of *atikrāntaḥ kārīṣagandhyām* (one who has surpassed Kārīṣagandhyā), the form *atikārīṣagandhyaḥ* [is established].

In the case of *tasya putraḥ* (his son), namely *atikārīṣagandhyāputraḥ* (the son of Atikārīṣagandhyā) or *atikārīṣagandhyāpatiḥ* (the husband of Atikārīṣagandhyā), [the rule] would also apply here. [The answer is: "Not so, because of the condition 'not being a feminine suffix' (*astrīpratyayena*) and 'not being a secondary member' (*anupasarjanena*). For that technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) applies where a feminine suffix is a secondary member (*upasarjana*), specifically in the context of the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇe*) where the compound is derived from it.
"Then there is the inclusion of that [term] and what follows it.

(P. 6.1.13.2) In the case of a word ending in *ṣyaṅ*, the *samprasāraṇa* substitution would apply to all the *yaṇ* sounds therein—for example, in *vārāhiputraḥ* and *tārṇakarṇīputraḥ*. Therefore, a prohibition must be stated for a *yaṇ* that does not reside in an affix (*apratyayastha*), according to how it has been formulated.

[Objection: It is established by the statement regarding substitution (*ādeśavacana*) that [the rule] does not apply when [the substitute] resides in a suffix (*apratyayastha*). Since substitutions occur for that which is being specifically pointed out (*nirdiśyamāna*), it will not apply to that which does not reside in a suffix. [Response: Or rather, [it applies] to that which is in the vicinity of the final letter (*antyasadeśa*) in cases where there is no modification of the non-final letter (*anantyavikāra*). Alternatively, this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) must be formulated: "In cases where there is no modification of the non-final letter, the operation applies to that which is in the vicinity of the final letter. [Question: But what is the difference here between this [rule] and the following technical rule? *Anantyavikāre 'ntyasadeśasya vā* ("In cases where there is no modification of the non-final letter, [the operation applies] optionally to that which is in the vicinity of the final letter"). Or else, *Anantyavikāre 'ntyasadeśasya kāryam bhavati* ("In cases where there is no modification of the non-final letter, the operation applies to that which is in the vicinity of the final letter")? [Response: There is no difference. Both are the same. However, the latter formulation is more concise. Furthermore, since the former rule would lead to the undesirable consequence that the elision of the final letter (*lopa*) would also apply to that which is in the vicinity of the final letter, the latter rule is preferable. Thus, the rule *anantyavikāre 'ntyasadeśasya kāryam bhavati* is established. This is the meaning.
Or rather, let the prohibition be stated for that which does not stand in the condition of being a *pratyaya*. This *paribhāṣā* must necessarily be formulated.

There are many purposes served by this *paribhāṣā*. What are they? The purpose is: "there is no *samprasāraṇa* when there is [already] a *samprasāraṇa*. It becomes unnecessary to state: "there is no *samprasāraṇa* when there is [already] a *samprasāraṇa*. How so? In the case of the root *vyadh*, we have the form *viddhaḥ*.

Thus, because an operation applies to that which is situated in the vicinity of the final [element] when there is no modification of the final [element], there is no fault. This purpose is not necessary; it is already accomplished in the very formulation (*nyāsa*). [The purpose is seen] in the case of the lengthening of a vowel following a word ending in *s* or the word *mahat*:
[e.g.,] *payāṃsi*.

[Objection: The rule *yaśāṃsi* etc. would also apply here [to forms like *yaśāṃsi*]. [Response: There is no fault, because of the principle that "when a modification applies to what is not final, it affects that which is in the vicinity of the final. [Objection: Even this is not a valid purpose, for the condition *nopadhāyāḥ* ("not when there is a penultimate vowel") continues to apply there. [Response: Even so, the rule would still apply in cases such as *anāṃsi* and *manāṃsi*. [Objection: This is not a fault; we shall qualify the penultimate vowel by means of the conjunction ending in *s*. That is, [the rule will apply] to the penultimate vowel of a conjunction ending in *s*. [Objection: Even so, it would still apply in *haṃsaśirāṃsi*.

[Objection: In this case, [the rule] would also apply to *dhvaṃsa-śiras*. [Reply: This is not a fault. *Haṃsa-* is derived from the root *ham* (to go). [Question: But who says that *haṃsa-* is derived from *ham*? [Reply: Rather, *haṃsa-* is derived from the root *han* (to kill), as in "it traverses the path" (*adhvānaṃ hanti*). [Reply:

In that case, the term *sarvanāmasthāne* (in the presence of a nominal suffix) is understood [from the preceding sūtra]. We shall qualify the conjunct consonant ending in *s* by its being followed by a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix.

[The rule] "there is no [substitution] for a *sa*-ending *saṃyoga* that follows a *sarvanāmasthāna*" applies when there is elision (*al-lopa*) of the final *an*. The purpose of the elision of the final *an* in a word ending in *an* is seen in forms such as *takṣṇā* and *takṣṇe*.

[Objection: In this case, the substitution [of *na* for *n*] would also apply here [to the *n* of *takṣṇ-ā*]. [Response: When a modification does not affect the final [element], the operation applies to that which is in the vicinity of the final element (*antya-sadeśa*).

Thus, there is no fault. But even this [solution] lacks purpose. We shall qualify the vowel *a* by means of the suffix *ana*: "the vowel *a* which belongs to that which ends in *ana*. Even so, it would still apply in cases such as *anasā* and *anase*. We shall qualify the stem (*aṅga*) by means of the letter *n*: "the vowel *a* which belongs to a stem ending in *n* that ends in *ana*. Even so, [it would still apply] in *anastakṣṇā*.

[An objection is raised: "In the case of *anastakṣṇe*, this [rule] would also apply. [The reply is: "In that case, let the technical definitions (*saṃjñā*) and interpretive rules (*paribhāṣā*) be operative at the time the grammatical operation takes place. Wherever the operation occurs, it should be understood as present there. When the rule *bhasya* is present, this [rule] *yaci bham* is also present. There, we shall qualify the *an* [of *bhasya*] by its being followed by a suffix beginning with *yaj* and so on; [we shall qualify] the *an* [as] that which follows a suffix beginning with *yaj*."

Regarding the statement "that which is *akāra*": in the rule prescribing *vṛddhi* for the root *mṛj*, there is a purpose [for the rule]. In the form *nyamārṭ*, *vṛddhi* would also apply to the augment *aṭ*. However, there is no fault, because when a modification does not concern the final phoneme (*anantyavikāra*), the operation applies to that which is in the position of the final phoneme (*antyasadeśasya*).
This too is not a purpose [for the rule], because according to the established paribhāṣā, "guṇa and *vṛddhi* [apply] to *ik*" (P. 1.1.3), *vṛddhi* applies only to an *ik* vowel.

It will be so. Even in this case, [the rule] would apply here in *mimārjiṣati*. Let it be so; by the reduction of the repetition (*abhyāsa*), there will be a short vowel. And there is a purpose for the *samprasāraṇa* of the *vasu* [root]: see *viduṣaḥ*.

[Otherwise], the [substitution] would also apply to the *v* of *vidi*. [But] because of the principle that "when a change does not affect the final [element], the operation applies to what is in the position of the final," it does not [apply].

There is a fault. This too is not a valid purpose. [Objection: There will be a prohibition by the rule "when there is a *samprasāraṇa*, [another] *samprasāraṇa* does not take place. [Response: Because it is separated by the letter *d* (or *id*), the rule does not apply. [Objection: In that case, since substitutes apply only to what is explicitly mentioned (*nirdiśyamāna*), it will not occur. And for the *yuvan*-class [of words], there is a purpose when there is *samprasāraṇa*.

In the forms *yūnaḥ*, *yūnā*, and *yūne*, the substitution would also apply to the letter *y*. [This is not the case] because of the principle: "When a modification does not concern the final sound, it applies to that which occupies the position immediately preceding the final sound. Thus, it does not apply here.

A fault arises. This objection also has no force. [One might argue: "When there is a *samprasāraṇa*, another *samprasāraṇa* does not occur," and thus it would not apply. [But] because of the intervention of the letter *u*, it does not apply. [If one says: "Once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been made, there is no intervention," [we reply:
because of the status as a *sthānivadbhāva*—whereby a single substitute is treated like the original in rules concerning what precedes—it remains an intervention indeed. Thus...

In that case, one might object here regarding the inclusion of the term "identical member" (*samānāṅga*) and the inclusion of the term "penultimate" (*upadhā*) for *r* and *v*. However, the inclusion of the terms "penultimate" for *r* and *v* need not be made. Why does [the rule] not apply here in the case of *abibhar bhavān*? There is no fault, because when a modification applies to what is not the final element, it takes effect on that which is in the position immediately preceding the final element (*antyasadeśa*). This objection, too, serves no purpose.
It is applied only in the context of *nyāsa*.

Due to the connection with rules concerning initial elements (*ādividhi*), there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding elision (*lopa*), *kutva*, *ḍhatva*, *bhaṣbhāva*, *ṣatva*, and *ṇatva*. There is over-extension in the case of rules concerning initial elements: [the rules] "The *ṣ* at the beginning of a verbal root is changed to *s*" (*dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ*) and "The *ṇ* is changed to *n*" (*ṇo naḥ*).
These would apply here [inappropriately]: as in *netā*.
The suffix *sotā* would not occur here; [but it occurs] in *namati* and *siñcati*, etc. The rule concerning *tyadādi* (the group beginning with *tyad*) would apply only here:
*tat*, *saḥ*, *tyat*.

In the case of *syaḥ*, the rule [for *tyadādi*] would not apply here; it is a *tyadādi* operation. The elision of the first member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*) would apply only here: *maṅktā*, *maṅktavyam*; it would not apply here. The substitution of *k* for *g* (*kutva*) would apply only here: *paktā*, *paktavyam*; the substitution of *bh* for *p* (*bhaṣbhāva*) would not apply here. The substitution of *ḍh* for *dh* (*ḍhatva*) would apply only here: *leḍhā*, *leḍhavyam*; it would not apply here.

[The rule for] *ḍhatva* would apply only here [in *abhutsi*], but not in *abhutsātām*. [The rule for] *bhaṣbhāva* would apply only here [in *abhutsi*], but not there. [The rule for] *ṣatva* would apply only here [in *draṣṭā*], but not in *draṣṭavyam*. [The rule for] *ṇatva* would apply only here [in *māṣāvāpeṇa*], but not in *māṣāvāpāṇām*. These...

The defects are either equal in number or more numerous; therefore, there is no purpose served by this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*). For a technical rule should not be formulated, nor should a grammatical definition (*lakṣaṇa*) be composed, simply because defects exist. Indeed, pots are not left unheated on the fire just because there are beggars, nor are barley seeds not sown just because there are wild animals. Furthermore, these defects are indeed present in their entirety.
The enumerated purposes are merely illustrative. Why is this so? Because there is no definition of faults (*doṣa*).

Therefore, this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) must be formulated for the sake of those purposes of this *paribhāṣā*, and a remedy (*pratividheya*) must be provided regarding the faults. This is the remedy: it is established by the mention of the acute accent (*udātta*). Wherever this *paribhāṣā* is intended [to apply].

In that case, an explicit mention of the acute accent (udātta) should be made. Then it should be stated: "When there is no modification of the final element, an operation applies to that which is in the position of the final element, provided there is an explicit mention of the acute accent. Well then, that explicit mention of the acute accent must be made. It need not be made;
for this paribhāṣā applies only where both that which is in the position of the final element and that which is not in the position of the final element are simultaneously present.

In the case of faults (*doṣa*), in one instance it concerns that which is in the vicinity of the final phoneme (*antyasadeśa*), while in another it concerns that which is not in the vicinity of the final phoneme (*anantyasadeśa*). In the case of purposes (*prayojana*), however, in that very same context there is both that which is in the vicinity of the final phoneme and that which is not in the vicinity of the final phoneme. Indeed, the Teacher has recorded such types of purposes as those which possess both characteristics. This is one example where, just as there is a fault, so too is there the mention of the *upadhā* (penultimate) vowel in the rule regarding *r* and *v*.
And that [suffix] is also applied only when there is a *nyāsa* (substitution).

(P. 6.1.14) [Example: *mātṛc*. One whose mother is Kārīṣagandhyā is *kārīṣagandhyāmātaḥ* or *kārīṣagandhyāmātaḥ*. [With the suffix] *mātṛka*: one whose mother is Kārīṣagandhyā is *kārīṣagandhīmātṛkaḥ*.
*kārīṣagandhyāmātṛkaḥ*, *mātṛkaḥ*, *mātṛ*, *kārīṣagandhīmātā*, *kārīṣagandhyāmātā*, *mātṛ*.
(P_6.1.16) Why is the mention of *vay* [in the rule] necessary? Is it not because *veñ* is included among the roots beginning with *yaj*?

It is recited that *vayi* is the substitute for *veñ*; in that case, it would already be established by the rule "for roots beginning with *yaj* before a *kit* suffix. To this, one might object: "This new rule is begun for the sake of the *ṅit* suffixes. But that is not so; for this substitution occurs before the *liṭ* suffix, and the *liṭ* is indeed *kit*. Therefore, he reads the following answer: "The mention of *vayi* is because of the prohibition regarding *veñ*. The mention of *vayi* is made [to prevent the application of the rule to *veñ*]."

Because of the prohibition regarding *veñ*. He will state a prohibition for *veñ* in the context of the *liṭ* [perfect tense]. That [prohibition] should not apply to *vay-* [the root meaning "to weave"]. For just as a rule is sought by virtue of the mention of *veñ*, so too would a prohibition apply. Alternatively, the prohibition of the *yakāra* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is no such prohibition. Or rather, this fault does not exist. Why? Because this [mention of *vayaḥ*] in the *liṭ* [is intended to indicate something else].

By thus prescribing the prohibition of *samprasāraṇa* for the root *vay-* (to weave), the Teacher indicates that the prohibition of *samprasāraṇa* does not apply [only] by virtue of the mention of the root *veñ*. This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*). This [prohibition] must be for the sake of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) when followed by a suffix beginning with *p* (*pit*); that is, so that there may not be *samprasāraṇa* of the *y* of the reduplicated syllable in the case of *vay-* when *pit* suffixes follow. But is it not [the case that...]?

And because of the inclusion of the word *veñ*, the prohibition of *samprasāraṇa* for the *yakāra* of the reduplicated syllable of *vay-* is established even in the case of *pit* suffixes. It is not established. Why? Because the term *kiti* (after a *kit* suffix) is understood to carry over there. Even so, *samprasāraṇa* would not apply to the *yakāra* of the reduplicated syllable of *vay-* even in the case of *pit* suffixes. Why? Because of the rule *halādiśeṣaḥ*.

It is obstructed. Here, the rule for the substitution of the first consonant (*halādiśeṣa*) does not apply. Why? Because he will state this: "The *samprasāraṇa* of the reduplication [of *vye*] takes precedence over the *halādiśeṣa* by way of conflict. Thus, this prohibition of *samprasāraṇa* for the *yakāra* of *vye* serves the purpose of the reduplication when followed by a *pit* suffix; it is not intended as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). If it is argued that it serves the purpose of the reduplication when followed by a *pit*, we say no, because there is no distinction [in the application].
If it is argued that [the rule applies] for the sake of the intensive (*abhyāsa*), that is not so. What is the reason? Because there is no distinction. The prohibition is made without distinction;

the rule "when a *kit* suffix follows" has already ceased to apply there. Furthermore, because there is no distinction, even for the root *veñ*, the substitution of semivowels for vowels (*samprasāraṇa*) in the reduplicated syllable is not desired in forms with *pit* suffixes, as in *vavau* and *vavitha*. Indeed, the mention of the modified form (*vikṛti*) is intended for the purpose of the prohibition.
And no modification is made that would take up the original form (*prakṛti*). (Pāṇini 6.1.17.1) Regarding the roots *grah*, *vṛśc*, *pṛcch*, and *bhṛjj*, there is no distinction [in their treatment].

As for what was said—that there is no distinction regarding the root *vṛśc*—that is not correct; for if the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the letter *r* did not occur here, [the rule would fail].
