Otherwise, the substitution of *v* would occur [in place of *u*]. However, when the *repha* (*r*) undergoes *samprasāraṇa*, because the *u* is not considered an *adatta* vowel due to its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, the prohibition "there is no *samprasāraṇa* of a *samprasāraṇa*" becomes established.
Therefore, it must be stated that there is no distinction for the root *grah*, and no distinction between the roots *prach* and *bhṛjj*.

(P_6,1.17.2) KA_III.25.11-22 Ro_IV. 333-334 Now, for what purpose is the mention of "both" (*ubhaya*)? [It is so that] the *samprasāraṇa* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) may occur for both classes: namely, for *vac*, *svap*, *yaj* and the rest, as well as for *grah* and the rest. This is not a necessary purpose, because the mention of "both" from the previous context continues here. If it does continue, then [the rule applies] to *grah*, *jyā*, *vye*, *vyadh*, *vaṣṭi*, *vicati*, *vṛścati*, *pṛcchati*, and *bhṛjjati*.

Regarding the rule *ṅiti ca*, it would follow that the [strengthening] applies to the roots beginning with *yaj* even before an affix marked by *ṅ*. This is not a fault, for the connection will continue to apply. [The rule is: "For *vac*, *svap*, and the roots beginning with *yaj* when a *kit* [affix follows]; and for the roots beginning with *grah* when a *ṅit* [affix follows]. Then [comes]: "In the case of the *liṭ* [perfect], there is [strengthening] of the reduplication for both classes. Thus, the terms "*kit*" and "*ṅit*" have ceased to apply. Alternatively, these governing rules (*adhikāras*) proceed like the leaps of a frog.

Just as frogs move by leaping again and again, so too are these governing rules (*adhikāras*). Alternatively, they may be treated as a single compound rule (*ekayoga*): "for *vac*, *svap*, *yaj* and the rest when followed by a *kit* suffix, and for *grah* and the rest when followed by a *ṅit* suffix," and then "of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) when followed by *liṭ*. Furthermore, there is no continued application (*anuvṛtti*) within a single compound rule. Or rather, both [the previous rules] have ceased; we shall refer back to them as needed.

In that case, this is the purpose of including both [the *abhyāsa* and the *samprasāraṇa*]: so that for both, there may be only the *samprasāraṇa* of the *abhyāsa*, and whatever else might otherwise apply, that shall not occur. And what else might apply? The rule of *halādiśeṣa*. For it will be stated that "the *samprasāraṇa* of the *abhyāsa* [takes precedence] over *halādiśeṣa* by way of a prior conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). That is a prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).
It should not be recited.

(P_6,1.17.3) KA_III.25.23-27.3 Ro_IV.334-336: The *samprasāraṇa* of the reduplication takes precedence over the *halādiśeṣa* by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The *samprasāraṇa* of the reduplication occurs in place of the *halādiśeṣa*.
[The phrase "it occurs in place of the *halādiśeṣa*" is repeated.]
By way of conflict: the scope for the *samprasāraṇa* of reduplication is seen in *iyāja* and *uvāpa*; the scope for the *halādiśeṣa* rule is seen in *bibhidatuḥ*.

They split. Here, both [rules] would apply: *vivyādha* and *vivyadhitha*. The vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the reduplicated syllable occurs by means of a prior exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Then that prior exception must be stated. Or rather, it need not be stated, because of the superior force of that which depends on vocalization; this applies elsewhere as well. Why?

The reason is that, because of the superior strength of that which depends on *samprasāraṇa*, it must be stated that elsewhere too, *samprasāraṇa* and that which depends on *samprasāraṇa* are stronger. It need not necessarily be stated only here; it applies elsewhere as well. What is the purpose? The purpose concerns *ram*, the elision (*lopa*) of *ā*, *iy*, *yaṅ*, and *aṇ*. Regarding *ram*: *bhṛṣṭaḥ*.

In the case of *bhṛṣṭavān*, both *samprasāraṇa* and *rambhāva* (the substitution of *ra*) would apply. Because it is subsequent, *rambhāva* would occur. It must be stated that *samprasāraṇa* is stronger so that *samprasāraṇa* takes place first. [Then] *ram*. [Next] *āllopa*: *juhuvatuḥ*, *juhuvuḥ*.
Both *samprasāraṇa* and *āllopa* would apply. Because it is subsequent, *āllopa* would occur. [Therefore, it must be stated that] *samprasāraṇa* [is stronger].

It must be stated that [the rule for] *samprasāraṇa* is stronger so that it may take effect. Once *samprasāraṇa* has been applied, both the substitution of the preceding vowel (*pūrvatva*) and the elision of the long *ā* (*āllopa*) would apply. Because it is subsequent, *āllopa* would occur. It must be stated that that which depends on *samprasāraṇa* is stronger so that the substitution of the preceding vowel (*pūrvatva*) may take effect. [Thus we have] *iyaṅ*: *śuśuvatuḥ*.

In *śuśuvuḥ*, both *samprasāraṇa* and the substitution of *iyaṅ* would apply. Because it is subsequent, the substitution of *iyaṅ* would occur. It must be stated that *samprasāraṇa* is stronger, so that *samprasāraṇa* takes place first. [Then] *yaṇ*. Once *samprasāraṇa* has been performed, both the rule for the preceding vowel (*pūrvatva*) and the substitution of *yaṇ* would apply. Because it is subsequent, the substitution of *yaṇ* would occur. [This is not the case, because the operation] depends upon *samprasāraṇa*.
It should be stated that [the subsequent rule] is stronger so that its priority may be established; thus, *iyaṅ* [is applied]. These are not valid purposes.
As for what was said regarding *ram*, this must be considered here:

"Let the substitution of *ram* be performed, or let the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) be performed. What should be done here? The substitution of *ram* [should take place], because it is subsequent.

The *samprasāraṇa* substitution is obligatory; it applies whether the *rambhāva* (the substitution of *ra*) has already taken place or not. The *rambhāva* is also obligatory; it applies whether the *samprasāraṇa* has already taken place or not. How so? Because it applies both to that *repha* (*r*) which stands in place of the *ṛ*-vowel and to the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). The *rambhāva* is non-obligatory (*anitya*), for it does not apply once the *samprasāraṇa* has already taken place.

What is the reason? The term *upadeśe* (in the original instruction) continues [to apply]. Furthermore, that mention of *upadeśa* must necessarily be carried over for the sake of forms such as *barībhṛjyate*. [The rule] "when there is elision of *āl*, and in the case of *iyaṅ* and *yaṇ*" [prescribes] a permanent (*nitya*) semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*). [However,] the status of being "prior" (*pūrvatva*) is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*). Therefore, it must be stated that this [substitution], which relies on semivowel substitution and serves no other purpose, is stronger; thus, there is a prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

Or it should be stated [as such]. Or neither should be stated. The purpose of including both [roots] has already been explained here: so that the *samprasāraṇa* of the reduplication of both may occur, and whatever else would otherwise result, that shall not happen. (P_6,1.17.4) The inclusion of *vyaci* among the *kuṭādi* roots is for the sake of *samprasāraṇa* before suffixes beginning with a vowel (*añ*) that are not marked with *ṇ* (*aṇit*).

It should be stated that *vyac* belongs to the *kuṭādi* group when followed by a suffix beginning with *a*. What is the purpose? To ensure *samprasāraṇa* occurs before suffixes beginning with vowels other than *ṇ*. Thus, so that there may be *samprasāraṇa* before suffixes beginning with vowels other than *ṇ*, as in *udvicitā* and *udvicitum*.
It should be understood that [the rule] must be applied. Why is "in *anaṅ*" mentioned? [Consider: *uruvyacāḥ kaṇṭakaḥ*.
(P_6.1.18) The mention of *caṅ* could have been omitted. How so? The term *ṅiti* continues [from the previous rule], and there is no other *ṅit* suffix for the root *svap* other than *caṅ*.

(P_6.1.20) There is a prohibition regarding *yaṅ* after the root *vaś*. A prohibition of *samprasāraṇa* must be stated for *vaś* in *yaṅ*. [Thus we get] *vāvaśyate*. Where should it not apply? [For example, in the case of *vāvaśyate* derived from *vaś* with *yaṅ*.]

[Objection: "They desire [it]. [Reply: In that case, such a prohibition must be stated. [Objection: It need not be stated. [Reply: The word "in the *yaṅ*" (*yaṅi*) is understood [from the previous rule]. [Objection:

If so, then he is merely restating that "the word 'in the *yaṅ*' is understood. [Reply: This need not be explained; for it is a well-known principle that governing rules (*adhikāra*) continue to apply. Indeed, this is precisely the correct principle: that governing rules should indeed continue to apply.
(P_6,1.27) KA_III.27.18–28.5 Ro_IV.337–338: What is prescribed as an irregular form (*nipātyate*)? The substitution of *śṛ* for *śrā* and *srā*.

The substitution of *śṛ* for *śrā* and *srā* is prescribed. It should be stated: "In the case of milk (*kṣīra*) and sacrificial oblation (*havis*). [Examples: *śṛtaṃ kṣīram* ("milk that has been boiled"), *śṛtaṃ haviḥ* ("oblation that has been boiled"). Where should it not apply? [It should not apply] in the case of *śrāṇā yavāgūḥ* ("boiled gruel").

Regarding the rule *śrapitā yavāgūḥ* ("the gruel has been cooked"): it should be stated that the form *śṛta* is used after the root *śrā* except when a causal agent (*hetu*) is involved. It must be stated that *śṛta* occurs after *śrā* except when a causal agent is present, so that it does not apply here: *śrapitaṃ kṣīraṃ devadattena yajñadattena* ("the milk was caused to be cooked by Devadatta and Yajñadatta"). Regarding the rule for words preceded by *āṅ*: it should be stated that [the suffix *kta* takes the form *ita*] after the roots *andh* and *ūdh*, when preceded by *āṅ*. Thus: *āpīno 'ndhuḥ* ("a well that has been filled").

The word *āpīnam* [is used for] the udder (*ūdhas*). What is the purpose? It is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*). [It applies] only after the prefix *āṅ* to the words *andhu* and *ūdhas*. Where should it not apply? As in *āpyānaś candramāḥ* ("the moon has waxed"). And this restriction should be understood as twofold: only after *āṅ* in the case of *andhu* and *ūdhas*, and only in the case of *andhu* and *ūdhas* when preceded by *āṅ*. Where should it not apply? As in *prapyāno 'ndhuḥ* ("a well that has been filled").

The word *ūdhas* [is substituted for *stanas*] after *prāpya*. This restriction should be understood as applying only when preceded by the prefix *ā-*. For indeed, we find such forms as *pīnaṃ mukham* ("a full face"), *pīnāḥ śambaṭyaḥ* ("full breasts"), and *ślakṣṇapīnamukhī kanyā* ("a girl with a smooth, full face").
(P_6.1.30) KA_III.28.14–29.6 Ro_IV.339–340: Regarding the root *śvi*, there is a prohibition of the characteristics of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) in the *liṭ* [perfect] tense.

In the *liṭ*, the *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) that constitutes the characteristic of the reduplicated syllable would invariably apply to *śvi*; its prohibition must be stated. Thus we have *śiśviyatuḥ*, *śiśviyuḥ*. Why is it said "of the characteristics of the reduplicated syllable in the *liṭ*" and not also "of the characteristics of the *ki* suffix"? [Because] the characteristic of the *ki* suffix...

For indeed, [the suffix] would always apply here. Which characteristic will sublate the characteristic of *śvayati*? In that case, just as the characteristic of *kill* sublates the characteristic of *śvayati*, so too it would sublate the characteristic of reduplication (*abhyāsa*). We do not say that the characteristic of *kill* sublates the characteristic of *śvayati* because it is an exception (*apavāda*); rather, it is because it is subsequent (*para*) to the characteristic of *śvayati*.
There is scope for the following verbal forms: *śuśāva*, *śuśavitha*,
and *śiśvāya*.
What is the scope for [the application of] the other *kita* suffixes? [The forms] *śūnaḥ* and *śūnavān*.

Here, both [rules] would apply: *śiśviyatuḥ* and *śiśviyuḥ*. The rule characterized by *śvayati* will prevail by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). But then, the rule characterized by *śvayati* will also prevail over the rule characterized by the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) by way of conflict. [This applies] to that which is characterized by the reduplication...

The scope [of the rule] for other roots such as *yaj* and so forth is *iyāja*, *uvāpa*. The scope for that which has the characteristic of the root *śvi* is when the form of the root follows [the suffix]; e.g., *śuśuvatuḥ*, *śuśuvuḥ*.

In *śuśuvitha*, both [rules] apply to the reduplication of the root *śvi*. [The forms] *śiśviyatuḥ* and *śiśviyuḥ* [would result]. [One might argue: "The characteristic of *śvayati* will apply by way of a conflict (vipratiṣedha). This conflict is not appropriate.

For there is no scope for other roots beginning with *yaj* in the case of the reduplication of *śvayati*. [Furthermore,] the inclusion of *śvayati* among the roots beginning with *yaj* [is for a different purpose].
That [rule] has no scope. Because it has no scope, the prohibition of the conflict is improper. Therefore, it has been well said:
"In the case of the root *śvi* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), there is a prohibition of the characteristics of the reduplicated syllable.
(P. 6.1.32–33; Kāśikā III.29.8–30.14; Rūpāvatāra IV.341–344). Regarding the rule *hvaḥ saṃprasāraṇe*, there is a separation of the yoga (yogavibhāga): *hvaḥ*.

A separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made regarding *samprasāraṇa*: "In the case of the root *hve*, there is *samprasāraṇa* when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇi*), as well as in the cases of the desiderative (*saṃ*) and the reduplicated aorist (*caṅ*). Then follows: "And also for that which is reduplicated (*abhyasta*). That is to say: "And for a reduplicated [root], there is *samprasāraṇa* of the root *hve*. For what purpose is this separation of the rule? It is for the sake of the domain of the causative suffix (*ṇi*), the desiderative (*saṃ*), and the reduplicated aorist (*caṅ*). Thus, there is *samprasāraṇa* of *hve* in the domain of the causative suffix, the desiderative, and the reduplicated aorist, just as follows: [examples].

It would be *juhāvayiṣati* and *ajūhavat*. But what is the reason it is not established? It is stated that [the substitution of *ū* for *o* applies] to the reduplicated form (*abhyasta*) of the root *hve*, and this [form in question] is not the reduplicated form of *hve*. Of what, then, is it the reduplicated form? It is the reduplicated form of *hvāyaya-ti*. This [root *hve*] is the reduplicated form of *hve*. How so? Because it consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*).

"Two [syllables] of the first [element]. If that is so, then it is stated [in the rule] "of the reduplicated *hvayati*," yet here *hvayati* is not reduplicated. What then? It is *hvāyayati*. [Objection: But *hvayati* itself is reduplicated here. [Question: How so? [Answer: By the rule "two [syllables] of the first [element] when it consists of a single vowel. Even so, [the rule is necessary] for the sake of the vocalization (*prasāraṇa*) of what is not reduplicated when there is a cause for reduplication. When there is a cause for reduplication...

Thus it should be stated. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of the *prasāraṇa* (vowel lengthening) of non-repeated (*anabhyasta*) roots, so that the *prasāraṇa* of the non-repeated root may occur—as in *juhūṣati* and *johūyate*. For if [the rule were applied] to the *prasāraṇa* of the repeated form, there would be no occurrence of *prasāraṇa* for the repeated syllable; indeed, in the case of the *prasāraṇa* of the repeated form, there is no *prasāraṇa* of the repeated syllable.

There would be non-attainment [of the rule]. The prohibition "when there is a *samprasāraṇa*, there is no *samprasāraṇa*" would apply. This is not a fault. Because of being separated [by other elements], it will not occur. [Objection:

Because of the prohibition of *samprasāraṇa* within the same member (*samānāṅga*), the prohibition would apply. [Response: Since the term "within the same member" (*samānāṅga*) will be raised as an objection there, [the prohibition does not apply here].

And it must be stated [in the rule] that "when there is a cause for the *abhyasta* [designation]" (*abhyastanimitta*), in order to prohibit [the application of the suffix *yaṅ*] to forms ending in a *kṛt* suffix.
What is the purpose? [Consider: one desires a *hvāyaka* (one who causes to call) → *hvāyakīyati*. From *hvāyakīyati*, the desiderative suffix (*san*) is applied → *jihvāyakīyiṣati*.
In that case, the word *nimitta* (cause) must indeed be included [in the rule]. For without the word *nimitta*, the sense of "being the cause" is not understood.

Even without the word "cause" (*nimitta*), the meaning of "cause" is understood. For example: "Curd and cucumber cause fever" (*dadhitrapusaṃ pratyakṣo jvaraḥ*); it is understood that these are the causes of fever. "Reed-water causes foot-disease" (*naḍvalodakaṃ pādarogaḥ*);
it is understood that this is the cause of foot-disease. "Clarified butter is life" (*āyuḥ ghṛtam*); it is understood that it is the cause of life. Now...

Alternatively, the suffix *matup* (expressing possession) is elided after *a*. That in which the reduplicated form (*abhyasta*) exists is called "the reduplicated" (*abhyasta*). Thus, [the rule applies] to "of the reduplicated.

Alternatively, the genitive in "of the reduplicated" (*abhyastasya*) is not a genitive of apposition with the verb *hvayati* ("to call"). What then? It is a genitive of relationship. [The meaning is: "that which is the verb *hvayati* belonging to the reduplicated. And what is the verb *hvayati* belonging to the reduplicated? It is the root (*prakṛti*). [That is,] the root *hve* belonging to the reduplicated.
Regarding the word *prakṛteḥ*: a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must indeed be made. Here, the root *hvayati* is not the base form (*prakṛti*) of the reduplicated stem; rather, it is *hvāyayati*.
(Pāṇini 6.1.36) What is the irregular formation (*nipātana*) in *apaspṛdhethām*? It is from the root *spṛdh*.

In the *laṅ* [aorist] tense, for the second person dual of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), the substitution of *āthām*, reduplication, vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*), and the elision of the vowel *a* are prescribed as irregularities (*nipātana*). As in: "O Indra and Viṣṇu, when you two contended" (*indraś ca viṣṇo yat apaspṛdhethām*). In the common language (*bhāṣā*), it is *aspṛdhethām*. Another says: following the root *spṛdh* preceded by the prefix *apa*, in the *laṅ* tense, for the second person dual of the middle voice, there is reduplication [of the root] in place of *āthām*.

The *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) and the elision of the vowel *a* are irregularly prescribed [in the following cases]: "O Indra and Viṣṇu, when you two contended" (*indraśca viṣṇo yad apaspṛdhethām*).

In the common language (*bhāṣā*), it is *apāspṛdhethām*. What is irregularly prescribed regarding *śrātāḥ* and *śritam*? In the case of the root *śrī* with the suffix *kta*, the forms *śrā* and *śri* are irregularly prescribed.
But where is there the form *śrā*, and where the form *śri*? The form *śrā* occurs in connection with *soma*; elsewhere, the form *śri* occurs. If that is so, [then...]
Now this occurs: *śritaḥ somaḥ*. In the plural, there is the absence of *śrā*. In that case, this does not occur now:
*śritāḥ naḥ grahāḥ*. When there is a plurality of *soma*, there is the absence of *śrā*; elsewhere, there is the presence of *śri*.

(P_6,1.37.1) KA_III.31.4–32.14 Ro_IV.345–347 For what purpose is this stated? The substitution of semivowels (*samprasāraṇa*) has been prescribed for *vaci*, *svapi*, *yaj* and so forth, as well as for *grah* and so forth. In that case, the substitution would apply to all the *yaṇ* sounds [in the root]. However, it is desired that it should apply to the subsequent [consonant] and not to the preceding one; and that cannot be accomplished without a specific effort.

"When there is a *samprasāraṇa*, [the subsequent] *samprasāraṇa* does not take place. Are there other rules of this kind? For example: "A long vowel is substituted before the suffix *yañ*" and "also before a *sup* ending," as in *ghaṭābhyām*. Why does the lengthening not occur for the mere vowel *a* [in *ghaṭa*]? There is a distinction here. This *paribhāṣā* applies: "The operation affects the final [element of the *alaṅga*]. But is it not the case that now...

It might be possible to apply this rule of exception here as well; [to this] he says "no. For there is no final *yaṇ* in words such as *vaci*, *spuṭi*, *yaj*, etc., nor in roots such as *grah* and others. If that is so, then according to the principle "when a modification does not affect the final letter, the operation applies to what stands in the vicinity of the final," it would be that which stands in the vicinity of the final [which is affected].

Whatever its purpose may be, there are no practical applications for this *paribhāṣā*. If that is so, then the activity of the Teacher (*ācāryapravṛtti*) indicates that not every *yaṇ* undergoes *samprasāraṇa*, since he teaches the change of *pyāy* to *pī*. How does this serve as an indicator? The purpose of teaching the change to *pī* is [to form] *āpīnaḥ andhuḥ*.

The form *āpīnam* is intended so that it may have the appearance of *ūdhas*. If, however, there were a *samprasāraṇa* for every *yaṇ* in this case, the explicit mention of the change to *pī* would be purposeless. For once the *samprasāraṇa* has been applied, and the substitution of the preceding vowel for the *samprasāraṇa* has occurred, the desired form would be established through the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) of the two *i*-vowels, resulting in *āpīnaḥ andhuḥ*.
"‘The udder is swollen’ (āpīnam ūdhaḥ). But the Teacher perceives that not every *yaṇ* undergoes *samprasāraṇa*;

therefore, he teaches this [root] *pyā-* the transformation into *pī-*. This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*). For a rule is intended as an indicator only when it is commenced while the matter is already established; however, the form of *pyā-* is not established by *samprasāraṇa*. For if *samprasāraṇa* were to occur, [the form would be *pīna*, not *āpīna*].
[Otherwise] it would apply to the final [element]. Even so, this is merely an indicator (*jñāpaka*). How? In the rule *pyāyaḥ*, this is not a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*).

What then? It is a genitive of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*): "that *yaṇ* which belongs to *pyā-*. By this, the Teacher indicates that not every *yaṇ* becomes a *saṃprasāraṇa*, since he teaches the substitution of *pī-* for *pyā-*. Even so...
This [argument] is inconclusive. All that is being indicated is that the *samprasāraṇa* substitution does not occur for every *yaṇ*.

In that case, why should it apply to the subsequent one and not to the preceding one? Even when this [rule] is stated, why should it apply to the subsequent one and not to the preceding one? For indeed, the *samprasāraṇa* shares a single grammatical operation (*ekayogakṣema*).
In that case, if the subsequent [moment] has already been produced, then the preceding one must also have been produced.

It is possible to effect the cessation of something that has arisen by negating its persistence, but not of that which has already been produced. For what could be achieved by someone saying "Do not eat" to one who has already finished eating? Furthermore, if the preceding [moment] has not been produced, then the subsequent one also has not been produced.

In that case, the reliance on a formal cause (*nimitta*) is untenable, as in the rule "a semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) does not take place when another semivowel substitution has occurred. This is not a fault. As for what was said—"Even when this [rule] is stated, how is it determined that it will apply to the subsequent [vowel] and not to the preceding one?"—in this matter, the intention of the Teachers is understood through a gesture, a movement, a blink, or through a great sequence of sūtras.

It is understood. This very fact indicates that [the rule] will apply to the subsequent [vowel] and not to the preceding one, since he teaches the prohibition: "When there is a *samprasāraṇa*, there is no [subsequent] *samprasāraṇa*. Furthermore, it is said that *samprasāraṇa* is indeed characterized by a single grammatical operation (*ekayogalakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, if the subsequent [vowel] has already been produced, the preceding one must also have been produced; for that which was applicable but not yet produced [cannot remain unproduced once the operation has occurred].

"It is possible to effect cessation by means of a prohibition. Let there be the production of both. We do not teach a prohibition of the former [element]. What then? We teach a prohibition of that which would otherwise apply based on the *samprasāraṇa*. Consequently, when the status of being "prior" has been prohibited, the result is established by means of the *yaṇ* substitution. As for what was also said: "Now, even if it is prior..."
Even that which is beyond what has not been produced is indeed not produced. In that case, reliance upon a cause is untenable. [To this we reply:

The designation will apply because it serves that purpose. Just as a pillar intended for Indra is called "Indra," so too here, the *samprasāraṇa* is for the sake of *samprasāraṇa*. That which is a *samprasāraṇa* for the sake of *samprasāraṇa*, in that [case]...
There will be a prohibition.

Now, while the term *samprasāraṇa* is still in force, what is the purpose of mentioning *samprasāraṇa* again? The mention of *samprasāraṇa* once more in this section on *samprasāraṇa* is for the following reason:
This is for the purpose of prohibiting *prasāraṇa* elsewhere. However, when *prasāraṇa* is mentioned again within the section on *samprasāraṇa*, this is the purpose:
so that there may be a prohibition even of that *samprasāraṇa* which is situated in a different location.

Regarding the rule *vyathaḥ liṭi* (P. 7.4.68): *vivyathe*. This is not a necessary purpose [for the rule]. Here, the *samprasāraṇa* substitution is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *halādiśeṣaḥ* (P. 6.4.2). In that case, consider the rule *śvayuvamaghonām ataddhite* (P. 6.4.133): *yūnā*, *yūne*. Even if this [rule] were stated, it would still not be established. Why? Because of the intervention by the vowel *u*. [This is so] because of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) operation.

Once [the substitution] has been performed, there is no intervention. Because of the status as a *sthānivadbhāva*—according to the rule that "a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated like the original (*sthānin*) for the application of a preceding rule"—there is indeed an intervention. If that is so, then the mention of "the same member" (*samānāṅga*) must be made. And the mention of "the same member" must be formulated: it should be stated that "in the case of a semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*), a semivowel substitution does not occur within the same member. In that regard, there is a fault in the case of *upoṣuṣi*. In that case...
The fault does not arise for one who has fasted.

Or rather, there is no such fault; for what reason? Because the prohibition applies to the occurrence of a second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) in respect to that member which is subject to the possibility of being expanded (*prasāraṇa*). And here, the root *vas* is a verbal base (*aṅga*) in relation to the suffix *kvasu*, while the form ending in *kvasu* is a base again in relation to the case-ending.

Alternatively, what is accomplished by the statement "of that stem which has reached the stage of expansion"? It means that the cessation of what is applicable but not yet fully realized can be effected through prohibition. And in this case, when there is *vasi*, there is no *kvasu*; and when *kvasu* has been fully realized, then *vasi* occurs. Or rather, of that stem...

What is accomplished by this [rule] *prasāraṇaprāptiḥ*? It amounts to saying: "That which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*). Because it is unestablished, the prohibition characterized as internal will not apply to the *samprasāraṇa* of *vasau*, which is characterized as external. In the Vedic verse (*ṛc*), there is the elision of the initial syllable of the subsequent member after the root *tri*; this occurs in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). In the Vedic verse...

The *samprasāraṇa* substitution for the vowel of *tṛc* should be stated. In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), the elision of the initial syllable of the following word should be stated. Examples: *tṛcaṃ sūktam* (a hymn consisting of three verses); *tṛcaṃ sāma* (a chant consisting of three verses). Why specify "in the Vedic language"? [Because in ordinary usage we find] *tryṛcāni*. Regarding the suffix *matup*: the *samprasāraṇa* substitution for the vowel of *rayi-* before the suffix *matup* should be stated as occurring diversely (*bahulam*).
Example: *ā revān etu naḥ viśaḥ* (May the wealthy one come to our people). And it does not occur: *rayimān puṣṭivardhanaḥ* (possessing wealth, increasing prosperity).

Regarding the term *kakṣyā* when it denotes a name (*sañjñā*): it should be stated that there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the vowel in *kakṣyā* before the suffix *matup* when it forms a name. [Examples: "Kakṣīvant, whom the Āśijas [praised]"; "Kaṇva Kakṣīvān. Why does it say "when it denotes a name"? [Counter-example: "A spotted elephant" (*kaṣyāvān hastī*). (Pāṇini 6.1.39) It would have been possible to omit the mention of *vaḥ* here; [the rule could have been formulated as] "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*).

It is established that there is no *samprasāraṇa* for the root *veñ*. How so? Once *samprasāraṇa* has occurred and the substitution of *uvaṅ* has taken place, reduplication follows, and then the long vowel by rule of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*). By this, the forms *vavatuḥ* and *vavuḥ* are established.

*ūvatuḥ*, *ūvuḥ*. Even for the root *vye*, there is a constant prohibition of the semivowel (*yakāra*) [from becoming a vowel], resulting in the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*): *ūyatuḥ*, *ūyuḥ*. And the threefold nature [of the forms] is to be established here; that is accomplished when this is so. If it is thus, then *vavau* [is also established].

The form *vavitha* is not established. By the word "also" (*ca*) in the rule *lyapi ca*, the suffix *liṭ* is also drawn in. Since that [rule] would necessitate a permanent prohibition of *prasāraṇa*, this optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) regarding a *kit* suffix is now commenced.
How is this to be understood:
as "that which is *ec* in its original instruction" (*upadeśe*), or rather "that which ends in *ej* in its original instruction"? And what follows from this? If it is understood as:

[Objection: If [the rule] is understood as "that which ends in *ej* in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*)," then [the suffix -aC] would undesirably apply here in the case of *ḍhaukitā* and *traukitā*. [Response: If it is understood as "that which ends in *ej* in its original enunciation," then there is no fault. [Objection: But even if it is understood as "that which ends in *ej* in its original enunciation," [the suffix -aC] would still undesirably apply here [in *ḍhaukitā* and *traukitā*]. For this too becomes something ending in *ej* by virtue of being treated like that which possesses the designation [of having such an ending].

In the context of grammatical instruction (*upadeśa*), that which possesses meaning (*arthavat*) is treated as if it were the principal element (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). Now, one might argue that even if the rule *ec ayan* is understood as *ec ayan upadeśe*, there would be no fault; for although it is stated "not before a śit [suffix]," we do not perceive a śit here. But surely the letter *k* itself is a śit here? It should not apply to the letter *k*. Why? Because of the principle: "That which is joined with a negative particle (*nañ*) or the word *iva* refers to something other than that which is similar to it."

For such is the understanding of the meaning: when a word is joined with the negative particle *nañ* or with the particle *iva*, it is understood that the operation applies to something else similar to that [original referent].

For such is the meaning perceived. Just as in common worldly usage, when one says, "Bring a non-Brāhmaṇa," one brings someone similar to a Brāhmaṇa; one does not become satisfied by bringing a clod of earth.

In this case as well, because of the prohibition [of the suffix] *śit* by the rule "not when *aśit*" (*aśiti*), the operation will be understood to apply to something other than *aśit* that is similar to *śit*. And what else is similar to *śit*? A suffix (*pratyaya*). In this case then:
from the root *glai*, [the form] *glānīyam*.
From *mlai*: *mlānīyam*;
from *veñ*: *vānīyam*; from *śo*: *niśāmīyam*.

Because they are subsequent [rules], the substitutions *āy* and so forth would apply. But even if it is understood that "that which ends in *ej* in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*) [is subject to the rule]," because they are subsequent, the substitutions *āy* and so forth would still apply. Let them be; once the substitutions *āy* and so forth have been made, by virtue of the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), the substitute will again be included by the mention of *ej*, and thus the substitution of *ā* will occur. But even if it is understood that "that which is *ec* in its original enunciation" [is subject to the rule], because they are subsequent...

When [the operations] *āya* and so forth have been applied, the substitution of *āt* will occur because, by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), it is included by the mention of *ej*. It will not occur; for the status of being a substitute applies only when the rule is not one concerning an *al* (phoneme), and this is a rule concerning an *al*. If that is the case, even if it is understood as "that which ends in *ej* in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*)," then in the case of *hūtaḥ*, [the rule would still apply].

[Objection: In this case [in *hūtavān*], the substitution of *ā* would also apply. [Response: Let it indeed be so that there is the substitution of *ā* here. Why does it not occur in the hearing? [Objection: It will have the status of being prior (*pūrvatva*). [Response: That is not established. Here, this must be deliberated: "Should the substitution of *ā* be applied, or the status of being prior? [Question: What should be done here? [Response: Because it is subsequent, the status of being prior [should take effect]. [Objection: If that is so, then this must be deliberated here: "Should the substitution of *ā* be applied, or the *samprasāraṇa*? [Question: What should be done here?

The substitution of *ā* occurs because it is subsequent. The *samprasāraṇa* is permanent; it applies both when the *ā*-substitution has been made and when it has not. The *ā*-substitution is also permanent; it applies both when the *samprasāraṇa* has been made and when it has not. The *ā*-substitution, however, is not permanent; for it does not apply once the *samprasāraṇa* has been made. What is the reason? Because the status of being "prior" (*pūrvatva*) is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*); therefore, it is sublated [by the *samprasāraṇa*]. Of that which...

A cause (*nimitta*) is sublated by another rule, yet that [cause] is not itself impermanent. Nor does the *samprasāraṇa* itself sublate the cause for the *āttva* (the substitution of *ā*). Another rule, namely the priority (*pūrvatva*), must necessarily be awaited. Since both rules are permanent, the *āttva* occurs first due to its posteriority; once the *samprasāraṇa* has occurred, the priority of the *samprasāraṇa* is established. Because the effect has already been produced, the *āttva* will not occur again.

Furthermore, even if the substitution of *ā* were somehow non-eternal (*anitya*), there would still be no fault; the mention of "instruction" (*upadeśa*) need not be made. If it is not made, then [the substitution] would apply here as well in the case of *cetā* and *stotā*. This is not a fault; for the activity of the Teacher indicates that the substitution of *ā* does not occur for that which is caused by a subsequent element, since he teaches the substitution of *ā* for the roots *krī*, *jī*, and *ṇau* (in the causative).

This is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*). This [rule] must be for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), namely: "for *krī*, *ji*, and *ṇī* only when followed by *ṇic*. If that is so, then why does [the author] carry forward the mention of *ej* in the rule *mīnātiminotidīṅāṃ lyapi ca*? Well then, consider here: *glai* → *glānīyam*; *mlai* → *mlānīyam*.

In *veñ* [the form] *vānīyam*, and in *śo* [the form] *niśāmīyam*, the suffixes *āya* and so forth would apply because they are subsequent [rules]. Here too, the activity of the Teacher indicates that the suffixes *āya* and so forth do not sublate the *ātva* (the substitution of *ā* for *i*); for this reason, he teaches the prohibition by stating "not before *śit*" (*aśiti*). For if they were to sublate it, [he would not have formulated such a rule].

Even in the case of *śiti* [affixes], they would cause [the substitution] to be barred. Or rather, let it be that "that which is taught [as having an indicatory letter *e*]" is what is meant. But has it not been said: *glai*—*glānīyam*;
*mlai*—*mlānīyam*;
*veñ*—*vānīyam*?

"Since this [root] *śo* is followed by a suffix beginning with a consonant (*paratvāt*), the substitutions *āya* and so forth would apply. Even here, the prohibition regarding *śit* suffixes is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the *āya* and other substitutions do not supersede the substitution of *ā*. Regarding the substitution of *ā*, there must be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the case of the suffix *eś*. An addition must be made for the substitution of *ā* when *eś* follows: *jagle*, *mamle*. [Objection: The prohibition "when not followed by *śit*" (*aśiti*) would then apply. [Response: This is not a fault. It is not understood in that way.

Śakāra is *it*; that which has this [śakāra] is *śit*. Not *śit* is *aśit*. [The objection: "In what sense, then, is it *aśiti*? [The answer: Śakāra is *it*; *śit* is not *śit*, thus it is *aśit*. [The objection: "If that is so, then in the case of *stanandhayaḥ* as well, [the rule] would apply. [The answer: Here too, *śap* becomes *śit*.

(P_6,1.45.2) KA_III.35.20–37.5 Ro_IV.355–358: Is this, moreover, an exclusion (*paryudāsa*)—meaning "that which is other than *śit*"—or is it a prohibitive negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*)—meaning "not when *śit* [follows]"?

And what is the difference here? There must be a prohibition regarding the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) when it is not *śit*, because [the substitute] would otherwise behave like the initial [element]. A prohibition must be stated regarding the single-substitute when it is not *śit*.

They become weary, they wither. For what reason? Because of the rule regarding the initial [element]. A single substitute for *śit* (a suffix beginning with *ś*) and *aśit* (a suffix not beginning with *ś*) should be treated like the initial element. Since there is another [rule] concerning *śit*, the substitution of *ā* (āttva) would apply. There is also the rule for suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*). And the rule for suffixes is not established: *suglaḥ*, *sumlaḥ*. The rule for suffixes characterized by a stem ending in long *ā* does not apply. This results in the occurrence of an undesired suffix.

[Otherwise] the substitution of *śravaṇa* (the original sound) would result; and it would take the form of an *abhyāsa* (reduplication). Furthermore, the form of an *abhyāsa* would not be established: in *jagle*, *mamle*, etc., the status of having an *ivarṇa* as the *abhyāsa* would follow [undesirably]. Moreover, there must be a prohibition regarding *aya*, *ava*, and *āya*: in the case of *glai*, [the form] *glānīyam* [would be incorrect].
From *mlai*: *mlānīyam*;
from *veñ*: *vānīyam*; from *śo*: *niśāmīyam*.

Because it is subsequent, the *āya* and other suffixes would apply. Let it then be a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (prohibitive negation): "not before a *śit* [suffix]. If there is a prohibition regarding a *śit*, an addition must be made for the cases of *ślau* and *luk*: *rarīdhvam*, *trādhvam*, and *śiśīte*. An addition must be made for the cases of *ślau* and *luk* when there is a prohibition regarding a *śit*.
[Examples: *divo naḥ vṛṣṭim maruto rarīdhvam* (O Maruts, grant us rain from heaven); [here there is] *luk*. *trādhvam naḥ* (protect us).

"The gods have struck down the wolf; he sharpens his two horns to gore the Rakṣas. This is not a fault. Here, first, in the phrase "O Maruts, grant us rain from heaven," the word *rai* does not have the form of the root *rā* ("to give"). Of what, then? It is of the root *rāti*, which has the sense of giving. In the phrase "he sharpens his two horns," this is not a form of the root *śyai*. Of what, then? It is of the root *śīṅ*; its meaning is that of sharpening (*śyati*).
It is indeed understood. But what is the meaning of the root *śyai*? The root *śyai* occurs in the sense of sharpening (*niśāna*). The root *śīṅ* also occurs in the sense of sharpening.

How, then, can one [root] occur in the sense of another? Roots have many meanings. For example, the root *vap*, though seen in the sense of scattering (*prakiraṇa*), also occurs in the sense of cutting (*chedana*), as in "he cuts the hair" (*keśān vapati*).

Regarding the word *vapati*: the root *īḍ* is seen in the senses of praising (*stuti*), inciting (*codanā*), and entreating (*yācñā*), and it also functions in the sense of moving (*īraṇa*). "Agni indeed prays for rain from here; the Maruts cause it to fall from yonder. This root *kṛ* is seen in the sense of the manifestation of what was previously non-existent (*abhūtaprādurbhāva*), and it also functions in the sense of cleansing (*nirmalīkaraṇa*).
"Make the back straight," "make the feet [straight]"—it is understood as "rubbing them clean. And it is also used in the sense of depositing (*nikṣepaṇa*).

It is also observed [in usage]: "Make a mat" (*kaṭe kuru*), "Make a jar" (*ghaṭe kuru*), "Move this stone from here" (*aśmānam itaḥ kuru*), which is understood to mean "Place it. This is the refutation for all [the objections]. It is stated that [the suffix] *śit* [is present], yet we do not perceive anything characterized by *śit* here. [This is due to] the characteristic of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*). [But] there is a prohibition of the characteristic of the suffix by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya*. As for *trādhvam*, this occurs in the *luṅ* tense by means of a transposition (*vyatyayena*).

It will be so. Or, alternatively, let it be a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion). But was it not said that there is a prohibition regarding the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) when followed by a non-*śit* suffix, because [the substitute] is treated like the initial [element]? This is not a fault. Because of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (treated like the original), according to the rule "a single-substitute is like the original in respect to an operation concerning what precedes it," there is an intervention.
As for the point regarding "the prescription of a suffix" (*pratyayavidhi*), the activity of the Teacher indicates that [suffixes] occur after roots ending in *ej*.

The rule for the application of suffixes is characterized by the presence of the letter *ā*; thus, when [Pāṇini] teaches *hvāvāmaśca* with the suffix *aṇ*, it is for the purpose of superseding *kap*. As for the statement "the form of the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsarūpam*), that rule (*yoga*) is rejected. Even if it were to be applied, there would still be no fault. How so? Because the term *liṭi* (in the context of the *liṭ* suffix) is understood to carry over; furthermore, this grammatical indication (*nirdeśa*) contains two *lakāra*s.

[The rule applies] "in the *liṭ* [tense], at the beginning of a *lakāra*. And by doing so, that which was stated—"an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for *eś* when there is *āt*-vṛddhi"—is also free from fault.

As for what was also stated—"and a prohibition regarding *ay*, *av*, *āy*, and *āv* [must be made]"—the prohibition concerning *śit* [suffixes] is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the *ay*-class substitutions do not sublate the *āt*-vṛddhi.
(Exclusion of nominal stems. An exclusion of nominal stems (*prātipadika*) must be stated: [the rule does not apply] to *gobhyām*, *gobhiḥ*, *naubhyām*.

[If it is argued that] it must be stated [in the rule for *naubhiḥ*], then it need not be stated. The activity of the Teacher indicates that the substitution of *ā* does not occur for nominal stems (*prātipadika*), since he teaches the substitution of *ā* in the rule *rāyo hali*. This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*).

It would serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): [the substitution of *ā* for *rāy-*] occurs only before a consonant (*hali*). If so, then what about the substitution of *ā* taught in the rule *ā otāṃ śasoḥ*?

He teaches [the rule]. There is also a purpose for stating this: it would serve both to prevent the application of *vṛddhi* and to prohibit [the substitution] before the suffix *śas*. Therefore, a prohibition regarding nominal stems (*prātipadika*) must be stated. It need not be stated.

Because of the governing context of verbal roots (*dhātu*), the [substitution] does not apply to the nominal stem. Due to the governing context of verbal roots, the *āt*-substitution will not occur for the nominal stem.

The term "dhātoḥ" (of the root) is understood [from the previous rule]. Where was it introduced? In the rule "liṭi dhātor anabhyāsasya" (in the periphrastic perfect, of a non-reduplicated root). Even if it has been withdrawn, there is no fault. It is stated that [the rule applies] "upadeśe" (in the original enunciation), and the mention of nominal stems (prātipadika) is not an original enunciation.

(P. 6.1.48) An addition [to the rule] is required for the root *lī* when the suffix *ṇic* follows, provided it means "deceiving" (*pralambhana*) or "causing to shrink/shame" (*śālīnīkaraṇa*), so that the vowel becomes long (*āt*).

An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the substitution of *ā* in place of the vowel of the root *lī* when followed by the causative suffix *ṇi*. What is the purpose? So that the substitution of *ā* may occur invariably in the sense of deceiving (*pralambhana*) and in the sense of making modest (*śālīnīkaraṇa*). First, regarding deceiving: *jaṭābhir ālāpayate* (he causes [him] to be deceived by means of matted locks);

*śmaśrubhir ālāpayate* (he causes [him] to be deceived by means of a beard). Regarding making modest: *śyeno vārtikam ullāpayate* (the hawk makes the quail modest/shameful); *rathī rathinam upalāpayate* (the charioteer makes the other charioteer modest/shameful).

Regarding the root *sidh* when it means "to be ignorant": it should be stated that [the rule applies] to the root *sidh* when it means "to be ignorant. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*). If it were stated [simply] as "in a non-transmigratory sense" (*apāralaukike*), an undesirable result would follow:
for example, "He prepares food, thinking, 'I will give it to the Brahmins. However, does this root *sidh* not occur elsewhere as well?
It exists; thus he says. Austerity accomplishes the state of an ascetic; knowledge reveals it to him. His own actions accomplish him; they reveal knowledge to him—this is the meaning.
(Regarding the rule Pāṇini 6.1.50: The statement that roots such as *mī* are taught with the vowel *ā* is for the purpose of the prescription of suffixes.

The status of being "like the original instruction" (*upadeśivadbhāva*) must be stated regarding the substitution of *ā* for the vowels of roots such as *mīnāti*. It must be stated that the substitution of *ā* occurs in the state of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*). What is the purpose? For the sake of the application of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*). So that the desired application of suffixes may take place once the substitution of *ā* has been made in the state of the original instruction. Which suffixes, then, necessitate this status of being like the original instruction?
Which [suffixes] then do not cause [the rule] to apply? What is the reason? It is stated that [the suffix applies] after an *ec* vowel, and yet there is no *ec* vowel among those [suffixes].
In that case, the rules for the suffixes *ṇa*, *ghañ*, and *yuC* cause it to apply. [Objection: No. [If so,] the suffix *ṇa* would be established by the rule "after *āt*" (*ātaḥ*) as in *avadāyaḥ*.
The suffix *ghañ* would also be established by the rule "after *āt*" as in *avadāyaḥ* occurring [there]. Furthermore, sir, what about the suffix *bhaÑ*? [Is it not also established by "after *āt*"]?

It is said: indeed, it is not stated that "ā" [is substituted] *from* (ātaḥ); rather, it is understood that [the substitution occurs] *after* (ātaḥ). How so? The suffix ghañ is prescribed as a general rule (*utsarga*) without distinction. To this, the suffixes *aj* and *ap* are exceptions (*apavāda*) when [the root] ends in an *i*-vowel or an *u*-vowel. In that case, once the substitution of *ā* has been made during the stage of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*), the cause for the application of the exception no longer exists; therefore, the suffix ghañ is established by the general rule.

And having established this, it is said that "it is not *āt*" (*na ca ātaḥ*), yet it is understood as *āt*. [The suffix] *yuc* [is applied]. "Slightly cut" (*īṣadavadānam*) is "well-cut" (*svavadānam*). Thus, the application of *yuc* after what ends in *āt* is established. But this is contradictory: "the teaching of *ec*. If there is no *ec* in the original instruction (*upadeśe*), then if there is an original instruction, there is no *ec*. To say "there is *ec* and there is an original instruction" is contradictory. This is not so.

This is contradictory. He says: "this *ec* [vowel] in the original instruction (*upadeśa*). If it is *ec* in the original instruction, then it is not *ec* in the original instruction; if it is not *ec* in the original instruction, then it is *ec* in the original instruction. We shall therefore understand the scope [of the rule] as being "in the case of *ec*. In that case, the mention of "original instruction" (*upadeśa*) must be made. It need not be made; the previously stated term continues by implication. Where was it previously stated? In the rule "from *āt* [comes *ai* and *au*] in the original instruction. That indeed...

In this context, the meaning is determined by both the qualification of the base (*prakṛti*) and the qualification of the object (*viṣaya*). Furthermore, that which is introduced for one purpose does not become something for another purpose.

Nor indeed does one thing, merely by being followed [by another], become something else; for a lizard, even while crawling, does not become a snake simply because of its crawling. As for what was said—that "that which is introduced for one purpose does not become something for another purpose"—[it is true].

Thus, even that which was introduced for one purpose serves another purpose; just as canals are constructed for the sake of rice, and from them water is both drunk and used for ritual rinsing, while the rice is also cultivated. Furthermore, it is said that indeed one thing does not become something else merely by following after what was previously introduced; for a lizard, though it crawls, does not become a snake simply because of its crawling.

"It becomes a snake"— this might be so in the case of physical substances; however, a word indeed becomes a qualifier for whichever specific attribute it is connected with, just as in the case of "the cow is white" and "the horse is white," where [the word "white"] is understood as qualifying the cow.

That "when there is the mention of the actual form of a verbal root, the rule is established by understanding it as including its suffixes. (P. 6.1.60). In the Vedic language, *śīrṣan* is a different base form. *Śīrṣan*.
In the Vedic language (*chandas*), another base form (*prakṛti*) should be recognized. What is the purpose? What is the purpose? It is for the sake of prohibiting the substitution (*ādeśa*).

Let the substitution not be understood; rather, let it be understood as another base form. And what would happen [if it were not so]? There would be no hearing of a word ending in *ask-* in the Veda. [For example: "May my head not shatter, nor my face. (R)
"It is shattered in the mouth.
"I split this head of yours! This, indeed, is the head of Atharvan.
[This refers to] those [substitutes] which serve as substitutes for *śiras* when a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix follows.

And in the rule *ca taddhite*, the inclusion of the word *śiras* must be made. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of substitution, so that it may be understood as a substitute (*ādeśa*), lest it be understood as a separate base (*prakṛti*). And what would happen [if it were not so]? In the case of a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *yakāra*, there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing the final vowel *a* of the stem [as it is]. For [the word] *śīrṣaṇya* refers to the head; [for example], *śīrṣaṇyaḥ kharaḥ* ("a donkey on the head"), or [alternatively], "on the hair" (*vā keśeṣu*).
Alternatively, the substitution of *śīrṣan* for *śiras* should be stated [as occurring] when referring to the hair of the head. Thus: *śīrṣaṇyāḥ keśāḥ* (hair belonging to the head), *śirasyāḥ*.

When an *ac*-vowel follows, *śīrṣa-* [is substituted for *śiras-*]. The substitution of *śīrṣa-* for *śiras-* should be stated when an *ac*-vowel follows. For example: *hāstiśīrṣiḥ*, *sthaulyaśīrṣiḥ*.

[The word] *pailuśīrṣiḥ*. [Vārttika: "And in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). And in the Vedic language, it should be stated that the substitution of *śīrṣa-* for *śiras-* occurs. [Examples: *dve śīrṣe* ("two heads").

Here, in the case of *hāstiśīrṣyā* and *pailuśīrṣyā*, since the term *śiras-* is included by the mention of *śiras-*, the substitution of *śīrṣan-* would apply. Let it be so. [Objection: The elision of the *ṭi* suffix will occur by the rule *na taddhite*. [Reply: It is not established. [Because of the rule: *ye ca abhāvakarmaṇoḥ*.

Thus, the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) would result [undesirably]. If, however, it were stated that "when *aci* follows a *taddhita* suffix," what would be achieved? [One might argue:

when the substitution of *śīrṣan* for *śiras* has been applied in the case of *iñ*, the desired form is established by the elision of the *ṭi* portion. But this cannot be maintained. For in the case of *sthūlaśirasaḥ idam* (belonging to one with a thick head), resulting in *sthaulaśīrṣam*, the preservation of the original form would undesirably apply because of the rule *anaṇi*. Therefore, it cannot be maintained in this way.

If it were not so, then because [the suffix] is included by the mention of *śiras*, the form *śīrṣan* would result. This fault is optional. In which alternative? There is a twofold view regarding the rule for *ṣyaṅ*: either *ṣyaṅ* is a substitute for *aṇ* and *iñ*, or *ṣyaṅ* follows after *aṇ* and *iñ*. Of these, when it is a substitute for *aṇ* and *iñ*, then this fault occurs; but when it follows after *aṇ* and *iñ*, [there is no fault].
In that case, no fault arises because [the suffix] is separated by *aṇ* and *iñ*.

It is stated [in the rule] "in the case of *śas* and so forth," yet it is also seen in cases other than *śas* and so forth: *śalā doṣaṇī*, *kakud doṣaṇī*, and *mahādevo yācate*. Regarding the words beginning with *pada*, there is the substitution of *māṃs*, *pṛt*, and *snū*.

An addition [to the rule]: an addition must be made for *māṃs*, *pṛt*, and *snu* when they occur at the beginning of words (*padādi*). *māṃs*: as in *yat nīkṣaṇam māṃspacanyāḥ* ("the vessel for cooking meat").

This is stated because one would otherwise expect *māṃsapacanyāḥ*. *pṛt*: as in *pṛtsu martyam* ("among the armies, the mortal"). This is stated because one would otherwise expect *pṛtanāsu martyam*. *snu*: as in *na te divaḥ na pṛthivyāḥ adhi snuṣu* ("neither from heaven nor from earth upon the ridges"). This is stated because one would otherwise expect *adhi sānuṣu*.

Regarding the word *nāsikā*: it should be stated that after the words *yat*, *tat*, *kṣudra*, and *para*, the substitution of *nas* for *nāsikā* occurs. Examples: *yat* + *nāsikā* = *nasyam*; *yat* + *tas* = *nastaḥ*; *tas* + *kṣudra* = *naḥkṣudraḥ*. It should be stated that this applies except when [the following word] begins with the vowel *a* or is the word *nagara*. This should not apply here: *nāsikyaḥ varṇaḥ* (a nasal sound).

[Nāsikya is] a city name. Then it should be stated [as such]. It need not be stated. First, regarding the statement "the *nāsikya* sound," its inclusion will be made in the list beginning with *parimukha*. Regarding "Nāsikya is a city," its inclusion will be made in the list beginning with *saṅkāśa*. (P_6.1.64) KA_III.42.8–43.10 Ro_IV.369–371 For what purpose is the mention of *dhātu*? So that it does not apply here: *ṣoḍan*,...

*ṣaṇḍaḥ*, *ṣoḍikaḥ*. Now, what is the purpose of including the word "beginning" (*ādi*)? [So that it does not apply] here: *peṣṭā*, *peṣṭum*. This is not a valid purpose. Let there be *satva* (the substitution of *s* for *ṣ*) here; once *satva* has been applied, the rule "of a substitute *s* following *iṇ*" will effect *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*). Then [consider] this:
"Desiring to desire" (*laṣitā laṣitum*). And this is also an example:

"one who desires to grind" (*peṣṭā peṣṭum*). But surely it was said: "Let there be *s*-substitution here; once *s*-substitution has been made, the *ṣ*-substitution will occur for the *s* of the substitute following *iṇ*. This cannot be so; for in the case of *pekṣyati*, because the *ṣ*-substitution would be considered unestablished (*asiddha*), [the rule would not apply].

The substitution of *k* for *ṣ* and *ḍh* before *si* (Pāṇini 8.2.41) would not apply here. There is a prohibition regarding the substitution of *s* for *ṣ* in the case of verbal roots ending in *su*, as well as the roots *ṣṭhivu* and *ṣvaṣk*.
A prohibition must be stated for the substitution of *s* for *ṣ* in the case of verbal roots ending in *su*, and for the roots *ṣṭhivu* and *ṣvaṣk*. Examples of verbal roots ending in *su*:
*ṣoḍīyati*, *ṣaṇḍīyati*. Example of *ṣṭhivu*: [ṣṭhīvati].

[The root] *ṣṭhīv* [is used]: *ṣṭhīvati*. [The root] *ṣvaṣk*: *ṣvaṣkate*. First of all, it need not be stated for the *subdhātu*s (roots beginning with *ṣ*). The term "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśe*) continues to apply; however, the mention (*uddeśa*) of nominal stems (*prātipadika*) is not the same as their original enunciation (*upadeśa*). If this is so, there is no purpose in mentioning "roots" (*dhātu*).
Why then does [the form] *ṣoḍan* not occur?

[The forms] *ṣaṇḍaḥ* and *ṣoḍikaḥ*. The term "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*) continues [to apply]. And the mention (*uddeśaḥ*) of nominal stems (*prātipadikānām*) is not the same as the original instruction (*upadeśaḥ*). Furthermore, in the case of the root *ṣṭhiv*, the second letter is *ṭha*. If it were *ṭha*, then the form *teṣṭhīvyate* would not be established. If that is so, then...

[Regarding] the letter *th*: if it is the letter *th*, then forms such as *ṭuṣṭhyūṣati* and *ṭeṣṭhīvyati* would not be established. If that is so, then there are these two roots *ṣṭhīv*: the second letter of one is *ṭh*, and the [second letter] of the other is *th*. For that one which has *th*, the substitution of *s* (*satva*) would apply. If that is so, then there are these two roots with two *ṣ*s: *ṣṭhivu* and *ṣvaṣkṛ*. What has been done?

[Objection: When the preceding [operation] has been performed, there will be the substitution of *ṣ* for *t* (*ṣṭutva*) upon contact with the following [sound]. [Reply: This cannot be maintained. For in cases such as *śvaliṭ ṣṭhīvati* and *madhuliṭ ṣvaṣkate*, because the substitution of *ṣ* for *t* (*ṣṭutva*) would be considered non-established (*asiddha*), the augment *dhuṭ* would apply by the rule *ḍaḥ si dhuṭ*. If that is so, then let the roots *ṣṭhivu* and *ṣvaṣka* have two *ṣ*s from the beginning. Why not [accept] the presence of the letter *y*? [Reply: No.

It is heard [in the tradition] that the letter *yakāra* has been elided and indicated. Now, for what purpose is the letter *sakāra* taught and then replaced by the substitute *ṣakāra*, rather than simply teaching *ṣakāra* itself? He says: "For the sake of brevity. How so? Having taught this *ṣakāra* without distinction and having stated the substitute *sakāra*, he effects the substitution of *ṣatva* by means of a concise method through the rule *adeśapratyayayoḥ*.

Thus [it is said]. For otherwise, those for whom the substitution of *ṣ* is desired would have to include them in that enumeration. Which roots, then, are taught with an initial *ṣ*? They should be recited. What is your effort in this matter? If something can be stated without such a recitation, let it be stated. Indeed, something can be stated even without a recitation.

How so? The roots *sad* and others that have *s* as their penultimate letter are taught with a *ṣ* as their upadeśa, as are *smi*, *svad*, *svid*, *svañj*, and *svap*, with the exception of *sṛp*, *sṛj*, *stṛ*, *styai*, *sekṛ*, and *sṛ*.

(Pāṇini 6.1.65) Now, for what purpose is the nasal *ṇ* taught [as the root-initial] and then replaced by the nasal *n*? Why not simply teach the nasal *n* itself? He says: "For the sake of brevity. How so? Without distinction...

Having taught the letter *ṇ* and stated the substitute *n*, [the author] effects the substitution of *ṇ* by means of a simple expedient through the rule: "The substitution of *ṇ* occurs after a prefix, even when not in a compound, for a root taught with *ṇ*. Otherwise, one would have to explicitly mention those roots for which the substitution of *ṇ* is desired. Which roots, then, are taught with *ṇ*? They must be listed. What is your contribution here?

If something can be stated even without the recitation [of the rule], let it be stated. Even without the recitation, something can be stated. How? All sounds containing *ṇ* are taught as having *ṇ* in their original form (*ṇopadeśa*), with the exception of the roots *nṛt*, *nand*, *nard*, *nak*, *nāṭ*, *nāth*, *nādh*, *nṝ*, and *nṝ*.
(P. 6.1.66.1) An addition must be made for the elision of *v* and *y* when *kvip* follows. [This applies to] *v* and *y*.
An addition must be made regarding the elision of *kvip*, so that [the rule] may apply here as well: from the root *kaṇḍūyati*, with the suffix *apratyaya* (i.e., *ap*), we have *kaṇḍūḥ*.
But what is the reason it is not established? It is said [in Pāṇini 6.1.66] "before a *val* [suffix]," yet here we do not see a *val*-initial [suffix].
But surely this *kvip* itself is *val*-initial? [Reply: Once the elision of *kvip* has occurred, because of the absence of a *val*-initial [suffix], [the substitution of *ū* for *u*] does not obtain.

This must be deliberated here: should the elision of *kvip* be performed, or the elision of *y*? What should be done in this case? The elision of *kvip* [should take place], because it is both subsequent and obligatory (*nitya*). Indeed, the elision of *kvip* is obligatory; for it applies whether the elision of *y* has already occurred or not yet occurred. Because it is both obligatory and subsequent, the elision of *kvip* takes precedence. Once the elision of *kvip* has been performed, there is an absence of the suffix beginning with *val*.

The elision (*lopa*) of *y* does not apply. If that is so, it will occur by virtue of the rule concerning suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). There is no application of the rule concerning suffixes when the operation depends on a phoneme (*varṇāśraya*). Or rather, some operations depending on phonemes do occur by virtue of the rule concerning suffixes; in that case, this too will occur. Alternatively, I shall state it thus: "There is elision of *v* and *y* before a consonant (*vali*). Then [the rule] for *vi*: "In the case of those ending in *vy*."

And there is the elision of *v* and *y*. Then, by the rule *apṛktasya*, there is the elision of that which is a single phoneme (*apṛkta*). [The rule applies] only to the *v* of *vi*. (P_6.1.66.2) KA_III.44.8–45.2 Ro_IV.374–375: The elision of *v* is not established because of the prescription of *ūṭ*. There is no establishment of the elision of *v* in the forms *āsremāṇam* and *jīradānuḥ*. What is the reason? Because of the prescription of *ūṭ*. By the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍ anunāsike ca*, *ūṭ* would apply.

There would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the *vraśc* and other roots. An over-extension occurs even with the *vraśc* and other roots; it would apply here as well in the cases of *vraścanaḥ*, *vrīhiḥ*, and *vraṇaḥ*. [Objection: This is established by the force of the original instruction (*upadeśasāmarthyāt*). By the force of the original instruction, the elision (*lopa*) will not occur in the case of *vraśc* and the others.

If it is argued that [the desired form] is established by the force of the original instruction (*upadeśa*), [we reply: there is indeed such force regarding the *samprasāraṇa* and the *halādi-śeṣa* operations. If it is argued that it is established by the force of the original instruction, there is another purpose for stating the original instruction: so that after the *samprasāraṇa* and *halādi-śeṣa* have been performed, the phoneme *v* may still be heard, as in *vṛkṇaḥ*.

[One might argue that] *vṛkṇavān* [is formed from] *vṛścati*, [and thus one would expect] *vivraściṣati*. But this is not so, because it is characterized as being external (*bahiraṅga*). Or rather, this is not even a valid purpose [for the rule]. Why? Because it is characterized as being external. The *samprasāraṇa* and the replacement by the first consonant (*halādi-śeṣa*) are external; [the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] is internal (*antaraṅga*).

There is elision. That which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is not established when [an operation] internal (*antaraṅga*) is to take effect. Or rather, there is no need for its formulation; indeed, the non-formulation of the elision of *val* is more logical. How so? In the cases of *āsremāṇam* and *jīradānuḥ*. [The forms] *āsremāṇam* and *jīradānuḥ* result from the elision of phonemes (*varṇalopa*). [Thus] *āsremāṇam*.

The form *jīradānuḥ* is established through the elision of a phoneme according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*), just as *saṃsphānaḥ* [is derived from] *gayasphānaḥ*. For example: *saṃsphayanaḥ*, *saṃsphānaḥ*, *gayasphānaḥ*.
Regarding the rule *gayasphānaḥ* (P. 6.1.67):

a prohibition must be stated for *darvi* and *jāgṛvi*: namely, *darviḥ* and *jāgṛviḥ*. Why is it said that "a prohibition must be stated for *darvi* and *jāgṛvi*, since [the rule] says 'of an uncombined suffix (*apṛkta*)'?"

Indeed, there are certain teachers who urge that even what is already established should be stated. Therefore, that [rule] must be formulated, or else a prohibition regarding *darvi* and *jāgṛvi* must be stated. [Objection: When there is elision (*lopa*) of the prefix *vi*, there is no prohibition regarding *darvi* and *jāgṛvi* because of the presence of a nasal (*anunāsika*).

[Response: When there is elision of *vi*, there is no prohibition regarding *darvi* and *jāgṛvi*. A prohibition that is purposeless is a non-prohibition. [In this case, it is simply] elision (*lopa*).

Why does it not occur? Because of the presence of a nasal (anunāsika). The word *vi* is understood here as being followed by a nasal, but in this case the word *vi* is not followed by a nasal; rather, the word *vi* here is followed by a pure [consonant]. If it is said that the word *vi* must be followed by a nasal, then [in the case of] *ghṛtaspṛk*,...

In the case of *dalaspṛk*, the rule does not apply here. For we do not perceive an *anunāsika* following this word *vi*. It is not understood thus: "that which has an *anunāsika* after it is *anunāsikapara*"; rather, [it means] that from which an *anunāsika* follows is *anunāsikapara*.
"Because of the presence of a nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) following [the *ṭutva* rule]. How then? "That in which a nasalized vowel follows is 'having a nasalized vowel following' (*anunāsikapar*);

[the rule applies] because of having a nasalized vowel following. Even so, it would apply here in the case of *priyadarvi*. The nasalization (*anunāsika*) is not yet established (*asiddha*) in this instance. Even so, a prohibition must be stated for the end of a verbal root (*dhātu*).
In the case of *divi* and *dhivi*, because of the rule "the inclusion of that which has meaning" (*arthavadgrahaṇāt*), there is the inclusion of the meaningful word *vi*.

However, the end of a verbal root (*dhātvanta*) is not meaningful. Alternatively, it is established by virtue of the nasalization (*anunāsikatva*) of the *v*. Or rather, this is the inclusion of the nasalized *v* itself; for among the semivowels (*yaṇ*), there are both those with nasalization and those without nasalization.

(P_6,1.68) KA_III.46.2–47.12 Ro_IV.377–380: If, however, this elision of the *apṛkta* were understood as the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), what would be accomplished? The mention of "having two consonants" (*dvihala*) and the mention of "the *apṛkta*" would not need to be made.

Since the elision of the *apṛkta* after a word ending in a consonant would be the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct, there would be no elision of the nasal (*nalopa*), as in the case of *pacan*.

When there is the elision of a single-consonant suffix (*apṛkta*) following a word ending in a consonant (*hal*), there is also the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*); however, in such cases, the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) does not occur. For example: *rājā*, *takṣā*. Because the elision of the final consonant cluster is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*), the elision of the nasal does not apply, just as in the case of *pacan*. Just as in *pacan* and *yajam*, because the elision of the final consonant cluster is unestablished, the elision of the nasal does not take place. This is not a fault.

The activity of the Teacher indicates that the elision of a consonant cluster at the end of a word (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is established by the rule *nalopaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.7], since he teaches an exception for the vocative case in the rule *na ṅisambuddhyoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.8]. If so, would this not also apply here in cases such as *pacan* and *yajan*? It serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for cases of a similar class. And what is of a similar class? That which follows immediately after the vocative ending. In the case of the suffixes *vas* and so on, the substitution of *d* occurs because the elision of the initial consonant of the cluster (*saṃyogādilopa*) is more powerful. In the case of *vas* and so on...

The substitution of *d* is not established, as in *ukhāsrat* and *parṇadvhat*. What is the reason? Because the elision of the initial member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*) is stronger than [the elision of the final member of a conjunct]. The elision of the initial member of a conjunct is stronger than the elision of the final member of a conjunct. For example, in *kūṭataṭ*.

Just as in *kūṭataṭ* and *kāṣṭhataṭ*, here the elision of the initial member of the conjunct is stronger than the elision of the final member of the conjunct. But [you might object] regarding the substitution of *d*:

It will not occur when [the suffix] *kṛt* has been applied. The substitution of *d* is unestablished (*asiddha*). Because it is unestablished, [the rule for lengthening] would apply. It is stated in the section on established rules (*siddhakāṇḍa*) that "the substitution of *d* occurs in *vasu* and so forth, when there is lengthening before the nominative singular (*su*). In that context, the mention of "lengthening before the nominative singular" need not be made; it should simply be stated: "the substitution of *d* occurs in *vasu* and so forth. Even so, because it is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*), the rule does not apply. Now, even in the case of the nominative singular, [the stem] becomes a word (*pada*), as in "rājā."

When the *nalopa* (elision of *n*) has been applied in the case of *takṣ*, the hearing of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) would follow. This results in a rope that is caught on both sides. The elision of the *r* [of the suffix] occurs by virtue of a restrictive rule (*niyamavacana*). One must state that there is elision of the *t* after an *r*. For example: *abibhar bhavān*, *ajāgar bhavān*. But for what reason is it not established? Because of the restrictive rule; specifically, because of this restriction: "after an *r*, [the *s* of the suffix is elided]."

It does not obtain. This is not a fault; for in the rule *rāt sasya*, the letter *t* is also indicated [as being included]. If this is so, then from the root *kīrt* (to proclaim), the form *kīḥ* would result without a suffix; however, *kīrt* is what is desired. [The principle is: "As prescribed by the grammatical rules, [the forms apply] when they are not actually used. And there is the substitution of *u* for *r*. The substitution of *u* for *r* must also be stated. [Thus we have] *abhinaḥ atra*.

In *acchinnaḥ*, because the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddhatva*), the substitution of *u* for *at* [by Pāṇini 6.4.110] would not apply. Or rather, it need not be stated [that it does not apply]. What is the reason? Because the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct is established (*siddha*) with respect to the substitution of *u*. The elision of the final consonant of a conjunct is established when the substitution of *u* is to occur, just as in *harivaḥ medinam*.

Thus, for example, in the case of *harivo medinaṃ tvā*, the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is established only after the substitution of *u* [for *v*] has taken place.

That very same fault remains; this is a double-edged sword. Therefore, it is impossible to understand the elision of the *apṛkta* as being the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct. If it cannot be so understood, then the mention of "having two consonants" (*dvihala*) and the mention of the *apṛkta* must indeed be made for both cases.

(P_6,1.69.1) KA_III.47.14–48.27 Ro_IV.380–383: A prohibition must be stated regarding the elision of the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi*) after words ending in *ḍatara* and so forth. [Objection: A prohibition regarding the elision of the vocative suffix after words ending in *ḍatara* and so forth must be stated;

for example, "he katarat" (O which of the two? and "he katamat" (O which of many?). Why is it said that a prohibition must be stated for words ending in *ḍatara* and so forth, when [the rule] "of that which is not followed by another vowel" (*apṛktasya*) already applies?

It follows [from the previous rule]. Since the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for *apṛkta* (single-consonant suffixes) has ceased, the *apṛkta* heading is withdrawn. [Question: Is the *apṛkta* heading withdrawn because one will state a prohibition for suffixes such as *-ḍatara*? [Answer: No, he says. And that is for the sake of *am*. That *apṛkta* heading must necessarily be withdrawn. For what purpose? For the sake of *am*, so that the elision of *am* may occur: "he kuṇḍa" (*kuṇḍa* + *am*).
Even though the section concerning *apṛkta* has concluded, the elision of *am* does not apply [here]. For elision does not remove everything.

Let there not be the elision of the whole; since "operations concern the final [sound] of an *al*-group," when the elision of the final [sound] is performed, the form would be established by the single-substitute rule (*pararūpa*) of the two *a*s, as in "he kuṇḍa."

Regarding the form *he pīṭha*: if this were obtainable, it would be correct; however, it is not so obtained. Why? Because here, by the rule *tasmād iti uttarasya ādeḥ parasya*, the elision (*lopa*) of the initial *a* [of the suffix] would apply. And when that *a* is elided, since the *m* remains, the rule *ataḥ dīrgho yañi supi ca* would require lengthening, resulting in the form *he kuṇḍām*.
Otherwise, the form *he pīṭhām* would result. If that is the case, then [the rule] "elision of the consonant" (*halo lopaḥ*) applies, as does "elision of the vocative" (*sambuddhilopaḥ*).

In that case, the mention of *hal* must be made. It need not be made; the previously established context continues. Where was it established? In the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisi apṛktam hal*. But that was specified in the nominative (*prathamānirdiṣṭam*), whereas here [in the present rule] it is specified in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdiṣṭena*).

The meaning is this: there is no such fault. The rule *eṅ hrasvāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.69) contains a fifth case (*pañcamī*), which will cause the first case (*prathamā*) of the word *hal* (from Pāṇini 6.1.71) to be interpreted as a sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), according to the principle that "from that [which is designated by the fifth case], the following [is affected]. Even so, once the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (long vowel homogeneous with the preceding) is applied to the two initial vowels, the form *he pīṭhā* would result. To this, the rule *ami pūrvatvam* (Pāṇini 6.1.107) will serve as the sublater.
It is called *ami*, yet we do not perceive the notion of "mine" (*mam*) here. [For] that which is modified in one part is not different from the original.

Alternatively, this must be considered here: should the elision of the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi-lopa*) be applied first, or the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*)? What should be done here? The single-substitute should take effect because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Even so, once the single-substitute has been applied, the elision of the vocative suffix cannot occur due to the absence of distinct separation (*vyapavarga*).

It does not obtain [the designation *sambuddhi*]. The status of being the "end" or "beginning" (*antādivadbhāva*) will apply [to the final consonant]. [Objection: When there is a dependence on both [the preceding vowel and the following consonant], the status of being the "end" or "beginning" does not apply. [Response: We shall not allow such a dependence on both. How so? It is not understood in this way: "There is elision of the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi*) that follows a short vowel. How then? "There is elision of the consonant (*hal*) that follows a short vowel."
If it is argued that [the rule] applies "after a *sambuddhi*," then that prohibition must be stated. It need not be stated; for it has already been said. What has been said?

That "it is established because of the presence of an *anunāsika* as the penultimate letter. Even so, the elision of *d* (*dalopa*) would still more strongly apply.
