Or rather, because of the use of the augment *du*. Or else, I shall state: "*du* [is the augment] for *itarādi* and others. Or rather, because of the use of the marker *ḍit*. Or else—

This word will be marked with the *ḍit* designation. In that case, the letter *ḍ* must be added. It need not be added; it is already included in the grammatical formulation (*nyāsa*) itself. The instruction "adḍ ḍatarādibhyaḥ" contains two *ḍ*s. Even so, the elision [of the final vowel] would still apply. The mention of the short vowel (*hrasva*) serves as a qualifier for what has been prescribed: namely, that the vocative suffix is prescribed after a short vowel.

(P_6,1.69.2) KA_III.49.1-10 Ro_IV.383-384: By the elision of the *apṛkta* [suffix] and by the elision of the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*), *luk* [elision] occurs by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope for the elision of the *apṛkta* is, for example, *gomān*, *yavamān*. The scope for *luk* is, for example, *trapu*.

In this case, both [rules] would apply: "that which is a Brāhmaṇa family" (*yat brāhmaṇakulam*) and "that Brāhmaṇa family" (*tat brāhmaṇakulam*). The scope for the elision of the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi-lopa*) is, for example, *he agne*, *he vāyo*. The scope for the zero-substitution (*luk*) is the same. Here, both would apply: *he trapu*.

The *luk* elision occurs by way of a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*). [Objection: Then that conflict of rules must be stated. [Response: Or rather, it is not necessary, because between *lopa* and *luk*, *luk* is determined to take precedence, as in the case of *anaḍvāhyate*. Or rather, there is no need for a conflict of rules. What is the reason? Because between *lopa* and *luk*, *luk* is determined to take precedence. For *luk* is determined to take precedence over *lopa*, *yaṇ*, *ayavāy-ekādeśa*.

Just as in the case of *anaḍuhyate*—that is, just as one acts like an ox (*anaḍvān*) is said to be *anaḍuhyate*—here too, the elision (*luk*) is determined through the [preceding rules on] elision (*lopa*) and elision (*luka*). (Pāṇini 6.1.70) This rule could have been omitted. How so? [In the verse: *agne trī te vajinā trī sadhasthā*.

Regarding the forms *tāni* and *tā*, this is established even by the rule for the homogeneous preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*). It is not established; because it is separated by the *num* augment, the *pūrvasavarṇa* does not apply. One must state that in the Veda, the neuter undergoes masculine behavior (*puṃvadbhāva*), for the sake of such examples as *madhoḥ gṛhṇāti* and *mahoḥ tṛptā iva āsate*. In that case, by means of masculine behavior, there is the disappearance of the *num* augment. [This occurs] when *num* is present.

When [the substitution] has ceased, it is established by the rule for the homogeneous preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*). It would be established in cases such as *agne*, *trī te vajrin*, and *trī ṣadhasthā*.

But this is not established: *ta tā piṇḍānām*. This too is established. How? When the seventh-case [rule] for the homogeneous preceding vowel has been applied, the sixth-case [rule] will apply again. Even so, the *guṇa* substitution would still occur before the suffix *jas*. [The author] will state [the solution].
This [is the case]. The statement that the Vedic usage applies to *jas* and so on is prior to [the rule] *ṇau caṅy upadhāyāḥ* (P. 6.1.31).

In the case of *tuk* being included in the *pūrvānta*, the shortening of the feminine when it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) of a neuter compound and the accent of a *dvigu* compound would not be established. In the case of *tuk* being included in the *pūrvānta*, the shortening of the feminine when it is a subordinate member of a neuter compound and the accent of a *dvigu* compound are not accomplished.

An umbrella made from an *ārāśastra*, an umbrella made from fried grain and cakes; an umbrella [measuring] beyond Kauśāmbī, an umbrella [measuring] beyond Vārāṇasī; an umbrella measuring five *aratnis*.

In the case of *daśāratni-chatram*, because the suffix *tuk* has been applied, these rules do not apply due to its infinity (*anantyāt*). Nor [is it because] they are characterized by being external (*bahiraṅga*).

Or rather, this is not a fault. What is the reason? Because they are characterized by being external. The suffix *tuk* is characterized by being external, whereas these rules are internal (*antaraṅga*). That which is external is considered unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal. In that case, consider *grāmaṇiputraḥ*.

When the short vowel [of the penultimate] is applied in the case of *senāniputraḥ*, the augment *tuk* would result; however, there is non-application in the case of *grāmaṇiputra* and similar forms. Why? Precisely because they are characterized by being external (*bahiraṅga*). Alternatively, it could be treated as beginning with the subsequent element (*parādi*). But if it were treated as beginning with the subsequent element, there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) due to the rule "of that which begins with a consonant cluster" (*saṃyogādeḥ*). There would indeed be over-extension if it were treated as beginning with the subsequent element.

Otherwise, the substitution of *e* would undesirably apply to another [element], such as a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) and so forth; furthermore, there would be the need for a statement regarding its elision. One must state: "And there is elision of *vi*. In the case of *agnicit* and *somasut*, the elision of *vi* would not be obtained by the rule "of that which is uncombined" (*apṛktasya*). This is not a fault. The mention of "uncombined" (*apṛkta*) will not be made. If it is not made, [the forms] *darviḥ*, etc., [would be problematic].

In the case of *jāgṛviḥ*, this [substitution] would also apply here. For the word *vi* is understood as being followed by a nasal (*anunāsika*), whereas here the word *vi* is followed by a pure [vowel].

Even so, the elision of the *t* along with its *u* (*satuk*) would result. This does not happen because "substitutes apply to that which is explicitly mentioned" (*nirdiśyamānasya ādeśā bhavanti*). Thus, it is not so.

It will be so; however, there must also be a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*. A prohibition of *iṭ* must be stated, for otherwise the *iṭ* characterized by the rule for roots beginning with a consonant (*valādi*) would apply to [the root] *parīt* when it has the augment *tuk*. If that is the case, then [the *tuk*] is not a part of the suffix (*abhakta*). If it is not a part of the suffix, then there is a fault regarding the accent (*svara*). If it is not a part of the suffix, then in the matter of accent there is a problem, as in the example *dadhi chādayati*.

In the expression *madhu chādayati*, the rule *tiṅ atiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28) does not result in the suppression of accent (*nighāta*). But is it not the case that the suffix *tuk* itself is *atiṅ*? No; the suppression of accent does not apply to what follows *tuk*. What is the reason? Because of the principle: "That which is joined with *nañ* or *iva* is understood as something else similar to it. For such is the way meaning is understood: when a word is joined with *nañ* or *iva*, the grammatical operation is understood to apply to something else that resembles it.

For indeed, the meaning is understood in this way. For example, when it is said, "Bring a non-Brahmin," one brings someone who is similar to a Brahmin; one does not consider the task accomplished by bringing a clod of earth. Likewise here, because of the prohibition of *tiṅ* (verbal endings) in the term *atiṅ*, the operation will be understood to apply to something other than *tiṅ* that is similar to *tiṅ*. And what else is similar to *tiṅ*? A word (*pada*).
(P_6,1.72) KA_III.51.8-11 Ro_IV.387-388 This rule could have been stated without it. How so?

The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is of three kinds: pervasive (*vyāpaka*), contiguous (*aupaśleṣika*), and objective (*vaiṣayika*). And what other connection can there be between one word and another than contiguity (*upaśleṣa*)? [In the rule] *ikaḥ yaṇ aci*, [the meaning is] "of that which is contiguous with a vowel."
Thus, even without the explicit mention of *saṃhitā*, [the rule] will apply only within *saṃhitā* (P.
6.1.74). Now, for what purpose is there the mention of *āṅ* and *māṅ* with their *anubandhas*?

The mention of *āṅ* and *māṅ* with their *anubandhas* is for the sake of ensuring the understanding that the prohibition [of the designation *gati*] applies specifically to *āṅ* and *māṅ* [when they are not *karmapravacanīya*]. Regarding *āṅ* and *māṅ*:

An instruction is given for the two [prefixes] *āṅ* and *māṅ* together with their suffixes (*sānubandhaka*), for the purpose of making known that *āṅ* is a *gati* or a *karmapravacanīya*, and for the purpose of making known that *māṅ* is a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). Let it not be so here: *ā chāyā*, *āc chāyā*; *pramā chandaḥ*.
In the Vedic language (*chandas*),
[the substitution of *u* for *ū*] occurs after a long vowel at the end of a word, optionally, in the case of *viśvajana* and others.
Regarding the rule "after a long vowel at the end of a word, optionally," an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made here for *viśvajana* and so forth in the Vedic language.
An umbrella for all people;
an umbrella for all people. The Kurus do not provide shade for others; the Kurus do not provide shade for others.

(P_6,1.77.1) KA_III.52.2–53.6 Ro_IV.389–391: What is the purpose of including the term *ig* [in the rule]? It is so that it does not apply here: *agnicit atra*, *somasut atra*. This is not a valid purpose, for *jaśtva* will serve as the sublater (*bādhaka*) here. But *jaśtva* is not established; look at the *yaṇ* substitution here. *Jaśtva* is not established here; because it is not established, the *yaṇ* replacement takes effect.

[The substitution] would apply to that which is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*) and precedes both a consonant (*hal*) and a vowel (*ac*). It would apply to that which is not at the end of a word and precedes both a consonant and a vowel, as in *pacati*. If this is so, then [the rule applies to] the *yaṇ* substitute for a long vowel (*dīrgha*). I shall state that the *yaṇ* is the substitute for a long vowel. In that case, the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) must be made. It need not be made; the previously established context (*prakṛta*) continues to apply. Where was it established?

Regarding the rule *dīrghāt padāntād vā*: that indeed is specified in the ablative case (*pañcamī*), yet here the purpose is served by what is specified in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). This locative case (*saptamī*) "in a vowel" (*aci*) will effect a transformation of the ablative "after a long [vowel]" (*dīrghāt*) into a genitive, according to the principle: "when [an element] is specified [by a locative], it refers to what precedes. Thus, the form *kumārī atra* would be established.

Regarding the phrase *brahmabandhvartham*: this [form] is not established; namely, *dadhi atra* and *madhu atra*. The term *hrasvaḥ* (short vowel) is a word that recurs from a previous rule. The mention of *hrasva* also continues to apply by *anuvṛtti* (carrying over). Where was it previously mentioned? In the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk*. If that [term] carries over, then [the rule applies] after a long vowel at the end of a word.

The particle *vā* (or) implies that [the augment] is optionally applied even after a short vowel at the end of a word. By means of its connection with the preceding rule (*sambandhavṛtti*), it will continue to apply: "The augment *tuk* is added after a short vowel before a *kṛt*-suffix ending in a *pit* letter" (*hrasvyasya piti kṛti tuk*); "In *saṃhitā*, the augment *tuk* is added after a short vowel before a *kṛt*-suffix ending in a *pit* letter" (*saṃhitāyām hrasvyasya piti kṛti tuk*); "And in the case of the suffix *cha*, the augment *tuk* is added after a short vowel before a *kṛt*-suffix ending in a *pit* letter" (*che ca hrasvyasya piti kṛti tuk*); "And after the particles *āṅ* and *māṅ*, the augment *tuk* is added after a short vowel before a *kṛt*-suffix ending in a *pit* letter" (*āṅmāṅoś ca hrasvyasya piti kṛti tuk*). [Furthermore,] after a long vowel at the end of a word, the augment is optionally applied.

[The rule] *piti kṛti tuk* [applies]. Then, *ikaḥ yaṇ aci*. The term *hrasvasya* (of a short vowel) is understood to carry over. The phrase *piti kṛti tuk* has ceased to apply here. In that case, it would follow here: *cayanam*, *cāyakaḥ*.

*Lavaṇam* [is derived from *lavaṇa*], *lāvakaḥ* [from *lavana*]. Here, the suffixes beginning with *ay* (Pāṇini 3.1.14) will be the exceptions. But in this case, it would apply to *khaṭvendraḥ* and *mālendraḥ*.

*khaṭvailakā* and *mālailakā*. [The rule] is sublated by *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Here, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* will be the sublaters. In that case, this is the purpose: that for *ika* before a vowel (*aci*), only *yaṇ* should occur; whatever else would otherwise result, let that not happen. And what else?

Something else is obtained: the *śākala* [substitution]. He will raise an objection regarding the prohibition of *śākala* in the case of *s-it* and in compounds; that [objection] need not be stated. (P_6.1.77.2) KA_III.53.7–54.4 Ro_IV.391–393: "The substitution of *yaṇ* [should be stated] even for that preceded by a protracted vowel (*pluta*). It must be stated: "The substitution of *yaṇ* [occurs] even for that preceded by a protracted vowel. For example: *agnā3i indram*, *agnā3y indram*.

paṭā3u udakam, paṭā3v udakam, paṭā3v āśā. What, then, is the reason that this is not established? It is because the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is unestablished [in this context], and these two are modifications of the protracted vowel.

The *pluta* vowel is established [as exempt from modification] in the context of vowel-sandhis (*svarasandhi*). How is this known? Because the Teacher teaches the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the *pluta* in the rule "the *pluta* and *pragṛhya* vowels remain as they are before a vowel" (*plutapragṛhyā aci*), he thereby indicates that the *pluta* is already established in the context of vowel-sandhis. How does this constitute an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? For an operation must apply to something that already exists as its subject. Then what is the purpose [of this teaching]?

"It is for the purpose of prohibiting both the lengthening and the Śākala rule; that is, so that neither the lengthening nor the Śākala [substitution] occurs. This too is not a valid purpose. The substitution of *yaṇ* for [the vowels] preceded by a *pluta* vowel is being introduced by the rule "for those two (*i* and *u*), *y* and *v* are substituted before a vowel in *saṃhitā*.
That [introduction] will serve the purpose of prohibiting both the lengthening and the Śākala rule. Therefore, it need not be stated. But surely, in that case...

Even though this has been stated, it still ought not to be said; for this must necessarily be stated for the sake of those *i* and *u* vowels that are preceded by a protracted (*pluta*) vowel and undergo the modification of becoming non-protracted (*apluta-vikāra*), as in: *bho3i indram*, *bho3y indram*.

"Bho3i iha bho3y iha. If there is indeed a basis for this, then this very thing should be stated. [Objection: That need not be stated. [Response: Even that must necessarily be stated for the sake of the accent (*svara*). For if this were present, the accent prescribed by the rule "yaṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.4) regarding the *udātta* and *svarita* vowels would apply. But if that [rule] is present, it will not occur because [the former rule] is considered non-existent (*asiddhatva*). If...
In that case, whatever the basis for it is, that alone should be stated; this [present rule] need not be stated.

But has it not already been said that this too must necessarily be stated for the sake of those *i* and *u* vowels which are preceded by a protracted (*pluta*) vowel and undergo the modification of becoming non-protracted? For example: *bho3i indram*, *bho3y indram*.

"Bho3i iha bho3y iha"—this is Vedic; in the Veda, one follows what is observed. But then, how is it that he sings the *sāman* "bho3y indram, bho3y iha," which is not Vedic? This too is an application following what is observed in the Veda. The substitution of *jaś* (the voiced unaspirated stops) is not established here; look at the *yaṇ* [substitution] in this case. And whatever consonant (*hal*) is not at the end of a word, provided it is preceded by a vowel (*ac*), [is subject to the rule]: "for a long [vowel], there is *yaṇ*."

The term *hrasva* (short vowel) refers to a metrical foot (*pāda*). By way of its connection [to the preceding rule], it is subject to the sublation of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. And this [term] was established by the Blessed One for the sake of that which is permanent in the *śākala* [substitution] within a compound; for, due to the application of logical necessity (*sāmarthya*), I do not see anything in this treatise that would be purposeless.

Regarding the substitution of *vān* (the sounds *au*): the mention of the original elements (*sthānin*) must be specified. In the case of the substitution of *vān*, the mention of the original elements must be made; it should be stated that this applies to the sounds *o* and *au*, so that it does not apply to the sounds *e* and *ai*. [Objection: Then it must be done. [Response: It need not be done. The term *vān* will not be employed. When a suffix beginning with *y* follows, the substitutes *ay*, etc., take the place of *ec*.

Thus it is established. Alternatively, if the mention of the word *vānta* were not made, then [the suffix] would also apply here in the case of *ceyam* and *jeyam*. The rule *kṣayyajayyau śakyārthe* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning that [the suffix applies] only to the roots *kṣi* and *ji*. In that case, however, it would still apply to those two even outside the sense of possibility (*śakyārtha*). For example: *kṣeyam pāpam* ("sin is to be destroyed").

Regarding the example *jeyaḥ vṛṣalaḥ* ("the low-born man is to be conquered"): it should be understood that there is a restriction (*niyama*) on both sides—that is, the substitution of *ai* and *au* occurs only for the vowels *e* and *o*, and those [substitutions] occur only when the suffixes have the sense of possibility (*śakya*). In this case as well, then, due to the restriction, [the substitution] would not apply: *lavyam* (to be reaped), *pavyam* (to be purified), *avaśyalāvyam* (necessarily to be reaped).

It must necessarily be stated: the restriction applies to that which is of the same class (*tulyajātīya*). And what is of the same class? That which is of the same nature as the *ec* vowels [substituted] for *kṣi* and *ji*. Of what nature is the *ec* for *kṣi* and *ji*? It is the vowel *e*. Even so, in the case of *rāyam icchati*, [we get] *raiyati*.
In this case as well, [the rule] would apply: *rāyiḥ* is Vedic; in the Veda, there is conformity with what is observed.

(P. 6.1.79.2) KA_III.54.17–22 Ro_IV.394: *goḥ yūtau chandasi*. An addition must be made for *goḥ yūtau chandasi*: "O Mitra and Varuṇa, sprinkle our pasture (*gavyūti*) with clarified butter. Elsewhere it is simply *goyūti*.

And regarding the measure of distance: an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the word *go* when used with *yūti* in the sense of a measure of distance. For example: "He has gone a *gavyūti* distance. But elsewhere, it is simply *goyūti*. (Pāṇini 6.1.80) [Question:
What is the purpose of the particle *eva*? [Answer: It is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). This is not so.

[Objection: There is no such purpose. A rule being formulated when [the desired result] is already established will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) even without the particle *eva*. [Response: Then it is for the sake of restriction according to what is intended, so that it might be understood thus: "only that which is caused by a verbal root. Let it not be understood thus: "only that which is caused by a verbal root. And what would be the consequence?
In the absence of that [suffix], there would not be [the application] of its cause: as in *śaṅkavyam dāru* ("wood for a stake") and *picavyaḥ kārpāsaḥ* ("cotton for a brush").

(P_6.1.82) KA_III.55.4-5 Ro_IV.395 By this word *tat*, what is being referred back? That very meaning of "he buys. Let it not be so here: *kreyaṃ naḥ dhānyam* ("our grain is to be bought"). And it does not exist...
Regarding the term *krayya* (P. 6.1.83):
in the section concerning *bhayya* and others, there should be an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for *hradayya*.
An addition for *hradayya* must be made in the section concerning *bhayya* and others. [Examples: *hradayyā āpaḥ* ("the waters of the heart"). [The suffix] *av* replaces *śara*.

And from *śara* and *hrada*, the suffix *av* is applied: *hradavyāḥ* (waters from a lake) and *śaravyāḥ* (arrows). Indeed, *tejana* (the point of an arrow) is *śaravya*. One would be a striker of the animals of the *śaravya*. Or rather, it is established by the usage of the word *śaru*. It is established again by the usage of the word *śaru*; for the expression "the speeding *śaru*" (*ṛñjatī śaruḥ*) is also seen. Thus, the application of the word *śaru* is [justified] by the phrase "the speeding *śaru*."
It is seen in common usage as *śarahastaḥ*. In common usage, they apply the designation *śarahastaḥ* to one who has arrows in his hand (*śarahastam*).

(P_6.1.84.1) Why is the singular number used? The singular number is for the purpose of prohibiting separate substitutes. The singular number is employed so that there may be a single substitute; [otherwise] there would be separate substitutes.

Let it not be so. Or rather, it is not the case [that a single substitute occurs] because, in the injunction of an action, one of two [words] is produced [as the substitute]. Nor indeed is there any purpose for this. What is the reason? Because, in the injunction of an action regarding substances, when one of two [words] is produced, a single substitute will occur. For example, in the case of substances, when there is an injunction of an action, one of two [words] is produced [as the substitute].

[It is said: "Make a mat from these two bundles of grass; make a jar from these two lumps of clay. And yet, although it is not explicitly stated that there is one [result], he produces only one. What, then, is the reason that when an action is enjoined regarding substances, the production of only one occurs from two?
It is because of their forming a single sentence (*ekavākyabhāvāt*). It is due to their forming a single sentence that, when an action is enjoined regarding substances, [only one result is produced].

The substitution of one [element] occurs for two [elements]. This is because they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*). For even in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), elsewhere, a single substitute (*ādeśa*) occurs for two substituenda (*sthānin*); as in the rules *jvaratvarasrivyavimavām upadhāyāś ca* and *bhrasjo ropadhayo ram anyatarasyām*. As for what was said—that it is because they form a single syntactical unit—that is not so; rather, it is by implication (*arthāt*).

Or, by virtue of the context, in common usage the manifestation of one of two [alternatives] occurs; and thus, either by implication or by context. For even in grammar, elsewhere, when there are two substituends, two substitutes occur: "After *r* and *d*, the *niṣṭhā* [suffix] becomes *na*, and the preceding *d* also [becomes *na*]; both [substitutes apply] for that which has a reduplication. How then is it said that this also applies in grammar?

For indeed, elsewhere, a single substitute occurs in place of two substituends. [As in the rules]: "In *jvara*, *tvara*, *sriv*, *av*, and *mav*, [the vowel] of the penultimate syllable [is replaced by *ū*];

and "In *bhrasj*, [the substitute] *ram* optionally takes the place of the *r* and the following vowel. Now, regarding the rule "In *jvara*, *tvara*, *sriv*, *av*, and *mav*, [the vowel] of the penultimate syllable [is replaced by *ū*]," let there be two instances of *ūṭh*. There is no fault; it is established by the rule for the lengthening of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*).

Regarding the rule *bhrasjo ropadhayo ram anyatarasyām*, this will indeed be stated: "In the case of the root *bhrasj*, there is the elision of the *r* and the *upadha* [vowel], and the augment *ram* is prescribed. As for what was said—that it occurs "either by implication (*arthāt*) or from the context (*prakaraṇāt*)"—that is not correct. Why? Because in common usage, the accomplishment of one thing out of two occurs precisely through syntactic unity (*ekavākyabhāva*). And therefore, it is due to syntactic unity.
"Indeed, sir, you might as well speak to a common villager with dusty feet who knows nothing of the context, saying:
'Make a mat from these two bundles of straw,' or 'Make a jar from these two lumps of clay. He would do only one thing. How so?
Because it is stated even in grammar that when there are two substituends, two substitutes may occur [in their place]. [As in the rule: *radābhyām*..."

"From the *niṣṭhā* [suffixes], there is *na* for the root-final *d*, and also for the preceding [consonant]. "Both [are replaced] when the reduplication is present. First, regarding this [sūtra]: "radābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ pūrvasya ca daḥ" consists of two sentences. How so? By means of a *yogavibhāga* (division of the rule). First: "radābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ"; then: "pūrvasya ca daḥ". Here, in the case of "ubhau sābhyāsasya," it is by virtue of the inclusion of the word "both" (*ubhau*) that [the rule applies].
There will be two [types of] substitutes.

In that case, there arises the understanding of the purpose of the grammatical rule as applying to a part [of the whole], just as in common worldly usage there arises the understanding of the purpose of a rule as applying to a part. For example, as in the world...

Regarding the injunction, "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in spring," once the fires have been established, the purpose of the scriptural rule is fulfilled; therefore, there is no further performance of it. Likewise, regarding the injunction, "A Brāhmaṇa is to be initiated in the eighth year from conception," once he has been initiated, the purpose of the scriptural rule is fulfilled; therefore, there is no further performance of it. Similarly, [the rite is performed] three times with water reaching the heart.

Regarding the rule "one should touch [the water] with sounds that are not audible," once one has touched it once, thinking that the purpose of the scripture has been fulfilled, there is no further application. Likewise here, too, thinking that the purpose of the scripture has been fulfilled by the word *khaṭvendra*, it would not apply to *mālendra* and so forth. But this is established: because the instruction regarding the property (*dharma*) is understood as a non-composite whole, just as in the case of worldly and Vedic [expressions]. This is established.

This [is so]. How? This treatise is an instruction on Dharma (*dharmopadeśana*). And in this treatise, which is an instruction on Dharma, the meaning of the treatise is understood in its entirety, just as it is in worldly and Vedic scriptures (*kṛtanta*). First, in the world: "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed; liquor must not be drunk. There, not merely any Brāhmaṇa is killed, nor merely any liquor.

And [the rule] would not be violated. Furthermore, if the meaning of the scripture were understood through a single part [of the whole], then by not killing even one Brāhmaṇa and not drinking even one [measure of] *surā*, there would be freedom of action elsewhere. Likewise, regarding the rule "an elderly Brāhmaṇa is to be saluted," only one who is merely elderly would be saluted. If the meaning of the scripture were understood through a single part, [then by the same logic,] one...
Having risen to greet one who is of an older age, one may act as one pleases otherwise. Likewise, it is indeed stated in the Veda:

"In the spring, a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma and other rites. Because the installation of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) is the occasion for this, the sacrifice is performed every spring. If the understanding of the scriptural meaning were based on a single part [of the injunction], then after sacrificing once, the performance of the sacrifice would not proceed again.

In this world, both ways are observed: the comprehension of the meaning of a treatise occurs both through its parts and without its parts. But how is it that both are obtained? He says: they are obtained. How so? First, in this case, regarding the rule "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in spring": the establishment of the fires is for the purpose of attaining the mouth of sacrifice (*yajñamukha*). Having established them once—
Since the purpose of the scripture has been accomplished by the thought that the sacrifice has been undertaken, there is no further activity;

therefore, in this case, the purpose of the scripture is understood through a single part [of the action]. Likewise, regarding the rule "A Brāhmaṇa is to be initiated in the eighth year from conception," the initiation is for the sake of consecration (*saṃskāra*). And once he has been initiated, he becomes consecrated. Therefore, in this case...

Furthermore, the meaning of a scriptural injunction is understood through its constituent parts. For example: "One should touch [the mouth] three times with water that reaches the heart, which is silent and not accompanied by sound. This touching is for the purpose of purification; and having touched it once, one becomes pure.
Therefore, even in this case, the meaning of the scriptural injunction is understood through its constituent parts. Now, in this context, it is said: "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed."

"Surā is not to be drunk. A great fault has been declared for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa and for the drinking of surā; that [fault] would apply to the mere killing of a Brāhmaṇa and to the mere drinking of surā. Therefore, in this case, the meaning of the scripture is understood as applying without exception. Likewise, "an elder Brāhmaṇa is to be saluted by rising"; a fault is declared for not rising to greet an elder, whereas in rising...

And it is a quality (*guṇa*). How so? "For the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of a youth depart when old age approaches; one regains them again by rising from one's seat and by salutation. And that [quality] would apply only to the mere state of being young. Therefore, even here, the meaning of the scripture is understood as being without limitation (*anavayavena*). Likewise: "In spring, a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices."

Thus, some purpose for sacrifice has been stated: namely, that "in the heavenly world, the Apsarases become his wives and lie with him. And that [purpose] ought to belong to the second and third sacrifices as well. Therefore, here too, the meaning of the scripture is understood in its entirety. Likewise, there is a purpose for the knowledge and application of the word as well.

It has been said: "A single word, correctly understood, in accordance with the treatises, and well-employed, becomes a cow of plenty in the heavenly world. If a single word, correctly understood, in accordance with the treatises, and well-employed, becomes a cow of plenty in the heavenly world, for what purpose are a second and a third employed? Indeed, there is no satiety regarding desires.

(P_6,1.84.3) KA_III.58.18–59.8 Ro_IV.402–403 Now, for what purpose is the mention of "prior" (*pūrva*)? The mention of "prior and posterior" (*pūrvapara*) is for the purpose of prohibiting the substitution of the subsequent [element]. The mention of "prior and posterior" is made for the purpose of prohibiting the substitution of the subsequent [element], so that there be no substitution of the subsequent [element] by the rule *āt guṇaḥ*. And how would it apply? For [the rule] is indicated by the fifth case (*pañcamī*).

[The term] *para* [is used] because an operation (*kārya*) is prescribed for that which follows what is indicated by the fifth case (*pañcamī*). For example: "after *dvi*, *antar*, and prefixes, *ap-* becomes *īt*" (*dvyantarupasargebhyaḥ apaḥ īt*). However, the mention of "prior" and "subsequent" (*pūrvaparagrahaṇa*) is made for the sake of what is indicated by the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).

That is, it is done so that the indication by the sixth case may be applicable. For if it were not indicated, the meaning of the sixth case would not be established. [This is said] when [the mention of "prior" and "subsequent"] is not being made.
For if both "prior" (*pūrva*) and "subsequent" (*para*) were included, the sense of the genitive case would not be established. Of what? Of the relation of substitution (*sthāneyoga*).

This is not a fault. This fifth-case form *āt* will effect a sixth-case interpretation of the seventh-case form *aci*, according to the rule "from that [the subsequent]" (*tasmād ity uttarasya*). And likewise, this seventh-case form *aci* will effect a sixth-case interpretation of the fifth-case form *āt*.

When "in that" (*tasmin*) is specified, [the rule] "of the preceding" (*pūrvasya*) applies. If this is so, then since the result is already established, the fact that the Teacher employs the term "preceding" (*pūrva*) indicates that both [the antecedent and the subsequent rules] cannot apply simultaneously as optional alternatives. What is the purpose of this indication? It is that which was stated:

Since both the seventh and fifth cases [the locative and ablative] exist due to the presence of the suffix *bhāva*, there would be an application of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in both instances, leading to the undesirable consequence of both operations occurring simultaneously. That is not a fault. (P_6,1.85.1) KA_III.59.10-60.6 Ro_IV.

404-406 For what purpose is this stated? The statement "as if it were the end or the beginning" (*antādivat*) is made because of the prescription of a substitute for that which is mixed (*āmiśra*). It is said to be "as if it were the end or the beginning" because of the prescription of a substitute for that which is mixed. For that which is mixed...
This is called a substitute (*ādeśa*). It is grasped neither by the mention of the preceding element (*pūrva*) nor by the mention of the following element (*para*).

For example, when milk and water are mixed together, because they are blended, it is not grasped by the mention of "milk" nor by the mention of "water. Yet, it is desired that there should be such a grasping; and since that is not accomplished without effort, the rule stating "as if it were the end and the beginning" (*antādivat*) is formulated.

This is stated for this purpose; there is indeed a need for it. What then? In that regard, the mention of that which is treated as if it were the end or the beginning must be made. That is to say, one must state: "it becomes like the end of this," or "it becomes like the beginning of this. However, it is established by virtue of the governing rules concerning what precedes and what follows. It is thus established.

This [is the case]. How so? Because of the governing influence of what precedes and follows. The phrase "of the preceding and the following" is understood [to apply here]. With respect to an operation concerning the preceding element, it behaves as if it were the final (anta-vat); with respect to an operation concerning the following element, it behaves as if it were the initial (ādi-vat). Now, where both [preceding and following] are relied upon, does it there behave as the final of the preceding, or as the initial of the following? [The rule applies] when there is reliance on both sides.

It is not like the case of the "end" and so forth. Should this be stated? No, it need not be. How is it understood without being explicitly stated? This is a worldly illustration. For example, in the world, when there is a servant belonging to two people of equal power, he performs their work for them alternately. But when both send him out simultaneously, and the tasks are in different directions—

In that case, if he is one who seeks non-contradiction, then he does not perform both. But what is the reason that he does not perform both? Because of the impossibility of simultaneity; there is no possibility of occurrence simultaneously.
Now, what are the purposes served by having a finite limit (*antavattva*)? Regarding having a finite limit:

The purpose [of this rule] is for the prescription of the suffix *ṭhac* after a compound whose prior member consists of more than two syllables (*bahvac-pūrvapada*). Regarding the status of the final element (*antavad-bhāva*) when the suffix *ṭhac* is prescribed after a compound with a multi-syllabic prior member: the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from the combination of the final vowel of the prior member and the initial vowel of the subsequent member is treated as the final element of the prior member. This is so that the suffix *ṭhac* may be applied according to the rule "after a compound with a multi-syllabic prior member. Where, then, would it apply? [For example: *dvādaśānyikaḥ*. (In *dvā-daśa-anya*, the substitution of *ai* for *a+a* is treated as the end of the prior member *dvādaśa*, thereby allowing the application of *ṭhac*. Where else would it apply?

In a case where, even after the substitution of a single substitute (*ekādeśa*), the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) remains polysyllabic (*bahvac*), [the rule applies]. For example: *trayodaśānyikaḥ*. The substitution of a single substitute for an affix (*pratyaya-ekādeśa*) serves as a basis for a preceding grammatical operation (*pūrva-vidhi*). The substitution of a single substitute for an affix is necessary for a preceding operation. For instance: *madhu pibanti*. In the case of the substitution of *śit* for *aśit*, the single substitute for *śit* and *aśit* is treated as if it were the final element of *śit*, so that the operation prescribed by the rule "when *śit*"—namely, the substitution of *piba*—can be performed. Where, then, [does this apply]?

It would apply where there is no single-substitute (ekādeśa). [Examples are: *pibati*; [and] regarding the substitution of *ṇ* for a case-ending (*vaibhaktasya ṇatve*). The purpose of the substitution of *ṇ* for a case-ending is as follows: *kṣīrapeṇa*, *surāpeṇa*. The single-substitute of the two case-endings belonging to the second member (*uttarapada*) is treated as if it were the final element of that second member, so that [the rule may] be applicable.

The suffix *ṇa* occurs when the following member (*uttarapada*) consists of a single syllable. Where, then, would it apply? Where a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) does not occur: for example, *kṣīrapāṇām* (those who drink milk) and *surāpāṇam* (the drinking of liquor). Regarding the substitution of *ī* and *ū* in *adas*: the purpose of the substitution of *ī* and *ū* in *adas* is as follows: *amī atra*, *amī āsate*.

*amū atra*, *amū āsāte*. The single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from the case-endings of *adas-* is treated as if it were the final element of *adas-*, so that the following rules may apply: *adaso 'ser dād u daḥ maḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.80] and *eta īd bahuvacane* [Pāṇini 8.2.81]. Where, then, would these apply? Where the single-substitute does not occur: *amībhiḥ*.

The purpose of the *svarita* accent in these two cases is as follows: in *kāryā* and *hāryā*, the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for *ti* and *tiroḥ* is treated as if it were the final element of the preceding part (*antavat*), so that the rule "the *tit* is *svarita*" can be applied. Where, then, would this apply? Where a single substitute does not occur, such as in *kāryaḥ* and *hāryaḥ*. Regarding the *svarita* accent, there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). Should the *svarita* be applied first, or the single substitute? What should be done here?
"The circumflex (*svarita*) will occur by virtue of its subsequent position through the rule of *vipratiṣedha* (mutual exclusion). "This *vipratiṣedha* is not logical.

The single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is permanent (*nitya*); for it applies whether the circumflex has already occurred or has not yet occurred. The single-substitute is non-permanent (*anitya*); for it applies to one kind of accent when the circumflex has occurred, and to another kind of accent when the circumflex has not occurred—thus, it applies to a different accent."
And if [the substitution] were to apply first, the rule would become non-eternal (*anitya*). In that case, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is *antaraṅga*. What is its *antaraṅga* status?
The single-substitute depends upon two phonemes (*varṇa*), whereas the *svarita* accentuation of the word depends upon the word as a whole. But the *svarita* accentuation is also *antaraṅga*. How so?

It has been stated that the mention of "word" (*pada*) is for the purpose of defining its extent. Between these two *antaraṅga* operations, the *svarita* accentuation prevails because it is subsequent.

Once the *svarita* accent has been applied, by virtue of proximity (*āntaryataḥ*), the single substitute for the *svarita* and the *anudātta* will itself be *svarita*. Alternatively, because of the inclusion of the gender-qualified form (*liṅgaviśiṣṭagrahaṇāt*), or rather, because when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, its gender-qualified form is also included, the *svarita* accent will thus apply here. Furthermore, the purpose is to ensure that the final syllable of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is accented acute (*udātta*). For example: *guḍodakam*.
In *mathitodaka*, the single substitute for both the preceding and following members (*ekādeśa*) is treated as the final element of the preceding member.

This is so that it may be possible to apply the rule: "In the case of *udaka* when it does not denote 'the whole,' the final syllable of the preceding member becomes acute. Where, then, would this apply? Where there is no single substitute (*ekādeśa*), as in *udaśvid-udakam*. And [there too] there is the acute accent on the final syllable of the preceding member; that is, the state of having the acute accent on the final syllable of the preceding member.

And because of the conflict [between rules]: "Let the acute accent on the final syllable of the first member be applied" and "let the single substitution (ekādeśa) be applied"—what should be done here?

Because it is subsequent, the acute accent on the final syllable of the first member takes effect. The scope for the acute accent on the final syllable of the first member is seen in *udaśvid-udakam*;
the scope for the single substitution is seen in *daṇḍāgram*.

In the case of *kṣupāgram*, both [rules] would apply here: *mathitodaka* and *guḍodaka*. By way of mutual exclusion (*vipratiṣedha*), the rule for the acute accent on the final syllable of the first member prevails. And this mutual exclusion must necessarily be resorted to; for otherwise, there would be no establishment of the circumflex accent (*svarita*) in the case of a single substitution (*ekādeśa*). Indeed, in the case of a single substitution, the circumflex accent would not be established.

It might be so. For one who thinks, "Let there be a single-substitute (ekādeśa) here; once the single-substitute has been made, the final syllable of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) will be udātta," for such a person the circumflex accent (*svarita*) is not established by the rule *svarito vānudātte padādau*. [Examples: *mathitodakam*, *guḍodakam*. Furthermore, the purpose is to establish the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the *kṛt*-derived stem: *prāṭitā*.

In the case of *prāśitā*, the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for the verbal prefix (*gati*) and the root (*kṛt*) is treated as if it were at the end of the preceding element (*antavat*), so that the rule "a *kṛt*-derived final member following a prefix, a *kāraka*, or a secondary word (*upapada*) retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*)" may apply. Where, then, would this apply? Where there is no single substitute (*akādeśa*), such as in *prakārakaḥ* and *prakaraṇam*. And there is also the retention of the original accent of the *kṛt*-derived final member; and this [retention of the *kṛt*-accent] prevails by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).

Let the accent of the base of the *kṛt*-derived stem apply; let the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [accent] apply. What should be done here? By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the accent of the base of the *kṛt*-derived stem prevails because it is subsequent. The scope of the accent of the base of the *kṛt*-derived stem is, for example, *prakārakaḥ* and *prakaraṇam*. The scope of the single-substitute [accent] is, for example, *daṇḍāgram*.

In the case of *kṣupāgram*, both [rules] would apply here: *prāṭitā* and *prāśitā*. By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the accentuation of the base of the *kṛt*-suffix applies. And that conflict must necessarily be resorted to; for if there were a single substitution (*ekādeśa*), the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) would not be established, because it is no longer "subsequent" [to anything]. For one who thinks thus...

Let there be a single-substitute (ekādeśa) here; once the single-substitute has been applied, the accentuation of the base of the *kṛdanta* [word] will occur. [But] its accentuation as the base of a *kṛdanta* is not established. What is the reason? Because the latter member (*uttarapada*) is no longer subsequent. For now, once the single-substitute has been applied, the latter member does not remain subsequent. [Objection: But surely it is subsequent by virtue of the rule regarding "as if preceding or following" (*antādivadbhāva*). [Response: Not so, because it is on both sides (*ubhayataḥ*).

In the case of a compound where the first member is a word ending in *ā*, the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel and the following initial vowel does not take place, as in the case of words like *anta*. Furthermore, the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the second member occurs by virtue of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule through the application of the *vipratiṣedha* (conflict) principle. The scope for the *vṛddhi* of the second member is seen in examples such as *pūrvatraigartakaḥ* and *aparatraigartakaḥ*. The scope for the single-substitute rule is seen in examples such as *daṇḍāgram* and *kṣupāgram*. In the present instance, both rules would apply: *pūrva-eṣukāmaśamaḥ*. [In this case, the *vṛddhi* of the second member prevails.]

In the case of *apara-eṣukāmaśam*, the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the final member occurs by way of a counter-exception (*vipratiṣedha*). However, there is the contingency of a single-substitute replacement (*ekādeśa*), because that which is internal (*antaraṅga*) is stronger. Thus, the single-substitute replacement would indeed apply. Why? Because the internal is stronger; the internal is more powerful. What is the fault in that? In that case, the rule for lengthening (*vṛddhi*) must be prescribed. Therefore, the lengthening must be enjoined there.

This is not a fault. The activity of the Teacher indicates that the grammatical operation takes place first between the preceding and following words, and only then does the single-substitute (ekādeśa) occur; this is shown by the fact that he teaches the prohibition "not when *indra* follows. How is this an indicator? In the word *indra*, there are two vowels (*ac*). Of these, one is removed by the elision rule "of that which has *ī* as its penultimate" (*yasyeti ca*), while the other is removed by the single-substitute rule.

Consequently, Indra becomes vowel-less (*anacka*). In that case, what occasion would there be for *vṛddhi*? However, the Teacher perceives that the operation [of *vṛddhi*] applies to both the preceding and following words before the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has taken effect; therefore, he teaches the prohibition "not when *indra* follows."

Now, what are the purposes served by [the status of] being like the first element (*ādivattva*)? Regarding the purpose served by being like the first element: it serves the purpose in the application of the technical term *pragṛhya*. When there is the status of being like the first element, the purpose in the application of the term *pragṛhya* is as follows: in the cases *agnī* and *vāyū*, the single substitute for two dual endings becomes like the first element of the dual ending, so that [the rule may apply].

[The rule] "the dual ending *ī*, *ū*, and *e* are *pragṛhya*" is intended for application [only where a single-substitute replacement does not occur]. Where, then, would it apply? Where a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) does not take place—as in *trapuṇī* and *jatunī*. [The sūtra] "in rules concerning *sup*, *tiṅ*, and *āp*" serves as the purpose [for the following]. Regarding *sup*: in *vṛkṣe tiṣṭhati* ("he stands on the tree") and *plakṣe tiṣṭhati* ("he stands on the fig tree"), the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of *sup* and *sup* is treated like the beginning of the subsequent *sup* so that the operation may be performed.

"A word (*pada*) is that which ends in a *sup* [case] suffix. Where, then, would this apply? Where a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) does not occur: *vṛkṣaḥ tiṣṭhati*, *plakṣaḥ tiṣṭhati*. [Regarding] *sup* and *tiṅ*:

in "pace" and "yaje," the single-substitute for *tiṅ* and *atiṅ* becomes like the beginning of the *tiṅ* [element], so that it may be possible to apply the rule "a word is that which ends in *tiṅ*. Where, then, would this apply? Where a single-substitute does not occur: *pacati*.

One sacrifices (*yajati*). A finite verb ending (*tiṅ*), and *āp* [as in] *khaṭvā*, *mālā*. Regarding the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) for *ap* and *āp*: the substitute for *āp* is treated like the initial element of that which it replaces, so that what can be done may be accomplished—namely, that the elision (*lopa*) of *su* occurs after a stem ending in long *ā*. Where, then, would this apply? Where the single-substitute does not occur—as in *kruñcā*.

The *uṣṇih* [meter] is the direction of the gods (*devadiś*). Regarding the mention of *āṅ* in rules concerning words (*padavidhi*): the purpose of mentioning *āṅ* in rules concerning words is as follows: in *adyāhate* and *kadāhate*, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) for both *āṅ* and *anāṅ* becomes like the initial element of *āṅ*. This is so that the rule *āṅo yamahanaḥ* may be applied.

Thus, the *ātmanepada* [middle voice] occurs. Where, then, would it apply? Where a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) does not occur. For example, in *āhate*. And there is a purpose for the augment *āṭ* in the rule prescribing *vṛddhi*: in *adyaihiṣṭa*. When did he go? [Answer:

*āṭ* and the word *adya* undergo a single-substitute; this substitute of *āṭ* and *adya* is treated as the initial element of *āṭ*, so that [the operation] may be performed, and also for the sake of *āṭ*.

"The *vṛddhi* [substitution] occurs for the vowel *a*. Where, then, would it apply? Where there is no single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [operation]. As in *aihiṣṭa*, *aikṣiṣṭa*. And regarding the status of a *kṛt*-derived nominal stem (*prātipadika*). And there is a purpose regarding the status of a *kṛt*-derived nominal stem: *dhārayaḥ*, *pārayaḥ*. When a single-substitute has been made between a *kṛt*-affix and that which is not a *kṛt*-affix, it is treated as if it were the beginning [of the subsequent element], so that it may be possible to treat the *kṛt*-derived form as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Where, then, would it apply? Where there is no single-substitute [operation]. As in *kārakaḥ*.

...the haraka. (P_6.1.85.4) KA_III.64.9–65.6 Ro_IV.413–414: "Not in the case of the shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) and others. It should be stated that when there is shortening of the reduplicated syllable and so forth, the rule of *antādivat* (as if it were the end of the preceding and the beginning of the following) does not apply. What, then, are the "reduplicated syllable and others"? They are: the shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), the [shortening] of *ūha*, *ambā*, words having the sense of *artha*, nadī-words, neuter words, and secondary members (*upasarjana*).
The shortening of the vowel in *abhy-ūha*: *upeyāja*, *upovāpa*. The shortening of the vowel in *ūh-*:
*upohyate*, *prohyate*.
It is produced. [The rules concerning] the shortening of the vowels in *amba*, words meaning "mother," rivers, and neuter upasarjana compounds apply:
*amba atra*, *akka atra*; *kumāri idam*, *kiśorī idam*; *ārāśastrī idam*.

In the cases of *dhānāśaṣkulī* (this), *niṣkauśāmbi* (this), and *nirvārāṇasi* (this), shortening would apply because [the words] *abhyāsa*, *ūha*, *ām*, *arthanadī*, and *napuṃsaka-upasarjana* are included [in the rule]. Or rather, it need not be stated. Why? Because it is characterized as being external (*bahiraṅga*). Or rather, this need not be said. What is the reason? Because it is characterized as being external.

The shortness (*hrasvatva*) is internal (*antaraṅga*), whereas these rules are external (*bahiraṅga*). That which is external is considered unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal. Furthermore, regarding a rule based on phonemes (*varṇāśrayavidhi*), it must be stated that the status of being "like the end" (*antavadbhāva*) or "like the beginning" (*ādivadbhāva*) does not apply. What is the purpose? The purpose is seen in the cases *khaṭvābhiḥ*, *juhāva*, and *asyai aśvaḥ*. Here, in the case of *khaṭvābhiḥ*:

Because of [the presence of] *mālābhiḥ*, the substitution of *ais* for *bhisaḥ* would apply, resulting in the form *mālābhaiḥ*. This is not a fault; it will not occur because of the force of the inclusion of the marker *t* (in *adbhis*). Is there another purpose for the inclusion of the marker *t*? Yes: [to account for forms such as] *kīlālapābhiḥ*.

In the case of *śubhaṃyābhiḥ* [from *śubham yābhiḥ*], the substitution of *au* by Pāṇini 7.1.34 (*ata au ṇalaḥ*) would apply. In the case of *asyai aśvaḥ*, the substitution of the preceding form by Pāṇini 6.1.109 (*eṅaḥ padāntād ati*) would apply. [Reply: Or rather, it need not be stated. Why? Because of the extension of non-identity (*atādrūpyātideśāt*). Here, identity of form is not being extended; for these [rules] depend upon the actual phonetic form.
The rules [concerning the substitution of *ṣ*] will not apply because the forms do not possess that specific nature.

(P_6.1.86.1) Why is this stated? The statement that the substitution of *ṣ* and the *tuk*-augment are "asiddha" (non-existent for the purposes of rule application) is for the purpose of prohibiting the application of characteristics based on the substituends (*ādeśa-lakṣaṇa-pratiṣedha*), and for the purpose of ensuring the occurrence of characteristics based on the original elements (*utsarga-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*). This is the non-existence (*asiddhatva*) of the substitution of *ṣ* and the *tuk*-augment.

It is said: [this is] for the purpose of prohibiting the characteristics of the substitute (*ādeśa*) and for the purpose of establishing the characteristics of the original form (*utsarga*). First, regarding the purpose of prohibiting the characteristics of the substitute: *kosiñcat*, *yosiñcat*. Once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, the rule "after *iṇ*" would require the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*]. Because [the single-substitute] is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), it does not occur. Furthermore, it is for the purpose of establishing the characteristics of the original form: *adhītya*.

When *pretya* is formed, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, the *tuk* augment [prescribed] by the rule "after a short vowel" (*hrasvasya*) does not apply. It does, however, apply because it is considered as if unestablished (*asiddhatvāt*). This is indeed a purpose [for the rule]. What then? In that case, there would be the non-establishment of the operation characterized by the general rule (*utsarga-lakṣaṇa*), due to the absence of the general rule itself. In that situation, the grammatical operation characterized by the general rule would not be established. [For example, in the case of] *adhītya*.

Regarding the word *pretya*: what is the reason? Because there is no general rule (*utsarga*) [applying here]. It is stated that [the substitution applies] to a short vowel, and we do not observe a short vowel here. But is it not the case that even here it is established by the statement of its being "not yet established" (*asiddha*)? If you say it is established by the statement of its being *asiddha*, we say no; for the existence of one thing does not follow from the statement of another being *asiddha*. If you say it is established by the statement of its being *asiddha*, that is not so.

What is the reason? Because the existence of one thing does not follow from the statement that another is unestablished (*asiddha*). Indeed, the manifestation of one thing does not occur simply because another is stated to be unestablished. For instance, when the killer of Devadatta is killed, it does not follow that Devadatta manifests again.

Therefore, both the rule regarding the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) and the status of being unestablished (*asiddhatva*) must be stated; thus, the state of being a substitute must be explicitly declared.

And [the rule regarding] *asiddhatva* (non-establishment): in the cases of *adhītya* and *pretya*, there is the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). In *ko siñcat* and *yo siñcat*, however, there is *asiddhatva*. The statement that the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* is purposeless because of the non-establishment (*asiddhatva*) of the grammatical operation (*śāstra*) is based on the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*.

[The rule] is purposeless. What is the reason? Because it is not established by the technical rules (*śāstra*). By this [rule], the non-establishment of the grammatical operation (*kāryāsiddhatva*) is not effected.

What then? By this, the non-establishment by the technical rules (*śāstrāsiddhatva*) is effected. That is to say, the rule concerning the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is considered non-established with respect to the rule concerning *tuk*.
[It must be stated: "The single-substitute is established (*siddha*) in the presence of *samprasāraṇa*, *ṅī*, and *iṭ*. For example, in *śakahūṣu*...

In the case of *parivīṣu*, there is *samprasāraṇa*. In *vṛkṣe cchatram* (or *vṛkṣe chatram*), the locative suffix (*ṅi*) applies. In *apace cchatram* (or *apace chatram*), the augment *iṭ* applies. [The rule for] *samprasāraṇa*, *ṅi*, and *iṭ* is established because of the statement that a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) occurring at the end of a word or the beginning of a word is treated as *asiddha*.

The single-substitute (ekādeśa) is established before *samprasāraṇa*, *ṅī*, and *iṭ*. Why? Because it is stated that a single substitute for [the final of] a word and [the initial of] a word is *asiddha*. It is said that a single substitute for [the final of] a word and [the initial of] a word is *asiddha*; however, this is not a single substitute for [the final of] a word and [the initial of] a word. If a single substitute for [the final of] a word and [the initial of] a word were *asiddha*, then in the case of "susasyā oṣadhīḥ kṛdhi,"...

In the case of *supippalā oṣadhīḥ kṛdhi*, the substitution of *ṣ* would apply. With respect to the rule for *tug* (the addition of *t*), the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from the combination of a word-final and a word-initial sound is considered *asiddha*. However, with respect to the substitution of *ṣ*, every single-substitute is *asiddha*. If, with respect to the substitution of *ṣ*, every single-substitute were *asiddha*, then [in the case of] *śakahūṣu*...

In the case of *parivīṣu*, the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) does not occur. Let it be then without distinction. [Objection: How is it in the cases *susasyā oṣadhīḥ kṛdhi* and *supippalā oṣadhīḥ kṛdhi*? [Response: This is not a fault. The mention of *bhrātuṣputra* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that [the rule applies] except when caused by a single substitute (*ekādeśa*).

Regarding the prohibition of *ṣatva*: the fact that the Teacher includes the word *bhrātuṣputra* in the list of *kaska*-type words indicates that *ṣatva* does not occur due to the cause of a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [operation]. If this were being indicated, then in forms such as *śakahūṣu* and *parivīṣu*, *ṣatva* would not apply. [The indication] applies to what is of the same class. And what is of the same class?
[Objection: If that is so, then in the case of *veñ*, when followed by a non-suffix (*apratyaya*), the substitution of *u* would apply [by P. 6.1.127], whereas *ut* is what is desired. [Response:

In the case of unattested usage, one follows the grammatical rule (*yathālakṣaṇam*). Or rather, it should not be understood thus: "of the preceding word-initial and the following word-final. How then? It should be understood as: "of the following word-initial and the preceding word-final."

(P_6,1.87.1) KA_III.66.25–68.3 Ro_IV.418–420: What is the purpose of mentioning *guṇa*? One might simply say, "When *āt* becomes one [with the following vowel], it is *guṇa*. If *āt* becomes one and that is *guṇa*, by what [rule] will this now occur? [In cases such as] *khaṭvendraḥ* and *mālendraḥ*.

*khaṭvodakam*, *mālodakam*. For in the place [of substitution], that which is most similar (*antaratama*) occurs. When several [substitutes] are applicable in a given place, the substitute that is most similar comes into being. In that case, would not *ai* and *au* also then result? *Ai* and *au* do not apply when *ec* follows; they have been so stated. Therefore, *ai* and *au* will not occur.

What is the reason? For here, *e* and *o* are said to be [substitutes for] *ai* and *au*. Well then, in this case—*khaṭvārśyaḥ*, *mālārśyaḥ*—the substitution of *ṛ* would apply. But *ṛ* is not intermediate between both [sounds]. That which is the most similar (*antaratama*) to both must be the substitute.

And the vowel *ṛ* is not the most similar (*antaratama*) to both [the preceding and following sounds]. In that case, the vowel *ā* would result. But *ā* does not apply before *ṛ* when it is part of a verbal root (*dhātu*). Thus, *ā* will not occur. What is the reason? The substitution of *ā* is prescribed before a verbal root ending in *ṛ*. That rule will therefore serve as a restriction: [the substitution occurs] only before a verbal root beginning with *ṛ*, and not elsewhere. In that case, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) would result. [But] the protracted vowel...

And [the substitution] is prescribed with respect to the object (*viṣaya*). When it is said "protracted" (*pluta*) with respect to the object, it means that when that object is to occur, then [the substitution] is by means of the protracted vowel.

By virtue of proximity (*āntarya*), those consisting of three morae (*trimātra*) and four morae (*caturmātra*) [would apply]. In that case, this is the purpose: so that, due to proximity, substitutes consisting of three or four morae do not occur in place of [sounds] consisting of three or four morae. For example, *khaṭvā indraḥ* becomes *khaṭvendraḥ*. [And] *khaṭvā*...
*udaka-khaṭvā-udakam*; *khaṭvā-īṣā* = *khaṭveṣā*; *khaṭvā-ūḍhā* = *khaṭvoḍhā*; *khaṭvā-elakā* = *khaṭvailakā*;

*khaṭvā-odanaḥ* = *khaṭvaudanaḥ*; *khaṭvā-aitikāyanaḥ* = *khaṭvaitikāyanaḥ*; *khaṭvā-aupagavaḥ* = *khaṭvaupagavaḥ*. Now, even when the term "guṇa" (vowel) is included [in the rule], why is it that here [only] those consisting of three or four morae [are affected]?

In their proper place, substitutes consisting of three or four morae do not occur; because they are marked by *ta* (taparatvāt), they are not remembered [as applying here]. [The rule] "guṇa and vṛddhi are followed by *ta*" applies. But surely, sir, that which has *ta* as its subsequent element is called *tapara*. He says: "No. It is also *tapara* when it is subsequent to *t*. If it were *tapara* only when subsequent to *t*, then [the substitution] would occur only here: *yavaḥ* and *stavaḥ* [from *yavau* and *stavau*], according to the rule *ṛdoḥ ap*.

In the case of *lavaḥ* and *pavaḥ*, [the rule] would not apply here. This is not the letter *t*; what then? It is the letter *d*. What is the purpose of the letter *d*? And what is the purpose of the letter *t*? If the letter *t* is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity, then the letter *d* is also [for that same purpose]. (P_6,1.87.2) KA_III.4-10 Ro_IV.420 An addition must be made regarding *ṅi*, *śī*, and *tām* before a *guṇa* vowel, for the purpose of preventing the application of the long vowel rule. An addition must be made regarding *ṅi*, *śī*, and *tām* before a *guṇa* vowel. *ṅi*: *vṛkṣe indraḥ*.
In *plakṣe indraḥ*, [the rule applies]. In *śīye indram*, [it becomes] *te indram*.

In *iṭ* [followed by] *apace indram*, [it becomes] *ayaje indram*. What is the purpose? To prevent the substitution of length (*dīrghatva*). Let there not be the long vowel resulting from the combination of similar vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*).

Thus [it is said]. Or rather, it need not be done, because it is characterized as being external (*bahiraṅga*). What is the reason? Because it is characterized as being external. The substitution of a long vowel by homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*) is characterized as external. That which is external is considered unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*). If [the question is asked]: "By what [rule] is the single [substitute] *guṇa* [determined]? [The answer is: It is the most similar (*antaratama*) in place.

For indeed: *e* and *o* are said [to be long] when followed by *ai* and *au*; *ṛ* is not included among both; *ā* is not [long] before *ṛ* when it is a verbal root (*dhātu*); and the protracted (*pluta*) vowel is also prescribed in its specific scope. Due to proximity (*āntarya*), those [vowels] consisting of three or four morae (*mātra*) are not considered [to be included] because they are marked by an inherent *t* (*taparatva*).

(P_6.1.89.1) KA_III.68.16–69.6 Ro_IV.421–422: Is this a reference to the specific forms of *eti* and *edhate*, or is it a reference to the verbal roots (*dhātu*) themselves? What follows from this? If it is a reference to the specific forms, then [the rule] is established.

The forms *upaiti*, *praiti*, *upaiṣi*, and *praiṣi* would not be established [by that rule alone]. However, if the term "dhātu" (verbal root) is included [in the definition], this becomes established. What, then, [is the purpose]?

Regarding the prohibition of *vṛddhi* before a root beginning with the vowel *i*: it must be stated that there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* before a root beginning with the vowel *i*, as in the cases of *upetaḥ* and *pretaḥ*. This is established by means of a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*). A split will be made: first, "vṛddhi [occurs] before *ec*" (Pāṇini 6.1.88). Then, "before *eti* and *edhati*" (Pāṇini 6.1.89). Thus, *vṛddhi* occurs before *ec* in the case of *eti* and *edhati*. Then, "and before *ūṭ*" (Pāṇini 6.1.90); *vṛddhi* also occurs before *ūṭ*.

Even so, [the rule] would apply here as well in cases such as *āitaḥ*, *etaḥ*, *upetaḥ*, and *pretaḥ*. In these instances, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) will serve as an exception. This is because this rule for *vṛddhi* is commenced when the substitution of the subsequent form has not yet taken effect; thus, just as it sets aside the substitution of the subsequent form in the case of *eṅ*, it likewise sets aside the substitution of the subsequent form in the case of *āṅ*.
It would subvert it; yet it does not subvert it. What is the reason? Because subversion occurs when [the rule] has not already applied.

This *vṛddhi* is not commenced when the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule for *eṅ* has not yet applied; however, in the case of *āṅ* + *pararūpa*, it applies both when [the *pararūpa* rule] has already applied and when it has not yet applied. Alternatively, according to the principle that "exceptions subvert the immediately preceding rules," this *vṛddhi* subverts the *pararūpa* rule for *eṅ*.

*na āṅi pararūpam* (P. 6.1.94): [The substitution of] the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) does not take place after *āṅ*. *akṣāt ūhinyām*: The rule *akṣāt ūhinyām* means that the *vṛddhi* [substitution] should be stated [after *akṣa*] before *ūhinī*. [Thus,] *akṣauhiṇī*. *prāt ūhoḍhoḍhyeṣaiṣyeṣu*: [The rule] *prāt ūhoḍhoḍhyeṣaiṣyeṣu* [means that *vṛddhi* is applied after *pra* before *ūha*, *ūḍha*, *ūḍhi*, *eṣa*, and *eṣya*. Thus,] *prauha*, *prauḍha*, ... [etc.]
In the case of these—*ūḍhi*, *eṣa*, and *eṣya*—vṛddhi should be stated. [Examples: *prauhaḥ*, *prauḍhaḥ*.
*pruḍhiḥ*, *praiṣaḥ*, *praiṣyaḥ*. After *sva*, [the suffixes] *īra* and *iṇa* [are applied]. After *sva*, *īra*...

The vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) must be stated for these two [roots] *īr* and *īri*: *svairaḥ*, *svairī*. The inclusion of *īri* could be omitted. How then [to derive] *svairī*? This is established by means of the possessive suffix *ini*. [Thus: "He who has freedom (*svairaḥ*) belonging to him" is *svairī*. And also in the case of *ṛte* in a third-case compound. And also in the case of *ṛte* in a third-case compound.

The substitution of *vṛddhi* must be stated [in these cases]: *sukhārtaḥ*, *duḥkhārtaḥ*. Why is *ṛte* mentioned? [To exclude cases like] *sukhetaḥ*, *duḥkhetaḥ*. Why is the mention of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) made? [To exclude cases like] *paramartaḥ*. Why is "in a compound" (*samāse*) mentioned? [To exclude cases like] *sukhenartaḥ*. [The rule applies] also to *prava*, *vatsatara*, *kambala*, and *vasana* when combined with *ṛṇa*: *prava-ṛṇam*, *vatsatara-ṛṇam*, *kambala-ṛṇam*, *vasana-ṛṇam*.
Furthermore, the suffix *vṛddhi* should be stated after the words *ṛṇa* and *daśan*. [Examples:
*prārṇam*, *vatsatarārṇam*, *vasanārṇam*. Furthermore, the suffix *vṛddhi* should also be stated after the words *ṛṇa* and *daśan*. [Examples: *ṛṇārṇam*, *daśārṇam*.

(P_6,1.90) KA_III.70.2-5 Ro_IV.423 What is the purpose of the particle *ca*? Its purpose is to carry forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the term *vṛddhi*. This is not a valid purpose; for the *vṛddhi* under discussion will continue to apply by way of *anuvṛtti*. Then what is the purpose? It is so that when *aci* follows an *āt*, only *vṛddhi* should occur, and whatever else would otherwise be applicable should not take place. And what else [would be applicable]?

The subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is obtained. [An objection will be raised that] the rule *usi omāṅkṣu* (P. 6.1.95) prohibits the subsequent form for *āṬ*; however, that need not be stated. (P. 6.1.91.1) [Question:

For what purpose is the mention of "in a verbal root" (*dhātau*)? [Answer: So that it does not apply here: *prarṣabhaṃ vanam*. [It has been] stated regarding the prescription of *vṛddhi* after a prefix (*upasarga*) when a verbal root is mentioned. What was stated? That the designations "motion" (*gati*) and "prefix" (*upasarga*) [apply].

Regarding the rule *kriyāyoge prādayaḥ tam prati*, it means that when a prefix is joined with an action, it is directed toward that [action]. Even if the mention of the verbal root (*dhātu*) were made, the form *prarchakaḥ* would still result. However, because of the statement "when a prefix is joined with an action, it is directed toward that," [the substitution] does not occur here. In that case, this is the purpose: so that there may be only *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) before a verbal root beginning with *ṛ* following a prefix; as for anything else...
[The rule] "tat" [is stated] so that it might not occur. Furthermore, what else would occur? Shortening (*hrasvatva*), by the rule *ṛti akaḥ*. [One might object:

"In the presence of *ṛ*, there is vṛddhi after a prefix ending in a short vowel, by way of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). That objection need not be stated. [Regarding the form] *che*: the augment *tuk* and the guṇa of the vocative (*sambuddhi*). [Regarding the form] *che-tuk*.

Because [the rule] "it occurs" exists, the *guṇa* substitution for the vocative (*sambuddhi*) occurs by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of the rule "there is *tuṅ*" is: *icchati*, *gacchati*. The scope of the *guṇa* substitution for the vocative is: *agne*.
O Vāyu! Here both [forms] occur: *agnéc chatram*, *agne chatram*, and *vāyóś chatram*.
In *vāyo chatram*, the guṇa substitution for the vocative case ending occurs by way of a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*). Then, that conflict of rules must be stated.

Or rather, it need not be stated, because [the guṇa] is characterized as being external (*bahiraṅga*). Why? Because it is characterized as being external. The *tuṅ* augment is characterized as external, whereas the guṇa substitution for the vocative case ending is characterized as internal (*antaraṅga*). That which is external is considered unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal.

This is established even without this prohibition and even without this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*). How so? This must be considered here: "Let the elision of the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi-lopa*) take place, or let the *guṇa* substitution take place. What should be done here? The *guṇa* [should take effect] because it is subsequent. The elision of the vocative suffix is obligatory (*nitya*), for it applies whether the *guṇa* has occurred or not. But the *guṇa* is also obligatory.

Even when the elision of the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi-lopa*) has been performed, [the *tuk* augment] applies; even when it has not been performed, it applies. The *guṇa* substitution is non-eternal (*anitya*). For indeed, when the elision of the vocative suffix has been performed, [the *guṇa*] does not apply. At that very moment, there is immediate succession (*ānantarya*) with the letter *ch*. In that case, the *tuk* ought to occur. Therefore, it is rightly said: "The *tuk* occurs before *ch*, [preventing] the *guṇa* of the vocative. Or rather, it is not so, because [the *guṇa*] is characterized as being external (*bahiraṅga*). [This also applies to] the lengthening due to *samprasāraṇa*, the elision of *ṇi* and *ya*, the *guṇa* of the reduplication, and so forth.

Furthermore, the substitution of semivowels for vowels (*samprasāraṇa*), lengthening (*dīrghatva*), the elision of *y* and *l* (*ṇyallopa*), the strengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsaguṇa*), and so forth, take precedence over the insertion of the augment *tuk* by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope for the substitution of semivowels and lengthening is, for example, in the forms *hūtaḥ* and *jīnaḥ*.
*saṃvītaḥ*, *śūnaḥ*. The suffix *tuka* [is applied]. *agnicit*, *somasut*. Here both [suffixes] would apply. *parivīṣu*.

Regarding the elision of *ṇi*: its scope is, for example, *kāraṇā* and *hāraṇā*. Regarding the *tuk* [augment]: its scope is the same. Here, both would apply: *prakārya-gataḥ* and *prahārya-gataḥ*. Regarding the elision of *a* [the penultimate vowel]: its scope is, for example, *cikīrṣitā* and *jihīrṣitā*.

6.1.93) A prohibition must be stated regarding the substitution after a word ending in long *o* when followed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). [Examples of the need: *acinavam*, *asunavam*. [Objection:

It follows [from the previous rule]. While that [rule] is in effect, it should also be stated: "Before *am*, the preceding [vowel is substituted]. Now, for what purpose is this stated separately? Why not state it here as one single rule: "In the case of the first two [cases], there is the *pūrvasavarṇa* [substitution], and also before *am*"? [Regarding the word] *plakṣam*: this is not a fault. The mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) will be set aside. And [the use of] *ca* is contradictory. Therefore, both [rules] must be commenced, and they must be formulated separately. The split of the rule "of the first two" must be made: "Of the first two, there is one long vowel of homogeneous sounds."

Then [the rule] "the same sound as the preceding" (*pūrvasavarṇaḥ*) applies. There occurs a long vowel identical to the preceding one by the rule "one [vowel replaces two] in the case of the first two cases. For what purpose is this split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*)? It is so that the substitution of a long vowel with a homogeneous sound (*savarṇadīrghatva*) may take place. For if there were a single combined rule (*ekayoga*), the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) would undesirably apply to the nominative plural suffixes *jas* and *śas*. Indeed, if there were a single combined rule, the substitution of the subsequent form would apply to *jas* and *śas*, as in *vṛkṣāḥ*.
