Now, one might object that the long vowel resulting from the substitution of the preceding sound with its homogeneous counterpart (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*) will supersede the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). [The answer is: It is not able to supersede it.

What is the reason? The substitutes *vṛddhi*, *savarṇadīrgha*, and *pūrvasavarṇa* are exceptions (*apavāda*) to the substitutes *guṇa* and *yaṇ* [prescribed by A 6.1.87 and 102]; in the case of vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*), the *pararūpa* substitute applies to them. The *guṇa* and *yaṇ* substitutes are the general rules (*utsarga*). The *vṛddhi*, *savarṇadīrgha*, and *pūrvasavarṇa* substitutes are their exceptions. For all of these, the *pararūpa* substitute is an exception. Therefore, it subverts everything. Because it subverts everything, it would apply.

Now, even if the separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*) is performed, why does *pararūpa* not subvert [the preceding rule] as an exception? The separation of rules is for the purpose of precluding other rules. It is understood that the separation of rules is for the purpose of precluding other rules. If the separation of rules is for the purpose of precluding other rules, then there is this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). The separation of rules is for the purpose of precluding other rules.
If this were the case, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

For example, in *vṛkṣam* and *plakṣam*, just as the split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) subverts the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), so too would it subvert the substitution of the preceding form (*ami pūrvatvam*). Furthermore, there would be an absence of the letter *n*, because of the immediate mention [in the rule] "from that" (*tasmāt*). And there would also be an absence of the change to *n* (*natva*). Thus, [the forms would be] *vṛkṣān*.

[The word] *plakṣān*. What is the reason? Because of the reference to what immediately precedes by means of the word *tasmāt* (from that). By this word *tasmāt*, the immediately preceding rule (*yoga*) is referred back. But what is the reason that the immediately preceding rule is referred back by this word *tasmāt*? So that it should not apply here: *etān gāḥ paśya*.

"Look at these four oxen. Let it be, then, that there is indeed a single *yoga* (rule). But was it not said that in a single *yoga*, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) would apply to *jas* and *śas*? This is not a fault. The mention of *ij* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the absence of *pararūpa*. In that the Teacher makes the mention of *ij* in the rule "na āt ici," he indicates [this].
"The single-substitute form (pararūpa) does not occur for the [suffixes] *jas* and *śas*. How is this a *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence)? The purpose of the mention of *ij* is as follows:
let it not apply here in the cases of *vṛkṣāḥ* and *plakṣāḥ*.

[Vṛkṣān, plakṣān]. If there were a single-substitute (pararūpa) for the nominative-accusative plural endings *jas* and *śas*, the mention of the suffix *ij* would be purposeless. However, the Teacher perceives that a single-substitute does not occur for *jas* and *śas*; therefore, he makes the mention of *ij*. This is not so.

This is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). This [mention of *ij*] would be for the sake of what follows: namely, that [the rule] "after a long vowel, before *jas* and *ic*" applies. If this were for the sake of what follows, he would have made this mention of *ij* right there [in that subsequent rule]. But even though it is made here, if it were for the sake of what follows, it would not be an indicator. In that case, if this were for the sake of what follows, he would certainly not have made this mention of *ij*.
Nor should there be the mention of *jaś* [and *śas*]. He should have said only this: "After a long vowel, before *śas*, there is a substitute homogeneous with the preceding.

That would then serve as a restrictive rule (*niyama*), meaning: "Only after a long vowel, before *śas*, and not elsewhere. Since this is established by such a more concise formulation, the fact that the Teacher includes the mention of *ij* indicates that [the substitution] does not apply to *jaś* and *śas*.

"The form of the subsequent [element] occurs. Alternatively, let there be a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). But was it not said that if the split of the rule is for the purpose of excluding other treatises, this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? This is not a fault. Even in the case of *ami*, a split of the rule will be made: "In the case of *ami*," meaning that what was previously stated does not occur. Then follows "the preceding": and the preceding [form] also occurs.

Regarding the phrase *ami iti*: as for what was said—that there is an absence of the letter *n* because of the immediate reference to "therefore" (*tasmāt*)—who indeed is capable of referring back to the immediately preceding rule by means of this word "therefore"? It is certainly referred back in this way: "therefore, from the long vowel homogeneous with the preceding" (*tasmāt pūrvasavarṇadīrghāt*). But that is not so; it is rather referred back thus: "therefore, from *ak*" (*tasmāt akaḥ*).

[The rule applies] "from a homogeneous vowel" (*savarṇāt*). Or rather, [it applies] "from that long vowel of the first two cases" (*tasmāt prathamayoḥ dīrghāt*). Or again, let there be a single application (*ekayoga*) with *ami*.
But was it not said that if the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the purpose of excluding other grammatical rules, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *ami*?
This is not a fault. For intermediate exceptions (*apavāda*) sublate preceding rules; thus is this division of the rule.

The subsequent form (*pararūpa*) will be sublated, but the substitution of *ami* for the preceding vowel (*ami pūrvatva*) will not be sublated. If this principle holds—that "exceptions [apply] in the middle" and "exceptions [apply] before"—then there is no need for even a single rule-separation (*yogavibhāga*). Since exceptions that precede sublate the immediately following rules, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) will thus sublate the homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrghatva*), while the homogeneous long vowel of the first two cases (*prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*) will remain unaffected.
It will not be obstructed. Alternatively, a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) will be made for the seventh [sūtra]: first, "from this [stem], a long vowel occurs before *yañ* and *sup*";
then one will state: "and in the plural. In the plural, a long vowel occurs from this [stem];
and in the plural, when followed by a *jhal* [consonant], the vowel *e* occurs. In that case, it would follow here as well: *vṛṣāṇām*.

In the case of *plakṣāṇām*, what is the fault? Once the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) has been applied, the augment *nuṭ*—which depends on a short vowel (*hrasva*)—would not apply. This must be considered here: should the lengthening be performed first, or the *nuṭ*? What should be done in this instance? The lengthening [should take place] because it is subsequent (*para*). Furthermore, the lengthening is indeed obligatory (*nitya*), for it applies whether the *nuṭ* has been applied or not. Because it is both obligatory and subsequent, once the lengthening has been performed, the *nuṭ* dependent on a short vowel does not apply.
If that is so, then the mention of *āt* (the suffix *ā*) from the previous rule is also carried over here by anuvṛtti. Where was it introduced? In the rule *āt jaser asuk*.

Therefore, even when the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) has taken place, the augment *nuṭ* will still occur. But then it would also apply here: *kīlālapām*, *śubhaṃyām*. The elision (*lopa*) of the *ā* [by *āto dhātoḥ*] will be the sublater of this. This must be considered here: [which should take precedence,] the elision...

"Let *nuṭ* be applied. What should be done here? Because it is subsequent, *nuṭ* [should apply]. If that is so, then in the rule *hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ*, the elision of *ā* (*ātaḥ lopaḥ*) from the rule *ātaḥ dhātoḥ* will be understood as continuing [into this context]. In that case, it would also apply here: *kīlālapānām brāhmaṇakulānām*. [To prevent this,] the phrase *na* from the rule *napuṃsakasya na* will be understood as continuing [into this context].

(P_6,1.103) KA_III.80.23–81.19 Ro_IV.446–448: Is this [the substitution of] *natva* [for *naḍ*] intended when there is plurality of males (*puṃsām bahutve*), or rather when there are many [referents] denoted by the word "male" (*puṃśabdāt bahuṣu*)? And what is the difference here? If *natva* is intended for males in the sense of plurality of males, then it would not be established in the feminine case, as in: *bhrūkuṃsān paśya*. It is likewise desired [not to apply] in the neuter.
That is not established. [The rule] "look at the eunuchs," "look at the impotent ones"—this would also apply to the word *strī* (woman).
From the word *strī*, it would follow: "look at the wooden dolls (*cañcāḥ*)."

"Look at the female slaves! Look at the female donkeys! If it is argued that [the suffix] occurs after a masculine word when denoting many, then if it is said "after a masculine word," the desired form *sthūrāpatyam* ("the offspring of Stūrā") would not be established; nor would the form *sthūrān paśya* ("look at the Stūrās") be established. Furthermore, the offspring of *Kuṇḍinī* or *Ararakā* would also not be established.

"Look at the *kuṇḍina*s; look at the *ararakā*s. [Objection: It is established on the basis of masculine predominance; these words have the masculine as their primary referent, and therefore the substitution of *na* will occur. [Response: If masculine predominance were the case, those very same faults previously cited would apply:
"Look at the *bhrūkuṃsa*s," "Look at the *ṣaṇḍha*s," "Look at the *paṇḍaka*s," "Look at the *cañcā*s," "Look at the *vadhrikā*s," "Look at the *kharakuṭī*s."

"Behold! Therefore, one should adopt that position in which there are fewer faults and apply a remedy against those faults. (Pāṇini 6.1.107) It is simply by the rule "vā chandasi" (in the Vedic language, there is optionally [substitution]) that we have *yamīm* and *yamyam*, *śamīm* and *śamyam*, *garuīm* and *gaurīm*, and *kiśorīm* and *kiśoryam*.

(P_6,1.108.1) Only the rule *vā chandasi* applies here: *mitrāvaruṇau yajyamānaḥ* (being sacrificed for Mitra and Varuṇa), *mitrāvaruṇau ijyamānaḥ* (being sacrificed to Mitra and Varuṇa). (P_6,1.108.2) Regarding the substitution of the preceding vowel (*pūrvatva*) after a semivowel (*samprasāraṇa*), the mention of "the same member" (*samānāṅga*) is for the purpose of excluding cases where the members are different. When the substitution of the preceding vowel occurs after a semivowel, the mention of "the same member" must be made.

What is the purpose? It is for the sake of prohibiting [the substitution] when the members are not identical. This is so that it does not occur in the case of non-identical members, such as *śakahvartham* and *parivyartham*. It is established by means of the term *asamprasāraṇa*. How is this established? By means of *asamprasāraṇa*.
The designation *samprasāraṇa* applies to the sentence (*vākya*), not to the individual phoneme (*varṇa*). Now, if the designation *samprasāraṇa* were applied to the phoneme, there would be a fault.

And thus, there is no fault in assigning the technical designation *saṃprasāraṇa* to the vowel. How so? Because this single [vowel] is prescribed in place of both the *saṃprasāraṇa* and the non-*saṃprasāraṇa* [vowels]. Or else, because the operation has already been performed. Alternatively, since the status of being "prior" (*pūrvatva*) has been effected once, it will not occur again. It is just as when it is said, "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in spring"; having established them once, [he does not do so again].

Thinking, "The purpose of the scripture has been accomplished," there is no further engagement [with it]. This is an unequal comparison. It is appropriate that for that [person] there is no further engagement; however, as for one who attains that which is based upon it, that cannot be sublated. For example, the injunction "In spring, a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma and other rites" serves as the cause for the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna).
It is sacrificed every spring; therefore, the previously stated solution—that it is established by virtue of not being a *samprasāraṇa*—remains valid.
If, however, this were not a *samprasāraṇa*, then the lengthening in the word *hūtaḥ* would not apply.

[Response: The lengthening occurs on the authority of the explicit statement (*vacanaprāmāṇyāt*). [Objection: That lengthening has no scope [elsewhere]. [Response: It will occur on the authority of that very statement, because [the word] has a finite number of syllables (*antavattvāt*).
Alternatively, since the preceding [element] becomes limited with respect to the operation, the lengthening will take place.

Regarding the rule *āṭo vṛddhiḥ*, the substitution of *iyaṅ* occurs by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) against the rule that "vṛddhi is substituted for the augment *āṭ*. The scope (*avakāśa*) of the rule "vṛddhi is substituted for *āṭ*" is, for example, in the case of *aikṣiṣṭa*.
The [substitution of] *iyaṅ* has its scope in cases such as *adhīyāte* and *adhīyate*. Here, however, both [rules] would apply:
*adhyaiyātām* and *adhyaiyata*. The substitution of *iyaṅ* occurs by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). This conflict is not appropriate.

The *vṛddhi* substitution for *āṭ* is internal (*antaraṅga*). What constitutes its internality? The *vṛddhi* of *āṭ* depends upon two phonemes (*varṇa*), whereas the *iyaṅ* substitute for the *aṅga* [depends upon three]. If this is so, then the following must be considered here: should *āṭ* be applied, or should the *iyaṅ* substitute be applied?

What should be done in this case? The *iyaṅ* substitute applies because it is subsequent (*para*). But the augment *āṭ* is obligatory (*nitya*); it applies both when *iyaṅ* has been applied and when it has not.

Is this *iyaṅ* substitution also permanent (*nitya*)? It would apply whether *āṭ* has been applied or not; thus, it is permanent. [Objection: *Iyaṅ* is not permanent, for it does not apply once *āṭ* has been applied. What is the reason? The *vṛddhi* substitution [of *āṭ*] is internal (*antaraṅga*). That whose cause is destroyed by another rule is not considered "permanent. And here, *āṭ* itself does not destroy the cause of *iyaṅ*; rather, another rule necessarily destroys it.

The substitution of *vṛddhi* for *āṭ* must be awaited. Between these two obligatory rules, the substitution of *iyaṅ* occurs because it is subsequent. Regarding the lengthening by *savarṇadīrgha* in place of the *guṇa* of *ā* [before] *āṅ* and the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), the lengthening by *savarṇadīrgha* takes place by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). Where? Before *āṅ* and the reduplication. This is the scope of the *guṇa* of *ā*:

*khaṭvendraḥ* (khaṭvā + indraḥ), *khaṭvodakam* (khaṭvā + udakam). The scope for the rule of homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrghatva*) is: *daṇḍāgram* (daṇḍa + agram), *kṣupāgram* (kṣupa + agram). Here, both [rules] would apply: *adya*, *ā*.
*ūḍhā*: *adyoḍhā* (married today); *kadā*, *ā*, *ūḍhā*: *kadoḍhā* (when was she married?).
upa, i, ijatuḥ: upejatuḥ, upa, u.

*upatuḥ*, *upopatuḥ*: here, the long vowel substitution (*savarṇadīrghatva*) occurs by way of a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*). First, there is no need for the doubling of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Let there be the *guṇa* substitution for *ā* [of the root], and then the replacement of *ay* and *av* [for *ai* and *au*]; thereafter, let the *halādiśeṣa* apply; finally, the *guṇa* substitution for *ā* will occur again. Thus, *upejatuḥ* would be established.

[The forms] *upejatuḥ* are established; however, this is not established: *upopatuḥ*, *upopuḥ*. For here, once the *guṇa* substitution has been applied [to form *upa-ū-atus*], the designation *pragṛhya* applies because it is a particle ending in *o*;

and by the rule "that which is *pragṛhya* remains in its original form" (*pragṛhyaḥ prakṛtyā*), the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) dependent on the *pragṛhya* status would result. [But this is not desired, as] the preservation of the original form occurs within the section concerning word-final sounds (*padāntaprakaraṇe*).

And this [visarga] is not at the end of a word (*padānta*). Being a part of the end of a word (*padāntabhakta*), it would be included by the mention of "end of a word. If that is so, then this very condition does not exist here: "a particle ending in *o*. What is the reason? Because between that which is taught by a general rule (*lakṣaṇokta*) and that which is taught as a specific form (*pratipadokta*), the specific form alone is taken. If so, then in this case as well, [in the example] *adyoḍhā*,...

The form *kadodhā* would be established [by this rule]. However, there is a fault regarding the vowel (*svara*). Indeed, a fault arises with respect to the vowel; for instance, the vowel [of the first member] would result in *adyodhā*, whereas *adyodhā* is what is intended. Furthermore, the prescription of the single-substitute (pararūpa) in the presence of *āṅ* would now be rendered purposeless. It is not purposeless; it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). What is indicated? The prescription of the single-substitute in the presence of *āṅ*.

But it is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) because of the principle that what is *antaraṅga* (internal) is stronger. By this, the Teacher indicates that "that which is *antaraṅga* is stronger. Now, what here is *antaraṅga* and what is *bahiraṅga* (external), since both the formation of a long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha* and the *guṇa* substitution for *āt* depend upon two words? That operation which pertains to a verbal root and a prefix is *antaraṅga*. Why is this so? Because [the prefix] precedes.
An *upasarga* (prefix) is joined with a verbal root (*dhātu*), not with the word *adya*. Why, then, is the word *adya* employed?

The word *adya* is also joined with the entire complex [of the prefix and the root]. What is the purpose of making this known? The purpose is that [the following rules] are internal (*antaraṅga*) compared to those characterized as external (*bahiraṅga*): the substitution of the homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*), the substitution of the preceding vowel (*pūrvatva*), the elision of *ta* and *hi*, the substitution of *ṭā*, *na*, *ṅī*, *yaṅ*, *is*, *min*, *ṅi*, *ṇal*, and the substitution of *au*.

Because of the modification of the phoneme (*varṇavikāra*), the "homogeneous with the preceding" (*pūrvasavarṇa*) is the purpose [of the rule]. In *agnī atra* and *vāyū atra*, both the "homogeneous with the preceding" (*pūrvasavarṇa*) and the modification of the phoneme *āvādeśa*—which is characterized as external (*bahiraṅga*)—would apply. However, by virtue of being internal (*antaraṅga*), the long vowel homogeneous with the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*) prevails. [The term] "preceding" (*pūrvatva*) [is used in the rule]. For example:
*śakahvartham*.

[The rule] *parivyartham* [is stated]. Furthermore, priority (*pūrvatva*) would apply, as would the external-conditioned (*bahiraṅga*) modification of the phoneme, namely *savarṇadīrghatva*. Priority occurs by virtue of being internal-conditioned (*antaraṅga*). [Examples: *tahilopa*: *akāri atra*, *ahāri atra*, *paca idam*. Both *tahilopa* and [the other operations] would apply; however, the external-conditioned modification of the phoneme, namely *savarṇadīrghatva*, [would supersede them]. [Thus,] both *tahilopa* and [the others] would apply.

From the perspective of internal operation (*antaraṅga*): *vṛkṣeṇa atra*, *plakṣeṇa atra*. Here, the substitution of *in* would apply, as would the external operation (*bahiraṅga*) characterized by the modification of phonemes, namely *savarṇadīrghatva* (lengthening by homogeneity). The substitution of *in* occurs because it is internal. *ṅerya*: *vṛkṣāya*, *plakṣāya atra*. Here, the substitution of *yā* for *ṅe* would apply, as would the external operation characterized by the modification of phonemes, namely *pararūpatva* (the single substitute of the subsequent form) according to the rule *eṅaḥ padāntād ati*. The substitution of *yā* for *ṅe* occurs because it is internal.

In the case of *asmin*: "in which this [is], in that this [is]. Here, the substitution of *-smin* would apply, as would the external modification of the phoneme consisting of the lengthening by *savarṇa-dīrgha*. However, the substitution of *-smin* occurs because it is internal (*antaraṅga*). [Likewise] the substitution of *-au* for *ṅi*. Thus: *agnau idam* ("this in the fire").

In the case of *yayau*, the substitution of *au* (autva) would be superseded by the substitution of *e* (*ṅiṇalautvam*), which is characterized as being external (*bahiraṅga*), while the lengthening of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatvam*) is internal (*antaraṅga*). Thus, the substitution of *au* occurs because it is more internal. These [other] purposes do not exist; for these are established even through the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).
However, this is the purpose: *vṛkṣāḥ atra*, *plakṣāḥ atra*. And [the rule for] the preceding homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇaḥ*) [is also required].

Furthermore, a phonetic modification (*varṇavikāra*) characterized as "external" (*bahiraṅga*)—namely, the substitution of *u* for *ru* according to the rule *ro 'plutād aplute*—is superseded by the "internal" (*antaraṅga*) substitution of the preceding homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*). Moreover, this is not the only purpose [for this rule]; in the first *yoga*, there are many purposes for which this *paribhāṣā* must be formulated. One must provide remedies for the defects [that arise].

(P_6.1.112) KA_III.84.25–85.3 Ro_IV.455–456: What is this [expression] "khyatyāt"? It is the mention of *sakhi* and *pati* in their modified forms. But what is the reason for mentioning *sakhi* and *pati* in their modified forms? Why not simply say "sakhipatibhyām"? It cannot be done in that way; for such a formulation would be more cumbersome, and it would lead to an over-extension here, as in *atisakheḥ*.

I am coming. [The forms] *atisakheḥ* and *svam* [are derived from the denominative *sakhiyati*]. And here there would not be [the following]: from *sakhiyati*, the suffix *apratyaya* [is added], resulting in *sakhyuḥ*; likewise *patyuḥ*. From *lunīyati*, the suffix *apratyaya* [is added], resulting in *lūnyuḥ*, *pūnyuḥ*.

(P_6,1.113) KA_III.85.5-24 Ro_IV.457-459 For what purpose is it stated, "after a non-protracted [vowel], before a non-protracted [vowel]"? It is so that [the rule] does not apply when a protracted vowel follows a protracted vowel, or when a protracted vowel follows [another] protracted vowel. [Examples: *susrotā3 atra nu asi* (where a protracted vowel follows a protracted vowel);

*tiṣṭhatu payaḥ ā3gnidatta* (where a protracted vowel follows a protracted vowel). Therefore, it is stated, "after this [short vowel], before a long vowel. What possibility is there for [the rule to apply] after a protracted vowel?
Or, [the rule applies] after a protracted vowel (*pluta*). A protracted vowel is not established (*asiddha*). Because it is not established, [the rule] would apply.

Now, if it is stated "after a non-protracted vowel (*apluta*)," since a protracted vowel is not established, why does [the rule] not apply here? It is understood thus: "after that which was originally a non-protracted vowel" and "into that which was originally a non-protracted vowel. This purpose is not necessary; the protracted vowel is established.

Regarding the rules for vowel coalescence (*svarasandhi*): how is this known? Because this rule—"the protracted (*pluta*) vowel remains in its original form" (*prakṛtyā*)—teaches that the *pluta* vowel undergoes the state of being its own original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). For an existing element that is subject to an operation must indeed be affected by that operation. [Objection: Regarding the statement "after a non-protracted vowel, [there is no substitution] when a non-protracted vowel follows," a prohibition must be stated for the case of the vowel *a* and the *haś* sounds (vowels and voiced consonants) within the same word (*samānapada*). For example: *payo3ṭ*.
[The objection: "No, because it is characterized by being external. [The response: Or rather, it need not be stated. What is the reason? Because it is characterized by being external.

The *pluta* vowel is external; the substitution of *u* (*uttva*) is internal. That which is external is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal. [Objection: In that case, this would also apply here: *susrotā3 atra nu asi*. Here too, the *pluta* is internal and the substitution of *u* is external.

But here, where is the internal (antaraṅga) *pluta* vowel, and where is the external (bahiraṅga) substitution of *ut*; or rather, where is the substitution of *ut* internal and the *pluta* external? The *pluta* at the end of a sentence before the beginning of another sentence is internal; the substitution of *ut* is external. Within the same sentence (*samānavākya*), the substitution of *ut* at the end of one word before the beginning of another is internal, while the *pluta* is external. But what is the reason for this externality?

Only the cause (*hetu*) is indicated, and not its being "unestablished" (*asiddhatva*) as well. For just as this [rule] is *bahiraṅga*, so too is it *asiddha*. This is the thought: the *pluta* vowel is unestablished, yet it becomes established by virtue of its basis (*āśrayāt*). Alternatively, that rule before which the present rule (*uttvam*) is commenced would be established by virtue of its basis. In which [rule]?

And it is not [applicable] when [the paribhāṣā] has not yet attained [its scope]. Regarding the *asiddhaparibhāṣā* and the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā*, whether they have attained or not attained [their scope]: (P_6.1.115) KA_III.86.2-20 Ro_IV.459-461 To what does this prohibition apply? "Not within a *pāda*" (*nāntaḥpādam*) is a universal prohibition. "Not within a *pāda*" (*nāntaḥpādam*)—this is a prohibition of everything. How so? The term *aci* ("before a vowel") is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
Whatever [a rule] applies, that is what is prohibited. If "not within a pada" (*nāntaḥpādam*) were a total prohibition, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that [the augment] *ru* is an initial element (*pūrvānta*) following a *k*-suffix, then there would be both a prescription and a prohibition regarding *ru*. If it is argued that [the augment] *ru* is an initial element following a *k*-suffix, then something must be prescribed and something else prohibited. For example, in the case of *saṃskartā*: *sam-* would be prescribed and *suṭ* would be prohibited. First of all, *sam-* need not be prescribed; for this will be stated: "The substitution of *s* for *sampuṅka* occurs in the rule prescribing *ru*, because otherwise an undesirable result would follow."

Furthermore, *suṭ* should not be prohibited. The rule *samaḥ suṭi* is a statement containing two *s*-sounds, meaning "when *suṭ* begins with an *s*-sound. Alternatively, it could be made to begin with the word (*padādi*). If it were at the end of the word (*parādi*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the application of *iṭ*. If it were at the end of the word, *iṭ* and *guṇa* would apply [in the following cases]: *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa*—here *iṭ* would apply by the rule *ṛtaśca saṃyogādeḥ*; and *saṃskriyate*.

[Objection: By the rule *guṇaḥ arti-saṃyogādyoḥ*, *guṇa* substitution would apply [to the vowel of the prefix]. [Response: In that case, it will be treated as non-separable (*abhakta*). [Objection: If it is non-separable, then the accentuation [of the verb] would not be established. [Example: *saṃskaroti*. [In this case,] the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) prescribed by the rule *tiṅ atiṅaḥ* would not apply. [Objection: But isn't *suṭ* itself [part of] the *atiṅ*? [Response: It is not the case that the following [verb] must undergo *nighāta* because of *suṭ*. Why?

This is the reason: "That which is joined with *nañ* or *iva* has its application in something other than that [to which it is joined], namely in what is similar to it; for such is the understanding of the meaning. That which is joined with *nañ* and that which is joined with *iva* are understood to apply to something else, namely to what is similar to it; for such is the meaning perceived. For example, when it is said, "Bring a non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇam ānaya*), one brings a Kṣatriya who is similar to a Brahmin. One does not become satisfied by bringing a clod of earth.

In the same way here as well, because of the prohibition *atiṅ*, the operation is understood to apply to something other than *tiṅ* that is similar to *tiṅ*. And what else is similar to *tiṅ*? A *pada*. (P. 6.1.142) Regarding the root *kṛ* [in the sense] of joy, livelihood, and making a dwelling: of the root *kṛ*.
It should be stated: "in the cases of making a joyful livelihood or making a lair. A bull leaps up out of joy; a cock leaps up seeking food; a dog leaps up seeking a place of shelter.
(P_6,1.144) KA_III.95.2-9 Ro_IV.480-481 What is this "continuity" (*sātatyam*)? Continuity is the state of being uninterrupted (*santatabhāva*).

If this is so, it should be *sāntatye*. Alternatively, there is the elision of *sama* before *hita* and *tati*: "The elision of *sama* before *hita* and *tati* must be stated. Thus: *saṃhitam*, *sahitam*.

*santatam*, *satatam*. Regarding *santu* and *mumu* in the sense of desire (*kāme*), their elision should be stated: *sakāmaḥ*, *bhoktukāmaḥ*. It should also be stated that this applies when *manas* follows: *samanāḥ*.

*bhoktumanaḥ* (desirous of eating). Regarding *avaśyam* with a *kṛtya* suffix: it must be stated that there is elision (*lopa*) of *avaśyam* when followed by a *kṛtya* suffix. Example: *avaśyabhāvyam*. (Pāṇini 6.1.145) This is explained too extensively; whether [the rule] is applied or not applied, [the result remains the same].
Regarding the term *pramāṇe*: it is already established that this refers to "the two measures that have been practiced. By what means, then, will it apply to those not practiced?

We shall understand it as a negation of "practiced" by means of the negative particle (*nañ*). This cannot be so; for [if it were], it would apply only in the case of what has been practiced, and would not apply to what has not been practiced. However, when the term *asevita* ("not practiced") is explicitly included, this will be understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound: "that in which practice does not exist."
Regarding the term *asevite*: therefore, the inclusion of the word *asevita* must be made [in the rule]. (P_6.1.150) Regarding *viṣkiraḥ śakunau vikiraḥ vā*:
it should be stated that "in the sense of a bird, *viṣkira* or *vikira* [is used]. For if it were simply stated "or in the sense of a bird," it would apply either to a bird or even elsewhere.

[Objection: Then it must be stated that [the suffix *ghañ*] is obligatory (*nitya*). [Response: It need not be stated. For the word *śakuni* (bird) is not connected by the mere absence of its being stated.
What then? The irregular formation (*nipātana*) is what is connected; that is, this irregular formation *viṣkiraḥ* is optionally applied in the sense of "bird."

(P_6,1.147) KA_III.96.2–9 Ro_IV.482–483: Regarding *āścarya* in the sense of "wonderful" (*adbhuta*). It should be stated that *āścarya* [is used] in the sense of "wonderful," so that it may also apply here: *āścaryam uccatā vṛkṣasya* ("It is wonderful how high the tree is!"), *āścaryam nīlā dyauḥ* ("It is wonderful that the sky is blue!"), and *āścaryam antarikṣe abandhanāni nakṣatrāṇi na patanti* ("It is wonderful that the stars, though unattached, do not fall from the atmosphere!"). Should that then be stated? It need not be stated; for [the usage] is non-eternal (*anitya*).

Thus it is established. Here, first of all, in the expression "it is a wonder that the tree is tall," the word "wonder" (*āścarya*) is not connected with the "tree" (*vṛkṣa*). What then? It is connected with "tallness" (*uccatā*), and that is impermanent. In the expression "it is a wonder that the sky is blue," the word "wonder" is not connected with the "sky" (*dyauḥ*). What then? It is connected with "blueness" (*nīlatā*), and that too is impermanent. [It is] a wonder.

"The stars do not fall from the atmosphere because they are unbound. In this case, the stars are not connected with the term "wonder" (*āścarya*); rather, it is the action of falling that is intended. And that [action] is impermanent (*anitya*). Therefore, the rule is already established by the very word "in the impermanent" (*anitye*).
(Pāṇini 6.1.154) The mention of *maskarī* could have been omitted. How so? [Because] *maskarī*...

Regarding the term *parivrājaka*: this is established by the suffix *-in*, which expresses possession (*matvarthīya*). [The derivation is: "he has a *maskara* (staff)" (*maskaro 'syāsti*). But it is not that he possesses a *maskara*; rather, [the meaning is] "do not perform actions" (*mā kṛta karmāṇi*). He says, "Peace is better for you. Therefore, the *parivrājaka* is called a *maskarī*.

The augment *suṭ* is to be seen as not prescribed by any specific rule (*avihitalakṣaṇa*) in the list beginning with *pāraskara*. *Pāraskara* is a country; *kāraskara* is a tree; *rathaspā* is a river; *kiṣkindhā* is a cave; *kiṣku* is a cubit.

In the case of *tad* and *bṛhat* combined with *kara* and *patya*, when they mean "thief" and "deity" respectively, there is the augment *suṭ* and the elision of the suffix *tal*: thus, *taskara* ("thief").
Bṛhaspati says: In the case of *prāyaścitti* and *citti*, the suffix *suṭ* with the augment *askāra* is optionally applied. Thus, *prāyaścittiḥ* and *prāyaścittam*.
(P_6,1.158.1) KA_III.97.2-6 Ro_IV.484-485 Are there words that consist of a single syllable which are unaccented? Yes.

He says "no," excluding [one vowel]. That is to say: those vowels in a word for which there would otherwise be the application of the acute accent become grave (anudātta), with the exception of one vowel. In that case, the rule should have been stated thus: "In a word, [all vowels] are grave."

Or rather, the rule *anudāttāḥ padasya* need not be stated. It is already established by the rule *anudāttaṃ padam ekavarjam*. How so? Here, the elision of the suffix *matup* should be understood. For example: *puṣyakāḥ* means "those who have merit" (*puṣyavantaḥ*), and *kālakāḥ* means "those who have blackness" (*kālavantaḥ*). Alternatively, the vowel *a* has the sense of the possessive suffix *matup*; for example: *tuṇḍaḥ* and *ghāṭaḥ*.

(P_6,1.158.2) KA_III.97.7-25 Ro_IV.485-486 For what purpose, then, is this stated? It is for the sake of preventing the separate accentuation of the augment (*āgama*), the modification (*vikāra*), the base (*prakṛti*), and the suffix (*pratyaya*); [it establishes] the accent of the word as a whole, with the exception of one [element]. Regarding the augment: "In *catur* and *anaḍuh*, the *ām* is acute. As in *catvāraḥ*.

[The substitution applies] to the word *anaḍvāh* [in the nominative singular], to a derivative (*vikāra*), and to the words *asthi*, *dadhi*, *sakthi*, and *akṣi* [where *anaṅ* is substituted for the final vowel and consonant, being accented acute]. Examples: *asthnā*, *dadhnā*. [The substitution applies] to the base (*prakṛti*): *gopāyati*, *dhūpāyati*. And it applies to the suffix (*pratyaya*): *kartavyam*.

In the Taittirīya [recension], a simultaneous accent would apply to these words. However, it is desired that there should be only one [accent]. Since this cannot be accomplished without an effort, it is stated: "A word is unaccented, with the exception of one. This is said for that purpose. But this is not a necessary requirement; for the simultaneity is already established by the rule *tavai* and *antaśca*.

Since simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) is already established by the word "simultaneously" (*yugapat*), the fact that the teacher teaches "simultaneity" indicates that the accent does not occur simultaneously. In that case, alternation (*paryāya*) would follow. Alternation results from a vacuous teaching; since alternation is already established by the rule "optionally when there is a gap" (*rikte vibhāṣā*), the fact that the teacher teaches "alternation" indicates that it is not merely an alternation [but rather that the two accents do not apply at all].

Thus [it is said]. But this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding the acute accent (*udātta*). This would be an indicator regarding the acute accent: [the rule] "it should enter into combination with the circumflex" (*svarita*); that is, the entry into combination with the circumflex would result. For even in the circumflex, there is an acute accent. Therefore, there is no purpose for this rule (*yoga*).
Even if this rule were commenced, [it would apply] to the grave accent (*anudātta*).
The impossibility of a conflict [of rules] arises because they can occur simultaneously in a single instance. A conflict regarding the *anudātta* accent is not possible;

for the Teacher will indeed state a conflict in the rule: "In the case of *je*, when a long vowel follows a word with more than two syllables. That conflict is not possible. What is the reason? Because they can occur simultaneously in a single instance. Indeed, a conflict occurs only when simultaneous occurrence is impossible.

And it is possible that both [properties] might exist. How is this possible? When it is stated that "a word is unaccented except for one [syllable]," that [restriction] does not apply here. What is the reason? By this [rule], accentuation is not prohibited; rather, by this, the state of being unaccented is produced. And it is indeed possible for both [the preceding and following syllables] to possess accentuation.

There might otherwise be the state of being *anudātta* (unaccented) for other [syllables] as well. But if this is understood as a governing rule (*adhikāra*), what is accomplished? The governing rule applies to each individual rule (*yoga-yoge*) so that it does not need to be explicitly stated; thus it stands over each rule: "In the case of a suffix beginning with *j*, the first syllable of a word ending in a long vowel becomes *udātta*. This [rule], "A word is *anudātta* except for one [syllable]," is present [as a governing rule]. From the last [syllable]...

Previously, for those with many vowels (*bahvacaḥ*), this [rule] was present: "A word is unaccented, except for one. In that case, as to whether the exclusion should be by the former [rule] or by the latter, it would be by the latter because of its posteriority. This cannot be so; for then only the single accent belonging to the sixth [chapter] would be included, while the other accents found in the seven chapters would not be included.

[The rule] "In *samānodara*, when followed by *śayita*, the vowel is acute" [is stated]. And [the rule] "In *asthi*, *dadhi*, *sakthi*, and *akṣi*, the substitute *anaṅ* is acute. But this is established by the fact that [a word] has only one non-acute vowel. This is established. How? By the fact that [a word] has only one non-acute vowel. It should be stated: "A word consists of only one non-acute vowel. What does this "by the fact of being non-acute" mean? It does not mean that what is not acute is non-acute; nor does it mean that what is not non-acute [is non-acute].

"Anudātta. That which has one anudātta [accent] is "ekānudāttam. Because of its having one anudātta, it is established. But then the sūtra is modified. Let it remain exactly as it was originally formulated. But was it not said that a conflict (vipratiṣedha) is impossible regarding the anudātta because it occurs simultaneously in a single [syllable]? This is not a fault, for it is a *paribhāṣā*.

What is accomplished by this? For technical definitions (*saṃjñā*) and paribhāṣās are operative at the time of their application; wherever an operation occurs, it should be understood that this [paribhāṣā] is present there. [In the rule] "the initial syllable of a word ending in a long vowel becomes acute," this [paribhāṣā] is present:
"a word is unaccented except for one syllable. [In the rule] "the penultimate syllable of a polysyllabic word [becomes acute]," this [paribhāṣā] is present.

"A word is unaccented (*anudātta*), with the exception of one [syllable]. In this regard, as to whether the exclusion (*varjyamānatā*) applies by the preceding rule or by the subsequent one, it shall apply by the subsequent one because of its posteriority. Alternatively, this is not a reference to the technical term *anudātta*; what then? It is a reference based on the literal meaning (*anvartha*): that which has no acute accent (*udātta*) is "unaccented" (*anudātta*). Furthermore, the expression "with the exception of one" (*ekavarjam*) would otherwise be unintelligible.

Because of doubt; and the phrase "with the exception of one" (*ekavarjam*) is not well-established. Why because of doubt? Because it is not known which one is to be excluded. But it is established that [the rule applies] with the exception of that *anudātta* (unaccented) syllable for which the prescription of an *udātta* (acute) accent would be redundant. This is established. How so? That *anudātta* syllable for which the prescription of an *udātta* accent would be purposeless is the one to be excluded.

Because both the accent of the base (*prakṛti*) and the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya*) have their own scope, there would be uncertainty (*aprasiddhi*). Since both the accent of the base and the accent of the suffix have their own scope, uncertainty would arise. The scope for the accent of the base is where the suffix is unaccented (*anudātta*), as in *pacati* and *paṭhati*. The scope for the accent of the suffix is where the base is unaccented, as in *samatvam*.

The status of being a *sima* (limiting accent) applies here, and both [rules] would apply: [the rule for] what is to be done, and [the designation] *taittirīyaḥ*. Because of the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the accent of the suffix will prevail. Because of the conflict, the accent of the suffix will occur. Not so; for it is stated that "in a conflict, the subsequent operation prevails. But the accent of the suffix is not subsequent. This is not [the case].

There is a fault. The word *para* signifies "desired. In a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), that which is desired is the one that prevails. If it is argued that, due to the conflict, the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) [should prevail], then the marker *cit* must be applied to the *kāmya*-suffixes and others. If it is argued that, due to the conflict, the accent of the suffix should prevail, then the *kāmya*-suffixes and others must be marked with *cit*. For example: *putrakāmyati*.

"He protects" (*gopāyati*), "he feels aversion" (*ṛtīyate*). This is not a fault. Here, the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*) will be the sublater. When there is a natural accent, there is an absence of the affix accent (*pratyayasvara*); when there is a natural accent, there is an absence of the affix accent.
[This] must be done.

[Taittirīya: This is established. But it is established because the accent of the base (*prakṛtisvara*) is stronger; thus, the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) does not occur. How so? Because the accent of the suffix is established as being stronger than the accent of the base. How so? The accent of the suffix is stronger than the accent of the base.

(P_6,1.158.4) KA_III.99.22–101.4 Ro_IV.491–493: "The accent remaining last is stronger" (*satiśiṣṭasvarabalīyastvam*). It must be stated that "the accent remaining last is stronger. And this is for the sake of multiple suffixes and compounds. Furthermore, this "strength of the accent remaining last" must necessarily be stated. What is the purpose? For the sake of multiple suffixes and for the sake of multiple compounds.

And [the purpose] is for the sake of multiple suffixes (*pratyaya*). First, regarding multiple suffixes: in *aupagavaḥ*, the accent of the primary element (*prakṛtisvara*) is superseded by the accent of the suffix *aṇ*. In *aupagavatvam*, the accent of the suffix *tva* supersedes the accent of *aṇ*. In *aupagavatvakam*, the accent of the suffix *ka* supersedes the accent of *tva*. Regarding multiple compounds: *rājapuruṣaḥ*, *rājapuruṣaputraḥ*.

In *rājapuruṣaputra-puruṣaḥ*, if it is said that the accent of what remains (*satiśiṣṭasvara*) is stronger, then the accent of *syādi* would override the accent of the *sārvadhātuka*. [Examples would be] *sunutaḥ*, *cinutaḥ*. However, there is no occurrence of the *syādi* accent because of the rule stating that what follows *tās* is unaccented (*anudātta*). Thus, there is no occurrence of the *syādi* accent. Why? Because of the rule stating that what follows *tās* is unaccented. Since this [rule] applies to the *lasārvadhātuka* following *tās*...

The fact that [the rule] teaches an *anudātta* accent indicates that the teacher [intends to convey]: even though it is subsequently prescribed (*satiśiṣṭa*), the accent of the *vikaraṇa* does not supersede the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka*. Alternatively, this is established through a conflict of words (*śabdavipratiṣedha*), because there is no fixed rule regarding conflicts between subsequent rules. Or rather, since not everything desired is encompassed by a conflict of subsequent rules, one resorts to a conflict of words.

It will be understood as follows: if there were a conflict of words (*śabdavipratiṣedha*), then the *kāmya*-suffixes and others would have to be applied after the root *cit*, as in *putrakāmyati*, *gopāyati*, and *ṛtīyate*. However, what is called a "conflict of words" occurs only where both [grammatical operations] apply simultaneously; and this is not the case with the *kāmya*-suffixes and others.

There is the contingency of simultaneous application. The accent of *nañ* is stronger than the accent of a case-ending. It should be stated that "the accent of *nañ* is stronger than the accent of a case-ending. This is the scope for the accent of a case-ending: *tisraḥ tiṣṭhanti*. This is the scope for the accent of *nañ*: *abrāhmaṇaḥ*, *avṛṣalaḥ*. Here, both would apply: *atisraḥ*. The accent of *nañ* occurs [and not the accent of the case-ending], because it is caused by the case-ending.

And it should be stated that the accent of *nañ* is stronger than an accent caused by a case-ending (*vibhakti*). This is the scope for the accent caused by a case-ending: *catvāraḥ*, *anaḍvāhaḥ*. This is the scope for the accent of *nañ*: the same [forms]. Here, both [accents] would apply: *acatvāraḥ*, *ananaḍvāhaḥ*.

It should be stated that when there is an *upapada* with a *kṛt*-suffix followed by the negative particle *nañ*, the accent of that [compound] is stronger. For example: *akaraṇiḥ hi te vṛṣala*. And it should be stated that when the negative particle *nañ* is mentioned together [with another word], its accent is stronger. For example: *avyathī*.

(P_6,1.159) Why is the root *kṛṣ* taken here in its modified form (*vikṛta*), rather than simply saying "after *kṛṣ*" (*kṛṣāt*)? [It is so that] it may apply to that *kṛṣ* which has this specific form in its verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*). It should not apply here: *halasya karṣaḥ* ("the pulling of the plough"). Furthermore, why is the reference made by means of the possessive suffix *matup*, rather than simply from *karṣa*?

Thus it should be stated. If only "after *karṣ*" were stated, then [the suffix] would apply only where *ghañ* follows immediately after the vowel *ā*: as in *dāyaḥ* and *dhāyaḥ*. But it would not apply here: *pākaḥ*, *pāṭhaḥ*. For nowhere does *ghañ* follow immediately after the vowel *ā*. Even in this case, *dāyaḥ*— The final answer is: Thus it should be stated. If only "after *karṣ*" were stated, then [the suffix] would apply only where *ghañ* follows immediately after the vowel *ā*: as in *dāyaḥ* and *dhāyaḥ*. But it would not apply here: *pākaḥ*, *pāṭhaḥ*. For nowhere does *ghañ* follow immediately after the vowel *ā*. Even in this case, *dāyaḥ*—

The word *dhāyaḥ* is separated by the suffix *yuk*. Even so, the mention of the vowel *ā* would be understood as a qualifier of that which is prescribed; that is, "that which is prescribed after [the vowel] *ā*. However, when the mention of *matup* is made, there is no fault. (P_6,1.161.1) Why is it said "of the anudātta"? [To exclude] *prāsaṅgam*.

The *prāsaṅgya* ox draws [the load]. Since there is an absence of both the circumflex (*svarita*) and the acute (*udātta*) when the acute is elided, the mention of the grave (*anudātta*) is purposeless. Because there is an absence of the circumflex and the acute when the acute is elided, the mention of the grave is redundant; for no acute is ever elided when it occurs upon an acute or a circumflex; rather, every [acute] is elided only when it occurs upon a grave. And this [acute] occurs upon a circumflex.

"It is elided. In the case of *prāsaṅgyaḥ* (meaning "one who carries a load on a pole"), even this [suffix] is elided as an unaccented vowel once the *nighāta* (elision) has been applied. Here, the following must be considered: "Should the *nighāta* be performed first, or the elision? What should be done here? Because it is subsequent, the elision occurs.
If that is so, then this accent of *nighāta* today is an exception (*apavāda*) to all other accents; and [an exception applies] not within the domain of another exception.

The general rule (*utsarga*) applies after the exception (*apavāda*). For exceptions apply first, and afterwards the general rules. Or rather, having first determined the domain of the exception, the general rule then applies. Therefore, in this case, the *thāthādi* accent never occurs at that point;

it awaits the exception, namely the *nighāta* (elision of accent). In that situation, even if one were to think, "Let the *nighāta* be applied, and let there be elision," [the general rule does not apply].

Because it is subsequent, that [element] is elided; being without an acute accent (*avidyamānodātta*), the grave (*anudātta*) is elided. (KA_III.102.3-20 Ro_IV.495-497) If

Regarding accent (*svara*): if it is argued that [the accent] applies to the end [of the word], then the accent would not be established in the case of the elision of *śnam*, *ksa*, *yuṣmad*, *asmad*, *idam*, and *kim*. *Śnam*: *vindate*, *khindate*. *Ksa*: *mā hi dhukṣātām*, *mā hi dhukṣāthām*. *Yuṣmad-asmad*: *yuṣmabhyam*, *asmabhyam*. *Idam-kim-lopa*: *iyān*.

In that case, let the initial syllable be [acute]. If it is argued that "the initial" is the rule, then in the case of *indhīta dvayam*, the final acute would not be established. If it is argued that "the initial" is the rule, then the final acute of *indhīta*—as in *dvayam trayam*—is already established at the beginning. Let it be then that the initial becomes acute. But was it not said: "If 'the initial' is the rule, then in *indhīta dvayam* the final [would be acute]"? This is because of the prohibition of the anudātta status for the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes after the roots *vid*, *indh*, and *khid*.

It is established for the *liṅ* [optative]. It should be stated that the lack of accentuation (*anudāttatva*) of the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes after the roots *vid*, *indh*, and *khid* does not apply in the *liṅ*. There is no purpose in mentioning the *liṅ* [separately]. Since the prohibition of the *lasārvadhātuka* accentuation after *vid*, *indh*, and *khid* applies without distinction, it is already established for the *liṅ*. It is simply: "the lack of accentuation of the *lasārvadhātuka* after *vid*, *indh*, and *khid* does not occur. This [is the point].

It is also established that [the suffix] *vindate* and *khindate* [are formed]. As for [the case of] *ayac*, how is it? Because of the marking with *cit* in *ayac*. By the force of the marking with *cit* in *ayac*, the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) will occur. (P_6.1.162) Is it the end of the root (*dhātu*) that becomes acute, or rather...

"Regarding the term *ādiḥ* (the beginning): what is the distinction here? If it is argued that [the rule applies to] the end of a root (*dhātoḥ antaḥ*), then there must be the mention of *ba* even in the case of the *anudātta* [rule]. If it is argued that [the rule applies to] the end of a root, then the mention of *ba* must be made even in the rule concerning the *anudātta*. It should be stated: "The beginning of reduplicated roots (*abhyasta*) is *anudātta* when followed by *ba*. Furthermore, the mention of *ba* must be made; it should be stated: "And the root *pib* ending in *ba* becomes *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable)."

It is *pibati*. And it should be *san* and *nit*. What is the purpose? So that in forms such as *cikīrṣati* and *jihīrṣati*, there may be the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) by virtue of the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.193] stating "it is *nit*. Let it be so then; let it be the beginning [of the word]. But in the case of roots ending in the suffix *ūrṇu*, the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*) would not be established for those roots beginning with *ūrṇu*. For example: *ūrṇoti*, *ūrṇute*.

The verbal roots *pratyaya*, *dhātu*, *gopāyati*, *dhūpāyati*, and *ṛtīyate* [are formed]. This is established by the rule regarding the final acute accent (*antodātta*). Let it then be that they have the final acute accent. But surely—

If it is argued that [the rule] "at the end of a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ antaḥ*) has already been stated, then the mention of *anudātta* (unaccented) must also include the mention of *ba*. As for what was said—that the mention of *anudātta* must be made—it is indeed included in the formulation (*nyāsa*) itself: "The initial [syllable] of reduplicated roots (*abhyasta*) is unaccented when followed by *anudātta*. Regarding the statement that the mention of *ba* must be made: it is because of the irregularity (*nipātana*) in the case of *piba*; an irregularity is made such that *piba* is acutely accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).

That accent of the suffixal particle (*nipātana-svara*) will be the sublater of the natural accent (*prakṛti-svara*). Furthermore, it must be stated that the *san* [suffix] is *nit*. Therefore, the letter *n* must necessarily be included in *san* for the purpose of specification. Where is there a need for this letter *n* for the sake of specification? In the rule *sanyaṅoḥ*. If it were stated merely as *sayaṅoḥ*, then in the case of *haṃsaḥ*— [the rule would undesirably apply].

"Vatsa, here too [the rule] would apply. [Objection: It will not apply because of the principle that 'when there is the mention of something meaningful, that which is meaningless is not included. [Reply: In that case, it would still not apply here: *jugupsate* (he feels aversion), *mīmāṃsate* (he investigates). [Objection: This [suffix] is indeed meaningful. [Reply:
No meaning whatsoever is taught [for it]. Even if some [meaning were taught]..."

The meaning [of the suffix] is not specified; since those whose meanings are not specified occur in their own sense (*svārthe*), it will ultimately occur in its own sense. And what is its own sense? It is the sense of the base (*prakṛtyartha*). In that case, it would also apply here: *haṃsaḥ*, *vatsaḥ*. [Reply: The *uṇādi* suffixes are underived nominal stems (*prātipadika*). Therefore, this letter *n* must be prescribed for no other purpose.

It should not be done. It is already accomplished by the rule of *nyāsa* itself. Alternatively, the word *dhātoḥ* ("of a root") is understood [from the previous rule]. Thus, it means "there is reduplication of a root that ends with the sound *s*. (P. 6.1.163) [The statement] "of a *cita* suffix, together with its stem" is for the sake of *bahu* and *akac*. It should be stated: "of a *cita* suffix, together with its stem. What is the purpose? For the sake of *bahu* and *akac*. That is, for the sake of *bahu* and for the sake of *akac*. First, for the sake of *bahu*:
In these cases, the suffix *ka* is applied for the sake of forming the feminine:
*bahubhuktam*, *bahukṛtam*; and for the sake of forming the masculine with the suffix *akac*: *sarvakaiḥ*, *viśvakaiḥ*.
Loudly, softly,
all together.
[Objection: Then that must be stated. [Response: It need not be stated. Here, the elision of the *matup* suffix (*matub-lopa*) is to be understood. For example:

"those for whom there is merit" (*puṣya*) are "meritorious ones" (*puṣyakāḥ*); "those for whom there is time" (*kāla*) are "timely ones" (*kālakāḥ*). Alternatively, the vowel *a* is used in the sense of the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*).

For example: "tunda" (one who has a protruding belly) and "ghāṭa" (one who has a prominent forehead). Furthermore, the reference to the preceding rule is due to the fact that it ends in the *cit* suffix, as in "the *cita* [accented] word."

(P_6,1.166) KA_III.104.9-22 Ro_IV.500-501: What is the purpose of [specifying] *jasaḥ*? [In the example] *tisṛkā*, [the mention of *jasaḥ* is unnecessary]. The mention of *jasaḥ* after *tisṛbhyaḥ* is purposeless. Why? Because it does not occur elsewhere. For nothing other than the suffix *jas* causes the word *tisṛ* to have a final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) other than this [case].

What is the reason? The word *tisṛ* has exclusively plural scope; therefore, the singular and dual case endings do not occur. In the nominative plural (*śas*), it must be subject to the rule: "The [vowel] following an *udātta-yaṇ* that is preceded by a consonant [is *udātta*]. All other case endings beginning with a consonant are those starting with *hal*. In those cases, the accent must be governed by the rule: "After words ending in *ṣaṣ*, *tri*, or *catur*, the penultimate vowel is *udātta* when a consonant-initial suffix beginning with *jhal* follows."

In that case, by not including *jas* [in the rule], it will apply only to *jas*. But was it not just now cited as *tisṛkāḥ*? The accent of the *nit* suffix will be the sublater here. No; for the accent of *tisṛ* is introduced even when another accent has not yet applied.
Just as it sublates the accent of the rule "sup and pit suffixes are unaccented" (*anudāttau suppitau*), so too does it sublate the accent of the *nit* suffix.

It might indeed cause sublation (*bādha*). This is not a fault, because sublation occurs only when [the rule] has not already taken effect. Furthermore, the accentuation of *tisṛ* is not commenced while the rule "anudāttau suppitau" (Pāṇini 3.1.4) has not yet taken effect; rather, the *nit*-accent applies both when that rule has taken effect and when it has not. Alternatively, according to the principle that "exceptions in the middle sublate preceding rules," the accent of *tisṛ* sublates the [application of] "anudāttau suppitau."

The *sup-pittva* accent will subvert [the accent], but the *nit-svara* accent will not be subverted. Some desire the mention of *jas* for the sake of including the compounded forms: *atitistrāḥ*, *atitistraḥ*. (P. 6.1.167) Regarding the *śas* [ending] in the feminine, a prohibition must be stated.

"Observe the four [forms]: *catasraḥ*, *caturaḥ* [in the accusative], and [the form] in the feminine. There is no prohibition regarding the feminine in the accusative plural (*śasi*), because of the specific accentuation as being acute on the first syllable (*ādyudāttanipātana*). [Question: "There is no prohibition regarding the feminine in the accusative plural (*śasi*). A prohibition that serves no purpose is 'no-prohibition' (*apratiṣedhaḥ*). Why does the accent not occur in the accusative plural? [Answer: "Because of the specific accentuation as being acute on the first syllable. This specific accentuation as being acute on the first syllable will be applied; it is an accent resulting from a specific rule (*nipātanasvara*)."

The *śas* [suffix] will be an exception (*bādhaka*) to the accent of the stem. Even so, the treatment as if it were the original instruction (*upadeśivadbhāva*) must be stated; for just as the accent of the irregularly formed word (*nipātana-svara*) sets aside the accent of the *śas*, it would likewise set aside the accent of the case-ending (*vibhakti-svara*), as in the case of *catasṛṇām*. And the occurrence of the accent of the case-ending is established by the inclusion of the term "beginning with a consonant" (*hal-ādi-grahaṇāt*). Why? Because the occurrence of the accent of the case-ending is thus accomplished.

Because of the inclusion of the term "beginning with a consonant" (*halādi*). When this [grammarian] includes the phrase "beginning with a consonant" in the rule *ṣaṭtricaturbhyaḥ halādiḥ*, the Teacher thereby indicates that the accent of a particle (*nipātana-svara*) does not supersede the accent of a case-ending (*vibhakti-svara*). How is this an indicator?

For if the accent were established by the rule for particles having the acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta-nipātana*), the inclusion of the phrase "beginning with a consonant" would be purposeless. Indeed, if the accent were established by the rule for particles having the acute on the first syllable, the inclusion of the phrase "beginning with a consonant" [would be redundant].

It would be purposeless. For no other [word] beginning with *hal* serves as a basis for the application [of this rule], except for the word *catasṛ*. First of all, the technical designation *ṣaṭ* does not apply [to it]. Why? Because it falls within the scope of the plural number; therefore, the dual and singular endings do not occur. Furthermore, the case-endings *jaś* and *śas* are elided here. All other case-endings beginning with *hal* are present. As for the word *tri*:

And yet it does not cause [the accentuation] to apply. What is the reason? Because its scope is the plural number (*bahuvacana*). Therefore, the dual and singular endings do not exist [in this context]. By the statement "not being a *sarvanāmasthāna*," it will not occur before the suffix *jas*. It ought to occur before *śas*, because of the rule "when there is a single substitute, the accent of the substitute is that of the udātta vowel. All other case-endings beginning with consonants (*hal*) are likewise excluded. Furthermore, the word *tisṛ* also does not [apply].
It causes [the application of the rule]. What is the reason? Because it has the plural number as its scope. Therefore, the dual and singular numbers do not exist [in this context].

Due to the statement "not a *sarvanāmasthāna*," it should not occur in the *jas* case-ending. It should occur in the *śas* case-ending by the rule "from that which has an udātta *yaṇ* preceded by a consonant. All other case-endings beginning with a consonant are likewise. This applies to both the word *catuḥ* and the word *tisṛ*.

It does not cause [the substitution]. For what reason? Because it is the domain of the plural number (*bahuvacana*). Therefore, the dual and singular numbers do not exist [in this case]. By the statement "not a *sarvanāmasthāna*," it should not occur before the suffix *jas*. It should occur before *śas*, according to the rule *caturaḥ śasi*. All other case-endings beginning with consonants (*hal*) are different. Among those, from the single word *catasṛ*, the suffix *śas* is a non-*sarvanāmasthāna*.

The case-ending beginning with *a* (the nominative plural) exists here. If there were a *nipātana-svara* (an accent assigned by specific rule) in this instance, the mention of "beginning with a consonant" (*hal-ādi*) would be purposeless.

Alternatively, the accent of the suffix *śas* does not apply here at all. Why? Because once the *yaṇ*-substitution has been made, there is no preceding element that is subject to become acute. If it is argued that the accent would then apply to what remains, [we reply] no, because it is separated from it by the vowel *ṛ*.

It will not be so. Once the substitution of *yaṇ* has been made, there is no intervention [of an element]. [Objection: There is indeed an intervention because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). [Response: Here, the status of being a substitute is prohibited; with respect to rules concerning accent (*svara*), it does not behave as a substitute. [Objection: This prohibition does not apply. It has already been stated that in the prohibition regarding accent, lengthening (*dīrgha*), and the elision of *y* and *l* (*yalopa*), a substitute for an elided element (*lopādeśa*) does not behave as a substitute.

Regarding the term *sau*: does this refer to the nominative singular (*prathamaikavacana*) or the locative plural (*saptamībahuvacana*)? From what does the doubt arise? Because the grammatical indication is identical. It refers to the locative plural. How is this known? Because [the author] teaches a prohibition for *go* and *śvan* in the rule *na gośvansāvavarṇa*, stating "not after *go* or *śvan* when followed by *s* or *au*. If it were the nominative singular, such a prohibition would be unnecessary. Therefore, it is the locative plural.

How does this function as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? If there were a reference to the nominative singular (*prathamaikavacana*), the statement of the prohibition regarding "cow" (*go*) and "dog" (*śvan*) would be purposeless. But is it not the case that this very [prohibition] establishes the meaning? We are indeed favored by those [grammarians] for whom, by relying on the nominative singular, the prohibition regarding "cow" and "dog" need not be stated. Indeed, the prohibition would not need to be stated.

But there are faults. What is the fault here? [In the case of] *svinā* and *khinā*, the udātta accent on the final syllable is not obtained. [However,] *svinkhinau* do not exist. This has been stated: "The two suffixes (*ini* and *iniṅ*) are not prescribed after a monosyllabic word, after a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, after a genus name, or in the locative case. Therefore, it should simply be *svavān* and *khavān*. But then, in this case, *yādbhyām*...

The form *yābhiḥ* is not established [by that rule]. Therefore, there is the inclusion of the locative plural (*saptamī-bahuvacana*). Regarding the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of a monosyllabic word (*ekāc*) before the nominative singular suffix *su*, a prohibition must be stated for *tvad* and *mad*. [Otherwise, one would get] *tvayā* and *mayā*. However, it is established as follows:

Because it begins with the third [case-ending] and lacks that [first case-ending], it is *sau*. This is established. How so? Because here the third case-ending and so forth do not exist for that which is *sau*; even though this does not possess *sau*, its base (*prakṛti*) does possess *sau*. And because the base has more than one vowel (*anekāctva*). Even though it has a base, that base becomes one with more than one vowel.

(P_6,1.169) KA_III.107.2-5 Ro_IV.506: What is the purpose of including the mention of "the latter member" (*uttarapada*)? It is so that the mention of "a single vowel" (*ekāj*) may be understood as a qualifier of the latter member, [meaning] "from a single-vowel [stem] that is the latter member. Now, if the mention of "the latter member" were not made, of what would the mention of "a single vowel" be a qualifier? It would be a qualifier of the compound (*samāsa*). And yet, there exists at present some [compound] consisting of a single vowel.
He says that there is a compound for which a rule would apply:
*śunaḥ ūrk* becomes *śvork*,
*śvorjā*, and *śvorje*.

(P_6,1.171) They employ forms ending in *nic* at the beginning of words. Other word-initial forms are established by the accent known as *udāttanivṛtti-svara*. Regarding the substitution of *ūṭh*, the mention of the *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) is for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of the rule] to the final letter. The mention of the *upadhā* must be made in the rule for *ūṭh*. What is the purpose? For the purpose of prohibiting [the rule from applying] to the final letter. Let it not apply to the final letter, as in *akṣadyuvā* and *akṣadyuve*.

(P_6,1.172) KA_III.107.13-22 Ro_IV.507-508: What is the purpose of including the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*)? [In the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*] one could say "after a long vowel" (*dīrghāt*) instead. Why does [the substitution] not apply in the case of "a Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires at eight steps" (*aṣṭasu prakrameṣu brāhmaṇa ādadhīta*)? The [substitution of] *ṣat* for *aṣṭan* will be the sublater. But it is not the case that the substitution of *ṣat* for *aṣṭan* applies when the [substitution of] *ṣat* for *ṣaṣ* has not yet been reached.

The accent (svara) is now commenced. Just as it excludes [the accent] from a long vowel, so too would it exclude it from a short vowel. However, the accent of "ṣaṭ" does not apply after a long vowel. What is the reason? Because once the substitution of *āt* has been made, the designation (*saṃjñā*) "ṣaṭ" no longer exists. Therefore, he recites the following reply:

"The mention of the long vowel in the case of *aṣṭan* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the designation 'ṣaṭ' for the sake of the augment *nuṭ* after that which ends in *ā*. This refers to the mention of the long vowel in the rule for *aṣṭan*.

It is formulated for the purpose of providing an explanatory indication (*jñāpaka*). What is to be indicated? The Teacher indicates this: that once the substitution of *āt* (for *aṣṭan*) has been applied, the technical designation *ṣaṣ* (six) still applies. What is the purpose of this indication? It is for the sake of the augment *nuṭ* after a stem ending in long *ā*. Thus, the *nuṭ* augment becomes established in the form *aṣṭānām* ("of eight"). But is not the substitution of *āt* obligatory? This very rule indicates that the substitution of *āt* is optional (*vibhāṣā*).
That he uses the term *dīrgha* (long vowel) here is for this reason: otherwise, he would have simply said *aṣṭanaḥ*.

Regarding the rule for the acute accent on the first syllable of words ending in *nadī* and *aja*, there must be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the words *bṛhat* and *mahat*. An addition must be made to the rule for the acute accent on the first syllable of words ending in *nadī* and *aja* to include *bṛhat* and *mahat*:
namely, *bṛhatī*, *mahatī*, *bṛhatā*, and *mahatā*.

(P_6,1.174) KA_III.108.6-16 Ro_IV.509-510: For what purpose is the phrase "preceded by a consonant" (*halpūrvāt*) stated? [In the examples] *agnaye* and *vāyave*, it would not apply. The mention of "a consonant" (*halgrahaṇa*) in the rule concerning the udātta-vowel (*udāttayaṇ*) is for the sake of words ending in *-n*. The mention of "a consonant" in the rule concerning the udātta-vowel must be made. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of words ending in *-n*, so that the rule may also apply after a word ending in *-n*, as in *vākpatnī* and *citpatnī*. [Objection: The mention of "preceded by a consonant" is redundant.

And because it is a substitute for the entire complex (*samudāya*). Furthermore, the mention of *halpūrva* (preceded by a consonant) is purposeless. Why? Because it is a substitute for the entire complex; here, the substitute is the whole complex. And because it is not stated [otherwise] regarding the circumflex accent (*svarita*): since the mention of *halpūrva* is not stated in the case of the circumflex accent, we consider the mention of *halpūrva* to be purposeless. As for what was said regarding the vowel with an acute accent (*udāttayaṇ*):
The inclusion of the term *hal* (consonant) is made for the sake of [words] ending in *n*, as stated in the *Nyāsa* itself. This is an instruction containing two *n*s:

*udāttayaṇo halpūrvād na ūṅ dhātvoḥ*. Furthermore, as for what is said—that the mention of *halpūrva* is redundant because it is a substitution of the whole (*samudāyādeśatva*)—this is indeed a simple substitution: *bahutitavā*.

Regarding the acute accent on the suffix *matup*: the mention of *re* must be made in the rule for the acute accent of *matup*. [Example: “*ā revān etu naḥ viśaḥ*. Furthermore, there is a prohibition concerning *tri*: a prohibition of *tri* must also be stated. [Example: “*trivatīḥ yājyānuvākyāḥ bhavanti*” (the invitatory and offering verses consist of three parts).

(P_6,1.177) KA_III.109.2-21 Ro_IV.510-512 Why does [the rule] not apply here: *kiśorīṇām*, *kumārīṇām*? [The word] "from a short vowel" (*hrasvāt*) is understood [to carry over]. In that case, it would still not apply here: *agnīnām*, *vāyūnām*. What is the reason? Because once lengthening (*dīrghatva*) has occurred, there is no longer a short vowel. This must be considered here: [which comes first,] the lengthening...

"Let the accent be applied. What is to be done here? By virtue of its being subsequent, the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs. If that is so, then the mention of "short" (hrasva) must be made in the rule for the accent on a *nām* [stem] ending in *matau*. The mention of "short" must be made in the rule for the accent on a *nām* [stem] ending in *matau*, as in: "after a stem ending in a short vowel in *matau*. Then it must be stated. It need not be stated. For he says this: [the suffix] follows a stem ending in a short vowel, and a *nām* [stem] does not end in a short vowel.

It exists. In that case, the principle of referring to what was previously so (*bhūtapūrvagati*) will be understood as "that which was previously short. A reference to what was previously so is understood when there is an absence of the present [form]; however, this [suffix] is present, as in *tisṛṇām* and *catasṛṇām*. This is not the case; for by the rule *ṣaṭtricaturbhyaḥ halādiḥ*, it ought to be followed by a vowel.
Since that [rule] would apply invariably, this option (*vibhāṣā*) is commenced. If that is the case, then a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made:

first, "after the words *ṣaṣ*, *tri*, and *catur*, the case-ending becomes acute"; then, "the case-ending beginning with a consonant (*halādi*)": thus, the case-ending beginning with a consonant after *ṣaṣ*, *tri*, and *catur* becomes acute. In that case, consider this: *tvam nṛṇām nṛpate jāyase śuciḥ*. But surely...

Even here, the accent prescribed by the rule *nṛ ca anyatarasyām* will be the sublater [of the preceding rule]. It is not established; it is not established. What is the reason? Because the mention of *jhal* (consonants) follows there [in that rule]. But what is the reason that the mention of *jhal* follows there? So that it does not apply here: *nrā*, *nre*. [In these cases,] the accent *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt* would otherwise apply.
In this case, the accent will be the sublater. Then consider the word *nari*. The mention of "short" (*hrasva*) does not serve as a purpose for citing only a single example.

If this were the only purpose, one would simply say *nām*; there, by virtue of that statement, the understanding of what was previously so (*bhūtapūrvagati*) would be recognized—namely, "that which was previously ending in a short vowel. Alternatively, it is not understood in this way: [the rule applies to] *nām* and the accents.

[Question: Should the mention of "short" (*hrasva*) be made in the rule for the suffix *matau*? [Answer: How then? [The answer is that] the phrase "after a short vowel in words ending in *nām*" (*nāmsvare matau hrasvāt*) continues [into this rule].

(P_6.1.182) KA_III.109.23-110.11 Ro_IV.512-513 [Question: Regarding the word *sau*, is it the nominative singular that is being referred to, or is it the locative plural? [Question: Why is there doubt? [Answer: Because the grammatical expression is identical. This [word *sau*] was used previously...

The conclusion is that there is the inclusion of the locative plural (*saptamī-bahuvacana*). Here too, that same [conclusion] ought to apply. If it were the inclusion of the locative plural, then in the case of *tābhyām brāhmaṇābhyām*, [the rule] would not apply to those two Brāhmaṇas mentioned here. Furthermore, the prescribed operation (*vidhi*) would not be established here. What is the reason? Because this is not the form produced by the suffix *sau*. Well then, consider the case of *tebhyaḥ*.

In the case of those Brāhmaṇas for whom the positive injunction (*vidhi*) is established but the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) does not apply, is something desired actually included, or is it merely the end of a fault? He says: "It is so. Here, in the case of those Brāhmaṇī women...

Thus, both the injunction and the prohibition regarding those Brāhmaṇī women are established. In that case, there is indeed the inclusion of the nominative singular. If there were an inclusion of the nominative singular, then by the rule *tena*, the accent would not be established in the masculine. But it is not necessarily only in the masculine; it occurs in the feminine, the masculine, and the neuter as well—as in *tena brāhmaṇena*.

[The objection is: "By that Brahmin woman, by that bowl"—even if the locative plural (*saptamī-bahuvacana*) is intended, this same fault remains. Therefore, in order to prohibit [the elision] for both, the mention of *yat* and *tat* must be made: *na gośvansāvavarṇarāḍaṅkruṅkṛdbhyaḥ yattadośca*. (Pāṇini 6.1.185). Regarding *titi*: the mention of the affix *ti* must be made. It must be stated: "*titi*" [meaning "when followed by an affix marked with *ti*"]. This is so that it does not apply here: *ṝta id dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100), as in *kirati*.

[The opponent says: "It swallows [the preceding vowel]. [The proponent replies: "In that case, it must be stated. [The opponent says: "It need not be stated. [The proponent asks: "Is this not the letter *t*? [The opponent replies: "What then? It is the letter *d*. [The proponent says: "If it is the letter *d*, then by internal similarity (*āntarya*), a long vowel would result for a long vowel. [The opponent replies: "This will not happen because of the rule: 'When a vowel is being taught (*bhāvyamāna*), there is no inclusion of its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). [The proponent asks: "If it is said that when a vowel is being taught there is no inclusion of its homogeneous counterparts, then [what about] *adas*?"
In the case of *aseḥ dāt u daḥ maḥ*,

[the rule] *amūbhyām* would not apply here. If that is so, then the activity of the Teacher indicates that a vowel being pronounced as *u* includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), since he makes the *u* in *divaḥ ut* a *tapara*.

"In that case, for this very purpose, the mention of the term *pratyaya* (suffix) must be made here so that [the rule] does not apply [to suffixes]. This is not the letter *t*. What then? It is the letter *d*. If it is the letter *d*, then it cannot serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Well then, by the rule *taparas tatkālasya*, the letter *d* is also indicated as having undergone the change to *c* (*cartva*). If this is so, then because the change to *c* (*cartva*) is considered unestablished (*asiddha*), [the rule] *haśi ca*..."
Thus, the substitution of *ū* would apply. This is a Vedic-style (sautra) formulation. Alternatively, the formulation will be made without sandhi (*asaṃhitayā*):
"An *aṇ* and an *udit* [vowel] denote their homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*), provided they are not suffixes; when followed by *t* or *tapara*, they denote those of the same duration."
