Regarding the rule *adupadeśāt*: how is this to be understood? Is it "that which is taught as the vowel *a*," or rather "that which is taught as ending in the vowel *a*"? What follows from this? If it is understood as "that which is taught as the vowel *a*," then [the rule] is destroyed in the case of [the word] *hataḥ*.

In this case, the designation *hathaḥ* would also result [as being included]. Now, if it is understood that "that which ends in /a/ in its original instruction (*upadeśa*)" is meant, then there is no fault. But even when it is understood that "that which ends in /a/ in its original instruction" is meant, the designation *hathaḥ* would still result here as well. For even this [word *hathaḥ*] ends in /a/ in its original instruction by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). [Reply: The principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" applies only to that which is meaningful (*arthavat*).

If, then, it is understood that "that which ends in *a* is the root as taught," then [the rule] would also apply here in the cases *mā hi dhukṣātām* and *mā hi dhukṣāthām*. Let it be so. Once the anudātta accent has been applied, the form is established by the "accent of the disappearance of the acute" (*udāttanivṛttisvara*) when the elision occurs.
It is not established. This must be considered here: should the anudātta accent be applied first, or the elision?

What should be done here? Elision [of the *s*] [should apply], because it is subsequent. If that is so, then this present rule regarding the anudātta accent of the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accent of the suffix. And the general rule (*utsarga*) does not apply where there is scope for an exception; for exceptions take effect first, and the general rules afterwards. Or rather, having first determined the domain of the exception, the general rule then applies.

It undergoes fixation (*abhiniviśate*). Therefore, in this case, the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) never occurs at that stage. It awaits the state of being unaccented (*anudātta*) for the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix, which is an exception (*apavāda*). In that situation, there arises the conflict: "Let the unaccentedness be applied" versus "Let the elision (*lopa*) be applied.

What should be done here? Elision takes effect because it is subsequent (*paratvāt*). Even though elision occurs due to its priority, that [elided element] is as if non-existent with respect to the udātta accent.
When an *anudātta* [vowel] is elided, an *udātta* [vowel] is substituted for it. (P.

6.1.186.2) Regarding the *anudātta* status of the roots beginning with *tasi*, the locative case (*saptamī*) is specified for the sake of the *abhyasta* and *sic* suffixes. The locative case must be employed when the roots beginning with *tasi* are designated as *anudātta*, in order to apply the designation *lasārvadhātuka*.

Thus it should be stated. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of the reduplicated roots (*abhyasta*). The initial syllable of reduplicated roots becomes acute (*udātta*) before a *lasārvadhātuka* suffix.

[Otherwise,] the initial syllable of a root ending in *sic* would become acute before a *lasārvadhātuka* suffix. If it were merely stated "before a *lasārvadhātuka*," then only that [root ending in *sic*] would have the acute accent on its initial syllable. If, however, the locative case is employed, then [the rule applies] to *tāsī* and the others as well.

Thus, the state of being unaccented (*anudāttatva*) would result [for the *tās* suffix]. This is not a fault. The ablative case in *tāsiyādibhyaḥ* will be interpreted as a genitive in place of the locative *lasārvadhātuke*, according to the principle "from that [the preceding], for the following.
Thus, the unaccented nature [of the *tās* suffix] follows from the accent of the *cit* element after *tās* and the others.

By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the lack of acute accent (*anudāttatva*) applies after roots such as *tās* (the marker of the periphrastic future) by way of conflict with the acute accent of a *cit* suffix. The scope of the *cit*-accent is, for example, *calanaḥ* and *copanaḥ*. The scope of the lack of acute accent after *tās* and so on is, for example, *āste* and *śete*. In the case of *āsīnaḥ* and *śayānaḥ*, both [rules] would apply; therefore, the lack of acute accent after *tās* and so on occurs by way of conflict. However, this conflict is not logical.

What is the reason? For a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) consists in the conjunction of two operations upon a single element; however, in this case, no single element is joined with two operations—namely, the low-pitched accent (*anudātta*) for the beginning and the high-pitched accent (*udātta*) for the end. Is it not the case that a conflict is necessarily only the conjunction of two operations? No; rather, impossibility (*asambhava*) is also [a cause of conflict]. But surely there is possibility here too: [the application of] the low-pitched accent to the beginning.

[The rule states: "The final [syllable] has the acute accent. And it is possible that both [the initial and the final] should be so. This possibility does not exist. For he will state this in the section on vowel accents: "A composite whole is the recipient of the grammatical operation. Furthermore, there must be an addition for the case of *muk*. An addition must be made for *muk*: as in *pacamānaḥ*.

In the case of *yajamānaḥ*, because it is separated by the augment *muk* and because it is not taught with an initial vowel (*adupadeśāt*), the rule "the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented" does not apply, and thus the unaccented nature is not attained. But surely this *muk* is part of what is taught with an initial vowel (*adupadeśabhakta*) and will therefore be included by the mention of "being taught with an initial vowel"? No, it is not established. The *muk* is said to belong to the stem (*aṅga*), yet the stem ends in the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*). Therefore, that [augment] belongs to the entire complex [of stem and suffix] and cannot [be considered part of the stem alone].

[The objection: It should be included by the mention of "an *adupadeśa*" (a verbal root taught with an initial vowel). Now, if this [root] were part of an *at* (containing the augment *at*), it would be included by the mention of "an *adupadeśa*. [The reply: Certainly, it would be included. [Objection: Then it will be part of an *at*. [Question: How so? [Reply: He will state the solution to this. Furthermore, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made from this point; an addition must be made because it is separated by the *it*-sounds.

The state of being unaccented (*anudāttatva*) would not be obtained in cases such as *pacataḥ* and *paṭhataḥ*. Furthermore, because they are non-exclusive (*anekānta*). The markers (*anubandhas*) are non-exclusive. If the markers are non-exclusive, then a prohibition must be stated for roots beginning with *ad-* and *juhotyādi*, as in *attaḥ* and *juhutaḥ*; otherwise, the rule "from a root having *a* as its upadeśa" would result in the unaccented status [of the affix]. Therefore, [a prohibition] from roots beginning with *ad-* and *juhotyādi* [is required].

There is no prohibition because there is no relationship between a substituendum (*sthānin*) and a substitute (*ādeśa*). In that regard, for the *adiprabhṛti* (beginning with *ad*) and *juhotyādi* (beginning with *juhote*) groups, there is no prohibition. "No prohibition" (*apratiṣedhaḥ*) means a prohibition that is purposeless. Why does the low-pitched accent (*anudāttatva*) not occur? Because there is no relationship between a substituendum and a substitute. We do not perceive a substituendum here, nor do we perceive a substitute. Alternatively, it is due to the mention of the term "having an *anudātta* or *ṅit* marker. Or else:

The fact that the Teacher includes the mention of *anudātta* and *ṅit* indicates that the state of being *anudātta* does not apply to those [roots] from which the *vikaraṇa* has been elided. This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*). This [mention] would be for the sake of *śnam*: as in *vindāte*, *khindāte*. But then, why does he include the mention of *ṅit*? For the *śnam*-suffix is not *ṅit*. If the *anudātta* status applies to what is *ṅit*, a prohibition must be stated regarding the *vikaraṇas*: as in *cinutaḥ*.
In *sunutaḥ*, *lunītaḥ*,
and *punītaḥ*, the rule *ṅitaḥ* would result in the [suffix] being unaccented (*anudātta*). Regarding the unaccented nature of what ends in *ṅit*, there is no prohibition for the *vikaraṇa* suffixes.

Because [the term] "of everything" (*sarvasya*) is a qualifier of "instruction" (*upadeśa*). Regarding the rule that [a root] ending in *ṅ* is unaccented (*anudātta*), there is no prohibition against the *vikaraṇas*. "No prohibition" (*apratiṣedhaḥ*) means a prohibition that is purposeless. Why does the unaccented state not occur? Because "of everything" is a qualifier of "instruction. We shall qualify "everything" by the mention of "instruction": "[roots] which are unaccented in their instruction (*upadeśe anudāttetaḥ*)."
Regarding the rule *upadeśe ṅitaḥ* and *upadeśe akārāntāt*:

an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the augment *s-* when it is *aniṭ*, *pit*, and has an udātta accent on its first syllable. An addition must be made for the augment *s-* when it is *aniṭ*, *pit*, and has an udātta accent on its first syllable.
"mā hi karṣam," "mā hi kārṣam. For what purpose is [the condition] "aniṭaḥ" (not having the augment iṭ) stated? [To exclude cases such as: "mā hi laviṣam.
Due to the optionality of the rule for roots beginning with *svap* (svapādīnām vā), the accent of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyastasvara*) prevails by way of supersession (*vipratiṣedha*).

By the rule "or for *svap* and so forth," the accent of the reduplicated (abhyasta) syllable prevails by way of opposition (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of the rule "or for *svap* and so forth" is, for example, *svapanti*, *śvasanti*. The scope of the accent of the reduplicated syllable is, for example, *dadati*, *dadhati*. In this case, both [rules] would apply: *jagrati*. By way of opposition, the accent of the reduplicated syllable prevails.
(P_6.1.190) KA_III.113.19–22 Ro_IV.521: The term *anudātte* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound intended for the purpose of [triggering] elision (*lopa*) and the substitution of *yaṇ*.

The term *anudātte* must be stated as a *bahuvrīhi* compound; it should be explained as "that which has no udātta accent" (*avidyamānodātta*). What is the purpose? It is for the sake of elision and the substitution of *yaṇ*, so that once elision and the *yaṇ*-substitution have been applied, the word-initial *udātta* accent may occur.
"Let him not place [it]"; here he does place it.

(P_6.1.191.1) Regarding the rule *sarvasvaro 'nackasya*: it should be stated that the *sarvasvara* (the acute accent on all syllables) applies to a monosyllabic word. This should not apply here in the case of *sarvake*.
(P_6.1.191.2) For what purpose is the mention of *bhyādi* ("beginning with *bhi*")? [It is so that] this [rule] should not apply here...
It occurs: *dadāti*, *dadhāti*. There is no need for this [separate rule]. Here, the accent of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyastasvara*) will be the sublater.

Thus, in the end, both would apply. Indeed, rules that have no scope (*anavakāśa*) are sublaters, and the accent of the reduplicated syllable does have scope. What is its scope? *mimīte*. Now, what is the purpose of mentioning "affix" (*pratyaya*)? [It is] from the affix.

[The purpose is] so that the acute accent (*udātta*) may belong to what precedes the suffix, and not to what precedes *āṭ*. [For example: *bibhayāni*. Nor is there any difference whether the acute accent belongs to what precedes the suffix or to what precedes *āṭ*. Furthermore, since [the augment] is a part of the *piṅ* [suffix], it will be included by the mention of *piṅ*. In that case, this is the purpose: so that the acute accent may belong to what precedes the suffix, and not to *āṭ*.
"Let it not be so"—this too is not a valid purpose, for that which is a portion of *pit* will be included by the mention of *pit*.

If this is the case, then since [the result] is already established, the fact that the Teacher employs the term "affix" (*pratyaya*) indicates that in the rules governing accent (*svaravidhi*), a composite whole (*saṅghāta*) is the recipient of the grammatical operation. What is the purpose of this indication? [It serves to establish that] the accent of *cit* applies to roots such as *tās* and others.

It has been stated that the status of being *anudātta* (unaccented) occurs by way of *vipratiṣedha* (conflict of rules). That is now established. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "pūrva" (preceding)? [Objection: When it is specified as "in that" (*tasmin*), the rule "of the preceding" (*pūrvasya*) will apply to the preceding element itself. [Response: If that is so, since the result is already established, the fact that the teacher employs the mention of "pūrva" serves to indicate that in rules concerning accents (*svaravidhi*), locative case endings (*saptamī*) [denote the locus of the operation].

"Thus, the locative case endings [denoting] 'at the end of that' occur. What is the purpose of this indication? [It serves for the rules: "In *rit*, the penultimate vowel of that which ends in *rit* [is lengthened]";

and "In *caṅ*, optionally, [the penultimate vowel] of that which ends in *caṅ* [is lengthened]. If this were indicated, then by the rule "caturaḥ śasi," the [lengthening] would also apply to that which ends in the suffix *śas*.
It will not happen, because of the force of the mention of *śas*. For otherwise, he would have stated this right there [in that rule].
[The rule states: "And [the augment *it* is applied] after four words: *ūḍ*, *idam*, *padādi*, and *apumraidryu*. Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *pit*?

It is so that it does not occur here: *jāgrati*. This is not a valid purpose, for the [augment] occurs here by the preceding rule. Then this is the purpose: *daridrati*. Because it is separated by the vowel *ā*, [the augment] will not occur; but once the elision (*lopa*) has been performed, there is no separation.

Because of the status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, there would indeed be an intervention; however, here the *sthānivadbhāva* is prohibited with respect to vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*) by the rule "it is not like the original element (*na sthānivat*). (P. 6.1.195).
An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) should be made regarding the suffix *yaki* when followed by *ra*. In the case of *yaki* followed by *ra*:
An addition must be made: [the rule applies to] "it is strewn by itself. This is established by the statement of the *upadeśa*.
It should be stated that [the rule applies] in the *upadeśa*. Regarding the statement of the *upadeśa*, the accent of roots such as *jan* is not established.

For example: *jayate svayam eva* ("it is born by itself") and *jāyate svayam eva* ("it is born by itself"). This is established through the division of the *yoga* (sūtra). The division of the *yoga* will be made.

For verbal roots ending in vowels, when the suffix *yak* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), the first syllable optionally becomes acute (*udātta*). For example: *cīyate svayam eva* (it is piled up by itself), *ciyate svayam eva*;

*jayate svayam eva*, *jāyate svayam eva*. Furthermore, in the case of instruction (*upadeśe*), for roots ending in vowels, when the suffix *yak* is used in the sense of the agent, the first syllable optionally becomes acute: *stīryate svayam eva*, *stīryate svayam eva*. That is so.
In that case, the mention of "instruction" (*upadeśa*) must be made; for without the mention of instruction, it does not become a limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*).
It need not be made, because the previous subject (*prakṛta*) continues to apply. Where was it previously stated? In the rule:

"The *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented after [roots] taught with a low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*), or marked with *ṅ*, *it*, or *at*, except for those ending in *han* and *iṅ*. But was it not already said that by the mention of "instruction," the accent of *jan* and so forth is intended?

"It is not established"—this is not a fault. It is not understood in this way: that the accent of *jan* and so forth is not established by the statement of the *upadeśa*. How then? The statement of the *upadeśa* must also be made for *jan* and so forth in order to establish their *āt*-vowel quality (*āttva*).
[Objection: In that case, the mention of *upadeśa* must be included there. [Reply: It need not be included; the previously mentioned term continues to apply. Where?

The present topic is: "There is the elision of the nasal [of roots] taught with an *anudātta* vowel, and of *van*, *tan*, etc., before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ* that begins with a *jhal* consonant" (P.
6.4.37). [Question: For what purpose is the mention of *seṭ* (having the augment *iṭ*)?
Why not simply say, "In *thali*, *iṭ* optionally"? [Answer: If it were said, "In *thali*, *iṭ* optionally," then this would undesirably apply here as well: *papaktha*. This is not so.

The purpose [of this rule] is as follows: the term *acaḥ* ("after a vowel") is understood [from the previous rule]. Then, what is the purpose [of this specific rule]? It is for forms such as *yayātha*. Why is this stated? Is it not already established by the rule *ñniti ādir nityam* ("when followed by a suffix marked with Ñ or Ṇ, the augment is always initial")? We say that it is stated [here] because we do not see a suffix marked with Ñ or Ṇ (*ñnit*) here; [the status of the suffix is determined] by means of the technical designation of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*).

The prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of suffix-based rules) by the rule *na lumatā tasmin* applies to that which is stated under the heading of *aṅga*. That prohibition—namely, *na lumatāṅgasya*—is restricted to what is taught within the *aṅgādhikāra*. Therefore, he recites the following reply: the statement that the first syllable of the *upamāna* is udātta is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* does not apply to an accent characterized by an *anubandha*. This is because of the statement that the first syllable of the *upamāna* is udātta.

It is formulated for the purpose of providing an indication (*jñāpaka*). What is indicated? The Teacher indicates this: "In the case of a vowel [accent] conditioned by a *anubandha*, the rule regarding suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not apply. What is the purpose of this indication? [The forms] *gargaḥ* and *vatsaḥ*.
Bida, Urvā, and Uṣṭragrīva.
The vowel in *vāmarajjuḥ* is not to be treated as having the acute accent on the first syllable by the rule *ñniti*; and here,
in the case of *atrayaḥ*, the same applies.

The rule *taddhitasya kitaḥ* does not apply to provide the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*). If it is argued that [the rule applies] when there is a marker (*anubandha*), then in the case of *pathipriyaḥ* and *mathipriyaḥ*, the rule *pathimathoḥ sarvanāmasthāne* would result in the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*). In that case, the Teacher indicates that the designation of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not apply with respect to accent. Even so, in the case of *sarpiḥ*...
In the case of *āgaccha*, *sapta āgacchata*, the rule *āmantritasya ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.198), which prescribes that the first syllable of a vocative is udātta, does not apply. And here too: *mahi datām*.

For [in the case of] *mahi dhātām*, this accent—[namely] the rule "the initial syllable of the suffix *sica* may optionally [be acute]" (*ādiḥ sicaḥ anyatarasyām*)—would not apply. If that is so, then the Teacher indicates that when an accent is prescribed with reference to a seventh-case form (*saptamīnirdiṣṭe*), the designation of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not take effect.
Even so, [in the case of] *sarvastomaḥ*...
Regarding *sarvapṛṣṭha*:

by the rule *sarvasya supi*, the initial udātta accent would not apply. Let it be, then, that [the accent] occurs only when characterized by an *anubandha*. How then do we account for *pathipriyaḥ* and *mathipriyaḥ*? This must indeed be stated as an exception.

In the case of *pathin* and *mathin*, when a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix is elided by *lumat*, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule does not apply. (P. 6.1.205). Regarding the lengthening [of the vowel] before the suffix *yañ* after a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), a prohibition must be stated. A prohibition regarding the lengthening before *yañ* after a *niṣṭhā* must be formulated; for example, *dattābhyām*, *guptābhyām*. Or rather, it need not be stated. Why? Because it is characterized as being external (*bahiraṅga*). In this case, the lengthening is external.

An internal element (*antaraṅga*) is [stronger]; that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is not established when an internal element is present. Without this prohibition and without this *paribhāṣā*, the rule is established. How so? It is not understood thus: "if the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) does not follow a stem ending in long *ā*. How then? It is understood: "if the past participle suffix does not come after [a stem] ending in *ā*. If this were the case, the grammatical formulation itself would be untenable.

For this fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) after the vowel *ā* is not logical [in this context]. And here it would apply: *āptaḥ*, *rāddhaḥ*. If that is so, then [the rule] "if the suffix *niṣṭhā* does not follow a vowel" would be a valid formulation. But here it would still apply: *āptaḥ*, *rāddhaḥ*; and here it would not apply: *yataḥ*.

[The opponent says: "In that case, the mention of the vowel *a* (*akāra*) is a qualifier of that which is prescribed (*vihita*). That is, [the rule applies] only if the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is prescribed after a root ending in the vowel *a*. [The proponent replies: Even so, it would not apply here in the case of *dattaḥ*, whereas it would apply where it should not, such as in *āptaḥ* and *rāddhaḥ*. [The opponent says: "In that case, the mention of the vowel *a* is a qualifier of the element that undergoes the grammatical operation (*kāryin*). That is, [the rule applies] only if the element undergoing the operation is something that ends in the vowel *ā*. [The proponent replies: Even so, [it would not apply] in the case of *adya aṣṭaḥ*.

When is it excluded? It does not apply here [in *aṣṭa*]. Therefore, it is rightly said: "There is a prohibition regarding lengthening in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffix *yañ*, or rather, there is no [prohibition] because [the cause of the lengthening] is characterized as being external (*bahiraṅga*)."

(P_6,1.207) KA_III.117.14–19 Ro_IV.530: What is the irregular formation (*nipātana*)? It is the irregular formation [of the word] *āśita* when it denotes the agent (*kartṛ*), consisting of the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrghatva*) and the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*). In the form *āśitaḥ*, the suffix *kta* is irregularly formed to denote the agent, and there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel. Thus, one who has eaten is called *āśitaḥ*. Furthermore, the acute accent on the first syllable is irregularly formed. However, the acute accent on the first syllable need not be irregularly formed; it is established by virtue of the governing rule (*adhikāra*). As for the lengthening of the penultimate vowel: [it is established].

It must not be elided; it is used with the prefix *ā*. If this is so, would it not follow that there should be an *avagraha*? No; the authors of the *pada-pāṭha* are not to be followed by the rules of grammar. On the contrary, the rules of grammar must be followed by the authors of the *pada-pāṭha*. The word-form (*pada*) must be established according to the grammatical rules. (P_6.1.208, 215; KA_III.117.22–118.3; Ro_IV.531) Is this an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding what is already established, or regarding what is not yet established? And how is it "regarding what is established," or how is it "regarding what is not yet established"? If [it applies] when there is a technical name (*saṃjñā*)...

Regarding the rule *upamānam*, *niṣṭhā* [ending], and *dvyac anāt*: since this would have been obligatory (*nitya*) by the previous rule, this new sūtra is commenced. It applies where it was previously unestablished, or where it was established elsewhere. In the case of *veṇu* and *rikta*, it was unestablished; for *veṇu* and *rikta*, which were unestablished, there is now an optional (*vibhāṣā*) rule, whereas the previous rule was obligatory. Thus: *veṇur iva veṇuḥ*. *Rikta* is the name of a certain person.

(P_6,1.217) KA_III.118.5–8 Ro_IV.531: What is the purpose of including the term *upottama*? One might simply say, "in *riti*, that which precedes [is long]. In that case, there would also be this further benefit: in the rule *matoḥ pūrvam āt sañjñāyāṃ striyām*, the mention of *pūrva* would not need to be made. If that is so, then the inclusion of *upottama* is for the sake of what follows: [the rule] *caṅi anyatarasyām*.

"Upottamam" (the penultimate vowel) alone [is intended]. Let it not apply here: *mā hi sma dadhat*. Why is this stated? It is not simply stated "except for *vatī*. If only "except for *vatī*" were stated, it would undesirably apply even in *rājavatī*. Now, if it is stated "except for *avatī*," why does it not apply here [in *rājavatī*]? Because it is unestablished (*asiddha*).

There is the elision of *n*. Because that [elision] is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), this is not the word *avatī*. What then? It is the word *anvatī*. Just as, because the elision of *n* is non-existent, it is not the word *avatī*, so too, because the substitution of *v* is also non-existent, it is not the word *avatī*.
[Objection: Its existence might be established by virtue of its dependence [on another rule].

Regarding the rule *coḥ ataddhite* (Pāṇini 6.1.222): it should be stated that the accent of the element *cu* applies when no *taddhita* suffix follows. This is so that [the accent] does not apply here: *dādhīcaḥ*, *mādhūcaḥ*. [Objection: Then that must be stated. [Reply: It need not be stated. Here, the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) will be the sublater. The accent of *cu* would have applied by virtue of its position, but it is superseded by the accent of the suffix. Furthermore, the rule *anudāttau suppitau* (Pāṇini 3.3.4) [which prescribes that suffixes ending in *su* or *pit* are unaccented] serves as an exception to the accent of the suffix.

Thus: by the rule *anudāttau suppitau*, there is the accent called *udāttanivṛttisvara*; for that *udāttanivṛttisvara*, there is the accent called *cusvara*. Just as that *cusvara* subverts the *udāttanivṛttisvara*, it would likewise subvert the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). But in this case, the *udāttanivṛttisvara* does not apply. What is the reason? Because of the prohibition: *na gośvansāvavarṇa*.

This is not a prohibition of the accent resulting from the removal of the acute (*udāttanivṛtti-svara*). Of what, then? Of the accent belonging to the third case and those following. But in cases where the accent of the third case and so on does not exist, such as in *dadhīcaḥ paśya*, [what then? In that case, we do not intend to prohibit the accent characterized by the third case and so on. What then? We prohibit the accent of the case-ending (*vibhakti-svara*) that is obtained by any rule whatsoever.

Regarding the prohibition: if this is a prohibition of the accent on the case-ending (*vibhaktisvara*), then [the accent] would not apply here in *vṛkṣavān* and *plakṣavān*. The mention of *matup* also follows as it was previously introduced. Where was it introduced? In the rule *hrasvanuḍbhyām matup*. If that [mention of *matup*] follows here, then [the accent] would undesirably apply in *vetasvān*. [Therefore,] the mention of *matup*...

And this *ḍmatup* also follows [from the previous rule]. If, however, the mention of *matup* does not include *ḍmatup*, then in the case of *vetasvān*, the substitution of *va* would not apply. In the rule for *vatva*, there is a reference to the general category; here, however, there is a reference to a specific one. If that is so, then in cases where there is no case-ending, such as *dadhīcī*, [the rule would fail]. Furthermore, if this [suffix] were subject to the accent known as *udāttanivṛtti-svara*...

Even if it were understood as a prohibition, it would not be possible [to apply it here]. For in this case too, it would undesirably apply to the word *kumārī*. Furthermore, the accent of the suffix *cu* is indeed taught as being more powerful (*satiśiṣṭa*). How so? It is stated that the accent applies when there is *cu*. This form of it occurs where, after the elision of the vowel *a* and the elision of the *n*, there is a suffix beginning with a vowel other than those of the *sarvanāmasthāna* class. Therefore, it is rightly said: "The substitution of *cu* occurs before a non-taddhita suffix."

(P_6,1.223) KA_III.119.16–120.24 Ro_IV.534–537: An addition must be made regarding the rule for the acute accent on the final member of a compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*) when it ends in a consonant. An addition must be made regarding the rule for the acute accent on the final member of a compound when it ends in a consonant:

*rājadṛṣat*, *brāhmaṇasamit*. Alternatively, when the accentuation of a consonant is to take effect, a consonant is treated as if it were non-existent. Or rather, when the accentuation of a consonant is to take effect...

The metarule (*paribhāṣā*) must be formulated as: "A consonant (*vyañjana*) is as if non-existent. Why are both of these stated? Why not simply say, "When *hal* (consonants) or *svara* (vowels) are to be applied, [the preceding element] is as if non-existent," or "When a *svara* is to be applied, a consonant is as if non-existent"? [It is because] what is twice bound is well-bound. If, when *hal* or *svara* are to be applied, the consonant...

Regarding the statement "as if non-existent": in the case of *dadhi*, since the rule states that a low-pitched (*anudātta*) vowel following a high-pitched (*udātta*) vowel becomes circumflex (*svarita*), the circumflex accent would not be obtained [if the consonant were present]. Therefore, this interpretive maxim (*paribhāṣā*) must be formulated: "In the prescription of accents, a consonant is as if non-existent after a high-pitched vowel. What are the applications of this maxim?

The purposes [of this rule]. The purpose is for the application of rules prescribing that an element ending in *li* is acute on the first syllable or acute on the final syllable. By the rule "that which precedes a suffix marked with *li* is acute," it would apply only in cases such as *bhaurikividham*.
In the case of *bhauliki-vidham*, [the suffix] would not apply to forms such as *cikīrṣakaḥ* and *jihīrṣakaḥ*. According to the rule *ñniti ādir nityam*, it would apply only here:
*āhicumbukāyaniḥ*.

In the case of *āgniveśyaḥ*, *gārgyaḥ*, and *kṛtiḥ*, [the rule] would not apply. According to the principle that "the final syllable of a verbal root (*dhātu*) is udātta," it would apply here in *ūrṇoti*, but it would not apply here in *pacati*. Now, as for what is said: "in the attainment of accent for consonants (*hal-svara-prāptau*), a consonant (*vyañjana*) is as if non-existent."

How indeed could a vowel obtain its accent when it follows a consonant? And one who asserts that must also state [the rule]: "In the prescription of accents, [a vowel] after an acute [vowel is acute]. Likewise, that which is prescribed for what begins with an unaccented vowel or ends with an acute vowel would not apply to what begins with a consonant or ends with a consonant. However, if in the prescription of accents a consonant is treated as non-existent...

Thus it might be said. Now, when it is stated that "in the rule for accents (*svaravidhi*), a consonant is as if non-existent," what is established by that which is prescribed for [words] beginning with an *anudātta* vowel and ending with an *udātta* vowel? Is that which is prescribed for [words] beginning with a consonant and ending with a consonant also established? Certainly it is established. How so? Because the term "rule for accents" (*svaravidhi*) is a compound whose final member is declined in all case-endings (*sarvavibhaktyanta*).
"An operation concerning accent is 'svaravidhi';

an operation of an accent is 'svaravidhi'. This cannot be so, for in this case a fault would arise: in *udaśvitvān ghoṣaḥ* and *vidyutvān balāhakaḥ*, the accent prescribed by the rule *hrasvanuḍbhyām matup* would apply. Let it be so.

"In that case, when a vowel-accent is to be applied, a consonant is treated as if it were non-existent. But has it not been said: "How indeed could a consonant receive a vowel-accent? [The answer is: In the rules "the high-pitched is udātta" and "the low-pitched is anudātta," the mention of the vowel (*aj*) specified by the genitive case has ceased to apply. When that has ceased, [the accent applies] to the consonant (*hal*).

Furthermore, there is the attainment of the *svarita* accent. As for what was said—that it should be stated that "after an acute (*udātta*) vowel, [the following] is subject to the rules for accents"—it need not be stated. This is not a reference to the technical term *anudātta*; rather, it is a reference based on the literal meaning (*anvartha*).

That which has no acute is *anudātta*. Of that, the *svarita* occurs. Furthermore, as for what was said regarding "that which begins with a consonant" (*tad-vyañjanādeḥ*), [it is explained as follows].

[An objection: "It would not apply after a word ending in a consonant. [Response: The activity of the Teacher indicates that this is established—namely, that it applies both after a word beginning with a consonant and after one ending in a consonant—since, having stated "not when the second member begins with an unaccented vowel," he teaches the prohibition "except in the case of pṛthivī, rudra, agni, pūṣan, and manthin. [Objection: "In that case, this *paribhāṣā* (metarule) must be formulated. [Response: It need not be formulated; it is established by the activity of the Teacher.

This indicates that there exists this *paribhāṣā*: "Since he teaches the prohibition of *nau* by means of the term *anāvaḥ*. Why is this stated? It teaches the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* because it has been well-composed as a rule for the suffixation of compound endings (*samāsānta*). The Teacher has composed it well; for when the rule for the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*) would otherwise apply, he [instead] teaches the accent of the *bahuvrīhi*.

He teaches an exception: "This purpose is not necessary; however, [the rule] *nañ-subhyām* is for the sake of restriction. That is to say, *nañ-subhyām* will serve as a restrictive rule: "Only after a *nañ*-compound or a *su*-compound does the final syllable of a *bahuvrīhi* become acute-accented, and not after any other. Even so, how is it known that the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvaratva*) will apply here, and not rather [the accent of the final member]?

Regarding the word *parasya*: because of the rule of Śitīśāna, the rule *nityābahvac* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning that [the suffix] occurs only after a stem ending in *śiti*, and not from any other [stem]. As for what was said—that the restriction applies to [compounds] with *nañ* and *su*—that is a rule concerning censure (*kṣepa*), whereas the [suffix] after *nañ* is not established [in that context]. Since the rule *udarāśveṣuṣu kṣepe* would otherwise apply, this [present rule] is stated thereafter. Furthermore, as for...
It is said: "Because of the subsequent rule *śiti-śāsanāt*," there would be a restriction for the subsequent [word]. This restriction would apply to the subsequent [word]:

*nityā-bahvac* after *śiti*. If this were to override the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*) in favor of the final acute accent of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*), then it would also apply in cases such as *capriyaḥ* or *vāpriyaḥ*, since the condition for the final acute accent exists in *cavāpriye*. Thus, the final acute accent is established for *cavāpriye*.

Why? Because of possibility. For indeed, sublation occurs only when there is no possibility [of both being true]; yet here there is the possibility that both might exist. Furthermore, sublation occurs even when there is a possibility. For example: "Let curd be given to the Brahmins; let buttermilk be given to Kauṇḍinya. Even though there is the possibility of giving curd, the giving of buttermilk sets aside the giving of curd.

It occurs thus: here too, even though the possibility exists, the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*) will supersede the natural accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*). If that is so, then [the rule] follows from the present injunction: "In a *bahuvrīhi*, the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). And what is the subject under discussion? It is "acute" (*udātta*), which continues to apply. Even so, in the case of *kāryapriyaḥ*,...

In the case of *hāryapriyaḥ*, [the rule] does not apply here. Even in a circumflex (*svarita*) vowel, there is an acute (*udātta*) element. Alternatively, the mention of *svarita* also follows as a carried-over reference from the context. Where was it previously mentioned? In the rule *tit svaritam*. It is established for a *bahuvrīhi* compound even without [the specific mention of] *ṛte*.

The mention of the *bahuvrīhi* is already established. Why does it not apply to the *tatpuruṣa*? It will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) for the *tatpuruṣa*, stating: "In a *tatpuruṣa*, [the feminine suffix ṅīṣ applies] after words meaning 'equal,' after those ending in the third or seventh case, after a word denoting a standard of comparison, after an indeclinable, and after those ending in the second case or a *kṛtya* suffix. Then why does it not apply to the *dvigu*? It will serve as a restrictive rule for the *dvigu*, stating: "In a *dvigu* ending in a *gota* vowel, [the feminine suffix ṅīṣ applies]. Then it would apply to the *dvandva*. [It applies] to a *dvandva* consisting of many *rājanya* [clans].

The rule *andhakavṛṣṇiṣu* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). [Objection: In that case, it would apply even in the case of an *avyayībhāva* compound. [Response: The rule *paripratyupāpāḥ varjyamānāhorātrāvayaveṣu* will serve as a restrictive rule. [Objection: Even so, how is it determined that this restriction applies only to these [words] in the case of *tatpuruṣa* compounds and the like, and not that the restriction applies to these [words] alone?

"Only in *tatpuruṣa* compounds and so forth"—this restriction is made according to what is desired. Indeed, the restriction will be according to what is intended. In that case, however, it would follow that these [words] are synonyms for *bahuvrīhi*. But a synonymy between *dvipād-diṣṭi* and *vitasti* is not possible. This is because of the rule: "After *dvi* and *tri*, when followed by *pād*, *dan*, or *mūrdhan* in a *bahuvrīhi*, and after them when followed by *diṣṭi* or *vitasti*."

Since the alternative [form] is already established, the Teacher teaches this alternative in order to indicate that it is not merely an optional variant. However, this is an indicator regarding the acute accent (*udātta*). This would be an indicator specifically for the acute accent. It would apply by merging with the circumflex (*svarita*). Thus, a merging with the circumflex would result. For even within the circumflex, there is an acute element. He teaches the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* compound as a rule for the final member of a compound (*samāsāntavidhi*), as in the word *sukṛt*.

The restriction [of the rule] after *nañ* and *su* is for the sake of limitation, because of the teaching regarding the suffix *śit* for what follows. The application of *nañ* in the sense of censure (*kṣepa*) is not established; there would be a restriction on what follows. Because of the possibility [of the term] "unpleasant" (*apriya*) within the compound, it [the restriction] applies to the prescribed rule (*vidhi*) from the context. In a *bahuvrīhi*, it is established except for the case of *ṛta*. And the determination is according to what is desired. Since two feet (*dvipād*) and a span (*vitasti*) are taught, a synonym (*paryāya*) is not possible.
This, however, is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding the acute accent (*udātta*): "One should enter [the compound] with the circumflex accent (*svarita*)" (P.

6.2.2). When there is the rule for the original accent of the case-ending (*vibhakti-prakṛti-svara*) in a *tatpuruṣa*, a prohibition must be stated regarding the *karmadhāraya*. That is to say, when there is the rule for the original accent of the case-ending in a *tatpuruṣa*, a prohibition must be stated regarding the *karmadhāraya*.

*paramam kārakam*, *paramakārakam*, *paramena kārakeṇa*, *paramakārakeṇa*, *parame kārake*, *paramakārake*. This is established because, between that which is taught by a general rule (*lakṣaṇa*) and that which is taught by a specific rule (*pratipadokta*), only that which is taught by a specific rule is accepted. How is this established? By the principle: "between that which is taught by a general rule and that which is taught by a specific rule, only that which is taught by a specific rule [is taken]."

The term *pratipada* refers to a compound consisting of a second, third, or seventh case; this [term] is also mentioned as a defining characteristic. Furthermore, an enumeration must be made regarding indeclinables (*avyaya*). [The rule] "in the case of indeclinables" should be stated as: "in the case of indeclinables, *nañ*, *ku*, and particles. Regarding *nañ*: *abrāhmaṇaḥ*.
*Avṛṣalaḥ*: the negative particle *nañ*. *Kubrāhmaṇaḥ*, *kuvṛṣalaḥ*: the particle *ku*. *Niṣkauśāmbiḥ*, *nirvārāṇasiḥ*: the particle *niḥ*. Let it not be where? *Snātvākālakaḥ*.

Regarding *pītvāsthirakaḥ*: there is an option for the prohibition in the case of the suffix *ktvā*. It should be stated that there is an option for the prohibition in the case of *ktvā*; [examples would be] *snātvākālakaḥ* and *pītvāsthirakaḥ*. Both [the rule and the option] need not be stated. This is established by means of a conventional irregularity (*nipātana*). This is established by means of a conventional irregularity. What is the irregularity? An irregularity must necessarily be applied here for the sake of forming a compound and for the sake of preventing the substitution of *lyap*.
By that very effort, the accent will be established. (P.
6.2.11) The mention of *sadṛśa* (resembling) is redundant because of the rule concerning the third-case compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*).
The mention of *sadṛśa* is purposeless. For what reason? Because of the rule concerning the third-case compound. A third-case compound is formed with the word *sadṛśa*.

It is said: in that case, it is already established by the rule that "in a compound where the third case is the prior member, it retains its original accent" (*prakṛtisvara*). If so, this [rule] must be stated for the sake of the genitive case, as in *pitṛsadṛśaḥ* ("resembling the father"). If it is argued that it is for the sake of the genitive, then the mention of the third-case compound would be purposeless.
If it is for the sake of the genitive, the statement regarding the third-case compound would be redundant. Why? Because here, by us...

The three-word derivation (*traisabdyam*) is what must be established: *pitṛsādṛśaḥ*, *pituḥ sādṛśaḥ*, and *pitḥsadṛśaḥ*. In that case, since two words have the same meaning, the analysis (*vigraha*) will be performed with one and the compound (*samāsa*) formed with the other, according to the maxim of the sheep and the ram (*aviravikanyāya*). For example, having analyzed it as "the meat of a sheep" (*aveḥ māṃsam*), the suffix arises from the word *avika*.

Regarding the word *āvikam*: if one analyzes it as *pituh sadṛśaḥ*, it will result in *pitṛsadṛśaḥ*; or if one analyzes it as *pitrā sadṛśaḥ*, it remains simply a sentence. A compound with the third case (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*) must necessarily be stated for cases where the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī-artha*) does not exist, such as *bhojanasadṛśaḥ*.

[The opponent says: "It is similar to the study [of the Veda]. [The proponent replies: If there is indeed a basis for that, then only that should be stated; this should not be stated. This too must necessarily be stated for the sake of that where the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī) is heard:
"similar to a female slave" (dāsyāḥ-sadṛśaḥ), "similar to a low-caste woman" (vṛṣalyāḥ-sadṛśaḥ).

(P_6.2.29) KA_III.124.14–19 Ro_IV.545: An addition must be made regarding the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) for stems ending in *ik* vowels when *yaṇ*-substitution and *guṇa*-strengthening have occurred. An addition must be made regarding the preservation of the original accent for stems ending in *ik* vowels when *yaṇ*-substitution and *guṇa*-strengthening have occurred:

*pañcāratnyaḥ*, *daśāratnyaḥ*. Once *yaṇ*-substitution and *guṇa*-strengthening have taken place, this accent—prescribed by the rule "in a *dvigu* compound ending in an *ik* vowel"—does not apply. It does not.
Or rather, it need not be stated. What is the reason? Because it is a rule characterized by being external (*bahiraṅga*).

The *yaṇ*-substitution and the *guṇa*-strengthening are external; the accent (*svara*) is internal. That which is external is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal. (P.
6.2.33) [In the case of compounds] after *pari*, *prati*, *upa*, and *āpa*, when followed by *vana*, [the accent is determined] by way of exception (*vipratiṣedha*).

Regarding the rule *paripratyupāpebhyo vanam samāse*, this occurs by way of a prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of the rule *paripratyupāpā varjyamānāhorātrāvayaveṣu* is, for example, *paritrigartam* and *parisauvīram*. The scope of the rule *vanam samāse* is, for example, *pravaṇe yaṣṭavyam*. In the present case, both rules would apply.

"parivana" and "apavana"—in a compound, this [designation] occurs by way of a prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*). Or rather, there is no need for a prohibition; the statement that "vana" has an udātta accent at the end is for the purpose of setting aside its exception. Or rather, there is no purpose for the prohibition. Why? Because the statement that "vana" has an udātta accent at the end is for the purpose of setting aside its exception. In this case, the udātta accent at the end is already established by the general rule (*utsarga*) itself. As for its being stated again...

This is the purpose: to set aside those other exceptions that would otherwise apply. Just as it sets aside the accent of the indeclinable (*avyayasvara*) which is an exception to that [rule], so too will this [present rule] set aside that. (P_6.2.36) Since even when there are multiple preceding members in a compound with *ācārya* as a subordinate element, they all constitute the *pūrvapada*.

There is doubt. When there is a compound with multiple members where the teacher's name is subordinate (*upasarjana*), doubt arises because several words function as prior members (*pūrvapada*). For example: *āpiśalapāṇinīyavyāḍīyagautamīyāḥ*.

With the exception of one word, all are prior members. In that case, it is not known which prior member should have its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). This is established through common worldly understanding. For instance, in the world:

Just as in the case of "Bring these Brahmins one by one from the beginning," where the very first one is brought, so too here, that which is the first member (*pūrvapada*) will have its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).

(Pāṇini 6.2.38) For what purpose is the rule stated that when the word *pravṛddha* is the second member (*uttarapada*), the first member retains its original accent? Is it not already established by the rule "In a *karmadhāraya*, [the first member retains its accent] except for a past passive participle" (Pāṇini 6.2.46)? It is not established.

What is the reason? [The rule] applies only to compounds such as *śreṇi* and so forth; let it not apply here in the case of *mahāniraṣṭo dakṣiṇā dīyate*. (Pāṇini 6.2.42) It should be stated that [the suffix -aṇ is applied] after *kuru* and *vṛji* when *gārhapata* follows: *kurugārhapatam*, *vṛjigārhapatam*.

[The rule applies to] *vṛjigārhapatam*. It should be stated that [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *kurugārhapatari*, *kataruru*, *vasūtajaratī*, *aślīla*, *dṛḍharūpa*, *apāra*, *ivaḍava*, *aśvatailika*, *drūpaṇyaka*, *mabala*, and those beginning with *dāsībhāra*. This is so that it may also apply here:
*devahūtiḥ*, *devanītiḥ*.

*Vasunīti*, *oṣadhi*, and *candramas*. If that is so, then it must be stated. It need not be stated. A split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: *kurugārhapata-rikta-ruru-vasūta-jarati-aślīla-dṛḍharūpa-apāra-ivaḍavā-tailika-drū-paṇyaka-mabalaḥ*.

Thus [ends the previous rule]. Then there is the rule *dāsībhārāṇāṃ ca*. There, because of the mention of the plural number, it should be understood as "of *dāsībhāra* and so forth. Regarding *paṇyakambalaḥ sañjñāyām*: it should be stated that "*paṇyakambalaḥ*" [is formed] when it is a name (*sañjñā*). A blanket which is to be sold is precisely what is called *paṇyakambala*. Another says:
It should be *paṇyakambalaḥ* (a blanket for sale), as it ought to be. Where should it not be? [In cases such as] *paṇyagavaḥ* (an ox for sale) and *paṇyahastī* (an elephant for sale).
(Pāṇini 6.2.47) Why is the term *ahīne* (not having passed over) used? [To exclude cases like] *kāntārātītaḥ* (one who has passed through a wilderness).

"Beyond a *yojana*. It should be stated: "The second case ending is used after a word denoting non-deficiency (*ahīna*) when no prefix (*anupasarga*) precedes it. This is so that [the rule] does not apply here: *sukhaprāptaḥ*, *duḥkhaprāptaḥ*. Then, must that be stated? Even if this were stated, or even if, at this point, the mention of "non-deficiency" (*ahīna*) is not made, then in cases such as *kāntārātītaḥ* and *yojanātītaḥ*, the form would be established by the very condition "when no prefix precedes it" (*anupasarge*).

(P_6,2.49) KA_III.126.22–128.14 Ro_IV.550–555. For what purpose is the term *anantara* ("immediately preceding") used? It is so that [the rule] does not apply here: *abhyuddhṛtam*, *upasamāhṛtam*. The mention of *anantara* with respect to a *gati* is redundant, because it has already been stated that a *gati* is unaccented (*anudātta*) when followed by another *gati*. The mention of *anantara* with respect to a *gati* is redundant. What is the reason? Because it has been stated that a *gati* is unaccented when followed by another *gati*. When a *gati* follows...

The fact that the prefix *gati* is unaccented is stated; that will serve as an exception. In that case, for whatever [word] does not have its original accent (*aprakṛtisvara*), there arises the possibility of it being accented on the final syllable. Thus, for whatever *gati* does not have its original accent, the rule "the end is accented in the case of suffixes *thā*, *tha*, *ghañ*, *kta*, *ac*, *ap*, *itra*, and *ka*" would result in final acute accent. However, because of the statement regarding the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*), it is not accented on the final syllable.

Indeed, by the force of the statement regarding the *prakṛtisvara* (original accent), the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) will not occur. For if it were [already] so, what would be the purpose of the statement regarding the *prakṛtisvara* at this point? If one asks, "What is the purpose of the statement regarding the *prakṛtisvara*?", it is for the sake of a single movement (*ekagati*). If one asks, "What is the purpose of the statement regarding the *prakṛtisvara*?", it is for the sake of a single movement; that is, it would be for the purpose of those cases where there is a single movement. [As in the example: *prakṛtam*.
[Objection: An inclusion of the word *ananta* (immediate) must therefore be made here so that [the rule] may apply in this case.

[Reply: Even if the inclusion of the word *ananta* is made, it is not established in this case. What is the reason? It is stated that "a *gati* which is immediate becomes the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*). And that which is the immediate *gati* here is not the preceding member.
And that which has a preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is not "immediately following" (*anantara*). In that case, this must be stated for the sake of [a compound] that does not have a preceding member:

so that even for a [compound] without a preceding member, the original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*) of the verb (*gati*) may occur. If it is argued that this is for the sake of [a compound] without a preceding member, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the *kāraka* [compounds].
If it is argued that this is for the sake of [a compound] without a preceding member, there is an over-extension regarding the *kāraka*, as in *āgataḥ*.

"He has come from afar" (*dūrād āgataḥ*). Just as [the rule] applies when the first member is a motion (*gati*), so too would it apply when the first member is a kāraka (participant in an action). But this is already established, because there is no possibility of the final syllable of a *gati* being accented. How so? Since there is no possibility of the final syllable of a *gati* being accented, the rule "of *thā*, *tha*, *ghañ*, *ktā*, *ac*, *ap*, *itra*, and *ka*" should not apply to a *gati*.

What is accomplished [by this]? This [rule] serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to the *kṛt-svara*. In that regard, the scope (*avakāśa*) of the rule "the preceding member retains its original accent when it is a *gati*" is, for example, *prakṛtam* and *prahṛtam*. The scope of the rule "the preceding member retains its original accent before suffixes ending in *tha*, *atha*, *ghañ*, *kta*, *ac*, *ap*, *tra*, and *ka*" is, for example, *dūrādgataḥ*.

When [the word] *dūrāt* has arrived, both [suffixes] apply here: *āgataḥ* and *dūrādāgataḥ*. By way of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the rule *antaḥ thāthaghañktājabitrakāṇām* applies. That [rule] must necessarily be applied to the verb *gam-* for the sake of forms such as *bhedaḥ* and *prabhedaḥ*. If that is so, then there is a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*).

The suffix *kta* will be applied according to the rule *antaḥ thāthaghañktājabitrakāṇām*. Consequently, the word ending in *kta* becomes an *uttarapada* (subsequent member) that is oxytone (accented on the final syllable). In this context, the mention of "an agent as a subordinate word" (*kārakopapada*) is understood to carry over, while the mention of "a motion-word" (*gatigrahaṇa*) has ceased to apply.
Alternatively, a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made later: first, there is this: "After a word denoting a comparison (*sūpamāna*), the suffix *kta* [is applied]."

Regarding the rule *sañjñāyām anācitādīnām*, and [the rule] *pravṛddhādīnām ca*: from that point I shall state *kārakāt*. After a word denoting a *kāraka* (agent, object, etc.), the final member ending in a *kta*-suffix is udātta-accented on its last syllable. From that point, [the rule] *dattaśrutayoḥ eva āśiṣi kārakāt* applies. And having done so, there is no purpose in the inclusion of the term *ananta*.

How is it "extracted" (*abhyuddhṛta*)? It qualifies the action of extracting; by means of *ud*, it qualifies *abhi*. In that regard, both the rule *gatiḥ anantaraḥ* ("a *gati* [term] [is compounded] with what follows immediately") and *gatiḥ gatau* ("a *gati* [term] [is compounded] with another *gati* term") would apply. The scope of *gatiḥ anantaraḥ* is, for example, *prakṛtam* and *prahṛtam*. The scope of *gatiḥ gatau* is, for example, *abhyud harati*.
He places [the fuel] together. Here one obtains both:

that which has been lifted up (*abhyuddhṛta*) and that which has been brought together (*upasamāhṛta*). This occurs by means of the rule "a motion [is compounded] with a motion" (*gatiḥ gatau*), despite the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). If this is so, then since it is already established—

The fact that the Teacher employs the term "immediately preceding" (anantara) indicates this *paribhāṣā*: "In the case of the mention of a *kṛt* [suffix], the rule applies even to that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*. What is the purpose of this indication? [The examples are: *avataptenakulasthitam te* ("this of yours is like a mongoose standing in heated [milk]") and *udakeviśīrṇam te* ("this of yours is scattered in water"). By means of this indication, the compound with the *gati*-preceded word *nakula* is established.

(P_6,2.50) KA_III.128.16–129.2 Ro_IV.555–556: What is the purpose of including the term *kṛt*? It is so that the mention of the letter *t* may be understood as a qualifier of the *kṛt* [suffix], namely: "when a *kṛt* suffix beginning with *t* and marked with *n* follows. Now, if the mention of *kṛt* were not made, of what would the mention of the letter *t* be a qualifier? It would be a qualifier of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). What fault would there be in that case? In this very instance: [text continues]

There might be [the forms] *prataritā* and *prataritum*, but here there would not be *prakartā* and *prakartum*. The mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] in the rule regarding a following *nit* suffix beginning with *ta* is purposeless. The mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] in the rule regarding a following *nit* suffix beginning with *ta* is useless. Even if the mention of *kṛt* were made, an undesirable interpretation could be understood:

namely, that it applies when a *kṛt* suffix beginning with *ta* follows a *nit* [augment]. And if it were not made, the desired interpretation would be obtained: namely, when a *nit* suffix beginning with *ta* ends [the word].

Regarding the rule *uttarapade*: since even when it is formulated an undesirable result is understood, whereas when it is not formulated the desired result is understood, we shall understand that it is indeed the non-formulation that is intended. Alternatively, the mention of *kṛt* [in the rule] is for the sake of those [roots] beginning with *ta* and for the sake of the augment *iṭ*. If that is so, then the mention of *kṛt* must be made for the sake of those beginning with *ta* and for the sake of *iṭ*; [the rule] should be understood as "that which begins with *ta* in the context of a *kṛt* suffix."

What is the purpose? It is for the sake of *iṭ*. Thus, it becomes established even in cases beginning with *iṭ*: *pralavitā*, *pralavitum*. Regarding the rule for the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) when the stem does not end in a long vowel (*aniganta*): there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the original accent applying after the substitution of *yaṇ*. When the stem does not end in a long vowel, the application of the original accent would occur following the substitution of *yaṇ*. For example: *pratyaṅ*, *pratyañcau*.

[The suffixes] are *pratyañcaḥ*. Now, for what purpose would the mention of "not having a penultimate vowel" (*aniganta*) be? If it is asked, "For what purpose is the mention of 'not having a penultimate vowel'?", [the answer is: it is for the sake of cases where there is no substitution of *yaṇ*. This would be for the sake of cases where there is no substitution of *yaṇ*. When is there no substitution of *yaṇ*? When there is the *Śākala* [variant]. Or rather, it has already been stated. What has been stated? That the *Śākala* [variant] does not occur in a compound. Where? In the following rule: *na samāse* (in a compound, [the Śākala variant does not apply]).
In that case, the letter *a* of the root *añc* is elided:
*pratīcaḥ*, *pratīcā*. There, the accent of the suffix *cu* will be the sublater [of the original accent]. This very result is desired. For he will state this:
"The suffix *cu* is not final when *añc* is followed by the suffix *vap*. As for the fact that he teaches the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*) for *ny-anc* and *ud-anc*, this is [the reason].

For an undertaking [of a rule] is indeed for the purpose of that which has not already been prescribed. This [present rule] would also be for the very same purpose of what has not yet been prescribed.

When is the *yaṇ* substitution not applied? And when is the *yaṇ* substitution not applied? When there is the *Śākala* [dissimilation]. Or rather, it has already been stated. What has been stated? That the *Śākala* [dissimilation] does not occur in a compound (*samāsa*). Well then, where the vowel *a* of the root *añc* is elided—as in *adhīcaḥ* and *adhīcā*—there the accent of the suffix *cu* [would apply].

It will be an obstructor [to the rule]. This very point is intended. He will say this: "In the case of *coḥ* (the suffix *cu*), when it is not ending in *i*, and when the suffix *vap* follows *añcati*.

If that is so, then why does he teach the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) for *ni-* alone? For this [teaching] is an undertaking for the sake of what is indicated by the *yaṇ*-substitution. This too would be for the sake of what is indicated by the *ayaṇ*-substitution. How so? Because the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratva*) is applied before the *yaṇ*-substitution has been made.

The accentuation "the *yaṇ*-substitute for an *udātta* or *svarita* vowel is optionally *svarita* when followed by an *anudātta*" is thus established. *Nyaṅ*. Therefore, it is rightly said: "If the original form (*prakṛti*) were to retain its accent when not ending in a suffix, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the original accent would apply even when the *yaṇ*-substitution occurs.
(P. 6.2.52.2) KA_III.129.22–131.14 Ro_IV.557–561: [This applies] to a word beginning with *cu-* which does not end in a suffix, when the suffix *añc* with the augment *v* follows.

By the rule *cu-svarāt an-igantaḥ añcato vapratyaye*, this accentuation takes effect by way of *vipratiṣedha* (conflict). The scope of the *cu-svara* is, for example, *dadhīcaḥ paśya*, *dadhīcā*, *dadhīce*. The scope of the rule *an-igantaḥ añcato vapratyaye* is, for example, *parāṅ*, *parāñcau*, *parāñcaḥ*. In the case of *avācā*, both [rules] would apply.

The form *avāce* occurs by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) with the rule for *avakāśa*. Or rather, it is not so, because there is a prohibition against the accent of the suffix *cu* when the preceding member is to retain its original accent; otherwise, it would be a universal exception (*sarvāpavāda*). Nor is this established even by way of conflict. How, then, is it established? By the prohibition of the accent of the suffix *cu* when the preceding member is to retain its original accent. [Thus,] the accent of *cu* [prevails].

The rule regarding the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member must be negated. Otherwise, the *cu*-accent would be a universal exception (*sarvāpavāda*). For if this negation were not made, this *cu*-accent would be a universal exception. How so? It would be an exception to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), [as prescribed] by the rule "the *sup* and *pit* [suffixes] are unaccented" (*anudāttau suppitau*). To that rule "the *sup* and *pit* [suffixes] are unaccented," there applies the accent of the disappearance of the acute (*udāttanivṛttisvara*). To that accent of the disappearance of the acute...

The *kṛtsvara* (the accent of a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix). Just as it subverts the *udāttanivṛttisvara*, so too would it subvert the *anigantasvara* (the accent of a word not ending in a long vowel). If there is equality in terms of numerical position, this [kṛtsvara] is also fourth. The *avyayasvara* (the accent of an indeclinable) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the final-accentuation of a compound. The *kṛtsvara* is an exception to the *avyayasvara*. This [kṛtsvara] is an exception to the *kṛtsvara*. Thus, between these two [rules], both being fourth in their respective series...

The contradiction is indeed justified. In that case, the accent of the *cu* suffix is what remains by virtue of being subsequently prescribed (*satiśiṣṭa*). How so? It is stated that the term *cu* applies where this specific form occurs—namely, when the initial vowel of the following member is not a case-ending (*asarvanāmasthāna*), and after the elision of the *a* and the *n* has taken place. Therefore, it is rightly said: "Or rather, [there is no fault], because the prohibition of the accent of *cu* applies only when the preceding member is to retain its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*); otherwise..."

For [the rule] "hi" is a universal exception (*sarvāpavāda*). The accent of a *kṛt*-suffix (*kṛtsvara*) takes precedence over the accent of a case-ending (*vibhaktisvara*) and the accent of a prefix (*īṣatsvara*) by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of the accent of a case-ending is, for example, *akṣaśauṇḍaḥ* and *strīśauṇḍaḥ*. The scope of the accent of a *kṛt*-suffix is...

Regarding *idhma-pravraścana*: here both [rules] apply—namely, the accent on the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) and the accent on the whole word (*kṛtsvara*). By the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the accent on the whole word prevails. The scope for the accent on the first member (*īṣatsvara*) is, for example, *īṣat-kaḍāraḥ* and *īṣat-piṅgalaḥ*. The scope for the accent on the whole word is the same as that previously mentioned. Here, both [rules] apply.

There is a slight distinction. The accent of *kṛt*-suffixes prevails by way of opposition. The accent of *hari* (the *hāri*-accent) prevails over the accent of *cit* (the *cit*-accent) by way of opposition. The scope for the *cit*-accent is, for example, *calanaḥ* and *copanaḥ*. The scope for the *hāri*-accent is, for example, [the following].
*yājñikāśvaḥ* (a horse for a sacrificer),
*vaiyākaraṇahasī* (a wife of a grammarian). Here, both [suffixes] would apply [simultaneously], as in *pitṛgavaḥ*.

*Mātṛgavaḥ*: *Hārisvara* (the accent on the first syllable of the second member) prevails by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). And from *kṛtsvara* (the accent on the first syllable of a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix): *Hārisvara* also prevails over *kṛtsvara* by way of conflict. The scope of *kṛtsvara* is, for example, *idhmapravraścanaḥ*. The scope of *hārisvara* is the same. Here, both would apply: *akṣahṛtaḥ*.

In the case of *vāḍavahṛtaḥ*, it becomes *hārisvara* by way of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). Or rather, the prohibition of "taking away" (*haraṇapratiṣedha*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that [the rule] does not sublate the accent of the whole (*kṛtsvara*). Or rather, there is no need for a conflict. What is the reason? The prohibition of "taking away" is an indicator that [the rule] does not sublate the accent of the whole. In that he teaches the prohibition "in the case of non-taking" (*aharaṇe*), that indicates...

"The teacher [states] that the accent of *anaḥ* when expressing the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) or an object (*karman*) does not subvert the accent of *kṛt*-suffixes. This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*). Since the accent of *anaḥ* expressing an abstract action or an object would [otherwise] apply by default, this is stated [as an exception]. If this is so, it is an even better indicator: the rule "the accent of *anaḥ* expressing an abstract action or an object" is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accent of *kṛt*-suffixes. Indeed, an exception subverts [a general rule]; how much more so [this specific case]? And the accent of the compound (*yuktasvara*) [also applies].

The accent of the *kṛt*-suffix prevails by way of prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope for the accent of the compound (*yuktasvara*) is, for example, *govallavaḥ* and *aśvavallavaḥ*. The scope for the accent of the *kṛt*-suffix is the same [in these cases]. Here, however, both would apply simultaneously.
*gosaṅkhyaḥ*, *paśusaṅkhyaḥ*,
*aśvasaṅkhyaḥ*. The accent of the compound member (*yuktasvara*) prevails by way of exception.

(P_6,2.80) KA_III.131.16-25 Ro_IV.561-562: For what purpose is the term *upamāna* [“standard of comparison”] included? If it were stated merely as “only when the word-meaning is the base form (*śabdārthaprakṛti*)”, this restriction would be understood because of the over-extension (*atiprasakta*) caused by the preceding rule. What would be the fault in that? In this case, [the suffix] would not apply: *puṣphārī*, *phalahārī*. However, when the mention of *upamāna* is made, [the fault does not arise].

There is a fault. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "the word and its meaning" (*śabdārtha*)? If it were stated merely as "the comparison [is used] only in the case of the base form (*prakṛti*)," then this would also undesirably apply here: *vṛkavañcī*, *vṛkaprekṣī*. However, when the mention of "the word and its meaning" is made, there is no fault. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "the base form"? [It is to exclude that which is] always the very nature of the word and its meaning.

In that case, it should apply where it ought to, but not here: *kokilābhivyāhārī*. Now, what is the purpose of the particle *eva*? It is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). But this is not necessary; since a rule is being commenced when [the desired form] is already established, it will serve as a restriction even without the particle *eva*. Then, is it for the sake of emphasizing what is intended (*iṣṭataḥ avadhāraṇārtha*)? So that it may be understood thus: [only in the intended cases].
"Upamāna [is used] only when it is the base form of the word's meaning. Let it not be understood thus:

"Upamāna alone [is used] when it is the base form of the word's meaning. For it is intended that both *upamāna* and *anupamāna* are udātta on the first syllable when they are the base forms of the word's meaning:
as in *sādhvadhyāyī* and *vilambādhyāyī*.

(P_6,2.92-93) KA_III.132.13–21 Ro_IV.562–563: What is the purpose of including the term *sarva*? [The suffix] *tarap* is obtained. A compound with a word ending in *guṇa* [expressing degree] occurs, and there is the elision (*lopa*) of *tarap*. *atikūlam*.

From *cela*, *rājya*, and so forth, the accent of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) prevails by way of conflict over the accent of *cela*, *rājya*, and so forth. [This applies] to the accent of *cela*, *rājya*, and so forth.

[Objection: It would then be a bad kingdom. [Response: In that case, a prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) must be stated. [Reply: It need not be stated. The word *para* expresses what is desired; in a conflict, that which is desired is the one that takes effect. (P.

6.2.136) Regarding the acute accent on *kuṇḍa* and so forth, there must be a mention of the entire complex. Regarding the acute accent on *kuṇḍa* and so forth, a mention of the entire complex must be made: it should be stated that "if the word *kuṇḍa* denotes a collection of forests."

Let it not be so here: *mṛtkuṇḍam* (a clay pot). Why [is the rule] stated as "after a prefix (*gati*), a kāraka, or a subordinate word (*upapada*)"? Let it not apply here: *paramam kārakam*, *paramakārakam*. Even when the rule "after a prefix, a kāraka, or an upapada" is stated, it would still apply there, for this is indeed a *kāraka*. Well then, consider this: *devadattasya kārakam* (the agent of Devadatta).

"Devadatta-kāraka. And this is also an example of "parama-kāraka," meaning "the supreme agent. This is not [itself] an agent; it is a qualifier of the agent. Just as one might say "an excellent agent" or "a beautiful agent," so too is this "parama-kāraka. Now, for what purpose is the mention of the *kṛt* suffix?

Let it not be the case here that [the rule applies] to *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* and *nivārāṇasiḥ*. Therefore, he recites the following answer: "If there is original accentuation (*prakṛtisvaratva*) for words beginning with 'gati', the mention of *kṛt*-affixes is purposeless, because there is no other [word] as the second member (*uttarapada*). If there is original accentuation for words beginning with 'gati', the mention of *kṛt*-affixes is useless.

What is the reason? Because there is no other subsequent member (*uttarapada*). For there is no other subsequent member following *gati* and the rest than what is formed by a *kṛt* suffix. What is the reason? Because two types of suffixes are prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*): *tiṅ* and *kṛt*.
Among these, a compound occurs with a *kṛt*-formed word, but not with a *tiṅ*-formed word. Therefore, without the mention of *kṛt*, [the rule would not apply].

It will indeed be accomplished. But was it not just now cited as *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* and *nirvārāṇasiḥ*? [The answer is: The designations "preverb" (*gati*) and "prefix" (*upasarga*) apply to that toward which [the particle] is connected with an action, and there is no connection of *nis* with the word *kauśāmbī* with respect to an action. Alternatively, since it is a preverb with respect to the verbal base (*prakṛti*) of the *kṛt*-derivative, the mention of *kṛt* is for the sake of a further purpose.

If that is so, then since a *kṛt*-prakṛti (verbal root) is already included under the category of "motion" (*gati*), the mention of *kṛt* should be made for the sake of a specific purpose. A *kṛt*-prakṛti is a verbal root (*dhātu*).

And with respect to a verbal root, there is a connection with action. In that case, by the rule "that which is connected with an action [is called a *gati*] with respect to that [root]," it would apply only here: *praṇīḥ*, *unnīḥ*. It would not apply here: *praṇāyakaḥ*.

[The opponent says: "There is no need for this [specification] 'unnāyakaḥ'. Nor is it understood from the rule *yatkriyāyuktāḥ* that the designations *gati* and *upasarga* apply toward that person whose action they are connected with. How then? It is understood that the designations *gati* and *upasarga* apply toward that action which they are connected with."

Furthermore, there is no single word whatsoever that could be the denoter of that meaning. Since there is no single word that denotes that meaning, it will belong to the *kṛt* affix along with its base. But is it not the case that the word *praṇīḥ* is the denoter of that very same meaning? Indeed, even this [word] denotes [the meaning] as qualified by the agent. Then what about this [word *praṇayanam*]? It belongs to that [meaning].

Thus, [the suffix] expresses the meaning of "origination" (*prabhavana*). Therefore, the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] must be made. If the mention of *kṛt* is made, then the accent does not apply to forms ending in *ām*, such as *prapacatitarām* and *prajalpatitarām*. However, if the mention of *kṛt* is not made, then the verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning; in the case of its intensification, there is the suffix *tarap*.

The suffix *ām* is introduced after a word ending in *tarap* in the sense of its own referent (*svārthe*). In that case, the phrase "those which are connected with an action" (*yatkriyāyuktāḥ*) indeed applies to the aggregate (*saṅghāta*), as there is a connection with the action toward that aggregate. Furthermore, there is no single word whatsoever that could be the designator of that specific meaning.
Since there is no single word that is the designator of that meaning, it will apply to the additional element (*adhika*). But is it not the case that...?

The word *prabhavana* is indeed expressive of that same meaning. This [suffix] also [expresses] that which is qualified by a substance (*dravya*). How is it that a state (*bhāva*) expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix becomes like a substance and also like an action (*kriyā*)?

[The rule applies] to the final member of the compound. Whence does this doubt arise? Both [factors] are under discussion; therein, either one can be specified. And what is the distinction here? It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "before *kap*" (*kapi pūrvam*), specifically by the rule "before a short vowel at the end, the accent falls on the syllable preceding the last" (*hrasvānte 'ntyāt pūrvam*). In that regard, concerning the case where a short vowel is at the end...

Since there is no preceding vowel that is to become acute (udātta) immediately before the final syllable, by the general rule, the word would naturally acquire an acute accent on its final syllable. Or rather, this is not a fault; for the mention of "the preceding" (*pūrvavat*) in the rule regarding the suffix *kap* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the final syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) does not receive the acute accent. Why? Because when the Teacher says "the preceding [vowel] in *kap*," he thereby indicates that the acute accent does not fall on the end of the subsequent member.

"It becomes acute (udātta). And by virtue of the context, this refers to the acute accent on the final syllable of a compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*). The term "compound" (*samāsa*), which was introduced in the current topic, continues to apply here. Where was it introduced? In the rule *cau samāsasya* ("in a compound ending in *ca*, the final syllable is acute"). But was it not said that if the final syllable of a compound is to be acute, then an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the suffix *kap*? This is not a fault, because the term "final member of a compound" (*uttarapada*) was also introduced in the current topic.
It follows [from the previous rule]. Where was it introduced? In the rule stating "the beginning of the second member [is acute]. There, the connection shall be made as follows:

"In a compound formed with *nañ* or *su*, the final syllable is acute. And: "After *idam*, *etad*, and *tad*, when used in the sense of the first ordinal number in counting actions, the second member [is acute]."

(P_6,2.148) KA_III.137.6-10 Ro_IV.573: A prohibition must be stated regarding the suffixes *datta* and *śruta* after a *kāraka* when not expressing a blessing (*anāśis*). "Let the final acute accent (antodāttatva) be applied [before] the compound-final suffix (samāsānta). What should be done here? The final acute accent [takes effect] because it is subsequent (paratva).
The compound-final suffix is obligatory (nitya); it applies both when the final acute accent has been applied and when it has not. The final acute accent is also obligatory;
