In the section concerning words with an udātta accent on the final syllable, an addition must be made for *tricakra* and others in the Vedic language.

It should be stated that [the compound] with *tricakreṇa*, *tribandhureṇa*, and *trivṛtā* as the *rathena* [is formed] as a singular (*ekavat*) and there is no elision (*aluk*). What is the purpose? So that when analyzing [the compounds] as *stokābhyāṃ muktaḥ* or *stokebhyo muktaḥ*, the resulting form would be *stokānmuktaḥ*. The mention of "as a singular" (*ekavad-vacanam*) is redundant.

And the treatment as a singular [ekavadbhāva] would be purposeless. Why does the non-elision (*aluk*) not occur in the dual and plural? Because there is no compound in the dual and plural. There is no compound for dual and plural endings. Should this be stated? No, for it will be understood even without being stated. Or rather, it has already been stated. What has been stated? That "it is because of non-expression" (*anabhidhānāt*). And that non-expression must necessarily be relied upon.

For if it were stated in the singular, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *goṣucara*. Indeed, if it were stated in the singular, there would be an over-extension in the case of *goṣucara*: [the form] *goṣucaraḥ* [would be incorrectly derived]. And after *varṣā*, there is an over-extension in the case of the suffix *ja*. [The form] *varṣāsujaḥ* [would be incorrectly derived]. And after *ap*, an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the suffixes *yoni*, *yat*, and *mat*. [This applies] to *ja* and *cara*.
And: *je* (in *je*), *care* (in *care*), there is the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [Examples: *yoni*: *apsuyoniḥ*; *yat*: *apsavyam*;
*mati*: *apsumatiḥ*; *je*: *apsujaḥ*; *care*: *apsucaraḥ*; *gahvareṣṭhāḥ*.
(P_6.3.2) In the section on the fifth case (*pañcamīprakaraṇa*), there is an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for *brāhmaṇācchaṃsinaḥ*.

In the section on the fifth case (*pañcamī-prakaraṇa*), an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the term *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*. [The word] *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī* [is formed]. And in the sense of "another" (*anyārthe*). Furthermore, this fifth case should be understood as having the sense of "another. [Thus,] one who recites the *brāhmaṇas* is called *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*.
Alternatively, the sense of the fifth case is indeed appropriate here: [it means] one who has taken [them] from the *brāhmaṇas*.

One who recites by repeatedly bringing forward [the verses] is called a *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*. (Pāṇini 6.3.3) The word *añjas* should be added to the list [of terms governing the suffix *ka*]. An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) of *añjas* must be made:
*añjasākṛtam*. Also, *puṃsānujaḥ*, *januṣāndhaḥ*, and *vikṛtākṣaḥ*. [Examples: *puṃsānujaḥ*, *januṣāndhaḥ*.
The addition "vikṛtākṣaḥ" (deformed-eyed) must also be included [in the list]. Examples: *puṃsānujaḥ* (born after a male), *januṣāndhaḥ* (blind from birth), *vikṛtākṣaḥ*.

(P_6,3.5) KA_III.143.2-8 Ro_IV. 585-586: And [the rule] regarding "ātmanaḥ" in the sense of a "pūraṇa" (ordinal). An addition must be made for "ātmanaḥ" in the sense of a "pūraṇa": *ātmanāpañcamaḥ* ("he who has himself as the fifth"), *ātmanādaśamaḥ* ("he who has himself as the tenth"). And also in the sense of "anyārtha" (something else). In the sense of "anyārtha," this third case (*tṛtīyā*) is to be understood: *ātmā pañcamo 'sya* = *ātmāpañcamaḥ*. Alternatively, the meaning of the third case is indeed applicable here: that which was done by him is his [deed] through himself (*ātmanā*).
This is the fifth [case]. How is it that Janārdana is "with himself as the fourth" (*ātmacaturtha*)? This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound: "he for whom the self (*ātman*) is the fourth.
An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made regarding the *ātmanebhāṣa* and *parasmaibhāṣa* [voices]. An addition regarding the *ātmanebhāṣa* and *parasmaibhāṣa* voices must be formulated.

[The terms] *ātmanebhāṣa* and *parasmaibhāṣa*. How should this be understood? If it means "belonging to grammar" (*vyākaraṇe bhavā*), then it is a feminine derivative: *vaiyākaraṇī*; and the name of those who are *vaiyākaraṇī* is *vaiyākaraṇākhyā* (or *vaiyākaraṇakhyā*). [In that case, the rule applies] "in the name of those who are grammarians. However, if *vaiyākaraṇākhyā* means "the name of the grammarians" (*vaiyākaraṇānām ākhyā*), then there is no purpose for the supplementary statement (*upasaṅkhyāna*). Even if...

"Vaiyākaraṇī" means "pertaining to grammar" (*vyākaraṇe bhavā*); the designation "vaiyākaraṇī" is thus *vaiyākaraṇākhyā*. Even so, there is no need for an additional rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*). It will be established by explicit statement (*vacana*). What is the purpose of the statement? [To account for] the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). This is established by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). What is the irregular derivation?
"The *ātmanepada* endings are used for roots marked with an *anudātta* vowel or the letter *ṅ*; the *parasmaipada* endings are used for the rest when denoting the agent" (Pāṇini 1.3.12–13).

[Vārttika: An addition must be made regarding the suffix *ṅi* after the words *hṛd* and *dyu*. An addition must be made regarding the suffix *ṅi* after the words *hṛd* and *dyu*: *hṛdispṛk*, [and *divispṛk*].

*divispṛk*. And in the sense of "another. This seventh case ending (*saptamī*) should be understood as having the sense of "another" (*anyārtha*). [Thus], *hṛdispṛk* means "that which touches the heart," and *divispṛk* means "that which touches heaven. [Objection: Under the heading concerning suffixes beginning with a consonant (*hal*) and ending in a vowel (*adanta*), an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) regarding the word *go* must be made.

[Reply: It need not be made. The substitution of *ava* for the elision (*luk*) takes precedence by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). Thus, [in the compound] *gaviṣthiraḥ*, the elision of the case-ending is replaced by *ava*.

Let there be elision (*luk*); by the rule "let there be the substitution of *ava*," the substitution of *ava* will take place by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). Once the substitution of *ava* has been made, the form is established simply by the rule "after a stem ending in a consonant. If it is argued that the substitution of *ava* occurs in place of elision by way of conflict, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *bhūmipāśa*. If it is argued that the substitution of *ava* occurs in place of elision by way of conflict, then an over-extension occurs in the case of *bhūmipāśa*: [the undesired form] *bhūmyām pāśaḥ* [would result].

The *bhūmipāśaḥ* [is formed by] "akaḥ ataḥ" or for the sake of the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*). If that is so, then having stated the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case without distinction, I shall state "akaḥ ataḥ. That will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): it occurs only after "akaḥ ataḥ," and not from anything else. By this, the formation of the diphthongs is established. It is established. [This is the purpose of the] Sūtra.

In that case, it would have to be split [into a separate rule]. Let it remain exactly as it is formulated. But was it not stated under the heading *haladanta* (consonants at the end) that an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) is required for the word *go*?

This is not a fault. This is established by means of a formal irregularity (*nipātana*). What is the irregularity? The word *gaviṣṭhira* is recited among the *vidādi* group. Furthermore, an irregularity is indeed stated more than once: namely, *gavi-yudhibhyāṃ sthiraḥ*.

(P_6,3.10) KA_III.144.19–145.13 Ro_IV.589–591: Is this an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding what is already established (*prāpta*), or rather regarding what is not yet established (*aprāpta*)? And how is it established, and how is it not established? If the term *saṃjñāyām* (in the sense of a name) continues [from the previous rule], then it is regarding what is already established;

if it has ceased [to apply], then it is regarding what is not yet established. What, then, is the distinction here? If it is for the sake of stating an option (*vāvacana*) regarding the names of causes (*kāraṇa*), then [it applies] when the suffix begins with a vowel other than *a*.

There is the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is for the purpose of stating a restriction (*vāvacana*) regarding the name of the cause, then there is over-extension in the case of suffixes beginning with *aj*; here too it would apply: *avikaṭe uraṇo dātavyaḥ* [would result in] *avikaṭoraṇaḥ*. Let it be, then, in a case where [the rule] is not otherwise obtained. It is a prescription of compounding (*samāsa*) where it was not previously obtained. If the compounding is to be prescribed where it was not obtained, then when it is already obtained, the compounding is already established by the very rule "in the sense of a technical name" (*sañjñāyām*).

This is not a fault; it indicates that there is indeed a compound here, since [the author] teaches the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case when the name of the cause is expressed. Even if the compound were established by this indication, the accent would still not be accounted for. For regarding the rule that "that which has a locative as its prior member takes its original accent" (*prakṛtisvara*), between that which is established by a general definition and that which is stated by a specific rule (*pratipadokta*), the specific rule prevails.

"Thus" means it is so. It should not have this accent here. What then? By the rule "in the sense of 'one who takes' when used in the locative case, provided it refers to a duty and not to taking," this accent should apply here. Furthermore, sir, are technical names (*saṃjñā*) even created in common usage? Common usage is not the authority for technical names. Moreover, in common usage, a name is based on a cause (*kāraṇanāman*). But was it not said [earlier] regarding a name based on a cause?

If it is argued that there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to vowels beginning with *a* due to the meaning of the word "optionally" (*vā*), this fault does not apply. It is established by means of a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). A split of the rule will be made: "And [there is no elision] in the case of the names of places belonging to the Easterners," and then, "In the case of [names] beginning with a consonant. Thus, when the name of a place begins with a consonant, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending. Now, for what purpose is this [second part] intended?

[The rule] is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*): [the suffix *ka* is applied] only when the following member begins with a consonant (*halādi*) in the case of a name of a cause (*kāraṇanāmni*), and not elsewhere. Where should it not occur? In *avikaṭe uraṇo dātavyaḥ* > *avikaṭoraṇaḥ*. Regarding the rule *gurau antāt ca*: it should be stated that [the suffix *ka* is applied] after a word ending in a heavy syllable (*gurau*) as well. As in *anteguruḥ*. Does the mention of "one's own limb" (*svāṅgagrahaṇam*) carry over [from the previous rule], or does it not? What follows from this? If it carries over, then *hastebandhaḥ* is established.

*hastabandhaḥ*. [The forms] *cakrebhandaḥ* and *cakrabandhaḥ* are not established. Now, having ceased, the established forms are *cakrebhandaḥ* and *cakrabandhaḥ*. [The form] *hastebandhaḥ*, [is not established].

The form *hastabandhaḥ* is not established. What is the reason? Because the prohibition "not in the case of *in*, *siddha*, or *badhnāti*" would apply. This is not a fault. For in all such cases where a *tatpuruṣa* compound with a *kṛt*-suffix as the final member is concerned, the rule "diversely" (*bahulam*) applies; it is in view of that [general rule] that the prohibition "not in the case of *in*, *siddha*, or *badhnāti*" is stated. While that [rule] is thus permanently applicable, this [present rule]...
The *vibhāṣā* (optional rule) is now commenced. Even so, it is not known in which case there is an option and in which case there is a prohibition.

This mention of the word *bandha* ending in *ghañ* is for the purpose of the prohibition; however, in the prohibition itself, the root (*dhātu*) is mentioned again. Thus, there is an option when it ends in *ghañ*, but elsewhere there is a prohibition.

(P_6,3.14) KA_III.146.4–16 Ro_IV.592–594: “In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, [the suffix] *kṛt* is frequently [retained], except in the case of a *karmadhāraya*. Regarding the rule ‘in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, *kṛt* is frequently [retained],’ it should be stated that this applies ‘except in the case of a *karmadhāraya*. This is so that it does not occur here: *parame kārake*, *paramakārake*. Then, must that be stated? It need not be stated. Because of the word ‘frequently’ (*bahula*), it will not occur. Now, for what purpose [is the rule stated]?”

The mention of *luka* and *aluk* is made because [the rule] "in a *tatpuruṣa*, after a *kṛt*-suffix, it is manifold" (*tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*) is not established [without it]. The mention of *luka* and *aluk* is for the sake of the fact that the statement "it is manifold" (*bahulavacana*) is incomplete. The mention of *luka* and *aluk* is made on the grounds that the statement "it is manifold" is incomplete. If it is incomplete, then whatever has been done by this [rule] remains undone. If that is so, then we do not say that it is "incomplete."
It is the whole, the agent, the accomplisher, and the producer; and whatever well-done deed has been performed by it—that is [the meaning].

Why, then, is the sequential enumeration of *luka* (elision) and *aluk* (non-elision) made? Because of the abundance of examples. Indeed, those rules are well-mastered in which there is both a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and an elaboration (*prapañca*). A mere definition alone—[is not sufficient].

Or rather, verbal proliferation (*prapañca*) is not the cause [of the Veda] in that way. Indeed, we must necessarily state this: "frequently," "optionally," "in both ways," or "for some"—for this scripture is the foundation of all the Vedas. In such a case, it is not possible to adhere to a single path.
In the section on the genitive case, an addition should be made: after the words *vāc*, *dik*, and *paśyat*, when combined with *yukti*, *daṇḍa*, and *hara* respectively.
[The examples are:
*vācoyuktiḥ*.

*diśodaṇḍaḥ*, *paśyatoharaḥ*. An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) should be made for *āmuṣyāyaṇa* and *āmuṣyaputrikā*. An addition must be made for *āmuṣyāyaṇa* and *āmuṣyaputrikā*: *āmuṣyāyaṇaḥ*, *āmuṣyaputrikā*. And it should also be stated that *āmuṣyakulikā* [is formed]: *āmuṣyakulikā*. [And] *devānāmpriyaḥ*.

And the addition "devānāmpriyaḥ" must be made [to the rule]. Example: *devānāmpriyaḥ*. Regarding the words "śepa," "puccha," and "lāṅgūla," the addition "śunaḥ sañjñāyām" (of *śvan* when it is a name) must be made. Examples: *śunaḥśephaḥ*, *śunaḥpucchaḥ*.

*śunolāṅgūlaḥ*. [The rule] *divaś ca dāse* requires an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*): it must be stated that [the substitution applies] after *divaḥ* before *dāsa*. Example: *divodāsāya gāyata*. [Regarding the rule P. 6.3.23: From words denoting a relationship through learning (*vidyā*) or procreation (*yoni*), there must be the mention of both the preceding and following members of the compound. From words denoting a relationship through learning or procreation, the mention of both the preceding and following members of the compound must be made.

It should be so that there is no confusion between those related by learning and those related by learning, nor between those related by birth and those related by birth. Now, must there not be such a confusion among them? Indeed, there must be. For example, the son of the Hotṛ priest—
The pupil of the father.
(P. 6.3.25.1) Where is this *n* heard? It is not heard anywhere.
Its elision occurs by the rule "there is elision of the *n* of a nominal stem" (*nalopaḥ prātipadikasya*). If it is not heard, for what purpose is it pronounced?

[Objection: "Let there not be the state of having *r* as a subsequent element (*raparatva*). [Response: Even when the letter *n* is applied, the state of having *r* as a subsequent element still occurs. What is the reason?

Because once the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) has been performed, this [vowel] is also taught as an *aṇ* substitute in place of *u*. [Reply: This is not a fault. It is stated that an *aṇ* being prescribed in place of *u* is one that has *r* as its subsequent element; however, this [vowel] is not taught as an *aṇ* substitute in place of *u*. What then? It is both an *aṇ* and a non-*aṇ*.
But how is this to be understood:

[does it mean] "the *dvandva* compound of those ending in *ṛ*," or rather "the *ṛ* sound within a *dvandva*"? And what is the distinction here? [The answer is: there must be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) regarding the word *putra* when it occurs in a *dvandva* compound of words ending in *ṛ*. There must be an addition regarding the word *putra* when it occurs in a *dvandva* compound of words ending in *ṛ*.

It must be formulated [as follows]: "Father and son" (*pitāputrau*). And the agent of the action (*kāryin*) is not specified. When the agent is not specified, it is not known which [of the two] should undergo the substitution *ānaṅ* in a *dvandva* compound of words ending in the vowel *ṛ*. Let us then assume that the rule applies to the vowel *ṛ* in a *dvandva*.

[If so,] there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to cases such as "father and grandfather" (*pitṛpitāmahau*), because no distinction is made. There would be an over-extension to cases such as "father and grandfather" because no distinction is made.

[The form] *pitṛpitāmahau* occurs. Let it be then that [the rule applies] to a *dvandva* compound of words ending in *ṛ*. But has it not been stated that there must be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the case of a *dvandva* of words ending in *ṛ* when followed by the word *putra*? This is not a fault. The mention of *putra* also follows as being established in the context. Where was it established? In the rule *putre anyatarasyām*. If that follows, then [the application of the rule] is optional (*vibhāṣā*).

[If it is argued that] because of the rule "in the case of the husband of a sister and in the case of a son," the option would also apply to the word *putra*, this is not a fault. The relationship [of the genitive] will continue to be understood.

[The rule] "the genitive in the sense of abuse" (*ṣaṣṭhyā ākrośe*) applies; specifically, "the genitive optionally in the sense of abuse when the word *putra* follows. [And further: "after words denoting a connection by learning or by birth, the genitive optionally in the sense of abuse when *putra* follows. [And finally: "optionally in the case of the husband of a sister and in the case of a son, the genitive optionally in the sense of abuse."

In the case of *ākrośe* (insult), the substitution of *ānaṅ* occurs for the final vowel of a word ending in *ṛt* when it is part of a *dvandva* compound. The mention of *putra* continues [from the previous rule], while the phrase "of the genitive in the sense of insult" (*ṣaṣṭhyā ākrośe*) is no longer applicable. As for the statement that "the subject of the operation (*kāryī*) is not specified," the subject of the operation is indeed specified. How so? Because the term "in the following member" (*uttarapade*) continues to apply. Furthermore, this substitute is marked with the indicator *ṅ*; therefore, even without an explicit mention of the subject of the operation, it applies specifically to that which ends in the vowel *ṛ*.

[The suffix] will occur [after the word *putra*]. But in that case, the word *putra* would not have been specified as the locus for the operation. And yet, *putra* has indeed been specified as the locus for the operation. How so? The mention of the vowel *ṛ* also continues by way of anuvṛtti from the previous context. Where was it mentioned? In the rule *ṛto vidyāyonisambandhebhyaḥ*. That [mention] was indeed made in the ablative case (*pañcamī*), whereas here the requirement is for a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus, the word *putre*—which is in the locative case—is used to convert the ablative *ṛtaḥ* into a genitive.
When it is stated, "it will apply to that," [the rule] "of the preceding" (*pūrvasya*) is indicated. (P.

6.3.26) In a *devatā-dvandva* (compound of deities), there is a prohibition regarding *vāyu* in both cases. It must be stated that in a *devatā-dvandva*, there is a prohibition of *vāyu* in both [the first and second members]. For example: *agnivāyū*. And in the case of *brahmaprajāpatyādi* (Brahmā-Prajāpati, etc.), there is also a prohibition. It must be stated that there is a prohibition for *brahmaprajāpatyādi* as well. For example: *brahmaprajāpatī*.
Śiva and Vaiśravaṇa;

Skanda and Viśākha. If that is so, then that prohibition must be stated. It need not be stated. While the term "in a dvandva compound" (dvandve) is already in force, the purpose of mentioning "dvandva" again is so that [the rule] may apply to those dvandvas which occur in both common usage (loka) and the Veda.

And what is the *dvandva* compound in both worldly usage and the Veda? Those [deities] that are prescribed as being offered together (*sahanirvāpanirdiṣṭa*) in the Veda—these are not prescribed as being offered together here.

(P_6,3.28) KA_III.149.4-5 Ro_IV.598: There is a prohibition regarding the lengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the vowel in *viṣṇu*. A prohibition regarding the lengthening of the vowel in *viṣṇu* must be stated. (In the rule for the offering of the *caru*): "One should offer a *caru* to Agni-Viṣṇu" (P_6,3.32-33). KA_III.149.8-10 Ro_IV.598: What is the irregular formation (*nipātana*)? It is the substitution of the long vowel *ṝ* for the vowels of both the preceding and the following members of the compound.

The two forms *arārau* are substituted [for *ara-arau*]. Examples: *mātarapitarau bhojayataḥ* ("He causes the mother and father to eat"); *mātarapitarāv ānaya* ("Bring the mother and father"). [Vedic examples: *a mā gantām pitarāmātarā ca* ("May the father and mother come to me");
*a mā soma amṛtatvāya gamyāt* ("May Soma come to me for the sake of immortality").
(Pāṇini 6.3.34.1) Regarding the rule *bhāṣitapuṃskāt*, how is this to be understood?

[The question is: "Is it that which has a masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) within the same class-form (*ākṛti*), or is it that which has a masculine form somewhere? What follows from this? If it is understood as "that which has a masculine form within the same class-form," then [the forms] *garbhibhāryaḥ* and *prajātabhāryaḥ* [would be correct].

In the case of *prasūtabhāraḥ*, the rule would not apply. Now, if it is understood that "having been mentioned as masculine" (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) applies in some instances, then [the rule] would also apply here in cases such as *droṇībhāryaḥ*, *kuṭībhāryaḥ*, and *pātrībhāryaḥ*. Let it be that [the term refers to] that which has been mentioned as masculine within the same form (*ākṛti*). How then [to account for] *garbhibhāryaḥ*?

"Prajātabhāryaḥ" (one whose wife has given birth) and "prasūtabhāraḥ" (one whose burden has been delivered)—effort must be made in this regard. Now, for what purpose is a separate prohibition stated for *ūṅ*? Why is it not stated in the very same place where the other prohibitions occur? [The answer is: It is not done by stating "not after a word ending in *ka*," etc. [and then adding *ūṅ*].
Then it would have to be stated that "also after *ūṅ*. Even in that case, this meaning—that the double prohibition need not be stated—would still hold.

But it cannot be done in this way, for the Teacher will state [the rule] "as in the masculine (*puṃvat*)" for the purpose of prohibiting [the feminine form] in a *karmadhāraya* compound. That masculine-like behavior (*puṃvadbhāva*) occurs here as follows:
Just as one says *kārikā vṛndārikā* and *kārakavṛndārikā*, so too here it would be:

*brahmabandhūḥ vṛndārikā* and *brahmabandhūvṛndārikā*. Now, even if a separate prohibition were stated, since that [prohibition] is for the purpose of what has already been forbidden, why does it not apply in this case? It is because of the force of the statement regarding a separate prohibition.
Alternatively, the term *anūṅ* will be carried over (*anuvartiṣyate*) from that [preceding rule]. Or rather, this is not a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).

What then? This is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), namely: "that which is other than *ūṅ*. And that [exclusion] serves the purpose of a prohibition; for its formulation is intended as a prohibition. But what is the purpose of mentioning the word "feminine" (*strī*) in this context regarding the treatment as masculine (*puṃvadbhāva*)?

Is it the inclusion of the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*), or the inclusion of the word "feminine" (*strīśabda*), or the inclusion of the feminine meaning (*stryartha*)? And what is the distinction here? If, in the rule for *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution), the term "feminine" (*strī*) refers to the inclusion of the feminine suffix (*strīpratyayagrahaṇa*), then in that case, when the rule states "like the masculine" (*puṃvat*), it should be understood as a prohibition regarding that [suffix] in the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Thus, in the rule for *puṃvadbhāva*, the mention of "feminine" (*strīgrahaṇa*) refers to the inclusion of the feminine suffix (*strīpratyayagrahaṇa*).
If, in that context, by the rule *puṃvat* (masculine-like), this prohibition were understood to apply to the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), [one might ask]: "Of what?

[The answer is: "It is a prohibition of the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*). But why is it said that it is a prohibition of the feminine suffix, when no other specific grammatical operation (*kārya*) pertaining to the masculine is prescribed for a word that has been stated in the masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) when followed by a coreferential subsequent member?

It would be extended [to the masculine]. Because there is no commencement [of such a rule] regarding the masculine: for indeed, no specific grammatical operation (*kārya*) is prescribed for the masculine word by its individual term (*pratipadam*) which could be extended to the case where the subsequent member is in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with a word that has been stated in the masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*). In that context, what else can be understood [as the purpose] other than the prohibition of the feminine suffix? But how, by this [rule] *puṃvat*, is the feminine suffix [negated]?

The negation can be understood. This is an instruction using the suffix *vati*, and in an instruction with *vati*, there is freedom of choice (*kāmacāra*) regarding the completion of the sentence. For example: "In the land of the Madras, barley exists like in Uśīnara; it may exist or it may not exist. Or: "Her artistic skills are like her mother's; they may exist or they may not exist. In the same way here as well, [the rule] means "it becomes like the masculine" or "it does not become like the masculine."

We shall justify the remainder of the statement: just as a woman's suffix does not occur for a male, so too it does not occur when there is a co-referential (samānādhikaraṇa) subsequent word that has been stated in the masculine. Furthermore, there must be a restoration of the nominal stem (prātipadika). Indeed, the restoration of the nominal stem must be stated. [For example: "enī bhāryā asya" (his wife is a female antelope).

In *etabhāryaḥ* and *śyetabhāryaḥ*, what is accomplished by the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*)? It is the removal of the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*). However, the meaning—namely, femininity—is not removed. Since that [meaning] has not been removed, why would the word ending in *naṅ* not be heard? [If it were applied,] the rule stating "when [the word refers to] a female" (*striyām*) would apply.

And there arises the contingency of being "as if in the original place" (*sthānivat*). That is, the status of being *sthānivadbhāva* would apply: in the case of *paṭvībhāryaḥ* (meaning "one whose wife is clever"), what is accomplished by the rule of "masculine-like behavior" (*puṃvadbhāva*)? It is the removal of the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*). Because that [suffix] would then have the status of being *sthānivadbhāva*, the substitution of *yaṇ* would result.

Why is this stated twice—namely, both "the restoration of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikasya pratyāpattiḥ*) and [the rule regarding masculine-like behavior]? Why not simply say "the restoration of the nominal stem"?

The status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) would also have been enjoined. Previously, this was observed by the Teacher: "And there is the contingency of [treating something] as a substitute," and that was recorded. Subsequently, this was observed: "And the restoration of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)," and that too was recorded. Furthermore, teachers do not compose and then subsequently revoke their own rules, as is seen in the case of the *vataṇḍī* and other such suffixes.

The rule regarding "masculine-like expression" (*puṃvadvacana*). In the case of *vataṇḍī* and others, the state of being masculine-like (*puṃvadbhāva*) must be stated. But who are *vataṇḍī* and the rest? They are those cases involving elision (*luk*), non-elision (*aluk*), and feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*) such as *dvī* and *strī*. [Example of] *luk*: *gārgyaḥ* [from *gārgī*], *vṛndārikā* [from *vṛndārikā*]; [the compound] *gargavṛndārikā*. What is accomplished by the state of being masculine-like? The cessation of the feminine suffix. The referent (*artha*) has not ceased; femininity (*strītva*) remains. Since that has not ceased, why would the sound *ya* not be heard?
For it is stated that elision (*luk*) occurs when [the word] is not feminine. Elision (*luk*), non-elision (*aluk*). *Vataṇḍī* or *vṛndārikā* becomes *vātaṇḍya-vṛndārikā*.
What is accomplished by the state of being like the masculine (*puṃvadbhāva*)? It is the removal of the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*). But the meaning—namely, femininity—is not removed.

Because that [femininity] has not been removed, the rule "there is elision of the *yakāra* after *vataṇḍa* in the feminine" (*luk striyām vataṇḍāt*) would result in the elision of the *yakāra*. If, however...

This elision (*luk*) would be stated as occurring only before the vowel *ī*. Therefore, the mention of *ī* should be made. It need not be made; it is already accomplished in the very formulation (*nyāsa*). This is a compound expression (*praśliṣṭanirdeśa*): *strī*, *ī* = *strī*.

In the rule for the suffix *ī*, the form *vataṇḍa* is recited without a suffix (*apratyayaka*). However, in the list beginning with *śārṅgarava*, it will be recited with a suffix (*sapratyayaka*). Indeed, that recitation with a suffix must be made. Furthermore, because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), elision (*luk*) would apply; [therefore,] there is no elision (*aluk*). It does not refer to the feminine domain (*astrīviṣaya*). For example: *kauṇḍīvṛsī*, *vṛndārikā*; *kauṇḍīvṛsyavṛndārikā*.

What is accomplished by the application of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment)? It is the removal of the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*). However, the meaning [of the feminine]—namely, femininity—is not removed. Since that has not been removed, by what means would the sound *ya* be heard? For the suffix *ñya* is prescribed [by Pāṇini 4.1.75] with the condition *astriyām* ("provided it is not feminine"). Thus, it would apply only when the object is not feminine. But in a case involving two feminine suffixes, such as *gārgyāyaṇī vṛndārikā*, the form *gārgyavṛndārikā* results; here, the *puṃvadbhāva* does not apply.

What is the reason? It is stated that "there is a substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) when a word denoting a feminine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) that does not end in the suffix *ūṅ* is followed by a co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) final member. However, in this case, that which follows a word denoting a feminine and does not end in *ūṅ* is not the final member; and that which is the final member does not follow a word denoting a feminine and end in *ūṅ*. Well then, let there be the mention of the word "feminine" (*strī*). [The meaning is: there is an extension of the masculine form to the feminine word.

If this is argued, there is the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of over-extension because there is no distinction. If it is argued that the word for "female" (*strī-śabda*) is extended by analogy from the word for "male" (*puṃśabda*), then the extension of the word for "male" would apply to every word for "female. This [undesirable consequence] would also apply here:
there are birds named *aṅgāraka*; their females are *kālikā*. [Thus, one would have to derive] *kālikāvṛndārikāḥ* and *aṅgārakavṛndārikāḥ*.

They obtain [their mates]: Kṣemavṛddhas who are Kṣatriyas; their women have fine hair; [thus] groups of women with fine hair; [finally] groups of women with fine hair who are Kṣemavṛddhas obtain [them]. The female mate of the swan is the varaṭā; of the tortoise, the ḍulī; of the antelope, the rohit; of the horse, the vaḍavā; of the man, the woman. What is the reason?

Because there is no distinction. For no specific qualification is stated such that the extension (*atideśa*) of the masculine term would apply to a feminine term of this kind. If no distinction is stated, the rule would over-apply (*prasaṅga*) everywhere. And how could it be that no distinction is stated, given that it is said "from that which has been spoken of as masculine" (*bhāṣitapuṃskāt*)? Furthermore, the condition of having been spoken of as masculine is impossible [in this case]. Moreover, the particle *ca* here has the sense of *hi* ("for").

It has been recited [in the sūtra]. For every word can indeed be made to follow one that is "bhāṣitapuṃska" (having a masculine form). Let it be, then, that there is the mention of "artha" (meaning). If there is an extension (*atideśa*) of meaning, a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is untenable. If there is an extension of meaning, a conflict does not hold. For the Teacher will state the conflict: "In the case of *khid*, *ghadi*, and so on, shortening takes place by way of conflict with the rule for *puṃvadbhāva*. That...

A conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is not possible here. For a conflict consists in the application of two grammatical operations simultaneously, and in this case, a single element is not joined with two operations: [one operation would apply] to the word’s short vowel (*hrasvatva*), while [the other] would apply to the meaning’s masculine state (*puṃvadbhāva*). Furthermore, there is the undesirable consequence that it would apply to all cases (*sarvaprasaṅga*) because there is no distinction; thus, the extension of the masculine term would apply to every feminine word. This undesired result would follow even for this [specific instance].

There are birds called *aṅgāraka*; their females are *kālikā*. [The compound] *kālikāvṛndārikāḥ* means "groups of female *kālikā* birds. [Thus] one obtains the form *aṅgārakavṛndārikāḥ* ("groups of female *aṅgāraka* birds"). The *kṣemavṛddhi*s are Kṣatriyas; their females are *tanukeśī*. [The compound] *tanukeśīvṛndārikāḥ* means "groups of female *tanukeśī* women. [Thus] one obtains the form *kṣemavṛddhivṛndārikāḥ* ("groups of female *kṣemavṛddhi* women"). The mate of a swan (*haṃsa*) is a *varaṭā*; the mate of a tortoise (*kacchapa*) is a *ḍulī*; [the mate] of a deer (*ṛśya*)...
The female of a *rohit* (red deer) is a *vaḍavā*; the female of a human is a *yoṣit*. What is the reason? Because there is no distinction.

For no specific distinction is introduced such that the masculine term would be extended to a feminine word of this class. But how is it that no distinction is introduced, when it is stated "from a word that has been used for the masculine" (*bhāṣitapuṃskāt*)? Indeed, the application of the term "used for the masculine" is untenable [in these cases].

It occurs. For there is no temporal sequence (paurvāparya) in the meaning. First of all, this is not a fault regarding what was said: that if the [operation] were extended to the meaning, a conflict (vipratiṣedha) would be impossible. A conflict does not necessarily consist only of the conjunction of two operations; rather, it is also impossibility (asambhava). And such impossibility exists here. What is the impossibility? It is the occurrence of the masculine-like treatment (puṃvadbhāva).

It destroys the cause of shortness (*hrasvatva*). Shortness, while being brought about, subverts the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment). A conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is appropriate only when there is an impossibility [of both rules applying simultaneously]. But then there is this fault: that it would apply everywhere because there is no distinction.
Therefore, let that very middle position be accepted. But was it not said that there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the masculine term to the feminine term?

If this is so, then there would be the undesirable consequence [of the rule applying] to all cases because there is no distinction. This is not a fault. This is a compound designation: "that which has an ūṅ-omission after a word that has a masculine form" is *bhāṣitapuṃskādanūṅ*. If this were the case, then elision (*luk*) would apply. It will not occur because of a specific technical injunction (*nipātana*). Or rather, non-elision (*aluk*) is the subject under discussion and it will be carried over [into this rule]. But how?

The mention of a feminine suffix by means of the term *anūṅ* can be understood [as referring to anything other than *ūṅ*]. "That which is joined with *nañ* or *iva* refers to something else similar; for such is the comprehension of the meaning. That which is joined with *nañ* and that which is joined with *iva* are understood to denote an operation upon something else that resembles it; for such is the meaning perceived. For example, when it is said, "Bring a non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇam ānaya*), one brings someone who resembles a Brahmin.

One does not become proficient merely by bringing a clod of earth. Likewise here, because of the prohibition of *ūṅ* in the term *anūṅ*, a grammatical operation similar to *ūṅ* is understood to apply to something other than *ūṅ*. Furthermore, what else is similar to *ūṅ* besides *anūṅ*? It is a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*). Even so, [in the case of] *iḍabiḍ-vṛndārikā* and *aiḍabiḍ-vṛndārikā*, [the rule would still apply].
Pṛthvī-vṛndārikā,
Pārtha-vṛndārikā, Darad-vṛndārikā.
Dāradavṛndārikā, Uśikvṛndārikā,
and Auśijavṛndārikā.

In this case, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not apply; an effort must be made here. (P_6.3.34.3) Now, how should it be in this instance: *paṭvīmṛdvyau bhārye asya* ("he whose two wives are clever and gentle")—should it be *paṭvīmṛdubhāryaḥ* or *paṭumṛdubhāryaḥ*? It should be *paṭvīmṛdubhāryaḥ*. Why is there a substitution of the masculine form?

[The rule] does not apply. It is stated [in the rule]: "from that which has been used in the masculine" (*bhāṣitapuṃskāt*). But surely, sir, the words *paṭu* and *mṛdu* are used in the masculine? [Answer: When they have the same form (*ākṛti*), they are those used in the masculine; and even when they appear in a different form, these two are still used in the masculine. Even when they have the same form, they are used in the masculine. How so? Because the elision of the suffix *matup* is prescribed. Thus it is.

In that case, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) occurs for a word that is *bhāṣitapuṃska* (having a corresponding masculine form), provided it does not end in the feminine suffix *ūṅ*, when followed by a co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) final member (*uttarapada*) to which the rule has been applied; however, that [word] for which the substitution has not been applied is not one that is *bhāṣitapuṃska*, does not end in *ūṅ*, and is followed by a co-referential final member. (P. 6.3.34.4) Regarding the mention of "the primary ordinal" (*pradhānapūraṇīgrahaṇa*) in the context of ordinals (*pūraṇī*), [it refers to] the ordinal.

The inclusion of the word *pradhāna* (principal) must be made [in the rule]. This should not apply here: *kalyāṇī pañcamī asya pakṣasya* → *kalyāṇapañcamīkaḥ pakṣaḥ* ("the fortnight having an auspicious fifth day"). Now, how should it be in this case: *kalyāṇī pañcamī āsām rātrīṇām*? It should be *kalyāṇīpañcamāḥ rātrayaḥ*. Here, the nights (*rātrayaḥ*) are the principal element.

(P_6,3.35) KA_III.154.6–155.24 Ro_IV.610–614. Here, certain suffixes beginning with *tasil* and ending with *kṛtvasuc* are listed, among which the masculine-like substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) is not desired; and certain others are listed elsewhere, among which the masculine-like substitution is desired. In this regard, what is the correct course? A complete enumeration (*parigaṇana*) must be made. [The suffixes] beginning with *tasil* are *tratas* and *sau*. [That is,] *tratas* and *sau*.
The suffixes *tasil* and others are to be understood [as follows]: he dwells in that hall (*tasyām śālāyām vasati*); he dwells there (*tatra vasati*);
of her (*tasyāḥ*), from there (*tataḥ*), in which (*yasyām*).

In the words *yatra*, *yasyāḥ*, and *yataḥ*. The suffixes *tara* and *tama* [are included]. The suffixes *tara* and *tama* should be understood as beginning with *tasil*. Examples: *darśanīyatarā* and *darśanīyatamā*. The suffixes *caraṭ* and *jātīyar* [are included]. The suffixes *caraṭ* and *jātīyar* should be understood as beginning with *tasil*.

*paṭucarī*, *paṭujātīyā*. [The suffixes] *kalpa* and *deśīya*: the suffixes *kalpa* and *deśīya* are to be regarded as belonging to the group beginning with *tasil*. Examples: *darśanīyakalpā*, *darśanīyadeśīyā*. [The suffixes] *rūpa* and *prāśa*: the suffixes *rūpa* and *prāśa* are to be regarded as belonging to the group beginning with *tasil*. Example: *darśanīyarūpā*.

The suffixes *tham* and *thāl* [are used] after words ending in *darśanīya*. *Tham* and *thāl* should be understood as beginning with *tasil*. [Examples: *kayā ākṛtyā* (by what form?), *katham* (how?);
*yayā*, *yathā* (by which, in which way). The suffixes *dārhil* and *dārhil* should be understood as beginning with *tasil*. [Examples: *tasyām velāyām* (at that time), *tadā* (then).

In that case, *til* and *thyan*—namely, the suffixes beginning with *tasil*—should be understood [as causing the masculine form]. For example: *vṛkī* becomes *vṛkatiḥ*; *ajathyā* becomes *yūthiḥ*. Regarding the suffix *śas*, when it expresses "many" or "few," the rule for becoming masculine (*puṃvadbhāva*) must be stated. For example: from *bahvībhyaḥ* (from many women), one says *bahuśaḥ* (in many ways); likewise, *alpaśaḥ* (in few ways). Regarding the suffixes *tv* and *tal*, when they follow a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*), [the same rule applies]. Regarding the suffixes *tv* and *tal*, when they follow a word expressing a quality...

The substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) should be stated. The state of being clever (*paṭvī*) is *paṭutvam* or *paṭutā*. Why [is it specified] "of that which expresses a quality" (*guṇavacanasya*)? [Consider: the state of being a Kaṭhī woman is *kaṭhītvam* or *kaṭhītā*. [The rule applies to] a *bha*-stem before a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) other than one beginning with *aṅ*. The substitution of the masculine form for a *bha*-stem should be stated before a secondary suffix other than one beginning with *aṅ*. [Example: A collection of female elephants is *hāstikam*. Why [is it specified] "other than one beginning with *aṅ*"? [Consider: *śyaineyaḥ*.
The son of Rohiṇī. If it is said "in the absence [of a specific deity]," then that which has Agnāyī as its deity is "āgneyaḥ," such as the *sthālīpāka* (cooked offering).
In this case, it would not apply; yet in these cases it should apply:

*kauṇḍinyaḥ* and *sāpatnaḥ*. If, however, it were stated as *anapatye* ("provided there is no offspring"), it could not be done in this way, for then it would not apply here: "The offspring of Gārgyāyaṇī is a young man, a rogue Gārga. Let it be so then.

[The rule applies] only when it means "rich. How is it that Kauṇḍinya is called *sāpatna*? It is established by means of a nipātana (irregular formation). What is the nipātana? It is the rule "in the case of Āgastya and Kauṇḍinya. But the word *sāpatna* is more of a primary form (*prakṛti*). [R 613: *Sāpatna* is a distinct primary form; the word *sāpatna* exists as a separate primary form. How is it that this sacrificial porridge has Agnāyī as its deity?

"The *sthālīpāka* offering belongs to Agni. Let it be so, then, "in the case of one who is childless. How is it that Gārgya is a fool? Gārgī and Āgneyī do not agree [phonetically]. Effort must be made here. Also, in the case of the suffixes *ṭhak* and *chaś*. It should be stated that the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) occurs also after the suffixes *ṭhak* and *chaś*: "the students of your ladyship" (*bhavatyāḥ chātrāḥ*).

"Your [bhāvatkāḥ], belonging to you [bhavadīyāḥ]. For what purpose is the mention of *ṭhak*? Why not simply say "when *ika* is applied, provided it begins with a vowel (*ajādau*)"? It cannot be done so. For if it were characterized by beginning with a vowel, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) as in the case of *māthitika* and others. Indeed, if it were characterized by beginning with a vowel, it would result in the same fault as in the case of *māthitika* and so forth. For example: *maṇitaḥ* (from *maṇi*), *vāritaḥ* (from *vāri*). If the suffix *ika* were applied here, the forms would have to be *maṇikaḥ* and *vārikaḥ*, which is incorrect. Therefore, the mention of *ṭhak* is necessary. Furthermore, if the suffix *ika* were applied, the feminine form would be *maṇikā* and *vārikā*, whereas the correct forms are *maṇikī* and *vārikī*. Thus, the mention of *ṭhak* is for the sake of obtaining the correct feminine forms. Moreover, if the suffix *ika* were applied, the accent would fall on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*), whereas with *ṭhak*, the accent falls on the final syllable (*antodātta*). Therefore, the mention of *ṭhak* is necessary. Furthermore, if the suffix *ika* were applied, the rule *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.117) would apply, causing the vowel *a* to be replaced by *vṛddhi*, resulting in the forms *maiaṇikaḥ* and *vaiaurikaḥ*.
