In the case of *mathitam* being the merchandise (*paṇya*) of someone, [the word] *māthitikaḥ* is formed; when the vowel *a* is elided, the substitution of *ka* by the rule *tāntāt* does not apply.
Likewise, it would not occur here either. (P.
6.3.36) For what purpose is the mention of *mānin*? The mention of *mānin* is for the sake of excluding the feminine.

And the mention of *mānin* is made for the sake of [forming] non-co-referential (*asamānādhikaraṇa*) meanings and for the sake of feminine forms. First, regarding the feminine form: *darśanīyām manyate devadatto yajñadattām* ("Devadatta considers Yajñadattā beautiful"); *darśanīyamānī ayam asyāḥ* ("he is one who considers her beautiful"). Regarding the non-co-referential meaning: *darśanīyām manyate devadattā yajñadattām* ("Devadattā considers herself more beautiful than Yajñadattā"); *darśanīyamāninī iyam asyāḥ* ("she is one who considers herself more beautiful than her").

Is this sequence of examples concerning the domain of the first rule (*yoga*), or rather concerning the phenomenon of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine substitution) in general? And what follows from this? If it concerns the domain of the first rule, then [the forms] *mādhyamkīyaḥ*, *śālūkikīyaḥ*, etc., [would not be valid].

In this case, [the rule] does not apply; even the positive injunction (*vidhi*) is not established here. What is the reason? It is stated that [the suffix *ṭāp*] is added after a word previously used in the masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃskāt*) provided it is not followed by the augment *ūṅ*. But this [word *vilepikā*] is not "previously used in the masculine and not followed by *ūṅ*. However, in the case of *vailepikam* (derived from *vilepikāyāḥ dharmyam*), the positive injunction is established and the prohibition does not apply. Now, regarding the mere absence of the masculine form...
In the case of *hastinīnāṃ samūhaḥ* (a herd of female elephants), the term *hāstikaṃ* results;

here, the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva-pratiṣedha*) based on the characteristic of the genus (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) would apply. If that is so, then the rule *na kopadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.51) is a subsequent enumeration intended for the scope of the first rule (*na karmadhārayājātīya-deśīyeṣu*), regarding the mere absence of the masculine form; it is not a prohibition specifically concerning [the application of] the rule *kopadhā-pratiṣedha*.

Regarding the mention of *taddhita* and *vu*: in the prohibition concerning words ending in *k* (*kopadha*), the mention of *taddhita* and *vu* must be made. That is to say, there must be a mention of the *k* that belongs to a *taddhita* suffix and the *k* that belongs to the *vu* suffix. This [prohibition] should not apply here: *pākabhāryaḥ*, *bhekabhāryaḥ*.

(P_6,3.40) KA_III.156.19–157.2 Ro_IV.616: It should be stated that [the suffix *vin*] follows a word denoting a body part (*svāṅga*) ending in *ī*, provided it does not end in the possessive suffix *mānin*. This must be stated so that it applies here as well: *dīrghamukhamānī* ("one who considers himself long-faced") and *ślakṣṇamukhamāninī* ("one who considers herself smooth-faced"). If it is said "provided it does not end in *mānin*," then forms such as *dīrghamukhamāninī* and *ślakṣṇamukhamāninī* would not be established. [Response: Since the mention of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) includes its specific gender-forms, this will be accomplished in that manner.

(P_6,3.42.1) KA_III.157.4-14 Ro_IV.616-617 For what purpose is this stated? It is for the sake of [applying] the masculine form (*puṃvat*) in a *karmadhāraya* compound where it has been prohibited. This undertaking is for the purpose of that which has been prohibited. It was stated [in P. 6.3.37]: "Not [for a feminine base] having *ka* as its penultimate letter" (*na kopadhāyāḥ*). Even in that case, the masculine form occurs: *kārikā-vṛndārikā* becomes *kāraka-vṛndārikā*; *jātīyā* becomes *jātīya*; *deśīyā* becomes *deśīya*. Thus: *kārakajātīyā*, *kārakadeśīyā*.

It has been stated that [the feminine suffix] is elided after *sañjñā* and *pūraṇī*. In those cases as well, the masculine form (*puṃvat*) occurs: *dattā vṛndārikā* becomes *dattavṛndārikā*; *dattajātīyā*, *dattadeśīyā*. *Pañcamī vṛndārikā* becomes *pañcamavṛndārikā*; *pañcamajātīyā*, *pañcamadeśīyā*. It has been stated that [the feminine suffix is elided] when caused by a *vṛddhi* vowel. In those cases as well, the masculine form occurs: *sraughnī vṛndārikā* becomes *sraughnavṛndārikā*.

Regarding *sraughnajātīyā* and *sraughnadeśīyā*: it has been stated that [the feminine suffix] *ī* following a word denoting one's own limb (*svāṅga*) does not become masculine when followed by the suffix *amānin*. In that case as well, the masculine form occurs:

*ślakṣṇamukhī vṛndārikā* becomes *ślakṣṇamukhavṛndārikā*, and *ślakṣṇamukhajātīyā* becomes *ślakṣṇamukhadeśīyā*. It has also been stated that [the feminine suffix] after a genus (*jāti*) does not become masculine when followed by *amānin*. In that case as well, the masculine form occurs: *kaṭhī vṛndārikā* becomes *kaṭhavṛndārikā*.
"Belonging to the Kaṭha school," "belonging to the region of the Kaṭhas.

(Pāṇini 6.3.42.2) Regarding the words *kukkuṭī* and others when combined with *aṇḍa* and others, there is the designation of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). It should be stated that for *kukkuṭī* and others, the masculine form occurs before *aṇḍa* and others. For example:
the egg of a hen is *kukkuṭāṇḍam*.
The track of a female deer is *mṛgapada*;

the young of a female crow is *kākaśāva*. Or rather, it need not be stated [as an exception], because the preceding member is intended not to be feminine (*astrīpūrvapada*). Why? Because the preceding member is intended not to be feminine. In this case, a feminine preceding member is not intended; what then? [It is intended to be non-feminine.]

"Not having a feminine word as the first member" (*astrīpūrvapada*). [The examples are: *ubhayoḥ aṇḍam* (the egg of both), *ubhayoḥ padam* (the foot of both), *ubhayoḥ śāvaḥ* (the young of both). Even if it can be argued that this [restriction] applies there, how is it in this case: *mṛgyāḥ kṣīram* (the milk of a doe) = *mṛgakṣīram*? Here too, the answer is simply: "Or rather, not so, because the status of having a non-feminine word as the first member is not intended to be expressed. But how can there be a non-intentional expression (*avivakṣā*) of something that actually exists? It exists.

Furthermore, there is the intention not to express [the actual meaning]. For example: "a hairless ewe" (*alomikā eḍakā*) and "a girl with no belly" (*anudarā kanyā*). And there is also the intention to express what is non-existent: "the ocean is a small water-pot" (*samudraḥ kuṇḍikā*) and "the Vindhya mountains are a *vardhitaka* (a type of cake)" (*vindhyo vardhitakam*).

By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the substitution of *ī* for *agni* takes precedence over the *vṛddhi* of *varuṇa*. By way of conflict, the substitution of *ī* for *agni* occurs in preference to the *vṛddhi* of *varuṇa*.

The scope for the substitution of *it* (short *i*) for *agni* is seen in *agnīṣomau*. The scope for the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) of *varuṇa* is seen in *vāyuvāruṇam*. In this instance, both [rules] apply simultaneously.

"One should sacrifice a bull dedicated to Agni and Varuṇa; there is an increase for Varuṇa by way of conflict. This is not a proper conflict. For a conflict consists in the application of two grammatical operations [to the same element], and here no single element is joined with two operations.
How so? [The rule states: "the substitution of *ī* for Agni and the substitution of *vṛddhi* for Varuṇa. A conflict is not necessarily restricted to the application of two operations alone.
What then? It is impossibility (*asambhava*). And that impossibility exists here. What is this impossibility?

The formation of *ī* for *agni* precludes the increase (*vṛddhi*) of *varuṇa*; the formation of the increase of *varuṇa* precludes the formation of *ī* for *agni*. This is the impossibility. When there is such impossibility, a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is appropriate; [the rule] prevails over the substitution of the prior form (*pūrvavadbhāva*).

Shortening occurs in the case of *khid*, *ghā*, and so forth. Shortening takes place by way of supersession (*vipratiṣedha*) because of the rule for becoming like the prior member (*pūrvavadbhāva*). The scope of the rule for becoming like the prior member is, for example, *paṭubhāryaḥ*.
Regarding the rule "a short vowel occurs before the suffix *khi*," this is its scope:
*kālimmanyaḥ*, *hariṇimmanyaḥ*. Here, both [rules] would apply.
*Kālimmanyā* and *hariṇimmanyā*. This [rule], "the short vowel occurs for the river-name (*nadī*) before the suffixes beginning with *gha*," finds its scope in examples such as *nartakitarā*.
The scope for the substitution of *pūrvavat* (the prior form) is,
for example, *darśanīyatarā* and *darśanīyatamā*. In this case, both [rules] would apply.

*paṭvitarā*, *paṭvitamā*. What is the scope for [the application of] the rule "a short vowel occurs"? It is, for example, *nartakikā*. What is the scope for [the application of] the rule regarding the substitution of the masculine form (*pūṃvadbhāva*)?
In the case of *dāradikā*, both [rules] would apply here:

*paṭvikā* and *mṛdvikā*. Shortening (*hrasvatva*) occurs by way of a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*). Now, once shortening has been applied, because of the principle of "reapplication" (*punaḥprasaṅga*), [the other rule would again apply].

Why does the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) not occur? Because once a rule has been superseded by a *vipratiṣedha* (conflict of rules), that which is superseded remains superseded for good. (P. 6.3.43) What is the purpose of including the mention of *ṅī* (the feminine suffix)? If it were stated simply as "a short vowel replaces [the final of] a polysyllabic stem" (*anekāco hrasvaḥ*), then it would undesirably apply here as well: *khaṭvātarā*, *mālātarā*. This is not a valid objection. The term *bhāṣitapuṃskāt* ("from a word that has a corresponding masculine form") continues to apply from the previous rule. Even so, [undesirable forms like] *dattātarā*, *guptātarā* would still result.

In this case as well, [the suffix] would apply. The word *ītaḥ* (from a stem ending in long ī) is understood [as a governing rule]. Even so, [the suffix] would undesirably apply here in *grāmaṇītaraḥ* and *senāṇītaraḥ*. The word *striyām* (in the feminine) is understood. Even so, [the suffix] would undesirably apply here in *grāmaṇītarā* and *senāṇītarā*. The words *striyāḥ* (of the feminine) and *striyām* (in the feminine) are understood. In that case, the mention of *ṅī* must be made for the purpose of establishing the "remainder" (*śeṣa*).

Regarding the rule *nadyāḥ śeṣasya anyatarasyām*: what is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*)? It is a river-name (*nadī*) that ends in the feminine suffix *ṅī*, as well as any monosyllabic word ending in *ṅī*. Even without explicitly mentioning the suffix *ṅī*, the remainder is established. How so? Because the term *ītaḥ* ("ending in *ī*") continues [from the previous rule]. Thus, it refers to a river-name that does not end in *ī* and a monosyllabic word ending in *ī*. Furthermore, the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) could even be omitted. How so? Because [the application of the suffixes] *gha* and the others would apply without distinction.

The general rule (*utsarga*) is that for the word *nadī*, there is optionally (*anyatarasyām*) shortening (*hrasvatvam*). The exception (*apavāda*) is that for a word with more than one vowel (*anekāc*), shortening is obligatory (*nityam*). When that obligatory [shortening] has been reached, the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) regarding words ending in *ugit* is commenced. If this were so, forms such as *lakṣmitarā* and *tantritarā* would not be established; rather, *lakṣmītarā* and *tantrītarā* would result. However, this very [result] is intended and thus correctly included.

It must be *lakṣmītarā* and *tantrītarā*. For the followers of Śākatayana read thus: "When the shortening of the vowel of a *nadī* [stem] occurs before suffixes beginning with *gh*, there is a prohibition of that shortening for a *nadī* [stem] ending in a *kṛt* suffix.
Why does this not apply here?

"The moon, which was not great, has become great; it is the 'Great Being' (mahadbhūta). But that which is of a different nature—being "not great" (amahān)—becomes "great" (mahān) when it exists within the category of the Great (mahatprakṛtau), that is, within the Great itself.

One is "great" [by nature], while another is "great" as it exists within the category of beings (bhūtaprakṛtau). [In the latter case,] the "great" exists only within the Great. Therefore, the substitution of *ā* (āttvam) should not occur; therefore, the substitution of *ā* will not take place. But how can there be the treatment as a masculine (puṃvattvam)?

In this case, even so, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would not be obtained: *amahatī mahatī saṃpannā mahadbhūtā brāhmaṇī* ("a Brāhmaṇī woman who was not great has become great"). If that is so, then [the objection remains]: in "not great" (*amahati*), the word "great" (*mahat*) indeed occurs, and here the word *bhūta* expresses that very thing.
For the word "great" (*mahat*) applies to what is not great, and here the word *bhūta* is employed to express that same thing. What, then, does it express?

[The word] *mahat* [is used] in the sense of greatness. Therefore, the masculine form is established; therefore, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is established. If this were so, then the substitution of *ā* (*āttva*) would also apply: as in *mahadbhūtaś candramāḥ* ("the moon has become great"). However, they consider that the substitution of *ā* must be set aside. [Objection: But the substitution of *ā* would still apply. [Response: This is not a fault. For that which was stated as a specific rule (*pratipadam*) regarding the compound of *mahat*, it is indeed based upon that.

They consider that the substitution of *āt* (the long vowel) should be applied; however, this [term *mahābāhu*] is mentioned by way of a grammatical definition (*lakṣaṇa*). If that is the case, then according to the principle that "between what is mentioned by a definition and what is mentioned by its specific form, the latter alone is taken," it would follow that only a compound specifically prescribed by its own rule is included. But this term is mentioned by way of a definition. Consequently, even in this instance, the rule would not apply: for example, in the case of *mahān bāhur asya mahābāhuḥ*. [The answer is: It does apply, because of the mention of the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*).

However, that *bahuvrīhi* which is formed through the rule of "recommencement" (*pratyārambha*) is established in that case; since it is already established by the rule "the *bahuvrīhi* is for the remainder" (*śeṣo bahuvrīhiḥ*), he says "many [words] in the sense of another word" (*anekam anyapadārthe*), whereby it applies to every specific instance. Or, because the compound occurs primarily based on the principal element. Or else, between the secondary and the primary, the operation is understood to apply to the primary. For example, [the word] "cow" (*gauḥ*).

The rule "the goat to be bound for Agni and Soma is called *anubandhya*" does not apply to a *bāhīka* (a person from the borderlands). How then do the terms *vṛddhi* and *ātva* apply to a *bāhīka*, as in "the *gauḥ* stands" or "bring the *gām*"? This occurs when the basis is the meaning (*arthāśraya*). For that which depends on the word (*śabdāśraya*) applies only to the word itself; and the rules for *vṛddhi* and *ātva* depend on the word.

(P_6,3.46.2) An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the words *mahat* and *ātta* when they are followed by *ghāsa*, *kara*, or *viśiṣṭa*; and the rule of masculine-like behavior (*puṃvadbhāva*) must also be applied for the sake of non-co-referentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇa*). An addition must be made for *mahat* and *ātta* when followed by *ghāsa*, *kara*, or *viśiṣṭa*, and the masculine-like behavior must also be applied for the sake of non-co-referentiality. For example: *mahatyāḥ ghāsaḥ* becomes *mahāghāsaḥ*.

The hand of a great person is *mahākara*; one who is distinguished among the great is *mahāviśiṣṭa*. Regarding the rule "after *aṣṭan*, [the suffix *ṭac* is added] when *kapāla* follows, provided it refers to an oblation (*havis*)," an addition must be made: "after *aṣṭan*, [the suffix *ṭac* is added] when *kapāla* follows, provided it refers to an oblation.
One should offer a sacrificial pap (*caru*) on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapālam*). Why specify "when it refers to an oblation"? [Consider: "eight potsherds for a Brāhmaṇa" (*aṣṭakapālam brāhmaṇasya*).

And [the suffix] must be added when "yukta" (yoked) follows "go" (cow). One should provide an addition for the case of "go" being followed by "yukta," as in *aṣṭāgavena śakaṭena* (a cart yoked with eight oxen). For what purpose is "yukta" mentioned? [To exclude cases such as] *aṣṭagavaṃ brāhmaṇasya* (eight oxen belonging to a Brahmin).
It should be stated that [this applies] prior to the hundred; let it not apply here: *dviśatam* (two hundred).
Two thousand,
eight hundred,
and eight thousand.

(P_6,3.48) KA_III.161.20–162.3 Ro_IV.629: What is the purpose of mentioning "all" (*sarveṣām*)? It is so that the option (*vibhāṣā*) may apply to all [numerals] from forty onwards, including *dvi*, *aṣṭan*, and *tri*. This is not a necessary purpose, because the mention of *dvi* and *aṣṭan* from the preceding context will continue to apply here. If that [mention] continues, then by the rule "for *tri* there is *trayaḥ*, and for *dvi* and *aṣṭan* as well," the substitution of *trayaḥ* would also apply to *dvi* and *aṣṭan*.

[The objection: "It follows [that the rule applies everywhere]. [Response: This fault does not arise. The governing rules (*adhikāras*) proceed like the movements of frogs; just as frogs move by leaping again and again, so too do the governing rules. Alternatively, a single yoga (sūtra) will be composed: "In a numeral, for *dvi* and *aṣṭan*, except in a *bahuvrīhi* or before *aśīti*;
for *tri*, [the substitute] *trayaḥ*; then optionally for all [numerals] beginning with forty. Or else, both [previous conditions] are withdrawn, and we shall rely upon that.

This mention of *yaṇ* is a mention of a suffix (*pratyaya*). In that context, according to the rule "when there is a mention of a suffix, there is a mention of that [suffix] and what begins with it," the application would occur when the suffix *aṇ* follows *yat*. Regarding the mention of *yadaṇ*, it is a mention of the form (*rūpa*), because of the mention of *lekha*. When there is a mention of *yadaṇ*, it should be understood as a mention of the form. Why? Because of the mention of *lekha*.

The fact that he employs the term *lekha* (writing) indicates that the Teacher [Pāṇini] does not intend for [the suffix] to occur when it ends in *aṇ*. Another says: "This is stated too little. In every case under the heading of 'subsequent member' (*uttarapada*), when there is a mention of a suffix, it should be understood as a mention of its form. Why? Precisely because of the mention of *lekha*. What is the purpose? [For example: *kumārī gauritarā* (a girl who is more white). This applies to the *gha*-class and others.

If it were taught that "the [final vowel] of *nadī* becomes short," then shortness would apply [inappropriately]. If this [rule] were to be indicated by the statement "of a non-indeclinable [ending] in *khiti*," then shortness would apply only to a non-indeclinable immediately preceding a *khiti* suffix. However, since there is no non-indeclinable immediately preceding a *khiti* suffix that is subject to become short, [the rule] will apply to that which ends in *khid*. But is there not such a case as *stanandhayaḥ*? In this instance...

There is indeed an intervention by the suffix *śap*. Once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, there is no intervention. However, because of the rule that "a single substitute is treated as the original in the formation of what precedes it" (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is indeed an intervention. Alternatively, the Teacher indicates this:

that [the suffix] does not apply immediately after a *khit* ending, since he teaches the prohibition "not after an indeclinable" (*anavyayasya*). For [the suffix] does not apply after a *khit* ending.
Immediately after, there is the indeclinable *avyayam*. (P_6,3.52) Regarding the substitution of *pada*, there is the technical designation (*nipātana*) of being oxytone.

[R: for the sake of the meaning of "struck by a word"]. In the case of the substitution of *pada*, the technical designation of being oxytone must be applied. What is the purpose? For the sake of the meaning of "struck by a word" (*padopahata*).

*Padopahataṃ* means "struck by the foot. The rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi* [Pāṇini 6.2.48] applies so that the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) may result in the final syllable of the first member being udātta. Furthermore, the statement "it should be treated as if it were taught" (*upadeśivadvacana*) is for the sake of establishing the accent. One must state that there is a treatment as if it were taught (*upadeśivadbhāva*). What is the purpose? For the sake of establishing the accent. Once the designation of the final syllable as udātta has been applied during the stage of the original teaching (*upadeśāvasthā*), the accent of the compound (*samāsasvara*) [takes effect].

So that there may be the substitution of *pad* [for *pāda*], as in *padājiḥ* and *padātiḥ*. (P_6.3.53) Regarding the substitution of *pad* before the suffix *ika* when it means "moving," an addition must be made: an addition must be made for the substitution of *pad* before *ika* in the sense of "moving. As in *pādābhyāṃ carati padikaḥ* ("he moves on foot"). An addition must also be made regarding the word *niṣka*: [an addition must be made] regarding *niṣka*. As in *panniṣkeṇa* and *pādaniṣkeṇa*.

It should be stated that [the rule] "of the second member" (*uttarapadasya*) applies when it is a name (*sañjñāyām*), so that it may also apply here in cases such as *lohitodaḥ* ("Red-water") and *kṣīrodaḥ* ("Milk-water").
For what purpose is the phrase "beginning with a single consonant" (*ekahalādau*)? [To exclude cases like] *udakasthānam* ("water-place").

Even when this [rule] is stated, it would still apply here; for this [word *gaur*] also begins with a single consonant (*ekahalādi*). What is the reason? Because speech resides in each individual phoneme (*varṇa*) and because phonemes perish as soon as they are uttered. Speech resides in one phoneme at a time; one does not utter two phonemes simultaneously. For example, when "gauḥ" is spoken, as long as the speech resides in the phoneme *ga*, it does not reside in the phoneme *au*.

Not in the case of *visarjanīya*. As long as there is no *au* or *a* phoneme, so long there is no *ga* phoneme and no *visarjanīya*. As long as there is no *visarjanīya*, so long there is no *ga* or *au* phoneme. This is because phonemes perish as soon as they are uttered; a phoneme, once uttered, has perished. Then another [phoneme] is employed. One phoneme is not an assistant to another phoneme. If that is so, then...

It is stated [in the rule] "beginning with a single consonant" (*ekahalādi*), yet every [compound] begins with a single consonant. In that case, a sense of excellence (*prakarṣa*) is understood: "that which begins with a single consonant more effectively. And what is more effective? That in which, after pronouncing a single consonant, a vowel (*ac*) is pronounced. (P. 6.3.61) The shortening of *ik* applies only when the second member (*uttarapada*) alone follows. The shortening of *ik* must be stated as applying only when the second member follows, so that it may also occur here: *śunaḥ skandhaḥ* → *śuṣkaṇdhaḥ*. *śunaḥ pucchaḥ* → *śupucchaḥ*. *śunaḥ phalam* → *śuphalam*. [Objection: Why is it not stated simply as "the shortening of *ik* occurs when the second member follows"? [Response: If it were stated thus, then in the case of *śunaḥ phalāni*, because the word *phala* is a neuter plural ending in *-āni*, the shortening would not apply. Therefore, it is stated as "only when the second member alone follows," so that the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*. [Objection: Even if it is stated as "only when the second member alone follows," the same fault remains; for in *śunaḥ phalāni*, since the word *phala* is a neuter plural ending in *-āni*, the shortening would still not apply. [Response: This is not a fault. For the word *mātra* in the expression *uttarapadamātre* is used in the sense of "exclusively" (*avadhāraṇa*). Thus, the meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when the second member alone follows, and not when it is accompanied by other words. Consequently, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "measure" (*parimāṇa*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when the measure of the second member is exactly one word. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there the measure of the second member is not exactly one word. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "mere" (*kevala*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when the second member is merely a single word. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there the second member is not merely a single word. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "non-excess" (*anatyaya*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when there is no excess over the second member. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there there is an excess over the second member. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "limit" (*maryādā*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only up to the limit of the second member. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there the shortening has not reached the limit of the second member. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "non-separation" (*aviyoga*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when there is no separation from the second member. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there there is a separation from the second member. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "non-distinction" (*avibhāga*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when there is no distinction from the second member. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there there is a distinction from the second member. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "non-difference" (*abheda*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when there is no difference from the second member. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there there is a difference from the second member. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "non-diversity" (*avaicitrya*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when there is no diversity from the second member. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there there is a diversity from the second member. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "non-mixture" (*asaṃsarga*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when there is no mixture with the second member. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there there is a mixture with the second member. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "non-combination" (*asaṃprayoga*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when there is no combination with the second member. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there there is a combination with the second member. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "non-connection" (*asaṃbandha*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when there is no connection with the second member. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there there is a connection with the second member. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "non-dependence" (*anapekṣā*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when there is no dependence on the second member. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there there is a dependence on the second member. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "non-relation" (*asambandha*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when there is no relation to the second member. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there there is a relation to the second member. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "non-attachment" (*asaṅga*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when there is no attachment to the second member. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there there is an attachment to the second member. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "non-union" (*asaṃyoga*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when there is no union with the second member. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there there is a union with the second member. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "non-conjunction" (*asaṃnipāta*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when there is no conjunction with the second member. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there there is a conjunction with the second member. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "non-coexistence" (*asahabhāva*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when there is no coexistence with the second member. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there there is a coexistence with the second member. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "non-simultaneity" (*ayugapadbhāva*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when there is no simultaneity with the second member. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there there is a simultaneity with the second member. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "non-identity" (*atādātmya*). The meaning is: "the shortening occurs only when there is no identity with the second member. Therefore, the shortening does not occur in *śunaḥ phalāni*, because there there is an identity with the second member. Alternatively, the word *mātra* is used in the sense of "non-difference-in-meaning" (*abhinna-arthatva*). The meaning is

"Alābukarkandhudṛnbhuphala. What, then, is the reason it is not established? Because the world's understanding [of compound formation] occurs at the very end; for according to the world's understanding, the shortening of the preceding member would apply only to that word which stands at the very end of the entire compound. Alternatively, the analysis (vigraha) may be made thus: "alābūśca karkandhūśca," [and so on].
alābu and karkandhu; alābu, karkandhu, and dṛnbhū; alābu, karkandhu, and dṛnbhvaḥ.

In the compound *alābukarkandhudṛnbhūnām phalam*, [the analysis is] *alābukarkandhudṛnbhūnām phalam*. If this were the case, the rule for prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) would require that *dṛnbhū* come first. [To avoid this,] it will be included in the list beginning with *rājadanta* (Pāṇini 2.2.31). Alternatively, the analysis will be made thus: the fruit of the *dṛnbhū* is *dṛnbhuphalam*.
*Karkandhūś ca dṛnbhuphalam ca* becomes *karkandhudṛnbhuphalam*;

*alābūś ca karkandhudṛnbhuphalam ca* becomes *alābukarkandhudṛnbhuphalam*. Even so, the connection with the word "fruit" (*phala*) is not established [as a compound]. The word *phala* is completed [as a separate item] with each preceding member. This is the prohibition of the *iyaṅ*, *uvaṅ*, and indeclinable (*avyaya*) substitutions.
A prohibition must be stated for the forms *iyaṅ*, *uvaṅ*, and *bhā* (the feminine suffix), as well as for indeclinables: *śrīkulam*, *bhrūkulam*,
and *kāṇḍībhūtaṃ vṛṣalakulam*.
The term *vṛṣala* (low-born) becomes *kuḍya* (wall). It should be stated that this applies to *bhrūkaṃsa* and others: *bhrukuṃsaḥ*, *bhrukuṭiḥ*. Another says:
it should be stated that the vowel *a* [is substituted] for *bhrūkaṃsa* and others: *bhrakuṃsaḥ*, *bhrakuṭiḥ*.

(P_6,3.62) KA_III.164.21 Ro_IV.635-636 What is an example [of this rule] regarding *taddhita* suffixes? "Oneness" (*ekatvam*), "oneness-ness" (*ekatā*). This is not a valid purpose, for this is already established by the rule of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment). How is there *puṃvadbhāva*? It occurs in the case of suffixes beginning with *tāsi* and ending with *kṛtvasuc*. Then what is the purpose? [The examples are]: "that which has come from one" (*ekasyā āgatam*) = *ekarūpyam*.

"Consisting of one" (*ekamaya*). This too is an example: "oneness" (*ekatva*), "the state of being one" (*ekatā*). But was it not said that this is already established by the rule for *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment)? It is not established. For it has been stated that [the rule applies] to a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) before the suffixes *-tva* and *-tal*. Now, what is an example when there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*)? "A single garment" (*ekaśāṭī*). This is not the case.

This is also established by means of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment). How is there *puṃvadbhāva*? It is characterized by having a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*). In that case, this is the purpose: *ekasyāḥ kṣīram* becomes *ekaṣīram*. And this is also an example: *ekaśāṭī*.
But was it not said that this is also established by *puṃvadbhāva*? It is not established; for [the rule] *na kopadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.37) prohibits it.

Thus, a prohibition would result. This is not a fault. For it has been stated [in the *Vārttika*] that in the prohibition regarding words ending in *kup*, there is an inclusion of the *taddhita* suffix *vuñ*.

(P. 6.3.66) The short vowel (*hrasva*) is not established in the case of the *khiti* suffix because the word does not end in a consonant (*anajantatvāt*). There is no establishment of the short vowel in the case of the *khiti* suffix, as in *kālimmanyā* and *hariṇimmanyā*. What is the reason? Because it does not end in a consonant. Once the augment *mum* has been applied, because it no longer ends in a consonant, the shortening of the vowel does not occur.

[The objection: It follows [that *mum* would apply even to long vowels]. [The reply: But it is established by the statement that *mum* applies to that which ends in a short vowel. This is established. How? It should be stated: "*mum* occurs for that which ends in a short vowel. Or else, by way of simultaneous prescription (*sanniyoga*). Alternatively, a simultaneous prescription will be made. What kind of effort is this being urged, called "simultaneous prescription"? The particle *ca* ("and") must be employed: "*mum* and [whatever else follows]. And what else? Whatever else [is prescribed].
It follows [the shortening]. And what else follows? Shortness (*hrasvatva*). It is established. But then the *sūtra* is violated.
Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. But was it not said: "Shortness is not established in the presence of *khit*, because [the stem] does not end in a vowel"?
This has been answered: "But it is established by the mention of *mum* for that which ends in a short vowel. Therefore, that mention of "short" (*hrasva*) [is necessary].

It should be applied; it should not be applied. The subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) continues. Where is the subject under discussion? It is "the *ika* vowel of an *aṅga* becomes short, according to Gālava. Now, that [rule] was stated in the nominative case, whereas here [in the present rule], there is a need for the genitive case. This word "in a *khit* suffix" (*khiti*), being in the locative case, will cause the nominative "short" (*hrasvaḥ*) to be understood as a genitive; for when something is indicated by the locative (*tasmin nirdiṣṭe*), [it governs the preceding element].

Regarding the word "pūrvasya" (of the preceding): Alternatively, it is stated that "there is shortening before a *khid* suffix. Since there is no [suffix] ending in *khid* that actually undergoes shortening, this must be understood as referring to what previously existed (*bhūtapūrvagati*). That is, it refers to that which previously ended in a vowel (*ajanta*). Or else, according to the principle that technical rules (*saṃjñā*) and interpretive rules (*paribhāṣā*) are applied at the time the operation (*kāryakāla*), the rule "there is shortening before a *khid*" should be regarded as being present wherever the operation occurs. Thus, [the rule] stands ready.

This [rule] is "acaḥ" (of a vowel). In that case, by virtue of the explicit statement, it will apply even to that which does not end in a vowel. But then, by virtue of the same statement, it would also apply here: *vāṅmanyaḥ*. This is not so; for the word "ikaḥ" (of a semi-vowel or a short vowel) is understood to carry over. Even so, it would not apply here: *khaṭvammanyaḥ*. This is not a fault, because the mention of "āp" (the feminine suffix -ā) is also understood as being carried over from the previous rule. Where was it introduced? In the rule "ṅyāpoḥ sañjñācchandasoḥ bahulam" (the substitution of ām for feminine stems ending in ṅī or āp occurs diversely in names and in the Veda). Even so, it would not apply here: *kīlālapammanyaḥ*.

One who considers [the suffix] *am* to be auspicious does not obtain [the desired result] here; therefore, the two solutions previously stated remain valid. (P_6.3.68.1) What is the purpose of treating *am* like an affix (*pratyayavat*) in this designation? The purpose of treating *am* like an affix in this designation is [to ensure the application of] the substitution of *ā* (*ātvam*), the homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*), the *guṇa* substitute, and the substitutes *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*. [This applies] in the treatment of *am* as being like an affix.

The substitution of *ātva*, the *pūrvasavarṇa* (homogeneous with the preceding vowel), *guṇa*, *iyaṅ*, and *uvaṅ* are the purposes [of the rule]. *Ātva* is a purpose: *gāmmanyaḥ*. The *pūrvasavarṇa* is a purpose:

*strīmmanyaḥ*. *Guṇa* is a purpose: *narammanyaḥ*. *Iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are purposes: *śriyammanyaḥ*, *bhruvammanyaḥ*. [Objection: If the suffix *am* were designated as being like a suffix (*pratyayavat*), there would be no establishment of *ātva* and *pūrvasavarṇa*, because it is not a nominative case (*aprathamātva*).

In the extension [of the rule] "like the affix" (*pratyayavat*), there would be non-establishment of the substitution of *ā* and the homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*). What is the reason? Because it is not the first case.

It is stated [in the sūtra] "of the first two," and we do not see the first case here. Furthermore, sir, is it said that the substitution of *ā* applies "to the first two"? Certainly not; it is not said "to the first two. Rather, it is understood as "of the first two. How so?

It is stated: "of *am* and *śas*. We shall understand it thus: that which is the word *am* accompanied by *śas*. And what is accompanied by *śas*? Only the nominative (*prathamā*). But surely it will be established through the extension (*anudeśa*) of the suffixes? It is not established. For what reason? Because in the case of an extension of a general property...
For there is no transfer of particulars. When a general property is being transferred, the particular is not transferred.

For example: "One should behave toward this Kṣatriya as one does toward a Brāhmaṇa. In this case, that which is the duty of a Brāhmaṇa—the general—is transferred to the Kṣatriya; however, that which is specific [to individuals], such as [the behavior toward] Māṭhara or Kauṇḍinya, is not transferred. Thus it is.

In this case as well, that which is common—the function of producing a cognition—is extended [by analogy], but that which is specific—namely, the rule "in the first two cases" (*prathamayoḥ*) which applies to the singular of the second case (*dvitīyaikavacana*)—is not extended. However, this is established by stating "like the singular of the second case. How so? It should be stated: "it becomes like the singular of the second case," because of the indication through *ekaśeṣa* (the grammatical device of retaining only one of several identical words).

Or rather, this is an indication by means of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member): *am* and *am* [are both referred to as] *am*. Thus, for a monosyllabic stem ending in *ic*, there is the substitution of *am*, and the operations prescribed for the suffix *am* apply to it.
Now, how should it be in this case: *śriyam ātmānam*?
Regarding the form *brāhmaṇakulam*: is it *śriyammanyam* or *śrimanyam*? It ought to be *śriyammanyam*.

Why does the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *svamoḥ napuṃsakāt* not occur here? [The answer is: The suffix *am* is introduced even before the elision (*luk*) has taken effect; therefore, just as it sets aside the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*, so too does it set aside the rule *svamoḥ napuṃsakāt*.

This [rule] would subvert the luk-elision; it does not subvert it. What is the reason? Because subversion occurs only when [the rule being subverted] has already become applicable. This [present rule] is commenced while that rule—"supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ"—is not yet applicable. However, the rule "svamoḥ napuṃsakāt" is both applicable and non-applicable. Alternatively, intermediate exceptions (apavāda) subvert the preceding rules.

Thus, this [rule] subverts the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*, but it will not subvert the rule *svamoḥ napuṃsakāt*. If that is so, then by the principle that "that which is external (bahiraṅga) is considered unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal (antaraṅga)," the elision (*luk*) characterized as internal will not occur because the *ām* characterized as external is unestablished. However, this maxim cannot be applied within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning the subsequent member of a compound.

In order to understand [the rule], for here a fault would arise: in *dviṣantapaḥ* and *parantapaḥ*, the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would not occur. Therefore, it must be *śrimanyam*. Let there be [an addition] regarding the word *kāra* following *astu-satya-agada*. An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) should be made for *kāra* after *astu-satya-agada*: *astuṅkāraḥ*, [satyaṅkāraḥ, agadaṅkāraḥ].

*satyaṅkāraḥ*, *agadaṅkāraḥ*. Regarding *bhakṣa* in the Veda (*chandas*): an addition must be made for *bhakṣa* in the Veda. [The example is] *tasya te bhakṣaṅkārasya*. Why "in the Veda"? [Counter-example: *bhakṣakārasya tat matam*. Regarding *dhenu* when followed by *bhavyā*.

An addition should be made for *dhenu-bhavyā*. [Example: *dhenumbhavyā*. An addition should be made for *lokasya-pṛṇe*. [Example: *lokamprṇasya dhanvinaḥ*. An addition should be made for *itye anabhyāśasya*. [Example: *anabhyāśamityaḥ*. [An addition should be made] for *bhrāṣṭrāgnyoḥ indhe*. [Example: *bhrāṣṭramindhaḥ*, *agnimindhaḥ*.

The addition of *indh-* must be stated [as a rule]. Examples: *bhrāṣṭramindhaḥ* (one who kindles a frying pan), *agnimindhaḥ* (one who kindles a fire). Regarding *gila-* [the rule] "of that which is not *gila*" must be stated as an addition. Example: *timiṅgilaḥ* (the fish that swallows whales). Why "of that which is not *gila*" (*agilasya*)? Example: *gilagilaḥ* (one who swallows a swallower). It should be stated: "and also after *gilagila*. Example: *timiṅgilagilaḥ* (one who swallows a *timiṅgila*).

Regarding the formation of *uṣṇaṃkaraṇa* and *bhadraṃkaraṇa*: an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the case of *uṣṇa* and *bhadra*. [The forms] *uṣṇaṃkaraṇa* and *bhadraṃkaraṇa* [are thus established]. Regarding the rule "after *sūta*, *ugra*, *rājan*, *bhojakula*, and *meru*, the suffix *putraṭ* optionally occurs after the word *duhitṛ*": it should be stated that after *sūta*, *ugra*, *rājan*, *bhojakula*, and *meru*, the suffix *putraṭ* optionally occurs after *duhitṛ*. [Thus: *sūtaduhitṛ* (or *sūtaputra*).
The daughter of a fierce man, the daughter of a fierce woman, the daughter of a king.
the king's daughter,
the son of the Bhoja, the daughter of the Bhoja.
Noble daughter,
noble daughter,
daughter of Meru!
*meruduhitā*.

(P_6.3.72) Is this an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding what is already established, or rather regarding what is not yet established? And how is it established, or how is it not established? It is either established by the rule *khiti* as obligatory, or not established elsewhere.

Regarding *rātreḥ*: when not yet applied, it is optional; when already applied, the rule is obligatory. Thus, we have *rātrimmanyaḥ*. When not yet applied, it is optional: *rātryaṭaḥ* or *rātrimaṭaḥ*.

(P_6,3.73) KA_III.168.22–169.8 Ro_IV.642–643: For what purpose is the inclusion of the *nañ* with its anubandha made? Why not simply say "of *na*" (*nasya*)? If it were said "of *na*," it would also apply in the case of *varṇaputraḥ*. This is not a fault; for when there is a mention of a meaningful element (*arthavagrahaṇa*), that which is meaningless (*anarthaka*) is not included, and thus this will not occur. Even so, [it would still apply] in the case of *praśnaputraḥ*.

[Objection: In this case as well, [the rule] would apply to *viśna-putraḥ*. [Reply: This is not a fault. According to the principle that "when a term without an *anubandha* is mentioned, it does not include one with an *anubandha*," this will not occur. [Objection: Even so, it would still apply in cases such as *vāmana-putraḥ* and *pāmana-putraḥ*. Therefore, the mention of the form with the *anubandha* must be made. [Addendum: An addition must be made for the elision of the *n* of *nañ* when a finite verb (*tiṅ*) follows in the sense of contempt (*avakṣepa*). An addition must be made for the elision of the *n* of *nañ* when a finite verb follows in the sense of contempt.
[The suffix] *kṛtya* [is applied]. "O wretch, you indeed do not cook" (*apacasi vai tvam jālma*). "O wretch, you indeed did not do it" (*akaroṣi vai tvam jālma*).

For what purpose is it stated as *tasmāt* ("after that")? Could it not simply be stated as *nuṭ aci* ("*nuṭ* after a vowel")? If it were stated as *nuṭ aci*, the augment *nuṭ* would apply only to *nañ*. Therefore, in this case, it is a *pūrvānta* (an element added at the end of the preceding item).

It will be so performed. In that regard, this is the meaning: the mention of *tadoḥ* (the genitive dual of *tad*) in the rule *tadoḥ saḥ sau anantyayoḥ* need not be made. For in that context, when there is a reference to the *tavarga* (the dental class), this purpose [of the mention] is to prevent it from occurring here in cases such as *aneṣaḥ karoti*.
To the extent that [the *s*] is a prior boundary (*pūrvānta*), that too is free from fault. It cannot be said thus; for in the case of *anuṣṇaḥ*, there would be the elision of *n* (*nalopa*).

By the rule *prātipadikāntasya*, the elision of the *n* would apply [to the final *n* of *rājñām*]. It will not occur because of the explicit mention of *nu*. In that case, however, the augment *ṅamuṭ* would apply. Therefore, it must be treated as part of the subsequent element (*parādi*). And when it is made part of the subsequent element, it must be stated that [the operation applies] "after that" (*tasmāt*). (P_6.3.76) KA_III.169.18–170.4 Ro_IV.644–645 For what purpose is *āduK* prescribed? Why not simply *aduK*? What is the resulting form?

"Ekānnaviṃśatiḥ" (nineteen) and "ekānnaśatam" (ninety-nine)—this is established by the rule for the lengthening of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*). It is not established; because of the rule *guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) would apply. If that is the case, then it will be stated as *aduṭ*. But *aduṭ* cannot be formulated, for nasalization (*ānunāsikya*) does not [apply here].

It would be so; for that [rule]—"when a non-nasal follows a *y* or *r*, a nasal may optionally occur"—is indeed restricted by the condition "of a word-final [consonant]. But what is the reason for this restriction to a word-final [consonant]? So that it does not apply here: *budhnaḥ*, *bradhnaḥ*.
[The rule] *badhnāti* [is applied]. If that is so, then *anuṭ* will be applied. But *anuṭ* cannot be applied. [Let there be] optional nasality (*ānunāsikya*).

By that, this form alone would result: *ekānnaviṃśatiḥ*. This form would not result: *ekānnaviṃśatiḥ*. Let it be, then, simply *aduk*. But was it not said that by the rule *ataḥ guṇe*, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) would apply? No, this is not so.
There is a fault. [Objection: It will not occur because of the functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the utterance of the vowel *a*. [Response:

Therefore, he recites the following answer: "The mention of *kvip* in the case of *añcati* and the *nahyādi* group is purposeless, because when there is a grammatical operation (*vidhi*), the reference to an *al* (vowel) pertains to that which begins with it. Three who are contemptible are *kattrayaḥ*. Or, what are these three? "Three who do not support [themselves] are *kattrayaḥ*. It is said: "The words beginning with *pṛṣodara* [are irregular]. What are the words beginning with *pṛṣodara*?

"Words of the *pṛṣodara* type. What, then, are words of the *pṛṣodara* type? Those in which elisions (*lopa*), augmentations (*āgama*), and modifications (*vikāra*) are heard, yet are not explicitly stated [by rule]. Now, what is this "as" (*yathā*)? It is the suffix *thāl* used in the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*). Now, what is this "taught" (*upadiṣṭa*)? It means "pronounced" (*uccārita*). Why so? Because the root *diś* has the action of pronunciation as its meaning. For having pronounced the phonemes, one says, "they have been taught" (*upadiṣṭāḥ*).

"These are the phonemes. By whom, then, were they taught? By the *śiṣṭas* (the refined). Who, then, are the *śiṣṭas*? The grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*). Why is this so? For refinement is preceded by the science (*śāstra*), and the grammarians are those who know the science. If, then, refinement is preceded by the science and the science is preceded by refinement, that results in a circular dependency (*itaretarāśraya*). And things that involve circular dependencies [are untenable].
They do not apply. If that is so, then [the term applies] by way of residence and conduct. And that conduct exists only in Āryāvarta.

But what is Āryāvarta? It is the region east of the Adarśa (or Adarśana) mountains, west of the Kālaka forest, south of the Himavat, and north of the Pāriyātra range. In this abode of the Āryas, those Brāhmaṇas who possess grain only in their jars and are free from greed—
Those venerable ones who have mastered some branch of knowledge without perceiving its specific cause are the *śiṣṭas* (the cultured).

If, then, the *śiṣṭas* are the authority regarding words, what is the purpose of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*? The *Aṣṭādhyāyī* is for the sake of making known who the *śiṣṭas* are. But how can the *śiṣṭas* be identified by means of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*? One who is studying the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* observes another [who has already mastered it].

He observes one who employs those words prescribed here that he has not studied. [He thinks: "Surely there is a divine favor or an innate disposition in him, since he employs the words prescribed in this [grammar] even though he does not study the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*. Surely he knows others as well. Thus, the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* is for the purpose of knowing the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
