[The rule applies] only when *śau* follows; then [only] when *sau* follows; and only when *sau* follows. In that case, even here, it would not apply by virtue of the restriction: *indraḥ vṛtrahāyate*. [Reply: There is no fault regarding the prescription of lengthening (*dīrghavidhi*) in the case of *me*, *hanta*, and *yi*. The restriction concerns lengthening characterized by the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), and this lengthening is not characterized by the penultimate vowel. This is so even in the case of *suṭ*.

Alternatively, the restriction (*niyama*) regarding *śi* has no scope (*anavakāśa*) within the present context; it will serve as a regulator for the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) even of that which is not under discussion. Or rather, while the term "sarvanāmasthāna" is being carried over [from the previous rule], the restriction regarding *śi* has no scope; it will be the regulator for the lengthening even of that which is not under discussion. How so? For that which has a restriction regarding *śi*, this [restriction] does not apply when *suṭ* is present; therefore, it would not be subject to regulation there. For that which has *śi*...

That which has *suṭ* does not have a *sarvanāmasthāna* [ending]; that which has *suṭ* does not have *śi*. Since there is no restriction established within this section on *sarvanāmasthāna*, it should be understood that the restriction applies without distinction to the *śi* ending. Having restricted here the rule for lengthening vowels (*dīrghavidhi*) that applies to *in* and so forth by specifying "when *suṭ* follows," the learned one should then likewise establish the restriction for the *śi* ending.

In the case of *bhrūṇahan*, it would likewise not be faulty [to apply the rule]. Or, having set aside the teaching [of Pāṇini 6.1.70] by saying "in *suṭ*," you might establish a restriction for *śi* without due consideration. Alas! Because of the restriction on the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) in the rule prescribing lengthening, there is no fault in my view regarding the prescription of lengthening in *yi*. Alternatively, even if *suṭ* is the subject under discussion, the restriction for *śi* has no scope; it serves to prohibit that which was not previously established. For that which...
The restriction [of the suffix *su*] applies when *suṭ* is present; therefore, that [restriction] would not apply there [in the case of *su*]. (P.

6.4.14) An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the long vowel of a stem ending in *at* or *asant* before a *pit* [suffix]. An addition must be made for the long vowel of a stem ending in *at* or *asant* before a *pit* [suffix]:
*gomān*, [yavamān].

The form *yavamān*. But what is the reason it is not established? For when there is a mention of a [term] without an *anubandha*, there is no mention of one with an *anubandha*; thus, [the suffix] *pit* would not apply. It is said, "when there is a mention of a [term] without an *anubandha*," yet this is a mention of one with an *anubandha*. If that is so, then when there is a mention of a [term] with that specific *anubandha*, there is no mention of one without that *anubandha*.

In this way, [the suffix] *pit* is not obtained. If that is so, then that supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be formulated. It need not be formulated. Once the letter *p* has been elided, it is no longer something ending in *at*, but rather something ending in *at*. Just as, when the letter *p* is elided, it is no longer something ending in *at*, so too, when the letter *u* is elided, it is no longer something ending in *at*. But surely, by way of its former state, it will still be considered something ending in *at*?

If that is so, then just as the form ending in *at* is accepted on the basis of its former state (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*), so too should the form ending in *atu* be accepted. If this is the case, then when relying upon the former state, one relies on the form ending in *at* and not on the form ending in *atu*; thus, it is not established. For in this grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), in all instances where there is a mention of a term with an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*), the actual phonetic form (*rūpa*) is what is relied upon.

Regarding the statement "wherein this is its form," the apprehension of a form does not occur without worldly usage (*laukika-prayoga*). And since in that worldly usage there is no usage of [words] accompanied by *anubandhas*, a second usage is resorted to. What is that? It is called "instruction" (*upadeśa*). And in instruction, this [word] ends in *at* (the suffix *ap*), not in *at* (the suffix *ac*). However, if it were the word *at*...

[Objection: One might say that [the suffix] is taken [as part of the whole] to express length. [Reply: This is not possible; for then it would follow here as well: *jagat* and *janagat*. [Objection: By the rule "when a meaningful element is mentioned, that which is meaningless is not included," this will not apply there. [Reply: In that case, it would still not apply here: *kṛtavān* and *bhuktavān*. [Question: Where, then, would it apply? [Answer: In *pacan*.

[If one were to] perform [the sacrifice], it is certainly not desired here. One would obtain what is undesired, and what is desired would not be accomplished. Therefore, a supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made.

Regarding the lengthening of the vowel in *gami*, the mention of *iṅ* is required. In the case of the lengthening of the vowel in *gami*, the mention of *iṅ* must be made. It should be stated as *iṅgameḥ*. This is so that [the lengthening] does not occur here: [in cases such as *gamayati*].

"The calf desires to go with its mother"—in this case, if *iṅ* were not included [in the rule], there would be the undesirable consequence of lengthening even for that which is not a substitute (*anādeśa*). For if the inclusion of *iṅ* were not made, lengthening would apply even to what is not a substitute, as in: "The calf desires to go with its mother. Alternatively, the inclusion of *iṅ* is unnecessary because in Vedic usage (*chandasi*), lengthening is observed even for that which is not a substitute. Thus, the inclusion of *iṅ* is not required.

It must be stated. What is the reason? Because in the Vedic language (*chandas*), lengthening is observed even where there is no formal rule (*anādeśa*). In the Vedic language, lengthening is seen even for the root *gam* where there is no formal rule: *svargam lokam sañjigāṃsat*. Since lengthening is observed in the Vedic language even where there is no formal rule, the mention of *iṅ* (the root *i*) is redundant. For in the same way as [lengthening occurs] in the Vedic language even where there is no formal rule...
The lengthening of *gam* occurs; thus, it would also apply in the common language (*bhāṣā*). Therefore, the mention of *iṅ* (the root *i*) must be made.
It need not be made. A split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be performed: "In the case of *ac* before *san*" (*acaḥ sani*). For roots ending in *ac*, there is lengthening before *san*.

Then: "And for *han* and *gam*" (*hanigamyoḥ*). And for *han* and *gam*, there is lengthening before *san*. [This follows] from the word "of *ac*" (*acaḥ*) alone. That is to say, when *han* and *gam* occur in place of an *ac*.
(P_6,4.16.2) Now, does the term *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) carry over [from the previous rule], or does it not?

What follows from this? If the designation *upadhā* applies to the lengthening in the context of the suffix *san*, then a prohibition regarding consonants must be stated. If the designation *upadhā* applies to the lengthening in the context of the suffix *san*, then a prohibition regarding consonants must be stated.

[The objection is: "But [the forms] *cicīṣati* and *tuṣṭūṣati* would have this same meaning. [The reply is: "In that case, [the rule] has been withdrawn; it was stated when [the topic of] *anadhikāra* (non-governing context) was being discussed. [Question: "What was stated? [Answer: "That in the rules concerning the lengthening of *han*, *gam*, and *dīrgha*, there is the mention of *ac* (vowels). [Objection: "This is not a fault. This has already been stated: wherever one says 'short,' 'long,' or 'protracted' (*pluta*), one should understand that the term *ac* (vowel) is present there."

(P_6,4.19.1) KA_III.185.9-16 Ro_IV.681-683 Now, why does *ūṭ* not become the initial [augment]? It would follow that it becomes the initial because of the rule "that which has *ṭ* as its marker is initial. But of what is it the initial? Of the letter *v*. Let it be so. What is the status of the *v*-bearing [element]? It will undergo elision by the rule "there is elision of *v* and *y* before a consonant" (*vyoḥ vali*). This cannot be maintained. [Because of the rule] "in the case of *jvara*, *tvara*, *sriv*, *yav*, and *mav*..."

According to the rule *upadhāyāśca*, there would have to be two instances of *ūṭ*. If that is so, then this [suffix] is not *ṭit*; what then? It is *ṭhit*. If it is *ṭhit*, then in the case of *dhautaḥ paṭaḥ*, the rule *etyedhatyūṭsu* would not result in *vṛddhi*. [Objection: Once *c* has been substituted for *t* (in *ṭhit*), it will occur. [Reply: The substitution of *c* for *t* (*cartva*) is considered *asiddha*. Because it is *asiddha*, the *vṛddhi* does not occur. [Objection: Its status as *siddha* will be established by virtue of its basis (*āśrayāt*).

If there were nothing else, [the substitution] would be established by virtue of its having a basis (*āśrayāt*); however, there is another established [substitute], namely *vāh* [for *vah*]. This too will be treated as *ṭhit*. In that case, once both have undergone the change to *c*, the status of being established by virtue of their basis will come into effect. (P_6.4.19.2) KA_III.185.17–186.15 Ro_IV.683–686 Now, does the mention of *kṅit* continue to apply, or not?

Ah, no. Furthermore, what follows from this? If the rule for *śū* and *ūṭ* applies under the governing heading of *kṅit*, then the substitution of *ṣ* for *ch* must be stated. If the rule for *śū* and *ūṭ* applies under the governing heading of *kṅit*, then the substitution of *ṣ* for *ch* must be stated [as in the forms] *praṣṭā* and *praṣṭum*.

It must be asked: there is also the contingency of *tuk*. For *tuk* would also apply. Even when the mention of *kṅit* has been withdrawn, an effort must certainly be made here to prevent *tuk*. For, due to its being *antaraṅga*, *tuk* would apply. [The rule] *cchvoḥ* is understood as containing the mention of *sannipāta* (phonetic contiguity). But even so, would it not apply to the final letter? No, because of the force of the mention of *sannipāta*.

It will apply to everything. Even so, it would still apply to the *aṅga* (the stem). [Objection: Substitutes occur for that which is explicitly mentioned; thus, it will not apply to the *aṅga*. [Reply: If this were the case, then from the root *ut-pucch* with the suffix *apratyaya*, the form *utpuṭ* would result, whereas *utput* is what is desired. Likewise, from the root *vāñch* with the suffix *apratyaya*, the form *vān* would result.
The form *vāṃśau* or *vāṃśaḥ* is not established. [This is] according to the rule (*yathālakṣaṇam*) regarding that which is not actually employed. However, there is this much distinction:

when the mention of *kṅit* is still in effect, it must be stated that the suffix *cha* undergoes the substitution of *ṣ*; and in that case as well, the principle of "proximate association" (*sannipātagrahaṇa*) is to be understood. When [the mention of *kṅit*] has ceased, the substitution of *ūṭh* for *div* would apply; thus, [one would get] *dyubhyām*.
[The forms] *dyubhiḥ* [and so on]. How [do you account for] *dyubhyām*, *dyubhiḥ*? Once *ūṭh* has been applied, the substitution of *ut* will take place for the word *div*. It is not established;
because of proximity (*āntarya*), a long vowel would result from a long vowel. For that purpose, the *tapara* (the *t* following the vowel) is made. It is made for this very purpose.

But where is the mention of *kṅit* established? It is in the rule: "For a nasalized vowel before *kvip* and *jhal*, when a *kṅit* follows. If that [mention] is carried over [to the present rule], then by the rule "for *aj*, *han*, and *gam* before *san*, *kvip*, and *jhal*," the lengthening would also apply before *kvip* and *jhal*. As for *jhal*, there is no fault; we shall qualify *san* by the mention of *jhal*: "before *san* beginning with *jhal*. Regarding *kvip* as well, this is the intention of the Teacher.

It indicates that lengthening does not occur [before] *kvip*, since he teaches lengthening in the rule: "There is lengthening for *kvip* after *vac*, *pracch*, *āyata*, *stu*, *kaṭapru*, *ju*, and *śrī*, and there is no *samprasāraṇa*.
(Pāṇini 6.1.15). For what purpose is the statement regarding "asiddha" [made]? In the statement regarding "asiddha"...

It has been stated. What has been stated? First, it was stated there that the declaration of "asiddha" (non-existent) for *ṣatva* and *tuk* is for the purpose of prohibiting the application of rules based on the original substitute (*ādeśa-lakṣaṇa-pratiṣedha*) and for the purpose of bringing about the application of rules based on the original general form (*utsarga-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*). Here too, the declaration of "asiddha" is for the purpose of prohibiting the application of rules based on the original substitute and for the purpose of bringing about the application of rules based on the original general form. First, regarding the prohibition of the application of rules based on the original substitute: *āgahi*, *jahi*, *gataḥ*.
[The root] *gam* has gone [to its elision]. When the nasalization (*anunāsika*) is elided and the *j* is substituted, both *ataḥ lopaḥ* (P.

6.4.48) and *ataḥ heḥ* (P. 6.4.105) would apply. However, because [the former rule] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), it does not take effect. Furthermore, this is for the sake of ensuring that the general rule (*utsarga-lakṣaṇa*) applies:

in *edhi* and *śādhi*, once the substitution of *e* for *asti* and the substitution of *śā* for *śāsti* have been made, the substitution of *dh* conditioned by a *jhal* consonant would otherwise not apply.

Because it is not established (*asiddhatvāt*), it occurs. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "here" (*atragrahaṇam*)? The mention of "here" is for the sake of specifying the domain (*viṣayārtham*).
The domain is being pointed out: so that within this very *ābhya* treatise, the *ābhya* treatise may be considered unestablished. Let it not be the case here: *abhāji*.
*rāgaḥ*,
*upabarhaṇam*. What, then, are the purposes of this grammatical rule?

The purpose [of the rule] is for *śit-tva* (the status of having *ś* as an it-marker) to apply when there is *dhit-tva* (the status of having *dh* as an it-marker). The absence of *ś* (*śābhāva*) and the substitution of *e* (*ettva*) are the purposes when there is *dhit-tva*, as in *edhi* and *śādhi*. Once the substitution of *e* and the absence of *ś* have been applied to the roots *as* and *śās*, the *dhit-tva* characterized by a *jhal* consonant would not otherwise obtain; however, it does occur because [the former operations] are considered *asiddha* (non-existent for the sake of the subsequent rule). First of all, the absence of *ś* does not serve as a purpose [for the rule]. I shall state it thus: "In the case of *śās* followed by *hau*, [there is] *śā-hau*. This is because [the root] has become one whose final letter is *y*.

There is the suffix *sakāra*. In that case, by the rule "sāt dhitvam dhi ca," there is the elision of the letter *s*. Alternatively, I shall state "ā hau. Even so, the elision of the letter *s* would still apply. [To this we reply: the term "of the penultimate" (*upadhāyāḥ*) is understood [from the previous rule].
Once the substitution of *ā* for the penultimate has been made, then by the rule "sāt dhitvam dhi ca," there is the elision of the letter *s*. Alternatively, I shall state "na hau."

In that case, when *ettva* (the substitution of *e*) is prohibited, there is the elision of the *s* by the rule *sāddhitvadhi ca*. It should be understood that *ettva* itself is an exception to this elision, and thus the elision of the *s* does not occur. Regarding the elision of *hi*: the elision of *hi* serves as the purpose for *uttva* (the substitution of *u*). In the word *kuru*, once the elision of *hi* has occurred, *uttva* would not apply because the *u* is followed by a *sārvadhātuka* suffix; however, [the elision of *hi* is treated as] non-existent (*asiddha*), and therefore [the condition for *uttva* is met].

This too is not a purpose [for the rule]. He will state there the purpose for the mention of *sārvadhātuka*: so that the substitution of *u* for *styā* occurs even when it was previously a *sārvadhātuka* suffix. The elision of *asti*, the substitution of *yaṇ* for *iṇ*, and the application of *aṭ* and *āṭ* augmentations are the purposes.
[Examples: *talopaḥ* (elision of *ta*), *astilopaḥ* (elision of *asti*), and the substitution of *yaṇ* for *iṇ* in the application of *aṭ* and *āṭ* augmentations: *akāri*.

Regarding the example *aihī*: when the *talopa* (elision of *ta*) has been applied, the augment *aṭ* and *āṭ* would not be applicable in the *luṅ* tense because [the elision] is treated as *asiddha*. However, they do occur. The purpose [of treating the elision as *asiddha*] is for the elision of the root *as-* and the *yaṇ*-substitution for *iṇ*. For instance, in *āsan* and *āyan*: once the *yaṇ*-substitution and elision of *iṇ* and *as-* have been performed, *āṭ* would not be applicable because the preceding portion is neither *aj-ādi* (beginning with a vowel) nor *an-ādi* (beginning with a non-vowel). Yet, it does occur because [the elision] is treated as *asiddha*. As for the elision of *as-*, it does not serve as a motive [for the rule]. The activity of the Teacher (*ācārya*) indicates that *āṭ* is stronger than elision.
Since he makes the vowel *a* long (using *tapara*) in the rule *śnasoḥ allopaḥ*, this does not serve as a purpose for [the substitution of] *iṇ* and *aṇ*.

Furthermore, the substitution of *yaṇ* will be established through a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). First: "In place of *iṇ*, *yaṇ* occurs. Then: "In place of *eḥ* that has more than one vowel (*anekāc*). That is to say:

"In place of *eḥ* that has more than one vowel and is *iṇ*, *yaṇ* occurs. Then: "In place of [a root] preceded by a non-conjunct consonant (*asaṃyogapūrva*), *yaṇ* occurs"—namely, in place of *eḥ* that has more than one vowel.

This is the solution for all [the objections]. The term "upadeśa" (in the original state) is understood [to carry over]. Thus, *aṭ* and *āṭ* occur precisely in the state of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*). Alternatively, the term "ārdhadhātuka" is understood [to carry over]. Or else, the rule "luṅ-laṅ-lṛṅkṣu aṭ" is a dual-marked (*dvilakāraka*) reference.

Regarding the statement "in *luṅ* and so forth, in the case of the *lakāra*s and so forth": in no way would forms such as *aijyata* and *aupyata* be established. This will be explained [later] with the rule: "The [forms] beginning with *aj* are established by means of *aṭ*. [Now follows the rule for] the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*).

The elision of the *anunāsika* and the substitution of *ja* for *ha*— namely, the elision of the *hil* suffix and the elision of the final *a*, as well as the substitution of *ja* for *ha*— are the purposes [of this rule]. When the *anunāsika* has been elided and *ja* has been substituted for *ha* in *āgahi* and *jahi*, the rule "the elision of *hi* after a short vowel" (*ataḥ heḥ*) would result in the elision of the suffix.

Because it is not established, [the elision] does not occur. First of all, the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) is not the motive [for the rule]. The phrase "in the case of *al* [elision]" (*allope*) continues to apply from the previous context. If "in the case of the original instruction" (*upadeśe*) continues to apply, then [the rule] would not apply here in the forms *dhinutaḥ* and *kṛṇutaḥ*. This is not a fault. The term "original instruction" (*upadeśa*) is not connected with the verbal root (*prakṛti*). What then? It is connected with the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.

Regarding the rule "that which ends in /a/ when taught as part of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix," the substitution of /j/ (jabhāva) does not serve as a motivation [for the elision]. The elision of *hi* will be established through a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). First: "after *ataḥ*" (from a root ending in /a/); then: "and after *utaḥ*" (from a root ending in /u/). Thus, there is elision (*luk*) of *hi* after both [roots ending in /a/ and /u/]. Then: "after a suffix" (*pratyayāt*). The term "after a suffix" is the remainder for both [preceding rules]. Now, for what purpose is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) [taught], rather than the elision of *hi* and the elision of the suffix? [The answer is: for the sake of the substitution of /j/ (*jabhāva*).

And it is said: "The non-existence [of the result] arising from the elision of the *anunāsika* does not apply to the elision of *at* and the elision of *hi*. This is stated so that there may be no application of the rule of numerical correspondence (*saṅkhyātānudeśa*). The elision of the *anunāsika* necessitates the elision of *hi*: "O Maṇḍūki, come here with them" (*maṇḍūki tābhir āgahi*); "and Rohita, come here" (*rohitaś cehāgahi*); "with the Maruts, O Agni, come" (*marudbhir agne āgahi*). "Vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) [occurs] when there is elision of *avarṇa*": vocalization occurs when there is elision of *avarṇa*.

The purpose [of the rule] is: look at *madhoḥ*, *maghonā*, *maghone*. Once the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) has been performed, the elision of the suffix *ya* (by the rule *yasya*) would apply; however, because it is considered as if not yet established (*asiddha*), it does not occur. This is not a valid purpose, for he will state this:
the word *maghavan* is an underived nominal stem (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*).

Thus [ends the discussion]. The substitution of *rebh* is for the purpose of the elision of the long *ā*. [Question: What is the purpose of the substitution of *rebh* when there is elision of the long *ā*? [Example: "What embryo did the waters first conceive? (*kiṃ svid garbhaṃ prathamaṃ dadhre āpaḥ*). Once the substitution of *rebh* has been applied, the elision of the long *ā*—by the rule "there is elision of *ā* before the augment *iṭ*" (*āto lopa iṭi ca*)—would not take place. [Answer: It does occur because [the substitution] is considered *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of subsequent rules). [Objection: Even this is not a valid purpose. The substitution of *rebh* is Vedic, and in the Veda, the *liṭ* (perfect tense) is treated as a *sārvadhātuka* (present-system) suffix.

It also occurs there. In that case, by the rule "a *sārvadhātuka* suffix that is not marked with *p* is treated as having the *ṅ*-marker," it acquires the status of being *ṅit*. Consequently, by the rule "the *ā* of *śnā* and of reduplicated stems [is elided]," the elision of the vowel *ā* takes place.
(P_6.4.22.3) KA_III.189.14–190.9 Ro_IV.693–695 If, then, this rule (*yoga*) were not commenced, [what would happen?]

But how is there the removal of the *u* in the case of the root *kṛ*? Here, in the forms *kurvaḥ*, *kurmaḥ*, and *kuryāt*, once the *u* has been elided according to the rule "when an *ukāra* follows a *sārvadhātuka* suffix," the substitution of *ut* does not apply. Furthermore, how is there the removal of the *ṇi* when *iṭ* is present? Here, in the forms *kārayate* and *kāriṣyate*, the elision of *ṇi*—which occurs by the rule "the elision of *ṇi* when a non-*iṭ* suffix follows"—would not apply. For you, who do not state this rule, there would have to be *luk*.
And how is it that *tarap* following *ciṇ* is not [subject to elision]?

Here, in the forms *akāritarām* and *ahāritarām*, there would be no elision (*luk*) of the *tarap* following *ciṇ*. But the Blessed One has indeed made [the rule] *caṅ* for that purpose; by that, when the augment *iṭ* occurs, there is the cessation of *ṇi*. Here, in the rules concerning the future suffixes *syati*, *sic*, *sīyuṭ*, and *tās* in the sense of the impersonal (*bhāva*) and passive (*karman*), when taught...

Or rather, [the rule] "for roots ending in *ad*, *an*, or *ghu*, as well as for those with *dṛś*, there is the augment *iṭ* as in the case of *ciṇ*" and "there is also the elision of *ṇi*"; furthermore, even when "also after *m* and *v*" (*mvoḥ api*) is supplied [from a previous rule], here too—in forms such as *kurvaḥ*, *kurmaḥ*, and *kuryāt*—the phrase "also after *m* and *v*" (*mvoḥ api ye ca*) will likewise be supplied.

Moreover, in the case of the elision of *ciṇ* (*ciṇ-luk*), the elision would apply only to that which has the marker *k* or *ṅ*. Even when there is the elision of *ciṇ*, the mention of "that which has *k* or *ṅ*" (*kṅit*) from the original context continues to apply.

Where is the subject under discussion? It is: "There is elision [of the penultimate nasal] of the roots *gam*, *han*, *khan*, and *ghas* before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*, except for *anaṅ*. Now, that rule is stated in the locative case (*kṅiti*), whereas here the requirement is in the genitive case (*ciṇaḥ*). This fifth case ending (*ciṇaḥ*) will effect a change of the seventh case (*kṅiti*) into a sixth case, according to the principle: "From that [which is denoted by the ablative], the subsequent [element is affected]. But how is it in the case of *ut* after the root *kṛñ* when there is the removal of *oḥ*? [It occurs] after the suffix *ṇi*.
Moreover, how could there be the cessation of *iṭ*? For you, who do not state this rule for *yogavibhāga*, how would there be the elision (*luk*) of *ciṇ* and not that of *tarap*?

The Blessed One, however, has employed *cam* for that purpose; by it, there would be the cessation of *iṭ* after *ṇi*. Furthermore, even if *mvoḥ* and *ye ca* were to follow, in the case of the elision of *ciṇ*, the elision would apply only to those [roots] marked with *k* and *ṅ*.

(P_6,4.22.4) Even when this rule (*yoga*) is being commenced, the *samprasāraṇa* of the *vasu*-suffix is established in the application of vowel rules (*ajvidhi*). It should be stated that the *samprasāraṇa* of the *vasu*-suffix is established in the application of vowel rules. What is the purpose? Behold those who have drunk (*papuṣaḥ*). Behold those who have stood (*tasthuṣaḥ*). Behold those who have led away (*ninyuṣaḥ*). Behold those who have accumulated (*cicyuṣaḥ*). Behold those who have cut (*luluvuṣaḥ*).
"Look at *pupuvuṣaḥ*. [This is said] so that, once the *samprasāraṇa* of the *vasu* suffix has been performed, the elision of the vowel *ā* and other operations may take place by the rule *aci*.

But what is the reason that these do not succeed? Because they are characterized as external (*bahiraṅga*) and because they are consequently considered non-existent (*asiddha*). For indeed, the *samprasāraṇa* of the *vasu* suffix is both external and non-existent; thus, in *paśuṣaḥ*, the substitution of *āt* does not occur, nor do the elisions of *y* and *l* occur, as in *na vājān*.

Regarding *cākhāyitā* and *cākhāyitum*: it must be stated that the substitution of *ā* (the *āttva*) is established even when the elision of *ya* (*yalopa*) and the elision of *a* (*allopa*) have occurred. What is the purpose? In the case of *paśuṣaḥ na vājān*, because the substitution of *ā* (*āttva*) would be considered not established (*asiddha*), the elision of the final *ā* by the rule *āto dhātoḥ* would not apply.
In the case of *cākhāyitā* and *cākhāyitum*, because the substitution of *ā* (*āttva*) would be considered not established, the elision of *ya* by the rule *yasya halaḥ* would not apply.

It is obtained. It is established by the statement regarding a common substratum (*samānāśraya*). However, a common substratum is not established here, for this involves different substrata (*vyāśraya*). For instance, in these cases: *papuṣaḥ paśya* ("look at the one who has drunk") and *tasthuṣaḥ paśya* ("look at the one who has stood").
Behold those who have led away;
behold those who have gathered; behold those who have torn asunder.

"Look at *pupuvuṣaḥ*. [In this form,] after the suffix *vas*, there is the elision of the vowel *ā* and so forth; in the case of *vasantaḥ*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) before the case-ending. In *paśuṣaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ā* for the suffix *viṭ*;
in the case of that which ends in *viṭ*, there is the elision of the vowel *ā* before the case-ending. In *cākhāyitā* and *cākhāyitum*, there is the substitution of *ā* for the suffix *yaṅ*;

and in the case of that which ends in *yaṅ*, there is elision before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. Is this something that needs to be stated? No, it is not. How is it understood without being explicitly stated?
It will be understood [from the context] here by virtue of the force of the mention of *atra*. But has it not been stated that there is another purpose for the mention of *atra*?

What was stated? That the mention of *atra* is for the sake of specifying the scope (*viṣaya*). This is also established by means of the governing rule (*adhikāra*). Here, in the forms *papuṣaḥ* and *cicyuṣaḥ*, [the suffix *vasu* is applied].

Regarding *luluvuṣaḥ*, two reasons were stated: being characterized by what is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) and being unestablished (*asiddha*). Among these, the state of being unestablished has been refuted, but the state of being characterized by what is extrinsic has not at all been refuted. This is not a fault, for [the rule] "what is extrinsic is [regarded as] intrinsic... [applies].
And these two meanings arise as mutual opposites. How so? When the internal (*antaraṅga*) exists, the external (*bahiraṅga*) [does not];
and when the external exists, the internal [does not]. Furthermore, there is no simultaneous coexistence here of the internal and the external.
The internal does not apply while the external has not yet been brought about; in that case, the external is merely the cause (*nimitta*).

Regarding the internal [operations]: "The shortening, the elision of *y*, and the elision of *ā* are established even when there is the substitution of *ay* for the semivowel in the suffix *lyap*; this must be stated. For example: *praśamayya gataḥ*, *pratamayya gataḥ*, *prabebhidayya gataḥ*, *pracecchidayya gataḥ*, *prastanayya gataḥ*.

Having caused [the root] *gad* to be preceded by *pra*, he departed. Because the operations of shortening (*hrasva*), the elision of *y* (*yalopa*), and the elision of *a* (*āllopa*) are considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the substitution of *ay* (by the rule *lyapi laghupūrvāt*) does not apply. Here too, this solution is established by the statement that they share the same basis (*samānāśraya*). How so? These rules apply when there is the suffix *ṇi*; the substitution of *ay* occurs when *ṇi* is replaced by *lyap*. The augment *vuk* and the augment *yuṭ* are established for the purposes of *uvaṅ* and *yaṇ* respectively; thus, *vuk* and *yuṭ* are established for *uvaṅ* and *yaṇ*.

The two [forms] *babhūvatuḥ* and *babhūvuḥ* must be stated; because the augment *vuk* is not established (*asiddha*), the substitution *uvaṅ* would otherwise apply. [Likewise,] *upadidīye*, *upadidīyāte*: [these forms must also be stated].

Because the suffix *yuṭ* is not yet established (*asiddha*), the substitution of *yaṇ* would apply. First of all, the addition of *vuk* need not be mentioned; I shall not state *vuk*. Instead, I shall state this: "After the root *bhū*, in the *luṅ* and *liṭ* [tenses], there is the substitution of *ūt* for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). Once the substitution of *uvaṅ* has taken place here, the substitution of *ūt* will apply to that which was the penultimate vowel.
Even so, how indeed is it certain that once the substitution of *uvaṅ* has taken place, the substitution of *ūt* will apply to that which was the penultimate vowel?

Furthermore, this would not apply to the *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) of the present [root] *bhū*. This is not a fault. The term *oḥ* is understood [from the previous rule]; therefore, it will apply to a vowel of the *u*-class (*uvarṇa*). Thus, *babhūvatuḥ* and *babhūvuḥ* would be established.
However, this [form] is not established: [namely, *babhūva*].

[The forms] *babhūva* and *babhūvitha* [are derived]. What is the reason? Because once *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* have been applied, there is no longer the vowel *u*. In these cases, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* do not apply. What is the reason? Because of the prohibition [stated in the rule] *kṅiti ca*. How is it that [the suffixes] have the *k*-marker (*kit*)? [By the rule] *indhibhavatibhyāṃ ca*. But we indeed reject that *kit*-status on account of the augment *vuk*; however, in this case, by means of the *kit*-status...
The suffix *vuk* is rejected. What, then, is the correct position here? The mention of *vuk* alone is correct.

For even if the *kit*-designation were present, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would still occur here. Why? Because that prohibition applies to *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* characterized by an *iK* vowel, and this *vṛddhi* is not characterized by an *iK*. If that is so, then there is no need for *vuk*, nor for the *kit*-designation; let them [the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*] occur here.

Regarding the rules for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*: when *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* have been applied, and when *ava* and *āv* have been applied, the substitution of *ū* will occur for that which was the *upadhā*. How so? Because in the rule "of *o*" (*oḥ*), the vowel *a* is also indicated. If that is so, then it would apply here as well: "look at *kīlālapaḥ*" and "look at *śubhaṃyaḥ*."

In this case, elision (*lopa*) will be the sublater. But then it would apply here: *kīlālapau*, *kīlālapāḥ*. If that is so, then the term *vyoḥ* (from the previous rule) is still in force; by that, we shall qualify the vowel *u*: "of *o* [and] *vyo*. Now, in this instance, *oḥ* is being carried over, while *vyoḥ* has ceased to apply. Furthermore, the mention of *yuṭ* need not even be stated, because of the force of the mention of *yuṭ* itself.

It will not [be necessary]. There is another purpose for the mention of *yuṭ*: what is it? So that there might be the hearing of two *y* sounds. There is no difference regarding the hearing of one or more *y* sounds when they follow a consonant.
But is it the case that [the preceding rule] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) prior to the application of *bh*? Or rather...

Along with that [objection]. But whence does this doubt arise? This instruction is made by means of the prefix *āṅ*, and furthermore, *āṅ* generates doubt. For example, there is a doubt regarding the statement: "It has rained as far as Pāṭaliputra."
[The question is: "Why [is it asked] 'before Pāṭaliputra, with him'? Likewise here too there is a doubt:

"before the brother, with him. And what is the distinction here? If it is "before the brother," then an addition must be made regarding names, wealth, non-existence, and qualities: if it is "before the brother," an addition must be made concerning names, wealth, non-existence, and qualities.

Look at *śunaḥ* [in the form] *śunā śune*. Once the *samprasāraṇa* has been performed, the rule *allopo 'naḥ* would apply. However, for one for whom that [substitution] is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) along with it, because of its *asiddha* status, the prohibition by the rule *na saṃyogād vamantāt* will take effect.
Even for one for whom the *asiddha* status applies prior to the *bh* [of *bha*-sañjñā], this is not a fault. How so? Because there is no *strī* here.

The distinction lies either in the non-elision of *a* or in its elision; this is the distinction. If there were elision by the non-elision of *a*, the accent known as *udāttanivṛtti-svara* would result. However, the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* does not apply here.
What is the reason? Because of the prohibition: "Not in the case of *go*, *śvan*, or a vowel (*avarṇa*) [at the end]. This [prohibition] does not apply to the *udāttanivṛtti-svara*.

[Question: Of what, then, is there a prohibition? [Answer: Of the accent of the third case-ending and those following it. [Question: But where then there is no accent of the third case-ending or subsequent ones, as in *śunaḥ paśya* ("look at the dog"), how is it? [Answer: In that case, we do not teach a prohibition of the grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) itself. Rather, this is a prohibition of the accent of the case-ending (*vibhaktisvara*) which has been obtained by any rule whatsoever. [Question: But where then...

There is no accent for the case-ending in *bahuśunī*. If, however, this were understood as a prohibition even of the *udāttanivṛtti* accent, it would not be possible; for then it would also apply here in the case of *kumārī*. In that case, the activity of the Teacher indicates that the *udāttanivṛtti* accent does not descend upon the word *śunī*, since he [uses] the word *śvan*.

In the *Gaurādi* list, he recites [the word *maghavan*] and makes an effort for the sake of making it oxytone; for [otherwise], it would be established simply by the suffix *ṅīp*. Consider: *maghonaḥ*, *maghonā*, *maghone*. Once the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) has been performed, the elision of the suffix *ya* (by the rule *yasya*) would apply.

However, for that [suffix *ya*] which is simultaneously [subject to the rule of] non-establishment (*asiddhatva*), there will be no [elision] because of that non-establishment. Even for that [suffix *ya*] which is non-established prior to the vowel (*bhāt*), [there is no elision].
This fault does not apply even to that [view]. How so? He will state this: the word *maghavan* is an unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*) nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

[In the case of] *bhūguṇaḥ* (the guna of *bhū*), [in the form] *bhūyān*, once the substitution of *bhū* has been made, the *guṇa* of *o* would apply. However, for one [view] where there is non-validity (*asiddhatva*) together with that [substitution], because of that non-validity, it will not occur. And for one [view] where there is non-validity prior to the *bhā* [substitution], for him too...

Even so, this is not a fault. How? By virtue of the power of the long vowel pronunciation, it will not occur. There is a purpose for the long vowel pronunciation. What is it? [The form] *bhūmā*. This is established by means of a nipātana (irregular formation). What is the nipātana? [It is the rule: "After *bahu*, when it has the sense of abundance (*bhūman*), it is treated like *nañ* with respect to the final member. Or rather, let it be that [the suffix *matup*] occurs together with that [long vowel]. If [it is argued] that [the forms] *susamprasāraṇa*, *yalopa*, *prastha*, etc., [are established] up to the word *ābhāt*...
The prohibition [applies] to forms such as *papuṣaḥ paśya*, *tasthuṣaḥ*,
*ninyuṣaḥ*, and *cicyuṣaḥ*.

In the forms *luluvuṣaḥ* and *pupuvuṣaḥ*, once the *samprasāraṇa* has been applied, the elision of the vowel *ā* and other operations [prescribed] by the rule *aci* would not be established. This is not a fault. It has already been stated that this is established by the mention of "having a common locus" (*samānāśraya*). How so? Because the elision of *ā* and other operations apply when there is *vas*.

In the case of the *vasantī* derivative, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) and the elision of *y*. [Thus we have] *saurī balākā*. Since the vowel *a* belonging to the *aṇ* suffix is elided, and because that elision is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the elision of *y* before the *ī* ending does not apply. Here too, the same solution applies: it is established by the statement that the rule depends on a common locus (*samānāśraya*). How so? The elision of the *a* occurs when the *aṇ* suffix is present; the elision before the *ī* occurs when what ends in *aṇ* is present. As in the case of *prastha* and others: *preyān*.
[Objection: Since *prastha* and the others are considered unestablished (*asiddha*), the rule "a monosyllabic base remains in its original form" (*prakṛtibhāva*) would not apply.

[Response: This is not a fault. Just as the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) does not apply because *prastha* and the others are unestablished, so too the elision of the suffixal *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*) will likewise not occur.

(P_6,4.23) Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the letter *ś* in the mention of *śnam* made? Why not simply state "there is no elision of *n* after *na*" (*nāt nalopaḥ*)? If only "there is no elision of *n* after *na*" were stated, it would undesirably apply even in cases such as *nanditā* and *nandakaḥ*.

If that is so, then I shall state it thus: "There is no elision of *n* after *na* for roots whose penultimate vowel is not *i* or *ī*" (*nāt nalopo 'niditām*). Then, [the rule] "after a consonant" (*halaḥ*) [will follow].

[The rule] *upadhāyāḥ kṅiti* [is governed by] *aniditām*. It cannot be so. For in this case, it would not apply: *hinasti*. Therefore, it cannot be so. If it were not so, then [the forms] *nanditā* and *nandakaḥ* would result. If that is the case, then [the word] *kṅiti* continues to apply. Even so, it would not apply here in *hinasti*. This [mention of *kṅiti*] is not a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*).

What then? It is a locative of existence (*satsaptamī*): "when there is *kṅit*. If that is so, then the word *naṣ* itself is qualified here by the status of being *kṅit*: "if *naṣ* is *kṅit*. Even so, [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *yajñānām* and *yatnānām*. [Objection: Lengthening (*dīrghatva*) will be the sublater (*bādhaka*) in those cases. [Reply: This must be considered here.

"Let lengthening be applied; [then] let there be the elision of *n* (*nalopa*)"—what should be done here? Because it is subsequent, the elision of *n* occurs. Therefore, the inclusion of the letter *ś* (*saśakāra*) must be made [in the rule]. But even if the inclusion of the letter *ś* is made, why does this not occur here in the cases of *viśnānām* and *praśnānām*? [It will not occur] because of the principle that "between that which is taught by a general rule and that which is taught as a specific form, the specifically taught one takes precedence. Thus, it will not happen.

(P_6.4.24) Regarding the elision of *n* in roots ending in a vowel other than *i* (*aniditām nalope*), an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the roots *laṅg* and *kamp* when they signify affliction and bodily change respectively. An addition must be made regarding the elision of *n* in roots ending in a vowel other than *i* for the roots *laṅg* and *kamp* in the senses of affliction and bodily change. [Examples: *vilagitaḥ*.
Regarding the rule for *vikapitaḥ*: [the question is] "for what purpose [is it stated] 'in the case of *upatapa* and bodily modification'?

[The examples are: *vilaṅgitaḥ*, *vikampitaḥ*. Regarding the rule for *bṛh* in the suffix *ac* when it is not an *aniṭ* [root]: an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for *bṛh* in the suffix *ac* when it is not an *aniṭ* [root]. [Examples are: *nibarhayati*, *nibarhakaḥ*. For what purpose is it stated "in the suffix *ac*"? [Counter-example: *nibṛṃhyate*. For what purpose is it stated "when it is not an *aniṭ* [root]"? [Counter-examples are: *nibṛṃhitā*, *nibṛṃhitum*.
But that supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be formulated. It need not be formulated. *Bṛh* is a separate root-form. How is this known?
Because elision is prescribed [only] before a vowel (*aci*). Yet it is observed even before what does not begin with a vowel: *nibṛhyate*.
It is prescribed [that the elision occurs] before a suffix lacking the augment *iṭ* (*aniṭi*). Yet it is observed even before a suffix having the augment *iṭ*: [e.g., *bṛḍha*].

It is stated [in the rule] that this applies when a root begins with a vowel (*aj-ādi*). However, it is not observed even in such cases: *nibṛṃhayati* and *nibṛṃhakaḥ*. An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the root *rañj* in the sense of "killing deer" (*mṛga-maraṇa*) when followed by the causative suffix *ṇi*: *rajayati mṛgān*. Why is it specified "in the sense of killing deer"? [So that we do not say: *rañjayati vastrāṇi* ("he dyes the clothes"). Furthermore, an addition must be made for the suffix *ghinuṇ*.

It must be formed. [The form] *rāgin* is established through a specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) in the suffix *ghinuṇ*. What is this irregularity? It is the rule "tyajaraja. However, it is impossible to rely on an irregularity as a governing principle (*tantra*) when referring to a verbal root (*dhātu*), for in that case a fault would arise: [the form] *daśahanaḥ* [would not be established] in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).

*Daṃṣṭrā*. This is not a case of a verbal root (*dhātu*) undergoing a specific phonetic substitution (*nipātana*). What then? This is the form of a word ending in a suffix (*pratyaya*). And when that suffix is present, there is elision (*lopa*) [of the nasal]. [This is established by the rule] *daṃśasañjasvañjām śapi*. An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the words *rajaka*, *rajana*, and *rajaḥ*. [Thus we have] *rajakaḥ*.

Regarding *rajanam* and *rajaḥ*: [the forms] *rajaka*, *rajana*, and *rajaḥ* are established because they possess the *kit* designation. These are indeed *auṇādika* (derivative) formations from the root *raj*. For example: *rucakaḥ*, *bhuvanam*, and *śiraḥ*.

(P_6,4.34) KA_III.195.8–196.2 Ro_IV.709–711: Regarding the substitution of *i* for the root *śās*, [the rule] "for *āśās* in the case of the suffix *kvip*" must be added as a supplement. [The form] is *āśīḥ*. Now, is this for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*) or for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartha*)?
How would it be for the purpose of restriction, and how for the purpose of an injunction? First, if it were for the root *śās* in general...

Therefore, the mention [of *śās*] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). For since the suffix *aṅ* is prescribed after *śās*, its mention is for the purpose of a specific injunction (*vidhyartha*). Even if there were a mention of *śās* in general, it would still be for the sake of an injunction. How so? It is stated that [the suffix applies] after roots ending in *a* or *hal*; however, we do not see anything beginning with *hal* here. But surely the *kvip* suffix itself begins with *hal*. [No,] because of the *kvip*...

Once the elision (*lopa*) has occurred, because the word begins with a consonant (*hal-ādi*), [the substitution] does not apply. This must be considered here: should the elision of *kvip* take place first, or should the substitution of *it* for the *a* and *h* of *aṅh-* take place? What should be done here? Because it is subsequent, the substitution of *it* for the *a* and *h* of *aṅh-* takes place. The elision of *kvip* is obligatory (*nitya*). Even when the substitution of *it* for the *a* and *h* of *aṅh-* has occurred, the elision of *kvip* still applies; and even when it has not occurred, it still applies. Because it is obligatory, once the elision of *kvip* has been performed, [the rule] does not apply due to the absence of a word beginning with a consonant.

It does not obtain. If that is so, then it will occur by virtue of the rule for suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). [Objection: There is no rule for suffixes that applies when based on a phoneme (*varṇāśraya*). [Response: Or rather, some operations based on phonemes also occur by virtue of the rule for suffixes; thus this case too will occur. Alternatively, I shall state it thus: "The substitution of *ī* for the root *śās* occurs before the suffixes *aṅ* and *hal*. Then, [the rule] "before *kvip*" [is stated]. And [the rule] "and before *kvip*, [the substitution of *ī* for *śās* occurs]."

It becomes *it*. In *āryaśīḥ* and *mitraśīḥ*, [the substitution occurs] after [the prefix] *āṅ*. Furthermore, when preceded by *āṅ*, the root *śās* becomes *it* before the suffix *kvip*; thus, *āśīḥ*. Now, for what purpose is this [rule]? It is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*). [The rule applies] only to *śās* preceded by *āṅ* before *kvip*. Where should it not apply? As in *āśāsyate*.

Regarding the form *āśāsyamāna*: if so, that must be stated. It need not be stated. Having stated that the root *śās* becomes *śāsi* without qualification, I shall subsequently state [the rule] "before the suffix *aṅ*. That will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning: "it occurs only before *aṅ* which begins with a vowel, and not before any other vowel-initial suffix. In that case, by this restriction, the substitution of *it* would still apply here: *āśāsyate*.

Regarding the term *āśāsyamāna*: the suffix *aṅ* is prescribed after the root *śās*, but it is not prescribed after this particular [root] *śās*. How then is the form *āśīḥ* established? It is established by means of a formal exception (*nipātana*). What is that exception? It is the rule: "In the case of *kṣiyā*, *āśis*, and *praiṣa*, a finite verb (*tiṅ*) is expected" (Pāṇini 2.3.60). [Now for the next sūtra: "In the case of roots taught with an *anudātta* vowel, there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*) before the suffix *lyap*. Regarding those taught with an *anudātta* vowel...

It should be stated that there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) even after the suffix *lyap*: *pramatya*, *pratatya*. Then, it should be stated: "optionally after *ama*. Thus: *prayatya* / *prayamya*, *praratya* / *praramya*, *praṇatya* / *praṇamya*. (P_6.4.40) It should be stated that this applies to the roots beginning with *gam* (*gamādīnām*): so that it may also apply here—*parītat sahakaṇṭhikā* (having a neck-ring), *saṃyat*.
Regarding *sanut*: it should be stated that the suffix *ūṅ* is applied to the roots *gam* and others. Thus: *agregūḥ* ("one who goes before") and *bhrūḥ* ("eyebrow").
Now, is this a conjunction (*samuccaya*) meaning "in *san* and [before] a suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant"? Or...

Or rather, is the mention of *jhal* a qualifier of the suffix *san*, meaning "when *san* begins with a *jhal* [consonant]"? And what follows from this? If it were a conjunction (i.e., both conditions apply), then [the suffix *saN*] would occur even after a root beginning with a non-*jhal* sound, as in *sisaniṣati*, *jijaniṣate*, and *cikhaniṣati*. If, on the other hand, the mention of *jhal* is a qualifier of *san*—as in the case of [the form] *jātaḥ*—then...

In the case of *jātavān*, [the rule] does not apply here. Let it be as you wish; let it be, for now, a conjunction (*samuccaya*). But was it not said that [the suffix *san*] would also apply when it begins with a non-consonant (*ajhal*)? This is not a fault. The mention of *jhal* from the preceding context is carried over (*anuvartate*). By means of that, we shall qualify *san*: "in *san* beginning with a *jhal*. Or rather, let it be a qualification of *san* once again. How so? *jātaḥ*.

[The word] "jātavān" [is the example]. The phrase "when a consonant (jhal) follows, provided it is marked with K or Ṅ" (jhali kṅiti) is understood from the previous context. If this is so, there is no purpose in mentioning "a consonant" (jhal). A division of the rule (yogavibhāga) will be made: "For the nasal (anunāsika) of the roots jan, san, and khan, the vowel 'ā' occurs when a consonant (jhal) follows that is marked with K or Ṅ.
Then, [the next rule is]: "In the case of the suffix san (sani). And in the case of san, for the nasal of jan, san, and khan, the vowel 'ā' occurs when a consonant (jhal) follows—this is all.
Therefore, there is no purpose in the inclusion of *jhal*.
By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the substitution of *ā* occurs in place of the nasal of the root *san*.
The substitution of *ā* for the nasal of *san* takes effect by way of conflict. [This refers to the nasal-elision of *san*.]

The scope for [the substitution of] *āt* is other than the roots beginning with *tan*; the scope for the substitution of *ā* is other than the roots beginning with *jan*. In the case of the root *san*, both rules would apply: as in *sātaḥ* and *sātavān*. [One might argue that] the substitution of *ā* occurs by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). This conflict is not logical;
for there are no other roots beginning with *tan* that provide scope for the elision of the nasal of *san*. [This is so] because of the root *san*.

The reading [of *san*] among the roots beginning with *tan* is without scope (*anavakāśa*). Indeed, there is no other scope for the substitution of *ā* (āttva) than the roots beginning with *jan*. Therefore, the inclusion of *san* under the rule for *āttva* is itself without scope. Because that [reading] is without scope, a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is improper. If this is so, then the reading among the roots beginning with *tan* does indeed have scope. What is its scope? Other operations belonging to the class of roots beginning with *tan*.

Regarding the rule *tanādibhyaḥ tathāsor halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.37), even though [the substitution of] *ā* has been prescribed, the mention [of the root] still has its scope. What is that scope? It is the case of the suffix *san* and the optionality [of the substitution]. Since both have their respective scopes, a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between them is appropriate. Even so, the conflict is inappropriate; for the Teacher will state: "When what precedes is not established (*asiddha*), there is no conflict, because of the non-existence of what follows."

[Objection: "In this way, there would be no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) in the absence of even one [of the two rules]; how much less so where both are absent? [Reply: This is not a fault. A conflict does indeed occur here. [Question: Is this something that needs to be stated? [Reply: Certainly not. [Question: How is it understood without being explicitly stated? [Reply: The activity of the Teacher (*ācāryapravṛtti*) indicates that a conflict occurs here, namely, when he [formulates the rule] *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām...* [P. 6.4.66].

He makes the mention of *hal* [in the rule] as "hali. How does this serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? The purpose of mentioning *hal* is so that the substitution of *ī* may occur when a consonant (*hal*) begins [the following element], but not in cases such as *godah*.

Regarding the term *kambaladaḥ*: if there were no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) here, the mention of the consonant (*hal*) would be purposeless. Let there be the substitution of *ī* (īttva) here; since that ī-substitution is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the elision (*lopa*) will take place. However, the Teacher perceives that a conflict does indeed occur here, and therefore he provides the mention of the consonant. This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*); it is for the sake of establishing a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*).

This might be the case: [the rule] would apply when a consonant (*hal*) follows so that *īttva* occurs, but it should not apply when a vowel (*ac*) follows. What would happen then? The substitution of *iyaṅ* would result. But surely, because it is *asiddha*, the substitution of *iyaṅ* will not occur. No, for it is not possible to understand *īttva* as *asiddha* with respect to the substitution of *iyaṅ*; for in this case, a fault would arise: [if *īttva* were *asiddha*, the following would be incorrect].
Regarding the forms *dhiyau*, *dhiyaḥ*, *piyau*, and *piyaḥ*: this is not the substitution of *ī*. What then? This is the *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the roots *dhyai* and *pyai*.
Furthermore, that which is established on the basis of a common locus (*samānāśraya*) is indeed considered *asiddha* (non-existent), yet this case involves different loci (*vyāśraya*). How so?

The substitution of *ī* occurs when the suffix *kvip* follows, whereas the substitution of *iyaṅ* occurs when a case ending (*vibhakti*) follows. Therefore, the mention of *hal* (consonant) must indeed be made for the sake of establishing this distinction.

For why should it be that, because the substitution of *ī* (īttva) is not established (*asiddha*), there is elision (*lopa*), and not, conversely, because the elision is not established, that the substitution of *ī* occurs? In that case, a circularity (*cakraka*) and lack of finality (*avyavasthā*) would result. There is no such contingency of circularity; for a grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) ought not to be something that causes a lack of finality. Indeed, finality is derived from the treatise itself. Therefore, because the substitution of *ī* is not established, the elision takes place.

The establishment [of the form] will occur by means of elision (*lopa*). Indeed, it is not the case that in that instance, that very [elision] remains unestablished. If so, then the mention of *hal* must be made for the sake of establishment, so that the substitution of *ī* occurs when [the suffix] begins with a *hal*, and does not occur when it begins with a vowel (*ac*). For why would this be? Because the substitution of *ī* is unestablished, the elision will take place; by means of that elision, the establishment [of the form] will occur, but not conversely, [by means of the elision of the *ī*].

Because it is not established (*asiddhatvāt*), the substitution of *ī* would be determined by the rule for *ī*. Indeed, that very [substitution] remains unestablished with respect to that [operation]. How so? For the Teacher will state: "The mention of *t* in the rule for the elision of *ciṇ* is purposeless, because a cluster [of sounds] is not an affix, and because the elision of *t* is unestablished. Thus, the elision of *ciṇ* is unestablished only with respect to the elision of *ciṇ*.

In that case, if this were for the sake of establishing a specific rule, he would not have included the mention of *hal* (consonant) at all. Having stated the substitution of *ī* (*īttva*) without distinction, he would simply have prescribed its elision (*lopa*) as an exception (*apavāda*) when followed by an affix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*). There is already this rule: "There is elision of the final *ā* [of the root] before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*, and also before an affix marked with *iṭ*. Following that, he could have stated: "There is elision of the final *ā* of roots ending in *ghu*, *mā*, *sthā*, *gā*, *pā*, *jahāti*, and *sā*, before an affix marked with *iṭ* and before an affix beginning with a vowel that is marked with *k* or *ṅ*. For what purpose [then] was it done otherwise?
Furthermore, this [term] *īt* will be stated for the purpose of superseding that [previous rule]. Then [comes the rule]: *īt*; and *īt* occurs for the roots beginning with *ghu*. Then: *eḥ liṅi*;

"optionally" (*vā*) for other roots beginning with a conjunct consonant; "not" (*na*) in the case of *lyap*; "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) for the root *māy* there is *it*; then [the rule]: *yati*. And *īt* occurs in the case of *yat*. Since this is established by such a concise formulation (*laghīyasā nyāsena*), why is the mention of *hal* (consonant) made?
The Teacher undertakes a more significant effort and indicates that there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) here. (P.

6.4.45) In this case, the mention of *anyatarasyām* could have been omitted. How so? Because it has been stated: "After the suffix *san*, when *ktic* follows, there is optionally both elision and the substitution of *āt*. Another says:

This entire yoga can indeed be stated [more concisely]. How so? Here, both *lopa* (elision) and *āttva* (the substitution of *ā*) are under discussion, as is the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionality). In that case, only a mere connection needs to be made:
after the suffix *san*, when *ktic* follows, there is optionally both elision and the substitution of *ā*.

What, then, are the purposes of the governing rule for *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes? The elision of *ataḥ*, the elision of *ya*, and the elision of *ṇi* are purposes; as are the elision of *āl*, the substitution of *ī*, the substitution of *e*, and the treatment as if it were *ciṇ* (*ciṇvadbhāva*) before the *sīyuṭ* augment. Regarding the elision of *ataḥ*: [examples are] *cikīrṣitā* and *cikīrṣitum*. Why is it specified that this occurs "before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix"? [Consider the case of: *cikīrṣati*.

This purpose is not valid. Let there be the elision of the vowel *a* of the suffix *san*; the vowel *a* of the suffix *śap* will then be heard. [Objection: In that case, let there be no *śap* at all. [Response: This too is not a valid purpose. The activity of the Teacher indicates that the elision of the letter *ś* of *śap* does not occur by this rule, since he [prescribes] *śap* for roots beginning with *ad*.

[The opponent says: "It teaches the elision (*luk*). [The proponent replies: "This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*). This would be for the sake of a grammatical operation (*kāryārtha*), as in *vittaḥ* and *mṛṣṭaḥ*. [The opponent asks: "What then of the fact that it teaches the elision after bases ending in long *ā*? [The proponent replies: "In that case, this is the purpose: *vṛkṣasya*, *plakṣasya*. The elision of the final vowel (*ataḥ lopaḥ*) would apply here. [The opponent says: "The elision of *y* (*yalopaḥ*) is also a purpose, as in *bebhiditā*, *cecchiditā*."
What is the purpose of the condition *ārdhadhātuke* (in a semi-vowel-affix)? [Consider: *bebhid-y-ate*, *cecchid-y-ate*. [Here,] there is the elision of the *ṇi*-affix (*ṇilopa*).

[Consider: *pāc-y-ate*, *yāj-y-ate*. What is the purpose of the condition *ārdhadhātuke*? [Consider: *pāc-ay-ati*, *yāj-ay-ati*. [Here,] there is the elision of the long *ā* (*āllopa*). [Consider: *ya-y-at-uḥ*, *ya-y-uḥ*. What is the purpose of the condition *ārdhadhātuke*? [Consider: *yānti*, *vānti*. [Here,] there is the substitution of *ī* (*īttva*). [Consider: *dī-y-ate*.

It is prescribed [that the substitution of *e* occurs] before an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix. Why is it specified "before an *ārddhadhātuka*"? [To show that it does not apply here: *adātām*, *adhātām*. [In these cases, the substitution of *e* for *at* does not occur. The substitution of *e* [occurs] as follows: *sneyāt*, *mleyāt*.

Why is it specified "before an *ārddhadhātuka*"? [To show that it does not apply here: *snāyāt*. And there is the treatment as *ciṇ* (*ciṇvad-bhāva*) before the *sīyuṭ* augment. What is an example of this *ciṇvad-bhāva* before *sīyuṭ*? *kāriṣīṣṭa*, *hāriṣīṣṭa*. Why is it specified "before an *ārddhadhātuka*"? [To show that it does not apply here: *kriyeta*.

It would be elided. This is not a valid example; because it is separated by the suffix *yak*, [the elision] will not occur. Then this is an example: *prasnuvīta*. And this also is an example: *kriyeta*, *hriyeta*. But was it not said that because of the separation by *yak*, it will not occur? In that case, let there simply be no *yak* at all. What would happen then? There would be *vṛddhi*. And once the *vṛddhi* has been applied—
[The rule] *yuk* would follow [as an unintended consequence].

(P_6.4.47) KA_III.199.17–200.11 Ro_IV.721–723 Why does this *ram* not occur in place of the *repha*? Because by the rule *mit acaḥ antyāt paraḥ*, it is placed after the final vowel (*ac*). What then of the *repha*?
Why does [the substitution] not occur by hearing [the original form]? Because of the force of the enunciation of the genitive case. The followers of Bhāradvāja recite:

"In the case of *bhrasj*, there is the elision of the *r* and the *upadha* (penultimate vowel), and the augment *ram* is prescribed. The vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) takes precedence over the substitute for *bhrasj* by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).
Vocalization occurs in place of the substitute for *bhrasj* by way of conflict. The scope of the substitute for *bhrasj* is as follows: [text continues].

*bharṣṭā* and *bhraṣṭā*. The scope for *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) is, for example, in *bhṛjjati*. Here, both [rules] would apply: *bhṛṣṭaḥ* and *bhṛṣṭavān*. By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), *samprasāraṇa* takes effect. Therefore, that "conflict with the preceding" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) must be stated.

It need not be stated. [The form is] established by the statement "or *ṛ* for *ras*. Or rather, I shall state: "after *ras*, *ṛ* occurs. Or, when *ṛ* is prescribed after *ras*, the substitution of *bhrasj* must be stated in place of the *vṛddhi* [augment] in the *sic* [suffix]. When the *vṛddhi* has been applied, this very form would result: [i.e., *babharja*].

[If it were so,] one would get *abhārṣīt*; this [form] *abhārkṣīt* would not exist. In every respect, we cannot escape the conflict with the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (the rule of priority for the preceding), and the Sūtra would be contradicted. Let it remain exactly as it was originally formulated. But was it not said that the *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) takes precedence over the substitute for *bhrasj* by way of *vipratiṣedha*? This is what is meant here.

This must be deliberated upon: "Let the substitution for *bhrasj* be applied; let there be vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). What should be done here? The substitution for *bhrasj* [is applied] because it is subsequent (*para*). Vocalization [is applied] because it is obligatory (*nitya*). Even when the substitution for *bhrasj* has been performed, [vocalization] applies; even when it has not been performed, it applies. The substitution for *bhrasj* is also obligatory: even when vocalization has been performed, it applies; even when it has not been performed, it applies. How so?

That which is the *repha* in the syllable *ṛ*, and [the substitution] for its *upadhā*, would also apply even when [the *samprasāraṇa*] has already taken place. The substitution for the root *bhrasj* is non-eternal (*anitya*). For it does not apply once the *samprasāraṇa* has occurred. What is the reason? Because parts of a phoneme (*varṇaikadeśa*) are not grasped by the mention of the whole phoneme. Even if they were so grasped, [the substitution] would still be non-eternal. How so? Because the term "original instruction" (*upadeśa*) continues to apply. That...
And the application of the rule for the inclusion of the *upadeśa* form must necessarily be followed for the sake of forms such as *barībhṛjjyate*.

(Pāṇini 6.4.48) The elision of the *ṇi* suffix (*ṇilopa*) and the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix (*yallopa*) take precedence by way of prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) over *iyaṅ*, *yaṇ*, *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and lengthening (*dīrghatva*). That is, the elision of *ṇi* and the elision of *yaṅ* occur by virtue of a prior counter-exception to *iyaṅ*, *yaṇ*, *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and lengthening.
The scope for the elision of *ṇi* (ṇilopa) is:
*kāryate*, *hāryate*. The scope for the substitution of *iyaṅ* is: *śriyau*, *śriyaḥ*. Here, both [rules] would apply: *āṭiṭat*.

He caused to eat (*āśiśat*). But surely, in this case, there ought to be the substitution of *yaṇ* [for the semivowel]. Well then, consider these: *atatakṣat*, *ararakṣat*. The scope for the substitution of *yaṇ* is, for example, *ninyatuḥ*, *ninyuḥ*. The scope for the elision of the *ṇi*-affix (*ṇilopa*) is the same. Here, both would apply: *āṭiṭat*.
[The rule] *āśiśat* [is formed]. The scope for the substitution of *vṛddhi* is:
*sakhāyau*, *sakhāyaḥ*. The scope for the elision of the *ṇi*-affix is the same. Here, both [rules] would apply:
from *kārayati*, [the form] *kārakaḥ*.

From the root *hṛ*, [the suffix] *ṇvul* forms *hārakaḥ*. The scope for *guṇa* substitution is, for example, *cetā* (one who knows) and *stotā* (one who praises). The scope for the elision (*lopa*) of *ṇi* is, for example, *āṭiṭat* and *āśiśat*. In this case, both operations would apply simultaneously:
*Kāraṇā* and *hāraṇā*. The scope for [the substitution of] length (*dīrghatva*) is: *cīyate*, *stūyate*. The scope for the elision of the *ṇi* suffix (*ṇilopa*) is:
*kāraṇā*, *hāraṇā*. In this case, both [rules] would apply:

It is caused [to be done] and it is taken away. There is the elision of the *ṇi* by way of a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*). Then that previous conflict of rules must be stated. It need not be stated. Let these rules [of substitution] apply here; once these rules have been applied, because of the status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the elision of the *ṇi* will occur since it is included by the mention of *ṇi*. This cannot be maintained. For there would be a fault regarding the substitution of *iyaṅ*; [the rule would affect] the final [element].

An elision would result. There is no conflict between the elision of *a* and the substitution of *iyaṅ* and *yaṇ*. The scope for *vṛddhi* is seen in: *priyam ācaṣṭe* → *prāpayati*. The scope for the elision of *a* is seen in:
*cikīrṣitā*, *cikīrṣitum*. In this case, both [rules] would apply:

In *cikīrṣakaḥ* and *jihīrṣakaḥ*, there is no conflict (*sampradhāraṇā*) between the application of the *guṇa* substitute and the elision (*allopasya*). The scope for lengthening (*dīrghatva*) is, for example, *api kākaḥ śyenāyate*; the scope for elision (*allopasya*) is the same. Here, both [rules] would apply:

In the forms *cikīrṣyate* and *jihīrṣyate*, the elision of the vowel *a* occurs by way of a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*). Then, that [rule] must be stated as a "prior conflict" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). It need not be so stated; for the word "subsequent" (*para*) expresses what is desired. In a conflict of rules, that which is desired is what takes effect. (P. 6.4.49) KA_III.201.8-202.2 Ro_IV.726-728 Is this mention of a phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*) intended for the elision of *ya*, or...?

It is a reference to a cluster [of sounds]. And what is the distinction here? If, when *y* is elided, there is a reference to a phoneme (*varṇa*), then a prohibition must be stated regarding the end of a verbal root (*dhātu*). If, when *y* is elided, there is a reference to a phoneme, then a prohibition must be stated regarding the end of a verbal root: as in *śucyitā* and *śucyitum*. Well then, let it be a reference to a cluster. If it is a reference to a cluster, the elision of the final [phoneme] would result. It is established.

[The rule] for the final [consonant] is by the preceding [sūtra] alone. In that case, by virtue of the force of the initial statement, it will apply to all [final consonants]. Even so, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), a restriction (*niyama*) must be understood: [the rule applies] only to that which follows a consonant (*hal*) and not from any other [vowel]. Where should it not [apply]? In *lolūyitā* and *popūyitā*. Why does a restriction arise? Because there is nothing else to be prescribed (*vidheya*). Since there is no further prescription, the restriction is established.

And here there is something to be prescribed. What is it? The elision (*lopa*) of the final [element] is obtained; that must be prescribed for the whole. In that case, let it be an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*) rather than a restrictive rule (*niyama*); thus, it will indeed be an original injunction and not a restrictive rule. Even so, the elision would still apply to the final [element]. For what reason? Because elision does not remove everything. But surely, by the force of the mention of the entire complex (*saṅghāta*), [the whole is intended]?

It will apply to the whole. If there is the inclusion of the entire cluster (*saṅghāta*), what is the fault in the option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding *ky*? If there is the inclusion of the entire cluster, there is a fault in the option regarding *ky*: [the forms] *samidhitā* and *samidhyitā*. When there is elision (*lopa*), then elision of the whole occurs;

when there is non-elision (*alopa*), then non-elision of the whole would result. This is established by the rule stating that [an operation applies] to the first letter of the subsequent element. [This applies] to a consonant (*hal*).

Thus ends the fifth [case]. Therefore, by the rule *tasmād ity uttarasyādeḥ parasya*, it will apply only to the letter *y*. Alternatively, let there be the mention of the "phoneme" (*varṇa*) again. But was it not said that if there is a mention of the "phoneme," there would be a prohibition regarding the end of a verbal root? This is not a fault, because the word *aṅgāt* (from the stem) continues to be understood. Nor is this a fifth case (*pañcamī*) [expressing an ablative sense] from the stem.
It exists. If that is so, then the genitive case in *aṅgasya* will be understood as a genitive of relation (*sambandha-ṣaṣṭhī*). [The meaning is: "that which is the *yakāra* of the *aṅga*.
And what is the *yakāra* of the *aṅga*? It is the cause (*nimitta*). In what does this [designation] "that in which the *aṅga* [occurs]" apply? It applies to an affix (*pratyaya*).
(P_6,4.51) Now, what is the purpose of the condition *aniṭi*? [Examples: *kārayitā*, *kārayitum*.

It could have been stated without saying *aniṭi*. Why does [the elision] not occur in *kārayitā*, *kārayitum*? This will be for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): "The elision of *ṇi* occurs only before a *seṭ* niṣṭhā suffix, and not elsewhere."
Let it not be so. [The word] *kārayitā* [is formed by] causing [the action] to be done. Alternatively, a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) will be made later: this [rule] exists:

"before a *niṣṭhā* suffix with the augment *iṭ*, [as in] *janita* in the sense of 'mantra' and *śamitṛ* in the sense of 'sacrificer'. Then follows: "there is the substitution of *ay* for *ṇi* before a suffix with the augment *iṭ*. Then it is simply: "there is *ay* in place of [the final element] before suffixes ending in *ām*, *āluc*, *āya*, *itnu*, and *iṣṇu*."

(P_6,4.52.1) Now, for what purpose is the mention of *seṭ*? The mention of *seṭ* in the rule regarding the *niṣṭhā* suffixes is for the purpose of prohibiting [the substitution of *kṛt*] in the case of roots that do not take *iṭ*. The mention of *seṭ* in the rule regarding the *niṣṭhā* suffixes is made so that the prohibition may apply in the case of roots that do not take *iṭ*, as in the example: *sañjñapitaḥ paśuḥ* ("the animal has been caused to be slaughtered"). Thus, the mention of *seṭ* in the rule regarding the *niṣṭhā* suffixes is for the purpose of prohibiting [the substitution of *kṛt*] in the case of roots that do not take *iṭ*.

If it is argued that this is established because of the absence of *iṭ*, [we reply: if it is argued that the mention of "having *iṭ*" (*seṭ*) in the rule for the *niṣṭhā* suffixes is for the purpose of prohibiting [the substitution] when there is no *iṭ*, then that is established even without the mention of "having *iṭ*. How? Because of the absence of *iṭ*. But is it not the case that by the rule "for that which has an optional [vowel]," there is a prohibition of *iṭ* for the root *jñap*? For the prohibition applies to monosyllabic roots; indeed, that prohibition applies to monosyllabic roots, and *jñap* is such a root.

And [the mention of] *anekāc* is for the sake of ensuring the presence of *iṭ*. However, since the elision (*lopa*) is caused by that [condition of having more than one vowel], the mention of *seṭ* is made for the sake of ensuring the presence of *iṭ*.
But how can *iṭ* be brought about by this [rule] "in the case of *seṭ*"? Because the elision is caused by that [condition of being *seṭ*].
In this case, the elision of *ṇi* should not occur as long as *iṭ* has not yet been applied. What is the reason? It is because it is stated "in the case of *seṭ*. If it were not so stated...

For if the elision of *ṇi* were to occur, there would be the undesirable consequence of the prohibition of *iṭ*. Indeed, if the mention of "having *iṭ*" (*seṭ*) were not made, then once the elision of *ṇi* had taken place, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "of that which has only one vowel" (*ekācaḥ*) would apply—as in *kāritam* and *hāritam*. If this is so, then there is no purpose for the mention of "having *iṭ*" nor for the rule itself. How so? Because there is a division of the yoga (sūtra) in the seventh [chapter].

It will be performed. This is the case: there is no *iṭ* augment in the *niṣṭhā* (past participle) suffix. Then, after a causative (*ṇi*) affix: there is no *iṭ* augment in the *niṣṭhā* suffix following a verb ending in a causative affix, as in *kāritam* and *hāritam*. Then, regarding *vṛttam*: the form *vṛttam* is also treated as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). What is the irregularity? [The absence of *iṭ*] after the causative affix in the *niṣṭhā* suffix.

The elision (*lopa*) is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). What is the purpose? For the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Only here, after the suffix *ṇi* before the *niṣṭhā* suffix, does the elision occur, and not elsewhere. Where should it not occur? In *kāritam* and *hāritam*. But then, would it not also apply here?

"Rolled food," "rolled alms"—thus [the forms are derived]. Then, regarding the root *adhi-i* (to study): if there is a *vṛtti* (occurrence/application) in the sense of studying, it is expressed as *vartate*. (P_6.4.52.2) An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the roots *vṛt*, *mi*, *śṛ*, and *dhī*, because they function as *sārvadhātuka* suffixes.
The addition of *vṛdhi* to the list of roots beginning with *mi* and *śṛdh* must be made. What is the reason? Because [the suffixes] would otherwise be treated as *sārvadhātuka*.

Thus, when one expects *vardhayantu* in the case of *vardhantu tvā suṣṭutayo giro me*, and when one expects *ramayatu* in the case of *bṛhaspatis tvā sumne ramṇātu*, and when one expects *śardhaya* in the case of *agne śardha mahate saubhagāya*.

In that case, it should be stated; yet it need not be stated. It is established because *vṛdhi*, *ami*, and *śṛdhi* possess the status of *ārdhadhātuka*. How do they have the status of *ārdhadhātuka*? For other suffixes following verbal roots are also seen in both ways [as *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka*] in the Vedic language. (Pāṇini 6.4.55) Furthermore, is this [suffix] *ktnu* or is it *itnu*? And what is the distinction here? The substitution of *guṇa* for the vowel of the prefix *ni-* must be stated [as a rule]: as in *gadaditnuḥ* and *stanayitnuḥ*. Let it then be *itnu*. [But] in the case of *itnu*, a separate suffix must be prescribed. If, then, a separate suffix *itnu* must be prescribed, then an addition must be made regarding the substitution of *ay* [for *i*]. An addition must indeed be made regarding the substitution of *ay*. Both [the prescription of the suffix and the addition] are performed within the very grammatical commentary (*nyāsa*).

(P_6,4.56) KA_III.203.22–204.9 Ro_IV. 732–733: If it is argued that [the rule] "when *lyap* follows, [the penultimate vowel is short] if preceded by a light syllable" applies, then an addition must be made for cases ending in consonants. And a prohibition must be stated for cases preceded by a heavy syllable (*guru*). [Example: *pracikīrṣya gataḥ*. This is established by the rule "after a light-prior [syllable] when *lyap* follows.

[Examples: *praśamayya gataḥ*; *pratamayya gataḥ*.

[The forms] *prabebhidayya*, *pracecchidayya*, *pragadayya*, and *prastanayya* have been explained. A prohibition must be stated regarding the substitute for *iṅ*. [Otherwise, one would have to say: "having taught (*adhyāpya*), he departed. [Objection:
