Regarding the rule *lakṣaṇapratipadoktayoḥ pratipadoktasyaiva*, it will not apply in this way [to the present case]. Concerning the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.65), how is this to be understood? Is it "those suffixes beginning with *si* which occur when there is a state (*bhāva*) or an object (*karman*) [as the denoted meaning]," or rather "those suffixes beginning with *si* that occur after a word expressing a state or an object"? What follows from this? If it is understood as "when there is a state or an object... [the following applies].

In the rule *ye syādayaḥ*, the augment *sīyuṭ* is specified [by the condition of being in the potential mood], while *sy*, *sic*, *tāsi*, and *yaḥ* are not specified. Alternatively, if it is understood as "those *sy*-beginning suffixes which occur after a verbal root expressing the sense of the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*)," then *sy*, *sic*, *tāsi*, and *yaḥ* are specified, and *sīyuṭ* is not specified. Let it be as you wish. Let it be for now that those *sy*-beginning suffixes occur after the action and the object; thus, *sy*, *sic*, *tāsi*, and *yaḥ* are also specified.

But was it not said that *sīyuṭ* is specified, while *syasictāsayaḥ* are unspecified? Yet *syasictāsayaḥ* are indeed specified. How so? In the rule "the suffix *yak* occurs in the sense of the impersonal (*bhāva*) and the passive (*karman*"), the suffixes beginning with *si* (i.e., *syasictāsayaḥ*) will also be carried over [by anuvṛtti]. Or alternatively, let it be that [the suffixes] beginning with *si* occur when they follow a verbal root expressing the impersonal or the passive. But was it not said that *syasictāsayaḥ*...?

"The *sīyuṭ* is specified, while [the *iṭ*] is not specified. But the *sīyuṭ* is also specified. How so? By considering that there is no *sīyuṭ* following an element expressing the sense of the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), it will be understood that the grammatical operation applies to the *sīyuṭ* when it expresses the sense of the action or the object. Now, if it is said "and the *iṭ*," to what does this belong?

The augment *iṭ* occurs. The term "of the stem" (*aṅgasya*) is understood [from the previous rule]. If this is so, then *iṭ* would apply at the very beginning, just like *aṭ* and *āṭ*. For example, just as *aṭ* and *āṭ* occur at the beginning because they possess the marker *ṭ*, so too would it be here. If that is the case, then [the augments] will belong to *sy*-affixes and the like themselves. Even so, it does not apply because of the absence of a genitive case [indicating the relationship between the stem and the augment]. But is this not the genitive case [implied] by the rule "in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*)"? This is not a genitive case.

What then? This locative case [in the rule *syādau*] is used in the sense of "specification of the object" (*arthanirdeśe*), meaning "in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). If that is so, then this locative case in *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* will cause the locative case in *syādau* to be interpreted as a genitive; for it is a principle that when something is specified in the locative, it refers to what precedes it. Even so...

It is not established. What is the reason? Because there is no temporal sequence (paurvāparya) with respect to the meaning; since it is impossible for that to exist in the meaning, the grammatical operation will be understood to apply to the word that expresses it. Even so, [the augment] *sīyuṭ* would not be obtained. If that is the case, then a separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made in the seventh [chapter]: "The *iṭ* augment belongs to the *ārdhadhātuka*. Whatever is called *iṭ*, all of that becomes the *iṭ* of the *ārdhadhātuka*.

Then, from the rule *valādeḥ*: "An *iṭ* augment occurs before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *val*. If this were so, then in the rule *syasicsīyuṭtāsiṣu iṭ bhavati*, the *ciṇvadbhāva* (the treatment as if it were *ciṇ*) would be without qualification. What would be the fault in that? [The fault is that] since the *iṭ* occurs before *sya*, *sic*, *sīyuṭ*, and *tās*, and because of the rule *ajjhanagrahadṛśām vā ciṇvat*, the *ciṇvadbhāva* would apply only in certain instances. If that is the case, then...

We shall depend upon the suffixes beginning with *syā*. [The rule] "the augment *iṭ* occurs before *sy*, *sic*, *sīyuṭ*, and *tās*, optionally like *ciṇ* after roots ending in *aj*, *han*, *grah*, and *dṛś* when *syā*-beginning suffixes follow" applies. Now, which [roots] cause this *iṭ* to be applied? Those that are *anudātta* (unaccented). But what about those that are *udātta* (accented)? It is established for them by that very [rule], because it is subsequent. Or rather, the *iṭ* should be desired even after *udātta* roots by this very [rule].

What is the purpose? [It is so that] from *kārayati* one may derive *kāriṣyate*, and from *hārayati* one may derive *hāriṣyate*. Because the augment *iṭ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the rule "when there is no *iṭ*" (*aniṭi*) applies, so that the elision of the *ṇi*-affix may take place. But how is it that even you, though desiring it, can obtain this *iṭ* only by this [rule], and not by the other? Or rather, let it be by that one instead?

Thus, by that very same prohibition, it would be so. But surely this [augment] is permanent (*nitya*); for it applies whether that [other rule] has been applied or not, yet it does not apply when this [other rule] has been applied. What is the reason? Because it begins with a vowel (*ava-ādi-tvāt*). Therefore, the augment *iṭ* will indeed occur by this [very rule].

What, then, are the purposes of this rule? [They are: *vṛddhi* [as in] *ceṣyate* and *cāyiṣyate*; the *yuk* augment [as in] *glāsyate*; and the change of *han* to *ghatva* [as in *jaghāna*]; and the lengthening mentioned in the rule *mitāṃ hrasvo vā ciṇi*. Lengthening is a purpose: *ceṣyate*, *cāyiṣyate*. The *yuk* augment is also a purpose: *glāsyate*.

[The root] *glai* will undergo elision [of its penultimate vowel]. Furthermore, the substitution of *gh* for *han* is a purpose [for this rule]: *haniṣyate* and *ghāniṣyate*. Moreover, the long vowel that was mentioned in the rule "the optional lengthening of the *mit* roots in the *ciṇ* [affix]" is also a purpose: *śamiṣyate* and *śāmiṣyate*, *tamiṣyate* and *tāmiṣyate*. And since the augment *iṭ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), by it my *ṇi*-affix is elided; furthermore, this [elision] is permanent and caused by a *val* sound, which would otherwise obstruct [the application of other rules]. Because the *iṭ* is non-existent, [the elision occurs].

The elision of the *ṇi* suffix [as prescribed by Pāṇini 6.4.51, *ṇer aniṭi*] should take place so that it may occur. But how is this [elision] obligatory (*nitya*)? Because it applies whether [the augment] has been applied or not (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅgitvāt*).
Even when that [augment] *iṭ* belonging to the seventh [chapter, Pāṇini 7.2.35, *ārdhadhātukasya iḍ vaLādeḥ*] has been applied, this [elision of *ṇi*] occurs again.

However, once this [elision] has been effected, the condition of being preceded by a consonant (*vaLāditva*), which was the cause for the application of the seventh [rule], is destroyed; therefore, the [augment] belonging to the seventh [chapter] does not apply.

(P_6,4.62.4) KA_III.206.18–22 Ro_IV. 740 Now, for what purpose is the mention of "upadeśa" (the original grammatical instruction)? Due to the substitution of *vadh*, the *ciṇvadbhāva* occurs in place of the *sīyuṭ* by way of conflict. The scope (*avakāśa*) of the substitution of *vadh* is: *vadhyāt*.
*vadhyāstām*, *vadhyāsuḥ*. The scope for the application of the *ciṇvadbhāva* rule is as follows:
*ghāniṣyate*.

"In the case of a conflict, that which is sublated remains indeed sublated. And there is a prohibition regarding the substitutes for *han*, *iṇ*, and *ṅī*. A prohibition must also be stated for the substitutes of *han*, *iṇ*, and *ṅī*: *haniṣyate*, *ghāniṣyate*.
he will go,
he will come,
he will study.

What is being referred to here is that which is an operation pertaining to the stem (*āṅgam*); and the substitutes for *han*, *iṇ*, and *niṅ* are not operations pertaining to the stem. Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *iṭ*? The mention of *iṭ* is for the sake of excluding *kṅit*. Regarding the examples *papitha* and *tasthitha*: since the governing rule for *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes applies, an addition must be made to the rule "and at the beginning of a *sārvadhātuka* suffix," because of that *ārdhadhātuka* governing rule. Now, while the condition "before a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ*" (*kṅiti*) is still in force, just as the mention of *iṭ* is for the sake of excluding those not marked with *k* or *ṅ*, so too...

Even though the term *ārdhadhātuke* is still in force, the mention of *iṭ* will be for the sake of the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes. [Objection: It is not established. Why? Because the vowel (*ac*) is not qualified by *k* and *ṅit*.

It occurs before *kṅit*. Before what? Before a vowel (*ac*). But for what reason is the *kṅit* qualified by the vowel? Just as the augment *iṭ* is also qualified by the mention of the vowel. [The forms] *dāsīya* and *dhāsīya* [are required]. In that case, a supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made. It need not be made; it is established by the mention of "ārddhadhātuka. How so? Regarding the substitution of *ī* [for *i*], there is a prohibition concerning the letter *v*. This is because we observe the forms *ghṛtam* and *ghṛtapāvānaḥ*. "Drink the clarified butter, O drinkers of clarified butter! Drink the fat, O drinkers of fat! That this is not the substitution of *ī*. What then? This is the *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the roots *dhyai* and *pyai*. In that case, that prohibition must indeed be stated.

It need not be stated that this will be *vanip* and not *kvanip*. To what does this prohibition apply? It would apply to *āṭ*. But it is also desired for *aṭ*. In that case, the mention of *aṭ* must be made. It need not be made; the previously established [term] continues by implication (*anuvartate*).

What is the subject under discussion? It is the rule: "In the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṅ* [tenses], the augment *aṭ* is acute. If that [rule] continues to apply here, then by the rule "āṭ is applied before vowels beginning with *a*, as well as *aṭ*," the augment *aṭ* would also be required. Let it be so. Once *aṭ* has been applied, *āṭ* will be applied again. But then, even in this case, once *aṭ* has been applied, *āṭ* would be required again: as in *akārṣīt*.

[The augment] *aṭ* will not apply because of the explicit mention of [the augment] *āṭ*. But then, in these cases as well, it would not apply due to the absence of *aṭ*: *aihiṣṭa*, *aikṣiṣṭa*. It will apply there because of the explicit mention of *āṭ*. But then, in these cases as well, it would apply because of the explicit mention of *āṭ*: *akārṣīt*, *ahārṣīt*.
This will be understood as "that which begins with a vowel (*ajādi*) when *aṭ* has not been applied. Is this something that needs to be stated? No.

If [the augment were applied] after *aṭ* has been added, such that [the root] begins with a vowel (*aj-ādi*), then the mention of *aj* would be purposeless. Alternatively, the term "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*) is understood to carry over. Or else, the term "in the *ārdhadhātuka* affixes" (*ārdhadhātuke*) is understood to carry over. Or else, the mention "in *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *luṅ* there is *aṭ*" (*luṅ-laṅ-lṅkṣu aṭ*) contains two *l*s; [the first *l* indicates the locative case, and the second indicates the genitive].

Regarding the statement "that which begins with *a* in the case of *luṅ* and so forth, [i.e.,] the *lakāra*s," in no way would forms such as *aijyata* and *aupyata* be established. If that is the case, then it is established for those beginning with *a* by means of *aṭ*; that is, by *aṭ* alone for those beginning with *a*.
Success! The augment *āṭ* serves no purpose. If that is so, then *āṭ* must be stated for the sake of *vṛddhi*. If it is said "for the sake of *vṛddhi*," then [the rule] will apply to *aṭ*.

I shall state that *vṛddhi* occurs after *aṭ*. If, then, *vṛddhi* is stated to occur after *aṭ*, then in the case of *asvavaḥ hasati*, *vṛddhi* would result when *utva* has been applied to *ru*. One should remember that *vṛddhi* applies to *aṭ* when it follows a verbal root (*dhātu*). [That is, *vṛddhi* applies to *aṭ*] when it follows a verbal root.

I shall explain the rule for *vṛddhi*. In that case, then, should the mention of "dhātu" (root) be made? It need not be made. A division of the *yoga* (rule) will be performed: first, "after *aṭ*, before a vowel, *vṛddhi* occurs"; then, "after a preposition (*upasarga*), before *ṛ*, *vṛddhi* occurs"; then, "before a root. The term "dhātau" (before a root) is the remainder for both [preceding rules]. In this case, then: *āṭīt*...

In the case of *āśīt*, the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116) results in the substitution of the single substitute for the preceding and following sounds (*pararūpa*) because of the presence of a *guṇa* vowel. [Response: I shall state: "This is the same as the case of *usi* following *om* and *āṅ*. Even if this is stated, or rather, at this point, the prohibition of *pararūpa* substitution for *āṭ* before *usi* and *om-āṅ* that was previously urged need not be stated. This is for the sake of the Vedic language (*chandas*).

In that case, the suffix *āṭ* must be stated [as a rule]. [Examples are: *araik u kṛṣṇāḥ*, *tritaḥ enam āyunak*, *surucaḥ ven āvaḥ*. For the sake of the meter (*chandas*), there is lengthening; in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), lengthening is observed frequently. For example: *pūruṣaḥ*, *nārakaḥ*. If that is so, then [the form] *āyan*—

[Objection: When the *yaṇ* and elision have been applied to the roots *iṇ* and *as*, the *vṛddhi* [substitution] does not apply because the root begins with a vowel other than *a*. One should remember: [the substitution of] the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) occurs in place of a *guṇa* vowel, except after the augment *aṭ*. In the case of *om* and *āṅ*, the rule applies before *usi*; that is equal [to the previous]. For the sake of Vedic usage, there is frequently a long vowel.
Between the roots *iṇ* and *asti*, the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) takes precedence.

(P_6,4.82) KA_III.209.24–210.15 Ro_IV.749–751 Now, why does this not occur here:

*punarbhvau*, *punarbhvaḥ*. This is stated too briefly. It should be stated: "after *varṣā*, *ṛtū*, *kāra*, or *punar* [as prefixes], the word *bhū* [takes the suffix *u*]": *varṣābhvau*, etc.

the mention of *hu* and *snuk* is purposeless. What is the reason? Because there is nothing else [to which it could apply]. For there is no other [element] before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix for which a *yaṇ* substitution would occur. But is this not the case: *yāti*?

Siddham. If it is argued that [the rule] is for the sake of forms with the *yaṅ* affix repeated (*yaṅluganta*), that is not so. What is the reason? It is established because [the affixes] belong to the *ārdhadhātuka* category.

[the agent is] a hider (*nigūhakaḥ*). Since the substitution of *guṇa* takes precedence, by virtue of internal proximity (*āntaryataḥ*), a long vowel will result from a long vowel. And this [is the case]. How so? When there is the suffix *ṇi*, there is the substitution of *ū*; when there is the suffix *lyap* after *ṇi*, there is the substitution of *ay*. An addition must be made [to the rule] regarding the forms with *ciṇ* and *ṇamul* suffixes, those separated by the causative (*ṇic*) affix, and those where the *yaṅ* affix has been elided: "he caused him to calm" (*śamayantaṃ prayojitavān*),
*aśami*, *aśāmi*.
śamam śamam, śāmam śāmam. From the root śam- (in the intensive form śaṃśamayati): aśaṃśami, aśaṃśāmi.

*śaṃśamam śaṃśamam*, *śaṃśāmam śaṃśāmam*. What, then, is the reason it is not established? It is stated that "when a causative suffix (*ṇi*) followed by *ciṇ* or *ṇamul* follows, there is lengthening of the vowels of those bases (*aṅga*) that have the marker *mit*. However, in this case, the base (*aṅga*) possessing the *mit* marker does not belong to that [causative suffix] which is followed by *ciṇ* or *ṇamul*; rather, it belongs to that [causative suffix] which is not followed by them.

And [the rule] "caṅ and mit are not [included] when followed by ciṇ or ṇamul" applies. When the elision (lopa) has been performed, [the root] becomes followed by ciṇ or ṇamul; however, because of the status of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva), it is not followed by ciṇ or ṇamul. Even so, because [the elision] is considered unestablished (asiddha), [the prohibition] does not apply. If that is the case, then [the rule applies] to those [roots] where the causative suffix (ṇic) intervenes between the root and ciṇ or ṇamul.
Furthermore, it is established by virtue of being an *antaraṅga* rule when there is elision (*yaṅlope*). What does this "by virtue of being an *antaraṅga* rule" mean?

It would mean that it is established by the statement regarding a common substratum (*samānāśraya*). But this case involves different substrata (*vyāśraya*). How so? The elision of the suffix *ṇi* occurs before another *ṇi*, while the lengthening of the short vowels (*mit*) of the stems (*aṅga*) is prescribed before a suffix beginning with *ciṇ* or *ṇamul*. Therefore, there is no need for an additional explanatory rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*).
It should be stated that [the rule] "of a prefix consisting of two or more [syllables]" applies here as well, so that [the form] *samupābhicchādaḥ* may also be obtained.

If that is so, then it must be stated. It need not be stated. Where there are three or more [prefixes], two are also present therein; thus, the rule is already established by the phrase "of a prefix not consisting of two [syllables]. Indeed, this [usage] does not exist in common worldly usage.

[This is] for the sake of clarity. For when it is said, "Let one who has two sons be brought," one who has three sons is not brought. The mention of *hal* is useless. Why? Because it is observed elsewhere as well; the elision occurs elsewhere too.
It is observed: "The fire devours the grass"; "the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) devours it in the bowl. (P.

6.4.101) It must be stated that there is a prohibition of *iṭ* [in this context]. In *rudihi* and *svapihi*, the substitution of *dh* by rule P. 6.4.100 would apply. Regarding the imperative suffix *hi*, because the rule for *dh* substitution is governed by the heading on consonants (*hal*), there is no prohibition of *iṭ*.

Regarding the substitution of *dh* for *gh*, since this falls under the heading (*adhikāra*) of "consonants" (*hal*), there is no prohibition of the augment *iṭ*. A prohibition that serves no purpose is called "non-prohibition.

Why does the substitution of *dh* not occur? Because of the heading of "consonants. The mention of "consonant" (*hal*) from the preceding context continues to apply here. Where was it previously mentioned? In the rule *ghasibhasor hali*. But that [rule] was specified in the locative case (*saptamī*), whereas here [the word *dhi*] is specified in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).

This is the meaning. That [objection] is indeed refuted there. Having been refuted there, it will follow here as being specified by whatever case-ending it is expressed with, provided it possesses meaning. Or else, [it refers to] that which is being specifically indicated.
The rule "there are substitutes" will not apply in this way. Why, then, does it not apply to that which is specifically indicated?
Because it is separated by the augment *iṭ*. If that is so, then in forms such as *chindhaki* and *bhindhaki*, the substitution for the *dh* sound would not be obtained.
Once the substitution for *dh* has been made, *akac* will occur. This must be considered here: should the substitution for *dh* be performed first, or should *akac* be applied?

What should be done here? The substitution of *dhi* [for *idam*] takes effect because it is subsequent. *Akac* is obligatory (*nitya*), for it applies both when the substitution of *dhi* has been made and when it has not been made. *Akac*, however, is non-obligatory (*anitya*), for it applies to one form when the substitution of *dhi* has been made, and to another form when it has not been made; and a rule that applies to different linguistic forms is considered non-obligatory. Since both are non-obligatory, the substitution of *dhi* occurs first because it is subsequent, and then *akac* is applied.
It will be so; or rather, there is the inclusion of the letter *h* itself by means of the letter *i* produced through incapacity (*aśaktija*). (P.
6.4.104) Regarding the rule for the elision of *ciṇ*, the mention of *t* must be made. What is the purpose? So that it does not occur here: *akāritarām*.

Regarding the statement *ahāritarām*: when there is elision (*luk*) of the *ciṇ* suffix, the mention of *ta* is useless because a composite [form] is not a suffix. When there is elision of *ciṇ*, the mention of *ta* is purposeless. Why? Because a composite is not a suffix. Why does the elision not apply to the composite? Because it is not a suffix. It is stated that elision (*luk*), substitution (*ślu*), and elision (*lup*) apply to a suffix.

And the *saṅghāta* (the entire complex) is not the condition [for the elision]. If, then, the elision of *t* is performed, it would follow that the [suffix] of the subsequent [element] occurs; however, because the elision of *t* is considered *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of grammatical operations), it will not occur. The elision of *t* is *asiddha*; because it is *asiddha*, it will not take place. Or else, because the effect has already been produced (*kāryakṛtatvāt*). Alternatively, having once applied the rule "there is elision (*luk*) of *ciṇ*," there will be no further elision. It is just as when a Brāhmaṇa [establishes] the sacred fires in the spring...

Regarding the injunction "one should establish [the fires]," once it has been established, the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled; therefore, there is no further engagement. This comparison is unequal. It is appropriate that there should be no further engagement with that very act itself; however, that which is obtained as its substratum cannot be sublated. For example, in the spring, a Brāhmaṇa [performs] the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices.

"One should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) refers to the sacrifice performed every spring as the occasion for the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*). Therefore, the two solutions previously mentioned apply here as well.

Alternatively, the rule *kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.24) is understood to carry over. Where was it introduced? In the rule: "There is elision [of the penultimate vowel] of the roots *gam*, *han*, *jan*, *khan*, and *ghas* before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*, except before *anaṅ*" (Pāṇini 6.4.98). That rule was indeed stated in the locative case (*saptamī*), whereas here the requirement is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). This is as in the rule: "The elision of *ciṇ*" (*ciṇo luk*, Pāṇini 6.4.104).

This fifth [rule], "eṣā pañcamī," will cause the seventh case [ending] to be interpreted as a sixth case, according to the principle "tasmād iti uttarasya" (from that which is designated by the ablative, the subsequent [element is affected]). (P_6.4.106.1) KA_III.215.2-11 Ro_IV.760-761 How is this to be understood? Is it "from the suffix *uk*," or rather "from a suffix ending in *u*"? And what follows from this? If it is understood as "from the suffix *uk*..."

Thus, *tanu* and *kuru* are established; however, *cinu* and *sunu* are not established. Likewise, by the inclusion of the term "not preceded by a conjunct consonant" (*asaṃyogapūrva*), the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) would apply only here: *takṣṇuhi*.

[The rule] *akṣṇuhi* [would apply]; [the forms] *āpnuhi* and *śaknuhi* would not occur here. Let it be as you wish. Let it be, for now, that [the suffix] follows from a suffix ending in *u*. How then [do we get] *cinu* and *sunu*? It will be by means of the rule of "extension to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*). Or rather, let it be that [the suffix] follows from a suffix ending in *u*. How then [do we get] *tanu* and *kuru*? It will be by means of the treatment as if possessing a designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*).

As for what is said—that by including the phrase "not preceded by a consonant cluster" (*asaṃyogapūrvagrahaṇa*), the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) would apply only here [in the examples *takṣṇuhi*, *akṣṇuhi*], and would not apply in cases such as *āpnuhi* and *śaknuhi*—this is not so. We do not qualify the suffix ending in *u* (*ukārānta*) by the phrase "not preceded by a consonant cluster. What then? We qualify the vowel *u* itself. The meaning is: "from a suffix that ends in an *u* which is not preceded by a consonant cluster."
(Regarding the rule *utaśca pratyayāt*): The phrase "optionally in the Veda" (*chandasi vā*) should be stated here as well.
Thus, for the rule *utaśca pratyayāt*, it must be said that it applies optionally in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). Examples: *ava sthira tanuhi yātujūnām*;
*dhinuhi yajñam dhinuhi yajñapatim*; *tena mā bhāginam kṛṇuhi*. Furthermore, [the mention of "optionally"] is for the sake of the subsequent rule.

Some say that the mention of *chandas* (the Vedic language) should be made; others say that the mention of the option (*vā*) should be made. In this way, in the rule "there is elision of this [nasal] optionally before *m* and *v*" (*lopaś cāsya anyatarasyāṃ mvoḥ*), the mention of "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) need not be made.
[Question: For what purpose is the term *sārvadhātuke* (before an affix having the marker *sārvadhātuka*) stated? [Answer: So that it does not apply here: [e.g., in *bhavati*].
*sañcaskaratuḥ*, *sañcaskaruḥ*. A prohibition must be stated for [the forms] ending in *-syā-*:
*kariṣyati*, *kariṣyataḥ*. Because the rule for *kṛñ* specifies the ending in *u* (*ukārānta*), there is no prohibition for those ending in *-syā-*. [This applies to] *kṛñ*.
Because of the instruction ending in *u* (in the word *ut*), there would be no prohibition for that which ends in *sy*. "No prohibition" (*apratiṣedhaḥ*) means a prohibition that is purposeless.

Why does the substitution of *u* (*uttvam*) not occur? Because of the instruction ending in *u*. It is impossible to rely on the instruction ending in *u* as a governing rule (*tantram*) in the case of the root *kṛ*; [if it were so], it would apply only here: "after *sam* and *pari*, when *kṛ* means 'adornment' or 'gathering'."

[The suffixes] *saṃskaroti*, *saṃkartā*, and *saṃskartum* would not [be formed] here. We do not say that [the rule applies] because of this specific mention of the form ending in *u* (*ukārānta*) as "that which performs" (*yaḥ ayam karoti*). What then? Because of the context of the vowel *u* (*ukāra-prakaraṇāt*), the stem (*aṅga*) ending in *u* is connected [to the rule]. The word *utaḥ* (from *ut*) is understood [as a governing term]. If this is so, there is no purpose in mentioning *sārvadhātuka*. Why does it not occur in *sañcaskaratuḥ*?
Regarding the rule *sañcaskaruḥ*: the word *utaḥ* is understood [from the previous rule]. In that case, the mention of *sārvadhātuka* must be made for the sake of the subsequent rule:

*śnasoḥ allopaḥ*. For *śnam* occurs only before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix. Furthermore, for the root *as*, there must be the substitution of *bhū* even before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. In that case, it is indeed for the sake of the subsequent rule: *śnābhyastayoḥ ātaḥ*. For *śnā* occurs only before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix.

Even though it has been taught [as having] an *ā* ending, there is no such form in an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. But is this not the case: *apsu yāyāvaraḥ pravapeta piṇḍān*? This is not an *ā*-ending; it is a *ya*-ending. In that case, it is indeed for the sake of what follows: the rule *ī hali aghoḥ*. Even there, it is simply by the rule *śnābhyastayoḥ*. Therefore, it is also for the sake of what follows.

In that case, [the rule] "this [is for] the root *daridra*" will be stated: "there is elision of the root *daridra* before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, and this elision is established for the purpose of the formation of the suffix. Therefore, this [mention of *daridra*] is also for the sake of what follows. [The rule] "optionally after *bhi*" follows "of a reduplicated (*abhyasta*) root"; therefore, this too is indeed for the sake of what follows. [The rule] "of *jahāti*"...

And: "of the reduplicated (abhyasta)"—this [rule] is for the sake of what follows as well. "Up to *hau*": the word "*hau*" is mentioned; "of the reduplicated"—this is for the sake of what follows as well. "Elision (*lopa*) before *yi*": "of the reduplicated"—this is for the sake of what follows as well. "In place of *ghu* and *vas*, *e* is substituted before *hau*, and there is elision of the reduplicated syllable": the word "*hau*" is mentioned; that indeed is the purpose.

Regarding the rule *śnasoḥ allopaḥ*: But was it not said that *śnam* occurs only before a *sārvadhātuka* affix? [And] since *asti* also undergoes the substitution of *bhū* before an *ārdhadhātuka* affix, it should likewise be replaced by *bhū*. To this, the wise remember that in the case of an auxiliary verb (*anuprayoga*), *asti* is not superseded by *bhū*, because of the specific mention of the agent (*kartṛ*). Indeed, in the case of an auxiliary verb, the non-supersession of *asti* by *bhū* is desired; as in: *īhām āsa*.

They formed *īhām āsatuḥ* and *īhām āsuḥ*. Furthermore, what would happen if there were elision (*lopa*) here? If there were elision, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) would not be established. Once elision is performed, reduplication would fail to occur because the syllable would lack a vowel (*anackatvāt*). [Objection: It will occur by virtue of the rule of "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāvāt*). [Reply: If you say it is by way of *sthānivat*...

If the doubling were performed first, then once doubling has been performed, elision would result. But in that case, there is elision of the subsequent [element]. Then the lengthening will apply to the *a* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). This is not established. Why? Because of its being a constituent part (*pratyaṅga*), the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) would occur. It is not established in this way. Why? Because of its being a constituent part, the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) would result. In that case—
And when [the substitution of] *pararūpa* has been applied, the elision (*lopa*) would also apply. In that case, the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) would be the sublater.
Therefore, the lengthening by the rule *ata ādeḥ* will be the sublater. If so, then this is the purpose: so that it may apply even when [the suffix] was previously a *sārvadhātuka*, as in *kuru*.

[Response: Some say that in the case of *didaridrāsati*, [the elision applies]. *Didaridriṣati*.

Or rather: it should be stated that [the substitution of *e* for *ai*] occurs optionally in the *adyatani* (aorist). Thus: *adaridrīt*, *adaridrāsīt*. (P_6.4.120.1) Regarding roots beginning with a substitute *ṇakāra* or *ṣakāra*, the substitution of *e* for *ai* must be stated in the *liṭ* (perfect). For roots beginning with a substitute *ṇakāra* or *ṣakāra*, the substitution of *e* for *ai* must be stated in the *liṭ*. Thus: *nematuḥ*.
They bowed;
he endured;
they endured.
It is established. But what is the reason it is not established? The prohibition [of *li*] by the rule *anādeśādeḥ* would apply.

Then it must be stated. It need not be stated. We shall qualify *ādeśādi* by means of *liṭ* here: "there is no [application of *li*] for that which begins with what begins with a substitute (*ādeśa*) when *liṭ* follows. There is another purpose for the mention of *liṭ*. What is it? So that it does not occur here: [example].

[The opponent asks: "Is it for the sake of *paktā* and *paktum*? [The proponent replies: "This is not a valid purpose. The term *kṅiti* continues to apply [from the previous rule]. Even so, [the substitution] would undesirably apply in cases such as *pakvaḥ* and *pakvavān*. The substitution of *e* is stated in conjunction with the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*), and we do not observe the elision of the reduplication here. [The opponent replies: "Even so, it would undesirably apply in *pāpacyate*. [The proponent replies: The long vowel (*dīrghatva*) will serve as its sublater (*bādhaka*) in this case."

This rule is not commenced because the modification resulting from repetition has not yet been reached. Just as it would supersede other modifications resulting from repetition, so too would it supersede lengthening. True, this is so; however, among the modifications resulting from repetition, there are superior, intermediate, and inferior types. In that regard, the rules for shortening and the retention of the initial consonant are general rules (*utsarga*), while lengthening is an exception (*apavāda*) to them.

And as for *ettva* (the substitution of *e*): by the rule of "prohibition of a prohibition" (*apavādavipratiṣedha*), the long vowel will take effect. But in this case, then—such as *babhaṇatuḥ* and *babhaṇuḥ*—since the substitute for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsādeśa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), *ettva* would apply. However, the inclusion of the roots *phal* and *bhaj* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the established status of the reduplicated syllable substitute; for by including *phal* and *bhaj*, the Teacher indicates [this].

It is established that the substitution of *et* occurs after an augment (*āgama*). If this is so, then for the first and third persons plural and so forth, there would be an absence of *ettva* because they begin with an augment.
Indeed, for the first and third persons plural and so forth, *ettva* does not apply because they begin with an augment, as in *pecatuḥ* and *pecuḥ*.

*debhatuḥ*, *debhuḥ*. Or rather, the prohibition regarding *śas* and *did* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that when there is no difference in form, the substitution of *et* is not to be understood [to apply]. Or rather, this is not a fault. Why? Because the prohibition regarding *śas* and *did* is an indicator that when there is no difference in form, the substitution of *et* is not to be understood [to apply].

In that the Teacher teaches this prohibition regarding *śas* and *did*, he makes it known that for those [elements] such as substitutes (*ādeśa*) which do not differ in form [from the original], there is no prohibition. (P. 6.4.120.2) KA_III.218.21–219.7 Ro_IV.768–769: The substitution of *e* for *dambh*. The substitution of *e* for *dambh* must be stated. [Examples: *debhatuḥ*, etc.

[The form] *debhuḥ* [is formed]. But what is the reason it is not established? Because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). Since the elision of *n* is non-existent, the substitution of *e* (*ettva*) does not apply. The substitution of *e* applies to the roots *naś* and *man* except in the *liṭ* [perfect tense]. It should be stated that the substitution of *e* applies to *naś* and *man* except in the *liṭ*. It should also be stated that in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), the substitution of *e* applies even to the roots *am* and *pac*. It should be stated: "In the Vedic language, [the substitution of *e* applies] even to *am* and *pac*."

What is the purpose? [The rule] *aneśam menakā* would have been included in the list of exceptions (*vyemāna*) under the *liṅ* suffix. As for *yaj*, *āyeje*, and *vap*, *āvepe*: the substitution of *e* in *dambh-* is not a defining characteristic. Because the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) is not yet established, the substitution of *e* in *dambh-* is not accomplished. However, the teaching regarding the substitution of *e* is indicated by the letter *t* in the rule for the substitution of *at* for *śn* and *as*. Thus, this rule is non-permanent (*anitya*).

(P_6,4.121) KA_III.219.9-19 Ro_IV.770-771 What is the purpose of mentioning *thal*? The mention of *thal* is for the sake of [the suffixes] other than *aṅit*. The mention of *thal* is made for the sake of those [suffixes] that are not *aṅit*, so that the substitution of *et* may occur in the case of non-*aṅit* suffixes, as in *pecitha* and *śekitha*. This is not a necessary purpose. The mention of *seṭ* itself will serve the same purpose here as the mention of non-*aṅit*. Then what [is the purpose]?

The purpose [of the rule] is so that the conjunction (*samuccaya*) may be understood, as in: "in *thali* when followed by *seṭ*, and in *kṅit* when followed by *seṭ*. What is the purpose? [Consider] *peciva* and *pecima*. Regarding these, he will state later that "the suffix *iṭ* is prescribed after roots such as *pac*. Thus, that [rule] need not be stated.
Why does it not apply here: [e.g., *papaktha*]?
[The rule] "lulavitha" [is established] because of the prohibition of *guṇa*. But then, it would not apply here either:

*pecitha*, *śekitha*. [Objection: It will be understood thus: "the *akāra* which belongs to the *guṇa*. [Reply: Even so, it would apply here: *śaśaritha*; for this [final *a*] is the *akāra* of the *guṇa*. [Question: How so? [Answer: Because [in the derivation] there is both *vṛddhi* and *guṇa*.

That which has the letter *repha* at its head undergoes the designation of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Alternatively, the activity of the Teacher indicates that the substitution of *et* does not occur for such types [of roots], since he makes the mention of *tṛ* in the rule *tṛphalabhajatrapaśca* (P. 6.4.123). Regarding the roots beginning with *rādh*, there must be a specification of the substituend (*sthānin*). It need not be specified; for it is already covered by the condition "in the middle of a single consonant" (*ekahalmadhye*).

It occurs. If it is so, then in the forms *tresasuḥ* and *tresuḥ*, the substitution of *e* for the sound *ra* would result. Let it be so; however, according to the rule that "operations apply to the final [element] of the *al*," it would affect the vowel *a*.

It will be so. [Objection: Since the suffix *al* is meaningless (*anarthaka*), the rule regarding the final letter (*antyavidhi*) does not apply; thus, this would not be obtained. [Response: This technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) has no purpose here. Or rather, the word *ataḥ* (from *āt*) continues to apply. [Objection: Even so, it would not apply to *rādheḥ*. [Response: The mention of the vowel *ā* also continues by way of context. Where was it introduced? In the rule *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ*. Or rather, it is from *śnas*.

In the rule *allopaḥ*, the use of the marker *t* (in *ataḥ*) is rejected. That [marker] which was under discussion will be carried over here. If that is carried over, then by the rule *ata ekahalmadhye 'nādeśāder liṭi*, the substitution of *et* would apply to the entire vowel *a*. [As in: *babādhe*. We shall qualify the vowel *a* with the *t*-marked *akāra* (*ataḥ*). [Thus, the rule becomes: *asya ātaḥ*.

In this context, "of this" (*asya*) continues to apply, while "from that" (*ataḥ*) has ceased to apply. (Pāṇini 6.4.127–128) The forms *arvaṇas* with the suffix *tṛ* and *maghonaḥ* need not be taught, for they are Vedic. The forms *arvaṇas* with the suffix *tṛ* and *maghonaḥ* need not be taught. What is the reason? Because they are Vedic. They follow the usage observed in the sacred texts (*dṛṣṭānuvidhiḥ*).

It occurs in the Veda (*chandas*), because of the prescription of the suffixes *matup* and *van*. Indeed, the suffixes *matup* and *van* are also prescribed in the Veda. Because both are seen in the Veda; for indeed, both are observed in the Veda: "these are the tracks of the steed" (*arvaṇaḥ*) and "the irresistible bull with the lovely tongue" (*anarvaṇam*).

(P_6.4.130) KA_III.221.2–222.17 Ro_IV.773–777: Regarding the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatva*) in the word *pāda*. It must be stated that there is shortening of the penultimate vowel in *pāda*. [Example: "Look at the two-footed one" (*dvipadaḥ paśya*). For if it were a substitute (*ādeśa*), there would be the undesirable consequence of it applying to the whole (*sarvādeśa-prasaṅga*). Indeed, if it were a substitute, it would follow that the substitute *pac* would apply to the entire word *dvipād* and the entire word *tripād*.

"By which [rule] there is a procedure for that which ends in it. Well then, that must be stated. Or rather, it need not be stated. What is the reason? Because this *paribhāṣā* (metarule) must be formulated:

"Substitutes apply to that which is being specifically pointed out (*nirdiśyamāna*). But what is the difference here: whether this *paribhāṣā* is made, or whether the shortening of the *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) is simply stated?

This technical rule (paribhāṣā) must necessarily be formulated. What are the many purposes of this technical rule? Its purpose is seen in the case of substitutes for *sup* and *tiṅ*. Regarding *sup*: [as in] *kumāryām*, *kośaryām*.
In the bed,
in the garland,
in that [garland].

When the augment *āṭ*, *yāṭ*, or *syāṭ* have been applied, the suffix *ām* would be required for that which has *āṭ*, *yāṭ*, or *syāṭ*. There is no fault, because the rule "substitutes apply to that which is explicitly mentioned" (*nirdiśyamānasya ādeśā bhavanti*) applies here. This must be considered: should *āṭ*, *yāṭ*, and *syāṭ* be applied first, or *ām*? Here, *ām* should be applied because it is subsequent (*paratvāt*). However, *āṭ*, *yāṭ*, and *syāṭ* are obligatory (*nityāḥ*), for they apply even when *ām* has already been applied.

[The suffixes] āḍ, āṭ, and syāṭ are also non-permanent (anitya). They are non-permanent because they apply when one [element] has been formed and do not apply when another has been formed; and since they apply to different words, they are non-permanent. Between these two non-permanent operations, the substitution of *ām* occurs by virtue of its being subsequent. Then consider this: *tasyai*, *yasyai*. When *syāṭ* has been applied, the substitution of *smai* would apply to that which includes *syāṭ*. However, substitutions take the place of what is specifically indicated [in the rule].

Thus, there is no fault. But why does it not apply to that which is specifically pointed out? Because it is separated by the suffix *syat*. [For example, in the forms] *aruditām*, *aruditam*, and *arudita*—which belong to the *sup* and *tiṅ* categories—once the augment *iṭ* has been applied, the substitutes *tām*, *tam*, and *tām* would apply to that which possesses the *iṭ*.
There is no fault, because grammatical substitutes apply only to that which is explicitly pointed out (*nirdiśyamāna*). This point must be considered here.

"Let *iṭ* be applied; let *tām*, *tām*, and *tām* be applied. What should be done here? By virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), the augment *iṭ* is applied. [But] *tām*, *tām*, and *tām* are *antaraṅga*. Then consider this: *kriyāstām*, *kriyāstam*.

When *sta* is applied with *sayāsuṭ*, the substitutes *tām*, *tām*, and *tām* would apply to that which includes *sayāsuṭ*. There is no fault, because substitutes apply to what is explicitly mentioned (*nirdiśyamāna*). And there is a purpose regarding the absence of *lyap*: in the case of *prakṛtya* and *prahṛtya*, *lyap* would apply to that which ends in *ktvā*. There is no fault, because substitutes apply to what is explicitly mentioned.

It occurs [in the following cases]: in the substitutes for *tri*, *catur*, *yuṣmad*, *asmad*, and the *tyadādi* group; and there is a purpose in the case of the substitutes for *tri*, *catur*, *yuṣmad*, *asmad*, and the *tyadādi* group. For example: *atitistraḥ*, *aticatasraḥ*. Here, the substitution of *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* would apply to that which ends in *tri* and *catur*. However, since grammatical operations apply only to what is explicitly mentioned (*nirdiśyamānasya*), there is no fault. [Likewise] in the case of *yuṣmad*:

*asmat*, *atiyūyam*, *ativayam*: the forms *yūyam* and *vayam* would apply to the endings of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. There is no fault, because grammatical substitutes (*ādeśa*) apply only to that which is explicitly mentioned (*nirdiśyamāna*). This is a modification of the *tyad*-class [pronouns]:
*atisyaḥ*, *uttamasyaḥ*.

In *atyasau* and *uttamāsau*, the substitutes for *tyad*-type stems would apply to the entire stem ending in *tyad* and so forth. Consequently, the substitution of *ka* would apply to the final syllable, as in *atikaḥ* and *paramakaḥ*. However, there is no fault here, because grammatical substitutions apply only to that which is explicitly indicated [by the technical marker]. This is also the case regarding the substitution of *ud* when it precedes [the root *pū*].

The purpose [of the rule] regarding *ud-* being the preceding element is as follows: in the case of *udasthātām*, once the augment *aṭ* has been applied, the substitution of the homogeneous vowel for the preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇa*) would apply to the entire form including the *aṭ* by the rule *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ*. However, there is no fault, because "substitutions apply only to that which is explicitly mentioned" (*nirdiśyamānasya ādeśā bhavanti*).
Why, then, does it not apply to that which is explicitly mentioned? Because it is separated by the intervening *aṭ*. In that case, this is indeed a general metarule (*paribhāṣā*).

[The substitution] should be made; it should not be made. It has been stated that "the genitive [case ending] denotes the element in place of which [something else is substituted]. The purpose of stating this rule is so that what ends in a genitive may be joined with the "place" (*sthāna*), because the genitive has been uttered. (P.
6.4.132) Why does *ūṭ* not become the initial [element]? Because [the substitute] is marked with the *ṭ*-diacritic.

The rule beginning with *bhavati* would apply. By the rule *samprasāraṇam*, the position of the *yaṇ* is taken over. If this is so, then the mention of *ūṭ* for *vāh* is redundant because it has already been effected by *samprasāraṇa*. The mention of *ūṭ* for *vāh* is purposeless. What is the reason? Because it has been effected by *samprasāraṇa*. It is already established by *samprasāraṇa* alone. What is the formation of the word?

Look at *praṣṭhauhaḥ*. [Objection: The *guṇa* substitution will occur because it is conditioned by the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇatvāt*). [Response: By virtue of being conditioned by the suffix, there will be *guṇa*.

[Objection: There will be *vṛddhi* because of the mention of *ej*. [Response: There will be *vṛddhi* because of the mention of *ej*. If this is so, then since the matter is already established, the fact that the Teacher teaches the substitution of *ūṭh* for *vāh* indicates that there exists this metarule (*paribhāṣā*): "That which is characterized by an external factor (*bahiraṅga*) is considered as not yet established (*asiddha*)."

Regarding the rule concerning internal characteristics (*antaraṅga-lakṣaṇa*): what is the purpose of making this known? [The example is: *pacāva idam*, *pacāma idam*. Because the external characteristic (*bahiraṅga-lakṣaṇa*)—namely, the substitution of *guṇa* for *ā*—is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the internal characteristic—the substitution of *ait*—does not take place. (P. 6.4.133) In the case of the *prasāraṇa* of *śvan* and others, the mention of "ending in *n*" is for the purpose of prohibiting those that do not end in *a*.

In the rule concerning the *prasāraṇa* of words beginning with *śvan* and others, the inclusion of the term ending in *n* must be made. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of prohibiting [the application of the rule] to those not ending in *a*.

Let it not apply to that which does not end in *a*, as in *mabhavā maghavate*. Likewise, when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, the inclusion of its gender-distinct form also occurs; thus, as it happens here:

One might argue that just as one says "look at the young men" (*yūnaḥ paśya*), so too should it be possible to say "look at the young women" (*yuvatīḥ paśya*). Regarding this, first, as for what was said—that the mention of the form ending in *n* (*nakārānta*) must be made—it need not be made. For it has already been stated: "The forms *arvan* and *maghavan* need not be taught [separately], for they are Vedic (*chāndasa*). Furthermore, as for what was said—that when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included—[that is correct].
It occurs just as it does here in "bhavati";
[one might argue that] just as one says "yūnaḥ paśye," so too would one say "yuvatīḥ paśya" in this case as well. Regarding the inclusion of forms qualified by gender, it has already been stated.

What was stated? Namely, "Or rather, not [is there an inclusion], because when a case ending follows, there is no inclusion of forms qualified by gender. Or else, [it will be explained] further below.
A division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: first, "of *śvan*, *yuvan*, and *maghavan* when a non-taddhita suffix follows. Then, "the elision of *at*" (*allopaḥ*);
that is, there is the elision of the letter *a*. Then, "of *an*" (*anaḥ*). The term "*anaḥ*" is the remainder for both [rules].
(P_6.4.135) Now, what is the purpose of this restatement of *ṣapūrvādīnām*?

Is it for the purpose of excluding *al*-elision, or is it for the purpose of restriction? How would it be for the purpose of excluding *al*-elision, and how would it be for the purpose of restriction? If that *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) applies without distinction to both *al*-elision and *ṭi*-elision, then it is for the purpose of excluding *al*-elision. But if the *prakṛtibhāva* applies only to *ṭi*-elision when an *aṇ* follows, then it is for the purpose of restriction. Furthermore, the restatement of the rule regarding words preceded by *ṣat* is for the purpose of excluding *al*-elision.

The repetition of the words "beginning with those preceded by *ṣ*" (*ṣapūrvādīnām*) is made for the sake of excluding elision (*allopārtham*). This preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāvaḥ*) applies without distinction to both elision of *a* (*allopa*) and elision of *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*). For if there were a restriction (*avadhāraṇe*), then in other cases where preservation of the original form occurs, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) would result. Indeed, if such a restriction were present, the elision of the penultimate vowel would follow in other instances where the original form is preserved. How so? If, first of all, the restriction were as follows: "only for those beginning with *ṣ*..."

In this case, by the rule [that *ṣyañ* applies only after certain bases], there would not be *sāmanaḥ* or *vaimanaḥ* when *aṇ* is used; rather, *tākṣaṇyaḥ* would result. Furthermore, even if the restriction were such that *ṣyañ* applies only after those bases beginning with *ṣat-pūrva*, still, by that very restriction, *tākṣaṇyaḥ* would not occur here, but rather *sāmanaḥ*.

However, [if the rule were not restricted], one would obtain *vaimanaḥ*. Furthermore, if there were a restriction from both sides—namely, that the suffix *aṇ* occurs only after roots beginning with *ṣ*, and that roots beginning with *ṣ* take only the suffix *aṇ*—even so, one would still obtain *sāmanyaḥ* and *vemanyaḥ*. Therefore, it is rightly said that the repetition of the rule regarding roots beginning with *ṣ* is for the sake of preventing the elision of the penultimate vowel (*allopārtha*). For if there were a restriction, there would be the undesirable consequence of the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) elsewhere where the stem remains unchanged (*prakṛtibhāva*).

Thus [it is said]. (P_6,4.140) *Ātaḥ anāpaḥ*. It should be stated: "After *ā*, except for *āp*. This is so that it may also apply here: "In a compound not preceded by *nañ*, *lyap* replaces *ktvā*. For what purpose is "except for *āp*" (*anāpaḥ*) stated? [Consider the example: *khaṭvāyām*.

In the *Mālā*: if it is stated that [the suffix] is not *āp*, how is it [applied] in the case of the *ktvā* suffix? This is established by means of a formal exception (*nipātana*). What is the formal exception? It is the rule: "there is a prohibition of *va* in the case of *ktvā*. If this is so, there is no need for the expression "not *āp*" (*anāpaḥ*). How then is it [applied] in the case of a compound where *nañ* does not precede, according to the rule "after a consonant, *lyap* replaces *ktvā*"? This is established by means of a formal exception. How is it [applied] in the rule "after a consonant, *śānac* replaces *śna* when *hi* follows"?

This is also established by means of an irregular grammatical form (*nipātana*). Alternatively, a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: first, "from *āt*" (*ātaḥ*), meaning that there is elision of the vowel *ā*;
then, "from a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*), meaning that there is elision of the vowel *ā* belonging to a verbal root as well.

(P_6,4.141) In the case of mantras, there is the undesirable consequence of [the elision] applying only when a suffix follows *ātman*. In the case of mantras, elision should be prescribed only when a suffix follows *ātman*. This is so that it may also occur here:
*tmanyā samañjan* and *tmanoḥ antaḥ asthaḥ*. If elision is stated to occur only when a suffix follows, how [is this explained]?

"Form it from the self alone. Therefore, there is no purpose in the elision of the suffix alone. How is there the application [of the suffix] to *ātman*? [In the form] *ātmanor antaḥsthaḥ*. This is established because it is Vedic; this is a Vedic usage. In the Veda, one follows what is observed. Furthermore, the mention of "the beginning" (*ādi*) is redundant because of the context of the vowel *ā*. And the mention of "the beginning" is indeed purposeless.

What is the reason? Because of the context of *ākāra* (the vowel *ā*). The word *ātaḥ* (after *ā*) is understood [from the previous rule]. (Pāṇini 6.4.142) Why is the mention of *ti* necessary? Could it not simply be stated as "there is elision (*lopa*) of *viṃśati* before a *ḍit* suffix"? It cannot be done so. If it were stated as "there is elision of *viṃśati* before a *ḍit* suffix," the elision would apply to the final letter [of the stem].

It is established that [the substitution] occurs for the final [element] by means of the elision of *ya*. In that case, by virtue of the force of the rule's formulation, it will apply to the word-form *ti*.
But why indeed, when the formulation serves no other purpose, should it apply to the word-form *ti* and not rather to the *aṅga*?
Therefore, the mention of *ti* must be made. Now, even if the mention of *ti* is made, why does it not apply to the final [element]?

Since substitutes (*ādeśāḥ*) occur for that which is being specified (*nirdiśyamānasya*), it will not be so [in this case]. (P_6.4.143) An addition (*upasaṅkhyānam*) must be made for [the word] *abha*. This is so that [the rule] may apply here as well:
*upasarajaḥ*.

[Regarding the forms] *mandurajaḥ* and so on: if that is so, then it must be stated [in the rule]. It need not be stated. How [do we derive] *upasarajaḥ*, *mandurajaḥ*? By virtue of the power of the formation of the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) even for what is not a vowel (*abhasya*). It will occur by virtue of the power of the formation of the *anubandha* even for what is not a vowel. When there is the elision of *ṭi* after a stem ending in *n*, [the rule applies] to *sabrahmacārin*, *pīṭhasarpin*, *kalāpin*, *kuthumin*, *taitilin*, *jājalin*, *lāṅgalin*, *śilālin*, *śikhaṇḍin*, *sūkara*, *sadmam*, and *suparvan*.

An addition [to the rule] must be made: for words ending in *n*, when the *ṭi*-suffix is elided, there is an addition of these—*sabrahmacārin*, *pīṭhasarpin*, *kalāpin*, *kuthumin*, *taitilin*, *jājalin*, *lāṅgalin*, *śilālin*, *śikhaṇḍin*, *sūkarasman*, and *suparvan*. *sabrahmacārin*: *sābrahmacārāḥ* (those who are fellow-students). *sabrahmacārin*: *pīṭhasarpin*: *paiṭhasarpāḥ* (those who are cripples who crawl on a bench).

Taitilāḥ; Taitilin; Jājalin; Jājalāḥ; Jājalin; Lāṅgalin; Lāṅgalāḥ;
Lāṅgalin; Śilālin; Śailālāḥ; Śilālin; Śikhaṇḍin; Śaikhaṇḍāḥ; Śikhaṇḍin; Sūkarasman.

*sauparva* from *suparvan*; *sauparvāḥ* from *suparvan*. Regarding *carmaṇaḥ kośe*: an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for "in a sheath made of leather"; thus, *cārmaḥ kośaḥ*. Regarding *āsmanaḥ vikāre*: an addition must be made for "a modification of stone"; thus, a modification of stone is *āśmaḥ*. Regarding *śunaḥ saṅkoce*: [an addition must be made for] "the contraction of a dog"; thus, *śaunaḥ saṅkocaḥ*.
And [the rule] regarding indeclinables: an addition must be made for indeclinables. What is the purpose? For the sake of forms such as *sāyamprātika*. [Examples are:

*sāyamprātikaḥ* (belonging to evening) and *paunaḥpunikaḥ* (repeated). A prohibition must be stated regarding the word *śāśvatika* (eternal). It need not be stated; this is established by means of a formal exception (*nipātana*). Which formal exception? [The one stating: "And [the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] after words whose opposition is eternal. Thus it is.
In that case, a prohibition must be stated for the case of *śāśvata*. [The word] *śāśvata*.
(P_6.4.148.1) KA_III.226.20-25 Ro_IV.785-786 What is an example for [the rule concerning] that which ends in an *i*-vowel?

"O Dākṣi," "Dākṣyāḥ," "Dākṣyaḥ. [In the vocative] "O Dākṣi": if there were no elision (*lopa*), once the substitution of the following vowel with a short one (*hrasvatva*) had taken place, there would be a long vowel by way of homogeneous lengthening (*savarṇadīrghatva*).

[Otherwise] it would follow that [the final vowel] is heard. Regarding *dākṣyā*: if there were no elision (*lopa*), once the *yaṇ* substitution has been applied to the subsequent [vowel], the hearing of the preceding [vowel] would follow, resulting in *dākṣeyaḥ*.

If there were no elision, even when elision is applied to the subsequent [vowel], the hearing of the preceding [vowel] would follow. These are not valid purposes [for the rule]. These are also established by means of the long vowel of homogeneous quality (*savarṇadīrghatva*).

In that case, consider these examples: *atisakher āgacchati* ("He comes from one who is very much a friend") and *atisakheḥ svam* ("The property of one who is very much a friend"). If there were no elision [of the final vowel], then after the shortening of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) had been applied, the prohibition "not [if it ends in] *sakhi*" (*asakhi*) would apply.
(Regarding Pāṇini 6.4.148.2) In rules such as "the [final vowel] of that which [ends in *ī*]" (*yasya īti*), there is a prohibition with respect to *śyā*. Of that which...

In such cases as "śyām," a prohibition must be stated; [as in] "kāṇḍe kuḍye" and "saurye nāma himavataḥ śṛṅge. Well then, that prohibition must indeed be stated. No, it need not be stated. Here, both "śyām" and "na" are understood from the context. Therefore, only their mutual connection needs to be made.

In the case of *yasya* and so forth, elision (*lopa*) occurs; [however], elision does not take place before the suffix *śya*. Elision takes precedence over *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). Elision occurs by way of conflict with *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*. The scope (*avakāśa*) of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* is, for example, *śriyau*, *śriyaḥ*, *bhruvau*, *bhruvaḥ*. The scope of elision is, for example, *kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ*.
In the case of *mādrabāheya*, both [operations] would apply here:

*vatsapreyaḥ* and *laikhābhreyaḥ*. By means of the rule of mutual exclusion (*vipratiṣedha*), there is elision (*lopa*). And there are also *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [substitutions]. By means of the rule of mutual exclusion, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* take precedence over *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*. This is the scope for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.
The word *cetā* [is derived from the root *ci*]; it is the same case for *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*. Here, both [rules] would apply:
*cayanam*, *cāyakaḥ*, *lavanam*.

*Lāvakaḥ*: Guṇa and vṛddhi [substitutions] occur by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). Or rather, it is not so; there is no need for conflict, because the substitution of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* is prescribed for a different domain. Why? Because the substitution of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* is prescribed for a different domain. The substitution of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* is introduced for a different domain. For which domain? For the domain of *yaṇ* and so forth. It is just as follows:

[If it were so,] the substitution of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* would subvert the substitution of *yaṇ*, and likewise it would subvert the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [substitutions]. Therefore, in those cases where *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are applicable, a prohibition must be stated. It need not be stated. For intermediate exceptions (*apavāda*) subvert preceding rules; thus, the substitution of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* will subvert the substitution of *yaṇ*, but it will not subvert the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.

(P_6,4.149.1) KA_III.227.21–228.12 Ro_IV.788–789: There is no application [of the suffix] *aṇ* after words such as *sūrya*, because the stem (*aṅga*) is different. There is no application of *aṇ* after words such as *sūrya*. For example, *saurī balākā* ("the crane of Sūrya"). What is the reason? Because the stem is different. This stem ending in *aṇ* becomes something else. When the elision (*lopa*) has been performed, there is no difference in the stem. [Objection: There is a difference in the stem due to the status of being "as if present" (*sthānivadbhāva*).

It is established, however, because of the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva*. This is established. How? Because of the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva*. Here, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prohibited; with respect to the rule for the elision of *y* (*yalopa*), it does not behave as a substitute.
Even so, it is not established. What is the reason? Because of the difference in the word-form (*śabdānyatva*). For the word *śūrya* is one thing, and [the other] is another.

[The word] *saurya* [is formed with the suffix -ya]. This is not a fault; for it will be established that "that which undergoes modification in one part is not different from the original. Furthermore, the mention of the "penultimate vowel" (*upadhā*) would be purposeless. And now that the status of being "like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) has been prohibited, the mention of the penultimate vowel is redundant. Why? Because in words such as *sūrya*, the letter *y* is indeed the final sound. What follows from this?

It is well said and correctly stated that if the lack of established status (*asiddhatva*) applies prior to the operation [of the rule], then indeed, because of that lack of established status, the elision (*lopa*) also lacks established status; consequently, the *yakāra* would not be final. Even if there were a lack of established status together with that [elision], there is still no fault. For it is not understood thus: "there is an elision of the *yakāra* of the bases beginning with *sūrya*. How, then, is it understood?

"The elision of *y* occurs for a member [of a compound] if that *y* belongs to *sūrya* and so forth. Even so, [the rule] would apply here in the case of *sūryacarī*. Therefore, the mention of "penultimate" (*upadhā*) must be made.
Furthermore, there must be an enumeration of the specific cases (*viṣayaparigaṇana*). There is indeed an enumeration of the specific cases.

And it should be stated: "The suffix *ṅīp* is applied after the words *sūrya* and *matsya*. Thus: *saurī*, *matsī*. It should be stated: "The suffix *cha* is applied after the words *sūrya* and *agastya*, as well as *ṅīp*. Thus: *saurī*, *saurīyaḥ*, *āgastī*.

[The suffix] *īya* [is applied after *agasti*]. Regarding *tiṣya* and *puṣya*, when they denote asterisms (*nakṣatra*), the elision [of the final syllable] must be stated: *taiṣam*, *pauṣam*. Regarding *antika*, when the suffix *tasi* follows, the elision of the *ka*-class [suffixes] and the acute accent on the first syllable must be stated. Regarding *antika*, when the suffix *tasi* follows, the elision of the *ka*-class [suffixes] must be stated, and the acute accent on the first syllable must also be stated: *antitaḥ* (not from afar). Regarding *tama*, when *tādi* and *kādi* [suffixes] follow... [the elision of the *ka*-class suffixes and the acute accent on the first syllable must be stated].

And the elision [of the suffix] must be stated: *agne tvam naḥ antamaḥ* ("O Agni, you are our nearest"). It descends as *antitamaḥ*. This [suffix] *tasi* need not be mentioned; for the elision of the suffix *gha* is also seen in the *Dāśataya*, where in *antiṣat* there is [the form] *antiṣat*. Likewise, in the *Atharvaveda*, there are those ending in *agha*: *anti ye ca dūrake* ("those who are near and far").

The mention of *cha* could have been omitted. Why does [the suffix] not apply here in *bilvakebhyaḥ*? [Because] the term *bhasya* (of a nominal stem ending in *bha*) is understood [from the previous rule]. Even so, it would undesirably apply here in *bilvakāya*. [Because] the term *taddhitasya* (of a secondary derivative) is understood. Even so, it would undesirably apply here in *bailvakaḥ*, which means "a modification or a part of a *bilvaka* tree. [Because] the term *taddhite* (when a secondary derivative follows) is understood. Even so, it would undesirably apply here in *bailvakaḥ*, which means "one who resides in Bilvakīyā."

In the case of *bailvakasya kiṃcit bailvakīyam*, [the suffix] would apply here [by the rule for *bilvaka*]. But that is not [the case], because it is stated that [the suffix] is prescribed after words beginning with *bilvaka*, and this suffix is not prescribed after the word *bilvaka*;
rather, it is prescribed after the word *bilvakīya*. This being so, since the desired form is already established, why is there the mention of the letter *cha*?
The Teacher indicates this by stating that there is a metarule (*paribhāṣā*):

"When elements are taught as being in obligatory conjunction (*sanniyoga*), the absence of one entails the absence of both. Therefore, the mention of *ch* must be made so that the elision (*luk*) applies only to *ch*, and not to *kuk*. [Objection:
But the elision of the whole [suffix] must be stated; otherwise, only the final letter would be elided.

"Let it not be so. Then it must be stated. "It need not be stated. [The rule] *tuḥ* is understood as the elision of all [sounds], because the mention of the final [sound] would otherwise be purposeless. By *tuḥ*, the elision of all [sounds] is understood. Why? Because the mention of the final [sound] would be purposeless. Since there is no purpose in stating the elision of the final [sound], it shall apply to the whole. Or else, it is *luk*.

The original [rule] is to be carried over. It is impossible to carry over the *luk* (elision). Why? Because the presence of the *guṇa* (vowel strengthening) is observed in the forms ending in *-iṣṭha* and *-kariṣṭha*. The *guṇa* is indeed seen in *-iṣṭha* and *-kariṣṭha*: for example, *vijayiṣṭhaḥ* ("most victorious") and *āsutikariṣṭhaḥ* ("most skilled at distilling"). [In the case of] the suffix *ṇi*, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is treated as if it were in the superlative (*iṣṭhavad*). Regarding the nominal stem in the context of the suffix *ṇi*...

The treatment as if it were the superlative suffix (*iṣṭhan*) should be stated. What is the purpose? For the sake of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), the substitution of *ra* (*rabhāva*), the elision of *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*), and for the sake of [the rule concerning] what follows *yaṇ*. First, for the sake of the masculine form: he describes her who is dark (*enī*)—he causes her to be "dark" (*etayati*). He causes her who is white (*śyetā*) to be "white" (*śyetayati*). Second, for the sake of the substitution of *ra*: he describes one who is broad (*pṛthuḥ*)—he causes him to be "broad" (*prathayati*).

It causes to spread; it softens. [The mention of] *ṭi* is for the purpose of its elision: one says "it is clever," *paṭayati*. [The mention of] *yaṇ* and so forth is for the sake of what follows: one says "it is thick," *sthavayati*; [one says] "it is small," *davayati*. But is this an exhaustive enumeration, or merely an illustration? He says: it is merely an illustration, for even words beginning with *pra* are intended [to be included]: *prādayaḥ*.
It expresses and brings about what is desired (*priya*). The followers of Bhāradvāja recite:

"In the case of the causative suffix *ṇi*, as if it were *iṣṭhan*, the rules for the masculine form of the nominal stem, the elision of the vowel *r*, the elision of *ṭi*, and the substitution of *yaṇ* for vowels beginning with *ā*, as well as the elision of *prādi* and the suffixes *vin* and *matuḥ*, are for the purpose of prescribing [these operations].

(P. 6.4.159) Is this the word *yi* or the letter *y*? What follows from this? If the elision (*lopa*) also continues [from the previous rule], then it is the word *yi*. If, however, it has ceased [to apply], then it is the letter *y*.

Then follows the letter *ya*. (P. 6.4.160) KA_III.230.15–22 Ro_IV.795–796: For what purpose is the substitution of *ā* for the *īyas* following *jyā* prescribed? Why not simply allow the elision (*lopa*) that was previously established to carry over? What would be the resulting form? *jyāyān*. [Objection: The lengthening will occur by the rule "before a suffix beginning with a consonant other than *k*" (*akṛtyakāre*). [Response: That being so, since the result is already established, why [is it stated] that the *ā* follows *jyā*?

The substitution of *ā* for the suffix *īyas* teaches that the Teacher intends to make known this metarule (*paribhāṣā*): "When an operation has already taken effect upon a stem (*aṅga*), a subsequent operation does not apply again. What is the purpose of making this known? The prohibition of *guṇa* for the root *pibati* was previously enjoined; that need no longer be stated. Now, for what reason is a long vowel (*dīrgha*) prescribed for the *īyas* following *jyā*, rather than an *akāra*?
Thus it might be said: what is the establishment of the form?

[The word] *jyāyān* [is formed]. By reason of proximity (*āntaryataḥ*), a long vowel will be substituted for a long vowel. If this is so, then since the goal is already established, the fact that the Teacher prescribes a long vowel indicates this metarule (*paribhāṣā*): "When a sound is being taught (*bhāvyamānena*), there is no inclusion of its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇānām*)."

(P_6,4.161) KA_III.231.2–23 Ro_IV.796–799 How is this to be understood: [does it mean] "of a stem (*aṅga*) beginning with a consonant (*hal*)," or rather "of an *ṛ*-vowel beginning with a consonant"? It is indeed appropriate to investigate this.
But surely there ought to be an unambiguous qualifier for the stem; for how could a consonant (*hal*) possibly belong to an *ṛ*-vowel?

One thing may be the beginning of another. This word *ādi* indeed exists as denoting a constituent part (*avayava*), as for example: "the beginning of the *Ṛgveda*," "the beginning of the half-verses," and "the beginning of the verses. It also exists in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpya*), as for example: "the meal of curd is the beginning of the accomplishment of one's purpose."
Near the eating of curd is the eating of ghee; the eating of ghee is the beginning of health. Near the eating of ghee, even though it exists in proximity, a deliberation arises:

"of an *ṛ*-vowel near a consonant, [and] of a base (*aṅga*) beginning with a consonant. What follows from this? If it is understood as "of a base beginning with a consonant," then it would not be more extensive.

In this case, the rule would not apply. Now, if it is understood as "of a ṛkāra belonging to a stem beginning with a consonant," then it would also apply to *anṛcīyān*. Furthermore, in both cases, it would apply to *svṛcīyān*. Let us assume, for now, that the rule applies to a stem beginning with a consonant. How then is *aprathīyān* formed? It will be a compound with a word ending in a taddhita suffix: *na prathīyān* = *aprathīyān*.

Thus it would be established when the compound is formed with a secondary derivative (taddhita) suffix at its end. However, when the secondary derivative is produced from the compound itself, then it is not established. Indeed, the secondary derivative should not be produced from the compound. What is the reason? Because the possessive sense (matvartha) has already been expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound. It might be that [the rule] does not apply when it is a *bahuvrīhi*; however, when it is indeed a *tatpuruṣa*, [it should apply].

Then [the suffix] *īyasun* is obtained: "not broad" (*apṛthuḥ*), "this also is not broad," "this also is not broad," and "this is less broad than these two" (*anayor aprathīyān*). It should not be that the suffixes beginning with *aj* (i.e., *īyasun* and *iṣṭhan*) occur after a compound. What is the reason? It is stated [in Pāṇini 5.1.123] that they occur "after a word expressing a quality" (*guṇavacanāt*), and a compound is not a word expressing a quality. But when, then, from a compound, the suffixes *vin* or *matup* are added, and from that which ends in *vin* or *matup*, [the suffixes *īyasun* and *iṣṭhan* occur]?
Then [the suffixes] *aj* and *ādi* would apply. "Not separate" (*apṛthu*) means those that are not separate (*avidyamānāḥ pṛthavaḥ*). "One who has non-separate things" is *apṛthumān*.

This is *apṛthumān*. This is *apṛthumān*. This is *aprathīyān* (wider) than these two. This is not a fault. Non-separate things simply do not exist; how could one say "one whose [things] are non-separate"? Why does it not occur here: *mātayati*?

*bhrātayati*. Here, elision (*lopa*) will be the sublater. This must be considered here: should the *ṭilopa* be performed first, or the substitution of *ra*? What should be done in this case? Because it is subsequent, the substitution of *ra* [takes effect]. But what if the substitution of *ra* were stated for the remainder? It cannot be so; for in that case, it would also undesirably apply here: [e.g., *bhrātṛ*].

[One] expresses that [the action] has been done, as in "he makes done" (*kṛtayati*). If that is so, then an exhaustive enumeration must be made; it should be stated: "In the case of *pṛthu*, *mṛdu*, *kṛśa*, *bhṛśa*, *dṛḍha*, and *parivṛḍha*.
(P. 6.4.163) [Question: Why is it said that a monosyllabic base remains in its original form (*prakṛtyā*) before the suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *īyasun*, and *ra*?

Or rather, [is it] without distinction? And what follows from this? If it were without distinction, then [the suffix] would also apply here in the case of *svī*, *khī*, and *śauvam*. But *svikhinau* do not exist at all. How so? This has already been stated: "The two [suffixes] are not prescribed after a monosyllabic word, after a word denoting a genus (*jāti*), or in the locative case. Therefore, it should be *svavān* and *khavān* only. As for *śauvam*, by virtue of its being subsequent [in the rules], the augment *aij* applies.
The elision of the *ṭi* suffix ought to occur. Now, the form *adhunā* is established as an irregularity (*nipātana*) in place of a base together with its suffix.

In that case, it would follow here: *dravyam*. [This is because] there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) for that which begins with *īti*. There is preservation of the original form for that which has the possibility of elision by the rule *yasyeti ca*; however, these [words] do not begin with *īti*. Even so, [the form] *śriye hitaḥ* [would require consideration].

In the case of *jña* as a deity, one would obtain the form *jñaḥ sthālīpākasya jñaḥ sthālīpākaḥ*. Therefore, there is original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) in the case of *iṣṭa*, *neya*, and *meya*. Now, what is an example of original form in the case of *iṣṭa*, *neya*, and *meya*? *preyān*, *preṣṭhaḥ*. This is not correct; because the prefixes [beginning with] *pra-* are considered unestablished (*asiddha*), it will not occur. In that case, here is an example: *śreyān*.

[The rule states: "An *ekāc* [stem] remains in its original form (*prakṛti*) before the suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *īyasun*, and *iyas*. If this is so, then because of the capacity for pronunciation of an *ekāc* stem, there would be no need for an explicit statement, and thus the original form would occur even without being stated. If it is argued that the rule applies when an *ekāc* stem occurs before *iṣṭhan*, *īyasun*, and *iyas*, that is not correct. What is the reason? Because of the capacity for pronunciation of an *ekāc* stem, the original form will occur even without an explicit statement. However, [the rule is necessary] for the purpose of the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *vin* and *mat*. [This refers to the case of stems ending in] *vin* and *mat*.
However, for the sake of the locative case, the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) must be stated: *sragvitaraḥ*,
*srajīyān*,
*sragvitamaḥ*.
*srajiṣṭhaḥ*: more sacrificial ladle-like; *srucīyān*: even more sacrificial ladle-like; *srugvattamaḥ*: most sacrificial ladle-like.

"sruciṣṭhaḥ. Now, one might object: "Will not the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *vin* and *mat* subvert the elision of the *ṭi* [portion]? How could that which is prescribed for one thing be a subverter of another? Indeed, subversion occurs only when coexistence is impossible; yet here, there is the possibility that both may exist. For just as the elision of *vin* and *mat* subverts the elision of the *ṭi*, so too does it [the elision of the *ṭi*] subvert [the *luk*] in a *taddhita* suffix.

This would also sublate that [rule]: "Whichever of us is more learned (*brahmīyān*), more possessed of sacred knowledge (*brahmavattara*). As for what was said—"How can that which is prescribed for one thing be a sublater of another?"—he should first be asked this:
"If, then, the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *vin* and *matup* were not prescribed, what would happen here? He says: "The elision of the *ṭi*. [That is,] the elision of the *ṭi*.

If that is so, then since the elision of *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*) has not yet occurred, the rule for the elision (*luk*) of *vin* and *mat* is commenced; it will therefore act as an exception (*bādhaka*). As for what was said—that an exception occurs only when there is no possibility [of both rules applying simultaneously]—and that there is indeed a possibility for both to occur:

even when such a possibility exists, an exception does take place. For example: "Let curd be given to the Brahmins. (In this case, although the two operations could theoretically apply, the specific instruction prevails.)
Just as in the case of "takram kauṇḍinyāya" (buttermilk for Kauṇḍinya), even though the giving of curd is possible, the giving of buttermilk serves to exclude it;
so too here, even though the elision [of the suffix] is possible, the elision of the *ṭi* element will set aside the elision of the *vin* and *mat* suffixes. Furthermore, as it is said:
"Just as the elision of *vin* and *mat* sets aside the elision of the *ṭi* element, it will likewise set aside this [rule] 'na taddhite' (not when a *taddhita* suffix follows)."

Thus, it does not sublate [the *ṭilopa*]. What is the reason? Because there is no sublation of that which has not already been reached.
