The elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *vin* and *mat* is not commenced when the *ṭilopa* has not yet been reached; however, in the case of the rule "naḥ taddhite" (Pāṇini 6.4.144), it applies both when [the *ṭilopa*] has been reached and when it has not. Alternatively, according to the principle that "exceptions (*apavāda*) sublate the immediately preceding rules," the elision of *vin* and *mat* will thus sublate the *ṭilopa*.

[The rule] *na taddhite* will not supersede this [rule]. If, however, *vinmatoḥ luk* supersedes *ṭilopa*, then *payiṣṭhaḥ* would not be established; rather, *payasiṣṭhaḥ* would result. [In such cases, one follows] the grammatical rule regarding what is not actually used in usage. Regarding the rule *prakṛtyā ake rājanyamanuṣyayuvānaḥ*: it should be stated that "the words *rājanya*, *manuṣya*, and *yuvan* remain in their original form (*prakṛti*) when followed by the suffix *aka*. Thus: *rājanyakam*.
*mānuṣyaka*, *yauvanikā*.

(P_6.4.170) Regarding the rule *mapūrvāt pratiṣedhe vā hitanāmnaḥ*: it should be stated that after a word preceded by *m* in a negative compound, the name *hitanāman* optionally [takes the suffix *aṇ*]. Thus, both *samānahaitanāmaḥ* and *samānahaitanāmanaḥ* are formed.

(P_6,4.171) KA_III.233.14–234.3 Ro_IV.805 Now, what is the purpose of this rule regarding the elision of the suffix *ana* after [the word] *brāhma* when there is no birth (*ajāti*)? Is it for the sake of elision, or is it for the sake of restriction? How would it be for the sake of elision, and how for the sake of restriction? If the term "in the sense of offspring" (*apatye*) continues to apply, then it is for the sake of restriction. If, however, that term has ceased to apply, then it is for the sake of elision. Therefore...

The author states the reply: "The statement is for the purpose of eliding [the suffix] of *brāhma* when there is no birth [of a descendant]. A statement is made for the purpose of eliding the suffix of *brāhma* when there is no birth [of a descendant]. The word "apatye" (in the sense of a descendant) is no longer operative. In that case, regarding the prescription of what was not previously established, there must be a prohibition of what was already established. That is to say, when the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) is prescribed for what was not previously established, a prohibition must be stated for what was already established [by default]. For example: *brāhmaṇaḥ*. Or rather, it is not necessary, because of the force of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
Or rather, it need not be stated. What is the reason? Because of the force of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), there will be an exclusion here.
Is there another purpose for the exclusion? What is it? [The purpose is to exclude] that which is a genus (*jāti*) and not a descendant (*apatya*), such as "the *brāhmī* herb.
But this is certainly not intended here. For what is undesired follows, and what is desired is not established. If that is so, then...

The term "in the sense of offspring" (*apatye*) follows [from the previous rule], but it is not connected with this specific *nipātana* (irregular formation) itself; that is, the form *brāhmaḥ* is irregularly formed in the sense of offspring when it does not denote a genus (*ajātau*). What, then, is connected? A prohibition is connected: the form *brāhmaḥ* is irregularly formed, [meaning] it is not [used] in the sense of offspring when it denotes a genus.

(P_6,4.172) Why is this stated? Is it not already established by the rule *na naḥ taddhite*? It is not so established; for if it were, the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi changes) would apply because of the condition *anaṇi*. Since the rule specifies *aṇi*, and this [suffix] is a *ṇa*-suffix, [the objection holds]. If that is the case, then since the matter is already established, the fact that the Teacher provides this irregular derivation (*nipātana*) indicates that [the rule applies] to those suffixes expressing a habitual characteristic (*tācchīlika*).

[The suffix] *aṇ* is applied. What is the purpose of this teaching? [It is so that] in the case of *caurī* and *tāpasī*, the vowel *ī* is established by the rule "after a stem ending in *aṇ*" (Pāṇini 4.1.15). Here, in the word *bhrauṇahatya*, what is the irregularity (*nipātana*)?

The substitution of *t* for the initial *y* in a *taddhita* suffix is prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregularity). [Objection: The prescription of the *t*-substitution in *bhrauṇahatya* is purposeless, because it has already been established by a general rule. [Response: The prescription of the *t*-substitution in *bhrauṇahatya* is indeed purposeless. What is the reason? Because it has been established by a general rule. In this case, the *t*-substitution will occur by the general rule itself: "In place of the root *han*, *ta* is substituted before an affix beginning with a vowel, except for *ciṇ* and *ṇamul*" (*hanaḥ taḥ aciṇṇamuloḥ*). However, there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*)...

Regarding the prohibition of *tattva* in a *taddhita* suffix: if this is so, then the Teacher indicates that *tattva* does not occur in a *taddhita* suffix. What is the purpose of this indication? [It is so that] in forms such as *bhrauṇaghnaḥ* and *vārtraghnaḥ*, *tattva* does not occur. Because of the difference in accentuation, the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) of *aikṣvāka* must be stated separately. Because of the difference in accentuation, the irregular derivation of *aikṣvāka* must be stated separately.

"Aikṣvākaḥ, aikṣvākaḥ. This is established by the indication through *ekaśruti* (monotone). *Ekaśruti* is the universal name for accent, just as the neuter is the universal name for gender. Now, what is irregularly formed (*nipātyate*) in the case of "Maitreya"? In the case of "Maitreya," there is the irregular formation (*nipātana*) consisting of the elision of the initial *y* when the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied.
In the case of *maitreya*, the elision of the initial *y* and subsequent sounds (*y-ādi-lopa*) is established as a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). This word *mitrayu* is mentioned four times:

first, it is listed among the *gṛṣṭy-ādi* group for the purpose of prescribing a specific suffix; second, it is included among the *yaska-ādi* group in the second chapter for the purpose of causing the elision (*luk*) of a suffix; third, it is mentioned in the seventh chapter for the purpose of substituting *iy* for *ya*; and this fourth instance is for the purpose of the elision of the initial *y* and following sounds.

The double mention [of *bidādayaḥ*] could be omitted. Its recitation in the *bidādi* list would be for the purpose of prescribing the suffix; however, in that case, there would be no need for elision (*luk*) nor for the deletion of *y* and so on, as the form would be established by the substitution of *iy*. This cannot be done. For in this case, in the example *maitreyakaḥ saṅghaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ*—as prescribed by the rule *añyañiñām aṇ* which applies to words characterized as *saṅgha*—would undesirably apply. [This would also affect] *hiraṇmaya*.

What is being prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātyate*)? The elision of *y* (*yalopa*) is prescribed for *hiraṇmaya*. That is, in the word *hiraṇmaya*, the elision of *y* is prescribed as an irregularity. Now, what is being prescribed as an irregularity for *hiraṇyaya*? It is established by the rule prescribing the elision of *m* (*malopa*) for *hiraṇyaya* in the Veda (*chandas*). In the Veda, the elision of *m* in *hiraṇyaya* is prescribed as an irregularity: *hiraṇyayī naḥ nayatu* ("May she, made of gold, lead us"), *hiraṇyayāḥ panthāna āsan* ("The paths were made of gold"), and *hiraṇyayam āsanam* ("A golden seat").

Regarding the rule *yuvoḥ anākau* ("for *yu* and *vu*, there are *an* and *āk*"), for which two [sounds] do *an* and *āk* occur? For the two suffixes (*pratyaya*). But how can they occur for the two suffixes when the term "of the stem" (*aṅgasya*) is being carried over [from a previous rule]? This [stem] ending in the sounds *yu* or *vu* becomes a stem (*aṅga*) before a case-ending (*vibhakti*).

It occurs as follows: if *an* and *āk* were to replace the final phonemes of a stem ending in *yu* or *vu*, they would result in substitutions for the whole [stem]. However, because the rule "substitutions apply to that which is specifically indicated" (*nirdiśyamānasya ādeśā bhavanti*) applies, this will not happen. But what about where there is no case-ending (*vibhakti*), such as in *nandanā* and *kārikā*? Even here, the case-ending exists by virtue of the characteristic of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*). But what about where...

The characteristic of a condition (*pratyaya*) does not exist [here]. [If one were to argue that] *nandanapriyaḥ* and *kārakapriyaḥ* [would be formed], let them not be so; for that which is the case-ending belonging to the compound (*sāmāsikī vibhaktiḥ*), and that which is the case-ending following from the compound (*samāsāt vibhaktiḥ*), in those two [cases], they will occur. Indeed, in that [case-ending], the stem (*aṅga*) does not end in the sounds *yu* or *vu*. It would be so for one who would qualify the stem by means of the sounds *yu* and *vu*; but for him, it would not apply to the two [suffixes] at the end of an infinite series (*ānantya*).

[The two suffixes] would be [the objects of the rule]. We shall indeed qualify the *yu* and *vu* sounds by means of the term "stem" (*aṅga*). That is to say: "In place of *yu* and *vu* belonging to a stem, *an* and *āk* occur, regardless of where they are situated. But what then of cases where there is no case-ending (*vibhakti*) following a compound, such as *nandanadadhi* and *kārakadadhi*? In that case, there is neither another cause nor a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) [for the preceding element], according to the rule of "as if a suffix were present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*). Nor...
In this case, the following is relied upon as the governing cause (*nimitta*):
"In this [context], after [an element], *yu* and *vu* become *an* and *āk*. What then? It means "the *an* and *āk* occur for the *yu* and *vu* of a stem (*aṅga*).

And the designation "stem" (*aṅga-sañjñā*) occurs by virtue of the characteristic of an affix (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*). Alternatively, it is that which is the stem of those two [affixes] itself which serves as the cause.

We shall take recourse [to this interpretation]. How? The genitive case in the word *aṅgasya* will be understood as expressing a general relationship. [The meaning is: "the *yu* and *vu* that belong to the *aṅga*. And what are the *yu* and *vu* belonging to the *aṅga*? They are the causes (*nimitta*). And of which two things does the term "belonging to the *aṅga*" apply? It applies to the two suffixes (*pratyaya*).

"If [it is argued] that *yu* and *vu* become *an* and *āk*, then there must be a prohibition regarding verbal roots (*dhātu*). If it is held that *yu* and *vu* become *an* and *āk*, then a prohibition must be stated for verbal roots:
[e.g.,] *yutvā*, *yutaḥ*, *yutavān*, *yutiḥ*. And [there must be a prohibition] for *bhujyu* and others; for *bhujyu* and others, too, there must be a prohibition.

It should be stated that *bhujyuḥ*, *kaṃyuḥ*, and *śaṃyuḥ* [are formed]. [This is] established because of the presence of a nasal (*anunāsika*). There is a mention of *yu* and *vu* when followed by a nasal, and these two [suffixes, *-yu* and *-vu*] are not followed by a nasal. If there were a mention of those followed by a nasal, then [the forms] *nandanaḥ* and *kārakaḥ* would not be obtained here, for we do not see a nasal following these words *yu* and *vu*.
Regarding the phrase "because of being followed by an *anunāsika*," it is not understood as: "the *anunāsika* is subsequent to these two; these two are 'followed by an *anunāsika*';

because they are followed by an *anunāsika*. How, then, is it understood? It is understood as: "the *anunāsika* is subsequent to these two; these two are 'those for which an *anunāsika* is subsequent'; because for them an *anunāsika* is subsequent. If there were a reference to those [sounds] for which an *anunāsika* is subsequent, then the designation *it* would apply to them. In that case—

What is the fault? In that case, there would be the prohibition of the *ṅīp* and *num* suffixes. A prohibition of the *ṅīp* and *num* must be stated: [otherwise] *nandanaḥ kārakaḥ* (the agent who causes delight) and *nandanā kārikā* (the female agent who causes delight) would result. The *ṅīp* and *num* suffixes characterized by the marker *u* would apply. And also for the end of a verbal root (*dhātvan-tasya*):

a prohibition must be stated for the end of a verbal root as well, such as in *divu* and *sivu*. However, the inclusion of the marker *ṭ* in *ṣiṭ* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the absence of operations conditioned by the marker *u*.

The fact that the Teacher makes these two suffixes, *yu* and *vu*, marked with the *ṣiṭ* indicatory letter (by stating "the suffix *ṣvuṇ* [is used] for an artisan; *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* [are used], and there is the augment *tuṭ*") indicates that no operation dependent on the *ugit* designation applies to *yu* and *vu*. How is this an indicator? The purpose of marking them with *ṣiṭ* is so that the vowel *ik* [of the suffix] may appear by the rule "that which is marked with *ṣiṭ*. If an operation dependent on the *ugit* designation were to apply here, the marking with *ṣiṭ* would be redundant.

[Otherwise, the rule] would be purposeless. However, the Teacher perceives that the operation conditioned by the marker *u* does not apply to the two [suffixes] *yu* and *vu*; therefore, he makes the suffixes *yu* and *vu* marked with *ṣ*. Alternatively, the addition of the marker *ṣ* is not for the purpose of prescribing the suffix *ṅīṣ*. This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*). For there is indeed another purpose for stating this. What is it? The addition of the marker *ṣ* is made for the purpose of prescribing the suffix *ṅīṣ*. Because they are marked with *ṣ*...

Thus, so that the suffix *ṅīṣ* may occur, the marker *ṭ* is added [to the end of the stem]. The addition of the *ṭ* marker is for the sake of excluding the case where the word is a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*). Even with the addition of the *ṭ* marker, there is another purpose: namely, so that the long vowel *ī* may occur by the rule "after a subordinate member ending in a *ṭ*-marked suffix. From a *ṭ*-marked suffix, the *ī* occurs when it is not subordinate; however, from a suffix marked with *ugit*, it occurs both when subordinate and when not subordinate. If this is the case, then by the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the suffix *ṭāp* is stronger.

But due to the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the suffix *ṭāp* will be stronger. The scope of *ṭāp* is *khaṭvā*, *mālā*; the scope of *ṅīp* is *gomatī*, *yavamatī*. Here, both would apply: *nandanā*, *kārikā*. By the rule of conflict, *ṭāp* occurs. This conflict is not logical; for it is said that "in a conflict, the subsequent [rule] prevails," yet *ṭāp* is prior and *ṅīp* is subsequent.

[If it is argued that] *ṅīp* [is taught first], then *ṭāp* will be applied after *ṅīp*, and thus a reversal of the order of the rules (*sūtra-viparyāsa*) would have been made. If that is so, then in the rule "after an *ugit*-stem, *ṅīp* occurs," the phrase "after *at*" (from the previous rule) will also be carried over (*anuvartisyate*). Even so, [the suffix] would apply here only to *ugit*-stems ending in *a*, such as *nandanā* and *kārikā*; it would not apply in cases like *gomatī* and *yavamatī*. If that is so, then there must be a continued connection (*sambandhānuvṛtti*) [of the condition].

It will be formed as follows: *ajādyataṣṭāp* [the suffix *ṭāp* is added after feminine stems beginning with vowels other than *a*, and after those ending in short *a*]; *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* [the suffix *ṅīp* is added after stems ending in *ṛ* or *n*]; *ataṣṭāp* [the suffix *ṭāp* is added after stems ending in short *a*]. *Ugitaśca* [the suffix *ṅīp* is also added after stems marked with the *ugit* designation]; *ataṣṭāp* [the suffix *ṭāp* is added after stems ending in short *a*]. *Vano ra ca* [after a stem ending in *van*, the suffix *ṅīp* is added and the final *n* is replaced by *r*]; *ugitaḥ* [the suffix *ṅīp* is added after stems marked with the *ugit* designation]; *ataṣṭāp* [the suffix *ṭāp* is added after stems ending in short *a*]. *Pādo 'nyatarasyāṃ ṅīp* [the suffix *ṅīp* is optionally added after the word *pāda*]; *ugitaḥ* [the suffix *ṅīp* is added after stems marked with the *ugit* designation];

*ataṣṭāp* [the suffix *ṭāp* is added after stems ending in short *a*]. Then, regarding *ṛci*: *ṛci ca ṭāp bhavati* [and the suffix *ṭāp* is added after the word *ṛc*]. The previously mentioned rule (*ataṣṭāp*) is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). Thus, it is established.

If the author of the Vārttika recites thus—"But because of the conflict (vipratiṣedha), the suffix *ṭāp* is stronger"—then this [previous argument] remains unaddressed. And this [following point] becomes addressed. How? The word *para* signifies "desired" (*iṣṭa*). That which is desired in a conflict is what takes effect. Furthermore, because the mention of *yu* and *v* refers to those that possess meaning, and because they possess meaning at the end of a verbal root...
And the inclusion [of the term] is not meaningful within the context of the verbal roots (*dhātu*).

7.1.1.3) Regarding the prescription of *num*, the mention of *jhal* must be made. In the prescription of *num*, the mention of *jhal* is required; it is intended that [the suffix] follows a stem ending in a *jhal* consonant or one marked with the *uṅit* designation.

[The rule] "ugidacām sarvanāmasthāne 'dhātoḥ" [Pāṇini 7.1.70] includes the word *jhalaḥ*. And that must necessarily be stated for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of the rule] to forms qualified by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭa*). Since it is a principle that when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, its form qualified by gender is also included, just as the forms *gomān* and *yavamān* occur here, so too would they occur in the case of *gomatī* and *yavamatī*. Or rather, [the rule need not be stated], because when a case ending (*vibhakti*) follows, there is no inclusion of a form qualified by gender.

Or rather, it should not be stated. What is the reason? This *paribhāṣā* must be formulated: "In a case involving a case-ending (*vibhakti*), there is no inclusion of that which is qualified by gender. But what is the difference here between formulating this *paribhāṣā* or including the mention of *jhal*?
This *paribhāṣā* must certainly be formulated; there are many purposes for this *paribhāṣā*. What are they?

The purpose [of the rule] regarding *śvan* is as follows: just as it occurs here in *śunā*, *śunaḥ*, so too should it occur here in *śunyā*, *śunyāḥ*. The purpose of the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of *yuvan* is as follows: just as it occurs here in *yūnaḥ paśya*, so too should it occur here in *yuvatīḥ paśya*. [The purpose of the rule] regarding the application of *num* to *ugit* stems and those ending in *ac* is as follows: *ugidacām*...

There is a purpose for [the rule regarding] the suffix *num*. Just as it occurs here in the forms *gomān* and *yavamān*, so too would it occur here in *gomatī* and *yavamatī*. And there is a purpose for [the rule regarding] the suffix *ām* after *anaḍuh*. There is a purpose for *ām* after *anaḍuh*. Just as it occurs here in the form *anaḍvān*, so too would it occur here in *anaḍuhī*. But it does not occur; rather, it is *anaḍvāhī*. It does occur.

By another effort [the rule] "ām anaḍuhaḥ striyām vā" applies; because of the inclusion of the specific gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭagrahaṇāt*), it would apply to that which ends in the vowel *ī*. Regarding the substitution of *ā* for *pathin* and *mathin*: the purpose of the substitution of *ā* for *pathin* and *mathin* is such that, just as *panthāḥ* and *manthāḥ* occur here, so too would it apply here in the forms *pathī* and *mathī*. However, the word *pathin* does not function in the feminine by itself.
In that case, it occurs when compounded. For example: *supathī*. Regarding the application of the suffix *asuṅ* for the word *pumān*: there is a purpose for the application of *asuṅ* for *pumān*.

Just as it becomes *pumān* here, so too would it be [the form] *puṃsī* in this instance as well. It is not only the word *pumān* alone that occurs in the feminine; rather, it occurs when compounded. For example: *supuṃsī*. Regarding the word *sakhi*, because of its being marked with the indicatory letter *ṇit*, the suffix *anaṅ* applies. [For example: *sakhyuḥ*.

The purpose of [the designation] *ṇit* is for the application of the suffix *-aṅ*. Just as here it occurs as *sakhā*, *sakhāyau*, *sakhāyaḥ*, so too would it apply here as well: *sakhī*, *sakhyau*, *sakhyaḥ*. The purpose of [the designation] *udātta* is for the occurrence of *ud* in the case of *bhavat*, *bhagavat*, and *aghavat*. Just as here it occurs as *bhoḥ*, *bhagoḥ*, *aghoḥ*, so too would it occur as *bhagavati*.

9–10. This *jhal*-grahaṇa (the mention of *jhal*) must be made for the sake of nothing else, or else a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) regarding *num* must be stated. Neither need be stated. The *jhal*-grahaṇa is performed later [in the rule], and it will be brought forward [to this point]. Even so, a reversal of the order of the rules (*sūtra-viparyāsa*) has been effected. If that is the case, then a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: "For *ugit* stems and for those ending in a vowel (*ac*), [the long vowel occurs] before a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix."

After [the vowel] *a*, [the augment *num* is added] after the root *yuj* when not in a compound. Then, [the rule] "of the neuter" (*napuṃsakasya*). The neuter takes the augment *num*. [The condition] "after a *jhal* [consonant]" (*jhalaḥ*) is the remainder for both [rules]. Then, "of a vowel" (*acaḥ*). The augment *num* also occurs for a neuter gender ending in a vowel.
Even though this [operation] concerning the *ugit* suffixes has been avoided, this other [rule] still applies:

In the case of *śātanitarā* and *pātanitarā*, since the rule "for a feminine stem ending in an *ugit* vowel, there is shortening before suffixes such as *gha*" would otherwise apply optionally, a constant shortening is desired. This is understood as follows: "the feminine stem (*nadī*) which is *ugit*. [If it were interpreted as] "this is a feminine stem that is *ugit*," then this fault would arise in the case of *aiṣumatitarā*, because here too this feminine stem is subsequent to an *ugit* vowel.

And [the suffix] is obtained. [The rule applies to] that which is prescribed after an *ugit* [stem]. This [suffix] is prescribed after an *ugit*. That which is prescribed by the word "after an *ugit*"—even so, there is a fault in the case of *bhogavatitarā*: namely, *bhogavatitarā* would incorrectly result as *bhogavatītarā*. Therefore, this should be understood as: "that which is a *nadī* [feminine] after an *ugit*, and which is prescribed after an *ugit*. When it is understood in this way, [there is no fault] in the case of *śātanitarā*.

11.2–13.2: *Upadeśivad-vacanam* (the statement "as if in the original instruction") is for the sake of establishing the correct accent (*svara*). It should be stated that in the case of *āyan* and so forth, there is the status of being "as if in the original instruction" (*upadeśivadbhāva*). It should be stated that *āyan* and so forth occur in the state of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*). What is the purpose? For the sake of establishing the correct accent. So that the desired accent may occur in *āyan* and so forth during the state of the original instruction. [Example: *śileyam*.

[Taittirīya: [The suffix] *taittirīyaḥ*. For if the status of being like the original instruction (*upadeśivadbhāva*) were not assumed, then once the acute accent on the first syllable had been applied by virtue of its being designated as a suffix (*pratyaya*), the substitutes would—by virtue of proximity (*āntaryataḥ*)—be toneless for those that are toneless. [Objection: Or rather, it need not be stated [that the status of being like the original instruction applies]. Why? Because of the application of the marker *cit* in certain instances. Since [Pāṇini] has marked certain elements such as *gha* and others with the *cit* marker.
By placing [the suffix] *ghacchau* at the beginning, the Teacher indicates that during the stage of grammatical instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*), the substitutions *āyan* and so forth take place.
How does this serve as an indicator? The purpose of adding the marker *c* is so that the rule "of a *cita*" (*citaḥ*) may apply the acute accent (*udātta*) to the final syllable.
If *āyan* and the others occur during the stage of instruction, then the addition of the marker *c* is meaningful.

It occurs; in that case, there is a prohibition regarding the *uṇādi* suffixes. In that context, a prohibition of the *uṇādi* suffixes must be stated, as in the examples *śaṅkhaḥ* and *śāṇḍhaḥ*. Alternatively, because of the prescription of *īyaṅ* for a verbal root—namely, that the Teacher teaches *īyaṅ* after the root *ṛti*—this indicates that the suffixes *āyan* and so forth do not apply to verbal roots. For if [they did apply],...

One should simply say that [the suffix] *chaṅ* occurs after the root *ṛ*. A rule being commenced when [the desired form] is already established serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Furthermore, it is not established by *chaṅ* after *ṛ*, because if *chaṅ* were present, the augment *iṭ* characterized by the condition of beginning with a consonant (*valādi*) would necessarily apply. Once *iṭ* has been applied, the substitute [of the root] would not occur because [the root] would no longer begin with [a consonant]. This must be deliberated here: "Let *iṭ* be applied; let there be the substitute"—what should be done in this case?

The augment *iṭ* [is applied] because it is subsequent. The substitute is permanent (*nitya*), for it applies whether *iṭ* has been added or not. The substitute is not impermanent (*anitya*), for it does not apply once *iṭ* has been added. Why? Because it lacks an initial point (*anāditvāt*). If so, the substitute is internal (*antaraṅga*). What constitutes its internality? For it was just stated that the rule "treat as original" (*upadeśivad-vacana*) regarding *āyan* and so forth is for the sake of establishing the correct accent.

This statement of *īyaṅ* for *ṛt* is merely an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the substitutions *āyan* and so forth do not apply to verbal roots and suffixes. Furthermore, this is established for the venerable teacher Pāṇini through his understanding of nominal stems (*prātipadika*); that is, by virtue of his understanding of nominal stems, [it is established that] the *uṇādi* formations are underived nominal stems (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*).

Regarding the substitution of *jha*, there must be a prohibition concerning the end of a verbal root (*dhātu*). [Otherwise, one would have to say] *ujjhitā* and *ujjhitum*. This is established by virtue of the governing context of "affix" (*pratyaya*). The term "affix" (*pratyaya*), which was previously introduced, continues to apply here.

What is the subject under discussion? It is: "The substitutes *āyan*, *ey*, *īn*, *īy*, and *iya* are for the initial sounds of suffixes beginning with *ph*, *ḍh*, *kh*, *ch*, and *gh*. If it is argued that this is established by the governing context (*adhikāra*) of "suffix" (*pratyaya*), [we reply: if it is established by the governing context of "suffix," then a rule must be stated regarding the substitution [of these sounds] when they do not belong to the beginning [of the suffix].
[For example: "Will even those who are about to give birth tomorrow lie down with their husbands? In that case, there must be an explicit mention of the term "suffix" (*pratyaya*).

The mention of "ādi" (beginning with) is carried over [from the previous rule], while [the rest] has ceased. But how can a single part of those [terms] mentioned in a compound be carried over, or a single part cease? This is established because they are not mentioned in a compound. A non-compound mention will be made: *pratyayasya ādīnām* ("of the beginning of an affix"). Then that non-compound mention must be made. It need not be made; it is done precisely in the formal statement (*nyāsa*).

How so? The instruction is without case endings: "of the suffixes and so forth. In that context, regarding the form *śayāntai*, because the stem (*aṅga*) does not end in the vowel *a*, the substitution of *ā* [for the final *i*] would be prohibited. While the mention of "suffix" (*pratyaya*) continues to apply there, the mention of "beginning" (*ādi*) has ceased;
thus, in the case of *śayāntai*, since the stem does not end in *a*, the substitution of *ā* would apply to the stem, and its prohibition must be stated.

This is established by virtue of non-immediacy (*anānantarya*); the substitution of *ad* does not occur after that which ends in a vowel other than *a*. This is established. How so? Because of non-immediacy, the substitution of *ad* will not occur after that which ends in a vowel other than *a*. How is this objected to, and how is it resolved? It is objected on the grounds that the mention of "that which ends in a vowel other than *a*" (*anakārānta*) is a qualifier of the suffix (*pratyaya*); it is resolved on the grounds that it is a qualifier of the phoneme *jha*.

The solution: If the inclusion of the vowel *a* (anakārāntagrahaṇa) were a qualifier of the letter *jh*, then [the rule] would not apply to forms such as *śerate*. In that case, it is established by the statement regarding the simultaneous occurrence (*sanniyoga*) with the augment *ruṭ*. That is, the simultaneous occurrence with *ruṭ* will be prescribed there. What kind of effort is this being urged, namely "simultaneous occurrence"? The letter *ca* must be added: "*ruṭ ca*" ("and *ruṭ*"). Furthermore, whatever else [elsewhere] is applicable [should also occur].
Furthermore, what else follows? The absence of *ad*. In that case, then, the letter *ca* should be inserted [in the rule]. It need not be inserted;

rather, a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: first, "of *śīṅ*"; that is, after *śīṅ*, the substitute *at* occurs for the following *jha*. Then, "ruṭ"; that is, *ruṭ* also occurs after *śīṅ*. Even so, an undesirable optionality (*paryāya*) would result. If that is the case, then [the rule] shall be: *ruṭ* for the vowel-sound (*ac*).

I shall explain this. That mention of the word *ac* must be made. It need not be made; the previous subject continues. Where was it previously stated? In the rule *ata abhyastāt*. But that [term *at*] was specified in the nominative, whereas here the sense requires a genitive. This fifth case [ending] in *śīṅaḥ* will effect a sixth case for the first case [ending] *at*, according to the principle "from that which is [stated] in the ablative, the following [is affected]."

In the case of the suffix *ruṭ*, there is a prohibition of the *guṇa* [strengthening] of the root *dṛś*. In the case of *ruṭ*, the *guṇa* of *dṛś* would apply—as in *adṛśran asya ketavaḥ*—but its prohibition must be stated. This prohibition will be established by the rule *kṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), which applies when a *kṅit* suffix follows.

Even so, the rule would apply here in the case of *evam api adṛśram asya ketavaḥ*. If that is the case, then let the restriction be applied to the *pūrvānta* (the preceding element). If it is restricted to the *pūrvānta*, then the prescription of *guṇa* for the root *śīṅ* must be formulated as: "In the *pūrvānta*, there is *guṇa* for *śīṅ*," as in *śerate*. However, this would result in a modification of the *sūtra*. Let it remain exactly as it was originally stated. But was it not said that when the augment *ruṭ* is present, there is a prohibition of the *guṇa* of the root *dṛś*?

Thus, this same fault applies even to the *pūrvānta* (the preceding element). How so? This suffix *dṛśi*, being introduced within the scope of the prohibition [by Pāṇini 1.1.5], just as it subverts that prohibition [stated in] "kṅiti ca" (Pāṇini 1.1.5), would likewise apply even to cases where there is no *anupadhā* (penultimate vowel). Therefore, a different suffix *ak* must be prescribed for the root *dṛś* by both [rules], as in "may I see my father and my mother."

The purpose is "let it be seen" (*dṛśeya*). Because of the rule for the substitution of *jh* [for *sip*], the augment *āṭ* occurs in the *leṭ* [subjunctive] by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of the substitution of *jh* is, for example: *lunate*, *lunatām*, *alunata*. The scope of *āṭ* is, for example: *patāti* (from *patāti*), *didyut* (from *didyaut*), *cyāvayāti* (from *cyāvayāti*). Here, both would apply: *api naḥ śvaḥ vijaniṣyamāṇāḥ patibhiḥ saha*.

The augment *āṭ* occurs [before the suffixes] beginning with *śay* by way of a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*). In that case, a "prior conflict" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) must be stated. Or rather, it need not be stated. Why? Because of the permanence (*nityatva*) of *āṭ*. The augment *āṭ* is permanent. How is it permanent? If the mention of "that which does not end in the vowel *a*" (*anakārānta*) is a qualifier of the letter *jha*, then [it is permanent]; for if it were a qualifier of the suffix, [the rule would not apply].

The substitution of *jha* is also obligatory, because it is characterized as *antaraṅga*. Indeed, the augment *āṭ* is also *antaraṅga*. How is it *antaraṅga*? If the governing rule for verbal roots (*dhātvadhikāra*) applies prior to the substitution of *l* (the suffixes), then both [the augment and the substitution] share the same basis. For even if the governing rule for verbal roots continues to apply after the substitution of *l*, both [the augment and the substitution] have the same locus. This holds whether the mention of "not ending in *a*" (*anakārānta*) is a qualifier of the suffix (*pratyaya*), or whether it applies at the stage of the substitution of *l*.
The heading *dhātu* (root) continues [from the previous rule]. Even in both cases, there is no need for a prior exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). How so?

By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* ("diversely in the Vedic language"), the elision (*luk*) of *śap* will not occur here; consequently, the prohibition by the rule *anataḥ* ("not after that which ends in a vowel other than *a*") will apply.
17.11–17. The rule *bahulam chandasi* is applied twice; one [occurrence] may be omitted. How so?

If, first of all, the former [application] is made and the latter is not, then in the rule *bhisa ais*, the term *bahulam chandasi* will continue to apply by way of *anuvṛtti*. If, on the other hand, the latter is made and the former is not, [the term] *bahulam chandasi* [will still apply].

In this case, the word *ruṭ* will also be carried over [from the previous rule]. Another says: both [instances of] the term *bahulagrahaṇa* [are unnecessary]; it is possible to omit one instance of the term *chandograhaṇa*. How so? Here is what exists: [the rule] *vetteḥ vibhāṣā*; then *chandasi*; then *chandasi ca vibhāṣā*; then *ataḥ bhisa ais bhavati*.
Regarding the rule *chandasi vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.1.9):
here, in the case of *vṛkṣaiḥ plakṣaiḥ*, the substitution of *et* would apply because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Where, then, will the substitution of *ais* take place?

When *ettva* (the substitution of *e*) has been applied, [the form] will undergo *ais* because it was formerly (*bhūtapūrva*) a stem ending in *a*. But since *ais* is obligatory (*nitya*), such being the case, when this is so, the obligatory application of *ais* occurs both when *ettva* has been applied and when it has not. Because it is obligatory, once *ais* has been applied, *ettva* will not occur, as its cause has been destroyed. [This refers to] *ettva*.

If it is argued that *ais* should occur because *bhisi* is subsequent, then where would *ais* apply? Once *ettva* has been applied, *ais* is nevertheless constant due to the principle of "having previously existed" (*bhautapūrvya*).

Thus, these two prohibitions are stated; both can be omitted. How so? I shall state it thus: "after *idam* and *adas*, [the substitution occurs] when *kā* follows. That will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) for *idam* and *adas*.
"Only from this, not from anything else.
7.1.12) Why is the substitution of *in* prescribed, rather than the substitution of *nā*? What would the resulting form be?

Regarding the forms *vṛkṣeṇa* and *plakṣeṇa*, the rule for the substitution of *et* will be formulated by means of a split in the yoga (*yogavibhāga*). How so? This is the [first] rule: "In place of *at*, when followed by a *jhal*-ending plural suffix or by *osi*, there is the substitution of *et*. Then follows: "And also before *āṅ*. That is to say, when *āṅ* follows, the substitution of *et* occurs in place of *at*. Thus we have *vṛkṣeṇa* and *plakṣeṇa*. Then follows: "And also for *āp* in the vocative. That is to say: "In place of *āp*, when followed by *āṅ* or *osi* [there is the substitution of *et*]. But it cannot be done in this way. For in this case, by this [rule]...

Thus, the elision of the form *id* would result as an undesirable consequence. [Objection: The elision will be applied before a *jhal* consonant. [Response: It is not possible to apply the elision before a *jhal* consonant; for in this case, a fault would arise in the forms *ayā* and *viṣṭāḥ*. [Objection: In that case, it shall be understood as an exception (*apavāda*) to the elision of *an*. [Question: How? [Response: I shall state it thus: "before *an*, and also before *ca*. [Objection: Then the mention of the letter *n* must be made. [Response: It need not be made.

It is applied in the very context of the *nyāsa*. The letter *n* is indicated by means of elision (*lup*). If this is so, then the rule "of the penultimate vowel" (*na upadhāyāḥ*) would result in lengthening. This is a Vedic (or scriptural) usage. Alternatively, it will be treated as a neuter indication. Now, for what purpose is "from *āt*" (*āt*) stated? Why not simply say "from *at*" (*ataḥ*)? What is the formal derivation (*rūpasiddhi*) for *vṛkṣāt*?

[From] *plakṣāt*. [The form is] established by means of *savarṇadīrgha* (lengthening of homogeneous vowels). It is not established. Therefore, by the rule "when a *guṇa* [is to be applied], the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) [takes its place]," the state of being the subsequent form would apply. [Objection: It will not occur because of the force of the pronunciation of the letter *a*. [Response: If a rule that would otherwise apply is set aside by the force of pronunciation, then even *savarṇadīrgha* would not apply. [Reply: This is not a fault, because the instruction [of the letter *a*] is with respect to that specific rule [which it intends to block].

That rule is set aside for which the purpose is rendered useless; however, that rule whose cause [for application] remains is not set aside. The utterance of the vowel *a* with respect to the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is useless, whereas it is indeed the cause for the long vowel by *savarṇa-dīrgha*.

20.5–10. Is this the mention of the singular dative case (*caturthī-ekavacana*), or is it the mention of the singular locative case (*saptamī-ekavacana*)? Whence arises the doubt? Because the grammatical indication is identical. It is the mention of the singular dative case. How is this known? By the rule that between a term defined by a general characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and one stated as a specific form (*pratipadokta*), the specific form alone is to be understood. If so, here too [the reference] must be to the singular dative case.

[Otherwise] there would be the inclusion [of the locative singular]. [The rule] *ṅer ām nady-āmnībhyaḥ* [would apply]. If that is so, then the understanding of the specific [meaning] comes from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*), for it is not the case that something is not a grammatical rule (*alakṣaṇa*) simply because of doubt. Therefore, we shall explain here that the fourth-case singular is not included, whereas in that [other rule], the seventh-case singular is [included].
An addition must be made [to the rule] regarding the substitution of *smāy* and other forms for *as*, when there is a single substitute (*ekādiṣṭa*). For instance:
*atho atra asmai*, *atho atra asmāt*, and *atho atra asmin*. This occurs when there is a single substitute.

Therefore, when [the substitution] has been made, the suffixes *smāy* and so forth do not apply. What, then, is the reason that the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) occurs first, rather than *smāy* and the others? It is not the case that they must occur because they are subsequent; they should not occur. Why? Because the single-substitute is obligatory (*nitya*). The single-substitute is obligatory; it applies both when *smāy* and the others have already occurred and when they have not yet occurred.

Furthermore, because [the substitution] is permanent (*nityatva*), once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, the rules for *smāy* and so forth—starting with *ataḥ*—would not apply. Why then is it said "after *aś*" (*aśaḥ*)? Should this not also be applied here, as in: *atra asmai*, *atra asmāt*, *atra asmin*? Once the single-substitute has been applied, the rules for *smāy* and so forth starting with *ataḥ* would not apply. This is established by the sequence of operations (*ānupūrvya*). It is not the case that *smāy* and so forth have not yet been applied here.

If a case-ending beginning with a consonant (*hal*) exists, and if there is elision of *rūpa* when that [ending] begins with a consonant, then a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) would not apply before such elision of *rūpa* has taken place.

That is established by the sequence of operations. In that case, an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made. Or rather, it need not be done, because it is characterized as being external (*bahiraṅga*). Why? Because it is characterized as being external; the single-substitute is external.
The internal [operations] are *smāy* and so forth; the external is not established when the internal is present.
(Pāṇini 1.4.2) Why is both *śībhāva* and *śibhāva* prescribed? Why not simply *śibhāva* alone be prescribed? What would the resulting form be?

[Objection: Those [forms] which are [already] established by the rule *ād guṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.87]. [Reply: It cannot be so. For in this case, in forms such as *trapuṇī*, *jatunī*, and *dīrghaśravaṇam*, the long vowel would not be heard. [Objection: In that case, let only the substitution of *śī* be stated. [Reply: It cannot be so. For in this case, in forms such as *kuṇḍāni* and *vanāni*, the short vowel would not be heard. Therefore, both the substitution of *śī* and the substitution of *śi* must be stated.

(P_7,1.18) KA_III,247.5–16 Ro_V, 22.2–23.6 For what purpose is the letter *ṅ* [used]? It is for the sake of including the general category (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*). If it were stated simply as *au*, it would apply only to the dual of the nominative case. Even if it were stated as *auṭ*, it would still apply only to the dual of the accusative case.

This would indeed be the case. There is this purpose [for the rule]. But what then? The operation conditioned by *ṅit* (ṅit-kārya) would apply. In the cases *khaṭve* and *māle*, the augment *yāṭ* would apply by the rule *yāṭ āpaḥ*. This is not a fault. It is not understood thus: "that which has *ṅ* as its *it* is *ṅit*; [the rule applies] when there is a *ṅit*. How then? "That which is *ṅ* itself as its *it* is *ṅit*; [the rule applies] when there is a *ṅit*. This being so, there is the mention of the phoneme (*varṇa-grahaṇa*).

This applies to the mention of phonemes (*varṇagrahaṇa*), and this principle applies: "In the mention of an *al* [phoneme], the rule applies to that which begins with it. Thus, there is no fault. Alternatively, this is a mention of phonemes, yet this principle does not apply to mentions of phonemes: "When there is a mention of a [phoneme] without an *anubandha*, it does not include that which has an *anubandha*. Or else, this is a reference to the preceding rules; it occurs within the preceding rules.

And those suffixes which are *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) do not perform their operations here. This vowel *au* is taken as having the *ṅit* designation in the rule for the formation of the *śī* affix;

yet for us, there is no such thing as a *ṅit* [suffix]. What kind of method is this? Its purpose is general, and when it is attached to this [vowel], the operation of a *ṅit* would apply to your *śī*;
that is the fault. One should understand that the *ṅit*-designation refers merely to the indication of the phoneme; whatever effect applies to the phoneme itself, that alone should be understood.

And one should know that this letter [the *ṅ*] occurs at the beginning; therefore, even though it is marked with the *ṅit* designation, there is no fault. This instruction may either be by means of the preceding rule [Pāṇini 7.1.20].

(Pāṇini 7.1.21) *auśaghau*. It should be stated: "*auśaghau*" [instead of "*auś" alone]. What is this "in *agha*" (*aghau*)? [It refers to] when it is not a final member of a compound (*anuttarapada*).

Thus [it is asked]: what is the purpose? So that it does not occur here in the cases *aṣṭaputraḥ* and *aṣṭabhāryaḥ*. Let there be *luk* (elision) in those cases. Let there be *auś* here; *luk* will take effect. [Objection: The same would then apply even after the word *ṣaṣ* (*ṣaḍbhyaḥ*). [Reply: Then it would also apply here: *aṣṭau tiṣṭhanti*, *aṣṭau paśya*. [Objection: It is an exception (*apavāda*). [Reply: Because it is an exception, *auś* applies here.

[The rule] will sublate the elision (*luk*). But then it would also sublate [the elision] here: *aṣṭaputraḥ*, *aṣṭabhāryaḥ*. [Answer: It is in the domain of that [elision]; it is an exception (*apavāda*) to that elision (*luk*) in whose domain the substitution of *auś* occurs. Or rather, it is an exception to that which immediately follows it.
Or else, it will be a sublater of the immediately following elision. Why is this so? Because a rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediately following.

Or rather: why does the substitution *auś* not occur here in the examples "aṣṭa tiṣṭhanti" and "aṣṭa paśya"? [The rule states: "Where there is *ātva*, there *auśtva* [should apply]. Only where there is *ātva* should there be *auśtva*. Why is this so? Because its inclusion is made in that manner; for its inclusion is made when it has become *ātva*, as in "aṣṭābhyaḥ."

26.2–28.6: "The elision of *su* and *am* [should be stated] after *tyad* and the others. It should be stated that there is elision of *su* and *am* after *tyad* and the others, so that it may apply here as well: *tat brāhmaṇakulam*. For if the substitution of *atva* (of *t* for *ta*) were made first, the elision would not occur; once *atva* has been applied, the elision does not take effect. This must be considered here: [which rule takes precedence?]

Let the substitution of *at* be made, and let there be elision (*luk*). What should be done here? The substitution of *at* [should apply] because it is subsequent. Elision is permanent (*nitya*), for it applies whether the substitution of *at* has been performed or not. Elision is not permanent, for it does not apply once the substitution of *at* has been performed. Therefore, by the rule *ataḥ am*, the form *am* must occur. Consequently, it should be stated: "and after *tyad* and so on. This is now considered:

In the rules for the application of *śi*, *śī*, *luk*, and *num*, the mention of "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*) may refer either to the word-form (*śabdagrahaṇa*) or to the meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*). What, then, is the distinction here? If, in the rules for *śi*, *śī*, *luk*, and *num*, the mention of "neuter" refers to the word-form, there is a prohibition regarding the "other member of the compound" (*anyapadārtha*). If, in the rules for *śi*, *śī*, *luk*, and *num*, the mention of "neuter" refers to the word-form...
An exception must be stated for the forms *bahutrapuḥ*, *bahutrapū*, and *bahutrapavaḥ*. Let it be, then, that there is a mention of "meaning" (*arthagrahaṇa*).

If there is a mention of "meaning," then in the case of *priyasakthnā brāhmaṇena*, the substitution *anaṅ* would not apply. Let it be, then, that there is only a mention of the "word-form" (*śabdagrahaṇa*). But was it not said: "If the mention of the neuter gender is intended for the rules regarding the suffix *śi*, the elision of *luK*, and the addition of *num*, then there is a prohibition when the compound has another word as its referent (*anyapadārtha*)"?

[Objection: This is established, however, because it is a qualifier of the subject under discussion (*prakṛtārthaviśeṣaṇatvāt*). This is established. How so? The meaning of the subject under discussion is qualified. And what is the subject under discussion? It is the *aṅga* (stem). The suffixes *śi*, *ślu*, and *num* occur for an *aṅga* that is functioning as a neuter. [Counter-example: How is it [explained] in the case of *priyasakthnā brāhmaṇena* ("by the Brahmin who has beloved thighs")? [Answer: In the list beginning with *asthi*, there is a mention of the word-form (*śabdagrahaṇa*). In the list beginning with *asthi*, there is a mention of the neuter gender (*napuṃsakagrahaṇa*).

The mention of "word" (*śabda*) should be understood [as referring to the meaning]. However, this is worthy of further investigation: surely, by this mention of "meaning" (*artha*), there ought to be no ambiguity, for there is no such thing as a neuter "word. Why, then, is it said that in the case of *asthi* and so forth, there is the mention of "word"? Even here, it is indeed the mention of "meaning. In this regard, the doubt is only this much: in what context does the original subject apply?

The meaning is specified as follows: "Of which [stem] being grasped? In the rules concerning the suffixes *śi*, *ślu*, and *num*, the meaning of the stem under discussion is specified as that which is being grasped among the group beginning with *asthi*.

28.8–29.5: A prohibition of the *pūrvasavarṇa* [substitution] when there is the substitution of *at*. When there is the substitution of *at*, a prohibition of the *pūrvasavarṇa* must be stated. [Examples: *katarat tiṣṭhati*, *katarat paśya*. It is established by virtue of the vowel having a nasalized (*anunāsika*) penultimate. This is established. How? The word *ac* will be treated as having a nasalized penultimate. Or else, because of the addition of the augment *ḍu*. Or rather, he will state "of *ḍatara* and so forth"; because of the addition of the marker *ḍit*.

Or alternatively, the word *ad* will be treated as having the marker *ḍ*. In that case, the letter *ḍ* must be added. It need not be added; it is already included in the formulation itself. The instruction contains two *ḍ*s: *adḍ* in the rule *adḍ ḍatarādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.26).

29.7–30.8: "The prohibition [of the neuter endings] applies to *itarāt* in Vedic; for *ekatarāt*, it applies everywhere. It should be stated: 'The prohibition applies to *itarāt* in Vedic; for *ekatarāt*, it applies everywhere. Examples: *ekataraṃ tiṣṭhati*, *ekataraṃ paśya*. Regarding the rules for the substitutes of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*: the case-endings (vibhakti) replace the neuter substitutes by way of conflict (vipratiṣedha). The case-endings of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* take the place of the neuter substitutes by way of conflict. The scope for the neuter substitutes is, for example: *trapu* (tin).
*trapuṇī*, *trapūṇi*. [This is] the scope for the substitutes of the case-endings (*vibhakti*) for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*: *tvaṃ brāhmaṇaḥ*, *ahaṃ brāhmaṇaḥ*.
"Yuvām brāhmaṇau," "āvām brāhmaṇau," "yūyam brāhmaṇāḥ," and "vayam brāhmaṇāḥ. In this case, both [forms] are applicable. "Tvam brāhmaṇakulam" (you, the Brahmin family).
I am in a brahmin family;
you two are in a brahmin family;
we two are in a brahmin family.
"You are Brāhmaṇa families;

we are Brāhmaṇa families. By the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the substitutes for the case-endings (*vibhaktyādeśa*) of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* take effect. Now, once the substitutes for the case-endings of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* have been applied, why do the rules for *śi*, *ślu*, and *num* not apply again due to the principle of recurrence (*punaḥprasaṅga*)?
They do not occur. That which is set aside by a prohibition in the case of simultaneous application (*sakṛdgatau*) remains set aside for good.

7.1.27) Why is the letter *ś* [in *śit*] used? It is for the purpose of making it a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). According to the rule *śit sarvasya*, that which has *ś* as its indicatory letter (*śit*) replaces the whole, as follows:

It might be so. But there is no need for this [restriction]. Even if the *śakāra* were not employed, since rules apply to the final letter of an element (*alaḥ antyasya*), when the *akāra* is applied to the final [letter], the form would be established through the three *akāras* by the rule *ataḥ guṇe pararūpatvam* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), as in *tava svam*, *mama svam*. If that were obtainable, it would be well enough; however, it is not obtainable. Why? Because here...
For otherwise, by the rule *hi tasmād iti uttarasyādeḥ parasya*, the substitution would apply to the initial *a* of the subsequent element. Therefore, he recites the following [sūtra]:

"The addition of the marker *ś* to the substitute for *ṅasi* is purposeless, because the utterance of an *a* for an *a* is purposeless. The addition of the marker *ś* to the substitute for *ṅasi* is purposeless. Why? Because the utterance of an *a* for an *a* is purposeless; that is, when an *a* is uttered for an *a*.

Since there would be no purpose [for it], the substitution will occur for the whole [word] even without the letter *ś*. [Objection: Because the substitute is meaningful, [the rule] is for the sake of elision (*lopa*). [Response: The mention of the vowel *a* is for the sake of the letter *k* which possesses meaning. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of elision in the substitute.

That which is the elision in the remainder (*śeṣe lopaḥ*) is understood to apply to the substitute. [Objection: But surely this is understood as "the case-ending (*vibhakti*) which is the substitute."

This case-ending is a substitute (*ādeśa*). How so? For Pāṇini, the son of Dākṣī, all [grammatical elements] are substitutes for entire words; for if there were a modification of only a single part, permanence (*nityatva*) would not be possible. Therefore, the letter *ś* is employed. Therefore, the letter *ś* must be made. It need not be made. It is indeed included in the formal statement (*nyāsa*). How so? This is a composite designation (*praśliṣṭanirdeśa*): *a*, *a*, *a*.
Thus, by the rule *anekāl śit sarvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.55), it will apply to the whole [word].
Regarding the statement "of the first two" (*prathamayoḥ*), of which two is this mention of "the first two"? Is it of the two case-endings (*vibhakti*), or...

[The question is: "Of two suffixes"? He says, "of two case-endings. How is this known? For elsewhere, when there is a mention of "the first two," it is understood as a reference to two case-endings, not to two suffixes. Where else? In the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*.
There is a reason why, in that case, it is understood as a reference to two case-endings. What is the reason? Because of the word *aci* [in that rule].
In that case, [the word *ajādi*] applies, yet the two initial vowels do not exist [as a single unit]. But surely it could be understood thus:

"those which are the first among vowels" or "those which are the first of the vowels beginning with *a*. If so, then the fact that the Teacher refers back to the previously mentioned rule "after that [stem], *śas* becomes *naḥ* in the masculine" (*tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi*) as being of the same quality as its predecessor (*pūrvasavarṇa*) indicates that the Teacher intends the mention of two case-endings (*vibhakti*). This is also the Teacher’s intention here.

He indicates that there is a mention of both case-endings when he teaches the prohibition "not [the substitution of *na*] for *śas*. This is not a prohibition; rather, this substitution of *na* is not being prescribed here. The substitution of *na* is already established in this instance by the rule "for *śas*, *na* is substituted in the masculine. It is for the sake of those cases where it would not be established by that [rule]. And where would it not be established by that? In the feminine and in the neuter.
And: "Look at you, O Brahmins; look at us, O Brahmins;
look at you, O Brahmin families."

"Look at us, O Brahmin families. Now, when the teacher says, "In the case of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, when there is no substitute (*anādeśa*), and in the second case," he thereby indicates that the mention [in the rule] refers to the case-endings (*vibhakti*).
(Pāṇini 7.1.30) KA_III,252.8-14 Ro_V, 33.10-34.6 Is this the word *bhyam*, or rather the word *abhyam*? From what does the doubt arise? Because the phonetic description is identical.

Furthermore, what follows from this? If, first of all, the word *abhyam* remains and there is elision (*lopa*) of the final letter, then the substitution of *etva* (the change to *e*) would apply. Or, if the word *abhyam* remains and there is elision, then there would be elision of the *ṭi* (the penultimate vowel) and the accentuation known as *udāttanivṛttisvara* would apply. Let it be as you wish.
Let us assume for now that the word *abhyam* remains and there is elision of the final letter. But was it not already stated that *etva* would apply?

Thus, this fault does not arise. For when there is a further application of an operation upon that which has already undergone an operation on its constituent parts (*aṅgavṛtta*), the rule "there is no prescription for what is already established" (*niṣṭhitasya*) will prevent it from occurring. Alternatively, let the word *abha* remain, and let there be elision of the remainder (*śeṣe lopaḥ*), which is the elision of the *ṭi* suffix. But was it not said that the accent of the disappearance of the acute (*udāttanivṛttisvara*) would apply? This is not a fault; for it has been stated that [this result] is established at the very beginning.

(P_7.1.33) KA_III,252.16–253.21 Ro_V, 34.8–38.4: For what purpose is the inclusion of the *sakāra* (the sound *s*) after *ām* made? Why not simply say "of *ām*, [there is] *ākam*"? By what means, then, will the form with the *sakāra* be produced? This *suṭ* augment belongs to *ām*; it will be included by the mention of *ām*.

Therefore, he recites the subsequent rule: "The inclusion of *sām* is for the sake of that which is grasped as it was originally stated, because of the statement regarding its substitution. The inclusion of *sām* is made [in the sūtra] on the principle that "substitutions apply to that which is being specifically pointed out" (*nirdiśyamāna*). Consequently, this would not apply to the form with the *sakāra* (i.e., *sām*). However, it is desired that it should apply;
and since that cannot be accomplished without an effort, the rule "of *sām*, *ākam*" is stated for this purpose.

Alternatively, there is no absence of the *sakāra* in the *āmu* [ending] because of the statement that [the substitution of] *akāra* applies only up to the dual. Nor is this a necessary purpose. Why? Because of the statement that the substitution of *akāra* applies only up to the dual. For it is taught that the substitution of *at* occurs for the pronouns beginning with *tyad* up to the dual;

therefore, the *sakāra* will not occur in the *āmu*. However, the prohibition of *suṭ* follows from the understanding that [the *akāra*] is a substitute [for the final letter]. Thus, there is a prohibition of *suṭ*.

But it must be stated [that the *suṭ* augment is not applied]. What is the reason? Because the elision (*lopa*) is understood to apply to the substitute (*ādeśa*). That which is the elision in the remainder (*śeṣe lopaḥ*) is understood to apply to the substitute. Or rather, it need not be stated; because of the mention of the elision of the *ṭi* suffix (*ṭilopa*), it serves to prohibit the *ṭāp* feminine suffix in the case of the substitute. Nor need the prohibition of *suṭ* be stated. What is the reason? Because of the mention of the elision of the *ṭi*. That which is the elision in the remainder when there is a substitute—that is the elision of the *ṭi*, and that must be stated. Why?

The purpose [of the rule] is to prohibit the suffix *ṭāp*. That is, [the suffix] *ṭāp* should not occur. In that case, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) must be stated. Or rather, it need not be stated; because there is no gender, the statement regarding the elision of the *ṭi* is purposeless. It need not be stated. Why? Because there is no gender. *Yuṣmad* and *asmad* are without gender. Is this something that needs to be stated? No, indeed. How is it understood even when it is not stated?

Indeed, there is no distinction between the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* whether they refer to a female, a male, or a neuter. There is a reason why this is so. What is the reason? It is because of the absence of that word which expresses a specific distinction. Come now, please pronounce that [specific word]; then that distinction will be understood. But surely, it cannot be so by this alone.
For it is not the case that a meaning must necessarily exist because of a word; rather, it is the word that must exist because of a meaning. Let this be seen in this way:
it is the very form of the object itself that is of such a nature that, by means of it, no distinction is perceived here. And this is necessarily so.

It should be understood in this way: for one who thinks that because the specific word [denoting the object] is not present here, the specific quality is not understood—here too its specific quality is not understood, namely, "a stone fuel" (*dṛṣatsamit*). Therefore, the prohibition of *suṭ* must be stated; therefore, the prohibition of *suṭ* must be stated by including the letter *s*.

Or it should be done. Now, even if the inclusion of the letter *s* is carried out, why does *suṭ* not occur here? By the force of including the letter *s*, it is understood that the substitute is for the *suṭ* that is about to occur.

39.2–8: Here, three operations—reduplication (*dvirvacana*), single-substitution (*ekādeśa*), and the substitution of *au* (*autva*)—simultaneously apply to the forms *papau* and *tasthau*. If the substitution of *au* were to obtain in all cases, the desired result would be achieved.
Even if reduplication were to be obtained, it would still be accomplished in this way; however, that [reduplication] is not actually obtained here. What is the reason?

For in this case, because it is subsequent, the single-substitute (ekādeśa) rule subverts the reduplication rule. Because it is subsequent, the substitution of *au* (*autva*) [subverts it]. The single-substitute rule is permanent (*nitya*), and thus it would subvert the substitution of *au*. But what scope do you consider to exist for the substitution of *au*, such that you say "the single-substitute rule is permanent"?

The substitution of *au* will set aside the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule as it finds no opportunity [to apply]. Even if, once the substitution of *au* has been made, one were to argue that the single-substitute occurs first because it is subsequent [to the rule for reduplication], and that reduplication will then take place by virtue of the substitute being treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), [this is not so].
(P. 7.1.36; Kāśikā III,254.6–13; Rgveda V)

40.2–41.1. *Videḥ vasoḥ kittvam*. It should be stated that the *kit* designation applies to the root *vid* when followed by *vasu*. What is the purpose? So that in the rules concerning the suffix *vasu*, there may also be the inclusion of the substitute for *liṭ*. And what is the reason it would not otherwise occur? For when there is a mention of a [root] without an *anubandha*, there is no inclusion of one with an *anubandha*; thus, the substitute for *liṭ* would not be included. Indeed, it is with an *anubandha*.

It is so formulated. But what is the reason that it is formulated with an *anubandha* (indicatory letter)? This [rule] is begun as a domain for the prohibition of *guṇa* in the case of roots ending in *ṛ* when the *liṭ* suffix follows; however, that [prohibition] is superseded by the fact of its being marked with the *kit* designation, as in the forms *ātistīrvān* and *nipupūrvān*. In that case, then, this *anubandha* must be attached to it for that purpose. It need not be attached. It is indeed included in the very formulation (*nyāsa*). The instruction contains two *s* sounds: [the first is for the sake of the *kit* designation, and the second is for the sake of the *ṣatva* substitution].
The substitute *vasu* is applied for the genitive suffix *śatṛ* when it occurs in a compound that does not have *nañ* as its prior member; the suffix *lyap* is applied for *ktvā*.

Regarding the substitution of *lyap*, there must be a statement that it behaves like the original form (*upadeśivad-vacana*). That is, the status of behaving like the original form (*upadeśivadbhāva*) must be stated for the substitution of *lyap*; [this applies] to the state of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthāyām*).

It should be stated that *lyap* occurs [in place of *ktvā*]. What is the purpose? To apply it even when no substitution has been prescribed, so that *lyap* may occur before those [substitutions] have been made. Which substitutions, then, necessitate the rule stating "as if taught" (*upadeśivad-vacana*)? They are: doubling (*hitva*), the substitution of *da* (*dattva*), the substitution of *t* (*tva*), the substitution of *et*, the substitution of *ettva*, lengthening (*dīrghatva*), and the substitution of *śūṭ*. The substitution of *t*: having cut (*chittvā*), having scattered (*kīrtvā*). The substitution of *t*. The substitution of *et*: having sprinkled (*siktvā*), having cooked (*paktvā*). The substitution of *et*. Lengthening: having sharpened (*śitvā*), having sharpened (*śiṣvā*). Lengthening. The substitution of *śūṭ*: having pierced (*viśitvā*), having entered (*praviśya*). The substitution of *śūṭ*. Thus, the rule "as if taught" is necessary for these purposes. *prapāya*: *īttva* (substitution of *ī*) and lengthening (*dīrghatva*). *śāntvā*, *praśamya*: lengthening and *śatva* (substitution of *ś*). *pṛṣṭvā*, *āpṛcchya*: *śatva*. *ūṭh*: *dyūtvā*.

*pradīvya*, *ūṭh*, *iṭ*, *devitvā*, *pradīvya*. But what is the reason that the substitutes (*ādeśas*) occur first and not the suffix *lyap*? It should not be the case that *lyap* occurs because it is subsequent; for there are indeed some subsequent substitutes here as well, and moreover, [the application of *lyap*] is characterized by being extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*).

The suffix *lyap* is external (*bahiraṅga*), while the substitutions (*ādeśa*) are internal (*antaraṅga*). That which is external is considered unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal. In that case, the treatment of the original form (*upadeśivadbhāva*) must be stated. It need not be stated. The activity of the Teacher indicates that the external *lyap* supersedes even internal rules, since he includes the mention of *lyap* in the rule "adaḥ jagdhiḥ lyapi kiti" (Pāṇini 2.4.36), even though it would have been established by the rule "ti kiti" alone.

[The suffix *ka*] is applied. Furthermore, a prohibition must be stated regarding [the formation of] *snātvākālaka*, etc.: "having bathed, he is black" (*snātvākālaka*), "having drunk, he is steady" (*pītvāsthiraka*), and "having eaten, he is satisfied" (*bhuktvāsuhitaka*). This is established by the mention of the word ending in that [suffix]. It is established by the mention of the word ending in that [suffix]. How so?

That which ends in *ktvā* ought to be changed to *lyap*, yet this [form] does not end in *ktvā*. Or rather, it is due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) of the compound. Alternatively, an irregular formation must necessarily be made here for the sake of the compound; by that very effort, *lyap* will likewise not occur. Or else, *lyap* should occur after what follows a negative particle (*nañ*), but here there is no negative particle.

We observe this. But surely the negative particle (*nañ*) itself is a verbal root (*dhātu*). It should not apply to what follows a verbal root. What is the reason? Because when joined with *nañ* or *iva*, there is a comprehension of meaning based on another similar locus. Just as with that which is joined with *nañ*, so too with that which is joined with *iva*, the grammatical operation will be understood to apply to something else similar to it. Why is this so? Because the meaning is understood in that way. That is the point.

And what else is there that is other than *nañ* and similar to *nañ*? He says: "A word (*pada*). Alternatively, in the case of the mention of an affix (*pratyaya*), [the rule applies to what is similar to it].

Here, first of all, regarding "the noble support of glories, of riches": the optional designation *nadī* for the case-ending *āmi* will be a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) in the Vedic language (*chandas*).
