And in the case of *grāmaṇī* and *sūtagrāmaṇī*, [the form] is established by the rule *hrasvanadyāpaḥ nuṭ*.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of *dhātoḥ* (after a verbal root)? [Consider: *abhaitsīt*.

*acchaitsīt*. Regarding the rule for the introduction of *num*, there is an instruction that it should be treated as if it were part of the original instruction (*upadeśivadvacana*) for the sake of the application of suffixes (*pratyayavidhyartha*). It must be stated that in the rule for introducing *num*, the status of being like the original instruction (*upadeśivadbhāva*) applies; that is, it must be stated that *num* occurs in the state of the original instruction. What is the purpose? For the sake of the application of suffixes. So that when *num* has been applied in the state of the original instruction, the desired application of the suffix may take place. As in *kuṇḍā*.

[The word] *huṇḍā*. For otherwise, the suffix would occur when the letter *a* is present. If the treatment as "taught" (*upadeśivadbhāva*) were not applied, then whatever suffix would apply when the letter *a* is present would indeed occur; while that [suffix] remains, the augment *num* would follow. What is the fault in that? In that case, there would be the contingency of undesirable results. There, something unintended would result: the augment *num* would occur while the unintended suffix remains.

There would follow the undesirable consequence of hearing [the augment] *num* after an affix. Alternatively, by the force of the mention of "root" (*dhātu*), the rule for *num* will apply when that [affix] is taught; that is, by the force of the mention of "root," *num* will occur when the root is taught. But has it not been stated that there is another purpose for the mention of "root"? What is it? [As in the case of] *abhaitsīt*.

57.2–58.6. Regarding the roots beginning with *tṛmp*: An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the roots beginning with *tṛmp* under the rule for the suffix *śa*. [Examples: *tṛmpati*, *tṛmphati*. For what purpose is this? Is it not the case that these are recited as already having the augment *num* attached? No, because their nasal has been elided.

Here, the nasal is elided by the rule "of those [roots] ending in a consonant and having a penultimate vowel other than *i*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel before *k* and *ṅ*. If, however, these were recited as having the marker *it* (i.e., as *idita*), [the following would apply].

It cannot be so; for in this case, the elision [of the *num* augment] would not occur in forms such as *tṛpitaḥ* and *dṛpitaḥ*. However, if these were recited among the roots beginning with *muc*, there would be no fault. Or rather, it should not be understood thus: "the *num* augment follows a root that has an *it* marker. How then? It should be understood as: "the *num* follows what has an *it* marker," and then "from the root" (*dhātoḥ*).
These two prohibitions are stated; both could have been left unspoken. How so? I shall state it thus:

"In the case of *liṭ* [perfect], when *iṭ* follows, *num* occurs after the root *radh*. This will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyama*), meaning that *num* occurs only after *radh* when followed by *iṭ* in *liṭ*, and not elsewhere.
"In another [word] beginning with *iḍā*, etc. (P. 7.1.65). Why does it not apply here? [Example: *iha*.
It is prescribed [that the *num* suffix is applied]. Let it be so. [One might argue: "The elision will occur by the rule *aniditām hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti*.

But then, in this case—*ālambhyā gauḥ*—when the *yat* suffix is present according to the rule *poḥ adupadhāt*, the *num* would apply. What is the fault there? The accent *ālambhyā* would result, whereas *ālambhyā* is what is desired. This is not a fault; for it has already been stated that [the application of *num*] is due to the force of the mention of the verbal root (*dhātu*).

Regarding the rule "upadeśe numvidhānam" (Pāṇini 7.1.68): Now, for what purpose is the mention of *kevala* (alone) used? Why not simply say "na na sudurbhyām" instead? [The answer is: [It would apply] to *su* and *dus*.

The inclusion of the word *kevala* (alone) is for the purpose of excluding other prefixes. The term *kevala* is employed after *su* and *dus* so that [the rule] does not apply when they are accompanied by another prefix. For example, *prasulambham*. This usage does not exist. Well then, consider this: *supralambham*. Because it is separated by the prefix *pra*, the rule will not apply. Well then, consider this: *atisulambham*. [This concerns] the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of a *karmapravacanīya*.

In this case, there will be an obstruction [to the application of the suffix], because of the rule: "The suffix *su* is used in the sense of honor (*pūjā*), and *ati* in the sense of transgression (*atikramaṇa*). But what happens when there is neither transgression nor honor? This too is an example: *supralambham*. Now, was it not said that [the suffix] will not apply because of being separated by the prefix *pra*? This is not a fault. In the rule *sudurbhyām*, this is not a locative (fifth case). What then? It is a third case.

Regarding the rule *sudurbhyām upasṛṣṭasya*: even that which is separated [by other words] is considered "preceded by" (*upasṛṣṭa*). (Pāṇini 7.1.69) Concerning the rule *ciṇṇamuloḥ anupasargasya*: it should be stated that [the prohibition applies] when there is no prefix (*anupasarga*) before the affixes *ciṇ* and *namul*. Here, [let there be] *mā...*
It occurred; it was obtained; it was obtained repeatedly. In that case, should it be stated? It need not be stated.
Here, although "after a prefix" (*upasargāt*) is also under discussion, and "not" (*na*) is also [under discussion] there, only a connection must be made:
"optionally after *ciṇ* and *namul*, not after a prefix."

(P_7,1.70) KA_III,263.7-13 Ro_V, 61-62: What is the purpose of [the condition] "not after a verbal root" (*adhātoḥ*)? [Examples: *ukhāsrat*, *parṇadhvat*. It could be said that "not after a verbal root" need not be stated. Why does [the suffix] not occur in *khāsrat*?

Regarding the example *parṇadhvat*: it is established by the inclusion of the term *ugit* in the rule for *añc*. Since it is established by the inclusion of *ugit* in the rule for *añc*, and because it applies to what is not a verbal root (*adhātu*), the mention of *añc* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). That is to say, [the suffix] applies only after a verbal root ending in *ugit* that is derived from *añc*, and not after any other verbal root ending in *ugit*. In that case, this is the purpose: so that it may apply even to that which was previously not a verbal root. As in *gomantam*.
[The word] *gomān* is derived from the root *gomat*, which is the form of *gomatyati* with the suffix *apratyaya*.

(Pāṇini 7.1.72). Regarding the rule for the addition of *num* after a stem ending in a consonant (*jhal*) or a vowel (*ac*), there must be a prohibition of that which is characterized by the marker *u* (*ugit*). [Otherwise, one would have to say: "the *brāhmaṇa* families possess cows" (*gomanti brāhmaṇakulāni*).

"Greater blessings, more numerous! [Objection: But surely the rule characterized by *jhal* will supersede the rule characterized by *ugit*. [Response: How can that which is prescribed for one thing be a superseder of another?
Indeed, supersession occurs only when there is no possibility [of both rules applying simultaneously], yet here such a possibility does exist.

If both were to apply, what would happen? If the rule characterized by *ugit* were also to apply here, the hearing of two *n* sounds would result. There is no difference in the hearing of one or many consonants that follow [the vowel]. But surely there is a difference in the technical designation (*pratijñā*)? What will a difference in technical designation achieve when there is no difference in the actual phonetic perception (*śruti*)?

But surely there is also a distinction established by scripture (*śruti*). Here, for instance, in the cases *śreyāṃsi* and *bhūyāṃsi*, when the *anusvāra* is applied to the following [consonant], the hearing of the preceding [nasal] would follow. Likewise, in *kurvanti* and *kṛṣanti*, once the *anusvāra* and the *parasavarṇa* have been applied to the following [consonant], the substitution of *ṇ* for the preceding [dental nasal] would follow. Now...

Why does the substitution of *ṇ* not occur even when there is a single *n*? [Because] having become an *anusvāra*, it transcends the condition for *ṇatva*. Why then does it not occur after the *parasavarṇa* has been applied? Because the *parasavarṇa* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). It is established by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). This is established by conflict: let the rule characterized by *jhal* apply, or let the rule characterized by *ugit* apply; thus, the rule characterized by *jhal* prevails.

There will be a conflict [between two rules]. The scope for the rule conditioned by *jhal* is, for example, *sarpīṃṣi*, *dhanūṃṣi*. The scope for the rule conditioned by *ugit* is, for example, *gomān*, *yavamān*.
In the present case, both [rules] would apply: *gomanti brāhmaṇakulāni*.
"Brahmin families possess barley;

they are better, they are more numerous. [In this case,] the *jhall* suffix will apply by virtue of the prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*). But surely, because of the understanding that there is a recurrence of the application (*punaḥ-prasaṅga*)?

The characteristic of being *ugit* would apply again. If it is argued that this constitutes a "reapplication" (*punar-prasaṅga*), it is the same as in the case of the suffixes beginning with *am*. If it is argued that this is a reapplication, it is equivalent to the following: when the suffixes beginning with *am* have been applied to *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the suffixes *śas*, *śī*, *luk*, and *num* do not occur because of reapplication. In the same way, once the characteristic of being *jhal* has been applied, the characteristic of being *ugit* would apply again due to reapplication.

It will not be so. As for what was said—that when there is no possibility [of both], there is indeed a sublation, but here there is a possibility that both might exist—nevertheless, even when there is a possibility, a sublation occurs. For example: "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, and buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya. Even though there is a possibility of giving curd, the giving of buttermilk [sublates it].

It becomes an annulment. Likewise here as well, even though both [possibilities] exist, that characterized by the *ugit* suffix will annul that characterized by the *jhal* suffix. Or rather, let there be the application of the rule characterized by the *ugit* suffix here as well. But was it not said that the hearing of the two *n* sounds of the *cvī* suffix would result?
This has been answered: there is no distinction regarding the hearing of one or many consonants following [the vowel].

It exists. But has it not been said that there would be a split in the proposition (*pratijñābheda*)? If there is no difference in the phonetic form (*śrutibheda*), what will a split in the proposition do? But has it not also been stated here that there is a difference caused by the phonetics—namely, in the case of "tāvat śreyāṃsi" and "bhūyāṃsi," when the *anusvāra* is applied to the following sound, the hearing of the preceding sound would result, as they say: "they perform"?

[Objection: In the case of *kṛṣanti*, once the *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa* have been applied to the following [sound], the rule for the change of the preceding [dental *n*] to *ṇ* would apply. [Response: This is not a fault. It has been stated that the teaching of the *ayogavāha* sounds is without distinction.

In this regard, first, in cases such as *śreyāṃsi* and *bhūyāṃsi*, once the *anusvāra* is applied to the following [sound], because that [following sound] is included by the mention of *jhal*, the *anusvāra* will occur for the preceding [sound]. As for *kurvanti*:

In the case of *kṛṣanti*, once the *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa* have been applied to the following [nasal], those two will apply to the preceding [vowel] because that [following nasal] is included by the term *jhal*. Alternatively, the designation *ugit* does not apply here at all. Why? Because it is stated that "the augment *mid* follows the final vowel," and there cannot be two *mids* following the final vowel.

The possibility exists. How then do these two *mit* vowels occur after the final vowel? As in: *bahvanaḍvāṃhi brāhmaṇakulāni*. These two are [added] without a specific cause. In that case, there is a prohibition regarding *bahūrji*. In that case, a prohibition regarding *bahūrji* must be stated: as in *bahūrji brāhmaṇakulāni*. Some [teachers] hold that the *num* augment occurs before the final vowel. From the final [vowel].
Some desire that *num* be inserted previously. Is this without distinction, or only in the case of *bahūrja*? And what follows from this?
If it were without distinction, then [the form] would have to be *kāṣṭhatakṣi*. But if only in the case of *bahūrja*, then [the form] would have to be *kāṣṭhataṅkṣi*.
Well then, it is only in the case of *bahūrja*. [In *bahūrja*,] *bahūrñji*.
In that case, this prohibition must be stated. It need not be stated. This [term] *acaḥ* is a fifth-case (ablative) form.

A neuter word ending in a *jhal* consonant that follows an *ac* vowel must take the augment *num*. However, that which follows an *ac* vowel here is not a *jhal*, nor is it a neuter word ending in such a [consonant];
and that which is a neuter word ending in [a consonant] does not follow an *ac* vowel. In this case...
But then, [the rule] would not apply to *kāṣṭhataṅkṣi*. In this case, that which follows the vowel (*ac*) is *jhal*, but the neuter word does not end in that;

and that which ends in the neuter word does not follow the vowel. This is not so. What is indicated is the class (*jāti*) of *jhal*. It means "that class of *jhal* which follows a vowel. If it were a fifth-case [ablative] construction, then in the case of *kuṇḍāni*, [the rule would not apply].

In this case, [the rule] "vana" does not apply. Well then, in the rule "ikaḥ aci vibhaktau," the phrase "acaḥ sarvanāmasthāne" will be carried over (anuvartate). Even so, because there is no genitive case, it still does not apply. This locative case "sarvanāmasthāne" will effect a change from the ablative "acaḥ" to a genitive; for when something is indicated by the locative, the rule "tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya" applies.

(P_7.1.73) KA_III,265.18–267.12 Ro_V, 66–69: What is the purpose of including the mention of *aj*? [It is so that] it does not apply when a vowel (*aci*) follows a consonant (*vyañjane*). Since it is stated "of *ik*, before a vowel" (*ikaḥ aci*), let it not apply when a consonant begins [the following word], as in *trapubhyām* and *trapubhiḥ*. Let there be elision (*lopa*). Let there be the augment *num* here. The elision of *n* will occur by the rule "elision of *n* at the end of a nominal stem" (*nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*). But how about the accent in *pañcatrapubhyām*?

In the case of *pañcatrapubhyaḥ*, this accent prescribed by the rule *igante dvigau* does not apply. [Objection: But surely the accent applies even when the augment *num* is heard; for even when *num* is heard, the accent occurs—as in *pañcatrapuṇā* and *pañcatrapuṇaḥ*. [Question: Why would it not occur when *num* is elided? [Answer: Now, why would it not occur when it is elided? [Question: What is the reason that the accent occurs even when *num* is heard? [Answer: Because that [augment] is a part of the entire complex (*saṅghātabhakta*), it is not capable [of being treated independently].
Considering that [the rule] is intended to prevent the final member from ending in an *ik* vowel, the accent occurs even when the *num* augment is heard.
But consider this: *atirābhyām*, *atirābhiḥ*. Once the *num* is applied, the substitution of *āt* by the rule *rāyo hali* would not apply. This is what must be deliberated here.

"Should the substitution of *ā* (ātvam) be applied? What must be done here? [The answer is: "Because it is subsequent (*paratvāt*), the substitution of *ā* takes place. "But then, in the case of *priyatisṛbhyām* and *priyatisṛbhiḥ*, once the *num* augment has been applied, the replacement by *tisṛ* would not apply. "This must be considered here: should the *num* augment be applied or the replacement by *tisṛ*?
What must be done here? [The answer is: "Because it is subsequent, the replacement by *tisṛ* takes place. Now, once the replacement by *tisṛ* has been applied...

Why does *num* not apply again? According to the principle that "when there is a conflict between two rules both of which apply simultaneously, that which is once superseded is superseded for good," [one might argue it does not]. Therefore, he recites the following answer: "The mention of the vowel (*aj*) in the rule *ikaḥ aci vibhaktau* is for the sake of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between *num* and *nuṭ*. The mention of the vowel in *ikaḥ aci vibhaktau* is made so that *nuṭ* may take precedence over *num* by way of conflict. For example: *trapūṇām*.

Regarding the term *jatūnām*: if the mention of *aj* (vowels) were not made, the augment *num* would be obligatory because its cause is constant; it would apply whether *nuṭ* has been applied or not. Since *num* is obligatory by virtue of its constant cause, there would be no occasion for *nuṭ* once *num* has been applied. Yet even this is not a valid purpose [for the rule].
For even if the mention of *aj* were made, an effort must certainly be made here to account for *nuṭ*, namely, by means of a "prior contradiction" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

It must be stated [as an exception]. In that case, the purpose is so that *num* does not occur once *nuṭ* has been applied. And what would happen? [In the forms] *trapūṇām* and *jatūnām*, because *num* would be a constant cause, there would be an absence of *nuṭ*; consequently, the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *nāmi* would not take place. Let it not be so. It will be accomplished by the rule *nopadhāyāḥ*. But in this case, *śucīnām*—[which belongs to the class] *inhanpūṣāryamṇām*—[the lengthening would fail].

Due to this restriction, "śau" and "sau," lengthening would not apply. [One might argue: "Since the rule concerns meaningful items (*arthavat*), it will not apply to that which is meaningless (*anarthaka*). [The author replies: This *paribhāṣā* cannot be understood as applicable here; for in this case, a fault would arise in the word *vāgmi*. [If you say: "In that case, between that which is taught by a general rule (*lakṣaṇokta*) and that which is taught by a specific rule (*pratipadokta*), the specific one prevails," [we reply: that is for the sake of the subsequent rules.

[Objection: Then the mention of *aj* (vowel) must be made for the sake of what follows [in the subsequent rule]. It is so that in the case of *asthi*, *dadhi*, *sakthi*, and *akṣi*, the substitution of *anaṅ* as an acute vowel may occur when a suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) follows; it should not occur here in forms such as *asthibhyām* and *asthibhiḥ*. If it were intended for the sake of what follows, he would have made this mention of *aj* right there [in the subsequent rule]. Since it is made here, [it serves a purpose for the present rule as well].

If there is some purpose [for this rule], let it be stated. Even here, when it is applied, there is a purpose. What is it? So that it may apply where a word beginning with *aja-* follows; but it should not apply here: *trapu*, *jatu*. This too is not a valid purpose, because it is stated that [the suffix must be] a case-ending (*vibhakti*), and we do not perceive a case-ending here.

By the rule *pratyayalakṣaṇena* [P. 1.1.62], the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations conditioned by a suffix) is stated in the rule *na lumatāṅgasya* [P. 1.1.63]. If this is so, then since the desired result is already established, the fact that the Teacher includes the mention of the term *aj* (vowel) indicates that there exists here another way in which *pratyayalakṣaṇa* operates. What is the purpose of this indication? [It is illustrated in the case of] "O *trapu*! (vocative singular of *trapus*).

"In *trapu*, the quality (*guṇa*) is established here. [Objection: "If [the rule] *ikaḥ aci* applies before a consonant, let it not be; but if there is elision (*lopa*), how can there be a vowel (*svara*)? [Response: Indeed, even when [a letter] is elided, if it is still being heard, why would the vowel not occur? [Objection: The substitution of *rāy-*, the change to *tisṛ-*, and even the *num* augment would be obstructed by the intervening *nuṭ* suffix. [Response: It should be stated that *nuṭ* occurs even with *num*; however, something is mentioned here for the sake of what follows, namely the case of *trapuḥ*."

(P_7.1.74) KA_III,267.14–268.14 Ro_V, 70.2–72.7: What is it that is extended here by means of the *puṃvadbhāva*? It is the prohibition of the *num* augment. But how can the prohibition of *num* be understood by this [rule] stating "as in the masculine" (*puṃvat*)? This is an indication using the suffix *-vat*, and in an indication using *-vat*, there is freedom of choice.
In order to justify the remaining part of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), it is as follows:

"In the land of the Madras, there are barley grains like those in Uśīnara—[one might say] they exist or they do not exist. "Her digits are like her mother’s—[one might say] they exist or they do not exist.
In the same way, here too, we shall justify the remaining part of the sentence: "it becomes like the masculine" or "it does not become like the masculine."

Just as the augment *num* does not occur for a masculine [stem], so too it does not occur for that which has been stated to have a masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) in the case of the third case endings and those following. Why, then, is it said that there is a "prohibition of *num*" rather than some other specific operation prescribed for the masculine which could be extended to that which has been stated to have a masculine form when followed by vowel-initial case endings beginning with the third case? Because no such operation has been prescribed for the masculine.

For indeed, no specific operation for a masculine noun is stated word-for-word that could be extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to the feminine forms beginning with *ajā-* in the third case and so on, which have been previously assigned a masculine form. In that context, what else could be understood [from the rule] other than the prohibition of the *num* augment? If "masculine-like" (*puṃvat*) means the prohibition of *num*, then it would also mean the prohibition of *guṇa*, *nābhāva*, *nuṭ*, and *aut*. Thus, "masculine-like" refers to the prohibition of *num*.

A prohibition must be stated regarding *guṇa*, *nābhāva*, and *nuṭ* [in the following cases]: 1. *Guṇa*: *grāmaṇye brāhmaṇakulāya*. 2. *Nābhāva*: *grāmaṇyā brāhmaṇakulena*. 3. *Nuṭ*: *grāmaṇyām brāhmaṇakulānām*. 4.

*Auttvam* (the substitution of *au*): *grāmaṇyām brāhmaṇakule*. The substitution of the short vowel (*hrasvatvam*) is not prohibited; therefore, the grammatical operations dependent upon that short vowel remain in effect.
And these rules would apply [undesirably]. Furthermore, it is for the sake of preventing shortening (*hrasva*), and also for the sake of prohibiting the *num* augment.
But how can a prohibition of shortening—which is neither under discussion nor explicitly mentioned here—be understood?
It is established by the extension of the meaning (*arthātideśa*). It is not understood in this way: "A male is expressed by this word; therefore, this [word]..."

[A word] that has a masculine form is [treated as] the masculine form of a word that has a masculine form. How then? That in which a male (pumān) is expressed is "bhāṣitapuṃska"; thus, for a meaning that has a masculine form, there occurs a meaning like that of the masculine. And there is a prohibition of the elision of the taddhita suffix. Furthermore, a prohibition of the elision of the taddhita suffix must be stated. For example: *pīluḥ* as a tree.

[The forms] *pīlu-phalam*, *pīlunā*, and *pīlunaḥ* [are established]. Or rather, it need not be stated. Why? Because there is the recognition of a word as having been previously mentioned in the masculine when the form (*ākṛti*) is the same. That which has been previously mentioned in the masculine within the same form—

And this [word] is one whose masculine form has been previously stated (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) in another form (*ākṛtyantara*). Is it necessary to state this? No, indeed. How will it be understood without being stated? This too is established by the indication of the meaning (*artha-nirdeśāt*).

72.9–73.8. What is the example? “akṣī te indra piṅgale” (O Indra, your two eyes are tawny). This is not [a valid example], for this is already established by the substitution of the preceding vowel’s quality (*pūrvasavarṇa*). Then what [is the example]? “akṣībhyām te nāsikābhyām” (from your two eyes and from your two nostrils). And this too is an example: “akṣī te indra piṅgale. But was it not said that this is also established by the substitution of the preceding vowel’s quality? No.

[The form] is established. Because [the *num* augment] intervenes, the substitution of the homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*) does not apply. It must be stated that in the Veda, the neuter undergoes the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*), for the sake of such forms as *madhoḥ gṛbhṇāmi* and *madhoḥ tṛptā iva asataḥ*. Through the masculine treatment, the *num* is eliminated; when the *num* is eliminated...

It is already established by the rule for the preceding homogeneous sound (*pūrvasavarṇa*). If so, the long *ī* must be stated for the sake of the accent, so that the acute accent (*udātta*) may apply and not the neuter accent (*napuṃsakasvara*). But surely the accent will be obtained simply through the extension of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*)?
It is impossible to rely on the extension of the masculine form as the basis for the accent; for in this case, a fault would arise: [if it were applied, the accent would be incorrect].

[The example] "madhur asmin asti" [is explained as] "madhumāsaḥ. In that case, then, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) must be stated. It need not be stated. The word "masculine" (*puṃvat*), which was previously introduced, continues to apply here. To what does this prohibition refer? He says: "To the *num* suffix. Therefore, the mention of *num* must be made. No, it need not.

It must be supplied. The context is being continued. Where is it found in the context? It is in the rule *idito num dhātoḥ* ("the augment *num* is added after a root ending in an *it* vowel"). But that [rule] has been interrupted by the mention of "more than one" (*aneka*), so it cannot be supplied. If that is the case, then regarding the term *sarvanāmasthāne*, the prohibition applies to whatever would otherwise apply when a *sarvanāmasthāna* follows. However, that too has been interrupted by a much more extensive mention and cannot be supplied.

To cause it to follow. Now, even that which is separated [by intervening rules] can be made to follow; having caused *num* alone to follow for the sake of this rule and for the sake of the subsequent one, the prohibition is established both here and there, and thus the mention of *num* in the rule *āt śīnadyoḥ num* need not be made.
Why does [the rule] not apply here in the cases of *adatī* and *ghnatī*?

[In the case of] *lunatī* and *punatī*, [the rule does not apply] because, when the elision (*lopa*) has taken place, there is no *a*-vowel present. What, then, is the example for this rule? [It is] *yāti* and *yāntī*.

Here too, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, the condition of "distinct separation" (*vyapavarga*) is absent, so [the rule] would not apply. [Answer: The distinct separation is established through the treatment of the preceding and following elements as if they were the end and the beginning [of a single unit].
In the case of a dual basis, it is not like [the rule concerning] the end and so forth. A dual basis will not be established here. It is not understood thus:
"num occurs after a śatṛ that ends in an *a*-vowel. How, then? Num occurs after an *a*-vowel, provided that *a*-vowel immediately precedes the śatṛ.

(P_7,1.81) KA_III,269.16–18; Ro_V, 75.6–8: What is the purpose of including the term *nitya*? [It is so that] the option (*vibhāṣā*) does not apply. This is not a valid purpose, for the desired result is already established here by the preceding rule alone. In that case, by the very force of its formulation, the rule will be obligatory (*nitya*). Therefore...
Let this mention of the word *nitya* regarding the suffix *sānnyāsika* stand aside for now.

[Regarding Pāṇini 7.1.82: There is a prohibition of *ām* after *anaḍuh* in the nominative singular (*sau*) because *num* has no other scope (*anavakāśatva*). [That is to say,] there is a prohibition of *ām* after *anaḍuh* in the nominative singular.

[The suffix] *num* would apply. What is the reason? Because *num* has no other scope [to apply]. *Num*, having no scope, subverts *ām*. Or rather, this is not a fault. Why? Because *num* is prescribed for that which has *a*-vowel as its penultimate (*avarṇopadha*).

I shall prescribe *num* for that which has *a*-vowel as its penultimate. [Objection: Then the mention of "that" (*tat*) must be made. [Response: It need not be made; it is understood from the context (*prakṛta*).

[The word] *anuvartate* [is used]. Where is it under discussion? In the rule *āt śīnadyoḥ num*. If that [rule] is being carried over, then in the case of *anaḍuh*, the augment *num* would apply after all the *a*-sounds. This is not a fault; for by the rule *mit acaḥ antyāt paraḥ*, it will occur after the final *a*-sound among all [the *a*s]. Or rather, it is established through the principle of "reapplication" (*punaḥprasaṅga*).
Alternatively, once again, due to the recurrence of the rule, when *num* has been applied, *ām* will occur, just as reduplication occurs in cases such as *attva*; for example:
*jagle*, *mamle*, *ījatuḥ*.

In forms such as *ījuḥ*, once the substitution of *ā* and so forth has been applied, reduplication occurs again because of the principle of "reapplication" (*punaḥprasaṅga*). One might argue that here too, once the augment *num* has been applied, the suffix *ām* will likewise follow by the same principle. This is not a valid solution. The principle of "reapplication" applies in cases of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), and a conflict occurs only when two rules each have their own scope of application. Here, however, *num* has no scope of its own and thus subverts *ām*. If this is the case, then [the following applies]:
This solution proceeds from the context. From what context? This objection arises:

"The prohibition of *ām* after *anaḍuh* is unnecessary because *num* has no other scope. The rebuttal to that is: "Not so, because *num* is prescribed for a word ending in a vowel (*avarṇa*). Thereupon, this further objection arises: "In that case, where there is no section concerning vowels (*avarṇa-prakaraṇa*), [what then?]"

Therefore, [the rule] *ām naḥ* is obtained as a sublation (*bādhana*) because there are many families of Brahmins. Consequently, this was recited at a later time [in the Aṣṭādhyāyī]: "Or it is established by the understanding of recurrence (*punar-prasaṅga-vijñāna*). (Pāṇini 7.1.84).

77.2–11. Regarding the substitution of *au* for *div*: a prohibition concerning verbal roots (*dhātu*) must be stated when *au* is substituted for *div*. [Otherwise, one would get] *akṣadyūḥ*. This is established by the governing rule of "not being a verbal root" (*adhātu*). The phrase "not being a verbal root" (*adhātu*) is understood [from the previous rule]. Where was it introduced? It was introduced in the rule: "For *ugit*-pratyayas and for those ending in *ac*, [the suffix *n* is added] before a nominal stem-ending (*sarvanāmasthāna*), provided they are not verbal roots. If it is argued that this is established by the governing rule of "not being a verbal root," then there is a fault in the case of the neuter gender. [This is because the governing rule of "not being a verbal root" applies there as well.]

If it is argued that [the rule] is established, there is a fault in the case of neuter nouns: *kāṣṭhataṅkṣi*, *kūṭataṅkṣi*. The prohibition [of the suffix *kvip*] by the rule "for a neuter [stem] ending in *jhal* or a vowel, provided it is not a verbal root" (*napuṃsakasya jhal acaḥ adhātoḥ*) would apply. But this has already been addressed. What was said? That "when a term without an indicatory letter (*ananubandhaka*) is mentioned, it does not include one with an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*).
Alternatively, the connection [from the previous rule] will continue to apply.

The mention of *it* here is purposeless because of the context of *ā*. The mention of *it* here is purposeless. What is the reason? Because of the context of *ā*. The term *āt* is understood [from the previous rule]. However, it is for the sake of cases preceded by *ṣ*. It is for the sake of cases preceded by *ṣ*.

78–79. Regarding the *asuṅ* [substitute], it should be stated that it behaves like the original form (*upadeśivad-bhāva*) for the sake of the correct accentuation (*svarasiddhi*), because it is an external characteristic (*bahiraṅga-lakṣaṇa*). It must be stated that the status of behaving like the original form applies to the *asuṅ* substitute; that is, it should be stated that the *asuṅ* occurs precisely at the stage of the original form (*upadeśāvasthā*). What is the purpose? For the sake of the correct accentuation. So that the desired accentuation may occur once the *asuṅ* has been applied at the stage of the original form—as in the case of *paramapumān*. If this were not done...

For if the treatment as if it were an *upadeśa* (original form) were applied, then when the final member of the compound is accented, the substitution *asuṅ* would—by virtue of internal proximity (*āntarya*)—be without accent, resulting in [the whole word] being without accent.
But what is the reason that the accentuation of the final member of the compound occurs first, rather than the substitution *asuṅ*? It is not the case that *asuṅ* must occur because it is subsequent;
for it is characterized by being external (*bahir-aṅga*). The substitution *asuṅ* is characterized by being external, whereas the accent is internal (*antaraṅga*).

An external operation (*bahiranga*) is not established when an internal operation (*antaranga*) is present. In that case, the status of being "like the original instruction" (*upadeśivadbhāva*) must be stated. It need not be stated. The initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) will be prescribed by way of an irregularity (*nipātana*); that irregular accent will be the sublater of the compound accent (*samāsasvara*). Even so, the status of being "like the original instruction" must still be stated. For in that very same way, the irregular accent sublates the compound accent.

In this way, it would also subvert the *prakṛtisvara*. [Example: *pumān*. Therefore, it is rightly said: "The instruction that [the substitution] is like the original (*upadeśivad-vacanam*) is for the sake of establishing the accent, because [otherwise] it would be a *bahiraṅga* rule.

79.7–81.7: Is it that the status of being *ṅit* is prescribed for the *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffixes] following a stem ending in *go*, or rather is the operation of being *ṅit* extended (*atideśa*) when a *sarvanāmasthāna* follows? And what is the distinction here? [The former view is: the extension of the *ṅit*-operation from *go* to the *sarvanāmasthāna*. [The latter view is: the operation of being *ṅit* is extended to *go* when a *sarvanāmasthāna* follows. For if one were to state that the *sarvanāmasthāna* itself has the quality of being *ṇit*, there would be a lack of comprehension (*asampratyaya*).
Because there is no mention of the genitive case. For if the term *ṇit* were stated [as a property] of the *sarvanāmasthāna*, there would be a lack of understanding. Why?
Because of the absence of the genitive. Substitutes are prescribed for that which is indicated by the genitive, and we do not see a genitive here.
If that is so, then this is an indication made by means of the suffix *-vat*.

"The substitute *got* becomes like that which has the marker *ṅ*. Well then, an instruction using the suffix *vat* must be made; for without *vat*, an extended application (*atideśa*) is not understood. Even without *vat*, an extended application is understood.
For example: "This is Brahmadatta. He says "Brahmadatta" regarding one who is not Brahmadatta. We think: [that this is so].

"Just as in the case of *brahmadatta*, this [suffix] becomes [treated as] having an indicatory letter *ṇ* (*ṇit*). Thus, here too, when it says "as if having an indicatory *ṇ*," it is understood that it is "like one having an indicatory *ṇ*" (*ṇidvat*).
Alternatively, let there be the status of having an indicatory *ṇ* for the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffixes following a stem ending in *go*. But was it not said:

"If the status of having an indicatory *ṇ* is stated with respect to the *sarvanāmasthāna*, there is no comprehension [of the intended meaning] because of the lack of a genitive indication"? This is not a fault; for the word "of *go*" (*gotaḥ*) is...

The rule *pañcamī sarvanāmasthāne* will cause the seventh case (*saptamī*) to be interpreted as a sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), [meaning] "from that" (*tasmāt*) and "of the subsequent" (*uttarasya*). Now, what is the purpose of the inclusion of the long vowel *ā* (the *tapara* marker) in *sarvanāmasthāne*? It is so that it would not apply here: *citraguḥ*, *śabalaguḥ*. This is not a valid objection; once the shortening (*hrasvatva*) has been applied, it will not occur. [But] it would still occur by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). Therefore, he recites the following reply:

The addition of *ta* (the long vowel marker) is purposeless because of the prohibition regarding the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). The addition of *ta* is purposeless. Why? Because of the prohibition regarding the status of the substitute. Here, the status of the substitute is prohibited by the rule stating that "the status of the substitute does not occur in the case of [the suffix] *niṭ*, the substitution of *āt* for the final vowel of *go*, and accent. And this prohibition must necessarily be resorted to; otherwise—

For there is a prohibition regarding the vocative singular (*sambuddhi*) and the nominative plural (*jas*). For one who thinks that [the substitution] will not occur here by virtue of the power of the inclusion of *t* (i.e., the *tapara* marker), a prohibition must be stated for the vocative and the nominative plural:
namely, *he citrago* and *citragavaḥ*. Now, even if the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* were in effect, once the *guṇa* has been applied...

Why does this [rule] not apply here? Because of the principle that "between that which is taught by a general definition and that which is taught by a specific rule, the specific one prevails. But one might object: even now, although the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) is absent, it should be possible to apply this paribhāṣā.
No, he says; for in that case, there would be no instance whatsoever where *sthānivadbhāva* could occur.

(P_7.1.95–96.1) KA_III,272.25–273.19 Ro_V, 81–84 Now, does the term *vibhaktau* ("in a case-ending") carry over here, or not? And what follows from this? If [the rule] "like one ending in *-tṛc* in the feminine when a case-ending follows" applies, then the form *kroṣṭrī-bhaktiḥ* would not be established. If [the rule] "like one ending in *-tṛc* in the feminine when a case-ending follows" applies, then *kroṣṭrī-bhaktiḥ* [is not established].

Thus, it is not established. If that is so, then I shall state the substitution of *tṛjvat* (as if it were the suffix *tṛc*) when the vowel *ī* follows. In that case, the mention of the vowel *ī* must be made. It need not be made; it is already accomplished within the very formulation (*nyāsa*). This is a *praśliṣṭanirdeśa* (a combined or contracted expression):

"strī" [is formed by] "ī" [joined with] "strī" [to mean] "in the feminine. That [substitution] occurs because of that [vowel *ī*]. But if it is in the vowel *ī*, then that [substitution] does not occur. What is the reason? Because it is caused by that [suffix].

That *ī*-vowel is caused by the substitution of the *tṛjvad-bhāva* [of *tud* for *tuda-*]. The *ī*-vowel does not apply as long as the *tṛjvad-bhāva* has not been performed. Why? Because it is stated that the suffix *ṅīp* applies after stems ending in *ṛ*, *an*, or *in*, whereas the *tṛjvad-bhāva* applies when there is an *ī*-vowel. Thus, this results in a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
And things involving mutual dependence are not logically established. If that is so, then the *ī*-vowel [is obtained] from its inclusion in the *gaurādi* group.
It will be so. [The word *bhāvanā*] is not listed among the *gaura*-group [of words that take the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*]. Indeed, no word ending in the suffix *tun* is listed among the *gaura*-group.

If that is the case, then the Teacher [Pāṇini] indicates here that the vowel *ī* occurs [in this formation], since he teaches the substitution of *tṛjvat* (the behavior of the suffix *tṛc*) when the vowel *ī* follows. If the state of being a *bhāvanā* were established by that alone, then even an undesirable result would follow. Even if there is no difference [between the two cases], [the undesirable consequence remains].

The suffix *ṅīp*, or *ṅīṣ*, or even *ṅīn* would apply here; yet it does not apply in this case: *pañcakroṣṭṛbhiḥ rathaiḥ* ("carts bought for five *kroṣṭṛ*s"). If that is so, then neither the other cause nor the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is subject to the rule of *pratyayalakṣaṇa*. Furthermore, no other cause is relied upon.

In this case, it is not that *tṛjvat* occurs after the word *kroṣṭu*; rather, the base (*aṅga*) *kroṣṭu* becomes like one ending in *tṛc*. And the designation "base" (*aṅga-sañjñā*) applies by virtue of the definition of an affix (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*). But is this a transfer of a grammatical rule (*śāstra-atideśa*)?

Is it the extension of the rule (*śāstra*) that "it is like *tṛc*" which is being extended, or is it the extension of the form (*rūpa*): is it the form of "like *tṛc*" that is being extended? And what is the distinction here? If it is an extension of the rule by the statement "like *tṛc*," then it follows that it would be just as it is in the case of *ciṇ*. If it is an extension of the rule by the statement "like *tṛc*," then it results in being exactly as it is in the case of *ciṇ*.

And how is it so in the case of *ciṇ*? It has been stated that because of the context [of the rule] "of the *aṅga*," this is established through the extension (*atideśa*) of the rules concerning the *aṅga*. Whatever operation pertains to the *aṅga* is extended here; thus, in this case as well, the *anaṅ*, the *guṇa*, and the *dīrgha* are extended, but the substitution of *ra* for the final letter (*raparatva*) is not extended. What is the fault in that? In that regard, there is the mention of *rapara*; therein, the substitution of *ra* for the final letter is not established.

That must be stated. This is not a fault. When a *guṇa* is extended by rule (*atideśa*), the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* (*raparatva*) is also extended. How so? A technical definition (*saṃjñā*) and a governing rule (*paribhāṣā*) are to be understood wherever the operation (*kārya*) occurs, according to the principle that "the time of the operation is the time of the definition. In the rule "for *ṛ* [ending in a stem], there is *guṇa* before the suffixes *ṅi* and the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffixes," this [other rule] presents itself: "an *u*-vowel followed by *aṇ* is followed by *ra*. If that is the case, then this is something else.
A fault arises: does the rule that consists of three verses apply by being directly stated (*āhatya*), or by being extended (*atideśa*) without being directly stated? And what follows from this?

If it is extended by being directly stated, then length (*dīrghatva*) is extended, while the absence of *aṅ* (*anaṅ*), the *guṇa* substitution, and the following of *ra* (*raparatva*) are not extended. On the other hand, if it is extended without being directly stated, then the absence of *aṅ*, the *guṇa* substitution, and the following of *ra* are extended, while length is not extended. Let it be by being directly stated. But has it not already been said?

"It is the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) that is extended [by analogy], while the *anaṅ* substitution, the *guṇa* substitution, and the subsequentness of *ra* (*raparatva*) are not extended. This is not a fault. When the lengthening is extended, the *anaṅ*, *guṇa*, and *raparatva* are also extended. How so? The term "of the penultimate" (*upadhāyāḥ*) is understood [in the rule], and the syllable becomes a penultimate only when these operations have not yet been performed. For indeed, how could this be [otherwise] regarding these rules?

The lengthening will apply to that which is the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) after [the substitution] has been made; it will not, however, be the lengthening of that which is the penultimate vowel after the closest internal substitute (*guṇa*) has been applied and the *av* replacement has occurred. Furthermore, a single example does not necessitate the commencement of a grammatical rule (*yoga*). In that regard, by the force of the statement "like *tṛj*" (*tṛjvat*), once these operations have been performed, that which is...
The lengthening will occur by means of that [term] *upadhā*. Or rather, what does it matter to us whether it is applied directly (*āhatya*) or not?
Whether applied directly or not, that which is the rule regarding the *tṛca* is extended by analogy (*atidiśyate*). Or again, let there be an extension of the form (*rūpātideśa*).
Now, when this extension of the form takes place, is that form which exists prior to the substitutions (*ādeśa*) that is extended, or rather...

Regarding the question of whether the substitution has already taken place or not: what follows from this? If the form existing prior to the substitutions were extended [by analogy], then only the *ṛ*-vowel would be extended, while *anaṅ*, guṇa, *raparatva*, and lengthening would not be extended. On the other hand, if the extension occurs after the substitutions have taken place, then the *ṛ*-vowel would not be extended, while *anaṅ*, guṇa, *raparatva*, and lengthening would be extended. In both cases, however, the accent (*svara*) remains unextended.

For a vowel does not possess form (*rūpa*). Let it be that the form which exists prior to the substitutions is what is extended [by analogy]. But was it not said that when the *ṛ*-vowel is extended, its *anaṅ* substitution, *guṇa*, *raparatva*, and lengthening are not extended? This is not a fault.
When the *ṛ*-vowel is extended, these rules will occur here by virtue of their own inherent basis (*svāśraya*). As for what is further stated regarding "in both ways" (*ubhayathā*)...
And the accent is not extended [to the substitute], for the accent does not possess a form; however, by the force of including the letter *ca* [in the rule], the accent will apply.

If it is argued that there is an extension of the form (*rūpātideśa*), then the undesirable consequence follows that it would be a substitute for the whole word (*sarvādeśa*). If there is an extension of the form, then a substitute consisting of the word *tṛ* would apply to the entire form ending in *tu*. But this is established through the extension of the form. It is established.

This [is the case]. How so? Because of the extension of form (*rūpātideśa*). This is an extension of form. But if it is argued that by doing exactly this, the objection is raised that "there would be the undesirable consequence of [the substitute] applying everywhere" (*sarvādeśaprasaṅga*), [we reply: it is established, however, through the understanding that when a suffix is mentioned, [it refers to] that which begins with what [the suffix] is prescribed after, and that which ends with it. This is established. How so? When a suffix is mentioned, [it denotes] that which begins with what it is prescribed after and that which ends with it.

The inclusion [of the word *bhū*] is for the purpose that, in this way, the suffix *-tṛc* shall serve as the substitute for that which ends in *-tu*. Even so, only a certain limited number of words ending in *-tṛc* would be obtained; this [undesired form] *paktā* would also be obtained. However, it is established by virtue of "nearest similarity" (*āntaratamya*): that which is most similar to *kroṣṭuḥ* will be the result. What, then, is that? It is that which ends in the suffix *-tṛc* prescribed after the root *kruś*.

The statement that the suffix *tṛc* is treated like *tṛj* is redundant, because in the domain of *tṛj*, the suffix *tṛc* already denotes a wild animal (*mṛga*). This [rule] regarding the domain of *tṛj* is intended to denote a wild animal. If it is argued that this must be stated for the purpose of excluding *tun*, so that there may be an exclusion of *tun* in the context of a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix], then if it is said "for the purpose of excluding *tun*," it is established as being applicable elsewhere as well; thus, it is for the purpose of excluding *tun*.

If this is argued, then it is established even without such a statement, just as elsewhere words prescribed without distinction are seen to have restricted domains. Where else? For example: although the root *ghṛ* is taught to him without distinction, it [is used] for *ghṛta*, *ghṛṇā*, and so forth.

"Gharma" refers to such an object. "Raśi" is taught for him without distinction; it refers to such objects as *raśi*, *raśmi*, and *raśanā*. "Luśi" is taught for him without distinction; it refers to a clod of earth (*loṣṭa*).

Thus, such is the scope [of the rule]. In that case, the purpose is this: "I shall state the option (*vibhāṣā*). [Namely,] "Optionally before vowels in the third case and those following. Furthermore, the mention of the word "optionally" (*vā*) is redundant because it is established by its very nature (*svabhāva*). And the mention of "optionally" is useless. Why? Because it is established by its very nature. By its very nature, in the third case and subsequent case-endings beginning with vowels, a word ending in *-tṛc* [is already understood].

And [the suffix] *tun* is used in the sense of "wild animal. (Pāṇini 7.1.95–96) The augment *num* takes precedence by way of prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣiddham*) over *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, *auttva*, and *tṛjvadbhāva*. That is to say, *num* occurs in preference to *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, *auttva*, and *tṛjvadbhāva* through prior contradiction. Among these, regarding *guṇa*: [Example: *praśām + ī* → *praśāmī* (where *guṇa* would otherwise apply). [Counter-example: *praśām + ī* → *praśāmī* (where *num* applies by prior contradiction). [Example: *praśām + ās* → *praśāmās* (where *guṇa* would otherwise apply). [Counter-example: *praśām + ās* → *praśāmās* (where *num* applies by prior contradiction). [Example: *praśām + īt* → *praśāmīt* (where *guṇa* would otherwise apply). [Counter-example: *praśām + īt* → *praśāmīt* (where *num* applies by prior contradiction). [Example: *praśām + īran* → *praśāmīran* (where *guṇa* would otherwise apply). [Counter-example: *praśām + īran* → *praśāmīran* (where *num* applies by prior contradiction). [Example: *praśām + īta* → *praśāmīta* (where *guṇa* would otherwise apply). [Counter-example: *praśām + īta* → *praśāmīta* (where *num* applies by prior contradiction). [Example: *praśām + īyāt* → *praśāmīyāt* (where *guṇa* would otherwise apply). [Counter-example: *praśām + īyāt* → *praśāmīyāt* (where *num* applies by prior contradiction). [Example: *praśām + īran* → *praśāmīran* (where *guṇa* would otherwise apply). [Counter-example: *praśām + īran* → *praśāmīran* (where *num* applies by prior contradiction). [Example: *praśām + īta* → *praśāmīta* (where *guṇa* would otherwise apply). [Counter-example: *praśām + īta* → *praśāmīta* (where *num* applies by prior contradiction). [Example: *praśām + īyāt* → *praśāmīyāt* (where *guṇa* would otherwise apply). [Counter-example: *praśām + īyāt* → *praśāmīyāt* (where *num* applies by prior contradiction). [For example, in] *jāgaritaḥ* and *jāgaritavān*. [The opponent replies: Even this is not a purpose. For the *guṇa* substitution is prescribed for *jāgṛ* in the domain of *vṛddhi*.

And it will serve as a sublater (*bādhaka*) in the domain of prohibition. In that case, once the *guṇa* has been applied and the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* (*raparatva*) has been applied, because the suffix is not followed by a nasal (*anugantatvāt*), the prohibition of *iṭ* will not take effect. If the substitution of *it* and *ut* were applied first, and then the substitution of *ra* for *r*, the suffix would end in a nasal (*anugantatva*), and thus the prohibition of *iṭ* would not apply. This is not a fault; this is established by the sequence of operations. For here, the substitutions of *it* and *ut* do not apply before the prohibition of *iṭ* has been effected.

What is the reason? Because of the prohibition of *kittva* by the rule *na ktvā seṭ*. Well then, consider these cases: *ātistīrṣati*, *nipupūrṣati*. Once the substitutions of *it* and *ut* have been applied, and the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* has occurred, the suffix *iṭ* would not be prohibited because [the root] no longer ends in a vowel (*anugantatvāt*). Let it not be so; rather, let it be governed by the rule *śryukaḥ kiti*. But then it will be governed by the rule *iṭ sani vā*. Well then, consider this: *āstīrṇam*.

The *piṇḍa* vowels have been filled in. Once the substitutions of *it* and *ut* have been applied, and the substitution of *ra* for *r* has also occurred, the prohibition of *iṭ* does not apply because the root is no longer monosyllabic (*anugantatvāt*). Let it be so; however, by the rule "the *iṭ* augment is optional before *san*" (*iṭ sani vā*), there will be a prohibition under the rule "there is a prohibition when an option has been prescribed" (*yasya vibhāṣā*). In that case, the mention of "monosyllabic" (*ekāj*) must indeed be made for the sake of this very point, namely for the prohibition of *iṭ* in the case of *vadha*. Thus, there is a prohibition of *iṭ* for *vadha*.

"Let it not be so"—that is, [let there be no need for the rule] *vadhiṣīṣṭa*. This too is not a valid purpose. For even if the mention of "ekāc" (monosyllabic) were made, the prohibition of *iṭ* would still apply to *vadha*, as in *vadhiṣīṣṭa*. What is the reason? Because the prohibition of *iṭ* applies to *vadha* when it is monosyllabic (*ekāctva*) upon the combination [of elements], and because the root is unaccented (*anudātta*). Indeed, it is precisely upon such a combination that *vadhi* is heard as monosyllabic.

And its original form (*prakṛti*) is unaccented (*anudātta*). But what is the reason for understanding it thus: "from a monosyllabic root that is unaccented in its *upadeśa* and is actually heard [in the derivation]"? It is for the sake of the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅlopārtha*). So that it may not apply when *yaṅ* is elided. [Otherwise, one would have to say] *bebhiditā*, *bebhiditum*.

[The forms] *cecchiditā* and *cecchiditum*. Because the prohibition does not apply. Once reduplication has occurred, the prohibition of *iṭ*—based on the rule "from a root that is unaccented in its original form (*upadeśa*) and consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*) as it is heard"—does not apply. When the prohibition of *iṭ* is absent, the restriction is not tenable. If the restriction is absent, what is the fault?

*pecima*, *śekima*. Furthermore, the prohibition of *iṭ* after the suffix *san* must be stated: *bibhitsati*, *cicchitsati*. [The rule] does not apply here. As for what was also said regarding "monosyllabic roots which are unaccented in their original enunciation" (*ekāca upadeśe 'nudāttāt*): [this too is resolved by the sequence].

If the word *upadeśa* were a qualifier of *anudātta*, then a restriction (*niyama*) regarding the *liṭ* [affix] after roots such as *kṛ* would be untenable, because the prohibition would not otherwise apply. [The rule] "thali ca seṭi kṅiti ca seṭi" [applies]. As for what is said, that there is a prohibition of *iṭ* after the suffix *san*, that is established because both are qualifiers. 119.16–120.10. Why is there the specific mention of *dṛḍha* as a nipātana? It should not simply be stated that "there is no *iṭ* after the root *dṛh*. The mention of *dṛḍha* as a nipātana is for the purpose of the elision of the *n* and the *h*, and for the purpose of the substitution of *ḍh* for the following [consonant]. The mention of *dṛḍha* as a nipātana is made for the purpose of the elision of the *n* and the *h*. So that the elision of the *n* and the *h* may occur. And it is for the purpose of the substitution of *ḍh* for the following [consonant]. So that the substitution of *ḍh* for the following [consonant] may occur.

It would be so. For if [the root] were stated as *aniṭ*, the substitution of *r* would not be established because of the lack of heaviness (*alaghutva*). Indeed, if it were stated as *aniṭ*, the substitution of *r* would not be established. As in *draḍhīyān*. What is the reason? Because of the lack of heaviness. And there must be a statement regarding the elision of *n* (*nalopa*). Furthermore, the elision of *n* must be prescribed;
otherwise, in the case of *paridraḍhayya gataḥ*, the substitution of *ay* (by the rule *lyapi laghupūrvasya*) would not occur. And in this case, [the form] would be *pāridṛḍhī*.
In the case of *kanyā*, the suffix *ṣyaṅ*—characterized by the guru (*g*) being followed by the penultimate (*upottama*) letter—would [otherwise] apply.
(Pāṇini 4.1.116) Why is *parivṛḍha* treated as an irregularly formed word (*nipātana*)? It is so that the augment *iṭ* does not occur after the root *vṛh* preceded by *pari*.

Thus it should be stated: "The substitution of *ḍha* for the following [consonant] and the elision of the *na* and *ha* are for the sake of the nipātana of *parivṛḍha*; furthermore, if the rule regarding the absence of the augment *iṭ* were not stated, the substitution of *ra* would not be established because [the stem] would not be light; and the mention of the elision of *na* is likewise [necessary]. Otherwise, in the case of *parivraḍhīyān*, the substitution of *ra* by the rule *raḥ ṛtaḥ halādeḥ laghoḥ* would not occur. And here, in the case of *parivraḍhayya gataḥ*, [the same difficulty would arise].

Otherwise, by the rule *lyapi laghupūrvasya*, the substitution of *ay* would not occur [in *parivārya*]. Furthermore, in the case of *pārivṛḍhī kanyā*, the suffix *ṣyaṅ*—which is conditioned by the penultimate syllable being heavy (*gurūpottama*)—would undesirably apply.
7.2.23) Why is it stated "when there is no naming" (*aviśabdane*)? For in the case of naming, the causative suffix *ṇic* must necessarily occur [as in *parivārayati*]. Thus...

Since this [the formation of *ghoṣita*] is already established, the fact that the Teacher says "in the sense of not making known" (*aviśabdane*) indicates that the suffix *ṇic* is optionally applied to the root *ghuṣ* in the sense of "making known" (*viśabdane*). What is the purpose of this indication? [The example: "Having heard the words of the king, the Puṣyamāṇavas proclaimed them" (*mahīpālavacaḥ śrutvā jughuṣuḥ puṣyamāṇavāḥ*). This usage thus becomes justified.

Is this a formal derivation (*nipātana*) made for the past participle (*niṣṭhā*) when it denotes the act of studying, or is it [meant] that [the suffix *kta*] occurs when there is an activity (*vṛtti*) regarding study? And what follows from this? If [it is meant] for the past participle denoting the act of studying...

An irregular formation (*nipātana*) is being made; [the forms] *vṛttaḥ*, *guṇaḥ*, *vṛttam*, *pārāyaṇam*, and *vṛttam* are established. However, [the forms] *guṇasya vṛttam* and *pārāyaṇasya vṛttam* would not be established. Now, if it is understood that "if the activity of learning (*adhyayana*) is present, there is the state of being occupied with it (*vṛttiḥ vartate*)," then there is no fault. Let it be so, in such a way that there is no fault—even when it is understood that "if the activity of learning is present, there is the state of being occupied with it."

It is not established. What is the reason? This root *vṛt* is intransitive (*akarmaka*). And even when intransitive roots are followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*, they become transitive (*sakarmaka*). Yet here, *vṛt* remains intransitive. How, then, is it known that *vṛt* is intransitive here?

The suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) for intransitive roots; thus, here the suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of the abstract action. In that case, [the rule] "of those marked with *u*" (*udit*)...
By the rule *ktvi vibhāṣā*, and by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*, there will be the prohibition of the augment *iṭ*. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *ṇi*?

The mention of *ṇi* in the rule for the formation of *vṛttanipātana* is for the purpose of prohibiting the restriction [that it applies] only to that which does not end in *ṇi*. The mention of *ṇi* is made in the rule for *vṛttanipātana* so that the restriction [of the preceding rule] should not apply to that which does not end in *ṇi*. A restriction arises because of the question "for what purpose? [The answer is: the thing to be prescribed.

Since it does not [otherwise] exist, there must be something to be prescribed here. What is it? The prohibition of *iṭ* after a root that has the suffix *ṇi* added to it (*ṇyadhika*) is what must be prescribed.
In this regard, let it be either a new rule (*apūrva-vidhi*) or a restrictive rule (*niyama*). It will be a new rule alone, not a restrictive rule.
Why indeed, when a rule is begun for the sake of an additional meaning, would it apply to that which has *ṇi* added (*ṇyadhika*) and not rather to that which has *san* added (*sanadhika*)?
Or it might be [the case] that there is an additional *yaṅ*. Therefore, the mention of *ṇi* must be made. Now, for what purpose is this irregular formation (*nipātana*) performed?

The irregular formation is for the sake of the suffix *ṇi*, for the sake of *lpa*, and for the sake of prohibiting *iṭ* and *guṇa*. The irregular formation is performed for the sake of *ṇi*, for the sake of *lpa*, and for the sake of prohibiting both *iṭ* and *guṇa*.

124.2–12. What is prescribed for *dānta* and *śānta*? For *dānta* and *śānta*, there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrghatva*). And what else? There is also the prohibition of the substitution of *ṭ* when the suffix *ṇi* is elided. Is the lengthening of the penultimate vowel not already established? It is established by [the general rule of] *vṛddhi*. It is not established; for by the rule "the short vowel replaces the final of roots ending in a *mit*," a short vowel ought to occur. If that is so, then [we rely on] the rule "for a nasalized vowel before *kvi* and *jhal*-beginning suffixes marked with *k* or *ṅ*."

Thus, in this case, the lengthening [of the vowel] would occur. But it is not established. Why? Because it is intervened by the *ṇic* suffix. Once the *ṇilopa* (elision of *ṇi*) has been performed, there is no intervention. [Objection: Due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is indeed intervention. [Response: Here, the status of being a substitute is prohibited with respect to the rule for lengthening; that is, "it does not behave as a substitute" (*na sthānivat*) regarding the operation of lengthening. Now, [regarding the forms] *spaṣṭa* and *cchanna*:

What is elided? The shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) in the words *spaṣṭa* and *channa*. And what else? The prohibition of the augment *iṭ* when there is the elision of the suffix *ṇi* (Pāṇini 7.2.28).

Regarding the roots *ghuṣ* and *svan*, there is an option (*vāvacana*) by way of a counter-exception (*vipratiṣedha*) to the prohibition of *iṭ*. [That is,] there is an option regarding the roots *ghuṣ* and *svan*.

Due to the prohibition of *iṭ*, [the rule] applies by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of the prohibition of *iṭ* after the root *ghuṣ* is when it is not preceded by *sam* and does not mean "making a sound": e.g., *ghuṣṭā rajjuḥ* ("a rope that has been sounded"), *ghuṣṭo mārgaḥ* ("a path that has been proclaimed"). The scope of the option (*vāvacana*) is when it is preceded by *sam* and means "making a sound": e.g., *saṃghuṣṭaṃ vākyam*.

Regarding the word *saṅghuṣita*: since it is derived from the root *ghuṣ* preceded by the prefix *sam*, both [the suffixes *kta* and *iṭ*] would apply. Thus, one would obtain both *saṅghuṣṭā rajjuḥ* and *saṅghuṣitā rajjuḥ*. The mention of the option (*vāvacana*) occurs by way of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of the prohibition of *iṭ* (by Pāṇini 7.2.18) is when the mind (*manas*) is denoted and the prefix *āṅ* does not precede: *svāntam manaḥ*. The scope of the optional rule (*vāvacana*) is when the mind is not denoted and the prefix *āṅ* does precede.
125.2–6 It should be stated that *hṛṣ* has the hair of the body (*loman*) and the hair of the head (*keśa*) as its agents. Thus: *hṛṣṭāni lomāni*, *hṛṣitāni lomāni*, *hṛṣṭam lomabhiḥ*.
The body hairs are bristling;
the hair on the head is thrilled;
the hair on the head is bristling.

*hṛṣṭaḥ* with respect to hair, *hṛṣitaḥ* with respect to hair. It should be stated that [the suffix *kta* is used] in the sense of "astonished" (*vismita*) and "repelled" (*pratighāta*). *Hṛṣṭo devadattaḥ*, *hṛṣito devadattaḥ*.

125.8–9. What is the purpose of the irregular formation (*nipātana*) of *apacitaḥ*? The substitution of *ci* for *cāy* is irregularly prescribed. Thus we have *apacitaḥ*. It should be stated that this applies invariably when the suffix *ktin* follows. Thus we have *apacitiḥ*. (P. 7.2.35) KA_III,291.2–17; Ro_V, 125.11–126.13.

For what purpose is the mention of "ārdhadhātuka" (affixes of the middle category) [in the rule]? Just as the mention of "valādi" (suffixes beginning with *v*) serves as a qualifier for the ārdhadhātuka affixes.

It would be understood [as]: "of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *val*. Now, if the mention of *ārdhadhātuka* were not made, of what would the mention of *valādi* be a qualifier? [The word] *aṅga* is understood [from the previous rule]. It would then be a qualifier of the *aṅga*. What fault would there be in that?
The augment *iṭ* would undesirably apply to the beginning of an *aṅga* that begins with *val*, just like *āṭ* and *āṭ*. For example, *āṭ* and *āṭ* [apply] to the beginning of the *aṅga*.

It is the same for you: even if the term *ārdhadhātuka* were included [in the rule], an undesirable interpretation could still be understood—namely, "that which is the base (*aṅga*) of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *val*. And when it is not included, the desired interpretation results: "that which begins with *val* belonging to the base. Furthermore, what is the *val*-initial element of the base? It is the cause (*nimitta*), in relation to which the designation "base" (*aṅga*) applies. And in relation to what does this [designation] apply?

Regarding the suffix: in a case where it is understood that if [the augment] were applied it would result in an undesirable outcome, whereas if it were not applied an acceptable outcome would follow, we shall understand that in such a case it must indeed not be applied. [Objection: Then this is the purpose: so that it does not occur here in *āste* and *śete*. [Reply: This too is not a valid purpose. The rule *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): the augment *iṭ* occurs after roots beginning with *rud* only before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, and not otherwise.

"From others"—even so, the suffixes *vṛkṣatva* and *vṛkṣatā* would result here. If that is the case, then the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) is a qualification of what is prescribed: [it refers to] that which is prescribed after a root.
But surely this [suffix] is prescribed after a root? It is not prescribed by the rule "after a root. Where, then, does the mention of "root" apply?

This is the subject under discussion: "after the root *ṛ*. Now, that which is designated by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdiṣṭa*) can indeed be qualified by that which is designated by the ablative case (*pañcamīnirdiṣṭa*). Furthermore, since that which is also prescribed after [the root] designated by the genitive can be qualified, it is possible to omit the mention of *ārdhadhātuka*.

(P_7.2.36) An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) should be made for the roots *snū* and *kram* when a *kṛt* suffix follows that does not cause the middle voice (*anātmanepada-nimitta*). An addition must be made for *snū* and *kram* when a *kṛt* suffix follows that does not cause the middle voice: *prasnavitā*, *prasnavitum*.
one should ask,
one who has set out,
in order to set out.

It should be stated. Then it must be stated. It need not be stated. Having stated the addition of the augment *iṭ* for the roots *snu* and *kram* without distinction, I shall state that it does not occur when followed by an *ātmanepada* [suffix]. Regarding the prohibition when followed by an *ātmanepada*, the prohibition must also be stated for those [suffixes] which follow that [first suffix], for the *sīyuṭ* [augment], and for the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [resulting from their combination]. And regarding the prohibition when followed by an *ātmanepada*, the prohibition must be stated for those [suffixes] which follow that [first suffix], for the *sīyuṭ*, and for the single-substitute.
Regarding those [roots] ending in *p*: *prasusnūṣiṣyate*, *pracikraṃsiṣyate*. With the suffix *sīyuṭ*:

*prasnoṣīṣṭa*, *prakraṃsīṣṭa*. In the case of a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*): *prasnoṣyante*, *prakraṃsyante*. Since the distinct separation (*vyapavarga*) [of the two sounds] ceases once the single substitute has been made, the rule would not apply. [Answer: The distinct separation is established through the treatment of the substitute as both the final element of the preceding and the initial element of the following (*antādivadbhāva*).

[The substitution] does not [apply] when both bases are involved, as in the case of "end" (*anta*) and so forth. If that is so, then because the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as the original (*sthānivat*) with respect to a preceding rule, there would be a separation (*vyapavarga*). In that case, a prohibition must be stated for the *sīyuṭ* affix that follows that [substitution]. However, this is established by the prohibition of *iṭ* for the *sn-* [augment] when it resides in the same word (*samānapada*) as the *ātmanepada*. How is this established?

It should be stated that the augment *iṭ* does not occur for *snu* when it resides in the same word as an *ātmanepada* [suffix]. If it is said that *iṭ* does not occur for *snu* when it resides in the same word as an *ātmanepada*, then [the form] *prasnavitrīyate*—meaning "he acts like one who is about to emit"—would not obtain [the desired result], because the *ātmanepada* suffix here is characterized by being extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). And also in the case of *kramu*: [the rule applies] to *kramu* when [it is followed] by an *ātmanepada*.

It should be stated that the augment *iṭ* does not occur [after a root] when it stands in the same word [as the suffix]. Now, for what purpose is *krami* mentioned separately? Why is it not simply said, "after *snu* and *krami*"? [The answer is: since it will be stated that [the augment *iṭ* is absent] after a *kṛt* suffix in the active voice (*kartari*) when the scope is the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), that [absence of *iṭ*] would apply only to *krami* and not to *snu*. [For example, one would get] *vyatiprasnavitārau*.

[This is] a section concerning over-extension (*vyatiprasaṅga*). Regarding the rule *kartari ca ātmanepadaviṣayāt kṛti*: a prohibition must be stated for the [augment] *iṭ* when a *kṛt* suffix follows a verb that has the scope of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). For example: *prakrāntā*, *upakrāntā*. In that case, much must be stated. It should be stated: "The augment *iṭ* does not occur after the root *snu* when it stands within the same word as a middle-voice [suffix]. It should also be stated: "[The augment *iṭ* does not occur] after the root *kram*. And regarding the rule *kartari ca ātmanepadaviṣayāt*...

It should be stated that [the suffix] *kṛt* [is intended]. But then the rule (*sūtra*) would be split. Let it remain exactly as it is formulated. But was it not said that there must be an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the roots *snū* and *kram* when a *kṛt* suffix follows that does not cause the middle voice (*ātmanepada*)? This is not a fault. We shall qualify the roots *snū* and *kram* themselves by their status as causes for the middle voice: "provided that *snū* and *kram* are not causes for the middle voice. But how can a verbal root (*dhātu*) [be a cause]?

The name [of the action] would be the cause for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). The verbal root (*dhātu*) alone is the cause. For the Blessed One has said: "The *ātmanepada* follows roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or the letter *ṅ*;

the *parasmaipada* follows the remainder when denoting the agent. But in cases where the verbal root is not relied upon, such as in the rule "for the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*")? Even there, the verbal root alone is relied upon; [the meaning is] "from a verbal root functioning in the sense of the state or the object. How, then, should one proceed?

The word *nimitta* occurs when there is an *ātmanepada* [suffix]. How so? [In the cases] *prakrāntā*, *upakrāntā*. Therefore, even when it is not present. How so? [In the case] *prakramitavyam*. Therefore, only when it is present. How so? [In the cases] *prakrāntā*, *upakrāntā*. This must indeed be stated: "And after a *kṛt* suffix that falls within the domain of *ātmanepada*, [the suffix *ktvā* becomes *lyap*]. Alternatively, the term "*kṛti*" is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
Regarding the lengthening of the vowel in *grah*, there is the mention of *iṭ*. When there is lengthening of the vowel in *grah*, the mention of *iṭ* must be made;
that is, it should be stated: "the *iṭ* is long. It need not be stated. The previously established [rule] continues to apply. Where was it established?

[The rule] "the augment *iṭ* is added to an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant of the *val* class" [is stated]. Even so, it must indeed be formulated. For if [the word *iṭ*] were not mentioned, there would be no comprehension [of what is to be augmented], because of the absence of a genitive case marker. Indeed, if the mention of *iṭ* were not made, there would be a lack of comprehension. What is the reason? Because of the absence of a genitive case marker. Substitutes are prescribed for that which is indicated by a genitive case marker, and we do not see a genitive case marker here. Furthermore, even if it were formulated...
Regarding the inclusion of *iṭ*: there is a prohibition of the *ciṇvadiṭ* augment. A prohibition of the *ciṇvadiṭ* must be stated [for this case], as in *grāhiṣyate*.
Also regarding the elision of *yaṅ*: a prohibition must also be stated for the elision of *yaṅ*, as in *jarīgṛhitā* and *jarīgṛhitum*.
It must be grasped as such. If, however, "the long *iṭ*" were understood as a separate augment, then if it is said that "it is the long *iṭ*," there is a contradiction.

If it is said that "it is the long *iṭ*," a contradiction arises: if it is *iṭ*, it is not long; if it is long, it is not *iṭ*. To say "it is both *iṭ* and long" is a contradiction. And when there is a restatement of what has been prohibited...
There is an absence of lengthening. When that which was prohibited is prescribed again, there is an absence of lengthening [in the alternative]. As in *vuvūrṣate*, *vivariṣate*, and *vavarīṣate*.
Here too, the rule "the augment *iṭ* is long" will continue to apply. Therefore, having prohibited it when it is situated elsewhere...

That re-statement does not succeed. By the rules *jṝvraścyoḥ ktvi* and *śryukaḥ kiti*, the long vowel is prohibited, and thus lengthening would not apply [to the forms] *jaritvā* and *jarītvā*. [If it were argued:
"The rule for *īṭ* is a prohibition of *iṭ*; the *iṭ* that occurs by default will become long. If...

In that case, when *iṭ* is mentioned, the mention of *īṭ* would not apply; thus, in *jarītvā*, the prohibition of *kittva* by the rule *na ktvā seṭ* would not take effect. Furthermore, in *agṛhīt*, the elision of the *sij* suffix by the rule *iṭa īṭi* would not take effect. And here, in *agrahīt*, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule *neṭi* would not take effect. Let it not be so; rather, it will be governed by the rule *hmyantānām*.

In this case as well, the term *neṭ* (not *iṭ*) continues to apply. Furthermore, that mention of *iṭ* must necessarily be carried over for the sake of forms such as *adhākṣīt*. Likewise, in *agrahīdhvam* and *agrahīḍhvam*, the cerebral [substitution] prescribed by the rule *vibhāṣā iṭaḥ* would not occur. Therefore, it cannot be said in this manner.

When there is the mention of *iṭ*, the mention of *īṭ* does not occur. These two roots, *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*, are acute-accented; therefore, the prohibition based on their original form (*prakṛtilakṣaṇa*) does not apply [to the rule concerning the substitution of the acute accent].
