150–151. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *ghas*? Is it not already established by [the rule] "ekāc" alone? The mention of *ghas* is for the sake of its being vowel-less (*anackatva*). The mention of *ghas* is made because, once the elision (*lopa*) has occurred, [the root] becomes vowel-less, and thus the augment *iṭ* would not apply. This must be considered here: should *iṭ* be applied first or the elision? What should be done in this case? The addition of *iṭ* is [governed by a rule] that follows [in the order of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*]. The elision is obligatory (*nitya*). Once [the elision] has been performed...

[Objection: The augment *iṭ* would apply even when [the reduplication] has not been performed; and since *iṭ* is obligatory, it would apply both when the elision has been performed and when it has not. [Reply: The *iṭ* is not obligatory, for it does not apply once the elision has been performed. Why? Because of the absence of a vowel (*anackatvāt*). [Objection: In that case, once the doubling has been performed, the *iṭ* will depend upon the vowel *a* that occurs in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). [Reply: It is not established. Why? Because of the doubling itself.
Because elision (*lopa*) has priority: "Let reduplication (*dvirvacana*) be performed, or let elision be performed"—what should be done here? Elision, because it is subsequent.

Once elision has been performed, reduplication does not apply because the root would lack a vowel (*anackatva*). However, if the mention of *ghas* is made again, there is no fault. How so? By virtue of the explicit statement, the augment *iṭ* will occur. Once *iṭ* has been applied, let reduplication be performed, and then elision.

Thus, even though the elision occurs because it is subsequent, the reduplication will take place by virtue of the status of being *sthānivadbhāva*. It should be stated that this applies to the root *dṛś* as well: *dadṛśvān*.
[One] has seen it. Then that must be stated. It need not be stated. [The word] *dṛśeḥ* (of the root *dṛś*) is understood [from the previous rule].

Regarding the rule *svarateḥ veṭtvāt ṛtaḥ sye vipratiṣedhena*: because of the optionality (*veṭ*) of the augment *iṭ* for the root *svar*, the rule *ṛtaḥ sye* takes effect by way of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) with the optional rule (*vā-vacana*) characterized by *svarati*. [This is so] because of the conflict with the rule characterized by *svarati*.
The scope for the use of the word "vā" (optionally) is as follows:
*svaritā*, *svaritā*. The scope for the rule *ṛtaḥ sye* [Pāṇini 7.2.41] is as follows: *kariṣyate*, *hariṣyate*. In the following case, both [rules] would apply: *svariṣyati*.
*asvariṣyat*. By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the form *artasya* occurs [in place of *svaritasya*].

they were distressed.

They have resided. And this too is an example:
*ayaṃsīt*, *vyaraṃsīt*, *anaṃsīt*.

if *iṭ* were not present here, the *vṛddhi* substitution would apply; but when *iṭ* is present, the prohibition "not before *iṭ*" (*neṭi*) applies.

The rule is established. [Objection: Let it not be so for roots ending in *hm* and *y*. [Response: It will be so; here too, the phrase "not before *iṭ*" (*na iṭi*) continues to apply. Furthermore, that mention of *iṭ* must necessarily be carried over for the sake of forms such as *adhākṣīt*. And examples of roots ending in long *ā* preceded by a word occur in the singular: *mā hi yāsīt*. If *iṭ* were not present here, [the rule] "of an unaccented [root]" (*anudāttasya*)...

Otherwise, the addition of the augment *iṭ* would result in an undesirable consequence. However, when *iṭ* is present, it has already been stated that "the acute accent of *iṭ* is due to the power of the *cit* designation of the suffix *sic*";
thus, by the rule "an *ekādeśa* [substitute] for an acute vowel is acute," the acute accent is established.

152.13–153.4. What is the purpose of this split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*)? Why not simply state: "In place of *īś*, *īḍ*, and *jan*, [the suffix] *s* becomes *dhve*"? [The answer is: so that it does not apply to *īś* in the case of *dhve*. But that is indeed desired: *īśidhve*. Then, [it is for] so that it does not apply to *īḍ* and *jan* in the case of *se*. But that is indeed desired: *īḍiṣe*, *janiṣe*. Then, [it is for] so that it does not apply to *īś* in the case of *sve*. But that is indeed desired: *īśiṣva*. Then, what about the *se* [suffix]?...

The term *svaśabda* (the word itself) is used here so that [the rule] may apply where there is a *svaśabda*, but not where there is a *svaśabda* in the sense of "intensive repetition of action" (*kriyāsamabhihāra*).

This too is intended: in the case of "May you, sir, rule" (*sa bhavān īśiṣva*), it is understood as "he rules" (*ayam īṣṭe*). Furthermore, this is indeed intended, for he says: "But it is established by the doubling of the second person singular of the imperative (*loṇmadhyamapuruṣaikavacana*) in the sense of intensive repetition of action."

(P_7.2.80) KA_III,302.20–303.2 Ro_V,154.1–6: Does the mention of *sārvadhātuka* continue [from the previous rule], or does it not? And what is the purpose of its continuation? There is certainly a purpose, provided that there exists an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *yā* after the vowel *a*. But surely such a case exists: *cikīrṣyāt*.
[One might argue: "The elision (*lopa*) will be the sublater (*bādhaka*) here. [Response: What, then, is the example for this rule? [Consider] *pacet* and *yajet*.

Here too, by the rule "lengthening occurs before *yañ* after *at*" (*ataḥ dīrgho yañi*), lengthening would apply. Just as that substitution of *ay* sublates the lengthening, it would likewise sublate the elision. Therefore, the mention of "sārvadhātuka" must be carried over [from the previous rule].

(P_7.2.82) KA_III,303.4–23 Ro_V,155.2–156.15: When there is *muk*, there is a fault regarding the vowel (*svara*). When *muk* is present, a fault occurs with respect to the accent: in *pacamānaḥ* and *yajamānaḥ*, because they are separated by *muk*, the status of being unaccented (*anudāttatva*) does not apply. [Objection: But surely this *muk* is part of the original instruction (*adupadeśabhakta*)?

It will be included by the mention of "having a low-pitched vowel as its upadeśa" (*adupadeśa*). [Objection: It is not established. For *muk* is said to belong to the *aṅga*, and the *aṅga* ends with the suffix (*vikaraṇa*);

thus, this [augment *muk*] is part of a composite whole (*saṅghātabhakta*) and cannot be grasped by the mention of "having a low-pitched vowel as its upadeśa. [Response: In that case, it shall be treated as non-partitive (*abhakta*). And if it is non-partitive, what happens? There is a fault regarding the accent (*svara*). [Example: *pacamānaḥ*.

In the word *yajamānaḥ*, because it is separated by the particle *mukā*, the status of being unaccented (*anudātta*) does not apply. If that is the case, then let [the accent] be applied to the beginning of the subsequent element (*parādi*). If it is applied to the beginning of the subsequent element, there is the undesirable consequence of a long vowel (*dīrghaprasaṅga*). If it is made the beginning of the subsequent element, then by the rule "a long vowel occurs before the suffix *yañ*," the lengthening of the vowel would apply. This is not a fault, for that [rule] applies specifically when a finite verb ending (*tiṅ*) follows. Thus, it is established. But in that case, the sūtra is altered.

Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. But was it not said that there is a fault regarding the vowel *muk*? This has been answered: because it is subordinate to the "instruction of *at*" (*adupadeśabhakta*), it will be included by the mention of "instruction of *at*" (*adupadeśagrahaṇa*). But was it not also said that *muk* is called an "augment" (*aṅga*) of the base (*aṅga*), and since the base ends with the suffix (*vikaraṇa*), this [augment] is subordinate to the entire complex (*saṅghātabhakta*) and cannot be grasped by the mention of "instruction of *at*" (*adupadeśagrahaṇa*)? What is the reason? Because the word *anta* has two meanings. How so? This word *anta* exists both as that which occurs together with something else and as that which occurs prior to it. For example: "Devadatta’s field is bounded by the limit" (*maryādāntam*). It is understood to mean "together with the boundary. And it exists as that which occurs prior to something: for example, "Devadatta’s field ends at the river" (*nadyantam*).
It is understood that [the term *anta*] means "prior to the river. Therefore, this mention [of *anta*] is intended so that it may be understood as functioning together with that [river].

This purpose is not necessary; for everywhere the word *anta* functions together with that. [Objection: How then is it said, "Devadatta’s field ends at the river" (*nadyantaṃ devadattasya kṣetram*)? [Response: Since a river cannot possibly be a field, [the meaning is understood as] "prior to the river" (*prāk*).

It is understood that [the rule applies] "of the river" (*nadyāḥ*). If so, then the mention of *pari-* must be made for the purpose of indicating the limit (*avadhi*). For if it were stated merely as "of that which ends in *m*" (*māntasya*), the substitutes would occur only where *yuṣmad* and *asmad* end in *m*. And where do *yuṣmad* and *asmad* end in *m*? [For example, in] *yuṣmān ācaṣṭe*.

If this is so, then [in the case of] *atijarasam*,...
Regarding the example *atijarasaiḥ*, [the rule] does not apply here;
it should be *atijaram*, *atijaraiḥ*. Gonardīya says: "This very desired form is indeed included [by the rule].
It should be *atijaram* and *atijaraiḥ* when this *paribhāṣā*—that 'an operation caused by a specific configuration' (*sannipātalakṣaṇa*)..."
"The rule is that there is no cause for its obstruction.

7.2.102) [This refers to] the substitution of *a* for the words beginning with *tyad* up to *dviparyanta*. [It means] the substitution of *atva* for those words beginning with *tyad* up to *dviparyanta*.
It must be stated. What is the purpose? So that [the substitution] does not occur for forms ending in *yuṣmad* or *asmad*, or those ending in *bhavat*.

Then it must indeed be stated. It need not be stated. Because the forms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are already established by the [application of] the *at* suffix to the *tyad*-class words, the elision (*lopa*) taught in the rule "in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe lopaḥ*) makes it known that the *at* suffix applies prior to that. Since this [elision] is already established by the *at* suffix of the *tyad*-class words...

The Teacher teaches the elision of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* in the case of the "remainder" (*śeṣe*); this indicates that the substitution of *atva* occurs prior to that [elision]. It does not apply to all cases. Alternatively, it might have been formulated for the sake of compounds because of the absence of *atva* there; however, this is not a valid purpose. This would rather be for the sake of compounds, as in *atiyūyam*.

The substitution of *at* [for *tyad* etc. is not desired when they are compounded: *atitat*, *atitadau*, *atitadaḥ*. It is traditionally taught that the elision of the *ṭi* suffix must be performed for the sake of preventing the feminine suffix *ṭāp*; however, the elision of the *ṭi* which occurs in the remaining cases [is different].

He should be asked: "What is the purpose? [The purpose is] for the sake of prohibiting the suffix *ṭāp*; that is, so that *ṭāp* does not occur. Then, that elision of *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*) must be stated. It need not be stated. Alternatively, by means of a locative of remainder (*śeṣasaptamī*), elision is prescribed for the remainder. Here, by the rule "there is elision of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*," the elision of the final [element] is established by this much alone. Since it is thus established, this [elision of *ṭi*]— [...is stated.]

The purpose of his employing the term *śeṣa* (remainder) is so that there may be the elision (*lopa*) of what remains. For the wise say that the accomplishment of its grammatical operation occurs when [only] the remainder is left. If this is so, then the activity of the Teacher indicates that the substitution of *atva* does not apply to all members of the *tyadādi* group; for he teaches the substitution of *ka* for *kim* by stating "the substitute *ka*" (*kimaḥ kaḥ*). Otherwise...
One should simply say, "The substitute *at* occurs for *kim*. Since this rule is being formulated even though [the result] is already established, it must serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
Furthermore, it is not established by the substitution of *at* [for *kim*] alone. For if *at* were applied, it would affect only the final phoneme.

But that [substitution of the final phoneme] is already established by the preceding rule; therefore, by the force of the present formulation, it will apply to the vowel *i*. Why, indeed, is this [rule] intended to exclude the final phoneme?
If there were an initial [application of the rule], it would apply to the letter *i*, but not to the letter *k*. Why, then, does he include the mention of *kim*?

For otherwise, he would simply have said "after *kaṭ*. Even so, the rule would still apply to what follows merely the letter *k*. [The word] *tyadādīnām* (of the *tyad*-class) is understood [from the context], and among the *tyad*-class words, there is no other word containing the letter *k* like *kim*. Thus...

Furthermore, this indicator (*jñāpaka*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). All that is indicated is that the substitution of *atva* does not occur for all members of the class beginning with *tyad*. In that case, how is it determined that it will apply only to those ending with *dvi*, and not to those ending with *yuṣmad* or *asmad*, or even those ending with *bhavat*? Moreover, the mention of *kim* must certainly be made for the sake of the subsequent rule.

[Objection: Why is it that *ku* [is used] for *kva*? Indeed, the substitution of *ka-* must necessarily be stated for the sake of forms with the augment *sakac*, such as *kaḥ*, *kau*, and *ke*. Therefore, the substitution of *at* should be stated for those ending in two vowels (*dviparyanta*). Since this is already established by the substitution of *akāra* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad* (i.e., *tyadādi*), [the rule applies] to *yuṣmad* and *asmad*;

thus, by the elision (*lopa*) of the remainder, it is understood that *at* occurs prior to that. Alternatively, it may have been formulated for the sake of compounds (*upasamasta*), because there is no substitution of *at* [in such cases].

178.11–180.5. Why is it said, "for the sake of the two non-final [sounds]" (*anantyayoḥ*)? [It is said] so that [the substitution] might not apply to the final sounds. This purpose is not necessary. The substitution of *a* (in rule 6.1.97) will serve as an exception (*bādhaka*) to the two final sounds. Rules that have no scope (*anavakāśa*) are exceptions, whereas the substitution of *a* has scope (*sāvakāśa*). What is its scope? The word *dvi*. The substitution of *sa* (in rule 6.1.63) also has scope. What is its scope?

[The substitute] is *anantya* (non-final). But how can there be the existence of a non-final [element] when a final [element] exists? It would be so for one who would qualify the stem (*aṅga*) by means of the letters *t* and *d*; for such a person, [the substitution] would not apply to the two non-final [letters]. We, however, shall indeed qualify the letters *t* and *d* by means of the stem. Even so, since both [rules] have their scope, the [substitution of] *satva* prevails because it is subsequent. Furthermore, what would happen if [the rule applied] to the two final [letters]?

[If the rule were stated as *tadoḥ saḥ* without qualification,] there would be the form *satvam*. In this case, in the word *saḥ*, the elision of the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi-lopa*) prescribed by the rule *eṅhrasvāt* would not occur. And here, in the word *yā sā*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* prescribed by the rule *ataḥ* would not occur. Therefore, it should be stated: "of the two non-final [sounds]. It need not be stated. I shall state it thus: *tadoḥ saḥ sau*; then *adasaḥ*; and then: "and for the letter *d* of *adas*, *s* occurs. Now, this [is the case]: *idam*.

For what purpose? For the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*): [it applies] only to the *d* of *adas*, not to any other *d*. If a restriction is made, then from the root *dvīyati* with the suffix *apratyaya*, the form *dvaḥ* would result; however, *svaḥ* is also desired. [The rule applies] according to the grammatical characteristics (*yathālakṣaṇam*) in cases where [the word] is not in common usage (*aprayukte*).

180–182. "The substitution of *au* for the *su* of *adas* would occur; why then is the elision of *su* prescribed? The substitution of *au* for the *su* of *adas* alone would suffice; for what purpose is the elision of *su* prescribed? [Otherwise] the vocative suffix would be elided after a short vowel. In the case of *he asau*, the elision [of the vocative suffix] would undesirably apply by the rule *eṅhrasvāt sambuddheḥ*. [Reply: No, because of the word *hal*. The elision of *hal* is the elision of the vocative suffix. That is the mention of *hal*."

It must be stated. For that is the subject under discussion. The mention of *hal* is the subject under discussion. Where was it introduced? In the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktam hal*. That [mention] was indeed indicated by the nominative case (*prathamā*), but here the sense requires it to be indicated by the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*).
This ablative case (*pañcamī*) in *hrasvāt* will effect the conversion of the nominative *hal* into a genitive; therefore [it is understood as *hrasvād halaḥ*].

Thus [it is said] regarding the subsequent rule. In that case, the substitution of *e* for *ā* would apply to the word *āpaḥ*. Here, in the example "he asau brāhmaṇi," the substitution of *e* for *ā*—by the rule "āṅi ca āpaḥ saṃbuddhau ca"—would undesirably follow. This is not so, because of the continued application (*anuvartana*) of the condition "before a consonant" (*jhali*). The term "before a consonant" (*jhali*) is understood there [in the previous rule]. Where was it introduced? In the rule "supi ca bahuvacane jhali et," which states that *e* is substituted for *ā* before a consonant in the plural of nominal suffixes. And also by the rule "pratyayasthāt ca kāt."
In this case, in the example *asakau brāhmaṇī*, the substitution of *ī* for the vowel preceding the suffixal *kā* would undesirably apply.
This is not a fault, for this is a composite designation: *ā*, *āp*, *āp*. [Objection: In that case, it would still not apply here: *kārike*.

In the case of *hārike*, the substitution of *śī* would also result; here too, the substitution of *śī* would apply. In the example *asau brāhmaṇī*, the substitution of *śī* would apply [by the rule] "for *auṅ* following *āp*, *śī* occurs. Therefore, the elision (*lopa*) of *su* must be stated.

(P_7.2.107.2) KA_III,312.14–313.4 Ro_V, 182: Regarding the prohibition of *aut* [for *s-au*] after [a stem] with the augment *sak*, or rather, the substitution of *ut* for *sāt*. It should be stated that the prohibition of *aut* applies after [a stem] with the augment *sak*; furthermore, it should be stated that the substitution of *ut* occurs for the following [element] *sāt*. Thus: *asakau*, *asukaḥ*. Regarding the substitution of those [pronouns] that have become the second member of a compound (*uttarapada*), there is the rule of "behaving like the original form" (*upadeśivadbhāva*). It should be stated that when the pronouns beginning with *tyad* have become the second member of a compound, they behave like their original forms. For example: *paramāham*.

"Paramāyam," "paramānena. What is the purpose? It is for the sake of cases where no specific rule has been prescribed. This is so that the substitutes may apply even when the single-substitute (ekādeśa) operation has not yet taken place. But what is the reason that the single-substitute operation occurs first rather than the substitutes? It is not because of priority; rather, it is because [the single-substitute] is prior to the substitutes.

It must be so, because it is characterized as being external (*bahiraṅga*). The substitutions (*ādeśa*) are external; the single-substitute operation (*ekādeśa*) is internal (*antaraṅga*). That which is external is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal. In that case, the treatment of the original form (*upadeśivadbhāva*) must be stated. It need not be stated. The activity of the Teacher (*ācāryapravṛtti*) indicates that first the operation of the preceding and following members (*pūrvapada-uttarapada*) takes place, and not the single-substitute operation—this is shown by the fact that he [does not apply the rule otherwise].

The rule *indrasya parasya* teaches a prohibition. How does it serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? In the word *indra*, there are two vowels (*ac*). Of these, one is removed by the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *yasya*, and the other is removed by the single-substitute operation (*ekādeśa*). Thus, *indra* becomes devoid of vowels (*anacka*). In that state, what occasion could there be for the application of *vṛddhi*? However, the Teacher perceives that the grammatical operation must first apply to both the preceding and the following members of the compound.
Since it does not occur when there is a single substitute (*ekādeśa*), it thereby teaches the prohibition [of *aut*] for that which follows *indra*.
Would the substitution of *au* apply to the *su* of *adas*, or is the elision of *su* being prescribed?

The vocative suffix (*sambuddhi*) would be elided after a short vowel, for that [elision] was indeed the subject under discussion; it would not be elided after a consonant. Furthermore, in that case, the substitution of *e* for the final vowel of words ending in *āp* would occur because of the continued application of the rule "not when followed by a *jhal* sound," and the substitution of *ī* (*śībhāva*) would also result from the rule "after a *k* situated in an affix.

183.4–184.4: An exception must be stated regarding the prohibition of *kvip* in the rule prescribing *vṛddhi* for the root *mṛj*. In the case of the forms *kaṃsaparimṛḍbhyām* and *kaṃsaparimṛḍbhiḥ*, which end in *kvip*, the *vṛddhi* substitution should not apply. Alternatively, when a verbal root is mentioned by its own form (*svarūpa*), the desired result is established through the understanding that the operation applies to the suffix attached to it. That is, when a root is mentioned by its own form, the grammatical operation is understood to apply to the suffix following that root. Thus, the operation occurs upon the suffix of the root.

Thus, this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) must be formulated. What are the purposes of this technical rule? Its purpose is for the sake of *sṛj*, *dṛś*, *masj*, *naś*, *han*, and *girati*. *Sṛj*: *rajjusṛḍbhyām*, *rajjusṛḍbhiḥ*. [The *ṣatva* is applied by this rule. *Sṛj*. *Dṛś*: *devadṛgbhyām*. [The *ṣatva* is applied by this rule. *Dṛś*.
*devadṛgbhiḥ*; *dṛśi*: *udakamagbhyām*, *udakamagbhiḥ*; *masji*. *naśi*: *pranaḍbhyām*, *pranaḍbhiḥ*;
*naśi*. *hanti*: *vārtraghnaḥ*.

*bhrauṇaghnaḥ* (the slayer of the embryo), *hanti* (he kills), *girati* (he swallows), *devagiraḥ* (those who swallow the gods). If it is said that [the rule] applies to the actual form (*svarūpa*), then in the case of *prasṛdbhayām* and *prasṛdbhiḥ*, the suffix *am* would apply by the rule *anudāttasya ca ṛdupadhasyānyatarasyām*. If this is so, then this is a *paribhāṣā* (a metarule).

"It is said that an operation prescribed for a verbal root (dhātu) occurs when that [root] is followed by its suffix. Well then, this technical rule (paribhāṣā) must be formulated. It need not be formulated. The activity of the Teacher (Ācārya) makes it known that this rule exists, in that he teaches the substitution of *t* for *th* in the word *bhrauṇahatya*.

Regarding the rule for *vṛddhi*: the mention of the vowel (*aj*) is for the sake of "cow" (*go*). The vowel is mentioned in the rule for *vṛddhi* so that *vṛddhi* may occur in the word "cow" (*go*). This purpose is not necessary; for by the very force of the designation as having the marker *ṇ*, *vṛddhi* occurs here.

It will be so. Now, for what purpose is the *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule)? Why not simply state: "When a suffix beginning with *ñ* or *ṇ* follows, [the penultimate vowel] of that [stem] is lengthened"?
What would be the resulting forms? *cāyakaḥ*, *lāvakaḥ*.

[The form] *kārakaḥ* is established by the application of the rule *guṇe kṛte*, followed by *ay-avaḥ* and *raparatve*, and finally by *ata upadhāyāḥ*. The division of the *yoga* (rule) is for the sake of [the forms] *sakhi-* and those beginning with a consonant. The division of the *yoga* is made for the sake of *sakhi-* and for the sake of those beginning with a consonant. First, regarding the sake of *sakhi-*: *sakhāyau*, *sakhāyaḥ*. Regarding the sake of those beginning with a consonant: *jaitram*.

*yautram*, *cyautram*. And if, by means of a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*), the suffix *i* is now applied for the sake of [forming] *sakhī* and words beginning with a consonant, then the mention of *ac* (vowel) must also be made.
What is the purpose? For the sake of *go*. But has it not already been stated that the vowel increase (*vṛddhi*) occurs here precisely by the force of the application of the marker *ṇit*?
"It will be so. There is another purpose for the designation *ṇit*. What is it?

[To ensure that] in the forms *gāvau* and *gāvaḥ*, once the substitution of *ava* has been made, the rule "vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel" (*ata upadhāyāḥ*) applies. As for the designation *ṇit* in the case of the nominative singular (*sau*), that is without scope;
and precisely because it lacks scope, the *vṛddhi* will take place by virtue of the power of the *ṇit* designation itself. Indeed, just as...

185–186. The mention of *aj* (vowel) must be made. But is it not already being done? It must be stated a second time so that the mention of the beginning of vowels (*acām ādi*) may be understood as a qualifier of *aj* (vowels), namely: "of the vowel at the beginning of vowels. Now, if the mention of *aj* were not made, of what would the mention of the beginning of vowels be a qualifier? He says: it would be a qualifier of *ik* (the short vowels *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, *ḷ*). [The rule would then read: "of the *ik* at the beginning of vowels. What would be the fault in that? Here...

[The suffix] would thus apply in cases such as *aitkāyanaḥ* and *aupagavaḥ*, but it would not apply here in cases such as *gārgyaḥ* and *vātsyaḥ*. Therefore, the mention of the letter *aj* must be made. It need not be made; the previously stated [rule] continues to apply.

What is the subject under discussion? It is "vṛddhi of a vowel (ac) before a suffix marked by Ñ or Ṇ" (*acaḥ ñṇiti*). If that [rule] were to follow here, then by the rule "vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel (upadhā) of *at*" (*ata upadhāyāḥ*), a vṛddhi would undesirably apply to every single vowel (*ajmātra*) that serves as a penultimate.
For example, in the word *chedakaḥ*. [Objection: We shall qualify the vowel (*ac*) by means of the letter *a* followed by *t* (*tapara*).
That is, it will mean "of a vowel which is *at*" (*acaḥ ataḥ*). [Response: In this case, only "of a vowel" (*acaḥ*) continues to apply, while "*ataḥ*" has ceased to apply. Or else:
The governing rules (*adhikāras*) proceed by "frog-leaps" (*maṇḍūkagatayaḥ*). Just as frogs go by leaping again and again, so do these governing rules.

Alternatively, they may be treated as a single rule (*ekayoga*): first, *acaḥ ñṇiti ata upadhāyāḥ*, and then *taddhiteṣv acām ādeḥ*. However, there is no continuous application (*anuvṛtti*) within a single rule.

Regarding the *taddhita* suffixes, when there is *vṛddhi* of the first vowel among the vowels (*acāmādivṛddhi*), a prohibition must be stated concerning the *vṛddhi* characterized by the final or penultimate [vowel]. For example, in *krauṣṭuḥ* and *jāgataḥ*. Now, [one might object]:...

And [the rule for] the *vṛddhi* of *ac* beginning with the first vowel will supersede the *vṛddhi* characterized by the final or penultimate [vowel]. How can that which is prescribed for one thing be a superseder of another? Indeed, supersession occurs only when coexistence is impossible; yet here, there is the possibility that both might occur. [Objection: It is established through worldly understanding that supersession occurs even when coexistence is possible. That...

Just as in the case of the injunction, "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, and buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya," where even though the giving of curd is possible, the giving of buttermilk serves to exclude it; so too here, even though it is possible, the *vṛddhi* of the initial vowel (*acāmādi*) will set aside the *vṛddhi* characterized by the final or penultimate letter. [Objection: This is an unequal comparison. For the giving of buttermilk is not commenced when the giving of curd has not already been established [as applicable].

In that case, [the rule] being commenced when [the condition] has already been reached would constitute an annulment (*bādhaka*). Here, however, while the *vṛddhi* characterized by the final vowel and the penultimate vowel (*antyopadhala-kṣaṇā*) has not yet been reached, the *vṛddhi* of the initial vowel of the vowels (*acām-ādi-vṛddhi*) is commenced, as in *suśruta-* and *sauśrutaḥ*. Or else, because of the inclusion of the word *puṣkarasat* [in the list]. Alternatively, the fact that the Teacher recites the word *puṣkarasat* in the *anuśatikādi* group indicates that, when the *vṛddhi* of the initial vowel of the vowels occurs, the [application of the] *vṛddhi* characterized by the final vowel and the penultimate vowel...

[The rule] "there is no increase" [applies]. (Pāṇini 7.3.1) Regarding the *devikā* group, there must be a mention of the initial element. In the case of the *devikā* group, a mention of the initial element must be made; it should be stated as "of those beginning with *devikā*," so that it may apply here as well: *dāvikākulāḥ*.

The *śālayaḥ*, the *śāṃśapāsthalāḥ*, and the gods (*devāḥ*). But what is the reason that [the rule] does not apply? Because elsewhere there is either the mention of that [word] itself or the mention of that which ends in it; yet here, this is neither that nor does it end in that.

It is established because [the word *devikā*] is a qualifier of the initial [vowel]. The words *devikā* and so forth qualify the initial [vowel] of the stem (*aṅga*). It is not understood in this way: "For stems beginning with *devikā*, an *ā* is substituted for the first vowel (*ac*) of the stem. How, then? [The rule means]: "When there is an affix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*, an *ā* is substituted for the first vowel of the stem, provided that it is the first vowel of *devikā* and so forth. Or else, [it is established] because [the rule] serves to exclude [substitutions] based on closest similarity (*āntaratamya*). Now...
Or rather, by this [rule], the closest possible *vṛddhi* is not produced; what then? By this, the closest possible [vowel] is excluded.

The *vṛddhi* is already established here by the rule "in *taddhita* suffixes, [the *vṛddhi*] of the first vowel among the vowels" (*taddhiteṣv acām ādeḥ*). In that case, it is by this [present rule] that the closest possible *vṛddhi* is excluded. This has been stated considering it to be yet another solution; and how is this another solution?

It would be so, if the words *devikā* and so forth were not qualifiers of the first member (*ādya-j-viśeṣaṇa*). And this must necessarily be understood in this way: that *devikā* and so forth are qualifiers of the first member. For if *devikā* and so forth were not qualifiers of the first member, then [the suffix] would also apply here:
*sudevikāyām bhavaḥ* → *saudevikaḥ*. Now, in this case as well, it is established precisely because they are qualifiers of the first member.

There is another way to avoid [this objection]. We do not say that an operation must be performed wherever its performance results in a fault; rather, it must be performed wherever its performance results in no fault.

And where is there no fault when it is performed? In the rule for technical designations (*saṃjñāvidhi*): "The term *vṛddhi* refers to *āt* and *aic*; [the term] *devikādi* refers to the vowel *ā*. Thus, [the rule] applies. But then, the Sūtra is contradicted.

Let it remain exactly as it was originally formulated. But has it not been stated that in the case of *devikā* and others, there is the inclusion of those beginning with them—because elsewhere there is inclusion of those [beginning with] them, or because there is inclusion of those ending with them? This has already been answered: it is established because they are qualifiers of the initial element (*ādyaj*). And because of the mention of the solitary *nyagrodha*. Because of the mention of the solitary *nyagrodha*, we understand that the *devikā* and others are qualifiers of the initial element.
Thus it is said. For this purpose of the mention of "kevala" (alone) is so that [the rule] might not apply here: *nyagrodhamūlāḥ śālayaḥ* ("rice plants rooted at a banyan tree").
And if the words beginning with *devikā* are qualified by having the first vowel as the marker (*ādyaj*), then the mention of "kevala" becomes meaningful.
How does this function as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? If the word *nyagrodha* is an underived nominal stem (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*).

It occurs. For since "nyagrodha" is derived from the root *ny-agra-rohati* ("grows downwards"), the rule regarding the word-final position (*padānta*) is for the purpose of restriction; therefore, it does not serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). It must be stated that there is the substitution of *it* for *vahīnara*. The substitution of *it* should be prescribed for *vahīnara*: the descendant of *vahīnara* is *vaihīnari*. However, Kuṇaravāḍava says: this is not *vahīnara*; what then? It is *vihīnara*.
This man is *vihīnaḥ*, meaning deprived of the enjoyment of desires (*kāmabhogābhyām*). The offspring of one who is *vihīna* is a *vaihīnariḥ*.
(Pāṇini 7.3.3) Regarding the rule that there is no *vṛddhi* after [the suffixes] *ya* and *va*: the absence of *vṛddhi* after *ya* and *va* is established.
Why? Because those two are exceptions to *vṛddhi*. For those two, *ai* and *au*, are stated as exceptions to *vṛddhi*.

The *vṛddhi* [rule] applies to them after the *ai* and *au* have already been established. Alternatively, the *ai* and *au* are permanent (*nitya*). They apply whether the *vṛddhi* has already taken place or not yet taken place.
Since the *ai* and *au* are permanent, even if the *vṛddhi* occurs, it belongs to those very same [sounds]. Why, then, is it not taught that "it is *na*" (the substitute *na*)?

Now, for what purpose is this prohibition stated? The statement regarding the connection with the prohibition is for the sake of defining the scope of *e* and *o*. For the sake of defining the scope of *e* and *o*, *ai* and *au* are prescribed in conjunction with that prohibition. Where there is a *vṛddhi* following *y* or *v*, there [the rule] does not apply, as in *adhyaśvaiḥ*. Where it is stated that there is no *vṛddhi* following *y* or *v*, there *ai* and *au* do apply.

So that [the rules] might apply here, but not there: *ādhyaśviḥ*, *dādhyaśviḥ*, *mādhvaśviḥ*. This purpose is not necessary; for those two [suffixes] follow from the first vowel (*ac*) after *y* and *v*. [The rule applies] by means of the initial vowel of the *ac*s.

In this context, we shall specify [the application of] *y* and *v*: "the *y* and *v* that belong to the beginning of vowels. Why do these two not apply in the case of *dvyāśītika*? Why do they not occur here in the word *dvyāśītikaḥ*? Where there is a *vṛddhi* substitute for the beginning of vowels, there *ai* and *au* are prescribed; in this case, however, the *vṛddhi* is according to the rule "of *ghu*" (*ghoḥ*). In that case, where the *vṛddhi* is according to the rule "of the beginning of vowels" (*acām ādeḥ*), there *ai* and *au* are stated; but here, the *vṛddhi* is according to the rule "of *ghu*" (*ghoḥ*).

"What is this [meaning of] *ghoḥ*? It means 'of the final member of a compound' (*uttarapadasya*)". Even though the governing rule for the "final member" (*uttarapada-adhikāra*) is present, the augment *aij* must necessarily be carried over for the sake of such cases as *pūrvatryalinde bhavaḥ = pūrvatrayalindaḥ*. This is not a fault. Here, by the word "final member" (*uttarapadena*), we shall qualify the initial vowels (*acām ādi*); and by the phrase "the initial of the vowels" (*acām ādinā*), we shall mean *y* and *v*. Thus, it refers to the vowels of the final member.

"Regarding the rule *āder yau yvau* (the semivowels *y* and *v* [are substituted] for the initials [of *ya* and *va*]): why then [is it said] 'from two word-final [consonants]'? Why is it stated 'from two word-final [consonants]'? So that [the substitution] would not occur for *iṇ*. Let there be no substitution of *yaṇ* for *iṇ*. As in *yataḥ chātrāḥ* and *yātāḥ*. But here, in *vaiyākaraṇaḥ*..."

In the case of *sauvaśvaḥ*, the substitution of *śākala* (the elision of *i*) would apply; furthermore, because of the status of the substituends (*sthānivadbhāva*), the substitutions *āy* and *āv* would also apply. Regarding the substitutions of *śākala*, *āy*, and *āv*, it has been stated. What was stated? First, regarding *śākala*, it was stated: "There is a prohibition of *śākala* in the case of [words ending in] *sin* and in eternal compounds. Regarding *āy* and *āv*, what was stated? "Because of the understanding of [the rule] as referring to vowels (*ac*), the [substitution of] *ai* and *au* is established. There is no *vṛddhi* for that which follows *y* and *v*.
For those two [substitutions] are exceptions to *vṛddhi*;
since *ai* and *au* are eternal (*nitya*), why is it not taught that *vṛddhi* applies to them? Where *vṛddhi* follows from *y* and *v*, there [the rule] does not apply to them, as in *adhyaśvaiḥ*.

For those two [substitutions] apply to the first vowel among the vowels following *y* and *v*; how then do they not apply in *dvy-aśītika*? Where *vṛddhi* applies to the first of the vowels, there *ai* and *au* apply; in this case, however, that [vṛddhi] belongs to *ghu*.
Now, why is it that [the substitution] does not occur for *yaṇ* from two [consonants] at the end of a word, as in the case of *iṇ*?
7.3.4) Furthermore, does the phrase "non-vṛddhi of the following" (*parasyāvṛddhiḥ*) carry over [from the previous rule], or does it not? And what follows from this? If it does carry over...

When the elision of *ṭi* has occurred in the word *śauvam* (dog-flesh), the augment *aij* does not apply. Now, if the word *svādhyāya* is recited among the *dvārādi* group, then the augment *aij* would apply before all the *yaṇ* sounds therein. Let it be as you wish. Let us assume for now that [the rule] continues. How then is *śauvam māṃsam* established? It is established by the proper sequence [of grammatical operations].

In this case, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) would not apply if the substitution of *aij* had not yet occurred. Why? Because by the rule *prakṛtyā ekāc*, there ought to be the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Thus, this is established through sequential application. Alternatively, let it be that [the prohibition] has been withdrawn.
But was it not said that the word *svādhyāya* is listed among the *dvārādi* group, and therefore, as many *yaṇ* sounds as there are, from all of them—?
The augment *ai* would apply to the former [word]. But who indeed is entitled to include the word *svādhyāya* in the list beginning with *dvāra*?

It is said that it should be read thus: "one's own study is *svādhyāya*. But that is not so; for *svādhyāya* is either "excellent study" (*suṣṭhu adhyayanam*) or "beautiful study" (*śobhanam adhyayanam*). Or else, one's own study is *svādhyāya*.
Even so, there is no fault. The phrase "of vowels, of the first" (*acām ādeḥ*) is understood [from the previous rule].
7.3.8) This word *śvan* is recited among the *dvārādi* group; what possibility is there that [the substitution] would apply to that which begins with it?

It is not the case that it is obtained [by the general rule], nor is there any purpose served by the prohibition; rather, it would be obtained by the rule concerning "that which begins with it" (*tadādividhi*). Yet, such a rule as "beginning with it" does not exist. Therefore, he recites the following reply: The mention of *śva* and so forth in the prohibition is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that elsewhere, when *śvan* is mentioned, the inclusion of what begins with it is intended for the sake of forms such as *śauvahāna*. The mention of *śva* and so forth in the prohibition is made for the purpose of providing this indication.
What is being indicated? The Teacher indicates that, other than in the case of the mention of *śvan*, the rule of "taking what begins with that" (*tadādividhi*) applies.

What is the purpose of this indication? It is for the sake of forms such as *śauvahāna*. *Śauvahāna* is the name of a city; [and] *śauvādaṃṣṭraḥ maṇiḥ* ("a gem from a dog's fang"). Furthermore, the mention of "beginning with the vowel *i*" is for the sake of forms such as *śvāgaṇikā*. Thus, the mention of "beginning with the vowel *i*" must also be made.

Why is this stated? [One might argue: "The rule *avayavād ṛtoḥ* will be stated later; [this present rule] is for the sake of ensuring that [the substitution] applies to the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) and not to the initial vowel (*ādi*) of the vowels. This purpose is not necessary. Since *avayavāt* is in the ablative case, even without the mention of *uttarapada*, it will apply to the subsequent member alone. [If you ask,] "Then it is for the sake of the subsequent rules," [it refers to] *susarvārdhāt*.

Regarding the rule *janapadasya*: the word *susarvārdhāt* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*). Regarding the rule *diśo 'madrāṇām*: the word *diśaḥ* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*). Regarding the rule *prācāṃ grāmanagarāṇām*: [the word *diśaḥ*] is likewise [in the ablative]. Regarding the rule *saṅkhyāyāḥ saṃvatsarasaṅkhyasya ca*: the word *saṅkhyāyāḥ* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*). Regarding the rule *varṣasyābhaviṣyati*: [the word *saṅkhyāyāḥ*] is likewise [in the ablative]. Regarding the rule *parimāṇāntasyāsañjñāśāṇayoḥ*: [the word *saṅkhyāyāḥ* is likewise in the ablative].

Thus [it is said]: "of a numeral" (saṅkhyāyāḥ) [is the rule]. This, then, is the purpose: so that [the suffix] *je* may apply to the *uttarapada* of the word *proṣṭhapadā*, but not to the *pūrvapada*. For example: one born under the *proṣṭhapadās* is a *proṣṭhapāda* Brāhmaṇa. Among *taddhita* suffixes, the vṛddhi of the *uttarapada* takes precedence over the vṛddhi of the initial vowel of the *ac*s [of the whole compound], by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), for the sake of forms such as *dvyāśītika*. Among *taddhita* suffixes...

In the case of *acām ādivṛddhi*, the *uttarapadavṛddhi* takes precedence by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). What is the purpose? It is for the sake of forms such as *dvyāśītika*. *Acām ādivṛddhi* has its scope in cases such as *aitikāyanaḥ* and *aupagavaḥ*. *Uttarapadavṛddhi* has its scope in cases such as *dviṣāṣṭikaḥ*.

In the case of *triṣāṣṭikaḥ*, both [rules] would apply here: *dvyāśītikaḥ* and *tryāśītikaḥ*. The vowel-increment (*vṛddhi*) of the final member occurs by way of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). But what is the difference here between the vowel-increment of the initial vowels (*acām ādivṛddhiḥ*) and the vowel-increment of the final member (*uttarapadavṛddhiḥ*)? This is the difference: if, in this case, there were vowel-increment of the initial vowels...
The augment *aij* might [undesirably] apply.
Why is the mention of *nagara-* [in the rule] necessary, since it would already be established by the phrase "of villages of the easterners"? It is not so established.

The village is one thing, the city another. How is this known? For instance, someone asks another: "From where do you come? and he replies: "Not from the village, but from the city. But surely, sir, that which is the village is the same as the city. How is this known? From common usage; for those rules that are not desired to apply to the village [apply] to the city.

It is even more effective that [certain things] are not done in the city. For example, when it is said, "The village cock is not to be eaten; the village pig is not to be eaten," then the city [cock or pig] is all the more not eaten. Likewise, when it is said, "One should not study in the village," it is even more effective that one does not study in the city. Therefore, that which is the village is indeed the city. How so? As it has been stated thus:

Someone asks another: "From where have you come? He replies: "Not from a village, but from a city. This person is referring to a specific type of settlement (*saṃstyāya-viśeṣa*). For these are indeed specific types of settlements: a village (*grāma*), a hamlet (*ghoṣa*), a city (*nagara*), and a caravan station (*saṃvāha*). If this is so, then since the matter is already established, the reason he mentions both "village" and "city" is this: [to indicate that the term applies to all such places].

The Teacher indicates that, apart from the mention of "village" (*grāma*), there is no mention of "city" (*nagara*). What is the purpose of this indication? In the rule *viśiṣṭaliṅgo nadīdeśo 'grāmāḥ*, the prohibition of "city" was prescribed;
that need not be stated [if this is understood]. If this is indicated, then [the rule] *udīcyagrāmāc ca bahvaco 'ntodāttāt* [applies].

Thus, in this case, the mention of "city" (*nagara*) should be made [in the rule for *bāhīka*]. And the mention of "city" should also be made [in the rule] for the villages of the Bāhīkas. For words denoting direction (*dikśabda*), when referring to villages, districts, names of persons, and the Cānarāṭas, the mention of "city" should be made. This fourth point is for the sake of providing an indicator (*jñāpaka*). There is no benefit in excessive insistence on that matter. Therefore, in whichever mention of "village" (*grāma*) the mention of "city" is included...
Its prohibition is not desired; it must be stated.

7.3.15) The mention of *saṃvatsara* is redundant because [the rule] has already been established by the phrase "of that which ends in a measure" (*parimāṇāntasya*). [Therefore,] the mention of *saṃvatsara*...

It is useless. Why? Because [the rule] *parimāṇāntasya* has already been established. It is already established by the rule *parimāṇāntasyāsaṃjñāśāṇayoḥ*. However, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the prohibition of *vṛddhi* in the case of measures of time. If that is so, the Teacher indicates that there is no *vṛddhi* for measures of time. What is the purpose of this indication? [For example: *dvairātrikaḥ*.

In *trairātrika*, there is no *vṛddhi* [substitution]. This serves no purpose; for there is no difference here whether the *vṛddhi* of the final member (*uttarapada*) occurs or does not occur. Then consider this: *dvasamikaḥ*, *traisamikaḥ*. And this too is a purpose: *dvairātrikaḥ*.

[The word] *trairātrikaḥ* [is formed]. Now, it was argued that there is no distinction here whether the vowel-increment (*vṛddhi*) of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) occurs or not. But this distinction does exist: if the vowel-increment of the subsequent member were to occur here, the increment of the first vowel among the vowels (*acām ādeḥ*) would not take place. Another says: "But this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that for measures of time, the term 'measure' (*parimāṇa*) is not included [in the rule]. If that is so, then the Teacher indicates that for measures of time...

"By the mention of *parimāṇa* (measure), there is no inclusion [of words like *varṣa*]. What is the purpose of making this known? It is for the sake of the rule: "After words denoting non-measure (*aparimāṇa*), as well as *bista*, *ācita*, and *kambalya*, [the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is not applied] when a *taddhita* suffix is elided.
Thus, in the cases *dvivarṣā* and *trivarṣā*, the exclusion does not apply by virtue of the exclusion of *parimāṇa*.

The phrase "there is no *vṛddhi* for the subsequent [element]" (*parasya vṛddhir na*) either continues to apply or it does not. What follows from this? If it continues to apply, then in the case of *pravāhaṇeyībhāryaḥ*—meaning "one whose wife is a *pravāhaṇeyī*"—the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would apply by virtue of the rule "of that which has *vṛddhi* as its cause" (*vṛddhinimittasya*).

It does not apply. If, however, it has ceased, there is no fault. Let it be so that there is no fault. Or rather, let it be that it continues to follow. But was it not said that in the case of *pravāhaṇeyī-bhāryaḥ* (one whose wife is a *pravāhaṇeyī*), because of the rule "of that which is caused by *vṛddhi*" (*vṛddhinimittasya*), the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would not apply? This is not a fault. [Let it be] *mā*.
It is indeed so. It will be understood thus: "from the genus" (*jāteḥ*).
(Pāṇini 7.3.31) This rule (*yoga*) can be omitted. How so? [Because] it would not be according to reality (*ayāthātathyam*).
*Āyathātathyam*, *ayāthāpūrvyam*, *āyathāpūrvyam*. When there is *vṛddhi* of the first member, then the analysis (*vigraha*) will be made thus: "not as it truly is" (*na yathātathā*).

203.5–8: A prohibition [of the substitution of *na* for *ṇa*] must be stated regarding the suffix *ta* when it is a *taddhita* following the root *han*. [The forms] *vārtraghna* and *bhrauṇaghna* [would otherwise require the substitution]. Or rather, it has already been stated. What has been stated? It has been stated that "when a grammatical operation concerns the specific form of a verbal root, it is established by understanding that the operation applies to a suffix attached to that root" (Pāṇini 7.3.33).

203.10–204.2. What is the purpose of including the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes]? [So that] it does not apply here: *dadau*, *dadhau*. This is not a valid purpose. [The rule] *aciṇṇaloḥ* continues to apply. If *aciṇṇaloḥ* continues to apply, then [the substitution] would not apply here in *adāyi* and *adhāyi*. It will apply in the case of *ciṇ* by virtue of the explicit statement. [But] *aciṇṇaloḥ* continues to apply. Even so, [it would not apply] in *cauḍiḥ*.
In this case, the form *bālākiḥ* would result. Here, the elision (*lopa*) will be the sublater. This must be considered here:

should the elision be applied, or the *yuk* augment? Because it is subsequent, the *yuk* augment applies. If that is so, the rule "of the vowel at the beginning" (*acām ādeḥ*) continues to apply; thus, *yuk* is applied where the first vowel is *ā*. Even so, in the case of *jñaḥ sthālīpākaḥ* (the sacrificial cake belonging to the deity Jña), [the *yuk* would not apply].
In this case, [the rule] would apply. Therefore, the mention of *kṛt* must be made.
(P_7,3.34) This that is stated is too little: [it should rather be: "when a *kṛt* suffix follows. (KA_III,323.5-7; Ro_V, 204.4-5)

204.6–10. In the section on *ṇic*, the augment *nuk* is prescribed for the roots *dhūñ* and *prīñ*. In the section on *ṇic*, it should be stated that *nuk* is added to *dhūñ* and *prīñ*: *dhūnayati*, *prīṇayati*. For the root *pā*, the elision (*luk*) is prescribed: *pālayati*.

204–205. What is the purpose of including the term *sth*? This will be examined: in the rule for the substitution of *it*, does the mention of *k* refer to the entire complex (*saṅghātagrahaṇa*) or to the individual phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*)? When it refers to the complex, the inclusion of *sth* must be made so that [the rule] may also apply here in the case of *kārikā*.

Regarding *hārikā*: when there is the apprehension of a phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*), since the mere letter *ka* is not a suffix (*pratyaya*), [the rule] will apply by virtue of the explicit statement. Now, how is this [rule] understood: "of that which does not have a *sup* [ending]"? Does it mean "of a stem (*aṅga*) that does not possess a *sub*" (*asu-b-vataḥ*)?
Or rather, "if *āp* does not follow a *sup*"? What follows from this? If it is understood as "of a stem that does not possess a *sub*," then [the form] *bahucarmikā* [would be incorrect].

In this case, [the rule] does not apply. Now, if it is understood that there is no fault provided that *āp* does not follow a *sup* [suffix], let it be so, in such a way that there is no fault. For in cases such as *vāpyaśvaḥ* and *vāpyoḍhaḥ*, the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule *supi ca* would apply; and in cases such as *vāpyāmaśvaḥ* and *vāpyāmoḍhaḥ*, the suffix *yuṭ* prescribed by the same rule *supi ca* would apply. It is stated [in the rule]: "The lengthening occurs when a *sup* [suffix follows]" and also "The suffix *yuṭ* occurs when a *sup* [suffix follows]. In that situation, how is it determined that the lengthening occurs because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), and not rather the *yuṭ* because it is external (*bahiraṅga*)? If that is the case, a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: "And when a *sup* [suffix follows]," meaning that a long vowel occurs after what ends in a *sup* suffix. Then: "Also when *ā* [follows, even] in non-*ap* [cases]," meaning that a long vowel occurs for an *ā*-ending [word] when followed by a *yar* [consonant] in non-*ap* cases and also when a *sup* [suffix follows]. What is the purpose of this? So that there may be a prohibition specifically of the lengthening prescribed by *supi ca*, according to the principle that "a rule or a prohibition applies to what has immediately preceded. However, the preceding rule is drawn over by the word *ca* itself. Well then, that division of the rule must be made. No, it need not be made. The teacher’s practice indicates that the lengthening does not occur by this rule, since he prescribes a prohibition against the lengthening by *supi ca*. But would it not be for the sake of prohibiting the subsequent *yuṭ*? No, because of the restriction to similar types. Because of the restriction to similar types. How is it an indicator? If there were lengthening here, the prohibition would be meaningless. But was it not said that it would be for the sake of prohibiting the subsequent *yuṭ*? This is not a fault. Because of the restriction to similar types. How is it an indicator? If there were lengthening in this case, the prohibition would be meaningless. But was it not said that it would be for the sake of prohibiting the subsequent *yuṭ*? This is not a fault. [For] he will state: "When *guṇa* is applied [by P. 6.1.87], *yuṭ* [is applied]. If that is so, then in *vāpyaśvaḥ*, the accent of the initial syllable (*ādyudātta*) will be applied. That accent will be a designated accent (*nipātanasvara*). If that is so, then in *vāpyaśvaḥ*, the designated accent would also apply. This is not a fault. He will state: "In this grammar, there is no connection with a circumflex (*svarita*) accent in the rules for accents. Therefore, it will not occur. 44. 1. *vāpyaśvaḥ*: *vāpī-aśvaḥ*. 2. *vāpyoḍhaḥ*: *vāpī-oḍhaḥ*. 3. *vāpyāmaśvaḥ*: *vāpyām-aśvaḥ*. 4. *vāpyāmoḍhaḥ*: *vāpyām-oḍhaḥ*. 5. *supi ca*: P. 7.3.102. 6. *yuṭ*: P. 7.3.33. 7. *ādyudātta-nipātana*: P. 6.1.197. 8. *svaravidhau ... nāsti*: Vārttika on P. 1.2.32. 9. *ād guṇe*: P. 6.1.87. 10. *yuṭ*: P. 7.3.33. 11. *vāpyaśvaḥ*: *vāpī-aśvaḥ*. 12. *vāpyoḍhaḥ*: *vāpī-oḍhaḥ*. 13. *vāpyāmaśvaḥ*: *vāpyām-aśvaḥ*. 14. *vāpyāmoḍhaḥ*: *vāpyām-oḍhaḥ*. 15. *supi ca*: P. 7.3.102. 16. *yuṭ*: P. 7.3.33. 17. *ādyudātta-nipātana*: P. 6.1.197. 18. *svaravid

206–208 This is now considered: regarding the substitution of *it*, does the mention of *k* refer to the entire cluster (*saṅghāta*) or to the individual phoneme (*varṇa*)? And what is the distinction here?

If the mention of *k* in the rule for *it* refers to the cluster, there would be no application [of the rule] in the case of words such as *etikāsu*. If the mention of *k* in the rule for *it* refers to the cluster...

If it is argued that there is no application [of the rule] when *e* follows *ti*, as in *etikāś caranti* ("those who go thus"), [the answer is: it will occur because of the explicit statement [in the rule]. There is a purpose for the statement; what is it? [The forms] *kārikā* and *hārikā*.

Let it be then that there is the mention of the phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*). But if there is the mention of the phoneme, there is no application because of intervention (*vyavahitatva*). If there is the mention of the phoneme, it does not apply because of intervention. In *kārikā* and *hārikā*, it does not apply because of the intervention by the vowel *a*. [Objection: Once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been made, there is no intervention. [Response: It is a single-substitute.

211.2–7. For what purpose is the feminine designation (*strīliṅga-nirdeśa*) employed? Why not simply say "not when preceded by *ya* or *ka*" (*na yakapūrvasya*)? [The answer is: so that the prohibition may apply to that short *a* which takes the place of the long *ā* that has a feminine referent (*strīviṣaya*). Let it not be the case here: from *śubham yāti* [we derive] *śubhaṃyāḥ*, and then *śubhaṃyikā*.
*Bhadrayikā*. A prohibition regarding the end of a verbal root must be stated when *yak* precedes. What is the purpose? *Sunayikā*, *aśokikā*, *apākikā*.

211.9–212.3: These two [compounds], preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, are not examples [of this rule], because of the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 7.3.48]: "not when [the first member] is not a case-ending (*asupaḥ*). Now, for what purpose is the mention of *bhastrā*? Is it not already established by the rule "not after that which has no corresponding masculine form" (*abhāṣitapuṃskāt*)? The mention of *bhastrā* is for the sake of the secondary member (*upasarjana*). This introduction is for the sake of the secondary member: *abhastrikā*.
Regarding *abhastrakā*: the mention of "preceded by the negative particle" (*nañpūrva*) is redundant because this rule applies to the final member of the compound alone.

Furthermore, the mention of "preceded by the negative particle" is purposeless. Why? Because the rule applies to the final member alone. It must be stated that the substitution of *it* (the short *i*) occurs for the final member alone, as in *nirbhastrakā*.
nirbhastrikā, bahubhastrakā, bahubhastrikā.

(P_7,3.50) KA_III,328.2-329.5 Ro_V, 212.7-215.1 Is this mention of the phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*) regarding the substitution of *ṭh*, or is it a mention of the whole word-form (*saṅghātagrahaṇa*)? And what is the distinction here? If it is a mention of the phoneme regarding the substitution of *ṭh*, there must be a prohibition for the end of a verbal root (*dhātvaṃta*). [The rule] regarding the substitution of *ṭh* is a mention of the phoneme.

If this is so, a prohibition must be stated regarding the end of a verbal root (*dhātu*). [Otherwise, one would derive forms such as] *paṭhitā* and *paṭhitum*. Alternatively, let there be the inclusion of the entire complex (*saṅghātagrahaṇa*). If there is the inclusion of the entire complex, however, a prohibition must be stated for those derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes and for words such as *māthitika*. If there is the inclusion of the entire complex, a prohibition must be stated for the *uṇādi* derivatives and for *māthitika* and the like. First, regarding the *uṇādi* derivatives: *kaṇṭhaḥ*,...

[The forms] *vaṇṭhaḥ* and *śaṇṭhaḥ*. And here, in the case of *māthitikaḥ*—meaning "one whose merchandise is churned" (*mathita-paṇya*)—once the short *a* is elided, the substitution of *ka* would apply by the rule *tāntāt*. However, when there is the mention of the letter *ṅ*, this becomes a rule concerning the phoneme *al* (the entire base). Therefore, there is a specific mention [of the letter *ṅ*].

Therefore, the specific letter *ṭha* must be mentioned [in the rule]. It need not be mentioned. Let it be that there is a mention of the phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*). But was it not said: "If there is a mention of the phoneme in the case of the substitute *ṭha*, there would be a prohibition regarding the end of a verbal root"? This is not a fault. The word "from the stem" (*aṅgāt*) is understood [to be supplied]. Or rather, there is no ablative case here in the word "from the stem. In that case, [the rule applies] to that which stands in a suffix.

Thus it continues. Where is the subject under discussion? It is: "The *it* [substitution] occurs for the *at* preceding a *ka* situated in an affix, before an *āp*, provided it is not part of a *sup*. Now, that [rule] was stated with the ablative case (*pañcamī*), whereas here the requirement is expressed with the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Therefore, by implication, there will be a change of case-ending. For example: "Devadatta’s houses are high; call him, Devadatta."

Thus it is understood: "Devadatta’s cows, horses, and gold; he is a wealthy son of a widow"—from this, Devadatta is understood. That which was previously indicated by the genitive case becomes, by implication, indicated by the nominative and the accusative. In the same way here as well, that which was previously indicated by the ablative will, by implication, become indicated by the genitive.

Even so, a prohibition must be stated regarding the *uṇādi* suffixes. It need not be stated; for the *uṇādi* suffixes are underived nominal stems (*prātipadika*). Even so, [the rule] would still apply in the case of *karmaṭhaḥ*. In that case, the genitive case in the word *aṅgasya* will be understood as a genitive of relation (*sambandha-ṣaṣṭhī*). [That is, it refers to] the *ṭhakāra* which belongs to the *aṅga*. And what is the *ṭhakāra* of the *aṅga*? It is the cause (*nimitta*). [The rule applies] when the *aṅga* [ends in *ṭhakāra*] because of which [suffix].
Thus it is so. And in what does this occur? In a suffix (*pratyaya*). Or rather, let there be the inclusion of the *saṅghāta* (the entire complex).

But was it not said that "if there is inclusion of the *saṅghāta*, there is a prohibition for the *uṇādi* [suffixes] and for words such as *māthitika*"? First of all, the prohibition of the *uṇādi* suffixes need not be stated; for it has already been resolved that the *uṇādi* suffixes are underived nominal stems (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*).

As for what is said here—that in the case of *mathita* and the word *māthitika* (meaning "one who deals in *mathita*"), once the elision of the vowel *a* has occurred, the substitution of *ka* [for the final syllable] would apply by the rule *tāntāt*—this is not a fault. Because of the status of the elided *a* as *sthānivat*, it will not occur.

[Objection: It is not established; for the status of being *sthānivat* applies to a rule concerning what precedes, and this is not a rule concerning what precedes. [Response: This too is a rule concerning what precedes.

215.3–5. Why does it not occur here: *āśiṣā tarati* → *āśiṣikaḥ*, *uṣā tarati* → *auṣikaḥ*? 7.3.54) KA_III,329.11–330.16 Ro_V, 215.7–217.13 What is this mention of *ñ*, *ṇi*, *n*, and *k*? Is it a qualifier of the root *han*?
Does this mean "the *hakāra* which follows [a letter] preceded by *ñ*, *ṇ*, *n*, or *nakāra* [belongs to] *han*"? Or rather, is it a qualifier of *hakāra*:

"if that *hakāra* which follows [a letter] preceded by *ñ*, *ṇ*, *n*, or *nakāra* belongs to *han*"? And what is the distinction here? If it means "belonging to *han* and following that [set of letters]," then there would be no application (*aprasiddhi*) in the case of *nakāra*. If it means "belonging to *han* and following that [set of letters]," then there would be no application in the case of *nakāra*, as in *ghnanti*.

"Let them kill," "they were killing. Let it then be a qualifier of the letter *ha*. If it means "of the letter *ha*," there would be no application [of the rule] in the case of *ñ* and *ṇit* suffixes. If it means "of the letter *ha*," there would be no application in the case of *ñ* and *ṇit* suffixes, as in *ghātayati* (he causes to kill) and *ghātakaḥ* (a killer). What is the reason? Because [the *ha*] is separated by the letter *na*.

It does not obtain [the designation of *it*]. It will obtain it by virtue of an explicit statement (*vacana*). Here too, it would obtain it by virtue of an explicit statement: "he desires to kill" (*hananīyati*), from *hananīya* with the suffix *ṇvul*, yielding *hananīyakaḥ*. Furthermore, due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is no application [of the rule] when the vowel is followed by the letter *n*. Due to the status of being a substitute, there is no application when the vowel is followed by the letter *n*: as in *ghnanti*.

"If it is argued that [the rule] will apply because of the explicit statement—that is, on the authority of the statement—then a prohibition must be stated regarding the elision (*alopa*). If it is argued that [the rule] will apply because of the authority of the statement, then a prohibition must be stated for cases where there is no elision (*alopa*), such as *hantā* and *hantum*. [Objection: It will not apply in the case of non-elision by virtue of the force of the inclusion of the letter *n*. [Reply: There is another purpose for the inclusion of the letter *n*.
What is it? It is to specify the audible [element]. It is so that the rule may apply only where the letter *n* is actually heard.

Let it not be the case here that [the forms] *hataḥ* and *hathaḥ* [would result]. But it is established by the statement "when there is elision of the penultimate vowel" (*upadhālope*). This is established. How? It must be stated: "and also when there is elision of the penultimate vowel" (*upadhālope ca*). Thus it is established. [Objection: Then the rule (*sūtra*) is split. [Response: Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. [Objection: But was it not said that if [the rule applies] to the root *han* followed by that [suffix], there would be no application when the suffix begins with *n*? [Response: By virtue of the explicit statement (*vacanāt*).

It will be so. Or, alternatively, let it be a qualifier of the letter *ha*. If it is argued that it has already been stated, "of the letter *ha*," and thus there would be no application [of the rule] in the case of *ñ-ṇ-it* suffixes, we reply: it will apply by virtue of the explicit statement. If it is further argued that by this same statement it would also apply here in the case of *hananīyakaḥ*, we say: this is not a fault. For that which is not separated [by anything else], even when there is an intervention, [the rule applies] by the authority of the explicit statement.
And there is no case where there is non-intervention by a constituent of a *dhātu*, while there is intervention by this *saṃghāta* [the whole word];

nor is there such a case. Furthermore, as for what was said—that because of the status of being a *sthānin*, the substitution does not apply when the vowel is followed by *n*—that will be established by the explicit statement [of the rule]. But has it not been stated that "if it is argued that it is due to the authority of the statement, then there is a prohibition regarding the elision (*alopa*)"? This is not so.

There is a fault. Here, immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is relied upon in the sense that the *n* replaces the *h*. In some cases, the immediate succession is produced by the combination [of sounds] (*sannipātakṛta*), while the non-immediate succession is produced by the grammatical rule (*śāstrakṛta*); in other cases, it is neither produced by the combination nor produced by the rule. When there is elision (*lopa*), the immediate succession is produced by the combination; when there is no elision, it is neither produced by the combination nor produced by the rule.
We shall adopt that [interpretation] from which the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) arises.

7.3.55) *Kutva* [occurs] after an abhyāsa, provided it is not followed by a case-ending (*asup*). It should be stated: "After an abhyāsa, *kutva* occurs, provided it is not followed by a case-ending. In this case...

Let it not be so. One might say: "He desires to kill" (*hananīyati*), and from *hananīya* with the desiderative suffix (*san*), one would get *jihananīyiṣati*. Therefore, that [rule] must be stated. It need not be stated. For it is said, "[the rule applies] after the reduplication of *han*," yet this is not a reduplication of *han*. This is indeed a reduplication of *han*. How? By the rule "for a monosyllabic root, the first part is doubled. If that is so, then regarding *han*:

It is said that [the substitution occurs] from that which is the reduplication of a member (*aṅga*); however, this is not a reduplication of a member of the root *han*. This is indeed a reduplication of a member of *han*. How so? By the rule "for a monosyllabic root, two [occurrences] of the first. If that is the case, then it is said that [the substitution occurs] from that reduplication which belongs to that wherein *han* is a member; and in this instance, *han* is not a member of that [base] wherein the reduplication occurs.
Furthermore, where there is repetition (*abhyāsa*), the *han* [root] does not become an *aṅga* [for that purpose].

The prohibition regarding *heḥ* in the case of *caṅ* is purposeless. Why? Because of the difference in the stem (*aṅga*). This stem becomes different when the causative suffix (*ṇi*) is present. Once the elision (*lopa*) has been performed, there is no difference in the stem. Due to the status of being "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), the difference in the stem persists. However, this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the understanding that elsewhere, when the suffix *ṇi* is added, the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *kutva*) applies. Thus, the Teacher indicates that elsewhere, when *ṇi* is added...

"It becomes *kutva*. What is the purpose of this teaching? [The answer is: In the form *prajighāyayiṣati*, *kutva* is established. Regarding the mention of *ji*: there is a prohibition for *jyā*. A prohibition for *jyā* must be stated regarding the mention of *ji*; [as in] *jijyatuḥ*.

[Objection: "They died" (*jijyuḥ*). In that case, this prohibition must be stated. [Reply: It need not be stated. According to the principle that "between what is taught by a general rule and what is taught by a specific rule, the specific rule prevails," this will not occur. [Objection: Then this *paribhāṣā* (metarule) must be formulated. [Reply:
It must certainly be formulated for the sake of forms such as *adhyāpya-gataḥ*.

Because *nyubja* has the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*), there is no prohibition [of the substitution of *ku* for *k*]. A prohibition that serves no purpose is called "no-prohibition" (*apratiṣedha*). Why does the substitution of *ku* not occur? Because it has the sense of an agent. This is not a word ending in the suffix *ghañ*; rather, this is an agentive suffix. [The derivation is: he bends down (*nyubjati*) = *nyubja*. Indeed, the suffix *ghañ* is observed here to have the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). It is called *nyubja* because people lie down bent over in it; thus, it is used in the sense of "affliction" (*upatāpa*).
For this [term *nyubja*] is also indeed a *kartṛ-sādhana* (an agentive derivation). It is "bent down" (*nyubja*) because he bends it down (*nyubjayati*).
The mention of *pravaci* is useless, because there is no technical grammatical term (*saṃjñā*) for the word *vaca*. [Therefore,] the mention of *pravaci* [is unnecessary].

It is purposeless. Why? Because there is no designation (*sañjñā*) of "word" (*śabda*) for the verbal root *vac*. A prohibition is stated regarding the non-designation of "word" for *vac*, and the root *vac* preceded by *pra* occurs in the sense of a non-designation of "word. In that case, this must be stated for the purpose of restricting the prefix:
so that the prohibition regarding the non-designation of "word" may apply only to *vac* preceded by *pra*. [Otherwise] here—*mā*...

It should be prescribed as "to be performed" (*kartavya*) and "to be abandoned" (*tyājya*).

(Pāṇini 7.3.69) Regarding *bhojya* in the sense of "that which is to be eaten": it should be stated that *bhojya* means "that which is to be consumed. This is so that it may also apply here: *bhojyaḥ sūpaḥ* ("the soup is edible").
"Gruel is to be eaten. But what is the reason it is not established? This root *bhakṣ* (to eat) occurs in reference to that which is hard and solid;
therefore, it does not apply to a liquid. Is it not the case that *bhakṣ* does not necessarily occur only in reference to that which is hard and solid?
What then? It also occurs elsewhere. For example: "one who subsists on water" (*abbhakṣaḥ*).

But surely, sir, the mention of *śyan* must also be made for the sake of subsequent rules, as in "śamām aṣṭānām dīrghaḥ" (the long vowel for the eight roots beginning with *śam* before a suffix marked with *ś*)?

The mention of *śyan* need not be made; here too, let it be simply "before a *śit* [suffix]. We shall qualify the *śit* by means of *śam* and the others: "that which is *śit* among *śam* and the rest. And what among *śam* and the rest is *śit*? That which is prescribed after *śam* and the others.

In the case of a prohibitive negation, there would be the undesirable consequence of prohibiting guṇa even for the *jus* suffix. In a prohibitive negation, the prohibition of guṇa would apply to the *jus* suffix, as in *ajāgaruḥ*. And in the case of the first person plural ending *ṇal*, in a prohibitive negation...

The prohibition of *guṇa* [substitution] would apply in cases such as *ajāgaruḥ*. Or rather, this is not a fault, because of the prohibition of what immediately precedes. Why? Because of the prohibition of what immediately precedes. That which is the prescription of *guṇa* immediately preceding [the present rule] is what is prohibited. In the case of *jusi*, the prescription of *guṇa* is by the preceding rule; for *guṇa* is prescribed before *jusi* by the rule "and in the case of *jusi*" (*jusi ca*).

And regarding the rule for *ṇal*: what [is the problem]? Or rather, it is simply because of the prohibition of the immediately preceding [rule]. For by the preceding rule, "guṇa is prescribed for *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes," guṇa would be applied even in *ṇal*. Alternatively, let there instead be a *paryudāsa* (exclusion). In the prescription for something other than this, there is the absence of guṇa in the case of *vā*. In the prescription for something other than this, there is the absence of guṇa in the case of *vā*. Or rather, it is not so, because of the force of the *paryudāsa*.

Or rather, it need not be stated. What is the reason? Because of the force of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the *guṇa* substitution will not occur here. There is another purpose for the exclusion. For in the prohibition regarding the word *vi* followed by a pure vowel, there is the inclusion of the word *vi* when followed by a nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) in the case of *kvip*. It may be so; [the forms] *jāgṛvāṃsaḥ* and *anu gman* [are examples]. If it is argued that this is not so because it has the status of a *sārvadhātuka* [suffix], [we reply: no. Why? Because it is established by virtue of its being a *sārvadhātuka*. How so?
The designation *sārvadhātuka* applies. The suffix *kvasu* is Vedic; furthermore, in the Veda, the *liṭ* [perfect] also becomes *sārvadhātuka*.

In that case, because it is also *sārvadhātuka*, it will be excluded by the rule "that which is *sārvadhātuka* is also *ṅit*" due to its *ṅit*-character.
