O ladles! O you of a hundred powers! O you of a hundred powers!
For the animal,
for the animal,
for the blue jay.
*kikidīvinā*.

(P_7.3.111) Regarding the prescription of *guṇa* for a stem ending in *gh*, there is a prohibition in the case of a *sarvadhātuka* suffix beginning with *ṅ*. When *guṇa* is prescribed for a stem ending in *gh* before a suffix beginning with *ṅ*, a prohibition must be stated regarding *sarvadhātuka* suffixes beginning with *ṅ*. [Example: *paṭvī*.

[The word] *mṛdvī* [is formed]; [the suffix] *kurutaḥ* is used. This is established by virtue of the governing rule for *sup*. The term *sup* is understood [from the previous context]. Where was it introduced? In [the rule]: "And before a *sup* ending that is a *jhal* [consonant], when there is a plural number, *et* [is substituted for the final vowel of the stem]. (Pāṇini 7.3.103).

238.5–13. Here, in the case of *atikhaṭvāya* and *atimālāya*, once the shortening (*hrasvatva*) has been applied, the suffix *yāṭ* would apply by virtue of the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*). A prohibition of this must be stated.

It need not be stated. In the rule prescribing *yāṭ*, there is no prohibition for *atikhaṭvāya* because it is a substitute for a short vowel (*hrasvādeśatvāt*). In the rule prescribing *yāṭ*, [the form] *atikhaṭvāya*...

Regarding the word *atimālāya*, there is no prohibition. A prohibition that is purposeless is considered "no prohibition. Why does the suffix *yāṭ* not occur? Because it is a substitute for a short vowel (*hrasvādeśa*). This is indeed a substitute for a short vowel; this has been stated [in the rule]: "In the application of the term *ṅy-āp*, what is not long [is included].
Now, even if the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) does not exist, once lengthening has been applied, this [suffix] was formerly *āp*. Thus, it is [included].

Why does [the substitution] *yāṭ* not occur? [Because of the rule: "Between that which is taught by a general characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and that which is taught by its specific form (*pratipadokta*), the latter alone [is taken]. But is it not possible for this paribhāṣā to apply even now, despite the existence of *sthānivadbhāva*? He says: "No.
For at that time, *sthānivadbhāva* would not occur anywhere at all.
The prescription of *ām* after [stems ending in] *i* and *u* takes precedence over the substitution of *au*. Thus, *ām* is to be prescribed after *i* and *u*: as in *śakaṭyām* and *paddhatyām*.
Regarding the form *dhenvām*: what is the reason it is not established? Because of the priority of the substitution of *au*. Due to its priority, the substitution of *au* would apply.

It is established by means of a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). A split of the rule will be made: first, “*ām* [is substituted] for *ṅi* after [stems ending in] *nadī*, *āp*, and *nī*” (Pāṇini 7.3.112).
Then, “after [stems ending in] *i* and *u*, *ām* is substituted for the following *ṅi*” (Pāṇini 7.3.113). Thus, *śakaṭyām*.
In the *paddhati*, it says "in *dhenu*. Then follows: "And *aut* [is substituted] for *ghī*. (Pāṇini 7.3.118–119).

239.9–241.1: *Auttve yogavibhāgaḥ*. A split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made regarding the substitution of *aut*. First: *aut*; after *id* and *ud*, *aut* occurs. Then: *at ca gheḥ*; and the vowel *a* also occurs after *ghi*. For what purpose is this split of the rule? It is for the sake of the substitution of *aut* after the words *sakhi* and *pati*. So that the substitution of *aut* may apply to *sakhi* and *pati*: *sakhyau*.

In the case of *patyau*, if there were a single rule (*ekayoga*), the substitution of *aut* would not apply because it is conditioned by the conjunction with the substitution of *at*. For if there were a single rule, the substitution of *aut* would not be obtained. Why? Because of its conjunction with the substitution of *at*. The substitution of *aut* is prescribed in conjunction with the substitution of *at*; therefore, it would only occur where the substitution of *aut* [would otherwise] apply. Alternatively, this is not a fault, because the substitution of *at* is stated as a secondary addition (*anvācaya*)—just as the elision of *s* occurs when the suffix *kyaṅ* follows. Or rather, there is no need for the substitution of *aut*.

[The rule is established] by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule). What is the reason? Because the vowel *a* is taught as a secondary (*anvācaya*) addition. The substitution of *au* is taught as the primary element, while the substitution of *at* is taught as a secondary addition, just as the elision of *s* occurs in the case of *kyaṅ*. For example: the suffix *kyaṅ* is taught as the primary element and applies to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in general;

however, where there is the letter *s*, there is elision [of the *s*]. Regarding the substitution of *at*, there is a prohibition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. The prohibition of *ṭāp* must be stated regarding the substitution of *at*. [Thus we have: *śakaṭau*.

In the case of *paddhati* and *dhenu*, once the substitution of *at* has been applied, the suffix *ṭāp* would be required. Or rather, it need not be stated. Why? Because that which is conditioned by a specific grammatical combination (*sannipāta*) does not serve as a cause for the destruction of that very combination. A rule conditioned by a specific combination [is not a cause for the destruction of that combination].

The suffix *ṭāp* will not occur because it is "without a marker" (*animitta*) for its prevention. Or else, because of the application of the marker *ḍ*. Alternatively, the vowel *au* will be made to have the marker *ḍ*;
thus, by the rule "and *au* with the marker *ḍ* is substituted for *ghi*" (Pāṇini 7.3.120).

241.3–6. Why is it stated "not in the feminine" (*astriyām*)? Could it not simply be stated "not in the masculine" (*nā puṃsi*)? What would the resulting forms be? *trapuṇā*, *jatunā*. [Objection: This is already established by the presence of the augment *num*. [Response: It cannot be so. For in the case of *amunā brāhmaṇakulena*, because the substitution of *mu* (*mubhāva*) is considered non-existent (*asiddhatvāt*), the *num* augment would not occur. However, when "not in the feminine" is stated, there is no such fault. How so?
He will say this: "Not when there is the substitution of *mu* and so forth" (*na muṭādeśe*).

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *ṇi*? Why not simply state "there is shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) when *caṅ* follows"? If it were stated merely as "there is shortening of the penultimate vowel when *caṅ* follows," [the desired forms would still be obtained].
In the case of *alīlavat* and *apīpavat*,

the shortening of the vowel *ū* alone would result [by the rule *ūkāl-śit-sarva-dhātu-kānām dīrgho 'ṇaḥ*]. This is not the purpose [of the present rule], for here the *vṛddhi* substitution is the sublater.

[It] will be so. If [the substitution of] *vṛddhi* is then performed, the shortening of the vowel *au* alone would result. This is not the case; because it is *antaraṅga*, the substitution of *āv* will take place here. For at this point, the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is no longer subject to shortening. Therefore, the mention of *ṇi* must be made. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *caṅ*? Not [for the sake of the rule] "of the penultimate vowel when there is *ṇi*."

Thus it is established. If the rule "there is shortening of the penultimate vowel before the causative suffix *ṇi*" were stated in this way, it would undesirably apply even in cases such as *kārayati* and *hārayati*. This objection is not valid; for the activity of the Teacher indicates [the intended meaning].

Since this [rule] prescribes the shortening of the *mit* vowels, it follows that shortening does not occur after the affix *ṇic*. In that case, it would not apply here either: *acīkarat*, *ajīharat*. [Objection: It will occur here by virtue of the explicit statement. [Reply: In that case, it would also apply here by virtue of the explicit statement: *kārayati*.

[The root] causes to take away (*hārayati*). Therefore, the mention of *caṅ* must be made. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *upadhā*? The mention of *upadhā* in the rule regarding *ṇau caṅi* is for the purpose of prohibiting [the shortening of] the final [vowel]. The mention of *upadhā* is made in the rule *ṇau caṅi* so that the shortening of the final [vowel] does not occur. If it were stated merely as *ṇau caṅi hrasvaḥ*, [the shortening would apply to the final vowel].
In the cases of *alīlavat* and *apīpavat*,
the shortening would apply only to the final vowel. This is not a valid objection, because [the desired result] follows here due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*).

The substitution of *ā* occurs. For now, there is no final vowel that undergoes shortening. Since there is no final vowel undergoing shortening, it will apply to a non-final vowel by virtue of this specific rule. Here too, it would apply by virtue of the rule: as in *acakāṅkṣat* and *avavāñchat*. Where there is no intervention [by another element], it applies even when there is intervention, on the authority of the explicit statement. And by what is there no intervention?

There is no intervention by a phoneme (*varṇa*). However, with this *saṃghāta* (cluster), there may or may not be intervention. In that case, the mention of "penultimate" (*upadhā*) must be made for the sake of what follows, so that the elision (*lopa*) and the substitution of *ī* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) may apply to the penultimate [phoneme] of the root *pibati*:
as in *apīpyat*.

*apīpyatām*, *apīpyan*. Now, how should it be in this case: *mā bhavān aṭiṭat* or rather *mā bhavān āṭiṭat*? It should be *mā bhavān āṭiṭat*. Why does the shortening not occur here? Because of the reduplication (*dvirvacana*).

On the grounds that it is intervened by another form when [the doubling] has been performed, this must be considered here: "Let there be doubling" or "let there be shortening"—what should be done in this case? Shortening, because it is subsequent. Doubling is obligatory; it applies both when shortening has been performed and when it has not. If this is so, then the activity of the Teacher indicates that shortening takes precedence over doubling.
The fact that he makes this [root] *oṇ* marked with *ṛt* (i.e., *oṇṛ*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). How does it function as an indicator?

The purpose of marking it with *ṛt* is so that the prohibition "not for those marked with *ṛt*" (*ṛditām na*) may apply. If reduplication were to occur first in this case, the marking with *ṛt* would be purposeless; for once reduplication has been performed, the shortening [of the penultimate vowel] would not take place because it is separated by the subsequent element.

245–247. Regarding the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatva*) after the suffix *ṇi*: an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the case of *ṇi* when it is followed by another *ṇic*. An addition must be made for the shortening of the penultimate vowel after *ṇi* when there is a subsequent *ṇic*: "He caused the lute-player to play the lute" (*avīvadad vīṇāṃ parivādakena*). But what is the reason that [the rule] is not established? Because of the intervention (*vyavahitatva*) by the [first] *ṇic*. Once the *ṇilopa* has been performed, there is no intervention. [Objection: There is still intervention due to the status of the substitute being as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*).

Thus, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prohibited here by the rule: "There is no *sthānivadbhāva* in the case of the elision [of a letter] following *caṅ*. Even so, the prohibition "not for those that have an elided *a*" (*aglopinām na*) would apply. [Objection: Once the *vṛddhi* has been performed, there is the elision;
therefore, the stem (*aṅga*) does not have an elided *a*. [Response: This must be considered here: "Let the *vṛddhi* be performed" or "let the elision be performed"—which of these two should be done?

The *vṛddhi* [substitution] takes precedence because it is subsequent. The elision (*lopa*) is permanent (*nitya*). Even when the *vṛddhi* has been applied, the elision applies; even when the *vṛddhi* has not been applied, it applies. The elision is impermanent (*anitya*).

When the *vṛddhi* is applied to one thing, it applies to another; since the rule applies to a different word-form when the *vṛddhi* has not been applied, such a rule is impermanent. Between these two impermanent operations, the *vṛddhi* takes precedence due to its subsequent status. Once the *vṛddhi* has been applied, the elision occurs.

Therefore, that [stem] does not become a base (*aṅga*) ending in *aglopa*. If this is so, then the activity of the Teacher indicates that elision (*lopa*) is stronger than *vṛddhi*, since he teaches the prohibition "not for those ending in *aglopa*" (*na aglopinām*). This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*).
There is another purpose for this statement. What is it? It is where [the suffix] is elided even after *vṛddhi* has already been applied.

It has already been explained. Now, as for why he employs the mention of *pratyāhāra* (the technical abbreviation): otherwise, he would have said "not for those [roots] that do not elide a vowel" (*alopinām na*).
Or rather, he would have stated: "the elision is stronger than *vṛddhi*. Alternatively, a prior exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) is commenced:
"the elision of *ṇi* and *ya*, and *iyaṅ*, *yaṇ*, *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and lengthening, is a prior exception [to the subsequent rules]. Therefore, an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made.

The prohibition regarding [roots] that lose a syllable (*aglopin*) is redundant because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). Furthermore, the prohibition concerning *aglopin* roots is purposeless. Why? Because of the status of being a substitute. Due to the status of being a substitute, shortening (*hrasvatva*) will not occur in this case.

In that case, this rule must be stated for the sake of those instances where the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply. Where does the status of being "as if the original" not apply? In the case of a substitute (*ādeśa*) for a consonant (*hal*) or a vowel (*ac*). For example: *atyararājat*. But what is the reason it is said that a substitute for a consonant or a vowel is not "as if the original"? It is because it is stated that "a substitute for a vowel is as if the original," and this [substitute in *atyararājat*] is not a substitute for a vowel alone.

What then? [The rule applies] to a vowel (*ac*) and to something else as well. But then, the prohibition "not for those that elide *ag*" would not apply. Why? Because it is stated "not for those that elide *ag*," yet here it is not only a vowel (*ac*) that is elided; rather, both a vowel and something else are elided. The prohibition will apply based on that vowel which is elided here. Just so, then...

Whatever vowel (*ac*) is elided here, the prohibition is based upon that; likewise, whatever vowel is elided here, the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) will be based upon that. If this is so, then since the matter is already established, the fact that the Teacher teaches the prohibition "not for those whose [vowel] is elided" (*aglopinām na*) indicates that from this point forward, the status of being "as if the original" does not occur. What is the purpose of this?

The purpose of this instruction is as follows: it has been stated previously that "when [an operation] is not established, [the substitute] is not like the original (na sthānivat)"; however, that need not be stated if this [present rule] is taught.
If this is taught, then from *ādīdhayati* we derive *ādīdhakaḥ*.

From the root *ā-vevī*, the form *āvevakaḥ* is derived. [If the rule] "there is elision of the *yī* and *ivarṇa* [of the roots] *dīdhī* and *vevī*" were applied, that elision would not occur here. Furthermore, in this case, in the word *pralunīhi*, this accent—namely, the rule "when a *tiṅ* ending is accented"—would not apply. This is not a fault. As for what was said regarding *ādīdhayateḥ* and *ādīdhakaḥ*:

Regarding the form *āvevakaḥ* derived from the root *ā-vev*, the elision [of the *y*] prescribed by the rule *yīvarṇayoḥ* would not apply; however, it will indeed occur here because of the explicit mention of the term *varṇa* (phoneme) in that rule *yīvarṇayoḥ*. Furthermore, as for what is said—that in the case of *pralunīhi*, the accent prescribed by the rule *tiṅi codāttavati* would not apply—[it does apply].

Thus, the substitution of *yaṇ* is external (*bahiraṅga*), while the vowel modification (*svara*) is internal (*antaraṅga*); "that which is external is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal" (P.

7.4.3). It should be stated: "and [the rule] regarding *kāṇi* and the others. But what are *kāṇi* and the others? They are *kāṇi*, *rāṇi*, *śrāṇi*, *bhāṇi*, *heṭhi*, and *lopi*. [Examples: *acakāṇat*,...
acīkaṇat, ararāṇat, arīraṇat.
aśaśrāṇat, aśīśraṇat,
ababhāṇat.
He did not revile, he did not harass,
he did not torment.
*alulopat*, *alūlupat*. Here: *avadigye*.

In the case of *avadigyāte* and *avadigyare*, once the substitution of *digi* has been applied, reduplication (dvirvacana) would be required; in that situation, it must be stated that [the substitution applies] "together with the reduplicated syllable" (*sābhyāsasya*).
But surely, once reduplication has taken place, the substitution of *digi* will apply to that which includes the reduplicated syllable? It is not established. For what reason?

Because the substitution for *digī* is subsequent, the rule concerning the substitute applies to the entire form including the reduplication. One might argue: "Let the substitution for *digī* be applied first, and then the reduplication," since the subsequent rule must take effect. To this, it must be stated that the substitute applies to the form "including the reduplication" (*sābhyāsasya*). If that is the case, then the substitution for *digī* will supersede the reduplication. However, due to the principle of "re-occurrence" (*punar-prasaṅga*), the reduplication would still apply.

If it is argued that there is a recurrence [of the application of rules], this is equivalent to the case of *am* and the other suffixes. If it is argued that there is a recurrence, this is just like the following: when *am* and the other suffixes have been applied, due to the recurrence [of the previous conditions], the suffixes *śi*, *ślu*, and *num* do not occur. In the same way, when the substitution of *diś* has been made, due to the recurrence [of the previous conditions], reduplication (*dvirvacana*) will not occur. Or else, in the case of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).

The objection "it would lead to a recurrence" refers to the fact that a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) occurs between two rules that both have scope. However, in this case, the substitution for the direction [of the prefix] (*digyādeśa*), which has no scope, will sublate the reduplication (*dvirvacana*). If, then, rules that have no scope are sublatives, [then consider the form] *babhūva*.

The substitution of *bhū* would subvert the reduplication (*dvirvacana*). But the substitution of *bhū* has its own scope. What is that scope? It is *bhavitā* and *bhavitum*. In that case, here [in the rule] "for *cakṣiṅ*, there is optionally *khyāñ* in the *liṭ*," the reduplication would subvert the substitution of *khyāñ*. And here too, in *babhūva*, if the reduplication occurs in place of the whole root, then the substitution of *bhū* would result in a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*). Or if...

Regarding the double application (dviḥprayoga) and reduplication: once the substitution of *bhū* for the subsequent [root] has been made, it follows that the preceding [form] should be heard. This is not a fault. The rules pertaining to *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes apply generally, while the specific suffixes have not yet been fixed. Therefore, when the substitution of *bhū* has been made in the general state of being an *ārdhadhātuka*, whichever suffix is applicable from whichever root shall occur from that very root.

Regarding the prescription of *guṇa* for roots beginning with a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*), the inclusion of the term "having a consonant cluster as a penultimate" (*saṃyogopadha*) is for the sake of the root *kṛ*. When prescribing *guṇa* for roots beginning with a consonant cluster, the inclusion of "having a consonant cluster as a penultimate" must be made. For what purpose? For the sake of the root *kṛ*, so that it may also apply here: *sañcaskaratuḥ*.

They have performed the action. If the inclusion of the term *saṃyogopadha* (having a conjunct consonant as a penultimate) is made, there is no purpose in including the term *saṃyogādi* (having a conjunct consonant at the beginning). Here too, in the cases of *sasvaratuḥ* and *sasvaruḥ*, it would be established by the rule itself for that which has a conjunct consonant as its penultimate. It might be established that *sasvaratuḥ* and *sasvaruḥ* are formed; however, this is not established: *sañcaskaratuḥ*.

They say *sañcaskaruḥ*. What is the reason? Because the augment *suṭ* is characterized as being external (*bahiraṅga*). *Suṭ* is external; the *guṇa* substitution is internal (*antaraṅga*). That which is external is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal. However, when the term "beginning of a conjunct" (*saṃyogādi*) is employed [in P. 7.2.43], the mention of "having a conjunct as a penultimate" (*saṃyogopadha*) is understood to serve no other purpose. By the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the *vṛddhi* substitution takes precedence over the *guṇa* substitution for roots ending in *ṛ* in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense. [This applies to] roots ending in *ṛ* in the *liṭ*.

Vṛddhi occurs before affixes marked with ñ or ṇ by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). The scope for *guṇa* substitution before the *liṭ* suffix is seen in *sasvaratuḥ* and *sasvaruḥ*. The scope for *vṛddhi* before affixes marked with ñ or ṇ is seen in *svārakaḥ* and *dhvārakaḥ*. In the present case, both rules would apply: *sasvāra*.
The *vṛddhi* [substitution] occurs by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Or rather, it is established through the principle of "repeated application" (*punaḥprasaṅga*).

Alternatively, because of repeated application, once the *guṇa* has been applied and the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* (*raparatva*) has occurred, the *vṛddhi* will take place by the rule "of the penultimate vowel, when preceded by *at*" (*ata upadhāyāḥ*).
This is not a valid resolution. For that which is called "repeated application" occurs only in cases where [the operation] is performed by that very same [rule].

And by that very [rule], it would apply even when [the suffix] has not been applied. Here, indeed, when the *guṇa* has been applied and *raparatva* (the substitution of *ra*) has occurred, the *vṛddhi* prescribed by "ata upadhāyāḥ" would apply;

and when [the suffix] has not been applied, the *vṛddhi* prescribed by "aco ñṇiti" would apply. Therefore, it is rightly said: "In the case of a suffix marked with *li*, the *vṛddhi* [prescribed] for a suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ* prevails over *guṇa* by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*)."

(P_7.4.12) Why is it stated as "or short" (*hrasvaḥ vā*) instead of being stated as "or *guṇa*"? In that case, this further purpose [is achieved]: the mention of *guṇa* need not be made. That which was previously introduced (*prakṛta*) is understood by way of anuvṛtti. Where was it introduced? It was introduced in the rule for *ṛtaḥ*.

And [the rule] "guṇa" applies to *saṃyoga* and so forth. The substitution of short *ṛ* for *ṛt* is for the purpose of prohibiting the substitution of *it*. The substitution of short *ṛ* for *ṛt* is stated for the purpose of prohibiting *it*; that is, so that *it* does not occur. If it were stated simply as "guṇa," then when *guṇa* is excluded, the occurrence of *it* would follow. If it were stated as "short vowel," then when the short vowel is excluded, the *guṇa* substitution that was applicable by default will take place.

Regarding the rule *ke 'ṇo hrasvaḥ*: why is the mention of *taddhita* included? The mention of *taddhita* must be made in the rule *ke 'ṇo hrasvaḥ*. What is the purpose? To exclude *kṛt*-suffixes; that [shortening] should not apply when a *kṛt*-suffix follows. For example: *rākā*.

[The word] *dhāka* [is formed]. In that case, then, it must be stated. It need not be stated. For *uṇādi* [suffixes] produce unanalyzed nominal stems (*prātipadika*). Why does [the rule] not apply here in the case of *prohyate*?

It is carried forward (*upohyate*). Because, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, there is an absence of distinct separation (*vyapavarga*). Even so, [the forms] *ā*, *ūhyate*, and *ohyate* [are established].
"It is confounded. The word *aṇaḥ* ("from a root ending in a vowel") is understood [from the previous rule].

(Pāṇini 7.4.24) Regarding the root *eti*, [the substitution of *ī* for *e*] occurs before the suffix *liṅ* when preceded by an *upasarga*. It should be stated: "Regarding the root *eti*, [the substitution of *ī* for *e* occurs before the suffix *liṅ*] when preceded by an *upasarga*. This is so that it does not occur here: *īyāt*.

"In that case, it must be stated. "It need not be stated. [The word] "from a preposition" (*upasargāt*) is understood [from the previous rule]. "In that case, the Teacher explains that the term 'from a preposition' is carried over (*anuvartate*). This need not be explained, for governing rules (*adhikāra*) do carry over; this is precisely the logical principle that governing rules should indeed carry over.

What is the purpose of the long pronunciation? Why not simply say *riṅ ṛtaḥ*? What would the resulting forms be? *mātrīyati*, *pitrīyati*. [One might argue that] the lengthening will occur by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*. If this is so, then since [the desired form] is already established...

The fact that [the Sūtrakāra] employs a long vowel pronunciation indicates that the Teacher intends this *paribhāṣā*: "When an operation has occurred within a stem (*aṅga*), there is no further application of a rule to what has already been established.
