Now, regarding the term *dvandvam*: what is here derived as an irregular form (*nipātyate*)? In the word *dvandvam*, there is the substitution of *am* for the first member (*pūrvapada*), the substitution of *a* for the second member (*uttarapada*), and neuter gender. That is to say, the substitution of *am* for the first member is irregularly prescribed, as is the substitution of *a* for the second member along with neuter gender. Or rather, it has already been stated. What has been stated? "Gender is not to be taught, because gender depends upon worldly usage."
In that context, the neuter gender is not to be applied [by rule].

8.1.16–17) From where does the governing heading for *pada* begin? The governing heading for *pada* extends prior to the governing heading for *apadānta*. [The rule] "the retroflex [substitute] occurs for what is not at the end of a *pada*" (*apadāntasya mūrdhanyaḥ*)...

Thus, up to this point, the governing rule (*adhikāra*) is "before a word" (*prāk padāt*). Now, from where does the governing rule "after a word" (*padāt*) extend? The governing rule "after a word" extends up to "before *sup* [affixes] when expressing contempt" (*prāk supi kutsanāt*). That is to say, the governing rule "after a word" extends up to "and when *sup* expresses contempt, provided it does not begin with *go-tra*" (*kutsane ca supy agotrādau*). However, the accent of the single-substitute *yaṇ* (*yaṇ-ekādeśasvara*) occurs after the governing rule for words. That is, the accent of the single-substitute *yaṇ* occurs after the governing rule for words.

It must be formulated. For in this statement, there would be no application for what is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*). Indeed, if it were formulated here, there would be no application for what is not at the end of a word;

[the rule] *udāttasvaritayor yaṇaḥ svarito 'nudāttasya* would apply only in cases such as *kumāryau* and *kiśoryau*, but it would not apply here in cases such as *kumāryaḥ* and *kiśoryaḥ*. Furthermore, [the rule] *ekādeśe udāttenodāttaḥ* would apply only in cases such as *vṛkṣau* and *plakṣau*.

In this case, there would not be [the designation] "trees" for *plakṣa*s; or rather, it is because the term "pada" (word) functions as a qualifier. Or else, the accentuation of the single-substitute *yaṇ* should not be applied after the section governing *pada*. What is the reason? Because the term "pada" functions as a qualifier.
The expression "of a word" (*padasya*) is not a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). What then? It is a genitive of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Should this be stated? No, indeed not.

How can it be understood [that this is so] when it is not explicitly stated? The genitive case here is one of locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). Or rather, because of the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) in the rule for the elision of *n*, [it follows that it is not a genitive of locus].

Alternatively, the fact that the Teacher includes the word "end" in the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* indicates that this is a genitive of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*), not a genitive of locus.

(P_8.1.18.1) KA_III,372.8–373.9 Ro_V, 322–324: What is the purpose of the mention of "all" (*sarva*)? The mention of "all" is for the sake of making the first syllable of a word that does not begin [with a prefix] unaccented. The inclusion of the term "all" is made so that even for a word that does not begin [with a prefix], the first syllable may become unaccented. Otherwise, the rule *tiṅatiṅaḥ* would apply only here [in the example]: *devadattaḥ*.

In this case, [the rule] would not apply to "pacati" (he cooks) or "devadattaḥ karoti" (Devadatta does). If it is argued that the mention of "all" (*sarva*) is for the sake of making the initial syllable unaccented (*anudātta*), that is not correct; why? Because there is a prohibition regarding the *luṭ* suffix.
If it is argued that the mention of "all" is for the sake of making the initial syllable unaccented, that is not so. What is the reason? Because there is a prohibition regarding the *luṭ* suffix.

Success! That the Teacher teaches a prohibition regarding the *luṭ* [future] tense by stating "not in *luṭ*" (*naluṭ*) indicates that even for a suffix that is not initial, the low-pitched accent (*anudātta*) occurs. How is this an indicator? For there is no form ending in *luṭ* that has the acute accent on its first syllable (*ādyudātta*). However, there would be the application of the rule concerning the final letter (*alo'ntyavidhi*); since rules apply to the final letter of the element (*alaḥ antyasya*), it would be a rule applying to the final [syllable].

It follows [the rule]. For where there is no initial operation (*ādividhi*), there must be an application according to the rule "of the final letter" (*alo'ntyavidhi*). What fault is there in that? [The fault is that] the rule *tiṅatiṅaḥ* would apply only here—*devadattayajñadattau kurutaḥ*—and would not apply here—*devadattaḥ karoti*.
[This is] established by the prohibition regarding the future tense (*lṛṭ*). That he teaches this prohibition regarding the future tense indicates [the following].

The Teacher [states] that even for what is not final, there is the state of being unaccented (anudātta). How is it known that this is an indicator (jñāpaka)? For indeed, there is no form ending in *lṛt* that has an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*). But is it not the case that this exists, namely *bhokṣye*? It has already been stated. What was stated? That "it is not so, because the governing term *pada* functions as a qualifier. If that is so, then this is the purpose: [the rule] *yuṣmadasmadoḥ ṣaṣṭhī-caturthī-dvitīyā-sthayor vāmnāvau*.
[The opponent says: "So that *vām*, *nau*, and so on, would apply to the form including the case-ending (*savibhaktika*). [The author replies: This too is not a purpose [for the rule].

For the term *pada* is understood [from the previous rule], and a word (*pada*) is that which ends in a case-ending; therefore, even without the mention of *sarva* ("all"), it will apply to the form including the case-ending.
[The opponent asks: It would be established in cases where the word ends in a case-ending; but what about where the word is [merely] within the case-ending?

In that case, it would not be established [that the substitution applies] in examples such as *grāmo vām dīyate* ("the village is given to you two"), *grāmo nau dīyate* ("the village is given to us two"), *janapado vām dīyate* ("the country is given to you two"), and *janapado nau dīyate* ("the country is given to us two"). [Objection: But surely the mention of the word *sthā* (in the rule *yuṣmadasmador sthāne*) is made so that [the substitution] will apply only to that which possesses a case-ending (*savibhaktika*).
[Reply: There is another purpose for the mention of *sthā*. What is it? So that it may be understood as a qualifier of the actually heard case-ending (*śrūyamāṇavibhaktiviśeṣaṇam*).

This is so that the [substitution] may apply where a case ending (*vibhakti*) is heard, but not where it is not; for example, in *yuṣmatputro dadāti* ("your son gives") and *asmatputro dadāti* ("our son gives").

324–325. The rules for *nighāta* (accentual suppression), as well as the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, apply within a single sentence (*samānavākya*). Having established the condition "in a single sentence," the rules for *nighāta*, *yuṣmad*, and *asmad* substitutes must be stated. What is the purpose? So that they do not apply in different sentences (*nānāvākya*). For example: *ayam daṇḍaḥ, hara anena* ("This is a stick; take with it"). *odanam paca, tava bhaviṣyati, mama bhaviṣyati* ("Cook the rice; it will be yours, it will be mine"). Furthermore, there is a prohibition [of these rules] in connection with verbs meaning "to see" (*paśyārtha*). And [this applies] with those meaning "to see."

The prohibition must be stated with reference to the phrase "within the same sentence" (*samānavākye*). Otherwise, the prohibition would apply only in cases where *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are the grammatical means (*sādhana*) of the verbs meaning "to see" (*paśyārtha*), as in: "The village went after having looked at you" (*grāmas tvāṃ saṃprekṣya saṃdṛśya samīkṣya gataḥ*) or "The village went after having looked at me" (*grāmo māṃ saṃprekṣya saṃdṛśya samīkṣya gataḥ*). In this case [the following], it would not apply: "The village [belongs] to you" (*grāmas tava*).

"Having looked at, having seen, having observed his own [property], he has gone; my village, having looked at, having seen, having observed its own [property], has gone. (Pāṇini 8.1.26) In the case of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, when there is no subsequent reference (*ananvādeśa*), either form may optionally be used. (Pāṇini 8.1.20)

Thus it should be stated: "In the village, the blanket is your property" (*grāme kambalas te svam*); "In the village, the blanket is your property" (*grāme kambalas tava svam*); "In the village, the blanket is my property" (*grāme kambalo me svam*); "In the village, the blanket is my property" (*grāme kambalo mama svam*). For what purpose is the restriction "when not used as a subsequent reference" (*ananvādeśe*)? [Consider: "Now, in the village, the blanket is your property" (*atho grāme kambalas te svam*); "Now, in the village, the blanket is my property" (*atho grāme kambalo me svam*). Another says:

All [words] such as *vām* and *nau*, etc., should be stated as optional (*vibhāṣā*) when not used in a correlative reference (*ananvādeśe*). For example: *kambalas te svam* ("The blanket is yours") or *kambalas tava svam*;

*kambalo me svam* ("The blanket is mine") or *kambalo mama svam*. Why is it said "when not used in a correlative reference"? Consider: *atho kambalas te svam* ("Now, the blanket is yours") or *atho kambalo me svam* ("Now, the blanket is mine"). In that case, this rule [regarding *vām* and *nau*] need not be stated for a pronoun preceded by another word (*sapūrvāyāḥ*).

Regarding the rule *prathamāyāḥ vibhāṣā* ("optionally [the genitive suffix] after the first case"), it should be stated: what is the purpose? It is for the sake of *anvādeśa* (subsequent reference). So that the option may apply in the case of *anvādeśa*: *atho grāme kambalas te svam* ("Now, in the village, the blanket is yours"), or *atho grāme kambalas tava svam*, or *atho grāme kambalo me svam*, or *atho grāme kambalo mama svam*.

Is this mention of "contempt" (*kutsana*) and "frequency" (*abhīkṣṇya*) in connection with *gotra* and so forth a qualification of the *pāṭha* (the list of words)? That is, do *gotra* and the others follow after a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) when they express the meanings of contempt and frequency, and are they [then] unaccented? Or rather, is it a qualification of the unaccented [vowel]?

The words *gotra* and so forth, which follow a finite verb (*tiṅ*), become unaccented when they signify contempt or frequency. The mention of "contempt" and "frequency" in the rule regarding *gotra* and so forth following a finite verb is for the purpose of qualifying the list [of items]. The mention of "contempt" and "frequency" is made in relation to the *gotra*-class and others as a qualification of the recited list; thus, the list itself is qualified. For if it were a qualification of the unaccented state, then in other instances where the *gotra*-class is mentioned, [the rule would not apply].

The mention of "contempt" (*kutsana*) and "frequency" (*abhīkṣṇya*) [is necessary]. For if [the term] *anudātta* were the qualifier, then in other instances where *gotra* and so forth are mentioned, the mention of contempt and frequency would have to be made. [Otherwise, one would have to state: "In the case of *cana*, *cit*, *iva*, *gotra*-class words, taddhita suffixes, and reduplication, when there is no understanding [of the meaning], [the particle is unaccented]; [and it is unaccented] in the cases of contempt and frequency"—thus it would have to be stated. Alternatively, one could simply state "the *anudātta* [particle]. Or else, one should state "those which are *anudātta*."

327–328. What is the purpose of the restriction *atiṅ*? [Examples: *pacati*, *karoti*. The mention of *atiṅ* is useless because of the governing rule concerning a single sentence (*samānavākya*). The mention of *atiṅ* is useless. Why? Because of the governing rule concerning a single sentence. The term "in a single sentence" (*samānavākye*) is understood [from the previous rule], and there cannot be two finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) in a single sentence.

What is the purpose of [specifying] "by means of particles" (*nipātaiḥ*)? [Examples: *yat kūjati śakaṭam* ("the cart creaks"), *yatī kūjati śakaṭī* ("the female cart creaks"), *yan rathaḥ kūjati* ("the chariot creaks"). It could have been stated without [mentioning] "by means of particles. Why does it not occur in the case of *yat kūjati śakaṭam*? Why [does it not occur] in *yatī*?

"The cart creaks" (*kūjati śakaṭī*); "the chariot creaks" (*yan rathaḥ kūjati*). [This is because of the rule] "Between that which is taught by a technical definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and that which is taught by its own specific form (*pratipadokta*), the latter alone [is affected].

This *paribhāṣā* cannot be understood to apply here, for in this case there would be a fault. [The rule] "by means of *yāvat* and *yathā*" would not apply here in cases such as: *yāvad asti atra eṣaḥ saraḥ* ("as far as this lake exists here") and *janebhyaḥ kṛṇavat* ("may he act for the people").

The particle *caṇ*, when distinguished by the marker *ṇit*, is to be understood in the sense of *ced* ("if"). For example: *ayam ca vai mariṣyati* ("If indeed he shall die") or *ayam cet mariṣyati* ("If he shall die"). [In such cases,] there would be no offering to the ancestors (*pitṛbhyas pūrvabhyas*) and no performance of expiation (*aprāyaścittikṛtau*).

What is the example for "multiple"? [The opponent suggests: "When he is intoxicated, then he burns. This is not correct. For here, one word is connected with *hi* and the other is connected with *yat*; therefore, there is no suppression (*anighāta*) of either. This...
In that case, [the rule applies]. For one who speaks untruth from me, evil purifies him. Indeed, even in the case of a single [verse]: "Agni indeed first won; Indra won after him.

ātmanepadaṃ bhavatīti vaktavyam /

While the term "in worship" (*pūjāyām*) is already in effect, what is the purpose of mentioning "worship" (*pūjā*) again? That [mention] is connected with the prohibition of non-unnasalized (*anighāta*) accent. If that were to carry over here as well, then the prohibition of non-unnasalized accent would undesirably apply even in this case. However, the prohibition of the unnasalized accent is desired here. For instance, in that [previous rule], since the non-unnasalized accent would have applied by virtue of the words *yāvat* and *yathā*, there was a prohibition of the non-unnasalized accent.

It is said: Now, when non-prohibition (*anighāta*) has already been established, why is the prohibition of non-prohibition (*anighātapratiṣedha*) stated here? [The answer is: Even here, it is by means of rules such as *yadvṛttānnityam* (P.

8.1.66). For what purpose is this stated? Is it not already established by the rule *na gatyarthaloṭā lṛṭ* (P. 8.1.51)? This undertaking is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). It is so that [the prohibition] may apply only in cases of jest (*prahāsa*) with the imperative *ehi manye*. Where should it not apply? [It should not apply] elsewhere.
"Come, I think you will go by chariot.

(P_8.1.47) KA_III,376.1-10 Ro_V, 331 Is this mention of *apūrva* a qualifier for *jātu*, meaning "after the word *jātu* that is not preceded [by another]," [the subsequent *tiṅanta* is unaccented]? Or rather...

It is a qualifier of a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). Because of the word *jātu*, [the rule] "a verbal suffix that has not occurred previously" applies; thus he says it is a qualifier of *jātu*. How is this known? From the fact that he states: "and [a word] ending in *kim* followed by *cit*. How does this function as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? Because here too the phrase "not having occurred previously" (*apūrva*) continues to apply, and there is no possibility for something to be both a word ending in *kim* and followed by *cit*.

"And *tiṅanta* (a finite verb) which has no preceding word. Here too, this is indeed a qualifier of *tiṅanta*. How so? [It means] "a *tiṅanta* following *cit* after an interrogative pronoun (*kiṃvṛtta*) which has no preceding word. If that is so, then why does [the author] employ the term "immediately following" (*anantara*) in the rule *yad āho utāho anantaram*? There is indeed a purpose for stating this as well. What is it? This would be for the sake of establishing the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). [The rule] *śeṣe vibhāṣā* [applies].

332–333. An addition should be made [to the rule] regarding the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the future suffix *lṛṭ* when there is a change in the agent, because of the change in the grammatical factor (*kāraka*). When there is a change in the agent, an addition must be made for that which is another grammatical factor than the agent. Example: "Come, Devadatta, to the village; you shall eat rice. Why, then, is it not established? Because of the change in the grammatical factor. If not...

It is said that "all others" (*sarvānyat*) are the *kāraka* (grammatical participant), and here all others are indeed the *kāraka*. But what is the reason for resorting to the negation of "all others" (*sarvānyat-pratiṣedha*), rather than resorting to the prescription of "not-all-others" (*asarvānyad-vidhāna*)? For in this case, the agent (*kartṛ*) is "not-all-other," and thus [the desired result] is established by virtue of the commonality of being an agent (*kartṛ-sāmānyāt*). If it is argued that it is established by virtue of the commonality of being an agent, then there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of the *sandhi* rule) even when there is a difference [in the agent], provided there is a commonality of being "other" (*anyasāmānye*).

If it is argued that [the rule] is established because of the commonality of the agent (*kartṛsāmānyāt*), then when there is a difference in that [agent], namely a difference in the agent, the status of being a base (*prakṛtibhāva*) would result even when there is another commonality of the factors of action (*kārakasāmānya*). For example: "Devadatta, bring the rice; Yajñadatta will eat this. If that is the case, then it must be stated explicitly: "Unless the agent is entirely different" (*na cet kartā sarvānyaḥ*). If it is argued that [this is necessary] when there is a designation of something else (*anyābhidhāne*)...

Some [hold that there is] a prohibition. If it is argued that "if the agent is not someone other than all [others]," then some desire a prohibition when another [agent] is denoted. [For example, in the case of] "Let the rice be carried by Devadatta; it will be eaten by Yajñadatta," it would follow that the verb form *bhokṣyante* [is used], yet *bhokṣyante* is what is intended. But this is established because two *tiṅ*-suffixes denote a single substance. This is established. How? Because two *tiṅ*-suffixes denote a single substance.
It should be stated that this applies where a single substance is denoted by two finite verbs (*tiṅ*).

(P_8.1.55) Of what is this a prohibition? It is a prohibition of the *ekaśruti* accent for the word *ām* when it is separated by one intervening word. [This applies] to the *ām* separated by one intervening word.

This is a prohibition of *ekaśruti*. But how can a prohibition of *ekaśruti*—which is neither under discussion nor explicitly mentioned—be understood? It is said: "in what is not near" (*anantike*). And what is "not near"? That which is distant. It is taught that *ekaśruti* occurs when addressing someone from a distance. This [prohibition] serves a purpose. What, then, is it? It is the contingency of the occurrence of *nighāta* (elision of accent).

But then the *nighāta* (the low-pitched accent) would indeed apply. [In the example] "ām bhoḥ devadatta3," the rule for the anudātta (low-pitched) accent of the vocative (*āmantrita*) would apply. However, this is established because of the statement of a prohibition within the section on prohibitions. How so? By the force of the statement of a prohibition within the section on prohibitions, the *nighāta* will not occur. Or rather, there is no single uniform pitch (*ekaśrutya*) here at all.

[The rule] applies. What is the reason? It is stated [in the sūtra] as "not near" (*anantike*); furthermore, one thing is distant and another is not near. If this is so, then the protracted vowel (*pluta*) would also not apply, for the protracted vowel is also said to be "from afar. This very point is intended to be included; thus it must be: "Ām, bhoḥ Devadatta! (with a protracted *ām*).

(P_8,1.56) KA_III,378.8-19 Ro_V, 336-338 For what purpose is this stated? Since it is taught that when these very vowels *yadādi* are joined with all those causes of non-elision (*anighātakāraṇa*), there is no elision— just as in the case of the preceding [vowels] joined, so too in the case of the following ones— it follows that he recites the subsequent [sūtra].

The rule stating that in the Veda (*chandasi*) there is no unaccented status (*anighāta*) for a word followed by *yat*, *hi*, or *tu* is intended to prohibit other cases. That is to say, it is meant so that the prohibition [of accentuation] does not apply to words followed by anything else.

For example, in the phrase *jāye svaḥ rohāva ehi*, why is it that the word *ehi* does not [remain unaccented] when it is joined with this [word *rohāva*], namely *atha idānīm*? [It would have been so if the rule were not restricted.]

[The rule] *bhavati* applies; and since [the rule] "a *loṭ* [ending] joined with a *loṭ* ending having the sense of motion" would apply, [one might object]. But *ruh* does not have the sense of motion. How is this known? Because [Pāṇini], in the rule *gatyarthākarmakaśliṣaśīṅsthāsavasajanaruhajīryatibhyaśca*, makes a separate mention of *ruh*. If *ruh* did not have the sense of motion, [he would not have done so]; for example: "Men mount the elephant" (*ārohanti hastinaṃ manuṣyāḥ*), [and thus one says] "He causes [them] to mount" (*ārohayati*).

In the case of "the elephant [goes] to the ground" (*hastī sthalam*) or "the men [go] to the ground" (*manuṣyāḥ sthalam*), the designation of *karman* (object) does not apply under the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmākarmakāṇām aṇikartā sa ṇau*, because the root *ruh* is not included therein. Therefore, it cannot be said that *ruh* does not have the sense of "going. Why, then, is the designation of *karman* not applied to the word *ehi* ("come") when it is joined with *rohāvaḥ* ("we two ascend")? Because it belongs to the Vedic language (*chāndasatvāt*).

344–347. What is the purpose of [mentioning] *gatau*? [Examples: *prapacati*, *prakaroti*. If *gati* were inherently unaccented (*anudātta*), the mention of *gati* would be useless because of the restriction regarding *tiṅ* suffixes. If *gati* were unaccented, the mention of *gati* would be redundant. Why? Because of the restriction regarding *tiṅ* suffixes. The rule *tiṅica udāttavati* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). That is to say, it applies only when there is a *tiṅ* suffix that possesses an acute accent (*udātta*).

[The rule] "the *gati* [particle] becomes unaccented (*anudātta*), and not otherwise" implies that the mention of *gati* must be made for the sake of the Veda (*chandas*). This is so that the unaccented status may apply when a *gati* follows in the Veda, but it should not apply to the word *mandra*. As in: *á mandrair indra háribhir yāhi máyūraromabhiḥ* ("Come, O Indra, with your delightful bay horses whose hair is like peacock feathers"). If it is argued that it is for the sake of the Veda, we say no, because it is not a *gati*. It is for the sake of the Veda.

If this is argued, it is not so. What is the reason? Because there is no [proper] derivation (*agati*). The designations *gati* and *upasarga* apply with respect to that toward which a verbal root (*kriyā*) is connected; however, here the prefix *āṅ* has no connection with the word *mandra*, but rather with the word *yāhi*. If that is the case, then [the designation would] not apply here either: in *abhyuddharati* and *upasamādadhāti*. For here too, [the prefix] *abhi-* [is not connected to the action].

[Objection: Is there a connection with action (*kriyāyoga*) toward *udam*? [Response: No; rather, there is a connection with action toward *haratim*. [Objection: This is not a fault. There is indeed a connection with action toward *udam*. How so? It qualifies the action of "taking up" (*uddharati*). By means of *ud*, it qualifies [the action] which is already qualified by *abhi*. In that case, since the rule "those which are connected with an action" (*yatkriyāyuktāḥ*) applies, there is certainly a connection with action toward the entire complex (*saṅghāta*). If so, then here too—

The action (*kriyā*) characterized by the means (*sādhana*) is expressed by the prefix *ā*, as in "Come with pleasant [songs]! (*ā yāhi mandraiḥ*). Now, it might be argued that first the verbal root (*dhātu*) is joined with the prefix (*upasarga*), and only afterwards with the means. This is not correct. First the root is joined with the means, and only afterwards with the prefix.
What is the reason? For the means brings about the action, and the prefix qualifies that action.
And once the meaning has been fully produced, it is possible to state its specific modification by means of a prefix (*upasarga*). This is indeed true.

However, having internalized that connection between the verbal root (*dhātu*) and the prefix, the root is then joined with the grammatical factor (*sādhana*). And this must necessarily be understood in this way; for he who thinks that the root is first joined with the *sādhana* [is mistaken].

It is logical that [the verb] becomes transitive through a prefix; thus, while *āsyate guruṇā* ("the teacher sits") is intransitive, *upāsyate guruḥ* ("the teacher is attended upon") would be transitive—by what?
But for that which is qualified by motion (*gati*), it is motion itself that serves as the qualifier. Why then would it not be [considered transitive] by means of the instrument (*sādhana*)?
For that [instrument] is indeed external, whereas that [motion] is internal.

What is the purpose of mentioning *tiṅ*? The mention of *tiṅ* is for the sake of delimiting that which possesses an acute accent (*udāttavat*). The mention of *tiṅ* is made for the sake of delimiting that which possesses an acute accent, so that [the rule] may apply when there is an acute-accented *tiṅ*, and not in the case of the word *mandra*.

"O Indra, come with your joyous bay horses. [In this case], "gati" (an indeclinable prefix) and "upasarga" (preverb) are designations applied to those [words] which are connected with an action and are directed toward it. However, there is no connection with an action for the word *āṅ* in relation to the word *mandra*; rather, [its connection with an action] is in relation to the word *yāhi*.

If it is argued that "gati" is [defined as] that which is connected with a verb (*yadyogāt*), then there would be a lack of application in the case of the accentuation of suffixes (*pratyayodāttatva*). If it is argued that "gati" is that which is connected with a verb, then there would be a lack of application in the case of the accentuation of suffixes.

[Otherwise] there would be non-application [of the rule]. Since it applies to that which performs an action, therefore the mention of *tiṅ* (verbal suffixes) must be made. If the mention of *tiṅ* is made, it would not apply to forms ending in *ām*, such as *prapacatitarām* and *prajalpatitarām*. However, if the mention of *tiṅ* were not made, since a verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning, the suffix *tarap* would arise to express excellence; and from that form ending in *tarap*, the suffix *ām* would arise in its own sense (*svārthe*). In that case...

Since the designations *gati* and *upasarga* apply to that [word] which is connected with an action, the connection with the action occurs toward this entire complex [of word and suffix]. Therefore, there is no purpose in mentioning *tiṅ*. Why does it not occur? [In the example: "O Indra, come with your mild, peacock-haired bay horses. [This would be so] because of the rule "that which is connected with a verb is a *gati*. But has it not already been stated that [the designation *gati* applies] because of its connection with a verb?

If it is argued that there would be a lack of established application regarding the accentuation of the suffix (*pratyaya-udāttatva*), this is not a fault. It is not understood in this way: "those which possess an action (*yatkriyāyuktāḥ*)—that is, for whom there is an action (*yasya kriyā yatkriyā*)—toward such [an agent], the designations 'motion' (*gati*) and 'prefix' (*upasarga*) apply.
How, then? It is understood thus: "toward that which possesses an action (*yā kriyā yatkriyā*)—toward such [an object], the designations 'motion' and 'prefix' apply."

(P_8,1.72.1) KA_III,382.16–382.18 Ro_V, 349: What is the purpose of using the term *vat*? It is so that [the operation] may also apply to its own locus (*svāśraya*). In the example *ām bhoḥ devadatta*, the rule *āma ekāntaram āmantritam anantike* ("an address separated by exactly one word from *ām* is considered proximate") ensures that there is a separation of exactly one word. (P_8,1.72.2) KA_III,382.19–382.25 Ro_V, 349: [The following is the commentary on the rule: The word *vati* is used here in the sense of "like that" (*tadvat*) to indicate similarity. This is because it is taught that *vat* is used in the sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*). If this were not the case, then since the word *āmantrita* ("address") is a technical term (*saṃjñā*), the rule would not apply to its own locus; for a technical term does not undergo operations pertaining to itself. However, when *vat* is employed, the operation applies to its own locus as well. For example, in *ām bhoḥ devadatta*, the status of being separated by exactly one word (*ekāntaratā*) is achieved through the application of the rule *āma ekāntaram...*. Otherwise, since the word *āmantrita* is a technical term, the operation would not apply to its own locus, and thus the separation of exactly one word would not be established. Therefore, the use of *vat* is intended to ensure that the operation applies both to the original element and to its own locus. Furthermore, the word *āmantrita* is mentioned here to indicate that the operation applies specifically to the address, and not to the entire sentence. If it were not mentioned, the operation would apply to the whole sentence, just as in the case of the rule *tiṅṅ atiṅaḥ*. Thus, the mention of *āmantrita* serves to restrict the scope of the operation. Moreover, the word *anantike* ("not far") is mentioned to exclude cases where the address is distant, such as *ām bho devadatta*, where the distance is greater than one word. If *anantike* were not mentioned, the rule would apply even in cases of greater distance, such as *ām bho devadatta*. Therefore, *anantike* is included to exclude such instances. Furthermore, the word *ekāntaram* is mentioned to exclude cases where the address is not separated by exactly one word, such as *ām devadatta*, where there is no intervening word. If *ekāntaram* were not mentioned, the rule would apply even when there is no separation or when there is more than one intervening word. 349–350. Because it exists as something already present (*vidyamānavat*) with respect to what precedes it, there is no established immediate succession (*ānantarya*) with respect to what follows. Since it exists as something already present with respect to what precedes it, there would be no establishment of immediate succession with respect to what follows. For example, in the mantra *imam me Gaṅge Yamune Sarasvati*, this word *Gaṅge* is, with respect to the word *Yamune*, as if non-existent (*avidyamānavat*). In that case, [the rule] for the vocative (*āmantrita*)...

Otherwise, the quality of being unaccented (*anudātta*) would not apply to what follows a word. However, this is established by the rule stating "of that which is preceded by a word" (*padapūrvasya*). How is it established? By the statement "of that which is preceded by a word. It must be stated that the status of being as if non-existent (*avidyamānavadbhāva*) applies to a vocative (*āmantrita*) that is preceded by a word.

What, then, are the purposes of this rule? The purpose of [treating the preceding word] as if it were non-existent (*avidyamānavat*) is for the sake of the vocative accent, the enclitic forms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, and the suppression of the accent (*nighāta*) of finite verbs (*tiṅ*).
Regarding the rule "a vocative following a word becomes unaccented (*anudātta*)," it applies here in the example: *pacasi devadatta*.

In the case of *devadatta yajñadatta*, [the substitution] does not occur because the vocative (*āmantrita*) is treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*). However, in accordance with the rule *yuṣmadasmadoḥ ṣaṣṭhīcaturthīdvitīyāsthayor vāmnāvau* ("for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* in the sixth, fourth, and second cases, *vām* and *nau* are substituted respectively"), it occurs here: *grāmo vām svam* ("the village is yours" / "the country is ours"). But in the case of *devadattayajñadattau yuvayoḥ svam* ("Devadatta and Yajñadatta, the property is yours both"), it does not occur because the vocative is treated as non-existent. Furthermore, in accordance with the rule *tiṅatiṅaḥ* ("a finite verb is followed by a pause after another finite verb"), it occurs here.
In the cases *devadattaḥ pacati* and *devadatta pacasi*, [the substitution] does not occur because the vocative (*āmantrita*) is treated as non-existent.

Regarding honorific usage, there is a prohibition of the immediately preceding [rule]. The purpose of the prohibition of the immediately preceding rule is for honorific usage. Thus, it is established even in such cases as *yāvat pacati śobhanam* and *yāvat devadatta pacati*. Regarding *jātu*, it is something unprecedented. *Jātu*.

An unprecedented purpose [is served]. [The forms] *jātu pacati* and *devadatta jātu pacasi* are also established here. Regarding *āho* and *utāho* in the rule concerning what immediately precedes: *āho* and *utāho* in the rule concerning what immediately precedes serve a purpose. [The forms] *āho pacasi* and *āho devadatta pacasi* are also established here. [The forms] *utāho pacasi* and *utāho devadatta* [are also established].

Why does this not occur here: *aghnye devi sarasvati iḍe kavye vihavye etāni te aghnye namāni*? A division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: first, "a word of general meaning [is not followed by a vocative] when it is in grammatical apposition with a vocative"; then, "optionally so, when it is a word of specific meaning."

(P_8,1.74) KA_III,384.1-8 Ro_V, 353 Why does [the elision] not occur here: *brahmaṇo vaiyākaraṇaḥ*? I shall state that it is "the plural number. It cannot be said that it is "the general term" (*sāmānyavacana*). How so? Because it is stated that "it is optional when there is a specific term" (*vibhāṣitaṃ viśeṣavacane*), and therefore, in relation to whatever constitutes a specific term...
Thus, this [term] will be [the general term] for that [specific one]. And with respect to what does this become so? With respect to the general term (*sāmānyavacana*). Another says:
it is possible to say "with respect to the specific term" (*viśeṣavacane*). How so? It is stated that "the general term is optional" (*vibhāṣitam*);

therefore, with respect to which [term] this becomes a general term, with respect to that very [term] this becomes a specific term. And with respect to what does this become so? With respect to the specific term.
"A general statement is made optional when there is a specific statement" (Pāṇini 8.2.1).
Within this *Sapādasaptādhyāyī* that has been enumerated, this [present] chapter— minus one quarter— is not established (*asiddha*).

It should be understood as follows: if it is argued that this "pādonādhyāya" (the final chapter minus one quarter) within the seven chapters plus one-quarter is unestablished (*asiddha*), then those rules expressed here by means of the seventh case (*saptamī-nirdeśa*), the fifth case (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*), and the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdeśa*) would also be unestablished. What would be the fault in that? [The rules] such as *jhalo jhali*, *hrasvādaṅgāt*, and *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* [would fail].

Because these [rules of] instruction are not established, the following *paribhāṣās* would not apply: "When that [word] is specified, it refers to what precedes; when from that [word], it refers to what follows"; and "the genitive case denotes the relation of substitution. This is not a fault. Even though this is unestablished there, it is established here. How so? The *saṃjñās* and *paribhāṣās* are to be understood at the time of their application; they are to be seen wherever the operation occurs.

*Jhalo jhali*, *hrasvādaṅgāt*, *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*. This [rule] presents itself: "When that which is specified by the locative case is mentioned, [the operation applies] to what precedes; when that which is specified by the ablative case is mentioned, [it applies] to what follows; and when the genitive case is used, it denotes a substitute. If it is said that technical terms (*saṃjñā*) and interpretive rules (*paribhāṣā*) apply at the time the operation is to be performed (*kāryakāla*), then this interpretive rule—"In case of conflict, the latter prevails" (*vipratiṣedhe param*)—would also present itself here. In that case, which [rule] would take effect?

There is a fault. In the case of *visphoryam* and *avagoryam*, the lengthening [of the vowel] would occur by virtue of the [subsequent] rule, through the principle of "conflict" (*vipratiṣedha*). To this, he recites the following reply: "When what precedes is not established, there is no conflict, because of the absence of what follows. When what precedes is not established, there is no conflict. What is the reason? Because of the absence of what follows. For a conflict exists only when two rules, each having its own scope, are simultaneously present.

There is a conflict [of rules], for when a preceding rule is not established, a subsequent rule does not apply with respect to that preceding one. If this were so, then in *dogdhā* and *dogdhum*, since the substitution of *gha* is not established, the substitution of *ḍha* would result; and in *kāṣṭhataṭ* and *kūṭataṭ*, since the elision of the first member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādilopa*) is not established, the elision of a final conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would result. These two [rules] are exceptions by virtue of the authority of the specific statement [of the sūtra]; they leave no room [for the application of the general rules].

[The technical terms and rules] will come into existence by virtue of the authority of the statement; therefore, there is no fault in the principle that "technical terms and paribhāṣās [apply] at the time they are needed.
(P_8.2.1.2) KA_III,386.1-11 Ro_V, 356-357: *pūrvatrāsiddham* is a governing heading (*adhikāra*). This should be understood as the governing heading *pūrvatrāsiddham*.
What is the purpose? It is for the sake of understanding that each subsequent rule is *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to each preceding rule.

This is so that each subsequent *yoga* (rule) may be regarded as *asiddha* in relation to each preceding *yoga*. For if there were no governing heading (*anadhikāra*), the status of being *asiddha* would be understood only with respect to a collective whole. Indeed, if there were no governing heading, the *asiddha* status would be understood only of a composite aggregate in relation to that same aggregate.

What is the fault there? There would follow the undesirable consequence (ayatheṣṭaprasaṅga). There, an undesired result would ensue: in the case of *yodhūmān* and *guḍaliṇmān*, once the substitutions of *gh* and *ḍh* have been applied, the substitution of *v* [for *dh*] by the rule *jhayaḥ* would undesirably apply. Therefore, this is a governing heading (*adhikāra*). Consequently, this should be regarded as a governing heading.
What is the purpose of the statement regarding *asiddha*? Regarding the statement on *asiddha*, it has been said: what has been said?

First, it was stated there that the mention of *asiddha* with respect to the substitution of *ṣatva* and *tuk* is for the purpose of prohibiting the application of rules based on the original form (*ādeśalakṣaṇa-pratiṣedhārtha*) and for the purpose of ensuring the occurrence of rules based on the general form (*utsargalakṣaṇabhāvārtha*).

And thus, here too, the statement "asiddha" (regarding what precedes) is for the purpose of prohibiting the application of rules based on substitutes (*ādeśa-lakṣaṇa-pratiṣedha*) and for the purpose of ensuring the presence of rules based on the original form (*utsarga-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*). First, regarding the prohibition of rules based on substitutes: in the forms *rājabhiḥ*, *takṣabhiḥ*, *rājabhyām*, *takṣabhyām*, *rājasu*, and *takṣasu*, once the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) has been applied, the substitution of *ais* and other changes would apply by the rule *ataḥ*. [However,] because [the elision] is treated as *asiddha*, they do not.

[These rules] exist for the purpose of establishing the meaning of the general rule (*utsarga*). In forms such as *amuṣmai*, *amuṣmāt*, *amuṣya*, and *amuṣmin*, once the substitution of *mu* has been applied by the rule *ato'm*, the suffixes *smāy* and so forth would not otherwise apply because [the original vowel] is no longer present. However, they do apply because [the application of *mu*] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) [for the purposes of subsequent operations]. In *suparvāṇau* and *suparvāṇaḥ*, once the substitution of *ṇa* (by *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām...*) has been applied, the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*nopadhāyāḥ*) would not otherwise apply. However, it does apply because [the application of *ṇa*] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).

(P_8.2.2.1) It is stated that, with respect to a secondary rule (*subvidhi*), the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*). This would be the case here in *rājabhiḥ* and *takṣabhiḥ*:

once the elision of *n* has occurred, the substitution of *ais* by [Pāṇini 7.1.9] "from *ataḥ*" would not take place. However, in these cases—namely *rājabhyām*, *takṣabhyām*, and *rājasu*—[the rule applies].

When the *nalopa* (elision of *n*) has been performed in *takṣasu*, the rules for lengthening (*dīrghatva*) and the substitution of *ai* (*aittva*) would apply. This is not a fault, because the term *subvidhi* is a compound ending in all case-terminations (*sarvavibhaktyanta*):
it means either "an operation concerning a *sup*" (*supaḥ vidhiḥ subvidhiḥ*) or "an operation [occurring] when a *sup* follows" (*supi vidhiḥ subvidhiḥ*).

(P_8.2.2.2) KA_III,387.4–18 Ro_V, 359–361 Now, what is an example regarding the formulation of technical names (*saṃjñā*)? [Consider] *pañca sapta*. In the case of *pañca sapta*, once the elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*) has occurred, the technical name "six" (*ṣaṭ-saṃjñā*)—as prescribed by the rule *ṣṇāntāṣaṭ*—would not apply. However, it does apply because [the elision] is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*). Thus, the explicit mention of "technical name" (*saṃjñā-grahaṇa*) is redundant.

And because the elision (*lopa*) is caused by that [designation]. Furthermore, the mention of the technical term (*sañjñā*) is purposeless. Why? Because the elision is caused by that. For as long as the designation "six" (*ṣaṭ*) has not been applied, there is no elision (*luk*) of *jaś* and *śas*; as long as the elision has not occurred, there is no designation of "word" (*pada*); and as long as the designation of "word" has not been applied, the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) does not take effect. Thus, this is established through a sequential process. This...

In that case, the purpose [of the mention of the technical term *sañjñā*] is so that this accentuation—namely, "by five or seven" (*pañcabhiḥ saptabhiḥ*) and "the penultimate syllable before *jhali*, beginning with a consonant, [is acute]" (*ṣaṭtricaturbhyo halādir jhaly upottamam*)—may occur. And because of the restriction regarding accent. Because of the restriction regarding accent, the mention of the technical term *sañjñā* is useless. For the restriction regarding accent is made with respect to the rules governing accent. What is the example for the rule concerning the *tug* augment?

In *vṛtrahabhyām* and *vṛtrahabhiḥ*, once the elision of the *n* has taken place, the augment *tuk* would apply by the rule *hrasvasya pitikṛti tuk*. It does not apply, however, because [the elision] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). And it has been stated regarding the prescription of *tuk*: what was stated? That "a grammatical operation conditioned by a specific configuration (*sannipātalakṣaṇa*) is not a cause for the destruction of that very configuration. If so, then this is the purpose: I shall state "before a *kṛt*-suffix" (*kṛti*). [Otherwise,] here [in the case of *vṛtrahabhyām*], it would not occur.
*bhūt* [is the example for *brāhmaṇahatya*]; *brahmahacchatram* [is the example for *bhrūṇahatyā*]. This is not characterized by a combination [of rules].
Here, it is stated that with respect to the operation (*kārya*) that would otherwise apply, the substitution of *m* is not *asiddha*; it is not a non-existence.
And thus, for now, [the rule] does not apply. If that is so, then it should be stated: "Not when there is the substitution of *m-ū*.

What is this "substitution of *ṭā*"? It means the substitute (*ādeśa*) of *ṭā*. If, then, it is said "when there is the substitute of *ṭā*," there is non-establishment [of the rule] when *ṭā* itself is the substitute. What is the fault in that? [The fault is that] in the case of *amunā*, because the substitution of *m-ū* would be considered as if it were not established (*asiddha*).

Consequently, by the rule *ato dīrgho yañi supi ca*, the lengthening of the vowel would apply [to the final *a* of *taddhita*]. This is not a fault. The compound [ṭādeśa] consists of all case-endings:

it means "the substitute for *ṭā*" (*ṭāyā ādeśaḥ*) or "the substitute in the case of *ṭā*" (*ṭāyām ādeśaḥ*). Thus, it is established. In that case, the sūtra is altered. Let it remain exactly as it was originally formulated.

But has it not been stated that "the substitution of *m* does not remain *asiddha* with respect to that operation which it itself undergoes"? It is replied: first of all, the non-existence (*abhāva*) [of the rule] does not even apply here. This is not a fault. In this matter, the intention of the Teachers is discerned through gestures, movements, winks, or by means of a great composition of Sūtras. This very fact makes it known that [the rule] indeed occurs.

In this regard, by stating "not non-existence" (*na-abhāvaḥ*), this [sūtra] teaches the prohibition of [the opponent's claim that a reason is] unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the subsequent [term]. Alternatively, reasons (*hetu*) can have two referents (*dvigata*). For example: "The mango trees have been watered and the ancestors have been gratified.
Likewise, sentences are also seen to have two referents, such as: "A white [dog] runs" and "He has gone to the Alambusas. Now...

Or this should be understood as being like the words of the old maiden. For example: An old maiden was told by Indra, "Choose a boon. She chose a boon, saying, "May my sons eat rice with plenty of milk and ghee from a bronze vessel.
Yet, at that time, she did not even have a husband; how then could there be sons, how cows, or how grain? In that regard—

By this single statement, "husband, sons, cattle, grain"—all of these are included. Likewise here too, by stating the prohibition of "being unestablished" (*asiddhatva-pratiṣedha*), "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is also included.

362–364. *Yaṇ-svara*: The accentuation of the *yaṇ* substitute is stated for the sake of the circumflex (*svarita*) accent. It should be stated that the accentuation of the *yaṇ* substitute is established [by this rule]. What is the purpose? For the sake of the circumflex accent of the *yaṇ* substitute; so that the circumflex quality may apply to the *yaṇ* substitute of a circumflex vowel. As in: *khalapvi aṭati*, *khalapvi aśnāti*. Then, must that be stated? No, it need not be stated.

He says: "This [rule] concerns the *svarita* *yaṇ*. But since a *svarita* is not established there, its establishment will occur by virtue of its dependence [on another]. If it is argued that its establishment is by virtue of dependence, then there is a fault regarding the *svarita* following an *udātta*. If its establishment is by virtue of dependence, there is a fault in cases such as *dadhyāśa* and *madhvāśa*. If this is so, then there must be a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*).

It will be formulated as follows: "After a *yaṇ* [consonant] that follows an acute (*udātta*), the following grave (*anudātta*) becomes circumflex (*svarita*). Then: "And after a *yaṇ* that is circumflex, the following grave becomes circumflex. [The rule] "after a *yaṇ* that follows an acute" remains the same. Alternatively, the mention of "circumflex" (*svarita*) need not be made. By what, then, would the following grave become circumflex after a *yaṇ* that is circumflex?
It will be so. [The rule] "of a *yaṇ* that is *udātta*" applies. But surely it does not apply because it is separated by a *svarita-yaṇ*?
In a rule concerning accent (*svara*), a consonant (*vyañjana*) is as if non-existent; thus there is no separation. Alternatively, it is not understood in this way:

"the *yaṇ* of a *svarita* is *svaritayaṇ*, [and the rule applies] to *svaritayaṇ*. How then? It is understood as: "the *yaṇ* within a *svarita* is *svaritayaṇ*, [and the rule applies] to *svaritayaṇ*."

The mention of *svarita* could be omitted. How so? It is already established by the rule: "When an *anudātta* follows, [the first syllable] at the beginning of a word becomes *udātta*. But then, how will the *svarita* arise in cases such as *gāṅge anūpe*? [It arises] through proximity (*āntaryataḥ*).

The single substitute for an acute (*udātta*) and a grave (*anudātta*) vowel will be circumflex (*svarita*). If so, this is the purpose [of the rule]: that there should be no exclusion by that [circumflex]. Now, even if the mention of *svarita* is made, why does there not occur exclusion by that circumflex which is already established, as in the case of *kanyā anūpe*? Because it is characterized as extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). That which is extrinsic is considered unestablished (*asiddha*).

[Objection: It will not be so in the case of *antaraṅga* [operations]. [Reply: Just as, when the mention of *svarita* is made, there is no exclusion by that *svarita* which is already established, so too, even when it is not made, there will be no such exclusion. Therefore, there is no purpose in the mention of *svarita*. [The result] is established because [the *svarita*] is characterized as *bahiraṅga*.

The single-substitute vowel (*ekādeśasvara*) is *antaraṅga*. It must be stated that the single-substitute vowel is established as *antaraṅga*. What is the purpose? For the sake of the *ay*, *av*, and *āy* single-substitutes; for the accent of the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*); for the *ekān* [accent]; and for the case where all syllables are unaccented (*sarvānudātta*). [Examples of] *ay*: *vṛkṣe idam*.

In *plakṣe idam*, there is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) for an acute and a grave vowel. Regarding that single substitute, the rule *udāttenodāttaḥ* applies. It must be stated that this [single substitute] is established by virtue of its proximity (*āntaryataḥ*), so that the substitution of *ay* for [the final of *plakṣe*] is acute, as required. There is no substitution of *av*. [The result is] *āy*: *kumāryai idam*. Here too, there is a single-substitute for an acute and a grave vowel. Regarding that single substitute, the rule *udāttenodāttaḥ* applies.
Thus, this situation arises. Its established status must be stated so that, by virtue of proximity (*āntaryataḥ*), the substitution of *ā* for [the final vowel] may be acute (*udātta*).

This purpose is not necessary; once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, the acute accent will occur by the rule "of an acute *yaṇ* preceded by a light vowel. This must be considered here: should the acute accent be applied first, or the single-substitute? What should be done in this case?

Because it is subsequent, [the rule for] acute accentuation is [considered later]. The single-substitute (ekādeśa) is permanent (*nitya*); for it applies whether the acute accent has already been applied or has not yet been applied. However, the single-substitute is also non-permanent (*anitya*). This is because a grammatical operation that applies when one kind of accent has been applied and also applies when another kind of accent—distinct from the former—has not been applied becomes non-permanent. In that case, the single-substitute is indeed *antaraṅga*.

What constitutes internal character (*antaraṅgatā*)? Substitution (*ekādeśa*) depends upon two phonemes (*varṇa*), whereas the accentuation of the word (*padodāttatva*) [depends upon] the word as a whole. If this is so, then the following must be deliberated here: let either *āṭ* be applied or the accentuation; what should be done in this case? The augment *āṭ* [is applied] because it is subsequent (*paratvāt*). The accentuation is obligatory (*nitya*); for it applies whether *āṭ* has been applied or not. But *āṭ* is also obligatory.

Even when the acute accent (*udātta*) has been applied, [the rule] applies; even when it has not been applied, it applies. Thus, *āṭ* is non-permanent (*anitya*). Otherwise, the rule applies to one thing when the acute accent has been applied, and to another thing when it has not been applied; since the rule applies to that which differs in accent, it becomes non-permanent. The acute accent itself is also non-permanent, for it applies to one thing when *āṭ* has been applied, and to another thing when it has not been applied.

Furthermore, a rule that applies to a different word (*śabdāntara*) becomes non-eternal (*anitya*). Between two such non-eternal rules, the augment *āṭ* prevails because it is subsequent. Once *āṭ* has been applied, the internal (*antaraṅga*) single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) takes effect. [In *vṛkṣa-vid-am*,] there is a single substitute for the acute (*udātta*) and grave (*anudātta*) vowels. Regarding that single substitute, the rule "the substitute is acute when followed by an acute" (*udāttena udāttaḥ*) applies. It must be stated that this [substitution] is established (*siddha*) on account of its proximity (*āntarya*).

So that the substitution of an acute (udātta) vowel may occur for an acute vowel, there is the accent of a single substitute (ekādeśasvara). As in *gāṅge anūpe*: here, there is a single substitute for an acute and an unaccented (anudātta) vowel; for that single substitute, the rule "when there is a single substitute [of an acute and an unaccented vowel], it is acute" applies. Its established status (*siddhatva*) must be stated so that the rule "or [the substitute] is circumflex (svarita) when the following word begins with an unaccented vowel" may apply. This is the accent of the present participle suffix -śatṛ, as in *tudati* and *nudati*; [here too, there is a single substitute] for an acute and an unaccented vowel.

There is a single substitute (ekādeśa). Regarding that single substitute, the rule "udāttena udāttaḥ" (an acute vowel is substituted for both) applies. It must be stated that this [substitute] is established as valid so that this accentuation—namely, the rule "śatṛ-anuṃ nady-ajādir antodāttāt"—may take effect. This is not necessary as a purpose.
The activity of the Teacher indicates that the accent of the single substitute is established as being the same as the accent of the *śatṛ* suffix, since he [uses the term] "anuṃ."

Thus he teaches the prohibition. How does this serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? For, without the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of an acute and a grave accent, there is no present participle ending in *śatṛ* with the nasal augment (*sanumka*) that has an acute accent on the final syllable. But is it not the case that such forms exist, namely *yántī* and *vantī*? Even in these cases, once the *nighāta* (suppression) has taken effect, there is no present participle ending in *śatṛ* with the nasal augment that has an acute accent on the final syllable without the single-substitute of an acute and a grave accent. This [is the point].

In this matter, it must be deliberated: "Let the *nighāta* (accentual suppression) be applied, or let the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) be applied"—what should be done here? Because it is subsequent, the *nighāta* should apply. But the single-substitute is obligatory; for it applies whether the *nighāta* has been performed or not. The single-substitute, however, is non-obligatory; for it applies when the accentuation is one way, and it applies when the accentuation is otherwise.

Furthermore, a rule that applies to a svarabhinnah vowel is non-permanent (anitya). If so, then the single-substitute (ekādeśa) is an internal operation (antaraṅga). What constitutes its internality? The single substitute depends upon two phonemes, whereas the suppression of accent (nighāta) belongs to the word. But the suppression of accent is also internal. How so? It has been stated that the mention of "word" (pada) is for the purpose of defining its extent. Since both are internal operations, [the single substitute prevails] by virtue of being subsequent.
When a *nighāta* (elision) has been applied, even this [result] does not occur without the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of the acute and grave accents; thus, it becomes an oxytone (*antodātta*).

This concerns the accent of the *śatṛ* suffix (present participle), which is monosyllabic and grave. For example: *tudanti*, *likhanti*. There is a single-substitute for the acute and the grave. Regarding that single-substitute, the rule "the substitute is acute when the original was acute" applies. It must be stated that this [substitute] is established as a fact, and by virtue of that, it is excluded from being treated as a mere elision (*varjyamānatā*).

For example: *sarvānudātta* (all unaccented), as in *brāhmaṇās tudanti* and *brāhmaṇās likhanti*. [In these cases,] there is a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for an acute (*udātta*) and an unacute (*anudātta*). Regarding that single substitute, the rule *udāttanodāttaḥ* (P. 8.2.5) applies. It must be stated that this [substitute] is established (*siddha*).
What is the purpose? So that the suppression (*nighāta*) prescribed by *tiṅatiṅaḥ* (P. 8.1.28) may occur. Why is it said to be "internal" (*antaraṅga*)?

For that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is indeed unestablished (*asiddha*). As in *prapacati* and *somasut pacati*. If so, then it must be stated [that the rule applies]. It need not be stated. Everywhere, the prohibition of *num* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the accent of a single-substitute (*ekādeśasvara*) is internal (*antaraṅga*). [Consider] *harivo medinaṃ tvā*: here the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) [occurs before the application of the rule]. [The rule for] the substitution of *ū* for *r* (*roḥ uttvam*) [is applied after the elision]. The elision of the final consonant of a conjunct [is thus established].

It must be stated that the substitution of *u* for *r* (the *rutva*) is established [as valid]. What is the purpose? In the example *harivo medinaṃ tvā*, because the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered non-established (*asiddha*), the substitution of *u* by rule P.
6.1.114 (*haśi ca*) would not apply. Furthermore, regarding protracted vowels (*pluti*): it must be stated that protraction is also established in relation to the substitution of *u*.
In the example *susrota3 atra nu asi*, because protraction is considered non-established, the substitution of *u* by rule P. 6.1.109 (*ato 'ti* [sic; actually *ato guṇe*]) would apply.

It need not be stated that [the rule applies] "from an *apluta* vowel to an *apluta* vowel. This is unnecessary. It is done precisely in the *nyāsa*: "The elision of *sij* is established before a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) vowel. The elision of *sij* must be declared as established before a single-substitute vowel. [For example: *alāvīt*, *apāvīt*. Because the elision of *sij* would otherwise be considered non-established (*asiddha*), the long vowel resulting from the homogeneity of similar vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*) would not apply. However, if...

It might be argued that the elision of the *sic* suffix after roots beginning with *iḍ* should be stated. But this cannot be done. Thus, the state of being acute (udātta) is established. 8.2.7.1) Why is the mention of "end" (*anta*) made? Regarding the elision of *n* (*nalopa*), the mention of "end" is for the purpose of qualifying the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the "word" (*pada*). In the case of the elision of *n*:

The term *antagrahaṇa* ("mention of the end") is employed. For what reason? Because the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning "word" (*pada*) functions as a qualifier. The governing rule concerning "word" is a qualifier. How so? The expression "of a word" (*padasya*) is not a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). What then? It is a genitive of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*).

375–376. Prohibition of the elision of *n* in *ahar*. It must be stated that there is a prohibition of the elision of *n* in *ahar*, as in the forms *ahobhyām* and *ahobhiḥ*. [Objection: Then that prohibition must indeed be stated. [Response: It need not be stated. Here, the substitution of *ru* will be the sublater.
[Objection: The *ru* is not established; because it is not established, the elision of *n* would apply. [Response: The *ru* being without scope will sublate the elision of *n*.

The *ru* [substitute] has scope. What is its scope? The non-final *a*. The activity of the Teacher indicates that the *ru* does not occur for a non-final [sound], since he makes the mention of *ahan*. If it is argued that the mention of *ahan* is for the sake of the vocative case, then this would be for the sake of the vocative: "O day" (*he ahaḥ*). As for what then...
The rule for *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) teaches this very point; it too must be for the sake of the vocative case alone, as in "he dīrghāho 'tra" (O Dīrghāhas, here).

As for the fact that the teacher provides a supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the words *rūpa*, *rātri*, and *rathaṃtara*, that indicates that the substitution of *ru* does not occur for a non-final [visarga]. How is this an indicator? For there is no difference between the substitution of *ru* or *re* for a non-final [visarga] in the words *rūpa*, *rātri*, and *rathaṃtara*.

(P_8.2.8) KA_III,394.20–395.18 Ro_V, 377–378: It should be stated: "Not [after] the suffix *ṅi* or in the vocative (*sambuddhi*), when not followed by another word. This is so that it does not apply here: *carmaṇi tilā asya carmatilaḥ* ("there are sesame seeds on his skin; he is a 'skin-seed'"). [Examples: *rājan*, *vṛndāraka*, *rājavṛndāraka*.

Thus [it is said]. Or rather, it should be stated: "or for neuter nouns. [Examples: *he carma*, *he carman*; *he varma*, *he varman*. Then, should it be stated that this applies "when not followed by another word"? It need not be stated. For it is said, "not before the genitive case-ending (*ṅi*) or the vocative singular (*sambuddhi*"), and we do not see the genitive or vocative here. [If you argue they exist] by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of the suffix as if it were still there), [we reply: no, because of the rule "when a suffix is elided by *lumat*, that which is conditioned by it does not take effect."
Thus, there is a prohibition regarding the characteristic of a *pratyaya* (suffix). Nowhere is the *ṅi* case-ending elided by means of *lopa*; rather, it is always elided by the marker *lumat*.

Just as here [in the examples] *ārdre carman* and *lohite carman* occurs, so too here [in the compound] *carmaṇi tilā asya* would result in *carmatilaḥ*. Therefore, an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made. If that is so, then by means of the sense of the *ṅya* suffix...

In that case, it serves no purpose. However, because it is designated as a *bha*, the prohibition regarding the locative suffix (*ṅi*) is redundant. The prohibition regarding the locative suffix is useless.

Why? Because of its status as a *bha*. The designation *bha* will apply here. If, then, the designation *bha* applies here, then in the case of *rathantare sāman*, the elision of the final vowel (*al-lopa*)—by the rule "the *an* [of *anaḥ*] is elided"—would result. This is not a fault. It has already been stated.

Vedic meters are also seen to possess both types of designation; for example, in the phrase *saḥ suṣṭubhā saḥ ṛkvatā gaṇena*, because it is treated as a *pada*, the substitution of *k* occurs [for *g*], and because it is treated as a *bha*, the substitution of *j* does not occur. Likewise here, because it is treated as a *pada*, the elision of the vowel (*allopa*) will take place, and because it is treated as a *bha*, the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) will not occur. Therefore, there is no purpose in the inclusion of the term *ṅi*. Nor is there any purpose for it in the sense of the vocative case (*sambuddhi*).

How so? [The rule] "there is no compound for words ending in *sambuddhi*" [applies to cases such as] *rājavṛndāraka*. Should this be stated? No, it need not be stated. How is it understood even when not explicitly stated? In this case, there ought to be a sentence and a compound with the same meaning; however, that meaning which is conveyed by the sentence here is never conveyed by the compound. [In the example, there is] the address of the individual parts.

The addressing of a collective group is understood through a sentence (*vākya*), or else it is expressed by a compound (*samāsa*). This [rule] "of neuter nouns" (*napuṃsakānām*) must indeed be stated.

(395.19–24) The substitution occurs even for the non-final [sounds] of the *niṣṭhā* suffixes and the *matup* suffix. That is to say, the substitution for the *niṣṭhā* suffixes and the *matup* suffix occurs even when they are not final.
378–379. A prohibition regarding *nārmata* must be stated; that is, a prohibition regarding *nārmata* should be formulated, as in the case of *nṛmataḥ* versus *nārmataḥ*.

Or rather, it has already been stated. What has been stated? First, regarding the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) and the suffix *matup*, it was stated: "Or rather, not [is there a need for a rule], because [the suffix] serves as a qualifier under the governing heading of *pada*. Regarding *nārmata* as well, it has been stated: "Or rather, not [is there a need for a rule], because it is characterized by being external (*bahiraṅga*)."

(P_8.2.11–12) KA_III,396.6–13 Ro_V, 379: Is this a single rule (*ekayoga*) or are they two separate rules (*nānāyogau*)? And what follows from this? If it is a single rule, then *hīvatī* and *kapīvatī* would not obtain [the suffix]. If, on the other hand, they are two separate rules, then *ikṣumatī* and *drumatī* would also obtain it. As you desire.

Let it be so. Let there be a single rule for now. How [is the form] *ahīvatī* and *kapīvatī* derived? The activity of the Teacher indicates that the suffix *-vat-* occurs after words of this class, since he says: "after *antavatī* and *īvatī*. Or rather, let there be two separate rules. But was it not said that [the suffix would undesirably apply] here as well in *ikṣumatī* and *drumatī*? The word will be read among the *yava*-group [of the *gaṇapāṭha*].

It is stated [in the rule] "iraḥ in the Veda" (*chandasi iraḥ*). In that case, [the substitution] would also apply here in the examples "te viśvakarmāṇam" and "te saptarṣimantam. This is not a fault. It is not understood thus: "iraḥ in the Veda. How then?

Regarding the rule *chandasi īraḥ*: even so, [the suffix] would undesirably apply here as well in cases such as *tviṣīmān* and *patīmān*. This is not a fault, because the mention of the vowel *ī* is a qualifier of what is prescribed (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*). That is to say, it refers to that which is prescribed after a stem ending in the vowel *ī*. Even so, [the suffix] would undesirably apply here as well in *sūram te dyāvāpṛthivīmantam*; and yet it would not apply here in *trivatīr yājyānuvākyā bhavanti*.
In that case, the enumeration should be performed as follows: *tri-hary-adhipaty-agni-re*. There are three *ṛc*s for the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. *Tri*:
"O Lord of Bay Steeds (*harivaḥ*), you who possess the earth. *Hari*: [The word] *hari*. *Adhipati*: He offers oblations containing the word *adhipati*.
*Adhipati*: [The word] *adhipati*. *Agni*: The *caru* offering contains the word *agni*. *Iva*: [The word] *iva*. *Re*: "May wealth come to our people" (*ā revat etu no viśaḥ*). If...
If that is so, then an enumeration must be made: *sarasvatīvān*, *bhāratīvān*, *apūpavān*, *dadhivān*, *caruḥ*;
[otherwise] this would not be obtained here. If this is the case, then it should be stated that "in the Veda, the suffix *matup* is applied diversely after the word ending in *ira*" (Pāṇini 8.2.16).

380–382. If, however, this *nuṭ* were made a prior element (*pūrvānta*), then there would be the prohibition of the rules for *vināma* and *ru* when *nuṭ* follows *an*. When *nuṭ* follows *an*, the rule for *vināma* (the substitution of *n* for *m*) must be applied; for example, in *akṣaṇvān*, the prohibition "not [if] at the end of a word" (*padāntasya na*) would apply. Furthermore, the rule for *ru* would also have to be prohibited; for example, in *supathintaraḥ*, the rule "after *na*, before a *ch*-beginning [suffix], except after *praśān*" (*naśchavyapraśān*) would apply. Let it be so, then.

[The suffix] *matup* begins with the following vowel (*parādi*). If it begins with the following vowel, the substitution of *va* must be prohibited, and there must also be an *avagraha*. If it begins with the following vowel, the prohibition of the substitution of *va* must be stated; for example, in *akṣaṇvān*. By the rule "the substitution of *va* occurs after *m*, *a*, or a short vowel in the penultimate position, except after words beginning with *yava* etc.," the substitution of *va* would apply [to *akṣan-vat*]. Furthermore, the *avagraha* would occur in an undesired place, as in *akṣaṇvān*. Well then, let it be that [the suffix] ends with the preceding vowel (*pūrvānta*). But was it not already stated that [the augment] *nuK* is applied to *anaḥ*?

[Objection: "There is a prohibition of the rules for *ām* and *ru*. [Reply: It is established by virtue of being a *bha*. [Question: The designation *bha* must be stated. [Reply: However, regarding the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of *an*, the mention of *matup* must be stated for the Vedic language. [Objection: In that case, here [in the word] *supanthintaraḥ*...

[Objection: Since the rule "the *ṭi* of the final member is elided before a *taddhita* suffix" applies, elision would result [of the final vowel]. And there must be the mention of the term *gha*. Indeed, the mention of the term *gha* must be made. [Response: In that case, much must be stated here: the augment *nuk* must be stated; the designation *bha* must be stated;

and regarding the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) for *anaḥ*, the mention of *matup* must be stated in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). Furthermore, the mention of the term *gha* must be made.

Thus it is said: "It need not be formulated. As for what was stated—"the suffix *nuk* must be mentioned"—this is the resolution regarding *nuk*: it is established by virtue of its being a *bha*-stem. However, the designation *bha* must be explicitly stated; it is therefore provided in the very formulation (*nyāsa*) itself: "In the Vedic language, [the forms] *ayasmaya* and so forth [are treated as *bha*].

Furthermore, as for what was stated—"in the case of the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form retention) of *anaḥ*, the mention of *matup* and the mention of *gha* must be made in the Vedic language"—[it is not required].

Thus, it need not be done. For Vedic texts (*chandāṃsi*) are seen to possess both designations [of *pada* and *bha*]. For example: *sa suṣṭubhā sa ṛkvatā gaṇena*. Because of the designation *pada*, there is the substitution of *k* (by *kutva*), and because of the designation *bha*, the substitution of *j* (by *jaśtva*) does not occur. Likewise here as well, because of the designation *pada*, the elision of *a* (*allopa*) and the elision of *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*) will occur; and because of the designation *bha*, the prohibition of the rules for *vināma* and *ru* will apply. It is established. [The rule is unnecessary. The *sūtra*...

In that case, it would be split. Let it remain exactly as it was originally stated. But was it not said that there is a prohibition of *vatva* (the substitution of *vat*) at the beginning of a subsequent word, and that there is an *avagraha*? As for what was said regarding the prohibition of *vatva*, since substitutes apply to that which is specifically indicated (*nirdiśyamāna*), it will not occur in that way. But then it would not apply to that which is actually being indicated. What is the reason? Because of the *nuṭ* augment.

382. *rathin-* [is formed] by adding *īt*. It should be stated that *rathin-* takes *īt*: *rathītaraḥ*. *bhūridāvn-* [takes] *tuṭ*. It should be stated that *bhūridāvn-* takes *tuṭ*: *bhūridāvattaraḥ janaḥ* (the person who gives much). (P_8.2.18) The prohibition for *kṛpaṇa* and others should be stated: *kṛpaṇaḥ*, *kṛpāṇaḥ*, *kṛpīṭam*. [The substitution of *i* for the vowel of] *vāla*, *mūla*, *laghu*, *alama*, and *aṅguli* [should be stated].
It should be stated that *la* optionally becomes *ra*. Thus: *aśvavālaḥ* / *aśvavāraḥ*; *mūladevaḥ* / *mūradevaḥ*;

*varuṇasya laghusyadaḥ* / *varuṇasya raghusyadaḥ*; *alam bhaktāya* / *aram bhaktāya*; *subāhuḥ svaṅguliḥ* / *subāhuḥ svaṅguriḥ*. It should be stated that for words such as *kapilaka*, the substitution is optional in both names (*sañjñā*) and Vedic meters (*chandas*). Thus: *kapirakaḥ* / *kapilakaḥ*.
*tilvirīkaḥ*, *tilvilīkaḥ*; *romāṇi*, *lomāni*; *pāṃsuram*, *pāṃsulam*; *karma*, *kalma*; *śukraḥ*, *śuklaḥ*.
(Pāṇini 8.2.19) KA_III,399.1-19 Ro_V, 383-384 What is this inclusion of the word *ayati* intended as a qualifier for the letter *r*?
Does this mean that "the *repha* (the sound *r*) following the root *ayati* becomes *la*, provided it belongs to a prefix"? Or rather, is it a qualifier of the prefix:
"the *repha* which belongs to a prefix following *ayati* becomes *la*"? And what is the distinction here?

If [the rule] were "the *repha* [becomes *la*] after *ayati*," then an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the prefix *pari*. If [the rule] were "the *repha* [becomes *la*] after *ayati*," then an addition must be made for the prefix *pari*.

It must be stated. [The form] *palyayate* will be accounted for by the explicit statement [of the rule]. There is a purpose for the statement. What is it? [To account for forms such as] *plāyate* and *palāyate*. Let it then be a qualifier of the prefix (*upasarga*). If it is argued that the term "of the prefix" (*upasargasya*) applies, there would be no application [of the rule] in the case of a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*).
If it is argued that the term "of the prefix" applies, there is no application in the case of a single-substitute, as in *plāyate* and *palāyate*, once the single-substitute has been effected.

[Objection: Because there is no separation [of the sounds], the rule does not apply. [Response: There is separation by virtue of the existence of the "end-of-word" (anta) and "beginning-of-word" (ādi) status. [Objection: When both [the preceding and following elements] serve as the basis [for the operation], it is not like the end-of-word or beginning-of-word status. [Response: In that case, since the single-substitute (ekādeśa) is treated as the original (sthānivat) for the sake of an operation concerning what precedes it, there is separation by virtue of this *sthānivadbhāva*. [Objection: Here, *sthānivadbhāva* is prohibited by the rule: "In the context of what is not established (*asiddha*) regarding what precedes, [an element] is not treated as the original."

These are indeed faults of that technical definition; the fault therein is [stated] in the rule *saṃyogādilopalatvaṇatveṣu*. Alternatively, let it rather be a qualifier of the *repha* (the letter *r*). But was it not said: "If it is argued that [the rule] *rephasyāyatau* applies, there must be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for *pareḥ*"? It will be established by the explicit statement (*vacana*). But was it not further said: "There is a purpose for the statement; what is it? *plāyate*, *palāyate*"?

Thus, here too, because of the intervention by the letter *a*, [the rule] does not apply. Once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been made, there is no intervention. However, because of the status of being "as if occupying the original place" (*sthānivadbhāva*)—according to the principle that "a single substitute is treated as the original in respect to a preceding operation"—there is indeed an intervention. In this case, the status of being "as if occupying the original place" is prohibited by the rule: "In respect to what is not established in what precedes it, there is no treatment as the original. These are precisely the faults of that *paribhāṣā*.

There is a fault in this rule regarding *saṃyoga*, elision (*lopa*), *la*-substitution, and *ṇatva* (Pāṇini 8.2.21). An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the case of the causative suffix *ṇi*: it should apply here as well, as in *nigāryate* and *nigālyate*. Why?

Furthermore, the reason is not established. It is stated that [the rule applies] *aci*, yet we do not see a vowel (*ac*) at the beginning here. [If it is argued that it applies] by virtue of the definition of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), [we reply: there is no application of the definition of an affix when the operation depends on a phoneme (*varṇāśraya*). If this is so, then it will occur by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). [We reply: the status of being a substitute is prohibited here by the rule: "In what is not established in the preceding, there is no status as the original" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat*). Therefore, he recites the subsequent [sūtra]: *girateḥ*.

It was stated regarding *ṇau* in [the section on] Latvia. What was stated? "The fault of that [rule applies] in the cases of the elision of the first member of a *saṃyoga*, the substitution of *l* for *r*, and the substitution of *ṇ*.
