I shall explain: "There is elision of a final conjunct [consonant] except when it follows /r/. There is elision of a final conjunct [consonant], provided it does not follow /r/. There is elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*). Then, regarding *s*: there is elision of a final *s* that is part of a consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntasya*). *Dhi* after the suffix *sic* is elided. It should be stated that there is elision of *sic* before the particle *dhi*. What is the purpose? The purpose is for [the form] *cakāddhi*. Let it not occur here: *cakāddhi palitaṃ śiraḥ*. If, then, [this applies] to *sic*...

This very form would result—namely *alaviḍḍhvam*—and this form [*alavidhvam*] would not occur. Therefore, the mention of *sic* must be made.
If, then, the mention of *sic* is made, however, it would not apply to the roots *ghas* and *bhas*. It would not apply to *ghas* and *bhas*.

[The rule] is established. [In the examples] *sagdhiś ca me sapītiś ca me* and *babdhām te harī dhānāḥ*, [the substitution of *dha* for *dhi*] does not occur. Therefore, the mention of *siC* is not intended there.
Consequently, in the rule *dhica*, the mention of *siC* need not be made. How then [to explain] *cakāddhi palitam śiraḥ*?

It is a form of the root *bandh*.

This is the form. Or rather, there is a Vedic elision of phonemes (*chāndaso varṇalopaḥ*), as in the case of *iṣkartāram adhvara*. When *āvyādhinīḥ sugaṇāḥ* is expected, [the form is] *iṣkartāram adhvarasya*; when *niṣkartāram* is expected, [it is as stated];

But it would not be established. Therefore, that mention of *sij* is not for that purpose. Alternatively, it is a Vedic elision of phonemes (*varṇalopa*), as in *iṣkartāram adhvara*. This is not a fault.

Regarding the rule stated as *dāder* (beginning with *da*), this [form] is not established there: *adhok*. Where, then, would it apply? [In the form] *mā sma dhok*. This is not a fault. from the root *gardabhayati*, after the suffix *ap* has been elided, we get *gardhab*. If the genitive expressed a relation to a part, it would not apply in cases such as *dogdhā* and *dogdhum*. However, this too [is accounted for] by the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), whereby the root is designated as beginning with *d*.
It becomes a member of a compound (*avayava*).
(Pāṇini 8.2.32.3) *hṛgrahoḥ bhaḥ chandasi hasya*. In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the substitution of *bha* for the *ha* of the roots *hṛ* and *grah* must be stated. [Example: *gardabhena*.

What is the purpose of the particle *ca*? It serves to carry forward (*anukṛṣyate*) the term *sdhvoḥ*. The drawing down [of the rule] is purposeless because of the prohibition regarding *sthānivadbhāva*. The drawing down of *dadhaḥ* and *tathoḥ* is purposeless.

For indeed, one who thinks that because of the capacity for attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*), the [augment] *at* occurs here even when there is no elision (*alopa*), by him a prohibition must be stated:
[as in] *dadhāti*, *dadhāsi*.

Furthermore, it is possible not to include the mention of *tathoḥ*. How so? It is stated that [the substitution occurs] "before a *jhal* [consonant] after a root ending in a *jhaṣ* [consonant]. And this [root] ending in a *jhaṣ* occurs before a *jhal* [consonant], and nowhere else.

Moreover, even if one were to argue that this [rule] does not exist because of the principle "when a preceding rule is not yet established, [the subsequent rule] does not behave as if it were in the place of the original" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat*), even so, the desired result would still not be achieved.

By the use of the particle *ca* for the purpose of inclusion (*anukarṣaṇa*), and not by the inclusion of *tath*, proximity (*ānantarya*) is resorted to here in the rule "of a word ending in a *jhaṣ* [consonant] when a *jhal* [consonant] follows. In some cases, proximity is produced by a phonetic conjunction (*sannipāta*), while non-proximity is produced by a grammatical rule (*śāstra*). In some cases, there is neither proximity produced by a conjunction nor proximity produced by a rule. In the case of elision (*lopa*), proximity is produced by a conjunction and produced by a rule.

In the absence of elision (*alopa*), there is neither that which is produced by *saṃnipāta* nor that which is produced by a rule of the grammar (*śāstra*). Wherever there is *ānantarya* (immediate succession) for whatever reason, we shall rely upon that. (P_8.2.40) KA_III,405.8-12 Ro_V,536.17-21; 537.1-2; 537.4-6; 537.9-11; 537.14-16;

[Question: What is the purpose of [specifying] *adhaḥ*? [Counter-example: *dhattaḥ*, *dhatthaḥ*. [Objection: It would be possible to omit *adhaḥ*. First, there is this rule: *dadhastathośca* ("and after *dadha*, [the *jhal* sounds are replaced by *jaś*] before *ta* and *tha*"). Following that, I shall state: *jhalām jaśaḥ* ("the *jhal* sounds become *jaś*"). That is to say: "The *jhal* sounds of *dadha* become *jaś* before *ta* and *tha*. Then, [the second part of the rule is: *ante* ("at the end").

And before [the suffixes], the *jaś*-sounds take the place of the *jhal*-sounds. Once the *jaś*-substitution has been applied there, [the rule] will not apply because [the preceding sound] does not end in a *jhaṣ* sound.

For what purpose is [the mention of] "from *ra* and *da*" (*radābhyām*)? [Consider the examples: *caritam*, *muditam*. But surely, even if "from *ra* and *da*" were stated, [the desired result would follow]?

In this case, it follows that here too the *niṣṭhā* suffix follows after the letters *r* and *d*. The *niṣṭhā* is not qualified by the letters *r* and *d*; rather, the letter *t* is what is qualified. [The rule means: "The *n* replaces the *t* that follows *r* and *d*, provided that it belongs to a *niṣṭhā* suffix. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "prior" (*pūrva*)? The mention of "prior" is for the sake of the substitute of the *niṣṭhā*.

It is for the purpose of prohibiting the substitution of the subsequent [element]. The mention of "prior" (*pūrva*) is made in the rule concerning the substitution of the *niṣṭhā* [suffixes] so that the substitution does not apply to the subsequent [element]. For example, in *bhinnavadbhyām* and *bhinnavadbhiḥ*. Indeed, [the rule] states "of what is designated by the fifth case (*pañcamīnirdiṣṭāt*)," and since it says "of what is designated by the fifth case," it would follow that the substitution applies to the subsequent [element].
(Exclusion due to the cause of *vṛddhi*). An exclusion must be stated regarding that which has as its cause *vṛddhi*. What is the purpose?
The purpose is [the forms] *kārti*, *kṣaiti*, and *phaulli*. In the case of *kārti*, once *vṛddhi* has been applied, the substitution of *n* by the rule *radābhyām* [would otherwise apply].

In the case of *kṣaitiḥ*, once the vṛddhi has been applied, the substitution of *n* [for the *y*] as prescribed by the rule *kṣiyodīrghāt* would apply. In the case of *phaulliḥ*, once the vṛddhi has been applied, the substitution of *l* for the *u*—which is taught as being conditioned by the presence of an *udupadha* (a root having *u* as its penultimate)—would not apply. Now, even if the prohibition is stated, how is this [rule *vṛddhinimittāt*] to be understood? Is "the cause of vṛddhi" (*vṛddhinimittam*) to be understood as "that which is the very cause of vṛddhi"?

Regarding the phrase *vṛddhinimittāt*: does it mean "from that which has an increase (*vṛddhi*) as its cause," or does it mean "that which has an increase as its cause is *vṛddhinimitta*, [and] from such a *vṛddhinimitta*"? What follows from this? If it is understood that the increase itself is the cause—that is, *vṛddhinimitta* means "having an increase as its cause"—then *kṣaitiḥ* is included [as a valid example], but *kārtiḥ* is not included. However, if it is understood that the increase is the cause of this [suffix], [then *kārtiḥ* is included].

This [term] *vṛddhinimitta* ("having *vṛddhi* as its cause") includes *kārti*, while it does not include *kṣaiti*. Furthermore, *phaulli* is not included in either case. Let it be as you wish. Let us first assume that "the cause of *vṛddhi*" (*vṛddhinimitta*) means "that which has *vṛddhi* as its cause" (*vṛddhinimittāt*). But was it not said that *kṣaiti* is included?

[The objection: "The suffix *kārti* is not included [in the rule]. [The response: But *kārti* is indeed included. How so? Because when it is said "there is *vṛddhi*" or "there is *guṇa*," that which has the letter *r* at its head (*rephaśiras*) is produced under the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Alternatively, let *vṛddhi* itself be the cause;

thus, this [suffix] is "that which has *vṛddhi* as its cause" (*vṛddhinimitta*), and the rule applies because of the phrase "from that which has *vṛddhi* as its cause. [Objection: But was it not already stated that *kārti* is included?

"The *kṣaiti* is not included" [in the rule]; yet the *kṣaiti* is indeed included. How so? Because that which is the rule for *vṛddhi* (the substitution of *ai*, *au*, and *āl*) contains the word *vṛddhi*. If that is so, then this prohibition must be stated. No, it need not be stated. Why? Because it is characterized as being external (*bahiraṅga*). The *vṛddhi* is external; [the *guṇa* substitution] is internal (*antaraṅga*).

[The substitution of] *natva* is not established, because that which is *bahiraṅga* is not established when [the *antaraṅga* rule is in operation]. And by adopting this view, even the substitution of *latva* becomes established in the case of *phaulliḥ*.

8.2.44) From the vowels *ṛ*, *l*, and so forth, the suffix *ktin* is treated like the *niṣṭhā* suffixes. That is to say, after the vowels *ṛ*, *l*, and so forth, the suffix *ktin* behaves like the *niṣṭhā* suffixes.

It should be stated: *kīrṇiḥ*, *gīrṇiḥ*; *lūniḥ*, *dhūniḥ*. It should be stated: "In the case of *du* and *gu*, there is lengthening. Examples: *ādūnaḥ*, *vigūnaḥ*. Regarding the root *pūñ*: it should be stated, "In the sense of destruction. Example: *pūnā yavāḥ* (the barley is destroyed). Why say "in the sense of destruction"? [To exclude: *pūtaṃ dhānyam* (the grain is purified). Regarding the root *sinoti*: when the object is a morsel and the agent is the subject [of the action]. Regarding *sinoti*...

It should be stated: "of that which has 'eating' as its object and agent. [Example: *sinaḥ grāsaḥ* ("the eating of the enemy"). Why is it said "of that which has eating as its object and agent"? [Counter-example:
*sitā pāśena sūkarī* ("the female pig was bound with a snare").

398–399. What is the purpose of [specifying] "from a long vowel"? [In the example: *akṣitam asi mā me kṣeṣṭhāḥ*. It could have been stated without [the condition] "from a long vowel. Why does [the substitution] not occur in *akṣitam asi mā me kṣeṣṭhāḥ*? This is made clear by the very formulation [of the rule] that the mention of a long vowel is intended. For if the intention were to include short vowels as well, he would have simply said *kṣeḥ*. It is not the case here.

An instruction can be made authoritative [only] when it applies where [something else] has not already been established. Just as the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is not established here, so too is the substitution of *iyaṅ*. But in this case, the case-ending is not unestablished; the case-ending is already established by the rule that "a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) [ends with] a case-ending. [Question: How is the technical designation "nominal stem" (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) established?
[Answer: By the rule "that which possesses meaning is a nominal stem. [Objection: But does not the prohibition "provided it is not a verbal root" (*adhātuḥ*) apply here?
This element is not an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of that element. If it were an imitation, the substitution of *iyaṅ* would not apply.

[Objection: An imitation is like its original form (*prakṛtivat*); thus, the substitution of *iyaṅ* will take place. [Reply: If it is said that an imitation is like its original form, then the derivation of case endings (*svādyutpatti*) would not apply. In that case, for those things that are based on extended application (*ātideśika*),...

Even their own bases (*svāśraya*) are not excluded. Furthermore, even if this [objection] does not hold—that "even the own bases of those [suffixes] prescribed by extension (*ātideśika*) are not excluded"—there is still no fault. In this case, one must necessarily state the suffixes (*vibhakti*) from all [rules] as being prescribed by extension (*nairdeśikī*). For example: *ner viśaḥ*, *parivyavebhyaḥ kriyaḥ*, *viparābhyāṃ jeḥ*. Moreover...

This is not so; it is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) like the original form (*prakṛti*), and thus there is no fault. That which is the form of a verbal root (*dhātu*) beginning with a vowel (*ajādau*) is what is being imitated. (Pāṇini 8.2.48) KA_III,408.11–409.2 Ro_V,563.17–564.10. [Objection: If this is an imitation, then by the rule *anukaraṇam ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.46), the final sound of the imitation should be treated as having an *udātta* accent. Consequently, the *svarita* accent of the word *asti* would be lost. [Response: This is not a fault. By the rule *anukaraṇam cānitiparam* (Pāṇini 8.2.46), the *udātta* accent applies only when the imitation is not followed by the word *iti*. However, in the present case, the word *iti* follows immediately after the imitation. Therefore, the rule *anudāttaṃ sarvam apādādau* (Pāṇini 8.1.18) applies, whereby the entire imitation becomes *anudātta*. Thus, the *svarita* accent of *asti* remains intact. Alternatively, one may argue that the word *asti* is not actually being imitated here. Rather, it is the *rūpa* (form) of the verbal root *as*—that is, its form at the beginning of a word starting with a vowel—that is being imitated. Since the form of the root *as* is inherently *anudātta*, there is no loss of the *svarita* accent. Furthermore, the word *asti* is used here merely for the sake of illustration (*upalakṣaṇārtham*). It serves to indicate that the same principle applies to all roots, such as *bhū*, *dā*, *dhā*, and others, as well as to nominal stems (*prātipadika*) like *gaurī* and *khaṭvā*. For example, in the case of *gaurī* and *khaṭvā*, the forms *gaurī* and *khaṭvā* themselves are imitated, and their respective *svarita* accents are preserved. Alternatively, one might consider the following: the word *asti* is indeed being imitated, but it is imitated as a complete word (*padarūpeṇa*). In this view, the *svarita* accent of the word *asti* is not lost. However, this interpretation is not tenable. If *asti* were imitated as a complete word, then according to the rule *anukaraṇam cānitiparam* (Pāṇini 8.2.46), the *udātta* accent would apply to the final syllable of the imitation. Consequently, the *svarita* accent of *asti* would be lost. Therefore, the first explanation—that the form of the root is imitated—is the correct one. In this context, the term *dhātu* refers to the verbal root (*dhātumātra*). The phrase "beginning with a vowel" (*ajādau*) means "at the beginning of a word whose initial sound is a vowel" (*ajādau pade*). The word *rūpam* (form) refers to the specific phonetic shape of the root. The word *tat* (that) refers back to the aforementioned form. The word *anukriyate* (is imitated) means that the form of the root is reproduced exactly as it is. Thus, the meaning is as follows: when a verbal root is followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel, the form of that root is imitated. For instance, in the expression *pacatu apacat vā*, the form *pacatu* or *apacat* is imitated. Similarly, in the expressions *gaurī khaṭvā vā*, the forms *gaurī* and *khaṭvā* are imitated. In these cases, because the imitation is followed by the word *iti*, the rule *anudāttaṃ sarvam apādādau* (Pāṇini 8.1.18) applies, and the entire imitation becomes *anudātta*. Consequently, the *svarita* accent of the original words remains. However, in the case of *asti*, since the word *iti* follows immediately after the imitation, the rule *anudāttaṃ sarvam apādādau* applies, and the entire imitation becomes *anudātta*. Therefore, the *svarita* accent of *asti* is not lost. This is the established conclusion. Alternatively, one may interpret the rule *anukaraṇam cānitiparam* (Pāṇini 8.2.46) as follows: the *udātta* accent applies to the final syllable of an imitation provided that the word *iti* does not follow immediately after it. In the case of *asti*, since *iti* follows immediately, the *udātta* accent does not apply. Instead, the rule *anudāttaṃ sarvam apādādau* applies, resulting in the entire imitation being *anudātta*. Thus, the *svarita* accent of *asti* is preserved. This is the correct interpretation. Alternatively, one might argue that the word *asti* is not being imitated here at all. Rather, it is the form of the root *as* that is being imitated. Since the form of the root *as* is inherently *anudātta*, there is no loss of the *svarita* accent. Furthermore, the word *asti* is used here merely for the sake of illustration. It indicates that the same principle applies to all roots, such as *bhū*, *dā*, *dhā*, and others, as well as to nominal stems like *gaurī* and *khaṭvā*. For example, in the case of *gaurī* and *khaṭvā*, the forms *gaurī* and *khaṭvā* themselves are imitated, and their respective *svarita* accents are preserved. Alternatively, one might consider the following: the word *asti* is indeed being imitated, but it is imitated as a complete word (*padarūpeṇa*). In this view, the *svarita* accent of the word *asti* is not lost. However, this interpretation is not tenable. If *asti* were imitated as a complete word, then according to the rule *anukaraṇam cānitiparam* (Pāṇini 8.2.46), the *udātta* accent would apply to the final syllable of the imitation. Consequently, the *svarita* accent of *asti* would be lost. Therefore, the first explanation—that the form of the root is imitated—is the correct one. In this context, the term *dhātu* refers to the verbal root (*dhātumātra*). The phrase "beginning with a vowel" (*ajādau*) means "at the beginning of a word whose initial sound is a vowel" (*ajādau pade*). The word *rūpam* (form) refers to the specific phonetic shape of the root. The word *tat* (that) refers back to the aforementioned form. The word *anukriyate* (is imitated) means that the form of the root is reproduced exactly as it is. Thus, the meaning is as follows: when a verbal root is followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel, the form of that root is imitated. For instance, in the expression *pacatu apacat vā*, the form *pacatu* or *apacat* is imitated. Similarly, in the expressions *gaurī khaṭvā vā*, the forms *gaurī* and *khaṭvā* are imitated. In these cases, because the imitation is followed by the word *iti*, the rule *anudāttaṃ sarvam apādādau* (Pāṇini 8.1.18) applies, and the entire imitation becomes *anudātta*. Consequently, the *svarita* accent of the original words remains. However, in the case of *asti*, since the word *iti* follows immediately after the imitation, the rule *anudāttaṃ sarvam apādādau* applies, and the entire imitation becomes *anudātta*. Therefore, the *svarita* accent of *asti* is not lost. This is the established conclusion. Alternatively, one may interpret the rule *anukaraṇam cānitiparam* (Pāṇini 8.2.46) as follows: the *udātta* accent applies to the final syllable of an imitation provided that the word *iti* does not follow immediately after it. 400–401. Regarding the substitution of *na* for the root *añc*, there must be an explicit prohibition of its manifestation. One must state an explicit prohibition of the manifestation [of the form] when it says, "he speaks a falsehood (*anṛtam*)"; [otherwise], it would be established through the recognition of the root *añj*. This is not a form of the root *añc*; it is a form of the root *añj*. Indeed, the meaning of *añc* is understood here. But what is the meaning of *añc*? The root *añc* signifies manifestation (*prakāśana*).

It occurs [in the sense that] one moves gracefully; it is understood as "one reveals oneself. Indeed, in common worldly usage, when one says "he moves gracefully," what is understood is not revelation, but rather composure—that is, "having become composed, he moves. If that is so, then from the root *añc* (to bend/move), there is the word *aṅka*, and *aṅka* means revelation. Thus it is said, "the cows are marked (*aṅkitāḥ*)."

[The forms] are manifested from other roots than *go*. If it is argued that [the root *añj*] has the meaning of "bending" (*añcati*), [we reply] that this is established because the root *añj* also has that meaning.

If it is argued that it has the meaning of "bending," the root *añj* indeed occurs in the sense of "bending. But how can one root occur in the sense of another? How does the root *añj* occur in the sense of "bending"? Roots indeed possess multiple meanings.
Furthermore, does the root *añj* occur elsewhere with the meaning of "to bend" (*añcati*)? He says: it does.

For the root *añj* signifies both "anointing" (*añjana*) and "manifestation" (*prakāśana*). That which is called "ointment for the eyes" (*aṅkteṣiṇī*) manifests what is white and black. Likewise, from the root *añj* comes "condiment" (*vyañjana*), and condiment is manifestation—that which [manifests] through its oily and sweet quality.

The stabilization of the dullened sense-faculties within their own respective domains is *rāga*; that is its *vyañjana*. Indeed, the etymological derivation is consistent with the meaning: it is called *vyañjana* because by means of it [the *rāga*] is manifested (*vyajyate*). (P_8,2.50) KA_III,409.3-6 Ro_V,517.1-4; Śbh_Sh 366.1-3; Śbh_t P.132b7-133a1; D.114b3-5; Ch.431c12-16; Ch'.515b29-c3; Tib.117b3-5; K.354.1-4; L.141.1-4; L2.127a2-4; L3.106b5-7; L4.103a1-3; L5.103b7-104a1;

401–402. Regarding the mention of *avāta* (without wind). It should be stated: "in the case of the mention of *avāta*. This is so that [the rule] may apply here as well: *nirvāṇo 'gnir vātena* ("the fire is extinguished by the wind"), *nirvāṇaḥ pradīpo vātena* ("the lamp is extinguished by the wind").

(P_8,2.55.1) KA_III,409.7–16 Ro_V, 402–403. It is stated [in the sūtra] "after a prefix" (*anupasargāt*). In that case, this is not established: *parikṛśam*. [This is derived from] the root *kṛś-*; what is this *ka-*?

It is prescribed [that the suffix *ka*] follows a root with an *iK* vowel in the penultimate position. This [word *parikṛśa*] does not end in a *niṣṭhā* suffix. What then? This *kṛśa* has the suffix *ka* prescribed after a root with an *iK* vowel in the penultimate position. For there would be a fault regarding the accent in *parikṛśa*. It cannot be so; for here, in the case of *parikṛśaḥ*, there would be a fault regarding the accent. By the rule "of words ending in semivowels (*antasthā*), *tha*, *ghañ*, *kta*, *ac*, *ap*, *itra*, and *aka*," this accent would undesirably apply. [Therefore,] there must be the elision (*lopa*) of the word.

This is the established view. If that is so, then the elision of the word must be understood [in this way]: "parikṛśaḥ" means one who has become emaciated through leanness (*kārśya*). For the *jagatī* meter is indeed complete and beautiful.

403. Regarding the substitution of *l* for the *ph* of the root *phal*, an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the root preceded by the prefix *ut*: *utphullaḥ*. One says "untruth" (*anṛtam*). It is said that this [rule] applies only when preceded by *ut*; however, it should be stated as "in the case of *utphulla* and *samphulla*": namely, *utphullaḥ* and *samphullaḥ*. Regarding the suffix *ka* prescribed after the root *kṛś* when it has an *iṭ*-class vowel (*igupadha*) as its penultimate, there is indeed a fault regarding the accent in the word *parikṛśa*. It is held that the elision (*lopa*) of the word [ending] is prescribed; for in the world, she is not deficient (*anūnā*).
*rucirā*.

(P_8.2.56) KA_III,410.1-11 Ro_V, 403-404 Is this a positive injunction (*vidhi*) or a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*)? And what follows from this? If it were an injunction, there would be no need for the mention of the letter *n*.

It must be stated: "It should not be done. The previous topic continues. Where was the previous topic? It was: "The *niṣṭhā* suffix [ta] following *rad* or *abhyas* becomes *na*, as does the preceding *d*.

But that rule has been interrupted by several *nipātana*s (irregularities) and cannot be made to continue. Now, if it is a prohibition, then the mention of *hrī* is useless, for there is no such rule from which this would follow. Let it be as you wish; let it be so.
Such is the rule. But was it not said that the mention of the letter *n* must be made? It need not be made; the previously stated [rule] is understood here by way of reference (*anuvartate*).

Where was it previously stated? In the rule: "After the roots ending in *r* or *d*, the *niṣṭhā*-suffixes take *na*; and after a root ending in *d* which has a preceding *u*, [the suffix takes *na*]. But that [rule] is interrupted by several exceptions (*nipātana*) and cannot be understood as applying here. [Reply: The connection will be understood by way of reference. Or rather, let it be explicitly stated.
In the very *Nyāsa*, the instruction contains two *nakāra*s (nasals): "after *nud*, *vid*, *und*, *trai*, *ghrā*, and *hrī*, [the augment *naṭ* is optionally applied] by the rule *anyatarasyām*;

however, it is not [applied] after *dhya*, *khyā*, *pṛ*, *mūrch*, and *mad*"—by this [the optionality is established]. Alternatively, let there be a prohibition. But was it not said that the mention of *hrī* is purposeless, since no rule applies after it? It is not purposeless; rather, the Teacher indicates this very point [through its inclusion].

The rule [for the substitution of *na*] occurs because of this, since he employs the mention of *hrī*. (P_8.2.58) Many such rules (*vidhi*) are recited; therein it is not known which [rule] always [requires] the substitution of *na*, and which does not.

Regarding the *vibhāṣā* (optionality), for what is there a prohibition and for what is there the augment *iṭ*? To this, he recites the following answer: "In the case of *vid*, when there is the *śnā* suffix, when there is the *tapara* [specification], and when there is the expression of the root itself (*tanavacana*), those two are indeed prohibitions. There is optionality for that which has the *śnā* conjugational class (*śnavikaraṇa*), and a prohibition for that which has the *śap* conjugational class (*śavikaraṇa*). The rule for the *na*-augment after *vid* with the *śyan* conjugational class is equal to that of *chid*. That is, the application of the *na*-augment to *vid* with the *śyan* conjugational class is equivalent to the case of *chid*.

The *lug-vikaraṇa* (the elision of the suffix) is included within the category of *val*. The *vidi* root, when followed by an affix beginning with a *val*, is included [in that same category]. This is precisely the meaning: for those two roots (*vid* and *vic*) for which *śna* and *śnā* have been prescribed, there are optionally *na*, *nañ*, and *u*. However, for those two for which *śya* and elision (*luk*) are prescribed, it is desired that they behave like *chid* and also take the augment *iṭ*. Another teacher says:

The suffix *niṣṭhā* is prescribed after the root *vid* [in the sense of "knowing"] as *vidita*; after *vid* [in the sense of "to exist"], it is desired as *vinna*; and after *vind* [in the sense of "to find"], it is both *vinna* and *vitta*. The word *vitta* [also] comes from *vind* in the sense of "possessions. The word *bhitta* means a fragment (*śakala*).
Regarding the statement "a fragment is called *bhitta*," this does not apply here in the case of *bhittam* and *bhinnam*. It is not so.

This is the fault: in all these cases, the root *bhid* denotes the general sense of splitting; therefore, one who seeks a specific meaning must necessarily employ a specific term [as a complement], such as "split" (*bhinna*) or "cleaved" (*bhitta*). If *tatva* were the expressive word, then the employment of *śakala* (fragment) would be redundant. Furthermore, since the meaning is already expressed by *śakala*, we conclude that *tatva* does not serve as the definitive expression.
*kvin-pratyayasya kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.62).
Why is the mention of *pratyaya* (suffix) used? Why not simply say *kvinaḥ kuḥ*? For with just *kvinaḥ kuḥ*, [the desired result would follow].

If [the rule] were stated [as *v*], the substitution of *k* would apply only to the letter *v*. But surely, once [the *v*] has been elided, it will not occur? The substitution of *k* would have no scope and would thus subvert the elision. [Reply: The substitution of *k* does have scope. What is its scope? It is when [the *v*] is not final. But how can there be a substitution of *k* for a non-final [letter] when a final one exists? The activity of the Teacher indicates that the substitution of *k* does not occur for a final [letter].

Thus, he provides this instruction regarding the *ka*-class (*kavarga*) by saying "kvinaḥ kuḥ. For otherwise, he would have specified that very [substitute] which possesses those [same] qualities. This, then, is the purpose: so that for those roots to which the *kvin* suffix is prescribed, the substitution of *ku* may occur at the end of a word even when they take other suffixes—as in *mā naḥ asrāk* and *mā naḥ adrāk*. [For if he had simply said] "kvinaḥ kuḥ," [the rule would not apply to these cases].

The mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) has been made [in the rule]. It is desired that the substitution of *k* for the *kvip* affix occurs everywhere at the end of a word (*padānte*). (Pāṇini 8.2.68) In the rule prescribing the substitution of *ru*, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made regarding the word *ahar* when followed by *rūpa*, *rātri*, and *rathaṃtara*. In the rule prescribing the substitution of *ru*, an addition must be made for *ahar* before *rūpa*, *rātri*, and *rathaṃtara*: *ahorūpam* ("the form of day"), *ahorātraḥ* ("day and night").
The *ahorātra* is a *sāman*.

In the case of the substitution of *r* for *ra*, there is a prohibition [of the elision of the final vowel] in an *upasarjana* compound when there is no *luk* elision of the case-ending (*asu*). In the case of the substitution of *r* for *ra* in an *upasarjana* compound, [the rule applies] when there is no *luk* elision.
The prohibition regarding *luk* must be stated [in the case of] "the summer (*nidāghaḥ*) has long days (*dīrghāhāḥ*). But this is established by means of the prohibition regarding a *sup* [ending].

How is it established? By the prohibition regarding a *sup* [ending]. This prohibition applies as a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*): "not when there is a *sup* [ending]. If that is so, then it would not apply here either: "he gives on the day" (*ahan dadāti*), "he eats on the day" (*ahan bhuṅkte*). It has already been stated regarding *luk*: what [is the point]?

It has been stated: "When [an affix] is elided by *lumat*, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the operation conditioned by the presence of an affix) does not apply to the word *ahar* when followed by *ravidhi*. (Pāṇini 8.2.70).

In both Vedic and common usage (*bhāṣā*), there is an extension (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the word *pracetasaḥ* when it refers to a king. In both Vedic and common usage, [there is an extension] for *pracetasaḥ*.

Why does [the substitution] not occur here in *papivān*, *tasthivān*? The term *saḥ* (of *s*) is understood [to carry over]. Even so, it would apply here as well. [Objection: Once the elision (*lopa*) has been performed, it will not occur. [Response: The substitution of *d* (datva) would block the elision because it would have no scope. [Question: But the substitution of *d* does have scope. [Question: What is its scope? [Answer: In *papivadbhyām*, *papivadbhiḥ*. [Objection: In these cases too, the substitution of *r* (rutva) would apply. Therefore...

Just as [the rule for] *ru* would sublate [the rule for] *lopa*, so too would it sublate *lopa*. But it does not sublate it. What is the reason? Sublation occurs when [a rule] is applied while another is not yet applicable; however, the substitution of *dat* for *rau* is not commenced while *lopa* is non-applicable—it is commenced while *lopa* is both applicable and non-applicable. If, then, [the condition] "of *s*" (*sasya*) continues to apply, then [the substitution] would not apply in the case of *anaḍudbhyām* and *anaḍudbhiḥ*.

[Objection: Because of the statement [in the rule], it will apply to *anaḍuh*. [Reply: If that is so, then there must be a prohibition of the letter *n* when the substitution of *d* occurs for *anaḍuh*. That is to say, when the substitution of *d* occurs for *anaḍuh*, a prohibition of the letter *n* must be stated; [otherwise one would get] *anaḍvān*. [Reply: But this is established by the fact that the augment *num* is prescribed as a specific rule (*pratipadavidhāna*). This is established. How? By the force of the fact that *num* is prescribed as a specific rule, the substitution of *d* will not occur.

If, then, whatever was applicable to *anaḍuh* is superseded by the *num* [augment] due to the force of its specific rule (*pratipadavidhāna*), then the substitution of *ru* would also not apply, as in the case of *anaḍvān tatra*. This is not a fault. That rule for which the teaching [of the augment] would otherwise be purposeless is superseded; however, that rule whose very cause [the form] remains intact is not superseded. [Thus, the substitution of] *datva* [remains].
And we pay homage [to the rule]; the prescription for each individual word (*pratipadavidhi*) would otherwise be purposeless, whereas for *ru* it is indeed a cause (*nimitta*).
Why is this stated? It is not established by the rule *hali* alone. It is not established because the term *dhātoḥ* (of a verbal root) is present there.

In that [rule], the verbal root (*dhātu*) is qualified by the letters *r* and *v*, meaning "of a verbal root ending in *r* or *v*. But what is the reason that in the preceding rule the verbal root is qualified by *r* and *v*? It is so that [the rule] does not apply here: *agniḥ*, *vāyuḥ*. If that is the case, then the mention of "verbal root" (*dhātugrahaṇa*) in the preceding rule is discontinued in the subsequent one.

Even so, [the rule] would apply here as well in the case of *kurkuraḥ* and *murmuraḥ*. If that is the case, then the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) continues there, but the root is not qualified by the letters *r* and *v*. What then? The *ik* vowel is qualified: "of a root ending in *r* or *v* which is an *ik* vowel. Even so, [the rule] would still apply here in the case of *kurkurīyati* and *murmurīyati*.
Therefore, the *dhātu* alone is the qualificand; and when the *dhātu* is being qualified, it must be stated: "and when there is a penultimate vowel (*upadhā*).

Regarding the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrghatva*), there is a prohibition for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), for *jṛ*, for *vṛ*, and for the four [roots beginning with *pra-vṛ*]. Regarding the lengthening of the penultimate vowel, there is a prohibition for the reduplicated syllable, for *jṛ*, for *vṛ*, and for the four [roots beginning with *pra-vṛ*].

A prohibition must be stated: *riyrtuḥ*, *riyuḥ*; *saṃvivyatuḥ*, *saṃvivyuḥ*; *jivraḥ*; *caturyitā*, *caturyitum*. And there must be a prohibition regarding the *uṇādi* suffixes: as in *kiryauḥ*, *giryauḥ*.
First of all, a prohibition regarding the reduplication need not be stated; for it is said [in the rule] "after a consonant" (*hali*), and here [the root] does not begin with a consonant.

We observe that [the rule] applies once the *yaṇ* substitution has been made. [Objection: It will not apply because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). [Reply: Here, the status of being a substitute is prohibited by the rule "it is not a substitute with respect to an operation concerning a long vowel. [Objection: This prohibition does not exist. For it has been stated regarding the prohibition: "In the case of accentuation, lengthening, and the elision of *y*, an elided substitute [is treated as non-existent]. And there is the prohibition concerning *jivri*.

It should not be stated [that the rule applies]. The *uṇādi* suffixes are underived nominal stems (*prātipadika*). [In the rule] "after a word ending in *catur*, before a case-ending beginning with a consonant other than *y*" (*supi na*), the term "*na*" (not) is understood. If this is so, then forms such as *gīrbhyām* and *gīrbhiḥ* would not be established. No, there is no fault; because the case-ending is modified, *gīrbhyām* and *gīrbhiḥ* are formed. Thus, the objection that "the prohibition regarding the *uṇādi* suffixes must be stated" has been refuted. The *uṇādi* suffixes...
"Unanalyzed nominal stems (*prātipadika*).

Regarding the rule *adaso 'nosreḥ*, it should be stated as *adaso 'nokārasya*. What is this "of that which does not have the vowel *o*" (*anosreḥ*)? It means "of that which does not have the phoneme *o*."

"Of that which does not have the letter *s* (asakārasya), of that which does not have the letter *r* (arephakasya)"—this refers to [the word] *adas*. Here, in the case of *adas*, it is "of that which does not have the letter *s*" (*asakārasya*). In the case of *adasyate*, it is "of that which does not have the letter *r*" (*arephakasya*). That being so, should this be stated? It need not be stated. It is already accomplished in the very grammatical formulation (*nyāsa*). The reference is made without case endings: *adas*, *o*.
Following the vowel *o*, there is first the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), then the letter *s*, and then the letter *r*. Now...

Or rather, it is not understood thus: "of the *adas-* [stem] that does not have the letter *s*. How then? It means: "the letter *a* belongs to this *s*; therefore, this is *asi-* (that which has *s*); [and the rule applies] to what is other than *asi-*, i.e., *ase-*. If this were the case, *amumuyaṅ* would not be established, and *adadryaṅ* would result. It should be *adamuyaṅ*, because when there is a modification of a non-final element, the operation applies to that which is in the position of the final element. [This concerns] *adas-*.

Some desire the substitution of *m* for the final letter of *adreḥ*, just as [the substitution of] *l* occurs; others [desire it] for that which is in the vicinity of the final letter (*antyasadeśa*). "No," say some, "for [the substitution] is seen in the case of *aseḥ*.

In that regard, because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the word (*pada*), the substitution would not apply to what is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*). Because of the governing rule concerning the word, it does not apply to that which is not at the end of a word.

[The objection is: "In forms such as *amuyā* and *amuyoḥ*, [the rule would apply]. [The reply is: "But it is established by the prohibition of the letter *s*. This is established. How? By the prohibition of the letter *s*.
In that the Teacher teaches the prohibition 'of anything other than *asi*,' he indicates that [the substitution] occurs even for that which is not at the end of a word."

414. The substitution of *ī* applies to that which ends in the plural. It should be stated: "the substitution of *ī* applies to that which ends in the plural. If it were stated simply as "in the plural" (*bahuvacane*), it would apply only in cases such as *amībhiḥ* and *amīṣu*; it would not apply here in cases such as *amī atra* and *amī āsate*. Therefore, it must be stated [explicitly]. No, it need not be stated. This is not a reference to the technical grammatical term (*pāribhāṣika*) for the plural.
What then? This is a literal designation: *bahuvacana* means "the expression of many meanings. [Regarding the rule] *bahuvacane* (Pāṇini 8.2.82).

What is the purpose of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning the sentence (*vākya*)? The governing heading concerning the sentence is for the purpose of excluding the word (*pada*). [The governing heading concerning the sentence...]

It is formulated for the purpose of excluding the word (*pada*). The governing scope (*adhikāra*) of "word" is excluded. For indeed, when it is said, "The crow caws," the governing scopes are not thereby excluded. Furthermore, there would certainly be a fault if the governing scope of "sentence" were to exclude the governing scope of "word. For word-level operations are indeed desired in what follows; they would not be established [otherwise]. [For example], the rule *naś chavy apraśān* [would fail] if it were for the purpose of excluding the word.
Thus, it is not understood as "for the sake of the cessation of the word" (*padasya nivṛttyartham*) or "for the sake of the cessation of the word" (*padanivṛttyartham*). What then?

It is "for the sake of the cessation [of the *ṭi*] within the word" (*pade nivṛttyartham*) or "for the sake of the cessation of the word" (*padanivṛttyartham*). For if it were otherwise, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) would apply to the final *ṭi* of all the words contained within a sentence. Yet, it is desired that it should apply to the final [element] of both the sentence and the word; and that is not accomplished without an effort.

Thus, this is the purpose of the section on *vākya* (sentence). Now, for what purpose is the mention of *ṭi*? The mention of *ṭi* is for the sake of those [elements] ending in a consonant, given that there is no restriction to the final [element] of the *al* (vowel). The mention of *ṭi* is made so that, even under the rule restricting [the substitute] to the final *al*, it may apply to that which ends in a consonant as well—such as *agnici3t* and *somasu3t*. This indeed serves a purpose. But what then? There is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it becoming a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*).

But then, a *pluta* [protracted vowel] would result as a replacement for the entire word-final syllable (*sarvādeśa*). What is the reason? Because of the mention of "vowel" (*acaḥ*), it would not apply to the final [phoneme] alone; and because it is not stated that the *pluta* applies to a non-final [phoneme], that *pluta* would consequently become a replacement for the whole. Or rather, this has already been explained. How has it been explained? It has been stated: "Wherever one says 'short,' 'long,' or 'protracted' (*hrasvaḥ*, *dīrghaḥ*, *plutaḥ*), there the term 'vowel' (*acaḥ*) should be understood as being present [by implication]."

(P_8.2.83.1) KA_III,416.7-15 Ro_V, 416-417 For what purpose is [the restriction] "not when [addressing] a Śūdra" stated? [Example: "Are you well, O grain-pounder? This which is stated—"not when [addressing] a Śūdra"—is too little. It should be stated: "not when [addressing] a Śūdra, a woman, or one who is envious. Among these, an example for a Śūdra has been given. For a woman: "I am Gārgī."
"O long-lived one, Bhavagārgī! [If you say:
'I am a cooking pot,' O long-lived one, then become a cooking pot! [The reply is: "This designation 'cooking pot' does not belong to me; rather, it follows the logic of the 'staff-bearer' (daṇḍin)."

Why does [the rule] not apply here: *devadatta kuśalī asi* ("Devadatta, are you well?")? In this case, something is said and something is replied;
something subordinate is said and something principal is replied. In that context, [the rule applies] to that which resides in the principal.

A prolation (*pluti*) should occur for that which bears the designation *ṭi*, yet here the *ṭi* designation does not reside in the principal element. If so, it would not apply here either: *ādheyaḥ agniḥ* / *na ādheyaḥ agniḥ*. This is not what is being deliberated—namely, whether the fire is to be established or not. What then? Here the action whose instrument is fire is being deliberated: "Is the fire to be established? or "Is the fire not to be established?"

"It should not be placed. If this is so, it follows that there should be a second use of the word *agni*. [Objection: This will not happen, because "that which has already expressed its meaning is not used again. [Response: If this is so, then likewise a second use of the word *ādheya* would not follow, since it is said that "that which has already expressed its meaning is not used again. [Reply: This is not a fault. Regarding those things whose meaning has already been expressed...
Furthermore, usage is observed as follows: "Bring two cakes," or "Bring two Brāhmaṇas.
(Pāṇini 8.2.84) It is said [in the rule] "when called from afar" (*dūrād dhūte*), yet this word *dūra* has an unstable referent; for that very reason...

It is distant in relation to one thing and near in relation to another. For instance, someone says to another: "This water-jar is by your side; bring it. He replies: "Stand up and take it; I cannot reach it because it is far. Another says: "Pāṭaliputra is far from Mathurā. He replies: "This is not far; it is near. In this way, it is so.

The word *dūra* (far) has an unstable referent; because its referent is unstable, it is not known in which state one should perform the leap (*pluti*). If that is so, then this indication is made by means of the verb *hvayati* (to call). That which is "far" occurs in the context of calling. But what is that? It is when there is a specific effort (*prayatnaviśeṣa*) compared to the natural effort (*prākṛta-prayatna*).

When [the word] is being taken up, there arises a doubt as to whether one will hear it or not; that is understood here as being distant. (P_8.2.85) Why is there the mention of *hai* and *he*? The mention of *hai* and *he* in the rule regarding their use is for the purpose of the protracted (*pluti*) vowel of *hai* and *he*.

The mention of *hai* and *he* is made in the rule regarding the use of *hai* and *he* so that the protracted vowel (*pluti*) may occur in the case of these two: *devadatta hai3*, *devadatta he3*. For if the mention of *hai* and *he* were not made, then when they are used, [the prolation] would apply to something else. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "use" (*prayoga*)? The mention of "use" is for the sake of including those that are meaningless, since [otherwise] there would be a mention only of those that have meaning. Thus, the mention of "use" is made.

When there is the mention of meaningful [words], it should also apply to those that are meaningless: *devadatta hai3*, *devadatta he3*. Now, again, for what purpose is the mention of *hai* and *he*? The mention of *hai* and *he* is made again for the sake of [applying the rule to] non-final [vocatives]. The mention of *hai* and *he* is made again so that it may also apply to non-final [vocatives]: *hai3 devadatta*, *he3 devadatta*.

(P_8,2.86.1) When the protracted (*pluta*) vowel is prescribed for a heavy syllable (*guru*), there arises the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the final light syllable (*laghu*) would also be protracted, because it is already prescribed by another rule. When the protracted vowel is prescribed for a heavy syllable—as in *de3vadatta*—the protraction would apply to the final light syllable. What is the reason? Because it is [already] prescribed by another [rule].

Because it is prescribed [by another rule]. For by another definition, the *pluta* vowel is prescribed for a short final syllable in the rule "dūrāddhūte ca. Or rather, the statement "or even for that which is not final" is intended to indicate both cases. Or there is no such fault. What is the reason? The statement "even for that which is not final" will serve to indicate both: namely, for a non-final long vowel as well as for a short one.

421–422. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "prior" (*prāk*)? The mention of "prior" is for the sake of optionality (*vibhāṣā*). The mention of "prior" is made so that there may be an option. Furthermore, the mention of "prior" is redundant because of the statement "of each one" (*ekaikasya*). Why? Because of the statement "of each one. The inclusion of the term "each one" is made for the sake of optionality.
It will be so. There is another purpose for the mention of "each one" (*ekaika*). What is it? So that the protracted vowel (*pluta*) does not occur simultaneously.

Because of the rule "a word is unaccented except for one [vowel]," there is no possibility of simultaneity. Since the protracted vowel is *asiddha* (not yet established), because of its being *asiddha*, the restriction (*niyama*) would not apply. This is not a fault; for even though this [rule] exists there...

But that which is unestablished elsewhere is established here. How so? Because the technical definitions (*saṃjñā*) and rules of interpretation (*paribhāṣā*) are operative at the time the grammatical operation takes place; thus, wherever there is an operation, those rules should be understood as present there. [In the rule] *guroḥ anṛtaḥ anantyasya api ekaikasya prācām*, this [rule] *anudāttaṃ padam ekavarjam* becomes present. In that case, would it not follow that there is a simultaneous application (*samāveśa*) [of both rules] even here?

Devadatta: These two, *siddha* and *asiddha*, are restricted to those cases where something is either definitely established (*siddha*) or definitely not established (*asiddha*). However, in that case, there would be an overlap with the circumflex (*svarita*) protracted vowel (*pluta*), according to the rule: "The circumflex [is used] for a repeated word when expressing envy, consent, anger, or censure.
For even in a circumflex vowel, there is an acute (*udātta*) element. Furthermore, there would be an overlap with the grave (*anudātta*) protracted vowel.
"An unaccented vowel [is used] at the end of a question or in expressions of respect. Therefore, the statement "prior to that" must be made.
8.2.88) Regarding the rule "ye yajñakarmaṇi," there is an over-extension; indeed, there is an over-extension in the case of "ye yajñakarmaṇi."

423. It is asked: what is called *praṇava*? What indeed is the name *praṇava*? Having elided the final syllable of either a *pāda* or a half-verse (*ardharca*), they prescribe in place of the remainder beginning with that [first] syllable either a three-mora *oṃ* or a three-mora *ok*;
that they call *praṇava*. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *ṭi*? The mention of *ṭi* is for the sake of making it a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*).

When it is the vowel *o*, then it should be a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). When it is the syllable *oṃ*, then by the rule "that which consists of more than one phoneme or ends in *ś* or *t* is a replacement for the whole" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.55), it will be a replacement for the whole.
(P. 8.2.90; Kāśikā III,519.13–16; Rūpāvatāra V)

424. What is the purpose of including the word *anta* (end)? The term *yājyā* refers to a collection of verses (*ṛc*) consisting of a group of sentences; in that case, the *pluta* [protracted vowel] would apply to the final *ṭi* (the last vowel among consonants) of every sentence. However, it is desired that it should apply only to the very last one. Since this cannot be established without a specific effort, the inclusion of the word *anta* is for this purpose.

Regarding the rule *agnītpreṣaṇe*, there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). There is an over-extension in the case of *agnītpreṣaṇe*; it would apply here as well: *agnīd agnīn vihara*. However, it is established by the statement *ośrāvaye parasya ca* ("one should cause [the word] *ośrāvaya* to be uttered for another"). Thus, it is established.
This [is the case]. How so? It should be stated: "One causes another to hear" (*ośrāvayet parasya*). *O3 śrā3vaya*. *Ā3 śrā3vaya*. Another says:
It should be stated as "in the case of *ośrāvaya* and *āśrāvaya*. *O3 śrā3vaya*. *A3 śra3vaya*.

424–425. It should be stated that [the doubling] occurs frequently elsewhere. For example: *uddhara3 uddhara* (pull out! pull out!), *āhara3 āhara* (bring! bring!). Then it must be stated? No, it need not be stated. A division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: "In the case of the command to the *agnīdh* priest, there is optionally [doubling] for the subsequent word as well. Then: "In the case of a response to a question, [doubling occurs] after *hi*. The term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) applies here too. Another says:

Every *pluta* [vowel] should be stated as optional (*vibhāṣā*) by one who does not desire the *sāhasa* [prolongation]. (P. 8.2.95) Regarding reproach (*bhartsana*), it should be stated that it occurs alternately (*paryāyeṇa*). For example: *caura3 caura*, *caura caura3*; *kuśīla3 kuśīla*, *kuśīla kuśīla3*.

(P_8.2.103) Regarding [the suffix] *vā* in the case of *asūyā* and others: it should be stated that *vā* applies in the case of *asūyā* and others. For example: *kanye3 kanye*, *kanye kanye*; *śaktike3 śaktike*, *śaktike śaktike*.

426–427. For what purpose is this stated? Because there would be the undesirable consequence of the expansion (*vivṛddhi*) of both [the *i* and *u* vowels] in the case of *ai* and *au*, the protracted (*pluta*) form is prescribed for *it* and *ut*. Since there would be the undesirable consequence of the expansion of both [vowels] in the case of *ai* and *au*, the protracted form is stated for *it* and *ut*. Why is it said "because there would be the undesirable consequence of the expansion of both"?
Because words are eternal, and in the case of eternal words, they must consist of phonemes that are immutable and unchanging.

[The objection: "Because of [the elements] which are subject to disappearance, appearance, and modification, this fault does not arise. [The reply: No, because it would entail the increase of both. It is not understood thus that "the increase of both" means "increase of both" (ubhayavivṛddhi), [and] "because of the entailment of the increase of both" (ubhayavivṛddhiprasaṅgāt). How then? "The increase of both occurs in this"; that is "the increase of both" (ubhayavivṛddhi), [and] "because of the entailment of the increase of both" (ubhayavivṛddhiprasaṅgāt). These two are *ai* and *au*.

Since the *samāhāra* vowels (*e* and *o*) consist of the *mātrā* of the vowel *a* plus the *mātrās* of the vowels *i* and *u*, when their *pluta* (protracted) form is prescribed, an increase of both [components] would result.

For example, just as an embryo growing increases with all its limbs fully developed. There is indeed this consequence; however, what then? In that case, there would be the undesirable contingency of it not being desired. Thus, an undesired result would follow there.

A *pluta* vowel would result in having four morae (*mātrā*). However, this is established by the rule stating that there is lengthening of *i* and *u*. How so? It should be stated: "There is lengthening of *i* and *u*. How, then, is this established? If the division is equal—that is, one mora for the *a*-vowel and one mora each for the *i*-vowel and *u*-vowel. But if [the division is unequal], there is half a mora [for the *a*].

If the vowel *a* (avarṇa) has one and a half morae (*adhyardhamātrā*), then the vowels *i* and *u* (ivarṇa- and uvarṇa) would result in having two and a half moraes (*ardhatṛtīyamātra*). Alternatively, if the vowel *a* has one and a half morae and the vowels *i* and *u* have half a mora each, they would result in having three and a half moraes (*ardhacaturthamātra*). Furthermore, the Sūtra would be contradicted.
Let it remain exactly as it was originally formulated. But was it not said that this leads to an undesirable consequence? To that, the venerable Saurya replied:

The Vāḍava, who knows the unintended [application], recites: "A *pluta* of four morae is indeed desired. (Pāṇini 8.2.107.1) Regarding the substitution of a *pluta* for *ec*, the mention of "word-final" (*padānta*) must be made; it should not apply here: [example omitted].
