When the substitution of *ṇ* applies to the end of a nominal stem, the mention of "the end of a compound" must be made. What is the purpose? It is for the purpose of excluding [the substitution] when it is not the end of a compound; that it should not occur in cases such as *gargabhaginī* and *dakṣabhaginī*. But does it not occur in *gargabhagiṇī*? [No, it does not.]

Thus, when the sentence is "the fortune of the Gargas is *gargabhagaḥ*; she possesses this *gargabhagaḥ*," [the suffix applies]. But when the sentence is "the sister of the Gargas is *gargabhaginī*," then it should not apply.
Let it not apply in that case. If the mention of the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) were made, then [it would apply] here in *māṣavāpiṇī* and *vṛīhivāpiṇī*.

[The suffix] is obtained. And it has been stated regarding the inclusion of [words] qualified by gender. What was stated? That there is a rule for the compounding of prepositions (*gati*), case-relation words (*kāraka*), and subordinate words (*upapada*) with *kṛt*-derived nouns prior to the arising of the nominal suffixes (*sub*).

496. Therein, the prohibition of *yuvan* and so forth: In that context, a prohibition of *yuvan* and the following must be stated. [Examples: *āryayūnā*, *kṣatriyayūnā*, *prapakvāni*, *paripakvāni*, *dīrghāhnī śarat*.
(P_8.4.13) Now, how should it be in these cases: *māṣakumbhavāpeṇa*, *vrīhikumbhavāpeṇa*? What [is the rule]?

Should there always be the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*], or is it optional? When the analysis of the compound is as follows—"the sowing of a jar" (*kumbhasya vāpaḥ*) is "jar-sowing" (*kumbhavāpaḥ*), and "the sowing of a jar of beans" (*māṣāṇām kumbhavāpaḥ*) is "bean-jar-sowing" (*māṣakumbhavāpaḥ*)—then the substitution of *ṇ* must always occur. But when the analysis is as follows—"a jar of beans" (*māṣāṇām kumbhaḥ*) is "bean-jar" (*māṣakumbhaḥ*), and "the sowing of a bean-jar" (*māṣakumbhasya vāpaḥ*) is "bean-jar-sowing" (*māṣakumbhavāpaḥ*)—[then it is optional].
Thus, in that case, there must be an option (*vibhāṣā*). (P.

8.4.14.1) Why is the mention of "non-compound" (*asamāsa*) made? The term "in a compound" (*samāse*) is understood [from the previous rule]; [the mention of *asamāsa*] is so that [the rule] may apply even in a non-compound. For example: *praṇamati*.

It undergoes modification. But where is the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) under discussion? It is in the rule *pūrvapadāt sañjñāyām agaḥ*. How, then, can the mention of "compound" be understood by means of that [rule]? By the force of the mention of "prior member" (*pūrvapada*); for it is only within a compound that there exists such a thing as a "prior member" and an "utter member" (*uttarapada*). Now, what is the purpose of including the word *api*? [It is so that the modification occurs] even in a compound.

It should be as follows: *praṇāmakaḥ*, *pariṇāmakaḥ*. If, then, [the substitution of ṇ] is desired both in a compound (*samāsa*) and in a non-compound (*asamāsa*), there is no purpose in including the mention of "non-compound" (*asamāse*). [The rule] "after a preceding word" (*pūrvapadāt*) has been removed. I shall state that the substitution of ṇ occurs after a prefix (*upasarga*) without distinction. Since it would not apply in a compound due to the restrictive rule (*niyama*), the substitution of ṇ after a prefix is considered unestablished (*asiddha*); and because of its being unestablished, the restriction does not apply.

"It will not exist. If that is so, then since [the desired result] is already established, the fact that the Teacher includes the word "also" (*api*) in the rule concerning non-compounds (*asamāsa*) indicates that it is not the case that one operation is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to every subsequent operation. Rather, it indicates that within a given section (*prakaraṇa*), a preceding operation is unestablished with respect to a subsequent one. What is the purpose of this indication? It is for the sake of [explaining] what was stated regarding the forms *niṣkṛtam* and *niṣpītam*, where [the substitution of] *satva* would otherwise be unestablished.
"The substitution of *ṣ* does not occur; therefore, that is not a fault.

With respect to the root taught as having *ṇ* (*ṇopadeśa*), there is no mention [of the prefix] because of the absence of a prefix (*upasarga*). A mention that is not understood is "non-mention" (*anirdeśa*). [The rule applies] to those [prefixes] which are connected with the action.

With respect to that [root], the designations *gati* and *upasarga* apply, yet there is no connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*) with respect to a root taught with the augment *ṇ*. If this is so, then he says: "After an *upasarga*, even in a non-compound, [the rule applies] to a root taught with *ṇ*" (Pāṇini 8.4.14). However, there is no *upasarga* with respect to a root taught with *ṇ*; in that case, it will occur by virtue of the explicit statement (*vacana*). If it is argued that [the rule applies] on the authority of the statement, [we reply: there is a prohibition regarding the elision of a word (*padalopa*), even on the authority of the statement. [This is because] it is on the authority of the statement [that the rule would otherwise apply].

If this is argued, then a prohibition regarding the elision of the word (*pada-lopa*) must be stated—as in *pranāyaka* (a village from which the leaders have departed). However, it is established by the rule stating that [the substitution] applies to the *ṇakāra* situated in that which the prefix (*upasarga*) is directed toward. This is established. How? It should be stated: "The substitution of *ṇa* occurs for the *ṇakāra* situated in that which the prefix is directed toward. Thus, it is established.

In that case, the Sūtra would be contradicted. Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. But was it not said that there is no designation [of the root] because there is no prefix (*upasarga*) with respect to the instruction of the *ṇ*? This is not a fault. "Instruction of the *ṇ*" (*ṇopadeśa*) is not understood in this way: "the instruction of *ṇ*" (*ṇa upadeśaḥ*) is "instruction of the *ṇ*" (*ṇopadeśaḥ*), [and then] "of the instruction of the *ṇ*" (*ṇopadeśasya*). How then? It means: "that which has the instruction of *ṇ*" (*ṇa upadeśo 'sya*) is "one for whom there is instruction of the *ṇ*" (*ṇopadeśaḥ*), [and then] "of one for whom there is instruction of the *ṇ*" (*ṇopadeśasya*)."

(P_8.4.15) Regarding the non-inclusion of *hi* and *mī*, there must be an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the modified forms. An addition for the modified forms must be made regarding the non-inclusion of *hi* and *mī*.
[Examples: *prahiṇoti*, *pramīṇīte*. This will be possible by virtue of an explicit statement (*vacana*). There is a purpose for such a statement. What is it?

[The forms] *prahiṇutaḥ* and *pramīṇāti* are established by virtue of the substitute being treated like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). This is established. How? By virtue of the substitute being treated like the original. Because of the status of being a substitute for a vowel (*acaḥ sthānivattvāt*), the substitution of *ṇ* will occur here. [Objection: But the treatment as a substitute is prohibited in this case by the rule "not a substitute when what precedes is not established" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat*). [Response: These very points are defects of that Paribhāṣā; its defect is stated in the rule: "its [the Paribhāṣā's] defect applies in the cases of the elision of the first member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*), the substitution of *l*, and the substitution of *ṇ*."

What is the purpose of [the mention of] *loṭ*? [Consider the examples: *prahimāni kulāni* and *pravapāni māṃsāni*. The mention of *loṭ* with regard to *āni* is purposeless, because of the rule concerning meaningful elements (*arthavadgrahaṇāt*). The mention of *loṭ* with regard to *āni* is useless. Why? Because of the rule concerning meaningful elements.

The word *āni* is included [in the rule] as one that possesses meaning, but this [word *prayāṇi*] is not meaningful [in that sense]. Or rather, it is because [the rule applies only after] a prefix (*upasarga*). Alternatively, the designations "motion" (*gati*) and "prefix" (*upasarga*) apply with respect to that action (*kriyā*) with which they are connected; however, there is no connection with an action with respect to this word *āni*. In that case, the designation would not apply even here: *prayāṇi*, *pariyāṇi*. For here too, there is no connection with an action with respect to the word *āni*.
In this context, the connection with action (*kriyā*) is with respect to the word *āni*. How so? It is not understood thus:

"The designations 'motion' (*gati*) and 'prefix' (*upasarga*) apply to that which is connected with the action of someone whose action [is being expressed]. Rather, it is understood thus: "The designations 'motion' and 'prefix' apply to that which is connected with whatever action [is being expressed]."

An addition must be made [to the rule] regarding *ni-* before the roots beginning with *gad-* when there is an intervention by *aṭ*. An addition must be made [to the rule] regarding *ni-* before the roots beginning with *gad-* when there is an intervention by *aṭ*:
*praṇyagadat*, *pariṇyagadat*. It should be stated that [this applies] also after *āṅ*: *praṇyāgadat*. But is this not already [covered by] *aṭ*?

"One who is part of a group beginning with *gada* will be included by the mention of *gadādi*. [But] it is not established. An *aṭ* is said to belong to the *aṅga*, and the *aṅga* ends in a *vikaraṇa*;

therefore, that which is part of such a composite (*saṅghātabhakta*) cannot be grasped by the mention of *gadādi*. If that is so, then the phrase 'in the case of separation by an *aṭ*' (*aḍvyavāye*) is understood [to apply here]. Where was it introduced? In the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye api*. But that [mention of *aṭ*] is a qualifier of the element undergoing the operation (*kāryin*)."

And here the meaning [of the rule] is determined by the specific condition (*nimitta-viśeṣaṇa*); in that case as well, it is indeed a specific condition. (P_8.4.19–20) KA_III,459.11–22 Ro_V, 500–501 For what purpose is the mention of "end" (*anta*)? The mention of "end" for the root *aniti* is for the sake of the vocative singular (*saṃbuddhi*). The mention of "end" for *aniti*—
It is formulated for the sake of complete understanding. O Prāṇa! Aprara said:

"The mention of 'end' (*anta*) in the rule *aniteḥ* is made because the prohibition "not [if] at the end of a word" (*padāntasya na*) would otherwise apply; it is intended to set that aside. Or rather, there is another [interpretation]: this word *anta* indeed signifies a constituent part (*avayava*). For example:"
"End of a garment" (*vastrāntaḥ*) means "end of a cloth" (*vasanāntaḥ*). It occurs in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpye*). For example: "He has gone to the end of the water" (*udakāntam gataḥ*);

it is understood as "he has gone near the water. Therefore, the inclusion of that which occurs in the sense of proximity is intended so that [the rule] may apply when there is a *n* following a *r* that is in proximity to the root *an* (to breathe). As in: *prāṇiti*. But here it should not apply: *paryaniti*.

What is the purpose of the phrase "not preceded by *a*" (*atpūrvasya*)? [Examples: *praghnanti*, *parighnanti*. It has been stated regarding the substitution of *han* when it is not preceded by *a*: "There is a prohibition [of the substitution of *gh*] when there is an intervening *k* or *v* in the case of the substitutes for *han*. (P. 8.4.22). What was stated? "There is a prohibition when there is an intervention by *k* or *v* in the case of the substitutes for *han*.
(P. 8.4.28). How is this to be understood? Is it that "that which follows *o* is *otpara*; that which is not *otpara* is *anotpara*"? Or rather...

"Okāraḥ paraḥ asmāt saḥ ayam otparaḥ, na otparaḥ, anotparaḥ. What follows from this? If it is understood that "otpara" means "that which has okāra as its subsequent [element]," and thus "not otpara" means "not having okāra as its subsequent," then [the rule] would apply even to *pra naḥ muñcatam*. Alternatively, if it is understood that "otpara" means "that which has 'o' as its subsequent [element] when 'o' follows this [okāra]," then [the rule does not apply].
Thus, the divine-bestowed gain does not reach us here; and in both ways, a fault arises at the outset:
"pra naḥ muñcatam," "pra naḥ muñcatam," and "pra u naḥ."

The substitution of *ṇ* is not desired even when there is the augment *api*. When there is the augment *api*, the change to *ṇ* is not desired. If that is so, then it should be stated: "after a preverb (*upasarga*), [the substitution of *ṇ* occurs] diversely" (Pāṇini 8.4.29). Regarding the substitution of *ṇ* for a letter standing after a *kṛt*-suffix, an addition must be made for the word *nirviṇṇa*. An addition must be made for *nirviṇṇa* in the rule concerning the substitution of *ṇ* after a *kṛt*-suffix: "I am weary of this dwelling."

Regarding the optional application (*vibhāṣā*) of the suffix *ṇi*, an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for cases where there is an intervention by a grammatical factor (*sādhana*). An addition must be made for the optional application of *ṇi* when there is an intervention by a factor:
[examples] such as *prāpyamāṇam* and *prāpyamāṇam*. This is established because that [suffix] is prescribed [in those instances]. The mention of *ṇi* is a qualifier of what has been prescribed.

[This is] because [the suffix] *ya* is prescribed after a root ending in *ṇi*. Or else, it is because of the governing scope (*adhikāra*) of *aṭ*. Or rather, the phrase "even when there is an intervention by *aṭ*" (*aḍvyavāye*) continues to apply. (P. 8.4.32) KA_III,461.8–462.6 Ro_V, 503–504 Why is this stated? It is not already established by the rule *na kṛtyacaḥ* (P. 8.4.29). This formulation is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*).

"Only from a root beginning with *ij* or the like that has the augment *nuṭ*, and not from any other [root] having the augment *nuṭ*. Where should it not apply? In *pramaṅkanam* and *parimaṅkanam*. Regarding the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* after a root with the augment *nuṭ*, the restriction is not established because there is nothing else to be prescribed. There is no application of the restriction regarding the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* after a root with the augment *nuṭ*. What is the reason? Because there is nothing else to be prescribed. A restriction occurs because of the purposelessness [of the rule otherwise]; [here], however, there is nothing to be prescribed.

[The objection is: "Since it is understood that [the substitution] does not exist, there is something to be prescribed here. What is it? Since an option (*vibhāṣā*) is obtained from a root with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), *ṇatva* must be prescribed as obligatory (*nitya*) in that case. In this regard, let it be either a new rule (*apūrvo vidhiḥ*) or a restriction (*niyama*). It will be a new rule, not a restriction. [The reply is: "But it is established by the inclusion of *san* within the governing heading of prohibitions (*pratiṣedhādhikāra*). This is established. How so?"
Because of the inclusion of *sanum* (a root with the augment *num*) in the section on prohibitions. In the section on prohibitions, the inclusion of *sanum* must be made [as follows]:
"Not for *bhā*, *bhū*, *pū*, *kami*, *gami*, *pi*, *āyi*, *vepi*, and roots with *num*. In that case, it would not apply here either: *preṅgaṇam*, *preṅgaṇīyam*. [Answer:

Regarding the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* when a *kṛt*-suffix follows, there is the inclusion of roots beginning with *ij* that have *num*. Regarding the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* when a *kṛt*-suffix follows, there is the inclusion of roots beginning with *ij* that have *num*.
The inclusion [of *sanum*] must be made. [Objection: In that case, the rule is established, but the sūtra is split. [Response: Let it remain exactly as it was formulated. [Objection:

But was it not said that when *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) applies to a *sanum* [suffix], there is no establishment of restriction because of the status of what is to be prescribed (*vidheya*)? [Response: This is not a fault. The word *halaḥ* (after a consonant) is understood [from a previous rule]. Where was it introduced? In the rule *halaścejupadhāt*. That [word *halaḥ*] indeed serves as a qualifier for the beginning [of the suffix] there, [but now it is connected] with the qualifier for the end.

And this is the purpose here. But how is it known that in that [rule] the prefixing element (*ādi*) is the qualifier? Because it is stated there as "from a root having *ij* as its penultimate" (*ijupadhāt*), there is no need for the suffixing element (*anta*) as a qualifier. That which was a qualifier of the prefixing element in that [rule] will serve as a qualifier of the suffixing element here. How so? Because it is stated there as "of those beginning with *ij*" (*ijādeḥ*), there is no need for the prefixing element as a qualifier. Or rather, [it refers to] "those beginning with *ij*, provided they have the augment *num*" (*sanumaḥ*).

Thus, here [in this rule], the phrase "optionally after the root *ṇī*" (Pāṇini 8.4.33) will be carried over (anuvartate). (Pāṇini 8.4.34) Regarding the roots beginning with *bhā*, there must be an inclusion of the root *pūñ*. An inclusion of the root *pūñ* must be made among the roots beginning with *bhā*; otherwise, [the substitution] would not apply here in the case of *prapavaṇam*.
Regarding *somasya*: there must be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the causative form (*ṇyanta*). An addition must be made for the causative form.

505. Regarding the rule concerning what follows *ṣa* and the beginning of a word (*padādi*): the mention of "following *ṣa* and the beginning of a word" must be made so that it applies only here, as in *niṣpānam* and *duṣpānam*. It should not apply here: *sasarpiṣkeṇa*, *sayajuṣkeṇa*. Then that [mention] must be stated. It need not be stated. For it is not understood thus: "the end of a word (*padānta*) is that which is within a word (*padasya antaḥ*); [the rule applies] from the end of a word. How then?

Regarding the rule *pade antaḥ padāntaḥ padāntāt* (Pāṇini 8.4.36): [The Vārttika] states that for the root *naś*, the substitute *aś* should be prescribed. It should be stated that for the root *naś*, *aś* is substituted; this is so that it may apply here as well: *pranaṅkṣyati*, *parinaṅkṣyati*.

In that case, it should be stated. It need not be stated; for here, the desired result is already established by the rule *naśeḥ ṣaḥ* alone. Since this is already established, the purpose of including the mention of the suffix *ant* is so that the substitution may apply even to that which previously had the letter *ṣ* at its end.

506. Regarding the rule *padavyavāye ataddhite*: it should be stated that this applies when there is an intervention by a word (*padavyavāye*) that is not a *taddhita* suffix. This [rule] should not apply here: *ārdragomayeṇa*, *śuṣkagomayeṇa*. Then it must be stated? No, it need not be stated. It is not understood as "an intervention by a word" (*padena vyavāye padavyavāye*). How then? It is understood as "an intervention within a word" (*pade vyavāyaḥ padavyavāyaḥ*), meaning "in the case of an intervention within a word."
The prohibition of the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*, which is not otherwise prescribed by a specific rule, is to be understood as applying to the group of words beginning with *kṣubhna*.

Why is the third case (instrumental) used in the formulation, rather than simply saying "ścau"? It is so that the substitution of *ścutva* (the change to *ś*) occurs whenever there is immediate sequence [of *s*], as in *yajñaḥ*, *rājñaḥ*, and *yācñā*. Now, why does the rule of "correspondence according to number" (*saṅkhyātānudeśa*) not apply here? The activity of the Teacher indicates that correspondence according to number does not apply in this instance, since he teaches a prohibition regarding the letter *ś*.

509. Regarding the rule *chatvam ami* (Pāṇini 8.4.65), it should be stated as *chatvam ami tacchlokena tacchmaśruṇā*. What is the purpose? [The examples are] *tacchlokena* and *tacchmaśruṇā*. (Question:

For what purpose is the mention of *savarṇa* (homogeneous sound) [in the rule *jharaḥ jhari savarṇe*]? (Answer: The mention of *savarṇa* in *jharaḥ jhari savarṇe* is for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of the rule] when the number of sounds is equal (*samasaṅkhyapratiṣedhārtham*).

509–512. For what purpose is this stated? This vowel *a* is taught in the traditional list of phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*) as being "open" (*vivṛta*); here, its restoration to a "closed" (*saṃvṛta*) state is effected. But what is the reason it is taught as open? The vowel *a* is traditionally remembered as being open for the sake of [grammatical] substitution (*ādeśa*) and for the sake of including its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). Likewise, the short form of the vowel *ā* is [open] for that same purpose; thus, for Pāṇini, *a* and *ā* are [homogeneous].

First, for the sake of substitution: in *vṛkṣābhyām* and *devadattā3*, so that by virtue of proximity (*āntaryataḥ*), a long or protracted vowel may replace an open [vowel] with another open [vowel]. And for the sake of including homogeneous sounds (*savarṇārtham*):
so that the letter *a* might include the letter *ā* through the mention of its own class (*savarṇagrahaṇena*), and likewise, the short [vowel] might include the long [vowel].

And likewise, in the cases *atikhaṭvaḥ* and *atimālaḥ*, when the shortening of the vowel *ā* is prescribed, it would result in that [vowel] being *vivṛta*; [therefore] the reversion (*pratyāpatti*) is for the purpose that it should instead be *saṃvṛta*. This is indeed a valid purpose. But what then? [The purpose is] regarding the reversion of the vowel *a*.

There is a prohibition regarding the long vowel. When the short *a* is restored, it must be stated that there is a prohibition of the long vowel. [Examples: *khaṭvā*, *mālā*. This is not a fault. Just as there is the inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) on the basis of the original form (*prakṛti*), so too must it be on the basis of the substitute (*ādeśa*).
In that case, by virtue of proximity (*āntarya*), a short vowel will be replaced by a short vowel, and a long vowel by a long vowel. Furthermore, because the substitute is not an *aṇ* sound.
There is no inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*). And because the substitute (*ādeśa*) is not *aṇ*, the inclusion of homogeneous sounds does not apply. Of which [sounds]?

Of the acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), circumflex (*svarita*), and nasalized (*anunāsika*) vowels. But this is established by the mention of the *tapara* vowel. This is established. How? By the mention of the *tapara* vowel. The mention of the *tapara* vowel must be made: *at aḥ*. Another says:

Regarding the restoration of the short vowel *a*, there must be a prohibition of the long vowel. When the short *a* is restored, a prohibition of the long [vowel] must be stated, as in *khaṭvā* and *mālā*. This fault does not arise; because of the force of the explicit utterance of the long [vowel], it will not occur. If so, then this is the purpose: in cases such as *vṛkṣābhyām* and *plakṣābhyām*, here too, by the force of the mention of the long [vowel], it will not occur.

In that case, then, even a crow behaves like a hawk (*kākaḥ śyenāyate*). But surely, here too, it will not occur precisely because of the force of the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) [in the rule]. There is another purpose for the mention of "long. What is it? *dadhyiyati*, *madhūyati*. And in this very instance, there is this fault: because the substitute is not *aṇ*, the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) does not apply. Of which [sounds]?

Regarding the acute, grave, circumflex, and nasalized vowels: it is established, however, by the mention of the *tapara* (the short vowel followed by *t*). This is established. How? By the mention of the *tapara*.

The mention of the *tapara* must be made as "at at" (meaning *a* and *ā*). Or rather, for the Venerable Pāṇini, it is established by the mention of *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) for those [vowels] distinguished by accent.
